**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical, of All the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers Who Flourished from the Apostolic Age to the Time of Innocent III; a Chronological Reissue of All the Existing Monuments of Catholic Tradition during the First Twelve Centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with certain manuscripts, and very carefully corrected; continually elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the completion of the most extensive editions produced in the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following individual volumes or authors of some importance; arranged with chapters properly placed within the text itself, and also with titles at the upper margin of each page distinguishing and indicating the subject treated; enlarged with works both doubtful and apocryphal, yet possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which one may see at a glance whatever each of the Fathers wrote on any topic; the other of Holy Scripture, from which the reader may readily ascertain which Fathers commented upon each text of each biblical book, and in what places in their works. A most accurate edition, readily to be preferred to all others, if the following are weighed: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the completeness of the correction, both the variety and the number of works reissued, the very convenient form of the volumes, consistently alike throughout the course of the whole work, the low price, and above all this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and small works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time brought together in our library, from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.**

# THE THIRTEEN BOOKS OF THE ECCLESIASTICAL HISTORY OF ORDERIC VITALIS, AN ENGLISHMAN, MONK OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT-EVROUL, DIVIDED INTO THREE PARTS

[Col. 0009]

## PREFACE

### I.

We publish in full Orderic Vitalis’s text as printed by Chesne [Note: [Col. 0009] *Ancient Writers of Norman History, explaining the deeds performed by them in Gaul, England, Apulia, and the East*. Paris, 1619, folio.] and by Dom Bouquet [Note: [Col. 0009] *Writers of French Affairs*, vol. IX, p. 10; vol. X, p. 234; vol. XI, p. 221; vol. XII, p. 585.]. We have retained the division of the work into three parts, established by Orderic himself and confirmed by the manuscripts. We have prefixed rubrics to the books and chapters, judging that readers will find them very welcome.

Anyone wishing to examine our author’s assertions should turn with the utmost confidence to the continuous and outstanding commentary with which the learned Le Prévost adorned his edition. [Note: [Col. 0010] *The Ecclesiastical History of Orderic Vitalis*, edited by A. Le Prévost, 4 vols., octavo, 1838–1852.]

Let us now say a few words about our Orderic.

### II.

Orderic Vitalis, a monk and eminent writer, English by nationality, was born at Ettingesham, now Atcham, on the River Sabrina or Severn, near the town of Schoresbury or Scrobesbury, commonly Shrewsbury, on the border of the lands of the Mercians and the Welsh, on 17 February 1075. His father was Odelerius, who, after his wife’s death, himself assumed the monastic habit in the Norman monastery of Saint Evroul at Ouche, where he had given his eleven-year-old son to God. Orderic seems to have died shortly after the year 1143; he had received the priesthood in the thirty-third year of his life. His name is presented in manuscripts thus: Odericus or Oldericus, Odelerius, Ordericus Vitalis Vitali.

The devout monk spoke thus of himself at the beginning of the fifth book of his *History*:

> “Carefully considering these and other matters of this kind, Father Guarin, [Note: [Col. 0010] Guarin of Essarts was abbot of the monastery of Saint Evroul at Ouche from 24 May 1123 until 20 June 1137.] I have decided simply to publish something that may be of service or pleasing to some of the faithful in the house of God; but I have resolved vigilantly to retain the charge undertaken, lest, like the slothful servant, I be condemned for a talent hidden in the earth when the Lord comes for judgment.
>
> “Accordingly, I first wished to obey the commands of the venerable Abbot Roger and afterward yours, beginning a little work [Col. 0011] on the condition of the Church of Ouche. Our predecessors encouraged one another to undertake it, but none of them wished to begin. For each preferred silence to speech and chose secure repose rather than the consuming care of investigating past events. They would gladly have read the deeds of their abbots and brethren, and a collection of their own modest possessions, which had been slightly increased from poor but devout founders by the great diligence of the fathers; but they declined to bend their talent to the task of composition or writing. At length I, an Englishman brought here from the remotest borders of Mercia at ten years old, a barbarian and unknown newcomer mingled with skilled natives, have, by God’s inspiration, attempted to set forth in writing Norman deeds and events for Normans.
>
> “With God’s help I have already composed two little books [Note: [Col. 0011] Here Orderic speaks of the third and fourth books of his work, for the first and second were added to the others later.] in which I briefly included a true account, gathered by careful inquiry from aged elders, of the restoration of our see, of our three abbots, and of certain events of that time.
>
> “Henceforth I shall begin the third little book from the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1075, and shall speak of my abbot, the community of Ouche, and events occurring during twelve years, namely until the death of King William.
>
> “It pleases me to begin this present little work from the aforesaid year, in which, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March, I was brought forth from my mother’s womb into this light; and on the Saturday of the following Easter, at Ettingesham, in the church of Saint Eatta the Confessor, situated on the River Sabrina, I was reborn at the sacred font through the ministry of the priest Ordric. After five years, my father entrusted me to the noble priest Siward to be educated in letters; receiving my first rudiments under his instruction, I was subject to him for five years.
>
> “But in the eleventh year of my life I was renounced by my own father for the love of God, and, a tender exile, was sent from England into Normandy to serve the eternal King. Thereafter, received by the venerable Father Mainerius, [Note: [Col. 0012] Mainerius, fourth abbot of Ouche, from 1066 to 1089.] clothed in the garment of the monastic habit, and joined to the sincere monastic community by an indissoluble bond, I have now for fifty-two full years gladly borne the Lord’s yoke; with those of my own age I have zealously walked, according to my ability, in God’s way under the Rule’s discipline. I have laboured to learn ecclesiastical custom and service, and have always applied my mind to some useful occupation.”

Orderic wrote this in 1128.

Again, at the end of Book XIII, he says:

> “Behold, worn down by old age and illness, I wish to finish this book; and evident reason requires this to be done for several causes. For I am passing the sixty-seventh year of my life in the worship of my Lord Jesus Christ; and while I see the great men of this age oppressed by severe and very adverse misfortunes, strengthened by God’s grace I rejoice in the security of subjection and poverty. Behold, Stephen, king of the English, is held lamenting in prison; and Louis, king of the French, conducting an expedition against the Goths and Gascons, is frequently troubled by many cares. Behold, since the bishop’s death, the see of Lisieux lacks a bishop, and I do not know when or what kind of pontiff it will have. What more shall I say?
>
> “Amid these things, almighty God, I turn my speech to you and doubly beseech your mercy to have pity on me. I give thanks to you, highest King, who made me freely and disposed my years according to your good pleasure. For you are my King and my God; and I am your servant and the son of your handmaid, who have served you, according to my ability, from the first days of my life.
>
> “For I was baptized on Easter Saturday at Attingesham, a village in England situated upon the great River Sabrina. There, through the ministry of the priest Ordric, you regenerated me from water and the Holy Spirit, and gave me the name of that priest, namely my godfather. Then, when I was five years old, I was entrusted to school at the town of Shrewsbury and offered you my first service in the clerical state in the basilica of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. There Siward, an eminent priest, taught me for five years the letters of Carmenta Nicostrata, and bound me to psalms, hymns, and other necessary instruction. Meanwhile, you exalted the aforesaid basilica, situated above the River Meole, which belonged to my father, and through the pious devotion of Count Roger built a venerable monastery.
>
> “You did not will that I should serve there longer, lest I suffer disturbance among relatives, who are very often a burden and impediment to your servants, or incur some injury to the observance of your law through carnal affection for kin. Therefore, glorious God, who commanded Abraham to leave his land, his father’s house, and his kindred, you inspired my father Odelerius to renounce me completely, that I might be wholly subjected to you. Accordingly, he gave me, weeping as I wept, to the monk Rainald, and sent me into exile for love of you; nor did he ever see me thereafter. As a tender boy, I did not presume to oppose my father’s will, but freely assented to him in all things, because he promised me on your behalf that, if I became a monk, after my death I would possess paradise with the innocent. Gladly entering into this covenant between you and me, my father [Col. 0013] declaring it, I left homeland and parents, all my kindred, acquaintances, and friends. Weeping and bidding me farewell, they commended me to you with kindly prayers, O highest God Adonai. I pray: receive their prayers, and, merciful King Sabaoth, graciously grant what they wished for me.
>
> “Thus, at ten years of age, I crossed the British sea and came as an exile into Normandy; unknown to all, I knew no one. Like Joseph in Egypt, I heard a language that I did not know. Yet, through the aid of your grace, I found every kindness and friendship among strangers. In the monastery of Ouche I was received into monastic life by the venerable Abbot Mainerius in the eleventh year of my life, and on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October, a Sunday, I was tonsured in the clerical manner. The name Vitalis was also given to me in place of my English name, which was judged discordant to Norman ears; it was borrowed from one of the companions of Saint Maurice the martyr, whose martyrdom was then being celebrated.
>
> “With your favour I have lived in the aforesaid monastery for fifty-six years, and have been loved and honoured by all the brethren and companions far more than I deserved. Having endured heat, cold, and the burden of the day, I have laboured in the vineyard of Sorech among your people, and, secure in your faithfulness, have awaited the penny you promised. Because they were your vicars, I revered six abbots as fathers and teachers: Mainerius and Serlo, Roger and Guarin, Richard and Ranulf. These lawfully presided over the community of Ouche; as men who would render an account for me and the others, they kept watch, exercised care within and without, and, with your accompanying and assisting help, provided us with necessities.
>
> “When I was sixteen, on the Ides of March, Gilbert, bishop of Lisieux, ordained me subdeacon by command of Serlo-elect. Then, two years later, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, Serlo, bishop of Sées, placed upon me the deacon’s stole. I gladly ministered to you in this rank for fifteen years. Then, in the thirty-third year of my life, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January, Archbishop William of Rouen burdened me with the priesthood. On that same day he consecrated 244 deacons and 120 priests; with them I devoutly approached your holy altar in the Holy Spirit, and for thirty-four years now have faithfully discharged your sacred ministries with eagerness of mind.”

### III.

[Col. 0013]

In this monastery of Saint Evroul at Ouche, Orderic, at the command of Abbot Roger and the request of his companions, decided simply to recount an annual history.

The work called the *Ecclesiastical History*, or *History of Ouche*, is tripartite and divided into thirteen books. The first two books—added later to those that follow—constitute the first part and briefly describe events from Christ’s birth to the year 1140.

The second part, from the third through the sixth book, follows the martial deeds of the Normans in France, England, and Apulia; it clearly sets forth the foundations of monasteries, the succession and deeds of bishops and abbots throughout almost all Neustria, and many other matters worthy of notice, especially under Duke William II, surnamed the Bastard.

Finally, in the third part, or from the seventh book through the final thirteenth, many matters are recounted concerning the death of William the Conqueror in 1087, his three sons Robert, William, and Henry, the expedition to Jerusalem in 1097, and various other events of those times.

Concerning our Orderic, Antonius Pagi writes thus under the year 1141, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, no. 7: “We have borrowed much from Orderic’s *History* to supplement the ecclesiastical annals. For although this author not infrequently errs in chronology, he nevertheless brings forward many things exceedingly worthy of knowledge and narrates them sincerely. I judge that he revised his work before his death; for, ending the first book, he says that Lothair then ruled the Germans, Louis the French, Stephen the English, and the monk Ramiro the Spaniards. Yet Emperor Lothair died in 1137, and in the same year Ramiro relinquished the kingdom of Aragon and returned to his monastery. Moreover, he completed his thirteenth book during the captivity of King Stephen.”

[Col. 0015]

# PROLOGUE OF ORDERIC VITALIS, AN ENGLISHMAN, MONK OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT-EVROUL, TO HIS ECCLESIASTICAL HISTORY

[Col. 0015A]

Our predecessors wisely considered, from ancient times, the course of the passing age; they recorded for human caution the good and evil events that befell mortals, and, always desiring to benefit those to come, piled writing upon writing. We see this plainly in Moses and Daniel, and in other sacred writers. We find it in Dares the Phrygian and Pompeius Trogus, and other historians of the Gentiles. We observe it also in Eusebius, Orosius’s *Ormesta of the World* [Note: [Col. 0015B] *History of the World.*], the Englishman Bede, Paul of Monte Cassino, and other ecclesiastical writers. I delight in examining their accounts, praise and admire the elegance and usefulness of their compositions, and urge the wise men of our age to follow their noteworthy undertaking. But since it is not mine to command others, I at least endeavour to avoid useless leisure and, exercising myself, to do something that ought to please my simple fellow-monks.

In the account which, by order of Abbot Roger, [Note: [Col. 0015B] Roger of Sappo, abbot of Saint-Evroul from 1096 to 1123, died in 1126.] I have undertaken to compose as simply as I can concerning the restoration of the monastery of Ouche, I desire truthfully to touch upon certain matters concerning the good and evil leaders of this wicked age. Not supported by literary skill nor endowed with eloquence, but prompted by the intention of good will, I now seek to write of those things which we see or endure. It is fitting indeed that, as new things daily happen in the world, so they should continually be committed to writing for God’s praise; and that, as past deeds were transmitted to us by those before us, so present events should now be transmitted by those living now to future posterity through the record of letters.

[Col. 0016A]

As a simple son of the Church, I intend to speak sincerely concerning ecclesiastical matters; diligently striving to follow the ancient fathers according to my measure and ability, I endeavour to investigate and disclose contemporary Christian events. I therefore desire this present little work to be called *Ecclesiastical History*. Although I cannot investigate Alexandrian, Greek, Roman, or other affairs worthy of report, since, as a cloistered monk, I am compelled by my own vow to bear the monastic observance without refusal, I nevertheless labour—with God’s assistance [Note: [Col. 0015B] Le Prévost: “with God’s consent.”]—simply and truthfully to explain for the investigation of posterity those things which I have seen in our own time or learned to have occurred in neighbouring regions. From conjecture based upon the past, I firmly believe that someone much more discerning than I will arise, and more able to investigate the outcomes of the manifold events [Col. 0016B] taking place throughout the world; perhaps he will draw from my notes and those of others like me what he may deign to insert into his chronicle and narrative for the knowledge of future generations.

For I have the chief confidence in this: that I began this work at the simple command of the venerable elder Abbot Roger, and present it to you, Father Guarin, [Note: [Col. 0016B] Guarin of Essarts, mentioned above, was abbot of Saint-Evroul at Ouche, 1123–1137.] his lawful successor according to the Church’s rite, so that you may remove what is superfluous, correct what is unformed, and secure what has been corrected by the authority of your discernment. I begin first from the Beginning without beginning, by whose aid I desire to attain the End without end, there to sing devout praises with those above forever [Note: [Col. 0016B] Le Prévost: “to be sung.”]: **ALPHA AND OMEGA.**

[Col. 0017]

# ECCLESIASTICAL HISTORY OF ORDERIC VITALIS, AN ENGLISHMAN, MONK OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT-EVROUL

## FIRST PART

In which the events from the Incarnation of the Saviour to the year 1140 are briefly described through the succession of Roman emperors, kings, and pontiffs.

## SUMMARY OF THE FIRST BOOK

I. The Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ. II. His life. III. His miracles and wonders. IV. Continuation. V. Continuation. VI. Continuation. VII. Continuation: his Transfiguration. VIII. Continuation. IX. Continuation. X. Continuation. XI. Jesus enters Jerusalem; parables. XII. The Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ. XIII. Continuation of the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ. XIV. Continuation of the Passion. XV. The death of our Lord Jesus Christ. XVI. His Resurrection and Ascension. XVII. The Holy Spirit descends upon the apostles. XVIII. Reigns of the Roman emperors. XIX. Succession of Roman emperors. XX. Roman emperors; persecutions of Christians; Constantine’s conversion. XXI. Roman emperors; invasions of Angles, Saxons, and Franks; origin of the Frankish kingdom. XXII. Clovis, king of the Franks, is baptized; kings of the Franks; kings of the English; Roman emperors. XXIII. Attempts to unite the Eastern and Western Churches; Council of Constantinople; Æthelthryth, daughter of Ine; Bishop Cuthbert. XXIV. Synod of Aquileia; Roman emperors; Charles Martel. XXV. Roman emperors; Pippin; Charlemagne; emperors of Constantinople. XXVI. King Lothair; King Charles; extinction of Charlemagne’s dynasty. XXVII. King Hugh; Council of Rheims; Pope Gerbert. XXVIII. Emperor Otto; Æthelred, king of the English; various events in England, Normandy, and Burgundy. XXIX. Restoration of the monastery of Ouche; conflicts between Franks and Normans; Council of Clermont; various events to the year 1138.

# BOOK I

[Col. 0017]

## I. The Nativity of Our Lord Jesus Christ

[Col. 0017A]

The almighty Word through whom God the Father created all things—the true vine and supreme master of the household, who planted the vineyard and, admitting labourers from the first hour until the eleventh, cultivates it so that he may gather abundant fruit from it—never ceases at any time to cultivate that same vineyard, [Col. 0018A] that is, the holy Church, and nobly to propagate its branches through every region of the world. Indeed, he who is the true King of all ages, the true high priest of good things to come, the true prophet, and Lord of human beings and angels, ineffably anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions [Col. 0019A] (Heb. 1:9), and the angel of the Father’s dispensation of inestimable counsel—according to the oracles of the prophets, who, taught by the Holy Spirit, shone like stars in the night of this age and, like cocks rousing sleepers by their pre-dawn crowing, foretold the mysteries of the Lord’s coming—chose from many thousands the royal Virgin Mary, born of the family of King David and gloriously distinguished by an abundance of every virtue, and made her his mother.

The noble Virgin, adorned with the marks of virtues, divinely betrothed to the righteous Joseph, greeted by the archangel Gabriel (Luke 1), and made pregnant by the Holy Spirit, gave birth to the Saviour desired by all nations—whom she conceived without sin—on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, without pain, for the world. Thus our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 0019B] was born at Bethlehem, a town of Judah, at the first census registration, while Quirinius governed Syria, in accordance with the whole order of prophecy that had foretold him. As truthful Scriptures report, splendid signs from heaven were displayed at Christ’s birth; and angels, devoutly rejoicing at humankind’s salvation, sang: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:1–14).

Accordingly, in the forty-second year of Caesar Augustus; in the twenty-eighth year from the destruction of Cleopatra and Antony, when Egypt also was turned into a province; in the third year of the 193rd Olympiad; and in the 752nd year from the foundation of the City—that is, in the year when Caesar Octavian, by God’s ordering, established the surest and truest peace after suppressing the disturbances of all nations throughout the earth—Jesus Christ, Son of God, consecrated the sixth age of the world by his coming.

From the beginning of the world to Christ’s birth, 3,952 years are counted according to the Hebrew truth; but according to the calculation of Isidore, bishop of Seville, and certain other doctors, 5,154 years are reckoned. Further, according to the calculation of Eusebius of Caesarea and Jerome, there are 5,231 years from Adam to the eighteenth year of Caesar Tiberius, when Christ suffered.

May the entire multitude of believers rejoice in the Holy Spirit and unceasingly worship the eternal Creator; and may it offer him, with all its strength, a sacrifice of praise—him who determined that his only Son, coeternal and consubstantial with himself and the Holy Spirit, should be incarnate, and who released the servant from liability to death by the undeserved death of the Son. [Col. 0019D] For the merciful Creator grieved that his creature, made in his own image and likeness, had fallen; and, by the inestimable counsel of his unfathomable depth, determined that his Son, equal to himself, should visit the servant condemned in prison, mercifully carry humanity from captivity upon his own shoulders back to his flock, and perfectly gladden the nine orders of angels through the restoration of their number.

Therefore the Son of God, made human, remained what he was and assumed what he was not; undergoing neither mixture nor division; governing all things in his divinity with the Father and the Holy Spirit, while enduring the infirmities [Col. 0020A] of our flesh through the humanity he had assumed. He kept inviolate the law which he had given through Moses, and, as Lawgiver, fulfilled all righteousness in every respect. For he was circumcised on the eighth day, and on the fortieth day was presented to the Father in the Temple with the legal offering (Luke 2:21–23).

Yet although the virgin mother wrapped the limbs of her divine offspring in swaddling clothes and bound his feet and hands with a tight band, and the tender infant, placed among the confined mangers, cried on account of the human misery which he had undertaken by the Father’s will, God most high was nevertheless revealed by the rising in heaven of a new star. He was sought at Bethlehem by eastern magi divinely enlightened; there he was found in the cradle and worshipped as God. The wise magi brought forth three precious gifts from their treasures and freely offered Christ gold, incense, and myrrh, thereby proclaiming him supreme King, true God, and mortal human being. In them were consecrated the firstfruits of the Gentiles’ election: they hastened to Christ at Bethlehem from Sheba and from other nations widely scattered throughout the world. Warned in a dream by an angel not to return to Herod, they joyfully went back into their own country by another way (Matt. 2:1–12).

At the time of her purification, the devoted virgin mother entered the Temple and presented to God the Father the child whom righteous old Simeon received in his arms. The blessed old man rejoiced in God because he saw, recognized through the Holy Spirit, and held in his hands the long-awaited Saviour of the nations; he declared to the peoples that Christ was Lord of life and death, and with great joy blessed him while many marvelled. Anna the prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, was joyfully present. This widow, mighty in virtues, recognized Christ and openly declared to all who awaited Jerusalem’s redemption that he had now come. His parents offered on his behalf a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons (Luke 2:24–38), by which the shining chastity and gentle simplicity of the Church were prefigured.

Behold: when the Lord was born in the flesh, not only the angels of heaven but every age and sex among mortals bore witness. The Virgin Mary conceived, gave birth, and nursed through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, and in every way effectively ministered to him by his own aid. John, in his mother’s womb, greeted his Lord with joyful movement; and Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, prophesied to the Church in a threefold prophetic manner concerning the Messiah and his mother. Angels glorified God, incarnate for human redemption; as they behold us redeemed, they rejoice that their own number is replenished. Shepherds, instructed by an angelic visitation, hasten to Bethlehem; they seek in the manger the living bread that came down from heaven, and find the infant who presides over the heavens wrapped in swaddling clothes. Through the shepherds’ proclamation, the hearts of those who hear conceive joy and wonder at the knowledge of Christ. The righteous elders Zechariah and Simeon confess Christ and foretell future things concerning him; blessed old Anna faithfully accompanies them in Christ’s love. While the good rejoice in happy gladness, Herod, hearing unprecedented reports, is troubled in his wickedness and orders all boys two years old and younger to be killed in Bethlehem and throughout all its territory. Jesus, with his inviolate mother, having been taken into Egypt by Joseph, Herod’s fury cruelly shed the blood of infants, and the fields of Bethlehem were drenched with the blood of the innocents (Matt. 2:13–16). But Christ transferred those slaughtered for his sake into his bridal chamber, where they rejoice eternally, happily crowned with victory.

## II. His Life

The Saviour lived on earth for thirty-two years and three months. Yet he was free from sin, spoke no deceit, and alone among the dead was found free from every fault.

[Col. 0021B]

At the beginning of his thirtieth year, he sought the channel of the Jordan; baptized by John, he sanctified the waters and thus showed his followers an example of utter humility. When Jesus had been baptized and was praying, heaven was opened. The Holy Spirit was seen to descend upon him in bodily form like a dove, and the Father’s voice was heard from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:1–17; Mark 1:9–11; Luke 3:21–22). John rightly surpasses all born of women: Christ entrusted himself to be baptized by him; the invisible Spirit made himself visible to him; and the Father from heaven commended his Son to him. Thus, in the Saviour’s baptism, the mystery of the Trinity was revealed to the blessed forerunner.

The Lord Jesus, who in the twelfth year of his life [Col. 0021C] sat in the Temple among the teachers and wished to be found not teaching but asking questions, was baptized at thirty years old and thereafter manifested as God by wonders. For three years he performed signs and instructed disciples. The age of three years [Note: [Col. 0021D] Le Prévost: “the age of thirty years.”] in our Saviour indicates the sacrament of our baptism, because of faith in the Holy Trinity and the operation of the legal Decalogue. Our Lawgiver also thus warns people not to dare to preach at an immature age or rashly to seek positions of pre-eminence, but humbly to strive to await the lawful and mature time for the priesthood or teaching.

Henceforth I wish to consider the succession of our Lord Jesus Christ’s miracles written in the four books of the Gospels and to set them down truthfully and briefly [Col. 0021D] on these pages. So that the matters there surveyed may more easily be recalled to mind wherever they occur, I investigate the sequence of events as the four evangelists described it; and, through the gift of him who makes the tongues of infants eloquent, I earnestly desire to offer it briefly. Since I have decided to compose a chronicle, it is right first of all that I diligently establish the certainty of the times, as the holy evangelists and other historians have long since explained in their writings.

Octavian Caesar Augustus, nephew and heir of Gaius Julius Caesar through his sister Octavia, was the second ruler of the Romans. He reigned fifty-six years and six months. In his forty-second year Christ was born.

[Col. 0022A] Tiberius, Augustus’s stepson, the son of his wife Livia by her former husband, reigned twenty-three years. In his eighteenth year Christ redeemed the world by his Passion.

After the death of Herod, offspring of Antipater the Ascalonite, who had usurped royal power in Judaea for thirty-four years, his son Archelaus exercised tyranny over the Jews for ten years. Fearing him, Joseph, as Matthew affirms, after returning from Egypt at the angel’s command, withdrew with the child and his mother into Galilee and lived at Nazareth. But Archelaus, accused before Augustus by the Jews because of his intolerable ferocity of spirit, was deposed and perished in perpetual exile at Vienne, a city of Gaul. Augustus, moreover, took care to divide the kingdom of Judaea among Archelaus’s brothers into tetrarchies, so that it might be less powerful. Pilate, sent into Judaea in the twelfth year of Tiberius Caesar, assumed the governorship of that people and remained there continuously for ten years, almost to Tiberius’s very end. Herod, Philip, and Lysanias, as Luke relates (ch. III, 1), governed Judaea with him; they were sons of the elder Herod, under whom the Lord was born.

The entire period during which our Lord is described as having taught on earth is confined within the space of four years. For then, as Josephus relates, after Annas had been removed, the Jewish high priesthood was held successively by Ishmael son of Baffi, Eleazar son of the high priest Ananias, Simon son of Canufus, and Joseph [Col. 0022C] Caiaphas, who prophesied that Jesus would die for the people. Eusebius of Caesarea, from the sixth year of Darius, who reigned after Cyrus and Cambyses, when the works of the Temple were completed, down to Herod and Augustus, counts in Daniel seven and sixty-two weeks, making 483 years, when Christ—that is, Hyrcanus, the last high priest of the Maccabean line—was slain by Herod, and the succession of high priests according to the Law ceased. Hippolytus, however, calculates 230 years for the Persian kingdom, 300 for the Macedonian, and thirty after them up to Christ; that is, from the beginning of Cyrus king of Persia to the coming of the Lord he reckons 560 years.

I have set forth these results of my investigation into the sequence of times for the attentive reader: that the Sun of righteousness arose in the sixth age, at [Col. 0022D] the last hour of this world. Now I shall undertake the work I have proposed concerning my Lord, in whose almighty goodness I trust; and I faithfully invoke his aid, that I may worthily carry my undertaking through to his praise.

### III. His miracles and mighty works

Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan into Galilee; and there, on the third day, he was invited with his disciples to a wedding at Cana. When the wine failed, at his mother’s request he ordered six jars to be filled with water and commanded the servants to carry it, changed into wine, to the steward of the feast (John II, 1–11). By this sign he first revealed his glory to his disciples; through it he indicated the transformation of carnal understanding under [Col. 0023A] the old Law, and its transfer through the grace of the Holy Spirit into newness of life. He was led by the Holy Spirit into the wilderness for the contest and was tempted by Satan, who, seeing a man of incomparable righteousness, marvelled. He fasted forty days and nights; and thus by his example he taught that every kind of demon is to be overcome by fasting and prayer (Matt. IV, 1–11; Mark I, 12–13; Luke IV, 1–13). The ancient serpent tempted the second Adam also by gluttony, vainglory, and covetousness—the means by which he had overcome the first Adam (Gen. II); but, defeated by him in three ways, he fled. And behold, angels came and ministered to the Son of God (Matt. IV, 11), who will reward Satan’s conquerors in heaven with everlasting joy.

[Col. 0023B] The Saviour went down with his mother and brothers to Capernaum and remained there not many days. Then, as Passover drew near, he went up to Jerusalem and entered the Temple. He found sheep, oxen, and doves being sold there, and money-changers sitting in the Temple; and, wonderfully radiant with the splendour of divinity, he drove them all out (John II, 12–17).

On the feast day of Passover many saw the signs Jesus performed and believed in his name. Then Nicodemus, a Pharisee and ruler of the Jews, came to Jesus by night, desiring to enjoy his private instruction. He was therefore granted teaching about the power of baptism, rebirth from water and the Spirit, Christ’s descent and ascent, the typological raising up of the bronze serpent, [Col. 0023C] and the undeserved Passion of the Son of Man (John III, 1–21).

After this the Lord came into Judaea. There he remained with his disciples and worked many signs of salvation. John, meanwhile, was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, where there was much water; and when his disciples and Jews disputed, he bore true witness concerning Christ (ibid. III, 22–23). Then Jesus left Judaea and went again into Galilee, passing through Samaria. In the Samaritan city called Sychar, near the estate Jacob gave to his son Joseph, was Jacob’s well. Jesus, weary from the journey, sat beside the well at the sixth hour and spoke mystical words with the Samaritan woman. The Samaritans received the Saviour joyfully, [Col. 0023D] earnestly begged him to remain with them for two days, and many, devoutly, believed in him (John IV, 5–42). From there Jesus went into Galilee in the power of the Spirit, and his fame spread through the whole region. He taught in their synagogues and was praised by all. On the Sabbath he entered the synagogue at Nazareth to read. The supreme reader stood up, unrolled the book of Isaiah the prophet, and read the prophecy he found: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to bring good news to the poor,” and the rest (Isa. LXI, 1). Having rolled up the book, he returned it to the attendant, sat down, and said: “Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.” They marvelled at the words of grace proceeding from his mouth (Luke IV, 14–22). Jesus himself bore witness that a prophet has no honour in [Col. 0024A] his own country (John IV, 44). He produced a true example from the past: although there were many widows in Israel, Elijah had been sent, in the time of famine, only to the woman of Zarephath; and although many lepers were left in poverty and affliction, Naaman the Syrian alone was cleansed in the Jordan at Elisha’s prophetic word. All who heard the Lord’s words in the synagogue were filled with anger (Luke IV, 28). Demonstrating by their sacrilegious action that what had been said was true, they rose up. Madmen drove the effective chief physician out of the city and led him to the brow of the hill on which their city was built, intending to throw him down. But he passed through their midst and went down from there to Capernaum (ibid. 29–31; Matt. IV, 13–16; Mark I, 21).

[Col. 0024B] He came again to Cana of Galilee. A royal official, whose son was ill at Capernaum, begged Jesus, who had come from Judaea into Galilee, to come down and heal his son. Jesus said to him: “Go; your son lives” (John IV, 46–50). Immediately the sick boy recovered; his father believed, returned home the following day, and found his household rejoicing in the son’s health. Learning what had happened, he believed with his entire household. This, John attests, was the second sign Jesus performed after coming from Judaea into Galilee (ibid. 54).

When Jesus heard that John had been handed over, he left Nazareth—whose name means “flower”—and dwelt at Capernaum, interpreted “most beautiful village,” by which [Col. 0024C] the Church is signified. Nazareth, from which Christ was called the Nazarene, is a village in Galilee near Mount Tabor. Capernaum, however, is a town in Galilee of the Gentiles, beside the lake of Gennesaret, in the territories of Zebulun and Naphtali (Matt. IV, 13), where the first captivity of the Hebrews was carried out by the Assyrians. From that point—that is, after John had been handed over—Jesus began to preach (ibid. 17), because after the voice has been silenced comes the Word, and after the Law has ended comes the Gospel, as the sun follows the dawn. “Repent,” he says, “for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (ibid.).

Walking beside the Sea of Galilee, Jesus found Simon Peter and his brother Andrew, and the sons of Zebedee, James and John, and called them. They at once left their nets and followed him (ibid. 18–22; Mark I, [Col. 0024D] 16–20; Luke V, 2–11). Simon means “obedient”; Peter, “acknowledging”; Andrew, “strong” or “manly”; James, “supplanter”; John, “God’s grace.” These interpretations fittingly apply to holy preachers. For without obedience no one enters the Lord; without strength no one perseveres; and one who supplants vices should ascribe every good thing he has to God’s grace.

Jesus travelled throughout Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, proclaiming the Gospel of the kingdom, and healing every sickness and infirmity among the people. His report went throughout Syria, a region extending from the Euphrates to the Great Sea, from Cappadocia to Egypt. They brought him all who were ill, seized by diverse sicknesses of soul and body and by torments—that is, acute sufferings—[Col. 0025A] as well as those who had demons, lunatics, and paralytics; and he healed them. Great crowds therefore followed him from Galilee and the Decapolis, from Jerusalem and Judaea, and from beyond the Jordan (Matt. IV, 23–25; Mark III, 7–8; Luke VI, 17), with a fivefold intention. Some, like the disciples, came because of heavenly teaching; others to have infirmities healed; some merely from report and curiosity, wishing to test whether what was said was true; others from envy, desiring to catch and accuse him in some matter; and some also followed him for bodily food.

Seeing the crowds, Jesus went up the mountain; and when he had sat down, his disciples came to him. Opening his mouth (Matt. V, 1–2)—he who had formerly opened the mouths of the prophets—he delivered a lengthy discourse [Col. 0025B] full of every perfection, in which he beautifully and profitably instructed and formed the apostles. Thus he who had given the Law through Moses on Mount Sinai might teach his own on Mount Tabor in Galilee and imbue them with the perfection of all righteousness.

For he spoke plainly of the eight beatitudes and the remaining commandments of the Law, which he came not to abolish but to fulfil (ibid. 17); and he declares the precepts of the new Law stricter than those of the Old Testament when he commands even enemies to be loved (ibid. 44), commands mercy to be performed in secret, and sets forth many other ordinances of the perfect life. Concerning treasure to be laid up in heaven; the impossibility of serving two masters; birds and lilies of the field (Matt. VI, 24, 28); the speck and beam in the eye; pearls not to be cast before swine; entrance into life through the narrow gate; the need to beware false prophets; and the house to be built upon rock (Matt. VII, 3, 6, 24; Luke VI, 18–49), the true Teacher of teachers spoke incomparably.

When Jesus had completed these words of perfection, the crowds marvelled at his teaching. For he taught them as one possessing authority, as God of all, not as the scribes and Pharisees (Matt. VII, 28–29; Mark I, 22; Luke IV, 31), who were servants of Moses and taught only what had been given to the weak.

When he came down from the mountain, great crowds followed him. The Saviour touched with his hand a leper who worshipped him humbly and immediately cleansed him, [Col. 0025D] commanding him to show himself to the priests with the sacrifice prescribed by the Law (Matt. VIII, 1–4; Mark I, 40–45; Luke V, 12–14). By this command he intimated confession and repentance for sins.

At Capernaum he approved the faith of the centurion and healed with a word his servant, who lay paralysed and grievously tormented, for whom he had humbly pleaded (ibid. 5–13; Luke VII, 1–10).

On the Sabbath, while he was teaching in the synagogue, a demon cried out through a man: “What have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know that you are the Holy One of God.” Jesus rebuked it, saying: “Be silent, and come out of the man.” The evil spirit, convulsing him, came out; and the man was healed, to the amazement of all present (Mark I, 23–28; Luke IV, [Col. 0026A] 33–37). Immediately he left the synagogue and entered Simon’s house. He saw Simon’s mother-in-law feverish and, asked by her friends, touched her hand. The fever at once fled; the woman rose in health and gratefully ministered to the heavenly physician. At evening, when the sun had set, they brought him many demoniacs and persons afflicted by various illnesses (Matt. VIII, 14–17; Mark I, 29–34; Luke IV, 38–41). The true chief physician laid hands on each, cast out spirits by a word, and healed all who were ill. The setting of the sun signifies the Lord’s death; afterwards the Gentiles, whom the demon possessed, are freed through faith, and the sick are healed from the diseases of sin by the remedy of a better life.

Seeing great crowds around him, he ordered his disciples late in the day to go across the sea; and, when he entered [Col. 0026B] the boat, his disciples followed him (Matt. VIII, 18, 23). It was fitting that, as he had performed miracles on land, so he should also perform them at sea, proving himself Lord of land and sea.

Having entered the boat, he caused the sea to be disturbed, stirred the winds, and raised the waves. He slept in body but watched in mind. When the storm arose, the disciples woke him, saying: “Lord, save us; we are perishing.” Then he rose, commanded the winds and the sea, and there came a great calm (ibid. 24–26; Mark IV, 35–49; Luke VIII, 22–25). Thus Emmanuel daily works in the stormy sea of this world, while the vessel of his Church is tossed by the storms of diverse tribulations and is almost endangered by the enormity of its perils. But because he is invoked tearfully by his own with faith, [Col. 0026C] he is immediately present, marvellously assists them by the power of his divinity, and, once temptations have been stilled, powerfully comes to their aid.

### IV. What follows

When he had crossed the sea into the region of the Gerasenes, two exceedingly fierce men possessed by demons came out from the tombs; meeting him, they cried: “What have we to do with you, Jesus, Son of God? Have you come here before the time to torment us? If you cast us out, send us into the herd of swine.” And he said to them: “Go.” Then they invaded the swine and drove the whole herd headlong into the sea (Matt. VIII, 28–32; Mark VI, 1, 17). Thus the herd, consisting of two thousand swine, was driven headlong by a legion of demons and drowned in the sea (Luke VIII, 26–37). [Col. 0026D] The herdsmen fled and, coming into the city, reported everything (Matt. VIII, 33). Thus, when the men had been healed and the swine driven headlong down, the Gerasenes of that city, exceedingly alarmed, came out; and foolishly begged the Lord to depart from their territory.

Gerasa is a city in Arabia beyond the Jordan, adjoining Mount Gilead, held by the tribe of Manasseh, not far from Lake Tiberias, where the swine were drowned. Its name is interpreted “expelling a colonist” or “an approaching stranger”; it signifies the Gentiles, to save whom the Son of God came when he assumed human flesh. The two men possessed by the legion of demons figure the two peoples, Jews and Gentiles, over whom the whole host of vices held sway. They dwelt among tombs because they served dead works—that is, sins. [Col. 0027A] Satan’s weakness is clearly displayed in this: he could not harm even swine without God’s permission.

Observe that when those predestined for life turn to the Lord and, using sound reason, are saved, filthy and puffed-up idolaters, together with all reprobates clinging to wickedness, who are signified by the swine, are condemned to the filth of the pool of muddy deeds.

Jesus entered the boat, crossed over, and came to Capernaum. While he was there, many gathered around him; filling the house, they heard his word. Then a paralytic was carried by four men; after the roof had been uncovered, the bed on which he lay was lowered before [Col. 0027B] him. The merciful Lord saw the faith of those carrying him, forgave the paralytic’s sins, and said to him, while the scribes murmured: “Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house.” Immediately he rose; taking up the bed before them all, he went home (Matt. IX, 1–7; Mark II, 3–12; Luke V, 18–26).

Passing on from there, Jesus called Matthew as he sat at the tax office; from being a publican he exalted him into a follower, apostle, and evangelist (Matt. IX, 9). While the Lord reclined in Levi’s house, the Pharisees murmured and criticized him for eating with publicans and sinners. But the gracious teacher observed their perverse thoughts and uttered this profitable saying: “Those who are well have no need of [Col. 0027C] a physician, but those who are ill. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners” (ibid. 10–13; Mark II, 15–17; Luke V, 29–32). The Lord frequented feasts of sinners in order to invite those who invited him by teaching them and to transfer them to the heavenly feast.

While Jesus spoke with John’s disciples and was reproached by the Pharisees because his disciples, unlike John’s, did not fast, he offered an apt comparison: that the bridegroom’s sons do not mourn while the bridegroom is with them; that unshrunk cloth is not sewn onto an old garment; and that new wine is not put into old wineskins (Matt. IX, 14–17; Mark II, 18–22; Luke V, 33–39). Thus he proves that the strict observances of the new Law should not be imposed upon those who are carnal and not yet [Col. 0027D] renewed, until spiritual renewal had been openly manifested through the mystery of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection.

As Jesus spoke to the crowds, Jairus, ruler of the synagogue, came, fell at his feet, worshipped him, and said: “Lord, my daughter has just died; but come, lay your hand upon her, and she will live.” The gracious creator rose and immediately went with him. A great crowd followed and pressed around him. But a woman who had suffered a flow of blood for twelve years, who had spent all her property on physicians—by whom false theologians, philosophers, and teachers of secular laws are signified—and could be cured by none, came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment. For she said within [Col. 0028A] herself: “If I only touch the fringe of his garment, I shall be healed.” Jesus turned, saw her, and said: “Take courage, daughter; your faith has made you well.” At once the source of her blood dried up and she was healed (Matt. IX, 18–22; Mark V, 22–34; Luke VIII, 41–48).

Then Christ, having come to the ruler’s house and seen the flute-players and tumultuous crowd, said: “Depart; the girl is not dead, but asleep.” And they mocked him. When the crowd had been put out, he entered the chamber, took with him Peter, James, John, and the girl’s father and mother, held her hand, and at his command the girl rose. He commanded that food be given to her, and this report went throughout all the land (Matt. IX, 23–26; Mark V, 35–43; [Col. 0028B] Luke VIII, 49–56). Jairus means “enlightening” or “enlightened,” and signifies Moses and the other teachers of the Law. His twelve-year-old daughter signifies the Synagogue; the woman with the haemorrhage signifies the Church of the Gentiles, which first touched Christ through faith and graciously obtained healing from the discharge of idolatry and carnal pleasures. At last, just as the girl is said to have come to life afterwards at the Lord’s command, so Israel will be saved when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered.

As Jesus passed on, two blind men followed him, crying: “Have mercy on us, Son of David.” He touched their eyes and gave them sight. As they went out, behold, they brought him a mute man possessed by a demon. When the demon had been cast out, the mute man spoke; [Col. 0028C] and the crowds marvelled, saying: “Nothing like this has ever appeared in Israel.” But the Pharisees said: “By Beelzebub, prince of demons, he casts out demons” (Matt. IX, 27–34).

The crowds sought Jesus in the wilderness and, when they found him, desired to keep him from leaving them (Luke IV, 42). When the crowds pressed upon him to hear the word of God, Jesus entered Simon’s boat and asked him to put out a little from land into the Lake of Gennesaret. Sitting there, he taught the crowds; and when he ceased speaking, he said to Simon, who had laboured unsuccessfully all night: “Put out into the deep, and let down your nets for a catch.” When they did so, they enclosed such an abundant multitude of fish that their net was heavily loaded and breaking (Luke V, 1–11).

[Col. 0028D] In those days he went out onto the mountain to pray and spent the night in the prayer of God. At daybreak he called his disciples and chose twelve of them, whom he named apostles—that is, “those sent.” The names of the twelve apostles are these: Simon Peter and his brother Andrew; James son of Zebedee and his brother John; Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew; James son of Alphaeus and Thaddaeus; Simon the Cananaean; and Judas Iscariot, who also betrayed him (Matt. X, 1–4; Mark III, 16–19; Luke VI, 13–16).

The sacred number of the apostles is not devoid of mystery. The number twelve signifies that they would proclaim the faith of the Holy Trinity through the four quarters of the world. The number four multiplied three times makes twelve; and its figure had appeared in many earlier things. The apostles were figured by Jacob’s twelve sons, the twelve princes of the people of Israel, the twelve springs found at Elim, the twelve stones of the altar, the twelve stones taken up from the Jordan, the twelve oxen beneath the bronze sea, the twelve stars in the bride’s crown, and the twelve foundations and twelve gates of the heavenly Jerusalem described in the Apocalypse. They were foreshadowed in many other figures, by which they stand out notably in dispensing God’s mysteries to the peoples.

The glorious Emmanuel travelled throughout Galilee; in villages, hamlets, and cities—that is, among the small and great alike—he preached the Gospel without respect of persons. He considered not the power of nobles but the salvation of believers; and after his honey-sweet preaching, [Col. 0029B] he healed every sickness and infirmity, so that the greatness of his works might persuade those whom his speech had not persuaded.

Seeing the crowds, Jesus had compassion on them because they were harassed and cast down, like sheep without a shepherd. He therefore called the Twelve together and gave them power to cast out unclean spirits and cure every infirmity. “As you go,” he said, “preach, saying that the kingdom of heaven will draw near. Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. Freely you have received; freely give. Do not possess gold, silver, or money in your belts; no bag for the journey, nor two tunics, nor shoes, nor staff” (Matt. IX, 35; X, 10; Mark VI, 6–9).

### V. What follows

[Col. 0029C]

The heavenly Master also gave many other most salutary admonitions, which his truthful fellow-disciples Matthew and Luke committed to writing for remembrance.

Jesus was going to a city of Galilee called Nain, situated two miles south of Mount Tabor, near Endor. As he approached the city gate with the great company accompanying him, behold, a dead young man, the only son of a widow, was being carried out. When the Lord saw her weeping, moved with compassion for her, he said: “Do not weep.” The bearers stopped; he came up, touched the bier, and said to the lifeless youth: “Young man, I say to you, arise.” Immediately [Col. 0029D] he came to life, sat up, and began to speak; and the restorer of life gave him back to his mother in health. Fear seized all who saw it. By divine ordering, a great crowd followed the Lord and a great crowd accompanied the widow, so that, seeing so great a miracle, many might become witnesses and many might become God’s praisers (Luke VII, 11–17).

Christ’s miracles were reported to John in Herod’s prison. Therefore John himself sent two disciples, that through them they might carefully investigate the hidden things of God’s wisdom concerning heavenly providence. When John’s messengers had returned, Jesus spoke much about John’s greatness and compared the Jewish generation to children sitting in the marketplace (Matt. XI, 2–19; Luke VII, 18–32). Then Jesus began to reproach the cities in which very many of his mighty works [Col. 0030A] had taken place because they had not repented at his preaching. Until this point he had reproved the Jewish generation generally; now he rebukes their cities almost by name, especially Chorazin—that is, “my mystery”—Bethsaida—that is, “house of fruits”—and Capernaum, because, though they had seen signs and works, they refused to turn (ibid. 20–24; Luke X, 12–15).

Then Jesus gives thanks to God the Father because he has hidden his secrets from the wise of this age and revealed them to little ones (Matt. XI, 25–30).

When the Pharisees reproached the disciples because they plucked ears of grain as they passed through fields on Sabbaths, rubbed them in their hands, and ate them, the Saviour excused them and, adducing the example of David and the priest Abiathar, said: “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. Therefore the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath” (Matt. XII, 1–8; Mark II, 23–28; Luke VI, 1–5).

Again, on the Sabbath, he entered the synagogue and healed a man with a withered hand. Moved by envy because Jesus did all things gloriously, the Pharisees went out and took counsel with the Herodians about how to destroy him. Therefore he withdrew from there, many followed him, and he healed them all.

Then a demon-possessed man, blind and mute, was brought to him, and he healed him, so that he spoke and saw. The scribes and Pharisees tried to corrupt Christ’s works by a malicious interpretation and asked him for a sign from heaven. He expounded deep and spiritual matters [Col. 0030C] by which he rebuked the evil and instructed the good. He also declared that no sign except Jonah’s sign would be given to the wicked generation; and in a comparison of merit he set above it the Queen of the South, who came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom, and the repentant Ninevites (Matt. XII, 9–45; Mark III, 1–5; Luke VI, 6–10). While his mother and brothers stood outside and sought to speak with him, he stretched out his hand toward his disciples and said: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matt. XII, 46–50; Mark III, 1–35; Luke VIII, 19–21).

That day Jesus went out of the house and sat beside the sea, and great crowds gathered to him.

[Col. 0030D] Entering a boat, he sat down, while the crowd stood on the shore; and he set forth many things in parables. In the farmer who went out to sow he presented a fitting likeness of his own activity, and likewise in the seeds themselves: part perished because some fell beside the way, was trampled by people, and eaten by birds of heaven; some fell on rocky ground, some among thorns, and were choked by differing outcomes. What these things signify I shall note briefly and plainly. The seed is the word of God; the sower is Christ; the birds are demons. The way is a perverse mind, worn and dried by the continual passage of evil thoughts. The rock is the hardness of an obstinate mind. The soil is the gentleness of an obedient soul. The sun is the heat of raging persecution. The thorns are hearts anxious from the ambition of riches. [Col. 0031A] The good soil is a devout and faithful mind, which yields fruit a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold. A hundredfold fruit is yielded by one who acts with the whole intention of eternity; sixtyfold—that is, perfect work with teaching, on account of six and ten; thirtyfold—that is, faith with teaching, on account of three and ten. Again, in another sense: the hundredfold fruit belongs to virgins and martyrs, because of their common manner of life or their contempt of death; the sixtyfold belongs to widows, because of inward leisure, since they do not struggle against the habit of the flesh. For rest is customarily granted to sixty-year-olds after military service. The thirtyfold belongs to married people, because this is the age of those who fight (Matt. XIII, 1–23; Mark IV, 1–20; Luke VIII, 4–15).

Then the true Prophet, as the crowds gathered, offered other parables: of good seed sown and tares, of the mustard seed, and of leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour until the whole was leavened. Sitting in the boat, the Saviour, like a rich householder, refreshed his guests with diverse foods, so that each might receive varied nourishment according to the nature of his stomach. He therefore uses diverse parables in order to satisfy diverse dispositions (Matt. XIII, 24–35; Mark IV, 26–33; Luke XIII, 18–21).

Having dismissed the crowds, he came into the house and explained the parable of the tares to the questioning disciples (Matt. XIII, 36–43; Mark IV, 34). Then he also added the parables of treasure hidden in a field, a merchant and a pearl, and nets cast into the sea, and explained what they signified. From there he crossed into [Col. 0031C] his own country and taught in their synagogues, so that all marvelled (Matt. XIII, 44–58; Mark VI, 1–6).

At a Pharisee’s invitation, the Saviour ate in his house. But a woman who had been a sinner watered the reclining Lord’s feet with tears, wiped them with the hair of her head, and anointed them with ointment. Everything she had previously used unlawfully for sin she wholly offers to God in devotion.

> [Note: [Col. 0031] Le Prévost: “penitent,” more correctly.]

As many delights as she had possessed in herself, so many burnt offerings did she find from herself. Swollen with false righteousness, the Pharisee reproved the sick woman for her sickness and the physician for his aid; he is rebuked by the parable of the two debtors and, like a madman carrying the rope with which he is to be bound, is convicted by his own judgment. The good deeds of the penitent sinner [Col. 0031D] are enumerated, and the evils of the falsely righteous man are corrected by the Judge, to whose eyes all inward things lie naked and open. At last Jesus forgave Mary’s sins, because, as he himself testified, she loved much. “Your faith,” he said, “has made you well; go in peace” (Luke VII, 36–50).

As the Lord and his disciples proclaimed the Gospel, women followed and supplied their needs from their own resources: namely Mary Magdalene, Joanna the wife of Chuza, Herod’s steward, Susanna, and many other women inspired by God. It was a Jewish custom, and was not regarded as blameworthy under the ancient usage of that people, that women should provide their teachers with food and clothing from their own substance. Paul recalls that he refrained from this because it might cause offence among the Gentiles. Susanna means “lily”; Joanna, “the Lord is her grace,” or “the Lord is merciful”; Mary, “bitter sea”; Magdalene, “of the tower.” The interpretations of their names plainly show by what prerogatives of merits the women who ministered to the Lord are adorned (Matt. XXVII, 55; Mark XV, 40–41; Luke VIII, 1–3).

Jesus went up to Jerusalem for a Jewish feast and healed a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years at the Sheep Pool, called in Hebrew Bethsaida, where priests washed the flesh of cattle used to offer sacrifices to God according to the legal rite. This pool had five porticoes, in which [Col. 0032B] lay a great multitude of sick persons—blind, lame, and withered—waiting for the movement of the water. For the angel of the Lord came down into the pool and the water was stirred; whoever first entered the pool after the water’s movement was healed of whatever infirmity held him. At Christ’s command the man was immediately healed and took up his bed on the Sabbath. When the Jews murmured and blasphemed over this, the Wisdom of the Father answered, manifested in many ways the mysteries of his divinity, as John the Theologian relates, and bore distinguished witness to John, his lamp, and to Moses.

> [Note: [Col. 0031] Here Orderic, in Le Prévost’s judgment, alludes to chapter IX, verse 5 of the First Epistle to the Corinthians.]

At that time Herod the tetrarch heard of Jesus’ fame and said to his servants: “This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead, and therefore mighty works operate [Col. 0032C] in him.” For Herod had seized John, bound him, and put him in prison because of Herodias, whom he had taken from his brother Philip and joined to himself despite John’s objection. The deceitful adulterer wished to kill the herald of truth, but he feared the people, by whom God’s prophet was revered. Herod also feared John, whom he knew to be a righteous and holy man; but love for the woman overcame him. By God’s strict judgment it came about that, because of his desire for the adulteress, he shed the blood of the holy prophet. Herod made a supper on his birthday for the leaders, tribunes, and chief men of Galilee. There Herodias’s daughter danced and pleased Herod and those reclining with him. The king swore that she would obtain from [Col. 0032D] him whatever she asked; prompted by her treacherous mother, she asked that John the Baptist’s head be given to her on a dish. The accursed king sent an executioner and ordered the Forerunner of Christ’s head cut off. It was promptly brought on a dish to the girl as the price of her dance, and the feast became bloody amid that impure banquet. John’s disciples buried his body in Samaria and, coming to Jesus, reported these things (Matt. XIV, 1–12; Mark VI, 14–29; Luke III, 19–20; IX, 7–9).

Having heard of the murder of his Baptist, the Saviour withdrew from there and went privately across the Sea of Galilee, that is, the Sea of Tiberias, into a deserted place. He did so not from fear of death, but sparing his enemies, lest they add murder to murder [Col. 0033A] if the frequent sight of his miracles provoked them to deadly zeal. He therefore postponed his death until the day of Passover and gave us an example of avoiding the rashness of those who betray.

When the crowds heard, they followed him on foot. Jesus, seeing the great crowd, had compassion on it and healed their sick. When evening came, he took five barley loaves and two fish; looking up to heaven, he blessed them, broke them, and gave them to the disciples to set before the crowds. He ordered the crowds to recline on the grass. As the apostles served them, five thousand men, besides women and little children, ate and were satisfied; and twelve baskets full of fragments from the leftovers were taken up (Matt. XIV, 13–21; Mark VI, 30–44; Luke IX, 10–17; John [Col. 0033B] VI, 1–13).

All this is full of mysteries. Jesus withdraws from Judaea and comes into the wilderness of the Gentiles. The crowds follow. Having compassion on their sick, he heals them. With the five barley loaves of the Mosaic Law and the two fish of prophecy and the Psalms, he fed them. And he did this at evening—that is, as the end of the ages approached—when he himself, the Sun of righteousness, set for us.

When the people saw the sign that he had performed, they said: “This is truly the prophet who is to come into the world.” Therefore Jesus, knowing that they were about to come and seize him and make him king, ordered the disciples to get into the boat and go before him across the strait; while he himself, having dismissed the crowd, withdrew to the mountain alone to pray. When evening came, the boat was tossed by waves in the middle of the sea, and, as they laboured at the oars for nearly the whole night, a contrary wind hindered them. In the fourth watch of the night, when they had rowed about twenty-five or thirty stadia, he came to them walking upon the sea; and, seeing him, they were afraid, because they thought that he was a phantom. As they cried out in fear, Jesus immediately said: “It is I; do not be afraid.” “Lord,” Peter said, “if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters.” But he said: “Come.” Peter descended from the boat and walked upon the water to come to Jesus. But when he saw the strong wind, he was afraid; and, beginning to sink, he cried: “Lord, save me.” Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand and caught him as he invoked him in danger: “You of little faith,” he said, “why did you doubt?” [Col. 0033D] When Jesus entered the boat, the wind ceased; and those who saw these things worshipped and confessed him to be the Son of God (Matt. XIV, 22–33; Mark VI, 45–52; John VI, 14–21).

Note that John describes the miracle of the loaves as having occurred near Passover, whereas Matthew and Mark report that it happened immediately after John had been killed. From this it is inferred that John was beheaded as Passover approached, and that in the following year, when Passover returned, the mystery of the Lord’s Passion was completed.

## VI. What follows

Jesus came with his disciples into the land of Gennesaret; welcomed gladly by its inhabitants, he healed their sick. Drawn by the Saviour’s kindness, they sent throughout the whole region and brought to him all who were ill; [Col. 0034A] and they begged him that they might only touch the fringe of his garment. And all who touched it were made well (Matt. XIV, 34–36; Mark VI, 55–56). There, against the scribes and Pharisees who had come from Jerusalem, he said many things and rebuked the superstitious traditions of the elders (Matt. XV, 1–9; Mark VII, 1–13).

The crowds boarded boats and came to Capernaum, seeking Jesus. To them he said: “Amen, amen, I say to you: you seek me not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled. Work not for food that perishes, but for that which endures unto eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you; for him God the Father has sealed” (John VI, 22).

These things, and many others like them, concerning the heavenly bread and eternal [Col. 0034B] life, he taught in the synagogue of Capernaum; but the Jews did not understand them, having hearts of stone. They therefore said: “This saying is hard.” Many, blinded by malice, murmured and took offence at him and departed. Jesus therefore said to the Twelve: “Do you also wish to go away?” Simon Peter answered: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life. And we have believed and known that you are Christ, the Son of God” (ibid., 61–70).

After this Jesus walked in Galilee, for he did not wish to go into Judaea, because the Jews sought to kill him. Then, as his fellow-writer John reports, his kinsmen—called his brothers according to Jewish custom—invited him to the Feast of Tabernacles (*scenopegia*), that he might show himself openly to the world. While they, who sought the glory of the world, went up, [Col. 0034C] he remained in Galilee. But when the feast was already half over, he went up into the Temple. To the amazement of all, he taught concerning his doctrine. The Pharisees heard the crowd disputing about him and sent officers to arrest him. Yet no one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come. On the last, great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried out, saying: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. He who believes in me, as Scripture says, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.” This he said concerning the Spirit, whom those believing in him were to receive. For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified. When they heard his words, some said: “This is truly the prophet.” Others said: [Col. 0034D] “This is the Christ.” But some said: “Does the Christ arise from Galilee? Does not Scripture say that Christ comes from the seed of David, and from the town of Bethlehem, where David was?” Thus a division arose in the crowd because of him. The officers who had been sent by the chief priests and Pharisees to seize Jesus, on hearing his words, forgot why they had come. They therefore returned without having committed the crime, filled with wonder. When their savage masters harshly asked why their agents had not brought them the Teacher of life in chains, those men, enlightened from heaven, bore true witness to Christ’s teaching. For they said: “Never has a man spoken as this man speaks.” For he who spoke was indeed God and man. When proud rulers wickedly disparaged the truth, Nicodemus restrained their impious audacity by the authority of the Law. Finally, having accomplished nothing, empty of faith and deprived of every benefit, they returned to their homes (John VII, 1–53).

Jesus then went to the Mount of Olives and again came early in the morning to the Temple. There, while the Lord sat and taught, all the people came to him; and by justice he condemned the woman brought before him, caught in adultery, but through the sweetness of his mercy acquitted her (John VIII, 1–4). Pharisaic deceit imagined that it was setting a trap for Christ, seeking to darken his reputation among the people and plausibly to show him either cruel or unjust. For if he condemned the guilty woman in accordance with Moses’ decree, they would mock him as harsh and forgetful of the mercy he preached, and thus make him hateful to the crowds by whom he was loved. But if, out of clemency, he forbade the adulteress to be stoned, they would condemn him as an opponent of the Law and a supporter of crimes. True Wisdom shattered the wicked men’s snares as though they were spiderwebs and, preserving royal dignity on both sides, passed through unhindered. For he said: “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her” (ibid., 7).

In the first clause is the restraint of one who has compassion; in the next, the justice of one who judges. Bending down, he wrote with his finger on the ground, and with the two-edged sword of his saying pierced the consciences of his plotters. Thus, behold, in every respect he preserved both the strictness of justice and the gentleness of mercy. At length the fraudulent questioners, [Col. 0035C] struck by the Lord’s sentence, were ashamed; they left the adulteress and departed, beginning with the elders. Then the supreme Judge mercifully raised up the woman left to him, who had been accused. “Go,” he said, “and sin no more” (ibid., 11). Behold: as merciful, he forgives past sins; and as just, he forbids her to presume to sin further.

In the treasury Jesus spoke much concerning the true light and freedom, his own exaltation and the slavery of sin, falsehood and truth. The Jews, raging against benefits blessed by Christ, answered: “You are a Samaritan and have a demon” (ibid., 48). Though insulted, he answered patiently, taught humbly, and proclaimed divine things for the salvation of those to be saved. Yet, growing more furious, they ran for stones [Col. 0035D] and picked them up to throw at him. But Jesus hid himself and went out of the Temple (ibid., 59).

As he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth. He spat upon the ground, made mud from the spittle, and smeared it on his eyes; and he said to him: “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam.” So he went, washed, and came back seeing (John IX, 1–7). This was done on the Sabbath, whence a great schism arose among the Jews. The man who had been enlightened bore witness to his Enlightener and was cast out of the synagogue; but he was recognized and received by him whom he rightly loved. Then Jesus spoke of the door, the sheepfold, and the sheep; of the good shepherd and the hireling. Many accepted his words, while more, on the contrary, wrongly rejected them (John X, 21).

[Col. 0036A] Departing thence, Jesus withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon. There a Canaanite woman repeatedly appealed to him on behalf of her demon-possessed daughter. Also at the disciples’ request, after some initial difficulty, he granted her plea; and, praising the mother’s faith and humility, freed the daughter from the demon (Matt. XV, 21–28; Mark VII, 24–30).

Leaving the territory of Tyre, the metropolis of the Canaanites, he came by Sidon, a city of Phoenicia, to the Sea of Galilee, through the midst of the territory of the Decapolis. There he took a deaf and mute man aside from the crowd, put his fingers into his ears, and, spitting, touched his tongue. Then, looking up to heaven, he groaned and said to him: “*Ephphatha*,” that is, “Be opened.” Immediately his ears were opened, the bond of [Col. 0036B] his tongue was loosed, and he spoke plainly. Those who knew him marvelled and said: “He has done all things well: he makes the deaf hear and the mute speak” (Mark VII, 31–37).

Coming beside the Sea of Galilee, he went up the mountain and taught many crowds that approached him. There he healed the mute and lame, the blind, the weak, and many others who had been cast at his feet; so that the crowds marvelled when they saw the mute speaking, the lame walking, and the blind seeing (Matt. XV, 29–31).

The Lord likewise works these things spiritually in the holy Church, through whose help the multitude of sinners is saved daily. The mute are those who do not praise the Lord or confess the faith. The blind are those who do not understand, even though they obey commands. The deaf are those who [Col. 0036C] do not obey, even though they understand. The lame are those who do not fulfil the divine commandments and travel by the byways of wicked deeds. Such persons are daily healed by divine power and led to the way of salvation. Those who feared the Lord, seeing bodily signs, joyfully magnified the King of Sabaoth. So too now the faithful rejoice at the conversion of the guilty and devoutly magnify the Lord of Israel, who does every good thing.

## VII. Continuation of the miracles: the Transfiguration

Jesus, having called his disciples, said: “I have compassion on the crowd, because they have now remained with me for three days and have nothing to eat; and I do not wish to dismiss them fasting, lest they fail on the way.” Then he ordered the crowd to recline upon the ground, took seven loaves and a few little fish, gave thanks, broke them, and gave them to his disciples. The disciples gave them to the people, and all ate and were satisfied. They took up seven full baskets of fragments that remained. Those who ate were four thousand men, apart from little children and women. Having dismissed the crowd, he entered a boat and came into the district of Magadan or Dalmanutha near Gennesaret (ibid., 32–39; Mark VIII, 1–10). There the Sadducees and Pharisees tested him and asked him to show them a sign from heaven, making little of the fact that he had fed four thousand people with seven loaves and filled seven baskets with the leftovers. But he rebuked their insolence, refused them any sign except the sign of the prophet Jonah, and, leaving [Col. 0037A] them, entered the boat and crossed the strait (Matt. XVI, 12; Mark VIII, 11–21).

At Bethsaida he was asked to touch a blind man. Taking the blind man’s hand, he led him outside the village; then, having spat upon his eyes, he laid his hands upon him and asked whether he saw anything. He replied: “I see men as trees walking.” Again he laid his hands upon his eyes. The man began to see and was restored, so that he saw all things clearly. Then he said to him: “Go to your home, and if you enter the village, tell no one” (Mark VIII, 22–26).

Jesus went out and came into the villages of Caesarea Philippi, and on the way asked his disciples what people thought about him. They said: “Some, John the Baptist; others, Elijah; others, Jeremiah, or one of [Col. 0037B] the prophets.” Jesus said to them: “But who do you say that I am?” Simon Peter answered: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God.” Jesus replied and said to him: “Blessed are you, Simon Barjona, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. And I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I shall give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. XVI, 13–19; Mark VIII, 27–29; Luke IX, 18–20). Then he ordered his disciples to tell no one that he was Jesus Christ. From that time Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and [Col. 0037C] suffer many things from the elders, scribes, and chief priests; be killed; and rise again on the third day. Peter took him aside and began, out of loving affection, to rebuke him, saying: “Far be it from you, Lord! This shall not happen to you.” But he turned and said to Peter: “Get behind me, Satan.
