You are a stumbling-block to me, because you do not savour the things of God, but those of men.” After the Lord had disclosed the mystery of his Passion and Resurrection, he urged them, together with the crowd, to follow the example of his Passion, promising a reward accompanying those who endure (Matt. XVI, 20–28; Mark VIII, 30–39; Luke IX, 21–27).

After six days he took Peter, James, and John his brother and led them apart up a high mountain, [Col. 0037D] and he was transfigured before them. His face shone as the sun, and his garments became white as snow. And behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them, speaking with him; and behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. And behold, a voice from the cloud said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him.” Hearing this, the disciples fell upon their faces and were greatly afraid. Jesus came, touched them, and said: “Rise, and do not be afraid.” Raising their eyes, they saw no one except Jesus alone. As they came down from the mountain, Jesus commanded them: “Tell the vision to no one until the Son of Man has risen from the dead.” Then, when the disciples asked, he said that Elijah had come; and they understood that he had spoken of John the Baptist. [Col. 0038A] On the following day, when he had come to the crowd, immediately all the people who saw him were astonished and ran to greet him. Then one man from the crowd approached him, fell on his knees before him, and said: “Lord, have mercy upon my son, for he has been lunatic from childhood and suffers grievously. The demon has often cast him into fire and into waters in order to destroy him; I brought him to your disciples, but they could not heal him.” When Jesus ordered him to be brought, and the sick man had been brought, immediately the spirit convulsed him; thrown to the ground, he rolled about foaming. When Jesus rebuked the demon and ordered it to come out of him and enter him no more, the demon cried out, tore him greatly, and departed. He fell thrown upon the ground, so that many said that he was dead. But Jesus, [Col. 0038B] taking his hand, raised him and restored him healed to his father. Then, when the disciples asked privately why they had been unable to heal him, he said: “Because of your unbelief. Amen I say to you: if you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you shall say to this mountain, ‘Move from here,’ and it will move, and nothing will be impossible to you. But this kind is not cast out except by prayer and fasting.” While they were staying in Galilee, he said: “The Son of Man is to be delivered into the hands of men, and they will kill him, and on the third day he shall rise.” And they were greatly grieved (Matt. XVII, 1–22; Mark IX, 1–26; Luke IX, 28–47).

When they came to Capernaum, those who collected the didrachma approached Peter and said: “Does your master not pay the didrachma?” He said: “Yes.” [Col. 0038C] When he entered the house, Jesus anticipated him, saying: “From whom do the kings of the earth receive tribute—from their sons or from strangers?” He answered: “From strangers.” Christ was the king’s son both according to the flesh and according to the Spirit: either as born from David’s stock or as the Word of the almighty Father. Therefore, as the king’s son, he did not owe the tax; but he who had assumed the humility of flesh wished to fulfil all righteousness. In every kingdom the sons, not the taxpayers, must be understood to be free. Jesus said to Peter: “The sons are free. But lest we give them offence, go to the sea and cast a hook; take the first fish that comes up; and, when you have opened its mouth, you will find a stater. Take it and give it to them for me and for yourself” (Matt. XVII, 23–26). This fish is Christ [Col. 0038D] in the sea—that is, in mortal life. The stater, that is, the didrachma, signifies confession, which is paid for Peter as for a sinner, but for Christ as for the immaculate Lamb who committed no sin.

When a question arose among the apostles as to which of them was greater in the kingdom of heaven, Jesus called a little child and placed him in their midst: “Amen I say to you, unless you are converted and become like little children, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven. Whoever therefore humbles himself as this little child, he is greater in the kingdom of heaven”; and the rest that he said concerning humility and meekness, avoiding scandals to the little ones, and gently correcting brothers. Then he dealt with fraternal forgiveness and proposed the parable of the [Col. 0039A] king who forgave ten thousand talents to a pleading servant, and of that same servant who would not remit a hundred denarii to his fellow servant (Matt. XVIII, 1–35; Mark IX, 32–49; Luke IX, 46–48).

Having completed his discourses after the tribute, concerning humility to be commended and innocence, correction and forgiveness, the merciful teacher departed from Galilee and came into the territory of Judaea beyond the Jordan. There he healed the crowds that followed him (Matt. XIX, 1–2).

When the Pharisees asked whether it is lawful for a man to dismiss his wife, he set forth the firm law of marriage, saying: “What God has joined, let not man separate” (Matt. XIX, 6; Mark X, 9). Then little children were brought to him, that he might lay his hands upon them and pray. But the disciples rebuked those who brought them. Jesus, indignant, said: [Col. 0039B] “Allow the little children to come to me, and do not hinder them; for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX, 13–15; Mark X, 13–16; Luke XVIII, 15–17). To a young man kneeling and seeking the way of eternal salvation, after he had declared the commandments of the Law, he added: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor; and you shall have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” But, hearing this, because he had many possessions, the young man went away sorrowful. Then Jesus said: “Amen I say to you that a rich man shall enter the kingdom of heaven with difficulty. It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX, 16–24; Mark X, 17–25; Luke XVIII, 18–25). Peter, delighted to hear praise of voluntary poverty, said sweetly to the Lord: “Behold, we have left all things and followed [Col. 0039C] you. What therefore shall we have?” Jesus said to them: “Amen I say to you that you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, shall yourselves also sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. And everyone who has left house, brothers, sisters, father, mother, wife, children, or lands for my name’s sake shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life. But many who are first shall be last, and the last first” (Matt. XIX, 25–30; Mark X, 26–31; Luke XVIII, 26–30).

Then he proposed the parable of the householder who hired labourers for his vineyard at different hours and gave each an equal wage of one denarius, [Col. 0039D] beginning with the last and ending with the first (Matt. XX, 1–16). The differing hours are understood typologically according to the ages of the passing world. Abel laboured in the early morning, Noah at the third hour, Abraham at the sixth, Moses the lawgiver at the ninth. At the eleventh hour Christ came and rebuked the Gentile peoples because they idled in the marketplace of this world; he commanded them through faith to work in the vineyard of his Church. Alternatively, the differences of the hours may be distinguished in each individual according to the stages of life. Morning is childhood; the third hour, adolescence; the sixth, youth; the ninth, old age; the eleventh is decrepit or very advanced age. In all these stages some are brought to conversion and rewarded with the denarius of everlasting life. On this comparison a modern versifier says:

[Col. 0040A]

> The vineyard was cultivated; its workers seek rewards.  
> Unequal was the labour; equal were the gifts.  
> The one who came last, summoned by the steward,  
> receives as much as the one who came before.  
> Thus God shows that, whenever we will,  
> if we undertake the work, we may be certain of the reward.

## VIII. What follows

Thus far I have examined, for the sake of a salutary exercise, the works which the Lord performed during the first two years of his preaching, insofar as I could learn them from the accounts of the evangelists; and I have attempted to set them down for myself in a brief narrative. Now I wish to investigate the events of the third year and to compress succinctly the weight of notable matters, after the Lord himself began to journey from Galilee into Judaea, in order to complete at Jerusalem the mystery of the Father’s [Col. 0040B] dispensation and reveal to us by his ineffable operation the secrets of the Law and the Prophets. First he taught in Judaea beyond the Jordan, on the eastern side; afterwards also on this side of the Jordan, when he came to Jericho and Jerusalem. For although the entire Jewish province, as distinct generally from other nations, is called Judaea, in a more particular sense its southern region was called Judaea, in distinction from Samaria, Galilee, Decapolis, and the other districts in the same province.

As Jesus went up to Jerusalem, he secretly foretold his Passion to his disciples. Then the mother of Zebedee’s sons asked that one of her sons might sit at his right hand and the other at his left in his kingdom (Matt. [Col. 0040C] XX, 17–24; Mark X, 32–45). But he invited them to patience and humility, and showed himself to be followed as the complete example of righteousness. He instructed John, when he asked, not to forbid one performing mighty works in his name.

As he went to Jerusalem, he sent messengers ahead of him into a city of the Samaritans; but they did not receive them. He rebuked James and John because they wished to ask for fire from heaven upon those who despised him, saying: “You do not know of what spirit you are. The Son of Man came not to destroy souls but to save them” (Luke IX, 51–56).

He appointed seventy-two and sent them two by two into every city and place where he himself was to come; [Col. 0040D] and he gave them instructions about what and how they ought to preach. He rebuked unbelieving cities. When the seventy-two returned rejoicing, he commanded them to rejoice not in the subjection of demons but in the inscription of their names in heaven. A confession of praise is offered to the Father. The Lord calls the eyes of the disciples blessed because they see what earlier righteous men and kings wished to see but did not see (Luke X, 1–24). To an expert in the Law who put him to the test he imparted the doctrines of true salvation, set out the parable of the man descending from Jerusalem to Jericho and his misfortunes, and plainly showed that the Samaritan who, after priest and Levite had passed by, helped the man wounded by robbers, had been his neighbour by showing mercy (Matt. XXII, 34–40; Mark XII, 28–34; Luke X, 25–37). [Col. 0041A] In a village Jesus entered as a guest and silenced Martha’s complaint that her sister was not helping her serve, declaring that she had chosen the better part (Luke X, 38–43).

Matthew thus sets out seven petitions in the Lord’s Prayer: “Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done, as in heaven also upon earth. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation. But deliver us from evil. Amen” (Matt. VI, 9–13).

In the first three petitions eternal things are sought; in the remaining four, temporal things, which nevertheless are necessary for attaining eternal things. But Luke (chapter [Col. 0041B] XI, 2–4) has comprised five petitions thus: “Father, hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our sins, since we ourselves also forgive everyone indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation.”

Behold: the seven petitions according to Matthew are abbreviated into five according to Luke. For God’s name is sanctified in the Spirit; but God’s kingdom is to come in the resurrection of the flesh. Then he adds the other three, concerning daily bread, forgiveness of sins, and avoidance of temptation. In these may fittingly be understood everything necessary to a human being in this life and the other.

Therefore, when the disciples asked Jesus, “Lord, teach [Col. 0041C] us to pray” (ibid., 1), he handed down not only a form of prayer, but also the urgency and frequency of prayer. He admonishes his followers concerning perseverance in continual prayer and gives the parable of the friend asking for three loaves at midnight; he urges them to ask, seek, and knock. For he exhorts them to ask for the food of God’s word, by which the friend—that is, the soul—is nourished; to seek the friend who gives abundantly, that is, the Lord; and to knock at the door of divine mercy, through which one enters the treasury of wisdom, where heavenly delights are preserved. The bread signifies charity, to which a stone is opposed—that is, the hardness of avarice. The fish is invisible faith because of the water of baptism, or because it is caught from invisible places and is not broken as it is tossed among the waves [Col. 0041D] of this world; a venomous serpent is opposed to it, by which faithless unbelief is represented. Hope is signified in the egg; for an egg is not yet a perfected offspring, but is hoped for as it is warmed. Despair is contrary to hope, and is represented by the scorpion, whose venomous sting strikes so far backward and, by its hidden prick, brings sudden destruction.

The Saviour rebuked blasphemers and men ungrateful for the benefits they saw. He offered the example of the armed man overcome by one stronger, and spoke of the unclean spirit returning sevenfold into a human being (Matt. XII, 31–45; Mark III, 27–30; Luke XI, 21–26). To the woman who cried out that blessed was the womb which had borne him, he replied that blessed was the person who kept God’s word (Luke XI, 27–28). After healing the man in whom three signs were performed at once—for the blind man sees, the mute speaks, and the man possessed by a demon is freed—Truth uttered many words of salvation, restrained the testing Pharisees by reason, said that a lamp ought not to be put under a bushel but upon a lampstand, and taught that the eye must be single (Matt. XII, 22–28; Mark III, 22–26; Luke XI, 14, 29–36).

Asked to dine at a Pharisee’s house, he noted that the Pharisee wondered why he had not been washed before dinner according to Jewish custom; he reproved external washing while inward parts were full of the filth of crimes, and, pronouncing “woe” six times against the Pharisees, added many of their evils (Matt. XXIII, 13–38; Luke XI, 37–52). He also commands his disciples to beware of the leaven of hypocrisy, [Col. 0042B] not to fear those who kill the body, and not to consider in persecution what they are to say (Matt. XVI, 6–12; Mark VIII, 15; Luke XII, 1–12).

When someone asked that an inheritance be divided between himself and his brother, he set forth the parable of the avaricious rich man. Then he commanded his disciples to avoid anxiety about food and clothing, an anxiety which birds do not have (Matt. VI, 25–34; Luke XII, 13–31). Promising the kingdom to the little flock, he ordered them to sell property, whether still to be acquired or already possessed, for almsgiving; and to have their loins girded and lamps burning. He also commands watchfulness, after mentioning the good and evil servant. He declares that the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it shall receive many stripes, but the ignorant servant few (Luke XII, 32–48). He says that he has come to cast fire upon the earth amid the necessity of those divided, and declares that those who discern the face of the sky ought to understand the evident time and to come to terms with an adversary on the way (Luke XII, 49–59). When some people slain by Pilate were reported to him, he said that all would perish likewise unless they repented, as also the eighteen crushed by the collapse of the tower. Setting forth the parable of the barren fig tree, he refers to those who defer repentance (Luke XIII, 1–9).

He raises up on the Sabbath a woman bent over for eighteen years, and refutes those who murmured at the cure on the Sabbath by the example of watering an ox; while the people rejoiced at his glorious miracles (Luke XIII, 10–17).

Comparing the kingdom of God to a mustard seed and leaven, and also speaking of the narrow way of life for the few, he says: [Col. 0042D] “The last shall be first, and the first last” (Matt. XIII, 31–34; Mark IV, 30–32; Luke XIII, 18–30). The Lord calls Herod a fox, by whom heretics are designated because of their deceit and snares; and he rebukes Jerusalem for refusing to be protected beneath his wings (Luke XIII, 31–35).

He heals a dropsical man on the Sabbath, as though delivering him from the pit of his fluid (Luke XIV, 1–4). He confounds the murmuring Pharisees by the example of drawing out an ass or ox that has fallen into a pit. Teaching also that humility must be pursued, he says that at a feast the first place must not be sought, and that one should feed not the rich but the poor, who cannot repay (Luke XIV, 5–14).

In many ways the Lord Jesus Christ, providing for human salvation, sets forth the parable of those invited who, seeking excuses, were not worthy of the supper. The first did not wish to come because of the estate he had bought; this signifies lovers of earthly wealth, who for its sake make light of striving after heavenly things. Another, detained by five yoke of oxen, did not go; this represents the inquisitive, who, enticed by bodily senses, care only to know outward things, and, while investigating others’ lives, neglect their own care and refuse to desire the feast of eternal salvation. The third refused to come because of a wife; this shows those entangled in the pleasure of the flesh. Thus, while earthly care occupies one person, shrewd reflection on another’s actions ravages another, and pleasure of the flesh stains still another’s mind, each fastidious person fails to hasten to the feast of everlasting life (Luke XIV, 16–20).

[Col. 0043B] To the crowds following him, the Saviour, speaking of those who were to leave even their close relations and their own life and follow him with the cross taken up, proposes the comparison of building a tower lest they fail, and offers the example of war between two kings (Luke XIV, 25–32).

## IX. What follows

When they murmured about the fellowship of sinners, he set forth the parables of the sheep and the drachma; just as their loss grieved the owner, so their finding brought joy. Thus joy among the angels over the salvation of one who repents is commended. Repentance is to lament evils committed and not repeat what must be lamented. Moreover, one who has committed forbidden things ought to cut off from himself even permitted things, in order to satisfy the divine will (Luke XV, 1–10).

[Col. 0043C] The Lord sets forth the parable of the sober and prodigal son, the return of the prodigal to his father, and the kindness with which the father received and kissed him; clothed him in the first robe, that is, the garment of innocence; and gave him the ring of sincere faith and shoes, that is, the office of proclaiming the Gospel. Thus God adorned the hands and feet of the convert—that is, his work and his course—and, after the fattened calf was killed, celebrated a feast. Hence, when the elder son—that is, the Jewish people—came from the field, that is, from external observance, and approached the house, he heard the symphony and dancing: that is, he perceived that the Church’s children, full of the Holy Spirit, were preaching the Gospel with harmonious voices. Learning the cause of the rejoicing, he was angry with his father and complained that he had killed the fattened calf for the destroyer of his property with harlots [Col. 0043D] and had preferred him to himself (Luke XV, 11–32).

Then the Lord presents, by contrast, the example of the steward of iniquity, who by more shrewd action reduced what was owed to his master (Luke XVI, 1–8). He declared that one cannot serve God and Mammon. He rebukes the avaricious Pharisees and, saying that the Law and the Prophets were until John the Baptist, introduces the unmerciful rich man clothed in purple and the poor man; showing what plunderers must suffer, if the miserly deserve to be punished in this way (Luke XVI, 13–31). He pronounces woe upon one who gives offence, but commands that a repentant brother be forgiven even seventy times seven (Matt. XVIII, 21–22; Luke XVII, 1–4). The apostles ask that their faith be increased, and hear of the power to move a tree; and, after offering [Col. 0044A] the comparison of a servant ploughing or feeding sheep, he teaches them to acknowledge themselves unprofitable servants, even when they have fulfilled what was commanded (Matt. XVII, 20; Luke XVII, 5–10).

While Jesus was going to Jerusalem, he was passing through the midst of Samaria and Galilee. At the entrance of a certain village he cleansed ten lepers, of whom only one—and he a foreigner—returned to give thanks (Luke 17:11–19). Asked about the time of the kingdom of God, he replied that it would not come with observable signs, and compared the coming of the Son of Man to lightning. He said that people would be overtaken on the sudden day of judgment, and likened that day to the days of Noah or Lot, when swift destruction came upon mortals. He also speaks of two in one bed, at the mill, and in the field: he declares that one of each will be taken and one left behind.

[Col. 0044B] By the name “bed” is figured the repose of the Church. He speaks of two as though of two persons; but this must be understood of two kinds of dispositions. For the person who, for God’s sake, pursues continence, so that, living without any anxiety, he may consider the things of the Lord, will be taken by God to eternal blessedness. But the person who, burning with love of human praise or with any other corruption of vices, damages the state of monastic life in which he has been instructed, must be left to eternal misery. This is suggested in the Lamentation of Jeremiah, which, under the figure of Judaea, describes the fall of every idle and sinful soul, saying: “Enemies saw her and mocked at her Sabbaths” (Lam. 1:7).

The two women grinding signify peoples occupied with the round and circuit of temporal affairs; as women are governed by men, so they ought to be governed by teachers. Labouring in various crafts, they serve the needs of the Church. One portion will be taken: that which enters marriage solely out of love for offspring and dispenses earthly property in order to acquire heavenly things. But that portion will be left behind which serves marriage for the allurements of the flesh, and which, if it has offered any earthly goods to the Church or to the poor, has done so in order that, as though it had bought off the Lord, it may abound the more in these things.

[Col. 0044C] The two in the field signify those labouring in the ministry of the Church, as in God’s field. The one who has sincerely preached God’s word will be taken; the one who has proclaimed Christ not chastely but from ulterior motive will be left behind (Luke 17:20–37).

The Church consists of these three kinds of persons, [Col. 0044D] each having two possible outcomes, because of being taken or left behind. Therefore the prophet Ezekiel saw three men delivered—Noah, Daniel, and Job (Ezek. 14:14)—in whom are signified preachers, the continent, and married persons. For Noah guided the ark amid the waters and therefore bore the figure of rulers. Daniel devoted himself to abstinence in the royal court and therefore represented the life of the continent. Job, however, established in marriage and exercising care for his own household, pleased God; through him the order of good married persons is fittingly figured.

Because one ought always to pray and not lose heart (Luke 18:1–8), the Lord sets forth the parable of the widow [Note: [Col. 0043D] Le Prévost: “widow,” correctly.], who sought vengeance against her adversary from an unjust judge and, through persistent prayers, obtained what she resolutely asked because of the annoyance she caused him.

[Col. 0045A] Having proposed the prayer of the Pharisee in the temple and that of the publican, he teaches that merits are not to be boasted of, but sins confessed (Luke 18:9–14). The good pray continually in order to obtain such vengeance upon their enemies that all the wicked may perish. For the wicked perish in two ways: either by conversion to righteousness, or by losing through punishment the power to do evil.

The Lord foretells that he will be handed over at Jerusalem and will suffer (Matt. 20:18–34; Mark 10:32–52; Luke 18:31–43). Near Jericho he heard a beggar beside the road; stopping, he had him brought to himself, and mercifully restored sight to the man who asked for it. Passing through Jericho, he saw Zacchaeus, chief of the publicans, up in a tree, and accepted lodging in [Col. 0045B] the house of one who earnestly desired to see him. When the Jews murmured because he had turned aside to a sinful man, Zacchaeus, standing firm in the truth of faith, said to the Lord: “Behold, Lord, I give half my goods to the poor; and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold.” Jesus said to him: “Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost” (Luke 19:1–11).

Then he gives the parable of a certain nobleman who went into a far country to receive a kingdom and return (ibid., v. 12), and of servants to whom he gave ten minas, that they might trade with them. When he returned, the first said: “Lord, your mina has gained ten minas.”

[Col. 0045C] The first servant is the order of teachers sent to the circumcision, who received one mina with which to trade, because they were commanded to preach one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God. Yet this same mina gained ten minas, because through teaching he joined to himself the people established under the Law. When that servant had been happily rewarded, another said: “Lord, your mina has made five minas” (ibid., v. 18). This servant is the company of those sent to evangelize among the uncircumcised; and those who, through them, were converted to the worship of the one God, having put to death the inclinations of the flesh, are deservedly set over them by divine appointment.

Moreover, the other servant who, though commanded to trade, stored away his master’s money in a cloth, denotes those who, though fitted to preach, refuse either to undertake, at the Lord’s command through the Church, the office of preaching, or at least to carry it out worthily.

[Col. 0045D] To bind money in a cloth is to hide gifts received beneath the idleness of sluggish torpor. In this parable, understand by the two faithful servants the teachers of both peoples; by the ten and five minas, the peoples who believe in the Lord; by the wicked servant, bad Catholics; by the enemies who did not wish the rightful heir to reign over them, the impiety of those who preferred either never to hear the word of faith or to corrupt it by falsely interpreting it; and by the sending of unsown seed, the examination even of those whom it did not happen to hear God’s word. In these five persons, indeed, every kind of humankind that will exist on the day of judgment is represented.

## X. Continuation

[Col. 0046A]

After these things had been said, Jesus went ahead to Jerusalem (ibid., v. 28). John alone records that, when the Feast of Dedication was being celebrated in winter at Jerusalem, the Jews said to Jesus as he walked in Solomon’s Portico: “How long will you keep us in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly.” Taking the occasion from this conversation, he said: “I and the Father are one,” and uttered other exalted sayings. Therefore the Jews, blinded by malice, took up stones to stone him. Then he again went beyond the Jordan, to the place where John had first baptized, and remained there. Many came there and believed in him (John 10:22–41).

At Bethany Lazarus was ill. His sisters Mary and Martha sent to Jesus for him, saying: “Lord, behold, he whom you love is ill.”

[Col. 0046B] On hearing this, Jesus said: “This illness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.” Then he remained there two days, and afterwards went with his disciples into Judaea, where he found Lazarus already four days in the tomb. When Martha heard of his coming, strong in faith, she met him and said: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.” She uses measured words, though she grieves without restraint over her brother’s death.

After her conversation with Christ and her true confession of faith, by which she believed him to be the Son of God, the life, and the resurrection, Martha called her sister Mary, speaking quietly: “The Master is here and is calling you.” She quickly rose,

[Col. 0046C] went outside the village, where the Saviour had stopped, and, seeing him, fell at his feet and said: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother Lazarus would not have died.” The fountain of compassion wept with his weeping friends over the death of his friend; but by weeping he brought forth inexhaustible joy for his own. Jesus, groaning within himself, came to the tomb, commanded the stone to be removed from the cave, and called in a loud voice the man who had been dead four days and was already stinking: “Lazarus, come forth!” Immediately he came out, bound hand and foot with bands; and the Lord at once ordered his disciples to loose him. After so glorious a miracle, to be proclaimed through all ages, had been performed, not all believed in Jesus; but many of the Jews who had come to console Mary and Martha, and had seen Lazarus’s unexpected resurrection, did believe (John 11:1–45).

[Col. 0046D]

There is no doubt that the Lord raised more dead persons; but the holy Gospel records that he raised only three for the sake of a definite mystery. By the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, who was raised within the walls of her home with few seeing it, are signified sinners who have sin shut up within their conscience and have not yet broken forth into action. These are commonly raised by divine inspiration when it recalls them from wrongful consent through private amendment.

By the widow’s son, who was carried out beyond the gates of the city and raised by Christ in the sight of many, are denoted guilty persons who, after consenting, proceed to commit the crime and, as it were, bring a dead person out from the hiding places of the soul, so that what was hidden in secret

[Col. 0047A] may appear in public. Such people are often healthfully admonished and divinely restored to life by the remedy of worthy conversion, while many know of it and rejoice.

By Lazarus, already buried and already stinking, are figured sinners entangled even in evil habit, so that the very habit of evil does not allow them to understand that what they do is evil. Hence they frequently defend the crime they commit and are now, as it were, buried beneath the huge weight of perverse habit. They grow insolently angry when reproved; and they stink while they are everywhere disparaged by the reproach of their evil reputation, and their neighbours, seeing them, are harmed by their example. Those whom human judgment considers deserving of condemnation are finally given life inwardly by God and afterwards absolved through priestly ministry.

In another sense, every human being is born dead through original sin. The first day of death is that given by the origin of descent. The second day of death is when the person grows into adolescence, reaches years capable of reason, and begins naturally to possess within himself the law by which people are naturally taught not to do to others what they do not wish done to themselves; yet they dare to transgress it.

[Col. 0047B] The third day of death is when the written Law is given to humanity, but is likewise despised. After all this Christ came, brought the Gospel, and preached the kingdom of heaven; he threatened Gehenna to evildoers and promised eternal life to those who lived well. The Gospel too is despised, and this is the fourth day of death, on which [Col. 0047C] Lazarus lay in the tomb.

Again, in another sense: first there is the stirring in the heart; second, consent; third, the deed; fourth, habit. By these modes, therefore, the guilty person dies and decays in the tomb. The grace of God calls back those made distant through sin and raises to life those oppressed by the manifold weight of sins.

When the marvellous miracle of the Godhead had been made public through the report of many who had carefully seen Lazarus unexpectedly come forth from the tomb by a law beyond nature, the chief priests and Pharisees gathered a council against Jesus; and, when Caiaphas prophesied, they determined to kill him.

Jesus therefore went away into the region near the wilderness,

[Col. 0047D] to a city called Ephraim, and remained there with his disciples. For the chief priests and their accomplices had given orders that, if anyone learned where he was, he should report it so that they might seize him. They feared, indeed, that the whole world would follow him and that the Romans, coming, would take away their kingdom from them (ibid., vv. 46–56).

Six days before Passover Jesus came to Bethany, and there they gave him a supper. Martha was serving, while Lazarus reclined at table. Mary took a pound of costly ointment of pure nard, anointed Jesus’ feet, and wiped them with her hair. Nard is a kind of aromatic. In Greek, *pistis* is called *fides* in Latin; hence the ointment is called *pisticum*, that is, “faithful,” because it preserves a corpse anointed with it unharmed from decay. The house is filled

[Col. 0048A] with the fragrance of the ointment when the Church is sprinkled with the good reputation of a religious life. Judas the unhappy man, who was a thief and kept the money-box, was offended by the sweetness of the fragrance that filled the house; he also criticized the service of the devout woman. But the Lord gently replied to his rash rebuke: “Leave her alone; for she has performed a good work upon me. Amen I say to you: throughout the whole world what she has done will be told in remembrance of her” (Matt. 26:6–13; Mark 14:3–9; John 12:1–8).

Many, led by curiosity, came to Bethany and saw Lazarus eating with Christ; rejoicing, they bore witness to the wonderful deed. Therefore the envious Pharisees planned to kill the man who had been raised, but they strove in vain to oppose Christ’s [Col. 0048B] omnipotence (John 12:9–11).

## XI. Jesus Enters Jerusalem.—Parables

On the next day a great crowd, which had gathered for the feast day, heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem; they took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him. As the hour of his immolation approached, the Lamb of God sought the place of suffering. When he came to Bethphage, at the Mount of Olives, he then sent two of his disciples, saying: “Go into the village opposite you, and immediately you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her. Untie them and bring them to me.” The disciples went and brought the donkey and colt; they put their garments upon them and made him sit upon them. Behold our king: as it was prophesied long ago concerning him,

[Col. 0048C] he does not sit in a golden chariot shining with purple, nor does he mount a fiery horse, a lover of discord and strife; rather, he sits upon the donkey, the friend of tranquillity and peace. He has no flashing swords around him, but comes meek; not to be feared because of power, but to be loved because of meekness. A very great crowd spread their garments in the road; others cut branches from the trees and spread them in the road. The crowds who went before and those who followed cried out: “Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Blessed is the kingdom of our father David! Hosanna in the highest!” Some Pharisees said to him: “Teacher, rebuke your disciples.” He said to them: “I tell you that, if these should be silent,

[Col. 0048D] the stones would cry out” (Matt. 21:1–9; Mark 11:1–10; Luke 19:29–44; John 12:12–15).

When he drew near and saw the city, he wept over it and, knowing beforehand the evils to come, foretold the calamities threatening it, because it had not recognized the time of its visitation. When he entered Jerusalem, the entire city was stirred, saying: “Who is this?” The people said: “This is Jesus, the prophet from Nazareth of Galilee.” He entered the temple of God and drove out all who were selling and buying in it. He overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those selling doves, saying: “It is written” (Isa. 56:7; Jer. 7:11), “‘My house shall be called a house of prayer’; but you have made it a den of robbers” (Matt. 21:10–16; Mark 11:15–17; Luke 19:45–46; John 2:13–16). Those who came to him,

[Col. 0049A] blind and lame, he healed in the temple. But when the chief priests and scribes saw the wonders he had done, and the children joyfully crying in the temple, “Hosanna to the Son of David!”, they were angered with the gall of envy and said to him: “Do you hear what these are saying?” Jesus replied: “I hear. Have you never read: ‘Out of the mouths of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise’?”

Having looked around at everything, he left the ill-disposed citizens and went out with the Twelve to Bethany, where he remained. Returning to the city in the morning, he was hungry. He came to a fig tree standing beside the road, but found on it nothing except leaves alone. Cursing it, he said: “May fruit never grow from you forever.” Immediately the fig tree withered, by which the Synagogue is signified: it had the words of the Law, not its fruits (Matt. 21:17–19; Mark 11:13–14).

When they asked by what authority he did such remarkable things in the temple, he asked whether John’s baptism was from heaven or from human beings. By so brief a question Christ confounded those who laid traps for him and stopped their mouths. For what they knew to be truly from heaven, they refused to confess because of malice; nor did they dare openly deny it because of fear of the crowds.

[Col. 0049B]

Then he gives the parable of the two sons whom their father sent into the vineyard and whose beginning and end were different. One obeyed his father not in word but in deed; the other, scorning him not with his mouth but with his actions, contradicted him (Matt. 21:23–32; Mark 11:27–33; Luke 20:1–8).

He added another parable concerning a husbandman

[Col. 0049C] who planted a vineyard, went abroad, and leased it to tenant-farmers. When his servants demanded the fruit of the vineyard, they seized them. They beat one, as Jeremiah; killed another, as Isaiah; and stoned another, as Naboth and Zechariah. Finally they crucified the Son of God. In a mystical sense, one servant and then another is sent whenever the Law, a psalm, and prophecy are read, so that people may act rightly through their admonition. But the messenger is beaten and cast out when the word is despised or, what is worse, blasphemed. So far as lies in his own power, he kills the heir who tramples the Son of God underfoot and insults the Spirit of grace. Once the evil cultivator has been destroyed, the vineyard is given to another, when the gift of grace that the proud person loses is received by the humble person (Matt. 21:33–41;

[Col. 0049D] Mark 12:1–9; Luke 20:9–16).

He set forth a third parable about the wedding which the kingly father made for his son, and punished the contemptuous invited guests by sending armies (Matt. 22:1–14).

The Pharisees, together with the Herodians, tested whether tribute might lawfully be paid to Caesar or not. When a coin was brought, Jesus answered: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22:15–22; Mark 12:13–17; Luke 20:20–26). The Sadducees also tested him concerning the woman who had seven husbands: whose wife she would be in the resurrection. Jesus answered: “You err, knowing neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. In the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven.” Behold, the good Teacher assures the children of the Church that those who rise again

[Col. 0050A] will enjoy the vision of God without the stain of corruption (Matt. 22:23–33; Mark 12:18–27; Luke 20:27–40).

When a doctor of the Law asked him what the great commandment in the Law was, he said: “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, with your whole soul, and with your whole mind. This is the greatest and first commandment. But the second is like it: You shall love your neighbour as yourself. On these two commandments hang the entire Law and the Prophets.” When they asked concerning the Christ whose son he was, he refuted them and showed that Christ was David’s Lord. He imposed such silence on them that no one dared from that day to ask him anything further; instead, they now openly strove to hand him over to Roman authority (Matt. 22:34–46; Mark 12:28–37; Luke 20:41–44).

[Col. 0050B]

Then Jesus spoke to the crowds and his disciples: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat. Therefore observe and do all that they tell you; but do not act according to their works. For they say and do not do. They bind heavy and unbearable burdens and place them on people’s shoulders, but they themselves are unwilling to move them with a finger. They do all their works in order to be seen by people. For they enlarge their phylacteries and make their fringes large. They love the first places at suppers, the first seats in synagogues, greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi by people. But do not be called Rabbi, for one is your teacher, and you are all brothers. And call no one your father

[Col. 0050C] on earth, for one is your Father, who is in heaven. Nor be called masters, for your one master is Christ. The greater among you will be your servant. Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted. Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who shut the kingdom of heaven before people! For you neither enter nor allow those who are entering to enter.”

Thus Jesus uttered many most healthful teachings: he taught the simple and rebuked hypocrites. He spoke of those swearing by the temple and the gold in the temple; of the altar and the gifts upon it; of divine compassion, which sent prophets, wise men, and scribes; and of the cruelty of the Jews, which put to death in various ways those sent by God.

[Col. 0050D]

He laments over Jerusalem; he mourns not stones but human beings. He repeated “Jerusalem” sorrowfully: she who kills the prophets and neglects to turn back from evil (Matt. 23). Jesus went out from the temple. When the disciples pointed out the great buildings of the temple, he answered: “Not one stone will be left upon another that will not be destroyed.” As he sat on the Mount of Olives, the disciples privately, as Matthew and Mark testify, asked about the time and signs of the destruction he had foretold. Answering their questions about the end, he said that many evils would come first: wars among nations, earthquakes in various places, pestilences and famines, terrors from heaven, and great signs. He prophesied much about future persecutions and his coming: believers must not premeditate what they will say when delivered up, but must possess their souls in patience.

[Col. 0051A] He foretold that Jerusalem would be surrounded by an army; woe to pregnant women; the sword and captivity; signs in heaven; and that he himself would come in a cloud with great power and majesty. “Look up,” he said, “because your redemption draws near.” Prohibiting drunkenness and the cares of this life, he commands watchfulness and prayer. He rebuked the pride of the scribes and affirmed that the widow who cast two small coins into the treasury had given more than all the others (Matt. 24; Mark 12:38–44; Luke 20:45; 21:4).

By the example of the fig tree he teaches concerning the coming of the consummation. He sets forth the parable of the ten virgins, and of the man who entrusted his goods to his servants and went abroad; of the coming of the Son of Man in his majesty with his angels; of the separation of sheep at the right hand and goats at the left; and he concludes with the retribution of the reprobate to eternal punishment and the reward of the just to eternal life (Matt. 24:32–33; 25; Luke 19:11–27).

## XII. The Passion of Our Lord Jesus Christ

On the first day of Unleavened Bread the disciples came to Jesus and said: “Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?” But he said to Peter and John: “Go into the city, to a certain man whom the man carrying a jar of water, who will meet you, shall point out to you. Follow him into the house which he enters, and say to the master of the house: ‘Where is the guest-room in which I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’ He will show you a large, furnished upper room; prepare it there.” They went and found things as he had told them, and prepared the Passover. When evening came, he came with the Twelve. As they reclined at table, he said: “I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. For I tell you that from now on I shall not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God” (Matt. 26:17–20; Mark 14:12–17; Luke 22:7–16).

[Col. 0051C]

According to John, supper having taken place, when the devil had already put into the heart of Judas, son of Simon Iscariot, that he should betray him, Jesus—knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going to the Lord—rose from supper and laid aside his garments. Having taken a towel, he girded himself. Then he poured water into a basin

[Col. 0051D] and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to dry them with the towel with which he was girded. After he had washed their feet and taken his garments, when he had reclined again, he said to them: “Do you know what I have done to you? You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for I am so. Therefore, if I, Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet,” and the rest as far as the place where he says: “He who receives me receives him who sent me” (John 13:1–20).

Matthew reports that, while the disciples were eating, Jesus said: “Amen I say to you that one of you is going to betray me.” Deeply saddened, they began one by one to say: “Is it I, Lord?” He answered: “He who dips his hand with me in the dish will betray me.” While they were dining, Jesus took

[Col. 0052A] bread, blessed and broke it, gave it to his disciples, and said: “Take and eat: this is my body.” Taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying: “Drink of this, all of you: this is my blood of the new covenant, which will be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. But I tell you: I shall no longer drink of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father” (Matt. 26:21–29; Mark 14:18–25; Luke 22:17–23).

The Lord, on the night on which he was betrayed, prayed three times, so that we too may pray for forgiveness of past sins, protection from present evils, and precaution against future dangers; and that we may direct every prayer to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Likewise, it should be noted that, just as there is a threefold temptation of desire,

[Col. 0052B] so also there is a threefold temptation of fear: the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and worldly ambition; likewise, fear of death, fear of humiliation, and fear of suffering. Against all these things he teaches that we ought to be fortified by prayer. Therefore the Lord’s three prayers may also be understood as corresponding to the threefold temptation of suffering.

John, the distinguished theologian, affirms that, after Jesus had washed the feet of Peter, who initially resisted strongly, and of the others, he first indicated the traitor still secretly among mystical words by the authority of prophetic Scripture, saying: “He who eats bread with me will lift up his heel against me.” Then, when he resolved to reveal him a second time, he was troubled in spirit and testified: “Amen, amen I say to you,

[Col. 0052C] that one of you will betray me.” The disciples looked at one another, uncertain of whom he spoke. Simon Peter signalled to John, who reclined upon Jesus’ breast, and John asked: “Lord, who is it?” “It is he,” he said, “to whom I shall give the dipped morsel.” And when he had dipped the morsel, he gave it to Judas, son of Simon Iscariot. After the morsel, Satan then entered into him, and Jesus said to him: “What you are doing, do quickly.” None of those reclining knew why he said this to him. Judas immediately went out after these things. And it was night. When he had gone out, Jesus said: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him” (John 13:18–31).

He also spoke many words of wonderful profundity concerning true love of God and neighbour, the unity of the Trinity,

[Col. 0052D] Peter’s threefold denial, the coming and consolation of the Holy Spirit the Paraclete, the keeping of God’s commandments and the happy reward of the good, the persecution of believers and the inexcusable condemnation of unbelievers, the scattering of the disciples, and his own passion now at hand.

Having concluded his incomparable discourse, Jesus lifted his eyes to heaven and graciously poured forth to the Father a prayer sure to be heard, for his disciples and for all who would believe in God through their word. In it, as a most merciful advocate, he asked the Father on our behalf for far greater things than human frailty would have dared to request (John 13:21–17:26).

## XIII. Continuation of the Passion

Then, according to Luke, a dispute arose among the disciples as to which of them seemed to be greatest.

[Col. 0053A] But the heavenly teacher urged them altogether toward humility by examples and words. Thus he compassionately restrained the contention of his weak disciples and declared himself, solely through compassion, to be their servant. To those who remained with him he also promises a kingdom; and, after some further words, says to Peter, who was boasting rashly: “Simon, behold, Satan has demanded you, that he might sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers.” Peter said to him: “Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death.” And he said: “I tell you, Peter: the cock will not crow today before you deny three times that you know me.” He said to them: “When I sent you without purse, bag, and shoes, did you lack anything?” They said:

[Col. 0053B] “Nothing.” Therefore he said to them: “But now let the one who has a purse take it, and likewise a bag; and let the one who does not have one sell his tunic and buy a sword.” They said: “Behold, here are two swords.” He said to them: “It is enough” (Luke 22:24–38).

And, as Matthew and Mark record, after a hymn had been sung they went out to the Mount of Olives. There he then said to them: “All of you will take offence because of me this night.” From there he came to the estate of Gethsemane, which is interpreted “valley of the rich,” or “of fatness.” He said to his disciples: “Sit here and pray, lest you enter into temptation.” Taking Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be afraid and to be distressed or sorrowful. He withdrew from them about a stone’s throw away;

[Col. 0053C] kneeling, he prayed, saying: “Father, if you will, take this cup away from me. Yet let not my will but yours be done” (Matt. 26:30–34; Mark 14:26–39; Luke 22:39–42; John 18:1).

An angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him; and, falling into agony, he prayed more earnestly. His sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground. We understand that there was a garden beyond the brook Cedron, into which he and his disciples entered; Judas knew this place. Having received a cohort and attendants from the chief priests and Pharisees, Judas came there with lanterns, torches, and weapons. Immediately approaching Jesus, he said: “Hail, Rabbi,” and kissed him. Then they came forward, laid hands on Jesus, and seized him. Then, as John records,

[Col. 0053D] Jesus said to them: “Whom do you seek?” They answered: “Jesus the Nazarene.” When he said, “I am he,” they went backward and fell to the ground, and so forth (Matt. 26:45–50; Mark 14:40–46; Luke 22:43–48; John 18:2–9).

Those who were about him, Luke says, saw what was about to happen and said: “Lord, shall we strike with the sword?” Then Peter struck Malchus, servant of the chief priest, and cut off his right ear. Jesus answered those who asked: “Allow it thus far” (Luke 22:49–51); and immediately added to Peter, who had struck: “Put your sword back in its place. For all who take the sword will perish by the sword. Or do you think that I cannot ask my Father,

[Col. 0054A] and he will provide me with more than twelve legions of angels? How then will the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must happen in this way?” (Matt. 26:52–54). To these words may be added what John records that he said in that place: “Shall I not drink the cup which the Father has given me?” (John 18:11). Then, as Luke says, he touched Malchus’ ear and healed it (Luke 22:51). In that hour Jesus said to the crowds: “Have you come out, as against a robber, with swords and clubs to seize me? Daily I sat among you teaching in the temple, and you did not seize me. But this is your hour, and the power of darkness.” Then all the disciples left him and fled. One young man, clothed in a linen cloth, followed him; when they seized him, he left the linen cloth behind and fled from them naked. In that crowd, when the tribune, cohort, and Jewish attendants were present,

[Col. 0054B] the Saviour was bound and first taken to Annas, the chief priest and father-in-law of Caiaphas (Matt. 26:55–57; Mark 14:47–53; John 18:12–13).

Peter, however, followed from afar as far as the courtyard of the chief priest. Having entered within, he sat by the fire with the attendants, for it was cold, in order to see the outcome. When a fire had been kindled in the middle of the courtyard and they were sitting around it, Peter was among them (Matt. 26:58; Mark 14:54; Luke 22:55; John 18:15–16). Peter is worthy of the greatest admiration because, even while afraid, he followed the Lord. His fear belongs to nature; his following, to devotion; his denial, to sudden weakness; his repentance,

[Col. 0054C] to faith.

The chief priests and the whole council sought false testimony against Jesus in order to hand him over to death, but found none, although many false witnesses came forward. The chief priest, while Jesus was silent, said: “I adjure you by the living God to tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God.” Jesus said to him: “You have said it.” Then the chief priest tore his garments, saying: “He has blasphemed. What further need have we of witnesses? Behold, you have now heard the blasphemy. What do you think?” They answered: “He is deserving of death.” Then they spat in his face and struck him with their fists (John 18). Others covered his face and struck his face with the palms of their hands, saying: “Prophesy to us, Christ: who is it that struck you?” The Lord is understood to have suffered these things at night in the house of the chief priest to whom he was first brought; there also Peter was tested amid these insults to the Lord.

[Col. 0054D] Peter’s threefold denial began before the first cockcrow and, according to Mark, was completed before the second. The other three Evangelists observed that before the first crow the whole denial had been conceived in Peter’s disposition and fear. At last Peter remembered the word of Jesus, who had said: “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.” And he went out and wept bitterly (Matt. 26:59–75; Mark 14:55–72; Luke 22:56–71; John 18:17–27).

The high priest questioned Jesus about his disciples and his teaching. Jesus answered him: “I have spoken openly to the world; I have taught openly in synagogue and in the Temple, where all the Jews assemble; and I have said nothing in secret [Col. 0055A]. Why do you question me? Question those who heard what I said to them. Behold, they know what I have said.” When he had said this, one of the attending servants struck Jesus, saying, “Is that how you answer the high priest?” Jesus answered him: “If I have spoken wrongly, bear witness concerning the wrong; but if rightly, why do you strike me?” And Annas sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest (John XVIII, 19–24).

When morning came, as Matthew relates, all the chief priests and elders of the people took counsel against Jesus, to deliver him over to death; and they brought him bound and handed him over to Pontius Pilate, the governor. (Matthew XXVII, 1–2.)

## XIV. What followed in the Passion of Our Lord Jesus Christ

[Col. 0055B] Luke connected the narrative concerning what was done to the Lord about morning, when the men who held him mocked him as they beat him; they covered him, struck his face, and spoke many blasphemies against him. When day came, the elders of the people, the chief priests, and the scribes assembled, and brought him into their council, saying: “If you are the Christ, tell us.” He said to them: “If I tell you, you will not believe me. But if I also question you, you will not answer me, nor let me go. Henceforth the Son of Man shall be seated at the right hand of the power of God.” All said: “Then are you the Son of God?” He said: “You say that I am.” But they said: “Why do we still require testimony? For we ourselves have heard it [Col. 0055C] from his mouth.” And their whole multitude arose and brought him to Pilate. Luke narrated all this (chapters XXII, 66–71, and XXIII, 1). Matthew and Mark, however, narrated the things done to the Lord up to morning; but afterward they returned to recount Peter’s denial (Matthew XXVI; Mark XIV). When that was finished, they returned to the morning, in order to connect from there the remaining things done to the Lord (Matthew XXVII; Mark XV).

John likewise says: “They bring Jesus from Caiaphas to the praetorium. It was morning, and they themselves did not enter the praetorium, so that they might not be defiled, but might eat the Passover.” Then the wicked assembly gathered there, and brought the Lord as though an already convicted criminal, Caiaphas urging it on, since he had already judged [Col. 0055D] that Jesus should die; no delay was allowed before he was handed over to Pilate for condemnation.

Matthew alone narrated the end of Judas the betrayer, saying: “Then Judas, who betrayed him, seeing that he had been condemned, moved by repentance, brought back the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, saying: ‘I have sinned, betraying innocent blood.’ But they said: ‘What is that to us? See to it yourself.’ Throwing down the silver in the Temple, he departed; and going away, he hanged himself with a noose. The chief priests, taking the silver, said: ‘It is not lawful to put it into the corban, because it is the price of blood.’ Having taken counsel, they bought with it the potter’s field, for the burial of strangers. Therefore that field was called Acheldemach—that is, Field of Blood—until the present day.” Thus was fulfilled [Col. 0056A] what had formerly been prophesied (Matthew XXVII, 3–10; Acts I, 18–19).

Thereafter the holy evangelists endeavor to recount in sequence the things done to the Lord through Pilate. Diligent readers ought carefully to investigate these matters and appropriately fit each thing into its proper place. In Christ’s Passion, as the diligent Augustine, bishop of Hippo, writes in the third book *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, many things were said and many answers given. Therefore each selected as much as seemed good to him and placed in his own narrative what he judged sufficient.

Jesus, as Matthew states, stood before the governor; and, when asked by him whether he was King of the Jews, answered: “You say it” (Matthew XXVII, 11). Pilate went out, [Col. 0056B] as John relates, to those who had not entered the praetorium, and said: “What accusation do you bring against this man?” They answered: “If he were not an evildoer, we would not have handed him over to you.” Pilate said to them: “Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law.” The Jews said: “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death.” Pilate again entered the praetorium, summoned Jesus, and said: “Are you King of the Jews?” Jesus answered: “Do you say this of yourself, or have others told you about me?” Pilate answered: “Am I a Jew? Your own nation and your chief priests have delivered you to me. What have you done?” Jesus answered: “My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would fight [Col. 0056C] so that I should not be handed over to the Jews. But now my kingdom is not from here.”

Pilate therefore said: “Then you are a king?” Jesus answered: “You say that I am a king. For this I was born, and for this I came into the world: to bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice.” Pilate said to him: “What is truth?” And having said this, he again went out to the Jews and said to them: “I find no charge in him” (John XVIII, 29–38). Then the enraged Jews, as Luke relates, began to accuse him, saying: “We have found this man subverting our nation, forbidding tribute to be given to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Christ, a king” (Luke XXIII, 1–25). And when, as Matthew says, he was accused by the chief priests and elders of the people, [Col. 0056D] he answered nothing, which he did out of meekness. Then Pilate said to him: “Do you not hear how many testimonies they speak against you?” And he answered him not a word, so that the governor marveled greatly. While he was seated upon the judgment seat, his wife sent to him, saying: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man. For today I have suffered much in a dream because of him” (Matthew XXVII, 13–19). When Pilate said, “I find no charge in the man,” the Jews, as Luke writes, became more insistent, saying: “He has stirred up the people throughout all Judaea, teaching from Galilee even to this place.”

But Pilate, hearing “Galilee,” asked whether the man was a Galilean; and when he learned that he was under Herod’s jurisdiction, he sent him to Herod, who was himself in Jerusalem in those days. Herod, seeing [Col. 0057A] Jesus, rejoiced greatly. For he had long desired to see him, because he had heard much about him and hoped to see some sign done by him. He questioned him at length. But Jesus answered him nothing. The chief priests and scribes stood there, persistently accusing him. Herod, with his soldiers, despised and mocked him, clothed him in a white garment, and sent him back to Pilate. Herod and Pilate became friends on that day; for previously they had been enemies toward one another.

Pilate, having summoned the authorities and the people, said to them: “You brought this man to me as one perverting the people; and behold, I have questioned him before you and found in this man no charge of the things of which you accuse him. Nor has Herod. For I sent [Col. 0057B] you to him, and behold, nothing deserving death has been done by him. Therefore I shall punish him and release him” (Luke XXIII, 16). For he knew that they had handed him over out of envy. At the feast the governor customarily released to the people one prisoner whom they wished. When they had assembled, he said: “Whom do you want me to release to you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ?” But the chief priests and elders persuaded the crowds to ask for Barabbas and destroy Jesus. Barabbas was a notorious robber, who had been cast into prison because of a sedition that had occurred in the city and murder. The governor said: “Which of the two do you want released to you?” They said: “Barabbas.” Pilate said to them: “What then shall I do with Jesus who is called Christ?” All said: “Let him be crucified.” The governor said to them: [Col. 0057C] “For what evil has he done?” But they cried out all the more: “Let him be crucified.” Pilate, seeing that he accomplished nothing and that rather a tumult was arising, took water and washed his hands before the people, saying: “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man; see to it yourselves.” And the whole people answered: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.” Then Pilate released Barabbas to them (Matthew XXVII, 15–26), but seized Jesus and scourged him.

John relates that the soldiers then plaited a crown of thorns, set it on his head, and clothed him with a purple robe. They came to him and said: “Hail, King of the Jews!” And they struck him. Pilate again went outside and said to them: “Behold, I bring him out [Col. 0057D] to you, that you may know that I find no charge in him.” Jesus therefore came out, bearing the crown of thorns and the purple garment. And he said to them: “Behold the man.” When the chief priests and servants saw him, they cried out: “Crucify, crucify him!” Pilate said to them: “Take him yourselves and crucify him; for I find no charge in him.” The Jews answered: “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.” When Pilate heard this statement, he was more afraid. He entered the praetorium again and said to Jesus: “Where are you from?” But Jesus gave him no answer. Pilate therefore said to him: “Will you not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to crucify you, and authority to release you?” Jesus answered: “You would have no authority at all against me [Col. 0058A] unless it had been given to you from above. Therefore the one who handed me over to you has the greater sin.” From that point Pilate sought to release him. But the Jews cried out: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend; for everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar.”

Pilate therefore, when he heard these words, brought Jesus outside and sat upon the judgment seat in the place called Lithostrotos, but in Hebrew Gabbatha. It was the Preparation of the Passover, about the sixth hour. And he said to the Jews: “Behold your king.” But they cried: “Away with him, away with him; crucify him!” Pilate said to them: “Shall I crucify your king?” The chief priests answered: “We have no king but Caesar.” Then he handed him over to them to be crucified (John XIX, 1–16).

John narrated these acts done through Pilate, which [Col. 0058B] Matthew and Mark recalled because they had passed them over. For Matthew says thus: “Then the governor’s soldiers, taking Jesus into the praetorium, gathered the whole cohort around him. Stripping him, they put a scarlet cloak around him. Plaiting a crown of thorns, they put it upon his head, and a reed in his right hand. Kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying: ‘Hail, King of the Jews!’ Spitting upon him, they took the reed and struck his head with it. After they had mocked him, they stripped him of the cloak—or, according to Mark, the purple robe (chapter XV, 17)—clothed him in his own garments, and led him away to crucify him” (Matthew XXVII, 27–31). John relates that Jesus, bearing his own cross, went out to Golgotha, that is, the Place of Calvary. But Simon of Cyrene, [Col. 0058C] father of Alexander and Rufus, whom three evangelists mention, was coming from the countryside and was compelled into service; afterward the cross was given to him to carry as far as the place mentioned (Matthew XXVII, 27–33; Mark XV, 16–22; Luke XXIII, 26–32; John XIX, 17).

## XV. The Death of Our Lord Jesus Christ

At Golgotha they crucified Jesus with two robbers, gave him myrrhed wine to drink, and placed above his head the written charge against him: “This is Jesus, King of the Jews.” This title was written in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew letters (Matthew XXVII, 34–37; Mark XV, 23–26; Luke XXIII, 33–38; John XIX, 17–22).

The soldiers therefore, after they had crucified him, took [Col. 0058D] his garments and made four portions, a portion for each soldier, and also took the tunic. Now the tunic was seamless, woven from the top throughout. They therefore said to one another: “Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it, to see whose it shall be,” so that the Scripture might be fulfilled (Psalm XXI, 19), saying: “They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots” (Matthew XXVII, 34–37; Mark XV, 23–26; Luke XXIII, 33–38; John XIX, 23–24).

The chief priests and scribes blasphemed him as he hung upon the cross; shaking their heads, they said: “Ha! You who destroy God’s Temple and rebuild it in three days, save yourself. If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross” (Matthew XXVII, 40; Mark XV, 29–30).

But one, according to Luke, of the robbers who hung [Col. 0059A] there blasphemed him, saying: “If you are the Christ, save yourself and us.” But the other rebuked him, saying: “Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same condemnation? We indeed justly, for we receive things worthy of our deeds; but this man has done nothing wrong.” And he said to Jesus: “Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom.” Jesus said to him: “Amen, I say to you: today you shall be with me in Paradise” (Luke XXIII, 39–43).

Standing beside Jesus’ cross were his mother, his mother’s sister Mary of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene. Therefore, when Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing there, he said to his mother: “Woman, behold your son.” Then he said to the disciple: “Behold your mother.” And from that hour the disciple received her into his own home (John [Col. 0059B] XIX, 25–27).

From the sixth hour darkness came over the whole land until the ninth hour; and about the ninth hour Jesus cried out in a loud voice, saying: “Eli, Eli, lama zababdani?” that is: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew XXVII, 45–46.) Afterward, knowing that all things had now been completed, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, Jesus said: “I thirst.” A vessel full of vinegar was standing there. They put a sponge full of vinegar around hyssop and offered it to his mouth (John XIX, 28–29). And, crying with a loud voice, according to Luke, he said: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke XXIII, 46).

Finally, according to John, when Jesus had received the vinegar, he said: “It is finished”; and, bowing [Col. 0059C] his head, he gave up his spirit (John XIX, 30). And behold, the veil of the Temple was torn in two from top to bottom; the earth shook, rocks were split, tombs were opened, and many bodies of saints who had fallen asleep arose. Coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they entered the holy city and appeared to many. The centurion and those with him who were guarding Jesus, seeing the earthquake and the things that occurred, were greatly afraid, saying: “Truly this was the Son of God.” There were there Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joseph, the mother of the sons of Zebedee, and many other women at a distance, who had followed Jesus from Galilee and ministered to him. All who had assembled for the spectacle, [Col. 0059D] seeing what occurred, returned beating their breasts (Matthew XXVII, 50–56; Mark XV, 37–41; Luke XXIII, 46–49).

When it had already become evening, Joseph of Arimathea, a distinguished councillor, a good and righteous man, waiting for the kingdom of God, yet a secret disciple because of fear of the Jews, boldly approached Pilate and asked him for Jesus’ body. When the governor had learned from the centurion that he was dead, he permitted it. Joseph therefore came and took Jesus’ body; having bought a linen shroud, he wrapped the body after taking it down. Nicodemus also came, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds. They therefore took Jesus’ body and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as is the Jewish custom in burial. Now in the place where he had been crucified [Col. 0060A] there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb cut in rock, in which no one had yet been laid. There, therefore, because of the Jewish Preparation, since the tomb was near, they placed Jesus. The aforementioned women, who loved him more ardently, sat opposite the sepulchre and watched where he was laid (Matthew XXVII, 57–61; Mark XV, 42–47; Luke XXIII, 50–55; John XIX, 38–42).

On the following day the priests and Pharisees maliciously suggested certain matters to Pilate concerning the words of the Lord Jesus; and, with his approval, they sealed the stone and secured the tomb by posting guards (Matthew XXVII, 62–66).

Certain matters are read in the Gospel narrative concerning what occurred at the Lord’s resurrection, which may seem contradictory if the order in which they happened [Col. 0060B] is not carefully considered. Therefore I wish to investigate what Augustine, the penetrating interpreter of Holy Scripture, says and discusses on this point in Book III of *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, and to record here the same passage as he published it. After clarifying many questions, he says:

> “Let us arrange in one narrative all that occurred around the time of the Lord’s resurrection, according to the testimony of all the evangelists, insofar as the Lord may help us, in the order in which it could have happened.
>
> ## XVI. His Resurrection and Ascension
>
> “Early on the first day of the week, as all agree, they came to the tomb. What Matthew alone mentions had already occurred [Col. 0060C]: the earthquake, the rolling away of the stone, and the terror of the guards, so that in some measure they lay as if dead. Then came, as John says, Mary Magdalene—undoubtedly with the other women who had ministered to the Lord, but more fervent than they in love, so that John not without reason mentions her alone while passing over those who were with her, as the others testify. She came, therefore; and when she saw the stone removed from the tomb, before examining anything more closely, she did not doubt that Jesus’ body had been taken away. She ran, as John himself says, and announced it to Peter and to John himself. For he is the disciple whom Jesus loved. They began to run to the tomb; [Col. 0060D] John arrived first, bent down, and saw the linen cloths lying there, but did not enter. Peter, coming after him, entered the tomb and saw the linen cloths lying there, and the cloth that had been over his head—not lying with the linen cloths, but folded separately. Then John too entered, saw likewise, and believed what Mary had said: that the Lord had been taken from the tomb. For they did not yet understand the Scriptures, that he must rise from the dead. The disciples therefore departed to their own homes. But Mary stood outside the tomb weeping—that is, before the site of that stone sepulchre, yet still within the space into which they had already entered. For there was a garden there, as John himself mentions (John XIX, 41). Then they saw an angel sitting at the right [Col. 0061A] upon the stone rolled away from the tomb; Matthew and Mark relate concerning this angel: Then he said to them: ‘Do not be afraid. For I know that you seek Jesus, who was crucified. He is not here, for he has risen, as he said. Come and see the place where the Lord was laid. Go quickly and tell his disciples that he has risen; and behold, he goes before you into Galilee. There you shall see him. Behold, I have told you beforehand.’ Mark too did not pass over similar words (Matthew XXVIII, 1–7; Mark XVI, 1–7).
>
> “At these words Mary, while she wept, bent down and looked into the tomb; and she saw, as John says, two angels seated in white, one at the head and one at the feet, where Jesus’ body had lain. They said to her: ‘Woman, why are you weeping?’ [Col. 0061B] She said to them: ‘Because they have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him.’ Here the angels must be understood to have risen, so that they were also seen standing, as Luke records them to have been seen; and they said to the frightened women, whose faces were bowed to the ground: ‘Why do you seek the living among the dead? He is not here, but has risen. Remember how he spoke to you while he was still in Galilee, saying that the Son of Man must be handed over into the hands of sinful men, be crucified, and rise on the third day.’ And they remembered his words (Luke XXIV, 1–8; John XX, 1–13).
>
> “After this Mary turned around and saw Jesus standing there, as John says, but did not know that it was Jesus. Jesus said to her: ‘Woman, why are you weeping? [Col. 0061C] Whom do you seek?’ Thinking that he was the gardener, she said to him: ‘Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.’ Jesus said to her: ‘Mary!’ Turning, she said: ‘Rabboni,’ which means ‘Teacher.’ Jesus said to her: ‘Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father. But go to my brethren and tell them: I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’ Then she departed from the tomb—that is, from that place where the garden’s open space was before the excavated stone—and the others with her, whom, according to Mark, trembling and fear had seized; and they said nothing to anyone. Then, according to Matthew, behold, Jesus met them and said: ‘Greetings.’ They approached, took hold of [Col. 0061D] his feet, and worshipped him. Thus we infer that they received the angels’ address twice when they came to the tomb, and likewise the Lord’s appearance twice: once there, when Mary thought him the gardener, and now again on the road, when he met them, so that by this repetition he might strengthen them and restore them from fear. Then he said to them: ‘Do not be afraid. Go, announce to my brethren that they are to go into Galilee. There they shall see me.’ Mary Magdalene therefore came announcing to the disciples that she had seen the Lord and that he had said these things to her; not she alone, but also the others whom Luke mentions. They reported these things to the eleven disciples and to all the rest. But their words seemed like nonsense to them [Col. 0062A], and they did not believe them. Mark also testifies to this. For after recounting that they had gone out from the tomb trembling and afraid, saying nothing to anyone, he adds that the risen Lord appeared early on the first day of the week first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons; that she went and announced it to those who had been with him, mourning and weeping; and that they, hearing that he lived and had been seen by her, did not believe. Matthew, moreover, inserted this too: when the women who had seen and heard all these things were departing, some of those guards who had lain as if dead came into the city and told the chief priests all that had occurred—namely, those things which they could themselves perceive.
