The chief priests, [Col. 0062B] gathered with the elders, took counsel and gave the soldiers a large sum of money to say that his disciples had stolen him while they slept. They also promised them security from the governor who had assigned them as guards. The soldiers, having received the money, did as they had been instructed; and this report was spread among the Jews until the present day. Luke alone of the four evangelists does not say that the Lord was seen by the women, but only the angels. Matthew, however, says that he met them as they returned from the tomb. Mark too says that he was first seen by Mary Magdalene, as does John; but he does not say how he was seen by her, which is explained by John (Matthew XXVIII, 8–15; Mark XVI, 8–11; Luke [Col. 0062C] XXIV, 9–12; John XX, 14–18 [Note: [Col. 0061] St Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, *Works*, vol. III, part I, col. 1201; *Patrologia*, vol. XXXIV.]).”

All four evangelists, just as they agree in truthfully reporting all that the almighty Emmanuel did before his Passion, likewise narrate his resurrection and ascension harmoniously, and record that the Lord risen from the dead was seen by people ten times.

Once he appeared to the women at the tomb; again to the same women as they returned from the tomb; thirdly, to Simon Peter. Although an evangelist does not specify when or where this occurred, he clearly records that it occurred. Fourthly, he appeared in another form, so that he would not be recognized, to two men going to the village of Emmaus. Traveling beside them on the road as a stranger, he asked the cause of their sadness and lamentation; [Col. 0062D] and, after hearing Cleophas’s lament concerning Jesus of Nazareth, who was a prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people, and concerning his condemnation, he gently rebuked them. Beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he expounded the Scriptures. Drawn by them to their lodging, he reclined with them, took bread at the meal, blessed it, broke it, gave it to them, and in the breaking of bread opened their eyes to recognize him; once recognized, he immediately vanished from their sight. Fifthly, as Luke and John testify, he appeared in the evening to several persons assembled in Jerusalem, where Thomas was absent. Jesus entered although the doors were shut, showed them his hands and side, and ate before them a portion of roasted fish and a honeycomb [Col. 0063A]; he breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit,” and the rest (John XX, 22). Sixthly, after eight days, Thomas saw him and said: “My Lord and my God” (ibid., 28). Seventhly, at the Sea of Tiberias, where seven disciples fishing saw him in the morning after their night’s labor, and after the miraculous catch of one hundred and fifty-three fish ate bread and fish with him on the shore. Eighthly, on the mountain of Galilee according to Matthew, where they saw him and worshipped him, though some doubted. Then he said to them: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you all days until the end of the age” [Col. 0063B] (Matthew XXVIII, 7). Ninthly, what Mark says: “At last Jesus appeared to them while they were reclining, and sternly reproached their unbelief” (Mark XVI, 12–14). He is called “at last” because they were no longer to dine with him on earth. Tenthly, on that same day, no longer on earth but raised in a cloud, the disciples saw him as he ascended into heaven; Mark and Luke record this (Mark XVI, 19; Luke XXIV, 51).

Thus he is recorded in the Gospel books as having been seen by people so many times before he ascended into heaven: nine times, namely, on earth, and once in the air as he ascended. But not all things were written, as John says (John XXI, 25). For his association with them was frequent [Col. 0063C] during the forty days before he ascended into heaven (Matthew XXVIII, 16–20; Mark XVI, 12–14; Luke XXIV, 13–49; John XX, 15; XXI, 4); yet he did not appear to them on all forty days continuously. For John says that, after the first day of his resurrection, another eight days intervened (John XX, 16), after which he appeared to them again. Thus, throughout those forty days, appearing whenever he wished, to whom he wished, and in whatever manner he wished, he confirmed in them faith in his resurrection.

Mark and Luke recount the final two appearances, together with what was said or done there. According to Mark, he rebuked the hardness of the unbelievers’ heart; and, having confirmed them in faith, said: “Go into all the world; preach the Gospel [Col. 0063D] to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved; but whoever does not believe shall be condemned. These signs shall follow those who believe: in my name they shall cast out demons; they shall speak in new tongues; they shall take up serpents; and if they drink anything deadly, it shall not harm them. They shall lay hands upon the sick, and they shall recover.” The Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God (Mark XVI, 15–19). But Luke says at the end of his Gospel: “He led them out to Bethany; and, lifting up his hands, he blessed them. And it came to pass, while he blessed them, that he departed from them and was carried up into heaven” (Luke XXIV, 50–51).

Likewise, at the beginning of the Acts of the Apostles, he says concerning the Lord’s ascension: “While eating with them, he commanded them [Col. 0064A] not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the Father’s promise, which, he said, you heard through my mouth. For John indeed baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.” Therefore those who had gathered together asked him, saying: “Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” But he said to them: “It is not for you to know the times or seasons which the Father has set by his own authority; but you shall receive the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you, and you shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem, throughout all Judaea and Samaria, and to the uttermost part of the earth.” When he had said this, while they watched, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their sight. And as they gazed into heaven while he went, behold, two men stood beside them in white garments, and said: “Men of Galilee, [Col. 0064B] why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, shall come in the same manner as you saw him go into heaven.” Then they returned to Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath-day’s journey away (Acts I, 12). There, as Luke testifies, the faithful disciples rejoiced particularly in the triumph of their heavenly Master; they persevered unitedly in prayer in the Temple and upper room, and confidently awaited, as he had commanded, the Father’s promise through the Son (ibid., 14).

For they had verified everything they had heard from him by the certain fulfillment of his works, and now visibly beheld it completed with their own eyes. For just as they had repeatedly heard from his own mouth that he would endure terrible suffering in his Passion and would himself rise victoriously on the third day, so they now joyfully behold the giver of life, death conquered and now immortal; and, as he is exalted above the heavens and seated at the Father’s right hand, they exult in blessed triumph. The angels too, appearing in white garments and addressing with wonder the Galileans intent upon heaven, signify the joy of angels and human beings, and announce his universal coming at the end of the age to judge the nations.

Peter and John, James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas of James, who remained with the Lord Jesus to the end, were called by him the salt of the earth and the light of the world (Matthew V, 13–14); and deservedly, because, despising the world, they followed [Col. 0064D] his footsteps, they were divinely established as rulers of the world and judges of the age. After the venerable assembly, in which there were about one hundred and twenty, had returned to Jerusalem, Peter, first in calling and greatest in dignity, rose in the midst of the brethren and spoke of Judas the traitor: how, hanging between heaven and earth, he burst asunder in the middle and his entrails poured out, because he was worthy neither of heaven nor of earth; and how the field bought at the price of Christ was called Haceldama, that is, Field of Blood. He then urged that, as David had foretold, another should be chosen in his place for the work of preaching and the heavenly ministry. All therefore accepted the former’s judgment; and, lest the sacred number of the apostles should seem incomplete, they put forward Joseph the Just and Matthias, and [Col. 0065A] cast lots for them. After prayer had been offered by Peter and confirmed by the others, the lot fell upon Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles (Acts I, 15–26).

These are the twelve hours of the day and the perfect twelve months of the year: the apostles, long ago signified by the prophets and patriarchs through many enigmas. All nations of the faithful venerate them; and they are deservedly accounted senators of heaven and glorious princes of the Church, because, as fruitful branches, they clung to Christ the true vine. For by voluntary poverty among humankind they especially imitated his footsteps in the fields, and shone with wondrous powers as his distinguished companions and fellow consecrated ones. Now they sit with him upon heavenly thrones and are the righteous judges of the twelve tribes of Israel. And just as on earth they constantly ran, as followers of Christ, toward the prize of life [Col. 0065B], and labored strenuously in the Church as his representatives and witnesses, so now, blessed co-heirs with him, they shine in heaven.

## XVII. The Holy Spirit Descends upon the Apostles

When the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, and the faithful disciples were assembled together at the third hour, there suddenly came a sound from heaven, and the Holy Spirit descended in tongues of fire upon those seated, filling them with all knowledge and divine gifts (Acts II, 1–4).

O how swift and effectual is this craftsman, and how sweet and life-giving the worker in the souls that desire his anointing! The divine fire came—not burning, but enlightening—and abundantly kindled the hearts of the disciples, emptying them of delight in carnal pleasures and of fear of punishments [Col. 0065C]. By the diversity of tongues he suddenly taught them in speech; by authority he strengthened them in mind; and he raised them to the summit of virtues against all the wiles of the enemy. In various languages the apostles spoke the mighty works of God, so that visitors from every nation marvelled that native Galileans could speak all languages fluently. When the envious Jews, deserving confusion, learned this—being accustomed always to distort Christ’s deeds and words by a sinister interpretation—they raved that those speaking the mighty works of God were full of new wine. But Peter, abundantly intoxicated with spiritual drink, rose up against the faithless; he poured forth words of saving wisdom, spoke eloquently of Christ’s incarnation, passion, and resurrection [Col. 0065D], and, with the Holy Spirit cooperating, overcame the confounded multitude of the malicious.

As he once struck Malchus, the servant of the high priest, with a sword and cut off his ear, so he pierced with the mystical word of God those who served carnally the mere letter of the Mosaic law, and cut away the old ceremonies and observances from the understanding of the newly baptized. Thus the Jews, whom treachery had shortly before compelled to rage for the Messiah’s death, Peter’s fervent preaching invited to repentance, faith, and baptism. And just as he had been accustomed to draw fish from the sea by the service of a net, so by the office of holy preaching he drew the erring from the pit of ignorance to the firmness of true faith. Accordingly, on that very day he baptized three thousand converts and renewed them, as they abandoned the oldness of their carnal life, into the new human being [Col. 0066A] (ibid., 41).

Behold, with God’s help I have simply pursued a kind of continuous account from Christ’s birth to the coming of the Spirit the Paraclete, and have briefly and in sequence gathered together each of the Saviour’s miracles from the Gospel books, insofar as I myself could investigate them according to my limited understanding, whether following the sharp-witted Augustine and other teachers, or setting them down in writing. In this sediment, as it were, I have sought to benefit myself and those like me: namely, to offer some profit to those who are weary of probing the depths and lengthy works of the learned. I have therefore arranged the Lord’s miracles, scattered through four books, into a connected work, and noted them down precisely in a short volume. Moreover, I have sometimes eagerly drawn upon the very words that I saw in the authoritative books; more often, for the sake of brevity, I have changed the wording. Yet I have taken the greatest pains everywhere to follow unconquered truth, and have never of my own accord departed from the authoritative sense [Col. 0066B].

## XVIII. The Reigns of the Roman Emperors

Now, because I have proposed to set forth a definite chronology in writing, so that the order of times may be clearer to the reader, I am pleased to insert certain matters which the ancient Fathers published in their little works on the same subject.

For Eusebius of Caesarea, Jerome skilled in three languages, Orosius also, the Iberian sophist, and Isidore of Seville, along with many others, wrote much about the course of the world’s ages. Especially among us, the priest Bede wrote in his book *On Times*; he was the latest to write for the English people [Col. 0066C] and endeavoured faithfully to follow the style of the ancients.

Tiberius, stepson of Octavian Augustus, the son of his wife Livia by her earlier husband, reigned twenty-three years. In his twelfth year Pilate was sent by him as procurator of Judaea. Herod the tetrarch, after holding the Jewish principate for twenty-four years, founded Tiberias-Livias in honour of Tiberius and his mother Livia.

In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, the Lord Jesus, after the baptism preached by John, announced the kingdom of heaven to the world. From the beginning of the world there had then elapsed, according to the Hebrews—as Eusebius records in his *Chronicles*—four thousand years [Col. 0066D], noting that the sixteenth year of Tiberius was the beginning of the eightieth jubilee according to the Hebrews. According to the same *Chronicles*, which Eusebius himself compiled, as it seemed good to him, from both editions, the years number five thousand two hundred and twenty-eight.

In the eighteenth year of Tiberius’s reign, the Lord redeemed the world by his passion; victorious over death, he rose on the third day, appeared manifestly to his faithful followers, and, while they watched, ascended into heaven on the fortieth day. Agrippa, surnamed Herod, son of Aristobulus, son of King Herod, accused Herod the tetrarch; having gone to Rome, he was cast into chains by Tiberius. There he attached many to himself in friendship, especially Gaius, son of Germanicus.

Gaius, surnamed Caligula, reigned three years, ten months, and eight days [Col. 0067A]. He made his friend Herod Agrippa, released from chains, king of Judaea; Agrippa remained king for seven years, that is, until the fourth year of Claudius. When Agrippa was struck by an angel, his son succeeded him in the kingdom and continued for twenty-six years, until the destruction of the Jews. Herod the tetrarch, likewise seeking Gaius’s friendship, came to Rome at Herodias’s urging. But, accused by Agrippa, he lost even his tetrarchy; fleeing into Spain with Herodias, he died of grief. Pilate, who had pronounced the sentence of condemnation upon Christ, was so oppressed by the anguish inflicted by Gaius that he killed himself by his own hand. Gaius enrolled himself among the gods and defiled the holy places of the Jews with the filth of idols.

[Col. 0067B] Claudius: thirteen years, seven months, twenty-seven days. In the fourth year of his reign, when the most grievous famine mentioned by Luke in the Acts of the Apostles occurred, he went to Britain—which no one before Julius Caesar, nor anyone after him, had dared to approach—and within a very few days received the greater part of the island into submission without a single battle or shedding of blood. He also added the Orkney Islands to the Roman Empire and returned to Rome in the sixth month after his departure. In the ninth year of his reign he expelled the Jews from Rome because of their disturbances, as Luke also relates. In the following year a very great famine seized Rome.

Nero: thirteen years, seven months, twenty-eight days. In his second year Festus succeeded Felix as procurator of Judaea [Col. 0067C]. Then Paul was sent in chains to Rome. Albinus succeeded Festus in the government of Judaea, and Gessius Florus succeeded Albinus. The Jews could not endure Florus’s luxury, greed, and other crimes; therefore they rebelled against the Romans. Vespasian was sent against them as commander of the army and captured many cities of Judaea. Nero was the first [Note: [Col. 0067D] Thus D. Le Prévost; Duchesne, however, reads otherwise.] who, beyond all his other crimes, also persecuted Christians; at Rome he put their most eminent men, Peter, to death by the cross, and Paul by the sword. He dared absolutely nothing in military affairs and nearly lost Britain; for under him two most noble towns there were captured and destroyed.

Vespasian: nine years, eleven months, twenty-two days. He was proclaimed emperor by the army in Judaea; entrusting the war to his son Titus, he departed for Rome by way of Alexandria [Col. 0067D], and, after Vitellius had been killed, obtained the throne. In his second year he overthrew the kingdom of Judaea and levelled the Temple to the ground, one thousand and eighty-four years after its first construction. This war was completed in four years: two while Nero was living and two afterwards. Among his other great achievements, while still a private citizen Vespasian was sent by Claudius to Germany and then to Britain. He fought the enemy thirty-two times, added to the Roman Empire two very powerful peoples, twenty towns, and the Isle of Wight, near Britain. A colossus was erected, one hundred and seven feet high.

Titus: two years, two months; a man wonderful in every kind of virtue, so much so that he was called the love and delight of the human race [Col. 0068A]. He built the amphitheatre at Rome and, at its dedication, killed five thousand wild beasts.

Domitian, Titus’s younger brother: fifteen years, five months. He was the second after Nero to persecute Christians, and shortly afterward was killed by the Senate as payment for his warfare against God.

Nerva: one year, four months, eight days. In his first edict he recalled all exiles. Thus the apostle John, freed by this general pardon, returned to Ephesus.

Trajan: nineteen years, six months, fifteen days. He initiated a persecution against Christians and made eminent servants of God into martyrs. Pliny the Second of Novum Comum [Col. 0068B], an orator and distinguished historian, is held in renown; many works of his talent survive. The Pantheon at Rome, which Domitian had made, was burnt by lightning; it received this name because that building is the dwelling-place of all gods. Jews stirring up revolt in various parts of the world were laid low in a deserved slaughter. Trajan extended far and wide the frontiers of the Roman Empire, which after Augustus had been defended more than nobly enlarged.

Hadrian, the son of Trajan’s cousin: twenty-one years.

Through Quadratus, a disciple of the apostles; Aristides of Athens, a man full of faith and wisdom; and the legate Serenus Granius, who had composed books on the Christian religion, Hadrian was instructed and commanded by letter [Col. 0068C] that Christians should not be condemned without an accusation of crimes. He also utterly subdued the Jews when they rebelled a second time, by a final slaughter, depriving them even of permission to enter Jerusalem. He restored Jerusalem to an excellent condition by building walls and ordered it to be called Aelia after his own name. Highly learned in both languages, he built at Athens a library of marvellous workmanship.

At Jerusalem Marcus was first appointed bishop from among the Gentiles, after the cessation of those who had been from among the Jews. Their names are these: James the brother of the Lord; Simeon son of Clophas; Justus; Zacchaeus; Tobias; Sextus; John; Matthias; Philip; Seneca; Justus; Levi; Ephraim; Joseph; and Judas. These fifteen were from the circumcision; they presided in Jerusalem [Col. 0068D] from the passion of the Lord until Aelius Hadrian, for nearly one hundred and seven years, and shone in faith and learning along with holiness. Then the following Gentiles succeeded them: Marcus, Cassianus, Publius, Maximus, Julianus, Gaius, Julianus, Capito, Valens, Dolicianus, Narcissus, Alexander, Mazabbanes, Hymenaeus, Zabdas, Hermon, Macharius, Maximus, Cyril, and John.

## XIX. Succession of the Roman Emperors

Antoninus, surnamed Pius, with his sons Aurelius and Lucius: twenty-two years and three months. The philosopher Justin presented Antoninus with a book composed in defence of the Christian religion and made him kindly disposed toward Christians [Col. 0069A]. Not long afterward, when his friend Crescens stirred up persecution, Justin shed his blood for Christ under Pius, bishop of Rome. Hermas wrote the book called *The Shepherd*, in which there is contained an Angel’s command that Easter should be celebrated on the Lord’s Day. Polycarp, coming to Rome, corrected many who had recently been corrupted by the heretical teaching of Valentinus and Cerdo.

Marcus Antoninus Verus, with his brother Lucius Aurelius Commodus: nineteen years, two months. They were the first to administer the Empire with equal authority, whereas until then emperors had ruled singly. They then waged war against the Parthians with admirable courage and success. When persecution arose in Asia, Polycarp and Pionius suffered martyrdom. In Gaul also Photinus [Col. 0069B], bishop of Lyons, and very many others gloriously shed their blood for Christ. Not long afterward a plague, avenger of crimes, devastated many provinces far and wide, especially Italy and Rome. When his brother Commodus died, Antoninus made his own son Commodus partner in the rule. Melito of Asia, bishop of Sardis, presented the emperor Antoninus with an *Apology* for Christians. Lucius, king of Britain, obtained by a letter sent to Eleutherius, bishop of Rome, that he might become a Christian. Apollinaris of Asia at Hierapolis and Dionysius at Corinth are renowned as bishops.

Lucius Antoninus Commodus reigned thirteen years after his father’s death. He successfully waged war against the Germans. But, wholly given over to luxury and obscenity, he did nothing resembling his father’s virtue and piety [Col. 0069C]. Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons, is held in renown. The emperor Commodus had the head of the Colossus removed and ordered the head of his own image placed upon it.

Helius Pertinax: six months. He perished through the crime of the jurist Julian, whom Severus killed at the Milvian Bridge in civil war in the seventh month after Julian had begun to rule. Victor, bishop of Rome, sent letters widely and decreed that Easter be celebrated on the Lord’s Day, as his predecessor Eleutherius had done, from the fourteenth moon of the first month to the twenty-first. Supporting these decrees, Theophilus, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, wrote against those who celebrated Easter with the Jews on the fourteenth moon, together with the other bishops present at the same council, a synodal letter of great usefulness.

[Col. 0069D] Severus Pertinax: seventeen years. He ruled the Empire bravely indeed, but laboriously, and exercised a most severe persecution against Christians. Clement, presbyter of the Church of Alexandria, and Pantaenus, the Stoic philosopher, are held to have been most eloquent in disputation concerning our doctrine. Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem; Theophilus of Caesarea; and Polycarp and Bacilus, bishops of the province of Asia, are held in renown. Very many Christians in different provinces were crowned with martyrdom. After killing Clodius Albinus, who had made himself Caesar in Gaul, at Lyons, Severus transferred the war to Britain. There, in order to make the recovered provinces safer against barbarian incursions, he drew a great ditch and a very strong rampart, further fortified with frequent towers, for one hundred and thirty-two Roman miles from sea to sea [Col. 0070A], and died at York.

Antoninus, surnamed Caracalla, son of Severus: seven years. Alexander, bishop of Cappadocia, had come to Jerusalem out of longing for the holy places. While Narcissus, bishop of that city—a man of extreme old age—was still alive, Alexander himself was ordained bishop there, the Lord indicating by revelation that this ought to take place. Tertullian of Africa, son of a proconsular centurion, is celebrated by the speech of all the Churches.

Macrinus reigned one year; with his son Diadumenian, with whom he had seized the Empire, he was killed in a military uprising at Archilaïs.

Marcus Aurelius Antoninus: four years. In Palestine [Col. 0070B] the city Nicopolis, formerly called Emmaus, was founded, through the diplomatic effort undertaken on his behalf by Julius Africanus, writer of chronicles. This is the Emmaus which the Lord, after his resurrection, deigned to sanctify by his presence, as Luke relates (chapter 24). Hippolytus the bishop, author of many treatises, brought down to this point the chronological canon which he wrote. He also reported that, by discovering the nineteen-year Easter cycle, he had furnished Eusebius—who composed a cycle concerning the same Easter—with an occasion for his work.

Aurelius Alexander: thirteen years. He was exceptionally devoted to his mother Mamaea and for this reason beloved by all. Urban, bishop of Rome, led many nobles to faith in Christ and to martyrdom. Origen is renowned at Alexandria—indeed, throughout the whole world [Col. 0070C]. Finally, Mamaea, Alexander’s mother, arranged to hear him and, having summoned him to Antioch, received him with the highest honour.

Maximinus: three years. He conducted a persecution against the priests of the Churches, and against clerics and teachers, especially because of the Christian household of Alexander, whom he had succeeded, and of his mother Mamaea; or particularly because of the presbyter Origen. Pontianus and Anterus, bishops of the city of Rome, were crowned with martyrdom and buried in the cemetery of Callixtus.

Gordian: six years. Julius Africanus is esteemed among ecclesiastical writers. In the chronicles that he wrote, he relates that he hurried to Alexandria, drawn by the very celebrated reputation of Heraclas [Col. 0070D], whom rumour declared most learned in sacred and philosophical studies and in every branch of Greek learning.

Philip, with his son Philip, reigned seven years. He was the first of all emperors to become a Christian, at the admonition of Pontius, a faithful soldier of Christ; and after the third year of his reign the thousandth year from Rome’s foundation was completed. The doors of the temples having been shut, the holy Church was freely opened with rejoicing for the praise of God; and thus this most august birthday year of all past ages was celebrated with magnificent games by a Christian emperor. Origen, son of the martyr Leonides, instructed at Caesarea in Palestine Theodore, surnamed Gregory, and Athenodorus, young brothers who later became the most distinguished bishops of Pontus [Col. 0071A], in divine philosophy. Against a certain Celsus, an Epicurean philosopher who had written against us, he replied in eight volumes. To state it briefly, he was so diligent in writing that Jerome recalls in one place that he had read five thousand of his books.

Decius: one year, three months. After killing the two Philips, father and son, he initiated a persecution against Christians because of his hatred for them. In it Pope Fabian was crowned with martyrdom in the city of Rome and left the seat of his bishopric to Cornelius. Alexander, bishop of Jerusalem, was killed at Caesarea in Palestine, as was Babylas at Antioch.

Gallus, with his son Volusian: two years, four months. As Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, testifies, when his reign flourished at its beginning and everything came to him as he wished [Col. 0071B], he persecuted the holy men who were praying to the supreme God for the peace of his reign; with them he drove away both his prosperity and his peace. Origen died before fully completing his seventieth year and was buried in the city of Tyre. Pope Cornelius, at the request of a certain matron Lucina, removed the bodies of the apostles from the catacombs by night and placed Paul on the Ostian Way, where he had been beheaded; Peter, however, near the place where he had been crucified, among the bodies of the holy bishops, in the Temple of Apollo, on the Golden Mount, in the Vatican of Nero’s palace, on the third day before the Kalends of July [29 June].

Valerian, with his son Gallienus: fifteen years. Having stirred up persecution against Christians, he was immediately captured by Shapur, king of the Persians [Col. 0071C]; there, deprived of his eyes, he grew old in miserable servitude. Gallienus, terrified by so manifest a judgment of God, therefore restored peace to our people. Yet, because of the demerit either of his own lust or of his father’s warfare against God, he endured countless losses to the Roman Empire as barbarians rose up. In this persecution Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, whose exceedingly learned treatises survive, was crowned with martyrdom. His deacon Pontius left an excellent volume concerning his life and passion; Pontius had endured exile with him until the day of his passion. Theodore Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, shone with great glory of miracles. One of these was that, to make room for building a church, he moved a mountain by prayers [Col. 0071D]. Stephen and Sixtus, bishops of Rome, suffered martyrdom.

Claudius: one year, nine months. He overcame the Goths, who had already for fifteen years been ravaging Illyricum and Macedonia; for this reason a golden shield was placed for him in the senate-house and a golden statue on the Capitol. Marcion, a most eloquent presbyter of the Church of Antioch, who had taught rhetoric in that same city, disputed against Paul of Samosata, who as bishop at Antioch taught that Christ had been a man of common nature. Notaries recorded the debate, and the dialogue survives to this day.

Aurelian: five years, six months. When he had begun persecution against us, lightning struck before him, to the great terror of those around him; and not long afterward he was killed by soldiers in the middle of the road between Constantinople and Heraclea [Col. 0072A]. Pope Eutychian was crowned with martyrdom at Rome and was buried in the cemetery of Callixtus; he himself buried three hundred and thirteen martyrs with his own hand.

Tacitus: six months. When he was killed in Pontus, Florianus held the Empire for eighty-eight days and was then killed at Tarsus. Anatolius, an Alexandrian by nation, bishop of Laodicea in Syria, trained in the disciplines of the philosophers, is much celebrated in writing. The greatness of his talent can be known most clearly from the book he composed on Easter and from his ten books of arithmetic instruction. The insane heresy of the Manichaeans and that of the Sabellians arose.

Probus: six years and four months. He completely liberated Gaul, long occupied by barbarians [Col. 0072B], through many severe battles, after finally destroying the enemy. Archelaus, bishop of Mesopotamia, composed in Syriac an account of the disputation which he held against Manichaeus when he came out of Persia; translated by Greeks, it is possessed by many.

Carus, with his sons Carinus and Numerian: two years. Gaius, bishop of the Roman Church, flourished; he suffered martyrdom under Diocletian. Pierius, presbyter of Alexandria, taught the people most successfully under Bishop Theonas. He achieved such elegance of speech and of various treatises—which survive to this day—that he was called the younger Origen. He was a man of remarkable frugality and a lover of voluntary poverty; after the persecution, he lived at Rome for the whole remainder of his life [Col. 0072C].

## XX. Roman Emperors. Persecutions of Christians. Constantine’s Conversion

Diocletian, with Herculius Maximian: twenty years. Carausius, having assumed the purple, seized Britain. Narseh, king of the Persians, brought war upon the East. The Quinquegentiani ravaged Africa. Achilleus seized Egypt; because of these events Constantius and Galerius Maximinus were made Caesars and admitted to the imperial rule. Constantius took Theodora, the stepdaughter of Herculius, by whom he later had six children, Constantine’s brothers. Galerius took Valeria, Diocletian’s daughter. After ten years Britain was recovered through Asclepiodotus, prefect of the praetorian guard.

In Diocletian’s nineteenth year, Diocletian in the East and Maximian Herculius in the West ordered churches to be destroyed and Christians afflicted and killed [Col. 0072D]. In the second year of the persecution Diocletian at Nicomedia and Maximian at Milan laid down the purple. Nevertheless, once begun, the persecution did not cease to rage until Constantine’s seventh year. In the sixteenth year of his reign Constantius, a man of the greatest gentleness and civility, died at York in Britain. This persecution burned with such cruelty and frequency that within one month eighteen thousand martyrs are said to have suffered for Christ. For, having crossed even the Ocean’s rim, it condemned Alban, Aaron, and Julius of Britain, with many other men and women, to their blessed bloodshed. Then the presbyter Pamphilus suffered [Col. 0073A], a close associate of Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea; Eusebius himself included Pamphilus’s life in three books.

In the third year of the persecution, in which Constantius also died, Maximinus and Severus were made Caesars by Galerius Maximus. Of these, Maximinus added his crimes and sexual excesses to persecutions of Christians. At that time Peter, bishop of Alexandria, suffered, together with many bishops of Egypt. Lucian also, a presbyter of Antioch, a man outstanding in character, continence, and learning, and many others suffered.

Constantine, son of Constantius by his concubine Helena, was made emperor in Britain and reigned thirty years and ten months. From the fourth year of the persecution, Maxentius, son of Maximian Herculius, was called Augustus at Rome [Col. 0073B]. Licinius, husband of Constantia, Constantine’s sister, was made emperor at Carnuntum. Constantine became a Christian from being a persecutor, and strove with all his power to exalt the Church of God. At the Council of Nicaea the Catholic faith was set forth. Constantine built many basilicas for the Lord. At Rome, where he was baptized, he made a basilica in honour of Saint John the Baptist, called the Constantinian Basilica; one for blessed Peter at the Temple of Apollo, and one for blessed Paul on the Ostian Way. In the Sessorian palace he made the basilica called Jerusalem, where he placed some of the wood of the Lord’s cross. At the request of his daughter he made a church for Saint Agnes the martyr, and likewise for blessed Lawrence the martyr on the Tiburtine Way in the Veranian field. He also made a basilica on the Lavican Way between the Two Laurels for the blessed martyrs Marcellinus and Peter [Col. 0073C], and a mausoleum in which he placed his mother in a purple sarcophagus. In the city of Ostia, near the harbour of Rome, he built a basilica of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and of John the Baptist. In the city of Albano he made a church of Saint John the Baptist, and also churches in the city of Naples. The same Constantine restored Drepanum, a city of Bithynia, in honour of the martyr Lucian buried there, and named it Helenopolis after his mother. In Thrace he established a city bearing his own name and willed it to be the seat of the Roman Empire and the capital of the whole East. He likewise decreed that pagan temples should be closed without any killing of persons.

Constantius, with his brothers Constantine and Constans [Col. 0073D]: twenty-four years, five months, thirteen days. James, bishop of Nisibis, is known, and by his prayers the city was often freed from danger. Arian impiety, supported by the patronage of Emperor Constantius, persecuted first Athanasius and then all bishops not of its party, by exiles, prisons, and various forms of affliction. Maximinus, bishop of Trier, is held in renown; when Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, was sought by Constantius for punishment, Maximinus received him with honour. The monk Antony died in the desert in the one hundred and fifth year of his life. When Constantius entered Rome, the bones of Andrew the apostle and Luke the evangelist were received by the Constantinopolitans with extraordinary favour. Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, who had been driven into exile in Phrygia by the Arians, presented a book on his own behalf to Constantius at Constantinople and returned to Gaul [Col. 0074A].

Julian: two years, eight months. He was baptized and raised through the sacred orders to the diaconate; but, abandoning the clerical state, he took up arms, seized the Empire, turned to the worship of idols, and persecuted Christians. At Sebaste, a city of Palestine, pagans invaded the tomb of John the Baptist and scattered his bones; gathering them again, they burned them and scattered them more widely. But by God’s providence certain monks from Jerusalem were present; mingling with those gathering them, they took away whatever they could and brought it to their father Philip. He immediately sent these relics through his deacon Julian to Athanasius, then chief bishop [Col. 0074B], since he considered so great a treasure beyond his own ability to guard. Athanasius received them and, with few witnesses, enclosed them in a hollowed-out wall of the sanctuary; in a prophetic spirit he consecrated them for the benefit of a later generation. This prediction was fulfilled under Emperor Theodosius through Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, who destroyed the tomb of Serapis and consecrated there a church of Saint John.

Jovian: eight months. A synod was held at Antioch by Meletius and his associates, in which the Macedonian doctrine blaspheming the Holy Spirit was condemned. After making peace with the Persians for twenty-nine years, Jovian returned to Roman territory. Warned by the fall of his predecessor Constantius, he sought Athanasius with honourable and most dutiful letters [Col. 0074C], receiving from him a statement of faith and a method for ordering the Churches. But untimely death in Cilicia ruined the pious and joyful beginnings of his reign.

Valentinian, with his brother Valens: eleven years. Apollinaris, bishop of Laodicea, composed writings of many kinds concerning our religion; later departing from the faith, he established the heresy bearing his own name. Damasus, bishop of Rome, built a basilica near the theatre for Saint Lawrence and another at the catacombs, where the bodies of the holy apostles Peter and Paul had lain. At that place he adorned in verse the very *platonia*, the burial-place where they had lain. Valens, baptized by Eudoxius, bishop of the Arians, persecuted our people. In Valentinian’s third year his son Gratian was made emperor at Amiens [Col. 0074D]. At Constantinople a shrine of the apostles’ martyrdom was dedicated. After the late death of Auxentius, Ambrose was made bishop at Milan; by his preaching all Gaul was converted to faith in Christ.

Valens, with Gratian and Valentinian, sons of his brother Valentinian: four years. Valens, having issued a law that monks should serve in the army, ordered those unwilling to do so to be killed by beatings. The nation of the Huns, long shut away in inaccessible mountains, suddenly stirred by raging fury, burst forth against the Goths and drove them, scattered and distressed, from their ancient homes. The Goths crossed the Danube as fugitives and were received by Valens without laying down their arms; soon, compelled by the greed of the commander Maximus to rebel through hunger [Col. 0075A], they defeated Valens’s army and, spreading through Thrace, overwhelmed everything alike with slaughter, fire, and plundering.

Gratian, with his brother Valentinian: six years. Theodosius, made emperor by Gratian, defeated in many great battles the mighty Scythian peoples—the Alans, Huns, and Goths. Unable to endure his concord, the Arians relinquished, after forty years, the churches which they had held by force. A synod of one hundred and fifty Fathers assembled in the imperial city against Macedonius, under Damasus, bishop of Rome. Theodosius made his son Arcadius partner in the Empire. From Gratian’s second year, when Gratian himself was consul for the sixth time and Theodosius was consul, Theophilus wrote a Paschal calculation. Maximus, indeed [Col. 0075B] a vigorous and upright man, worthy of the imperial title, had he not risen through tyranny in violation of his sworn allegiance: in Britain he was made emperor by the army almost against his will; he crossed into Gaul, where he ensnared Augustus Gratian by deceit and killed him at Lyons, then expelled his brother Valentinian from Italy. Yet Valentinian paid the most just penalty of exile with his mother Justina. Arian heresy had polluted both her and him; and he harassed Ambrose, the most eminent stronghold of Catholic faith, with a treacherous siege. Only after the incorrupt relics of the blessed martyrs Gervasius and Protasius had been brought forth at God’s revelation did he abandon his wicked designs.

Theodosius, who while Gratian lived had already ruled the East for six years, reigned eleven years after Gratian’s death [Col. 0075C]. He and Valentinian, whom he had kindly received when expelled from Italy, killed the tyrant Maximus at the third milestone from Aquileia. Because Maximus had stripped Britain of almost all its armed youth and military forces—which had followed the traces of his tyranny into Gaul and never returned home—the fierce peoples from overseas, the Scots from the northwest and the Picts from the north, saw the island deserted of soldier and defender, came upon it, and for many years overwhelmed it with devastation and plunder. Jerome, interpreter of sacred history, carried the book which he wrote *On Illustrious Men of the Church* down to the fourteenth year of Theodosius’s entire reign.

[Col. 0075D] Arcadius, son of Theodosius, with his brother Honorius: thirteen years. The bodies of the holy prophets Habakkuk and Micah were revealed by divine disclosure. The Goths attacked Italy, and the Vandals and Alans Gaul. Innocent, bishop of Rome, dedicated the basilica of the most blessed martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, from the pious provision of the will of a certain distinguished woman, Vestina. Then Alexis, servant of Christ, died. Pelagius the Briton attacked the grace of God.

Honorius, with Theodosius the Younger, his brother’s son: sixteen years. Alaric, king of the Goths, invaded Rome and burned part of it by fire on the ninth day before the Kalends of September [24 August], in the 1,164th year from its foundation; on the sixth day after entering it, he left the city after plundering it.

[Col. 0076A] Lucian the presbyter, to whom the Lord revealed, in the seventh year of Emperor Honorius, the site of the tomb and relics of the blessed protomartyr Stephen, Gamaliel, and Nicodemus—who are read of in the Gospel and in the Acts of the Apostles—wrote out that revelation in Greek for all the Churches. Avitus, a presbyter and a Spaniard by origin, translated this revelation into Latin and, adding his own letter, delivered it to the western Churches through the presbyter Orosius. Orosius himself, having reached the holy places, whither Augustine had sent him to Jerome to learn concerning the nature of the soul, received relics of blessed Stephen and, returning to his homeland, was the first to bring them to the West. The Britons, unable to endure the assaults of the Scots and Picts, sent to Rome and, promising submission [Col. 0076B], begged for aid against the enemy. A legion was immediately sent; it struck down a great multitude of barbarians, drove the rest beyond Britain’s boundaries, and, about to return home, ordered its allies to raise a wall across the island between the two seas to repel enemies. Built without a skilled master-builder, more of turf than stone, it benefited its builders not at all. For as soon as the Romans departed, the former enemy, conveyed in ships, cut down, trampled, and devoured everything that met it, like a ripe harvest. When aid was sought again, the Romans hastened back, drove the defeated enemy across the seas, and, joined with the Britons, placed a wall—not an earthen, dusty one as before, but one solidly of stone—from sea to sea between the cities that had been established there because of fear of the enemy [Col. 0076C]. On the southern seacoast also, because an enemy was feared from that direction, they established towers at intervals chiefly for observation. Thus they bade farewell to their allies, as though never to return. Boniface, bishop of Rome, made an oratory in the cemetery of Saint Felicitas and adorned her tomb and that of Saint Silvinus. Jerome the presbyter died in the twelfth year of Honorius, on the second day before the Kalends of October [30 September], in the ninety-first year of his life.

Theodosius the Younger, son of Arcadius, reigned 26 years. Valentinian the Younger, son of Constantius, was made emperor at Ravenna. His mother Placidia was styled Augusta. The savage nation of the Vandals, Alans, and Goths, crossing from Spain into Africa, defiled everything with sword, fire, plundering, and likewise with Arian impiety. [Col. 0076D] But blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo and the outstanding doctor of all the Churches, lest he should see the ruin of his city, departed to the Lord in the third month of its siege, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September [28 August]. He had lived 76 years and had completed nearly 40 years in the clergy or episcopate. At this time the Vandals, having captured Carthage, also ravaged Sicily. Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum, mentions this captivity in the letter which he wrote to Pope Leo concerning the calculation of Easter.

Palladius, ordained by Pope Celestine as the first bishop for the Scots who believed in Christ, was sent in the eighth year of Theodosius. When the Roman army withdrew from Britain, the Scots and Picts, having learned that its return was refused, themselves returned; and, driving out the natives, they occupied the whole northern part of the island as far as the wall. Nor was there delay: the guards of the wall having been slain, captured, or put to flight, and the wall itself broken through, the cruel plunderer raged even within it. A letter full of tears and miseries was sent to Aetius, thrice consul, the man of Roman power, in the twenty-third year of the Emperor Theodosius, begging for help; but help was not obtained. Meanwhile a dreadful and most notorious famine afflicted the refugees. Forced by this, some surrendered themselves to the enemy. Others fought back bravely from mountains, caves, and wooded places, and inflicted slaughter upon the enemy. The Scots returned home, intending to return again before long. The Picts occupied the farthest part of the island, then for the first time and thereafter. The aforementioned famine was followed by a great abundance of crops; [Col. 0077B] abundance by luxury and negligence; negligence by a most severe pestilence; and soon afterward by the still harsher blow of new enemies, that is, the Angles. By unanimous counsel, the Britons chose to invite these men, with their king Vortigern, to themselves as defenders of their country; but, once received, they soon found them assailants and conquerors.

Sixtus, bishop of Rome, built the basilica of Holy Mary, Mother of the Lord, which the ancients called Liberius’s. Eudocia, wife of the Emperor Theodosius, returned from Jerusalem and brought with her the relics of the most blessed Stephen, the first martyr; these are venerated where they were placed in the basilica of Saint Lawrence. Bleda and Attila, brothers and kings of many nations, laid waste Illyricum and Thrace. [Col. 0077C]

## XXI. Roman Emperors. Invasions of Angles, Saxons, and Franks. Foundation of the Frankish Kingdom.

Marcian and Valentinian, 7 years. The nation of Angles or Saxons was conveyed to Britain in three long ships. When report at home declared that their expedition had prospered, a stronger army was sent. Joining the first arrivals, it first drove away the enemies whom it had been suffering; then, turning its arms against its allies, it subdued almost the whole island, from its eastern side to its western, by fire and sword, inventing the pretext that the Britons did not give sufficient pay to those fighting for them.

John the Baptist revealed his head beside the former dwelling of King Herod to two eastern monks [Col. 0077D] who had come to Jerusalem for prayer. It was subsequently carried to Emesa in Phoenicia and honored with fitting reverence.

The Pelagian heresy troubled the faith of the Britons. Seeking assistance from Gallic bishops, they received as defenders of the faith Germanus, bishop of the Church of Auxerre, and Lupus, bishop of Troyes, likewise endowed with apostolic grace. These distinguished athletes of the Lord confirmed the faith both by the word of truth and by signs of miracles; moreover, they repelled by divine power a war undertaken at that time by Saxons and Picts united against the Britons. For Germanus himself, having become leader of the army, put the huge enemy host to flight not with a trumpet blast but with the cry “Alleluia,” as the voice of the entire army [Col. 0078A] was raised to the stars. Later, arriving at Ravenna, he was received with the highest reverence by Valentinian and Placidia and departed to Christ. His body was conveyed to Auxerre in an honorable procession, accompanied by works of miraculous power. Aetius the patrician, the salvation of the western commonwealth in the West and once the terror of King Attila, was killed by Valentinian. With him the western empire fell and has not hitherto been able to rise again.

About this time the kingdom of the Franks began. For in the time of Theodosius the Younger, son of Arcadius, and Pope Celestine, Pharamond, son of Sunno, duke of the Franks, was the first king of the Franks and reigned five years. At his death, his son Clodio [Col. 0078B] reigned seven years.

Then the devil appeared to the Jews in Crete in the form of Moses and promised to lead them dry-footed through the sea to the land of promise. Thus very many perished, while the remainder were converted to the grace of Christ.

In the second year of Marcian and Valentinian, King Merovech died after reigning 13 years. After him, his son Childeric held the Frankish kingdom for 23 years.

Leo, 17 years. On the Chalcedonian Tome, he sent throughout the whole world to each orthodox bishop an individual letter agreeing with the others, requesting them to write back what they thought of that Tome. [Col. 0078C] He received replies from all of them so harmonious concerning Christ’s true incarnation, as though all had been written at one time and under a single dictation. Theodore, bishop of the city called Cyrrhus, named after Cyrus king of Persia, wrote concerning the true incarnation of the Lord and Savior against Eutyches and Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, who denied Christ’s human flesh. He also wrote an Ecclesiastical History from the end of Eusebius’s books down to his own time, that is, to the reign of this Leo, under whom he also died.

Victorius, at the command of Pope Hilary, wrote an Easter cycle of 632 years.

Zeno, 17 years. The body of the apostle Barnabas and the Gospel of Matthew written in his own hand were discovered, Barnabas himself revealing them. [Col. 0078D] Odoacer, king of the Goths, took possession of Rome, which their kings thereafter held for a long time.

After the death of Theodoric, son of Triarius, another Theodoric, surnamed Valamer, assumed the kingdom of the Goths. He devastated both Macedonias and Thessaly, set fire to many places in the imperial city, and hostilely occupied Italy as well. Huneric, the Arian king of the Vandals, after exiling and dispersing more than 334 Catholic bishops in Africa, closed their churches and subjected the people to various punishments. Indeed, he cut off the hands of countless persons and severed their tongues, yet was unable to take away their speech of Catholic confession.

The Britons, under Ambrosius Aurelianus, a modest man [Col. 0079A] who perhaps alone of Roman stock had survived the Saxon massacre—his parents, clothed in purple, having been killed in it—challenged their victorious nation to battle and defeated it. From that time onward, now these, now those held the victory, until the stronger newcomer gained possession of the whole island for a long period.

In the year in which Zeno began to reign, Childeric having died, his son Clovis began to reign in Gaul, and reigned vigorously for 19 years.

Anastasius, 28 years. Thrasamund, king of the Vandals, closed the Catholic churches and sent 220 bishops into exile in Sardinia. Pope Symmachus, among the many works for churches which he either created from their foundations or renewed from antiquity, built dwellings for the poor at Saint Peter, Saint Paul, and Saint Lawrence; and every year he supplied money and clothing throughout Africa and Sardinia to bishops who were in exile. Anastasius, because, favoring the Eutychian heresy, he persecuted Catholics, perished by a divine thunderbolt.

## XXII. Clovis, King of the Franks, Is Baptized. Kings of the Franks. Kings of the Angles. Roman Emperors.

Clovis, king of the Franks, was baptized in the fifteenth year of his reign, together with 3,000 nobles, by blessed Remigius, archbishop of Rheims. Four years afterward he died, and his son Theodoric succeeded him.

> [Note: [Col. 0079D] Thus in the manuscripts and in the edition of Le Prévost.]

When he died, his brother Clothar reigned in Gaul for 51 years. Then Gildardus and Flavius flourished in the see of Rouen; and Mamertus of Vienne [Col. 0079C], because of the manifold plague by which the people were afflicted, instituted the solemn litanies, that is, Rogation processions, before the Ascension of the Lord.

Justin the Elder, 8 years. Pope John came to Constantinople; at the gate called the Golden Gate, when crowds met him, he restored sight before all men to a blind man who begged it. On returning, when he arrived at Ravenna, Theodoric killed him and his companions through the affliction of imprisonment, moved by envy because Justin, defender of Catholic piety, had honorably received him. In the same year he killed the patrician Symmachus at Ravenna; and he himself perished there the following year by a sudden death. His grandson Athalaric succeeded him in the kingdom. Hilderic, king of the Vandals, commanded bishops to return from exile and restore the churches, [Col. 0079D] after 74 years of heretical profanation. Benedict the abbot shone in the glory of virtues, which blessed Pope Gregory recorded in the book of the *Dialogues*.

Justinian, nephew of Justin through his sister, 38 years. The patrician Belisarius, sent by Justinian into Africa, destroyed the nation of the Vandals. Carthage too, in the ninety-sixth year after its loss, was recovered, the Vandals having been expelled and defeated, and their king Gelimer captured and sent to Constantinople. The body of Saint Antony the monk, found by divine revelation, was carried to Alexandria and buried in the church of Blessed John the Baptist. Dionysius the Little wrote Easter cycles, beginning from the year of the Lord’s Incarnation. Then the code of Justinian was promulgated to the world. [Col. 0080A] Victor, bishop of Capua, also, writing a book on Easter, exposed the errors of Victorius.

King Clothar died in old age, and the Frankish kingdom was divided into four kingdoms: Paris fell to Charibert, Orléans to Guntram, Soissons to Chilperic, and Metz to Sigibert. Finally, in the thirty-sixth year of Justinian’s reign, King Sigibert, who had begun war with his brother Chilperic, was killed through his brother’s treachery. His son Childebert, still a very young boy, together with his mother Brunhild, assumed the governance of his father’s kingdom and reigned 25 years.

Justin the Younger, 11 years. Narses the patrician defeated and killed Totila, king of the Goths, in Italy. [Col. 0080B] Afterwards, accused before Justin and his wife Sophia through the envy of the Romans—for whom he had labored greatly against the Goths—of oppressing Italy with servitude, he withdrew to Naples in Campania and wrote to the nation of the Lombards, asking them to come and take possession of Italy. Pope John completed and dedicated the church of the apostles Philip and James which his predecessor Pelagius had begun. Then the warlike Alboin, son of Audoin, king of the Lombards, came from Pannonia into Italy and, with his Winili (Guinili), took possession of it with the permission of Narses the patrician.

Tiberius Constantine, 7 years. Gregory, then apocrisiarius at Constantinople and afterward bishop of Rome, composed books expounding Job and proved, in the presence of Tiberius, that Eutychius, bishop of that same city, had erred concerning the faith of our resurrection. [Col. 0080C] The emperor himself so refuted Eutychius’s book on the resurrection with Catholic arguments that he declared it ought to be burned in the flames. For Eutychius taught that in the glory of that resurrection our body would be impalpable and more subtle than winds and air, contrary to the Lord’s saying: “Handle me and see; for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39). The nation of the Lombards, accompanied by famine and mortality, invaded all Italy and, laying it waste, besieged Rome itself. Their king at that time was Alboin.

Maurice, 21 years. Hermenegild, son of Liuvigild, king of the Goths, because of his unconquerable confession of the Catholic faith, was deprived by his Arian father of the insignia of royalty and cast into prison and chains. At last, on the night of the second Sunday after the Lord’s resurrection, he was struck on the head with an axe and entered the heavenly kingdom as king and martyr in exchange for the earthly one. [Col. 0080D] His brother Reccared, as soon as he received the kingdom after his father, converted to the Catholic faith the whole Gothic people over whom he ruled, at the urging of Leander, bishop of Seville, who had also instructed Hermenegild. Maurice had as wife the daughter of Tiberius Constantine and was the first of the Greeks to bear the Roman fasces. Gregory, pontiff of the Roman Church and outstanding doctor, in the thirteenth year of Maurice’s reign, the thirteenth indiction, [Col. 0081A] convened a synod of 23 bishops at the body of the blessed apostle Peter and decreed matters necessary for the Church. The same Gregory, sending Augustine, Mellitus, John, and many other God-fearing monks with them to Britain, converted the Angles to Christ. Æthelberht indeed was soon converted to the grace of Christ, together with the people of Kent over whom he ruled and the neighboring provinces; he also endowed Augustine, his bishop and teacher, and the other holy bishops with episcopal sees. But the peoples of the Angles living north of the river Humber, under Kings Ælle and Æthelfrith, had not yet heard the word of life. In the eighteenth year of Maurice, Gregory, in the fourth year of his pontificate, writing to Augustine, decreed that the bishops of London and York, on receiving the pallium from the Apostolic See, ought to be metropolitans; [Col. 0081B] and four years later he died.

Phocas, 8 years. At the request of Pope Boniface, he decreed that the see of the Roman and Apostolic Church should be the head of all Churches, because the Church of Constantinople described itself as first among all Churches. At the request of another Pope Boniface, he further ordered that in the ancient shrine called the Pantheon, once the filth of idolatry had been removed, a church of Blessed Mary ever Virgin and All Martyrs should be made; so that where once worship was offered to all, not gods, but demons, there should thereafter be a commemoration of all the saints.

The Persians, waging most grievous wars against the commonwealth, seized many Roman provinces and Jerusalem itself. Destroying churches and profaning every holy thing, among the ornaments of places both sacred and common which they carried off, they also took away the standard of the Lord’s cross. [Col. 0081C]

Heraclius, 31 years. Anastasius the Persian monk suffered a noble martyrdom for Christ. Born in Persia, he learned magical arts from his father as a boy; but when he had learned Christ’s name from captive Christians, he was immediately converted to Him with his whole mind. Leaving Persia, he sought Christ at Chalcedon and Hierapolis, and then went to Jerusalem. There, after receiving the grace of baptism, he entered, four miles from that city, the monastery of Abbot Anastasius. Having lived there according to the rule for seven years, he came to Caesarea of Palestine for prayer, was captured by the Persians, and endured many beatings over a long period, amid prisons and chains, under the judge Marzaban. At last he was sent to Persia to their king Chosroes. [Col. 0081D] Beaten by him three times at intervals, he was finally suspended by one hand for three hours of the day and then beheaded with 70 others, thus completing his martyrdom. Soon afterward, a demoniac who put on his tunic was healed. Meanwhile Emperor Heraclius arrived with an army, defeated the Persians and King Chosroes, brought back rejoicing the Christians who had been taken captive, and restored the wood of the Holy Cross to Jerusalem. The relics of the blessed martyr Anastasius were first carried to his monastery and then to Rome, where they are venerated in the monastery of Blessed Paul the Apostle, called *ad Aquas Salvias*.

In the sixteenth year of Heraclius’s reign, the fifteenth indiction, Edwin, most excellent king of the Angles in Britain, received with his people of Northumbria the word of salvation preached by Bishop Paulinus. Paulinus had been sent from Kent by the venerable Archbishop Justus. This occurred in the eleventh year of Edwin’s reign, approximately the 180th year after the arrival of the Angles in Britain; Edwin granted Paulinus the episcopal see of York. [Col. 0082A] To this king, indeed, as a foretoken of the faith to come and of the heavenly kingdom, power in his earthly kingdom also increased, so that he brought under his authority all the boundaries of Britain inhabited either by the Angles themselves or by Britons—something no king of the Angles before him had done.

At that time Pope Honorius rebuked by letter an error that had arisen among the Scots concerning the observance of Easter. John also, who succeeded Severinus, Honorius’s successor, while he was still elected to the pontificate, wrote to them at the same time concerning that Easter and concerning the Pelagian heresy, which was reviving among them. [Col. 0082B]

In Gaul, after the deaths of Kings Theudebert and Theodoric, Lothar the Great, son of Chilperic, flourished and alone held the monarchy of Francia. At his death his son Dagobert succeeded him and governed the kingdom vigorously for 12 years. Then his son Clovis reigned 26 years and, at his death, left the diadem to his three sons, Lothar, Theodoric, and Hilderic. In the times of these kings, holy men shone in Francia through virtues and signs: Romanus and Audoenus, Ansbert and Eligius, Ebrulf and Launomarus, Maurus and Columbanus, Philibert and Wandrille, [Col. 0082C] and many others, powerful in faith and preaching, resplendent in holiness and miracles.

Heracleonas with his mother Martina, 2 years. Cyrus of Alexandria, Sergius and Pyrrhus, bishops of the imperial city, restoring the heresy of the Acephali, taught as doctrine one operation in Christ’s divinity and humanity and one will. Of these, Pyrrhus came from Africa to Rome in these times, that is, under Pope Theodore. With a repentance that later proved false, he presented to that pope, in the presence of all the clergy and people, a written statement bearing his subscription, in which all things written or done by himself or his predecessors against the Catholic faith were condemned. He was therefore kindly received by him as bishop of the imperial city. But because, after returning home, he resumed [Col. 0082D] his native error, the said Pope Theodore summoned all priests and clergy to the church of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and condemned him under the bond of anathema.

Constantine, brother of Heraclius, 6 months. Paul, Pyrrhus’s successor, tormented Catholics not only with frenzied doctrine, as his predecessors had done, but with open persecution. He subjected the apocrisiaries of the holy Roman Church, sent to correct him, partly to prison, partly to exile, and partly to beatings. He also overthrew and plundered their consecrated altar in the house of Placidia, a venerable oratory, forbidding them to celebrate Mass there. Therefore he too, like his predecessors, was condemned by the Apostolic See with the just punishment of deposition.

[Col. 0083A] Constantine, son of Constantine, 28 years. Deceived by Paul, just as his grandfather Heraclius had been deceived by Sergius, bishop of the same imperial city, he issued the *Typos* against the Catholic faith. It defined that neither one nor two wills or operations in Christ were to be confessed, as though Christ were to be thought incapable of willing or acting at all. Accordingly Pope Martin, having convened at Rome a synod of 105 fellow bishops, condemned under anathema the aforesaid heretics Cyrus, Sergius, Pyrrhus, and Paul. After this Theodore the exarch was sent by the emperor; he took Pope Martin from the church of Constantine and brought him to Constantinople. Afterwards exiled to Cherson, Martin ended his life there, still shining to this day with many signs of miraculous power in that place. [Col. 0083B] The aforesaid synod was held in the ninth year of Constantine’s reign, in October, in the eighth indiction.

Emperor Constantine, after Pope Vitalian had recently been ordained, sent to Blessed Peter the Apostle golden Gospels adorned around the edges with white gems of marvelous size. Some years later, in the sixth indiction, he himself came to Rome and offered upon that altar a pallium woven with gold, while his whole army entered the church carrying candles. In the following year an eclipse of the sun occurred at about the tenth hour of the day, on the fifth day before the Nones of May [3 May]. Archbishop Theodore and Abbot Adrian, a man likewise most learned, sent by Vitalian to Britain, made very many Churches of the Angles fruitful with the harvest of ecclesiastical learning. After many unprecedented devastations inflicted upon the provinces, Constantine was killed in a bath in the twelfth indiction; and not long afterward Pope Vitalian also sought the heavenly kingdoms. [Col. 0083C]

## XXIII. Efforts to Unite the Eastern and Western Churches. The Council of Constantinople. Æthelthryth, Daughter of Anna. Bishop Cuthbert.

Constantine, brother of the preceding Emperor Constantine, 17 years. The Saracens invaded Sicily and, having taken enormous booty with them, soon returned to Alexandria.

At the request of the most devout emperors Constantine, Heraclius, and Tiberius, Pope Agatho sent his legates to the imperial city. Among them was John, then deacon of the Roman Church and not long afterward its bishop, for the purpose of bringing about the union of God’s holy Churches. [Col. 0083D] They were received most graciously by Constantine, the most reverend defender of the Catholic faith, and were commanded, laying aside philosophical disputations, to investigate the true faith through peaceful discussion. All the treatises of ancient Fathers which they requested were supplied to them from the library of Constantinople. There were also present 150 bishops, with George, patriarch of the imperial city, and Macarius of Antioch presiding. Those who asserted one will and operation in Christ were convicted of having falsified very many sayings of the Catholic Fathers. When the conflict was ended, George was corrected; but Macarius, with his followers and also his predecessors Cyrus, Sergius, Honorius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter, was anathematized. In his place Theophanius, an abbot from Sicily, was made bishop of Antioch. [Col. 0084A] Such grace accompanied the legates of Catholic peace that John, bishop of Porto, one of their number, publicly celebrated Mass in Latin in the church of Saint Sophia on the Sunday of the octave of Easter, before the emperor and patriarch.

This was the sixth universal synod, celebrated at Constantinople and composed in the Greek language, in the time of Pope Agatho; the most devout Emperor Constantine conducted and presided over it within his palace, together with the legates of the Apostolic See and 150 bishops sitting in council.

For the first universal synod was assembled at Nicaea against Arius: 318 Fathers, in the time of Pope Julius under Emperor Constantine. The second was at Constantinople: 150 [Col. 0084B] Fathers, against Macedonius and Eudoxius, in the time of Pope Damasus and Emperor Gratian, when Nectarius was ordained bishop of that city. The third was at Ephesus: 200 Fathers, against Nestorius, bishop of the imperial city, under Emperor Theodosius the Great and Pope Celestine. The fourth was at Chalcedon: 630 Fathers, under Pope Leo in the time of Emperor Marcian, against Eutyches, bishop of the most impious monks. The fifth likewise was at Constantinople, in the time of Pope Vigilius under Emperor Justinian, against Theodore and all heretics. The sixth is this one of which we have just spoken.

Saint Æthelthryth, the perpetual virgin of Christ, daughter of Anna king of the Angles, was first given as wife to a most eminent man, [Col. 0084C] named Tondberht, prince of the southern Gyrwe, and afterward to Ecgfrith king of the Northumbrians. After preserving her marriage-bed undefiled for 12 years, she took the veil after being queen and became a consecrated virgin. Soon she also became the pious mother and nurse of holy virgins, receiving a site for the building of a monastery which they call Ely. Even her dead flesh testifies to her enduring merits: after 16 years in the grave, it was found incorrupt, together with the garment in which it had been wrapped.

Justinian the Younger, son of Constantine, 10 years. He established peace with the Saracens for ten years by land and sea. The province of Africa, which had been occupied by the Saracens, was also subjected to the Roman Empire, Carthage itself having been captured and destroyed by them. Because Sergius, pontiff of the Roman Church of blessed memory, refused to favor and subscribe Justinian’s errant synod held at Constantinople, Justinian ordered his protospatharius Zacharias to carry him off to Constantinople. [Col. 0084D] But the militia of Ravenna and the neighboring districts forestalled the emperor’s wicked orders and drove Zacharias out of Rome with insults and injuries.

In the fourth year of Justinian, Pippin became the first mayor of the royal household in Francia. Pope Sergius ordained the venerable man Willibrord, surnamed Clement, bishop to the people of the Frisians. An Englishman by birth, he had left Britain as a pilgrim and, among the barbarians, daily caused countless losses to the devil and increases to the Christian faith. Justinian, deprived of royal glory because of the crime of perfidy, withdrew into exile in Pontus; Abbot Cyrus supported him there.

Leo, 3 years. Pope Sergius, by the Lord’s revelation, found in the sacristy of Blessed Peter the Apostle a silver chest which had long lain in a very dark corner. Within it was a cross adorned with various precious stones. Removing the four petals in which gems of marvelous size were enclosed, he saw within a portion of the life-giving wood of the Lord’s cross. From that time onward, every year in the basilica of the Savior, called the Constantinian, on the day of its Exaltation, it is kissed [Col. 0085B] and adored by all the people.

In Britain, Cuthbert, the most reverend bishop of the Church of Lindisfarne, formerly an anchorite, lived from childhood to old age a life made illustrious by signs of miracles. When his body had been buried for 11 years, it was afterward found incorrupt, as though he had died that very hour, together with the garment that covered it. King Cædwalla of the West Saxons voluntarily left the kingdom of Ine and, arriving at Rome, was baptized by Pope Sergius on Easter Saturday. Still wearing his white baptismal garments, he was seized by illness and died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May [20 April]. At the pope’s command—he had named him Peter in baptism—he was buried in the church of the Holy Apostle, and this epitaph was inscribed upon his tomb:

> The royal height, wealth, offspring, mighty realms, triumphs,  
> Spoils, nobles, walls, strongholds, and home—  
> Whatever his fathers’ valor, and whatever he himself had gathered,  
> Cædwalla, mighty in arms, left behind for love of God,  
> So that, a king and stranger, he might behold Peter and Peter’s see,  
> And in its fountain, blessed, receive pure waters.  
>
> [lacuna]  
>
> For he came unharmed from Britain’s utmost world,  
> Through diverse peoples, straits, and ways;  
> He saw the city of Romulus and beheld  
> Peter’s dread sanctuary, bearing mystical gifts.  
> White among Christ’s sheep he will enter in fellowship,  
> For in body he holds a tomb, but in mind the things above.  
> You would think that he had exchanged the insignia of sceptres—  
> He whom you see to have earned Christ’s kingdom.

## XXIV. Synod of Aquileia. Roman Emperors. Charles Martel. Bede.

[Col. 0085D]

Tiberius, 7 years. A synod was held at Aquileia. Through ignorance of the faith it hesitated to accept the fifth universal council, until, instructed by the salutary admonitions of the blessed pope, it too consented to agree with the other Churches of Christ. Gisulf, duke of the Lombard people at Benevento, devastated Campania with fire, sword, and captivity. Since there was no one able to resist his assault, Pope John, successor to Sergius, sent priests and very many gifts to him, redeemed all the captives, and made the enemy return home. He was succeeded by another John, who, among many illustrious works, made a most beautiful oratory for the holy Mother of God inside the church of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. Aripert, king of the Lombards, [Col. 0086A] restored to the jurisdiction of that see many estates and patrimonies in the Cottian Alps which had once belonged by right to the Apostolic See but had long been taken away by the Lombards, and he sent this donation to Rome written in letters of gold.

Justinian a second time, with his son Tiberius, 6 years. Regaining the kingdom with the help of Terbel, king of the Bulgars, he killed the patricians who had expelled him, and Leo, who had usurped his place, and Leo’s successor Tiberius, who had held him in custody in that city throughout his own reign after driving him from the kingdom. He sent the patriarch Callinicus to Rome after tearing out his eyes, and gave the episcopate to Cyrus, who had been abbot in Pontus and had supported him in exile. Ordering Pope Constantine to come to him, [Col. 0086B] he honorably received and dismissed him, so that on a Sunday he commanded him to celebrate Mass for him and received communion from his hand. Prostrate upon the ground, he asked the pope to intercede for his sins and renewed the privileges of the whole Church. When he sent an army into Pontus, despite the pope’s strong prohibition, in order to seize Philippicus, whom he had exiled there, the entire army went over to Philippicus’s side and made him emperor. Returning with him to Constantinople, it fought Justinian at the twelfth mile from the city; and, Justinian having been defeated and killed, Philippicus assumed the kingdom.

Philippicus, one year and six months. He expelled Cyrus from the pontificate and commanded him to return to Pontus to govern his own monastery under the title of abbot. [Col. 0086C] He sent Pope Constantine letters of perverse doctrine, which the pope rejected with the counsel of the Apostolic See. For this reason Constantine had pictures made in the portico of Saint Peter depicting the acts of the six holy universal synods. Philippicus had ordered such pictures removed when they were in the imperial city. The Roman people also decreed that they would receive neither the name of the heretical emperor in documents nor his likeness on coinage. Hence his image was not introduced into the churches, nor was his name spoken in the solemnities of Mass.

Anastasius, 3 years. He captured Philippicus and deprived him of his eyes, but did not kill him. He sent letters to Pope Constantine at Rome through Scholasticus, patrician and exarch of Italy, declaring himself a supporter of the Catholic faith and a proclaimer of the holy sixth council. Liutprand, king of the Lombards, at the admonition of the venerable Pope Gregory, confirmed the donation of the patrimony in the Cottian Alps which Aripert had made and which he himself had reclaimed. Wulfram, archbishop of Sens and monk of Fontenelle, flourished; preaching the word of the Lord to the Frisians, he performed many miracles. Ecgberht, a holy man of the English people, adorning his priesthood with monastic life while living as a pilgrim for the sake of the heavenly homeland, converted by devout preaching the chief provinces of the Scottish people to the canonical observance of Easter, from which they had long strayed, in the year 717 from the Lord’s Incarnation. [Col. 0086D]

[Col. 0087A] Theodosius, 1 year. Elected emperor, he defeated Anastasius in a hard battle near the city of Nicaea. After receiving an oath from him, he made him become a cleric and be ordained priest. Theodosius himself, as soon as he assumed the kingdom, being Catholic, immediately restored in the imperial city to its former place the venerable image which depicted the six holy synods and which Philippicus had cast down.
