The river Tiber overflowed its bed and caused much destruction to the city of Rome, increasing in the broad street to a height of one and a half statures, while the waters flowing from Saint Peter’s Gate joined those extending to the Milvian Bridge. It remained so for seven days, until the citizens made frequent litanies, and at last returned on the eighth day. In these times many nobles and common people of the English nation, [Col. 0087B] men and women, leaders and private persons, were accustomed, at the prompting of divine love, to come from Britain to Rome.

Leo reigned 9 years. In his third year, Charles Martel, son of Pippin, became mayor of the royal household; in the following year he defeated the tyrant Ragenfrid in battle at Vinchy, and after defeating him took possession of Angers. The Saracens, gathering with an immense army against Constantinople, besieged the city for three years, until, as its citizens cried earnestly to the Lord, many of them perished through hunger, cold, and pestilence, and so, wearied by the siege, withdrew. Returning, they attacked in war the nation of the Bulgars, which lives beyond the Danube. Defeated by them too, they fled and returned to their ships. As they put out to sea, a sudden storm arose; many were drowned, [Col. 0087C] or killed when their ships were wrecked along the shores. Hearing that the Saracens, after laying waste Sardinia, were even profaning the places where the bones of Saint Augustine the bishop had long ago been transferred and honorably deposited because of the devastation of barbarians, King Liutprand sent and, at great cost, acquired them. He transferred them to Pavia and there deposited them with honor due to so great a Father.

Thus far I have followed the chronography of the Englishman Bede, who wrote down to the year 734 from the Lord’s Incarnation. Bede himself, a priest, and Paul of Monte Cassino, a monk by religious profession and deeply imbued with learning, among their other good studies published and eloquently set forth the history of their own people in five books: whence the Winili (Guinili) and Angles had come, and how the Lombards subdued Italy and the Angles Britain to themselves. [Col. 0087D]

## XXV. Roman Emperors. Pippin. Charlemagne. Emperors of Constantinople.

Henceforth I am compelled laboriously to search out the records of other Fathers, and I undertake to continue the account of the times down to our own age, which is now made grim by many and various calamities: for two prelates have ambitiously contended over the Roman pontificate for six years already, while, after the death of Henry, king of the English, his nephew Stephen and his son-in-law Geoffrey have pursued their enmity with threats and arms over his kingdom, to the detriment of many.

[Col. 0088A] Constantine, son of Leo, reigned fifty-eight years. Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, flourished, and presided over the bishoprics of Paris and Bayeux, and also over the abbeys of Jumièges and Fontenelle. Charlemagne and Pippin obtained the mayoralty of the palace, and their brother Remigius, after Ragenfrid had been expelled, became archbishop of Rouen. Constantine and Abdallah, Emir and king of the Saracens, alike raged against the orthodox. Constantine assembled a council of 330 bishops at Constantinople.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 754, Pope Stephen, harassed by the malice of Aistulf, king of the Lombards, fled into Gaul. Honorably received by the Franks, he fell ill at Paris; upon recovering, he dedicated an altar at Saint-Denis. He consecrated Pippin and his sons, Charles and Carloman, as kings, and entrusted to them the defense of the whole holy Church against all its enemies.

Pippin, king of the Franks, having ruled vigorously for sixteen years, died on the eighth day before the Kalends of October [24 September], leaving his kingdom to his son Charles. Charles the Great reigned forty-seven years and accomplished many things worthy of praise, both in ecclesiastical and secular affairs. His merits before God and men were great; many recount his deeds with admiration and sing of them with the highest approval to eager listeners. For he himself went to Rome with a noble army of Gauls, and on his return captured Desiderius, king of the Lombards. [Col. 0088C] He subjected Pavia and the other cities of Italy to himself; destroyed Pamplona; took Saragossa by force of arms; crushed Saxons, Spaniards, and Saracens in wars; humbled the heathen powers through fear of Christian might; and raised high the banner of the cross in Christ’s name.

Leo, son of Constantine, reigned five years. Charles again went to Rome, and then penetrated Capua and Apulia by military force.

Constantine, together with his mother Irene, reigned seventeen years. Then someone at Constantinople found a stone coffin, and in it a man lying with this inscription:

> Christ will be born of the Virgin Mary, and I believe in him. Under the emperors Constantine and Irene, O sun, [Col. 0088D] you will see me again.

Charles came through Alemannia to the borders of Bavaria, and in the third year took possession of Bavaria. Then he marched against the Slavs called Vulti, and in the following year devastated Hungary.

In these times Adrian and Leo presided over the apostolic see for forty-eight years, shone brightly in very good works in their episcopacy, and benefited the Church of God. Then Constantine and Leo, and another Constantine, as has been said, ruled. For from the time of Constantine the Great, son of Helena, who founded Constantinople, down to the time of Constantine, son of Irene, the emperor at Constantinople ruled the Roman Empire, and presided over Illyricum, Italy, and many other nations and languages. But because several [Col. 0089A] of these emperors were heretics, and had not been raised to the empire by the people’s election according to lawful rite, but wickedly usurped the imperial stock by the cruel murder of their lords or their own kinsmen, and because they could not adequately defend even half of so vast a dominion against barbarians rising on every side, Pope Leo and an assembly of the senators and people of Rome met and took salutary counsel concerning the condition of the commonwealth. By common resolution they cast off from their necks the yoke of the ruler of Constantinople, chose the vigorous king of the Franks, Charles—who had already zealously protected them in many ways—and decreed to set him upon the Roman eminence.

Accordingly, in the fifth year of Pope Leo, which was the year 808 from the Incarnation [Col. 0089B] of the Lord, King Charles the Great was made the eighty-third emperor from Augustus and was called Augustus by the Romans. He condemned to death those who had dishonored Pope Leo, by whom he had been consecrated; but, at the pope’s prayers, he remitted their death sentence and confined them in exile. About that time there was a great earthquake, which shook almost all Italy and cast down a great part of the roof of the blessed apostle Paul, together with its beams.

Nicephorus, Irene’s brother, reigned six years. He made peace with Charles. Aaron also, king of the Persians, sent envoys and gifts of friendship to Charles.

Michael, son-in-law of Nicephorus, reigned three years and sent envoys of peace to Emperor Charles.

[Col. 0089C] Leo, son of Bardas, reigned six years. Charlemagne died at Aachen, and his son Louis the Pious succeeded him, born of Hildigard, daughter of Wittekind, king of the Saxons; he ruled vigorously for twenty-seven years. In his time a storm of tribulations raged exceedingly over the inhabitants of earth. Paschal, the hundredth pope from Peter, crowned Louis the Pious at Rome on Easter Day.

Theophilus reigned eleven years. Lothair rebelled against his father Louis and, as the power of the faithless increased, disturbed the land. Then the Northmen devastated Brittany and other lands, and the bodies of Saints Samson and Philibert, and of many others, were moved for fear of the pagans.

Michael, son of Theophilus, reigned twenty-seven years. In the second [Col. 0089D] year of his reign Emperor Louis died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July [20 June] and was buried by his brother Drogo, archbishop of Metz. Then, in the third year, which was the year 842 from the Incarnation of the Lord, the battle of Fontenoy was fought near Auxerre between his three sons, Louis, Lothair, and Charles the Bald. In it the Christian people were laid low on both sides by mutual slaughter on the sixth day before the Kalends of July [26 June]. At last the lot of victory fell to Charles. In that same year the Northmen devastated Rouen and burned the monastery of Saint Ouen the bishop on the Ides of May [15 May].

Basil, having killed his lord Michael, reigned twenty years. Severe famine, mortality among human beings, and plague among animals raged everywhere throughout the world.

After King Louis’s death, Rollo entered Neustria with his men on the fifteenth day before the Kalends [Col. 0090A] of December [17 November]. In the year 876 from the Incarnation of the Lord he entered Normandy, and for thirty-seven years waged war against the Gauls, until he was baptized by Archbishop Franco.

Leo and Alexander, sons of Basil, reigned twenty-two years. After Emperor Charles died, King Arnulf was made emperor and held the empire for ten years.

In the year 900 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the third indiction, King Zendebald killed Arnulf’s son.

Then Rollo besieged Chartres. But Walter, bishop of that city, a religious man, went out carrying in his hands the tunic of Saint Mary, Mother of God; with divine help he put the enemy to flight and freed the city. For he had summoned to his aid Richard, duke of Burgundy, and Ebles, count of Poitou; and, when the enemies had been put to flight and God triumphed, the Christian people rejoiced.

Alexander reigned one year. The Huns devastated Saxony and Thuringia. Constantine Porphyrogenitus, son of Leo, reigned with his mother Zoe for four years. In the third year Louis, Arnulf’s son, died; Conrad, son of Conrad, was raised to be king and reigned seven years.

Romanus the Armenian reigned with the aforesaid Constantine for twenty-six years.

Then Rollo became a Christian and made peace with Charles, king of the Franks, having received his daughter Gisla in marriage. While Henry was ruling, King Charles died in prison at Péronne, held by Count Herbert, and [Col. 0090C] a great dissension disturbed the Franks. At last, after five years, Louis, son of King Charles, took as wife Gerberga, daughter of Henry, king of the Germans.

Constantine reigned with his young son Romanus for fifteen years. Then Otto, son of Henry, began to reign; he ruled thirty-six years and had as wife the sister of Athelstan, king of the English. Then William Longsword defeated Rithulf of Évreux at the place called the Meadow of Battle; and eight years later, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January [17 December], Arnulf, governor of Flanders, killed William. William was succeeded in the duchy by his son Richard the Elder, who held the principality vigorously for fifty-four years and performed praiseworthy deeds.

[Col. 0090D] Stephen and Constantine, sons of Romanus, deposed their father from the royal throne. But Constantine likewise deposed both of them, and himself ruled with his son Romanus for sixteen years.

While Edgar, son of Edmund, ruled the English, graciously aided the worshippers of God, and faithfully obeyed teachers in all matters pertaining to the edification of the Church, Dunstan, archbishop of Canterbury, Oswald of York, and Æthelwold of Winchester shone in holiness and learning and governed the peoples entrusted to them carefully and beneficially. Wholeheartedly embracing the establishment of religious life, they flourished successfully and founded twenty-six abbeys of monks or nuns in England. For the Danish devastation which [Col. 0091A] some years earlier had martyred Saint Edmund, king of the East Angles, had also raged exceedingly over virtually the whole flock of Christ throughout the island of Britain; having destroyed the sacred buildings, it had torn apart or scattered the Lord’s sheep in wolfish fashion.

Emperor Nicephorus reigned ten years. Excessive disturbances raged in the world, and greedy magnates, with the armies subject to them, rose in war against their equals.

John, having killed Nicephorus, ruled through his wife; her niece Theophanu married Emperor Otto. In the fifth year of his reign Otto the younger died, and his son Otto ruled after him for eighteen years. Then Hugh the Great and other nobles of the Franks rebelled against [Col. 0091B] King Louis. That duke, indeed, followed in the footsteps of his father Robert, who rebelled against Charles the Simple and was anointed king. King Charles, however, when he saw that he was despised by the perjured duke, before a year had elapsed gathered forces from every side, rose against the deserter, defeated him in battle at Soissons, and killed him.

### XXVI. King Lothair. King Charles. Extinction of Charlemagne’s dynasty.

In the month of May, on Friday, blood rained upon the workmen. In the same year, in September, King Louis died after many tribulations and was buried at Rheims in the basilica of Saint Remigius. His son Lothair [Col. 0091C] was anointed king at Rheims and held the kingdom vigorously for seven years. Then Hugh the Great, duke of the Franks at Orléans, surpassed all the magnates in wealth and power. He had as wife a daughter of Emperor Otto, who bore him three sons—Hugh, Otto, and Henry—and a daughter named Emma. She married Richard the Elder, duke of the Normans, but died childless.

In the second year of King Lothair, in August, Hugh the Great besieged the city of Poitiers. But the Lord thundered terribly through the merits of Saint Hilary, bishop and patron of that city. A violent whirlwind tore apart the duke’s tent; great terror seized him and his army and immediately drove them [Col. 0091D] from the siege of the city. In the same year Gilbert, duke of Burgundy, died, and Otto, son of Hugh and his son-in-law, obtained the duchy. Yet not long afterward he too died childless, and his brother Henry succeeded.

Then Ansegisus, bishop of Troyes, was expelled from his city by Count Robert and went to Saxony to Emperor Otto. Having brought Saxons from there, he besieged Troyes for a long time. For the two dukes Helpo and Bruno aided him with their armies. Once, when they came to plunder Sens, Archbishop Archembald and the aged Count Rainard met them with their forces; battle was joined, and they killed Duke Helpo and many Saxons. When his companion Bruno saw this, [Col. 0092A] he abandoned the siege and returned sorrowfully to his own country.

King Lothair recovered Lothair’s kingdom and came with a large army to the palace at Aachen, where Emperor Otto was staying with his wife; at mealtime he entered without anyone opposing him. Otto fled with his wife and people and abandoned the palace. Then, after Lothair had returned victoriously to Francia, the aforesaid emperor gathered an army, came to Paris, burned its suburb, and there the emperor’s nephew, with many others, perished by the arms of the Gauls. King Lothair therefore summoned Hugh, duke of the Franks, and Henry, duke of Burgundy, and attacked the enemy. He did not cease pursuing the fugitives as far as Soissons. But they, [Col. 0092B] terrified by their pursuers, rushed into the bed of the river Aisne; not knowing the ford, many perished there. Thus water consumed more than the sword, for the river had filled its banks; so many died there by drowning that the water overflowed with the corpses of the dead. King Lothair steadfastly pursued the enemy for three days and as many nights. Then, in that same year, the aforesaid king made peace with the emperor at Rheims, against the will of the dukes and army of the Franks; and he granted him Lotharingia, greatly distressing the Franks.

In the year 976 from the Incarnation of the Lord, King Lothair died and was buried at Rheims in the basilica of Blessed Remigius. His son Louis held the kingdom for eleven years [Col. 0092C] and, when dead, was buried at Compiègne in the basilica of Saint Cornelius the martyr. His brother Charles wished to rule, but Hugh the Great, son of Hugh the Great, rebelled against him and, having gathered a large army, besieged Laon, where Charles was living with his wife. At last Charles, angered, rushed out from the city with armed men, put Hugh and his army to flight in battle, and burned their huts. Seeing, therefore, that he could not overcome Charles by force, Duke Hugh formed a plan with Ascelin, the aged bishop of Laon and Charles’s adviser. Forgetful of his rank, his age, and his imminent death, that man imitated Ahithophel and Judas and was not ashamed to become a traitor. For at night, [Col. 0092D] while everyone was asleep, he betrayed Laon; Hugh bound Charles with his wife—the daughter, namely, of Herbert, count of Troyes—and consigned them to long imprisonment in a tower at Orléans. There Charles begot two sons, Louis and Charles, and from that time the progeny of Charlemagne ceased to rule in Francia.

### XXVII. King Hugh. The Council of Rheims. Pope Gerbert.

Accordingly, in the year 993 of the Lord’s Incarnation, Duke Hugh was anointed king at Rheims. In the same year his son Robert was also appointed king and exercised royal government for thirty-eight years. A certain vision encouraged Hugh to so great a deed. For Saint Walric appeared in a dream to the aforesaid duke while he was in the city of Paris, [Col. 0093A] clearly revealing who he was and what he wanted, namely commanding him to undertake a military expedition against Arnulf of Flanders and to remove his body from the monastery of Sithiu, where the body of Saint Bertin rests, and restore it to the monastery of Leuconaus in the district of Vimeu. Moreover, he promised him that, if he did these things, he and his descendants would rule in Francia to the seventh generation. Hugh therefore gladly obeyed the command, and, by the force of his power, with God’s will, terrified Arnulf; he recovered the bodies of the venerable men Walric and Richarius, which had been removed through a certain clerk named Erchembald for a great price, and reverently restored them to their proper places. The duke himself went [Col. 0093B] to Leuconaus with his magnates, established the soil containing Saint Walric at the monastery situated on the river Somme, and, having expelled the secular canons, installed regular monks. Not long afterward, as has been said, he received the kingdom, and his line has endured in the kingdom down to the present day. For four kings of his stock have now ruled: Robert, Henry, Philip, and Louis. At the beginning of his reign King Hugh convened a synod at Rheims, invited Sewin, archbishop of the city of Sens, with his suffragans, and caused Lord Arnulf, archbishop of Rheims, to be deposed. For he said that one born of a concubine ought not, according to the canons, to be a bishop. He envied Arnulf because he was of the royal lineage of Charlemagne, [Col. 0093C] brother of King Lothair, though born of a concubine; yet he was illustrious in character, because he was good and modest.

But the venerable Sewin feared God more than Hugh and therefore did not consent to Arnulf’s unjust deposition; rather, so far as he could, he reproved the king himself. Hence the royal wrath boiled against him and burned fiercely to carry out the rash design it had conceived. The other bishops, however, though unwilling, deposed Arnulf out of fear of the king and appointed Gerbert, a monk and philosopher who had been King Robert’s teacher. Arnulf was indeed deposed by the king’s violent command, expelled with great dishonor from the church of Blessed Mary, Mother of God, [Col. 0093D] at Rheims, and confined for three years in prison at Orléans. All these things were reported to the Roman pontiff. Greatly indignant at them, he suspended all the bishops who had deposed Arnulf and installed Gerbert in his place. He also sent Abbot Leo from the apostolic see into Gaul to exercise his authority and correct the unlawful ordinations according to rule. Finally, the pope’s legate first approached Sewin of Sens, whom he knew above all others to be a strict guardian of righteousness, and communicated the apostolic commands to him. When the council at Rheims was again gathered by apostolic command, Archbishop Arnulf [Col. 0094A] was recalled from custody and received back into his own see with great honor. The disputation of Bishop Gerbert and Abbot Leo is considered very useful and is carefully preserved in the deeds of the bishops of Rheims.

Gerbert was most learned in sacred and secular books, famous in his school, and had distinguished pupils: King Robert, namely, Leotheric, archbishop of Sens, Remigius, [Note: [Col. 0093] Remigius, bishop of Auxerre, is not that Remigius, the monk who was truly Gerbert’s disciple. On him consult, for example, Le Prévost.] bishop of the people of Auxerre, Haimo and Hubold, and very many others shining in the choir of learned men.

Bishop Remigius produced an eloquent exposition on the Mass and usefully explained the art, or edition, of the grammarian Donatus. Haimo too commendably expounded the epistles of Saint [Col. 0094B] Paul the Apostle and treated many other matters from the Gospels and other sacred Scriptures in a spiritual manner. Hubold, skilled in the art of music, resounded in the church to the praise of the Creator; he sang a sweet Office concerning the Holy Trinity and composed many other delightful chants concerning God and his saints.

Gerbert taught these and many others, whose manifold learning greatly benefited the Church of God in the following age. After he had been deposed from the see of Rheims, which he had unlawfully usurped, he left Gaul in shame and indignation and went to Emperor Otto; by him and by the people he was elected to the bishopric of Ravenna. [Col. 0094C] From there, after some years, he was transferred to the apostolic see and, in the year 999 of the Lord’s Incarnation, was elevated as Pope Sylvester. It is reported of him that, while he was a scholar, he spoke with a demon and asked what fate awaited him. From it he immediately heard this ambiguous monadic utterance:

> Gerbert passes from R to R; afterward, as pope, he flourishes at R.

The oracle of the deceitful one was then sufficiently obscure to understand; nevertheless, afterward we plainly see it fulfilled. For Gerbert passed from the see of Rheims to the bishopric of Ravenna and afterward became pope at Rome.

### XXVIII. Emperor Otto. Æthelred, king of the English. Various events in England, Normandy, and Burgundy.

[Col. 0094D]

In the year 1002 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Emperor Otto died and Henry succeeded him.

Then, in 1024, Emperor Conrad ruled. In the third year of his rule Richard II died, who deserved to be called father of monks because of his devotion to religion.

Then, while Æthelred, son of Edgar, was king, many adversities arose in the kingdom of England. For Sweyn, king of the Danes, invaded England with a huge fleet; when the English defected to him, King Æthelred fled into Normandy with his wife and sons. His wife Emma was sister of Richard, duke of Normandy, son of Gunnor, [Col. 0095A] and of Robert, archbishop of Rouen. Not long afterward the pagan king Sweyn was killed by Saint Edmund, king and martyr, and his body, embalmed with spices, was taken to Denmark. For the Danes were still pagans, and the death of their fierce lord—whose body could not remain buried in English soil—had terrified them. King Æthelred, on hearing of Sweyn’s death, at once returned to his native land, reconciled to himself his deserters by words and promises, and encouraged them to defend themselves better than before against enemies restored to life, as it were. But Cnut, Sweyn’s son, was greatly angered against his own people because they had fled and had womanishly abandoned the noble kingdom of England, already subdued for him. At last, having prepared a fleet, he crossed into England with Lacman, king of the Swabians, and Olaf, king of the [Col. 0095B] Norwegians, and besieged London. There King Æthelred fell ill and died; and his son Edmund, surnamed Ironside, that is, “Iron Side,” was raised to be king.

The English and Danes fought many times, and as the lot of victory changed, much blood was shed on both sides. At last, when capable and prudent men arranged peace, the two rulers made a necessary treaty for their peoples. Cnut became a Christian and took as wife Emma, widow of King Æthelred, together with half the kingdom. She bore him Harthacnut, king of the English, and Gunnhild, wife of Henry, emperor of the Romans.

[Col. 0095C] At Satan’s instigation—for he continually strives to disturb the human race unto death—King Edmund, after seven years, perished in a privy through the treachery of the cruel Eadric Streona. Cnut gained the whole of England and possessed it until his death. He banished Edmund’s sons Edward and Edmund, handsome little boys, into Denmark and ordered his brother Sweyn, king of the Danes, to kill them. But he refused to murder the noble and innocent boys wickedly; rather, when an occasion arose, he gave them to the king of the Huns as hostages, as if they were his own grandsons. There the ætheling Edmund died an untimely death. But Edward, by God’s providence, married the king’s daughter and ruled over the Huns. He begot Edgar Ætheling, Margaret, queen of the Scots, and Christina, a nun; Edward, [Col. 0095D] son of King Æthelred, after he had gained his hereditary right, summoned them and kindly reared them in England as though they were his own offspring.

In the year 1031 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Robert, king of the Franks, died. His son Henry, though Queen Constance, his younger brother Robert, and other Franks strongly opposed him, obtained the kingdom of Gaul with the help of Duke Robert and the strength of the Normans, and ruled twenty-nine years.

In the fifth year of his reign Robert, duke of the Normans, died on his journey to Jerusalem, near the Bithynian city of Nicaea, on the Kalends of July [1 July]. His illegitimate son William, a boy of eight, succeeded to the duchy and held it vigorously for fifty years.

During his minority, the Normans, stirred by their innate restlessness, [Col. 0096A] rebelled and fought among themselves for a long time, causing enormous slaughter of nobles and common people. For Count Gilbert of Brionne, Osbern the steward, Walchelin of Ferrières, Hugh of Montfort, Roger of Spain, Robert of Grandmesnil, Turchetil, the duke’s tutor, and many others died by mutual blows. Guy, son of Renaud, duke of Burgundy, by a daughter of Richard II, and a count appointed by Duke William, also rebelled against him and enticed by promises many Normans prone to treachery. Having associated them with himself, he strove to take the duchy from the duke. Therefore the young duke was compelled to hasten to Poissy, where he threw himself at King Henry’s feet and sought aid from him against his wicked nobles [Col. 0096B] and kinsmen. Henry, being merciful, pitied the distressed youth, summoned the strength of the French army, and went into Neustria to aid the duke.

In the year 1039 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Emperor Conrad died, and his son Henry ruled seventeen years. In the fourth year of his reign there was a great mortality among human beings.

In the year 1047 from the Incarnation of the Lord, a fierce battle was fought at Val-ès-Dunes. But Guy, unable to bear the force of King Henry and Duke William, was defeated and compelled to flee from the battle with his men, not without great shame and loss. In these times Bruno, bishop of Toul, serving as envoy for the Lotharingians, went to Rome. As he prayed one night on the way, [Col. 0096C] he heard angels singing: “Thus says the Lord: I think thoughts of peace, and not of affliction,” etc. (Jeremiah 29:11.) When Bruno reached Pope Damasus, he was honorably received by him and appointed cardinal-bishop in the Roman senate. For he was handsome and noble, wise and eloquent, and adorned with many virtues.

In the same year Pope Damasus died, and Bruno was elected Pope Leo. He endeavored everywhere to restore the decrees of the holy canons, which in the preceding times of the aforesaid kings and pontiffs had fallen greatly into disuse and had almost vanished from human knowledge. Thus, in the year of the Lord 1050, he held [Col. 0096D] a useful council at Rheims, treated of the chastity and justice of God’s ministers, and renewed salutary decrees which bishops and priests no longer knew. Then, with Abbot Herimar directing the work, he dedicated the church of Saint Remigius, archbishop of Rheims, on the Kalends of October [1 October], and translated the body of that bishop; its feast is celebrated with the greatest solemnity in Francia every year on the first day of October.

### XXIX. Restoration of the monastery of Ouche. Conflicts between the Franks and Normans. The Council of Clermont. Various events down to the year 1138.

In the following year the monastery of Saint Evroul at Ouche was restored by William, son of Giroie, and his nephews Hugh of Grandmesnil and Robert his brother; the venerable monk Theodoric of Jumièges [Col. 0097A] became its first abbot.

In these times a serious conflict and seedbed of war arose between the king of the Franks and the duke of the Normans. For William of Arques, the duke’s paternal uncle, rebelled against him and, on the advice of his brother Mauger, archbishop of Rouen, invited King Henry to assist him. The resolute duke immediately besieged Arques, forestalled and killed Count Enguerrand of Ponthieu as he sought to enter the stronghold against him, took the fortification, disinherited William, and had Mauger, instigator of the dissensions, deposed from ecclesiastical office.

Therefore the king of Gaul roared with intense indignation. In the year of the Lord 1054 he entered the district of Évreux with a great army and sent his brother Odo [Col. 0097B] with many troops of knights through the district of Beauvais across the Seine. But the duke followed the king’s force along its flank and had sent ahead against Odo the troop of Caux under Count Robert of Eu and Roger of Mortemer. Immediately they met the French, joined battle at Mortemer, and, after great slaughter on both sides, the Franks fled. Having captured Guy, count of Ponthieu, who had come to avenge his brother’s death, the rejoicing Normans reported their victory to the duke. When the king heard that his men had turned their backs to the Normans, he was ashamed and at once returned sadly to his own land. Some time later lawful negotiators of peace went back and forth between the discordant lords; [Col. 0097C] Guy and the others who had been captured were restored, the aforesaid princes made a treaty, and their subject peoples rejoiced greatly.

In the year 1060 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Henry, king of the Franks, died; his son Philip held the sceptre of Gaul after him for forty-seven years.

In the sixth year of his reign Edward, son of Æthelred, king of the English, departed this life; after him Harold, son of Godwin, seized the diadem of England. In the following year a comet appeared. In autumn Duke William of Normandy crossed the sea and, battle having been joined, killed Harold on the second day before the Ides of October [14 October], gained the kingdom, received the royal sceptre on Christmas Day, and held it for twenty years and eight months.

In his times the holy Church increased and was magnified, [Col. 0097D] and was fostered by religious men and good rulers. For Maurilius, John, and William presided over the metropolitan see of Rouen; Lanfranc over Canterbury; Thomas over York; and other religious Fathers and teachers were placed over monasteries and bishoprics.

In the year 1087 from the Incarnation of the Lord, King William died, and his son William Rufus ruled twelve years and ten months.

In these times, in the year 1095, Pope Urban held a great council at Clermont and urged Christians to undertake the journey to Jerusalem against the pagans.

There were then drought, famine, and mortality among human beings.

[Col. 0098A] In the year 1099 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Jerusalem was taken by holy pilgrims after they had defeated the nations which had long held it. Then Pope Urban died and Paschal succeeded him. In the following year William Rufus, king of the English, died in the hunt, struck by an arrow. His brother Henry succeeded him and reigned thirty-five years and four months. In the seventh year of his reign he fought a battle at Tinchebray, in which he captured his brother Robert, duke of the Normans, and subjected the duchy to himself. Then Emperor Henry died on the seventh day before the Ides of August [7 August], and his son Charles Henry succeeded him.

Then, in the third year, Philip, king of the Franks, died, and Louis Theobald succeeded and had now ruled twenty-nine years.

[Col. 0098B] In the following year Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, and Hugh, abbot of Cluny, departed this life; shortly afterward William, archbishop of Rouen, followed them in death.

During these three years there was a great famine in Gaul, and a multitude of people was afflicted by the torment of the sacred fire.

In the year 1118 from the Incarnation of the Lord, a violent wind in the western regions, on the vigil of Christmas, threw down many buildings and forest trees. In the following year a battle was fought at Brémule, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September [20 August], between Henry, king of England, and Louis, king of the Franks. The army of the Gauls was put to flight, while the English and Normans triumphed. In that same year Pope Calixtus II held a very great synod of bishops at Rheims and labored strenuously to reconcile those at variance. At last peace was made between the kings; as the king of England was returning to his realm, his sons William and Richard, with a great multitude of nobles from many lands, perished by shipwreck on the seventh day before the Kalends of December [25 November].

In the year of the Lord 1123, in the first indiction, when certain Normans—Amaury of Évreux, Waleran of Meulan, and their accomplices—rebelled, King Henry besieged, burned, and took their strongholds: Montfort, Brionne, and Pont-Audemer. After many losses, Count Waleran was captured in battle with eighty knights and was bound for five years in the prison of King Henry, [Col. 0098D] who had raised him and against whom he had insolently taken up arms.

In the year of the Lord 1125, there was a change among many rulers. Charles Henry V, emperor, died, and Lothair, duke of the Saxons, succeeded to the empire. Then also the eminent dukes William of Poitou and William of Apulia died. In the third year afterward Charles, duke of Flanders, was killed in church while praying at Mass, on the Kalends of March [1 March]; he was succeeded by William, son of Robert, duke of the Normans, who was killed at Aalst in the following year. Then Garmond, patriarch of Jerusalem, and Geoffrey, archbishop of Rouen, died.

In the year 1130 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Baldwin II, king of Jerusalem, died on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September [15 August]; [Col. 0099A] his son-in-law Fulk, count of Anjou, succeeded him.

In the second year Pope Honorius died at Rome, and immediately an exceedingly great schism arose in the Church. For during the night certain persons elected as pope Gregory, a deacon born at Pavia, and called him Innocent; the Church established in the western regions accepted and followed him. But on the third day others enthroned Peter, son of Leo, and called him Anacletus. Because he was supported by powerful brothers, kinsmen, and very many friends, he has now effectively acquired possession for seven years of the city of Rome and of the pope’s revenues and dominions; Apulia, Sicily, and a great region of the world have followed him.

In the year 1136 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the fourteenth [Col. 0099B] indiction, Henry, king of the English and duke of the Normans—a vigorous lover of peace and justice, a faithful worshipper of God, protector of the unarmed people, and ardent defender of the holy Church—died in the castle of Lyons on the Kalends of December [1 December]. His body, embalmed with spices, was brought to England and buried at Reading in the basilica of the Holy Trinity which he himself had built for monks.

Stephen, his nephew through his sister Adela, succeeded to the kingdom; and he is now completing the sixth year of his reign, a year which has brought grievous reverses, many sorrows, and losses affecting many. For he fought at Lincoln against the consuls who had rebelled against him, was defeated and captured, and was kept in sorrowful chains in the prison of Robert of Bristol. [Col. 0099C]

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1138, Peter Anacletus suddenly died.

The emperor Lothair, while returning from Apulia after subduing it to himself, died; Conrad, nephew of Emperor Henry and of Charles, succeeded him. Roger, king of Sicily, meanwhile gradually entered Apulia; and, after the death of the most excellent duke Ranulf, to whom the pope and the emperor had entrusted the region against him, he vigorously recovered the cities which had been taken from him. He captured Pope Innocent, who had recently publicly anathematized him, through his son Roger, and made peace with him on his own terms. Finally, from the unwilling and modest pope he received the kingdom of Sicily and the duchy of Apulia; absolved by him, he appointed his son Roger duke of Apulia. [Col. 0100A]

Following in the footsteps of my predecessors, I have attempted to write a chronicle. In the first book of my Ecclesiastical History I began the thread of the narrative with the Incarnation of the Saviour and carried it, through the succession of emperors and kings, down to the present day, in which John Augustus, son of Alexius, rules at Constantinople; Lothair rules the Germans; Louis the Franks; Stephen the English; and the monk Remigius the Spaniards. [Col. 0100B]

Now, in the second book, with God’s help, I consider matters concerning the holy apostles and apostolic men, published by the ancient doctors and written down from copies; and I desire briefly to assemble their deeds, insofar as the inspiration of the divine Spirit shall disclose them to me.

I am pleased to investigate carefully the succession of the Roman pontiffs and their fellow-workers in the vineyard of Sabaoth, and to set it forth in truthful writing for companions who ask this of me. The Roman bishops, indeed, from most blessed Peter—to whom the Lord Jesus Christ first said: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 16:19)—down to Pope Innocent, who today presides over the apostolic see, number 141. [Col. 0100C]

Concerning all these, whose mention is inserted in the Deeds of the Pontiffs, I earnestly desire to disclose something in the following book.

## SUMMARY OF THE SECOND BOOK

[Col. 0099]

I. The origins of the Church of Jesus Christ. The acts and miracles of the apostles. The disciples increase in number. II. Stephen, the first of the martyrs. Persecution of the Church at Jerusalem. Paul’s conversion. Peter’s miracles. III. The opinion of the Roman Senate concerning Christ. The crimes of King Herod against Christians. IV. Christ’s word is propagated. The Church at Antioch. The preaching of Paul and Barnabas. V. Notices concerning Christ’s apostles. The history of Peter. VI. Paul. VII. Continuation: Peter and Paul residing at Rome. VIII. Continuation: the death of the apostles Peter and Paul. IX. Andrew. X. Andrew: continuation of his life. XI. James and John. XII. James the Less. XIII. Philip. XIV. Thomas. XV. Bartholomew. XVI. Matthew. XVII. Simon, Jude, or Thaddaeus. XVIII. Matthias. XIX. History of the disciples: Barnabas. XX. Mark. XXI. Luke. [Col. 0101] XXII. Martial of Limoges. XXIII. Continuation of the life of the apostle Martial. XXIV. History of the Roman pontiffs: Peter and his successors. XXV. Continuation of the history of the Roman pontiffs. XXVI. Continuation. XXVII. Continuation. XXVIII. Continuation. XXIX. Continuation. XXX. Continuation.

# BOOK II

## I. The origins of the Church of Jesus Christ. The acts and miracles of the apostles. The disciples increase in number.

[Col. 0101A]

When the fullness of time came, heavenly grace mercifully bestowed upon humankind the saving visitation which it had foreseen before the foundation of the world; and, near the final hour of the age, it illuminated the shadowed hearts of mortals with the rays of a new light. For our Saviour Jesus Christ, as the lofty voice of the holy Gospel truly instructs us, in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar received baptism from John in the Jordan; and for three and a half years shone forth as the true sun by manifest signs and wonders, displaying to the world his divinity, by which he is equal, consubstantial, and coeternal with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Then, in the thirty-third year of his age, he mercifully endured the passion of the cross for the salvation of humankind; and, having destroyed death—which had held the human race entangled for five thousand years in the bond of just condemnation—he despoiled hell, conquered Satan, the ancient serpent, and rose victorious from the dead on the third day. Finally, on the fortieth day, after confirming his followers as true witnesses of his resurrection by clear manifestations, and commanding them to preach the Gospel to all nations with the performance of signs, he led his disciples out to Bethany. Standing upon the Mount of Olives, he blessed them; and, while they looked on and rejoiced, he ascended into heaven. After ten days, while his friends were fasting and praying together, he sent the Paraclete Spirit. As he had promised, by inward anointing he taught them everything in a moment; happily endowed them with the abundance of every grace; strengthened them against every assault of opponents; and made them unconquerable athletes and teachers of all nations. [Cols. 0101B–C]

Luke, a Syrian by birth, a physician by profession, and a faithful disciple of Christ, filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit, after writing the Gospel for Greek-speaking believers, added for Theophilus the distinguished book concerning the Acts of the Apostles. Theophilus, moreover, means “one who loves God”; by him is signified every diligent and discerning person who ardently perseveres in continual meditation upon the divine law. To such a person the word of God is rightly addressed; by such a person it is received with life and steadfastly retained by the bond of true love. To him the Gospel—that is, the good message—is fittingly communicated, and the triumphs of the invincible apostles and martyrs are recounted, because he is considered worthy to share in such heavenly mysteries. [Cols. 0101C–0102A]

The eloquent Arator also strove to follow Luke’s narrative. From it he drew special material for versification, and he presented to Pope Vigilius a poem beautiful in metrical resonance, leaving for posterity an illustrious memorial of his own composition. I strive to look upon such great and distinguished forerunners; and, like a lame man proceeding step by step, I can scarcely follow from afar the swiftest runners. Yet I must begin at the outset with their subject matter, since I have the wish to speak about the apostles and their blessed fellow-soldiers.

Luke relates in a lucid narrative that, on the holy day of Pentecost, the apostles were filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the mighty works of God in the various languages of the nations, to the astonishment of Jews who had gathered from different peoples. When their jealous rivals, murmuring out of envy, said, “These men are full of new wine” (Acts 2:13), Peter, inflamed with zeal for faith, stood with the eleven companions, raised his voice, and gave an orderly exposition of the coming of the Paraclete Spirit, foretold long before through the prophet Joel. Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, whom God the Father had declared by mighty works, signs, and wonders, and had raised from the dead on the third day after the passion of the cross, he spread a most true testimony, citing persuasive examples from the Psalmist. The Jews, therefore, were pierced in heart, received the saving word, and were baptized; and on that day about three thousand souls of believers were added (ibid., 1–41). Thus proceeded the primitive Church, which heavenly grace abundantly flooded. [Cols. 0102B–C]

Many signs and wonders were performed through the apostles in Jerusalem, and all who saw these unprecedented things were afraid. All who believed also lived together and held all things in common. They sold possessions and property and distributed them to everyone according to each person’s need. Daily the faithful grew in virtue; and, as the Lord added those who were to be saved, their number increased (ibid., 41–47).

Peter and John went up to the Temple at the ninth hour. There they saw a lame man, forty years old, lame from his mother’s womb, begging. Though he denied that he possessed riches, Peter offered the needy man something better: taking him by the hand, he immediately healed him by his word in the name of Jesus Christ. At once, his feet and ankles strengthened, the man leapt up and ran; he entered the Temple with them and joyfully praised the Lord openly. When all the people saw the special miracle performed in Christ’s name upon the lame man who was placed daily at the Beautiful Gate of the Temple, they were filled with astonishment and ecstasy. While the apostles were being held there, the people ran to Solomon’s Portico to see the lame man, now healed through the power of Christ’s name. When the crowd had assembled, Peter began to speak. In a wholly humble argument he diverted praise for the healing completely from himself and attributed it entirely to the power of the divinity of Christ Jesus. He gently rebuked the Jews, Christ’s persecutors; but afterward, trusting in the untiring mercy of his Master, he mildly excused them because they had acted through ignorance. Finally, he invited them to repentance for their crimes and plainly showed that the Saviour and true prophet, as Moses, Samuel, and all the prophets thereafter had foretold, had now come (Acts 2:42; 3:26). [Cols. 0103A–B]

While they were speaking to the people, the priests, the captain of the Temple, and the Sadducees came upon them, seized them, and put them in custody. Filled with the wickedness of gall, they were distressed because the apostles were teaching the people and proclaiming resurrection from the dead in Jesus. Many of those who heard the word believed, and the number of men came to five thousand. On the following day Annas, the chief priest, Caiaphas, John, Alexander, all who were of priestly descent, together with rulers, elders, and scribes, assembled in Jerusalem. Setting the apostles in their midst, they asked: “By what power or in what name have you done this?” Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, gave the most excellent testimony that the sick man had been healed in the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, and that no other name under heaven had been given by which salvation must be obtained. When the opponents saw the boldness of Peter and John, and learned that they were unlettered and ordinary men, they marvelled and were troubled. They certainly recognized that they had been with Jesus. They also saw the man who had been healed standing before them and could say nothing in opposition; but because of the sign evident to everyone in Jerusalem, they wasted away with anger. [Cols. 0103B–D] Finally, after taking counsel, they summoned the apostles and ordered them never again to speak or teach in the name of Jesus. Peter and John strongly opposed their command, saying: “Judge whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to the Lord. For we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard.” They threatened them and released them, not daring to punish persons whom they saw were exceedingly pleasing to the people because of the great miracle (Acts 4:1–22).

Released, they came to their own people and reported what had happened to them. When these heard it, they unanimously raised their voice to the Lord. Inflamed with divine zeal, they poured forth a particular prayer pleasing to God; and when they had prayed, the place in which they stood was shaken. All were filled with the Holy Spirit, and with the nets of sacred preaching drew many from the depths of error to the light of faith and righteousness. [Col. 0104A]

The multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul. No one possessed anything as private property, nor was anyone among them needy. All things were common to them. Owners of houses or fields sold them and placed their prices at the feet of the apostles; these were distributed to each according to individual need. Thus the congregation first established in Jerusalem shone forth, its whole attention always blazing toward heaven. Divine blessing consecrated this most joyful assembly, and from it a gracious pattern of good conduct flowed down to us. Joseph, surnamed Barnabas by the apostles—that is, “son of consolation”—a Levite and Cypriot by origin, ready for a good work, sold the field he possessed, brought the price, and laid it at the apostles’ feet (Acts 4:23–37). [Cols. 0104A–B]

But Ananias sold a field and, with the knowledge of his wife Sapphira, deceitfully withheld part of its price; bringing a certain portion, he laid it at the apostles’ feet. When Peter learned by the Holy Spirit of the fraud, he rebuked the deceiver for his lie. As soon as Ananias heard the apostle’s rebuke, he fell down and died. About three hours later his wife, unaware of what had happened, entered. Questioned by Peter about the price of the field, she lied. Rebuked in turn by the apostle, she immediately fell at his feet and died. Therefore great fear came upon the whole Church and upon all who heard these things (Acts 5:1–11). [Cols. 0104B–C]

Many signs and wonders were performed among the people through the hands of the apostles, and all were unanimously in Solomon’s Portico. None of the rest dared to associate with them, though the people extolled them. The multitude of believers in the Lord, both men and women, increased still more. The sick were laid in the streets upon little beds, so that, as Peter came by, at least his shadow might fall upon some of them and they might be freed from their infirmities. A multitude from the neighboring cities also came running to the apostles at Jerusalem, bringing the sick and the possessed; and the desired healing came to all (ibid., 12–16). [Col. 0104C]

The chief priest and all who were with him were filled with jealousy. They laid hands upon the apostles and put them in the public prison. But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors and, leading them out, said: “Go, stand in the Temple, and speak to the people all the words of this life.” At daybreak they entered the Temple and spoke the word of God boldly. The chief priest and those with him convened the council and sent to the prison for the apostles to be brought. The officers found the prison securely shut with every care, but no one inside. At length they heard that those whom they sought were teaching in the Temple. Then the captain, with his attendants, brought them without force, for they feared the people might stone them. The chief priest rebuked those set before the council because they had filled Jerusalem with a teaching contrary to the general decree of the elders. The apostles replied: “It is necessary to obey God rather than men. The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree. God exalted him at his right hand as Leader and Saviour, to grant repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins. We are witnesses of these words, as is the Holy Spirit whom God gave to all who obey him.” When they heard this, they were cut to the heart and considered killing them (Acts 5:17–33). [Cols. 0104D–0105A]

Then Gamaliel, a Pharisee and a teacher of the law held in honour by all the people, rose in the council. Wishing to aid the apostles, he had them removed and publicly recalled how, a few days before, Theudas with four hundred accomplices had been reduced to nothing; and how Judas the Galilean, with his followers, who drew the people away after himself, had perished in the days of the registration. Finally, after offering such examples, he said: “Now therefore I tell you: withdraw from these men and leave them alone. For if this counsel or work is from men, it will be destroyed; but if it is from God, you will not be able to destroy them, lest you perhaps be found to be resisting God also.” Hearing this, they agreed; and, summoning the apostles, they had them beaten, ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and released them. The apostles went away rejoicing from the presence of the council because they had been judged worthy to suffer dishonour for the name of Christ. Every day, in the Temple and from house to house, they did not cease teaching and proclaiming Jesus Christ (ibid., 34–42). [Cols. 0105A–B]

In those days, as the number of disciples increased, the Greeks murmured against the Hebrews because their widows were neglected in the daily service. Therefore the Twelve summoned the multitude of disciples and said: “It is not right for us to leave the word of God and serve tables. Therefore, brothers, select from among yourselves seven men of good reputation, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this work; but we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word.” As all agreed, they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit; Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timotheus, Parmenas, and Nicolas, a convert from Antioch. They set these before the apostles, who prayed and laid their hands upon them. The number of disciples in Jerusalem multiplied greatly, and a large multitude of priests also submitted to the faith (Acts 6:1–7). [Cols. 0105C–D]

## II. Stephen, the first of the martyrs. Persecution of the Church at Jerusalem. Paul’s conversion. Peter’s miracles.

Stephen, full of grace and power, performed great wonders and signs among the people. The Jews, therefore, envying him, rose up against him; disputing with him, they could not withstand the wisdom and Spirit by which he spoke. Then they suborned false witnesses to say that they had heard him utter blasphemous words against Moses and God; and they stirred up the people, elders, and scribes. Then they rushed together, seized him, brought him before the council, and accused him. All who sat in the council saw his face as though it were the face of an angel (ibid., 8–15). [Cols. 0105D–0106A]

Questioned by the chief priest, he responded eloquently and fearlessly set forth with wisdom the ancient deeds of the fathers. He offered a fitting encomium upon Abraham, Moses, and the other patriarchs, and brought a narration of great events to a close in brief speech. Finally, he rebuked the unbelievers and despisers of the law, openly calling them stiff-necked and uncircumcised in hearts and ears: persons who had always resisted the Holy Spirit and persecuted the prophets. Hearing these things, they were cut to their hearts and ground their teeth at him. But Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looked intently into heaven, saw the glory of God, and said: “Behold, I see the heavens opened and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.” Crying out with a loud voice, they stopped their ears, rushed upon him together, drove him out of the city, and stoned him. The witnesses laid their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul; and they stoned Stephen as he prayed and said: “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” Then, kneeling, he cried with a loud voice: “Lord, do not lay this sin against them.” And when he had said this, he fell asleep in the Lord (Acts 7:1–59). [Cols. 0106A–B]

This took place in the second year after the Lord’s Ascension, on 26 December. God-fearing men carried the body of the protomartyr to Gamaliel’s estate, called Caphargamala, mourned greatly over him (Acts 8:2), and buried him there reverently. Nicodemus, Gamaliel, and Abibas were later buried with him. This great treasure lay hidden there for more than three hundred years, until the priest Lucian discovered it by God’s revelation and John, bishop of Jerusalem, translated it to Jerusalem in the seventh year of Emperor Honorius. [Cols. 0106B–C]

After Stephen was stoned, a great persecution arose against the Church in Jerusalem, and all except the apostles were scattered throughout the regions of Judaea and Samaria. Yet, strengthened by the Holy Spirit in that dispersion, they passed through many places and preached the word of God. Then Philip preached Christ in Samaria and showed his hearers many signs, healing paralytics, lame persons, and the possessed in Christ’s name. The Samaritans unanimously listened to what Philip said and received the true faith with great eagerness. Then Simon Magus, who had long before deceived the Samaritans and for a long time made them mad by his magic—so that those whom he deceived considered him great and called him “the great power of God”—believed Philip preaching concerning the kingdom of God. Baptized in the name of Jesus Christ with other men and women, he attached himself to Philip. For he saw great signs and mighty works being done and marvelled in amazement at such unheard-of things (ibid., 2–13). [Cols. 0106C–D]

When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. Upon arriving, they prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit. Then they laid hands upon the baptized, and they received the Holy Spirit (ibid., 14–17). From this arose the ecclesiastical institution that, after baptism, which is given to catechumens through the ministry of a priest, the bishop should lay on hands with prayer and anointing with chrism; and thus full confirmation is bestowed upon the baptized through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0107A]

When Simon saw that the Holy Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money, saying: “Give me also this power, so that anyone upon whom I lay hands may receive the Holy Spirit.” But Peter said to him: “May your money perish with you, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed with money. You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God. Therefore repent of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that perhaps this thought of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity.” Simon, however, disregarding the apostle’s words, departed; having become an apostate, he long provoked the Lord’s wrath by countless crimes. But the apostles, after speaking the word of the Lord, returned to Jerusalem and proclaimed the Gospel in many Samaritan regions (cf. Acts 8:18–25). [Cols. 0107A–B]

At the command of an angel of God, Philip met the eunuch of Candace—[Note: [Col. 0107] Read *Candacis*: this is the name of the queen of the Ethiopians, not of the eunuch. Le Prévost.]—who was over all the treasures of the queen of the Ethiopians and was returning from Jerusalem. Philip climbed into the chariot with him and began to explain the prophet Isaiah whom he was reading. Beginning with the prophecy concerning the slaughter of the gentle lamb, Philip preached Jesus to him. The eunuch heard gladly, understood attentively, believed willingly, found water, and was baptized. He returned joyfully to his homeland, renewed through sacred regeneration. But the Spirit of the Lord snatched Philip away; and from Azotus as far as Caesarea he preached the Gospel in every city (ibid., 26–40). [Cols. 0107B–C]

Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, requested letters from the chief priest to the synagogues at Damascus, so that he might devastate the Lord’s Church, bind men and women of the sect of the Nazarenes, and bring them to Jerusalem. As he approached Damascus, a light from heaven shone around him. Falling to the ground (Acts 9:1–4), he heard the Lord rebuke him, was corrected, and was beneficially transformed both for himself and for many others. Led by the hand into Damascus by his companions, who heard the Lord speaking with him but saw no one, he did not see, eat, or drink for three days. Ananias, sent by the Lord, laid hands on Saul, strengthened him, restored his sight, and baptized him. Thus, by a wonderful change, the wolf and savage persecutor became a lamb and a most valiant ram, a chosen vessel and teacher of the nations. Immediately, entering the synagogues, he preached Jesus, that he is the Son of God, to the astonishment of all who knew his former obstinacy, when he had been an even more zealous adherent of ancestral traditions (ibid., 4–21). [Cols. 0107C–D]

Saul grew still stronger and confounded the Jews living at Damascus. Therefore immense hatred was stirred against him because of his faithful witness; and, after some time, the Jews earnestly sought to kill him, guarding the gates of Damascus by night and day so that he could not escape. But when Saul became aware of the hostile plot, the disciples, while the enemies plotted in vain, lowered him by night in a basket through the wall. When he came to Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples; but all feared him, not believing that he was a disciple. Barnabas, however, took him, led him to the disciples, and told them how Saul had seen the Lord on the road and what else had happened. As they gave thanks to God, Saul faithfully joined them and went in and out among them, acting boldly in the name of the Lord Jesus. He disputed with Greeks and refuted the Jews, and, aided by God, surpassed all others. Envious persons, defeated by one more exalted than themselves, tried to kill Saul. When the brethren learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him away to Tarsus. The Church throughout Judaea, Galilee, and Samaria enjoyed peace. Walking in the fear of the Lord, it was built up, filled with the consolation of the Holy Spirit, and increased in the multitude of believers (ibid., 22–31). [Cols. 0108A–B]

The apostle Peter healed at Lydda Aeneas, a paralytic who had lain upon a bed for eight years. All the inhabitants of Lydda and Sharon who saw this turned to the Lord. At Joppa, Tabitha, full of good works and almsgiving, died and was laid by the brethren in an upper chamber. Hearing that Peter was at Joppa, near Lydda, the disciples sent two men to him and begged him to come. As soon as he heard the brothers’ message, he humbly obeyed. When Peter arrived, all the weeping widows stood around him and showed him the tunics and garments that Dorcas had made for them. Sending everyone outside, Peter knelt and prayed; then, turning to the body, he said: “Tabitha, arise.” She opened her eyes and, seeing Peter, sat up. Giving her his hand, he raised her and presented her alive to the saints and widows. When this miracle was made known throughout all Joppa, many believed in the Lord (ibid., 32–42). [Cols. 0108B–C]

Cornelius at Caesarea, a centurion of the cohort called the Italian, was a devout man who feared God with all his household and diligently gave alms and offered prayers for everlasting salvation. About the ninth hour of the day he plainly saw in a vision an angel of God. Looking at him, he was struck with fear and heard him say: “Cornelius, your prayers and alms have ascended as a memorial before God.” The angel then commanded him to summon Simon Peter, from whom he would hear saving counsel. Cornelius immediately obeyed and sent three men to Peter. On the next day, as they approached the city, Peter went up to the upper rooms about the sixth hour to pray. As he grew hungry and yearned after heavenly things, in an ecstasy of mind he saw heaven opened and a certain vessel, like a great linen sheet, lowered from heaven to earth by its four corners. In it were every kind of four-footed creature, creeping thing of the earth, and bird of heaven. A voice came to him: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat.” But Peter said: “By no means, Lord, for I have never eaten anything common or unclean.” The voice came to him again a second time: “What the Lord has purified, do not call common.” This happened three times, and immediately the vessel was taken up into heaven. By this revelation the conversion of the nations was divinely indicated to Peter—a conversion accomplished in every language and tribe throughout the four regions of the world—and he was clearly instructed by God not to reject anyone wishing to be converted. Secure and rejoicing, Peter received Cornelius’s messengers as guests in the house of Simon the Tanner and went with them the next day to Caesarea in Palestine. [Cols. 0108D–0109A] On entering there, he found Cornelius, his relatives, and close friends; and, asked by those who were ready to hear and obey to speak the word of life, he piously complied (Acts 10:1–33). [Col. 0109B]

For Peter opened his mouth and said: “Truly I have learned that God is not a respecter of persons; but in every nation the one who fears him and does righteousness is acceptable to him. He sent the word to the children of Israel, proclaiming peace through Jesus Christ. He is Lord of all.” While Peter preached these and many other things concerning the Saviour’s coming and everlasting life, offering copious draughts of life from the fountain of heavenly teaching to those who thirsted greatly, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard the word and suddenly granted them knowledge of languages. Peter then baptized Cornelius and all who had believed with him, to the astonishment of those of the circumcision who had come with him (ibid., 34–48). [Cols. 0109B–C]

After remaining at Caesarea for several days at the request of the distinguished newly baptized believers and confirming them, Peter went up to Jerusalem and recounted the conversion of the nations to his fellow apostles. Then certain persons of the circumcision disputed with him, saying: “Why did you enter the house of uncircumcised men and eat with them?” Peter began to explain in sequence how he had prayed while fasting at Joppa; how, there in an ecstasy, he had seen the vision in which God showed him the calling and conversion of the nations and his own assistance; and he truthfully made known the rest of what had occurred. Hearing this, they were silent; and, because they burned with brotherly love, they rejoiced and glorified the Lord, who saves even the nations through repentance. [Cols. 0109C–D]

Believers from Cyprus and Cyrene, and others who had been scattered in the persecution arising over Stephen, travelled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, speaking the word of faith only to Jews. But upon entering Antioch, they proclaimed the Lord Jesus to Greeks, and a great number of believers turned to the Lord. When the Church at Jerusalem heard this, it rejoiced in the Lord and sent Barnabas, a good man full of the Holy Spirit and faith. When he arrived and saw the grace of God, he rejoiced; after strengthening them all, he departed for Tarsus to seek Saul. From there the two came together to Antioch, remained for a whole year in the Church, and taught a great crowd. There the disciples were first called Christians (Acts 11:1–26). [Cols. 0109D–0110A]

Then Agabus the prophet, one of those who had come from Jerusalem, foretold by divine prophetic oracles that a great famine would occur. Saul and Barnabas were sent to Jerusalem with the ministry contributed by the brethren for the needs of the saints (ibid., 27–30).

## III. The opinion of the Roman Senate concerning Christ. The crimes of King Herod against Christians.

Meanwhile Tiberius Augustus reigned for about twenty-two years. In the eighteenth year of his reign, as reliable testimony truly affirms, our Lord Jesus Christ suffered, rose again, and performed many wonders in an ineffable manner. Pilate reported these events, already widely publicized far and near, to Tiberius; and added that, because innumerable mighty works had been performed in Christ’s name, very many people already believed him to be God. Tiberius reported what he had learned to the Senate. But the Senate is said to have rejected Christ, as Tertullian writes in his *Apology*, because its judgment on the matter had not first been referred to it, but its authority had been anticipated by the people’s decision. For an ancient law had been enacted that no one should be regarded as a god among the Romans unless confirmed by decree and judgment of the Senate. Yet, as Eusebius of Caesarea states in the second book of his *Ecclesiastical History*, this occurred in truth so that the divine power might not be thought to need human advocates. Although the Senate rejected him, according to what we have said above, Tiberius nevertheless maintained his decision, that no one should devise anything hostile to Christ’s teaching. [Cols. 0110A–C]

Divine wisdom surely impressed this upon Caesar’s mind at that time so that, without any obstacle, the proclamation of the Gospel might spread everywhere in its very beginnings. Thus it came about that, like a light suddenly displayed from heaven or a bursting ray of the sun, it illuminated the whole world with the brightness of heavenly light, fulfilling also that prophecy which said: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:5; Rom. 10:18). Thereupon, in every city and village, immense crowds gathered to the churches, as grain at harvesttime is gathered to the threshing floors. All who were held in the bonds of the sickly superstition handed down to them from their parents, through Christ’s teaching and the miracles of power which they saw performed, and upon receiving knowledge of the word of God, came as though freed from tyrannical masters to the one true God and Lord, their Creator, repenting of their old error with faithful confession. [Cols. 0110C–D]

After Tiberius’s death, Gaius Caligula assumed the empire and held it for four incomplete years. He granted the Jewish principate to Herod Agrippa, son of Aristobulus, and at the same time bestowed upon him the tetrarchies of Philip and Lysanias; shortly afterward he also added that of Herod. But Herod himself—the man who had instigated the death of John the Baptist or had been present as a mocker at the Lord’s passion—he tortured in many ways and condemned to perpetual exile in Spain, as Josephus, the distinguished Jewish historian, writes. [Cols. 0110D–0111A]

Then Philo the Jew, a most distinguished writer and foremost among those eminent in Greek philosophy, left to posterity illustrious monuments of his learning; and among other things that he wrote, he maintains, concerning the cruelty and madness of Gaius, that he was so puffed up with pride that he wished to be called a god and profaned the holy places of the Jews with idols. The Jews also, because of the crimes which they dared commit against Christ, endured excessive disasters and tribulations, as the aforesaid learned men Philo and Josephus report in their writings. For from the time of that sacrilege they were never free from the frenzy of seditions, never from wars and deaths, until the final destructive evil enclosed them during the siege under Vespasian. [Col. 0111B] Pilate, who had been made procurator of Judaea in the twelfth year of Tiberius Caesar and had pronounced the sentence of condemnation against Christ, suffered such anguish at Gaius’s instigation that he killed himself by his own hand. Matthew, preaching in Judaea, wrote the Gospel in the Hebrew language.

After Gaius Caesar was killed, Claudius reigned for thirteen years and eight months. Under him a very severe famine seized the whole world, as Luke describes the prophet Agabus as having foretold.

At that time, under Claudius, when there was famine, King Herod laid hands upon certain members of the Church to afflict them. Then James, son of Zebedee, apostle of our Lord Jesus Christ, was visiting all Judaea [Col. 0111C] and Samaria and performing many signs by Christ’s power. In the synagogues he disputed against unbelievers and expounded the holy Scriptures, showing that all things foretold by the prophets had been fulfilled in the Lord Jesus Christ.

Hermogenes the magician, hearing the report of his miracles, became envious and sent his disciple Philetus to him in order to investigate. Philetus came with certain Pharisees and attempted to withstand James and overthrow, by his objections, his preaching concerning the Lord Jesus Christ. But the apostle acted confidently in the Holy Spirit, refuted every assertion of his opponent, and showed him from the divine Scriptures that Jesus of Nazareth is the true Son of God. Returning to Hermogenes, Philetus began emphatically [Col. 0111D] to praise James, to approve faithfully his arguments concerning the true faith, to extol him as unconquerable, and to publicize the many miracles which he had seen or heard of. Finally, he urged his master that they should both immediately go to him, ask his forgiveness, and become his disciples. Hermogenes, therefore, filled with jealousy, bound Philetus so that he could not move. But when the apostle learned this through Philetus’s servant-boy, he sent him his handkerchief and directed that he should be touched with it in the Lord’s name. When this was done, Philetus was at once freed from the magician’s bond, ran to James, and joyfully mocked the demons’ evil arts. The magician, deeply grieved, stirred up demons by his wicked art and ordered them to bring James and Philetus to him bound. But when they came, they began [Col. 0112A] to howl in the air and complain horribly that they were being tormented there by an angel of God, bound in fiery chains. At last, by the apostle’s command, they were released; and in turn they returned to Hermogenes, bound his hands behind his back with ropes, and led him bound to the apostle.

The blessed apostle rebuked him, declaring that fellowship with demons is detestable and wholly harmful to humankind; and he ordered Philetus to release the magician, who stood before him humbled and confounded. Once freed, Hermogenes took the apostle’s staff as protection against the demons’ rage and brought from his house wallets full of books, placed upon the necks of his disciples. Then he began to burn all the books in the fire; but at the apostle’s command, lest the smell of the burning sorceries [Col. 0112B] should trouble the unsuspecting, he filled the wallets with stones and lead and sank them in the sea. Thus stripped of every burden of sorceries, Hermogenes returned, humbly clasped the apostle’s feet, offered true repentance to God, and, cleaving to the blessed apostle, obeyed him in all things. Indeed, he began to be so perfected in the fear of God that the Lord also performed many miracles through him; seeing these, many abandoned their errors and crimes and were converted to the Lord.

But the Jews, persevering in wickedness, when they saw that the magician whom they considered invincible, together with his friends, believed in Christ, offered money to Lysias and Theocritus, centurions of Jerusalem, and had James seized and put under guard. When [Col. 0112C] a disturbance had arisen, he was brought for a hearing, and all marvelled at his constancy in the Lord. Questioned by the Pharisees, he answered most excellently and treated the holy Scriptures wisely and eloquently. Accordingly, he proved incontrovertibly the birth from the inviolate Virgin, the Passion and Resurrection, and all other things concerning Christ which the Catholic Church confesses. When the apostle happily concluded his address, all believed and, confessing their sins, faithfully adhered to the Church of God.

After several days Abiathar, the high priest, seeing that so great a people had believed in the Lord, was grieved; and, having given money, he stirred up a very bitter disturbance, so that Josias the scribe put a rope around the apostle’s neck and led him to the praetorium of King Herod, son of Aristobulus. [Col. 0112D] Herod, wishing to please the Jews, ordered him beheaded. As James was being led to execution, he saw a paralytic lying there, earnestly asking to be healed by him; and he said to him: “In the name of my crucified Lord Jesus Christ, for whose love I am being led to be beheaded, rise whole and bless your Saviour.” He immediately rose and, rejoicing, began to run and bless the Lord. When Josias saw this, he fell at the apostle’s feet and humbly asked his forgiveness.

James, understanding that his heart had been visited by God, rejoiced; and Josias confessed that the Lord Jesus was the true Son of the living God. Then Abiathar had him seized and his mouth beaten with fists. Afterwards, having sent [Col. 0113A] a report concerning him to Herod, he obtained that he too should be beheaded. When James had kissed him, he laid his hand upon his head and, making the sign of the cross upon his forehead, blessed him. Thus, perfected in faith, he was beheaded with the apostle; and to both the almighty Emmanuel granted eternal reward.

After, therefore, the martyrdom of the blessed apostle James, the eminent brother of John the Evangelist—a martyrdom which the devotion of the Church solemnly celebrates on the eighth day before the Kalends of August [25 July]—seven of his disciples, who had been instructed by him in the true faith and had witnessed his Passion, divinely instructed, placed his body in an old ship and, upon the deep sea, entrusted themselves, under God’s providence, without a pilot or the necessary equipment. In this miraculous manner they arrived in [Col. 0113B] Spain and, received by the king of Galicia, first preached the faith and religion to the Iberians; there they obtained a venerable burial-place for their master. Many miracles were there performed through the merits of Saint James the apostle, and the inhabitants of the whole province had long since received Christ’s faith. In the episcopal see, canonical followers reverently guard the most precious body of the apostle; and faithful worshippers of Christ flock there from every region of the world and assemble to implore the merciful Adonai through the apostle’s intercessions.

King Herod, whom Josephus calls Agrippa, seeing that the Jews were pleased because he had killed James, also put Peter in prison and handed him over to four [Col. 0113C] squads of soldiers to be guarded. Peter was kept in prison in order that after Passover he might publicly be brought forth to death. The prayer of the Church was incessantly striking at the ears of the divine majesty, lest the tender flock should be deprived of the aid of its loving shepherd. But merciful God quickly heard the prayers of His bride and faithful friend for His beloved steward: heavenly help came to His own and, by frustrating it, forestalled Herod’s impious undertaking. By night, while Peter slept between two soldiers, bound with two chains, and guards stood before the prison door, an angel of the Lord appeared with a light; striking Peter’s side, he awakened him. “Rise quickly,” he said.
