At once the chains fell from his hands. Girded, shod, and clothed with his cloak, he went out; following the angel, he passed through the guards as far as [Col. 0113D] the iron gate, which opened to them of its own accord. He thought that these things were happening in a dream. When the angel departed, he came to himself, recognized the truth of what had happened, and gave thanks to his deliverer for his rescue (Acts 12:3–11).

He came to the brethren gathered in the house of Mary, mother of John surnamed Mark. When he knocked at the door, the maid Rhoda came out to see who it was. Recognizing Peter’s voice, she did not open the door for joy, but ran inside and announced that Peter was standing outside the gate. When he had at last entered, he encouraged the astonished disciples, explained how the Lord had brought him out of prison, and immediately departed to another place. Then there was great agitation among the soldiers concerning Peter; and, when he was not found, [Col. 0114A] King Herod was exceedingly angry with the guards. The king’s crime committed against the apostles did not permit vengeance to be delayed: the avenging right hand of Divinity was immediately present, as Luke teaches in the Acts of the Apostles (ibid., 13–23), and Josephus in the nineteenth book of the *Antiquities*. For when he had gone down to Caesarea, formerly called Straton’s Tower, and on a solemn day was providing games for the citizens in honour of Caesar, he entered the theatre clothed in a magnificent garment wonderfully woven with gold and silver, sat down upon the tribunal, and addressed them from on high. As the people cried out, “The voice of a god, and not of a man,” the angel of the Lord immediately struck him because he had not given glory to God; and, swarming with worms, he died after five days.

## IV. The word of Christ spreads. The Church of Antioch. The preaching of Paul and Barnabas

[Col. 0114B]

His son Agrippa reigned for twenty-six years, that is, until the destruction of the Jews, and was at peace with the Romans and Christians. The word of the Lord grew and multiplied.

At Antioch, in the Church, there were prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simon Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen, foster-brother of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. While they were ministering to the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work [for] which I have chosen them.” Then, fasting and praying and laying hands upon them, they sent them away. Thus sent by the Holy Spirit, they went to Seleucia [Col. 0114C] and from there sailed to Cyprus. At Salamis they preached the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews and traversed the whole island as far as Paphos (Acts 13:1–6).

There the proconsul Sergius Paulus, a prudent man, summoned Barnabas and Saul and, eagerly hearing the word of God, believed. Then Saul, by command, struck Elymas the magician, who was resisting the doctrine of faith, with temporary blindness; and he deserved to be called Paul, after the first man from the Gentiles whom he conquered for the faith, just as Scipio Africanus was surnamed from conquered Africa. Then they came to Perga in Pamphylia and to Antioch in Pisidia; entering the synagogue on the Sabbath day, they sat down. After the reading of the Law and the Prophets, with the rulers of the synagogue assenting, Paul stood up and, motioning with his hand for silence, [Col. 0114D] gave an excellent account of the history of the patriarchs and firmly declared that the promises long ago made by God through the prophets had now been perfectly fulfilled in Christ (ibid., 7–43).

On the following Sabbath almost the whole city assembled to hear the word of the Lord. Therefore the jealous Jews tried to obstruct apostolic preaching by blasphemous contradiction. Then Paul and Barnabas said resolutely: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles. For thus the Lord has commanded us: ‘I have set you as a light to the Gentiles, that you may be for salvation unto the uttermost part of the earth.’” Hearing this, the Gentiles rejoiced, and those who were predestined to life believed. But the Jews, having stirred up [Col. 0115A] persecution against Paul and Barnabas, expelled them from their territory; and they, filled with joy, came to Iconium (ibid., 44–52) and spoke in the synagogue to Jews and Greeks. There they stayed a long time, acting boldly in the Lord; and, as He worked with them, signs and wonders were performed through their hands. Therefore the envious wicked Gentiles and Jews planned to mistreat and stone them. But they fled to the cities of Lycaonia, Lystra and Derbe, and to all the surrounding region, and there they preached the Gospel. The whole city was stirred by their teaching (Acts 14:1–6).

At Lystra a certain lame man, who had never walked, heard Paul speaking; and when Paul invoked the name of the Lord Jesus, he was immediately healed, leaped up, [Col. 0115B] and, believing, glorified the Lord. The people, seeing this, marvelled and said in Lycaonian: “The gods, made like men, have come down to us.” They called Barnabas Jupiter, but Paul Mercury. When the priest of Jupiter and the people wished to sacrifice to them, the apostles immediately sprang into the crowd, tore their tunics, and in humble words ascribed the glory of the miracle to the Lord; humbling themselves, they scarcely calmed the crowds so that they would not sacrifice to them. Jews came from Antioch and Iconium, persuaded the crowds, stoned Paul, and dragged him outside the city, thinking that he was dead. When the disciples stood around him, he rose and entered the city; the following day he departed for Derbe. Then both returned to Lystra, Iconium, Antioch, and Pisidia, [Col. 0115C] preaching the word of life, strengthening the souls of the disciples through exhortation, appointing presbyters in every church, and commending them to the Lord with fastings and prayers. From Pamphylia they went down to Attalia and from there sailed to Antioch (ibid., 7–25).

There they remained for a long time with the disciples (ibid., 27). Then certain men who had come down from Judaea were urging Gentile believers to be circumcised and observe the Law of Moses. Paul and Barnabas resisted them in argument; and, by common decree, they were sent to Jerusalem to the apostles and presbyters in order that this question might be decided. Passing through Phoenicia and Samaria, they reported the conversion of the Gentiles and [Col. 0115D] brought great joy to all the brethren. At Jerusalem they were received by the Church and announced how much God had done with them. Since those who had believed from the Pharisees were very eager to Judaize, Simon Peter, James, and the other elders carefully discussed the question proposed; and finally they decreed that chosen and approved brethren should be sent to the Gentiles and that by them a written message should be dispatched at the prompting of the Holy Spirit, directing that, other burdens being removed, they should abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what had been strangled, and from fornication (Acts 15:1–29).

Paul and Barnabas, Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas were therefore sent to Antioch and conveyed the letter of the apostles and elders to the multitude [Col. 0116A] of Gentile believers. When they had read it, they rejoiced at the consolation. Judas and Silas, being prophets, encouraged and strengthened the brethren with many words; afterwards they returned in peace to Jerusalem. But Paul and Barnabas preached the word of the Lord at Antioch for some time, and, departing from there, separated from one another. Barnabas sailed to Cyprus with John Mark. Paul, having chosen Silas, traversed Syria and Cilicia, strengthened the churches, and commanded them to keep the ordinances of the apostles and elders (ibid., 30–41). From there he came to Derbe and Lystra, and there, because of the Jews who lay in wait, circumcised Timothy, whose father was a Gentile. He passed through Phrygia, Galatia, and Mysia, went down to Troas, [Col. 0116B] and, warned by a vision in the night, crossed into Macedonia. At Philippi, which is the principal city of Macedonia, he preached; Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth who worshipped God, heard him and, baptized with her household, believed, and by urgent entreaties compelled the faithful to stay with her (Acts 16:1–15).

As Paul was going with his companions to prayer, a certain girl having a spirit of Python met them; by divination she brought her masters much profit. Following them, she cried out: “These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of salvation.” When she had done this for many days, Paul, grieved, said to the spirit: “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.” And it came out that same hour. But when [Col. 0116C] her masters saw that their hope of profit had gone, they became angry, seized Paul and Silas, brought them into the marketplace before the magistrates, and accused them of disturbing the city by proclaiming a custom unfamiliar to Romans. The agitated populace also rushed against the innocent men. By command of the magistrates they were beaten with rods, cast into the inner prison, and their feet fastened in stocks. At midnight Paul and Silas, worshipping the Lord, praised Him and experienced His aid in a special way. A great earthquake suddenly occurred, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken. All the doors immediately opened and everyone’s bonds were loosed. Seeing these things, the jailer was greatly terrified; and, after hearing from Paul the account of faith, he believed and was baptized with his whole household. When the city magistrates [Col. 0116D] heard that they were Romans, they were afraid; bringing them out of prison, they asked them to leave the city (ibid., 16–40). From there they entered Lydia [perhaps “the house of Lydia”] and, by way of Amphipolis and Apollonia, came to Thessalonica. There, for three Sabbaths, Paul entered the synagogue of the Jews and publicly argued from the Scriptures, opening and demonstrating that Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead, and that “this Jesus whom I proclaim to you is the Christ.” Many Jews and Gentiles believed and joined Paul and Silas. The jealous Jews therefore stirred up a mob and, dragging Jason and certain other brethren before the city authorities, accused them. But after receiving satisfaction from Jason and the others, they released them. The brethren immediately sent Paul and Silas by night to Beroea; [Col. 0117A] and from there, because of the riot among the populace stirred up by the Jews, the brethren escorted Paul as far as Athens. There he awaited Silas and Timothy, whom he had left at Beroea. Meanwhile he argued in the synagogue with Jews and worshippers, and every day in the marketplace with all who heard him. Certain Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also debated with him. The Athenians and resident foreigners devoted themselves to nothing else but either telling or hearing something new. But Paul, standing in the midst of the Areopagus, rebuked the Athenians as addicted to the superstition of idolatry and began to speak of an altar on which was inscribed: “To an Unknown God.” From this he took the beginning of the preaching laid upon him, proclaiming the true God, formerly unknown to the world; and, comprehending much in a brief discourse, he earnestly preached faith [Col. 0117B] and the hope of resurrection (Acts 17:1–31).

Then Dionysius the Areopagite, his wife Damaris, and others who joined them believed the apostle (ibid., 34). Afterwards Paul departed from Athens and came to Corinth; bearing witness to Jews and Greeks that Jesus is the Christ, he devoted himself to the ministry of preaching. He disputed in the synagogue every Sabbath. Silas and Timothy came there from Macedonia; and while Paul was preaching, Crispinus [Crispus], ruler of the synagogue, believed with his entire household, and many Corinthians who believed were baptized. Paul entered the house of a certain just man named Titus [Note: [Col. 0117D] Vulgate: “of a certain man named Titus Justus.”], adjoining the synagogue; and, commanded by God through a vision [Col. 0117C] in the night, he remained a year and six months, diligently teaching the word of God there. There Aquila, a Jew by birth from Pontus, dwelt with his wife Priscilla. Since Paul shared their trade of tentmaking, he worked with them and earned his livelihood by his own hands. Then Paul bade the brethren farewell, sailed for Syria, and came to Ephesus. From there he went down to Caesarea and afterwards travelled to Antioch. Having spent some time there, he set out and travelled in order through Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples (Acts 18:1–23).

## V. Notices concerning Christ’s apostles. The history of Peter

Up to this point I have made a summary extract for myself concerning the primitive Church, namely, of those matters which Luke set forth in the Acts of the Apostles, as far as the narrative of how [Col. 0117D] Paul baptized at Ephesus, in the name of the Lord Jesus, those who had been baptized with John’s baptism; how he remained there with those same persons, who, filled with the Holy Spirit, spoke in tongues and prophesied; how, disputing concerning the kingdom of God for three months, he benefited many; and how, departing from there, he evangelized all in Asia so vigorously for two years and performed many miracles upon the sick and demoniacs in the name of Jesus Christ (Acts 19:1–10). Henceforth it pleases me to examine other books and briefly record for myself certain matters concerning the same apostles which I may find in authoritative books and those commonly used in the Church.

[Col. 0118A] The Creator of all alone knows the rank of the apostles and the merit of each; He who searches the hidden things of the human heart distributes to each the recompense of his labours. For *apostoli* means “those sent”: Christ sent them to evangelize throughout the whole world, so that, as fishermen draw out a multitude of fish from the sea with nets, so they might draw lost people, through preaching, from the depth of vices to the light of life. Their names are these: Simon Peter and Andrew his brother; James of Zebedee and John his brother; James of Alphaeus and Philip; Thomas and Bartholomew; Levi Matthew and Simon the Cananean; Judas Thaddaeus and Matthias (Acts 1:13, 26).

[Col. 0118B] First in calling and greatest in dignity, Peter the key-bearer attained the seat at the summit of the apostolic office. He obeyed Christ ardently and followed Him with his whole heart. Born of a father named Jona or John, and native of the village of Bethsaida in the province of Galilee, which is beside the Lake of Gennesaret, he had three names, so that his future dignity and the power in which he shines exalted might be made manifest; and the manifold grace bestowed on him from heaven was made evident by the meaning of his three names. For Simon means “obedient,” Peter “acknowledging,” and Cephas “head.” Thus Simon, through obedience—by which, as soon as he heard the Lord’s command, he eagerly strove, leaving all things, to follow Him unencumbered even unto death—ascended to the knowledge of the ineffable Deity. And because, inspired from heaven, he ardently sought, beyond human understanding, [Col. 0118C] the vision of God and faithfully uttered the lofty voice of glorious confession, saying, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16), he deserved, Christ Himself rewarding him beyond compare, to be honoured and appointed head and foundation of the Church. For the generous rewarder, who had divinely inspired knowledge of Himself, rewarded with chief authority the faith of a pure heart uttered in the confession of the mouth: “Blessed are you,” He said, “Simon Bar-Jona, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (ibid., 17).

Truly blessed is Simon—that is, “obedient”—who is called Bar-Jona, that is, “son of the dove,” by which the Holy Spirit is signified. “An obedient man,” as Solomon says, “speaks victories” (Proverbs 21:28). Since he continually observes the divine commands, he is attacked in daily conflicts by diverse temptations; and as he perseveres in God’s commandments, Satan is overcome. For what else does the divine law command or teach except that every human being should serve his Creator, fight against the ancient serpent who always lies in wait for us, and labour to obtain the prize of the heavenly calling? Then the mighty athlete of God undoubtedly speaks victories, when, having overthrown the enemy, he celebrates thanks to God his protector, saying with the Prophet: “You have girded me with strength for battle, and have made those who rise against me fall beneath me” (Psalm 17:40); and many other similar things. No one can please God the Father by holy works unless, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0119A] he has attained the virtue of obedience.

Then the Saviour, magnificently completing the reward of Peter’s devout confession, said to Simon: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18). *Petrus* in Latin and *Cephas* in Syriac are names in each language derived from “rock,” namely from Christ, who is the firm rock upon which the Church is founded. Thus Simon attained through obedience to the acknowledgment of the Son of God, which flesh and blood did not reveal to him, but the heavenly Father; and therefore he deserved to be surnamed by the Saviour Himself Peter, that is, “acknowledging.” Finally, having been given the keys of the heavenly kingdom, he was appointed Cephas—that is, head [Col. 0119B] of the Church—by the King of Sabaoth: namely, prince of the apostles and supreme pontiff, endowed with the power of binding and loosing, pre-eminent in teaching and holiness, illustrious in signs and miracles, the first shepherd of Christ’s sheep in the Church, and its special vicar.

For seven years he preached among the circumcised; and Luke shows in the Acts of the Apostles, as I noted above, the special deeds that he performed then. At the Beautiful Gate of the Temple he raised up a lame man aged forty, and baptized five thousand converted Jews. By a censorial command he punished Ananias and his wife Sapphira, guilty of fraud and falsehood, and thus frightened those present and those to come, so that [Col. 0119C] they might be chastened for their good. As he passed through the streets, his shadow touched a crowd of sick people upon their beds and healed them through the merits and power bestowed upon him from heaven.

At Lydda he healed in the Lord’s name Aeneas the paralytic, who had lain on a pallet for eight years; and those who saw and marvelled at the novelty of the miracle he led to faith. At Joppa he raised from death the venerable widow Tabitha and restored her alive to the saints and widows. The remaining deeds which he performed from Judaea as far as Antioch, and how vigorously he pursued Simon Magus and repeatedly overcame him in disputation, Clement of Rome, son of Faustinus, has set forth in detail in the books of the *Recognitions*, from which he entitled the same work *The Itinerary of Peter*. For he himself, leaving behind everything he possessed at Rome, sailed for Palestine and, at Caesarea Stratonis, found the apostle Peter through the guidance of Barnabas, whom he had kindly entertained at Rome as an excellent guest and friend. Welcomed tenderly by Peter as a son by a father because of the goodwill of them both, instructed diligently in the faith of the true Prophet, and reborn in the sacred font, [Col. 0119D] he was inseparably joined to him.

At Caesarea Peter disputed with Simon Magus. When Simon departed in the evening with a thousand men, Peter encouraged those who remained and, invoking God’s name, healed demoniacs and sick persons. The next day the debate was renewed, and, with God’s help, Simon was defeated on many points. At last, confused, he departed in the evening with a few men, while the rejoicing people prostrated themselves before Peter; [Col. 0120A] through his prayers the demoniacs and sick were healed, and they departed rejoicing, as though they had received the teaching and mercy of the true God. On the third day Peter refuted Simon by sound reasoning when he denied the immortality of the soul, and convincingly exposed his crimes. The people, enraged, expelled the blasphemer from the court and drove him outside the courtyard; of the many who had formerly followed him, scarcely one continued to follow him. Simon then placed his polluted and abominable secret things upon his companion’s shoulders; and, fearing that if detected he would be subject to the public laws, threw them into the sea by night. The companion refused to accompany him, having now recognized him as a most wicked impostor, and fled.

Peter remained at Caesarea for three months, ordained Zacchaeus bishop there, and [Col. 0120B] baptized ten thousand believers on a festival day. He also sent twelve brethren after Simon, that they might investigate his journeyings. For Zephaniah and Joseph, Micah and Eleazar, Phinehas and Lazarus, Elisha and Benjamin son of Saba, Ananias son of Sapphira and Rubelus brother of Zacchaeus, Nicodemus and Zacharias the builder, were chosen by the apostle so that, in the number twelve of the brethren of the faithful, they might assist in the worship of the Deity; and that, especially supported by God’s grace and by their help as well, he might pursue Simon Magus and other enemies of righteousness.

When the three months had been completed, Peter went by way of the town of Dora to Ptolemais, where [Col. 0120C] he stayed ten days, instructing the people in God’s law. Then at Tyre, Sidon, and Berytus he was likewise occupied in sowing the divine seed; afterwards, with a very great multitude of chosen persons from the individual cities, he entered Tripolis. There he was received in the house of Maro with the greatest eagerness of the citizens, who freely supplied every kindness and lodging to all Peter’s companions. In the morning a great crowd ran to Maro’s garden to hear Peter. First, he drove out unclean spirits crying aloud from possessed bodies; then, after his discourse, he healed the sick. There he abundantly sowed words of salvation for three months, baptized Clement and many others in springs situated close to the sea, and appointed his host Maro, now perfect in all things, bishop.

From there he came to Antaradus and divided the following multitude of believers into two parts. He commanded Nicetas and Aquila to lead them and go ahead to Laodicea, lest so great a crowd of followers should seem to provoke hostility among those alien to the faith. After they had gone on, Clement, in friendly conversation, told Peter where he was from, described his lineage, and related the misfortunes of his parents. The following day he went to a neighbouring island to see enormous columns of glass; and there, after twenty years, he recognized his mother Matidia through Peter. Peter healed Matidia’s paralytic hostess by prayer, and Clement gave her a thousand drachmas as payment.

[Col. 0121A] Then Peter came to Balaneae and from there to Paltus, and thereafter to Gabala and so to Laodicea, where he remained ten days. There occurred the recognition of Matidia and her three sons, Clement, Faustinus, and Faustus. The recognized twins reported that after the shipwreck, while they clung to a fragment of planking and were tossed about upon the sea, pirates found them, took them aboard their little vessel to Caesarea Stratonis, and there, after changing their names, sold them to a certain honourable woman. She brought them up as sons, had them educated in liberal and Greek letters, and, once grown, committed them to philosophical studies.

While Peter remained at Laodicea and was continually occupied, as was his custom, in worthy pursuits, an old man named [Col. 0121B] Faustinianus, dressed as a poor man, came to him and began to argue that there is neither God, nor worship, nor providence in the world, but chance and *genesis* govern everything. Against him his three sons, whom he did not yet recognize, argued outstandingly for three days before the people and instructed their hearers with many doctrines in their answers.

On the first day Nicetas wisely argued that there is one God, holding all things, who made the world and governs it by His providence—a just God, who will one day repay each according to his deeds. On the second, Aquila eloquently argued that the just God orders all things justly. On the third, Clement held a discussion concerning the rationale of *genesis*: whether all things happen from it, or whether there is [Col. 0121C] something in us governed not by *genesis* but by God’s judgment. Then, by God’s prompting, without whom nothing exists, the recognition of the obstinate old man, his wife, and his sons occurred after twenty years.

The leading man of the city tried with all his force to retain Peter and his companions as guests, and his daughter, who had for twenty years been cruelly possessed by a demon, was released and healed.

In those days, when Faustinianus had visited Anubion and Appion, his friends who were lodging with Simon, and had dined with them, his appearance was transformed by magical art into the likeness of Simon; and consequently all his friends were seized with great fear lest, by Caesar’s command, he should be arrested and punished as a magician. Then Peter came to Antioch and, received by the people [Col. 0121D] with immense joy, preached the word of God. He healed the sick brought to him, paralytics, those harassed by demons, and persons suffering various perils. For the multitude of sick persons was innumerable. Before all the people Peter poured out prayer to the Lord; suddenly an immense light, by God’s grace, appeared in the midst of the people, and immediately restored all the sick to health. Therefore all the Antiochenes confessed the Lord with one voice, and within seven days more than ten thousand persons, believing in God, were baptized.

Theophilus, who was pre-eminent above all the powerful men in the city, burned exceedingly with love for God; and he gladly offered to God an immense basilica belonging to his own household, which was consecrated under the name of a church. In it [Col. 0122A] a chair was established for the apostle Peter by the whole people. Faustinianus, moreover, when he had seen the miracles and understood the heavenly mysteries, openly fell at the apostle’s feet; renouncing his former errors, he asked to be baptized. The apostle Peter imposed a fast upon him and, when Sunday came, baptized him. Taking occasion from his conversion, Peter recounted before the people all that had befallen him. This narrative pleased many, both for delight and instruction, and strongly commended the aforesaid old man with his family to the people of Antioch. The whole city happily increased in divine worship, and holy mother Church rejoiced in Christ Jesus as the number of the faithful increased daily.

Accordingly, the blessed apostle Peter first held his seat at Antioch for seven years [Col. 0122B] and preached in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia. Then, when Simon Magus made for Rome, Peter organized the Church of Antioch and consecrated Evodius there as bishop in his place. At last he went to Rome with several chosen disciples; and, entering the city in the time of the emperor Claudius, he found the aforesaid wonder-worker deceiving the people by many apparitions through a demonic power which they call a *paredrus*—a familiar attendant spirit. Simon had become so insolent that he boasted that he was a god and received from Roman citizens, as though a god, the honor of a statue placed in the river Tiber between the two bridges. Satan had wholly possessed this utterly mad instigator of every evil and first armed him with a wicked heresy [Col. 0122C] to overthrow the Church’s right faith. Against him, therefore, the almighty Emmanuel prepared the distinguished commander of His host to fight at close quarters—I mean Simon Peter, to whom Christ handed over the keys of the kingdom of heaven and whom He appointed prince of the apostles and worthy ruler of the Church. Thus, on coming to Rome, Peter dispersed the darkness of falsehood by the radiance of truth and justice; and there, judging justly as a worthy censor, he held his seat for twenty-five years, two months, and three days.

When the bright light of God’s word had shone upon the city of Rome, and the discourse of truth preached through Peter had enlightened the minds of all his hearers, it pleased them so greatly that hearing alone no longer sufficed to those who listened daily. Mark, [Col. 0122D] the apostle’s disciple, compelled by innumerable daily requests, wrote the Gospel; what Peter preached orally, Mark gathered in writing and passed down to posterity for the perpetual admonition of readers. When Peter learned through the Holy Spirit that he had been robbed by this devout theft, he was delighted; considering their faith and devotion in these things, he confirmed the work and gave the writing to the Churches to be read forever, together with the two letters called Canonical. During the reigns of the emperors Tiberius, Gaius Caligula, Claudius, and Nero, he labored manfully in Christ’s vineyard. He trained outstanding disciples, endowed with virtues and learning, and sent them to various places: namely Mark, his little son and disciple, to Aquileia and later Alexandria; Martial to [Col. 0123A] Limoges; Apollinaris to Ravenna; Valerius to Trier; and many others. In different places these worked many miracles in Christ’s name, drew very numerous assemblies of gentiles to the light of faith, and placed them, regenerated in the water of holy baptism, in the bosom of pious mother Church.

Once at Rome, while a great many brethren were dining together, Titus said to the apostle Peter: “Since all the sick are healed by you, why do you allow Petronilla to lie paralysed?” The apostle replied: “This is expedient for her. But, lest the impossibility of her recovery be thought excused by my words,” he said to her, “Rise, Petronilla; serve us.” At once she rose up whole and served them. When the service was finished, he ordered her to return to her bed. But when [Col. 0123B] she began to be perfect in the fear of God, not only was she herself healed, but by her prayers she also recovered many others to health and a better state.

## VI. Paul

Paul, the distinguished athlete of the all-powerful *Adonai* (“Lord”), the chosen vessel, teacher of the gentiles, and preacher of truth—who deserved to occupy the twelfth throne among the apostles, and, caught up into paradise, to hear secret words which it is not permitted for a human being to utter (2 Cor. 12:4)—is truly worthy of glory and of continual honor from the children of the Church as a skilful teacher. He was called Saul, that is, “temptation” in Hebrew, because he had first been engaged in the trial of holy mother Church. Afterwards, when his name was changed, he was called from Saul Paul, that is, [Col. 0123C] “wonderful”; and in a wonderful manner he was made from a ravening wolf into a gentle lamb. In Latin, moreover, *Paulus* is understood as “small”; hence he openly testified of himself: “I am the least of the apostles” (1 Cor. 15:9).

He was born of the tribe of Benjamin, a Pharisee of Pharisees, born at Tarsus in Cilicia, raised from childhood in Jerusalem, and instructed in God’s Law by Gamaliel. In the second year after the Lord’s ascension, while he was excessively zealous for the traditions of the fathers and consequently raged fiercely against Christians, he set out for Damascus with letters from the high priest in order to slaughter all Christ-worshippers there. As he approached the city, he was suddenly surrounded by an unfamiliar light and unexpectedly struck by the heavenly voice of the Lord Jesus. Wholesomely [Col. 0123D] he fell to the ground; abandoning his former ferocity, he rose and was led by his fellow travellers into Damascus, where for three days he remained helpless. Then, by God’s command, Ananias visited him after three days; he received the faith which he had persecuted and was baptized. He boldly preached that same faith to Jews and gentiles; beginning from Jerusalem, he went as far as Illyricum and Italy, and to the Spains (Rom. 15:24, 28), and made Christ’s name known to peoples of many nations to whom it had not been declared.

Luke the Evangelist, Paul’s companion and fellow-laborer, spoke diligently and worthily of him to the end, and carefully narrated especially his deeds, omitting others. Arator also, subdeacon of the holy Roman Church, subsequently produced a second book [Col. 0124A] and devoutly sang the Acts of the Apostles in heroic verse, relating Paul’s contests, endurance, and shipwreck. I have briefly noted above certain extracts from his deeds; nor am I weary here of recalling them again in praise of the Creator.

Saul, who is also Paul, set apart at the Holy Spirit’s warning, preached at Paphos; by command he struck Elymas the magician blind when he resisted the words of faith, and converted the proconsul Paul to the faith. Entering the synagogue at Antioch, he signaled for silence with his hand and there spoke of how the Israelite people went out of Egypt through the sea, and of the various miracles performed in the wilderness. On another Sabbath he commemorated Christ’s Passion and Resurrection, established them by prophetic proofs, [Col. 0124B] and increased the Church’s flock as many came to faith. At Lystra he healed a man lame from his mother’s womb, who gave heed to the words of God; and when the Lycaonians, in their old superstition, wished to sacrifice to him, he restrained them by tearing his garments and delivering eloquent reasoning. After many struggles in preaching, he endured a dispute raised by baptized Jews: that gentile believers should not be baptized before being circumcised. Paul therefore conveyed the embassy of the faithful to Jerusalem, consulted Peter, James, and the other elders, and communicated their decision by letter: that they should abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what was strangled, and from sexual immorality.

At Philippi he expelled an unclean spirit from a slave-girl possessed by a python-spirit, and, casting out the demon that gave answers to those who consulted it, deprived greedy seekers of the profit of divination. Therefore, accused by those same men and sent to prison at the command of the city’s chief men, [Col. 0124C] he cried aloud by night to the Lord of light in prayer, and the gracious helper of the faithful swiftly heard him. For when an earthquake occurred, everyone’s chains were loosed; and after the prison-keeper and his household were baptized, Paul and Silas, servants of the King of Sabaoth (“Hosts”), were permitted to depart free. Preaching at Athens, Paul was called a “seed-picker” (*seminiverbius*) by the people, and was thus named by those in error with a fitting term. From his words a spring of eternal life arose for the thirsty, and the seed of salvation was freely scattered to all who desired to receive it. He debated with Epicurean and Stoic philosophers [Col. 0124D] and eloquently proclaimed to them the true God, whom the Cecropids—that is, the Athenians—called “the unknown God.” Dionysius the Areopagite, together with his wife Damaris, believed and was baptized; because of his pre-eminence in wisdom and justice, he was joined to Paul among his chief friends. Later, as Aristides of Athens asserts, he was ordained bishop for the Athenians by the same apostle; and after many outstanding works of power, he was crowned with a distinguished martyrdom. From there Paul came to Corinth, found Aquila preaching with his wife Priscilla, and, while staying with them, practiced the trade of tent-making, in which they were skilled. There Christ warned him not to cease preaching; and as he faithfully obeyed, many were converted.

At Ephesus the Holy Spirit, filling twelve men whom Paul baptized in the name [Col. 0125A] of the Lord, immediately granted them various languages. There, while Paul healed sufferers from various diseases in the name of the Lord Jesus, seven Jews—the sons of Sceva, a chief priest—presumed to lay hands on a demoniac, adjuring him by the name of the Lord Jesus whom Paul preached. But the demon, speaking through the possessed man, openly acknowledged Jesus and His disciple Paul. Then it suddenly rushed upon the unbelieving exorcists and drove them away torn to pieces. Many Ephesians, hearing the preaching of truth, believed and were baptized; and some of those who practised magical arts burned their books of magic, whose value they reckoned at fifty thousand denarii. Thus the word of God grew mightily and prevailed; as believers were strengthened in God’s grace, the party of the impious [Col. 0125B] wasted away and was put to shame. Paul sent Timothy and Erastus into Macedonia, but himself remained in Asia for a time (Acts 19:1–22).

Demetrius the silversmith saw that, through Paul’s teaching, the Ephesians had abandoned the shrine of Diana; grieving that the profit of his craft had come to nothing while idols were condemned, he summoned his accomplices, set forth their common complaint, and stirred up a loud popular riot. Therefore the mad crowd rushed furiously into the theatre and seized Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonian companions of Paul; but the uproar of the madmen, turned back upon itself, accomplished nothing (ibid., 23–40).

Paul summoned the brethren, bade them farewell with an exhortation, and then set out for Macedonia. He stayed in Greece for three months. His companions [Col. 0125C] were Sopater, son of Pyrrhus, a Berean; of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; Gaius of Derbe and Timothy; and also the Asians Tychicus and Trophimus. Paul, with Luke, after the days of Unleavened Bread, sailed from Philippi to Troas in five days and stayed there seven days. On the first day of the week, when many had gathered to break bread and had listened until midnight to Paul’s lengthy discourse—for he was to depart on the next day—a young man, Eutychus, sitting in a window, overcome by sleep, fell down from the third storey. But, restored to life by Paul’s prayers, he lived again, to the joy of all who had seen it (Acts 20:1–12).

[Col. 0125D] From Miletus Paul sent to Ephesus and summoned the elders of the Church. He set before them many things beneficial for the salvation of souls; when he had finished speaking, he knelt and prayed with them all. There was great weeping among all, and, after kissing the brethren, Paul was escorted by them to the ship. Boarding the ship, he sailed on a direct course to Cos, then to Rhodes and Patara; through Syria he came to Tyre and stayed there seven days with faithful friends in Christ. Then he came from Ptolemais to Caesarea and entered the house of Philip the Evangelist, who had four virgin daughters who prophesied (ibid., 13–38; Acts 21:1–9).

Then the prophet Agabus came down there from Judaea, bound his own feet and hands with Paul’s belt, and openly [Col. 0126A] foretold through the Holy Spirit that the Jews would thus bind Paul in Jerusalem and hand him over to the gentiles. While everyone wept and begged him not to go up, Paul said: “I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem, for the name of the Lord Jesus” (Acts 21:10–13).

Trusting in the steadfastness of faith, he accordingly came to Jerusalem and told James and the other elders what God had done among the gentiles through his ministry. When they heard of the conversion of the gentiles, they glorified God, the Creator of all. Then Paul entered the Temple for purification and began to perform the rites of the Mosaic Law, so as to remove every occasion of scandal from zealots for the ancestral Law and, becoming a Jew to Jews, thus to win them all. [Col. 0126B] But the Jews from Asia, when they saw him in the Temple, stirred up all the people by hostile cries and laid hands on him. The entire city was agitated, and there was a gathering of the people. They seized Paul, dragged him outside the Temple, immediately shut the doors, and, beating him, sought to kill him. Claudius Lysias, tribune of the cohort, hearing that the city was thrown into confusion by sudden disorder, immediately ran down to them with soldiers and centurions. He rescued Paul by force so that he should not be killed; having bound him with two chains, he removed him from the riot and brought him into the barracks to inquire who he was and what he had done. With the tribune’s permission Paul went up the steps; speaking in Hebrew, he set out in a sure sequence the story of his conversion and gave an excellent account of his former way of life [Col. 0126C] in Judaism and afterward in the grace of Christ. As he spoke very wisely, the Jews could not bear the force of his words; shouting and raging, they cried: “Take such a man from the earth, for it is not right that he should live.” The tribune therefore ordered that he be brought into the barracks, scourged, and tortured. Then Paul said to the centurion standing by him: “Is it lawful for you to scourge a Roman citizen who has not been condemned?” When the tribune learned that he was a Roman citizen, he was afraid because he had bound him (ibid., Acts 21:14–40; 22:29).

On the following day Paul was brought before the council; standing in their midst, he spoke reasonably in his own defense (Acts 22:30). But Ananias the high priest [Col. 0126D] ordered those standing beside him to strike him on the mouth. Then Paul said to him: “God will strike you, whitewashed wall! And do you sit judging me according to the Law, yet contrary to the Law order me to be struck?” Those standing by said: “Do you curse God’s high priest?” Paul replied: “I did not know, brethren, that he was the high priest. For it is written: ‘You shall not curse a ruler of your people’” (Exod. 22:28). Knowing that one party was Sadducean and the other Pharisaic, Paul cried out in the council: “Men and brethren, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. I am being judged concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead.” When he said this, dissension arose between the parties and the assembly split. For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, angel, or spirit, whereas the Pharisees confess both. Some Pharisees [Col. 0127A] argued, saying: “We find nothing evil in this man. What if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him?” Therefore, when a great dissension had arisen, the tribune, fearing that Paul would be torn to pieces by them, rescued him from their midst with the help of soldiers and brought him into the barracks (Acts 23:2–10).

The next night the Lord stood beside him and said: “Be steadfast; for as you have testified of me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also at Rome.” When day came, more than forty Jews went to the chief priests and elders and bound themselves by a vow that they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul when he was brought before the council. When the tribune learned this through Paul’s sister’s son, he cleverly foiled [Col. 0127B] the plots of the impious. For at the third hour of the night he sent Paul, bound, to Caesarea with two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen, and two hundred spearmen; and in a letter he explained Paul’s case to Felix the governor. Brought there, Paul was kept in Herod’s praetorium, and after five days was brought out for a hearing (ibid., 10–35). Ananias the priest was present with the Jewish elders, and the advocate Tertullus craftily brought forward an accusation against Paul. At the governor’s signal, Paul answered briefly and immediately refuted the accusations with a prudent reply. Governor Felix postponed their case until the tribune should come down, and ordered the centurion to keep Paul in good conditions. Some days later Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish, summoned Paul, and heard from him the faith that is in Jesus Christ. [Col. 0127C] As Paul reasoned about righteousness, chastity, and the judgment to come, Felix trembled; hoping to get money from him, he frequently sent for him. When two years had passed, Felix received Porcius Festus as his successor; wishing to confer a favor upon the Jews, he left Paul in bonds (Acts 24).

Not long afterwards Festus came down to Caesarea and directed the Jews to accuse Paul. They brought many serious charges against him, which they could not prove, while Paul answered: “I have committed no offense whatsoever against the Law of the Jews, nor against the Temple, nor against Caesar” (Acts 25:7–8). At last, because of the Jews’ plots and the evasiveness of the judge, who was attempting to favor them, he was compelled [Col. 0127D] to appeal to Caesar. He was brought before King Agrippa and Governor Festus, and, stretching out his hand, he gave an account of his calling and of Christ’s faith in a very eloquent testimony. Finally all admired his prudence, and the leading men, having withdrawn, said to one another: “This man has done nothing deserving death or bonds. He could have been released, if he had not appealed to Caesar” (Acts 26:31). He was therefore handed over to Julius, centurion of the Augustan cohort, and was accompanied by Aristarchus the Macedonian and Luke. There were 276 persons on the ship, and for fourteen days they endured a stormy and exceedingly dangerous voyage. They saw neither sun nor stars, nor did they take food, since every hope of safety had been removed. Paul had urged that they winter in Crete, but [Col. 0128A] the counsel and efforts of the helmsman and shipowner had prevailed, to whom the centurion and soldiers had given greater credence. Thus reckless haste rashly encountered winter storms and nearly drowned all of them, unless Paul’s merits had come to their aid. They suffered excessive fear and hardship when they fell into the Syrtes; the ship’s equipment was broken up, and with their own hands they threw overboard the grain and other things that burdened the stern. Amid these events an angel of the Lord stood by Paul, saying: “Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar; and behold, God has granted you all who sail with you” (Acts 27:23–24).

After the shipwreck, they reached the island of Mytilene with the greatest difficulty, and the barbarians showed them great kindness; lighting a fire [Col. 0128B] because of the rain and cold, they revived them. There, while Paul was placing sticks on the fire and a viper, driven out by the heat, fastened upon his hand, the barbarians who watched declared him to be a murderer and believed without doubt that he would shortly die. But he threw the viper into the fire and, to the amazement of all, suffered no harm (ibid., 25; Acts 28:6).

Publius, the ruler of the island, graciously received the shipwrecked men there for three days. Paul went in to Publius’s father, who was afflicted by fevers and dysentery; when he prayed and laid hands on him, he healed him. The other islanders who were sick also came to him and were healed. Therefore, in recognition of Paul’s merits, they honored the shipwrecked men with many honors and supplied them, when they sailed, with what was necessary. After three months they boarded an Alexandrian ship [Col. 0128C] which had wintered on the island; guided by God, they reached Rome not long afterward. Some of the brethren, learning of Paul’s arrival, came to meet him with rejoicing. There Paul was permitted to live by himself with the soldier guarding him. After three days he summoned the leading Jews and complained to them of his imprisonment and of the evils he had suffered from his brethren in Jerusalem. Then he faithfully spoke about the true faith which is in Jesus Christ. For a full two years he remained in his own rented lodging, preaching God’s kingdom to everyone and teaching, with all confidence and without hindrance, the things concerning the Lord Jesus Christ (Acts 28:7–31).

## VII. Continuation: Peter and Paul Living at Rome

[Col. 0128D] Thus far I have followed the narrative in the Acts of the Apostles by Saint Luke the Evangelist, who, passing over other matters, reports that Paul came to Rome and preached God’s word there for two years without anyone hindering him. He entered Rome in Nero’s second year and defended himself before him while Nero was still gentler in the beginnings of his reign. Strengthened by God, Paul was delivered from the mouth of Nero, whom he figuratively calls a lion; afterward he left and went among the western peoples as far as Narbo, a city of Gaul. There, as is reported, he built a basilica and dedicated it in honor of the Maccabean martyrs. There still appears on a wall the sign of the cross, traced by that apostle with his thumb in oil. Then he ordained his disciple Paul [Paulus] as bishop and sent him to that city; laboring greatly [Col. 0129A] in good works, he completed his life in a blessed end.

So also many others shone wonderfully in God’s Church. Instructed in the catholic faith by the blessed Teacher of the Gentiles, they were wisely appointed in the teaching-seat to govern God’s people in various places. For Luke spread the net of faith in Bithynia; Titus in Crete; Carpus in Troas; Timothy and Archippus in Asia; Trophimus at Arles; Onesimus at Ephesus; Sosthenes at Corinth; Tychicus at Paphos; Dionysius the Areopagite at Athens; Epaphras at Colossae; and Erastus at Philippi. Like fish from the depths of the sea, they drew gentile multitudes out of the darkness of ignorance into the light of truth. As they taught others the path of righteousness, so they followed it in their own words and deeds. Their names are therefore inscribed in the book of life, and all peoples will proclaim their wisdom and praise.

Now it is fitting that I should speak of the triumphant death of the saints and truthfully continue the narrative sequence from the teachings of the Fathers: how the glorious princes of the earth, nobly bearing the banner of the true Joshua, gained the land of promise; and how, as they loved one another in life, so they were not separated in death, but, burning with one spirit, contended at Rome against the emperor Nero and Simon Magus, and on one day, after the enemy had been defeated, sought the heavenly kingdoms.

Marcellus the Roman, son of Marcus the prefect, baptized by the apostle Peter, wrote in an Epistle to the holy martyrs [Col. 0129C] Nereus and Achilleus—who, while exiled for Christ’s faith on the island of Pontia, fought daily there against the sorcerers Furius and Priscus, disciples of Simon Magus, with invincible assertions of truth—about the perversity of Simon Magus and the innocence of Peter. For he relates that one day, while Simon was accusing Peter, calling him a magician, and stirring the Roman people to hate him, a widow suddenly passed by with a great crowd, carrying out her only son amid lamentation and loud cries. Peter then said to Simon’s flatterers: “Come to the bier and set down the dead man. Let the true faith be judged to belong to the one who raises him.” When the people had done this, Simon said: [Col. 0129D] “If I raise him now, will you kill Peter?” The crowd replied: “We will burn him alive.” Then Simon, invoking demons, began through their agency to make the body move. Seeing this, the people began to shout in Simon’s praise and for Peter’s destruction. But Peter, having barely obtained silence, said to the people: “If he lives, let him speak, walk, take food, and return to his home. Otherwise, know that Simon is deceiving you.” The people cried out with one voice: “Unless Simon does this, let him suffer the punishment he imposed upon Peter.” Simon, pretending anger, attempted to flee. But the people held him with great reproach. Then Peter, stretching out his hands to heaven, said: “Lord Jesus Christ, who said to us, Your disciples: ‘Go; in my name cast out demons, heal the sick, raise the dead’: raise this boy, that this whole crowd may know that You are God, and that there is no other besides You, who live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ages of ages. Amen.” The boy rose up and, worshipping Peter, said: “I saw the Lord Jesus Christ commanding the angels and saying: ‘At the petition of my friend Peter, let the only orphan be restored to his widowed mother.’” As the people cried with one voice, “One is the God whom Peter preaches,” Simon transformed himself into a dog’s head and began to flee. But when the crowd held him and wished to throw him into the fire, Peter placed himself among them and saved him. “Our Master,” he said, “taught us to return good for evil.” Having escaped, [Col. 0130B] Simon came to Marcellus, whom he had long ago deceived, and tethered at the entrance a savage dog which he could scarcely keep fastened even with an iron chain. “Let us see,” he said, “whether Peter, who is accustomed to visit you, can enter.” Then, after an hour, Peter came; making the sign of the cross, he loosed the dog and said: “Go and speak to Simon: cease deceiving the people, for whom Christ shed His blood, by the ministry of demons.” Marcellus, seeing such great marvels, ran to Peter, fell at his knees, received him into his house, and drove Simon out in disgrace. The dog became gentle toward everyone, but pursued Simon alone. When it had thrown him beneath itself, Peter ran up and cried: “I command you, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, not to fix your bite upon any part of his body.” It could touch none of his limbs, but it so worried his clothing with its bites that no part of his body remained covered. All the people—and especially the children—ran after him together with the dog and, howling, drove him like a wolf beyond [the] city walls. He, unable to endure the disgrace of this shame, appeared nowhere for one year. Afterwards he became known to Nero Caesar and, joined in friendship to that malignant man—worse than the worst—clung closely to him.

As the end of the apostolic contest approached, the Lord appeared to the apostle Peter in a vision and said: [Col. 0130D] “Simon and Nero, filled with demons, are plotting against you. Do not be afraid, for I am with you; and I shall give you the consolation of the apostle Paul, who will enter Rome tomorrow. With him, after seven months, you will together wage war against Simon. And after you have conquered and cast him down and consigned him to hell, you will both come to me together as victors.” And so it happened. For Paul came on the following day. In what order they met and, after seven months, engaged in conflict with Simon, Saint Pope Linus recounted and wrote the entire text of their Passion in the Greek language for the Eastern Churches.

## VIII. Continuation: The Death of the Apostles Peter and Paul

From this point, as I began long ago, I wish to excerpt certain matters and, interrupting the copious prolixity of words, to gather a concise sequence of the deeds accomplished.

When Peter heard that Paul had come to Rome, he rejoiced greatly, rose at once, and went to him. When they saw one another, they wept for joy; lingering a very long time in each other’s embrace, they bathed one another with tears. Then the greater part of the peoples believed through such great preachers of God’s word; nor could the mad assembly of Jews or gentiles openly resist them, upon whom the nurturing Spirit richly poured the abundance of all wisdom.

While innumerable peoples were being converted to the Lord through Peter’s preaching, Nero’s wife Libia and Agrippina, wife of Agrippa the prefect, were also converted, so that they withdrew themselves from their husbands’ sides and devoted themselves to chastity for love of the eternal King. [Col. 0131B]

Paul too shone with manifold grace and became very well known throughout the Roman world by signs, miracles, teaching, and wondrous holiness. Outside the city he rented a public garden, where he discussed the word of life with Luke, Titus, and other faithful persons. Meanwhile he began to gather a very great multitude; with God’s help, many souls were added to the faith through him, so that the sound of his preaching and holiness spread through the entire city and his fame went out through all the surrounding region. Many from Caesar’s household flocked to him and, hearing his preaching, believed in the Lord Jesus Christ. Many also came to him from Caesar’s private chamber; becoming Christians, they abandoned military service and, so inflamed with inward zeal, clung to Christ that they would not return to their military service or the palace, but preferred the glory of true faith and virtues to all arms, wealth, and honors. [Col. 0131C] Thus the devil’s loss increased greatly each day, while wholesome joy increased among the faithful. Seneca also, Nero’s tutor, seeing divine knowledge in Paul, was joined to him in such friendship that he could scarcely refrain from conversing with him. Thus, if he could not speak with him face to face, he might enjoy Paul’s sweetness, friendly conversation, and counsel through frequent letters sent and received. Thus indeed, through the work of the Holy Spirit, Paul’s teaching multiplied and was loved, so that he could teach there lawfully and was very gladly heard by many. For he debated with gentile philosophers and refuted the Jews, so that very many yielded to his instruction. Caesar’s tutor read some of Paul’s writings before Caesar and declared all of them admirable. The Senate, too, held no slight opinion of him.

Accordingly, when this divine brightness had shone through the eminent apostles not only upon the Romans but had also enlightened all who flocked to Rome from diverse nations as to the capital of the world, the leaders of the synagogues and rulers of the gentiles were stirred by bitter envy. With impious slanders they incited the turbulent mob against the apostles. They therefore brought Simon Magus before Nero as he came out of the palace, and tried falsely to accuse the blessed apostles. Simon began [Col. 0132A] to speak many evils of Peter, asserting that he was a magician and deceiver. Perverse people believed him and were deceived, foolishly marveling at his illusory signs. For he made a bronze serpent move, stone dogs bark, and bronze statues laugh and move; and he himself would run and suddenly be seen in the air. Against these things Peter healed the sick by a word, gave sight to the blind by prayer, and drove away demons by command alone. Meanwhile he also raised the dead, and withdrew all whom he could from the magician’s most wicked fellowship. Therefore all religious people detested the magician; the criminally minded, on the contrary, his accomplices, falsely accused Peter by their testimony. At last such report reached Nero, and he ordered Simon Magus to enter his presence. Immediately on entering, Simon began to deceive those watching and to alter his appearances before Nero, so that he suddenly became a boy, then an old man, and at another time a younger man. Thus through many forms he raved by the agency of the devil. Seeing these things, the emperor supposed him to be God’s Son. Then, as the deceptive magician and his accomplices accused the apostles, Nero ordered Peter and Paul to be brought quickly before him. On the following day the apostles and the Magician disputed before Caesar and, as the truthful narrative relates, set forth divergent arguments. The disciples of truth uttered truths and exposed the magician as a thief and criminal in every respect; they declared him base and apostate, lest the heedless obey him to their own condemnation. When Simon threatened to send his angels to punish Peter, Peter [Col. 0132C] secretly asked Nero to order a barley loaf brought to him and handed to him privately. When this was done, Peter took the bread, blessed it, broke it, and hid it beneath his sleeve. Then, as the Magician boasted that he was God’s Son, Peter urgently asked what he had done. Simon, indignant that he could not disclose the apostle’s secret, cried out and ordered great dogs to come forward and devour Peter in Caesar’s presence. Behold, dogs of marvellous size immediately appeared and rushed at Peter. But Peter knelt upon the ground, stretched out both hands, and displayed the bread that he had blessed. When the dogs saw it, they immediately disappeared entirely. Thus the magician was plainly exposed to the mockery of all: though he had promised angels coming against the apostle, he produced dogs, thereby showing that he had not divine angels but canine ones.

At last, after Simon Magus had been refuted by the apostles in many arguments concerning words, Nero ordered a lofty wooden tower to be built in the Campus Martius. On the following day the Emperor, the senate, the Roman knights, and all the people assembled for the spectacle, and, at Nero’s command, the apostles were brought forward. Then Simon climbed the tower before them all; crowned with laurel, he stretched his hands upward and began to fly aloft. Paul, kneeling before all the people, prayed to the Lord; but Peter watched Simon’s contrivances and confidently awaited the fitting moment for divine vengeance. At length he said to his faithful companion: “Paul, raise your head a little and look.” Paul, full of tears, [Col. 0133A] lifted his head, saw Simon already flying high in the air, and said: “Peter, why do you delay? Complete what you have begun. For the Lord Jesus Christ now calls us.” But Peter, looking toward Simon, said: “I adjure you, angels of Satan, who bear him through the air to deceive the hearts of unbelieving people, by God the Creator of all things, and by our Lord Jesus Christ, His Son, whom He raised from the dead on the third day: from this hour bear him no longer, but let him go.”

At Peter’s words Simon was immediately dropped from on high, fell in the place called the Sacred Way, and, broken into four pieces, joined together four stones. This event bore witness to the apostolic victory even to the present day. Then, at the sound when he crashed, [Col. 0133B] Paul raised his head and gave thanks to God, the righteous Judge. Nero, filled with great anger, had Peter and Paul kept in chains. He ordered Simon’s body to be guarded carefully for three days and as many nights, for he thought that he would rise again on the third day. But Peter declared that he had been damned for ever. While the apostles rejoiced in the Holy Spirit and openly confessed the Lord Jesus as their master, Nero, filled with great wrath, said to Agrippa his prefect: “These irreligious men must be destroyed miserably; therefore take iron clubs and order them to be killed in the Naumachia.” Agrippa said: “You order them to perish by an unsuitable example. Since Paul seems to be innocent, it is right that his head should be cut off for irreligion. But Peter, because he committed homicide, order to be raised upon a cross.” The Emperor assenting, the teachers of eternal salvation were immediately led away from his presence and delivered to Paulinus.

Paulinus, a most distinguished man invested with magisterial authority, received the apostles of Christ and committed them to the Mamertine prison, under the charge of Processus and Martinianus and other soldiers. There they remained in prison for nine months, and by their prayers healed many sick persons and demoniacs who came to them. At last, when all who were in custody cried out urgently and unanimously asked them for water because they were endangered by thirst, the most blessed apostles prayed to God and were swiftly heard by Him to whom they clung. For when the blessed apostle Peter made the sign of the cross on the Tarpeian Hill, waters sprang from the hill at that same hour. Then Processus and Martinianus, and all who were in custody, prostrated themselves at the feet of the apostle Peter, and forty-seven persons who believed in the Lord were baptized. Then he offered for them a sacrifice of praise and made them all partakers of the Lord’s Eucharist.

Accordingly, when they had seen so many miracles, the guards Processus and Martinianus said to the apostles: “Go where you wish, for Nero, forgetting you, has despaired of you.” Urgently entreated by the brethren to depart, they left after nine months and came by the Appian Way to the gate. Then Paul visited acquaintances and friends in the city of Rome [Col. 0134A] and strengthened in the faith the Romans and other believers, who greatly rejoiced at his rescue. According to his accustomed practice, he abundantly scattered the word of God and, with God’s help, increased the number of believers over several days. But blessed Peter, while he had an iron shackle broken from his leg and a bandage fell from him before a fence on the New Way, came near the Appian Gate and saw the Lord Jesus Christ. When he recognized Him, he worshipped Him and said: “Lord, where are you going?” And the Lord said to him: “Follow me, Peter, for I am going to Rome to be crucified again.” Peter immediately followed Him and returned to Rome; and the Lord said to him: “Do not be afraid, for I am with you until I bring you into the house of my Father.”

When he returned in the morning, behold, the guards [Col. 0134B] seized him and dragged him before Caesar’s tribunal. Nero, recalling what had happened, ordered Peter to be raised upon a cross and Paul to be beheaded. When Peter came to the cross, wholly intent upon heavenly things, he carefully considered in his spirit that the Lord Jesus Christ, who had descended from heaven to earth, had been raised high upon an upright cross. He therefore asked the executioners to turn his cross around and crucify him with his head downward. They turned the cross and fastened his feet upward and his hands downward. Then an innumerable multitude of people assembled, so filled with fury that they wished even to burn Nero the emperor himself. But Peter restrained them, saying: “Do not, my little children, do not hinder my journey. My feet now walk the heavenly way. [Col. 0134C] Do not grieve, but rejoice with me, because today I obtain the fruit of my labours.”

Then, after a long exhortation in which he subtly explained the form of Christ’s cross, which he was imitating, he prayed and gave thanks to God, saying: “I thank you, good shepherd, because the sheep whom you entrusted to me suffer with me. I ask, Lord, that they may share with me in your grace in your kingdom.” And he added: “I commend to you, good shepherd Christ, the sheep whom you entrusted to me, so that those who have you may not feel themselves to be without me, through whom I was able to shepherd this flock.” Saying this, he gave up his spirit.

Immediately men who had never been seen there appeared; no one could see them there either before or afterward. They said that they had come from Jerusalem because of him. Together with Marcellus, a distinguished man, they secretly took away his body and placed it beneath a terebinth near the Naumachia, in the place called the Vatican. They testified that mighty patrons and friends of the Lord Jesus Christ had been given to the Romans.

Now concerning the Teacher of the Gentiles—how he fought the good fight, completed his course, and obtained the prize of the heavenly calling—I wish to excerpt briefly from the history of his Passion and insert it here, in true praise of the ineffable Adonai. After Paul came out of prison, as stated above, he returned to the garden where he had previously lodged; and a very large company of friends joyfully gathered there to him. [Col. 0135A] One day, while he was engaged in saving teaching and, toward evening, instructed crowds in an upper chamber, Patroclus, the king’s cupbearer, invited by his companions and withdrawing himself from Caesar’s sight, went in the evening to Paul’s lodging to hear teachings of eternal life. But, because of the crowd, he could not get in to the teacher in order to hear more conveniently the word of God, which he fervently loved. He therefore climbed up to a higher window and sat beside it. Yet, as the abundant discourse was drawn out at length and the young man grew weary with sleep, through the devil’s envious snare he began to doze a little; falling from the window of the quite lofty upper chamber, he breathed out his spirit. This was promptly reported to Nero as he was returning from the bath; and he, [Col. 0135B] because he loved the young man greatly, was saddened, and another was appointed in his place to the office of wine. Paul, who was teaching the people within, immediately knew by the Spirit what had happened, announced it to the people present, and ordered the lifeless body to be brought to him at once. When the corpse had been brought, Paul addressed the people and exhorted them to pray to the Lord Jesus with full faith for the dead man’s resurrection. When all had prostrated themselves in prayer, Paul said after finishing the prayer: “Young Patroclus, arise and tell how great are the things the Lord has done for you.” Patroclus immediately arose as if from sleep and began to glorify almighty God. Paul dismissed him rejoicing with the others who belonged to Caesar’s household. While Nero mourned Patroclus and was overwhelmed by immense sorrow, [Col. 0135C] he heard from those attending him that Patroclus was alive and standing before the doors. On hearing this Caesar was terrified in his heart and refused to allow him to enter or stand before his eyes. At last, persuaded by his friends, he permitted him to enter; seeing him restored to health and bearing no signs of death, he was astonished. Speaking with him, he learned that he was a Christian. Hence he became very angry and struck him on the cheek; and Patroclus therefore rejoiced all the more in the Lord Jesus. Then Barnabas and Justus, Paul’s soldier, Arion the Cappadocian, and Festus the Galatian—Caesar’s attendants and friends—said to him: “Why do you strike an upright young man who speaks wisely and with complete truth? For we too serve the unconquered King, Jesus Christ our Lord.” When Caesar [Col. 0135D] heard them with one mind and voice call Jesus the unconquered King, he shut them up in prison, in order to torture severely those whom he had formerly loved greatly. He also ordered that the preachers of that great King be sought out with utmost diligence and issued a deadly edict that, wherever they were found, they should be punished by various tortures without examination. The faithful were therefore sought out by the officers of the state in a thorough search; very many were found and brought before Caesar.

Among them Paul was led in chains, bearing his customary chains for Christ’s name. All the others regarded him as their teacher, rightly honoured him whom the Lord had judged a vessel of election, and placed him before themselves in every respect. From this [Col. 0136A] Nero could easily infer, without anyone’s informing him, that Paul presided over the soldiers of the great King. When he asked why he had secretly entered the Roman realm, drawn his soldiers away from Nero, and subjected them to the dominion of his own king, Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, steadfastly proclaimed before all present the power of almighty God. He invited all to the bounty of His hand, who can distribute the richest gifts according to each person’s merit, and admonished Caesar himself faithfully to obey the highest King. Moreover, he declared that his King would come to judge the living and the dead and destroy the form of this world by fire. On hearing these things Nero Caesar was inflamed with anger and ordered all Christ’s soldiers to be burned with fire. But Paul, [Col. 0136B] by decree of the senate, as one guilty of treason, was ordered to be beheaded according to Roman laws. He was handed over to the prefects Longinus and Megistus, and to Acestus the centurion, to be put to death outside the city; on the way Paul preached the word of salvation without ceasing. Nero also dispatched servants and officers in haste, who diligently searched out Christians in hiding in order to kill them. Thus so vast a multitude of Christians was slain that the Roman people broke violently into the palace and strove to stir up a revolt against Caesar himself. Nero then feared the people’s cries and issued another edict ordering Christians to live in peace. Therefore Paul was again brought before him. But when Nero saw him, he cried out most vehemently: [Col. 0136C] “Take away the magician; take away the sorcerer; behead the deceiver; remove from the face of the earth this changer of minds!” But Paul firmly promised that after death he would live eternally and remain with his unconquered King; and that he would visibly show himself alive to Nero after his beheading, to prove the truth of his words. Then Paul was joyfully led to execution and abundantly imparted words of life to his executioners and the others accompanying him. For, with the Holy Spirit working with him, he exposed the vanity of idolatry, proved by reasoning that it was nothing, wonderfully set forth the true faith and knowledge of the true God, and magnificently expounded the condemnation of the reprobate and the glorification of the righteous. [Col. 0136D] Nor was this without effect. For the divine word immediately bore fruit: it touched and inflamed the hearts of the crowds who heard it and turned the voice of the converted into lamentation for their former sins.

Meanwhile, while there was delay because of such holy occupations and a great crowd sent cries upward, Nero sent Parthenius and Feritas to see whether his order had been fulfilled; through them he hastened the apostle’s Passion if he were still alive. Paul likewise offered them the seed of salvation, but it did them no good, their hearts being hardened through the prevailing power of wickedness. As he proceeded to the place of martyrdom with innumerable companions, he met the most noble matron Plautilla at the gate of the city of Rome. [Col. 0137A] “Farewell,” he said, “Plautilla, daughter of eternal salvation.” Then he asked her to lend him the cloth with which her head was covered, so that he might bind his eyes with it at the hour of his Passion. Weeping, she commended herself to his prayers, hastily offered him the cloth, and withdrew a little to one side because of the obstruction caused by the crowd, as the apostle instructed her. When pagans mocked her for believing a magician and deceiver, Paul encouraged her, ordering her to await his return apart, for she would receive in the little cloth certain signs of his death. In a few words he taught Longinus and his companions, who believed, how and by whom they were to be baptized after his death. On reaching the place of Passion, he turned toward the east, stretched his hands to heaven, and for a very long time prayed in Hebrew with tears [Col. 0137B] and gave thanks to God. Then, bidding farewell to the brethren, he blessed them, bound his eyes with Plautilla’s *mafora*—head-cloth—and bent both knees to the ground and stretched out his neck. The executioner struck forcefully and cut off his head. After it had been severed from his body, the name of Jesus Christ resounded in Hebrew with a clear voice. Immediately a stream of milk came from his body onto the soldier’s garment, and afterward blood flowed out. But the cloth with which he had bound his eyes could not be seen. So great an immensity of light and sweetness of fragrance shone forth from heaven at the moment of his beheading that mortal eyes could not bear its brightness and human speech could not describe its fragrance. All who saw these things marvelled greatly and for a long time praised the unconquered King Sabaoth. Parthenius and Feritas, returning, came to the City Gate, where they found Plautilla glorifying the Lord. Immediately they asked her mockingly why she did not cover her head with the *mafora* she had lent to Paul. But she, inflamed by the fervour of faith, answered magnanimously: [Col. 0137C] “O vain and wretched men, who do not know how to believe what you see with your eyes and touch with your hands! Truly, I have the very cloth which I gave him, made glorious by the pouring out of precious blood.” Then, rejoicing, she related that Paul had come from heaven accompanied by innumerable companies of white-robed ones, had brought the *mafora*, returned grace for the kindness shown him, and added a promise of eternal recompense. Immediately [Col. 0137D] Plautilla drew the cloth from her bosom and showed it to them soaked with rosy blood. Seized by overwhelming fear, they hurried to Caesar and reported to him what they had seen and heard. On hearing it, he was horribly astonished; stunned by immense dread, he began to discuss these reported matters with philosophers, friends, and officers of state.

About the ninth hour, while they marvelled at these things among themselves and questioned and conversed with one another, Paul came although the doors were shut. Standing before Caesar, he said: “O Caesar Nero, behold, I am Paul, a soldier of the eternal and unconquered King. Even now believe that I am not dead, but live to my God. But upon you, wretch, unspeakable evils will come before long, together with the greatest punishment; eternal destruction awaits you, because, among the other terrible deeds you have done, you have unjustly shed much blood of the righteous.” [Col. 0138A] Having said this, he suddenly disappeared. Nero, hearing these things, was stricken with fear beyond expression and became like a madman, not knowing what he could do. At last, on his friends’ advice, he ordered Patroclus, Barnabas, and the others who had been chained with them to be released. Longinus and his companions also came in the morning, as Paul had arranged for them, to his tomb. There they saw two men praying, with Paul standing between them. In marvellous fear they were terrified and dared not come nearer. When they saw the prefects and centurion, who had been agents in Paul’s death, hurrying toward them, [Col. 0138B] overcome with human fear, they immediately turned to flee. But when the latter humbly pleaded, they stopped; hearing their confession of faith, they baptized them with spiritual joy.

At that time a great persecution of Christians broke out, and the first sufferers furnished those who followed with an outstanding example of courage and steadfastness. In Tuscany Torpes, a high official of Nero, was beheaded after many tortures. At Rome Processus and Martinianus, and their forty-six companions, were baptized by the blessed apostle Peter. Longinus and two others were converted through Paul and received the saving washing from Titus and Luke. These indeed followed their teachers, step by step, in faith and martyrdom. At Milan Nazarius, Gervasius, Protasius, and the boy Celsus suffered martyrdom. [Col. 0138C] Nero thus added warfare against God to his innumerable crimes and deservedly incurred the hatred of his army and of the Roman people. They resolved publicly to beat him with *cathomi* (scourges) until he expired. When he heard this and unbearable trembling and fear came upon him, the wretch fled so that he was never seen again. Some report that, while he was still wandering in flight, extreme cold and hunger caused him to stiffen to death, and that he was devoured by wolves.
