Behold, what I have investigated here and there concerning the chief senators of the Church, I have gathered in simple brevity; from very many books I have committed their notable deeds to the memory of posterity in a truthful style. Peter preached among the circumcised for seven years, then held his see at [Col. 0138D] Antioch for seven years. Under the Emperor Claudius, intending to contend against Simon Magus, he went to Rome, preached the Gospel there for twenty-five years, and was the first to hold the pontificate of that world. In the thirty-sixth year after Christ’s Passion, on the third day before the Kalends of July [29 June], he was crucified and buried on the Aurelian Way, near Nero’s palace, in the Vatican. On the same day Paul, after having endured innumerable and notable contests and labours, was beheaded on the Ostian Way, at the second milestone, in gardens at the Waters of Salvia. They suffered together at Rome under the Emperor Nero, in the consulship of Bassus and Tuscus. The former is honoured in that city near the triumphal way with the veneration of the whole city; the latter receives equal honour on the Ostian Way.

## IX. Andrew

[Col. 0139A]

Rome, the head of the world, glories that she has such exalted patrons, to whose thresholds faithful people strive to hasten from every part of the world, so that, aided by such powerful advocates, they may be protected without ceasing against every adversary and hostile power. All who suitably and devoutly request their intercession experience their help at hand, through the gift of God the highest King, who, three and one, lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, according to Hebrew etymology, is interpreted as “handsome” or “answering.” [Col. 0139B] In Greek speech, from ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀνδρός, “from a man,” he is called “manly.” In the allotment of preaching he received Scythia and Achaia; in the latter, at the city of Patras, he died suspended upon a cross on the second day before the Kalends of December [30 November]. We possess an excellent little book concerning his deeds, in which many wonderful things are related about blessed Andrew. The author of the book is not known to me; but its account of marvellous events is, I think, deservedly most pleasing. I therefore wish briefly to excerpt certain matters from it in praise of the all-powerful Messiah and insert them into this little work of ours. Accordingly, when the apostle and evangelist Matthew announced the word of salvation to the Myrmidons, he was seized by the cruel inhabitants; his eyes were torn out, and he was confined in prison bound with chains. At an angel of God’s command, the apostle Andrew came to the strait. Finding a ship on the shore, [Col. 0139C] he immediately boarded it, and, with favourable winds, sailed to the city where Saint Matthew was held amid the filth of prison. Seeing his fellow apostle sitting in intense sorrow with other prisoners, he wept most bitterly. When they prayed together, that place at once shook and a great light shone in the prison. The blessed evangelist’s eyes were restored, and everyone’s chains were loosed. Thus Matthew and all the others imprisoned with him were freed and went away. When Andrew preached God’s word to the inhabitants, they seized him and dragged him through the city streets with his feet bound. Blood flowed from his head, his hair having been torn out. At length, as the apostle prayed, great fear came upon the inhabitants of Myrmidonia, and they promptly released him. Then, prostrate on the ground before the apostle’s feet, they received his preaching and, divinely inspired, believed in the Lord and were baptized. Departing from there, Andrew came into his own region, where he touched the eyes of a certain blind man, who immediately received sight. Demetrius, chief man of the city of Amasus, hearing of the signs Andrew performed in Christ’s name, fell weeping at the apostle’s feet, asking him to restore alive his Egyptian boy, whom a fever had killed. The gentle apostle pitied his grief, went with him to the house of mourning, and, after prayer, the boy immediately rose up well. All who saw it rejoiced and, believing, were baptized.

Sostratus, a Christian boy, solicited by his mother for sexual intercourse, fled to the apostle. She, moved by bitterness, accused her son before the proconsul. While the boy was silent from shame, Saint Andrew defended him and openly reproved the shameless woman for her wickedness. The angry proconsul ordered the boy shut in the sack prescribed for parricides and cast into the river, while Andrew was thrown into prison. As the apostle prayed, there was a great earthquake with heavy thunder; the proconsul fell from his seat, and all the rest fell to the ground. The boy’s mother was struck, withered, and died. Then the proconsul, prostrate at the apostle’s feet, said: “Have mercy on us who are perishing, servant of God, lest the earth swallow us.” As the apostle prayed, the earthquake ceased, calm returned to the air, and he went among those in distress and healed them. The proconsul received the word of God and, [Col. 0140B] believing in the Lord, was baptized by the apostle with all his household.

Gratinus of Sinope, seized by fever, became seriously ill, while his wife swelled with dropsy. Their son also, while bathing in the women’s bath, was grievously tormented by a demon after losing his senses. Asked by the proconsul, Andrew came to the city in a vehicle. Entering Gratinus’s house, he drove out the demon and healed the cleansed boy. He rebuked the husband and his wife, polluted by the contagion of adultery; after receiving from them a promise of amendment, he healed them. Finally, restored to health, they received faith in Jesus Christ and were joyfully baptized with all their household.

[Col. 0140C] At Nicaea seven demons hid among the tombs beside the road; at midday they stoned passers-by and had already killed many. At length, when the apostle arrived there, the whole city rejoiced and came out to meet him with palm branches, crying: “Our salvation is in your hand, man of God.” Then they explained the entire matter; and they in turn immediately heard from the apostle the order of faith and religion. Straightway, rejoicing, they believed in the Lord and confessed Jesus Christ as the Son of God. Andrew gave thanks to God for their ready faith; he ordered the demons to stand before the people in the likeness of dogs and afterward drove them into dry and barren places, lest they harm anyone. Thus, by God’s power, he delivered the city, [Col. 0140D] baptized its believing citizens, and appointed for them as bishop Coelestinus, a good and wise man.

At the gate of Nicomedia he encountered a dead young man on a bier and saw his parents, burdened with age and following their son’s corpse with excessive weeping. Moved by compassion for their tears, he asked how the youth had died. But as they answered nothing through fear, he heard from the servants: “While he was here alone in his room, seven dogs suddenly came and attacked him. Torn most miserably by them, he fell dead.” Then Andrew recognized this deed as the work of the seven demons whom he had driven from Nicaea. Sighing toward heaven, he asked God [Col. 0141A] for life for the dead man. Having prayed, he turned to the bier and said: “In the name of Jesus Christ, arise.” To the people’s amazement, the boy rose up and clung to his reviver. The apostle brought the believing youth with him as far as Macedonia and instructed him in saving words.

Leaving there, he boarded a ship, entered the strait of the Hellespont, and intended to go to Byzantium. Behold, the sea was stirred up, a violent wind came upon them, and the ship was sinking; the sailors awaited the danger of death. At last blessed Andrew prayed to the Lord. At His command the wind immediately fell, calm returned, and a favourable voyage brought them, delivered from danger, to Byzantium. As they hurried from there, a multitude of men appeared in Thrace, carrying spears in their hands with swords drawn and desiring to rush upon those they encountered. But blessed Andrew made the sign of the cross against them and prayed to God for the salvation of his companions. An angel of the Lord passed by in great splendour, touched their swords, and, as those swords fell to the ground, the man of God passed by unharmed with his followers. Andrew the apostle reached Berinthus, a maritime city of Thrace, and there found a ship hurrying to Macedonia. An angel of God ordered the apostle to board it. Having embarked, he preached God’s word, and the sailor with all the shipmasters believed in God.

There was at Thessalonica a noble and very wealthy young man named Exous. Unknown to his family, [Col. 0141C] he came to the apostle, heard him preaching God’s word, believed in the Lord, despised his parents and possessions, and attached himself to Andrew. His parents sought him and found him at Philippi. They tried very hard, through gifts and threats, to separate him from the apostle, but could not. When the apostle preached, they rejected the word of salvation; gathering a band, they set fire to the house and, bringing bundles of rushes, reeds, and torches, began to burn it down. Then the young man poured a flask of water from above with an invocation of Christ’s name, and divine power immediately extinguished the whole fire, as though it had never been kindled. Then, furious, they brought up ladders to climb them and kill Andrew and Exous with the sword; but they were divinely blinded so that they could not see the ascent of the ladders. Then a certain Lysimachus, one of the citizens, perceived the divine work and boldly rebuked the neighbours’ madness, saying: “Why, men, do you exhaust yourselves in useless labour? God fights for these men and you do not recognize it. Stop this folly, lest heavenly wrath consume you.” At these words all were pierced in heart; as the dark night came on, they themselves were illuminated from heaven. They went up, found the apostle praying, and, prostrate upon the floor, asked and received forgiveness from him. The apostle graciously raised them up; strengthened in the faith, they praised the Almighty. Only the boy’s parents did not believe. Cursing the young man, they returned to their homeland; fifty days later they both expired together in a single moment. [Col. 0142A] But their fellow citizens, because they loved the young man greatly, granted him his whole inheritance. Remaining with the apostle, he distributed the proceeds of his estates to the poor.

After some time both went together to Thessalonica, where citizens joyfully assembled for them in the theatre. Exous preached God’s word to them, while blessed Andrew, admiring his wisdom, listened in silence. Then, at the crowd’s request, he ordered the sick Adimathus, son of Carpianus, to be brought. But when the message of his healing was given him by his father, he believed; he put on his clothes, rose sound from his bed after twenty-three years, and, [Col. 0142B] outrunning his parents, went to the theatre. There he fell at the apostle’s feet and, to the amazement of the people, gave thanks for his recovered health. When one of the Thessalonians asked the apostle on behalf of his demon-possessed son, Satan, skilled in a thousand devices, suffocated him in a private room. When the father found him dead and wept greatly for this reason, he nevertheless remained strong in faith and prevailed in hope; he had friends carry the corpse to the theatre and related what had happened to the apostle. Andrew turned to the people and said: “O men of Thessalonica, what will it benefit you, when you see miracles performed, if you do not believe?” When they promised that they would believe upon seeing the miracle, the apostle Andrew said to the dead youth: “In the name of Jesus Christ, arise, boy.” He immediately rose, [Col. 0142C] and the astonished people faithfully kept their promise to receive the faith.

Medias of Philippi begged the apostle with tears on behalf of his sick son. The most gentle man kindly received his prayers, took his hand, and went to Philippi. As they entered the city gate, an old man met them and pleaded for his sons, whom Medias had tortured in prison because of an offence. At the apostle’s urging, Medias fell at his feet and released not only those two but also seven others for whom nobody spoke, provided only that his son might be healed. When they had been freed, the apostle healed Philomed, who had been disabled for twenty-two years.

[Col. 0142D] Then, as the people cried out for him to heal their sick as well, Andrew, trusting in the Lord, said to the healed boy: “Go through the houses of the sick, and in the name of Jesus Christ, in whom you have been healed, command them to rise.” The boy obeyed the apostle’s orders. Seeing these miracles, the people believed and offered the apostle many gifts; but, preaching the word of life freely to all, he accepted nothing. He also freely healed the sick daughter of Nicolaus, for whom her father offered much, and invited everyone to faith.

## X. Andrew: The Continuation of His Life

The apostle’s fame concerning the miracles which he performed upon the sick spread everywhere through Macedonia. [Col. 0143A] Virinus [Note: [Col. 0143D] Read: Quirinus. Le Prévost], therefore, the proconsul, was stirred up against him and sent soldiers to Thessalonica to seize him; but, seeing the radiance of his countenance, they did not dare touch him. When the people who believed in God heard that the soldiers had come there to harm the apostle, they became angry and wished to kill them with swords and clubs; but at the apostle’s prohibition, they scarcely restrained their hands from slaughter. The proconsul again sent soldiers, but when they saw the apostle they were troubled and said nothing. At last the proconsul sent a multitude of soldiers a third time. One of them was seized by a demon and uttered savage words against the absent proconsul. Then the demon departed, and the soldier fell down dead. Meanwhile the proconsul came in great fury and, standing beside the apostle Andrew, [Col. 0143B] could not see him until he heard him speaking. At length, wretched man that he was, when he saw the saint of God, he heaped insults and threats upon him. But the kindly man strove to calm the furious judge with gentle words; after pouring out prayers to the Lord, he raised the dead soldier. Yet the proconsul remained in his madness. At daybreak he ordered wild beasts to be admitted into the stadium, the blessed apostle dragged in, and cast to the beasts. His furious servants dragged him by the hair, threw him into the arena, and released a fierce and terrible boar. It circled the saint of God three times but did him no harm. Again at the proconsul’s order, a boar was brought by thirty soldiers and set upon him by two hunters; it did not touch Andrew, but tore the hunters to pieces. Finally, [Col. 0143C] uttering a dreadful grunt, it fell and died. While the people praised the Lord, an angel was seen descending from heaven and strengthening the saint of God in the stadium. At last the savage proconsul, burning with anger, ordered a most fierce leopard to be released. Once released, it left the apostle alone, went up to the proconsul’s seat, seized his son, and suffocated him. Yet excessive madness possessed the proconsul: he neither grieved over what had happened nor said anything. Then the blessed man strengthened the people in God’s love and promised, in order to confirm their faith, that he would raise the dead son of the proconsul. Prostrate upon the ground, he prayed for a very long time; taking the suffocated man’s hand, he raised him in the Lord’s name. Seeing this, [Col. 0143D] the people magnified God and wished to kill Virinus the proconsul, who in unbelief resisted the saint of God; but the apostle did not permit them. The ashamed proconsul departed from the praetorium.

A certain woman entreated him, and blessed Andrew came to a field where there was a serpent, fifty cubits long, laying waste the whole district. As the apostle approached, it gave forth great hisses; and, while all present were exceedingly terrified, it raised its head and came to meet him. Then the holy man of God said to it: “Lower your head, accursed creature, which from the beginning you raised for the destruction of humankind; submit yourself to the servants of God and [Col. 0144A] die.” Immediately the serpent uttered a dreadful roar, wound itself around a large oak nearby, and, vomiting out a stream of venom with blood, expired. Then the apostle came to the woman’s estate, where a little boy whom the serpent had struck lay dead; and he sent his parents to see their son’s killer dead. When they had gone, the apostle said to the proconsul’s wife: “Go and raise the boy.” Without any doubt, she came to the body and said: “In the name of my God Jesus Christ, rise unharmed.” At once he rose, while all rejoiced and gave thanks to God. On the following night blessed Andrew saw Peter and John in a vision, in which it was revealed to him that shortly afterward he would hang upon a cross [Col. 0144B] and follow the Lord Jesus in the passion of the cross. He summoned the brethren, explained the account of the vision, comforted them as they mourned his imminent departure, instructed them beneficially for five days, and by devout prayers commended the flock of the Church to God. From there he set out for Thessalonica.

Lisbius the proconsul attempted to resist the way of God; though he repeatedly sent soldiers to seize Andrew, he was miserably frustrated in his purpose. At last, when the apostle arrived, he was beaten with whips by two demons. Afterwards he summoned the man of God and confessed his wickedness to him before all the people. Then he gladly heard the word of God from the apostle; healed of his sickness, he believed in God [Col. 0144C] and diligently walked in God’s law.

But Calista, the proconsul’s wife, was deeply jealous of Trophima, who had formerly been her concubine but was now joined to another husband and adhered to apostolic teaching. Therefore, without Lisbius’s knowledge, she summoned the procurator and ordered that Trophima be condemned as a prostitute and taken to a brothel. Trophima was accordingly led to the brothel, handed over to the brothel-keeper, and there prayed continually to God. When lewd men came, she set the Gospel—which she kept against her breast—before them; and immediately their lascivious desire failed. At last a most shameless young libertine came and tried to use violence; but she resisted, and the Gospel fell to the ground. Then Trophima, grieving, stretched both hands to heaven and said weeping: “Do not allow me, Lord, [Col. 0144D] to be defiled, for whose name I love chastity.” At once an angel of the Lord appeared to her, and the impudent young man fell at her feet and expired. Strengthened by God, she blessed God and raised the youth in Christ’s name; and the entire city ran to witness this sight.

Calista and her procurator went to the baths. While they were bathing together, a most hideous demon appeared to them; struck by it, both died. There was therefore great mourning, and the sudden event was reported to the apostle and the proconsul. An old nurse, who because of age was carried in others’ arms, begged the apostle to restore Calista to life. [Col. 0145A] Although her husband raged over the grave crime committed, the gentle apostle ordered the body to be brought into the midst; approaching it after prayer, he touched the woman’s head. “Rise,” he said, “in the name of Jesus Christ my God.” Immediately the woman rose and sought reconciliation with Trophima. Thus Lisbius the proconsul, having seen God’s miracles, advanced in faith through the apostle and faithfully obeyed the apostle’s counsel in all things.

One day, while they sat together on the shore and many people there diligently heard the word of God from the apostle’s mouth, behold, a corpse was cast up from the sea at the apostle’s feet. At once, after prayer had been poured out to God, it was restored to life. The young man was called Philopator, son of Sostratus, a Macedonian citizen. [Col. 0145B] He wept for companions swallowed by the waves and pleaded with the apostle, who prayed; and, as the wave obediently brought them, he raised thirty-nine bodies to life. He ordered each of the brethren to hold one dead person and say to him: “May Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, raise you.” Thus thirty-nine men returned to life and glorified almighty God.

After many signs and good works, which I cannot recount one by one, the blessed apostle Andrew came to Patras, where Maximilla, wife of Aegeas the proconsul who had succeeded Lisbius, was gravely ill. Then Effidima, who had been converted through the teaching of Sosia, asked the apostle to visit Maximilla, who was feverish. He came to the sick woman’s chamber, with Effidima preceding him; after he prayed, the fever was driven away and the woman [Col. 0145C] was healed. The proconsul offered the holy man of God a hundred silver coins, but he would not even look at them. Since many signs were performed by the blessed apostle at Patras, and many were drawn to faith in Christ by manifestations of bodily aid, Stratocles, the brother of Aegeas the proconsul, arrived from Italy. His servant, named Algmana, whom he loved dearly, lay foaming in the courtyard under a demon’s assault. Amid great tumult, with Stratocles shaken by overwhelming grief, Maximilla and Effidima advised that blessed Andrew be summoned. As he prayed, the demon-possessed boy was healed. Stratocles therefore believed in the Lord and, strengthened in faith, attached himself to the apostle to hear the word of God. Aegeas [Col. 0145D] had gone to Macedonia; Maximilla, aflame with spiritual love, daily sought an opportunity to receive heavenly teaching from the apostle and came to him in devotion. The proconsul was therefore greatly enraged against the apostle because his wife, after receiving the doctrine of salvation, did not wish to unite herself with him.

I shall now briefly record the passion of the most blessed apostle Andrew and strive to include it truthfully in my little book, as the devout devotion of holy Mother Church has preserved it in her libraries from ancient times and faithfully recites it. The presbyters and deacons of the churches of Achaia, who were present, saw it, and wrote it usefully and elegantly for all the churches established throughout the four regions of the world.

[Col. 0146A] The proconsul Aegeas returned from Macedonia and came to Patras, a city of Achaia, and began to compel those who believed in Christ to sacrifice to idols. Holy Andrew confronted him and earnestly sought, with reasonable arguments, to invite him to the true faith. But wisdom did not enter into his malevolent soul. Yet the generous dispenser of divine wisdom, though he had not benefited the impious Aegeas, poured out abundant nourishment of heavenly teaching for others who were predestined to life. He treated the mystery of the cross with great discernment, clearly explained why God became human and suffered, and eloquently set forth the order of the Lord’s passion and the common benefit of the human race. Enraged, Aegeas seized the apostle and shut him in prison. A multitude [Col. 0146B] from nearly the whole province came to him, so that they wished to kill Aegeas and free the apostle by breaking down the doors. But Andrew restrained them with salutary admonitions, taught them throughout the whole night, recalled the patience of the Lord Jesus to their minds, and earnestly begged the people not to hinder his passion.

On the following day the proconsul Aegeas sent for the apostle and brought him before himself. Sitting on the tribunal, he sought to lead him astray; but, founded in God, Andrew stood firm against threats and blandishments. At last Aegeas ordered him, stretched out, to be beaten with the whips of seven squads of three men; but after the blows, the valiant athlete of Christ proclaimed praise of the cross and steadfastly declared true affirmations to the raging tyrant.

Then Aegeas, indignant, ordered him to be fastened to a cross [Col. 0146C] and instructed the torturers that, with feet and hands bound, he should be stretched as though upon a rack, so that, not fastened with nails, he might not die quickly but instead be tormented by prolonged suffering. As the holy man was led by the executioners, a crowd gathered, crying and saying: “What has this righteous man and friend of God done, that he is being led to the cross?” Andrew, however, went secure and joyful; he begged the people not to hinder his passion and did not cease from salutary teaching. When he had reached the place of contest and saw the cross from afar, he cried out in a loud voice:

“Greetings, O cross, consecrated in the body of Christ and adorned from his limbs as though with pearls! O good cross, which received beauty and loveliness from the limbs [Col. 0146D] of the Lord—long desired, earnestly loved, sought without interruption, and now at last prepared for a soul that longs for you!”

Saying these and many other things full of love and devotion, he stripped himself and handed his garments to the executioners. Approaching, they raised him upon the cross, stretched his whole body with ropes, and suspended him; thus they carried out the command of the impious proconsul by a cruel act. A crowd of nearly twenty thousand people stood by and cried that the holy man was suffering this by an unjust judgment; among them was Stratocles, Aegeas’s brother. Holy Andrew strengthened the minds of the faithful and exhorted them to endurance in time, teaching that no suffering was worthy to be compared with eternal recompense.

[Col. 0147A] Meanwhile all went to Aegeas’s house and cried out together: “What is this judgment of yours, proconsul? You have judged wickedly. Grant us the righteous man; restore to us the holy man; do not kill the man dear to God.” As the people said these and many other things, Aegeas was frightened; promising to take him down, he began to go with them. Seeing him, holy Andrew urged him to believe in Christ and, while he still could, to run to the faith for his salvation. Hanging upon the cross, he himself rejoiced in security, and, exceedingly joyful at the sight of Christ, whom he had loved with all his mind and long desired, said: “Now I see my King; now I worship him; now I stand in his presence.” But when the executioners put their hands to the cross, they could not touch him, [Col. 0147B] and again and again others pressed forward to release him; but the arms of those attempting to take him down became numb. Then holy Andrew cried out in a loud voice and poured forth a most devout prayer before God. After he had prayed for a long time to Jesus, his good master, an immense brightness like lightning came from heaven and so surrounded him, in the sight of all, that human eyes could not look upon him because of the brightness. When the brightness had remained for about half an hour, Andrew, the renowned champion of Christ, gave up his spirit as the light departed, going with that same light to the Lord. Maximilla the noblewoman reverently took his body, anointed it with spices, and buried it in an excellent place.

Before Aegeas came to his house, he was seized by a demon and died on the road, before everyone’s eyes, under demonic torment. Stratocles, Aegeas’s brother, took nothing of his property but departed holding the body of the holy apostle Andrew. Such fear also seized everyone in that province that no one remained who did not believe in our God and Savior. It is said that manna, like flour, and oil of most sweet fragrance flow from his tomb; by these the inhabitants of the region are shown what the fertility of the present year will be. If it flows sparingly, the earth yields sparingly; but if it comes forth abundantly, a great abundance of fruits is supplied.

Behold, compelled by love of you alone, glorious apostle [Col. 0147D] of Jesus Christ, I have briefly reviewed the course of your life, happily adorned with divine gifts, to the praise of your almighty master, to whom you faithfully clung unto death. Therefore, gentle Andrew, kindly receive this devoted service, and commend me, a sinner, by devout prayers to the mercy of the Creator. In his worship, amid joys and sorrows, I desire, with his help, to persevere. And you who, hanging upon the cross, exhorted Aegeas, your cruel killer, to faith, unceasingly aid the faithful children of the Church who sing to you with utter devotion of heart and melody of voice:

> Holy Andrew, gentlest of saints,  
> Obtain pardon for our errors;  
> And raise us up by your intercessions,  
> Weighed down as we are by the burden of sins.
>
> Amid the miseries of this unsteady age  
> We are often shaken and groan in weakness.  
> Plead for us before the majesty of the Lord,  
> That he may grant us to enjoy the true light.

Amen.

[Col. 0148A] XI. James and John.

James and John, sons of Zebedee, were called by Christ Boanerges—or, as it is better read, Boanereem—that is, “sons of thunder,” because of the strength and greatness of the faith by which they held inviolate and taught the spotless law of the Lord. James is interpreted “supplanter,” while John means “the grace of God,” or “one in whom there is grace.” Rightly were brothers of such election called by such illustrious names: by overthrowing vices in the arena of this frail life, they eminently conquered the crooked serpent [Col. 0148B]; becoming special friends of God and filled with his manifold grace, they illuminated holy Mother Church with the teaching of truth. Concerning blessed James—how he evangelized in Judaea and Samaria and suffered martyrdom under Herod, son of Aristobulus, when accused by the chief priests and Pharisees—I have, as I found it set forth by ancient writers, simply inserted an abridgement into the preceding book of this work. I now investigate writings about John the Theologian, friend of Jesus Christ, and desire briefly to gather them for the praise of the King Sabaoth: those which Mellitus wrote to the Laodiceans and other faithful throughout the world, and which other distinguished antiquaries published about him, especially Jerome, interpreter of the divine law, who marked them out in [Col. 0148C] the prologue to the Apocalypse.

John the apostle and evangelist was a virgin, chosen by the Lord Jesus Christ and loved by him more than the others. He was held in such affection that at the supper he reclined upon Christ’s breast; and, when he alone stood by the cross, Christ entrusted his own mother to him. Thus he who had called John, when he wished to marry, to the embrace of virginity, entrusted to him also a virgin to guard. Therefore, when John was publicly preaching the word of God in Asia and earnestly proclaiming the testimony of Jesus Christ to Jews and Gentiles, he was accused at Rome by the envious reports of opponents of the truth. By command of the emperor Domitian—who, after Nero, was the second to persecute Christians—he was seized at Ephesus and brought before the emperor and [Col. 0148D] senate at the Latin Gate. Since he persisted in the true faith, steadfast as a firm and lofty mountain, on 6 May, by the emperor’s command, he was cast into a vat of boiling oil. Yet, protected by divine grace, he emerged unharmed; and on that day his feast is devoutly celebrated every year by the faithful. From there he was carried into exile on the island of Patmos. There the Apocalypse, shown to him by the same Lord, was written down; in it the state and order of the Church are displayed sevenfold, as are the great pressures of tribulations and the recompenses of merits.

Finally, by the providence of God, who disposes all things justly, the Roman senate killed Domitian in the very year in which John was exiled, because of his bloody deeds. Then, by general resolution, it decreed that whatever Domitian had ordered should be annulled. Therefore holy John the apostle, who had been deported by Domitian’s will with disgrace, returned to Ephesus with honor and to the joy of many. [Col. 0149A] All the Ephesian people came out to meet him as he returned, and the single voice of faithful, exulting men and women rang out: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!”

As John entered the city, behold, Drusiana, who had ardently desired to see him, was being carried out dead. Widows and poor people, together with relatives and orphans, wept and cried: “Holy John, apostle of God, behold, we are carrying out Drusiana. Obeying your holy counsels, she supported us all and served God in chastity and humility. Longing for your return, she said each day: ‘Would that I might see the apostle of God with my own eyes before I die!’” Then blessed John ordered the bier set down and her body unwrapped, and said in a clear voice: “May my Lord Jesus Christ awaken you, Drusiana. Rise, return to your house on your feet, and prepare refreshment for me.” Immediately she rose and joyfully obeyed the apostle’s command. Rightly so, for it seemed to her that she had been awakened not from death but from sleep. Then the people cried out for three hours: “One is the God whom holy John preaches; one is the true Lord Jesus Christ.”

At that time two exceedingly wealthy young brothers, persuaded by the philosopher Crato, sold their property [Col. 0149C] and bought individual jewels, which they shattered in the marketplace in everyone’s sight. They staged this spectacle as a vain display of contempt for the world. As blessed John the apostle passed through the market, he saw this; pitying the folly of those who had gone astray, he kindly gave wiser counsel. He summoned Crato, the teacher of error, reproved the ruinous destruction of property, and taught useful contempt for the world according to Christ’s command, recalling the teaching of his own master, who said to the young man seeking from him counsel concerning eternal salvation: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21). The philosopher Crato accepted the apostle’s salutary counsel and begged that the gems which had been shattered [Col. 0149D] might be restored whole.

[Note: [Col. 0149D] Le Prévost, vainly.]

Therefore blessed John gathered the fragments of the gems and, holding them in his hand, raised his eyes to heaven and prayed for a long time. When the prayer was ended, after the faithful present answered “Amen,” the fragments of the gems were so perfectly joined that no sign whatever remained of their having been broken. Then the philosopher Crato, together with all his disciples, threw himself at the apostle’s feet, believed, and was baptized with them all. Publicly preaching the faith of the Lord Jesus, he began to be a true philosopher. The two brothers, who had formerly squandered their property to no purpose, then obeyed [Col. 0150A] the Gospel: they sold the gems and distributed the proceeds to Christ in the poor. An innumerable multitude of believers began to attach themselves to the apostle and follow in his footsteps.

Atticus and Eugenius, two brothers of standing in the city of Ephesus, followed the example of the aforementioned young men. They sold everything they could possess, gave it to the needy, and, unencumbered, followed the apostle as he went through the cities preaching the word of God. It happened that they entered the city of Pergamum and saw their servants proceeding in silk garments and shining in worldly splendor. Struck by the devil’s arrow, they became deeply sad because they themselves were poor, clothed in one cloak, while they saw their servants powerful [Col. 0150B] and resplendent. But blessed John, understanding Satan’s deceits, ordered straight rods to be brought to him in separate bundles and small stones from the seashore. When this had been done, he invoked the Lord’s name: the forest rods were turned into gold and the stones into gems. Then the holy apostle said to them: “Go to the goldsmiths and jewelers for seven days, and, when you have tested whether this is true gold and these are genuine gems, report to me.” The two went round the workshops of the craftsmen; after seven days they returned and reported to the apostle that the goldsmiths had pronounced the gold excellent and the jewelers had confirmed that the stones were precious. Then holy John said: “Go and buy back the lands which you sold, [Col. 0150C] for you have lost the rewards of heaven. Buy yourselves silk garments, so that, like a rose, you may shine for a season. Yet while its flower displays both fragrance and redness, it suddenly withers. You sigh at the sight of your servants and have lamented your own poverty. Be flourishing, that you may wither; be rich for a time, that you may beg forever. Is the hand of the Lord not able to make his servants abundant in riches and incomparably splendid? But he has ordained a contest for souls, that those who refused to possess temporal wealth for his name’s sake may believe that they will possess eternal riches.”

While blessed John spoke these and similar things for edification, elaborating splendidly on the misery and contempt of the world, apostasy, and perseverance in goodness, [Col. 0150D] behold, a young man named Stacteus was being carried out dead by his widowed mother. The grieving mother and the crowds conducting the funeral rites threw themselves at the apostle’s feet and, with many tears, begged him in the name of his God to raise this young man, as he had Drusiana, and mercifully relieve his widowed mother and the wife whom he had recently married. Then the apostle prostrated himself and prayed weeping for a long time. Three times rising from prayer, he stretched his hands to heaven and poured out silent prayer for a long time. Then he ordered the wrapped body to be unbound, called the young man by name, and commanded him to rise and become a true messenger concerning the things [Col. 0151A] he had seen while dead.

Then Stacteus rose, worshipped the apostle, and began to rebuke his disciples. “I saw your angels,” he said, “weeping; I saw Satan’s angels rejoicing at your downfall. I also saw the kingdom now prepared for you, and zetas—chambers—furnished with flashing gems, full of joys, banquets, riches, perpetual life, eternal light, and delights—all of which you have lost. And, alas, you have acquired places of darkness, full of dragons and narrow constraints, full of hissing flames and torments, full of foul smells and pains.” As Stacteus said these and similar things, the multitude of people present was astonished.

Atticus and Eugenius, with the man who had been raised, prostrated themselves before the apostle and together [Col. 0151B] begged him to intercede for them with the Lord. At last, in answer to their supplication, holy John instructed them to offer repentance to God for thirty days; during this period they were especially to ask God that the golden rods might return to their own nature and that the stones might return to the baseness in which they were born. When the thirty days had passed, neither the gold changed into rods nor the gems into sand. At length the troubled brothers came to the apostle and with many prayers and tears begged his mercy. Moved with compassion for their weeping and repentance, while all also interceded for them, he ordered the rods to be carried back to the forest and the stones to the shore, for they had returned to their own nature. Then the aforesaid [Col. 0151C] brothers received back the grace that they had lost: they drove out demons as before, healed the sick, gave sight to the blind, and performed many miracles in the Lord’s name.

When the whole city of Ephesus—indeed, the entire province of Asia—honored and proclaimed holy John, the worshippers of idols stirred up a sedition. The frenzied pagans dragged John to Diana’s temple and tried to compel him into the foulness of sacrifice. Filled with the Holy Spirit, he proposed that they go to Christ’s church and, invoking the powers of their Diana, make Christ’s church fall; or, if they could not do this, he himself, invoking his God’s name, would make Diana’s temple collapse and [Col. 0151D] her idol be smashed. Once this had happened, they should consider what was right, abandon the superstition of vanity, and take up the path of true faith and righteousness. The people approved this condition, though a few opposed the decision. Then blessed John gently urged the people to withdraw far from the temple; he himself prayed with devout mind and clear voice. At once the temple and all its idols fell down and became like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth. On that same day twelve thousand pagans, excluding little children and women, were converted and received baptism in the name of the Holy Trinity. Then Aristodemus, chief priest of all the idols, under the prompting of a most wicked spirit stirred up the people so that, once sedition had arisen, people [Col. 0152A] prepared to wage war upon people. But John, lover of peace, said: “Tell me, Aristodemus, what shall I do to remove indignation from your heart?” He replied: “If you wish me to believe in your God, I will give you poison to drink. When you have drunk it, if you do not die, your God will be shown to be true.” The apostle accepted this agreement. Aristodemus, wishing to frighten him, went to the proconsul and asked him for two men who were to be beheaded for their crimes. At last he consented; they were brought into the middle of the marketplace, and there, before the apostle and all the people, drank poison and immediately gave up the spirit. Blessed John, as the men who had drunk the poison lay dead, fearlessly took the cup; making the sign of the cross over it, [Col. 0152B] he prayed devoutly and faithfully recounted before all who heard the ineffable works of God. Then he armed himself with the sign of the cross, drank all that was in the cup, and, giving thanks to the Lord, remained joyful and cheerful. Seeing this, the people cried: “One is the true God whom John preaches.”

But after Aristodemus had intently watched the apostle of God for three hours and found no trace in him of pallor or trembling, he nevertheless refused to believe, although the others reproached him; with hardened heart, he still resisted the truth. At last he asked that those dead from poison might be restored to life by divine power and promised that then his heart would be cleansed of every doubt. The people rose against him, saying that they would burn him and his house if he dared further to vex God’s apostle. But John, seeing that a most bitter sedition was arising between believers and unbelievers, asked for silence and said in the hearing of all: “Patience is the first virtue that we must imitate among the divine virtues. Therefore, if Aristodemus is still held in his unbelief, let us loosen the knots of his unbelief. For I shall not cease from this work until healing can come to his wounds. I must have the perseverance of a skilled physician, who diligently seeks to apply various remedies to a sick person. Thus, since this sufferer has not yet been healed by what has been done, let us do for him something that has not been done.” Then he summoned Aristodemus and gave him his tunic. He himself stood clothed in a cloak and instructed him: “Go, lay it upon the bodies of the dead, and say this: ‘John, apostle of our Lord Jesus Christ, has sent me to you, that you may rise in his name and all may know that death and life serve my Lord Jesus Christ.’” [Col. 0152D] As soon as Aristodemus obeyed these commands and saw the restored men rise, he worshipped the apostle and hastened to the proconsul. Shouting in a loud voice, he told him of the miracles he had seen. Then he formed a salutary resolve and said to the proconsul: “Let us go and, falling at the apostle’s knees, seek pardon.” Then together they came to the apostle and, prostrating themselves, begged forgiveness. He received them kindly, offered God a prayer with thanksgiving, [Col. 0153A] and directed them to undertake a fast of one week. When it was completed, he baptized them with all their relatives, connections, and servants. They broke all the images and built a basilica in the name of Saint John, in which he himself was assumed.

When blessed John was ninety-nine years old, the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him with his disciples and said: “Come to me, for it is time that you feast at my banquet with your brothers.” John rose and began to go, but the Lord said to him: “You shall come to me on the Sunday of my resurrection, which will be five days from now.” Having said this, he was received into heaven. When Sunday came, the whole [Col. 0153B] multitude assembled around John in the church that had been built in his name. From the first cockcrow, celebrating the mysteries of God, he addressed the whole people until the third hour of the day, saying: “My brothers and fellow servants, heirs and sharers in the kingdom of God, recognize our Lord Jesus Christ and consider how many powers, prodigies, signs, and gifts, as well as teaching, he has bestowed upon you through me. Therefore persevere in his commandments, for the Lord now deigns to call me from this world.”

After this he ordered a square grave to be made beside the altar and its earth cast out of the church. Then he descended into it and, stretching out his hands to the Lord, [Col. 0153C] said: “Invited to your banquet, I come giving thanks, because you have deigned, Lord Jesus Christ, to invite me to your feast, knowing that I have desired you with my whole heart. I saw your face and was as though raised from a tomb. Your fragrance awakened eternal desires in me. Your voice is honey-sweet, full of sweetness, and your speech incomparable with the utterances of angels. I wrote down your works, which I saw with my eyes, and the words that I heard with my ears from your mouth. Now, Lord, I commend to you your children, whom your virgin mother, the Church, regenerated to you through water and the Holy Spirit. Receive me so that I may be with my brothers, with whom you invited me when you came. Open for me the gate of life and bring me to the banquet of your feast, where all your friends [Col. 0153D] feast with you. For you are Christ, Son of the living God, who saved the world at the Father’s command. To you we give thanks through ages of ages without end.” When all the people answered “Amen,” such a light appeared over the apostle for about one hour that no one could endure the sight.

[Note: [Col. 0153D] Duchesne and Le Prévost: *nullus* (“no one”).]

Afterward that grave was found full, containing nothing but manna, which that very place produces to this day, where through the merits of the special friend of Jesus Christ a great abundance of miracles continually occurs. Many hasten there, pour out vows and prayers to God, and through the merits of Saint John, apostle and evangelist, receive the desired fulfillment of their prayers; and, with infirmities [Col. 0154A] and dangers driven away, they beneficially experience the power of his prayers. With them I too, a sinner, come and trembling offer my devotion; and, devoted in faith and hope to the Savior’s excellent friend, I pour out this prayer:

> O most blessed John, intimate friend of Christ, chosen as a virgin by the same Lord Jesus Christ, more beloved than the rest, and beyond all others imbued with heavenly mysteries, made his most illustrious apostle and evangelist: I humbly beseech you. Love me, wretched though I am, yet loving you; and mercifully be present as a hearer of my prayers. Look upon my labors and afflictions, by which I am continually distressed, the many infirmities of my body, and the troubles of my character; and by your living merits and prayers devoutly [Col. 0154B] offered to the Lord for me, effectively remove them. Thus, cleansed of faults, may I deserve always to cleave to divine worship and, joined to the snow-white company of the faithful, praise the King Sabaoth forever. Amen.

XII. James the Less.

James the Less, son of Alphaeus, who in the Gospel is called the Lord’s brother because Mary, the wife of Alphaeus, was aunt to the Lord’s mother—whom John the Evangelist calls Mary of Cleophas—was immediately ordained bishop of Jerusalem by the apostles after the Lord’s ascension, and held the governance of that see for thirty years. All the apostles honored him, both because of his surpassing holiness and because of his kinship with the Savior. When they had dispersed to preach in different regions, they returned to him at suitable times as to a father and humbly sought from him, as from a master, whatever necessary counsel reason required. [Col. 0154C]

At last, in the seventh year of Nero’s reign, while he was preaching Christ the Son of God at Jerusalem, he was thrown from the Temple by the Jews and stoned; he was buried there near the Temple on the Kalends of May [1 May].

Hegesippus, a holy and learned man, near to the time of the apostles, mentions James the Just in the fifth book of his *Commentaries*. He relates that after Festus, the governor and successor of Felix, died in Judaea, and the province was without a governor and ruler before Albinus succeeded, James, the brother [Col. 0154D] of the Lord, suffered the cruelty of the Jews and passed to the Lord. He was holy from his mother’s womb. He drank neither wine nor *sicera* (strong drink), and ate no animal food. No iron came upon his head; he was not anointed with oil and did not use baths. He wore no woolen garment, but only linen. He entered the Temple alone and cast himself upon his knees, praying for the people’s forgiveness, so that by praying, continually bending his knees, and never ceasing from prayer, he formed calluses on his knees like those of a camel. Therefore, because of his extraordinary self-restraint and consummate righteousness, he was called “the Just” and *Oblias*, which is interpreted “bulwark of the people.”

[Col. 0155A] Certain persons from the seven Jewish sects questioned him as to what the door of Jesus was. He replied that this was the Savior. For the Jews differ among themselves in seven divisions and depart from the line of truth. The Pharisees and Sadducees, Essenes and Galileans, Hemerobaptists, Basbuthaeans, and Samaritans glory in being called by their particular names, and stubbornly maintain and follow diverse doctrines according to their own inclination. Some of these believed through James that Jesus is the Christ. And when many of the rulers had believed in Jesus, a great disturbance arose among the Jews, Scribes, and Pharisees, who said: “Nothing remains but that the whole people will believe in Jesus, that he himself is the Christ.”

Then, by common counsel, they approached James and reverently [Col. 0155B] asked him to ascend, on the feast-day of Passover, to the lofty place of the Temple’s pinnacle, and to affirm true testimony concerning Jesus before the multitude of Jews and Gentiles who had gathered from neighboring and distant cities. He, however, rejoiced at having an opportunity to make the truth manifest, and promised his compliance to those who entreated him—though not in accordance with the desire of the malicious. For the righteous man understood that this was brought about by divine prompting, and therefore consented to their request. Set on high, he cried out with a loud voice to all the people and firmly and plainly declared that Jesus, the Son of God, had fulfilled all that the prophets had foretold concerning him.

Finally, when James had faithfully finished his discourse, the crowds rejoiced and, glorifying the Lord, said: [Col. 0155C] “Hosanna to the Son of David!” But the Pharisees and other enemies of the truth were greatly distressed; and, having entered into a most wicked counsel among themselves, they cried: “Oh! Even the righteous man has gone astray!” Then they fulfilled what is written in the Book of Wisdom: “Let us take away the righteous man, because he is useless to us” (Wisdom 2:12). For the Pharisees, going up to him, said: “We asked you to remove the people’s error concerning Jesus, and you have increased it.” James said to them: “I have removed error and shown the truth.” But while the crowds rejoiced at his preaching and believed in Jesus, they cast him down from on high and began to press him with stones. Thrown down, he fell upon his knees and prayed: “I beg you, Lord God the Father, forgive [Col. 0155D] them, for they do not know what they are doing.” And while they continued to assail him from above with stones as he prayed thus, one of the priests, of the sons of Rechab, cried out: “Spare him, spare him, I beseech you. What are you doing? This righteous man whom you are stoning is praying for you.” Then a certain Pharisee, enraged, seized a fuller’s club and struck him violently on the head, spilling out his brains. Thus the witness of Jesus Christ was brought to completion by such martyrdom, and there he was buried near the Temple on the Kalends of May [1 May]. Not long afterward came the siege by Vespasian, which prudent Jews believed had occurred by divine action in vengeance for James the Just, as is plainly read in the books of Josephus, the distinguished historian of the Hebrews. While the unbelieving Jews were endangered by a twofold destruction, the Church [Col. 0156A] of God, rejoicing in the true faith and saving powers, invokes with pure devotion a mighty warrior to aid its long contest, and cries in clear voices:

> James the Just, brother of the Lord Jesus,  
> May you have gracious compassion upon us,  
> Whom proud boasting makes guilty  
> And the world’s wantonness has defiled.  
> Mercifully hear our prayers,  
> Obtaining for us the joys of the true light—  
> You who prayed to the Lord for your enemies.  
> Grant aid to those devoted to you,  
> That they may attain the everlasting reward.  
>
> Amen.

## XIII. Philip

Philip is interpreted “mouth of the lamp,” a name showing that he was wholly open to the outpouring of twofold charity and obedient to the divine commands. [Col. 0156B] Endowed and instructed with sacred gifts, like a shining lamp he illumined barbarian peoples by radiant examples and the teaching of truth. He was born at Bethsaida, a city of Galilee, and was among the first to follow Christ’s footsteps. After the Lord’s Ascension, he preached the Gospel for twenty years among the Gauls—or Galatians—and the Scythians, and drew diverse peoples to the knowledge of the true light.

Once in Scythia, while he was being held by Gentiles and was led to the statue of Mars to be compelled to sacrifice, a huge dragon emerged from beneath the base of the statue and struck the son of the priest who was attending the sacrificial fire; it also struck two tribunes who governed that province and whose officers held the holy apostle Philip in chains. By the dragon’s breath all [Col. 0156C] became diseased and began to suffer severely. Then Philip urged them all to believe in the Lord, overthrow and break Mars, and set up in the place where he appeared to stand the cross of the Lord, and worship it. He added that, if these things were done, the sick would be healed, the dead raised, and the deadly dragon put to flight in the name of Jesus Christ. Then those who were tormented, compelled by pain, began to cry: “Let strength be restored to us, and we shall overthrow this Mars.”

When silence had been made, the apostle commanded the dragon immediately to depart in the name of the Lord, to go into the wilderness and harm no one, and to dwell where there was no human access. Then the most savage dragon [Col. 0156D] came out, hurried away, and never appeared anywhere thereafter. The apostle raised in the Lord’s name the priest’s son and the tribunes, who had died, and restored to health the whole diseased crowd. Therefore all who had persecuted the apostle Philip did penance, and, believing him to be a god, wished to worship him. But he continuously taught them for one year, diligently instilled in them knowledge of the supreme God, and eagerly sowed in believing hearts all things that pertain to the true faith. Thus many thousands believed and were baptized by that apostle.

Philip the apostle, aided in many ways by God’s grace, built many churches and ordained bishops and priests, together with the remaining sacred orders, in the Church [Col. 0157A]. Then, returning to Asia by revelation, he remained in the city of Hierapolis and extinguished the malignant heresy of the Ebionites, who deny that the Lord Jesus is the Son of God and deny that he truly took a human body from the Virgin. His two most holy virgin daughters were there, through whom the Lord gained a multitude of virgins.

Seven days before his departure, he summoned to himself priests, deacons, and bishops of neighboring cities, and foretold to them that he would breathe the air of life for only seven more days. Then he exhorted them all to stand manfully in the faith and always to remember the Lord’s teaching. Finally, after abundantly exhorting the people, the blessed apostle departed to the Lord at the age of eighty, on the seventh day before the Kalends of May [25 April]; [Col. 0157B] and his most holy body was buried at Hierapolis. Some years later his two daughters were buried at his right and left; and there, through his merits, many benefits are granted to those who faithfully ask, as the Bridegroom’s friends approach him and sing with exultant voices:

> Bowed low, we beseech you, Philip, mouth of the lamp:  
> Strike the merciful ears of the heavenly Judge,  
> That he may repel the punishments we deserve  
> And grant the heavenly joys for which we pray.  
>
> Amen.

## XIV. Thomas

Thomas means “abyss,” and Didymus means “twin”: he was like the Savior and adorned with many kinds of gifts of virtue. He preached the Gospel [Col. 0157C] to the Parthians and Medes, Hyrcanians and Persians, Bactrians and Indians; and he completed his martyrdom in the city of Calamina, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January [21 December], under King Mesdeus. Not long afterward, he shone forth from there at the city of Edessa through many miracles.

There is much divergence in accounts concerning the apostles, both because of the antiquity of the time and because of the remoteness of the regions where Christ’s husbandmen preached to barbarians, whose differing barbarism departs greatly from Roman customs and usage of speech. Hence we doubt certain things that we read about the holy apostles, because they were published by uncertain authors and transmitted down to us—especially since Pope Gelasius and other great teachers have termed them apocryphal. The eminent bishop Augustine [Col. 0157D] likewise doubted writings of this sort and, with cautious scruple, brought forward a certain example concerning the acts of Saint Thomas against Faustus the Manichaean.

[Note: [Col. 0157D] Saint Augustine, *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, XXII.79. Le Prévost.]

I have said this concerning the discord among writers found here and there throughout the world in ancient volumes, not to disparage the wondrous works of the saints, but so that whatever has been written concerning the apostles or other blessed persons by earlier authors may be examined with subtle caution, for the strengthening of faith and the edification of conduct. Now, in the Lord’s name, I shall briefly continue the narrative that recounts Saint Thomas the apostle’s fruitful journey, his blessed and glorious [Col. 0158A] preaching of Christ, and his laborious passion unto the prize of everlasting life.

When Thomas Didymus was at Caesarea, the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him, commended him to Abbanes, the steward of Gundaforus, king of the Indians, and sent him with Abbanes to India to build the king a palace in Roman workmanship. While they sailed across the sea, Thomas spoke much mystically concerning his knowledge of the craft and promised that he would perform marvelous works in marble and wood in every kind of construction. On the seventh day they prosperously arrived at Andrinopolis; and when they came down from the ship, they heard the voices of singers with organs, pipes, and lyres. The king of that city was celebrating the marriage at which he gave his daughter Pelagia to Dionysius. Heralds went around the city [Col. 0158B] crying that everyone—rich and poor, noble, citizen, and stranger—should attend the royal banquet; whoever did not come would offend the king.

Abbanes therefore attended the banquet with Thomas; but Thomas, according to his usual practice, devoted himself not to amusements or feasting, but to heavenly contemplation. Meanwhile a Hebrew singing-girl carrying a pipe went around beside the meal and sang for each person whatever pleased that one. When she came to Thomas, she lingered longer before him; and seeing a man neither eating nor drinking, but keeping his eyes fixed upon heaven, she understood that he was a Hebrew and a worshipper of the God of heaven. Rejoicing with him as with a compatriot, she began to sing in Hebrew: “There is one God of the Hebrews, who created all things; he made heaven and earth, and he founded the seas.” [Col. 0158C]

On hearing this, the apostle prayed more earnestly and urged the girl, who was singing words of truth, more attentively to repeat the same words. Then the cupbearer rebuked him for neither eating nor drinking, and struck his face with the palm of his hand. But the apostle immediately foretold in Hebrew what would happen to him at once, before the banquet was ended. When the cupbearer went out to fetch water from a spring, a lion attacked him and departed after drinking his blood. Dogs devoured his limbs; and one black dog, holding his right hand in its mouth, brought it into the midst of the banquet. While the guests who beheld this were astonished, the Hebrew singing-girl—who alone had understood his prophecy—threw down her pipe and ran to begin kissing his feet. [Col. 0158D] She said to all present: “This man is either a prophet or an apostle of God.” For when the cupbearer struck him, he foretold in Hebrew the misfortune he suffered: “I shall not rise,” he said, “from this banquet unless I see that very hand brought here by a black dog.”

When the king inquired into the commotion of the people and heard what had happened, he had the apostle summoned to him and asked him to bless his daughter [Note: read: “his daughter’s”] together with her bridegroom.

[Note: [Col. 0158D] Read: *filiae suae*, “his daughter’s.” Le Prévost.]

Thomas therefore entered the bridal chamber with the king, placed his hand upon both their heads, and blessed them in prayer in God’s name, invoking the names of the patriarchs. [Col. 0159A] As the apostle left the bridal chamber and the bridegroom accompanied him, a palm branch full of large dates appeared in his hand. The young man joyfully ran to his bride and gave her some of its fruit to taste. When both had tasted that fruit, they suddenly fell asleep and saw one dream. A mighty king adorned with gems appeared, standing between them and embracing them both, and saying: “My apostle has blessed you [Note: read: ‘for you’], that you may become partakers of eternal life.”

[Note: [Col. 0159D] Read: *vobis*, “for you.” Le Prévost.]

When they awoke and told one another what they had seen, behold, Thomas appeared to them and said: “My King, who has just spoken to you in the vision, himself brought me in through closed doors, so that my blessing [Col. 0159B] may bear fruit upon you. For you have integrity, which is queen of all virtues and the fruit of perpetual salvation. Virginity is the sister of angels and the possession of every good. Virginity is victory over lusts, the trophy of faith, triumph over enemies, and the security of eternal rest. For from corruption arises defilement, from defilement guilt, and from guilt shame.”

After Thomas had spoken these and many other things about the praise of virginity and the ugliness of lust, and had related many unseemly consequences that arise for most people from carnal intercourse, Dionysius and Pelagia gratefully heard all that the apostle taught. Two angels then appeared to them there: “We,” they said, “are angels given to you by God because of the [Col. 0159C] blessing of his apostle, so that, while you keep his admonitions, we may offer to the Lord all your petitions.”

The bridegroom and bride were instructed by these and other pious admonitions. Falling at the apostle’s feet, they said: “Strengthen us in all truth, so that we may lack nothing of the knowledge of God.” He said to them: “I shall come to you on the following night and, after instructing you more fully, shall depart.” Accordingly, as he had promised, he came and carefully instructed both of them in all mysteries of eternal life, and sanctified them with the water of baptism. When this had been done, he sailed away. After some time he sent one of his disciples, whom he ordained priest and established there to remain in that city and organize a church, in which a great people had been gained for God. There is the seat of Thomas [Col. 0159D] the apostle, and the Catholic faith remains there to this day.

Dionysius became a bishop and consecrated his bride with the sacred veil. After his death she underwent a double martyrdom, because she disdained to have a husband and refused to sacrifice to idols. Thus she was beheaded in confession of Christ; and over her tomb was written in Greek language and letters: “In this place rests the bride of Dionysius the bishop and daughter of Thomas the apostle.”

When they came to Hierapolis, a city in India, Abbanes entered before King Gundaforus and announced that Thomas was present, a craftsman of the highest skill. The king [Col. 0160A] discussed with him the construction of a palace and showed him the site for the building. Thomas took a reed and, measuring, said: “Behold, here I shall arrange the doors and the entrance facing the rising sun: first, a forecourt; second, a reception hall; third, an audience chamber; fourth, a three-apsed hall; fifth, winter apartments; sixth, summer apartments; seventh, a heated room and dining rooms with reclining couches; eighth, baths; ninth, gymnasia; tenth, a kitchen; eleventh, swimming pools and flowing water-basins; twelfth, a hippodrome and, around it, arched promenades.”

[Note: [Col. 0159D] Compare Mabillon, *Iter Italicum*, II, p. 11; Muratori, *Annali d’Italia*, IV, 11; and Le Prévost, II, 11, where the palace of the dukes of Spoleto, under the year 814, is described.]

The king considered this and said: “Truly, you are a craftsman, and you deserve to serve kings.” Then, leaving him limitless sums of money, he departed.

The apostle began to travel about provinces and cities, [Col. 0160B] preaching the word of the Lord, baptizing believers, and giving abundantly to the needy. He gained an innumerable people for the Lord, ordained clergy, built churches, and throughout the full two years during which King Gundaforus was absent strengthened the churches. When the king returned and discovered what the apostle had done, he ordered Thomas and Abbanes bound with iron and cast into the depths of prison. Since Gad, the king’s brother, was wasting away at the point of death, he postponed their execution. While he planned to flay them alive and then hand them over to the flames, Gad, his own brother, died. Because he was greatly loved, unbearable mourning ensued. The barbarians, according to the custom of their people, wrapped the dead man in purple and fine linen and adorned his whole body with gems. The king also ordered a memorial [Col. 0160C] built for him from purple stones and the body placed in a purple sarcophagus.

Meanwhile, as craftsmen performed their splendid work and his burial was therefore delayed, Gad himself, who had died, rose again on the fourth day, at the first hour of daylight. Fear, astonishment, and silence came over all who, according to Indian custom, were giving lamentation at the royal funeral. Gad rebuked King Gundaforus because he had intended to flay and burn a friend of God, whom angels serve. He also reported that he had seen in heaven an indescribable palace, built according to the order Thomas had laid out; and he revealed much concerning Thomas’s merits and heavenly secrets. Then he hastened to the prison, freed the apostle from his chains, fell weeping at [Col. 0160D] his feet, and begged forgiveness for his brother.

As the apostle came forth, the king himself, now more restrained, met him and, throwing himself at his feet, begged pardon. Then the apostle, taking a fitting opportunity, began to instruct the barbarians. Proclaiming the truth, he said among other things: “My Lord Jesus Christ has bestowed much upon you, who has shown you his secrets. Behold, your provinces are full of churches. Therefore be ready to be sanctified.” He conveyed these and similar matters to the rulers and instructed them in faith and sacred religion.

[Col. 0161A] Great fame of the miracles the Lord was working through the apostle spread through India; and an immense gathering of people from distant and nearby cities came to him. They wished to sacrifice calves and rams to him according to divine custom, because they thought him to be a god. Gundaforus the king, however, at the apostle’s advice, ordered them to wait for one month until the people of the entire province had gathered together, and then to do what he commanded. When thirty days had been completed, a multitude assembled in a field near the ascent of Mount Gazi; among them was a great multitude afflicted with various illnesses. The apostle ordered all the sick to be gathered in one place, and he stood in their midst, stretched his hands to heaven, [Col. 0161B] and prayed for them.

When the apostle’s prayer was ended, a flash came upon them and terrified them so greatly that they feared they would perish by a lightning stroke. All lay prostrate with the apostle for nearly half an hour and perceived God’s most welcome goodness present with them. Many suffering from fevers, deaf persons, blind persons, and the lame were healed; other infirmities too were driven from people by the Creator’s power. At the apostle’s command, they all rose from the ground and, rejoicing in restored health, glorified the Lord.

Then blessed Thomas climbed upon a rock so that he might see everyone and be seen by everyone; and, when silence had been made, he abundantly gave them true teaching. On the following Sunday, nine thousand [Col. 0161C] men were baptized, apart from children and women. The apostle proceeded by revelation to Upper India, and all peoples hastened to him because of his reputation. They saw the signs and wonders he performed. Therefore, astonished, they did not dare despise his preaching. For he cast out demons, gave sight to the blind, and cleansed lepers. He also drove away every pain, fever, and chill, and even raised the dead.

A certain woman named Sintice, who had been blind for six years, was healed so thoroughly that she retained no sign of her former infirmity. Then Mygdonia, the wife of Carisius, a kinsman of King Mesdeus, was greatly stirred. Changing her dress, she joined her maidservants where Saint [Col. 0161D] Thomas was delivering a most saving discourse concerning the true God. As the apostle taught, the whole multitude believed and, after a fast of seven days, received baptism. But Mygdonia, having heard the word from the apostle’s mouth, no longer wished to touch her husband’s bed. Carisius, enraged, went to the king and obtained from him an order that the apostle be seized and sent to prison. Sintice then led Mygdonia to the prison; after giving a gift to the jailer, she entered to him.

When the apostle heard of Mygdonia’s belief, he ordered her to return quickly to her house and await him there in a locked chamber. At midnight the apostle came, fulfilled his promise by entering the room, strengthened Mygdonia, instructed her in the faith, and ordered her to fast for seven days. On the eighth day he returned in the same manner and baptized the faithful woman [Col. 0162A] with all who had believed.

Carisius, whose sister King Mesdeus had as his wife, asked that Queen Treptia be sent to his wife, so that through her Mygdonia might be recalled to the marriage bed. King Mesdeus consented. Queen Treptia went to her, addressed Mygdonia with crafty blandishments, and strove with all her might to draw her back to her former way of life. But Mygdonia, now founded in Christ, resisted bravely; strong in faith, she fought back as a valiant warrior and vigorously brought the queen, overcome by reason, to Christ. For she answered her with sweet speech, skilfully implanted the apostle’s love in her mind, and thus quickly kindled the woman’s heart by preaching. She said:

“O sister Treptia, if you knew what I have learned, you would [Col. 0162B] not think him a man, but a god. For he gives hearing to the deaf, restores health in every sickness, and sometimes even raises the dead to life. He has shown another life, immortal and knowing no pain or sorrow. This very night a dead man was raised by him. For Simforus, a military commander, went to the prison, received the apostle from the jailers in faith, and took him to his house. The apostle prayed and raised the commander’s only son, who had died. Behold, he now sits in the commander’s house, teaches all who come in to him, and cures every infirmity.”

Treptia replied: “If it is as you assert, let us go; and if I prove that it is truly so, I shall at once believe him. [Col. 0162C] For it is foolish not to seek eternal life and not to believe in such great miracles.” Therefore they went to the commander’s house; having entered, they could not then speak with him, for he was occupied in laying hands upon various illnesses. When the queen saw such great wonders, she said in astonishment: “Accursed by God are those who do not believe in works of salvation.”

Then a man with elephantiasis, horrible in appearance, with a scabby face and a most hoarse voice, was brought in at the apostle’s command. The apostle looked upon him, wept, knelt for a long time in prayer, laid his right hand upon him, and humbly invoked God. Then a boy of radiant appearance appeared, took the leper aside into a hidden corner, stripped him of his garments, and stripped away his skin as though it were a bodily tunic—[Col. 0162D] as one flays a calf—and brought him back to the apostle. Thomas sealed him with the sign of the cross, baptized him, and had him clothed in new white garments. Seeing this, the people magnified God, and the queen, kissing his feet, asked to be baptized. Then the apostle, foreknowing that the time of his departure from the body was near, baptized the queen with all who were present there.

When the queen returned, she admonished the king concerning the faith and steadfastly declared herself a Christian. Then the king’s heart was alarmed, and he angrily cried against Carisius: “While I strive to recover your wife for you, I have lost my own. For Treptia has become worse for me than Mygdonia for you.” He immediately ordered Thomas sent for and brought before him with his hands bound behind his back. When he was brought, the king commanded [Col. 0163A] him to restore the women deceived by his persuasion to the marriage bed. When Thomas refused to do this and preferred to save his persecutors themselves through faith, the angry king ordered iron plates heated and the apostle’s feet stripped, so that, standing barefoot upon them, he might be overcome by pain. At once water burst forth and extinguished the plates.

Then, on Carisius’s advice, he was sent into the furnace of the baths; but the baths could no longer become hot, and on the next day the apostle came out unharmed. Finally, they compelled him to offer sacrifice to an image of the sun. The statue of the sun was made of gold and had a golden four-horse chariot and a car, in which it appeared to be driven rapidly toward the heavens with its reins streaming loose. In the temple the Gentiles danced in barbarian fashion, and virgins sang with [Col. 0163B] lyres, pipes, and drums, with *tituli* [perhaps read *citolis*, a kind of musical instrument] and censers.

[Note: [Col. 0163D] Here *citolis* is perhaps to be read, a kind of musical instrument. See Du Cange’s *Glossarium*, under *Citola*.]

When the king and his friends brought the apostle there and urged him to sacrifice to the image of the sun, he commanded the demon in Hebrew to come out, appear to him, and carry out what had been commanded. The demon came out and stood before him, so that Thomas alone saw him. The apostle spoke with Zabul in Hebrew, and no one knew what he said or to whom he spoke.

At last, when Saint Thomas had bent his knees in worship of the Lord in the temple, and in the king’s presence commanded the demon in Christ’s name to harm no one but to shatter the metal of the image, immediately the idol melted like wax placed by a fire [Col. 0163C] and dissolved. All the priests raised a howl. Then the chief priest of the temple pierced the apostle with a sword. But the king fled with Carisius. A great division arose, since the greater part of the people cried out for the apostle, so that his assailant was sought in order to be burned alive. They honorably carried the apostle’s body into the church with praises and hymns and embalmed it with costly spices; and there great signs and wonders occurred. For demoniacs were freed and every disease was cured.

After a long time, the Syrians petitioned Alexander, Roman emperor, who was returning victorious from the Persian campaign after defeating King Xerxes, and obtained leave for him to send to the rulers of India so that they might return the dead man to his fellow citizens. Thus the apostle’s body was transferred from India and placed in the city of Edessa in a silver coffin suspended by silver chains. [Col. 0163D] No idol-worshipper, no heretic, and no Jew can live there.

Abgarus was king and toparch of that city; he was worthy to receive the letter written by the Savior’s own hand. A baptized child, standing above the city gate, reads it whenever a barbarian people comes against the city. On the very day it is read, the barbarians are either appeased or driven away, being terrified both by the Savior’s writing and by the prayers of Saint Thomas the apostle, [Col. 0164A] or Didymus, who touched the Lord’s side and said: “You are, Lord, my God.”

The venerable archbishop Georgius Florentius Gregorius of Tours writes that he heard the following concerning Saint Thomas from a certain Theodore, who had then travelled as a pilgrim to India and, after returning, related among other things:

> “In India, in the place where the body of the blessed apostle Thomas formerly rested, there is a monastery and a temple of marvelous size, carefully ornamented and constructed. In this building, then, the Lord displays a great miracle. A lamp placed there and lit before the place of his burial continually shines by divine ordinance, day and night, receiving no replenishment of oil or wick from anyone. It is not extinguished by wind, does not fall by accident, and is not diminished by burning. Through the apostle’s power it has an increase unknown to human beings; this is known only to divine power.
>
