> “In the city of Edessa, where we have said that his blessed limbs are buried, when the festival of his translation arrives, a great gathering of people assembles. Those coming from different regions with vows and business are granted permission to sell and buy for thirty days without any levy of toll. During these days, which occur in the fifth month, great and unusual benefits are bestowed upon the people. No disturbance arises among the populace; no fly touches dead flesh; no water fails the thirsty. For although on other days water is drawn there from wells more than a hundred feet deep, now, if [Col. 0164C] you dig only a little, you find abundant waters overflowing. There is no doubt that this is granted through the apostle’s power. When the festival days are over, the toll is restored to the public treasury, the absent fly appears, and the nearness of water disappears. Thereafter rain sent by God cleanses the entire courtyard of the temple so thoroughly from the dirt and varied filth produced during the festival that you would think it had never been trodden.”

[Note: [Col. 0164D] Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, I.32.]

Truly our God, almighty, just, and merciful Judge, and patient rewarder, wondrously glorifies his saints and crowns them ineffably with everlasting honor; he corrects humankind by terrifying it and saves it through repentance by punishing it. Therefore, let us ourselves, groaning in the valley of weeping, give thanks for his ineffable benefits [Col. 0164D] and hasten to him by cleaving to his commandments. Let us also entreat the blessed apostle Thomas, who is called Didymus, and confidently sing to him:

> O Thomas, explorer of Christ’s side,  
> By those holy wounds we beseech you,  
> Which washed away all the world’s crimes,  
> Wipe away our guilt by your prayers.  
>
> We feel the grievous wounds of sins,  
> For which we utter anxious sighs.  
> Weeping, we pray: graciously offer  
> For us prayers to the Thunderer in your power. Amen.

## XV. Bartholomew

Bartholomew is a Syriac [name], and is interpreted [Col. 0165A] “son of him who suspends the waters.” In his allotted preaching he received Lycaonia; then he evangelized in Assyria and Third India. At last, while living in Albanus, a city of Greater Armenia, he was flayed by barbarians and beheaded at the order of King Astyages; and thus he was buried on the ninth day before the Kalends of September [24 August]. His most sacred body was first translated to the island of Lipari, then to Benevento, in the year 809 from the Lord’s Incarnation, and is honored by the faithful with devout veneration. Now it is fitting carefully to investigate the whole course of his passion and briefly insert it into our narrative from ancient codices.

Historiographers assert that there are three Indias, in which there were said to be five thousand towns and nine thousand peoples. The first India extends toward [Col. 0165B] Ethiopia, the second toward the Medes, and the third forms the boundary, because on one side it has the region of darkness and on the other the Ocean Sea. Into this India, therefore, the apostle Bartholomew came and entered a temple in which there was an idol of Astaroth; and there he began to remain as a stranger.

When the apostle arrived, Astaroth fell silent: he gave no answers to those consulting him and could not aid those whom he had afflicted. The temple was already full of sufferers, and though sacrifices were offered daily Astaroth gave no answer. The sick, brought from far-off regions, piteously bewailed their pains; and the worshippers of the idol gained nothing either by sacrifice or by lacerating themselves in their custom. [Col. 0165C] They went to another city where another demon, named Beerith, was worshipped; offering sacrifice to him, they asked concerning the silence of their god and their other circumstances. He said to them: “Your god is held captive and bound in fiery chains, so that he does not dare even sigh or speak, since the apostle of God, Bartholomew, entered there.”

When they asked who this Bartholomew was, the demon replied: “He is a friend of God Almighty, and he has come into this province to abolish the divine powers worshipped by the Indians.” The worshippers of Astaroth said: “Tell us his signs, so that amid many thousands we may recognize him.” He answered: “His hair is black and curly; his flesh fair; his eyes large; his nostrils even and straight; [Col. 0165D] his ears covered by the hair of his head; his beard long, with a few gray hairs; his stature well proportioned, so that it is not noticeably either short or excessively tall. He is clothed in a white tunic striped with purple; he wears a white cloak with a single purple jewel at each corner. It is twenty-six years since his garments have ever become dirty or old. Likewise, the sandals on his feet have never worn out during twenty-six years. He prays to God with bent knees a hundred times by day and a hundred times by night. His voice is powerful like a trumpet. Angels of God walk with him; they do not allow him to become weary or hungry. He remains always of the same countenance and spirit, always cheerful and glad at every hour. He foresees all things, knows all things, and both speaks and [Col. 0166A] understands every language of all peoples. Behold, even what you ask and what I answer concerning him, he already knows. Angels of God serve him and report these things to him.” Having spoken these and many other things, the demon fell silent.

On returning, they went around the lodging places of all strangers and inspected every individual’s face and attire, but for two days they did not find God’s apostle. Finally, a certain demoniac named Seusticus cried out: “Apostle Bartholomew, your prayers burn me.” The apostle said to him: “Be silent and come out of him.” Immediately the man was freed, though he had been tormented by the demon for many years.

When Polemius, king of that province, heard this, he sent to him, asking him to heal his daughter, who was possessed by the moon-madness; she used to seize with her bite, tear, and strike everyone whom she could lay hold of. [Col. 0166B] The apostle therefore rose and went with the king’s messenger, and ordered the girl, who was tightly bound in chains, to be loosed. But when the servants were afraid to approach her, the apostle said: “I hold bound the enemy who was within her. Go and release her; wash and refresh her, and bring her to me tomorrow morning.” They went and did as the apostle commanded, and the demon could no longer torment her. Then the king loaded camels with gold and silver, gems and garments, and sought the apostle; but, since he was not found, all was carried back to the palace.

When dawn began on the following day and the king was shut up in his chamber, the apostle appeared to him alone and instructed him in the true faith and saving doctrine. [Col. 0166C] For he set forth in order the incarnation of the Word of God from the undefiled Virgin Mary, and carefully expounded the threefold temptation and the threefold victory.

King Polemius accepted the apostolic preaching and deliberately ordered the priests of the idols to sacrifice on the next day. As they sacrificed at the first hour of the day, the demon spoke and complained of the torments by which angels afflicted him. At the apostle’s command, he also openly confessed his deceits, by which he wounded the wretched.

Then the apostle said to the people: “Behold him whom you thought a god, who cared for you. Hear now the true God, your Creator, who dwells in heaven; and if you wish me to pray for you and for all the sick who are present to receive health, cast down and [Col. 0166D] break this idol. When you have done this, I shall consecrate this temple in Christ’s name.” Therefore, at the king’s command, all the people brought ropes and pulleys, but they could not overthrow the image. The apostle said to them: “Untie its bonds.” And when they had untied everything, he commanded the demon to go out and smash the image. At once it went out and shattered every kind of idol. Therefore all who saw this cried with one voice: “One is the almighty God, whom his apostle Bartholomew preaches.” Then the blessed apostle stretched out his hands to the Lord and prayed long for the salvation of all who were present. When all had answered Amen, an angel of the Lord appeared, radiant as the sun and having wings; he flew around the four corners of the temple and with his finger [Col. 0167A] carved the sign of the cross upon the squared stones. Then he commanded them to make the sign of the cross upon their foreheads with their finger. And he displayed an enormous Egyptian, blacker than soot, with a sharp face, a long beard, hair reaching to his feet, and fiery eyes flashing sparks like heated iron. From his mouth and nostrils issued a sulphurous flame. He had thorny feathers and wings like a sphinx, and his hands were bound behind his back and tightly fastened with fiery chains. After malignant Satan had been seen by all the people and was released by the angel, who commanded him to go to a desert place where there was no human habitation and there await the Day of Judgment, he gave forth a most dreadful howl in a terrible voice, flew away, and was nowhere seen. The angel of the Lord, in the sight of [Col. 0167B] all, then flew up to heaven.

Then King Polemius, together with his wife and two sons, with his whole army and all the people who had been saved, with all the people of his city and of the neighboring cities belonging to his kingdom, believed and was baptized; and, laying aside the diadem from his head along with the purple robe, he began to attach himself to the apostle. Meanwhile, the worshippers and priests of all the temples assembled and complained to King Astyages, his elder brother, as follows: “Your brother has become the disciple of a magician, who claims our temples for himself and destroys our gods.” As they reported this weeping, behold, priests from other cities likewise came and made the same report with tears. King Astyages, therefore, angered, sent a thousand armed men with the priests [Col. 0167C] to bring the apostle bound before him wherever they found him. When he had been brought before the king and had steadfastly answered questions concerning the true God, it was reported to the king that his god Waldach had fallen and been broken into pieces. Then the king tore the purple garment which he wore, had the holy apostle beaten with clubs, and commanded that, after being beaten, he be beheaded. Countless people from twelve cities who had believed came; with hymns and every honor they bore away his body, built for him a basilica of marvelous size, and placed his most sacred body in it. On the thirtieth day after his burial, King Astyages and all the priests were seized by a demon; coming to his shrine, [Col. 0167D] they confessed the apostle and, by God’s judgment, died. Therefore great fear fell upon all unbelievers. All, seeing the manifest vengeance of God, believed and were baptized by the presbyters whom the apostle Bartholomew had ordained.

King Polemius was ordained bishop by the apostle through a revelation, with the acclamation of all the people and clergy. Performing signs, he lived twenty years in the episcopate; and when all things had been accomplished, well ordered, and firmly established, he passed to the Lord.

After many years had elapsed, persecution again came upon the Christians. When the pagans saw [Col. 0168A] all the people thronging to the tomb of blessed Bartholomew and bringing there incense for continual supplication, they were enticed by envy, took away his body, put it in a lead sarcophagus, and cast it into the sea. But through God’s providential aid, the lead sarcophagus was raised and borne by the waters from that place to the island of Lipari; and there it was revealed to the Christians that they should receive it honorably. It was gathered up and buried there, a great church was built over it, and a community of monks devoted to divine worship was established.

## XVI. Matthew

Matthew Levi, as he himself relates in his Gospel, was a tax collector; but he was called by the Lord from among the publicans, [Col. 0168B] added to the number of the apostles, and adorned with manifold grace. He first evangelized in Judaea, afterward preached in Macedonia, and finally in Ethiopia. After converting King Eglippus with many thousands of his people and baptizing them into Christ, he suffered martyrdom under Hyrtacus Adelphus while celebrating Mass; and thus, blessed, he passed to the Lord on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October [21 September]. The course of the preaching and passion of the blessed Evangelist is found in ancient books as follows.

After the apostle Matthew had written the Gospel in Judaea in the Hebrew tongue, he went to the Ethiopians at God’s command and, performing divine works, saved many. For, entering the great city Nadaber, he exposed the impostures of the magicians Zaroes and Arphaxath, [Col. 0168C] who said that they were gods and thus deceived King Eglippus and his people. They caused people to remain motionless for as long as they wished. They restrained human sight and hearing from their functions. They commanded serpents to strike, and then in turn healed by incantation. Thus their reputation spread throughout Ethiopia and drew peoples from remote parts of Ethiopia to hurry to the magicians and, deceived, to worship their deceivers. Indeed, as the common saying has it, the wicked are shown greater reverence through fear than the good through love.

Therefore the merciful Lord, caring for humankind, sent the apostle Matthew, through whom he aided the Ethiopians stained with a double blackness. When an Ethiopian eunuch named Candacis saw him—[Note: [Col. 0167D] Cf. above, chap. 11.]—he who [Col. 0168D] had been baptized by Philip, deacon of the apostles, joyfully fell at his feet and, worshipping him, received him into his house. All the friends of Candace’s eunuch came to him; hearing the word of life, they believed in Christ Jesus the Lord, and very many were baptized, seeing that the apostle of God nullified every evil which the magicians inflicted upon people. For they injured those whom they could so that the injured would seek them out; and they were thought to heal because they ceased from inflicting injury. But Matthew, apostle of Christ, not only healed those whom they harmed, but also cured all who were brought to him, afflicted by various illnesses. He preached the truth of God [Col. 0169A] to the people, so that all wondered at his eloquence, because he spoke Greek, Egyptian, and Ethiopian speech excellently. When Candace asked confidently and affectionately, he eloquently explained how, through human presumption at the tower of Babel, the confusion of languages had occurred; and, conversely, how the incarnate Godhead, through Christ’s humility, redeemed the human race, crushed the ancient enemy, kindled his chosen servants with the fire of the Holy Spirit, and fully taught them knowledge of every language and all the wisdom of the Scriptures. While the holy apostle gladly brought forth many salutary things from the treasury of wisdom for the people who listened willingly, someone came saying that the magicians were arriving, each with a dragon. The dragons wore helmets, and their breath issued flaming heat; they breathed sulphurous vapors from their nostrils, whose smell killed people. Then Saint Matthew signed himself with the cross and, though Candace’s eunuch tried to prevent him, went out without fear. As soon as the two magicians appeared, both dragons fell asleep at his feet. Then the apostle said to the magicians: “Where is your art? If you can, awaken them.” But they tried to awaken the dragons by magical art and could not do so at all. Meanwhile the people gathered, and seeing this were astonished. Finally the blessed apostle, in the Lord’s name, commanded the savage serpents to return to their place in complete gentleness and depart without injuring anyone. Immediately the serpents raised their heads, [Col. 0169C] began to go, and, leaving the city through open gates, were nowhere seen.

Then the holy Evangelist addressed the rejoicing people in a kindly discourse and recounted the sequence of the creation of the first human being and the delightfulness of Paradise, the envy and deception of the apostate angel, the fall of the first-created Adam through transgression, and his restoration through the Passion of the Son of God. While the apostle discoursed further upon this abundant subject matter, suddenly a mournful tumult arose: Euphranon, son of King Eglippus, was mourned as dead. The magicians stood at his funeral and, because they could not raise him, maintained to the king that he had been taken away by the gods into their company; they urged that he should be counted as one of the gods and that an image and temple should be made for him. But Queen Euphenisia, having received sounder counsel from faithful Candace and having contemptuously rejected the magicians, sent honorable barons reverently to summon the apostle Matthew to the king. When he entered, she immediately prostrated herself at his knees [Col. 0169D] and faithfully and devoutly begged that he would raise her son. The blessed apostle rejoiced in her good faith, prayed to the all-powerful Lord for the dead boy’s resurrection, then took the boy’s hand and commanded him in the name of Jesus Christ to rise; immediately the boy rose.

When the king saw so great a miracle, his heart trembled. He ordered crowns and purple garments to be brought to him at once, and sent heralds through the cities and diverse provinces of Ethiopia, saying: “Come to the city and see [Col. 0170A] the Lord hidden in the likeness of a man.” When the entire multitude had come with candles and lamps, incense and various kinds of sacrifices, Saint Matthew addressed them all thus: “I am not God, but the servant of almighty God, who sent me to you so that you might abandon error and, knowing the true Lord, worship him. Remove gold, golden crowns, and silver from before my eyes. Go, build a temple for the Lord, that there you may assemble and together hear the word of God.”

Hearing this, they went away rejoicing. Sixty thousand people began to build a temple for God, and within thirty days they completed the holy church. Matthew named it Resurrection, because of the raising of the king’s son. He sat there for twenty-three years, appointed presbyters and [Col. 0170B] deacons, ordained bishops in cities and villages, and built many churches. The king and queen and diverse peoples of the Ethiopians received Christ’s baptism, and the frightened magicians fled to the Persians. Countless miracles were performed through blessed Matthew, which cannot all be recounted individually. For many blind people received sight, paralytics were healed, demoniacs were saved, and even the dead were raised.

The most Christian King Eglippus, having completed old age, went to the Lord, and Hyrtacus Adelphus received his kingdom. He wished to take as wife Ephigenia, daughter of the dead king, who had already been consecrated to Christ, had received the sacred veil from the apostle’s hand, and was superior of more than two hundred virgins. [Col. 0170C] Hoping that through the apostle he could sway Ephigenia’s mind, he began to negotiate with him, saying: “Take half my kingdom, if only I may unite Ephigenia in marriage with myself.” Then blessed Matthew commanded the king, Ephigenia, and all the people to be present in church on the Sabbath, in order that they might hear the words of almighty God. This was done. When great silence had been made in the assembly, he began to speak, wisely and eloquently discussing continence, good marriage, and reasonable conduct. For he clearly demonstrated that gluttony in eating flesh or marital intercourse involves defilement but is free from guilt. “For bodily uncleanness is washed away by God through almsgiving and works of mercy, but not crimes, [Col. 0170D] which are not washed away except by tears of repentance. If anyone, on the same day after taking fleshly food, should presume to partake of the spiritual food of the Lord’s body, he becomes guilty through both of sin, impropriety, and presumption—not because he ate, but because, contrary to order, justice, and God’s rule, he appropriated the good of the Eucharist. Thus homicide and lying, although evil by their own nature, nevertheless seem to become good on account of their purpose. For if someone lies in order to hide an innocent person and protect him from an enemy by lies, or if a judge condemns one criminal in judgment lest he kill many innocents, a good and useful fruit springs from it. This is plainly apparent in the killing of Goliath, Sisera, Haman, and Holofernes. Thus marriages, when contracted, arise in the honorableness of a good work, if they are joined in holiness and justice. But if a king’s servant should dare to appropriate his lord’s betrothed, he is known to have incurred not merely an offense but so great a crime that he rightly is delivered alive to the fires of the flames. This happens not because he took a wife, but because he wronged one who was his superior.”

By these and other plain examples the apostle Matthew dissuaded King Hyrtacus from marrying Ephigenia, who was consecrated to God, lest he incur the wrath of the heavenly King by rashly joining her to himself in marriage. Hyrtacus, inflamed with anger, departed; but the apostle continued steadfastly and cheerfully in teaching and prayer. Then he blessed Ephigenia, who lay prostrate at his feet before all the people, and placed a veil upon the heads of all the virgins who were there. [Col. 0171B] When the mysteries of the Lord had been received by the entire church after Mass had been celebrated, and everyone had returned home, he remained beside the altar where he had consecrated the body of the Lord; there, praying with hands outstretched, he received martyrdom. For an executioner sent by Hyrtacus struck the apostle from behind with a thrust of the sword and thus made him Christ’s martyr. On hearing this, the whole people proceeded with fire toward the palace, but the presbyters and deacons, along with other religious men, scarcely restrained them by sacred admonitions from burning the king with all his household. Ephigenia, however, gave whatever gold, silver, and gems she could possess to the priests and clergy, that they might build from them a basilica worthy of the apostle and distribute the remainder to the poor. Hyrtacus, meanwhile, [Col. 0171C] first tried to tempt her through noblewomen, then strove to seduce her through magicians. At last, when nothing had advanced his desire, he ordered the residence in which she dwelt with Christ’s virgins, serving her God day and night, to be surrounded with fire. But as fire burned all around it, the angel of the Lord appeared with Saint Matthew the apostle, strengthened the sacred virgins, and promised swift deliverance. Immediately God stirred up a very strong wind, turned the whole blaze away from the house of his virgin, and consumed the king’s palace with its possessions. He himself barely escaped with his only son; but even from this he gained no joy. For a most violent demon filled his son and, rushing rapidly, brought him to the tomb of the apostle Matthew; with his hands bound behind him by the devil himself, he compelled him to confess his father’s crimes. The king himself became elephantiasic [afflicted with elephantiasis], fell upon a sword, and died; piercing his own stomach with his hand, he paid the penalty for the apostle’s death. All the people mocked at his death, seized Behor, Ephigenia’s brother, who had been baptized by the apostle, and raised him to be their king. He began to reign in the twenty-fifth year of his age and ruled for sixty-two years, maintaining the firmest peace with the Romans and Persians. All the provinces of Ethiopia were filled with catholic churches, and great wonders occur at the confession-shrine of the blessed apostle Matthew. He was the first to write the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ in the Hebrew language; it was discovered in the time of Emperor Zeno, through his own revelation. [Col. 0172A] Holy Mother Church solemnly celebrates his memory on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October [21 September], and sings to him in the sweet melody of voice and mind:

> Holy Matthew, mighty in a double office,  
> Intercede diligently with Jesus by your prayers,  
> That he may guide us amid the world’s storms,  
> Lest everlasting destruction afterward swallow us up.

Amen.

## XVII. Simon Jude, or Thaddaeus

Simon the Canaanite—that is, the Zealot—was from Cana, a village of Galilee, where the Lord changed water into wine. This distinguishes him from Simon Peter and from Judas the betrayer, who was also called Simon Iscariot. He received primacy in Egypt.

Judas of James bore three names. For he was called Judas, Thaddaeus, [Col. 0172B] and Lebbaeus. He preached in Mesopotamia and in the interior regions of Pontus. Then both entered Persia together, and, after subjecting an innumerable multitude of that nation to Christ, completed their martyrdom on the fifth day before the Kalends of November [28 October].

Craton, a disciple of the apostles, wrote at length concerning what they did during thirteen years and what they suffered in Persia; he included everything in ten books. Africanus the historian translated this into Latin. Abdias also, bishop of Babylon, who had been ordained by them, wrote an account of them in the Hebrew language. All these things were translated into Greek by Eutropius, their disciple; and all were likewise rendered into Latin by Africanus. From this an abridgment was extracted, welcome to those [Col. 0172C] wishing to know what the beginnings of their preaching were, and by what end they left the world and passed into the heavenly kingdoms.

The holy apostles Simon and Jude therefore entered Persia by revelation of the Holy Spirit. There they found two magicians, Zaroes and Arphaxat, who had fled from Ethiopia before the face of the holy apostle Matthew. Their teaching was perverse and full of deadly blasphemy against the Lord and the prophets. As the apostles entered Persia, Warardach, governor and commander of Xerxes, king of the Babylonians, met them. He had undertaken war against the Indians, invaders of the frontiers of Persia. When the apostles arrived, the demons that gave answers of their deceit to those sacrificing at each station fell silent. Therefore their worshippers went to the shrine of a neighboring city to consult them. The demon gave the inquirers a bellowing reply, announcing that, while the apostles of God Simon and Jude were present, their gods could not speak. Then Commander Warardach caused the apostles to be sought out. When they were found, he asked who they were and whence they had come; he heard that they had come there from the Hebrew race for the common cause of salvation. When he asked them to grant his gods power to answer, and they had permitted it after pouring forth prayer, their frenzied devotees were immediately seized by demons and prophesied that a great war would take place and that many would fall on each side. The apostles laughed, but the commander was frightened; yet, at their persuasion, [Col. 0173A] he awaited envoys of peace there until the following day. Since the profane priests raged against the apostles and asserted that ragged, contemptible persons ought neither to speak nor be heard amid Babylonian riches, the commander ordered the apostles and the mad priests to be kept under guard until the next day, and there, following apostolic counsel, considered the outcome of the affair.

On the next day the word of the apostles was fulfilled. For the commander’s messengers returned at full speed on dromedaries with the Indian envoys and reported that all was as the apostles had declared. The Indians had restored the lands they had invaded, paid tribute, and established a most firm treaty of peace. Finally, after the commander had proved the apostles truthful by the attesting manifest event, he angrily ordered a great fire to be kindled and commanded that the priests with their accomplices be thrown into the fire.

But the apostles, mindful of the Lord’s command, prostrated themselves before the commander and, scattering dust upon their heads, pleaded for their enemies not to perish. To the astonishment of all, they plainly declared that this was the teaching of our God.

At last Warardach ordered the priests to be counted and all their property investigated, so that it might be given to the apostles. There were found to be one hundred and twenty temple priests. Each received from the treasury one pound of gold in each month; but the chief priest received four times as much gold [Col. 0173C] as the others. Their wealth in gold and silver, garments and beasts of burden was so great that it could not be counted. The commander offered it to the apostles, but they entirely rejected it and instead ordered it distributed to the needy.

Then, while the commander praised before King Xerxes his successes and the apostles’ proclamations, Zaroes and Arphaxat, who were with the king, began to disparage the apostles and tried to stir everyone against them unless they worshipped their gods. But the commander always spoke well on behalf of the apostles. At last a public dispute was arranged in the king’s presence. When the magicians had spoken openly before all, every advocate was rendered mute, and for almost an hour no one among those who had recently been noisy and eloquent could utter anything. Then they were permitted to speak, but could not walk; and afterward, when their steps had been restored, they saw nothing though their eyes were open. Those who saw this were terrified and held the magicians in reverence more through fear than love. Such a spectacle lasted from early morning until the sixth hour, and the advocates returned sadly and in confusion to their homes.

The commander then told the apostles, whom he greatly loved, all these things. He summoned the aforesaid advocates to his house and presented to them the apostles of God, Simon and Jude, through whom they could overcome the magicians if they obeyed their counsels. But when the advocates saw men dressed in very shabby clothing, they began to hold them almost in contempt. Simon rebuked their swelling [Col. 0174A] insolence in a most salutary discourse. He clearly showed that some worthless things are shut away in chests of gold and gems, while precious jewels are stored in the meanest wooden boxes; that beautiful vessels are filled with vinegar, while vessels most ugly in appearance are filled with excellent wine. Thus great virtues sometimes flourish in persons contemptible to the eye, and by their eminent merits please the highest Creator in every respect.

Then the holy apostles instructed the advocates with salutary admonitions, commended them to God in holy prayers, and marked their foreheads with the sign of the cross. Zebedee and the other advocates boldly entered the king’s presence and mocked the magicians; but the magicians could not harm them in any way. The angry magicians therefore caused a multitude of serpents to come, and all who saw this were exceedingly terrified. At the king’s command the apostles were hurriedly summoned. On arriving, they filled their cloaks with serpents and boldly threw them upon the magicians; immediately the serpents began to devour their flesh. The magicians howled like wolves, while all who openly watched the torments of the impious rejoiced. The king and all the people said to the apostles: “Allow them to die.” But they replied: “We were sent to lead people from death to life, not to hurl them from life into death.” Then they prayed and commanded the serpents to take all their venom from the magicians and return to their places. Therefore the magicians suffered greater torments when [Col. 0174C] all the serpents again ate their flesh and sucked their blood in order to draw out their venom. When the serpents had departed and, by the apostles’ sentence, the magicians had spent three anxious days without eating, drinking, or sleeping, the apostles came to visit them and, “not returning evil for a curse” [Rom. 12:17], healed them. Yet they remained in their perfidy; and just as they had fled Ethiopia before the holy apostle Matthew, so they withdrew from these two, covered with shame, and stirred up idol-worshippers throughout Persia to hostility toward the apostles. They themselves sacrificed in all the temples and by their tricks made people suddenly rigid and suddenly released, suddenly blind and then seeing, suddenly deaf and then hearing. Thus they made sport of those who sacrificed to idols and were like themselves.

At the request of the king and commander, the apostles remained in Babylon, performing great wonders in the Lord’s name: restoring hearing to the deaf, movement to the lame, sight to the blind, cleansing lepers, and driving demons out of possessed bodies. They therefore had many disciples, from whom they ordained presbyters, deacons, and clergy in the churches.

There a daughter of a very wealthy satrap was endangered in childbirth after being defiled, and the deacon Eustosinus was accused of the crime of incest. When they heard this, the apostles ordered the girl’s parents and the deacon to be present, and the infant [Col. 0175A] born at the first hour of that same day to be brought. When they commanded the infant to speak, it said in perfectly clear speech: “This deacon is a holy and chaste man and has never defiled his flesh.” When the parents pressed it to inquire concerning the person guilty of incest, the apostles said: “It is fitting for us to acquit the innocent; it is not fitting to expose the guilty.”

Nicharon, a friend of the king, received an arrow in his knee during military exercise, and it could not by any means be drawn from the bone. Then blessed Simon invoked the Lord Jesus; as soon as he applied his hand, he removed the arrow, and the man was immediately healed, so that not even a mark of the wound appeared.

[Col. 0175B] Two most ferocious tigers escaped from separate cages and began to devour whatever they could find. Then all the people fled to the apostles of God. The apostles invoked the name of the Lord Jesus, and the beasts, which had never been accustomed to become tame, became gentle as lambs. By day they remained among the people like sheep; by evening they returned to the apostles’ little cell. When the apostles moved on to other cities, the tigers themselves guarded their dwelling. The gracious preachers therefore took from this material for discourse and taught the people what rational human beings should do and how they ought to obey God; they set before their eyes, as if with a finger, the example of brute animals.

At the king’s and people’s request, they remained in Babylon for one year and three months. During that time more than sixty thousand men, excluding children and women, were baptized. First the king and all his dignitaries received the faith. For they saw every sickness cured by a word, blind persons enlightened, and dead persons raised. Abdias, who had come with them from Judaea and had himself seen the Lord Jesus with his own eyes, was ordained bishop, and the city was filled with churches. When these matters had been duly arranged, they departed. Crowds of disciples followed them—two hundred men and more. They traversed the twelve provinces of Persia and their cities.

Now it is time to relate how the holy apostles suffered [Col. 0175D] martyrdom. The aforementioned magicians Zaroes and Arphaxat committed crimes through the cities, declared themselves to be of the race of gods, and always fled before the apostles. They remained in whatever city they were in only until they learned that the apostles were coming there. At Sanir there were priests of seventy temples; each received one pound of gold from the king four times yearly [Note: [Col. 0175D] Duchesne and Le Prévost: “one pound of gold each”], when they celebrated a feast of the sun—that is, at the beginning of spring, summer, autumn, and winter. The aforementioned magicians stirred up everyone they could against the apostles everywhere and earnestly made this their prior concern.

After the holy apostles had traversed all the provinces and lodged at Sanir in the house of their disciple Sennes, behold, at about the first hour all the priests together rushed in and, shouting horribly at Sennes, ordered the enemies of their gods to be brought out. Meanwhile the holy apostles were seized and led to the Temple of the Sun. As they entered, demons cried out through possessed persons: “What have we to do with you, apostles of the living God? At your entry we are burned with flames.” In one eastern chamber of the temple stood a cast-gold quadriga of horses, in which stood a likewise cast representation of the sun’s radiance. In another chamber stood a cast-silver moon, with a two-ox chariot, likewise cast in silver. As priests and magicians with the people compelled the apostles to worship, they spoke together in Hebrew about the vision of our Lord Jesus [Col. 0176B] Christ, whom they contemplated calling them amid angels. An angel of the Lord also appeared to them and strengthened them. Then, when silence had been made, they spoke to the people and reasonably exposed their error: they uselessly bestowed on a creature the honor due to God alone, and, not without insult, enclosed in man-made dwellings the sun and moon, which God had created in heaven from the beginning and ordained to stand open to the whole world and shine. While all were astonished, Simon commanded the demon to go out and shatter the image of the sun and its quadriga. Likewise, Jude commanded the image of the moon to be broken. Then two Ethiopians, black and naked and terrible in appearance, were seen to come out before all the people; as they broke the images, they uttered a terrible-voiced howl. The frenzied priests therefore rushed upon the apostles and killed them while they rejoiced and gave thanks to God. Their host Sennes also suffered with them, because he scorned to sacrifice to idols. At that very hour, although the sky was very clear, tremendous lightning occurred, so that the temple was split in three from the summit of its roof to its lowest foundation. Zaroes and Arphaxat were scorched by a thunderbolt and turned to ashes.

Three months later King Xerxes blinded all the priests, transferred the apostles’ bodies with immense honor to his own city, and built there a basilica in an octagonal circuit, each of its eight sides eighty [Col. 0176D] feet long, so that the circuit measured eight times eighty feet, while its height was one hundred and twenty feet. He built it all of squared marble and *synmatic* stonework [uncertain term], and overlaid its vaulted ceilings with sheets of gold. In the middle of the octagon he set up a sarcophagus of pure silver. He labored constantly on the building for four years, and, completing it on their feast day—that is, the fifth day before the Kalends of November [28 October]—was granted to dedicate the basilica in honor of the saints. In that place believers receive divine benefits who venerate their martyrdoms, which they bore witness to our Lord Jesus Christ even unto death. We also, who in hope of the Lord recall these things in writing, [Col. 0177A] joyfully praise the blessed apostles as companions and guests of the highest King; and in the courts of Jerusalem, which is our mother, we devoutly sing with the children crying “Hosanna” to the Redeemer:

> Blessed Simon and renowned Thaddaeus,  
> Behold our groans with tears;  
> We who through the Fall deserved the abyss,  
> Through you may we deserve entrance into heaven.

Amen.

## XVIII. Matthias

Matthias, one of the seventy disciples, was chosen by lot by the apostles to take Judas’s place. He preached in Judaea and suffered there for Christ. His feast is celebrated on the sixth day before the Kalends of March [24 February], and the consecrated company, devoutly approaching, prays to him in song:

> [Col. 0177B] Righteous Matthias, seated by lot upon the twelvefold throne,  
> Loose us from every bond of guilt,  
> That through your holy prayers  
> We may enjoy the joys of the true light.

Amen.

Judas Simon Iscariot was born of the tribe of Issachar and was numbered among the twelve apostles. But because, inflamed by deadly greed, he sold his own master and lord to the Jews for thirty pieces of silver, he lost the dignity of the apostleship; and, a wretch who repented wrongly, he hanged himself with a noose. Even now he has many followers in the Church: those who wish to be called by the sacred name without righteous deeds. Though unworthy, Judas indeed bore names worthy and mystical, by which false Christians are figuratively denoted in the Church. For Judas means “confessing,” and by this name are foreshadowed those who, as the Apostle says, “profess that they know God, but deny him by their deeds” (Titus 1:16). Moreover, Simon means “obedient”; by this designation are represented hypocrites, deceivers, and falsely obedient persons, who serve the Lord’s commandments not out of love for God and longing for heaven, but outwardly comply with the commands of their superiors for empty glory, human favour, and a passing reward. Many of these, like Judas Iscariot, are blinded by excessive greed and, abandoning the pursuit and fellowship of good things, willingly fall into detestable crimes; ensnared beyond release in the cords of their sins, they perish. For they rejoice in a passing reward in this present age, and here swell proudly at a recompense received for certain honourable and conspicuous observances; but in the world to come, bound in an inextricable knot, they will mourn in Tartarean filth-pits and, tortured with an unspeakable kind of punishment for their crimes, will be deprived of every hope of forgiveness.

When Judas the traitor departed from the company of the apostles, what did those who remained with the Lord Jesus deserve? Ineffable glory and everlasting blessedness. Holy Mother Church believes, and every Catholic faithfully declares, that the twelve apostles are truly blessed and exalted, and sharers in eternal happiness. For they are the sun [Note: [Col. 0177D] Duchesne and Le Prévost: “sal.”] of the earth and the light of the world, the twelve hours of the unending day, the fruitful branches of the fertile vine, Christ’s fellow-workers and his co-heirs in the heavenly kingdom. They are everywhere commemorated in the celebrated memory of the faithful and honoured among all nations where the true faith rules; and they are reverently called teachers of the nations and governors of the churches: namely, judges of the world appointed by Christ, stern censors of the reprobate, merciful helpers of the devout, and unceasing intercessors. For, despising all worldly things, they clung inseparably to Christ, who is the true vine and life. Now they reign in heaven with that same King of kings; they rejoice with the angels in his everlasting praise; and, seated upon twelve thrones, they judge the twelve tribes of Israel with the Lord. I have investigated their deeds as they are read in the Church, and have made an abbreviated compilation of them from what I found in ancient books.

Henceforth I desire to treat of their companions and successors, and, with God’s help, shall devoutly entrust the memory of certain of them to this work. I do this not because they need my praise, whose praise is God himself, who reigns as Three and One in eternity and blesses his own with himself through eternal recompense, but so that by doing this I may show them my devotion and obtain their favour, that through their intercession I may piously attain my salvation.

## XIX. History of the Disciples: Barnabas

Joseph, therefore, who was surnamed Barnabas—that is, “son of consolation”—was by birth from the city of Cyprus, [Col. 0178C] which was founded by Cyrus, king of the Persians. In the third year after the Lord’s Passion he received the apostleship among the Gentiles with Paul (Acts 4:36). He was one of Christ’s seventy-two disciples, lived with the apostles in joyful and sorrowful times alike, and, in accordance with his name, afforded the greatest consolation to believers.

At the beginning, when he owned a field, he sold it and laid the price at the apostles’ feet (ibid., 37). After Paul’s conversion he welcomed him as a friend and brought him to the apostles, to whom he was still unknown and suspect, recounting for those who did not know it the course of his calling (Acts 9:27). He was sent by the apostles to Antioch; there, seeing the grace of God among the disciples, he rejoiced, and, through his exhortation, a great multitude was added to the Lord. From there he went to Tarsus to seek Saul; having found him, he brought him to Antioch, and there for a whole year they lived together and taught a great multitude. Then the disciples were first called Christians at that place (Acts 11:22–26).

Because Barnabas and Saul were compassionate and kindly, they brought to the brethren in Judaea the alms of Gentile believers (ibid., 29–30). When they had returned from Jerusalem, their ministry completed, taking with them John who was surnamed Mark (Acts 12:25), they were at Antioch among the prophets and teachers. While they were ministering to the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.” Sent indeed by the Holy Spirit, they came to Seleucia and from there sailed to Cyprus. After they deprived the magician Barjesus, also called Elymas, of sight for a time and converted the proconsul Sergius Paulus to the true faith, they led a very great multitude of Gentiles to the light of truth (Acts 13:1–48).

When, therefore, those running toward faith and righteousness had been chosen, the reprobate, more inflamed with anger, stirred up a riot and drove the apostles from their territory. But they, rejoicing and filled with the Holy Spirit, preached the word of God and converted a plentiful multitude of Jews and Greeks to the Lord (ibid., 49–52).

Arriving at Lystra, they cured a man lame from his mother’s womb. When the crowds saw this miracle, they considered them gods, saying: “Gods made like men have come down to us.” They called Barnabas Jupiter, but Paul Mercury. The priest of Jupiter, whose temple was before the city, brought bulls and garlands before the gates and wished, with the people, to offer sacrifice. But the apostles, utterly abhorring such an act, drove them away; tearing their tunics, they sprang into the crowds and cried out, and with many reasonable words scarcely restrained the crowds from sacrificing to them (Acts 14:6–17).

From there they came to Derbe, preached the Gospel, and, teaching many, instructed them in virtues. Having travelled through many provinces, proclaiming the word of the Lord, they finally reached Jerusalem. Received by the holy apostles, they joyfully reported how great were the wonders God had worked with them. Then certain wicked men at Antioch raised a dispute about the necessity of circumcision. Therefore the holy apostles took counsel and sent Barnabas and Paul to uproot such wickedness. They hastened to Antioch with the apostolic letter and, preaching, destroyed the impious heresy (Acts 14:6; 15:1–31).

Like true shepherds, they preached the word of God, taught the ignorant, healed the sick, and exercised every care for holy religion. They took the greatest precaution that neophytes should fall into no heresy; therefore they frequently visited the churches in which they had preached the word of God. For they knew Satan’s cunning craftiness, and therefore took care lest it should defile the renewed hearts of the saints with the deadly seed of tares. Afterwards, as Luke the Evangelist says, it seemed good to them that Paul should return to Jerusalem, while Barnabas should revisit Cyprus, his native city (Acts 15:39). He had with him in ministry John surnamed Mark. This man, indeed, while he was a pagan and, with his companion Orduo, served Cyril, priest of the utterly abominable Jupiter, was baptized by Barnabas and Paul in the place called Iconium and faithfully accompanied them through many places.

Finally, while the aforesaid apostles were preaching in Pamphylia and many Jews and Gentiles had believed in the Lord, Paul was shown in an angelic vision by night that he should hasten more quickly to Jerusalem and permit Barnabas to go to Cyprus. When the vision had been related, they knelt in prayer; kissing one another, they took farewell with many tears, and, separated in body, never afterwards saw one another in this life.

Barnabas and John went down to Laodicea and thence came to the city called Anemoria. There certain discerning and well-disposed pagans heard their preaching, believed in Christ, and, having been baptized, received the power of the Holy Spirit. Then they sailed to Cyprus and found there Timon and Aristion, servants of the Lord. Timon, however, was burning with severe fevers. When Barnabas laid his hands and the holy Gospel upon him, through invocation of our Lord Jesus the fever immediately fled; and the man was so strengthened that he at once followed the saints of God joyfully.

By the teaching of the apostles, blessed Barnabas carried with him the Gospel of the holy apostle Matthew; wherever he found sick persons, he placed it upon them, and immediately they were healed from whatever illness afflicted them. Barnabas appointed Heraclius, whom the apostle Paul had baptized, bishop for the strengthening of the faithful. Then, wishing to enter Paphos, he was recognized by the Jewish sorcerer Barjesus, whom Paul had long before deprived of sight for a time. Moved by malice, Barjesus resisted as much as he could and prevented him from entering Paphos.

[Col. 0180C] Accordingly, the blessed man turned aside to a certain place, where he saw pagan men and women running naked in sport. Barnabas, therefore, indignant, immediately cursed the temple; and at once part of it collapsed utterly from its foundations, and its fall crushed many of the pagans to death. But the rest who escaped fled to the temple of Apollo. The distinguished athlete of Christ entered the city of Salamis, where he found a synagogue of Jews. He steadfastly preached the Gospel of Christ to it and converted very many Jews to faith in Christ. When Barjesus learned of this, he displayed all his malice and stirred up a riot against the holy apostle of God. The Jews wished to hand him over, once seized, to the consul of Salamis; but first they afflicted him with many punishments and various tortures.

Then, as they were taking him, worn down and shattered by punishments, to be judged, they learned that Eusebius, a great and exceedingly powerful man of imperial lineage, was coming to the island. Fearing greatly that he might rescue him from their hands, they tied a rope around his neck, dragged him by night from the synagogue to the hippodrome and thence outside the gate, and afterwards surrounded him with fire and cruelly burned him. Thus the blessed apostle, after many struggles and prolonged contests, passed through burning, for love of Christ, to everlasting joys. But the impious Jews, not satisfied with his death, took his body and, enclosing it in a lead coffin, intended to cast it into the sea. Meanwhile John Mark, with Timon and Rhodon, secretly carried away the holy body in the nighttime [Col. 0181A] and placed it, on the third day before the Ides of June, in a crypt which had formerly been a dwelling-place of the Jebusites. Because of this concealment, the venerable body lay hidden for the course of many years and could not be found by worshippers of Christ. At last, in the time of the emperor Zeno and Pope Saint Gelasius, it was found through the revelation of that same holy apostle and, with hymns and praises, marvellously placed in honour of God. Through the merits of the holy apostle Barnabas many benefits are bestowed upon those who ask devoutly. May the abundant grace of our God, which works unweariedly and efficaciously assists those whom he has predestined to life, make us also sharers in them through all ages. Amen.

## XX. Mark

[Col. 0181B] Mark the Evangelist was the disciple and interpreter, and in baptism the son, of the blessed apostle Peter; he wrote from Peter’s mouth the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ. As is reported, he caused his thumb to be cut off so that he might be considered unfit for the priesthood. Yet he was not rejected by the apostles, but by their choice was appointed bishop of Alexandria. When blessed Peter was in the city of Rome, he summoned him and sent him to Italy to preach to the Gentiles: “Why,” he said, “do you remain here with us? Behold, you have been instructed in all that Jesus of Nazareth did. Rise, go to Aquileia, and there sow among the peoples the doctrines of true salvation.”

Then Mark received his first allotment of preaching and the staff of the episcopate; he set out on the journey imposed upon him and came to Aquileia, which is the first among the cities of Italy. There he found a leprous youth named Ataulf, son of the illustrious Ulfinus, the foremost man of the city. Speaking with him, he took hold of his hand and arm. At once the leprosy was cleansed from his hand and arm. Seeing this, the youth quickly ran to his father and joyfully told him everything Mark had done for him. Ulfinus therefore came in great haste with a large crowd and found Mark sitting at the Western Gate; he began to beg him to heal his son. When Mark promised healing if he believed, Ulfinus declared that he would believe in the Lord Jesus. Then Mark baptized the youth, and all leprosy departed from him. When he had been healed, Ulfinus was baptized with his whole household. A multitude of people also was baptized that day.

After some years Mark desired to see Peter and wished secretly to leave the people and go to Rome. The people, learning this by God’s will, ran together at dawn and, crying out, begged him to give them a shepherd. Then Hermagoras was chosen by the people and brought by blessed Mark to Rome. There he was made by the blessed apostle Peter proto-bishop of the province of Italy; and, after many miracles that God worked through him among the people, under Nero’s reign, he was martyred with Fortunatus the archdeacon under the governor Sevastus, on the third day before the Ides of July.

But blessed Mark, at the command of the holy apostle Peter, assumed the government of the see of Alexandria and first preached Christ in the land of Egypt. In the regions of Libya, Marmarica, Ammonica, and Pentapolis he proclaimed the true faith. All who then lived in those lands were uncircumcised, idolaters, and full of every impurity. When Mark came to Cyrene, which is in Pentapolis, and found the inhabitants accursed because of their excessive crimes, he began the divine discourse by bestowing, in the Lord’s name, healing upon the sick. For he cleansed lepers and expelled many utterly wicked spirits by word alone. Very many, seeing these things, believed; they destroyed their idols, cut down their sacred groves, and were baptized in the name of the Lord who is Three and One.

Then it was revealed to him by the Holy Spirit that he should go to the sanctuary of Alexandria. Mark therefore bade farewell to the brethren and disclosed what had been divinely revealed to him. But they accompanied him as far as the ship and, eating bread with him, dismissed him, saying: “May the Lord Jesus Christ make your journey prosperous.” On the seventh day he came to Alexandria and, leaving the small ship, hastened to the city. As soon as he entered it, his sandal broke. “Truly,” he said, “my journey is proceeding favourably.”

Then the blessed man gave his sandal to a certain cobbler of old age, named Anianus, to be repaired. While doing the assigned work, the cobbler severely wounded his left hand and immediately cried out: “There is one God.” When blessed Mark heard this, rejoicing within himself he said: “The Lord has made my journey prosperous.” Immediately he spat into his right hand and, anointing the man’s hand, said: “In the name of Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, let this hand be healed.” It was healed at once. The cobbler, considering the power of so great a man, the effectiveness of his word, and the austerity of his life, begged him to turn aside into his house and eat bread with him. Mark entered gladly, gave a blessing, offered prayer, preached the true faith to those who heard, and declared that the wisdom of this world is foolishness before the Lord. With truthful words he then added accounts of signs and wonders done in the Lord’s name. And Anianus, with his entire household and a multitude of neighbours, believed, was baptized, and became the helper of the teacher in preaching.

The idolatrous Alexandrians, however, when they saw their rites and ceremonies being destroyed by the Galilean preacher, sought to kill him and laid many snares for him. Blessed Mark, recognizing their plans, ordained Anianus bishop there, and three presbyters—Melinus, Sabinus, and Cerdon—seven deacons, and eleven others belonging to ecclesiastical ministry. Then he went to Pentapolis, remained there two years, strengthened the brethren who had formerly believed there, and ordained bishops and clerics throughout those regions. He returned to Alexandria and found the brethren multiplied in grace and faith. Seeing that they had built a church in the place called Bucoliae, [Col. 0183A] that is, “the cowherds,” beneath the rocks beside the sea, he rejoiced greatly; kneeling, he glorified the Lord and graciously added his aid in words and prayers.

When the time was now fulfilled, the Christians were multiplying in faith, and the images were being overthrown, the pagans learned that the saint had arrived and were filled with intense envy because of the miracles which they had heard were being performed by him. For he healed the sick, preached to unbelievers, restored hearing to the deaf, and granted sight to the blind. They sought to seize him but could not find him. Therefore, at the spectacles of their idols, they gnashed their teeth and, holding their revels, cried: “Great is the power of this magician.” At last, on the Sunday of the Lord’s Passover, that is, the eighth day before the Kalends of May, when the festival of Serapis was being celebrated, the conspirators assembled and immediately went forth. They found the man of God celebrating the most sacred offering to the divine majesty. At once the profane men seized the servant of God, put a rope around his neck, and dragged him so cruelly over rocks that his flesh fell to the ground and the rocks were stained with his blood. While they raved and said, “Let us drag the buffalo to the places of Bucoliae,” Saint Mark gave thanks to God, saying: “I give you thanks, my Lord Jesus Christ, because I have been judged worthy to suffer these things for your name.”

As evening drew on, they put him into prison, [Col. 0183C] until they should determine by what death to destroy him. But about midnight, with the doors shut and the guards sleeping before the entrance, behold, there was a great earthquake. An angel of the Lord descended from heaven and, touching him, said: “Servant of God Mark, prince and propagator of the most holy decrees throughout Egypt, behold: your name is inscribed in the book of heavenly life, and your memorial shall not be abandoned for ever. For you have become a companion of the powers above. Indeed, in heaven they shall receive your spirit, and in you repose shall not perish.” Hearing this, blessed Mark stretched his hands to heaven and said: “I give you thanks, Lord Jesus Christ, because you have not abandoned me, but have remembered me among your saints. I beseech you, Lord Jesus Christ, receive my soul in peace, and do not allow me to be separated from you any longer.”

When he had said this, the Lord Jesus came to him in the clothing and appearance in which he had been with his disciples before he suffered, and said: “Peace be with you, Mark, our Evangelist.” But he said: “I give you thanks, Lord Jesus Christ.” When morning came, the multitude of the city assembled; throwing him out of custody, they again put a rope around his neck and dragged him, saying: “Drag the buffalo to the places of Bucoliae.” As he was dragged, he gave thanks to God and said: “Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit.” Saying this, he gave up his spirit. Then the immense crowd of pagans kindled a fire in the place which was called “by the angels” [Note: [Col. 0183D] Le Prévost reads: “to the angels.”], and wished to burn the holy remains. But then, by God’s providence, a mighty storm arose, a violent blast of wind came, the sun withdrew its rays, and heavy thunder sounded. A very great rain also poured from morning until evening, so that the dwellings of many collapsed and many perished by death. The guards, terrified, abandoned the holy body and fled. Others said mockingly that Serapis was doing these things and was thus visiting his enemy during his own festival.

Then religious men came, took the righteous body, and buried it gloriously, on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, in the place of the hewn stone. Thus blessed Mark the Evangelist, first bishop of Alexandria, suffered for Christ, and his body was laid in the eastern part. After the course of many years, because of the incursions of pagans who covered the whole East like locusts and subdued to themselves the greatest part of the world to south and north, faithful Christians transferred it to Aquileia, where he had first proclaimed Christ. Therefore the bishop of Aquileia now holds the insignia of the patriarchate once possessed by the Alexandrian pontiff, and shines as the fourth primate in the world out of reverence for him: namely, Saint Mark, whom Peter, the key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven, sent into Egypt and entrusted with the primacy of the southern region for the salvation of many souls. The natives of Venetia and western peoples rejoice in possessing the body of the blessed Evangelist and ceaselessly venerate it to the praise of almighty God, praying that they may deserve to be numbered for ever in the fellowship of the blessed. Amen.

## XXI. Luke

Luke the Evangelist, a Syrian by birth, eminent in the medical art at Antioch, and a disciple of Christ’s apostles, afterwards followed the apostle Paul even to his confession. Remaining without blemish in virginity, he chose to serve the Lord. Stirred by divine command, he wrote the Gospel in the regions of Achaia and, in a faithful narrative, showed Greek believers the Lord’s incarnation and demonstrated that he descended from the stock of David. Then he published another separate book, in which he clearly unfolded the acts of the apostles and the beginnings of the rising Church. Thus Luke composed two books for Theophilus—that is, “one who loves God”—and, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, presented them to all who burn with a twofold love.

For in the former book he described Christ’s true priesthood, by which the Lamb of God, shedding his precious blood, expiated the world’s sin. In the following book he set forth the majesty of the ineffable Godhead, through which the Son of God ascended to the Father’s right hand in the humanity he had assumed; he also narrated the coming of the Paraclete Spirit upon the apostles in tongues of fire, by which the primitive Church, enlightened, shines gloriously. In these two books of Luke, the spiritual chief physician, true medicine is found: by it the deadly diseases of sins are driven away, and the remedy of life-giving righteousness is administered to those who devoutly seek it. Thus by his writings and discourses blessed Luke proclaimed the Lord and made known the light of truth to the ignorant. Among other miracles he performed, it is reported that he raised a dead person in the Lord’s name. At last, when he was eighty-three years old, filled with the Holy Spirit, he died in Bithynia on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November. His bones, together with those of Saint Andrew the apostle and Timothy, disciple of the apostle Paul, were transferred to Constantinople in the twentieth year of the emperor Constantius, on the seventh day before the Ides of May.

Behold, by the Lord’s own bestowal of help, I have now gladly made mention of the holy apostles and evangelists who were the Saviour’s table-companions and associates. I have collected their pious deeds, as briefly and truthfully as I could, from diverse books, and gathered them together into one work.

## XXII. Martial of Limoges

It remains to recall something concerning blessed Martial of Limoges, who, powerful in outstanding virtues, is reckoned among the greatest and most illustrious after the apostles. Aurelian, whom he raised from the dead in the Lord’s name, narrates many things about him in truthful writing and with diligent care, in due sequence. From these I desire to collect certain matters, and I call upon the Holy Spirit to deign to grant his help to my endeavour.

In Judaea, while our Lord Jesus Christ was preaching and a great crowd of Jews flocked to him, bringing what was necessary for human use and diligently learning by hearing from him the path of salvation, a most noble Jew of the tribe of Benjamin, named Marcellus, came to him, bringing with him his wife Elizabeth and his only son Martial, fifteen years old. Seeing the extraordinary things that he did and hearing the saving things that he preached, they were pierced in heart and believed in him; at his command they were baptized by the blessed apostle Peter. When all returned to their homes, Martial committed his whole self to the Lord Jesus and continually adhered to his discipleship. Constantly associated with the apostle Peter, to whom he was connected by close kinship, he followed the Lord Jesus. He saw the raising of Lazarus, who had been dead four days, and was present at many other miracles. With Cleophas he served in the ministry of the sacred supper and in other mystical services; with the other disciples he was present at certain appearances after the Resurrection and at the glorious Ascension. He also happily experienced the coming of the Paraclete Spirit and, richly anointed with divine chrism, shone forth; equipped with faith and grace for evangelizing, he grew strong in manly fashion.

After the dispersal of the apostles, Martial went with his kinsman the blessed apostle Peter to Antioch, and from there, after seven years, he made for Rome. There Peter and his companions were received as guests by the consul Marcellus; they lived in his house for many days and publicly preached to the Romans the most saving precepts of life. Then the Lord Jesus appeared there to blessed Peter and ordered him to send Martial to preach in the provinces of Gaul. Peter summoned Martial to himself and related in order the commands given him by God. When Martial heard this, he wept bitterly, since he greatly feared the distant region and the barbarity of its people. Blessed Peter gently consoled him and, sending him to preach, recalled to him the divine signs. Without delay Martial, with the two presbyters Alpinianus and Austriclinianus, set out on the journey enjoined upon him. But once the journey had begun, Austriclinianus died. Martial, grieving, returned to Rome and reported his companion’s death to Peter. At Peter’s command he returned to his deceased brother; he touched the dead priest’s body with the apostle’s staff, and the man, by the merits and prayers of the saints, immediately rose alive again.

Then Martial came with his disciples to the fortress of Tullum. There he was received as a guest by a wealthy man named Arnulf, remained for two months, and diligently proclaimed the word of God. A great crowd came to him daily, gladly heard his saving counsels, and saw signs unfamiliar to them. Then Arnulf’s daughter, who was tormented daily by a demon, vomited forth the unclean spirit at Martial’s command and became as if dead. But the man of God took her hand, raised her, and restored her unharmed to her father. For holiness, kindness, human humility, and constant prayer were in him.

The ruler of the aforesaid fortress, named Nerva, was a kinsman of the emperor Nero; his son was suffocated by the devil. The dead youth’s father and mother, and all the people present, prostrated themselves at Saint Martial’s feet. With great lamentation and wailing from all, they cast the body of the youth before him and said tearfully: “Man of God, help us.” The most holy bishop had compassion upon the people’s tears. He too wept with his disciples and, with them, implored almighty God to raise the dead man. Finally, when the prayer was finished, the holy bishop commanded that the dead man should rise sound in the name of the crucified Saviour. At once he rose, cast himself at the blessed man’s feet, [Col. 0186D] and began to cry: “Baptize me, man of God, and seal me with the sign of faith.” Then he added: “Two angels came to me with great force, saying that I was to be raised by the prayers of blessed Martial. Hell has no measure. There are weeping and bitterness; there are darkness, bellowing, lamentation, and great sorrow; great and dreadful cold and fire, never at any time failing; the bites of serpents, unbearable stench, decay and misery, and the worm that does not die. There are infernal jailers, who torment the souls they seize with diverse scourges.” As he said these and similar things, all the people began to confess the Lord; and there three thousand six hundred persons of both sexes were baptized. They also offered many gifts to the blessed man, all of which he ordered to be given to the poor. Afterwards he went to the representations of idols, shattered every carved image, and reduced them to nothing.

Then the blessed bishop came with his disciples to the village of Agedunum [Note: [Col. 0187D] Commonly Ahun.] and preached the true faith to idolaters deceived by diabolical error. The priests of the idols came and struck the holy preachers severely. But while they blessed the Lord, patiently endured adversities for his sake, and confidently sought his aid against the impending affliction, their assailants were suddenly made blind. Leading one another by the hand, they sought the image of Mercury. In accordance with custom they consulted it, but Mercury gave them no answer, because the demon had been bound by the angels of God [Col. 0187B]. Going to another idol, they heard that their god could not answer them because he had been bound with fiery chains by the angels of God.

Then the blinded priests came to Saint Martial and, prostrate at the saints’ feet, asked forgiveness. The blessed bishop restored their sight; then he went with all the people to the statue of Jupiter and adjured the demon in the Lord’s name immediately to depart from it and to shatter the statue before all the people. The demon fulfilled the command and broke the image into tiny pieces. Then two thousand six hundred were baptized there.

When a paralytic heard of this miracle, he had himself carried to the man of God. He was of a great family and very rich in gold, silver, and possessions. When the man of God heard his prayers and recognized his faith, he took his hand and, after prayer, healed him. Once healed, he glorified God and offered gifts to the blessed man. Martial refused to accept them, ordering that they all be given to the poor.

While Saint Martial remained there, the Lord appeared to him in a vision and said: “Do not fear to go down to the city of Limoges, for there I shall glorify you and shall always be with you.” Then the blessed bishop strengthened those whom he had baptized, commended them to the Lord, and went with his disciples to the city. They were lodged in the house of a noble matron named Susanna [Col. 0187D], and on the following day began publicly to preach the Lord.

At the lodging of the man of God, a certain madman was confined in chains, and no one dared release him. Susanna begged the bishop to heal him also, as he had healed the other sick persons. He assented to her plea and made the sign of the cross over the sick man. Immediately the chain broke and the man was made well. The noble mother and her daughter Valeria, seeing this sign, believed and were baptized by the blessed bishop with six hundred persons of their household.

While the saints were preaching in the theatre, the priests of the idols became indignant, beat them severely with whips, and put them into prison. But Saint Martial and his companions bore what had been inflicted upon them patiently and gave thanks to God. At about the third hour of the following day Martial prayed, and immediately a great light, like the brilliance of the sun, shone in the prison. Everyone’s chains were broken and the doors were opened; all who were present asked to be baptized. There was also an earthquake in the city; lightning flashed and thunder sounded; the pagans fled in vain to the temples of their idols; and the priests who had struck the saints of God were killed by a stroke of lightning. Therefore all the citizens, struck unanimously by terror, went to the prison. Falling at the bishop’s feet, they asked forgiveness for their sins and sought his help. As the blessed bishop prayed with his fellow-workers, [Col. 0188B] Aurelian and Andrew were raised and, bowed low, sought pardon; with all the people who gazed in wonder at these unfamiliar things, they confessed the true Lord. On the following day blessed Martial summoned everyone, from the least to the greatest, and, after giving fitting exhortation, baptized them all. Then twenty-two thousand believed in the Lord and gladly submitted themselves to the saving *theusebia*, “reverence for God.”

The sacred bishop came with all the people to the temple in which stood the statues of Jupiter, Mercury, Diana, and Venus. Having broken the idols, he dedicated there a church in honour of Saint Stephen the first martyr.

[Col. 0188C] Blessed Susanna, however, happily died in the Lord and was buried by blessed Martial with great veneration. She also bestowed many gifts and countless benefactions upon the blessed man, and placed a multitude of servants at his disposal. Moreover, Valeria, her daughter, vowed her virginity to the Lord; and, filled with the Holy Spirit, she always showed herself approved in every good work. When she heard that Stephen, her betrothed, the duke, was coming to the city of Limoges, knowing for certain that she had deeply offended him by her vow of chastity, she distributed all her wealth in gold and silver, in many kinds of clothing, and in precious stones, to the poor. For she had long since granted her estates, slaves, and household-born servants, together with her mother, to the holy bishop, so that after her death [Col. 0188D] her holy body might be buried there.

Stephen the duke held dominion from the river Rhône to the Ocean Sea, and possessed the whole region on this side of the Loire, all Aquitaine, and also the peoples of the Gascons and Goths. Yet he was not called king, because no one claimed this title for himself except Nero alone, who held the Roman Empire. He entered the city of Limoges and ordered Valeria, his betrothed, to come to him. When, in conversation with her, he learned of her rejection of him and had certainly established that, because she herself refused, he could not join her to himself in marriage, he gnashed his teeth fiercely. He would not allow her to speak with him any longer, [Col. 0189A] but, filled with rage, ordered her led outside the city and immediately beheaded.

When she had been led to the place of execution, she foretold the executioner his imminent death; then, stretching out her hands to heaven, she prayed and confidently commended herself to the Lord God. While she prayed, a voice was heard from above: “Do not fear, Valeria, for those await you in a glory enclosed by no end.” Hearing this voice, the virgin rejoiced, and, raising her eyes to heaven, said: “Lord, into your hands I commend my spirit.” Having said this, she freely extended her neck and was beheaded by the gladiator’s trainer with a single blow. Many saw her radiant soul, departing from the body like the sun, borne to heaven in a fiery globe, while the harmonious choir of angels sang: “Blessed are you, Valeria, [Col. 0189B] martyr of Christ, who kept the commandments of the Lord. You shall remain continually in his presence, in the splendor of light that knows no end.”

On hearing this, the armour-bearer of Duke Stephen, who had beheaded her, hurried with the greatest haste to report to his lord everything he had seen and heard. Finally, just as the virgin’s word concerning his approaching death had foretold, he was struck by an angel, fell at the duke’s feet, and immediately expired. Great fear and trembling seized the duke and all his people. Therefore, clothed in haircloth, the duke asked blessed Martial to come to him. When Martial had come into his presence, the duke prostrated himself at his feet and began to say with great weeping: “I have sinned, most holy man, by shedding innocent blood; but I beg you, raise [Col. 0189C] this my armour-bearer and make me believe in your God.”

Then the holy bishop summoned the entire people of the Christians and urged them all to beseech God for the resurrection of the dead man. Then, when silence had been made, he himself prayed in a clear voice. When his prayer was finished, he went to the dead man’s body and, taking his hand, commanded him to rise in the name of the Lord. He immediately rose, fell at the bishop’s feet, and asked to be baptized. Duke Stephen too, seeing this sign, likewise fell before the holy man’s footprints and implored pardon for the crime he had committed. The blessed bishop imposed penance upon him for the killing of the virgin and martyr, and baptized him, all his companions and commanders, the whole army, and all the people of both sexes—fifteen thousand in number. The aforesaid duke gave his teacher many gifts of gold and silver, so that he might build churches from them in honor of the Lord. He also granted vast estates and many benefactions, with vineyards and household servants, in the province of Limoges, so that the bishop might thereby provide endowments for the churches he was going to build and supply every need of the clergy who would serve God in them. Afterwards he established a hospital for the poor in alms of blessed Valeria, in which he arranged for three hundred poor people to be fed every day. He also established another, in which he decreed that a multitude of six hundred poor people should receive daily refreshment; and he built a church over the tomb of Valeria, virgin and martyr.

## XXIII. Continuation of the Life of the Apostle Martial

[Col. 0190A]

Meanwhile Stephen, prince of the Gauls, went to Italy by command of the emperor Nero and served him there for six months with four legions of soldiers. Yet amid military service he did not forget the divine law; rather, he so trained his army that each man should be content with his own pay, and that anyone who stole anything should suffer capital punishment.
