When his time of service had been completed, he received permission to return; but he did not wish to revisit his own country before seeing blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.

Accordingly he and his entire army hastened to Rome. On entering the city, they found the apostle teaching great crowds of people in the place called the Vatican. Immediately, barefoot [Col. 0190B] and clad in haircloth, they prostrated themselves at his feet and humbly requested his blessing. When Peter saw so illustrious a people from Gaul and heard that all had been taught the Gospel of God and baptized by blessed Martial, he rejoiced exceedingly, gave thanks, and blessed the Lord. When the apostle carefully inquired concerning the character, grace, and manner of life of the aforesaid bishop, the devoted duke kindly related much concerning his virtues and miracles and the conversion of the peoples who flocked to the fountain of holy baptism.

After the duke obtained absolution from the apostle for the shedding of Valeria’s innocent blood, he offered him two hundred pounds of gold, which he had received as a gift from the emperor Nero. [Col. 0190C] But Peter ordered the duke to bring that gold to the holy bishop, that he might build churches with it or distribute it to the poor. At last, having received the apostle’s blessing, they returned together to Gaul; and, on the duke’s advice, before revisiting their own homes, they went again to their common patron.

When they came to a royal palace called Jocunciacum, they pitched tents and pavilions above the river Vinzenne. While they were going to the river, overheated by the sun, to escape both heat and sweat, Hildebert, son of Archardius, count of Poitiers, came to the place called Garricus. There he was suffocated by the devil and died, and the entire army, searching for his corpse, did not find it. Then Archadius, with his whole army, was overcome by excessive [Col. 0190D] grief; weeping, he came to Limoges to blessed Martial and humbly implored him on behalf of his son.

At that time great crowds of Goths and Gascons had come to Limoges, and many peoples from various regions had assembled there, wishing to hear from the blessed man the words of true salvation. Archadius and the whole people threw themselves at the feet of the man of God and, with great weeping, begged for the young man drowned in the river. Martial too began to weep and, barefoot and clad in haircloth, went to the place. While all prayed, the man of God adjured the demons hiding in the pit, commanding them to bring the young man’s body to the riverbank and themselves to appear openly before the people. Immediately the body was cast upon the bank of the river, into dry ground, some six stadia away; and the demons were seen in the likeness of pigs.

[Col. 0191A] Then, as the people begged and the bishop uttered an imprecation, they emerged from the river with great violence and came before the feet of holy Martial. They were like Ethiopians, blacker than soot; their feet were huge, their eyes dreadful and bloodshot, their hair covered their whole bodies, and sulphurous fire issued from their mouths and nostrils. When they spoke, they seemed to imitate the voice of ravens. When the bishop asked their names, one of them said: “I am called Thousand-Artificer, because I have a thousand arts for deceiving humankind.” Another said: “I am called Neptune, because I have hurled many people into this pit and drowned them in the punishments of hell.”

The holy bishop said: [Col. 0191B] “Why do you wear fiery chains in your nostrils?” The demons replied: “When we deceive human souls, we lead them to our master with these chains.” When the bishop asked what their master was called, they said: “Rixoaldus, because he always desires quarrelling and remains in anger and indignation.” Finally, since they begged him not to speak further with them in Latin or send them into the abyss or the Ocean Sea, he commanded them in Hebrew to go into a desert place and harm no creature until the Day of Judgment. The demons immediately flew away through the air and were never seen again.

The duke, the whole populace, and the entire army gathered from various provinces and assembled for this spectacle threw themselves at the holy bishop’s feet, tearfully begging for the resurrection of the dead man. Moved by so much weeping, he ordered them all to beseech the Lord together. Taking the dead man’s hand, he said: “Hildebert, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, arise.” He immediately rose and thereafter lived devoutly for twenty-six years. As all glorified the Lord who had displayed so glorious a miracle, holy Martial summoned Hildebert and asked him, for the edification of the hearers, about the things he had seen while already lifeless. When questioned—[Note: [Col. 0191D] Read: “when questioned.”]—he related many things.

“When, weary,” he said, “from the heat of the sun, I was washing my body of sweat, the demons immediately threw me into a pit and suffocated me. When they wished to bind me with fiery [Col. 0191D] chains, an angel of the Lord standing near at once snatched me from their hands. As we began to proceed eastward, two companies of demons came toward us and hurled fiery arrows. One of them went before us and another behind. I was utterly terrified, but the angel accompanying me gently strengthened me.

“With a resonant voice and sweet melody the angel began to sing to the Lord, saying: ‘Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, his holy name. He who forgives all your iniquities and will redeem your life from hell.’ Then we came to purgatorial fire, in which Christians are tormented for their daily [Col. 0192A] transgressions, provided they are not burdened with grave crimes. For purgatorial fire is a river, with a bridge laid over it. Leading me there, the angel of the Lord set me upon it; then, taking my hand, he said: ‘You shall stand here until, cleansed of all sins, you deserve to become a participant in the heavenly kingdom.’

“When these things had been done, we came to the gate of paradise, beside which we found a multitude of demons assembled. I feared their savagery and accusation exceedingly. Then a voice was heard from heaven: ‘Let the soul of this boy return to his entrails, and let him live twenty-six years.’ The angel who led me was of incredible beauty and surpassed human nature in the sight of his appearance. When I also asked about our teacher Martial, the angel answered: ‘He possesses great merit in heaven, because he remains a virgin and is free from, and has resolved to remain free from, desire for women. From youth he began to serve the Lord and to cling to blessed Peter. He did not return to his father’s house. As he is known to be removed from the desire of the flesh, so he will be exempt from the pain of death. Twelve angels have been assigned to him by the Lord; walking always with him, they do not allow him to grow weary, hungry, or thirsty, but guard him from every evil and render him wholly exempt from every contagion of suffering.’”

As Hildebert related these things and others like them, the bishop and duke rejoiced with all the assembled people and gave thanks to the Lord for the benefits bestowed. Hildebert, observing the angel’s admonitions, [Col. 0192C] shaved his head and, attaching himself to the blessed bishop, remained in God’s service. He drank no wine and ate no meat. He used no footwear. In food he was content with bread and water alone, and in clothing with haircloth. He devoted himself to continual prayer, frequent fasts, and uninterrupted performance of good works. Whatever his parents gave him he distributed to the needy; he kept nothing for the morrow. Many followed his example, renounced their own wills, and ran to Christ by the narrow way.

Duke Stephen issued a decree and sent it through all the peoples subject to his authority: all temples and idols were to be broken into pieces and burned with fire, and they were to devote themselves to and strive to serve God alone. [Col. 0192D] He himself faithfully observed before God the religious life that he had learned from his good teacher. He was devoted to almsgiving, just in judgment, solicitous toward the poor, humble and devout toward priests and all God’s ministers; a most prudent father of Christians and a most fierce persecutor of pagans. From the day he received baptism, he was not defiled with a woman, but lived in chastity until the day of his death.

In the city of Bordeaux there was Count Sigibert, who had been severely ill with paralysis for six years. On hearing of the wonders performed by blessed Martial, he commanded his wife Benedicta to go [Col. 0193A] swiftly to the man of God, taking with her twenty-six pounds of gold and a sufficient quantity of silver, and, having made her petition, to obtain God’s favor for him through God’s friend. She made fitting preparations for what had been commanded with the greatest speed and went to the man of God with two thousand eight hundred horsemen. Arriving before him, she confidently sought the recovery of her husband. Delighted by her faith, the blessed man promised health to the sick man. Then he handed his staff to the noblewoman and ordered her to place it upon her husband so that he might be healed. He refused to accept the gold and silver, but freely bestowed divine benefits according to the Lord’s command. He baptized noble Benedicta and all her travelling companions, and sent them home strengthened in the faith.

[Col. 0193B] Meanwhile, when the people of the city of Bordeaux had gone to the shrines of idols and the priest was burning incense, the demon said through a certain Jew named Martial that he would depart from him, and sorrowfully proclaimed openly the great powers of the holy bishop and his dignities before God. At last, as the noblewoman entered the city, the elders of the people came out to meet her and told her all that they had heard from Jupiter. Then the countess summoned to herself the chief priest of the idols and ordered him to go through every temple and break them all into small pieces, except the temple of the unknown God.

Then, with her Christian companions, she implored God’s mercy; and, in his name, came to her husband’s bed and placed the blessed bishop’s staff upon him. The limbs which had been afflicted by the contraction of sinews and the destructive complication of fevers were immediately restored as though they had never been deprived of their natural strength. When the aforesaid Count Sigibert was healed, he went with a great retinue of people to the holy bishop and was reborn by him in the water of sacred baptism, together with all his followers. [Col. 0193C] He brought abundant gifts of prayers and thanksgiving for the heavenly benefits bestowed upon him, and afterwards lived happily for many days in God’s service.

Once, when the aforesaid city, pressed by human insolence, was already about to be consumed in a conflagration of fire and seemed almost to threaten its own destruction by burning, devout Benedicta faithfully set the man of God’s staff against [Col. 0193D] the fire. Confessing the Creator’s omnipotence, she invoked his aid. Immediately the fire was so completely extinguished that no trace of it could be seen.

At that time, divinely prompted, Martial, bishop of Christ, went to the river Garonne and, in the place called Mauritania—[Note: [Col. 0193D] Commonly: Mortagne-sur-Gironde.]—preached God’s word to many who had assembled there. He remained there for three months, engaged in the most salutary work of divine service. Nine demoniacs, bound with chains and brought from the city of Bordeaux by their parents, were healed by holy Martial when the demons had been expelled. For the demons who had been expelled from Bordeaux through the power of Christian faith, enraged against the wretched idolaters whom they had subjugated, had invaded them and, violently assailing their bodies, tormented them excessively. They were therefore dragged by their parents to the man of God; when he prayed and commanded, the malignant enemies emerged from their mouths with blood and were never seen anywhere again.

Once, while blessed Martial preached in Mauritania and an immense multitude of peoples flocked together to hear the true doctrines, Count Sigibert resolved to come to him with a great force of soldiers and cordially provide him with a suitable supply of food and drink. He desired therefore an abundance of fish and sent servants to the sea to fish. At last, while the fishermen were carrying back many kinds of fish and wished to see the desired shore, a sudden tempest arose on the sea that began to threaten them with death and the ships with shipwreck. [Col. 0194B] But Countess Benedicta, standing on the shore with a multitude of people and waiting, saw the alarming danger in fearful agitation. When the men and ships had already begun to sink, the devout woman stretched her hands to heaven and, crying aloud, invoked God. At once the storm was calmed and ceased. The fishermen reached harbor unharmed with their ships, fish, and nets, and all who saw it glorified the wondrous God.

The gracious bishop, returning from Mauritania, went back to Limoges [Col. 0194C] and thence proceeded to a village called Asiacum—[Note: [Col. 0193D] Perhaps Axia (Aixe) near Limoges. Le Prévost: Ansiacum, an unknown place.] There an image of Jupiter was held in veneration by the pagans, and a great multitude of sick persons, oppressed by various infirmities, lay there. When the bishop arrived, the demon fell silent; but, at the inhabitants’ request, the man of God commanded him to leave the image, break the statue, and visibly appear before the people. Immediately he came out of the statue like a little black boy, darker than soot; his foul, very thick hair reached to his feet, and through his mouth, nostrils, and eyes there issued [flame?] with a foul heat. Finally, after the saint had shown the people whom they had worshipped as lord and again ordered him to shatter the statue, he reduced the broken statue to dust and afterwards was never seen anywhere.

The venerable bishop had all the sick brought together before him and, making the sign of the cross over them, healed them in God’s name; and he baptized all who were seen to be residing there. Returning thence to his own see, he caused oratories to be constructed and carefully adorned them with distinguished ornaments. He consecrated one in honor of Saint Stephen, the first martyr, his kinsman; he established another in honor of Saint Peter the apostle, his teacher; and he clothed the entire altar round about with plates of gold. When the basilicas had been built, the blessed bishop announced a fixed day for their dedication, [Col. 0195A] and Duke Stephen ordered a sufficient provision prepared for all who would come to the sacred solemnities.

While the holy bishop celebrated the solemnities of Mass, Arveus, count of the city of Tours, was possessed by a demon together with his Christian wife. The man of God did not permit the people to be harassed long, but ordered them brought to him and rebuked the demons for daring to enter them. The demons replied that this had been permitted them because of a transgression: contrary to his command, the man and his wife had defiled themselves by carnal impurity throughout the night. As the duke and people begged for the afflicted, the holy bishop expelled the demon in the Savior’s name and restored the people to the strength of their former health. The Basilica of Saint Peter was consecrated on 2 May, [Col. 0195B] in the time of the emperor Nero; and such brightness shone there on the day of its dedication that one could scarcely see another person standing nearby.

When these rites had been duly performed, blessed Martial ordained Aurelian and appointed him over the city of Limoges after his own departure. He placed the priest Andrew in charge of the church of Saint Peter the Apostle, and established there with him Hildebert, son of Count Archadius, and thirty-six other clerics. Duke Stephen generously gave them revenues from his own resources for food and clothing. Many things indeed have been written about the deeds of blessed Martial, but they cannot all be individually set forth. For he was filled with divine learning, eminent in religion, powerful in uprightness of character, and wondrous in the performance of miracles. [Col. 0195C] He was a despiser of the world, a lover of God and neighbor, one for whom to live was Christ and to die gain. As we have often said, he restored sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, walking to the lame, speech to the mute, and recalled the dead to life. There are many other things worthy of commemoration, as Aurelian says, which Christ’s grace worked through him; if they were written down, unbelievers would call them apocryphal.

In the fortieth year after the Lord’s Resurrection, while blessed Martial the bishop was praying as usual, behold: the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to him in splendor with his disciples. Greeting him amicably, he called him and foretold that the fifteenth day would be the end of his departure from the world. Therefore the holy man, [Col. 0195D] filled with great joy, gave thanks to God and prepared for his death through two weeks of continual fasts, vigils, and prayers. At the appointed time of night, after a brief rest that refreshed his weary limbs, he rose to prayer and continued in prayer and divine praise until the second hour of the day. Then, at the second hour, he offered sacrifice to the Lord for himself and for the whole Church, and afterwards preached continually until evening. When night had fallen, he took the severe nourishment prescribed for him: namely, bread and water.

As the end of his summons approached, the man of God called the brethren together and announced that the day of his death was imminent. He sent messengers throughout all the regions and provinces [Col. 0196A] that he himself had won for the Lord. Many came together with great lamentation: namely, the people of Poitiers, Bourges, Auvergne, the Gascons, and the Goths. As the day of his death drew near, at everyone’s request he went outside the city gate called Calcinea. There he delivered a discourse on the true faith and divine works, and profitably reviewed the blessed virtues by which wholesome conduct is adorned. When his exhortation was ended, he blessed the people and commended them to the Lord God with devout prayers. Then he had himself carried to the oratory of blessed Stephen; there, lying upon ashes and haircloth, he awaited his end and, kneeling with his hands lifted toward heaven, made provision that his departure should be fortified by prayers.

At last he uttered this prayer to the [Col. 0196B] Lord: “Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit.” As all wept and prayed, he made a gesture with his hand for them to be silent and said: “Be silent. Do you not hear what great praises are coming from heaven? Surely the Lord comes as he promised.” Immediately a great light shone in that place, and the voice of the Lord calling him sounded: “Come forth, blessed soul.” Then he went to heaven with that same splendor, and meanwhile the choir of angels was heard.

On the following day, at the third hour, a paralytic touched his bier and was immediately made well. When his body was being carried for burial, at the hour when it was carried out to the Basilica of Saint Stephen, the heavens opened; and, while those carrying the holy body proceeded to the burial-place, they remained open continuously. [Col. 0196C] Moreover, as many sick persons flocked to the funeral, blessed Alpinian, taking the holy bishop’s cloth, touched the bodies of the sick and healed them all at the invocation of Christ. Among the rest, a dropsical man was brought from the city of Toulouse with six blind persons and four demoniacs. They were presented at the saint’s tomb on the day after the holy bishop’s death and were healed by the touch of the sacred cloth.

Countless miracles were performed through this most holy bishop after his burial, all of which cannot individually be comprehended in writing because of their immense number. Perhaps for one whom these things do not suffice, even larger volumes, if written, would not suffice.

[Col. 0196D] May the gracious bishop Martial intercede for us who speak of him: he who was Christ’s table-companion and the apostles’ associate, who proved a pious shepherd to the people of Limoges and their first preacher among the western peoples; so that, fortified by his holy prayers, we may deserve to be admitted as participants in the eternal inheritance. Amen.

## XXIV. History of the Roman Pontiffs: Peter and His Successors

Because I have resolved to compile a chronography according to the writings of the ancients, and, beginning an ecclesiastical narrative, have briefly appended at its beginning certain matters concerning the holy apostles, I now strive, with God’s help, to present a continuous succession of the Roman bishops and shall attempt to begin with the blessed apostle Peter, to whom Christ entrusted the keys of the kingdom of heaven. I judge this work necessary and consider it useful to earnest dependants and to other teachable persons. As I have truly ascertained, during the eleven hundred years since the mighty Emmanuel came to us, clothed in a cloud of flesh through the undefiled Virgin, many eminent champions, by God’s aid, have held the reins of ecclesiastical government in the city of Rome. From its very beginning Rome had labored to raise its standards above all its neighbors and, by God’s ordering, had extended its boundaries to the Euphrates and the Ocean. It is pleasing for good people, amid worldly waves, to examine the triumphal courses of those champions, so that, walking in the heroes’ footsteps, they may strive to imitate their vigorous and saving deeds.

Blessed Simon Peter, prince of the apostles, [Col. 0197B] son of John, born in the village of Bethsaida in the province of Galilee, first occupied the see at Antioch for seven years. Then, under Claudius, he went to Rome against Simon Magus, and there governed the Church while preaching the Gospel for twenty-five years. He disputed many times against Simon before Nero and the people; having defeated him, he was martyred with Paul under Nero, in the thirty-sixth year after the Lord’s Passion, on 29 June.

Linus of Tuscany, son of Herculanus, occupied the see for eleven years, three months, and twelve days; he was martyred on 26 November. By command of the apostle Peter he decreed that a woman should enter church with her head veiled.

Cletus the Roman occupied the see for twelve years, one month, and [Col. 0197C] eleven days. He suffered under Domitian on 26 April, and the episcopal see was vacant for twenty days. Rufinus, the presbyter of Aquileia, says in the prologue to his history of Clement that Linus and Cletus ministered while the apostle Peter was alive and succeeded him. I greatly wonder that so prudent a translator and historian, so highly learned in both Greek and Latin, did not consider that both completed their blessed course by martyrdom and that no one suffered persecution in the city for Christ until Nero’s thirteenth year, after the downfall of Simon Magus. Linus, indeed, suffered in the time of Vespasian, while Cletus suffered in the persecution of Domitian.

Clement the Roman, from the Caelian Hill, son of Faustinus, occupied the see for ten years, two months, and ten days. [Col. 0197D] Under Trajan he was cast into the sea on 23 November, and the episcopal see was vacant for twenty-one days. Following the discipline of the blessed apostle Peter, he was outstandingly endowed with the adornments of good character; for this reason he pleased Jews, Gentiles, and all Christians. He kept a written register by name of their destitute persons, and did not permit those cleansed by the sanctification of baptism to be subjected to public begging. He consecrated with the sacred veil the virgin Flavia Domitia, niece of Caesar Domitian and betrothed of Aurelius; and he confirmed Theodora, wife of Count Sisinnius, in her purpose of chastity.

Her husband, moved by jealousy, secretly followed her as she entered the church; but when Clement prayed, he immediately became blind and deaf. When his servants wished to cast him out of the church, they wandered around for a long time and could not find the door, until Theodora, praying earnestly for her husband, obtained that he and his boys might leave. He was finally brought home and remained blind. After Mass, Theodora informed Saint Clement the pope of what had happened. Clement urged the people to pray to God. Then he went with the woman to the sick man and, praying, immediately restored his sight and hearing. But when he had recovered his bodily senses, the man became insane and ordered Bishop Clement, whom he thought had entered his wife, seized and dragged away. His servants tied up stone columns and pulled them now from inside to outside, now from outside to inside. While Sisinnius and his servants were thus mad, [Col. 0198B] Clement withdrew, and Theodora prayed all day with tears for her husband.

At last, toward evening, the apostle Peter appeared to her and comfortingly said: “Through you Sisinnius will be saved, so that what my brother Paul the apostle said may be fulfilled: ‘The unbelieving husband shall be sanctified through the believing wife’” (1 Cor. 7:14). Immediately Sisinnius, having recovered his senses, summoned Clement through Theodora. Confessing his madness, he believed in almighty God; and, strengthened in the following Easter season, he received baptism together with 323 persons of both sexes. Many noble and distinguished people believed in the Lord through him and, receiving the true faith, were baptized.

Publius Torqueanus, an official of the sacred rites, envied the multitude [Col. 0198C] of Christians; having given money to the patrons of the city districts, he stirred up a sedition against the Christian name. During Mamertinus’s administration of the prefecture of the Roman people, a disturbance took place; and, by Publius Torqueanus’s order, Clement was secretly brought before him. Clement attempted, by reasoned answers, to turn the judge himself toward the true faith. Finally, as the seditious party rioted, a report concerning him was sent jointly to Nerva and Trajan. Trajan replied with an order that, if Clement refused to sacrifice, he should undergo exile beyond the Black Sea, which adjoins the city of Cherson. The Lord granted blessed Clement such favor that even the pagan governors wept for him. The governor Julian commended him to God with tears and provided him with a ship laden with every necessity. [Col. 0198D] Many religious men, from both laity and clergy, followed him.

In exile the blessed pope found more than two thousand Christians condemned to cut marble. When he learned that they had been banished for God’s name, he rejoiced and furnished them with abundant instruction concerning the preservation of faith and patience. Then, learning that they carried water on their shoulders from the sixth milestone, he prayed to the Lord and asked for water. When his prayer was finished, he saw a lamb standing upon a mountain. With a small hoe he lightly struck the spot indicated by the lamb’s raised right foot, and opened a spring adorned with flowing veins, which suddenly burst forth and made a river. The whole province flocked to this report, and an immense multitude received Saint Clement’s teaching, so [Col. 0199A] that five hundred souls or more were baptized in a single day. Within one year, after believers had broken the idols, seventy-five churches were built there.

After three years, at the pagans’ instigation, a hostile report was sent to the emperor Trajan; and the commander Aufidianus, dispatched by him, killed many Christians by various punishments. When the multitude had been slaughtered, he ordered Clement alone brought to the sea, an anchor tied about his neck, and himself thrown into the middle of the sea, so that Christians might not find him and venerate him as a god. When this had been done, Phoebus and Cornelius, disciples of Saint Clement, stood upon the shore with a multitude of Christians and prayed with weeping. The sea withdrew into its own bed for nearly three miles, and the people entered by dry ground and saw wonders. [Col. 0199B] They found a dwelling fashioned like a marble temple by angelic hands, and there the body of Saint Clement lay in a stone shrine through the ministry of angels, with the anchor by which he had been cast in placed beside him. It was revealed to his disciples not to remove him, because on every anniversary of his martyrdom the sea would recede and for seven days afford dry passage to those who came. Many marvels having been done there, all the surrounding Gentiles believed in Christ and serve him who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

Clement decreed that an altar-cloth, chair, or candlestick, if consumed by age, should be burned.

[Col. 0199C] Anacletus the Greek, of Athens, occupied the see for nine years, two months, and ten days. When he died on 13 July, the episcopal see was vacant for sixteen days. He decreed that an accusation against priests should not be made except by suitable and thoroughly tested men, free from suspicion.

Evaristus, a Jew of Bethlehem, son of Judas, held office for nine years, ten months, and two days, in the times of Domitian, Nerva, and Trajan. After his martyrdom, the episcopal see was vacant for eighteen days. He ordained seven deacons to attend upon the bishop as he preached with the pen of truth, and to be like eyes for him in every place. He also decreed that a man should not put away his wife, nor a woman her husband, and that the Church should not accept another [bishop] while its bishop is alive.

Alexander, a Roman from the district of Caput Tauri, son of Alexander, [Col. 0199D] [held office] for ten years, seven months, and eleven days. He blessed water for sprinkling, with salt, in the dwellings of people, and incorporated the Lord’s Passion into the prayer of priests while Masses are celebrated. Through him the Lord performed many miracles and granted salvation to many souls. At last he was beheaded on the Nomentan Way, on 3 May, and the episcopal see was vacant for thirty-five days.

Sixtus, a Roman, son of a shepherd, from the Via Lata, held office for ten years, two months, and one day. He decreed that sacred ministries should not be touched except by ministers. During the liturgical action, the priest is to sing among the people the hymn of angels and men:

> Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth.  
> Heaven and earth are full of your glory.  
> Hosanna in the highest.  
> Blessed is he who comes [Col. 0200A] in the name of the Lord;  
> Hosanna in the highest!

First, the person, faith, life, and conduct of an accuser must be carefully investigated in detail. For accusers who do not know the faith of truth, who do not lead a life of upright conduct, or who come from the household of enemies, are not to be believed. Finally, he was martyred on 5 April, and the episcopal see was vacant for fourteen days.

Telesphorus, a Greek, held office for eleven years, three months, and twenty-one days, in the time of Antoninus and Marcus. He decreed that a fast of seven weeks should be observed before Easter; that Mass should be sung at night on the Nativity of the Lord; and that at the beginning of the sacrifice the angelic hymn—that is, “Glory to God in the highest”—should be said. At last he was martyred on 5 January, and the episcopal see was vacant for seven days.

[Col. 0200B] Hyginus of Athens, formerly a philosopher, held office for four years, three months, and four days, in the time of Verus and Marcus. He established, indeed, that a metropolitan should not hear the cases of others without the presence of all the bishops of the province. A bishop, moreover, is not to decide anyone’s case without his clergy; otherwise the judgment of both shall be void. He was buried on 11 January, and the episcopal see was vacant for three days.

Pius, an Italian from Aquileia, held office for nineteen years, four months, and three days, in the time of Antoninus Pius. Instructed in the guise of a shepherd, he ordered that Easter be kept on Sunday. He died on 11 July, and the episcopal see was vacant for fourteen days.

Anicetus, a Syrian, held office for eleven years, four months, and three days, in the time of Severus and Marcus. He decreed that a cleric should not wear his hair long. A bishop is not to be ordained by fewer [Col. 0200C] than three bishops. A metropolitan, however, is to be consecrated by all those over whom he ought to preside. He was martyred on 20 April, and the episcopal see was vacant for seventeen days.

Soter, a Campanian, son of Concordius, from the city of Fundi, held office for nine years, seven months, and twenty-one days, in the time of Severus. He died on 17 April, and the episcopal see was vacant for twenty-one days.

## XXV. Continuation of the history of the Roman pontiffs

Eleutherius, a Greek, son of Abundius, held office for fifteen years and three months, in the time of Antoninus and Commodus. He determined that an absent person should not be judged, nor should the slander or testimony of an informer be heard against him. No food that is nevertheless human and rational is to be rejected by Christians. [Col. 0200D] Then he died on 26 May, and the episcopal see was vacant for five days.

Victor, an African, held office for ten years, two months, and ten days. He was crowned with martyrdom on 1 August, and the episcopal see was vacant for twelve days. He decreed that no one should be judged on uncertain evidence.

Zephyrinus, a Roman, held office for eight years, seven months, and ten days, in the time of Antoninus and Severus. He was buried on the Appian Way on 26 August, and the episcopal see was vacant for seven days. He decreed that one who has been unjustly despoiled should first recover what is his, and thereafter answer lawful accusers; and, if necessary, should receive no small period of respite.

Callixtus, a Roman from the district of Ravenna, held office for seven years, two months, and ten days, under Macrinus and [Col. 0201A] Elagabalus. He decreed that a bishop should neither judge nor excommunicate the parishioner of another. For no one is to be bound or condemned by the judgment of anyone but his own bishop. One who has fallen into sin, if he has undertaken worthy penance, is not to be deprived of the rank of his former office; indeed, even if he has not yet held it, he may obtain it. The fast of Saturday is to be observed three times yearly, consisting of wheat, wine, and oil, in accordance with the prophecy of the fourth, seventh, and tenth [months]. Finally, he was martyred on 13 October under the emperor Alexander, and the episcopal see was vacant for six days. Then the priest Calepodius, Asterius, and the consul Palmatius, with two hundred members of his household, suffered martyrdom.

Urban, a Roman, held office for four years, ten months, and twelve days. He decreed that all believers should receive the Holy Spirit after baptism through the laying on of the hands of bishops, so that they might be complete Christians. Then Tiburtius, Valerianus, Maximus, and Caecilia suffered martyrdom. He himself was martyred on 6 June.

Pontianus, a Roman, held office for nine years, five months, and two days, in the time of Alexander, by whom he was compelled to go into exile in Sardinia with the priest Hippolytus. He died on 30 October, and the episcopal see was vacant for ten days.

Antherus, a Greek, held office for twelve years, one month, and twelve days. He was martyred on 3 January, and the episcopal see was vacant for thirteen days.

Fabian, a Roman, held office for fourteen years and eleven months. Among other things he said: “An angry man’s insult is not to be regarded as an accusation. Everyone who alleges a crime must prove it; and whoever fails to prove it shall suffer the punishment which he wished to inflict.” [Col. 0201C] He suffered martyrdom on 19 January, and the episcopal see was vacant for seven days.

Cornelius, a Roman, held office for two years, two months, and three days. At the request of Saint Lucina, he secretly raised the bodies of the apostles. He placed the body of blessed Paul on the Ostian Way, and deposited that of Peter in the temple of Apollo, on the Golden Mount, in the Vatican. Under Decius he was exiled at Centumcellae. Then, having been brought to Rome, he saved many persons and was beheaded on 14 September; the episcopal see was vacant for thirty-five days. He decreed that priests should not take an oath except on account of the faith.

Lucius, a Roman, held office for three years, three months, and three days, in the time of Gallus and Volusianus. By God’s providence he returned from exile. He was beheaded by Valerian on 5 March, and the episcopal see was vacant for thirty-five days. He decreed that two priests and three deacons should always and everywhere be with a bishop as ecclesiastical witnesses.

Stephen, a Roman, held office for seven years, five months, and two days, in the time of Valerian, Gallicanus, and Maximus. He gave sight to Lucilla, who had been blind from the cradle, and baptized her father, the tribune Nemesius, together with sixty-two others of both sexes. After the martyrdom of Simpronius, Olympius, Exuperia, and Theodolus, he sent before him in martyrdom, on 1 August, twelve priests—Bonus, Faustus, Maurus, Primitius, Calumniosus, John, Exuperantius, Quirillus, Honoratus, and many others—and he himself, after celebrating Mass, was beheaded [Col. 0202A] on 2 August; the episcopal see was vacant for twenty-seven days. He decreed that persons of ill repute should not accuse priests. Priests and levites are not to use consecrated garments in ordinary daily life except in church.

Sixtus, a Greek and former philosopher, held office for one year, ten months, and twenty-three days, in the time of Gallienus and Decius. He established that anyone who, disregarding his own judge, appeals to another should be excommunicated. At last, on 6 August, he was beheaded with six deacons: Felicissimus, Agapitus, Januarius, Magnus, Vincentius, and Stephen; and the episcopal see was vacant for thirty-five days. Then Lawrence the archdeacon, Hippolytus with his household, Abdon and Sennes, petty kings of the Persians, and many others were martyred by various torments.

[Col. 0202B] Dionysius, formerly a monk, held office for six years, two months, and four days. He assigned churches to priests and established cemeteries, parishes, and dioceses. He was martyred on 27 December, and the episcopal see was vacant for five days. This is found in the decrees of Dionysius: “A confession produced by compulsion is not credible; for it ought not to be extorted, but rather freely offered.”

Felix, a Roman, held office for four years, three months, and twenty-five days, in the time of Claudius and Aurelian. Then he was crowned with martyrdom on 30 May, and the episcopal see was vacant for five days. He decreed that a bishopric should not be taken from a bishop before his case has been examined.

[Col. 0202C] Eutychianus, a Tuscan from Luna, held office for one year, one month, and one day, in the time of Aurelian. He died on 27 July, and the episcopal see was vacant for eight days.

Caius, a Dalmatian, held office for eleven years, four months, and twelve days, in the time of Carinus, Diocletian, and Constantius. He established seven grades of orders: porter, reader, exorcist, subdeacon, deacon, priest, bishop. He was martyred on 22 April, and the episcopal see was vacant for eleven days.

Marcellinus, a Roman, held office for nine years, four months, and sixteen days, in the time of Diocletian and Maximian. He decreed that a superior should not be judged by an inferior; that a layman should not accuse a cleric; and that a cleric of any rank should not bring anyone before a secular court without the permission of his own bishop. He was martyred on [Col. 0202D] 25 April. Within thirty days, eighteen thousand people were put to death with him for the faith of Christ. Then there was an excessive persecution of Christians, and the episcopal see was vacant for seven years, seven months, and twenty-five days.

Marcellus, a Roman from the Via Lata, held office for ten years, seven months, and twenty-one days, in the time of Maxentius and Maximinus. By command of the tyrant he served for a long time among horses in a stable, and at last died on 16 January. Then the episcopal see was vacant for twenty days.

Eusebius, a Greek and former physician, held office for six years, one month, and three days, in the time of Constantine. He died on 2 October, and the episcopal see was vacant for seven days. In his time, the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ was discovered on 3 May, and Judas Cyriacus was baptized.

[Col. 0203A] Melchiades, an African, held office for four years. He decreed that none of the faithful should fast on Sunday, nor on the fifth weekday, following the pagan rite. He was buried in the cemetery of Callixtus on the Appian Way on 10 December, and the episcopal see was vacant for sixteen days.

Silvester, a Roman, son of Rufinus and Justa, held office for twenty-three years, ten months, and eleven days. The priest Cirinus instructed him at Rome; imitating his life and conduct, he attained the highest summit of the Christian religion. From youth Silvester devoted himself piously to hospitality and other good works. He received at Rome as his guest Timothy, arriving from Antioch, and assisted with all his strength while Timothy publicly preached Christ. Thereafter, when that same man, after one year and three months, had been martyred for the truth by Tarquinius, prefect of the city, Silvester secretly removed [Col. 0203B] him and brought Bishop Melchiades, with holy priests and deacons, to his house to bury him as a witness of Christ. Thus Timothy was honorably buried in the garden of Theona, a Christian woman, beside the burial place of the apostle Paul. Silvester was seized by Perpenna Tarquinius and sent to prison, to be tortured on the following day for confessing the Godhead. Meanwhile, while the prefect was dining, a fish bone lodged in his throat and he died; and while Silvester’s persecutor was carried with mourning to his grave, Silvester came joyfully out of prison. When he was thirty years old, he was made a deacon; and shortly afterward, at the request of all the people, he was ordained a priest by Saint Bishop Melchiades. When Melchiades [Col. 0203C] died, Silvester was unanimously elected pope by all. He shone in every virtue, and by the merit of his holiness pleased all alike.

There was a monstrous dragon on the Tarpeian Mount, where the Capitol is situated. Once each month magicians, with sacrilegious virgins, descended to it by three hundred and sixty-five steps, as though into hell, bringing sacrifices and lustral offerings. It suddenly rose up, and although it did not come forth, it nevertheless poisoned the nearby air with its breath; from this came a deadly plague among people and the greatest lamentation over the death of infants. At last, when the pagans asked Silvester for help, he proclaimed a three-day fast to the Christians. Afterward, instructed by the blessed apostle Peter in a vision, he descended with three priests and two deacons, and by the power of [Col. 0203D] God shut the dragon in completely. From that day onward the whole city, delivered from its breath, gave thanks to God. When many pagans at Rome saw these things and were rescued from the dragon’s plague, they believed in Christ and were baptized.

When the Emperor Constantine was compelling Christians to sacrifice to idols and inflicting widespread slaughter upon those unwilling to worship images, Silvester withdrew from the city with his clergy. For some time he lay hidden on Mount Soracte, devoting himself to fasts and prayers. But the avenging hand of God struck Constantine with elephantine leprosy and so restrained him from shedding the blood of His servants. Therefore the Augustus, grieved by so great a [Col. 0204A] calamity, earnestly sought to discover what might benefit him. Then, on the advice of the impious priests of the Capitol, he ordered a company of nearly three thousand infants to be killed, so that a bath might be made from their shed blood and, immersed in the steaming gore itself, he might obtain a remedy for his leprosy. As Constantine left the palace for the bath and saw a multitude of women weeping most bitterly over the killing of their children, he asked the cause of such grief; and, when he learned of the crime, he immediately recoiled in horror. In a long and carefully reasoned address he condemned this barbaric cruelty and praised the mercy of the Roman Empire. He therefore commanded that the sons be restored unharmed to their mothers, added very generous gifts, vehicles, and provisions, and thus sent them joyfully back to their homes.

[Col. 0204B] On the following night he saw in a vision the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Admonished by them, he recalled Silvester and his clergy, heard from him instruction in true salvation, and willingly assented to him in all things. Then the pope prescribed a fast of one week for Constantine himself and for all the Christian people. When it was completed, he ordered that on the evening of Saturday the saving font should be prepared in the Lateran palace and sanctified according to custom. Constantine was then baptized; and immediately, as an extraordinary light flashed forth for nearly half an hour, he was cleansed from leprosy and confessed that he had seen Christ.

During Constantine’s reign, a council of forty-four bishops was held in the city of Rome. There Pope Silvester [Col. 0204C] disputed against twelve most learned leaders of the Jews and, with God’s help, overcame those who opposed him by a shower of authoritative pronouncements. Against the rabbis Abiathar and Joas, it was argued that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God. Against Godolias and Anna, scribes, it was plainly demonstrated from the books of the prophets that Christ was born of a Virgin, tempted by the devil, betrayed by a disciple, seized by enemies, mocked, scourged, given vinegar to drink, sold, crowned with thorns, stripped, had his garments cast by lot, was fastened to the cross, died, and was buried. Against Dohet and Chusi, teachers, and Bonoim and Arohel, interpreters of the Law, the great benefit of Christ’s incarnation, temptation, and passion was shown. Against Jobal and Thara, [Col. 0204D] Pharisees, it was authoritatively proclaimed that Jesus Christ is perfect God and perfect man: according to his humanity, in order to grant salvation to all, he was tempted, suffered, and died; but his all-powerful Godhead is untouched by every passion, just as the sun’s radiance upon a tree remains unaffected by the cut when the tree is cut with iron. To the priest Seleon an abundant explanation was set forth that the Son of God is rightly called the spotless lamb because he was sacrificed for the offense of the whole people. [Note: [Col. 0203D] Better: “offenses.” Le Prévost.] He was also born of a virgin, so that we might be born from the womb of the virgin Church. He was tempted in three ways, that he might deliver us from similar temptation; seized, that we might be released; bound, that we might be freed from the knot [Col. 0205A] of the curse; mocked, that he might rescue us from the mockery of demons; sold, that he might redeem us; humbled, that he might exalt us; captured, that he might take us away from the captivity of demons; stripped, that the nakedness of the first man, through which death entered, might be covered; crowned with thorns, that he might remove from us the thorns and briars of the first curse; fed with gall and given vinegar to drink, that he might bring us into the land flowing with milk and honey; and finally sacrificed upon the altar of the cross, that he might blot out the sins of the whole world. Here the devil’s argument failed: he who had set calf against calf and goat against goat could not find a lamb to set against the spotless Lamb. Thus our King died in order to take captive the dominion of death; he was buried in order to bless the graves of the saints; he rose again in order to restore life to the dead; he ascended into heaven in order not merely to restore to humankind the paradise it had lost, but also to open the gates of heaven. He now sits at the Father’s right hand in order to grant the prayers of believers. He will come to judge the living and the dead, to render to each according to his works. This is the true faith of Christians.

When Silvester had argued these and many other points forcefully, and Seleon, while the other Jews were silent, had praised the pope’s arguments, Zambri, the twelfth, a most skillful magician, resisted. He chose to contend not with the authoritative words of the Scriptures but through magical acts, and demanded that a most ferocious bull [Col. 0205C] be brought before him in the sight of all. Immediately, at the command of the pope and Augustus, the bull of Terentius was brought, though scarcely one hundred exceptionally strong soldiers could hold it. When Zambri whispered a certain secret into its ear, the wretched beast immediately gave a bellow, its eyes burst out violently, and it expired. Then all the Jews greatly insulted Silvester, and their uproar resounded for nearly two hours. Finally, when the Augustus had ordered silence, Silvester addressed the sorcerer, demanding that, as he had killed the bull alive, so he should restore that same bull to life from death in God’s name. He could not do this, but openly began to vow and to affirm by the safety of the Augustus that, if Silvester raised the bull from death, all would abandon the Jewish law and surrender themselves to the Christian religion. Then the holy pope stretched out his hands and, kneeling, prayed with tears for a very long time. When his prayers were ended, he approached the young bull and cried out loudly: “In the name of Jesus Christ, who was crucified by the Jews under Pontius Pilate the governor, arise and stand in all gentleness.” Immediately it rose, and the holy bishop came forward and released all the bonds from its horns. “Go,” he said, “in all gentleness to your herd.” And at once the bull returned gently to its herd. Then all the Jews, falling at his feet, asked to be regenerated by the water of baptism.

Helena Augusta herself also appeared publicly after the curtains of the court had been drawn aside, and, kissing the pope’s knees openly before all, [Col. 0206A] asked that a place of penance be granted to her. In that same hour many demons came out of possessed bodies and confessed that they had been compelled to depart at the command of Saint Silvester.

In the aforesaid disputation between Christians and Jews, Zenophilus and Craton were chosen by the Augustus and senate as the chief assessors and official arbiters; one was Greek and the other Latin. Both were highly accomplished orators, forthright lovers of truth, and men long proven in the Roman court as guardians of rectitude and despisers of greed. Both were pagans, so that they might favor neither side on grounds of religion, but seek only to serve justice, and so that neither Christians nor Jews might regard them with suspicion because of their own sect.

[Col. 0206B] When Christ triumphed through Saint Silvester, many Jews and pagans believed. Since these events took place at the beginning of the first month, they enrolled their names and were baptized at Easter. From that time the name of the Lord began to be magnified by all the Roman people, the flock of believers was strengthened throughout the world, and everywhere was greatly exalted by God’s power.

At Constantine’s command Pope Silvester assembled three hundred and eighteen bishops at Nicaea in Bithynia, and convened two hundred and seventy-seven bishops in council in the city of Rome. He decreed that no layperson should bring an accusation against a cleric. An oppressed person is to have the judges whom he chooses. Deacons are to wear dalmatics, and their left side is to be covered with a linen pallium. No cleric is to enter a court for any cause, nor plead his case before a judge except in the Church. The sacrifice of the altar at Mass is not to be celebrated upon silk or dyed cloth, but only upon linen, as it is written that the Lord’s body was buried by Joseph [Col. 0206C] in linen. If anyone wishes to serve or advance in the Church, he is to be a reader for twenty years, an exorcist for thirty days, an acolyte for five years, a subdeacon for five years, a deacon for seven years, a priest for three years, and then, if he deserves it, become a bishop. Finally, after countless good works, Silvester died on 31 December. The episcopal see was vacant for one hundred and sixty-five days.

## XXVI. Continuation of the history of the Roman pontiffs

Marcus, a Roman, son of Priscus, held office for two years, eight months, and twenty days. He built two basilicas: one on the Ardeatine Way in the cemetery of Balbina, where he rests; and another in the city of Rome near the Palatine. [Col. 0206D] He ordained twenty-seven bishops in various places. He died on 7 October. The episcopal see was vacant for twenty days.

Julius, a Roman, son of Rusticus, held office for fifteen years, two months, and seven days. In the time of Constantius the heretic, he endured many tribulations and was in exile for the Catholic faith for ten months; but after the tyrant’s death he returned gloriously to his see. He built two basilicas and three cemeteries. He ordained nine bishops. He died on 12 April. The episcopal see was vacant for twenty-five days.

Liberius, a Roman, son of Augustus, held office for six years, three months, and four days, in the time of Constantius. He spent three years in exile for the faith. Later, having agreed with the Arians, he was recalled through the heretical priests Ursatius and Valens [Col. 0207A] and violently persecuted Catholics. Finally, he was buried on 25 April on the Salarian Way in the cemetery of Priscilla. The episcopal see was vacant for six days.

Felix, a Roman, son of Anastasius, held office for one year, three months, and three days while Liberius was in exile. In a council of forty-eight bishops, he anathematized Constantine Augustus, rebaptized by Eusebius of Nicomedia, and the heretics Ursatius and Valens. He was therefore deposed and suffered martyrdom in the city of Corona on 11 November; the episcopal see was vacant for thirty-seven days. He ordained nineteen bishops, and his days are counted within the tenure of Liberius. For the enactments that Liberius made before his exile are authoritative; but those made after his return, because he had agreed with heretics, [Col. 0207B] are void.

Damasus, a Spaniard by birth, son of Antonius, held office for eighteen years, three months, and eleven days. Ursinus was ordained in rivalry with him, but was expelled from the city and established as bishop in Naples. Damasus, however, became praiseworthy in his virtues. He sought out and discovered many bodies of saints, and identified their tombs in verse inscriptions. He was maliciously accused of adultery by two deacons, Concordius and Callixtus, but after a synod was held he was cleared, as forty-four bishops condemned his accusers. He decreed that psalms be sung in church by day and night, and issued a decree about this to priests, bishops, and monasteries. He loved Jerome, interpreter of the divine law, strongly supported him with pontifical authority, [Col. 0207C] and urged him to investigate the certainty of the Scriptures. He ordained sixty-two bishops in various places. He was buried beside his mother on the Ardeatine Way, in the basilica which he himself built, on 11 December. The episcopal see was vacant for thirty-one days.

Siricius, a Roman, son of Tiburtius, held office for fifteen years. He made and disseminated many beneficial enactments throughout the world, because he was very solicitous for the Lord’s flock. He consecrated thirty-two bishops in various places. He was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way on 22 February. The episcopal see was vacant for twenty days.

Anastasius, a Roman, son of Maximus, held office for three years and ten days. He decreed that whenever the holy Gospels are read, priests should not sit but stand bowed. No overseas cleric is to be ordained without a written authorization from his bishop. He built the Basilica of Crescentiana in the second district of the city of Rome and consecrated eleven bishops. He was buried in his own cemetery at Ursumpileatum on 27 April. [Col. 0207D] The episcopal see was vacant for twenty-one days.

Innocent, from Alba, son of Innocent, held office for fifteen years, two months, and twenty-one days. He made many enactments, discovered many Cataphrygians and banished them into exile, and condemned the heretics Pelagius and Celestinus. He decreed that anyone born of a Christian woman should be baptized, a proposition which Pelagius condemned. He dedicated the basilica of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, in accordance with the pious provision in the will of Vestina, an illustrious [Col. 0208A] woman, and honored it with many gifts. He ordained fifty-four bishops. He decreed that the Saturday fast should be observed, because on Saturday the Lord was laid in the tomb and the disciples fasted. He was buried at Ursumpileatum on 28 July. The episcopal see was vacant for twenty-two days.

Zosimus, a Greek, son of Abramius, held office for one year, three months, and eleven days. He made many regulations in the Church, ordered deacons to have their left side covered with linen pallia, and ordered a candle to be blessed in the parishes. He consecrated eight bishops.

Boniface, a Roman, son of the priest Jucundus, held office for three years, eight months, and seven days. He and Eulalius were ordained in rivalry on the same day, and there was dissension in the clergy for seven months and fifteen days. Eulalius [Col. 0208B] was ordained in the Constantinian basilica, while Boniface was ordained in the Basilica of Julius. But by the authority of Honorius Augustus and of Valentinian, son of Placilla Augusta, both were expelled. When Easter came, Eulalius entered the city, baptized in the Constantinian basilica, and celebrated Easter. Therefore the emperors, angered by such presumption, drove Eulalius into Campania; but recalled Boniface to the city of Rome and established him as bishop. He decreed that no nun or woman should touch or wash the consecrated altar-covering, nor should anyone but a minister place incense in church. A slave, a person bound to the curia, or anyone subject to any other obligation is not to become a cleric. Pope Boniface built an oratory in the cemetery of Saint Felicitas the martyr, beside her body, and [Col. 0208C] ordained thirty-six bishops in various places. Then he was buried on the Salarian Way beside the body of Saint Felicitas on 25 October, and the episcopal see was vacant for nine days. Then clergy and people requested that Eulalius be recalled, but he did not consent to return to Rome.

Celestinus, a Roman, son of Priscus, held office for eight years, ten months, and seventeen days. He made many good enactments. He decreed that the one hundred and fifty psalms of David should be sung antiphonally before the sacrifice. For previously only Paul’s epistle and the holy Gospel were read, and Masses were celebrated. He consecrated forty-six bishops. He was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on 10 April. The episcopal see was vacant for twenty-one days.

Sixtus, a Roman, son of Xistus, held office for eight years and nineteen days. He was accused by a certain vassal. [Col. 0208D] Therefore Valentinian Augustus assembled a synod of fifty-six bishops, by whom the pope was cleared and the vassal condemned. The latter died within three months, and the pope buried his body at Saint Peter’s. Pope Sixtus adorned the basilicas of the saints with many ornaments and ordained fifty-two bishops. He was buried on the Tiburtine Way in the crypt beside the body of blessed Lawrence. The episcopal see was vacant for twenty-two days.

Leo, a Tuscan, son of Quintianus, held office for twenty-one years, one month, and thirteen days. At Chalcedon, aided by the Catholic emperor Marcian, he assembled two hundred and fifty-six priests, received and approved the written subscriptions of four hundred and six bishops, and, having set forth the Catholic faith, condemned the heretics Eutyches and Nestorius. He diligently issued many [Col. 0209A] letters concerning the faith, by which he repeatedly strengthened the Council of Chalcedon. He wrote twelve letters to Emperor Marcian, nine to Augusta Pulcheria, and eighteen to the bishops of the East. Zealous in sacred matters, he did many good works. He ordained one hundred and eighty-five bishops. He was buried beside the blessed apostle Peter on 11 April. The episcopal see was vacant for seven days.

Hilary, a Sardinian, son of Crispinus, held office for six years, three months, and ten days. He circulated letters concerning the Catholic faith throughout the East; confirmed the three synods of Nicaea, Ephesus, and Chalcedon; and condemned every heresy with anathema. He provided many precious ornaments for the basilicas of the saints and ordained twenty-two bishops. After many good works he was buried beside blessed Lawrence [Col. 0209B] in the crypt, near the body of Saint Bishop Sixtus. The episcopal see was vacant for fifteen days.

Simplicius of Tibur, son of Castinus, held office for fifteen years, one month, and seven days. He ordained thirty-six bishops. He was buried in the Basilica of Saint Peter the Apostle on 2 May. The episcopal see was vacant for six days.

Felix, a Roman, son of Felix, priest of the title of Fasciola, held office for eight years, eleven months, and seventeen days, from the times of Zeno Augustus and Odoacer, king of the Goths, until King Theoderic. He excommunicated Peter, bishop of Alexandria, and Acacius of Constantinople for deviating from the true faith, and sent two bishops, Misenus and Vitalis, from the Apostolic See against them. When they entered the city [Col. 0209C] of Heraclea, they were corrupted by money and did not carry out the pope’s instruction. When Pope Felix learned this, after an investigation he excluded both from communion. He ordained thirty-one bishops. He was buried in the Basilica of Saint Paul the Apostle, in the time of King Theoderic and Zeno Augustus. The episcopal see was vacant for five days.

Gelasius, an African, son of Valerius, held office for eight years and eighteen days. He loved the poor, enlarged the clergy, and delivered Rome from famine and danger. He made regulations for the whole Church. He composed tracts and hymns like Ambrose, and issued books against Eutyches and Nestorius, which are still kept stored in the archive of the library. He ordered the Manichaeans whom he found in the city of Rome to be deported into exile, and [Col. 0209D] burned their books before the doors of the Basilica of Saint Mary. He condemned Peter and Acacius forever unless they repented, because through them many evils and killings occurred. He ordained sixty-seven bishops. He was buried in the Basilica of the blessed apostle Peter on 21 November. The episcopal see was vacant for seven days.

Anastasius, a Roman, son of Peter, from the fifth district, Caput Tauri, held office for one year, eleven months, and twenty-four days. Many of the clergy withdrew themselves from communion with him because he wished secretly to recall Acacius; but he could not do so, because he was struck by God’s providence. He consecrated twenty bishops. He was buried in the Basilica of Saint Peter the Apostle on 19 November. The episcopal see was vacant for four days.

[Col. 0210A] Symmachus, a Sardinian, son of Fortunatus, held office for fifteen years, seven months, and twenty-seven days, in the time of King Theoderic and Emperor Anastasius. He and Laurentius, bishop of Nuceria, were ordained in rivalry; but by the judgment of Theoderic, since Symmachus had been ordained earlier and by the larger party, he was confirmed in the Apostolic See. After three years, however, he was falsely accused through Roman envy, and Peter, bishop of the city of Altinum, invaded the Apostolic See contrary to the canons. Then a very great schism arose in the Church and the clergy was again divided. Pope Symmachus, when a synod of one hundred and fifteen bishops had assembled, was cleared; and Peter of Altinum, invader of the Apostolic See, and Laurentius of Nuceria were condemned. Then, by all the bishops and the whole clergy and people, Symmachus was restored with glory to the Apostolic See at [Col. 0210B] Saint Peter’s. But Festus, head of the senate, and Probinus, former consuls, began to fight in the city with other senators. Through envy they persecuted all who communicated with Symmachus so extraordinarily that they even expelled consecrated women from their monasteries or dwellings, stripped women naked, and wounded them with the blows of beatings. In the middle of the city there was daily fighting against the Church, and many priests and other believers were killed. Among them the priests Dignissimus and Gordianus were seized and killed with clubs and the sword, along with many other Christians. Thus no member of the clergy was safe in the city, by day or by night. Faustus, a former consul, alone fought for the Church. Symmachus nevertheless endured [Col. 0210C] from the consulship of Paulinus to that of Senator. He banished into exile the Manichaeans whom he found in the city of Rome, and burned their images and books before the doors of the Constantinian basilica. He adorned the basilicas of the saints with diverse ornaments and ordained one hundred and seventeen bishops. He decreed that the angelic hymn should be sung every Sunday. Every year he supplied money and clothing to bishops confined in exile throughout Africa and Sardinia. He redeemed captives with money throughout Liguria and various provinces, and gave many gifts to the needy. After many good works, he was buried in the Basilica of Saint Peter on the nineteenth day of July. The episcopal see was vacant for seven days.

## XXVII. Continuation of the history of the Roman pontiffs

[Col. 0210D]

Hormisdas of Campania, son of Justus, from the city of Frision, held office for eight years and seventeen days. At the counsel of King Theoderic, he sent Ennodius of Ticinum and Fortunatus, bishop of Catania, to Constantinople, and absolved the Greeks who had been anathematized on account of the heretics Peter of Alexandria and Acacius of Constantinople. But the Emperor Anastasius, because he favored the Eutychian heresy, rashly expelled them; and, among other things, wrote back to the pope with arrogance: “We wish to command, not to be commanded.” Not long afterward, by God’s nod, he perished when struck by lightning. Justin, however, a Catholic, reigned after him, willingly obeyed the pope’s commands in everything, and honorably received Germanus, bishop of Capua, [Col. 0211A] and others sent from the apostolic see; accompanied by the consul Vitalian and a multitude of monks and distinguished men, he conducted them from the Round Castle as far as Constantinople. Then certain clergy who were accomplices of Acacius wickedly begrudged this glory, shut themselves up in the great church of Holy Wisdom, and, after taking counsel, informed the emperor that unless Acacius, their bishop, were restored to them absolved, they would not obey the apostolic see. Then Clovis, king of the Franks, became a Christian and sent a gift, with precious gems, to the blessed apostle Peter. The aforesaid pope flourished from the consulship of Senator to that of Symmachus and Boethius, and ordained fifty-five bishops in various places. He was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter on the eighth day before the Ides of August [6 August]. [Col. 0211B] The episcopal see was vacant for seven days.

John of Tuscany, son of Constantius, held office for two years, nine months, and sixteen days, from the consulship of Maximus to that of Olybrius. Then Justin, an orthodox believer, wished to extirpate all heretics and consecrate their churches to God. For this reason Theoderic Gualamer, because he was a heretic, burned with excessive anger and resolved to destroy all Italy by the sword. Pope John, therefore, asked by the king at Ravenna, undertook an embassy; although ill, he went to Constantinople and there restored sight to a blind man. Then, received with glory, he crowned the Emperor Justin and obtained from him indulgence for the heretics, for the deliverance of Italy. Meanwhile the heretical king put to the sword the illustrious senators and [Col. 0211C] former consuls Symmachus and Boethius. He also treacherously seized, on their return, Pope John and the senators who had been honorably received at Constantinople by the emperor; he made the pope a martyr in confinement at Ravenna on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June [18 May], and himself, by God’s nod, suddenly expired ninety-eight days later. [Note: [Col. 0211D] The manuscript reads *intravit* (“entered”); the expression has no sense.] Pope John consecrated fifteen bishops. His body was brought from Ravenna to Blessed Peter. The episcopal see was vacant for fifty-eight days.

Felix Samius, son of Catorius, held office for four years, two months, and three days, in the times of Theoderic, his grandson Athalaric, and the Emperor Justinian, from the consulship of Tiburtius to that of Lampadius and Orestes. He was ordained peacefully and consecrated twenty-nine bishops. He was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Paul on the fourth day before the Ides of October [12 October]. [Col. 0211D] The episcopal see was vacant for three days.

Boniface of Rome, son of Sigibuld, held office for two years and twenty-five days, in the time of the heretic Athalaric and the Emperor Justinian. During his ordination, there was great dissension among the clergy and senate for eighteen days. For Dioscorus was ordained together with him in the Constantinian basilica. But shortly afterward, by God’s nod, Dioscorus died on the second day before the Ides of October [14 October]. A very large multitude indeed supported him. Boniface bestowed small dishes upon presbyters, deacons, and notaries from inheritances, and aided the clergy with many provisions during a danger of famine. In the basilica of the apostle Saint Peter he convened a synod, [Col. 0212A] and chose the deacon Vigilius as his successor; but later repenting of this, he burned the written instrument of his subscription in the presence of the clergy and senate. He was buried in the basilica of the apostle Saint Peter on the seventeenth day of October. The episcopal see was vacant for two months and fifteen days.

John Mercurius of Rome, son of Projectus, of the Caelian Hill, held office for two years, four months, and six days, in the times of Athalaric and Justinian. The devout emperor, out of the highest love for the Christian religion, set down his faith in writing and sent his own written declaration, together with precious gifts, through Eparchius and Demetrius to the apostolic see. John consecrated twenty-one bishops. He was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter on the sixth day before the Kalends of June [27 May]. The episcopal see was vacant for six days.

[Col. 0212B] Agapetus of Rome, son of the presbyter Gordian, held office for eleven months and eighteen days. He was sent by Theodahad, king of the Goths, who had killed Queen Amalasuntha, daughter of King Theoderic, to the Emperor Justinian; by whom he was honorably received at Constantinople. There he exiled Anthimus, bishop of that city, because he denied the two natures in Christ, and consecrated the Catholic Menas as bishop. He then died at Constantinople on the tenth day before the Kalends of May [22 April]; his body was brought to Rome in a lead coffin and buried at Blessed Peter’s on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October [20 September]. The episcopal see was vacant for one month and twenty-eight days.

Silverius of Campania, son of Hormisdas, bishop of Rome, [Col. 0212C] held office for one year, five months, and six days. He was elevated by Theodahad the tyrant, not lawfully but through payment, force, and fear. After two months, however, Theodahad was destroyed by God’s nod; and Witigis forcibly took the daughter of Amalasuntha as his wife and was elevated as king. The Emperor Justinian sent the patrician Belisarius against the Goths to free Italy. The patrician accordingly took Naples, which resisted him, and killed all the Goths and citizens, so that not even priests or consecrated women were spared in the churches. Witigis, quickly gathering an army of Goths, besieged Rome for one year and killed innumerable persons by the sword or by famine—which was then extreme throughout the whole world. No one was permitted to enter or leave Rome. Then all private, fiscal, and Church possessions [Col. 0212D] were consumed by fire. Men were slaughtered by the sword; others perished from famine or disease. At length, by God’s grace, Belisarius put the Goths to flight and protected Rome.

When the empress asked Silverius to restore the heretic Anthimus, he steadfastly persisted in God and did not comply; rather, by his own authority he firmly confirmed the judgment of his predecessors. But she ordered the patrician Belisarius to send Pope Silverius into exile and substitute Vigilius, the *apocrisiarius*—papal representative—in his place. Belisarius reluctantly carried out the command. Certain false witnesses accused the pope of intending to surrender the city of Rome to the king of the Goths through the Asinarian Gate near the Lateran, [Col. 0213A] and Belisarius seized him in the Pincian Palace. Then, while the patrician Antonina severely rebuked the pope, the subdeacon John took the pallium from his neck and, stripping him in a chamber, clothed him in a monk’s habit. Silverius was thus sent into exile to Ponza; there he was sustained on the bread of tribulation and water of affliction, and was buried on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July [20 June]. He consecrated eighteen bishops and, after his death, performed many healing miracles. The episcopal see was vacant for fourteen days.

Vigilius of Rome, son of John the consul, held office for fifteen years, six months, and twenty-six days. Then Belisarius defeated Witigis in war, and John Sanguinarius, commander of the troops, pursued and captured him by night. Led to Constantinople, he was joyfully received by [Col. 0213B] the Emperor Justinian, who made him a patrician and a count and sent him near the Persian frontier, where he remained until death. The emperor also elevated the patrician Belisarius, granting him military rank, and sent him to Africa. Belisarius treacherously killed Guittarit, king of the Vandals, restored Africa to the commonwealth after ninety-nine years, and, coming to Rome, bestowed much of the Vandal spoils upon God, Saint Peter, and the poor. The Empress Theodora pressed Pope Vigilius in writing [Note: [Col. 0213D] Read: *urget*, “presses.” Le Prévost.] to restore Anthimus the heresiarch. He wholly refused, indeed holding unshakably to the judgment of his predecessors. Accordingly, when envious Romans made accusations and charged the pope, as though a murderer, with the death of Silverius, [Col. 0213C] the notary Anthimus was sent; Pope Vigilius was seized in the church of Saint Cecilia and conveyed by ship through Sicily to Constantinople. For two years the Greeks strove, by imperial power, to have the heretic restored, as Vigilius had promised while he held the rank of deacon. But the pope would by no means consent, preferring to die well rather than live badly. At length, after he had spoken firmly before Justinian and Theodora, someone slapped his face amid insults; the pope fled into the church of Saint Euphemia, to the pillar of the altar. But he was driven out from there, a rope was put around his neck, and he was dragged through the whole city until evening. He was then placed under strict guard, and the Roman clergy who had come with him were dispersed among various mines.

[Col. 0213D] Then the Goths made Baduila Totila their king, and not long afterward besieged Rome. The famine in the city became such that even women wished to eat their own children. At length Totila entered the city and, while the people hid in churches, held it for some time. Then Narses, a eunuch and chamberlain, was sent to Italy by the emperor; after King Totila had been killed with his army, Narses gained the victory. Hearing this, the Emperor Justinian rejoiced greatly and, at the request of the Romans together with Narses, sent Pope Vigilius back with his clergy; but Vigilius himself died at Syracuse from the pain of the stone. Finally he was buried on the Via Salaria near Saint [Col. 0214A] Marcellus. The episcopal see was vacant for three months and five days. He consecrated eighty-one bishops; and, to govern the clergy during his exile, he sent to the Lateran the presbyter Ampliatus, his *vicedominus* or deputy administrator, and Valentinus, bishop from Sicily.

Pelagius of Rome, son of John the vicar, held office for eleven years, ten months, and twenty-seven days. Two bishops—John of Perugia and Bonus of Reverentum—and Andrew, presbyter of Ostia, ordained him pope. [Note: [Col. 0213] Read: “of Ferentino.” An episcopal city in the Campagna of Rome.] For a multitude of religious, learned, and noble persons had withdrawn from communion with him, saying that Pelagius had involved himself in the death of Pope Vigilius, so that he might be afflicted by such great punishments. Pope Pelagius and Narses therefore took counsel. [Col. 0214B] After a litany had been appointed at Saint Pancras, they came with hymns and spiritual songs to the blessed apostle Peter. Pope Pelagius, holding the Gospel and the cross of the Lord over his head, ascended the ambo and thus satisfied all the people that he had committed no evil against Vigilius. He consecrated forty-nine bishops. He was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter on the sixth day before the Nones of March [2 March]. The episcopal see was vacant for three months and twenty-five days.

John of Rome, son of the illustrious Anastasius, held office for twelve years, eleven months, and twenty-six days. Then the Heruli made Sindual their king and began to oppress all Italy. But Narses, after killing the king, manfully subdued them. With God’s help he also killed Amingus and Butilinus, [Col. 0214C] leaders of the Franks who were pressing upon Italy, and kept all Italy in peace and gladness. But the Romans, from envy, accused him before Justinian and unjustly stirred the emperor against him. When Narses perceived that the emperor had stripped him of his former dignity, he summoned the Guinilian Lombards, who inhabited Pannonia, to invade Italy. This was done. Not long afterward Narses died and was brought in a lead coffin, with all his riches, to Constantinople. Pope John consecrated sixty-one bishops and was buried in the basilica of the apostle Saint Peter on the third day before the Ides of July [13 July].
