The episcopal see was vacant for ten months and three days.

Benedict of Rome, son of Boniface, held office for four years, one month, and twenty-eight days. In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord [Col. 0214D] 568, Alboin, king of the Lombards, brought the Lombards into Italy. Then famine also assailed the Italians and compelled them to surrender themselves to the Guinilians. Hearing this, the Emperor Justinian sent to Egypt and dispatched grain-laden ships to Rome, assisting those endangered by famine. On account of his frequent victories over hostile peoples, he was surnamed Alamannic, Gothic, Alan, Vandalic, and African. Within the city of Constantinople he built a church for Christ the Lord, which he named in Greek *Hagia Sophia*, “Holy Wisdom.” Its construction surpasses all buildings so completely that nothing like it can be found throughout the whole expanse of the earth. [Col. 0215A] This ruler was Catholic in faith, upright in works, and just in judgments; therefore prosperity attended him in everything. In his time Cassiodorus Senator, afterward a monk, shone in the city of Rome in both secular and divine learning. Among the other works he wrote nobly, he especially disclosed the hidden meanings of the Psalms with great power.

At that time Dionysius the abbot, established in the city of Rome, also composed the Paschal computation by remarkable reasoning.

Priscian of Caesarea likewise investigated, as one might say, the depths of the art of grammar at Constantinople.

Arator also, subdeacon of the Roman Church, [Col. 0215B] a remarkable poet, set down the Acts of the Apostles in hexameter verse.

At that time too, the most blessed father Benedict shone forth first in the place called Subiaco, forty miles from the city, and later at the fortress of Cassino, through the great merits of his life and apostolic powers. As is well known, the blessed Pope Gregory composed his life in graceful language in his *Dialogues*.

XXVIII. Continuation of the history of the Roman pontiffs.

Pope Benedict died, worn out by many labors and afflictions, and was buried in the basilica of the apostle Saint Peter on the second day before the Kalends of August [31 July]. He consecrated twenty-one bishops. The episcopal see was vacant for three months and ten days.

[Col. 0215C] Pelagius of Rome, son of Winigild, held office for ten years, two months, and ten days. He was ordained without the emperor’s command because the Lombards were besieging Rome and devastating Italy severely. Then there were excessive disasters and rains. A plague of the groin suddenly struck down the pope on the seventh day before the Ides of February [7 February]; he was buried at Blessed Peter’s. He ordained forty-eight bishops in various places. The episcopal see was vacant for six months and twenty-five days.

Gregory, a philosopher by training, son of Gordian, the most illustrious praetor, and of the blessed Silvia, presided for thirteen years, six months, and ten days, in the times of the Emperors Tiberius Constantine, Maurice, and Phocas. He expounded forty homilies on the Gospels, Job, and Ezekiel; he produced the *Pastoral Rule* and the *Dialogues*, [Col. 0215D] besides many other works which we cannot enumerate. For he shone as an incomparable teacher and, with great sagacity and immense diligence in speaking and writing, labored profitably and greatly benefited the children of God’s Church. He added to the prayer of the canon: “And dispose our days in your peace,” etc. Romanus, patrician and exarch, came to Rome and stirred up great disturbance among the Roman citizens. For, as he was returning to Ravenna, he occupied the cities held by the Lombards—namely Sutrium, Polimartium, Ameria, Perugia, and many others. Therefore King Agilulf, greatly enraged, advanced with a strong army against Perugia. There he besieged Maurisio, leader of the Lombards, who had surrendered himself to the Romans, and, after [Col. 0216A] several days, captured and immediately killed him. Not long afterward, when Agilulf returned to Ticinum, through the efforts of the blessed Pope Gregory he concluded a most firm peace with the Romans.

At the same time, the blessed Pope Gregory sent servants of God—Mellitus, Augustine, John, and many others with them who feared the Lord—to preach to the English people, so that he might convert them to our Lord Jesus Christ. After many great works, he was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter before the secretarium on the fourth day before the Ides of March [12 March]. He ordained sixty-two bishops in various places. The episcopal see was vacant for five months and eighteen days.

Sabinian of Tuscany, from the city of Blera, son of Bonus, held office for one year, five months, and nine days. Then [Col. 0216B] there was a severe famine in the city of Rome. The pope, after peace had been made with the Lombard people, ordered the Church granaries opened and grain sold at one solidus for thirty modii of wheat. He was buried in the church of the blessed apostle Peter on the sixth day before the Kalends of March [24 February]. He ordained twenty-six bishops. The episcopal see was vacant for eleven months and twenty-three days.

Boniface of Rome, son of John of Cappadocia, held office for eight months and twenty-two days. He obtained from Prince Phocas that the apostolic see should be head of all Churches, because the Church of Constantinople preferred itself to the Roman Church and styled itself the first of all Churches. He was buried in the church of the apostle Saint Peter on the second day before the Ides of November [12 November]. [Col. 0216C] He consecrated twenty-one bishops. The episcopal see was vacant for ten months and six days.

Boniface, a Marsian by nationality, from the city of Valeria, son of John the physician, held office for six years, eight months, and thirteen days. In his time there were severe famine, pestilences, and floods. Pope Boniface then asked Prince Phocas for the temple called the Pantheon, obtained it, and dedicated it in honor of All Saints. He was buried at the blessed apostle Peter’s on the eighth day before the Kalends of June [25 May]. He ordained thirty-six bishops. The episcopal see was vacant for six months and thirty-five days.

Deusdedit of Rome, son of the subdeacon Stephen, held office for three years and twenty-three days. He greatly loved and honored the clergy. Then Eleutherius, patrician and [Col. 0216D] chamberlain, stormed Naples and killed the rebel John of Compsa, who had killed many people. Peace was thus made throughout all Italy. Then there was a great earthquake. Such an outbreak of scabs followed among the people that no one could recognize his own dead. Pope Deusdedit was buried at the blessed apostle Peter’s on the sixth day before the Ides of November [8 November]; for his funeral he left one complete *roga*—a distribution or gift—to all the clergy. He ordained twenty-nine bishops. The episcopal see was vacant for one month and sixteen days.

Boniface of Campania, from the city of Naples, son of John, held office for five years. He was the gentlest of men and established many good things in the Church. Then Eleutherius the patrician invaded the realm as an *intarta*—that is, a rebel. [Note: [Col. 0215] I.e., “rebel.” See Du Cange’s *Glossary*, under *antartes*. Duchesne reads *in Tharsia* instead of *intarta*.] [Col. 0217A] But, coming to Rome, he was killed at Luceoli by soldiers from Ravenna. The pope was buried at the blessed apostle Peter’s on the eighth day before the Kalends of November [25 October]. He ordained twenty-nine bishops. The episcopal see was vacant for thirteen days.

Honorius of Campania, son of the consul Petronius, held office for twelve years, eleven months, and twenty-two days, in the time of the Emperor Heraclius. He did and taught many good things and adorned the basilicas of the saints with many ornaments. He decreed that every Saturday a litany should go forth from Blessed Apollinaris and that all the people should assemble at Blessed Peter’s with hymns and spiritual songs. He consecrated eighty-one bishops and was buried on the fourth day before the Ides of October [12 October] in the church of the blessed martyr Agnes, which he himself built from the ground up. The episcopal see was vacant for [Col. 0217B] one year, seven months, and seventeen days.

Severinus of Rome, son of Abienus, held office for two months and two days under the Emperor Heraclius. He was gentle and generous, greatly loving the clergy and the poor. Then the Lateran episcopal residence was violently plundered by the chartulary Maurice, the patrician and exarch Isaac, and the Roman army. After ordaining four bishops, the aforesaid pope was buried at Blessed Peter’s on the fourth day before the Nones of August [2 August]. The episcopal see was vacant for three months and twenty-four days.

John of Dalmatia, son of Venantius the scholar, held office for one year, nine months, and eighteen days. Through the most holy Abbot [Col. 0217C] Martin, he sent large sums throughout Dalmatia and Istria for the redemption of captives, and caused relics of saints to be brought thence with proper honor. He was buried at Saint Peter’s on the fourth day before the Ides of October [12 October]. The episcopal see was vacant for one month and thirteen days.

Theodore the Greek, son of Theodore the bishop, from the city of Jerusalem, held office for six years, five months, and eighteen days. Then the abominable chartulary Maurice rebelled against the patrician Isaac and bound all the judges and the army to himself by oaths. Isaac sent against him Donus, master of the troops and his treasurer; after capturing Maurice, Isaac had him beheaded and his head set upon a stake in the circus at Ravenna, while he kept the *imboiati*—perhaps “the shackled men”—in a strict prison to be punished. Isaac himself soon afterward perished suddenly by God’s nod; Theodore Calliopas, sent by the emperor, succeeded to [Col. 0217D] the government of Italy. Pope Theodore was very pious and good and deposed Pyrrhus and Paul, heretical bishops of Constantinople. He ordained forty-six bishops. He was buried at the blessed apostle Peter’s on the Ides of May [15 May]. The episcopal see was vacant for one month and sixteen days.

Martin of Todi held office for six years, one month, and twenty-six days. In his time Paul, bishop of Constantinople, rose against Catholic doctrine and, rashly overthrowing and plundering the altar of the Roman see which had been consecrated in the house of Placidia, forbade Roman *apocrisiarii* to worship there, to offer the immaculate sacrifice to God there, or to receive the sacraments of communion. Admonished by them and by other orthodox bishops, [Col. 0218A] he raged still more madly: he imprisoned some of them, deported others into exile, and subjected others to beatings. Pope Martin then gathered one hundred and five bishops in the city of Rome and, after condemning the heresies, confirmed the Church of God. Later, at Paul’s instigation, the Emperor Constantine sent the exarch Theodore into Italy and caused Pope Martin to be taken by him into exile at Cherson, where the holy bishop died on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October [17 September].

Eugenius of Rome, from the first Aventine district, a cleric from infancy, son of Rufinianus, held office for two years, nine months, and twenty-four days. He was very good and anathematized Peter, bishop of Constantinople, for heresy. He ordained twenty-one bishops. He was buried on the fourth day before the Nones of July [4 July] at [Col. 0218B] the blessed apostle Peter’s. The episcopal see was vacant for one month and twenty-one days.

Vitalian of Segni in Campania, son of Anastasius, held office for fourteen years and six months. He was well disciplined and consecrated ninety-seven bishops. Then the Emperor Constans besieged Romuald, son of King Grimoald, at Benevento; but, defeated there, he fled to Rome. There he was honorably received by the pope with the clergy, remained twelve days, and stripped away everything made of bronze for the city’s adornment. He inflicted many evils upon Italians and other peoples subject to him, and was afterward killed by his own men in Sicily while bathing. After him the tyrant Mezenzius seized the kingdom. Then the Saracens made a great slaughter of Christians in Sicily. Moreover, [Col. 0218C] Pope Vitalian was buried at the blessed apostle Peter’s on the sixth day before the Kalends of February [27 January]. The episcopal see was vacant for two months and thirteen days.

Adeodatus of Rome, formerly a monk, son of Jobianus, held office for four years, two months, and five days. Then Mezenzius was killed by the army of Italy in the city of Syracuse; many of the judges were mutilated, and his head was brought to Constantinople. The Saracens afterward captured the aforesaid city, slaughtered many of its people, carried away an immense booty—which the Emperor Constans had recently brought there with him—and returned to Alexandria. The aforesaid pope ordained forty-six bishops and was buried at Blessed Peter’s on the sixth day before the Kalends of July [26 June]. [Col. 0218D] The episcopal see was vacant for three months and fifteen days. Then there were unheard-of rains and thunder; legumes could not be gathered, but in the following year they grew again of themselves.

Donus of Rome, son of Maurice, held office for one year, five months, and ten days. Then, in the East, a comet appeared in August and for three months terrified those who beheld it in many regions from cockcrow until morning; death among human beings followed from the East. Pope Donus enlarged the [clergy] with various honors and consecrated six bishops. He was then buried at the blessed apostle Peter’s on the third day before the Ides of April [11 April]. The episcopal see was vacant for two months and fifteen days.

Agatho of Sicily held office for two years, six months, and four days, in the time of the Emperors Constantine, Heraclius, and Tiberius. [Col. 0219A] Then the moon underwent an eclipse in June for eighteen days, and a remarkable mortality followed. Parents and children, two or three at a time, were carried to burial. Then envoys of the apostolic see were honorably received by the emperors in the imperial city, and they gathered one hundred and fifty bishops from the eastern regions in a general synod to discuss the Catholic faith. There George of Constantinople, convicted of heresy, submitted. But Macarius of Antioch, stubborn in his error, deserved to be condemned with his followers; for he was deposed by the general judgment and sent into exile to Rome. Theophanius was appointed abbot of the Sicilian island. Pope Agatho consecrated eighteen bishops. He was buried at the blessed apostle Peter’s on the fourth day before the Ides of January [10 January]. The episcopal see was vacant for one year, seven months, and five days.

XXIX. Continuation of the history of the Roman pontiffs.

Leo the Younger, a Sicilian by nationality, son of Paul, held office for ten months and seventeen days. He was very eloquent, learned in the divine Scriptures, educated in the Greek and Latin languages, outstanding in chant and psalmody, and very zealous in every good work. He received the Sixth Synod, held in the palace of the Emperor Constantine called the Trullo, and translated it with the greatest diligence from Greek into Latin. Then, on the sixteenth day of April, in the eleventh indiction, after the Lord’s Supper, the moon underwent an eclipse and was almost the whole night in a blood-red appearance; after cockcrow it gradually began to grow bright again. Pope Leo ordained twenty-three bishops. He was then buried on the fifth day before the Nones of July [3 July] at [Col. 0219C] the blessed apostle Peter’s. The episcopal see was vacant for eleven months and twenty-two days.

Benedict the Younger of Rome, son of John, held office for ten months and twelve days. From childhood he served the Church and devoted himself to good works. He flourished in the time of Justinian and Heraclius. Then, at Theophany, the moon was entirely darkened as if under a cloud, though the sky was clear. In February a star appeared from the west by day and turned toward the eastern regions. After this, in March, Mount Bravius in Campania erupted for ten days, and all the neighboring places were devastated by its ash. The aforesaid pope ordained twelve bishops and was himself buried at Blessed Peter’s on the eighth day before the Ides of May [8 May]. The episcopal see was vacant for two months and [Col. 0219D] fifteen days.

John the Syrian, of Antioch, son of Cyriacus, held office for one year and nine days, in the time of the Emperor Justinian. While still a deacon, he had been sent by Pope Agatho, with other priests, to the imperial city. He was buried at Blessed Peter’s on the fourth day before the Nones of August [2 August]. The episcopal see was vacant for two months and eighteen days. He was afflicted by a prolonged illness and ordained thirteen bishops.

Conon of Sicily, son of Traceseus, held office for eleven months. At his election there was great contention: the clergy favored Peter the archpresbyter, while the army favored his follower, the presbyter Theodore. But suddenly, by God’s nod, abandoning Peter and Theodore, all elected Lord Conon, a handsome and devout [Col. 0220A] old man. He was afflicted by a prolonged illness and ordained sixteen bishops. He was buried at the blessed apostle Peter’s on the tenth day before the Kalends of October [22 September]. The episcopal see was vacant for two months and twenty-three days.

Sergius the Syrian, of Antioch, son of Tiberius, from Palermo in Sicily, held office for thirteen years, eight months, and twenty-three days, in the time of the Emperor Justinian, son of Constantine. When Pope Conon died, one party of the people elected Theodore the archpresbyter and another Paschal the archdeacon. But while the dissension was excessive, Sergius was elected by the clergy. Paschal secretly gave money to John Platinus, exarch, wishing through him to seize the papacy by force, but in vain. Not long afterward, because of certain incantations to which he adhered, he was expelled from the archdeaconry and died unrepentant after five years. The Emperor Justinian ordered a council to be held in the imperial city, and sent its acts, ratified by imperial hand, to Rome for Pope Sergius through Sergius the *magistrianus*. But because certain things contrary to ecclesiastical doctrine had been inserted there, Sergius refused to subscribe; consequently great turmoil arose. For Zacharias, the *protospatharius*, was sent by the emperor to Rome to seize the pontiff and take him to Constantinople. But, God stirring them up, the troops of Ravenna and the people of the Pentapolis assembled at Rome and shut the city gates in order to kill Zacharias. Trembling, he fled into the pope’s chamber and, fearful of death, hid anxiously beneath the bed. When the [Col. 0220C] army of Ravenna entered the Lateran episcopal residence armed through the gate of the blessed apostle Peter and threatened to throw down the doors of the patriarchium unless they were opened, the blessed pope went out and honorably received the soldiers and people who had hastened to his aid. By giving a gentle answer, he soothed their hearts. But they, inflamed by zeal for God and love for their bishop, did not leave the guard of the patriarchium until they had expelled the aforesaid spatharius from the city with insults. Moreover, he who had sent him was, at that very time, through the Lord’s requital, justly deprived of his kingdom; and the Church of God, with its bishop, was preserved unharmed through Christ’s favor.

Pope Sergius, with God showing the way, found in the sacristy of Saint Peter a large [Col. 0220D] portion of the holy Cross in a silver casket and decreed that it should be venerated by the people every year on the feast of its Exaltation. At the breaking of the Lord’s body he decreed that *Agnus Dei*—“Lamb of God”—should be sung three times by clergy and people. He ordained Damian, archbishop of Ravenna; Berhtwald, archbishop of Canterbury; Clement Guillebrord among the Frisian people; and other bishops in various provinces, ninety-seven in all. He was buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter on the sixth day before the Ides of September [8 September], under the Emperor Tiberius. The episcopal see was vacant for one month and twenty days.

John the Greek held office for three years, two months, and twelve days. By his counsels he saved Theophylact, exarch of Italy, from being killed by a riotous people in the city of Rome. He also induced Gisulf, duke of the Lombards, [Col. 0221A] who was committing arsons and many evils in Campania, to return to his own territories, after many gifts had been given for captives. He consecrated fifteen bishops and was buried at Blessed Peter’s. The episcopal see was vacant for one month and eighteen days.

John the Greek, son of Plato, held office for two years, six months, and seventeen days. He was very learned and eloquent, flourished in the time of Tiberius and Justinian, and diligently repaired many things in cemeteries of the saints and churches which had been ruined or left uncovered. Then Aripert, son of Raginbert, duke of the Taurini, king of the Lombards, restored the Cottian Alps to Saint Peter and renewed the grant inscribed in letters of gold. The Emperor Justinian, with the aid of Terbel, king of the Bulgars, recovered the kingdom which he had lost [Col. 0221B] and caused Leo and Tiberius, usurpers of the empire, to be beheaded in the circus before all the people. Pope John ordained nineteen bishops. He was buried at the blessed apostle Peter’s before the altar of Saint Mary, Mother of God, which he himself built, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November [18 October]. The episcopal see was vacant for two months.

Sisinnius the Syrian, son of John, held office for twenty days. He was resolute in spirit and concerned for the Romans, but was greatly afflicted by gout. On the twentieth day after his ordination he suddenly died and was buried at Blessed Peter’s. The episcopal see was vacant for one month and eighteen days.

Constantine the Syrian, son of John, held office for eight years and fifteen days. [Col. 0221C] He was a very good man. Then a great famine occurred at Rome for three years, followed by the greatest abundance. The Emperor Justinian sent the patrician Theodore into Italy; he captured Ravenna and caused the proud Archbishop Felix, deprived of sight, to go into exile in Pontus. At the request of the aforesaid ruler, the pope went with many persons to Constantinople, where he was received with great honor by Justinian, his son Tiberius, and the people. Not long afterward Philippicus killed Justinian and seized the kingdom. But shortly afterward Philippicus himself was expelled; Anastasius assumed imperial power and assented to the true faith. The aforesaid pope consecrated sixty-four bishops and was buried at Blessed Peter’s on the sixth day before the Ides of January [8 January]. The episcopal see was vacant for [Col. 0221D] forty days.

Gregory the Roman, son of Marcellus, held office for sixteen years, nine months, and eleven days, in the time of the Augusti Anastasius, Theodosius, Leo, and Constantine. He built many churches and abbeys and performed many other good works, impossible to enumerate. Through Bishop Boniface he converted Germany to faith in Christ. At that time the moon was seen blood-red until midnight; the River Tiber flooded and occupied Rome for seven days, so that, having passed out through the Flaminian Gate, it rose in the Via Lata to a depth of one and a half human heights. While Pope Gregory repeatedly conducted litanies with clergy and people, God at last took pity and removed the water after the eighth day. Anastasius, deposed from the empire, fought against Tiberius, [Col. 0222A] but was defeated and made a cleric. The abominable people of the Hagarenes ravaged Spain for ten years; when they sought to cross the Rhône into Francia, Eudes, duke of the Aquitanians, defeated them and killed 300,000 of them. It is recorded, however, that only fifteen hundred Franks fell there. Then, in a certain part of Campania, rain like fire was seen falling from heaven and burned up wheat, barley, and legumes.

Under Prince Leo, Constantinople was besieged by the Hagarenes for two years, but, under God’s protection, was not taken. Nevertheless, 300,000 of the city’s people died through famine or pestilence.

Liudprand, king of the Lombards, was then oppressing the Romans; but, restrained by the bishop’s exhortation, prayers, and holiness, he afterwards desisted.

Duke Basil, Exarch Paul, and other evildoers, by command of Leo Augustus, sought to kill Pope Gregory. But the Romans and Lombards, by God’s will, resisted with all their strength and protected the blessed bishop. They killed Jordanes the chartularius, John Barion, Duke Exclaratus, and his son Adrian, and entirely thwarted the emperor’s wicked designs. For he had decreed that no church should contain an image of the Savior, of His holy Mother, of any holy martyr, or of an angel. He asserted that all such things were accursed. Accordingly, he ordered sacred images in the imperial city to be removed and compelled them to be burned publicly in the midst of the flames. Those who resisted he condemned to be deprived of their heads or other limbs. He deprived Germanus, [Col. 0222C] bishop of Constantinople, who opposed him in this matter, of his episcopal office, and installed the priest Anastasius in his place. In January, for ten days, the star called Antefer shone in the west with rays. After this, Tiberius Petasius attempted to seize the throne, but was killed while Exarch Eutychius and the Romans fought against him. Pope Gregory ordained 150 bishops and, after many good works, was buried beside the blessed apostle Peter on the third Ides of February [11 February]. The episcopal see then stood vacant for one month and five days.

Gregory the Syrian, son of John, held office for ten years, eight months, and twenty-five days, while Leo and Constantine ruled. He was exceedingly renowned for holiness, devotion, wisdom, [Col. 0222D] and eloquence in Greek and Latin; he built many things and adorned many churches of God in various ways. In the city of Rome he assembled a synod of ninety-three bishops against the heretical emperors Leo and Constantine, who removed the sacred images of God and His saints from churches and irreverently burned them. He added to the canon that the priest should say: “Whose solemnity is celebrated today before the sight of your majesty, O Lord our God, throughout the whole world”; and he caused this to be written upon stone in the oratory. King Liudprand besieged Rome. On this account the pope sought aid from Charles, king of the Franks. Then, because of Transamund, duke of Spoleto, who had fled to Rome, four cities were taken from the Romans. The blessed pope consecrated eighty bishops and was buried on the fourth day before the Kalends [Col. 0223A] of December [28 November] in the church of the apostle Saint Peter. The see stood vacant for eight days.

Zacharias the Greek, son of Polochronius, held office for ten years, three months, and fourteen days. Adorned with every virtue, he benefited the Church of God. Italy was then greatly troubled. Therefore the pope went to King Liudprand, established peace for twenty years, and restored captives. Liudprand died in the thirty-second year of his reign, and Ratchis, son of Pemmo, duke of Friuli, assumed the kingdom. Then, while Emperor Constantine had gone out against the Hagarenes, a certain man named Artavastus secretly seized the empire. Constantine, however, assembled the army of the East, courageously assaulted the city, captured the king, and deprived the rebel and his accomplices of their eyes. Then Carloman, son of Charles Martel, king of the Franks, [Col. 0223B] became a monk at Monte Cassino. King Ratchis likewise, at the pope’s urging, came to Rome and, by God’s will, laid aside the royal diadem and became a monk. Pope Zacharias translated the four books of Dialogues of the blessed Pope Gregory from Latin into Greek, and ordained eighty-five bishops. On the Ides of March [15 March] he was buried beside the blessed apostle Peter. The see stood vacant for twelve days.

Stephen the Roman, son of Constantine, held office for five years and twenty-eight days. Then the priest Stephen was elected by the people. But on the third day, after rising from sleep and cheerfully sitting down to arrange his affairs, he suddenly lost his senses and speech, and died on the following day. Stephen the deacon was then ordained, adorned with every virtue. At that time Aistulf, king of the Lombards, [Col. 0223C] grievously persecuted the holy Church and strove to subject Rome entirely to his dominion. Therefore, when the pope could achieve nothing with him by prayers or gifts, he was compelled to go to Gaul in defense of the holy Church. King Pippin and the Franks received him honorably and had him spend the winter at Saint-Denis in Paris. Afterwards Pippin besieged Pavia with the army of the Gauls and compelled Aistulf to swear peace to the Romans. But after Pippin had returned home, Aistulf broke his oath. For he besieged Rome for four months and, digging up many bodies of saints, violated the cemeteries. Again Pippin, moved by the pope’s prayers, besieged Pavia and compelled the perjurer to restore to Saint Peter Ravenna, Narni, Rimini, and many other places that [Col. 0223D] had been taken away. Not long afterwards Aistulf perished while hunting, struck by a divine blow, and Duke Desiderius seized his kingdom. Pope Stephen ordained fifteen bishops and consecrated Pippin, king of the Franks, Bertrada the queen, and their sons Charles and Carloman. Then he was buried beside the blessed apostle Peter on the Kalends of May [1 May]. The see stood vacant for five days.

Paul the Roman, Stephen’s brother, held office for ten years and one month. In the time of Constantine and Leo, he performed many good works. He ordained sixty bishops; after his death the see stood vacant for one year and one month, when Constantine the transgressor seized the Apostolic See.

### XXX. Continuation of the History of the Roman Pontiffs

[Col. 0224A]

Stephen the Sicilian, son of Olibus, held office for three years, five months, and twenty-eight days. A vigorous, good, and wise man, he greatly benefited the Church of God. Before his election an unheard-of crime was committed at Rome. For Toto, duke of Nepi, compelled George, bishop of Palestrina, against his will to consecrate his lay brother Constantine pope. After that ordination George fell ill and, weakened beyond measure, never afterwards sang Mass. For his right hand withered and contracted, and he could not even bring it to his mouth; in that same year he died from a most grievous illness. After a year Rome was handed over to Christopher the primicerius and Sergius the sacellarius, and Duke Toto was treacherously killed by Demetrius and Gratiosus. [Col. 0224B] After this Pope Stephen was lawfully elected by all. Not long afterwards Constantine the usurper, his brother Passibius, Theodore the bishop, and the vicedominus were seized and blinded by certain malign men; and Christopher, his son Sergius, and many others perished through the deceit and instigation of King Desiderius. Meanwhile Pope Stephen, at the beginning of his pontificate, sent Sergius the secundicerius to Charles the Great, king of the Franks, and requested counsel and assistance from him. Charles willingly sent him twelve bishops from among the Franks, men of the highest repute and learned in Holy Scripture and the ordinances of the sacred canons.

In April, a synod of many bishops was assembled in the basilica of the Holy Savior beside the Lateran; and Constantine, who had suddenly been made a cleric [Col. 0224C] and pontiff from being a layman, was condemned by the judgment of all. Then a general decree was issued under an anathema forbidding any layman, or anyone from another order, to be promoted to the episcopate except through the successive grades; and ordering that all that the same Constantine had done in ecclesiastical matters for divine worship should be repeated, except baptism and sacred chrism. Pope Stephen consecrated thirty bishops and was buried at Saint Peter’s. The see stood vacant for eight days.

Adrian the Roman, son of Theodore, of the region of the Via Lata, held office for twenty-three years, ten months, and seventeen days. He was noble and handsome, steadfast, devout, and holy. Then Desiderius, king of the Lombards, inflicted countless [Col. 0224D] evils upon Rome, Ravenna, and their subjects. Therefore, at the pope’s request, Charles the Great came into Italy, besieged Pavia for six months, and, with God’s help, took it. On Holy Saturday he was honorably received at Rome with his followers. He sent the captured King Desiderius and his wife to Francia, and restored to Saint Peter what had been taken from him. Pope Adrian built churches, furnishings, and many remarkable works, and by his prayers compelled Emperor Constantine to assemble 350 bishops at Nicaea; he caused that synod to be translated from Greek into Latin. Then, in the twentieth year of this pope’s pontificate, the River Tiber reached the gate of Saint Peter’s and brought great loss upon the citizens. But the pope instituted litanies, and the Lord, taking pity, removed the water. He ordained 185 bishops and was buried [Col. 0225A] beside Saint Peter on the seventh day before the Kalends of January [26 December]; on that same day Pope Leo succeeded him.

Leo the Roman, son of Aizuppius, held office for twenty years, five months, and sixteen days, like his predecessors in all things. While he was diligently doing what was good, and one day was proceeding with the people in a litany to the blessed apostle Peter, Paschal the primicerius and Campolus the sacellarius sprang from ambush with their armed retainers, drove the unarmed people away in fear of their weapons, and attempted before the altar of Saint Peter to deprive the pope of his eyes and tongue. But after several days Albinus the chamberlain rescued him from prison, and the Lord Almighty restored him to complete health. Winigis, duke of Spoleto, came to his aid, and, seeing the pope—[Col. 0225B] who had been torn with clubs and had lain half-dead, weltering in blood before the altar—miraculously healed, he glorified the Lord with other faithful men. Afterwards the pope went to Charles the Great, king, and set forth to him his complaint concerning what had been done. Charles received so great a man honorably and sent him back with two archbishops, Idilwald and Arno, six bishops, and three counts. The king himself later came to Rome, and on the day of the Lord’s Nativity was crowned by that pope in the church of Saint Peter; by all, Romans and Franks alike, he was made Roman emperor.

After this, in the ninth indiction, on the second day before the Kalends of May [30 April], a great earthquake occurred and destroyed the whole church of the apostle Saint Paul; Pope Leo restored it most excellently. [Col. 0225C] This bishop also ordered litanies to be celebrated for three days before the Ascension of the Lord. None of his predecessors did more than he in churches of saints, ornaments, or other necessary things. He ordained 126 bishops. He was buried in the basilica of the apostle Saint Peter on the second Ides of June [12 June]. The see stood vacant for one month.

Stephen the Roman, son of Marinus, held office for seven months. To secure the peace of the holy Church, he went into Gaul to Emperor Louis, obtained from him whatever he wished, and mercifully brought thence the exiles who had been banished for the crime committed against blessed Pope Leo. He consecrated five bishops and was buried beside the blessed apostle Peter. The [Col. 0225D] see stood vacant for twenty-six days.

Paschal the Roman, son of Bonosus, held office for seven years, four months, and eighteen days. He proved a most holy imitator of his predecessors and did many beautiful and useful things for the Church and its people. He consecrated forty bishops. He was buried in the church of Saint Peter. The see stood vacant for four days.

Eugenius the Roman, a good and holy man, held office for four years. Then great abundance and peace prevailed throughout the world.

Valentine the Roman, son of Peter, of the region of the Via Lata, abounding in every virtue, held office for forty days. He was chosen in the Lateran palace by one hundred bishops, the Roman nobles, and all the people; he was taken from the church of Holy Mary [Col. 0226A] Mother of God and placed upon the pontifical throne, but shortly afterwards died a holy death.

Gregory the Roman, son of John, handsome and noble, wise and holy, held office for sixteen years. Then the Hagarenes came forth from their own territories and grievously devastated islands and regions of Christians; after killing men, they plundered basilicas and dwellings of the faithful and, raging wildly, destroyed them. Therefore Pope Gregory built walls for Ostia, which for this reason was afterwards called Gregorianopolis. He performed countless other good works. For he built many basilicas, transferred many bodies of saints, and carefully placed them in suitable locations. He consecrated 185 bishops and was buried in the basilica of the apostle Saint Peter. The see stood vacant for fifteen days.

[Col. 0226B]

Sergius the Roman, son of Sergius, held office for three years. When he had been elected according to custom, John the deacon, with a rustic band armed with weapons of war, broke down the doors and, transgressing the established law and order, forcibly entered the patriarchium. But after one hour his troop fled in terror, and John the usurper was captured, beaten, and deprived of the diaconate. At that time Lothair Augustus sent Drogo, archbishop of Metz, and his son Louis, with many bishops, abbots, and counts, to Rome. They wrought much slaughter in towns and countryside along the way, and by tyrannical cruelty terrified the native inhabitants and compelled them to flee into hiding. One day, therefore, a dark mass of clouds arose, and certain leading men of Drogo [Col. 0226C] were struck by lightning and died. Louis then came to Rome, and Pope Sergius anointed him with holy oil and consecrated him king of the Lombards. Pope Sergius ordained twenty-three bishops and founded several abbeys and churches. He was buried beside the blessed apostle Peter, and the see stood vacant for two months and fifteen days.

Leo the Roman, son of Raduald, held office for eight years, three months, and six days. He shone like the sun in the world through innumerable good works, and greatly benefited the Church of God in buildings, ornaments, and other useful undertakings. Soon after the death of Pope Sergius, the Saracens plundered the basilicas of the apostles Peter and Paul. But when they wished to return by ship to Africa, [Col. 0226D] they perished in storms at sea. Then such an earthquake occurred in Rome that everything seemed shaken by the elements. Pope Leo forbade laymen to be in the presbytery during Masses. In the first year of his pontificate, through his merits and prayers he drove away a basilisk, which, hiding in the foul caverns of Rome, killed many by its breath. The blessed pope also extinguished, by making the sign of the cross against it, a fierce fire raging in the quarter of the Saxons. He made many churches and ornaments, restored ancient cities, renewed the wall of Rome, enclosed the church of Saint Peter with a wall, and fortified it like a city, called Leonine from his name. With all the Roman people, amid great rejoicing, he dedicated it on the fourth day before the Kalends of July [28 June].

Behold, in this little work I have recorded the succession of one hundred pontiffs who governed the Apostolic See after the blessed [Col. 0227A] apostle Peter, insofar as I have investigated it in the writings of Saint Pope Damasus to Jerome and in the Acts of the Pontiffs.

As for the other forty who presided over the Apostolic See after Leo IV down to our own time, I have not hitherto found complete accounts of their deeds; therefore I scarcely dare to say a few things concerning them. I strive only to set forth their names in order; but I am wholly compelled to be silent concerning their lineage and deeds, until, by God’s gift, I can find fuller writings about them, as I desire.

Pope Benedict held office one year, six months, and ten days. Pope Nicholas, nine years and ten months. Pope Adrian, five years. Pope John, ten years. [Col. 0227B] Pope Marinus, one year and four months. Pope Adrian, one year and four months. Pope Agapitus, one year.

Basil Stephen, one year. Then Formosus, John, and Stephen flourished in the time of Louis from overseas. After them came Marinus, Agapitus, Octavian, Leo, Benedict, John—who blessed Otto the Younger—Benedict, Benedict, Gerbert Silvester, Agapitus, and Benedict. Thus, for nearly 110 years, eleven fathers presided over the Apostolic See, but I have not yet found their genealogy or the certain dates of their elevation or death.

Clement Suidger, who was bishop of Bamberg, held office for nine years and blessed Emperor Henry and Agnes.

[Col. 0227C]

Opo Damasus, who had been bishop of Aquileia, held office one year.

[Col. 0228A]

Leo the Lotharingian held office for five years. He was Bishop Bruno of Toul. He came into Gaul and held a great council at Reims. He renewed the ancient decrees of the holy Fathers which had fallen into neglect, and made many salutary and useful corrections in both orders.

Gebehard Victor held office for three years.

Frederick Stephen, son of Duke Gothelo, held office one year.

Gerard Nicholas, the first chosen from among the Franks, held office for two years.

Alexander of Lucca held office for eleven years.

Gregory Hildebrand, a monk from boyhood, held office for fourteen years. In his time Emperor Henry intruded Guibert of Ravenna and, having expelled the pope, greatly troubled the Roman Church.

[Col. 0228B]

Desiderius Victor, formerly abbot of Cassino, held office for two months.

Urban Odo, formerly a monk of Cluny and bishop of Ostia, held office for twelve years; he directed a Christian army to Jerusalem against the pagans.

Paschal Rainerius, a monk from the valley of the Bruttii, held office for twelve years.

Gelasius John of Cádiz held office for two years.

Calixtus Guido, son of William, duke of Burgundy, who had been archbishop of Vienne, held office for six years.

Honorius Lambert, who had been bishop of Ostia, held office for five years.

Innocent Gregory of Pavia held office for twelve years. In the ninth year of his pontificate he assembled a great council at Rome and enacted many measures, although few are preserved.

[Col. 0228C]

End of this book.

[Col. 0227]

## Second Part of the *Ecclesiastical History* of Orderic Vitalis, Monk of the English Nation, of the Monastery of Saint Evroul at Ouche

In it the warlike achievements of the Normans in Francia, England, and Apulia; the foundations of monasteries; the succession and deeds of bishops and abbots throughout almost all Neustria; and many other matters worthy of remembrance are clearly set forth under Duke William II, surnamed the Bastard.

## Summary of Book Three

I. Prologue. II. The foundation of the monastery of Saint Evroul at Ouche and of various monasteries in Neustria. The invasions of the Normans into this province. [Col. 0229] III. The baptism of Rollo. The rule of his successors. Foundations of monasteries. IV. The restoration of the monastery of Ouche. V. Gervais, benefactor of the monastery of Ouche, and his family. VI. History of the monastery of Ouche. VII. Continuation of the history of the monastery of Ouche: Abbot Theodoric. VIII. Migrations of the Normans into Apulia. Their first settlements there. Anschetillus the monk. IX. Continuation of the history of the monastery of Ouche and Abbot Theodoric. X. Abbot Theodoric’s journey to the East. His death. XI. Continuation of the history of Ouche: Robert of Grandmesnil, abbot. XII. Wars between Franks and Normans. Various events. XIII. Dissensions in Normandy. Osbern is imposed as abbot upon the monks of Ouche in Robert’s place. Abbot Robert goes into Apulia to Robert Guiscard. Various events. XIV. Continuation of the history of Ouche: Abbot Osbern. XV. William, duke of the Normans. Robert of Vitot or Wace. Extinction of the line of Geroi. XVI. William, count or marquis of the Normans. The dispute between Hugh of Grandmesnil and Ralph, count of Mantes. Death of Abbot Osbern. XVII. Comets. Events in England. Harold’s usurpation. William, marquis of the Normans, prepares to cross the sea into England. XVIII. Continuation of the history of Ouche. Further concerning Osbern’s death. Election of Abbot Mainer. XIX. Saint Josse, son of Juthail, king of the Bretons. XX. Events in England. The Norwegians are defeated by the English. William, duke of the Normans, invades England. The famous battle. XXI. Effects of the battle. William subdues the whole land. He is crowned king of the English.

# Book Three

## I. Prologue

[Col. 0229A]

We ought unceasingly to apply ourselves to praising the Creator in all His works; for we cannot probe His ineffable power and greatness, nor do we possess the capacity by which His sublimity and tireless goodness may be narrated by us. The pages of the Old and New Testaments treat of this; every wise person searches and reflects upon it; but no one penetrates the immensity of the depths of God. The knowledge of Christ’s love surpasses all human wisdom; to seek it out, embrace it, and pursue it with all one’s strength is just and full of eternal salvation. For this reason blessed men, whose praise is found in authoritative books and who rejoice with the angels in [Col. 0229B] heaven, despised transitory things and longed for those that endure; abhorring fleshly things, they beneficially enjoyed spiritual ones. They followed the Savior’s footsteps by the arduous path of virtues and left us a saving example, so that, as their followers, we may hasten by the path of righteousness to the everlasting inheritance—a work for which, burdened by sins, we are exceedingly sluggish and weak. Yet we ought, as far as we can, to strive sincerely to follow their footsteps, so that, joined to their merits, we may someday deserve to be added to the company of the blessed. In the earlier part I gladly spoke of certain friends of God and lords and rulers of His [Col. 0230A] people; to meditate or speak faithfully about them is pleasant to the soul and a useful remedy for inward maladies. Now, however, my masters impose another work upon me and furnish material concerning Norman events, since the Normans, coming forth from Denmark, devoted themselves not to letters but to arms, and until the time of William the Bastard labored more at warfare than at reading or composition. Dudo, dean of Vermandois, eloquently narrated the military deeds of three dukes; abounding in many words and verses, he composed a panegyric concerning them and sent it to Richard, Gunnor’s son, seeking his favor. William, surnamed Calculus, a monk of Jumièges, followed him and elegantly abridged his work; he also briefly and clearly set forth the deeds of the four dukes [Col. 0230B] who succeeded them.

## II. The Foundation of the Monastery of Saint Evroul at Ouche and of Various Monasteries in Neustria; the Invasions of the Normans into This Province, Where They Settled

First I shall undertake a work concerning the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth, which He Himself cultivates and protects throughout the world by His mighty right hand against the snares of Behemoth. In the region which was formerly called Neustria and is now called Normandy, this vineyard, tended by laboring cultivators, spread abroad [Col. 0231A] its shoots and offered God abundant fruit in persons who persevered in holiness. For many monasteries were built there by good husbandmen, where the branches of that vine—that is, good Christians—gave themselves up, that they might fight more safely, to the end, against the snares of spiritual enemies. Thus Saint Audoenus, the bishop who flourished in great excellence, both secular and spiritual, in the time of Dagobert, king of the Franks, and Louis his son, founded one convent of nuns at Fécamp and another of monks at Rouen. There he himself was buried in the year 678 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and there he lay concealed for 165 years, until the Normans devastated Rouen. In the days of that bishop, Saint Wandrille gathered a great host of monks at Fontenelle, and blessed Philibert, the strong standard-bearer of a distinguished battle-line, shone forth at Jumièges. In an earlier time also, that is, while Chilperic and his nephew Childebert ruled the Franks and by royal authority defended the innocent from wicked men, Evroul of Bayeux, taught by an angelic revelation, established a monastery in the forest of Ouche. He reformed the rustic inhabitants, who had formerly served robbery and brigandage, and by the nourishment of teaching and the working of miracles summoned them to a better way of life. Thus the Lord also spread abroad His vineyard in other places through good cultivators and abundantly infused the sweetness of His salvation into Gallic hearts.

[Col. 0231C]

After the kingdom of the Franks had, by God’s favor, been greatly exalted above neighboring peoples and enlarged by the frequent victories of its kings Pippin, Charles the Great, and Louis the Pious, excessive greed, pride, and lust seized nobles, men of middling condition, and the lowly alike. Plunging them into the snares of wickedness, these vices led them to act against the author of their salvation, so that they did not faithfully obey Him. The whole order of clergy and laity, assaulted by the aforesaid calamities, fell from its former strength and, yielding to the world’s enticements, languished after abandoning the splendor of its former rigor. Yet divine mercy long spared sinners and invited them to repentance in many ways. To those turning back from the snares of wickedness it graciously granted forgiveness; but upon those persisting in evil it brought the scourge [Col. 0231D] of its wrath.

In the time of Charles, king of the Franks, surnamed the Simple, Brier, called Iron-Rib, son of Lothbrok, king of the Danes, went forth from his sheath with his foster-father Hasting and a vast multitude of young men to despoil nations. Suddenly, like a violent whirlwind from the sea, he entered Gaul, swiftly burned towns and cities together with the monasteries of saints, and for thirty years raged insatiably against Christians with his accomplices. Then Rouen, Noyon, Tours, Poitiers, and other principal cities were burned. Unarmed peoples were killed; monks and clerics were scattered; and the bodies of saints were either left without veneration in their tombs, after their buildings had been destroyed, or carried by devout guardians to foreign places.

[Col. 0232A]

But by the dispensation of divine mercy, consolation soon came from the same people from which the desolation of Neustria had come. For nearly thirty years after Hasting’s devastation had passed, Duke Rollo entered Neustria with a strong force of Danish youths and strove to crush the Franks through prolonged incursions. In battle with the Franks, he killed their standard-bearer Roland and put to flight Rainald, duke of Orléans, together with the Frankish army, after defeating them in war. He besieged the city of Paris for four years, but, God preventing it, did not gain it. He assaulted and captured Bayeux, killed its count Berengar, and took his daughter Poppa in marriage; by her he begot William surnamed Longsword. By these and innumerable other conflicts he wore down the Franks and, through constant plunder and burning, devastated almost the whole of Gaul as far as Burgundy. Since the Franks could not endure such attacks and all jointly begged for peace, King Charles gave Rollo his daughter, named Gisela, in marriage and left him the entire land from the river called Epte to the Ocean Sea, to possess forever.

## III. Rollo’s Baptism; the Rule of His Successors; Foundations of Monasteries

Therefore, in the year 912 from the Lord’s Incarnation, Duke Rollo [Col. 0232C] was baptized by Lord Franco, archbishop of Rouen; having despised the idols which he had formerly served, he devoutly embraced Christianity with his whole army. Having completed five years from his baptism, he died. His son William, who after him held the duchy of the Normans for twenty-five years, restored to its former condition the monastery of Jumièges, which Saint Philibert had built but Hasting had destroyed.

In the year 942 of the Lord’s Incarnation, while Louis ruled as king of the Franks, Duke William was killed through the treachery of Arnulf, lord of Flanders. His son Richard, then ten years old, became duke of the Normans and, amid varied circumstances, now prosperous and now adverse, vigorously held the duchy for fifty-four years. Among the other good works he performed, he built three monasteries: one at Fécamp in honor of the Holy Trinity; another on Mont-Tombe in honor of Saint Michael the Archangel; and a third at Rouen in honor of the apostle Saint Peter and Saint Audoenus, archbishop.

[Col. 0232D]

Then, in the year 996 of the Lord’s Incarnation, after the death of Richard the Elder, his son Richard, Gunnor’s son, succeeded and held the duchy of Normandy piously for thirty years. He rebuilt the monastery of Fontenelle, which Saint Wandrille had built but Hasting had destroyed; and his wife Judith, sister of Geoffrey, count of the Bretons, founded a monastery at Bernay [Col. 0233A] in honor of Holy Mary, Mother of God.

After Richard Gunnorides died, his son Richard the Younger succeeded. He died after holding the duchy for barely one year and a half. Then his brother Robert assumed the principate of Normandy and held it illustriously for seven and a half years. Following in the footsteps of his fathers, he began to restore the abbey of Cerisy. But, pierced by the fear of God, he relinquished earthly honor and, taking up a voluntary pilgrimage, went to the Lord’s tomb at Jerusalem. On his return journey he died at the city of Nicaea in Bithynia, in the year 1035 from the Lord’s Incarnation. His son William, then eight years old, assumed the duchy of the Normans and, assailed by the plots [Col. 0233B] of many rivals, held it energetically for fifty-three years. He took pains to follow the endeavors of his parents in the worship of God and, with God’s favor, surpassed all the glory of his fathers in wealth and power. At Caen he built two monasteries: one for monks, in honor of Saint Stephen the first martyr, and the other for nuns, in honor of the Holy Trinity.

Seeing such zeal for holy religion in their princes, the barons of Normandy desired to imitate them and urged themselves and their friends to similar works for the salvation of their souls. Each hastened to outdo another in good works and worthily to surpass him in generosity of almsgiving. Every powerful man judged himself deserving of ridicule if he did not support clerics or monks upon his estate with the necessities of life for God’s service.

[Col. 0233C]

Thus Roger of Tosny built the monastery of Châtillon, otherwise called Conches, where Abbot Gilbert, a man of great integrity and wisdom, flourished praiseworthily.

Goscelin of Arques founded outside the walls of Rouen, on the hill of the Holy Trinity, the monastery commonly called Saint Catherine’s; the venerable Abbot Isembert, eminent in wisdom and religious devotion, presided over it.

William, count of Eu, at the prompting of his devout wife Lescelina, built the abbey of Saint Mary upon the stream of the Dives; Ainard the German, a man endowed with holiness and learning, governed it for a long time.

[Col. 0233D]

In the time of Duke Robert, Count Gilbert of Brionne led an expedition of three thousand armed men into the district of Vimeu; but the outcome did not prosper according to his desire. For Count Enguerrand of Ponthieu met him with a strong force and, after battle was joined, compelled him and his men to flee in defeat; among the fugitives he captured many, killed others, and disabled others with wounds. There a certain knight named Herluin, fearing danger and fleeing with all his strength for his life, vowed to God that, if he escaped safely from the imminent peril, he would thereafter serve as a knight no one but God alone. By God’s will he honorably escaped the danger and, mindful of his vow, left the world and founded, on his hereditary estate at the place called Bec, a monastery dedicated to Holy Mary, Mother of God. [Col. 0234A] The shepherds of God’s holy Church chose this man because of his nobility and piety and set him over the new monastery which he had begun. During his governance Lanfranc and Anselm, with other profound scholars, went there to the schools of Christ; and there William, son of Geroi, Hugh, count of Meulan, and other distinguished knights took up Christ’s warfare. There, to this day, many clerics and laymen live under the monastic habit and, fighting against Zabulun, serve God praiseworthily.

Humphrey of Vieilles, son of Turold, began two monasteries at Préaux, one for monks and the other for nuns. His son Roger of Beaumont loved them greatly and willingly [Col. 0234B] enriched them from his own revenues.

William, son of Osbern, founded two monasteries on his own land, one at Lyre and the other at Cormeilles, where he himself lies buried. Many other Norman nobles also built houses of monks or nuns in various places, according to their means.

Greatly stirred by their example, Hugh of Grandmesnil and Robert vowed that they too would build, from possessions which they held by hereditary right, a monastery for their own salvation and for the salvation of the souls of their forebears.

Accordingly, when they had resolved to build a monastery at Nuceret, their estate near Grentemaisnil, and were already setting about the work, word reached the ears of William, son of Geroi, their maternal uncle, that his nephews Hugh and Robert had begun to build a monastery. This man had indeed been in secular life a knight of great eminence, terrible to enemies and faithful to friends. He had many sons and brothers and nephews powerful in arms, and very formidable to enemies both near at hand and far away. William, surnamed Talvas, son of William of Bellême, invited him to his wedding and, while he suspected no evil, deprived him of his eyes without any offence on his part, and cruelly mutilated him by cutting off his genitals and the tips of his ears. For this great crime he became hated by all; and after some time he was even expelled from all his honor by his own son, Arnulf by name.

[Col. 0234D] William of Geroi loved the Church of God throughout his life, and honored monks, clerks, and other religious persons. Twice he sought the Lord’s Sepulchre at Jerusalem: once while safe and prosperous, and again after the misfortune which we have related as having befallen him. After returning from his second pilgrimage he abandoned the world; going to Bec, he assumed the monastic habit there and devoutly granted to that house the church of Saint Peter at Ouche. Thus Abbot Herluin sent the monk Lanfranc—who afterwards became archbishop of Canterbury—with three monks to Ouche, and through them caused the service of God, which had fallen away, to be restored there. At that time the place was deserted, and ivy growing up covered the walls of the church. Only two aged clerks, Restold and Ingrannus, dwelt there; in so great a wilderness, amid poverty, they served God according to their ability.

After some time, when William learned of his nephews’ plan to construct the abbey, as mentioned above, he came to them and said:

> “I rejoice greatly, my dearest ones, that Almighty God has deigned to inspire your hearts to build a house in His name. But you see that this place where you have begun to build is not suited for the dwelling of monks, because water is lacking there and woodland is far away. It is certain that monks cannot exist without these two resources. But if you are willing to accept my counsel, I shall point out to you a more suitable place. There is a place in the district of Ouche where Saint Ebrulf, formerly the friend of God and an abbot, lived, and from there, after performing many miracles, happily passed to Christ. Restore, therefore, his monastery there, which was destroyed by pagans; there you will find an abundance of water. I have woodland adjoining the place, from which I shall supply sufficiently everything necessary for the church. Come and see the place; and if it pleases you, let us build there together a house for God, gather faithful men who may pray devoutly for us, and give them from our possessions and rightful revenues enough that they may always be free to devote themselves to divine praises.”

Hearing this, Hugh and Robert approved his counsel and came with him to inspect the aforesaid place. When they arrived, a little book of the Life of Saint Father Ebrulf was presented to Robert. [Col. 0235C] He read it carefully and expounded it wisely to Hugh and his other companions. In short, the place at Ouche pleased both brothers. But because that place had already been granted to the monastery of Bec, and some monks of that monastery, as we have said, were living there, they gave Abbot Herluin and the monks of Bec, by way of exchange, the estate called Rosseria, and thus rendered the aforesaid place free.

## IV. Restoration of the Monastery of Ouche

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1050, in the fourth indiction, after their plan to restore the monastery at Ouche had been confirmed, William and Robert, sons of Geroi, and Hugh and Robert, sons of Robert of Grentemaisnil, approached William, [Col. 0235D] duke of the Normans. They disclosed their intention to him and asked him to assist their salutary undertaking by his princely authority. By common agreement they also surrendered the oft-mentioned place freely into his protection, so that neither they nor any others might ever be permitted to demand from the monks or their men any customary due or revenue whatsoever, apart from the benefit of prayers. The duke gladly assented to their good intention, confirmed the charter concerning the possessions which his magnates were giving to Saint Ebrulf, and entrusted it to Malger, archbishop of Rouen, and to the suffragan bishops, to be strengthened by their subscriptions.

Then Hugh and Robert, having received from the duke permission to choose an abbot, went to Jumièges and requested from Lord Robert, abbot of that church, the monk Theoderic to govern their abbey. The abbot willingly favored the just request of the noble men and granted them the monk whom he knew to be fit for pastoral care. Rejoicing, they presented him to the duke. The duke received him with fitting reverence and, giving him the pastoral staff according to custom, appointed him over the church of Ouche. Then Hugh, bishop of Lisieux, went to Ouche with Osbern the archdeacon and his other clerks; he brought with him the venerable monk Theoderic and solemnly consecrated him there on the third Nones of October [5 October], a Sunday.

Having been ordained, he was not raised up in pride, but showed by words and deeds the way of religious life to those over whom he was set. [Col. 0236B] From childhood he had been brought up in the house of the Lord and, through long discipline, had learned to lead a religious life continuously. He was assiduous in holy prayers and vigils, and also in abstinence. He afflicted his own body with cold so severely that he sometimes went through an entire winter without a fur garment. One day, therefore, when according to his usual custom he wished to offer sacrifice to God, he found upon the altar a fur garment of remarkable whiteness. Not doubting that it had been placed there not by human hands but by angels, he gave thanks to God, put it on, and joyfully completed the divine service. We heard from truthful monks who were then dwelling in the aforesaid monastery that this occurred in the church of Jumièges, while he was still a cloistered monk.

The venerable Theoderic, abbot of Jumièges, had lifted this man from the sacred font and had greatly loved him, reared under the monastic yoke in the school of Christ. When he had reached mature strength and was conspicuous for good character, the abbot made him his deputy for the spiritual benefit of the brethren and advanced him to the instruction of children and the guardianship of the cloister’s priorship. Then, as has been said above, this man of God was taken from Jumièges in the time of Abbot Robert and placed over the newly planted abbey at Ouche, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1050, the fourth indiction: the nineteenth year of King Henry of France and the fifteenth of Duke William’s rule in Normandy.

[Col. 0236D] For the construction of the new house, with his father’s permission, he brought with him from Jumièges his nephew Ralph, Hugh the cantor, and other suitable brethren. With them and through them he zealously established regular observance, restrained rigor, and a fitting order in divine worship. He received persons of differing ages and conditions who came for conversion, and diligently instructed them according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. First, he humbly taught Gunfrid, Rainald, Fulk son of Fulk the dean, and several others skilled in grammar, the reformation of life in the school of Christ. He also treated kindly the old man Riculf, the rustic priests Roger and Durand the gardener, Goisfred and Ulric, and other simple disciples. Since they could not grasp the profound systems of Scripture, he gently fed them with the milk of pious encouragement; by displaying holy deeds, he strengthened them beneficially in faith and religious life.

He likewise carefully instructed Herbert and Berengar, Goscelin and Ralph, Gilbert and Bernard, Richard and William, and many other boys of good promise in the house of the Lord: to read well, sing, write, and diligently practice the other good studies appropriate to servants of God seeking true contemplation. [Col. 0237A] When the country people saw such zeal for holiness in a barren countryside, long previously deserted, they began to marvel. Some thereby gained salvation, while others brought loss upon themselves. Some, seeing their way of life, imitated them; others, envying them, pursued them with various troubles. Yet both received their due reward, God the most equitable judge rendering it. Noblemen and men of middling rank, inspired by God, flocked there and devoutly commended themselves to the prayers of God’s servants. Bringing gifts of charity, they blessed God, who sustained His servants upon unfruitful ground.

Therefore, while the church of Ouche was rising through the merits of Saint Father Ebrulf, and growing everywhere in honor of God through the zeal and labor of Geroi’s family, Roger of Montgomery, viscount of Hiesmois, began to envy his kinsmen because they burned ever more fervently [Col. 0237C] in God’s love. He determined entirely within himself to perform a similar work for the salvation of his soul. Accordingly, he summoned Abbot Gilbert of Châtillon with his monks. They had begun to maintain the monastic order at Nuceret but, when Hugh and Robert changed their plan, as related above, had refused to follow their wishes; indeed, accusing them of fickleness for altering the project of construction, they had left them. Roger summoned these men and gave them Troarn in order to build an abbey; there he expelled twelve canons whom his father Roger had established there. Having expelled the clerks—because they had served gluttony, lust, and other pleasures of the flesh, as well as secular gain—he installed there monks trained in regular discipline.

[Col. 0237D] By command of Father Gilbert, the monks took up the strict way of religious life in the church of Saint Martin and entrusted it to their followers to be observed until death. Their successors, under the learned fathers Gerbert, Durand, and Arnulf, have diligently endeavored to maintain it laudably down to the present day.

## V. Concerning Geroi, Benefactor of the Monastery of Ouche, and His Family

Concerning Geroi, son of Ernald the Fat of the court of Sedal, son of Abbo the Breton—whose descendants conferred many benefits upon the monks of Ouche—it is pleasing here briefly to inform posterity who and what manner of man he was.

He sprang from the great nobility of the Franks and Bretons and flourished nobly through remarkable worth and courage in the times of Hugh the Great and Robert, kings of the Franks. [Col. 0238A] His sister Hildiard had three sons and eleven daughters; married to honorable men, these daughters bore many sons, who in the ensuing age were a great terror to enemies in arms in Gaul, England, and Apulia. Among the other brave deeds which Geroi performed, he fought with William of Bellême against Herbert, count of the people of Le Mans. When William was defeated and fled with his men, Geroi stood firm and manfully sustained the battle until he compelled Herbert and all his men to flee. Having gained victory, he deserved to be praised for it to this day by those who know of it.

A powerful Norman knight named Helgo offered him his only daughter in marriage and gave him Monasteriolum, Escalfoi, and all his land lying between these two strongholds. But Helgo died shortly afterward; Geroi possessed all his honor, while the maiden who had been betrothed to him was overtaken by untimely death and died before the wedding. Then William of Bellême brought Geroi to Rouen before Richard, duke of Normandy. Recognizing his valor, the generous duke honored him and granted him all Helgo’s land by hereditary right. Returning from there, Geroi took as wife Gisela, daughter of Turstin of Bastembourg. By her he begot seven sons and four daughters, whose names were: Ernald, William, Fulk, Ralph Malacrown, Robert, Hugh, and Geroi; Heremburgis, Hadwisa, Emma, and Adelaide.

The often-mentioned hero, though he flourished abundantly in this world with offspring, riches, [Col. 0238C] and extensive possessions, nevertheless faithfully loved God, who grants all things, and honored His Church, its worship, and its ministers. From his own resources he built six churches in the Lord’s name. At Vernuciae he built two churches: one to Mary, holy Mother of God, and the other to Saint Paul, Doctor of the Gentiles. In the village called Gloz, in the district of Lisieux, he founded a third for Saint Peter, prince of the apostles; at Escalfoi, a fourth for the apostle Andrew; at Monasteriolum, a fifth for Saint George the martyr; and at Haute-Rive he restored a sixth for Saint Martin the confessor. With such patrons assisting him, the aforesaid man lived honorably for a long time in this world; after death, through their merits, he obtained, as we believe, forgiveness of sins and blessed rest in the company of the faithful.

When Geroi died, his sons were still boys, and only Ernald and William were knights. Gilbert, count of Brionne, trusting in his own strength and desiring to enlarge his territories, boldly attacked the orphans with a powerful force and sought to take Monasteriolum from them by force of arms. But they gathered a band of kinsmen and retainers, resisted him bravely in open country, and, after great slaughter, forced him to flee defeated. Avenging themselves, they soon afterward violently took from him the borough called Sappus. Duke Robert, however, reconciled them; sympathizing with the orphans and rejoicing in their valor, he obtained Sappus for them from Count Gilbert by his counsel, so that a firm peace might be made. [Col. 0239A] But the same count, because after some years he was hostile to the aforesaid seven sons of Geroi and wished to take back from them Sappus, which he had granted them at Duke Robert’s counsel, met his death through their courage and strength, although surrounded by a great multitude of men.

All these brothers were energetic and generous, skillful and agile in war, terrible to enemies, and kind and gracious to companions. They rose through differing fortunes and nevertheless—such being the human condition—fell. It would be lengthy and impossible for me to recount the various deeds of each; I wish only briefly to make known to posterity the end of each one.

Ernald, the firstborn, a strong and worthy man, was one day playing at Monasteriolum and wrestling with a young man when he happened to fall upon a sharp bench. Three ribs were broken, and he died three days later. William, second by birth, lived a long time and ruled all his brothers throughout his life. He was very eloquent and witty, generous and spirited, beloved by dependants and feared by opponents. None of his neighbors dared in any way invade his land or exact any customary exaction from his men. He held the episcopal dues of the estates of Monasteriolum and Escalfoi, nor did any archdeacon dare there to harass the priests of that honor.

[Col. 0239C] For after his father Geroi had obtained Helgo’s estate, as stated above, he asked the inhabitants of that region to what bishopric they belonged. They answered that they belonged to no bishopric. But he said: “This is altogether unjust. Far be it from me to be without a shepherd and the yoke of ecclesiastical discipline!” He then investigated which of the neighboring bishops was more religious; recognizing the virtues of Roger, bishop of Lisieux, he subjected all his honor to him. He also persuaded Baldwin of Balgenzai and his sons-in-law, Wascelin of Pont-Erchenfroi and Roger of Merula, likewise to submit to that bishop their lands, which enjoyed a similar freedom.

Bishop Roger, seeing that the aforesaid magnates were voluntarily humbling themselves to him, rejoiced over them and gave a privilege that the clerks of their lands should not go outside their jurisdiction to plead cases, nor be oppressed by the unjust encroachments of archdeacons. William of Geroi firmly maintained this privilege and obtained it from Lord Bishop Hugh for the monks of Ouche.

He married Hiltrude, daughter of Fulbert of Bèna, who had built the castle of Laigle in Duke Richard’s time, and by her begot Ernald of Escalfoi. Then he took in marriage Emma, daughter of Walchelin of Tanet; she bore William, who afterwards in Apulia was surnamed “the Good Norman.”

[Col. 0240A] The oft-mentioned man was loved by Richard and Robert, dukes of the Normans. Because of the fidelity which he kept toward his lords Robert of Bellême, Talvas, and Geoffrey, and toward other heirs or friends, he endured very many losses and dangers. For he voluntarily destroyed his own castle of Montaigu to ransom his lord Geoffrey of Mayenne, whom William Talvas had captured and would not permit to leave prison unless the aforesaid castle, which he greatly feared, were demolished. After Geoffrey escaped Talvas’s bonds, he built for the baron of Geroi the castle of Saint-Céneri upon the Sarthe, in return for the great fidelity which he had found in him. I could relate much about William, but because I am occupied with many concerns, I am compelled to pass to other matters. I shall discuss his end more fully later. Now I shall briefly set forth the affairs of his brothers, as I promised above.

Fulk, the third, held half of Monasteriolum and begot two sons, Geroi and Fulk, by a concubine. After Duke Robert’s death he was killed with his godfather, Count Gilbert, whom he was escorting. Robert held the castle of Saint-Céneri with the surrounding region for a long time. Duke William gave him in marriage his cousin Adelaide, by whom he begot a son named Robert, who now serves King Henry of England. But after many remarkable and admirable exploits, when great hostilities had arisen between the Normans and the Angevins, he held the castle of Saint-Céneri against Duke William. There, in the twenty-fifth year of that duke’s rule, he was besieged; having eaten poisoned fruit which he had forcibly taken from his wife, he died five days later.

[Col. 0240C] Ralph, the fifth brother, was surnamed “the Clerk,” because he was exceptionally well educated in letters and other arts. He was also called Malacrown, because in his youth he had been occupied with military exercises and frivolities. He was highly skilled in medicine and learned the profound secrets of many matters, of which old men still speak to their children and grandchildren with wonder. At length, abandoning the world’s allurements, he fled to Marmoutier; there, having become a monk under Abbot Albert, he humbly prayed to God that his body might be disfigured by the disease of incurable leprosy, so that his soul might be cleansed from the filth of sins. He obtained what he had piously prayed for and died happily about six years after his conversion.

Hugh, the sixth brother, flourishing in youth, was carried off through envious fortune. One day, as he was returning from the castle of Saint Scholastica with his brothers and many retainers, and was practicing jousting with his companions beside the church of Saint German in the territory of Escalfoi, his squire, carelessly casting a missile, struck him grievously. Being gentle by nature, he immediately called the same squire to him and secretly said:

> “Flee quickly, for you have gravely wounded me. May God have mercy on you! Flee before [Col. 0241A] my brothers notice this and kill you for what has happened.”

Thus the noble young man died that day.

Geroi, the youngest of all, while still blooming in the first flower of youth, seized plunder in land belonging to the church of Lisieux. Returning from there to Monasteriolum, he fell into madness and died. Thus, though in different ways, one death took all the sons of Geroi and allowed none of them to reach old age.

Heremburgis, the eldest daughter, was given to Wascelin of Pont-Erchenfroi; by her William and Ralph were born, and they later gave great assistance to Robert Guiscard, duke of Calabria, in Apulia and Sicily. Then Hadwisa was joined to Robert of Grentemaisnil, and bore him Hugh, Robert, Ernald, and an equal number of daughters. After his death, she was joined to William, son of Archbishop Robert, and bore him Judith, who later became wife of Count Roger of Sicily. [Col. 0241B] Geroi’s third daughter was Emma, given to Roger of Merula; by her were born Ralph and William, the father of our neighbors Ralph and Roger. The fourth, Adelaide, was joined to Solomon of Sablé and bore him Rainald, whose descendant, named Lisiard, now gives King Henry of England great assistance against the Angevins. Let this suffice concerning Geroi’s descendants.

Now let us return to the subject from which we have digressed for a while.

## VI. History of the Monastery of Ouche

[Col. 0241C]

In the first year in which the abbey of Ouche was founded, William and Robert, sons of Geroi, and Hugh and Robert, their nephews, assembled at Ouche with their sons, nephews, and barons.
