Discussing the welfare of the new monastery which they had begun, they jointly decreed that each of them, at his death, should grant himself together with all his property to Saint Ebrulf; and that none of them should give or sell elsewhere any tithe, church, or anything else belonging to a church without first offering it to the monks of Ouche for purchase. This was willingly confirmed by the priest Fulk, Osmund Basseth, Lupetius and Fulk, sons of Fredelendis, Odo Rufus, Richard son of Guibert, Robert of Torp, [Col. 0241D] Geroi of Logis, and their other barons. Then the aforesaid founders of the monastery reckoned the extent of their possessions and, according to their means, gave a good portion to the church which was being begun.

The possessions which Robert, Hugh, and Ernald, sons of Robert of Grentemaisnil, granted to the church of Ouche for their salvation were these: at Nuceret, the church with the entire tithe, the priest’s land with arable land of three ploughlands, and the estate called Solengiacus; at Oillei, with the entire benefice which the clerk Tezscelin held, including the tithe of the mills of that estate; likewise the English estate with its chapel; the church of the estate called Villaris, with one tenant; and at the estate called Oth, [Col. 0242A] the chapel and the priest’s land with one tenant and the tithe of the mills of the same estate. In the chapel of Waipré they gave also such a share as their father Robert had held; moreover, the tithe of Buinna; and at Belmes, a third part of the mill with its tithe; the benefice of the priest Fulk—namely, the church and tithe of Grentemaisnil—and the tithe of the mill of Olivet; one tenant at Collavilla with the tithe of the whole estate; also the tithe of wax and of Saint Peter’s pence “between the mountains”; further, the church in the settlement called Fogei and a share of the tithe of Coluncella, which their father Robert had held.

Hugh gave to that monastery the land of Cueleio, at the voluntary request of the lords of that estate, whose allod it was; indeed, he also gave its tithe from all ploughlands and livestock, and the tithe of Mont Calvet, both from toll and from grain; the church of Lovignei with the priest’s land; moreover, the land called Noer Mainard; at the place called Maisnil Bernard, land for one plough and the land of the estate of Tanacet; besides these, the chapel of Mancelles with the priest’s land, and at Sappus the toll-tithe; also the estate called Maisnil Dode, the church of Limboth with the priest’s land, and the share which their mother Hadwisa held at Vieux-Maisnil. At Neuf-Marché, Hugh gave a fourth part of the chapel of Saint Peter and the tithe of half the toll of the entire estate, and likewise of the mills; [Col. 0242C] at Seiri-Fontaine, the chapel and a third part of the tithe with all first-fruits, and five crofts.

William, son of Geroi, with the consent and gift of his sons Ernald and William and of his brothers Robert and Ralph Malacrown, gave to the aforesaid monastery the chapel of Escalfoi and the tithe of the toll of that estate, together with the priest’s land and that of Adelelm; also the tithe of the whole woodland belonging to that estate, both from swine and money, and the woodland itself for every necessity. He further gave all the chapels which he then held in his lordship: one built in honor of Saint George at the estate called Monasteriolum; two at Vernuciae, one in honor of Saint Mary and the other [Col. 0242D] in honor of Saint Paul; and two at Sappus, one in honor of Saint Peter and the other in honor of Saint Martin. He bestowed all these with their tithes and associated lands; in addition, the toll-tithes and all customary dues, both from woods and from other matters, which were then owed him at Escalfoi, Monasteriolum, and Sappus.

Therefore, after Abbot Theoderic of the aforesaid monastery had been appointed by God’s granting grace, he bought from Ernald, son of the said William, with the consent of his uncle Robert and at the command of Count William, the land of Balgenzai, as Baldwin, the same count’s treasurer, had held it; the part of the land of Escalfoi lying between the Black Water and Carentonne; Henry’s cleared land; and the tithe of the mill of Escalfoi. Ernald further gave that monastery the land of Haute-Rive and everything pertaining to it, with all its chapels and the priests’ lands, and the land of Dorthmusi.

Finally, his brother William, son of the aforesaid William, with the approval of his brother Geroi and of his kinsmen, namely Geroi and Fulk, granted to the said place all the chapels within his power, having received a considerable sum from the abbot of the aforesaid monastery. One of these was situated at Maisnil Bernard in honor of Saint Sulpicius; another at Roilville in honor of Saint Leodegar; another at Moenai in honor of Saint Mary; [Col. 0243B] and half of that same Moenai, which Robert held, with his approval as well; one at Ternant; one at Exarz in honor of Saint Peter; one at Algerun together with the whole estate; and one at Bois-Herbert. William himself, along with the lords of these chapels—Roger Gulafret of Maisnil Bernard, Herfred of Roilville, Robert of Moenai, Henred of Ternant, William the priest of Exarz, William the provost of Algerun, and Roger Faitel of Bois-Herbert—willingly granted all these to the aforesaid monastery for the redemption of their souls, with all tithes and priests’ lands.

Likewise, William gave the same monastery at Vernuciae land of one ploughland for the redemption of the soul of Emma, his mother. He further gave half the mills of Vernuciae, with the consent of his brother Ernald; what he held there in his lordship; Warin’s land; the grove of Landigula; at Vernuciae, Burnend’s land; two fishermen of Ternant; and at Monasteriolum, three ovens and one burgess. Then William, son of Wascelin of Pont-Erchenfroi, gave the aforesaid monastery the church of Blessed Mary and whatever the priest Osbern held, with the re-tithe of toll, and the tithe of mills or ploughlands which he held there and elsewhere, or would hold; at Roilville, the portion which he himself held.

Afterwards Robert, son of Helgo, with the consent and gift of his lords William and Robert, together with their sons and nephews, [Col. 0243D] sold to the monks of the aforesaid monastery the church of Saint Martin on the river Waiol. In the same place he also gave the priest’s land with another tract of land amounting to eight ploughlands, which they purchased for no small price. He also gave half the chapel of Saint Andrew at Sappus with the priest’s land, and half of all his land in that estate. Robert, son of Teodelin, gave the other half of the same chapel with half of the whole estate.

Finally, Abbot Theoderic bought from William and Robert, sons of Ralph surnamed Fraisnel, for eighteen pounds, the church of Saint Mary of the Wood, built in former times by the aforesaid monastery, together with the woodland there; he bought it as a monk named Placidus had held it. Furthermore, Hubert of Uncins sold the aforesaid abbot the church of the same estate and arpents of land. [Col. 0244A] Their lord William, son of Osbern the seneschal, granted all these things.

After this Robert, son of Geroi, approving and confirming everything which his brothers, nephews, they themselves, and their men had given to the aforesaid place, also gave from his own estates to that place Saint-Céneri, Saint Peter of Potestas Nidi, all tithes pertaining to those places, half the thicket of Saint-Céneri, fishing rights in the Sarthe at the discretion of the monks dwelling there, Saint Mary of Mont Wantelen, the entire tithe of Siralais, and the tithe of all honors which he himself might acquire. Then Ralph, son of Geoffrey, his knight, gave the same place the church of Radon with his consent. Meanwhile a worthy knight of Dreux, named Wado, hearing of these things, gave the church of Saint Michael situated upon the Avre in the district of Évreux, with the consent of his lords, sons, kinsmen, and friends.

These are the donations which William and Robert and their other kinsmen gave to the monastery of Ouche. Having made a charter concerning them, they presented it to William, duke of Normandy, for confirmation. He gladly received their requests and kindly granted their donations to the aforesaid monastery. By the privilege of a princely charter he also distinguished the church of Ouche, that it might remain forever free and immune from every alien subjection. Concerning the election [Col. 0244C] of an abbot for that place, he granted everything to the counsel of the brethren, while preserving the requirements of regular discipline: namely, that no affection for friendship, kinship, or indeed money should corrupt the votes of the electors.

Finally, the aforesaid prince inserted this at the end of the charter and confirmed it in these words:

> “I, William, count of the Normans, caused this little charter of donation to be written and entrusted it to the hands of the archbishop of Rouen, bishops, abbots, and princes—whose names and marks are written below—to be confirmed under excommunication, so that it may remain henceforth and forever unshaken and supported. If anyone should presume to infringe it, or by himself or through another should wish by any device to inflict any injury upon it, let him know that, by the authority of God and of all the saints, unless he makes amends, he is excommunicated from all Christendom and accursed forever.”

Having said this, Duke William signed the charter with the sign of the cross. Then subscribed: Malger, archbishop of Rouen, son of Richard, duke of Normandy, and Gunnor; Hugh, bishop of Lisieux, son of William, count of Eu; Odo, bishop of Bayeux, uterine brother of Duke William; William, bishop of Évreux, son of Gerard Flaitel; Gilbert, abbot of Châtillon; William, Robert, and Ralph, sons of Geroi; their nephews Hugh of Grentemaisnil, Robert and Ernald, and William son of Wascelin; Ralph of Tosny; [Col. 0245A] Ralph Tesson; Roger of Montgomery; William son of Osbern; Richard of Belfou; Richard of Saint Scholastica; and very many other magnates of Normandy. Gathered in the forest of Lyons at the duke’s court on the river Loire, before the church of Saint Denis, they confirmed the charter of the church of Ouche in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1050, the fourth indiction.

In the same year Robert of Grandmesnil exchanged secular dress and, under the rule of Abbot Theoderic at Ouche, assumed the monastic habit. He was, indeed—as we have mentioned above—the son of Robert of Grandmesnil, a most valiant baron, born of Hadwisa, daughter of Geroi. In childhood he learned letters abundantly, and among his companions was notably distinguished by a retentive memory for them [Col. 0245B]. But when he reached the years of youth, scorning the leisure of study, he turned to the labor of arms and served as Duke William’s squire for five years. He was then fittingly equipped with arms by that duke, made a knight, and nobly honored with many gifts.

But, considering the vicissitudes of mortals, he chose rather to remain lowly in the house of the Lord than to flourish for a time like grass in the tents of sinners. For he often recalled the perils of secular warfare, which his father and countless others had experienced: while bravely attacking their enemies, they fell into the snare that they had prepared for others. For his father Robert fought, with Roger of Tosny, against Roger of Beaumont [Col. 0245C]. In that conflict Roger was slain with his sons Elbert and Elinancus, while Robert received a mortal wound in the bowels. Carried home, he survived for three weeks and divided his land between his sons Hugh and Robert. He then died on 18 June [1050] and was buried beside the church of St Mary at Norrey.

His son Robert was moved by this and strove to serve in a better warfare. Therefore, as has been sufficiently said above, he resolved to build a monastery in the aforesaid village for the salvation of himself and his own, and, with the consent of his brother Hugh, generously to subject to it his entire share of the inheritance. But, changing his plan at the persuasion of his maternal uncle William, son of Geroi, he made a general testament with his brother Hugh concerning the goods [Col. 0245D] mentioned above, came to Ouche, and there devoutly professed monastic life according to the Rule of St Benedict.

He endured many labors for the support of the poor church, and repeatedly took away the wealth of his parents, who abounded in riches, distributing it charitably for their salvation to the aid of the faithful. Having given his mother Hadwisa sixty Rouen pounds, he obtained from her his marriage-portion—namely Norrey of Mainard, Vieux-Mesnil, Tansy, and Mesnil-Dodé—and handed it over to the church of Ouche. At that time he also bestowed upon the men of Ouche a great psalter adorned with varied paintings, the gift of his mother; to this day the assembly of monks, intent upon psalmody, frequently chants it [Col. 0246A] in praise of God.

Emma, wife of King Æthelred of the English, had presented this volume to her brother Robert, archbishop of Rouen; and William, son of that prelate, had privately taken it from his father’s chamber and brought it to his beloved wife Hadwisa, wishing in every way to please her. The aforesaid man also acquired many other good things for his church, and was acceptable to the brethren both in providing ecclesiastical ornaments and in securing necessary supplies.

## VII. Continuation of the history of the monastery of Ouche: Abbot Theoderic

The venerable Abbot Theoderic zealously devoted himself to monastic observance and sought to benefit the community entrusted to him by words and deeds [Col. 0246B]. He was a Norman by birth, originating from the district of Talou [Note: [Col. 0245D] Today Talou.], of medium height, agreeable in speech, ruddy in face, learned in sacred letters, and dedicated to divine worship from childhood to grey hairs.

But just as tares arise unseasonably in a wheat harvest, to be wholly uprooted by the diligent reaper at harvest-time and handed over to the unspared fire, so wicked sons grow up among the company of the devout; but at the appointed time they shall be exposed by the just Judge and sternly subjected to deserved punishments.

Under the aforesaid abbot, a monk named Romanus was maintained among the flock at Ouche. At the devil’s instigation, he stole tunics, breeches, and other such things. When Father Theoderic repeatedly rebuked him [Col. 0246C] for committing such crimes, he utterly denied that he had stolen, though shortly afterwards he often confessed it. One night, while lying in his bed, he was possessed by a demon and violently tormented. Hearing him crying out horribly, the monks approached him; driving the demon away and sprinkling him with holy water, they could scarcely at length rescue him from demonic affliction. Returning to himself, he understood that the devil had received such power over him because of the thefts he had committed, and promised thereafter to guard himself from this wickedness. But afterwards, like a dog returning to its vomit, he returned to it. Therefore Abbot Theoderic had his hood cut off [Col. 0246D] and expelled him from the monastery. Cast out from the fellowship of the brethren, he set out, as they say, for Jerusalem; but we do not at all know what end he afterwards met.

A certain priest named Ansered lived in the territory of the village called Sappo and led a frivolous life in many ways. When he was afflicted by illness, he asked the monks of the aforesaid monastery to give him the habit of St Benedict. Having received it, he was brought to the monastery and placed in the infirmary. But after recovering from the illness, he resumed, as far as he could, the frivolity which he had practised in his secular way of life [Col. 0247A]. And, as a certain wise man says of such people:

> “They change their sky, not their soul, who run across the sea.”

[Note: [Col. 0247] Read: “They change their sky, not their mind, who run across the sea.” Horace, *Epistles* I.11.27. (Le Prévost).]

This man changed only his habit, not his character. When Abbot Theoderic saw that his life and conduct were highly blameworthy, and heard that he hated the sacred order—for he had instructed his father and mother to slander him and remove him from the monastery—he feared that the man’s wretchedness might corrupt the other brethren. He therefore wished to fulfill in his case the apostolic command: “Remove the evil from among yourselves” (1 Cor. 5:15); and: “If the unbeliever departs, let him depart” (1 Cor. 7:15). Thus he allowed him to leave the monastery and return to the world.

Adding sins to his sins [Col. 0247B], he joined himself to a certain little woman. But, since she did not suffice for him, he invited another woman, named Pomula, into his love, and made an agreement with her to take her with him to Saint-Gilles. For he wished his parents and friends not to know that he loved her. Having appointed for the woman a place where they should meet and travel together, he set out with certain pilgrims going to Saint-Gilles. But she, without his knowledge, withdrew from this arrangement and attached herself to another cleric.

When Ansered came to the place which he had assigned to the woman and did not find her, he said to those with whom he was travelling: “I must return home, because I have forgotten something necessary to me [Col. 0247C]. But do not delay on your journey, for I shall quickly catch up with you.” Entering by night the house in which the woman lived, he found them reclining together. She immediately informed her lover of his arrival. The lover seized an axe and struck him on the head, leaving him dead. Then he put him into a sack, dragged him some distance away, covered him with earth, and concealed him.

When he was found many days later—for beasts had uncovered him and eaten his thigh and shin—such a stench issued from him that no one could approach him. Indeed, he was discovered because the smell was perceived at a distance. His father and mother, who loved him more than the others did, took him and buried him outside the cemetery of the church [Col. 0247D]. See what a death punished this man, who preferred to return to the vanity of the world rather than live among God’s servants, by which life he might have ascended to the heavenly kingdom.

Another priest, named Adelard, having assumed the monastic habit during an illness, handed over to God, St Ebrulf, and that saint’s monks, to possess forever, the church of Sappo together with the tithe which he held in fief. But after he recovered his health, he began to regret what he had done and resolved to return to the world. When Abbot Theoderic heard this, he caused the Rule of St Benedict to be read to him and said: “Behold the law under which you wish [Col. 0248A] to serve. If you can observe it, enter; but if you cannot, depart free.” For he did not wish to retain such a man by force.

But the other, badly hardened in his obstinacy, left the monastery and resumed the secular habit which he had abandoned. When he wished to take back the church of Sappo which he had given to the monks, Hugh of Grandmesnil, who then held the honor of Sappo, did not permit him. He went to Friardel, to his relatives—for he was of good family—and afterwards lived there for almost fifteen years. Yet he was never wholly well thereafter, but was afflicted by continual illnesses. Finally, seeing death approaching and fearing eternal punishments because of the guilt of apostasy, he begged Abbot Mainer, who was the fourth ruler of that monastery after the venerable [Col. 0248B] Theoderic, to restore to him the habit of St Benedict, which through his sins he had abandoned. Having received it, he survived for three weeks and ended his life there. For his illness was so severe that he could not do without a woman’s attendance; therefore he could not be carried alive to the monastery from which he had departed.

In the days of William, duke of Normandy, Ivo, son of William of Bellême, governed the bishopric of Sées and, by hereditary right through paternal succession, possessed the town of Bellême after the failure of his brothers Warin, Robert, and William. He was learned, handsome in body, shrewd, eloquent, witty, and very fond of jokes. He loved clerics [Col. 0248C] and monks as a father loves sons, and among his chief friends he reverently esteemed Abbot Theoderic. They often met in private conversation, for the city of Sées is only seven leagues distant from the abbey of Ouche.

The aforesaid bishop’s niece, named Mabel, was married to Roger of Montgomery, viscount of the Hiémois; through her he had obtained a great part of the possessions of William of Bellême. At the prompting and advice of the aforementioned bishop, Roger handed over to Abbot Theoderic of St Ebrulf the church of St Martin at Sées, and he and his wife earnestly begged him to establish a monastic community there. The abbot promptly began the assigned work in the Lord’s name. He installed there Roger, a priest and monk of Ouche, Morin, Engelbert, and other disciples of his. He himself also often visited the place, sometimes remaining for three or four weeks, and applied all his efforts, for the love of God and the benefit of those to follow, to bringing the undertaking to completion [Col. 0248D].

The aforesaid Mabel was very powerful and worldly, shrewd and talkative, and exceedingly cruel. Yet she loved the man of God, Theoderic, greatly; and, although she was very harsh toward other religious people, she obeyed him in certain matters. She offered her firstborn son Robert of Bellême—whose cruelty in our own days raged with excessive violence against miserable peoples—to him [Col. 0249A], to Roger, and to the other monks living at Sées, that he might be washed in the sacred font of baptism.

True charity makes a person in whom it reigns lovable to the good and fearsome to the perverse. Therefore the often-mentioned abbot was deservedly loved by the good and feared by the wicked. He avoided external cares as far as he could and devoted himself with fervent diligence to divine worship. He was constant, indeed, in prayer and in such manual labor as was appropriate to him. For he was an excellent scribe, and left the young men of Ouche distinguished memorials of the art planted within him. With his own hand he wrote in that monastery a Collectary, a Gradual, and an Antiphonary. He also urged his companions who had come with him from Jumièges, by sweet exhortations, to produce precious manuscripts of the divine law [Col. 0249B]. Thus his nephew Ralph wrote the Heptateuch and the Missal in which Mass is sung daily in the community; his companion Hugh wrote a commentary on Ezekiel and the Decalogue, and the first part of the *Moralia*; while the priest Roger wrote Chronicles, the books of Solomon, and the third part of the *Moralia*.

Thus, through the above-mentioned scribes and other copyists whom he could induce to undertake this work, the aforesaid Father, during the eight years in which he presided over the monks of Ouche, procured for their library every book of the Old and New Testaments and every work of the most eloquent Pope Gregory. From his school also came outstanding scribes: Berengar, later advanced to the bishopric of Venosa; Goscelin and Ralph [Col. 0249C], Bernard, Turketil, Richard, and many others. They filled the library of St Ebrulf with the writings of Jerome and Augustine, Ambrose and Isidore, Eusebius and Orosius, and other doctors; and by their examples they wholesomely encouraged the youth who would follow to undertake similar study.

The man of God Theoderic taught these men and often warned them wholly to avoid the idle leisure of a wandering mind, which is generally very harmful to body and soul. He was also accustomed to relate this to them:

> “A certain brother in a monastery was blameworthy for many transgressions against monastic discipline. But he was a scribe and devoted to writing, and of his own accord copied a certain enormous volume of the divine law. After he died [Col. 0249D], his soul was brought before the tribunal of the just Judge for examination. While malignant spirits fiercely accused it and produced its countless sins, the holy angels, in contrast, displayed the book which that brother had written in the house of God and counted, one by one, the letters of the huge book against the individual sins. At last a single letter exceeded the number of sins; against that letter the efforts of the demons could bring forward no sin. Therefore the Judge’s mercy spared the brother, commanded his soul to return to its own body, and graciously granted him time to amend his life. Reflect often upon this, dearest brethren. Cleanse your hearts from empty and harmful desires, and continually offer to the Lord God the works of your hands as sacrifice [Col. 0250A]. Avoid idleness with all your strength as a deadly poison, for, as our holy Father Benedict says, ‘Idleness is the enemy of the soul.’

> “Also frequently ponder among yourselves what is said in the *Lives of the Fathers* by a proven teacher: one demon alone, in temptation, afflicts a monk laboring in good works; but a thousand demons attack the idle person. Pricked on every side by countless arrows of temptation, they compel him to grow weary of the monastic enclosure, to desire the ruinous spectacles of the world, and to seek experience of harmful pleasures. Since you cannot support the poor by abundant alms, because you have no earthly wealth, nor can you raise great churches as kings and other powerful men of the world do—for you are enclosed within regular cloisters and deprived of every worldly power—at least, according to Solomon’s exhortation, guard your hearts with all vigilance [Col. 0250B], and strive without ceasing, with all your strength, to please God. Pray, read, sing psalms, write, and devote yourselves to other such occupations; and thus wisely arm yourselves against the temptations of demons.”

With such admonitions Father Theoderic instructed his disciples; exhorting, entreating, and rebuking, he vigilantly incited them to good works, to which he himself first arose by praying, writing, and doing other good things. For these pursuits he was slandered by certain monks who set worldly concerns before divine offices. Alas! The very reason for which they ought to have revered him made them disparage him all the more [Col. 0250C]. For they said:

> “Such a man ought not to be an abbot: he neither understands nor attends to external affairs. From what will those who pray live, if those who plough fail? He is a fool who desires more to read or write in the cloister than to secure the means by which the brethren’s food may be supplied.”

These things and others like them were said by certain proud men, who inflicted many injuries on God’s servant. But William, son of Geroi, always held him in reverence because of his holiness, restrained with fitting severity the disturbances raised by persons whom I do not wish to name, and promptly gave answers, within and without, to every complaint on behalf of the man of God. Some time later, this aforesaid nobleman resolved to go to Apulia for the benefit of the church of Ouche. When he departed and did not afterwards return, the man of God Theoderic remained greatly desolate in Normandy [Col. 0250D].

Just as the life of the wicked is most displeasing to the good, so the life of the good is generally burdensome to corrupt morals. Accordingly, as the good, inflamed by the divine Spirit, strive in many ways to urge the wicked toward uprightness, so the perverse, stirred by demonic malice, frequently strive to bend the upright toward perversity. Although they cannot utterly cast them down, they nevertheless sometimes disturb them in God’s way and, by harassing them in various ways, often make them slower in holy activity.

Thus certain infamous men, while the church of Ouche was rising and shining before God and men through its increase in good works, began to collect various pretexts for hostility against it and, troubling the resources given for the food, clothing [Col. 0251A], and common meal of God’s servants, to afflict it. But gracious Jesus, the true bridegroom of the Church, though the waves of the sea raged to overwhelm the Church’s ship, marvellously shone forth in rescuing his own by repressing the efforts of their opponents.

I shall truthfully explain, though out of chronological order, what happened at that time to Mabel, daughter of William Talvas. While monastic order was at first regularly observed at Ouche, and duties of charity were shown to all visitors, as is still the custom there, she devised and inflicted upon the place many wickedly contrived troubles because of the hatred she bore toward the founders of that monastery. For her father, she herself, and all his descendants maintained a lasting hatred against the Geroians. Therefore, since her husband Roger of Montgomery loved and honored the monks, and she did not dare openly to harm them with malice, she often turned aside to the monastery with a multitude of knights, ostensibly for lodging; thus she burdened monks already distressed by poverty in barren country [Col. 0251B].

Once, while she was lodging there with a hundred knights, Lord Abbot Theoderic rebuked her for coming with such ostentation to poor monks and admonished her to restrain herself from this folly. Enraged, she replied: “Henceforth I shall bring a greater number of knights than I have brought.” The abbot said to this: “Believe me: unless you repent of this wickedness, you will suffer what you would not wish.” And so it happened. On the following night an illness seized her and began to torment her severely. She immediately ordered herself carried away from there.

As, terrified, she hastened to flee from the land of St Ebrulf, and passed before the house of a certain burgess named Roger Suisnarius, she ordered a nursing infant to be brought out from there and gave her own breast to the child’s mouth to suck, in which the greater part of her disease had gathered. The infant therefore sucked and shortly afterwards died; but the woman recovered and returned home. She lived for nearly fifteen years afterwards, but, after being chastised there by God’s scourge, as we have said above, she never dared visit Ouche again. As long as she afterwards lived amid the troubled felicities of this life [Col. 0251D], she carefully kept herself from in any way harming or benefiting the inhabitants of that monastery. Yet she loved Abbot Theoderic and entrusted to him, more than to the church of Ouche, the cell of St Martin, as we said in anticipation.

## VIII. The Norman migrations into Apulia; their first settlements there; the monk Anschetillus

While Pope Benedict occupied the apostolic see, Saracens from Africa came by ship into Apulia every year and, with impunity, exacted whatever tribute they wished from the indolent Lombards and Greeks inhabiting Calabria, throughout the cities of Apulia.

In these days Osmund, surnamed Drengot, killed William Repostel in the presence of Duke Robert, in the forest where he was hunting [Col. 0252A], because William had arrogantly boasted before the magnates of Normandy that he had violated Osmund’s daughter. For this crime Osmund fled from the duke’s presence, first to Brittany, then to England, and finally to Benevento, with his sons and nephews. He was the first Norman to choose a settlement in Apulia, receiving from the prince of Benevento a town in which he and his heirs might reside.

Then a certain Norman knight named Drogo went on pilgrimage to Jerusalem with a hundred knights. As he returned from there with his companions, Duke Guaimar detained them at Salerno for several days, out of hospitality, to refresh themselves.

At that time twenty thousand Saracens landed on the Italian coast and began, with extreme threats, to demand tribute from the citizens of Salerno. While the duke with his retainers was collecting the levy from the citizens [Col. 0252B], the Saracens disembarked from their fleet and, with great security and rejoicing, sat down to dine on the grassy plain lying between the city and the sea. When the Normans learned this and saw the duke collecting money to appease the barbarians, they reproached the Apulians in friendly fashion: they were redeeming themselves with money like unarmed widows, rather than defending themselves like brave men by the strength of arms.

Then they took up arms and suddenly attacked the Africans, who were confidently awaiting tribute. Having killed many thousands, they compelled the rest to flee in disgrace to their ships. Laden with vessels of gold and silver and much other precious spoil, the Normans returned. The duke earnestly asked them to remain there with honor [Col. 0252C], but, desiring to revisit their homeland, they did not comply with his requests. They nevertheless promised either to return to him themselves or soon to send him some chosen young men of Normandy.

After reaching their native soil, they reported to their compatriots many things they had seen, heard, done, and suffered. Then some of them fulfilled their promise, retraced their path to Italy, and by their example stirred the fickle hearts of many to follow them. Thus Turstin surnamed Citellus; Ranulf; Richard, son of Anschetillus of Quadrelli; the sons of Tancred of Hauteville—Drogo, Humphrey, William, Herman, Robert surnamed Guiscard, Roger, and their six brothers [Col. 0252D]; William of Montreuil; Ernald of Grandmesnil; and many others left Normandy and went to Apulia, not together but at different times.

Upon arriving there, they first became paid soldiers of Duke Guaimar and other powerful men against the pagans. Later, when certain causes of conflict arose, they attacked those whom they had previously served and, by manly arms, subdued for themselves Salerno, Bari, Capua with all Campania and Calabria. In Sicily they also acquired Palermo, the city of Catania, the castle of John, and other cities and illustrious towns which their heirs possess to this day.

Among the Normans who crossed the Tiber, William of Montreuil, son of William Geroianus, flourished most greatly. Made commander of the Roman army, he bore the banner of St Peter and subdued fertile Campania [Col. 0253A]. As brother and friend of the men of Ouche, to whom, as said above, he had made many gifts before migrating from Normandy, he instructed them to send him a faithful envoy to receive the gifts he was preparing for them.

When his father William heard this, he willingly offered himself for this embassy, for the benefit of the holy Church. Abbot Theoderic was thereby both glad and sad: glad at the great devotion of the elder lord, which burned within him and prompted him to undertake so laborious a journey; sad at the great support that he was losing in the aforesaid elder, since he was ready for every good work. Finally, the man of God, Prior Robert, and the whole community commended Lord William to God and assigned to him the highly skilled monk Gunfrid, the excellent scribe Roger of Jumièges, and twelve other honorable attendants [Col. 0253B].

Crossing the Alps, he made for Rome. Then, continuing his journey, he found in Apulia his son and other friends, relations, and kinsmen. Greatly rejoiced at seeing him, they retained him with them for some time in great honor and gave him many great gifts for the support of the Church for which he was begging. But he, wishing swiftly to relieve his needy brethren, sent back the monk Gunfrid with a large sum of money. Yet by God’s hidden judgment, the outcome was otherwise than had been hoped.

For Gunfrid came to Rome and resolved to spend the winter there in the monastery of St Paul the Apostle. Because of greed for the gold he carried, the Romans poisoned him; thus the venerable pilgrim died, confessing Christ, on 13 December [Col. 0253C]. Not long afterwards William also began his return journey with a vast sum of money. But, arriving at the city named for Caieta, nurse of the Trojan Aeneas, he fell sick with a deadly illness.

Then he summoned to himself two knights, Anschetillus of Norrey, son of Ascelin, and Theodelin of Tansy, and said to them:

> “Behold, as you see, the twelve companions who left Normandy cheerfully with us have died in this country; now a grave illness has seized me too and impatiently drives me to my last end. Therefore, Anschetillus, in the presence of Theodelin as witness, I entrust to you the money that I have obtained, so that without fraud you may carry it to Lord Abbot Theoderic, to my nephew Robert, and to the other monks of St Ebrulf, for whom I am now an exile. You are both men of St Ebrulf and ought to keep faith with him. Let no greed deceive you. Consider carefully that, since all your companions have died, by the merits of St Ebrulf you alone survive—perhaps so that you may faithfully render him this service. Give the men of Ouche, whom I love in Christ as myself, my final farewell; and humbly urge them faithfully to pray to the almighty Lord for me.”

Saying this and much else, he brought forth [Col. 0254A] gold, precious cloths, a silver chalice, and other valuable objects; counted them carefully; and entrusted them to Anschetillus. Not long afterwards, as his illness worsened, the noble lord died, confessing Christ, on 5 February. He was honorably buried in the church of St Erasmus, bishop and martyr, where the episcopal see is situated.

Then Anschetillus and Theodelin went to Gaul and returned safely to their homes. After some days Anschetillus came to Ouche and told the brethren of the death of Lord William and his companions, but said absolutely nothing about the money entrusted to him, which he had already wickedly spent on his own uses. When the monks heard of the death of the founder of their church, they were deeply grieved and faithfully offered prayers, Masses, and other good works to God, to whom all things live, for his soul [Col. 0254B]; their successors endeavor to observe these fervently even to this day.

As Anschetillus returned to his house, his companion Theodelin came to Ouche and asked the monks what had been brought to them from Apulia. Discovering that they had received nothing but the mournful news of their friends’ deaths, he was astonished and disclosed the whole truth about everything that had happened to him, favorably or adversely, during the journey. Abbot Theoderic immediately summoned Anschetillus and demanded the money entrusted to him. At first he began to deny it, but afterwards, convicted by Theodelin, acknowledged the truth of the matter.

“The money which you demand,” he said, “I received from my lord William. I spent one part for our own uses, but another part I deposited at Reims, on the advice of my lord Ralph Mala-Corona, who met me there.” On hearing this, the monks sent to Reims twice concerning the deposited money: first Rainald, monk of Sappo, and afterwards Fulk, to Archbishop Gervase. The aforesaid metropolitan graciously received the monk of St Ebrulf and assisted him, as far as he could, in the business for which he had come [Col. 0254C]. For while he had been bishop of Le Mans and frequently attended the court of William, duke of Normandy, with whom he was very intimate, he had often been honorably received at Ouche and treated as a friend with his entire household. Thus, on seeing the monk Fulk, he wished to repay benefits with benefits.

But because a long time had already passed and Anschetillus had foolishly deposited the things now demanded, he could scarcely recover a few and less valuable items from what he had received in Apulia. With difficulty he exacted only the silver chalice, two chasubles, an elephant’s tooth, a griffin’s claw, and certain other objects. The monks then considered Anschetillus’s frauds and brought him to judgment in the court of St Ebrulf. Richard of Avranches, son of Turstin, and many other nobles were there to assist him. But as the monks made a reasonable complaint, it was determined by just judgment that he should lose the entire fief which he held from St Ebrulf [Col. 0254D].

At last, by the advice of friends, the following agreement was made between the two parties. Anschetillus publicly confessed his guilt, gave security to Abbot Theoderic, and humbly begged the monks to have mercy on him. In compensation for the loss which he had caused them through his own misconduct, he granted St Ebrulf, before many witnesses, the third part of the borough of Ouche which he had possessed through paternal inheritance. He placed the deed of gift upon the altar, accompanied by a silk cloth from which the cantor’s cope was made. Moved by pity, the monks mercifully forgave his faults and generously promised him all the remainder of his fief, except for that which he had offered at the urging of his friends [Col. 0255A]. Not long afterwards he went to Apulia, where he was killed.

## IX. Continuation of the history of the monastery of Ouche and Abbot Theoderic

[Col. 0255B]

The ancient enemy never ceases to assail the Church’s peace with the goads of diverse temptations and, through those whom he can subject to worldly vanity, cruelly to harass those who keep prudent watch in the simplicity of the Catholic faith and stand manfully at the summit of virtues. Therefore, when he saw that, with God’s help, a regular monastery had risen in the forest of Ouche and that Abbot Theoderic, by word and deed, was benefiting very many souls, young and old, he burned with the envy by which he expelled the first-created Adam from paradise through the tasting of forbidden fruit. After William Geroianus’s departure, he insolently stirred Prior Robert against his abbot, and while the great discord endured long, he grievously disturbed the unstable minds of those subject to them [Col. 0255C].

This Robert, as has been sufficiently said above, was of distinguished nobility, namely brother of Hugh of Grandmesnil. Yet he still possessed youthful frivolity, untamed strength, and worldly ambition. He was praiseworthy in chastity and certain other sacred gifts; but, on the other hand, as Flaccus says:

> “[Lacuna] Nothing is blessed in every respect.”

[Note: [Col. 0255] Horace, *Odes* II.16.27. Cicero: “Nothing is perfect and blessed in every respect.” (Le Prévost).]

He was blameworthy in certain faults. In whatever good or evil he desired, he was swift and ardent in carrying it out; when he heard or saw what he disliked, he was quick to anger; and he desired more to rule than to be subject, and to command rather than obey. His hands were open to receive and to give [Col. 0255D], and his mouth was ready to satisfy his anger with disorderly speech.

Since, as has been said, he shone with the splendor of lofty birth, had founded that monastery from his own inheritance, enriched it by gathering brethren from every quarter for God’s worship, and provided the necessary resources, he could not be restrained beneath the yoke of regular discipline in the new foundation. He therefore frequently disparaged his Father in secret, because the man of God attended more to spiritual than to secular affairs. At times he openly quarrelled with him and criticized certain of his ordinances concerning external matters, made in good faith.

Consequently, God’s servant often withdrew to the refuge at Sées [Col. 0256A], where he lived for six or eight weeks, performed God’s work in peace, and diligently promoted human salvation as far as he was able. Thus he awaited the correction of his abusive brother and fulfilled the Apostle’s command: “Give place to wrath” (Rom. 12:19). But when he perceived that resentment and scandals were not diminishing but rather increasing to the brethren’s harm, he wished to surrender the pastoral staff, together with the whole abbey, to William, duke of Normandy. The duke, however, using prudent counsel, entrusted the entire ordering of this affair to Maurilius, archbishop of Rouen, that he should carefully investigate the cause of the dissension and, with the counsel of wise men, rightly determine what ought to be done.

Accordingly, in the year 1056 from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the eighth indiction [Col. 0256B], while Pope Victor occupied the apostolic see, Henry, surnamed the Good, emperor of the Romans, son of Emperor Conon, died; his son Henry succeeded him and reigned fifty years. In that same year Bishop Maurilius, his counsellor Fulbert the scholar, Bishop Hugh of Lisieux, Abbot Ansfrid of Préaux, Lanfranc, provost of Bec, and many other men of profound discernment assembled at Ouche. There they celebrated the feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, on the third day before the Kalends of July [29 June].

Then, after the causes of dissension had been heard and carefully examined, they ordered Abbot Theodoric to remain in authority as he had hitherto been; Robert the prior they earnestly exhorted to follow Christ’s poverty and, for God’s sake, humbly obey his spiritual father in all things [Col. 0256C]. When the aforementioned admonishers had returned home, the flock of Ouche rested for a while in peace. But after one year, when the death of William Giroie became known, the old quarrel arose anew; and discord, hostile to the welfare of body and soul, grievously disturbed the monks.

Theodoric, a lover of peace, was beset on every side. At Sées he could neither advance the salvation of souls nor bring to completion the cell begun there by Roger and his wife, because they were then occupied with many secular concerns and attacked on every side by their enemies. At Ouche he could not benefit himself or others as fully as he wished [Col. 0256D], because of the harassments inflicted on him by certain more powerful monks.

At last, after long deliberating with himself what he ought to do according to God, he resolved to leave everything and go to the Lord’s tomb at Jerusalem. Thus, on the fourth day before the Kalends of September [29 August], he came from Sées, where he had then stayed for a long time, to Ouche. Having called the brethren into chapter, he disclosed his intention; he admonished them all, gave them absolution and his blessing, and commended them to God. Afterwards he went to Lisieux and surrendered the care of souls to Bishop Hugh, by whom he was greatly loved. Thus, while many friends wept, he undertook the holy pilgrimage for Christ [Col. 0257A].

Herbert of Le Monasteriol, the first monk whom he himself had received into the church of Ouche, set out abroad with him; so too did the clerk William, surnamed Bona Anima (“Good Soul”), son of Radbod, bishop of Sées, who in the following period held the metropolitan see of Rouen for nearly thirty-six years.

## X. The journey of Abbot Theodoric to the East; his death

In those days there was an honourable hospice on the frontier of the Bavarians and Hungarians, established by faithful and powerful Christians from the surrounding provinces for receiving the poor and pilgrims. At that time Ansgot the Norman presided over this hospice by election of the inhabitants. He was a kinsman of Roger of Tosny, called “the Spaniard” [Col. 0257B], and had served nobly in war under the Norman dukes Richard and Robert. But, pierced by the fear of God, he had abandoned all worldly things and embraced for Christ pilgrimage and voluntary poverty, to be maintained throughout his life.

When he saw Abbot Theodoric and his companions, he recognized him very well. He lovingly kept them for several days as fellow-countrymen and showed them every kindness.

Meanwhile a certain devout bishop of the Bavarians, travelling abroad, arrived there. Hospitable Ansgot, as was his custom, retained him in the same place for several days with all his retainers. Then he earnestly commended venerable Theodoric and his attendants to him, and eloquently recounted how great was Theodoric’s holiness before God [Col. 0257C] and his distinction among men in his homeland. Having heard of the holy man’s character, the bishop gave thanks to God; he received him kindly, as befitted such a man, and reverently conducted him with him as far as Antioch.

There different intentions arose among the pilgrims. Some wished to continue by land, as they had begun, as far as Jerusalem. Others, fearing the barbarity of the peoples, resolved to cross the sea by ship. The bishop and the abbot, with many others, accepted their counsel. While the bishop was seeking a ship and experienced sailors, and while a devout archimandrite of the monastery of Saint Symeon at the Syrian port was honourably detaining Theodoric and his companions [Col. 0257D], Herbert, the monk of Ouche, grew impatient from his desire to hasten the journey and strove more eagerly to seek the holy places by land than by sea. His abbot therefore gave him leave to go where he wished.

Taking the land route, he reached Laodicea with a troop of foot-travellers. There, falling seriously ill, he remained a long time after his companions departed. When he had scarcely risen from his bed, he did not press onward, but, leaving the eastern regions, returned as quickly as possible to western Normandy.

Then the bishop, Theodoric, William Bona Anima, and their companions boarded a ship in the harbour of Saint Symeon. Crossing the sea, they sailed to the island of Cyprus, where on the seashore they found the abbey founded in honour of Saint Nicholas the Confessor, archbishop of Myra [Col. 0258A]. When they entered the church and had prayed there to God as heavenly grace inspired each one, Theodoric rose from prayer after many tears. Broken by the burden of old age, the weariness of the sea, and other discomforts, he sat down anxiously in the church.

When the bishop, his most faithful companion, asked what had happened to him, he answered: “My Father, I had resolved to visit the earthly Jerusalem, but I believe that the Lord is disposing otherwise for me. I am grievously afflicted by bodily distress; therefore I judge that the heavenly Jerusalem is to be sought rather than the earthly.”

The bishop said to him: “My dearest brother, I shall now go and procure lodging for you; meanwhile sit here and rest.” The bishop went out to seek lodging, while Theodoric approached the altar [Col. 0258B] and prayed there for a long time to God, whom he had faithfully served from childhood. Then he prostrated himself before the altar toward the East, arranged the garments about himself decently, lay down upon his right side as though wishing to sleep, rested his head upon the marble step, and placed his hands crosswise upon his breast. Thus, on the Kalends of August [1 August 1058], he rendered up his faithful spirit to God his Creator.

When the lodging had been prepared, the bishop summoned the servant of the man of God and sent him into the church for the holy man. But when he found God’s servant dead in the church, he returned in terror to the bishop and tremblingly reported the unexpected event. The bishop, however, did not believe that the man of God had departed so suddenly. “The good old man,” he said, “is very weary from the sea’s discomfort and excessive heat [Col. 0258C], and so is now held in sweet sleep upon the cold marble in the church’s coolness. Let us go and visit him.”

The bishop therefore entered the church with his clergy. When he carefully touched his peer and found him cold in death, he was astonished and grieved. At once he ordered all the pilgrims, who were already arranging to dine in different lodgings, to assemble in the church; and he faithfully related to the inhabitants of that place the life of the dead pilgrim. When they learned of his religious character, they rejoiced and kindly offered their services and expenses to the other pilgrims.

Then the bishop performed the funeral rites for the dead man with his clergy and ordered the remaining pilgrims to make a grave before the church doors [Col. 0258D]. They made a pit where the bishop directed, using their staffs. They approached the dead man’s body, with the bishop present, and wished to carry it away for burial. But by God’s will the body became so heavy that it could by no means be moved from the place where it lay.

Seeing this, the bishop and all present were greatly astonished. After prolonged discussion with his amazed companions concerning what they should do, he was at last instructed by divine inspiration and said: “This man was of great holiness, and, as is now plainly made manifest, his life pleased God. Therefore, I think, he ought to be buried in a worthier place and henceforth receive from us, as far as we are able, more solemn reverence. I shall now celebrate the Mass with the clergy for his soul before the divine Majesty [Col. 0259A]; meanwhile prepare a suitable grave for him beside the altar.”

They gladly obeyed his command. When the Mass had been reverently completed and the grave carefully prepared, they lifted the body to be buried without difficulty and fittingly interred it beside the altar. There afterwards many suffering from fevers and other ailments were healed through his merits.

When the monks of Ouche learned of their revered father’s death from the account of his companions returning to Normandy, they were deeply saddened. They faithfully celebrated the service due to God for his soul, and each year to this day they solemnly observe his commemoration on the Kalends of August [1 August]. They also diligently observe to this day the religious institutions which he had learned from the teaching of the venerable abbots Richard of Verdun, William of Dijon [Col. 0259B], and Theodoric of Jumièges, and had faithfully delivered to the new church entrusted to him; and they carefully impart them to novices converted to the religious life.

## XI. The history of Ouche continues: Robert of Grandmesnil, abbot

In the year 1059 from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the twelfth indiction, the men of Ouche elected Robert of Grandmesnil as their abbot. In electing this man, they reasonably considered the many advantages: his illustrious lineage, his ardent devotion to monastic affairs, and his effectiveness and vigour in action.

When the whole community’s consent had been confirmed, they took him to Évreux [Note: [Col. 0259D] Or “Ebroicas,” Évreux.] [Col. 0259C], presented him there to Duke William, and made known to him the monks’ election and petition. The duke granted their request, and through the pastoral staff of Ivo, bishop of Sées, entrusted to the chosen man the abbey’s external authority. William, bishop of Évreux, spiritually committed to him the inner care of souls by episcopal blessing on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July [21 June].

Now made abbot, Robert began diligently to administer the monastery’s affairs and generously supplied God’s servants with necessary support from his parents’ wealth. The just observances which his pious predecessor had established he not only did not diminish, but increased, as circumstances and the time required [Col. 0259D], prompted by the authority of his elders and by the example of neighbouring communities.

While still a novice, he had gone, by venerable Theodoric’s permission, to Cluny, where Abbot Hugh—at that time the special glory of monks in our age—presided over the monastic host. On his return after some time, through the generosity of great-hearted Hugh, he brought with him the distinguished monk Bernefrid, who later became a bishop. Robert honourably retained him for some time, that he might acquaint the men of Ouche with Cluniac customs.

Under Robert, Mainerius, son of Gunscelin of Escalfoy, entered the religious life [Col. 0260A]. Some years later he assumed the government of the same monastery and held it usefully for twenty-one years and seven months.

At the same time Ralph, surnamed Mala-Corona (“Evil Crown”), came to Ouche and remained there for a long time with Abbot Robert, his nephew. As we briefly mentioned somewhat above, from childhood he had studied letters abundantly and, by searching out the schools of Gaul and Italy, attained remarkable knowledge of hidden matters. He was nobly educated in grammar, dialectic, astronomy, and music. He possessed such extensive knowledge of medicine that in the city of Salerno, where the greatest schools of physicians had existed since ancient times, he found no equal in medical art except a certain wise matron.

Yet, although he possessed such learning [Col. 0260B], he did not devote himself to leisure but long submitted himself to the labour of warfare. He was often proved outstanding among his companions in military danger, both by hand and by counsel. The people of Le Monasteriol still recount many things which seem wonderful to us: subtle experiments of his against diseases or other unexpected occurrences, which they themselves saw or heard from their fathers, to whom he was well known through long familiarity.

At last, fearing the collapse of the unstable world and wisely guarding against it by withdrawing, he trampled underfoot worldly luxury and sought the Great Monastery of Saint Martin at Tours. There, under the venerable Abbot Albert, he served seven years in the monastic Rule. After he had become established in the order [Col. 0260C], with his abbot’s permission he came to Ouche to comfort his nephew, who had now undertaken the government of the new church.

Because this same nobleman, on account of many sins by which he felt himself heavily burdened, had obtained from the Lord through many prayers the disease of leprosy, he received from his nephew a chapel constructed in honour of Saint Ebrulf. There, having the monk Goscelin for God’s service and his own assistance, he lived for a very long time; and he profitably offered counsel of piety to many who came to him on account of his wisdom and noble rank.

At his earnest urging, Abbot Robert summoned Hugh, bishop of Lisieux, the monks’ faithful master and father. Robert caused the aforesaid chapel to be dedicated by him, on the second day before the Nones of May [6 May], in honour of the holy confessors Ebrulf [Col. 0260D], Benedict, Maurus, and Leudfrid.

They relate that this church had been founded in the time of Saint Ebrulf, and that he himself was accustomed to retreat there when he wished to adhere more ardently to heavenly contemplation, setting aside external cares. The place is pleasant and quite suitable for solitary life. In the valley flows the barren stream of the Carentonne, which separates the bishopric of Lisieux from that of Évreux. On the mountain’s summit, a wood receives the gusts of wind in its dense foliage; and on the mountain slope, between stream and wood, a garden surrounds the church. Before the church doors rises the spring called Ouche [Col. 0261A], from which all the surrounding region receives the name Uticensis, “of Ouche.”

No one should wonder that we have said the bishop of Lisieux performed a dedication within the bishopric of Évreux. In those days three noble bishops, men of great refinement, governed three adjoining dioceses. Hugh, son of Count William of Eu, presided over the people of Lisieux; William, son of Gerard Flaitel, administered ecclesiastical law to the people of Évreux; and Ivo, son of William of Bellême, supplied care for eternal salvation to the people of Sées. These three were then especially powerful in Normandy through zeal for divine worship and unanimity of purpose; they were bound by such love that each of them, within his neighbour’s diocese as though it were his own, performed every divine office as occasion and reason required, without litigation or envy [Col. 0261B].

## XII. Wars between the French and the Normans; various events

At Satan’s prompting, who never ceases to harm the human race, excessive conflict flared up between the French and Normans. King Henry of France and Geoffrey Martel, the very powerful count of Anjou, entered Norman territory with a strong force and inflicted very many losses upon the Normans. But William, the most resolute duke of the Normans, often vigorously avenged these injuries. He captured many Frenchmen and Angevins, killed some, and long afflicted many others shut up in prison.

Whoever wishes carefully to investigate the individual conflicts and losses which they inflicted upon one another in turn should read the books of William, monk of Jumièges, surnamed Calculus, and of William of Poitiers, archdeacon of the church of Lisieux [Col. 0261C]. They wrote diligently concerning the deeds of the Normans and presented their works to William, now king of the English, wishing to win his favour.

During this stormy period Robert, son of Giroie, rebelled against Duke William. Having summoned the Angevins, he strongly fortified his castles—Saint-Céneri and La Roche-Mabile—and held them for a time against the duke besieging them with a Norman army. But because mortal strength is frail and suddenly withers like a grass-flower, this nobleman, after innumerable proofs of courage, was sitting cheerfully by the fire in winter [Col. 0261D]. Seeing his wife Adelaide, who was the duke’s cousin, holding four apples in her hand, he playfully snatched two of them and, unaware that they were poisoned, ate them despite his wife’s objections. He was immediately infected by the poison and died five days later, on the eighth day before the Ides of February [6 February 1060], amid the great grief of his people.

After his death Ernald, son of William Giroie, arose in his uncle’s place, strengthened the townsmen by prayers and admonitions, and ordered them to resist the duke manfully for their paternal inheritance. The shrewd duke softened his bold spirit with flattering appeals and persuaded him, by many promises, to make peace. Accepting his friends’ advice, Ernald yielded to the duke, swore fealty to him, and received from him Le Monasteriol, Escalfoy [Col. 0262A], Saint-Céneri, and the whole inheritance of his fathers.

After peace had been made, Abbot Robert asked the duke to permit his uncle’s body, which had lain buried at Saint-Céneri for three weeks, to be transferred to Ouche. The duke, mindful of hostile hatred, at first refused; afterwards, ashamed to rage against a dead man, he granted permission. The energetic abbot immediately transferred Robert Giroie’s body to Ouche in a coffin and honourably buried it in the monks’ cloister. All who were present wondered that no stench was perceptible from the body, although it had been dead for three weeks. Some say that the force of the poison by which he had been killed dried up all moisture in the dead body, and that therefore no offensive smell could issue from it to trouble the nostrils of the living [Col. 0262B].

When Ernald returned to his rightful position, the monks of Ouche rejoiced and, strengthened by his aid, resisted their insolent neighbours who unjustly oppressed them while they were unarmed. In the times of Abbot Theodoric and his successor Robert, Baldwin and Wiger of Balgençay, with their men, behaved insolently toward the monks. They not only did not obey them as lords, but frequently troubled both the monks and their people with very many vexations.

After Robert had assumed governance of the abbey, he judged it unworthy to endure this longer. With the brethren’s counsel, he therefore handed these rebels over to his kinsman Ernald because of their contumacy, so that Ernald might crush by military force, for as long as he lived, the stubbornness of those who disdained peacefully to endure the monks’ gentleness [Col. 0262C]. Ernald burdened them with many and various services and compelled them and their people to guard his fortifications at Escalfoy and Saint-Céneri.

They therefore earnestly asked Abbot Robert and the monks to deserve restoration to the monks’ authority, promising them complete submission and amendment. The abbot and monks granted their request and asked Ernald to restore them to the Church’s service, which is truly freedom for the humble and meek.

In these days Roger, the firstborn son of Engenulf of Laigle, was killed. Engenulf and his wife Richuerada, deeply afflicted by his death, came to Ouche. They requested and received the monks’ benefaction [Col. 0262D] and prayers for their own salvation and that of their son Roger, and offered Roger’s finest horse to God and the monks for his soul. Because the horse was valuable, Ernald asked that it be given to him; and he granted Baldwin, his men, and the land of Balgençay back to the monks’ former authority. And so it was done. Ernald received from Abbot Robert the horse of his cousin Roger, and restored Baldwin and all the land of Balgençay to the church’s lordship.

Baldwin, rejoicing that he had escaped Ernald’s burdensome services, gave the monks the lordship which he held in the village of Saint Ebrulf, the land which he held above the stream of Ductus Villaris, and the land of Norman Mica and Benignus. Then [Col. 0263A] Baldwin clasped hands with Abbot Robert and swore fealty; he promised submission and justice concerning himself and his men, and earnestly requested that Robert no longer remove his honour from the monks’ jurisdiction. When the monks confirmed this, it stood ratified; and both Baldwin himself and his son Robert have, to the present day, rendered military service solely to the monks for the land of Balgençay.

For the abbey of Ouche is situated in the fief of Balgençay, and the aforementioned Baldwin was of noble birth. Count Gilbert of Brionne, nephew of Richard, duke of the Normans, gave his niece in marriage to Baldwin the German, who had come with his brother Wiger to Normandy to serve Duke Richard. By her were born six sons and several daughters: Nicholas of Basqueville, Fulk of Aulnay, Robert of Courcy, Richard of Neuville, Baldwin of Balgençay, and Wiger the Apulian [Col. 0263B]. Under Duke William these men flourished in great valour, were enriched by him with much wealth and many honours, and left extensive possessions in Normandy to their heirs.

Baldwin, who held the honour of Balgençay with his brother Wiger, gave his sister Elizabeth in marriage to Fulk of Bonneval, a vigorous knight. He granted him as her marriage portion the church of Saint Nicholas, which his father had built, with its adjoining estate.

Mindful of the world to come, Fulk offered to God for monastic life in the monastery of Ouche his son Theodoric, whom Abbot Theodoric had lifted from the sacred font. In Abbot Robert’s presence he granted to Saint Ebrulf both the boy and the aforesaid church of Saint Nicholas, for his own soul and the salvation of his friends [Col. 0263C]. Baldwin, Wiger, William of Bonneval, and their other relatives likewise gladly consented to this. They themselves, and many others who were present, became lawful witnesses of the above-written grant, for the church’s benefit.

At that time Roger, son of Tancred of Hauteville, was present there on his way to Italy. Later, with God’s help, he acquired a great part of Sicily and attacked, crushed, and conquered by arms the Africans, Sicilians, and other peoples who did not believe in Christ and who were ravaging that island.

The boy Theodoric, withdrawn from the world and given to God, lived fifty-seven years in the monastic habit. Advancing lawfully through every grade as far as the priesthood, he honourably served God [Col. 0263D].

At the same time Guy, surnamed Bollein, great-grandson of the elder Giroie, flourished honourably in the district of Corbon with his wife Hodierna. Enlarged in wealth through the military estate, he administered his property honourably. He had several sons: Norman and Walter, who served in the labours of warfare; and Geoffrey and William, surnamed Gregory, who, instructed in letters, attained the rank of priesthood.

By God’s will and at the prompting of Abbot Robert, his kinsman, the aforesaid Guy greatly loved the men of Ouche. On the feast of All Saints, he renounced his son William, then nearly nine years old [Col. 0264A], to the world and to himself, and gave him to serve God under the monastic yoke in the church of Ouche. Then William the provost, an outstanding knight and the boy’s maternal uncle, gave the church of Algeron with the entire village to Saint Ebrulf; and at his death he faithfully devoted himself and all his property to the same patron.

God’s grace adorned the boy William with good manners and made him diligent in worthy studies; hence his superiors deservedly surnamed him Gregory. Carefully reared in the bosom of holy mother Church, and entirely removed from worldly clamour and carnal luxury, he flourished nobly in the useful learning especially appropriate to sons of such a church. He was a skilled reader and singer, and an outstanding writer and illuminator of books [Col. 0264B]. The works of his hands still greatly help us in reading and singing, and by the excellence of like activity teach us to banish idleness from ourselves.

From childhood he was constant in prayers and vigils. Until old age he applied himself moderately to fasts and other mortifications of the flesh; he was a diligent observer of monastic order and zealous in rebuking transgressors of the holy Rule. He had committed to a tenacious memory the letters of Paul, Solomon’s Proverbs, and very many other collections of Holy Scripture, which he brought forth in his daily conversation to exhort those with whom he spoke. Engaged in studies of this sort, he has now spent fifty-four years in the monastic order, and still, under Abbot Roger, pursues good works in his customary manner, so that through a good end [Col. 0264C] he may pass into the stability of eternal rest.

As the monastery of Ouche was gloriously strengthened by an enlarged community of forty monks, and monastic order was there regularly observed according to the norm of divine law, its fame spread far and wide and invited many to love that church. But some were infected by destructive envy and wounded by the harmful weapon of their own malice.

Abbot Robert, endowed with innate generosity, gladly received all who came from anywhere seeking conversion, and vigorously provided whatever the brethren needed for food or clothing. The revenues of the church of Ouche, standing in an unproductive district [Col. 0264D], were not sufficient for the great liberality of this Father. Yet, as we have said, he came from noble parents and frequently received their wealth for the monks’ use as he wished, with their affectionate consent.

In the first year of his government, because the old church which Saint Ebrulf had built was small and of rustic workmanship, he began an immense basilica of remarkable construction. He resolved to build it in honour of Mary, holy Mother of God, and enlarge it with many altars of saints. Since relics of saints had been deposited in the old church in Saint Ebrulf’s time—though, owing to their antiquity, the names, deeds, and places of burial of these saints are unknown to those now living [Col. 0265A]—he planned to make the new building so large that it would wholly surround the old one and always contain with honour the bones or tombs of the saints hidden there. But when storms of troubles came upon him, he was forced to cease the work he had begun. None of his successors dared to carry it forward on the same scale, in the same arrangement, or at the location which he had intended.

In the year 1059 from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the thirteenth indiction, Henry, king of the French [Note: [Col. 0265] It is established that King Henry died in the year 1060, on 29 August.], after many achievements through which he had flourished gloriously in his kingdom, received from John, physician of Chartres, who from an occurrence was surnamed “the Deaf,” a potion intended to give him a longer and healthier life. But because he followed his own desire rather than his chief physician’s command, and while his inward parts were being grievously distressed by the searching poison he thirstily and secretly asked a chamberlain for water, drinking before the purge and without the doctor’s knowledge—alas!—he died the next day amid the great sorrow of many.

He left the sceptres of the French to his son Philip, who was still of childish age, and entrusted the boy and kingdom to Baldwin, duke of the Flemings, for protection. Such guardianship well suited so great a duke, since he had in marriage Adela, daughter of Robert, king of the French. By her he had begotten Robert the Frisian, the queen of the English, Odo metropolitan of Trier, and other men of great nobility.

In the same year Frederick, son of Duke Gothelon, who was also called Pope Stephen, died [Col. 0265C]; Gerard, also called Nicholas, succeeded him. This was the third year of Henry IV, son of Emperor Henry Conrad and Empress Agnes, who began to reign as the eighty-seventh ruler from Augustus and reigned fifty years.

In the year 1063 from the Lord’s Incarnation Pope Nicholas died, and Alexander, bishop of Lucca, succeeded him. At that time Siegfried of Mainz, Gunther of Bamberg, and very many other bishops and nobles travelled to Jerusalem with a large retinue.

## XIII. Dissensions in Normandy; Osbern is imposed upon the monks of Ouche as abbot in Robert’s place; Abbot Robert goes to Apulia to Robert Guiscard; various events

[Col. 0265D] At the same time a grave dissension arose between William, duke of Normandy, and his magnates. For, with greed raging, each sought to undermine the other, and severe disturbances arose from various causes to the injury of the wretched. Some of harsher temper therefore rejoiced, while lovers of piety and moderation were deeply saddened.

Then Roger of Montgomery and his wife Mabel rejoiced at the outbreak of hostility, drew the duke to themselves by flattering blandishments, and, by cunning intrigues, more fiercely inflamed his anger against his neighbours. The spirited duke, giving the reins to anger beyond measure, disinherited the leading knights Ralph of Tosny [Col. 0266A], Hugh of Grandmesnil, Ernald of Escalfoy, and their barons, and forced them into exile for a long time without demonstrable charges.

Then also Robert, abbot of Ouche, was summoned to the duke’s court and commanded to answer on an appointed day concerning certain accusations of which he had been falsely charged. Rainerius, a monk of Castillon, whom Robert had appointed prior over the men of Ouche and summoned without hesitation to his most private counsels as a faithful friend, had accused him before the duke of certain mockeries and imprudent remarks disparaging the duke in private.

When Robert perceived that the duke was furiously enraged against him and all his kindred and desired to injure them, and when, from information supplied by his friends, he learned with certainty of the duke’s ill will, which intended to inflict bodily mutilation upon him [Col. 0266B], he chose, on Bishop Hugh of Lisieux’s advice, to avoid the impending fury before suffering irreparable harm.

Therefore, in the third year of his rule, on the sixth day before the Kalends of February [27 January], after he had recited at Saturday Vespers the antiphon “My sins, O Lord,” he departed. Mounting horses with two monks, Fulk and Urso, he made for France and from there went to Pope Nicholas to disclose his circumstances.

Meanwhile the Norman duke, upon the advice of the venerable Abbot Ansfrid of Préaux, Lanfranc, prior of Bec, and other ecclesiastical persons, requested Osbern, prior of Cormeilles, from Abbot Rainerius of Holy Trinity of Mont-Rouen [Col. 0266C]. Osbern suspected nothing of this. In a synod at Rouen the duke entrusted to him, through the pastoral staff of Archbishop Maurilius, the care of the abbey of Ouche.

Then, at the duke’s order, Bishop Hugh brought him to Préaux and there suddenly consecrated him abbot, without the knowledge of Saint Ebrulf’s monks. Afterwards he brought him with him to Ouche and imposed him, by the duke’s command, upon the grieving men of Ouche. They were troubled by a double dilemma. Their own abbot was still alive: he had founded the aforesaid church and received them into monastic life, and had been expelled without demonstrable charges, not by synodal judgment but by the tyranny of a raging marquis. They hesitated to accept another abbot, yet they did not dare openly refuse because of the duke’s wrath [Col. 0266D].

At last, on the advice of the aforesaid bishop, they chose to suffer violence and give obedience to the master forced upon them without their consent, lest, by remaining without a yoke, they offend God’s power and, by resisting, stir up the duke’s more grievous ill will toward the destruction of the new monastery.

Moreover, Ernald of Escalfoy fiercely avenged the wrong of his disinheritance. For three years he disturbed the district of Lisieux by plundering, arson, and the capture or killing of men. One night he came to Escalfoy with four knights and secretly entered the castle with his men. He burst out in a great shout; when sixty of the duke’s knights [Col. 0267A] heard it, they imagined that a great army was present with Ernald. Terrified, they abandoned the castle which they ought to have guarded and fled. Ernald set fire to it and inflicted great damage on his enemies.

He also burned the borough of Ouche and, with his followers brandishing bare swords in their right hands through every corner of the church, searched long for Abbot Osbern in order to kill him. But Osbern was absent by God’s providence.

A few days later Herman the cellarer visited Ernald privately and kindly rebuked him for seeking to destroy the abbey which his father had constructed for the salvation of his own soul. Ernald received the servant of God’s admonitions piously. Remembering his father’s piety, he wept for his misdeeds against the monastery of Saint Ebrulf and, repentant [Col. 0267B], promised fitting amends.

Not long afterwards he came to Ouche, laid a pledge upon the altar for his misconduct, sought forgiveness, and gave security to Abbot Osbern. For the aforesaid monk had carefully and truthfully explained to him that the abbot had not seized his kinsman’s place through greed, but, compelled by princely force and the prompting of his superiors, had reluctantly undertaken the governance of a deserted church.

Finally, Abbot Robert found Pope Nicholas at Rome and carefully explained to him the purpose of his journey. The pope received his compatriot kindly—for he too was French by birth—heard his complaint compassionately, and promised him faithful assistance in his need [Col. 0267C]. Robert then went on to his relatives in Apulia, where they had gained possession of very many cities and towns by force of arms. After conferring with them, he returned to Normandy with apostolic letters and two cardinal-clerics, and boldly approached Julibon, where Duke William was then holding his court.

But when the duke heard that Abbot Robert had arrived with the pope’s legates to claim the abbey of Ouche, and that he intended to challenge Osbern—installed as abbot by the duke’s command—as an intruder upon another’s right, he said in great anger that he would gladly receive the pope’s legates concerning the Christian faith and religion, as representatives of the common father; but if any monk from his land brought against him a complaint hostile to his interests, he would have him irreverently hanged by the neck from the tallest oak in the neighboring wood [Col. 0267D]. On hearing this, Bishop Hugh informed Robert and warned him to avoid the presence of the enraged prince.
