Robert promptly departed and withdrew to the Paris region, to the venerable Hugh, abbot of the monastery of Saint Dionysius, apostle of the Gauls. Since Hugh was his kinsman, Robert lived honorably for some time with him and with other friends and relatives influential among the nobles of France.

From there he directed Abbot Osbern that both should appear before the Roman cardinals in the district of Chartres, and that, after their respective cases had been carefully investigated there, they should unquestionably submit to the judgment pronounced by ecclesiastical persons in accordance with the ordinances of the holy canons. He appointed also the day and place at which they should meet [Col. 0268A]. Osbern received the summons and said that he would gladly go to the Roman court; but, adopting another plan, he did not come at the appointed time and place. Robert therefore sent letters through one of the men of Ouche whom Ernald had captured; in them, by the pope’s authority, he excommunicated Osbern as an intruder and imperiously summoned all the monks of the monastery of Ouche to follow him.

Who could relate by how many tribulations the church of Ouche was then shaken within and without? Behold: Robert, its founder and ruler, had been unjustly driven from his seat and was compelled to wander among foreign households; while in his place a stranger succeeded to secular power [Col. 0268B]. Though diligent, religious, and zealous in his order, this man was nevertheless suspicious and apprehensive, and did not sufficiently trust the native brethren. Therefore some of them, upon hearing of the excommunication inflicted upon the substituted abbot and at the exhortation of Father Robert—who, with the pope’s consent, had ordered his sons to come after him—left Normandy, accompanied their abbot, and sought the Apostolic See.

Nearly all wished to leave; but the boys and the weaker brethren, held under closer guard, remained unwillingly. Others, being stronger and claiming greater freedom, voluntarily went into exile after their father. Their names are these: Herbert and Hubert of Mosterol; Berengar, son of Ernald, an outstanding scribe (these three, carefully reared from childhood in the house of the Lord and trained in worthy studies, remained throughout their lives useful to divine worship) [Col. 0268C]; Rainald the Great, skilled in grammar; Thomas of Anjou, renowned for noble birth; Robert Gamaliel, an excellent singer; Turstin; Rainald Capreolus; and Walter the Little. They left Neustria, their native soil, and sought Sicily, destined to undergo diverse fortunes. Some later returned; others, aiding their shepherd to the end, closed their last day in Calabria.

Moreover, Lord Mainerius, whom Abbot Robert had appointed claustral prior before his first departure, had, a few days after Robert’s departure, gone to Bec [Col. 0268D] and first discussed with Lanfranc, prior of the monks of Bec, the substitution of another abbot; thereby he had irreconcilably offended the very man to whom he had made profession. Frightened by Robert’s threats and shamefully assailed by the reproaches of his supporters, he went, with the counsel and permission of Abbot Osbern, to Cluny. There, for one year, he zealously learned by experience the strict discipline of the Cluniacs under the venerable archimandrite Hugh.

In this change, however, the church of Ouche was grievously desolated and stripped of many possessions which it had formerly held. Neighboring knights, men or kinsmen of the Geroians, after driving out the natural heirs, inflicted severe harassment and losses upon the monks of Saint Evroul [Col. 0269A]. For each seized land, or a church, or a tithe; and the new abbot, as an outsider, did not know the grants of property. He hesitated to seek reliable information from those in whom he had no confidence concerning the possessions seized by Robert son of Helgo, Geroie son of Fulco of Mosterol, Roger Gulafra, and other perverse kinsmen. Thus the church of Ouche then lost much which it has been wholly unable to recover even to this day.

After Pope Nicholas died, Alexander succeeded him. Abbot Robert came to him with eleven monks of Saint Evroul and clearly set forth the wrongs done to himself and his followers. The pope kindly refreshed them with paternal consolation and gave them the church of Saint Paul the Apostle in the city of Rome, so that, dwelling there, they might maintain their order until they found a suitable habitation [Col. 0269B]. Robert then sought aid from his cousin William of Mosterol and found him most ready to help. For that knight was the pope’s standard-bearer; by arms he had gained Campania and had subjected to Saint Peter the Campanians, who had departed from Catholic unity through various schisms. He gave his exiled kinsman and his monks half of the ancient city called Aquino.

Afterward Robert approached Richard, prince of Capua, son of Aschettin of Quadrelli. Richard indeed favored him with many flattering expressions, but did not fulfill the promises he had made. When Robert saw that he had been deceived by empty promises [Col. 0269C], he angrily reproached Richard with his ignoble lineage, which he knew well; then, leaving him, he went to Robert Guiscard, duke of Calabria. Guiscard honorably received him as his natural lord and earnestly begged him and his monks always to remain with him.

Guiscard’s father was Tancred of Hauteville, from the district of Coutances. By two lawful wives whom he married, Tancred had twelve sons and several daughters. To one son, named Geoffrey, he granted lands from the paternal inheritance; he admonished all the others to acquire for themselves, outside their native soil, by force and intelligence whatever they needed. They went to Apulia not all at once but at different times, carrying wallets and staffs in the guise of pilgrims [Col. 0269D], lest they be captured by the Romans. All prospered through various turns of fortune and became dukes or counts in Apulia, Calabria, or Sicily. Geoffrey the monk, surnamed Malaterra, recently composed an elegant little book about their worthy deeds and valiant achievements, at the request of Count Roger of Sicily.

The greatest and most powerful of them was Robert Guiscard. After the deaths of his brothers Drogo and Humphrey, he held the principality of Apulia for a long time. Having subdued by military strength the Lombards and Greeks, who, relying on their great cities and towns, strove to defend their ancient rights and former liberty, he acquired the duchy of Calabria. Crossing the Ionian Sea with a small but brave force of Normans and peoples from this side of the Alps, he invaded Macedonia [Col. 0270A], fought twice against Alexius, emperor of Constantinople, and, having defeated him in war by land and sea, put him to flight with an enormous multitude.

This hero, as we have said, honorably received Abbot Robert and his monks. He gave him the church of Saint Euphemia, situated above the shore of the Adriatic Sea, where the ruins of an ancient city called Brixa are still visible, and ordered a monastic house to be built there in honor of Saint Mary, Mother of God. The duke himself and other Normans gave great possessions to the aforesaid church and commended themselves to the prayers of the faithful gathered, or yet to be gathered, there for the warfare of Christ [Col. 0270B].

There was buried Fredesendis, wife of Tancred of Hauteville; for her sake her son Guiscard bestowed a certain great estate on that church. The same prince entrusted to the aforesaid Father the monastery of the Holy Trinity in the city of Venosa. Robert chose Berengar, son of Ernald son of Helgo, a monk of Ouche, and presented him to Pope Alexander to receive the government of the monastery of Venosa. After receiving blessing, he honorably held charge of the abbey of Venosa for as long as Alexander, Gregory, and Desiderius governed the Apostolic See; then, in the time of Pope Urban, he was elected by the people and received the bishopric of that same city.

Born of noble lineage, he had served Christ from infancy at Ouche under Abbot Theodoric, and excelled in the skill of reading, singing, and especially fine writing [Col. 0270C]. Then, as we have said, he followed his abbot and was raised by him to pastoral responsibility. He received a small flock of twenty monks, found it greatly occupied with worldly vanities and exceedingly sluggish in the worship of God, and afterward, with God’s grace helping him, increased it to one hundred monks. He also ennobled them by such zeal for good virtues that many bishops and abbots were chosen from among them and placed over holy mother Church, for the honor of the true King and the salvation of souls.

Furthermore, the great-hearted duke gave Abbot Robert a third monastery, built in honor of Saint Michael the Archangel in the city of Melfi. Robert entrusted it [Col. 0270D] to William, son of Ingran, who had been born at Ouche and promoted to clerical rank, but had received monastic profession at Saint Euphemia. Thus in these three monasteries of Italy the chant of Ouche is sung, and the monastic order is observed to this day, insofar as the circumstances of that region and the devotion of its inhabitants permit.

Two sisters by the same mother of Abbot Robert, Judith and Emma, lived at Ouche in the chapel of Saint Evroul. Under the sacred veil they were believed to have renounced the world and to cleave to God alone in purity of heart and body. But when they heard that their brother Robert was flourishing in Apulia with considerable secular power, while they saw themselves despised and without assistance in Normandy, they set out for Italy [Col. 0271A]. Casting off the veil of holiness, they embraced the world with all their strength and both married husbands who did not know that they had been dedicated to God. Count Roger of Sicily took Judith as his wife; another count, whose name I do not remember, united Emma to himself in marriage. Thus both abandoned the veil, the token of holy religion, for love of the world; and because they broke their first pledge, both remained barren in this world, enjoyed temporal happiness only for a brief moment, and offended their heavenly Bridegroom.

After Abbot Robert’s departure, his maternal uncle Ralph Malacrown saw harsh tribulation grievously raging against his relatives and strangers exercising lordship in the house of Ouche, which he and his brothers had built for God [Col. 0271B]. He therefore left the chapel of Saint Evroul, where, as stated above, he had lived, and went to Marmoutier, where he had made monastic profession. There, not long afterward, having completed seven years in the monastic order, he rested in a glorious death on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February [19 January].

At the same time Geoffrey Martel, count of the Angevins, died after many valiant deeds in worldly affairs. Because he had no children, he left his honor to his nephew Geoffrey, son of Alberic, count of the Gâtinais. After some time Geoffrey’s brother Fulk, surnamed Rechin, treacherously captured him, seized his principality, and confined him in prison for thirty years in the castle called Chinon [Col. 0271C].

At this time Duke William of Normandy was growing greatly in worth and power and surpassed all his neighbors in generosity and magnificence. He married the noble Matilda, daughter of Baldwin, duke of the Flemings, namely the niece through a sister of Henry, king of the Franks. By God’s gift he had by her sons and daughters: Robert, Richard, William, and Henry; Adeliza, Constance, Cecilia, and Adela. Eloquent historians may weave a great history from their lives, if, setting leisure aside and applying themselves to study, they strive to make known to posterity the diverse deeds of the illustrious. But we, since we do not attend upon secular courts but live in a monastic cloister [Col. 0271D] and apply ourselves to monastic concerns, shall briefly record what belongs to our purpose and return to the matter begun.

When war arose between the Normans and their neighboring Bretons and men of Maine, Duke William, on the counsel of his elders, resolved to establish peace among his dissenting nobles and recall the exiles. Accordingly, softened by the entreaties of Simon of Montfort, Waleran of Breteuil in the Beauvaisis, and other powerful friends and neighbors, he recalled his nobles Ralph of Tosny and Hugh of Grandmesnil—whom, as stated above, he had disinherited and driven beyond his territory with their retainers—and restored their paternal inheritances to them [Col. 0272A]. Ernald also, after a three-year war, received a truce from the duke and went to Apulia to friends and relatives who enjoyed great wealth there. Not long afterward he returned with much money and brought the duke a precious cloth.

## XIV. The History of Ouche Continues: Abbot Osbern

After the storms by which the church of Ouche had been grievously assailed had somewhat subsided, Osbern, its ruler, was oppressed by great turmoil of anxieties and inwardly afflicted by a biting conscience because of the apostolic anathema under which he had been compelled to lie. With the counsel and consent of the brethren, he recalled Mainerius from Cluny and, deposing Fulcher, whom Abbot Robert had appointed prior, substituted Mainerius in his place [Col. 0272B].

Osbern was the son of Herfast, born in the district of Caux.

> [Note: Col. 0271D. Commonly, the Pays de Caux.]

He had been thoroughly educated in letters from childhood, was eloquent in speech, and keenly ingenious in every craft: carving, construction, writing, and many similar works. He was of middling stature and mature age, with a head abundantly covered in black or gray hair. He was harsh toward fools and the stubborn, merciful toward the sick and poor, and suitably generous to both those within the community and outsiders. He was zealous in his order and an exceedingly diligent provider of everything which the brethren needed bodily or spiritually. He sternly restrained the young and compelled them, with words and blows, to read, chant, and write well. With his own hands he made writing-desks for boys and the uneducated, and daily required from each the prescribed measure of work [Col. 0272C]. In this way, driving away idleness, he shrewdly burdened youthful minds with useful application and prepared them to be enriched in later times with the treasures of knowledge.

He had been a canon of Lisieux under Bishop Herbert. Later, wishing to be bound by a stricter rule, he left secular dress and fled to reform his conduct according to God’s well-pleasing will at the new monastery which Goscelin of Arques had established for the Holy Trinity on the hill of Rouen. There the venerable Abbot Isembert, a man of marvelous learning and in our age incomparably eminent, then flourished. Rainerius, Isembert’s successor, sent Osbern, now tested in the order, to build the monastery of Cormeilles, where at that time the renowned noble William, son of Osbern [Col. 0272D], steward of the Normans, had begun to found an abbey for Saint Mary, Mother of God. After Abbot Robert had been driven from his place, as has been sufficiently related above, Osbern was ignorantly and unwillingly raised to govern the church of Ouche. He administered it diligently and profitably for five years and three months, insofar as the savagery of the wicked time allowed.

From there he brought with him, by his abbot’s permission, a monk of his church named Witmund, very wise and devout. He used Witmund’s advice and help for as long as he lived at Ouche. This monk was highly skilled in grammar and music, as the antiphons and responsories which he composed still testify [Col. 0273A]. He composed many sweet-sounding chants in the troper and antiphonary. He completed the history of Saint Father Evroul, adding nine antiphons and three responsories. For Vespers, over the psalms, he composed four antiphons; in the second nocturn he added the last three; he also composed the fourth, eighth, and twelfth responsories, an antiphon for the canticles, and a most beautiful antiphon for the Gospel canticle at second Vespers.

Arnulf, cantor of Chartres and disciple of Bishop Fulbert, had already composed that same history according to clerical use at Abbot Robert’s request, and had first sung it to two young monks, Hubert and Ralph, whom the aforesaid Father had sent to Chartres [Col. 0273B]. Moreover, Rainald the Bald composed the responsory in praise of the Lord sung at Vespers, and seven antiphons, which are found written in the antiphonaries of Ouche. Roger of Sappo and other studious brethren also devoutly composed several hymns concerning that same Father and entrusted them to their successors in the library of Ouche.

Deeply troubled by excessive concern because of the apostolic anathema to which he had been forced to submit, Abbot Osbern decided, on the advice of wise men, to send a legate to Rome and humbly seek the blessing of the Apostolic See. He ordered the wise monk Witmund to dictate a supplicatory letter and the young Bernard, surnamed Matthew, a noble scribe, carefully to write it [Col. 0273C]. The text of this letter is as follows:

> “To Lord ALEXANDER, Apostolic Lord, most eminent father of the whole world in the place of blessed Peter:
>
> [Note: Col. 0273D. Alexander II, 30 September 1061–21 April 1073.]
>
> “OSBERN, a certain abbot dwelling far away, of the monastery of Saint Evroul in the land of Normandy, sends true greeting, most humble submission, and prayer as devout as his ability permits.
>
> “Because above and before all prelates of the Church, lord Father, it is your office to bear concern throughout the world for all Christendom, to seek with ardent desire the gain of souls, and by your authority to recall the discordant to concord, therefore I, an unknown abbot yet remaining within the bosom of your protection, cry aloud to you as to a most merciful comforter. With all the effort of my mind I pour out prayers and implore help, that through your grace you may deign to rescue me, in accordance with the justice of authority, from a certain disturbance of our order which I am suffering [Col. 0273D].
>
> “The cause of this disturbance is as follows. The abbey of Saint Evroul, which I now hold, was once held before me by Lord Abbot Robert, kinsman of William, a Norman knight and your faithful servant. But after something adverse befell him, he left it and departed. The prince of the province and the prelates of the Church installed me as abbot in that place; and, as they declared and still declare to me while I trembled over the matter, they rightly and according to God ordained me. Whether they speak the truth, I do not know. This alone I firmly know from my own conscience: that, so far as concerns me, I received the name and burden of abbot neither by request, price, personal influence, service, nor the device of any cunning, but solely by command of obedience; and, in receiving it, I heard no complaint.
>
> “The aforesaid Abbot Robert, carried far from us, has become father of a certain monastery in the province of Calabria; there he is grievously stirred against me with anger and hatred, brings accusation, and threatens, saying that I invaded his place against God. From this discord the souls of those subject to us are certainly endangered, and I, tossed between the two parties, waver greatly. For I dare not be disobedient to my superiors, who assert that I stand rightly in this place and command me to remain [Col. 0274A]; yet I greatly fear the anger and hatred of the brother who accuses me, especially since we are both priests and monks.
>
> “For when the apostolic voice resounds terribly to all, saying, ‘Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer’ [1 John 3:15], who can sufficiently describe how grave a murder a monk and priest commits when he hates his brother? And if he thus offers sacrifice at the altar, who does not know that he damns his own soul? Therefore, most reverend apostolic lord, Father of all Christendom, prostrate upon the ground at the feet of your mercy, I earnestly beg with tearful groans from the depths of my heart that you—who, in the place of blessed Peter, ought with utmost vigilance to feed the Lord’s sheep and guard them from the snares of wolves—may hasten, out of zeal for God, to destroy through the judgment of equity the evil of this wolfish discord between myself and the brother of whom I speak, Robert; and may utterly remove all this disturbance from my heart [Col. 0274B].
>
> “That is: by the command of your authority, cause both me and the authors of my ordination, and also the same Robert who accuses us, to meet together for the fairest examination of the matter before competent and lawful judges; so that, if I am found to be rightly placed in the abbey, I may remain, but if wrongly, I may depart. If through your grace you do this, you will commendably fulfill your office and lead us both, brothers, into the sweetness of peace. For whether I am to remain or to depart, certainly my brother’s indignation, softened by the decision of judgment, will rest; and I, freed from disturbance, shall thereafter be able to serve God in security.
>
> “O ruler of the rulers of the Church and Father of fathers, appointed as a refuge for all the troubled, receive these my words with the ear of your heart, by the blessed power of binding and loosing which you possess above all earthly people; and insofar as they rightly sound, do what they ask. And, that you may believe that I speak simply, I call upon God, who knows all things, as witness to my conscience: he sees that I speak from my whole heart and mouth what I say. Finally, at the end of my words, pious lord, bowed and suppliant, I most earnestly ask that through this same legate whom I send to you [Col. 0275A], you will graciously take care to send me word in letters sealed with your seal how you understand or receive these words of mine, what you intend to do concerning them, and when and where; so that, when you have given a certain answer to my disturbance, I may rejoice that I have cried out to a most merciful comforter.
>
> “Farewell, glorious Father, most excellent ruler, supreme head of the Church on earth. Farewell, and keep watch over the Lord’s sheepfolds. Would that you may act so that you come secure to the final judgment. Amen.”

William, priest of Saint Andrew of Échauffour, carried this letter and presented it to Pope Alexander at Rome. When it had been read before the Roman senate and carefully examined with prudent inquiry, the venerable pope, at the request of Abbot Robert, who was present, absolved Osbern and sent back the bearer of the aforesaid mission rejoicing in the apostolic blessing [Col. 0275B]. Robert had already despaired of returning to Normandy because of Duke William’s ferocity. As stated above, he was honorably retained in Calabria by Guiscard and other Normans who were seizing foreign wealth. Having moderated the anger which he had formerly held against Osbern, he now acted as Osbern’s kindly intercessor before the pope—he whom earlier, by subtle accusations, he had cruelly attacked. When the mission had been completed, the priest William successfully returned to those who had sent him; reporting what he had seen and heard at Rome, he gladdened the men of Ouche.

Osbern, now more secure, exercised in a praiseworthy manner the inward and outward care of the church committed to him. Because of the storms of persecution which he had endured, he had admitted only four novices to conversion; but those whom he found received by his predecessors he diligently and profitably trained in sacred arts [Col. 0275C]. He established a general anniversary to be held each year on the sixth day before the Kalends of July [26 June] for the fathers and mothers, brothers and sisters, of all the monks of the monastery of Ouche. In a very long roll are written the names of all the brethren as they enter the order at God’s call; beneath are written the names of their fathers and mothers, brothers and sisters. This roll is kept by the altar throughout the year, and diligent commemoration of those inscribed is made before the Lord, while the priest says to him in the celebration of Mass:

> “Deign to join to the fellowship of your elect the souls of your servants, male and female, whose names appear to be written before your holy altar.”

The anniversary of which we speak is observed on 26 June as follows. All the bells are rung for a long time, evening and morning, for the Office of the Dead. The roll of the dead is unfolded and spread openly upon the altar. Prayer is faithfully offered to God first for the dead, afterward for living relatives and benefactors, and for all the faithful. The morning Mass is solemnly sung by the abbot [Col. 0276A], and with him all the ministers put on sacred vestments. On that day the almoner gathers in the monastery as many poor persons as there are monks, and the cellarer adequately feeds them in the guesthouse with bread, drink, and wine from the common provision. After chapter, the entire community performs the washing of the poor’s feet, as at the Lord’s Supper. What Abbot Osbern thus established, the church of Ouche observes vigilantly to the present day and zealously transmitted to the monks of Nogent, Bourgueil, and its other followers.

The often-mentioned man of God, as stated above, greatly loved the poor and the sick, and relieved their needs by giving generously what was necessary.

> [Note: Col. 0275. The passage is corrupt; it should here read “their necessities,” etc., or something similar.]

He therefore established that seven lepers should be supported permanently by the monks of Ouche for the love of God, and that every day they should receive from the brethren’s cellar the bread and drink allotted to seven monks [Col. 0276B]. He himself and his successor Mainerius gladly maintained this practice as long as they drew the breath of life while in office. But afterward Serlo, their successor, altered this institution, as human wills change; and Roger, who succeeded them, restored in the name of the Lord the number of three sick persons.

## XV. William, Duke of the Normans. Robert of Vitot, or of Vassy. Extinction of the Geroian Line

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1064, after the death of Herbert the younger, count of the men of Maine, Duke William crossed the river Sarthe with a strong force of armed men. He graciously received many of the men of Maine who submitted themselves to his authority and thereafter held them by right for the twenty-four years of his life that remained [Col. 0276C].

The aforesaid young man, after the death of his father, Herbert the elder—who was commonly surnamed “Wake-the-Dog,” because of the most grievous attacks which he continually suffered from his treacherous Angevin kinsmen—had, on the counsel of his mother Bertha, commended himself and his patrimony to the most powerful duke of the Normans. He had given his sister Margaret in marriage to Robert, son of the same duke, and with her had granted his inheritance, namely the county of Maine, should he die without children. But Walter, count of the Vexin, son of Count Drogo—who had gone to Jerusalem with Robert the elder, duke of the Normans, and died as a pilgrim on that journey—had married Biota, daughter of Hugh, count of the men of Maine, and aunt of the aforesaid young man. Walter consequently claimed the whole county of Maine and possessed part of it [Col. 0276D]. For Geoffrey of Mayenne, Hubert of Sainte-Suzanne, and other powerful men firmly held the city itself, the capital of the province, in Walter’s allegiance, because they greatly feared to submit to the Norman yoke, which is exceedingly burdensome to those upon whom it is imposed.

Therefore, while the great-hearted duke repeatedly attacked the rebels in expeditions and, as the fortune of war requires, both suffered losses and inflicted losses on his enemies, Count Walter and his wife Biota were, it is said, together treacherously poisoned to death through the schemes of their enemies [Col. 0277A]. After they had died, the duke, now more secure, attacked the rebels with great strength and received the city of Maine amid immense rejoicing, its citizens surrendering voluntarily. Lord Ernald, bishop of that city, honorably came out to meet him with clergy and monks clad in vestments and carrying Gospel-books and crosses.

Geoffrey of Mayenne, however, envied the duke’s great good fortune and tried to harm him by stirring up opponents against him as far as he could and by devising evils in other ways. The duke endured Geoffrey’s insolence for some time, so that he might correct him personally without great loss to many; but when Geoffrey persisted in wickedness, he raised a huge army against him, captured his town of Ambrières, and burned Mayenne after a long siege [Col. 0277B]. Having thus subdued these two castles, he broke Geoffrey’s obstinacy and compelled him to serve himself, although Geoffrey was the bravest man in Maine and urged the other proud men to resist with him. Once he had been overcome, nearly all his accomplices and supporters in rebellion were bowed down by fear; compelled to fear and obey Prince William, whom the divine hand protected.

William entrusted the beautiful virgin Margaret for upbringing to Stigand, a powerful man of the household of Odo. But before she reached marriageable years, she was happily taken away from the mockeries of the world by death and rests buried at Fécamp, where the monastic house of the Holy and Undivided Trinity flourishes gloriously [Col. 0277C].

At the same time Robert of Vassy, son of Ralph son of Archbishop Robert, died childless; and Duke William, his kinsman, obtained his entire inheritance into his own lordship. Then the duke gave the land of Robert of Vitot, who was in exile for the killing of Count Gilbert, to Geoffrey of Maine, brother of Viscount Hubert. From him Lord Osbern, abbot of Saint Evroul, bought the estate called Ducts Ertu, together with Trunchet and Mesnil-Roscelin. Duke William granted this and confirmed it in a charter before the leading men of Normandy: William son of Osbern, Richard of Avranches son of Turstin [Col. 0277D], Roger of Montgomery, and many others named in the charter.

After a long time Robert of Vitot was reconciled with the duke, recovered his honor, and laid claim to the aforesaid land of Saint Evroul. But not long after the English war, in which he himself was wounded in the knee, had ended, he contracted a fatal illness. When he felt death approaching, he generously granted to the faithful of God, for the redemption of his soul, all the land which, as we have already said, he had claimed from them. This grant was made to Saint Evroul at Dover, before Odo, bishop of Bayeux; Hugh of Grandmesnil; Hugh of Montfort [Col. 0278A]; Hugh son of Fulco; and many other persons of high and middling rank.

Then, because this knight had nearly eleven nephews made fierce by the titles of knighthood, and because they raged against one another, his inheritance could scarcely ever remain at peace down to the present day. For Matthiellus, his brother Richard, Nigel, and Rualod the Breton, Nigel’s son-in-law, succeeded at different times and committed many evil acts, accompanied by misfortunes. Each of them laid claim to the aforesaid possession from Saint Evroul; but, through the impending judgment of God, who powerfully protects his Church everywhere, each was forced to desist from his unjust claim. Under the great Duke William, Matthiellus and Richard, and under Duke Robert and his brothers William Rufus and Henry, the other claimants, attempted with many threats to despoil the Church of God of the possessions it held [Col. 0278B]; but, with the King of kings aiding his own, they could not accomplish the wickedness they desired.

Ernald of Escalfoy, son of William Geroian, after returning prosperously from Apulia, approached Duke William, presented him with a most precious cloth, and humbly requested from him the restoration of his inheritance. The duke, considering the man’s nobility and outstanding worth, and recalling the shortage of valiant knights on his own side against the men of Le Mans, the Bretons, and others resisting him, became more lenient and pardoned his offence. Having granted a truce, he promised to restore Ernald’s patrimony, and until the appointed [Col. 0278C] term gave him free and safe passage to travel to and from through his territory. Ernald therefore rejoiced at receiving the duke’s empty promise—but vainly, as became clear shortly afterward.

For Mabel, daughter of Talvas, poisoned food and drink with deadly venom and ordered it to be served to him as he was returning from the duke’s court into France. But this enormous crime was disclosed to him by a friend who knew of the plot. Thus, while he was conversing with certain friends at Escalfoy, and was invited with the utmost urgency to a feast by the retainers of the aforesaid woman, he remembered his friend’s warning and in no way consented, but wholly rejected the food and drink in which he feared death lay concealed. Gilbert, however, brother of Roger of Montgomery, who was accompanying Ernald, [Col. 0278D] being entirely ignorant of the plot, took a cup and, seated on horseback, drank unmixed wine. Poisoned thereby, he died on the third day at Raimalast [Note: [Col. 0277D] Today Remalard (Orne).]. Thus the treacherous woman, thinking to destroy her husband’s rival, killed her husband’s only brother, a man outstanding in the years of his youth for great honour and knightly prowess.

Not long afterward, lamenting that her first attempt had failed, she again rose, with another effort no less deadly, to commit the crime she desired. She enticed by prayers and promises a knight named Roger Gulafra, Ernald’s chamberlain, and quickly bent that deceitful attendant to her wicked purposes. Then [Col. 0279A] she prepared her deadly draughts; and he administered them to his lord Ernald, to Geroie of Corbeville, and to William called Goiet of Montmirail. Thus three nobles were poisoned together by one infection at Corbeville. But Geroie and William, carried back to their own houses and able there to arrange their care as they wished, recovered, God giving efficacy to the physicians’ remedies. Ernald, however, being an exile and unable adequately to procure care for himself in foreign lodgings, was ill for several days; at last, as the illness grew worse, he died on the Kalends of January.

On the day before he died, while lying alone in bed in his chamber, he clearly saw—not in a dream—a certain very beautiful old man, whom he believed to be St Nicholas the bishop. From him he heard these words: “Brother, do not concern yourself about your bodily health, for tomorrow you will certainly die; but exert yourself with all your strength to ensure that your soul may be saved at the judgment of the just and eternal Judge.” Having said this, the old man suddenly disappeared. The sick man immediately sent to Ouche and asked to be visited by the brethren of that place. They promptly sent Fulk of Warlenville to Corbeville. For there the aforesaid knight had stayed for three years during his exile with Geroie, lord of that town, his kinsman and friend; and from there he had vigorously avenged the wrong of his expulsion by warfare through the Corbonnais, the Drouais, the Morini, and others whom he could summon to his aid. [Col. 0279C]

When Fulk arrived at once, the sick man rejoiced greatly. Having disclosed the revelation which he had seen the previous day, and renounced the world with gracious devotion of spirit, he became a monk. Then, mourning his sins and rejoicing in God, he died that same day. His body was brought to Ouche and honourably buried in the monks’ cloister by Lord Abbot Osbern and the community of St Ebrulf.

After Ernald’s death, the whole nobility of the Geroians nearly collapsed, and none of his descendants has been able, down to the present day, fully to attain the standing of their forebears. He had married Emma, daughter of Turstin called Halduc; by her he had William, Rainald, Petronilla, and Geva, as well as other sons and daughters. Bereft of their father while he was still flourishing in the full vigour of youth, [Col. 0279D] and placed in foreign households, as we have sufficiently shown above, they were compelled from childhood to suffer poverty and many injuries. Their mother withdrew to her brother Eudo, steward of the Norman duke, who stood eminent among the magnates of Normandy in wealth and power in the Cotentin. She lived honourably in widowhood for almost thirty years, both with him and with her other friends. She was praiseworthy for chastity, gentleness, and other honourable virtues; and at last, near the end of her life, she laid aside secular dress and devoutly received the sacred veil from Lord Roger, abbot of Holy Trinity at Exmes.

William of Escalfoy, Ernald’s eldest son, when he reached adolescence, went to the court of Philip, king of the Franks. Made the king’s armiger, he served him until he received knighthood from him. Then he made for Apulia, where he had relatives of high rank. Retained there in friendship by them, he advanced greatly in many ways through his acts of prowess. There he married a noble wife of Lombard stock and obtained possession of thirty castles under Count Robert of Loritello, namely the nephew of Guiscard. By his fertile wife he had many children of both sexes; and, forgetting the Normans, he lived honourably among the Winili for nearly forty years.

Rainald, however, Ernald’s youngest son, was entrusted to Abbot Osbern three months before his father’s death. He was carefully raised under regular discipline in the church of Ouche and was named Benedict by the aforesaid abbot, on account of his sweetness. [Col. 0280B] When his father offered him to God for the monastic life, he granted St Ebrulf one ploughland at St Germanus in the parish of Escalfoy. Because of the misfortunes which, as we have related, he and his heirs endured, the church long ago lost this land. The aforesaid boy was five years old when he assumed the monastic yoke, and for fifty-two years, under four abbots, he bore it bravely through adversity and prosperity.

He himself learned reading and singing in abundance; and, after reaching mature strength, freely imparted this learning to others without any stain of deceit. His memory for recounting what he had seen or heard was remarkably strong; and by his delightful narration of matters which he had investigated in sacred books or in the assertions of learned persons, he often refreshed his companions. He always strove to please the gentle, the modest, and untaught novices through friendliness and service; but he resolved manfully to resist the proud, hypocrites, and inventors of novelties with bold opposition.

Twice, by permission of Abbot Roger and for the benefit of the church of Ouche, he travelled to Apulia. There he found his brother William and many others of his kindred, who abounded in wealth in that foreign land. He remained in Calabria for almost three years with Abbot William of St Euphemia, son of Humphrey of Telliolo; and, when returning, he brought St Ebrulf a cope of white purple as a gift from the aforesaid abbot, who was his cousin. From childhood he honourably observed monastic practices and adhered fervently, night and day, to divine worship. [Col. 0280D] We often saw him maintain psalmody so tirelessly that scarcely a single verse was sung by the others in his choir while he himself was silent.

But, as it is written, “Many are the afflictions of the righteous” (Ps. VII, 20), he endured many adversities through the importunity of disturbances within and without. For, because he was stern and harsh toward the rash, and disdained to flatter hypocrites, he was often troubled by their manifold attacks. And because the eye of God beholds all things and by subtle judgment reproves even what seems praiseworthy to human beings, God struck the aforesaid brother from childhood with bodily infirmity and, so that the righteous person may yet be made righteous, has not ceased to increase the weakness of his limbs.

For in boyhood, because he was immoderate and rose to every task with all his strength in order to seem stronger than the other brethren, he was injured by a rupture of the intestines while carrying earth. Since he did not spare himself, the same injury became incurable. Finally, for seven years now he has been oppressed by such a grave affliction that he can no longer raise even his hand to his mouth, nor by his own strength perform any service for himself. Most high God, who healest the broken in heart, mercifully have pity on him; cleanse him from every sin; and, delivered from the oppressive prison of the flesh, receive him into the fellowship of thy servants in eternal rest!

The two daughters of Ernald, after their father’s death and the desolation of their family, chose rather to please God by the modest ordering of their conduct than to be subject to the world through the corruptible beauty of their bodies. Therefore both dedicated their virginity [Col. 0281B] to God; despising the world, they became religious women. Petronilla received the veil in the monastery of St Mary at Angers. For a long time she carefully observed the sacred order according to the custom of the other virgins; then, having now been enclosed for ten years, she became widely known to many through her reputation for holiness and the example of her virtue. Her sister Geva, in the monastery of the Holy Trinity which Queen Matilda built at Caen, long bore and taught the sacred rule under Abbess Beatrice, advancing honourably both herself and others. These things have been said concerning the founders of our church and their descendants.

## XVI. William, Count or Margrave of the Normans. The Conflict between Hugh of Grandmesnil and Ralph, Count of Mantes. The Death of Abbot Osbern

[Col. 0281C]

Now let us return to the narrative of history. The renowned margrave of Normandy, William, entrusted to a number of his barons the defence of the castle called Neufmarché against the Beauvaisis, who were trying to ravage his borders, after expelling Geoffrey, the natural heir, for some slight offence. Yet scarcely any of them could hold it for one year because of the attacks of the men of Milly, the Gerberrois, and other neighbouring peoples. At length the high-spirited duke, on the advice of Roger of Montgomery—who greatly envied Hugh of Grandmesnil’s very near and formidable power, and desired by every contrivance or circumstance to prepare trouble for him—entrusted the aforesaid town jointly to Hugh of Grandmesnil, eminent for bold prowess and generosity, and to Gerald the steward, giving Hugh one half of it. [Col. 0281D] Hugh gladly accepted the defence of the fortification and, with God’s help, within one year captured two very great nobles of the Beauvaisis. Having terrified the other enemies, he pacified the entire region in that district.

At Neufmarché four canons possessed the church of St Peter the Apostle, but negligently performed God’s worship and led excessively secular lives. Therefore the high-spirited Hugh granted to the church of St Ebrulf, that is, to its monks, the half belonging to himself, on this condition: when the canons failed, whether through death or any other event, monks would succeed them. And so it occurred. For when two canons who belonged to Hugh’s portion departed thence, monks [Col. 0282A] succeeded them and have possessed half the church down to the present day. Robert the Bald, Ralph of Rosseria, John of Belnay, and other worthy men have lived there.

At one time a serious conflict arose between the often-mentioned Hugh and Count Ralph of Mantes, stepfather of Philip, king of the Franks. When Hugh boldly engaged the aforesaid count, he was compelled to flee because he had an inferior number of knights. During this flight Richard of Heldric’s Court, a noble knight from the Vexin, was wounded. For when, fleeing rapidly on horseback, he entered a ford of the River Epte, the lance of a pursuing knight struck him most fiercely from behind, over his horse. He was immediately carried to Neufmarché [Col. 0282B] by his fellow-knights. Fearing death, he vowed, on Hugh’s advice—for he had served in Hugh’s military household—that henceforth he would serve under the monastic rule through exercises of virtue. He therefore summoned the monks of Ouche and committed himself to Abbot Osbern’s instruction.

Afterward, through God’s gift—God who draws sinners back from the abyss of destruction by diverse occasions—Richard recovered somewhat, though not completely. For nearly seven years he lived fervently in the order and benefited the church in many ways. Because he had neither wife nor children, after being wounded he voluntarily brought to St Ebrulf the patrimony he possessed in the Vexin. He obtained from his uncle Fulk, from Herbert the Butler, his feudal lord, [Col. 0282C] and from his other relatives a complete grant of this property.

Although his wound was never closed, and matter flowed from it daily in a quantity, as those who saw it reported, sufficient to fill an eggshell of a goose, he earnestly strove to follow the community’s rulefully ordered life and cheerfully performed the services required by the order. He went on foot or rode wherever he was commanded, and diligently served ecclesiastical interests to the extent of his ability, in word and deed. Abbot Osbern loved him more than the others and greatly trusted in him as in his own person. He therefore entrusted to Richard the supervision and expenses, and the direction of the masons, for the new basilica which he intended to begin.

[Col. 0282D] At the prayers and exhortation of this Richard, the aforesaid father went to France and invited Robert the Eloquent, Herbert of Serranz, Fulk of Caldreio, and other knights and common people of the Vexin to meet with him in friendly conference. With the assent and rejoicing of the aforesaid nobles and neighbours, he received the estate of Heldric’s Court into the lordship of St Ebrulf. Returning from there, he took to his bed. After some days, as his illness worsened, he came, supported, into the chapter-house and ordered the letter—which, as we said above, he had sent to Pope Alexander—to be read publicly. This was done so that all might know that he had not seized the abbey from Abbot Robert, but had accepted its governance unwillingly and under compulsion.

Finally, he strengthened the brethren by exhortation and begged them to forgive his errors and remember him. Thus, after making confession and receiving the communion of the most holy body of the Lord, he died on the sixth day before the Kalends of June [27 May 1066], while the brethren devoutly sang litanies for him. He had governed the church of Ouche for five years and three months. On the next day Vitalis, abbot of Bernay, came to bury his friend, and interred him in the cloister of the monastery beside the church of St Peter, prince of the apostles. Seventeen years later, his successor Mainerius transferred him to the new chapter-house together with the bones of his companion Witmund.

## XVII. Comets. Events in England. Harold’s Usurpation. William, Margrave of the Normans, Prepares to Cross to England

[Col. 0283B]

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1066, in the fourth indiction, in April, for about fifteen days a star called a comet appeared in the north-western quarter. As discerning astrologers, who have subtly investigated the secrets of natural science, assert, it signifies a change of kingdom. For Edward, king of the English, son of King Æthelred by Emma, daughter of Richard the Elder, duke of the Normans, had died shortly before; and Harold, son of Earl Godwine, had usurped the kingdom of the English and had already held it for three months, to the injury of many, stained by perjury, cruelty, and other wickedness.

This unjust invasion stirred up excessive discord among certain peoples, and brought death and mourning to many mothers for their sons and to wives for their husbands. Edward had granted full possession of the English kingdom to his kinsman Duke William of the Normans, first through Robert, supreme bishop of Canterbury, and afterward through that same Harold; and, with the consent of the English, had made him heir to all his rights. Indeed, Harold himself at Rouen had sworn an oath to Duke William before the magnates of Normandy; having become his man, he had sworn upon the most sacred relics everything demanded of him. The duke had also taken Harold with him on an expedition against Conan, count of the Bretons, and had splendidly equipped him and his fellow-knights with gleaming arms, horses, and other insignia.

For this Englishman was remarkable for stature, elegance, bodily strength, courage of spirit, eloquence of speech, and many charms and worthy qualities. But what did such gifts avail him without faithfulness, the foundation of all good things? On returning to his homeland, through desire for the kingdom he broke faith with his lord. For he deceived King Edward, who, as his illness worsened, was already near death, and related to him an account of his crossing, journey into Normandy, and embassy. He then added, by deceitful assertions, that William of Normandy had given him his daughter in marriage and granted him the right to the entire English kingdom as his son-in-law. Hearing this, the sick ruler was astonished; nevertheless, he believed and granted what the crafty tyrant had fabricated.

[Col. 0284A]

After some time, King Edward of pious memory died in London on the Nones of January, in the twenty-fourth year of his reign. He was buried in the new monastery which he had founded in the western part of the city and had caused to be dedicated in the preceding week, near the altar which St Peter the Apostle, in Bishop Mellitus’s time, had consecrated with visible signs. On the very day of his burial, while the people were still drenched in tears at the obsequies of their beloved king, Harold secretly seized the splendour of diadem and purple. He was consecrated only by Archbishop Stigand, whom the Roman pope had suspended from divine offices for certain crimes, without the common consent of the other bishops, earls, and magnates.

When the English heard of Harold’s rash seizure, they were angry; some of the more powerful, prepared to resist stoutly, entirely withheld themselves from his subjection. Others, not knowing how to escape his tyranny, which had already become too powerful over them, and considering in turn that they could neither depose him nor, while he reigned, set another king in his place for the good of the kingdom, submitted their necks to his yoke and strengthened the crime he had begun. He immediately defiled the kingdom which he had wickedly invaded with horrible crimes.

Edwin and Morcar, earls, sons of Earl Ælfgar, attached themselves to Harold in friendship and strove with all their strength to assist him, because he had as wife their sister Eadgyth, [Col. 0284C] who had previously been the wife of Gruffydd, the very powerful king of the Welsh. She had borne him Bleddyn, heir to the kingdom, and a daughter named Nest. Then Tostig, son of Earl Godwine, seeing his brother Harold’s crime prevail and the kingdom of England burdened by various oppressions, took it bitterly, opposed him, and resolved openly to resist. Harold therefore violently took from him their father’s earldom, which Tostig, being the elder, had long held under King Edward, and forced him into exile.

Tostig, now an exile, went to Flanders. There he entrusted his wife Judith to her father Baldwin, ruler of the Flemings; then he hastened to Normandy and sharply reproached Duke William for allowing his perjurer to reign. He promised faithfully that, if William crossed to England with Norman forces, he would secure for him the honour of the kingdom. They had long loved one another greatly and had married two sisters, through whom their friendship was often renewed. Duke William received his arriving friend with joy, thanked him for his friendly rebuke, and, stirred by his exhortations, summoned the magnates of Normandy and openly consulted them on what ought to be done in so great and momentous an undertaking.

At that time Normandy flourished brilliantly in wise church prelates and nobles. For the holy Maurilius, once a monk and now metropolitan, presided as bishop over the see of Rouen; Odo, Duke William’s maternal half-brother, over Bayeux; Hugh, brother of Count Robert of Eu, over Lisieux; William over Évreux; Geoffrey over Coutances; John, son of Ralph, count of Bayeux, over Avranches; and Ivo, son of William of Bellême, over Sées. All these men excelled alike in distinguished nobility of birth, religious renown, and manifold worth.

Laymen also were pre-eminent: Count Richard of Évreux, son of Archbishop Robert; Count Robert, son of William, ruler of Eu; Count Robert of Mortain, Duke William’s maternal half-brother; Ralph of Conches, son of Roger of Tosny, standard-bearer of the Normans; William, son of Osbern, the duke’s kinsman and steward; William de Warenne and Hugh the Butler; Hugh [Col. 0285B] of Grandmesnil and Roger of Mowbray; Roger of Beaumont and Roger of Montgomery; Baldwin and Richard, sons of Count Gilbert; and many others, fierce in knightly lineage and powerful in prudent understanding and counsel. They yielded neither in courage nor mature judgment to the Roman senate, but endeavoured to equal it in enduring toil and in conquering an enemy through both intelligence and courage.

All were summoned by the duke’s command to a common council. When they heard of so great a matter, being diverse men, they held differing views. The more spirited, eager to support the duke, urged their companions to go to battle and praised the immediate undertaking of so great an enterprise. Others advised against beginning such a laborious work, set forth many troubling and perilous objections to their excessive and death-rushing designs, raised the dangers of the sea and the difficulty of assembling a fleet, and maintained that the small number of Normans could not overcome the multitude of Englishmen.

At length William sent Gilbert, archdeacon of Lisieux, to Rome and sought Pope Alexander’s counsel about what had occurred. When the pope heard the facts, he supported the lawful duke, directed him boldly to take arms against the perjurer, and sent him the banner of St Peter the Apostle, by whose merits he would be defended from every danger.

Meanwhile Tostig received leave from the duke to return to England and firmly promised his assistance, both personally and through all his friends. [Col. 0285D] But, as it is written, “Man proposes, God disposes,” events turned out very differently from what he had hoped. He entered the sea from the Cotentin, but could not reach England at all. For Harold had fortified the sea with a multitude of ships and soldiers, so that no enemy could enter the kingdom he had fraudulently seized without severe conflict.

Tostig was therefore pressed on every side by great difficulties, unable either to invade England by war with a few men against innumerable foes or to return to Normandy because of contrary winds. Driven in turn by the west wind, south wind, and other winds, he endured many distresses and, wandering over the waters, feared many dangers; until, after many hardships, he at last came to King Harald of the Norwegians, surnamed Hardrada. [Col. 0286A] Honourably received by him, he saw that he could not fulfil the promises which he had made to Duke William, changed his purpose, and said:

> “Most magnificent king, I humbly approach your highness and faithfully offer myself and my service to your majesty, that through your support I may be restored to the honour due to me by paternal succession. For my brother Harold, who ought by right to obey me as the first-born, has treacherously risen against me and dared to usurp the kingdom of England by perjuries. Therefore I request manly assistance from you, whom I know to flourish especially in strength, arms, and every excellence, as being your man. Crush in war the insolence of my faithless brother; retain one half of England for yourselves, and secure the other half for me, who shall faithfully serve you from it as long as I live.”

Hearing this, the greedy king rejoiced greatly. He then ordered an army to be assembled, military equipment prepared, and the royal fleet to be diligently equipped in every respect over six months. The errant exile stirred the tyrant to so great a labour and, by crafty evasion, so deceived him that he was not seized by him as a spy upon his kingdom, but might somehow through him avenge upon his faithless brother the injury of his expulsion.

Nevertheless, the margrave of the Normans was preparing his expedition, unaware of the misfortune that had overtaken his forerunner and driven him far beyond his appointed course [Col. 0286C] to the north. In Neustria many ships, with their equipment, were carefully prepared; clergy and laity alike applied themselves to their construction with effort and expenditure. By a princely levy, numerous warriors were summoned from Normandy. Fighting men also, stirred by reports, assembled from neighbouring regions and prepared themselves with military equipment for battle. For Frenchmen and Bretons, Poitevins and Burgundians, and other peoples from this side of the Alps hastened to the overseas war; longing for English plunder, they exposed themselves to diverse fortunes and dangers by land and sea.

## XVIII. The History of Ouche Continues. Again on the Death of Osbern. The Election of Abbot Mainerius

[Col. 0286D]

While these things were being done, Osbern, abbot of Ouche, died, as we have related above. Before crossing the sea, the monastic community asked the duke concerning the appointment of a successor. He held counsel concerning the matter with his magnates at Bonneville. Finally, at the urging of Bishop Hugh and other wise men, he chose Mainerius, the prior, entrusted him with external administration by the pastoral staff, and instructed the aforesaid bishop to supply whatever belonged to his spiritual care. The bishop willingly completed everything.

On the same day the duke ordered Lord Lanfranc, prior of Bec, to appear before him, and entrusted to him the abbey which the duke himself had honourably founded at Caen in honour of St Stephen the first martyr. [Col. 0287A] Lanfranc thus became the first abbot of Caen, but shortly afterward was promoted to the archbishopric of Canterbury. He was a Lombard by nation, richly trained in the liberal arts, endowed with kindness, generosity, and every religious virtue, and greatly devoted to almsgiving and other good works. From the day when he first received the government of the church at Bonneville, as we have mentioned, he shone nobly for twenty-two years and nine months, benefiting many faithful persons in the house of God.

The venerable Bishop Hugh, by the duke’s command, brought Mainerius, the great-hearted servant of God, to Ouche, and according to the canons blessed him before the altar of St Peter the Apostle on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August [16 July]. [Col. 0287B] Having received the name and burden of abbot, he lived praiseworthily and usefully held the government entrusted to him for twenty-two years and seven months. With God’s help, he improved the monastery committed to him in many ways, inwardly and outwardly.

By prudence and reason he kindly calmed the brethren, who had been somewhat disturbed at his election. They had chosen two monks, both eminent in religious life and double learning—namely Rainald of La Roche and Fulk of Warlenville—to govern them, and therefore had dissented considerably from the man placed over them by the bishop and their neighbours without their consent. In affairs of this kind, disturbance commonly arises through inferior men. For while wicked men strive violently to impose their own judgment, regular order and sounder counsel are often impeded. But almighty God powerfully protects his Church in every affliction, corrects those who err, and mercifully affords necessary consolation as and through whom he wills.

His providence therefore advanced the aforesaid Mainerius—as later became plainly clear—to govern the monastery of Ouche, situated in barren country among very wicked fellow-countrymen. He was a native of the neighbouring castle called Escalfoy, abundantly trained in grammar, dialectic, and rhetoric; skilful and severe in cutting away vices, fervent in implanting and imparting virtues to the brethren. A constant observer of monastic rule, he showed those entrusted to him the way of life in words and deeds, and became an encourager, guide, and vigilant companion to many in labouring in the vineyard [Col. 0287D] of the Lord Sabaoth.

He began a new basilica in honour of St Mary, mother of the Lord; St Peter the Apostle; and St Ebrulf the confessor. Therein seven altars are consecrated to the divine majesty in honour of saints. For the old church which St Ebrulf had built for the prince of the apostles while Chilperic and his nephew Hildebert bore the sceptres of the Franks had been largely ruined by age and did not suffice for the monastic community, which was increasing daily. Yet building in stone at Ouche was very laborious, since the quarry at Merlerault, from which squared stones were brought, lay six miles away. Thus the administrators faced great difficulty in assembling horses, oxen, [Col. 0288A] and carts through which the loads of stone and other equipment necessary for so great a work were transported.

The aforesaid abbot never rested throughout his administration, but, anxiously occupied with the care of many matters, greatly benefited both those subject to him and posterity. With the aid of God, and through the support and generosity of brethren and friends, he completed a bright and spacious church, suited to those freely celebrating God’s service; the cloister and chapter-house; dormitory and refectory; kitchen and cellar; and other workshops appropriate to the monks’ needs.

For Archbishop Lanfranc, when he attended the dedication of the church at Caen in the twelfth year after the English war [1077], gave Abbot Mainerius forty-four pounds of English money [Col. 0288B] and two marks of gold. Later, from Kent, he sent forty pounds sterling through Lord Roger of Sappo, whom he knew and counted as a friend because of his literary learning. With these gifts the church tower was raised and the monastic dormitory built. Queen Matilda gave a precious mitre, a cope for God’s service, and one hundred Rouen pounds for the production of a *tricorium* [materially uncertain term]. William of Ros, a clerk of Bayeux who enjoyed a threefold dignity in that church—for he was cantor, dean, and archdeacon—gave forty pounds sterling to the men of Ouche. Not long afterward, voluntarily leaving the pomps of the world, he became a monk at Caen; and from there, before completing one year in monastic life, he was raised to govern the monastery of Fécamp. Because of the many benefits he conferred upon the men of Ouche, his name was written in the general roll; and it was decreed that masses, prayers, and alms should be performed for him altogether as for a professed monk. With the support of very many benefactors, therefore, the fabric of the new basilica was raised, and the work begun, both of the church and the buildings, was honourably completed.

During Abbot Mainerius’s administration, ninety monks of diverse character and condition, whose names are recorded in the volume of the general register, laid aside secular dress in the school of Ouche. Stirred by inspiration and the praiseworthy example of good men, they undertook to go by the arduous way. Some of them, while the father himself was still alive, obtained the reward of good conduct; others remained long in their holy purpose and courageously performed a long military service, striving to please God by devotion and to benefit people through the practice of good works. Some, distinguished by noble birth, assisted their monastery in many ways and obtained from their relatives, acquaintances, or friends tithes, churches, and ecclesiastical ornaments for the brethren’s use. I cannot set down individually everything which each contributed to his house; yet, insofar as I find a suitable ability to recount it, I desire, with God’s aid, truthfully to communicate some things for the common benefit of posterity.

Accordingly, the first of the monks, Roger of Altaripa, by order of the aforesaid abbot, went into the district of the Vexin and took possession of Heldric’s Court, which, as we have related above, Richard the Wounded had given to Saint Ebrulf. [Col. 0289A] He found the land uncultivated and almost empty of cultivators. Therefore, first he built there an oratory of wattles in honour of St Nicholas, bishop of Myra; and for this reason the village now standing there is still called by its inhabitants the Chapel of St Nicholas. It often happened, as he himself used to tell us, that at night, while he was chanting Matins in the wattle chapel, a wolf stood outside opposite him and, as though responding to the psalm-singer, answered with a murmur.

Thus the venerable man, aided by God, bound to himself Herbert the cupbearer by the bond of affection. After the death of his kinsman Herbert, namely the brother of Richard the Wounded, Herbert granted half his fief to Saint Ebrulf. [Col. 0289B] There Roger, labouring with the assistance of his benevolent patron, cultivated the place itself, which had long previously been abandoned because of war and other misfortunes. After some years Roger of Sappo succeeded the aforesaid lord there and began to build a church of stone.

For this aforesaid knight was very powerful throughout the whole Vexin; enlarged by wealth, sons, and strong parents and relatives, he surpassed almost all his neighbours. His wife was named Rollandis, daughter of Odo of Calvimont. She bore him Geoffrey, Peter, John, and Walon, and several daughters, from whom arose a great abundance of descendants. All these—the father, that is, and the aforesaid brothers—were knights of great worth and, so far as outward appearance showed, of approved loyalty towards God and men. [Col. 0289C] The aforesaid woman, moreover, was throughout her life of exceptional honour, and is still alive, though her husband and children have long since been taken from this world. By their generosity and support, the chapel of the blessed bishop Nicholas was restored, and a suitable dwelling for monks, who live according to the Rule and love peace, was made there and remains to this day.

At the same time Fulcoius, son of Ralph of Caldreio, greatly loved the venerable Roger because of the many kinds of goodness in which he excelled, and kindly offered him his son to lift from the sacred font of baptism; Roger gladly received him. Then, as their acquaintance and affection gradually increased, Fulcoius granted his fellow-countryman the church of [Col. 0289D] St Martin of Parnes, at which the parish assembled on appointed days from seven neighbouring villages, to render their vows to God and to hear, as was fitting, the praises and commandments of God. Roger then summoned Abbot Mainerius.

After the aforesaid father arrived at Parnes, Fulcoius, with the consent of his brother Wascelin, granted to Saint Ebrulf the church and all the customary rights belonging to that church; in the same village, land sufficient for one plough, the tithe of his plough-team, two holdings of houses, and one mill called Tollens-Viam (“Toll-the-Road”). He also gave the monks the archdeaconry which he held in fief from the archbishop of Rouen through his forefathers, and he granted them lordship over all the tenants dwelling at Parnes, on the condition that, if they committed offences against [Col. 0290A] the monks, he should punish them not in their own houses but by another fiscal penalty. The people of Parnes rejoiced that they were subjected to the monks, hoping to be protected by their patronage against the neighbouring Normans, by whose attacks they were frequently harassed.

Later, while Goisbert the physician held the priory, Fulcoius gave the entire cemetery so that a new basilica might be begun. Then the foundation of the new work was laid; but because of very many obstacles arising over thirty-four years, the work has not yet been completed.

The aforesaid knight was strong, high-spirited, and ardent in everything that he desired; quick to anger and fierce in military exercises. He was ready to seize other men’s goods insolently and to squander his own imprudently, that he might deserve the empty praise of lavishness. [Col. 0290B] He had a wife named Ita, daughter of Heremar of Ponthieu, who bore him Walter and Mainerius, Hugh and Gervase, Hermar and Fulcoius, and a daughter named Luxovia. Mainerius and Fulcoius were bound by the monastic rule from childhood; the other four pursued the freedom of military life.

Fulcoius the monk, because, as I have already said, he was unstable in character, sometimes loved greatly and stoutly defended against all opponents, but at other times himself grievously oppressed. At Parnes the aged Roger, Goisbert the physician, Robert the Bald, Haimericus, John, Isembard, and many others [Col. 0290C] served God in the monastic life. Among them Bernard, surnamed Michael, Rainald, Theodoric, Walter the Bald, and William of Caen, who was surnamed Alexander, lived in great religious devotion; and there they reached the end of their lives and were honourably buried.

Robert the Eloquent of Calvimont, their lord paramount, confirmed to the monks all that Fulcoius had given. Not long afterwards, while he was violently carrying off booty from the land of Saint Ouen, he fell from his horse in armour; his helmet was fixed in the ground, his neck was broken, and he died miserably. Abbot Mainerius buried his body at Alliariae in the chapter-house of the brothers of Flavigny dwelling there. Then his sons Otmund of Calvimont, Wazso of Pexei, and Robert of Beauvais [Col. 0290D] granted to Saint Ebrulf everything that, as stated above, had been given or granted by their predecessors.

## XIX. Concerning Blessed Josse, Son of Juthail, King of the Bretons

Thus the church of Parnes was entrusted to the monks of Ouche. It was anciently built in honour of St Martin, metropolitan bishop of Tours, and there the body of St Josse, confessor of Christ, has long been reverently kept.

Who this man was and whence he came, I shall briefly insert into this account of ours, drawing truthfully certain things from the book written concerning his holy manner of life.

Blessed Josse, son of Juthail, king of the Bretons, and [Col. 0291A] brother of King Judicael, when he was being sought for the kingdom, left the studies that he was pursuing at Lanmailmon and set out as a pilgrim with eleven pilgrims travelling to Rome. On the way Haimo, duke of Ponthieu, detained him, recognizing his nobility, and had him ordained priest as his own chaplain.

After seven years Josse served God for eight years in the wilderness of Braic by the stream of the Altea. There birds of various kinds and little fishes he fed with his own hand like tame livestock. When he had divided his only loaf among four poor persons, despite the murmuring of his servant Vulmar, he received from God four little boats, drawn along the waters of the Altea and laden with an abundance of food and drink. Afterwards, at Runiac on the river Canche, he built an oratory to St Martin and lived there for fourteen years. [Col. 0291B] An eagle carried off eleven of his hens; finally, when it had carried off the cock, the man of God made the sign of the cross and prayed. At once the eagle returned, set down the cock unharmed, and immediately died.

Once, while Josse and Duke Haimo were seeking a suitable dwelling for him in a dense forest, and the duke, exhausted by hunting and burning with excessive thirst, had fallen asleep, the man of God thrust the staff that he used into the ground and, after pouring out prayers to God, brought forth a spring. Sick persons who come there venerate it, and, drinking from it, are quickly healed. The servant of God built two oratories with his own hands in the forest out of wood. One he dedicated to Peter, key-bearer of heaven, and the other to Paul, mighty in speech. Afterwards he went to Rome and brought back from there many relics of saints.

Juliula, [Col. 0291C] a girl blind from birth, was instructed in a vision to wash her face with the water in which Josse washed his hands. When she did so, she received sight. This occurred while the man of God was returning from Rome; a wooden cross was set up there, and hence the place itself was called the Cross.

Meanwhile, while Josse had gone to Rome, Duke Haimo built a stone church in the wilderness. After the man of God’s return, he had it dedicated in honour of Blessed Martin and, as an endowment, gave it a certain village from his own property with all its appurtenances. There the faithful athlete of God, Josse, served God for a long time; having happily completed the course of holy life, he passed to Christ on the Ides of December.

[Col. 0291D] His two nephews, Winnoch and Arnoch, succeeded him there. They regularly washed and anointed the holy body, which remained incorrupt for a long time. Duke Drochtricus, Haimo’s successor, heard this but doubted it. Wishing insolently to investigate the matter, he caused the sacred tomb to be opened by force. Looking within irreverently, he was immediately terrified and said, “Ah, holy Josse!” At once he became deaf and dumb, and until his death was weakened in his whole body. His wife, terrified by her husband’s misfortune, groaned to God and, for the salvation of his soul, gave two villages, Crispiniacum and Netrevilla, to St Josse. These things occurred in the time of Dagobert, son of Lothair the Great, king of the Franks.

[Col. 0292A] Isembard of Fleury, at the urging of the monk Adelelm, writes to Abbot Herbold that in the year 977 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the time of Lothair, son of Louis, king of the Franks, the body of St Josse was found as follows. A certain peasant named Stephen, who earned his living by operating a mill, was instructed in a dream by a man in splendid clothing and came to the place of St Josse. Leaving his wife and children, he became a cleric. The body of St Josse, whose whereabouts were then unknown to all mortals, he began to seek within the church, prompted by the vision. At the direction of Pridianus Sigemanus, he found a sarcophagus on the right side of the altar of St Martin. While all rejoiced and sang praises to God, the tomb containing the holy body was excavated and raised [Col. 0292B] from the earth.

News of this spread everywhere. A great crowd hurried from all directions to see the elevation of the saint’s body and to offer him vows and gifts. Many miracles occurred there, and many kinds of infirmities were cured. At length, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, the body of St Josse was reverently placed upon the altar of St Martin.

In that same year a monastery was begun there from the foundations, the monastic order began to be restored, and the reverend Sigebrand was appointed abbot. One night, while the body of St Josse was kept in the church of St Peter, seven candles stood before the relics. Only one had been lit by the sacristan; the other six, while the guards slept, were lit from heaven. [Col. 0292C]

Likewise, on another occasion, the body of St Josse was in its church. In the presence of Sigemanus, a light extinguished by the force of winds and the flooding of rains was divinely rekindled.

On a Sunday, while Pridianus was solemnly celebrating Mass, a vassal of Count Hilduin named Guarembert, full of evil intent, wished violently to take whatever he pleased from the possessions of the saint and, after driving Sigemanus out, to substitute another more compliant with his own ways. Therefore, when the Gospel was being read, “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” (Matthew 9:4), the wretch began to cry out loudly, struck invisibly. Tormented a third time, he finally fell down under divine compulsion and vomited a clot of blood from his mouth. [Col. 0292D] After Mass, by order of Sigemanus the sacristan, he was carried outside; and on the following day, through the merits of St Josse, he recovered his right mind. This happened in the time of Hugh the Great.

That same day, a certain woman, Ostrehildis, was trying to leave the basilica after Mass, but the soles of her feet adhered so firmly to the threshold of the doorway that no one could possibly pull her free. She suffered no evil except that she felt intense cold from her knees down to the soles of her feet. The next day she vowed herself as a handmaid to God and St Josse, and immediately healed, she piously fulfilled her vows.

The truthful men Adelelm and the monk Richer relate that, when Stephen was carrying the relics of St Josse to the monastery of St Riquier for the construction of its basilica, [Col. 0293A] the renowned Bertsendis, the marriageable daughter of Alsindis, had for two years been grievously burdened by an affliction of the kidneys extending down to her feet, so that she could neither go anywhere nor even move without a bearer. But when mother and daughter had poured out a prayer in faith before the relics of the holy confessor, the sick girl was healed. Her mother, seeing her daughter restored to health, rejoiced greatly and gave a costly cloak to the swift physician.

A certain Robert, travelling alone at midday, was completely blinded upon seeing an evil spirit in human form. After a long time he sought St Josse and gave himself as a servant before Abbot Guy. Blood flowing from his eyes, he received sight that very day, and at Vespers openly declared that he had seen the monks seated in their stalls.

[Col. 0293B] Gunzso, a priest of Laon, was crippled for seven whole years by a dreadful infirmity of hands and feet. In a vision, someone advised him to seek Josse the physician in Ponthieu. He immediately obeyed the command. On a Sunday, at about the third hour, he entered the basilica, prayed prostrate, moistened the pavement with tears, and, when his prayers were finished, rose up sound. Then joyfully he at once sang Mass and truthfully recounted to the people, with thanksgiving, the course of his healing.

Wandelmar of Laon lost his right eye through illness and, persuaded by friends, resolved to visit Blessed Josse. But, ignorant of the right path, he happened to come with a companion to the spring which Josse, while still alive, had brought forth by his merits. Wandelmar [Col. 0293C] saw the very clear spring, stopped his companion, sat down there, washed his hands and face in the spring water, and suddenly recovered the sight he had lost. He then went joyfully to the monastery and, while his friends rejoiced, gave thanks to God.

Two demoniacs named Maginard were cleansed at the tomb of St Josse and afterwards lived for a long time sound in the world.

Sieburgis, wife of the most distinguished man Bertran, suffered a flow of blood from her nostrils for ten continuous months.
