Her friends brought her to the shrine of St Josse so that she might be healed. She prayed there but was not healed at once, and therefore, having left the basilica, uttered many complaints. At length, as she was returning home with resentment in her heart [Col. 0293D] and had passed the cross set beside the road, the blood immediately ceased to flow from her nostrils. At once, rejoicing, she retraced her steps to the monastery of the holy man and, after giving thanks, was completely healed.

Robert of Thérouanne, while at midday in summer he was alone inspecting work on his field, was suddenly seized by a demon and so tormented that the enemy urged him almost without ceasing to devour men and break everything in pieces. His three brothers therefore brought him bound to the tomb of St Josse during the June Ember fast, and they remained there from Wednesday until Saturday. Thereafter the sick man began to be more at peace; when he had recovered complete health, he gave himself permanently as a servant to St Josse. [Col. 0294A] At this man’s request, on the feast of St John the Baptist, Abbot Guy mounted the pulpit, recounted the event to the people, and presented the man himself, who was present and openly declared his experiences.

A certain man of mature age remained so deaf for seven years that he heard absolutely nothing. His wife brought him to the tomb of the holy man, where she prayed for some time. Then, by Pridianus’s instruction, the woman brought her husband to the spring of St Josse and three times poured the spring water over his head with her own hands. He immediately recovered his hearing and, returning to the church, heard the Mass which he had not heard for seven years.

Isembard of Fleury wrote all these things that occurred in the times of Hugh the Great or King Robert, at Adelelm’s request. [Col. 0294B] But afterward Blessed Josse did not cease to perform many great works for those who sought him, though they were not recorded because of negligence. When the rulers of the realm changed and the nobles disturbed one another in mutual conflict, the body of St Josse was again covered over with earth for fear of enemies. It lay so until all who had hidden it had died, and a general ignorance enveloped its whereabouts.

In the time of Henry, king of the Franks, while the monks frequently lamented that they did not know where their patron Josse rested, the holy body was divinely revealed to a certain simple layman. When he uncovered it, it was solemnly elevated through the care of the abbot and brethren. Afterwards the monks admitted the discoverer of the relics to the monastic life, [Col. 0294C] appointed him guardian of the sacred treasure, and entrusted the offerings of the faithful to him.

But when the abbot died, his successor did not love the sacristan as he ought, nor did he treat him amicably as his predecessor had done. Deeply offended, the sacristan took the holy body by night and carried it with him into France. Geoffrey, burgess of Gomery, honourably received him together with the treasure that he bore and granted him, until his death, the office in the castle church, where there were four canons.

After some time King Henry of the Franks, when certain disturbances of war had arisen, besieged Gomery. With the forces of the Frankish army he overcame Geoffrey and burned the town. While a devouring flame consumed the basilica and the buildings of the castle, [Col. 0294D] and the terrible cries of attackers and defenders, as is customary in such events, resounded from every side, one of the canons took the bones of St Josse from their shrine and fled hastily from the fire.

By chance a royal retainer met him on the bridge and asked what he was carrying wrapped in cloth. When the canon confessed that he was carrying sacred vestments and his books, the retainer violently took everything and carried this treasure with him into the territory of Parnes. This man was called Robert and was surnamed Meslebren, that is, “mixing bran”; he was among the retainers of Ralph of Caldreio, who at that time was considered one of the foremost knights in the Frankish army. The aforesaid knight therefore greatly rejoiced in such booty, and it was carefully placed in the church of St Martin by the priest and parishioners. [Col. 0295A] It has now been reverently kept there for more than seventy years. Countless miracles have been performed there upon the sick, and even to this day, as the whole neighbourhood attests, they frequently occur through the meritorious faith of those who ask.

Concerning the translation of the sacred body, which we have here just touched upon briefly, and the many healings of the sick that occurred at Parnes, William of Mureaux, a venerable monk and distinguished priest, composed an excellent work, in which he truthfully and clearly discusses the wondrous events performed at the holy bones.

King Philip of the Franks suffered from fever for two years and could not be healed by any medical art. Therefore, after two years, he came to Parnes, drank water sanctified by contact with the relics [Col. 0295B] of St Josse, and spent two nights in prayer before the holy body. There, when the pain ceased, he recovered health. Once healed, the king offered fifty Pontoise shillings to St Josse, and consented and established by an ordinance of royal authority that a fair should be held there every year on the Tuesday of Pentecost in honour of St Josse.

Moreover, through the merits of St Josse, many miracles have occurred at Parnes and occur daily. Some have been written down; more have been hidden in silence through the negligence of those who knew them or the inexperience of those who saw or experienced them. Although we hasten to recount other matters, we have willingly touched briefly upon a few things concerning you, holy Josse, [Col. 0295C] and inserted in this little work the gifts of grace bestowed upon you from heaven. According to the measure of our smallness, we devoutly exalt you.

We pray, therefore, glorious son of the king of the Bretons and companion of angels, that through the efficacy of your merits you may commend us to God and obtain for us the fellowship of the saints, with whom, beholding in his splendour the Creator of all things, we may joyfully praise him through all ages of ages. Amen.

## XX. Events in England: The Norwegians Are Defeated by the English; William, Duke of the Normans, Invades England; the Famous Battle

In the month of August, Harold, king of the Norwegians, with Tostig and an immense fleet entered the boundless sea and, [Col. 0295D] with the wind Aparctias, or Boreas, blowing, landed in England and first invaded the province of York. But when Harold the Englishman heard that the Norwegians had arrived in England, he left Hastings, Pevensey, and the other ports lying opposite Neustria across the sea—which he had shrewdly guarded with many ships and soldiers throughout that year—and hurried with a great army to meet the northern enemies, who had suddenly appeared.

Then a most fierce battle was joined by both sides. A great quantity of blood was shed on either side, and an innumerable multitude of men raging with beastly fury was slaughtered. At last victory fell to the pressing English, and Harold, king of the Norwegians, perished with Tostig and all his forces. The battlefield is also plainly visible to passers-by, [Col. 0296A] where a great heap of the bones of the dead lies even to this day and bears witness to the manifold destruction of both peoples.

Meanwhile, while the English were occupied with the battle of York and, as we have said, had abandoned the guard of the sea by God’s will, the Norman fleet, which had awaited the south wind for a month in the mouth of the Dives and neighbouring harbours, was carried by a westerly breeze to the anchorage of St Valery. There many vows were made for themselves and their friends, and prayers and countless tears were poured out. For household companions, loved ones, and relatives who were to remain at home were anxious with tears, sighs, and many cares—both fear and desire, for themselves and their friends—while fifty thousand soldiers with a host of footmen strove to cross the dreadful sea to conquer an unknown people in their own [Col. 0296B] land.

There Duke William and the whole army commended themselves to God with prayers, gifts, and vows, and carried the body of St Valery, confessor of Christ, outside the basilica to obtain a favourable wind. At last, when the prosperous wind desired by the vows of many suddenly blew by God’s will, the duke’s burning urgency immediately summoned everyone to the ships and ordered them manfully to embark. Thus the Norman army crossed the sea on the third day before the Kalends of October [29 September 1066], on the night when the Catholic Church festively celebrates the commemoration of St Michael the Archangel, and joyfully seized the seashore [Col. 0296C] without resistance. Then it occupied Pevensey and Hastings, entrusting them to selected knights so that they might serve as a refuge for the army and a defence for the ships.

The English tyrant, swollen with joy after spilling the blood of brother and enemy, returned victoriously to London after the great slaughter. But Harold—for the prosperity of this world quickly vanishes like smoke before the wind—soon lost the joy of his deadly triumph when the burden of a graver calamity threatened. Nor could he long rejoice in fratricide or remain secure, because a messenger promptly announced to him that the Normans were present. When he heard that the Normans had entered England, he again prepared himself for battle. He was very bold and valiant, strong and most handsome in body, eloquent and gracious to his supporters. [Col. 0296D]

When his mother Gytha, deeply sorrowful at the death of her son Tostig, and other faithful friends urged him not to go to war, his brother Earl Gyrth said to him:

> “Dearest brother and lord, your valour must be restrained by the moderation of prudence. You have now returned exhausted from battle with the Norwegians, and you are again hurrying to fight the Normans. Rest, I beg you. Be willing prudently to consider with yourself what you promised Duke William under oath. Beware lest you incur perjury and, for so great a crime, you fall together with the strength of our people and become the enduring disgrace thereby of our descendants. I, free from every oath, owe nothing to Count William. Therefore I am prepared to fight him boldly for my native land. But you, my brother, remain at peace wherever you may be and await the outcome of the war, lest the renowned liberty of the English fall through your destruction.” [Col. 0297A]

Having heard these words, Harold became violently angry. He rejected this advice, which seemed salutary to his friends, and provoked with insults his brother, who had given him faithful counsel. He also insolently struck with his foot his mother, who was earnestly striving to keep him with her. Then for six days he summoned peoples from every side to war, assembled an innumerable multitude of Englishmen, and hurried with them to battle against his enemies. He intended to overwhelm them by a nocturnal or sudden attack while they were less on guard; and, lest they escape by flight, he had placed seven hundred ships loaded with armed men in the sea.

When Duke William heard of his approach, he ordered all his men to arm on the morning of Saturday. He himself heard Mass and fortified body and soul with the Lord’s sacraments, humbly hanging about his neck the holy relics upon which Harold had sworn. Religious men from Normandy had also accompanied those about to fight. For two bishops, Odo of Bayeux and Geoffrey of Coutances, were there with many monks and clerics, [Col. 0297B] whose duty was to fight with prayers and counsel.

The battle began on the second day before the Ides of October [14 October], at the third hour; throughout the whole day both sides fought most fiercely, to the destruction of many thousands. The Norman duke placed foot-soldiers armed with bows and crossbows in the front line, then armoured infantry in the second line, and finally squadrons of cavalry. In their midst stood the duke himself with his strongest force, so that he might direct every quarter by voice and gesture.

On the other side, English forces from every region had gathered at the place anciently called Senlac. One part gave its service to Harold, but all to their country, which they wished to defend against foreigners. There they immediately gave up the aid of horses and all stood closely massed on foot. Turstin, son of Rollo, bore the Norman standard. The dreadful blare of trumpets sounded the signals of battle from both sides. The cheerful boldness of the Normans began the fight. [Col. 0297C]

The Norman infantry, advancing nearer, challenged the English and directed wounds and death against them with missiles. The English stoutly resisted, each according to his ability and skill. For some time both sides fought with their utmost strength. Terrified by the stubborn ferocity of the English, the Breton infantry and cavalry alike, and all the auxiliaries in the left wing, turned away; almost the whole battle line of the duke, believing that he had already been killed, gave ground. But the duke, seeing a large part of the enemy force rush out and pursue the rear of his men, confronted the fugitives and stopped them by striking or threatening them with his spear. Then, uncovering his head and taking off his helmet, he cried: “Look at me! I live, and, with God’s help, I shall conquer.”

At once, encouraged by the duke’s words, those who had given ground regained courage and, surrounding several thousand who had pursued them, destroyed them in a moment. [Col. 0298A] In the same fashion, twice more the Normans feigned flight, then suddenly wheeled their horses and cut off the pursuing English, slaughtering those enclosed on every side. Thus they deceived the English through a dangerous stratagem, killed them after separating them from one another, and, having slain many thousands, attacked the survivors more vigorously. The men of Le Mans, Franks, Bretons, and Aquitanians pressed them, and the English fell in miserable death.

Among those present at this battle were Count Eustace of Boulogne; William, son of Count Richard of Évreux; Geoffrey, son of Rotrou, count of Mortain; William, son of Osbern; Robert, a young knight, son of Roger of Beaumont; Haimeric, ruler of Thouars; Hugh, count of the stables; Walter Giffard and Ralph of Tosny; Hugh of Grandmesnil and William de Warenne; [Col. 0298B] and very many others, most renowned for excellence in arms and whose names deserve to be commended among the most warlike in the volumes of history.

Duke William surpassed them in courage and prudence. He led the army nobly, restraining flight, giving courage, sharing danger, and more often shouting for men to come than commanding them to go. In the battle three horses were pierced and fell beneath him; three times he fearlessly leapt down, and the death of his mount did not long remain unavenged. With his angry sword, scorning delay, he pierced shields, helmets, and coats of mail; he struck down some with his shield, and was the aid and salvation of many of his own men, just as, on the other hand, he was destruction to the enemy. [Col. 0298C]

From the third hour of the day the battle was fiercely joined, and in the first clash of the soldiers King Harold was killed. Then his brother Earl Leofwine died by the same fate with many thousands. Finally, as the day was now declining, the English saw that their king, the leading men of the realm, and many legions of their own had perished, while the Normans still stood defiantly and savagely assailed those who opposed them with terrible arms. They turned in flight and departed as quickly as possible, suffering varied fortunes. Some seized horses; others went on foot, some by roads and most through pathless country, trying to save themselves.

When the Normans saw the English fleeing, they pressed their pursuit all through Sunday night, to their own detriment. [Col. 0298D] For tall grass covered an old embankment, where the Normans, running at full speed with horses and arms, fell headlong and, as one suddenly fell upon another, killed one another in turn. There indeed confidence returned to the fleeing English. Seeing the advantage of the steep bank and numerous ditches, they gathered together, unexpectedly made a stand, and inflicted a great slaughter upon the Normans. There Engenulf, a townsman of Aigle, and many others fell; and, as is reported by those who were present, nearly fifteen thousand Normans perished.

Thus almighty God, on the day before the Ides of October [14 October], punished innumerable sinners of both hosts in different ways. For, while the Normans’ cruelty raged intolerably, he punished many thousands of Englishmen on Saturday—men who long before had unjustly killed innocent Alfred with his followers on foot, and who, on the preceding Saturday, had mercilessly slaughtered King Harold of Norway, Earl Tostig, and many others. The same judge also avenged the English on Sunday night and hurled the raging Normans into a blind pit. For, contrary to the commandment of the Law, they had immoderately coveted another’s property; and their feet, as the Psalmist says, were swift to shed blood. Therefore they encountered ruin and misery in their ways (Psalm 13:3). [Col. 0299A]

Duke William, seeing the English companies unexpectedly gathered together, did not halt. He called back with a manly voice Count Eustace, who had turned away with fifty knights and wished to sound the signal for retreat, lest he depart. Eustace, however, quietly urged retreat into the duke’s ear and foretold that, if he continued, death was close at hand. While these words were being exchanged, Eustace was struck between the shoulders by a resounding blow, whose severity was immediately shown by blood from his mouth and nostrils; almost dying, he escaped with the help of his companions.

When victory had been completed, the duke returned to the battlefield. There he looked upon the pitiable slaughter, a sight not without compassion. The flower of English nobility and youth, stained with blood, covered the ground far and wide. Harold was recognized by certain marks, not by his face, and was carried to the duke’s camp. By order of William, surnamed Malet, he was entrusted for burial near the seashore which he had long guarded with arms. [Col. 0299C]

## XXI. The Result of the Battle: William Subdues the Country; He Is Crowned King of the English

As fortune, ever changing, supplies mortals on earth with circumstances exceedingly harsh and unforeseen, some rise from the dust to the heights of great power, while others, suddenly cast down from the highest summit, lament in immense sorrow. Thus Gytha, widow of Earl Godwin, once rejoicing in wealth and power, is now overwhelmed with excessive grief because she has been violently afflicted by grievous misfortunes.

For she bore seven sons to her husband: Sweyn, Tostig, Harold, Gyrth, Ælfgar, Leofwine, and Wulfnoth. All these were earls and flourished in great bodily beauty and worldly merit; but separately they experienced diverse and terrible fates. Ælfgar and Wulfnoth, loving God, lived piously and lawfully; the former died at Reims as a pilgrim and monk, in true confession, and the latter died honourably at Salisbury. [Col. 0299D] But the other five died in arms, in different places and while pursuing diverse aims.

The sorrowful mother offered Duke William gold equal in weight to Harold’s body, but the great-hearted victor refused such a bargain, considering it unworthy that Harold should be buried at his mother’s pleasure when, because of his excessive greed, countless men remained unburied. He ordered great care to be given to the burial of his own men, and granted all Englishmen who wished it free permission to bury whomsoever they chose. After burying his own men as was then fitting, he went to Romney and, having overcome those within, avenged the destruction of his men, whom that savage people, after they had been driven there by error, had attacked in battle and routed, with very great loss on both sides. [Col. 0300A]

Then the duke hastened to Dover, where a great multitude had assembled, relying on the fortress as impregnable, as it seemed to them, because that castle stands on a very steep cliff adjoining the sea. But while the garrison feared the besieging duke and were preparing a suppliant surrender, Norman men-at-arms, greedy for plunder, set fire to it; and, as the devouring flame spread lightly through the air, most buildings were caught and burned. The duke, however, pitied the loss of those who wished to submit themselves to him [Col. 0300B], gave payment for rebuilding their houses, and compensated their other losses. Having received the castle, he fortified it wherever its defences were deficient, for eight days.

Many soldiers there, eating fresh meat and drinking water, died of diarrhoea; and very many were weakened for the rest of their lives. Leaving a garrison there, as well as those weakened by dysentery, the duke set out to complete the subjugation of those whom he had defeated. The people of Canterbury, not far from Dover, came out voluntarily to meet him, swore loyalty, and gave hostages.

After Harold had been slain, Stigand, archbishop of Canterbury, and the distinguished earls Edwin and Morcar, with other leading Englishmen who had not taken part in the battle of Senlac, established as king Edgar the Ætheling, son of Edward, king of the Huns, son of Edmund Ironside—that is, “Iron-Side” [Col. 0300C]—and declared that, with him, they would fight bravely against foreign enemies for their country and people. But Duke William, when he heard of their numerous assembly, approached with a strong force and encamped not far from London, sending five hundred horsemen ahead. They compelled the force which had marched out of the city against them to retreat within the walls; and, after making great slaughter among their sons and friends, they inflicted immense grief upon the citizens. They also added fire to the slaughter in the city, burning every building on this side of the river. The duke crossed the river Thames and came to the town of Guarengefort.

There Archbishop Stigand and other noble Englishmen [Col. 0300D] arrived. Setting Edgar aside, they made peace with William and accepted him as their lord. He received them kindly, and they recovered their former ranks and honours. Nevertheless, the Londoners, adopting prudent counsel, submitted themselves to the duke’s obedience and brought the hostages he had commanded, both those he specified and in the number he specified. Edgar Ætheling, whom the English had appointed king, distrusting his ability to resist, humbly yielded himself and the kingdom to William. Since the boy was gentle and sincere, and a kinsman of King Edward the Great—for he was the son of Edward’s nephew—William embraced him warmly and honoured him throughout his life as one of his own sons.

By God’s ordering, within the space of three months all England [Col. 0301A] was pacified. All the bishops and magnates of the kingdom made an agreement with William and urged him to receive the royal crown, as the custom of English rule required. The Normans pressed for this most urgently, since they had undergone the immense dangers of sea and battle so that their lord might obtain the royal insignia. The native inhabitants too, subdued by divine direction, desired it, since hitherto they had been accustomed to serve only a crowned king.

At that time Aldred was metropolitan of York. A great lover of justice, mature in years, wise, good, and eloquent, he shone in many virtues and continually desired to approach the King of kings in the footsteps of the Fathers. Stigand of Canterbury, however, was excessively occupied with worldly cares and affairs [Col. 0301B], and had been interdicted by Pope Alexander on account of certain offences.

Finally, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord [read: 1066], in the fifth indiction, on Christmas Day, the English assembled in London to ordain a king. Norman companies, armed and mounted, were posted around the monastery as a guard, lest any treachery or sedition arise. Therefore Archbishop Aldred, in the basilica of St Peter, chief of the apostles, called Westminster, where King Edward lies honourably buried, consecrated Duke William of the Normans as king of the English in the presence of the bishops, abbots, and magnates of the whole kingdom of Albion, and placed the royal crown upon his head.

[Col. 0301C] Meanwhile, at Satan’s instigation—he who is opposed to every good—a troublesome occurrence for both peoples, and a portent of future calamity, suddenly arose. For while Bishop Aldred addressed the English and Geoffrey of Coutances the Normans, asking whether they consented that William should reign over them, and all declared their joyful assent with one voice, though not in one language, the armed soldiers outside, stationed for the protection of their people, heard at once the shouting of the rejoicing congregation in the church and the noise of an unfamiliar language. Taking it for something sinister, they rashly set the buildings on fire. As the blaze hurried through the houses, the people rejoicing in the church were thrown into confusion, and the multitude of men [Col. 0301D] and women of every rank and condition, pressed by the disaster, quickly left the basilica.

Only the bishops and a few clergy with the monks, exceedingly terrified, remained standing before the altar. They barely completed the rite of consecration over the king, who was trembling violently. Almost all the others ran to the raging fire: some to resist the force of the blaze manfully, and more to seize plunder for themselves amid such confusion. The English, judging this unexpected affair to be a plot, were greatly enraged; afterwards they always regarded the Normans with suspicion and, judging them unfaithful to themselves, longed for a time of vengeance upon them.

XV. Having thus received the sovereignty, King William governed it vigorously and effectively in adversity and prosperity [Col. 0302A], and ruled it commendably for twenty years, eight months, and sixteen days. William of Poitiers, archdeacon of Lisieux, treated copiously of his excellence, exceptional character, favourable fortunes, vigorous and admirable deeds, and produced a book remarkable for polished style and profound thought. He was for a long time chaplain to the said king, and diligently sought to explain fully and without doubt, in a lengthy and copious narrative, what he had himself seen and events in which he had participated, although misfortunes prevented him from carrying his book through to the king’s end. Bishop Guy of Amiens also composed a poem in metre, in which, imitating Virgil and Statius as poets of heroic deeds, he described the battle of Senlac, censuring and condemning Harold [Col. 0302B], but praising and magnifying William.

John of Worcester, a monk from childhood, English by birth and venerable in character and learning, set forth honourably, in the material which he added to the Chronicles of Marianus Scotus, accounts of King William and of events occurring under him and under his sons William Rufus and Henry down to the present day. Marianus had been a monk in the monastery of St Alban the martyr near Mainz. There, following Eusebius of Caesarea, Jerome, and other historians according to his ability, he devoted himself kindly to study and charitably offered to the children of the Church—who could not themselves investigate such matters—the sweet fruit of long study and of the great labours he had borne in far-off pilgrimage.

[Col. 0302C] After diligently examining ancient and modern manuscripts, he composed a chronography in which, beginning with the creation of the world, when God formed Adam from the clay of the earth, and proceeding through all the books of the Old and New Testaments and through Roman and Greek histories, he gathered together the best material. Having set out the years by the reigns of kings and terms of consuls, he commendably arranged an annalistic history down to the day of his death. Continuing him, John wove together the events of nearly a hundred years and, by order of the venerable Bishop and monk Wulfstan, inserted them into the aforementioned Chronicles. In these he usefully and concisely disclosed many matters worthy of narration concerning the Romans, Franks, Germans, and other peoples known to him.

Indeed, these Chronicles [Col. 0302D] contain all the judges, kings, and high priests of the Hebrews from Moses to the destruction of Jerusalem, when, under Titus and Vespasian, the Jewish kingdom was justly destroyed for the murder of the Saviour and his martyrs. There are named all Roman consuls and dictators, emperors and pontiffs; likewise all the kings who ruled the kingdom of England from the time when Hengist and Horsa served Vortigern, king of Britain, to the scandal of the Welsh. The bishops who held ecclesiastical government in England are likewise recorded in these chronicles, from the time when Pope Gregory sent Augustine, Mellitus, and other preachers of God’s word into England. Through them God brought King Æthelberht of Kent, King Edwin of Northumbria [Col. 0303A], and other princes of that people to faith in the truth. From these little works Engelbert, monk of Gembloux, excerpted certain notable passages; he omitted much that had been written in the same Chronicles concerning the islands of the Ocean, but nevertheless added much concerning the Goths, Huns, Persians, and other barbarian peoples.

I have included these matters freely in this book so that eager readers may seek out these manuscripts for themselves, since they bear a great fruit of wisdom and can scarcely be found. For they have been produced by modern writers and have not yet been widely distributed throughout the world. I saw one of them at Worcester in England and the other at Cambrai in Lotharingia. There the prudent Fulbert, abbot of the monastery of the Holy Sepulchre, kindly showed it to me [Col. 0304A]. That monastery was carefully built in the northern part of Cambrai at the expense of Liébert, bishop of the same city, where that bishop deserved honourable burial.

> [Note: [Col. 0303] Liébert, bishop of Cambrai, founded the monastery of the Holy Sepulchre in the year 1064.]

Now, weary and longing for rest, I intend here to end the first little book of the ecclesiastical history which I have drawn forth with a truthful pen concerning contemporary and neighbouring princes and teachers.

In what follows I shall discuss King William more fully, and shall report, without flattery, the unhappy changes undergone by English and Normans, seeking no honour or reward from victors or vanquished.

## SUMMARY OF BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0303]

I. Deeds of King William in England. II. King William returns to Normandy. Archbishops of Rouen. III. The English, oppressed by the Normans, plan rebellions. IV. King William returns to England. Rebellion of the city of Exeter. V. Other rebellions in England against the Normans. VI. Many Norman soldiers leave England and return to Normandy. Norman tyranny. Rebellions of the English. VII. The sons of King Harold, Danes, and Saxons struggle unsuccessfully against the Normans. VIII. William defeats his enemies. The royal crown is sent to him by the pope. IX. The Council of Windsor. King William’s piety and praiseworthy conduct. On the origins of the monastic order in England. X. The care of the Roman pontiffs in instructing and refining the English. Relaxation of morals. King William restores ecclesiastical discipline. Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury. XI. Peace and concord are gradually established between English and Normans. The unhappy fate of Earl Morcar. On William of Poitiers, the writer. XII. King William divides English lands among the Normans. Norman pride and luxury. XIII. Norman churchmen also seek riches. The praiseworthy abstinence of the monk Guitmund. XIV. Disputes among the heirs of the county of Flanders. Queen Matilda governs Normandy. XV. The Council of Rouen. XVI. Abbots of Norman monasteries under King William. XVII. Pope Alexander II. Pope Gregory VII. On the bishopric of Le Mans. XVIII. Herbert, count of the people of Le Mans. Disturbances in Maine. XIX. The rebellion against King William of Earls Roger of Hereford and Ralph of Norwich. The punishment of Count Waltheof. XX. Life of the blessed hermit Guthlac. XXI. Death of the blessed hermit Guthlac. Miracles and prodigies at the saint’s tomb. Building of Crowland monastery. XXII. History of Crowland monastery. XXIII. Miracles at the tomb of Earl Waltheof. XXIV. King William attempts unsuccessfully to subdue the Bretons. Ainard, first abbot of St Peter of the Dive. His successor Fulk. XXV. Disputes among the sons of King William.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0303]

## I. Deeds of King William in England

[Col. 0303B]

In the time of Pope Alexander II

> [Note: [Col. 0303B] Alexander: 30 September 1061–21 April 1073.]

very many kingdoms throughout the world were shaken by calamities, and repeated eruptions of peoples raged to their own destruction. The inhabitants of the western regions felt these things and suffered very grievous losses. For after the deaths of the excellent kings Henry [Col. 0304B], king of the Franks, and Edward of the English, the Franks and English long mourned their funerals, because after them they scarcely obtained rulers comparable to them in virtue and in the sweetness of their character. When the fathers of their countries had been removed, tyrants succeeded, abusing the rein of royal power. England then collapsed, polluted by Harold’s cruelty and perjury; bereft of its rightful heirs [Col. 0305A], it lay subject to foreign plunderers, favouring William the conqueror. Thus it furnished pious historians with a mournful theme for recording its ruin.

Eloquent scholars who spent longer at King William’s court had abundant material for making several books: they knew his deeds, his various and famous successes, and his intimate and profound counsels, and, sharing in his wealth, were raised far above their birth. The churches which were made under him or by him for God’s praise in Neustria or England bear praiseworthy witness to his devotion and generosity in divine worship and offer to posterity an example of good zeal worthy of imitation. He also devoutly built many monasteries; he greatly improved those founded by himself or by others; enriched them, rejoicing in treasures of many kinds [Col. 0305B]; and protected them by his patronage against every adversary. These things are openly attested by the monks of the two monasteries at Caen, monks in one and nuns in the other. While still duke, he had built these two monasteries in favour of the eternal King; in one he chose burial for himself, and in the other for his wife.

After the battle had been concluded, after he had bravely subdued his enemies and received the royal crown at London, he built the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Senlac, where the battle had taken place. As befitted royal munificence, he endowed it with many riches and estates. There he appointed as abbot Goisbert, a religious monk of Marmoutier; under his direction the monastic order and regular discipline prospered fittingly. For Marmoutier was founded by the most holy Martin, archbishop of Tours, and there, by God’s inspiration, the religious life of good men grew and multiplied. In our time the abbots Albert and Bartholomew, Bernard and Hilgot, and William of Nantes presided over this monastery; through holiness and integrity they benefited many, and, famous far and wide, shone usefully upon neighbours and strangers alike. After Goisbert’s death Henry, prior of Canterbury, assumed the office of abbot and held the monastery of Battle honourably. At his death Ralph, prior of Rochester and monk of Caen, succeeded [Col. 0305C]. By his zeal for holiness and saving teaching he strove to benefit himself and many gathered with him; and even in old age he continued fervently in spiritual pursuits. At last, in the twenty-fifth year of King Henry of the English, the religious old man passed happily from the world to God.

After his coronation, King William arranged many matters at London wisely, justly, and mercifully: some for the advantage or dignity of the city itself; others for the benefit of the whole people; and some to provide for the churches of the land. Whatever laws he enacted, he established on the best grounds. No one ever asked him in vain for a just judgment. He condemned no one whom it would not have been unjust to condemn. He also imposed commands upon his leading men with fitting dignity and gravity, and diligently urged justice upon them. They must keep always before their eyes the eternal King, by whose aid they had conquered; the conquered, equal to the conquerors by profession of Christianity, ought not to be oppressed excessively, lest those whom they had justly subdued should be driven by injuries into rebellion. He prohibited seditions, restraining killing and every kind of plunder; he restrained the peoples by arms and arms by laws. He imposed a moderate rate upon taxes and all payments due to the royal treasury, so that it would not be burdensome. He allowed no place within his territories for robbery, invasions, or crimes. He commanded that harbours and every road should be open to merchants and that no injury should be done to them. Thus wholly upright were the beginnings of his reign; the growth of his good qualities shone clearly for the benefit of his subjects, and perseverance in good deeds and a praiseworthy end confirmed them by manifest indications.

[Col. 0306B] Leaving London, the king remained for several days at the nearby place of Barking, while certain fortifications in the city were being completed against the fickleness of its great and fierce populace. Edwin and Morcar, sons of Earl Ælfgar, almost the greatest of all Englishmen in lineage and power, came to the king, asked pardon if in any matter they had opposed him, and entrusted themselves and all that they possessed to his mercy. Then came Earl Copsi, exceptional in courage and worth, and Turchil of Limis; Siward and Aldred, sons of Æthelgar and great-grandsons of King Edward; also Eadric surnamed *Guilda*, that is, “the Wild,” nephew of the pernicious duke Eadric surnamed *Streone*, that is, “the Acquirer”; with many other nobles, wealthy in possessions. They made peace with William, gave oaths, and all recovered their possessions with honour. The king then proceeded through different parts of the kingdom and everywhere arranged what was beneficial for himself and for the inhabitants of the land. He installed vigorous Frenchmen as guards in the castles and distributed wealthy benefices, for which they would willingly endure labours and dangers.

Within the walls of Winchester, a noble city rich in resources, strong in fortification, and adjoining the sea, he built a powerful citadel. There he left William, son of Osbern, foremost in his army, appointing him to govern the whole kingdom northward in his stead. He entrusted Dover and all Kent to his brother, who was eminent for great liberality and worldly ability. To these two he committed the government of England and left with them [Col. 0306D] Hugh of Grandmesnil, Hugh of Montfort, William of Warenne, and other most resolute warriors. Some of them governed those subject to them commendably; others, lacking moderation, oppressed their men without restraint.

## II. King William Returns to Normandy. Archbishops of Rouen

The king, having entrusted the care of the kingdom, withdrew to Pevensey, where a large force of English cavalry gathered around him. There, with a generous hand, pay was given to soldiers returning to their homeland.

The ships having been launched, in March King William was carried prosperously to his native land. With him he honourably brought Stigand the archbishop, Edgar Ætheling, kinsman of King Edward [Col. 0307A], and the three most illustrious earls, Edwin, Morcar, and Waltheof; also Ægelnoth, the Kentish magnate, and many others of lofty nobility and remarkable beauty. He used kindly cunning, so that, while these leaders were with him, nothing might be altered in his absence, and the whole people, stripped of its chiefs, might be less able to rebel. Finally, he displayed to them his riches and honours in Normandy so that he might keep them with him in his power as hostages, since their authority or safety was of the highest importance to their kinsmen and compatriots.

At King William’s arrival in great worldly glory, all Normandy rejoiced exceedingly. The days were wintry and Lenten; but in bishoprics and monasteries where the new king came, Easter festivals were begun [Col. 0307B]. Nothing customary in the effort to offer such honour was omitted. Moreover, whatever novel thing could be devised was added. He immediately repaid this devotion with manifold gifts, granting cloths, pounds of gold, and other great offerings to altars and servants of Christ. Churches which he did not visit in person he gladdened by sending gifts.

He celebrated Easter at the monastery of the Holy Trinity of Fécamp, where a great gathering of bishops, abbots, and noblemen assembled. Then Count Ralph, stepfather of Philip, king of the Franks, and much of the French nobility were present. They curiously observed the long-haired youths of British England and marvelled at the king’s and royal attendants’ garments woven and embroidered with gold. They praised vessels of gold or silver and buffalo horns adorned at both ends with yellow metal. In short, the French took note of many such things befitting royal magnificence, so that on returning home they might report them because of their novelty.

When the Easter solemnity had been celebrated, the king ordered the basilica of St Mary above the Dive to be dedicated. He himself attended reverently with a great company of magnates and commoners on the Kalends of May [1 May 1067], and, through the voice of a herald, promulgated enactments highly beneficial to the whole people. Then, on the Kalends of July [1 July], he ordered the church of St Mary at Jumièges to be dedicated and attended the sacred rite reverently. He richly endowed both [Col. 0307D] from the estates of his own demesne and devoutly exalted them by his presence while the sacred rite was celebrated. Maurilius, archbishop of Rouen, with his suffragan bishops, performed this dedication humbly and devoutly. Soon afterwards, in the twelfth year of his episcopate, he took to his bed. Having fulfilled everything appropriate to a religious servant of God, he passed on the fifth day before the Ides of August [9 August] to God whom he had long served. His body was carried into the episcopal church, which he himself had dedicated to St Mary, Mother of God, five years earlier, in the first indiction, and was honourably buried before the crucifix. His epitaph, composed by Richard, son of Herluin, canon of that church, was inscribed over him upon copper plates in gold as follows:

> Citizens of humankind, do not refuse a tear  
> To your bishop, Maurice the monk.  
> Rheims gave him birth; Liège, nurse of learning,  
> Gave him drink from philosophy’s threefold spring.  
> For you he brought this church, begun, to completion;  
> With great rejoicing he celebrated its dedication.  
> While Christ’s sober people keep vigil, O Lawrence,  
> He passes on and celebrates the laurel-crowned feast in heaven.

After the death of its bishop, the Church of Rouen elected Lanfranc, abbot of Caen, as its prelate; and King William, with his magnates and all the people, most willingly consented. But the man devoted to God and intent upon humility refused the burden of such primacy [Col. 0308B], striving with all his power to place before himself at this height John, bishop of Avranches. In order that this union might be accomplished canonically, he went to Rome, obtained from Pope Alexander permission for the aforesaid appointment, and carried away with permission the sacred pallium, in which both he and all Normandy could take pride.

Accordingly John was transferred from the see of Avranches, which he had governed for seven years and three months, and became metropolitan of Rouen. He burned intensely with the ardour of virtues in word and deed, and, like Phinehas, raged with excessive zeal against vices. In secular dignity he was conspicuous by the distinction of great nobility. For he was the son of Ralph, count of Bayeux, who was the half-brother of Richard the Elder, duke of Normandy. For ten years, therefore, he governed the metropolitan see vigorously and diligently. He laboured greatly to remove mistresses from unchaste priests; when, in synod, he forbade them under anathema to keep concubines, he was struck with stones and fled. Fleeing from the church, he cried loudly: “O God, the nations have come into your inheritance” (Psalm LXXI, 1).

In his place Michael, an Italian by birth, trained in literary learning and venerable for his religious zeal, was raised by lawful election to the summit of the bishopric of Avranches. He flourished as a praiseworthy shepherd for more than twenty years and died a blessed old man in the time of Duke Robert. On his death Turgis succeeded and held the bishopric for almost thirty years [Col. 0308D].

> [Note: [Col. 0307] In Le Prévost’s judgment, this passage was written in the year 1123.]

## III. The English Are Oppressed by the Normans and Plan Rebellions

Meanwhile the English were oppressed by Norman arrogance and grievously wronged by proud governors who despised the king’s warnings. Lesser officials who guarded the fortresses burdened native nobles and commoners with unjust exactions and many insults. Bishop Odo and William, son of Osbern, swelled with excessive haughtiness; they disdained to hear the English complaints reasonably or to support them with the balance of justice. They protected by force their men-at-arms who committed excessive plunder and incestuous ravishments [Col. 0309A], and raged still more against those who, afflicted by grievous insults, made complaints.

Having lost their liberty, the English groaned deeply and considered among themselves how they might cast off the intolerable yoke, hitherto unfamiliar to them. They therefore sent to Sweyn, king of the Danes, asking him to reclaim the kingdom of England, which Sweyn and Cnut, his grandfathers, had won by arms. Some voluntarily fled into exile, so that, as exiles, they might either be free from Norman power or return, enriched with foreign resources, to renew the contest against them. Others, flourishing in the flower of handsome youth, travelled to distant lands and boldly offered themselves for service under Alexius, emperor of Constantinople [Col. 0309B]. He was very wise and marvellously generous. Against him Robert Guiscard, duke of Apulia, had taken up arms with all his men in support of Michael, whom the Danes had driven from the imperial throne through the hostility of senatorial power.

The English exiles were therefore received favourably by the Greeks and set against the Norman legions, which bitterly opposed the Pelasgians. Emperor Alexius began to build beyond Byzantium for the English a city called Chevetot; but, because the Normans harassed them excessively, he brought them back to the imperial city and entrusted to them the principal palace with the royal treasures. For this reason the English Saxons sought Ionia; they and their heirs faithfully served the sacred empire and, among the Thracians, have remained to this day in great honour, dear to the emperor, senate, and people.

Provoked to rebellion by the Normans’ many forms of oppression, the English sent envoys to Boulogne. They instructed Count Eustace to hasten with a fleet carefully equipped with soldiers and arms to take Dover. Formerly they had had fierce enmities with him; but now, because hostilities had arisen between him and the king, and because experience had shown him skilled and fortunate in war, they made peace with him and tried to deliver the fortress of Dover to him against the king. Eustace, taking on board a Kentish guide, embarked upon his ready fleet and, at the dead of night, hurried across with his men [Col. 0309D] to seize the town by surprise. He took many soldiers with him but left behind all but very few horses. The entire neighbourhood was under arms, especially the Kentish force, which had endeavoured with all its strength to support Eustace.

The bishop of Bayeux and Hugh of Montfort, the foremost guardians of the fortress, had gone beyond the river Thames and had taken the greater part of the soldiers with them. A larger number of enemies would have arrived from farther districts if the siege had lasted two days. But when the enemy vigorously attempted to assault the town, its guards proved tireless in defence and resisted with the greatest energy wherever the place could be attacked. For several hours of the day the battle was fought most fiercely on both sides. But Eustace lost confidence and feared a sortie by the defenders, by which he might be driven off more shamefully [Col. 0310A]; he therefore ordered the signal for retreat to the ships to be sounded. Then the townsmen at once opened the gates and, eagerly but cautiously pursuing, cut down the rearmost men.

The fugitives believed that the bishop of Bayeux had suddenly arrived with a great force. In that terror, like madmen, they hurled themselves down the precipice of a trackless cliff and perished by such a shortcut more disgracefully than by men’s swords. In that flight many died in different ways. Most, having cast away their arms, were killed by sharp stones. Some, falling together, killed themselves and their companions with their own weapons. Many, mortally wounded or dashed to pieces, rolled down alive into the sea. Many more, breathlessly rushing to the ships, panicked in excessive desire for safety and sank the vessels by their own multitude, perishing suddenly by drowning [Col. 0310B]. Norman horsemen captured or killed as many as they could pursue. Eustace himself was saved by his horse’s speed, knowledge of the path, and a readier ship. His most noble nephew was captured there. The English escaped by many byways, because the few defenders could not pursue many fugitives in different directions.

Not long afterwards Count Eustace was reconciled with King William and thereafter enjoyed his friendship for a long time. For this count was of very great nobility, being descended from Charlemagne, the most vigorous king of the Franks. He was also of great power, as the eminent lord of three counties: Boulogne, Guînes, and Thérouanne. He had as wife the high-born and devout Ida, sister of Godfrey, duke of Lotharingia. She bore him three sons—Godfrey, Baldwin, and Eustace—and a daughter, who married Henry IV, emperor of the Germans.

While very many Englishmen planned rebellion because of their lost former liberty, which they longed earnestly to recover, many of the same people kept faith with God and honoured the king established by him, according to the command of the Apostle: “Fear God; honour the king” (1 Peter 2:17). Earl Copsi, foremost among the English in lineage and power, and still more exceptional for the singular quality of a prudent and wholly honourable mind, faithfully [Col. 0310D] supported King William and strongly approved his cause. But his retainers dissented from him because they were the worst advocates and accomplices of factions. They assailed him in various ways, attacking him with prayers, threats, and entreaties that he should abandon the foreigners and comply with the will of good men of his own nation and kinship. But because a mind firmly fixed upon the course of good could not be moved from rectitude, he was killed by treachery, when fellow-countrymen had been stirred up against him, for the integrity of his loyalty. Thus this excellent man demonstrated by his fate that the majesty of one’s lord must always be dear to faithful subjects.

Then Aldred, first of York, and certain other bishops worked for the advantage of the king, because, knowing the admonition of the wise man, they obeyed justice: “Fear God, my son, and the king” (Proverbs 24:21). At that time also some very wise townsmen, certain freeborn soldiers whose names and wealth had influence, and many common people strongly rose against their own countrymen on behalf of the Normans.

Meanwhile King William, while remaining in Normandy, looked far ahead for its tranquillity with the greatest concern. With the counsel of wise men, he established just laws and right judgments equally for rich and poor, and appointed excellent judges and governors throughout the provinces of Neustria. He freed holy monasteries and lands granted to them from unjust exactions through royal privileges and protections. He proclaimed peace throughout his whole land, by the voice of a herald, to strangers and natives alike [Col. 0311B], and sternly decreed severe and just punishments against thieves, rebels, and despisers of their country’s peace.

Meanwhile varied rumours came flying from across the sea. Mingling troubles with welcome news, they disturbed the king and announced that, through English ill will aided by the efforts of Danes and other barbarian peoples, a great disaster would befall the Normans. The king therefore entrusted the rule of Neustria to his wife Matilda and to his young son Robert, leaving with them devout bishops and vigorous magnates to defend the region. Then, on the sixth night of December, he came to the mouth of the river Dieppe beyond the town of Arques. In the first watch of the cold night he gave his sails to the south wind, and in the morning, with a most favourable voyage, reached the harbour of the opposite shore called Vincenesium [Col. 0311C]. Already the wintry wind had made the sea extremely violent, but the Church of God was celebrating the feast of St Nicholas, bishop of Myra, and was faithfully praying in Normandy for its devout prince. Thus divine omnipotence, which everywhere and always prospers whom it wills, guided the benevolent king with joy through winter storms to the harbour of safety.

On this crossing the king brought with him Roger of Montgomery, whom, when he had set out for the overseas war, he had left as guardian of Normandy with his own wife. To Roger he first gave Chichester and Arundel, and after some time the county of Shrewsbury.

## IV. King William Returns to England. The Rebellion of the City of Exeter

[Col. 0311D]

They came out to meet the arrival of the king of England and exalted him with both monastic honours and secular services. He celebrated Christmas Sunday in London, and there shrewdly won the favour of the English bishops and magnates. He soothed everyone with courteous affection, graciously invited them to kisses, and showed affability to all; he kindly granted whatever they requested and readily listened when they brought messages or made suggestions. Men who have defected are sometimes won back by such artifice. With equal diligence and skill he now instructed the French, now secretly warned the English always and everywhere to be ready against every deceit and snare of individuals. All the cities and regions [Col. 0312A] which he had visited or occupied with garrisons obeyed his command. But around the borders of the kingdom, toward the west or the northern quarter, unbridled fierceness still proudly prevailed; and under King Edward and other earlier kings it had formerly disdained to serve the king of England except on its own terms.

Exeter was the first to strive to assert its independence; but when the bravest warriors attacked it vigorously, it was reduced to subjection. This city is wealthy and ancient, situated on level ground and laboriously fortified, about two miles distant from the seacoast, which is reached by a very short passage from Ireland or Lesser Britain. Its citizens held it in a frenzy: a numerous people, intensely hostile to men of French race, both the young men and the elders. They eagerly [Col. 0312B] summoned allies from neighbouring districts, retained visiting merchants fit for war, and added or repaired battlements and towers and whatever else they judged necessary in their defences. They also urged other towns by embassies to join the same conspiracy, and prepared themselves with all their strength against the foreign-born king, with whom they had previously had no dealings in any matter. When the king learned these facts more certainly, he ordered the leading men of the city to swear him fidelity. But they sent back this reply, saying: “We shall neither swear an oath to the king nor admit him into the city; but we shall pay him tribute according to the former custom.” The king in turn sent them this reply: “It is not my custom to hold subjects on these terms.” Then he approached their borders with an army, and for the first time in that expedition brought out the English.

As soon as the leading men learned that the king was approaching with an army, they went out to meet him; they asked for peace, said that the gates would be opened to him, promised to do whatever was commanded, and immediately produced as many hostages as the king required. Having returned to their fellow citizens, who were exceedingly afraid of punishment for their offence, they nevertheless contrived the hostile measures which they had begun and encouraged one another for many reasons to undertake a siege. On hearing this, the king, who was encamped four miles from the city, was filled with anger and astonishment.

Accordingly, the king first hurried forward with five hundred horsemen, in order to inspect the place and its walls and discover what the enemy were doing. The gates were barred, and dense crowds stood upon the fortifications and all around [Col. 0312D] the circuit of the wall. Finally, at the king’s command, the army was moved against the city, and one of the hostages was blinded near the gate. The obstinacy of the raging people was bent by no fear or pity for any of the remaining hostages; rather, it was sharpened to defend themselves and their homes with utter determination. But the king strongly enclosed the city in siege, assaulted it with military ferocity, and for many days laboured strenuously to attack the citizens from above and undermine the wall from below. At last the townsmen, compelled by the heavy pressure of the enemy, adopted a useful course and resorted to supplication, and the fairest youth, the elders, and clergy carrying sacred books and such ornaments went out to the king. The restrained prince immediately spared those humbly prostrate, mercifully forgave the people who confessed their offences, as though he did not know that they had stubbornly resisted him and cruelly and insultingly mocked the soldiers whom he had sent from Normandy and whom a storm had driven into their harbour.

The people of Exeter rejoiced and gave thanks to God that, after such anger and terrible threats, they had made peace, better than they had hoped, with the foreign-born king. The king, however, abstained from interfering with their property and secured the city gates with a strong and trustworthy guard, lest common soldiers should suddenly enter and violently plunder the citizens’ wealth. He selected a site within the walls for building a castle, and left there Baldwin of Meules, son of Count Gilbert, and other distinguished soldiers to complete the necessary work and remain as a garrison. He then advanced farther into Cornwall. Having settled everywhere the disturbances he encountered, he dismissed the army and returned to Winchester to spend the Easter festival there.

### V. Other rebellions in England against the Normans

In the year 1068 from the Incarnation of the Lord, King William sent honourable envoys into Normandy and ordered his wife Matilda to come to him. She at once gladly obeyed her husband’s command and crossed the sea with a great company of men and noblewomen. Among the clergy who ministered to her in divine matters, the renowned Guy, bishop of Amiens, stood out; he had already described in verse the contest of Harold and William. Ealdred, metropolitan of York, who had anointed her husband, anointed Matilda to share in royal honour [Col. 0313C] on the day of Pentecost in the second year of the reign of the aforesaid king. Adorned with the royal diadem, the queen bore a son named Henry before the year had ended, and he made him heir to all his land in England. When he reached his teachable years, he learned the knowledge of letters; after the death of both parents, he vigorously undertook the struggles of warfare. At length, illustrious with titles earned by manifold excellence, he held his father’s principality for many years.

In the same year the distinguished young men Edwin and Morcar, sons of Earl Ælfgar, rebelled, and many others rose fiercely with them; their uprising violently disturbed the kingdom of Albion. For when Earl Edwin had made peace with King William, and had submitted to him his brother and nearly a third part of England, the king had promised that he would give him his daughter in marriage; but afterwards, through the deceitful counsel of the Normans, he refused the noble young man the maiden he desired and had long awaited. Therefore, angered, Edwin was driven into rebellion with his brother, and a great part of the English and Welsh followed him. The aforesaid brothers were ardently devoted to the worship of God and to reverence for good men. They possessed great beauty, noble and extensive kinship, widely effective power, and extraordinary popular affection. Clerics and monks offered frequent prayer for them, and crowds of the poor made daily supplication.

Earl Ælfgar founded the monastery of Coventry [Col. 0314A] and generously enriched it with great revenues for the maintenance of the monks living there. The devout Countess Godiva, moreover, bestowed all her treasure on the same church; summoning goldsmiths, she devotedly distributed all that she possessed in gold and silver for making sacred textiles, crosses, images of saints, and other marvellous ornaments of the church. Parents devoted to God and worthy of religious praise produced a distinguished offspring worthy of much commendation: Edwin, Morcar, and one daughter named Aldith, who first married Gruffydd, king of the Welsh, and after his death was joined in marriage to Harold, king of the English.

At the time of the Norman calamity, which crushed the English without restraint under excessive oppressions, Bleddyn, king of the Welsh, came to the aid of his uncles [Col. 0314B] and brought with him a multitude of Britons. When many English and Welsh nobles had assembled together, a general complaint arose concerning the injuries and oppressions by which the English were intolerably afflicted by the Normans and their associates. By embassies they secretly and openly incited against the enemy all whom they could throughout the borders of Albion. By the agreement of all, an audacious conspiracy arose to recover their former liberty, together with a determined sworn league against the Normans. A violent disturbance broke out in the regions beyond the Humber. The rebels held forests, marshes, estuaries, and several towns as fortified positions. The city of York raged most fiercely, and the holiness of its bishop was unable to calm it. [Col. 0314C] Many lived in tents; they disdained to rest in houses lest they become soft, and thus some of them were called “woodland men” by the Normans.

The king therefore more carefully surveyed the remote parts of the kingdom and fortified suitable places against enemy raids. For very few fortifications, which the French call *castella*, had existed in the English provinces; consequently the English, although warlike and courageous, had proved weaker in resisting enemies. The king accordingly founded a castle at Warwick and entrusted it to Henry, son of Roger of Beaumont, for defence. Then Edwin and Morcar, considering the doubtful hazard of battle with their men, sought the king’s favour and obtained it, outwardly at least. Afterwards [Col. 0314D] the king built Nottingham Castle and entrusted it to William Peverel.

When the people of York heard this, fearing violence if they delayed their submission, they gave the king the keys of the city with hostages. Yet because he held their loyalty suspect, he established a fortification in the city itself and entrusted its guard to chosen soldiers. Then Archil, the most powerful man of Northumbria, made peace with the king and gave him his son as a hostage. The bishop of Durham also came into the king’s favour, intervened as a mediator of peace on behalf of Malcolm, king of the Scots, and carried the agreed terms into Scotland. Malcolm, although summoned by the English and prepared to undertake a strong expedition to help them, nevertheless, [Col. 0315A] having heard the peace embassy, remained at rest and joyfully sent back his envoys with the bishop of Durham, through whom he swore faithful service to King William. Thus he prudently provided for himself and greatly pleased his people by preferring peace to war. For the Scottish people, though harsh in battle, nevertheless love leisure and tranquillity; they do not wish to be disturbed by neighbouring kingdoms, being more intent upon the pursuits of Christian religion than upon arms. Afterwards, on his return, the king established castles at Lincoln, Huntingdon, and Cambridge, and entrusted their protection to very brave men.

### VI. Many Norman soldiers leave England and return to Normandy. The tyranny of the Normans. Rebellions of the English

At this time certain Norman women burned with the cruel flame of desire and repeatedly demanded by messengers that their husbands return quickly, adding that unless they hastened home, they themselves would procure other husbands. For they did not dare cross the sea to their husbands because sea-voyaging was still unfamiliar to them, nor seek them in England, where they were continually under arms and repeatedly undertook daily expeditions, not without a great shedding of blood on both sides. Amid so many movements of war, the king wished to retain his soldiers with him; he generously offered them lands with revenues and great powers, and promised greater things once the whole kingdom had everywhere been freed from enemies. Lawful barons and vigorous champions [Col. 0315C] were deeply troubled as they watched their king surrounded by wars, together with his brothers, friends, and loyal companions; and they feared that, if they departed, they would openly be deemed faithless traitors and cowardly deserters. On the other hand, what were these honourable warriors to do if their wanton wives polluted their marriage-bed by adultery and brought upon their descendants the enduring stigma and disgrace of infamy?

Therefore Hugh of Grandmesnil, who had already held the governorship of the Gewissae—that is, the region of Winchester—and his brother-in-law Humphrey of Tilleul, who had undertaken the defence of Hastings from the first day of its construction, departed with many others, sadly and reluctantly abandoning the king as he laboured among foreigners. Then they returned to Normandy to serve their wanton ladies; but neither they nor their heirs were ever afterwards able to recover the honours which they had already acquired and had abandoned for this cause.

England was grievously worn down by manifold desolations and heavily oppressed both by natives and by foreigners. Fires, plunder, and daily killings attacked, struck down, overthrew, and shattered the wretched people. Adverse fortune ensnared alike the conquered and the conquerors in its trap, now hurling them heedlessly down by the sword, now by famine, now by pestilence, as the almighty Judge allotted to each. But the king, having observed the hardships of the land, summoned his paid soldiers and, having rewarded them all with royal generosity for their military service, kindly allowed them to go home.

[Col. 0316A] In the third year of his reign, King William granted the earldom of Durham to Robert of Comines, who soon confidently approached the city with five hundred soldiers. But on the first night the citizens assembled and slaughtered him and all his soldiers except two who escaped by flight. These very brave men were unable to defend themselves, overwhelmed by timing, treachery, and numbers.

Not long afterwards Robert, son of Richard, commander of the garrison at York, was killed with many others. Thereafter the English gained confidence against the Normans, by whom they saw their companions and friends being excessively harassed. Loyalty, oaths, and the safety of hostages were cheap in the eyes of men angered by the loss of their fathers’ estates and the killing of their relatives and compatriots.

[Col. 0316B] Marius, Swegen, Cospatric, Edgar Ætheling, and other powerful and factional men gathered together; joined by a force of citizens and neighbours, they dared to attack the king’s fortification at York. William, surnamed Malet, commander of the castle, informed the king that he would be lost unless he brought prompt aid to the exhausted men. The king arrived swiftly, fell upon the besiegers, and spared none. Many were captured, most were killed, and the rest were put to flight. The king remained eight days in the city, established another garrison, and left Count William, son of Osbern, to guard it. He himself returned joyfully to Winchester and celebrated Easter there. Again, after the king’s departure, the English gathered against both garrisons; but while Count William fought bravely with his men in a certain valley, they did not prevail. Many of them were captured or slaughtered, while the rest postponed death by flight.

Pressed hard by the storms of war rising everywhere, King William sent his much-loved wife Matilda back to Normandy, so that, removed from English tumult, she might peacefully devote herself to religious works and preserve the security of the province with the boy Robert. She was a kinswoman of Philip, king of the French, and traced her descent from the kings of France and emperors of Germany; she was famed for the exceptional nobility of both birth and character. By her distinguished husband she bore the desired offspring of both sexes: Robert and Richard, William [Col. 0316D] Rufus and Henry, Agatha and Constance, Adelaiza, Adela, and Cecilia. In this changeable life different fortunes befell them, furnishing sharp-tongued sophists with abundant material for composing great books. This queen was adorned alike by beauty, lineage, learning, every grace of character and virtue, and—what is worthier than these of immortal praise—steadfast faith and zealous love of Christ. The almsgiving to which this lady daily devoted herself with fervour aided her husband, struggling in the array of war, more than I can express.

### VII. The vain attempts of the sons of King Harold, of the Danes, and of the Saxons against the Normans

The two sons of Harold, king of England, grieving for [Col. 0317A] their father’s death and their own expulsion, had fled to Diarmait, king of Ireland. They were aided by his support and that of the magnates of the kingdom; bringing sixty-six ships laden with armed men, they landed at Exeter. Then, advancing from the shore, they began more boldly to ravage the countryside, and, raging with sword and fire, attempted to inflict the greatest damage. Immediately Brian, son of Count Eudes of Lesser Brittany, and William of Eu, met them under arms; in two engagements on one day they reduced that dreadful multitude to so small a number that the survivors escaped in two boats and filled Ireland with mourning. Had night not ended the battle, not even a messenger of the disaster would have returned home. This omen justly attended sons seeking vengeance for their tyrannical father and those assisting that purpose.

Meanwhile Gytha, Godwin’s wife and Harold’s mother, secretly took away an immense treasure and crossed into Gaul, never to return, out of fear of King William.

In that season Swegen, king of the Danes, most carefully equipped a great fleet with Danes and English, set over it his two sons, his brother Osbern, two bishops, and three most beloved counts, and sent it to England. For he had often been solicited by the English with money and earnest requests; he was moved by the ruin of his own men, recently killed in Harold’s battle; and, moreover, he was incited to desire the kingdom by close kinship, being, as son of Harthacnut, nephew of King Edward. He possessed great power [Col. 0317C] and gathered all the forces of his kingdom, adding substantial assistance from neighbouring lands and friends. Poland, Frisia, and Saxony assisted him. Lutici also sent auxiliary bands for the sake of English wealth. There lived among them a very populous nation which, still held in the error of paganism, did not know the true God; entangled in the snares of ignorance, it worshipped Guoden, Thunor, and Frea, and other false gods—indeed, demons. This people was skilled in warfare by land and sea; Swegen had often defeated it with its king and subjected it to his dominion. Thus, elevated by many triumphs and wishing further to increase his power and glory, Swegen, as we have said, sent a great fleet against King William into England.

When they landed at Dover, an encounter with royal soldiers drove them back. Likewise they were repulsed by the Normans at Sandwich. Having found an opportunity to disembark, they spread out in plunder around Ipswich; but the provincials assembled, killed thirty of them, and forced the rest to flee. Ralph of Gaël attacked those who had landed at Norwich for a similar raid; he deprived many of life by the sword and many by water, and compelled the rest, shamefully taking to their vessels, to depart into the sea. King William was then in the Forest of Dean, occupied there in hunting as was his custom. On hearing there of the Danes’ arrival, he immediately sent a message [Col. 0318A] to York, warning his men to prepare more cautiously against them and to summon him should necessity require it. The guardians of the garrisons sent back word that they did not need his assistance for a year. By then Ætheling, Waltheof, Siward, and other exceedingly powerful Englishmen had joined the Danes.

They came to the mouth of the broad River Humber. There Ætheling had gone apart from the allied force with some of his men to plunder. The king’s household from Lincoln fell upon them and captured them all, except two who escaped with Ætheling, and destroyed the ship which its frightened guard had abandoned.

The Danes approached York and were greatly reinforced by the company of its inhabitants. Waltheof, Cospatric, Marius, Swegen, Elnoc, Archil, and the four sons of Carl, their standard-bearer, led the Danes [Col. 0318B] and the men of Northumbria. The castle garrison rashly went out against them and fought unsuccessfully within the city walls. Unable to resist the multitude, all were either killed or captured. The deserted castles lay open. The calamity of his men was reported to the unsuspecting king; rumour, magnifying it, reported that the enemy’s numbers were greater than they were and that they confidently awaited battle with him. The king was disturbed by grief and anger alike and prepared to hasten against the enemy with an army. But they, fearing the great warrior, fled to the Humber and put in at the bank adjoining Lindsey. He hurried there with cavalry, found certain wicked men in nearly inaccessible marshes, punished them with the sword, and destroyed several hiding places. The Danes escaped to the opposite bank, awaiting [Col. 0318C] a time when they could avenge themselves and their allies.

At that time the western Saxons of Dorset and Somerset, with their neighbours, attacked Montacute, but were thwarted by divine providence. For men of Winchester, London, and Salisbury came up under the leadership of Geoffrey, bishop of Coutances; they killed some, mutilated some whom they had captured, and put the rest to flight. The Welsh and men of Chester besieged the king’s garrison at Shrewsbury; they were aided by the inhabitants of the city, together with Edric the Wild, a powerful and warlike man, and other fierce Englishmen. The inhabitants of the county of Exeter did the same at Exeter, joined by a crowd gathered from every direction and by Cornwall. [Col. 0318D] For the furthest territory of the English toward the west and Ireland is called Cornwall—that is, Cornuallia. The citizens of Exeter supported the king, not forgetting the hardships they had once suffered. As soon as the king received this news, he ordered the two counts William and Brian to help those in difficulty. But before they reached Shrewsbury, the city had been burned and the enemy had departed. The defenders at Exeter likewise suddenly sallied out and by their attack drove away those besieging them. William and Brian met the fugitives and punished their rashness with great slaughter.

Meanwhile, at Stafford, the king easily destroyed very many men of the rebellious [Col. 0319A] party. In so many conflicts much blood was shed on both sides, and both unarmed and armed common people were pitiably shaken here and there by various misfortunes. God’s law was everywhere violated, and ecclesiastical discipline was almost universally dissolved. The killings of wretches multiplied; souls were wounded by the goads of greed and anger and were carried off in crowds here and there to hell, God condemning them—God whose judgments are proved to be most just.

When King William returned from Lindsey, he left there his half-brother Robert, count of Mortain, and Robert of Eu, to repel Danish raids. The Danes hid themselves for a time. But once they thought themselves secure, attracted by the feasts of the provincials, commonly called *firma*, they came ashore. The two counts attacked them unexpectedly, mingled their banquets with blood, pressed the panic-stricken men, and pursued them with slaughter as they fled all the way to their ships. News again spread that these same raiders had come to York to celebrate the Lord’s Nativity there and were preparing for battle. The king hurried there from Nottingham but was held up at the water of Pontefract, impassable by ford and unsuitable for navigation. When men advised returning, he did not agree; when others wished to build a bridge, he replied that this was not expedient, lest the enemy suddenly fall upon them and find in the very work an opportunity to inflict disaster. They were detained there three weeks.

At last a bold knight named Lisois, surnamed “of the Monasteries,” explored the river most carefully, seeking a ford above and below. After great difficulty he finally discovered a passable place and crossed with sixty high-spirited horsemen. A multitude of enemies fell upon them, but did not prevail because they resisted most fiercely. On the following day Lisois returned and revealed the ford; without delay the army was brought across. They proceeded through forests, marshes, mountains, and valleys by a very narrow path that did not permit two men to travel side by side.
