Thus they approached York, but received word that the Danes had fled. The king sent tribunes and commanders with a force of armed men to restore the castles in the city, and likewise left others on the bank of the Humber to resist the Danes. He himself advanced into certain wooded and most difficultly accessible places [Col. 0319D] and zealously pursued enemies hidden there. His army spread over a hundred miles. He struck very many with the avenging sword, destroyed others’ hiding places, devastated lands, and burned houses with all their possessions. Nowhere did William exercise such cruelty; here he shamefully yielded to vice, refusing to restrain his anger and killing guilty and innocent alike by the same punishment. For, goaded by anger, he ordered crops, livestock, vessels, and every sort of foodstuff to be heaped together and all utterly burned at once after fire was set to them, so that all sustenance throughout the entire region beyond the Humber might likewise be destroyed.

Consequently, in the following period so severe a famine raged widely in England and involved the unarmed and simple people in such misery of hunger that more than one hundred thousand people of the Christian nation, of both sexes and every age, perished. In many matters my account has willingly extolled William; but in this matter, in which he alike pierced the just and unjust with the spear of wasting famine, I do not dare to praise him. For when I see innocent infants, flourishing youths, and grey-haired old men endangered by hunger, moved by pity I grieve more for the sorrows and anxieties of the wretched people than I uselessly endeavour to favour him with frivolous flatteries. Moreover, I state without doubt that so deadly a slaughter will not go unpunished. For the almighty Judge beholds high and low alike, and as the eternal law of God makes plain to all, the most rigorous avenger will examine and punish the deeds of everyone equally.

### VIII. King William routs his enemies. A royal crown is sent to him by the pope

[Col. 0320B]

Amid the wars, William ordered the crown and other royal ornaments and vessels brought from the city of Winchester. Leaving the army in camp, he went to York, where he celebrated the Nativity of our Saviour. Again he learned that a hostile band was hiding in a corner of the region, protected everywhere by sea or marshes. A single entrance led in over firm ground, only twenty feet wide. They had gathered abundant plunder; they acted without concern and thought that no force could harm them. Yet when they heard the royal column approaching, they departed by night with all possible haste. The king, burning to pursue enemies hostile to him, followed them to the River Tees [Col. 0320C] and forced his way through trackless places, whose roughness sometimes compelled him to go on foot. He remained on the Tees for fifteen days. There Waltheof, present in person, and Cospatric, absent, were reconciled by an oath offered through envoys.

The Danes, recently the comrades of these men, were already in danger, tossed like wandering pirates by waves and winds. Famine pressed them no less than the storm. Some perished in shipwreck. The survivors sustained life on the cheapest gruel—not merely common soldiers, but even their leaders, counts, and bishops. Meat had entirely failed; for a long time they had fed upon it rancid and rotten. They did not dare land to gather plunder or reach the shore anywhere because of fear of the inhabitants. At last the scanty remnants of the great fleet returned to Denmark and tearfully related to their King Swegen the grave perils they had endured, the extreme fierceness of their enemies, and the destruction of their companions.

In January King William returned from the Tees to Hexham by a route hitherto untried by an army, a route where very sharp ridges and the lowest hollows of valleys, though the neighbouring country enjoys springlike mildness, are covered with snow. Yet he crossed in the bitterest cold of winter and strengthened the soldiers’ spirits by his own cheerfulness. That journey was completed with difficulty, and an immense loss of horses occurred. Each man was anxious for his own safety and gave little thought to lord or friend. In this hardship the king [Col. 0321A] became separated with only six horsemen and spent the whole night ignorant where the men he had led might be. Returning to York, he restored several castles there and arranged matters beneficial to city and region.

He then launched an expedition against the men of Chester and the Welsh, who, besides other offences, had most recently besieged Shrewsbury. But the army which had endured hardships feared that much harsher ones remained in this march. It feared the roughness of the country, the severity of winter, the shortage of provisions, and the terrible fierceness of enemies. The Angevins, Bretons, and men of Le Mans were grievously burdened by services they called intolerable; therefore, stubbornly seeking leave to depart, they complained. For his own men asserted in excuse that they could not always obey a lord who dared new and excessive things and commanded too much. But the king followed the constancy of Julius Caesar in such necessity and did not think fit to retain them by much entreaty or new promises. He boldly began the undertaking and ordered the cohorts faithful to him to follow; he made little of deserters, should they depart, as sluggish, cowardly, and weak men. After the most difficult exertions he promised rest to the victors, affirming that no one can attain honours except through labours.

Thus he proceeded tirelessly by a route never before tried by horsemen, in which were steep mountains and deepest valleys, dangerous brooks and rivers, and yawning valley-bottoms. Those travelling that way were often severely afflicted by excessive rain, sometimes mixed with hail. At times horses drowned in marshes supplied a crossing for all. The king himself often nimbly went on foot ahead of everyone and vigorously helped the struggling men with his hands. At last he brought the army safely as far as Chester and restrained hostile disturbances throughout all Mercia by royal power. He then established a fortification at Chester and, on his return, another at Stafford, placing soldiers and ample provisions in both places. Arriving thence at Salisbury, he distributed very generous rewards to the soldiers for such endurance, praised those who deserved well, and dismissed them with great favour. But in indignation he detained the deserters for forty days beyond the departure of their fellow soldiers, and by that punishment chastised an offence which deserved worse.

[Col. 0321D] After this King William celebrated Easter Sunday in the city of Winchester, where cardinals of the Roman Church solemnly placed a crown upon him. At his request Pope Alexander had sent him, as to his dearest son, three suitable vicars: Ermenfrid, bishop of Sion, and two cardinal canons. William retained them with him for nearly a year, hearing and honouring them as angels of God. In different places and in many affairs they acted as they judged those regions to require canonical examination and ordering.

### IX. The Council of Windsor. King William’s piety and praiseworthy conduct. On the origins of the monastic order in England

[Col. 0322A]

A very great and most useful synod was held at Windsor [Note: [Col. 0321] Today Windsor. In this place—or rather in the city of Winchester, commonly called *Guenta*—the council was held.] in the year 1070 from the Incarnation of the Lord. The king and the cardinals presided over the council, and there they deposed Stigand, long condemned, by anathema. For he was stained by perjuries and homicides, and had not entered the archiepiscopate by the door. Rather, through the wicked ascent of ambition and usurpation, he had risen through two bishops, the bishop of Norwich and the bishop of Winchester. Several suffragans also were deposed, unworthy of the episcopate because of their criminal lives and ignorance of pastoral care.

In their place two Norman royal chaplains were appointed as notable bishops: [Col. 0322B] Walchelin of Winchester and Thomas of York, one in place of a deposed bishop, the other of one deceased. Both were prudent, full of gentleness and humanity, venerable and beloved by men, revering and loving God from the depths of their hearts. Others likewise were substituted, brought over from Gaul: learned men, distinguished in conduct and devoted lovers of divine things.

King William showed himself worthy of praise in many respects through his pursuit of manifold uprightness, and especially because he always loved true religion in God’s ministers—a religion which peace and worldly prosperity sometimes serve. Numerous reports attest this, and the evidence of his deeds most certainly proves it. Whenever any pastor passed from this world at the completion of his life and the Church of God mourned, bereft of its own ruler, the diligent prince [Col. 0322C] sent prudent envoys to the orphaned household and had all the Church’s property inventoried, lest it be dissipated by secular guardians. He then summoned bishops and abbots and other wise counsellors and, by their counsel, investigated most carefully who seemed better and more useful for governing God’s household in both divine and secular matters. Finally, the benevolent king appointed as administrator and ruler of the bishopric or abbey the man whom the provision of wise men chose for the merit of his life and the learning of his wisdom.

He maintained this practice for fifty-six years, during which he held rule in the duchy of Normandy or the kingdom of England, and he left it to posterity as a religious custom and example. [Col. 0322D] He utterly abhorred the Simoniac heresy, and therefore in choosing abbots or bishops he considered not so much persons’ wealth or power as their holiness and wisdom. He placed men proven in virtue over the monasteries of England; through their zeal and strictness the monastic life, which had already grown somewhat lukewarm, revived, and what had seemed to fail rose again to its former strength.

For Augustine and Laurence, and the other first preachers to the English, were monks; and in their bishoprics, in the place of canons—a practice scarcely found in other lands [Col. 0323A]—they devoutly established monks. They built many splendid monasteries and handed down regular observances to converts by word and example. Thus the monastic order flourished magnificently in England for more than two hundred years, and the Christian religion happily restrained the English kings Æthelberht and Edwin, Oswald and Offa, and many others, and beneficially raised them to the height of virtues; until Edmund, king of the East Angles, fell as a martyr by the sword of the pagans, together with two other kings of England. Then the heathen Danish kings Oskytel and Guthrum, Hámund and Halfdan, Ivar and Ubba, with their bands, invaded England, burned the churches of monks and clerics, and slaughtered the people of God like sheep.

[Col. 0323B] After some years Alfred, king of the Gewisse, son of King Æthelwulf, rose against the pagans and, by God’s power, either killed, expelled, or subdued the enemy; and he was the first of all kings to hold alone the monarchy of all England. In integrity, generosity, and praiseworthy foresight he surpassed, I think, all the kings of England before and after him; and after spending twenty-nine years praiseworthily in the kingdom, he left the sceptre to his son Edward the Elder. When the condition of the realm had thus been pacified, religious princes and bishops began again to restore monasteries. Since all the monks of the whole of Albion had been killed or driven away in the aforementioned rage of the heathen, they sent the distinguished young man Oswald to the monastery of Fleury, which Leodebodus of Orléans built in Gaul above the Loire River [Col. 0323C] in the time of Louis, son of Dagobert, king of the Franks. That place is exceedingly venerable because of the bones of Saint Benedict, father and master of monks, which the monk Aigulf, sent by Abbot Mummolus, brought from the province of Benevento into the district of Orléans. This happened after the devastation of the monastery of Cassino, which blessed Benedict foretold with tears to Theoprobus, a monk and noble servant of God, as we read in the second book of the *Dialogues*, which the illustrious Pope Gregory elegantly composed for Peter the subdeacon.

After the death of King Cleph, before his son Authari was fit to rule, and while the whole Lombard people was without a king and subject to thirty-four dukes, [Col. 0323D] the raging raiders of the Winnili attacked by night and devastated the monastery of Cassino; but, under God’s protection, all the monks escaped unharmed with their abbot Bonitus. Thereafter the same desolation remained there for 110 years, until Petronax, bishop of Brescia, came to Mount Cassino and, with the assistance of Pope Zacharias, restored the noble monastery there; raised magnificently, it continues to increase daily down to the present day. While the aforesaid desolation endured and Mount Cassino lacked worshippers, the house of Fleury, by God’s will, was enriched with the precious body of the foremost Father Benedict. The monks on this side of the Alps solemnly and devoutly celebrate its translation every year on 11 July, the fifth day before the Ides of July. The reverend young man Oswald went there [Col. 0324A] to become a monk, learn the monastic rule, beneficially discipline his life according to God’s will, and lead other lovers of this order, following in the apostles’ footsteps, toward the prize of the heavenly calling. And so it happened.

After some years Oswald was returned from Fleury by its archimandrite, who graciously yielded to the requests of the English. Since he possessed abundant sagacity as well as goodness, he was set over all the monasteries of England. The venerable men Dunstan and Æthelwold also assisted him most earnestly, and first equipped Glastonbury and Abingdon with regular observances. The English kings Æthelstan, Eadred, Edmund, and [Col. 0324B] especially Edgar son of Edmund faithfully obeyed these teachers. During Edgar’s reign Dunstan became metropolitan of Canterbury and Æthelwold was enthroned as bishop of Winchester. Oswald, meanwhile, first governed the bishopric of Worcester and afterwards the archbishopric of York. At their request Abbo of Fleury, a wise and devout monk, was sent across the sea; he taught the monastic observance at Ramsey and other English monasteries, as it was observed in Gaul at that same time. Zeal for holiness and every kind of uprightness enlightened the aforesaid bishops; it shone forth aptly through their teaching and the miracles displayed through them, and benefited many unlearned and learned people.

Then Bishop Æthelwold, under King Edgar, restored at the settlement now called Burgh the monastery of Medeshamstede, which Bishop Sexwulf had formerly built in the time of Wulfhere, king of the Mercians [Col. 0324C]; and he enriched with great wealth the basilica built in honour of Saint Peter, chief of the apostles. Thereafter Thorney, Ely, and many other monasteries were constructed in numerous places, and communities of monks, clerics, or nuns were diligently placed in them. An abundance of revenues was generously apportioned to each monastery, so that sufficient food and clothing might be provided for the *theorici* [apparently a scribal reading; perhaps “clerics”], lest, through lack of necessities, they should falter and fail in divine worship.

Thus the monastic order was renewed in England; in many monasteries the glorious host of monks [Col. 0324D], armed with the weapons of virtues against Satan, was nobly trained to fight steadfastly in the Lord’s battle until it gained victory. But after some time, in order to purge the wheat where the abundance of tares had multiplied too greatly, a most severe storm again arose from the north against the English under King Æthelred, son of Edgar. For Swein, the mad idolater king of the Danes, came to England with a powerful pagan fleet and immediately fell upon the unsuspecting people like a violent whirlwind; and the frightened King Æthelred fled to Normandy with his sons Edward and Alfred and Queen Emma. Not long afterwards, while Swein was raging excessively against Christians, he was killed by Saint Edmund at God’s command; and Æthelred, hearing of his enemy’s death, returned to his own land. Then [Col. 0325A] Cnut, king of the Danes, learning the differing fortunes of his father, summoned to his side two kings, Lachman of the Swedes and Olaf of the Norwegians, and came to England with an immense army. Finally, after many massacres, when King Æthelred and his son Edmund Ironside had died, he obtained England; he himself afterwards possessed it, as did his sons Harold and Harthacnut, for more than forty years.

During these storms the metropolis of Canterbury was besieged and burned, and Saint Ælfheah the archbishop was martyred by diverse tortures at the hands of the heathen Danes. Then other cities were burned, and episcopal and monastic churches were destroyed with their books and ornaments. The flock of believers too, battered by so many tempests in diverse places and exposed to the teeth of wolves, was horribly torn to pieces in various ways [Col. 0325B].

## X. The Supreme Concern of the Roman Pontiffs to Instruct the English. Relaxation of Morals. King William Restores Ecclesiastical Discipline. Lanfranc, Archbishop of Canterbury.

I have prolonged a lengthy digression, but, unless I am mistaken, not a useless one; and I have rehearsed matters gathered from ancient annals, so that the attentive reader may plainly see why the Normans found the English uncultivated and almost illiterate, though Roman pontiffs had once diligently instructed them with the best institutions.

For Gregory and Boniface sent outstanding teachers to the English, with books and every ecclesiastical implement, and educated and instructed them in every [Col. 0325C] good thing as their dearest sons. Then Pope Vitalian, in the time of Kings Oswiu and Egbert, sent to England the most learned men Theodore the archbishop and Adrian the abbot; through their skill and zeal, the English clergy flourished wonderfully, abundantly imbued with both Latin and Greek learning. In the following age the flourishing Abbot Albinus and Bishop Aldhelm succeeded them; their diligence and religion taught many people, and in writings they impressed for posterity praiseworthy memorials of their virtues. The discerning Bede extolled all these, and many others, with praises, and by investigation of the liberal arts and hidden matters strove to be counted equal to the perfected. He broke for the children of the Church the saving bread of the Old and New Testament by expounding it clearly [Col. 0325D]; in more than sixty books of explanation he unlocked hidden things; and thus he won lasting remembrance for himself among his own people and foreigners alike.

After precious stones had been happily placed in the wall of the heavenly Jerusalem and grains of wheat carefully stored in the granary of the true Joseph, flints were strewn in the streets and chaff cast onto the dungheap, irreverently trampled by passers-by. So, by the just ordinance of almighty God, after the elect had passed from transitory things to eternal ones, while the Danes, as I have already described, raged for a long time through England without fear of God or humanity, countless transgressions against God’s law were rashly committed. Human pursuits, always inclined to wrongdoing, when rulers with the rod of discipline had been removed, became abominable through unspeakable [Col. 0326A] deeds. Such dissolution had relaxed clergy and laity and inclined both sexes to every wantonness. Abundance of food and drink nourished luxury; the fickleness and softness of the people easily drove anyone into shameful conduct. When monasteries had been destroyed, monastic religion was weakened, and canonical strictness was not restored until the time of the Normans. Thus for a long period beforehand monasticism had declined among the people across the sea, and the conduct of monks differed little from secular life. They deceived by their dress and by the title of their profession, being devoted to feasting, innumerable private possessions, and foul transgressions. This order, therefore, was corrected into regular observance at the prompting of King William, and, brought to blessed customs, was held in great honour. A number of abbots [Col. 0326B] were newly appointed by the king, and many monks were suitably trained in French monasteries. Set over the English by royal command, they established discipline and set forth examples of religious life. Over the monastery of blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, which Augustine, first teacher of the English, had built, was placed the famous Abbot Scotland, eminent in learning and goodness. Born of a distinguished family in Normandy and regularly educated at the Mount of Michael the Archangel “at the peril of the sea,” he was set over Canterbury by the Normans for the correction of morals. Likewise, a rapid change of masters occurred in other monasteries, beneficial to some but dangerous to others, both masters and subjects.

The see of Canterbury, in which Augustine, sitting by decree of Pope Gregory, had presided over all bishops of Britain, was assigned, after the deposition of Stigand, to Lanfranc, abbot of the men of Caen, by the willing election of the king and all his magnates [Col. 0326C]. Born of noble parentage among the citizens of Pavia in Italy, from childhood he pursued study in the schools of the liberal arts; eagerly devoted to a secular purpose, he thoroughly learned the expertise of secular law according to the custom of his homeland. As a young advocate, he often overwhelmed aged opponents in litigation; in speaking aptly, he surpassed old men by the torrent of his eloquence. At that age he resolved to deliver legal opinions, which jurists, judges, and city magistrates gladly received. But while in exile he pursued philosophy, like Plato once at the Academy, eternal fire set his mind ablaze and love of true wisdom shone upon his heart. With Ecclesiastes he perceived—though he had not yet learned it through the use of ecclesiastical reading—that worldly goods are vanity. Therefore, in a sudden contempt of spirit, casting aside the world and himself and embracing the religious profession, he submitted himself to the regular yoke. He chose the small monastery of Bec in Normandy, poor in situation and resources; by his prudence and most vigilant care he enriched it and raised it to a condition of most beautiful order. While he governed the brotherhood by strict yet gentle discipline and assisted the holy abbot, Herluin, a novice exile, with humble and useful counsel, God, the examiner of thoughts, made him known—while he mortified himself to vices and the world and laboured especially for inward [Col. 0327A] and heavenly things—so that he might be set as a lamp upon a lampstand and fittingly illuminate the Lord’s spacious house. Drawn from cloistered quiet by the compulsion of obedience, he came forth as a teacher; under his teaching the library of philosophical and divine literature shone brightly. In both he was most powerful at untying the knots of questions. Under this teacher the Normans first investigated literary learning, and from the school of Bec proceeded eloquent scholars in divine and secular matters. For formerly, during the time of the six dukes of Neustria, scarcely any Norman adhered to liberal studies, nor was a teacher found, until God, provider of all things, brought Lanfranc to the Norman shores. The fame of his learning became widely known throughout [Col. 0327B] Europe; therefore many gathered at his school from France, Gascony, Brittany, and Flanders.

In grammar they recognized in Lanfranc an Herodian; in dialectic, an Aristotle; in rhetoric, a Cicero; in sacred Scripture, Augustine and Jerome and the other interpreters of law and grace. Had Athens, while still flourishing and most excellent as a seat of instruction, known his genius and Lanfranc’s learning, it would have risen before him in every kind of eloquence and discipline and desired to be instructed by the useful arguments it received from him. This monk was likewise zealous to destroy with the sword of the word any sects that assailed the Catholic faith. Indeed, at the Roman and Vercelli synods he pierced with the blade of spiritual speech Berengar of Tours, whom some considered a heresiarch and whose doctrine they condemned because, concerning the saving sacrifice, it administered death to souls. There he most devoutly expounded and most truthfully demonstrated that the bread and wine set upon the Lord’s table, after consecration, are the true flesh and true blood of the Lord and Saviour. By profound disputations he publicly defeated Berengar at Rome and Tours and compelled him to anathematize every heresy and profess the true faith in writing. Then the blasphemous heresiarch, ashamed and grieved because at Rome he had thrown into the fire with his own hands the little books of his perverse doctrine, lest he himself be burned, corrupted disciples by money as well as deceit; he composed a new work at home and sent it abroad through the same persons, so that the old error might be supported more approvingly and extended more enduringly into future years [Col. 0327D]. To refute this, Lanfranc published a clear and elegantly written treatise on the Eucharist: weighty with sacred authorities, unshakeably firm in the sequence of its arguments, rich in establishing the true understanding, brilliant in eloquent speech, and not tedious through prolixity. Many churches desired Lanfranc for their abbot or bishop with incredible longing. Even Rome, head of the Christian world, solicited him by letters and tried to retain him by entreaty and force. Thus he shone honourably before all, adorned by exceptional virtue and wisdom.

Accordingly, after the bishop of Sion had deposed Stigand, [Col. 0328A] as has already been said, he invited Lanfranc to episcopal government and announced the petition of the Church of God in a council of the bishops and abbots of Normandy. Lanfranc, however, troubled, judged so weighty a burden to be beyond him and asked for time to deliberate, firmly holding that a monk’s repose and an archbishop’s business could not be pursued together. Abbot Herluin commanded—the one whom he used to obey as Christ. The queen with her princely son entreated him. The great men assembled for this purpose also earnestly urged him. He did not refuse with a hasty decision, since the rule of discretion guided all his deeds and words. He took care not to offend obedience, nor at the same time so many men who asked, supported, and exhorted him. Sorrowfully, therefore, he crossed the sea, hoping to excuse himself and to find joy in [Col. 0328B] returning. The king reverently received with joy this helper in Christian cultivation, and, contending nobly against his reluctance with humility and majesty, overcame his excuse.

Therefore, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1070, Lanfranc, first abbot of the men of Caen, was given by divine appointment as instructor to the English; by a most honourable election and faithful consecration, he was enthroned as archbishop of the Church of Canterbury on 29 August, the fourth day before the Kalends of September. Many bishops and abbots attended his ordination, with a very great multitude of clergy and people. All inhabitants of Albion, present and absent, would have rejoiced and given many thanks to God with great gladness, had they recognized how great a good was then bestowed on them from heaven [Col. 0328C].

In the Church of Caen William, son of Radbod, bishop of Sées, succeeded Lanfranc; after nine years, I think, King William advanced him from there to govern the metropolitan see of Rouen. He was cousin to William, bishop of Évreux, son of Gerard Flaitel, whose power was especially strong in Neustria during the time of the Richards. A canon and archdeacon of Rouen, he served Bishop Maurilius; burning more ardently with love of God, he travelled abroad with Abbot Theodoric of Ouche and reverently visited the glorious tomb of the Saviour at Jerusalem. Returning from there, and taking care not to lose his former labours, he wholly withdrew himself from the world’s enticements and gladly attached himself to God’s service in the monastery of Bec. [Col. 0328D] Then, with Lanfranc, he was drawn out for the instruction of the novices flocking to the fortress of Caen for Christ’s service; shortly afterwards he himself became their praiseworthy father and teacher.

When William, bishop of Évreux, died, Baldwin, the duke’s chaplain, succeeded him and governed the bishopric regularly for almost seven years.

When he died, Gilbert, son of Osbern, canon and archdeacon of Lisieux, succeeded and held the bishopric usefully for more than thirty years; he increased and improved the Church’s possessions in many ways by his diligence.

When Ivo, bishop of Sées, died, Robert, son of Hubert of Ryes, succeeded; for almost twelve [Col. 0329A] years he presided over the bishopric and, fervent in God’s worship, greatly loved religious persons.

> **Note [Col. 0329].** Bishop Michael is omitted by Orderic, since he presided over the Church of Sées only for a few days. —GUIZOT.

## XI. Peace and Concord Gradually Established between English and Normans. The Unhappy Fortunes of Earl Morcar. On William of Poitiers, the Writer.

At this time, with God’s grace assisting, peace reigned in England, and some degree of security refreshed the inhabitants of the land, robbers having been driven far away.

English and Normans lived together peaceably in boroughs, castles, and cities, joining one another mutually in marriage. You might see some villages or urban markets filled with French merchandise and traders; everywhere you might see Englishmen who had formerly seemed uncouth to the French in their native dress, now transformed by foreign attire. No one dared plunder [Col. 0329B]; each person safely cultivated his own fields and cheerfully lived in harmony with his neighbour—though not for long. Churches were built and repaired, and in them sacred ministers endeavoured to render God the service owed to him. The reigning king’s zeal for good was wakeful, and he earnestly stirred up to good all whom he could. He often endeavoured to learn the English language, so that without an interpreter he might understand the complaint of the subjected people and affectionately declare to each person the enactments of justice, as reason dictated. Yet advanced age made him less capable of such learning, and the tumult of manifold occupations necessarily drew him to other matters.

But because the adversary of humankind, like a roaring lion, goes about the earth seeking someone [Col. 0329C] whom he may crush with the tooth of his cruelty, a great disturbance again arose for English and Normans; for a long time the treacherous Fury raged to the ruin of many. King William, making ill use of evil counsel, brought damage upon his reputation when he deceitfully shut up the illustrious Earl Morcar on the Isle of Ely and besieged him, though Morcar was his ally and was neither plotting nor suspecting any evil. Sly messengers ran back and forth between them and wickedly concluded a deceitful agreement: namely, that the earl should surrender himself to the king and the king should receive him peacefully as a faithful friend. The besieged man could indeed have defended himself there for a long time by the site’s inaccessibility, or, if overwhelming force came upon him, could have escaped by boat down the encircling river [Col. 0329D] to the Ocean. But he simply accepted false assurances and came peacefully from the island to the king with his men. The king, fearing that Morcar might avenge the injuries wickedly inflicted upon himself and his countrymen and that, through him, irreconcilable seditions might arise in the kingdom of Albion, put him in chains without any manifest charge, kept him confined in prison all his life, and entrusted him to the custody of Roger, the townsman of Beaumont. When the very handsome young Earl Edwin heard this, he preferred death to life unless he should free his brother Morcar, unjustly taken captive, or avenge himself upon the Normans with copious bloodshed. For six months [Col. 0330A] he sought assistance from Scots, Welsh, and English. Meanwhile three brothers, his intimate companions and chief retainers, betrayed him to the Normans, and they themselves killed him while, with twenty knights, he defended himself with all his strength. In this deed the sea’s flooding assisted the Normans: it forced Edwin to delay at a certain stream and wholly deprived him of escape. When the death of Edwin was heard throughout England, great mourning arose not only among the English but also among Normans and French, who mourned him with many tears as a companion or kinsman. For, as said above, he had been born of a religious family and, insofar as he could amid the many hindrances of worldly responsibilities, had devoted himself to many good works. His bodily beauty stood out among many [Col. 0330B] thousands, and he was a kindly lover of clerics, monks, and the poor. But King William, learning of the treachery by which the often-mentioned earl of the Mercians had perished, was moved to pity and wept; sternly, he drove into exile the traitors who brought him the head of their lord in hope of his favour.

Thus far William of Poitiers wove his history, in which, imitating the style of Sallust Crispus, he expounded William’s deeds with subtlety and eloquence. A Norman by birth, he came from the village of Préaux and had there a sister who presided over the nuns in the monastery of Saint Leodegar. He was called “of Poitiers” because at Poitiers he was abundantly imbued with the fountain of philosophy. Having returned to his own country, he shone more learned than all neighbours and companions, and assisted the bishops of Lisieux, Hugh and Gilbert, in ecclesiastical affairs through the office of archdeacon [Col. 0330C]. Before entering the clergy he was formidable in military matters, served an earthly prince protected by martial arms, and was able to report the dangers he had seen all the more reliably because he had taken part amid arms in fearful conflicts. In old age he devoted himself to silence and prayer, and had more power in composition or versification than in conversation. He frequently produced subtle, elegant, and readily recitable verses, generously sharing them without envy for the instruction of younger people, by whom they might be corrected. In some matters I have briefly followed his composition concerning William and his followers; I have not, however, attempted to pursue everything he said, nor to do so as subtly [Col. 0330D]. Henceforth, with God’s help, I shall record what occurred in later times in our own regions, firmly believing that, just as I gladly examine what earlier writers have published, so younger persons—and those not yet born—will diligently seek out the events of the present age.

## XII. King William Divides English Lands among His Normans. Norman Pride and Luxury.

King William, having overthrown, as we have said, the greatest earls of the Mercians—Edwin, that is, having been killed and Morcar confined in chains—distributed the renowned regions of England among his helpers and raised the lowliest Norman retainers into exceedingly wealthy tribunes and centurions [Col. 0331A]. He gave William the Steward of Normandy, son of Osbern, the Isle of Wight and the county of Hereford, and set him, together with Walter de Lacy and other proven warriors, against the Britons eager for war. Their boldness first invaded Brycheiniog and overthrew the Welsh kings Rhys, Cadwgan, and Maredudd, besides many others. The king had long before given Chester and its county to Gerbod of Flanders, who there endured great and difficult opposition from both English and Welsh enemies. Then, compelled by an embassy from those he had left in Flanders and entrusted with his hereditary honour, he obtained from the king leave to go and return quickly; but there, ensnared by adverse fortune, he fell into his enemies’ hands and, confined in chains and deprived of worldly prosperity, learned to utter laments of long misery [Col. 0331B]. Meanwhile the king granted the earldom of Chester to Hugh of Avranches, son of Richard surnamed Goz, who with Robert of Rhuddlan, Robert of Malpas, and other fierce magnates shed much Welsh blood. He was not generous but prodigal; he always led not a household but an army. He observed no measure in giving or receiving. He devastated his land every day, and gave more favour to fowlers and hunters than to cultivators of the land or those who prayed to heaven. He served the greed of his belly excessively and, weighed down by extreme corpulence, could scarcely walk. By concubines [Col. 0331C] he begot a great many children of both sexes, almost all of whom perished, swallowed up by various misfortunes. He married Ermentrude, daughter of Hugh of Clermont in Beauvaisis, and by her begot Richard, heir to the earldom of Chester. Richard, still a young man and childless, perished by shipwreck with William Ætheling, son of Henry king of the English, and many nobles, on 25 November [1119], the seventh day before the Kalends of December.

King William first gave Roger of Montgomery the castle of Arundel and the city of Chichester; later he added for him the county of Shrewsbury, situated on a hill above the River Severn. Roger was wise, moderate, and a lover of justice, and loved the company of wise and modest men. He long kept with him three wise clerics, Godebald, Odelerius [Col. 0332A], and Herbert, and profitably followed their counsel. To Warin the Bald—small in body but great in spirit—he gave his niece Amieria and the command of Shrewsbury. Through him he boldly subdued the Welsh and other opponents and pacified the entire province entrusted to him. He set William surnamed Pantulf, Picot, and Corbet, together with Roger and Robert his sons and other loyal, most valiant men, over his county; kindly aided by their judgement and strength, he flourished pre-eminently among the greatest magnates.

King William gave Earl Waltheof, son of Siward, the most powerful of the English, the county of Northampton and joined to him in marriage his niece Judith, so that firm friendship might endure between them [Col. 0332B]; she bore her husband two beautiful daughters. He also gave Walter surnamed Giffard the county of Buckingham; to William de Warenne, whose wife was Gundred, Gerbod’s sister, he gave Surrey. To Odo of Champagne, nephew of Count Theobald, who had a sister of the same king—namely, a daughter of Duke Robert—he gave the county of Holderness.

> **Note [Col. 0331D].** This Odo, son of Stephen II, count of Champagne, having been deprived of his paternal inheritance by his uncle Theobald III, count of Chartres, fled about the year 1050 to his kinsman William the Bastard, duke of Normandy. William gave him in marriage his half-sister Adelaide, daughter of Herluin of Conteville and Herleva, William’s own mother. Odo then followed William into England in 1066 and rendered him vigorous service in acquiring this kingdom by arms. Nor was this without reward: besides granting him the county of Holderness in England, William also arranged that the land of Aumale in Normandy—which Odo had received from John of Bayeux, archbishop of Rouen, under specified conditions—should be honoured with the title of a county. Thus Odo became the founder of the counts of Aumale. After William I died and his inheritance was divided between his sons William Rufus and Robert [Col. 0332D], so that the former received the kingdom of England and the latter the duchy of Normandy, Odo became bound in vassalage to each by reason of his respective dominions. Since, when the brothers disagreed, he could not discharge the duties of this double obligation equally, he attached himself, as though given a choice, to King William and thereafter admitted an English garrison into Aumale Castle. But he did not stand long in this loyalty. Deceived by ambition, he agreed with Robert of Mowbray and many other English barons who had conspired to remove William and set up Stephen, Odo’s own son, as king. Warned in time, William forestalled this treachery, seized Odo, and cast him into prison, where he spent the remainder of his declining life. We have assembled this account here from various passages in Orderic. Dom Bouquet, book IV, pp. 587–588.

And to Ralph de Guader, son-in-law of William son of Osbern, he gave the county of Norwich. He entrusted the jurisdiction of Leicester to Hugh of Grandmesnil; and he wisely distributed among other noble men the jurisdictions of cities and commands, with great honours and powers. To Henry, son of Walkelin de Ferrières [Col. 0332C], he granted the castle of Stafford, which Hugh of Avranches had formerly held; and he bestowed many great honours upon other newcomers who had adhered to him. He advanced some to such an extent that they had in England retainers richer and more powerful than their parents had been in Neustria.

What shall I say of Odo, bishop of Bayeux, who was a palatine earl, fearsome everywhere to all the inhabitants of England, and who, like a second king, dispensed justice throughout the land? He held primacy over all earls and magnates of the kingdom and possessed Kent with the treasures of the ancients. There Æthelberht son of Eormenric, Eadbald, Eorconberht, Egbert, and his brother Lothair had long ago reigned; they were the first of the English kings to receive the faith of Christ from the disciples of Pope Gregory [Col. 0333A], and by observing the divine law earned the prize of eternal life. In this man, I think, vices were mingled with virtues; but he adhered more to worldly business than to the gifts of spiritual contemplation. The monasteries of the saints complain greatly that Odo inflicted many injuries upon them and violently and unjustly took away estates granted to them long ago by faithful English people.

> **Note [Cols. 0333B–0333D].** This may be true of the monasteries of England. Yet many monasteries of Gaul acknowledge him as their benefactor, especially Saint-Bénigne of Dijon, on which he bestowed very many gifts, as the following record, copied from the old martyrology of Saint-Bénigne and printed in Labbé, vol. I of the *Bibliotheca Manuscriptorum*, p. 658, attests:
>
> “The death of Lord Odo, bishop of the city of Bayeux. We rightly count the day of his anniversary among the principal commemorations of our benefactors. For he both inherited from his forebears their devotion toward us and, as no degenerate heir, himself increased it with more abundant fruit. He was descended from the stock of the counts of Normandy, who loved this Church of Dijon with singular affection and advanced it greatly in property and possessions. Having become their imitator, he strove so to renew their affection in his own time that the remembrance both of himself and of them ought deservedly to remain ever fresh among us. To touch upon some indications of his devotion: when on one occasion he was seeking Pope Urban, who was then in Gaul, he came to Dijon and was received by Lord Jarenton and the brothers of this place with such honour that he thought himself wholly unworthy unless he responded to so great a service by a corresponding act through which he might establish by lasting testimony his affection toward them. Therefore, at the urging of William, dean of the Church of Bayeux, and Richard, archdeacon of Rouen, he gave to Saint Bénigne, patron of the Church of Dijon, through the hand of the above-mentioned abbot, the monastery of Saint Vigor, situated outside the city of Bayeux on Mount Chrism, with all its appurtenances, etc. [lacuna] Having governed the see of the holy Church of Bayeux happily for forty-eight years, he undertook the journey to Jerusalem, completed the course of his life in Apulia in the resolve of a holy life, and thus received burial there, in the church of Blessed Mary, Mother of God.”
>
> Dom Bouquet, book IV, pp. 587–588.

Geoffrey, bishop of Coutances, also, born of noble Norman stock, was a keen supporter and comforter at the battle of Senlac and in other conflicts which afterwards crushed newcomers and natives on both sides. As commander of troops he received from King William’s gift 280 [Col. 0333B] villages, commonly called *manors* from the fact of residence; when dying, he left them all to his nephew de Mowbray, who, because of his wickedness and rashness, was not to possess them for long.

Eustace of Boulogne likewise [Note: [Col. 0333D] Eustace II, count of Boulogne from about 1049, was the second husband of Goda, daughter of Æthelred II, king of England, after the death of her first husband Walter, count of Mantes. After she had died childless, he married, in a second marriage in 1057, Ida, daughter of Godfrey the Bearded, duke of Louvain. In the battle of Hastings he was nearly killed, being severely wounded by an axe between the shoulders. Yet in the following year, forgetful of the gifts with which the conqueror had honoured him, and instigated by Philip, king of France, he attempted to seize from William the kingdom which he had helped him acquire by his own valour. Accordingly, having formed an alliance with the inhabitants of Kent, he landed a fleet at Dover while William was in Normandy. But the treachery of the men of Kent having meanwhile been exposed, he was so received by the garrison that, after part of his men had been slain, he was compelled in great disgrace to hasten back to his ships with the rest. Made wiser by that defeat, he sought, through the assistance of friends, to regain William’s angered favour—and not unsuccessfully. For he recovered the prince’s friendship and cultivated it in such a way that he never afterwards lost it. Eustace outlived King William I. How he conducted himself toward William’s successor we shall see elsewhere. ID., book IV, p. 588.], Robert of Mortain, William of Évreux [Note: [Col. 0334D] William, son and successor of Richard, count of Évreux, followed his father on the English expedition of William the Bastard, his kinsman. He received such great rewards for his services in England that the king, as though by way of compensation, took from him the castle of Évreux in Normandy. As soon as its usurper died, he repaired this loss by expelling the royal garrison from the fortress. ID., book IV, p. 588.], Robert of Eu [Note: [Col. 0334D] Robert, successor to his father William in the county of Eu, had already, twelve years before the battle of Hastings, given great assistance to his kinsman William the Bastard against Henry, king of France. In 1054, with the aid of Robert, count of Mortemer, he had routed the forces of Henry, led by Odo, Henry’s brother, after they had entered the district of Vexin. ID., book IV, p. 588.], Geoffrey, son of Rotrou of Mortagne, and other counts and magnates whom I cannot name individually, received great revenues and honours in England from King William. Thus foreigners were enriched with England’s wealth, while her sons were wickedly slain on their account, or driven irretrievably into exile through foreign kingdoms.

[Col. 0334A] The king himself, it is said, received every day one thousand and sixty pounds of sterling money, thirty shillings, and three halfpennies from the lawful revenues of England, apart from royal gifts, redemptions of offences, and the many other sources of business which daily increased the king’s treasury. King William made a careful inquiry into his whole kingdom, and caused all its estates to be faithfully recorded as they had been in King Edward’s time. He so distributed the lands among his knights, and so arranged their ranks, that the kingdom of England continually possessed sixty thousand soldiers, ready to present themselves swiftly at the king’s command as circumstances required.

Having thus acquired the excessive wealth amassed by others, the Normans swelled with unrestrained arrogance and impiously slaughtered the natives, smitten by the divine scourge for their sins. In their case we see the complete couplet of Mantuan Maro fulfilled:

> The mind of man [variant: “men”] knows not fate or the lot to come,  
> nor how to keep measure when raised by favourable circumstances.
>
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* X.501.)

Noble maidens were exposed to the mockery of contemptible squires, and, violated by filthy scoundrels, bewailed their dishonour. Matrons distinguished by refinement and noble birth groaned in desolation; deprived of the comfort of their husbands and almost all their friends, they preferred death to life. Untaught parasites marvelled, and through pride became as if senseless [Col. 0335A] at the source from which such power had flowed to them; they thought themselves permitted to do whatever they pleased. Why did these foolish and wicked men not reflect with complete contrition of heart that they had conquered their enemies not by their own strength but by the will of God, who governs all things, and had subdued a nation greater, wealthier, and older than themselves—a nation in which many holy and wise men and mighty kings had shone, and which had flourished nobly in many ways, at home and in war? They ought continually to have feared, and implanted in the depths of their hearts, the sentence of Truth: “With the same measure with which you have measured, it shall be measured back to you” (Luke 6:38).

## XIII. Norman churchmen also seek riches. The praiseworthy abstinence of the monk Guitmund

Some ecclesiastical men also, who seemed wise and religious, zealously served the royal court in pursuit of desired dignities, and by various forms of flattery shamefully fawned, to the discredit of their religious reputation. As military pay was bestowed by princes upon their recruits, so bishoprics and abbeys, provostships of churches, archdeaconries and deaneries, and other powers and dignities of the Church were bestowed by laymen upon certain tonsured men in payment for their service—offices which only the merit of holiness and the teaching of wisdom ought to secure. Clerics and monks now attached themselves to an earthly prince for such rewards, and indecently rendered manifold service for temporal advantage, service unsuitable to divine worship. The old abbots were intimidated by threats of secular power [Col. 0335C] and unjustly driven from their seats without synodal hearing; in their place hirelings—not monks but tyrants—were intruded contrary to the ordinances of the holy canons. The arrangement and advancement that existed between flocks entrusted to men of this kind and their archimandrites was such as commonly exists between wolves and two-year-old sheep without a defender.

This can readily be proved by those who were present at the case of Thurstan of Caen and the community of Glastonbury. For when that violent abbot compelled the Glastonbury monks to abandon the chant which the English had learned from the disciples of blessed Pope Gregory, and to learn an unfamiliar chant, never before heard by them, from Flemings or Normans, a most bitter quarrel arose, soon followed by an outrage against the sacred order. When the monks refused to accept the new observances [Col. 0335D] and the stubborn master persisted in his obstinacy, laymen came to the aid of their lord, carrying spears. The assembly of monks was unexpectedly surrounded by them; some were cruelly beaten and, as is reported, mortally wounded. Many similar matters might be related, if they would usefully edify the reader’s mind. But since these things are less pleasant, I shall omit them and turn my pen to other matters.

The venerable Guitmund, a monk of the monastery called the Cross of Helton, where the glorious confessor of Christ Leudfred is recorded to have served the Lord happily for forty-eight years in the time of the young kings Hildebert and Chilperic, was summoned by royal command, crossed the sea, [Col. 0336A] and wholly declined the burden of ecclesiastical government offered to him by the king and magnates of the realm. He was mature in years, religious, and most learned in letters. A clear proof of his outstanding ability appears in his book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord against Berengar* [Note: [Col. 0335] Guitmund, bishop of Aversa, *On the Truth of the Body and Blood in the Eucharist*.], and in his other short works. Therefore, when the king asked him to remain with him in England, while awaiting a suitable time to promote him, he considered the matter carefully and, showing that the vow of his religious purpose was otherwise, replied to the king:

“Many reasons deter me from ecclesiastical rule, and I neither wish nor ought to set them all out one by one. First, I consider my weaknesses, under which I am continually oppressed in body and soul. Having carefully considered them, I greatly fear the divine judgment, grieving that I labour daily on the way of God and waver from the truth. And when I cannot rightly govern myself, how can I direct the lives of others into the way of salvation?

[Col. 0336B] “Having surveyed everything with watchful mind, I see no rule by which I could worthily preside over the company of men whose foreign customs and barbarous speech I do not know, whose fathers, dear parents, and friends you have killed by the sword, or whom you oppress after disinheriting them through exile, unjust imprisonment, and intolerable servitude. Search the Scriptures and see whether any law ordains that a shepherd chosen by enemies should be violently imposed upon the Lord’s flock.

“An ecclesiastical election ought first to be made sincerely by the faithful subjects themselves, and afterwards, if canonical, reverently confirmed with the assent [Col. 0336C] of fathers and friends; otherwise it ought to be corrected in charity. By what right can you, without fault, share with me and other despisers of the world—who have voluntarily stripped ourselves of our possessions for Christ’s sake—what you have savagely seized through war and the shedding of much blood? The general law of all religious persons is to abstain from plunder and, in observance of justice, to refuse spoil even when it is offered. For Scripture says: ‘The offering of one who sacrifices from unjust gain is defiled’ (Ecclesiasticus 34:21). And shortly afterwards: ‘He who offers sacrifice from the substance of the poor is like one who sacrifices a son in the sight of his father’ (ibid., 24).

“Considering these and similar proclamations of the divine law, I tremble and judge the whole of England to be like a very great spoil; I fear to touch it and its treasures as though they were burning fire. And because God commands each person to love his neighbour as himself, I shall tell you without deceit what has been divinely instilled in me. What I judge advantageous for myself, I also believe salutary for you. Therefore, do not consider my friendly speech bitter; but you, vigorous prince, and your fellow-soldiers, who entered upon grave danger with you, receive with kindly heart the utterance of our admonition.

“Consider carefully the works of God on every day of your lives; fear His judgments, which are incomprehensible, in all your actions; and strive thus to regulate your lives in the balance of equity according to God’s will, so that He, the eternal Judge who orders all things justly, may be merciful to you in the final judgment. [Col. 0337A] Let not flatterers deceive you with vain security, nor insolently urge you, because of the successful events of this present life, to fall into deathly sleep amid worldly prosperity. If you have conquered the English in battle, do not grow proud on that account; rather, wage with greater caution the more grievous and dangerous struggle against spiritual wickedness which still remains and threatens you daily.

“Changes of kingdoms have frequently occurred throughout the world, as we read here and there across the many fields of Scripture, to which God has granted knowledge of the liberal arts. Under King Nebuchadnezzar the Babylonians subdued Judaea, Egypt, and very many other kingdoms; but after seventy years they themselves, with their king Belshazzar, were conquered and subjected by the Medes and Persians, ruled by Darius and his grandson Cyrus. Then, after two hundred and thirty years, the Macedonians under Alexander the Great defeated Darius, king of the Persians, with his many legions; yet they too, after some years, were conquered together with their king Perseus when the Romans sent their phalanxes throughout the world.

“The Greeks under Agamemnon and Palamedes besieged Troy; they slew King Priam, son of Laomedon, and his children—Hector and Troilus, Paris and Deiphobus, and Amphimachus—and after a ten-year siege devastated and destroyed the famous kingdom of Phrygia with fire and sword. One part of the Trojans, under the leadership of Aeneas, acquired the kingdom of Italy; another part, with Antenor, after a long and difficult journey reached Dacia, settled there, and dwelt there until the present day.

“The Romans overthrew the kingdom of Jerusalem, which David [Col. 0337C] and his other mighty successors had enriched with the spoils of foreign peoples and exalted by subduing the barbarian nations around it. Under Vespasian and Titus they destroyed the noble Temple, 1,089 years after its first construction, when eleven hundred thousand Jews perished by sword or famine. In the time of Duke Sunno, the Franks joined themselves to the Gauls, manfully cast the Roman yoke from their necks, and began to rule over them. The Anglo-Saxons, led by Hengist and Horsa, took dominion by cunning and force from the Britons, now called Welsh, almost six hundred years ago. The *Guinili*, expelled by lot from the island of Scandinavia, invaded under King Alboin, son of Audoin, that part of Italy now called Lombardy; after long resistance to the Romans, they have held it until now.

“All these peoples whom I have recalled as swollen by victory soon afterwards underwent miserable destruction, and, tormented by the same crushing ruin as those they conquered, groan without remedy in the sewers of Erebus. Under Duke Rollo, the Normans took Neustria from Charles the Simple, and have now held it for one hundred and ninety years despite the opposition of the French and their frequent hostile attacks. What should I say of the Gepids and Vandals, Goths and Turks, Huns and Heruli, or of the other barbarians? Their efforts tend to nothing except theft and plunder and continual raging after peace has been trampled underfoot. They disturb the earth, burn dwellings, harass the world, scatter wealth, slaughter people, and defile and unsettle everything. These signs therefore foretell the end of the world, as we are plainly taught by the voice of Truth itself: ‘Nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom; and there shall be great earthquakes in various places, pestilences and famines, terrors from heaven, and great signs’ (Luke 21:11).

> Thus is the world continually oppressed by countless disasters.

“Having carefully considered these and many similar revolutions in human affairs, let no victor glory in the ruin of his equal; for he too will not stand except for as long as the ordinance of the Creator commands. I shall now turn my speech to you, O king; I beg you to drink it in kindly for the sake of eternal salvation. None of your fathers before you bore royal lineage; nor has so great an honour come to you by hereditary right, but by the gratuitous gift of almighty God and the friendship of Edward, your kinsman. Edgar Ætheling and many others descended from the royal line are nearer heirs to the English crown according to the laws of the Hebrews [Col. 0338B] and of other peoples. When they had indeed been set aside, the lot of advancement fell to you; but God’s judgment hangs over you, the more terrible because it is the more hidden, to require an account of the stewardship entrusted to you.

“I have spoken these things from a kindly heart to your highness, humbly entreating that your mind may always remember the last things, and that the prosperity of the present may not entangle you too greatly, since intolerable pain, great mourning, and gnashing of teeth are accustomed to follow it. I commend you to the grace of God, together with your friends and faithful men; and, with your permission, I intend to return to Normandy, leaving England’s rich spoil like refuse to lovers of the world. I love Christ’s free poverty, embraced by Antony and Benedict, more than the riches of the world, which Croesus and Sardanapalus loved excessively and afterwards, when they perished miserably, left to their enemies. For Christ the good shepherd threatens woe to the rich of this world, who here enjoy vain and superfluous pleasures; but He promises blessedness in the kingdom of heaven to the poor in spirit. May He grant it to us, He who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.”

The king and his magnates marvelled at the eminent monk’s constancy. In supplication and devotion, the king paid him fitting reverence and ordered that he should return suitably honoured to Neustria, and there await the king’s presence wherever he wished. After Guitmund had returned within the enclosure of his monastery, it was widely reported that he had preferred monastic poverty to the riches [Col. 0338D] of bishops; that, before the king and his magnates, he had called the conquest of England plunder; and that he had accused of rapacity all bishops and abbots set over churches in England against the will of the English. His words were therefore widely circulated and keenly discussed throughout England. They displeased many who despised the prospect of becoming his followers and burned with immense envy against him.

Not long afterwards, when John, archbishop of Rouen, died, the king and many others elected Guitmund to the archbishopric. But his rivals, whom he had criticized, did all they could to prevent his becoming archbishop. They could find nothing to object against so great a man except that he was a priest’s son. But he, wishing to be cleansed of all avarice, and preferring to be burdened by poverty among strangers rather than to foster dissensions among his own people, reverently approached Odilo, abbot of his monastery, and humbly asked and received from him permission to go on pilgrimage. The unlearned abbot, however, did not know how great a treasure of wisdom lay hidden in the aforesaid scholar. He therefore readily let that desirable philosopher depart from his monastery. Pope Gregory VII joyfully received him when he came, appointed him a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, and Pope Urban, after he had already been proved in many matters, solemnly ordained him metropolitan of the city of Aversa.

This city was built in the time of Pope Leo IX by the Normans who first settled Apulia, and was called Aversa by the Romans because it was built by bands hostile to them. This city, wealthy in riches, warlike through the ready valour of its people on this side of the Alps, feared by enemies, cherished by loyal dependants and allies, gladly obeys, by the Normans’ choice, the pope alone. From him it received as its bishop the scholar Guitmund, splendidly invested with the pallium, the garment of mystical dignity. The aforesaid archbishop governed the Church entrusted to him for a long time and rejoiced that, by apostolic privileges, it was free from every exaction of mortals. He diligently taught the people, protected them by his merits and prayers, and, after many struggles in the exercise of virtues, went to the Lord.

## XIV. Disputes among the heirs of the county of Flanders. Queen Matilda governs Normandy

In the fifth year of his reign [Note: [Col. 0339D] A.D. 1071.], King William sent William, son of Osbern, to Normandy, that he might protect the province together with [Col. 0339C] Queen Matilda.

Then a great quarrel arose in Flanders among the heirs to the principality. Baldwin, son-in-law of Robert, king of the Franks, was a most powerful ruler of the Flemings, and by his wife Adela had many sons and daughters endowed with various qualities. Robert the Frisian, Arnulf, Baldwin, Odo archbishop of Trier, Henry the cleric, Queen Matilda, and Judith, wife of Count Tostig, were the children of Baldwin and Adela. Scholars could compose great volumes about their characters and various fortunes.

Robert, the firstborn, had long ago offended his father. Rejected and expelled by him, he withdrew to Florence, duke of the Frisians, his father’s enemy, faithfully served him, and took his daughter in marriage. The duke of Flanders was consequently furious; in anger he nicknamed him “the Frisian,” declared him wholly an exile, and appointed Arnulf heir to his rights. Not long afterwards Duke Baldwin died, and Arnulf held the duchy of the Morini for a short time. For Robert the Frisian assembled a huge host of Frisians and other peoples and vigorously attacked Flanders. Philip, king of France, their kinsman, gathered an army of Frenchmen to assist Arnulf and summoned Count William of Normandy as guardian. William came to the king with only ten knights [Col. 0340A] and cheerfully entered Flanders with him as if going to a game.

Robert the Frisian joined the army of Emperor Henry to his own divisions. On Septuagesima Sunday, in the morning, on the tenth day before the Kalends of March, he forestalled the imperial forces; King Philip fled with the French, and Robert caused his own brother Arnulf, his nephew Baldwin, and Count William to be killed by the missiles of his men. Thereafter he held the duchy of the Morini for a long time and at his death left it to his sons, Robert of Jerusalem and Philip. Count William’s body was carried into Normandy by his own men and buried in the monastery of Cormeilles amid the great mourning of his followers.

He had built two monasteries of monks on his own patrimony in honour of holy Mary, Mother of God. One was at Lyre beside the river Risle, where his wife Adeliza was buried; the other at Cormeilles, where, as we have said, he himself was interred. All greatly mourned this baron of the Normans, foremost in valour, who had known his generosity, wit, and remarkable virtues. King William divided his inheritance among his sons. William the elder received Breteuil and Pacy, with the remaining part of his paternal right in Normandy, and held it almost thirty years throughout his life. But his younger brother Roger received the earldom of Hereford and all his father’s landed estate in England; yet shortly afterwards he lost it because of his treachery and insolence, as will be explained below.

Although Queen Matilda reigned powerfully and abounded in innumerable riches, a great sorrow arose for her [Col. 0340C] from her father’s death, her mother’s desolation, and the cruelty of one brother, by which the other brother and her dear nephew, with many friends, suddenly perished. Thus almighty God strikes earthly people who forget Him, casts down the proud, and clearly shows that the Most High rules over all the earth. Robert the Frisian therefore subdued all Flanders and possessed it for almost thirty years; he easily won the friendship of Philip, king of France. They were cousins by their ancestors’ descent, and both had wives who were daughters of Florence, margrave of the Frisians; their sons too remain bound by this tie of kinship until now.

But renewed discord arose between the Normans and the Flemings, and continued for a long time because of the murder of the queen’s brother and other relatives, and especially because of the fall of Count William. With affairs in Normandy disturbed, the king of England put his kingdom in excellent order and hastened to Normandy so that he might settle all matters there rightly and usefully. When news of the king’s approach was heard everywhere, lovers of peace rejoiced; but the sons of discord, foul with crimes in their evil consciences, trembled at the coming of the avenger. He then assembled the leading men of the Normans and the people of Le Mans and strengthened them all by royal exhortation to maintain peace and justice. He also admonished bishops and ecclesiastical men to live rightly, continually to meditate upon God’s law, to care jointly for God’s Church, [Col. 0341A] to correct the conduct of their subjects according to the decrees of the canons, and to govern all with prudence.

## XV. The Council of Rouen

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1072, a council was assembled at the metropolitan see of the city of Rouen, in the basilica of blessed and glorious Mary, ever-Virgin Mother of God. John, archbishop of that city, presided; following in the footsteps of the Fathers, he attended in every way to the interests of the Church. With him were his suffragans Odo of Bayeux, Hugh of Lisieux, Robert of Sées, Michael of Avranches, and Gilbert of Évreux.

First, the faith in the holy and undivided Trinity was discussed. In accordance with the decrees of the holy councils—namely, Nicaea, Constantinople, the first Council of Ephesus, and Chalcedon—they strengthened and ratified it, and professed that they believed it with all their heart. After this profession of the Catholic faith, the following chapters of Catholic doctrine were appended.

First, we decree that, according to the statutes of the Fathers, the consecration of chrism, baptismal oil, and oil for anointing shall take place at the proper hour—that is, after None—in accordance with the statutes of the holy Fathers. The bishop must also ensure that at this consecration he has with him twelve priests, or as many as possible, clothed in priestly vestments.

Likewise, in certain provinces a detestable custom has arisen: some archdeacons whose see is without a pastor receive portions of oil and chrism from some bishop and mix them with their own oil. This too is condemned. Rather, every archdeacon shall present all his chrism and oil to the bishop who is to consecrate it, as to his own bishop.

Likewise, the distribution of chrism and oil shall be carried out by deans with the greatest diligence and propriety. While distributing them they shall be clothed in albs, and the substances shall be distributed in such vessels that none of them may be lost through any negligence.

Likewise, it is decreed that no one shall celebrate Mass who does not communicate.

Likewise, no priest shall baptize an infant unless he is fasting and clothed in alb and stole, except in case of necessity.

There are some who keep the viaticum and holy water beyond the eighth day; this too is condemned. Others, having no consecrated hosts, consecrate them again; this is strictly forbidden.

Likewise, it is decreed that the gift of the Holy Spirit shall be given only to those who are fasting and by persons who are fasting, and that confirmation itself shall not take place without fire. It is also decreed that we should not be found transgressors of apostolic authority in conferring holy orders. For we read in the Decrees of Pope Leo that holy orders are not to be conferred indiscriminately on every day, but that after Saturday, at the beginning of the night which dawns into the first day of the week, the sacred blessing is to be conferred by fasting persons upon those to be consecrated, who are fasting. The same observance applies if it is celebrated in the morning of Sunday itself, the Saturday fast having been continued. This time does not depart from the beginning of the preceding night, and undoubtedly belongs to the day of the Resurrection, as is also made clear at the Lord’s Passover.

Likewise, we shall observe the Ember Days at their proper times, according to divine institution and in common observance: the first week of March, the second of June, the third of September, and the same week of December, out of reverence for the Lord’s Nativity. For it is most unworthy that the institution of the saints should be neglected through any occupations or worldly cares.

Likewise, clerics who, without being elected or called, or without the bishop’s knowledge, intrude themselves into holy orders; those upon whom a bishop lays hands, as on deacons; and others who, having no other orders, are ordained deacons [Col. 0342B] or priests: these are worthy of deposition.

Likewise, those who have received blessed tonsures and abandoned them shall be excommunicated until they make worthy satisfaction. Clerics who are to be ordained shall come to the bishopric on Thursday.

Likewise, monks and nuns who, leaving their churches, wander through the world, and others who have been expelled from monasteries for their wrongdoing, must be compelled by pastoral authority to return to their monasteries. If the expelled abbots refuse to receive them, they shall provide them with food from alms, which they shall also acquire by the labour of their hands, until they appear to have amended their lives.

Likewise, pastoral charges—that is, parish churches—are bought and sold by laymen and clerics, and even by monks. This is forbidden henceforth. Likewise, marriages are not to take place secretly or after a meal; rather, bridegroom and bride, fasting, shall be blessed by a fasting priest in a monastery. Before they are joined, the ancestry of both shall be carefully investigated. If any blood relationship is discovered within the seventh degree, or if either has been previously dismissed, they shall not be joined. A priest who acts contrary to these provisions shall be deposed.

Concerning priests, Levites, and subdeacons who have taken women to themselves, the Council of Lisieux shall be observed: they shall govern no churches, either personally or through assistants, and shall receive nothing from benefices. Archdeacons, whose duty it is to govern them, shall not be permitted to have any [Col. 0342D] concubine, any woman introduced into their household, or any mistress; rather, they shall live chastely and justly, offering their subjects an example of chastity and holiness. Deans too must be chosen who know how to rebuke and correct their subjects, whose life is not infamous but, by merit, is set above their subjects.

Likewise, it is forbidden that anyone who, while his wife lives, has accused her of adultery should ever marry the woman of whom he has made that accusation after his wife’s death. For many evils have resulted from this; very many have killed their wives for this reason.

Likewise, no one whose wife has taken the veil shall ever take another wife while she lives.

Likewise, if the wife of a man who has gone abroad or elsewhere marries another man before she has certainty of the first man’s death, she shall be excommunicated until worthy satisfaction.

Likewise, it is decreed that those found publicly fallen into criminal sins shall not be restored too quickly to holy orders. For, as blessed Gregory says, if those who have fallen are granted permission to return to their order, the vigour of canonical discipline is undoubtedly broken, since through hope of restoration no one fears to conceive desires for wrongful action. Therefore this must remain established: one publicly fallen into crime is in no way to be restored to his former rank before completing penance, unless in the utmost necessity, and then only after worthy satisfaction by a long penance.

Likewise, if anyone who has fallen is found deserving of deposition, and the number of fellow bishops required by authority cannot be present for his deposition—namely, six for the deposition of a priest and three for that of a deacon—each person who cannot be present shall send his representative with his authority.

Likewise, it is decreed that no one in Lent shall dine before beginning Vespers after the ninth hour has passed. For one who eats earlier does not fast.

Likewise, it is decreed that on Holy Saturday the office shall not begin before None. For it looks toward the night of the Lord’s Resurrection, in reverence for which “Glory to God in the highest” (*Gloria in excelsis Deo*) and “Praise the Lord” (*Alleluia*) are sung; this is also shown at the beginning of the office, namely in the blessing of the candle. The book called the *Official* relates that no celebration of the sacrament takes place on these two days. It calls this two-day period Friday [Col. 0343C] and Saturday, on which the grief and mourning of the apostles are commemorated.

Likewise, if the feast of any saint falls on a day upon which it cannot be celebrated, it shall be celebrated not earlier, but within the octave.

Likewise, following the decrees of the holy Fathers, namely Pope Innocent and Pope Leo, we decree that general baptism shall take place only on Holy Saturday and the Saturday of Pentecost. This is to be observed while ensuring that the laver of regeneration is not refused to infants at whatever time or on whatever day it is requested. We strictly forbid anyone to be baptized on the vigil or day of Epiphany except from necessity of illness.

This council was accepted by John, archbishop of the Church of Rouen; Odo, bishop of Bayeux; Michael, bishop of Avranches; Gilbert, bishop of Évreux; and also by very many venerable abbots, by whom the monasteries of Normandy were at that time nobly flourishing and preserving monastic strictness.

## XVI. Abbots of monasteries in Normandy under King William

I judge it worthwhile to make known to posterity the memory of the Fathers who wisely governed the monasteries of Normandy under King William and strove until death worthily to obey the eternal King, who reigns without change. Their followers, I believe, left many things written about them for posterity; yet it is pleasant for me, on this page at least, to name with my teachers certain men whom I love above the rest—not for temporal reward, but solely for love of the wisdom and religion divinely instilled in them.

The monastery of Fécamp, situated in sight of the sea and dedicated to the holy and undivided Trinity, Creator of all, was nobly founded by Richard I, duke of the Normans, and richly enlarged by the second Richard with many honours and riches. After William of Dijon, a wise man most fervent in religion, the venerable Abbot John governed it for fifty-one years. After him William of Ros, a cleric of Bayeux but a monk of Caen, held it for almost twenty-seven years. Like mystical nard in the house of the Lord, this man gave forth fragrance through charity, generosity, and manifold virtue. The works which he diligently performed openly, or secretly offered to almighty God before few witnesses, testify what spirit dwelt in him and, possessing him wholly, brought him to be crowned before the throne of the Lord of Hosts.

From the monastery of Fontenelle [Note: [Col. 0343D] Afterwards Saint-Wandrille.] the monk Guntard was chosen by the election of wise men; after the death of Abbot Robert he was appointed ruler over the monks of Jumièges. He carefully supplied the food of spiritual teaching to the sheep entrusted to him and manfully maintained the rigour of monastic order.
