He gently cherished and honoured the meek and obedient as a father does sons; but against the reprobate and stubborn, and against despisers of the Rule, he wielded the rod as a stern master of discipline. Finally, the aforesaid Father went, with his fellow pastors of Normandy, to the council held by Pope Urban at Clermont in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1095, in the third indiction. There, by God’s command, he ended his life on the sixth day before the Kalends of December; Tancred, prior of Fécamp, fierce as a lion, succeeded him.

After the death of Herluin, who had been founder and first abbot of the monastery of Bec, and who, flourishing in many graces, had during his life beneficially served the children of the Church without deceit, the venerable Anselm, thoroughly furnished with manifold learning, succeeded him. By God’s gift he commendably filled the aforesaid monastery with learned and devout brethren. Then, as the number of God’s servants increased, there was no lack of material resources; rather, as noble friends and kinsmen gathered together, an honourable abundance of necessities accrued to the brethren [Col. 0344D]. Clerics and laymen flocked to the counsel of this most accomplished scholar, and the sweet words of truth flowing from his mouth pleased the supporters of justice like the utterances of an angel of God.

An Italian by birth, he followed Lanfranc and sought Bec; and, like the Israelites laden with the gold and riches of the Egyptians—that is, with the secular learning of philosophers—he eagerly approached the land of promise. Having become a monk, he attached himself in every way to heavenly contemplation, and from the most fruitful fountain of wisdom poured forth abundant honey-sweet streams of teaching. He diligently investigated the obscure meanings of Holy Scripture, vigorously elucidated them in speech and writing [Col. 0345A], and wholesomely unravelled the intricate sayings of the prophets. All his words were useful and edified well-disposed hearers. His receptive disciples preserved in writing his letters and figurative sermons; having drunk their fill of these, they profited greatly not only themselves but many others also.

This was repeatedly experienced by his successors William and Boso, who richly drew in the compositions of so great a teacher and generously offered from them a desirable draught to the thirsty. Anselm was approachable and gentle, and answered charitably all who asked questions simply. At the pious request of friends he published books of remarkable subtlety and profundity on the Trinity, truth, free will, the fall of the devil, and why God became man [Col. 0345B]. The fame of this teacher’s wisdom spread throughout the Latin world, and the western Church was nobly intoxicated by the nectar of his good repute.

A great seed-bed of the liberal arts and sacred learning began in the Church of Bec through Lanfranc and grew magnificently through Anselm, so that from it proceeded many excellent teachers, prudent sailors, and spiritual charioteers, to whom the reins for governing the Church in the arena of this world were divinely entrusted. Thus the monks of Bec, through good custom, have become so devoted to literary studies and so diligent in discussing or expounding sacred riddles and useful discourses, that nearly all seem philosophers; and from their conversation even those who appear among them unlearned and are called rustics [Col. 0345C] may learn profitable things from grammarians foaming with learning. They rejoice in the worship of the Lord through mutual friendliness and the sweetness of charity, and, as true wisdom teaches them, they excel in untiring religious devotion.

I cannot adequately speak of the hospitality of the men of Bec. Let Burgundians and Spaniards, and others arriving from far or near, answer and declare without deception how kindly they have been received by them; and let them endeavour sincerely to imitate them in like circumstances. The door of the men of Bec stands open to every traveller, and their bread is denied to none who asks for it in charity. What more should I say of them? May he who freely began, and carries out, the good that shines forth in them [Col. 0345D] preserve them in good things as they persevere, and bring them unharmed to the harbour of salvation.

Gerbert of Fontenelle, Ainard of Saint-Évroult, and Durand of Troarn: as three stars shine in the firmament of heaven, so these three archimandrites shone in many ways in the citadel of Adonai. They excelled in religious devotion, charity, and manifold skill, and continually devoted themselves to the study of divine praise in God’s temple. Among the foremost singers, they possessed the art of music for sweet modulation, and composed melodious chants for antiphons and responsories. Concerning the supreme King, whom cherubim, seraphim, and all the host of heaven praise; concerning the undefiled Virgin Mary, who bore for us the Saviour of the ages; concerning angels, apostles, and martyrs; and concerning confessors and virgins, they brought forth honey-sweet praises flowing from their most sweet hearts [Col. 0346A]. These they faithfully handed down to the children of the Church, that they might sing in harmony to the Lord with Asaph and Heman, Ethan and Jeduthun, and the sons of Korah.

Nicholas, son of Richard III, duke of the Normans, a monk of Fécamp from childhood, governed for almost sixty years the monastery of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, in the suburbs of Rouen. He began a basilica of marvellous scale and elegance, in which rests the body of Saint Ouen, archbishop of that city, together with many other relics of saints. There were also then many other fathers of monks in Neustria, whose numerous graces I am compelled to pass over, lest excessive length produce weariness in the reader.

XVII. Pope Alexander II. Pope Gregory VII. On the bishopric of Le Mans.

[Col. 0346B]

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1073, in the eleventh indiction, Pope Alexander II, after governing the Roman and Apostolic See for eleven years, departed from the world. Gregory VII, who at baptism had been named Hildebrand, succeeded him and sat in the papal chair for seventeen years. A monk from childhood, he studied the law of the Lord earnestly and, being very zealous for justice, endured many persecutions. He sent apostolic decrees throughout the world, and, sparing no one, thundered terribly with heavenly pronouncements, inviting all by threats and entreaties alike to the wedding-feast of the King of Sabaoth.

At the pope’s request, the venerable Hugh, abbot of Cluny, sent to Rome Odo, prior of the aforesaid monastery [Col. 0346C], who had been a canon of the Church of Rheims, together with other suitable monks. The pope joyfully received them as helpers sent to him by God. He chose Odo in particular as his counsellor and appointed him bishop of the Church of Ostia. It is the prerogative of that see to receive one elected by the Roman clergy and to bless him as pope. The pope also promoted other monks, as reason prescribed, and worthily set them over the care of various churches.

After the death of Ernald, bishop of the people of Le Mans, King William said to Samson, his Bayeux chaplain: “The see of the bishopric of Le Mans has been bereft of its bishop, and, God willing, I now wish to appoint you in his place. Le Mans, said to be named from a dog’s madness, is an ancient city [Col. 0346D], and its people are insolent and bloodthirsty toward their neighbours, always defiant of their lords and eager for rebellion. Therefore I resolve to entrust to you the episcopal reins: you whom I have carefully brought up and loved from childhood, and whom I now desire to exalt among the greatest nobles of my realm.”

Samson answered: “According to apostolic tradition, a bishop must be blameless. But throughout my life I have been very blameworthy; before the sight of the Godhead I am polluted by every vice of mind and body. Wretched and contemptible because of my sins, I cannot attain so great an honour.”

The king said: “You are shrewd, and you clearly see that you ought rightly to confess yourself a sinner. Yet I have fixed my decision concerning you and shall not rescind what has been settled: you must accept the bishopric, or put forward another who may become bishop in your stead [Col. 0347A].”

On hearing this Samson joyfully said: “Now, my lord king, you have spoken excellently, and, with God’s assistance, you will find me ready to act accordingly. In your chapel there is a certain poor clerk, but noble and of good conduct. Entrust the episcopal office to him in the fear of God, for I judge him worthy of such honour.”

When the king asked who he was, Samson replied: “He is called Hoel and is a Breton by birth; but he is humble and truly a good man.” Immediately, by the king’s order, Hoel was summoned, still unaware why he was being called. When the king saw the young man, emaciated and in humble dress, he despised him; and turning to Samson, said: “Is this the man whom you commend so highly?”

Samson replied: “Yes, lord. Without doubt I faithfully commend this man; I rightly place him above myself and men like myself [Col. 0347B]. He is mild and kindly, and therefore more worthy of the episcopal office. Let his bodily thinness not make him contemptible. His humble dress makes him more acceptable to the wise. God does not look merely upon outward things, but beholds what lies hidden within.”

The prudent king listened attentively to the wise man’s words and began to consider them shrewdly. Returning to himself, he gradually restrained his scattered thoughts by the bond of reason; he immediately summoned the named clerk before him and entrusted him with the care and temporal jurisdiction of the bishopric of Le Mans. The king’s decree was communicated to the clergy, and the good-life testimony concerning the aforesaid clerk was examined by those who knew him. For so pure and straightforward an election, the faithful offered devout praise to God [Col. 0347C], and the elected shepherd was honourably conducted to the folds of his sheep by bishops and other faithful persons to whom this had been commanded by the king.

Yet he was no less amazed at this sudden elevation to the episcopate than David had been at his advancement to the kingdom, after Samuel rejected his elder brothers. Thus Hoel became bishop of Le Mans and discharged the episcopal office holy for fifteen years. He began to build the episcopal basilica, in which rests the body of Saint Julian the Confessor, the first bishop of Le Mans, along with other good works necessary for God’s Church; and as circumstances allowed, he strove to complete what he had begun. After his death the distinguished poet Hildebert succeeded him and commendably held the episcopal office for almost thirty years [Col. 0347D]. He completed the episcopal basilica begun by his predecessor and dedicated it reverently amid the great rejoicing of the people. Not long afterward, namely in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1125, in the fourth indiction, when Gislebert, archbishop of Tours, died at Rome with Pope Callistus II, he ascended the metropolitan see of the city of Tours under Pope Honorius, compelled by the prayers and commands of Holy Church; and there he still applies himself to praiseworthy studies and deeds.

XVIII. Herbert, count of Le Mans. Disturbances in Maine.

Just as the sea never rests safely in fixed solidity, but flows according to its nature disturbed by ceaseless agitation, and, though at times it appears calm to those who look upon it [Col. 0348A], nevertheless terrifies sailors by its customary surging and instability; so the present age is continually vexed by its mutability and plainly changed in countless ways, sad or joyful. Among the insolent lovers of the world, for whom the world itself is not enough, a monstrous quarrel often arises and grows without measure. While each strives to be superior and crush his rival, forgetful of equity he transgresses God’s law; and human blood is cruelly shed in pursuit of that which each man desires to obtain. The ancient books of historians report this abundantly; modern reports affirm it unceasingly through lanes and streets. Hence some now rejoice, while others nevertheless weep and grieve. I have briefly touched on certain such events in this little book of ours [Col. 0348B], and I wish truthfully to add others, as I learned them from elders.

Herbert, count of Le Mans, traced his descent, it is said, from the lineage of Charlemagne, and deserved to be called by the common, though not very Latin, name “Wake-the-Dog” (*Evigilans-Canem*) on account of his great valour. For after the death of his father Hugh, whom Fulk the Elder had violently subjected to himself, Herbert took up arms against the same Fulk, frequently made night expeditions, frightened men and dogs of Anjou in the city itself or in the more fortified towns, and compelled the terrified to keep watch under dreadful assaults.

Hugh, Herbert’s son, after Alan, count of the Bretons, died in Normandy after being poisoned by the Normans [Col. 0348C], married Alan’s widow Bertha, sister of Theobald, count of Blois. She bore him a son named Herbert and three daughters. One of these was given to Azzone, marquis of Liguria. Another, named Margaret, was betrothed to Robert, son of William, duke of Neustria; she died a virgin under the guardianship of that duke. The third married John, lord of the castle called La Flèche; she bore her husband three children, Goisbert, Elias, and Enoch.

After the death of Geoffrey Martel, the most powerful count of Anjou, he was succeeded through his sister by two nephews, sons of Alberic, count of Gâtinais. Of these, Geoffrey, simple and tractable in disposition, obtained the principality by right of primogeniture. But William [Col. 0348D], prince of the Normans, acquired Herbert the younger’s inheritance after his death; and Count Geoffrey granted Robert the younger, together with Herbert’s daughter, the entire honour, receiving from him homage and the due fealty in the presence of his father at Alençon. Not long afterwards Fulk, surnamed Rechin, rebelled against Geoffrey, his brother and lord; he captured him by treachery and kept him imprisoned in the castle of Chinon for more than thirty years. Amid so great a change, worldly affairs in Anjou and its borderlands were thrown into disorder, and the nobles of the country turned to diverse pursuits as each was led by his own will.

Because Fulk was greatly distressed that the Normans ruled at Le Mans [Col. 0349A] and possessed, against his wishes, a county which he claimed as his right, seditious citizens, neighbouring townsmen, and common soldiers unanimously formed a plan against the foreigners. Armed, they boldly surrounded the city’s citadel and other fortifications, attacked and expelled Turgis of Tracy, William of La Ferté, and other royal garrison commanders. Some who resisted them stoutly they killed; others they cruelly cast into chains. Triumphantly asserting their liberty, they took such vengeance upon the Normans. Then the entire region was disturbed, Norman power there was obscured, and it was attacked everywhere by almost everyone as though by a general plague. Geoffrey of Mayenne and other nobles of Le Mans rose in a like conspiracy against the Normans. Some, however, though few [Col. 0349B], supported and obeyed King William because of differing circumstances and motives.

The magnanimous King William, hearing the dreadful reports of the slaughter of his men, became angry and prepared to restrain the enemy’s invasion and exact by arms the deserved punishment for the traitors’ rebellion. By royal command he swiftly summoned Normans and Englishmen, assembled many legions of armed men into one body, prudently arranged cavalry and infantry with their commanders for war, and came in terrible array with them into the district of Le Mans. First he besieged the castle of Fresnay with his force and there girded Robert of Bellême with the belt of knighthood. Hubert, however, a townsman, made peace with the king [Col. 0349C], surrendered his castles of Fresnay and Beaumont, and thereafter served him for some time. The king then besieged Sillé; but the lord of the castle humbly sought the king and obtained the peace he desired.

No one dared resist the king as he advanced with such immense power. All townsmen and country people, with the clergy and all religious persons, resolved worthily to receive the peaceful ruler and gladly submit their necks to his lawful authority. At length the king came to Le Mans, besieged the city with many companies, made his royal edicts known to his men at a suitable moment, and imperiously ordered the townspeople to take prudent counsel and surrender the city to him peacefully before assaults, killings, and burnings occurred. The next day, having adopted sound advice, the citizens came out and humbly brought the keys of the city to the king; surrendering themselves, they were received graciously by him [Col. 0349D]. The remaining people of Le Mans were terrified when they saw so great a flood of a mighty army spread through their territories, and now knew that their accomplices and supporters had failed before the face of that most proven warrior. They too sent envoys of peace to the victor; joining hands on both sides, they joyfully united their banners with the royal standards. Thereafter they were permitted to dwell and, if they wished, to enjoy themselves in peace, each in his own house and beneath his vine.

Thus the people of Le Mans were pacified without great loss and lived peacefully under the authority of King William. But Count Fulk, wickedly infected by harmful envy, attempted to rise against certain supporters of the Normans [Col. 0350A]. John of La Flèche, one of the most powerful men of Anjou, was then especially hostile to him because he adhered to the Normans. When John learned for certain that the aforesaid count was hastening against him with armoured forces, he sought out allied kinsmen and requested and obtained King William’s help. The energetic King William sent John William de Moulins, Robert de Vieux-Pont, and other very brave warriors who had been tested many times. John carefully stationed them with his own retainers to defend his towns.

When Fulk heard this, he was greatly distressed and, having gathered forces from every quarter, besieged John’s castle. Count Hoel too came to Fulk’s assistance with a multitude of Bretons and strove with him fiercely to constrain John’s power and resources [Col. 0350B]. When King William learned that so great a multitude had surrounded his men, he again summoned Normans and Englishmen by royal edict, assembled other peoples subject to him like a strong commander, and, as they say, led sixty thousand horsemen with him against the hostile formations. But the men of Anjou and the Bretons, learning of the king’s arrival with his army, did not flee. Instead, they boldly crossed the river Loire; once across, they destroyed their boats, lest the hope of flight make the more timid fight less vigorously.

As both battle-lines prepared for an uncertain engagement, and dreadful fears concerning death and the miseries that follow the death of the wicked filled many minds, a cardinal-priest of the Roman Church and religious monks arrived by divine prompting [Col. 0350C]. Divinely inspired, they approached the leaders of both armies, beseeched and rebuked them. Individually, on God’s behalf, they forbade war and urged peace by admonition and prayer. William of Évreux, Roger, other counts, and vigorous nobles gladly joined them. As these men had been ready and bold for lawful contests, so they rightly shuddered to enter into detestable conflicts through pride and injustice. Therefore, while Christ’s messengers sowed the seeds of peace, the excessive swelling of the ambitious subsided, and the pallid fear of the frightened gradually diminished. At last many consultations were held, various negotiations conducted, and words opposed to words; but God prevailed, and envoys of peace were received on both sides.

The count of Anjou granted Robert the younger, the king’s son, the jurisdiction of Le Mans with the entire honour which Robert had received from Count Herbert together with his betrothed Margaret [Col. 0350D]. Finally Robert lawfully rendered Fulk the homage due from a lesser to a greater. John and the other men of Anjou, who until then had rebelled against their count on the king’s behalf, were reconciled to their ruler; likewise the people of Le Mans, who had risen against the king for the count, were pacified. Thus, by God’s grace softening the hearts of princes, the guilt of penitents on both sides was pardoned; and the well-disposed peoples openly rejoiced as clear peace drove far away the stormy blackness of tumults. This peace, made between the king and the aforesaid count at the place commonly called Blancalande [Col. 0351A] or Bruyère, endured throughout the king’s lifetime for the benefit of both provinces.

XIX. The rebellion of Counts Roger of Hereford and Ralph of Norwich against King William. The punishment of Count Waltheof.

But at the same time another most grievous storm arose, exceedingly savage and harmful to many in England. Two most powerful English counts, Roger of Hereford and his brother-in-law Ralph of Norwich, jointly resolved openly to rebel and, after taking the sovereignty of England from King William, to assume for themselves a right—or rather, a tyranny [Note: [Col. 0351C] Henry of Huntingdon assigns the date of this conspiracy: “In the ninth year of King William,” he says, “that is, A.D. 1075, Ralph, to whom the king had given the earldom of East Anglia, planned beforehand to expel the king from the kingdom, with the counsel of Earl Waltheof and Roger, son of William FitzOsbern. Ralph had married the sister of this Roger; and at the wedding itself they proclaimed this treason.”

Roger of Howden: “In the year 1074, in which Pope Hildebrand held a Roman council, Roger, earl of Hereford, son of William, earl of the East Angles, gave his sister in marriage to Earl Ralph contrary to the command of King William; and, celebrating magnificent nuptials with a very great multitude of nobles . . . [Col. 0351D], they formed a great conspiracy against King William, with very many consenting, and compelled Earl Waltheof, caught unawares by their plots, to swear conspiracy with them.”

Add William of Malmesbury, *De gestis regum Anglorum*, book III: “Ralph of Gaël,” he says, “was by the king’s gift earl of Norfolk and Suffolk, a Breton in part, with a mind twisted away from every good. Since he had betrothed a kinswoman of the king, daughter of William FitzOsbern, he entertained ambitions beyond what was proper and meditated embarking upon tyranny. Therefore, on the very day of the wedding, a banquet was held with great display . . . When the guests were drunk and swollen with wine, he set forth his purpose in a long speech. Since all reason was clouded in their minds by drink, they loudly applauded as he spoke. There were Earl Roger of Hereford, Ralph’s wife’s brother; there was Waltheof; and there besides very many others conspired to kill the king.” Dom Bouquet, book IV, p. 593.].

Accordingly they strengthened their castles in rivalry, prepared arms, gathered soldiers, frequently sent envoys to neighbours and distant persons in whom they trusted, and invited by promises and prayers all whom they could into their support [Col. 0351B]. Considering changes in circumstances and opportunities of the times, they said to their confederates and supporters: “All wise men determine that one must wait for a fitting time, and that when a welcome and favourable time comes, men of worth should illustriously begin a famous undertaking. For attaining the glory of a kingdom, we have never seen a time more suitable than that now granted us by God’s ineffable gift. The man called king is base-born, as being a bastard; and it is plainly shown by God that he displeases God, since such a master presides over the kingdom. He is surrounded on every side by conflicts beyond the sea; he is attacked not only by outsiders but even by his own offspring, and is abandoned amid dangers by his own dependants. This has been deserved by his wickedness, which has been too widely made known throughout the world. For he disinherited William Guerleng, count of Mortain, over a single word and drove him entirely out of Neustria [Note: [Col. 0352C] William of Jumièges, book VII, chapter 33, testifies likewise: “At the time when Duke William was preparing to go to England and claim it for himself by arms, the bold Conan, count of Brittany, tried to frighten him by sending this embassy: ‘I hear,’ he said, ‘that you now wish to cross the sea and acquire for yourself the kingdom of England. But Robert, duke of the Normans, whom you pretend was your father, when departing for Jerusalem entrusted his whole inheritance to my father Alan, his own cousin. You and your accomplices, however, poisoned and killed my father Alan at Winmusterium (Fiscannum) in Normandy, and invaded his land, which I, because I was a boy, could not possess. Therefore either restore to me the Normandy due to me, or I shall make war upon you with all my strength.’

“On hearing this, Duke William was somewhat alarmed; but God soon deigned to deliver him when the enemy’s threats came to nothing. For one of the Breton nobles, who had sworn fealty to both counts and carried such messages between them, smeared poison inside Conan’s hunting-horn, reins, and gloves; he was Conan’s chamberlain. At that time the same Breton count was besieging Château-Gontier in the county of Anjou; and, when the soldiers of the town surrendered to him, he was bringing in his own men. Meanwhile Conan carelessly put on his gloves; having touched the reins, he raised his hand to his mouth. By that touch he was poisoned, and soon afterwards died, while all his men mourned.” Ibid., book IV, p. 593.]; he lodged Walter, count of Pontoise [Col. 0352A], nephew of King Edward, at Falaise together with his wife Biota, and killed both of them on the same night by a wicked potion. He also poisoned the very vigorous Count Conan, whose death all Brittany mourned with unspeakable grief because of his great valour. William committed these and many other crimes against his kinsmen and relatives, and he does not cease to commit similar deeds against us and our peers. He rashly invaded the noble kingdom of England, unjustly slaughtered the rightful heirs or cruelly drove them into exile. Nor did he honour as was fitting those helpers through whom he was exalted above his entire lineage; rather, he was ungrateful to many who shed their blood in his service, and for trivial pretexts punished them as enemies even to death. To wounded victors [Col. 0352B] he gave barren estates desolated by the enemy’s ravaging, then later, when restored, took them away or diminished them under the compulsion of avarice. Therefore all hate him, and if he perished, many would rejoice. Behold, the greater part of his army remains beyond the sea, held fast in fierce and continual wars. The English cultivate only their fields; they attend to feasting and drinking, not battles. Yet they ardently desire to see vengeance for the ruin of their parents.”

Thus spoke the rebels and others like them, encouraging themselves in every way toward their desired crime. They summoned Count Waltheof of Northampton to a conference and, trying him in many ways, said: “Behold, brave man, you now see the much-desired time in which to recover the honours taken from you and exact the vengeance due for the injuries recently inflicted upon you. Agree with us and adhere to us unceasingly, and without doubt you will be able to have with us a third part of England. For we wish the condition of the kingdom of Albion to be restored in every respect, as it once was in the time of the most pious King Edward [Col. 0352C]. Let one of us be king and two dukes; and thus all English honours will be subject to us three. William is overwhelmed beyond the sea by countless burdens of war, and we know for certain that he will not return to England again. Come, noble hero: prudently secure what is most advantageous to yourself and your family, and what will bring salvation to all your people, who have been laid low.”

Waltheof answered: “The greatest caution is necessary in such matters, and every man must preserve whole faith toward his lord among every people. King William lawfully received my fealty, as a greater from a lesser, and joined me in marriage to his niece so that I might always remain faithful to him. He also gave me a rich county and numbered me among his familiar companions at table [Col. 0353B]. How then can I be faithless to so great a prince unless I choose utterly to betray my pledged faith? I am known in many regions, and—may it never happen!—it would be great disgrace if I were publicly proclaimed a sacrilegious traitor. Nowhere has a good song been sung of a traitor. All peoples curse an apostate and traitor like a wolf, judge and subdue him as worthy of hanging, and, if occasion permits, fasten him to the gallows amid shame and many reproaches. Ahithophel and Judas devised the crime of betrayal, and by the same punishment of hanging, worthy neither of heaven nor of earth, killed themselves. English law punishes a traitor by decapitation and wholly deprives all his descendants of their natural inheritance. Far be it that my nobility should be stained by wicked treason and that so shameful an infamy concerning me should be proclaimed throughout the world. The Lord God, who powerfully delivered David from the hand of Goliath and Saul, Hadadezer and Absalom, has freely delivered me too from many dangers on sea and land. I faithfully commit myself to him, and confidently hope in him that I shall not commit treason in my life nor, through apostasy, become like the angel of Satan [Col. 0353C].”

The Breton Ralph and Roger, hearing this, were greatly distressed; and by a terrible oath of conspiracy they bound him not to disclose their counsel. Not long afterward the conspiracy of rebellion suddenly broke out through the regions of England, and open opposition to the royal officers spread widely. William de Warenne and Richard de Bienfaite, son of Count Gilbert, whom the king had made chief justiciars of England in the affairs of the realm [Col. 0353D], summoned the rebels to the king’s court. They, however, scorned to obey their commands; attempting to carry on their insolence, they chose to fight the king’s forces. Without delay William and Richard assembled the army of England and fought fiercely against the rebels in the field called Fagaduna. By God’s power they defeated those opposing them and, having captured all, of whatever rank, cut off their right feet as a mark of identification.

They pursued the Breton Ralph as he fled to his castle, but could not capture him. Then, gathering a multitude, they besieged and attacked Norwich, strengthened their allies by courage and military skill, surrounded the enclosed enemies with repeated assaults and varied engines of war, and pressed and exhausted them relentlessly for three months [Col. 0354A]. The avenging army outside daily increased and gained strength, and abundant supplies of food and other things were provided to them lest they depart through want. Ralph de Gaël, seeing himself so confined by the siege and expecting no help from his accomplices, cautiously entrusted his fortress to loyal guards; he himself entered the nearby sea and sailed to Denmark for assistance. Meanwhile the king’s deputies William and Richard compelled the townsmen to surrender; sending messengers across the sea, they urgently begged the king, on account of the disturbances described above, to return quickly for the protection of his realm [Col. 0354B].

The energetic king, when he heard the messages of his men, prudently arranged affairs in Normandy and Maine; having put everything in the best order, he swiftly crossed to England. After summoning all the nobles of the kingdom to his court, he greeted with kind words the lawful heroes and those proved faithful; but he reasonably asked the instigators and supporters of rebellion why they preferred wickedness to justice. Norwich was surrendered, its garrison having made peace with the king; and Ralph de Gaël, earl of Norwich, was forever disinherited from England. Expelled, he returned with his wife to Brittany. There his excellent castles of Gaël and Montfort lay under his authority, and his children possess them by hereditary right to this day [Col. 0354C]. After many years, in the time of Pope Urban, he took up the cross of the Lord, went with Robert II, duke of the Normans, against the Turks to Jerusalem, and died with his wife as a penitent and pilgrim on the way of God.

Roger of Breteuil, earl of Hereford, was summoned to the king’s court and came; when examined, he could not deny treason manifest to the whole world. Therefore he was judged according to the laws of the Normans, lost all earthly inheritance, and was condemned to perpetual imprisonment in the king’s prison. There also he repeatedly slandered the king and offended him irreconcilably by obstinate conduct. For once, while the people of God were duly celebrating the feast of Easter and the king sent to Earl Roger in prison, through suitable attendants, a set of precious garments [Col. 0354D], Roger ordered a huge pyre prepared before him and immediately burned there the royal ornaments: the cloak, silk tunic, and furred robe of precious skins of foreign mice. When the king heard this, he angrily said: “He is very proud, since he has done me this dishonour; but by the splendour of God, he shall not leave my prison throughout my lifetime.” The king’s sentence remained so fixed that Roger did not leave his chains, even after the king’s death, except as a dead man. His sons Rainald and Roger, excellent young knights, serve King Henry and await his mercy—mercy which has seemed very slow to them—in severe struggles.

Truly, the glory of the world falls and withers like the flower of hay, [Col. 0355A] and like smoke it fails and passes away. Where is William, son of Osbern, Earl of Hereford and the king’s viceroy, steward of Normandy and warlike commander of soldiers? He was indeed the first and greatest oppressor of the English [Note: [Col. 0355D] The notice concerning the foundation of the monastery of Blessed Mary of Lyre asserts the same: When William, Duke of the Normans, had sought counsel and heard that all the barons of Normandy were unanimous in favour of conquering England, he rejoiced greatly. When they again assembled to deliberate, William, the duke’s steward, son of Osbern, was present. Declaring the expedition for taking England, and the English nation, to be exceedingly formidable, he argued most vigorously against the very few who wished to go into England. [Col. 0356D] When the magnates heard this, they rejoiced greatly and pledged him their word that they would all agree to whatever he said. Then, coming before them at daybreak, he said: “I am prepared to set out on this expedition with all my followers.” Therefore all the Norman princes had to support his proposal, as they had promised him. Among the documents of the *Gallia Christiana Nova*, vol. XI, col. 123. Dom Bouquet, book IV, p. 595.], and through his rashness he fostered an enormous cause, by which the ruin of a wretched death fell upon many thousands. Yet the just Judge sees all things and fittingly repays each person according to his deserts. Alas for grief! Behold, William fell: the bold champion received what he had deserved. As he slaughtered many with the sword, so he too suddenly perished by the sword. Finally, before five years had elapsed after his fall, the spirit of discord stirred up his son and son-in-law in hostility against their lord and kinsman, just as it stirred up the Shechemites against Abimelech, [Col. 0355B] whom they had set over themselves after killing the seventy sons of Jerubbaal.

Behold, the offence has been truthfully described by me, for which William’s offspring was so uprooted from England that, unless I am mistaken, it now possesses not even a footstep of land there.

Earl Waltheof was summoned before the king and, through the accusation of his wife Judith, was charged with having known of and supported the aforesaid treason, and with having proved unfaithful to his lord. He, however, fearlessly acknowledged publicly that he had heard from them the most wicked purpose of the traitors; but that in so heinous a matter he had given them no assent whatsoever. Upon this confession an inquiry was held, and, as the judges [Col. 0355C] disagreed among themselves, it was prolonged through several adjournments until the following year. Meanwhile the aforesaid hero was in the king’s prison at Winchester, and often bewailed his sins, recounting them there frequently and weeping to devout bishops and abbots. Thus, for the space of one year, he did penance at the priests’ counsel, and every day in prayer sang to God the one hundred and fifty Psalms of David which he had learned in childhood. This man was large and handsome in body, surpassing many thousands in generosity and courage; he was a devout worshipper of God, a humble hearer of priests and of all religious persons, and a kindly lover of the Church and of the poor. For these and many other gifts which he especially possessed in the lay estate, he was greatly beloved by his own people and by foreigners who knew how to love what pleases God; [Col. 0355D] and during the year-long delay every possible effort was made to procure his release from prison. At last a powerful gathering of his enemies assembled at the royal court, and after many deliberations it was decided that he was guilty of death: he had consented to companions discussing the death of their lord, and had neither struck them down [Col. 0356A] for plotting their lord’s destruction nor revealed their criminal conspiracy by an open denunciation. Without delay, Waltheof was led by the Normans—who greatly feared his escape and desired to acquire his estates and rich honours—outside the city of Winchester, in the morning while the people still slept, to the hill where the church of Saint Giles, abbot and confessor, now stands. There he devoutly distributed the clothes in which he had gone forth honourably dressed as an earl to the clerics and poor persons who happened to be present at the spectacle; then, prostrating himself on the ground, he prayed to the Lord for a long time with tears and sobs.

When the executioners feared that the citizens might be roused and obstruct the king’s command, and, coming to the aid of so noble a fellow-countryman, kill the royal officers, they said to the prostrate earl: “Rise, [Col. 0356B] that we may fulfil our lord’s command.” He replied: “Wait a little, for Almighty God’s mercy, at least until I say for myself and for you the Lord’s Prayer.” They permitted this. He rose and, kneeling only, with his eyes fixed upon heaven and his hands outstretched, began aloud: “Our Father, who art in heaven.” When he reached the final clause and had said, “And lead us not into temptation,” abundant tears burst forth with lamentation and did not allow him to finish the prayer he had begun. But the executioner was unwilling to wait longer: drawing his sword, he struck forcefully and cut off the earl’s head. After it had been severed, the head said in a clear and articulate voice, heard by all [Col. 0356C] who were present: “But deliver us from evil. Amen.” Thus Earl Waltheof was beheaded at Winchester on the second day before the Kalends of May, in the morning. His body was thrown contemptuously into a pit there and hastily covered with green turf. When the citizens awoke and learned the reports, they were deeply grieved; men and women raised a great lament over the fall of Earl Waltheof. After fifteen days, at Judith’s request and by the king’s permission, Ulfketel, abbot of Crowland, came and took up the corpse, which was still whole and fresh with blood, as if the man had died that very moment. With the great mourning of many, he conveyed it to the monastery of Crowland and reverently buried it in the chapter-house of the monks.

## XX. Life of Guthlac the Hermit

[Col. 0356D] I now wish to insert into this little work an abridgment which I recently made, at the request of the venerable Prior Wulfino, from the life of Saint Guthlac the hermit.

A certain Felix, bishop of the East Angles, Burgundian by nation but venerable for holiness, [Col. 0357A] composed the deeds of the most holy anchorite in an extended and somewhat obscure style. At the kindly request of the brethren, with whom I stayed five weeks at Crowland by the charitable command of the venerable Abbot Geoffrey, I have clarified them briefly to the best of my ability. The occasion for speaking of the blessed hermit arose in our narrative through Earl Waltheof, who was a faithful brother and helper of the monastery of Crowland, as I shall truthfully set forth at the end of this epitome from the account of the elders. I firmly believe that the holy deeds of the Saxons or English beyond the Alps will profit the faithful on this side of the Alps no less than those of Greeks or Egyptians, concerning whom lengthy but delightful and profitable compilations are frequently read, gathered through the zeal of learned saints. Moreover, [Col. 0357B] I think that the less this matter was formerly known among our people, the more pleasingly it will be received by those burning with the fire of charity and grieving from their inmost heart over sins already committed.

In the time of Æthelred, king of the English, Guthlac was born of his father Penwald, of the lineage of Icel, lord of the Mercians, and of his mother Tette. At his birth a heavenly portent was openly displayed to the people: from the clouds a hand was stretched toward a cross, which appeared to stand before the door of the house where Tette was giving birth. After eight days the child was baptized and named Guthlac—that is, “gift of battle”—from the tribe called the Guthlacingas. After a gentle childhood, when he felt the ardour of youth and considered the brave deeds of heroes, he gathered companies of retainers and turned to arms. He devastated and destroyed with fire and sword [Col. 0357C] the villages and fortresses of those opposed to him; and, after plundering immense spoils, he voluntarily restored for God’s love a third part to those from whom it had been taken. Then, after nine years in which he had grievously afflicted his enemies with slaughter and robbery, he reflected upon the frailty of mortal life and the instability of transient things. Alarmed, he returned to himself, examined himself as though he saw death before his eyes, and strove to enter upon the path of a more reformed life. He therefore left his accomplices, despised for Christ’s sake his parents, homeland, and companions of youth, and, in the twenty-fourth year of his age, renouncing worldly pomp, went to the monastery of Repton. There, under the abbess named Ælfthryth, he received the tonsure and [Col. 0357D] clerical habit. Thereafter he avoided drunkenness and every form of excess with all his strength, and devoted himself, as far as humanly possible, to every kind of uprightness and religious observance. For two years he was instructed in sacred letters and monastic disciplines, but he was not satisfied with these alone. For he sought to undertake the distinctive contest of the eremitical life, in which he wrestled hand-to-hand with the enemy.

At last, having obtained permission from the elders, he was brought by a fisherman named Tatwine in a little boat to the island called Crowland. In the inland regions of England lies a vast and most forbidding marsh, beginning at the banks of the River Granta and extending from south to north in a very long course as far as the sea, now in pools, now in marshy flats, sometimes in dark waters, and amid frequent wooded islands and the winding turns of streams. [Col. 0358A] Many had tried to live there, but had abandoned the gloomy dwelling because of the unknown monsters of the wilderness and terrifying shapes of many kinds. Guthlac therefore explored Crowland in summer, then set out to revisit his brethren and masters whom he had left without farewell. Three months later he returned, with two boys, to the chosen wilderness, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, when he was twenty-six years old. At that time the feast of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle is celebrated; Guthlac most earnestly prayed to him as his companion and helper in every adversity. For fifteen years he wore not woollen or linen garments but coverings of skins alone, and he took only a little barley bread and muddy water, after sunset. Satan tempted him in countless ways and laboured to ensnare him or drive him from the wilderness.

Once, when for three days he was weary with despair over the work he had undertaken, behold: Bartholomew, his faithful helper, visibly appeared at the morning watches; strengthening the frightened man with spiritual commands, he promised him help in all things and faithfully fulfilled his promise in many temptations.

On another day two demons came to him in human appearance, tempting him and urging him, by excessive fasting, to imitate Moses, Elijah, and the other Egyptian fathers. But he, singing psalms in contempt of them, [Col. 0358C] began to eat a portion of barley bread.

At another time, while the man of God was perseveringly engaged in prayers during the dead of night, he saw companies of demons entering his cell from every side. Binding his limbs, they led him outside his cell and plunged him into the muddy marsh. Then they carried him through the harshest places of the marsh among dense thorny thickets; after tearing his limbs, they ordered him to leave the wilderness. When he refused, they beat him with iron whips and, after enormous torments, bore him aloft among the storm-clouded regions of the cold air. From there, countless bands of demons arriving from the north threatened him even to the jaws of Tartarus. Guthlac then, seeing the punishments of Gehenna, was terrified; yet, scorning the demons’ threats, [Col. 0358D] he sighed from the depths of his heart to God. Without delay Saint Bartholomew, shining with heavenly light, came to him and commanded that he be restored in great peace to his own dwelling by those enemies. Groaning, they obeyed the apostle’s commands, while angels rejoicingly sang sweetly to meet him: “The saints shall go from strength to strength” (Psalm 83:8).

The demons often endeavoured in many ways to terrify Guthlac, but, with the Lord’s help, he frustrated them and all their contrivances. Fearless, he stood in the citadel of virtues, endured hard labours in the struggle, and overthrew diabolical attacks. In the time of Coenred, king of the Mercians, Beccelinus [Note: [Col. 0357D] Read: *Beccelinus*. Le Prévost.] the cleric, [Col. 0359A] incited by a demon to kill the man of God while cutting his hair, was rebuked by him for harbouring so great a crime in his heart. As soon as he saw that he had been anticipated, he blushed, fell at the saint’s feet, confessed his crime, begged forgiveness, and, having received pardon, promised that he would be his companion.

A raven dropped a stolen little sheet in the middle of the marsh; yet, through the merits of the man of God, the water did not damage it as it hung upon a reed. He returned it unharmed to its grieving writer.

Two ravens living on the island were very hostile to blessed Guthlac, so that whatever they could break, drown, carry off, or defile, they would recklessly ruin, cursing it indoors and out. The man of God bore them kindly [Col. 0359B] through the virtue of patience. Birds of the uncultivated wilderness and fishes wandering through the muddy marsh came swiftly, flying and swimming, to his voice as to a shepherd, and received food from his hand according to the need of each creature’s nature.

While the venerable man Wilfrid was present, two swallows joyfully visited Guthlac according to their nature, settling with song upon his arms, knees, and breast. He placed a straw in a little window and thus indicated a nest for the birds in his cell. For they did not dare to build their nests in Guthlac’s hut without his permission.

Once, when the aforesaid Wilfrid had brought the exile Æthelbald to the man of God, he forgot his sleeves in the boat in which they had arrived, and rapacious ravens carried them away. The man of God, sitting in the entrance of his house, immediately recognized this in the Spirit of God and mentioned it to Wilfrid in the course of their conversation. Not long afterward, through the power of faith and prayer, he made good the loss.

Wehtred, a distinguished young man of the East Angles, was possessed by a demon and miserably tormented for four years. He tore himself and all whom he could reach with wood, iron, nails, and teeth. Once, when a crowd tried to bind him, he seized a battle-axe and killed three men. After four years he was brought to Crowland. Taking him by the hand, the man of God led him into his oratory and, fasting and praying continuously there for three days, healed him of every disturbance [Col. 0359D] caused by the evil spirit.

Egga, companion of the aforesaid exile Æthelbald, was possessed by an unclean spirit, so that he did not know at all what he was, where he sat, or what he did. His companions brought him to Guthlac’s threshold. Then, as soon as he girded himself with the belt of the man of God, he regained his sound mind and thereafter kept both that belt and his sane mind throughout his life.

Moreover, Guthlac, the man of God, being endowed with the spirit of prophecy, was accustomed to foretell future things and to report absent matters to those present. To a certain abbot who had come to him for devout conversation, he related in full order the matter of two clerics who, before the third hour, had turned aside to a widow’s house in pursuit of drunkenness.

[Col. 0360A] He rebuked two other brethren because they had hidden beneath the marsh sand two flasks filled with ale; and when they marvelled at the man of God’s great discernment and fell to the ground, he kindly pardoned them.

As the fame of blessed Guthlac quickly flew far and wide, many persons of different ranks came to him—abbots, monks, earls, rich people, afflicted people, and poor people—from the neighbouring borders of Mercia and from parts of Britain, seeking health of body or soul. Each one beneficially obtained the thing for which he had come in faith. The sick received a remedy, the sorrowful joy, the penitent consolation, and every anxious person relief through the man of God’s conversation and effective prayer.

Obba, companion of the distinguished exile Æthelbald, while walking through [Col. 0360B] rough country fields, was wounded in the foot by the prick of a thorn concealed under the grass of the untilled ground. His whole body swelled from the sole of the foot to the loins, and the new pain allowed him to sit, stand, or lie quietly in no position. Thus he barely reached Crowland. As soon as he was brought to the man of God and the cause of his suffering was related in order, Guthlac wrapped him in the sheepskin garment in which he was accustomed to pray. Immediately, faster than speech, the little thorn sprang out of his foot like an arrow released from a bow. In that same hour, when all the swelling had subsided, the sick man recovered; joyfully, with those who had seen it, he gave thanks to God.

Once Bishop Headda came to Guthlac with certain clerics and laymen, among whom there was incidental conversation on various matters concerning the blessed man. But the aforesaid bishop, [Col. 0360C] having learned the brilliance of divine grace in the venerable man and his abundance of wisdom in expounding the holy Scriptures, dedicated the church of the island of Crowland on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September. Then, by an inviolable command of obedience, he compelled the same servant of God to receive the rank of priesthood. Thereupon the holy man was compelled, contrary to his custom, to attend the bishop’s meal. When he saw the scribe Wigfrid sitting at a distance, he began to ask him about the promise he had made the day before, boasting to his companions on the road that he would test whether the same man possessed true or feigned religion. Wigfrid immediately blushed and, falling to the ground, sought and obtained pardon. All marvelled that their entire conversation on the road had been clearly revealed to the man of God through the Spirit [Col. 0360D].

The most reverend Abbess Egburgh, daughter of King Aldwulf, humbly petitioned through a messenger. Guthlac received from her a lead coffin and, in it, linen in which to be wrapped after death. When she asked who would be heir of that place after him, he replied that he was still a pagan. And so it came to pass: Cissa, who succeeded him in possession of his seat, received baptism in Britain some years later.

The prince Æthelbald, whom King Ceolred was pursuing here and there, came as usual to the man of God amid doubtful dangers, when his own strength and that of his followers had failed, so that divine counsel might be present where human counsel was wanting. Blessed Guthlac kindly consoled him and, through the Spirit of God, promised him lordship [Col. 0361A] over his own nation, rule over peoples, and the trampling-down of his enemies; and promised that he would have all these things not by force of arms or shedding of blood but from the hand of the Lord. Everything was fulfilled in the order in which the man of God had foretold it. For King Ceolred died, and Æthelbald acquired his kingdom.

## XXI. Death of Blessed Guthlac the Hermit; Miracles and Portents at the Saint’s Tomb; Building of the Monastery of Crowland

After completing fifteen years in the wilderness, the venerable Guthlac began to fall ill on the Wednesday before Easter. On Easter Day, nevertheless, rising beyond his strength, he sang Mass. On the seventh day of his illness he commanded his servant Beccel [Col. 0361B] to arrange that his sister Pega should come there after his death, and that she should wrap his body in a shroud in the sarcophagus which Egburgh had sent him. Then Beccel began to entreat the man of God under adjuration to tell him before his burial who it was whom he heard speaking with him every day, morning and evening. The gracious champion of God, after pausing briefly and breathing heavily, said: “My son, do not trouble yourself about this matter. What I was unwilling to reveal to any human being while living, I shall now make known to you. From the second year in which I began to inhabit this wilderness, the Lord always sent the angel of my consolation to speak with me morning and evening. He showed me mysteries which it is not permitted for a human being to tell; he lightened the harshness of my labour by heavenly revelations; by showing me absent things, [Col. 0361C] he made them present to me. O son, preserve these words of mine and report them to no one else except Pega or Egbert the anchorite.” When he had spoken thus, a sweet odour was perceived to issue from his mouth, so that a nectar-like fragrance filled the whole house. On the following night, while the aforesaid brother was occupied with the night vigils, he saw the whole house surrounded by fiery brightness from midnight until dawn. At sunrise, the man of God, raising himself somewhat as if to rise and stretching out his hands toward the altar, strengthened himself with communion of Christ’s body and blood. Then, lifting his eyes to heaven and stretching his hands upward, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 715 [Note: [Col. 0361D] Read: 714. (Le Prévost.)], he gave up his soul to everlasting joy.

[Col. 0361D] Meanwhile Beccel saw the house filled with heavenly splendour and a tower as though of fire raised from earth to heaven, in comparison with which the sun seemed to grow pale like a lamp in daylight. He also heard the whole expanse of the air resounding with angelic songs, while the island was fragrant with the scented breaths of diverse spices. The aforesaid brother, therefore, greatly terrified and unable to bear the extraordinary brilliance, took a boat and went to Pega, Christ’s virgin, recounting to her in order the brother’s commands. Hearing these things, she groaned deeply. The next day she came with the aforesaid brother to Crowland and, on the third day, buried the blessed limbs in the oratory according to his command, [Col. 0362A] where afterward the Lord performed many miracles of healing the sick because of the merits of His friend.

On Saint Guthlac’s anniversary, his sister Pega assembled priests and other men of ecclesiastical rank and opened his tomb to transfer his body to another mausoleum. They then found the whole body intact, as though he still lived; and all the garments in which it was wrapped shone with their original brightness in an ageless newness. As all marvelled, were amazed, and trembled at the miracle they saw, Pega, spiritually moved, reverently wrapped the sacred body anew in the shroud which Egbert the anchorite had sent for this purpose while Guthlac was alive. She placed the sarcophagus above the ground as a memorial, [Col. 0362B] where it rests honourably to this day.

When the aforesaid exile Æthelbald heard of the holy man’s death, he went there mourning. After tears and a long prayer, while sleeping in the nearby hut, the holy man appeared to him, consoled him, and promised him the royal sceptre before the year’s end. He also gave, at Æthelbald’s request, a sign: on the following day, before the third hour, unexpected provisions of food would be given to the inhabitants of Crowland. Without delay, events followed his words. Therefore, after obtaining the kingdom, Æthelbald adorned the mausoleum of the venerable Guthlac with wonderful constructions of ornaments.

A certain householder in the province of Wissey lost the sight of his eyes for a year [Col. 0362C] and could not recover it by any applications of medicines. At last, brought in faith to Crowland, he sought an audience with Pega, Christ’s virgin. With her permission he lay down in the oratory beside the holy body. She scraped a lump of salt, previously blessed by the holy man, into water, and from it dripped water drop by drop within the blind man’s eyelids. At the touch of the first drop sight was restored to his eyes; hence the enlightened householder gave thanks through the merits of Saint Guthlac. Many others also, burdened by diverse illnesses, hearing reports of blessed Guthlac’s miracles, come to marshy Crowland, where the holy body rests; having obtained complete health through his merits, they give thanks to God.

[Col. 0362D] Thus far I have briefly followed the writings of Bishop Felix concerning the venerable Guthlac and inserted them into this little work for the praise of God and the moral edification of the faithful. What remains concerning the building of the monastery of Crowland and the dwelling of the cenobites I shall set forth from the truthful account of Ansgot the subprior and other elders.

## XXII. History of the Monastery of Crowland

King Æthelbald, when he learned that his blessed comforter was shining in miracles, joyfully sought the place of his burial, and he granted in perpetuity to those serving him the gifts he had already bestowed upon the blessed man after gaining the kingdom. [Col. 0363A] For once, while the same king came to Crowland to visit his patron before he departed this life, and the man of God asked him to grant a quiet dwelling for himself on that island, the king granted five miles eastward, that is, as far as the ditch called Asendic; three westward; two southward; and two northward. He freed it in every way from all rent and secular customary dues, and confirmed this in a charter sealed with his seal in the presence of his bishops and magnates.

And because the marshy ground of Crowland—as its very name indicates, for *Crulandia* means “raw,” that is, muddy, land—could not support a stone mass, the aforesaid king had huge oak piles of countless number driven into the ground. He ordered hard earth to be brought in boats over nine miles by water from Uppalond, that is, “higher land,” and mixed with the marshes. Thus, since holy Guthlac had been content with a wooden oratory, he began and completed a stone basilica. Then he assembled religious men there, founded a monastery, and enriched the place with ornaments, estates, and many other riches, to the honour of God and of the holy anchorite whom he had greatly loved, because of the sweet consolation which he had often received from him while he was in exile. He loved him throughout his life, and, since the first restoration made by that king, the seat of Crowland has never lacked [Col. 0363C] an inhabited community of religious monks down to the present day. A certain Kenulf was of great renown in those days and governed the monastery of Saint Guthlac for some time; after him the stone which he set as a boundary against the people of Deeping is still called Kenulf’s stone.

Afterward England was disturbed by diverse storms of war. When barbarians arrived from Denmark or Norway under the leaders Inguar, Halfdene, and Gudrun, and other tyrants, and the native English kings who had ruled England were displaced, the monastery of Crowland was plundered like many others. Its ornaments were taken away, its estates devastated, and they were reduced into lay possession contrary to canon law. But divine mercy, which permits hypocrites to rule for a time because of the sins of the people, also knows how to restore tranquil times to chastened children through the governance of lawful princes. Accordingly, after the aforesaid tyrants—who killed Saint Edmund, king of the East Angles, with many other faithful men, and set fire to the churches of the saints and the dwellings of Christians—had by divine providence been killed or otherwise overthrown, Alfred, son of King Æthelwulf, prevailed with God’s help and alone became the first of all kings to obtain the monarchy of all England. After him his son Edward, surnamed the Elder, reigned usefully for a long time; dying, he left the kingdom to his three sons, Æthelstan, Edmund, and Eadred. They all held the kingdom of England in succession, and each in [Col. 0364A] his own time strove to reign commendably and to benefit those subject to him.

In the time of King Eadred, there was a London cleric named Turketel, who asked the aforesaid king to grant Crowland to him. The king willingly assented to what he requested. This cleric was of royal descent, a kinsman of Osketel, metropolitan of York, and possessed much wealth and extensive estates, all of which he regarded as little for the sake of eternal dwellings. For, as we have said, he had not asked the king for Crowland in order to enlarge his lands; rather, because he knew that religious men were there in the solitude surrounded on every side by marshes and pools, he resolved, despising all the delights of this world, to dedicate himself to divine worship. Having therefore prudently arranged his affairs, he became a monk at Crowland; and, when through his zeal the community of monks there had increased, he was made their master and abbot by God’s will and the election of the good. [Col. 0364B] He was a most intimate friend of the holy bishops then governing God’s Church: Dunstan, Archbishop of Canterbury; Æthelwold of Winchester; and Oswald of Worcester, later Archbishop of York. He strove with all his strength to follow their counsels. As we have said, he was of very noble birth and possessed sixty manors from the patrimony of his parents. For their souls he gave six estates to the Church of Crowland: Wenliburg and Bebi, Wiritorp and Elmington, Cotehham and Oghington. He confirmed this by a testament sealed with the seal of the most vigorous King Edgar, son of King Edmund. Archbishop Dunstan also, together with his suffragans, confirmed the donation of the aforesaid properties by making the sign of the cross upon the charter; and he excommunicated with the anathema of everlasting curse anyone who should take from the aforesaid Church any of the named possessions unless he made amends through worthy satisfaction.

Finally, long afterward, when Turketel died on the fourth day before the Ides of July [975], his nephew Elgeric succeeded him. At the completion of his life, Elgeric left the abbey of Crowland to another Egelric, who was of his kindred. Upon his death, Osketel, a monk of great nobility, was made abbot of the same church. His sister Leofwynn was lady of Eynesbury, [Col. 0364D] where at that time lay the body of Saint Neot, abbot and confessor; but service worthy of so great a man was not then performed there. Therefore the aforesaid woman went to Whittlesey and summoned her brother, Abbot Osketel, with certain Crowland monks, to come there. She gave them the body of Saint Neot, which she had reverently brought with her, judging them worthier custodians. They gratefully received the gift bestowed on them by God and honourably placed it beside the altar of Saint Mary, Mother of God, on the north side. There it is still reverently venerated by the faithful, and his feast is celebrated on the second day before the Kalends of August. When Osketel died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November [1005], Godric succeeded him. When he entered the way [Col. 0365A] of all flesh on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February [1018], Brihtmer received the abbey.

At that time there was a monastery at Peakirk, over which the noble Abbot Wulfgeat presided. There holy Pega, sister of Saint Guthlac, had long served the Lord. After her venerable brother died, she strove earnestly to test her life by a more austere labour for Christ’s love. Therefore she went to Rome, humbly visited for herself and her own the thresholds of the holy Apostles, and there gloriously ended her life on the sixth day before the Ides of January. She rests buried in the church which the faithful founded there in her honour, shining venerably and mercifully assisting with many miracles those who faithfully call upon her.

After Brihtmer, abbot of Crowland, died on the seventh day before the Ides [Col. 0365B] of April [1048], Wulfgeat, father of Peakirk, asked King Edward, son of Æthelred, to permit the flocks of the two monasteries to be united and, for God’s praise, to become one convent under one abbot and one rule. The king promptly granted this kindly. Wulfgeat therefore, after governing Crowland for a long time, died on the Nones of July [1052]. Ulfketel, monk of the church of Peterborough, received the governance of Crowland from King Edward at the command of his abbot Leofric. He presided over Crowland for twenty-four years and began to build a new church because the old one threatened ruin. In this undertaking he was assisted, by God’s inspiration, by Earl Waltheof of Northampton, son of Siward, earl of the Northumbrians, who gave the estate called [Col. 0365C] Barneack to those serving God and Saint Guthlac. Not long afterward, through the malice of the Normans—who greatly envied him and feared him because of his exceptional worth—he was unjustly beheaded at Winchester, amid the grief of many, on the day before the Kalends of June. At the request of his wife Judith and by King William’s permission, his body was brought to Crowland by Abbot Ulfketel.

Not long afterward, because the aforesaid abbot was English-born and hated by the Normans, he was accused by enemies, deposed by Archbishop Lanfranc, and assigned to the cloister at Glastonbury. Then Ingulf, a monk of Fontenelle, received the abbey of Crowland as a gift from King William and governed it through very many adversities for twenty-four years. He was English by birth, had been the king’s secretary, and afterward had gone to Jerusalem. Returning from there, he sought Fontenelle and received the monastic habit from Gerbert, the exceedingly learned abbot of that monastery. Under him, already trained in the order, he administered a priory. The king, who had known him earlier, requested him from his abbot and placed him over the people of Crowland. After receiving the governance of Crowland, he strove by kindly petitions to assist his predecessor before King William. Ulfketel therefore, by the king’s permission, returned to Burgh—that is, to his own church—and died there some years later on the seventh day before the Ides of June.

But Abbot Ingulf strove, as he could, to aid the monastery entrusted to him; [Col. 0366A] yet by God’s will he endured very many adversities. For part of the church, together with its buildings, vestments, books, and many other necessary things, was consumed in a sudden fire. He himself, held by the severe disease of gout, languished long before his death, but did not cease to benefit those subject to him with a vigorous mind. He ordered the body of Earl Waltheof to be moved from the chapter-house into the church and water to be warmed in which the bones might be washed. But after the covering of the sarcophagus was removed, in the sixteenth year after his death the body was found whole as on the day when it had been buried, with the head joined to the body. The monks and many lay people who were present saw only a reddish thread, as though a sign of the beheading. When the body had been transferred into the church [Col. 0366B] and honourably buried near the altar, miracles were performed there very frequently. The sick truly experience this: seeking in faith, they often obtain the joy of the health they desire.

At last, when Abbot Ingulf died on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January [1109] [Note: [Col. 0365] Ingulf died on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January, not on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December. (Le Prévost.)], Geoffrey succeeded him and, with zeal for goodness and integrity, greatly benefited the church of Crowland and its inhabitants. He was a Frenchman by birth, from the city of Orléans. From childhood he had pursued the schools of the liberal arts and was abundantly imbued with literary learning. Despising the world and burning with heavenly desire, he assumed the monastic habit in the monastery of Saint Evroul, the abbot, which that same saint had founded at Ouche in the time of Childebert, king of the Franks [Col. 0366C]. There, indeed, because that place abounds more in religion than in worldly riches, Geoffrey as a novice took on the monastic yoke under Abbot Mainer, renowned for his great fervour. He bore it for a long time; having been tested in various offices, after fifteen years from his conversion he deserved promotion to the ministry of prior.

Finally, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1119, by command of Henry, king of the English, he undertook the governance of the church of Crowland. He began a new basilica of most beautiful workmanship, together with very many other good works, and throughout the fifteen years in which he held the office of abbot, with God’s help, he strove to bring them to completion for the salvation of himself and those subject to him.

## XXIII. Miracles at the tomb of Waltheof

In the third year of his rule miracles first began to be displayed at the tomb of Count Waltheof [Col. 0366D]. On hearing reports of them, the English rejoiced greatly; and English people frequently flocked to the tomb of their fellow countryman, whom they heard was now glorified by God through many signs, both in joy at this new occurrence and to pray for their own needs.

When a certain Norman monk named Audin saw this, he was greatly angered. He mocked those who came and disparaged the aforesaid count with derision, saying that he had been a worthless traitor and deserved to be punished for his crime by the loss of his head. When Abbot Geoffrey heard this, he gently reproved him, since he was a foreigner, saying that he ought not to disparage the works of God [Col. 0367A], since God has promised to manifest his presence to his faithful until the consummation of the age, and promises to give from the fountain of his unfailing mercy a draught to those who repent from the depths of their hearts.

Immediately, while the same abbot was trying by such words to restrain the rashness of the foolish man, and he was uttering increasingly unsuitable words, he was struck by a sudden illness in his vitals in the presence of the oft-mentioned Father. After a few days he died in the church of Saint Alban, protomartyr of the English, where he had made his monastic profession.

On the following night, as Abbot Geoffrey rested in bed and pondered closely within himself the events mentioned above, he soon saw in a vision that he stood at the coffin of Count Waltheof. He also saw the saints of God, Bartholomew [Col. 0367B] the apostle and Guthlac the hermit, standing there with him and shining in white garments. The Apostle, as it seemed, took up the count’s head, restored to the body, and said: “He is not headless.” Guthlac, standing at the feet, replied in turn: “This man was a count.” The Apostle then completed the beginning of the monastic saying: “But now he is a king.”

Having heard and reported these things, the abbot gladdened the brethren and glorified the Lord God, who never ceases at all times to bestow his mercy upon those who believe in him. When fifteen years of his rule had been completed, the venerable abbot and priest Geoffrey died on the Nones of June. He was succeeded by Waltheof the Englishman, monk of the monastery of Crowland, brother of Gospatric, of high English nobility.

As miracles became more frequent at Crowland, the monks rejoiced [Col. 0367C]. To the extent of their ability they gladly honoured the body of so great a count, and commissioned Vitalis the Englishman to compose his epitaph in heroic verse. He promptly obeyed their command and uttered aloud what he had meditated in his heart:

> Behold, this stone covers a man of great worth!  
> The bold son of Siward, count of the Danes,  
> Waltheof, an outstanding count, lies buried here.  
> He lived worthy of honour, formidable in arms and spirit;  
> Yet amid perishable riches and honours  
> He loved Christ and strove to please Christ.  
> He cherished the Church and reverently loved the clergy,  
> Especially the monks of Crowland, faithful to him.  
> At last, slain by the sword of Norman judges,  
> At the end of May he seeks the fields of light, freed from his limbs.  
> Watery Crowland rejoices in the soil of her lord,  
> Whom, while he lived, he loved with deep reverence.  
> May the Almighty grant his soul rest in the citadel of heaven!

For the killing of Count Waltheof King William was reproved by many; and, with many rising against him, he suffered many adversities by the just judgment of God [Col. 0368A], nor did he ever afterward enjoy lasting peace. Indeed, he resisted all men manfully, because he was spirited; but he no longer exulted in prosperous success according to his wishes as he had before, nor rejoiced in frequent triumphs of victory. In the thirteen years for which he lived thereafter, he did not drive an armed battle-line from the field, nor, while besieging a town, capture it by martial valour.

The almighty Judge orders all things justly and leaves no crime unpunished, for he punishes all things either in this world or in the world to come.

## XXIV. King William vainly attempts to subdue the Bretons. Ainard, first abbot of Saint Peter of Dive. His successor Fulk

[Col. 0368B]

King William, wishing to enlarge his territories and to subjugate the Bretons, so that they might obey him as they had formerly served Rollo and William and the other Norman dukes, besieged the town of Dol with a great army. By many terrors and threats he intimidated those in the castle, and swore that he would not depart until he had gained possession of the fortress.

Yet, by the will of God who governs all things, events turned out otherwise. For while the aforesaid king remained proudly in his tents and gloried in his riches as a mighty man, he heard that Alan Fergant, count of Brittany, was hastening to assist the besieged with many troops of armed men [Col. 0368C]. Terrified, he made peace with the garrison, who as yet knew nothing of the help coming to them, and immediately withdrew, not without great loss of goods. In their hasty departure they left behind tents and baggage, vessels and weapons, and equipment of many kinds; they reckoned their loss of these possessions at fifteen thousand pounds sterling, with many groans.

[Note: [Col. 0367D] It is remarkable that Orderic is silent about Philip, king of France, having brought assistance to the count of the Bretons in this expedition—a fact affirmed by the other historians who mention it, whose accounts are as follows.

Symeon of Durham, under the year 1075: “Having crossed the sea, King William launched an expedition into Lesser Brittany and besieged the castle of Count Ralph, called Dol, until Philip, king of the Franks, drove him from it.”

Matthew Paris, under the year 1075: “King William, crossing into Armorican Brittany, besieged the castle of Dol. But the king of the Franks came upon them in hostility and cut off all supplies. Therefore the king abandoned the siege and, in his retreat, lost there many soldiers and horses together with wealth.”

Moreover, we have already observed above, p. 566, note B, that Orderic wrongly conflates two sieges of the castle of Dol begun by William. For, in fixing the date of this same siege of Dol, he combines both the death of Ainard, abbot of Dive [Col. 0368D], which certainly occurred in 1076, and the marriage of Constance, William’s daughter, with Alan Fergant, which is equally certainly known to have been celebrated in 1086; he plainly confuses two events separated by a full decade.

Furthermore, what he relates about the siege of Dol conflicts with what other writers report concerning it. The Breton and Briocense Chronicle do not say that William besieged the castle of Dol in order to compel the Bretons to render him fealty; on the contrary, they testify that he had been summoned by Hoel, duke of Brittany, to join him in overcoming Bretons in that castle who had rebelled against him. It is therefore clear that different sieges are related here and there. DOM BOUQUET, vol. IV, pp. 595–596.]

Then the prudent king, perceiving that he could not overcome the Bretons by force, carefully devised another course advantageous both to himself and to his descendants. He confirmed a treaty of friendship with Alan Fergant and honourably united his daughter Constance to him in marriage at Caen. She lived with her husband in honour for nearly fifteen years and strove with all affection to benefit her subjects and companions [Col. 0369A]. For she continually sought the nectar of peace, loved the poor, and reverently honoured all worshippers of God. Dying childless, she caused them grief.

The lovers of justice in Brittany would greatly rejoice if a fortunate offspring provided them with praiseworthy heirs, who by native goodness might instil the balance of justice into the untamed Bretons and compel them to follow the rule of divine law and human reason.
