After Constance’s death, Count Fergant took as wife the daughter of the count of Anjou. By her he begot a son named Conan, to whom King Henry of the English recently gave his own daughter in marriage to secure peace.

About this time the reverend Ainard, first abbot of Dive [Col. 0369B], took to his bed and, having fulfilled in himself the things fitting for a servant of God, died on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of February [1078]. He was German by nation and thoroughly learned in both arts, versifying and composing melodies, and exceptionally skilled in producing sweet chants. This can be clearly demonstrated in the histories of Kilian, bishop of Würzburg, and of Catherine the Virgin, and in very many other chants which he elegantly composed in praise of the Creator.

In his youth, burning with religious zeal, he sought out the venerable Abbot Isembert and gladly submitted himself to his discipline for the love of God. He became a monk in the monastery of the Holy Trinity, which Goscelin de Arches had built on the hill of Rouen toward the east [Col. 0369C]. Thence, by divine will, he was selected by the governors of the Church in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1046 and set upon the lampstand, that he might give light to all who are in the house. Once ordained, he undertook the care of the abbey of Dive, which Countess Lescelina, wife of Count William of Eu, had founded. He governed it profitably for thirty-one years, living well and teaching well; then, an old man and full of days, he finished the course of this present life.

The venerable Durand, abbot of Troarn, buried his body in the basilica of Saint Mary and composed the memorable poem to be engraved upon the plate of his tomb. In it he set forth clearly as follows the character and virtues of the aforesaid archimandrite and the graces divinely bestowed upon him:

> [Col. 0369D] Here lies Ainard, fragrant as spikenard,  
> With many flowers and merits of virtue.  
> By him this place was founded and built  
> With immense zeal and no small expense.  
> He was a man great in uprightness, gentle as a lamb,  
> Distinguished in life, pre-eminent in doctrine;  
> Sober and chaste, prudent, simple, and honourable,  
> Strong in counsel, illustrious in office.  
> His mind possessed gravity and mature age,  
> Grey hair, but a thin face.  
> On the nineteenth day before the Kalends in the month of February,  
> His final lot took him away and swift death carried him off.  
> You who pass by, remember to pray for him in supplication,  
> That the gracious countenance of God may be his satisfaction.

The church of Dive, bereft of its own ruler, was given to Fulk [Col. 0370A], prior of Ouche, to govern; and he was consecrated abbot by Robert, bishop of Sées. From the time of King William and Duke Robert II, the aforesaid house was governed for many years and magnificently advanced as the circumstances of the time allowed.

The aforesaid leader brought with him four monks from Ouche: Bernard, surnamed Matthew, his kinsman; Richard; William of Montreuil; and Turchetil—ready and useful scribes, most skilled in divine worship. They were indeed peaceful helpers to him. They were the first eagerly to place their shoulders under the yoke of the Lord night and day, and they said cheerfully to their companions, both in word and unfailing example: “Come with us to Bethel.”

[Note: [Col. 0369] Perhaps a corrupt passage, which you will look for in vain in Holy Scripture.]

## XXV. Dissensions among the sons of King William

[Col. 0370B]

The instigator and cause, it is said, of the turbulent storms which we have stated were stirred up by the people of Le Mans and the Normans was Robert, the king’s son.

For Duke William, before the battle of Senlac, and again during one of his illnesses afterward, had made Robert, his firstborn child, his heir and commanded all the magnates to do homage and swear fealty to him. They gladly obeyed his command. But after the death of his betrothed, Margaret, the young man, urged on by youthful ambition and the harmful promptings of his companions, demanded the honours due to him from his father [Col. 0370C]—namely, dominion over the people of Le Mans and Neustria.

The prudent father, looking carefully in every direction, refused his requests and persuaded his son wisely to await the proper time for obtaining what he sought. But Robert bore it ill that he could gain nothing from his father and often quarrelled arrogantly with him. He was talkative and prodigal, bold and highly capable in arms; a strong and reliable archer; loud and uninhibited in voice, eloquent in speech, full-faced, stout-bodied, and short in stature. Hence he was commonly surnamed Gambaron and Short-Boot.

Once, when the king was preparing to make an expedition against the men of Corbon and was lodging in the town of Richer, called l’Aigle because, while the castle was being built by Fulbert, an eagle’s nest was found there in an oak tree [Col. 0370D], a devilish quarrel arose among the king’s sons. From it many disputes and crimes afterward sprang up.

The two brothers, William Rufus and Henry, supported their father. Judging their strength equal to their brother’s, they considered it unworthy that he alone should seek to possess his paternal right and should eagerly desire, with a troop of retainers attending him, to be considered the equal of his father. Therefore they came to Robert’s lodging in the castle of l’Aigle, which he had taken in the house of Roger Calcege, and there began, as soldiers commonly do, to play dice in the upper chamber. Then they made a great noise and [Col. 0371A] poured water over Robert and his followers, who were below.

Then Ivo and Alberic de Grandmesnil said to Robert: “Why do you endure such an injury? Behold, your brothers have climbed above your head and are defiling us with you by filth, to show their contempt for you. Do you not see what this signifies? It is perfectly obvious even to the bleary-eyed. Unless you quickly punish this disgrace inflicted upon you, you are cast down and cannot rise again.”

On hearing this, Robert rose in fury and hastened to break into the upper chamber against his brothers. Immediately, when a cry arose, the king ran from his lodging and for the moment checked the quarrel among his sons by royal authority.

On the following night Robert [Col. 0371B] deserted the king’s cavalry with his foot-soldiers, went to Rouen, and tried secretly to seize the royal fortress in advance. But Roger of Ivry, the king’s butler, who guarded the tower, learned of the plotters’ attempt. He diligently fortified the stronghold against their treachery and sent envoys swiftly to inform his lord the king of the matter. The king was exceedingly angry and ordered all the conspirators to be seized. Hearing this command, they were greatly terrified. Some were captured, while the rest fled into exile and found safety abroad.

Then Hugh of Châteauneuf, nephew and heir of Albert Ribaldi, was the first to receive the aforesaid exiles. He opened to them Châteauneuf, Rémalard, and Sorel [Col. 0371C], together with his other fortified places, for the devastation of Neustria. He was Roger the count’s son-in-law, having married Mabel, sister of Robert of Bellême, who had followed the king’s son with Ralph of Conches and many others.

By a wicked undertaking, the deserters—an abominable crime!—began their course. For an empty hope and promises to be despised, they abandoned towns and rich estates. The king, however, reduced their lands to his own control and, from their revenues, paid mercenary soldiers to fight against them.

[Col. 0372A] By these disturbances inhabitants and neighbours were terribly agitated and everywhere took up arms either against the king or for him. Frenchmen and Bretons, men of Le Mans and Angevins, and other peoples wavered, not knowing whom they ought justly to follow. Wars therefore breaking out on every side, the resolute king gathered an army. As he went against his enemies, he made peace with Rotrou, count of Mortagne.

This count had often plundered the lands of the church of Chartres, which is dedicated to the perpetual Virgin Mary. He had been frequently rebuked for it by the bishop and clergy; yet, persisting incorrigibly, he was excommunicated. By divine punishment he became deaf and thus remained deaf until his death.

[Note: [Col. 0371C] In earlier times the father of this Rotrou, Geoffrey, count of Mortagne and also viscount of Châteaudun, had similarly harassed the clergy of Chartres, as we learn from these words of Fulbert’s twenty-fifth letter, in Chesne, vol. IV, p. 182:

> “That evildoer Geoffrey, whom I had excommunicated for many crimes, uncertain whether desperate or driven into madness, gathered a multitude of soldiers who did not know where they were being led, suddenly burned our villages with fire, [Col. 0371D] and devises against us every kind of plot in his power.”

Rotrou himself teaches us, in a charter [Col. 0372D] for the monastery of Saint Denis in the Perche, that Geoffrey was killed by citizens of Chartres who had laid an ambush. Of him he says:

> “Unexpected death, as he returned from the church of the Mother of the Lord in the city of Chartres, assailed him with hidden swords.”

See Aegidius Bri de la Clergerie, *History of the Perche*, p. 148. DOM BOUQUET, vol. IV, p. 597.]

King William hired this man for payment and brought him with himself to the siege, since Rémalard [Col. 0372B] was held of his fief. He fortified four castles in a ring and suitably stationed soldiers there to keep the garrison in check.

Meanwhile, one day Aimeric of Villeray had escorted the seneschal of the king of France, who had lodged with him. As he returned with three knights to his own castle, where enemies of the king had taken refuge, four horsemen happened to emerge from the royal troop. Meeting him, they barred his entry into his nearby fortress and, striking him, killed him at once. Then they hoisted the corpse of the ill-fated plunderer onto a horse as though it were a slaughtered pig and, having brought it before the tents of Count Roger, against whom he had long raged in hostility, threw it down.

His son Wulfric, terrified by so dreadful a misfortune to his father, made peace with the king [Col. 0372C] and afterward remained faithful to him and to his heirs for nearly fifty years.

Many misfortunes threaten the people of this land. If all were written down diligently, they would fill enormous volumes. Now, stiff with winter cold, I shall turn to other occupations and, weary, determine to end this present little book here. But when the calm serenity of spring returns, I shall recount in what follows the matters I have discussed less fully, as well as those that remain; and, God helping me, I shall explain copiously in a truthful style the events of war and peace among our people.

## Summary of Book V

[Col. 0371]

I. Prologue. II. Various events in Normandy. III. The wretched event at Lisieux. Death of Hugh, bishop of Lisieux. IV. Gilbert Maminot, Hugh’s successor. V. John, archbishop of Rouen; William, his successor. VI. The council of Lillebonne. [Col. 0373] VII. On the city of Rouen; on the city of Évreux; deeds of Blessed Taurin. VIII. Mallon and Avitian, apostles of Normandy. Distichs in honour of the forty-seven first bishops of Rouen. IX. Continuation of the distichs. X. Continuation of the distichs. XI. Continuation of the distichs. Epitaphs of Rollo and William Longsword. XII. Sequence of events in Neustria under King William. Revolts of Robert, son of King William. XIII. Sequence of events. XIV. Other sons of William become distinguished by good character. His daughter Adela. XV. The author returns to the history of the monastery of Ouche. Administration of Abbot Mainer. XVI. Account of gifts made to the monastery of Ouche. XVII. Digression on the monastery in the land of Odelerius, father of Orderic Vitalis, near the city of Shrewsbury in England. XVIII. Continuation of the account of gifts made to the monastery of Ouche. Charters of donation. Distinguished men buried in the church of Ouche. XIX. John, monk of Ouche. Poem of Orderic Vitalis in his praise. Gift of Goisbert the physician to the monastery of Ouche. XX. Continuation of the account of gifts made to the monastery of Ouche. Various events. Gifts made to the monks of Manly. On the lords of Manly. XXI. Continuation of the account of gifts. On the lords of Manly. XXII. Continuation of the accounts of gifts.

# Book V

## I. Prologue

[Col. 0373A]

Following the examples of our elders, we must unceasingly avoid deadly idleness and zealously labour in useful study and wholesome exercise. Through these an attentive mind is cleansed of vices and gloriously armed by life-giving discipline against every wickedness. “Every idle man is in desires,” as Solomon says.

[Note: [Col. 0373C] You will look for this passage in vain in the Vulgate translation of the sacred books.]

And: “Desires kill the sluggard” (Proverbs 21:25). For the slothful and idle person is one who, lacking good will, has voluntarily submitted himself to vices. He is rightly judged to be miserably oppressed by indolence if he does not meditate day and night on the law of the Lord—that is, in prosperity and adversity—and does not attempt, by resisting Satan’s snares and struggles, to oppose them, so as to deserve to attain the prize of the heavenly calling. Harmful desires undoubtedly kill such a man when they draw him, languishing in goodness, into crime [Col. 0373B], and plunge him by the broad way of his own pleasure into the abyss of perdition.

Therefore our forefathers utterly condemn sloth and idleness, enemies of the soul, and invite their followers by words and examples to beneficial labour and exercise. In this matter not Christians only, but pagan poets also agree. Virgil says:

> “What avail labour or good deeds? Relentless labour conquers all,  
> and pressing poverty in harsh circumstances.”

[Note: [Col. 0373C] This passage should be restored as follows:

> “What avail labour or good deeds?” VIRGIL, *Georgics*, III.525.  
> “Relentless labour conquers all,  
> and pressing poverty in harsh circumstances.” VIRGIL, *Georgics*, I.145.]

Ovid likewise instructs one wishing to resist desire against Venus, saying:

> Idleness consumes minds and breaks bodies.  
> By my first counsels, make haste to flee idleness.  
> If you remove idleness, Cupid’s bow is gone,  
> [Col. 0373C] and his torches lie despised and without light.

[Note: [Col. 0374C] The first verse is not found in Ovid. The others are from the poem entitled *Remedies for Love*, V.135, 139, and 140. They should be restored as follows:

> “By my first counsels, make haste to flee idleness . . .  
> If you remove idleness, Cupid’s bow is gone,  
> and his torches lie despised and without light.”]

[Col. 0374A] Carefully considering these and other things of this sort, Father Warin, I have resolved simply to publish something that may benefit or please some of the faithful in the house of God, while vigilantly holding fast to the undertaking I have begun, lest, like the slothful servant, I be condemned for a talent hidden in the earth when the Lord comes for judgment.

Accordingly, I wished first to obey the commands of the venerable Abbot Roger, and afterward yours, by beginning a little work on the state of the church of Ouche—something which our predecessors urged one another to do, but none of them was willing to begin. For each preferred silence to speech and placed secure repose above the consuming care of investigating past events. They would gladly have read accounts of the deeds of abbots and brethren, and a collection of their modest possessions, increased from slender beginnings by needy yet devout founders through the great solicitude of the Fathers [Col. 0374B]; but they refused to bend their minds to the task of composing or writing.

At last, brought here at the age of ten from the farthest borders of Mercia, an Englishman, a barbarian and unknown newcomer mingled with knowledgeable natives, I have attempted, at God’s inspiration, to set down in writing for Normans the deeds and events of the Normans.

With God’s help I have already produced two books, in which I have truthfully related the restoration of our house and the careers of our three abbots, adding briefly certain events of that age, insofar as I diligently learned them from aged elders.

Henceforth I shall begin a third book from the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0374C] 1075, and speak of my abbot, the community of Ouche [Col. 0375A], and the events that occurred during twelve years, namely until the death of King William.

It pleases me to begin this present little work with the aforesaid year, in which I came forth from my mother’s womb into this light on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March; and on the Saturday of the following Easter I was reborn at the sacred font at Atcham, in the church of Saint Eata the confessor, situated on the river Severn, through the ministry of the priest Ordric. Five years later my father entrusted me to the noble priest Siward to be educated in letters; receiving my first rudiments under his instruction, I was subjected to him for five years.

But in the eleventh year of my age I was given up by my own father for the love of God and sent, a tender exile, from England into Normandy, that I might serve the eternal King [Col. 0375B]. Then I was received by the venerable Father Mainer, clothed in the robe of the monastic habit, and joined to the sincere community of monks by an indissoluble bond. For forty-two years now I have gladly borne the light yoke of the Lord and, together with my contemporaries, have walked as cheerfully as I could in the way of God according to the Rule’s ordinance. I have laboured to learn ecclesiastical custom and service, and always applied my intelligence to some useful undertaking.

If our bishops and other rulers of the world possessed such holiness that miracles were divinely wrought for and through them, as were frequently accomplished in former times by the ancient Fathers and, scattered throughout books, sweetly instruct readers’ hearts and recall to the present the glorious signs of earlier teachers [Col. 0375C], I would shake off my torpor, exercise myself, and transmit in writing to the eager knowledge of posterity matters worthy of record. But now is that season in which the charity of many grows cold and iniquity abounds; miracles, the signs of holiness, cease; while crimes and mournful lamentation multiply in the world. The quarrels of bishops and bloody battles of princes give historians richer material for writing than theological treatises, or the frugality and wonders of those who eat dry food. The time of Antichrist approaches; before his face, as the Lord teaches blessed Job, scarcity of miracles will go before, and the frenzy of vices will rage excessively [Col. 0376A] among those who carnally love themselves.

Now, venerable abbot, I shall boldly continue in the Lord’s name what I have begun, kindly trusting that your wisdom will correct whatever my ignorance has done amiss.

## II. Various events in Normandy

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1075, the thirteenth indiction, King William celebrated holy Easter at Fécamp and presented his daughter Cecilia through the hand of Archbishop John to be consecrated to God. She was brought up with great care and instructed in many ways in the monastery at Caen. Dedicated there to the holy and undivided Trinity, she remained a virgin under the venerable Abbess Matilda, faithfully subject to the holy Rule.

When the aforesaid mother died after forty-seven years of her rule [Col. 0376B], Cecilia succeeded her and governed the nuns commendably for nearly fourteen years. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1127, on the third day before the Ides of July, she departed from this world. Thus, for fifty-two years after her father offered her to God, she served commendably as a nun in habit, order, and devout zeal; and she died in the twenty-sixth year of the reign of her brother Henry.

[Note: [Col. 0375C]

An authentic instrument establishes that Abbess Matilda died on 6 July 1120. Compare Le Prévost:

“Matilda I,” say the authors of the new *Gallia Christiana* (vol. XI, col. 432), “born of royal ancestors, was consecrated to God almost at birth in the monastery of Saint Leodegar of Rettel. Thence, chosen to govern, not by years but by compelling merits, the monastery built at Caen by Queen Matilda, she died old and full of days on the day before the Nones of July, in the fifty-fourth year of her prelacy.” This is explicitly stated by the circular letter sent immediately after her death by the nuns of Caen to various churches in France and England. The same is contained in the roll, as it was called, later sent to those same nuns from Saint Martin of Tours. The original of this roll, and of 254 others sewn together into a single roll approximately seventeen ells long, preserving the character of Matilda’s age, is kept in the abbey of the Holy Trinity.

This authority of the document conflicts with the contemporary authors Orderic Vitalis and William of Jumièges, who write that Matilda died in 1112 [Col. 0376C] after presiding for forty-seven or nearly forty-eight years. But how often these writers are mistaken! . . .

“Our authors continue: Cecilia, firstborn daughter of King William of England and Matilda, the founders, was offered by them to God on the very day of the dedication of the church, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July 1066, to serve God perpetually in that place. This is also attested by the charters of William and Matilda concerning the dedication, foundation, and endowment of the monastery, to which greater faith seems due than to contemporary writers who assert that Cecilia was offered to God by her father through Archbishop John in the church at Fécamp on Easter Day 1075. In this matter, as in many others, those writers were mistaken: they confused Cecilia with her sister Matilda, who had died before Matilda, the first abbess. Cecilia, however, presided for many years after Matilda—Orderic assigns nearly fourteen in Book VIII—and departed this world in 1127, on the third day before the Ides of July, in the twenty-sixth year of her brother Henry. The Chronicle of Caen gives 1126.” DOM BOUQUET, vol. V, p. 598.]

While King William remained in Neustria and, with God’s help, defended his land against all adversaries, the English bishops Lanfranc of Canterbury, Thomas of York, and Remigius of Lincoln went to Rome and were most honourably received by Lord Pope Gregory and the Roman senate. They gave abundant and lavish gifts from English wealth to the covetous Romans [Col. 0376C], and by their generosity, eloquence, and double learning appeared remarkable to the Latins. The pope and Roman clergy received most gladly King William’s embassies, which the bishops just mentioned had brought with gifts, and willingly granted the privileges which he had requested and which had formerly been conceded to his predecessors.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1077, the fifteenth indiction, the aforesaid bishops gladly returned from Rome. At their arrival the king and all the Norman natives rejoiced magnificently. Then many basilicas in Normandy were dedicated with immense rejoicing. The king and queen attended them with their sons Robert and William, together with a great multitude of magnates and people. The mother churches of the bishoprics of Bayeux and Évreux, and the monastery of Bec, were dedicated in honour of Saint Mary, Mother of God and perpetual Virgin [Col. 0377A].

In the same year the monastic basilica in honour of Saint Stephen, protomartyr, was dedicated at Caen, and the king and his nobles gave it a rich endowment and an abundance of many treasures. John, archbishop of Rouen, and his suffragan bishops of Normandy solemnly conducted the dedications of these churches; with them were the reverend metropolitans Lanfranc and Thomas, many abbots, and a wonderful multitude of people.

The venerable Abbot Herluin, rejoicing greatly at the dedication of the church of Bec and having seen what he had intensely desired in this world, disdained to remain longer among mortals [Col. 0377B]. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1034, at the age of forty, he abandoned secular knighthood, changed his life, and received the habit of holy religion from Lord Herbert, bishop of Lisieux. Three years later he was ordained by the same bishop and established as abbot. Thus the monastery of Bec began.

Finally, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1078, at the age of eighty-four, in the forty-fourth year of his monastic life, he died on the seventh day before the Kalends of September and was honourably buried in the chapter-house of the monks. A few days after his death Anselm, then prior of the same place, was elected abbot. In the following year, on the feast of Saint Peter called the Chair, he was consecrated abbot by Lord Gilbert, bishop of Évreux, in the basilica of Bec.

He took on the monastic yoke in the twenty-seventh year of his life and lived for three years as a cloistered monk without office. Then he was prior for fifteen years after Lanfranc; after Herluin, first abbot of the monks of Bec, he flourished for another fifteen years as abbot. Thereafter he was raised to the archbishopric of Canterbury after the venerable Lanfranc. He governed it for sixteen years and suffered many adversities. In the seventeenth year of his archiepiscopate, the forty-ninth of his monastic profession, and the seventy-sixth of his life, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, Wednesday [1109] before the Lord’s Supper [Maundy Thursday], he passed from the world [Col. 0377D].

## III. The wretched event at Lisieux. Death of Hugh, bishop of Lisieux
Because unskilled people are excessively elated by deceitful prosperity and, fragile as reeds, are easily swayed this way and that by the changing blast of adversities, God, governor of all things, wisely mingles hardships with pleasant things, in order to restrain and wholesomely moderate the shifting impulses of mortals.

Accordingly, while King William was greatly puffed up with secular pomp, and the people of Neustria were shamefully steeped in manifold luxury, without providing for what was to come in view of their huge accumulation of sins, a terrible crash of thunder resounded in the sanctuary of the basilica of Lisieux, and an unbearable stroke of lightning struck down the congregation standing in the episcopal church. For on a certain Sunday in summer, while the sacred mysteries of the Mass were being celebrated in the morning, and a vested priest named Herbert stood at the altar, there suddenly came an immense flash of lightning, immediately followed by a dreadful noise and a heavy blow. It struck, shattered, and cast down the cross which stood above the tower pulpit. Then it descended terribly into the holy building and fell upon the Crucifix; it struck its hand and foot and, in a wondrous manner, tore the iron nails from the cross. A dark gloom dulled the sight of the trembling people, sparkling fire flew throughout the whole basilica, and killed eight men and one woman. It scorched the beards, private parts, and other hair of men and women, and filled the nostrils of the crowd with a most foul stench. One woman, named Mary, stood in a corner of the church, not without great terror; herself frightened, she looked upon the whole people lying across the pavement as though lifeless. [Col. 0378A–B]

An event of this sort occurred before the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, and immediately at that same time Hugh, bishop of Lisieux, began to fall ill. In July, as his sickness grew worse, the bishop perceived that unavoidable death was at hand; and, as a servant of God about to go to the court of his Lord, he examined himself diligently and prepared himself in great fear to render an account for his stewardship. Purified by confession and penitence, washed by prayer and a shower of tears, and happily strengthened by communion in the saving mystery, he admonished, absolved, and blessed the clerics and laypeople who were with him. Finally, he recalled a matter over which he was especially grieved, and thus begged all who stood by him:

“I know that I am now about to enter upon the way of all flesh; but I am greatly distressed because I am far from my see and do not see my bride, to whom, by God’s ordering, I have been lawfully joined for almost forty years. Therefore I now beg all of you whom I formerly loved, nourished, advanced, and honoured: carry me from here and lead me to my dearest bride. I completed the church of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, which my venerable predecessor Herbert had begun; I adorned it diligently, dedicated it honourably, and richly endowed it with ministers, vessels necessary for divine service, and other furnishings. [Col. 0378C–D] I commend it in supplication to its heavenly Lord, and desire to rest in its bosom; there I shall await the coming of the Saviour.”

When he had said this, all immediately rose, placed the bishop upon a fitting bier to carry him, and brought him from the village called Pont-l’Évêque to Lisieux. Distinguished clerics and honourable laymen themselves bore their most beloved father onward. At last, as they hastened toward the city, while death was swiftly drawing near, they turned aside into a grassy plain; there, with tears and prayers, they awaited beneath the open sky the departure of their bishop.

> The sun, shining in Cancer with flashing splendour,  
> Veils the dying bishop in its scattered rays.

In such brightness and loveliness of place the noble bishop Hugh lay, commended to God in the hands of his own people, and breathed his last on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August [17 July]. [Col. 0379A]

> Thus died a man beyond replacement in our age,  
> Hugh the Father, jewel of priests and glory of his country.

May Christ, the supreme pontiff, whose office he bore on earth for a time, ever look kindly upon him! Pont-l’Évêque is four leagues distant from Lisieux. In the field beside the road where the bishop died, a cross was raised, which to this day is called the Cross of the Bishop. His body, however, was brought to Lisieux; but his burial was delayed for eight days because of a dispute between the canons and the nuns. The clerics wished to bury him in the episcopal residence; but the religious women most fiercely opposed them, saying:

“Our father Hugh built the abbey of Saint Mary our Lady, gathered us there for the service of God, and, as a father his daughters, brought us up in the fear of God. Mindful of death, he chose for himself a place of burial in the church which he founded. May he be punished with eternal death who attempts to take the body of our father from his daughters!” [Col. 0379B]

They therefore went to Rouen, to the king’s court, and both parties set forth their complaint; but the royal judgment had greater compassion on the weaker sex. Finally, the king summoned Archbishop John and charged him to go quickly to Lisieux and suitably bury the bishop’s body in the chapel of Saint Mary. But he, being fierce and arrogant and having long harboured a harmful resentment in his heart against the aforesaid bishop, furiously disregarded the king’s command and would not go to bury his fellow bishop. [Col. 0379C] As he was returning from the king’s court through the city upon his mule and, speaking proudly about the matters at hand, approached his house, a sudden stroke, by divine dispensation, struck him down to the ground in public sight of the crowd and rendered him speechless throughout the two years he lived thereafter. Then Gilbert, bishop of Évreux, went to Lisieux with a great company of faithful people and fittingly buried the bishop’s body in the choir of the nuns, Robert, count of Eu, Hugh’s brother, being present.

A suitable stone was placed upon the tomb of so great a bishop, and an epitaph composed in the Adonic metre, consisting of a dactyl and a spondee, was inscribed as follows in golden letters upon sheets of copper:

> Here lies Hugh of Lisieux, renowned for the honour  
> Of the episcopate, likewise noble by the blood of his fathers.  
> Endowed also with the distinction of character, not without the twofold  
> Gift of understanding, worthy of glory for his devotion.  
> At his passing Philip was king; then William  
> Was king of the English. On the following day Phoebus entered  
> The sign of Leo. May God grant this man the joys of heaven. Amen.  
> [Col. 0379D]

## IV. Gilbert Maminot, Hugh’s Successor

To govern the bishopric of Lisieux, Gilbert, surnamed Maminot, the king’s chief physician and chaplain, was chosen and consecrated by Michael, bishop of Avranches, in the presence of Archbishop John, who, as we have said, had already become speechless. He was the son of Robert de Curvaspina, a valiant knight. He held the bishopric for twenty-three years and vigorously maintained the interests of the Church. He was exceedingly skilled in the art of medicine, [Col. 0380A] but could never sufficiently attend to himself in his episcopal office. He was distinguished by learning and eloquence; he abounded continually in wealth and luxuries and served his own will and the care of the flesh too much. He devoted himself excessively to leisure and repose and commonly indulged in games of dice and tables. In ecclesiastical worship he was sluggish and negligent, but eager and ardent in hunting and catching birds. Thus he clung throughout his life to secular pursuits and activities, and so lived into extreme old age.

I could write more concerning his deeds, but I restrain my pen because I was promoted by him, together with, I think, more than three hundred others, to the rank of subdeacon. Therefore, just as I have related certain blameworthy things concerning him, so it is fitting that I should set forth what is praiseworthy and worthy of imitation. [Col. 0380B] He willingly gave alms to the poor; he flourished diligently and honourably in generosity and liberality. In judgment he investigated truth carefully, zealously sought to defend rectitude, and freely administered justice to all who asked for it. He received gently sinners who humbly confessed their offences and prudently gave sound and saving counsel to those truly penitent. He performed holy orders, dedications, and other ministries of this kind devoutly and carefully; but he was slow to undertake them and scarcely stirred himself, nor would he begin unless compelled by the many entreaties of many persons.

At that time, in the Church of Lisieux, there were honourable persons and distinguished archdeacons and canons: William de Glanville, dean and archdeacon; Richard de Angerville and William of Poitiers, archdeacons; Geoffrey de Tregaville, treasurer; Turgis, cantor, and his son Ralph; and many others whom Hugh had reared and honoured by granting ecclesiastical offices. [Col. 0380C] The aforesaid successor associated these men with himself, instructed them by fruitful teaching in arithmetic, astronomy, diverse natural philosophy, and other profound subjects, and graciously attached them to himself as intimate companions in feasts and conversations.

## V. John, Archbishop of Rouen; William, His Successor

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1079, Archbishop John died in the eighth year of his rule and was buried in the baptistery of the basilica on the north side. [Col. 0380D] His monument was made of white stone, and this epitaph was carefully inserted upon it:

> Your metropolitan lies here, city of Rouen;  
> By his death you fall from your lofty height.  
> The Church’s resources diminish; the sacred order grows cold—  
> He whom prudent religion had established.  
> Long neglected, he reformed these decrees of the canons  
> And ordained that priests should live chastely.  
> Under him none of God’s gifts were for sale;  
> Therefore he bestowed abundant wealth upon the Church.  
> Eloquent speech, birth, wisdom, and a sober life  
> Were his, whom this small stone covers.  
> It was the ninth day of September when John,  
> Stripped of the flesh, departed. May true rest be his! Amen.

Upon the death of John, the metropolitan, William, abbot of Caen, [Col. 0381A] was canonically elected and brought from his monastery—where he served God according to the Rule as a proven monk—to protect the Church of Rouen. In the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God, he was consecrated by the great Gilbert, bishop of Évreux, and became the forty-sixth metropolitan of Rouen after blessed Nicasius, whom Saint Denis, bishop of Paris, had appointed as the first bishop over the people of Rouen.

He was good, pleasant, and gentle, and guarded for thirty-two years the flock divinely committed to him. He richly furnished the mother church with every ornament necessary for divine worship, and elegantly rebuilt from the foundations the episcopal cloister and its suitable houses. He gloriously translated the body of Saint Romanus the bishop [Col. 0381B] from its own church into the metropolitan basilica and reverently placed it in a shrine elaborately overlaid with gold, silver, and precious stones. He also ordained that his feast on the tenth day before the Kalends of November [23 October] should be celebrated festively throughout his diocese, and by a general decree established an annual solemn gathering outside the city at the body of the holy bishop. He invited almost all parishioners to it by exhortations, absolutions, and blessings.

Like a kindly father, he was beneficent toward monks, clerics, and all subject to him. He devoted himself continually to psalms, hymns, spiritual songs, and sacred mysteries. All deceit and bitterness were far from him. He sought to harm no one, [Col. 0381C] but to assist every needy person as reason required. He was a most skilled singer and possessed a voice excellently suited for singing. He was most learnedly trained in ecclesiastical observance and was strong in clear and suitable speech for preaching the word of God to the unlearned. With patience and kindness he soothed all who lived with him; without envy he distributed a great part of his burden among deans and archpriests, while eagerly admitting worthy men to share in honour.

## VI. The Council of Lillebonne

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1080, King William held court at Lillebonne on the feast of Pentecost and ordered Archbishop William, all the bishops and abbots, the counts, and the other magnates [Col. 0381D] of Normandy to be present together there. What the king commanded was done. Thus, in the eighth year of the pontificate of Pope Gregory VII, a celebrated council was held at Juliobona, and, through the king’s foresight and the counsel of his barons, useful deliberation was held concerning the state of God’s Church and of the whole realm. I wish to insert here the statutes of the council, faithfully recorded by those who attended, so that later generations may learn what laws existed in Normandy under King William.

1. The Peace of God, commonly called the *trevia* [Truce], as Prince William himself established it at the beginning, shall be firmly maintained and renewed in every parish by the pronouncement of excommunications. Those who disdain to observe it, or violate it in any way, shall be subjected by the bishops to judicial justice, as was previously established. If anyone is disobedient to his bishop in this matter, the bishop shall report it to the lord in whose land he lives, and that lord shall submit him to episcopal justice. If the lord too refuses to do this, the king’s sheriff, when requested by the bishop, shall do it without any excuse.

2. Concerning those who have wives from among their own kindred, or the wives of their parents, the bishops shall administer canonical justice. For the king neither tolerates nor protects anyone in this matter; rather, by aiding the bishops, he urges that the law of God be firmly kept. [Col. 0382A]

3. Priests, deacons, subdeacons, and all canons and deans shall have no woman at all. If anyone is subsequently found to have incurred the same offence, and is first accused of it by the bishop’s officials, he shall clear himself in the bishop’s court. But if he is first accused by one of his parishioners or lords, the accused shall have a delay in order that he may speak with the bishop; and if he wishes to clear himself, he shall do so in the parish he serves, in the presence of several parishioners, before the bishop’s officials and by their judgment. If he cannot clear himself, he shall lose his church irrevocably. The aforesaid king established this, not permanently taking from his bishops their due jurisdiction, but because at that time the bishops had done less in this matter than was fitting, until, seeing their reform, he should restore to them as a reward for good conduct what he had temporarily taken from their hands because of their offence. [Col. 0382B]

4. No layperson shall have any share in altar revenues, burial fees, or the third part of the tithe; nor shall he receive money in any way for their sale or grant. Nor shall a priest perform service on this account, unless he carries his lord’s message, so that he returns on the same day to the service of the Church. Within Normandy only, he may accompany his lord for prayers, receiving his lord’s maintenance if the lord wishes; meanwhile the priest shall see to the service of the Church. [Col. 0382C]

5. Priests shall not be compelled by bishops or their officials, by force or threats, to give anything beyond the bishop’s lawful dues. No monetary fine shall be exacted on account of their women. Archdeacons shall, once a year throughout their archdeaconries, inspect the vestments, chalices, and books of the priests subject to them, at only three places in each archdeaconry designated by the bishop, where the neighbouring priests shall be summoned to display these things. When the archdeacon comes to make this inspection, he shall receive maintenance for three days, if necessary, from the priests who assemble, retaining a fifth share for himself. [Col. 0382D]

6. If a priest commits an offence against the forests of the king or his barons, the bishop shall receive no fine for it.

7. Once a year, around Pentecost, priests shall come with their processions to the mother church; and from every household wax worth a denarius, or its equivalent, shall be offered at the altar for lighting the church. Whoever refuses to do this shall be compelled by his priest, through his own official means, to pay it without a monetary penalty. A layperson shall neither appoint nor remove a priest from a church without the bishop’s consent. Yet the bishop shall not reject one who ought to be received, nor retain one who ought to be rejected. [Col. 0383A]

8. In churchyards situated in cities, castles, or boroughs, bishops shall recover whatever they possessed in the time of Count Robert or of King William, with his consent. In churchyards situated in frontier districts, if war arises and persons establish dwellings there for the duration of the war, and remain in the precinct because of the war, the bishop shall receive from them no fine except what he would have received before they took refuge in the precinct. But when peace has been made, those who fled there because of war shall be compelled to leave the precinct or be subjected to episcopal law. Those who had lived from ancient times in the aforesaid churchyards shall remain in their former freedom. [Col. 0383B]

9. Village churches shall retain as much churchyard as they had in the time of Count Robert, or as much as they had until the above-written council; and bishops shall retain in them those customary rights which they possessed in the time of Count Robert or of King William, with his consent, unless bishops, with King William’s approval, have granted some exemption. If, after the council, a new church is built within a village, the bishop shall establish a churchyard with the agreement of the lords and parishioners of that church. If a new church is built outside a village, it shall have five perches of churchyard on every side. [Col. 0383C]

10. If a church is granted to monks, the priest who holds that church shall honourably retain whatever he held from it before the monks received it, and shall be all the better off inasmuch as he is associated with holier men. Upon his death or other incapacity, the abbot shall seek out a suitable priest and present him to the bishop either personally or through his messenger. If the man is to be received, the bishop shall receive him. But if the priest wishes to live religiously with the monks, he shall ensure that the church into which he entered by episcopal permission is honourably maintained, in vestments, books, and all other things necessary for the church’s service, according to that church’s means. If the priest does not wish to live with the monks, the abbot shall give him enough from the church’s goods for the priest both to live well and suitably fulfil the service of the church. If the abbot refuses, he shall be suitably compelled by the bishop to do so. The priest shall be lawfully subject to his bishop and shall pay the episcopal dues. What remains over, the abbot shall have for the use of his monastery. The same shall be observed in churches belonging to canons. [Col. 0383D]

11. Violation of a church or its precinct, as determined above, and offences for which the divine office is omitted, shall be compensated to the bishops by a monetary payment. An assault on the road to church shall be treated likewise.

If anyone angrily pursues another into a precinct or into a church, likewise.

If a layperson ploughs or builds in a precinct without episcopal permission, likewise.

If a cleric commits rape or theft, strikes, wounds, or kills anyone; if he undertakes a duel without the bishop’s permission, takes a distraint, commits an assault, unjustly seizes anything, or commits arson; or if his household dependent or a resident of the precinct does so: likewise, he shall compensate the bishops by a monetary payment. [Col. 0384A]

If a cleric commits adultery or incest, likewise.

If a priest commits an offence in respect of his ministry, likewise.

Priests who neglect to attend the synod, likewise.

And whoever does not pay the synodal and visitation dues at the appointed times, likewise. [Col. 0384B]

If a cleric abandons his tonsure, likewise.

If a monk or nun not living under a rule abandons the religious habit, likewise.

If priests excommunicate persons other than violators of the Truce of God and robbers without the bishop’s permission, likewise.

If an estray, commonly called *Weridif*, comes into the court of a priest or cleric living in the precinct, it shall belong to the alms of that church, or to the bishop’s precinct.

Whatever is left behind as a result of a dispute in the house of a priest or cleric, or in a clerical or priestly precinct, or with their household dependent, shall belong to the bishop.

Whatever is found or left in a church or precinct shall belong to the bishop. [Col. 0384C]

If anyone assaults, strikes, captures, or kills a priest, monk, or nun, or burns their houses in the precinct, he shall likewise make compensation.

Whatever is found or left in a church or precinct shall belong to the bishop.

If anyone commits adultery or incest, or has intercourse with a godmother, mother, or daughter, likewise. If a woman does the same, likewise. If anyone leaves his wife, or if any woman leaves her husband, without the judgment of the bishop, likewise. Those who consult the dead or practise sorcery, likewise. Whoever, denying or repudiating an accusation made against him, is convicted by the ordeal of iron—excepting violation of the Truce of God—likewise. Whoever resists justice and permits himself to be excommunicated, likewise. [Col. 0384D]

Crimes of parishioners falling under episcopal jurisdiction shall, where this has been customary, be examined by the judgment of the bishops.

If a challenge is made to a judgment, it shall be decided before the bishop.

If an ordeal of iron is adjudged, it shall be completed at the mother church.

If an ordinary legal proceeding is to be held, it shall be held where the court previously sat.

No one shall dare to preach in a bishop’s parish without his permission.

If anyone falls into the aforesaid offences and comes voluntarily to penitence, penance proportionate to the nature of the crime shall be imposed, and no money at all shall be exacted.

If a layperson commits rape in a precinct, he shall compensate the bishop. But if he does it elsewhere, in whatever manner he does so, the bishop shall receive nothing. [Col. 0385A]

12. Bishops shall have these customary rights in those places in which they have possessed them hitherto, by concession, in the time of Count Robert or King William. Places which have been exempt shall retain the exemption which they have firmly held until now. In all these jurisdictions and customs, the king retains what he has possessed hitherto.

If a priest contests his lord’s judgment in an ecclesiastical case and, by going to the bishop’s court, unjustly causes him trouble, he shall compensate his lord with ten shillings.

If bishops can show in the king’s court that they possessed anything not written here in the time of Count Robert or King William, by his concession, the king does not deprive them of possessing it; provided only that they in no way seize it until they show in his court that they ought to possess it. Likewise, on account of this written settlement, the king takes nothing from laypeople which they can show in his court that bishops ought not to possess; provided only that they do not dispossess bishops of it until it has been shown in the king’s court that bishops ought not to possess it. [Col. 0385B]

This synod was held in a royal village beside the Seine, where there had been an ancient city called Caletus by its inhabitants. From it the surrounding district, from the sea as far as Talou, has to this day been called the Pays de Caux. As is recorded in ancient Roman histories, Gaius Julius Caesar besieged this city and destroyed it because of the excessive obstinacy of the warriors within, who resisted most fiercely. Then, after he had subdued the enemies there at his pleasure, considering the site’s convenience, he prudently established a Roman garrison and called it Juliobona after his own name; the barbarians now call it, with the name corrupted, Ille-Bona [Lillebonne].

> [Note: Sigebert in his *Chronicle* gives almost the same account as Orderic concerning the origin of Lillebonne [Col. 0385C–D]. But Valesius, in the *Notitia Galliae*, under “Julio-Bona,” p. 256, maintains that both are mistaken in this matter. “Caletus,” he says, “is a city unknown to all ancient geographers. It never existed anywhere; and the district of Caux received its name not from this city Caletus, which never existed, but from the Caletes, a very well-known people of Gallia Lugdunensis. Sigebert and Vitalis were misled by some resemblance, whatever its value, between the names Juliobona and Illebona. Turnebus too was misled: in Book IX of his *Adversaria* he calls Juliobona ‘Villambona,’ and wishes the name Villaebona to designate no place other than Illebona, which some have mistakenly called Insula-bona. Masson also followed Turnebus. But all of them are convicted of error by the single itinerary of Aethicus, from which Juliobona lies ten Roman miles from Carocotinum or Corocotinum [Le Crotoy], and thirty from Rouen. This does not fit Illebona at all, which is about twenty or thirty Roman miles distant from Carocotinum. Therefore I agree with Philipp Clüver, who says that Juliobona, the capital of the Caletes, is Dieppe, so named from the river washing it. [Col. 0386C–D] In Aethicus, the route from Juliobona to Milan is thirty-four Roman miles; the route from Juliobona to Dreux is sixty-eight Roman miles, as follows: Breviodorum, or Breviodurum, seventeen Roman miles; Noviomagus, seventeen; Condate, twenty-four; Dreux, ten Roman miles. The same route is similarly described in the Peutinger Table . . . Clüver identifies Breviodurum as Pont-Audemer, Noviomagus as the capital of the Lexovii [Lisieux], and Durocasae or Durocasses as Dreux.” These are Valesius’s words. But the most eminent d’Anville refutes this opinion, even from the traces of Roman roads, which, since they led to Lillebonne, plainly demonstrate that it was Juliobona, capital of the Caletes. He further shows that Valesius’s error in locating Juliobona arose because he took Carocotinum to mean the town of Le Crotoy, whereas Harfleur should rather be understood by this name (*Notitia Galliae*, p. 393). Dom Bouquet, Book V, p. 600.]

Finally, the same Caesar carefully explored the whole of Neustria and ordered the city of Rouen to be built upon the river Seine in a most suitable place, where at the eastern end of the city the river Albula flows into the Seine with the Robec, and the Maronne flows in from the west. [Col. 0386A] Rouen was named by its founders as though *Romanorum domus*, “house of the Romans,” for there a legion of Roman citizens lived securely, governing and restraining the provincials on every side.

## VII. Of the City of Rouen; of the City of Évreux; Deeds of Blessed Taurinus

The city of Rouen is exceedingly rich in people and commercial activity, most delightful for the convergence of its harbour, the murmur of its streams, and the beauty of its meadows, most abundant in fruits, fish, and all things, surrounded on every side by hills and woods, very strong in walls, ditches, and fortifications, and most beautiful in its ramparts and in the buildings of its houses and churches. To this city blessed Nicasius the bishop was sent by Saint Denis [Col. 0386B] in the time of the emperor Domitian, together with his companions. But on the way, in a certain market-place called Scamnis, he was seized by Sisinnius Fescenninus and, steadfastly persisting in the faith of Christ, was beheaded with Quirinus the priest and Scuviculus the deacon on the fifth day before the Ides of October [11 October]. Their bodies were left by their persecutors to be devoured by birds, savage dogs, and wild beasts; but, by command of almighty God, they were guarded untouched by angels.

Then, after the profane attendants had departed, on the following night the holy martyrs were wondrously raised by divine help; taking up their heads, they crossed the river Epte at a ford unknown to human beings and rested in a most pleasant island in that river. In memory of the saints, the place has from then until the present day been called Vani—that is, “the ford of Nicasius”—and God has granted there many benefits to those who faithfully ask through the martyrs’ merits. Ancient paganism, after the preacher had been martyred on his way, possessed Rouen for a long time and filled it with countless idolatries until Saint Mellonus became archbishop.

At that time the faith of Christ possessed and savingly enlightened the city of the Evantici, that is, Évreux, situated upon the river Iton. Blessed Taurinus had been sent there by Denis Macharius and, strengthened by God, had performed many miracles. For God was always with him and gloriously directed all his works; therefore he endured the hard and harsh things of this world with equanimity. [Col. 0387A] He had left in Rome his father, the Roman Tarquinius, and his most devout mother Euticia, a worshipper of Christ, together with other friends and relatives; and at the command of Pope Clement he had entered Gaul in youthful exile with Denis the Ionian.

When the second persecution, which raged under Domitian against Christians, was raging most fiercely, the aforesaid Denis, bishop of Paris, ordained his spiritual son Taurinus—now forty years old—as bishop. Having prophesied many things that he would suffer, he sent him to the people of Évreux in the Lord’s name. As the man of God approached the gates of the city, a demon opposed him in three apparitions: namely, in the forms of a bear, lion, and buffalo, wishing to terrify Christ’s champion. But Taurinus stood firm in faith like an unconquerable wall [Col. 0387B] and completed the journey he had begun, receiving lodging in the house of Lucius.

On the third day, while Taurinus was preaching there to the people and the sweetness of faith greatly pleased the new hearers, the grieving devil began to torment Euphrasia, Lucius’s daughter, and cast her into the fire. She immediately died; but shortly afterward, when Taurinus prayed and commanded her to rise in the Lord’s name, she was restored to life. No mark of burning appeared upon her. All who saw this miracle were suddenly terrified and astonished, and believed in Jesus Christ. On that day 120 persons were baptised, eight blind persons received sight, four mute persons were healed, and many others were cured of diverse illnesses in the Lord’s name. [Col. 0387C]

Then Taurinus entered Diana’s shrine and, by God’s power, compelled Zabulus—the Devil—to stand visibly before the people. At the sight, the pagan crowd was greatly afraid. For there plainly appeared to them an Ethiopian, black as soot, with a long beard and casting fiery sparks from his mouth. Then an angel of the Lord, shining like the sun, arrived and, in the sight of all, led the demon away with his hands bound behind his back. On that day, therefore, two thousand men were baptised, and all the sick were healed by divine aid. Deodatus, Euphrasia’s brother, saw this, believed, was baptised, became a priest, and faithfully recorded these things in writing.

Then Taurinus entered Diana’s foul shrine, cleansed it with exorcisms and prayers, and dedicated it as a temple to God in honour of Saint Mary, Mother of God. [Col. 0387D] He then began everywhere to destroy idols, consecrate churches to Christ, travel throughout the whole diocese, ordain according to canon law, and establish hospitality in all places.

Envious Satan, seeing so many good things, was grieved and strove by various contrivances to injure the man of God, stirring up many opponents against him. Two magicians, Cambisses and Zaraa, were priests of Diana; when they saw the people’s conversion to God, they groaned and incited twenty of their disciples to kill Taurinus. As they approached, the man of God saw and recognized them from afar; and when he made the sign of the cross against them, they immediately stood fixed in place. At his command they were released; falling at his feet, they believed and were baptised in the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. [Col. 0388A] But when the magicians discovered that their devices had no power against Christ’s soldier, they killed themselves with their own knives.

Meanwhile Licinius the consul heard of the holy bishop’s fame and had him brought before him at the village of Gisay. As Taurinus was being led away, he encountered a paralytic and the paralytic’s sister, who was blind, deaf, and mute. Taurinus immediately blessed water, sprinkled the sick persons with it, and at once restored them to health. The executioners saw this and immediately believed in the Lord. While bishop and consul disputed vehemently about idolatry and *theusebia*—godliness or divine worship—and, by command of the irrationally raging consul, the bishop was stripped and beaten with rods, he faithfully prayed to God and was at once strengthened by a voice sent to him from heaven. The hands of the executioners immediately withered; [Col. 0388B] Licinius, however, inflamed with anger because his wife Leonilla spoke for the man of God, ordered her to be tortured.

While these things were taking place, a messenger arrived saying that Licinius’s son had died in a fall during a hunt near the castle of Alerci, together with his armour-bearer. Licinius, therefore, and his entire army were deeply grieved, and, by God’s prompting, he was compelled to entreat the man of God whom he had begun to torture. After Taurinus had prostrated himself in prayer in the church of Saint Mary, he went with the people to the bodies of the dead. There he devoutly implored God; when his prayers were ended, he took the hand of the young man Marinus, his cousin, and restored him from death to life in the Lord’s name. When Licinius, his wife, [Col. 0388C] and all his nobles saw this, they rejoiced and, falling at the bishop’s feet, asked that holy baptism be given to them. On that day 1,200 men were baptised.

Then, at Marinus’s request for his armour-bearer, Taurinus consented. He approached the body, invoked God, called Paschasius by name, and restored him to life by God’s power. Both men, surviving after this experience, recounted to the living what the dead had seen among the dead. Paschasius foretold to Marinus that he would die on the day when he put off his white baptismal garments; and so it happened. For Marinus was seized by a slight fever and died on the eighth day after his baptism.

By these and many other miracles Taurinus, first bishop of the Ébroïciens, shone forth, and led many thousands of people [Col. 0388D] to knowledge of truth and righteousness. Finally, while Pope Sixtus sat in the apostolic see and Aelius Hadrian governed the commonwealth, Taurinus, full of days and virtues, was called by heaven on the third Ides of August [11 August]; and the church, with the people standing by, was filled with a thick and fragrant mist. After the space of one hour had passed, the mist withdrew, and the bishop appeared seated in his chair, as though praying, with hands outstretched and eyes turned toward heaven. The fall of their shepherd caused immense grief among the parishioners; and by command of an angel, who had appeared to the people in the form of an honourable man, the man of God was buried outside the city, about one third of a mile to the west. That place was long afterward left without honour. But now, by God’s grace, a chosen flock of monks has been established there in a saving warfare [Col. 0389A].

At the burial of the venerable bishop an unprecedented thing occurred. While the bishop was being placed in the mausoleum according to custom and the people were weeping bitterly, he raised himself from the grave as though alive and said: “My little children, what are you doing? Do not be afraid. Listen to a righteous man.” Then, bowing his head, he was silent.

When the servant of Christ had therefore been buried, the angel of God said to the people: “Depart quickly, lest you be overwhelmed by enemies. This city will now be destroyed, but none of you will be endangered. For many ages this place will remain unknown.” Having said this, he appeared nowhere again, and everything was fulfilled as he had foretold. For the tomb of the holy bishop and the anniversary of his death remained unknown to men for a long time. Some signs, moreover, are still daily wrought through him at Évreux. For the demon [Col. 0389B] whom he expelled from Diana’s shrine still dwells in that same city; often appearing in various forms, he harms no one. The common people call him Gobelin, and affirm to this day that, through the merits of Saint Taurinus, he has been restrained from injuring human beings. And because, at the saintly bishop’s command, he complied by breaking his own images, he was not immediately plunged into the abyss; rather, he suffered punishment in the place where he had reigned, seeing those people saved whom he had long assaulted in many ways to their ruin.

The inhabitants also relate—and it is true—that no venomous creature can live in the city of Évreux. For the rich soil, soaked by the streams of the river Iton, produced adders and serpents, and the city of Évreux abounded excessively in creatures of this sort [Col. 0389C]. When the citizens complained of this plague, blessed Taurinus prayed to the Lord to free the city from this inconvenience and no longer allow a poisonous reptile to live within its walls. He prayed and was heard. If by chance a snake or toad is carried in a bundle of grass, it dies immediately upon coming within the city walls.

After a long time the Christian religion increased, and the clergy of Évreux, together with the faithful inhabitants, sought the burial-place of their first bishop Taurinus and, God showing the way, found it. It was then reverently raised from the ground and, after some time, was transported by the faithful to Fécamp. There a venerable monastery of monks was built for the continual worship of the Deity [Col. 0389D], and there the holy man’s body was reverently placed in a precious shrine.

May God, through the prayers and merits of the kindly bishop Taurinus, deliver us from every poison of vices; adorn us with the perfect radiance of holy virtues; and join us in the holy dwellings to the fellowship of His saints, where we may worthily praise the King of kings Himself through all ages of ages. Amen.

While Aelius Hadrian and Antoninus Pius were emperors, the newly planted Christianity in Gaul was grievously afflicted by hostile fury, and holy Mother Church was greatly humbled for nearly 160 years. No history plainly tells us what people this was, whence [Col. 0390A] it came, or under what prince or tyrant it raged, oppressing Christians and idolaters intolerably. Yet in many accounts of the saints of that period it is clearly evident that, under the aforesaid rulers, a certain cruel and barbarous army severely devastated the kingdom of Gaul. At that time there was no king in Gaul; rather, the emperor of the Romans, from the time of Gaius Julius Caesar, ruled over all lands this side of the Alps and appointed governors and other authorities to individual cities at his own pleasure.

There was a great silence concerning God in Neustria after the death of Saint Taurinus the bishop, until the times of Diocletian and Maximian. By them was brought about the tenth calamity of diabolical fury, which raged more grievously and for a longer time than the others against Christ’s Church. Yet He who [Col. 0390B] always promised to be present with His own wonderfully strengthened and delivered His bride amid the immeasurable storms of tribulations, protected and exalted her, and openly glorified her by honourable triumphs. Moreover, before His Father in the heavenly Jerusalem He will reward her with an eternal crown. Therefore, the one whom He loves so greatly He did not cease for a long time to leave bereft of illustrious teachers amid the frenzies of persecutors.  
[Note: For *desiit* (“did not cease”), perhaps *permisit* (“allowed”) should here be read.]

VIII. Mallonus and Avicianus, apostles of Normandy. Couplets in honour of the first forty-seven bishops of Rouen.

While the tenth persecution fiercely threatened Christians for ten years, slaughtering innumerable thousands of martyrs by many kinds of tortures and sending them gloriously adorned with precious blood to heaven, [Col. 0390C] Quintinus and Lucianus, Valerianus, Rufinus and Eugenius, Mallonus and Avicianus, and many others of the Roman clergy and nobility left Rome and dispersed throughout Gaul, confidently preaching the word of God. Quintinus then went to Amiens, Lucianus to Beauvais, and Mallonus, with Avicianus and certain other suitable men, to Rouen.

When Diocletian and Maximian Herculius voluntarily laid down the reins of empire, Constantius, a man of great courtesy, assumed in the western regions the imperial power which Herculius had resigned. He exercised much clemency toward men and the greatest devotion toward God. For neither, from rage shared with his colleague, as Eusebius of Caesarea [Col. 0390D] relates, had he stained his kingdom with the blood of the godly; nor had he destroyed houses of prayer and assemblies of Christ’s worshippers by hostile devastation, as Maximian had done. In Neustria he founded a city, which he called Constantia after his own name; and in that province he had a concubine named Helena, by whom he begot Constantine the Great, afterward founder of Constantinople.

At that time the venerable Mallonus dwelt at Rouen with certain other faithful people and, by God’s will, first obtained the episcopal chair there; after him the metropolitan dignity has remained there to the present day. Six cities [Col. 0391A] are subject to it: the city of the Bessin, that is, Bayeux; that of the Ébroïciens, that is, Évreux; Lisieux; Avranches; Coutances; and Séez. The church of Rouen has now had forty-six bishops, and its clergy has composed for posterity a heroic couplet concerning each bishop. I shall not shrink from inserting these in order into this work, in charitable fashion, together with certain necessary additions.

[1.]

Holy bishop Mallonus, first in the succession,  
Cultivated the people of Rouen by teaching.

He flourished in the time of Popes Eusebius and Melchiades, and passed to the Lord on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November [22 October]. He lay buried for a long time in the crypt of the basilica of Saint Gervasius the martyr outside the city. His mausoleum is preserved there to this day; but after a long time his body was removed from there for fear of the Danes and transported to the castle of Vilcassini, called Pontoise [Col. 0391B]. There it is reverently kept in a royal church dedicated in his name, and a community of canons solemnly serves him.

[2.]

After him the distinguished, devoted Avicianus  
Obtained the governance and directed the pastoral charge.

[Note: [Col. 0391D] Le Prévost: “with honour” in the Chesne edition.]

He attended the Council of Arles, held in the time of Pope Sylvester under Constantine Augustus, who began to reign in the 1061st year from the founding of the City. Then was celebrated the Nicene synod of 318 Fathers, among whom Nicholas of Myra in Lycia and other most eminent bishops shone.

[3.]

Severus, a bishop radiant in virtue, succeeded,  
Distinguished in character, gentle to those entrusted to him and to himself.

He flourished for fifteen years in the time of Constantine and Constantius, under Popes Mark and Julius. Then Maximinus of Trier, Hilary of Poitiers, Athanasius of Alexandria, Eusebius of Vercelli, and Dionysius of Milan shone like stars [Col. 0391C].

[4.]

Eusebius too, gentle and steadfast in the episcopal order,  
Shone with the kindly flowers of virtues.

He flourished for twenty-five years in the time of Popes Liberius and Felix, under Constantine, Julian the Apostate, Jovinian, and Valentinian.

[5.]

Marcellinus succeeded him by Christ’s appointment,  
A distinguished shepherd, adorned by uprightness of character.

He laboured well in the Church for twenty years in the time of Pope Damasus, while Valentinian and Valens reigned with Gratian and Valentinian [Col. 0391D]. Then Antony the monk, most renowned among the Egyptians, died. At Saragossa Peter, an eminent orator, flourished. Ambrose of Milan stood as an unconquerable wall against the Arians. Under Pope Damasus the Constantinopolitan synod of 102 Fathers against Macedonius and Eunomius was held.

[6.]

Peter, ever watchful among the people and a worthy guardian,  
Holily governed the episcopate entrusted to him.

He flourished for nineteen years in the time of Popes Siricius and Anastasius, under Theodosius and Arcadius. Then Martin of Tours [Col. 0392A] and Maurilius of Angers, Basil of Caesarea, the eminent orator Augustine of Hippo, and Jerome, interpreter of the divine law, shone forth.

[7.]

Victricius, mighty conqueror and avenger of vices,  
Instructed the Lord’s Church with kindly precepts.

He flourished for eleven years in the time of Pope Innocent, under Arcadius and Honorius. Then Donatus, bishop of Epirus, and John of Jerusalem shone. The discovery of the body of Saint Stephen the proto-martyr took place, God revealing it to Lucian, priest of Caphargamala. Then the priest Orosius, who wrote the book *On the Ormesta of the World*, was sent by Augustine to Jerome concerning certain profound questions; he visited Lucian, from whom he first brought to Spain the relics of Saint Stephen sent to the priest Avitus [Col. 0392B].

[8.]

The kindly bishop Innocentius succeeded him,  
Restoring the Lord’s Church and reforming the people.

He flourished for nine years in the time of Popes Zosimus, Boniface, and Celestine, under Honorius and Theodosius, son of Arcadius. Then the Ephesian synod of two hundred bishops, presided over by Cyril of Alexandria, was assembled. Palladius, ordained by Pope Celestine, was sent as the first bishop to convert the Scots to Christ.

[9.]

Full of sacred eloquence, Evodus succeeded,  
Strong and harmless, prudent, devout, and modest.

He flourished for eight years in the time of Popes Celestine and Sixtus. Then the Gauls rebelled against the Romans [Col. 0392C], and the Franks, descended from Trojan stock, allied themselves with them; united together, they made Francus Pharamond, son of the duke Sunno, their king. Maximus, bishop of Turin, was held eloquent in composing sermons.

[10.]

Holy Silvester honourably presided over the Church;  
He wisely and justly governed and enlarged it.

[Note: [Col. 0391D] Le Prévost: “with honour” in the Chesne edition.]

He flourished for eight years in the time of Pope Leo, while Clodio and Meroveus ruled in Francia.

[11.]

Bishop Malsonus, sustained by divine doctrine,  
Was everywhere a venerable shepherd among the people.

He flourished for nine years under Marcian and Valentinian, when Pope Leo held at Chalcedon a synod of 630 bishops against Eutyches and Dioscorus [Col. 0392D]. Then Hengist and Horsa, with Saxons and Angles, were carried to Britain in three long ships and received by King Vortigern against the Picts. Then Germanus of Auxerre flourished wonderfully.

[12.]

The renowned bishop, an enduring guardian of the people,  
Germanus, received the episcopal see.

He flourished for eight years, while Childeric ruled the Gauls and Leo the Latins. Then Theodorus, bishop of Syria, wrote an Ecclesiastical History from the end of Eusebius’s books to his own time, that is, to the reign of Leo, under whom he died.

[13.]

Crescentius cultivated and adorned those entrusted to him  
With outstanding manners and made them grow in virtue.

He shone for twenty-six years in the time of Popes Hilary and Simplicius, during Leo’s reign [Col. 0393A]. Then Childeric, son of Meroveus, reigned in Gaul.

[14.]

Gildardus shone, a holy and gracious shepherd,  
Generous and steadfast, aflame also with the light of the word.

He flourished for fifteen years in the time of Popes Felix, Gelasius, Anastasius, and Symmachus, under the Emperor Zeno; and he consecrated blessed Laudus, bishop of Coutances. Then Remigius of Reims, Solemnis of Chartres, and Vedastus of Arras flourished, and in the year 488 from the Lord’s Incarnation baptized Clovis, the Merovingian king of the Franks. Three years later Mamertus, [Col. 0393B] archbishop of Vienne, established solemn litanies—that is, rogations—before the Lord’s Ascension because of an impending disaster. Victorius, at Pope Hilary’s command, wrote the 532-year Paschal cycle. Odoacer, king of the Goths, took Rome; thereafter their kings Theodoric Triarius and Theodoric Walamer held it for a long time. Huneric, the Arian king of the Vandals in Africa, drove out more than 336 Catholic bishops, closed their churches, and afflicted the people with various punishments. Gildardus of Rouen and Medardus of Soissons were born to Nectardus, father from Noyon, and Protagia, mother; both passed to the Lord on the sixth Ides of June [8 June].

The distinguished Audoenus composed the following verses concerning them:

[Col. 0393C]

These are Gildardus and Medardus, twin brothers.  
One day saw them born from the womb and consecrated,  
Clothed in white and released from this flesh.

[15.]

Flavius shone brightly with the notable flower of virtues;  
And filled those entrusted to him with divine law.

He flourished for thirty-five years in the time of Popes Symmachus, Hormisdas, John, Felix, Boniface, John, and Agapetus, under Anastasius, Justin the Elder, and Justinian. After Clovis’s death Sigismund, Childebert, and his other sons succeeded. Lotharius, however, surviving them all, ruled in Francia for fifty-one years; in his time Launomarus and Ebrulfus, and other holy men, flourished in his kingdom. Transamund, king of the Vandals, closed the Catholic churches and sent 220 bishops into exile in Sardinia; [Col. 0393D] Pope Symmachus supplied them with money and clothing every year. Emperor Anastasius, because he favoured the heresy of Eutyches and persecuted Catholics, perished by a divine thunderbolt. Pope John, under Justin the Elder, gave sight to a blind man at Constantinople; as he returned to Ravenna, Theodoric killed him. He also killed the patrician Symmachus and Boethius; and he himself perished by a sudden death in the following year. His nephew Athalaric succeeded him in the kingdom. Hilderic, king of the Vandals, ordered the bishops to return from exile and the churches to be restored, after seventy-six years of heretical profanation. Abbot Benedict shone in glory of virtues, which blessed Pope Gregory wrote in the book of the *Dialogues* [Col. 0394A]. The patrician Belisarius, sent by Justinian into Africa, destroyed the Vandal people and sent their captive king Gelimer to Constantinople. Carthage too was recovered in the ninety-sixth year after its loss. Dionysius Exiguus wrote Paschal cycles beginning from the year 532 of the Lord’s Incarnation; in that year Justinian’s Code was promulgated. Victor, bishop of Capua, writing a book on Easter, criticized the errors of Victorius. Cassiodorus the senator, Priscian the grammarian, and Arator the subdeacon flourished.

[16.]

The martyr Praetextatus fell, at the instigation of  
Queen Fredegund, for the name of Christ Jesus.

He flourished for forty-eight years in the time of Popes Agapetus, Silverius, Vigilius, Pelagius, John, and Pelagius, under Justin and [Col. 0394B] Tiberius Constantine. The patrician Narses defeated and killed Totila, king of the Goths, in Italy. The Lombard people, accompanied by famine and mortality, invaded all Italy under King Alboin.

[17.]

Melantius governed the Church for many years.  
He taught those subject to him and made them live justly.

He presided over the people of Rouen for twelve years in the time of Popes Pelagius, Benedict, and Gregory the Great, the teacher, while Maurice, first of the Greeks, ruled the Romans; but unworthily, since, as they say, he had been the betrayer of his master Praetextatus, whom Fredegund, wife of King Chilperic, had caused to be killed.

IX. Continuation of the couplets.

[18.]

The noble Hyldulfus sat in the aforesaid episcopal office  
And cultivated the doctrines of the divine word.

[Note: [Col. 0393D] Le Prévost: *dogmate*, “by doctrine.”]

He flourished for twenty-eight years in the time of Gregory the Great, the teacher, and of Popes Sabinian, Boniface, Deusdedit, Boniface, and Honorius, while Maurice, Phocas, and Heraclius ruled. Then Childebert and his sons Theodoric and Theodebert, and Lotharius the Great, reigned in Francia. In England Æthelberht of Kent, Edwin of Northumbria, Rædwald of the Gewisse, and Penda of Mercia reigned; Gregory sent to them preachers of God’s word—Augustine, Mellitus, John, and many other God-fearing monks—through whom the English were converted to Christ. In Italy Authari son of Cleph and Ago Agilulf ruled the Lombards, together with the praiseworthy queen Theodelinda [Col. 0394D].
