In Neustria, in the twelfth year of King Childebert, Saint Ebrulf, abbot of Ouche, already an octogenarian, died on the fourth day before the Kalends of January [29 December 596]. About the same time the monastery of Monte Cassino was attacked by Lombards at night and, after the monks had fled, was destroyed in the time of Bonitus, its fifth abbot. Benedict, Constantine, Simplicius, Vitalis, and Bonitus had already presided over that monastery. Chosroes, king of the Persians, grievously devastated the commonwealth by wars and fiercely afflicted the holy Church by burnings, plundering, and slaughter. Anastasius the Persian, a monk, was crowned with glorious martyrdom together with seventy others. Heraclius defeated the Persians, killed Chosroes, brought the Lord’s cross back to Jerusalem [Col. 0395A], and restored all Christians from captivity.

[19.]

Saint Romanus, noble in illustrious action,  
Shone in character and in the light of the sacred word.

He worked miracles for thirteen years in the time of Popes Honorius, Severinus, and John, while Heraclius reigned; and on the tenth day before the Kalends of November [23 October] he gloriously passed to the Lord. Then Dagobert and Louis, Christian princes, flourished in Gaul; Oswald, Oswine, and Oswiu in England; and Agilulf, Adaloald, Arioald, Rothari, and Rodoald in Italy. Under Arioald, blessed Columbanus, a Scot by birth, after building the monastery of Luxeuil in Gaul, founded Bobbio in the Cottian Alps of Italy.

[20.]

Audoenus succeeded him, shining in episcopal  
Rank and resplendent with virtues.

He shone gloriously for forty-three years in the time of Popes Theodore, Martin, Eugenius, Vitalian, Adeodatus, Donus, Agatho, Leo, Benedict, and John, while Heracleonas, son of Heraclius, and three Constantines ruled. He lived long and well, laboured much, and benefited God’s Church wonderfully. My power to relate how greatly this man excelled in nobility, holiness, and every excellence fails me. Pope Martin held in Rome a synod of 105 bishops; afterward, for the Catholic faith, he was seized by the exarch Theodore at the command of Constantine, grandson of Heraclius, and exiled at Cherson, where he rested in a holy end [Col. 0395B]. Archbishop Theodore and Abbot Adrian, a man likewise most learned, were sent to Britain by Pope Vitalian and made many English churches fruitful with the harvest of teaching. From the time when Pope Gregory sent dispensers of the divine seed to England, Augustine and Laurence, Mellitus of London and Justus of Rochester, Honorius and Deusdedit, governed the church of Canterbury and drew the kings of Kent—Æthelberht and Eadbald, Eorconberht and Egbert—with their subject people to Christ’s faith. The seventh chosen for the episcopacy was Wighard, elected by Kings Oswiu and Egbert and sent to Rome for ordination. There, while awaiting the appointed day of consecration, he died; in his place Theodore the Greek, pre-eminent in holiness and wisdom, was ordained. In Neustria Philibert, glorious in nobility, holiness, and the splendour of miracles, by permission of King Louis and Queen Balthild, built at Jumièges a monastery of 800 monks [Col. 0395D]; after some years he placed over it Saint Aichadrus, whom he had taken from the monastery of Hério. Then Wandrille founded the monastery of Fontenelle and gathered there almost 400 monks for God’s service; from these the Church of God later gladly took many suitable bishops and abbots to govern her. Sidonius and Ribertus, Geremarus, Leudfredus, and many other monks also flourished in the diocese of Rouen. The zeal and aid of the venerable Archbishop Audoenus favoured them all in every good work, as ardent readers may clearly observe in their deeds [Col. 0396A]. In Italy, when King Aripert died at Pavia after nine years, his two sons, still adolescents, succeeded: Godebert held the royal seat at Pavia, while Bertharith held it in the city of Milan. Not long afterward Grimoald, vigorous duke of Benevento, killed Godebert with the sword and drove Bertharith into exile; he took their kingdom along with their sister and held it powerfully and profitably for nine years. After his death Bertharith reigned for eighteen years and made his son Cunipert, whom he had received from Queen Rodelinda, partner in the kingdom. Both were lovers of justice, benevolent worshippers of God and His Church, and defenders of the poor. Alahis, duke of Brescia, rebelled against them and repeatedly disturbed the entire region for a long time, until he was killed while Cunipert fought him and ceased from malice [Col. 0396B]. At the request of the most devout rulers Constantine, Heraclius, and Tiberius, Pope Agatho sent John, bishop of Porto, John the deacon, and other envoys of the holy Roman Church to Constantinople. There, through them, he held a council of 150 bishops against George, patriarch of the imperial city, Macarius of Antioch, and other heretics. When the controversy ended, George was corrected, while the obstinate Macarius and his accomplices were anathematized.

[21.]

Renowned Ansbertus, endowed with the height of virtue,  
Governed the Church, which he nobly adorned in holiness.

He flourished for eighteen years in the time of Popes Leo, Benedict, John, Conon, and Sergius, under Constantine and [Col. 0396C] Justinian the Younger. Then Lotharius, Theodoric, and Childeric reigned in Gaul, while Leodegar, Ebroin, and Pippin the First held the mayoralty of the royal household.

[22.]

Distinguished Grippo succeeded in the holy order,  
Outstanding in deeds, a shepherd venerable for his merits.

He flourished for thirty-four years in the time of Popes John, Sisinnius, Constantine, and Gregory. Then Leo, Tiberius, Justinian, Philippicus, Anastasius, Theodosius, and Leo governed the commonwealth; and Clovis, Childebert, and Dagobert the Younger reigned in Gaul. The most reverend Cuthbert, bishop of the church of Lindisfarne in Britain and formerly an anchorite, led a life illustrious for miraculous signs from childhood to old age. In the time of Henry, king of the English, Ralph, bishop of Rochester, found his body incorrupt; in the presence of King Alexander of the Scots, who stood by and looked reverently on, together with monks and clerics, he changed Cuthbert’s garments [Col. 0396D].

[23.]

The just and illustrious Radilandus shone in the order,  
Compassionate toward all and filled with rich merits.

He flourished for three years in the time of Pope Gregory. Leo then ruled. The Franks, after Dagobert’s death, raised the cleric Daniel to be king. The Saracens besieged Constantinople for three years with a vast army; but, conquered while the citizens fought more by prayers than arms, they fled in peril from hunger, cold, and pestilence. Liutprand, king of the Lombards, at Pope Gregory’s urging confirmed the grant of the patrimony in the Cottian Alps, which Aripert had sent to Rome inscribed in golden letters and which he had reclaimed [Col. 0397A]. He also purchased the bones of Saint Augustine the teacher at a great price and transported them from Sardinia, which the Saracens had ravaged, to Pavia, where he honourably deposited them.

[24.]

The venerable Hugh benefited the Lord’s people  
And bestowed upon those subject to him the doctrines of holy life.

He was a cousin of Pippin, prince of the Franks, and was archbishop for eight years in the time of Pope Gregory II. He also presided over the churches of Paris and Bayeux and over the abbeys of Jumièges and Fontenelle. His body, together with that of Saint Aichadrus, was carried by the monks of Jumièges into Lotharingia and is still honourably preserved there in a silver shrine, in the village called Hasprès in the territory of Cambrai [Col. 0397B]. Constantine then ruled. Bede the Englishman, servant of Christ and priest of the monastery of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, which is at Wearmouth in Jarrow, flourished. He was born in the territory of that monastery and, at the age of seven, was given by his relatives to be educated under the most reverend Abbot Benedict and afterward Ceolfrith. He spent the whole remainder of his life dwelling in that monastery and gave all his effort to meditation upon the Scriptures. Amid observance of the regular discipline and daily responsibility for singing in church, as he himself declares in writing, he always found it delightful either to learn, to teach, or to write. In the nineteenth year of his life [Col. 0397C] he received the diaconate, and in his thirtieth the priesthood, both by command of his abbot Ceolfrith and through the ministry of the most reverend Bishop John. From the time he received the priesthood until the fifty-ninth year of his age, he never ceased from beneficial study. He made brief notes upon much of holy Scripture from the small works of the venerable Fathers, taking care to add material in accordance with their understanding and interpretation. The fruit of his labours and studies was most useful and delightful to God’s Church: he produced seventy-two books upon God’s law and necessary inquiries, all of which he himself carefully enumerates and describes at the end of his history of the English. Then in Lombardy the monk Paul of Monte Cassino flourished, and in Gaul Fortunatus the poet, kindly bishop of Poitiers [Col. 0397D].

[25.]

Radbertus, having worthily received the shepherd’s seat,  
Shone with holy powers and lived a holy life.

He flourished for four years in the time of Pope Gregory II, while Constantine ruled. Then Charles Tudites—that is, Martel—held power in Francia. With Duke Eudo he fought the Saracens in Aquitaine and overthrew 375,000 of them; likewise, in the province of Narbonne, he courageously repelled them in battle and devastated them with a very great slaughter.

[26.]

Grimo, a devoted shepherd—pious and eminent in deed—  
Received the Church to govern by divine right.

[Note: [Col. 0397D] Le Prévost: *cultu*, “by worship.”]

He flourished for four years in the time of Pope Gregory III. In [Col. 0398A] England, after the death of Berhtwald, archbishop of Canterbury, Tatwine succeeded. Then two English kings, Coenred of Mercia and Offa, son of Sighere, king of the East Saxons, abandoned earthly sceptres for Christ, set out for Rome, and, with Pope Constantine’s blessing, became monks. They remained at the thresholds of the apostles in prayers, fasts, and almsgiving until their final day. The venerable Wilfrid, archbishop of York, died in the forty-fifth year of his episcopate, in the province of Oundle, on the fourth Ides of October [12 October], while Coenred and Osred son of Aldfrith, king of the Northumbrians, reigned. Not long afterward Adrian, the most learned abbot, died; his pupil Albinus, thoroughly instructed in many ways, succeeded him.

[27.]

Rainfridus shone in the summit of pastoral office, in every  
Action magnificent, a builder of the episcopate.

He flourished for seventeen years in the time of Popes Zacharias and Stephen. Carloman and Pippin obtained the mayoralty of the palace.

[28.]

Bishop Remigius, born of royal stock,  
Lived devoutly and instructed those entrusted to him in doctrine.

He was son of Charles Martel and brother of King Pippin. After Ragenfrid had been expelled, he held the see of Rouen for seventeen years in the time of Popes Paul, Constantine, and Stephen. Constantine, son of Leo, emperor, assembled at Constantinople a synod of 330 bishops. Pope Stephen, harassed by the persecution of Aistulf, king of the Lombards, [Col. 0398C] went to Francia and consecrated King Pippin and his sons Charles and Carloman. Then Boniface, archbishop of Mainz, and Wido, abbot of Fontenelle, flourished. Constantine and Abdallah, emir and king of the Saracens, together raged against the orthodox. Leo, son of Constantine, ruled as Augustus in the seventy-first place for five years. In the year 778 from the Lord’s Incarnation, King Pippin died on the eighth day before the Kalends of October [24 September], and his son Charles the Great succeeded him.

[29.]

Bishop Meinardus, full of the fragrance of goodness,  
Taught those subject to him and cleansed them from the filth of vices.

He flourished for eight years in the time of Pope Hadrian. In the sixth year of his reign Charles went to Rome; returning thence, he captured Pavia, led Desiderius, king of the Lombards—who had inflicted many persecutions upon Pope Hadrian—captive into Francia [Col. 0398D], and expelled his son Adalgis from Italy. This Desiderius was indeed the thirty-first king of the Lombards; in him the royal dignity failed because of its sins, and thereafter the Lombard people never had a king of their own, but were always subject to kings of the Franks or emperors of the Germans.

The first dukes of the Winnili were Ibor and Aio, who, with their mother Gambara, led the Winnili by lot from the island of Scandinavia. Their subsequent kings were Agelmund, Lamissio, Lethu, Hildehoc and Godehoc, Claffo and Tato, Wacho, Waltarith, Audoin, and Alboin. Agelmund led the Lombards into [Col. 0399A] Bulgaria, Audoin into Pannonia, and Alboin, aided by the patrician Narses, into Italy. After King Alboin was killed by his armour-bearer Helmechis at the prompting of his wife Rosemund, Cleph gained the kingdom by election of the people. His son Flavius Authari reigned after him and married Theodelinda, daughter of Garibald, king of the Bavarians. Authari died of poison after six years of his reign; Ago Agilulf, duke of Turin, acquired both queen and kingdom and, dying after twenty-five years, left the kingdom to his son Adaloald. But after Adaloald had reigned ten years with his mother Theodelinda, Arioald held the kingdom over the Lombards for twelve years; Rothari succeeded him, a man strong in power but stained by the treachery of Arian heresy [Col. 0399B]. When he had reigned sixteen years, he left the kingdom to his son Rodoald; after five years, having been discovered in adultery, Rodoald was struck by a Lombard rival and died.

[Note: [Col. 0399D] Le Prévost: “months.”]

Aripert, son of Gunduald and grandson of Queen Theodelinda, succeeded; after nine years, dying, he left the kingdom to his sons Bertharith and Godebert. Then Grimoald, duke of Benevento, took Rodelinda, daughter of King Aripert, as his wife, killed her brother Godebert with the sword, and drove Bertharith from the kingdom. When Grimoald died after nine years, Bertharith recovered the kingdom and expelled Garibald, Grimoald’s son, who had reigned three months after his father. After Bertharith’s eighteen years, Cunipert reigned twelve years; when he died, the Lombard people had four kings in two years [Col. 0399C]: Liutpert, son of Cunipert; Raginbert, duke of Turin and son of Godebert; Aripert, Raginbert’s son; and Rothari, duke of Bergamo. Finally Aripert, stronger than them all, killed Liutpert and Rothari, drove Ansprand, Liutpert’s guardian, from the island of Comacina, and deprived his son Sigisbrand of his eyes. He then reigned for nine years and restored to Saint Peter many things which his predecessors had taken away. Later, while swimming in the Po, weighed down with gold, he sank and was drowned. Ansprand, a wise man, reigned only three months; his bold son Liutprand sat upon the royal throne for nearly thirty-two years. His nephew Hildebrand was raised to be king, but died before two years had passed [Col. 0399D]. Then Ratchis and Aistulf, sons of Pemmo, duke of Friuli, reigned; the former voluntarily laid down the diadem and became a monk at Rome. Aistulf, however, in the time of Pope Stephen, opposed God’s Church in many ways, but at last, by God’s just judgment, was struck by an arrow while hunting. Finally Duke Desiderius, aided by Pope Stephen, was made king of the Lombards; having gained the kingdom, he persecuted the pope, clergy, and people of Rome. Hence Pope Hadrian was compelled to seek the strength of the Franks; by them the horn of the Lombard kingdom’s cruelty was broken and cast down, even to the present day [Col. 0400A]. This happened in the time of Meinardus, archbishop of Rouen, in the year 774 from the Lord’s Incarnation.

[30.]

The bishop whom Guillebert succeeded, in every…

Constant and gentle, and a faithful shepherd of the people. He flourished for forty-eight years, in the time of Popes Adrian, Leo, Stephen, and Paschal. Then Constantine, Leo, Nicephorus and his son Stauracius, Michael, Leo, and Michael flourished as emperors at Constantinople. Charles, king of the Franks, was wonderfully powerful, and his excellence increased praiseworthily. He destroyed Pamplona, subdued Saragossa by siege, subjected Gascony, Spain, and Saxony, and devastated Bavaria, the regions of the Slavs called Vults, and those of the Huns. In the time of Constantine and his mother Irene [Col. 0400B], a certain man at Constantinople discovered a stone chest, and in it a man lying down with this inscription:

> Christ shall be born of the Virgin Mary, and I believe in him. Under the emperors Constantine and Irene, O sun, you shall see me again.

Under Pope Leo there was a great earthquake which shook almost all Italy and brought down a large part of the roof of the church of St Paul together with its beams. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 800, in the eighth indiction, King Charles was consecrated emperor by Pope Leo and was called Augustus by the Romans. Having completed forty-seven years of reign, Charles died, and his son Louis reigned for twenty-seven years; Archbishop Guillebert was his secretary [Col. 0400C].

## X. Sequence of distichs

**[31.]** Rainoward succeeded him, fortunate in due order.

He nourished the gentle and restrained the rebellious.

He flourished for ten years, in the time of Popes Eugenius, Valentine, and Gregory IV, under the Emperor Theophilus. In his time dissension arose in Gaul when Lothair rebelled against his father Louis the Pious. Then for the first time the Northmen ravaged Brittany and other lands, and the body of St Philibert was transferred from the island of Noirmoutier.

**[32.]** Gumbald maintained the governance of a righteous life,

A venerable shepherd, providing everywhere for his people. [Col. 0400D]

He flourished for eleven years, in the time of Popes Gregory and Sergius, while Michael, son of Theophilus, ruled as emperor. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 840, Emperor Louis died on 20 June. His brother Archbishop Drogo conveyed his body to the city of Metz for burial. A division of the kingdom took place, and a battle was fought near Auxerre on 25 June between Louis’s three sons, Louis, Lothair, and Charles the Bald; in it the Christian people on both sides were laid low by mutual slaughter. The body of St Ouen was transferred when the Northmen ravaged Rouen and devastated his monastery on 15 May.

**[33.]** Illustrious Paul, worthy of a shepherd’s summit,

Shone in the word of teaching and in the worthiness of his life. [Col. 0401A]

He flourished for six years, in the time of Pope Sergius, under the Emperor Michael. Lothair held and ruled that part of the Frankish kingdom which his father had freely given him; it is called to this day Lotharingia, that is, “Lothair’s kingdom.” Charles the Bald, king of the Franks and emperor of the Romans, a good and strong man, was established.

**[34.]** Wanilo, a prudent man, mighty in divine teaching,

Taught those entrusted to him the laws of eternal salvation.

He flourished for eleven years, in the time of Popes Leo, Benedict, and Nicholas. In the fifth year of his rule, it froze from the day before the Kalends of December [30 November] until the Nones of April [5 April].

**[35.]** Adalard, outstanding in character and resplendent in goodness,

As a gracious paternal shepherd maintained the laws of the priesthood. [Col. 0401B]

He flourished for three years, in the time of Pope Nicholas. Basil killed his lord Michael and ruled Constantinople in his place for twenty years. Severe famine, human mortality, and a pestilence among animals raged throughout the world for three years.

**[36.]** Riculf, blessed and upright, of distinguished stock,

Bestowed very many landed estates upon the Church.

He flourished for three years, in the time of Popes Nicholas and Adrian.

**[37.]** John, a noble bishop by divine right,

Shone in the rank of pontiff with the brilliance of virtues.

He presided over the people of Rouen for two years.

**[38.]** Vitto [Note: [Col. 0401D] *Vilto*, in the edition of Chesne.], ascending to the episcopal office entrusted to him,

Shone among the people, a prudent man of holy doctrine. [Col. 0401C]

He governed the Church for one year, in the time of Pope Adrian and the Emperor Basil.

**[39.]** Franco succeeded, a good helper of the people,

Who consecrated Rollo at the font of holy baptism.

He flourished for forty-four years, in the time of Popes John, Marinus, Adrian, and Stephen. Then Leo and Alexander, sons of Basil, reigned for twenty-two years. In the year of the Lord 876, Rollo entered Neustria with his men and grievously afflicted Gaul for thirty years by wars, plundering, and fires. He fought against Duke Richard of Burgundy, Ebles of Poitiers, and other princes of Gaul; elated by frequent victories, he inflicted many losses upon Christians. Finally Charles the Simple, son of Louis the Do-Nothing, unable to bear Rollo’s warfare, made peace with him, gave him his daughter Gisela as wife [Col. 0401D], and granted him Neustria. Then Alexander and Constantine ruled at Constantinople with their mother Zoe, as did Romanus the Armenian.

**[40.]** Gunthard in due order assumed the pontifical seat,

Useful among the people and likewise a prudent counsellor.

He flourished for twenty-four years, in the time of the Emperor Romanus the Armenian and Constantine. Then in Gaul Duke Robert assumed the crown for himself. King Charles fought against him in the same year and killed the perjurer; yet Hugh, son of the slain duke, won the victory. Not long afterwards Count Herbert of Péronne, brother-in-law of Hugh the Great, deceitfully captured the king and held him in prison for three years—indeed, until the king’s death [Col. 0402A]. Louis, the king’s son, went with his mother Eadgifu into England to seek his uncle Æthelstan, king of the English and son of Edward the Elder. Rudolf, noble son of Richard, duke of Burgundy, and nephew of Charles, reigned for seven years. When he died, William Longsword, duke of the Normans, at the request of the Franks brought Louis back from England and lawfully restored him to his ancestral throne.

In this time Agapetus, Basil, Stephen, Formosus, John, and Stephen flourished in the apostolic see. William, son of Rollo, restored the monastery of Jumièges and ardently desired to become a monk there under Abbot Martin; but the abbot refused to receive him until his son should be fit to hold the duchy of Normandy [Col. 0402B]. Meanwhile, after this duke had ruled the duchy of Normandy courageously for twenty-five years and had subdued enemies and neighbours by craft or force, he went confidently to a conference with Arnulf, prince of Flanders. He was killed by Arnulf’s treachery on an island in the River Somme, on 18 December. His son Richard Sprotæus, who was then ten years old, possessed the duchy for fifty-four years after his father. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 942, while Louis Overseas reigned, Duke William and Gunhard, archbishop of Rouen, died.

**[41.]** Hugh succeeded, a violator of the law of the Lord,

Born of illustrious stock, but bereft of Christ’s light.

He exercised the episcopate for forty-seven years, but he is praised by none of the writers who have spoken of him or of his bishopric [Col. 0402C]. They openly report that he was a monk in habit, not in deed. Then Marinus, Agapetus, Octavian, Leo, Benedict, and John presided over the apostolic see, and excessive disturbances shook the kingdoms of the earth.

For King Louis subjected Rouen to himself and deceitfully brought Duke Richard to Laon, where he imprisoned him; but Richard escaped through God’s will and the prudence of his guardian Osmund. Afterwards King Harald of the Danes, on the counsel of Bernard the Dane, came with an army into Normandy and fought against King Louis in revenge for William Longsword. In this battle Count Herluin of Montreuil was killed with his brother Lambert and sixteen other counts of Gaul, beside the River Dives [Col. 0402D]; Louis was captured and sent to the fortress of Rouen to be held there. Therefore Gerberga, queen of the Franks and daughter of Henry, emperor beyond the Rhine, made peace with the Normans on the counsel of Hugh the Great. She sent her son Lothair as a hostage and two bishops, Hildierius of Beauvais and Guy of Soissons, as pledges for the observance of faith. Thus the king was released from his chains, and Count Richard, the father of his country, was strengthened.

Emperor Otto subjected Italy to himself. Stephen and Constantine, sons of Romanus, deposed their father from the throne of Constantinople; but Constantine likewise deposed both of them and himself ruled with his son Romanus for sixteen years. Nicephorus succeeded them as emperor [Col. 0403A]. Liudolf, son of King Otto, died after subduing Italy to himself, and the boy Otto was raised as king in the palace at Aachen. John, having killed Nicephorus, ruled through Nicephorus’s wife; her niece Theophanu married Emperor Otto. In England King Edmund was murdered by treachery in the sixth year of his reign, and his brother Eadred obtained the kingdom. Upon Eadred’s death, Edgar, son of Edmund, succeeded and reigned long and beneficially for himself, the people, and the Church of God. Then Dunstan of Canterbury, Oswald of York, and Æthelwold of Winchester shone in the governance of the Church of God. Through their zeal and labour, with King Edgar favouring and obeying these bishops, twenty-six monasteries were built in England. When Louis died, his son Lothair reigned for six years; in him the line of Charlemagne was completely deprived of the kingdom [Col. 0403B]. For Charles and the other sons of King Lothair were captured, and Hugh Magnus, son of Hugh the Great, was raised as king.

**[42.]** An illustrious bishop, born of distinguished parents,

Blessed Robert rested in a devout end.

He was the son of Duke Richard the Elder by Gunnor, and for forty-eight years ruled the archbishopric of Rouen and the county of Évreux, in the time of Robert, king of the Franks, and his son Henry. Then Agapetus and Gerbert-Sylvester, John and Benedict, and likewise John and Benedict, presided over the Roman Church. Otto, Henry, and Conrad, meanwhile, ruled the commonwealth by lawful succession [Col. 0403C].

Archbishop Robert abounded exceedingly in worldly wealth, was excessively occupied with secular affairs, and did not abstain, as befitted a bishop, from carnal enticements. For, like a count, he had a wife named Herleva, by whom he fathered three sons, Richard, Ralph, and William; he apportioned to them, according to secular law, the county of Évreux and other very great honours. At last, in old age, mindful of his errors, he repented and greatly feared for his many and grave offences. He therefore distributed many alms to the poor and began from the foundations the metropolitan church in the city of Rouen in honour of the holy Mother of God, completing it in large part.

Duke Richard II held the duchy of Normandy praiseworthily for thirty years [Col. 0403D]. Like a pious father, he aided Christ’s poor, clerics, and monks; and he enlarged and defended the three monasteries founded by his father: Fécamp, St Ouen in the suburb of Rouen, and St Michael in peril of the sea. The aforesaid duke also restored Fontenelle, and ratified by his own grant whatever Thurstan or Gerard Flaitel and other nobles had given it. When dying, he left the principality to his sons, young Richard and Robert; the dignity granted them endured no more than nine years. For Richard III died of poison before two full years had elapsed, and his brother Robert went on pilgrimage to Jerusalem after seven and a half years. Robert left his duchy, since he would not return, to William, an eight-year-old boy, and entrusted him to his kinsman Alan [Col. 0404A], count of the Bretons.

Then the æthelings Alfred and Edward were exiles in Normandy. Richard II had given his sister Emma in marriage to Æthelred, king of the English; she bore Alfred and King Edward. After her husband’s funeral, she sent her children into Neustria and married Cnut, king of the Danes. She bore him Harthacnut, king of the Danes and English, and Gunnhild, who married Henry, emperor of the Romans.

**[43.]** Malgerius, a young man, received the throne of honour,

Illustrious by birth, but noble in no deed.

He was the son of Duke Richard II by his second wife, named Papia. For seventeen years, in the time of Popes Clement, Damasus, and Leo, he ruled the people of Rouen without apostolic blessing or pallium [Col. 0404B]. He clung unworthily to fleshly pleasures and worldly concerns, and fathered a worthy and legitimate son, named Michael, a knight whom King Henry, now old, honours and loves in England.

Then many tribulations arose in the world and severely shook its inhabitants with affliction. The Saracens invaded Sicily, Italy, and other Christian regions, committing many massacres, plunderings, and burnings. Emperor Manichetus of Constantinople rose up after gathering the forces of the empire; having driven back the idolaters after much destruction, he liberated the frontiers of Christendom. He also reverently transferred the bones of St Agatha, virgin and martyr, and the bodies of other saints from Sicily to Constantinople, lest the returning pagans defile them [Col. 0404C]. When Diogenes succeeded him, Osmund Drengot, Drogo, and other Normans began to inhabit Apulia and to wield arms courageously against the Hagarene Saracens or pseudo-Christians. Finally Robert, surnamed Guiscard, after many hazards of war, received Apulia as a grant against the adversaries of St Peter—first from the Lombard Harduin and his nephew Melo, and later from Pope Leo—on condition that he should defend it perpetually. With God’s help he subsequently held it bravely, extended the boundaries of his dominion as far as Sicily, Calabria, and Bulgaria, and left it to his sons by hereditary right.

In Normandy many wicked deeds were perpetrated in this time [Col. 0404D]. The Normans killed by poison Count Alan of the Bretons, guardian of their duke, and cruelly slew his successor Count Gilbert, son of Geoffrey, by force of arms. They killed one another in reciprocal conflicts almost daily and beyond belief. Then Turchetil of Neufmarché, Roger of Tosny, Osbern the seneschal of Normandy, the two sons of Roger of Montgomery—William and Hugh—Robert of Bellême, Galchelin of Ferrières, and many others powerful in arms, killed one another and brought great confusion and grief upon a region bereft of its necessary protectors.

In England, after King Harthacnut died, Edward, his brother by the same mother, succeeded and reigned beneficially and praiseworthily for twenty-three years [Col. 0405A]. In Brittany Eudo succeeded his brother Alan and exercised the principality for fifteen years with such independence that he was subject to no one’s lordship. God also gave him seven sons, famous for diverse fortunes, to whom fortune proved excessively changeable. A long history, delightful for its variety of events, might truthfully be composed about them by diligent writers.

## XI. Sequence of distichs. Epitaphs of Rollo and William Longsword

**[44.]** Bishop Maurilius, filled with the light of learning,

Shone conspicuously in outstanding morals and nourishing deeds.

A native of Mainz, he presided as abbot over a monastic house in the city of Florence. Hated by transgressors because of his severity in discipline, he detected poison administered to him in a drink. Therefore, following the most holy Father and teacher Benedict, he abandoned the incorrigible and came to Fécamp in Neustria with Gerbert, a wise and devout monk, in the time of Abbot John, his fellow-countryman. There he chose for himself a permanent dwelling devoted to the worship of the supreme and undivided Trinity. After some time he was chosen by ecclesiastical election, Malgerius having been deposed, and ascended to the metropolitan dignity. He flourished for twelve years in the time of Popes Victor, Stephen, Nicholas, and Alexander; in the ninth year of his episcopate he dedicated the metropolitan basilica [Col. 0405B].

He reverently transferred the bodies of the dukes Rollo and William into the sacred building, buried Rollo near the south door and William beside the north door, and inscribed their epitaphs above them in golden letters. The inscription for Rollo is as follows [Col. 0405C]:

### Epitaph of Rollo

> Duke of the Normans, terror of his enemies and weapon of his own,
>
> Rollo lies enclosed beneath this inscription in the tomb.
>
> His worth advanced his forebears, so that neither
>
> grandfather, father, nor great-grandfather had served him.
>
> Meeting the Danish battle-line, he defeated a king leading
>
> two hundred brave men and many companies.
>
> Frisians, Walcheren men, men of Halba, men of Hainaut—
>
> all these allies Rollo put to flight.
>
> By many wounds he compelled the conquered Frisians
>
> to swear allegiance to him and render tribute.
>
> He captured Bayeux and twice overcame the men of Paris;
>
> none was harsher against Frankish battle-lines.
>
> For thirty years he filled the fields with the slaughter of Gauls,
>
> waging war against sluggish Charles.
>
> After many devastations, plunderings, burnings, and killings,
>
> he made a profitable treaty with the willing Gauls.
>
> Supplicating Bishop Franco, he deserved to be washed in baptism;
>
> thus every crime of the old man perished.
>
> As he had formerly been a wolf, so afterwards he became a lamb among the gentle.
>
> May peace thus soothe him, changed before God!

Likewise, funeral dirges over the mausoleum of William Longsword, situated on the northern side, were set forth in letters of gold as follows [Col. 0405D]:

### Epitaph of William Longsword

> None oppressed those whom William defended;
>
> he whom he wished to harm was deprived of help.
>
> His hand was feared by kings and dukes;
>
> warlike Emperor Henry feared him.
>
> He ruled the Normans for twenty-five years,
>
> prompt in the duties of knight and duke.
>
> He splendidly restored the monastery of Jumièges,
>
> and resolved there to bear the monk’s yoke.
>
> He fervently cultivated the rule of unconquered Benedict,
>
> [Col. 0406A] under whom, full of love for God, he sought to be subject.
>
> Abbot Martin delayed this; divine power
>
> chose for him the portent of dying cruelly by arms.
>
> For, unarmed and ensnared by the treacheries of Count Arnulf,
>
> he fell—may he be able to possess the heavenly God! Amen.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1063, in the second indiction, Archbishop Maurilius joyfully dedicated in October the metropolitan basilica in the city of Rouen, which Robert had begun, in honour of St Mary, Mother of God. This was the eighth year of Emperor Henry IV and the fourth of Philip, son of Henry, king of the Franks; in that year Le Mans was subdued by the Normans. It was also the tenth year from the battle which William and Guy fought at Val-ès-Dunes. Then Michael overthrew his stepfather Diogenes from the imperial throne and seized the sceptre of Constantinople, though shortly thereafter he would disgracefully lose it [Col. 0406B]. In England, after King Edward died, great disorder arose when the perjured Harold, son of Godwin, who was not descended from the royal line, gained the kingdom by force and fraud.

> In the year one thousand and sixty-six
>
> from the birth of the Word, the proud king being crushed,
>
> the bounds of the English felt the comet’s blazing hair.

In that same year the battle of Senlac was fought; after Harold was slain, William won his victory on 14 October and was crowned king on the day of the Lord’s Nativity.

**[45.]** John, ever-vigilant bishop in the same see,

Strove to uphold the precepts of apostolic law.

He was son of Ralph, count of Bayeux, and had been bishop of the church of Avranches [Col. 0406C]. Thence he was raised to the archbishopric and flourished for ten years, in the time of Popes Alexander and Gregory VII.

**[46.]** After him came William, a noble and kindly man,

Who governed the people of Rouen in catholic fashion.

He was the second abbot of Caen, and was brought thence to the archbishopric, in which he flourished for thirty-two years in the time of Popes Gregory, Victor, Urban, and Paschal. This William buried King William and Queen Matilda at Caen; their sons Robert and William obtained the duchy of Normandy and the kingdom of England, respectively.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1095 there was drought and human mortality, and on a certain night in May stars appeared to fall from heaven. Pope Urban held a great council at Clermont [Col. 0406D] and exhorted Christians to undertake the journey to Jerusalem against the pagans. Then there was a great famine in Gaul. In the year of the Lord 1099, in the seventh indiction, Jerusalem was captured by the holy pilgrims after they defeated the gentiles who had long held it; and the church of St Evroul at Ouche was dedicated on 13 November. In the following year, King William Rufus of the English died while hunting, struck by an arrow, on 2 August. After he was buried at Winchester, his brother Henry was crowned at London on 5 August and received the royal sceptre; he is now spending his twenty-seventh year in office. By God’s gift he possessed abundant worldly prosperity, and nevertheless endured adversity in the various fortunes of children and friends and in the manifold disturbances among his subjects [Col. 0407A]. Philip, having exercised the kingdom of the Franks for forty-eight years, died; his son Louis succeeded him in the ninth year of King Henry.

**[47.]** Geoffrey the Breton, wise, eloquent, and stern,

Holds the episcopal summit and gives sustenance to the people.

He was dean of the church of Le Mans in the time of the venerable bishops Hoel and Hildebert, and has now governed the metropolitan see of Rouen for seventeen years, in the time of Popes Paschal, Gelasius, Calixtus, and Honorius. Henry V and Lothair presided over the Latins, and Alexius and his son John over the Greeks. In this time many memorable things occurred throughout the world, which, if life remains my companion, attended by heavenly favour and grace, shall truthfully be committed by the service of my pen, in their proper places, for the knowledge of posterity [Col. 0407B].

## XII. Succession of events in Neustria under King William. The rebellions of Robert, son of King William

Kind reader, I beg you, spare me as I wish to return to the course of the proposed narrative. I have already made a lengthy digression concerning the bishops of Rouen, charitably desiring to set out their unbroken succession fully for posterity. For this reason, I have composed a chronography of nearly eight hundred years and have named in sequence all Roman pontiffs from Pope Eusebius to Lambert of Ostia, called Honorius, who now presides over the apostolic see. I have also included in this little work all emperors from Constantine the Great, founder of Constantinople [Col. 0407C], as far as John, son of Alexius, who now reigns at Constantinople, and Lothair the Saxon, who is now protector of the Roman Empire. Henceforth I shall return to the affairs of our own time and region and begin to recount what was done in Neustria under King William after the council of Lillebonne.

Seditious young men flattered the young Robert, the king’s son, and provoked him to useless ventures, saying:

> Most noble son of the king, why do you live in such great poverty? Your father’s retainers guard the royal treasury so closely that you can scarcely give even a single denarius from it to your own followers. This is a great disgrace to you, a loss to us, and to many others, that you are thus alienated from royal wealth. Why do you tolerate it? He ought rightly to possess wealth who knows how to distribute it liberally to every petitioner. Alas! Your very great generosity is miserably thwarted, since excessive poverty oppresses you through your father’s stinginess; he has preferred his retainers—indeed, your retainers—to you. How long, valiant man, will you endure this? Come, rise manfully. Demand from your father a portion of the kingdom of Albion, or at least reclaim the duchy of Normandy, which he granted you long ago before the assembled company of magnates who are still present. It does not become you to endure longer that your natural servants should rule over you and, like strangers there, deny hereditary wealth to you while you beg. If your father agrees to your request and grants what you ask, your vigour and incomparable worth will be magnificently revealed. But if he persists in obstinacy [Col. 0408A] and, prompted by avarice, refuses you the honour due to you, assume a lion’s courage, reject this unworthy dependence, and avail yourself of the counsels and assistance of your friends. Without doubt, you shall have us ready for all that you wish.

At such encouragement the young Robert was fiercely inflamed with anger and desire. Approaching his father, he spoke thus:

> My lord king, give me Normandy, which you granted me long ago, before you crossed into England against Harold.

His father answered:

> What you ask, my son, is unfitting. By Norman valour I obtained England. I possess Normandy by hereditary right, and while I live I shall not let it be taken from my hand.

Robert said:

> What then shall I do, or what shall I give to my followers?

His father answered:

> Serve me fittingly in all things, and rule wisely everywhere with me, as a son with his father.

Robert replied:

> I do not wish always to be your hired servant. At some time I want to have resources of my own, so that I may reward those who serve me with worthy payments. Therefore, I beg you, grant me a suitable duchy, so that, as you preside over the kingdom of England, I may preside over the duchy of Normandy, always subject to you.

The king said:

> What you desire, my son, is perverse. Do not rashly seek to command your father concerning a dominion which you ought, if you prove worthy, to receive from him at the proper time, with the favourable wishes of the people and in God’s blessing. Choose the best counsellors for yourself, and wisely beware reckless men who spur you on and imprudently incite you to wicked acts [Col. 0408B]. Remember what Absalom did, how he rebelled against his father David, and how badly it ended for him, Ahithophel, Amasa, and his other counsellors and supporters. The Normans provoke you to foolish undertakings so that, once affairs are thrown into disorder, they may act without discipline and commit wicked deeds with impunity. Do not yield to the persuasions of insolent young men; seek counsel rather from the archbishops William and Lanfranc, from other learned men, and from mature nobles. If you carefully observe this, you shall in due course rejoice at the good outcome. But if you imitate Rehoboam, who scorned the counsels of Benaiah and other wise men and obeyed the commands of young men, you shall obtain the abasement and rejection by which he himself, despised by his own people and foreigners alike, mourned for a long time.

Robert said:

> My lord king, I did not come here to hear speeches, with an abundance of which grammarians have frequently filled me to nausea [Col. 0408D]. Instead, give me a satisfactory answer concerning the honour due to me, which I await, so that I may know what I ought to do. This is certainly fixed in my mind, and I wish it known to all, that henceforth I shall serve no one in Normandy under the worthless condition of a slave.

On hearing this, the angry king said:

> I have already told you plainly enough; yet I do not begrudge explaining to you once more, still more fully, that I do not wish to surrender the native soil of Normandy from my hand during all my life. Nor do I wish, and it would not be prudent for me, to divide while I live the kingdom of England, which I acquired with great labour; for, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste” [Luke 11:17]. He who made me king shall alter my kingdom for me according to his will. Let this be most certain to all: while I live, I shall hand my principality over to no one, nor make any mortal a participant in my kingdom. The sacred and renowned diadem was placed on my head by Christ’s vicars, and to me alone was entrusted the bearing of Albion’s royal sceptre [Col. 0409A]. It is therefore unfitting and wholly unjust that, so long as I enjoy the breath of life, I should permit anyone to be my equal or superior in my dominion.

Then Robert, having heard his father’s irrevocable decision, said:

> Compelled to go abroad like Polynices of Thebes, henceforth I shall try to serve strangers. If fortune attends me, perhaps I may obtain in exile the rank which is disgracefully denied me in my ancestral home. Would that I might now meet an old Adrastus, to whom I may eagerly offer the service of my loyalty and from whom I may receive welcome recompense!

Having spoken thus, Robert departed in anger; leaving his father, he went out of Normandy. Then Robert of Bellême and William of Breteuil, Roger son of Richard of Bienfaite, Robert of Mowbray, William of Moulins, William of Rupierre, and many others went away with him—men eminent in noble birth and knightly prowess, monstrous in pride, terrible to their opposing enemies in ferocity, and excessively ready to undertake grievous wickedness. The young Robert was uselessly attended by their company and wandered through foreign kingdoms for nearly five years [Col. 0409C]. He had already freely granted his companions ancestral estates and vainly promised numerous additions to their patrimonies. They nevertheless exalted him with empty promises, and thus, encouraging one another with lying assurances, deceived themselves.

Having departed from his native soil, Robert first visited his uncles: Robert the Frisian, prince of the Flemings, and his brother Udo, archbishop of Trier. Then he sought other noble kinsmen—dukes, counts, and powerful townsmen—in Lotharingia, Alemannia, Aquitaine, and Gascony. He set forth his complaints to them, repeatedly mingling falsehood with truth. Many gladly heard his grievances, and generous barons gave him many gifts [Col. 0409D]. But whatever he received from liberal friends for his support, he foolishly distributed to minstrels, parasites, and prostitutes. Having recklessly squandered these things, he was oppressed by severe want, begged, and as a needy exile sought borrowed money from foreign moneylenders.

Queen Matilda, moved by maternal compassion for her son, often sent him great sums of gold and silver and other precious things without the king’s knowledge. When he discovered it, he sternly forbade her to do so again. When she brazenly repeated the same act, the angry king said:

> The saying of a certain wise man, highly convincing to me, is true:
>
> “A wife faithless to her husband is the shipwreck of his fortunes.”
>
> Who henceforth in this world shall find for himself a faithful and useful companion? Behold my consort, whom I love as my own soul, whom I have placed above all treasures and powers in my whole kingdom: she supports my enemies who plot against my life, enriches them greatly with my resources, and zealously arms, consoles, and strengthens them against my welfare [Col. 0410A].

She answered:

> My lord, I beg you, do not wonder if I lovingly cherish my firstborn child. By the power of the Most High, if my Robert were dead and hidden in the depths of the earth, seven feet from the eyes of the living, and could be restored to life by my blood, I would shed my own blood for him and endure anguish beyond what female weakness dares promise. By what reasoning, do you suppose, could it delight me to abound in riches while I allow my son to be crushed by extreme poverty? Let such hardness be far from my heart, nor should your power command this of me!

On hearing this, the fierce prince turned pale, and his anger burned so hotly that he ordered a certain royal courier of the queen, Samson by name, a Breton by birth, to be seized and immediately blinded [Col. 0410B]. But when Samson learned through the queen’s friends of the king’s fury, he escaped by flight, avoided the deadly decree, and immediately fled to the monastery of Ouche. There, at the queen’s request, he was received by Abbot Mainerius, and beneficially put on the monastic habit for the salvation of body and soul. He was shrewd, eloquent, and chaste, and lived for twenty-six years in the monastic order.

## XIII. Succession of events
In those days, in the German region, there was a certain [Col. 0410C] good and holy anchorite who, among his other marks of virtue, possessed the spirit of prophecy. Queen Matilda sent messengers and gifts to him, humbly asking him to pray to God for her husband and her son Robert, and adding the request that he should communicate to her what prophecy might befall them in the future. He received the messengers of so great a lady kindly and asked for a delay in answering until the third day. When the third day dawned, he summoned the queen’s envoys and said:

“Go and convey these things from me to your lady. In accordance with your request I prayed to God, and, as He revealed it, I learned these things in a vision. I saw a certain meadow most beautifully clothed in grasses and flowers, and a most spirited horse grazing in the meadow. [Col. 0410D] On every side stood a multitude of cattle, which greatly desired to graze upon the meadow; but the fiery steed drove them all away and permitted no animal to enter there, either to pluck the flowers or to trample the grass.

“Alas! The handsome and strong hoofed beast suddenly failed and disappeared, and a playful cow undertook the guardianship of the flourishing meadow. At once the whole multitude of animals standing around ran freely into it; grazing upon the meadow from every side, they devoured all its former beauty without fear of its defender, trampled it everywhere beneath their feet, and befouled it with the foulness of dung. Seeing this, I was astonished and asked my guide, who showed me these things, what they signified. He carefully explained everything and said to me:

“‘The meadow which you see signifies Normandy, and the grasses signify the multitude of common people within it, enjoying peace and abundance of goods. [Col. 0411A] The flowers, moreover, are the churches, where there are chaste companies of monks, clerics, and nuns, and where faithful souls unceasingly cleave to faithful contemplation. The unbridled horse signifies William, king of the English, under whose protection the sacred order of the devout serves securely the King of Angels.

“‘The greedy animals standing around are the French and Bretons, the Morini and Angevins, and other neighboring peoples, who greatly envy the prosperity of Normandy and stand ready, like wolves for prey, to attack its wealth; but they are wholly repelled by King William’s invincible strength. Yet after he fails according to the human condition, his son Robert will succeed him in the duchy of Normandy. Immediately enemies will surround [Col. 0411B] it on every side; and, its guardian having fallen, they will enter the noble and wealthy land, despoil it of beauty and riches, and, despising its foolish ruler, wickedly trample all Normandy underfoot.

“‘He himself, like a frolicking cow, will serve lust and sloth; and he will be the first to plunder ecclesiastical wealth and distribute it to filthy pimps and other lechers. He will grant his rule to such men and seek counsel from them in his necessities. In Robert’s duchy catamites and effeminate men will rule; under their dominion wickedness and misery will spread. Cities and villages will be burned; basilicas of the saints will be rashly violated. Assemblies of faithful people of both sexes will be scattered, and many thousands of people will perish by sword or fire. Many of these will fall without repentance and without the viaticum, and for their sins [Col. 0411C] will be drawn down to cruel Tartarus. Normandy will be subjected to these events; and just as formerly, victorious over neighboring peoples, it swelled beyond measure, so under a slippery and indolent duke it will become contemptible and will lie miserably, and for a long time, exposed to the weapons of its neighbors. The foolish duke will be called ruler only in name; but the power of rascals, and of those to whom the province has been given over, will rule it, to the ruin of many.’”

Such was the vision which lately appeared to me while I was praying, and which my spiritual instructor disclosed to me, as has been explained. Nevertheless, O venerable lady, you will not see the dreadful things threatening the Normans. For after a good confession you will rest in peace, and you will behold neither the death of your husband, nor the misfortune of your offspring, nor the desolation of your beloved land.

[Col. 0411D] When these things had been said by the anchorite, the messengers returned and reported to the queen the prophecy, which contained glad things together with sad. Men of the succeeding age, however, who endured the slaughter of Neustria, or experienced its burnings and other losses, truly found the prophet truthful through their own disasters and dreadful misfortunes.

At length Robert repented of his folly after many useless wanderings; but he could not freely return to his angry father, whom he had insolently left. Therefore he turned aside to Philip, king of the French, namely his kinsman, and earnestly sought assistance from him. Philip received him and sent him to the castle of Gerberoy. That castle is situated in the district of Beauvais and borders upon Neustria; [Col. 0412A] by its position, walls, and defensive works it is exceedingly strong. Helias the viscount likewise gladly received the royal exile with his colleague and promised assistance in all matters to him and his companions. For it is the custom of that castle that two equal lords rule there, and that all fugitives, from whatever place they come, are received there.

There Robert gathered common soldiers, and promised them and many barons of Gaul far greater things than he could give, should aid come to him. On this occasion, therefore, many evils sprang up, and sons of perdition came forth by fraud or force against the unarmed and innocent, devising countless wicked acts. Many of those who seemed peaceable and flattered the king or his retainers unexpectedly joined the enemies [Col. 0412B] of the commonwealth, by whom their kinsmen and lords were deprived of their inheritances. Thus Normandy was more grievously afflicted by its own people than by foreigners, and was devastated by an internal plague.

But the high-spirited king prudently prepared strong armies, stationed them in castles along the frontier of the province adjoining the enemy, resisted all adversaries manfully on every side, and permitted no one to plunder his land with impunity. He also judged it intolerable that his enemies had chosen a seat so close to his border, and did not endure it longer without a terrible charge. Therefore, after Christmas, in the winter months, he assembled his iron-clad ranks and went to visit at Gerberoy the enemies who uttered dire threats against him. For nearly three weeks he restrained those in the castle with a strong [Col. 0412C] force by siege. Distinguished champions served on both sides, and men chosen for courage and military skill frequently came together in battle. On one side Normans and Englishmen, together with the king’s auxiliaries from neighboring regions, pressed fiercely; on the other, Frenchmen and neighboring enemies adhering to Robert resisted stoutly. As they fought, many were struck down, horses were killed, and great losses accumulated for the combatants.

When the king had returned to Rouen, prudent magnates took counsel how they might reconcile father and son. Roger, earl of Shrewsbury; Hugh of Grandmesnil; Roger of Beaumont with his sons Robert and Henry; [Col. 0412D] and many others attended this counsel and said to the king:

“Great-hearted king, we humbly approach Your Highness and beg that you may graciously hear our prayers. Young Robert has been grievously deceived by the evil counsel of perverse young men, and thereby great danger and loss have arisen for many. He repents of his error, but does not dare to come here without your command. He most humbly implores your clemency to have mercy upon him, and through us, whom he knows to be faithful to you, he seeks to obtain this. He is guilty and has sinned in many things; but he repents and promises fitting amendment. Therefore we all beseech your clemency to grant, in godly compassion, pardon to your suppliant son. Correct your erring offspring; receive him as he returns; kindly spare him as penitent.”

For their sons, brothers, [Col. 0413A] and kinsmen who were in exile with Robert, the distressed magnates earnestly appealed to the king. He answered them:

“I marvel that you so earnestly plead for a faithless man who has dared to begin unheard-of wickedness in my kingdom. He stirred up internal tumults against me; he carried off my young warriors, whom I had reared and equipped with the arms of knighthood. He procured for me Hugh of Châteauneuf and other foreign enemies on every side. Which of my predecessors, from the time of Rollo onward, endured such warfare from his own offspring as I do? Consider William, son of great Rollo, and the three Richards, dukes of Normandy, and my lord and father Robert; see how faithfully sons served their fathers unto death. This man strives to take from me the duchy of Neustria and the county of Maine. [Col. 0413B] He has terribly stirred up against me the French and Angevins, together with Aquitanians and countless others. Had he been able, he would have moved the whole human race against me and slaughtered me together with you. Under the divine law given through Moses he is guilty of death, and, guilty like Absalom, he must be punished by the same death.”

In repeated conferences the Norman magnates addressed the king, seeking by sweet speech and prayers to soften his resentment. Bishops and other religious men broke down the hardness of his swollen heart by divine words. The queen, the envoys of the king of the French, and neighboring nobles and friends came to compose the peace. At last the strong prince yielded to the assaults of so many magnates and, overcome by compassion, [Col. 0413C] received back his offspring with his companions. He again granted him the duchy of Normandy, as he had formerly granted it to him at Bonneville, when ill, after his own death, with the counsel of his magnates.

> [Note: [Col. 0413] Le Prévost: incorrectly “Juliam Bonam” in the edition of Chesne.]

When peace had indeed been made, the Normans and men of Maine rejoiced exceedingly, having long been severely worn down by the toil of war for many years.

## XIV. The other sons of King William become distinguished by good conduct. His daughter Adela.

The calm of peace, long sought between the king and his son, was quickly clouded over. For the insolent young man disdained to follow or obey his father. The spirited prince, however, publicly reproached and insulted him with frequent rebukes and taunts because of his indolence. [Col. 0413D] Therefore, after some time, relying upon a few companions, he again withdrew from his father and did not return thereafter, until his father, returning, sent Count Alberic to him in France to recover the duchy of Neustria.

Just as the angered father, because of the attempts already described, sometimes cursed his rash offspring and often wished many misfortunes upon him, so he affectionately blessed the offspring obedient to him, William and Henry. For his son Richard, who had been born after Robert but had not yet received the belt of knighthood, was hunting near Winchester in the New Forest. As he obstinately pursued a certain beast while his horse was running, he was tightly squeezed against the saddle by a stout hazel branch and mortally injured. [Col. 0414A] Thereupon, in that same week, he repented, received absolution, and was strengthened with the sacred viaticum; not long afterward he died in England, to the great grief of many.

William Rufus and Henry, however, favored their father and obtained their father’s blessing; they held the height of kingship and the duchy for many years. Agatha, the king’s daughter, who had first been betrothed to Harold, was later sent to be betrothed to Amfurcius, king of Galicia, who sought her through emissaries. But she who had not rejoiced in her first intended husband according to her wish greatly abhorred being joined to the second. She had seen and loved an Englishman; but she greatly feared to be joined to an Iberian whom she had never seen. She therefore poured out a tearful prayer to the Almighty, that she should not be [Col. 0414B] led into Spain but that He Himself should rather receive her. She prayed and was heard, and the maiden died soon afterward. Her body was then brought back to her native land by her attendants and buried in the church of Saint Mary Ever-Virgin in the city of Bayeux.

Adelais, a most beautiful maiden now of marriageable age, devoutly commended herself to God and came to rest in a holy end under the protection of Roger of Beaumont. Constance was given by her father with great rejoicing at Bayeux to Fergant, count of the Bretons, son of the count of Nantes; she died in Brittany without a child.

Stephen of Blois, count palatine, [Col. 0414D] wishing to establish friendship with King William, asked him for his daughter Adela in marriage. [Col. 0414C] By the counsel of prudent men she was granted to him by her father, and with very great rejoicing she was joined to him. He betrothed her at Breteuil and celebrated honorable nuptials at Chartres. He was son of Theobald, count palatine, and grandson of Bertha, countess of the Bretons and of the men of Maine. He had the distinguished counts Odo and Hugh as brothers, and by the aforesaid wife begot four sons: William, Theobald, Stephen, and Henry. The first three are powerful counts and are numbered among the greatest nobles of the French and English.

For the first-born, William, son-in-law and heir of Gero of Sully, is a good and peaceable man, mighty in offspring and resources. Theobald, heir to his paternal inheritance, flourishes in manifold virtue and excellence. Stephen, however, son-in-law and heir of Eustace, count of Boulogne, received from the gift of King Henry, his maternal uncle, the county of Mortain in Normandy and many honors in England. Henry, from childhood dedicated to the divine warfare in the monastery of Cluny, was fully instructed under monastic rule in the writings of the sacred law. If he perseveres well in it, he will be an heir of the heavenly kingdom and, through contempt for the world, will appear eminent among worldly rulers. Let this brief sketch of the offspring of King William suffice for the present, for ardent desire continually urges me to fulfil my promise and does not cease to compel me to render my vow.

## XV. The author returns to the history of the monastery of Saint-Evroul. The administration of Abbot Mainerius.

[Col. 0415A]

The eternal disposer of things powerfully bears His ship amid the storms of the age and wisely steers it; in His vineyard He kindly aids the laborers who work each day, and strengthens them by an infusion of heavenly grace against their labors and perils. Behold: amid warlike tumults and military uproar, He providently guides His Church and beneficially advances it by increasing it in many ways. The monastery of Saint-Evroul experienced this conspicuously: planted in barren countryside and among the worst neighbors, it was nevertheless defended by the aid of heavenly mercy against the threatening attempts of faithless men.

Abbot Mainerius assumed the care of this church in July 1066 [Col. 0415B] and ruled it profitably for twenty-two years and eight months. He prudently placed ninety-two monks in its fold to perform the work of God, and zealously instructed them how they ought to conduct themselves there. He began to build a new basilica and the houses necessary for the monks, and, with God’s help, completed them quite elegantly in that deserted region. The good reputation of their religious life greatly ennobled the men of Saint-Evroul and moved many powerful and middling persons to love them. Many hastened to them in order to bind themselves to their fellowship and deserve to become participants in benefits before God. They gave earthly things in order to receive heavenly things from God.

Some, fervent in the love of God, abandoned the world and handed their possessions over to [Col. 0415C] the monastery according to the statute of the Rule; by admonitions and prayers they urged their friends and kinsmen toward the same purpose. Among these were Roger of Sappo and his brother Odo; Serlo of Orgeres and Razso, son of Ilbert; Odo of Dol; Geoffrey of Orléans and John of Reims; and many others trained in literary learning and fit for the worship of the Deity. Some were eminent by birth and were active in external concerns concerning the affairs of the church. For Drogo, son of Geoffrey of Neufmarché; Roger, son of Erneis of Coulonces and nephew of William de Warenne; Ernald, son of Humphrey of Tillières and nephew through his sister of Hugh of Grandmesnil; and Goisbert the physician were men of the court, and by their management acquired lands, churches, and tithes for their brethren. Mainerius indeed employed these helpers, [Col. 0415D] and through them the church increased in revenues, possessions, and worthy inhabitants.

The aforesaid abbot chose Fulk of Guarleinville, a diligent and capable man, as his associate in governing the house, and entrusted him with the provostship of his monastery. This Fulk was the son of Fulk, dean of Évreux; fervent in the religious order, he diligently helped his abbot in all matters, and drew both his father and a great part of his patrimony to his church. The aforesaid dean had been among the disciples of Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, and held from his paternal inheritance a knight’s fief. According to the custom of that age, he also had a noble companion named Orieldis, by whom he begot abundant offspring. He had eight sons [Col. 0416A] and two daughters, whose names were Guarin, Christian, Ralph, William, Fulk, Frodmund, Hubert, and Walter, surnamed Tirel; Alwisa and Adelais.

For in Neustria after the coming of the Normans, the chastity of clerics was so corrupted that not only priests but even bishops freely used the beds of concubines and openly gloried in their numerous progeny of sons and daughters. Such a custom grew up in the time of the neophytes baptized with Rollo, who violently occupied the desolated region armed not with letters but with weapons. Thereafter priests of Danish stock, scantily educated in letters, held parishes and, bearing arms, defended a lay fief through military service. At last [Col. 0416B] Bruno of Lorraine, bishop of Toul, was summoned to Rome and, by God’s ordering, became Pope Leo. While traveling to Rome, he heard angels singing: “The Lord says: I think thoughts of peace and not of affliction,” etc.

This pope strove for many good things and notably benefited his subjects both by good conduct and good teaching. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1049 he came into Gaul, dedicated the church of Saint Remigius, archbishop of Reims, on the Kalends of October, and, at the prompting of Abbot Hermar, gloriously translated his body to the place where it is now venerated. He then held a general council there and, among the other benefits he established for the Church, prohibited priests from bearing arms and having wives. From that point the deadly custom began gradually to decline. Priests have indeed now gladly ceased to bear arms, [Col. 0416C] but still refuse to abstain from mistresses or to cleave to chastity.

The aforesaid Dean Fulk, defiled by the festering corruption of long-standing vice, raised his mind toward better things. Already an old man, by the counsel and admonition of his son Fulk he fled to Saint-Evroul and obtained the monastic habit—not so much abandoning the world as abandoned by the world. When he became a monk, he gave Saint Evroul the church of Guarleinville and the land belonging to it; he likewise gave another tract in the same vill which Hugh, bishop of Bayeux, had given him and which he had long held from William, son of Osbern and nephew of the aforesaid bishop. William, Fulk’s son and heir, publicly granted these things in chapter; with his father he placed the gift upon the altar [Col. 0416D] of Saint Peter, and then received an ounce of gold from the monks’ charity in acknowledgment.

William of Breteuil and Gilbert Crispin, with his two sons, likewise granted these things. The witnesses then present were Roger of Clères and Hugh Asinus, Robert of Stuteville and Ralph of Lalande, Ralph of Fornelles and Walter of Calmont, William of Longueville, and Gernenguilus. William Guastinellus granted these things before Richer of Laigle and received an ounce of gold for the grant. The witnesses present were William Alis and Morin of Le Pin; Robert, son of Helgo; and Ralph Cloethus.

Here I wish briefly to record the possessions of the church of Saint-Evroul [Col. 0417A], so that alms faithfully given may be made known to novices, and that those who use them may know by whom, at what time, or for what price they were given or acquired. For greedy possessors of earthly things crave perishable goods and think little of those which are highest and eternal; therefore very many attempt scarcely anything in hope of heavenly reward unless they perceive some temporal benefit. The tithes which the Lord required from the Israelites through Moses for the use of the sanctuary and the Levites are retained by our laymen, who do not wish to restore them to the ministers of the Church unless they are redeemed for a high price. Therefore the diligent administrators of hospices admonished laymen to restore tithes to the Church of God and, burning to take them from them by whatever means, gave them great sums of money, unaware that the sacred canons wholly forbade such selling [Col. 0417B] and buying. Moreover, in recent councils sacred bishops condemned this unlawful commerce by anathema; yet, in consideration of mercy, they pardoned past offences and granted by pontifical authority that the things then possessed by the Church should be possessed perpetually.

## XVI. Account of gifts made to the monastery of Saint-Evroul.

Men of middling rank began to establish the abbey of Saint-Evroul in barren countryside, contributing for the brothers’ sustenance modest resources, widely scattered, in proportion to their means. The neighbors all around are oppressed by poverty and assailed by want and wickedness; they endeavor to persist in deceit, theft, and [Col. 0417C] robbery. Hence the monks of Saint-Evroul are compelled to procure sustenance for themselves and visiting guests from afar. Yet because they were devoted to regular discipline from the beginning of their foundation, the highest magnates and religious bishops loved them and, giving necessary resources in tithes, churches, and other gifts, faithfully honored them.

Ralph of Conches, son of Roger of Tosny, who was the renowned standard-bearer of the Normans, when intending to depart for Spain came to Saint-Evroul, into the chapter of Saint Evroul. He asked forgiveness from Abbot Mainerius and from the community of monks because he had long before assisted Ernald of Exmes while Ernald was burning their borough. Making due reparation to the monks for this, he placed his pledge [Col. 0417D] upon the altar and devoutly promised many things if he should return safely. He also commended to them his physician Goisbert, whom he loved greatly. After Ralph’s departure, Goisbert immediately made monastic profession there and steadfastly kept it for nearly thirty years until the end of his life.

After some time the aforesaid lord returned home; mindful of his promise, he came to Saint-Evroul and gave Saint Evroul two arpents of vineyard which he held at Tosny for the use of masses. He also granted whatever he had at Guarleinville, namely land and pannage, on the condition that the first pannage of servants should not be paid, but the second or third should be paid, while no pannage at all should be paid by the monks. Moreover, he gave the monks three tenants: one at Conches, another at Tosny, and the third at Achinneio, [Col. 0418A] whom Gerold Guastinellus had held from him and freely given to blessed Father Evroul.

After several years this same Ralph took the monk Goisbert with him to England. Through Goisbert’s agency he gave the monks of Saint-Evroul two estates: one in Norfolk, called Caldecote; the other in Worcestershire, called Alwinton. King William granted all these things and confirmed them by royal authority in a charter before his magnates. Elizabeth, wife of the aforesaid knight, and his sons Roger and Ralph likewise kindly granted all of them. Witnesses to these gifts were Roger of Clères, Walter of Spain, William of Pacy, Robert of Romilly, Gerold Guastinellus, Gilbert son of Turold, Roger of Mucegros, and Walter of Calmont.

[Col. 0418B] Then Robert of Vals gave Saint Evroul one half of two thirds of the tithe of Bernières. After his father’s death, his son Roger confirmed the aforesaid alms by his own grant; for this confirmation he received forty shillings of Dreux, and his wife received ten shillings from the monks’ charity. The often-mentioned Ralph, who was the overlord, gladly assented to this and kindly secured the grant from his wife and offspring. He was illustrious in knightly prowess and flourished preeminently among the chief magnates of Normandy in wealth and honors; for nearly sixty years he served the rulers of Neustria, King William and his son Duke Robert, vigorously.

He secretly carried off his half-sister Agnes, daughter of Richard, count of Évreux, [Col. 0418C] and gave her in marriage to Simon of Montfort. In recompense he himself took as wife Simon’s daughter Isabel, who bore him noble offspring: Roger and Ralph, and a daughter named Godehildis. Godehildis first married Robert, count of Meulan, and afterward Baldwin, son of Eustace, count of Boulogne. At last the aged Ralph, after very many happy and unhappy events, died on the ninth day before the Kalends of April; his son Ralph held his paternal right for nearly twenty-four years. When cruel death subjected both to itself, burial received them with their fathers in the monastery of Saint Peter of Castillon. Isabel, however, [Col. 0418D] after remaining a widow for a long time, repented of the deadly wantonness to which she had been too devoted in youth, abandoned the world, received the veil in a monastery of holy nuns at Haute-Bruyère, and there beneficially reformed her life, persevering praiseworthily in the fear of God.

After Count William, son of Osbern, fell by Flemish arms, King William divided his honor among that count’s sons: Breteuil and all his father’s possessions in Normandy to William, and the county of Hereford in England to Roger. William, the more moderate man, greatly loved the monastery of Saint-Evroul and bestowed many benefits upon it for the souls of his parents. He sent, through the monk Roger of Sappo, a Gospel-book adorned with gold, silver, and precious stones; [Col. 0419A] and he granted all that his men had given or sold to Saint Evroul. He also granted henceforth one hundred shillings each year from his toll at Glos and gladly confirmed a charter to this effect before his magnates.

“I, William of Breteuil, son of Count William, give to blessed Evroul and his monks one hundred shillings in coin from the toll of Glos, to buy fish every year at the beginning of Lent, for the redemption of the soul of my father and my mother; and so that their anniversaries and mine may be celebrated solemnly by all the monks, and that on the anniversary of each of us the food and drink of one monk may be given to the poor on their behalf. During my lifetime, moreover, one Mass of the Trinity shall be sung for me in the monastery every Sunday [Col. 0419B]. I give the monks one burgess at Breteuil, and grant them whatever my men Richard Fresnel, William Alis, Ralph of Lacunela, and others have given them. I presently give these things, and henceforth faithfully promise them counsel, aid, and many benefits. And whoever removes these things after my death shall be excommunicated.”

The aforesaid William of Breteuil and Ralph the chaplain, William the steward son of Barnon, Ernald son of Ernald, and Robert of Louviers confirmed the present charter by their subscriptions.

At last, in the year 1099 from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the seventh indiction, the aforesaid William attended the dedication of the church of Saint-Evroul. He added one hundred shillings from [Col. 0419C] the revenue of the rent of Glos to the hundred shillings he had formerly given Saint Evroul; and in the presence of three bishops and five abbots, and of all the people standing with the clergy, he laid the gift upon the altar, still wet with its most sacred consecration. Not long afterward, in the time of Duke Robert, he died at Bec on the second Ides of January and lies buried in the cloister of the monastery of Lyre, which his father had founded upon his own land. His anniversary is celebrated solemnly each year in the monastery of Saint-Evroul.

The charter for the gift of the aforesaid ten pounds was afterward sealed with the seal of Henry, king of the English; and William’s successors, Eustace and Ralph of Gaël and Robert of Leicester, granted it to the monks and have rendered it most faithfully down to the present day.

[Col. 0419D] William of Moulins, with the assent of his wife Albereda, gave blessed Evroul the church of Mahéru, together with its tithe, all the priest’s land belonging to that church, and the cemetery. At the castle of Moulins he also gave the church of Saint Lawrence with the land which he held in demesne near the castle, as he himself held it. He made this gift in chapter before his magnates Walter of Asnières and Ebrard of Rues, and certain others; and thereby merited the benefit of the church as its brother and generous helper. Then Abbot Mainerius, through the liberality of the brethren, offered the aforesaid marquis fifteen pounds in coin and brought him with [Col. 0420A] Albereda, daughter of Guidmund, from whose patrimony the property came, to the altar to confirm the gift. They willingly granted before the whole community all the things set forth above and duly confirmed them in a charter upon the altar of Saint Peter.

After some time the aforesaid lord gave Saint Evroul the church of Bonmoulins, together with the whole tithe of crops, mill, and oven. Rainald Parvus, who at that time, by command of the monks, safeguarded their possessions there, generously contributed thirty shillings to Saint Evroul.
