After Albereda had borne her husband two sons, William and Robert, a divorce was made between the aforesaid man and woman on account of consanguinity. When the separation had been completed before a bishop, William took another wife, named [Col. 0420B] Duda, daughter of Waleran of Meulan. She bore him two sons, Simon and Hugh, both of whom cruel death swallowed in youth without offspring. Albereda received the religious habit and ended her life in a certain monastery of holy virgins.

The aforesaid William was the son of Walter of Falaise and was exceedingly powerful in arms; hence Duke William granted him the daughter of Guidmund with the entire honor of Moulins. He clung excessively to futile and vain glory, for which he became guilty of many homicides. It is reported that he shed much blood and was marked by a fortune of such dreadful cruelty that no one escaped impending death who had been [Col. 0420C] wounded by him, however slightly. He lived through prosperity and adversity into a very old age and, so far as the world was concerned, flourished honorably. At last he died in his castle on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November and lies buried in the chapter-house at Saint-Evroul.

His son Robert, after obtaining the ancestral inheritance, mindful of future salvation, came to Saint-Evroul and granted whatever his father and mother had given or granted. He also kindly assented to whatever men of that honor had given or sold to Saint Evroul. He carried this grant by means of a Gospel-book onto the altar and afterward received from the monks’ charity five marks of silver and an excellent war-horse. He then lawfully governed his paternal honor for nearly fifteen years and, because he was a most valiant, though dull-witted, fighter, defended it most vigorously against neighboring enemies. Transgressing King Henry’s prohibition, he attacked Enguerrand, [Col. 0420D] surnamed Oison, with arms and repeatedly fought against him in military campaigns. Therefore the king’s anger, inflamed by the malicious accusations of informers, disinherited him and expelled him from Normandy with Agnes, daughter of Robert of Grandmesnil, whom he had recently married. He went to Apulia, wandered among foreign encampments, and after some years succumbed to death there. Thus, after the elder brother had been driven out by the ruler’s violence, Simon succeeded and, together with his wife Adelina, gladly granted all that his predecessors had given to the men of Saint-Evroul.

[Col. 0421A] Roger of Montgomery, after the line of Geroia had fallen, possessed the whole patrimony of Exmes and Montreuil for almost twenty-six years. At first, so long as his wife Mabel lived—she had always hated the descendants of Geroia, founders of the monastery of Saint Evroul—he proved troublesome to the monks of Ouche in many ways, at her instigation. At length the just Judge, who mercifully spares sinners but sternly strikes the unrepentant, permitted the cruel woman, steeped in much blood and having violently disinherited many nobles and forced them to beg abroad, to perish by the sword of Hugh, from whom she had taken the castle situated on the rock of Jaligny, thus unjustly depriving him of his paternal inheritance. In his great grief, he undertook a daring action; having joined to himself [Col. 0421B] his three brothers, men distinguished in martial prowess, he came by night to the countess’s chamber and, at the stronghold upon the Dives called Bures, cut her down with the sword as she lay luxuriating in bed after a bath, in recompense for his patrimony. Once this murder of the deadly mistress had been committed, many rejoiced at her downfall, and the perpetrators of so great a deed immediately departed for Apulia.

Hugh of Montgomery was in the same village with sixteen knights; but when he heard of his mother’s death, he could pursue the fleeing killers but could not catch them, because their prudent cunning had destroyed behind their tracks the bridges across the rivers, lest avengers overtake them. The wintry season, dark night, and flooding rivers also hindered the pursuers; and, their vengeance accomplished, the fugitives immediately left Normandy. Finally, the community of Troarn, over which Abbot Durand presided, buried her body, torn limb from limb, on the Nones of December [5 December 1082]; and, not because of the pre-eminence of her merits but through favour to her friends, inscribed these funeral verses above her tomb:

> Born of a lofty line of illustrious parents,  
> Greatest Mabel lies covered by this tomb.  
> She, more renowned among celebrated women,  
> Shone throughout the wide world by her own merit.  
> Keen in intellect, alert in mind, unwearied in action,  
> Effective in speech, provident in counsel;  
> Slight in form, yet altogether great in dignity;  
> Generous in expenditure, sufficiently refined in dress:  
> She was her country’s shield, the march’s defence,  
> Welcome or terrible to her neighbours.  
>
> [Col. 0421D] But because we mortals cannot all do everything—  
> Alas! she perished by the sword, slain by treachery at night.  
> And because aid must now be brought to the dead woman,  
> Let every friend who is present prove it by rendering help!

After Mabel’s killing, Count Roger took another wife, named Adelaide, daughter of Everard of Puiset, one of the most noble magnates of the French. By his former wife the aforesaid count had five sons and four daughters: Robert of Bellême, Hugh of Montgomery, Roger the Poitevin, Philip, and Arnulf; Emma, a nun and abbess of Almenêches; Countess Matilda, namely wife of Robert, count of Mortain; Mabel, wife of Hugh of Newcastle; and Sibyl, wife of Robert, son of [Col. 0422A] Haimo. By his second wife he had one son, named Everard, educated in letters, who has remained until this day among the royal chaplains at the court of William and Henry, kings of England. The later wife differed in character from the former. For she flourished in maturity and devotion, and often encouraged her husband to love monks and defend the poor.

The aforesaid lord therefore recalled the wrongs he had often inflicted upon the monks of Ouche and prudently strove to efface his former offences by amendment of his later life. Thereafter he vigorously aided the monks, bestowed many possessions upon them in Normandy and England, and voluntarily confirmed the following charter before his magnates.

[Col. 0422B] “I, Roger, by the grace of God earl of Shrewsbury, desire to honour the monastery of the holy father Evroul; and for ever grant to it the following from my possessions, for the salvation of myself and my people. Every year, at the beginning of Lent, I command that thirty shillings in money of Le Mans be given from the revenues of Alençon, to provide light day and night in the church of Ouche before the Crucifix of the Lord. I also grant its passage-toll at Alençon and all customary dues, throughout all my land, upon the monastery’s own property; and in all my woods I grant forever pannage for the monks’ swine.

“At Exmes I give land for one plough, and I irrevocably confirm the tenth of the mill and the tenth of all revenues of that castle; and I willingly [Col. 0422C] add my portion of the tenth from the fair of Les Planches. Odo of Piret confirms the church of Radon and the whole tithe which William Sor gave to Saint Evroul; likewise the church of Saint-Jouin and the whole tithe which the priest Rainald gave. In the church of Bailleul, I grant of my own free decision, for love of God, the altar of Saint Leonard and one portion of the tithe of that village, together with the land which Rainald of Bailleul and his wife Amieria, my niece, gave.

“In England also I give two manors, Onne and Mersiton, in Staffordshire; the tenth of my cheeses and wools from Pulton; whatever I possess at Melbourne in Cambridgeshire; one hide of land at Grafham in Sussex; and the land of Wulfwine the goldsmith of Chichester. I further [Col. 0422D] confirm whatever Viscount Warin, William Pantulf, Hugh of Mesdavid, and my other men have hitherto given Saint Evroul in England or Normandy. All these things, with the consent of my sons Robert of Bellême, Hugh, and Philip, I grant before God for the redemption of the soul of myself, of Mabel and Adelaide my wives, of my predecessors, and of my future heirs; and I confirm this testament by the sign of the holy Cross, so that whoever diminishes, violates, or takes away anything from these gifts may be accursed.”

Count Roger made and confirmed this testament by subscribing it. After him, at Alençon, his sons Robert, Hugh, and Philip the grammarian subscribed, along with his other magnates: Robert son of Theobald, and his son Hugh; Gilbert the constable and Hugh son of Turgis; Fulk of La Ferté and Engelbert the provost; Rainald of Bailleul and William Pantulf; Odo of Piret; and many others.

[Col. 0423A] Moreover, Count Roger gave much to other churches—to Troarn, Sées, Almenêches, Cluny, Caen, and very many others—from the honours which he had received, though he had not obtained them from his paternal inheritance.

### XVII. Digression concerning the monastery on the land of Oderic, father of Orderic Vitalis, near the city of Shrewsbury in England

He also began to build a new monastery at the eastern gate of his own city, that is, Shrewsbury, in honour of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, beside the river called the Meole, which flows there into the Severn. In former times a wooden chapel had been founded there by Siward, son of Æthelgar and kinsman of King Edward. At that time it was possessed, by the gift of the same earl, by Oderic of Orléans, son of Constantine, a man pre-eminent in intelligence, eloquence, and learning. This Oderic, a fervent lover of justice and useful confidential counsellor of the aforesaid earl, kindly urged him to build a monastery. When the earl hesitated over how or where to begin so great a work, Oderic gave him this advice:

[Col. 0423B] “Many men, vigorous lord, attach themselves to your high rank; yet with different intentions they try to serve you in word or deed. Some desire more to obtain your possessions for themselves according to their own pleasure than to exhort you soundly to gain enduring honours. But one who truly strives to obey you ought always to love you more than your possessions, and unceasingly offer your soul those things which are more healthful.

“You have begun, noble lord, to consider building a monastery; but among those who burn more to receive gifts for themselves than to have them given to others, you have found no helpful encouragement for so arduous a work. It seems to me most salutary to erect a monastic house, carefully to establish there the authoritative rule according to the institution of the most holy Father Benedict, and liberally to provide true poor men of God with food and clothing out of your abundance. Consider carefully now what learned servants do in [Col. 0423D] regular monasteries. Innumerable good works are performed there daily, and Christ’s soldiers fight manfully against the devil.

“No one doubts that for a worthy combatant, the fiercer the battle, the more glorious the victory and the greater the reward of triumph in the heavenly court. Who can recount the monks’ vigils, hymns and psalmody, prayers and alms, and their daily offerings of Mass amid showers of tears? Christ’s followers devote themselves wholly to this: crucifying themselves, they may please God in all things. They reproach the world and its worldly parasites, avoiding worldly delights as dung and contemptuously trampling worldly wealth underfoot in hope of what is above. They have harshness and lowliness in clothing, dryness and frugality in food, and the cutting off of their own wills for love of the Lord Jesus.

[Col. 0424A] “What shall I say of chastity and every form of self-restraint, of the monks’ silence and modesty, and finally of obedience? The abundance and greatness of such virtues overwhelms my intellect; I confess that I cannot adequately express it by the office of speech. In royal cloisters true cenobites are enclosed like daughters of a king, lest, if they wander shamelessly abroad, like Dinah daughter of Leah, they be shamefully violated by Shechem son of Hamor the Hivite (Gen. 34:1), to the injury of their stern father and the disgrace of their fierce brothers. They become their own guardians lest they fall within their enclosures; and if they have fallen through transgression, they are their own accusers in their inner chambers. They strive by every means, like gold in a furnace, to purge themselves from every dross of vice.

[Col. 0424B] “Therefore I think that their prayers, poured out for any of the faithful, immediately ascend before the throne of divine majesty, and that they are to be believed to obtain from the very King of Hosts whatever they ask. Since my youth I have long been privy to the monks’ secrets and, through familiar inquiry, have learned their customs. Therefore, when I examine the way of life of all mortals upon earth and carefully consider the lives of hermits and canons, I judge all inferior to the life of monks who live canonically and are governed in order.

“Accordingly, glorious earl, I faithfully urge your nobility that, while it is possible, a monastic fortress against Satan be built for God within your earldom, which you did not receive by hereditary right from your fathers; there hooded champions will continually resist Behemoth in combat for your soul. Behold, beside the river Meole stands a house which you recently gave me. Near it, in fulfilment of the vow which I made last year before the altar of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, at Rome, I have begun to build a stone basilica.

[Col. 0424C] “The basilica which, as I have said, freely bound by a vow, I lately undertook to make, and my house with all my equipment, I joyfully offer to the Almighty. I promise, according to my ability, to be a helper in all things in the name of Jesus Christ. Rise quickly; begin manfully; carry out God’s work splendidly.

> Delay no more: delay has always harmed those ready to act.”  
> —Lucan, *Pharsalia* I.281

“Many fellow-workers will surely be present; and, even after your burial, pious men will pray for you. First, when monks and masons arrive to lay the foundations of the monastery, I shall provide fifteen pounds sterling for the beginning of this undertaking. Then I shall give myself, my son Benedict—now five years old—and all that is mine to the monastery, on this condition: one half of all my possessions shall, with me, be subjected to the monks’ lordship, while the other half shall be given to my son Everard under the monks’ protection.

[Col. 0424D] “Moreover, I have long since entrusted my firstborn, namely Orderic, to a free schoolmaster to be instructed in letters; and I have secured for him a place of safe residence among God’s young household servants at Ouche in Neustria. For him I willingly bestowed gifts of blessing—namely thirty marks of silver—from my own resources upon his future teachers and companions. Thus, for love of the Redeemer, I renounce my firstborn son and send him across the sea into exile, that, a voluntary exile among strangers, he may serve the heavenly King; there, free from every care of parents and from deadly affection, he may flourish outstandingly in monastic observance and the service of the Lord. Inspired by God, I have long desired these things and have earnestly wished to devote myself and my offspring to such pursuits, so that, by the help of God’s grace, I may deserve to be numbered with my children among the elect at the Last Judgment.”

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1083, in the fourth indiction, Count Roger, having found the counsels of his faithful adviser profitable, summoned Viscount Warin, Picot of Say, and his other magnates on the fifth day before the Kalends of March, a Friday [Col. 0425B]. When the matter had been explained and approved by all, he went with them to the church of the blessed apostle Peter. There, before many witnesses, he publicly vowed that he would build an abbey; he gave Saint Peter the entire suburb lying outside the eastern gate, and placed the donation upon the altar by means of his gloves. In the same year monks of Sées, Rainald and Frodo, first assembled there and began to establish monastic workshops, assisted by Oderic, Warin, and many others.

The first abbot of that monastery, during the reign of William Rufus, was the eloquent Fulchered; Godfrey succeeded him during Henry’s reign. Both were learned and devout shepherds, and for almost forty years strove diligently to rear the Lord’s flock. With great care [Col. 0425C] they increased externally the resources of the new monastery, and inwardly established praiseworthy rules of conduct for their disciples’ salvation. Oderic, father of Vitalis, likewise completely fulfilled what he had promised. Having given two hundred pounds of silver, he offered his son Benedict there to God; and after Count Roger’s death he himself assumed the monastic habit. There he served God as a monk for seven years according to the rule of the holy Father Benedict; then, on the Friday in Whitsun week, after many labours which he had endured for God, he covered [i.e. expiated] his offences by tearfully confessing them, and, anointed with holy unction and strengthened with the viaticum, died on the third day before the Nones of June [3 June 1108].

Count Roger lived for six years after the death of King William the Bastard; as an aged lord he flourished among the foremost nobles of England, and moderately endowed with lands and revenues the abbey which, as I said, he had built. He died there in 1094, on the sixth day before the Kalends of August [27 July], and was honourably buried in the new basilica between the two altars. His son Robert alone obtained all his fief in Normandy; and because he was cruel, proud, and very wicked, he committed innumerable wrongs. Hugh of Montgomery held the earldom of Shrewsbury, but after some years he was suddenly pierced by a missile shot by Magnus, brother of the king of the Northmen, and fell on the seashore. The community of Shrewsbury carried him away with great mourning and buried him in the cloister. During his lifetime the crafty lord also secured individual earldoms for his two other sons, Roger and Arnulf; after his death, however, under King Henry, treachery immediately took both from them.

[Col. 0426A] Behold, I have made this brief digression concerning the building of the monastery in my father’s estate, where Christ’s household now dwells, and where my own father, as I remember, already sixty years old, voluntarily bore the Lord’s yoke until the end. Good reader, spare me, I pray; do not, I beg, be annoyed if I have committed something concerning my father to the record of letters—him whom I have not seen since he drove me into exile, as a hated stepson, for love of the Creator. It is now forty-two years, during which many changes of affairs have occurred far and wide throughout the world. As I often think upon these matters and commit some of them to writing, cautiously resisting idleness, I exercise myself by thus [Col. 0426B] composing.

### XVIII. The account of donations made to the monastery of Ouche is continued. Instruments of donation. Distinguished persons buried in the church of Ouche

Now I shall return to the subject begun, and explain to my younger native-born brethren, who are strangers to these matters, the affairs of their own community which they do not know; in this way, by God’s help, I shall usefully serve them.

Goisbert, a citizen of Chartres, as has been said, entered religious conversion; he sold for thirty pounds of Chartres currency the excellent house which he had possessed in the city, and joyfully brought the whole price to the monks of Ouche. He was tall and slender in stature, kind and approachable in character, high-minded and generous. Since he was exceedingly skilled in the art of medicine, he was known to many and was necessary and a familiar friend to them. Through him, therefore, Fulcher of Chartres, Peter of Manli, and many others came to know the monks of Ouche; revering their honourable character together with their religious life, they bestowed on them a fitting portion of their possessions.

[Col. 0426C] The aforesaid Fulcher was distinguished by noble birth, possessed a great estate from his patrimony, was abundantly educated in letters, and was a canon of the holy Mother of God. He made a charter concerning the gift of the possessions which he had given Saint Evroul. As he himself composed it with subtlety and elegance, Robert Andrew, an excellent scribe, recorded it thus:

“I, Fulcher, son of Gerard, unworthy and insignificant canon of the church of Blessed Mary of Chartres, often considering with myself the condition of my own state and that of other mortals, have found that almost all things under the sun, as Solomon says, are subject to vanity. Nothing exists on earth that can make men blessed after the miseries of this life, unless, while they live, they have done something good for themselves. Moved by consideration of this and greatly terrified by the enormity of my sins, because every person will one day render an account to God for what he has done, it has seemed to me—so I believe, by God’s inspiration—that I should transfer some of my possessions to Blessed Evroul for the salvation of myself and my friends. Thus my brothers and friends dwelling there may have however small a support for their bodies, and may more willingly make remembrance of me from it; for the things which we leave to our descendants by hereditary right, I say, not only do not benefit us after death, but indeed harm us greatly because we have disposed of them badly.

[Col. 0427A] “Let all faithful members of holy Church know, therefore, that I willingly and freely, providing for my salvation in the future, convey to Blessed Evroul and those serving him, in perpetual right, all these things—though they are small—which I shall take care to enumerate here: namely, the church of Mont-leiscent and half the tithe of that village; the cemetery; three acres of land behind the cemetery; likewise the monastery’s right of archage [uncertain term], to the extent held by Goscelin; and the tenth of my mill. If I establish a market there, I likewise grant them the tenth from it. The monk who dwells at Mont-leiscent shall never pay milling dues for his grain. If he wishes to grind at his own mill, let him do so; if not, let him grind at mine and retain his milling due.

“At Marchesville also, whatever I possess there—land, monastery, and mill—I give them forever. In the village called La Landelle I likewise give land for one plough and a monastery. I also give the tenth of my wood, namely of pannage, bees, and wild beasts caught there. The monks’ pigs shall in no way pay pannage in my wood; nor shall the monks ever render to me or to my heirs any labour, service, or military expedition. If any of my men wishes to give or sell anything to Blessed Evroul, I grant all of them full permission to do this without fear of me.

[Col. 0427C] “Should any foolish or envious person ever dare, openly or secretly, violently to diminish, violate, or remove these donations of whatever sort, which I freely offer to almighty God, who granted me existence, and to Blessed Evroul, the outstanding confessor, let him, eternally punished by anathema, not see the Lord’s good things in the land of the living unless, repenting, he returns to his senses through a most worthy satisfaction. Lord Robert, bishop of the church of Chartres, in whose fief lie the properties mentioned above as given, willingly confirmed this donation of our small means at my simple request. My brothers, the canons of that same church, also confirmed it, as did my wife Alpes and my sons.”

The monks of Ouche held for fifty years the property which, as stated, the aforesaid lord had given them, and his successors Bartholomew, surnamed Boellus, and his son Gerard willingly confirmed it. There dwelt Aimeric, Radulf, Hugh the Englishman, William of Merle, and many other monks flourishing in eloquence and integrity. The bishops of Chartres—Robert, Geoffrey, Ivo, and Geoffrey—bestowed kindly protection upon them. Thus, through the monks’ diligence and the aid of good men, the basilica at Marchesville was founded and consecrated to Saint Mary, Mother of God, through whom the salvation of the world came.

[Col. 0427D] At the same time, Landric, Geoffrey, and Gunher gave all the land of Jarenzai to Blessed Evroul. Because Isnard, from whom they had long held it, granted it entirely free to the monks, he received six pounds from Abbot Mainer. Then Landric and the other men named above received half the land from the aforesaid father, and in Isnard’s presence became the abbot’s men by joining hands. There also, before Isnard and many others, those three confirmed the church of that village, everything belonging to it, and the entire tithe; and they wholly confirmed, before the priest Gerard and many others, the tithe of all the land, both that belonging to Isnard and that belonging to Blessed Stephen or to anyone else.

In the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1073, in the tenth indiction, during the reign of William the Great, king of the English and duke of the Normans, the knight William, surnamed Pantulf, following the counsel of his venerable friend Abbot Mainer and with the consent of his lord Count Roger, gave Saint Evroul the churches of Noron: one built in honour of Saint Peter, the other in honour of Saint Cyricus the martyr. He then also gave the whole tithe of Noron, his own enclosure, a part of the wood from Ogeret Bridge, his share of one tract of land called Molenx, and of another located beyond the stream and commonly called Ruptices.

[Col. 0428B] Later he granted the entire fief of William of Maloi, in which there are almost thirty acres of land; from the monks’ charity he received sixteen pounds of Rouen currency to undertake a journey to Saint-Gilles. The same man granted Saint Peter all the land which Walter, son of Rufa, sold to the monk Robert; for this the aforesaid monk gave him one hundred shillings of Rouen currency. Besides these gifts, William gave the monks in that same village sixty acres of land, the mill of Helmet, and the tenth of half the mill of Noron.

He also gave the church of Esmiville, together with its tithe and all revenues belonging to the church; in the same village, the land of one vavasour; two sheaves from the tithe of his own estate and that of all his men of Maisnil-Bachelier; and the entire mill-tithe of Roreville. He gave Saint Peter all the land which his mother Beatrice held in demesne at Fosses, and also the tenants belonging to the alms of Saint German of Aubervic. Helvis, William’s sister, gave Saint Peter all her marriage-portion from Aubervic, which he then confirmed. Moreover, in that same village he added the tithe of his men, Raimbold, Robert the Heretic, and Gualo son of Safred.

[Col. 0428D] Furthermore, this same William granted Saint Peter of Noron all churches and tithes in every place in England or Normandy, or wherever his honour might increase, and the tenth of all his possessions—namely mares, cows, cheeses, and every thing from which he could give a tenth. He likewise confirmed whatever his men might wish to give or sell to Saint Evroul, provided that he did not lose service owed to himself. He granted his entire share of his property, so that after his death the cenobitic monks of Saint Evroul should possess one half and the monks of Noron retain the other half.

William and his wife Leelina, as we have said, freely granted all these things to God for their salvation and that of their friends, and generally confirmed this grant in the chapter-house of Saint Evroul before the community of monks and many witnesses. Then William himself immediately gave forty marks of silver to support the brethren who were going to establish a cell at Noron.

After this, Abbot Mainer, Prior Fulk, and William Pantulf went to Count Roger, who was then staying at Bellême, and humbly asked him to confirm by his consent the gifts of the aforesaid knight. Since he was liberal and upright, Roger graciously favoured their just petition and approved all that they had requested before everyone who had then assembled at his court on various affairs.

[Col. 0429B] At that time the feast of Saint Leonard the confessor was being celebrated there. Many had come, at the generous count’s invitation, to observe it solemnly: Hoel, bishop of Le Mans; Hugh, bishop of Lisieux; Robert, bishop of Sées; Ainard, abbot of Dive; Durand of Troarn; Robert of Sées; Hugh of Longueil; Emma, abbess of Almenêches; Hervey, chaplain of the bishop of Lisieux; Roger Faidel; Hugh son of Fulk; Robert son of Theodelin; Roger Gulafra; and many other clerics and laymen were present at the above-written confirmation.

In the year of the Incarnation 1077, in the fifteenth indiction, the noble Abbot Robert, brother of Hugh of Grandmesnil, came to Normandy for a conference with William, king of the English. He pardoned the king, who sought forgiveness because he had formerly unjustly driven him into exile. King Philip of France had summoned Robert, wishing to give him the bishopric of Chartres; but because the French avoided the rule of the Normans, Geoffrey, nephew of Eustace, count of Boulogne, forestalled the episcopate.

[Col. 0429C] The illustrious Robert, after attending the sacred dedications of the churches at Caen, Bayeux, and Bec, which were consecrated that same year, and after completing friendly discussions with King William and with other friends and kinsmen whom he had not seen for many years, returned to Apulia. He took with him William Pantulf, his nephew Robert of Corday, and other distinguished knights. Robert Guiscard then ruled Calabria and was acquiring the duchy of Gisulf, duke of Salerno. He was the son of Tancred of Hauteville, a man of modest station; but, powerful in greatness of spirit and good fortune, he had subdued the Italians. With his brothers and immigrant compatriots he pressed strongly upon the Apulian settlers; after magnificently accomplishing unexpected deeds, he surpassed all his kinsmen and, rich in much wealth, unceasingly enlarged his borders. He honourably received William Pantulf and, promising him much, strove to retain him because of his worth. On Easter Day he seated him beside himself at dinner and promised him three cities if he remained with him in Italy.

[Col. 0430A] Meanwhile Countess Mabel was killed by the sword of the bold knight Hugh of Jaligny. When William Pantulf returned from Apulia, great trouble arose on account of her killing. He was charged with the crime of treason and was severely assailed by hostile attacks from many enemies. The aforesaid woman had taken from William the castle of Piret, which had been given to him; because of this injury a stubborn hatred had long raged between them. Hence it was suspected that she had perished through the counsel of the aforesaid knight, especially because great intimacy and frequent conversation had united William and Hugh.

Count Roger and his sons therefore seized all William’s land and sought his death. William, his wife, and their children fled to Ouche, where they remained a long time under the monks’ protection and in great fear. The aforesaid knight boldly denied the crime charged against him, but no one proved it against him by certain evidence, nor would they accept the denial of a man who wished to clear himself according to law.

[Col. 0430B] At length the judgment of many magnates established in the king’s court that the accused man should undergo at Rouen, in the presence of the clergy, the ordeal of red-hot iron, to remove the stain of a heinous deed. This was done. He carried the glowing iron in his bare hand and, by God’s will, appeared unburned; therefore the clergy and all the people praised God aloud. Malicious enemies, armed for the spectacle, were present so that, if the accused should be found guilty by the judgment of fire, the crime might immediately be punished by the sword, his head having been cut off.

In these distresses which William and his household suffered, Abbot Mainer and the monks of Ouche kindly comforted him and helped him with all their efforts before God and men. His friendship for them consequently grew stronger, and from the cloths which he had brought from Apulia he offered four of the more precious to Saint Evroul. From these four copes for the singers were made in that church; they are preserved there to this day for the adornment of divine worship.

[Col. 0430C] After the death of William, king of the English, William again went to Apulia; on his return he brought relics of the body of the most blessed confessor of Christ, Nicholas, and placed them in the church of Blessed Peter at Noron, to adorn that place. Afterwards he gave the monks dwelling there a manor in England called Traditona, together with the mill and church of that village and the entire tithe of six villages belonging to that church.

Then, in the year of the Incarnation 1112, in the fifth indiction—the twelfth year of Henry, king of the English, and the fourth of Louis, king of the French—this same William, in the fortieth year after he had begun the monastic cell at Noron, came to Ouche. Remembering the old friendship and the gifts which, as stated above, he had made, he reviewed them all and confirmed them in a general act of grant before the community of monks, together with his wife Leelina.

[Col. 0431A] Then also his sons Philip, Ivo, and Arnulf confirmed whatever their father had given to the monks of Saint Evroul; William and Leelina and their three sons, Philip, Ivo, and Arnulf, together placed the gift upon the altar. During the time of four bishops—Robert, Gerard, Serlo, and John, who presided over the see of Sées—Robert the Bald, Geoffrey, Ascelin, and many other devout monks lived in the aforesaid cell. Persevering in the fear of God and charity, they furnished ordinary people with an example of honourable conduct.

The oft-mentioned William also lived a long time, honoured the poor and the clergy, devoted himself to almsgiving, was great-hearted in adversity and prosperity, and prevailed over all enemies, flourishing in wealth and honours. He gave sixty marks of silver for beginning a new basilica. He began a very beautiful work to God’s praise, but, overtaken by death, could not complete it. His sons succeeded to his patrimony, Philip in Normandy and Robert in England, but they neglect to follow their father’s undertakings with equal virtue.

[Col. 0431B] Ralph of Montpinçon, steward of William the Great, king of the English, wholly and faithfully dedicated himself to Saint Evroul. He humbly asked Lord Abbot Mainer that some clerk, fit for God’s service, should be received into monastic life in the monastery of Ouche, to pray faithfully to God for the salvation of himself and his wife. This was done. For, by God’s will, a schoolman of Reims named John was then seeking monastic life. Brought to the king’s court, he granted the aforesaid knight his prayers and the labours which he would endure for Christ. Delighted by this, Ralph humbly kissed John’s feet openly before all.

The monks then gladly received the aforesaid John. Having received him, they rejoiced greatly, because he was skilled in grammar and persistently devoted to worthy studies even into old age. The aforesaid lord gave Saint Evroul, for John’s maintenance in perpetuity, the tenth of five mills: three at Jort, a fourth at the place commonly called Hurtavent, and a fifth at Montpinçon; two sheaves from the villagers’ tithe at Gualdreslogiis; half the tithe at Spanais; and, [Col. 0431D] at Ermentrude’s village, two acres of meadow.

After some years, on the Ides of February, the same Ralph died. His body was brought to Ouche and honorably buried by the monks in the cloister there. His two sons, Hugh and Ralph, were present with their mother Adeliza; before many witnesses who had assembled for the burial of so great a baron, they willingly confirmed both themselves and all that their father had given to Saint Evroul. Almost thirty years later, Hugh of Montpinçon came to Ouche to visit his spiritual brethren. He brought with him his eldest son Ralph, and mourned his wife Matilda, daughter of Hugh of Grandmesnil, and his sister Adeline, who had recently died. [Col. 0432A] Then Hugh renewed the brotherhood of the monks which he had received formerly in childhood, and begged them to pray for his brother Ralph, who had died as a pilgrim on the road to Jerusalem. The boy Ralph likewise was associated wholly with the monks, as his parents had been; and, led through the chapter-house by Walter the Bald, an eloquent knight, he kissed the brethren and then confirmed to them all that his father and grandfather had given to Saint Evroul.

Finally, when the aforesaid Hugh was already sixty years old, he died at Rouen on the Nones of March; and his corpse, at the command of his wife and sons, was brought to Ouche. Then the monks honorably buried the body of their brother in the chapter-house; and his sons, Ralph, William, and Arnulf, confirmed themselves and everything [Col. 0432B] that had been bestowed on the church of Ouche by their forebears. Ralph, the first-born, married the daughter of Ranulf, Chancellor of King Henry; after he died shortly afterwards, the convent of Ouche buried him in its chapter-house beside his father. William then inherited his father’s right in Normandy. Arnulf, however, went to Apulia for the profit of his uncle William of Grandmesnil. Their mother Matilda, after the death of her husband, fell in love with an exiled young knight named Mathiellus; leaving her kinsfolk and friends in Neustria, she set out with him on the road to Jerusalem, and greedy death swiftly swallowed both of them on their journey in the same year. Mathiellus died in Apulia [Col. 0432C] while travelling onward; Matilda died at Joppa while returning.

## XIX. John, monk of Ouche. A poem by Orderic Vitalis in his praise. The gift of Goisbert the physician to the monastery of Ouche.

Now I wish to make clearer to the reader’s understanding who John was, whom I have already mentioned briefly above, and how and how long he lived under the monastic rule.

He was keen of intellect and steadfast in study. He lived in the monastic habit for nearly forty-eight years and laboured intensely in searching out the hidden mysteries of books. Received as a young man by Abbot Mainer, he entered God’s sheepfold. Under Serlo and Roger, after he had already been promoted to the priesthood, he served as a soldier, and courageously taught others to contend [Col. 0432D] by word and example. In the time of Abbot Warin, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, he died confessing Christ. For a long time he held the office of subprior, and often discharged the abbot’s part in expounding the divine law. By command of Abbot Roger he went to Rome, with the deposed Fulk, to Pope Urban. On that journey he endured grievous illnesses and many adversities. In old age he languished for more than seven years under the torment of stone; groaning in prolonged illness, he did not lie abed, but rose daily for the divine office, gave thanks to God, and, well prepared, as I believe, died at the beginning of the dark night.

And because he himself composed many verses, Vitalis the Englishman, his disciple, wrote poetry concerning him and, amid tears on the day of his death, after the burial had been performed, composed the following poem:

> When March had completed three weeks, John departed  
> On a dark night of winds and rain.  
>
> Born at Rheims, he sprang from the Franks;  
> Ilbert was his father, Poncia his mother.  
> Though his family fed the boy from the profit of the awl,  
> The liberal art raised him to famous honours.  
>
> From his childish years he was devoted  
> To profitable studies; therefore he left Rheims and his own people  
> And came to the strangers at Ouche. Joined to them,  
> He was a monk for almost ten lustres, and renowned throughout.  
>
> He was subtle in intellect and swift in making verse,  
> Fashioning in metre or prose whatever he wished.  
> He shunned idleness and read the writings of the ancients,  
> Gathering the profitable teachings of men of old.  
>
> He watched praiseworthily in the worship of Christ;  
> [Col. 0433B] Night and day he strove to render his vows to God.  
> In deed and word he was an example of piety;  
> He often unfolded the obscurities of the divine law  
> And explained its mysteries to his pupils in welcome speech.  
>
> Like bees, he bore both sting and nectar in his mouth:  
> With his point he pierced the proud, and gave honey to the innocent.  
> By sweet counsel he soothed the sad and sick;  
> By sternness, rebuking the frivolous, he instructed the foolish.  
>
> He was a skilful and provident abridger, aptly  
> Compressing a vast subject into few verses.  
> He devoutly and honourably composed many poems  
> Concerning Christ and Mary the Virgin Mother.  
>
> He beautifully resounded many poems concerning the holy friends [of God].  
> In verse he described the life of Saint Evroul  
> For his beloved father, Archbishop Ralph.  
> Many who live together possess works drawn from his meditations.  
>
> Although he was distinguished by gracious virtues,  
> Yet he was not altogether without envy or anger.  
> Who can pass through this life without sin?  
>
> [Col. 0433C] He alone, having a mother without a father, a father without a mother,  
> Passed the course of life without the wound of fault.  
> Wounded and burdened by human failings,  
> Corrected by the divine scourge, he wept bitterly.  
>
> He groaned beneath the painful tormenting sickness of strangury,  
> And for seven years uttered frequent sighs.  
> Thus his sinful flesh, subjected to stripes for its faults,  
> Endured the deserved, vigorous lash of the healer.  
>
> He deserved to be struck by the rod of Father and Master;  
> To Him, breathlessly and with tears arising, he cried,  
> That after death his spirit might deserve to behold  
> The appeased countenance of the heavenly Judge.  
>
> This holy monk, while night was equal to day,  
> Went forth from darkness and the storms of the world and death.  
> May Christ give him light and everlasting rest  
> In the homeland of light and the pleasant dwelling of repose! Amen.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1076, in the fourteenth indiction, [Col. 0433D] when Goisbert the physician had visited his countrymen and friends in Gaul and had bestowed the service of his art on those in need and those who sought it, he approached many friends and dependants to whom he had formerly given faithful service by his skill. He kindly urged them to make alms from their abundance for eternal salvation, and especially exhorted them to give to the monks of Saint Evroul those things which do not belong to a lay person. He turned aside to Peter of Mantes, son of Ansold the Rich of Paris; amid their other conversations of familiarity and friendship, he approached him and begged him to give the churches of Mantes to the monks of Ouche. Peter, being cheerful and generous, and readily inclined to undertake difficult things, whether good [Col. 0434A] or evil, easily assented to the persuasion and confirmed a charter of donation before his nobles. The text of the deed which he made is as follows:

“The brevity of mortal life, the faithlessness of men, the changeableness of times, and the desolation of kingdoms daily warn us that the end of the world is at hand. Truth taught us this when it said to the disciples: ‘When you see these things happening, the kingdom of God is near’ (Matt. 24:33; Mark 13:29). Therefore the prudent ant, in proportion as it perceives winter to be approaching more quickly, ought to foresee diligently, so that it may store its grain safely and have, in the cold season, not grass but abundant flour. For it is said somewhere to those who are sluggish concerning their salvation: ‘See, see that your flight [Col. 0434B] be not on the Sabbath or in winter’ (Matt. 24:20).

“Therefore, considering these matters, I, Peter, though a sinner and unworthy, desiring to provide for myself in the future, have wished God’s bees to make honey in my gardens on this condition: that, when their baskets are filled with combs heavy with honey, they may render praise to their Creator from it and may sometimes remember their benefactor. Thus, from the goods that I have possessed until now, I have freely given some things, though few, to blessed Evroul, so that the brethren dwelling there may have some bodily support and may remember me more willingly. For, whether we will it or not, we leave all these things behind; and after death nothing benefits anyone unless he has done some good in life.

“These are the things which I have granted and grant to blessed Evroul, and which, for the sake of my salvation, I confirm to him for ever by hereditary right [Col. 0434C] in this my charter. Namely, in the village called Mantes, I give two churches: the church of Saint Mary, and the church of Saint Germanus and Saint Vincent; the burials of the churchyards; and everything belonging to the priesthood. I also give the land of one ploughland, four tenants, land on which the monks may dwell, one orchard, and the rent of three and a half arpents, which Walter the Blind and his nephew Hugh, surnamed Muscosus, gave to Blessed Mary in Mainer’s vineyard. All these things I grant in perpetuity to the monks of Saint Evroul, as free as I myself held them.

“And if any of my men wishes to give anything in alms to the saints and monks, whatever may be given without harm to my service and without impairment of my justice, I most willingly consent with my sons, on such terms and with so firm a grant that, if any one of them loses his fief for any offence, the Church of God shall by no means lose the alms which it possesses. My wife Windesmoth and my sons Ansold, Theobald, and William have granted all these things, and they piously promise, so long as they live, to defend this alms against the assaults of all men to the best of their ability. Moreover, when my men saw my good will toward God’s servants, stirred by this wholesome example, they entrusted themselves to the fellowship of the monks and gladly bestowed gifts upon them from their goods. Indeed, all the knights of Mantes earnestly sought their fellowship in life and death, and became their brethren, so that by monastic prayer [Col. 0435A] they might be able more strongly to resist the host of demons.

“Hugh son of Odo, who surpassed his fellow townsmen in wealth and worth, gave to the church of Saint Mary and the monks of Saint Evroul the whole tithe of his land which he held at Mantes: namely, of grain, wine, mill, oven, pigs, sheep, wool, geese, hemp, flax, and all things from which a tithe is due. And if by chance his men should cultivate other land, the monks are to have the tithe from it exactly as Hugh himself would have had it. Pagan Odo, his son, at first refused to grant this; but later, having been captured by the Normans at Meulan, he ransomed himself. Thus compelled by God, he, his wife Elizabeth, and their sons Hugh and Simon wholly granted the aforesaid [Col. 0435B] tithe to Saint Mary and placed the act of donation on the altar before me, my son Ansold, the boy Peter, and many others. The monks gave Pagan ten pounds in money and his wife twenty shillings.

“Adelelm of Gazeran likewise entrusted his son Amalric, together with the tithe of Puseaux, to the monks; and, if the boy should die before reaching seven years, he granted the tithe to the church in perpetuity for seven pounds. The boy afterwards grew up and attained the priesthood; he possessed the tithe of Puseaux for a long time, and at his death left it by right to the monks, who had fed and diligently taught him in return for it. Hugh son of Walon, surnamed Fresnellus, before becoming a monk, gave three tenants to Saint Mary; and Stephen son of Gislebert gave the monks land of half a ploughland at Goupillières. Although this was not of my fief, I nevertheless ratified the gift in my own charter by my own hand.

“Therefore I firmly grant to the monks these things which have been given by myself or my friends, and I, as a kindly supporter, consent to everything else that any of my men may give to Saint Evroul without diminution of my right or service. And I earnestly pray that if any envious or perverse person, at the devil’s prompting, presumes to violate or diminish our gifts, he may immediately recover from such madness, lest for the guilt of wicked invasion and sacrilege he be condemned on the day of judgement with the reprobate and the violently dead (*biothanati*) by the most just Judge.”

The aforesaid lord confirmed the foregoing charter with [Col. 0435D] his subscription and, before many suitable witnesses, handed to Abbot Mainer investiture of the aforesaid properties. His sons Ansold, Theobald, and William were present, as were his sons-in-law Walter of Pexey and Baldwin of Dreux; the leading men of Mantes, Hugh and Stephen; Walter the priest; Walter the knight surnamed Costatus; Richer the reeve and Fulk, sons of Fulcher; Hugh and Odo, sons of Walon; Hervé, son of Heroard; and a great part of the parish of Mantes. There Abbot Mainer appointed Goisbert prior. Goisbert soon completed the small church which Godfrey, a priest of great simplicity and innocence, had begun. Not long afterwards, as the monks prospered within and without, and the worthy parishioners rejoiced in [Col. 0436A] their advancement, the old church of Saint Mary was demolished and a new one of fine workmanship was begun. As circumstances permitted, it was elegantly completed over twenty years under the priors Goisbert, Widmund, Roger, and Hugh. Many monks remained there until the present day and laboured piously in divine worship.

## XX. The account of gifts made to the monastery of Ouche continues. Various events. Gifts made to the monks at Mantes. Concerning the lords of Mantes.

Peter, lord of Mantes, lived into old age; and through the zeal of its generous patron, the church’s property and the common people of Mantes prospered suitably. He was greatly loved by his dependants and neighbours, because he was armed with simplicity rather than crafty cunning. [Col. 0436B] He loved alms and gave them often, but he feared fasts and, abhorring them, excluded them from himself as far as he could. He readily made many promises, and sometimes sold things of great value at a cheap price. He was at once greedy and prodigal. He did not care whence abundant dishes might be set before him, nor did he consider whether the necessary resources came from plunder or honest gain; likewise, he thought little of to whom things acquired in whatever manner might be offered. He therefore never abounded in wealth.

By his wife Guindesmoth he had four sons, Ansold, Theobald, Warin, and William, and as many daughters, Hubelina, Eremburga, Odelina, and Hersende. From them there sprang an abundant multitude of descendants who, ranging about the unstable wheel of the revolving world, by the dispensation of God, who governs all things, underwent diverse fortunes. [Col. 0436C] At last Peter, worn out by age, died on the second day before the Ides of January, and rests buried in the monks’ cloister beside the southern wall of the church. John of Rheims composed the following epitaph for him:

> After one thousand and one hundred years of the heavenly Lamb,  
> Peter, flower of the nobles, fell near the Ides of January.  
> He was generous, cheerful, and very witty,  
> More devoted to banquets than to the contest of warfare.  
>
> He stood highest among the nobles and was heir of noble men.  
> He lived honoured and lies buried in the earth where he rests;  
> And he gave this site for the church of Christ’s Mother.  
>
> The cloudy sun of January had shone twelve times upon him;  
> But may the Sun of righteousness shine brightly upon him through Mary’s prayer.  
> Paris mourns; may Paradise compose a song over him  
> [Col. 0436D] Through the saints to whom he granted this site and church.

Ansold, Peter’s son, was in some respects very unlike his father in character; yet he was greater in manifold virtue, or, to speak more moderately, his equal. He was of outstanding intellect and high courage, strong and tall in body, most excellent in knightly prowess, exalted in authority, and just in judgement; bold and eloquent in debating questions, and almost the equal of philosophers. He frequented the thresholds of churches and diligently lent attentive ears to sacred sermons. He learned the deeds that had been recorded in ancient books, carefully investigated them from learned narrators, and committed the lives of the Fathers which he heard to a retentive memory. He hated lying narrators, those who adulterated God’s word, and those greedy for shameful gain; when their wicked sophistries were exposed, he openly refuted them lest they deceive the innocent. [Col. 0437A]

He always honoured his devout mother Guindesmoth and, as a faithful son, obeyed his pious mother in all things. She came from a noble family of the territory of Troyes and, devoted to God, outlived her husband in widowhood for almost fifteen years. Blessed old woman, who was piously supported in her husband’s marriage-bed by faithful offspring until old age and, seeing there the safest comforter for herself, died after receiving the viaticum. Thence she was reverently borne to burial by her dear son, and her body was honorably interred in the bosom of the church beside the companion of her bed.

The aforesaid knight shone by worthy deeds during his time as a young warrior. Leaving friends, kindred, and beloved parents, [Col. 0437B] he exercised his inborn valour among strangers. He therefore went to Italy and, joined to the most valiant Duke Guiscard, invaded Greece. In the battle in which the emperor Alexius of Constantinople was defeated and fled, he fought nobly. After some time, at his father’s earnest request, he returned to Gaul and married a noble and well-behaved young woman named Odelina, daughter of Ralph, surnamed Malvicinus, a burgess of Mantes.

By his frugality this military man encouraged all associated with him toward honourable conduct, and by the modest restraint of his economy offered an example even to religious persons. He never ate apples in an orchard, grapes in a vineyard, or hazelnuts in a wood. [Col. 0437C] He took only at the canonical hours what was set before him at table, saying that it belongs to brute animals, not to man, to eat whatever chance presents without regard to place and time. Content with lawful marriage, he loved chastity; he condemned the obscenity of lust not, like a layman, with common abuse, but openly, like a teacher of the Church, with arguments. He praised fasts and every bodily continence in all persons, and himself manfully observed them according to the measure of a layman. He abstained entirely from plunder and shrewdly preserved the goods acquired by his own labour. He lawfully paid the tithes, first-fruits, and alms which his predecessors had given to God’s ministers. To unruly and jesting vagabonds or prostitutes he not only gave no gifts, [Col. 0437D] but even denied them his company and familiar conversation.

By his lawful wife, whom he had married while she was young and had religiously trained to obedience in every modesty, he had seven sons and two daughters: Peter, Ralph, Warin, Lisiard, Guy, Ansold, and Hugh; Mary and Guindesmoth. The historical narrative may relate more in its proper places concerning their fortunes.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1106, at the end of February, when a comet with a very long tail appeared in the western regions, the famous Duke Bohemond, after the capture of Antioch, came to Gaul and married Constance, daughter of Philip, king of the Franks. He celebrated splendid nuptials at Chartres, Countess Adela generously providing an adequate establishment. [Col. 0438A] Then the third expedition of Westerners to Jerusalem took place, and a very great massing of many thousands advanced against the Thracians, threatening to trample underfoot the Byzantine sceptre. But God’s most just providence frustrated the designs of those who coveted the invasion of their neighbour’s possession; hence the proud multitude of ambitious men attained none of the things it had vainly expected.

In the same year, within the three weeks in which the comet shone, Ansold of Mantes, pricked by the spur of divine fear, humbly approached the court of Saint Mary and freely made satisfaction to God with many tears for certain disputes which he had had against the monks. Then [Col. 0438B] before all his barons, assembled in the monks’ dormitory, he granted to the Church of God and Saint Mary of Mantes everything which his father Peter, Hugh, Pagan, Anastasius, Robert son of Hubelina, Hervé son of Heroard, Odo son of Walon, Fulk and Richer sons of Fulcher, and any other men of his, whatever their rank, had given or might give, provided that he did not lose their service. The agreement was that, should any one of them lose his fief for any offence, the church should in no way be deprived of its gift of alms.

Ansold also granted, by the rod which he had handed into the hand of John, monk and priest, the tithe which his sister Hersende had held as marriage-portion and had restored to Blessed Mary before her death, so that after the death of his nephew Peter the church might receive the tithe free. [Col. 0438C] He also gave Saint Mary the site of the mills in Bole Wood, so that two denarii from each mill should be given for the church lights, and whoever committed fraud in this matter should pay five shillings. Previously sixty shillings had been paid for such an offence; but because ecclesiastical law is milder than secular law, fifty-five shillings are remitted and five received. Ansold, his wife Odelina, and his two sons Peter and Ralph placed the gift of these things upon Saint Mary’s altar by means of the missal-book; all the knights of Mantes were also present at this ceremony. [Col. 0438D]

Then Ansold appointed his eldest son Peter heir to all his possessions. The boy, while Goislen of Marolles proclaimed and made the announcement, received the homage and fealty of the knights of Mantes. Present were William, Ansold’s brother; Robert, his nephew; Guibald the knight, son of Ralph Malvicinus; Hugh of Marolles; Odo Pagan, son of Hugh; Gislebert son of Haimon; Odo son of Walon and his sons Peter and Arnulf; Fulk son of Fulcher and his two nephews Josfred and Odo; Grimold son of Almannus; and Walter son of Fulk.

After his father’s death, the often-mentioned lord lawfully governed his paternal right for eighteen years, showed the monks faithful patronage in all things, and zealously devoted himself daily to their conversation for the improvement of his conduct. He diminished none of their possessions, but increased some, as stated above, and composed the charter of his donation as follows:

“I, Ansold, grant and confirm everything which my father Peter gave, for his forebears Ansold and Warin and his other relatives, to God, Saint Mary, and the monks of Saint Evroul, in the same manner and on the same terms as he granted it. I also willingly [Col. 0439B] grant, insofar as concerns myself or my children, the tithe of Mantes which my two sisters hold as marriage-portions—namely Eremburga, wife of Baldwin of Dreux, and Hersende, wife of Hugh of Vicinis—if the monks can obtain it from them or from my nephews by prayer or payment. For I know that the tithe is God’s portion, which from ancient times He has deigned to reserve for Himself through Moses for the support of the Levites. Hence, I think, it is concealed from none who are wise that whoever obstinately feeds upon such plunder earns a terrible punishment in the future.

“Moreover I give Saint Mary the site of the mills in Bole Wood, so that two coins from each mill may be given for the lights of the church. Whoever commits fraud shall pay five shillings; for this offence sixty shillings have hitherto been paid. My wife Odelina and my sons Peter and Ralph grant these things. From this we received the benefactions and fellowship of the brethren; and as a token, I received as a gift from the monks one horse worth one hundred shillings, which had belonged to Grimold of Salmarches. [Col. 0439C] Therefore I make this charter of grant with my wife and sons, by which, upon my faith and without deceit, I make God’s Church an inviolable gift, that, through God’s mercy, I may deserve to be joined to the fellowship of the faithful. Amen.”

Germund the Red of Montfort, at his death, gave Saint Mary and the monks living at Mantes half of all that he possessed at Puseaux, for the salvation of his soul, with the consent of his wife Eremburga, from whose marriage-portion the land came, and of his sons Hugh and Walter. It was then established that the heirs holding the land should perform all service due to the lord from whose fief it was held. The revenues which arose from wood and open land were to be assembled wherever both parties jointly thought fit and divided equally. [Col. 0439D] On that day Hugh of Guacejo was prior of Mantes; in his presence and that of many others, the gift was placed upon Saint Mary’s altar before the aforesaid man’s body was committed to the bosom of the earth.

Later, when Walter, the aforesaid Germund’s son, was made a knight, he denied that he had assented to this donation, wishing to maintain that his father had given the property to him before he gave it to the monks. Therefore the monks approached Count Amalric, lord of Montfort, and complained to him of Walter’s disturbance. Compelled by the count’s justice, the disputants came to this agreement: the monks gave forty shillings at Montfort to Walter, then a young knight, and he granted them all the matters stated above in the presence of Richelde, Amalric’s wife. On the following Sunday, at Mantes, both brothers Hugh and Walter [Col. 0440A] confirmed the aforesaid grant; in the presence of Prior David, the other brethren, Ansold and his son Peter, and all the clergy and people assembled in the church, they placed the donation upon the altar. Afterwards their brothers Engenold and Hervé granted the same things. This was done in the year in which King Henry of England attacked the castle of Saint-Clair in France and King Louis of France, in return, built the castle of Gournay in Normandy; from this occasion savage battles raged between them, to the harm of many.

Nivard of Hargeville gave the monks of Mantes all the land which he possessed at Punctelville, together with half the tithe of that land; in return he received twenty-eight shillings from the monks’ charity. His brother Simon granted this, and Prior Hugh gave him Cordovan slippers in return. Peter and Guarimbold, Nivard’s sons, granted what their father had given, and each received slippers worth six denarii in return. On the following Sunday Nivard himself came to Mantes and placed the gift upon Saint Mary’s altar before the entire parish. [Col. 0440B]

When Geoffrey of Marc came to Mantes to assume the monastic habit, he gave the monks of Blessed Evroul the entire church situated at Marc, half the churchyard, and the tithe. His wife Emmelina and their sons—William, Simon, Hugh, Stephen, and Pagan—granted this. Then Hugh the Red of Fresnay, from whose fief Geoffrey had held it, came to Mantes and, at the monks’ request, granted that all which Geoffrey had given the monks should be free from every service. Thus, if the heirs at Marc served him or withheld service due to him, the monks should nonetheless always hold the property freely. His brother Walter also granted this. [Col. 0440C]

Walter, son of Heldeburgis, after receiving a mortal wound, gave the monks of Mantes the whole tithe which he possessed at Puseaux from the fief of Hervé, son of Heroard. His wife Isemburgis, together with Walter’s three brothers Richard, Theobald, and Geoffrey, was present there and consented. Hervé, son of Heroard, likewise assented to all the tithes which he possessed at Puseaux; and Simon of Thoiry granted the monks the part of the tithe which was from his fief. [Col. 0440D] To ensure that no claim remained, the monks gave Hervé one house with many furnishings for four pounds in money, and one arpent of vineyard as a wardship, which Walter son of Alps had given to Saint Mary; they gave his wife Odelina, from whose marriage-portion it came, one fustian cloth; Simon received twenty shillings, and his wife, from whose inheritance it came, three shillings.

Baldwin the Red of Montfort, when he became a monk, gave the monks of Mantes the revenue which he possessed at Mantes: namely, ten shillings and one sextary of salt. The monks of Fécamp, who lived at Mantes, paid this to him on the feast-day of Saint Remigius. The same Baldwin also gave all that he possessed in the church and tithe of Jumelville, [Col. 0441A] and the twelve denarii which the sons of Burga paid him as rent from Concita. His wife granted these things and received one cow in return. His son Geoffrey likewise assented to the aforesaid possessions of the monks and received from them for this one horse worth sixty shillings and twenty shillings. Firm witnesses to this were Ansold, lord of Mantes, and his son Peter; Geoffrey son of Richer; Grimold son of Almannus; Amalric Floenel; and many others.

But after Baldwin died, his son denied all the things aforesaid; therefore, after twenty shillings had again been given him, he made a renewed grant. He accordingly went to Mantes with Prior David and commanded the monks of Fécamp dwelling at Saint George’s that, from that day onward, they should pay every year to the monks of Mantes the ten shillings and sextary of salt which they had been accustomed to pay his father. [Col. 0441B] William also, son of Henry of Richebourg, from whose fief it was held, granted it to the monks and received from them, in charity, ten shillings and half a measure of wine.

Eremburga, daughter of Peter of Mantes, and her son Amalric restored to God the half of the tithe which they had unjustly held, and placed the gift upon the altar of Saint Mary, Mother of God, before the people. The lord Ansold, supporter and faithful instigator of this gift, was present and granted it with his sons Peter and Ralph. Then, in order to redeem the tithe, since William of Mantes held it in pledge for twenty pounds, the monks gave Eremburga ten pounds and granted to her [Col. 0441C] and her heir three arpents of vineyard.

After this same Eremburga had taken the veil, she and her aforesaid son Amalric again restored their share of the frequently mentioned tithe to God; as before, they placed the gift upon the altar of the Lord’s Mother by means of the book of the Gospels. William of Mantes, his nephew Robert, his brother-in-law Geoffrey, Odo Pagan, Odo son of Walon, Fulk the clerk, and Geoffrey son of Richer were present and gave thanks to God, who had relieved the woman, burdened with the deadly load of wicked rapacity.

## XXI. The account of gifts continues. Concerning the lords of Mantes.

Through the industry of its inhabitants and the gifts that flowed into it, [Col. 0441D] the house at Mantes grew and became wealthy; but after a while it was weakened by the decline of its praiseworthy patron Ansold. For after bearing the arms of knighthood for fifty-three years, and now reaching old age, he began to fall ill. Sick for almost seven weeks and about to go before the tribunal of the Most High, he prepared himself by confession and repentance. Although he did not lie abed but went daily to church, and remained vigorous in memory and eloquence, he nevertheless recognized that he had lost the bodily constitutions by which physicians foretell men’s destruction or health, and that he could not escape the condition of approaching death. Mindful therefore of eternal salvation, he turned wholly to the Lord and eagerly hastened to perform for everlasting life those things which he had heard from wise men and had willingly [Col. 0442A] retained.

One night, hearing the sound of the bell, he rose and came to church with one of his attendants. He prayed to God to accept his satisfaction and fulfil his will. When the matins service had ended, he summoned the monks, disclosed his vow to them, and sought from them the monastic habit. David was then prior there, and had with him honourable monks and priests, namely John of Rheims, Osbern, and Odo.

Ansold earnestly wished to be joined to these men in habit, as he already was in mind. He said that he had lost all affection for wife and children, could no longer retain lordship of the land in any way, and knew death to be near; therefore he wished to cling to God alone, and they ought not to refuse his request. The monks, hearing this, rejoiced at the man’s good will; [Col. 0442B] nevertheless, because his eldest son and future heir was absent, they postponed for two days what he had asked. He took this delay very ill, longing for the invisible things which the father of the household gives to watchful servants. For he declared that this was his whole desire and entire will: to live with Christ’s poor and to end his life with them, so that he might obtain the promise which God makes to His own.

Finally, when the two days had passed and he heard that his son had arrived, he ordered his wife to come at once to him with their son. When they were present, before many knights he made many declarations to his son, and before a large gathering of persons of different ages and sexes he admonished him as follows:

[Col. 0442C] Dearest son, whom I have reared delicately, wishing to leave you as my heir and successor acceptable to God and to men, now keep with the utmost care the things which I most devoutly enjoin upon you. First of all, always love God above all things. Fear and venerate your bishop and your king as your patrons; and do not forget, so far as you are able, to obey their commands. Pray to God daily for their prosperity, that through the merits and protection of a good bishop everlasting salvation may be granted to your soul, and that under the governance of a peaceful king you may possess temporal honour tranquilly and justly. Render to your men the loyalty that you owe them, and rule them not as a tyrant but as a gentle patron. Prudently preserve your lordship in fields, woods, meadows, and vineyards, and avoid diminishing it by making grants to others. Do not practise robbery; utterly drive thieves [Col. 0442D] and plunderers away from you. Guard your own property lawfully, and do not take another’s property by force or invasion. From such things come wrath, then discord; robbery, slaughter, and arson follow, with losses, murders, and countless other evils. Wise is he who knows how to guard against the causes of evils which he sees befalling others, lest they happen to himself. Keep these, my final commands. Always love and attend our mother, the holy Church. Reverently hear daily the word of God, which is the food and life of the soul, the Masses, and the service owed to God. Honour the servants of God in word and deed; especially venerate and assist, as far as you can, our lords and brothers the monks, ministers of this Church; support them with your counsel and aid should they need it. Freely allow them to possess in peace and quiet the property which my father [Col. 0443A] and I have given them for our salvation. Never wish to diminish them in their possessions and revenues, nor suffer any violence to be inflicted upon them by your dependants. For if you take care to be their faithful supporter, they will pray to God for you without ceasing. Therefore never hate them or their possessions, but always love them; and, if the Lord grants you life and prosperity, cause them to increase. If you observe and do these things, I grant you on God’s behalf the blessing which our holy fathers left to their heirs, and I pray God that it may come and remain upon you. But if, God forbid, you act otherwise, I leave you the curse by the authority of God and the holy Fathers.

[Col. 0443B] When he had ended this address to his son, the memorable hero addressed his wife Odelina in these words: “Dear sister and beloved wife Odelina, I beg you kindly now to hear my entreaties. Until now we have lawfully kept faith in marriage with one another, and, with God’s help, have lived together for more than twenty years without quarrel or shameful complaint. Through lawful union we have begotten honourable offspring; encourage them with diligent exhortations to submit wholesomely to their Creator. Behold, I am being led to my end, and, whether I will or no, I am approaching the bounds of death. Behold, according to the lot of all flesh I am wasting away, and am compelled to pay the common debt. I do not wish to draw you out with many words. Since your life can be an instruction to many, add only this to [Col. 0443C] your customary virtues: from henceforth live chastely in holy widowhood. Grant me leave to become a monk and, abandoning the splendid garments of the world, to receive the vestments of the holy Father Benedict, though they are black. I desire to join the fellowship of those who forsake the world’s allurements for Christ. Therefore, lady, I beg you to release me from the marriage bond and faithfully commend me to God, so that, freed from every worldly burden, I may be found worthy to be marked by the monastic habit and tonsure. This I ask from the depths of my heart; this I desire with every wish: that my soul may be reckoned in the monastic fellowship and, having assumed the form of religious life and been renewed, may already sing in this present age: ‘I am black, but beautiful’ (Song of Songs 1:4). I am black through the blackness and unbeautifulness of rough clothing, but beautiful through the humility [Col. 0443D] of a holy purpose and devotion pleasing to God.”

As Ansold spoke these and similar words, his good wife, accustomed never to oppose his wishes, bathed in many tears but without cries, strong in reverent modesty and obedient to her husband in her customary manner, granted what he requested. Then the holy Church was festively observing the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord; and a violent wind was shaking the world intolerably, overthrowing woods, houses, and other buildings, causing great damage on sea and land, and marvellously terrifying human hearts. Once consent had been given, the recruit of Christ was immediately tonsured; the neophyte was clothed in sacred vestments, and, wearing them for three days, was buried with Christ so that he might rise with him. Finally, on the third day, [Col. 0444A] sensing death, he had the brothers summoned and asked them to perform for him the commendation of the dying. When this had been completed, he asked that holy water and a cross be brought to him. When they had been brought, he sprinkled himself with the water, adored the cross, and commended himself thus to Christ who hung upon the cross, while a certain learned man prompted the words:

> Into your hands, Lord God, though once a sinner but now penitent, I commend my spirit, as a servant ought to entrust himself to his lord.

Having said this, he happily breathed his last, as we believe. Then vigils were sung, psalms and prayers were said at his departure with many sighs, and Masses were devoutly celebrated. When these had duly been performed, he was committed to mother earth, to be kept and restored, while the Church of God celebrated the Assumption of Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist. [Col. 0444B] Odo of Monasterolum was present at these funeral rites and performed the priestly office there. In a short verse he thus recorded his name and office, the day of his death, and a great prayer for him:

> If anyone should wish to know, while he was alive,  
> Who he was whom the tomb covers, and what name he bore:  
> This man’s name was Ansold, and his title that of knight.  
> The fifth day at the end of December became his rest.  
> May the reward of rest be granted him through God’s mercy! Amen.

Peter, renowned in warfare and daring, feared by his neighbours, presided over Manlia; but in some of his actions he strayed from his father’s footsteps. For, given to youthful frivolity, he loved actors and gamblers; yielding to the persuasion of young men, he cultivated greed and often oppressed poor peasants, both his own and others’. He rashly seizes what belongs to others and heedlessly squanders his own. Therefore, just as he harms his fellow inhabitants, so neighbouring raiders lie in wait greedily and do harm both to him and to his men. When angry he readily threatens the harshest things; when pleased he rashly promises difficult things; in both cases he is often proved a liar. After his father’s death he married a most noble wife, named Ada, niece of Burchard of Montmorency and daughter of the count of Gisors. He honours monks and clerics in speech and patiently endures their rebukes; but he veils his shamelessness under the excuse of youthful age and promises amendment of life in more mature years—may it indeed come to pass! [Col. 0444D] Now I shall briefly record the things given to the monks by him or under him.

As he died, Ansold left the monks an excellent palfrey; in return for it Peter, at his father’s request, gave the monks land at Mont-Marcenii, and then confirmed to them everything which his predecessors had given. He also restored to Saint Mary, free of every due, the vineyard of Clarofons, which John of Saint-Denis, his wife Mary, and their son Ernulf had formerly given freely; but afterwards, intending to go to Jerusalem, they had sold it to a Breton of Montfort named Fulk, who was disputing the monks’ claim. Peter took it from the Breton by episcopal justice into his own hand; but shortly thereafter, struck by illness through divine action, he restored it in his confession to Saint Mary, free from every payment. [Col. 0445A] He also offered the yield of the vineyard for that year to the holy Virgin, to repair an image.

Grimold, nephew and heir of Stephen of Manlia, gave the monks the entire tithe from his land, both from Ansold’s fief and from Pagan’s fief, together with the tithe of his mill and vineyards; and he placed the gift upon the altar with his wife Petronilla. Then, upon the death of his aforesaid wife, he granted the monks two arpents of land at Mont-Tedbert. He went to Jerusalem with Count Stephen of Blois, endured many severe hardships on that journey, and after returning lived lawfully.

## XXII. The accounts of donations continue.

Gerold, surnamed Costatus, brother-in-law of the aforesaid Grimold, fell ill and, terrified by a divine stroke, gave the monks a certain tithe which he possessed in the district of Marolium, together with his share of the courtyard of that same village. His wife consented, since it was part of her dowry; Peter, lord of Manlia, likewise wished and granted it, since it was held from his fief. Alberic of Marolium gave the monks twelve jugera of land, situated on the brow of the hill westward in the territory of Marolium. [Col. 0445B]
