Odo, son of Gualo, an honourable knight, upon the death of his son Arnulf gave the monks of Manlia three jugera of land, which at that time the priest Fulk cultivated. He also gave two modii of wine and established that they should be delivered yearly from his vineyards, so that the Church of Manlia should in no way lose this aforesaid gift through succession or change of heirs, and should worthily pray without ceasing to God for the souls of his sons Peter, Arnulf, and Milo, and for his other friends. A few days later the aforesaid Odo fell ill. Desiring to profit from this illness as a good son from his father’s chastisement, he summoned to himself his wife Beliarda, his daughter-in-law Cornelia, and his daughter Sicilia with her husband Geoffrey. With their assent, he gave all his tithes to God and Saint Mary. Accordingly, at Odo’s command the aforesaid women, together with Geoffrey, went to the Church and placed the gift upon the altar. When this was done and his sickness grew worse, he became a monk there and lay in the monks’ infirmary for ten [Col. 0445D] days. Meanwhile his son Walter Audax arrived from Troyes, where he had long remained, and found his father still alive. Asked by him, Walter granted all that his father had given to the Church of God and that his relatives had approved: namely, three jugera of land, two modii of wine each year, and all the tithes that his father had possessed in grain, wine, and first-fruits. After his father’s death and burial, Walter sent the gift of all these things upon the altar of the Holy Mother of God by means of a book; and, imitating his father, he has remained to this day a good neighbour to the monks.

In the time of Hugh of Vacy, David, and the other priors who laboured usefully at Manlia, it was known to many—and we wish it to be known to posterity—[Col. 0446A] that Tesza, wife of Bernard the Blind, gave the monks of Saint Ebrulf dwelling at Manlia one half of the land of Saint Columba, both open land and woodland, in addition to two arpents of land which she gave them, where they might build a house and, if they wished, have settlers without another’s share. She did this with the consent of her lords: namely Goislen, who then held the other half of the land in demesne because service was deficient, and Guaszo of Pexei, who was the chief lord. At various times the monks gave these patrons much money, wishing to increase the Church’s property in lawful peace and to provide some advantage for the brethren who would follow. Thus the first of these, eager and magnanimous, began this business during his priorship and gave the aforesaid Tesza ten shillings, her son Odo one fustian cloth, and her son-in-law William ten shillings. He also gave Goislen a horse valued at four pounds and twenty shillings to his wife; to Guaszo twenty-five shillings and a horn cup, and another horn cup to his wife. [Col. 0446B] The aforesaid persons received these and many other things from the monks’ charity; and, placing the gift upon the altar of the Lord before many witnesses, they firmly granted everything. But afterwards, prompted by wickedness and having broken the agreement in many ways, they acted falsely. Guaszo in particular, who was stronger than all the others and ought to have corrected them if they strayed, disturbed the alms-gift, seized the settlers’ property as plunder, and overthrew their houses. Hence the place became deserted, as it had once been. For the monks left the place for a time under such compulsion. Finally, after many years had passed, Amalric, Guaszo’s son, was killed. Then the monks approached Guaszo, mourning for his son’s death, and asked him to make amends for the damage he had inflicted upon them. Stricken by his son’s death, he humbly replied and promised that he would repair the wrong he had committed. He therefore summoned the aforesaid Goislen and Amalric of Belveder, to whom he had recently restored that same fief and from whom Goislen then held it. They met at Fraxini and discussed the redress of the offence. At Guaszo’s request on behalf of the monks, Amalric confirmed the gift which Tesza had made and Guaszo and Goislen had granted. [Col. 0446D] When the assent and consent of all had been secured, the aforesaid lords—Guaszo, Amalric, and Goislen—openly put the monks in seisin; and Grimold of Manlia, his son Roger, and many others saw and heard this. On the appointed day Amalric came to Manlia, placed upon the altar of Saint Mary the gift he had granted to the monks at Fraxini, and received twenty Medantine shillings from the monks’ charity.

Thus, through the diligent administration of the monks, the cell of Manlia rose, and through the abundant contributions of those who gathered there it grew fittingly to the praise of God. For that village was most excellently planted with vineyards and fertile fields, watered by the river Mauldre flowing through its midst, [Col. 0447A] and strongly defended by an abundance of noble knights. During their lives these men willingly give the Church land and other resources; they reverently honour the monastic order, and, in the fear of death, seek it with all their affection as an aid to the soul. There knights keep cloister with the monks, often discussing practical and theoretical matters together. Thus it becomes a school for the living and a refuge for the dying.

In the time of the elder Peter, Abbot Mainerius petitioned Philip, king of the French, and humbly requested from him the things granted to the monks of Saint-Evroul within his kingdom. The king kindly confirmed what had been granted and graciously and cheerfully urged those with him to give more abundantly. This took place on a journey [Col. 0447B] between Épône and Medan. Then, in the time of the younger Peter, King Louis came to Manlia. Angry with that same Peter for certain offences of insolent youth, he demolished the stone fortification with which prudent Ansold had enclosed his house, together with the house itself. The king then lodged in the monks’ house and confirmed by royal grant everything that had been given to them in the time of the three lords—Peter, Ansold, and the other Peter—or which they had purchased themselves. At that time Guarinus of Sées, a shrewd and well-educated man, held the priory; through his service and personal conversation with the king, he procured royal confirmation of all the things which Goisbert and Guidmund, William [Col. 0447C] and Hugh, David and Rannulf, and the other priors of the same cell had provided for that place. Let what has here been said concerning Manlia suffice.

The celebrated physician Goisbert, after beginning the church at Manlia, as we have said, sought to confer with certain close friends and associates about the common benefit of his monastery. When they agreed, he earnestly asked his abbot to entrust the priory of Manlia to another, so that he himself might proceed more freely to administer other affairs. This was done. Guidmund, formerly a priest at Solignac, a good man, was appointed in his place; and the aforesaid physician, for the benefit of his brethren, applied himself with all his energy to many French knights. Some he attracted by medical care [Col. 0447D] and aid, others by gifts, but both groups by eloquent exhortations.

Accordingly Unfrid, surnamed Harenc, his wife Havisa, Havisa’s sons Pagan and Alexander, Roger of Rolla Crota, his wife Basilla, and Basilla’s son Guiard granted to God and Saint Ebrulf the church of Villiers-Vastatus, its appurtenant tithe, and land sufficient for one plough-team. They also granted the whole village’s right of lodging, free and undisturbed by anyone’s share; likewise land, both in established holdings and newly broken ground throughout the parish, to be cultivated by persons settled there, reserving to themselves only the field-share (*campartum*). This gift was made before Lord Robert at Ivry, [Col. 0448A] with his consent and that of his sons Ascelin Goel and William. Robert granted everything that he possessed in that village, for which he received the entire benefice of the place and one ounce of gold. Not long afterwards, divinely struck in his genitals by the stimulus of a serious disease, and fearing death, he became a monk of the abbey of Bec. His son Ascelin Goel inherited his patrimony by hereditary right and for a long time surpassed all his fellow countrymen in notorious crimes. He built a very strong castle at Breherval and filled it with savage bandits, to the ruin of many. He secretly seized the fortress of Ivry with great cunning, captured his lord William of Breteuil after defeating him in battle, and harshly confined him in a most stringent prison. He violently extorted from him a thousand Dreux pounds and the refuge of the aforesaid tower as his ransom; and he married William’s daughter Isabel, by whom he begot seven sons. With his wife and sons he granted all the property which Saint Ebrulf held from his fief—namely Villiers-Vastatus and half the tithe of Montinnei—and received sixty shillings from the monks’ charity. He confirmed his charter of grant at Breherval. On another occasion, in the house of the monks at Saint Hellerius, he granted Saint Ebrulf that all his lordship should be free from passage-dues in that place and throughout all his land. His sons Robert and William, surnamed Lupellus, later also granted this, and long maintained its firm terms. [Col. 0448C]

Hugh Paganus Crassa-Lingua (“Thick-Tongue”), his wife Agnes, and their son Guy granted Saint Ebrulf the viscounty—that is, the road-dues—which they held at Villiers-Vastatus. For this they once received ten shillings and a stag’s hide from the monks, and on another occasion twenty shillings. Their son received ten Medantine shillings for his consent. John of Reims drafted the charter of this agreement before the tower of Breherval, Hugh of Fresnel dictating it; Hugh Paganus confirmed it with his people. Some time later the aforesaid Hugh became a monk, and his sons Ralph, Simon, and Robert attempted to take the viscounty from the monks. But that they might possess it in peace, [Col. 0448D] the monks gave Ralph, the eldest, one hundred and ten Medantine shillings, Simon five shillings, and Robert Cordovan slippers.

In the year in which Goel died, Alexander and Gislebert gave Saint Ebrulf a field from the holding of a certain peasant Robert, in the presence of Robert of Saint Nicholas. Robert himself complained that he had not land sufficient for one plough-team. Whatever Fulk of Saint-Aubin gave Saint Ebrulf from his land at Villiers, his heirs Theodoric and Rainer confirmed, as did their wives Emmelina and Tescelina, from whom the inheritance came; they retained some share for lodging, with the assent of their lord Alexander.

[Col. 0449A] I have extended this lengthy narrative concerning the property given to the Church of Saint-Evroul, but I have not yet been able to include everything here. For these properties are small, acquired from persons of modest rank either through entreaties, by force, by purchase, or in some other way, and scattered across very many dioceses. In them the number of monks is determined according to the extent of the possessions, and they serve the Lord daily on behalf of their benefactors in hymns, prayers, and a life of continence. The remaining matters will truthfully be collected in the following work and clearly disclosed for the knowledge of the brethren who succeed us in labouring in the Lord’s field.

## SUMMARY OF BOOK VI

[Col. 0449]

I. Prologue: various events. II. Digression: history of the blessed Count William, monk of Gellone. III. Concerning Gerold, chaplain of Hugh, count of Avranches: through his counsel very many knights receive the monastic habit in the monastery of Saint-Evroul. IV. Abbot Mainerius’s journey to England. Charter of King William for the monastery of Saint-Evroul. Concerning the three brothers. The monks of Saint-Evroul. V. Continuation of the account of donations made to the monastery of Saint-Evroul. A new cell at Almenêches is given to the monks of Saint-Evroul. Various histories. VI. Meditations. Life of the blessed Father Ebrulf. VII. Continuation. VIII. Continuation. IX. Death of the blessed Ebrulf. X. Obscurity of the history of Saint-Evroul after the death of the blessed Ebrulf. Depredations of the Normans. XI. How and when the Franks acquired the relics of the blessed Ebrulf. XII. The monks of Saint-Evroul resolve to follow the body of their founder. The relics of the blessed Ebrulf are divided. XIII. Deeds of Ascelin in the wilderness of Saint-Evroul. XIV. Saint-Evroul is ravaged and destroyed. How the monastery of Saint-Evroul is restored from its ruins. The first abbots of Saint-Evroul. XV. The monks of Saint-Evroul obtain certain relics of their patron. Succession of the abbots of Saint-Evroul.

# BOOK VI

## I. Prologue: Various Events

[Col. 0449B]

The keenness of human intellect always needs to be suitably exercised upon a useful subject-matter; by recalling the past and examining the present, it must be happily trained in virtues for the future. Everyone ought to learn daily how to live, and to appropriate for his own benefit the strong examples of heroes who have passed away. Many things thought unheard-of often sound in untrained ears, and events new to people of the present frequently arise in sudden crises; without the recurrence of past events, the inward eyes of the inexperienced are darkened in such matters. Therefore diligent people investigate hidden things; embracing piously whatever they judge useful for a kindly mind, they value it highly. They labour from goodwill and disclose the past to posterity without envy; [Col. 0449C] yet the indolent sometimes tear their diligence apart with canine teeth. Hence some envious persons, injured by the bites of the envious, often grow sluggish and abandon an undertaking whose model may perhaps be shut away in eternal silence. Thus, at times, a mournful loss comes to the world through a trivial occasion—a loss which benevolent posterity, if it could restore it and recover what was left unfinished, would energetically rise from its cast-off lethargy to repair, eagerly seek with determined will the flower and fruit of the work it had missed, and search it out ardently with diligent discernment. We frequently read this in the complaints of the ancients, and lament with eminent teachers grieving over the attacks of their rivals. We see Jerome, Origen, and other teachers complaining in their writings of the quibbles of barking detractors; and we grieve that for this reason many outstanding things have been withdrawn from our view, since witty sophists preferred to rest in idleness rather than labour to bring hidden things forth eloquently and expose themselves to the slanderous barking of those who gnaw at them. I beg those who neither publish works of their own, nor receive those of others generously, nor peacefully correct what displeases them, to be silent and at rest. Let them learn what they do not know; and if they cannot learn, at least let them allow their fellow-students to publish what they think.

Concerning the human condition and fall, the changeability of the declining age, the vicissitudes of our prelates and princes, peace or war, and the manifold, unceasing accidents of mortals, every writer has an abundant theme. But writers nowadays need not toil to recount the miracles and wonders of saints, because these are now exceedingly scarce upon the earth. For the ancient fathers—Martial and Taurinus, Silvester, Martin, and Nicholas, and other wondrous men whose tongues became keys of heaven—full of divine gifts and shining in the Church like Phoebus, ruled by the power of the Almighty over the elements [Col. 0451A] of the world and the powers of the air. Now, having received the heavenly reward with their King, they stand blessed in heaven. Their successors, however, who hold the summit of authority, are called Rabbi, and sit in Moses’ seat, possess in many ways the secular pomp and wealth which most of them covet too eagerly; but they do not shine equally in the merit of holiness or the power of virtues and wonders. Nevertheless, the course of the age and human affairs ought to be written truthfully, and chronicle ought to be composed for the praise of the Creator and just governor of all things. For the eternal Creator works even now and marvellously orders everything; let each person piously set forth from His glorious deeds whatever has been divinely inspired in him, according to his wish and capacity.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1066, in the fifth indiction, William duke of the Normans, since the line of King Edward capable of holding the royal sceptre had failed, crossed the sea to the English with many thousands of armed men and killed Harold, invader of the kingdom of Albion, in battle on the field of Senlac. Then, at the desire of Franks and English alike, on Christmas Day at Westminster, he was consecrated king by Aldred, archbishop of York, and held the English kingdom vigorously for twenty years, eight months, and sixteen days. He broke, put in chains, disinherited, expelled, and dispersed beyond the boundary of their native land the rebellious sons of the kingdom. But he exalted his dependants and supporters, enriched them with great honours, and magnified them by placing them over the affairs of the realm. [Col. 0451C] Among these Hugh of Avranches, son of Richard surnamed Goz, shone out above the other magnates. After Gerbod the Fleming returned to his own people, the king prudently granted him the earldom of Chester by counsel. Hugh was indeed a lover of the world and of worldly splendours, which he regarded as the greatest portion of human happiness. He was ready in warfare, excessively lavish in giving, delighted by games and luxuries, actors, horses and dogs, and other vanities of that sort. A very great household was always attached to him, noisy with a numerous throng of boys of noble and base birth. Honourable men, clerics, and knights lived with this earl, whom he rejoiced to have as partners both in his labours and in his riches. A cleric of Avranches named Gerold served in his chapel, endowed with piety, uprightness, and learning. He performed the Lord’s service daily and frequently offered the most holy oblation devoutly. He urged as many courtiers as he could to amend their lives by setting before them examples of their predecessors. He saw and deservedly condemned carnal licentiousness in many; he mourned the immense negligence towards God’s worship found in very many. To leading barons, moderate knights, and noble youths he offered salutary admonitions, amply adducing from the Old Testament and from recent Christian history the exemplary service of holy soldiers. [Col. 0452A] For he eloquently narrated the conflicts of Demetrius and George, Theodore and Sebastian, Duke Maurice and the Theban Legion, and the eminent commander Eustace with his companions, who deserved to be crowned in heaven through martyrdom. He also spoke of the holy champion William, who after a long military career renounced the world and served the Lord gloriously under the monastic rule. Thus his exhortation benefited many, drawing them from the worldly sea to the safe station of the regular life.

## II. Digression: History of the Blessed Count William, Monk of Gellone

Now, since mention of Saint William has occurred, I should like briefly to insert his life into this little work. I know that it is rarely found in this region, and a truthful account of such a man will please some readers. [Col. 0452B] Antony, monk of Jumièges, recently brought it and showed it to us when we thirsted to see it. A lay is commonly sung about him by minstrels; but rightly preferable is the authoritative account, diligently composed by religious teachers and reverently read by attentive readers in the common hearing of the brethren. Yet because its bearer was hastening on his way and winter frost prevented me from writing, I shall now endeavour to commit to parchment in summary form the faithful abridgement which I briefly recorded on tablets, and to make known the fame of the bold marquis.

In the time of Pippin, king of the Franks, William was born to Count Theodoric and his mother Aldana. In childhood he was instructed in letters, and he was devoted to military service under Charlemagne. He received the title and office of count and, in military affairs, the command of the first cohort. Then Charles appointed him duke of Aquitaine and entrusted him with a mission against King Theodebald and the Spaniards and Hagarenes. Entering Septimania eagerly, he crossed the Rhône, besieged the city of Orange, and, driving out the invaders, recovered it. Then he fought many battles with barbarians from overseas and neighbouring Hagarenes; by divine help he saved God’s people with his sword, enlarged the Christian dominion, and subdued the Saracens. In the territory of Lodève, in the valley of Gellone, amid innumerable rocks, he built a monastery in honour of the Saviour and the Twelve Apostles. There [Col. 0452D] he established religious monks with an abbot, generously supplied all their necessities, and confirmed their charters by his own and royal instruments. His two sisters, Albana and Bertana, became nuns there and persevered well in God’s service.

After a long time, summoned by Charles, he sought France. Received with honour, he disclosed his wish to become a monk. The king granted this with many tears and ordered him to take from his treasures whatever he wished to carry to his church. But William rejected all earthly wealth and requested—and obtained—a certain reliquary containing wood of the Holy Cross. The patriarch of Jerusalem had sent it to King Charles, by Zacharias, a priest of great repute, when Charles was staying at Rome in the first year of his empire. On hearing of William’s change of life, the entire royal household rose up and all the city suddenly poured forth. A great multitude of nobles was present; they entered weeping and in a throng, and begged William with mournful complaint not to leave them. But he, burning with the fire of God, left everything. Escorted with great honour, he bade all farewell and at last departed from the army of the Franks amid its tears and sighs. Reaching the settlement of Brioude, he offered his arms at the altar of Saint Julian the martyr: his helmet and splendid shield in the church by the martyr’s tomb; outside, at the doorway, he presented to God his quiver and bow, a great spear, and a double-edged sword. Then Christ’s pilgrim hastened through Aquitaine to the monastery [Col. 0453B] which he himself had shortly before built in the wilderness. He approached it barefoot, wearing a hairshirt next to his flesh. When his arrival was heard, people came out to meet him at a distance where the roads divided; despite his vigorous resistance, the brethren made a festive procession. There he offered the reliquary, more precious than all gold, together with gold and silver chalices and many other varied ornaments; and, after making his request, he abandoned the world with all its pomps and enticements.

Thus, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 806, the fifth year of Charles’s empire [Note: [Col. 0453D] Read: sixth. Le Prévost.], on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, Count William became a monk and was suddenly transformed and changed in Christ Jesus. Having become a monk, he was taught and was not ashamed; he was rebuked but did not become angry. At times he was beaten and injured by insults, yet did not resist or threaten. He rejoiced in subjection and delighted in every humiliation, ready to serve, comply with, and obey everyone. He advanced daily in every holiness and religious observance, and in every observance of the holy Rule, like gold in a furnace under wondrous refining. The monastery, which he had not entirely completed before becoming a monk, he completed as he had begun it, with the assistance of his sons Bernard and William [Note: [Col. 0453D] Read: Gautcelin, or Gocelin.], whom he had placed over his counties, and of neighbouring counts. He made passable the difficult road to the aforesaid monastery because of the roughness of the mountains. Ingeniously cutting the rock with hammers, axes, and various kinds of iron tools, and casting a foundation of stones beside [Col. 0453D] the river Araris, he raised the road higher and joined it to the mountain.

Louis, son of Charles, king of Aquitaine, in all generosity, from the estates under his jurisdiction, at William’s request, granted property to the monastery and confirmed it by a royal charter and the authority of his ring. Around the monastery William had vineyards and olive-groves planted, many gardens laid out, and the valley itself, after its unfruitful trees had been cleared away, more suitably planted with fruitful orchards. He himself laboured at these and similar tasks, dedicating his own hands to rustic work for the love of God, and thus continually exercised himself in true humility and religious devotion.

[Col. 0454A] Before the abbot and brethren he frequently cast himself to the ground, asking that, for God’s mercy’s sake, he might be permitted to be further abased and humiliated. He sought the lowliest duties in the monastery. He wished to become most contemptible and to be held in contempt. He wished to be like a beast of burden and, like an ass’s colt, to carry the brethren’s loads in the house of the Lord. Once a most powerful duke, he was not ashamed to ride a mean little ass with his flasks. Behold, Lord William, from a count, becomes a cook; from a great duke, he is made a household servant, carrying wood on his neck, bearing a jar of water, striking and kindling the fire. With his own hands he washes the dishes, gathers vegetables, seasons pottages, and soaks legumes. At the very hour of the meal, without any delay, he sets before the brethren everything generously prepared; while continuing his fasts, he tends and watches over the hearths [Col. 0454B]. He himself, acting as baker, heats the oven, puts in the loaves, and draws them out when baked.

Once, because of a shortage of firewood for baking bread, he gathered vine-prunings and straw and whatever his hand found, quickly threw it into the furnace, and heated it vigorously. Since the time pressed hard upon the servant of God, and he rebuked himself deeply because the brethren’s meal-hour was being delayed somewhat, while he had nothing with which to clear the ashes from the oven, he invoked Christ, fortified himself with the sign of the Cross, entered the middle of the furnace, and, wholly unharmed, carefully prepared everything that needed to be done there. He threw out the coals with bare hands, removed the ashes with his scapular unharmed, arranged the hearth, and regulated it for putting in the loaves. Thus William stood for a long time in the fire and suffered [Col. 0454C] no burning whatever in either body or clothing. Afterwards, on the brethren’s advice, the abbot altogether forbade him servile work, but commanded him to devote himself to prayer and holy meditation, and assigned him a suitable cell. Thus, long exercised in the active life, he began to rest in the contemplative life; and after Martha’s service and frequent ministry, he delighted with Mary in perpetual contemplation.

At length William, perfected in virtues, was granted the spirit of prophecy, and his life was attested by divine revelations. He foretold the day of his death to the abbot and brethren, made it known also in writing to many neighbours, sent a messenger to King Charles, and most clearly indicated the sign that would occur when he died. [Col. 0454D] Finally, after all things had been duly completed, Blessed William departed on the fifth day before the Kalends of June [Note: 28 May, in the year 812.], while angels rejoiced and those of earth wept. Then throughout all the surrounding provinces, through all lesser and greater churches, there came a very great and unusual ringing of bells, a long pealing and wondrous sound, though no human beings pulled the ropes or moved the bells, except by the sole divine power that came from heaven. The holy body of this outstanding man was honourably buried there, and, after many miracles had been gloriously wrought, the praise of God was faithfully sung.

That venerable monastery endures there even to the present [Col. 0455A] day, and a great host of monks serves the Lord God of Hosts there with rejoicing; through the merits of Saint William, a devout monk who had been an illustrious knight, the multitude of the sick who recover exults in Christ Jesus, who glorifies eternally all who cleave to him.

### III. On Gerold, chaplain of Count Hugh of Avranches. By his counsel many knights receive the monastic habit in the monastery of Ouche.

Gerold of Avranches often recounted the trophies of most unconquered warriors, and by entreaties and threats urged his fellow athletes and noble squires toward a similar manner of life.

First, therefore, five distinguished men left the count’s household. Their names were these: [Col. 0455B] Roger, son of Ernéis, nephew of Count William of Warenne of Surrey; Ernald, son of Humphrey of Telliol, nephew of Hugh of Grandmesnil, viscount of Leicester; Guy of Medan, his own squire; Drogo, son of Geoffrey of Neufmarché; and Odo, the count’s chaplain, son of Ernulf of Dol. These men, indeed, at Ernald’s instigation—for his parents had built the abbey of Ouche—went to Ouche and were gladly received into the monastery by Abbot Mainer. There they lived regularly for a long time and, by their energy and diligence, suitably increased the church’s possessions.

Gerold, however, who, as a cock awakens sleepers in [Col. 0455C] the deep night by crowing, had likewise, by sowing the word of God, raised to better things those seduced in the darkness of Lethean forgetfulness and the depths of worldly allurements, finally struck himself with his own wings and vigorously shook off his lethargy. Following the disciples mentioned above, he strove to go to Ouche. Yet, by God’s will, he was compelled to remain in England. For when he arrived at Winchester, he began to suffer a grave illness; fearing death, he devoutly received the monastic habit in the Old Minster of Saint Peter, and for a long time lived according to the Rule under Bishop Walkelin and Geoffrey, a most learned and devout prior. Thereafter, after some time, he was canonically advanced to ecclesiastical office; and at Tewkesbury, while Samson of Bayeux was presiding over the bishopric of Worcester, [Col. 0455D] he became the first abbot. There Robert, son of Haimo, had built the monastery of Saint Mary on the River Severn, and in the time of William the younger, king of the English, had richly endowed it with many possessions. Gerold, having been placed at the height of pastoral government, diligently cultivated the office of holy preaching which he had gladly exercised while a cleric, by which he had drawn many from the mire of lust and rapacity to the purity of an innocent life; and, with God’s help, he benefited many. He established the new monastery under the ordinances of the regular order, committed a multitude of novices to the monastic rule, and handed down to neophytes the best practices of rigorous life. He lived among those subject to him in spiritual exercise, sometimes even went ahead of the younger men in arduous work, and [Col. 0456A] with diligent care prudently arranged the monastery’s affairs within and without.

After many years envious Satan rose up against the Lord’s flock, and, after wickedly troubling the shepherd, cruelly harassed the tender sheep. For Robert the Breton, after the death of Robert, son of Haimo, his abbot, by whom he had been received into monastic life, accused him before King Henry of certain false crimes. The abbot, summoned before the king, refused to employ lengthy arguments; content with his innocent conscience, he voluntarily surrendered the lordship of the abbey to the king, and, after Martha’s laborious service, returned to Mary’s better part within the seclusion of the Winchester cloister. Finally, when after some time he had been invited by the venerable Ralph, bishop of Rochester, and had himself visited that same bishop at the request [Col. 0456B] of many for the sake of holy conversation, there, when God called him, he took to his bed and, after completing all that properly pertains to a servant of God, died reverently.

Roger of Warenne, whom we have said was converted through the exhortation of the aforesaid priest and had hastened to Ouche, as though from the flames of Sodom, with four fellow-knights to become a monk, lived there nearly forty-six years. Fervent in the Order, he flourished in manifold honour. He was handsome in body, and by choice wore a lowly, humble habit. In his whole bearing he possessed venerable modesty, a clear voice, and eloquent speech. He was strong in enduring labours, willing in singing psalms and hymns, and, in his way of life, accommodating and well-mannered toward his companions. [Col. 0456C] He was sparing toward himself in food and generous toward others; ever ready for vigils and indescribably sober. He did not swell with the pride of carnal nobility; rather, standing in humility, he submitted to the Rule and chose gladly to perform every lowly service for the brethren. For many years he willingly made it his practice to oil all the brethren’s shoes, wash their stockings, and gladly perform other services which seem contemptible to certain dull and puffed-up persons. He adorned a Gospel-book with gold, silver, and gems, and provided many vestments, singers’ copes, tapestries with curtains, and many other ornaments for his church. Whatever he could, he opportunely seized from brethren and kinsmen, and, taking it away [Col. 0456D] from bodily use, gladly assigned it to divine worship for the salvation of souls.

Richard of Coulonces, brother of the aforesaid Roger, came to Ouche and gave to Saint Ebrulf the church of Estolveio, which he had redeemed from a certain man of his, Ernéis; he also added the tithe of two mills. With his wife Adelaide and the aforesaid Ernéis, he laid this donation of property upon the altar. For this grant the monks gave Richard eight pounds of money; they also gave one hundred shillings to Robert of Mowbray, who was the chief lord, and he, without hesitation, in the orchard of Thurstan of Soligny, granted to Saint Ebrulf the church of Estolveio, as the monks requested. The aforesaid Richard became very wealthy [Col. 0457A] and, being a friend of King Henry, was held in high honour among his peers. He lived prosperously until old age and had by his wife eleven sons and five daughters, to whom these names were given: Hugh, Geoffrey, and Richard; John and Robert; Odo and Henry; Ivo and Ralph; William and Henry; Rohese and Adelaide, Matilda and Avicia. Of these, two were dedicated to God from childhood. John was committed to monastic life in the church of Ouche, and Adelaide became a nun in the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Caen.

Then, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1125, the aforesaid Richard died on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October; and in the following year his son Hugh came to Ouche, offered a silver dish to God upon the altar, willingly confirmed everything [Col. 0457B] that his father, as stated above, had given, laid the gift upon the altar, and devoted himself wholly as well.

### IV. Abbot Mainer’s journey to England. Charter of King William for the monastery of Ouche. On three monk-brothers of the monastery of Ouche.

While the calm of prosperous times smiled upon him, Abbot Mainer crossed to England in the fourteenth year of his rule [Note: In the year 1081.] and took with him Roger of Warenne and Drogo of Neufmarché. He visited the court of King William, by whom he had often been summoned, and charitably visited Archbishop Lanfranc and others most dear to him. He was honourably received by the king and his magnates, and with prudent speech exhorted the brethren of the church of Ouche—namely, those [Col. 0457C] who had left Normandy and in England had been raised to more abundant hope. Distinguished monks also were joyfully received by the noble magnates of the realm and were honoured, as the favour shown to foreigners demands, from wealth violently acquired in a foreign land. Therefore the king and magnates gladly gave them estates, money, and ornaments for the church, and faithfully and devoutly commended themselves to their prayers. The possessions, churches, and tithes which friends and kinsmen of the men of Ouche bestowed upon them were recorded in a charter for the knowledge of future posterity. For the magnificent William made the following grant to Saint Ebrulf, in which he willingly confirmed by royal authority, in these words, the gifts of himself and his men:

> “WILLIAM, by the grace of God king of the English and duke of the Normans and prince of the men of Maine, to all supporters of the Catholic faith and guardians of peace in the Church, the highest and inexhaustible gift of joy.
>
> “Since mortal life is brief, and all things pass from generation to generation, we wish to confirm by the testimony of letters the decrees of our time, so that none of our successors may dare to violate what we rightly do from our own right and from the power given by God, lest he oppose Him who disposes all kingdoms according to His will. I therefore, William, [Col. 0458A] by God’s grace king, purpose to grant to the monastery of Blessed Ebrulf an alms that may profit me forever in the kingdom divinely entrusted to me; and I grant those things which our faithful men, for the common salvation of all, lawfully give to God from possessions which I gave them. By this present charter I make known our confirmation to all God’s faithful, present and future.
>
> “First, therefore, to the monastery of Ouche, which the blessed confessor of Christ Ebrulf built in the wilderness, I give from my own lordship, for the love of God, in Gloucestershire the estate called Rawella, that is, ‘Goat’s Spring’; and in Northamptonshire a certain church with all that belongs to it in the village called Nethleham.
>
> “Moreover, our magnates have granted Saint Ebrulf the following from their own goods and requested that they be inserted in a charter of royal [Col. 0458B] authority against the attacks of all. Roger, earl of Shrewsbury, gave all that he held in Melbourne, in Cambridgeshire; also Othnam and Mereston in Staffordshire; one hide of land in Graphan; the land of Wulfwin the goldsmith in Chichester; the tithe of cheeses and wool from Pulton; and the tithe from Senegai in Cambridgeshire. Mabel, the same earl’s daughter, gave Saint Ebrulf each year, from her revenues in England, sixty shillings sterling for her tithes, for the lighting of the church. Warin, sheriff of Shrewsbury, gave Saint Ebrulf Newton and the church of Hales with its tithe, and the tithe of Gueston in Staffordshire; and his lord, Earl Roger, confirmed these gifts.
>
> “Further, Hugh of Grandmesnil, who with his brother Robert and his uncles William and Robert, sons of Geroi, had restored the monastery of Ouche, gave it the following in England as a perpetual inheritance: all the land that he held in Little Pilardenton in Warwickshire; two-thirds of the tithes of all his land; sixteen peasants to safeguard those tithes; and nine churches. For he gave three villeins in Shelton, three in Wares, two in Belgrave, one in Stoton, one in Kirkby, one in Merston, one in Ostersley, one in Charlton, and another in the other Charlton. He also gave the church of Wares and the whole tithe belonging to it, with land for two plough-teams; the church of Turchillston [Col. 0458D] and the tithe belonging to it, with two virgates of land; the church of Clenefeld with its entire tithe and two virgates of land; the church of Charlton with its tithe and five virgates of land; the church of Noveslai with its tithe and two virgates of land; the church of Merthegrave, now called Belgrave by another name, with its entire tithe and eleven virgates of land; Guillecote; and whatever Hugh the Clerk of Sappo held from him in England; the church of Merston with its entire tithe and land belonging to the church; the church of Cotefford with its tithe and one hide of land; and the church of Pellingis, with all that Leofric held there from him.
>
> “[Col. 0459A] These are the things which Hugh of Grandmesnil, with my consent, gave Saint Ebrulf in England. Ralph of Conches likewise gave the same saint two manors: Alwington in Worcestershire and Caldicote in Norfolk. Hugh, son of Constantine, gave the church of Guafra and one hide of land. Hugh, earl of Chester, offered his son Robert to God for monastic life in the church of Ouche, and gave that church one hide of land in Little Pilardenton, a tithe and one peasant in the village called Brichella, and the tithe of Sanley in Buckinghamshire. Robert of Rodelent, with the consent of his lord, the aforesaid Hugh, earl of Chester, gave Saint Ebrulf Kirkby with two churches—one, namely, in the village itself, and [Col. 0459B] another near that manor on an island in the sea; the church of Saint Peter the Apostle with all belonging to it in the city of Chester; in Merston, in Northamptonshire, the church of Saint Lawrence with all that belongs to it; and in the same county the church of Bivella with two carucates of land. Other men of Earl Hugh also gave their tithes to the church of Ouche: in Northamptonshire, Rozscelin of Stenton, Osbern son of Tezzo of Neubela, Baldric of Farefort, a tithe with one peasant; Roger of Millai, Brisard, and Robert Pultrel in Leicestershire. All these gave their tithes to Saint Ebrulf, and the aforesaid earl willingly confirmed them.
>
> “Therefore I confirm by this present charter, made in the city of Winchester in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1081, in the fourth indiction, those things which I gave from our [Col. 0459C] lordship to the often-mentioned church, and all those things which I have confirmed as given to it by our barons. I deliver this testament, to be consecrated by the sign of the holy Cross, to my magnates who have made their alms or are witnesses to them, so that this grant may remain established forever by royal authority and that an irredeemable curse may strike sacrilegious violators of sacred things, unless they repent of their guilt.”

In this charter William the Great, king of the English, first made the sign of the holy Cross, and the following magnates subscribed, whose names are written below: Robert and William, [Col. 0459D] sons of the king and greatest counts; Roger of Shrewsbury and Hugh of Chester; Ralph of Conches and William of Breteuil; Hugh of Grandmesnil and his nephew Robert of Rodelent; Robert son of Murdac and Waleran of Villeray; William of Moulins and Richer of Laigle; Eudo the steward and Warin, sheriff of Shrewsbury.

Having returned from England, Abbot Mainer brought this charter with him and delivered it for preservation in the church archives. Then Queen Matilda, having heard the praiseworthy report of the conduct of the men of Ouche, came to Ouche for prayer; honourably received by the brethren, she offered a mark of gold upon the altar, commended herself and her daughter Constance to the brethren’s prayers, and, after providing funds, ordered a stone refectory to be built where they might [Col. 0460A] eat together. She gave Saint Ebrulf a chasuble adorned with gold and pearls and an elegant singer’s cope, and promised more if she lived long; but death intervened, and she could not fulfil her promises. Adeline also, wife of Roger of Beaumont, bestowed upon the men of Ouche an alb richly adorned with gold embroidery, in which the priest is accustomed to celebrate Mass on the principal feasts. Thus many others of both sexes gave gifts of various kinds from their resources to the aforesaid monastery and greatly desired spiritually to share in the benefits bestowed there upon the Architect of heaven.

At this time three brothers, born of the same parents, served there worthily in the monastic habit: Robert, surnamed Nicholas, Roger, and Odo. [Col. 0460B] They were sons of a certain priest named Gervase of Monasterol, whom Abbot Theoderic had long before transferred from Sées to govern the diocese of Sappo. The three aforesaid brothers came to conversion in their youth and, distinguished among the brethren by good conduct, were esteemed pleasing to God and men. The first of them was unlettered but a fervent lover of virtue, and he diligently supervised the work on the new basilica that was being built. The other two were learned grammarians and conspicuous priests, vigorous helpers of their abbot and distinguished deputies both within and without. The aforesaid archimandrite appointed Odo—who was younger in age, but more eloquent and stronger in enduring labour—as prior of his monastery. Roger, who was older in age and literary learning, [Col. 0460C] he sent to England on ecclesiastical business. Roger himself diligently fulfilled his master’s commands and procured the construction of a shrine in which saints’ relics might suitably be deposited; he elegantly adorned it with gold and silver. By his industry he acquired many goods for his church: various furnishings, singers’ copes and vestments, candlesticks and silver chalices, and other ornaments fitting for divine worship. He was gentle and modest, temperate in food, drink, and sleep, and beloved by all for his habitual mildness. Thus he was exercised for twenty years in various offices, as the monastic order requires; and in the succeeding period, after Mainer and Serlo, he was advanced by the common election of the brethren to hold [Col. 0460D] the rule of the abbey of Ouche. He held it for thirty-three years through adversity and prosperity; broken by old age, he entrusted it to one of his disciples named Warin, and, so far as lay in his power, made him his deputy and successor three years before his death. But if life accompanies us and opportunity is supplied with God’s help, a clear narrative in our subsequent writing will unfold their deeds to posterity.

### V. Continuation of the account of gifts made to the monastery of Ouche. The new cell of Alençon is given to the monks of Ouche. Various narratives.

Now I return to discuss the things given to Saint Ebrulf.

When Ralph the young knight, son of Albert of Cravent, first began to bear military arms, he attacked the monk Guitmund, who was travelling with his servant Manlia in the valley of Guy; having thrown down the monk, he carried off the horses. The monk then went on foot to Pacy and, grieving, asked Albert to assist him against his son. The aforesaid knight answered him insolently and immediately refused every assistance for the restoration of the horses. Seeing this, his wife Alberada began to weep, wring her hands, tear her hair, and lament her son as though already dead. In a loud voice, like one mad, crying out and wailing amid many tears, she said:

> “[Col. 0461B] My son Ralph, what have you undertaken to practise—not knighthood, but madness? Alas, you are wickedly governed by detestable instructors, whose deadly sophistries now foolishly deceive you and miserably drag you into the abyss of destruction. Oh, what sad news you have sent me, what bitter grief you have caused me! Deceived youth, what am I to say to you? By wickedly wronging an unarmed servant of Christ, you have earned a deadly overthrow for yourself. My son Ralph, what have you done in raging thus, you who have exercised the beginnings of your knighthood against the Almighty? I know with complete certainty that I shall have brief joy and long sorrow because of your crime. Do not all teachers alike agree and everywhere proclaim with one voice that the Most High dwells in his saints and lovingly endures prosperity and adversity with them? Help, father, your frenzied son; strive with every effort that the stolen steeds be sorrowfully restored to the monk, lest your only [Col. 0461C] son be immediately delivered to the devil for so great a crime.”

As this prudent matron pleaded for her son’s salvation and strove faithfully to console the desolate monk, Albert and all his household, moved with fear, trembled. He gave his mule to the monk, sent his squires with him to Breherval, and, binding his son under a terrible adjuration, ordered him without delay to restore everything that had been taken. Guitmund, therefore, having recovered the horses, returned to Pacy, thanked Albert and his wife, from whom each sought and obtained pardon for the offence committed. The aforesaid woman was the daughter of Hugh, bishop of Bayeux, and among her kin flourished, according to her station, in much honourable conduct.

[Col. 0461D] In the same year the aforesaid young knight fell ill and, repenting of his deed, sought pardon from the men of Ouche and devoted himself and all his possessions to Saint Ebrulf. After he died, his grieving father had his body brought to Ouche and granted Saint Ebrulf one half of the tithe of Ulmey, wholly free, just as he himself had held it. The monks of Coulombs held the other half of the tithe under this arrangement: they were to pay on his behalf all episcopal customary dues and all fiscal obligations. This grant was made to the men of Ouche in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1070, in the time of Philip, king of the French, and Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, namely nephew of Renaud, bishop of Paris. Ralph, surnamed Bad Neighbour, who was the chief lord, willingly assented at Medan [Col. 0462A] to Abbot Mainer’s request concerning the tithe of Ulmey, which, as stated, had passed into the right of the Church.

Not long afterwards the aforesaid Albert died, and his body was brought to Ouche. His heirs—namely his son-in-law Guy, son of Ebrard of Rui, Ralph of Cunella, and the others who have succeeded down to the present day—confirmed the tithe that he had given Saint Ebrulf. With God’s help the monks of Ouche possessed it peacefully for almost sixty years under three bishops, Geoffrey, Ivo, and Geoffrey.

Now it is fitting to make known in writing to posterity how and at what time the cell of Alençon was built in the county of Talou and subjected to the men of Ouche in the time of King William and Archbishop John, and to append to this work the charter of donation and confirmation ratified in King Henry’s time.

Since mortal life slips away daily and mortal man irretrievably loses the worldly honours which he gains with the greatest labour, everyone ought, while living and able, faithfully to obey God’s commands, so that, despising transitory things, he may by God’s grace obtain eternal ones. Carefully considering this, a certain noble knight of Normandy, named Gulbert, son of Richard of Hugleville, at the prompting of his wife Beatrice, decided to establish monks on his patrimony at Alençon, so that he might be aided by their prayers and merits at the last judgment. Since his nephew Drogo had recently [Col. 0462C] abandoned secular knighthood and assumed monastic life at Ouche, he greatly loved Abbot Mainer and the monks of Ebrulf, and gave them the church of Saint Mary of Alençon with all its prebends, on the condition that six monks should be appointed in place of the six canons then serving there, and that, whenever the canons left the world in any manner, or by the pious endeavour of a more reformed life, the monks should receive their prebends. The aforesaid lord also gave those monks the whole village of Parc, with its church and the whole tithe of that village, as free and exempt from every burdensome customary obligation as he himself had hitherto held it. He wholly released the men of Parc so that they should render him no compulsory service and should not go except upon the general expedition of the duke of Normandy. From the mill at Alençon he gave them each year, as a tithe, two modii of wheat, and from another mill on the Seine half a modius of every grain. He also granted that the monks might take each day from the wood of his forest, called Harulsart, two ass-loads of fuel for their fire. The aforesaid knight held annually from the prince of the Normans two cartloads of wine as a fief; from these he permanently granted the monks one modius for celebrating Masses. He gave, indeed, two churches with their whole tithes and the lands belonging to them: one, that of Parc, built in honour of Saint Mary, Mother of God; the other, that of Belnay, founded in honour of Saint Peter, prince of the Apostles. [Col. 0463A] Since these were prebends of the church of Alençon, two canons then possessed them. Ralph served the church of Parc; after some time, while returning from England, he was overtaken by a sea-storm and, when his ship was wrecked, was swallowed by the waves with all his companions. Walter held the church of Belnay and later became a monk of Saint Ebrulf.

Gulbert, with his wife Beatrice, willingly bestowed all these things upon the Church of God for eternal salvation, and repeatedly entreated his men and friends kindly to increase his alms. Geoffrey, therefore, his knight, gave Saint Mary the church of Saint Denis with its whole tithe; and by persuasion and gifts he recovered for the Church of God the shares of the tithe which three knights held from him: Osbern Capes [Col. 0463B] and the two sons of Aszo, Bernard and Ralph. He also granted land, villeins, and every customary due from those villeins in Vico Silvatico. Robert, knight of Hugleville, granted the monks the church of Saint Alban with its whole tithe, and received sixteen Rouen pounds from their charity for it. Bernard, son of Geoffrey of Neufmarché, gave Saint Mary the church of Speinis, with all land belonging to it and its entire tithe, held by the priest Ebrard; and, in exchange for the churches of Burchella and Bruneshopa, granted twenty shillings from the rent of Neubury at the feast of Saint Michael. Baldric, son of Nicholas, gave one burgess at Dieppe; and Ralph, son of Ansered, gave one lodger at Hotot.

Therefore, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1079, in the second indiction, namely the fourteenth year of William the Great, king of the English and duke of the Normans, the aforesaid Gulbert and his wife Beatrice laid the donation of the above-written things upon the altar of Saint Mary. The witnesses present were: Gilbert and Ralph, Walter and John, the four canons of the same church; Bernard of Neufmarché and Geoffrey of Saint-Denis; Osbern Capes and Osbern Buflo; Eustace of Carquita and Eustace of Torcy; Robert of Hugleville and Roger of Parc; and many others.

Finally, when Gulbert died on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September [Col. 0463D] and was honourably buried by the monks whom he had established on his estate, his son Walter obtained his paternal honour and confirmed everything which his father and his father’s men had given to Saint Mary. Again, in the time of Robert, duke of the Normans, after he had married Avicia, daughter of Hebran of Salcheville, at her prompting he confirmed by his own grant the alms of his father and mother. He also added the tithe of the toll of Alençon, granted six burgesses and all their customary dues, and so fully released them that he should exact nothing from them except the general service owed to the count of Normandy. He also granted the whole of his water for fishing, as the monks might choose.

Besides this, his wife Avicia, fervent in the love of God, [Col. 0464A] granted the monks each year sixty shillings from her rent, payable on the Kalends of October, so that they might buy wax, oil for the church lights, and incense throughout the year; and with her husband she laid the donation upon the altar of Saint Mary. Witnesses to these donations are Adam and William, sons of Tedfred; Osbern Buflo and Eustace of Torcy; Robert of Cropus and Robert son of Godmund; John Catus; and many others. After several years, Walter and his wife Avicia, advancing in the love of God, requested twelve monks from Roger, abbot of Saint Ebrulf; and for their necessary sustenance they gave them the mill of Parc, which yielded eleven modii, five acres of land at Hugleville, three lodgers having fifteen shillings a year, and, at the village called Hundred Acres, [Col. 0464B] the church of the Holy Trinity with its entire tithe.

All these things which I have related as given to the men of Ouche by Gulbert and his men were confirmed by the grants of William, king of the English, and John and William, archbishops of Rouen. Then whatever Walter, Gulbert’s son, added to his father’s alms was granted to the monks of Saint Ebrulf by Robert II, duke of Normandy. He also allowed them to establish at Parc a fair on the Nativity of Saint Mary, and through the lord Walter, surnamed Giffard, wholly forbade anyone to claim any customary due or privilege therein without the monks’ consent. His brothers William Rufus and Henry, kings of the English, and Archbishop Geoffrey likewise confirmed all the matters written above to the monks of Ouche, who had then possessed them peacefully for many years. The canons yielded to the monks because they saw that the virtues of those whom they could not equal excelled in every respect. For Guinimar and Benedict, together with John, the latter’s son, remained with the monks for many years and finally died when illnesses grew severe. Gilbert, however, who stood out as wiser than all his companions, and Walter freely undertook monastic life; having promised amendment of life, they departed when already broken by old age.

Now I should like to record briefly something concerning the noble lineage and character of the men of Alfage. Gulbert, surnamed the Advocate of Saint-Valery, [Col. 0464D] married the daughter of Duke Richard; by her he fathered Bernard, the father of Walter of Saint-Valery, and Richard of Hugleville. Richard long served his maternal uncle, the Duke of Normandy, and by his gift received the noblewoman Ada, widow of the elder Herluin of Hugleville, together with all her inheritance. The duke gave him much, promised him much more, and would generously have fulfilled his promises if Richard had pleased him by humbly serving him. On the Sée, in the village once called Isnelliville, he established a borough, naming it Alfage after the lofty mountain thickly covered with beech trees that rose before it. He also imposed the laws of Cormeilles upon its settlers. He flourished in martial prowess and great generosity; hence he was formidable to his enemies and faithful to his friends.

[Col. 0465A] In the time of the young William, son of Duke Robert, when William of Arques rebelled against the duke and the like defection of nearly all the men of Talou abandoned the illegitimate prince, Richard alone stood firm against the rebels in his castle beside the church of Saint-Albin, and, out of loyalty to the duke, took care to defend the surrounding district against the incursions of the men of Arques. His helpers in that conflict were his son-in-law Geoffrey and Hugh of Montmorency, sons of Turchetil of Neufmarché. The men of Arques suddenly surrounded Hugh and all his followers near Montmorency and killed him as he defended himself manfully.

Geoffrey, moreover, by Ada, Richard’s daughter, begot Bernard and Drogo, whose fortunes differed. Drogo [Col. 0465B] abandoned soldiering, lived devoutly at Ouche, learned letters in the monastic life, and rose through the sacred grades of orders to the priesthood. Bernard, however, adhered to military service until old age and fought valiantly under three kings of England. Finally, in the time of William Rufus, he fought against Resen, king of the Welsh; after killing him, he founded the castle of Brecon and possessed for many years the kingdom of the Britons, whose capital is called Talgarth. He also built a church in his town in honour of Saint John the Evangelist, established monks there, and gave them tithes of all his possessions.

Gulbert, Richard’s son, married Beatrice, [Col. 0465C] daughter of Christian of Valenciennes, an illustrious tribune. She bore her husband Walter, Hugh, and Beatrice. This aforesaid hero, a kinsman of the duke, was always faithful to him, and, accompanied by his chief retainers, endured the principal dangers with him in the war in England. But after the kingdom had been pacified and William was reigning, although the king offered Gulbert many estates in England, he returned to Neustria; possessing straightforward integrity, he refused to hold anything acquired by plunder. Content with his own goods, he rejected those of others and devoutly offered his son Hugh to ecclesiastical discipline in the monastery of Ouche, under the instruction of Abbot Mainer. He lived long with his devout wife, who was a cousin of Queen Matilda, and until the end commendably devoted himself to almsgiving, prayer, and other [Col. 0465D] good works. The venerable Beatrice survived her husband by three years and died in holy confession on the second day before the Nones of January [4 January].

Walter, however, was a handsome boy but not very wise, and for this reason readily submitted himself to Godmund and other deceitful guardians. He admitted a company of rogues into close familiarity; by their wicked persuasion he foolishly squandered his paternal honour and repeatedly disturbed monks, clerics, and lawful tenants with injuries. At last, having become a knight, he married the beautiful and eloquent Avicia, daughter of Herbrand. By her counsel and shrewd exertion he began to be drawn back somewhat from his former [Col. 0466A] depravity. For she was prudent and eloquent, devoted to God from childhood, and, so far as she was able, devoted to many good works. She had three brothers, distinguished knights: Jordan, William, and Robert. With their help their brother-in-law prevailed against the deceitful advisers and recovered many things which he had fruitlessly alienated and lost through fraudulent stratagems.

The aforesaid woman bore her husband twelve sons and daughters, most of whom untimely death soon swallowed up in infancy. Then she herself, after completing fifteen years with her husband, died on the eighth day before the Kalends of February [25 January]. [Note: Read “March,” that is, 22 February, as may be seen in the epitaph itself.] She was buried in the cloister of the monks, whom she had loved greatly, beside the doorway of the basilica. Prior Guarin caused a stone arch to be constructed over her, [Col. 0466B] and Vitalis, the Englishman, composed the following epitaph:

> Here lies the body of noble Avicia;  
> May Christ grant her secure life in heaven without end!  
>   
> While she lived, upright and richly endowed with praise,  
> She eagerly pursued—and by unceasing effort sought to gain—justice.  
> She was exceedingly beautiful, sufficiently eloquent, and wise.  
> She diligently strove always to attend the worship of God.  
> Each day she endeavoured to hear Mass and the Hours.  
> Thus, of her own free will, the honourable maiden began to live.  
>   
> At last she was married to the noble husband Walter,  
> With whom she lived happily for fifteen years,  
> And bore the desired offspring, twelve in number.  
> This lady shone especially in outstanding virtues;  
> Striving greatly to exalt the worship of the Church,  
> She bestowed her own ornaments for the altar’s use.  
> Priests, monks, widows, the sick, and the poor  
> She always honoured and sustained with abundant assistance.  
>   
> She was so chaste that no rogue ever dared  
> [Col. 0466C] openly to defame her by notorious accusations.  
> In February, on the day when Peter ascended  
> The pontifical chair, she suffered mournful and dark death.  
> The people of Alfage mourn the fall of so great a lady;  
> But may God grant Avicia’s soul the joys of life! Amen.

Walter lived for almost three years after his wife’s burial. Tormented by a long illness, he put on the monk’s cowl; and shortly afterward, having made confession and received penance, died on the sixth day before the Kalends of June [27 May]. Prior Hildegarius buried his body at the feet of his aforesaid wife, and Vitalis composed the following lament over him:

> Here rests Walter, lord of Alfage;  
> May his place be forever in true repose!  
> May had already counted twenty-seven suns  
> When this man, in a monk’s tunic, departed from the prison of the body.  
> [Col. 0466D] Long illness had tortured him; having confessed  
> His own sins, may he be absolved through you, O Christ! Amen.

After Walter’s death, four bereaved orphans remained: Richard, Jordan, Walter, and Elias. King Henry took them into his guardianship and ordered Robert the viscount to administer the lordship of Alfage for two years. Jordan of Salcavilla, however, having secured the king’s favour by services and gifts, obtained the whole lordship. He recovered his nephews, to be brought up together with their patrimony, and maintained and augmented it honourably for four years. Meanwhile Richard, a boy of twelve, died and rests buried in the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God. [Col. 0467A] His brother Jordan succeeded him: a handsome young man endowed with good character. He served among his contemporaries in King Henry’s court, and the aforesaid king gave him as wife the prudent and beautiful Juliana, daughter of Godescalch, who had come to England with Queen Adeliza from the region of Louvain.

## VI. Meditations: The Life of the Blessed Father Ebrulf

Thus far I have spoken at length of the affairs of Saint Ebrulf, which for the most part fill our little book. Therefore, I ask my readers not to take offence if, mindful of benefits received, I recall our benefactors. I indeed desire to commend the founders and their kindly collaborators to the enduring memory of posterity in writing, so that the children of the Church may remember before God in the sight of angels those by whose benefits they are sustained in this mortal life, in order to carry out the service of the Creator of all things.

Accordingly, after the victorious Abraham returned from the slaughter of the four kings and brought back his nephew Lot, together with his fellow captives of both sexes and their property, he directed his companions to take their shares from the spoils of the Sodomites. By Abraham—whose name is interpreted “Father Most High”—are signified perfect men, who daily fight against evil spirits and the vices of the flesh, overcome the world and the prince of the world, trample underfoot earthly pride and fleshly enticements, and account them as dung. By Lot, led captive by barbarians but nobly delivered through the living strength of his spiritual uncle, [Col. 0467C] whose name is interpreted “bound” or “declension,” is signified the carnal mind or brutish people: ensnared in Sodom—that is, in pleasurable vices—bound in the chain of sin, turning away from God, and taken captive by evil spirits. By Abraham’s companions, who are recorded to have fought, are rightly understood the faithful laity, who, at his command, are said to have taken for themselves a share of the spoils. For thus it is written in the book of Genesis:

> The king of Sodom said to Abraham: “Give me the persons, but take the rest for yourself.” He answered him: “I will take nothing of all that is yours, except what the young men have eaten and the shares of the men who came with me—Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre. Let them take their shares!”  
> —Genesis 14:21–24

Many laypeople are adorned with gentle and modest habits; they join themselves to Christ’s perfect warriors by faith and good will, and kindly rejoice with them as they fight manfully against demons. Yet they do not leave behind the fragile world; they are unwilling wholly to forsake worldly things, but remain in lawful marriage, offend God in many respects by transgressing the law, and nevertheless redeem their sins by alms, according to Daniel’s counsel. These, indeed, receive their shares from the enemies’ spoils when they build monasteries for God’s servants from earthly possessions, devoutly establish hostels for the poor and sick from unrighteous mammon, and provide food and clothing from their own substance to those who pray to heaven.

The king of Sodom, flattering the triumphant Abraham, represents the devil, who daily tempts the saints by a thousand devices for harm; night and day he attacks them with blandishments and terrors, and craftily supplies every worldly pleasure, riches, and honours in order to draw their souls alone down with himself into the abyss of destruction. Abraham, however, despised the flattering king’s fawning, considered neither praises nor any gifts from him worthy of acceptance, and allowed only his fellow soldiers to take their shares and what was necessary for food. Thus holy men, while they complete the time of their warfare in this life, despise all worldly things because of their desire for heaven and seek no reward as recompense for their holiness. But they admonish worldly rulers who accompany them in Catholic faith and desire for eternal goods to give churches their shares from their patrimonies [Col. 0468B] and revenues, and to support the needy and those who despise the world by their benefactions, so that they may claim for themselves everlasting glory from Christ, who declares that he is present in the poor.

Many authorities and examples can demonstrate that people retain for the profit of eternal salvation only as much as they distribute mercifully in almsgiving, according to the Saviour’s command. For what they lavishly squander for the pleasure of the flesh, or uselessly pour out for the empty splendour of worldly prosperity, unquestionably passes away irreparably like flowing water. Others, however, who increase and store up immense treasures for their heirs, alas, often accumulate for themselves an increase of wickedness and misery, and diligently train their children to injure many people. For they themselves are zealously devoted to thefts, robberies, and many kinds of evil, and, deservedly punished by retributions worthy of their wickedness, perish. Thus it happens that they are judged worthy neither of heaven nor of earth; ungrateful successors obtain ample honours; and many curse the predecessors who provided excessive riches for corrupt heirs.

Prudent sophists make friends for themselves from the mammon of iniquity: while these receive their benefactors’ material goods for the support of this present life, they repay them eternally with spiritual goods through merits and prayers. Ebrulf of Bayeux eagerly sought for himself such debtors. I have already related very much concerning his affairs in the present work. Henceforth I shall begin with the father himself, briefly pursuing his deeds as they have been handed down by the writings or reports of the ancients; and I shall endeavour here to insert his life for the refreshment of readers.

The venerable Father Ebrulf, therefore, born of a most noble lineage, was a native of the city of Bayeux. His parents, raising him with excessive care, entrusted him to instruction in the Catholic faith. With remarkable speed he diligently pursued divine and human studies and, while still a boy, is said to have surpassed his teachers in learning. For heavenly grace, foreseeing that he would become a teacher of religion, made him most effectively teachable in all things. Nor, through arrogance—as is the custom of this age—did he corrupt the dignity of such ability by acting proudly. [Col. 0469A] Distinguished in appearance and sweet in speech, he was troublesome to no one through any frivolity.

As has been said, illustrious through the radiance of nobility and already known to the foreknowledge of the immortal God, he soon came to the attention of King Clothar, son of Clovis, the first of the Frankish kings to become Christian, who was baptized by Saint Remigius, archbishop of Reims, together with three thousand nobles. When Clothar learned who Ebrulf was and of what nobility, he immediately ordered him to be brought before him, judging that one elevated by brilliance of mind was worthy to serve in royal offices. Through the service of humility, however, the heavenly Emperor granted him such favour with the earthly ruler that, being preferred above the rest, he held a very high place in the palace. Endowed with an advocate’s eloquence, he sat among the most learned courtiers to plead causes. Yet he attended to secular affairs in such a manner that he never withdrew his mind from the contemplation of inward love.

But since there was a fitting hope of continuing his line in his father’s house, urged by the frequent and honourable persuasion of friends, he arranged to marry a wife worthy of his birth. Receiving her for the sake of offspring, not for the pleasure of the flesh, he devoutly fulfilled the divine commandments and frequently pondered them with careful meditation. Thus the man full of God enjoyed temporal things, cautiously taking thought lest he displease the Creator through the things he had received. As he became exceedingly wealthy, he rejoiced more in good works than in material wealth. He laboured with the utmost zeal to translate into his own life the deeds of the ancient Fathers, [Col. 0469C] which he had read in many books. Devoting himself to almsgiving, prayer, and vigils, he summoned the wife whom he had married to the same work of holiness, so that through a faithful husband the devotion of the woman, though herself faithful, might increase. Thus, while still living in lay dress, he ordered his life so that he seemed in no respect different from those whom monastic rule restrained.

While that most blessed man was thus living praiseworthily under a rule of his own and ardently serving the Lord’s commands, it happened that he heard the Lord commanding his followers in the Gospel: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9:23). The man of God had also laid up in his lofty memory, as the crowning point of perfection, what Truth itself promises to those who despise the world: “Amen, I say to you: you who have left all things for my sake shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matthew 19:29). [Col. 0469D] Inflamed, therefore, by these truthful promises, he sold his possessions and distributed to the poor everything he could have, doing without reservation what he had previously done with discretion. Consecrating with the sacred veil the wife whom he had taken in order to preserve his father’s name, he gave her to the heavenly Bridegroom. He himself, as though having escaped shipwreck, hastened to a monastery; becoming a monk, he remained there for some time in all humility, serving God. In him the desire for holy conduct grew more and more.

The narrator of the Life does not identify by its proper name the monastery to which the aforesaid man fled. I therefore judge it worthy briefly to explain for future readers what I have learned about it from the report of elders. The venerable Martin, abbot of Vertav, had built an abbey in a place which the common people from ancient times call “The Two Twins,” because antiquity recalls that twins were restored to life there. For premature death had carried off, without baptism, the twin children of a powerful lord; great grief therefore overcame both parents. But Martin, returning from England, found his friends mourning, sought consolation from heaven, restored the twins to life by his merits and prayers, and dedicated them as monks to God upon their own patrimony. The name derived from that ancient event persists for the village to this day; and the great mass of stones in the foundations of buildings and the ruins of walls bears evident witness that the district of Bayeux was made illustrious by a dwelling of people of high rank. [Col. 0470B]

Ebrulf, while still a layman powerful in wealth and honours, was, as they say, a suitable collaborator in the building of the aforesaid monastery. He helped those who were beginning with counsel, strengthened those who hesitated, and enlarged the newly begun undertaking through wealth, estates, and many means. At last, stripped of everything, he renounced himself there; a true poor man of God, he assumed the monastic habit there, fought for God with the arms of obedience, and shone as an example to those who saw him.

But when the glorious confessor Ebrulf began, because of the grace of his holiness, to be honoured by the brethren, he feared falling into the danger of pride. Taking with him three monks whom he had joined to himself in familiar conversation and had found readier for the struggle toward that perfection, he earnestly hastened with all speed to seek the wilderness, desiring to devote himself solely to the contemplation of God. Passing through the district of Hiémois, they came to a place called Montfort. Since it was a pleasant place, abounding in woods and springs, they stayed there and lived holy lives in solitude for some time. But because two castles, Exmes and Gacé, were nearby, to which many people came to pursue legal cases outside court, God’s servants often endured disturbances from the crowds of arrivals. These towns, indeed, are said to have existed in Caesar’s time and to have resisted him stoutly; there too the seats of princes remained for many centuries. Hence crowds of great and middling men, to whom the noble hero had formerly been known amid worldly eminence, visited him as he now zealously devoted himself to special contemplation; and, engaging in lengthy conversation about useful matters, they disturbed him while he meditated upon heavenly things. They therefore abandoned that place of the venerable man, where later generations built a basilica in honour of Saint Ebrulf which still remains.

Then these lovers of the wilderness entered the forest which the inhabitants call Ouche. This forest, dreadful in its density of trees, frequently traversed by bands of robbers, provided a dwelling-place for savage beasts. As they fearlessly travelled through the vast places of the wilderness and found nowhere to establish a lodging suited to their devotion, blessed Ebrulf, burning with the spirit of a pure conscience, prayed to the Lord, saying:

> “Lord Jesus Christ, who showed yourself as the most faithful guide to your people Israel as they travelled through the wilderness, in a pillar of cloud and fire, graciously deign to show us, who wish to escape the condemnation of Egyptian bondage, a place of freedom suited to our frailty.”

As soon as the prayer was completed, an angel of the Lord appeared to the faithful man, coming to show what he had sought. Following this guide, they came to springs most suitable for drinking, which, diverted a little, gathered into a large pool. There they bent their knees and gave immeasurable praise to God, who showed them the way and never despises his servants who hope in him. [Col. 0471B] Having celebrated their thanksgiving and invoked the Lord’s name, they built a hut of brushwood and leaves large enough for the number of inhabitants. Surrounding it with a small cloister of the same material, they remained there, having obtained the refuge of their desired repose. Their service proved to be as free as it was pleasing to God. Trampling every worldly tumult beneath their feet, they clung only to heavenly things; and, having despised all else, they possessed nothing except God.
