Thus they deserved rightly to sing with the Psalmist: “I have said, O Lord, that my portion is to keep your law” (Psalm 118:57). For, obeying the law of the highest God, they endeavoured to acquire him alone as their portion.

While, therefore, with all vigilance they sought the advancement of the inward person, and neither the harshness of the place nor the savagery of beasts frightened them from their purpose, it happened that one of the robbers who lived in the forest turned aside to them. Amazed by their constancy and perseverance in Christ’s service, he said:

> “O monks, what disturbance has compelled you to come into these parts? Or how have you dared to lodge in such great solitude? You have not found a good place. Do you not know that this is a place for robbers, not hermits? The inhabitants of this wood live by plunder, and, living by their own labour, are unwilling to endure partners. You cannot remain safe here for long. Moreover, you have found fields uncultivated and unfruitful, unfriendly to your labour.”

To this the venerable Father Ebrulf, being an eloquent man, responded by addressing each point of his statements:

> “Truly, brother, it was not the violence of disturbance but the foreknowledge of almighty God that drove us here. Nor have we come to these places through any usurpation, but rather in order to weep more freely for our sins. Since the Lord is with us, placed under his protection we do not fear human threats, for he himself said: ‘Do not fear those who kill the body but have nothing they can do to the soul’ (Matthew 10:18). As for what you proposed last concerning labour, know that the Lord is able to prepare for his servants in the wilderness a table of refreshment. You too can share in his abundance if you abandon the wickedness you practise and most devoutly promise, my son, to serve God, who is living and true. For our [Col. 0472A] God, as the prophet says, on whatever day a sinner is converted, consigns to forgetfulness all the evils he has done (Ezekiel 18:21). Therefore, brother, do not despair of God’s goodness because of the enormity of your crimes. Rather, following the Psalmist’s admonition, ‘Turn away from evil and do good’ (Psalm 33:15), know for certain that the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous and his ears are open to their prayers. But we do not wish you to be ignorant of what the same prophet immediately proclaims in a dreadful statement: ‘The face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth’ (ibid., 17). If the regard of divine mercy is present to the righteous so as to hear their prayers, it is plainly beyond doubt that it turns away from the unjust in order at some time powerfully to punish their shamelessness.”

Then that man, pierced by heavenly grace in these words, returned to his own home. At daybreak, renouncing everything that he possessed, he carried with him only three ash-cakes of bread and a honeycomb and quickly returned by the same path to God’s servants. Falling before Saint Ebrulf’s feet, he offered gifts of blessing; immediately, inspired by the Holy Spirit and promising a reformed life, he became there the first to make monastic profession. Many robbers of the same forest followed his example: through the blessed man’s admonition, they either became monks or, abandoning robbery, became cultivators of the soil. From neighbouring places, too, once the fame of the blessed man’s name and merit had spread abroad, some came to him, desiring to behold his angelic face and hear his most delightful speech. When they supplied him with what was necessary for the body, refreshed by spiritual things, they returned joyfully to their homes. Some among them, having merited to enjoy his conversation, begged to be enrolled in so spiritual a fellowship; and because of the multitude now arriving, the aforesaid forest lost the name of solitude.

## VII. Continuation of the Life of Blessed Ebrulf

As the number of brethren grew, the grace of virtues also increased in blessed Ebrulf. He was exceptional in patience, praiseworthy in abstinence, frequent in prayer, and cheerful in exhortation. Prosperity could not puff him up, nor adversity break him. Whatever was offered to him by the faithful people he ordered distributed to the poor [Col. 0472D] who came to him, saying that monks ought not to be anxious about anything for the morrow.

One day, then, when the supply of bread was exhausted, a poor man came to the gate and began to ask for alms. When he loudly protested that the steward denied having anything he could give away, the venerable Father said: “Brother, why do you disregard the poor man’s cry? Please give alms to the needy man.” But the steward said: “Father, I have nothing except half a loaf, which I am keeping for our little ones. For I have distributed the rest according to your command.” Ebrulf answered: “You must not hesitate, my son. Have you not read the Prophet saying, ‘Blessed is he who understands the needy and poor; the Lord will deliver him in the evil day’ [Psalm 40:1]? Surely the faithful Creator will never cease to feed those for whom, nailed to the cross, he deigned to shed his precious blood.”

On hearing this from the venerable Father, the steward gave the half-loaf he had kept for the little ones to one of the servants, saying: “Run quickly and give it to the poor man, but do not call him back.” Obeying the command, the servant ran until he found the needy man nearly one stade from the monastery. When he said to him, “Receive, sir, the alms which the abbot sends you,” the man drove the staff he carried in his hand into the ground and, giving thanks to God, received the gift with both hands. When he drew the staff from the ground, while the bearer of the alms had not yet departed, a great spring suddenly burst forth, following the point of the staff, [Col. 0473B] and it still bubbles and flows there to this day. In that place many healings of the sick were performed, and fever sufferers were summoned there from distant regions out of desire for cure. In visions, too, many were commanded, in order to obtain health, to seek the forest of Ouche and drink from the spring of Saint Ebrulf which flows there. Thus many left Burgundy, Aquitaine, and other regions of Gaul, sought Ouche with utmost difficulty, and, only after searching, scarcely found it, since the place was then obscure, as though deserted. At last, when they had found the spring, drawn water, and drunk faithfully from it while invoking the holy name—or washed their heads or other limbs—they rejoiced in recovered health and, giving thanks to God, returned gladly to their homes.

These things were frequently done there over many centuries, down to the time of Henry, king of the Franks, while the district of Ouche, after the devastation of the Danes, was inhabited only by scattered cultivators. Then a certain local man named Berengar received that field by paternal succession and enclosed the spring with a hedge, lest sick people who came there should damage his crops. For the peasant was often angrily distressed because strangers who flocked there for healing trampled the meadows, gardens, and other things situated around it. From that time the miracles of healing ceased to occur there, for as long as the aforesaid Berengar and his heirs Letherius, William, and Gervase possessed that estate.

After Saint Ebrulf had given away the bread to the poor man, behold, before sunset a packhorse-driver was seen standing outside the door of the cell, sufficiently laden with bread and wine. The man who had brought him, calling himself a moneylender, summoned the steward. Handing over what he had brought, he said: “Go, brother, and give this to your abbot.” Having said this, as though hurrying on his journey, he mounted his horse and departed quickly. When the father asked who the giver was, he was told how swiftly he had departed. He understood, therefore, that these things had been brought to him by God; rejoicing in spirit, he gave thanks to God’s boundless mercy, who multiplies his compassion for his servants and returns much for little. From that [Col. 0474A] day onward, they never lacked what human frailty requires.

But as, through the gracious Lord’s help, they gradually began to increase in temporal goods, two fierce robbers from another province, hearing that their possessions were increasing, made their way to the blessed man’s cell. Having seized a herd of pigs, as they hastened to leave the forest, they turned back and began to wander around that same wilderness. Unable to find a free way out, amazed at why this had happened, and already weary from wandering, they heard the signal by which the brethren were summoned to gather for prayer. Struck by great terror at its sound, they abandoned the pigs and hastened to the man of God. Having confessed the crime they had committed, [Col. 0474B] they became his monks.

To commend the master’s illustrious glory, however, we have judged it should not be passed over that the outstanding grace of the sevenfold Spirit was displayed through one of the disciples of this most honourable man. A raven that had made its nest near the monastery used stealthily to steal eggs; entering the refectory through an open window, it caused general disorder and carried off to its nest whatever it could take. Then one of the brethren whose duty this was said in simple prayer: “Lord, avenge us upon the enemy who takes away what your mercy gives us.” Without delay, they found the bird dead under the tree in which it had made its nest. Thus whatever wished to harm them either quickly perished [Col. 0474C] or, repenting, assumed the habit of a better way of life.

Accordingly, when God, the inspector of all, graciously looked upon the glorious contest of his beloved Ebrulf, he strengthened his heart with the firmness of faith so that, persevering in his work, he might become an example of regular discipline to others. Although he burned intensely with desire to go to more remote places in the wilderness and avoid human company, he decided on wiser counsel to benefit the community presently before him, whose leader and master he had become in their chosen way of life. Fearing, that is, lest, if the founder withdrew himself, the work of the building might become somewhat unstable because of its newness, he took care that, while providing a place of rest for himself, he should not bring harm to others. The leader of the striving host therefore remained, fighting in the battle line as a soldier and, outside it, advancing as a strong commander and raising himself through increases of virtue. [Col. 0474D] The widespread fame of his holiness, travelling through many provinces, attracted happy, vigorous, God-fearing persons to the contest of the same profession. They gave the blessed man houses, estates, possessions, and households, asking him to order monasteries built for them and to impose whatever rule of life the prudent shepherd wished. The holy man consented to their petitions, regularly founded fifteen monasteries of men and women, and placed persons of most proven life over each of them. He himself presided over the monastery he had first built and remained there continually in God’s service, exhorting the brethren “to advance to higher things and fear the devil’s many forms of ambush.” The fame of so great a father’s holiness reached the ears of the rulers who held the reins of the Frankish kingdom in those days, a people who had only recently been brought under the gentle yoke of Christianity.

For Clothar the Elder reigned fifty-one years and, dying, left the kingdom divided into four parts among his four sons. Charibert accordingly established his royal seat at Paris, Chilperic at Soissons, Guntram at Orléans, and Sigibert at Metz. Sigibert, the youngest of them all, was the first to marry, namely Brunhild, daughter of the king of Galicia. She bore him King Childebert, Ingund—wife of Hermenegild, king and martyr of the Visigoths—and Bertha, [Col. 0475B] wife of Æthelberht, king of the people of Canterbury, as well as Bova, a virgin consecrated to God. Then, eight years later, he was killed through the treachery of his brother Chilperic, and Childebert, still a boy, obtained the kingdom with his mother Brunhild. He held it vigorously for almost twenty-five years, as is read in his deeds. After enduring many labours, he perished by poison and left his father’s two portions of the kingdom to his sons Theudebert and Theuderic. With them Clothar the Great, son of Chilperic, carried on hostilities for nearly twenty years. At last he killed King Theudebert in war and cruelly caused the aged Brunhild to be tied to the tails of unbroken horses; thus he tore to pieces the powerful queen to whom Pope Gregory had once, as is stated in the *Papal Deeds* [Col. 0475C] and the *Register*, given earnest support. Thus, with all rivals removed, he alone obtained the monarchy of Francia; and at his death he left it to his son Dagobert, whose deeds are very well known among the Franks.

In that period, while these men held primacy among the Gauls, the Roman Empire was held by Justinian and Justin the Younger, and also by Tiberius and Maurice, Phocas and Heraclius. The Apostolic See was then governed by Hormisdas and John, Felix and Boniface, John and Agapetus, Silverius, Vigilius and Pelagius, John and Benedict, Pelagius and Gregory, the great teacher, Sabinian and Boniface, Deusdedit and Boniface, renowned for the feast of All Saints. In those days the metropolitan see of Rouen was held by Flavius and Praetextatus, Melantius, Hildulf, and Romanus, the distinguished offspring of Benedict.

VIII. Continuation.

I have investigated these matters in chronicles and have briefly noted them, wishing to satisfy my reader, so that it may be sufficiently clear in what times the eighty-year life of the holy Father Ebrulf flourished in the world. Now I shall strive to return to recounting certain matters which I learned not from writing but from the accounts of elders. For in the excessive storms that raged terribly in the time of the Danes, the writings of the ancients perished in fire together with basilicas and dwellings; and the ardent studies of younger men, though they thirst insatiably, cannot recover them. Moreover, some things that had been skillfully rescued from barbarian hands through the diligence of former generations perished through the damnable negligence of their successors—shame upon them!—who neglected to preserve the penetrating depth of spiritual matters contained in the books of the Fathers. When the manuscripts were lost, the deeds of the ancients were given over to oblivion; modern people can recover them by no art, because the memorials of the old pass from the memory of the present along with the passing world, as hail or snow flows away in waters with a rapidly and irretrievably running stream.

The names of the places in which Father Ebrulf built fifteen monasteries, and the names of the fathers whom he appointed as Christ’s vicars over monastic companies, have been effaced by the various changes of events across four hundred years—events occurring under many rulers, from Lothair the Great and Childebert down to Philip and his son Louis, who reigned in Gaul. Yet venerable old men related with eloquent speech to their sons certain things that they had seen or heard; these sons likewise retained them with the tenacious glue of memory and passed them on to the succeeding age. Thus, sowing things worthy of report, they impart them to their brethren, by which they stir the hard hearts of mortals to love of the Creator, lest, like the sluggish servant with the talent hidden in the ground, they incur condemnation. Therefore listen to what I learned long ago as a boy from the fathers of old, and with me magnify the wondrous God in his saints.

As the fame of the blessed Father Ebrulf spread far and wide, it reached the ears of Childebert, king of the Franks. Desiring greatly to see him, he went to Ouche, with his wife and several members of his household. When he had come near the monastery of the man of God—to the place, namely, where there is now a basilica built in honor of the blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of God—he reverently dismounted from his horse and commanded that all make fitting preparations to meet the servant of God. Then the clerics accompanying him stood robed, put their hands upon the relics and crosses which they had laid upon cloths, and wished to take them up again; but they could not move them at all. Therefore all, seized by deep sorrow, threw themselves upon the ground and humbly implored the Lord’s mercy.

The queen, binding herself by a vow, said: “If almighty God grants us the power safely to recover the sacred things we have placed here, I shall cause a venerable church to be built in this place in honor of his Mother.” When she had said this, the clerics put their hands upon the sacred objects, but gained nothing. Then the queen, exceedingly sorrowful, said with tears: “I know that my sins deserve that I should be unable to behold the servant of God. Yet if, through the intercession of that saint, God the Creator of all things looks upon us and permits us to remove the holy relics, I shall provide a marble altar at my own expense and have it conveyed to that blessed man.” As soon as these words had left her mouth, all the relics moved of themselves. Taking them up, they went joyfully to meet the man of God.

For the blessed man was now approaching, attended by the assembled company of brethren; and with him a crowd of people of both sexes hurried joyfully to greet the king. The king was received and remained there for three days. On the third day he granted ninety-nine estates to Blessed Ebrulf by charter, and then returned joyfully to his own home.

The queen, mindful of her vow, caused an honorable church to be built for the undefiled Mother of God, Mary, on the hill lying between the stream of Carentonne and the forest. As she had promised, she sent the venerable man a marble altar, which remained in that place for many years. Then, after the passage of many years, a certain petty fellow wished to move part of that marble to another place; but by accident he broke it in two. That deed, to make clear to all that it had displeased God, was not allowed to remain unpunished for long: before the year had turned, the said man was deprived of life.

In the basilica which I have said the queen built, two altars are consecrated: one dedicated to the holy and undivided Trinity, the other to the untouched Virgin, Mother of God. It is said that there was there a convent of nuns, as well as a cemetery for monks and eminent men, whose bodies were carried there for burial, because the soil in the valley was marshy and, whenever it was dug in winter, water at once sprang up, and the flowing spring filled the grave. Hence the aforesaid shrine of the Virgin Mother displays many indications of a distinguished habitation, and honorable sarcophagi are preserved there to this day, believed without hesitation to have belonged to persons of rank. This being so, let us proceed to tell what remains.

When the man filled with God saw that he could not endure the crowds coming to him, he duly arranged his monastery, withdrew secretly from it, and concealed himself for three years in a certain crypt, so that no monk at all knew of it, except one named Malchus, the spiritual son of the man of God, who, being more intimate than the rest, knew his secrets. The crypt was beneath a leafy hill near a brook, and was about half a league from the monastery. But the devil, enemy of all good things, seeing the brethren increase in good works, strove wickedly to intoxicate them with the gall of his malice and to sadden them all alike by a dreadful disturbance. Accordingly, he once introduced dissension among them, which grew so strong that two of them were killed and all the others afflicted by unspeakable grief.

Therefore the spiritual son of the servant of God, seeing an incurable wound in the body of the brethren, hurried at a run to the physician. When the holy man saw him coming from afar, he understood that he was hurrying so urgently not without cause. He came to meet him and asked why he had come. Malchus then set out in order how the brethren had been stirred into sedition by the devil’s instigation. Hearing this, he groaned, inflamed by zeal for God, and hastened with the messenger. When he drew near the monastery and came to the place where there now stands a church founded in his own honor, all the bells of the monastery began to ring of themselves. Likewise, bells rang from the church of Blessed Mary and from the basilica of St Martin, called “the Elegant,” where the parish assembled, in the place commonly called Bercoteria.

Then the devil, perceiving that the saint was coming, assumed human form and began to flee. Seeing this, the blessed man said to his godson: “Brother, do you see that man running?” But he answered: “I do not see him, lord.” “Look,” he said, “the devil, transformed into the form of a man, is fleeing, afraid to remain there any longer.” Saying this, he pursued fleeing Belial. When he came to the place now called Escalfou by the inhabitants, Satan, no longer permitted to flee farther, stopped. Blessed Ebrulf boldly approached, threw him into a blazing oven prepared for baking bread, and immediately blocked the oven’s mouth with an iron lid which he happened to find there. From that event the place was afterwards called Escalfou.

When the women who had brought their bread for baking saw this, astonished, they said to the man of God: “What shall we do, lord, about our bread?” He replied: “God is able to bake your bread without bodily fire. Carefully sweep the ground before the oven; lay your loaves there one by one; and, once they are fully baked, carry them to your own homes.” This was done, while all who saw it praised God.

Then Blessed Ebrulf returned to his monastery and ordered the two brethren who had been killed to be brought before him. Throwing himself upon the ground, he devoted himself to prayer until they awoke from the sleep of death. Having made confession and received communion of the Lord’s body, they again gave up the spirit, to the amazement and rejoicing of all who saw it. The venerable Father ordered them honorably buried and, certain of their salvation, devoutly gave thanks to God.

The elders report these and many similar deeds performed through Ebrulf, adding that they had seen at Ouche an aged monk named Natalis, who possessed a large volume concerning miracles and deeds performed by that oft-mentioned servant of almighty God. Once, after Mass was finished, a burning candle was carelessly left upon the altar. While the inhabitants attended to other matters, its flame consumed the wick down to the altar-cloth; then devouring fire accidentally caught the altar linens, the book—of which no copy can anywhere be found by us—and everything there that could burn, whether around or upon the altar. All therefore mourned the irreparable loss of knowledge concerning the past. Since the hermits were unlettered, they did not restore it in writing, but communicated orally to younger men what they had learned by sight or hearing. When these too failed, a darkness of ignorance covered their descendants and irretrievably concealed the investigation of bygone things, except for those matters which the skill of a certain sophist briefly assembled, for reading in church, in the Life of the holy Father.

Now, just as I inserted the beginning of that reading in my little work, so I shall also usefully compose the end of his works and life without the embellishment of falsehood.

Meanwhile, in the twenty-second year after their beginning in that wilderness, a pestilential calamity of sudden death entered that monastery through the assault of the ambusher of the human race. But Blessed Ebrulf, not like a hireling who fled in the midst of wolves after abandoning the sheep, entered the struggle with them; and, fulfilling the Apostle’s injunctions, he rejoiced with those who rejoiced and wept with those who wept (Rom. 12:15). Addressing them with words of exhortation, he said:

> “O brethren, strengthen your hearts and be ready. Act manfully and be strengthened in the Lord (1 Cor. 16:13), knowing that tribulation produces patience (Rom. 5:3). Be renewed in the spirit of your minds, and fight against the ancient serpent. Let there be one heart and one soul among you in the Lord. Behold, our summons draws near, and our works shall be revealed; and the true Judge will render according as each person’s merits demand. Therefore watch and pray, because you know neither the day nor the hour. Blessed is that servant whom, when the Lord comes, he finds watching” (Matt. 24:41).

With these and similar divine persuasions the wise preacher stirred the consciences of the brethren, adding also what joys await the good and what torments are owed to those who live wickedly.

As they began to die quickly, so that the holiness of the blessed man might shine forth more fully, one of the brethren, named Ansbert, died without viaticum. His attendant came to the abbot and said: “Pray, Father, for your son, who has now miserably departed from human affairs. May your prayer grant him guidance, since communion in the saving sacrifice did not fortify his journey.” Because of this, Blessed Ebrulf, greatly accusing himself as though it had happened through negligence, came to the dead man’s bed. With tears preceding him, prostrate in the dust, he took up the weapons of prayer which he was accustomed to wield. When he sensed that the protection of divine favor was present, he rose from the ground and called out to the dead man. At his voice, the man who had lost the light raised his head; opening his eyes and beholding the author of his freedom, he said:

> “Welcome, my liberator; welcome. For your prayer saves me, whom the enemy had claimed as his own because he found me uncommunicated; it dissolves the artifices of his cunning. Deprived of the banquet of the blessed, I had received the sentence that, lacking viaticum, I must be miserably tormented by the punishment of hunger. Therefore, gracious Father, I beg you: do not delay to make me a participant in the saving sacrifice.”

What more need be said? The sacrifice was ordered to be brought. As soon as he received it, to the astonishment of all that he had returned to life, he again gave up the spirit through God’s providential dispensation. The glorious Father rejoiced, having been made more certain of his brother’s salvation; the brethren rejoiced, praising God for the new miracle. He was glad because he had restored to the life of life a brother rescued from death through the life received; they gloried that they possessed a Father at whose prayers hell itself trembled. Though they saw the danger of the approaching pestilence, yet under such a great leader they now feared less the destruction of sudden death. But while that affliction of mortality was raging, seventy-eight monks died, as well as a considerable multitude of servants.

Furthermore, what happened to one of them should not be passed over in silence. On the very day of the Lord’s Nativity, the soul was taken from a man very necessary to the monastic household. When his body had been carefully prepared for burial, it was carried outside the monastery to the place of burial. Having laid him there, they waited until, after the proclamation of the Masses had been completed, he might be committed to the grave. The whole congregation of the church wept over the death of so great a servant. For he was an exceedingly diligent steward, administering the brethren’s affairs most devotedly, and for that reason was loved by all with great affection.

As all wept together, Blessed Ebrulf, receiving the Holy Spirit with all his mind, groaned; and, compassionating the brethren’s grief, he resorted to his familiar aids. He devoted himself to prayer, beat his breast violently, and afflicted himself in tearful prayer until the servant for whom he prayed rose again and, giving thanks for restored life, fell down before the feet of the one who had raised him. At this, a cry rose to heaven and the name of the Holy Trinity was blessed by all together. Ebrulf was regarded by everyone as illustrious and apostolic because he had raised the dead. The man who had been restored to life, returned to his former office, lived for many years thereafter. At last, by the consenting will of heavenly mercy, that deadly sickness ceased.

Yet when the illness ceased, the pious shepherd did not cease to pray for the dead, understanding that true charity labors more for the soul than for the body. Although he shone with venerable gray hair, he did not know how to yield to old age; by praying or reading, he joined day to night, according to what the Psalmist says among other things concerning the blessed man: “He shall meditate in the law of the Lord day and night” (Ps. 1:2). Filled with the fire of charity, he persisted most diligently in every exercise of virtue. Merciful toward sinners, he stood the firmest guard over his own mouth. Neglecting the care of his skin, he had his hair cut only three times a year. He never returned evil to anyone in revenge. If someone reported to him any loss of temporal goods, he immediately replied: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away: blessed be the name of the Lord!” (Job 1:21).

Such power to restore peace was in him that whoever came to him in discord returned peaceful, softened by his honey-sweet words. He received all who came to him—noble and lowly, poor and pilgrims—with a cheerful countenance. He wished always to be most joyful before all, and rarely, indeed scarcely ever, allowed anyone whom he received to depart from him without some small gift. The sick too, restored to health by his blessing, returned with immense joy, blessing God. In short, salvation came to all who sought the blessed man, according to their desire. Many also, so grievously afflicted by a most violent force of fevers that they could not come into the presence of the most blessed man, sent messengers to request his kindness, that they might be worthy, for charity’s sake, to receive the belt he had made for himself from a cord, or some article of his clothing. Those who obtained this through faith were granted their former health.

A certain housewife, whom no physician could heal, having heard of the powers of the most blessed man, asked that a fringe of his garment be brought to her by a messenger. When she received it, she escaped her illness, as did very many others. Behold the praiseworthy physician, who, present among those present, bestows the benefits of health, and, absent from those absent, does not cease to provide the same. Those who have not known his face feel his power.

Since all came to him for definite reasons, among them there arrived from another region a certain poor man. When the most compassionate old man saw him, wasted throughout his body by severe illness and walking bent over upon his legs, he said: “Brother, how have you been able to complete such a laborious journey when you are afflicted with such weakness?” The man replied: “Compelled by a double necessity, lord, I resolved to come to your holiness: namely, that you might both satisfy a hungry man and heal a sick one by the power you possess.” Ebrulf ordered him to remain there, immediately restored him to health, made him a monk, and commanded that he be a gardener. Thus the man who had come seeking two things rejoiced that he had been endowed with a threefold gift. Having escaped the danger of hunger, he found a remedy for illness and gained the purpose of a better life.

IX. Death of Blessed Ebrulf.

Amid these signs of virtue, when Christ’s veteran soldier was already eighty years old, he desired with all his heart to behold the face of him whom he had devoutly served, judging that servant faithless who should wish to avoid the Lord’s presence. Stricken with fever, he was seen to take no food for forty-seven days, except at times the sacrament of the body of the Lord Jesus; and, as though suffering no weakness, he unceasingly distributed to the brethren the mystery of the divine word. When religious men from neighboring places came eagerly to see him and begged him with tears to restore his little body by taking something from the charity offered to him, he said: “Be silent, brothers, be silent. Do not, by urging me, impose upon me a distaste which I do not desire at all.” For he had no need of earthly food, since the Holy Spirit nourished him within. He was fed by hope of eternal sweetness, certain that in exchange for his labor he would be granted blessed immortality.

Finally, when the day approached on which he desired to be released and enjoy the longed-for face of the Creator, he summoned the brethren. They were grieving at his departure and crying out what they should do when their shepherd was dead. He addressed them thus:

> “My little children, persevere with one mind, joined by the bond of charity. Let spiritual love be among you toward one another. Do not let the subtle deceit of the ambusher steal you away, and strive to fulfill what you promised to God. Love sobriety, preserve chastity, maintain humility, avoid pride, and let each hasten to surpass the other in good work. Receive guests and pilgrims with kindly spirit, for the sake of him who said: ‘I was a stranger, and you received me’” (Matt. 25:43).

As glorious Ebrulf spoke these and other such words, and had also given peace to the brethren, his most holy soul departed from the body. At once his face shone with such brightness that no one doubted that the liberated spirit was triumphing in heaven. He departed from the world on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, in the time of Rodobert, bishop of Séez, in the twelfth year of the reign of King Childebert.

> **Note:** [Col. 0481] Read: “of Clothar.” For it is established that Blessed Ebrulf died on 29 December, in the twelfth year of Clothar II.

The brethren carried him with great reverence into the church. For three days and nights, singing hymns and praises to God, they appear to have carefully watched over his holy body, awaiting the assembly of God’s servants. Once it became known that the comforter of the entire country had departed this life in the aforesaid city, everyone rushed to the monastery to take part joyfully in the blessed funeral. The poor mourned the true poor man of God; the rich, the rich man; boys, their father; old men, an old man. Since he had been a common good to all, the mourning was deservedly common.

But that outstanding act of mercy which the most pious man performed, now that he enjoyed eternal light, I do not think should be passed over in silence. A certain brother, conspicuous for his religious devotion and obedience, served in that monastery, elevated to the rank of deacon. The Father had loved him exceedingly because of his preeminence in holiness. Seeing himself deprived of so great a Father, he was overwhelmed by sorrow and said: “Alas! What shall I do, wretch that I am? Why do you abandon one whom you confessed that you loved, Father? Why do you allow me, who shared your most intimate counsels, to be torn away from you? Why do you scorn as one hated the man you treated as a son? Surely I never deserved from you that you should wish to be given to burial before me.”

He persisted in speaking such words and in shedding tears. And behold: on the very night of the Lord’s Circumcision, by divine will, he gave up the spirit. This was undoubtedly done through the prayers of most blessed Father Ebrulf, so that the man whom he had loved should not lie subject to the mockery of this world, and so that he might show himself most ready to be present in answer to the prayers of those who prayed. Thus that monk, according to his prayer, was laid out for burial on the next day with his abbot.

O glorious death, more precious than life! For what it took away from the world, it undoubtedly assigned to heaven. Indeed, as far as I can judge, it was better for him to die in this way than to be raised from death once more only to die again. Now, certain of salvation, he fears no defilement by sin. If he had been raised, he would have labored in anxious hope amid an uncertain peril. Therefore this should not be considered less significant than the above-mentioned restoration of the dead to life.

Accordingly, the venerable Father Ebrulf was magnificently buried in a marble tomb in the basilica of St Peter, chief of the apostles, which he himself had built of stone. There various illnesses are healed to this day, and consolations come to the grieving through the favor of our merciful Savior, to whom belong honor and power, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

Behold, I have truthfully described the life of the holy Father Ebrulf and carefully inserted it into this little work as it was transmitted by earlier writers, so that knowledge of so great a patron may benefit readers, and so that my labor and devotion may please the Lord God, as I strive to make known the glorious deeds of my nourisher, to the praise of him in whom we live and move and are.

X. The Obscurity of the History of Ouche after the Death of Blessed Ebrulf. The Depredations of the Normans.

From the time when the aforesaid hero departed from the world, I know absolutely nothing concerning who or how many successors he had during four hundred years in the monastery of Ouche, or what events the people of the province or the monks endured. For in the following time, as I have already fully explained in several places, pirates came forth from Denmark and, first under the leadership of Hasting and afterwards under Rollo, came into Neustria. Ignorant of the Christian faith and divine worship, they raged savagely against the faithful people. They burned Noyon and Rouen, along with many other cities, towns, and villages; they destroyed many monasteries flourishing in great religious observance; innumerable killings ravaged many regions terribly; and, after the inhabitants had been driven away or killed, cities and estates were reduced to wilderness.

In such devastation, unarmed monks, not knowing what to do, often trembled. Afflicted by misery, they assiduously gave their sorrow expression in weeping and, groaning in hiding places, awaited their end. Some, fearing the intolerable savagery of the barbarians, fled to foreign kingdoms which the martial power of the pagans had not yet reached. They carried with them the bodies of their fathers, whose souls reign with the King of Sabaoth, whom they had devoutly served in this world. The fugitives also carried abroad writings concerning the deeds of those Fathers, and concerning the possessions of their churches—what and how great they had been, or by whom they had been bestowed. The storms of so many disturbances swept away a great part of these writings, which, alas, were irreparably lost amid such grave and dangerous upheavals.

The monks of Jumièges and Fontenelle did this, but overtaken by sad misfortune they never brought back what had been taken away. The monks of Jumièges transferred the bodies of the holy Archbishop Hugh and of Aichadrus, abbot, to Haspas; the inhabitants of Cambrai and Arras reverently preserve and venerate them in precious shrines to this day. Likewise, the monks of Fontenelle brought to Ghent the relics of the holy confessors, Abbot Wandrille and the Archbishops Ansbert and Wulfran; preserved by the Flemings to this day, they are held there in great veneration. The same happened to many others. I omit to set forth their names one by one, either through ignorance, because not everything is known to me, or to avoid extending words that would be wearisome through excessive length and less necessary.

Dudo, dean of Vermandois, wrote diligently concerning the arrival of the Normans and their cruel barbarity, and sent his work to Richard II, duke of the Normans, son of Gunnor. William, surnamed Calculus, a monk of Jumièges, also elaborated Dudo’s material with discernment, elegantly abridged it, and added the deeds of his successors down to the subjugation of the English. He completed his narrative after the battle of Senlac and presented it to King William, the most exalted man of his people. I too, as others have produced elevated works about elevated places for exalted persons, and gratefully magnified great things in a magnificent manner, am encouraged by their example to undertake a like study. I have already composed much concerning the monastery in the forest of Ouche, honorably restored in the time of Duke William, later king.

For I could find nothing written concerning ancient times after the passing of Father Ebrulf. Therefore I shall especially endeavor to commit to writing what I have heard from elders: how the body of St Ebrulf the confessor was translated from its place. A short reading is indeed found at Rebais, but I do not approve of it greatly; it was produced, to be sure, by an ignorant author, to whom, in my opinion, the certainty of events and times was not fully apparent. Therefore, since I do not assent to another’s report, I must reveal in a clear written account what I learned from the native elders of Ouche: how and when the Franks obtained the precious earthly remains of venerable Ebrulf.

XI. How and When the Franks Obtained the Relics of Ebrulf.

In the year 943 from the Incarnation of the Lord, after Arnulf, ruler of Flanders, treacherously killed William, duke of the Normans, surnamed Longsword, and Richard “Sprotaides,” his ten-year-old son, assumed the duchy of Normandy and received the homage and fidelity of all the nobles at Rouen before his father’s burial, Louis, king of the Franks, surnamed “Overseas,” came with an army into Normandy. He deceitfully took the boy duke with him to Laon, promising the Normans under oath that he would rear him as his own son and educate him in the royal court to govern the commonwealth. But the event had a different outcome. King Louis, prompted by the traitor Arnulf, resolved either to kill the aforesaid boy or to mutilate him by cutting off his limbs so that he could no longer bear arms.

When Osmund, the boy’s tutor, learned this through Ivo of Credou, the king’s crossbowman, he carefully persuaded him to pretend sickness. By feigning illness, he made the guards less watchful. One day, while the king was dining and everyone was providing for his own or his companions’ comfort, Osmund bought a bundle of green grass, carried it to the tower, and wrapped Duke Richard in it. He then came down, hurried to his lodging, spread the grass before his horse, and hid the boy. At sunset he carefully carried him with him out of the city, went to Coucy, and there left the boy duke under the protection of Bernard, count of Senlis, who was his uncle.

Bernard the Dane, who was defending Normandy, sent envoys to Denmark and informed Harold, king of the Danes, of the death of Duke William and the disinheritance of his offspring. Harold immediately hastened with a great fleet to Normandy. Received by the Cotentin men at Bernard’s command, he waited for two years for an opportunity harmful to the Franks, and at last exacted a cruel revenge for the murder of his kinsman and the exile of that man’s child. For, when dissension arose during a conference between Danes and Franks, he captured King Louis; he killed Herluin and Lambert, sixteen other counts, and a multitude of common people.

Meanwhile, while the boy Richard lived in exile for almost three years, and the king of France thought that Normandy had been completely subdued to him, he feared that Hugh the Great, duke of Orléans, might help the Normans. He therefore gave Hugh the Hiémois and the Bessin, with the whole district of the Cotentin as far as Mont-Saint-Michel in the Peril of the Sea, and imperiously ordered him to attack the rebellious Normans with a strong hand and vigorously bring their towns under his rule. Hearing this, the greedy marquis rejoiced, willingly broke the treaties formerly made with the Normans, and invaded their lands hostilely with a great army. The duke himself lodged at Guaceium with his own household, while his army was scattered throughout the province.

Then Herluin, the duke’s chancellor, and Ralph of Dragey turned aside to Ouche and lodged in the monastery of St Ebrulf the confessor. Both were religious men, diligent in the fear of God. The simple monks rejoiced at the arrival of such great men and kindly offered them every service of charity within their power. They familiarly led them through their chapels, oratories, and private quarters, and, to their own injury, showed them their reliquaries containing saints’ relics. At that time the visitors reverently inspected the monks’ private precincts and departed with gifts and prayers offered; but shortly afterwards, like the Chaldeans in Jerusalem, they returned and cruelly carried away the vessels of God’s temple and all its precious things.

Hugh the Great indeed besieged the Hiémois with his army, but the military strength of the townspeople stoutly resisted him and blocked his path so that he could proceed no farther. The king of the Franks, however, entered the district of Évreux with great force and began to ravage all Normandy with plundering and fire. When Bernard the Dane heard this and received certain reports of Neustria’s devastation, he was anxious because he could not, by fighting with Norman forces alone, withstand such powerful princes. He therefore made a shrewd plan and exercised his keen intelligence in carefully devising how to avert the twofold danger from himself and his people.

He immediately met the king and said in supplication: “What are you doing, lord king? You are doing a wicked thing, utterly unbecoming to your dignity. Is all Normandy, which you are destroying, yours? Behold, Rouen and the other cities, with their villages and towns, stand open to your command; all their inhabitants, rich and of middling condition, serve you, and, having no other lord, revere and love you. Who gave you such grievous counsel, that with the sword of evildoers you should destroy your own flock and slaughter the people devoted to you? He may be proved hostile and faithless to royal majesty who gave you the advice to lay waste your own lands with sword or flame.”

By these and other gentle words the king’s heart was softened; he dismissed his army, and the king himself entered Rouen with Bernard [Col. 0486B]. There Bernard received the king amid the great rejoicing of the citizens, prepared a lavish banquet, and retained him for many days with the highest favour. One day, after dinner, when the king sat in the principal hall and cheerfully discussed affairs of the realm with those seated beside him, the shrewd Bernard craftily introduced a speech that was ambiguous to many.

“Great joy, O Norman nobles,” he said, “has arisen for us, for which we ought, as is fitting, to give thanks to God. Until now we have served a duke descended from Rollo; now, by God’s will, we obey a great king descended from the emperor Charlemagne. Until now we were ducal; now we are royal—or rather, what is greater, imperial.”

[Col. 0486C] When all had applauded such words and had beguiled the French with flattering sophistries, Bernard again asked for silence; and when all were quiet, he said:

“In many matters I approve the shrewdness of the French; nevertheless my lord the king has done one thing which I do not praise, in which I see both his loss and very great dishonour. It is known to all that Hugh the Great is faithless and the son of a traitor. Our king has increased his power excessively—to his own dishonour, unless I am mistaken—by giving him the district of Oximin and the Cotentin with many thousands of armed men. This pestilent counsellor has deceitfully deceived his simple master and, justice weighing the matter, has fixed a dagger in his own soul, by persuading his lord to strengthen his enemy against himself.

“I greatly wonder, my lord [Col. 0486D] king, that you are so forgetful of the past. It was sufficiently plain to all beneath heaven—for so great a crime could not have been committed in secret—that Robert, Hugh’s father, was a traitor, rebelled against Charles your father, seized the crown, and, perjured against his lord, fought against him; and, rightly struck down in battle, he perished. Hugh took part in these schemes; and while you were in exile in England with your uncle King Æthelstan, he disturbed Gaul for seven years. Is it not clearer than daylight to every sensible person that he is guilty of treason against royal majesty who maliciously advises the king to strip himself of his own possessions, diminish his lordship, and increase the strength of his enemy to his own ruin? Far be it that anyone should take a share in the duchy of Normandy; rather, let the king [Col. 0487A] of the Franks alone rule over all Normandy, with all Normans gladly favouring him!”

On hearing this, the king became anxious about the gift which he had voluntarily bestowed on Hugh without being asked. As he sought counsel on what should be done, the wily Dane suddenly persuaded him utterly to revoke all that had been promised, and by a threatening command to compel Hugh to withdraw from the siege of Oximin; if he persisted in rebellion against the command, the united strength of all should attack him there in war.

Bernard at once prepared two knights for this embassy, and the king charged them with imperious words to carry to Hugh. The messengers hastened to Hugh and firmly conveyed the king’s words:

“You have presumed upon abominable [Col. 0487B] rashness, in invading the dominion of the lord king of the Franks and now besieging the town of Oximin, where his own seat has stood from ancient times. Hear now his command on this matter, and obey it without delay by the fealty which you owe him. Before sunset withdraw from the siege; and, for the offence of your rashness against the king, make amends to him at Laon at such time as he himself shall appoint, by the judgment and counsel of the magnates. Otherwise be prepared, with your men, for battle. For the king, your lord, if he finds you, will fight against you this week with the forces of the French and the Normans.”

Hearing this, Hugh was violently enraged, and in a fury of anger addressed his men thus:

“How has such madness seized the foolish king that he sends such orders to me, who am aiding him with all my strength [Col. 0487C]? I have not coveted the rule of Normandy, nor asked any part of it from him; rather, he himself freely offered me the whole country on this side of the Seine as far as the sea, and asked my assistance in subduing the unruly pirates. Is it not plainly evident to all that he has resolved to fight me on the very account for which I serve him, as he himself commanded me? Wretched is he who serves an unjust man, and weak is he who is subjected to a deceitful and foolish man. Now withdraw quickly; devastate this whole region; destroy the churches; burn the houses; pull down the ovens and mills; carry off the flocks and herds; take away every kind of spoil, since you will not return here again; and [Col. 0487D] leave them accursed, burdened with plunder.”

When he had said this, the unrestrained plunderers spread through the province, surrounded the unsuspecting country people, who already believed themselves safe under Hugh’s protection, and mercilessly carried out the duke’s orders. Then Herluin the chancellor and Ralph of Dragey did not concern themselves with the peasants’ livestock or household goods; remembering the hospitality of Ouche, they returned there and unexpectedly descended upon the monastery with their followers.

They entered the basilica with armed violence, while the monks were astonished and suspected no evil. They immediately approached the sanctuary of the church and the sacred tombs, removed from their mausolea the three bodies of Saints Ebrulf, Ebremund, and Ansbert, and carried away their bones, wrapped in deerskins, together with other [Col. 0488A] saints’ relics. Their retainers scattered everywhere and irreverently seized, despite the monks’ weeping and cries, whatever they found useful to human life. There indeed, wholly loosening the reins of greed, they spared no one; they pillaged books, garments, and various possessions of both the monks and their dependants, and, searching through everything which they had previously learned about when the monks themselves—as has been said—showed it to them, they took it away. At last they joined the rest of the multitude, departed from the borders of Neustria, and all together hastened back to their native land with their spoil.

## XII. The Monks of Ouche Resolve to Follow Their Founder’s Body. The Relics of Blessed Ebrulf Are Divided.

[Col. 0488B] The monks of Ouche, rendered exceedingly mournful by so great a desolation, did not know what to do or where to go, having lost everything. Yet, considering the events, when their holy Father had been carried away they resolved to go into exile.

A venerable old man named Ascelin was prior of Ouche and diligently discharged the office of prior according to the needs of the time. Seeing the monks and their servants overwhelmed by extreme grief, all wishing alike to abandon the desolated place and to follow their blessed Father abroad with the hostile army, he turned many matters over in subtle meditation and resolved to await his end there in the fear of the Lord.

At last he summoned all the brethren, and, when they had assembled [Col. 0488C] together, said:

“For our sins and the sins of our fathers, the divine stroke has descended upon us; falling terribly upon us, it has utterly crushed us and all that is ours, and has cast us down beyond repair. Behold: as the almighty Judge destroyed Jerusalem and Solomon’s Temple through the hands of Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans, and justly humbled his sanctuary, so through the hands of Hugh and the French he has punished this place by afflicting it in many ways—above all, which is more grievous than anything else, by depriving us of the bones of our blessed Father Ebrulf and of other saints’ relics.

“But I do not dare forbid you, whom I see following the pledges of our father, to do so, for many reasons: this whole region is now deserted, and unarmed, hooded men lack necessary food amid the arms [Col. 0488D] of warring princes. Go with God’s blessing, and faithfully serve the gracious Father who has hitherto fed you in his own land, journeying with him in a foreign land. But I shall not leave the place of Ouche. Here, where I have enjoyed many benefits, I shall serve my Creator, and I shall not depart while vital warmth remains in me. I know that many bodies of saints rest here, and that an angelic vision designated this place to the holy Father, where he ought to exercise himself in spiritual warfare for the edification of many. Many faithful people here offered pleasing offerings of holy life to the highest King, for which they have now received crowned rewards in the Elysian abodes. Here, as you depart, I shall remain in good hope; following my predecessors, I shall preserve this woodland place [Col. 0489A] in the Lord’s name, until a more prosperous time smiles upon us, through the gift of the Lord of lords himself.”

At these words the sorrowful brethren parted from one another. The men of Ouche, therefore, then abandoned their native countryside with their dependants; joining the enemy, they followed their master’s bones in tears. In all, monks and their servants alike numbered almost thirty; gathered together, they followed the chapel-clerks on foot. The latter indeed knew them well, but showed them no familiarity, since they feared them as suspects and were afraid that the French might secretly deprive them of the precious treasure.

But the gracious Lord, who chastises those who stray in order to bring them back to the right path, comforts the converted with fatherly affection and in wondrous ways gives aid to those in need.

On the first night after leaving Neustria, the army encamped in a place called Campus. After supper, some parasites began jesting and making improper remarks. A certain buffoon therefore said jokingly to the duke:

“Do you know, lord duke, what Herluin the chancellor and Ralph the chamberlain have done? They dug up the corpses of certain peasants in Normandy and, grossly deceived, believing them to be holy relics, placed them in your chapel and are reverently carrying them with them into France.”

When the duke asked their names, the jester said: “Ebrulf, Ebremund, and Ansbert.”

[Col. 0489C] Since these names were unfamiliar to the French and they did not know how great was the glory before God in heaven of the men just named, they broke out into much idle and mocking talk. Then, during the first watch of the night, when the repose of sleep oppressed mortals, the Most High thundered terribly from heaven, hurled lightning amid violent flashes, and struck the jester with his fellow scoundrels who had disparaged the holy relics. When they had been killed, he greatly terrified the duke and his whole army.

The next morning the duke summoned the entire army, ordered the chancellor reverently to carry the holy bodies before him, and commanded the whole army, before leaving that place, devoutly to make offerings to the holy relics. He also summoned the grieving monks with their little household, asked them who and what manner of men Ebrulf and his companions had been, willingly heard their answers and accounts of the venerable men’s deeds, and eagerly invited the magnates of Belgica to listen. Meanwhile, piously considering the maturity and simplicity of the men of Ouche, and moved by God’s prompting—for God has mercy everywhere on his own—he pitied them and said:

“[Col. 0489D] “I regard the bones of your Father, which you voluntarily follow, as more precious than all gold and silver. I also favour you for love of them; and, taking care for you, I order the chancellor to treat you honourably in his company and to grant you all the offerings that shall be made to the holy relics, until you reach Orléans, which is the capital of my duchy. There I shall provide for you the means to have sufficient sustenance.”

[Col. 0490A] Thus the men of Ouche were treated more hopefully among strangers, and every day received a great abundance of gifts from the faithful. With God’s help, they were amply refreshed by the offerings prompted by the needs of the sick and by the good will of the devout. When they reached Orléans, the bands of fighting men having occupied houses throughout the city with their attendants and horses, the monks turned aside with the saints’ pledges into a certain oven, and there necessarily lodged on the first night.

Later the citizens built there a basilica in honour of Saint Ebrulf; and through the saints’ merits many benefits of healing were divinely granted to the sick. Herluin the chancellor was abbot of Saint Peter of Le Pont, and by Hugh the Great’s command he placed the venerable relics there.

[Col. 0490B] Then Ralph of Dragey claimed his share of such booty and was unwilling to yield his portion to anyone at any price. He was indeed a distinguished citizen of Soissons, the duke’s chief chamberlain, powerful in extensive possessions, honours, and riches, and renowned for faith and other virtues. No one dared inflict injustice upon so great a baron. Therefore, by common decree, the relics were brought before judges and divided.

Herluin, because he was a priest, abbot of the canons of Saint Peter, and chief of the chapel-clerks of the duke’s chapel, kept for himself the head and the larger portion of Saint Ebrulf’s bones; also his book, a small altar covered with silver, his staff and girdle, and charters of donations. The remaining [Col. 0490C] part of the body he handed over to Ralph. There was no difficulty in dividing the other bones. The men of Orléans chose for themselves the bones of Saint Ebremund the abbot; Ralph received the bones of Saint Ansbert the monk. Ralph hastened with so great a treasure to Rebais and, being its brother and friend, devoutly offered them to that monastery.

The men of Rebais, clad in white silk garments, came forth with burning candles and smoking censers, received the relics with rejoicing, and have reverently guarded them to this day. Then Ralph, so that the church might be increased through his benefactions, gave Port-Alnon and Bonolio; and, lest anything be lacking for making their shrines, he gave a great quantity of gold [Col. 0490D] and silver. For these gifts the same nobleman deserved to be buried in the church when he died.

In exchanges of this kind foreign devotees are mistaken; yet, being full of good will, they readily obtain pardon for an error that is not malicious. Having acquired relics by chance, they exalt them to the best of their ability; but in their investigation of the foreign Ansbert they are mistaken, advancing him beyond what is right and supposing him to have been archbishop of Rouen. But I confidently affirm what I have learned beyond doubt through extensive inquiry.

That Ansbert of Ouche was the young man who suddenly died without viaticum, but was immediately restored to life by Saint Father Ebrulf. Finally, after receiving communion, he departed to the Lord and [Col. 0491A] happily attained the fellowship of the saints. The Ansbert of Rouen, however, rests at Fontenelle with Abbot Wandregisel and Gwlfran, archbishop of Sens, and is daily honoured with due reverence by his own people. I have truthfully recorded these matters concerning the division of Saint Ebrulf’s body, as I heard them long ago from religious and truthful old men.

## XIII. The Deeds of Ascelin in the Wilderness of Ouche

After Hugh the Great’s death, his son Hugh the Great succeeded to the duchy; and when certain conflicts arose between Charles and the magnates of the realm, Hugh obtained the kingdom and left it to his heirs down to the present day. Geoffrey, son of the count of Anjou, was the godson of the aforesaid Hugh. Brought up by him, he grew to manly strength and, when adult, received from him the arms of knighthood.

[Col. 0491B] When he heard at the king’s court of his father’s death, he sorrowfully claimed from the king his hereditary right; and, because he had often seen the miracles of Saint Father Ebrulf, whose relics were kept at Orléans, he earnestly requested that something of his bones be given him. Hugh, because he greatly loved the young man, granted him his father’s honour and bestowed a portion of Saint Ebrulf’s relics upon him. He was thus the first to present Saint Ebrulf’s relics to the people of Anjou; devotion of the faithful cultivates them to this day in the church of Saint Maimbod.

The monks of Ouche who had gone into exile with the holy body, aided by God, found kind affection among foreign hosts and had an abundance of bread, wine, and fish supplied by the river Loire. Having experienced many changes of fickle fortune, they met their end in France [Col. 0491C].

But the old man Ascelin lived in the wilderness of Ouche with a few poor inhabitants. He brought up his nephew Ascelin, Guitbert of Gacé, Haimo of Tellières, and other boys, and taught them elementary letters, so that they might render daily service to God in that place. One day he summoned the hermits dwelling around him from every direction, announced to them a feast day, and on the appointed day celebrated the solemnity according to his means. During the celebration of Mass he addressed the people standing by:

“We ought to have feared the divine threats; but, with hardened heart, we heard what was said and made light of it, until, like wicked servants, we felt the rod of him who strikes. Severely smitten, we weep and mourn with pain from the depths of our being. Long ago, when the Danes, still pagans, devastated Neustria with Hasting, and again when Rollo raged with his men, many churches, cities, and towns were laid waste. By God’s assistance, we lay hidden in woodland and barren country, and, although in great fear and want, escaped the swords of the ravagers unharmed.

“Now, alas, a time of wrath has fallen upon us; unexpectedly the Creator’s vengeance has surrounded us and, through the hands of those in whose bond of hospitality we trusted, has stripped us of the sacred bones, dearer than all riches. We read in the sacred Scriptures [Col. 0492A] that the Lord rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh and delivered his tabernacle—where he dwelt among human beings—into the captivity of the uncircumcised Philistines [Note: [Col. 0491D] That is, calumniators.] (Psalm 77:60). A like judgment has now befallen us. We have lost the bodies of the saints, in which we placed our chief hope; and while our companions go abroad following the many tombs of the Fathers, we few and weak persons remain in an uncultivated wilderness.

“Yet although the French have carried away the holy bones, and plundered our books, garments, and other precious necessities, they have left us the tombs and dust of the most holy flesh, and other sacred things which they could not carry away; by God’s favour, they have unwillingly left these for our great consolation. We must not treat them negligently; rather, let us carefully store up what the enemy has left us [Col. 0492B] and preserve it reverently. By God’s mercy we still possess a hair from the beard of Saint Peter the Apostle, which the Roman pope sent to Blessed Ebrulf for the dedication of this church. We also know of other precious relics, deposited in this basilica by the ancient fathers. I propose, if it pleases you all, that we now inspect everything, and hide it safely because of sacrilegious persons, until God reveals it to future worshippers.”

All assenting and approving, the old man completed Mass. When Mass was over, he dismissed the people with a blessing, retaining the schoolboys for the service of the censer and candles. Then, with a mason [Col. 0492C], he approached Saint Ebrulf’s tomb, reverently removed its slab, and gathered the dust of the holy flesh in little heaps like cakes. He brought forth several boxes and reliquaries in which sacred pledges lay with their inscriptions. At last he told the boys to go and eat; and he, with the mason and mature, necessary assistants, concealed the relics in the wall, compelling the boys to remain away so that the secret might be hidden from them.

We heard these things from the boys themselves many years later, but we could not learn the precise place where the relics had been laid, because, as we have said, those informants had been excluded from the depositing of the pledges.

These things occurred in the time of Duke Richard I, who ruled Normandy for fifty-two years [Col. 0492D] and, as stated above, first suffered exile and great tribulations, but later, with God’s help, bravely prevailed after subduing his enemies. Amid savage storms the good old man Ascelin preserved the monastic life until decrepit old age; and, dying, entrusted the care of Ouche to Ascelin the clerk, his nephew. The latter, burning with youthful frivolity, began to hate the woodland life, removed from urban refinements, and went to France in order to learn. Finding an abundance of luxuries, he lived there for nearly fifty years and rose through various grades to the priesthood. Thus ensnared by carnal pleasures and puffed up in France by unbroken prosperity, [Col. 0493A] throughout his life until old age he forgot all that his predecessors had left him in Normandy.

## XIV. Ouche Is Plundered and Destroyed. How the Monastery of Ouche Was Restored from Its Ruins. The First Abbots of Ouche.

Meanwhile, as the inhabitants died or departed, Ouche returned to solitude. With people gone, a great forest grew up amid its chapels and houses, and wild beasts inhabited it there for a long time. In the district of Beauvais, a certain priest named Restold was then told in a vision:

“Go to Saint Ebrulf in Normandy, and there you shall enjoy length of days and the delight of a happy life.”

He therefore left his native country, wandered through Neustria [Col. 0493B], and sought Saint Ebrulf’s dwelling. Though searching many days, he found no one to show it to him. At last he found an old basilica of Saint Ebrulf at Montfort; he lived there for a long time, believing that the heavenly oracle had indicated that place to him and his offspring.

In the territory of Balençay, a certain countryman possessed a bull named Fala. Often leaving the herd of cattle, it ran into the forest. Although its owner searched for it for a long time with his household and dogs, it could not be found; but after five or seven days, when it was thought irretrievably lost, it suddenly returned safe. This happened frequently, and the matter became habitual [Col. 0493C]. The neighbours watched it as a sport, and the young bull was freely allowed to go and return.

After some time the curiosity of the herdsmen was aroused, and they tried persistently to discover the bull’s wanderings, following it through the thick wood. They also took with them a skilful tracker named Duilet, who, like a dog, shrewdly traced the bull’s footsteps until he found it lying before the altar of Saint Peter the Apostle, as though praying there. The walls were covered with turf, except where ivy nets concealed them, and the ruins of ancient buildings lay visible to those looking on. Thick forest had grown within and without, where no one had lived for fifty years. Then white-haired old men, hearing this, remembered that, as their fathers [Col. 0493D] had told them, Saint Ebrulf and many other despisers of the world had lived there.

A renewed vision, returning to Restold, reproved him because he had not yet fully obeyed the first command. When the priest anxiously inquired how he might more acceptably obey the command, he was told that he ought to go to Ouche and there, as a follower of Saint Ebrulf, serve God. Restold therefore left his former dwelling at Montfort, went to Ouche, and was the first to settle there with his wife and his son Ilbert.

At that time Guazso of Montfort was a noble knight. Filled with the fear of God, he devoutly resolved in his heart to restore all the churches in his neighbourhood which had been ruined by age and neglect in the many devastations mentioned above, and to devote all his ingenuity, resources, and substance wholeheartedly to so praiseworthy an undertaking. He repaired at his own expense the old basilica of Saint Peter the Apostle, desiring by such zeal to make almighty God favourable to him.

One morning, while his oxherd kept the oxen on the hill above the stream of Carentonne and rested among the ruins where the grass was richer, a certain pilgrim appeared before him. There, as though weary from the labour of travel, he sat down and began to converse with him for some time.

“Go quickly,” he said, “to Guazso, and tell him to come to me at once.”

When the oxherd ran to his master and reported the pilgrim’s [Col. 0494B] words, Guazso, held back by laziness, did not obey the command but ordered the pilgrim to come to him at once through the servant. The latter sent the dependant again and a third time; but the obstinate nobleman, occupied by I know not what, did not go. When the oxherd returned for the third time and announced that his master would not come, the old man said:

“Come and attend carefully to what I say. This place has been sanctified by divine blessing from ancient time and is most richly endowed with most holy relics.”

As he spoke, the radiant informant rose and pointed out, in the middle of the open space, the site of the altar of Saint Mary, Mother of God; likewise he showed to the east the altar of the Holy and Undivided Trinity. Then he added to the astonished oxherd:

“If your lord had come to me when I summoned him through you, I would have shown him a hidden treasure by which he could restore the old basilica here; and I would have disclosed another secret that would have brought immense joy to all Normandy.”

When the servant finally heard these things and, retracing his path, reported them to Guazso, Guazso then hastily mounted his horse. Reaching the desired place, he did not find the messenger. Greatly saddened at his delay, he eagerly questioned the servant about what he had heard concerning the site’s consecration and the two altars.

Then he conferred with Ralph Fraxmel, son of Turold, who was then chief lord of the same place, and, with God’s help, attempted to restore the basilica in honour [Col. 0494D] of the perpetual Virgin Mary. The workmen excavated the old ruin and found an immense supply of stones, with which they promptly completed the work begun. There they found many tombs of noble persons; old men asserted that, because of certain insignia found there, bodies of kings and bishops had been buried in them.

Certain signs also were divinely performed there. A knight named Harduin saw a huge stone among the church’s stones. Coveting it for his own work, he carried it to his house and wished to make it into a water trough for himself and his beasts of burden. But after beginning to hollow it out, he fell ill. While he lay sick, Gumfold of Tolcheta, a country knight, saw a vision. Instructed by it, he visited the sick Harduin and advised him to have the sacred stone carried back to its former place, predicting that otherwise he would inevitably die.

Hearing this, the sick man immediately summoned his household, ordered a four-wheeled wagon with oxen to be made ready, and earnestly asked that the stone be returned to the church of the Holy Virgin Mother. Thus the stone was lifted onto the cart and he himself placed upon it; having restored the stone which he had stolen from the sacred building, he confessed his offence, implored the mercy of almighty Lord (Adonai), and was immediately healed.

Many other signs indeed occurred there, but they have been consigned to oblivion because the people of that time have died away; for want of writers—of whom Neustria was then especially deprived—they were not written down [Col. 0495B].

At that time William, son of Geroi, held the lordship of Échauffour. He heard that in the forest there were Saint Ebrulf’s spring and, above the stream of Carentonne, the old church of Saint Peter the Apostle. Led by curiosity, he inspected everything, saw that the place was suitable for worshippers of God, reverently approved it, assigned Restold and Ingerann, priests, to that place, and provided them sufficient sustenance from the revenues of Échauffour. In the course of time, as is fully recorded in the third book of this work, the monastery of Ouche was restored by the aforesaid William, his brothers, and his nephews, and was regularly established through the labour and care of the monks of Jumièges [Col. 0495C].

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1051, Theodoric, a monk of Jumièges, undertook the care of the abbey. For eight years he piously and prudently trained the newly planted flock, and worthily taught it to walk in the law of the Lord according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. Then, as has been said above, he grew weary of the burden of government and voluntarily laid it down, to the sorrow of the bishops Maurilius of Rouen and Hugh of Lisieux. Despising earthly life, he sought exile; longing for the heavenly Jerusalem, he laboured to see the earthly one. At last, on the Kalends of August, he died before the altar in the church of Saint Nicholas on the island of Cyprus. There he deserved honourable burial by the community of monks, and shone through frequent miracles in the healing of the sick [Col. 0495D].

I have also composed the following heroic epitaph concerning him:

> Theodoric first ruled the church of Ouche,  
> And taught the good works which he had himself first done.  
> For thirty years he bore the rigour of monastic life,  
> And triumphantly endured the struggle against Satan.  
> For eight years he exercised a father’s office  
> Among woodland folk, where he remained poor.  
> With his own hand, writing many volumes,  
> He gave the church’s children an example of goodness.  
> At last, a pilgrim, he began his journey toward Jerusalem.  
> In Cyprus he received life’s end and burial.  
> The last light of July saw him die;  
> May Christ cherish him, radiant, in the Father’s bridal chamber.

## XV. The Monks of Ouche Obtain Certain Relics of Their Patron. Succession of the Abbots of Ouche.

The monks of Ouche grieved that they did not possess their patron’s body [Col. 0496A] and sought in many ways how it might be restored to them, but had not yet been able to find a way. Since they had not fulfilled their entire desire in this matter, they nevertheless acquired many relics by various means and, at different times, brought them back with God’s favour.

Fulco, provost of the church of Ouche, who later became abbot of Dives, was sent by William the Bastard, king of the English, to Countess Bertha in Brie on private business. Through a chaplain of the countess, whom he recognized as Norman by birth and as familiar with the church of Rebais, he obtained a tooth of Saint Ebrulf. Returning to the church of Ouche, he brought it with him to the rejoicing of all.

During the reign of King Louis, there was at Paris a canon named [Col. 0496B] Fulbert who possessed an entire bone from Saint Ebrulf’s spine. A chaplain of the chapel of Henry, king of the Franks, had taken it and had long ago given it to him as a pledge of affection. Fearing, for various reasons, to keep it, Fulbert, through the mediation of Fulco, priest of Mantes, summoned William of Montreuil, prior of Mantes, and gave him the relic to carry to the church of Ouche. William joyfully accepted the gift and completed the commission as quickly as possible.

While hurrying on his journey, he experienced the aid of the holy Father. The aforesaid prior unknowingly ate poison in food, which immediately spread through the limbs and entrails of the rider. But when he felt death close to his heart, he cried out in fear to God [Col. 0496C] and prayed that, through Saint Ebrulf’s merits, God might have mercy upon him. Having made prayers and vows, he vomited up the poison, was quickly healed, gave thanks to his Saviour, joyfully presented the relics to the monastery of Ouche, and fittingly enclosed them in silver.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1130, Guarinus, the seventh abbot, went to Rebais, where he had heard that half the body of Saint Ebrulf was kept. Two monks went with the aforesaid Father—Odo of Montreuil and Guarinus of Sées—to seek the holy pledges of their Father; and many difficulties befell them. For Natalis, abbot of Rebais, was absent; the will of the community was to beware of them, not as guests but as enemies. The inhabitants’ equal hostility discouraged them with disheartening words, bidding them depart [Col. 0496D]. Yet their good desire grew and drew them all the more toward its accomplishment.

The abbot therefore, leaving his two companions at Rebais and laying aside the outward marks of prelacy, set out on a laborious journey. Riding as though a poor monk, he was not ashamed to meet those who came his way; but earnestly seeking Abbot Natalis, he went to the town of Rignac, to the court of Count Theobald.
