On the following day he came to the abbot, and disclosed neither who he was nor what he sought. Natalis said that he intended to go to Clairvaux and agreed that Guarinus might go with him. Thus both, with their attendants, went to Clairvaux and were kindly received by the brethren of that monastery, who strive to observe the Rule of Saint Benedict wholly to the letter.

They sought Lord Bernard [Col. 0497A], father of that monastery, spoke with him, and, asking many questions, found in him great wisdom. He discussed the holy Scriptures eloquently and satisfied their wishes and inquiries. When he heard the cause of the men of Saint-Evroult, he kindly assisted Abbot Guarinus and sent a letter of exhortation to the community of Rebais.

At length Abbot Guarinus returned with Abbot Natalis and found Odo and Guarinus cheerful, and dear and agreeable to the men of Rebais. Both were indeed mature, affable, and modest, and trained in the twofold learning of letters. Although both excelled in eloquence and learning, Odo, in the ardor of charity, made every effort to put Guarinus before himself. For Guarinus possessed grace and wisdom in divine discourse and, during eight days of hospitality, at the prompting of Prior Amalric, gave exhortation to all in the cloister; he won the goodwill of the whole community, no longer as an enemy but as a faithful friend [Col. 0497B].

Abbot Guarinus then produced the letter of the venerable Abbot Bernard. The community of Rebais gladly received it and resolved still more gladly to fulfill what it had heard. Stephen, bishop of Paris, and Burchard, bishop of Meaux, were present by God’s will, and earnestly urged the men of Rebais to refresh the men of Saint-Evroult with the nectar of charity. Therefore, with all assenting, the bishops appointed a day upon which the pledges of many saints kept there should together be brought forth; the people of the land should assemble to behold them [Col. 0497C], be strengthened and gladdened by manifold blessing, and afterward the men of Saint-Evroult should receive what they desired and so return to their own home.

But Abbot Natalis changed his plan and, with crafty fickleness, disturbed the men of Saint-Evroult, saying that, unless Count Theobald granted permission, he would never hand over what the community had approved. Therefore, by common counsel, Odo of Saint-Evroult was sent into Normandy to the count, who had then gone to speak with his uncle, King Henry. The obedient monk undertook the difficult journey, followed the count, came to Vernon, and first disclosed his secret to the king, asking his help. The king promised him assistance and entreated his nephew the count on behalf of the monks’ affair. The count granted his uncle’s request [Col. 0497D] and sent his consent to the men of Rebais through his steward Andrew. Andrew did not come on the day when the relics were displayed, but remained at Coulommiers, the count’s castle.

The abbot of Saint-Evroult, Guarinus of Sées, and Andrew of Colombes went there to Andrew. On seeing them, he received them kindly, commended himself to their prayers, declared the count’s consent, and announced himself as the count’s envoy and guarantor in the matter. Then Abbot Guarinus joyfully returned with his companions to Rebais. When Abbot Natalis heard the count’s consent, moved to repentance because he had greatly troubled the men of Saint-Evroult, he assented to their wishes.

Accordingly Prior Amalric awakened the community in the morning and led it with the men of Saint-Evroult to the church; and the whole community, in ordered procession [Col. 0498A], went to the sanctuary. The silver vessel in which the pledges of blessed Ebrulf were enclosed was broken open; the relics were reverently taken out; and the right arm, with a pyx full of fragments of bone, was bestowed upon them. The men of Saint-Evroult returned to Neustria and arrived at Saint-Evroult on 26 May [1130]. A great multitude of both sexes, nearly four thousand, assembled and came to receive the benefits of so great a patron, striving by outpoured prayers to merit his intercession before God. Sick persons, heavily burdened by the affliction of various infirmities, hastened there and sought remedies for their pains from the Most High through the merits of the gracious Father Ebrulf. Very many obtained what they sought and devoutly sang thanks and praises to God. Those dwelling there experienced many benefits of God, and rejoicing deservedly, exulted and placed their confidence in the merits of blessed Father Ebrulf [Col. 0498B].

A certain man of Breton birth, named Goisfred, lived in the district of Corbon. As he himself related, in his youth he had devoted himself to many robberies and acts of brigandage; but after some time, God inspiring him, he changed his life for the better. He took a lawful wife named Hildeburg, complied with her salutary counsels, renounced cruel and death-dealing company, and procured his necessities by the labor of his hands. From the goods acquired with sweat, moreover, he gave alms: he distributed to the poor, clerics, hermits, and monks, and bestowed on such persons the surplus profit of all his earnings, reserving only necessities for his own sustenance and that of his household [Col. 0498C]. He sought fellowship with the men of Saint-Evroult and, becoming a brother in Christ, kept that fraternity excellently. On the principal feasts of the saints he came to the monastery of Saint-Evroult, but, mindful of the commandment of the Law, he did not wish to visit the brethren empty-handed.

Once, two years before the death of King Henry, a remarkable event occurred. On the night of the Feast of the Holy Innocents, an unexpectedly heavy snow fell, such as no mortal of that age had seen, or had ever heard from his teachers to have been seen. It blocked the entrances of houses, covered the surfaces of roads, leveled hills and valleys, suffocated birds and animals, overwhelmed even human beings, and on that day wholly denied countless faithful persons entrance to churches.

In such severe weather the aforesaid Goisfred [Col. 0498D] arose, disregarded the excessive snowfall, loaded a beast of burden with fine wheaten loaves, and, taking his son with him, hastened to the feast of holy Father Ebrulf. When he came to a certain river named the Risle, he could not ford it, because there was no bridge and its waters had swollen. Anxious in fear and trembling, he sighed to the merciful Lord and prayed that He would assist him. Burning with pious desire, he immediately experienced divine aid and found himself alone beyond the bank, without any visible guide; but he realized that his son, with the beast and its load, had remained on the other bank.

Then his son, perhaps unequal in faith and merit, fearfully entered the water up to his navel, drew with him the beast [Col. 0499A] laden with loaves, and, though with difficulty, came out safe. The bread carried to the servants of God had been in the water, but remained untouched and unwetted by it. Thus bread fit for the use of Christ’s servants was preserved from heaven and, in a wondrous manner, drawn dry from the midst of the waves. Finally father and son reached their appointed destination. Joyfully he recounted how he had escaped the dangers of roads and waters and ascribed it to the merits of holy Father Ebrulf, whose feast he was seeking. When many who had assembled for the celebration heard these things, they glorified the Lord God of Sabaoth, who always comforts His own.

## XVI. Succession of the Abbots of Saint-Evroult

At that time Abbot Guarinus governed the monastery of Saint-Evroult [Col. 0499B]. Because of the great devotion with which Goisfred burned toward God, he loved him deeply and honored him reverently. This same Father was ardent in the worship of God and gave proof of such disposition in constant exercises. He honored religious persons and reverently placed them before himself; he diligently devoted himself to good pursuits. Although he was very thoroughly furnished with literary skill, he humbled himself; setting aside the dignity of a master, he eagerly hastened to various duties appropriate to juniors as though he were one of them, and performed them cheerfully, thereby offering his subjects a praiseworthy example.

He was of middling stature, thin and lean; unburdened by any corpulence, he was nimble and quick in all fitting tasks [Col. 0499C]. For humility’s sake he eagerly listened to words of teaching and instruction from others, and often carefully asked his equals or subordinates about matters that he himself knew better, listening humbly as a pupil. He abounded in eloquence when expounding readings from the divine law, and lucidly opened up profound compositions by examining them. At about twenty-three years of age he entered monastic life, in which he served the highest King for forty-six years. He made known the fruits of his keen intellect and diligent disposition in metrical poems, pointed letters, and other compositions.

From these I propose to insert into this little book one miracle which he learned in England while staying at Thorney with Abbot Robert, and committed to writing at the request of the bishop of Ely together with the monastic community. The text of the letter is as follows:

> “To all sons of holy Church, especially those obedient to the commands of the Rule of the outstanding Father Benedict: may Hervey, least servant of the servants of God and unworthy minister of the church of Ely, bring the purpose well begun to a better end.
>
> “For the praise and honor of Saint Benedict, patron of monks, we have wished to make known an event recently reported among us, worthy of hearing, deservedly pleasant to those who hear it, useful to those who retain it, and perhaps profitable to those who do not yet know it.
>
> “In the time of Henry, king of the English and duke of the Normans, in the sixteenth year of his reign in England and the tenth of his countship in Normandy, there was on the estate of our church [Col. 0500A] a man named Briestan, in the village called Catriz. According to the testimony of his neighbors, he wronged no one unjustly; he did not seize what belonged to others, but lived peacefully content with his own. Neither very rich nor excessively poor, he honorably supported himself and his small household from a moderate holding, according to the condition of laymen. He lent money to needy neighbors, though not at interest; but because of the untrustworthiness of many people he retained pledges from debtors. Thus he conducted himself between the two extremes, so that he was judged neither better than the best men nor worse than the wicked.
>
> “Although he thought himself secure on every side and believed that he was an object of envy to no one, divine grace inspired him—as the outcome of the matter proved—to desire to bind himself with the bonds of Saint Benedict’s Rule and to be clothed in its habit [Col. 0500B]. What more need be said? He came to our monastery, built in honor of Saint Peter the Apostle and Saint Etheldreda, asked mercy from the monks, and promised to surrender himself and his possessions to their authority.
>
> “But alas! That wicked one through whose envy Adam fell from Paradise will by no means cease to envy Adam’s descendants until the last man who is to come. Yet God, who mercifully and gently orders all things, ever as the Almighty makes good things out of evils and better things out of goods. When many heard of this—for though the man was not of high rank, he possessed some small reputation—a servant of King Henry, but especially a servant of the devil, came rushing up armed with wolfish teeth.
>
> “[Col. 0500C] But, so that you may know who and what this man was, let us digress a little from our subject. His name was Robert, and he was surnamed Malarteis, which in Latin we render ‘evil craftsman,’ and not without reason. He had absolutely no occupation except lying in wait. I mean, for everyone: monks and clerics, knights and peasants, people of every rank, whether renowned for religion or living otherwise. Yet, lest I seem to incur the charge of falsehood, I should say that he did this frequently wherever he was able to spread his malice. He accused all alike to the extent of his power, striving with all his might to bring everyone to ruin. Whenever he injured one or several persons, he was numbered among those of whom it is said: ‘They rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in the worst things’ (Proverbs 2:14) [Col. 0500D]. If he could not secure a condemnation by truth, then through the devil speaking in him he became an inventor of falsehood, a liar, and its father. But since no one—not even one who had remained inseparably with him from childhood—could either write or even recount this man’s evils, for he might justly be called a master of a thousand devices, let us return to what we began.
>
> “Hearing, as we have said, the report that the aforesaid man wished to take up the religious habit, Robert came, following the teaching of his master, who always lies or deceives. Intending to tell a lie, he began with a lie and said to us: ‘Know that this man, Bricstan, is a thief; that he possesses and conceals the king’s own money obtained by robbery; and that he seeks monastic life not for the sake of any other salvation, but in order to escape the judgment and punishment for this crime [Col. 0501A]. For he found a hidden treasure and, secretly taking it away, became a moneylender. Guilty, therefore, of such great crimes—namely robbery and usury—he fears to stand before the king or the judges. Therefore, sent here to you by the king’s command, I forbid you to dare receive him into your fellowship.’
>
> “But we, having heard the king’s prohibition and fearing to incur his wrath, refused to join this man to our community. What more need be said? Sent under sureties, he was led to judgment. When Ralph Basset sat in judgment, and all the men of the shire had assembled at Huntingdon, as is the custom in England, I myself, Hervey, was present with Abbots Rainald of Ramsey and Robert of Thorney, as well as many clerics and monks. Not to detain you too long: the accused man was produced with his wife, and the crimes falsely imputed to him were repeated. He did not deny deeds that had not been done; he could not confess what he had not done. On the contrary, he was charged with lying and mocked. For he was somewhat stout, of middling size, and had, if I may say so, an honorable countenance [Col. 0501B].
>
> “After many insults unjustly inflicted upon him, they condemned him, like Susanna, to be delivered with all his possessions into the king’s power. After such judgment, when compelled to surrender his property, he surrendered what was at hand; he stated where the absent property was and who his debtors were. But when he was compelled to surrender more and name greater amounts, he answered in English: ‘That wat min lauert godel mihtin that ic sege soth.’ This we Latins say: ‘My lord, God Almighty knows that I speak the truth.’ Repeating this phrase often, he said nothing else.
>
> “When all that he possessed had been disclosed, relics were brought forth. As he was required to swear, he said to his wife: ‘My sister, by that bond of charity which binds us, I adjure you: do not allow me to incur perjury. For I fear danger to my soul more than torture of the body. If, therefore, your conscience reveals to you anything remaining, do not delay to bring it forward. For our spiritual enemy desires the damnation of souls more than the tearing of flesh.’ To this she replied: ‘My lord, apart from what has been declared, I have absolutely nothing except sixteen shillings and only two rings [Col. 0501D], weighing four pence.’ When these had been brought forward, the woman added: ‘Dearest husband, now swear without fear. I shall afterward, confirming with my conscience as witness that you have sworn truly, carry red-hot iron in my bare hand, if you order it, before all who wish to see.’
>
> “What more need be said? He swore, and then, bound in custody and taken to London, was cast there into a dark prison. There, harshly and disgracefully confined in iron fetters more than sufficiently heavy, he endured for no small time the prolonged torments of hunger and cold. Set in such misery, compelled by this very grave need, he asked according to his ability and knowledge that divine aid might be present to him. But since he despaired of obtaining this through his own merits—which he believed very slight, or, more truthfully, nonexistent—he ceaselessly invoked with tearful heart and such voice as he could Saint Benedict, to whose precepts, as stated, he had vowed without pretense to submit himself; and also the holy virgin Etheldreda, in whose monastery he had foreseen that he would do this [Col. 0502A].
>
> “Thus burdened and bound by iron on one side, tortured by cold on another, and worn down by fasting on another, he endured a miserable life in darkness for a full five months, mourning—by my judgment—as one who would certainly rather die than live unhappily. Seeing no human help at all present for him, he did not cease to urge Saint Benedict and Saint Etheldreda by continuous groans, sighs, sobs, and sometimes tears, pondering their names in heart or voice.
>
> “What more need be said? One night, when bells were being rung through the city for the night praises, and he in prison had continued fasting from all food for three days amid his other distresses, he was now almost failing and wholly despairing of bodily restoration, repeating the saints’ names in a mournful voice. But God, gracious and merciful, who remains the unfailing source of all goodness, who despises no one in need and chooses no one because of power or riches, at last showed His mercy to the petitioner—a mercy greatly desired, delayed both to increase desire and that, once obtained, it might be loved the more.
>
> “Saint Benedict and Saint Etheldreda, with her sister Saint Sexburga, came to the man who cried out. Terrified at the unfamiliar presence of the light going before the saints [Col. 0502C], he covered his eyes with his hand. When the saints came with that light, Saint Etheldreda spoke first: ‘Bricstan,’ she said, ‘why do you so often summon us with tears? Why do you stir us with such cries?’ Already weakened by fasting, as though brought out of his mind and filled with joy at so great a miracle, he could make no answer at all.
>
> “Then the saint continued: ‘I am Etheldreda, whom you have so often invoked. Here is Saint Benedict, under whose habit you vowed to serve God, and from whom you have often sought aid. Do you wish to be freed?’ At hearing this voice his spirit revived, and as though waking from sleep he said: ‘My lady, if I could somehow live, I would wish to leave this execrable prison. But I see myself so afflicted by various distresses that, having lost all bodily strength, I no longer have any hope of escape.’
>
> “Then the holy virgin, turning to Saint Benedict, said: ‘Saint Benedict, why do you not do what the Lord has commanded you?’ At these words the venerable man Benedict put his hand to the fetters and broke them on both sides, removing them from the bound man’s feet so that he felt nothing at all. He appeared to have broken them more by command than by action [Col. 0502D]. Having taken them off him, he threw them indignantly from his hand and struck so powerfully the beam supporting the floor above that prison that he made a considerable crack in it. Frightened by the sound of so great a blow, all the guards lying on the floor above awoke. Fearing that the prisoners had escaped, they hastened with lights to the prison. Finding the doors wholly intact and secured, they entered with keys. Yet when they saw him whom they had sent in bound now unbound, they were even more astonished.
>
> “When they asked about the great sound they had heard—who had made it and who had freed the man in fetters—another man, imprisoned with him, answered while Bricstan remained silent: ‘I do not know what persons entered the prison with a very great light and spoke at length with this companion of mine. But ask him himself, who knows better, what they said or did to him.’ Turning to him, they said: ‘Tell us what you heard or saw.’ And he said: ‘Saint Benedict, with Saint Etheldreda and her sister Sexburga, was here and removed the fetters from my feet. If you do not believe me, at least believe your own eyes’ [Col. 0503A].
>
> “Seeing the miracle and not doubting it, they reported it in the morning to Queen Matilda, who happened then to be in that city. She sent to the prison Ralph Basset, who had ordered Bricstan condemned and still said that this deed had been accomplished by magical art. When he came there, he began, as he had before, to speak with Bricstan as if mockingly: ‘How are you, Bricstan? Has God spoken to you through His angels? Has He come down to you in prison? Tell me about these sorceries of yours.’ But Bricstan, as though dead, made no response at all.
>
> “Then Ralph, seeing how those fetters had been broken, hearing also from Bricstan’s companion about the three persons who had entered the prison with light [Col. 0503C], about the words they had spoken and the sound they had made, and recognizing that these things had undeniably happened by divine power, began to weep profusely. Turning to Bricstan, he said: ‘Brother, I am a servant of Saint Benedict and the holy virgin Etheldreda; speak with me for love of them.’ He answered: ‘If you are servant of the aforesaid saints, your coming is good. Know that the things you see or hear done about me are true, not magical.’
>
> “Ralph took him and brought him, rejoicing and weeping, before the queen and many barons who were present. Meanwhile the report, swifter than any bird, flew through the whole city of London and reached the ears of almost all the citizens. Then citizens everywhere raised their cry to heaven [Col. 0503D]; every sex and age together blessed the name of the Lord and ran to the court where they had heard he had been taken. Very many shed tears of joy, while others wondered at what they saw or heard.
>
> “The queen, filled with joy—for she was a good Christian—because of the novelty of so great a miracle ordered bells rung in all the monasteries of the city and praises to God sung by every assembly of the ecclesiastical order. As he visited very many churches in the city, devoutly giving thanks to God in the abundance of his joy at liberation, a great crowd followed and preceded him through the streets, and everyone wished to see him as though he were a new man.
>
> “When he came to the basilica of Saint Peter, called in English Westminster, Abbot Gilbert of that place [Col. 0504A], a man most learned in liberal and sacred letters, led forth a procession outside the monastery to meet him, with the whole flock of monks and the church’s full ceremonial. For he said: ‘If the relics of any dead person should be received festively in the Church, much more should we honorably receive these living relics—this man, namely. Concerning a dead man, where his spirit is, we who are still set in this frail life remain uncertain. But concerning this man we do not fail to know that he has in our presence been visited and freed by God, who does nothing unjustly.’
>
> “When they had rendered to God, according to their ability and judgment, due veneration for his deliverance, the queen sent him back to the church of the holy virgin Etheldreda on the island of Ely with great honor and joy [Col. 0504B]. I and the entire community of monks went out in procession to meet him with candles and crosses, singing *Te Deum laudamus*—‘We praise thee, O God.’ As we brought him fittingly and festively into the church, and had celebrated divine praises, we gave him the monastic habit, which he had long desired, in honor of his deliverer, most holy Benedict.
>
> “The fetters in which he had been shackled, in honor of Saint Benedict who broke them and in veneration of the virgin Etheldreda who had stood beside him, we hung in that same church as a memorial of so great a miracle, to be seen by the people; and they were seen to hang there for no small time, so that the event might be learned through them.
>
> “We wished to make these deeds of the venerable Father Benedict known to the sons of holy Church, not because he had not accomplished greater things, but because these are more recent and seem unusual in our times and in the lands of England [Col. 0504C]. Let none wonder concerning our blessed Father Benedict if he performs great and even immeasurable things: for, according to the testimony of Pope Gregory, he is made equal to Moses in drawing water from the rock; likened to Elijah in the obedience of the raven; called Elisha in recalling iron from the deep abyss; and joined to Peter in a disciple’s walking on water by command. He too, as is known, was a prophet in foreseeing the future and an apostle in working miracles; or, to put it more briefly, he was filled with the spirit of all the righteous.
>
> “Since, therefore, we know without doubt concerning him that whatever he wills he obtains from the Lord [Col. 0504D], let us joyfully remain in his service, knowing that by his prayer we are not deprived of our penny. If Saint Benedict did not deny aid to this man, who vowed that he would become his monk, what help will he grant to those who are already voluntarily bound by the bonds of his Rule? Many evident proofs openly show that this kindly master, now glorified by God in heaven, unceasingly intercedes for his suppliant disciples and effectively helps them daily in their necessities.
>
> “Therefore we, who have now received Christ’s gentle yoke and bear, laboring in His vineyard, the burden and heat of the day, must remain steadfast and persevering in the goodness of God, certain that the almighty Lord will protect and save us through the merits and prayers of the banner-bearing teacher [*signipotens didascalus*] [Col. 0505A]. Let us earnestly pray to Him, the maker of all things, that almighty and merciful God may cause us to come forth from Babylon and the borders of the Chaldeans, and to run in Jerusalem in the fellowship of the citizens above—He who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.”

Thus far, ranging through diverse subjects, I have grown weary with writing, and I now set an end to this sixth book of the *Ecclesiastical History*. In another volume, with God’s help, I have already completed seven books, in which I have published much concerning the death of King William and his three sons; and, recounting them, have added the journey to Jerusalem and various events occurring in our times.

As the almighty Creator ordained from the beginning, so He wondrously orders the course of the ages; instructing the receptive minds of earthly people, He recalls them from the harmful desire for low things [Col. 0506A] and summons them to better things through the presentation of memorable deeds. For by the casting down of the exalted and the raising up of the humble, the condemnation of the reprobate and the salvation of the righteous, the human race is continually instructed, lest through execrable warfare against God it become profane; rather, may it always fear divine judgment and love divine rule, avoid the guilt of disobedience, and continually offer faithful service to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—one God, king of the ages and Lord of all things—who lives and reigns through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

Virgin Mother, lead all peoples  
[Note: [Col. 0505A] Le Prévost: “Evvrigenas”]; O gate of heaven;

In your mercy remove such great afflictions from the oppressed!

## TO THE READER

If you seek arms, leaders, monks, and priests,

This fourth part of Vitalis will give you these things.  
[Note: [Col. 0506A] Rather: “second.”]

[Col. 0505] **THE THIRD PART OF THE ECCLESIASTICAL HISTORY OF ORDERIC VITALIS, AN ENGLISHMAN, MONK OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT-EVROULT:** in which much is related concerning the death of King William and his three sons; and the journey to Jerusalem and various events that happened in those times are added.

## SUMMARY OF BOOK SEVEN

I. A brief compendium of events in the kingdom of the Franks from the coronation of King Pippin to the end of Charlemagne’s dynasty.  
II. The reigns of Hugh, Robert, Henry, and Philip.  
III. Edward, king of the English. Henry, king and emperor of the Germans. The conflicts of Emperor Henry and Pope Gregory VII.  
IV. Disturbances in the empire of Constantinople. Robert Guiscard’s expedition against Dyrrhachium.  
V. Robert Guiscard comes into Italy to assist Pope Gregory against Emperor Henry. He captures Rome. At Gregory’s urging, he spares the city.  
VI. The Greeks attack the Normans while Robert is absent. Robert Guiscard returns to Greece. The Normans return to Italy.  
VII. The vain confidence of Odo, bishop of Bayeux, seeking the papacy. King William orders him detained.  
VIII. Death of Queen Matilda. Her epitaph. The rebellion of the men of Le Mans. King William orders the number of English soldiers to be registered.  
IX. Translation of the body of blessed Nicholas of Myra.  
X. Very many churches acquire relics of blessed Nicholas.  
XI. The author returns to the narrative of events. Wars between Normans and Franks over the district of the Vexin.  
XII. Death of King William.  
XIII. The king’s funeral. Pious reflections.

# BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 0507]

## I. A brief compendium of events in the kingdom of the Franks from the coronation of King Pippin to the end of Charlemagne’s dynasty

[Col. 0507A]

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 688, Pippin the Austrasian, mayor of the royal household, assumed the leadership of the Franks.

In the year of the Lord 711, Childebert, king of the Franks, died.

In the year of the Lord 712, Pippin the elder died; and his son, called Charles Martel, seized the leadership.

In the year of the Lord 715, King Dagobert the younger died on 19 January; he had reigned in Francia for five years.

In the second year after his death [Col. 0507B], Prince Charles Martel first fought Radbod near Cologne, while Theuderic, son of the above-mentioned Dagobert the younger, was reigning. At that time the impious people of the Vandals began to devastate Gaul. At that time churches were destroyed, monasteries overthrown, cities captured, houses laid waste, fortresses demolished, countless massacres of people committed, and much human blood shed everywhere.  
[Note: [Col. 0507D] Thus in the manuscript of Saint-Ouen of Rouen. The edition reads: “blood of the human race.”]

In that tempest the Vandals raged most grievously throughout all Gaul, laying everything low with flames and sword. Coming to the city of Sens, they began to attack it by every device, with missiles and engines. Seeing this, Eboba, bishop of that city, went out from the city with his people, trusting in divine power; he drove them from the siege of the city and pursued them in their flight until [Col. 0507C] they had departed from his territory.

In the year of the Lord 741, Prince Charles Martel died and was buried in the basilica of Saint Denis at Paris. Because of the constant wars, he handed over church property to laymen. After his death, his sons Carloman and Pippin assumed the leadership.

In the year of the Lord 750, Pippin was elected king, and Childeric, who remained of the line of King Clovis, was consecrated. Here the offspring of King Clovis failed.

In the year of the Lord 768, King Pippin died, and his sons Charles, who was called the Great Emperor, and Carloman were chosen for the kingdom.

In the year of the Lord 771, Carloman died.

[Col. 0508A]

In the year of the Lord 809, Alcuin the philosopher, abbot of Saint Martin of Tours, died.

In the year of the Lord 814, the great Emperor Charles died, and his son Louis, called the Pious, assumed the kingdom of the Franks and the Roman Empire. In his time pagans spread through the district called Ponthieu. In the twentieth year of the reign of the most pious lord Emperor Louis, his son Lothair rebelled against him and took from him the kingdom of the Franks. In the same year, gathering a very large army, Louis the father restored to himself the kingdom that his son had taken away.

In the year of the Lord 840, Emperor Louis the Pious died on 20 June. In the same year there was an eclipse of the sun on Wednesday before the Ascension of the Lord [Col. 0508B], at the ninth hour of the day, on 6 May. As the year turned, on the day of the Ascension of the Lord, the battle of Fontenoy was fought in Burgundy by the four sons of the aforesaid Louis—Charles, Lothair, Louis, and Pippin—and much human blood was shed there. Of these, Charles, called the Bald, obtained the kingdom of the Franks and the Roman Empire. Lothair claimed for himself that part of Francia which to this day is called the kingdom of Lothair after his name. Louis, however, claimed Burgundy and was anointed king.

In the year of the Lord 867, Emperor Charles, called the Bald, son of the most pious Emperor Louis, while making his second journey toward Rome, died at Vercelli on 29 September [Col. 0508C].

[Note: [Col. 0507D] This epitaph of Charles the Bald was carved in the abbey of Nantua:

> This tomb preserves the limbs of Lord Charles,  
> conspicuous in the sovereignty of Rome,  
> and not leaving behind the sceptres of the Dardanian race,  
> but rather peacefully holding other kingdoms;  
> and he governed Christ’s Church with pious rule,  
> ever an outstanding guardian in adversity.  
>
> Journeying into Italy, he was consumed by dark fevers,  
> and, returning, died within our [lacuna] borders.  
> May God deign to join him to the hosts on high  
> and unite him with the holy choirs of saints.  
>
> When the fifth day of the month disclosed its light to the world]

In October, after an interval [spatium; reading uncertain], he yielded his spirit to God, as supplied by Le Prévost. There he was buried in the basilica of Saint Eusebius the martyr, and rested for seven years. Afterwards his body was, by a vision, brought into France and honourably buried in the basilica of Saint Dionysius the martyr at Paris. His son Louis succeeded to the kingdom. In the following year John, pope of Rome, came to Gaul with Formosus, bishop of Porto, carrying with him most precious relics. Having first arrived by ship at Arles, he proceeded through Lyons and other cities to the city of Troyes; there he spoke with King Louis, son of Charles the Bald, and returned to Italy. Afterwards Louis, king of the Franks and son of Charles the Bald, died. He left his little son Charles, called the Simple, with the kingdom under the guardianship of Prince Odo.

At that time the unbelieving people of the Northmen spread through Gaul, raging in slaughter, plundering, and every kind of cruelty. Then the nobles of the Franks, Burgundians, and Aquitanians assembled together and chose Prince Odo as their king. When Odo died on the Kalends of January [898], Charles the Simple, son of Louis, received the kingdom. In his time the Northmen came into Burgundy, to Saint-Florentin. Richard, duke of Burgundy, met them with his army in the district of Tonnerre; charging them, he struck down a multitude of them by the edge of the sword, and the rest fled, on 1 June.

At that time there was an earthquake around the monastery of Saint Columba the Virgin, on 9 January. At this time the pagans besieged the city of Chartres. Richard, duke of Burgundy, and Prince Robert therefore gathered an army and charged them. Having slain 6,800 of the pagans, and taken hostages from the few who remained, on 20 July, a Saturday, they prevailed through the aid of heavenly mercy and the intercession of Saint Mary, Mother of God. Afterwards, in the middle of March, a star appeared in the north-west, sending forth a great ray for nearly fourteen days.

In the following year there was a great famine throughout all Gaul. Then, nearly five years later, on the Kalends of February, fiery battle-lines of various colours were seen in the sky—a remarkable sight—following one another in turn. In that same year there was great dissension between the king and his princes. Because of this, very many massacres of the Christian people were committed; but, by God’s favour, all that opposition ceased.

In the third year after this persecution, Rodulf, duke of Burgundy, died on the day before the Kalends of September and was buried in the basilica of Saint Columba, in the oratory of Saint Symphorian the martyr. In the second year after his death, Prince Robert rebelled against Charles the Simple and was anointed king in the basilica on 29 June. Before the year was complete, on 15 June, a battle took place at the city of Soissons between Charles the Simple and Robert himself, who had seized the kingdom of the Franks; Robert himself was killed there. As Charles returned victorious from the slaughter of the battle, Herbert, most wicked among the faithless, met him and, under the pretence of a false peace, compelled him to turn aside as a guest into the castle called Péronne; thus, captured by deceit, he detained him. Robert had married the sister of this Herbert, and by her he had begotten Hugh the Great.

Charles, being thus confined, raised Rodulf, the noble son of Richard, duke of the Burgundians—whom he had received from the sacred font—as king, acting with the counsel of Hugh the Great, son of the aforesaid Robert, and of the Frankish nobles. Charles the Simple himself, after the prolonged misery of imprisonment, died in that confinement and was buried in the basilica of Saint Fursey the Confessor, which stands in the same castle of Péronne. Rodulf was anointed king on 12 July at the city of Soissons.

In these times the pagans again ravaged Burgundy, and a battle took place between Christians and pagans on Mount Chalo. Many thousands of Christians were slain by the pagans, on 6 December.

When King Rodulf died on 15 January, they buried him in the basilica of Saint Columba the Virgin. After King Rodulf’s death, Hugh the Great, together with the Franks, summoned Duke William, called Longsword, and sent him to Ovia, wife of the aforesaid Charles the Simple, in order to bring back her son Louis from there. For she had fled to her father, the king of the English, through fear of Herbert and Hugh. William went there and, after giving hostages to Louis’s mother under oath, brought Louis back into France.

Thus, on 19 June, Louis, son of Charles the Simple, was anointed king at Laon. In the second year thereafter, on 14 February, from cockcrow until daylight, blood-red battle-lines appeared across the whole face of heaven. In the following month, on 24 March, the Hungarians, still pagans, began to lay waste France, Burgundy, and Aquitaine with sword and fire. Afterwards the Frankish nobles rebelled against King Louis, Hugh the Great above all. In that year a severe famine occurred throughout the whole kingdom of the Franks, so that a modius of wheat was sold for twenty-four solidi.

Then, not many days later, King Louis, son of Charles the Simple, was deceitfully captured at the city of Bayeux by the Northmen, many of the Frankish people being killed, with the concurrence of Hugh the Great. Afterwards, in May, on a Tuesday, blood rained upon workmen. In that same year, in September, King Louis—having led all his life amid distress and tribulations—ended his final day [954], and was buried at Rheims in the basilica of Saint Remigius.

In the following month, on 12 November, his son Lothair, now a young man, was anointed king at Rheims, and Hugh the Great was made duke of the Franks. In the second year thereafter, in August, the aforesaid Hugh the Great besieged the city of Poitiers, but gained nothing by it. For while he was besieging that city, on a certain day the Lord thundered with great terror, and a whirlwind tore his tent from top to bottom. Great astonishment seized him and his army, so that they could not live. They immediately turned to flight and withdrew from the siege of the city. God did this through the intercession of blessed Hilary, who is always the guardian and defender of that city.

In that same year Gislebert, duke of Burgundy, died, leaving the duchy to Otto, son of Hugh the Great. Otto had married the daughter of Gislebert. In the second year Hugh the Great, duke of the Franks, died at the estate of Drodingam on 16 June and was buried in the basilica of Saint Dionysius the martyr at Paris. His sons succeeded him: Hugh, Otto, and Henry, born of the daughter of Otto, king of the Saxons. Hugh became duke of the Franks, and Otto duke of the Burgundians. When Otto, duke of the Burgundians, died, his brother Henry succeeded him.

In his time contention arose between Ansegisus, bishop of Troyes, and Count Robert. Bishop Ansegisus, expelled from the city by Count Robert, went to Saxony to Emperor Otto; and, bringing Saxons with him, he besieged the city of Troyes for a long time in October. When they came to plunder Sens, Archbishop Archembald and Count Rainard the Elder met them with a great army at the place called Villare. The Saxons were killed, together with their duke, named Helpo, and the men of Sens were victorious. Helpo had declared that he would burn the churches and villages along the river Vanne as far as the city, and would plant his lance in the gate of Saint Leo. But after he and his people had been killed by the men of Sens, his servants carried him back to his homeland, Ardenne. This had been commanded by Helpo’s mother, named Warna. Count Rainard and Archbishop Archembald mourned with great lamentation, for he was their kinsman. When Duke Bruno, Helpo’s companion, who had besieged the city of Troyes, saw that Helpo and his men had died, he returned to his own country.

Then, not many days later, King Lothair assembled a very large army and restored the kingdom of Lotharingia to his authority. Coming to the palace called Aachen, where Emperor Otto was staying with his wife, he entered the palace at mealtime without opposition and ate and drank whatever they had prepared for their own use. Emperor Otto, fleeing with his wife and people, abandoned the palace. King Lothair therefore plundered the palace and the whole province, then returned to France in peace, with no one pursuing him.

Afterwards Emperor Otto assembled his army and came to Paris. At the gate of the city Otto’s nephew was killed with many others, after its suburb had been burned. For he had boastfully declared that he would plant his lance in the city gate. King Lothair therefore summoned Hugh, duke of the Franks, and Henry, duke of Burgundy, and charged against them. He pursued them as they fled as far as the city of Soissons. Entering the channel of the river called the Aisne without knowing the ford, very many of them perished there. The water consumed far more than the sword would have devoured, and so many died there that the water itself overflowed with the corpses of the dead: it had filled its banks. King Lothair steadfastly pursued them for three days and three nights, as far as the river flowing beside Ardenne or Argonne, and killed a very great multitude of the enemy. Having ceased to pursue them, King Lothair returned to France with a great victory. Emperor Otto, with those who had escaped, returned in great confusion to his own lands. Thereafter Emperor Otto, whether himself or with his army, made no further attempt to come into France.

In that same year King Lothair made peace with King Otto at the city of Rheims, against the will of Hugh and his brother Henry, and against the will of his own army. King Lothair granted King Otto the kingdom of Lotharingia as a benefice. This cause greatly saddened the hearts of the Frankish princes.

In the year 976 King Lothair died, now old and full of days, and was buried in the basilica of Blessed Remigius at Rheims. His young son Louis succeeded him.

In the year 977 the young King Louis died, having reigned in France for six years. He was buried in the basilica of Blessed Cornelius at Compiègne. His brother Charles, son of King Lothair, succeeded him. In that same year Hugh, duke of the Franks, rebelled against Charles because Charles had taken the daughter of Herbert, count of Troyes, as his wife. Hugh gathered a very large army and besieged Laon, where Charles was living with his wife. Charles came out from the city and put Hugh and his army to flight, burning the lodgings where the enemy had been staying. When Duke Hugh saw that he could in no way overcome Charles, he conferred with the old traitor Ascelin, the false bishop of Laon and Charles’s counsellor. Thus Bishop Ascelin betrayed Laon by night, while all were asleep, to Hugh, duke of the Franks. Charles and his wife were bound and taken into custody at the city of Orléans. Charles himself had not yet been anointed king, because Duke Hugh opposed it. While Charles remained in custody in a tower at Orléans, his wife bore him two sons, Louis and Charles.

## II. The reigns of Hugh, Robert, Henry, and Philip in France

In that same year Duke Hugh was anointed king at the city of Rheims. In that same year his son Robert was appointed king. Here the kingdom of Charlemagne comes to an end.

In those days there was at the city of Rheims an archbishop, a good and modest man, Lothair’s brother by a concubine, named Arnulf. King Hugh envied him and wished to exterminate the descendants of King Lothair. Gathering a synod in the city of Rheims, King Hugh invited the archbishop of Sens, named Sewinus, with his suffragans. In that council, through the treachery of Arnulf’s nephew, whom he held in prison, he caused Lord Arnulf, archbishop of Rheims, to be deposed, declaring that one born of a concubine ought not to be bishop. In Arnulf’s place he had Lord Gerbert, a monk and philosopher, consecrated. Gerbert had been the teacher of King Robert, son of Hugh, and of Lord Leotheric, archbishop and successor of the venerable Sewinus. Hugh had Arnulf committed to custody at the city of Orléans.

The venerable Archbishop Sewinus did not consent to Arnulf’s deposition or Gerbert’s appointment. Yet the king’s command exerted pressure. The other bishops, although unwilling, deposed Arnulf and appointed Gerbert through fear of the king. But Sewinus, fearing God more than an earthly king, would not consent to the king’s wickedness. Rather, insofar as he could, he rebuked the king himself; for this reason the king’s anger burned fiercely against him. With great dishonour the king ordered Arnulf to be expelled from the church of Blessed Mary, Mother of God, at Rheims, and thus, bound, to be thrust into prison. Bound in prison at the city of Orléans, where his nephew Charles was detained, he remained there for three years.

All these matters were reported to the Roman pontiff, who was greatly indignant at them. He placed under interdict all the bishops who had deposed Arnulf and appointed Gerbert. He also sent Abbot Leo from the apostolic see to Lord Sewinus, archbishop of the city of Sens, so that in his place he might convene a synod at Rheims. He ordered him without delay to recall Arnulf from prison and depose Gerbert. Therefore, after the council had assembled, Arnulf was again recalled from custody in the city by apostolic command and received with great honour into his own see. Gerbert, understanding that he had received the pontifical dignity unjustly, was moved to repentance. You will find a fuller account of the very useful dispute between Bishop Gerbert and Abbot Leo in the *Deeds of the Bishops of Rheims*.

Afterwards Lord Gerbert was elected bishop at Ravenna by Emperor Otto and by the people of that city. After serving as bishop in the same city for many years, the pope of Rome died; immediately the entire Roman people cried out that Lord Gerbert should be given to them. Taken from Ravenna, he was appointed supreme pontiff in the city of Rome.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 918, King Hugh died and was buried in the basilica of Blessed Dionysius the martyr at Paris. His son Robert succeeded him, most pious and modest among kings.

In the year of the Lord 999, the venerable Archbishop Sewinus began from the foundations to restore the monastery of Saint Peter at Melun. Sending monks there, he placed Abbot Gautier over them. In that same year the knight Gualterius and his wife surrendered the castle of Melun to Count Odo. King Robert gathered a very large army, and Count Burchard summoned the Northmen with their duke Richard; they besieged the castle of Melun. When the castle was captured, Gualterius and his wife were hanged on the gallows. Count Burchard recovered the castle of Melun, as he had held it before. Then Rainald, the aged count of Sens, died after committing many evils and was buried in the basilica of Saint Columba the Virgin. His son Fromund succeeded him, having married the daughter of Rainald, count of Rheims.

In the year of the Lord 1000, in the thirteenth indiction, on 17 October, the venerable metropolitan Bishop Seguinus passed to Christ. After his death, the church of Sens remained without priestly consecration for one year. The entire people called for Lord Leotheric to be appointed: he was born of the noblest lineage, then archdeacon, and distinguished by every virtue. But very many clerics opposed this, desiring to ascend the episcopal rank. Above all Count Frotmund, son of Rainard the Elder, sprung from an evil root, would not allow it, because he had a clerical son named Bruno and wished to make him bishop. But by God’s providence the suffragan bishops of the church of Sens assembled; with apostolic consent and authority, setting aside all human fear, they solemnly ordained Lord Leotheric to preside over the church of Sens from the episcopal see.

In the year of the Lord 1001 Henry, duke of Burgundy, died without sons, and the Burgundians rebelled against King Robert, unwilling to receive him. Count Landric entered and held the city of Auxerre.

In the year of the Lord 1003 King Robert, having taken with him the Northmen and their duke Richard, together with a very large army, ravaged Burgundy and besieged Auxerre for many days. But the Burgundians, wholly unwilling to submit to him, unanimously resisted him. He besieged the castle of Avallon for nearly three months and captured it through the pressure of famine. Then he returned to France.

When Frotmund, count of Sens, died, his son Rainard succeeded him, most wicked among the faithless. He inflicted upon the churches of Christ and upon His faithful a persecution such as had not been heard of from the time of the pagans until the present day. Archbishop Leotheric, greatly distressed by this matter, did not know at all where to turn. Committing himself wholly to the Lord, in prayers and vigils he begged Christ that His heavenly mercy might deign to provide help.

Thus, in the year from the Passion of the Lord 1016, in the thirteenth indiction, on 22 April, the city of Sens was taken by Archbishop Leotheric through the counsel of Rainald, bishop of Paris, and restored to King Robert. Rainard fled and escaped naked. But his brother Frotmund and the other knights from the city entered and held the tower that stands in the city. The king assailed it for many days, took it, and led Frotmund, brother of Count Rainard, into prison at the city of Orléans, where he also died.

Robert, king of the Franks, reigned for thirty-seven years. His wife Constance, renowned for virtue and wisdom, bore him a noble offspring: Henry, Robert, and Adela. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1031, in the fourteenth indiction, King Robert died, and his son Henry reigned for nearly thirty years. Robert held the duchy of Burgundy and begot three sons, Henry, Robert, and Simon. Henry, the first-born, begot Hugh and Odo, but died before his father. Hugh succeeded his grandfather in the duchy and, outstanding in great virtue, held it for three years. Then he voluntarily made his brother Odo duke, while he himself, pierced by the love of God, served God devoutly as a monk of Cluny for nearly fifteen years. Adela, daughter of King Robert, was given in marriage to Baldwin, ruler of Flanders; she bore him numerous children: the counts Robert the Frisian, Arnulf, and Baldwin; Udo, archbishop of Trier; Henry, a cleric; Matilda, queen of the English; and Judith, wife of Duke Tostig.

In these times, while Robert and Henry ruled the Gauls, ten popes succeeded one another in the apostolic see: Gerbert the Philosopher, called Sylvester; John; Benedict; John his brother; Benedict their nephew; Clement; Damasus, fervent in nobility and zeal for the good; Leo; Victor; Stephen; and Nicholas. Henry, king of the Franks, took as wife Bertrada, daughter of Julius Claudius, king of Russia. She bore Philip and Hugh the Great, count of Crispeii. After his father’s death Philip reigned for forty-seven years. He married Bertrada, daughter of Florentius, duke of the Frisians, who bore Louis, Theobald, and Constance.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1047, in the fifteenth indiction, William the Bastard, duke of the Normans, brought King Henry into Neustria. With his aid, he fought against his kinsmen at Val-ès-Dunes, overcame and subjected Guy of Burgundy and other rebels, and put others to flight. Afterwards, firmly established in power, he married Matilda, daughter of Baldwin, margrave of Flanders. She bore him four sons and five daughters: Robert, Richard, William, and Henry; Agatha, Adeliza, Constance, Adela, and Cecilia. Various fortune drove so illustrious a progeny through diverse courses and cast each one down into his appointed end, as our pen has sufficiently recorded elsewhere. Afterwards, seditious men arose and sowed dissension among the aforesaid princes; a great war broke out between the Franks and the Normans, in which an excessive slaughter of many occurred.

At last, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1054, King Henry entered the district of Évreux and began, by plundering and burning, to inflict vast damage. He sent his brother Odo, with many thousands, through the district of Beauvais beyond the Seine. Duke William, with his troops, followed the king at his side and waited for an opportunity to resist. He summoned Roger of Mortemer and all the men of Caux, commanding them to advance swiftly against the royal army. They promptly obeyed the orders, met the Gauls, and fought at Mortemer. Gaining the victory, they captured Count Guy of Ponthieu and put Odo and Count Ralph of Montdidier to flight, after killing many. Then Pope Leo died in the sixth year of his pontificate. In his second year the abbey of Ouche was restored, and Theodoric was consecrated first abbot of Saint Évroult on the Nones of October. After eight years he went abroad and died on the Kalends of August in the island of Cyprus. An abundance of miracles was celebrated at his tomb.

## III. Edward, king of the English. Henry, king and emperor of the Germans. The conflicts of Emperor Henry and Pope Gregory VII

[Col. 0516B]

Edward, king of the English, after reigning for twenty-three years, departed this life in the sixth year of Philip, king of the Franks. His genealogy descends as follows from the stock of Shem, son of Noah. Shem begot Arphaxad and Beadumg. Beadumg begot Wala. Wala begot Hatra. Hatra begot Itermod. Itermod begot Heremod. Heremod begot Sceldunea. Sceldunea begot Beaw. Beaw begot Cetuna. Cetuna begot Geat, whom the pagans long ago worshipped as a god. He begot Finggoldwlf, father of Fidhulput; from whom came Frealaf, father of Frithowald; from whom Woden was born, after whom the English name the sixth day of the week Woden’s day [Wednesday]. He was a man of great eminence and power among his own people. [lacuna]

Here some material is lacking; it nevertheless appears to have been a kind of recapitulation of the matters which he has already related more fully in the preceding books, namely from Duke William’s crossing into England down to the year of Christ 1083.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1084, Henry, king of the Germans, gathered together a multitude of Saxons, Alemanni, Lotharingians, and other peoples. He forcibly penetrated Italy, besieged and stormed Rome. When the Romans surrendered themselves because of their greed for the gifts he had promised them, he captured the city. He expelled Gregory VII from the apostolic see and wickedly put in his place Wibert, metropolitan of Ravenna. Gregory then withdrew to Benevento. A great dissension arose throughout the world, causing great harm to the children of the Church and remaining long to the destruction of many.

Pope Gregory, who had been called Hildebrand at baptism, had been a monk from childhood and devoted his entire life greatly to wisdom and religion, waging an unceasing struggle against sin. He ascended through every grade of ecclesiastical orders to the height of the supreme pontificate, in which for sixteen years he strove vigilantly to observe the law of God. Inflamed with zeal for truth and justice, he rebuked every crime and spared no one acting against rectitude through fear or favour. Thus he endured persecution and exile from men untamed and opposed to the yoke of the Lord; yet by no device could they overcome him until his death.

He often admonished and rebuked Henry, king of the Germans, because he was an incorrigible transgressor of divine law; finally he excommunicated him. For the aforesaid prince left his wife, the daughter of Eustace, the distinguished count of Boulogne, and clung to the foul pleasures of adultery like a pig delighting in mud. Thoroughly hostile to God’s laws and to the exhortations of good men, he resisted them. Godfrey, duke of Lotharingia, grieved by the shameful repudiation of his sister, made war against Henry. Having gathered many thousands together, he fought him, routed him shamefully from the field, and thus avenged his sister’s injury.

The same king often deceitfully summoned to his court those nobles whose wives, daughters, or estates he desired; having secretly sent his retainers ahead, he had them killed without suspicion on the road. By these and many other crimes the foul king defiled himself and drew innumerable accomplices in treachery with him to destruction. When Pope Gregory heard the complaints about such great crimes, he repeatedly begged the aforesaid man to amend his life. But Henry wickedly mocked the physician and teacher, and nothing was achieved. Gregory often convened synods of many bishops and deliberated how he might correct the Christian empire, which Henry was so shamefully and wickedly polluting. At last, by judgment of a synod, he excommunicated Henry, repeatedly warned and stubbornly persisting in wicked deeds; under an anathema he stripped him of the kingdom which he had damnably usurped, and by apostolic authority consecrated Count Conrad king through the hands of many bishops.

Thus deprived, Henry lay low for one year in his own house, holding the county which he had received by hereditary right from his parents. But he procured much assistance by lavishly distributing from the treasure he had greedily amassed long before. Then, having assembled many thousands of accomplices, he scorned the common decree, rebelled as a public enemy, fought King Conrad, overthrew and killed him, and shattered his army by various disasters.

Henry, elated by this victory, seized the empire that he had lost, subdued rebels, and, having greatly increased his forces, besieged Rome and directed his whole effort against Pope Gregory. I think that it had utterly escaped his mind that Absalom had gathered great companies against David his father, taken up arms on the counsel of Ahithophel the Gilonite, invaded Jerusalem as his father departed with his followers, and at last destroyed many thousands of warriors; but, though his wicked will had been accomplished in many things, he perished miserably. So this man took up arms against his father, and deservedly afterwards endured dreadful persecution from his own offspring. When people asked why he had presumed such horrors against the head of the Church, he asserted with a laugh that this was the cause of so great a discord between himself and the pope: a physician had tried too harshly to treat an impatient sick man.

The unbridled king therefore laid a strong siege around Rome. He terrified the Romans by threats and force, softened them by gifts and promises, and by these means won over the citizens and gained the city. When the Romans failed him, Pope Gregory made for Apulia; there he was honourably received by the Normans, lived for four years, ministered the commands of life to the children of the Church, and completed the end of his labours. Henry Augustus then unlawfully introduced Wibert, metropolitan of Ravenna, whom they called Clement, into the Lord’s fold. Because of this a grievous and long-lasting dissension in the world punished many with a double death. The Milanese, the people of Mainz, and many others who favoured Wibert anathematized all the Gregorians and cruelly attacked them with arms. Conversely, Gregory and his followers summoned the erring Wibertines back to the unity of the Church, and excommunicated according to ecclesiastical law those who scorned to return.

Odo, count of Sutri, was a nephew of the usurper Wibert. He laboured by force and entreaties to turn to the wicked party all foreigners and natives whom he could; those who resisted and refused undue submission to the heretic he tortured or punished with a deadly death.

## IV. Disturbances in the Constantinopolitan Empire. Robert Guiscard’s expedition against Dyrrhachium

In such great darkness the Catholic Church groaned, praying the Lord, who is true light and justice, that, after the authors of discord had been overthrown and removed, He would grant peace and truth on earth to people of good will.

In those days eloquent Greece was shaken by a grievous storm of wars. Afflicted by vast losses, it was filled to overflowing with fear and grief. For Bitinacius, a Greek, inflamed by a spirit of excessive greed and arrogance, seized the empire, expelled Michael, emperor of Constantinople, from the kingdom, deprived of sight Michael’s son, who ought to have succeeded him in the empire, and bound him in chains in prison. He also committed to custody the two daughters of Robert Guiscard, one of whom that same young man had betrothed. The distressed Michael fled into Italy and humbly begged the Normans for aid for himself and his offspring.

The great-hearted Duke Guiscard honourably received the imperial exile, comforted him with services and favours, and eagerly promised him abundant aid. Nor was there delay: as he had promised, he made vigorous preparations for vengeance. Yet he threatened many arduous things in vain, God not willing; he was not permitted to bring to fulfilment the matter he most urgently sought.

Alexius, commander of the army, had gone into Paphlagonia at Michael’s order and had led with him the army of Greece against the Turks, who were holding Nicaea, a city of Bithynia, under siege. When he heard of the expulsion of the noble emperor and the rash tyranny of the treacherous usurper, he addressed the army and asked what ought to be done. For he was prudent and upright, bold, generous, and beloved by all. Everyone therefore favoured him and showed themselves ready at his command. He immediately urged them to besiege Byzantium unanimously and manfully wrest it from the witless tyrant ruling over them. Constantinople was accordingly enclosed by siege for several days. But through Raymond the Fleming, who was the city’s chief guard and gatekeeper, the city was opened by arrangement with the citizens. Alexius entered the imperial palace, cast Bitinacius from the royal throne, cut off his long beard, and committed him unharmed to prison custody.

Amid the rejoicing of all, Alexius took up the imperial sceptre and diadem and ruled the kingdom vigorously and nobly for thirty years, in adversity and prosperity alike. He was very wise and merciful to the poor, a strong and magnanimous warrior, gracious to soldiers, a most lavish giver of gifts, and a most devoted observer of the divine law. As soon as he began to reign, he released from chains Michael’s son, whom, as I have related, had been blinded, and gave him to the abbot of the monastery of Saint Cyrus to be guarded. Since he was, as it were, useless to the world, he became a monk there and spent all his life among God’s servants. The aforesaid hero also loved Guiscard’s daughters as though he had begotten them himself, treated them gently and piously, and raised them for nearly twenty years amid delights under his protection. Their duty was, in the morning, when the emperor rose from his bed and washed his hands, to bring a towel and an ivory comb and comb the emperor’s beard. These noble girls were assigned this easy and welcome service by the generous prince; after a long time they were restored to Count Roger of Sicily, whom the emperor favoured as a friend.

Daily the wheel of the unstable world turns;

The true words of the Thunderer prove to be fulfilled among mortals: “With the same measure with which you have measured, it shall be measured back to you” (Luke 6:28). Behold: just as Michael drove his stepfather Diogenes from the royal throne, so he himself was cast down from that same height by Bitinacius; and Bitinacius in turn was cast down by Alexius through a like expulsion.

Alexius, together with the patriarch of the imperial city and the wise men and senators of the Greek realm, determined that the holy empire should not be restored to Michael, who had fled to the public enemies and had committed himself and all that was his to the faithless Normans [Col. 0519D]. For it is their custom not to restore an empire to their allies, but to seize it; and, having stripped them of their honours, utterly to subjugate in cruel fashion those whom they ought to liberate from others and assist in obtaining the offices due to them. Therefore Alexius admitted into his friendship the English who, after King Harold had been slain, had left Albion with the magnates of the kingdom and sailed from the face of King William through the Pontus into Thrace. He openly entrusted to them the principal palace and the imperial treasures; indeed, he appointed them guardians of his person and possessions. From the four quarters of the world companies of warriors assembled against him in military service, and made many attempts to deprive him of life and empire. Yet they laboured mightily in vain. For, under God’s protection, he escaped many snares of his enemies [Col. 0520A], and in his old age made his son John partner in the empire. Thus all who consider wisely may plainly perceive that no one can cast down or destroy him whom God defends and sustains.

While, therefore, as we have said, storms of so many disturbances raged in Illyricum, and Michael, with tears and complaints, was urging the Italians to come to his aid, Robert Guiscard assembled from the whole duchy of Apulia and Calabria a strong army of Normans and Lombards. Having prepared a powerful fleet, he entered the harbour of Otranto; then, favourable winds blowing, he crossed the sea and landed at Dyrrhachium. The townsmen resisted manfully, but at the end of June he besieged the city. In his army, indeed, he had no more than ten thousand [Col. 0520B] fighting men. He terrified his adversaries not by numbers but by the strength of his men, and invaded Greece—warlike from the ancient times of Adrastus and Agamemnon. Robert Giffard, William of Grandmesnil, and other most valiant young warriors who had recently come from Neustria were present on this expedition. Mark Bohemond, Guiscard’s son by a Norman mother, assisted his father; he led part of the army under prudent command while his father was absent, acted wisely in all things, and gave proof of the valour he would later display. His brother Roger, surnamed Borsa, remained in Apulia by his father’s command and guarded the duchy due to him by inheritance from his mother.

Emperor Alexius, aroused by the lamentation of the Dyrrhachians, gathered a great army and endeavoured by land and sea battle to crush those besieging [Col. 0520C] his city. Meanwhile, while imperial couriers were sent in every direction and troops of warriors were being gathered from the islands of the sea and the neighbouring provinces, one day Mark Bohemond went out for forage with fifty knights and happened to meet five hundred knights who were advancing in light order before the army in order to assist the besieged. As soon as they saw one another, they entered into real combat. But the Danaans could not withstand the Norman attack; they turned their backs and lost much booty. Then they lost the bronze cross which the Emperor Constantine, when about to fight Maxentius, had caused to be made after seeing a cross in heaven. Thus the Normans returned from the encounter bringing immense joy and hope of victory to their companions. [Col. 0520D] The Pelasgians, however, felt most grievous sorrow and despondency at the loss of the Lord’s cross, and laboured hard to ransom it for a talent of the greatest weight in gold. But Guiscard judged such a bargain unworthy, because he valued the bronze in the cross, for the power of Christ, more dearly than all gold. He therefore carried this cross with him amid many dangers. After his death the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Venosa reverently preserves it to this day and venerates it with other relics of the saints.

In October Emperor Alexius approached Dyrrhachium and drew up for battle his legions summoned from many nations. Battle was joined; there was great shedding of blood, and, savage Mars raging, immense loss was inflicted [Col. 0521A] upon both sides. At last the Lord looked down from heaven upon the faithful small number and steadfastness of the western pilgrims, granted them victory, and struck terror into the eastern forces that trusted in their own strength, putting them to shameful flight. Then Duke Robert, rejoicing in so noble a triumph, left Dyrrhachium and advanced farther with his army, wintering in Bulgaria. For by a siege of three months he had devastated the region around Dyrrhachium and had left there nothing by which men or horses could subsist.

## V. Robert Guiscard comes to Italy to aid Pope Gregory against Emperor Henry. He takes Rome by assault. At Gregory’s urging, he spares the city.

[Col. 0521B] Then envoys of the Romans came to Duke Robert with apostolic letters, and, respectfully greeting him, said:

> “Pope GREGORY, most valiant duke, humbly and earnestly entreats you, as a father his son, that your unconquerable excellence swiftly come to the aid of the Apostolic See, and that for the love of God you place no excuse before this assistance. For Henry, king of the Germans, is besieging Rome and holds the pope, together with the clergy adhering to him, confined in the fortress of Crescentius. There, indeed, the pope, surrounded with a company of faithful people, fears that he may be deceived and irreverently delivered into the hands of his enemies through the defection of the Quirites, who are exceedingly greedy and treacherous. We have therefore been sent to you by him, [Col. 0521C] and request your prompt help in so great a necessity. Your strength has been divinely exalted above all your enemies, and no mortal hand can withstand it so long as you serve God and obey the vicar of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles.”

On hearing this, the high-minded hero was deeply troubled. He wished to aid the venerable pope, beset by arrogant lions, as Peter had been in Herod’s prison; yet he strongly hesitated to leave his army, which he reckoned very few in number among many crafty and cruel enemies, without a leader in a foreign land, like lambs among wolves. At last, lifting the eyes of his mind to the Lord, from whom all good proceeds, he summoned his companies [Col. 0521D] with his son Bohemond and said:

> “We must always obey God, who speaks to us through the universal shepherd of the Catholic Church. With God’s help, I shall obey the pope’s command, and I shall strive to return to you as soon as I can. Meanwhile, rest prudently in this province, and be watchful among enemies on every side. If anyone presumes to attack you in war, resist manfully in the power of God. But take care not to begin hostilities, nor give the enemy an occasion for battle, nor provoke the natives until I return. I shall undertake the service laid upon me by the Lord; and, if life accompanies me, I shall return swiftly. By the soul of my father Tancred I swear, and by this oath I firmly assure you, that until I have returned to you I shall not use a bath, [Col. 0522A] my beard shall not be shaved, nor my hair cut.”

After these words the warlike soldier immediately took to sea with a few fellow-soldiers and, God guiding him, went to Apulia. From there, having gathered armed bands, he attacked Rome. When Emperor Henry learned by reliable report that Duke Robert had overcome the emperor of Constantinople and had suddenly arrived, like lightning, with immense force to aid the pope, he carefully considered the various possibilities and became greatly afraid. Having already made peace with certain Roman nobles, he withdrew from part of the city and afterward returned to the western parts of his realm. He preferred to depart honourably, sound and free, rather than await the furious president of the contest and be caught in the whirlwind of sudden conflict.

While such grave tumults and so many storms of war raged in the world, and the kingdoms of the earth were tossed like a ship amid the waves of the sea, the venerable Robert, abbot of Saint Euphemia, after returning to Calabria from the war at Dyrrhachium, began to fall ill on the second day before the Kalends of December, having, as was reported, taken poison in food. A certain man, a Saracen by birth, served the monastery of Brixia in the baker’s craft. He had married the sister of Prior William, son of Ingrannus, and, for some hidden and quite trifling reason, bore secret hatred against the abbot. Therefore, at the devil’s prompting, he poisoned the abbot’s dish, imitating his forefather Ishmael, who sought by deadly sport [Col. 0522C] to afflict innocent Isaac. The man of God then lay ill for thirteen days, while the monks mourned; having made confession and received holy communion, he died on the second day before the Ides of December. He was buried in the church of Saint Mary the Mother of God, which he himself had built from its foundations. It was decreed that his anniversary should be reverently celebrated each year in remembrance of him. This is gladly done by the monks, whom he had endeavoured to rear in God’s house like a father raising his sons. It is also customary on that day to distribute abundant alms to the poor for their departed pastor.

As Guiscard approached, the swelling Romans assembled and judged it intolerable that the head of the world should be attacked by foreign persecutors. Encouraged, therefore, by many exhortations, they advanced to meet him under arms. But at once, when the Normans—exceedingly hardened in warfare—charged, they were repulsed. Then the victors, mingled with the fleeing citizens, entered the city and, by command of the impetuous duke, set fire to the buildings. Thus Guiscard opened for himself a way into Rome by sword and flame, and thereafter none of the citizens dared utter a word against him. Then, as he came to the tower of Crescentius, the pope came out to meet him with the clergy, gave thanks for his exertion and aid, absolved him from his offences in return for his obedience, and fervently wished for him God’s eternal blessing.

After their reciprocal conference, and after the pope had set forth an account of his complaints, the angry duke added this threat:

> “The Roman [Col. 0523A] citizens are most wicked and faithless, and for the innumerable benefits bestowed upon them they have been, and always will be, ungrateful to God and His saints. Rome, once called the head of the world and the remedy for sinners, has now become a habitation of dragons and a pit of every wickedness. Therefore I shall destroy this den of thieves by sword or flame and put its filthy, criminal inhabitants to death. The persecution of the bishop which the Jews began, the Romans have persistently sought to complete. Did not the Jews crucify Christ, and the Romans likewise make martyrs of Christ’s members, Peter and Paul? What shall I say of Linus and Cletus, Clement and Alexander, Sixtus and Telesphorus, Callistus and Urban, Cornelius and Fabian? All these strove through pastoral care to heal the sick, [Col. 0523B] and were wrongfully slain by their own fellow citizens, whom they were endeavouring to save. Finally, what shall I relate concerning Sebastian, whom they shot with arrows and hung in a sewer on a *gumfus* [reading uncertain]? What of Lawrence, whom they placed upon an iron gridiron and, with coals beneath, roasted like a fish? What of Hippolytus, whom they tore apart after binding him to untamed horses? What of Hermes, Tiburtius, Zeno, Valentine, and the other saints, whose number is beyond human knowledge? Report maintains, and the testimony of many confirms, that all Rome is drenched with the precious blood of martyrs, and that innumerable bodies of saints lie hidden in the Romans’ latrines. The same cruelty which then raged among pagans now raves among false Christians, [Col. 0523C] who, lured by greed, favour the profane and assist mad heretics against the Catholic Church. Therefore no mercy should be shown them. I shall punish the wicked with the avenging sword, set the blood-stained city on fire, and, with God’s help, repopulate it with peoples from beyond the Alps and restore it in better condition.”

Then the pope fell at the duke’s feet and, pouring forth tears, said:

> “Far be it from me that Rome should be destroyed on my account! For I was chosen not for the destruction of the city but for the salvation of the people. I prefer to follow our Lord Jesus Christ in death rather than wickedly avenge my own injuries by having sinners punished. Those who despise His ordinances and savagely obstruct the order of the Church, scattering the Lord’s flock like ravening wolves, are indeed opposed to our Creator. [Col. 0523D] The injury and vengeance belong to Him, as also service and recompense. He knows His devout servants and abhors raging adversaries. Therefore we commend ourselves and what is ours to His omnipotence, and with a well-disposed heart pray that He may cut away with the censorial sword what opposes the sacred law, and direct us according to His good pleasure.”

Thus the pope calmed the angry duke. Having accepted his counsel, he left the tower of Crescentius with the clergy who followed him and, escorted by the duke with a strong force, went to Alba. Ascanius Julius, son of Aeneas, founded this city, and the Emperor Constantine gave it to Pope Saint Silvester. The duke, having received the apostolic blessing, hastened his journey to the sea and [Col. 0524A] swiftly made for his troops across the strait, as he had sworn to them.

## VI. In Robert’s absence the Greeks attack the Normans. Robert Guiscard returns to Greece. The Normans return to Italy.

Meanwhile the crafty emperor of the Greeks, when he learned that Robert had gone to Italy, thought that he could weaken the Normans, deprived of their duke’s presence.
