He rose up, assembled many companies, and compelled the unwilling Normans to battle. Once battle was joined, the Normans were initially found weak and, for many reasons, were frightened and almost defeated at the beginning of the struggle. For when they weighed their own small numbers, the absence of their fortunate duke, and the multitude of their enemies, they nearly took flight before fighting. But when Bohemond wavered and trembled in the conflict with his troops, [Col. 0524B] anxiously calling upon God from his heart, the assistance of divine mercy came, and a voice of this kind thundered from above:

> “Bohemond, what are you doing? Fight bravely. For He who aided your father will likewise aid you, if you trust in Him and faithfully serve Him.”

Revived and strengthened by this voice, the Normans advanced and fiercely charged the Pelasgians. By their attack the Achaeans were suddenly driven back and, turning their backs, left much spoil to the needy pilgrims.

On returning from Tuscany, Guiscard found his men sufficiently elated by this victory. He too, rejoicing in so noble a triumph, gave thanks to God. But Bohemond, who had been wounded in the battle, he sent to the physicians of Salerno to be treated, [Col. 0524C] for their exceptional medical skill was renowned throughout the world.

Now the people of Dyrrhachium, seeing that the Normans had advanced far into Bulgaria and by military force acquired several provinces of the Byzantine empire, while they themselves were completely cut off from aid from the Thracians, Macedonians, and all their neighbours, often discussed anxiously among themselves how they might provide for their own desperate situation. At last the more audacious among them decided together what to do: they secretly sent envoys to the duke, asked for peace, and sincerely promised to hand over the citadel of the city to his troops. He granted their request and sent three hundred knights to receive the city. When the Normans came by night, therefore, the city [Col. 0524D] was opened; once they had been admitted, peace and security between the two parties were established.

Sichelgaita, wife of Robert Guiscard, was daughter of Guaimar, duke of Salerno, and sister of Gisulf, who had been deprived of his duchy through the greedy aggression of his brother-in-law. She hated her stepson Bohemond, fearing that through him—because he was stronger and possessed intelligence and great excellence—her son Roger would lose the duchy of Apulia and Calabria, which belonged to him by hereditary right. Accordingly, she prepared a deadly potion and sent it to the chief physicians of Salerno, among whom she had been brought up and from whom she had learned the art of poisons. They immediately understood the will of their lady and former fosterling, and [Col. 0525A] administered the poison of death to Bohemond, whom they ought to have cured. Having received it, he fell sick almost to death and at once informed his father of his illness by messenger.

The crafty duke immediately perceived his wife’s plots. Sadly summoning her before him, he questioned her thus:

> “Is my lord Bohemond alive?”

She answered: “I do not know, lord.”

But he said: “Bring me the text of the Holy Gospel and a sword.”

When these had been brought, he took the sword and swore over the sacred book:

> “Hear, Sichelgaita! By this Holy Gospel I swear that if my son Bohemond dies of the sickness by which he is held, I shall kill you with this sword.”

Terrified beyond measure by this accusation, she prepared a healing antidote and immediately dispatched a messenger to Salerno to her physicians, through whom she had prepared death. By pressing flatteries and prayers he urged them to aid her in her peril. When the chief physicians heard that their mistress’s fraud had been discovered and that she was in danger, and prayed that the duke’s terrible threats might not be carried out against them in the future, they strove with every resource of the medical art to cure the youth whom they had harmed. Through the help of God, who had decreed through him to crush the Turks and Hagarenes, enemies of the Christian faith, the sick man recovered. Yet throughout the rest of his life he remained pale because of the poison with which he had been infected.

Meanwhile this deceitful and ingenious woman turned many things over in her mind; endlessly goaded by extreme fear, she considered that if her messenger delayed in crossing [Col. 0525C] the sea and the sick man died before his arrival, she would not escape the death by her husband’s sword which had been sworn upon her. Accordingly, she devised another evasive scheme, brutal and altogether detestable. Alas! she poisoned her husband. As soon as he began to fall ill, and she did not doubt his inevitable end, she gathered her retainers together with the remaining Lombards, rose by night, went to the sea, and boarded the best ships with all her people. She burned all the other ships so that the Normans could not pursue her. But when she reached the Apulian shore, a knight of her following slipped away secretly, came by night to Salerno, hurried to Bohemond, and said:

> “Get up quickly, flee, and save yourself.”

When Bohemond asked the reason, the messenger replied:

> “Your father is dead, and your stepmother is in Apulia. She is hurrying here to kill you.”

Without delay Bohemond, disturbed by so grave a report, mounted an ass, secretly left the city, and fled to Jordan, prince of Capua, his cousin. Received there in friendship, he escaped the plots and threats of his stepmother. When she arrived at Salerno and learned that the man she sought had escaped, she recognized that she had been deceived and was deeply grieved. Her son Roger, surnamed Crumena, obtained by succession from his ancestors the broad duchy on this side of the sea.

The Normans in the foreign land were burdened on every side by overwhelming anxieties. They saw their greatest and most valiant [Col. 0526A] duke endangered by a woman’s treachery; they saw the strength of their army diminished by the departure of the Lombards, who had secretly left with their mistress; and, since their ships had been burned, they could not depart for Italy without serious delay and difficulty. Therefore the high-minded duke summoned to himself Count Robert of Loritello, Geoffrey of Conversano, his nephews, Hugh the one-eyed of Clermont, William of Grandmesnil, his brother-in-law Odo Bonus-Marchisus, and his other kinsmen and nobles, and asked what they intended to do. As all whispered among themselves and offered no settled opinion, he said:

> “Divine vengeance strikes us for our sins and restrains our excessive desires. The Lord justly chastises us as His servants and plainly shows us that worldly glory ought not to be sought. Let us give Him thanks for all that He has deigned to bestow upon us, and seek with all our heart that He may always have mercy on us. Behold: we came from poor and most humble parents; we left the barren land of Constantine and homes empty of necessary things, set out, and with great fear scarcely passed through Rome. Then, by God’s gift, we acquired many great cities. Yet we must ascribe this not to our strength or merits, but to divine ordinance. Finally, because of the offences of the natives, we invaded as much of the empire of Constantinople as could be traversed in fifteen days. You know well that I was invited to defend Emperor Michael [Col. 0526C], whom his own citizens wickedly drove from the throne of empire, because I had lawfully given my daughter to his son. If it pleased God, I had resolved to subdue Constantinople, which is possessed by an unwarlike people enslaved to luxury and wantonness, to Catholic warriors, so that they might take the holy city of God, Jerusalem, from the Turks, drive back the heathen in war, and extend Christian rule. For this desire I undertook so great a labour and so perilous a struggle. But the blameless will of almighty God ordained otherwise. David wished to build God’s temple in Jerusalem, but God ordained that it should be accomplished by his son Solomon with immense rejoicing. So, as I suppose, my labour will be completed in times to come; the fruit of my labour will someday be revealed, and the incitement of such great courage will be profitably offered to our descendants. Therefore, brave men, take wise counsel and do not lose your former courage, which I have often proved in arduous and difficult circumstances. I am one man of earth and, like the rest, mortal. But you are many and flourish, by God’s bounty, in many gifts. The famous deeds proclaimed far and wide were performed by you; never in any histories have greater deeds been recorded as accomplished by so few and humble men than those which you, with God’s help, have done. Therefore choose from among yourselves one stronger and wiser, and appoint him your leader. Do not lose, in a short time, the fertile land gained through great labour. [Col. 0527A] My son Bohemond, if he still has life and health, will strive to come to your aid as quickly as possible.”

As the duke continued these and similar words, Peter the Frank and the other members of his household, carefully considering his speech, said:

> “In the matter which you command us to undertake, there is immense danger and the greatest difficulty. The enemies are innumerable and we are few; the powerful and crafty emperor is greatly opposed to us, and, while you restrained us, we have often grievously offended him in many ways. We cannot resist his strength and broad power, for he rules many kingdoms and nations. Would that we might return in peace and safety to the homes from which we departed!”

[Col. 0527B] Hearing this, the duke groaned deeply, began to call upon God with tears, and lamented his son thus:

> “Alas, wretched me, surrounded by so many misfortunes! In former times I harmed many and committed unjust evils. Now the evils which I long deserved have found me all at once. Supreme God, spare me now! Merciful God, have pity on me, a sinner! Mighty God, help Your people whom I have brought here! My son Bohemond, equal in courage and wisdom to Epaminondas of Thebes, where shall I find you? Noble champion Bohemond, fit to be compared in warfare with Thessalian Achilles or Frankish Roland: do you live, or are you held fast by destruction? What has befallen you? What has become of your excellence? If you were safe and present here as I left you when I went to Tuscany, you would possess the rich region of Bulgaria won by our arms. For I know that, if you live, you possess such vigour that, should you be present at my death by God’s decree, you would by God’s help in no way lose the right which I acquired by war. Come then, excellent fellow-soldiers, provide cautiously for yourselves, and consider how far you are from your homes. Remember how great were the deeds of the Normans, and how our parents often withstood and bravely overcame the Franks, Bretons, and men of Le Mans. Recall how great were the things you accomplished under my leadership in Italy and Sicily. You gained Salerno and Bari, Brindisi and Taranto, Bisignano and Reggio, Syracuse and Palermo, Cosenza and Castrogiovanni, with many other cities and towns. Under my leadership and with God’s help [Col. 0527D] you overcame Gisulf, duke of Salerno, Wazo, count of Naples, and other most powerful princes. Therefore do not become base now that the effort of your former greatness of spirit has been lost. By common election appoint one of yourselves, as I have said, as leader, and keep for yourselves with distinction the rich provinces which you have already gained.”

None of those who were present at these events dared undertake such a duchy; all preferred to consider the security offered by flight. Then, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1085, Robert Guiscard, illustrious duke of Apulia and almost without equal in our age, having made confession, been cleansed of his sins, and fortified by reception of the saving Eucharist, was taken from the world when the hour of death came. He was not cast down by military strength but undone by a woman’s malice—by which the first Adam was driven from the seat of Paradise—not injured by weapons but by poison. After his death, the Normans embalmed his body with salt and requested from the emperor permission to return peacefully to their homeland. Although the emperor rejoiced that he had been delivered from a terrible enemy, he nevertheless mourned deeply in pity for the dead duke, who had never fled from battle. He graciously granted leave to those who wished to return to Italy with the corpse of their prince and all their possessions. To others, who wished to remain with him and serve him, he promised generous pay. Thus those who had formerly fought bravely against Byzantium thereafter served it faithfully. Returning to Apulia, they carried the duke’s body [Col. 0528B] to Venosa and buried it there with great mourning in the monastery of the Holy Trinity. The venerable Abbot Berengar, son of Ernald, son of Helgo, presided over that monastery. The pious archimandrite Theodoric had raised him at Utica, and Abbot Robert had then brought him with himself to Calabria. Afterwards Pope Alexander consecrated him abbot of the monastery at Venosa; and some years later, because of the merit of his life and his wise learning, Pope Urban promoted him to the episcopate of the aforesaid city.

## VII. The vain confidence of Odo, bishop of Bayeux, who aspired to the papacy. King William orders him detained.

[Col. 0528C] While the storms previously mentioned raged in the world, certain Roman diviners investigated who would succeed Hildebrand in the papacy, and learned that after Gregory’s death Odo would be Roman pope. On hearing this, Odo, bishop of Bayeux, who with his brother King William ruled the Normans and the English, thought little of the powers and riches of the western kingdom unless he also ruled more extensively over all men on earth by right of the papacy. He sent to Rome, bought himself a palace, bound the senators of the Quirites to himself in friendship by great gifts, and adorned his palace at great expense with superfluous furnishings. He enlisted Hugh, count of Chester, and a great company of distinguished knights, entreated them to go with him to Italy [Col. 0528D], and lavishly added enormous promises to his entreaties. Since the Normans are fickle and eager to see foreign lands, they immediately agreed with the presumptuous bishop, for whom rule over Albion and Neustria was insufficient. They resolved to abandon the great estates they possessed in the western regions and promised on oath to accompany the aforesaid bishop beyond the Po.

The prudent King William learned of this preparation, but did not approve of it, judging that it would greatly harm his kingdom and many others. Therefore he swiftly crossed to England, and unexpectedly encountered Bishop Odo on the Isle of Wight as he wished, with great pomp, to sail to Normandy. There [Col. 0529A] the king assembled the leading men of the kingdom in the royal hall and spoke thus:

> “Excellent nobles, listen carefully to my words and, I pray, give me sound counsel. Before I crossed into Normandy, I entrusted the government of England to my brother, the bishop of Bayeux. In Normandy many rose against me, and, so to speak, both those close to me and outsiders attacked me. My son Robert, and the young warriors whom I had raised and armed, rebelled against me; my faithless dependants and neighbouring enemies gladly joined them. Yet under the protection of God, whose servant I am, they achieved nothing, nor gained anything from me except iron in their wounds. I cowed by terror the Angevins massed against me and prepared for battle, and in the same manner restrained the rebellious men of Le Mans by arms and force. Occupied beyond the sea with these affairs, I remained there a long time and laboured diligently in the public interest. Meanwhile my brother grievously oppressed England, despoiled churches of their lands and revenues, stripped them of ornaments furnished by their predecessors, and seduced my knights, who ought to have defended England against the Danes, Irish, and other enemies most hostile to me. He plans, in contempt of me, to draw them across the Alps into foreign kingdoms. Excessive anxiety presses upon my heart, especially on account of God’s churches, which he has afflicted. The Christian kings who ruled before me loved God’s Church and enriched it with honours and gifts of many kinds; hence, as we believe, they now rest in [Col. 0529C] a pleasant abode, rejoicing in blessed recompense. Adelbert and Edwin, Saint Oswald, Æthelwulf and Alfred, Edward the Elder and Edgar, and my kinsman and most dear lord Edward gave riches to the holy Church, the bride of God. But my brother, to whom I entrusted guardianship of the whole kingdom, violently plundered its wealth, cruelly oppressed the poor, enticed my knights away by a frivolous hope, and harassed the entire kingdom, shaking it with unjust exactions. Consider carefully what should be done in consequence, and, I pray, tell me.”

> [Note: [Col. 0529D] Let the churches of Worcester and Evesham serve as examples of all. Their complaints are preserved in the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 133, col. 1, where the following is read: “A certain Odo, bishop of Bayeux and earl of Kent, namely the brother of King William, asked for and received from his brother the king all the lands . . . which rightly belonged to the abbey [of Worcester] . . . and thus we lost them.” Likewise, from the Register of Evesham, [Col. 0530D] ibid., p. 151: “In the year of the Lord 1077 . . . the king sent here a certain monk from the monastery called Cerasii, named Walter, most thoroughly educated in both liberal and grammatical letters. This abbot, through the unjust power of Odo, the king’s brother, bishop of Bayeux, lost twenty-eight vills.” Dom Bouquet, book VII, p. 614.]

Since all feared so great a man and hesitated to pronounce judgment against him, the high-minded king said:

> “Harmful rashness must always be restrained, and no one should be spared for any favour to the detriment of the commonwealth. Therefore seize this man who disturbs the land, and carefully guard him so that he may not grow stronger for worse.”

Since no one dared lay hands upon a bishop, the king himself first seized him. When Odo protested, “I am a cleric and a minister of the Lord; it is not lawful to condemn a bishop without the pope’s judgment,” the prudent king said:

> “I [Col. 0530A] do not condemn a cleric or prelate, but seize my earl, whom I set over my kingdom in my stead, because I wish him to render an account of the stewardship entrusted to him.”

Thus royal power captured the aforesaid bishop, had him taken to Normandy, and imprisoned him in the fortress of Rouen. There he was kept in confinement under careful guard for four years, that is, until the end of the king’s life. Once the head of unrest had been removed, the agitation of the knights subsided, and the king’s foresight strongly fortified his realm within and without.

Behold, in this man we see openly fulfilled what Fulgentius says in the book of *Mythologies*: “He who seeks more than is permitted will be less than he is.” The bishopric of Bayeux, the earldom of Kent abounding in immense wealth, and royal power shared with his brother throughout England and Normandy were insufficient for one cleric who strove to be set over the whole world. No divine calling or canonical election compelled him to this; rather, it was the unrestrained presumption of an incurable greed. Therefore he lost what he had, groaned in prison, and left an example for posterity not to gape after honours.

## VIII. Death of Queen Matilda. Her epitaph. Rebellion of the men of Le Mans. King William orders the number of English soldiers to be enrolled.

At this time, in the seventh indiction, [1083], Matilda, queen of the English, fell ill. Troubled by a prolonged sickness, she acknowledged and earnestly bewailed her sins; after all that Christian custom requires had duly been performed, strengthened by the saving sacrament, she died on the third day before the Nones of November. Then her body was carried to the monastery of the Holy Trinity, which she herself had built for nuns at Caen, and was reverently buried between choir and altar by many bishops and abbots. Monks and clerics celebrated her funeral rites, together with a multitude of poor people to whom in life she had often given help in Christ’s name.

A memorial above her was wonderfully constructed of gold and gems, and the following epitaph was graciously inscribed in letters of gold:

> This splendid structure of a beautiful tomb covers  
> Matilda, distinguished in character, royal offspring.  
> Her father was the Flemish duke; her mother was Adela,  
> [Col. 0530D] daughter of Robert, king of the French people,  
> and sister of Henry, who possessed the royal throne.  
> Joined in marriage to the magnificent King William,
Present seat and present church she made,

enriching them from her own resources with so many lands  
and so many honorable possessions, and dedicating them under her care.

She was a comforter of the poor, a lover of piety,  
scattering her wealth—poor for herself, rich for the needy.

Thus she entered into the fellowship of life without end,  
on the first day of November, after first light.

[Col. 0531A] The abbey at Caen, dedicated to the holy and undivided Trinity, was vigorously governed for forty-seven years by Abbess Matilda. She carefully brought up and regularly instructed Cecilia, the king’s daughter, and many others in the service of God. Upon Matilda’s death, the noble Cecilia succeeded her and, during the reign of her brother King Henry, fulfilled a mother’s office for many years. Afterwards the daughter of William the consul, son of Stephen of Blois, assumed the government of the same church, but, overtaken by an untimely death, held it only a short time.

After the death of the glorious Queen Matilda, King William, during the almost four years that he survived her, suffered grievously as many storms of tribulation rose against him. For certain men of Maine, who are always stirred, as it were, by a natural restlessness, and by their instability disturb peace and are themselves disturbed, [Col. 0531B] took up arms against King William and brought great losses upon themselves and many others. Humbert the viscount, son-in-law of Count William of Nevers, first offended the king on certain minor grounds; but when these later grew more serious, he abandoned his castles of Beaumont and Fresnay and, with his wife and all his followers, withdrew as a public enemy to the castle called Sainte-Suzanne. This stronghold, to which he fled, stands above the river Erve, on a steep rock, at the border of Maine and Anjou. There he summoned a force of soldiers and relentlessly inflicted losses, and the fear of losses, upon the Normans who were attempting to defend the district of Maine. For he was illustrious by birth, outstanding in intelligence and worth, ardent in great courage and boldness, and widely famous for these distinctions. The guardians of the city of Le Mans and of the surrounding towns, frequently harassed by Humbert’s attacks, reported their misfortune to King William and sought his assistance.

King William therefore promptly summoned an army of Normans and called up that portion of the men of Maine who adhered to him; with a strong force he entered the hostile country. But he could not besiege the castle of Sainte-Suzanne, inaccessible because of the cliffs and the dense vineyards that surrounded it; nor could he constrain the enemy within it as he wished, because Humbert provisioned himself vigorously and had broad routes of access. The king therefore built a certain fortified post in the valley of Beugy and stationed there a great force of soldiers to restrain the enemy; he himself returned to Neustria because of important affairs of the kingdom. The king’s household, commanded by Alan Rufus, count of the Bretons, excelled in wealth, feasts, and military expenditure. But the garrison force strove to match them in courage and numbers. For proven soldiers came running to Humbert from Aquitaine, Burgundy, and other provinces of France, eagerly desiring with all their strength to assist him and display their own prowess. Consequently the castle of Sainte-Suzanne was enriched from the losses of the men of Beugy and grew daily stronger and stronger for resistance. Many wealthy Norman and English magnates were captured; by their ransoms the viscount, Robert of Burgundy, whose granddaughter he had married, and his other supporters were honorably enriched. Thus for three years Humbert resisted the Normans and, enriched by the resources of his enemies, remained unconquered.

[Note: [Col. 0531D] This Robert, brother of William I, count of Nevers, withdrew to Geoffrey Martel, count of Anjou, who had married Agnes, the sister of Matilda, Robert’s paternal grandmother. Geoffrey granted him the lordship of Craon, which he had taken from Suhard because of Suhard’s treachery. Having also received in marriage from Geoffrey Havise or Blanche, daughter and heiress of Geoffrey I, lord of Sablé, Robert became head of the lords of Craon and Sablé. Humbert married Robert’s granddaughter, also named Ermengard—daughter of William I, count of Nevers, and Ermengard, countess of Tonnerre [Col. 0532D]—and by her had three children: Ralph, son-in-law of King Henry I of England and viscount of Beaumont; Humbert; and Godchildis, abbess of Étival. (Anselm, *Historia genealogica magnorum Franciae officiorum*, vol. III, p. 197; Dom Bouquet, book VII, p. 616.)]

[Col. 0532B] In this war Robert of Vieux-Pont, Robert of Uxey, and other distinguished and deeply lamented Norman knights were killed. For on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December, while a Norman troop was making an attack upon the enemy, a certain beardless boy, hidden beside the road among thorns, loosed an arrow and struck Richer of Laigle, son of Engenulf, mortally beneath the eye. His enraged companions rushed together, immediately seized the boy, and wished to kill him in vengeance for the most noble baron. But the dying Richer came to his aid. As they were about to cut the boy’s throat, the wounded man cried out with all the effort he could muster: “Let him go, for the love of God. It is because my sins require it that I must die thus.” The assailant was at once released. [Col. 0532C] The lamented hero confessed his sins to his companions; before he could be brought to a town, he died. His body was then carried to a monastery of monks which his father Engenulf had built on his own estate in honor of Saint Sulpicius, bishop of Bourges. There it was buried, amid the immense grief of his parents and kinsmen, by Gilbert, the venerable bishop of Évreux.

This man was rightly mourned by those who knew him, because he was adorned in his life with many virtues. He was strong, handsome, and agile in body; faithful to God’s law; submissive and humble toward religious persons; prudent and eloquent in secular affairs; and calm and generous in all his conduct. He had as wife Judith, daughter of Richard Goz of Avranches, and thus sister of Hugh, count of Chester. By her he fathered Gilbert of Laigle, Engenulf, Matilda, and many other sons and daughters. Gilbert alone, after the others had died, succeeded as heir to his father’s worth and honor. He married Juliana, daughter of Geoffrey, the most vigorous count of Mortain, [Col. 0533A] who bore Richer, Engenulf, Geoffrey, and Gilbert. The two middle sons perished by shipwreck, on the seventh day before the Kalends of December, with William Ætheling, son of King Henry, and many other nobles. Matilda married the powerful Robert de Mowbray, earl of Northumbria, who in the same year rebelled against William Rufus, king of England. But shortly afterwards he was captured and grew old childless, spending almost thirty-four years in the prison of the aforesaid king and of Henry, his brother. Now I shall return to the matter from which I have digressed briefly.

In January, William de Warenne, Baldric of Châteaureil, son of Nicholas, and Gilbert of Laigle, wishing to avenge the death of his brother Richer, attempted with a strong force of Normans to attack the townsmen. But they gained nothing except steel in their wounds. Then William, count of Évreux, was captured, and Matthiellus of Guitot, son of Geoffrey the Little, was mortally wounded. He was then carried to his lodging by grieving squires and fellow-soldiers. A priest was immediately summoned; he confessed his sins, received the holy viaticum, and prepared himself to await death.

The Normans who guarded the fortification in the valley of Beugy, afflicted by severe losses and diminished by the swords of very brave young warriors, feared still worse things for themselves. Since they could overcome Humbert neither by courage [Col. 0533C] nor by fortune, they changed their purpose and plan and attempted to recall him to the king’s friendship. Humbert nevertheless, although this war had greatly strengthened him in wealth and power, preferred the security of tranquil peace and prudently assented to the efforts of the mediators. Without delay envoys were sent to the king in England. When the king heard that Hervey the Breton, whom he had appointed commander of the troops, and Richer and other most valiant champions had perished, and learned that his adversary was advancing with good fortune and being strengthened daily against him, he took precautions lest the affairs of his men, through excessive stubbornness, be plunged into a worse condition. He therefore prudently forgave Humbert all his former offenses. Humbert, having received security, crossed the sea [Col. 0533D] to the king; friendship was made between them, and he honorably recovered all his paternal right. The Normans and the men of Maine rejoiced, having been variously harassed by four years of conflict. Thereafter, as long as King William lived, the aforesaid hero remained faithful to him, gladly held his honor, rejoicing in freedom, and at his death left it to his sons Ralph and Humbert.

At this time [1086] King William caused the military force of the English kingdom to be enrolled and found sixty thousand soldiers, whom he ordered all to be ready whenever necessary. For Cnut the Younger, king of the Danes, was then preparing a huge fleet and intended to come to England—which his forefathers Swein and Cnut had formerly subdued for themselves—and reclaim his right. He was devout before God in piety, great among men in power, and worthy of praise for many virtues. By his threats and preparations he had frightened the Normans who inhabited England. But, hindered by various events while King Noth was alive, he had not accomplished his purpose. Under the reign of William the Younger, when many ships stood ready on the shore and a favorable wind was already blowing, and sailors were placing the armed army aboard the ships for England, King Cnut, wishing to discover God’s will, entered a church, humbly prostrated himself before the altar, and with tears prayed God to direct his journey according to His good pleasure. [Col. 0534B] Then his brother entered the church. Seeing the king alone prostrate before the altar, he began to reflect how great a labor and how grave a danger threatened so many thousands through one man, and how, if that man were removed, a swift and violent change would follow. Without delay he drew his sword, cut off the praying king’s head, and immediately fled into exile. At this sad news the army was at once dispersed and each man returned to his own business. Finally the elders of the people made Calomanoth, brother of the king, king, while the parricide remained in exile. They honorably buried the body of King Cnut in a basilica; many miracles were divinely performed at his tomb. A great monastery of monks was built there, and a monastic order was regularly established, as it is observed at Evesham in England. From there the first monks came to the Danes and diligently demonstrated monastic practice, while the barbarians marvelled.

The aforesaid king is rightly honored by monks and other men of religious life. For he was the first to reform the customs of his people, who were newly converted and exceedingly undisciplined; he established metropolitan and episcopal sees according to the decrees of the canons; and he invited monks, formerly hated and unknown among the Danes, generously assigning them a suitable place of habitation in his kingdom.

## IX. Translation of the Body of Blessed Nicholas of Myra

[Col. 0534D]

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1087, in the tenth indiction, on the ninth day of May, the body of Saint Nicholas, archbishop and confessor, was translated from Myra to Bari. John, archdeacon of the church of Bari, gives an eloquent account of this translation—how and by whom it was accomplished.

[Note: [Col. 0533D] *The Translation of Saint Nicholas, Bishop, from the Lycian city of Myra to the Apulian town of Bari or Barum*, written by John, archdeacon of Bari, at the command of Urso, archbishop of Bari and Canosa, about the year of the Lord 1088 or thereabouts; in Surius, 9 May.]

From his account I am pleased to extract a little and insert mention of so glorious an event in this small work, for the knowledge of diligent readers who have not yet seen John’s work, should it happen that they deign to examine this.

[Col. 0535A] In the time of Emperor Alexius, the Turks and other pagan peoples, desiring to exercise their fury, crossed their borders; and, God permitting it, they devastated Lycia and other Christian regions, destroyed churches because of the sins of the Christian people, violated crosses, images of Christ, and sanctuaries in many ways, and consigned many cities with their inhabitants to fire. Thus they raged for many years and inflicted countless massacres upon Christians.

Myra, therefore, the metropolis of Lycia, was brought under Turkish dominion and, because its citizens’ sins required it, was emptied of its own inhabitants. Meanwhile men of Bari, who had set out with three ships for Antioch on business, approached the harbor of Myra joyfully and sent ahead a certain stranger to discover the condition of the basilica of Blessed Nicholas, which stood in the fortress. On his return he reported that many Turks were present and had assembled for the funeral rites of the lord of the fortress, who lay dead there. Hearing this, the men of Bari immediately spread their sails and turned their ships’ prows toward Antioch; after a few days’ favorable voyage, they reached Myra. There they found a Venetian ship and, as is customary, began mutually to inquire about various matters. Certain men of Bari were known to and friendly with the Venetians, and they began in turn to discuss the saint’s body. The Venetians did not hesitate to express what they had long conceived in their minds. They confessed that they had iron crowbars and hammers ready and, since they ought to attempt their intended plan, did not delay dining there. When the men of Bari heard this, they were inflamed with an even greater desire to begin and complete the undertaking—not so much for their own glory and honor and the greatness of their whole country as from love for so eminent a confessor. They therefore completed the business for which they had gone to Antioch and, guided by God, returned from there as quickly as possible. As they prosperously approached the shore of Myra and, their first zeal now failing, wished to sail on past it, God commanded otherwise: a contrary north wind rose, while the south wind lay still, and compelled the sailors of Bari to remain there. Understanding God’s will, they at once took up their weapons, left a few men drawn up in formation to guard the ships in the meantime, and the rest, armed and cautious as though going to meet enemies, hastened toward the church, which was about three miles from the shore. At last they entered the church enclosure, laid down their arms, humbly entered the holy building, and earnestly invoked the holy bishop. When each had finished praying, they began to ask the sacristans where Saint Nicholas’s body lay. The latter immediately showed them the place and, drawing out some of the holy liquid, gave it to them. Then Lupus, a priest of Bari, received some of the holy oil in a glass flask and placed it aloft for safer keeping. By chance, while they were speaking, it fell onto the marble pavement, but remained unbroken, to everyone’s astonishment.

[Col. 0536A] Then the men of Bari began, as if merely attempting conversation, to speak with the three monks who had been left to guard the relics: “We wish to remove the holy body from here and transport it to our own country. For this purpose the Roman pontiff sent us, and we have come in three ships. If you will consent to this, we shall give you one hundred gold solidi from each vessel.”

On hearing this, the monks were immediately astonished and afraid, and said: “How dare we begin this, when no mortal has hitherto wished to attempt it with impunity? Who would be rash enough to become buyer or seller in so great a transaction? What thing so precious and wonderful could be purchased for so great a treasure? If the lords of the lands have not dared to undertake this except by prayers and supplications, how will you be able to accomplish it? Therefore cease to pursue such a crime any further, for it is not pleasing to the divine majesty. Yet make the attempt: behold the place.” Saying this, they thought that what the others wished could not be done. For nearly two hundred Olympiads had passed since Blessed Nicholas—who is recorded to have attended the synod of Nicaea, held under Pope Saint Sylvester and Emperor Constantine—departed from the world; and until then no one had been able either secretly to steal any of his relics, openly to carry them off by force, or obtain them from the Lord through prayers. The men of Bari, however, were afraid because they were few among many in a foreign place, the sun was inclining toward sunset, and the return to their ships was dangerous. [Col. 0536C] But strengthened by God, they first seized the monks and guarded them carefully under restraint. They also stationed lookouts more cautiously, who watched for people approaching from every direction; they themselves, divided here and there with weapons, stood along the paths. Thus forty-four most valiant young men stood outside prepared to resist, while the two priests Lupus and Grimoald, with a few others, carried out what had to be done in the church and began the prayers called litanies. But overwhelmed by excessive fear, they could not utter clearly what they had begun.

Meanwhile Matthew, one of the sailors, boldly seized an iron hammer, struck and broke the marble pavement, beneath which he found cement. When this had been reduced and removed, the upper part of a marble sarcophagus at once appeared. Joy arose from this, and they dug more and more eagerly, delaying neither to break up and scatter the old joint fastened with mortar by means of a small axe nor to cast out the fragments. When these were thrown outside and the stone vessel was uncovered, the leading young man struck it with a hammer and broke one side. A most fragrant odor issued out, filling those present with the wonderful delight of its sweetness. The aforesaid young man then put in his hand and first felt that a great quantity of liquid was present, so that the same sarcophagus, which was not small, seemed filled nearly to the middle. He then immersed his right hand, found the most precious treasure that he sought with the utmost desire, and boldly began to draw it out quickly. At last, in seeking the head, he entered wholly into the mass of liquid and, searching here and there with feet and hands as necessary, found the head; finally he emerged, his garments and whole body wet with the life-giving liquid. This was done, therefore, nearly eight hundred years after the death of Saint Nicholas, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May [1087].

Since no chest was available and the unexpected event had occurred so quickly, the men of Bari wrapped the relics as best they could in the tunic of the priest Lupus; they all immediately followed Lupus as he carried the sacred burden. Praising the Lord for their most holy spoil—which they had taken not from enemies but from the Lord’s treasury—they hurried to the shore. Some also carried off fragments of the marble sarcophagus which they had broken; from these, many altars and altar-slabs throughout Italy were rashly consecrated by many bishops. When they came to the harbor, a dispute arose as to in whose ship the cherished burden should be placed. For all desired to have with them so great a companion and patron. At last all peacefully agreed that Matthew’s ship should carry it, provided that he first pledged to them by oath his good fellowship. This was done.

They gladly boarded the boat, wrapped the relics in another new white cloth, and placed them in a wooden vessel in which sailors customarily kept their wine. There is no need to relate at length the grief of the people of Myra when they learned of the loss done to them. For as soon as the inhabitants of the fortress of Myra—which is situated upon a hill about one mile from the church—heard this report, they hurried together from every direction. Bitterly angry and deeply sorrowful, they hastened to the shore; mourning their shepherd and lord taken away, they tore out their hair and beards and, wailing, sang this mournful song:

> What time is this—alas!—that has brought  
> Such misery upon us?  
> Why do we behold the disgrace  
> Of our homeland?
>
> For God’s gifts, preserved through many years,  
> We have now suddenly lost  
> Through an easy act of theft.
>
> Until now the land of Lycia was enriched  
> And exceedingly adorned by this heavenly treasure;  
> Celebrated throughout the whole world  
> With outstanding praises,  
> And defended by the merits of its great-hearted father.
>
> Unhappy Myra, despoiled of your worship  
> And your gifts, you shall remain sorrowful forever.
>
> O Father Nicholas, venerated throughout the world,  
> [Col. 0537D] Why do you forsake our country—indeed, your own?
>
> Here you were born and raised by holy parents;  
> Here you were a devout child and youth,  
> A devout man and old man.
>
> Here you were father and lord, shepherd and gracious guardian,  
> In this homeland, hitherto both living and dead.
>
> Whenever adversities oppressed this wretched place,  
> It immediately sought your aid, gracious Father.
>
> You were present in adversity, our sole hope of salvation,  
> Giving protection to the suppliant peoples.
>
> To whose prayers, venerable protector, you then showed favor,  
> Receiving their vows and granting what they asked.
>
> From every quarter, from all parts of the world,  
> They often ran to your sacred, life-giving tomb.
>
> Alas! Let the faithful multitude know at once that it is empty:  
> All worship and all honor will cease.
>
> For God’s gifts will be lacking, and former grace;  
> Only the name of an ancient story will remain.
>
> Shepherd, to whom do you entrust your own sheep to be fed?  
> When you leave the flock, the wolf will quickly come.
>
> [Col. 0538A] Our strength, consolation, every glory, and relief—  
> You, our sole hope, salvation, and cause of joy—
>
> Alas for us wretches! We lose all these things;  
> Hence grief and perpetual sorrow come upon us.
>
> Alas! To whom was such power granted  
> To commit so great a crime  
> And so violate this holy place?
>
> Whose rash hand treated you so badly?  
> What sacrilegious person has now committed this theft?
>
> Yet fortunate are you who bear off the rich spoil!  
> Every evil has taken possession of us unhappy people!

While the people of Myra mourned exceedingly and could not avenge their loss, the joyful men of Bari quickly cast loose their ropes. Rowing, they reached that night the island called Cacabus, and from there proceeded to the islands of Maiestra. Departing thence, they rowed with excessive haste to the places called Macri, where they remained for three days because the north wind was against them. Greatly disturbed, they began to doubt whether they had Saint Nicholas’s body with them, or whether he himself no longer wished to be carried by them. Then Eustace, one of them, was reproved for his doubt in a vision and was greatly terrified while, in the vision, his tongue was made bloody by the bites of swallows.

Thereafter, by common resolution, they brought forth the small portions of the relics which some of them had secretly taken for themselves, and swore that they retained nothing of the relics as private property. Romuald revealed two teeth and small joints which he had kept concealed. Thus all the others brought the particles that they had covertly set apart for themselves [Col. 0538C] and restored them to the remaining limbs. At last, with a favorable wind blowing and their ships ploughing the broad sea, Saint Nicholas appeared in a dream to Disigius, one of the sailors; he encouraged him and foretold that, on the twentieth day after they had taken away his body, they would enter the harbor of Bari. Disigius told his companions of the vision, and they consequently conceived great confidence. A little bird unexpectedly appeared, fluttering among the sailors in the ship, and gladdened them by its repeated visits. The sailors also frequently smelled a most sweet fragrance; strengthened by these and other pleasing signs, they rejoiced and drew near their own shores in gladness.

Led by God, they came to the harbor of Saint George, about five miles from the walls of Bari. From there they sent messengers to the clergy and people of Bari. The entire city was immediately filled with unexpected joy, and at once persons of both sexes and every age went out to the shore. The sailors entrusted the casket containing the relics to the religious Elias, abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict situated above the harbor. He reverently received the sacred pledges, placed them with the brethren in the aforesaid church on the ninth day of May [1087], and diligently guarded them for three days.

Urso, archbishop of Bari, a religious man worthy of God and well known and an intimate friend of the Italian lords, was then absent. A ship stood ready for him at Trani, which the bishop intended to board two days later in order to go to Jerusalem for prayer. But an envoy from the citizens came to him with a letter and immediately conveyed the news of so great a joy. Abandoning the journey he had begun, Urso gladly hastened without delay to Bari. The body of Saint Nicholas was received by the men of Bari, and the feast of his translation was established on the seventh day before the Ides of May. It was then carried to the court of Catapano and reverently placed, at the sailors’ request and with all the citizens present, in the church of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, built by the archbishop three years earlier.

They then began a basilica proper to Saint Nicholas and entrusted the holy body, the offerings of the faithful, and the work of the basilica to the venerable Abbot Elias. [Col. 0539B] With the archbishop’s consent and everyone’s favor, they appointed him overseer of all that had to be done. Immediately diverse multitudes gathered from every province of the entire West. Countless signs and miracles were daily performed by divine power. For on the first day, when the holy body had been placed in the church of Saint Benedict, as stated, more than thirty sick persons, of both sexes and every age, were freed from various illnesses; restored to perfect health, they gladly and safely returned home with thanksgiving. We have declined both to record individually and to number how many demoniacs, deaf persons, lame persons, mute persons, blind persons, and others afflicted by illnesses of many kinds were wholly relieved and healed on subsequent days. For the number is infinite and unknown to us, as we have indicated by an equivalent expression.

## X. Very Many Churches Acquire Relics of Blessed Nicholas

The aforementioned John, archdeacon of Bari, from whose book I have briefly excerpted this account, set down in writing twelve notable miracles. Yet neither he nor anyone else could make known to posterity all the healings and other aids which Almighty God, through the merits of the most holy bishop Nicholas, has most mercifully bestowed even to this day upon his servants who faithfully ask. Finally, God permitting, many churches obtained relics of the aforesaid bishop. Not only Italians and Greeks, [Col. 0539D] but other peoples also, possessing these holy pledges, sing thanks to God.

For a certain knight, Christopher, who was present at the translation of the noble Nicholas, kept a rib for himself in his sleeve. Not long afterwards, when ill, he fled to the monastery at Venosa, sought and obtained the monastic habit from Berengar, the archimandrite, presented to the Holy Trinity the rib of Saint Nicholas which he had with him, and recovered from his illness.

At the same time Stephen, cantor of the monastery which Count Fulk the Elder had built at the city of Angers in honor of Saint Nicholas, went to Apulia. With permission of his lord Abbot Natalis, he deliberately put aside the monastic habit; then he lived at Bari as a cleric, acquired great familiarity with the sacristans of the basilica of the holy bishop, and afterwards authority among them. [Col. 0540A] Finally, seeing an opportunity, he secretly seized the arm of Saint Nicholas, which was suitably covered with silver and preserved outside the mausoleum for blessing the people. He attempted to flee to Gaul and enrich his country and monastery with so great a treasure. But as soon as the men of Bari learned that such a theft had been committed against them, they sent mounted couriers far and wide to their frontiers and to their friends and patrons, carefully seeking to guard every route leading to France so that such a thief could not escape. Stephen turned aside to Venosa and, wishing to lie concealed there in fear, remained through the winter; while awaiting the clear spring weather, he fell ill. Then, when his necessary funds failed, he was compelled to sell the silver covering of the holy arm for food. Meanwhile the report spread throughout all Italy and Sicily that the arm of Blessed Nicholas had been stolen by Gauls. Finally, while frequent talk of such a theft stirred the people, and certain inhabitants of Venosa and servants of the monks had seen and recognized the silver workmanship, and rumor of the affair rang through the monastic community, Erembert, an energetic monk, hurried with servants of the monastery to the sick former monk. In a sudden, furious onset, he fiercely demanded the arm of Saint Nicholas as though it had been entrusted to him. When Stephen saw himself discovered and, in such a storm, did not know where to turn, pale and trembling he produced the precious pledge for the insistent monk. [Col. 0540C] Erembert received it with great joy and immediately carried it to the monastery of Holy Trinity, while the monks and all the citizens praised God. There Saint Nicholas even to this day wonderfully aids, in many necessities, those who faithfully ask for his pledges. The aforesaid Erembert was a Norman by birth, a vigorous knight before his conversion, and afterwards a monk fervent in the order.

In the same period, a certain Norman knight, William surnamed Pantulf, went to Apulia. Because he loved Saint Nicholas greatly, he sought many relics of him and, through God’s aid and the good offices of those who had translated the relics, obtained one tooth and two fragments of the marble tomb. He was valiant in arms, endowed with intelligence, and widely known among neighboring lords and the great lords of England and Italy for his good sense and great wealth. Having acquired the tooth of so great a lord, he returned to Normandy and announced a day on which he summoned many persons to his own estate, called Noron, so that they might fittingly receive the relics.

Accordingly, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1092, in the fifteenth indiction, the tooth of the gracious confessor Nicholas, together with other saints’ relics, was brought from Apulia by William Pantulf and honorably received in the basilica of Noron, founded in ancient times in honor of Saint Peter. Roger, abbot of Ouche, and Ralph—then abbot of Sées, but afterwards archbishop of Canterbury—were summoned to this reception. [Col. 0541A] With the great devotion of the monks and rejoicing of the laity, they received the holy relics in June and carefully placed them in a silver pyx generously prepared by the aforesaid knight. The aforesaid pledges were frequently sought by people suffering fevers and other sick persons; through the merits of the gracious bishop Nicholas, those who devoutly asked obtained their desired health.

Not long afterwards the aforesaid hero began the foundations of a new basilica and, having given twenty marks of silver, completed a great portion of the work. But many misfortunes arose, the work was impeded, and, when its first founder died, it was not brought to completion. William died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May, and his wife Leelina on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October; they rest buried there in the monks’ cloister. [Col. 0541B] But Philip, Robert, Ivo, and Arnulf, their sons, had not yet devoted themselves to fully carrying out their parents’ undertakings in ecclesiastical matters. We have therefore truthfully inserted in our work these matters concerning the translation of Saint Nicholas’s body. We faithfully beseech him, the worker of wonders, that, mindful of those who remember him, he may have mercy on us and pray God for us without ceasing.

## XI. The Author Returns to the Narrative of Events—Wars between Normans and French over the District of the Vexin

Let us now return to the matter which we began and from which we have digressed somewhat.

When the ancient hostility between Normans and French was renewed, the conflagration of wars arose, bringing a most grievous burden of losses disastrously upon clergy and laity. For Hugh surnamed Stavelus, Ralph Malusvicinus, and other inhabitants of the castle of Mantes rose against King William. Having gathered a great band of raiders, they made many incursions into Normandy. By night they crossed with their followers the river Auctura, which separates Neustria from France, and immediately rushed into the diocese of Évreux, cruelly prepared to do harm. They especially devastated the lands of William of Breteuil around Pacy and of Roger of Ivry; driving off herds of cattle and capturing people, they swelled with unbounded arrogance in their scorn for the Normans. The warlike King William, therefore, [Col. 0541D] deeply enraged, began to lay claim to the whole province of the Vexin. He demanded from Philip, king of the French, the restoration of Pontoise, Calvimont, and Mantes, and, unless his right were restored, he issued terrible threats against his enemies. The ground of this claim was as follows.

King Henry, son of Robert, king of the Franks, although after his father’s death he ought by right of primogeniture to have been crowned with the burdens of kingship, was pursued with stepmotherly hatred by his mother Queen Constance, who sought to set his brother Robert, duke of Burgundy, above him in the kingdom of the Gauls. On the advice of Amaury the Elder of Montfort, son of William Panoensis, he came to Fécamp with twelve retainers and humbly asked Duke Robert of Normandy to assist him in his pitiable exile caused by his mother’s treachery [Col. 0542A]. The aforesaid duke received him generously, as his natural lord, and gladly kept him with him until the feast of Easter had passed. Then he gathered Norman forces from every quarter, made a most vigorous expedition into France, and set fire to and burned the city of Orléans with a Norman assault. By incomparable losses he thus broke the stubbornness of the Franks. Having subdued them, he restored the expelled prince to his kingdom.

Once established in the kingdom, Henry thanked Duke Robert and, in return for his service, granted him the whole of the Vexin from the river Oise to the Epte. Drogo, count of that province, willingly consented to this; and, having done homage, faithfully served the aforesaid duke for as long as he lived [Col. 0542B]. Both counts flourished in the distinction of virtues, loved one another deeply, and rejoiced in mutual honour and advancement.

The aforesaid Drogo, as is said, was descended from Charles the Great, king of the Franks; and the oft-mentioned duke gave him in marriage his kinswoman Godgifu, sister of Edward, king of the English. By her were born Counts Ralph and Walter, and the venerable Fulco, bishop of Amiens. This maiden was living in exile in Neustria with her brother when Cnut, king of the Danes, invaded England by military force, drove out the twin heirs Alfred and Edward, and through Eadric’s treachery slew the princes Edmund and Edwin.

[Col. 0542C] Some years later, after Duke Robert died at Nicaea, a city of Bithynia, the magnates of Normandy rebelled against the child William. When his father had undertaken the journey to Jerusalem with Count Drogo, William was only eight years old and had been entrusted by his father to the guardianship of his kinsman Alan, count of the Bretons. Therefore, after Robert and Drogo had died on pilgrimage, and after Alan had been fatally poisoned by Norman treachery while besieging Montgomery, and their heirs had wickedly been deprived of necessary protection, King Henry, at the counsel of the Franks, who are always hostile to the Normans, greedily reclaimed the district of the Vexin and thereafter always subjected it to his own right. William [Col. 0542D], however, because of his boyish weakness, could not then vindicate his right. Later, as more pressing concerns arose for him among the people of Maine and the English, he kept silence and delayed taking up arms against his lord Henry or Henry’s son Philip for the district of the Vexin.

Accordingly, in the twenty-first year after he began to reign over the English, he made to Philip, king of the Franks, a claim and legal complaint concerning the county of the Vexin. But Philip resorted to the frivolous quibbles of rebels and, utterly scorning the king of the English’s demands, sent him away disappointed. Therefore, in the last week of July, William came unexpectedly with his army to Mantes and entered the castle mingled with its garrison. For the soldiers had secretly gone out to see the trampling down [Col. 0543A] of their crops and the uprooting of their vineyards, which Ascelin Goël had devastated with Norman forces on the day before the king arrived. The king’s army therefore burst in with the townspeople, passed through the gates, and, with fire set in the frenzy of the men-at-arms, burned the castle together with its churches and houses. As is reported, a multitude of people perished by the violence of the fire.

There King William, exceedingly corpulent, fell ill from excessive heat and exertion, and lay grievously afflicted for six weeks. Some who opposed peace rejoiced at this and awaited free permission to steal and plunder others’ possessions. Others, who expected the security of peace, greatly feared the death of their peaceful protector. But he, who throughout his life [Col. 0543B] had always used the counsel of wise men, had feared God as a faithful servant, and had been an untiring defender of holy Mother Church, remained vigorous in praiseworthy memory even unto death; and as his life was venerable, so too was his end. During his illness, until the hour of death, he retained sound understanding and vigorous speech. Repenting of his sins, he disclosed his offences to God’s priests and humbly strove, according to Christian custom, to make God favourable to him. Bishops, abbots, and devout men remained about him and gave the dying prince wholesome counsel for eternal life.

Since the noise of Rouen, a populous city, was intolerable to the sick man, the king ordered himself to be carried outside the city [Col. 0543C] to the church of Saint Gervais, situated on the western hill, which Duke Richard, his grandfather, had given to the abbey of Fécamp. There Gilbert, bishop of Lisieux, and Guntard, abbot of Jumièges, with certain other physicians, kept diligent watch and carefully attended to the king’s spiritual and bodily welfare.

## XII. Death of King William

At last, when his illness had become very severe and the king saw inevitable death threatening him, he was inwardly terrified as he pondered the future things that were unseen, and repeatedly groaned with sighs. He summoned his sons William Rufus and Henry, who were present, together with certain friends, and began wisely and very prudently [Col. 0543D] to deliberate on the ordering of the kingdom. His son Robert, the elder by birth, had long and often quarrelled with his father and had recently, angered in like fashion by certain foolish matters, departed to the king of the Franks.

[Col. 0544A] Yet the wise hero did not delay making provision for his own future good and that of many others. He ordered all his treasures to be distributed among churches, the poor, and God’s ministers. He shrewdly fixed the amount to be given to each person and ordered the notaries to record it in his presence. He also humbly sent great gifts to the clergy of Mantes, so that the churches which he had burned might be rebuilt from them. He admonished all present concerning the preservation of faith and justice, the observance of God’s law and peace, the privileges of churches, and the decrees of the Fathers; and, with tears sometimes mingled in, he delivered the following eloquent address, worthy of perpetual remembrance:

> “Burdened, my friends, by many and grievous sins, I tremble; and, soon to be carried away to God’s dreadful [Col. 0544B] judgment, I do not know what I shall do. For from childhood I was nurtured in arms, and I have been greatly defiled by the shedding of much blood. I cannot possibly number the evils that I have committed during the sixty-four years in which I have lived this troubled life; for these I am now compelled without delay to render account to the most just Judge. When my father, voluntarily setting out into exile, entrusted the duchy of Normandy to me, I was a tender child, only eight years old; and from that time until now I have always borne the burden of arms. I have now held this duchy itself for nearly fifty-six years amid the hazards of wars. Those over whom I ruled often plotted against me and wickedly inflicted losses and grievous injuries upon me. They treacherously killed Turchetil, my guardian, Osbern son of Herfast, steward [dapifer] of Normandy, and Count Gilbert, father of the country, along with many others necessary to the commonwealth.

> [Note: “William,” says Eadmer, “when in the twenty-first year of his reign he was detained at Rouen by the illness of which he died, intended in every way to commend himself to the merits and intercessions of Anselm. He had Anselm come to him from Bec and lodge not far from him. But while he delayed speaking with him concerning the salvation of his soul, because he felt his illness somewhat eased, the prince’s body happened to be overcome by such great weakness that he could endure the disturbances of the court in no way. Having therefore crossed the Seine, he took to his bed at the estate of Ermentrude, which lies opposite Rouen on the other side of the river. Whatever luxuries were brought to the sick king, half of them was sent by him to the sick Anselm [Col. 0544D]. Yet he was not granted to see him again in this life, nor, as he had intended, to speak with him at all concerning his soul. For such illness seized them both that neither could Anselm reach King William nor William reach Abbot Anselm. William indeed died thus, yet not, as is said, unconfessed; and Anselm was immediately relieved of his illness.” From Eadmer the monk, *History of Recent Events*, book I, p. 33, at the end of the Works of St Anselm; Dom Bouquet, book VII, p. 618.]

> “By these events I have tested the loyalty of my people. Many times at night, out of fear of my kinsmen, I was secretly carried out of the principal chamber by my uncle Walter and taken to the homes and hiding-places of the poor, lest I be found by the faithless men who sought my death.

> “If the Normans are governed by firm and strict rule, they are most valiant; in difficult affairs they are unconquered, excel all others, and strive to prove themselves stronger than every enemy. Otherwise they tear one another apart and destroy one another. For they desire rebellions, seek seditions, and are ready for every wickedness. [Col. 0544D] They must therefore be restrained by the strong discipline of righteousness and compelled by the bridle of discipline to walk the path of justice. But if they are allowed to go their own way without a yoke, like an untamed wild ass, they and their princes [Col. 0545A] will await shameful want and confusion. I have long learned this from many experiences. My own relatives and kinsmen, who ought in every respect to have defended me against all mortals, rose against me in repeated conspiracies and almost deprived me of my father’s whole inheritance.

> “Guy, son of Renaud, duke of Burgundy, by my aunt Adeliza, repaid me evil for good. I had kindly received him when he came from another region, honoured him as an only brother, and given him Vernon, Brionne, and no small part of Normandy. Yet he disparaged me in words and deeds; he declared with scorn that I was a bastard, degenerate, and unworthy of rule, [Col. 0545B] and vilified me as an enemy. Why say more? He broke faith with me, rebelled against me, drew away from me my magnates Ranulf of Bayeux, Haimo Dentatus, and Nigel of the Cotentin, with many others, and by wicked counsel compelled them to become perjured men with him. Forgetful therefore of the homage and loyalty which he had sworn to me, he strove to take away the whole of Normandy. Thus, while still beardless, I was compelled to take up arms against him and fight my kinsman and vassal on the plain near Val-ès-Dunes. Then, with the help of God, the just Judge, I defeated the enemies between Caen and Argences; and, when they had been overthrown by God’s will, I freely possessed my paternal right. Afterwards I besieged the fortress of Brionne, shut up Guy—wounded and escaped from battle by flight—and did not depart from there [Col. 0545C] until I had driven the public enemy out of Neustria and taken all his fortresses.

> “Not long afterwards another most grievous adversity arose against me. My uncles Malger, archbishop of Rouen, and his brother William—to whom I had freely given Arques and the county of Talou—despised me as a bastard and summoned King Henry and Count Enguerrand of Ponthieu against me. As soon as I heard these reports in the Cotentin, I set out, despite many dissuading me. I sent ahead to Arques some knights who were more eager to strike blows; and I myself followed with no large army and besieged the lofty fortress. But before I had reached the lands lying between the two rivers, the Saâne [Col. 0545D] and the Varenne, my scouts forestalled Count Enguerrand as he hurried to enter the castle. They killed him while he fought bravely—for he was a most fierce knight—and put his forces to flight. By a severe siege I subdued the garrison and forced the perjured count into exile; nor did I ever permit him, throughout his life, to return to what he had lost. I also deposed the insolent bishop, who was devoted neither to God [Col. 0546A] nor faithful to me, from his episcopal seat by decree of the pope.

> [Note: Malger, son of Richard II, duke of Normandy, by his second wife Papia, succeeded his uncle Robert, who died in 1036, as archbishop of Rouen; he had previously been a monk of Fécamp. “Without apostolic blessing,” says Orderic, “and without a pallium, he ruled the people of Rouen; he clung unworthily to carnal pleasures and worldly concerns, and begot a son named Michael, a worthy knight and legitimate son, whom King Henry in England, now in his old age, honours and loves.” About May 1055 William arranged at the council held at Lisieux for Malger to be deprived of office and for Maurilius to be substituted in his place. More concerning Malger is related in the *Acts of the Bishops of Rouen* and the *Deeds of William*, pp. 70, 89, and 90 of our volume XI. Dom Bouquet, book VII, p. 619.]

> “And I put in his place Maurilius, a venerable monk, whom God had sent to me from the city of Florence in Italy.

> “Henry, relying on royal power, ardent in military boldness, and intensely provoked by the disparagements of my enemies, often seemed to trample me down as though I were unarmed, to crush me in many ways, and to impose unlawful claims upon me. He repeatedly entered my land with a great host of armed men, but never rejoiced in plunder and spoils taken from me or in the capture of my people. Often he entered my borders with great pomp and terrible threats; but never returned to his own land happy or without disgrace [Col. 0546B]. He brought here with him many men distinguished in valour, but because they perished by the sword of myself and my men—alas!—he did not bring them back.

> “Once, furiously inflamed against me, King Henry divided the great army of France into two parts so as to oppress our lands by twin invasions. He himself led one division into the diocese of Évreux, to devastate everything as far as the Seine. The other he entrusted to his brother Odo, Renaud of Clermont, and two counts, Ralph of Montdidier and Guy of Ponthieu, so that they might quickly enter Neustria through the fords of the Epte, invade Bray, Talou, and the whole district of Rouen, and utterly lay waste with sword, fire, and plunder everything as far as the sea. When I learned this [Col. 0546C], I did not respond sluggishly. I continually opposed myself with my men to the king’s encampments along the bank of the Seine; and wherever he attempted to ravage my soil, I met his aggression with arms and sword. I sent Count Robert of Eu, Roger of Mortemer, and other most proven knights against Odo and his legions. When they met near the castle called Mortemer, with the forces of both sides drawn up, a terrible battle was joined with much bloodshed on either side. For the warriors on both sides were valiant and knew not how to yield even unto death. On one side the French raged in desire for acquisition; on the other the Normans struck, burning with hope of escape [Col. 0546D] and of defending themselves and their homes. At last, with God’s help, the Normans won and the French fled. This battle across the Seine was fought in winter before Lent, in the eighth year after the battle of Val-ès-Dunes. Then Count Guy of Ponthieu was captured, and Odo, with Renaud and others whose feet were swift, was put to flight. Count Ralph likewise would have been captured, had not Roger, commander of my forces, come to his aid; [Col. 0547A] for he had long before done homage to him. In such necessity Roger rendered him fine and fitting service, protecting him in his castle for three days and afterwards escorting him safely to his own lands. For this offence I expelled Roger from Normandy; but shortly afterwards, reconciled with him, I restored his honour to him. Yet I took from him, as I think was right, the castle of Mortemer in which he had saved my enemy; but I gave it to William de Warenne, his kinsman, a lawful knight. I kept Count Guy in prison at Bayeux as long as I pleased; and after two years I received homage from him on the condition that from then on he should always be faithful to me and should provide military service, wherever I commanded, with one hundred knights every year. Then I gave him great gifts and dismissed him honourably and in peace.

> “After the battle was concluded, as soon as I received certain news, I sent word through Ralph of Tosny to the king of the Franks about what had happened beyond the Seine. When he heard it, he immediately rose by night and fled swiftly with his army; nor thereafter did he ever spend a night securely in my land. Thus, from my childhood I was beset everywhere by countless pressures, but by God’s grace I was honourably delivered from all of them. I therefore became an object of envy to all my neighbours, yet, with the help of God, in whom I always placed my hope, I was defeated by none. The Bretons and the Angevins often experienced this; the French and Flemings attest it; the English [Col. 0547C] and the people of Maine have felt it grievously. Count Geoffrey Martel of Anjou, Conan prince of the Bretons, and Robert the Frisian, lord of the Morini, laid many snares against me. Yet, though they desired it greatly and spread many plots, God guarded me, and they never attained their wish.

> “I gained the royal crown which none of my predecessors wore; divine grace alone, not hereditary right, conferred it upon me. It is difficult to relate how many labours and dangerous conflicts I endured beyond the sea against the men of Exeter, Chester, and Northumbria; against the Scots and Welsh, the men of Norwich and the Danes; and against the other adversaries who strove to deprive me of the kingdom of England. In [Col. 0547D] all these matters victory fell to my lot. Yet, although human greed rejoices in triumphs of this kind, inwardly I am pierced and bitten by anxious fear, as I consider that cruel rashness has raged throughout them all. Therefore I humbly beg you, priests and ministers of Christ, [Col. 0548A] to commend me in your prayers to almighty God, that he may forgive the sins by which I am heavily burdened and, through his tireless mercy, save me among his own. I also order my treasures to be given to churches and the poor, so that what has been amassed through wrongful deeds may be scattered for the holiest uses. For you ought to remember how lovingly I loved you and how strongly I defended you against all rivals.

> “I never violated the Church of God, our mother; rather, wherever reason required, I eagerly honoured her. I never sold ecclesiastical dignities. I always detested and rejected simony. In the election of persons I examined merit of life and instruction in wisdom and, so far as lay in my power, [Col. 0548B] entrusted the government of the Church to the person most worthy of all. This may indeed be truly proved in Lanfranc, chief bishop of Canterbury; in Anselm, abbot of Bec; in Gerbert of Fontenelle and Durand of Troarn; and in many other teachers of my kingdom, whose famous praise resounds, I believe, to the ends of the earth. I chose such companions for conversation; in their fellowship I found truth and wisdom, and therefore I always joyfully desired to benefit from their counsels.

> [Note: “Anselm, abbot of Bec,” says Eadmer in Eadmer’s *History*, p. 33, “was a good man, exceptionally strong in learning, and, because of the merit of his outstanding holiness, known, eminent, and esteemed throughout Normandy and France. He was also held in great renown in England and was joined in most holy friendship with the aforesaid king and with Archbishop Lanfranc. Whenever he came to the king’s court on various business concerning the Church or other matters, the king himself, putting aside the fierceness by which he seemed savage and terrifying to many, became so yielding and affable that, to the amazement of all, in Anselm’s presence he became altogether another man than he usually was. He always held Anselm and Lanfranc—men alike supported by divine and human prudence—in high regard for his own sake, and in all matters which they were to do for him, insofar as their office concerned them, he listened to them with a more affectionate attention than to others. Thus by their counsel he very often and greatly relaxed the severity of his disposition toward certain persons.” Dom Bouquet, book VII, p. 621.]

> “With God’s assistance, nine abbeys of monks and one of nuns, founded by my fathers in Normandy, grew and were gloriously enlarged by the many endowments which I gave [Col. 0548C]. Then, during my duchy, seventeen monasteries of monks and six of nuns were built, where great service and many alms are daily performed for love of the supreme King. Normandy is fortified by such strongholds, and within them the people of the land learn to fight against demons and the vices of the flesh. For, inspired by God, I was either their founder, or a zealous helper and willing encourager of their foundation. I also graciously confirmed, in Neustria and England, all property in land and other revenues that my magnates gave to God and his saints for spiritual salvation, and by princely authority freely confirmed their charters of donation against all rivals and assailants.

> “I have pursued these concerns since my earliest years, and I leave them to my heirs to be maintained for all time. In these matters, my sons, follow me continually, so that you may be honoured before God and men here and for ever. I especially admonish you, my own flesh, to cling without ceasing to the fellowship of good and wise men, and in all things, if you wish to remain glorious for long, [Col. 0549A] to obey their authority. The teaching of devout wise men is to distinguish good from evil, to hold fast to justice in every way, to avoid wickedness by every effort, to spare and assist the weak, the poor, and the just, to restrain and subdue the proud and unrighteous and protect the simple from their attacks, to attend holy church devoutly, to love the worship of God above all riches, and tirelessly to obey the divine law night and day, in adversity and prosperity.

> “Before I fought Harold on the height of Senlac, I granted the duchy of Normandy to my son Robert, because he is the firstborn. He has already received the homage of almost all the barons of this land. An honour once granted cannot be taken away. Yet I know without doubt [Col. 0549B] that the land subject to his rule will truly be miserable. For he is proud and a foolish wretch, destined long to suffer cruel misfortune. I appoint no heir to the kingdom of England; rather, I commend it to the eternal Creator, whose I am and in whose hand all things are. For I did not possess so great an honour by hereditary right, but took it from the perjured King Harold through dreadful conflict and much shedding of human blood, and, after killing or driving out his supporters, subjected it to my rule. I bore excessive hatred toward the native sons of the kingdom. I cruelly oppressed nobles and common people; I unjustly disinherited many; I killed countless persons, especially in the district of York, by hunger or the sword. For the peoples of Deira and beyond the Humber received the army of Swein, king of the Danes, against me, and slew Robert de Comines within Durham with a thousand knights, together with other of my magnates and most proven knights in various places. Therefore, stirred by immoderate rage, I hastened upon the northern English like a mad lion.
