I ordered their houses, crops, and all equipment and household goods to be immediately burned, and abundant herds of cattle and flocks to be slaughtered everywhere. Thus I punished a multitude of both sexes with the sword of such terrible famine; and so, alas, I brought many thousands of that most beautiful people—old men and young men alike—to a dreadful slaughter [Col. 0549C]. Therefore I dare entrust the insignia of this kingdom, which I acquired amid so many sins, to no one but God alone, lest after my death yet worse things happen because of me. I desire that my son William, who has always remained close to me from his earliest years and has willingly obeyed me in all things as far as he could, may long flourish in the Spirit of God and, if it be God’s will, prosperously shine upon the royal throne.”

When King William had said these things and many similar ones, and astonishment seized those standing by as they shrewdly weighed the future, Henry, the younger son, hearing that nothing from the royal treasures was being given to him, sorrowfully said to the king with tears: “And what do you give me, father?” The king replied: “I give you five thousand pounds of silver from my treasury.” Henry said: “What shall I do with treasure if I have no place to live?” His father answered: “Be patient, my son, and be strengthened in the Lord. Bear it peacefully while your elder brothers go before you. Robert shall have [Col. 0550A] Normandy, and William England. But in your time you shall have the whole honour that I have acquired, and you shall surpass your brothers in riches and power.”

Having said this, the king, fearing lest sudden disturbance might arise in a kingdom so extensive, wrote a letter to Archbishop Lanfranc regarding the appointment of a king. He gave it, sealed with his own seal, to his son William Rufus, ordering him to cross at once into England. Then he kissed and blessed him and sent him hastily across the sea to receive the crown. William soon reached the harbour called Wissant, where he heard that his father had already died. Henry, meanwhile, hurried to receive the money assigned to him, carefully to weigh it lest anything should be lacking, to summon trusted companions who were necessary to him, and to procure a secure treasury [Col. 0550B].

Meanwhile the physicians and royal servants attending the sick prince, together with the magnates who came to visit him, began to speak to him on behalf of the prisoners whom he held in custody, humbly begging that he might pity and release them. He said to them:

> “I have long kept Morcar, a noble English earl, bound in prison, and unjustly, yet because I feared that, if he were free, the kingdom of England might be disturbed through him. But I put Roger of Breteuil in chains because he raged very stubbornly against me and incited his brother-in-law Ralph of Gael, with many others, against me; and I swore that he should not leave them in my lifetime. Thus I cast many into chains because of their own perversity, and many others through fear of future [Col. 0550C] sedition. For the discipline of righteousness requires this, and God’s law through Moses commands the rulers of the world to restrain the guilty lest they destroy the innocent. But now, placed at the point of death, as I hope to be saved and absolved from my guilt through God’s mercy, so I order all prisons to be opened at once and all prisoners, except my brother the bishop of Bayeux, to be released and set free for God’s sake, that he may have mercy on me. Yet let those released proceed from prison on this condition: first, let them give the ministers of the commonwealth security under oath that they will preserve peace in England and Normandy by every means and will manfully resist, to the best of their ability, the enemies of peace.”

When Robert, count of Mortain, heard the king’s [Col. 0550D] judgment that his brother was to be bound for ever, he was deeply grieved. For Herluin of Conteville had married Herleva, concubine of Duke Robert, and by her had fathered two sons, Odo and Robert. Duke William, and later king, had enriched his stepfather with great and numerous honours in Normandy and England; he had also raised to very great possessions his sons Ralph, whom Herluin had fathered by another wife, and his uterine brothers Odo and Robert. For after he had expelled from Neustria, for trifling reasons, William surnamed Werlenc, count of Mortain, son of Count Malger, he had given the county of Mortain to Robert, son of Herluin, his brother. After the death [Col. 0551A] of Hugh, bishop of Bayeux, son of Count Ralph, he had granted that bishopric to his brother Odo, whom he later placed over the kingdom of Kent in England. Finally, because of Odo’s excessive conduct, as was related in full above, King William seized him on the Isle of Wight, kept him in prison for four years, and, because of his insolence, did not wish to release him even at his death. The aforesaid count of Mortain therefore grieved greatly and made humble intercession for his brother both personally and through his friends, wearing out the sick man with prayers.

When many earnestly petitioned for the bishop of Bayeux, the king, wearied by the entreaties of so many, said:

> “I am amazed that you do not wisely inquire who and what sort of man he is for whom you plead. Do you not ask for a man [Col. 0551B] who has long been a despiser of religion and a shrewd instigator of deadly sedition? Have I not already restrained this bishop for four years, who, when he ought to have been the most just ruler of the English, became the worst oppressor of peoples and destroyer of monastic communities? In freeing a seditious man you act wrongly and seek enormous harm for yourselves. It is evident that my brother Odo is frivolous and ambitious, attached to fleshly desires and immense cruelties, and will never change from his seductions and harmful vanities. I have proved this clearly in many instances; therefore I have confined not a bishop but a tyrant. Without doubt, if he escapes, he will disturb the whole land and bring ruin upon many thousands. I say these things not from hatred, like an enemy, [Col. 0551C] but as a father of the country making provision for the Christian people. For if he behaved chastely and modestly, as is fitting everywhere for a priest and minister of God, there would be in my heart a joy greater than I can describe.”

When all promised the bishop’s amendment, the king again said:

> “Whether I wish it or not, your request shall be granted, because after my death a violent and sudden change of affairs will occur. Against my will I consent that my brother be freed from prison. But know that through him death or grave affliction will be inflicted upon many. As for Baldwin, son of Nicholas: because he foolishly abandoned my service and went to Spain without my permission, I took all his land from him as punishment. But now I restore it to him for God’s sake. I think no better knight in arms can be found than he; but he is prodigal and frivolous, wandering in many different directions.”

Thus King William, though he was grievously afflicted by excessive pain, nevertheless retained sound understanding and vigorous speech, and in all matters requiring attention for the kingdom gave prompt and useful counsel.

At last, on the fifth day before the Ides of September, Thursday [9 September 1087], when Phoebus was already scattering his bright shafts of rays over the world, the awakened king heard the sound of the great bell in the metropolitan church. When he asked what was ringing, the attendants replied: “Lord, the first hour is now being sounded in the church of Saint Mary.” Then the king, with the utmost devotion, raised his eyes to heaven and, stretching his hands upward, said: “To my Lady, [Col. 0552A] Mary, holy Mother of God, I commend myself, that by her holy prayers she may reconcile me to her most dear Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.” Having said this, he immediately breathed his last.

The physicians and the other persons assembled there, who had watched the king resting throughout the night without groan or outcry, and now unexpectedly saw that he had so suddenly departed, were intensely astonished and became as though out of their minds. The wealthier among them immediately mounted their horses, departed, and hastened to protect their own property. But when the lesser retainers saw their masters thus make off, they seized weapons, vessels, clothing, linen, and every article of royal furnishing, and fled, leaving the king’s nearly naked corpse on the floor of the house. See, I pray you all, what worldly faith is like. [Col. 0552B] Each man seized what he could of the royal equipment like a kite and immediately fled with his booty. Thus, when the administrator of justice fell, impiety came forth shamelessly and first practised rapacity by plundering the very avenger of plunder.

The report of the king’s death flew on swift wings and poured joy or sorrow far and wide into the hearts of those who heard it. For the death of King William, on the very day on which he died at Rouen, was announced in the city of Rome and in Calabria to certain disinherited persons, as they afterwards truthfully reported in Normandy. The evil spirit indeed rejoiced greatly when it saw its clients, who eagerly desired to seize and steal, freed through the death of the judge.

## XIII. The King’s Funeral. Pious Meditations

[Col. 0552C]

O worldly pomp, how contemptible you are, because you are so utterly vain and unstable! You are rightly said to be comparable to rain-bubbles, which rise very swollen in a moment and suddenly are reduced to nothing. Behold: the mightiest hero, whom more than a hundred thousand soldiers had lately eagerly served, and whom many peoples feared with trembling, has now been shamefully stripped by his own men in a house not his own and left naked on the bare ground from the first hour until the third. For the citizens of Rouen, hearing of the ruler’s fall, were greatly terrified; almost all lost their wits as if drunk, and were disturbed as though they saw a host of enemies threatening the city. Each withdrew from the place where he was [Col. 0552D], sought advice about what to do from his wife, a chance-met companion, or a friend, and either moved his possessions or resolved to move them; fearing they might be found, each hid them.

At last the religious men—clerks and monks—gathering their strength and deepest feelings, arranged a procession. Properly vested, they went with crosses and censers to Saint Gervasius and, according to the custom of holy Christianity, commended the king’s soul to God. Then Archbishop William ordered that his body be carried to Caen and buried there in the basilica of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, which he himself had founded. But his brothers and kinsmen had already departed from him, and all his servants had shamefully abandoned him as though he were a barbarian. Thus [Col. 0553A] not one of the royal retainers could be found to take care of the rites for his body. Then Herluin, a knight of the *pagus*, moved by natural goodness, manfully undertook responsibility for the funeral out of love of God and honour for his people. At his own expense he therefore hired embalmers, bearers of the dead, and a conveyance, and brought the king’s corpse

> [Note: [Col. 0553D] “He possessed such power,” says Eadmer in his *Life*, “that throughout all England, all Normandy, and the whole land of Le Mans, no one dared raise a hand against his authority. Yet, as soon as he lay upon the ground about to breathe out his spirit, his corpse was, as we have learned, abandoned by every person, except for one attendant alone; without any pomp it was carried down the Seine in a little boat [Col. 0554D]. And when he was to be buried, we have heard that the very ground of his burial was claimed by a certain peasant, who, asserting a hereditary right to it, complained that it had long ago been wrongfully taken from him by that same man.” Dom Bouquet, vol. VII, p. 623.]

to the port on the Seine; placed it on a ship and conveyed it by water and land as far as Caen.

Then Lord Abbot Gilbert, with the community of monks, reverently came out to meet the bier; a weeping and praying crowd of clergy and laity joined them. But immediately adverse fortune brought great terror upon them all alike. For a huge fire suddenly burst out from a certain house and [Col. 0553B] belched forth immense masses of flame, devastatingly engulfing a great part of the borough of Caen. Therefore all the clergy and laity ran to check the fire. The monks alone completed the office they had begun and, chanting psalms, brought the king’s bier to the monastic basilica.

Finally, for the burial of the great duke and father of his country, all the bishops and abbots of Normandy assembled. Of these, it is pleasing to name a few and record them briefly on this page for the knowledge of posterity.

William, Archbishop of Rouen; Odo, Bishop of Bayeux; Gilbert of Évreux; Gilbert Maminot of Lisieux; Michael of Avranches; Geoffrey of Coutances; and Gerard [Col. 0553C] of Sées.

The abbots likewise were these: Anselm of Bec; William of Ros, of Fécamp; Gerbert of Fontenelle; Guntard of Jumièges; Mainer of Ouche; Fulk of Déville; Durand of Troarn; Robert of Sées; Osbern of Bernay; Roger of Mont-Saint-Michel-in-Peril-of-the-Sea.

The archimandrites of Rouen, Nicholas of Saint-Ouen and Walter of Mont-Sainte-Trinité, and many others, whom it would take too long to name individually. All these came to the funeral of the renowned baron and buried him in the presbytery, between the choir and the altar.

When Mass had been completed and the sarcophagus had already been [Col. 0553D] set in the ground, though the body still lay in the bier, the great Gilbert, Bishop of Évreux, ascended the pulpit and delivered at length an eloquent address on the magnificence of the deceased prince: how he had vigorously extended the bounds of Norman jurisdiction; raised his people higher than all his predecessors had done; maintained justice and peace throughout his dominion; usefully chastised thieves and robbers with the rod of rectitude; and strongly defended clerks, monks, [Col. 0554A] and the unarmed populace with the sword of valour. Having finished his address, he appealed to the people and, while many wept compassionately and affirmed his words, added:

> “Since no mortal person can live in this life without sin, we beseech you all, in the charity of God, to endeavour to intercede with almighty God for the dead prince, and kindly forgive him if he committed any wrong against you.”

Then Ascelin, son of Arthur, rose from the crowd and loudly made the following complaint in the hearing of all:

> “This land on which you stand was the courtyard of my father’s house. This man for whom you pray, while he was still Count of Normandy, violently took it from my father and, with all justice denied, forcibly founded this church upon it. Therefore I challenge this land and openly lay claim to it; and, lest the body of the despoiler be covered by my turf or buried in my inheritance, I forbid it on God’s behalf.”

When the bishops and other magnates heard this, and learned from his neighbours, who testified that he had spoken the truth, they summoned the man. Setting all violence aside, they soothed him with gentle entreaties and made peace with him. For the site of the burial alone they immediately paid him sixty shillings; for the rest of the land which he claimed, they promised him equivalent compensation, and not long afterwards, for the salvation of their beloved special lord, they fulfilled the agreement. Moreover, as the body was being put into the sarcophagus and forcibly compressed because the vessel, through the carelessness of the [Col. 0554C] masons, had been built too short, its exceedingly fat belly burst; an unbearable stench filled the persons standing around and the rest of the crowd. Smoke from incense and other aromatics rose abundantly from the censers, but could not overcome the foulest odour. The priests therefore hurried to complete the funeral rites and swiftly returned in terror to their own dwellings.

Behold: I have carefully investigated and truthfully explained what God’s providence foreshadowed in the duke’s downfall. I do not hawk a fabricated tragedy, nor do I flatter parasites laughing at a talkative comedy; rather, I faithfully set forth diverse events to studious readers.

Adversity appeared amid prosperity, so that the hearts of [Col. 0554D] earth-dwellers might be afraid. A king once powerful and warlike, feared by many peoples across many provinces, lay naked in a courtyard, abandoned by those whom he had begotten or nourished. He needed borrowed money for his funeral array; he required the aid of a common man to hire a bier and corpse-bearers—he who hitherto had abounded excessively in such great and superfluous wealth. He was carried to the basilica past a fire by frightened men; and he who had been lord of so many cities, towns, and villages lacked free ground [Col. 0555A] for his burial. The fat of his belly, nourished on so many delights, was exposed to shame and taught prudent and foolish alike what the glory of the flesh is. For, when they behold the corruption of a muddy corpse, all are admonished zealously to seek, through the labour of saving self-restraint, things better than the pleasures of the flesh, which is earth and shall return to dust. The condition of rich and poor is alike: death and decay likewise seize them both. Therefore, O children of men, do not put confidence in false princes (Ps. 145:3), but in the living and true God, the creator of all things. Turn over the sequence of the Old and New Testaments, and take from them abundant examples of [Col. 0556A] what you ought to avoid and what you ought to seek. Do not hope in iniquity, nor desire plunder. If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them (Ps. 62:11). For all flesh is as grass, and all its glory as the flower of grass. The grass has withered, and its flower has fallen (1 Pet. 1:24; Isa. 40:6; Ecclus. 14:8). But the word of the Lord remains for ever.

Here, with the end of the king, I think it fitting to set a limit to the seventh book of the *History of Ouche*; and in the eighth I wish to impart something to posterity concerning his sons and the manifold disturbance which for a long time severely afflicted Neustria and England.

> [Note: [Col. 0555A] Le Prévost: “to explain” (*enodare*).]

## Summary of Book Eight

[Col. 0555]

I. Duke Robert succeeds his father in Normandy and William Rufus in England. Very many discords arise after the death of King William. II. Odo, Bishop of Bayeux, is released from custody. Henry, for a payment, receives from his brother Duke Robert part of Normandy. III. A rebellion is raised in England by Bishop Odo in order to elevate Duke Robert to the throne. William Rufus defeats the rebels. IV. Grithfrid, king of the French, invades England. History of Count Robert of Rhuddlan. V. Duke Robert’s bad government. At Bishop Odo’s instigation, he invades the people of Le Mans. VI. Roger, Count of Le Mans, makes peace with Duke Robert. The wickedness of Count Robert of Bellême. The magnates of Normandy wage war among themselves. VII. Death of Durand, Abbot of Troarn. Pope Victor is elected. Pope Urban II. VIII. Various events in Apulia, Normandy, and England. Deaths of certain magnates. The restricted rule of William Rufus. IX. King William plans an attack on his brother Robert in Normandy. The people of Le Mans rise against the aforesaid Robert. Fulk, Count of Anjou. X. Fulk, Count of Anjou, devises a new shape for shoes. Customs, clothing, games, and so forth of this period. XI. The people of Le Mans rise against the Normans. XII. Dissensions and wars among the magnates of Normandy. XIII. Discordant disturbances and wars continue in Normandy. XIV. Discordant disturbances continue in Normandy. War between the men of Évreux and those of Conches. XV. Conan’s conspiracy to surrender the city of Rouen to the king of England. XVI. Conflict and defeat of the people of Hiémois. William comes to Normandy and makes peace with Duke Robert. XVII. Remarkable case of a certain priest of the diocese of Lisieux. XVIII. Agreements made between King William and Duke Robert. Affairs of the diocese of Lisieux. Roger, Abbot of Ouche. XIX. Bertrada, Countess of Anjou, leaves her husband and marries Philip, king of the French. Prelates of France eminent in religion and learning. Council of Rouen. XX. Malcolm, king of the Scots, undertakes war against the kingdom of England. He is killed. Concerning his wife and children. XXI. Conspiracies formed against William Rufus in England. XXII. Discords and private wars among the magnates of Normandy. XXIII. Robert of Bellême harasses the monks of Ouche. XXIV. The religious life and death of certain knights. Concerning Anfrid, first abbot of Préaux. Abbots, prelates, and monks distinguished in virtues and learning. XXV. Concerning the new garments of monks: how and by whom they were invented. XXVI. Abbots and monks conspicuous for piety in new monasteries. Concerning founders of new orders. XXVII. The illustrious Hugh of Grandmesnil receives monastic profession on his sickbed from Geoffrey, prior of the monks of Ouche, and dies shortly afterward. Concerning his children.

## Book Eight

[Col. 0557]

### I. Duke Robert succeeds in Normandy and William Rufus in England.—Very many discords arise after the death of King William

[Col. 0557A]

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1082, in the tenth indiction, William the Bastard, king of the English, died at Rouen on the fifth day before the Ides of September; and his body was buried at Caen in the church of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr.

His son Robert became duke of the Normans and prince of the people of Le Mans in name only for many years; but, subject to sluggishness and idleness, he never exercised rule, as he ought, with strength and justice.

William Rufus brought his father’s letter to Archbishop Lanfranc. After reading it, that prelate [Col. 0557B] hurried with the young man to London and consecrated him king, at the feast of Saint Michael, in the ancient basilica of Saint Peter the Apostle called Westminster. He reigned for twelve years and ten months.

> [Note: [Col. 0557D] William Rufus reigned from 29 September 1087 to 2 August 1100.]

He sought to imitate his father in certain worldly respects. For he was vigorous in martial courage and secular generosity, but excessively subject to pride, lust, and other vices. Yet he was cold in his attitude towards God, attendance at church, and worship.

He bestowed an abundance of gold, silver, and gems upon Otto the goldsmith and ordered a marvellous memorial to be made above his father’s tomb.

> [Note: [Col. 0557D] That goldsmith Otto is recorded in the *Domesday Book*, [Col. 0558D] among the king’s goldsmiths.]

Obeying the royal commands, Otto fashioned an outstanding work, which to this day shines fittingly with gold, silver, and gems [Col. 0557C]. Excellent poets, finding in such a man such abundant matter for verse, composed many elegant and splendid poems. But, in keeping with metropolitan dignity, only the following verses of Thomas, Archbishop of York, were set in gold:

> He who ruled the stern Normans, and boldly conquered  
> And bravely held the Britons;  
> Who by his prowess restrained the swords of the men of Le Mans  
> And brought them under the laws of his rule—  
> The great King William lies here in a small tomb.  
> A small house suffices for a great lord.  
> Phoebus had turned seven times three courses and two  
> In the Virgin’s womb, and here he died.

In the same year many Norman nobles followed their king in death. For while the king was still [Col. 0557D] ill, his kinsman Gilbert of Aunou, son of Richard of Heugleville, a good and simple man, died on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of September and was buried in the church of Saint Mary, where he had established six monks from the monastery of Ouche. There also, four years later, his pious wife Beatrice was buried on the second day before the Nones of January. When their duke died, the Normans shed many tears—if not for [Col. 0558A] him, at least for their friends and kinsmen who then died. Simon of Montfort, son-in-law of Richard, Count of Évreux, and William Pagnel; likewise the most valiant young Hugh, son of Hugh of Grandmesnil, and his kinsman Robert of Rhuddlan; William of Avranches, son of Witmund; and other illustrious men died. Blessed are those who died well, who did not see the miseries of a desolated land bereft of its defender!

Then an excessive change of circumstances occurred in Normandy: a chilling fear clung to the unarmed people, while burning ambition went unpunished among the powerful. Robert of Bellême was hurrying to the king’s court to speak with him about necessary matters. On reaching the entrance to Brionne, he heard that the king was dead. He immediately turned his horse [Col. 0558B] and came to Alençon, where he at once expelled the unsuspecting royal retainers from the fortress. He did the same at Bellême and at all his other castles; and not only at his own, but also in the strongholds of his neighbours, whom he disdained to regard as his equals. These he either subjected to himself by introducing his own retainers or utterly destroyed, lest they ever be able to resist him. William, Count of Évreux, likewise expelled the royal guards from Dangion; William of Breteuil and Ralph of Conches, together with all the others, brought the fortifications in their territories under their own power, so that each might freely pursue his damnable enmities against his neighbour and bordering lord. Thus the magnates of Neustria expelled all the king’s [Col. 0558C] guards from their fortifications and in turn despoiled by their own strength a country rich in wealth. The riches which they had violently seized from the English and other peoples they deservedly lost through brigandage and plunder.

Everyone knew Duke Robert to be weak and idle; consequently criminals despised him and pursued deceitful schemes as they pleased. The duke himself was indeed bold and strong, worthy of much praise, and eloquent in speech; but he was imprudent in governing himself and his own people, lavish in giving, excessive in promising, ready and heedless in lying, merciful to suppliants, gentle and lenient in executing justice upon wrongdoers, changeable in decisions, and altogether too affable and pliant towards everyone in maintaining agreements. Therefore he was contemptible to the perverse and foolish. In body he was short and thickset, and was consequently called by his father *Brevis-Ocrea*, “Short-Boot.”

> [Note: [Col. 0558D] In French, *Courte-Heuse*.]

He strove to please everyone and gave, promised, or granted each person what he asked. Being lavish, he daily diminished the dominion of his forefathers, foolishly granting to everyone what he requested; he himself became poorer and thereby strengthened others against himself. He gave Ivry, [Col. 0559A] where the fortress built by his great-grandmother Albereda is extremely strong, to William of Breteuil. And to Roger of Beaumont, who had been accustomed to guard Ivry at King William’s command, he granted Brionne, a very strongly fortified town situated in the heart of the land.

### II. Odo, Bishop of Bayeux, is released from custody.—Henry, for a payment, receives from his brother Duke Robert part of Normandy

After he emerged free from prison, Odo, Bishop of Bayeux, recovered all his former honour in Normandy and became adviser to his nephew, the duke. He was eloquent and high-minded, generous and very energetic in worldly matters. He diligently honoured religious men; he fiercely defended his clergy by sword and word; and he lavishly adorned the church in every respect with costly ornaments. The buildings which he constructed testify to this, as do the remarkable vessels and vestments of gold and silver with which he adorned the basilica and clergy. In his youth, on account of his brotherhood with the duke, he was given the bishopric of Bayeux. There he flourished for more than fifty years and did diverse things. In some matters the spirit laudably ruled him; in others the flesh miserably held dominion over the spirit. Thus, impelled by carnal passion, he fathered a son named John, whom we now see at the court of King Henry, distinguished by eloquence and great ability. Yet although worldly frivolity held the aforesaid Odo in certain respects, he nevertheless greatly [Col. 0559C] improved ecclesiastical affairs outwardly. He began from the foundations the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God, completed it elegantly, and richly endowed it with many treasures and ornaments. At the church of Saint Vigor, bishop of Bayeux, situated beside the city wall, he installed monks and set over them as father the religious and wise Robert of Tombelaine. Among other monuments of his learning, Robert left to the church a brief and lucid exposition on the *Song of Songs*, profound in meaning. But after the aforesaid bishop, as has been said, was confined in prison, the aforesaid abbot left everything and went abroad; arriving at Rome, he was honourably retained by Pope Gregory VII and faithfully served the Roman Church until his death. Thus, when the founding bishop had been committed to chains [Col. 0559D] and the abbot had gone to Italian parts, the newly planted flock of monks was scattered. Each sought a dwelling as he could, and they never returned to that monastery.

Finally Bishop Odo gave the aforesaid monastery to Jarent, abbot of the monks of Dijon.

> [Note: [Col. 0559D] Read “at Jarent” (*Jarentoni*). Le Prévost.]

There, to this day, a cell of the monks of Dijon flourishes. Thus it is plainly evident that Bishop Odo greatly loved the monastic order. He also sent promising clerics to Liège and to other cities where he knew the studies of philosophy especially flourished, generously supplying them with abundant funds so that they could apply themselves continuously and for a long time to the fountain of philosophy. Among the pupils whom he thus [Col. 0560A] supported were Thomas, Archbishop of York; his brother Samson, Bishop of Worcester; William of Ros, Abbot of Fécamp; Thurstan of Glastonbury; and many others who flourished in the Church of God in our own times, and diligently benefited the flocks entrusted to them by the nourishment of doctrine and the rays of virtue. Thus Bishop Odo, though greatly entangled in secular concerns, mingled many praiseworthy acts with unlawful ones, and bestowed upon churches and the poor what he had criminally amassed. At last, by the will of almighty God, in the year 1096 from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth indiction, he left everything and undertook the journey to Jerusalem with his nephew Duke Robert, as, God willing, we shall relate more fully below. In the presence of Gilbert, Bishop of Évreux, he died [Col. 0560B] in the city of Palermo. His body was buried in the basilica of Saint Mary, over which Count Roger of Sicily had an outstanding work made.

Robert, Duke of Normandy, distributed the wealth he possessed liberally among knights and bound a multitude of young warriors to himself through hope and desire of gifts. When his treasury failed, he asked his brother Henry to give him money from his treasury. Henry wholly refused. The duke then sent word that, if Henry wished, he would sell him a portion of his land. Henry, hearing what he had desired, gladly accepted his brother’s offer. Thus a firm agreement was made between the brothers. Henry paid the duke three thousand pounds of silver and received from him the whole *pagus* of the Cotentin, which is [Col. 0560C] a third of Normandy. Thus Henry first acquired Avranches, Coutances, Mont-Saint-Michel-in-Peril-of-the-Sea, and the entire estate of Hugh, Earl of Chester, which he possessed in Neustria. Henry governed the province of Coutances well and commendably trained his youthful powers. In childhood his parents had entrusted him to literary studies, and he was nobly instructed in both natural ability and learned knowledge. When Lanfranc, Archbishop of Canterbury, saw him attain the strength of youth, he raised him to arms for the defence of the realm, clothed him in a hauberk, placed a helmet on his head, and girded him with the belt of knighthood in the Lord’s name, as a king’s son and a man born of royal stock. During the twelve years [Col. 0560D] in which William Rufus reigned over the English, Henry passed a toilsome life, tossed through the various turns of fickle fortune; tried by sorrowful and happy circumstances, he learned much. Finally, when his brother died, he ascended the summit of royal power, which he held for nearly thirty-three years. If life remains my companion, I shall explain his character and deeds in their proper places, with God’s help. But now I determine to return to the order of the narrative and to make known to posterity what was done in our times.

In the first year of the rule of the two brothers, the magnates of both realms met and strove to deliberate concerning the two kingdoms, now divided, which one hand had formerly held.

> “A vast burden has suddenly grown upon us,” they said, “and a great diminution of our power and wealth has befallen us. Until now we have held honourable position in Normandy under mighty dukes, possessing the paternal inheritance which our forebears—who came from Denmark with Rollo two hundred and twelve years ago—won with great courage. Then we crossed the sea with Duke William, overthrew the English Saxons by our strength and arms, and acquired their estates with all their riches, not without great peril to our own blood. Alas! A violent change has arisen for us, and a sudden overthrow of our high estate. What are we to do? Behold, our lord is dead; two young men succeed, and have suddenly separated the lordship of [Col. 0561B] England and Normandy. How can we adequately serve two such different lords, so far apart from one another? If we serve Robert, Duke of the Normans, as we ought, we shall offend his brother William and thus be deprived by him in England of great revenues and chief honours. Again, if we fittingly obey King William, Duke Robert will deprive us in Normandy of our paternal inheritances. We must take the greatest care lest under these princes there happen to us the kind of division that befell the Israelites under Rehoboam and Jeroboam. One people, divided against itself under two rulers, fell into apostasy when God’s law, temple, and ceremonies had been overthrown. Thus, through an abominable dissension, the Hebrews wickedly armed themselves against their own flesh and, serving Baal, slaughtered many thousands of their own people. At last, one part of them—who never afterwards returned—was carried captive by the Assyrians into Media; the other suffered Babylonian captivity under the Chaldeans. And what happened to the Thebans under the two brothers Eteocles and Polynices? Did not many thousands on both sides fall? At last the brothers themselves fell by mutual wounds and left their hereditary right to foreign successors. We must carefully consider these things and many like them, and prudently guard against perishing through youthful counsel. Let us firmly enter into an inviolable pact; let us depose or kill King William, who is younger, insolent, and owes us nothing, and establish Duke Robert—elder in age, more accommodating in disposition, and the man to whom we long ago swore fealty while their father was alive—as ruler of England and Neustria, in order to preserve the unity of both realms.”

This plan was jointly adopted by Odo, Bishop of Bayeux, Eustace, Count of Boulogne, Robert of Bellême, and many others; they disclosed their resolution to Duke Robert. He, being fickle and thoughtless, took great pleasure in their useless promises and pledged himself to them that, if they began, he would be present in every matter and would soon furnish effective aid to accomplish so splendid an undertaking. Therefore, after the Nativity of the Lord, the aforesaid magnates crossed into England, fortified [Col. 0562A] their castles with abundant equipment, and in a short time stirred up a great part of the country against the king.

### III. A rebellion is raised in England by Bishop Odo in order to elevate Duke Robert to the throne.—William Rufus defeats the rebels

Odo, as stated above, was palatine earl of Kent and had under him several earls and powerful men. Earl Roger of Shrewsbury, Hugh of Grandmesnil, who held the command of Leicester, his nephew Robert of Rhuddlan, and many other most valiant knights favoured the insurgents. They abundantly equipped their strongholds with ditches, men, and provisions for men and horses. Already greedy plunderers were invading the property of country people, exultantly awaiting Duke Robert. He had planned that his advance forces should be followed, when spring returned, by himself with many legions of soldiers. Then Osbern, son of Richard surnamed Scrope, Bernard of Neufmarché, his son-in-law, and their other accomplices, who held the borders of Mercia, wickedly persisted in robberies and killings in the territory of Worcester, despite the prohibitions and excommunications of Wulfstan, the man of God and bishop. When King William saw that his own men were plotting the worst against him in his land and were proceeding, as evils multiplied in every quarter, from bad to worse, he did not plan, like a timid fox, to flee into dark dens; rather, like a strong and bold lion, he planned terribly to crush the rebels’ efforts. He therefore summoned Archbishop Lanfranc with the suffragan [Col. 0562C] bishops, the earls, and the native English, and disclosed to them the attempts of his adversaries and his intention of overcoming them. They urged the king to suppress the disturbers of the peace and promised themselves wholly ready to assist. Thirty thousand Englishmen then came voluntarily into the king’s service and urged him to punish the faithless traitors without regard, saying:

> “Act manfully, as the king’s son and as one lawfully raised to the throne; rule securely over all in this kingdom. Do you not see how many are with you and gladly obey you? Command throughout all Albion, and overthrow every rebel by royal justice. We shall fight for you to the death and never set another above you. It is altogether foolish and impious to prefer a foreign enemy to a known king. Detestable is the people that is faithless to its ruler. Let the battle-line be near death which rejoices in its lord’s ruin! Carefully examine the histories of the English, and you will find the English always faithful to their rulers.”

Encouraged by the natives’ exhortation, King Rufus became more resolute. Having assembled a great army, he marched out to fight the rebels. Then Odo of Bayeux shut himself within the city of Rochester with five hundred knights and intended to wait there for Duke Robert and his auxiliaries, in accordance with the arrangements they had made. For the insurgents, though very numerous and furnished with much treasure, arms, and vast equipment, had not dared to fight openly against the king in his own kingdom. They chose the town of Rochester with careful forethought, because, if the king did not besiege them in the city, they could, situated in the middle, devastate London and Canterbury with loose rein, and swiftly send messengers across the nearby sea and to the neighbouring islands to hire aid. But the resolute king forestalled their plans: in the month of May he powerfully besieged the town with a great army and, after fortifying two castles, denied the enemy every opportunity of leaving. The aforesaid town, as we have mentioned, was held by Bishop Odo, Count Eustace, Robert of Bellême, and many noble and lesser men; they waited in vain for the assistance of Duke Robert, who was held fast by idleness and softness. [Col. 0563B] Roger, Earl of Mercia, however, and many Normans who were besieging outside with the king, secretly strove to assist the men shut in as far as they could. Yet they did not dare openly to take up arms against the king. All the bishops of England aided the king sincerely with the English and laboured for the clear peace of the country, ever dear to good men. Hugh, Earl of Chester; Robert of Mowbray, Earl of Northumbria; William de Warenne; Robert, son of Haimo; and other lawful and mature barons faithfully adhered to the king, and usefully supported him by arms and counsel against the public enemies.

In the town of Rochester there appeared a plague like the plague of Egypt, by which God, who always cares for and justly orders human affairs, showed ancient miracles fresh even in our own times. For just as gnats afflicted the Egyptians with their importunity and did not cease for a moment from troubling them, so flies grievously harassed the besieged with unceasing annoyance. The besieged could not go outside the castle, and many of them perished from various misfortunes as disease raged. Countless flies were therefore bred from the filth of men and horses, fostered by the heat both of the season and of the breath of those living together, and horribly forced themselves upon the eyes and nostrils, food and drink of those shut in. Thus the proud band of rebels was stung by so great an infestation of flies that they could never eat by [Col. 0563D] day or night unless a large part of them took turns defending their companions’ faces from the flies’ disturbance with fans. Therefore Odo of Bayeux and his accomplices could not endure the siege any longer. They accordingly asked King William by messengers to make peace with them and receive the town from them on the condition that they should receive back from him their lands, estates, and all that they had hitherto held, and that from then on they should faithfully serve him as their natural lord.

On hearing this, the king became angry and swelled with great severity. Unmoved in any respect, he did not grant the ambassadors’ requests, but swore that the faithless traitors would be captured in the town by force, immediately hanged on gallows, and exterminated from the land by other various kinds of death. But when those who [Col. 0564A] were besieging with the king saw his mind raging so fiercely toward the death of their kinsmen and friends who were under siege, they approached him with great supplication and tried to soothe him by many entreaties and much persuasive favour. Thus they said:

> “Praised be God, who always helps those who hope in him and grants good fathers an outstanding offspring to succeed them. Behold, the swollen young men and old men blinded by greed have now learned sufficiently that the royal strength has not yet failed in this island. For those who flew upon us from Normandy like kites upon prey, supposing that the royal stock had failed in England, have now, by God’s restraint, found William the younger to be no weaker than William the elder. Almost overcome, they yield to your strength and, failing, humbly implore your greatness. We also, who have stood with you in the greatest dangers, as we stood with your father, now stand humbly before you and earnestly plead for our fellow-countrymen. For as you conquered the fearful and cowardly by courage, so it is fitting that you spare the humbled and penitent by gentleness. Let clemency temper royal severity, and let a celebrated victory suffice for your glorious valour. David, the great king, spared Shimei when he cursed him, and earnestly begged Joab, Abishai, and the other warriors not to kill Absalom, who had opposed him (2 Kings 18). The sacred books abound in examples of this kind; nor does the perceptive poet differ from them in his little work *On the Wonders of the World*:

> [Col. 0564C] Let the noble anger of the lion spare the fallen!  
> Do likewise, whoever rules the world.”

As they spoke thus, King William said:

“I acknowledge that I have overcome the enemies by your strength and, through God’s help, have gratefully approached the trophy of victory through your exertions. Yet you must take all the more care lest, by your prayers, you compel me to depart from the strictness of justice. Whoever spares perjurers and robbers, kidnappers and accursed traitors, takes peace and tranquillity away from the innocent and sows countless killings and losses among the good and unarmed. What have I done against these criminals? What harm have I caused them? Why have they pursued my death with all their strength and, to the utmost of their ability, raised whole peoples against me, to the injury of [Col. 0564D] many? I left them all that was theirs, nor did I bring any charge against them. Yet they became my bitterest enemies. Therefore I judge it altogether right that we should unshakably uphold the judgment of the great King David, whom you proposed to me for imitation. Just as Baanah and Rechab, sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, who beheaded King Ish-bosheth in his own house, were put to death by hanging at Hebron at David’s judgment (II Kings 4), so these plotters against the kingdom should be punished by a terrible sentence, so that present and future generations may be frightened and corrected by the report of this vengeance!”

To this the magnates said to the king: “All that you say, lord king, we judge true and just, nor can we contradict your reasoning by a single word. Yet affection compels us humbly [Col. 0565A] to beg Your Majesty to consider who those are for whom we make such earnest intercession. Odo of Bayeux is your uncle, and is endowed with episcopal consecration. He subdued the English with your father and gave him dangerous assistance in many anxieties. What ought to be done with so great a man? Far be it from you to lay hands upon the Lord’s priest and shed his blood in such a matter! Remember what Saul did at Nob, and what he suffered on Mount Gilboa (II Kings 22 and 31). Who would dare wickedly advise you to condemn the Lord’s bishop and your own uncle? No one. Therefore we all pray that you grant him your favour and permit him to depart unharmed for Normandy, to his diocese.

“The Count of Boulogne also was sufficiently faithful to your father and, in difficult affairs, a vigorous helper [Col. 0565B] and companion. Robert of Bellême likewise, greatly beloved by your father and formerly promoted by him with many honours, now possesses a large part of Normandy and, strengthened by very powerful castles, surpasses nearly all his neighbours and the magnates of Neustria. If, therefore, you remit the resentment of your heart toward these men and retain them kindly with you, or at least dismiss them from you in peace, you will still make useful use of their friendship and service in many eventualities. He who harms today may perhaps later obey as a friend. In their following are distinguished young knights of power, who offer themselves to you; illustrious king, you must not make light of their service. Therefore, subdue by [Col. 0565C] magnificence and mercy those whom you have already overcome in power, riches, and great courage.”

Thus the magnanimous king, overcome by the prayers of his faithful men, consented. He spared the besieged destruction and mutilation, and granted them leave to depart from the town with horses and arms. But he utterly cut off every hope of holding inheritances and lands in his kingdom for as long as he should reign.

Then Bishop Odo tried to obtain from King Rufus that, at their departure, trumpeters should not sound their trumpets, as is customary when enemies are defeated and a town is taken by force. But the king, angered, wholly refused what was requested, openly declaring that he would not grant it even for a thousand marks of gold. Therefore, as the townsmen departed in sorrow and shame and the royal trumpets sounded in celebration, the multitude [Col. 0565D] of Englishmen who adhered to the king cried aloud for all to hear:

“Bring torques, bring torques, and hang the traitor bishop and his accomplices from the gallows! Great king of the English, why do you permit the instigator of evils to leave safe and sound? The perjured murderer ought not to live, he who by deceit and cruelties has destroyed many thousands of men.”

The sorrowful bishop heard these and other reproaches with his companions. But though he uttered bitter threats, he could not satisfy his indignation. Thus the irreligious prelate was expelled from England and stripped of his very extensive possessions. Then, by God’s just judgment, he lost with immense disgrace the great gains which he had acquired through wrongdoing; ashamed, he returned to Bayeux and never afterward came back to England.

[Col. 0566A] Therefore, in the first year of King William Rufus, at the beginning of summer, the city of Rochester was surrendered to him, and the wicked uprising of all who had taken up swords against the peace was crushed. For the unjust and all evildoers, seeing the king’s boldness and strength, trembled, because they had eagerly embraced plunder, slaughter, and other crimes; and during the twelve years of his reign they afterward did not dare utter a word. He, however, conducted himself shrewdly and awaited a fitting time for vengeance. He punished the factions of some by very severe laws, but deliberately overlooked the guilt of others. He craftily spared certain old barons, whose wickedness had made them somewhat disloyal to him, for love of his father, to whom they had long faithfully adhered, and out of reverence for their old age; knowing well [Col. 0566B] that disease and death itself would not allow them to flourish for long. Moreover, some men, the more gravely they knew that they had offended against the royal majesty, served him all the more zealously thereafter and strove in many ways to please him by gifts, services, and flattery.

## IV. Gruffydd, King of the Welsh, Invades England. The History of Robert, Count of Rhuddlan

While England was being violently shaken on every side by the aforesaid storm, and the inhabitants of the kingdom daily slaughtered one another with mutual wounds—for some tried to depose the king, while others, on the contrary, fought manfully for him—Gruffydd, king of the Welsh, invaded the borders of England with his army. Around Rhuddlan he inflicted a great slaughter of men and set fires; he also took immense [Col. 0566C] booty and carried people off into captivity.

But Robert, lord of Rhuddlan, returning from the siege of Rochester and learning of these terrible and damaging reports affecting himself, groaned in deep grief and openly displayed his anger in dreadful threats. For he was a knight strong and active, eloquent and formidable, generous and praiseworthy for many virtues. He had been King Edward’s squire and received the belt of knighthood from him. His father Humphrey was son of Amfrid, of Danish stock; his mother Adeliza was sister of Hugh of Grandmesnil, of the illustrious lineage of the Giroie family. This outstanding champion, amid the labours of knighthood, was a supporter of the Church; loving clerics and monks greatly, he honoured them and willingly devoted himself, according to his means, to almsgiving [Col. 0566D] for the poor.

Moreover, he loved greatly the monastery of Ouche, where his brothers Ernald and Roger were monks and where his father, mother, and other relatives lay buried, and he enriched it to the best of his ability. He gave it the church of Telliolo, together with what he possessed in the church of Damblainville and its priesthood; and he granted what he possessed in the church of Corner, with its priesthood. He added the tithe of his mills and of all his revenues, and a second tithe of his stores. In England, the same Robert gave Saint Evroul and his monks Cumbinella, land of two ploughlands and twenty villeins, with the church and its priesthood; and [Col. 0567A] the whole tithe and the village called Chercabia, with its church and priesthood; the church of Insula; and, in the city of Chester, the church of Saint Peter of the Market, with three tenants. So that Saint Evroul might hold all these things securely and peacefully, as Robert himself had given them, he came to the chapter of Ouche and, before Abbot Mainer and the convent of monks, confirmed his grant of all the things mentioned. Razso the dean, Hugh of Milly, William the Butler son of Grimold, Roger son of Giroie, Durand, Brunel, Osbern of Orgeres, and Walter the provost were then present with him. They were present when Robert went into the basilica and laid upon the altar the deed of gift of the aforesaid possessions. I have touched briefly on the gifts which the aforesaid [Col. 0567B] hero bestowed upon the church of Ouche; and, I pray, let not the discerning reader mock me thoughtlessly if, while there is occasion, I pursue the subject of the work undertaken within the narrative.

Robert, son of Humphrey, crossed to England with his father while still a boy, and served King Edward at court and in warfare until he was made a knight by that king. Then, once clad in shining arms and honourably enriched with royal gifts, he desired to revisit his relatives; having obtained the king’s permission, he joyfully returned home to his own people. But when the battle of Senlac had been fought and King William was occupied by the many uprisings of his enemies, this same young knight crossed again to the English with his cousin Hugh, son of Richard of Avranches, surnamed Goz, and always [Col. 0567C] flourished among the foremost in every military duty. Then, after many struggles, the county of Chester was granted to the aforesaid Hugh, and Robert was made commander of his army and governor of the entire province.

At that time the neighbouring Britons, commonly called Welsh or Welshmen, raged excessively against King William and all his supporters. By the king’s decree, therefore, a fortress was built against the Welsh at Rhuddlan and granted to Robert, that he might oppose the barbarians in defence of the English kingdom. The warlike marcher-lord fought very often against this turbulent people and shed much blood in frequent battles. Having repelled the native Britons in savage warfare, he extended his borders and built a very strong castle on Mount Dagaunoth, which lies beside the sea. For fifteen years he oppressed the Britons intolerably and invaded the territories of those who, swelling with their ancient freedom, owed absolutely nothing to the Normans. He pursued his enemies through woods, marshes, and steep mountains, defeating them in many ways. Some he killed at close quarters, without respect, like cattle; others he held long in bonds or cruelly subjected to unlawful servitude. It is not lawful for a worshipper of Christ thus to oppress his brothers, who have been reborn in the faith of Christ through holy baptism.

Pride and avarice, which possess the hearts of mortals throughout the world, spurred Margrave Robert without restraint toward plunder and homicide, [Col. 0568A] through which he was afterward plunged into a dreadful abyss. For on a day in July Gruffydd, king of the Welsh, landed with three ships beneath the mountain called Hormaheva, and immediately his pirate army spread out like ravening wolves to ravage the region. Meanwhile the sea withdrew its waves, and the pirates’ fleet stood upon the dry shore. Gruffydd and his men ranged along the coast, seizing people and cattle, and hastened back to the beached ships.

Meanwhile the cry of the people awakened Robert, who was sleeping at noon, and informed him of the enemy’s raid through his land. As he lay, he rose promptly and immediately sent heralds throughout the country to assemble a force of armed men. [Col. 0568B] But he himself, with a few warriors and unprepared, pursued the Welsh; from the summit of Mount Hormaheva, which is exceedingly steep, he saw captives being bound by the pirates and thrown with the livestock into the ships. Therefore the margrave, bold as a noble lion, roared fiercely and urged the few unarmed men with him to fall upon the Welsh on the dry shore before the tide returned. But they pleaded the smallness of their number and the difficulty of descending the precipice of the steep mountain.

At last Robert, seeing the hostile force with its booty waiting for the return of the sea in order to escape, was greatly distressed. Impatient of delay, he descended the difficult slope without a mail-coat, accompanied by one knight only, named Osbern of Orgeres, toward the enemy. [Col. 0568C] When they saw him protected only by a shield and attended by a single knight, all together directed their missiles against him, overloaded his shield intolerably with javelins, and mortally wounded the distinguished knight. Yet while he stood and held his shield, none dared approach him at close range or attack him with a sword. At length the warlike hero, pierced with spears, bent his knees; exhausted in strength, he dropped his shield, excessively burdened with missiles, and commended his soul to God and to Mary, holy Mother of God. Then all rushed upon him, cut off his head before the eyes of his men, and hung it upon the mast of a ship as a token of victory. Many from the mountaintop beheld this with immense weeping and [Col. 0568D] sorrow but could not aid their hero.

Afterward fellow-countrymen assembled from the entire region, but in vain, since they could not help the margrave once he had been slain. Nevertheless, having prepared a fleet, they pursued the pirates fleeing by sea, in profound grief as they looked upon their lord’s head above the mast of the stern. When Gruffydd and his accomplices looked back and saw that their pursuers were greatly angered by the wrong done to their lord, they took down the head and threw it into the sea. When Robert’s knights saw this, they ceased vainly to pursue the murderers. But they took up his body with the exceeding lamentation of English and Normans, brought it to Chester, and buried it there in the monastery of Saint Walburga the Virgin. [Col. 0569A] Hugh, earl of Chester, had recently built that monastery; Richard, a monk of Bec, presided over it as abbot and there nourished for God a flock of monks amid brutal multitudes.

After some years Ernald the monk, son of Humphrey, crossed to England and, with the permission of Robert de Limesey, bishop of the Mercians, removed the bones of his brother Robert. Abbot Roger received them honourably with the convent of brethren and buried them in the monks’ cloister beside the church, on the south side. This Ernald, accompanied by four noblemen—Guy, Roger, Drogo, and Odo—abandoned knighthood in youth and became a monk. In monastic life he laboured harder than all his companions and lived fervently in the monastic order for almost fifty years. He devoted himself earnestly to the [Col. 0569B] welfare of his church, for which he crossed the British sea many times and travelled through Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily, in order to provide aid for his church from the possessions of his relatives. There he visited his brother William, abbot of Saint Euphemia, his cousin William of Grandmesnil, and other kinsmen enriched in Italy, and by kindly force extracted from them, as much as he could, gifts for his monastery. Thus he secured adornments and other benefits for his church from his relatives’ possessions and made those kinsmen serve the interests of the monastery. He endured many injuries and rebuffs in many places, yet could not be driven from his undertaking, although he was sometimes and often [Col. 0569C] obstructed by many adversities. The aforesaid man zealously applied himself to these and similar efforts; through his diligence, the stone arch erected over his brother’s tomb remains standing to this day.

Rainald the painter, surnamed Bartholomew, painted the arch and tomb in varied colours; and Vitalis, an Englishman, earnestly requested by Ernald, composed the following epitaph in elegiac verse:

> In this mausoleum Robert of Rhuddlan  
> Is buried, in the bosom of the earth, as men must be.  
>   
> Son of Humphrey, born from Danish seed,  
> This young man was brave and illustrious.  
>   
> Generous and warlike, active, handsome, and bold,  
> He was a knight in the world while life was granted him.  
>   
> A munificent marcher-lord and a faithful friend to his companions,  
> [Col. 0569D] He obeyed the Church, Christ’s bride.  
>   
> Priests, monks, orphans, and pilgrims  
> He always honoured and gave generous gifts.  
>   
> He built a castle and long held Rhuddlan,  
> Strongly set against the raging natives.  
>   
> Against barbarian peoples he bore arms,  
> Freely enduring a thousand dangers with a noble spirit.  
>   
> Mount Svaudunum and the swift river Colvenum  
> He crossed many times with armed men.  
>   
> Having put the fair king Blidenus to flight,  
> With a few men he seized splendid booty in an ambush.  
>   
> He took Hoel captive and bound him with cords,  
> Who then ruled the Welsh host as king.  
>   
> He captured King Gruffydd and defeated Trehellus.  
> Thus he shone through frequent titles of warfare.  
>   
> Yet, daring rashly to attack the Welsh,  
> He died at the beginning of July, in summer.  
>   
> [Col. 0570A] Owen betrayed him  
> [Note: [Col. 0569D] Read: “went forth” (*prodiit*), not “betrayed” (*prodidit*). Le Prévost.]  
> Hoel the king rejoiced,  
> Vengeance having been accomplished beneath Mount Hormaheva.  
>   
> Gruffydd cut off his head with the sword and threw it into the sea.  
> This tomb indeed holds what remained of his body.  
>   
> He rests in the cloister of holy Father Evroul;  
> For whose merits may full salvation be his!  
>   
> Once vigorous, he now lies here lifeless.  
> Hence sorrow, alas, resounds through the whole land.  
>   
> He is now turned to dust; he accomplishes nothing further.  
> Therefore, devout reader, remember him.  
>   
> Pray with worthy prayer and tears to the true God,  
> Who rules all things, that He may place him in the heavenly citadel.  
>   
> Christ, splendour of God, giver and restorer of the life  
> Of the world, be merciful to this your servant.  
>   
> Rescue Robert, O Christ, from Tartarean fires!  
> He is indeed exceedingly guilty; erase, I pray, his sin.  
>   
> Spare him, because, crying aloud in supplication to holy Mary,  
> He fell pierced with hard javelins.  
>   
> [Col. 0570B] Forgive his faults; grant enduring treasures,  
> That he may always dwell among the shining choirs. Amen.

## V. The Misgovernment of Duke Robert. At Bishop Odo’s Instigation He Invades the Men of Le Mans

While William Rufus ruled throughout all regions of the English and everywhere vigorously restrained rebels by princely authority, the swollen Odo, expelled from England, returned to the diocese of Bayeux. As Duke Robert acted weakly, Odo strove to dominate all Normandy. The whole province was in disorder. Bands of robbers roamed through villages and countryside, and gangs of thieves raged excessively against the defenceless. Duke Robert exercised no discipline over evildoers, and for eight years under a weak prince marauders vented their fury upon [Col. 0570C] a helpless people. They harassed holy Church without restraint and violently seized or devastated possessions which good predecessors had freely given. Desolate monasteries groaned, and monks and nuns were oppressed by great want. Amid the pestilence of such conflicts, no honour or reverence was shown to things consecrated to God. Fires, plundering, and murders occurred daily, and the people mourned, distressed by excessive calamities. Worthless sons emerged in Normandy, eagerly ready for every monstrous crime, and cruelly devoured their mother’s entrails.

Meanwhile wanton lust went unpunished; sodomitical Venus shamefully polluted effeminate men worthy of burning in flames. Adulteries publicly defiled the marriage bed, and manifold negligence prevailed concerning the observance of divine law. Bishops, by God’s authority, anathematized outlaws; theologians admonished the guilty in sermons. But pride and avarice, with their followers, resisted all these things without restraint. Illicit castles were founded everywhere, and there sons of robbers were reared like wolf-cubs to tear sheep apart. The wicked sought occasions for enmity so that neighbouring settlements might be repeatedly visited by mutual conflicts, while rapacity and incendiarism were pursued with irreverent zeal. [Col. 0571A] The devastated land feels this grievously and bears witness for me, as does the groaning multitude of widows and weak persons, overwhelmed by many evils. Thus through the sloth of a feeble duke, in a short time all that had been accomplished and long developed in Neustria through the energy and zealous care of its diligent lord and his supporters perished, falling into great poverty, disturbance, and disgrace.

In the summer, after certain report of the surrender of the town of Rochester had resounded across the sea, Henry the prince, count of the Cotentin, crossed into England and claimed from his brother his mother’s land. King William received him kindly, as befitted a brother, and granted fraternally what he could [Note: [Col. 0571D] Read: “what he had requested” (*petiverat*). Le Prévost.]. Then, once he had accomplished the matters for which he had gone, in autumn [Col. 0571B] he took leave of the king and intended to return to Normandy with Robert of Bellême, who had by then been reconciled to the king through powerful friends.

Meanwhile certain ill-wishers, sowers of discord, forestalled them and, mingling falsehood with truth, reported to Duke Robert that his brother Henry and Robert of Bellême had been reconciled with King Rufus and had even bound themselves by oath to an alliance for the duke’s injury. The duke, knowing them to be powerful and exceptionally strong knights and greatly fearing their designs, took counsel with the bishop of Bayeux and forestalled the aforesaid magnates. For before they could undertake anything, while they disembarked unsuspectingly from their ships onto the seashore, he sent a strong force of knights, seized them, [Col. 0571C] bound them in chains, and committed one to custody at Bayeux and the other at Neuilly, under the hand of the tyrant of Bayeux.

When Roger, earl of Shrewsbury, heard that his son Robert had been captured, he obtained leave from the king, hastened to Neustria, and fortified all his castles with military forces against the duke. Odo of Bayeux, like a fire-breathing dragon cast down to earth, was exceedingly angry at the king’s insolence and stirred Normandy with various seditions, in order somehow to devise revenge against his nephew, by whom he had been shamefully expelled. The duke greatly feared Odo and complied with some of his counsels, while making light of others.

As rebels raged everywhere in Normandy, desiring [Col. 0571D] to add many evils, the utterly wicked Bishop Odo came to Rouen to the duke. Having considered the affairs of the entire province, he said:

“Whoever ought to hold the helm of a realm and preside over God’s people, scattered among diverse customs, must be gentle and stern as reason demands: everywhere gentle as a lamb toward the good, the subject, and the humble; but stern as a lion toward the wicked, rebellious, and obstinate. Consider this wisely, lord duke, so that you may rule well over the noble duchy of Normandy which you have received from God through paternal succession. Take courage and act manfully. Behold: the insolent and lawless rage throughout the whole land, and by their most wicked and continual deeds have [Col. 0572A] nearly become like pagans and, if it may be said, equal them in the enormity of their crimes. Monks and widows cry out to you, and you sleep. You hear unheard-of crimes again and again, and make light of them.

“Holy David did not act thus, nor great Alexander; neither Julius Caesar nor Severus the African; neither Hannibal of Carthage nor Scipio Africanus, Cyrus the Persian, nor Marius the Roman. Why linger over a recital of barbarians whose very names are obscure and unknown to you? Let us recount matters better known and nearer to our own blood. Remember your fathers and forefathers, whose greatness of spirit and courage the warlike people of the Franks feared: I mean Rollo, William Longsword, the three Richards, your grandfather Robert, and finally your father William, loftier than all his predecessors. [Col. 0572B] I beg you, emulate their severity and effectiveness, just as they followed the vigour and diligence of their own predecessors, who obtained the kingdoms of the world through immense labours, crushed tyrants, and subdued savage peoples.

“Awake, gather the unconquered army of Normandy, and march to the city of Le Mans. There are your townsmen in the castle which your father built, and the whole city, with the venerable Bishop Hoel, gladly obeys you. Order all the magnates of the Manceaux to come to you there, and receive the obedient with joyful words and a favourable mind. Attack those who despise you with military force, and immediately besiege their fortifications [Col. 0572C] unless they quickly surrender. Once the Manceaux have been subdued, attack Count Roger and utterly expel him and his offspring from the borders of Normandy. Do not fear, but trust in God’s strength. Take up manly courage and use the counsels of wise men. You already hold Robert, Roger’s firstborn, in prison. If you persist stubbornly in the struggle, as becomes a good duke, you will be able utterly to expel the Talvas family, destroyers, from your duchy.

“Their lineage is accursed: it nourishes wickedness and contrives it as though by hereditary right. Indeed, their dreadful deaths bear witness to this; for none of them, so far as is known, has died by the common and customary end, like other men. Unless you now root out the stock of Talvas, it will still, in my opinion, prove harmful to you [Col. 0572D] and unconquerable. They possess, indeed, exceptionally strong castles: Bellême, Luberçon, Essay, Alençon, Domfront, Saint-Céneri, Roche d’Igé, for which Mabel fought with bold Hugh, Mamers, and Verneuil, as well as many others which William of Bellême, Robert, Ivo, Guarin, and their other successors arrogantly built or seized from their lords or neighbours by force or fraud. They have always devoted themselves to deceits and criminal schemes, and have kept faith with none of their friends or kinsmen. Having therefore overthrown their innocent neighbours by killing or capturing them, they grew exceedingly powerful and built great houses and very strong fortifications [Col. 0573A] by the extreme toil of the peasants.

“Now, excellent duke, you will be able to take all these things from them by right, if you prove a worthy and strong emulator of your great-hearted father and his deeds. For your father held all the aforesaid strongholds in his lifetime and entrusted them for safekeeping to whomever he wished. But Robert, whom you now hold bound, as soon as he heard that the king had died, arrogantly drove your townsmen out of your fortifications and subjected those strongholds to his own lordship in order to disinherit you. Consider wisely all that I have said; and, as a good prince, rise praiseworthily for the peace of holy mother Church and for the defence of the poor and weak, and crush those who resist by force. Once the horns of the foremost men who have raised their necks against you are broken, the rest, [Col. 0573B] seeing the downfall of their companions, will fear you and serve your commands without opposition. Then God’s people will rejoice securely in peace beneath the shelter of your protection and will devoutly pray almighty God for your salvation. The worship of God will be continually celebrated in your land by every order, and God’s law will be beneficially observed with common security.”

All present praised the bishop’s exhortatory address and cheerfully offered themselves for the duke’s duty, in defence of the whole homeland. Duke Robert therefore assembled an army, marched to Le Mans, and was received with rejoicing by clergy and citizens alike. After his messages had been heard, [Col. 0573C] Geoffrey of Mayenne, Robert the Burgundian, Elias son of John, and many others came to him, ready for the duke’s service. The bishop of Bayeux and Count William of Évreux commanded the Norman forces, together with Ralph of Conches, his nephew William of Breteuil, and other military men distinguished by many valiant deeds.

Payen of Montdoubleau, with other recalcitrants, held the castle of Ballon and fiercely resisted the approaching duke with his troops. There, on the Kalends of September, Osmund of Gasprée, a very handsome and honourable knight, was killed. Ernald the monk brought his body to Ouche, and it was buried in the porch before the doors of the church.

After many losses on both sides, the men of Ballon [Col. 0573D] made peace with the duke. Afterwards Normans and Manceaux together besieged the castle of Saint-Céneri with the duke. Robert of Bellême’s household was there, commanded by Robert Quarrel, a most fierce knight conspicuous for great strength; at Count Roger’s urging he vigorously opposed the besiegers. But when provisions failed, the castle was taken, and by command of the angry duke the aforesaid garrison commander was immediately deprived of his eyes. Many others who had obstinately resisted the prince of Normandy there likewise had their limbs mutilated by sentence of the court.

Then Geoffrey of Mayenne came to the duke with the leaders of the Manceaux and presented to him Robert Giroie, son of Robert of the Giroie family. [Col. 0574A] “This man,” he said, “lord duke, is your cousin, and has long lived in Apulia with your relatives, who wield great power there. He now comes confidently to you, his lord and kinsman, faithfully offering you his service, and rightly claims from you this castle, which his father possessed and held by hereditary right throughout his life, and where he died.”

Duke Robert readily assented to these requests and restored the castle of Saint-Céneri to Robert Giroie. He held it for nearly thirty-six years afterward, fortified it with walls, ditches, and palisades, and at his death left it to his sons William and Robert.

The inhabitants of this fortress were almost always without rest and peace, while neighbouring Manceaux [Col. 0574B] and Normans pressed upon them. The winding course of the river Sarthe surrounds on three sides the rocky hill on which Saint Céneri, the venerable confessor, lived in the time of Milehard, bishop of Sées. There he founded a monastery for monks and, having served the Lord with a glorious company and happily completed the course of his life, migrated joyfully to the Lord on the Nones of May. Finally, while Charles the Simple was reigning, when the Dane Hasting ravaged Neustria with a host of pagans, the holy body was taken by the faithful to Château-Thierry, the monks were scattered, and the monastery was destroyed.

In the succeeding period the inhabitants changed. Bloodthirsty robbers made there a den of thieves, where, under [Col. 0574C] Saint Céneri’s rule, despisers of the world had formerly lived modestly and borne the Lord’s yoke in the monastic order to the end. One hundred and forty labourers, it is said, worked there in the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts under the aforesaid archimandrite. Their stone tombs, visible to those approaching between and around the basilica, bear witness to the merit and reverence of the men who rest there. The wicked inhabitants therefore deservedly suffered many misfortunes and were frequently afflicted by killings, burnings, manifold oppressions, and overthrows.

When the townsmen of Alençon, Bellême, and other strongholds heard how badly matters had gone for Robert Quarrel and his accomplices, they were greatly frightened and took counsel about surrendering their due fortifications to the approaching duke [Col. 0574D]. But Robert quickly failed in the courage he had begun to show and, yielding to softness, eagerly returned to shelter and rest; he dismissed his army, each man to return home.

## VI. Count Roger of Le Mans Makes Peace with Duke Robert. The Wickedness of Count Robert of Bellême. The Magnates of Normandy Make War upon One Another

When the Norman and Manceau forces had been disbanded, Count Roger rejoiced. By mocking envoys he sought peace from the duke and the release of his son, making many false promises. But the duke, improvident and unstable, prone to fall and lax in maintaining the rigour of justice, unexpectedly accepted the frivolous agreements of unfaithful men. [Col. 0575A] He made peace with Count Roger, granted his request, and released Robert of Bellême from chains.

Once free, Robert swelled with pride, valued the duke’s commands and threats less highly, and, mindful of the injury he had received, exercised a long and manifold vengeance. During the fifteen years in which they afterward lived together in Neustria, he raged greatly and disturbed the duke’s whole land in many ways. By cunning evasions he turned many away from the duke’s assistance and service, and diminished the duke’s dominion, which his predecessors had possessed and greatly enlarged. For he was subtle in intellect, deceitful and double-faced; large and strong in body; bold and powerful in arms; eloquent; excessively cruel; insatiable in greed and lust; an astute contriver of serious schemes [Col. 0575B] and most enduring in the harsh labours of worldly undertakings; an ingenious craftsman in constructing buildings, engines, and other difficult works; and an inexorable executioner in torturing men. He did not honour, assist, and clothe holy Church as a son honours his mother; rather, like a stepson, he defiled, oppressed, and despoiled his stepmother. At last, after innumerable crimes and deceitful factions, King Henry, the most just judge, specially inspired by God and a vigorous avenger of the wretched, confined him in chains by God’s judgment. But of these matters elsewhere.

The aforesaid man, through the intervention of King William, who loved him greatly for the sake of his parents, Roger and Mabel, married Agnes, daughter of Guy, Count of Ponthieu. By her he begot a son named William, who later securely possessed, by hereditary right, extensive estates in Neustria and Ponthieu. [Col. 0575C]

For Robert surpassed all his brothers as much in tyranny as in wealth. Having disinherited his brothers, he seized the whole patrimony of his forefathers in Normandy and the district of Maine, and held it alone for a long time. With utmost effort he strove to subjugate his kinsmen, his equals in nobility; and, as his insatiable greed dictated, he bent some beneath his dominion by deceit and intolerable wars, or by treacherous assaults. Hugh of Nonant, Paganellus, Robert of Saint-Céneri, Bernard of La Ferté, and many others experienced this; he frequently distressed them, [Col. 0575D] terrified them in many ways, and afflicted them. Indeed, he humbled many by taking away their honours and burning their fortifications; or, after devastating their estates, he reduced them to extreme want; or, what was worse, he rendered them useless by maiming their limbs, making them crippled or lame, or depriving them of sight.
