Thus the wretched region was returning to desolation, while the blazing tyranny of the bloody marquis sought to trample down all its neighbours; against him men, swollen with equal nobility of birth, strove to defend their ancient freedom unto death. So immense losses grew daily; and, for revenge or acquisition, losses added to losses ruined human affairs and threatened the inhabitants of the land with famine. [Col. 0576A]

Geoffrey, son of Rotrou, Count of Mortagne, took up arms against Robert, burned Excalfoium and many other villages round about, and carried off much booty and many people. This count was high-minded, handsome and strong in body, fearing God and a devout worshipper of the Church, a vigorous defender of clerics and God’s poor; in peace quiet and gracious, endowed with good habits; in war formidable and fortunate, intolerable to neighbouring rulers and an enemy to all. Through the nobility of his parents and of his wife Beatrice, he was conspicuous among the illustrious; [Col. 0576B] and he had under his authority valiant barons and townsmen fierce in war. He also gave his daughters in marriage to comital husbands: Margaret to Henry, Count of Covarevicum, and Juliana to Gilbert of the town of L’Aigle. From them sprang a noble and distinguished line of descendants.

[Note: Justellus, *History of the House of La Tour d’Auvergne*, book I, p. 31, adds a third daughter of Geoffrey, namely Matilda, wife of Raymond of Turenne, relying on the testimony of Geoffrey of Vigeois, chapter 23 of his chronicle: “Raymond, whose name is written on the denarius of public coinage, begot Boson by Matilda, who was sister of the Count of Perche.” Since the count’s name is not expressed, we leave undecided whether she was the daughter or the sister of Count Geoffrey. Dom Bouquet, book VIII, p. 633.] [Col. 0575D; 0576D]

Count Geoffrey, therefore, was adorned by so many genealogical distinctions, supported by arms and courage, wealth and friends, and—above all—fortified by the fear of God; fearing no one, he advanced like a lion. He claimed Danfront, a very strong castle, and other estates as his lawful due, and strove to take them from his kinsman Robert. He was grieved that Robert oppressed the unarmed and undeserving, but could not find in the open field [Col. 0576C] a public enemy upon whom to inflict the deserved vengeance. For Robert, who crushed almost everyone, nevertheless feared everyone, and therefore did not dare to engage the enemy hand-to-hand in open battle. He hid cunningly in his fortifications and, though he was most courageous in warfare, often sorrowfully allowed raiders to range through his lands, not venturing to meet them. For he wisely guarded against being abandoned by his own men into the enemy’s hands if he marched out. Thus the long quarrel between the two powerful marquises endured and produced many losses and killings among their subjects. Indeed, a like tinder of evils sprang up everywhere throughout Normandy among the other magnates and prepared an enormous medley of tragedies. [Col. 0576D]

While Neustria was everywhere disturbed by the swollen seditions of magnates under a weak prince, and while the peaceful children of the Church groaned amid fires and frequent plundering, the most merciful ruler of humankind had compassion on His servants. He removed certain veterans from the pit of misery and the valley of tears out of the fellowship of mortals, and, as we believe, graciously joined them in the desirable delightfulness of paradise to known fellow-soldiers engaged in a similar pursuit of religion.

## VII. Death of Durand, Abbot of Troarn.—Pope Victor elected.—Pope Urban

[Col. 0577A]

Durand, the aged abbot of Troarn, a monk from childhood, eminent in religious devotion and wisdom, most skilled teacher of ecclesiastical chant and sacred doctrine, a harsh chastiser of himself and a gentle benefactor of others, lay down upon his bed after many labours in God’s service. Well prepared, like a prudent and faithful servant, to go to the court of his lord, he departed this world on 11 February [1088].

At his death an occurrence not to be passed over took place. When the aforesaid Father died, a divided colour was seen in his body. For on the left side of his face and of his entire body, down to the feet, snowy whiteness appeared; while a leaden lividity covered the whole right side and occupied the entire right half [Col. 0577B] from the crown of the head to the feet, just as the whiteness occupied the left. This unusual division of visible colour struck terror into those who saw it and offered diligent inquirers into the cause of the unprecedented phenomenon an occasion to display the subtlety of their discernment. Accordingly different men said different things. But it is not for this brief account to insert every interpretation that eloquent men, from the abundance of their thought, advanced in many forms. Some interpreted left and right as the active and contemplative life, or as the present and future life. Others believed that this prodigy was a presage of future events.

His venerable disciples reverently buried the body of their religious teacher in their chapter house, and added this epitaph to the white stone laid over him:

> In this tomb lies the good and venerable abbot,  
> Durand, the model of our monastery.  
> For the praise of the Lord he built this present church,  
> In which we believe God is favourable to him.  
> Under February’s eleventh light, released from the bond  
> Of flesh, he is borne to the angelic homeland.

After the shepherd’s burial, the flock of Troarn chose Arnulf, prior of the monastery of Sées, and requested ecclesiastical governors and their princes to set him over them. When these rejoiced and willingly consented to what was asked, Arnulf accepted the government of the Troarn community. He held it diligently for nearly twenty-two years and instructed those subject to him by words, writings, and wholesome examples. The two aforesaid monasteries [Col. 0577D] had received the beginning of their foundation from one prince, and likewise derived from one source their observance of divine service and the institution of monastic order. For Roger of Montgomery dedicated both monasteries to monks, and the rule of Fécamp committed both to monastic observance. One affection joined these communities of monks alike, and Martin, the banner-bearing archbishop of Tours, keeps safe those entrusted to his service. The monks of Sées first received their abbot from Troarn; and now, while that same father still lived, they obtained a friendly return from among his disciples. Having gained him, they gave thanks to God and prospered well through the diligence of their good shepherd.

Then Robert, duke of Normandy, yielding to the entreaties of his magnates, released his brother Henry from the bonds in which he had been confined with Robert of Bellême. [Col. 0578A]

About this time [1085], Pope Gregory died in the city of Benevento, and Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, was elected and enthroned as Victor, pope of Rome. The dead pope’s body was buried in the sanctuary of St Bartholomew the Apostle, where, through his merits, an abundance of miracles was divinely shown to faithful petitioners. Lepers asked for water with which his body had been washed; when they obtained it, they washed faithfully and were immediately cleansed by God’s help.

After Pope Victor had ascended the height of the pontificate, he began solemnly to sing his first Mass on the holy day of Pentecost. But, by God’s hidden will, he was suddenly seized by a grave sickness. Driven by diarrhoea, he was led away from Mass three times to the latrine; thus in his papacy he had barely celebrated a single Mass. He was a man of great nobility, wisdom, and religious devotion, and had long governed the monastery of the holy father Benedict, built at Monte Cassino. Thence he was raised to the episcopate, but suddenly fell ill, as we have said. He languished from Pentecost until August and then died. [Col. 0578B]

After his death the Roman clergy assembled and elected Odo, formerly a monk and bishop of Ostia, as Urban, pope of Rome. God of Israel appointed him a great prince against the Philistines, and entrusted to him David’s tower with its bulwarks, facing Damascus. He was French by nation, distinguished for noble birth and gentleness, a citizen of Rheims, a monk of Cluny, of middle age, great in body, discerning in moderation, supreme in religious devotion, and eminent in wisdom and eloquence. Guibert, the usurper of the Apostolic See, still troubled God’s Church, drawing all whom he could, whether by flattery or persecution, away from the unity of peace into his schism. Odo, Count of Sutri, was Guibert’s nephew and restrained the supporters of ecclesiastical peace by many forms of oppression. [Col. 0578C]

Pope Urban, trusting in the Lord of heaven, who does not leave the sceptre of sinners over the lot of the righteous, sent envoys and letters under Roman authority to the Franks, Greeks, and other peoples throughout the world, urging them to persevere unwaveringly in the Catholic faith and prudently to guard against every rupture from the law of God and the body of Christ, which is the Church. Henry alone, ruler of the Germans, and his followers adhered to Guibert. But the Franks, the English, and almost all other peoples throughout the world devoutly obeyed Urban. [Col. 0578D]

## VIII. Various events in Apulia, Normandy, and England.—Deaths of certain magnates.—William Rufus’s restricted administration

In Apulia all the Normans unanimously supported the Catholic pope. Yet among themselves they quarrelled savagely, and brothers repeatedly waged wars more than civil. Roger, surnamed *Crumena*, that is, “the Purse,” held the duchy of Calabria alone with his mother. This his brother Bohemond, living in exile with Prince Jordan of Capua, endured with difficulty. Therefore, with the assistance of his brother-in-law Jordan and of his other relatives and friends, he took up arms against his brother and began manfully to reclaim the portion of his paternal honour which he himself had conquered in war together with his father. His brother and stepmother could not withstand this war and were compelled to seek more advantageous counsel from their friends. Accordingly, through the persuasion of Count Roger of Sicily and other kinsmen, they made peace and handed over to him Bari and Taranto, together with two other cities and many towns.

After making this agreement, the brothers gave their sister Mabel in marriage to William of Grandmesnil and subjected many castles to his authority, because he was very worthy. By this bond of kinship the Normans were prudently tied together in mutual connection, and they have possessed to this day a great part of Italy, which Drogo, Humphrey, Richard, and, above all, Robert Guiscard had held. [Col. 0579B]

In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1089, in the twelfth indiction, Robert, the first abbot of the monastery of Sées, a good and simple man, took to his bed in January. Having received the Lord’s sacraments, he departed this world on 15 January. Ralph, son of Seifred of Échauffour, a monk of the same monastery, succeeded him in the administration. He was highly learned, eloquent, and agreeable, and therefore loved by all. In youth, though of an illustrious family, he entered monastic life and served humbly in the monastery for ten years through the various ranks of office. In the eleventh year, at the command and consecration of Gerard, bishop of Sées, he accepted the care of the abbey. He governed vigorously for sixteen years amid the fierce storms of war and, relying on God’s aid, carefully increased the Church’s possessions as opportunity allowed. Later, when Robert of Bellême’s cruelty became too threatening, he fled to England. King Henry retained him honourably with himself and, through Bishop Gundulf, placed him over the bishopric of Rochester. [Col. 0579C] Thereafter, having been promoted after some years, he succeeded the venerable Archbishop Anselm and presided over the metropolitan see of Canterbury for nine years. [Col. 0579D]

In the third year [1089] of William Rufus, king of the English, Lanfranc, bishop of the metropolitan see of Canterbury, died and was buried before the Crucifix in the basilica of the Holy Trinity, which he himself had built with marvellous workmanship. Anselm of Bec, moreover, mournfully committed the aforesaid memory of his compatriot to a volume in heroic verse. By God’s will, three years later, raised by ecclesiastical election, he ascended the chair of Canterbury. Then, within the ten years during which William Rufus thereafter reigned, Thomas, metropolitan of York, followed his fellow bishop in death, together with many other bishops [Col. 0580A] and abbots. For Bishop Wulfstan of Worcester, Robert of Hereford, Osmund of Salisbury, Walkelin of Winchester, Baldwin, archdeacon and abbot of St Edmund the King and Martyr, Thurstan of Glastonbury, Rainald of Abingdon, and many other bishops and abbots died; I do not wish to name them one by one, lest readers grow weary.

At this time a certain clerk named Ranulf gained the intimacy of King Rufus. By ingenious accusations and manifold flatteries, he obtained from the king authority over all the royal officials. He was sharp in intellect, handsome in body, swollen with eloquence, given to banquets, drunkenness, and excessive lust, cruel and ambitious, lavish toward his own dependants, but a most rapacious plunderer of strangers. [Col. 0580B] He sprang from a rather obscure and poor family, and, raised far above his birth to the injury of many, grew proud. He was the son of Thurstan, a common priest from the district of Bayeux. From childhood he was reared among the foot-servants of the court together with low parasites, applying himself more to cunning evasions and clever verbal contrivances than to the art of letters. Because he dared arrogantly to prefer himself in the court of the great King William above distinguished men, he undertook many things without the king’s knowledge or command, insolently accused many in the king’s hall, and rashly ordered his superiors about as though supported by royal power. Hence Robert, the royal steward, surnamed him Flambard; the name was bestowed upon him, as it were prophetically, according to his habits and deeds. For, a blazing flame, through many actions he imposed new practices upon the people, cruelly oppressed their assemblies, and changed the Church’s temporal chants into lamentations. [Col. 0580C]

He disturbed the young king with fraudulent goadings, urging him to revise the survey of all England and advising him to repeat the apportionment of English land, cutting back from subjects, newcomers and natives alike, whatever should be found beyond a fixed measure. With the king’s consent, he measured and recorded with a cord all the ploughlands which the English call *hides*; disregarding the measures that the free English had liberally distributed by King Edward’s command, he reduced them, accumulated the royal revenues, and cut down the peasants’ fields. [Col. 0580D] Thus, by the diminution of land they had long possessed and by the severe increase of an unfamiliar levy, he shamefully oppressed the people, suppliants to royal fidelity; stripping them of their goods, he impoverished them and reduced those once greatly affluent to extreme want.

On his counsel the young king, whenever prelates died, seized churches with the estates once given to them. In abbeys he subjected monks, and in bishoprics episcopal deans and canons, to any of his retainers. He assigned them a scant allowance for their livelihood and made the remaining revenues subject to his own dominion. Thus the king’s greed flared exceedingly within God’s Church, and that wicked custom, then begun and continuing to the present day, brings destruction upon many souls. [Col. 0581A] For this reason the covetous king delayed appointing pastors to churches; the people, lacking a ruler, and the flock, lacking a shepherd, lay exposed to wolves’ teeth and perished, wounded by the poisoned missiles of manifold sins.

The prince, therefore, burning with excessive greed, brought into his treasury the abundant wealth which earlier kings of the English—namely Æthelberht and Edwin, Offa and Æthelwulf, Alfred and Edgar, and other princes with their magnates—had gladly and devoutly given to God’s Church. Newly converted to the faith, they had faithfully worshipped God and liberally bestowed from their abundance upon monks and clerics, so that the special ministers of the sacred law, nourished by abundant food, might rejoice, diligently perform God’s worship night and day without any refusal, and unceasingly offer God solemn watches in the places appointed. [Col. 0581B] There pilgrims and travellers came safely; after their labour they found prompt rest there, and after hunger they found plentiful sustenance by princely institution. Thus unexpectedly comforted, they gave thanks to God and devoutly besought the Creator of all for their benefactors, who long before had prepared so great a help for them.

Before the Normans gained England, it was customary that, when governors of churches died, the bishop should carefully inventory the possessions of monasteries in his diocese and keep them under his authority until abbots were lawfully appointed. Similarly, upon the death of a bishop, the archbishop safeguarded the property of the bishopric and, with the counsel of those belonging to that church, expended it on the poor, the construction of churches, or other good works. [Col. 0581C] William Rufus, at the beginning of his reign, abolished this custom by Flambard’s persuasion. He allowed the metropolitan see of Canterbury to remain without a bishop for three years and carried its revenues into his own treasuries. It seems unjust indeed, and contrary to every principle of reason, that what was given to God through the faithful generosity of princes or laudably increased through the diligence of stewards of ecclesiastical property should again be withdrawn under lay control and expended upon the wicked uses of the world.

We must undoubtedly believe that, just as those who devoutly gave God of their possessions have now received, by God’s gift, the reward of their merits, so sacrilegious invaders of sacred things will be punished by God the avenger and stripped, with lasting disgrace, of the wealth they unjustly possess. [Col. 0581D] For the law of the Almighty is eternal and true. As it graciously promises rewards to those who cultivate justice, so it threatens terrible punishments to transgressors for their wickedness. Mercy and truth are proclaimed on every page of divine authority and are clearer than light to every learned person. It is therefore astonishing that the human heart so readily declines into wickedness and desires present, perishable things more than future, enduring ones, although it knows that all things lie open to the divine gaze and that nothing escapes God’s judgment unexamined.

After the metropolitan see of Canterbury, bereft of its bishop, had spent three years in fear and mourning, the just Judge, who looks down from heaven upon the children of men and sees them all embrace vanities of vanities, struck the king of the English—defiled with the manifold dregs of crimes—with a grievous sickness. [Col. 0582A] Punished by illness, he summoned the Lord’s priests, laid bare the wounds of his soul by confession before these spiritual physicians, promised amendment of life, and ordered the ecclesiastical governors to elect an archbishop according to the Lord’s will.

At that time Anselm, abbot of the monks of Bec, had by chance crossed into England on business of his church. When the king’s order concerning the election of a metropolitan was heard, holy Church rejoiced, gathered an assembly of elders, and began to deliberate concerning the matter for which they had assembled. At last, considering the holiness and wisdom of the venerable Anselm, they unanimously elected him in the Lord’s name and, despite his strong resistance, set him over the metropolitan see of Canterbury according to ecclesiastical custom. [Col. 0582B] Once enthroned, the diligent shepherd often groaned, wisely weighing how heavy and dangerous a burden he had undertaken to bear. He did not grow proud of his elevation but trembled over the perdition of many whom, under his government, he saw straying from God’s law. He perceived many things in his diocese that needed correction. He often rebuked the sinful king and the grim magnates. Therefore he suffered many adversities from them and went into exile twice for zeal for justice. By wholesome words and examples he strove to reform the perverse habits of those subject to him; but because of the hardened wickedness of some, he did not succeed in many things as he wished. [Col. 0582C] For the perverse, as Solomon says, are difficult to correct, and “the number of fools is infinite” (Ecclesiastes 1:15).

## IX. King William plans to attack his brother Robert in Normandy.—The men of Maine rise against the aforesaid Robert.—Count Fulk of Anjou

In those days [1089], the lamp of true holiness shone more dimly in almost every order, and the princes of the world, with the bands subject to them, clung to works of darkness. William Rufus, king of Albion, was an arrogant and dissolute young man, eagerly followed by crowds of people of shameless habits. He was commanding, bold, and martial, and strutted magnificently with a multitude of soldiers. He applauded military titles and greatly favoured their holders because of worldly pride. He neglected to defend country people against soldiers, allowing their possessions to be ravaged with impunity by his young warriors and men-at-arms. [Col. 0582D] He had a retentive memory and a burning will for good or evil. He pressed hard upon thieves and robbers, inspiring terror, and vigorously compelled tranquil peace to be maintained throughout the land subject to him. By generosity, or by force and fear, he either enticed or subdued all the inhabitants of his kingdom, so that no one dared in any way to murmur against him.

Strengthened in his kingdom, he summoned bands of magnates; when they had gathered at Winchester, he spoke aloud what he had inwardly been pondering:

> “You know, noble barons,” he said, “how my brother Robert’s loyalty has acted toward me and how many hardships he has caused me. There is no need of many words to recount how many of my men he has stirred up against me in my own kingdom, and how earnestly he has plotted to deprive me of kingdom and life. It is sufficiently clear to all what intolerable harm he would have done me in the first year of my reign, had not divine power in its mercy driven it away from me. [Col. 0583A]
>
> “Behold: holy Church sends me a lamentable complaint from the lands across the sea, because, greatly sorrowing, she is daily soaked with tears; lacking a just defender and protector, she stands among evildoers like a sheep among wolves. He strives by fraud and force to take my land from me, though he neglects to defend his own land from wicked raiders. Therefore I urge all of you who were my father’s men and held your fiefs in Normandy and England from him, without deceit to support me courageously and unanimously in this work of worth. We must not allow bands of robbers to oppress the faithful or destroy the monasteries of the saints, which our fathers built with utmost effort in Neustria. The whole region is exposed to slaughter and plundering, often from necessity recalling William, the great prince, who delivered it from foreign and internal wars. [Col. 0583B] It is fitting, therefore, that as I bear his name and crown, so I should adhere to his purpose in defending the fatherland. Gather, I pray, in counsel; prudently form your deliberation; pronounce your judgment concerning what must be done in this crisis. If you approve, I shall send an army into Normandy and repay in kind the injuries which my brother has without cause devised against me. I shall aid God’s Church, protect unarmed widows and orphans, and punish thieves and murderers with the sword of justice.” [Col. 0583C]

When he had said this, all gave their assent and praised the king’s high-mindedness. Then King William made William de Warenne count of Surrey; soon afterward death, sparing no one, carried him away. The monks of Cluny, whom he had honourably established at Lewes, buried his body in their chapter house and indicated, in these verses carved on a white stone above his grave, who and what kind of man rested there:

> [Col. 0584A] Here, Count William, is a place whence praise springs for you.  
> You founded this house and loved it with lavish generosity.  
> This place honours your funeral, since the gift  
> You gave with ready heart to Christ’s poor pleased God.  
> Pancras, the heir, preserves your ashes,  
> And will join you to the heavenly host of saints.  
> Best of Pancrases, bring aid to him who glorifies you,  
> And grant a dwelling in heaven to him who gave you such a house.

The sons of the aforesaid count, William and Reynold, succeeded with their mother Gundrada and long flourished in worth and power under Kings William and Henry of England. King William also bestowed great honours upon Robert, son of Haimo, and raised him among the greatest magnates of England. He married Sibyl, daughter of Count Roger, who bore him a daughter named Matilda; Robert, son of King Henry, later married her. [Col. 0584B]

Stephen of Aumale, son of Odo, Count of Champagne, was the first of the Normans to attach himself to the king. At royal expense he strongly fortified his castle on the river Aucie, receiving there a very powerful royal garrison against the duke. Gerard of Gournay soon followed him. He handed Gournay, La Ferté, Fontaine-le-Bourg, and his other fortifications over to the king, and strove to subject his neighbours to the royal party. Then Robert, Count of Eu, Walter Giffard, Ralph of Mortemer, and nearly all who dwelt beyond the Seine as far as the sea joined the English, and received abundant money from the royal resources for strengthening their houses with arms and retainers. [Col. 0584C]

Then Duke Robert prepared a defence against so many enemies. He gave his daughter, whom he had had by a concubine, as wife to Helias, son of Lambert of Saint-Saëns, and granted him Arques, with Bures and the adjoining region, as a marriage portion, so that he might resist the adversaries and defend the county of Caux.

[Note: Robert also summoned King Philip of the French to assist him against the English king—something which, remarkably, Orderic either did not know or passed over in silence. This is clear from the notice of excommunication issued by Pope Urban II against William, archbishop of Rouen, in the dispute concerning the monks of Fécamp, among the documents in *Gallia Christiana*, XI, col. 18:

“For in the year 1089 from the Incarnation of the Saviour, at the time when war existed between the brothers William, king of the English, and Robert, Count of the Normans, that count, wishing to reward King Philip of the French because he had assisted him in besieging the king’s castle of La Ferté, and having nothing of his own that he could give, took away the manor called Gisors from St Mary of Rouen and bestowed it upon the king.”

William, who had then passed from being abbot of Caen to preside as archbishop, took this harshly; because he could not induce the count to restore what had been taken, he commanded all churches throughout Normandy to cease divine praise. When he likewise ordered the church of Fécamp to cease, the prior and monks—for Abbot William III was then absent in England—answered that they could not cease, etc.

William of Malmesbury, book IV, p. 121, likewise testifies that Philip was summoned by Robert for assistance, but adds insultingly: “He, indolent and belching forth his daily drunken revel, came to war gasping from gluttony; but the English king’s money, promising much, met him, and, defeated by it, he unfastened his belt and returned to his feast.” Roger of Howden states the matter more moderately under 1089: “King William, secretly sending King Philip a considerable sum of money, obtained his request that he should withdraw from the siege—perhaps of a certain castle, La Ferté.” Dom Bouquet, book VIII, p. 636.] [Col. 0583D–0584D]

Helias began manfully to carry out his commands. He was always loyal to Duke Robert and Robert’s son William; under the two kings, William and Henry, he endured much—labours and disinheritance, losses, exile, and many dangers.

When the men of Maine heard of the Normans’ dissension, they thought to shake off their haughty yoke, [Col. 0584D] as they had often attempted under William, [Col. 0585A] the great king of the English. As soon as Duke Robert learned this, he sent envoys and gifts to Fulk, ruler of the Angevins, earnestly begging him to restrain the men of Maine from their rash undertaking and come to him in Normandy, where he was seriously ill. Fulk willingly agreed to the request and found the duke already recovering. After many discussions of peace and friendship, Count Fulk said to Duke Robert:

> “If you do for me one thing which I greatly desire, I shall subject the men of Maine to you and shall faithfully serve you as a friend at all times. I love Bertrada, offspring of Simon of Montfort, namely the niece of William, Count of Évreux; Countess Helvise is rearing and keeping her under her protection. I beg you, give her to me as wife, and I shall keep all that I have pledged to you.” [Col. 0585B]

Immediately, on the duke’s behalf, the Count of Évreux was consulted about the matter. He at once took counsel with his close friends and carefully investigated the outcome of the affair. Finally, after diligent consideration, he came to the duke’s court and said to him among other things:

> “My lord duke, you ask of me a thing very contrary to my interest: that I give my niece, still a tender virgin, to a twice-married man; yet my brother-in-law entrusted her to me to be reared. You prudently seek your own advantage but make little account of mine. You wish to gain the county of Maine through my niece, while taking away my inheritance. Is what you propose just? I shall not do what you ask unless you restore to me Bathventum and Nogent, Vassy and Gravençon, Sacey, and the other estates of my uncle Ralph, who was jokingly called ‘Ass’s Head’ because of the size of his head and the mass of his hair; and restore to my nephew William of Breteuil Pont-Saint-Pierre and all else which we can reasonably and lawfully prove ought to be ours by hereditary right. [Col. 0585C] I have lawful and wholly competent witnesses that Robert of Gacé, son of the aforesaid Ralph, my uncle, made me heir to his entire right. But King William, our cousin, because he was more powerful than we, made all portions of our inheritance his own, like a lion in the division of a stag. Having wisely considered these matters, my lord duke, uphold justice for us, and we shall obey your commands.” [Col. 0586A]

When the duke had heard this answer, he resolved on the advice of the wise to grant the lesser things, lest he lose the greater. Edgar Ætheling, Robert of Bellême, and William of Arques, a monk of Molesme, were then the duke’s principal counsellors. The duke therefore acceded to the petitions of William of Évreux and his nephew William of Breteuil and granted the aforesaid towns with their territories, except Sacey, which Gerard of Gournay possessed, he being of the same kindred. For he was the son of Basilia, daughter of Gerard Flaitel, and of such power that no one could use force against him.

Then the count of Anjou joyfully received the girl he had desired and, while two wives were still living, married a third. She bore him a son named Fulk. Mindful of his compact, Fulk went to the men of Maine and endeavoured to restrain them more by prayers and promises than by force; he postponed their concerted rebellion for at least a year. [Col. 0586B]

## X. Fulk, Count of Anjou, devises a new form of shoes.—The customs, clothing, games, etc., of this period
He was in many respects blameworthy and notorious, and yielded to many pestilent vices. Because he had misshapen feet, he caused long shoes, extremely pointed at the tips, to be made for himself, so that they covered his feet and concealed their swellings, commonly called bunions. [Col. 0586C] From this an unusual fashion spread through the western world and greatly pleased the frivolous and lovers of novelty. Thus shoemakers made upon their shoes, as it were, scorpions’ tails, commonly called *pigaciae*.

[Note: [Col. 0585D] These *pigaciae* seem to be the same kind of footwear as *Poulainiae* or *Pouleanae*, or beaked shoes, concerning which Du Cange offers a copious and learned discussion in his notes on Anna Comnena’s *Alexiad*, pp. 202–204, and a briefer one in his *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin*, under “Poulainia” and “Rostra.” Orderic, as he observes, makes Fulk Rechin the originator of such pointed shoes—not because he first invented them, but because he first introduced their use into France. For Cato in Festus, Cicero in *On the Nature of the Gods*, Tertullian in *On the Pallium*, ch. 5, and others show that curved and hooked shoes were in use among the Romans. Their shape ended in an arched point, turned upward like hooks; hence Tertullian calls those who wore hooked shoes “hook-footed” (*uncipedes*). This ridiculous fashion lasted in France until the time of King Charles VI, as the continuator of Nangis testifies under the year 1365:

“They wore shoes having exceedingly long beaks in the forepart, extended lengthwise in the manner of a horn; others bore them slantwise, as griffins have behind and naturally carry for claws. These beaks they commonly wore, and call them *Pouleanas* in French. And because the thing was very ugly and, as it were, contrary to the natural formation of the limbs about the feet—indeed, it seemed an abuse of nature—the lord king of France, Charles, caused a public proclamation to be made by heralds in Paris that no person whatsoever should dare to wear such things. He further ordered, under a heavy penalty, that artisans should thereafter neither presume to make such shoes or similarly pointed boots, nor sell them to anyone. For in like manner Pope Urban V had very strictly forbidden them in the Roman Curia.”

Dom Bouquet, book VIII, p. 637.]

Nearly everyone, rich and poor alike, excessively desired this kind of shoe. Formerly, at all times, shoes were rounded in the shape of the foot, and men of high and middling rank, clerics and laymen, used them suitably. But now worldly people, through perverse customs, proudly desire an unsuitable shape; and what honourable men once judged most disgraceful and wholly rejected as dung, modern people esteem as sweet honey and wear as they embrace it as a special ornament.

[Col. 0587A] A certain rascal, Robert, at the court of King Rufus was the first to stuff long *pigaciae* with tow and twist them here and there like a ram’s horn. On this account he was surnamed Cornard, “the Horned.” A great part of the nobility soon followed his foolish invention as though it were some notable work of excellence and valour. Then effeminate men ruled everywhere in the world and raged without discipline; foul catamites, worthy of being burned in flames for Sodomitic filth, shamefully indulged themselves. They cast aside the practices of heroes, mocked the exhortations of priests, and maintained a barbarous fashion in dress and life. They parted their hair from the crown toward the forehead, let their locks grow long like women, and took the greatest care of them. They delighted in being clad in long, exceedingly tight shirts and tunics. [Col. 0587B] Some arrogated all time to themselves and lived as they pleased, outside the law of God and ancestral custom. At night they devoted themselves to feasts and drinking-bouts, idle talk, dice and gaming, and other amusements; by day they slept.

Thus, after the death of Pope Gregory and William the Bastard, and other devout rulers, the honourable custom of the ancient fathers was almost wholly abolished in the western regions. For they wore modest garments, excellently fitted to the measure of their bodies. They were suited for riding and running, and for every task which reason suggested should be done. But in these days the practice of the ancients has been almost wholly changed by new inventions. Insolent youth embraces womanly softness, [Col. 0587C] and courtly men lavishly flatter women in every wantonness. On the joints of their feet, where the body ends, they impose the likeness of serpents’ tails, which they behold before their eyes like scorpions. They sweep the dusty ground with the superfluous trailing length of their undergarments and cloaks; they cover their hands with long, wide sleeves for every task; and, burdened by these excesses, they can scarcely walk quickly or do anything useful. They are shaved at the crown like thieves, but nourish long hair at the back of the head like prostitutes. Formerly penitents, captives, and pilgrims were customarily unshorn and wore long beards, displaying by that sign their penitence, captivity, or pilgrimage to observers. [Col. 0587D] Now, however, nearly all common people are shaggy-haired and bearded, openly showing by this appearance that they delight in the filth of lust, like stinking goats. They curl their hair with curling-irons. They cover their heads with a band, without a cap. Scarcely any man of the military class appears in public bareheaded and shorn lawfully according to the Apostle’s command (1 Cor. 11). Thus by outward dress and bearing they reveal what kind of consciences they have within, and how they run toward God through their narrow adornment.

Therefore the Most High Judge, seated upon a lofty throne, seeing that human intention clings excessively to wickedness, strikes the untaught people and undisciplined populace with many scourges. He allows earthly men to be wasted by diseases and troubled by wars, and subjects them to hypocritical [Col. 0588A] rulers, whom He sees to be hostile to Him and voluntary transgressors of His law. But the elect, inflamed with the zeal of Phinehas, are often angry among the reprobate and complain to the Lord with the Prophet: “I saw transgressors and wasted away, because they did not keep Thy words” (Ps. 118 [119]:158). Therefore good teachers rebuke, entreat, and reprove them with all patience and teaching. But against all these things there stubbornly stands the wicked hardening of an evil heart, which is accustomed to foster and defend every contagion of crime. If Persius and Plautus and the other biting satirists were now present, and carefully investigated how our contemporaries fulfil their desires secretly and openly, they would find abundant matter for rebuke and mockery in plain view.

[Col. 0588B] Having therefore observed countless falls in the world, Geroius Grossivus wrote, among other things, in a certain letter to Gilbert Maminot, bishop of Lisieux:

> The lamp of virtues by which the former age shone  
> Has wholly transferred all its radiance to the stars.  
> In our times the world is wrapped in darkness,  
> Nor can its extinguished head now lift itself again.  
> There is no good man today, none who cares for goodness—  
> No reward, no honour, no love of virtue.

The ardent scholar inveighed hyperbolically against the enormity of wickedness which he saw spreading everywhere. Blittero the Fleming likewise, in the poem which he recently published concerning Emperor Henry, clearly described in elegiac verse the world and the wretched fortunes of mortals. [Col. 0588C] Many other learned writers also uttered great complaints concerning the crimes and miseries of this age. Following them, I have briefly noted in this present little work the time when, on this side of the Alps, the folly of *pigaciae* began, together with the excessive length of hair and garments that uselessly swept the earth’s dirt.

I should much rather write of the holiness and miracles of the saints than of the trifles of fools and frivolous revelries, if our princes and bishops earnestly cultivated holy gifts and possessed miracles proclaiming holiness. But I cannot compel them to become holy. Therefore, leaving these matters aside, I make a truthful account of the things that occur. Now I return to the order of my narrative.

## XI. The Men of Le Mans Rise against the Normans

[Col. 0588D]

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1090, in the thirteenth indiction, the people of Le Mans rebelled against the Normans. Having expelled their guards from the fortifications, they set up a new ruler for themselves. For those who, while King William lived, had often attempted to rebel against him, immediately began to devise rebellion upon his death. They therefore sent an embassy to the sons of Azzo, marquis of Liguria, and, making known their wish through an envoy, said:

“Why are you so sluggish and cowardly that you do not reclaim your inheritance, which we willingly preserve for you? All the lawful heirs of the lordship of Le Mans are dead, and now no heir is closer to us than you. [Col. 0589A] William also, the violent invader of many, has now fallen. Through Margaret, daughter of Herbert, whom he wished to unite to his son Robert, he long subjected us to his dominion. Behold, his sons—one ruling the kingdom of England and the other the duchy of Normandy—are disturbed by mutual slaughter, oppose one another, rage through plunder and burning, and, savagely fighting, are almost proceeding to mutual destruction. But we possess the city of Le Mans and its towns in peace, and faithfully bid you come here without delay and rule over us by hereditary right.”

The people of Le Mans sent this message to the Ligurians, not from love for them, but in order, under some plausible pretext, to shake from themselves the Norman yoke which for nearly thirty years had grievously worn down [Col. 0589B] their proud necks.

The Ligurian brothers, hearing the embassy, rejoiced and, taking counsel with their closest friends, considered what should be done. At length they determined that Fulk, the elder, should retain his father’s dignity in Italy, while his brother Hugh should claim the lordship of Le Mans for himself through his mother’s inheritance. Finally Geoffrey of Mayenne, Elias, and other citizens and townsmen received the arriving Hugh and for a time supported him in obtaining the right due to him from his maternal inheritance.

[Note: [Col. 0589D] Orderic here recounts Hugh’s second arrival in Le Mans. His first occurred about the year 1067, when the people of Le Mans, weary of the Norman yoke imposed upon them by William the Bastard, summoned Azzo, count of Liguria, to govern them while William was occupied in recently conquered England. Azzo brought with him, together with [Col. 0590D] his wife Gersende, his underage son Hugh. When Azzo returned to Liguria, Hugh remained among the people of Le Mans under his mother’s guardianship as his father’s successor, but was later compelled to return there, as may be seen above from the acts of the bishops of Le Mans. Dom Bouquet, book VIII, p. 639.]

But the venerable bishop Hoel, who held the episcopate by the gift of King William, always remained faithful to him and his sons and, so far as he could, [Col. 0589C] dissuaded them from their savage resistance. He placed the stubborn under interdict, anathematized them by pontifical authority, and excluded them from the thresholds of holy mother Church. Therefore the instigators of rebellion were exceedingly angry with him and terribly threatened to injure him. Meanwhile, as he rode through his diocese with his clergy and diligently exercised his office in episcopal fashion, Elias of La Flèche seized him and kept the bishop bound in prison until Hugh had been received in the city of Le Mans. The church of that bishop mourned his affliction. It laid the holy images of the Lord with the crosses, and the shrines containing holy relics, upon the ground; stopped up the doors of the churches with thorns; and, like a mourning widow, ceased from the ringing of bells, solemn chant, [Col. 0589D] and customary ceremonies, and devoted itself to tears.

After the people of Le Mans discovered that their new count was poor in wealth, sense, and courage, they repented of their imprudent deed [Note: [Col. 0590D] Le Prévost reads *imprudentes*, “imprudent [people],” in place of *imprudentis*, “of an imprudent [deed].”] and held him in contempt and hatred, as the Shechemites did Abimelech (Judges 9). For he was foolish, cowardly, and indolent, and knew not how to govern the reins of so great a dignity. [Col. 0590A] He had married a daughter of Robert Guiscard; but the cowardly husband, unable to endure the high spirit of his noble wife, repudiated her. For this Pope Urban publicly excommunicated him. All the Allobroges cursed him and, finding an opportunity, sent him into exile among the fierce peoples beyond the Alps. Appointed count, ignorant among the knowledgeable and fearful among brave knights, he was held in contempt. He was frequently anguished and almost bloodless with manifold terror, and meditated flight, which he considered his chief remedy. Observing this, the people of Le Mans rejoiced greatly and continually instilled greater fear into him.

At last his cousin Elias approached him and, discussing the pressing circumstances with him, [Col. 0590B] said:

“I hear the people whisper, my lord, that you wish to return to your native land and abandon the harsh customs and county of an untamed people. Certainly none of your friends should dissuade you from this. For as your manners are gentle and love the tranquillity of peace, so the inhabitants of this region are occupied with wars and impatient of rest. Moreover, the implacable Normans lay claim to Le Mans and, with immense fierceness, threaten dreadful things against its people. The sons of King William, who formerly disagreed among themselves, have now been reconciled and are assembling in Normandy with a great army, so that they may suddenly rush into our land and attack and punish us, who rebelled against them, with cruel arms. Believe without doubt that this is the chief cause for which King William has come into Neustria with great pomp; and his arrival, I think, will bring us grave fear and the greatest distress.”

As he spoke thus, Hugh plainly disclosed to Elias that he wished to sell his county and revisit his ancestral home. Elias said:

“I am your kinsman, my lord, and by my support you were raised to the dignity of the county, which you can give or sell to no one but me. For the daughter of Count Herbert married Lancelin of Beaugency, and bore him Lancelin, father of Ralph, and John, my own father. I have stated this openly, so that you may know me, like yourself, to be descended from the line of Count Herbert. Now therefore accept from me whatever we agree between ourselves upon, and leave me the emblem of the county, [Col. 0590D] which ought to be mine by right of kinship. What I seek is indeed grave and laborious, because while the three sons of King William live, I shall scarcely, or never, possess it in peace. It seems very disgraceful for such great rulers, who can surround us with a hundred thousand soldiers, to suffer with impunity any insult from neighbouring fellow-countrymen, or in any way to lose without terrible retaliation any right which their father acquired by whatever agreement. Love of freedom likewise spurs me on, and the justice of ancestral inheritance supplies me with confidence in God to fight for it.”

Having heard this, the cowardly Allobrox agreed, and received ten thousand solidi in the money of Le Mans for the county of Le Mans. When the Ligurian departed, Elias became count of the people of Le Mans and held the acquired county vigorously for twenty years. He also became heir to his father-in-law Gervase of Château-du-Loir, whose daughter he had married; by her he fathered a daughter named Eremburga, whom he joined in marriage to Fulk, count of the Angevins, the son of his lord. Once he had received power, he greatly reformed his conduct [Col. 0591B] and flourished in many virtues. He honourably revered the clergy and the Church of God, and attended Mass and the service of God daily with fervour. He preserved justice for his subjects and maintained peace for the poor, so far as he could.

## XII. Dissensions and Wars among the Magnates of Normandy

At this time the frenzy of wickedness grew exceedingly in Normandy, overflowed beyond measure in all its regions, and miserably disturbed the unhappy native inhabitants of the land. Frequent clashes of arms rang out in conflicts, and the earth was soaked with the blood of many.

In the second year after King William died [1089], Ascelin, surnamed Goel, treacherously stole the fortress of Ivry from his lord William of Breteuil [Col. 0591C] and delivered it to Duke Robert. William, unwilling to lack the castle, paid the duke 1,500 pounds for its redemption. When he had recovered the tower, he deprived Goel of the lordship of Ivry in vengeance and stripped him of every possession that he held under William’s authority. A long war then arose between them; the neighbouring land suffered through plunder, burnings, and the slaughter of men. Amalric of Montfort, surnamed the Strong because of the prowess in which he excelled and because all his kinsmen dwelling about him feared his boldness and ferocity, rushed like a raging lion into William of Breteuil’s land and undertook battle alone against two knights. One of them struck him in the side with a lance, and he died that same day. When he died, his brother Richard inherited the paternal honour [Col. 0591D] and made the greatest effort to avenge his brother’s death upon William.

(1090–1092.) Duke Robert frequently imposed military duties upon Gilbert, son of Ingenulf of Laigle, because he was very valiant, and gave him the castle of Exmes as a reward and for the defence of the country. Accordingly Robert of Bellême, stirred by the gall of envy and anger, assembled an army and besieged the castle for four days in the first week of January, attacking it with fierce assaults amid winter rains and frosts. Gilbert, with few but courageous fighters, stoutly resisted within; hurling missiles and stones, he drove back the enemy, cast them into the ditch, wounded some, and even [Col. 0592A] killed others. Meanwhile Gilbert, lord of Laigle, came to his assistance. At night he entered the castle with eighty knights, furnished it with food, arms, and defenders, and by such aid strengthened his uncle. But the tyrant of Bellême, seeing the strength of the place and the firm resistance of its defenders, did not dare to remain in a prolonged siege; furious and deeply grieved, he withdrew, gaining nothing but the wounds of his own men.

The following year, when the aforesaid knight Gilbert came from Sainte-Scholasse and had stopped at Moulins to confer with Duda, lady of that castle, he happened after the conference to leave his arms there with Anthony surnamed Haren. Unarmed, he himself hastily departed with his squires toward evening. [Col. 0592B] Gerard Capreolus, Roger of Ferrières, and nearly thirteen other knights of Corbon immediately pursued him and tried to take him alive. As he rode swiftly and strove to escape the hands of his enemies, one of them pierced his side with a lance. To the grief of those who committed the deed, the noble hero died that day. On the morrow, the leap-day, his body was brought to Saint-Sulpice and there buried with his kinsmen, amid great mourning, by Gilbert bishop of Évreux and Serlo abbot of Ouche. Geoffrey, count of Mortagne, considering that his men, who had committed this grievous crime, had through the killing of a most valiant baron produced the seed of immense damage for his land, made peace with Gilbert of Laigle, his nephew, [Col. 0592C] and gave him his daughter Juliana in marriage. She bore him Richer, Geoffrey, and Gilbert. Thus the wise count provided fittingly for his subjects and heirs: through the sweetness of marital union he buried the crime which had arisen, lest a more abundant evil should sprout from the root of the wicked act and continually grow worse anew among their descendants. Thus the compact between the kindred heirs remains unbroken to the present, and serene peace binds them gently and peacefully.

In the same week in which Gilbert, as has been said, perished between Moulins and Laigle, Goel fought a pitched battle against his lord William of Breteuil. Having with him Richard of Montfort and a great multitude of Frenchmen, [Col. 0592D] he crushed the hostile army. He cast William, captured with many others, into chains and cruelly afflicted him with the squalor of prison during the following Lent, compelling him against his will to undergo the rigour of Lenten penance for his sins. Finally, on this occasion Richard of Montfort, Hugh of Montgomery, Gervase of Neufchâtel, and many other Frenchmen and Normans assembled and made peace between William and Goel at Breteuil. Then William, as the agreement required, joined his daughter Isabel to Goel in marriage and gave, for his ransom, one thousand pounds of Dreux money, horses, [Col. 0593A] arms, and many other things. He even added the castle of Ivry, sad and sorrowful. Thus this wicked robber, greatly enriched by these resources, grew proud. He enclosed his castle—which was truly a den of thieves—with ditches and dense hedges for the harm of many, and there spent his entire life in plundering and killing his neighbours. By his wife he fathered seven sons, whose wickedness grew exceedingly and whose savage deeds caused many tears among widows and the poor.

## XIII. Discordant Disturbances and Wars Continue in Normandy

At the same time another disturbance arose in Neustria. Robert, count of Meulan, puffed up by the gifts and promises of King William, came from England, approached the duke at Rouen, [Col. 0593B] and insolently demanded back the castle of Ivry from him. The duke replied: “I gave your father Brionne, a noble castle, in exchange of equal value for the castle of Ivry.” The count of Meulan said: “I do not accept that exchange, but I want to possess what your father gave to mine. Otherwise, by Saint Nicaise, I shall do something displeasing to you.” Angered, the duke immediately ordered him seized and bound in prison, and entrusted Brionne to Robert, son of Baldwin, to guard.

[Note: [Col. 0593C] The monk of Bec gives another reason for the removal of the castle of Brionne from Count Robert of Meulan, in his notice concerning the liberty of his church, published by Mabillon in the appendix to volume V of the *Annals of the Benedictine Order*, p. 635:

“In the time of the venerable Father Anselm, Robert, count of Meulan, by his cunning obtained from Robert, duke of Normandy, the castle of Brionne under his own lordship, although it had hitherto belonged to the dukes of Normandy. Having attained his desire, he wished to possess the monastery of Bec under his lordship because that monastery was known to have been built in the fiscal district of Brionne castle. First, like the crafty man he was, he privately sought Father Anselm’s consent through messengers, asking and, as though humbly entreating, that he allow this, while promising many endowments for the Church from his own property, especially in that castle. Father Anselm [Col. 0593D] answered them: ‘It is not mine to grant this. That abbey is not mine, but belongs to the lord prince of Normandy: what pleases him shall be done.’ They answered: ‘Our lord hopes easily to obtain the prince’s consent, but he wishes to know your will and secure your assent.’ The abbot said: ‘I can do nothing in this matter on my own authority; but I tell you that the lord count, in my judgment, is undertaking a difficult business.’ The envoys asked, ‘How so?’ The abbot immediately explained the reasons. When he had finished, the envoys returned to their lord without any dispute.

“When the count heard Anselm’s reply, he was astonished at the man’s prudence. When these things had come to the monks’ notice, … they hurried to Duke Robert and made known the business for which they had come. When the duke heard this, angered, he said loudly: ‘By God’s wonders! What is this? What madness is this that I hear? Does the count of Meulan wish to take my abbey from me—indeed, that one which I love above all others? Does this traitor wish to withdraw it from me? By God’s wonders, he shall not enjoy for long the gift [Col. 0594C] which I gave him.’ Then William Crispin, William of Breteuil, and Roger of Bienfaite happened to arrive. When they learned the matter, they were greatly indignant and declared with loud voices and terrible oaths that they would take away whatever their ancestors had given to the church of Bec if Count Meulan in any way held the monastery of Bec under his lordship. At the same time they sharply rebuked the duke because he had entrusted the key of his province to an unfaithful man. What more need be said? Having obtained leave, the monks returned, strengthened by the promises of the duke and princes.

“After a few days Count Meulan … went to court. When the monks learned this, greatly fearing the duke’s fickleness, they selected some of their number and sent them hastily to court. They informed the duke beforehand of the count’s arrival and implored him with many prayers [Col. 0594D] not to alter by any word his promises toward the church of Bec. While they were conversing together, the count arrived. When the duke saw him, laughing, he said: ‘Lord Robert, what is the matter? How stands it between you and the monks of Bec?’ Seeing the monks present, the count lowered his face and replied: ‘Well; for they will graciously grant whatever you order.’ The duke answered: ‘You are plainly lying.’ Raising his voice angrily, he said again: ‘By God’s wonders, you most falsely hope that I am so dull as to wish to give you my abbey.’ His words then ran on, as was his custom when he was angry, although rarely; and he reproached the count exceedingly over this matter. Seeing that his endeavour in this affair would be fruitless, the count entirely abandoned his hope. Not many days later the duke demanded back his castle and took it from the count’s hand, giving it to Roger of Bienfaite, who claimed it by hereditary right. Thus the church of Bec had peace in this matter.”

Dom Bouquet, book VIII, p. 641.]

The crafty old man Roger of Beaumont, when he heard that his son had been captured, for several days appeared to attend to other matters as though he had not cared about the misfortune of his child, and sorrowfully concealed the grief of his sad heart [Col. 0593C] under a cheerful countenance. Then, when he judged the duke appeased, [Col. 0594A] he sent presents in advance, approached him, and greeted him honourably. When the duke had returned his greeting, he said:

“I thank your highness, my lord duke, because you have punished my son’s arrogance with princely severity. I ought long ago to have done this myself, if the necessary strength had remained to me in this old age. For his excessive insolence has often grieved me, and he has frequently despised my warnings. He therefore needed correction and instruction in how he ought to speak to his lords and superiors.”

Roger gently said these and similar things to gain the duke’s favour. The duke, failing to foresee what would happen, welcomed the flatterer. Roger was now admitted familiarly to all the duke’s counsels and thus afterward appeared to act prudently concerning the recovery of his offspring. [Col. 0594B] For he was one of the ancient and foremost magnates of Duke Robert and King William; son-in-law of Count Waleran of Meulan and brother-in-law of Hugh; worthy of well-founded praise for fidelity and loyalty; supported by friends and kinsmen, wealth and broad honours, fortified towns, worthy men, and powerful, eminent sons. One was count of Meulan in France; the other was earl of Warwick in England. Thus furnished with wisdom, resources, and friends, he approached the duke and said:

“You ought, my lord duke, to deal mercifully with me and frequently remember that I have always been faithful to the lords of Normandy. I have never defrauded my lord, but have borne great and dangerous labours for him. [Col. 0594C] You can see this more clearly than light in your own war, [Col. 0595A] in what I did before your father against the rebels. In it Roger of Spain fell, with his sons Elbert and Elinant, and many others. From childhood I chose always to persist in fidelity. I received this hereditary principle from my grandfather Torf and my father Humphrey, and throughout my life I have fervently maintained it in adversity and prosperity. Far be it from me, now that I am an old man, to begin to practise the treacheries which I have hitherto hated and from my earliest youth avoided with all my power! Since your father never found me straying from his side, but enduring stoutly in his fidelity and bearing very great adversity for him with manly strength, he always admitted me, above his other magnates, to all his secrets.”

As Roger spoke thus, the duke said:

“Lord Roger, I know very well, from the testimony of many, your great loyalty, in which you flourished splendidly in the time of my fathers. Therefore, as they loved you and profitably accepted your worthy counsels, so I likewise rejoice in your wisdom and embrace your advice. As for my having put your son in chains, I certainly did this not from contempt for you, but because of his foolish and excessively insolent anger, with which he pressed me threateningly and importunately.”

Roger said:

“Because you have corrected a rash young man, I gladly gave thanks, and again give great thanks to your highness. Henceforth, if it please your serenity, he should be spared. Release him now that he has been punished, and he will render you faithful service.”

Thus won over by such words, [Col. 0595C] the duke released the count of Meulan from his chains and allowed him to depart free with his father.

Not long afterward Roger and his son asked the duke to restore Brionne to them and promised for this an immense sum of money. The duke, eager for money, readily assented to the request and ordered the aforesaid governor to restore the town to Roger. But he replied to the duke:

“If you wish to retain Brionne for yourself, as your father held it as his own property, I do not delay in restoring it to you. Otherwise I shall keep my inheritance and surrender it to no one while I live. For it is plainly known to all the inhabitants of this province that Richard the Elder, duke of the Normans, gave Brionne with the whole county to his son Geoffrey, [Col. 0595D] who in turn left it at his death to his own son Gilbert. Then, after Count Gilbert had been wickedly killed by evil men, and the guardians of his sons fled with the boys to Baldwin of Flanders for fear of their enemies, your father subjected part of my grandfather’s county to his own lordship and distributed part of it to outsiders as he pleased. Long afterward, when he had married Baldwin the Fleming’s daughter, at Baldwin’s request he restored Moles and Sapp to my father Baldwin and gave him as wife the daughter of his aunt. To Baldwin’s brother Richard he restored Bienfaite and Orbec. Finally, by your favour, my lord, whom I desire to obey in everything, I now possess Brionne, the chief town of my grandfather Count Gilbert; and, with God aiding [Col. 0596A] the justice of my claim, I shall hold it to the end.”

On hearing this, Roger sharply urged the duke not to abandon the matter, but suddenly to assemble a force of armed men, crush the rebels, and reduce by siege the very strongly fortified castle situated in the middle of the land. Accordingly Duke Robert besieged Brionne in Whitsun week. Robert, son of Baldwin, strove to defend it against armed battalions with only six knights. Yet the lord of Beaumont and the count of Meulan had assembled great companies of warriors, suddenly surrounded the aforesaid fortification so that it could receive neither the aid of allies nor provisions, and, pressing vigorously, attacked the town most fiercely after the ninth hour. [Col. 0596B] The great heat and extreme dryness of early summer then prevailed, greatly helping those attacking from outside. The ingenious besiegers heated iron missiles in a smith’s furnace which had been built ready at hand, then suddenly hurled them upon the roof of the principal hall within the stronghold. With all their strength they lodged the red-hot iron heads of arrows and javelins in the dry old thatch of the roof. A great fire quickly arose and was greatly strengthened while the defenders of the town fought fiercely and did not know of the stratagem, until the flame advanced above their heads. As soon as they saw it seize everything over them, their strength failed; and, while balls of flame raged everywhere within, [Col. 0596C] they surrendered themselves to the duke’s mercy. Thus Duke Robert took Brionne from the ninth hour until sunset—though his father William, with the aid of King Henry of France, had scarcely been able to subdue it in three years, when Guy, son of Rainald of Burgundy, had established his garrison there after the battle of Val-ès-Dunes.

In the assault upon the aforesaid castle, Gilbert of La Pigne was commander of the force, and prudently directed the besiegers’ companies from Pont-Audemer and Beaumont, boldly urging them to make an irresistible attack. Meanwhile, struck mortally on the head by a javelin falling from above, he was immediately carried, almost lifeless, by his grieving companions out of the crush of the combatants [Col. 0596D]. Shortly afterward the wounded man recovered from his fainting fit, and began to cry out terribly to those around him:

> “O wretched men, wretched men! What are you doing? Why do you squander our time? Why do you love the vanities of the world and consign to oblivion those things which are truly health-giving and enduring? If you knew the miseries and torments which you deserve by living wickedly, and if for even one hour you felt the horrors that I have just seen, you would assuredly count all the pleasures of this passing age as nothing.”

As he said this and wished to add more, he fell silent; and thus the renowned commander, failing in the midst of his words, put off mortality.

After these events the duke restored Brionne to Roger and, taking pity on Robert the castellan, promised him his paternal fief. For he was very strongly supported by friends and kinsmen [Col. 0597A], and had many advocates with the duke. As stated above, King William held dear Richard and Baldwin, the sons of Count Gilbert; and, both because they were near kinsmen and because of the valour of both, he raised them high and enriched them with many estates, honours, and powers in England and Normandy. The aforesaid brothers were also blessed with good wives and honourable offspring.

Richard married Rohais, daughter of Walter Giffard, who bore him sons and daughters: Roger and Gilbert, Walter and Robert, and Richard, a monk of Bec, to whom King Henry entrusted the monastery of Ely. Baldwin, moreover, begot Robert and William, Richard, and the illegitimate Guigier. These men, indeed, flourished through the strenuous excellence of their worldly lives in the time of King William and his sons [Col. 0597B]; tossed by the shifting blasts of unstable fortune, they were perilously buffeted on the sea of this world. Wigerius, however, the youngest of them, voluntarily abandoned the hazards of secular knighthood, cut his hair at the monastery of Bec, and lived as a monk for nearly forty years under the venerable archimandrists William and Boso.

## XIV. Continuing Disorders in Normandy.—War between the Men of Évreux and Conches

While battles resounded everywhere in Neustria, the territory of Évreux could enjoy no security of peace. There a conflict worse than civil war arose between wealthy brothers, and was greatly intensified by the wicked rivalry of proud women [Col. 0597C]. For Countess Helvise, angered against Isabel of Conches over certain insulting words, strove with all her might, in wrath, to rouse Count William and his barons to arms. Thus, through women’s suspicions and quarrels, the hearts of brave men were inflamed with fury; shortly afterward much human blood was mutually shed by their hands, and the roofs of many houses were burned in villages and hamlets.

Both women who stirred up such wars were talkative, high-spirited, and handsome; they commanded their husbands, oppressed their dependants, and terrified them in various ways. Yet their characters differed greatly. Helvise was clever and eloquent, but fierce and avaricious. Isabel, on the other hand [Col. 0597D], was generous, bold, and merry, and therefore beloved and welcome among those who lived with her. On campaign she rode armed among the knights like a knight, and showed no less courage among mailed horsemen and spear-bearing retainers than Camilla, the maiden glory of Italy, among Turnus’s soldiers. She rivalled Lampedo and Marpesia, Hippolyta and Penthesilea, and the other warrior queens of the Amazons, whose battles Pompeius Trogus, Virgil, and other writers of histories recount; kings of Asia contended with them, and for fifteen years subdued the peoples of Asia by arms.

The men of Évreux had many helpers and commonly inflicted many burnings and plunderings upon the people of Conches. But at times the latter, no weaker, rendered reprisals to their enemies. Ralph approached Duke Robert [Col. 0598A], set before him complaints concerning the losses he had suffered from his fellow-countrymen, and requested his lord’s assistance; but in vain, for he obtained nothing. Therefore he turned elsewhere and was compelled to seek useful protection. Through his envoys he appealed to the king of England, informed him of his misfortunes, and promised himself and all that he possessed if the king would assist him. Hearing this, the king rejoiced and promised effective aid to the needy man. He then ordered Count Stephen, Gerard of Gournay, and other tribunes and centurions who commanded his households in Normandy to help Ralph with all their efforts and to furnish his castles with every necessity. They eagerly obeyed the royal commands and supported Ralph [Col. 0598B], striving in every respect to please the king.

In November 1090, Count William gathered a huge army and began to attack Conches. His two nephews, powerful men, William of Breteuil and Richard of Montfort, were with him and attacked the men of Conches with their companies. There Richard of Montfort, while attacking the monastic court of St Peter of Castillon, refused to desist from what he had undertaken even out of reverence for the monks, who cried out weeping and appealed to the Lord. Suddenly struck by an enemy missile, he died that very day, amid the deepest mourning of both parties. For he was Isabel’s brother and Count William’s nephew through his sister. Thus both parties mourned the formidable marquis [Col. 0598C], who, through excessive arrogance and insolence, perished while stubbornly doing evil. The body of the aforesaid knight was carried by his men to his native soil and buried at Asparlone, in the cemetery of St Thomas the Apostle. There regular monks of Marmoutier serve God, and there the elder Simon, son of Amalric, and his sons are buried.

Not long afterward the men of Évreux assembled again and, desiring to avenge their grief, set about ravaging the territory of Conches. Ralph then had a very strong force of his own men and of the king’s household. To the eager young soldiers preparing to sally out, he said:

> “Arm yourselves and be ready; but do not leave the fortification until I command you. Let the enemy load themselves with plunder; then, as they withdraw, pursue them manfully with me.”

They obeyed their leader, who was most worthy and skilled in warfare, and pursued the departing men, burdened with plunder, at a measured pace. When they attacked, the men of Évreux abandoned their booty and fled. William of Breteuil was then captured with many others, and this victory was followed by peace. Ashamed that they had proudly begun the war and had consequently suffered the crushing weight of great loss with disgrace, the men of Évreux accepted peace terms after a three-year war. Meeting together, they confirmed the following agreement: William gave his uncle Ralph three thousand pounds for his ransom and made Roger, his cousin, Ralph’s son, heir to all his rights. The count of Évreux likewise appointed that same Roger, as his nephew, heir to his county [Col. 0599A].

But divine providence, which is not subject to human wishes, ordained otherwise. The young man was distinguished by excellent character and was exceedingly beloved by all his companions, dependent retainers, and neighbours. He loved clerics and monks and honoured them suitably. He disdained to wear costly garments, by which the proud grow excessively arrogant, and strove to govern himself modestly in every aspect of his life.

Once idle knights were playing and conversing together in the hall at Conches, speaking before Lady Elizabeth, as is customary on such occasions, about various subjects. One of them said:

> “Recently I saw a dream that greatly terrified me. I saw the Lord fixed upon the cross, bruised over His whole body and, as if excessively tormented by anguish, writhing; and He looked at me with a dreadful countenance.”

Those present said to the teller of this tale:

> “This dream is grave and terrible, and appears to portend for you the fearful judgment of God.”

But Baldwin, son of Count Eustace of Boulogne, said:

> “I too recently saw in a dream the Lord Jesus hanging upon the cross, but radiant and beautiful, smiling joyfully upon me and blessing me with His right hand, and graciously making the sign of the cross above my head.”

Those standing by answered:

> “By such a vision the sweetness of great grace seems to shine upon you.”

On hearing this, the young Roger said to his mother [Col. 0599C]:

> “I know a man, not far away, who has beheld similar things in a vision.”

When his mother pressed him and carefully asked who it was and what he had seen, the young man blushed and did not wish to disclose the matter openly. At last, much entreated by his mother and the friends present, he replied:

> “A certain man recently saw in his vision the Lord Jesus laying His hand upon his head, blessing him mercifully, and calling him in these words: ‘Come quickly, my beloved, to me, and I shall give you the joys of life.’ I therefore declare boldly that he whom I know to have been so summoned by the Lord will not live long in this life.”

Not long afterward the three aforementioned young men, as their differing reports foretold, experienced differing outcomes. The first was badly wounded on an expedition [Col. 0600A] and died without confession or viaticum. Baldwin, Ralph of Conches’s son-in-law, took up the Lord’s cross on his right shoulder and, at Pope Urban’s command, undertook a second pilgrimage against the heathen. On that journey he was raised above all his peers and gloriously supported by the power of the crucified Creator, as he had beheld in his dream. For he was first made ruler of Rages—that is, Edessa—the most noble city; and after some years, upon the death of his brother Godfrey, he possessed the kingdom of Jerusalem for a long time. He fought the pagans many times and, with God’s aid, won glory through many triumphs.

Roger, however, in the same year in which these visions occurred, took to his bed and, having devoutly attended to all that befits a faithful man in that condition, departed from the world on the Ides of May, 1090 [Col. 0600B]. Amid the mourning of many, he was buried at Castillon with his parents and rests there.

## XV. Conan’s Conspiracy to Hand Over the City of Rouen to the King of England

At the same time Henry the Clito ruled the Cotentin vigorously and continued resolute against his brothers. He bore hostility toward the duke because of the unjust imprisonment which, as related above, he had suffered from him the day before yesterday. He was nevertheless also an enemy of the king of England because of his mother’s land, from which the king had disseised him in England and given it to Robert, son of Haimo. For these reasons he steadily fortified his castles and shrewdly gained many supporters among the leading men of his father’s former following [Col. 0600C].

He possessed Avranches, Cherbourg, and Coutances [Note: [Col. 0599D] Concerning the city of Coutances, the matter is not altogether certain. Among the documents in volume XI of *Gallia Christiana*, col. 221, there survives a historical fragment from the Black Book of the chapter of Coutances, which reads as follows:

> “When the glorious King William, faithful in Christ, had died at Rouen and had been solemnly buried in the monastery of St Stephen which he himself had built at Caen, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1088, indiction 11, his elder son Robert succeeded him as duke in Normandy, while his middle son William became king in England. There was contention and war between them for many days in both lands. At that time the aforesaid Robert gave his younger brother, Count Henry, the whole district of Coutances together with that of Avranches, and likewise the bishoprics, now and henceforth. When therefore the bishop of Avranches had accepted the lordship of the aforesaid prince, Geoffrey of Coutances wholly refused it, and declared by word and fulfilled by deed that the church of Coutances, of which he was minister, should during his lifetime have no lord except him whom the church of Rouen had [Col. 0600D]: ‘not because, as he said, he disdained that the son of the king his lord should be his own lord, but lest the dignity of the Church should in future be diminished by this precedent; and because he would rather lose every temporal possession more honourably than suffer, even in the slightest matter, the abasement of the Church.’

> “Accordingly, he endured courageously and for a long time the protracted enmities of that lord himself, of powerful barons, and of parishioners; the frequent plundering of his goods, the burning of houses, and the destructive breaking down of his parks. Yet, supported by greatness of spirit, zeal for justice, and faith, he kept the Church wholly intact in its rightful status and under the lordship of the duke of Normandy, despite that duke’s wish to ruin it.”

For this reason Orderic excludes Robert of Mowbray, the bishop’s nephew through his brother, from the number of barons who favoured Henry. Dom Bouquet, book VIII, p. 644.] and Gavray, as well as other fortresses; and he had with him Count Hugh, Richard of Reviers, and other men of the Cotentin, except Robert of Mowbray. Gathering strength everywhere by entreaty and payment, he increased daily. Neustria was troubled by so many scourges, and infernal fury gave men, villages, and houses over to slaughter and flames.

The power of the English king ranged through almost all Normandy; with Norman nobles favouring him because of his money, he made the province, bereft of its ruler, subject to himself.
