The citizens of Rouen too, enticed by royal gifts and promises, discussed changing their prince and planned to betray the metropolis of Normandy to the king along with its indolent duke [Col. 0601A]. The instigator of this faction was Conan, son of Gilbert Pilatus, who stood foremost among the citizens as the richest of them. He had made an agreement with the king to surrender the city. Enriched with immense wealth, he flourished in the city and, puffed up, continually maintained a great household of knights and retainers against the duke. Most of the townspeople agreed with him. Some, however, resisted in fidelity to the duke and, by timely delays and evasions, obstructed the detestable crime.

But Conan, confident of his fellow citizens’ agreement, fixed a deadline. On the appointed day he summoned the king’s army from Gournay and other royal camps and commanded it to come swiftly to Rouen. When the duke learned of so great a plot against himself, he summoned the friends [Col. 0601B] in whom he trusted. He also made a treaty of friendship with his brother Henry and with certain others who had deserted him, and by urgent messengers announced his distress to Count William of Évreux, Robert of Bellême, William of Breteuil, Gilbert of Laigle, and his other faithful men. Henry therefore came first to his aid, first bringing help to his brother and then manfully inflicting punishment upon the traitor.

On the third day of November, 1090, Gilbert of Laigle led a troop of the duke’s knights to service and approached the southern part of the city by the bridge over the Seine. At the same time, from the other side, Rainald of Warenne hurried with three hundred knights to the Cauchie gate [Col. 0601C]. Conan then said to his men:

> “Rise at once and arm yourselves, for this is no time to wait any longer. Behold, enemies are coming from the south to attack us, while our eager allies hasten from the west to aid us. Therefore meet friends and enemies as is fitting: open the entrance to our comrades, and sharply bar the way to our enemies with arms.”

Accordingly, one party of citizens ran to repel Gilbert and his men, while another tried to unbar the western gate in order to admit Rainald and his force. Moreover, some of the king’s retainers had long since entered the city and, ready and silently awaiting the rebellion, bore the delay of the uprising impatiently.

At last, as military and civic tumult arose [Col. 0601D], an immense cry was raised on both sides, the whole city was thrown into utter confusion, and it raged cruelly against its own entrails. Many citizens fought at both gates against their kinsmen and neighbours, one party favouring the duke and the other the king. When the duke perceived that they were in a frenzy in the city, as has been said, he came out of the citadel with his brother Henry and his own comrades and hastened to assist his followers. But as the great turmoil of confusion threw everything into disorder, and it was impossible to know which side each citizen had chosen, the duke, persuaded by his friends not foolishly to incur a shameful destruction and bring enduring disgrace upon all Normans, fled with a few men through the eastern gate. He was immediately received faithfully by the inhabitants of the suburb called Mala Palus as their special lord [Col. 0602A]. Then, with a boat made ready, he entered the Seine and, leaving the conflict behind him, sailed in alarm to the estate of Ermentrude. There he was received by William of Arques, a monk of Molesme, and there, in the basilica of St Mary of the Meadow, awaited the end of the uprising.

After Gilbert of Laigle, through the valour of himself and his men and through the aid of citizens who were not parties to the treason, had secured the southern gate, he joined Henry and the duke’s other auxiliaries and engaged the rebels in battle within the city. As the presumptuous criminals failed in their impious undertaking, the duke’s party gained strength and, striking its adversaries stoutly with the sword, prevailed. Then a violent slaughter of burgesses took place [Col. 0602B], and Conan, standard-bearer of the traitors, was captured with many others. Fear and grief were immense in the city; as men fought, fell, or fled, women cried aloud in tears. Innocent and guilty alike were everywhere slain, fled, or were captured. Since, as said above, the citizens were divided against one another and endangered by the storms of a grievous calamity, the terrified royal troop fled. Eagerly seeking the hiding places of the nearby woods, it concealed itself and, with difficulty, escaped the danger of death or capture through the aid of night.

The victors led Conan into the citadel. Henry took him through the upper chambers of the tower and, taunting him, addressed him thus:

> “Consider, Conan, what a beautiful fatherland you attempted to bring under your power. Behold, to the south a delightful park lies open to your sight. Behold a wooded country, abounding in wild beasts. Look: the Seine, a river full of fish, washes the walls of Rouen and daily brings here ships laden with many kinds of merchandise. Behold, on the other side is a populous city, beautiful with its walls, sacred churches, and urban houses, to which all Normandy has rightly been subject from ancient times” [Col. 0602C].

Terrified by Henry’s ironic taunt, Conan groaned and, begging mercy as a suppliant, said:

> “By my own guilt, lord, I deserve condemnation; but now I beg mercy for the sake of God, Creator of all. For my ransom I shall give my lord gold and silver, as much as I can find in my own treasures and those of my kinsmen; and for the fault of my disloyalty I shall render faithful service until death.”

Henry said to him:

> “By my mother’s soul! There shall be no ransom for a traitor, but the swift infliction of the death he deserves.”

Then Conan groaned and cried aloud:

> “For the love of God, permit me confession!”

But Henry, the fierce avenger of an injury done to his brother, raged in anger; spurning the wretch’s supplications, he pushed him with both hands and hurled him down through the tower window. The man was shattered in a moment by the miserable fall and died before he reached the ground. Then his corpse was tied to a horse’s tail and disgracefully dragged through all the streets of Rouen, to terrify deserters. The place where this punishment was inflicted [Col. 0603A] was called Conan’s Leap down to the present day.

When Duke Robert returned from the Meadow to the citadel and learned what had occurred, he was moved by pity and grieved for the misfortune of the citizens. But the more severe judgment of the magnates prevailed, and he was unable to spare the guilty. Robert of Bellême and William of Breteuil were then present; they carried off the inhabitants of Rouen as captives like foreign robbers and grievously afflicted them in the squalor of prison. William, son of Ansger, the richest of the Rouennais, was taken captive by William of Breteuil and, after long prison misery, ransomed himself for three thousand pounds. Thus the men of Bellême and Laigle and the duke’s other auxiliaries savagely vent their rage upon them, dragging away in chains the citizens of the metropolis of Neustria [Col. 0603B] and, stripping them of all their goods, cruelly afflicting them as barbarian enemies.

Behold by what miseries proud Normandy is brought low: Normandy which, having long ago conquered England, gloried excessively, and, after killing or driving out the native sons of that realm, seized their possessions and dominions. Behold the mass of riches which she snatched from others and by which, in her power, she swelled insolently to her own ruin: now she miserably disperses it not for her own pleasure but rather for her torment. Now, like Babylon, she drinks from the same cup of tribulations from which she wickedly used to make others drunk. At the sight of so many evils, the poor clergy groan, communities of monks weep, and the unarmed people, desolated everywhere, mourn. Only those rejoice—though neither for long nor happily—who can persistently steal or plunder [Col. 0603C].

Alas for grief! Priestly reverence is almost annihilated, and obedience is denied it by nearly everyone, while the violence of evil men rises and rages furiously. Why does such an unbridled Fury rage in Neustria, trample down its native Normans, and overwhelm them in ruin? Because in those days there was no king or duke in Jerusalem, and the rebellious people sacrificed to Jeroboam’s golden calves at Dan and Bethel. Therefore Joel laments and exhorts the transgressors of the Law, consumed by the caterpillar (*eruca*), grub or palmerworm (*bruchus*), locust (*locusta*), and blight or rust (*rubigo*). By these four calamities, set forth by the prophet, are signified four passions of the mind: fear and desire, grief and joy. Fear and desire goad and consume human hearts, then cast them down by subjecting them to deadly joy or grief [Col. 0603D]. Joyful passions submit to lust; sorrowful ones adhere to cruelty. Virgil mentions these in his poem:

> Hence they fear and desire, grieve and rejoice, and do not behold the light,  
> shut up in darkness and a blind prison.  
> (*Aeneid* VI.732)

For those enveloped in the darkness of disturbances can no longer contemplate the clear light of wisdom, nor free themselves from the glue of vices. I observe many things in sacred Scripture that, subtly fitted to the events of our time, seem similar. But I shall leave allegorical citations and interpretations suited to human conduct for learned readers to investigate, and shall endeavour to continue somewhat further [Col. 0604A] the straightforward history of Norman affairs.

## XVI. Conflict and Disaster of the Men of Hiémois (*Oximenses*).—William Comes to Normandy and Makes Peace with Duke Robert

Having described the troubles of the men of Évreux and the factions and perils of the Rouennais, I shall now relate the conflicts and losses of the men of Hiémois (*Oximenses*). Robert of Bellême built a castle on an elevated site commonly called Les Fourches, transferred thither the inhabitants of Vignats, and strove to subjugate all his neighbours to himself by tyranny. He also built another stronghold, called Château-Gontier, on the River Orne near Curba, through which he thought to bring the whole region of Houlme utterly under his sway, though unjustly. Thus [Col. 0604B], raised excessively above his own birth and that of his ancestors, he rose up; throughout almost all Normandy, deprived of the protection of a just advocate, he opposed his equals and began to oppress all his neighbours.

At this the Norman magnates were troubled and deeply grieved, and for a long time deliberated extensively about resistance. Above all, because they were nearest to the tyrant’s territories and impious undertaking, Hugh of Grandmesnil and Richard of Courcy were the first to rise up. They fortified their strongholds with arms, provisions, and the assistance of knights. These men were advanced in years, eminent in courage and nobility, and powerful through neighbourhood and kinship. For Robert, Richard’s son, had married a daughter of Hugh, who bore her husband five sons.

The high-spirited Hugh had flourished in great excellence in his youth. He had married the most beautiful Adeliza, daughter of Count Ivo of Beaumont, who bore him Robert, William, Hugh, Ivo, and Alberic [Col. 0604C]; and Adeline, Hawise, Rohese, Matilda, and Agnes. Diverse fortune enveloped so numerous and beautiful an offspring and permitted none of them except Robert to live to old age. He was the firstborn and, all his brothers and sisters having died, grew old as the husband of three wives. First he married Agnes, daughter of Ranulf of Bayeux; then Emma, daughter of Robert of Stuteville; finally Lucy, daughter of Savaric, son of Cani.

William and Ivo, moreover, had wives. The former married in Apulia Mabel, daughter of Robert Guiscard; the latter married in England a daughter of Gilbert of Ghent [Col. 0604D]. Adeline married Roger of Ivry, and Rohese Robert of Courcy; Matilda married Hugh of Montpinçon, and Agnes William of Say. Hawise, however, died when already of marriageable age.

Therefore the eminent Hugh, relying on his sons, sons-in-law, and many friends, began war fiercely against Robert and stoutly resisted his tyranny through the conspicuous valour of his helpers. But Robert, swelled by the strength of his brothers Roger and Arnulf and of many dependants, despised his neighbours, and began by many efforts to crush them and devastate their possessions. Count Matthew of Beaumont, William of Warenne, and many others came to their conflicts [Col. 0605A], to display their valour in such an arena. There Theobald, son of Waleran of Breteuil, and Guy the Red were killed. The former was called the White Knight because his horse and all his equipment were white; the latter was likewise surnamed the Red because he was clothed in red.

Robert, seeing that he could not conquer such distinguished neighbours by himself, because nobility, courage, and strength for enduring or undertaking hard things prevailed in them, humbly won over the duke of the Normans with promises and earnestly begged him to come against his rivals.

Accordingly, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1091, in the fourteenth indiction [Col. 0605B], Duke Robert of the Normans besieged Courcy in January. But sparing his freeborn magnates, he neglected to press the besieged hard. Robert, however, attacked the enemy by every device and force for three weeks and assailed the stronghold with various engines. Yet, often repelled by the abundance of knights within, he was put to shame. He erected against the fortification a great machine, called a *berfredus*—a siege tower—and furnished it abundantly with military equipment. But not even so did he constrain the townspeople as he wished. Whenever he began an assault upon Courcy, the military force from Grandmesnil hurried to assist and violently dragged the assailants back from their enterprise.

Meanwhile the castle defenders captured William de Ferrières, William de Rouvrai, and many others [Col. 0605C], and were richly aided by their ransoms. But the fortune of war changes, and the victor is often overcome by the conquered. Ivo, son of Hugh, and Richard, son of Gilbert, were captured by the outside enemy, along with many others who experienced Robert’s dreadful prison.

Hugh no longer bore arms because of old age, but he excelled all others in keen wisdom and counsel. Greatly distressed by being burdened for so long with the siege, he sent word to the besieging duke:

> “I served your father and grandfather for a long time, and endured many hardships in their service. I have always likewise been faithful to you. What have I done? How have I sinned against you? Why have I deserved to be attacked by you so hostilely? I publicly acknowledge you as my lord, and therefore shall not fight against you. But now accept two hundred pounds from me, and withdraw for only one day, wherever you please, so that in your absence I may fight Robert of Bellême. It is clear that Robert puts excessive confidence in the duke’s protection, and that the besieged are more constrained by reverence for their allegiance than by the terror of hostile forces” [Col. 0605D].

An oven stood outside the fortification between the siege tower and the gate of the town, and there a baker baked bread to support those shut in, because, in order to hasten the siege, it had not been permitted to the townspeople to build an oven in the new fortress. It therefore happened that very frequent slaughter took place around the oven, and, with much blood shed [Col. 0606A], many souls brutally departed from the prison of flesh. For the men of Courcy defended the bread in the oven by force of arms, while the men of Bellême strove to take it from them; and for this reason much cruel carnage occurred. One day, while bread was baking in the oven and violent anger arose from insolence between the hostile parties, armed lines assembled on both sides. A battle began; nearly twenty men were killed and many wounded, who did not taste, with their own blood, the bread for which they had paid.

Before the eyes of the besiegers, the comrades of the besieged entered the castle daily and strengthened their allies with arms and food, so that they should not fail, while the duke did nothing to prevent it.

Once, when Robert fled from an engagement with his men [Col. 0606B], the pursuers made one of their squires climb the siege tower and set fire to it from the north side. Thus, by God’s just judgment, the machine was burned—the machine which had been insolently built by tyrannical command during the days of the holy Nativity of the Lord.

The diligent Gerard, bishop of Séez, came to the siege to make peace among his divided parishioners and established his lodging at the monastery of Dives. He offered peace to the contending parties; but, since discord prevailed, he groaned at being rebuffed. Robert further committed a great injury against him and deeply distressed him. A boy who served the bishop was riding playfully through the army in a childish manner when Robert threw him from his horse, seized him, thrust him into prison, and retained the horse for himself [Col. 0606C]. This boy was called Richard of Guaspreia, son of Sevold, whose kindred had long been striving to defend itself against Robert with all its strength. When the bishop heard that his cleric had been captured by Robert without offence, he ordered that he be restored immediately; and unless he were restored, he placed the entire army under interdict.

After several days the beardless cleric was released free, and the ailing bishop was carried back to his own see at Séez. There he was fortified by the Lord’s sacraments and died in the hands of his disciples on 23 January 1091, the tenth day before the Kalends of February. His body was buried in the church of St Gervasius the Martyr.

In that same week William Rufus, king of the English [Col. 0606D], crossed into Normandy with a great fleet. On hearing of his arrival, the frightened duke withdrew at once with Robert and the other besiegers, and everyone returned to his own home. Immediately almost all the Norman magnates hastened to the king, bringing him gifts with the greatest favour in expectation of greater gifts in return. When the French, Bretons, and Flemings, and many others from neighbouring provinces, heard that the king was staying at Eu in Neustria, they too came to him. They eagerly experienced his magnificence and, returning home, ranked him above all their princes in wealth and generosity.

At last the two brothers came peacefully together at Rouen and, assembling as one, were reconciled after abolishing their previous complaints [Col. 0607A]. [Note: [Col. 0607D] Roger of Hoveden states the terms of this peace in these words:

> “In the year 1091 King William the younger went to Normandy in February, in order to wrest it from his brother Robert; but while he remained there, peace was made between them upon this agreement: the count was to grant the king, in good faith, the county of Eu, Fécamp, the abbey on Mont-Saint-Michel, Keresburg (Cherbourg), and the castles which had revolted from him; and the king was to subject to the count’s rule [Col. 0608D] the province of Le Mans and the castles which were then resisting the count in Normandy. He was also to restore to all Normans the lands which they had lost in England because of their loyalty to the count, and to give the count in England as much land as had been agreed between them. They further agreed between themselves that, if the count died without a son born in lawful marriage, the king should become his heir; and likewise, if the king should die, the count should become his heir. Twelve barons on the king’s side and twelve on the count’s side swore this agreement.”

Dom Bouquet, book VIII, p. 648.]

Duke Robert then received great gifts from the king and granted him the county of Eu and Aumale, together with the whole land of Gerard of Gournay and Ralph of Conches, with all their castles and those subject to them. There the aforesaid king resided in royal fashion with his followers from January until the Kalends of August.

## XVII. The Remarkable Experience of a Certain Priest in the Diocese of Lisieux
What befell a certain priest in the bishopric of Lisieux at the beginning of January, I do not think should be passed over or suppressed in silence. In the village called Bonneval there was a priest, Gualchelmus, who served the church of Saint Albinus of Angers, formerly a monk and bishop and confessor. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1091, at the beginning of January, he was summoned, as duty required, to visit by night a sick man at the farthest bounds of his parish. As he was returning alone, far removed from human habitation, he began to hear a tremendous noise, as though of a very great army, and thought it was the household of Robert of Bellême, hastening to besiege Courcy. For the moon, eight days old, was then shining clearly in the sign of Aries and showing the way to those who travelled. The aforesaid priest was young, bold, and strong, large and agile in body. Hearing the tumult of the hurrying multitude, he became afraid and began to ponder whether he should flee, lest he be attacked by base parasites and shamefully plundered, or raise a strong hand in his own defence if he were assaulted by anyone. At last he saw four medlar trees in a field, some distance from the road, and wished quickly to turn aside to them in order to hide until the cavalry had passed by. But a man of enormous stature, carrying a huge club, overtook the hurrying priest and, lifting his staff above his head, said: “Stand still, and go no farther.” At once the priest froze in place, and, leaning on the stick he carried, stood motionless. The tall bearer of the staff stood beside him and, doing him no harm, waited for the army to pass.

Behold, a vast crowd of foot-soldiers passed by, carrying on their necks and shoulders cattle, clothes, goods of many kinds, and diverse utensils—things that robbers are accustomed to carry off. All of them lamented, urging one another to hasten. The priest also recognized there many of his neighbours who had recently died, and heard them mourning under the great punishments by which they were tortured for their crimes. Then followed a troop of bier-bearers [Col. 0608A], with which the aforesaid giant suddenly joined himself. Nearly fifty biers were being carried, each borne by two carriers. Upon the biers sat little men like dwarfs, but with great heads like barrels. A huge tree-trunk too was carried by two Ethiopians, and upon it a wretched man, bound cruelly, was being tortured. Amid dreadful agonies and cries he howled aloud. For a most hideous demon, sitting upon the same trunk, relentlessly prodded the bloodied man in the loins and back with fiery spurs. Gualchelmus recognized him as the murderer of Stephen the priest, and saw him suffering intolerably for the innocent blood which he had shed two years before, dying before he had completed penance for so great a sin [Col. 0608B].

Then followed a company of women, whose multitude seemed innumerable to the priest. They rode in the feminine manner, seated on women’s saddles in which burning nails had been fixed. A wind frequently raised them by a space of about one cubit, then immediately allowed them to fall back upon the spikes. They were wounded in the buttocks by the glowing nails; horribly tormented by piercing and burning, they cried, “Woe! Woe!” and openly confessed the shameful acts for which they paid such penalties. Thus, indeed, for the obscene allurements and pleasures in which they had indulged without restraint among mortals, they now suffer terribly flames, stenches, and many other punishments beyond recounting [Col. 0608C], and with piteous cries confess their penalties. In this troop the aforesaid priest recognized certain noblewomen, and saw the palfreys and mules, with the women’s litters, of many women who still breathed the air of life.

Standing there, the priest trembled at such sights and began to turn many things over in his mind. Not long afterward he noticed a numerous host of clergy and monks, their judges and rulers, bishops and abbots with pastoral croziers. The clerics and bishops were clothed in black copes; likewise the monks and abbots were wrapped in black cowls. They groaned and wept, and some called out to Gualchelmus, begging him, because of their former acquaintance, to pray for them. The priest reported that he saw there many persons of great reputation [Col. 0608D], whom human opinion asserted had already been joined with the saints in heaven. He saw Hugh, bishop of Lisieux, and the principal abbots, Mainer of Saint-Evroul and Gerbert of Fontenelle, and many others whom I cannot recall by name or endeavour to set down in writing [Col. 0609A]. Human sight is often deceived, but the eye of God sees to the depths. For man sees the face, but God sees the heart. In the kingdom of eternal blessedness perpetual brightness illuminates all things; there perfect holiness, having attained every delight, rejoices in the children of the kingdom. There nothing is done in disorder; nothing defiled is admitted there. Nothing unclean or contrary to honour is found there. Therefore whatever the dregs of the flesh have committed unbecomingly is boiled away in purgatorial fire and cleansed by various purifications, as the eternal Judge ordains. And as a vessel cleansed of its rust by fire and carefully polished on every side is placed in a treasury, so the soul, cleansed from the contagion of every vice, is admitted into Paradise, where, endowed with every happiness [Col. 0609B], it rejoices without fear or care.

Terrified by these visions, the priest was greatly alarmed, and, leaning upon his staff, awaited still more terrible things. Behold, a great army of knights followed; no colour was visible among them but blackness and gleaming fire. All rode the largest horses, armed with every weapon, as though hastening to battle, and carried the blackest banners. There were seen Richard and Baldwin, sons of Count Gilbert, who had recently died; and many others whom I cannot enumerate. Among the rest, Landric of Orbec, who had been killed that same year, began to address the priest. Shouting horribly, he conveyed his messages and urgently begged him to report his commands to his wife. But the companies following and those going before [Col. 0609C] hindered him by interrupting his words and said to the priest: “Do not believe Landric, for he is a liar.” This man had been viscount and advocate of Orbec and had risen far above his birth through ability and merit. In business and lawsuits he judged as he pleased, perverted judgments in return for gifts, and served greed and falsehood rather than justice. Accordingly, he was deservedly condemned to disgraceful punishments and openly called a liar by his companions. At this judgment no one flattered him, nor did anyone entreat for him by means of his clever eloquence. Rather, because when he was able he was accustomed to stop his ears against the cries of the poor, now in his torments [Col. 0609D], as an abominable man, he was judged wholly unworthy to be heard.

After the immense troop of knights had passed, Gualchelmus began to think within himself: “This is without doubt the household of Herlechin. I have heard that many have seen it in former times; but, unbelieving, I mocked the reports, because I had never seen certain evidence of such things. Now indeed I truly see the spirits of the dead; yet no one will believe me when I recount what I have seen, unless I show the people of earth a sure proof. Therefore I shall seize one of the riderless horses which follow the troop, mount it at once, lead it home, and show it to my neighbours so that belief may be secured.” Immediately he seized the reins of a coal-black steed; but it violently shook itself free from the hand that seized it and went away through the company of Ethiopians with winged speed [Col. 0610A]. The priest grieved that he had not attained his desire. He was young in years, bold and impetuous in spirit, swift and strong in body. Therefore he stood ready in the middle of the road, and, facing a very spirited steed as it came, stretched out his hand. The horse stopped to receive the priest, and, breathing from its nostrils, cast forth a great cloud as long as a very tall oak. Then the priest put his left foot in the stirrup, placed his hand upon the saddle-straps after grasping the reins, and suddenly felt beneath his foot an excessive heat like burning fire; through the hand holding the reins an incredible cold penetrated to his inmost breast.

While these things were happening, four dreadful horsemen arrived and said in terrifying shouts: “Why do you attack our horses? You shall come with us. None of us harmed you, whereas you began to seize what is ours.” But he, exceedingly frightened, released the horse. As three knights were about to seize him, the fourth said: “Leave him; let him speak with me, because I shall send messages to my wife and children through him.” Then he said to the greatly frightened priest: “Hear me, I beg you, and tell my wife what I command.” The priest replied: “I do not know who you are, nor do I know your wife.” The knight said: “I am William of Glos, son of Baron, once the renowned steward of William of Breteuil and of his father William, count of Hereford. Among mortals I thirsted for unlawful gains and plunder, and sinned in more crimes than can be told. But above all [Col. 0610C] usury tortures me. I lent my money to a certain needy man and received one of his mills as a pledge. Since he could not pay the rent, I kept the pledge throughout my life; having disinherited the lawful heir, I left it to my own heirs. Behold, I carry in my mouth the glowing iron of the mill, which without doubt seems to me heavier to bear than the castle of Rouen. Tell therefore Beatrice, my wife, and Roger, my son, to help me and quickly restore to the heir the pledge from which they have received far more than I gave.” The priest replied: “William of Glos has long been dead, and no such message would be acceptable to any of the faithful. I do not know who you are or who your heirs are. If I presume to tell such things to Roger of Glos, or his brothers [Col. 0610D], or their mother, they will mock me as a madman.” William, however, persisted earnestly in his entreaties and carefully impressed upon him many very familiar signs. Though the priest understood all that he heard, he pretended not to know it. Finally, overcome by much pleading, he agreed and again promised that he would do as requested. Then William recapitulated everything and, in a long conversation, repeated many matters to him. Meanwhile the priest began to consider that he would not dare announce the abominable commands of one who had died a violent death. “It is not fitting,” he said, “to make such things public. I shall by no means tell anyone what you enjoin.” At once the other, furious, stretched out his hand, seized the priest by the throat, and began to threaten him, dragging him along the ground. The captive [Col. 0611A] felt the hand by which he was held burning like fire; in that distress he suddenly cried: “Holy Mary, glorious mother of Christ, help me!” Immediately, at the invocation of the most merciful Mother, the Son of God’s aid was present, as the ordinance of the Almighty had appointed. For a knight arrived, bearing a sword in his right hand; brandishing his sword as though he meant to strike, he said: “Why are you killing my brother, accursed men? Leave him and go away.” At once they flew off and pursued the Ethiopian phalanx.

When all had gone, the knight remained on the road with Gualchelmus and asked him: “Do you recognize me?” The priest answered: “No.” The knight said: “I am Robert, son of Ralph, surnamed Blond, and I am your brother.” Since the priest was deeply astonished at so unexpected a thing and was greatly distressed, as has been said, by what he had seen and felt, the knight began to recount many things concerning the childhood of both of them and to rehearse familiar signs. The priest remembered perfectly what he heard, but dared not acknowledge it aloud and denied everything. At last the aforesaid knight said: “I marvel at your hardness and dullness. After the death of both our parents I brought you up and loved you above all mortals. I sent you to school in France and supplied you abundantly with clothes and money, striving sufficiently to benefit you in many other ways. Now you have become forgetful of these things and disdain even to recognize me!”

[Col. 0611C] Then the priest, after a full statement of truthful words, was convinced by certain proofs and openly, with tears, acknowledged his brother’s speech. The knight then said to him: “You deserved to die and now to be dragged with us as a sharer in our punishments, because with wicked rashness you attacked our possessions. No one else has dared to begin this. But the Mass which you sang today saved you from perishing. I too have now been permitted to appear to you and to make known to you my misery. After I had spoken with you in Normandy and been bid farewell by you, I went to England; there, by the Creator’s command, I received the end of life, and endured monstrous punishments for the sins with which I was too heavily burdened. The weapons we bear are fiery; they infect us with a most foul stench, oppress us excessively with immense weight [Col. 0611D], and burn us with unquenchable heat. Until now I have been tortured unspeakably by punishments of this kind. But when you were ordained in England and sang your first Mass for the faithful departed, your father Ralph was released from his punishments, and my shield, by which I was grievously afflicted, fell away. As you see, I carry this sword; but I confidently expect release from this burden within a year.”

As the knight said these and other such things, and the priest listened attentively to him, he saw around his ankles, by the spurs, something like a swollen mass of blood in the form of a human head. Astonished, he asked: “Why does so great a coagulation of blood hang from your heels?” The knight answered: “It is not blood but fire; and it seems to me of greater weight than if I carried Mount Saint-Michael upon myself. Since I used costly and sharp spurs in order to hasten to shed blood, I justly bear on my ankles this enormous burden [Col. 0612A]. So intolerably weighed down by it, I cannot express to any man the measure of my punishment. Mortals ought unceasingly to meditate upon these things and fear—indeed, guard against—paying such dreadful penalties for their offences. I am not permitted to speak longer with you, brother, because I am compelled to pursue the miserable troop in haste. I beg you: remember me and aid me with devout prayers and alms. For from Palm Sunday until one year hence I hope to be saved and, through the Creator’s mercy, freed from every torment. But be solicitous for yourself and amend your life prudently, for it is stained with many vices; know also that it will not be long. For the present, keep silence. What you have now unexpectedly seen and heard, conceal in silence, and for three days do not presume to tell anyone.”

Having said this, the knight departed in haste. The priest was seriously ill throughout the whole week. Then, after he began to regain strength, he went to Lisieux, recounted everything in order to Bishop Gilbert, and obtained from him the remedies necessary for himself. Thereafter he lived in health for almost fifteen years. I heard from his own mouth these things which I have committed to writing, together with many others that have been erased by forgetfulness; and I saw his face, injured by the touch of that dreadful knight.

I have written these things for the edification of readers: that the righteous may be strengthened in good things and the perverse may turn back from evil. [Col. 0612C] I now return to the subject I had begun.

## XVIII. Agreements concluded between King William and Duke Robert.—Affairs of the bishopric of Lisieux.—Roger, abbot of Saint-Evroul

In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1091, in the fourteenth indiction, in January, William Rufus, king of the English, crossed the sea into Normandy with a great fleet. On hearing of the king’s arrival, Duke Robert immediately abandoned the siege of Courcy, and Robert of Bellême fled with his accomplices. The king remained in Neustria until August and, by royal authority, pacified those who were at variance and wished to submit to him. Henry, however, because he brought forward grave complaints against both his brothers and claimed a portion of his magnificent father’s extensive inheritance, yet obtained nothing because of their excessive obstinacy, gathered Bretons and Normans, fortified Coutances, Avranches, and other towns, and rose with all his strength to resist. But Hugh, count of Chester, and Henry’s other supporters, observing his poverty and fearing King William’s great wealth and terrible power, abandoned the distinguished prince in his distress of war and surrendered their fortresses to the king.

In the middle of Lent, therefore, King William and Duke Robert besieged Mont-Saint-Michel and shut up their brother Henry there. For nearly fifteen days they distressed him and his followers particularly through lack of water. But the shrewd young man, thus constrained by his brothers, abandoned on every side by kinsmen, friends, and allied relations, and afflicted by a manifold scarcity of nearly everything human beings need, prudently considered within himself the various reversals of mortal life. Having restrained his ungoverned impulse, he resolved to reserve himself for better times. At last he asked the besiegers to allow himself and his companions free departure from the Mount. They were greatly pleased and honourably allowed him to go out with all his equipment. Henry therefore surrendered his fortifications, travelled through Brittany, thanked the Bretons who alone had given him help, and afterward sought the neighbouring French. The noble exile remained in the Vexin for not quite two years, seeking various lodgings [Col. 0613B]. Content with only one knight, one clerk, and three squires, he lived a poor life. Thus royal offspring learned poverty in exile, so that, when he became king, he might know well how to pity the wretched and needy, and with royal power or generosity support their humiliation or want; having experienced the condition of the weak, he might mercifully show mercy to them.

Then Duke Robert conceded a large part of Normandy to King William, and Normandy rested from war for nearly two years. After the feast of Pentecost, Archbishop William assembled a synod of bishops and abbots at Rouen, and began to deliberate with Duke Robert and the suffragan bishops concerning the bishopric of Séez. At last, when the consultation had ended [Col. 0613C], he chose Serlo, head of the monks of Saint-Evroul, and entrusted to him, though he strongly resisted, the bishopric of Séez. Finally, on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, he summoned the aforesaid monk to Rouen and canonically consecrated him in the church of Holy Mary, Mother of God. The venerable Serlo then bore vigorously the burden of the episcopate entrusted to him for thirty-two years and four months, and earnestly strove to benefit God’s Church in prosperity and adversity. But he had exceedingly harsh and unruly parishioners: Robert of Bellême, Rotrou of Mortagne, and their accomplices. They cruelly quarrelled among themselves, frequently violated the peace of God’s Church, scattered amid the tumults of war the sheep of the Lord’s flock whom Christ redeemed with his own blood, and, oppressing them by manifold factions [Col. 0613D], tore them apart. Against them he boldly drew the sword of God’s word and frequently excommunicated those hardened in wickedness; but he could scarcely, or never, instruct or retain his rebellious disciples in firm peace. Therefore, for as long as he held the episcopate, he laboured constantly amid tumult and disturbance; and often, when Robert’s fury raged excessively, he lived in exile in England or Italy, groaning in much anxious fear.

After its aforesaid head had assumed the episcopate, the abbey of Saint-Evroul, concerned for a shepherd, summoned its former pastor on the seventh day before the Kalends of August and, after a three-day fast, began to deliberate on choosing an abbot. Three abbots were also present [Col. 0614A]: Fulk of Le Désert, Arnulf of Troarn, and Ralph of Sées. After the reading concerning the ordination of an abbot according to the Rule of Saint Benedict had been read, they chose Lord Roger of Sap, a monk of that same monastery, who excelled in simplicity and literary learning, and in much probity and sweetness of good manners. Herman the prior, Ernald of Telliol, and several others then brought him to the duke’s court, but did not find the duke in Normandy. For, on suddenly hearing of secret plots which men overseas were devising against the peace and security of the realm, both brothers had unexpectedly crossed from Neustria to England, to the astonishment of all. Herman then returned to Saint-Evroul to govern the house, while Ernald followed the rulers of the realm by sea with the abbot-elect. Having arrived at the royal residence called Windsor, they presented to the duke the election by the monks’ convent, with the authority of the bishop of Sées and of the three abbots. He gladly gave his assent, and entrusted to the aforesaid Roger, by the pastoral staff—as was then customary—the care of the monastery in external affairs. By his letters he commanded the bishop of Lisieux to advance him canonically in all respects. King William too then graciously received that monk there, confirmed everything which his father and his nobles had formerly given to the church of Saint-Evroul, and ratified it by royal authority in a charter. Having accomplished the purposes for which he had gone, Roger returned to Saint-Evroul on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January and, honourably received by the brethren [Col. 0614C], presided over the abbey for thirty-four years. He admitted one hundred and fifteen disciples to monastic life, whose lives shifting fortune variously tossed about. Some of them, flourishing in virtues, attained, with God’s aid, the prize of the heavenly calling. Others, through Satan’s snares, fell back into the foul abyss of vices and would receive from the just Judge what they deserved.

We saw six abbots among those whom we have said were subject to the venerable Roger: Guarin of Sées, Geoffrey of Orléans, Gilbert of Glos, Robert of Préaux, William Bassus, and Louis. Guarin succeeded his master and held the government of the church of Saint-Evroul for many years [Col. 0614D]. Robert of Préaux vigorously governed the monastery of Thorney in England. Geoffrey of Orléans presided for nearly fifteen years over the church of Euland.

> [Note: [Col. 0613D] Read “Crulandensis”: Croyland. (Le Prévost.)]

William Bassus long governed the Benedictine monastery of Holm. Louis, after the canons had been expelled from Balcheriville by the judgment of his elders, first established the monastic order with ten monks in the basilica of Saint George the martyr. Gilbert of Glos, a noble and eloquent man, governed the monastery of Lyre for nearly ten years and reformed much there. Thus the monks of Saint-Evroul were regularly drawn forth from the inner precincts of the monastery and raised to the summit of prelacy for the benefit of many [Col. 0615A], so that, shining like lamps upon a lampstand, they might show the way of salvation to those desiring to enter the house of the Lord by the path of righteousness. But disturbances in external affairs, caused by the negligence or wickedness of secular rulers, are very often an obstacle to ecclesiastical order and monastic strictness. All who desired to serve religion in Normandy or its borderlands experienced this all too greatly in the time of Duke Robert and Philip, king of the French.

In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1092, in the fifteenth indiction, Henry, son of King William, obtained the town of Domfront through God’s help and the support of friends, and from there strove boldly to assert his hereditary right [Col. 0615B]. For while he was younger, he was treated by his brothers not as a brother but rather as an outsider; he was compelled to seek the aid of foreigners, that is, Frenchmen and Bretons, and for five years was severely harassed by the fluctuations of diverse events. At last the people of Domfront, by God’s will, took pity on the sufferings of so distinguished an exile. They summoned him from France through Harecherius, received him honourably, shook off the rule of Robert of Bellême, by whom they had long been grievously oppressed, and established Henry as their lord. He then took up arms manfully against Robert, count of Normandy; by burnings and plundering he avenged the injury of his expulsion, seized many men, and committed them to prison.

Meanwhile, after he had captured a man named Rualedus from the land of Saint Evroul [Col. 0615C], he placed him in Domfront castle. While the man sat by the fire—for it was winter—he began with tears to invoke Saint Evroul and say: “I beseech you, Saint Evroul, friend of God, rescue me from this captivity. For you know that I have always served you faithfully.” Having said this, he suddenly fell asleep.

And behold, someone seized his hand and began to draw him. When he awoke, he felt that all pain had departed from his body. For he was greatly weakened, so much so that he could not move from his place without another’s help. He had fallen from the beast on which he was bound while travelling. He therefore began to consider within himself what he should do and how he might get out of the house [Col. 0615D]. For he had seen that the knight who had placed him there had very firmly fastened with a wedge the door through which one could go out into the garden. Nevertheless, gathering strength through faith, he went to the door and laid his hand upon the bar. Then—marvellous to tell!—the wedge, which had been firmly driven in, fell to the ground. Opening the door, he reached the garden exit and, looking out, saw a multitude of knights standing before him in the street. Stretching out his hand, he is said to have said: “Saint Evroul, lead me.” And thus, barefoot, clothed only in a linen garment and cloak, he passed through the midst of their ranks as though they had no eyes. No one asked who he was or where he was going. I think that by the power of that most holy man they had been unable to see him [Col. 0616A]. At about the sixth hour, looking behind him, he saw the knight who had captured him coming at a swift run. Stricken with great fear, he hid himself among some thickets that presented themselves to his sight. When the said knight came near that place, he asked the oxherds ploughing there whether they had seen a man fleeing, promising that he would promptly give three solidi to anyone who informed him. But they, warned by fear, although they knew the man, denied knowing. After the knight had gone away from the place where he was hidden, the captive rose and, trusting in God’s help and Saint Evroul’s, returned unharmed to his own home, surviving bodily down to our own time. We learned what we have related from his own mouth, and because he is a man of lawful and praiseworthy life, we believe him without hesitation [Col. 0616B].

## XIX. Bertrada, countess of Anjou, abandons her husband and marries Philip, king of the French.—Prelates of France distinguished for religion and learning.—The Council of Rouen

At about this time [1092–1093], a shameful disturbance arose in the kingdom of France. Bertrada, countess of Anjou, feared that her husband would do to her what he had already done to two others, and that she would be left in contempt or become a worthless prostitute. Conscious of her nobility and beauty, she sent a most trusted envoy to Philip, king of the French, and plainly made known to him what she contemplated in her heart. For she preferred voluntarily to leave her husband and seek another rather than be left by her husband and exposed to everyone’s contempt [Col. 0616C]. At last the effeminate prince, having learned the wanton woman’s desire, consented to the disgrace and joyfully received her as she came into France, having abandoned her husband. He dismissed his noble and devout wife Bertha, daughter of the noble Duke Florentius of Frisia, who had borne him Louis and Constance, and took Bertrada to himself, though she had lived with Fulk of Anjou for nearly four years. Odo, bishop of Bayeux, performed this execrable marriage; consequently, as a gift from the adulterous king in recompense for his shameful service, he held for a time the churches of the town of Mantes. No French bishop deigned to perform the execrable consecration [Col. 0616D]; rather, standing firm in the strictness of ecclesiastical rectitude, they strove to please God rather than man and unanimously detested the shameful union, pronouncing the same anathema upon it. Thus the wanton concubine left her adulterous count and clung to the adulterous king until his death. The abominable crime of adultery—alas!—was perpetrated upon the throne of the kingdom of France. Hence a great commotion of threats and attempts at battle arose among wealthy rivals. Yet the wily woman restrained the hostility between the rivals and by her ingenuity joined them in such peace that she prepared a splendid banquet for them and served them fittingly, as pleased them.

Pope Urban sent legates of the Apostolic See into France and, through letters and the preaching of priests, reproved, entreated, and rebuked the erring king, who had repudiated his lawful wife and associated with himself an adulteress contrary to God’s law. But, hardened grievously in his disgrace, like the deaf asp that stops its ears against the voice of the charmer, he despised the fathers’ exhortations of correction. He lay long rotting in the stench of adultery, until he had begotten two sons by the adulteress, Philip and Florus. Therefore, during the pontificates of Urban and Paschal, he remained under interdict for nearly eleven years. During that time he never wore a crown, put on purple, or celebrated any solemnity in royal fashion. Whenever the king came into any town or city of France, as soon as the clergy heard of it, every ringing of bells and the public chanting of clerics ceased [Col. 0617B]. Public mourning was observed, and divine worship was conducted privately for as long as the transgressing prince remained in that diocese. Yet, by permission of the bishops whose lord he was, he had a chaplain for the sake of royal dignity, from whom he heard Mass privately with his private household.

At that time France flourished with devout and learned prelates. The aged Leutherius presided over the metropolitan see of Bourges, and Daimbert over Sens. The illustrious Renaud presided over Reims; after his death Ralph, surnamed the Green, succeeded him in that diocese. The most learned Ivo also presided over the church of Chartres, to whom the good repute of his life and sound teaching bears plain witness. Walo likewise presided over the Parisians [Col. 0617C], and many other bishops shone in their regions, so that France greatly rejoiced in their devotion and sacred teaching. Nevertheless, King Philip brazenly resisted their admonitions to amend his life and, rotten with adultery, persisted in wickedness. Therefore he deservedly suffered toothache, scabies, and many other sicknesses and disgraces. With the consent of the French, he gave his son Louis Pontoise, Mantes, and the whole county of the Vexin, and entrusted him with the care of the whole kingdom while he was coming into the first bloom of youth. He had earlier given his daughter Constance to Hugh, count of Troyes, before later giving her at Chartres to Bohemond, the most mighty duke of Antioch [Col. 0617D]. This duke came into France in the year from the Incarnation 1106 and, as the foremost standard-bearer of the Christian army, was everywhere received with distinction by the peoples of the West. He took the aforesaid daughter of the king with him to the eastern lands and led many thousands of westerners with him against the pagans. But on that expedition, all things fell out as pilgrims wished.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1108, in the first indiction, Archbishop William assembled a council of bishops and abbots at Rouen, and for several days discussed the necessary affairs of the Church with his suffragans. Then Ralph, bishop of the city of Coutances, came to the lodging of Serlo, bishop of Sées, who was wiser, and, having spoken with him on many matters, heard an ample account concerning the matters under discussion. At length, among other things, the aforesaid bishop related, saying:

> “In our city there is a basilica, built from ancient times in honour of the blessed apostle Peter, where many miracles were formerly wrought by divine power. Many sick persons have there received healing, and burning candles have often been seen descending from above. A certain nun, believed to be of great religious devotion, frequents this church daily, and repeatedly recounts that she has seen very many such things. To furnish a sure proof of her account, once, while she was keeping vigil alone in the oratory and saw a burning candle lowered from on high without human assistance, she reverently approached the altar, extinguished the candle, wrapped it in a clean linen cloth, and shut it up in her chest. When, at a fitting time, she related what she had seen and opened the chest to show what she had deposited, she found only ashes as evidence of its burning; but she saw that the entire candle had been consumed, without injury to the cloth or to the other things which were there.
>
> “Recently, in the same basilica, while God’s people were celebrating the feast of the blessed apostle Peter and the clergy stood in the choir for the celebration of the evening synaxis, all saw three brightly burning wax tapers descend from above as far as the altar, and, marvelling at the unusual event, were astonished. The tapers burned until the end of Matins, and were consumed at dawn. They stood in the air in proper order above the altar, yet did not touch the altar-cloth. The middle one was largest and square; the other two were of medium size and round. The report of this event spread throughout the whole city, and after Vespers nearly all clerics and laypeople hurried to see the spectacle. No one dared touch the tapers; but on the square taper the clerics read the following writing. On the first side: ‘Command, Peter, wrath from heaven.’ On the second: ‘The people, *tarisum* with sin.’ On the third: ‘Have mercy on him.’ On the fourth: ‘Tears.’
>
> “The letters were very well formed for reading, and learned readers diligently investigated the meaning of this inscription. Supplying the necessary implied words, they interpreted it according to their understanding. For it seemed to them that Peter—head of the world, judge of the age, and keeper of the keys of the heavenly kingdom—was being divinely addressed thus: ‘Command, Peter, wrath from heaven, that it may be poured out upon the people *tarisum*, that is, wholly parched by sin. I would have mercy’—that is, ‘I would have mercy on him’—if he offered me tears of worthy repentance. For divine speech is not subject to the rules of grammarians, nor can it be compelled of necessity to follow the idiom of human speech. Therefore, terrified by these things seen at Coutances, amid the pestilences and storms of war which we endure, we perceive dangers threatening us and fear still worse things in the future.”

When Ralph, bishop of Coutances, reported these things, his hearers marvelled; and shortly afterwards many calamities of war, storm, and famine followed in Normandy. For that same bishop died not long thereafter, and a deadly scourge raged throughout his whole diocese.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1089, in the tenth indiction, the venerable Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, died; and the ecclesiastical property belonging to the metropolitan was subjected to royal control for three years. Thereafter the holy Anselm, abbot of Bec, succeeded by God’s dispensation; enduring many labours and adversities, he governed holily for seventeen years.

## XX. Malcolm, king of the Scots, undertakes war against the king of England.—He is slain.—Concerning his wife and children.

At that time much wickedness arose in the lands and increased greatly. Men of military rank abandoned the customs of their fathers in dress and in the cutting of their hair; shortly thereafter burgesses, peasants, and almost all the common people imitated them. Because transgression of the divine law had overflowed exceedingly, the punishment of heavenly wrath justly crushed the guilty under many and varied calamities.

At that time Malcolm, king of the Scots, rebelled against the king of the English and refused the service due from him. King William, however, after he had made peace in Normandy with his brother Robert, as we have related above, and had taken him with him against the faithless traitors who had conspired against the king, assembled an army from all England and led it as far as the great river which the Scots call Watra. But because the crossing was inaccessible, he encamped upon its bank. The king of the Scots stood opposite with his legions, ready for battle, and sent this message to the king of the English through envoys:

> “King William, I owe you nothing except battle, if I am provoked by your injuries. But if I see Robert, the first-born son of King William, I am prepared to render him whatever I owe.”

Having heard this, Robert the duke crossed the river with a few knights, on the advice of the wise.

The king of the Scots received him kindly and kept him with him in friendship for three days. Then he led the duke up a high mountain and showed him from there, on a plain, a huge army of armed men. Afterwards, from another side between two mountains, he threatened him and showed him a greater army in another field.

> “With such Scottish companies,” he said, “I am prepared to receive your brother if he dares cross over here to me. Would that he wished to attack us and test the sharpness of our missiles! I confess that King Edward, when he gave me his great-niece Margaret in marriage, gave me the earldom of Lothian. Thereafter King William confirmed what his predecessor had given me, and commended me to you, his first-born son. Therefore I shall keep what I promised you. But I promised your brother nothing, and I owe him nothing. As Christ says, no one can serve two masters.” (Matt. 6:24.)

Robert replied:

> “It is as you assert. But circumstances have changed, and my father’s ordinances have in many respects wavered from their former firmness. Now, therefore, illustrious king, yield to me and come with me to my brother; you will find with him kindness and an abundance of good things, because he is nearer and more powerful and has a greater store of riches.”

By these promises the king was made trusting, and, after their conference, he was reconciled with the king. The kings then dismissed their forces, and themselves set out together for England.

After some time, when King Malcolm wished to return to his own land and was peacefully making his way home, honoured by the king with many gifts, Robert de Mowbray encountered him near his borders with his nephew Morel and armed knights, and unexpectedly killed him while unarmed. When the king of the English and the magnates of the realm heard this, they were greatly grieved and deeply ashamed that so foul and cruel a deed had been committed by Normans. An ancient crime was repeated by men of the present day. For just as Abner, son of Ner, returning peacefully from the house of David, was treacherously killed by Joab and Abishai, so King Malcolm, returning in peace from the court of King William, was slaughtered by the Mowbrays.

Margaret, queen of the Scots, struck by the grievous news of her husband’s death, trembled. She summoned all the nobles of her kingdom, commended to them her sons Edgar, Alexander, and David, and besought them to honour them as sons of a king. When her requests had been received with great favour by the court, she ordered crowds of poor people to be gathered and all her treasure distributed to them for the love of God; and she asked everyone diligently to pray to the Lord for herself, her husband, and her children. She was the daughter of Edward, king of the Hungarians, who was the son of Edmund, surnamed Ironside, brother of Edward, king of the English; while in exile he married, together with the kingdom, the daughter of Solomon, king of the Hungarians. This high-born woman sprang from the blood of royal forefathers; but she shone more gloriously through goodness of character and holiness of life. At last, after arranging matters fittingly and distributing her riches among gatherings of the poor, she entered the church and requested her chaplains to celebrate Mass. Thereafter she devoutly attended the sacred solemnities and, after receiving the holy Eucharist, expired amid the words of prayer.

Among the other good works performed by this noble lady, the faithful queen rebuilt the monastery of Iona, which Columba, servant of Christ, had built in the time of Brude, king of the Picts, son of Meilocon, but which had fallen into ruin through the ravages of wars and long antiquity. Having supplied suitable resources for the work of the Lord, she restored it for the monks.

She had sent her two daughters, Edith and Mary, to her sister Christina, a nun of the abbey of Romsey, to be educated and instructed in sacred letters. There they were long nurtured among the nuns and learned both the art of letters and the observance of good morals. Having reached marriageable age, the devout virgins awaited God’s consolation. For, as has been said, bereft of both parents and deprived of the help of brothers and of other friends or kinsfolk, they experienced the mercy of God, who disposes all things well, as a ready helper. Alan Rufus, count of the Bretons, sought from King Rufus the hand in marriage of Matilda, formerly called Edith; but, forestalled by death, he did not obtain her. Afterwards William de Warenne, earl of Surrey, sought Matilda; but she was reserved by divine providence and married another more illustriously. Henry, having acquired the kingdom of the English, married the aforesaid virgin, and by her begot William Ætheling and Matilda the empress. Eustace, count of Boulogne, took Mary as his wife; she bore him an only daughter, whom Stephen, count of Mortain, joined to himself together with her paternal inheritance.

After Malcolm, king of the Scots, had been killed by the Normans, a grave sedition concerning the succession arose in their kingdom. Edgar, the king’s first-born son, rightly assumed his father’s authority. But Donald, brother of King Malcolm, having seized tyrannical power, cruelly resisted him for some time. At last the vigorous young man was killed by his uncle. But Alexander, his brother, killed Donald and obtained the kingdom. Thus, as avenger and successor of his brother, Alexander reigned for several years and took as wife a daughter of Henry, king of the English, by a concubine. Dying childless, he left the kingdom to his brother David. Thus all these brothers reigned in turn in Scotland; flourishing in good morals and the love of God, they lived commendably according to their capacity, as young men and laymen.

David, the youngest of the brothers, prudently avoiding the violent assaults of the Scots, sought the court of Henry, king of the English. While internal disaster afflicted the Scots and they armed, in the fury of war, relentlessly against their own vitals, he clung inseparably to the court of his brother-in-law. Brought up among the household youths, he grew up and won the familiar friendship of the wise and powerful king. From him he received splendid arms of knighthood and, enriched with many gifts, took his place among the chief magnates at his court. He also married the daughter of Count Waltheof and of Judith, the king’s cousin, and obtained the two earldoms of Northampton and Huntingdon, which Count Simon of Senlis had held with the aforesaid woman. She bore him a son named Henry and two daughters, Clarice and Hodierna. But a wretched cleric cruelly killed David’s first male child, while still young, with iron fingers. Because of an unheard-of crime which he had committed at Norwich, he had been punished by the loss of his eyes and the cutting off of his feet and hands. For, while a certain priest was celebrating Mass, after the reception of the sacrament and after the people had departed, this man struck him violently in the belly with a great knife and, horribly spilling his entrails, slaughtered him upon the altar. Later, received in England by Count David for the love of God and sufficiently maintained in food and clothing, together with a little daughter, this man—using iron fingers because he was maimed—savagely stabbed the two-year-old son of his benefactor while pretending to caress him, and so, at the devil’s instigation, unexpectedly spilled the infant’s entrails in the nurse’s arms. Thus David’s first child was killed. The criminal was therefore tied to the tails of four unbroken horses, which pulled violently in different directions and tore him apart as a terror to evildoers.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1125, Alexander, king of the Scots, departed this life, and his brother David assumed the reins of the kingdom. Melcofus, Alexander’s illegitimate son, sought to wrest the kingdom from his uncle and stirred up against him two very fierce wars. But David, who was superior in intelligence, power, and wealth, overcame him and his followers.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1130, while King David was cautiously examining a judicial proceeding at the court of King Henry and diligently investigating the charge of treachery which Geoffrey de Clinton, as they say, had committed against the king, Angus, earl of Moray, entered Scotland with Melcolf and five thousand armed men and sought to subdue the whole region. Edward, son of Siward, who had been earl of the Mercians under King Edward, commander of the army, and cousin of King David, gathered an army and suddenly met the hostile host. At last, battle having been joined, Angus slew the earl and overthrew, captured, and routed his troops.

[Note: [Col. 0621D] Read “Angus.” Le Prévost.]

Then, with his companies already exalted by victory, he eagerly pursued the fugitives and entered Moray, bereft of defender and lord, obtaining, with God’s help, the entire lordship of that extensive region. Thus David, his power enlarged, was exalted above his predecessors; and through his zeal the realm of the Scots was adorned with religious and learned persons.

Behold, on account of the Scots, who from ancient times adhered to the Catholic faith and gladly served Christian simplicity, I have prolonged somewhat the resumed thread of my narrative. But now I strive to return to the intended work concerning our own people.

## XXI. Conspiracies formed in England against William Rufus.

Many Normans, enriched in England by wealth acquired through the labour of others, became excessively swollen with pride; they were intensely goaded by the troublesome unrest of burning greed and arrogance. For they envied and resented the fact that William Rufus flourished especially in boldness and prowess, feared no one, and ruled all his subjects harshly. The arrogant men therefore gathered together and formed a wicked conspiracy against the king; forgetful of the faith which they had promised their lord, they basely fell into the crime of treason.

Robert, son of Roger de Mowbray, was very powerful in influence and wealth. Proud in his boldness and military ferocity, he despised his equals and, puffed up by vain haughtiness, considered it beneath him to obey his superiors. He was large-bodied, strong, dark, and hairy; bold and deceitful, with a grave and stern expression. He made a practice of thinking more than speaking and scarcely ever laughed in conversation. He possessed two hundred and eighty estates in England, which King William the Great had given to Geoffrey, bishop of Coutances. For that bishop was distinguished by noble birth and excelled more in military skill than in clerical learning; he therefore knew better how to train armoured soldiers for war than vested clerics for chanting. Accordingly, he often took part in battles against Danes and Englishmen and acquired great possessions by the subjugation of enemies; at his death he left them to Robert, his nephew, earl of Northumbria.

Robert, wishing to extend his borders in every direction and, strengthened through his alliance with powerful men joined to him by kinship among his wealthiest companions, to attempt great enterprises, married Matilda, a high-born maiden, daughter of Richard de l’Aigle. She was the niece, through a sister named Judith, of Hugh, earl of Chester. Robert was the first to adopt this vain scheme with his accomplices, and began open rebellion as follows. Four great ships, called *Canardos*, arrived in England from Norway. Robert, his nephew Morel, and their followers met them and violently took from the peaceful merchants all that they possessed. Having lost their goods, the merchants came to the king and tearfully set forth their harsh complaint. He immediately commanded Robert imperiously to restore without delay what had been taken from the merchants. But this command was wholly disregarded. The magnanimous king inquired into the value of what they had lost and restored everything to them from his own treasury.

He then summoned Robert to his court, but Robert refused to come. The king, perceiving the wickedness of the fierce man, assembled an army and led a strong military force against him. At last, as the king approached Robert’s territory, Gilbert de Tonbridge, a powerful and wealthy knight, called the king aside, fell prostrate at his feet, and said to him, who was greatly astonished:

> “I beseech you, my lord king, forgive my offence, and I shall disclose to you a matter of great benefit for your safety.”

As the king marvelled, hesitated, and deliberated somewhat within himself, he finally pardoned the suppliant graciously and eagerly awaited what had been promised. Gilbert said:

> “Stay your step, noble king, I pray, and do not enter this forest before us. Enemies await there, armed and ready, who are now trying to attack you. We have made a conspiracy against you and devised your death under oath.”

Hearing this, the king halted and, as the aforesaid baron pointed them out, learned both the fact and the identities of the traitors.

Thus the assassins who had planned to kill the king were thwarted; the armed companies safely passed through the places of ambush and besieged the very strongly fortified castle called Bamburgh. Since that stronghold was impregnable, seeming inaccessible because it was surrounded by marshes, waters, and other obstacles to travellers, the king built a new fortress for the defence of the province and the confinement of the enemy, and filled it with soldiers, arms, and provisions. Those conscious of the treason, and their supporters, fearing exposure, fell silent; bloodless with fear because they perceived that their plans had come to nothing, they mingled with the king’s companies and eagerly undertook the service of him whose death they had desired.

Meanwhile, while the king stood armed with his troops ready for war and compelled commanders of thousands and hundreds, other magnates of Albion, and the peoples subject to them to labour without ceasing on the new fortification, Robert sadly watched the opposing work from his own battlements. He loudly called his accomplices by name and openly reminded them to keep the oath of their fellowship in treason. The king and his faithful men, hearing this, laughed; but the guilty mind, aware that its crime had been publicly exposed, tortured those who knew of it and shared in it with fear and shame. When the king had successfully returned to his own affairs and was diligently discussing the governance of the realm with his friends, Robert, sickened by the weariness of the long siege, leapt out by night. Wishing to move from castle to castle, he fell into the hands of his enemies. Captured by the king’s retainers, Robert brought the war to an end; he lived in chains for almost thirty years and there grew old, paying the penalty for his crimes.

His wife Matilda, who had scarcely ever been happy with him because she had been married at a time of disturbance and had lain trembling in her husband’s bed for only three months amid the disasters of war, was quickly deprived of marital comfort and, afflicted with many sorrows, grieved for a long time.

Her husband, as has been said, lived in prison. While he was alive, she could not lawfully marry another according to God’s law. At length, with the permission of Pope Paschal, to whom the matter, examined closely by inquisitive persons, had become known, Nigel de Aubigny took her as his wife after many days and for some time held her honourably out of regard for her noble family. But after Gilbert de l’Aigle, her brother, had died, the crafty man sought an occasion for divorce and repudiated her, because she had been the wife of his kinsman; he married Gundreda, sister of Hugh de Gournay.

[Note: [Col. 0623D]]

The following genealogy, copied from the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, declares who and how great this Nigel de Aubigny was:

> “Roger de Mowbray,” says the author, “who founded the abbey of Byland, did not bear the surname of his father Nigel de Aubigny. In the time of King Henry, son of William the Bastard, after he had obtained England while his brother Robert Curthose was active in the regions of Jerusalem, there were two valiant brothers of the king’s household: one was earl of Clare, the other earl of Arundel; and their third brother was Nigel de Aubigny, then a young man of good disposition and great promise, bearer of the king’s bow. When he had been made a knight, King Henry, because of his merit, first enfeoffed him with Egmanton in his forest, with its parks and appurtenances. Soon afterward Nigel gave that estate to Robert de Ayvile. When the king heard this and asked Nigel whether it was so, he answered that it was, and that the king now had two worthy knights where he had previously had only one. The king approved the act and enfeoffed him with the vavasories of Cauvil and Wivil.
>
> “Moreover, when Robert Curthose returned from Syria and learned that his brother King William Rufus had died, he wished to be crowned king but found his brother Henry crowned. In the course of time he resolved to fight Henry at Tinchebray in Normandy, where Nigel de Aubigny killed Robert Curthose’s charger and thus delivered him captured to King Henry. Then King Henry enfeoffed Nigel with the whole English land of Robert de Frontboeuf, who had deserted the king and gone over to Robert Curthose.
>
> “At that time Nigel married the daughter of Hugh de Gournay in Normandy, named Gundreda, who was the foundress of Byland Abbey. Afterwards the same King Henry besieged a castle in the overseas regions, which Nigel de Aubigny, entering first, captured. The king then proposed to enrich him further and gave him all the Norman lands of Roger de Mowbray—this Roger being earl of Northumbria—and immediately granted him seisin of Mowbray Castle, the Castle of Bayeux, and the castle of Caen, with their great possessions and appurtenances. Nigel then had one hundred and twenty enfeoffed knights in Normandy and one hundred and forty in England. When he had received the lord king’s writ to take seisin in the earldom of Northumbria and had begun his journey, he fell ill at Rouen. Shortly afterwards he died and was buried at Rouen in Normandy. When King Henry gave the said Nigel the land of Roger de Mowbray, he commanded that Nigel’s son and heir should bear the surname Mowbray.
>
> “The son and heir of the said Nigel de Aubigny was Roger de Mowbray, who founded Byland Abbey and several other holy places. Marked with the cross, he went to the Holy Land; captured by the Saracens, he was ransomed by the Knights Templar, and died in the Holy Land, being buried at Sures. Roger de Mowbray’s first-born son was Nigel de Mowbray, who succeeded him. This Nigel married Mabel and begot by her four sons: William, Robert, Philip, and Roger. Later this same Nigel, marked with the cross, died in the Greek Sea, thrown into the sea in a cask containing [an account of] what sort of man he had been. William, the first-born and heir, … begot Nigel and Roger. Nigel married the daughter of Roger de Caneville, died at Nantes without an heir, and was buried at Neufbourg, etc.” (*Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 775.) Dom Bouquet, vol. VIII, p. 653.

Morel, however, with his lord cast into indissoluble chains, fled sorrowfully from England. Wandering through many regions, he grew old poor and hated in exile.

Elated by the trophy won over the rebels, the king rewarded his friends, dealt with the factious, and punished the convicted in various ways. He expelled Roger de Lacy from England, utterly disinherited, and gave his inheritance to Hugh, Roger’s brother, who had faithfully served justice. He privately rebuked Hugh, earl of Shrewsbury, and, having received from him three thousand pounds, craftily received him into friendship. In like manner he punished many others by accepting great sums of money; out of respect for their noble kinsmen, who might repay retaliation in Normandy, he prudently concealed his intentions. William of Eu was then openly convicted of wickedness; the king deprived him of his eyes and emasculated him by cutting off his testicles. He suffered this at the instigation of Hugh, earl of Chester, whose sister he had married but to whom he had not kept due faith, since he had begotten three children by a concubine beside her.

Counts and men of consular rank were aware of, and were instigators of, the detestable conspiracy. But when the evil conspiracy had been detected, they were ashamed as they reflected upon many things among themselves; and, with their most powerful member broken, they became quiet, lest they too should be shaken in the same fashion. The king learned this carefully and, on the advice of the wise, spared such men. He did not publicly summon them to judgment, lest their fury should increase for the worse, and they should again be roused into a general attack upon the commonwealth, whence many losses, destruction, and public grief might be produced for many.

## XXII. Discords and private wars among the magnates of Normandy.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1094, the attempt of the rebels in England was suppressed, and the powerful William, with no one resisting, was established in his father’s kingdom.
