But Normandy, its inhabitants everywhere terrified and disturbed, was miserably troubled; and Duke Robert, while seditions raged fiercely, became contemptible because of his softness. Then an excessive war arose between William of Breteuil and Ascelin Goël. Its occasion was as follows. William, Goël’s brother, a young knight, committed an injury against a certain woman at Pacy. When she complained, William of Breteuil, as befitted a just lord, enforced lawful justice against the contumacious young man. Ascelin therefore became angry at his lord because he compelled his brother to plead publicly. Not long after, by ingenious fraud, he stole from him the castle of Ivry and handed it over to Robert, duke of the Normans; William redeemed it from Robert by the payment of a great weight of silver. Afterwards a savage feud raged between them over this theft, and each desired to harm the other.

In February [1092], Ascelin enlisted Richard de Montfort and the household of King Philip, and boldly received William, his lord, as he came against him to battle. He defeated and captured him and routed his army, taking some knights captive. Exalted by this victory, he became excessively arrogant and cruelly tortured his lord, Roger de Glos, and others whom he had captured. For three months he confined them in prison in the castle of Bréval; and often, while a severe winter raged, he exposed them at the window of a high hall to the north wind or the northwest wind, clothed only in shirts soaked abundantly with water, until every garment around the prisoners’ bodies stiffened into a single mass of ice. At length, friends intervened and peace was made between them, upon the following terms: William was allowed to leave prison; he gave his daughter Isabel to Goël as wife; he paid three thousand pounds, with horses, arms, and many other expenses; and he promised the castle of Ivry. When these matters had been arranged, William was free. But the peace which they had made lasted only a little while.

In the following year William, goaded by restlessness, renewed the war and stationed his soldiers in a fortification within the monastery of monks which Roger of Ivry had built in honour of Saint Mary. Goël, who held the castle, hired a force of knights, approached the monastery—which had then, alas, become a den of robbers—and during the torrid heat of summer around Pentecost attacked fiercely, set fire to it, and consumed in devouring flames the basilica and the monks’ buildings, with their furnishings. William Alis, Ernald son of Popelina, and eight other knights were then captured, and for a long time experienced all too keenly Goël’s cruelty in his prison. William of Breteuil barely escaped by flight and desired with his utmost effort vengeance for such great injuries. The wealthy lord, inwardly pierced by excessive grief, was angry that his man was advancing against him with such force and that for three years his strength had been greatly increased through ransoms of captives and the plundering of peasants. At last he pledged seven hundred pounds to Philip, king of the French, and promised Duke Robert of Normandy and many others a great sum of money if they would faithfully assist him and subdue the hostile forces.

Accordingly, in Lent [1094], the king of France and the duke of Normandy besieged Bréval, labouring there for almost two months. Priests came there with their parishioners bearing banners, and abbots were compelled to gather there with their men. Robert of Bellême brought there a most ingenious engineer, whose inventive skill had aided the Christians in taking Jerusalem. He constructed engines, moved them on wheels against the enemy fortification, hurled great stones into the town and upon its inhabitants, and taught the warriors to make assaults by which they destroyed the enclosing rampart and palisade and threw the roofs of houses down upon those dwelling within. By such great calamities he compelled the adversaries to surrender.

An old hatred between Robert and Goël had long grown strong because of ancient offences. When this Robert saw an opportune time for vengeance, he aided William of Breteuil with counsel and assistance more than all his other peers. Goël, however, was capable and shrewd, but a wicked robber and violator of churches. He had noble and high-spirited kinsmen; with their assistance he had fortified Bréval, a castle in a wild and wooded region, and by courage and supplies had vigorously endured such great burdens of war. At last, seeing such great and spirited princes most vehemently opposed to him, he sought peace from his lord and father-in-law and obtained it, to William’s joy. He then honourably restored the castle of Ivry to him, after kings and dukes had long been harassed.

This is the famous tower, huge and most strongly fortified, which Albereda, wife of Ralph, count of Bayeux, built; and which Hugh, bishop of Bayeux, brother of John, archbishop of Rouen, held for a long time against the dukes of Normandy. They relate that, after the aforesaid lady had completed the oft-mentioned castle with much labour and expense, she caused Lanfred the architect to be beheaded, lest he should build a similar work anywhere else. His inventive genius was praised above all craftsmen then in Gaul, and after constructing the tower of Peverel he had been master of this work. At last she herself was killed by her husband because she had also attempted to keep him away from that fortification. Behold how fickle fortune is daily turned, and how the condition of the world is variously stirred. He is exceedingly foolish and blinded who continually sees such things and is not corrected, but trusts in that which quickly falls. One mortal drives another into death, and in the same course follows him whom he has sent beforehand to destruction; and, alas, deservedly loses the power to aid himself or others.

Once peace had been made between the contending adversaries, to the joy of many, Robert of Bellême alone was greatly angered, because he had not been invited to the council of peace, lest he impede it—he who had been foremost in directing the military preparations for the defeat and humiliation of that fierce and insolent enemy. For Robert’s cunning and strength surpassed and overawed all others; by marvellous stratagems he terrified that notorious brigand, formidable alike in intellect and warfare, whom kings and dukes had previously been unable to restrain from laughter as he sported in his stronghold and mocked his enemies with many wiles. [Col. 0628C]

At last, when the aforesaid knight learned that concord had been made between the discordant parties, he immediately summoned his troops, revealed his heart’s treachery to no one, hurried back, and suddenly swooped down upon Saint-Céneri against Robert Géroie. The inhabitants, believing that Robert was away on the general expedition with the duke, had gone out and were wandering freely and confidently, each as he pleased, through the fields. When the crafty ambusher suddenly attacked with his forces, striving to enter the town and bring its garrison under his control, Géroie, by God’s prompting, forestalled the hostile assault, quickly entered the fortification with his men, and Robert of Bellême grieved that his desire to seize the castle had been frustrated. He then turned to plunder, killed one knight, and inflicted very great damage. Thus his wickedness and deceit were exposed, and open war began thereafter. Géroie had Geoffrey of Moulins, William of Sillé, and many other helpers; and for three months he devastated the whole district around Alençon. Henry, son of William the Great, king of the English, held Domfront and made war against Robert, from whom he had taken that castle—indeed, against his own brothers, the king and the duke, by whom he had been expelled as an exile from his paternal inheritance.

At the beginning of July [1094], Robert Géroie made an expedition with Henry’s household and his other companions-in-arms; having taken immense booty, he began to pursue the enemy with his forces. While [Col. 0629A] Géroie was escorting his allies as they hastened homeward, and was going farther on in cheerful conversation with acquaintances and friends, a report suddenly arose that he had been killed. Great grief immediately struck everyone, and a dreadful outcry resounded in the castle. The garrison turned pale and lost all counsel and manly courage. Pagan of Mondoubleau, Rotrou of Montfort, and other defenders of the castle therefore deserted; and, as some relate, in order to favour Robert of Bellême, they abandoned the castle without a defender, though no one compelled them. His wife Radegund, shaken by these dreadful reports, turned pale and resolved to await certainty of the matter in the castle with her people. But one woman could not defend what seemed good to her against insolent men. When they left the castle [Col. 0629B] and shouted shamelessly, Robert of Bellême, learning of this affair, immediately appeared, found the fortification empty of defenders, entered easily, thoroughly plundered it, and burned the remainder with flames.

Having entered the castle, they found cauldrons boiling over fires, full of meat; tables covered with cloths; and food laid out with bread upon them. The monks of Sées took the arm of Saint Céneri from the church and reverently transferred it to the monastery of Saint Martin. The rest of his body is preserved at Château-Thierry upon the river Marne and is reverently honoured by the French with celebrated devotion.

As Géroie was returning joyfully from his friends and vainly considering how again to inflict harm on his enemies, [Col. 0629C] he was unexpectedly crushed by adverse reports—for no mortal power endures long. Thus that noble knight was immediately disinherited and forced, as an exile, to seek the hospitality of strangers. In the same year his wife Radegund, an upright and honourable woman, died. Shortly afterwards she was followed in death by their son, the child William, whom Robert of Bellême had held as a hostage and, as they say, had destroyed by poison through the agency of Robert of Poilley. Géroie, then, afflicted by so many misfortunes, fled to his friends and sought help; strengthened by the consolation of relatives and friends, he raised his hope toward better things. In the following year [1095] he fortified a castle upon Montaigu and exercised the sharpest [Col. 0629D] vengeance against Robert of Bellême.

But Bellême, raging excessively, ran to the duke; by many complaints and promises he incited him and brought him with the army of Normandy to besiege Montaigu. Then Geoffrey of Moulins and other leading men of Maine approached the duke and gently entreated him on behalf of Géroie, their kinsman. Since the duke was readily moved to mercy, they immediately obtained from him that the castle, which had [Col. 0630A] recently been built, should be demolished and Géroie’s entire inheritance restored to him in peace. And so it was done. As serenity returns after an excessive storm and gladdens men, so divine justice often chastises the guilty; merciful goodness relieves the afflicted, justifies the penitent, and piously rewards those who have been purified.

Géroie, instructed by many calamities, therefore gave thanks to God, by whose aid he recovered his former honour after many struggles. For almost thirty years thereafter he spent his life amid joys and sorrows. He took as wife Felicia, daughter of Guarnier of Connerré, who bore three sons and as many daughters: William, Robert, and Matthew; Agatha, Dameta, and Avelina.

## XXIII. Robert of Bellême harasses the monks of Ouche

[Col. 0630B]

The knight of Bellême strove with all his might to destroy the new castle and compelled the peasants throughout all his jurisdiction and neighbourhood to forced labour for the work of its projected demolition. Since the men of Saint Evroul had not come to destroy the castle—for they were by no means obliged to submit to his authority—he swelled violently against the monks and for one year inflicted enormous damage upon them. He forcibly compelled the men of the holy father Evroul to work on his own castles. He seized the goods of those who fled and cruelly threatened that he would destroy the monastery itself unless they surrendered themselves wholly to him in every respect as to their lord. Finally, his madness grew to such a degree that nearly all [Col. 0630C] ecclesiastical possessions in the neighbourhood were ravaged by his violence.

Accordingly the cloistered monks were pressed by severe want, and Abbot Roger was compelled to seek assistance in England from King William for the needs of the destitute, whose necessary food had been taken away by the tyrant’s devastation. He cruelly threatened other servants of God who were subject to him or in his vicinity, and often afflicted them mercilessly with many injuries and troubles. The people of Sées and Troarn attest this, as do those of Maine, who frequently turned pale in grieving anger and sorrow because of his cruelty and unjust exactions.

Robert also oppressed the bishopric of Sées contrary to law and right; he claimed that it had been given by Duke Richard to his grandfather William of Bellême, and he heavily burdened ecclesiastical properties with many oppressions and losses. Therefore the venerable Bishop Serlo excommunicated him and, with episcopal rigor, placed all his land under interdict: no divine office was to be celebrated there, nor were bodies of the dead to be buried.

> **Note:** [Col. 0629D] We learn from Letter 120 of Ivo of Chartres that he did not wholly approve such a censure: “If divine service has unjustly been forbidden you by the bishop of Sées, it displeases me, both on account of him who acts and of him who suffers. But since I ought not to do to my neighbour what I should not wish him to do to me, [Col. 0630D] do not wonder if, for the present, you do not receive the chrism which you request from us. For it is an ecclesiastical law that those who have been interdicted or excommunicated by one church are not received by another.” Dom Bouquet, book VIII, p. 656.

Robert, who because of his hardness was rightly called Talvas, [Col. 0631A] was hardened like Pharaoh. Episcopal blows or ointments did not soften him; instead he increased daily, abominably, in every wickedness. Like Ishmael, he fiercely raised armed hands against all his neighbours; he terrified monks, clerics, and the unarmed populace by savage tyranny, and miserably afflicted them with frequent losses and insults. In those times the chief ecclesiastical censure could not prevail over him, because secular power exalted him too greatly and the monstrous enormity of his character made him intolerable to relatives, friends, and dependants.

He made little of disfiguring people by depriving them of their eyes or cutting off feet or hands. Rather, like the Sicilian Phalaris, he delighted in devising unheard-of tortures for the suffering. [Col. 0631B] Those whom he confined in prison for some offence he tortured indescribably—more cruel than Nero, Decius, or Diocletian—and from this he boastfully made jokes and raised laughter with his parasites. He gloried in the pleasure of the tortures he inflicted on prisoners; because of the extremity of the punishments, he cruelly rejoiced in the mutilation of men. He preferred inflicting torments upon wretches to increasing his wealth by ransom for captives. Yet, with God’s aid, many often escaped from his bonds and afterwards vigorously avenged their wrongs—persons from whom, had he been touched by human reason and mercy, he might have received great tribute and honourable service.

Terrible to many, he feared many; because the pricking of conscience made him suspect a great number, he laboured anxiously in troubles night and day and scarcely believed anyone faithful to him. He was indeed a great and very fierce warrior, endowed with intelligence and eloquence as well as strength. But by excessive pride and cruelty he polluted everything, and by a wicked accumulation of crimes darkened the gifts divinely bestowed upon him. Through insolence and greed he began many wars against his neighbours, but was often defeated and fled with loss and dishonour.

The men of Corbon and Maine knew this well; so did the neighbouring Normans and the nearby men of Hiémois, who became victors when the tyrant fled. Geoffrey, count of Mortain, and his son Rotrou experienced it happily; so also did Elias of Maine and other [Col. 0631D] neighbours, against whom he always devised hostile injuries but who, by God’s judgment, justly made him suffer harder things. He possessed thirty-four very strongly fortified castles and held lordship over many thousands of people. Yet Hugh of Nonant, a poor townsman and neighbour, resisted him for many years and frequently inflicted immense losses and injuries upon him.

He had as wife Agnes, daughter of Guy, count of Ponthieu; she bore William Talvas, heir to all his honour. The savage husband did not honour his noble wife, as he should have done, for the sake of their beloved [Col. 0632A] child; rather, he afflicted her with many troubles as if she were a hated slave. Indeed, for a long time he consigned her to confinement in the castle of Bellême, as though she were a robber. At last, rescued through the help and resourcefulness of a faithful chamberlain, she secretly escaped from prison, fled to Adela, countess of Chartres, and thence withdrew to Ponthieu, never to return to the tyrant.

Through the dreadful enterprises and evasions of this aforesaid butcher, Neustria was often disturbed, and the region of Maine and the surrounding country were grievously ravaged with plunder, slaughter, and fire. Bishoprics and monasteries cried out against him to the Lord of Hosts, in whose lands castles had been forcibly planted and the possessions of the saints diminished or despoiled by his rash invasion. But the monks of Ouche, after many losses, labours, and fears, could not bear his warfare. Therefore, compelled to do so, they granted him throughout all their land—which until then had been free from evil customs—and gave Robert sixty pounds of Mans money from the rent of the peasants, so that he should no longer harass the monastery and its settlers, but should permit the worshippers of God to rejoice in peace through lawful *theosebia* (“godliness”). Other monks and unarmed clerics likewise ransomed themselves for a similar price; at great expense they appeased the raging tyrant, because at that time kings and dukes refused to restrain his immense cruelty by their chief jurisdiction for the peace of the churches.

## XXIV. The religious life and death of certain knights. Of Anfrid, first abbot of Préaux. Abbots, prelates, and monks illustrious in virtue and learning

[Col. 0632C]

In those days the ancient nobles who had served under Duke Robert or his son, King William, put off the human being in the manner of human mortality. Roger of Montgomery devoutly took the monastic habit at Shrewsbury and remained for three days in divine conversation and prayer among the servants of God in the basilica of Saint Peter the Apostle, which he had founded outside the city between the two rivers Meole and Severn. At last, on the sixth day before the Kalends of August, he died and was buried in the basilica of Saint Peter, after his son Hugh of Montgomery [Col. 0632D] had become earl in England and Robert of Bellême had acquired all his father’s honour in Normandy.

> **Note:** [Col. 0631D] In the year 1075, according to Le Prévost.

Moreover, Roger of Poitou, Arnulf, Philip, and Everard received nothing of their paternal inheritance, because the two elder sons, Robert and Hugh, as stated above, held all their father’s rights on this side of the sea and beyond it. Yet Roger and Arnulf, who enjoyed distinction among their comrades in arms by their military and personal merit, took noble wives by their father’s counsel and through their own management.

> **Note:** [Col. 0631D] Roger, having married Almodis, sister and heiress of Boso III, count of La Marche, who died in 1091, first established his seat at Charroux in Poitou and was thence surnamed “of Poitou.” Summoned afterwards to England by King William II, he obtained the earldom of Lancaster there. This occurred no later than 1094, as is clear from the following charter transcribed by Aegidius Bry in his *History of the Counties of Alençon and Perche*, p. 83: “Let all know . . . that Count Roger, surnamed of Poitou, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1094, for the souls of himself, his predecessors, and his successors, gave in alms to the Lord God and Saint Martin, and to the brethren dwelling now and hereafter in the monastery of Sées . . . the church of Lancaster with all things belonging to it.” Afterwards Henry I, brother and successor of William, deprived him of his honours and expelled him from England for rebellion in 1102; he returned with his wife to Aquitaine. Arnulf, however, having been made earl of Pembroke, married Lafracot, daughter of the king of Ireland. For this reason, after his father-in-law’s death, he sought the kingdom of Ireland, though with unsuccessful efforts. Dom Bouquet, book VIII, p. 657.

Both became counts and flourished for a while, strong in power and wealth. But before [Col. 0633A] death they lost the honours they had acquired because of their treachery. Philip and Everard, however, applied themselves variously to the study of letters and to the course of their declining life from childhood [reading uncertain].

> **Note:** [Col. 0634D] A corrupt passage, scarcely intelligible even if *peritia* (“skill”) is accepted in place of *pueritia* (“childhood”), as the learned A. Le Prévost proposes.

Philip went abroad with Duke Robert and died at Antioch. Everard, who was born of Countess Adelaide, performed a modest clerical office in the chapel of King Henry.

Roger of Beaumont also, a wise and moderate nobleman who had always been faithful to his lords, the dukes of Normandy, submitted his neck to monastic life at the monastery of Préaux after completing his military service. His father, Humphrey of the Vieilles, had founded that monastery on his own estate; and Roger himself, after his father’s death, had enriched it with many properties and ornaments. There [Col. 0633B] lies buried Robert of Beaumont, son of Humphrey, whom Roger de Clare killed; and Roger himself, his brother, already an old man, rested there after some years of conversion, with a good end.

He left his sons Robert and Henry as invested heirs of his honour, and God’s grace greatly exalted them in this world. They were distinguished by friendship and intimacy with kings and powerful counts; enriched by noble and eloquent wives, notable offspring of both sexes, and abundant wealth together with honours. Robert held by hereditary right, after Hugh—the brother of his mother Adeline—the county of Meulan in the Vexin; and by King Henry’s gift he happily obtained the earldom of Leicester in England, together with many other estates and treasures. [Col. 0633C] His brother Henry, through his own energy and lawful conduct, earned the earldom of Warwick and took as wife the elegant Margaret, daughter of Geoffrey, count of Mortain. The fame of her piety and integrity is celebrated and widely proclaimed in the neighbouring regions among the foremost women. She bore her husband Roger and Robert of Neubourg, whose eminence shone especially in England and Neustria during King Henry’s reign.

The aforesaid counts lawfully loved and generously endowed the monastery of Préaux, which their ancestors had built in a most favourable place near the seaport and Pont-Audemer, where the Risle swiftly seeks the sea. [Col. 0633D] There monks were called by God to the praise and worship of almighty God and were piously instructed in regular discipline by devout and wise teachers.

The epitaph shining in the cloister above his tomb, by the door of the basilica on the south side, clearly shows to those who look upon it who and how great was Anfrid, first abbot of the church of Préaux:

> Behold, beneath this tomb lies buried a dove without gall,  
> Abbot Anfrid, a good and pious man.  
> Ever watchful, he fulfilled what the divine law commanded—  
> That law which was his counsel and his pursuit.  
> For the weak, the uncertain, the blind, the lame, and pilgrims,  
> He was shelter, foot, eyes, counsel, and staff.  
> When he died, Phoebus had for thirty days  
> Scorched the fishes. May God grant him rest.

Richard of Fourneaux governed that same monastery in more recent times. Robert of Tombelaine had received him into monastic life at Bayeux, in the church of Saint Vigor. But while Bishop Odo, founder of the new monastery, languished in King William’s prison, and Robert the scholar returned to Mont-Saint-Michel [Col. 0634B] of the Peril of the Sea, whence he had been a monk—or rather migrated to the regions of Latium, as I have related above—the new and unfinished foundation was quickly destroyed, and the assembly of faithful people that had flocked there from various places was soon dispersed for want of a leader.

Richard, one of their number, was exceedingly learned in sacred letters. Amid that great devastation of the tender flock, he sought religious scholars, in whose fellowship he dwelt reverently, adhering to wholesome teachings. At that time Anselm of Bec, Gerbert of Fontenelle, Gontard of Jumièges, and many others flourished in Normandy, shining lamps in the temple of God. Greatly enlightened by them, he drank in the abundant nourishment of salutary teaching.

After the death of Abbot Geoffrey, Richard was chosen to govern the abbey of Préaux. He held it for almost twenty-four years during the time of Duke Robert and King Henry and died there. [Col. 0634C] He applied himself especially to the sacred books, ran from youth in the way of God, chanting as he followed in the footsteps of the ancient Fathers, kindly broke the enigmatic bread in the house of the Lord for hungry boys, liberally and cheerfully distributed to those who stretched out their hands, and even compelled the sluggish and reluctant to eat.

He produced a commentary on Genesis for Maurice, the most learned abbot of Saint-Laumer at Blois, and wrote another for Lord Adelelm, a most learned priest and monk of Flavigny, who grew old in reverent service to the Holy Trinity with the monks of Fécamp. For Pons, distinguished abbot of Cluny, he composed an excellent exposition of Solomon’s Proverbs. For other venerable persons he lucidly expounded Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, and Deuteronomy, and wrote many treatises explaining allegorically or tropologically the obscure [Col. 0635A] problems of the prophets.

Nicholas, deacon and abbot of the holy bishop Audoen, was son of Richard III, duke of Normandy. He flourished in great kindness, charity, and other virtues, and shone conspicuously in the Church of God until the fourth year after the death of King William, his cousin. At the urging of Duke Robert, his uncle, he became a monk as a boy in the monastery of Fécamp under Abbot John. After some years, however, Duke William appointed him, while still young, to rule the aforesaid abbey. Once placed in authority, he strove to benefit those subject to him, both within and without, rather than merely to rule them.

After returning from worshipping at the Lord’s tomb in Jerusalem, he died in the fifty-sixth year of his rule, on the fourth day before the Kalends of March. He was buried before the altar of Saint Mary, Mother of God, in the church of Saint Peter the Apostle, which he had begun from the foundations; there he awaits a better state in the resurrection. Above him shines a structure made of beautifully painted wood, upon whose summit the monk Maurice elegantly inscribed in golden letters this epitaph:

> Here love and piety, the flower and honour of monks—  
> Nicholas—having laid aside his body, lives for the Lord.  
> He ruled his flock in love; he built the church you behold.  
> This light set when Phoebus scorched the fishes.

Helgot, prior of Caen, eminent in learning and the practice of virtues, succeeded the venerable Nicholas and held the governance of the abbey of Saint Audoen for almost twenty years. [Col. 0635C] In his time the community of that church increased commendably in number and religious discipline. Then a certain layman, Gilbert, came from Jerusalem to Rouen; received into monastic life by the aforesaid father, he served his church worthily. He undertook the work of the basilica, long since interrupted despite its marvellous scale. There he spent liberally the money of his lady Alberada the Fat, who, dying in the way of the Lord, had entrusted her treasure to him; aided also by contributions from other faithful persons, he laboured to complete the notable work.

When Abbot Helgot died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December and was buried before the altar of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, situated in the vestibule on the north [Col. 0635D] side, William of Balot, a monk of the same church from childhood, succeeded him in office and governed for almost fourteen years. During his time, the huge basilica once begun by Nicholas was completed only with difficulty after sixty years and was dedicated by Archbishop Geoffrey, with many other prelates and subjects, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November.

In the same year [1126], Abbot William died and Ragemfrid, a monk of the same church, assumed government. In his time the cloister, together with other monastic buildings, was completed and particularly distinguished. Then Fulbert, archdeacon and dean of Rouen, fell ill and devoutly took the monastic habit. On his death he was buried in the cloister of Saint Audoen before the chapter house and fittingly covered with a white stone. The inscription engraved there declares what manner of man he was:

> Glory of the metropolis, ornament and crown of the clergy,  
> In your death, Fulbert, fell. There fell the deep  
> Wisdom of an inexhaustible spring, an eloquent tongue.  
> This man was archdeacon of the metropolitan church,  
> First a canon, last a monk.  
> It was the fourth day before that day on which Christ,  
> Born of the holy Virgin, shone upon the world, when so great  
> A pillar of the Church fell—second to none in piety.

At the blessed departure of fathers who pass away in Christ, the pious love of their children mourns upon earth. Though it confidently hopes that they ascend to the heavenly kingdom, it nevertheless affectionately laments their absence, fearing the excessive desolation of those who remain here in exile. Yet divine mercy often visits its Church and consoles it by the invisible action of its sweetness, lest it fail on the way; daily it strengthens the Church for struggle by sending strong champions. Hence the Prophet says: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you” (Psalm 44:17).

When the apostles flew beyond the stars, apostolic teachers succeeded them, shining in word and deed as they stood in the courts of Jerusalem; to this day they offer God acceptable fruits of their labours. Behold: while wickedness abounds in the world, the devotion of the faithful grows more abundantly in religious life, and the multiplied harvest rises in the Lord’s field. Monasteries are built everywhere in woods and open country, and bands of hooded men, clothed in new observances and varied habits, travel through the world. They particularly use whiteness in their clothing, so that they may appear distinct from and conspicuous among others. [Col. 0636C]

In many passages of Holy Scripture blackness signifies humility; for this reason religious zeal has until now gladly worn that colour. But modern people reject the blackness used by the ancient Fathers—as a token of humility—both by regular clergy in capes and monks in cowls, as though to display a greater righteousness. They also seek to differ from others through an unfamiliar cut of their garments. Voluntary poverty, contempt for the world, and, in my opinion, true religion burn fervently in many of them; but many hypocrites and deceiving pretenders are mixed among them like tares among wheat. Pagan, canon of Chartres, surnamed Bolotinus, recently composed a fine poem in Adonic metre, [Col. 0636D] in which he subtly and copiously exposed the cloaked superstitions of these hypocrites.

## XXV. Concerning the new clothing of monks: how and by whom it was devised

In the present chronicle I now endeavour openly to explain how and by whom the recent alteration of the ancient habit first began to arise, because I think this will be pleasing to future readers.

In Burgundy there is a place called Molesme. Hence Rainald, bishop of Langres, said:

> “And, as it were, a baptism to those in love with Molesme.”

There, in the reign of Philip, king of the French, the venerable Abbot Robert founded a monastery. Inspired by the grace of the Holy Spirit, he gathered disciples of great religious devotion and kindly trained them in the pursuit of virtues and holy poverty, according to the practice of other monasteries. After some years, having carefully investigated the Rule of Saint Benedict and examined the teachings of other holy Fathers, he summoned the brothers and addressed them thus:

> “Dearest brothers, we have made profession according to the Rule of our holy father Benedict. But, as it seems to me, we do not keep it in its entirety. We observe many things not prescribed there, and, neglecting many of his commands, omit them. We do not labour with our hands, as we read that the holy Fathers did. If you do not believe me, friends, read the lives of the holy Anthony, Macarius, Pachomius, and, before all others, Paul the Apostle, teacher of the nations. We have abundant food and clothing from the tithes and offerings of churches, [Col. 0637B] and by craft or violence we take away things belonging to priests. Thus indeed we feed upon human blood and share in sins. I therefore urge that we observe the Rule of Saint Benedict completely, taking care not to turn aside from it either to the right or to the left. Let us obtain food and clothing by the labour of our hands. Let us abstain, in accordance with the Rule, from drawers, woollen undergarments, and furs. Let us leave tithes and offerings to the clerics who serve the diocese. And thus let us diligently labour to run after Christ in the footsteps of the Fathers.”

At these words the community of monks did not agree; rather, they set against these measured innovations the examples and institutions of their predecessors, whose lives had clearly shone with evident miracles, and the paths trodden by venerable men. [Col. 0637C] They said:

> “We have long observed, and earnestly desire to preserve until death with all our strength, the way of life in which the holy Fathers formerly lived religiously in Gaul, and whose holiness, pleasing to God, was attested by miracles both during their lives and after their burial, according to their rite and traditions. As to your rebuke, venerable Father, that we stray from the strictness of the monastic Rule and do not walk the harsh path of the Egyptian Fathers, who lived in the Thebaid and in the Holy Land among barbarians in ancient times, examine carefully by subtle inquiry the necessary reason for this.

> “No teacher rightly compels the faithful in a time of peace to endure all that holy martyrs were compelled to suffer in persecutions by pagans; for the martyrs themselves did not voluntarily undergo before the pressure of the impious the same things which they afterwards bore while struggling for the faith under necessity. The Lord plainly declared this to Peter when he said: ‘When you were younger, you girded yourself and walked where you wished; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish’ (John 21:18).

> “According to the commands of the divine law, consider wisely how fittingly you ought to guide in God’s way those who have freely converted from worldly wickedness and desire, under your instruction, to undertake a more upright life. On what ground can it be approved that you should forcibly drive those who voluntarily wish to change their own evil state into good to the hiding places of Paul or Anthony? For they fled from their ancestral homes, even out of fear of their parents, lest they be killed. A provident physician nurses a sick person with tempered medicine, lest, by tormenting him with the pain of an excessively harsh treatment, he seem to destroy the one whose cure he undertook. No prudent person lays an unbearable burden upon one who is weak, lest the weary bearer, crushed beneath the load, perish on the road.”

When the monks thus openly resisted, Abbot Robert said:

> “I mention the inimitable life of the Egyptian Fathers as an example for good; but no violent exaction is imposed upon you from it—rather, a wholesome persuasion is offered. Yet I invite you to keep in all things the Rule of Saint Benedict, which, according to what you have professed, I truly recognize that you violate in many respects. Therefore I fear the judgment of the heavenly Judge, lest in the dreadful judgment he rage against us for the guilt of transgression.”

In reply the monks said:

“Blessed Father Benedict, as is plainly evident to us all, sent the blessed Maurus, prior of his monastery, whom he had reared from childhood, into Gaul; and through him he sent to the Franks the book of the Rule which the man of God himself had written in his own hand, together with a pound of bread and a hemine of wine. Received there by King Theodebert, Maurus remained in Gaul until his death; and, with the assistance of Florus, a counsellor of the king, he built a monastery and there regularly trained one hundred and forty monks in the place called Glanifolium.

“But the discerning Father Maurus did not imitate the customs of the Egyptians, who are continually scorched by the excessive heat of the sun [Col. 0638C]; rather, with pious consideration, he took account of the practices of the Gauls, who often shiver in the wintry frost of the West, as he had beneficially learned from his spiritual master. For Saint Benedict says: ‘Let clothing be given to the brethren according to the nature of the places in which they live and the temperature of the air. Those in cold regions need more; those in warm regions, less. This consideration therefore belongs to the abbot.’ Thus likewise he prudently moderates and orders food and drink and every aspect of human life, so that all things may be done in measure on account of the weak, and without murmuring. He also most earnestly admonishes the abbot to consider the weakness of every person. He directs that such work or craft be assigned to sickly or delicate brethren [Col. 0638D] that they may neither be idle nor be crushed and broken by the force of their labour.

“Paul and Antony, and many others who first sought the wilderness and built monasteries for themselves in the remote places of the desert, were driven there, as has been said above, through fear of the pagans. They chose an exceedingly rigorous life and, through the cooperation of God’s grace, transformed necessity into willingness. Then, through the praiseworthy example they offered, the number of those renouncing the world grew greatly; and, according to differences of places and the varied customs of men, it proceeded under diverse observances. Yet, as Pope Gregory says, diversity of custom accomplishes nothing against the unity of the holy Church’s faith.

“A great part of mankind in warm regions does without breeches and wears loose, ankle-length tunics like women [Col. 0639A]. The body of monks descended from such people and dwelling among them does not reject but adopts their custom. But all peoples in the western climate wear breeches, and they know that they cannot do without them, both because of the cold and because of decency. For these reasons the same custom prevails in our order, and we do not wish to abandon what is useful and honourable. Thus concerning all other matters learned teachers who preceded us in the sacred habit have handed down reasonable grounds to us.

“In Italy, Palestine, and certain other regions olives are plentiful enough; enriched by their fruit, people do not need fat to season various foods. But this has mercifully been granted to us here, who lack the richness of oil. Because we do not daily labour with our hands, we are severely reproved by many [Col. 0639B]; but we confidently adduce the sincere labour of divine worship, which we learned long ago from authoritative masters proven by long observance of the divine law. King Dagobert, Theoderic, and Emperor Charlemagne, with other kings and emperors, devoutly founded monasteries. From their revenues they lavishly provided food and clothing for the servants of God; they subjected a multitude of dependants to perform external services fully; and they ordained that monks should devote themselves to reading, holy prayers for all their benefactors, and heavenly mysteries.

“Accordingly, by the institution of princes and longstanding custom, it has become customary in Gaul that peasants should perform rural labours, as is fitting [Col. 0639C], and servants should everywhere carry out servile duties; while monks, who of their own will have abandoned the vanities of this world and serve the King of kings, should sit quietly within the cloister’s enclosure like the king’s daughters; should seek out the secrets of sacred law by reading; should persevere delightfully in silence while continually meditating upon it; should restrain their mouths from corrupt and idle talk; should sing Davidic hymns and other mystical chants to the Creator night and day; and should apply themselves to other pure and fitting works to be performed daily, as reason requires, according to the precepts of their elders. Such, to this day, is the work usually done by monks in the West; and all without doubt know and attest that their pursuits ought to be of this kind.

“Far be it that peasants should languish in idleness, and, sated and wanton, should occupy themselves with laughter [Col. 0639D] and empty sport, when their natural lot has been assigned to continual labour. Yet excellent soldiers, subtle philosophers, and witty scholars, if they renounce the world, are compelled to occupy themselves with servile and unsuitable pursuits or labours, after the fashion of base slaves. Tithes of the faithful and offerings are granted by general authority to clergy and ministers of God for their own sustenance, as the Apostle Paul says to the Corinthians: ‘Those who minister in the sanctuary eat what belongs to the sanctuary; those who serve at the altar share with the altar’ (1 Cor. 9:13). Thus too the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live by the Gospel. We, moreover, are clergy both by order and office, and we offer clerical service to the supreme pontiff who has passed through the heavens, so that, with his aid, we may obtain the portion of the heavenly inheritance [Col. 0640A].

“Therefore we possess ecclesiastical benefices by right, and by common ordinance we determine always to retain them. Let this, O reverend Father, be unquestionably known to your holiness: we have learned from former cenobites, who lived religiously, that these things must be maintained, and we possess them as heirs of our order and profession. So long as the Cluniacs, the monks of Tours, and other regular men retain them, we shall not abandon them; nor do we wish, as rash inventors of novelties, to be condemned far and wide by our brethren.”

While the monks steadfastly said these things and much else of like kind, the abbot, sufficiently obstinate in his own opinion, withdrew from them with twelve who agreed with him. For a long time he sought a place suitable for himself and his companions, who [Col. 0640B] had resolved to observe the Rule of Saint Benedict in every respect literally, as the Jews observe the Law of Moses. At last Odo, son of Henry, duke of Burgundy, took pity on them and granted them an estate in the place called Cîteaux, in the diocese of Chalon. There Abbot Robert dwelt for some time in the wilderness with the chosen brethren and began to build a monastery of excessive strictness and religious observance. By God’s gift, he soon had many imitators of holiness.

When the cenobites of Molesme had for some time lacked a shepherd, and, after the departure of a man famous for the virtues of God, had become more contemptible in the eyes of neighbours and acquaintances, they humbly approached Pope Urban. Having laid before him the complete sequence of events which I have recounted above, they sought counsel and aid from him [Col. 0640C]. He, however, provided for both parties with fatherly affection. By apostolic authority he commanded the abbot to return to his former monastery and govern it according to the Rule, lest it should collapse; and in the other monastery, which he had begun later, to appoint in his place any suitable man from among his own followers. Then he established by firm decree that each man should first adopt whichever form of life he desired, and thereafter hold to it throughout all his life without contradiction.

Thus the prudent pope issued a useful decree upon this matter, saying:

“It must most carefully be guarded against that a dreadful schism should be fostered in the house of God, springing up and spreading to the harm of many; and likewise that a good thing, divinely inspired for the salvation of souls, should culpably be stifled. Therefore, in a salutary fatherly manner [Col. 0640D], we provide and by apostolic authority command that the monks of Molesme, who choose the general customs of monks, shall preserve them inviolate and shall no longer dare, after abandoning their own abode, to pass over to other observances. But the Cistercians, who boast that they will observe the Rule of Saint Benedict in all things, must never return—after falling back again—to those things which they now abandon through voluntary contempt. For stability in a community, and perseverance in every good work, must always be exalted and firmly maintained; since it is acceptable to the Creator, who requires the tail of the sacrificial victim in the offering, and fittingly pleasing to men, who, at the sight of an example of holiness, are incited to the summit of virtues.”

Accordingly, compelled to do so, Abbot Robert returned to Molesme [Col. 0641A], where he commendably served God until the end of his life. He chose Alberic, a man of great religious devotion, as his deputy for the work at Cîteaux; and he made him abbot of Cîteaux over John and Hilbod of Arras and twenty-two other brethren. Alberic lived there for ten years in great poverty and laboriously served God with his companions, from whom he confidently expected an inestimable reward.

After his death Stephen, an Englishman, a man of great religious devotion and wisdom, succeeded him, and held the office for more than twenty-four years, gloriously eminent in teaching and holy action. During his time the monastery in the wilderness grew in many ways. While Stephen was still alive and at his command, Guy was elected abbot of Trois-Fontaines; and not long afterward his venerable predecessor [Col. 0641B] died. Guy, however, for some time held in a blameworthy manner the paternal office he had assumed, and foolishly abandoned it after two years. Then the young man Renaud, son of Milo, count of Bar-sur-Seine, was elected and consecrated abbot by Walter, bishop of Chalon.

It is now nearly thirty-seven years since Abbot Robert, as has been said, settled at Cîteaux; and within so brief a time so great a multitude of men has flocked there that sixty-five abbeys have arisen from it, all subject, with their abbots, to the archimandrite of Cîteaux. All do without breeches and furs, abstain from fat and the eating of meat, and shine in the world with many good works, like lamps shining in a dark place. They practise silence at all times; they do not wear dyed garments; they labour with their own hands and secure their own food and clothing. Every day, except Sunday, they fast from the Ides of September until Easter. They keep their entrances closely barred and conceal their secrets most carefully. They admit no monk of another church into their inner precincts, nor permit him to enter their oratory with them for Mass or other services. Many noble champions and profound sophists have flocked to them because of the novelty of their distinctive way, and, willingly embracing an unfamiliar strictness, have joyfully sung hymns of gladness to Christ upon the straight way. In desert and woodland places they built monasteries by their own labour, and with thoughtful provision bestowed sacred names upon them [Col. 0641D], such as House of God, Clairvaux, Bonmont, and La Charité, and many others of this sort. By the nectar of the name alone, hearers are invited eagerly to discover how great is the blessedness there denoted by so distinctive a title.

Many thirsty people have drunk from their spring, and many streams have flowed from it through the various regions of Gaul. Imitators of the new observance have spread through Aquitaine, Brittany, Gascony, and Ireland. Hypocrites mingle with the good; clad in white or variegated garments, they deceive men and furnish an immense spectacle to the people. Many desire to resemble true worshippers of God in habit rather than virtue; by their multitude they disgust beholders, and, insofar as the deceptive gaze of men is concerned, make approved cenobites appear more contemptible [Col. 0642A].

## XXVI. Abbots and monks conspicuous for piety in new monasteries. On the founders of new orders.

At the same time the venerable Andrew of the Valley of Bruyères, a monk, flourished. In the district of Bourges he built the monastery called Casale Benedicti and taught disciples to serve God in great poverty and continence. He was Italian by birth, fully trained in literary learning, and, through God’s grace, suited to winning souls for God.

Then Aldebert, abbot of Dol, was raised to the archbishopric of Bourges. Abounding in many virtues, he furnished those following Christ with an example of holiness in word and deed [Col. 0642B]. Guarnerius of Montmaure, brother of the aforesaid prelate, was a distinguished knight and afterwards a monk of La Maison-Dieu; for nearly sixty years he served God. While he was still under arms, serving the world, he was once returning from the pilgrimage of Saint James. At the entrance to a certain forest, alone with his armour-bearer, he suddenly encountered a sick beggar. When the latter asked for alms, Guarnerius had no coins at hand to give; but he devoutly offered him valuable gloves sent to him by a beloved woman.

After a long time an angelic vision appeared to a certain religious servant of God, who, after Matins, was praying in the oratory, and specially commanded him to perform certain acts. When the monk diligently inquired by whose authority such commands were given to him, the vision said: “He sent me [Col. 0642C] to you and gave you these commands—the one whom Martin clothed with a portion of his cloak, and to whom Guarnerius gave his gloves.”

The brother reported this to the abbot. The story of Martin’s divided cloak was well known to the elders: while still a catechumen at Amiens, he covered Christ in a poor man with a portion of it. But the matter of Guarnerius’s gloves remained entirely hidden for a long time. At last, when some questioned him, Guarnerius simply disclosed how he had helped the needy man for love of Christ; and from them he likewise heard the revelation, and gave thanks to God, who is ever present to those doing good.

About this time Bernard, abbot of Quincay, left the territory of Poitiers because he refused to subject the aforesaid monastery, which had hitherto been free, to Cluny [Col. 0642D]. And because, as it is written, “The righteous is as confident as a lion” (Prov. 28:1), he contended in a Roman synod against Pope Paschal for its liberty, and, since the pope had not rendered him complete justice, summoned him to the divine judgment. The pope, fearing his formidable resolve, asked him to remain with him for the protection of the Roman Church.

Bernard, however, wholly abandoned worldly concerns and travelled through many places with certain religious brethren who eagerly followed him. At length, after many wanderings, he turned aside to the venerable Bishop Ivo. Kindly received by him, he settled with several brethren on an estate of the church of Chartres; and in a woodland place called Tiron he built a monastery in honour of the Holy Saviour [Col. 0643A]. A great multitude of faithful people of both orders flocked there, and the aforesaid Father received all who hastened to conversion in a loving embrace. He directed each person to practise in the monastery the lawful crafts which he knew. Therefore carpenters and smiths, sculptors and goldsmiths, painters and masons, vintners and farmers, and highly skilled artisans of many occupations gladly assembled around him. They carefully carried out what the elder’s command enjoined upon them, and contributed to the common benefit whatever they earned.

Thus, where shortly before robbers had been accustomed to lurk in a dreadful forest and slaughter unwary travellers in sudden attacks, a noble monastery quickly arose through God’s aid [Col. 0643B]. Theobald, count palatine, and his mother Adela; Rotrou, count of Mortagne, and his mother Beatrice; as well as distinguished and lesser men of Chartres, Dreux, Corbon, and other neighbouring faithful people, having truly tested the innocent simplicity of the monks, kindly cherished them in the fear of the Lord. They gave them the strongest support in funds and counsel, in order to strengthen the fortress of God which they had begun.

The venerable Vitalis, formerly chaplain to Robert, count of Mortain, and a canon of Saint-Evroul at Mortain, set aside the burdens of worldly concerns and riches. He resolved to bear Christ’s light yoke in the footsteps of the Apostles [Col. 0643C], and lived for some time in desert places with certain religious men. There he subdued the former habits of a softer life and learned the practices of stricter observance. At last he considered the village of Savigny, where vast ruins of ancient buildings are visible, chose it as a dwelling place for himself and his companions, and began to found a monastery in the adjoining wood in honour of the holy and undivided Trinity.

He did not imitate the practices of the Cluniacs or of others who had long been devoted to monastic observances; rather, he adopted, as he pleased, the modern observances of neophytes. He was exceptionally well schooled in letters, endowed with courage and eloquence, and bold in uttering whatever he wished. In preaching to the people he spared neither lowly persons nor powerful ones; like a trumpet, in accordance with Isaiah’s prophecy (58:1), he raised his voice, declaring to the Christian people their crimes and to the house of Jacob their sins [Col. 0643D].

Kings and dukes accordingly revered him. Great crowds flocked to hear his words, but afterwards returned from his presence sorrowful and ashamed when they heard from him deeds of wickedness secretly committed long before. Every rank was inwardly pierced by his truthful accusations. All the people trembled before his rebukes, and both sexes, covered with shame, blushed at his reproaches. He openly assailed bare vices and goaded those conscious of hidden sins with reproaches that brought them disgrace [Col. 0644A]. Thus he often subdued proud champions and untamed crowds of the populace, and made wealthy ladies, delicately dressed in silken clothes and furs from Canosa, tremble as he fiercely attacked crimes with the sword of God’s word, severely struck consciences polluted by filth, and terrified them by the resounding thunder of divine punishment.

Thus the diligent sower of the word benefited many, gathered many to himself, served God for seven years in the monastery which he had built, and persevered in a good life to a good end. After some illness, during which he had faithfully confessed and devoutly received the viaticum of holy communion, he was in the oratory at Matins of the Blessed Virgin Mary. He gave the blessing requested by the reader, and, when all present had said “Amen,” immediately breathed out his spirit [Col. 0644B]. After his death Geoffrey of Bayeux, a monk of Cerisy, succeeded him; he too cultivated excessive innovations and placed a harsh yoke upon the necks of his disciples.

I have recorded these things for posterity concerning modern teachers, who prefer new traditions to the observances of the ancient Fathers, call other monks secular, and rashly condemn them as transgressors of the Rule. Considering their zeal and strictness, I do not greatly blame them; nevertheless, I do not rank them above the greater and approved Fathers. I think they do not know that the blessed Father Columbanus, born in Ireland, was a contemporary of Saint Benedict [Col. 0644C]; that, leaving his father’s house and native land, he sailed into Gaul with eminent monks; that he was received by Childebert, king of the Franks and son of Sigibert; that he built the monastery of Luxeuil in Burgundy; and that, later expelled by the most impious Queen Brunhild, he withdrew into Italy and, received by Agilulf, king of the Lombards, founded the monastery of Bobbio.

This Father of wondrous holiness laboured among the foremost men, shone gloriously among mortals by signs and miracles, and, instructed by the Holy Spirit, issued a monastic Rule and was the first to hand it on to the Gauls. Most flourishing monks came forth from his school and shone in the world by their virtues like stars in the firmament. Eustace of Luxeuil, Agilus of Rebais, Faro of Meaux [Col. 0644D], Audomar of Boulogne, Philibert of Jumièges, and many other bishops and abbots of most excellent religious devotion came forth from it. Their holiness was shown from heaven through evident miracles, and through their zeal the Church was notably extended in her children.

They, I think, knew the blessed Maurus and his companions and disciples, being neighbours, and received from them, as from others, written copies of the Rule of Saint Benedict for the edification of the learned. Yet they did not reject the ordinances of their own master, namely the venerable Columbanus. From him, indeed, they learned the manner and order of divine service, and the form of prayers for all ranks within the Church of God. They adopted the blackness of their garments and other observances, which they maintained for the sake of his religious life and honour [Col. 0645A], and which their followers down to the present day desire reverently to observe. The book of his life, full of signs and virtues, shows what a man and how great a man the aforesaid teacher was before God and men. He is also frequently mentioned in the deeds of Audoenus, archbishop of Rouen, Eligius of Noyon, and other men gathered by him and advanced, through his instruction, to the peace of virtues.

## XXVII. The distinguished man Hugh of Grandmesnil enters monastic life on his sickbed through Geoffrey, prior of the monks of Saint-Evroul, and dies shortly afterward.—On his children.

I recently began the subject of my writing with the church of Saint-Evroul; but, as though carried away into ecstasy, I looked out upon the vast realms of lands, flew far and wide in discourse, and, surveying very many things, prolonged a very lengthy recapitulation. Now, weary, I shall return to my couch—which is Saint-Evroul—and at the end of the book clearly unfold something concerning matters that belong to us.

In the year from the Incarnation 1098, indiction 1, Hugh of Grandmesnil, a renowned hero, took to his bed in England. Broken by old age and sickness, he drew near his end. Then he entered monastic life through Geoffrey of Orléans, prior of the monks of Saint-Evroul, whom Abbot Roger had long before sent to England for the protection of that same monastery. On the sixth day afterward—that is, on the eighth day before the Kalends of March—he died. Then Bernard and David, monks of Saint-Evroul, conveyed his salted body, carefully sewn into oxhide, to Normandy [Col. 0645C]. The often-mentioned abbot and the community of monks honourably buried it in the chapter house, beside Abbot Mainerius, on the southern side.

Moreover Ernald of Rodelent, his nephew, covered the stone sarcophagus with a slab; and Vitalis composed this epitaph in heroic verse:

> Behold, beneath this inscription rests valiant Hugh,  
> Who flourished for many years in many virtues.  
> The stronghold of Grenton was called his dwelling,  
> Whence came the surname well known to many.  
> In the time of mighty William, king of the English,  
> This hero shone among the foremost magnates.  
> Strong in warfare and faithful in virtue,  
> Terrible to enemies and a lordly protector to friends,  
> Enlarging by his expenditures, offices, and rich estates,  
> He greatly advanced the monastery of Saint-Evroul.  
> While the pious people celebrated the chair of Saint Peter,  
> [Col. 0645D] the veteran died, clothed in the habit of a monk—  
> A worshipper of the Church, a generous giver, a revealer, and  
> gentle toward the poor. May he rejoice in the citadel of heaven! Amen.

Seven years earlier Adeliza, the wife of the aforesaid nobleman, had died at Rouen on the fifth day before the Ides of July and had been buried in the chapter house of Saint-Evroul, at the right hand of Abbot Mainerius [Col. 0646A]. She was the daughter of Ivo, count of Beaumont, and of Judaea, her mother, and bore her husband six sons and as many daughters, upon whom diverse fortune fell amid the shifting instability of the world.

Robert, the eldest, grew old as the husband of three wives. Under his hand the patrimony he had received from his father in considerable abundance declined. At last, thirty-eight years after his father’s death, he died on the Kalends of June and was buried in the chapter house of Saint-Evroul with his two wives, Agnes and Emma.

His brother William was greatly esteemed at the court of King William, and the king loved him so much [Col. 0646B] that he offered him his niece, the daughter of Robert, count of Mortain, in order to retain the young man, thus joined to his own kindred, in great honour. But the proud young knight rejected the king’s counsel and, led by fickleness, went to Apulia with Robert Giffard and many others. There he married Mabilia, daughter of Robert Guiscard, surnamed Short-Wolf, receiving fifteen castles with her; and there, after his return from Antioch, he died, leaving two sons, William and Robert, heirs to his rank.

Hugh, a valiant and honourable knight, died in youth and was honourably buried in the chapter house of Saint Father Evroul.

Ivo at first retained his paternal honour in England for some time [Col. 0646C], but later, in the reign of King Henry, pledged it to Robert, count of Meulan. He twice undertook the journey to Jerusalem; on his first expedition he endured hardships with his companions at Antioch, but on the second he died.

Alberic, who was younger in age, studied letters in childhood; but in youth he abandoned the clerical state and took up knighthood, in which he strove manfully to accomplish many deeds. He wounded Tancred, son of Odo the Good, Marquis, who was distinguished by titles of many virtues. As a result, the aforesaid captain limped for the rest of his life.

All these sons of Hugh were handsome and tall in body [Col. 0646D], and valiant. But, pursued by misfortune, they enjoyed neither long life—except Robert—nor peaceful prosperity for long.

## Summary of Book Nine

[Col. 0645]

I. Prologue. Remarkable events of this period.  
II. Various portents. The Council of Clermont.  
III. Councils held in regions of Normandy. The holy war is preached.  
IV. The condition of Normandy. Peter the Hermit and soldiers marked with the cross set out for Palestine.  
V. Duke Robert of Normandy, Duke Godfrey of Lorraine, his brother Baldwin, Bohemond, Count Raymond of Toulouse, and very many magnates set out. First battles of the cross-bearers against the Turks.  
[Col. 0647] VI. Various journeys of the cross-bearers. Treachery of the Greeks.  
VII. The capture of Nicaea. Advance of the very great army of cross-bearers. Battles against the Turks.  
VIII. New battles. Capture of Iconium and Heraclea.  
IX. Siege of Antioch.  
X. The siege of Antioch continues. The cross-bearers capture this city.  
XI. The Turks, led by Kerbogha, attack the Franks at Antioch.  
XII. Discovery of the Holy Lance. Great joy among the Christians. They prepare for a general battle. They defeat the Turks.  
XIII. On the deeds of Baldwin. He obtains the principality of Edessa.  
XIV. After Antioch is captured, Hugh the Great is sent by the Christians to the emperor of the Greeks. The Christian leaders determine to remain in that city for the summer. Various expeditions.  
XV. Duke Bohemond and Count Raymond contend for dominion over the city of Antioch. Numerous Christian victories over the pagans. The army of cross-bearers advances toward Jerusalem.  
XVI. Internal dissensions. The cross-bearers continue the journey they have begun to Jerusalem.  
XVII. The Christian army reaches Jerusalem. Siege of that city.  
XVIII. Jerusalem is captured by the cross-bearers.  
XIX. The cross-bearers establish their seats in the city of Jerusalem. Godfrey is elected king.  
XX. The battle of Ascalon. Victory falls to the Christians. On Baldric, archbishop of Dol.

# Book Nine

## I. Prologue. Remarkable events of this period.

[Col. 0647A]

The eternal Creator wisely and beneficially orders the changes of times and events. He does not arrange and alter human affairs according to the whim of the unbridled, but mercifully holds them in his mighty hand and exalted arm, fittingly advances them, and administers them. We plainly see this in winter and summer; we likewise experience it in cold and heat; we observe it in the arising and passing away of all things, and can properly investigate it in the manifold variety of God’s works. Hence many histories arise concerning the many kinds of events occurring daily in the world, and abundant material for discourse is furnished to eloquent historians.

[Col. 0647B]

I consider these matters deeply and commit my reflections to writing because in our times an unforeseen transformation is taking place, and a remarkable theme for narration offers wonderful material to the industry of writers. Behold: the journey to Jerusalem is divinely undertaken; one flock is wondrously gathered from many peoples of the West, and one army is led against the heathen into eastern lands. Holy Zion is rescued by her children, who voluntarily came forth from distant regions, after the defeat of the foreigners by whom the holy city had formerly been trampled down and God’s sanctuary wickedly defiled. For the detestable Hagarites, permitted by divine judgment, long ago crossed the borders of Christendom, seized the holy places, killed Christian inhabitants, and abominably polluted sacred things with their filth [Col. 0647C]. But after many years they worthily paid the deserved penalty through the swords of the Cisalpine peoples.

No subject, I think, ever came forth more glorious for writers of warlike affairs than that which the Lord has now offered to our poets and writers, when through a few Christians he triumphed in the East over the pagans. He stirred them from their homes by the sweet desire of pilgrimage. Indeed, God recently renewed Abraham’s ancient miracles when, by the mere ardour of seeing the Messiah’s tomb, he drew the faithful of the West; without king or secular compulsion, through Pope Urban he exhorted them; from the ends of the earth and the islands of the sea he drew them forth, as Moses drew the Hebrews out of Egypt [Col. 0648A]; and he led them through foreign peoples as far as Palestine. There he overcame kings and princes gathered with many nations, and gloriously subdued them, along with their most strongly fortified cities and towns.

Fulcher of Chartres, chaplain of Godfrey, duke of Lorraine, who shared the labours and dangers of the praiseworthy expedition, composed a reliable and truthful work on the commendable warfare of Christ’s army. Baldric, archbishop of Dol, likewise eloquently wrote four books in which he truthfully and eloquently set forth a complete account from the beginning of the pilgrimage to the first battle after Jerusalem’s capture. Many other Latins and Greeks also treated this memorable matter [Col. 0648B] and made known to posterity, in enduring writings, the illustrious deeds of heroes.

I too, least among all who follow the Lord in a life under the religious habit, because I love Christ’s valiant champions and desire to exalt their worthy deeds, seek in this little work which I have begun on ecclesiastical affairs to commence the account of the Christian expedition in the Lord Jesus. I fear to undertake the whole work concerning the holy pilgrimage and do not dare promise so arduous a task; yet I do not know how I can pass over untouched so noble a subject. I am hindered by old age, being sixty years old and a monk reared in a regular cloister from childhood. Nor can I henceforth endure the great labour of writing. I have no scribes [Col. 0648C] now to take down my words, and therefore I hasten to finish this present little work. I shall now begin the ninth book, in which I shall endeavour to relate in due order and truthfully certain matters concerning Jerusalem, God granting me the necessary aid.

In the deserts of Idumaea I cry to you, good Jesus, mighty king, Nazarene: I beseech you, help me. Grant me the strength worthily to proclaim your glorious right, by which you exalted your own and crushed the rebellious. You are leader and ruler of your own, and protector in straits. You are the helper of your own and the rewarder of the victorious. Highest God, I worship you; now I implore your aid. To the King of kings [Col. 0649A] be everlasting praise through endless ages! Amen.

## II. Various portents. The Council of Clermont.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1094, indiction 2, seditions and the tumults of wars resounded almost throughout the whole world, and cruel earthborn men inflicted immense losses upon one another by killings and plunder. Wickedness in manifold form abounded excessively and supplied innumerable calamities to its servants. Then a great drought scorched the grass of the earth and damaged grain and legumes; after these perished, a very great famine followed.

Emperor Henry attacked the Roman Church; and when many rose against him with good cause, he was overcome by God’s will. Pope Urban held a council at Piacenza and diligently dealt with peace and the other interests [Col. 0649B] of the holy Church.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1095, indiction 3, on the day before the Nones of April, Wednesday, the twenty-fifth day of the moon, a movement of stars so great was seen in Gaul by countless observers that, because of their density, they would have been thought hail, were it not that they were stars. Many also thought that stars had fallen, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled which says that at some time the stars will fall from heaven (Matt. 24:29).

Gislebert, bishop of Lisieux, an aged physician most expert in many arts, was accustomed every night to contemplate the stars for a long time and, as a shrewd astrologer, carefully mark their courses. Accordingly this natural philosopher attentively observed the portent of the stars [Col. 0649C], and summoned Walter, the watchman who guarded his household while the others slept.

“Do you see, Walter,” he said, “this remarkable sign?”

The other answered: “Lord, I see it; but I do not know what it portends.”

The old man said: “A migration of peoples from kingdom to kingdom is, I think, foreshadowed. Many will depart who will never return, until the stars return to their proper stations, from which, as it appears to us, they are now plainly falling. Others will remain in a lofty and holy place, like stars shining in the firmament.”

After a long time Walter of Cormeilles related this to me exactly as he had heard it from the mouth of the prudent chief physician concerning the course of the stars, and exactly as the prodigious event occurred.

Philip, king of the French, abducted Bertrada, countess of Anjou, and, having abandoned his noble wife, disgracefully married the adulteress. Rebuked by the bishops of Gaul because he had voluntarily deserted his wife and she her husband, he refused to repent of his foul offense; but, wasted by old age and illness, he miserably rotted in the filth of adultery.

Pope Urban, during Philip’s reign, came into Gaul, dedicated the altar of St Peter at the monastery of Cluny and many basilicas of saints, and exalted them by privileges of apostolic authority to the praise of Christ. At that time a mortality among men raged in Normandy and France, emptying many houses of inhabitants, while a great famine wasted the wretched.

In the same year, 1095, in the fourth indiction, in the month of November, the aforesaid pope assembled all the bishops of Gaul and Spain and held a great council at Clermont, a city of Auvergne, which in antiquity was called Arverni. [Col. 0650A] He corrected many matters then being conducted there, and established many measures useful for the reform of morals. At the Synod of Auvergne there were thirteen archbishops and 225 bishops, with a multitude of abbots and other persons to whom God had entrusted the care of holy churches.

The decrees of the council held at Clermont were as follows:

The Church shall be catholic, chaste, and free: catholic in faith and in the communion of saints; chaste from every contagion of wickedness; and free from every secular power.

No bishop, abbot, or member of the clergy shall receive an ecclesiastical dignity from the hand of princes or of any laymen.

[Col. 0650B] Clerics shall not hold prelacies or prebends in two cities or churches.

No one shall be both bishop and abbot.

No priest, deacon, subdeacon, or canon of any rank shall engage in sexual intercourse.

No priest, deacon, or subdeacon shall minister after a lapse.

Ecclesiastical or canonical dignities shall neither be sold nor bought by anyone.

Pardon shall be granted only to those who bought canonries in ignorance of the authority of the canons, or without knowing that this had been forbidden.

But those who knowingly possess offices bought by themselves or their relatives shall be deprived of them.

No layman, after receiving ashes at the beginning of the fast, [Col. 0650C] shall eat meat until Easter.

The first fast of the Ember Days shall always be observed in the first week of Lent.

Ordinations shall always be celebrated either on the eve of Saturday or while the Sunday fast continues.

On Easter Saturday the office shall not end before sunset.

The second fast shall always be observed in the week of Pentecost.

From the Advent of the Lord until the octave of Epiphany; from Septuagesima until the octave of Easter; from the first day of the Rogations until the octave of Pentecost; and at all times from Wednesday at sunset until Monday at sunrise, the Truce of God shall be kept.

[Col. 0650D] Whoever seizes a bishop shall altogether be held an outlaw.

Whoever seizes or despoils monks, clerics, religious women, or their companions shall be anathematized.

Whoever plunders the goods of deceased bishops or clerics shall be anathematized.

Whoever contracts marriage within the seventh degree of consanguinity shall be anathematized.

No one shall be elected bishop unless he is a priest, deacon, or subdeacon, and has the support of noble birth—unless there is extreme necessity and permission from the supreme pontiff.

The sons of priests or concubines shall not be promoted to the priesthood unless they have first entered the religious life.

[Col. 0651A] Whoever takes refuge in a church or at a cross, if guilty, shall, after immunity of life and limb has been granted, be handed over to justice; if innocent, he shall be set free.

The Body of the Lord and the Blood of the Lord shall be received separately.

Each church shall possess its own tithes, and they shall not pass into the right of another church, whoever may give them.

No layman shall sell or retain tithes.

No stipulated price shall be demanded or paid for the burial of the dead.

No lay prince shall have a chaplain unless he has been assigned by a bishop.

If such a chaplain commits an offense, he shall be corrected by the bishop and another substituted.

These enactments Pope Urban generally sanctioned at the Synod of Auvergne, [Col. 0651B] and he strongly urged persons of every rank to keep God’s law. Then he set forth at length, with tears, a complaint concerning the desolation of Christendom in the East, recounting the calamities and savage oppressions inflicted upon Christians by the Saracens. Regarding also the trampling-down of Jerusalem and the Holy Places, where the Son of God bodily dwelt with his most holy companions, the tearful narrator openly wept in the sacred assembly. Thus he compelled many hearers to weep with him through intense feeling and pious compassion for their brethren. He delivered to those present a long and very useful discourse, eloquent and rich in words, and warned the magnates of the western regions, together with their dependants and fellow-soldiers, [Col. 0651C] to keep peace firmly among themselves, to take the saving sign of the cross upon their right shoulders, and to exercise fully against the pagans the prowess for which their military service was renowned:

“For the Turks and Persians,” he said, “the Arabs and Hagarites, have invaded Antioch and Nicaea, Jerusalem itself, made illustrious by Christ’s tomb, and many other cities of Christians; and they have already extended enormous power through the empire of the Greeks. Securely possessing Palestine and Syria, which they have now subjected to themselves, they destroy basilicas and slaughter Christians as sheep. In churches in which divine sacrifices were formerly celebrated by the faithful, the heathen have made stables for their animals; they have installed their superstitions and idolatry also, and disgracefully expelled the Christian religion from the sanctuary consecrated to God. [Col. 0651D] Estates of saints assigned for stipends, and inheritances of nobles entrusted for the support of the poor, are subjected to pagan tyranny; their cruel masters convert them to their own uses and abuse them. They have already carried many captives away into distant barbarian lands and, fastening them with straps beneath yokes, subject them to rural labours. While these people drag ploughs laboriously like oxen, they break up the fields; and they are inhumanly subjected to other brutish tasks suitable to beasts, not men. As they toil continually amid these things, they are beaten with whips, pricked with goads, and abominably enslaved by countless persecutions. In Africa alone ninety-six bishoprics have been destroyed, as those who come from there report to us.”
