Therefore, as soon as Pope Urban eloquently brought this lament [Col. 0652A] to Christian ears, with God’s grace assisting, an overwhelming love of pilgrimage seized innumerable people and persuaded them to sell their estates and leave everything they possessed for Christ. A remarkable willingness to go to Jerusalem, or to assist those going, possessed rich and poor, men and women, monks and clerics, townsmen and peasants. Husbands resolved to leave their beloved wives at home. Yet the women, lamenting, though leaving behind their children together with all their wealth, greatly desired to follow their husbands on pilgrimage. Estates formerly dear were now sold cheaply, and arms were bought by which divine vengeance might be exercised upon the Philistines. Thieves, pirates, and other criminals, touched by the Spirit of God, rose from the depths of wickedness, abandoned their confessed crimes, made satisfaction to God for their sins, [Col. 0652B] and set out on pilgrimage. The provident pope urged all who were suitably able to bear arms into war against God’s enemies; and by God’s authority he absolved every penitent, from the hour at which he took up the Lord’s cross, of all sins, and piously remitted every burden imposed by fasts and other mortifications of the flesh. For, as a prudent and kindly chief physician, he clearly considered that those setting out on pilgrimage would very often be harassed on the road by many protracted dangers and would daily be distressed by manifold happy or unhappy events; through these, Christ’s well-disposed servants might be cleansed from every stain of sin.

While the pope was preaching magnificently in the council and vigorously exhorting the sons [Col. 0652C] of Jerusalem to rescue their holy mother, a man of great renown, Haimar, bishop of Le Puy, rose and approached the apostolic pontiff before all with a joyful expression. Bending the knee, he asked leave to go and a blessing, and obtained them amid the rejoicing of all. Moreover, the pope promulgated an order that all should obey him and appointed him the apostolic vicar in God’s expedition. For he possessed the highest nobility, great valour, and singular diligence. Envoys of Raymond Berengar, count of Toulouse, were likewise immediately present; they reported to the pope that he would go with many thousands from his duchy and testified that he had already fastened the cross upon himself in the council.

[Col. 0652D] Behold—thanks be to God! Voluntary leaders eagerly came forth for the Christians about to depart. Behold, priesthood and kingship, clerical order and lay order, agree in leading the battle-lines of God. Bishop and count represent anew for us Moses and Aaron, whom divine assistance accompanies alike. On the tenth day of February [1096], an eclipse of the moon occurred from midnight until dawn, and darkness arose over the northern part of the moon.

Odo, bishop of Bayeux; Gislebert of Évreux; Serlo of Sées; and the envoys of other Norman prelates attended the Council of Auvergne with letters of excuse. Returning thence with the apostolic blessing, they brought synodal letters to their fellow bishops.

### III. Councils held in the regions of Normandy. The holy war is preached.

[Col. 0653A]

Archbishop William therefore assembled a council at Rouen and discussed ecclesiastical concerns with his suffragan bishops. Then all came to Rouen in February [1096], and unanimously considered the chapters of the synod held at Clermont. They confirmed the apostolic enactments and left the following document to posterity.

1. The holy synod decreed that the Truce of God be firmly observed: from Sunday before the beginning of the fast until Monday after the octave of Pentecost, at sunrise; and from Wednesday before the Advent of the Lord, at sunset, until the octave of Epiphany; and throughout [Col. 0653B] every week of the year, from Wednesday at sunset until Monday at sunrise; and on all feasts of Holy Mary and their vigils, and on all feasts of the apostles and their vigils. Thus no person shall assault, wound, or kill another; no one shall take damage or plunder.

2. It also decreed that all churches and their precincts; monks, clerics, religious women, and women; pilgrims, merchants, and their servants; oxen and horses ploughing; men driving carts and harrowers, and the horses with which they harrow; people fleeing to carts; and all lands of saints and the money of clerics, shall be in perpetual peace. Thus on no day shall anyone dare to assault, seize, plunder, or in any manner molest them.

[Col. 0653C] 3. It also decreed that all persons aged twelve and over shall swear that they will observe in full this ordinance of the Truce of God as here defined, by the following oath:

> “Hear this, you, N.: from this time forward I shall faithfully keep this ordinance of the Truce of God as here defined; and against all who disdain to swear it or refuse to keep this ordinance, I shall give aid to my bishop or archdeacon. Thus, if they summon me to proceed against such persons, I shall neither flee away nor evade the matter, but shall go with my arms together with him and shall assist against them by every means in my power, in good faith and without evil intent, according to my conscience. So may God and these saints help me.”

[Col. 0653D] 4. Furthermore, the holy synod decreed that all who refuse to take this oath or violate this ordinance shall be struck with anathema, as shall all who communicate with them or sell goods to them—whether smiths, other tradesmen, or priests who admit them to communion or perform the divine office for them. Counterfeiters, robbers, purchasers of plunder, those who gather in camps to commit robberies, and lords who henceforth keep them in their camps are likewise struck with this anathema. By apostolic authority and our own, we prohibit any Christian worship from being performed in the lands of those lords.

5. The holy synod also decreed that all churches shall be seised of their possessions exactly as they were in the time of [Col. 0654A] King William, and with the same customary rights; and that no layman shall have a share in the third part of the tithe, in burial, or in altar offerings, nor exact from them service or any exaction, except that established in King William’s time.

6. It also decreed that no layman shall appoint or remove a priest of a church without the bishop’s consent, or sell the office or receive money from it; and that no man shall grow his hair long, but shall be tonsured as befits a Christian. Otherwise he shall be excluded from the thresholds of holy Mother Church; no priest shall perform the divine office for him or attend his burial. No layman shall possess episcopal customs or jurisdiction belonging to the cure of souls.

[Col. 0654B] 7. No priest shall become the man of a layman, because it is unworthy that hands consecrated to God and sanctified by sacred anointing should be placed between unconsecrated hands—those of a man who may be a murderer, adulterer, or guilty of any criminal sin. But if a priest holds from a layman a fief that does not belong to the church, he shall render him such fealty that the layman may be secure.

Gislebert, bishop of Évreux, surnamed “the Crane” from his tall stature, and Fulbert, archdeacon of Rouen, publicly promulgated these decrees of the fathers. Archbishop William and the other prelates confirmed them by their authority. Odo of Bayeux, Gislebert of Lisieux, Turgis of Avranches, Serlo of Sées, [Col. 0654C] and Ralph of Coutances sanctioned the aforesaid synod. The abbots of the whole province were also present, together with the clergy and some of the magnates desirous of peace. The prelates undoubtedly established highly beneficial measures from good will. But because royal justice was lacking, they achieved little for the benefit of ecclesiastical tranquillity. For all that they then determined, as stated above, was almost rendered void.

### IV. The state of Normandy. Peter the Hermit and soldiers marked with the cross set out for Palestine.

For at that time there was a remarkable faction among the Norman magnates, and throughout the region the disorderly made a great and violent practice of stealing and plundering. Arson and robbery devastated the whole country. [Col. 0654D] They drove very many natives into exile; parishes were destroyed, and priests abandoned churches made desolate by their flight.

The Norman people are untamed and, unless restrained by a stern ruler, extremely ready for crime. In every community wherever they are found, they seek mastery; violating the course of truth and faith, they have often been swept away by the heat of ambition. The French, Bretons, Flemings, and other neighbouring peoples have often felt this; Italians, the Winili [reading uncertain], and English Saxons have experienced it even to destruction.

The origin of the Trojans, as is related, came from the fierce people of the Scythians. When they had been reduced to ruin, Antenor the Phrygian penetrated the Illyrian regions and, with neighbouring exiles, sought long and far for a place to dwell. At last he settled above the shore of the Ocean Sea in the northern region; he inhabited the maritime land with his companions and heirs, and from Dan, his son, that people, sprung from the Trojans, received the name Danes.

This people was always cruel and warlike and had very powerful kings, but scarcely consented to receive Christ’s faith until late. Rollo, a most fierce leader, came from that stock with the Normans, and was the first to subdue Neustria to himself; it is now called Normandy after the Normans. *North* in English means “the north wind,” while *man* means “a human being.” Thus *Norman* means “a northern man,” whose bold harshness has proved excessively hostile to delicate neighbouring peoples, as the cold north wind is to tender flowers. [Col. 0655B] For natural savagery still grows within that people, and an inborn passion for fighting rages, which does not allow peasants and peaceable workers to remain quietly in their homes.

From Rollo onward mighty dukes ruled the warlike Normans: namely William Longsword; Richard the Elder; Richard II, son of Gunnor; his two sons Richard the Younger and Robert of Jerusalem; and William the Bastard. The last of these in time surpassed all his predecessors in strength and eminence; at his death he left the duchy of Normandy to Robert and the kingdom of England to William.

Robert, however, a soft and yielding duke, fell away from the vigour of his predecessors and languished in idleness and softness. He feared his provincial subjects more than he was feared by them, and consequently ruinous disorder spread everywhere through his land. Henry, the duke’s brother, held Domfront, a very strong castle, and had brought a great part of Neustria under himself by favour or arms; he obeyed his brother only at his own pleasure and in no other fashion. [Col. 0656A] Another brother, who wore England’s crown, held, I think, more than twenty castles in Normandy and had drawn powerful magnates and townsmen to himself by gifts or threats. Robert [Note: [Col. 0655C] Rather, Henry.] count of Eu; Stephen of Aumale; Gerard of Gournay; Ralph of Conches; Robert, count of Meulan; Walter Giffard; Philip of Braose; Richard of Courcy; and very many others, with all their subject strongholds and townsmen, obeyed the king and, because he was feared, clung to him with all their efforts. Thus Normandy was miserably disturbed by its own sons raging against one another, and the unarmed common people were left desolate without a protector.

At last Duke Robert, anxiously perceiving such misfortunes [Col. 0656B] and fearing still worse, since he had been abandoned by almost everyone, resolved on the advice of certain religious men to leave his land to his brother the king and, taking up the Lord’s cross, to go to Jerusalem to make satisfaction to God for his sins. When the king of the English learned this, he rejoiced greatly, approved the plan, accepted Normandy to keep for five years, and paid his brother ten thousand marks of silver to carry out the Lord’s journey.

Pope Urban, in the following Lent [1096], held another council at Tours and confirmed the matters he had treated at Clermont. In mid-Lent he dedicated the basilica of St Nicholas at Angers [Col. 0656C] and honoured it with apostolic privileges. At the urging and by the authority of the pope he released Geoffrey Martel, [the Bearded — Note: [Col. 0655C] Dom Bouquet.] count of Anjou, from chains. Geoffrey had been captured by the treachery of his younger brother Fulk Rechin, who had deprived his own lord of his rank and confined him in prison for nearly thirty years at the castle of Chinon.

[Note: [Col. 0655C] We learn from the following charter of Hugh, archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See, concerning the absolution of Fulk, count of Anjou—among the documents of the new *Gallia Christiana*, IV, col. 10—that Urban had attempted the Bearded One’s liberation two years earlier:

“Hugh, archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See, to his most beloved brothers in Christ—the archbishops, [Col. 0655D] bishops, abbots, and faithful of God’s holy Church—greetings.

“We judged it worthy to make known to all the orthodox how, by command of our lord Pope Urban, we undertook the duty of travelling to the territories of Anjou in the case of Fulk, count of the Angevins, in order to absolve him from the bond of anathema in which he had long been entangled because of the capture of his brother Geoffrey, whom he had taken in open war. Yet the count himself did not evade rendering an account, making satisfaction, or undergoing judgment; indeed, he was always ready to do so.

“From the report of trustworthy clerics and laymen, we learned that his aforesaid brother, at the time when he was captured, had been excommunicated by Stephen, cardinal and legate of the Roman See, because of the manifold injury which he inflicted upon the church of Tours and the abbey of St Martin of Marmoutier; and that the principality of the county of Anjou had been granted to this Fulk by that same legate on behalf of St Peter. We also learned, from the truthful report of reliable men among his nobles, that it had been granted to him by his uncle [Col. 0656C] Geoffrey.

“Therefore, having undertaken this legation, and so that the force of apostolic obedience might be handled by us with greater authority, we associated with ourselves in carrying it out our venerable brother, the archbishop of Bourges. Having thus come together, we deliberately visited the count’s brother, whom we heard was held captive. We found him so deranged, as everyone reported, that it seemed altogether useless and vain to entrust to his governance the rule of a country, since by his folly he had become useless both to himself and to all others—to such an extent that he would not even allow himself to be freed from captivity through our hands.

“We therefore came to the monastery of St Florentius; and on the feast day of the Nativity of St John the Baptist, before religious men—bishops and abbots who had come when invited—we unanimously absolved Count Fulk, who was ready to make satisfaction or render an account, with the approval and praise of all. We received securities from him that, should his brother recover soundness of mind, he would, by the command of our lord the pope or by ours, either make peace with him or be ready to undergo judgment; and that he would not marry a wife, concerning the number of whom he was accused, without our counsel.

“We judged it proper to lay open to you the course of this action. The names of the religious men present are these: Aldebert, archbishop of Bourges; Revellus, bishop of Le Mans; William, abbot of St Florentius; Bernard, abbot of SS. Sergius and Bacchus; Gerard, abbot of St Albinus; Nualdus, abbot of St Nicholas; Baldric, [Col. 0657D] abbot of Bourgueil; Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme. Done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1094, at the abbey of St Florentius, on the feast day of St John the Baptist.”

[Col. 0658D] Dom Bouquet, book IX, pp. 663–664.]

[Col. 0657A] Therefore, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1096, in the fourth indiction, in March, Peter of Acheris, a monk distinguished for learning and generosity, set out on pilgrimage from France. He brought with him Walter of Pexeio, with his nephews Walter surnamed “Without-Possessions,” William, Simon, and Matthew, other distinguished French knights, and nearly fifteen thousand foot soldiers. Then, on Easter Saturday, he arrived at Cologne and rested there through Easter week, but did not cease from his good work. He preached to the Germans and drew fifteen thousand of them into the work of the Lord. Two distinguished counts, Berthold and Hildebert, and one bishop joined him; with him they went on pilgrimage through Germany and Hungary. But the proud Frenchmen, while Peter [Col. 0657B] remained at Cologne and wished to enlarge and strengthen his companies by preaching God’s word, refused to wait for him and set out upon the journey through Hungary. Coloman, king of the Hungarians, favoured them then and supplied the necessary assistance in his land. After crossing the Danube, they came through Bulgaria as far as Cappadocia, where they waited and joined themselves to the Germans following with Peter.

The fame of the apostolic command swiftly flew through the whole world and moved those predestined from every people toward service in the army of the highest Messiah. That mighty thunderclap could not escape England and the other maritime islands, although the abyss of the wave-resounding sea separates them from the world. Indeed, the rapidly spreading report encouraged and armed Britons, Gascons, [Col. 0657C] and the remotest Galicians among humankind. Venetians, Pisans, Genoese, and those who lived along the shore of the Ocean or Mediterranean Sea covered the sea as they ploughed it with ships laden with arms and men, siege engines and provisions. Those who went by land covered the surface of the whole earth like locusts. In July Walter of Pexeio died at Finipoli in Bulgaria, and the sign of the holy cross appeared in his flesh after death. On hearing of this sign, the duke and bishop of the city went out; carrying Walter’s body reverently into the city with all the citizens, they buried it, and granted the other pilgrims access to the city, which they had previously forbidden, [Col. 0657D] and a market.

In the same year [1096], Hugh, count of Crépy, entrusted his land to his sons Ralph and Henry, gave his daughter Isabel to Count Robert of Meulan, and, setting out on pilgrimage, brought with him a noble company of Frenchmen. Then Stephen, count of Blois, son of Theobald, count of Chartres, who was son-in-law of William, king of the English, took up the Lord’s cross and departed on pilgrimage. Other counts and men of consular rank—Guy Trousseau, nephew of Guy, count of Rochefort; Milo of Bray; Centorius of Bière; Ralph of Baugency; [Col. 0658A] Everard of Puiset; William the Carpenter; Drogo of Monceaux; and many other magnates and renowned knights—went on pilgrimage for Christ’s love with many squadrons of Frenchmen.

Peter the Hermit, preceding the following host with many Germans and Frenchmen, had reached the imperial city. He found there many Lombards, Langobards, and Germans who had preceded him and were awaiting the coming army in accordance with the emperor’s reply. Meanwhile, the emperor ordered a market to be supplied for them, as was proper in the city. He also commanded them not to cross a certain arm of the sea, called the Arm of St George, until the very large army which followed had arrived. “For,” he said, “if you act otherwise, [Col. 0658B] savage heathens will rush upon you and destroy this unwarlike multitude.” This indeed happened later. For that people, without king or leader and gathered from diverse places, lived without discipline, greedily laid hands on others’ property, stripped and sold the lead with which churches had been roofed, destroyed palaces, and behaved wickedly in all things.

When he learned this, the emperor was very angry, since he had already found them ungrateful for his benefits. He therefore compelled them to be driven from the city and to cross the sea. After crossing, they again committed many unlawful acts against Christians. They ravaged their land like enemies and burned their houses and churches. At last they came to Nicomedia. The Ligurians and other peoples were separated there from the French. The French [Col. 0658C] were indeed fiercer and more unmanageable and therefore more inclined to every evil. The others set a certain Rainald over themselves and entered Romania under his command. Having advanced four days’ journey beyond Nicaea, they entered the castle of Exerogorgan and remained there for lodging. It was full of every kind of provision, but it is uncertain whether it had been left empty of inhabitants through fear or deliberately. There the Germans were surrounded by the Turks and almost annihilated, as will be made clear in what follows.

### V. Robert, duke of Normandy; Godfrey, duke of Lorraine; his brother Baldwin; Bohemond; Raymond, count of Toulouse; and very many magnates set out. — The first battles of those signed with the cross against the Turks.

[Col. 0658D]

In September Robert, duke of the Normans, entrusted Neustria to King William and, receiving from him ten thousand marks of silver, set out on pilgrimage, bringing with him a multitude of knights and foot soldiers terrible to his enemies. For there went with him Odo, his uncle, bishop of Bayeux; Philip, cleric and son of Count Roger; Rotrou, son of Geoffrey, count of Mortain; Walter of Saint-Valery, grandson through his daughter Papia of Richard the Younger, duke of the Normans; Gerard of Gournay; Ralph the Breton of Gaël; [Col. 0659A] Hugh, count of St Pol; Ivo and Alberic, sons of Hugh of Grandmesnil; and many other knights of outstanding valour.

Godfrey, duke of Lorraine; his brothers Baldwin and Eustace, count of Boulogne; Baldwin, count of Mons; Robert, margrave of Flanders, nephew of Matilda, queen of the English; and Rainald the German, with many thousands of armed men, left their possessions for Christ’s love. They gladly sought exile to confound the pagans and relieve Christians, and travelled with their troops through Hungary. Haimar, bishop of Le Puy, with Raymond of Toulouse, passed prosperously through Slavonia, and Bodin, king of the Slavs, treated them kindly. But Robert [Col. 0659B] the Norman, his brother-in-law Stephen of Blois, Hugh the Great, Robert of Flanders, and many others, after crossing the Alps, entered Italy; passing peacefully through the city of Rome, they wintered in Apulia and Calabria. Duke Roger, surnamed Borsa, honourably received the duke of Normandy and his companions as his natural lord and supplied them abundantly with necessities.

While Marquis Bohemond was besieging a certain castle with Roger, his uncle, count of Sicily, and heard of the movements of the dukes and of many peoples, he promptly inquired carefully into the prowess and badges of each. Having examined these closely, he at last ordered the finest cloak to be brought to him; he cut it into pieces and distributed a cross to each of his men, retaining one for himself. A vast crowd of knights therefore suddenly gathered around him, and old Roger was left almost alone at the siege; grieving that he had lost his people, he returned to Sicily with a few men. But Bohemond, provident and skilful, modestly prepared his route and transport, crossed the sea with his magnates and abundant armed forces, and at last arrived in the regions of Bulgaria under calm oars.

His chief companions were these: Tancred, son of Odo the Good Marquess; the count of Rosinolo with his brothers; Richard of the Principate and his brother Ranulf; Robert of Anza and Robert of Sourdeval; Robert, son of Turstan; Herman of Cannae; Humphrey, son of Ralph; Richard, son of Count Ranulf; Bartholomew Boel of Chartres; Albered of Cagnano; and Humphrey of Monte Scabioso. [Col. 0659D] All these adhered unanimously to Bohemond with their retainers and swore that they would most devoutly and inseparably obey him on God’s journey.

Hugh the Great and William, son of the Marquess, hurriedly embarked upon the sea at the port of Bari and, sailing, arrived at Dyrrachium. The duke of the city, thinking them great barons, ordered them seized and carefully brought under watchful guard to Constantinople before the emperor. Thus the flattering duke wished to commend himself to Caesar by faithless service [Col. 0660A] and to demonstrate his devotion toward him by such proofs.

Soliman, leader of the Turks, when he learned that Christians had come against the heathen, assembled a great army and besieged the castle of Exerogorgan, where the Germans were. The Turks hastened to surround the town and, when Rainald came out with his men to lay an ambush for those approaching, put him to flight in battle. Then many Christians fell by the sword. Those who could escape by flight withdrew into the castle. Once it was surrounded on every side, the enemies immediately cut off the water from those shut in. The spring and well by which the castle was supplied lay outside; a legion of Turks, strongly posted around both, watched them unceasingly. Thus the besieged endured the extreme hardship of thirst [Col. 0660B] for eight days; but, distressed by the enormity of their sins and hardness of heart, they did not deserve God’s help. At last their leader conferred with the Turks and arranged, if possible, the betrayal of his brethren. Rainald therefore, pretending to go out to battle, departed with many men and fled as a deserter to the Turks. The rest, compelled, made a disgraceful surrender and, despairing, committed an abominable apostasy against God. But those who bore witness to their faith suffered capital sentence: they were either set up as targets and shot with arrows, or separated from one another and sold cheaply, or carried away into captivity with Count Berthold.

On the third day before the Kalends of October [29 September 1096], the Christians suffered this first persecution [Col. 0660C]; and thus the Germans and other peoples were led captive into Chorosan or Aleppo. But those who remained steadfast in the faith of Christ found rest in a glorious end. The Franks had already advanced far ahead and entered the city of Chevetot, which Emperor Alexius had recently begun to build and had intended to hand over to the English who had fled from the face of William the Bastard; but, prevented by the Turks, he had left it unfinished. Soliman, however, elated by his defeat of the Allobroges and Germans, approached Chevetot, near Nicaea, secure in his triumph, with his men, who now thirsted for nothing but blood, and rushed upon the Gauls with great force.

For Peter had already returned to Constantinople, because his company refused to obey him [Col. 0660D]. The unbridled Turks suddenly came up, encountered the distinguished knight Walter, leader of the army, and his fellow soldiers, and easily cut him down with many others, because they were unprepared. They wounded his brother William and some others. There too they beheaded a certain priest of the Lord as he devoutly celebrated the rites of Mass. Those who could escape alive fled into the city or hid in thickets, woods, or mountains. But the few who held the fortress in order to defend themselves killed many of the besiegers. The Turks brought together a great quantity of wood from every direction and prepared to set fire to the fortress and its occupants. The Christians, now brought to the uttermost extremity of despair, became more courageous and boldly hurled firebrands onto the wood [Col. 0661A]. Thus they escaped the fire. Very many on both sides perished, and this happened in October.

Many of the pilgrims returned as fugitives and reported their misfortunes to those who were still encamped on this side of Byzantium. The emperor bought all their weapons, so that, being unarmed, they might do less harm to the inhabitants in a foreign land. The others waited for one another, so that, after taking counsel together, relying upon auxiliary leaders and supported by military forces, they might make themselves acceptable to God through prayers and confessions, and thus enter the land of their enemies.

After Soliman had overcome the Franks, slaughtered some in battle, and sent very many others into captivity, he besieged the few who were resisting most fiercely in the city [Col. 0661B]. But on the following day, when reliable informants told him that Duke Bohemond had invaded Macedonia against the emperor and had armed a huge army of Normans and Apulians against the Turks to avenge Christian blood, he was greatly frightened. He left Chevetot and swiftly withdrew his forces to defend his own land. Thus the rash Gauls disdained to await the assistance of Bohemond and the other faithful men; placing excessive confidence in their own strength, they approached the Turkish frontiers and there, by God’s permission, as we have said, were worn down in a grievous battle.

## VI. The Various Routes of the Crusaders. The Treachery of the Greeks

[Col. 0661C] Duke Godfrey, the first of all the dukes, came to Constantinople and encamped near it on the tenth day before the Kalends of January [23 December 1096]. Bohemond, however, waited for his followers who were striving to join him; he advanced slowly, cunningly awaiting them day by day as he travelled. Soon afterward Emperor Alexius ordered lodging to be provided for the duke in a suburb of the city. The squires of the ducal army obtained provisions for themselves in the customary way; they rode securely outside the city to fetch straw and other necessities. But Turcopoles and Pincenati, lying in ambush by the emperor’s command, killed them daily. They did not yet suspect anything unfavourable of the emperor, since he had voluntarily provided them lodging.

The duke was deeply distressed by the loss of his men [Col. 0661D] and by the unexpected ambushes of the Turcopoles. Baldwin therefore went out to protect his men, found the enemies pursuing them, attacked the unsuspecting men by surprise, overcame them, killed some, and presented sixty captives to his brother. When the emperor heard this, he became very angry and began to devise evil against the pilgrims. The prudent duke, guarding against treachery, left the city and again pitched his camp where he had first set up his tents. When night came, the duke’s camp was attacked by Caesar’s order, and his army was subjected to many injuries. The most shrewd duke and fiercest warrior feared stratagems; he had wisely stationed sentries to keep watch over the tents and commanded every man to remain alert [Col. 0662A]. The attackers were speedily repulsed; after seven of them had been killed, the duke boldly pursued the fugitives as far as the city gate. Then he returned to his tents and remained there five days.

Meanwhile the emperor was thinking how to plot evil against the duke, while the duke anxiously took counsel for himself and his men. The emperor prevented him from passing through the imperial city; the duke awaited the arrival of the nobles who were following. At length the perceptive and energetic emperor, leaving no measure untried, made peace with the duke: if he crossed the Arm, he would always send him an abundant market and supply all who were in need with the necessary assistance—provided only that he could be secured by an oath from him. The crafty man devised this [Col. 0662B] in order to remove the duke and his forces from the Byzantine region, lest he be able to make use of the counsel and assistance of the princes who were yet to arrive. The duke accordingly crossed over, repeatedly pledging fidelity to Caesar and receiving the same pledge from him.

Bohemond came into the valley of Andronopolis, and there diligently exhorted his men in an address to conduct themselves cautiously; to remember the pilgrimage undertaken for God; to restrain their greedy hands from plundering the homes of Christians; to keep God always present before their eyes; and for the richer to aid the poor and the stronger the weak, supporting them with their strength and resources for the love of God. At last they reached Castoria from the valley, where they solemnly celebrated the Nativity of the Lord [Col. 0662C]. They remained there for several days but could not obtain the market they sought, because the citizens regarded them not as pilgrims but as gladiators and tyrants. Compelled by hunger, they were forced to seize oxen, horses, and asses, and whatever else suitable for eating they could find.

After leaving Castoria, they encamped in Pelagonia. There they attacked from every side a very strongly fortified castle of heretics—[Note: [Col. 0661D] That is, Greeks.]—abundantly stocked with every good thing, utterly destroyed it, and burned its inhabitants together with it. For all these travellers equally hated Jews, heretics, and Saracens, all of whom they called God’s enemies. From there they came to the River Vardar, which Bohemond crossed with part of his army [Col. 0662D]. But the Count of Rosinolo remained behind with his brothers. Immediately the emperor’s troops, who watched the roads and lay in wait as scouts, saw that the army was divided and rushed upon the count and his men.

Tancred, who was not yet far away, learned of the disturbance, urged his swift horse with his spurs, flew to them like lightning, crossed—or rather swam—the river between them, and promptly brought the count assistance. At once two thousand knights followed Tancred across the stream; they quickly overcame the Turcopoles, drove them from the battle, and gloriously triumphed over the fugitives. They killed some and bound many more whom they had captured [Col. 0663A], presenting them to Bohemond. When asked why they acted so wickedly, since he was not hostile to their emperor, they answered: “Stationed at the emperor’s command, we can do nothing other than what he commands.” This unwilling war was waged against the pilgrims on the fourth weekday, at the beginning of the fast [18 February 1097].

Though angered by Caesar’s wickedness, Bohemond restrained himself. He released the captives without punishment but checked them with threats, lest they thereafter harm his men. “We,” he said to his close companions, “who are about to pass through the emperor’s territory, must curb our swelling anger and, so far as we can, avoid provoking him unjustly. It is the height of folly for a man to spend all his breath where an aroused mind will achieve no result [Col. 0663B]. Yet it is the measure of prudence for a man subject to power to conceal himself when his own power cannot satisfy his desire. It is prudent to defer until its time what one cannot accomplish immediately. Again, he deserves rebuke for sluggishness and cowardice who, when he can do no more, thunders threats, but when he can act, forgets the wrong that was done him. If we can, let us overcome the emperor with benefits; if not, let us calmly overlook the evils inflicted upon us.” So he spoke, silently contained his anger, and sent envoys to the emperor to obtain security for the pilgrims of Jesus Christ.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1097, in the fifth indiction, Robert, Duke of the Normans, Hugh the Great [Col. 0663C], Stephen of Blois, Robert of Flanders, and other nobles who had set out from many provinces and wintered in Italy with their companies, made ready eagerly. In the mild spring they crossed the Adriatic Sea and joined Bohemond in Macedonia. When such nobility assembled in one place and incomparable virtue offered itself without pretence for God’s work, there was great rejoicing among all those present who feared God.

But Emperor Alexius, who had long since experienced the arms of the men from beyond the Alps to his great cost, was exceedingly alarmed when he heard of the arrival of such great barons. Having discerned the method by which he might escape danger, he attempted to deceive them by treachery under a guise of peace. For he was shrewd and eloquent, generous, and an ingenious artist in deceit. Therefore he sent envoys [Col. 0663D] to the noble pilgrims, humbly requested peace from them, and promised on oath to give them free passage through his land, together with the necessary business arrangements and aid.

But Duke Bohemond, who had long known his frauds well and had twice defeated him in war, did not accept his feigned promises. Instead, he vigorously urged his companions to besiege Constantinople, clearly showing by many plausible arguments that this would be most advantageous to them. The Franks, however, said: “We have left behind our wealth and willingly undertaken this pilgrimage, in order, for Christ’s love, to confound the pagans and liberate Christians. But the Greeks are Christians [Col. 0664A]. Therefore let us make peace with them and restore to them what the Turks have taken away.”

Thus the shrewd Bohemond was compelled by the Franks’ counsel to make peace with the emperor of the Greeks, to the great harm of Christians, as later became clear. When approached, the emperor strove with flattering gestures to show favour to our people. He sent Corpalatium, a man very close to him, with other envoys to Bohemond, that they might conduct him safely through that land and furnish them everywhere with a market. Then, as circumstances required, they pitched camp from place to place and came by way of the city of Serra to the city of Rusa. There, the Greeks having supplied all necessities adequately, they pitched their tents on the fourth weekday before the Lord’s Supper [Wednesday of Holy Week, 1097; Col. 0664B].

Bohemond left his people there and went with a few men to speak with the emperor. Tancred led Christians impoverished by the expedition by another route into a fertile valley rich in bodily sustenance, where they celebrated the Lord’s Passover. Alexius, hearing that Bohemond had arrived—the man he greatly feared, having twice been defeated by him in battle—received him honourably and supplied him abundantly outside the city, as befitted them both.

Meanwhile Duke Godfrey, having left his companions beyond the Arm, had returned to Constantinople because the emperor was sending none of the market provisions he had promised. The Bishop of Le Puy and the Count of Toulouse, having again left their multitude behind them, were present [Col. 0664C]. The emperor, on the advice of the Greeks, who greatly feared that the Franks, if gathered together, might rise against them and deprive them of their goods, addressed each leader through intermediaries and demanded homage and fealty from them. If they did so, he promised them a market and a safe conduct, and that he himself would follow after them and aid them with all his forces.

The Franks were hard pressed and did not wish to swear; nor would the Pelasgians otherwise permit them passage. The Franks did not wish to fight Christians, yet they could not obtain peaceful passage. They abhorred returning home with the task for which they had come unfinished. Finally, compelled by many necessities, they swore to Emperor Alexius his life and honour [Col. 0664D], that they would take neither from him, so long as he faithfully observed what he had sworn. The Count of Toulouse resisted more than the others; indeed, restlessly he considered how he might avenge himself upon the emperor. Nevertheless, the common judgment of the leaders prevailed, and they scarcely recalled the high-spirited count from this purpose. He swore, therefore, but was never brought to perform homage. Immediately orders were given for embarkation.

Meanwhile Tancred had arrived with the army committed to him. Hearing that Alexius had required an oath from the elders, he hid among the common people with Richard of the Principate and hurried across in swift ships. Bohemond and the Count of Toulouse [Col. 0665A] remained until they were supplied with market provisions. Duke Godfrey came with the others to Nicomedia and remained there three days with Tancred. Then the duke, learning that no road lay open by which so many and such great peoples could advance, sent three thousand men to level the precipitous places of cliffs and mountains. Taking axes, adzes, mattocks, and many other tools, they cleared thickets and brushwood, levelled the mountain steep places, and prepared a road for the army. They set up high markers which those following might recognize, lest they go astray; thus they reached Nicaea in Bithynia.

## VII. The Capture of Nicaea. The Advance of the Crusaders’ Vast Army. Battles against the Turks

[Col. 0665B] Having encamped on the day before the Nones of May [6 May], and having positioned the tents of the westerners, they besieged Nicaea, capital of all Romania, a city most strongly fortified. Its walls, rising toward heaven, and the adjoining lake surrounding one side of the city, made it appear impregnable. At first the shortage of bread was so disastrous, before the emperor sent them a market, that whenever a single loaf could be found, it was bought for twenty or thirty denarii. But God provided for His own: Bohemond quickly arrived and brought up an abundant army by land and sea. Thus an unforeseen abundance of provisions suddenly arose throughout Christ’s army.

On the feast of the Lord’s Ascension they began [Col. 0665C] to assault the city and to erect wooden engines against the height of its walls. For two days they fiercely attacked the city and attempted to undermine the wall. The pagans within, on the other hand, pressed on bravely, defended their walls and homes with great force, hurled stones and missiles, sheltered behind shields, and boldly exposed themselves to the descending storm of weapons. Opposite them, the Gauls left nothing unattempted, hid beneath the tortoise-shell formation of interlocked shields, thereby evaded the downpour of missiles, and repeatedly harassed the exhausted besieged.

Meanwhile the citizens sent messengers and summoned help from their fellow tribesmen and relatives, saying: “Hurry! Enter confidently by the southern gate, which as yet is free from every siege; fear nothing!” But, with God’s help [Col. 0665D], events turned out very differently for those who expected this. On that very day, namely the Saturday after the Lord’s Ascension, the Bishop of Le Puy and the Count of Toulouse arrived there, and the southern gate was entrusted to them by the other princes. The count, unexpectedly confronting the Saracens as they came confidently forward, met them armed; his entire army, splendid in arms, courageously repelled barbarian folly. The Saracens, having lost many of their men, fled shamefully and were easily defeated by the Franks.

The citizens of Nicaea again summoned their neighbours, confirming by oath their certainty of victory. The latter therefore came boldly with ropes, by which they imagined that they would take Christians captive and bind them for their own country. But the Franks met the approaching heathen in close formation, attacked them again [Col. 0666A], defeated and routed them, and returned victorious after killing many. Then Count Raymond and Bishop Aimar laboured greatly with their armies and assailed the city in many ways, while the besieged citizens opposed them with all their strength.

At last the Christian leaders assembled and besieged Nicaea, the Bithynian city, in the following disposition. On one side Bohemond and Tancred besieged it; beside them stood Duke Godfrey with his brothers. Next was Robert, Count of Flanders, a vigorous man and most daring knight. Beside him were Robert, Duke of the Normans, Stephen, Count of Chartres, Hugh, Count of Saint-Pol, Conan the Breton, son of Count Geoffrey [Col. 0666B], Ralph of Gael, Roger of Barneville, and their companies. At the southern gate the Count of Toulouse and the Bishop of Le Puy kept watch. Thus they had surrounded the city so that no one could enter or leave, except by the lake which encircled it. For, in full sight of the Christians, the pagans sailed safely across the lake and conveyed by ship whatever they needed.

Yet Christ’s army commendably besieged Nicaea, wisely arranging its splendid camps and imposing tents in Christ’s name. The Christians shone in arms and were especially becoming in the adornment of their conduct. Pure in habits, vigorous in body, and courageous in heart, they served as soldiers. They guarded their souls and renounced every unlawful thing arising from the desires and pleasures of the flesh [Col. 0666C]. The leaders themselves served as soldiers; while disposing all matters and encouraging the others, they themselves kept watch. There was a great community of all goods among them. Each day bishops preached continence and condemned every prostitute and abuse from the midst of the camp.

Meanwhile the Turks laboured to defend the city and went and returned safely across the lake in sight of the Christians. The Franks, distressed, devised a way to take the lake from them. They sent envoys to Constantinople and diligently informed the emperor what, in their judgment, should be done against the enemy. As soon as the emperor heard their request, he assented and ordered everything to be done in accordance with their plan. By the emperor’s command, oxen were quickly brought [Col. 0666D], and sailing vessels reached the harbour of Chevetot. Turcopoles also arrived. Boats were placed upon wagons and, with oxen serving this operation, laboriously drawn to the lake shore. When night fell upon the land, the vessels were launched into the lake and entrusted to the Turcopoles. At daybreak, the ships, ploughing the lake in ordered formation, made for the city.

Seeing from afar the lake covered with ships, the citizens marvelled and supposed that perhaps aid had come to them. But once they learned the truth, they stiffened with fear, became bloodless, and despaired. All had happened contrary to their expectation, and they were dismayed by the sudden reversal. For a city besieged by land and lake, no hope of safety remained. Therefore they sent envoys to the emperor [Col. 0667A], earnestly begging him to spare the now conquered people, receive the surrendered city, and protect it as his own from enemies, lest their property become booty for foreigners.

When the emperor heard this, secretly begrudging the Christians’ success, as the outcome later proved, yet satisfying the embassy of the besieged, he commanded Tatano, commander of the army—whom he had earlier appointed to go before our men with forty thousand troops—and his other officers to conduct safely to Byzantium those surrendering themselves and their goods, and carefully to arrange for the preservation of the city. Everything was done in accordance with the emperor’s command: the city was surrendered, and the pagan people were conveyed unharmed to the imperial city.

The emperor received the defeated people with the honour of freedom, maintained them with great generosity [Col. 0667B], and gave many gifts to poor Christians. Once the city had been surrendered, the Christians withdrew from the siege. Many indeed died there from hunger, the sword, or some other destruction; these, as we believe, were crowned with the blessed martyr’s wreath, because they gave their bodies for compassion toward their brethren. Many pagans too were slaughtered by various fates, and their unburied corpses lay scattered everywhere.

The Christians stayed there seven weeks and three days; when the city had been handed over, they directed their sorrowful steps elsewhere. They regretted the long siege because they had not obtained dominion over the city according to the custom of a subjugated city. For if at least the enemy’s resources had been confiscated, the poverty of the needy would have been relieved and the expenses consumed somewhat restored. The Christians did not patiently endure Alexius’s order forbidding the confiscation of the possessions of Nicaea [Col. 0667C], where they had long spent their resources in vain, shed their blood, and diminished beyond measure the wealth they had brought. Thus they experienced the emperor’s deceitful conduct to their loss. Yet, because they could achieve nothing at that time, they kept silent for the present.

Here the seedbed of hatreds first appeared; here the nourishment of enmities became known; here the incentives of discord began to sprout; here the shapes of rivalries seemed to grow. For because Alexius had not acted rightly toward them, they began to consider vengeance against him.

On the day on which the siege of Nicaea was lifted, they reached a certain bridge [Col. 0667D], where the Christian people pitched their tents. They stayed there two days, and on the third, before daylight, set out in haste. Because the night was dark, they followed an uncertain road without knowing it. Thus separated from one another, they completed two days’ journey.

Bohemond, Robert the Norman, Stephen Count of Blois, Tancred, Hugh of Saint-Pol, Gerard of Gournay, Walter of Saint-Valery and his son Bernard, William son of Ranulf the viscount, William de Ferrières, Hervey son of Dodeman, Conan son of Count Geoffrey, Ralph of Gael and his son Alan, Riou of Lohéac, Alan the seneschal of Dol, and many others were in one division. In the other were the Count of Toulouse [Col. 0668A] and the Bishop of Le Puy, Duke Godfrey, Baldwin, Hugh the Great, and Robert of Flanders, with abundant columns of travellers.

That same week, Turks as innumerable as the sand of the sea gathered against Bohemond. Trusting in their great multitude, they unanimously attacked the Christians. Their leader was Dalimannus, and rage against the foreigners animated them because the latter had dared to capture Nicaea and ravage their possessions. There were Turks, Saracens, Persians, and Agulani; their number was reckoned at 360,000, besides Arabs, whose gathering was beyond calculation.

But the noble Bohemond, when he saw the innumerable multitude of enemies threaten and assail his men with rabid mouths and savage swords [Col. 0668B], stood undismayed. In a short but most wise address he admonished his men and commendably strengthened them for an honourable contest. He quickly ordered his companions, who had moved some distance away, to hurry to help them in their great need. He commanded the infantry to pitch the tents vigorously and wisely, and the knights to advance with him to meet the pagans in battle and endure tirelessly the labour of fighting.

Meanwhile the Turks came shouting and attacked the Christians most fiercely with arrows, javelins, and close combat. No rest was given to the exhausted men; one could see all Christian bodies flowing with blood or sweat. Conversely, the Franks bore the burden of battle unceasingly, prudently deferred charges against the enemy at times [Col. 0668C], sometimes resisted with their swords, waited for their summoned companions, and did not falter in any respect. They endured this violence of combat from the third hour of the day until the ninth.

That day women were especially necessary to the combatants. They swiftly offered water to the thirsty and strengthened the fighters through exhortation. The field of Mars glowed hot; both sides fought with all their strength. The Christians were hard pressed, for they were frequently attacked in their very camp. The other army distrusted Bohemond’s envoys and doubted whether there was truly a battle. It could not believe that any people would dare breathe for battle against even a tenth part of its army. Yet after this report spread throughout the whole army [Col. 0668D], and envoys were added to envoys, Duke Godfrey, a most fierce knight, Count Stephen, a prudent and moderate man, Hugh the Great, Baldwin, and Eustace flew fearlessly to the aid of their fellow soldiers. The Bishop of Le Puy followed behind, together with Raymond, Count of Toulouse.

The hearts of the exhausted Christians marvelled at the source from which so great and sudden a host had unexpectedly poured upon them. The mountains and valleys were covered, and every level place was crowded with dense wedges of troops. With God’s help the Christians fought bravely; the matter was decided only by drawn swords wielded for death. The companions whom they had summoned arrived suddenly. The Bishop of Le Puy, with his great army [Col. 0669A], took the enemy in the rear. On another side the Count of Saint-Gilles, Baldwin, and Eustace rode forward swiftly. On the right Duke Godfrey charged, together with Hugh the Great and Robert of Flanders, a knight most active in every respect. Robert the Norman, Stephen of Blois, Tancred, and Bohemond fought on and had long borne the burden of battle.

The pagans, astonished because they were unexpectedly pressed by enemies in front and behind, entrusted themselves to flight and turned their backs to those striking them. The Christian sword cut them down to destruction, and many met death in many ways. Those who could do so hid themselves. Thousands of barbarians were killed there, for the Christians fell fiercely upon men who had cruelly pursued them throughout the day [Col. 0669B].

William the Marquis, Tancred’s brother, and Geoffrey of Mont-Scabieux, men greatly experienced in war, of good character and distinguished, fell, as did many others, knights and foot soldiers. For the Turks, exceedingly powerful in cunning, possess bold hearts and fight with untiring swords. They inflict death upon enemies at long range very frequently, because they employ bows and rely on many instruments of war. They boast that they derive their genealogy from the stock of the Franks and that their forefathers departed from Christianity. They also say that no one is naturally fitted for warfare except themselves and the Franks. This battle took place on the Kalends of July [1 July 1097], and the day was solemnly celebrated with devout praises to almighty God, who orders all things well [Col. 0669C].

Once the heathen had thus been overthrown and driven far away, the Christians turned to plundering their tents and found there a great abundance of gold and silver. In their pavilions they discovered draught animals, mules and horses, oxen and camels, sheep and asses, and plentiful household goods. Laden with diverse treasures, they returned to their own people in triumph and with inexpressible joy. The report of so great a victory began to frighten distant and foreign nations and to pour the name of Christianity into the ears of remote peoples. All and each feared the glorious deeds of the Christians and their army that was approaching them.

## VIII. New Battles. The Capture of Iconium and Heraclea

Soliman, fleeing from Nicaea, found ten thousand Arabs [Col. 0669D] and gave them a splendid account of the exceeding valour, courage, unconquered strength, multitude, and most richly equipped array of the Christians; by this report he compelled them all to flee with him. Yet, as human ingenuity devises many things and meditates vain schemes, the Turks contrived a stratagem harmful to the simple worshippers of Christ. Soliman and other pagans came to cities or castles inhabited by Syrian Christians and deceitfully said to them: “We have defeated the Franks; they have utterly perished, and any who remain are hidden in holes.” In this manner they addressed the unsuspecting people and were admitted within their gates. Once inside the towns of those who knew nothing [Col. 0670A], they plundered houses and churches. They carried off everything precious and desirable, sons and daughters alike. Thus, deceiving people everywhere, they forestalled the Franks’ arrival.

When the Christians heard these things, they pursued them. They entered a waterless and uninhabitable land, where they suffered from hunger and thirst almost to death. If they happened to find unripe grain, they plucked the ears, rubbed them, chewed them, and swallowed them. Many men died there, as did draught animals; many glorious knights were compelled to go on foot. Those who could do so yoked oxen to carry themselves or their possessions in place of vehicles. Not long afterward they entered a very fertile land, full of provisions and every good thing, except that they could not replace their lost horses [Col. 0670B].

Arriving at Iconium, at the persuasion of the inhabitants they filled their skins with water; after completing a day’s journey, they came to a certain river, where they lodged two days and recovered their strength. Scouts, who always went before the army to make provision for it and to seize straw and other necessities, advanced to the city of Heraclea. There a large assembly of Turks waited in case it could harm the Christians. They had laid ambushes for the scouts, but the Franks boldly attacked them and readily scattered the fugitives. Thus, after the Turks had been expelled, Heraclea was quickly brought under Christian dominion, and they spent four days there.

There Tancred and Baldwin separated themselves from the others and entered the valley of Botentrot with their forces [Col. 0670C].

Tancred, again separated from Baldwin, came to Tarsus with his knights. The Turks came out from the city and met them, prepared to resist. Tancred, a man indeed of extraordinary courage, bravely struck down those who attacked as enemies, drove them back in flight into the city, and besieged it. When night followed, the Turks fled, and at the very onset of night the citizens cried aloud: “Franks, conquerors and lords of the world! The Turks have withdrawn; the city lies open—come! Run, most invincible Franks, to receive the city! Run; do not delay! Why do you linger?”

The sentries of the camp heard this clearly. But because it was night, counsel and action were postponed until daylight [Col. 0670D]. At dawn the leading citizens came, surrendering themselves and their possessions to the Christians and choosing Tancred as their lord. There a great quarrel arose between the princes. Baldwin, whose army had greater numbers, was wholly intent on plundering the inhabitants’ goods or claiming half the city. Tancred, however, being moderate by nature, preferred to lack dominion over the city rather than plunder the property of citizens who had kindly entrusted themselves to him. He therefore gave his men the signal and, with trumpets sounding, departed somewhat embittered; Baldwin alone occupied all Tarsus.

Without delay two excellent cities, Azera—[Note: [Col. 0669D] Adana.]—and Mamistra, together with very many castles [Col. 0671A], surrendered to Tancred. Other Armenian nobles had entered the land with their armies. At their arrival the city of Alfia was surrendered, and the inhabitants of that land entrusted it to a military man named Simeon to defend. The main army came to Caesarea of Cappadocia, which had been destroyed down to the ground. Yet the surviving ruins still testified to how great it had been.

Plastencia, a beautiful city, rich in fertile soil, which the Turks had besieged three weeks earlier but had been wholly unable to capture because it was impregnable, immediately opened itself gladly to the Christians. Peter of Alfia sought this city and readily obtained it from the nobles, to defend and conquer the land in fidelity to the Holy Sepulchre and Christianity [Col. 0671B]. Bohemond, an energetic man in military affairs, summoned such of his own knights as he wished and diligently pursued the Turks who had besieged Plastencia and were marching not far ahead in order to cause harm; but he did so in vain, because he could not find them.

They came to Coxon, a noble and wealthy city, which its inhabitants gladly surrendered to the Christians, their brethren. There the weary army rested three days. The Count of Toulouse was told that the Turks who had been guarding Antioch had departed in flight. Therefore, after consulting with his men, he selected persons to send ahead in order to investigate the route diligently and reconnoitre everything else carefully. Men of standing and skilled in military discipline were sent for this purpose: the Viscount of Châtillon [Col. 0671C], William of Montpellier, Peter of Roasa, and Peter Raymond, with many knights, came into the valley of Antioch and learned there a different report. For the Turks were making abundant preparations to defend the city.

Peter of Roasa, separating from the others, entered the valley of Rugia; finding a great many Turks, he dealt them a severe blow, overcame them, and put them to flight. When the Armenians heard of the Christians’ favorable successes and likewise of the pagans’ frequent reverses, they surrendered to Peter the city of Rusa and certain castles. The main army undertook a difficult route. There they advanced slowly through exceedingly rough and rocky mountains, where, in distress, they suffered remarkable losses. They were dashed against and battered about, struggling [Col. 0671D] and failing along the trackless road. Horses slipped into a vast precipice. Many, having there lost their horses or pack-animals together with the goods loaded upon them, were impoverished. When they had scarcely escaped those calamitous straits, they turned aside to a certain city called Marafim. Its inhabitants brought the men of our side an abundant market supply. They remained there for a while, until they had somewhat recovered their strength. After this they entered a famous, broad, and fertile valley, in which lies the royal and renowned city of Antioch, the metropolis and chief city of all Syria, where Peter, chief of the apostles, held his episcopal see. Now, by God’s hidden judgment, though a just one, very many churches in it have been destroyed and irreverently applied to certain human uses.

As the scouts drew near the Iron Bridge, they found innumerable Turks hastening to reinforce Antioch. Therefore, making a sudden attack upon them—for the Christians always travelled armed—they unexpectedly engaged and threw them into confusion. Having destroyed many, they brought back to their own camp, which they had pitched on the banks of the river, the Turks’ mules, which they were leading to their city heavily laden in many ways with provisions and various treasures. There was therefore immense rejoicing in the camp, both for the victory and for the rich spoils which the scouts had brought back. Thus they daily and continually rendered praises and thanks to God, who so excellently protected them among heathen battle-lines while, for love of Him, they lived far from their native land as exiles.

## IX. The Siege of Antioch

[Col. 0672B]

Bohemond, never yielding to idleness or sleep—for he was a restless man—came stealthily and cautiously with four thousand soldiers near the gate of Antioch, waiting in case any persons might secretly enter or leave.

At earliest dawn the army struck the tents from the place where they had been; it approached Antioch on Wednesday, the twelfth day before the Kalends of November [21 October], pitched its tents, and stoutly besieged the city from three gates until the third day before the Nones of June [3 June]. For it was not besieged on the other side, since that side was hemmed in by cliffs and mountains so extended and inaccessible that no one could approach there, nor was the place susceptible of siege. Excessive fear seized [Col. 0672C] the Antiochenes and all the inhabitants round about, and none of them dared await an encounter with the scouts. Accordingly, for nearly fifteen days they kept quiet.

The land adjoining Antioch, being a fertile valley, was most productive: full of vineyards, pleasant with fruits and crops, wooded with trees, rich in gardens, and abundant in pasture. Many Armenians and Syrians from the city—Christians, but subject to the Turks—pretended flight and boldly went out into the camp. Begging, they reconnoitred the state of the camp; returning, they reported it to the Turks, and so did the Christians much harm. The Antiochenes therefore, having learned the plans of the camp, gradually began to venture forth boldly, to hem in the pilgrims by attacks, slaughter the unwary, and harass them with plundering and other stratagems. Thus [Col. 0672D] they blocked every road round about and shut off from the Christians everything from sea and mountain country. Those outside were therefore more grievously besieged than those who lay concealed within.

From a nearby and rather strongly fortified castle called Arech, the Turks rushed upon the Christians, and many had perished through the ambushes of the natives. The Christian leaders, therefore, compassionately concerned, went out to meet the Turks, challenged them to battle, and, feigning flight, deliberately withdrew to the place where Bohemond and his men lay concealed in ambush. There two thousand Christians were slain. Then Bohemond, a most valiant warrior, swiftly rose from ambush and attacked the Turks, killing many and taking some alive. These he solemnly beheaded before the city gate as a spectacle. Then the men in camp built a castle on the summit of the mountain called Maregard, which, in the succession of days, each of the leaders guarded in turn according to his allotted watch.

Meanwhile provisions grew scarce, because they neither dared make foraging raids nor had a market. What they had found in the valley they had consumed lavishly. All foodstuffs were therefore exceedingly expensive; famine became dreadful, since fodder failed day after day, while the adversaries inside jeered and rejoiced.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1097, in the fifth indiction, after the celebration of Christ’s Nativity, Duke Bohemond and Robert of Flanders set out, not without the tears of those remaining behind; and more than twenty thousand horsemen and foot soldiers with them spread out through [Col. 0673B] the settlements of the Saracens. Arabs and Turks from Jerusalem and Damascus, and from towns in many other regions, had assembled to aid Antioch. When they heard that the Christians were dispersed throughout their territory, they rejoiced greatly, hoping certainly to prevail against them, since they believed them few and foreign. Therefore, in the dead of night, they arranged two battle-lines in ambush, one in front and the other behind.

The warlike Count of Flanders and Bohemond rushed unanimously upon them at dawn; invoking the name of Jesus and bearing the sign of the cross, they fought most steadfastly, and many pagans died. Yet the Christians gained little wealth from their spoils, because they had no leisure either to pursue or plunder them. [Col. 0673C] Meanwhile, the Turks who were stationed in the city’s garrison, hearing that Bohemond had departed, came out boldly and were already ranging through the camp itself. For they had reconnoitred which tents seemed weaker. One day they burst unanimously into the camp and struck the Christians at close quarters, not yet knowing that their own people had been defeated. That day the Ishmaelites raged violently in the camp, and many Christians were killed. Among them fell the standard-bearer of Le Puy. Had it not been for muddy rough ground separating the city from the camp and allowing no passage, or only a difficult one, they would have ridden down the tents with loose reins and wreaked havoc among the Christian people, who had already somewhat languished.

Bohemond, returning after the Saracen battle had been concluded, [Col. 0673D] but finding little to plunder, ascended other mountains. Yet the land had already been reduced to such desolation that many returned empty-handed. Their labor had therefore been in vain, except that they had solemnly triumphed over the Turks. But no victory extinguishes hunger where everything fit for eating is lacking. Joy lasts but little when want of bread brings sorrow. They returned to the camp, which dreadful starvation afflicted. The Armenians and Syrians, insatiably greedy for profit, seeing that the Christians had returned empty-handed, hurried to suitable and more distant places; purchasing whatever food they found, they brought it to the camp and sold at a high price what they had bought cheaply. The pestilence of disease infected the camp.

[Col. 0674A] The wealthier gave many gifts to those in need and begging from door to door; nevertheless, for many days they could not sustain so many thousands. Some therefore planned to slip away from the camp. William the Carpenter and Peter the Hermit fled secretly; Tancred found and seized them, rebuked them disgracefully, and compelled them to return to the army. Then Bohemond brought them before himself, restrained them with shameful words, and punished them with fitting forced services. At that time men and horses suffered alike from hardship and wavered in despair of escape. The Christians’ horses had failed so badly that, in that great and entire army, scarcely a thousand knights could be found who had mounts. Tatanus, a Greek by nation and commander of the emperor’s guards, grew pale from fear of death amid so many disasters. Promising his companions much that would be useful, he undertook an embassy to the Emperor and, having departed, never afterward returned to them.

[Col. 0674B] He gave Alexius Caesar a vivid account of the valor and loyalty, and the manifold sufferings, of those besieging the city; and he summoned Guy, son of Duke Guiscard, and the distinguished Frankish nobles who followed with many companions, though they were being honorably detained by the Emperor at Constantinople, to hasten to their allies. On hearing reliable reports, the emperor assembled a huge army and set out with many forces to assist the worshippers of Christ. But through evil counsels, as we shall relate later, he did not bring his good undertaking to completion.

Meanwhile the impoverished people secretly departed, going [Col. 0674C] wherever they thought they might survive. No one dared approach the sea, because roads and pathless places were guarded. Then once more a fresh report spread abroad: innumerable Turks were coming, and the onset of death was immediately threatening all. They were so many that even a broad expanse stretching in every direction for many stadia would scarcely contain them. The bloodless Christians turned pale, and many hung their drooping heads. Yet the nobility dared deliberate about battle. All the leaders had assembled and encouraged one another. Seeing this, prudent Bohemond warmly congratulated them; setting forth wise counsel, he urged them eloquently to battle. He ordered the foot soldiers to remain in camp and carefully watch the city gates [Col. 0674D] lest, once they were opened, the citizens might range about freely.

All the knights, armed with invocation of the name of the Lord Jesus and fortified by Holy Communion, left the camp amid much lamentation from both groups. Neither side trusted in itself: neither priest nor woman, commoner nor soldier. Neither these nor those hoped ever again to enjoy one another’s sight. Both sides rushed into their loved ones’ kisses, and all were moved to tears. The knights encamped between the river, called in ancient times Daphnes, which flows past Antioch, and the lake. They had heard that the Turks had assembled at Arech castle beyond the Iron Bridge. The energetic Christian leaders gathered before dawn, [Col. 0675A] and as the first light of dawn appeared, they sent forward experienced scouts. Swiftly returning, these cried out that the Turks were present and had drawn up two numerous battle-lines. For they had seen them advancing from the other bank of the river.

Then the Christian princes discussed how to arrange the battle and entrusted the matter to Bohemond. Six battle-lines were accordingly drawn up. Five of them advanced to bear the weight of battle and effectively drive back the enemy host by striking it. Bohemond, with his own line, moved slowly last, intending to watch over and support all; and, should the Turks prevail against the foremost lines, to receive the full violence of battle. Trumpets sounded; bugles echoed. The shouting of both multitudes was heard, and a most fierce contest was fought on either side. Both armies pressed hard at close quarters. Shield now repelled shield, boss struck boss, and, when the spears had broken, swords were hacking.

Turkish reinforcements arrived and began vigorously to press the Christians. The Franks could not sustain so great an attack by so many battle-tested nations, but, wavering, were forced to give ground. The shouting, uproar, and shower of missiles were so great that they darkened the very air. Bohemond groaned, for he watched them on every side as though he were all eyes, and said: “Christ, sustain your Christians!” Then he added: “Robert”—for Robert, son of Gerard, bore his standard—[Col. 0675C] “urge your swift warhorse hard with the spurs, and be fearless aid to the wavering Christians! I pray you, remember our forefathers, and do not tarnish the bright renown of the Franks! Know that help will immediately come to us from heaven. Yet God wishes us, like strong athletes, to deserve and gain the prize.”

Robert, fortified with the sign of the holy cross and surrounded by supporting companies, hurried to the scene and, a most daring knight, resisted the bloodthirsty Turks. He attacked the faithless enemy so fiercely that he made the streamers of Bohemond’s standard flutter before the Turks’ faces, and somewhat frightened them by his loud cry. At the onset and loud cry of that chief standard-bearer, the Franks recovered courage and rushed unanimously upon the Turks. There was a great crash of weapons, and fire struck from bronze helmets flashed. Wounds struck against wounds, and the fields were purple with excessive blood. One might see entrails hanging out, severed heads, mutilated bodies, and men falling everywhere. The Turks were therefore terrified by extreme fear, and suddenly, as their formations gave way, fled; our men promptly pursued them beyond the Iron Bridge.

Many Turkish soldiers were killed there, because that battle had no infantry. The Christians, having won a great trophy, returned joyfully to their people, bringing with them many horses, of which they had special need, and much spoil gained in battle. The Turks returned in great disgrace to their castle of Arech; stripping it entirely, they set it on fire and fled. The Armenians and Syrians, [Col. 0676A] seeing this, occupied the narrow places and killed many of them, while bringing back some alive. They surrendered the aforementioned castle, now subdued, to the Christians. The Franks also brought a hundred heads of the slain into camp, for the consolation of their own side and the discouragement of those under siege. All this was seen by envoys of admirable Babylon, who had then been sent from Babylon and were staying in tents near them. Those who had remained in camp had fought the Antiochenes all day and had continuously guarded the city’s three gates, lest they break out. This battle took place on the Ides of February [13 February], Tuesday, preceding the beginning of the Lenten fast.

Although the multitude of citizens had always been defeated in battles and diminished by death, wounds, or captivity, [Col. 0676B] it was so great in the city that, rendered all the more furious by anger, they attacked the Christians more fiercely, constantly disturbed the camp itself, frequently made sorties, and inflicted every sort of death. Besides this, the Christians were afflicted by serious hardships, because they neither could abandon the siege nor dared venture far from camp. The surrounding regions had already been reduced to such desolation that they supplied them with no provision of fodder. The Turks, indeed, knowing the advantageous places of the country, ranged about gathering grain and more diligently laid ambushes for the Christians. Moreover, whatever cities, castles, or towns there were, every man and woman, all those near [Col. 0676C] or far away, were hostile to the Christians. Every place was blocked, lest merchants perhaps reach them. Thus they faced the dreadful danger of a shortage of food. The nobility therefore anxiously and compassionately sought to provide for the common people.

They adopted the plan of fortifying Machomaria and depriving the Turks of passage across the bridge. They also decreed that Duke Bohemond and Raymond, Count of Toulouse, should go to the Port of Saint Symeon and bring to the siege the people waiting there. Therefore those who remained in camp, girded with swords, unanimously prepared themselves to begin the castle. But the Turks, inferior neither in number nor arms, boldly met the Franks [Col. 0676D] and attacked so strongly that they forced them to flee and killed many. Finally, learning that the two greatest princes had gone to the port, they aptly laid hidden ambushes and savagely attacked those returning from the Port of Saint Symeon. The Saracens assailed the Christians with arrows, swords, lances, missiles, and every kind of shower of weapons; they mercilessly cut down the Christians and, gnashing their teeth at them, shouted. For a body of people had returned with the aforesaid leaders, neither sufficiently armed nor very ready for battle. The few Christians could not long endure the cruelty of their raging enemies; after more than a thousand had been killed in that encounter, the rest fled.

Such are the outcomes of wars; such are the changes of men and times. No one has ever succeeded always happily; no one will ever rejoice, or has rejoiced, in uninterrupted prosperity. For this reason adversity must be feared and guarded against in prosperity, while prosperity must be hoped and wished for in adversity. The report that the Christians had been defeated greatly saddened those who remained, especially because it gave no certain number of survivors or slain. Very many escaped by crawling through the mountains and returned to the tents as quickly as possible.

Bohemond, returning by a shorter route, arrived before the Count of Toulouse and gave a truthful report of his men’s reverse. The Christians, more angered than frightened, unanimously attacked the Turks; stirred by the slaughter of their fellow soldiers, they manfully [Col. 0677B] assaulted the pagans. The battle was exceedingly fierce on both sides. The Turks had crossed the bridge and boldly met the Christians, by whom, beyond expectation, they were horribly received and struck down. They tried to escape by flight, but, once flight began, found death. The narrow bridge and the swift, deep river hindered the fugitives. There was no other crossing for them; no one could ford the river about the bridge, and scarcely anyone could swim it. A great multitude of horsemen mounted the bridge together, and the Franks, desirous of vengeance for their brethren and of victory, strove to kill the cruel beasts. The insatiable killers pressed upon them with lances and used swords against them at close quarters. Some they hurled into the river; others they pierced with deadly swords. The river was made bloody with blood and covered over with corpses.

[Col. 0677C] The illustrious leader Godfrey struck a certain mighty warrior clad in a golden hauberk on the back with his sword and, with a powerful blow, cut him in two through the middle as though he were a tender leek. The head, shoulders, and upper part of the body from the belt upward fell into the river, while the lower part remained on the exceedingly swift warhorse.
