The horse, lacking its rider, was harshly urged by its spurs; with loose reins, outstripping the fugitives, it entered the city. When the whole populace standing on the walls and fortifications saw this, they trembled in great grief and poured forth many words of lament over so mighty a stroke by the valiant baron.

That day of manifold death had dawned for the pagans, [Col. 0677D] on which scarcely anyone assembled there could escape death. Women watched their people’s miseries from the walls and fortifications, and begrudged the Franks their successive successes. In that battle twelve princes, whom they call admirals, and fifteen hundred principal soldiers died; and others, greatly terrified lest they should undertake anything arrogantly against the Christians, were cowed. The dead of night ended the battle. Rejoicing in the Lord Jesus, the Christians returned victoriously to their people, bringing many horses and abundant spoils. On the next morning the Turks collected the bodies of their men and buried them beyond the bridge at Machomaria before the city gate. They also buried with them garments and costly equipment, adding bows, [Col. 0678A] quivers, and many bezants for the burial provision of the dead. When the Christians learned this, they dug up the buried, seized the desirable wealth, and contemptuously threw the collected bodies into one pit. They sent four mules laden with the heads of the slain to the gate. Seeing them, the citizens and the Babylonian envoys grieved violently and were sorrowful even unto death.

On the third day the Christians began to build the castle mentioned above, fortifying it with stones taken from the graves of those who had been disinterred. Once it was well fortified, they hemmed in their enemies more closely. The Franks then ranged more safely into the mountains and now freely attended to carrying back straw and all kinds of provisions.

## X. The Siege of Antioch Continued—The Crusaders Take This City

The Christians had not yet placed their tents on the other side of the river, and there the Turks ranged about more safely. By common counsel, therefore, a castle was built beyond the river; and the magnanimous Tancred agreed with the leading Franks to guard that castle. For all the others refused such a charge. Accordingly, summoning his fellow soldiers and supporters, he fortified the castle, stoutly opposed the besieged city, and tirelessly watched roads and trackless places. One day he found Syrians and Armenians, as was their custom, carrying plentiful necessities into the city; swiftly attacking them, he took everything [Col. 0678C] they carried and, gloriously enriched by rich spoils and provisions, aided his companions. The Antiochenes, therefore, and all their supporters were greatly terrified and overwhelmed by repeated misfortunes and disasters. The Franks were fiercer in disposition, more courageous by nature, more expert through experience in war; and they had set out with endurance for distant regions and foreign peoples for this purpose. In their straits they sighed to God, called upon Him as their helper in their necessities, and often made devout satisfaction to Him for human transgressions.

Pirrus Datianus, a certain *admiratus*—that is, a commander—of Turkish descent, possessed three towers in the besieged city. Through trustworthy messengers he had made a pact of friendship [Col. 0678D] with Bohemond, of whom widespread report had brought him many favorable accounts. They therefore frequently spoke with one another through faithful interpreters and recognized signals. Bohemond sometimes urged him toward Christianity, sometimes persuaded him with manifold promises to surrender the city; and, as a shrewd man, left nothing untried. At one moment he frightened him with the disasters impending over the city; at another he attracted him to Christianity by the abundant rewards gloriously appointed by God. At last Pirrus assented to his renowned friend, offered him his three towers, promised to give his son as a hostage, and urgently urged that they hasten the undertaking.

Prudent Bohemond cautiously concealed his inward joy [Col. 0679A] and for a time controlled his expression and speech. He then addressed the leaders concerning the difficulty of taking the city, the great weariness of the long siege, and the praiseworthy constancy of the victorious expedition. He urged that the lordship of Antioch be granted by all to whichever of their number could obtain it by price, force, friendship, or any contrivance. The elders did not then agree with him, but said that it ought to belong to all in common, because all had labored there by a common effort. The wise hero, having heard much, fell silent and awaited an opportunity for the desired outcome.

A little later, a report foretelling evil spread through the camp: Turks, Publicans, Agulans, Azimites, and very many pagan nations were coming and had declared war upon the Christians. [Col. 0679B] Reliable messengers had already arrived who testified to the certainty of the impending danger. The Christian leaders therefore spoke among themselves and of their own accord said to Bohemond: “You see that our cause stands at a crisis. If, therefore, by prayer or price, even with our help, you can obtain this city, we unanimously grant it to you, saving in every respect the oath which, with your approval, we made to the emperor. If the emperor comes to help us as he promised and keeps the sworn agreements, we do not wish to live as perjurers; but, with your consent, we shall surrender it to him. But if he does not, let it always be subject to your authority!”

Bohemond immediately approached Pirrus again; and Pirrus, asking no questions, sent his son as a hostage. “Let your herald,” he said, [Col. 0679C] “cry aloud in your camp that the Frankish people, prepared today, are tomorrow to enter the Saracens’ land to plunder it; thus the reason for our undertaking will be concealed from both ours and yours. Once our people believe that the enemy host has gone farther away, and rest less watchfully in the silence of night, you meanwhile must hasten secretly, place a ladder against the wall, suppress every sound, quickly and confidently climb the wall, and take possession of my towers, as I promised. Afterwards decide what must be done and bring the affair to its conclusion with swords; do not, like idle men, neglect anything that should be done. I, wakeful and anxious, shall await your arrival.”

Bohemond therefore ordered his herald, surnamed Malam-Corona, to proclaim throughout the camp that all were to go plunder the enemy’s lands. He entrusted the entire secret to Duke Godfrey, the Count of Flanders, the Norman, the Count of Toulouse, the bishop of Le Puy, and certain other leaders; Tancred and his advisers, however, had known the whole matter from the beginning. Stephen of Chartres was absent: detained, as he claimed, by severe illness, he had gone to Alexandretta to recover until he regained health. The Christian army, ignorant of this affair, left camp at evening; led through certain byways, it returned by short winding routes near the city before dawn. Meanwhile Bohemond ordered his close companions cautiously to set against the wall [Col. 0680A] the ladder he had prepared, silently and confidently to climb it, and, vigorous in arms and spirit, prudently to do whatever else was necessary.

A Lombard named Paganus was the first to ascend, not without great fear. Fulcher of Chartres, Roger of Barneville, Godfrey Parented of the castle of Secred, and nearly sixty others followed him. Pirrus carefully received them and placed them in his towers. Then, when Pirrus saw that no more were following, he became very sorrowful and is said to have spoken in his mother tongue: “Alas, alas! *michro Francos ethome*—that is, ‘we have few Franks.’” The Lombard then quickly descended the ladder and called from a distance to the waiting Bohemond: “What are you doing? Are you asleep? Send quickly those whom you intend to send, for we have now secured the three towers unharmed. [Col. 0680B] Otherwise you have lost both us and the city, and your friend, who has poured all his hope and soul into your bosom.”

On hearing this, Bohemond and those with him ran more swiftly than words can tell. Many seized the ascent and, under Pirrus’s guidance, entered seven other towers. Killing all whom they found within, they now resounded through the walls and streets, ran everywhere, and spared no one they encountered. The citizens, wearied by the labors of the long siege, scarcely awoke; still drowsy, they came unarmed from their homes. Stunned by sleep and the sound of shouting, the unsuspecting encountered the wary; ignorant of the situation, they summoned their enemies as though they were their own dependents. Wherever they were met, they fell and were cut down like sheep. [Col. 0680C] Then Couterinus, Pirrus’s brother, was also slain.

Meanwhile so many had begun to climb the ladder that the ladder itself split and broke apart, and those below beside the walls could not help their companions fighting above. While they grieved at this turn of events, God’s mercy came to their aid. For, not far from the ladder, by God’s will, they felt along the left side and found a certain gate which scouts had observed in previous days; breaking it down, they entered with all speed. Then a tremendous din arose, and a fuller opportunity for fighting opened to the Christians, while a crueler threat of death came upon the Turks, buried in sleep and wine. As the pagans tried to escape the imminent danger, they ran into the Christians; striving unknowingly to avoid the attack, they fell into sudden peril of death. At Bohemond’s command, his banner was raised in the city and placed opposite the citadel, which stood on a higher hill within the city.

The Christians took Antioch on the third day before the Nones of June [3 June], Wednesday, and killed innumerable pagans there. No allowance was made that night for age, sex, or any condition. The night was uncertain, and therefore spared no mixed company of either sex. Day dawned, and those staying in camp, roused by the populace’s tumult and the echoing trumpets, saw and recognized Bohemond’s banner; they rejoiced at the capture of the city. They ran to the gates, entered, and helped their companions with all their strength. Any Turks they found attempting to escape [Col. 0681A] they energetically struck down. Some Turks did escape through the gates, because they were unrecognized by the impetuous Franks.

Cassianus, lord of the Turks and *admiratus* of Antioch, hid among the fugitives and fled into Tancred’s territory. There, when his horses and those of his companions were completely exhausted, he was forced to halt and turned aside into a hut. When the Syrians and Armenians who inhabited that region—against whom Cassianus had done much evil—learned this, nearly twenty of them rushed upon him, seized him, cut off his head, and presented it to Bohemond. Thus they obtained both his favor and the liberty they desired. Deceived by unhappy fortune, Cassianus perished thus. It is uncertain [Col. 0681B] whether he departed deprived of every refuge, or hurried about seeking help from his fellow countrymen. This is certain: had he entered his citadel, he would have provided more advantageously for himself and his people. The streets and all the city’s passageways were occupied so densely with corpses that no one could walk freely. Crossroads and lanes were blocked by slaughtered bodies, so that terrible horror and stench oppressed every passerby.

## XI. The Turks, Led by Curbaran, Attack the Franks in Antioch

Hearing reports of the city’s capture, many who had gathered, or were still gathering, to aid it were killed. Others escaped by withdrawing into the citadel. Others sought safety for their lives in flight. Sensadolus, Cassianus’s son, met Curbaran, commander of the army of the Soldan, king of the Persians, and with many tears recounted the dreadful fate of his father and homeland. While Cassianus was being besieged by the westerners, he had summoned this man by many embassies for Antioch’s relief. On the third day after the city had been subdued to the Christians, Sensadolus surrendered to Curbaran the citadel overlooking the city, himself, and all that was his; by many complaints, tears, and promises he incited him against the Christians. Curbaran was bold and warlike, prudent and wealthy, and eager for glory. He had received from the Caliph, the apostolic head of his people, permission to rage against the Christians, [Col. 0681D] and had sworn that he would not return until he had subjected Syria, Romania, and Apulia also to himself. He had great confidence in his forces, because he had innumerable peoples with him. The king of Damascus and the *admiratus* of Jerusalem had also joined him. Turks and Hagarenes, Arabs and Publicans, Azimites, Kurds and Persians, as well as three thousand Agulans, adhered to him. They were armored everywhere in iron and feared neither arrows nor lances; they brought no weapons into battle except swords.

Such and so great enemies encamped at the Iron Bridge and immediately captured that fortification. They killed everyone at once, except the lord of the castle, whom they bound in iron chains; after the battle he was found alive and bound. The Hagarenes seized from certain poor people the cheapest weapons—a rusty sword, a small lance, and a contemptible bow—and presented them to Curbaran with great mockery, as an insult to the Franks. Nevertheless, with scoffing reproaches, he sent them to Khorasan and by empty boasts stirred the mad idolaters against Christ.

While these things were taking place, Curbaran’s mother came from the city of Aleppo to her son and began sternly to rebuke him for what he had undertaken. She plainly foretold that he would be defeated by the Christians and, in that same year, would die suddenly—not in battle. For she was an old woman, being a hundred years of age, and a foreknower of the future. This sorceress also drew many conclusions from the constellations and was versed in divination by the knees and in many other disciplines. [Col. 0682B] The boastful hero restrained his mournful mother with proud promises, and on the third day came armed, with very great forces, to the town entrusted to him.

The Christians went out to meet the Ishmaelites, but could not overcome their immense multitude and strength. They were immediately forced to take refuge in the city, and many perished, suffocated by the sudden crush in the narrow entrance of the gates. For the Turks attacked them fiercely. Great despair therefore fell upon the Christians. Yet they comforted one another and spoke publicly of battle on the following day. Some, however, more fearful than right and honour allowed, disgracefully considered flight by night. William of Grandmesnil and his brother Alberic, Guy Trousseau, and Lambert the Poor, [Col. 0682C] together with several others, were terrified by the previous day’s battle; anxious to flee on the morrow, they were lowered by ropes over the wall. Hence, to their lasting shame, they were called the stealthy Rope-Walkers. All night they travelled over steep precipices, and with many companions reached the port of Saint Symeon on foot, their hands and feet stripped raw.

There they found many ships, and frightened the sailors wavering in the harbour with cruel news, saying that Antioch had been captured by the Turks and that the Christians there had been exterminated by the pagans. On hearing this, some sailors, breaking their anchors, were already ploughing the sea and spreading their crackling sails to the slanting winds; others lingered indecisively. [Col. 0682D] Yet all alike were disturbed and pale. While this was happening, behold, the Turks suddenly flew in, scouting the shore; they slaughtered the unprepared and frightened sailors, plundered the vessels lingering in the harbour, burned them after setting fire to them, and tore the idle men to pieces at their pleasure.

The fighting defenders of the city bore the weight of the Turkish war throughout the day, and, suddenly acting on the counsel of wise men, built a wall of unworked stones without mortar between the city and the citadel. That wall afforded the Christians timely aid in defending themselves, while it created an inconvenient obstacle for the Turks in attacking. The Franks stood armed by the wall with every diligence, yielding neither to sleep nor to any other need. Meanwhile [Col. 0683A] hunger gradually grew stronger and compelled the besieged to devour horses, asses, and whatever else was unclean. In such want the faithful called upon the Lord, and he heard them.

The Lord Jesus appeared, while a certain priest was spending the night in the basilica of Saint Mary and praying for God’s afflicted people, when he was half asleep, accompanied by a company of saints. He complained of the fornications by which the Christian bands had been defiled with foreign or Christian prostitutes, and added harsh threats against the multitude given to brothels. Meanwhile a shining cross shone above his head, by which the priest recognized the Redeemer of the world and fell devoutly prostrate in adoration. Then blessed Mary, mother of mercy, and Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, fell [Col. 0683B] at the feet of the Lord and Saviour and, with pious prayers for the Christians’ affliction, softened the wrath of him who threatened. They complained of the pagans, who had foully polluted God’s holy house with their filth.

When the prayers of the supplicating Mother and apostle had ended, the Holy of Holies relented; with a more cheerful countenance he commanded the priest publicly to rebuke the whole people, to invite them by every means to repentance, and securely to promise, on God’s behalf, that God would provide them fitting help within five days if they faithfully converted. The priest attested these things, under oath upon the holy Gospel and the cross, before the bishop of Le Puy and the entire multitude. The people immediately turned to lamentation, and [Col. 0683C] encouraged one another to confess their guilt. Their faces drenched with tears, their heads covered in ashes, and their feet bare, all prayed everywhere in the churches, sought the Lord’s aid, and asked for counsel.

All the leaders swore by a common decree that none, while he lived, would withdraw from that fellowship until they had reached Jerusalem and kissed the Lord’s sepulchre. Tancred also swore that, so long as he had forty knights, he would not turn aside from the journey to Jerusalem. This inspiration therefore greatly encouraged, strengthened, and gladdened the Christians.

Peter Abraham, a certain cleric from Provence, related the following vision to his companions:

> “When Antioch was besieged,” he said, “and we were oppressed outside by severe distress and manifold scarcity, Saint Andrew the apostle appeared to me. When I asked, he revealed his name and led me into the church of Saint Peter, which is in this city. There, showing me a certain place, he said: ‘I want you to know that, after you have entered this city, you will find here the lance which pierced the side of the Lord and Saviour upon the cross. This is a most holy safeguard, and one especially to be embraced by Christians.’”

Having said this, the apostle disappeared, and I lacked confidence to reveal to anyone what I had seen. But after the city had been captured, I again saw the same apostle. “Why,” he said, “faint-hearted man, have you not taken up the lance?” And I replied: “Lord, if I spoke of it, who would believe me?” “Do not despair,” said the apostle, “do not despair; but know with certainty that all is true, as I told you and showed you. This revelation will indeed greatly benefit the exhausted Christians, [Col. 0684A] for saving confidence will flow to them through the lance. Within five days the Lord will visit them and powerfully deliver them from the hands of their persecutors.”

Peter disclosed to his companions this counsel divinely communicated to him. But the people disbelieved and mocked him as he testified. He nevertheless persisted and affirmed it under oath; at last the people believed the man who swore, and recovered their former strength for enduring suffering.

Meanwhile the Turks who were in the citadel diligently made sorties against the Franks, and the latter resisted them to the extent of their power. In the first encounter Roger of Barneville was killed and buried by the Christians in the church of Saint Peter with great mourning. He was a noble Norman, a handsome and most worthy knight. One day the Turks shut three Christians within a tower, [Col. 0684B] and the Franks, wasting away under afflictions, did not dare to help those enclosed. Two of them emerged from the tower grievously wounded. Hugh the Mad alone, a most vigorous fighter from the army of Godfrey of Mont-Scabieux, defended himself bravely throughout the day. He also laid low two Turks; aided by no assistance, he with his own hand alone withstood the pursuing bands.

Truly this man was bold and high-spirited, worthy among all warriors of the highest praise. At that time our men were broken by overwhelming calamities: they saw one of their own fighting all day and did not come to his aid; they heard him shouting and did not answer. When the leaders summoned the knights, they did not assemble; when the trumpets sounded, they hid in their houses. Indeed, unarmed and spiritless, they shrank from the battle for which they had long prayed; [Col. 0684C] already, like lifeless men, inglorious and unwarlike, they preferred death.

Bohemond and the other leaders, seeing that the army had so utterly failed that they could not bring the men even as far as the wall which separated the city from the citadel by a slender division, ordered fire to be set in the city. Thus they dragged out the emasculated men lurking in houses and hiding places. The fire was accordingly kindled in the city, on the side where Cassian’s palace stood out, and did not cease from the third hour of the day until midnight. About two thousand houses or churches were burned. The fire then died down because all violence of the winds had vanished.

The Christians, with fierce flames in their lodgings and scarcely able to seize their possessions, were compelled to flee to the leaders; [Col. 0684D] each took a position at the city gates for the purpose of keeping watch. There was continual conflict between the Franks and the Turks of the citadel. By now the affair was carried on only by arm and hand. They fought hand-to-hand on both sides, and the battle was not interrupted for an instant. The Turks, more numerous and strengthened by more plentiful food, relieved one another in turns, omitted no possible measure, attacked the Franks boldly, voluntarily pressed themselves into engagements, and encouraged one another. The Franks, on the other hand, excessively distressed, wavered and could take neither food nor sleep, since no rest was granted to them. They therefore began to raise a high wall of stone and lime mortar, because the other one, which they had erected without mortar, had been easily thrown down by the Turks.

[Col. 0685A] One night, a fire was seen from the west to hang in the sky and to rage as though falling within the Turkish camp. Although the fire then caused the heathen no harm, it nevertheless struck them with great fear and sadness, while bringing comfort and joy to the Christians; that sign from heaven shone forth for both peoples. The men of the citadel pressed them all day with lances and missiles, adding wound to wound. The besieging army outside so encircled the city that no one could enter or leave by day. At night someone might sometimes go out, but secretly and with great fear.

Hunger increased day by day and afflicted the Christians beyond belief. Many indeed died of hunger. Hard and very coarse bread, when it could be found, was bought for a Byzantine gold coin. [Col. 0685B] Horseflesh and ass-flesh were reckoned imperial delicacies. A hen cost fifteen solidi; an egg was valued at two solidi, and a walnut at one denarius. Every cheap item cost many staters. I am weary of enumerating one by one the manifold hardships, all the miseries, and the sufferings endured by the Christian defenders for thirty-six days in the besieged city. Thus God tested his athletes and examined them in the furnace of affliction, so that they might be cleansed from their own sins; and, having cleansed them, he honoured them gloriously.

Meanwhile Stephen, count of Chartres, detained, as he said, by a slight illness, had withdrawn, as stated above, to Alexandretta to recover. All awaited his return, [Col. 0685C] since all the leading men had appointed him their leader and counsellor. For he was eloquent and exceptionally learned. When he heard that the Turks had encircled the city, he secretly climbed the heights from Alexandretta, which is not far from Antioch. He saw countless Turkish tents, and the Turks themselves spread out like the sand of the sea over many stadia; he recognized the city as surrounded and the small company of Christians as shut in.

Terrified with his companions by overwhelming fear, he began to flee in haste and secretly departed at speed; returning to his castle, he stripped it. As he fled, he met Emperor Alexius at the city of Philomelium, as the emperor was coming with a great army to aid the besieged. Calling him aside, [Col. 0685D] he said:

> “Know for certain that Antioch has been captured by the Christians. But the Turks retain for themselves the citadel, which rises most strongly fortified above the city. And behold, they are besieging and assaulting our men in the city—or rather, as I think, have already taken it and all our men have perished. Therefore take counsel for yourself and for the people whom you are leading.”

Guy, Bohemond’s brother, and many other Franks and Greeks were hastening to help the besieged. The emperor summoned them and disclosed his plan. He then ordered all of them immediately to return, to lay that region utterly waste, and to transfer its inhabitants into Bulgaria, so that, if the Turks pursued, they might find no provisions in the depopulated country. The terrible rumours spread by the rumour-mongering count brought immeasurable grief upon God’s people. [Col. 0686A] For bishops, abbots, and priests ceased almost three days from prayers and praises of God, sighing with deep groans. The emperor, too ready to believe the words of the count of Chartres, returned to Constantinople; and the glory of victory and triumph over the Turks was divinely reserved for others who had fought lawfully. The Franks returned most unwillingly and lamented most bitterly. Many of the poor pilgrims also died everywhere.

Guy, son of Robert Guiscard, made much lamentation for the death of his brother and friends, moved many acquaintances and strangers to tears, and poured forth many insults against Count Stephen along the way. Yet compelled to do so, he returned sadly with the emperor and the other helpers.

[Col. 0686B] The warriors of God who struggled in the city placed all their hope in heaven and confidently discussed seeking the Lord’s lance. They therefore came to the church of Saint Peter and carefully marked the place; they debated it there for a long time. At last, the opinion of the majority prevailing, thirteen industrious and vigorous men were ordered to dig carefully. From morning until evening they dug, and, with that same Peter to whom it had been revealed present, they found the lance. When it was reverently raised, a public cry arose; there was a famous rush toward it, and it was kissed with the greatest devotion. Such joy arose among them that, all sloth cast aside, they thereafter remembered no sadness and from then on dared to deliberate concerning battle.

## XII. Discovery of the Holy Lance. Great Joy of the Christians. They Prepare for a General Battle. They Defeat the Turks.

[Col. 0686C]

By common counsel of the Christians, the able men Peter the Hermit and Herluin, skilled in the Turkish language, were sent to Curbaran. On behalf of God and his people they urged him and his followers peaceably to depart with all their people from the city which Saint Peter the apostle had subjected to Christ. If they longed for the sacrament of baptism, they would receive them as true brothers and bind with them a covenant of everlasting friendship. But if not, let them gird themselves with the sword and, if they dared, consider battle.

Then Curbaran looked at the envoys with a grim countenance, utterly rejected Christianity, despised the crucified king, called the apostle Peter a superstitious deceiver, and declared our faith to be a most foolish sect. [Col. 0686D] He invited the Christians to the worship of Muhammad, and warned those who despised it to flee. The envoys quickly set out on their return journey and came back in haste; they made the army of the baptized certain of the impending battle.

Meanwhile hunger grew worse, and fear of the Turks still somewhat unmanned the hearts of those who trembled. At length, at the command of the priests, they completed a three-day fast, held processions through the churches with litanies, and each Christian, fortified with the most holy viaticum, made ready for battle. They therefore formed seven battle-lines within the city.

[Col. 0687A] In the first line was Hugh the Great, with Count Robert of Flanders and thirty thousand Franks and Flemings. In the second was Duke Godfrey, with his brother Eustace, Count Conon, and thirty thousand most valiant warriors from among the Germans, Lorrainers, and men of Boulogne. In the third was Robert, duke of the Normans, with fifteen thousand men of Le Mans, Angevins, Bretons, and Englishmen. In the fourth was Aimar, bishop of Le Puy, with other bishops and ordained clergy; with them was Peter Abraham, who carried the Lord’s lance, which the Christians wished to have borne before them and believed to be a great defence and protection there. In the fifth was the most valiant count Raynald, with four thousand Germans and Bavarians. In the sixth was Tancred [Col. 0687B] with four thousand Apulians. In the seventh was Bohemond, duke of Apulia, with thirty thousand Lombards and Italians. He departed from the city last, so that he might provide for all and be wholly present in the need of each.

Raymond of Toulouse remained with twenty thousand to guard the city, lest the heathen—of whom many thousands held the citadel of Saint Peter beside the walls—should invade it. As the Christians went out, bishops and priests preached and prayed; standing in elevated places, they signed them all with the sign of the venerable cross.

As they departed in order from the city through the gate before the Mosque, earnestly imploring the effective aid of the merciful God, a slight shower fell divinely, like [Col. 0687C] a dewy drop. Like morning dew, it refreshed the wetted horses and riders. Thus the horses, as though gladdened, began to neigh; the riders’ spirits, sweetened, became more vigorous and eager; and all felt themselves readier and freer of encumbrance. Yet that rain was so fine and slight that they could scarcely call it rain, but perceived certain dew-like drops more than they saw them. This, indeed, was reported by many trustworthy men who were present.

When Curbaran saw them advancing to battle, he said: “These men are hurrying more toward flight than battle. Let them come this far, so that we may freely swallow them up in our power. Let them come out, let them come out! For we shall immediately surround them, prevail, and crush them.”

But the Christians advanced step by step, and no one rashly hurried before another out of order. When Curbaran saw them marching properly armed, not turning aside anywhere like frightened men but proceeding at a measured pace, he again did not blush to say: “Will these contemptible little dogs perhaps dare to undertake battle?” Then he grew rigid with fear; his bodily strength failed and his courage chilled. He therefore secretly instructed his commander, whom they call the admiral, that if he saw a fire kindled and smoking at the head of Curbaran’s army, he should know for certain that his men were defeated. The commander was then to withdraw immediately, after giving the signal and taking all his own men away, lest the people with him, or those in the tents, should all perish.

Then, when Curbaran saw battle-lines in formation and forces greater than he had heard of, [Col. 0688A] he deliberately began gradually to withdraw toward the mountains, so that the Franks, thinking him in flight, might pursue recklessly and, being thereby disordered, be more easily harmed. When this plan achieved nothing, the Turks separated from one another. One force came from the sea; others stood in position, hoping that they could enclose the Christians. But the Franks took a detachment from the line of Duke Godfrey and Robert the Norman, established it as an eighth line, and put a certain Raynald over it. They met the heathen approaching from the sea. The Turks fought fiercely against them and struck many with arrows or inflicted upon them other deadly kinds of destruction.

The other Christian divisions formed themselves in a line extending from the sea to the mountains, an interval of about two miles. From the mountains and from the sea the Turks pressed them skilfully, surrounding the Christians and harassing them from every direction.

Behold—thanks be to God—an innumerable army was seen coming out from the very mountains, riding white horses and carrying white banners in their hands! Many Christians saw this, and, as they believe, heathens also; they hesitated and wondered what it could be. At last both sides recognized that a sign had been made from heaven and recognized the leaders of that host, bearing their standards, as the holy martyrs George, Demetrius, and Mercurius. Great fear therefore seized the Saracens, while better hope grew among the Christians. Not all saw this, but many who did see it [Col. 0688C] bore witness to it. It appeared from heaven to some for confusion and to others as a manifestation of imminent triumph.

The heathen fighting on the sea side, after they could no longer bear the weight of battle, set fire to the grass, as Curbaran had arranged. When those in the tents recognized the sign mentioned above, they fled swiftly and restlessly, trembling as they carried off the more valuable goods. The Christians fighting opposite them now turned the battle toward the Turkish tents, where they knew the greater part of the enemy’s strength remained. The Turks still resisted with all the obstinacy they could muster. Some fought, while others devoted themselves to plundering the tents.

Duke Godfrey, Robert of Flanders, and Hugh the Great rode beside the river, [Col. 0688D] where they knew that a very great multitude of combatants was again assembled. Attacking the heathen steadfastly, they drove them back in unity. The heathen pressed stubbornly, and battle was fought relentlessly on both sides. Bronze helmets resounded like anvils struck by hammers. Fire sparkled in tiny flashes; swords were shattered. Men, their skulls crushed, fell to the ground. Mail-coats broke; entrails spilled out; exhausted horses sweated; no rest was given to horses or riders. The closely packed formations were scarcely separated from one another by the slight interval of their weapons. Men struck men at close quarters, pushing hand against hand, foot against foot, and body against body.

Yet fear, divinely cast upon the Turks, terrified them; the Christians’ invincible steadfastness caused them [Col. 0689A] to marvel and be stunned, and forced them into flight. The entire army therefore began to collapse; neither trumpet, drum, clarion, nor herald could call them back. The fleeing Turks turned toward the tents, where they supposed that many of their own whom they had left there remained in reserve; but, as has been said, while these men were fighting, those others had fled once the fire was lit. Finally the Christians drove the pagans before them, killing them cruelly, as far as the Iron Bridge, and pursued them, slaughtering them here and there, as far as Tancred’s castle. Then they returned to the enemy’s tents and plundered everything desirable. They carried into the city with great joy every kind of treasure, wool-bearing sheep, countless beasts of burden, abundant foodstuffs, and whatever was necessary for those in need.

For it is the custom of the heathen to bring abundant wealth against an enemy: horses, asses, and camels to carry loads; sheep and cattle for food; and not to omit grain, flour, beans, oil, and wine. [Col. 0689B] The Christians were enriched abundantly by all these things along with their desired triumph. They blessed God with worthy praises, recognized him as their protector visibly present, and joyfully raised hymns to heaven.

The Syrians and Armenians, inhabitants of that region, seeing that the Turks had been irretrievably defeated in battle, blocked the familiar winding mountain paths and occupied the narrow tracks, inflicting immense slaughter upon them with drawn swords. They butchered them like wandering sheep, the Turks having, through excessive fear, forgotten every means of defence.

The admiral also, who had remained in the fortress entrusted to him by Curbaran, when he saw his people shamefully scattered far and wide, took counsel for himself in terror. Before the Franks returned, he requested and received a Christian banner, and placed it in the fortress at a higher point, so that his own men and he himself might thus be spared and there might be no uncertainty about surrendering the fortress. [Col. 0689C]

Then, when the victorious Christians had returned and the Lombards saw the banner of the count of Saint-Gilles, because it was more readily at hand when requested, they were greatly indignant and began to rage with fierce threats. To settle the dispute, the admiral gave the banner back to the count and raised Bohemond’s banner on the tower for the peace and safety of himself and his fellow soldiers. Then the agreement which Bohemond and the admiral had made with one another was confirmed by all, and the fortress was immediately surrendered to the Christians. Not long afterward the admiral, as he himself maintained he had long desired, was baptized, and was endowed with the Franks’ generous bounty.

Thus, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July—28 June—1098, the Christians triumphed in battle with God’s help and obtained Antioch free and at peace. The Turkish inhabitants who surrendered the fortress but resisted the Christian faith, which is the light of the soul and the beginning of salvation, returned to their own land under Bohemond’s escort, as had been promised them. [Col. 0689D]

As the Franks who had escorted them according to the agreement were returning, and the Turks were now approaching their own borders without fear, Baldwin of Rages suddenly met them. Battle having been joined in the Lord’s name, he struck down and killed the barbarians and destroyed almost all of them. Then, laden with spoils, he came with his household to Antioch and brought his friends joyful news.

[Col. 0690A]

## XIII. The Deeds of Baldwin. He Acquires the Principality of Edessa.

But since an occasion now presents itself to recount what befell Baldwin, the pen of our narrative will briefly set it forth in the Lord’s name. So great a matter must not be passed over in silence.

After Baldwin, as was said above, had taken possession of Tarsus, [Col. 0690B] a city of Cilicia, while Tancred departed in bitterness, he left the army of his brother Godfrey and of the other leaders, and made his way with three hundred knights and his men-at-arms to the city of Edessa. He approached the Turkish ruler who governed that province and eagerly offered his military service for his lordship. The ruler, with his citizens, gladly received the Frankish knights; he assigned them rich lodgings in the city, provided ample food and abundant pay, and entrusted to them the defence of his entire territory.

When Duke Godfrey and our other men heard that Baldwin had become protector of the Edessene principality, they rejoiced greatly and, out of regard for him, took care not to enter the territory of that province. For Baldwin was a tall, handsome, and high-spirited knight, endowed with learning, eminent in manifold virtue and honour, and outstanding in noble birth, being descended from the line of Emperor Charlemagne. [Col. 0690C] With the Edessenes, he made frequent expeditions against the neighbouring Turks, crushed the heathen by arms, brought back great booty and captive enemies, and thereby made the duke of Edessa formidable to all his neighbours.

That city, as is read in ancient books, was called Rages; but in the mad storms of wars it was destroyed under the tyrannies of the Assyrians and Chaldeans. In a later age Seleucus Nicator, one of the four principal commanders of Alexander the Great, restored the aforesaid city after Alexander’s death and called it Edessa. The Tigris and Euphrates flow there, bringing an abundance of delights to its inhabitants. Abgar, toparch of Edessa, reigned there. To him the Lord Jesus sent a sacred letter and the precious cloth with which he wiped the sweat from his face, and upon which the image of the same Saviour shines forth miraculously depicted; it displays to beholders the appearance and dimensions of the Lord’s body. Thaddaeus, disciple of Jesus Christ, came to this city, baptized King Abgar with all his people, and first established there the worship of God, God working with him. [Col. 0690D]

Greeks, Armenians, and Syrians live there together and, from Christianity’s beginning until the present day, serve the King of Heaven. Yet, sins demanding it, God recently wielded the rod of his discipline and allowed the Christians’ transgression to be punished by the ravaging of the heathen. Thus the aforesaid city, like the surrounding region, fell under Turkish dominion. Nevertheless, the inhabitants freely devoted themselves to divine worship, nor were they compelled by any pagan coercion to abandon God’s law. The citizens rejoiced at the arrival of the Franks, and the Franks in turn embraced them in every respect as brothers.

Prince Turgidus, blinded by envy and treachery, laid plots for the Christians. He commanded his groom, as he went on an expedition, that on their return he should attack Baldwin and his companions while they were unarmed and kill them without mercy. That faithless contriver of deceit prepared the crime of his wicked conspiracy. This did not escape Baldwin, because he was much loved by many. On their return from the expedition, [Col. 0691B] the pagans, as though jesting, urged the Christians to lay down their arms and proceed more freely. But they perceived the plot and did not comply. At last, as they neared the city and the Franks rode cautiously in armour, the heathen suddenly attacked them at a signal and shamefully exposed their wicked scheme by striking their companions.

The Christians, invoking God, resisted; they struck the enemy bravely, put them to flight, killed some of the fugitives, and pursued others while striking them as far as the city gate. Baldwin then immediately ordered his men to pitch their tents there and besiege the city.

At once there arose much tumult in the city, and the people assembled from every side into one body. Then Tobias, the foremost among the city’s leading men, said: “Good citizens, I ask you to be quiet for a little while. I and three fellow citizens will now go to the Franks and discover why they besiege us.” The four chief men of the city accordingly went out and asked the cause of so sudden a siege. Baldwin replied:

> “I left my brothers, friends, and the noble army of Christians in Cilicia; I came here with three hundred distinguished knights to serve you, and have been a faithful defender in every matter both to you and to your ruler. For my sake the Christians were afraid even to enter the borders of your territory and did you no harm whatever. I and my men fought fiercely against your neighbouring enemies and, for your peace and safety, gained frequent victories over your enemies. [Col. 0691D] You yourselves have certainly seen these things, and, I think, will truthfully bear witness to them for us.
>
> “What, then, have my companions and I done wrong today? As we were safely returning to your homes, as yesterday and the day before, our fellow soldiers unexpectedly attacked us with drawn swords and missiles, intent on killing us. But when we resisted in so great a crisis and invoked God in the Christian manner, Christ our God—ever a ready helper to his own—swiftly aided us as we awaited aid from heaven. Our comrades who attacked us as enemies felt our weapons drawn in defence of our lives; they turned their backs and fled. Some of them, as you may see, lie cold upon the road, abandoned by their companions.
>
> “These things having happened, we remain in our tents and await your aid and counsel. We still regard you not as enemies, but as lawful hosts.”

When Tobias heard these and similar words, he called aside the neighbouring men who stood near, conferred briefly with them, and quickly returned to the Franks. “There is no need for many words, noble knights,” he said. “We beg you to wait here peacefully for us now, and we shall conduct your affair beneficially in the city.”

With these words spoken and accepted by both sides, the envoys entered the city and reported to their fellow citizens what they had heard and done. The people approved what they heard together, sent the four principal men ahead to the ruler’s palace, and themselves followed gradually with arms. They found the stern ruler sitting privately in his hall. The first four greeted him in the customary manner [Col. 0692B] and said:

> “We now need great counsel, because we greatly fear as enemies those whom until now we have had as faithful helpers. The Franks boldly besiege us and fiercely desire to assault us. They call us traitors and summon us to judgment. They say that, while returning from hostile territory, they were betrayed by their fellow soldiers and harmed more cruelly by companions than by enemies. Unless we render them justice, they terrify us with dreadful threats: they will bring against us all the forces of the Christian army.
>
> “We must therefore deliberate prudently and profitably, lest we perish or unjustly provoke against ourselves the intolerable fury of the Christians. This treachery was committed without our knowledge, and so great a crime must swiftly be punished. The common judgment of the citizens is therefore that the faithless traitors should be severely punished according to the ancient laws, and that these excellent companions—indeed, protectors—should be honourably reconciled to us.”

Meanwhile, while Tobias spoke thus, a band of citizens cautiously entered the palace in silence. But the profane ruler arrogantly despised the measures of those seeking peace and openly showed himself the defender and accomplice of the traitors. The angry citizens therefore immediately rushed upon him and irreverently cut off his head. Then Tobias took the severed head and said to the neighbouring citizens: “Guard this palace unharmed, with all the things contained within it, and I with my companions will bring in the Franks with joy and peace.”

Having said this, Tobias went out; after greeting the Franks, he spoke as follows:

> “The citizens of Edessa, deeply grieved by the injury done to you, demanded justice from the ruler. [Col. 0692D] But because he revealed himself as the author of the treachery, they cut off his head. And behold: through us they have sent you the head of God’s enemy and yours.”

While all rejoiced at this, Tobias added: “Come, distinguished knight, and take the ruler’s daughter in marriage. Be our prince, and possess the duchy of Edessa for ever.”

Baldwin, therefore, entered the city rejoicing with his men, and was received in the chief palace amid the great joy of all the citizens. The distinguished daughter of the wicked duke was baptized at the fitting time and joined in marriage to the noble Baldwin, whom, while her father still lived and without his knowledge, she had desired from the depths of her heart. The native Christians, rejoicing that they were to be subject to a Christian prince, gave thanks to God; [Col. 0693A] and the Turks, deprived of the dominion by which they had hitherto oppressed the worshippers of Christ, were cast down. A vast basilica of Saint Sophia had been built there in ancient times. Under Baldwin’s rule, faithful newcomers together with the natives began reverently to worship there in honor of the Holy Savior, who is the power and wisdom of God the Father. The order of divine worship was splendidly restored at Edessa; and, far more than our pen can record, divine mercy worked marvelously in His people, inwardly and outwardly.

Baldwin, occupied with many affairs to Christ’s praise, could not bring assistance to the Christians besieging Antioch. Yet, on hearing reports [Col. 0693B] of the extreme oppression they had suffered there, he and his fellow-knights deeply sympathized with the worshippers of Christ; and, having put their own affairs in the best possible order, they hastened as quickly as they could to their aid. Meanwhile, with the Lord Jesus helping them, they triumphed victoriously over Curbaran and his men; and Baldwin and his companions put to confusion the Turks retreating, as has been said, from the stronghold of Antioch. Having killed them and seized their spoils, they visited their brothers and friends. Then all rejoiced as each side recounted its prosperous successes, and with mouth and heart gave boundless praise to God the conqueror, who orders all things gloriously.

After the brothers and friends had conversed together, [Col. 0693C] Duke Baldwin went to Rages and governed the Church of God and the people entrusted to him like a gracious patrician. By frequent engagements he subdued the neighboring Turks, and, overthrowing evildoers, enlarged the borders of the Christians. He also nobly increased the clergy and supplied them with necessary resources; and he earnestly urged them to perform divine worship daily for the salvation of believers. For nearly five years he held the duchy bravely. Thereafter he succeeded his brother Godfrey in the kingdom of Jerusalem, which he vigorously ruled for nearly fifteen years, performing many valiant deeds against the pagans. By the Turkish wife whom he had taken he had no offspring. Therefore he appointed Baldwin of Burg, his kinsman, as his successor in the duchy and kingdom. Thereafter Fulk, Count of Anjou, journeyed as a pilgrim to Jerusalem [Col. 0693D] and received in marriage, together with the kingdom, Melisende, daughter of the second Baldwin.

## XIV. After Antioch Was Taken, Hugh the Great Is Sent by the Christians to the Greek Emperor. The Christian Leaders Resolve to Remain in This City for the Summer. Various Expeditions.

In July [1098], after the longed-for victory and the acquisition of Antioch through the power of God’s grace, the Christian leaders assembled and, by common counsel, sent Hugh the Great to Emperor Alexius at Constantinople, urging him to hasten to receive the city which they had won for him through calamitous sufferings, and likewise to preserve inviolate the sworn agreements made with them—namely, that the count himself should come unhesitatingly with them to Jerusalem. Hugh the Great discharged this office [Col. 0694A] of embassy and went. But although on this expedition he performed many deeds energetically by force and counsel, he nevertheless failed grievously in that, having been sent as an envoy of raven-kind, he did not afterward return to his brethren as he had promised and ought to have done.

After Hugh’s departure, the leaders convened a council and deliberated on conducting God’s people to Jerusalem. They said:

> This people, which has endured many misfortunes in order to deserve to see the tomb of the Lord its God, now exhausted by many disasters, openly complains that the journey must be hastened; and we too, worn down by great fatigue, complain. Let us therefore provide what is most useful for them. We judge that no further delays should be introduced except those imposed by unavoidable necessity. Yet each matter [Col. 0694B] must be considered not rashly but carefully and moderately. The land through which we are to travel is waterless. The summer heat is excessive. At present we cannot endure the harshness of the climate. We have been exhausted in resources and strength by the long siege. Let us therefore remain quiet and rest, restore the wounded and sick, and meanwhile have compassion on our poor. Let us await the moist season after the solstice and avoid the harmful course of Cancer and Leo. In November the weather will grow cooler; then, assembled unanimously, let us undertake the appointed journey. Otherwise we should afflict the whole people with untimely heat. Let this counsel be explained more fully to the demanding crowds. We must avoid an unmanageable season, and recognize that this is most advantageous for all.

This was announced throughout the whole army [Col. 0694C] and was finally approved by all.

The leaders and their households accordingly dispersed through the neighboring districts to spend the summer; and the needy followed them in order to live. For the leaders had said: “If anyone is needy and sound in body, let him join us; and we shall support all, giving each person wages. Let the sick be maintained at public expense until they recover.” Then Raymond Pilet, a member of the household of the Count of Saint-Gilles and a high-spirited knight, gathered many knights and foot-soldiers. Having assembled this force, he boldly entered, as far as he could, the land of the Saracens and passed beyond two cities to a certain Syrian castle called Talamania. The Syrians who inhabited it voluntarily [Col. 0694D] surrendered themselves to the Christians, and the Franks rested there for about eight days.

Then, girded with military belts, they attacked the neighboring castle of the Hagarenes, hemmed it in, and prevailed. They plundered it and destroyed its inhabitants. Yet those who wished to convert to the faith of Christ they preserved unharmed. Having done this, they rejoiced and returned to the first castle. Again, on the third day, they went out and reached the city of Maʿarra, which lay near them. Many pagans who had assembled from Aleppo and other surrounding cities then rushed out to fight them. Thinking they meant to give battle, the Franks prepared themselves for combat in the manner of soldiers in camp; but the enemies’ vain hope deceived them. For the Turks cautiously withdrew toward the city, [Col. 0695A] neither fleeing nor fighting hand-to-hand. Instead, by a certain stratagem of war, they drew back from battle and then attacked the Franks again with swift movements, assailing them and turning about in the easiest of circles; their horses, brought back, again wheeled without difficulty. The Franks endured repeated attacks and could not safely avoid the charges of their assailants. For if they tried to withdraw, the pagans would press upon their rear as they retreated—as afterward happened. They therefore bore the hardship and the burning thirst until evening. The heat was indeed extreme. Finally, since they could no longer endure the hardship or restrain the burning of thirst, because no water for refreshment could be found, they resolved and agreed to return in a close body and by stages [Col. 0695B] to their castle.

But the weak and undisciplined people—that is, the infantry and the Syrians—disregarding formation and neglecting the soldiers’ command, were seized by excessive fear and began to flee in scattered groups. The pagans pressed after them tirelessly, pursued and struck down those who turned their backs, and, fiercer than wolves, spared no one. The prospect of the desired victory and the favorable opportunity of the moment gave them strength. Many of the common and faint-hearted people were killed by the sword; others perished from extreme thirst. Those who escaped alive returned with Raymond to Talamania and remained there for several days. This slaughter occurred in July, and the insolence of the proud was chastised by God. Thus, indeed, we frequently read in the sacred books that the children of Israel were afflicted [Col. 0695C] and defeated in war by the Philistines, Edom, Midian, and other neighboring peoples, so that they might be compelled always to return to God and persevere in keeping His commandments.

At Antioch, Haimar, bishop of Le Puy, fell ill; and, like a father, comforted his mourning children. Entering upon the way of all flesh, on the Kalends of August [1 August 1098] he departed to the Lord. Accordingly, immoderate mourning arose throughout Christ’s whole army, because he had been the counsel of the nobles, the hope of orphans, and the support of the weak. A man of war among soldiers, he instructed and trained clerics in a clerical manner; he excelled in singular prudence and was eloquent and agreeable to all in every respect. Therefore the sobbing army celebrated his funeral rites and buried his body, embalmed with spices, [Col. 0695D] in the church of Saint Peter the Apostle.

The Count of Saint-Gilles, yielding in no way to idleness or indolence in his zeal against the pagans, immediately entered the land of the Saracens, attacked and violently seized Albara, one of their noble cities. He killed almost all the city’s inhabitants of both sexes and subjected the conquered city to his own dominion. The Christians established there a suitable bishop and arranged those matters which pertained to the worship of true religion. The bishop of Albara was sent to Antioch and there worthily consecrated according to the rite of the Church.

## XV. Duke Bohemond and Count Raymond Contend over the Lordship of Antioch. Numerous Christian Victories against the Pagans. The Army of the Cross-Bearers Advances toward Jerusalem.

[Col. 0696A] As the agreed time for going to Jerusalem approached, all began to discuss the impending undertaking, lest they be further delayed from their journey. But an unappeasable dispute over the lordship of the city persisted between Duke Bohemond and Count Raymond; nor could the experience of the elders restrain it by many grave and profound admonitions. One demanded dominion over the entire city, as it had been granted to him while the city, though not yet taken, was under siege. The other invoked the oath which, as Bohemond himself had approved, they had made to the emperor; nor could he in any way be softened, as he claimed, in order to avoid perjury.

Bohemond therefore fortified with provisions, men, weapons, and guards the castle which had been handed over [Col. 0696B] to him. The count likewise most carefully held the palace of the emir Cassian, which he had occupied beforehand, and the tower over the bridge from the port of Saint Symeon. Their ambitions and rivalries were so great that neither trusted the other, each suspecting that the other, beneath a veiled ambition, was seeking to seize the city for himself. Nor was this surprising, considering its honor and advantage.

Antioch is indeed a most beautiful, strongly fortified city, exceedingly rich in abundant revenues. Within it are four rather high mountains; on one of them—the loftiest—stands a castle which overlooks the whole city. Below, the city is finely built and surrounded by a double wall. The inner wall is broad and rises high into the air. It is constructed and fitted together from great squared stones. In the circuit of this wall are four hundred and fifty towers, beautiful in the splendor of their fortifications and defended by battlements. The outer wall is not so high, but is nevertheless of admirable beauty. It contains three hundred and forty churches. Because of its great primacy, it has a patriarch to whom one hundred and fifty-three bishops are subject. It is enclosed on the east by four mountains, while on the west the river Farfar flows past the city walls. In antiquity, as Jerome writes in his exposition of the prophets, it was called Reblatha; but later it was enlarged by Seleucus Nicator and named after his father, namely Antiochus the Illustrious.

And because it possessed such authority and nobility, [Col. 0696D] being the head and metropolis of all Syria, the Franks did not wish to abandon it rashly after conquering it. Through it they hoped to extend their supremacy far and wide and to subject even distant regions to Christianity. They had besieged it for eight months and one day, and, after taking it, had themselves been besieged in it for three weeks. During that long siege so vast a multitude of pagans gathered that no one remembered seeing or hearing of a more numerous assembly of peoples. They rested there for five months and nine days. With so many concerns confronting them, they did not wish to leave it carelessly, but entrusted it to faithful protection. The count and Bohemond, however, each gave special thought to making it his own. [Col. 0697A] They therefore fortified the city, as stated, and in November, intending to depart elsewhere, left Antioch after arranging all necessary matters.

Count Raymond departed with his army, passed through the two cities of Rugia and Albara, and on the fifth day before the Kalends of December [27 November] reached the fortified and prosperous city of Maʿarra, full of many peoples of the Hagarenes. On the following day he began with his men to attack the city; but because of the walls and defenders he accomplished nothing then. Bohemond followed him and reached the aforementioned city on Sunday. On the next day they vigorously attacked the city and harassed the defenders of its walls with various assaults, but did them little harm. Ladders stood raised against the wall, but, with the Turks shouting and fighting against them, no one dared climb. For the citizens thought they could withstand them as they had earlier resisted Raymond Pilet.

Count Raymond had a wooden siege-engine constructed and, so that it might be more easily moved, placed upon four wheels. It was so tall that it looked down upon the summit of the walls and equaled the height of the towers. They brought this structure up beside a certain tower. Trumpets and horns sounded their martial calls; armed formations surrounded the walls. Crossbowmen and archers shot missiles, while those in the wooden tower hurled huge stones. William of Mont-Pèlerin and many others fought in the engine, battering the citizens from above with stones and other missiles and easily killing those struck on shields, [Col. 0697C] helmets, or heads. Others continually assailed one another with iron hooks. From the towers the Turks labored to attack the Christians with arrows and stones. They also threw into the engine the fire called Greek fire and left nothing untried. Conversely, the Christians poured out oil, which especially extinguishes Greek fire; they attempted the ascent and drew back their feet, fearing those remaining upon the walls, but failed in nothing. Thus the battle was prolonged until evening. Such was the untiring valor of the Hagarenes that they boldly repelled the Christians’ stratagems.

At last Gulferius of Towers, a Limousin, a man of noble birth and remarkable courage, was the first to climb the ladder and set foot upon the wall. Some, though not many, climbed after [Col. 0697D] him; for the ladder broke apart and split. Gulferius nevertheless defended the wall bravely, fought off the pagans, and summoned his companions by gesture and voice. Meanwhile they hurriedly erected another ladder; and through it so many knights and foot-soldiers climbed that they occupied a large part of the wall and drove back the citizens by fighting. Yet the pagans rose up with all their strength and attacked the Christians, charging them several times with such force that some Franks, overcome by fear, threw themselves down from the wall. Many, however, remained on the wall and endured frequent assaults until the Christians undermined the wall and opened an entrance. When the Turks learned this, they were frightened to the point of despair and rushed into irreversible flight.

Accordingly, on the Ides of December [13 December 1098], on the evening of Saturday, Maʿarra, a wealthy city, was taken. The Christians entered the conquered city and greedily carried off whatever treasures they found in houses or pits. They devoted themselves with all their effort to killing Saracens and scarcely allowed anyone to live. No place in the entire city was free of corpses; even the steps of those walking were painfully impeded by the dead and heaped-up bodies. After the city was taken, a great part of the inhabitants, with their wives, children, and household goods, gathered in the palace above the gate and there fell under the Christians’ power. Some of them were killed; others, by Bohemond’s command, were taken to Antioch for slavery or sale; [Col. 0698B] and all, after their possessions had been plundered, were scattered. The Franks remained in that city for a full month and three days.

There the bishop of Orense fell ill, departed from those below, and flew to those above. Then severe famine overtook the army and forced everyone to put to their unwilling teeth things shameful, unfamiliar, harsh, or unlawful. Some then ate Turkish flesh. When the elders and more honorable men heard of this, they blushed and were grieved, but in view of the extreme famine they suspended punishment. For it was not reckoned against them as a very great crime, because for God’s sake they cheerfully endured such hunger and fought the enemies of God with teeth and hands. They indeed committed unlawful acts; but constricting necessity compelled the law to be broken. For the hunger of an army craves everything and rejects nothing. Some cut open the bodies of Turks because they found in their bodies bezants and gold which they had swallowed, and took it. Very many also perished there from overpowering hunger.

## XVI. Internal Discord. The Cross-Bearers Continue Their Begun Journey to Jerusalem.

There the magnates again spoke of agreement between the duke and the count, but accomplished nothing. Bohemond, therefore, enraged, immediately returned to Antioch, and the journey to Jerusalem was disrupted to the harm of the people. The private rivalries of rulers ruin and afflict their subjects when they disagree among themselves. For while each seeks what is his own, he grows cold toward the common good. Peoples also are abandoned to common destruction when their leaders do not bring consolation even to themselves. Thus the Jerusalem-bound people were greatly delayed by the particular quarrels of their leaders.

Again, the count sent envoys after the princes who were at Antioch and addressed them, asking that they meet him at Rugia for a conference. Duke Godfrey, Robert of Normandy, Robert of Flanders, and other summoned leaders therefore came to Rugia and brought Bohemond with them. They again said much about reconciling the magnates, but accomplished nothing toward hastening the journey. Bohemond would not go unless the whole city were given to him; nor would the count go unless Bohemond accompanied them. The count returned to Maʿarra, where the Christian army was endangered by famine. At last, pierced in heart, he generously mastered his own inclinations and undertook the journey to Jerusalem in order to provide for God’s soldiers. He placed God’s cause before his own will or advantage. It is indeed the highest virtue in rulers if they rule themselves; for excessive obstinacy in leaders endangers all their subjects. The count therefore commanded himself, lest he harm all Christendom. He ordered his men carefully to fortify Cassian’s palace. He left Maʿarra on the Ides of January [13 January 1099], barefoot, and voluntarily joined himself to God’s pilgrims. In his humility the count displayed this token of the pilgrimage he had undertaken. [Col. 0699B] Great joy therefore arose among God’s people; and as they proceeded, the duke of Normandy joined them at the city of Capharda. There they rested three days, and the king of Caesarea made peace with the leaders. For he had often previously sent his envoys to Maʿarra, firmly promising that he would be peaceful toward the Christians, would gladly provide much from his own goods, and would furnish an abundant market throughout all his kingdom, unless the untamed Frankish people aimed to dispossess him or devastate his realm. The king accordingly gave the Christians his pledge. Then they all left Capharda and encamped along the river Farfar near Caesarea.

But seeing the Franks encamped near his city, the king was greatly distressed and quickly sent them this message: “Unless at first light you remove your camp from the suburb of our city, you will violate the treaty made with us, and we shall deny you the market promised to you and provide for ourselves.” When morning came, he sent two of his men to show them how to cross the river and lead the army into fertile country. They entered a rich and prosperous valley over which stood a castle; its lord immediately gave the leaders a guarantee of safety. They plundered nearly five thousand animals. There also much food of various kinds was found, and the whole army of Christ was refreshed by its freely available abundance. The people of the castle also gave the army horses, very pure gold, and much money, and swore that henceforth they would in no way harm the pilgrims [Col. 0699D] or afterwards forbid them a market. They remained there five days.

Leaving there, they came to a certain Arab castle. Its lord immediately came out to speak with them and made a peace pleasing to both sides. They moved on from there to the city of Cephalia, most beautiful in its walls and rich in every good thing, situated in a valley. Its citizens, trembling in fear of the Franks, left the city and abandoned gardens filled with vegetables and houses full of provisions and wealth; in their panic they fled. The Christians gladly took possession of all their goods and joyfully gave thanks to God, giver of good things. On the third day they proceeded from there, [Col. 0700A] crossed in descent a very high mountain range, and again came down into a fertile valley, where they rested for twelve days. Then they vigorously attacked the Saracens’ castle nearest the valley and would indeed have conquered it, had not the pagans driven out herds of animals, beasts of burden, and livestock. The Christians plundered these and thus returned to their tents laden with spoil. The pagans, exceedingly terrified, withdrew by night; and at dawn the Franks entered the castle, empty of people.

There they found abundance of wheat, wine, flour, barley, and oil, and celebrated the Purification of Saint Mary with the greatest devotion. There the king of the city of Camela sent the leaders generous gifts through his messengers and offered his peace to the Christians, promising [Col. 0700B] that he would never harm Christians but would love and honor them—provided only that the Christian people repaid him in good with like measure. The king of Tripoli also sent the Christians ten horses, four mules, and an immense weight of gold, and through envoys requested peace and friendship from them. The counts neither made peace with him nor accepted his offers; indeed, they answered confidently: “We reject all these things from you until you strive to become a Christian.”

After leaving the rich valley, they came to a castle called Arqa, beside which they pitched camp on the day before the Ides of February [12 February]. That town was defended by an innumerable multitude of pagans, crowds of Arabs and Publicans, who stoutly resisted the Christians’ assaults. [Col. 0700C] Fourteen Christian knights went toward Tripoli, which was not far from the army, and found sixty Turks leading before them many people—Saracens, Arabs, and Kurds—about fifteen hundred in number, and a great many animals. The Christians fiercely attacked them, killed six of them, took as many horses, put the others to flight, and carried off the animals. The unconquerable ferocity of the Franks terrified all their neighbors, both near and far. For God thus worked in them, He who is ever present to His champions. By God’s power the event turned out happily for the faithful: fourteen Christians overcame sixty Turks, routed the remaining multitude, and snatched the animals from their jaws.

[Col. 0700D] From Count Raymond’s army, Raymond Pilet and Viscount Raymond went out with not many knights and ranged before the city of Tortosa, where there was no small multitude of pagans. When it was already late, they withdrew to a secluded place, spent the night in advantageous positions, and kindled many fires as though the whole army had arrived. At sunrise the Franks assembled to attack the city; they found it empty of inhabitants and lived there as long as they besieged the castle.

The emir of the city of Maraclea, which was not far away, made peace with the Christians and brought their banners into the aforesaid city. Meanwhile Duke Godfrey [Col. 0701A] and the Count of Flanders and Bohemond came as far as Laodicea, commonly called Lycia. Bohemond again separated from them and returned to Antioch, which he greatly desired to be his own. The duke and count then besieged the city of Gibelet. Count Raymond heard that the pagans were approaching in great bodies of fighting men and were preparing an unmistakable battle against the Christians. He therefore sent to his companions who were besieging Gibelet, saying:

> A certain battle threatens us, and troops of pagans are coming against us. Therefore make terms of peace with the city you are besieging, and come more readily to protect your brethren. It is better to assemble and fight than to be separated from one another and defeated. In war the delay is slight, but the gain for victors is very great. Sieges consume much time, and besieged strongholds are scarcely subdued. Wars will subject nations and kingdoms to us. Enemies conquered in war will vanish like smoke. When the war is completed and the enemy defeated, a vast dominion will lie open to us. It is therefore good that we assemble, because if we can deserve to have God as our leader and forerunner, we shall undoubtedly triumph at once over our enemies. Hurry, I say, lest our rivals, when they arrive, find us unprepared.

The duke and count gladly heard this embassy, for they eagerly hungered for battle. They therefore made peace with the emir of Gibelet and received from him many gifts together with agreed terms. Then they set out at once to render aid. But they did not then find the Turks whom they expected. [Col. 0701C] They encamped beyond the river and from that side besieged the castle. Not long afterward, some Christians rode to Tripoli to see whether they might undertake anything harmful against the pagans. They found Turks and Arabs, together with the Tripolitans themselves, gathered outside the city, likewise awaiting the Christians’ sortie and lurking as if in ambush. At once the opposing sides fiercely attacked each other. The Hagarenes endured the first attacks for a while and resisted longer. At last they turned their backs under the blows and, in that retreat, lost many of their own men. Many of the city’s more distinguished inhabitants also fell there. From the spectacles atop the battlements, wives, mothers, and maidens called down evils upon the Christians and were anxious for their own people. They groaned, and some among them even applauded the valor of the Franks. From the slaughter of the pagans and the shedding of blood, the river flowing by the city seemed to have turned red. The cisterns within the city, supplied by the river, were defiled with blood. Thus the deepest grief fell upon the Tripolitans, both for their leading men slain and for their cisterns polluted by the foul invasion of blood. They suffered two losses in one day and deserved to shed double tears. They were distressed because the Franks had unexpectedly won the trophy of victory. They were saddened by the bloody defilement of their cisterns, which they valued highly. The Tripolitans were therefore terrified to the point of collapse and, besieged without a siege, [Col. 0702A] no longer dared leave their city. Their neighbors suffered the same disasters. The Franks, rejoicing in their victory and singing hymns to God, returned to their own men.

On the following day, knights from the army rode beyond the valley of Sem to plunder the country. Finding oxen, asses, sheep, and camels, numbering nearly three thousand, they returned joyfully to their camp laden with such great spoil. They remained before the castle of Arqa—for it was exceedingly impregnable—for three months and one day. They also celebrated the Lord’s Easter there on the fourth day before the Ides of April [10 April 1099]. Christian ships had arrived at a certain rather safe harbor near the castle; they supplied the camp with wheat, wine, cheese, [Col. 0702B] oil, beans, bacon, and a market of every abundance. The Christians also frequently went out to plunder the rich countryside, since they were in no way disappointed of their desire; for this reason they returned more cheerfully and were stirred more vigorously to make further raids. Many Christians were also killed there, for the Saracens’ swords were not always blunted, nor was their soldiery always inactive or their hand weak. Thus they killed Anselm of Ribboth-Mont and William the Picard, men of noble birth and skilled in war, whose notable deeds in that army of Christ were plainly known; and many others fell whose names may God preserve in the memorial of His life.

The king of Tripoli frequently addressed the Christian leaders through intermediaries [Col. 0702C] and tried by every means to test their minds, so that, by giving them gifts, he might make peace with them, induce them to abandon the castle, and pay them agreed sums of money. The Christians proposed Christianity to him, and they could not be moved otherwise from their purpose. But he strongly resisted Christianity and feared to abandon the laws of his fathers and the customs of his forefathers. As time went on, the new crops had turned white. For that tract of land is warmed by greater heat than the region on this side of the mountains; and therefore a quicker summer ripens its harvests more quickly. In the middle of March fresh beans were gathered; on the Ides of April wheat was cut; and the autumn of the vintage returned.

Duke Godfrey, therefore, and the count of Normandy, the count of Flanders, the count of Toulouse, and Tancred discussed proceeding on the journey, because the favorable time was now pressing—indeed, almost passing. [Col. 0702D] They therefore abandoned the castle which they had long besieged, came to Tripoli, and concluded a treaty with the Tripolitans. The king of Tripoli gave them fifteen thousand bezants and fifteen horses of great value, and returned three hundred pilgrims whom he had long held captive. Finally, under the pretext of peace, he provided them with a market.
