Therefore all were refreshed; and he solemnly promised them that, if they should ever defeat the war which the emir of Babylon was then preparing against them, he himself would become a Christian and thereafter hold his land in allegiance to them.

Thus, in the middle of May, they departed from the city and traveled all day by a narrow, steep, and trackless road, reaching the castle of Betheren late in the day. Then they approached Zebari, a city situated on the seacoast. There, because of a lack of water, they suffered the intolerable distress of excessive thirst; greatly weakened by it, they hurried to the river Braim, where men and beasts of burden were refreshed with drink.

On the Sunday of the Ascension, they had to proceed by a narrow road. All day they feared raids by pagans, yet did not cease moving forward. Standard-bearers and armed knights went ahead and guarded the entire army against ambushers. Behind them came those responsible for the baggage and the helpers of the pack-animal drivers. The military formation hastened behind, and every man was present for everyone’s needs. Thus [Col. 0703B] every day the baggage-carriers and porters hurried on, while groups of unarmed people clung to them. Trumpets sounded, and they advanced by stages, lest the weaker fail on the road. They kept watch by turns at night, and wherever greater fear threatened, there they prepared more vigilant guards. They admitted nothing rash or disorderly. The undisciplined were punished, the ignorant instructed, the rebellious rebuked, and the incontinent reproved for their talkativeness; all alike were urged to almsgiving. All also cultivated frugality and chastity, and, so to speak, there was in the camp a kind of school of moral discipline. Such was the rule and such the pattern of those traveling to Jerusalem. Therefore, while they maintained this rigor of discipline and abounded in charitable affection, [Col. 0703C] God plainly dwelt among them and fought His wars through them. We have said this in order that, by extolling these men, we may rebuke the life and conduct of those undisciplined persons who presumptuously succeeded to this glorious expedition. For among human beings nothing is more useful than discipline.

Finally, having crossed the mountainous country, where enemies had been feared but none encountered, they passed along the sea by four cities: Baruch; Sarepta, commonly called Sagitta; Tyre, which is named Sor; Acharon, called Acra; and thence to the castle called Caiphas. From there, seeking lodging, they came near Caesarea, where they rested on the day of Pentecost, 10 June. Then they came to Diospolis, called Ramatha, or Arimathia, or Ramula; [Col. 0703D] and there, wearied by the journey, they halted, while its citizens escaped in flight through fear of the pilgrims. Long ago the mother Church there had enjoyed episcopal rank; but now, bereft of the dignity of a bishop, she groaned in great sorrow, because that place lay ignobly beneath the stiff-necked Saracens. The Christians restored a bishop to the aforesaid city and offered him tithes of their resources, so that, from the abundance collected, he might live and restore the church, long desolate. There the blessed champion George had fought conspicuously and nobly completed the course of his martyrdom; near the small city rises his basilica, where the precious body of that same athlete had rested. Him whom the Christians had seen as guide and forerunner in the battle of Antioch, and as a mighty defender against the erring people, they wished also always to win as companion and defender. They reverently honoured his basilica and, as we have said, established a bishop at Ramula.

## XVII. The Christian army reaches Jerusalem. The siege of the city.

Divinely inspired, they set out at dawn and, at the signal, entered upon the road, hastening toward Jerusalem; and, as they had long desired, on that day they came as far as the city. Jerusalem is about twenty-four miles from Ramula. Once they reached the place from which they could see turreted Jerusalem, they wept for overwhelming joy; they stopped, worshipped God, and, kneeling, kissed the holy ground. All would have walked barefoot, had fear of the enemy not required them to proceed armed. They went and wept; and those who had assembled for prayer, about to fight first, carried weapons instead of bags.

> **Note:** [Col. 0703D] Thus in Chesnius; that is, *peris* in place of *perarum* [“bags”], apparently required by the sense.

The Christians besieged Jerusalem on 6 June [1099], not as stepchildren besiege a stepmother, but as sons a mother. Her friends and sons surrounded her in order to hem in strangers and adulterous intruders—not to capture her while free, but to free her while captive. Robert, duke of the Normans, besieged Jerusalem on the northern side, near the church of St Stephen the Protomartyr, where he fell asleep in the Lord after being stoned by the Jews. Beside him the count of Flanders [Col. 0704C] pitched his tents. Godfrey the duke and Tancred besieged her from the west. From the south Count Raymond besieged her on Mount Sion, near the church of Blessed Mary, Mother of God, where the Lord Jesus supped with his disciples. Jerusalem, therefore, was enclosed under siege by her sons, while within she was profaned by the Manzerine peoples.

Then Hugh Bunel, son of Robert of Jalgeio, fully equipped with arms, came to the duke of the Normans and faithfully offered him his following, as to his natural lord. Graciously received by him, he vigorously aided, by hand and counsel, those besieging Aelia—that is, Jerusalem. For long before, in Normandy, he had cut Countess Mabel to pieces, because she had violently deprived him of his paternal inheritance. Therefore that knight, with his brothers Ralph, Richard, and Goislen, fled after committing so great a crime into Apulia, then into Sicily, and afterward withdrew to Emperor Alexius. But nowhere could he remain safe for long. William the Bastard, king of the English, together with all the descendants of that woman, sent out searchers throughout the world to seek him, promising honours and gifts to the pursuers who should kill the exiled murderer wherever they found him. Thus worthy Hugh, fearing the mighty hands and far-reaching arms of so great a king, left the whole Latin world and, fearing the flock of the baptized, lived for a long time in exile among foreign peoples, learning their customs and speech for twenty years.

> Le Prévost: *properis una voce*; this yields no sense.

Received by the Norman duke, he greatly benefited his men, explaining the pagan customs, evasive tricks, and deceits by which they cunningly worked against the faithful. Cosan also, a noble and powerful hero of Turkish stock, voluntarily approached the Christians and assisted them in many ways to take the city. For he faithfully believed in Christ and earnestly desired regeneration through holy baptism. Therefore, as friends and brothers, he strove with all his strength to assist our people in gaining the glory of Palestine and the capital of David’s kingdom.

On the third day of the siege, knights left the Christian camp—namely Raymond Pilet, [Col. 0705B] Raymond of Taurina, and many others—to reconnoitre or plunder. They attacked, overcame, and put to flight two hundred Arabs whom they found. They killed many and seized thirty horses there. Having done this, they returned cheerfully to their own side.

On Monday they vigorously attacked the city and would indeed, as they thought, have prevailed, had they prepared ladders in sufficient number. Nevertheless, they levelled the outer wall and set one raised ladder against the inner wall. Christian knights took turns climbing it and fought hand-to-hand upon the wall with the Saracens, striking them with swords and lances. Many on either side were killed in that engagement, though more of the pagans perished. [Col. 0705C] When the trumpet sounded the withdrawal, the Christians finally desisted from that assault and returned to camp.

Meanwhile, the provisions they had brought with them had failed. Bread was no longer to be found for purchase, nor could they go out to forage for grain. That country is not at all watered; rather, it is parched and exceedingly harsh, and therefore poorly suited to beasts of burden and animals, being scant in pasture. Nor is the land wooded, and therefore it is less productive. It produces only palm and olive, though it also bears vines. The Jordan, as they suppose, is separated from Jerusalem by about thirty stadia. It has six lakes at a distance. The city has its cisterns, from which it is supplied. At the foot of Mount Sion is the spring of Siloam; but it could scarcely support a few people. Yet it was helpful, and even a little water was purchased at great expense. They led their horses to drink six miles away, not without very great fear.

Meanwhile it was reported in the camp that Christian supply-ships had put in at the harbour of Joppa, which we think was called Joppe in the ancient name. This greatly pleased all in the camp. The leaders deliberated about how to make safe the journeys out and back for those bringing necessities from the ships. Joppa is about eight miles from Ramula. The people of Ascalon or the natives, roaming in the hill-country or in the cut-out passages of steep ravines, repeatedly attacked and slaughtered travellers. This disturbance or rumour disrupted the merchants’ supplies. To carry out this task, at earliest dawn [Col. 0706A] Raymond Pilet, Achard of Montmerlo, William of Sabra, their fellow-knights, and certain foot-soldiers set out from Raymond of Toulouse’s army toward the sea. Trusting in their courage, they marched to the harbour; but they became separated from one another—whether by design or through ignorance of the road, we do not know.

Thirty knights, taking another road and separated from their companions, encountered one hundred Arabs, Turks, and Saracens from the admiral’s army. They boldly attacked and joined battle. Their opponents, however, stubbornly resisted and, trusting in their numbers, surrounded the few with many. This is the Saracens’ manner of fighting. They had already enclosed the Christians and were confidently talking of their deaths, when a messenger, shouting for Raymond Pilet, roused him thus: “Unless you fly with the utmost speed to bring aid to your fellow-knights, you have certainly lost them all. They are already encircled by enemies, though they are still somehow defending themselves.”

At this, they let loose the reins, spur their war-horses, and all fly to the rescue faster than speech. With shields set before their breasts, they drive back the crowds with their lances, scatter those opposing them, and each man lays his opponent upon the ground. The enemies are caught unawares; the whole matter is committed to swords; and, with God’s help, they prevail. The pagans again drew up two battle-lines, thinking that they could resist, but achieved nothing. The Franks again attacked them fiercely and thus freed their own men from that assault, though they lost there Achard, a most courageous knight, and some foot-soldiers. [Col. 0706C] They pursued the fleeing Turks for nearly four miles and pierced many with sharp spear-points. They also retained one hundred and three horses, and one living man, who under compulsion related in order everything being prepared against the Christians.

Meanwhile, during the siege, violent thirst afflicted and pressed hard upon the Christians. When they led horses six miles away to water, the pagans lay in ambush and severely harassed them from narrow places. The Kidron and other streams had dried up in the extreme heat. Barley-bread was expensive in the camp. The natives, hiding in caves or caverns, had concealed all supplies.

The appointed leaders came together in council and stated what ought to be done amid such disasters. They said: “We are hemmed in on every side; bread fails, water is lacking. We ourselves are gravely besieged while we suppose that we are besieging this city. We scarcely dare leave the camp, and then return empty-handed. Our long delay has brought on this want; unless we take precautions, we shall incur still worse. By weapons and strength alone, without engines, we cannot take this city. Its walls, battlements, and towers stand in the way; so do its defenders, abundantly supplied within. What, then, do you advise? Let us undertake something that will benefit all of us and harm the citizens who are shut in. Let us strive to make wooden engines with which to attack the walls or towers. Since this land bears no timber, let us seek beams from houses or carry off timbers from churches; let us raise our engines once assembled and attack this city with all our strength. Otherwise we waste our time in vain.”

At length the faithful champions found timber far from the place and brought it back with great labour. Carpenters were summoned from the whole army: some shaped the rough surface of the wood, others hewed it, others bored it, and others joined timber to timber. Duke Godfrey was building one engine from his own resources; Count Raymond of Toulouse had ordered another to be erected at his own expense. The Hagarenes were no less busy fortifying the city. At night they laboured to heighten the towers and worked without rest to defend the city.

On a certain Sabbath, in the dead of night, they moved Duke Godfrey’s engine; at sunrise they raised it on the eastern side [Col. 0707B] and for three days prepared and fitted it together with utmost diligence. The count, however, brought his engine up near the wall on the south side—a thing that we may call a wooden castle. But a deep ravine prevented its being joined to the wall. Such an engine cannot be brought down slopes or directed against mountainous ground; it always requires level plain ground in order to be moved. Therefore heralds cried throughout the army that whoever cast three stones into that ditch should receive one denarius for the stones cast. Thus all whom delay had wearied eagerly and vigorously devoted themselves to the undertaking.

Bishops and priests addressed the people, speaking excellently of Christ’s death and of the place of his Passion, which they pointed out before their eyes; and they spoke piously and eloquently of the heavenly Jerusalem, of which the earthly city gives a figure. All the laymen, girded with arms, therefore attacked the city unanimously, pressing it by night and day on Wednesday and Thursday. Then, after prayers and fasts, sobs and almsgiving had gone before, strengthened by communion of the sacred viaticum, they attacked the city at earliest dawn on Friday, the Ides of July [Friday, 15 July], but could not then prevail. Those upon the towers and walls assisted one another and continually hurled fire and stones. Raymond of Toulouse, after the ditch had been filled—for they had completed it in three days and nights—brought his castle to the wall. He angrily reproached his men for their delay until Monday, because of the excessive labour that they had endured throughout the whole week.

After the morning’s work, at the duke’s command, the Franks rested a little from fighting, and the pagans from defence. But the admiral Guinimund and his nephew Frigolendis the Persian were in the Tower of David, and had summoned the magistrates and leading men of the city there for conference. Meanwhile the women of the city climbed upon the flat roofs of the houses, according to Palestinian custom, and, arranging dances, sang this song loudly in their own language:

> Sing worthy praises to Mahomet, our god,  
> and offer sacrifices with joyful festivity,  
> that the fearsome strangers may be conquered and perish.
>
> They ravage and swell with barbarous spirit;  
> they spare no one, but resist the people of the East,  
> and crave the spoils which our land has nourished.
>
> Pressed by misfortune, they have come here  
> to despoil our delights and rich provinces.  
> They condemn all our peoples and judge us beasts.
>
> They worship a crucified God, washed in baptism.  
> They scorn our rites, our worship, and our gods with disgrace.  
> But suddenly they shall be overwhelmed by punishments and destruction.
>
> Brave Turks, by fighting drive the Franks hence.  
> Recall the famous deeds of your ancient fathers.  
> Your enemies shall flee or perish today.

These and many similar things the Turkish women sang on high. The worshippers of Christ listened in astonishment and with close attention, diligently learning from their interpreters what the Turks were saying. Then Cono, a German count, an upright man and wise counsellor, who had the sister of Duke Godfrey as his wife, said: “My lord duke, do you hear what these women say? Do you understand why they do this? Women’s exultant exhortation means a fearful failure of the men. Look: through weariness and fear the men are weakening, while the women rise up and, as though in reproach and disgrace of the warriors, chatter against us. They have dared, not without penalty, to terrify and deceive us with frivolous arguments. Let us, in contrast, use manly—indeed heavenly—counsel. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, who suffered here on Friday, let us take up arms, attack the city gloriously, and today reach the Lord’s tomb.”

## XVIII. Jerusalem is taken by those signed with the cross.

[Col. 0708C]

At the third hour, when the Jews condemned the Lord before Pilate, the Christians, mindful of that Passion, as though their strength had been renewed, and with a new boldness coming upon them—as if they had laboured not at all before—began to fight. Duke Godfrey and his brother Eustace fought bravely, and the rest followed them. Then Letald and Raimbold Croton, worthy knights, climbed the wall and, fighting resolutely, shouted aloud. Others immediately followed them. Those who until then had defended the walls there fled in all directions and no longer concerned themselves with protecting the city. The multitude of Christians entered the city, pursued the fugitives, and spared no one.

[Col. 0708D] The Armenians, Greeks, and Syrians, who had formerly been subject to the Turks in Aelia—that is, Jerusalem—and had nevertheless somehow served Christian worship amid great oppression, fled together in a body to the basilica of the Holy Sepulchre when they saw the Christians bursting violently into the city. With the utmost devotion, crying *Kyrie eleison*—“Lord, have mercy”—and other supplications appropriate to the occasion, they awaited the outcome. Tancred, with his troop, ignorant of the streets, came there by God’s guidance. From their prayers and religious actions he recognized the aforesaid people as worshippers of Christ. “These,” he said, “are Christians. Therefore let none of you harm them in any way. We have not come here to injure worshippers of Christ, but to rescue them from cruel oppressors. They are our brothers and friends, faithful persons hitherto tested, like gold in a furnace, through many tribulations.”

Then the distinguished champion left Ilgerius Bigod, commander of his force, there with two hundred knights, appointing him guardian of the place so that pagans might not enter there further. He himself, with the remaining squadrons, proceeded to attack the other fortifications and assisted his comrades who were running through the city and busied in killing foreigners.

Meanwhile, the faithful inhabitants who had remained with Ilgerius in the church addressed him privately. Seeking his protection, they favourably led him and his companions to the holy places: namely, the Lord’s tomb and other sacred objects; and they showed them certain things which, through fear of the pagans, they and their forebears had long hidden in secret places. There [Col. 0709B] Ilgerius found, among other relics, in a marble capital hollowed out like a shrine beneath an altar, a little ball of hair of Holy Mary, Mother of God. He afterward carried it into Gaul and reverently divided it among sacred places of bishoprics and monasteries.

For the Virgin Mother, untouched, grieved greatly at the Passion of Christ, her Son and Lord; and, in the ancient custom of her people and that age, she tore her garments, pulled out her hair, and reverently uttered mournful laments for the death of so great a friend. The neighbouring women who were present—namely, devout women who had long adhered to the divine discipleship—piously supported and embraced the Mother of the heavenly King as she wept, and gently comforted her as the occasion required. They devoutly gathered and carefully preserved the hair then pulled out, which John the Theologian and other lovers of Christ afterward placed in a safe location, knowing that this would benefit the salvation of many.

Our pen has inserted this into the work because the aforesaid Ilgerius gave two of the sacred hairs to Ernald the monk, his cousin, at Chartres; and Ernald presented them to the church of Manlian, where many healings of the sick occurred through them. Now I return to the continuation of our narrative.

The admiral, who held the Tower of David, terrified with the leading men of the city and many others whom he had there with him, surrendered to Count Raymond and immediately opened the gate to him. In former times pilgrims had purchased access through that gate with their money, because they used to pay tolls there; otherwise they were mercilessly detained at the gate. The citizens fled together to Solomon’s Temple and still presumed to defend themselves in it. They renewed heavy attacks upon the Christians. But when they saw that they had accomplished nothing, they threw down their swords and submitted their necks to slaughter. No one knows the number of those killed. Their blood, flowing through the Temple, reached the calves of those walking there, and vast heaps of corpses increased throughout the city, because the victors spared neither age, sex, rank, nor any condition. They persecuted and killed them with such hatred because they had polluted the Lord’s Temple and the basilica of the Holy Sepulchre, [Col. 0710A] had appropriated Solomon’s Temple and other churches for their unlawful uses, and had defiled them indecently.

Some had fled onto Solomon’s Temple and sought Tancred’s banner, so that they might at least be saved in this way; having received it, they awaited whatever fate might come. But this helped them little or not at all, because the Christians did not spare even them. Except that some were kept alive for a time to carry out the dead, they were eventually sold or alienated from their homeland. Tancred was greatly saddened by this, but did not on that account rage against his companions.

Count Raymond of Toulouse ordered the admiral, who had entrusted himself to him and surrendered the Tower of David, along with the others who were with him, to be conducted unharmed as far as Ascalon. For he had made this agreement with them and kept his compact inviolate. The victors did not plunder or burn that city in the manner of a subdued city. Rather, finding the houses furnished with every kind of good, they kept them for their own needs; and many shared their abundant discoveries with poorer people. Each person freely and peacefully possessed, with all the treasures within it, whatever house—great or small—he had first entered and cleared of pagans, and retains it to this day by hereditary right.

## XIX. The crusaders establish their residences in the city of Jerusalem. Godfrey is chosen king.

[Col. 0710C] The Christians, having attained the triumph long desired, washed their hands from the slaughter. Many, barefoot, rejoicing and weeping for joy, hastened in crowds to kiss the holy tomb of the Holy Saviour, and there offered joyful gifts and sacrifices of peace. Then there was immense joy among the faithful, because all had obtained what they had long awaited and sought through many labours and dangers. There, cheerful, they saw the end of their toil; now more secure because of their present fortune, they imagined that rewards of future good things would come to them. They also made provision for removing the corpses, because horror was increasing and the stench was enormous. The bodies of the slain were heaped upon pyres by captive pagans and poor Christians, paid for the task; when these had been burned, our men cleansed the city of its impurities.

The faithful soldiers of Christ sat secure in the city of Jerusalem and gave worthy thanks to God, by whose free aid they had gained victory over the pagans. They restored their dignities to the churches and fitted each one for the work of prayer. They instituted a feast on Friday, 15 July, the day on which they recovered the city. They also deliberated about establishing a king there; and on the eighth day after the capture of the city, by common counsel they elected Duke Godfrey as king. He was a man of royal blood, descended from forefathers of Christian profession. Eustace, count of Boulogne, who fought the battle of Senlac in England with William, married Ida, sister of Godfrey, duke of Lorraine. By her he fathered Godfrey, Baldwin, and Eustace, whom God’s grace honoured in many ways in this world with wealth and virtues, and especially proved, strengthened, and exalted in the Jerusalem expedition. Godfrey, therefore, being the elder, was raised to the throne of King David’s realm, because he was glorious in vigour, skilled in warfare in the French manner, most effective in military affairs in heart and arm, generous and serene, and abounding in clemency.

Arnulf of Zocris, a most learned man, was also elected to fulfil the office of bishop. Meanwhile Tancred and Count Eustace, with many retainers and dependants, went to Neapolis, having been voluntarily invited by its citizens; and the people of Neapolis surrendered their city to them in peace. They stayed and rested there joyfully for several days, until the king sent swift envoys to them with this message: “We have heard—and it is certain—that the Babylonian admiral is at Ascalon and is preparing a great war there against us. Hasten, therefore, and come, so that we too may boldly meet them before they can shut us up in the city. For those shut in have difficult entry and exit, and unsuitable fear frequently troubles them. Let us meet in the open, free field; and, with God directing us, the outcome will be freer and easier for us. We are more ready than they in arms and strength, and we wish to meet them where they as yet expect nothing to fear.”

On hearing this, Tancred and Eustace came to Ramula by the sea, where they found many Arabs riding ahead of the admiral’s army. They attacked them confidently and quickly scattered them. They killed some and kept others alive, from whom they obtained reliable reports about the admiral and his army. They investigated every point precisely: who they were, how innumerable their people were, what they were preparing, and where they intended to fight.

Tancred sent the following carefully elicited information from the captives to the king by messengers: “Know beyond doubt that battle is prepared against us at Ascalon, and that nearly the whole world has assembled and conspired, intending violently to crush and subjugate us. Come, therefore; gather all your forces, and let us attack the synagogue of Satan. For if, as you ordered, we meet them unafraid and by surprise, God helping us, we shall easily prevail; for they are occupied with their arms and much equipment and are carrying engines to attack the city.”

The king therefore proclaimed through a herald that all should prepare themselves for war and zealously follow the king’s banner. The king, the patriarch, the appointed count of Flanders, and the bishop of Martarona left the city on Tuesday. Count Saint-Gilles and the Norman would not leave until they had more certain information concerning the admiral’s incursion. But after seeing all that was being prepared, [Col. 0712A] the king sent the bishop of Martarona to Jerusalem, that he might testify to the leaders concerning everything being prepared. After speaking with the Toulousan and the Norman, the bishop of Martarona, hurrying to report the counts’ declared words to the king and patriarch, fell into the hands of the pagans. It is uncertain whether he was carried off or killed, but he never appeared afterward.

The Toulousan and the Norman set out to battle with many men and left Jerusalem on Wednesday. The clergy devoted themselves to Masses and prayers; Peter the Hermit, the scant remnant of weak people who had stayed behind, and the unwarlike sex of women carried processions from church to church, devoutly persisting in prayers and almsgiving so that God, propitious to his people, might mercifully help them [Col. 0712B] and irretrievably overthrow their enemies with a strong hand.

The leaders, with their armies, assembled at the stream opposite Ascalon. There they found abundant herds and were enriched with rich plunder. Three hundred Arabs pursued the Franks, but they immediately rushed upon them and, after capturing two of them, put them to flight as far as their army. After this sortie the Christians returned to camp and rested that night—except that all rather devoted themselves to watches and prayers. Late in the day the patriarch publicly forbade anyone who would fight on the next day to concern himself in any way, before battle, with plundering spoils.

## XX. The battle of Ascalon. Victory falls to the Christians. Concerning Baldric, archbishop of Dol.

[Col. 0712C] At sunrise, on the day before the Ides of August, Christ’s sacred host entered a valley beside the sea, made beautiful by a lovely plain, and there formed six battle-lines. The king and the count of the Normans, the Toulousan, the Fleming and Guaston, Eustace and Tancred commanded the troops; and each carefully arrayed his archers and foot-soldiers. Setting these in front, they advanced slowly, instructing them how to shout the war-cry, how to withstand attack, how by striking to pierce enemies thought impenetrable, how to look back often without fear to their standards, and how to harden themselves to endure hostile blows—although they had learned all these things in other battles successfully fought.

No less, opposite them, the pagans massed in wedges more numerous than stars; their countless legions stretched from side to side in ranks. They put Ethiopians in front, stationed them in position, and ordered them to remain unmoving. These men, with knees fixed to the ground but the right foot set behind, protecting their upper bodies with shields, used bows and swords. They had been commanded neither to retreat even for a moment nor to move a single step beyond the position occupied. The military companies held the assigned positions in the array in which they had been drawn up. Since they feared excessive thirst because of the heat, the cloud of dust, the exertion, and the duration of the fighting, they had suspended full drinking-vessels from their necks, refreshed by which they might stand more steadily or pursue fugitives more tirelessly. There was no mention of their own flight: they trusted in their countless multitudes, in the courageous hearts of barbarian peoples, and in imperial decrees that they should never flee. “Let fugitives,” said the emperor, “be punished by the penalty of death!”

With battle very carefully prepared on both sides, when they approached the place of combat, the Christians paused a little, raised their eyes devoutly to heaven, and prayed with their knees fixed upon the ground. They hoped for aid from heaven, which they had often experienced as present to them in many needs. When they had prayed briefly and reverently touched their foreheads with the sign of the saving cross, they rode forward with greater confidence and manfully attacked the pagans in the name of the Lord Jesus. [Col. 0713B] The pagans had already halted and waited unmoving.

On the right wing beside the sea rode the Toulousan. On the left side the king advanced with his legions. In the centre fought the Norman, the Fleming, Tancred, and others; yet ten thousand foreigners rose against each thousand of ours. When battle began, Robert, duke of the Normans, saw from a distance the admiral’s standard, which had a golden apple at the tip of its spear, while the spear itself shone white, handsomely sheathed in silver. Once he recognized where the admiral was, he boldly charged through the middle of the battle-lines upon him and grievously wounded him, nearly to death. This struck very great fear into the pagans. The count of Flanders also attacked them as an enemy, and Tancred fearlessly attacked them through the middle of the camp. The pagan soldiers immediately took to flight. The Ethiopians stood stupefied. The king and certain Franks turned against the Ethiopians and, lingering there for a while, cut them down crosswise with swords as if they were grain, mutilating and dismembering their bodies. The fields were flooded with blood, and pagan corpses lay everywhere.

The Christians pursued the fugitives. The pagans, terrified by God’s power, had no place for recovery. Their eyes, as was later reported by those who escaped, became so dim that, even with open eyes, they could scarcely see the Christians and could do them no harm at all. Many did not dare to bark against few, and strove by many means to escape. But our men, prevailing, punished the pagans without distinction and spared no one. Thus a deadly day had come upon the pagans, in which no opportunity to escape was granted to anyone, because throughout the trees, rocks, and hiding places of caves they perished under the weapons of the victorious hand.

Count Raymond, fighting from the seaward side, killed innumerable men and forcefully barred the fugitives from the city, which was some distance away from them. Thus exhausted, they either remained behind, were immediately struck down and died, or threw themselves into the sea; and so, headlong, they rushed from death into death. The admiral’s fleet covered the whole sea, and that people waited for the outcome of the battle. But when they saw a fate other than that which they had hoped coming upon their men, they boarded skiffs, set their sails slantwise to the wind, [Col. 0714A] and rowed homeward.

They say that the admiral, scarcely still breathing, groaned deeply and lamented thus:

> “O Creator of all, what is this? What has happened, that a hostile fate has harmed us? Alas for me! What unspeakable disgrace, what lasting reproach has befallen our people! A beggarly people, a small people, has prevailed over our people. How has this happened? Having made an agreement, I led here two hundred thousand soldiers, with foot-soldiers beyond number, whom I believed a match for all the world. Yet now, if I am not to lie, they have been so shamefully overcome by fewer than a thousand knights and thirty thousand foot-soldiers. Either their God is almighty and fights for them, or ours is angry with us and punishes and rebukes us in excessively harsh wrath. Whatever it may be, one thing is certain: I shall not rise against them again, but shall return dishonoured to my homeland for as long as I live.”

Having said this, he lamented tearfully and grieved from his inmost heart.

The people of Ascalon, when they saw the fleeing Hagarenes entering the city in a mass, and Count Raymond with his Provençals relentlessly pursuing and slaughtering them, shut the gates and excluded alike their enemies and their auxiliaries. For they feared that the invincible enemies, together with their supporting forces, would enter Ascalon and utterly subdue it after killing its citizens. But the man of Toulouse stood undaunted before the city with his troops, and destroyed to the point of extermination the Philistines who lingered before their refuge, as though they were sheep.

Moreover, the citizens, looking down from the battlements [Col. 0714C] upon the Christians’ persistence, and fearing that they might suffer the destruction which they had seen or heard had befallen their neighbours, asked for the count’s banner and faithfully promised him their certain surrender. They reflected, indeed, that he was nearer and bore down upon them more urgently for their destruction, and that he had saved Admiral Guinimund and the others who had entrusted themselves to his good faith. He therefore sent them his standard-bearer at their request; and, after all those outside the city had been put to flight or killed, he went to his peers. When they had ceased from slaughter and assembled together, he said:

“Behold, thanks be to God, victory has come to us favourably, and Ascalon, with its citizens subdued, lies almost open. The Ascalonites have now received my banner [Col. 0714D]; and, if you consent, they will favour me as their lord and obey my commands for their own safety.”

The king replied: “Far be it from me to yield the lordship of this city to anyone; rather, by taking it by assault I shall presently subject it to my own dominion! Ascalon lies near Jerusalem, and it is fitting that it be subject to the rule of him who presides over Jerusalem.”

Robert the Norman and the Fleming, together with other magnates, said to the king: “We all know well enough that the Count of Saint-Gilles willingly left rich lands and strongly fortified towns for God’s sake; that in God’s expedition he has performed many brave deeds with the utmost vigour; and that he has surpassed us all in enduring more grievous perils. Therefore, if he resolves steadfastly to complete the pilgrimage which he began, and to defend the holy city which he fiercely captured in order to win it for God, you ought willingly [Col. 0715A] to offer him the city which you do not yet possess and which he claims. For when we return to our own lands, he will undoubtedly be very necessary to you in counsel and in arms. The city will be nobly and profitably subject to royal majesty, for so great a hero will do homage to it and serve it in arms.”

Since the king did not yield to the magnates’ persuasions, the count departed angrily and ordered the Ascalonites to defend themselves resolutely. The king wished to besiege the city; but, as all the nobles withdrew because of anger and weariness, he could accomplish nothing alone, and sorrowfully left the town unharmed. Shame! Neither he nor the other kings who reigned after him for forty years could capture the aforesaid metropolis of the Philistines down to the present day; [Col. 0715B] indeed, through it they lost more than a hundred thousand men, besides innumerable other losses. Thus insatiable ambition gains its reward. If true charity had possessed the king, and if he had loved his neighbour as himself according to God’s law, he could have gained the hostile town that very day, through which a free passage as far as Babylon would have lain open to the worshippers of Christ. I praise King Godfrey greatly; but, as the Apostle Paul writes to the Corinthians (1 Cor. 11), in this I do not praise him.

It is reported that the admiral had two hundred thousand soldiers and countless companies of infantry in the battle. The Christians, however, had scarcely one thousand cavalrymen and thirty thousand infantry. With God’s help, when the slaughter had been accomplished, they returned to plunder the tents of the Ishmaelites. There they found, [Col. 0715C] to put it briefly, whatever fine equipment can be imagined: silver and gold, provisions, flour and oil, herds of innumerable beasts, every magnificence of ornament, heaps of weapons, and anything else that could be better. Having plundered all these things, they returned to the holy city of Jerusalem and offered God worthy thanks in every church. Robert, duke of the Normans, bought the standard from those who had retained it from the wounded admiral, for twenty marks of silver, and placed it in the Lord’s Sepulchre as a memorial of the memorable victory. Another bought the sword of the same admiral for sixty bezants.

Thus indescribable joy arose throughout all Christendom. In this manner the Christians liberated Jerusalem from the hands of the impious [Col. 0715D] Turks in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1099, and, with Christ as their leader, triumphed over them many times. This great battle was fought on the second Ides of August [12 August 1099], and Christendom [Col. 0716A] throughout the world was exalted in giving thanks to God.

Thus far I have followed in the footsteps of the venerable Baldric and have given a truthful narrative of Christ’s renowned host, which, with God’s help, distinguishedly defeated the swarms of heathens in the eastern lands. In many places I inserted in my work the very words of that rhetorician, as he himself had produced them, not daring to publish his statements otherwise, since I did not believe that I could improve them. Yet, lest the prolixity of our account burden readers with weariness, I cut away certain things by abridging them; and I truthfully added some matters, deserving to be made known to posterity, which he had omitted, according as I learned them from those who took part in the labours and dangers.

I have resolved reverently to honour the aforesaid elder, whom I knew well. He was a citizen of Orléans, [Col. 0716B] a monk and abbot of Bourgueil, trained in the liberal studies and venerable for the merits of his religious life. Thereafter, because of his piety and wisdom, he was raised by ecclesiastical election to the rank of archbishop of Dol. As bishop he preserved monastic life, and generally lived with monks as circumstances allowed. For he governed the unruly Bretons, whose perversity he could not endure. Therefore he often left those insolent and lawless people and fled to Normandy, where the church of Dol had estates on the river Risle from the time of Saint Samson, during the reign of Hildebert, king of the Franks, and possessed them quietly and peaceably. There, by his writings and teachings, he incited his hearers to God’s worship; he visited the neighbouring monasteries—namely Fécamp, Fontenelle [Col. 0716C] and Jumièges, along with many others—and strengthened them by sacred sermons in the fear of God. At length he died in a good old age and was buried at Préaux, in the basilica of Saint Peter the Apostle, before the crucifix.

Here, wearied by writing and investigating matters remote in place, namely events performed in eastern climates, and eagerly desiring rest, I resolve to end the sixth book [Note: [Col. 0715D] “Sixth” in the first division of the work.] of the *Ecclesiastical History*. In the seventh, if I live safe and free, with the help of our Saviour, in whom I place my chief hope, I shall truthfully treat of the varied events, favourable and adverse, which occurred over thirty years, and shall simply communicate them, to the best of my ability, for the knowledge of posterity. For I suppose that there will be some like myself who [Col. 0716D] will eagerly search chronographers for the sequence of this generation, and for transient deeds, so that they may recount to themselves the past vicissitudes of a declining age for instruction or pleasure.

## Summary of Book Ten

[Col. 0715]

I. Pope Urban II dies. Paschal II; Emperors Henry IV and Henry V; their conflicts with the supreme pontiffs.  
II. Narrative of English and Norman affairs. The character of William Rufus. Deaths of certain prelates. On Blessed Anselm, bishop of Canterbury.  
III. Crusading knights, bishops, and abbots. [Col. 0717]  
IV. Frankish and Norman magnates contend with one another over the Vexin.  
V. The great king of the Norwegians wages war against the Irish. War between the English and the Welsh.  
VI. On Count Elias of Maine. William Rufus harasses the people of Maine. On Hildebert, archbishop of Tours.  
VII. Elias, count of Maine, is captured. King William occupies the city of Le Mans. Count Elias recovers his freedom.  
VIII. Blessed Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, comes to the pope in Italy. Elias, count of Maine, renews war against King William.  
IX. Serlo and Roger of Sées, abbots of Saint-Evroul. Disputes arise between the monks and the bishop of Lisieux. Consecration of the church of Saint-Evroul.  
X. On the crusaders. Godfrey, king of Jerusalem. Greeks and Syrians, having expelled the Franks, seize the city of Laodicea. Raymond of Toulouse remains at Constantinople with Emperor Alexius. The duke of Normandy departs from Syria.  
XI. Bohemond recovers Laodicea. Duke Robert travels through Italy, intending to return to Normandy. New knights prepare themselves for the holy war. On the mournful event which occurred in the New Forest.  
XII. Evil omens concerning King William. The aforesaid king dies.  
XIII. Henry, father of William Rufus, succeeds him on the throne.  
XIV. Count Elias of Maine recovers the county of Maine.  
XV. Rivalry and dissensions arise between King Henry and Duke Robert. On Ranulf Flambard, bishop of Durham. Duke Robert crosses to England with an armed force.  
XVI. Peace is arranged between the two brothers, Henry and Robert.  
XVII. The duke of Poitou, the duke of Burgundy, and many other magnates take the cross. Their conflicts with the emperor of Constantinople.  
XVIII. The treachery of Emperor Alexius. The army of crusaders is destroyed by the Turks in Asia Minor.  
XIX. The rule of Godfrey, king of Jerusalem; Baldwin, his brother and successor; the battle of Ramla.  
XX. Harpin of Bourges is captured by the Saracens.  
XXI. Bohemond is captured by the Saracens. Melaz, daughter of Daliman, their prince, frees him from prison by subtle artifice.  
XXII. What follows.  
XXIII. Melaz becomes a Christian and is joined in marriage to Roger, son of Richard of the Principate, Bohemond’s kinsman.

# Book Ten

## I. Urban II dies. Paschal II; Emperors Henry IV and Henry V; their conflicts with the supreme pontiffs

[Col. 0717A]

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1098, in the sixth indiction, the almighty Creator of all things openly displayed certain signs in the world, by which He divinely terrified human hearts and, through unprecedented manifestations, foretold that more terrible things were to be expected. For on the fifth day before the Kalends of October [27 September], the sky seemed to burn for almost the entire night. Then, in the seventh indiction, on Saturday, the day of the Lord’s Nativity, the sun turned to blackness. After this, many changes of rulers immediately took place throughout the world, and dreadful disasters, seditions, and grave perils raged in the world.

Pope Urban, after he had governed the apostolic [Col. 0717B] see vigorously and profitably for ten years, fell ill at Rome at the time when Jerusalem was captured, and, about to receive from God the reward for the good labours in which he especially flourished, departed this life on the fourth day before the Kalends of August [29 July 1099]. How praiseworthy his works had been was attested even by the lamentations of his enemies after his death, as were the splendour and renown of his greatness, widely spread throughout the world. Peter Leo composed three elegiac verses upon him and briefly commended his memory thus:

> Cluny had taken as monk Odo, a canon of Rheims;  
> Rome calls him and makes him bishop of Ostia.  
> When, his name changed, he becomes Pope Urban,  
> the City’s whole honour, once expelled, is restored.  
> Here Rome celebrated his famous funeral,  
> [Col. 0717C] on the fourth day before August.

Another distinguished versifier likewise considered the [Col. 0718A] life, character, and death of the aforesaid pope, and composed this poem:

> Odo, canon of Rheims, whom Hugh of Cluny  
> made a monk, becomes an eminent pope.  
> Living, he was the City’s light; dead, its eclipse:  
> the City stood while Urban stood; when he fell, it fell.  
> Ruling by law and fostering peace, he blessed you, Rome,  
> guarding you within from vices, without from the enemy.  
> Neither wealth, renown, nor power ever bent, exalted, or frightened him—  
> neither gifts, praise, nor threats.  
> Eloquence adorned his tongue, wisdom his heart, uprightness  
> his character, and beauty his outward form.  
> Behold, through him the holy city lies open, our law triumphs,  
> nations are conquered, and faith grows throughout the world.  
> But the rose which blooms most richly in the garden is snatched away sooner;  
> so fate bore off the man while he flourished.  
> Death receives the man, rest the soul, and the tomb the body.  
> [Col. 0718B] Among us nothing remains but fame.

While Pope Urban still shone in the house of God and worthily drove darkness from the hearts of mortals by his preaching and example, Guibert of Ravenna, whom they called Clement, died. Peter Leo, mocking him in verse, bestowed upon him the following epitaph:

> Neither Rome nor Ravenna gives you a place, Guibert.  
> Set in neither, you are now deprived of both.  
> You who, alive at Sutri, were an accursed pope,  
> lie dead in the town of Castellana.  
> But since you were a name without reality, for your empty name  
> Cerberus of hell now prepares the gates.

After Pope Urban’s death, Rainer, a monk of Vallombrosa, was elected Pope Paschal and was canonically consecrated on the sixteenth day after his predecessor’s death [Col. 0718C]. He governed the apostolic see for nearly twenty years and laboured to benefit God’s Church from its supreme seat. [Col. 0719A] In the time of Philip, king of the Franks, he came into Gaul, celebrated Easter at Chartres, and, at the request of the venerable Bishop Ivo, confirmed the privileges of that church.

Henry IV, emperor, who from his youth had disturbed the holy Church, violently usurped ecclesiastical investitures for a long time, intruded profane opponents of ecclesiastical unity into the house of God, and cruelly armed them with secular power, was already cast down from the royal throne by Charles, his son. Ashamed of the enormity of his crimes, he died, deserted by all friends, in wretched old age on the seventh Ides of August [7 August 1106]. But because he died struck by apostolic anathema for his crimes, his corpse, like that of a beast, decayed outside the bosom of mother earth [Col. 0719B], and was not deemed worthy of being covered or honoured with the common burial of mortals. He reigned nearly fifty years, but received the dreadful wages of shameful servitude.

Charles Henry V, emperor, began to reign in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1106, in the fourteenth indiction. He embraced his father’s tyranny, reigned for nearly nineteen years, and walked in his father’s path, as is read in *Paralipomenon* concerning the faithless heir of a wicked father. In the fifth year of his reign, with thirty thousand horsemen and an immense multitude of infantry, he besieged Rome; and, having agreed terms, he was received by the Romans, entered the basilica of Saint Peter the Apostle, and, by the pope’s command, sat in the imperial throne. He immediately ordered the pope to celebrate Mass. [Col. 0719C] But the pope refused unless four magnates of the emperor, whom he had expressly anathematized, left. The enraged emperor therefore commanded that the pope be seized before the altar. Immediately one of Caesar’s retainers laid hold of the pontiff; but another, bolder than the rest and an imitator of Simon Peter, drew his sword, attacked the pope’s assailant with greater force, and struck him down there at once with a single blow—more harshly than Peter struck Malchus. There was therefore great tumult in the city, fierce conflict on both sides, and bloodshed without reverence in the sacred buildings. Two thousand Normans from Apulia had come to the Romans’ aid. They promptly sallied out with Latins and Romans and slaughtered the multitude of Germans and other peoples who had already lodged securely in the old city across the Tiber. [Col. 0719D] They drove the emperor and his retainers out of the city three times. Yet they could not rescue the captive pope because he had been hidden from their sight.

The emperor tried forcibly to march with his army through the middle of the city into Campania; but military valour compelled him shamefully to depart elsewhere, and many wept for the killing of the many whom, as we have said, were suddenly slain from his battle-lines in the city. Then the pope, held under careful guard and deprived of every comfort, granted the emperor whatever he demanded. Consequently, after his release, he was held in less esteem by many. For Robert of Paris, Gualo, bishop of León, Pons, abbot of Cluny [Col. 0720A], and many other cardinals and prelates of churches reproached the pope and unhesitatingly judged that whatever he had granted the emperor by word or writing ought to be invalid. They maintained that for truth and justice he should have desired to die, innocently following Christ unto death, and should have greatly preferred to suffer chains and lashes rather than assent to secular power in anything contrary to law and the decrees of the Fathers. He, however, patiently endured the reproaches of the learned men and declared that their arguments were lawful and true. Not long afterward he assembled a council of bishops at Rome, publicly condemned, on the advice of jurists, all the agreements which he had ratified under compulsion for the emperor, and excommunicated the emperor himself for violating [Col. 0720B] God’s house, seizing Christ’s priest, and shedding Christian blood.

Thus in the sixth year of his reign the emperor stained the glory of Latium with so great a crime and vainly afflicted many peoples in carrying out so great an outrage. How severe and dangerous that winter was with rain, snow, and ice; what perils the army endured on narrow and uneven roads and at river crossings; and how the emperor, having assembled his forces, took the besieged city more by threats than weapons—these matters a certain Irish scholar committed to writing in an elegant account. In that expedition the emperor attacked Milan, but was repulsed and achieved nothing there. He also ravaged the broad territory of the powerful lady Matilda, who possessed Pavia, [Col. 0720C] Piacenza, and a great part of Italy now called Lombardy; she had long and vigorously resisted him and his father, and had always supported the rightful popes Gregory, Urban, and Paschal.

Henry, king of the English, gave his daughter Matilda in marriage to the emperor. Roger, son of Richard and kinsman of the king, brought her from England to Germany with a noble retinue. The wealthy king also gave her ten thousand marks of silver and sent magnificent gifts in royal fashion. The emperor loved his high-born wife exceedingly; but, because of sin, he lacked offspring worthy of the empire. Therefore the imperial line passed, by God’s command [Col. 0720D], into another family. For after his death Lothair, duke of the Saxons, was elected by the magnates of the realm and, because of his moderation and goodness, was raised to the imperial throne. The Empress Matilda, after her husband’s death, returned to her native land and preferred to live among her own people, although she was much loved by foreigners. Her father, the king of the English, betrothed her to Geoffrey, count of Anjou. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1133, she bore her husband a son named Henry, whom many peoples expect to become their lord, if almighty God, in whose hand all things are, grants it.

Now, since I have wandered somewhat from my subject and lingered over matters done beyond [Col. 0721A] the Alps in Italy and Palestine, I shall return to our affairs, which occurred in Neustria and England.

## II. Narrative of English and Norman affairs. The character of William Rufus. Deaths of certain prelates. On Blessed Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury

William Rufus, renowned in war, reigned in England after his father’s death. He vigorously restrained rebels by the rod of justice, and for twelve years and ten months subjected everyone under his dominion to his will. He was generous to soldiers and foreigners, but he oppressed the poor inhabitants of his kingdom excessively, violently taking from them what he prodigally bestowed upon newcomers. Under him many of his father’s nobles died, men who had warred to vindicate their forefathers’ inherited rights. In their places [Col. 0721B] he installed certain degenerates and raised them to great honours, bestowed as rewards for flattery. He never had a lawful wife, but clung insatiably to filthy fornications and frequent adulteries; polluted by disgraceful acts, he damnably set his subjects an example of shameful licentiousness. When bishops and abbots died, the king’s retainers seized ecclesiastical possessions and all treasures, and committed them wholly to the king’s control for three years or more. Thus, indeed, because of greed for revenues stored in the king’s treasury, churches remained vacant and the Lord’s sheep, lacking necessary shepherds, lay exposed to wolfish bites.

[Col. 0721C]

At the same time the venerable bishops Osmund of Salisbury, Walkelin of Winchester, William of Durham, Remigius of Lincoln, and many other reverend pontiffs died. Flambard, his brother Fulcher, and other retainers of the king long possessed their estates and all their wealth. Likewise, when Baldwin, abbot of Saint Edmund the king and martyr, Simeon of Ely, and other Fathers departed from this mortal world, royal officials throughout England seized the monasteries with all their appurtenances and parsimoniously supplied the monks with food and clothing. At length, after a long interval, the king granted ecclesiastical dignities to court clerics or monks as though wages to hirelings; in them he considered not so much [Col. 0721D] religion as favour and service agreeable to himself in a secular manner.

Accordingly Robert, surnamed Bloet, who had been the elder William’s chaplain, and who after his death crossed the sea from the port of Toi with the younger William and carried to Archbishop Lanfranc the king’s letter concerning the crowning of his offspring, received the bishopric of Lincoln after Remigius’s death and held it for more than twenty years. Gerard, nephew of Walkelin of Winchester, was first bishop of Hereford, and later, in King Henry’s time, became archbishop of York. William of Warelwast held the bishopric of Exeter, John the Physician that of Bath, Ralph surnamed Luffa that of Chichester, Ranulf Flambard that of Durham [Col. 0722A], and Herbert Losinga that of Thetford. Thus the king’s chaplains and friends gained the English bishoprics, and some of them also held provostships, both to oppress the poor and to increase their own wealth. Others, however, divinely alarmed by the burden of ecclesiastical government which they had undertaken, strove to benefit those entrusted to them spiritually and materially, and praiseworthily reformed their lives according to the pleasing will of God. For human beings often sinfully do many things to fulfil their own will, seeking nothing but their own pleasure in committing wickedness; but the wise judge of all things, in His ineffable mercy, wisely directs these acts for the benefit of many. Frequently men who are frivolous and unlearned are chosen to hold the governance of the Church, not for holiness [Col. 0722B] of life, training in ecclesiastical doctrine, or proficiency in liberal letters, but through favour granted to noble relatives and powerful friends. Yet when they have been promoted in this way, merciful God spares and pities them; afterward the abundance of heavenly grace is poured into them, the house of God is illumined through them by the light of heavenly wisdom, and many are saved through beneficial pursuits.

The venerable Anselm, primate of Canterbury, seeing continual transgressions, was often grieved; and, imitating John and Elijah, frequently denounced what he sorrowfully saw being done contrary to divine law. But the proud king, who scorned to be beneficially governed by the bridle of his spiritual charioteer, became entangled [Col. 0722C] in the malice of evil and insolent counsellors, and grew angry at the wholesome exhortations of his pious admonisher. Therefore, during his reign, the prudent archbishop twice went into exile, first seeking Pope Urban and afterward Paschal. The causes of his exile, and the manner in which he undertook his dangerous journey, were carefully narrated by Eadmer, his chaplain and travelling companion, in the book which he published eloquently concerning Anselm’s character, deeds, and nectar-like teachings. On that journey Baldwin of Tournai, a noble hero, and the aforesaid Englishman accompanied him; those who have closely investigated their private affairs esteem the virtuous prowess of both as worthy of praise.

In Apulia Anselm found Pope Urban and, received by him reverently, lived with him there for some time. [Col. 0722D] Then Roger, son of Tancred, count of Sicily, had come into Campania, was besieging Capua, was striving to restore his nephew Richard, son of Jordan, to his paternal right, and was pressing the rebellious Lombards, who had excluded the aforesaid young man, with a siege. The pope was there as mediator, and together with the venerable Anselm carried embassies of peace between the disputants. At length the count, having subdued the rebels, restored his nephew to his former honour; and the pope commended Lord Anselm to the count, and the count to Anselm. When a council had been assembled at Bari by papal command, and the Greeks had proposed an abundance of difficult questions concerning the faith and other mysteries, Father Anselm, by the pope’s command, addressed them all in a general discourse and satisfied the proposed [Col. 0723A] inquiries with a subtle and lucid answer for Greeks and Latins.

When the aforesaid pope had rendered his apostolic service to God and the catholic people, and had resolved spiritually to benefit his own people in the regions of Gaul from which he had come, he held a great synod at Clermont, a city of Auvergne; admonishing the people of God to fight against the heathens, he ordered them to bear upon their shoulders the Lord’s cross, which is a terror to the devil and all evil. Then there arose the vast movement of peoples, as has been sufficiently related in the preceding little book.

## III. Crusading knights, bishops, and abbots

Then Godfrey, duke of Lorraine, pledged the castle of Bouillon with all its appurtenances to the bishop of Liège, his lord, and received from him seven thousand [Col. 0723B] marks of silver. Thus many others, wealthy and poor, sold their lands and revenues and procured money for undertaking the journey to Jerusalem.

Robert II, duke of the Normans, jokingly surnamed Curthose, likewise handed over all his land to his brother King William for five years and received from him ten thousand marks of silver to fulfil the pilgrimage he desired. In the ninth year of his reign King William, unwilling to exhaust his own treasures, despoiled the ornaments of the churches, which the devoted generosity of earlier kings and magnates had adorned with gold, silver, and gems and left to holy Mother Church for the praise of God and their own [Col. 0723C] remembrance. In September William crossed the sea, received Normandy upon payment of money, and harshly oppressed it for nearly five years—that is, throughout the rest of his life. Then Odo, bishop of Bayeux, went on pilgrimage with his nephew Duke Robert. For such bitter hostility existed between him and the king because of past quarrels that no mediators could reconcile them.

The king was high-spirited, irascible, and tenacious in memory; he did not readily forget without vengeance an injury done to him. The proud prince bitterly recalled that Bishop Odo, his uncle, had been the first to resist him at the beginning of his reign and had drawn a great multitude of magnates into rebellion against him. [Col. 0723D] At Odo’s instigation Count Robert of Mortain held Pevensey; but later, when his nephew the king besieged him, he made peace and, surrendering the fortress, returned to favour. Gilbert, son of Richard, likewise fortified Tonbridge with his brother Roger; but in Easter week the king besieged the town, which yielded to him at the first assault. Finally the bishop himself, with Eustace of Boulogne, Robert of Bellême, and a distinguished force of armed men, held Rochester Castle; there, hemmed in by two fortified positions which the king had constructed around it, he yielded in disgrace and departed, irrecoverably disinherited from the whole kingdom of Albion.

Thereafter in Normandy, when the king sought vengeance and attacked his brother, who had unjustly and vainly attacked him, [Col. 0724A] and, having drawn the barons to himself by greed or fear, gained a great portion of Normandy and triumphed, Odo of Bayeux resisted him for a long time with all his strength and did not fail to aid the duke until he himself failed him. Consequently, after King William prevailed, as has been said, the bishop preferred pilgrimage to subjection to an enemy. At Rome the bishop and the duke spoke with Pope Urban; having received his blessing, they crossed the Tiber and spent the winter in Apulia.

From there the bishop withdrew to the city of Palermo, commonly called Palerna, where he departed this life in February. Gilbert, bishop of Évreux, buried him in the metropolitan basilica of Holy Mary, Mother of God. From his youth [Col. 0724B] this man had been promoted to the office and had held the governance of the church for almost fifty years. He enriched the episcopal church with many honours and ornaments, honoured the clergy, despoiled many persons of their possessions, and prodigally gave what he had taken from some to others. When King William heard of his death, he gave the bishopric to Turold, brother of Hugh of Évreux. After seven years, for certain private reasons, Turold voluntarily relinquished the episcopate and subjected himself to the monastic Rule in the abbey of Bec under Abbot William. There he served God in observance of the Rule for a very long time until the end of his life. Richard, son of Samson, succeeded him for twenty-six years.

King William therefore possessed Normandy and made subject to himself the domains of his father which his brother had foolishly alienated. [Col. 0724C] He entrusted churches deprived of shepherds to rectors chosen according to his own measure. For the monasteries of Jumièges and Saint-Pierre de Préaux were vacant. Guntard, vigorous abbot of Jumièges, had died at Clermont on the sixth day before the Kalends of December [26 November], while the famous synod was being held there. In his place the king installed Tancard, provost of Fécamp. After several years, when a disgraceful disturbance arose between him and the monks, he departed in infamy; Ursus of Rouen, a monk of that church from childhood, succeeded him for twenty years. Meanwhile Fulco, monk of Saint-Evroul and abbot of Préaux, had gone to Pope Urban and lived in exile at Monte Cassino. His successor, named Benedict, a monk of Saint-Ouen [Col. 0724D] of Rouen, had died. Therefore King William gave the men of Préaux as abbot Étard, a gardener of Jumièges and a monk from childhood. For several years he diligently tended God’s flock. But when Fulco returned with papal letters, Étard willingly relinquished the monastic office and, returning to the place of his conversion, died in extreme old age. Fulco, who before his deposition had ruled the monastery of Préaux rigorously for twenty years, increased the number of brethren through his diligence, and advanced the Church in many ways, was unjustly accused and deposed through Satan’s envy and instigation, and lived in exile for seven years. Then, having returned, he successfully governed his abbey for another seven years, and died an old man at Winchester in England on the third day before the Nones of April [3 April].

## IV. Frankish and Norman magnates contend with one another over the Vexin

[Col. 0725A]

In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1097, in the fifth indiction, William Rufus, having learned of his father’s death and the causes of the wars, began to lay claim against Philip, king of the Franks, to the whole district of the Vexin, and demanded the notable towns of Pontoise, Chaumont, and Mantes. Since the Franks would not comply with his demand, but instead were eager to resist him fiercely in battle, a great war arose between the fierce peoples, bringing mournful death to many. Yet the entire weight of the losses fell and accumulated upon the Gauls. For King Philip was indolent, corpulent, and unsuited for war. His son Louis, still held in childish immaturity, could not yet perform [Col. 0725B] military service. But the English king was wholly devoted to warfare, especially loved the best and proven champions, and honourably led with him chosen troops of knights. Surrounded by them, if Gaius Julius Caesar himself had stood against him with Italian cohorts and attempted to inflict some injustice upon him, he would undoubtedly have dared to test at close quarters against Caesar the strength and courage of his own young warriors. Robert of Bellême was the commander of this army; his influence with the king and his cunning surpassed those of the rest. The distinguished Count Henry, the king’s brother, Count William of Évreux, Hugh of Chester, Walter Giffard, count of Buckingham, and many other English counts, tribunes, and centurions led the king’s forces and frequently performed notable deeds, [Col. 0725C] as changeable fortune allowed.

Most of the French, who were compelled to obey two lords, were anxious for the estates by which, richly endowed, they flourished under the dominion of both kings; and since no one can serve two masters (Matt. 6:24), they chose the fiercer and wealthier in resources, and with their men and fortified places willingly obeyed him. Robert, therefore, count of Meulan, received the English into his strongholds and opened to them a free passage into France; their military power inflicted very great losses upon the French. Guy of La Roche also, coveting English silver, favored them and surrendered his fortresses of La Roche and Vetheuil. Thus did several others, faithless to their own people and greedily obedient to foreigners.

[Col. 0725D] Then King William ordered the exceedingly strong castle of Gisors to be built, which to this day, situated opposite Calvimont, Trie, and Boury, encloses Normandy. Its site and construction were planned by the ingenious craftsman Robert of Bellême. One day, while the Normans were attacking the French and the latter nevertheless met them with distinction, Theobald-Pagan of Gisors, Walter of Amfreville, and Gerald of Évreux were captured. The French, needing ample ransoms for them, were encouraged to fight. Robert of Maldestorn and Odmund of Calvimont, Gualbert of Boury and his brother Richard, Godfrey and Peter, sons of Herbert of Sérans, commanded the knighthood of the Vexin and at times fiercely resisted their enemies.

[Col. 0726A] Indeed, that province possesses an abundance of excellent soldiers, endowed with free birth and great valor. They would not allow the distinguished renown of the French to perish; for the defense of their country and the glory of their people, they exposed themselves to their enemies even unto death. Accordingly, from all Gaul they enlisted chosen champions and bold young warriors, and, repeatedly resisting the enemy, profitably earned their pay.

Once, while the household of the king of England was ravaging the borders of Calvimont and the courage of the soldiers displayed its strength on both sides, the French captured Gilbert of l’Aigle with very many others of high nobility, and the English captured Pagan of Montgai with others of his party.

[Col. 0726B] In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1098, in the sixth indiction, in September, King William assembled a great army and, advancing into France, took up quarters at Conches on the fifth day before the Kalends of October [27 September]. That night a terrible sign was revealed to the world. For nearly all the western sky appeared red as blood, as though it were burning. Then, as we afterwards heard, Christians fought against pagans in the eastern regions and, with God’s help, triumphed.

King William ranged through France as far as Pontoise, devastating that noble province, abundant in every kind of produce, with fires, plundering, and the seizure of people. He also surrounded the walls of Calvimont with many legions of armed men and ordered terrible assaults to be launched by mailed companies.

[Col. 0726C] The distinguished townsmen vigorously defended their fortifications, yet they did not forget the fear of God and human fellow-feeling. They spared, prudently and mercifully, the persons of those attacking; but they directed the violence of their anger against the enemy’s valuable horses. For they killed with arrows and missiles more than seven hundred horses of enormous value; Gallic dogs and birds fed on their carcasses until they were nauseated. Thus many foot-soldiers returned home with the king, though they had crossed the Epte as proud horsemen upon foaming steeds.

Although the spirited Frenchmen had been unable to defend the open villages against the royal raiders, whose numbers were excessive, and had not dared to engage hand-to-hand, without a king and lawful commander, against the powerful king surrounded by countless bands, they nevertheless held their fortresses, strongly fortified, and awaited better times through the bounty of the good Creator.

[Col. 0726D] King William, with William duke of the Poitevins, under the guidance of the young Amaury and Nivard of Septoculo, led a very great multitude against Montfort and Épernon and devastated the surrounding district. But the younger Simon, with God’s help, kept his fortresses unharmed. The elder Simon held Neauphle; Peter likewise, with his sons Anseau and Theobald, held Mantes; and other townsmen, whom I cannot name individually, boldly retained their strongholds. Meanwhile, while King William was returning to England on business of the kingdom, a truce having been granted on both sides, tranquil peace gave the French the joy of security.

## V. King Magnus of the Norwegians wages war against the Irish. War between the English and the Welsh.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1098, Magnus, son of Olaf, king of the Norwegians, rose against the Irish and prepared a fleet of sixty ships to sail against them. King Magnus was strong and handsome in body, bold and generous, active and worthy, conspicuous for many honorable qualities. He possessed great power in the islands of the Ocean and was abundantly supplied with many riches and resources of many kinds. In lawful marriage he begot Eystein and Olaf, to whom he left the kingdom and great power. A third son, named Sigurd, was borne to him by an English captive woman of noble birth.

[Col. 0727B] Sigurd was reared by Turer, son of Ingherr, foster-father of King Magnus. Outliving his brothers, he reigned for a long time and established in the Norwegian kingdom bishoprics and monasteries of monks which his predecessors had not known. Before he reigned, he sailed to Jerusalem. He besieged by sea Tyre, a wealthy city situated in the heart of the sea, and Sigurd, with his men upon the waters, took it while the Jerusalemites attacked it by land. Returning through Russia, he married Malfrid, the king’s daughter; and, after returning home, soon afterwards received the kingdom by God’s gift.

Five cities are situated around Norway upon the seacoast: Bergen, Cuneghella, Copenga, Borg, and Alsa. Tønsberg is the sixth city; it is situated eastward opposite the Danes.

[Col. 0727C] In the interior of the island are large lakes rich in fish, and country villages are set around the edges of the pools. The inhabitants abound in the flesh of fish, birds, and every kind of wild animal. They also observe the religious rites of the Christian law; peace and chastity are maintained among them; crimes are punished under very stringent laws and severe penalties. The Orkney Islands, Finland, Iceland, and Greenland—beyond which no land is found to the north—and many others as far as Gotland are subject to the king of the Norwegians; riches from all the world are brought there by ship.

Now my mind endeavors to unfold the cause and outcome of the war which King Magnus undertook against the Irish and by which he inflicted much loss and slaughter upon many people.

[Col. 0727D] He had married the daughter of the king of Ireland. But because the Irish king had not kept the agreements they had made, King Magnus, angered, sent his daughter back to him. War therefore arose between them. In the fifth year of William Rufus, king of the English, the king of the Norwegians drew military forces from every side and, while the east wind blew, traversed the Ocean. He visited the Orkney Islands, sailed around Scotland from the northwest, and passed through the other islands subject to his authority as far as Anglesey. He wished to enter Ireland; but since the Irish were ready for battle on the coastal shores, he turned elsewhere.

He settled the island of Man, which was deserted, filled it with inhabitants, and furnished it extensively with houses and other necessities for human use.

[Col. 0728A] He also explored other Cyclades, set in the great sea as though beyond the world, and by royal command compelled them to be inhabited by many peoples. For several years he devoted himself to this enterprise, for the increase of his kingdom and the expansion of its population.

Once the commander of King Magnus’s forces directed his course toward England with six ships; but he raised a red shield—the sign of peace—above the mast of his ship. When the coastal populations dwelling in England on the shore of boundless Amphitrite in the northern climate saw barbarian peoples and unfamiliar ships hastening toward them, they cried out in extreme fear, and all the armed men of the region of Mercia assembled. At that time there was a great disturbance of war between the English and the Welsh. Therefore every sudden cry immediately summoned everyone to arms.

[Col. 0728B] Two counts, to whom the region of Mercia was especially subject, both marked by the omen of the single name Hugh, quickly sent messengers throughout the land and ordered every armed Frenchman and Englishman to hasten, against the foreign ranks, for the defense of their country. A very great multitude from the counties of Chester and Shrewsbury accordingly assembled and prepared for battle beside the sea in the district of Deganwy.

Hugh of Montgomery hastened there first with his companies and, awaiting his allied companions, remained there for many days, prudently guarding the country lest the Welsh or Norwegians should fall upon its inhabitants. But one day, while the troubled natives were moving about upon the shore and preparing themselves against the Norsemen whom they saw raging against the English from their ships,

[Col. 0728C] Count Hugh, spurring his horse, was gathering his bands and keeping them under strict command against the enemy, lest they should be attacked while scattered and divided. Meanwhile, when a barbarian Norwegian saw the count riding swiftly, prompted by the devil he suddenly launched a whizzing missile and, alas, struck the noble count. He immediately fell and died amid the now-heaving waves of the sea. Great grief consequently arose.
