When King Magnus learned of his death, he lamented bitterly with his men and sent peace and security to Hugh Dirgane—that is, “the Fat.” “I am raising an army,” he said, “not against the English but against the Irish; nor am I invading another’s territory, but settling islands that belong to my authority.”

[Col. 0728D] At last the Normans and English searched long for Hugh’s body and, only when the tide had ebbed, scarcely found it. Then, on the seventeenth day after his death, they conveyed it to Shrewsbury and buried it in the monks’ cloister with immense mourning. Of Mabel’s sons he alone was gentle and lovable. For four years after the death of his father Roger he governed his paternal honor with the greatest moderation, and he was killed near the end of July.

After his death his brother Robert of Bellême approached William Rufus and offered him three thousand pounds sterling for his brother’s earldom. Having been made count, he perpetrated monstrous deeds against the Welsh for four years. He transferred the town of Quatford

[Col. 0729A] and founded Bridgnorth, a most strongly fortified castle, upon the river Severn. He also claimed as his right Blymhill and the whole land of his kinsman Roger of Bully, and purchased it from the king for a great weight of silver. Yet just as this man was enriched with many landed possessions, so, swollen with the still greater arrogance of pride, as a follower of Belial he insatiably sought shameful and cruel acts.

The English and Welsh, who had long heard of his deadly games with laughter as if they were a fable, now, flayed by his iron claws, groaned in tears and experienced as true the things they had learned. For the more he swelled with increased wealth and household dependants, the more fiercely he burned to take their estates from his neighbors, whatever their rank, and he appropriated for himself lands which ancient predecessors had given to saints.

[Col. 0729B] Long before this, in the county of Maine, he had violently built castles on another’s land—namely, on the estates of Saint Peter of La Couture and of Saint Vincent the Martyr—and there grievously oppressed the tenants. When the worthy Count Elias learned of this, he did not bear it weakly; armed with his men, he met Robert by the stream of Ruille in the district of Sillé and, in the name of the Lord, invoking Saint Julian the bishop, fought him. Though Robert had the greater forces, Elias shamefully drove him, defeated, from the field. There Robert of Courcy was wounded and lost his right eye. Gualcher of Villers, William of Moulins, Godfrey of Guacé,

[Col. 0729C] and many others were captured. The men of Maine obtained very great ransoms for them and thus avenged the wrongs done to the saints and the losses of their own people. The conflict between them continued for a long time and brought destruction to countless people and bitter captivity.

## VI. Concerning Elias, count of Maine. William Rufus harasses the people of Maine. Concerning Hildebert, archbishop of Tours.

Now I wish to retrace the sequence of events and the genealogy of a family line already hoping for royal honors. Elias, son of John and Paula, cousin of Hugh, count of the people of Maine, flourished in many virtues devoted to the worship of God and wholesomely maintained the governance of the people in the fear of God. He married the noble Matilda, daughter of Gervase, who was the son of Robert, surnamed Brochard, brother of Gervase, archbishop of Reims.

[Col. 0729D] He had six brothers. The first two, Goisbert and Enoch, became monks after military service. The remaining four—Geoffrey and Lancelin, Milo and William—were overtaken by premature death. Elias possessed from his paternal inheritance the castle of La Flèche; from his wife’s patrimony he held four castles: Liger, Mayet, Lucé, and Ussé. His wife bore him a daughter named Eremburga, who, when she reached marriageable age, married Fulk, then count of Anjou and now king of Jerusalem. She bore a noble offspring: Geoffrey and Elias, Matilda and Sibyl, who solemnly married sons of kings;

[Col. 0730A] but, with God ordering all things without fault, they were soon widowed.

At the time [1096] when Duke Robert entrusted Normandy to his brother and received from him a great quantity of silver to accomplish his journey to the sepulcher of our King, Count Elias came to the king’s court at Rouen. After consulting with the duke for a long time, he approached the king and humbly said to him:

“My lord king, by the counsel of the pope I have taken up the cross of the Lord for His service, and with many noble pilgrims I have vowed to the Lord God a journey to Jerusalem. As your faithful man, I seek your friendship and wish to undertake this journey with your peace.”

The king answered him: “Go where you wish; but leave me the city of Le Mans with the whole county, because I wish to possess whatever my father possessed.”

[Col. 0730B] Elias said: “By hereditary right I possess the county of my forefathers, and, with God’s help, I shall leave it free to my children as I now hold it free. If you wish to plead the matter, I will gladly submit to judgment and, according to the decision of kings, counts, and bishops, shall either lose or retain my ancestral right.”

The king replied: “I will plead with you by swords, lances, and countless missiles.”

Elias said: “I wished to fight in the name of the Lord against pagans; but behold, I now find a nearer battle against the enemies of Christ. For everyone who resists truth and justice is proved an enemy of God, who is true Truth and the Sun of Justice. He has deigned to entrust to me the stewardship of the people of Maine, which, through any frivolity, I ought not foolishly to abandon,

[Col. 0730C] lest the people of God be handed over to robbers as sheep to wolves without a shepherd.

“Now hear openly, all you nobles standing here, the resolve which I have conceived in my mind through heavenly inspiration. I shall not relinquish the cross of our Savior, with which I have been marked in the manner of a pilgrim; rather, I shall place the same upon my shield, helmet, and all my weapons, and shall fix the sign of the holy cross upon my saddle and bridle. Armed with such a mark, I shall go forth against the enemies of peace and right, defending Christian lands by warfare. Thus my horse and my arms shall be marked with the holy sign, and every adversary who rises against me will fight against a soldier of Christ. I trust in Him who governs the world: He knows the secret of my heart, and through His mercy I shall await the fitting time when I may perform my desired vow.”

[Col. 0730D] King William said: “Go wherever you please and do what you wish. I do not wish to fight against bearers of the cross, but I shall claim for myself the city which my father acquired on the day of his death. Therefore repair with the greatest care the collapsed ramparts of your fortifications; quickly assemble masons and stonecutters eager for wages; and restore, however you can, the old ruins of neglected walls by repairing them. For I shall visit the citizens of Le Mans very soon and display before their gates one hundred thousand lances with banners. Nor will I yield you my inheritance without a legal challenge. I shall also have carts loaded with spears and arrows drawn there by oxen. But I myself, with many legions of armed men, shall precede to your gates the ox-drivers shouting cheerfully.”

[Col. 0731A] “Believe this most certainly, and proclaim it to your accomplices.”

When these statements had been uttered by both parties, the count withdrew and manfully fortified his county. The lofty nobles who heard the quarrel of such great heroes dared introduce nothing on either side, because they feared their swollen king and lord and sympathized with the distinguished count, who firmly set forth his claims. For he was worthy and honorable, beloved for many virtues. He excelled in body: strong and tall, slender and stately in stature, dark and hairy, and well tonsured like a priest. His speech was also agreeable and eloquent; he was gentle to the peaceful and stern toward rebels, a rigorous cultivator of justice and fervent in the fear of God for good works.

[Col. 0731B] How great his piety in prayers and devotion was, his cheeks, often wet with tears, showed. He devoted himself greatly to the defense of churches, alms for the poor, and fasting; every week, on the sixth day, in reverence for Christ’s Passion, he abstained completely from all food and drink.

Moreover, King William was occupied with many concerns regarding the French, Bretons, and Flemings; postponing the fulfillment of his threats for two years, he forgot the people of Maine. Meanwhile Elias strengthened a castle at Dangeul against Robert Talvas and stationed there his retainers to defend the inhabitants of his land. The aforesaid tyrant was distressed because he could not ravage the neighboring fields at will.

[Col. 0731C] Therefore, at an untimely season, in January, he disturbed the king, inflamed him with bitter verbal provocations, and at the beginning of February brought him with a Norman army to the aforesaid castle. For he said to the king: “The guards of the enemy town, made sluggish by security, are scattered in every direction. They observe the winter rains and storms and suppose that you, with your army, are entangled in other campaigns. Therefore, if we now hasten there suddenly, we shall find the inhabitants and townsmen unprepared and shall easily take the town.”

For several reasons the king reluctantly undertook the expedition; but, at Robert’s urging and because he promised success, he was ashamed to delay lest he be thought cowardly. Yet a resounding rumor preceded the king’s arrival, and the lordly command assembled the provincials, equipped with suitable arms,

[Col. 0731D] and posted them against the enemy at river crossings, hedges, and difficult approaches through the woods. The king was then unable to harm his enemies; but, angered by resentment, he became more furious against them. He ordered Robert to assemble a great household of warriors in his towns and expended abundant sums of money, so that his towns might everywhere be enclosed by ditches, walls, and many palisades, and generous gifts might be lavishly distributed to warlike mercenaries.

Accordingly the lord of Bellême, ready for these tasks, founded new towns and greatly strengthened old ones by surrounding them with steep ditches. In that county he possessed nine castles: Bellême and Peray, Mont-de-Noue and Sillé; Saint-Rémy-des-Plains and Orthez, Allières and the Motte of Walter of Clincamp, Mamers, and very many other fortified residences.

[Col. 0732A] This shrewd contriver had cunningly acquired that region for himself as a source of revenue. In these places he settled tenants of bestial cruelty and neighbors faithless to their fellows, through whom he satisfied his arrogance and waged cruel war against the people of Maine. During Lent, while sinners touched by divine grace abandon evil ways and tremblingly flee to the remedy of penitence for their past crimes, more than three hundred prisoners perished in Robert’s jail. They offered him much money for their lives; but, cruelly rejected by him, they died from hunger, cold, and other miseries.

At this time [29 July 1097], Hoel, a man of venerable life and Breton birth, bishop of the people of Maine, died. Count Elias elected Geoffrey the Breton, dean of that church, to the bishopric; but the clergy, acting first, compelled Hildebert of Lavardin, the archdeacon, to sit in the episcopal chair and, exulting with joyful loud voices, sang:

[Col. 0732B] “We praise thee, O God,” and the other things required by ecclesiastical usage at the election of a bishop.

When Elias learned of this, he was greatly angered and wished to resist. But when the clerics told him, “You ought not to prefer your own election to the Church’s election,” he showed reverence because he feared God, remained silent, and agreed with the canons, lest a deadly schism arise among the members of the Church.

[Col. 0732C] Geoffrey, indeed, was already confident of obtaining the episcopate and had already prepared abundant dishes for his own elevation. The prepared dishes were certainly consumed by greedy diners. But the people of Maine completely refused to have him as their bishop. He was the brother of Judicael, bishop of Alet, and after the death of William, archbishop of Rouen, he presided over the people of Rouen for seventeen years.

After the death of Gilbert, archbishop of Tours, Hildebert was elected by clergy and people and, by God’s will, rose from the see of Maine to the metropolitan see. He was gentle and devout, and zealous for learning in both sacred and secular letters. In our times he flourished as an incomparable writer of verse and composed many poems equal or superior to the poems of the ancients, which the ardent enthusiasm of scholars eagerly seeks to investigate with subtlety and strives diligently to acquire for itself above gold and topaz.

[Col. 0732D] For he speaks elegantly and wisely concerning Christ and the Church, body and soul, the deeds of saints and their virtues, the praise of virtues and the censure of vices. Very many poems of Hildebert are brought to Rome by Roman cardinals, who frequently visit regions of Gaul because they find people there mild and obedient to themselves; these poems are judged admirable by the schools and teachers of the Romans. This holy hero exercised the office of bishop for almost thirty-five years and devoted himself especially to worthy studies in teaching and action. He laudably adorned in many ways the church of Saint Gervase, where the body of the outstanding confessor of Christ, Julian,

[Col. 0733A] rests. He later dedicated it, in the time of his successor Guiumar the Breton, who was also called Guy of Étampes. Yet, because sins demanded it, the church which the practice of good works had richly adorned and enriched with varied ornaments for God’s honor was, eight years after its dedication, disfigured and horribly devastated by a fire which consumed a great part of the city.

## VII. Elias, count of Maine, is captured. King William occupies the city of Le Mans. Count Elias recovers his liberty.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1098, in the sixth indiction, Count Elias, during the week preceding Rogationtide, made an expedition against Robert and, after making a raid,

[Col. 0733B] ordered his men to return after None. As they were returning, the count, separated from his troop with seven knights, turned aside near Dangeul. There he noticed certain men hidden among dense trees and thickets, and at once charged upon them with a few companions. But Robert lay hidden there in ambush. When the crafty man, experienced in warfare, saw a few men ranging about incautiously, he suddenly sprang forth with many others and immediately captured the count, Hervé of Montfort, his standard-bearer, and almost all the rest.

When the advance part of the army cheerfully reached Ballon, they heard from those who had escaped that he had been captured; and after their vain joy they were suddenly all overwhelmed with immense grief. Robert then presented Elias to the king at Rouen,

[Col. 0733C] and the king ordered him to be honorably guarded. For he was not cruel to soldiers, but gracious and generous, pleasant and affable.

With Fortune smiling favorably upon him, King William rejoiced; having summoned the barons of Normandy together, he said: “Until now I have acted negligently in acquiring my paternal inheritance, because in my desire to enlarge my lands I did not wish to harass peoples or kill men. But now, as you see, without my knowledge my enemy has been captured and, by God’s will—who knows my right—is delivered to me. What do you commend? What do you advise me now? Investigate what course should be taken, and inform me of what you judge most beneficial.”

After examining the matter, the magnates replied:

[Col. 0733D] “By common counsel, lord king, we decree that by your command the entire Norman army be assembled. With it we shall all go boldly and eagerly to obtain the region of Maine.”

Hearing this, the king rejoiced. Swift couriers were then sent far and wide through the provinces, proclaiming the king’s wish that his subjects, dependants, and friends should aid him without deceit. Thus Frenchmen and Burgundians, Morini and Bretons, and other neighboring peoples gathered to the generous prince and multiplied his ranks in many ways.

In June [1098], King William led his army through Alençon and, surrounded by many knights, entered the enemy’s country in a manner that inspired terror. At the king’s command, troops of soldiers suddenly came to Fresnay

[Col. 0734A] and fought for a while before the castle gates in military exercise with the townsmen’s horsemen. But Ralph, viscount of Beaumont, hastened humbly to the king and earnestly requested a treaty of peace until the date he had specified:

“From your highness, lord king, I request a truce until you return safely from Maine. For there the bishop and the assembly of senators are gathered; there a common daily deliberation and provision concerning the condition of the commonwealth is made. Whatever may there be agreed with you, we shall gladly follow, and we shall obey your commands in all things. I say this, lord king, by counsel of my elders, because if, without war, I were the first to abandon the cause and, deserting my peers, the first to make peace, I should undoubtedly bring disgrace and reproach upon all my family.

[Col. 0734B] The limbs ought to follow the head, not precede it; and well-bred, legitimate household servants prefer to obey their lord rather than command him.”

The king praised him as he said these and many similar things, and granted what had been requested.

Geoffrey of Mayenne, Rotrou of Montfort, and many others through whose lands he was to pass acted similarly, obtaining security from him by suppliant words until his return. Gilo of Solesmes, one of the noblest Frenchmen, an ancient warrior of the household of King Henry of France, who had seen many great assemblages of peoples, stood upon a high hill and surveyed the armed companies on every side. He estimated that there were five hundred thousand men there and declared that he had never seen such a great army assembled anywhere on this side of the Alps.

[Col. 0734C] The king’s first halt in hostile territory was at Rouessé; on the following day he encamped and spent the night at Montbuzot. On the third day he came to Coulaines and ordered the tents of the multitude to be pitched in the meadows of the Sarthe. Crossbowmen and archers were stationed in the vineyards beside the road; they carefully watched the route so that enemies might not pass unpunished and harassed passersby with frequent missiles.

Fulk, surnamed Rechin, count of Anjou, on hearing that Elias had been captured, promptly came to Maine, because he was its chief lord. Gladly received by the citizens, he fortified it with soldiers and slingers. When the king arrived, soldiers came out of the city to meet him

[Col. 0734D] and fought manfully against the Normans throughout the day, performing deeds of war on both sides. Famous fighters on either side strove to display their strength and to earn bloody praise from their lords and comrades-in-arms.

Pagan of Montdoubleau, formerly familiar with the Normans, made peace with the king and handed over to him the very strong motte which he possessed at Ballon. Through it the whole town, subdued by its opponents, obeyed. The king made Robert of Bellême commander of the forces there and assigned him more than three hundred knights equipped in courage and arms. He raged violently against the resisting inhabitants and severely afflicted them with incomparable losses.

[Col. 0735A] For he uprooted their vineyards with a great multitude of armed men, trampled their crops, and devastated the surrounding region; but he could not sustain a long siege. For severe shortage of food pressed upon men and horses, since the season then lay between the old and the new harvests. A sextary of oats was sold for ten solidi of Maine, without which the strength of hoofed horses can scarcely be sustained in western climates. Therefore the king dismissed his legions, ordered his harvests to be stored in granaries, and instructed them to be ready after the gathering of crops to besiege the enemy’s strongholds.

While King Rufus was returning to Normandy with a strong army, Count Fulk besieged Ballon. Having gathered the Angevins with the men of Maine, he strove for several days

[Col. 0735B] to crush the enemy. The garrison at once reported this to the king; when the report spread, spirited nobles hurried with all speed to assist their countrymen. Meanwhile, while the count and his army were dining in their tents and beggars from the town, having received alms, reported to the besieged that the besiegers were then eating—namely, about the third hour—ordered ranks of soldiers suddenly rushed out in arms. They unexpectedly drove away the unarmed men sitting at table and, capturing many, put all the others to flight.

There Walter of Montsoreau and Geoffrey of Briollay, John of Blaison and Berlais of Montreuil, with nearly one hundred and forty other knights and countless foot-soldiers, were captured. The victors plundered the enemy’s spoils—arms,

[Col. 0735C] clothing, and varied equipment. Among those captured were many noble townsmen who, as possessors of great estates, were prominent among the chief barons of their native country and, by hereditary right, had precedence over many knights of great valor.

In the third week of July [1098], King William came to the aid of his men and brought with him armed masses terrible to his enemies. On the king’s arrival the townsmen received him with rejoicing. Hearing this, the prisoners all cried out together with a great shout: “William, noble king, free us!” When he heard it, he ordered all to be immediately released, to be abundantly fed with their companions outside in the court, and, upon his word, to be dismissed free after the meal.

[Col. 0735D] When his retainers objected that amid so great a crowd of people they would flee openly, the king opposed their harshness and, rebuking them on the prisoners’ behalf, said: “Far be it from me to believe that a worthy knight would violate his pledged word! If he does so, he will always be contemptible, as one outside the law.”

[Col. 0736A] Count Fulk had withdrawn from the siege to the city and awaited the outcome in the monasteries of the saints. The Angevins, however, conferred with the men of Maine and found themselves inferior to the Normans in every respect; accordingly, they arranged a conference between the king and the count. There, with God’s help, a necessary peace was made between them, from which immense joy arose among both peoples for many reasons. It was requested and granted that Count Elias and all those captured on either side should be returned; and that Le Mans, together with every castle which King William had held, should be subjected to Rufus, his son. 

When the terms of peace had thus been duly confirmed, the king summoned Robert, commander of the forces, son of Hugh of Montfort, and ordered him to enter the tower of Le Mans

[Col. 0736B] and the other fortifications. He assigned him seven hundred selected knights, gleaming in mail-shirts, helmets, and every kind of armor. At once, after the guards had departed, they took possession of all the city’s fortifications and raised the king’s banner in the principal tower with great triumph. On the following day the king sent after them a thousand distinguished knights and, imposing laws as he pleased, took possession of the whole city. The royal tower, Montbarbet, and Little Montbarbet were subjected to the king, and rightly so, since they are known to have been founded by his father. All the citizens likewise, in peace, congratulated the new prince with applause, songs, and varied demonstrations.

Then Bishop Hildebert, the clergy, and all the people went out with great joy to meet the king and, singing psalms, led him into the basilica of Saint Gervase the Martyr, where rest the bodies of the holy bishops and confessors Julian, Turibius, Victor, and very many others.

Released from prison, Elias of Bayeux came before the king at Rouen, dark and shaggy, and humbly said to him:

> Most illustrious king, who give aid to many, I beg you, by your distinguished prowess, help me. I have long been called a count, because by hereditary right I possessed a noble county; but, with the omen changed, I have been deprived of the title of name and honour. Therefore I beseech you to receive me into your household with the designation of my former dignity, and I will render you services worthy in return. I do not ask for the city or towns of Le Mans until I have earned them from your magnificence by suitable service. I long only to be counted among your retainers and to enjoy royal friendship.

[Note: [Col. 0735D] Orderic expressly states that Elias was held in prison from May until the end of July; nevertheless William of Malmesbury writes that he was immediately released by the king. These are his words, book IV, p. 124: “A certain Elias, the author of the disturbances, is captured. When he was brought before him, the king said mockingly: ‘I have you, master!’ But he, whose lofty nobility did not know, even in so great a danger, how to speak humble words, said: ‘You have caught me by chance; if I could escape, I know what I would do!’ Then William, nearly beside himself with rage and glaring at Elias, said: ‘You scoundrel—what would you do? Depart, go, flee! I grant you leave to do whatever you can; and by the face of Luke, if you conquer me, I shall make no peace with you on account of this favour.’ Nor was the deed inferior to the word: he immediately let him escape, marveling at rather than pursuing the fugitive. But greater credit is due to Orderic, with whom the deeds of the bishops of Le Mans agree. Dom Bouquet, book X, p. 674.]

The generous king decided readily to grant this; but Robert, count of Meulan, dissuaded him out of the venom of envy. For the crafty old man presided over the king’s counsels and judgments. Therefore he feared to endure an equal or superior in the chief court [Col. 0737A]. He said to the king:

> The men of Le Mans are deceitful and faithless; what they cannot accomplish by force they accomplish by tricks and evasions. Behold: the defeated enemy makes supplication and fraudulently longs to become your familiar. Why does he seek this? So that, the nearer he is admitted to your secrets, the more fiercely he may rise against you when an opportunity suits him, and join himself more dangerously to your enemies.

When this had been said, the king’s will was changed, and the valiant hero was rejected from being counted among the king’s household. From this there afterwards arose great trouble, with many dangers and losses.

Again Elias tried to soften the king with flattering words, but in vain. He then firmly added:

> Gladly, lord king, would I serve you, if it pleased you and I found favour with you. From this time on, I beg you, do not reproach me if I undertake something else. I cannot patiently endure seeing my inheritance taken from me and every right denied me while violence prevails. Therefore let no one wonder if I make a claim, if I strive with all my strength to recover my ancestral honour.

The angry king replied:

> Go, and do whatever you can do against me.

Elias therefore requested and received safe-conduct through the king’s territory. Free to depart, he returned to his own lands amid the rejoicing of his friends. He fortified his five towns with their adjacent villages, repaired the losses through careful administration, and diligently attended to his own affairs. From August until Easter he remained quiet in peace. Yet he shrewdly considered by what demonstration he might reveal his purpose to his enemies [Col. 0737C], and frequently deliberated with his faithful kinsmen.

After King William had obtained Le Mans, as has been said, without much shedding of blood, he entrusted the guarding of the city to William, count of Évreux, Gilbert of Laigle, and other worthy nobles. He committed the royal tower—abundantly supplied with arms, food, and every necessity—to Walter of Rouen, son of Ansger. Viscount Ralph, Geoffrey of Mayenne, Robert the Burgundian, and the other magnates of the entire province allied themselves with the king; having surrendered their fortifications, they diligently obeyed the laws he imposed.

## VIII. Saint Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury, comes to the Pope in Italy. Elias, Count of Le Mans, renews war against King William.

[Col. 0737D]

While these events were taking place across the sea in Neustria, and excessive expenditure was prodigally squandered on superfluous displays, Ranulf Flambard, now bishop of Durham, other royal attendants, and royal stewards despoiled England. Worse than robbers, they mercilessly plundered the stores of peasants and the accumulated goods of merchants; nor did they restrain their bloody hands even from sacred things. When prelates of the Church died, they immediately succeeded to their possessions by royal power and irreverently seized whatever was found in their treasuries. They subjected the estates of monasteries and the revenues of bishoprics to the king’s lordship, and exacted an enormous money-payment [Col. 0738A] from surviving archimandrites or bishops. Thus they accumulated the burdens of boundless exactions by right and wrong alike, and sent them across the Channel to the king, to be spent on wicked or advantageous purposes.

By collections of this kind great gifts were presented to the king, by which foreigners were enriched for vain glory. But the sons of the realm, unjustly stripped of their possessions, grieved and lamented, crying to God, who delivered Israel from the hand of Moab through the ambidextrous Ehud, after he had slain the very fat King Eglon.

Seeing this, the holy Archbishop Anselm was deeply distressed and tried to aid the oppressed. He strove courageously to stand as a wall for the house of Israel against those who worshipped Baal. Therefore, on account of the manifold afflictions of the churches, he sent faithful envoys and suppliant letters to appeal to the king [Col. 0738B] and make complaint. But the king, hardened in heart and unsound in mind, did not obey his humble teacher. Anselm therefore asked his leave to go to Rome.

The proud prince allowed him indeed to depart for Rome, but forbade him to enter Normandy. Alas, how foolishly, blinded by profane arrogance and soon to fall, he refused to see God’s servant fleeing from before his tyranny! He was never able to see him afterwards, because he himself soon fell by a cruel death.

The venerable man, obeying the prince’s command, passed through Boulogne. His honoured travelling companions were Baldwin of Tournai, a monk of Bec, and Eadmer of Canterbury, an Englishman by birth, who afterwards diligently wrote the life of this father for the edification of souls. The aforesaid prelate completed his arduous journey as far as Capua, chief city of fertile Campania [Col. 0738C], where he found Pope Urban. Received kindly and honourably by him, Anselm explained the reason for his arrival.

The Pope was then very busy there, for he was striving to reconcile the people of Capua to their lord Richard, son of Jordan, against whom they had rebelled. That young man, aided by the support and courage of his uncle Roger the Elder, count of the Sicilians, had stubbornly compelled them to surrender. Thus the venerable old man lived in exile among the Italians, from whom he was descended, and among other peoples for nearly two years; and, as an eloquent sower of the word, he gave spiritual benefit to foreign hearers. Whoever wishes more fully to investigate his deeds or sayings may find them in the book of the aforesaid Eadmer at Bec of Herluin, his predecessor [Col. 0738D].

In autumn King William, having subdued the people of Le Mans as stated and arranged Norman affairs as he pleased, returned with a south wind blowing to the very wealthy kingdom of Albion.

In the following year, 1099, after Easter, Elias began war anew. With the secret assent of the natives, he sought to ravage the borderlands and provoke the king’s soldiery. Finally, in June, he came with a distinguished multitude of knights, crossed the ford of the river Huisne at Godfrey’s Planches, and challenged the royal warriors who guarded the city to battle. The bold Normans burst out and fought long [Col. 0739A]; but, overwhelmed by the numerous strength of the enemy, they were driven back into the city.

Then the enemy entered with them as well, for the townsmen, constrained by their violence, were unable to shut the gates. Fleeing through the city, they could scarcely gain entrance to the citadel and the other fortifications. The citizens greatly loved Elias and therefore desired his lordship more than that of the Normans. Yet the townsmen who held the king’s strongholds had every necessity in abundance, and thus strove to fight unto death in loyalty to their lord.

Elias was received in the city by rejoicing townspeople; but immediately grave disaster arose for them all. Walter, son of Ansger, keeper of the citadel, ordered the craftsmen whom he had with him to work, and blazing slag to be hurled violently by crossbowmen upon the roofs of the houses [Col. 0739B].

Then the ruddy Titan was traversing lofty Gemini, and the world was parched by immense drought; a fiery whirlwind settled upon the roofs of the halls. Thus an excessive fire was kindled; when it gained overwhelming force, the entire city was burned. Clarembald of Lusières, Walter, and the other retainers carefully held the fortifications. Elias and his men laboured greatly but vainly with engines and assaults, yet accomplished nothing against the impregnable defences.

Robert of Bellême fortified Ballon and immediately dispatched his messenger Amalric to the king in England. Having crossed the sea, the latter came to Clarendon [Col. 0739C], met the king riding with his household in the New Forest, and, when the king eagerly asked for news, replied:

> Le Mans has been seized by treachery. But my lord holds Ballon, and the royal household diligently guards all the fortifications assigned to it. It urgently desires the aid of royal power against the hostile force which surrounds and attacks them from every side.

On hearing this, the king said:

> Let us cross the sea to help our men!

At that very moment, without consulting anyone, he wheeled his horse around by the reins and, spurring him on, hurried to the coast. Finding by chance an old ship, he entered it without royal equipment, like a common man, and immediately ordered the oarsmen to row. Thus he waited neither for a favourable wind, nor companions, nor anything else befitting royal dignity [Col. 0739D]. Fearless, he entrusted himself to fortune and the sea, and by God’s guidance reached the harbour of Touques safely at daylight on the following day.

There, as is customary in summer, many people of both ranks were standing about and, seeing a vessel sailing from England, eagerly waited to learn some news. When they asked first about the king, he himself stood there as certain messenger concerning himself. Because he unexpectedly answered the questioners with a laugh, astonishment and then joy immediately arose among them all. Then, mounted on the mare of a certain priest, he made for Bonneville, attended by a great crowd of clergy and peasants, who accompanied him on foot with loud applause. His presence greatly terrified the enemies raging throughout Neustria.

At last, after dispatching embassies, he assembled a great army in a short time [Col. 0740A] and hastened to ravage the hostile province. As soon as the enemy host and its leader Elias learned that the king had come across the Channel, they fled without delay and abandoned the captured city, far worse than they had found it. Bishop Hildebert humbly approached the king in Normandy and was kindly received as a familiar friend; for he had taken no part in the disturbances just described, either by counsel or by his presence.

When the spirited king heard of the enemies’ retreat, he followed them slowly and did not consider Le Mans worthy even of one night’s lodging. Passing through the burned city, he ordered tents to be pitched in a broad meadow beyond the bridge over the Huisne. On the following day he grievously avenged his wrongs with sword and fire [Col. 0740B].

Before the king reached the enemy camp and could commit it to flames, the hostile force itself burned everything and voluntarily stripped its whole territory bare, lest malicious raiders find anything to plunder or dwellings in which to prepare beds for rest. Thus Valles and Ostilliacum were destroyed, and many other towns and rural places utterly ruined.

Robert of Montfort, commander of the troops, advanced before the army with five hundred knights, extinguished the fire at the castle of Valles, and strengthened the fortification for the king’s use. Elias meanwhile remained with a great force at the castle of Liger, reserving himself for better times [Col. 0740C] and awaiting the outcome.

Finally, on Friday the king besieged Mayet and ordered his army to storm the castle on the following day. But on Saturday, while the fighters eagerly armed themselves and prepared to deliver a fierce assault upon the garrison, the king, at the counsel of wise men, gave glory to God. Out of reverence for the Lord’s burial and resurrection, he spared his enemies and granted them a truce until Monday.

Meanwhile they strengthened the inner castle with all their energy and set wicker screens against the assault, to meet the blows of missiles and stones. They were resolute men and faithful to their lord, and therefore fought stubbornly for him to the death, deserving praise as an example of approved courage. While the outside attackers laboured hard to fill the surrounding ditch with an immense mass of timber [Col. 0740D], making a public approach to the palisade for themselves by laying down many supports, the townsmen dropped down flasks full of burning coals and, aided by the summer heat, utterly burned the heaps of material amassed for their injury. They harassed one another in this conflict until Monday, and the king was greatly distressed at the sight.

While he was tormented by anger and grief because all his efforts there came to nothing, someone threw a stone down upon him from a lofty tower. By God’s will it struck not him, but terribly struck the head of a warrior standing nearby, mingling bone and brain with a blow that spared neither. As the man miserably died before the king, the garrison at once mocked him with a loud and dreadful cry [Col. 0741A]:

> Behold, the king now has fresh meat; let it be carried to the kitchen and served to him for supper.

The grieving king therefore summoned his nobles apart, took their advice, and ordered his men at daybreak to leave for Lucé. The prudent counsellors foresaw that high-spirited warriors were resisting in a very strong fortification, and, secure within stout enclosures, could easily prevail in many ways against exposed men. The shrewd advisers openly gave this useful judgment: that, in the present crisis, it was salutary for the unarmed subjects that the prince should depart safely with his distinguished companies and punish the enemy by another kind of vengeance, thereby prudently securing the safety of his own people and the humiliation of the enemy [Col. 0741B].

In the morning they rose quickly and employed various instruments to devastate the enemy country. They uprooted vineyards, cut down fruit-bearing trees, demolished walls and stone boundaries, and ravaged by fire and sword the entire very fertile region. Then the king entered Le Mans in triumph and granted the tribes of many provinces permission to return home.

These things occurred in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1099, in the seventh indiction, in July. Then Jerusalem, after the defeat of the Gentiles who had long held it, was taken by the holy pilgrims on the eighth day before the Ides of July, as I explained in the preceding book. Pope Urban too, joyfully celebrating the restoration of Christ’s sepulchre to Christ’s worshippers, died on the fifth day before the Kalends of August [Col. 0741C]. Pope Paschal succeeded him, enthroned on the sixteenth day after his predecessor’s death.

## IX. Serlo and Roger, abbots of Saint-Evroult. Disputes arising between the monks and the bishop of Lisieux. Consecration of the church of Saint-Evroult.

Gilbert, bishop of Lisieux, was repeatedly asked by the monks of Saint-Evroult to bless their abbot. He refused unless the abbot presented him with a written declaration of canonical profession. Mutual contention consequently continued between them for ten years; neither would endure defeat, and each hoped for victory.

For Serlo, who was elected to govern the abbey after Mainer, presided over the monks for two years without blessing because he refused to make an unprecedented profession to the church of Saint-Evroult. Likewise Roger of Sap presided over the brethren for more than seven years. But because the bishop stubbornly persisted in his opinion, Roger did not bear the pastoral staff. In this matter the royal authority, appealed to by the monks, prevailed by right and ordered the obstinate bishop to observe the customs which his predecessors in Normandy had maintained under the king’s father [Col. 0742A], and to consecrate the abbot without demanding any innovation. The king’s order was granted by the unwilling prelate, and the ancient custom was confirmed for the monastery.

[Note: [Col. 0741D] “A grave and long-lasting controversy,” says Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, Preface to Part I of the sixth century, p. IX, “arose from the end of the tenth century between bishops and certain abbots concerning the profession of subjection which bishops required from them when they were to be ordained abbots.” He subsequently gives a detailed history of this controversy. From it it appears that, although abbots who invoked either custom alone or even simony were finally defeated, others vigorously persisted in refusing the promise—namely those who had obtained privileges of liberty from Roman pontiffs, as also those who professed themselves subject to the king alone. Moreover, bishops customarily demanded chiefly four things from monasteries subject to them: obedience; an annual payment, called synodal due or *ciriadae*; procurations, or the right of lodging in those monasteries; and solemn processions—that is, the right to celebrate masses and solemn assemblies in their churches. Dom Bouquet, book X, p. 676.]

Ralph, abbot of Sées, brought the elected brother to Lisieux and, on behalf of the monastic community, dictated the election. Robert, a monk of Sées and an outstanding writer, drew up the charter; and Herluin, the bishop’s chaplain, read it aloud thus before everyone, while the clergy kept silence:

> Christ, the assisting bishop and shepherd of the ecclesiastical flock and of shepherds, makes his flock perpetual from mortals through continuous succession. Since he is the power and wisdom of God, he likewise perpetuates the pastoral order itself by appointing many priests [Col. 0742B], because death prevents them from remaining. We do not doubt that their consecration is effected by God through the ministry of bishops in spiritual blessing; nevertheless we firmly hold that election too is dispensed by the same Holy Spirit through the mouths of subjects.
>
> Therefore we, the unanimous congregation of Saint Evroult, following examples and apostolic traditions, after the departure of our Father Mainer and after our father Lord Serlo had been made bishop, with divine mercy going before us, have elected as abbot our lord Roger, our brother, known to us by his manner of life and united with us by profession. We are supported by the presence and suffrages of eminent men: namely the aforesaid Bishop Serlo, Anselm abbot of Bec, Ralph of Sées, Arnulf of Troarn, and others. With them, so far as we are able to see, considering the worthiness of the person according to the Apostle’s instruction [Col. 0742C], we choose a Catholic man, instructed in divine law, chaste, sober, humble, gentle, merciful, beneficent, and endowed with the other qualities fitting for a pastor.
>
> Offering him, thus elected, to be consecrated to the divine Majesty, we present him to Gilbert, our bishop of Lisieux, requesting the episcopal consecration and canonical blessing according to ecclesiastical custom.

When this election of the monks had been carefully read and gratefully received both by the prelate and the clergy, Roger was consecrated abbot on the feast of the Beheading of Saint John the Baptist. On the following day he was honourably received by the brethren at Saint-Evroult.

On that day, while the brethren sat in conversation in the cloister and exchanged many observations as they investigated matters carefully, a discussion arose, as I believe by God’s inspiration, concerning the dedication of the church of Saint-Evroult. Through much discussion an ardent desire to do this greatly increased in all. At last, with friends rejoicing and encouraging them, the plan was settled [Col. 0743A], and, with God’s help, the basilica of Saint-Evroult was dedicated on the Ides of November, 1099.

Three bishops performed this office. Gilbert of Lisieux consecrated the principal altar in honour of Holy Mary, Mother of God, Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and Saint Evroult the confessor. Gilbert of Évreux consecrated the southern altar in honour of all the apostles; and Serlo consecrated the altar in honour of all martyrs. On the following day Serlo blessed the crucifix and its altar in honour of the Holy Saviour and Saint Giles the confessor, while Gilbert of Évreux consecrated the altar for the morning mass in honour of all saints. Finally, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November, the bishop of Évreux consecrated the southern altar in honour of all confessors [Col. 0743B]. When the celebration of Mass was completed, he came into the chapter-house and strengthened the brethren in God’s service with holy exhortations, devout prayers, and blessings.

At the end of the same year, on the second day before the Kalends of January, Serlo of Sées dedicated the altar in the northern chapel in honour of all virgins. Thus seven altars were reverently dedicated on appointed days by the three bishops and, according to ecclesiastical custom, assigned to the glorious orders of saints in praise of God, who stand before that same Holy of Holies in the heavenly kingdom, rejoicing for ever.

Many Norman magnates attended this dedication, and faithful people of both orders offered God the first-fruits of their prayers. William, abbot of Bec, Ralph of Sées, Arnulf of Troarn, Geoffrey of Coutances, Richard of Ansger’s ville, William of Glanville, Etard, William of Évreux, Hugh son of Safred, William of Arenis, archdeacons and deans, and other honourable clergy were present [Col. 0743C], and with their bishops solemnly completed the service of divine worship.

Then William of Breteuil gave this church ten pounds yearly from the revenues of Gloz. Robert of Grandmesnil also gave the greater church of Saint Samson at Mont-Calvet, land for one plough-team, and the tithe of the fair of that town, its mill, and its woodland to God. Gilbert of Laigle granted half of the town of Laigle to Saint Evroult on this condition: that the knight Richard should hold it thereafter from the monks as he had held it from the aforesaid knight. The other half, by the gift of Richer, father of that Richard, they had long already possessed in demesne.

Ralph of Conches also granted Saint Evroult Caldecote and Alwinton, which are in England, three arpents of vineyards at Toeni, everything he possessed at Guarlenville, and six tenants in his three towns [Col. 0743D]; and, gladly consenting, he confirmed what his men had given.

At the same time there was great disturbance among many people in the West, and shameful confusion in the sight of all for those who had deserted. Pope Urban had decreed by general authority and compelled all Latin Christendom, by apostolic command, inviolably to observe this: all who had taken up Christ’s cross but had not completed the journey to Jerusalem through failure of will must undertake the journey anew in the Lord’s name, or, struck by anathema, pay the penalty outside the Church.

Stephen, count of Blois, constrained by many such pressures, groaned and prepared himself anew for pilgrimage; and the same desire fervently took root in countless knights.

[Note: [Col. 0743] The edition reads “thousands” (*millibus*), which, from the interlinear correction in the manuscript itself, seems to us to require correction.]

For they had heard favourable reports of the glorious deeds of Christ’s followers, who fought against the battle-lines of heathen peoples, armed with faith in the Holy Trinity, and gained a happy victory through the power of the pious Saviour, deserving eternal praise through all ages [Col. 0744B].

## X. Concerning those marked with the cross. Godfrey, king of Jerusalem. Greeks and Syrians, having expelled the Franks, occupy the city of Laodicea. Raymond of Toulouse remains at Constantinople with Emperor Alexius. The duke of Normandy leaves Syria.

Now, with the aid of the Holy Spirit, I wish to return to our pilgrims, briefly to relate the fortunes and end of those who remained after the triumph in Judaea or Syria, or of those who returned to their homes by a difficult road.

In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1099, in August, Godfrey, son of Eustace, count of Boulogne, and Ida, assumed David’s kingdom in Jerusalem and reigned for three years. In that same month, still relying upon the united help of all his fellow soldiers [Col. 0744C], he fought at “Admiravisum” [reading uncertain] and, with God’s help, won a happy triumph near Ascalon.

In autumn, after the heathen had been overthrown by the warfare of the supreme King Sabaoth, the eminent nobles resolved to return. Taking leave of friends and companions, they set out on the homeward road. Duke Robert of the Normans, Count Robert of Flanders, and Count Raymond of Toulouse returned, and the Turks had thoroughly experienced their valour.

As they returned, they met on the way many groups of pilgrims who had been unable to accompany them on the first expedition, but, when opportunity was given, fulfilled their vow to go to the Lord’s sepulchre whenever they could. These endured extreme want on the journey and almost perished of hunger. For the earlier pilgrims, who in preceding years had devastated the regions between Antioch and Jerusalem, sowed destruction by starvation along the road for the pilgrims who followed; after the inhabitants of the provinces had been killed or driven away, they found in the untilled fields nothing to eat [Col. 0744D].

Those who were returning heard from the pilgrims they met that Duke Bohemond was besieging Laodicea and that within it the emperor’s garrison was resisting him with all its strength.

Nearly twenty thousand pilgrims had arrived there [Col. 0745A], having hastened from England and other islands of the Ocean to the Lord’s sepulchre, at the time when the heathen were besieging Antioch and constraining the Christians within the city. The people of Laodicea gladly received the island Christians and entrusted themselves to their protection against the Turks.

Among them Edgar Ætheling was pre-eminent, the man whom the English had once vainly set over themselves as king after Harold’s death. He undertook to defend the city, held it in loyalty to Duke Robert, and assigned it to him after the victory over the pagans. He was handsome in body, eloquent in speech, generous and noble, as the son of Edward, king of the Huns; but he was sluggish in action, and he loved the duke, who was of his own age and almost like a foster-brother.

Duke Robert therefore acquired Laodicea in Syria and remained there for some time with Normans, Englishmen, and Bretons [Col. 0745B]. He also placed his own guards in the fortifications while he completed his pilgrimage to the tomb of the Lord Jesus Christ.

Meanwhile Ravendinus, protospatharius of Emperor Alexius, and other commanders came by ship and besieged the city with a great army. The townspeople, favouring their compatriots, expelled the westerners, and Greek and Syrian imperial governors were admitted. When Bohemond heard this, he immediately hurried there with an army and attacked the long-besieged city with repeated assaults.

When the people of Laodicea and the Thracians learned of the return of those from Jerusalem [Col. 0745C], fearing that, if united, they would form an irresistible army, they shrewdly sent envoys and gifts ahead to entice them. They instructed them to hasten securely to defend their city. Hearing this, they rejoiced and came; the citizens peacefully received them into the city.

After they had discussed what had happened and settled everything on both sides, Duke Robert and his companions told Bohemond to withdraw in peace, or else promptly prepare for war. Bohemond, on hearing this, summoned his men and considered what should be done amid such incursions. All urged him to withdraw in peace, content with what was his, and not unjustly invade another’s possessions: lest he fight against brothers and brave equals and thereby provoke God’s anger against himself; lest he create scandal for Christians and laughter for pagans; and lest he stain the glory of his courage by the shedding of Christian blood [Col. 0745D].

The moderate duke therefore perceived the depth of their reasoning and, wisely understanding the very useful counsels of the sages, accepted them. Though sorrowful, he withdrew with his men out of respect for his companions.

The Greeks and Syrians, now safer, deliberated about their interests. After some days they summoned the westerners separately and addressed them thus:

> Illustrious lords, whose faith and courage the whole world has now recognized, hear the words which we now speak to you in good will. We plainly know that you left wealthy kingdoms for the cause of pilgrimage and that, now your vows have been nobly fulfilled, you wish to revisit them—especially since the sweet love of wives and beloved children urges you, and affection for parents and friends, whom you forsook for Christ, moves you.
>
> Now, to accomplish this purpose, graciously accept our advice, which, under God’s direction, you will without doubt find sound and advantageous. Leave to us, for the Emperor’s use, the cities and towns that you possess in Syria or Romania. We shall prepare an excellent fleet for you. We shall convey you, and all who wish to follow you, without fare to Constantinople and the Emperor; until you arrive there, we shall supply in abundance bread, wine, and whatever else you need. We know the Emperor’s will in this matter and are eager to please him by such service [Col. 0746A]. He greatly desires to have Franks with him and admires and loves their constancy and vigorous effort. Go confidently, by our counsel, to him; you will find this advice beneficial.

The Franks likewise deliberated together, considering many matters shrewdly, according to each man’s thought. The princes withdrew with their retinues and spoke among themselves:

> Behold, we are far removed into a foreign land and greatly desire to return to our own country. But a double difficulty constrains us. We cannot remain here honourably, as our nobility requires; nor can we return to Gaul without grave danger. Bohemond, possessing Antioch and the surrounding provinces, rules everywhere and does not deign to tolerate anyone as his equal in these regions. We lack a ship for crossing the sea, and we have no overland route except through the Emperor’s territory [Col. 0746C]. That route is dangerous unless we have his goodwill; among barbarous inhabitants, the uncertain paths are fearful.
>
> We are pressed by manifold poverty and troubled by fear of many misfortunes. We are worn out by immense labour and, as has already been sufficiently said, earnestly desire to return to our homeland. Yet we cannot accomplish this by sea or land except through the Emperor’s means. What then shall we do? We have no wish to remain longer here, and every sort of want is ready at hand for sick and weary exiles. Let us therefore accept the Greeks’ promises, although they are deceitful; and since they are Christians, let us gladly receive what they peacefully offer us, though we ought to have begged them with earnest prayers to do it.

At last the Gauls commended themselves to God, in whose hand are all things, and graciously agreed to the inhabitants’ promises in every respect. The latter rejoiced greatly and faithfully fulfilled what they had promised. The Emperor honourably received the arriving Franks and, having heard the agreements which the Achaeans had made and the Gauls had accepted, rejoiced and confirmed them by imperial authority. He offered great honours to those wishing to remain with him, and bestowed generous gifts upon those returning westward.

Raymond, count of Toulouse, remained with him for as long as he lived [Col. 0747A], being numbered among his intimate table-companions and counsellors. The Emperor especially loved him and gladly listened to him, because he knew that Raymond had steadfastly resisted Bohemond at Antioch out of loyalty to him.

Raymond’s wife, daughter of King Alfonso of Galicia, completed the same long pilgrimage with him and bore at Constantinople a son named Alfonso. After his brother Bertrand, this son held his father’s right as count of Toulouse and, down to the present day, subdued the Goths in Provence. Count Raymond long kept in his chapel at Byzantium the Lord’s lance which Peter Abraham found at Antioch. The Emperor also honoured with many gifts and enriched with great stipends other knights who wished to dwell among the Greeks [Col. 0747B].

Rodbert of Normandy, however, and Robert of Flanders, with their fellow-soldiers who were hastening to return, he bestowed with very many gifts, and granted them free passage and trade through his land. Those indeed who were leaving the eastern regions he either retained with himself or sent with all urgency into the Italian lands, because he strove with all his might to weaken the forces opposed to him in Syria and to obstruct all who were hastening to aid those resisting him.

## XI. Bohemond recovers Laodicea. Duke Robert sets out through Italy on his return to Normandy. New knights prepare themselves for the holy war. Of the mournful event that occurred in the New Forest.

[Col. 0747C] Tireless Bohemond, when he heard the events we have related—that is, that the emperor’s agents and all the Franks with their forces had ploughed the sea in ships—swiftly gathered a numerous host of Normans, Armenians, Allobroges, and men of other peoples. He besieged Laodicea, vigorously captured it, held it for twelve years after its capture, and left it to his successors down to the present. He likewise splendidly subjected to himself Tarsus and Mamistra, Albara and Marra, and other strongholds, among which Reblata stands, to the praise of God and the support of Christians. He honoured Greeks, Armenians, and Syrians who maintained monastic life in monasteries according to their own rite, and faithfully granted them the possessions they had formerly held. Moreover, certain [Col. 0747D] monasteries that the cruel Turks had despoiled and from which they had driven out their religious inhabitants, the vigorous hero assigned to Latin monks or clerics, generously allotting them ample possessions, so that they might abound in every good thing in God’s service and render worship to the divine Majesty according to Latin custom.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1100, the aforesaid leaders, honoured by the emperor, as has been said, with many gifts, departed with their followers and were received amicably by the Normans in Italy, who possessed great wealth there. For Roger the Elder, count of Sicily, his nephew Roger, duke of Apulia, Geoffrey of Conversano, nephew of Duke Guiscard, and their other compatriots and kinsmen rejoiced at their safe return [Col. 0748A] and endeavoured to cheer these champions, wearied in many struggles for Christ. There Robert, duke of Normandy, fell in love with a noble maiden, Sibyl, daughter of Geoffrey of Conversano; he betrothed her and brought her with him into Neustria. She flourished in good character and, adorned with many virtues, was beloved by those who knew her. In the third year thereafter she bore a son at Rouen, whom William, archbishop of that city, baptized and called by his own name. While Duke Robert was in exile, he did not forget that he had received ten thousand marks of silver from his brother and had mortgaged Normandy to him for five years. Therefore he obtained from his father-in-law, lord of Brindisi—the city in which, as Lucan relates, Gaius Caesar shut up Pompey the Great [Col. 0748B]—and from other friends a supply of gold, silver, and precious objects. From their gifts he amassed a vast sum of money, which he prudently intended to repay to his creditor, so that he might peacefully recover his duchy.

Memorable deeds solemnly performed in the East to Christ’s honour by princes and other faithful persons were swiftly reported in the West by flying rumour; and the children of the Western Church rejoiced at the glorious deliverance of Jerusalem and the humiliation of Babylon. William, duke of the Poitevins, on hearing of the noble triumphs, was kindled with the desire to make pilgrimage. An army of three hundred thousand from Aquitaine, Gascony, and other regions [Col. 0748C] of Hesperia followed his banner. He resolved to mortgage the duchy of Aquitaine and all his land to William Rufus, king of the English, and to draw a plentiful payment from that king’s treasury, by which he might nobly undertake the journey he wished to begin. He therefore sent eloquent envoys to the king and made known through them what he had in mind.

But the pompous sceptre-bearer, who, like a thirsty dropsical man, desired ever more the more he possessed, greedily received the messengers’ proposals and eagerly sought to add the ample possessions of the aforesaid duke to the former dominions of his paternal duchy and kingdom. He therefore ordered a very large fleet to be prepared and a great body of cavalry from England to accompany him, so that, having crossed the sea, he might stand ready in arms [Col. 0748D] like a lion over its prey; drive his brother by war from entering Neustria; purchase the duchy of Aquitaine with many masses of silver; and, having subdued by war those who opposed him, extend the boundaries of his dominion as far as the River Garonne. Such were the thoughts and arrogant ambitions of the swollen young man. But the almighty Creator, who governs all things, ordained otherwise.

Then, about the Rogation Days [1100], a mournful event occurred in the New Forest. While the king’s knights were engaged in hunting and were trying to wound does or stags with crossbows, one knight loosed an arrow to strike a wild beast and by chance struck the noble youth Richard, son of Duke Robert. He fell dead at once, and great mourning arose from this among many people. Terrified by the grave misfortune, the horseman immediately fled to Saint Pancras and there promptly became a monk, thus escaping a twofold punishment. As one who despised the world, he expiated the guilt of homicide by penance; and he avoided the hostile resentment of the parents and friends of the illustrious young knight. Many deemed the said knight extraordinarily fortunate; but men often deceive themselves and others, because the King of Sabaoth ordains otherwise: clouded by the darkness of ignorance, human thoughts are vain.

It is pleasing briefly to speak of the origin of the aforesaid young knight. While Duke Robert, in his youth, had foolishly rebelled against his father and, with a great band of robbers, ravaged Neustria in exile with plunder and many crimes, he loved the beautiful concubine of an elderly priest on the border of France, and by her begot two sons, Richard and William. Afterwards she carefully reared the children for a long time; when they were grown, she presented them to the duke in Neustria as his sons and recalled to him very clear signs of the intimate association of his youth with her. Since he recognized some things but nevertheless hesitated to acknowledge his offspring, their mother openly carried red-hot iron and, unharmed by any burning, proved that she had conceived by the king’s son. These two brothers were indeed upright and lovable, but in a moment they withered quickly like a flower of hay. One, as has been said, was wounded and killed while hunting; the other, after [Col. 0749C] Henry captured Robert at Tinchebray, sought Jerusalem and there quickly fell in honourable military service.

Now, reader, see why the forest in which the aforesaid young knight perished was called “New.” From ancient times it had been a populous region and abounded in villages suitable for human habitation. A numerous people diligently and earnestly cultivated the district of Southampton; thus the southern province served the city of Winchester in many ways with the fertility of its fields. But William the First, after obtaining the kingdom of Albion, being a lover of forests, deliberately devastated more than sixty parishes, forced country-dwellers to migrate elsewhere, and established wild beasts there in place of men, so that he might enjoy hunting. [Col. 0749D] There he lost two sons, Richard and William Rufus, and, as has been said, his grandson Richard; and a manifold vision appeared terribly to certain persons, by which the Lord plainly showed that the consecrated buildings abandoned for the breeding of wild animals displeased Him.

## XII. Evil portents concerning King William; the aforesaid king dies.

In July [1100], while the royal fleet was being equipped with the apparatus of royal pomp and the king himself, stubbornly gathering immense weights of precious metal from every quarter, was waiting near the strait, dreadful visions concerning the king were seen in monasteries and bishoprics by members of both orders. Hence public reports spread everywhere among the people in marketplaces and cemeteries. Nor did they remain wholly unknown to the king himself.

There was in the monastery of Saint Peter at Gloucester a monk of good reputation but better life, who reported that he had seen the following dream in a nocturnal vision:

> “I saw,” he said, “the Lord Jesus seated upon a lofty throne, with the glorious host of heaven and the choir of saints standing beside Him. While I was caught up above myself in ecstasy, amazed and intently observing these unfamiliar sights, behold, a most radiant virgin fell before the feet of the Lord Jesus and humbly entreated Him with these prayers: ‘Lord Jesus Christ, Saviour of humankind, who, hanging upon the Cross, shed Your precious blood, look mercifully upon Your people, miserably groaning [Col. 0750B] beneath William’s yoke. Avenger of crimes and most righteous Judge of all, I pray: avenge me upon William, and rescue me from his hands, because he has shamefully defiled me, so far as lies in him, and cruelly afflicted me.’ But the Lord answered: ‘Bear it patiently; wait a little, for sufficient vengeance upon him will soon be granted to you.’”

On hearing this, I trembled, and did not doubt that heavenly wrath was soon threatening our prince, understanding that the cries of the holy virgin and mother, the Church, had reached the Lord’s ears because of robberies, shameful adulteries, and the intolerable burden of other crimes by which the king and his followers did not cease daily to transgress the divine law.

When he heard this, the venerable Abbot Serlo issued admonitory letters and sent them amicably from Gloucester to the king, clearly inserting in them those things which the monk had learned in the vision. In the same monastery, on the Kalends of August, the feast of Saint Peter in Chains was solemnly celebrated, and an immense crowd of persons from both orders gathered there. Then Fulcher, a fervent monk of Sées, first archimandrite of Shrewsbury, an eloquent expositor in theological treatises, chosen from the company of elders, mounted the pulpit and addressed the people concerning the Salvation of God. There he openly rebuked transgressors of the divine law and, as if full of the prophetic spirit, among other things steadfastly prophesied:

> “England is given as an inheritance for profane men to trample, because the land is filled with iniquity. The entire body is stained by the manifold leprosy of wickedness; the sickness of evil has occupied it from head to foot. Unbridled pride flies everywhere and tramples all things—if it may be said—even the stars of heaven. Unrestrained lust defiles vessels of clay and likewise of gold, while insatiable greed devours everything it can. Behold: a sudden change of affairs is imminent. Effeminate men shall not rule long. The Lord God will come to judge the public enemies of His bride; He will strike Moab and Edom with the sword of manifest vengeance and overthrow the mountains of Gilboa with a terrible upheaval. God’s wrath will spare transgressors no longer. Heavenly vengeance will now rage against the children of unbelief. Behold, the bow of the heavenly fury is drawn against the reprobate, and the swift arrow has been drawn from the quiver to wound. It will strike suddenly; let every wise person avert the blow by reforming himself.”

These and many similar things were said to the people on Wednesday in God’s temple; and immediately the scourges began to follow upon the display of their deeds.

On the next day King William ate in the morning with his parasites and, after dinner, prepared to go hunting in the New Forest. While he was merrily making sport with his retainers and putting on his boots, a certain smith came there and presented him with six crossbows. The king immediately accepted them cheerfully, praised the craftsman for his work, and, unaware of what was to come, kept four for himself and handed two to Walter Tirel. “It is right,” said the king, “that the sharpest arrows should be given to the man who knows how to inflict deadly [Col. 0751B] wounds with them.” This man was a noble knight from France, a wealthy townsman of Poix and Pontoise, powerful among the magnates and very valiant in arms; therefore he was the king’s familiar table-companion and constant associate everywhere.

Finally, while they were talking idly about many matters and the household retainers were gathering around the king, a monk from Gloucester arrived and handed the king his abbot’s letter. When it had been read aloud, the king burst into laughter and mockingly addressed the aforesaid knight: “Walter, make right of what you have heard.” He replied: “I shall do so, lord.” Thus he made light of the warnings of the elders, forgetting that the heart is exalted before ruin, and said concerning the contents of the letter he had heard: “I wonder whence this desire to tell such things arose in my lord Serlo, who is indeed, in my opinion, a good abbot and a mature elder. Out of excessive simplicity he has reported to me, though I am occupied with so many affairs, the dreams of snoring men, and has even sent them, set down in writing, across so many regions of the earth. Does he suppose that I follow the custom of the English, who abandon their journey or business because of a sneeze or old women’s dreams?”

Having said this, he rose quickly, mounted his horse, and hurried into the forest. His brother Count Henry, William of Breteuil, and other nobles were present; they went into the wood, and the hunters were duly scattered through different places. When the king and Walter of Poix, with a few companions, stood in the forest armed and eagerly awaiting prey, a beast suddenly ran between them. The king moved from his position, and Walter loosed an arrow. It flew swiftly, grazing the bristle along the beast’s back, and mortally wounded the king, who was standing opposite. He immediately fell to the ground and, alas, expired without delay. Thus, when one earth-born man had fallen, a great commotion arose among many, and a terrible cry over the prince’s death rang through the forest.

Henry hurried at full speed to Winchester Castle, where the royal treasury was kept, and as the true heir demanded its keys from the guards by royal command. William of Breteuil also arrived there breathless and, anticipating him by cunning calculation, opposed him:

> “We ought lawfully to remember the fealty we promised to Duke Robert, your brother. He is the first-born son of King William, and both I and you, my lord Henry, have done homage to him. Therefore loyalty must be kept by us in all things toward him whether absent or present. He has long laboured in God’s service, and God now restores to him, without the tumult of war and together with his father’s diadem, his duchy, which he left as a pilgrim for God’s love.”

Meanwhile a fierce dispute began to arise, and a multitude of men gathered there from every side; the strength of the present heir, whose claim was being challenged, increased. Henry swiftly laid his hand upon the hilt and drew his sword, nor did he allow any outsider, through frivolous delay, to seize his father’s sceptre beforehand.

At last, when friends and wise counsellors had assembled, the dispute was softened on both sides; by the sounder counsel, lest a worse rupture should arise, the castle with the royal treasures was surrendered to Henry, the king’s son. This had long before been prophesied by the Britons, and the English desired to have as lord the man whom they knew had been nobly born to the throne. When the king was dead, many magnates withdrew from the forest to their homes and arranged their affairs against the future disturbances they feared.

Certain retainers covered the bloodied king as best they could with cheap cloths and carried him from the forest to the city of Winchester like a fierce boar pierced with hunting-spears. Clerics, monks, and citizens—but only the poor—together with widows and beggars, came out to meet him and, out of reverence for the royal dignity, quickly buried him in the old monastery of Saint Peter. But ecclesiastical teachers and prelates, considering his foul life and grim end, then dared to judge him; they declared him, as one who had died a violent death, unworthy of ecclesiastical absolution, since while he breathed the breath of life they had been unable effectively to restrain him from wickedness. The bells did not even ring for him in certain churches, though they were frequently and long rung for the humblest poor and little women. From the vast treasury, in which many heaps of coins had been amassed through the toil of the wretched, no alms were distributed to the needy for the soul of its once-greedy owner. Mercenary soldiers, hangers-on, and common prostitutes lost their gains at the fall of the adulterous prince [Col. 0752D] and bewailed his miserable death, not so much from pity as from their detestable desire for his vices. They earnestly sought Walter Tirel in order to tear him limb from limb for the fall of their patron.

But he, after committing the deed, hastened to the sea; having crossed it, he sought the strongholds he possessed in Gaul and there safely mocked the threats and curses of his ill-wishers. He had as wife Adelaide, daughter of Richard, of the lofty lineage of the Giffards; she bore to her husband Hugh of Poix, a most valiant knight. Finally, after many years, he sought Jerusalem, and Walter died repentant on the way of God.

Therefore, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1100, on Thursday, the fourth day before the Nones of August [2 August], William Rufus died in the New Forest by the stroke of an arrow, after possessing the kingdom of England for twelve years and almost ten months.

## XIII. Henry, brother of William Rufus, succeeds him on the throne.

Henry hastened to London with Robert, count of Meulan, and on the following Sunday at Westminster, in the basilica of Saint Peter the Apostle, received the royal insignia; the venerable Maurice, bishop of London, consecrated him. For Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, as stated above, was in exile; Thomas, archbishop of York, had recently died, and the metropolitan see was still vacant. Henry was thirty years old when he began to reign, [Col. 0753B] and he reigned thirty-five years and four months. Amid prosperity and adversity he governed wisely and fittingly the kingdom divinely entrusted to him, and was regarded as illustrious among the foremost princes of all Christendom, shining by reason of peace and justice.

In his days the Church of God flourished vigorously in wealth and honours, and every religious order increased manifoldly to the Creator’s praise. This is attested by monks and clerics, who increased in number and eminence during his reign; hermits also can rightly bear witness, for they cleared the dense woods and, raising lofty peaks of monasteries and palaces, rejoiced there and sweetly sang glory to God where lawless robbers had formerly been accustomed to lurk in order to commit every crime.

From the beginning of his reign he wisely reconciled all men to himself and invited their affection by royal generosity. He honourably treated the magnates, increased their wealth and honours, and by thus softening them made them faithful to himself. He fostered the subject peoples by establishing just laws and, protecting them by his patronage, defended them from unjust tax-gatherers and robbers. Thus the eminent nobleman shone among all western princes and rulers of kingdoms and won the favour of all—clerics and laymen alike—who rejoiced in a rational king.

He began to comfort churches bereft of pastors and, by the counsel of elders, appointed learned teachers over them. To William, surnamed Giffard, who had been chancellor of the dead king, he committed the episcopal see of Winchester; and he promoted Gerard, bishop of Hereford, to the metropolitan see of York. He also sent swift messengers across the sea, through whom he summoned the venerable Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, back to his own see, from which, as said above, King William had expelled him by unwarranted persecutions. He gave the monastery of Ely to Richard, son of Richard of Bienfaite, a monk of Bec; the abbey of Saint Edmund, king and martyr, to Robert, a young monk of Ouche, son of Hugh, count of Chester; Glastonbury to Herluin of Caen; and Abingdon to Faricius of Malmesbury. Hugh, count of Chester, Robert of Bellême, and other magnates [Col. 0754A] who were in Normandy, hearing of the unfortunate prince’s death and the sudden change of affairs, settled their concerns in Neustria, hastened to England, did homage to him, and received from him their estates and all their dignities with royal gifts.
