King Henry did not, like Rehoboam, follow the counsels of foolish young men, but wisely embraced the arguments of the prudent and the admonitions of elders. He admitted Robert of Meulan, Hugh of Chester, Richard de Redvers, Roger Bigod, and other energetic and shrewd men to his counsels; because he humbly complied with wise counsellors, he deservedly ruled many lands and peoples. In the fourth month after he began to reign, the aforesaid prince, unwilling to indulge shamefully like a horse or mule without understanding, married in royal fashion a noble maiden named Matilda, by whom he begot two children, Matilda and William. She was the daughter of Malcolm, king of the Scots, and Queen Margaret; her descent came from the line of King Alfred, son of King Egbert, who first gained the monarchy of all England after the Danish disaster and the death of Saint Edmund, king and martyr. For previously, after the Angles had come into Britain from the island of Angeln, where the metropolis of Saxony lies, and after conquering or destroying those now called Welsh, they named the island they had occupied in war “England,” after their native land, under Hengist as their first leader; five kings had reigned in it, as is read in the writings [Col. 0754C] of the Briton Gildas and the Englishman Bede.

Thus wise Henry, recognizing the maiden’s noble birth and having long desired the manifold propriety of her character, chose such a companion in Christ for himself and raised her with him in the kingdom, Gerard, bishop of Hereford, consecrating her. I have offered a few preliminary remarks on events in England; nevertheless, I wish to add some material on the Normans to this work.

In August 1100, as soon as the ill-starred king’s death became known in Neustria, the fury of the swelling Normans was aroused against its own vitals. In that same week William, count of Évreux, and Ralph of Conches with a great force invaded the territory of Beaumont and carried off immense plunder from the lands of Robert, count of Meulan, in revenge for certain injuries that he had inflicted upon his peers through deceitful counsels which he had long sought to suggest to King Rufus against them. Likewise many others, who had long conceived anger and ill-will but had not dared, because of the rigour of princely justice, to reveal them in open revenge, now, with the reins loosened, rose against one another with all their strength and devastated the miserable land, bereft of a ruler, through reciprocal slaughter and destruction of property.

In September Duke Robert came to Normandy and, received by his own men, went with his wife Sibyl to the Mount of Saint Michael the Archangel of the Perilous Sea. There he gave thanks to God for his safe return from his distant pilgrimage; afterwards he consummated his marriage with his bride, the daughter of Geoffrey of Conversano. In the following year she bore him a son, whom Archbishop William baptized and named after himself. Duke Robert recovered his duchy without anyone preventing him and held it, in name only, for nearly eight years. He was ruinously given over to sloth and softness, and therefore became contemptible to restless and lawless inhabitants. Theft and robbery were committed without cease, and evils multiplied everywhere to the injury of the whole country.

## XIV. Count Helias recovers the county of Maine.

[Col. 0755B]

Helias, son of John of La Flèche, when he heard the news for which he had hoped—that King William had indeed died—came to Le Mans with a troop of armed men. Voluntarily received by friendly citizens, he peacefully took possession of the city. He summoned his lord, Fulk, count of Anjou; with his help he besieged the castle for a long time. Hamery of Morée and Walter of Rouen, son of Ansger, guarded the tower with the retainers they needed; they had a sufficient supply of food, arms, and everything necessary for besieged men to resist. Yet every day they spoke together and threatened each other, though jokes were often mingled with the threats.

They granted Count Helias the privilege of putting on a white tunic whenever he wished and thereby safely approaching those who guarded the tower. Trusting their good faith, since he knew them to be exceptionally worthy and loyal, he often approached his enemies conspicuous in the whiteness of his clothing, and did not hesitate to converse with them alone for a long time. Those shut in and those outside engaged each other in various banterings; many jests were exchanged on both sides with no malicious intent, and people in that region will speak of them in future with wonder and delight.

At last Walter and Hamery addressed Helias after several days:

> “We are guarding this most strongly fortified castle, rich in every resource, as our lord entrusted it to us. We shall fear neither you nor all your engines of war, so long as we wish to resist you. We can indeed harm you with stones and arrows, since, stationed in the higher fortress, we have the advantage over you. Yet from fear of God and natural affection we spare you, especially as we do not know for whom, as soldiers, we are preserving this tower. Therefore we judge it just and expedient that we should mutually grant and receive a truce until our envoy returns from our lords, the rulers of England and Normandy. When he has returned, we shall do what reason directs us.”

Hearing this, Helias gladly reported it to Fulk. All were greatly pleased and willingly agreed to the Normans’ proposal. The envoy sent to the duke of Normandy said:

> “Walter and Hamery, with their loyal companions, are keeping the castle of Le Mans as King William ordered them. Besieged by the men of Le Mans and Angevins, they seek your aid, wishing to know what they ought to do according to your will. If you wish to possess this castle, come with a strong force of warriors to help them and free them from their encircling enemies. Otherwise instruct them how they may escape the danger of death.”

But the duke, worn out by the hardships of his long pilgrimage and more eager to embrace the repose of bed than the labour of war, sent word through the envoy that the besieged should make an honourable peace with their besieging enemies:

> “I am exhausted by long labour, and the duchy of the Normans is enough for me. The nobles of England also invite me to hasten across the sea, because they are ready to receive me as king.”

Finally, having heard this, the envoy did not make the return journey; rather, swiftly crossing the sea, he went to the king of Albion and clearly reported in due order what, as I have written, he had just said to the duke. But the king, occupied with the affairs of his realm overseas, shrewdly preferred lawfully to embrace what was due to him rather than, from pride, to burden himself excessively with foreign and unwarranted labours. He thanked the guardians of the castle for their goodwill and sent the envoy back honoured with worthy gifts. The messenger therefore returned to his people and reported to them in order the replies of King William’s sons.

The guardians, now proven in commendable loyalty, ordered Helias to put on a white tunic, for which reason they were accustomed to call him “the White Bachelor.” [Col. 0756C] He immediately obeyed their command. The townsmen received him swiftly as he came and jokingly said:

> “White Bachelor, you may rightly rejoice now, because the time you have long desired is at hand. If you have plenty of money in your treasury, you can make a happy bargain with us. Powerful William, king of the English, built this castle, and his heir entrusted it to us; but lately—alas!—he has died. We give you this castle and henceforth grant that you shall be count of the people of Le Mans. We have not been frightened or overcome by fear of your strength, nor would strength to resist you have failed us for a long time if we had still wished to resist. We have arms, bold courage, and sufficient provisions. But we lack our natural lord, on whom to bestow the service of our valour. Therefore, vigorous man, recognizing your worth, we choose you; and, by surrendering the castle, we today make you ruler of the people of Le Mans.”

These worthy champions spoke thus to Helias, made peace with him, and surrendered to him the most strongly fortified tower with all the resources which William Rufus had gathered there. Peace having been made, the brave townsmen departed with their arms and all their goods; they were received by the counts not as conquered enemies, but as faithful friends. Count Helias escorted them safely through the city with two hundred knights and vigorously protected them from being harmed by the citizens whose homes they had burned in the previous year. Thus Count Helias recovered his county in the third year and held it honourably until his death for almost ten years.

Meanwhile, after several years, he gave his daughter Eremburga to Fulk, son of his lord, count of Anjou, and appointed him his successor and lord of the men of Le Mans. Later he formed a treaty of friendship with Duke Robert and King Henry; he took manfully part in their wars, doing great harm to one and giving great assistance to the other. After his wife died, he refused to live celibately, but married Agnes, daughter of William, duke of the Poitevins, the repudiated wife of Alfonso the Elder, king of Galicia.

> [Note: [Col. 0757] In the year 1080 Alfonso repudiated Agnes because of kinship. GUIZOT.]

He celebrated the marriage with great rejoicing, but died in the following year, mourned by many. Bishop Hildebert reverently buried his body in the basilica of Saint Peter the Apostle at La Couture.

## XV. Rivalry and dissensions arise between King Henry and Duke Robert. Of Ranulf Flambard, bishop of Durham. — Duke Robert crosses to England with an armed force.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1101, in the ninth indiction, a great disturbance arose in England and Normandy.

For seditious magnates, fearing the magnanimity of King Henry and preferring the indolent softness of Duke Robert, so that they might wickedly fulfil their desires, began to devise deceitful schemes in turn and sent him word to cross quickly with a fleet prepared. Robert of Bellême and his two brothers, Roger the Poitevin and Arnulf; William de Warenne, earl of Surrey; Walter Giffard; Ivo of Grandmesnil; Robert son of Ilbert; and many others ratified the plan of treachery and supported the duke’s party, at first secretly and afterwards openly. But the foolish duke did not preserve his own dominions; for the sake of the kingdom, which his more cunning brother possessed, he recklessly alienated them.

He then gave Robert of Bellême the bishopric of Sées, the castle of Argentan, and the forest of Gouffern; he granted the fortress of Gisors to Theobald Pagan because he had once entertained him. He also gave very much from his own treasury to other magnates and promised many men, if he became king, greater things than he could give. Since he did not reject the company of prostitutes and buffoons, but shamelessly indulged them and squandered his possessions, amid the riches of a vast duchy he often lacked bread; because of want of clothing he did not rise from bed until the sixth hour, nor did he go to church to hear the divine office because he was naked. For prostitutes and parasites, knowing his indulgence, continually surrounded him and often stole his breeches, stockings, and other garments with impunity. Thus there was openly fulfilled in him what a certain wise man said:

> “Those who squander their own possessions afterwards seek what belongs to others.”

But the Norman magnates, despising their duke and more eagerly desiring to favour the English king, resolved to transfer the duchy of Neustria to him and repeatedly encouraged him toward this ambition through embassies. Thus both peoples, under the pressure of treachery, were corrupted and plotted how they might harm their own lord, to whom they were unfaithful. Certain rebels undertook open war against their faithful neighbours and stained the bosom of their kindly motherland with rapine, fires, and bloody slaughter. The venerable Archbishop Anselm, all the bishops and abbots with the sacred clergy, and all the English adhered inseparably to their king and continually prayed to the King of Sabaoth for his safety and the stability of the kingdom. Robert of Meulan also, and many other loyal and prudent barons, faithfully remained attached to their lord and supported him with their strength and counsel.

Ranulf Flambard, bishop of Durham, was the principal instigator of this madness. He, indeed, having risen from a common stock, flattered William Rufus excessively; and by favouring him with cunning schemes, he was exalted by him above all the magnates of the realm. He was made chief administrator of the royal revenues and justiciar; and, having frequently practised countless cruelties, he became hated and terrible to many. But he himself, having amassed wealth from every quarter and enlarged his honours, became exceedingly rich; and even to episcopal rank, though he was almost illiterate, he advanced—not by merit of religion, but by secular power. Yet because no power in mortal life lasts long, when his king had been killed, he, the long-standing despoiler of his country, was imprisoned by the new king. For the many injuries by which he had harassed Henry himself and other children of the realm, poor as well as rich, and had repeatedly afflicted and grievously distressed them in many ways without respect, he was, by divine ordinance, when the wind changed, cast down from the lofty summit of power and handed over, in chains, to William de Mandeville to be guarded in the Tower of London. But, as Ovid says of Daedalus:

> “Adversity often stirs ingenuity . . .”

[Col. 0758D] The ingenious bishop strove to escape the harshness of imprisonment, and cunningly secured an exit through friends. For he was shrewd and eloquent; and although cruel and wrathful, he was nevertheless generous and generally agreeable, and for this reason pleasing and beloved by very many. By the king’s command he had two sterling shillings daily for his maintenance. Thus, with the help of friends, he made merry in prison, and each day ordered a splendid banquet to be served for himself and his guards. One day a rope was brought to him in a jar of wine, and an abundant feast was furnished at the bishop’s expense. The guards ate with him and, having drunk Falernian wine freely, became cheerful. When they were thoroughly drunk [Col. 0759A] and snoring securely, the bishop fastened the rope to a pillar in the middle of the fortress-window; taking his pastoral staff with him, he descended by the rope. But because he had forgotten to wrap his hands in gloves, they were flayed as far as the mouth by the roughness of the rope; and since the rope did not reach the ground, the corpulent prelate fell heavily and, almost shattered, groaned piteously. His faithful friends and tried retainers waited at the foot of the tower; not without great fear, they had prepared excellent horses there for him. Mounting them, he fled swiftly, and met his loyal companions with his treasure; with them he hastened by sea to Duke Robert in Normandy.

Flambard’s mother, however, was a sorceress and frequently conversed with a demon; through this wicked familiarity she had lost one eye. She was being carried in another ship across the sea to Neustria with her son’s treasure, and there her companions mocked her everywhere with derisive gestures because of her criminal enchantments. Meanwhile pirates encountered them on the sea and plundered the entire treasury; and the witch, an old woman, was put ashore naked and mourning on the coast of Normandy with the sailors and passengers. Finally the fugitive bishop was received by the duke and made governor of Normandy; and the duke himself, so far as his indolence allowed, used his counsels. He especially incited the duke to conflict with his brother and exerted every effort to foster hostility against the king. He advised the duke how he might obtain the kingdom of England [Col. 0759C] and promised him his assistance in all matters.

At last, in the autumn of 1101, Duke Robert crossed to England and, welcomed by illustrious and wealthy men who had allied themselves with him and awaited him, prepared for war against the king. His fleet was very unlike the fleet of his father William; it reached Portsmouth not through the strength of the army but through the agency of traitors. The duke was immediately brought into the province of Winchester by the nobles of the realm, who had long before rendered him homage; and he challenged his brother to battle through the incitement of seditious men, unless he laid down the crown. Many who had formerly adhered to the king only in appearance willingly received the arriving duke and filled out his ranks with their forces. Robert of Bellême, William, earl of Surrey, and many others deserted the king; and many, in order to force an occasion for separation, made unjust demands upon him, threatening that unless he satisfied their petitions they would desert him [Col. 0760B]. Robert of Meulan, Richard de Redvers, and many other valiant barons surrounded their king. All the English likewise, knowing no rights of another ruler, remained steadfast in loyalty to their king, for which they eagerly desired to enter battle.

Meanwhile Hugh, earl of Chester, took to his bed; after a long illness he assumed the monastic habit in the monastery which he himself had built at Chester, and three days later died, on the sixth day before the Kalends of August [27 July]. Richard, however, a most beautiful boy, whom he alone had begotten by Ermentrude, daughter of Hugh of Clermont, held his earldom for nearly twelve years, beloved by all; he married Matilda, daughter of Stephen, count of Blois, by Adela, sister of King Henry [Col. 0760C]. With her he perished by shipwreck in the White Ship, alas, as will later be sufficiently explained, on the seventh day before the Kalends of December [25 November], 1101.

> **[Note: Col. 0759C]**
>
> The following genealogy gives the succession of the earls of Chester from this Norman Hugh:
>
> In the year of the Lord 1089, Lord Anselm, abbot of the church of Utica [read: Bec], came into England. At the request of Hugh, the first earl of Chester, he came to Chester and there founded an abbey in honour of St Werburgh; having gathered monks there, he appointed Richard, a monk of Utica [read: Bec], as its first abbot. When this had been done, in the same year, on his return from Chester, he was made archbishop of Canterbury (in the year 1093).
>
> On the sixth day before the Kalends of August died Hugh, first earl of Chester, who lies in the chapter-house of the church of Spalding, at its southern extremity. After his death his son Richard, a boy seven years old, received the earldom. On the seventh day before the Kalends of December he was drowned with his wife and many others at Barfleur. After him succeeded Ranulf de Meschines, nephew of the aforesaid Earl Hugh, who, dying on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, lies to the south beside the first Hugh. After him succeeded his son Ranulf de Gernon, who, dying on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January, lies beside his father. After him succeeded his son Ranulf, who, dying on the seventh day before the Kalends of November, lies beside his father. After him succeeded his nephew John of Scotland, who, dying on the seventh day before the Ides of June, lies beside the aforesaid earl.
>
> Now Ranulf had four sisters: the eldest, Matilda; the second, Mabel; the third, Agnes; the fourth, Hawise. The first Matilda was married to Count David and had a son John, surnamed “of Scotland,” who was earl of Chester and had four daughters. The first, Margaret, was married to Alan of Galloway and had a daughter, Dervorguilla, who was the wife of John Balliol. The second, Isabella, was married to Robert de Brus and had a son Robert de Brus. The third, Matilda, died without children. The fourth, Alda, was married to Henry of Hastings and had a son Henry Hastings.
>
> Mabel, the second sister of Earl Ranulf, was married to the earl of Arundel and had four daughters: namely, Mabel, married to Robert Tateshall, by whom she had a son Robert Tateshall; the second sister, Nicola, married to Roger de Somery, by whom she had a son Ralph, who died before his father, and four daughters: namely, Margaret, married to Ralph Basset the younger; the second, Joan, married to John le Strange; the third, Elizabeth, married to Walter de Sully; and the fourth, Matilda, married to Henry of Herdington. Cecily, the third daughter of the earl of Arundel, was married to Roger de Montalt. Isabella, the fourth daughter of the same earl, was married to John, son of Alan, and had a son John.
>
> Agnes, the third sister of Earl Ranulf, was married to William Ferrers the elder and had a son William the younger, who was earl of Derby. William the younger had a son Robert.
>
> Hawise, the fourth sister of Earl Ranulf, was married to Robert de Quincy and had a daughter Margaret, countess of Lincoln, who was married to John de Lacy, constable of Chester. By her John begot Edmund; Edmund begot Henry Lacy, earl of Lincoln, and Edmund himself died before his mother. The said Henry, by the daughter of the earl of Salisbury, begot Edmund, who died before his father, and a daughter named Alice; she was married to Lord Thomas, earl of Lancaster and Leicester, and after his death to Lord Ebulo le Strange. .

### XVI. Peace is arranged between the two brothers, Henry and Robert.

[Col. 0761A]

The earl of Meulan, foreseeing the intrigues and defection of his fellow-countrymen, and striving to preserve his faith to his royal friend in prosperity and adversity, turned over many matters subtly in his silent heart, now on one side, now on another; and he laboured anxiously lest the condition of the kingdom should waver. He therefore said to the king:

“Every honourable man, endowed with justice, when he sees a friend assailed by troubles, ought, if he wishes to be held worthy through lawfulness, to assist his beloved friend in need with all his efforts. In such a concern, one ought not so much to weigh the profit of a future reward as to consider the relief of a needy friend. Yet we see many acting very differently and staining, by disgraceful treachery, the honour of the faith which they pledged to their lord. This indeed [Col. 0761B] we plainly see and feel as sharp pricks in our own sides.

“We therefore, to whom the care of the common good has been divinely entrusted, must watch everywhere for the safety of the realm and of God’s Church. Let it be our greatest care that, by God’s grace, we may conquer peacefully; that we may gain victory without the shedding of Christian blood; and that the faithful people may remain in the serenity of peace. Therefore now, my lord king, hear my counsel and do not disdain to obey my advice. Address all your knights gently; flatter all as a father his children; soothe everyone with promises; grant whatever they ask; and thus skilfully draw all to favour you. If they ask for London or York, do not delay to promise great things, as royal generosity requires. [Col. 0761C] For it is better to give up a portion of the kingdom than to lose victory and life amid a multitude of enemies. And when, with God’s help, we have successfully reached the end of this affair, we shall offer useful advice on recovering the estates which rash deserters have usurped during the war.

“It is certain that whoever freely deserts his lord when he is in danger of death, seeks another from greed of gain, makes saleable to his king the military service which he ought voluntarily to render for defence of the kingdom, and strives to despoil him of his own estates, shall by the judgment of reason and equity be judged a traitor; he shall deservedly be stripped of his hereditary possessions and driven into exile.”

All the magnates standing by King Henry praised the earl’s words and urged the king to follow his advice. [Col. 0761D] The king, surpassing in wisdom, thanked his well-disposed advisers and willingly accepted their salutary exhortations; by promises and gifts he reconciled to himself many whom he regarded as suspect. At last he advanced with a great army to meet his brother and sent envoys through whom he carefully asked why Robert had presumed to enter the bounds of England with an armed army. Duke Robert, through his representatives, spoke thus:

“I have entered my father’s kingdom with my nobles, and I claim it as due to me by right of primogeniture.”

For several days the two brothers remained upon a certain plain and daily sent distinguished messengers to one another [Col. 0762A]. The seditious traitors desired war rather than peace; and because they pursued private advantage more than the public good, the crafty couriers distorted their messages and sowed quarrels rather than concord between the brothers. But shrewd Henry perceived this, and therefore asked for a face-to-face conference with his brother. When they met, the sweetness of brotherly love filled them both. A noble circle from the immense army stood around, and there the fearful splendour of Normans and English in arms shone forth. The two brothers alone spoke in the midst of the watching people, and without deceit uttered with their mouths what they had pondered in their hearts. Finally, after a few words, they embraced one another and exchanged sweet kisses; without any mediator, they became reconciled.

I cannot set down here the words of this conference, because I was not present; but I learned by report the agreement which resulted from the counsel of such great brothers.

First, Duke Robert remitted to his brother the claim which he had made in the kingdom of England, and released him, in consideration of his royal dignity, from the homage which Henry had rendered him long before. King Henry, however, promised to pay the duke three thousand pounds sterling every year; and he surrendered the whole district of the Cotentin and whatever he possessed in Neustria, except Domfront. He kept only the castle of Domfront for himself, because, when the people of Domfront admitted him, he had pledged by oath never to cast them out of his hand nor alter their laws or customs. With all arbiters removed, [Col. 0762C] the brothers alone ratified their decisions; while all those around watched them with amazement, they decreed that they should help one another, as brothers ought, recover all their father’s dominions, and punish together, on both sides, the wicked sowers of strife.

When peace had thus been made, confusion covered the faithless men. It made them contemptible even to those whom they had unjustly flattered, inglorious, and pale with fear; it compelled them to hide from the king’s presence. But the sincere common people and those engaged in just labours rejoiced. The armed bands, having received the king’s leave, were disbanded and returned joyfully to their homes. The whole kingdom of Albion, rejoicing in the tranquillity of peace, was quiet; and the Church of God, flourishing in prolonged repose, shone in the divine law and, secure in God, served as a soldier without the turmoil of battles [Col. 0762D]. Clear testimony to our narrative is borne by new churches, the many chapels recently founded in the villages of England, and the laborious cloisters of monasteries with the other workshops of monks, built in King Henry’s time. For every religious order, enjoying peace and prosperity, strives inwardly and outwardly to show diligence in all things belonging to the worship of the all-powerful Godhead. Hence the fervent devotion of the faithful undertakes to pull down churches and houses, rebuilding them in improved form. Thus ancient buildings, constructed under Edgar, Edward, and other Christian kings, are demolished so that they may suitably be made better in scale, [Col. 0763A] size, or elegance of workmanship, to the praise of the Creator.

After Duke Robert had remained with his brother the king for two months, honoured with royal gifts, he returned to Neustria as winter approached, taking with him William de Warenne and many others who had been disinherited on his account.

Not long afterwards Gilbert the Old, surnamed Maminot, bishop of Lisieux, died in August; and Fulcher, Flambard’s brother, was consecrated bishop of that see by Archbishop William in June. This man, almost illiterate, had been snatched from the court to the episcopate through his brother’s influence. Having held it for seven months, commendable for his lavish generosity, he died in January 1102. [Col. 0763B] Then Ranulf Flambard, who was an exile in Normandy and lacked the bishopric of Durham because of his hostility to the king whom he had opposed, obtained the bishopric of Lisieux for his young son Thomas and governed it for three years, not as bishop but as administrator. Meanwhile William de Pacy, having given a great price to the earl, tried to seize the bishopric; but, condemned first at Rouen and afterwards at Rome for the taint of simony, he miserably paid for his rashness. Thus Lisieux lacked a ruler for almost five years, and the Lord’s flock, lacking a worthy shepherd, lay open to wolves’ teeth, until God’s grace sent John as bishop, for the consolation of his people.

### XVII. The duke of Aquitaine, the duke of Burgundy, and very many other magnates take the cross. Their disputes with the emperor of Constantinople.

[Col. 0763C]

Having heard good reports of the illustrious champions who had gone abroad and, fighting gloriously in Christ’s name against the heathen in the East, had triumphed, the western nobles emulated their unconquered valour and unexpected successes. Their cousins and kinsmen were stirred by the example of their prowess to a like undertaking. For the ardour of pilgrimage—to visit the Saviour’s tomb and the holy places, and to exercise their strength and knighthood against the Turks—kindled many. Fear of apostolic malediction also compelled many to make the pilgrimage; for Pope Paschal publicly anathematized and excluded from all Christendom all who had freely taken the Lord’s Cross [Col. 0763D] and returned without completing their journey, unless they took the road back again and, making satisfaction to God, devoutly fulfilled their vows.

Therefore, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1101, William, duke of the Poitevins, gathered a huge army from Aquitaine and Gascony and cheerfully undertook the journey of the holy pilgrimage. He was bold and worthy, exceedingly agreeable, and surpassed even witty entertainers in manifold jesting. It is reported that three hundred thousand armed men followed his banner when he departed from Aquitaine. Stephen, count palatine of Blois, was almost universally reproached and continually ashamed because he had shamefully fled from the siege of Antioch and abandoned his glorious companions struggling in Christ’s martyrdom [Col. 0764A]. Many persons repeatedly rebuked him, and both fear and shame compelled him to resume Christ’s military service. His wife Adela also frequently admonished him and, amid the endearments of their loving marriage, said:

“Far be it from you, my lord, to consent for long to endure the reproaches of so many men. Recall the renowned valour of your youth, and take up the arms of praiseworthy knighthood for the salvation of many thousands, so that from this there may arise throughout the whole world great rejoicing among Christ’s worshippers, terror among the heathen, and the public overthrow of their wicked law.”

The shrewd and spirited woman spoke these and many like things to her husband. But he, knowing the dangers and difficulties, feared to undergo the harsh labours again. At last he recovered courage and strength, set out with many thousands [Col. 0764B] of Franks, and went as far as Christ’s Sepulchre, although very grievous obstacles stood in his way. Then Harpin sold the city of Bourges to Philip, king of the Franks, and began the journey to Jerusalem with Joscelin of Courtenay and Milo of Bray. Duke Stephen, Stephen, count of the Saône country, and another Stephen, son of Richeldis, with very numerous companies of warriors from Burgundy, swiftly joined Christ’s army. The archbishop of Milan also, and Albert of Biandrate, a most powerful Italian, with bands of Ligurians, undertook the journey to Jerusalem. All these travelled abroad for the love of God; when they reached Macedonia, they sent envoys to Emperor Alexius, by whom they asked him for safe-conduct and a market [Col. 0764C].

The prudent Augustus, hearing that the immense strength of the westerners was approaching, was alarmed; granting without hesitation everything that they requested of him, he skilfully treated them with courtesy. He had often experienced the boldness and courage of the Italians under Guiscard and Bohemond, and therefore took great care not to offend them or provoke them to war. He consequently decreed that they should have free passage through his land and generously acceded in every respect to their requests. He bestowed great gifts upon the leaders and had all of them conducted safely as far as Cappadocia, which lies beyond Constantinople. There all the western companies were counted, and more than five hundred thousand combatants were found. The prudent men took counsel concerning the journey to be completed, but also considered beforehand the dangers to be avoided. Thus in their meetings they examined what threatened them and spoke to one another as follows:

“Up to this point we have been secure, because we have dwelt among brothers whose customs and speech we know. For ever since we left our homes until now, Christians have kindly received us for love of the supreme Father. From this point another condition awaits us. Between the emperor and Bohemond, who rules Antioch, the mighty storms of war rage fiercely. The regions through which we must travel are uncultivated, and the Turks roam frequently through them as far as the sea. Just as wolves naturally thirst for the blood of sheep, so they desire to destroy every race of Christians. Let us humbly beseech Almighty God to protect us, for we are surrounded on every side by diverse dangers. Behold, we have left behind us the treacherous emperor and his peoples, whom we greatly suspect. On our right is the sea, in which are Crete, Cyprus, famous Rhodes, and many other islands, all subject to the emperor and hostile to us because of the misdeeds of our countrymen who went before us. To the east and north barbarous nations possess the world even to earth’s bounds, and burn with insatiable desire to shed Christian blood. Through uncultivated places the journey to Antioch is more than thirty days, where every kind of food fails us because the fertile regions have been devastated by the war which has long endured between the emperor [Col. 0765B] and Bohemond. What shall we do amid so many dangers? We are desolate on every side.”

At last, after many inquiries into diverse opinions, the duke of Aquitaine said:

“Let us send envoys to the emperor and unanimously ask him to send Count Saint-Gilles with the Saviour’s lance, so that he may safely lead us through provinces unknown to us as far as Christ’s Sepulchre. He is wise and of great authority, and in the first expedition was counted among the foremost in every respect. By long experience he knows the difficulties and roads that we do not know, and his proven valour has long been very well known to Christians and pagans. Therefore, if we set this man over us as a Maro [guide] and counsellor, we shall have security from the Augustus and prudence against the heathen.”

Messengers were sent with everyone’s consent, and eloquently presented their embassy to the Augustus. When he heard the requests of the westerners, he immediately conveyed them to Count Raymond. Hearing this, Raymond replied:

“By God’s grace, I have laboured greatly in taking Jerusalem; broken by old age and many labours, I now desire to enjoy rest. I have fled to the refuge of your Majesty, lord Augustus. Spare me, I beg you; do not compel me to make pilgrimage further.”

But the emperor said to the envoys:

“I urged Count Saint-Gilles to travel with you. But he pleads old age and his infirmities, which prevent him from being able to go out with you. Go securely under my peace. I do not wish—and ought not—to drive away the excellent count who has fled to the protection of our peace.”

The envoys immediately returned and reported what they had heard.

Then all were troubled and murmured different things among themselves. William of Aquitaine said:

“Take up arms swiftly; return and besiege Constantinople. We shall not withdraw while vigorously storming the city until we either kill the treacherous emperor or forcibly extort from him against his will what has been asked. By his frauds he has destroyed countless thousands of the faithful; therefore, I think, he who by whatever means takes the life of one who occupies the land for the ruin of many will offer a sacrifice pleasing to God.”

Stephen of Blois and the other moderate barons did not assent to such an order but jointly opposed it, reasonably advancing arguments of plain truth. But the Aquitanians [Col. 0766A], Gascons, and other unruly men, who, in their youthful recklessness, sought royal power, supported the youthful impudence of their insolent duke. They therefore returned presumptuously and besieged Byzantium for three days. When the emperor heard of their undertaking and considered the populous city opposite them, enclosed by a triple wall, he at first treated the hostile arrival lightly. But when he understood their persistent obstinacy, he ordered three very fierce lions and seven leopards released between the middle wall and the outer defensive wall. He stationed guards upon the third wall, to which the palaces of the nobles were attached on the inner side, and commanded the gates to be left open. Thus he hoped, by means of wild beasts, mockingly to frighten the Franks and defend the imperial city without human hands.

[Col. 0766B] But man’s crafty thought has no force except insofar as divine providence decrees. When the Franks stood armed in their camp and saw no one resisting them, they entered through the first gate seeking battle, and, looking curiously about in every direction, waited for defenders. Immediately on their first entry savage lions met them and, raging with teeth and claws, wounded some and tore to pieces the unwary, ignorant of combat with beasts.

But the contest of beasts could not long withstand human skill. The armed warriors pierced the animals with hunting-spears and whistling missiles; having killed the lions, they put the leopards to flight and pursued them as they fled to the middle wall. Then [Col. 0766C] the leopards, climbing like wall-runners, leapt over the wall; the Frankish divisions entered through the gate of the second wall and attempted vigorously to storm the third. A great shouting arose in the city among the citizens, with dreadful confusion and a rushing together of all who did not know what to do in so sudden an emergency. Hearing the tumult of the unprecedented assault, the emperor was terrified and groaned that he had been deceived by a false hope. At last, through his envoys, he begged the noble pilgrims and, with many promises, calmed their anger and restrained them from storming the imperial city, into which they had almost already broken.

As the Franks returned to their tents in victory, the mournful Augustus summoned the count of Toulouse [Col. 0766D] and said to him, sad and greatly cast down:

“Confounded, glorious count, I flee to you and ask your counsel concerning what should be done amid this unexpected uproar. Behold, the insolence of the Franks has dared with brazen hand and arms to attack the imperial city, which is the head of the East. It has violated the eminence of the holy empire and, lest worse should happen, bent it to its supplication; by spilling the blood of faithful subjects, it has provoked the wrath of Almighty Wisdom. Imperial majesty, which once used to give laws to strangers and inhabitants, alas, is now compelled to submit to conditions imposed by insolent pilgrims.”

Count Raymond replied:

“My compatriots often make attacks of this sort, and I know well their tumultuous assaults in such matters against those assembled with them. The wisdom of your greatness has no need of long circumlocutions. Let a timely peace be made with these insolent men. Thus public necessity demands, for whose sake, unless I am mistaken, many will breathe out their souls. The wicked Gascons demand me as leader of their journey; against my will, they rashly compel me to continue on pilgrimage.

> They shall not go unpunished, since they persist in such deeds.

“I am greatly grieved, mighty emperor, over the injury inflicted on the holy empire; but I shall not now disclose all that I intend. We shall wait for the time of vengeance, when the impious rashness of the wicked will be expiated. Behold, the wall of Constantinople is wet and defiled with the blood of her own sons, as at this very moment, shame upon it, we sorrowfully behold.”

The Augustus and the count exchanged these and other such words [Col. 0767B] and devised how to exact retaliation from their enemies for the trouble they had caused them. The emperor selected distinguished envoys, who, with an oath, conveyed his message to the Franks, humbly entreating them to depart peacefully and wait for the count with twenty thousand Turcopoles in Cappadocia. Having received the emperor’s pledge with an oath, they withdrew and, preparing themselves, rested for some time. After several days the count followed them. The emperor then sent many ships loaded with *tartarones* and ordered these to be distributed to all according to their ranks and dignities. The people of Thrace call *tartarones* square copper coins, with which provincials in Thrace or Bithynia conduct trade, as they do with *philippi* or Byzantine coins [Col. 0767C]. The needy pilgrims eagerly accepted the emperor’s gifts, not knowing the deceit and cunning malice of this most wicked traitor. For the crafty spy discovered their number by this method, calculating the number of recipients from the measure of money he gave to each. He then sent an account of their number to Daliman and Soliman, and other Turkish princes, ordering them to meet the pilgrims in Paphlagonia with the combined forces of all paganism.

### XVIII. The treachery of Emperor Alexius. The army of cross-bearers is destroyed by the Turks in Asia Minor.

The men of our country, ignorant of the fraud, rejoiced at the count’s arrival; with the Turcopoles leading them, who knew the Getic language, the local customs, and the roads [Col. 0767D], they set out and, wandering through extreme hardships for three weeks, reached the great city of the barbarians called Gandras. For they entirely left on their right the route which leads through Romania and Syria to Jerusalem, and took byways through Pontus—formerly the kingdom of Mithridates, king of twenty-two kingdoms—northward as far as Paphlagonia. I do not know whether Count Saint-Gilles thus went astray through ignorance, or whether, out of malice and for revenge, he led his companions astray in this way. When the Christians had crossed rough country, dangerous rivers, and pathless forests, and after three weeks had scarcely reached the city of Gandras [Col. 0768A], they decided to rest there for a while after many labours. Then, behold, a multitude of pagans, as innumerable as the sand of the sea, came against them and challenged men unprepared and exhausted by very many hardships. They brought with them their wives and herds of cattle and dragged huge stores of riches in wagons: that their own presence might protect the mass of their wealth to the utmost; that they might display their treasures to enemies and kinsmen alike, so as to inspire terror in all by the enormity of their riches; and finally that, everywhere, both at home and on campaign, they might abound in every kind of pleasure.

But the Christians, worn out by hunger, thirst, and other hardships, when they began to be pressed into battle, forgot their former sufferings, marched out armed, recovered courage [Col. 0768B] and strength, drew up their battle-lines, and fought bravely for five days in the Lord’s name. There, as trustworthy pilgrims report, were five hundred thousand Christians; and, unless I am mistaken, one million pagans attacked them terribly. The fighting was most fierce on both sides, and many thousands were slain. On the fifth day, when the Turks saw that their divisions were failing and unexpectedly feared the unconquered strength of the Christians, they ordered by public decree their wives in the tents, the eunuchs, and the other servants who guarded the leaders’ possessions, carefully to pack all equipment with their treasures and be ready the next night to flee from the enemy.

But the Christians, ignorant of the Turks’ weakening, alas for shame! weakened themselves. At nightfall Count Raymond, with the emperor’s Turcopoles and his own provincials, turned their backs and began to flee secretly, without the other leaders’ knowledge [Col. 0768C]. Seeing this, the armour-bearer of the count of Toulouse, piously sympathizing with the Christian army, struck down his lord’s tent so that his deceived fellow-soldiers might learn of his sudden flight. Albert of Biandrate, a most valiant hero, was killed in the battle with many thousands, whose exact number is not known to me. The duke of Aquitaine, Stephen of Blois, and other nobles with their troops, when they learned of the faithless flight of their companions, were themselves terrified by loss of courage and attempted to flee in different directions. The Turks, very exhausted and intending to seek refuge in flight, discovered [Col. 0768D] that the Franks were fleeing; their spirits were roused, they pursued their enemies under arms, slaughtered all the rearmost men, and massacred many thousands. Some, however, in the flower of youth, they carried away captive. Nearly four hundred thousand Christians perished in body; but in spirit may they live in eternal rest with Christ, in whom they died.

The Count of Toulouse, with his followers and the Turcopoles, fled back to Constantinople; and, on reporting the Christians’ disastrous outcome, they brought great joy to the emperor. Meanwhile Dalimannus and Solimannus, with the other princes of the hostile people, celebrated in triumphal pomp their victory; and they restored intact to him the quantity of tartarons which the emperor had deceitfully given the Christians under the false name of charity, and sent him half of all the spoils which they had taken from the defeated enemy. For this was the agreement which that faithless traitor had made with the Turks; by these terms he had sold the faithful to the unbelievers, and, receiving as the price of his treachery an immense heap of tartarons for the blood of the baptized, he danced in foolish exultation.

The distinguished dukes of Aquitaine and Burgundy, and other valiant nobles, fled and hid, as opportunity allowed, in caves, the recesses of caverns, or the thickness of forests. For Syrians and Armenians, mingled with barbarians, lived in those regions. Dwelling here and there in hamlets, they served the Turks, publicly paid an annual tribute to purchase peace and security, and nevertheless devoutly observed the Christian law—proved by persecutions like gold in a furnace. They were therefore deeply grieved by the Christians’ overthrow; they compassionately aided those wandering by trackless ways as brethren, and, so far as they could under fear of the unbelievers to whom they were subject, mercifully supported them. They concealed fugitives in their hiding places, fed those in concealment, and guided them through the darkness of night onto the road leading to Antioch; bringing them to known relatives and compatriots, they kept them safe. Many were taken captive by barbarians into unknown lands, and remained for some time in slavery or chains among people whose speech they did not understand. There, duly serving the supreme Deity, they experienced His grace and were wondrously aided in many ways, like the Israelites among the Assyrians or Chaldaeans. Thus very many returned from captivity, either by escape or with the permission of Persian princes and of other peoples.  
[Note: [Col. 0769D] These events occurred in the year 1102.]

Thus, with the aid of the gracious Creator, who is near to all who love Him, nearly one hundred thousand Christians escaped. Some turned back through Illyricum; others completed the journey they had begun amid enormous fears and hardships. The Duke of Poitou, who had left the lands of the Limousins attended by three hundred thousand armed men, and who, in his excessive arrogance while Constantinople was under siege, had terrified the emperor, entered Antioch with six companions, scarcely arriving there as a poor beggar. Likewise other dukes, distinguished counts, and tribunes lost their forces; deprived of their beloved retainers and their possessions, they were left utterly desolate in savage barbarian lands. Yet restored by constancy in the true faith and love of gracious Jesus, they hastened to His tomb. Although, by God’s hidden judgment, they had been delayed by hardships of many kinds, inwardly strengthened by spiritual nectar they tried by every means to visit the holy places, so that they might become companions of the holy bloodstained martyrs, who, having shed their blood for Christ, rejoice crowned in heaven.

## XIX. The rule of Godfrey, king of Jerusalem. Baldwin, his brother and successor. The battle of Ramla.

[Col. 0770A]

Godfrey, king of Jerusalem, reigned for two years [Note: [Col. 0770D] From the year 1099 to the year 1100.], and, almost continually prepared for war, stood against the Philistines; relying upon great prowess, he enlarged the boundaries of his kingdom. The native Gentiles kept a treacherous peace in cities and villages, and dared not openly murmur against the Christians. Yet, sorrowing, they secretly devised evil against them and, full of guile, awaited the time for carrying it out. At last the citizens of Joppa poisoned King Godfrey while he was staying there and thus killed the glorious prince, to the great grief of the Christians. He was the first Christian, since the Saviour suffered for us in Jerusalem, who was compelled by ecclesiastical election to wear a diadem there, in praise of Him who deigned to wear thorny crowns for humankind’s salvation, and to be called king of Jerusalem, to the terror of the Gentiles. Upon his death, as has been said, counsel was immediately taken concerning the appointment of a king. Messengers were therefore at once sent to Rages; the king’s death was reported to Baldwin, his brother, and he was summoned to govern the kingdom of Jerusalem in his brother’s place. He immediately entrusted the duchy of his own province to Baldwin of Bourcq, his kinsman, and himself penetrated hostile lands and barbarous nations like lightning. Near Sarepta, a city of the Sidonians, he encountered nearly forty thousand pagans; with a few men he charged bravely among them, struck them with marvellous terror, and by God’s power put them all to flight, then joyfully made his way into Judaea. The Turks had indeed foreknown his coming and therefore lay armed in ambush, awaiting the joy they hoped for. But disappointed in their vain hope, those who could escape hurried tremblingly home, with loss and disgrace.

The aforesaid hero, received by the Jerusalemites, took the helm of David’s throne and held it bravely for almost twelve years. He was handsome in body, tall in stature, pre-eminent in courage and strength, great-hearted in enduring hardships, trained in literary learning, gifted with eloquence of speech, and becomingly adorned with many virtues. During his reign Stephen of Blois and the nobles mentioned above came to Jerusalem through many dangers, and were honourably received by the aforesaid king and by Patriarch Ebremar. The Duke of Poitou, having completed his prayers in Jerusalem, returned to his own country with some of his companions; and later, supported by prosperity, he repeatedly recounted the miseries of his captivity before kings, magnates, and Christian assemblies, as he was a pleasant and witty man, in rhymed verses with amusing tunes. But Stephen of Blois and many others remained in Judaea for Christ’s love and resolved to offer God the courage and worth of their military service; they waited for the king of Babylon, whom they had learned was approaching with innumerable armies.

[Col. 0771A] At last, having heard reliable reports that the Admirable One [Note: [Col. 0771D] Rather, “the Admired One,” commonly *émir*.] of Babylon had come to Ascalon and had resolved on the following day to attack the Christians with many legions, King Baldwin, Stephen, and the other faithful encouraged one another in the Lord Jesus. They faithfully armed themselves to win triumph in His name, whether by their own death or that of the enemy. They sent part of the army to Joppa; the king and the greater part of the nobility went to Ramla. They did not wish to be shut up in Jerusalem, and moreover did not know which city the Turks would attack first. At last, with a sudden assault, the Admirable One and his immeasurable army surrounded Ramla, set about attacking its wall with missiles and various engines, and undermining it with mattocks and digging-tools. Inside were excellent but few knights, and they could not withstand so great a mass of such astonishing multitude.

Stephen therefore, Harpin, William Sans-Avoir, and all the others persuaded the king to depart with all speed for Jerusalem. “Hasten,” they said, “valiant man, hurry to the holy city, lest so many troops surround it without a defender and consume that mother with all her children by sudden assault. Behold, we too are enclosed here together, and confidently await our end in confession of Christ, praying our Creator with all our hearts that we may be His true martyrs; that through the shedding of our blood in His name we may be cleansed from all sins; and that we may be able to behold His desirable and propitious countenance with His own. Farewell, good king, and depart at once, although escape through such numerous and cruel ranks of enemies is difficult unless divine mercy accompanies you.”

The anxious barons said this and much else like it to the king, forcing him to leave one danger for a greater one. Though unwilling, he yielded to the exhortations of so many heroes. With one knight he mounted a swift and very powerful mare called Farisia, and, riding out, passed unharmed by night through the enemy bands under God’s protection. When he had crossed the pagan camp by night and was hastening through various winding paths toward Helia, the watchmen on guard discovered that unknown knights had passed by. They cried out and, rousing the companies, pursued the fugitives for two miles with great clamour and howling. But the king fled by paths he knew and, with God’s help, escaped unharmed with the utmost difficulty. Leaving in terror the mountain road which he had begun to take toward Jerusalem, he came with difficulty by steep tracks to the town called Arsuf, where he found its frightened guards keeping watch. He immediately spoke with them, but when he wished to enter, he was repulsed. For although he repeatedly said to them, “I am Baldwin; do not fear; receive me among you,” the garrison, dreading the many forms of enemy deception, did not believe him, until they kindled a fire above the walls and, seeing his uncovered head, recognized him. Then they joyfully admitted him; he encouraged them and, reporting the news, warned the garrison to defend themselves.

From there the king mounted his gazelle with his fellow knight and came hastily to Joppa. Recognized by the citizens, he entered and reported the sad news: “Innumerable troops of pagans surround Ramla and attack it until those inside are utterly destroyed. The glorious hero, Count Palatine Stephen of Blois, Milo of Bray, Harpin of Bourges, William Sans-Avoir and his brother Simon, and other valiant nobles are becoming Christ’s martyrs at Ramla; and they forcibly sent me away, so that I might strengthen you and our other brethren for like things. The enemies pursued us insolently and, I think, will hasten to come here. Now, if it pleases you, let us send a messenger to Jerusalem and order the patriarch and all our brethren to bring us aid without delay in fitting array, as we shall direct them.”

When all approved this counsel, the king summoned a courageous squire. “Dear brother,” he said, “go to Jerusalem and bring us the armed multitude of our brethren; and, if you return alive when we have assembled, I shall make you a knight.” At once he carried out the entrusted embassy most successfully and duly gained the arms of the promised knighthood.

The accursed pagan army destroyed Ramla and killed or carried into captivity all whom it found within. Then, swollen with victory, it came to Joppa on the same day and covered the surface of the earth with its multitude like locusts; it sent Count Stephen and the others thought more noble to Ascalon. It silently besieged the city for two days, and on the third departed with loss and disgrace. For the guards of the fortress of Jaffa saw the Jerusalemites’ banners over the hills and joyfully reported to the king that they were near the castle of the Burgundians. The king then assembled the band of the faithful and, strengthening them with a manly exhortation, said:

“Behold a time desirable for valiant recruits, fitting for illustrious athletes to avenge their loved ones, and terrifying enough for the timid and idle, who resemble foxes in cunning and sloth. Behold before your gates an accursed people, hateful to the Lord God and to all His faithful. Come, brave men, take up arms and rise gloriously against the enemies of all good things. Arm yourselves manfully to execute God’s vengeance; as our allies approach, go forth from the city and, strong in faith, fight under God’s protection. Recall from your very marrow your injuries and losses, and let the foreigners feel that your hands are not sluggish. They have slain Count Stephen and Harpin and other great barons; they have taken from us our excellent knights and commanders—barons, I say with tears, than whom none better can be found in the world. Let recent grief at our friends’ death inflame and sharpen you for the destruction of the enemies. Remember David, that mightiest king, and his warriors—Joab and Abishai, Benaiah and Uriah the Hittite; Jonathan and Judas Maccabaeus; and many praiseworthy athletes of your own people. As we go forth from here, we shall begin the battle, while the Jerusalemites who come to our aid will strike the foreigners from the other side. May mighty Emmanuel be with you, the Son of the holy Virgin Mary—your King and guide, and the unconquered defender of His Church!”

Meanwhile the Jerusalemites approached Ernald’s castle, and their banners appeared to the Turks. King Baldwin and the men of Joppa adored the Lord’s holy Cross; carrying it with them, they immediately rushed out under arms and began terribly striking the unarmed men. When the foreigners saw war arising against them from both sides, unprepared and without counsel, they took flight in the terror sent by God and, like the army of Holofernes, suffered an equal disaster. King Baldwin and the Christians pursued the heathen as far as Ascalon; cutting down all they could, they made a great slaughter and rescued every captive whom the enemy were dragging bound. Yet those of higher rank whom they had sent ahead to Ascalon were lost; and rumour-bearers gave us no certain information concerning them except concerning Harpin. Thus the Christians, after many anguishes, triumphed in Christ’s name and returned to Jerusalem with much spoil from the Gentiles, joyfully giving thanks to God the victor. Then they restored Ramla to a better condition than it had been before, and devoutly renewed in the Lord’s name the episcopal see with suitable revenues. I do not know how to record on paper the certain number of those slain, for I was not present. But those who were present took care not to count, but to kill; and on their return they stripped the slain of their spoils.

## XX. Harpin of Bourges is captured by the Saracens.

Harpin of Bourges was taken captive to Babylon, where he was held for many days in the prison of the Admirable One. Remembering the martyrs who endured innumerable contests even unto death for Christ’s name, he often invoked Him; strengthened by Him and restored to his former freedom, he rendered Him devout thanks. The manner of his liberation was as follows.

Merchants from Byzantium came to Babylon with merchandise of many kinds. There, as the laws of nations required, they paid the established customs dues to the officials of the state and stayed for a considerable time. Since they were Christians and abounded in riches, they frequented Christ’s churches, visited the dwellings of poor Christians, and called upon Christians in chains. Harpin accordingly had a conversation with them, entrusted an embassy to them, and sent this message to Emperor Alexius:

“Harpin of Bourges, your servant, has for a long time groaned in grievous affliction in a Babylonian prison, and humbly beseeches the magnificence of your imperial majesty to pity and assist him, and, by an order directed to the Admirable One on his behalf, rescue him from the miseries of imprisonment.”

Hearing this, the emperor compassionately pitied the noble Frenchman and immediately commanded the Admirable One to restore Harpin to him at once; otherwise, he would order all Babylonian merchants and paid agents throughout the Constantinopolitan Empire to be seized. Frightened by an order backed by such indignation, the Admirable One immediately released Harpin from his bonds. Keeping him with him for several days, he showed him certain extraordinary things; finally, honouring him with precious ornaments and other gifts, he sent him to the emperor. Thus released, Harpin came to the emperor at Constantinople, thanked him for his effective assistance, and afterwards, having received rewards from him, returned to Gaul.

Meanwhile he went to Pope Paschal, reported to him his arduous fortunes and struggles, and carefully sought his counsel for the ordering of his life. The wise father, hearing of the athlete’s harsh labours, said:

“One must take the greatest care that no one, washed and clean from the baths and clothed in snowy or silken garments, should walk along a muddy road at the time of dark night, lest perhaps he fall into the mire and, foully stained, blush before those who see him. My son, consider yourself through this image and turn this example to your own correction. You have been cleansed through penitence and confession; through arduous pilgrimage and the struggles of martyrdom, you have been crowned with the emblems of virtues. In the miseries of prison you made satisfaction to God for your offences; in suffering you learned patience, chastity, and other virtues. The present life is a grim night, wholly covered by the darkness of ignorance: ‘A man does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred’ (Ecclesiastes 9:1), nor can he foresee what the coming day will bring him. Secular life is a muddy road, which you must avoid with all your strength, lest you be defiled and lose the crown of sufferings in which you glory. Take care, then, that you are not like ‘a dog returned to his own vomit, and a washed sow to wallowing in the mire’ (2 Peter 2:24). Never again bear arms against Christians; but, as a true poor man of Christ, despise worldly pride. Thus, an imitator of Christ’s footsteps, by works of righteousness rejecting your own will in hope of eternal recompense, you will happily attain the prize of the heavenly calling with the faithful in Abraham’s bosom.”

Harpin therefore received the pope’s blessing and, with his permission, made for Gaul. There he was honourably received by his own people but did not remain with them long. For, following the pope’s counsel—or rather Christ’s—he left the world, went to Cluny, became a monk, and persevered in God’s service until death.

## XXI. Bohemond is seized by the Saracens. Melaz, daughter of Prince Dalimannus, releases him from prison by subtle contrivance.

At about this time another most grievous event befell the Christians in Syria. The famous duke Bohemond led an expedition against the Turks. Dalimannus unexpectedly fell upon him with an immense multitude, killed many, and seized Bohemond, together with Richard of the Principate and some other noble and most worthy men; he kept them for a long time chained in prison. But Tancred, prince of the army, heard of the misfortune of his lord and kinsman and was grieved, yet did not turn in womanish fashion to fruitless tears or lamentations. Rather, from every surrounding province he summoned the whole military force of the faithful, fortified Antioch and all its surrounding villages and towns with careful guards, and, as long as the duke remained in chains, defended them irreproachably against every assault of the enemy—indeed, he nobly enlarged their frontiers.

When Emperor Alexius learned that Bohemond had fallen into Turkish hands, he rejoiced and sent envoys to Dalimannus with many gifts, earnestly begging him to accept a very great ransom for Bohemond and, upon receiving one hundred thousand *philippei*, to hand him over to him. He did this not in order to free the imprisoned duke and restore him to his former liberty for the protection of Christendom, but to keep him forever confined in his own chains. For he deeply regretted that Bohemond had taken Antioch from him. It is certain that that metropolis belonged to the Constantinopolitan Empire; but it had been taken away from the emperor by Turkish violence fourteen years before the men from beyond the Alps, after capturing the city, killed Cassianus. The emperor had always asserted his claim, but was prevented from fulfilling his desires by the vigorous resistance of the Normans. He made many attempts and laboured fruitlessly in many ways, by entreaty and payment among pagans and Christians; for, when his efforts were frustrated, the city remained with its conquerors—those, namely, who had won it by extraordinary courage after defeating the Hagarenes, and had marvellously defended what they had gained by God’s power. Dalimannus, however, rejected the emperor’s request and resolved to keep Bohemond, whom the Turks called “the Little God of the Christians,” in chains forever; he regarded this as a supreme honour to his law, not as a trifling matter.

A certain Greek held the patriarchate of Antioch during the time of the Turks, and he was intractable toward the victorious Normans. For after they had obtained the principality, they determined to order clergy and people according to Latin rites; the Pelasgians, following their ancient customs, rashly judged this very unsuitable. But when Bohemond was captured, a rumour arose among the people that this prelate was preparing to betray Antioch to the emperor. When he learned that such a rumour was current about him, he was exceedingly angry and—whether indignantly, I do not know, through the innocence of a clear conscience, or driven by accusation and fear of a wicked offence—left his bishopric and withdrew into the wilderness. He determined never to return to those whose customs he abhorred. The Norman rulers of the city rejoiced at the Pelasgian’s departure; they informed the captive Bohemond of the entire course of events and asked his advice concerning the appointment of a patriarch. He ordered Bernard the Provençal—formerly chaplain of Aimar, bishop of Le Puy, and especially commended to him by that bishop, when dying, as a special friend to a special friend—to be transferred from the bishopric of Mamistra to the patriarchate of Antioch. Accordingly, by the duke’s order, clergy and people elected Bernard and placed the pontiff in the chair of Saint Peter the Apostle. He was indeed endowed with learned skill; but after he became known to those subject to him, he became hated, because he was avaricious and, through the natural harshness of the Gothic people from which he sprang, excessively austere. He presided over God’s Church for many days and occupied the office of rule until decrepit old age. In his time, as has been said and will be told more clearly still, the storm of many tribulations thundered forth.

Throughout the whole world it was heard that Bohemond had been ensnared in pagan chains. All Christians mourned him, and even pagans honoured him in prison. The whole Church prayed to God for him, that He would graciously save him from the hands of his enemies. But gracious God, who created all things, knows both how to chastise His servants with tribulations for the sins of human frailty and how marvellously to help those who humbly invoke Him in supplication, aiding them even through their enemies better than they hope. Abraham and Joseph experienced this under Pharaoh among the Egyptians; Tobias and Raguel under Shalmaneser, Sennacherib, and Asarhaddon among the Assyrians; Daniel and the three youths, with other children of the Exile, under Nebuchadnezzar and Evil-merodach among the Chaldaeans; Ezra, Nehemiah, and Mordecai with his niece Esther under Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes among Persians and Medes. The apostles also, and other holy preachers, experienced it happily: when they suddenly came into foreign lands of barbarians, they were first considered contemptible, as strangers and beggars; shortly afterwards, as signs shone forth and tongues thundered, they appeared wondrous, and brought the inhabitants, previously untamed, under the yoke of the sacred law and trained them in every good thing. Thus He who said, “My Father works until now, and I work” (John 5:17), recently visited in prison His athletes, of whom I write for the knowledge of posterity because of the wondrous divine works, and richly gladdened them with the honey-sweet nectar of His goodness. For earth-dwellers are scourged with the lashes of affliction for the offences of human frailty, and, afflicted by the heavenly rod, are compelled tearfully to beseech the Creator’s mercy. But God our King, who saves those hoping in Him, powerfully heard the prayers of His bride, the Church, and helped the captive duke and his companions through the ingenuity and aid of his enemy’s daughter—as He once helped the thirsty people in Bethulia through the strength of Judith, the bold widow, when the proud throat of Holofernes had been cut.

Melaz, daughter of Prince Dalimannus, was beautiful, very wise, and possessed great authority throughout her father’s household, much wealth, and many servants for her attendance. Hearing of the valour of the Franks, she loved them ardently and sought their acquaintance so eagerly that, after lavishly paying their guards, she frequently descended to the prison. There she subtly conversed with the captives about the Christian faith and true religion, investigating it through shrewd discussion, sometimes with deep sighs. She preferred the sweetness of their affection to all love for her parents; and she supplied them abundantly with everything needed for food and clothing. Her father, occupied with many other affairs, either did not know these things or perhaps, considering it an approved act of frugality in his beloved child, did not concern himself with them.

After two years, a war more than civil arose between brothers. Solimannus, swollen with excessive ferocity, rose against Dalimannus, gathered an immense multitude of armed men, entered the borders of his brother’s principality, and insolently challenged his brother to battle. Stirred by such an attack, Dalimannus procured support for himself from every quarter. He too, elated by the many trophies he had won hitherto, thirsted for bloody conflict and, when the hour of battle came, stood ready on the field with his legions. Meanwhile Melaz spoke privately with the Christians and addressed them thus:

“For long I have heard many praising the military prowess of the Franks. Now, in my father’s pressing need, I would like to test it, so that sight’s experience may prove what hearing approves.”

Bohemond replied: “Fortunate and honourable lady, if it pleases your exalted highness to allow us to go forth armed onto the field of war, we shall without doubt openly display Frankish blows of sword and lance and show you, before your eyes, our strength against your enemies.”

The girl said: “Promise me, by the faith in which you are Christians, that in this affair which we are arranging you will do everything according to my counsel and will presume to do nothing contrary to my command. Confirm this promise to me by your faith, and afterwards I shall not delay in opening to you the secret of my heart.”

Bohemond was the first to promise on his faith what she asked; all the others followed him, pledging what the girl commanded. Then she said, dancing for joy: “Now I am secure concerning you, because, as I believe, you are honourable men and will in no way violate your pledged faith. Aid my father, who is now to fight in the field, and readily display your worth to support him. And if victory falls to you—as may it indeed happen!—do not pursue the fleeing enemy. Return here quickly under arms, and do not lay down your weapons until I order you. Meanwhile I shall make all the guards descend from the lofty station of the tower to the lower gates and stand with me in the courtyard, as though awaiting you. When you return and I order the guards to bind you in your accustomed chains, lay your strong hands manfully upon them, seize them all without delay, and shut them up in prison as substitutes for yourselves. On seeing this, I shall flee from you as from deadly wolves. You, however, take possession of the very strong citadel and guard it carefully until you make a suitable peace with my father. The citadel has lofty gates through which you will be able to descend by stone steps into the palace and gain possession of all my father’s treasures and dwellings. But if my father, angry at these offences, wishes to punish me, I beg you, friends whom I love as my own heart, come quickly to my aid.”

## XXII. Continuation.

Having said this, she armed the knights and immediately sent them out. She had previously deceived and bribed the guards of the citadel, and, having instructed them in the matter, had said among other things: “Great fear for my father troubles me, for a multitude from many nations is arrayed to fight against him. But because he is a high-minded warrior, he has disdained to ask help from captives. Yet know that he has entrusted me with the authority to arm Christians and send them to battle in support of our forces. If they conquer the enemy bands, the honour and advantage will be ours. But if they fall and perish by the sword of the enemy, we shall feel no grief over the downfall of foreigners, whose customs and ceremonies the entire race of Hagarenes abhors.”

Hearing this, they gladly assented and greatly praised the prudent foresight of the maiden. She immediately released the captives, drew them from the prison-house, and sent them armed to battle. They found the fighting already fierce and confidently shouted the Norman cry: “God, help!” As they cried out and struck terrible blows, Solimannus’s formations wavered. There were some Christians in his army; when they recognized the famous leader Bohemond, they rejoiced, abandoned Solimannus, and joined the Catholics.

Marciban, Solimannus’s proud young son, heard that Bohemond was there and sought him in battle, calling him aloud by name; he desired to fight him in single combat. At last they met face to face before Dalimannus and struck one another fiercely. But the warlike Norman threw down the Turk, drew his sword, and cut off his head. Dalimannus cried, “Spare him, spare him! He is my nephew.” When the Christian champion learned the fact, sadness of face covered joy of heart, and he replied mockingly: “Forgive me, lord, for what I did in ignorance. I thought him not your nephew but an enemy, whose life I extinguished in order to please you.”

After great slaughter on both sides, Solimannus’s army was crushed; the hostile battle-line pursued it in flight throughout the day. But the Christians, as had been agreed, immediately returned and found their lady waiting with the archers before the tower. At once she said to the guards: “The Franks are undoubtedly honourable men and have kept their pledged word perfectly. Go out to meet them; receive their weapons from them and bring them back to their former place, until my father comes and gives them the rewards due to their military service.”

The Turks were departing to obey the girl’s commands, but the Franks enclosed them among themselves, cautiously barred the gates with bolts, and took possession of all the inner chambers of the tower without public tumult. Without shedding blood, they attained their object. For the city was empty of fighting men because they had gone out to battle; only women with infants remained, anxiously guarding the houses. The prison stood in the very strong citadel, and there a supply of rich treasure, varied household furnishings, and abundant wealth was kept; the chief palace was joined to the same tower.

On the following night, Melaz brought the Christians down from the citadel into the palace, showed them every chamber and hidden inner room, and instructed them what they ought to do when Dalimannus arrived. On the next day the victor returned with his satraps, tribunes, and nobles. His daughter met him, dancing with companions of her own age: “Hail,” she said, “glorious conqueror!” [Col. 0779B] But he answered furiously: “Be silent, most vile harlot. I do not care for your feigned greetings; I count your deceitful flatteries as nothing. By the divine lineage of Muhammad, who gave me victory, tomorrow I shall have you perish with your lovers. For, to my disgrace, you gave arms to my enemies; with them, as a most wicked traitress, you shall be burned in devouring flames.”

He did not yet know that his archers were confined in the darkness of the prison, while the Franks, standing proudly on a higher seat, rejoiced in freedom and, with Christ’s help, planned rebellion against him. Trembling and bloodless with fear, the girl fled from the raging man’s presence and, sorrowful and terrified, sought the hiding-places of her chamber.

After some hours, when the furious prince was seated in judgment and had with him only the chief [Col. 0779C] magnates—for the remaining populace, squires, and other retainers were dispersed through their lodgings, preparing their horses, arms, and other appropriate equipment—he ordered certain men to go into the chamber and bring before him the reckless traitress. When she had been summoned and stood before the raging tyrant, hearing alone and without assistance his terrible threats together with insults, Bohemond looked down through a window from the tower; and, seeing his deliverer standing abandoned for judgment, he grieved.
