“Behold,” he said, “our helper is in distress. Now we must go out from here and support her with all our strength.”

At once they went down step by step from the citadel into the hall. Armed, they surrounded Dalimannus [Col. 0779D] and all his tribunes and companions, blocked the doors of the house, and occupied every defensive position around it. All alike became anxious and uncertain what they should do. The Turks, with the doors barred, could turn nowhere; unarmed and few, they could not resist in battle men superior to them in numbers and weapons. The Christians could then have cut down all the heathen; but, because of the oath which they had made to the girl, they did not dare, without her command, to strike or injure anyone in any way. Therefore all looked toward her and waited to learn what she would order, taking care not to violate their pledged faith.

At last Melaz, now more confident, began to laugh, and, presiding among the Franks as though a lady, said to Dalimannus [Col. 0780A]:

“Dear father, you are unjustly angry with me; with excessive threats you frighten me and revile me for the salutary assistance which, consulting for your welfare, I cleverly provided in great kindness. For while the Franks struck in battle, your men took heart and the enemy quickly faltered. Consider how faithful the Christians are. They loyally assisted you in battle, and while they fought, the enemy turned their backs. They had ample opportunity to depart, as is clear even to the bleary-eyed; yet, unwilling to leave you without a farewell, they returned of their own accord and confidently demand from your generosity the rewards of their military service. Already they have their hands upon the sword-hilts; already, if they wish, they can slaughter us all. They already possess the tower, the palace, and all your wealth that is in them; and your townsmen, held in bonds, do not dare [Col. 0780B] murmur against them. In these circumstances, father, consider what must be done, and seek sound advice from the counsellors who are present.”

After she had spoken thus, the lady presided over the Christian party. Dalimannus, however, having withdrawn apart, sought counsel with his men. Then, taking his seat again, he said: “First, daughter, we wish to hear your counsel.”

She replied: “I shall not delay to state what I believe useful. Make peace with the Christians, and let there be an inviolable treaty between you for as long as you live. Release all their captives who are in the lands under your rule, and let them likewise restore all those of your people who are in their power. Grant to Bohemond and his fellow-soldiers, through whose fortunate aid you obtained victory, rewards worthy of their glorious service. Know this further [Col. 0780C]: I am a Christian, and I wish to be reborn according to the sacrament of the Christian law; nor shall I remain here with you any longer. For the law of the Christians is holy and honourable, whereas your law is full of vanities and polluted by every impurity.”

Hearing this, the Turks were greatly angered; with grim looks and stern gestures they showed themselves fierce. But, God hindering them, they were unable to carry into action the malice of their profane hearts.

While they discussed what should be done, Melaz summoned the Christians apart and said: “Come, worthy soldiers, proved in many necessities and distresses, who have voluntarily come here from distant lands and, enduring many labours and [Col. 0780D] dangers manfully, have escaped them: act manfully in the name of your God, whom you declare omnipotent. Now courage and arms are needed, so that you may laudably complete what you have bravely begun. My father is exceedingly angry and with all his efforts plots destruction for us with his followers. Until now you have kept excellently the stipulated condition imposed upon me. From henceforth I release you from the promise confirmed by your oath. Fortify now the citadel, the palace, the wall round about, and the lesser and greater *zetas* [probably defensive enclosures]; search carefully and guard the entrances, lest anyone go out or come in without your inspection. For if my father goes out from here, he will gather all the surrounding nations and force you, by a cruel siege, into shameful surrender or destruction. Therefore shut him and all his men together in a single chamber, [Col. 0781A] and there compel all of them to peace with necessary severity; but, as far as you can, restrain your hands from the shedding of blood. I entrust the oversight and direction of these matters to you, Lord Bohemond, since you have been tested in many things, and the praise of your prudence and judgment is throughout the world. Henceforth I shall be your inseparable sister, and in the faith of the Lord Jesus Christ I shall endure with you things both joyful and sad.”

Bohemond, rejoicing, therefore thrust Dalimannus and all his men by force into a certain chamber, and assigned armed guards to watch that lodging. He then stationed other soldiers in different places, instructed each man what he ought to do, and thus governed the principal palace, with all who were within it, for nearly fifteen days. He allowed their wives, female attendants, and unarmed eunuchs to enter, and to supply them with an adequate provision of food and other necessities. Dalimannus groaned deeply because his own house had become a prison for him and his daughter a censor, sternly restraining him. Hence he fiercely cursed Muhammad, his god, and execrably condemned all his friends, servants, and fellow-soldiers, who allowed him, in the midst of his own kingdom, to be miserably handled by a few captives and foreigners. The enclosed barons persuaded him to make peace with the Christians, so that he might at least be permitted to live a little longer. At last his hardness was softened by fear. Speaking with Bohemond, he sought peace, agreed that Bohemond and all his men should depart freely, released from captivity all captives who groaned under his dominion, and promised him his daughter also.

When cunning Melaz heard this, she replied to the reporting Bohemond: “All words are easily spoken, but not all always seem credible. Receive my father’s pleasing but ambiguous promises gladly; nevertheless, keep watchfully what you hold until you triumph, secured by the firm assurance of certain safety. Let well-known messengers from both sides be sent to Antioch, and let an armed troop of your soldiers be brought, escorted honourably by whom you may be conducted without deceit into your own territory and escape the treacherous deception of every enemy.”

This counsel pleased everyone. Richard of the Principate and Sarcis of Mesopotamia [Col. 0781D] were therefore sent to Antioch, and, to the rejoicing Antiochenes, explained the outcome of events. Then Tancred, commander of the army, immediately sent collectors and gathered soldiers and captive pagans; he assigned the assembled men to the aforesaid barons to conduct them. Then the daughter of Cassian, admiral of Antioch, was restored, having been brought out of the Christians’ prison with much weeping. Asked why she wept so, she answered that she wept because she would not be eating the excellent pork which Christians use. For the Turks and many other Saracen peoples abhor swine’s flesh, although they eagerly devour the flesh of dogs and wolves. Thus they are proved to lack every law of Moses [Col. 0782A] and Christ, and to adhere neither to Jews nor to Christians.

### XXIII. Melaz becomes a Christian and is united in marriage with Roger, son of Richard of the Principate, kinsman of Bohemond

Meanwhile Bohemond spoke frequently with Dalimannus and, being wise and moderate, treated him courteously. For the relief of many whom that same tyrant was able greatly to oppress, he suitably flattered him. By services and sweet words he softened both him and all who were with him, and by the diligence of his modest conduct drew them into affection for himself. Gradually the provincial tribunes and nobles came to know the new ruler and eagerly sought to observe the foreign prince, the master of their native prince; [Col. 0782B] conversing with their lord by his permission, they praised him highly. They urged him, as though he were their natural lord, to promote the public good, exhorted him in every way to seek the friendship of so great a leader, and frequently recalled that saying of the comic poet:

> …Since what you want cannot be done,  
> Want what can be done…  
> (Terence, *Andria*, II.1.)

They added this also: “We were grievously deceived by the victory lately won, because we had the opponents of our law as effective helpers in the slaughter of our people, and wickedly and foolishly rejoiced in our common loss. Behold, accursed Mahomet, our god, has utterly abandoned us and has fallen before the God of the Christians, stripped of all strength! Behold, in a wondrous way, Christ crucified—whom they declare almighty, and rightly so, as all their enemies experience and suffer to their harm—has unexpectedly released through your daughter those whom you believed held fast in chains in prison and intended to confine for all time without release. He has glorified them, armed in war, with notable trophies, and has stained their swords with the blood of our brothers and nephews. Moreover, he has delivered to them the chief stronghold, where all your treasures are, and has shut you and the principal nobles of your kingdom beneath their hands, reducing you, without battle, to captivity in your own palace, groaning like helpless slave-women. We cannot approach you from outside without the consent of the foreigners, [Col. 0782D] nor can we bring you any aid. We do not dare rise against them in a body, because they would immediately avenge their wrath upon you. Even if the great king of the Persians, the sultan, came with all his power and strove to storm this fortification, such is the prowess of the Franks and so great the strength of the stronghold that they would dare resist him there and, before they were taken, inflict immense losses upon our people. It is better, therefore, to pacify an enemy by affection than to provoke him by rashness to deadly fury.”

Dalimannus accordingly accepted counsels of this kind. Having gained the friendship of the vigorous leader, he now freely gave orders in his own house concerning their common advantage, and from his treasures voluntarily distributed generous gifts to the Christians. He also ordered all captives throughout his territory to be released. They were earnestly sought, brought in when found, well clothed by Dalimannus, and handed over to Bohemond. He immediately united them with their countrymen and assigned them to various offices, to increase and protect their companions, lest they should be deceived by any malicious stratagem of the pagans.

Richard and Sarcis, their embassy completed, returned after fifteen days and brought a large Christian force. Dalimannus ordered them all to be received with great honour, abundant provisions to be prepared for them according to their native customs, and everything necessary to be supplied in plenty. Then Bohemond [Col. 0783B] and Dalimannus confirmed perpetual peace between themselves and prepared for three days an equipment sufficient for them in all respects. Thereupon Bohemond, Richard, and their fellow-captives joyfully emerged from captivity and, like Zerubbabel and Nehemiah, blessed the Lord God of Israel.

Dalimannus and his nobles accompanied them for some distance, rejoicing because they too had been released from confinement—yet deceitfully, since along the way they plotted by every means to injure the Christians. But, God protecting His own, they could not do so. For they feared these faithful men, who therefore proceeded armed and as if prepared for battle; moreover, they carefully retained hostages for security until they reached the safe places which they had determined upon. [Col. 0783C] At last Dalimannus asked leave from his allies to return as a friend; having received it, he returned sorrowful because he had been unable to harm them by any stratagem on the road.

Prudent Melaz left her father’s house with her female attendants, eunuchs, and noble household, and with all her *progenies* [Note: [Col. 0783D] *Progenies*, that is, household or house.] willingly and devoutly joined herself to the worshippers of Christ, just as Bithia, Pharaoh’s daughter, beneficially accompanied Moses and the Hebrews when the Egyptians perished. The Antiochenes joyfully came out to meet those whom they had long desired to see, and the clergy and all the people faithfully blessed King Adonai, who saves all who hope in Him. Bohemond then sent Richard, his companion in captivity, to Gaul, and through him sent silver fetters to Saint Leonard the confessor [Col. 0783D] and devoutly gave thanks for his deliverance.

After noble Melaz had been reborn by holy baptism in the Catholic Church, Bohemond addressed her thus at a suitable time in an assembly of nobles [Col. 0784A]:

“Noble maiden, while still a pagan you wonderfully came to our aid unexpectedly; you wisely preferred the Lord Jesus to all your kindred, kindly cherished Him in us, who are His members and servants, and thereby incurred your father’s anger almost to the danger of death. Choose from among us whichever husband you wish in Christ’s name. It is not right that we should in any degree resist your just requests, since, because of your preceding merits, we are deeply indebted to you. First listen now to my counsel, which, sweet friend, I hope will be profitable to you.

“I confess that your father gave you to me; but I desire to provide for you more advantageously. Hear carefully why. From my youth I have been a restless man, living amid labours; I have endured many severe things and fear that I shall yet endure more severe ones. For I have conflict with the emperor and with pagans on every side. Besides, when I was in prison I made a vow to the Lord that, if I were released from the bonds of the heathen, I would go to Saint Leonard, who is in Aquitaine. From sincere affection I offer you these excuses, because I do not wish to see you in any way abandoned more than I would my own daughter or sister, nor to enter a marriage-bond of which you would shortly repent. What joy or pleasure could there be for you in our union, when immediately after the wedding I must set out over sea and land upon an immense journey and travel abroad to a distant region, near the ends of the earth? With these matters considered, lady, choose what is better from among many possibilities. Behold Roger, offspring of Prince Richard [Col. 0784C] and my cousin: he is younger than I, outstanding in beauty, and my equal in nobility, wealth, and power. I commend him for you to have as husband, and desire that you may live with him for a long time.”

All those present approved the wise leader’s advice. The prudent maiden readily accepted the agreement of so many great men. Roger therefore honourably betrothed the girl with joy and celebrated the wedding with great applause and dancing throughout all Antioch; at it Bohemond, as steward, served together with the chief men of the land. This Roger, six years later, after the deaths of Bohemond and Tancred, obtained the principality of Antioch; two years thereafter, on the field of Sarmatan, he was killed by the Persian Amirgazis with seven thousand Christians.

[Col. 0784D] I have already said very much concerning the changes of temporal affairs and the fortunes of men; and, if life accompanies me, much still remains to be said in what follows. Here this book of the *Ecclesiastical History* ends; let some little rest now be granted to me, who am weary!

## Summary of Book Eleven

[Col. 0785]

I. Prologue. Philosophical maxims.  
II. Various events in England and Normandy under King Henry and Duke Robert.  
III. Disputes and wars between King Henry and Robert of Bellême. This count is compelled to submit to the victor.  
IV. Robert of Bellême crosses into Normandy and commits many evils there. He rises against Duke Robert. On the deaths of certain men.  
V. Ivo, bishop of Chartres. The offspring of Countess Adela of Chartres. Various events in England and Normandy.  
VI. King Magnus of the Norwegians is killed on campaign.  
VII. Louis of France, son of King Philip, crosses over into England. Bertrada, his stepmother, plots against him. King Henry crosses into Normandy and visits Duke Robert, his brother.  
VIII. Troubles of the Church. Serlo, bishop of Séez, urges King Henry and his nobles to have their beards and hair cut.  
IX. Bohemond, duke of Antioch, comes into France. Various events. King Henry and his brother Robert labour unsuccessfully to make peace.  
X. Discord between the two brothers: by what evil men it is stirred up. King Henry joins battle with Duke Robert, defeats and captures him at Tinchebray.  
XI. Robert of Bellême again attempts to stir the Normans against King Henry.  
XII. Bohemond, aided by Robert of Montfort and many other barons, undertakes an expedition against the emperor of Constantinople. Death of Mark Bohemond. Antioch is defended by Baldwin against the Saracens.  
XIII. King Baldwin is captured by the Saracens.  
XIV. Particular adventures of Baldwin and certain other knights.  
XV. Events in the principality of Antioch.  
XVI. Events in Normandy and elsewhere. William of Ros, abbot of Fécamp. Roger of Bayeux succeeds him. John, archdeacon of Séez. On the deaths of certain persons.  
XVII. Various events. Abbots and priors distinguished for piety.  
XVIII. Philip I, king of the Franks, dies. His son Louis succeeds to the kingdom. The count of Beaumont and the lord of Montmorency invade the lands of Saint-Denis. King Louis acts vigorously against the rebellious barons.  
XIX. King Henry keeps his brother Robert captive. Various events. Plague and other calamities rage in certain regions of Gaul.  
XX. Anselm of Canterbury, Hugh of Cluny, William archbishop of Rouen, and several other illustrious prelates and doctors die.  
XXI. King Henry visits the monastery of Saint-Evroult. Wars between the peoples of the kings of France and England. The two kings meet and make a treaty.

# Book Eleven

## I. Prologue. Philosophical Maxims

[Col. 0785A]

Gracious God of Hosts, mighty King governing all things,  
Preserve Thy creature, O deity reigning through the ages.  
Crush the power of Satan, who rages continually against Thee  
While everywhere he plots to afflict Thy servants.  
Look kindly, Maker of the world, I pray, upon my petitions.  
I worship Thee, seek Thee, and rightly labour to please Thee.  
Now, an old man, I write the deeds of pontiffs and kings;  
At sixty years of age I make them known to the young.  
For such labour I ask no payment from them,  
But offer it freely, content with the love of my brethren.  
If new signs clearly occurred in these days,  
I would strive truthfully to include them in my work.  
I believe that they would be more welcome to those now living and to posterity,  
More profitable to me, and more pleasing to others,  
[Col. 0785B] than uselessly investigating or generously recounting  
Earthly excursions and perishable pedigrees.  
While I breathe, I should wish to write illustrious and wondrous things,  
Filling my parchment with marvels in Christ’s name.  
I love the praises of Him beneath whom the whole world lies subject,

[Col. 0786A]

Who has power gently to remove from us every disease.  
We are compelled to speak of the dark things which we see or endure;  
we recount the unstable actions of changeable men.  
For worldly love draws the host of men downward,  
and the file of justice does not polish away their rust.  
Prone to evil, they devise earthly things;  
they despise heavenly things and do not behold them, bent as they are.  
Behold, sinners bear deadly burdens!  
The bright mighty deeds of saints justly cease.  
Transgressors who violate the law  
deserve the punishments of heavenly wrath, not signs.  
Very many things can be related concerning lawsuits and wars,  
which the savage passion for possessing inflicts upon men too grievously.  
Murders, incest, and a thousand crimes may be recorded,  
[Col. 0786B] if learned men deign to speak of shameful matters.  
The foolish man is troubled in vain and loses his leisure,  
but no wise man is eager to squander his time.  
For he wastes time who publishes a useless poem,  
and the labour itself is lost that yields no benefit.

[Col. 0787A]

But the elect, fervent for good things, run diligently;  
watchful, they eagerly press on toward praiseworthy study.  
Those who voluntarily undertake what must be borne need not be compelled—  
those who gather the sheaves of harvest and carry them into barns.  
A spirited horse that goes willingly enough needs no spur,  
but must be governed by a moderate rein lest it stumble.  
A hard rider urges a horse with sharp spurs  
and strikes it with frequent lashes to make it run.  
The law is like the Church’s kindly teachers:  
by their admonitions they spur the slow and restrain the swift.  
The evil beast bearing ten horns now rules;  
the savage people everywhere are stained with the leprosy of crimes.  
The Lord showed Behemoth to Job as a type;  
the crafty devil rages wickedly in this world.  
Raging Erinnys ranges over the earthborn,  
[Col. 0787B] and every day thrusts her own into the depths of Erebus.  
Amphisilena plays with and deceives mortals,  
and by deceiving them takes away the delights of Paradise.  
Alas! the deadly serpent wickedly infuses its poison into them,  
makes them mad, and causes them to destroy one another.  
The foolish undergo sicknesses and plagues, and the wicked,  
moreover, wickedly add the worst evils to themselves.  
We see human misfortunes and wretched ruins,  
from which a discerning author can fill parchment skins.  
If he wishes to pour forth idle words upon diverse subjects,  
he finds abundant material amid bitter things.  
In divinely accomplished writings, the envious enemy of humankind  
is called by many names:  
lion, wolf, dragon, partridge, basilisk,  
[Col. 0787C] kite, boar, fox, dog, bear, leech, horned viper,  
and fierce snake, when he lies in wait for us  
and by deceit or force plots destruction for the foolish.  
A thousand other names are plain to ingenious readers,  
according to the various arts which the enemy employs.  
He defiles countless people with vices and often slaughters them.  
Alas for sorrow! mighty hosts commonly perish.  
Holy King, rescue us, good Jesus, supreme priest,  
lest the ancient serpent infect us with the condemned.  
But draw us, cleansed from vices, out of the sea of the world,  
and mercifully associate us with the saints in the heavenly court. Amen.

## II. Various Events in England and Normandy under King Henry and Duke Robert

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1102, in the ninth indiction, Henry, king of the English, having made peace with his brother Robert [Col. 0787D], was established in his kingdom and gradually attempted to take vengeance upon the traitors who had wickedly deserted him in his time of need. For he summoned Robert called Malet, Ivo of Grandmesnil, Robert of Pontefract, son of Ilbert de Lacy, and Robert of Bellême, more powerful than all of them, as well as many others, to his court; not all together but separately and at different times, he charged them with many kinds of breach of faith. Some of those unable to clear themselves of the crime alleged he condemned to heavy fines; others, whom he regarded as more suspect, he disinherited beyond recovery and compelled into exile.

In the following year [1103], William de Warenne [Col. 0788A] went sorrowfully to Robert, duke of Normandy, and described the great loss he had suffered through him: he had lost the county of Surrey, which yielded him a thousand pounds of silver each year. He therefore asserted that it was proper for the duke to make peace with his brother the king and, through his favour, recover his former honour. The duke readily accepted such words and crossed into England.

On hearing this, the king was angry and spoke thus to his followers and sworn companions: “What ought I to do with my enemies, who have dared, without my safe-conduct, to rush upon me and invade the boundaries of my kingdom?” His men gave the king differing answers. He sent private retainers to meet his brother and through them clearly made known his will.

Then the unbridled duke learned through secret embassies [Col. 0788B] that he had entered the confines of England without consultation, and that unless he adopted prudent and wise counsel, he would be enclosed within the island’s bounds and unable to return home as he pleased. Yet by order of the crafty king he was honourably brought in with his fellow-knights; and, through their shrewd counsel, the matter was concealed, lest foreigners perceive any bitterness between the brothers. The frightened duke therefore concealed his fear beneath feigned cheerfulness, while the king likewise hid his inward rage under a cheerful face.

Among other matters the king reproached the duke for violating the treaty: he had as yet exacted no vengeance on public traitors, imposed no princely discipline of severity upon the unruly, and in that same year had received Robert of Bellême amicably in Normandy and granted him his father’s dominions—namely the castle of Argentan, the bishopric of Séez, and the forest of Gouffern. For that aforesaid butcher had crossed into Normandy and acquired the county of Ponthieu for William Talvas, because Guy, count of Abbeville, his father-in-law, had died. At last the duke, frightened by such reproofs, humbly promised to amend everything. At the queen’s industrious intercession, he also granted him a fixed payment of three thousand pounds. The appeased king then confirmed friendship with him, renewed their former treaty, and restored the county of Surrey to William de Warenne. After William recovered the paternal right which he had foolishly lost, he remained faithfully attached to the king for the thirty-three years during which they lived together, chastened to good purpose, and flourished as one of the king’s chief and intimate friends.

Duke Robert then returned to Normandy and became more contemptible to his men than he had been before. In this expedition he gained for himself nothing but fear, labour, and disgrace. But the king, flourishing in prosperity in all things, was greatly exalted; his fame flying far and wide, he was named among the greatest kings throughout the four quarters of the world. No king in the realm of Albion was more powerful than he, none wealthier in extent of lands within the island, and none happier in abundance of everything available to mortals. Our narrative, if life accompanies us and God helps, will demonstrate this plainly in what follows. [Col. 0789A] By wisdom or force he subdued all his enemies to himself, and rewarded those serving him with wealth and honours. Thus he cast down many notable men from the lofty summit of power because of their rashness, condemning them to irrecoverable loss of their hereditary right. Conversely, he ennobled men of low birth who served him favourably; he raised them, so to speak, from the dust, and, granting them ample resources, exalted them above counts and illustrious townsmen.

Of this Geoffrey de Clinton, Ralph Basset, Hugh of Buckland, Cuillegrip, Rainer of Bada, William Trossebot, Haimo of Falaise, Guigan Algazo, Robert de Bostare, and many others are witnesses for me: having amassed wealth [Col. 0789B] and built houses surpassing all that their fathers possessed, they themselves surpassed those fathers—men who had often been oppressed by those same persons on false or unjust pretexts. The king ennobled these and many others whom it would be tiresome to name one by one; though they were of the lowest stock, he raised them from low estate by royal authority, set them on the heights of power, and made them formidable even to the distinguished princes of the kingdom.

But as he was a magnificent rewarder of the faithful, so he was an implacable enemy to the unfaithful, and scarcely pardoned established offences without punishment in body, honour, or money. Those who died in his chains experienced this lamentably; they could not be redeemed by kinship, nobility of birth, or payment of money. He prosecuted Robert of Pontefract [Col. 0789C] and Robert Malet in lawsuits, stripped them of their honours, and drove them into exile. He also burdened Ivo—because he had begun war in England and burned the fields of his neighbours by fire, a crime unusual in that region and not expiated without severe punishment—with the payment of an enormous sum. A stern judge, he had accused him and, since he had not cleared himself, afflicted and made him sorrowful with great distress.

Therefore the aforesaid knight sought help from Robert, count of Meulan, who was chief among the king’s counsellors; pressed by extreme anxieties, [Col. 0790A] he committed himself to that man’s protection. First, he was ashamed of the mocking reproaches made against him—that he had left Antioch over the wall like a tightrope-walker. Then, fearful and with much reflection, he considered that he would scarcely, or never, regain the king’s friendship that he had lost. He therefore decided to repeat his pilgrimage. An agreement was made: the count was to reconcile him with the king, provide him with five hundred marks of silver for setting out, and hold all his land in pledge for fifteen years. When those years had elapsed, he was to give Ivo’s son a daughter of Henry, count of Warwick, his brother, in marriage, and restore his paternal inheritance. This compact was confirmed by oath and fortified with royal approval. Ivo set out abroad with his wife, died during the journey, and his inheritance passed under the control of strangers.

The city of Leicester had had four lords: the king, the bishop of Lincoln, Count Simon, and Ivo, Hugh’s son. The aforesaid count of Meulan, acting through Ivo—who was burgess, sheriff, and the king’s farmer—entered by cunning, and, by the king’s aid and his own shrewdness, subjected the whole city to himself. Thus he became a count in England, surpassed all the kingdom’s magnates in wealth and power, and exceeded almost all his relatives. He also had as wife the beautiful Isabel, the king of France’s niece, who bore him twin offspring, Waleran and Robert.

[Note: [Col. 0789C]

The following genealogy records the part of Robert I’s descendants which established itself in England:

“It should be remembered that Robert, count of Meulan, coming into England with William, duke of Normandy, obtained the earldom of Leicester by gift of the said duke and conqueror [Col. 0789D] of England. After first destroying the city of Leicester together with the castle and the church within the castle, he rebuilt, in the time of the aforesaid conqueror, that church of St Mary within the castle, establishing there twelve secular canons and one dean: … After Robert’s death, Robert le Goczen [le Bossu], his son and heir, succeeded him; by the counsel of Lord Alexander, then bishop of Lincoln, and other discreet persons, he founded this abbey of the Meadows of Leicester … This Robert, with the consent of Amicia his wife, assumed the habit of our religious order in this abbey, living justly and holily for fifteen years and more. His wife Amicia also became a nun at Eton.

“After the death of this Robert, our founder (in the year 1167), his son Robert succeeded to the inheritance and was called Robert ‘with the white hands’ (*as blanches meyns*). This Robert took as wife Petronilla, daughter of Hugh de Grandmesnil, with the honour of Hinckley and the other possessions [Col. 0790C] of that Hugh which he held in England; and from that time the honour of Hinckley was first joined to the earldom of Leicester. By the said Petronilla he begot three sons and two daughters: Robert, called ‘Petronilla’s son’ to distinguish him from the aforesaid men, who [Col. 0790D] succeeded his father in the inheritance but had no heir begotten from himself; William the Leper, the second son; Geoffrey, bishop of St Andrews in Scotland, the third son; and Amicia, the eldest daughter, and Margaret, the younger.”

Robert (called *as blanches meyns*, “with white hands”) also died while returning from the Holy Land and was buried at Durazzo, overseas. He was succeeded in the inheritance by his aforesaid son and heir Robert, called “Petronilla’s son.” When he too died without an heir, the inheritance was divided between the aforesaid sisters Amicia and Margaret, since their two brothers had already died. Amicia was betrothed to Lord Simon de Montfort, father of that Simon who died at Evesham; Margaret was betrothed to Sayer de Quincy. Thus two earldoms were created, Leicester and Winchester, from what had formerly been the earldom of Leicester. (*Monasticon Anglicanum*, I, p. 312.)

Dom Bouquet, book XL, p. 687], bore [children], namely Hugh, surnamed “the Poor,” and five daughters. Blinded in mind amid so much wealth, he did not keep his oath to his son Ivo, because the young man did not receive, at the appointed time, the woman to whom he had been pledged and the hereditary land.

### III. Conflicts and wars between King Henry and Robert of Bellême. The count is compelled to submit to the victor.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1102, in the tenth indiction, King Henry summoned Robert of Bellême, a most powerful count, to his court, and charged him with forty-five offences committed in deed or word against himself or his brother, the Duke of Normandy; he ordered him to answer publicly to each charge. For during a whole year he had diligently caused inquiries to be made, disgraceful acts to be cautiously investigated by secret agents, and all of them most carefully recorded in writing. When Robert had requested and obtained leave, as was customary, to withdraw and take counsel with his own men, he went out and realized that he could not clear himself of the crimes alleged. He quickly mounted his horse and fled, frightened and breathless, to his castles. While the king and his barons awaited an answer, a royal officer reported that Robert had departed at once.

The king then grieved that he had been deceived, but confidently awaited the time for vengeance. He publicly denounced Robert, accused in general complaints and not legally acquitted; and unless he returned to submit to judgment and do what was right, he declared him a public enemy. Again he summoned the rebel to an assembly, but Robert wholly refused to come. Rather, he fortified his castles everywhere with ditches and walls and sought assistance from his Norman kinsmen, foreign Welshmen, and all his relatives.

The king summoned the army of England and besieged Arundel Castle, situated near the sea-shore. Having established his camp there, he dismissed the labourers with their households for three months. Meanwhile the guardians of the stronghold humbly requested a truce from the king, so that they might demand from their lord either aid for defence or permission to make peace. With the king’s consent, messengers sought Robert in the region of the Mercians. Having found him, they anxiously revealed that the king’s intolerable attack threatened them. For he was then building Bridgnorth, a most strongly fortified castle on the river Severn, and was vainly seeking auxiliaries with all his strength for resistance.

On hearing of his followers’ defection, Robert groaned. Since he was unable to assist them, he released them from their pledged faith and, much saddened, granted them leave to make terms with the king. When the envoys returned, the garrison gladly surrendered the castle to the king; he received them graciously and honoured them with many gifts. The king then advanced his army to Blyth Castle, once belonging to Roger of Bulkeley. Immediately the joyful townsmen came out to meet him and, acknowledging him as their natural lord, received him gladly. When this had been done, the king allowed the people a brief rest; and the assembled great men greatly feared his prudence and courage.

Meanwhile the king sent envoys to Neustria, informing the duke in truthful letters how Robert had offended against both brothers and secretly fled from his court. He then urged that, as they had agreed in England, they should both punish their traitor by a common vengeance. The duke therefore assembled the army of Normandy and besieged the castle of Vignats, held by Gerard of Saint-Hilaire. The townsmen desired a military assault, because, if a vigorous attack were made, they were prepared to surrender the stronghold. They did not think it honourable to surrender without force, lest they deservedly be judged faithless deserters.

But because the duke was indolent and weak, lacking princely firmness, Robert de Montfort and other accomplices in the rebellion—who in turn were at odds with one another—set fire to their own tents and burned them. They threw the whole army into confusion and deliberately fled without pursuit, forcing into shameful flight those others who wished to press hard upon the hateful Robert. When the defenders saw this great disgrace of the Norman army, they mockingly shouted after them with loud howling. Thereafter, fearing less, they began a cruel war throughout the district of Ouche.

Robert de Grandmesnil, Hugh de Montpinçon, Robert de Courcy, and their men resisted the savage raiders as best they could and strove to defend their country. But the public enemies, enticed by plunder, rose with greater ferocity. Proudly occupying Gontier’s Castle, Fourches, and Argentan, they were exceedingly enraged that any of their neighbours had dared even to bark against them without a leader. Throughout the whole province they seized the plunder of the country people; having pillaged everything, they gave the houses to the flames.

The king of the English, unlike his brother, did not languish in idleness. In autumn he assembled the forces of all England, marched into Mercia, and besieged Bridgnorth for three weeks. Robert had withdrawn to Shrewsbury and entrusted the aforesaid town to Roger, son of Corbet, Robert de Novavilla, and Ulger the Huntsman; he had attached to them eighty paid knights. He had also made peace at that time with the Welsh and enlisted their kings Cadwgan and Gervase, sons of Rhys, who repeatedly sent forces to drive off the king’s army.

Robert had disinherited William Pantulf, an honourable and valiant knight, and had completely rejected from his service a man who promised him much assistance in his pressing need. William, despised by Robert, turned to the king. Since the king had long known his energetic spirit, he welcomed him gladly. At once he entrusted two hundred knights to him and assigned him the custody of Stafford Castle, which was nearby. Above all others, this man injured Robert and stubbornly opposed him in counsel and arms until his overthrow.

The earls and leading men of the realm then assembled and discussed at length making peace between the quarrelling man and his lord. They said: “If the king violently subdues this magnificent count and, by excessive obstinacy as he intends, disinherits him, he will henceforth trample all of us beneath his feet like helpless serving-women. Let us therefore zealously sow peace between them, so that we may duly advance the interests of both our lord and our equal, and, by calming disturbances, make each of them indebted to us.”

Accordingly, one day they all approached the king together. In the open field they held earnest negotiations for peace and attempted by many arguments to soften the royal severity. Then, on a nearby hill, stood three thousand country knights. Understanding well the endeavours of the nobles, they cried aloud to the king: “Lord King Henry, do not trust these traitors. They are striving with all their might to deceive you and to take from you the severity of royal justice. Why do you listen to those who urge you to spare a traitor and let the conspiracy for your death go unpunished? Behold, we all stand faithfully with you and are ready to obey you in everything. Assault the town fiercely; press the traitor from every side; and make no peace with him until you hold him in your hands, alive or dead.”

Hearing this, the king took courage; and when the assembly soon dispersed, the schemes of the faction were brought to nothing. He then summoned the aforesaid Welsh kings through William Pantulf. By gifts and promises he won them over and prudently stole them away from the enemy, associating them and their forces with his own side. He also summoned three principal townsmen and swore before all that, unless they surrendered the town to him within three days, every one of them whom he could capture would perish by hanging.

Terrified by such determination in the king, they began to seek a plan for their safety. They summoned William Pantulf, their kinsman, intending to listen to his persuasion. He came as mediator between them and the king and, in an eloquently composed speech, urged them to surrender the stronghold to their lawful king. On the king’s behalf, he promised under oath to increase their estates by land worth one hundred pounds. Considering the common advantage, the townsmen consented and obeyed the will of the royal majesty, lest resistance bring them peril.

Finally, with the king’s permission, they sent an envoy to their lord Robert, informing him that they could no longer endure the might of the unconquered prince. But the paid knights knew nothing of the peace which all the townsmen and burgesses, unwilling to perish, had concluded without consulting them.

When the knights learned of this unexpected development, they were indignant and took up arms, attempting to prevent the work already begun. The force of the townsmen shut them up in one part of the fortress, while the royal troops, bearing the king’s banner, were admitted amid general rejoicing. Since the paid knights had kept faith with their lord, as was fitting, the king granted them free departure with their horses and arms. As they went out through the companies of besiegers, they wept and openly lamented that they had been wickedly overthrown by the treachery of the defenders and their commanders. Before the entire army, lest their misfortune should bring reproach upon other hired soldiers, they exposed the deceit of their accomplices.

When Robert heard that the most strongly fortified castle of Bridgnorth, in which he had chiefly trusted, had been subdued by the king, he groaned in anguish and, almost driven mad, did not know what to do. The king ordered his columns to pass through Huvell Hegen and besiege the town of Shrewsbury, set upon a hill and surrounded on three sides by the river Severn. The English call a certain passage through the wood “Huvell Hegen,” which Latin-speakers might call “an evil path” or “an evil road.” For a hollow track, a thousand paces long, rough with great stones and so narrow that it could barely hold two riders abreast, lay there; a dark forest shaded it on either side, and archers hid within it, suddenly striking passers-by with whizzing missiles or arrows.

There were then more than sixty thousand foot-soldiers on the expedition. The king ordered them to cut down the forest with axes and make for himself and all future travellers a very broad road, to last forever. The royal command was quickly fulfilled: the woodland was levelled, and the multitude made a very broad way across it.

On hearing this, Robert was greatly terrified. Seeing himself surrounded everywhere by misfortune, he was humbled and compelled to implore the mercy of the unconquered king. The stern king, on the contrary, mindful of injuries, resolved to attack him with a fighting host and in no way spare him unless he surrendered as conquered. At last Robert wasted away in grief over his unhappy condition. On the advice of his friends, he went out to meet the king, now near the city; confessed the crime of treason; and offered the keys of the city to the victor.

The king therefore took possession of the whole honour of Robert and of those of his men who had persisted with him in rebellion. He allowed Robert himself to depart unharmed with his horses and arms and had him safely escorted through England to the sea. All England rejoiced at the exile of the cruel tyrant, and many congratulated King Henry with flattering words: “Rejoice, King Henry, and give thanks to the Lord God, because you have begun to reign freely since you conquered Robert of Bellême and expelled him from the borders of your kingdom.”

### IV. Robert of Bellême crosses into Normandy and commits many evils there. He rises against Duke Robert. On the death of certain men.

When Robert had been expelled, the kingdom of Albion was quiet in peace. King Henry reigned prosperously for thirty-three years; afterward no one in England dared rebel against him or hold any stronghold against him. Robert, filled with anger and grief, crossed into Neustria and cruelly attacked his countrymen, who had refused to help their weak lord. He grievously afflicted them with slaughter and fire. For just as the dragon of whom John the visionary writes in the Apocalypse, cast down from heaven, savagely unleashed his rage upon the inhabitants of earth, so this cruel butcher, driven from Britain, furiously rushed upon the Normans. After plundering their estates, he set their lands ablaze and tortured to death or mutilation any knights or others whom he could capture. His cruelty was so great that he preferred inflicting torments upon captives to becoming rich through large ransom payments for them.

Roger the Poitevin and Arnulf, Robert’s brothers, were wealthy earls in England and enjoyed great honours through the provision of their father, Count Roger of Montgomery. Arnulf had married a daughter of the king of Ireland, named Lafracoth, through whom he desired to acquire his father-in-law’s kingdom. Immoderate greed seeks more than it ought and therefore suddenly takes away from many what they have justly acquired. The powerful king of the English, because of Robert’s wickedness, hated all his offspring and kindred and resolved to root them all out of his kingdom. He therefore sought occasions against the aforesaid brothers, persistently pursued whatever he found, and drove them, disinherited, from Britain.

The land which the elder Count Roger had given to the nuns of Almenêches—because Abbess Emma was the sister of the aforesaid counts—the impatient avenger mercilessly took from the church of virgins and granted to Savaric, son of Chama, in return for military service.

When they had thus been driven out of England, the violent bitterness of wickedness increased in Neustria and committed innumerable crimes during three years. Many villages were devastated, and churches were burned together with the people who had fled to them as children flee to their mother’s bosom. Nearly all Normandy had risen against Robert and conspired to resist him in a common league, but in vain, because it lacked a sound head against so great a robber. For he was powerful in resources and ability, and possessed a mass of wealth which he had long accumulated in twenty-four very strong fortresses, formerly built for rebellion. He alone possessed his paternal inheritance completely and allowed no share to his aforesaid brothers, who had been disinherited because of him.

Roger therefore withdrew to Carrouges Castle, part of his wife’s patrimony. There he remained until old age and, at the end of his life, left worthy sons as his successors. Arnulf, after many labours which he had borne fruitlessly for his brother, indignantly went over to the duke. Seizing Almenêches Castle by surprise, he handed it over to him and drew many of his brother’s supporters to his side. Then great disturbance arose in the territory of Sées. Many provincials abandoned Robert with Arnulf and surrendered their towns to the duke’s supporters. Robert, deserted by his own brother, scarcely trusted anyone anywhere, being afraid on every side; and because he was terrible to almost everyone, he distrusted even those who still adhered to him.

In June [1103], the duke’s soldiers attacked the abbey of nuns. Eager to plunder the region, they made stables for their horses within the sacred buildings. When Robert learned this, he flew there and set fire to the monastery. He seized Oliver de Frêne and many others; some he miserably afflicted with long and severe imprisonment, while others he condemned to death or mutilation.

Duke Robert came with the army of Normandy to Ouche and ought to have assisted his supporters. Roger de Lacy was then commander of the troops, and by his command Malger, surnamed Malaherba, held the aforesaid fortress. Many rejoiced at the impending misfortune of the hateful tyrant and eagerly assembled to attack him. Count William of Évreux, Count Rotrou of Mortagne, Gilbert de l’Aigle, and all the men of Ouche had conspired together against him, but they could not exact as they wished a retaliation proportionate to the evils he had so often inflicted on them.

But Robert de Saint-Céneri, his steward Burchard, and Hugh de Nonant resisted him for a long time and distressed him more than all other Normans by losses and injuries. When the duke arrived with his army, Robert drew up his battle-lines and tested his indolent lord in many ways. Attacking boldly upon the causeway, he finally put him to flight and captured William de Conversana, brother of Countess Sibyl, together with many others.

The more spirited Normans were greatly ashamed that those who had flourished as conquerors of foreign peoples in barbarian lands were now defeated and put to flight in the bosom of their own country by one of their own sons. Robert, greatly puffed up by his successes, rose in greater ferocity. Scorning the duke thereafter, he strove to bring all Normandy everywhere beneath his own power. The provincials, lacking a ruler and unable to endure the harsh tyranny of this warlike count, bowed their necks beneath his yoke, though unwillingly. They adhered wholly to him, not so much from love as from fear; relying on his protection, they waged cruel war against their neighbouring rivals.

Thus, as the duke’s strength failed, Robert rose more violently; and when neighbouring men of Ouche defected to him, he took possession of the fortress of Ouche. He also made Gontier’s Castle and many other surrounding strongholds subject to himself.

After the monastery of nuns at Almenêches had been burned, as stated, the tender community of virgins was miserably dispersed. Each returned, according to such resources as chance had granted her, to the homes of parents or friends. Abbess Emma fled with three nuns to Saint-Évroult and lived there for six months in the chapel where the holy father Ebrulf had dwelt alone, intent upon the vision of heaven. In the following year she returned to her church and, with the help of God and His faithful people, attempted to restore what had been destroyed.

She lived for nearly ten years thereafter. During them, she diligently rebuilt the basilica of the Virgin and Mother and the regular buildings, and worked hard to recall the dispersed nuns within the monastic enclosure. After her death, Matilda, daughter of her brother Philip, succeeded her and laboriously repaired the monastery and its buildings after it had again been burned in a sudden fire.

At the same time [1102–1103], the leading magnates of Normandy—Walter Giffard, William of Breteuil, and Ralph de Conches—died, and young men succeeded them. Walter Giffard, Earl of Buckingham, died in England and was carried thence into Normandy, as he himself had ordered. He was buried at the entrance of the basilica of the Blessed Virgin Mary at Longueville. Upon the painted and decorated wall above him was written the following epitaph:

> Walter, noble stock of the noble Giffards,  
> Possesses in burial the tomb he deserved while living.  
> Founder and builder of this present church,  
> He lies here, as though in a tomb of his own making.  
> He proved himself magnificent and a friend to his country,  
> A leader mighty in valour and abounding in piety;  
> But especially a patron of religious persons and monks,  
> He benefited the Church in many ways.

The monks of Cluny accordingly honoured the vigorous baron with due reverence and continually commended his soul to the Lord God in prayer, mindful of the abundant benefits they had received at Longueville from his alms. His wife Agnes was sister to Anselm of Ribemont. Fifteen years after her marriage she bore her husband a son, Walter. After her husband’s death, she carefully reared the boy to manhood and prudently governed his paternal honour for many years.

This woman, excessively inflamed by female desire, fell in love with Duke Robert and unlawfully entangled him for herself in the treacherous nets of love. Through herself and her powerful kinsmen, she promised him much assistance against all enemies. She soon drew the sluggish man into agreeing that, if his wife died, he would marry the aforesaid woman and entrust to her the government of all Normandy.

Not long afterward, Countess Sibyl, poisoned, took to her bed and died during Lent, while many mourned her. William, archbishop of Rouen, performed her funeral rites and honourably buried her, with clergy and people, in the metropolitan basilica of Saint Mary, Mother of God. A polished slab of white stone covers her tomb in the nave of the church, bearing this epitaph for attentive readers:

> Nobility, beauty, praise, glory, and great power  
> Do not make a human being live forever.  
> For noble, powerful, wealthy Countess Sibyl  
> Lies buried in this tomb, reduced to ashes.  
> Her generous hand, provident mind, and chaste life  
> Would have benefited her country, had they endured longer.  
> The Normans mourn their lady; the Apulian people their foster-child;  
> At her setting, great glory fell.  
> When the star of Titan entered the Golden Fleece,  
> She suffered death and fell. God, be life to her!

After this, the tumults of the wars long since begun suddenly increased greatly across almost the whole of Neustria, certain causes arising. While these raged with deadly violence, the duke was prevented from taking another wife; and Agnes, remaining a widow, vainly desired to ascend the princely marriage-bed.

Then a great war arose between the men of Breteuil and Évreux and their other neighbours. William de Breteuil had married Adeline, daughter of Hugh de Montfort, but had had no child by lawful marriage. When he died at Bec on 12 January [1103] and was buried at the monastery of Lyre, which his father had built upon his own estate, his nephews William de Guader and Rainald de Graceio contended to succeed him. But the Normans accepted Eustace, his son by a concubine, because they preferred to have a native-born illegitimate man as their lord rather than a Breton or Burgundian, though legitimate.

Thus a grievous war arose between hostile parties, and the devastation of the country was greatly increased. William de Warenne soon died; Reginald gained strength, and Count William of Évreux, with many others, joined him in support. Ralph de Conches, son of Isabel, Ascelin Goël, and Amaury de Montfort gathered their forces and, favouring Reginald, wickedly inflicted immense losses upon their neighbours, devastated their own country as enemies, and gave little help to the man whom they tried to assist.

Eustace, having with him William Ales, Ralph Rufus, Theobald, and his other barons, resisted bravely. By their counsel he sought aid from the king of England against so many enemies. The king gave him his daughter Juliana as wife and promised invincible assistance against Goël and all other enemies. At that time he also married another of his children to Count Rotrou of Mortagne; she bore her husband a daughter named Philippa.

### V. Ivo, bishop of Chartres. The children of Countess Adela of Chartres. Various events in England and Normandy.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord [1103], Pope Paschal came into Gaul. Honourably received by the French, he faithfully performed the divine service. At that time the venerable Ivo, bishop of the city of Chartres, flourished among the foremost teachers of France in learning, both sacred and secular. Invited by him, the pope celebrated the solemnity of Easter at Chartres.

Countess Adela also supplied generous expenses for the pope’s service and obtained from the Apostolic See a blessing for herself and her household forever. This praiseworthy lady, after her husband’s pilgrimage, honourably administered his county and carefully brought up her young children for the protection of holy Church.

William, the eldest, married the daughter of Gilo de Sully. Possessing his father-in-law’s inheritance, he lived long in peace and fathered worthy offspring, Odo and Raher. Theobald, however, Count Palatine, was distinguished in arms, strong in his love of peace and justice, and shone forth among the foremost princes of France as supreme in wealth and valour. He married Matilda, daughter of Duke Engelbert; after the death of his uncle King Henry, he took possession of the duchy of Normandy and restrained the raging disorderly men by striking them with the necessary rod of discipline.

> **Note:** “[Col. 0797D] On hearing of the death of King Henry,” says Robert de Monte in his Appendix to Sigebert under the year 1135, “the Count of Anjou and his wife Matilda, daughter of the same king, obtained without any difficulty the castles of Normandy, namely Domfront, Argentan, Ouche, Ambrières, Gorron, Mont-Cenis, etc. The magnates of Normandy immediately sent for Count Theobald, that he might come and take Normandy. [Col. 0799D] He therefore came to Rouen, and afterwards to Lisieux on the Saturday of the fast of the tenth month. On the next day, while he and Robert, Count of Gloucester, were conferring, a messenger came from England saying that his brother Stephen was already king. On hearing this, Robert, Count of Gloucester, brother of Matilda, surrendered the castle of Falaise which he held.” Matthew Paris relates the same matters under 1136 and adds for the following year: “To his brother Theobald, Count of Blois, who complained that Stephen had unjustly invaded England though he was the younger in age, Stephen agreed to pay two thousand marks yearly; and so the brothers departed reconciled with one another.” Theobald therefore possessed Normandy, or a part of Normandy, for nearly a full year before restoring it to his brother under an agreement. Dom Bouquet, book XI, p. 692.

Stephen, the third child of Stephen of Blois, received the arms of knighthood from his uncle the king. After William, Count of Mortain, had been captured at Tinchebray, Stephen received that county as a royal gift. He married Matilda, daughter of Eustace, Count of Boulogne, by her mother Mary, and possessed her entire honour by hereditary right. Finally, after King Henry died at the castle of Lyons on 2 December, Stephen crossed the sea and, at the beginning of the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1136, assumed the sceptres of England.

Henry, the youngest in age, was from childhood a monk of Cluny and in youth was elevated to become abbot of Glastonbury in England.

> **Note:** “[Col. 0800D] In administering the church of Glastonbury, Henry earned the following praise, which is read in *Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 18: ‘Henry, brother of Theobald, Count of Blois, nephew of King Henry, a monk of Cluny, in the year of the Lord 1126, presided over the church of Glastonbury: a man whom abundant learning made illustrious and uprightness of character especially adorned. His industry brought such great benefits to the church of Glastonbury that his memory there will deservedly flourish for ages,’ etc.” Dom Bouquet, book XI, p. 692.

Thereafter, following William Giffard, he was promoted to the bishopric of Winchester.

Finally, when the mother of so great an offspring began deeply to contemplate the pale season of dark death, she voluntarily abandoned, after much wealth and pleasure—in which an abundance of sins stains and destroys souls—the slippery allurements of the world and its swollen pride. Becoming a nun at Marcigny, under the strict rule of the Cluniacs, she served the King of Sabaoth. These matters concerning the noble mother and fortunate offspring have been said by anticipation. Now I wish to return my pen to the sequence of the narrative, from which I have digressed briefly.

The king of the English sent Robert, Count of Meulan, into Normandy to quiet domestic disputes. He ordered Duke Robert and the other magnates to spare his son-in-law and fight against that man’s enemies; otherwise they would feel the hostility of royal power. Observing the king’s goodwill toward Eustace, many kept quiet, and those who had previously harmed him strove eagerly to assist him.

Nevertheless Reginald, Goël, and other rash men obstinately persisted in their wickedness. Not even at the king’s request, out of respect for his royal dignity, did they cease attacking his son-in-law; rather, with impious rashness, they perpetrated killings and burnings. Among other cruel acts committed by the aforesaid Reginald, he persistently attacked a hostile stronghold, captured every person within as they came out, and mercilessly killed them like brute animals by thrusting his own sword into their entrails. For this reason he became especially hateful to everyone. Eustace grew notably stronger and obtained the whole honour of his father; Reginald was expelled from Neustria.

Having returned to his native land, Reginald began plotting against his elder brother William. But by the just judgment of God, amid the tumults he was devising, he fell into his brother’s hands and paid in his prison the due penalty for his wicked acts.

Goël also watched John, son of Stephen of Meulan. As John returned from a conference with his lord, the count, who was staying at Beaumont in Normandy, Goël seized him and confined the greedy moneylender in prison for nearly four months. Therefore the aforesaid count laboured earnestly to rescue his burgess, who was very rich, but could not free him from the wolf’s mouth except by conciliating several persons.

The resourceful Count Robert accordingly made peace with William, Count of Évreux, and promised his daughter—who was one year old—to William’s nephew Amaury. In that peace he brought together Ralph de Conches, Eustace, Goël, and the other warlike border lords. Once this peace was made, John was restored, and security and the calm of peace were extended to many others.

In the following year—

> **Note:** “[Col. 0800D] That is, 1104.”

—Isabel, wife of the Count of Meulan, gave birth to twins, Waleran and Robert. For certain intervening reasons, Amaury was prevented from marrying the girl promised to him.

When the sleepy duke saw the excessive desolation of his country and could not defend the region of his duchy against Robert of Bellême, he violated the agreement he had made with the king. Without the king’s counsel he made peace with the aforesaid Robert and granted him his father’s lordships, namely the bishopric of Sées and the other possessions mentioned above.

The venerable Serlo, bishop of Sées, therefore considered it unworthy to endure Robert’s tyranny and preferred to withdraw from his bishopric rather than live under him. Leaving his own see, he wandered abroad and, striking Robert and his helpers with an anathema, cursed them.

The aforesaid man also grievously harassed in many ways Ralph, abbot of Sées, a pleasant, witty, and lovable man. He oppressed the men of Saint Martin, the holy bishop, with unjust exactions and drove the abbot away through the undeserved afflictions imposed upon his subjects. Thus bishop and abbot, worn down by the tyrant’s yoke, fled to England and were graciously received by King Henry for relief.

At this time the venerable Gundulf, bishop of Rochester, died. In his place Abbot Ralph was appointed by an ecclesiastical election. He was consecrated bishop of Rochester by the reverend Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, and after some years became Anselm’s successor in the see of Canterbury.

### VI. Magnus, king of the Norwegians, is killed on campaign.

At that time Magnus, the very powerful king of the Norwegians, sailed around the islands of Britain and entered the deserted islands as far as Ireland with a great fleet. Having shrewdly established settlers there, he ordered towns and villages to be built after the manner of other peoples. The Irish, therefore, envied him greatly and attempted with all their strength to harass him, plotting by treachery or force to destroy their enemies.

The magnanimous king rose against the Irish and brought his fleet to the shores of Ireland. But they, terrified by fear of so great a king, summoned the Normans; Arnulf and his auxiliaries hurried to bring them aid. All of them, once assembled, feared formidable Magnus and did not dare fight him hand-to-hand; instead, they strove to devise a wicked treachery against him.

At length certain witty and eloquent men came to him deceitfully, deceived him with frivolous promises, and persuaded him to leave the ships with only a few men, in order to inspect the province and receive it into his allegiance. But he, disastrously credulous toward traitors, left his armoured troop-formations on the shore and, following his deceivers for two miles, sought his own destruction. For there he found great bands of enemies lying hidden; when they leapt out from their ambushes, the bold Norwegian, scorning flight, began to fight bravely. But a few could not withstand innumerable foes. King Magnus stood with his back against a tree, and, shielded by his buckler, wounded many with missiles; but overwhelmed by the multitude, alas, he perished. [Col. 0801C]

A wealthy citizen of Lincoln kept the treasure of King Magnus, supplying him with ornaments and vessels, arms and implements, and other things necessary for royal service. When he learned of the king’s death, he hurried home and, trading with the royal treasure, amassed immense wealth. [Col. 0801D] When the king of the English heard of the death of the aforesaid king, he rejoiced as though relieved of a great burden; and after some time he demanded from the Lincoln citizen the treasury of the said prince. At first the citizen concealed the truth of what he had done. Therefore the king suddenly seized him when he was convicted, and took from him, it is said, more than twenty thousand pounds of silver.

Having tasted the blood of King Magnus and his companions, the Irish became more savage, and suddenly turned to destroy the Normans. For their king took his own daughter away from Arnulf and unlawfully joined the wanton woman to a certain cousin of his. He also resolved to kill Arnulf himself as recompense for the affinity. But Arnulf, learning the accursed treacheries of that barbarous people, fled to his own men, and thereafter lived for almost twenty years without a settled abode. At last, now an old man and outwardly reconciled to the king, he took a wife; and, after the wedding, on the following day he fell asleep after eating and met his last day, leaving his wedding attendants mourning-threnodies instead of ribald wedding songs. While enemies everywhere were being overwhelmed by the play of changing fortune, King Henry grew strong; above all, the death of King Magnus made him safer, and, enriched by a vast revenue, he swelled with pride. [Col. 0802A]

## VII. Louis of France, son of King Philip, crosses to England. His stepmother Bertrada plots against him. — King Henry crosses into Normandy and visits his brother Duke Robert.

[Col. 0802B]

At the same time [Note: [Col. 0801D] That is, in the year 1100.], the young Louis, with his father’s permission, crossed to England with a few but wise men, and came to King Henry’s court, intending to serve King Henry as a distinguished young knight. Henry received him honourably as a king’s son and treated him kindly in every respect. Meanwhile a messenger of Bertrada, his stepmother, followed him gradually and delivered to King Henry letters sealed with the seal of Philip, king of the French. The learned king read the letter; after reading it, he summoned his counsellors and began to deliberate with them cheerfully and at considerable length. For in the letter he had read that Philip, king of France, ordered him to seize Louis, his son, who had come to his court, [Col. 0802C] and confine him in prison for all the days of his life. The wise bearer of the sceptre carefully discussed with his lawful barons how absurd and improper was the command which the king of the French had sent him through female impudence, and he rejected from himself and all his men so wicked a plot, utterly unworthy of a king.

William of Bosc-Le-Hard, however, a wise knight who was with Louis, perceived the matter while it was still hidden. Therefore, as if intending to jest, he came uninvited to the assembly of magnates. At once the king kindly sent word through him to Louis that he should depart peacefully; and he sent both Louis and his companions back to France, honoured with many gifts.

[Col. 0802D] Louis, therefore, having learned of his stepmother’s treachery, angrily approached his father and reproached him because he had procured such dreadful treatment for him through his letters in a foreign land. The king, ignorant of the wicked betrayal, denied everything; and the young man, burning with anger, wished to kill his stepmother. But she laboured by many means to forestall him with death; summoning three sorcerers from among the clergy, she agreed upon a great price for bringing about his destruction. The sorcerers began to perform certain wicked secret rites for several days and promised the cruel adulteress Louis’s death within nine days, if they completed what they had begun. Meanwhile one of them disclosed the magical practices of his companions; the other two were captured, and the plot, unfinished, perished by God’s will. Then the shameless stepmother employed poisoners, enticed by promises of great rewards, and infected the royal offspring with poison. [Col. 0803A]

Accordingly, the illustrious young man took to his bed and for several days could neither eat nor sleep. Almost all the French were saddened that the king’s legitimate heir was in danger. At last, when all the chief physicians of the French were failing, a certain shaggy man from Barbary came and began to demonstrate his medical skill upon the youth, whose case was desperate. By God’s will he succeeded, to the envy of the native physicians. This man had indeed long lived among pagans and had carefully investigated the profound secrets of medicine from teachers whom long investigation of philosophy had raised, beyond all [Col. 0803B] barbarian sophists, through knowledge of things. The royal offspring finally recovered, but remained pale throughout the rest of his life.

As her stepson recovered, the stepmother groaned. Fear, because of the evils she had formerly brought upon him, produced hatred and increased it daily in many ways. She therefore greatly desired his destruction and had sought it by many efforts through many accomplices in wickedness: so that she herself, freed from fear of the man whom she had grievously offended, might glory in power, and that, should he die, she might more securely place her own sons Philip and Florus upon the royal throne. At last the father came as a suppliant for the poisoness, requested from his son remission of the guilty stepmother’s offences, promised amendment, and granted Pontoise and the whole district of Vexin [Col. 0803C] for reconciliation. Louis, on the advice of bishops and barons, whom he knew to be quite favourable to him, and out of reverence for his father’s exalted rank, pardoned the crime. But she trembled at his command because her crime had been uncovered; covered with shame, she became his servant, obtained pardon, and unwillingly ceased to harass the man whom she had tried with so many afflictions.

Five years later, after his father’s death, Louis obtained the kingdom of France and reigned for twenty-seven years. He always loved Henry, king of the English, in whom, as has been said, he had found great faithfulness; and he never quarrelled with him except unwillingly and through slanderous traitors.

[Col. 0803D] After his father’s death Ralph of Conches crossed the sea. Kindly received by the king, he recovered his paternal estates and took as wife Adeliza, daughter of Count Waltheof and Judith, the king’s cousin; she bore Roger, Hugh, and several daughters. Thus other prudent magnates abandoned their sluggish lord and profitably sought the sensible king; weeping, they begged him to aid the languishing Church of God and the miserable land. Moved kindly by the petitions of many Normans, and earnestly requested by many honourable persons of both clerical and lay rank, he was asked to visit his paternal inheritance, which was being miserably ravaged; to gladden by his presence [Col. 0804A] the province lacking a ruler; and to take up the rod of justice in order to defend it against profane robbers.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1104, Henry, king of the English, crossed to Normandy with a great fleet and visited Domfront and other towns subject to his authority with a great military force. He was honourably received by his magnates and honoured in royal fashion with abundant gifts. For Count Robert of Meulan, Richard of Chester, Count Stephen of Aumale, Henry of Eu, Rotrou of Mortagne, Eustace of Breteuil, Ralph of Conches, Robert son of Haimo, Robert of Montfort, Ralph of Mortemer, and many others held great estates from him in England; and in Neustria they had already turned to him with their nobles and were eagerly prepared to fight with him against all natives of the land. [Col. 0804B]

Then, after several days, the king summoned his brother to a conference. In the presence of the assembled flatterers, he accused him of having annulled the treaty made between them in England: because he had made peace, without the king’s counsel, with Robert of Bellême, traitor to them both, and had given him his father’s domains contrary to law and agreement; because, sluggish in idleness, he had given himself over to thieves, robbers, and other evildoers [Note: [Col. 0803D] Le Prévost; Cheanius reads: “had abandoned” (*deseruerit*).]; because, obeying shameless rascals, he had left all Normandy to them unpunished; and because he had occupied the place of shepherd or prince in vain, since he had not performed the office of ruler for the benefit [Col. 0804C] of the Church of God and the unarmed people, whom he had voluntarily abandoned, like sheep to wolves’ teeth, to their undisciplined persecutors.

The king’s speech set out his case reasonably and very wisely, asserting that the duke, his brother, had broken the treaty through many grave offences. The duke could not deny these charges while attempting to clear himself through his shameful associates. For he lacked understanding and friends, because he despised the company of good men and the counsel of wise men, while miserably seeking what was contrary, to the damage of himself and many others. Thus caught in various entanglements of accusations, the duke took counsel with his men and, as befitted the weaker party, sought the friendship of the stronger. He granted to him William, [Col. 0804D] count of Évreux, together with his county and all subject to him. For both the duke and his supporters feared that he might be exposed by a public examination and deservedly stripped of the duchy which he bore in name, not in action, or else suffer a terrible war through the arms of his sceptre-bearing brother, ending in irreparable overthrow.

When the distinguished count heard that he was to be given away like a horse or an ox, wishing to preserve his integrity and loyalty, he said openly before all:

> Throughout my life I have served your father faithfully, and I have never in any respect violated the faith pledged to him. I have likewise kept it until this day for his heir, and have resolved always to keep it with all my strength. But because, as God himself [Col. 0805A] says in the Gospel—and as I have often heard from learned men—it is impossible peacefully to serve two masters at variance with one another, I earnestly desire to be bound to the authority of one, lest, occupied by two services, I be acceptable to neither. I love the king and the duke. Both are sons of my lord the king, and I seek to honour them both; but I shall do homage to one and lawfully serve him as my lord.

This statement by a generous man pleased everyone. Then Duke Robert delivered him to the king by the hand; peace having been made between the brothers, the king returned to England before winter. Soon the mad robbers renewed the war and rashly violated whatever the king and the leading men had established for the common safety of the country. For Robert of Bellême, exceedingly envious of the success of the king whom he hated bitterly, was distressed [Col. 0805B] and, with his nephew William, count of Mortain, and all others whom he could seduce, attempted to oppress the king’s supporters by war.

Then the pestilent natives became more savage than can be told. At once they stained the province with slaughter and plunder; after carrying off booty and killing people, they burned houses everywhere. The peasants fled with their wives and children into France and endured immense miseries in exile. Thus the Normans, who gloried that they had conquered the English and Apulians in their own lands, now laboured and lamented as mournful wretches in French fields. In their gardens, reduced to wilderness for want of cultivators, thistles and nettles with other useless herbs filled everything and multiplied exceedingly. [Col. 0805C]

## VIII. The tribulations of the Church. Serlo, bishop of Séez, urges King Henry and his magnates to cut their beards and hair.

Meanwhile holy Church was grievously oppressed; and, while she frequently beheld the deaths of her innocent offspring and the irreparable ruin of souls, she raised pure hands with her heart and prayed her Bridegroom, who presides in heaven, for her own aid. The lamentable mourning of sorrowful Normandy spread across the sea, and the king of the English was summoned by the complaints of the desolated. Gunher of Aunay, who held Bayeux, Rainald of Warenne, who favoured the duke’s party, and other retainers [Col. 0805D] of the duke broke the agreements of peace. They captured Robert son of Haimo and several others of the king’s household, keeping them long in prison both from greed for ransom and from contempt and hatred of their lord.

When the energetic king heard this, he ordered a fleet prepared. In the spring he crossed into Neustria and, in the last week of Lent [1105], made harbour at the port called Barfleur; on Holy Saturday he lodged and rested beyond the fords of the Vire, in the village called Carentan.

Then the venerable Serlo, bishop of Séez, came there. First among the Normans to offer his service to the king, he met him and there celebrated the newly begun Paschal solemnities for the King of kings.
