As he stood in the church with the king, vested in sacred garments and about to begin the sacred [Col. 0806A] office, while patiently waiting for the gathering of the people and the king’s household, he saw the basilica occupied by the baggage of country people, with various utensils and a great variety of household goods. Drawing long sighs in sorrow, he said to the king, who sat very humbly in a lowly place among peasants’ chests, with certain magnates:

> The hearts of all faithful people ought rightly to mourn when they see the trampling of holy mother Church and the overthrow of her afflicted people. Behold, this house plainly shows how Constantine’s realm is miserably ravaged! Indeed all Normandy, subjected to profane robbers, lacks a suitable ruler. The basilica of God, once called a house of prayer, you can now see shamefully filled with unclean household goods; and the building in which [Col. 0806B] divine sacraments alone ought to be performed has, through lack of a just defender, become the people’s storehouse. Those who gather cannot reverently bend the knee before the altar, nor stand fittingly, joyfully, and devoutly before the divine majesty, because of the many kinds of goods which the defenceless populace has brought here into the Lord’s house through fear of criminals. Thus the church has become a refuge for the people, although even within it they have no complete safety.
>
> This very year Robert of Bellême burned the church of Tournai, in my own diocese, and killed there forty-five persons of both sexes. I recall these things with groaning in the presence of God. I tell them also in your hearing, lord king, so that your mind may be inflamed with zeal for God and may endeavour to imitate Phinehas (Num. 25:7), Mattathias [Col. 0806C] (1 Macc. 2:24), and his sons. Rise without delay in the Lord’s name; gain your paternal inheritance by the sword of justice, and rescue from the hand of the worst men your ancestral possession and the people of God. For your brother does not possess Normandy, nor does he rule his people as a duke should, leading them along the path of uprightness. Instead, he lies sluggishly idle and is subject to William of Conversano, Hugh of Nonant, who governs Rouen, Gunher his nephew, and other unworthy men. Alas, while he squanders the wealth of the great duchy on trifles and vanities, he himself often fasts until the ninth hour for lack of bread. Often he does not dare rise from bed, nor can he go to church because he lacks breeches, stockings, and shoes. [Col. 0806D] Buffoons and prostitutes, who often accompany him, steal his clothes by night while he snores, sodden with drink, and boast with laughter that they have stripped the duke. Thus, when the head is sick, the whole body becomes weak; when the prince is foolish, the whole country is endangered and the miserable people are wholly desolated.
>
> From the time of Rollo, who was the first ruler of Neustria over the Normans and from whom your lineage sprang, down to this deficient man, Normandy was subject to vigorous dukes. For the distress of so great a native land, worthy king, be usefully angry; and, as David the prophet and king admonishes, “do not sin” (Ps. 4:5): take up arms for the defence of your country, not from a desire to increase earthly power.

The king was encouraged by the bishop’s words, and, after hearing [Col. 0807A] the opinion of the magnates who were present, he spoke as follows:

> In the name of the Lord, I shall rise to labour for peace, and, with your help, shall seek with all my might the tranquillity of the Church.

The count of Meulan was present to strengthen this counsel; nor did the agreement of the other nobles present oppose it. Indeed, they vigorously urged and encouraged the chief magnate to undertake war against the devourers of the people for the general protection of Neustria.

Again the eloquent bishop continued his holy preaching and, beneficially mindful of his office, added:

> We ought continually, each day, to seek the way of life and in all things obey the divine law, which is without reproach. Although we cannot completely correct everything that is done culpably in secret, [Col. 0807B] we ought at least to cut off with the sword of the Spirit those things that are openly done against God, and wholly remove them from among ourselves according to God’s commands and the ordinances of the holy Fathers. You all wear long hair in womanly fashion, which does not become you, who were made in God’s likeness and ought to possess manly strength. How improper and detestable it is for men to wear long hair: Paul the apostle, vessel of election and teacher of the nations, says thus to the Corinthians: “A man indeed ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but woman is the glory of man” (1 Cor. 11:7). And shortly afterward: “If a man grows his hair, it is a disgrace to him; but if a woman grows her hair, it is her glory, because hair has been given her for a covering” (ibid., 15). [Col. 0807C]
>
> Penitents are enjoined not to shave or cut their hair, not for adornment or pleasure, but so that, just as they appear before God hairy and inwardly unkempt through their crimes, so they may walk outwardly bristly and unshorn before men, showing through outward disgrace the deformity of the inner person. By their long beards men are made like goats, by whose filthy wantonness fornicators and catamites are shamefully defiled and are rightly judged abominable to honourable people by the loathsome stench of impurity. But by growing their hair they are regarded as imitators of women, whose softness draws them away from manly courage into wickedness and often miserably casts them down into detestable apostasy.
>
> [Col. 0807D] Alas! Behold, the salutary medicine which the doctors of the Church, who are spiritual physicians, long ago wisely ordained under divine prompting for the health of souls, the children of perdition have appropriated at Satan’s instigation, to increase their condemnation, and have now by long practice violently changed into custom. Roman pontiffs and other bishops forbade this rash usurpation and condemned it in their synods by divine authority. But transgressors hardened in wickedness think perversely and stubbornly hold up the shield of malice against the goad of holy preaching. They avoid shaving their beards lest their clipped hairs prick their female friends during kisses; and, being hairy, they make themselves appear more Saracens than Christians. Behold, they have turned the squalor of penitence into an exercise of luxury! These obstinate sons of Belial dress their heads with women’s hair and wear scorpions’ tails at the ends of their feet, [Col. 0808A] thereby showing themselves womanish through softness and serpentine through their stings. John the mystic saw this kind of people in the appearance of locusts a thousand years ago and plainly expounded it to us in his Apocalypse, which he published on the island of Patmos. Many indeed follow this practice of such wickedness, not knowing how great is the sin in the hair of which they glory. Therefore, glorious king, I beseech you to set your subjects a praiseworthy example, so that they may first see in you how they ought to prepare themselves.

When he had said this, the king and all the magnates joyfully assented. The eager bishop immediately drew shears from his bag and cut the king’s hair first, then the count’s, and then with his own hands the hair of many magnates. All the king’s household and those assembled from every quarter competed in having their hair cut; fearing the royal edict, they cut off their formerly precious hair and trod underfoot, like worthless rubbish, the locks they had long cherished. [Col. 0808B]

After the Paschal festival had been celebrated, the king of the English sent envoys to Philip, king of the French, summoned Geoffrey Martel, count of Anjou, and manfully inflicted vengeance upon the enemies of the Church of God.

## IX. Bohemond, duke of Antioch, comes to France. Various events. — King Henry and his brother Robert labour fruitlessly to make peace.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1106, changes of rulers occurred in the world and many memorable events happened in various places. For in the last week of February [Col. 0808C] a remarkable comet appeared in the western regions, sending its very long hair toward the east. It terrified many hearts and, glowing in the evening for three weeks, elicited much talk concerning human secrets.

In March Duke Bohemond came to France, as he had vowed to the Lord while in the prison of Dalaman; in the district of Limoges he solemnly fulfilled his vow at the tomb of St Leonard the Confessor. Before reaching France, he had sent envoys into England and informed the king in England of the reason for his arrival, intimating that he wished to cross to his court. But the prudent king, fearing that Bohemond might draw away from his dominion the knights he had selected, [Col. 0808D] ordered him not to hazard a winter voyage—especially since the king himself would cross into Neustria before the feast of unleavened bread and could speak with him there at leisure. And so it happened.

After Bohemond left Nobiliacum, where the holy confessor’s mausoleum stood, having completed his prayers, he travelled through the cities and towns of France during Lent. Everywhere he was reverently received by clergy and people alike, and he recounted the various events in which he had participated. He reverently presented relics, silken pallia, and other desirable objects to holy altars; he himself was favourably received in monasteries and bishoprics, rejoiced, and gave thanks to God for the kindness of the western peoples. [Col. 0809A] He had with him a son of Emperor Diogenes and other distinguished Greeks and Thracians. Their complaint against Emperor Alexius—who had through treachery taken from them the ancestral lineages of their forebears—further incited the fierce French to anger against him.

Many nobles came to him and offered him their infants, whom he gladly received from the sacred font and upon whom he bestowed his own name. For he had been named Mark at baptism; but after his father heard at a feast the jocular tale of the giant Bohemond, the name was pleasantly given to the boy. This name thereafter resounded throughout the whole world and became widely known among innumerable people in the world’s threefold clime. Thus this famous name was disseminated in France, though it had previously been almost unknown to all westerners. [Col. 0809B]

The oft-mentioned hero held a conference with King Philip and sought in marriage his daughter Constance. At last, after Easter, he became betrothed to her at Chartres; Countess Adela prepared for them a feast abundant in everything. There the king of the French attended with a great multitude of his men and gave Bohemond his daughter, whom, for some reason unknown to me, he had taken away from Count Hugh of Troyes. Then the same duke, conspicuous among illustrious men, proceeded to the church and there ascended the pulpit before the altar of the Virgin and Mother. He recounted to the great crowd assembled there his misfortunes and exploits, urged all armed men to march with him against the emperor, and promised exceedingly rich cities and towns to the approved volunteers. [Col. 0809C] Therefore many were greatly inflamed; taking the cross of the Lord, they left all that they possessed and set out for Jerusalem as though hastening to a banquet. Ralph of Pont-Echanfray, surnamed Rufus, and his brother Guascelin, Simon of Anet, Robert of Manley with his cousin Hugh Sine-habere, and many others departed; I cannot set down all their names individually in writing.

In the same year [1105], an event of this kind occurred in Normandy. Robert of Stuteville, a strong and powerful man, strongly favoured the duke and managed his households and strongholds in the region of Caux. [Col. 0809D] On Easter Day, while his chaplain was communicating him and his household, and a certain knight came properly to the altar to receive the Eucharist, the priest took the heavenly bread and wished to put it into the man’s open mouth, but was wholly unable to move his hand away from above the altar. Both were greatly terrified by this difficulty. At last the priest said to him: “If you can, receive it. For I am entirely unable to move my hand or offer you the Lord’s body.” The knight stretched his neck over the altar, leaned earnestly toward the chalice, and with gaping mouth received the consecrated offering from the priest’s hand. Ashamed by the unusual occurrence, and ignorant of what was to come, the knight feared misfortune; therefore he distributed many of his garments and other possessions among clergy and poor people. Then, in the first encounter after Easter, [Col. 0810A] he was killed at Maromme, near Rouen. His chaplain, also named Robert, related to me this same thing which, as stated, happened to himself and the unfortunate knight during the life-giving mysteries.

Then Fulk, abbot of Jumièges, died on 3 April [1105] at Winchester in England, and a certain wretched little man named Robert, having given the duke 140 marks of silver, was intruded into his place. Though a professed monk of St Denis the Martyr, he became not a shepherd but a scatterer of the Lord’s flock, harmful to many as a follower of Simon Magus. The monks fled from the face of the devouring wolf and scattered among other monasteries, desiring to save their souls. But he built a castle in the monastery above the Dives and gathered a household of knights, thus making God’s temple into a den of thieves. He also sold the ecclesiastical ornaments which the faithful had carefully provided, and disposed of Simonian possessions to support his retainers. [Col. 0810B]

In May a phlegmatic epidemic spread throughout all the West. With catarrh grievously afflicting them, every eye wept, and throughout all France, where I then was, every cheek was wet with tears. Summer, extremely harsh in heat, brought the crops to maturity; a similarly hot autumn gradually followed. Burning fever, fevers, and other illnesses severely afflicted the inhabitants and laid many sick people low in bed.

In the same month Geoffrey Martel, count of Anjou, besieged and manfully stormed the town of Condé held by the Norman of Montrevel. [Col. 0810C] This Geoffrey was a vigorous and strong administrator of justice, sternly threatening the necks of thieves and robbers with the rod of discipline. His father had long been accustomed to spare them, because he frequently rejoiced with them in their plunder and robberies, receiving shares from them. But when the young man had grown up and perceived enormous wickedness boiling over in the Angevin province through his father’s detestable negligence, he was pierced by zeal for God and took pity on the miserable region, which would abound in every good thing if it possessed peace.

At last, by command of his uncle Geoffrey, who was the rightful heir—though [Col. 0810D] the perjured Fulk had taken from him the dignity of the county and held him imprisoned at the castle of Chinon for almost thirty years, whence he scarcely emerged free when the venerable Pope Urban was present and commanded it—and with his father’s consent nonetheless, he received the county of Anjou. With the utmost endeavour he dispensed justice to the simple and poor and commendably preserved the sincere peace of the Church of God. With God’s help he quickly pacified the entire province and gloriously surpassed almost all his predecessors in courage and justice; but, though brought to perfection in a short time, he fulfilled many years. After three years of his rule he besieged Condé, as I have said above, and conspicuously compelled the rebels shut within by military prowess. When the leaders of the castle had come out to him and were negotiating peace [Col. 0811A] and the town’s surrender on the following day, a crossbowman, prompted by the devil, suddenly shot a bolt from the fortification and struck the most valiant young man, who was mediating a conference among the magnates, mortally wounding the good administrator of justice in the arm. On the next day the lawful defender of his country died, and amid the mourning of many was buried in the monastic basilica of St Nicholas the Bishop.

After his death, Philip, king of the French, granted the county of Anjou to Fulk, his stepson, and entrusted the beardless boy to William, duke of the Poitevins, who happened then to be at court, so that he might protect him on the journey and conduct him safely to his father. But William led the youth entrusted to him as far as [Col. 0811B] the boundary of his own land and there, forgetful of justice and of the future reproach, seized him and held him in prison for more than a year. When the corpulent king of France heard this, he was greatly distressed and tried by prayers and threats to free the boy from confinement. For Bertrada, mother of the said youth, was the king’s wife; she continually spurred him on and vainly stirred up many people to aid the captive. The king, pricked by repeated goads, wished to punish so great a crime by the terror of threats. But the arrogant duke despised the heavy king and held the young man longer, until he obtained from the father, for the rescue of his son, the towns situated on the boundary of the two counties. Not long afterwards the old father died, and the young count married Eremburga, daughter of Helias, count of Maine, who bore him noble children of both sexes. [Col. 0811C]

In the same year [1105–1106], King Henry, as has been said above, sailed into Neustria in spring and laboured to reclaim his paternal inheritance, which perjurers, robbers, and rascals were trampling underfoot. He hired Helias of Maine with his forces and besieged the city of Bayeux, held by Gunher of Aunay. Gunher came out to the king and, for his favour, restored free to him Robert son of Haimo, whom he himself had formerly captured; but he scorned to surrender the city when the king imperiously demanded it. Therefore the king immediately stormed the city, set fire to it, burned it completely, and captured the aforesaid townsman with his foot-soldiers and fellow-knights. [Col. 0811D]

When they heard of the destruction of so great a city, the remaining burgesses trembled greatly and feared to await, in defiant resistance, the king who was advancing with such determination. Thus the men of Caen, learning of the disaster at Bayeux and fearing that they might suffer a like destruction, sent to the king, who was now hurrying against them with great fierceness, and made peace with him on his terms. At once they expelled Enguerrand the townsman, son of Ilbert, with his men, and surrendered the fortress to the king. The king gave Dalston in England, which yields eighty pounds annually, to four leading men of Caen; it is called “Traitors’ Village” to this day, though it is no longer subject to them. [Col. 0812A] Then the king went to Falaise, but did not storm it because Count Helias withdrew at the Normans’ request. Nevertheless, a military engagement occurred there in which Roger of Gloucester, a valiant knight, was killed.

The German princes, king and duke, met at Saintes in the week of Pentecost and spoke for two days about making peace. But because rebellious dissidents caused disturbance, they departed after all agreements had been broken. Afterwards they began everywhere to wage war with all their strength; magnates and worthy young knights chose the parties to which they would adhere and persisted in burnings and plunder from Pentecost until the feast of St Michael.

Then Henry, emperor of the Germans, died on 7 August [1107]; but because, as God bore witness, he had not made satisfaction to the Church for his many offences, he was denied burial in the earth and for many years did not deserve to be buried according to human custom. His son, Emperor Henry V, succeeded him; three years later he married Matilda, daughter of Henry I, king of the English, but had no lawful successor by her. [Col. 0812B]

## X. By what evil men discord between the two brothers is stirred up. King Henry joins battle with Duke Robert, defeats him at Tinchebray, and captures him.

[In the year 1106.] Robert, the usurper of the abbey of Dive, added Judas’s nefarious crime to the wickedness of Simon, among the other evils he had committed. [Col. 0812C] He made an agreement at Falaise with Duke Robert and his magnates: he would suddenly bring the king to them with few men, and they should be ready to receive him. Having thus arranged the treachery, Robert went to Caen and, finding the king, familiarly said: “If it pleases you to come with me, I surrender to you the stronghold which I possess above the Dives.” When this pleased the king, Robert said: “There is no need now to lead a large army, lest the noise of the multitude be heard and our undertaking be impeded. Only a few retainers are within, and they obey me completely.” The king therefore rose by night and rode all night with seven hundred knights; at dawn he halted near the place.

Meanwhile Rainald of Warenne and the young Robert of Stoteville, with another hundred and forty knights, [Col. 0812D] seized the stronghold of Dive; and as dawn rose, while the king approached, they shouted with laughter and insults. Many other knights also followed from Falaise and the surrounding towns, intending to fight the king and his followers at close quarters. But when he perceived the trick, the king angrily ordered his men immediately to assault those within the castle. The royal knights accordingly launched a fierce attack at once, set fire to the place, and burned both castle and monastery. Then Rainald and Robert, worthy young warriors, and many others were captured. Many likewise who had fled to the church tower were burned to death. Moreover, their adherents, hurrying to assist them, saw the huge pyre and immediately fled back to Falaise. The victorious king [Col. 0813A] pursued them slowly, but none dared come out against him. They suffered deservedly, according to the Apostle’s saying: “If anyone destroys the temple of God, God will destroy him” (1 Cor. 3:17). Behold: these men rashly made God’s house a den of thieves and irreverently polluted it with the shameful filth of men and horses; deservedly they perished by the sword or devouring flames!

Then the traitor Robert was captured and brought before the king, laid crosswise over a horse like a sack. The king said to him: “Faithless man, flee from my land. Were it not for reverence for the sacred order whose habit you outwardly wear, I would at once have you most miserably torn limb from limb.” The apostate, thus released, immediately fled in disgrace to the French, from whom he came; and, since he neglected to endure the quiet of monastic life with poverty in the cloister, he obtained the provostship [Col. 0813B] of Argenteuil. In the same year, while he was binding a certain John by legal proceedings and violently exacting from him certain customs—I know not what—he was struck in a fit of rage by the aforesaid man of the district and thus, as his sins required, was miserably slain without repentance.

That autumn in Normandy was stormy with thunder, rain, and warfare; and the fuel of battles, nourished by many causes, openly burst forth. For Robert of Bellême, William, count of Mortain, and many others adhered resolutely to Duke Robert, because they feared the king, wholly refused to submit to his yoke, and opposed him with all their strength. Therefore the king, having assembled a multitude of his men, built a castle opposite Tinchebray [Col. 0813C] and stationed there Thomas of Saint-Jean, with many cavalry and infantry, to keep the garrison in check. When William, count of Mortain, whose town was under siege, heard this, he assembled a noble company of knights and brought in a great supply of food and other necessities which he knew the besieged lacked, while the king’s soldiers looked on in sorrow. He also had the green crops cut in the fields and furnished them to his townsmen as fodder for their horses. The said young man possessed such remarkable courage and so great a force of military strength that the royal sentries did not dare leave their fortification [Col. 0813D] or challenge those entering it.

When he heard this, the king was greatly angered and endeavoured to rise more vigorously against his enemies. Having gathered an army, he came to Tinchebray and held it under siege for some time.

Meanwhile Count William sought out the duke, Robert of Bellême, and his other friends, and urgently procured aid against the king. The duke accordingly assembled an army and ordered his brother to raise the siege in his own land; otherwise he declared war. But Henry, with hardened heart, persisted in the siege and undertook a war more than civil for the sake of peace. He had with him four counts: Elias of Maine, William of Évreux, Robert count of Meulan, and William [Col. 0814A] of Warenne; and other principal barons—namely Ranulf of Bayeux, Ralph of Conches, Robert of Montfort, Robert of Grandmesnil, and many others with their retainers. On the other side Duke Robert had with him Robert of Bellême and his nephew William of Mortain, Robert of Stoteville, William of Ferrières, and many others with their forces. He had fewer knights than his brother, but brought forward a more numerous band of infantry. On each side brothers and kinsmen stood armed, and some prepared wounds for one another. Treacherous deserters also bore weapons, but did not adhere to their lord with steadfast hearts; from ill will they inclined more toward flight than battle.

[Col. 0814B] Many religious men indeed tried to prevent so great a crime and greatly feared to see the shedding of fraternal blood. Vitalis the hermit, who was then pre-eminent among venerable persons, more fervent than the rest, became mediator between the quarrelling brothers. He boldly forbade them to fight at close quarters, lest they seem to imitate the deed of the sons of Oedipus, detested in every age, and thus deservedly incur the accursed and horrible fate of Eteocles and Polynices.

At length the king carefully considered the many contingencies and, having taken the sophists’ arguments to heart, thoughtfully pondered different counsels. He therefore sent this message to his brother:

“My brother, I have not come here through desire for earthly honour, [Col. 0814C] nor have I resolved to deprive you of the rights of your duchy. Rather, summoned by the tearful complaints of the poor, I wish to aid the Church of God, which, like a ship without a helmsman, is endangered amid the storms of the sea. For you occupy the land like a fruitless tree and offer no fruit of justice in sacrifice to our Creator. You are called duke in name only; your retainers openly mock you, and you do not avenge the injuries of their contempt for you. Thus cruel sons of iniquity, under your shadow, wickedly oppress Christian people and have already made almost deserted of inhabitants many parishes in Normandy. Seeing this, I burn with zeal for God, who rules us, and demand to lay down my life for the salvation of my brothers, my beloved people, and my country.

“Therefore, considering these things, I ask you to adopt my counsels; and you will plainly be able to prove that I undertake this not from greed but from good will. Give up to me all fortresses, the whole administration of justice and governance of all Normandy, and half the duchy; possess the other half without toil or care, and each year receive from my treasury in England the equivalent value of the other half. Thereafter you may safely enjoy feasts, games, and every pleasure. I, meanwhile, shall endure the labours impending for peace, provide without failure for your promised repose, and, with God’s help, justly restrain the rage of the wicked so that they may not oppress God’s people.”

Hearing this, the duke summoned his advisers and reported the king’s message. They immediately recoiled from the king’s proposals and, with defiant words, turned the duke [Col. 0815A] away from accepting terms of peace. When the envoys reported that the duke and his supporters desired not peace but war by every means, the king, commending himself to God, said: “Almighty God, in whom I believe, knows that I undertake this conflict for the aid of the desolated people. From the depths of my heart I entreat our Maker to grant victory in today’s battle to him through whom He has decreed to give protection and peace to His people.”

Having said this, he summoned the commanders of his household, equipped all for battle, and briefly exhorted them as the circumstances of place and time required. He released Rainald of Warenne and all the others captured in the church at Dive, and vowed to God that he would restore the church which had been burned. [Col. 0815B] Then the armoured battle-lines were drawn up and advanced in disciplined close order. Ranulf of Bayeux commanded the first line; Robert, count of Meulan, the second; and William of Warenne the third. The latter rejoiced greatly at his brother’s release and boldly urged all his companions to fight invincibly. The king kept the English and Normans on foot with himself; he placed the men of Maine and the Bretons, under Count Elias, farther away in the open field. On the opposing side Count William of Mortain led the first line, and Robert of Bellême the last.

When the armies met and Count William’s squadrons strove to strike Ranulf’s force, [Col. 0815C] they were packed together so densely and stood so inseparably joined in armour that they could do one another no harm; their reciprocal efforts strove in vain against an impenetrable resistance. While both sides howled and shouted, Elias with his men suddenly charged, struck the duke’s unarmed infantry in the flank, and immediately killed 225 men. Seeing this, Robert of Bellême took flight, and the duke’s broken force yielded to the victors.

Then Gualdric seized the duke and committed him to royal custody. He was the king’s chaplain, who had stood in battle alongside the knights; not long afterward he became bishop of Laon [Note: [Col. 0815] Chesnius reads *Landavensis*, corrected by the learned Le Prévost from a manuscript.], greatly oppressed his parishioners, and was therefore struck down by his own citizens in an orchard on Good Friday, together with seven chief ministers of the church. [Col. 0815D] The Bretons captured Count William, from whom the king and his friends scarcely rescued him. Robert of Stoteville, William of Ferrières, and many others were captured. Some, released by the king’s favour, rejoiced at their freedom obtained; others, as their sins deserved, remained bound in chains until death.

The king, rejoicing in victory, summoned his companies, prudently arranged his affairs, and ordered the captured enemies to be carefully guarded. The duke said to him: “Treacherous Normans deceived me by their frauds and drew me away, my brother, from your counsels, which would indeed have been beneficial to me had I followed them. As I departed from the men of Falaise, I bound them by oath not to surrender the fortress of Falaise to anyone except me or William of Ferrières, whom I have found faithful in all things. Therefore hurry now, my brother, and send William to take possession of the stronghold, lest Robert of Bellême forestall you by some stratagem and, having seized this very strong fortress, resist you for some time.”

The king brought his brother with him amicably but cautiously and swiftly sent the aforesaid knight to gain the town. Following him at once, he hastened to Falaise and, at the duke’s command, received the fortress and the allegiance of the burgesses. Then the boy William, who was being brought up there, was brought to the king. Seeing him tremble in fear and assailed by various misfortunes in his tender age, [Col. 0816B] the king comforted him with gentle promises. Then, lest any ground for reproach arise against him should the boy be harmed by any hostile accident while in his hands, he did not wish to keep him under his own special guardianship, but entrusted him to Elias of Saint-Saëns to be educated. The duke had long before given this knight a daughter born to him by a concubine and, granting him the county of Arques, had raised him among the chief barons of Normandy.

When reports of the king’s victory were heard, all religious persons rejoiced. But outlaws and lovers of wickedness grieved and mourned, because they knew for certain that a yoke had been divinely placed upon their unbroken necks. For when the seditious robbers learned that the sceptre-bearing ruler [Col. 0816C] whom they had formerly found a strong dispenser of justice had, with God’s help, proved superior to his enemies in war, they recognized the man’s power, immediately scattered to different places, and through fear of him alone ceased their customary attacks. Thus, their wicked associations dispersed here and there, they changed their appearances, fearing greatly to be found or recognized by those whom they had crushed.

The king went with the duke to Rouen and, favourably received by the citizens, renewed his father’s laws and restored the city’s former dignities. At the duke’s command, Hugh of Nonant surrendered Rouen castle to the king; he recovered by royal force his own honour, which the lord of Bellême had taken from him, and thereafter possessed it peacefully all his life. [Col. 0816D] Other holders of castles throughout Normandy likewise were released by the duke and, surrendering all their castles with his consent, were reconciled to the victor.

In mid-October [1106], the king came to Lisieux, summoned all the magnates of Neustria, and held a council most beneficial to God’s Church. There he decreed by royal ordinance that firm peace be kept throughout the borders of Normandy; that, with robbery and rapacity altogether suppressed, all churches should possess their holdings as they held them on the day his father died, and that other lawful heirs should likewise possess theirs. He also made all his father’s lordships subject to his own authority and, by the judgment of wise men, declared void whatever his brother had heedlessly granted to unworthy persons. [Col. 0817A] He sent to England the enemies whom he had captured in battle and condemned William of Mortain, Robert of Stoteville, and certain others to perpetual imprisonment. He remained unyielding toward them; although pressed by the prayers, promises, and gifts of many, he could never be softened.

## XI. Robert of Bellême again attempts to incite the Normans against King Henry

Robert of Bellême, whose hope had been disappointed otherwise than he expected, groaned deeply and, still striving to wage war against King Henry, approached Count Elias. “My lord count,” he said, “I beg you, help me; for I am your man and place great confidence in you. Behold, I now need your assistance, because excessive disorder prevails in the world. Behold, the younger brother has risen against the elder; the servant has overcome his lord in war and put him in chains; he has taken from him his ancestral inheritance and thus, perjured, has subjected his lord’s rights to himself. Yet I have kept faith with my natural lord and, as I faithfully obeyed his father, so throughout my life I shall serve his offspring. So long as I live, I shall never endure that he rule Normandy in peace who has bound my lord—indeed, his own—in prison. I still possess thirty-four most strongly fortified castles, from which I can certainly inflict most grievous attacks upon the invader. I ask only your aid, that through you I may help my imprisoned lord and restore him, or his heir, [Col. 0817C] to the duchy of Normandy.”

When this had been said, Elias replied: “Every prudent person must provide from the beginning that he does not undertake what he cannot, or ought not, complete. Again, he must take care not to wish to raise anyone unworthy higher than is fitting, or prefer him to others in authority, when he does not know how to govern himself. For, as the common proverb says: ‘He who strives to uphold a fool on high presumes to contend against God.’ I am allied to King Henry and can find in him no cause for breaking with him. I do not wish foolishly to offend so great a prince, nor ought I to listen to you or anyone else in such a matter. For he is endowed with intelligence, power, and wealth; and, I think, no one in the West can equal him in his particular prerogatives.

“If, as you say, he fought against his elder brother and lord, the greatest necessity compelled him to do so, and the supplication of religious persons, miserably trampled by the *biothanati* [violent wrongdoers], summoned him. Moreover, as the people say in daily speech, evil must be done so that a worse evil may cease. I say this according to popular usage, but do not affirm it on divine authority. The two brothers fought once for this very reason: that the yearly conflicts which daily drenched the earth with the blood of sons might henceforth cease. For since the duke returned from Jerusalem and received the duchy of Normandy, he has been excessively given over to sloth and idleness. Provoked by his negligence, transgressors of the law have hitherto raged intolerably in Normandy in every wickedness, secretly and openly; and for six years holy mother Church has been afflicted by their fires and robberies. [Col. 0818A] Crowds of poor people have consequently been driven into exile in foreign kingdoms, and monastic communities have been stripped of the goods and estates which pious barons had formerly bestowed. The violence of the wicked spared no one. Fear and mourning filled everything. As the wickedness of evils increased in many forms every day, nearly all reverence for divine worship was perishing.

“It is unnecessary to prolong the account with further details. Behold, we see basilicas burned in many places of Normandy, dioceses emptied of parishioners, and cities and villages everywhere filled with crimes and sufferings. You and your accomplices have therefore defiled a noble province and provoked God’s wrath against yourselves. By God’s just judgment victory was bestowed from heaven upon the lover of peace and justice, and the opposing party utterly overthrown. I shall make no attempt whatever to rise against him, lest, by offending God who is his protector, I seem to provoke Him against myself. But if you abandon your efforts at malice and hostile schemes, and seek the friendship of the powerful sceptre-bearing king, you may find me a ready helper with him.”

When Robert found Elias inflexible toward unsuitable factions and recognized that his counsel was full of utility and sound judgment, the crafty man, as though wholly changed, thanked the wise counsellor and sought reconciliation with the king through him. Since there was very great intimacy between the king and the count, he obtained Argentan and surrendered whatever he had seized from the princely domain. [Col. 0818C] He obtained the viscounty of Falaise and the other possessions which had belonged to his father. For King Henry, with God’s help, humbled all his enemies and demolished the adulterine castles which Robert or the rebels had built. He sent his brother to England, lest turbulent men under cover of his assistance disturb the simple and peaceable; he kept him in prison for twenty-seven years and supplied him abundantly with every luxury.

Meanwhile Henry governed the duchy of Normandy together with the kingdom of England firmly; until the end of his life he always devoted himself to peace and, enjoying uninterrupted prosperity as he wished, never declined from his former strength or severity of justice. He shrewdly subdued eminent counts, castle-holders, and bold tyrants so that they might not rebel; but he always gently cherished and protected the peaceable, the religious, and the humble people. Established in supremacy on this side and beyond the sea in the eighth year after he began to reign, [Col. 0818D] he continually sought peace for the peoples subject to him and sternly punished transgressors of the laws with harsh penalties. Abounding in wealth and pleasures, he was excessively given to lust; from youth to old age he culpably remained subject to this vice and begot many sons and daughters by concubines. Possessing vigorous industry, he multiplied his secular gains in many ways and amassed for himself immense treasures of desirable things. He claimed as his own the hunting of every wild animal in all England; he even had the feet of dogs belonging to those who lived near the forests partly cut off; and he scarcely permitted the privilege of hunting in their own woods to a few nobles and intimates. A curious investigator, he examined everything and committed what he heard to a tenacious memory. He wished to know every affair of his officials and dignities and, as a diligent judge, scrutinized the varying circumstances of Albion and Neustria. He learned all concealed matters and whatever was done secretly, to the astonishment of those responsible, who wondered how the king knew the hidden investigation. Having carefully reviewed the histories of the ancients, I boldly assert that no king in the English realm was richer or more powerful than Henry in respect of worldly splendour.

## XII. Bohemond, aided by Robert of Montfort and many other barons, undertakes an expedition against the emperor of Constantinople. The death of Marcus Bohemond. Antioch defended by Baldwin against the Saracens

[Col. 0819B]

In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1107, King Henry summoned his magnates and charged Robert of Montfort in legal proceedings with breach of faith. Feeling himself guilty, Robert received leave to go to Jerusalem and left all his land to the king. He then departed with certain of his fellow knights. He found Bohemond in Apulia and joyfully recognized his countrymen there. Hugh of Puiset and Simon of Anet, Ralph of Pont-Echanfray and his brother Guascelin, with many other men from this side of the Alps, were with [Col. 0819C] Bohemond. Very many men of other nations were awaiting passage across the sea; all wished to fight with the aforesaid duke against the emperor, and during that waiting received provisions for themselves and their horses from his generosity. For two years he fed so many companies, nearly exhausted all his treasury, and cheerfully supplied ships to all without fare. He honourably received Robert of Montfort and, not knowing why he had left his native land, elevated him among his chief men because Robert had held by hereditary right the office of marshal of the Norman army. He had long kept ships and pilgrims waiting in the sea-ports, provided abundant food for all from his revenues, and prepared with the utmost effort a most formidable fleet for August.

At last the army of Christ sailed with favourable winds into Thessaly and besieged Dyrrachium for a long time. The high-spirited duke attempted in many ways to take the town, but those who most ought to have helped him obstructed him. For his brother Guy and Robert of Montfort, in whom he trusted above the rest, had treacherously gone over to the emperor’s side; bribed by him with great gifts of money, they craftily frustrated their lord’s efforts. Whenever he had prepared siege-engines and fixed a day for an assault, they, underhandedly alleging some pretexts, would seek a truce or secretly inform the enemy by what evasions they could avert the imminent danger. Thus Bohemond was long deceived by the treachery of his own men together with [Col. 0820A] his companies; and, food failing, Christ’s army was reduced to nothing in a foreign land. At last, unable to endure severe hunger, they gradually withdrew, scattered through Macedonia, and accepted the emperor’s peace. Received by him, they were given free leave either to remain under him or go wherever they wished. Indeed, most of them also received many gifts from him; enjoying his generosity and restored after extreme want, they gave thanks.

Bohemond saw that he could not accomplish his excessive ventures and grieved; though daily urged by his companions to seek the Augustus’s favour, he held out for some time. For they said: “We suffer the penalties of our rashness, we who undertook proud enterprises beyond our native places and our strength, and presumed to raise our hands against the holy empire. No hereditary right induced us to such ventures, nor did any prophet sent by God summon us by a heavenly oracle; rather, greed to rule in another’s dominion persuaded you to begin these arduous undertakings, and likewise the desire for gain drew us into bearing the intolerable burden of labours and perils. But because ‘God is not mocked’ (Gal. 6:7), neither deceives judgment nor overturns what is just, He has graciously heard the prayers of the righteous who cry to Him against us in Greece, and has scattered our companies, worn down not by battle but by hunger, and abolished our strength without bloodshed. Therefore, we beseech you, make peace with the emperor before you are captured or condemned to death, and all your followers, when you fall, are immediately assigned to inextricable miseries.”

Hearing this, the worthy duke understood the manifest defection of his men and finally, lest he incur irreparable disgrace together with loss, unwillingly yielded and made peace with the Augustus [1108]; from there he returned sadly to Apulia. He was ashamed before the French, to whom he had promised very great kingdoms, and with embarrassment allowed them to complete their pilgrimage [1109]. Then Hugh of Puiset and Ralph of Pont-Echanfray, with his brother Guascelin and many others, went to Constantinople; they were honoured with many gifts by Emperor Alexius and then departed for Jerusalem. In the imperial city the wife [Col. 0820D] of Ralph, daughter of Goislen of Leugis, died and was honourably buried there. Some, after completing their devotions, returned to their native land and met the end of their lives through various chances. Guy soon afterward fell ill and openly acknowledged the treachery he had committed, but was never able to obtain absolution from his brother. Robert also, a participant in the same treachery, then died and was praised by no one’s lips, as his deserts required.

In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1111, in the fourth indiction, Marcus Bohemond died in the name of Jesus after many struggles and triumphs. The praiseworthy knight Tancred succeeded him for some years, to confound the pagans. After Tancred’s death, Roger, son of Richard and cousin of the aforesaid princes, assumed the principality of Antioch [Col. 0821A] but, hindered by misfortune, held it only a short time.

The death of these unconquered princes was heard throughout the world. Great mourning therefore arose among Christians and joy among pagans. Accordingly the amir Ghazi, nephew of the sultan, prince of Persia, undertook war against the Christians and besieged Sardanas, a Christian castle ten leagues from Antioch, with a huge multitude. Roger, son of Richard and prince of Antioch, went to war [in the year 1119] despite Patriarch Bernard’s prohibition and would not wait for Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, whom they had summoned. He was indeed a bold and ready knight, but inferior to his predecessors, being wicked, obstinate, and rash.

[Col. 0821B] The pontiff, solicitous for his people in a fatherly manner, said to the overly hasty duke: “Brave duke, govern your courage prudently, and wait for King Baldwin, Joscelin, and the other faithful nobles, who are urgently making their way to our aid. Rash haste has grievously harmed many and deprived the greatest princes of life and victory. Search ancient and modern histories, and carefully consider the wondrous fortunes of kings. Recall Saul, Josiah, and Judas Maccabaeus; recall also the Romans defeated by Hannibal at Cannae. Take diligent precautions lest you and those subject to you be hurled into a like ruin. Wait for your venerable companions, who excel in faith and manifold virtue; with them fight the pagans in the strength of almighty God, and, with God’s help, you shall enjoy the victory you desire.”

The provident prelate spoke these and many similar things. But the proud prince despised everything, departed, and made camp at Sarmada with seven thousand men. Then the amir Ghazi and the great masses of pagans suddenly raised the siege and quickly descended from the neighbouring hills to the plain, covering the surface of the earth with their multitude like locusts. They then rushed upon the Christians’ tents, savagely fell upon the unprepared men, and killed Prince Roger with seven thousand men in the plain of Sarmada. Robert of Vieux-Pont and other knights or squires who had gone out in the morning to forage, hunt birds, or for other reasons [Col. 0821D] had left the tents, saw the sudden attack, fled seven leagues to the city, and roused the citizens with dreadful reports to defend their homeland. Nearly one hundred and forty escaped outside the camp; through God’s salvation they were preserved for the protection of the faithful.

When this became known, Patriarch Bernard, with all the clergy and laity whom he could find, rose manfully for the city’s defence. Cecilia also, daughter of Philip king of the French and formerly Tancred’s wife, made Gervase the Breton, son of Haimon, viscount of Dol, a knight and equipped many other squires in military armour against the pagans. [Col. 0822A] Exalted by so great a slaughter of Christians, the pagans rushed in a mass to the city, intending unexpectedly to enter Antioch after its defenders had been killed. But God intervened, and by the hands of a few faithful men they were wholly driven back from Antioch’s barriers.

After fifteen days, the king of Jerusalem and Pons, count of Tripoli, gathered with their forces at the castle of Harim; having engaged in battle in the name of gracious Jesus, they won and broke the horns—the power—of the pagans. There the young warrior Gervase killed the amir Ghazi [Note: [Col. 0821D] Chesnius: “Amir Ghazi killed the nephew of Sultan Ghazi.”], and Christian valour routed the pagan forces. The Christians were enriched with the spoils of the nations and eagerly gave thanks to God.

Then King Baldwin took possession of Antioch because the line of Tancred had failed [Col. 0822B] and held it for some years against the pagans. At last the young Bohemond of Apulia came to Syria; received by all with great rejoicing, he married the king’s daughter and recovered all his father’s possessions. For about four years he flourished brilliantly, following in his father’s footsteps, but, like a most beautiful flower, soon withered. [Note: [Col. 0822D] Young Bohemond died in the year 1130.]

## XIII. King Baldwin is captured by the Saracens

Meanwhile [in the year 1123], Balad Sahanas—that is, the *vicecomes* [viscount] of Baghdad—who had married the daughter of Roduan, king of Aleppo, and obtained her kingdom with her, had long fought fiercely against the Christians. This veteran warrior, while besieging the city of Mambij and thirsting also for the Christians’ destruction, [Col. 0822C] learned that King Baldwin, Joscelin, and very many others intended to go to Raqqa and had resolved to celebrate the Easter solemnities there. In the last week of Lent he secretly departed from the siege with forty thousand men and captured Joscelin of Turbessel and Gualeran of Puiset, who had gone ahead, on Maundy Thursday. Then, like a wolf, he hid with his men in a thick olive grove and waited in ambush at the bridge of Toreis over the Euphrates for King Baldwin on Easter Saturday, who did not know what had happened to the companions sent before him. The crafty scout saw the chaplains and unarmed crowd, but, eagerly seeking richer prey, allowed them to pass unharmed. At last he captured the king, who was confidently following his men with thirty-five knights; then he sent all his troops after the unarmed men like rabid tigers and ordered them all immediately killed. And so it happened. All the king’s chaplains and unarmed men who had gone ahead were slaughtered like sheep on Easter Saturday.

Balad, elated by such success, rejoiced and led the king and bound knights to Harran, and thence to Carpetras, where he kept them for a long time. There is there a very great, wealthy, and exceptionally fortified tower, one of the principal strongholds in the world by which tyrants exalt themselves. There King Baldwin, Joscelin, Gualeran, Pons [Col. 0823A] of Gavarret the viscount, the young warrior Gervase, Guiumar the Breton, son of Count Alan, and thirty-two knights were chained together for one year, with forty Armenian and Syrian Christians whom they found already captured there. Balad entrusted the tower and prisoners to three hundred and fifty soldiers for guarding. He ordered the king to be constrained by fasting in order to compel the surrender of the fortresses he especially desired; he assigned the others to diverse services and daily labour under guard. Then he assembled a great army and hurried against Christendom, which he thought without a ruler, and confined Sardanas, the castle near Antioch, in a prolonged siege; but, as the most mighty King of Hosts (Sabaoth) strengthened its defenders, he could not take it.

[Col. 0823B] Meanwhile the captives served the pagan guards; with one foot fastened in a shackle, they obeyed their commands. Every day they carried water from the Euphrates for a mile, and cheerfully performed the other tasks imposed upon them. The pagans therefore loved them as good beasts of burden, treated them affably, and, so that they should not fail, fed them abundantly as good servants and laborers. King Baldwin and Joscelin alone were exempt from work, but were closely guarded. By Balad’s order, moreover, the king ate only on Sunday and Thursday each week; and on those days he fed the three hundred and fifty soldiers guarding him. He also provided abundant sustenance for all his companions and for the forty captives whom he had found imprisoned there, [Col. 0823C] both from royal generosity and in order to win the favor of the guards. Such liberality benefited them greatly. For the pagan soldiers kept them honorably and, contrary to Balad’s command, often secretly satisfied the king with plentiful feasts. The admiral of Caloiambar, his wife’s uncle, assisted him, sending him a hundred bezants each week.

The cunning of the pagans often appeared favorably disposed toward the Christians; but may their dog-like faith perish forever! For twice, during solemn celebrations of their own rites, they chose by lot Christian knights, bound them to a stake, shot them with arrows, and killed them amid immense mockery. At this sight the prisoners were grievously distressed, and preferred to die nobly rather than live miserably. Therefore, after one year, the Christians took courage; and on a certain Sunday they made their guards drunk after those men had been lavishly refreshed by royal fare. While the pagans snored, the Franks took their weapons; joined by the forty Armenian and Syrian Christians who had long been captives, they killed all the Turks. Having also slain the gatekeepers, they gained possession of the entire fortress. On the following day they boldly burst into the city, slew many thousands of pagans, and, carrying off plunder with them, held the exceptionally strong citadel for nearly eight months. Then they sent Joscelin and Geoffrey the Slender out, and through them sought help from all Christendom.

At about this time [1123–1124], the queen of Jerusalem, [Col. 0824A] who was of Armenian birth, sent a hundred most loyal Armenians, wearing Turkish arms and clothing, to aid her husband. Arriving at Carpitras, they entered the tower; skilled in the Turkish language and in cunning, they gave notable assistance to the Franks.

As Joscelin and Geoffrey travelled along an unknown road and, in a barbarous land, all alike feared one another as enemies, they joined a certain peasant who was going from Mesopotamia into Syria, his wife riding upon an ass. As they travelled and conversed together, the peasant immediately recognized Joscelin. At the barbarian’s words the most valiant hero trembled and denied that he was Joscelin. But the other said: “Do not deny what you are, brave knight. I know you very well as my lord, [Col. 0824B] Joscelin. I often served you in your household, and rejoiced when I was permitted to serve your humbler retainers. I carried water, kindled fire, and among your household servants earned food and clothing through your generosity. After some years I returned to my Turkish parents; but I now leave them again as profane people and seek the Christians, among whom I deem it far happier to live than among my kinsmen and fellow countrymen. I heard of your misfortunes, worthy man, and long ago grieved deeply over your downfall and that of your people. But now, since you have been released from bonds and are returning to your own home, I shall give you faithful companionship and shall guide your journey as far as Antioch.”

The pagan spoke these words and many others like them, and Joscelin with his companion rejoiced greatly. Immediately they exchanged clothes. [Col. 0824C] The barbarian went before them as master and talked with those they met; while the Christian nobles followed as lowly slaves and silently prayed to the King of Sabaoth for their common safety. The Saracens, moreover, joyfully carried their six-year-old daughter in their arms by turns, and thus passed unknown through towns and cities.

Now hear what befell those who struggled at Carpitras. Three wives of Balad were concealed in the citadel, and for fifteen days the Christians had not discovered that they were there. Fatumia, daughter of Halis, king of the Medes, surpassed the others in beauty and power; another was the daughter of Roduan of Aleppo; and the third was the daughter of the admiral of Caloiambar. The daughter of Roduan wrote a letter and sent a pigeon, carrying the letter tied about its neck, [Col. 0824D] to her husband, who was besieging Sardanas with a hundred thousand men. From the tower she clearly reported everything concerning the capture of the citadel, the slaughter of the guards, and the ravaging of the country. Balad was immediately alarmed, broke off the siege, and hurried back to Carpitras; having gathered forces from every side, he besieged it for eight months.

Then Joscelin, with his companions, passed unrecognized through the midst of Balad’s battle-lines; reaching his own home, he rewarded his guide most generously. He caused them all to be regenerated at the sacred font, enriched the husband and wife with great possessions, and gave in marriage, with great honor, to a Christian knight the little girl whom he had carried while unknown and by means of whom he had deceived the pagan tribes. Balad long surrounded Carpitras with an immense [Col. 0825A] host, while Baldwin and his men resisted with distinction. In the citadel were many spacious and beautiful halls, and chambers enclosed by very strong walls, containing huge treasures: abundance of gold and silver, precious stones, purple cloth and silk, and a wealth of every kind. There also arose there an abundant stream from the Euphrates, conducted by marvellous art through a subterranean channel and supplying all the besieged in abundance for necessary uses. The supply of bread, wine, and fresh or salted meats would have sufficed a thousand knights for ten years. Thus the courage of the Franks could confidently await Joscelin’s return with Christian aid.

Balad, therefore, in his anxiety, often sent eminent [Col. 0825B] envoys to entreat King Baldwin, promising much and sometimes rebuking him with harsh reproaches:

“You commit a shameful deed, O king, by which your honor will now and in future generations be held more contemptible. Shame! You cruelly torment and improperly oppress noble ladies, a thing fitting neither royal magnificence nor Christian religion. Why do you hold my unarmed wives—who have never injured you in any respect—bound in prison like captives? Why do you confine queens of royal blood in chains as though they were thieves or traitors? What you do is the greatest disgrace to your people and a detestable crime against your religion for all ages. I beg you, soften your iron heart; pity my old age and spare female [Col. 0825C] frailty. Restore my wives to me, I pray; and under oath I will give security to you and yours that I shall inflict no injury upon you for one year, until Goscelin, your envoy whom you sent out, returns and brings the help that you require. Meanwhile, if you restore to me the marriage bond which I desire, I shall withdraw from here and attend to the affairs of my own country, and you shall have my peace until the stated term. Have free trade throughout my whole province; and from my immense treasure which you may perhaps have obtained, buy freely everywhere whatever you please.”

Gazis and Bursethinus, with other distinguished men, delivered these messages and sought by eloquent persuasion to induce king to yield to king.

King Baldwin summoned everyone held in the citadel, [Col. 0825D] explained Balad’s demands, and sought their common counsel. Since different persons held different views and hesitated to give a settled judgment in a doubtful matter, Queen Fatumia said:

“I see, most valiant men, that you hesitate over what answer to make to my lord’s arguments. Now I beg you not to disdain to hear me. Make light of all my lord’s commands, for there is no truth in them. Everything that he promises is false, and he seeks thus to deceive you. So long as you hold this fortress, which is impregnable, and keep me and my fellow wives with you, he will undoubtedly fear you and will not dare in any way to attack you. For he considers cunningly within himself, and often discusses in his synagogues with his familiar followers, that if by reason of some injury done to you [Col. 0826A] you should kill us, he will never thereafter be free from war. All our kindred, who possess the greater part of the East, will rise against him until his death. Therefore confidently await help from heaven and from faithful friends, and prudently guard against the deadly evasions of your wily enemy. You are superior, and can repel attackers with javelins and stones. What do you lack, if you possess greatness of spirit? You have weapons in abundance along with plentiful food. You have bread, water, wine, and meat in an impregnable stronghold. Recall Troy’s ten-year siege and recount the marvellous deeds of heroes which your minstrels daily proclaim; draw strength from them and strengthen your hearts. Fight bravely in the manner of the Gauls and persevere until victory, lest [Col. 0826B] a shameful song about you be sung throughout the world. Until now the glorious praise of Western valor has resounded throughout the whole world, and the fame of the Franks has penetrated the Persian kingdoms. We do not regret being enclosed with you, though King Balad counts it as a reproach to you. We endure this confinement more gladly than observe demonic worship with idolaters. For we embrace your kindly customs and rejoice in your faith and religion, hoping that, if by divine favor we can escape safely from here with you, we shall indeed be imbued with the heavenly sacraments of the Christians.”

### XIV. The remarkable fate of Baldwin and certain other knights

The other queens readily affirmed Fatumia’s words, [Col. 0826C] and the Christians greatly welcomed such encouragement from these foreign women. Strengthened by it, they held the tower and resisted for many days. At last King Baldwin, worn down by Balad’s entreaties and extensive promises, yielded. Although they wished otherwise, he returned his three wives and sent them away under the escort of five brave knights. But when these men presented Balad with his wives, properly adorned, and wished to return to their companions in the tower, the tyrant immediately detained them, to the great grief of many. Thus Guiumar the Breton, Gervasius of Dol, Robert of Caen, Muschedus of Le Mans, and Rivallo of Dinan were captured by lying Balad and given as a gift to Hali, king of the Medes. That ruler was exceedingly powerful, and after keeping the Franks honorably for nine months [Col. 0826D] gave them as a gift to the caliph of Baghdad. On the following day the sultan received them from the caliph and immediately granted them liberty and great riches. There the four champions made Guiumar, son of Count Alan, their lord; and they remained under the sultan for three and a half years with great honor, returning to Antioch in the fourth year.

In exile the gracious God did not withhold His help from His own. For the aforesaid five knights, though carried so far into captivity, enjoyed great favor among the barbarians. The king of the Medes entrusted them to the city prefect and ordered that, dressed in Frankish fashion, they should attend him daily. They were adorned with silken and gold-embroidered garments, possessed horses, arms, and varied equipment, and received whatever they asked of the king [Col. 0827A] or prefect. They appeared splendidly before the Persians, and the Medes, admiring Frankish dress, praised them. Daughters of kings desired their beauty and smiled upon their wit. Kings and dukes themselves wished to have grandsons of Frankish stock. Yet no one compelled them in any respect to abandon the worship of Christ or depart from their own rite.

They tell marvellous things about the sultan’s riches and about unknown kinds of things which they saw in the East. The sultan is said to mean, as it were, “sole lord,” because he stands over all princes of the East. In the fourth year he granted them leave to return and bestowed upon them a golden arrow, the principal token signifying their release. He offered them the daughters of very powerful nobles, if they wished to remain, [Col. 0827B] as well as immense treasures and estates. When they finally wished to depart, he showed them his immense treasure and varied riches. At length, rewarded with many gifts, they bade farewell to acquaintances and benefactors and returned to Antioch under the escort of David, king of the Georgians, and Turold of Montanis. Joyfully they told their friends how they had stayed in Nineveh, Baghdad, and Babylon, and of many things unknown to us which they had seen in the eastern regions.

There they learned that Balad was besieging Monbec and was still holding King Baldwin, after the killing of his companions, tightly confined in prison. Joscelin, who had escaped from Carpitras and had sent faithful envoys to Emperor John, to the Greeks, and to the Armenians, hurried after eight months with a great army to [Col. 0827C] relieve the besieged king whom, as has been said, he had left in the tower of Carpitras. Meanwhile Balad besieged the fortress and frequently sent his nephew Gazin and the young commander Bursechinus to the king. With an oath he promised that, if Baldwin peacefully surrendered the fortress, he would receive liberty to go wherever he wished with all his men, along with everything he asked. But the king, exhausted by long confinement and too hastily trusting the deceitful pagan, surrendered the fortress—to the scandal of Christians and the rejoicing of pagans. When the king came out, Balad ordered four of his teeth pulled out; ordered Waleran of Pusacio’s left eye torn out and the veins of his right arm cut, so that he could never again bear a lance; and ordered all their [Col. 0827D] companions beheaded. This was done. Waleran died after the mutilation of his limbs, and the king was again shut up in prison, where for four years he suffered worse things than before. Moreover, twenty-four knights and one hundred and forty Syrians or Armenians were killed by decapitation. But they live with Christ, whom they confessed and whom they served while living. When Joscelin heard in passing of the king’s surrender and his companions’ slaughter, he lamented bitterly and halted with the whole Christian army. After counsel was taken there, each man returned to his own affairs. News of this disaster was heard throughout the world; the followers of Christ mourned, while immense joy arose among the pagans.

Therefore, after everything in the matters just mentioned had fallen out according to Balad’s wish, and while Christians throughout [Col. 0828A] Syria and Palestine were resisting bravely as though the king had been abandoned, he dispatched couriers throughout the pagan world to kings and admirals. Having summoned them, he again besieged the city of Monbec with his legions. Joscelin and all Christians, hearing this, rejoiced and eagerly assembled to fight against them. Then also, by the will of our merciful Savior, the five distinguished knights were present, having returned that same week, as we have said, from barbarian captivity. A great battle occurred upon the broad plain between Monbec and the castle of Trehaled. Balad, Musci, Heron his brother, and many other admirals fought and strained with all their strength to crush the Christians. There Balad instructed Geoffrey the monk, count [Col. 0828B] of Marash, to take two asses laden with gold and withdraw alone from the battle, lest both should perish in battle that same day. For his sister, exceedingly skilled in divination, had seen in the constellations that Geoffrey and Balad would fall by each other’s blows that day; weeping, she had told her brother to guard himself. But the religious count despised the tyrant’s gifts as dung and joyfully offered himself in confession of God for sacrifice. Avenging the blood of many saints, he killed Balad; and himself fighting devoutly for Christ, he fell gloriously. His standard was found upon Balad’s body. When Balad fell, a dreadful and grievous burden was cast from the Christians’ necks. Then nine hundred Christian knights fought against three hundred [Col. 0828C] thousand pagans; and, with the most mighty God of Israel powerfully helping His own, they prevailed. Of the Christians, six knights and eleven foot-soldiers fell; but of the pagans thirteen thousand were slain, whose names were found written in Balad’s register. Almighty Emmanuel, son of the untouched Virgin, happily strengthened His Israelites, cheered them after defeating the enemies through whom, like a hammer or rod of His wrath, He had crushed the guilty, and after the storms of tribulation provided the calm of prosperity. Now, as God thundered, the horns of the nations were broken, and the Christians, praising the unconquered King of Sabaoth, raised their heads.

The admiral Gazis, nephew and heir of Balad, king [Col. 0828D] of Aleppo, succeeded him. But because of the newness of the change and the diminution of his resources, he could neither attempt arduous enterprises nor endure difficult ones—things which his predecessor, trained by long experience and skilled through manifold ingenuity, had undertaken and been able to bear and accomplish. Therefore Gazis released King Baldwin from prison for a ransom of one hundred and fifty thousand bezants, took forty hostages chosen from among the leading boys of Jerusalem and the surrounding province, and demanded a guarantee that all pagans whom the faithful held in prison should be restored. These terms having been granted, he released the king and waited at the appointed time near the castle of Gis, in the territory of Caesarea Philippi. Then the Christians went with the gold agreed as the king’s ransom and, boldly making an assault in Christ’s name, [Col. 0829A] captured the admiral, the fortress, and his hostages. Singing joyful thanks to God, they returned to Jerusalem. Gazis redeemed himself for one hundred thousand gold bezants and made a firm peace with the Christians, but he did not remain long in power.

Meanwhile [1124], while King Baldwin, as stated, was held in prison and nearly all hope of his release had been altogether denied to the Christians, the bishop of Jerusalem urged clergy and people not to fail amid tribulations, but, trusting in Christ, to resist the pagans bravely and enlarge their territories by arms of war, to the praise of the Creator. Envoys were therefore sent to Italy to summon the doge of Venice with a great fleet. They besieged Tyre, a city famous in both divine and [Col. 0829B] secular books, pressing it by sea and land until it surrendered. Finally, after subduing the city, they ordained as bishop a certain cleric, an Englishman by birth, and built outside the city a church in honor of the Holy Savior, at the place where the Lord Jesus preached to the peoples the word of eternal salvation. They made an altar from the great stone upon which He sat when teaching. For He would not enter the city of the Uncircumcised, lest He seem to give the Jews occasion for stumbling if He, being a Hebrew, had entered a city of Gentiles and held fellowship with them. From fragments which stonecutters had knocked off the unshaped stone with hammers, the faithful gathered pieces [Col. 0829C] and carried them through the regions of the world in reverence for the Lord’s sitting; they were placed in consecrated places among sacred relics.

### XV. Events in the principality of Antioch

Ravendinos, a powerful Greek, came to Antioch and delivered to Prince Roger—the man mentioned above—the embassy of Emperor Alexius: namely, he sought Roger’s daughter as wife for John, son of the Emperor. Alexius’s long-standing resentment had gradually subsided, because, endowed with wisdom, he had plainly seen that mortal fate had swallowed up Bohemond, Tancred, and other rebels; he feared intensely that the same fate would shortly threaten him.

Therefore he decided to join his offspring to the line of a warlike people, so that at least in this way [Col. 0829D] his heir might obtain the principality of Antioch through kinship, which he had no confidence of obtaining by force of arms. He accordingly sent the aforesaid Pelasgian to the Normans. While awaiting the common answer, he suffered a grave misfortune. For while this aforesaid hero remained at Antioch and waited for an honorable answer agreed in general consultation, and while Amir Gazis the Persian, as I have related above, violently invaded Christian territory, Ravendinos went with Roger against the enemy, was captured, and ransomed for fifteen thousand bezants. Since he was Greek, the Turks did not harm him; out of regard both for their knowledge of the neighboring people and for the Emperor’s favor, they spared him and, after receiving the ransom, released him safely, as has been said. But he, seeing that Roger with all his force [Col. 0830A] had perished and that King Baldwin had acquired the kingdom of Jerusalem and the principality of Antioch, approached him also on the emperor’s behalf and requested his daughter in marriage for John. King Baldwin rejoiced at this, received the embassy, granted the request, sent the suitor to Jerusalem so that he might see his daughter, and conveyed through him secrets known only to the queen. Ravendinos accordingly came to Jerusalem. The queen received him and her child very gladly and obeyed her husband’s commands. The beautiful girl came out in public, greatly pleased those who beheld her, and, hearing favorable reports, rejoiced in vain. For nothing is stable except what the sole Maker of all things ordains. The emperor’s envoy sailed with his retainers and foreign companions to the island of Cyprus. [Col. 0830B] The duke of Cyprus decided to go with him to Constantinople after fifteen days, and ordered them all to be honorably lodged there until Pentecost.

Thus they were quartered far from his palace in a quite honorable hall. While they awaited the appointed time with difficulty, they received abundant food from the duke. Meanwhile the duke was killed in his house by a conspiracy of his own people, and one plank was removed from each ship lying at anchor along the seashore. Death was openly decreed for the envoys and pilgrims also by the murderous killers; but through a certain wise man who participated in their counsels, it was cunningly prevented and repeatedly deferred. For he said:

“I beseech you, brothers and friends, spare these men for your own safety, [Col. 0830C] and restrain your hands from shedding the blood of persons who have never harmed you in any way. Moderate your acts with the bridle of discretion and the balance of justice, lest through the enormity of your crimes you provoke God and men against yourselves and incur the wrath of great rulers on both sides. Behold, you have already committed an abominable offense against the Emperor: by nocturnal murder you have killed his kinsman and the duke of the empire of Constantinople. Yet you may still flee from his punishment to the Jerusalemites, whom you have not injured. But if you offend the magnanimous Frankish king of Jerusalem, and war presses you from both sides, what will you do? Where will you flee?”

By these and other words the wise hero restrained the murderous men and scarcely kept their bloody hands from the throats of innocent people. Around the feast of Saint John he scarcely secured for them leave to depart.

At last they were barely permitted to enter two old ships; and, with immense difficulty, after many days [Col. 0830D] they reached Illyricum. From there, safer, they made for Byzantium through cities renowned in poets’ songs—through Athens, mother of eloquence and inventor of the liberal arts, and through Thebes, nurse of tyrants thirsting for civil wars. Ravendinos reported to the lords who had sent him the harsh outcome of his embassy; in turn, he learned that many changes had occurred in his own country. During these inquiries, King Baldwin, as I have related fully above, was captured by Balad. After a short time Emperor Alexius died, and John became emperor. Consequently, amid so many changes, the preparation of the aforesaid marriage alliance came wholly to nothing.

The noble offspring of Philip, king of the Franks, Constance bore Bohemond a son. She carefully raised him at Taranto in Italy and, in maternal fashion, properly guarded him until the age of puberty. Bohemond, a boy of good disposition, grew prosperously; when he reached his youthful years, to the rejoicing of many, he took up arms. He strove to emulate and imitate his father’s courage and character, and by many proofs of valor and integrity allowed those who watched him to hope great things of him. When the Antiochenes [Col. 0831B] heard this, while King Baldwin was held by Balad in prison at Carpitras for nearly six years, they repeatedly sent envoys to summon the rightful heir, so that he might safely cross to Syria and receive his paternal principality with the favor of his subjects. But his anxious mother held him back until the king, as stated above, came forth from his bonds. At length, when Baldwin learned the Antiochenes’ wishes and judged that this arrangement would also benefit the peoples by the authority of Bohemond’s forefather, he offered his daughter to the young Bohemond with the counsel of his nobles and directed him to assume successfully the eminence of his paternal duchy. Thus the beloved youth, while all prayed to God for him, embarked on a ship, crossed to Antioch, received his father’s principality amid the rejoicing of many, and married the king’s daughter.
