She bore him a female child. Once made prince, he was gentle toward all his subjects; but he undertook wars against the pagans and, alas, endured only a short time. He ruled for nearly three years and then, by sudden fate, fell amid much mourning and loss.

For after certain quarrels had arisen among the Christian princes, Bohemond and Leo the Armenian, their blameworthy rashness brought the pagans joy in a victory won through the slaughter of the faithful. The aforesaid Leo was the son of Turold of Montanis and maternal uncle of Bohemond’s wife. Against him the young man gathered an army and began to lead it into enemy country. When [Col. 0831D] he came to the Euphrates and made camp there, he heard from a certain Armenian that Amir Sanguin was approaching with a great host of Turks and intended to invade Christian territory. At first unbelieving, he sought confirmation of the report; trusting none of the other informants, he left his forces and climbed a high mountain with two hundred young men to scout. From there he saw seven squadrons of foragers advancing. Thinking little of them, he attacked and fought very fiercely; he killed almost all of them, but lost all his own men except twenty knights. Meanwhile an innumerable army approached. When those who remained saw the enormous companies arriving and begged the reckless young knight—stupefied in mind by grief—saying:

“Go quickly to your troops; marshal your battle-lines, attack the enemy, and defend your country with distinction,”

he did not yield, but, having lost his fellow soldiers, chose to die rather than flee. Thus the beardless youth raised his hand against innumerable foes and, fighting in Christ’s name, met his final fate. The few who could escape crossed the Euphrates and rejoined their comrades. In sorrow they reported the terrible news that their leader had been killed, and immediately all withdrew in bodies to the towns and stoutly fortified the entire province against the pagans. When Baldwin, king of Jerusalem, learned of his son-in-law’s death, he hastened into Syria with his forces against the pagans. Received there by the faithful, he defended the whole land against its enemies and [Col. 0832B] long held the principality of Antioch, until he left it to Fulk of Anjou, his successor, whom he had made his heir.

These things concerning the fortunes of Christians exiled in the East for Christ Jesus I learned and have simply committed to writing for the knowledge of posterity, in a truthful style, as I heard them from those who took part.

### XVI. Events in Normandy and elsewhere. William of Ros, abbot of Fécamp. Roger of Bayeux succeeds him. John, archdeacon of Sées. On the death of certain persons

I now return to recount matters which occurred in Italy, France, Spain, England, and Flanders.

[Col. 0832C] In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1107, in the fifteenth indiction, Henry, king of the English, after subduing Normandy by war, often summoned the magistrates of the people to his court. Since they had long been accustomed to disturbances and wars, he wisely pacified them and urged them all, with prayers and threats, to walk rightly.

In January an assembly of nobles was held before the king at Falaise. There Robert, abbot of Caen, was struck by a sudden illness and died; Eudo, a monk of that monastery, afterward fulfilled his office for many years.

In March the king again held a council at Lisieux. With the counsel of the great men, he prudently enacted necessary decrees for the subject peoples and, by royal power, [Col. 0832D] having calmed the storms of war, beneficially brought Neustria under control. On his return, William of Ros, the third abbot of Fécamp, fell ill and happily passed away before the end of that same month. This venerable man, rich in good character, lived praiseworthily. From childhood he flourished, filled with the nectar of many virtues; in clergy and monastic life he shone upon the world as an example of good works. While still a novice in monastic habit, he took charge of the aforesaid monastery, governed it for nearly twenty-seven years, and corrected many things both within and without. He demolished the chancel of the old church built by Duke Richard, rebuilt it better with work of exceptional beauty, and fittingly enlarged it in length and breadth. He also elegantly enlarged the nave of the basilica where [Col. 0833A] the chapel of Saint Frodmund stands. When the work was finally completed, he had it consecrated on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July [15 June 1106] by Archbishop William and four other bishops. When he died, he was fittingly buried in the new work that he himself had built, before the altar of the glorious Virgin Mary.

Many wise and distinguished men, drawn by love of this gentle archimandrite, gathered at Fécamp and under him reverently served the supreme and undivided Trinity in the school of divine worship. Faithful friends and disciples therefore wrote much concerning him, in prose and verse. They especially chose the epitaph composed by Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, and set it above him, engraved in golden letters:

> Rich toward the poor, William, abbot of the holy name,  
> worshipper of the soil only in his body,  
> returned from Egypt and left the desert behind;  
> now, victorious and rejoicing, he possesses Jerusalem.  
>
> He made an enduring friendship with upright conduct,  
> and hatred of vices; steadfast in both, he was.  
>
> On that all-too-grievous day, the sixth before April,  
> his spirit was restored to its homeland, his bones to the earth.

Adelelm, monk of Flavigny, who lived reverently at Fécamp for a long time and was abundantly versed in a twofold learning, both divine and human doctrine, remained united to the aforesaid father in ardent affection until the end of his life, as may be seen from the subtle writings he produced. He composed, with considerable eloquence, a memorial upon William’s mortuary roll [Col. 0833C] and fitted to that venerable life splendid flowers from Holy Scripture. When these were read, their emotion of honeyed piety drew many tears from readers’ eyes. There, I think, not merely human talent rang out so blessedly; heavenly grace displayed its gifts to well-disposed readers, gloriously adorning its faithful guardian of the bride for the benefit of many and granting that a shining lamp should gleam in this world upon a lampstand. Many who read the title of the roll wept devoutly; marveling at the gift of heavenly dew, they poured out tearful prayers to God for the faithful soul. The aforesaid writer composed three elegiac verses which, in remembrance of the servant of the Almighty, I shall not hesitate to insert here:

> William, benefit and honor of the clerical order,  
> was at Bayeux illustrious with threefold honor.  
> Having sent his wealth ahead, he entered Caen; from there Fécamp,  
> that place itself, celebrates him brought back.  
>
> When the sixth day before April was still remaining,  
> strife found its end and rewards their beginning.

Finally, after the death of the oft-mentioned Father, Roger of Bayeux was elected and consecrated by William, the aged metropolitan, on 21 December; thus he obtained the rule of the church of Fécamp as its fourth abbot. For the first, William of Dijon, diligently and religiously established that same monastery under Duke Richard; John the Italian succeeded him for fifty-one years. In the third place William of Bayeux, surnamed *Puella* (“the Girl”) for his beauty, presided; [Col. 0834A] his successor, received by him into the monastic habit, learned what he was to teach.

Then, on the feast of Saint Thomas the Apostle, the very aged bishop ordained the aforesaid Roger and another 120 priests; and on the following day at Rouen he performed over him the abbatial blessing. Thus the new priest and abbot returned to Fécamp to celebrate the Nativity of the Lord, and held the government now received for almost thirty-two years. I have spoken without doubt of this ordination, because I was present and, by order of my lord Roger, my abbot, though unworthy, received the burden of priesthood. A great multitude of clergy had then assembled at Rouen, and the household of Christ had prosperously increased, nearly seven hundred clerics being ordained there that day in various ranks.

Then I, fervent with youthful ardour, devoted myself to dactylic verse, in which I thus comprised in a few lines the number of priests and deacons:

> The Lord caused me to have one hundred and twenty companions  
> To receive the crown of priesthood;  
> And the Levitical order he adorned with two hundred stoles,  
> And forty-four ministers for Christ’s sacred rites.

Amid the storms of tribulation endured by Normandy while it lacked a suitable ruler, the bishopric of Lisieux remained long desolate after the death of Bishop Gilbert Maminot. It lay open rather to wolves than to shepherds, and wretchedly subjected to robbers rather than defenders. But when King Henry was triumphant at Tinchebray, Ranulf Flambard, the king’s enemy, who resided as ruler in the city of Lisieux, discerning an opportunity [Col. 0834C] and the cunning by which he might escape, sent swift messengers to the king, rejoicing in his recent victory. He humbly sought peace from him and offered the city which he held, if he were reconciled.

The wise king, who preferred peace to war—which is wont to generate losses—pardoned the bishop, who asked for concord, for his past offences; quickly recovered Lisieux; and restored to the reconciled prelate the bishopric of Durham. He entrusted the see of Lisieux to John, archdeacon of Sées; and, having prudently arranged Normandy, crossed into England to attend to the affairs of the realm.

The aforesaid archdeacon was the son of Norman, dean of Sées. He grew up, having been educated from childhood in the church of Sées; he flourished in association with the bishops of that see, Robert, Gerard, and Serlo; and was strong in manifold learning, trained in both secular and ecclesiastical studies. Therefore, having distinguished himself sufficiently in reasoning and eloquence under the aforesaid masters, he was promoted to the office of archdeacon. He sat among the foremost to pronounce judgments of right according to law, and for a long time discussed ecclesiastical business reasonably.

At length the fury of Robert of Bellême boiled up against Bishop Serlo; and because the aforesaid archdeacon especially assisted his bishop, Robert hated him and began to pursue him with deadly threats and assaults. Since Robert was at that time exceedingly powerful, and scarcely anyone in Normandy could withstand his war, the unarmed cleric, greatly afraid, fled to England [Col. 0835A] and lived honourably in exile, having been warmly received by the king, to whom he had long been known. For he was counted among the king’s principal chaplains and was often summoned into the intimate royal councils. Finally, as has been said, the king loved him for the virtues set forth above and granted him the see of the aforesaid city.

In September Serlo, bishop of Sées, ordained John the Levite priest; shortly afterwards Archbishop William consecrated him bishop. He ruled the government entrusted to him vigorously for almost thirty-four years, and reformed the church, clergy, and people of God in many ways.

At the same time Maurice, bishop of London, a good and religious man, died. In his time the basilica of Saint Paul the Apostle was burned, together with a great [Col. 0835B] part of the city. Richard of Belmeis, sheriff of Shrewsbury, succeeded him in the bishopric. He laboured most earnestly on the construction of the aforesaid basilica, which his predecessor had begun, and completed the work in great part.

Then the magnates of England, Richard de Redvers and Roger surnamed Bigod, died and were buried in the monasteries of monks which they themselves had founded on their own lands. Roger was buried at Thetford in England, Richard at Montbourg in Normandy. The Cluniacs wrote the following epitaph for Roger, whom they called an *alonax* [uncertain term]:

> Roger Bigod, you are enclosed in a little tomb,  
> And only a small portion of things falls to your share.  
> Wealth, lineage, eloquence, royal favour—  
> All perish. No one can evade death.  
> Wealth overturns minds; therefore may piety,  
> Virtue, and God’s counsel raise you up!  
> The Virgin was wed to the Sun for three times eight nights  
> When, by your death, you paid death’s due.

William, count of Évreux, now mature in age and rightly fearing the chance of inevitable death, resolved at the prompting of his wife Helvise to build on his own land a house where chosen *alonazontes* [uncertain term] might fittingly serve the King of kings in true religious observance. Accordingly, husband and wife sought Roger, abbot of Saint-Evroul, for his counsel and assistance in this undertaking, and specifically requested twelve monks [Col. 0835D] to build a monastery at Nogent. Therefore an equal number of brethren gathered there with the aforesaid abbot on 13 October 1107. In a wilderness place which the inhabitants called Boucheron, they began to live according to the Rule at the chapel of Saint Martin the archbishop.

They kindly received there many people of differing ages who came for conversion, and willingly showed them the way of life according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. But just as crops suffer many injuries from sowing until harvest, and not all grains prosper with equal fortune or perish through similar misfortune, but grow only with difficulty after being afflicted by various injuries amid winter rains and summer heat, so human beings in every order or congregation [Col. 0836A] are buffeted by diverse tempests: they are not all blessed by common prosperity, nor again shattered by the same misfortune.

## XVII. Various events. Abbots and priors distinguished for piety

In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1108, the first indiction, the aforesaid count and his wife began a great basilica in honour of Saint Mary, Mother of God, and spent a large sum of their own money to complete the work. Yet they could not finish it, being seriously hindered by worldly troubles. For the count himself was becoming somewhat impaired by nature and old age, while his wife governed the whole county; she placed more confidence than she ought in her own shrewdness. She was indeed beautiful and eloquent, and in bodily stature surpassed almost all women living in the county of Évreux. As daughter of the illustrious William, count of Nevers, she possessed very notable nobility.

This woman, abandoning the counsel of her husband’s barons, preferred her own judgment, generally undertook matters too difficult for secular affairs, and hastened to attempt immoderate things. Consequently, because of her womanly boldness, she was disliked by Count Robert of Meulan and other Normans. Their hostility disparaged her before the king and stirred him to hate her by corrosive slanders. At length, because the aforesaid count and Countess Helvise utterly demolished the king’s dungeon at Évreux, and offended the king in certain other matters [Col. 0836C] in which their fidelity to their lord had wavered, they were disinherited in Normandy and twice exiled into Anjou.

These disturbances greatly damaged the building of the monastery, and not long afterwards the deaths of both followed, to the desolation of many. The countess died first and rests at Nogent. The count later suffered a stroke and died without viaticum; his corpse decays with that of his father at Fontenelle.

Since the aforesaid nobleman died childless, and his nephew Amaury lacked the king’s favour because of his rashness, the king appropriated the county of Évreux to his own domain. Hence, as I shall clearly relate below, great wickedness arose, and the city [Col. 0836D] with all the surrounding country lay open to devastation and fire. The monastery which the aforesaid count had begun at Nogent, as stated, remains unfinished to this day under the priors Robert, Roger, and Ranulf.

The first of these, Robert of Préaux, was son of Haimon of Prunet, a lawful knight. Through his great literary learning he shone among eloquent philosophers in the schools of grammar and dialectic. Summoned by the king from his priory, he crossed to England and, after Abbot Gunter, undertook the government of the monastery of Thorney, which he ruled vigorously for twenty years.

Thorney is called in English the “island of thorns,” because it is surrounded on every side by the waters of abundant streams flowing through groves of various trees. [Col. 0837A] There is there a monastic monastery in honour of Saint Mary, Mother of God, which flourishes in the worship of the supreme Deity through welcome religious observance and is wholly removed from secular habitation. The venerable Æthelwold, bishop of Winchester, built it in the time of King Eadred and transferred there, after the Danish devastation, the body of Saint Botulf, abbot of Iken, with many other relics of saints. In that devastation blessed Edmund, king of the East Angles, fell as a martyr in confession of Christ.

Only the monks, with their servants, live in Thorney’s shaded enclosure and faithfully serve God in safety. No woman enters the island except for prayer, nor is any permitted to remain there for any reason; indeed, through the religious zeal of the community, women’s habitation is entirely kept at least nine miles away.

After Norman power subdued England and King William suitably brought it under his laws, he appointed Fulcard, a monk of Saint-Bertin of Sithiu, a man of great learning, over Thorney. For almost sixteen years he performed the duties without an abbot’s blessing. He was gracious, pleasant, and charitable, most skilled in grammar and music. Therefore he left precious memorials of his learning in England for future generations. He issued many compositions worthy of remembrance and sweetly composed delightful chant-histories of Saint Oswald, bishop of Worcester, and of other saints whose line sprang from Albion.

Later, certain disputes arose between him and the bishop of Lincoln, [Col. 0837C] and he withdrew. Gunter of Le Mans, a monk of Battle who had been archdeacon of Salisbury, succeeded him. He regularly established the monastic community of Thorney according to the order of Marmoutier, and carefully built from the foundations a most beautiful basilica with the monks’ service buildings. There, after his death, he rests, buried by his faithful disciples.

The epitaph composed for him in a few verses thus briefly informs readers what manner of man he was:

> The renowned founder of this church of Thorney,  
> The illustrious Abbot Gunter, lies in this tomb.  
> He was ruler for twenty-six years and benefited  
> This monastery in many ways.  
> All whom he could, he subjected by virtues  
> [Col. 0837D] Through which he hoped to ascend the star-bearing kingdom.  
> At last he died, fittingly, on 18 August.  
> O kindly Christ, cherish him in repose!

Robert, his successor, surpassed him in literary learning and shone among the chief prelates of all England through great steadfastness and eloquence. Roger, who succeeded him in the priory of Nogent, laboured for almost twenty-four years in building the new work and advancing those subject to him. Finally, he took to his bed and died, well fortified, on 21 December. A friend composed this short poem about him:

> Roger, blessed fourth prior of Nogent,  
> Died lately on the twentieth day of December.  
> As a boy he learned grammar and read sound doctrine;  
> Beardless, he abandoned the fleeting world.  
> [Col. 0838A] For almost forty years, a praiseworthy monk,  
> He ardently bore the burden of the Lord above.  
> For twice twelve years he was a kindly prior,  
> Ever benefiting the brethren by good example.  
> He loved peace and strove to benefit many;  
> He was suited to everyone, that he might benefit them.  
> He strove with all his might to build for God  
> A special church of the excellent Virgin Mary.  
> Supreme God, I pray, forgive his offences;  
> Merciful King, grant him everlasting life. Amen.

Having said these things about friends and familiar companions, I return to the course of annalistic history, from which I have digressed somewhat.

## XVIII. Philip I, king of the Franks, dies. His son Louis succeeds him in the kingdom. The count of Beaumont and the lord of Montmorency invade the lands of Saint Denis. King Louis vigorously punishes rebellious barons

[Col. 0838B]

In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1108, the first indiction, Philip, king of the Franks, took to his bed. After prolonged illnesses, when he saw that death was imminent, he made confession faithfully and summoned the magnates of the Franks and his friends.

“I know,” he said, “that the burial-place of the kings of the Franks is at Saint-Denis. But because I know myself to be an exceedingly great sinner, I do not dare to be buried beside the body of so great a martyr. I greatly fear that, as my sins deserve, I may be delivered to the devil and that what Scripture relates once happened to Charles Martel may happen to me. I love Saint Benedict; I humbly implore the pious Father of monks, and desire to be buried in his church upon the Loire. For he is merciful and kind, and graciously receives all sinners who seek a more reformed life and strive to be reconciled to God according to the discipline of his Rule.”

After these and many other words had been suitably concluded, King Philip died in the forty-seventh year of his reign, on 29 July 1108. As he had wished, he was buried in the monastery of Saint Benedict at Fleury, between the choir and the altar. On the following Sunday, his son Louis Theobald was enthroned at Orléans and held the sceptre of the Gauls for twenty-eight years, amid prosperity and adversity. He married Adelaide, daughter of Humbert, lord of Maurienne, who bore him four sons: Philip, Louis Florus, Henry, and Hugh.

As human affairs stand, he experienced many changing fortunes and was often deceived in military conflicts by Fortune, which moves like a turning wheel. The magnates of the realm frequently rebelled against him and harassed him and his supporters with losses and repeated injuries. Even while his father lived—when he had long grown cold in military vigour and justice—they raged arrogantly against both father and son and despised the commands of each.

Therefore, because King Philip had fallen from royal eminence through old age and illness, and the rigour of princely justice against tyrants had become too weak, Louis was initially compelled to seek the aid of bishops throughout all Gaul to suppress the tyranny of robbers and rebels. The bishops therefore established a popular association in France, so that [Col. 0839A] priests should accompany the king to a siege or battle with banners and all their parishioners.

In his youth Louis had been betrothed to the daughter of Guy the Red, count of Rochefort, and he strove to bring under his own rule the county which was due to her by hereditary right. He besieged Chevreuse, Montlhéry, Béthelcourt, and other strongholds; but, resisted vigorously by many nobles, he did not obtain them, especially because he had given the maiden Lucienne, to whom he had been betrothed, to Guichard of Beaujeu.

Then Matthew, count of Beaumont, and Burchard of Montmorency devastated the lands of Saint Denis the martyr; despite the royal prohibition, they did not refrain from arson, robbery, or killing. Louis, therefore, to whom his father had entrusted the guardianship of the kingdom, heard the complaints which Abbot Adam poured out to him in tears. He besieged Montmorency and fiercely attacked its three gates at once. Young Simon of Montfort, who had succeeded his brother Richard in the lordship, strengthened the Frankish army by his courage and energy.

Countess Hadala had sent the king one hundred fully equipped knights, because her husband Count Stephen had gone abroad and her eldest sons, William and Theobald, were still held in the weakness of childhood and could not command military bands. At length treacherous fellow-soldiers, who favoured the rebels and desired impunity for plunder and killing, mocked military discipline. They fled and, not through fear of the enemy but through deceitful evasion, frightened their comrades [Col. 0839C] and compelled them to flee, to raise the laughter of their enemies.

There the most valiant knight Raimbald Créton, who was the first to enter Jerusalem in its conquest, was suddenly—alas!—killed. Richard the Centurion of Lagny, a Jerusalemite, also fell.

Again, in the following year, Louis gathered Frankish battle-lines and besieged Chambly against the count of Beaumont. But deceived by similar treachery, he lost many of his men and fled in disgrace. He could not exact full revenge for so many crimes, because his father was still alive while these things were taking place, and his stepmother, through secret machinations, contrived many evils against him and wickedly armed numerous enemies against him.

After King Philip died, Louis became king. Now more secure in wielding the royal staff, he raised his head and lifted his right hand against rebels. First he besieged Puiset and brought Hugh—warlike, but unjust—under control by military strength. There brigands and outlaws had a special den, committed unheard-of crimes, and did not abstain from wicked deeds through fear of the angry king’s wrath and threats or of the bishop’s anathema.

One day, while the royal force pursued Hugh along a narrow path and he tried in flight to enter the fortress, he happened to encounter Anselm of Garlande, commander of the French militia. Hugh immediately struck him with a lance and suddenly killed him. Count Theobald of Blois came to aid the besieged [Col. 0840A] and compelled the king and his men to withdraw by force of arms.

Finally, having recovered his army, the king returned to Puiset and compelled the rebels to surrender through the superior strength of his forces. At the prayers of those who intervened, he spared the besieged. He granted impunity to men unworthy of life, but utterly demolished the fortress. The neighbouring villagers and travellers therefore rejoiced greatly.

He also besieged Gournay-sur-Marne and severely pressed the besieged through lack of bread. Hugh of Crécy, son of Guy the Red, held it, and would not restore it at the king’s command to the heirs of the Garlandes, who claimed it.

One day in 1118, Count Theobald came with many knights to the stream of Torcy and began to fight against the royal forces. But when they prevailed, the count [Col. 0840B] and his companions were compelled to turn their backs; they were driven in flight as far as the entrance of Lagny, and many who hid in vineyards and hedges were captured. The townspeople were exceedingly frightened and soon, peace having been made, surrendered themselves.

The aforesaid count, descended from the blood of kings and counts, flourished among the foremost magnates of Gaul, powerful in wealth, power, and conspicuous nobility. He had many powerful and fierce men who were very hostile to their fellow-countrymen and neighbours. Some of them, as the evidence of their deeds made public, showed no fitting reverence either for God or for human beings. Therefore the king, hearing frequent reports of their wickedness, was angry and sought to restrain them by royal power from harassing those beneath them.

But they, fearing that the king would oppress them and check their fulfilment of perverse desires, fled to the protection of their powerful patron. Confident in him, they often presumed to devise impious acts against God and the Church. For this reason frequent hostility arose between the king and the count, and, while their malignity persisted, many people were killed on both sides.

Once the king attacked Theobald in the district of Meaux, having with him Robert, ruler of Flanders, and other nobles. There he happened to be attacked by the count’s household. Since a greater number of men prevailed, he was put to flight. While the king [Col. 0840D] and his men were fleeing, the margrave of Flanders fell in a narrow pass. Trampled beneath the iron-shod hooves of horses, he could not rise; with his limbs badly crushed, he was lifted up only with difficulty and died a few days later.

Kings, princes, and many people wept for his death; Christians and pagans as far as Arabia mourned the fall of this warlike Jerusalemite. His body was borne in great lamentation by the men of the Morini to the city of Arras, which he had shortly before fortified against Emperor Henry and surrounded on every side with an imposing wall of white stone. It was buried in the church of Bishop Saint Vedast, founded in penitence by King Theuderic for the unjust killing of Saint Leodegar, bishop of Autun.

[Col. 0841A] His son Baldwin, still a boy, succeeded him and with his mother Clementia governed his paternal principality for several years. The signs of virtue already displayed gave his friends great hope of his future excellence; but, like a most welcome flower touched by a slight injury, he withered in a moment.

## XIX. King Henry keeps his brother Robert captive.—Various events.—Pestilence and other calamities rage in certain parts of Gaul

After returning victorious to England, King Henry consigned Duke Robert, his brother, and several others captured with him to perpetual imprisonment. On the advice of his intimates, he ordered the seizure of the boy William, whom he had entrusted to Hélie of Saint-Saëns for upbringing. To carry this out, he suddenly sent Robert of Beauchamp, sheriff of Arques, to the castle of Saint-Saëns.

The aforesaid official arrived there on a Sunday morning, and the people, seeing him suddenly in church, were astonished. Although Hélie, the boy’s guardian, was absent, the sleeping child was nevertheless suddenly lifted from his bed by faithful friends and removed from the hands of those seeking him, lest he be bound in chains with his father. When Hélie heard this, he swiftly sought the beloved little William and, having found him, carefully reared him in exile among foreigners.

The sheriff subjected Hélie’s castle to the king’s authority. The king afterwards gave it to his kinsman William de Warenne, [Col. 0841C] that he might remain faithfully attached to him and firmly resist his enemies. Hélie, wandering through various places, saved the boy and brought him up as his own child until he reached the years of puberty. He led him through many regions and displayed his distinction to numerous magnates and noble townsmen. By prayers and promises he zealously drew as many as he could to love the young man, openly proclaimed the grievance of his dispossession, and thus inclined many hearts to pity his downfall.

Many Normans strongly favoured him and fervently wished to set him over themselves. Accordingly, some offended the powerful sceptre-bearer then ruling them and rendered themselves suspect in many ways. Robert of Bellême especially, recalling the friendship and intimacy he had enjoyed with the duke and the enormous power in which he had flourished under him over the greatest Normans, strove with all his might to aid the illustrious exile, the duke’s son.

Messengers frequently travelled between them and tireless couriers disclosed secrets to each in turn. Thus Robert and Hélie strengthened one another by mutual encouragement and worked earnestly, deliberating about the advancement of the duke’s offspring. They continually approached King Louis of France, Duke William of Poitou, Duke Henry of Burgundy, Alan, prince of the Bretons, and other powerful rulers of regions; frequently importuning them with envoys and letters, they invited them by every means to aid William Clito.

[Col. 0842A] At length Fulk of Anjou betrothed to him his daughter Sibyl and granted him the county of Maine, and for some time gave the oft-mentioned young man substantial help. Yet King Henry’s excessive resourcefulness prevailed, and the proposed marriage was completely broken off by threats, entreaties, and the weighty abundance of gold, silver, and other valuables. Clever advocates were also sent, and consanguinity was debated; on that ground it was decided that they ought not to be joined according to Christian law.

For Richard, son of Gunnor, duke of Normandy, begot Robert; Robert begot William the Bastard; and William begot Robert, father of William Clito. Robert, archbishop and count, brother of Duke Richard, begot Richard, count of Évreux; Richard begot Agnes, wife of Simon, who bore Bertrada, mother of Fulk; and Fulk begot Sibyl. Thus the kinship of William and Sibyl was investigated, and the long-desired union of the illustrious young people was frustrated.

The distinguished young man was again expelled by the Angevins and forced to seek assistance from strangers amid fear and hardship. Finally, after many wanderings, he turned aside to his kinsman Baldwin of Flanders and tested his loyalty, boldness, and support. Baldwin received him warmly, promised him every aid, and, as I shall relate below, perseveringly sustained the struggle for him until death.

In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1109, the second indiction, [Col. 0842C] divine vengeance punished human crimes with many scourges and struck mortals with their customary terror tempered with mercy, in order to invite sinners to repentance and mercifully offer pardon and salvation to those who repented. In Gaul, especially in the provinces of Orléans and Chartres, a fiery plague attacked many, weakened them, and killed some. Excessive rains smothered the fruits of the earth; the barrenness of the soil became dreadful; and nearly the entire vintage perished. Thus, with Ceres and Bacchus failing, a severe famine everywhere afflicted the inhabitants of the world.

This grievous year was the third of the reign of Louis, son of Philip, king of the Franks, and the ninth of Henry, son of William the Bastard, duke of the Normans and king of the English.

[Col. 0842D] In the same year King Henry gave his daughter Matilda in marriage to Charles, son of Henry, emperor of the Germans. Buchard, bishop of Cambrai, received her from her father and conducted her to her husband. Roger, son of Richard, and many other Normans accompanied her, and through this marriage hoped to rise to the Roman summit; they also wished one day, through their boldness or fierceness, to win for themselves the dignities of magnates.

For in this way their forebears had ruled in England through Emma, daughter of Duke Richard, and had raged in Apulia, through Sichelgaita, daughter of Guaimar, duke of Salerno, against the rightful heirs. The shrewd emperor, who had investigated many matters, learned this and took care not to place the foreign-born men’s presumptuous and unwarranted arrogance upon his neck. Therefore, at the counsel of the Germans, he dismissed them all to their own lands after giving them gifts.

## XX. Anselm of Canterbury, Hugh of Cluny, William archbishop of Rouen, and several other illustrious prelates and teachers die

At that time many teachers of the churches, eminent in holiness and wisdom, departed: namely, Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury; William, archbishop of Rouen; the venerable rulers of monasteries Hugh, abbot of Cluny, Gervase of Redon, and William of Cormeilles; and many others were taken from this light. Their blessed souls, as we believe without doubt, are in the hand of God. Therefore the world itself seems to mourn the passing of such great barons, in the denied abundance of fields and vineyards. Even the ungodly, who did not grieve devoutly at the departure of such fathers, were nevertheless compelled to groan under the many calamities which, through God’s justice, they suffered for their impiety.

Anselm governed the church of Canterbury canonically for sixteen years and shone pre-eminently in our times as the flower of good men. Lord Eadmer, who was the blessed man’s monk and companion in exile, wrote a useful and elegant book concerning his life. At last the sacred hero, about to receive from the Lord the reward of his labours, died on 21 April 1109 [Col. 0843C] and was buried before the Crucifix in the basilica of the Holy and Undivided Trinity.

Then the venerable Hugh, abbot of Cluny, after celebrating Christ’s Passion and Resurrection, was struck by illness on Monday and took to his bed. For three days he prepared his journey to the Lord through confession and prayer. He commanded the community to elect a successor and confirmed the elected young man, named Pons, by the testimony of his authority. He then had himself carried to the infirmary in the hands of the brethren, and there, on Wednesday, the aged hero passed to Christ, whom he had served from childhood.

He governed the monastery of Cluny, it is said, for sixty-four years, received more than ten thousand monks into the service of the Lord of Hosts, [Col. 0843D] and after his death was buried in the basilica which he himself had begun from the foundations. Thus two pillars of the churches were at once transferred from the earthly Jerusalem, still a pilgrim among foreigners, and, as we believe, were planted immovably in the heavenly Zion on account of their long-standing holiness.

Anselm, the glorious archbishop of Canterbury, died before Easter and, adorned with the mitre, entered the court of almighty Lord (*Adonai*) on Wednesday. During the very solemnities of Easter his dear friend Abbot Hugh likewise passed from the world on Wednesday. Ralph, bishop of Rochester, received the crown of the see of Canterbury and held it for nine years, being for some time confined by grave illness. Pons, son of the count of Melgueil, assumed the government of Cluny; after a time, for various reasons, [Col. 0844A] as will be related below, he relinquished it. He went as a pilgrim to Jerusalem and, after returning thence, died at Rome in the prison of Pope Calixtus. His sanctity shines honourably at his tomb through evident miracles.

In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1110, the third indiction, Archbishop William died in a good old age on 9 February 1110, after governing the metropolitan church of Rouen laudably for thirty-two years. He was buried in the chapter-house of the canons which he himself had built, and the following epitaph, declaring what kind of man he was, was inscribed on the eastern wall:

> Your devotion, generous hand, and holy meditation,  
> William, bid us mourn your death.  
> That you were a pious bishop and kind to the clergy,  
> Your inward qualities teach and your outward deeds prove.  
> Light of the Church, honour and defender of the clergy,  
> You were prudent and ready for every good work.  
> You built this house and cloister for the brethren,  
> Nor was your door closed to the poor.  
> Your generosity provided for the brethren’s sustenance  
> Churches, tithes, lands, dues, and houses.  
> By your example you taught your subjects to cease  
> From speaking shameful words and following foul deeds.  
> Blessed in a good end, you were released six days  
> Before the Fishes would follow the course of the Sun.

In that same year a comet was seen in the highest region of the sky from 10 June until 30 June. Soon afterward Hélie, count of Maine, died.

For three continuous years, namely from the second [Col. 0844C] indiction until the fourth, an exceedingly harsh famine occurred in Gaul, by which a multitude of people was grievously reduced.

In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1111, the fourth indiction, Geoffrey the Breton, dean of Le Mans, was summoned to England by King Henry and appointed bishop over the people of Rouen. Strong in eloquence and learning, he instructed clergy and people in the Catholic faith and governed the Church of God profitably for seventeen years.

In the same year Emperor Charles captured Pope Paschal and violently disturbed the Church of God, as has already been related elsewhere.

In the year 1112 Gilbert, the aged bishop of Évreux, died in a good old age on 29 August, after living thirty-four years in the episcopate. He was buried in the basilica of Saint Mary, Mother of God, which he himself completed and had dedicated; he enriched it with estates and ornaments, enlarged its clergy, and assigned them to ecclesiastical worship night and day. In the following year Audin of Bayeux, the king’s chaplain, succeeded him. Trained in literary learning, he regularly showed those entrusted to him the way of God.

## XXI. King Henry visits the monastery of Ouche.—Wars between the peoples of the kings of France and England.—The two kings meet and make a treaty.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1113, in the sixth indiction, Henry, king of the English, attended by a multitude of his magnates, came to Ouche, and there celebrated the Purification of the holy Mother of God Mary with great rejoicing [Col. 0845A]. He sat for a long time in the monks’ cloister, carefully observed their way of life, and, having seen the moderation of their religious observance, praised them. On the following day he came into the chapter-house, humbly sought and received their confraternity. There were present his nephews Theobald and Stephen, Conan the Breton, William, bishop of Exeter, and many other counts and nobles with their retainers. Then, on the counsel of Count Robert of Meulan, the king ordered a charter to be drawn up, in which everything possessed by Ouche Abbey on that day should be briefly set down. This was done. Afterwards Prior Ernald and Gilbert of Sées carried the charter to the king at Rouen. He gladly confirmed it by making the sign of the cross, and handed it to the magnates present that they too might confirm it with the sign of the cross [Col. 0845B]. Thus Count Robert of Meulan subscribed, and Count Richard of Chester, Nigel d’Aubigny, and Goël d’Ivry, William Peverel, Roger of Thibouville, William de la Londe, Robert the king’s son, and many others.

This charter was indeed made on the counsel of wise men against covetous heirs, who every year plundered the alms of their parents and, to the great detriment of ecclesiastical property, repeatedly compelled the monks to plead in court. Therefore the king sealed the aforesaid testament with his seal and, by general authority, forbade anyone to summon the monks to court concerning the possessions which he had established by royal decree, except in the royal court. He also gave the monks of Ouche sixty bacons [Col. 0845C] and ten measures of wheat, and commanded John, bishop of Lisieux, to distribute the wheat to the monks at Argentan. The bishop willingly carried this out without delay. When, as stated, the festival at Ouche had been celebrated, the king went on to inspect the borders of his realm and to fortify the weaker parts of the land against enemies and brigands.

At this time [1112–1113], while the sons of light rejoiced in peace and tranquillity and the sons of darkness were likewise goaded by wickedness and unrest, a great dissension arose in the kingdom of the Franks, through which the blood of many was cruelly shed. For Fulk the Younger, count of Anjou, who was son-in-law and heir of Elias, count of Maine, at the instigation of his uncle Amalric [Col. 0845D] strove to inflict losses upon King Henry and with all his strength implored King Louis to aid him. But Henry, endowed with intelligence and wealth and abundantly supported by military resources, with God’s help frustrated the enterprises of his enemies as though they were spiders’ webs, and rejoiced that they had been trampled down without the shedding of his own men’s blood. Against Gervase of Neufchâtel, who stubbornly strove to resist him, he fortified two strongholds, one called Nonancourt and the other Illiers, and gained possession of a third above it, called Sorel. Moreover, many of the magnates of Maine came over to King Henry; having made their fealty, they surrendered their fortifications to him. In the same year Theobald, count of Blois, resisted King Louis manfully [Col. 0846A] and inflicted many severe losses upon him. Indeed, while the king was besieging the castle of Puteaux, Theobald compelled him to flee by force of arms. Thus, by occupying his youth with these exertions, he kept the king of the Franks engaged, so that he could not trouble his uncle, the king of the English, by attacking Normandy.

Then Robert of Bellême brought forth the enormous malice which he had long cherished in secret and openly raised his head against the king, whom until then he had flattered with poisonous pretences. This man was powerful and cunning, excessively avaricious and cruel, an implacable oppressor of the Church of God and of the poor, and, if it is permissible to say so, in every form of wickedness without equal in Christian times. For, having broken the bond of fidelity, he openly incurred perjury when he deserted his natural lord Henry [Col. 0846B], who was then assailed on every side by many men, and aided Fulk of Anjou and the other public enemies of his lord with counsel and forces.

Accordingly, on the day before the Nones of November [4 November 1112], at Bonneville, he was reasonably charged before the aforesaid king: why he had acted unjustly against his lord; why, having been summoned three times to his court, he had not come; why, as the king’s vicomte and official, he had not rendered account of the royal revenues belonging to the vicomtés of Argentan, Exmes, and Falaise; and with other offences. By the just judgement of the royal court, for his immeasurable and innumerable crimes, which he could not deny, committed both against God and against the king, he was delivered into the strictest bonds. When the tyrant [Col. 0846C] who disturbed the land and, through many robberies and burnings, was still preparing to add worse evils, had been captured, the people of God, freed from the yoke of the robber, rejoiced, gave thanks to God their deliverer, and wished King Henry a long and happy life. Then the king besieged Alençon, recovered the fortress after several days, granted Geoffrey, Adam Sore, and the other knights guarding the citadel free permission to depart, and released from their chains Hugh de Mes-David and two other knights who had been captured with Robert.

The French and Normans, with those who bordered upon them, gradually rested from arms; and soon afterwards, through peaceful envoys passing between them, they mutually confirmed a complete peace [Col. 0846D]. In the first week of Lent Fulk of Anjou came into the district of Alençon, and there at Pierre-Pécoulée conferred with King Henry. He swore fealty to him, became his man, received from him the county of Maine, and gave his daughter to William Adelin, the king’s son. Then King Henry restored the county of Évreux to Count William, who had been exiled among the Angevins for fourteen months. He likewise graciously pardoned Amalric of Montfort and William Crispin for what they had done against him. He recalled also the exiles whom the impious Robert had driven out and mercifully restored to them their paternal lands. He relieved with serene protection the churches of God—namely Ouche, Sées, and Troarn—which had long groaned [Col. 0847A] beneath the grievous oppression of their fierce lord; and restored to them churches, tithes, and other possessions which they had unjustly lost. For he restored to Saint Ebrulf thirty Mancelle shillings from the revenues of Alençon for the lights of the church, which Count Roger, with the consent of his son Robert, had given each year at the beginning of Lent, together with all the rest which that count had confirmed in a charter but which the wicked heir had wickedly taken away.

Finally, King Louis, having learned in many ways the eminence, great energy, and worth of King Henry, rejected the traitors who preferred seditions to peace, sought a conference with him, and resolved to establish a lasting peace for the advancement of the holy Church. Therefore, in the sixth indiction, in the last week of March [1114], both kings met at Gisors [Col. 0847B] and, after peace had been sworn on both sides, embraced one another in a bond of affection, to the great joy of many. Then Louis granted Henry Bellême, the county of Maine, and all Brittany. For Fergan, prince of the Bretons, had already become the man of the king of the English. The king had moreover betrothed his daughter to Fergan’s son Conan. Now Amaury of Verneuil and other magnates of Bellême, to whom William Talvas, Robert’s son, had entrusted the town while he himself had gone away to defend his county of Ponthieu, relying on the great strength of the fortress and the multitude of armed men, vigorously prepared themselves to resist any attacker. But King Henry assembled an army from all Normandy [Col. 0848A], besieged Bellême on the Kalends of May, and there fortune proved more favourable than he had hoped. Count Theobald of Blois, Fulk of Anjou, Rotrou of Mortagne, and other distinguished nobles came to assist the Normans; with their forces they surrounded the town and entered it victorious on the third day. It was the Feast of the Invention of the Holy Cross, and the king had ordered the entire army to refrain from assaulting the town and from the work of war. But the knights of Counts Theobald and Rotrou, who had not heard the king’s command, took up arms. The townsmen’s knights likewise came out of the castle to fight in single combat. When the besiegers charged them fiercely and they in turn fled at speed on their reined-in horses toward the eastern gate, they were struck down by their pursuers at the very entrance [Col. 0848B] of the gate. The gates were held up by the multitude of the enemy’s lances so that they could not be shut, and were thrown entirely open. At once the royal army entered with immense shouting and manfully seized a great part of the fortress. Then, because those holding the citadel persisted, fire was set; and the noble town, which Robert had long before fortified and enriched at great cost, was burned utterly to the ground.

Thus Henry, victorious and having confirmed peace with all his neighbours, returned to England. For five years he governed in great tranquillity the kingdom beyond the sea and the duchy on this side, while his faithful friends devoutly praised the Lord God of Sabaoth, who orders all things mightily and sweetly (Wisdom 8:1). Amen.

## Summary of Book Twelve

[Col. 0847]

I. Pope Gelasius II and Burdinus, antipope. Disputes between the Apostolic See and the emperor. Wars between Louis, king of the Franks, and Henry, king of the English. Various portents. II. The various events of the war are continued. III. Council of Rouen. Events of the war. Rising of the burgesses of Alençon against King Henry. IV. Pope Calixtus II. Eustace of Breteuil rises against King Henry. Rebellion of the men of Exmes. V. The account of the war waged between the kings of France and England is continued. VI. Calamities and portents. Events of the war. VII. Battle of Brémule. King Louis suffers defeat. VIII. King Louis renews the war. IX. Council of Rheims held by Pope Calixtus. It treats of the disputes between the emperor and the Apostolic See. X. The Council of Rheims continued. XI. King Henry brings certain rebellious Normans back to obedience. On ancient Rouen. XII. King Henry has a conference with Pope Calixtus. Peace is arranged between the kings of France and England. XIII. Council of Rouen. Clerics rise against the archbishop. XIV. King Henry crosses to England. The dreadful wreck of the White Ship. XV. Pope Calixtus returns to Italy. King Henry’s marriage. Various events. Dissensions arise in the abbey of Cluny. XVI. On the monasteries of Crowland, Ouche, and certain others. On the archbishopric of Canterbury. The English’ extraordinary favour toward monks. XVII. New rebellions against King Henry. XVIII. Death of Serlo of Sées. XIX. Henry, having chastised rebels and traitors, pacifies Normandy. XX. Rainald, archbishop of Rheims. Pope Honorius II. Death of Emperor Henry, son of Charles. Lothair is elected emperor. XXI. King Louis again undertakes the protection of Henry Clito, son of the duke of Normandy, and tries to defend his rights [Col. 0849] against the king of England. The duke of Flanders is killed by Burchard of Lille and other conspirators. Henry Clito receives the duchy of Flanders. Wounded in battle, he dies. XXII. King Henry pardons the supporters of his nephew Henry Clito. Normandy is brought back to peace. Prophecies of Merlin. XXIII. Germond, patriarch of Jerusalem. Ecclesiastical affairs. On the Council of Rouen. Events in France and in the kingdom of Jerusalem.

## Book Twelve

[Col. 0849]

### I. Pope Gelasius II and Burdinus, antipope.—Disputes between the Apostolic See and the emperor.—Wars between Louis, king of the Franks, and Henry, king of the English.—Various portents.

[Col. 0849A]

I. In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1118, in the eleventh indiction [Note: [Col. 0849] “In the year 1117 and in the tenth indiction,” according to Le Prévost.], on the eve of the Nativity of the Lord, a violent wind threw down very many buildings and woods in the western regions.

After the death of Pope Paschal, John of Gaeta, long-standing chancellor and master of the Roman pontiffs, was elected Pope Gelasius [Note: [Col. 0849] Pope Gelasius II was elected on 15 January 1118.]; and, despite the emperor’s opposition, was canonically consecrated by the Roman clergy. At the same time Burdinus, archbishop of Braga, who was called Gregory VIII by his supporters, was intruded into the Church [Col. 0849B] of God with the emperor’s connivance. A grave dissension then grew up from this, a fierce persecution broke out, and the Catholic people were violently disturbed.

At that time there was grave hostility between Louis, king of the Franks, and Henry, king of the English; the enmity of such great princes repeatedly ruined one another’s lands with losses. King Louis aided the exile William in gaining his inheritance, and a great part of the Normans strove with all their strength to support him. Henry, however, seized the castle of Saint-Clair and long held it against Odmond and other neighbouring marauders, thereby greatly harassing the French. Louis, moreover, deceitfully approached Vaux-de-Niçois, commonly called Vani, and unexpectedly entered it disguised as a monk, accompanied by fellow knights clad in black cowls [Col. 0849C]. There he fortified a castle in the cell of the monks of Saint-Ouen and shamefully made the house of the Lord, where prayers alone ought to be offered to God, into a den of thieves. When the king of the English heard this, he swiftly came there with an army and established two forts, which the enemy’s mockery disgraced with shameful names: one was called “the Bad Seats” (*Malassis*), and the other “the Hare’s Trap” (*Trulla Leporis*). Thus the fury of war raged wickedly for almost four years, afflicting both lands with fires, plundering, and savage killings.

Pope Gelasius was exceptionally well educated and, through long practice—for he had served with distinction as the *apocrisiarius*, or envoy, of bishops for almost forty years—was experienced. Yet he presided over the Roman Church for not quite two years. Burning excessively with greed, he came into Gaul and began to oppress the churches in those regions with the unrestrained [Col. 0850A] excesses of the Romans; but, like the morning frost, he quickly passed away when God breathed.

At that time in Britain the devil appeared to a woman lying in after childbirth, in the likeness of her husband, from whom she had asked for food, and brought it to her. Deceived by the appearance of her husband, she ate; and he vanished after the meal. A little later her husband came, heard what had happened, was greatly alarmed, and told a priest. The priest invoked the name of the Lord, touched the woman, sprinkled her with holy water, and taught her what to say if the deceiver came again. Satan came a second time, and she asked him what she had been taught:

> “That violent wind which roared terribly shortly before the Nativity of the Lord and greatly [Col. 0850B] frightened us—what does it portend? It stripped the roofs from churches and houses, threw down the tops of towers, and felled countless mighty trees in the woods.”

He replied:

> “The Lord had decreed that a great portion of humankind should perish. But the effective supplication of those above obtained that people should be spared and that a great fall should instead threaten the trees. Yet before three years have passed there will be fearful tribulation on earth, and very many persons of high rank will fall in destruction.”

After he had said this, the woman sprinkled holy water, and the demon immediately vanished. At the same time a prodigy was seen in England. At Ely a pregnant cow was bought from a peasant and, by command of Hervey the Breton, bishop of that diocese, slaughtered and opened. But—wonderful to relate!—three piglets instead of a calf were found in it. A certain Jerusalemite [Col. 0850C], who happened to meet the man leading the animal from market, reported this and added, before the bishop and others standing by, that three persons of high rank under King Henry’s power would die that same year, and that many bitter troubles would follow thereafter. The outcome of events proved what this foreign prophetic figure had foretold at that time.

For William, count of Évreux, died on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May [18 April 1118] and was buried at Fontenelle, in the monastery of Saint Wandrille, with his father Richard. Then Queen Matilda, who at baptism was called Edith, died on the Kalends of May [1 May], and lies buried in the basilica of Saint Peter at Westminster. Robert, count of Meulan, died on the Nones of June [5 June] and rests at Préaux, in the monks’ chapter-house, with his father and brother. Upon their deaths a great tribulation arose among the Normans.

[Col. 0851A]

For Amalric of Montfort, son of Simon and Agnes and nephew through his sister of Count William, claimed the county of Évreux, which King Henry wholly refused him on the advice of Audin, bishop of that city. He therefore rose with all his strength and stirred up nearly all France against King Henry. He was warlike and powerful, possessing very strongly fortified castles and powerful townsmen; moreover, because his parents flourished in wealth and influence, he stood high among the greatest magnates of the Franks. In the same year, in October, William Punctellus surrendered to him the citadel of Évreux, and the whole city lay open to plunderers. The entire episcopal estate was also plundered, and Bishop Audin was compelled to flee with his clergy and retainers. Then Hugh of Gournay [Col. 0851B], Count Stephen of Aumale, Eustace of Breteuil, Richer of Laigle, Robert of Neubourg, and many others rebelled against King Henry and attempted to restore the exile William, son of Duke Robert, to his paternal rank.

Baldwin, a fierce young man and lord of Flanders, rose with all his might against King Henry in order to restore his kinsman William to his paternal inheritance. Henry, count of Eu, was among the first to assist the rebels by his support. But when the prudent king learned of this, he seized him at Rouen with Hugh of Gournay and forced him by chains to surrender his fortifications. Then Baldwin came with a multitude of Morini into Normandy as far as Arques [Col. 0851C], and, while the king watched the flames with the Normans, burned villages in Talou. The restrained king accordingly fortified Bures and stationed there, because he regarded most Normans as suspect, mercenary Bretons and Englishmen with abundant equipment. Baldwin, gnashing with excessive ferocity, often came there and challenged the Bretons to military action. At last he was wounded by a certain Hugh Boterel and returned from there to Aumale, because Count Stephen and Countess Hawise were exceedingly favourable to him. There, as stated, on the following night he ate tender meat, drank honeyed wine, and lay with a woman. Thereafter a deadly illness seized the incontinent wounded man and forced him, miserably languishing from September until June [Col. 0851D], to his end. All, therefore, who had hoped in him could at once learn that hope ought not to be placed in man, but in the Lord.

After Baldwin’s death, Charles of Anchin, his kinsman through a daughter of Robert the Frisian, succeeded him and, solicitous for his own affairs, made peace with the king of the English and his other relatives.

Hugh, son of Gerard of Gournay, whom the king had raised as a son, equipped with knightly arms when he came of age, elevated among the magnates after restoring to him his paternal honour—which his stepfather Drogo had governed for some time—received as a friend, on the faith of royal trust, the castles committed to him. But he did not repay the benefits of his magnificent patron with fitting thanks [Col. 0852A]. Instead he joined the traitors and dared to rebel against his lord and foster-father.

In June [1118] he negotiated with the king concerning his sister, named Gundred, and, on the king’s counsel, gave her in marriage to the powerful man Nigel d’Aubigny. When the betrothal had been made, the bridegroom and bride celebrated their wedding; but Hugh with his accomplices hastily withdrew from there and on that same day took up arms against the king. He unexpectedly entered the stronghold of Le Plessis and suddenly killed a worthy man, Bertran surnamed Rumicen, who was a faithful guardian both to the king and to himself; he entrusted the fortification to Bertran’s nephew Hugh Talbot. Yet not long afterwards the king recovered this castle [Col. 0852B], strongly fortified it, and stationed there Robert and William, sons of Amalric, with a distinguished company of knights for the defence of the region.

Hugh, however, stubbornly maintained the rebellion he had begun. He fortified his castles of Gournay, La Ferté, and Fontaine-le-Bourg with men and arms and utterly ravaged the whole country between the Seine and the sea with fires and plundering. For Robert Hachet by surname, Gerard of Fécamp, Enguerrand of Guascole, Anthelme and Gilbert of Cressy, and other greedy plunderers adhered to him; they waged a most cruel war in Talou and the district of Caux. In winter nights they ranged far afield, seized knights and peasants with their wives and even their infants in cradles, and cruelly exacted enormous ransoms from them in prison [Col. 0852C]. They had many accomplices there, refreshed by whose hospitality and concealed, when necessary, for longer periods, they would suddenly rush out to crime and crush the country people everywhere with immense losses. Thus they harmed the Rouen province of Bray, troubled it excessively by threats of worse things, and, aided by numerous French and Norman auxiliaries, harassed their neighbours.

William of Roumare, castellan of Neufmarché, and his companions alone opposed them. Often the booty which the others had brought from afar was carried by these men from the meadows green beside the Epte to their own homes. At that time eighteen castellans, the chief nobles of Neustria, whose renown and power particularly surpassed those of others [Col. 0852D], were benumbed by the frost of treachery, favoured the party of the exile William, and rejoiced at the weakening of the royal side.

### II. The account of the various events of the war is continued.

At that time Fulk, count of Anjou, came at the invitation of Robert Giroie, who was defending the castle of Saint-Céneri against the king. With five hundred knights he besieged La Motte-Gautier, which the king had fortified, and after eight days, at the end of July, took the stronghold by assault with great persistence. When King Henry heard this, he came to Alençon and, sending out mounted messengers, assembled the divisions of all Normandy for battle.

Meanwhile, by frequent assaults the Angevins exhausted the Normans [Col. 0853A] and battered down the fortification with powerful blows of stones. Thus one hundred and forty knights, without loss of limbs or arms, were compelled to surrender; their leaders were Roger of Saint-Jean and his brother John, chosen by the king. On the Kalends of August [1 August 1118], the Angevins razed the fortification to the ground and, joyful in victory, returned to their homeland. The garrison, saddened by its misfortune, came to Alençon, but were deeply ashamed because the king was angry at their surrender. Yet they reasonably excused their failure: although they had frequently sought help through messengers and had long awaited it, the ally had delayed far too much in arriving with the necessary force, while the immense violence of constant assaults had pressed upon those enclosed within. Then King Henry gave Sées, Alençon, and all Robert of Bellême’s land in that region to Count Theobald [Col. 0853B]. With the king’s permission, Theobald gave the same honour to his brother Stephen, as a share of the paternal inheritance which lay in France. The young Stephen therefore possessed Sées, Alençon, Moulins-sur-Sarthe, Almenêches, and La Roche-Mabile; he changed their arms, fortified them with his own retainers, oppressed the inhabitants with forced services and exactions, and, changing the customs which they had previously had under the king, made himself hateful and them disloyal. In those days the sons of wickedness sat in the seat of pestilence, and through them many evil deeds were done in the land.

Then Richer of Laigle claimed from the king his father’s land in England [Col. 0853C], but the king wholly refused him, saying that his brothers Geoffrey and Engenulf served in the king’s household and confidently awaited that same honour by hereditary right. Since the young man repeatedly asserted his claim and, by importunately coming again and again, became troublesome to the king, the king, occupied with many matters, entirely denied him what he sought and further disparaged him with disgraceful words. The angry and inflamed young man therefore left the Norman court and immediately made an agreement with the king of the Franks: unless his paternal right were restored to him, he would abandon the king of the English. King Louis promised Richer that, if he favoured his party, Louis himself would keep sixty knights and Amalric fifty permanently in Laigle castle.

Thus confident, Richer came to court and again requested the king of the English [Col. 0853D] concerning his inheritance; but he obtained nothing and left sorrowfully. On the following day his uncle Count Rotrou repeated the request to the king concerning the matter aforesaid and kindly offered counsel lest the sedition grow. The king accepted his advice and sent word through him that he would restore to Richer everything he had requested. Hearing this, Richer rejoiced and went out to meet King Louis, who was already hastening forward with a great army.

> “My lord,” he said, “I recently made an agreement with you which I cannot keep. For my lord, the king of the English, has restored to me all that I requested. Therefore it is right that in all things I should preserve entire faith toward him.”

King Louis said: “Go, and I shall do what I can.”

Richer immediately returned to his own home [Col. 0854A], while the king, slowly advancing with all his force, came to the gates of Laigle. The townsmen wished to defend themselves, but the king pressed them; and a violent wind greatly fed a fire, set by someone unknown, so that the devouring flame burned the whole town. Compelled by such misfortune, Richer went to the king and, after an agreement was confirmed, surrendered the fortification to the French on the third day before the Nones of September [3 September 1118]. The king of France and his men remained there three days in great want; departing on the fourth, he left Count Amalric, William Crispin, and Hugh of Neufchâtel to guard the castle. Then William of Rette and Sancy, William of Fontenilles, and Isnellard of Scublay, for fidelity to King Henry, went to the bridge of Erchenfred [Col. 0854B] and, abandoning everything they had held under the violator of peace, attached themselves to Ralph the Red against the king’s enemies. Seeing the burning of the whole town, the French were not fearful like fleeing hares but secure in courage like lions. They held the streets, emptied of houses, and pitched their tents there, intending to seek their food by arms.

When these events had been reported, King Henry hastened there with a huge army the following day. He eagerly prepared to besiege Laigle, now utterly devastated, while all within trembled. But a sorrowful report prevented his undertaking: William of Tancarville, in whom the king had placed excessive confidence. Catching up with the king in the town called Lived [Col. 0854C], he said:

> “Where are you going, lord king? Behold, the men of Caux send me to you, that you may hasten back to them with your forces. For Hugh of Gournay and Stephen of Aumale, with their accomplices, are stationed on the hill of Rouen and are striving to build a castle in the monastery of Holy Trinity. There they await your nephew, who is coming with a multitude of Frenchmen, so that the city may be betrayed to him by its citizens.”

Immediately upon hearing this, the king returned from there and pursued the bands of castle-men as they scattered in different directions. Then they captured nearly forty men of the Moulin district and, strengthened by booty gathered from everywhere, fortified Laigle castle and held it stoutly for a full year.

King Henry came swiftly to Rouen, but did not find the enemies there as he had heard; he had been deceived by his chamberlain, who had turned him back from Laigle [Col. 0854D]. The chamberlain had certainly brought great assistance to those who were trembling beneath dreadful fear and anxiety by, on the pretence of another false occasion, vainly drawing the king away with his troops.

Then the king made an expedition against Hugh in Bray with a thousand knights and began to storm Hugh’s castle called La Ferté. But an extraordinary inundation of rain soon broke out. At last, after the province had been utterly devastated, he withdrew and then moved against Robert, who had rebelled, attacking and completely burning Neubourg. For the aforesaid Robert was the son of Count Henry and Margaret; he brought claims against Waleran, count of Meulan [Col. 0855A], son of Count Robert, that is, against his own paternal uncle. But because royal power protected his kinsman, he could not press his claims as he wished. Enticed therefore by public enemies, he rose against the king; but after losing much wealth through devastation and burning, he recovered nothing. He was indeed endowed with eloquence, but feeble in the right hand, and gained more by his tongue than by his lance.

At that time King Henry did not wish to maintain a prolonged siege because, with everything disturbed, as usually happens in conflicts among relatives, he did not trust his own men. For those who ate with him favoured his nephew and his other enemies, and, exposing his secrets, earnestly procured help for them. This was more than a civil war [Col. 0855B], since ties of kinship bound brothers, friends, and relatives on both sides; therefore neither side strove to harm the other. At that time many in Neustria imitated Ahithophel and Shimei, and other deserters, doing deeds like those of men who deserted the king divinely appointed through Samuel and joined the parricide Absalom. So did most men who abandoned the peaceful ruler, consecrated by episcopal election and blessing; while falsely professing the faith which they had pledged to him as their lord, they willingly, not from obligation but of their own accord, attached themselves to the beardless petty lord in order to commit evil.

### III. Council of Rouen.—Events of the war.—Rising of the burgesses of Alençon against King Henry.

[Col. 0855C]

In the eleventh indiction, on the Nones of October [7 October 1118], a council was assembled at Rouen. There King Henry discussed the peace of the realm with Ralph, archbishop of Canterbury, and the other barons whom he had gathered. There Geoffrey, archbishop of Rouen, spoke about the state of the Church of God with four suffragan bishops—Richard of Bayeux, John of Lisieux, Turgis of Avranches, and Roger of Coutances—and with many abbots. Present were Roger of Fécamp, Ursus of Jumièges, William of Bec, Eudes of Caen, Richard of Préaux, Andrew of Troarn, William de la Croix, Osbern of Ultrisport, and many others whom there is no need to name. There Conratius [Col. 0855D], a Roman cleric and legate of Pope Gelasius, made, in most eloquent speech—as one who had drunk from the Latin fountain from childhood—a complaint concerning Emperor Charles, the wicked destroyer of Pope Paschal’s good works and buildings and the cruel persecutor of Catholics. He also added a lament concerning Burdinus the false pope, invader of the Apostolic See, and concerning the manifold tribulation of the Church in the regions of Tuscany. He further reported the exile of Pope Gelasius, who had already come this side of the Alps amid rising storms, and requested from the Norman Church the assistance of prayers, and still more of money. Serlo, bishop of Sées, did not attend this synod, but his legate stated that he was absent because of illness and old age.

Audin, bishop of Évreux, sent word through [Col. 0856A] his legate that he had not attended because he was defending his country against public enemies. But “unless the Lord guards the city, the watchman keeps watch in vain”; for on that very day the tower was surrendered to Amalric of Évreux.

William Punctellus, nephew of Ralph de Guitot, to whom the king had entrusted the citadel of the city of Évreux, remembered the old association which he had enjoyed with Amalric at the court of Count William. Thinking, according to his understanding, that so great a man had been unjustly deprived of his ancestors’ inheritance, he unexpectedly admitted faithful companions with him into the tower and, scorning the common peace of all the people, deserted the king and joined Amalric. Elinancius of Auteuil soon joined him with many others, and a great sedition disturbed the whole region [Col. 0856B] on every side. The occupiers of the citadel seized the bishop’s estate and the city, plundered all the bishop’s household goods together with books and ornaments, and by military force brought the surrounding district under their power. Bishop Audin fled with his household to avoid being killed, and wandered in exile here and there for a year. He did not shave his beard; by his dress he displayed mourning for the Church’s desolation. Such tribulation afflicted Évreux, and, after the clergy had been driven out, the divine office ceased there for a year.

In the second week of November [1118], King Henry came to Laigle with a strong force of knights and infantry and devastated the surrounding countryside. The garrison [Col. 0856C], who took great pride in their valour, came out and vigorously exercised themselves against the royal men in military fashion. There they captured Count Theobald after he had been thrown from his warhorse; but the king and Count Stephen pursued with a force of knights and nobly rescued the count from the enemies’ hands. Then such a fierce and powerful contest occurred that the king himself was struck on the head by a stone; but his metal helmet harmlessly turned away the blow.

At that time the townsmen of Alençon rebelled against King Henry; and I shall record the reason why they offended the king by so great a crime. Stephen, count of Mortain, who then ruled them, was young and did not love the townsmen as he ought, [Col. 0856D] nor honour them according to their due rights. Like Rehoboam, he deferred to the favour of flatterers rather than to the counsel of elders, and judged the townspeople disloyal both to himself and to the king. Hence he oppressed them with injuries and unprecedented exactions, giving insufficient thought to what might follow. At last he assembled them all and demanded that they give him their sons as hostages. Unwillingly and under compulsion they obeyed his command; but filled with ill-will, they longed for the time of vengeance. They cleverly concealed their anger, but before long planned an open retaliation.

The count received the hostages but did not treat them honourably. He placed the wife of a certain worthy man, daughter of Pagan of Cacé, a famous knight, in custody in the tower; entrusted there to pimps, she groaned bitterly. [Col. 0857A] Her husband Amiot, deeply enraged, was ashamed, and secretly united in pledged trust many men who had a grievance like his own. Yet the imprudent men feared to appeal to the king, a lover of justice, lest he disdain to hear their complaint against his own nephew. Therefore they approached Arnulf of Montgomery, brother of Robert of Bellême, and through him asked Fulk, count of Anjou, to receive Alençon, which they were ready to surrender, expel the count’s guards from the tower, and obtain liberty for its inhabitants.

The count gladly accepted this proposal. He gathered his knights, archers, and infantry; came to Alençon; entered with his men by night; and, fiercely attacking those in the tower, besieged them. Rumour—than which nothing moves more swiftly upon earth—spread the news far and wide, and [Col. 0857B] it immediately reached the ears of the anxious king amid the concerns of his realm.

When the magnanimous king learned the reliable reports, he summoned Normans, Englishmen, and many others by royal authority; he also called Count Theobald of Chartres and his followers to his aid. In December innumerable men assembled near Alençon and laboured earnestly to relieve the besieged. The distinguished brothers Theobald and Stephen preceded the king and attempted, through the force of fighting troops, to bring provisions into the tower, but could not prevail. For the count of Anjou came out against them, drew up his battle-lines, and began to fight them vigorously. There he killed some, took and bound many more, [Col. 0857C] put others to flight, and returned joyfully to the town with abundant spoils.

Thereupon he assailed the besieged more securely, depriving them of water by concealed cuts made through underground works. The natives knew the passage through which the builders of the castle had conveyed a water-channel thither from the Sarthe. But those shut up in the fortress, seeing that their provisions were failing and that no aid was coming from any quarter, made peace and, surrendering the tower with everything in it, departed safely. These disasters incited many to plundering, and many violated the observance of Advent. Thus evils increased everywhere; they defiled Neustria on every side with slaughter, robbery, and fire. And as the young of the viper, by bursting forth before the appointed time of birth, kill their mother, [Col. 0857D] so the Normans, before the lawful end of Duke William’s rule, polluted their own land and miserably ruined it by monstrous deeds.

While the Christian people celebrated the feast of the Apostle Thomas, an excessive wind caused the inhabitants of the earth immense damage and portended future disorders among men and changes of powers.
