Not long afterward the greatest troubles followed in the world: many fell from on high, while others, by the disposition of God, “who raises the poor from the dunghill” (1 Sam. 2:8), were honourably exalted.

## IV. Pope Calixtus II.—Eustace of Breteuil rises against King Henry. The revolt of the people of Exmes.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1119, in the twelfth indiction, [Col. 0858A] Pope Gelasius II died and was buried at Cluny on the fourth day before the Kalends of February [29 January 1119]; and Guido, archbishop of Vienne, was elected Pope Calixtus on the fourth day before the Nones of February [2 February]. Lambert of Ostia, Boso of Porto, Cono of Palestrina, John of Crema, and many other clerics of the Roman senate were present; to them the special prerogative of electing and consecrating the pope had been granted. Thus Guido was enthroned: chaste from youth, devout, generous, ardent in God’s work, and endowed with many virtues.

He was the son of William Tête-Hardie, duke of Burgundy, whom Adela, daughter of Richard II, duke of the Normans, bore to Duke Rainald. This Guido was the grandson of the fierce Guy who had tried to claim the duchy of the Normans for himself, fought at Val-ès-Dunes against William the Bastard and Henry, king of the French, and held Vernon and Brionne stoutly against them for three years. Thus, born of royal stock, brother of dukes, kinsman of kings and emperors, and imbued with the nectar of praiseworthy manners, he was advanced to the supreme pontificate. He held it vigorously for five years and instituted and accomplished much good in the house of God.

In the same year [1119], Eustace of Breteuil, the king’s son-in-law, was repeatedly urged by his fellow-countrymen and kinsmen to withdraw from the king unless he restored to him the tower of Ivry, which had belonged to his ancestors. The king for the present deferred [Col. 0858C] granting this, but promised it for the future and pacified him with soothing words, buying him off. Since he did not wish to incur the hostility of a man who was among the more powerful nobles of Neustria, surrounded by friends and retainers and possessed of very strong fortresses, he gave him as a hostage the son of Ralph Harenc, who guarded the tower, in order to make him more secure and faithful; and in exchange he received from Eustace two of the latter’s daughters—his own granddaughters—as hostages.

Eustace treated his hostage badly. At the counsel of Amaury of Montfort, who craftily devised ever-greater wickedness and promised Eustace many things on his faith which he did not perform, Eustace put out the boy’s eyes and sent him to his father, a most worthy knight. The angry father came to the king and told him of his son’s misfortune. The king was greatly grieved [Col. 0858D] and for this reason entrusted his two granddaughters to him so that vengeance might immediately be taken. Ralph Harenc, with the angry king’s permission, took Eustace’s daughters and cruelly tore out their eyes in retaliation for his son; he also cut off the tips of their noses. Thus innocent childhood paid miserably, alas, for the parents’ crime; on both sides parental affection lamented the disfigurement of the children along with its own loss.

At last Ralph, strengthened by the king and honoured with gifts, returned to guard the tower of Ivry; and he caused Eustace to be informed that the royal severity had exacted retaliation from his daughters. When he learned of his daughters’ blindness, their father and mother grieved exceedingly. He fortified his castles of Lira and Glos, Pont-Saint-Pierre, and Pacy, carefully blocking them so that neither the king nor his faithful men [Col. 0859A] could enter. He sent his wife Juliana—who was the king’s daughter by a concubine—to Breteuil and assigned to her the troops necessary to defend the town.

Since the townsmen were faithful to the king and did not wish in any way to offend him, as soon as they understood that Juliana’s arrival would harm many people, they immediately sent word to the king to come swiftly to Breteuil. The provident king, remembering the saying addressed by a bold courtier to Caesar concerning the business of war:

> “Away with delays: delay has always harmed those prepared.”  
> —Lucan, *Pharsalia* I.281

on hearing the townsmen’s embassy, hastened to Breteuil. The gates were gladly opened to him, and he entered the town. Then he thanked the faithful inhabitants for their devotion to their allegiance, [Col. 0859B] forbade his soldiers to seize anything there, and besieged the stronghold in which his insolent daughter had shut herself up.

She was then distressed on every side and did not know what to do. Knowing certainly that her father had arrived there exceedingly angry with her and would not abandon the siege around the castle without a triumph, she at last conceived in advance the plan of laying her hand upon the Lord’s anointed, as Solomon says: “There is no wickedness greater than a woman’s wickedness” (Ecclus. 25:26). She therefore deceitfully requested a conversation with her father.

The king, unaware of so great a woman’s treachery, came to the parley; his unhappy offspring wished to kill him. For she drew a crossbow and loosed [Col. 0859C] an arrow at her father, but, God protecting him, did not wound him. The king therefore immediately ordered the castle bridge destroyed, so that no one might enter or leave. Seeing herself surrounded on all sides and supported by no one, Juliana surrendered the castle to the king, but could by no means obtain free departure from him. Compelled by royal command, she leapt down from above without bridge or support and descended in shame, bare-buttocked, into the depth of the ditch.

This occurred at the beginning of Lent, in the third week of February, while the castle ditch overflowed full of wintry water and the water, constrained by severe frost, fittingly supplied intense cold to the tender flesh of the fallen woman. The unhappy female warrior escaped thence as best she could, disgraced, and returned to her husband, who was staying at Pacy; sorrowfully she gave him a truthful account of the event. [Col. 0859D] The king summoned the townsmen, praised them for preserving their fidelity, honoured them with promises and benefits, and, on their counsel, entrusted the castle of Breteuil to their protection.

Not long afterward, because Ralph de Gaël, a bold champion, was nephew through a sister of William of Breteuil, the king restored to him the entire honour of his ancestors, except Pacy, which Eustace held. Ralph diligently guarded the castle received as the king’s gift; he was faithful to the king in all things, conspicuous and praiseworthy for many noble deeds, and boldly attacked public enemies on every side.

At the same time [1119], the people of Exmes deliberated rebellion. For the men of Courcy and other townsmen [Col. 0860A] in the vicinity, hearing that almost all the Normans had deserted the king and supported his nephew, resolved to do the same. First, therefore, Rainald of Bailleul went to Falaise, renounced his allegiance to the king, and haughtily refused the king’s demand that he surrender his house at La Maison Renouard. Then the king said: “You have come to my court; I shall not arrest you. But you will repent of having begun this crime against me.” As soon as Rainald departed, the king summoned his troops and came almost alongside him at his fortification that evening.

Rainald, seeing that he was unable to sustain such a burden, came out in the morning, sought the king’s mercy, and surrendered the stronghold. The king immediately committed the stone house to the flames with its stores of food and everything within it. [Col. 0860B] On learning this, the men of Courcy, of Grandmesnil, and of Montpinçon abandoned their attempts at rebellion, immediately repressed their ill-willed designs lest they suffer the same fate, and thereafter did not presume to raise their horns against their lord the king.

## V. Continuation of the account of the war between the kings of France and England

Geoffrey, archbishop of Rouen, fiercely assailed Ascelin, son of Andrew, in several lawsuits and greatly burdened him by unjustly taking away his possessions, as some thought. Ascelin, therefore, inflamed with bitter resentment, approached the king at Pontoise and promised to betray Les Andelys to him, if he came to take it by force of arms. The French were exceedingly delighted [Col. 0860C] and urged the king not to be sluggish. Once the agreement was confirmed on both sides, Ascelin brought with him very worthy companions and at night admitted them into his granary, where he concealed them secretly beneath straw. King Louis followed him slowly with a body of warriors.

In the morning, when the king was seen, the people’s shouting resounded, and a great disturbance suddenly seized the inhabitants at so unexpected an event. Those hidden beneath the straw burst out suddenly; shouting “Regale,” the English standard, with the populace, they ran to the stronghold. But once inside they in turn cried, “My joy,” the French standard. The natives having thus been shut out, the Gauls occupied the inner castle, and the king’s squadrons forced their way through the gates and took the whole town. [Col. 0860D] Richard, the king’s son, and the other inhabitants, caught by this unforeseen attack and deprived both inside and outside of every hope of defence, fled to the church of Saint Mary the Virgin.

At last King Louis, after taking possession of the garrison and the entire borough, ordered Richard and his fellow soldiers, out of reverence for the undefiled Mother who bore the Saviour of the world, whose aid and basilica he had faithfully sought, to go freely wherever they wished. When the king departed, the French carefully held the town they had taken in the heart of the region and subdued to themselves all the surrounding province along the Seine. Geoffrey of Sérans and Enguerrand of Trie, Alberic of Boury and Baldwin of Bray, and other distinguished French knights remained there. The archbishop [Col. 0861A] excommunicated them because of the ecclesiastical property which they had seized; but, hardened in obstinacy by the opportunity of the time and the cause of war, they resisted for a while. King Henry strongly fortified the castle at Noyon against the French and stationed there one hundred knights, commanded by William, son of Theodoric, leader of the force.

Richard Fraxinellus, blessed with eight sons but made foolish by the frivolous incitement of his wife Emma, though already close to death, took up tyranny with his sons against the common welfare of the people. In the territory of L’Aigle he constructed a fortification upon the king’s demesne, followed his lord Eustace, strove to ravage his neighbours’ fields, and, although an old man, was not ashamed to be marked out among the public enemies.

[Col. 0861B] Then the Lenten observance was damnably polluted by the sons of men.—Robert, son of Ascelin Goël, was the first among the king’s enemies to come to his senses. Repenting of the faction he had begun, he sought the friendship of the sceptre-bearing prince and, having obtained it, preserved it faithfully and advantageously until his death, which was near at hand. Many beneficially followed his example.

The king also ordered Amaury to make peace with him and, once the fortress had been restored to the king, to receive the whole county of Évreux in peace. But Amaury, being a restless man, foolishly rejected what royal generosity freely offered. Since the loss of his paternal inheritance gave him a greater cause for war, [Col. 0861C] he often hurried breathlessly through towns at night, stirring everyone by excessive anxiety, strengthening and urging his allied companions to guard their fortifications carefully, keep sleepless watch against cunning scouts, harry the neighbourhood prudently and vigorously, strip everything bare except churches, or manfully subdue it to themselves. He persistently pursued the labour of war for the hereditary countship which the king would not permit him to hold.

But Ralph Rufus sometimes made himself a serious obstacle to them and powerfully frustrated their designs. He was courageous, skilled in warfare, and distinguished and renowned for valour and boldness. Once, while the king’s household was campaigning in the Vexin and French strength, as the fortune of war had it, was superior and put the enemy to flight, [Col. 0861D] the warhorse of Richard, the king’s son, was suddenly killed beneath him, and the young man was almost captured by the enemy. When Ralph saw this, he immediately leapt down from his own horse and said to the king’s son: “Mount at once and flee, lest you be captured.” Richard immediately departed; Ralph was taken prisoner, but after fifteen days was released in exchange for Galo of Trie. This knight was Enguerrand’s full brother and had shortly before been captured; he groaned, gasping, in the king’s harsh prison. Not long afterwards he died from the wounds and beatings he had suffered; Ralph was judged faithful by the king and honoured. Thereafter he was counted among the king’s chief and intimate friends; and the king promised him many honours, had he lived for some time longer.

[Col. 0862A] Once three townsmen—Eustace, Richer, and William of La Ferté-Porcen—assembled with their forces, burst into Normandy while plundering as far as the spring of Ternant, and set fire to and burned the houses of Vernueil in the land of Saint Evroul. Ralph, stationed at Pont-Ercenfroi, saw the smoke and immediately set out to fight the enemy, having gathered knights from every side. The king had stationed thirty horsemen at Sap and as many at Orbec because of the raids of plunderers converging upon wickedness from every quarter. Ralph collected them all together, attacked three hundred horsemen with a small band of his own at the crossing of the Charentonne, recovered the great booty they were carrying, captured certain knights, and pursued them as far as La Ferté-Fresnel. Had the enemy’s garrison not been nearby, [Col. 0862B] he would have inflicted very great damage upon them.

Not long afterward the same courageous knight courteously prevailed upon the king and humbly requested that he merely show his presence against the Fresnels, who had proved cowardly and lawless. At last, after Pentecost, the king was induced by Ralph’s repeated entreaties to inspect the stronghold by which the district of Ouche had been devastated. At the king’s arrival the men of Fresnel were greatly terrified and began anxiously to consider in turn what they should do. When Ralph of Pont-Ercenfroi boldly began a warlike assault, they presented the keys of the gates to the king and, after a judgment was pronounced and accepted for their undertaking of rebellion, were reconciled.

Near the end of June, old Richard came to Ouche, took the monastic habit while sick, and died shortly afterward at the beginning of July; he lies buried in the chapter-house of the monks. He gave Saint Evroul a share of the church at Gomfredi and half of his tithe, and obtained the consent of William his eldest son and his other sons to what he had given.

Amid so many and such great storms raging fiercely, sceptre-bearing Henry stood firm in royal dignity. He guarded all his own fortresses excellently, having shrewdly placed faithful keepers in them; hostile cunning could not enter them at will. For Rouen the metropolis, Bayeux, [Col. 0862D] Coutances, Avranches, Sées, Arques, Nonancourt, L’Aigle, Caen, Falaise, Exmes, Fécamp, Lillebonne, Vernon, Argentan, and the other towns subject solely to royal authority did not allow themselves to be torn from his rightful lordship by deceitful persuasions. The lawful nobles also—Count Richard of Chester and his kinsman and successor Ranulf of Bricquessart; Ralph of Conches and William of Warenne; William of Roumare and William of Tancarville; Ralph of Saint-Victor and Walter Giffard; Nigel of Aubigny and his brother William; and other chief men—remained attached to the king in adversity and prosperity and disdained to be branded with the charge of disgrace, treachery, and perjury.

The beardless sons of Count Robert of Meulan, Waleran and Robert, likewise adhered to the king; their nobles, with their strongly fortified castles, obeyed him in all things and vigorously resisted the attacking adversaries. [Col. 0863A] Pont-Audemer, Beaumont, Brionne, and Goisville supported the king, while the magnates just named faithfully served in warfare with their forces.

In May [1119], William Adelin, the king’s son, crossed from England into Normandy. His father rejoiced at his arrival and at once made known what he had previously concealed in his heart. He sent peaceful negotiators to Fulk, count of the Angevins, and, after arranging advantageous treaties of peace, kindly invited him to his court.

[Col. 0863B] In June William Adelin was betrothed at Lisieux to the count’s daughter. This noble union pleased many who desired peace; and although the thread of the young husband’s life was, by his final fate, soon cut short in the depths of the sea, it nevertheless bound the dissenting peoples together in a necessary peace for the immediate time. Then, at the count’s request, the king received William Talvas, son of Robert of Bellême, into friendship and restored to him all his father’s land in Normandy. He granted him Alençon, Almenêches, and Vignats and other castles, except for the keeps, which he assigned to his own guards. He also pardoned Robert of Saint-Céneri, the king’s cousin, at the prayers of the father-in-law of his son, for having recently deserted his allegiance [Col. 0863C] and gone over to the enemy; and he restored Moulins and Excalfurnum [probably Exmes-related locality; reading uncertain].

A great assembly of bishops and nobles met at Lisieux. There the premature death of Baldwin, ruler of the Morini, became known to all, and for the absolution and repose of his soul the king ordered the clergy to ring the bells and pray. In Neustria this produced joy in some and sorrow in others: the Fleming, the king’s bitterest enemy, had fallen, while the Angevin, the king’s friend and lord of three cities, had joined the powerful crowned ruler.

In summer, after long waiting and many kinds of persuasion that the perjured might repent, King Henry made a terrible progress through Normandy, [Col. 0863D] burned Pont-Saint-Pierre and other enemy castles with their towns, and exercised harsh vengeance upon his enemies and those who agreed with them.

## VI. Calamities and portents.—The course of the war

Meanwhile almighty God displayed marvellous works in the world, warning the hearts of those who saw them to be corrected from wickedness. In the preceding winter excessive rains fell, and river floods invaded human dwellings more than usual. The people of Rouen and Paris, as well as other citizens and peasants, are witnesses, for they experienced the raging surges of the overflowing Seine to the destruction of their houses and crops.

In the following Lent [1119], an excessive wind blew upon the Seine and for some time dried it up. From [Col. 0864A] bank to bank a person could have crossed, had anyone dared to attempt that unusual journey. Paris saw this and rightly trembled.

In August, late in the evening, while it was winter [sic; the reading is materially uncertain], the moon appeared red as blood; and in Gaul men saw circles around it like the bottom of a great cask. Then it seemed divided in the middle by a sapphire-coloured line, and the space between its equal halves appeared so broad to observers that, if a similar thing were displayed upon the earth, it would be judged a path fit for human footsteps. After an interval of an hour, however, it appeared whole again, and, as the redness gradually faded, the crescent of the new moon shone in its customary fashion.

At the same time a very great redness was seen to move through Neustria from Pacy by Meulan; and for three nights many Gauls saw such a sign in the sky. [Col. 0864B] Those who saw it interpreted it in different ways and, as each pleased, asserted his own opinion to listeners. The folly of the proud foolishly gloried in future events as though they were past, boldly declaring that King Louis—then staying with the French at Andely—would consume the Normans like a flame and, with the sword cutting its way, subject the whole region of Neustria to himself. Thus the insolence of the arrogant brazenly claimed the prophecy for its own desire; but the outcome of events furnished those same men with something very different. Setting these matters aside, I shall continue the course of the narrative.

King Henry, no longer willing to spare the rebels, entered the district of Évreux and began to attack Évreux with a strong force. But he could not enter, because the townsmen within fought manfully together with the citizens. With him were his son Richard, his nephew Count Stephen, Ralph de Gaël, and a great force of Normans. Having gathered them all before him, the king said to Bishop Audin: [Col. 0864C] “Do you see, lord bishop, that we are driven back by our enemies and cannot subdue them except by fire? Yet if fire is sent in, churches will be burned and immense harm will be inflicted upon the innocent. Therefore now, shepherd of the Church, consider carefully and advise us wisely what you judge more useful. If victory is divinely granted us through burning, then, with God’s help, the losses of the churches will be repaired; for from our treasures we will gladly provide suitable expenditures by which, I think, the houses of God will be rebuilt better than before.”

Anxious in so great a crisis, the bishop hesitated. He did not know what command best accorded with the divine dispensation; he did not know what he ought rather to wish or choose more beneficially. At length, by the counsel of prudent men, he ordered fire to be set and the city burned, that it might be freed from excommunicated traitors and restored to its lawful inhabitants. Ralph de Gaël was the first to cast fire in from the northern side; the unbridled flames at once raced through the city, and, because it was the dry season of autumn, consumed everything. Then the basilica of Saint Saviour, served by nuns, was burned; so too was the celebrated church of the glorious Virgin and Mother Mary, [Col. 0865A] served by the bishop and clergy, where the parishioners attended the episcopal court. The king and all his magnates humbly gave the bishop a pledge concerning the burning of the churches and openly promised abundant expenditure from their wealth for their restoration.

As stated above, the provident king had made peace with Robert Goël, entrusted the fortress of Ivry to him for the maintenance of good faith, and taken his brothers as hostages for appropriate security. Ralph Rufus was a useful link in this peaceful arrangement, for he was brother-in-law of the aforesaid knight and bound to him by so close a relationship. Before the king went to Évreux, he ordered Ralph to challenge Amaury and his fellow-countrymen to battle and conduct military manoeuvres beside the river Avre near Ivry. [Col. 0865B] He also named the day on which this was to occur. Ralph obeyed the king in all things, and the outcome occurred exactly as the king had wished.

When the king saw the city wholly in flames, he immediately sent a messenger to Robert and reported what had happened. Robert at once cried out in the battle: “Lord Amaury, hear the news I am telling you, in which you will gain nothing but grief: the king today has burned the city of Évreux, and the guards of the fortress face the imminent fear of death.” On hearing this, Amaury gathered his fellow soldiers and returned sorrowfully to his own lands because of his city’s destruction.

[Col. 0865C] Philip and Florus, sons of King Philip of France and nephews of Amaury through their mother Bertrada, as well as William Punctellus and Richard of Évreux, son of Fulk the provost, and other valiant knights defended the fortress. With the entire city ablaze, they resisted more confidently and eagerly, since the citizens having fled, they now had less to defend. The inhabitants of the destroyed city were scattered everywhere and, having lost all they possessed, were forced miserably to wander abroad in temporary shelters.

The moderate king ordered those in the tower to surrender it to him, promised much and forgave all their offences. When they consented, he hastened to other business of the realm. But after several days he returned by night with a great force and, before dawn, by candlelight, began suddenly to fortify the castle; he entrusted it to warlike defenders. [Col. 0865D] Ralph Rufus and Simon de Moulins had been appointed commanders there, along with Gilbert of Exmes and very many others outstanding for their proven valour. In them the king placed confidence; through them he restrained his enemies and recovered the country that had been taken from him.

Amaury and Eustace, Odo of Gomerz, Guy Malvoisin, and other very valiant knights stayed at Pacy. With great boldness and courage they visited their followers, strengthened them by their visit, and frequently harassed the king’s garrisons with fierce raids. Nevertheless, the latter were never unprepared, since they constantly and cautiously guarded against hostile enemies. Armoured in mail and helmets, they met their adversaries [Col. 0866A] as fierce as lions and exchanged notable blows with lances and swords. Neither side wished to be defeated by the other; each burned to be thought the bravest, and therefore daily fighting cast down many men.

There William, knight and son of Roger of Saint-Laurent, was killed. His body was buried in the cloister of Saint Victor the martyr. His nobility derived from the most illustrious barons of Caux, and his renowned courage had many times been demonstrated among the foremost warriors of the Talou. Thus the frequent exercise of savage Mars shed much blood and cruelly tore life from handsome young men, inflicting mournful loss upon many.

King Louis besieged the castle of Dangu and fiercely pressed Robert, its defender, with the strong force of the French. At last the townsman, by the counsel of friends besieged outside, burned the castle by setting fire to it; departing, he left the enemy nothing but ashes. In the same week he rushed with the garrison of Gisors against the French and carried off immense booty from Calvimont and its villages. King Louis of France, delighted by Dangu’s conflagration, celebrated exultantly and besieged Neufchâtel, which William Rufus had built at Fosselmont near the Epte; [Col. 0866B] but he did not gain everything he desired. For Walter Riblard stoutly resisted with the royal retainers and inflicted very severe wounds upon the besiegers by missiles he directed at them.

After fifteen days Amaury sent the king a messenger, who informed him of the burning of Évreux and other misfortunes [Col. 0866C] and urgently requested his swift aid. Hearing this, the king departed immediately and, after burning the huts, left joy to his enemies. There Enguerrand of Trie, a most worthy knight, was wounded in the brow and, after some days, became insane and died miserably.

Meanwhile King Louis swiftly completed a progress through France, again suddenly entered Normandy from Étampes, and brought several warlike knights with him. On the twentieth day of August [1119], King Henry heard Mass at Noyon and went out with his greatest magnates to campaign against the enemy, unaware that the king of France had then come to Andely. The sceptre-bearer of Albion advanced with a distinguished host of armed men; his rapacious men-at-arms harvested the grain around Étrépagny, and he ordered very large bundles to be carried on the backs of warhorses to the castle of Lyons. The king had stationed four knights above Guarclives to keep watch lest anyone from another direction devise any hindrance against them. Seeing helmeted men with banners making for Noyon, they immediately reported it to their king.

## VII. The battle of Brémule. King Louis suffers defeat.

On the same day King Louis left Andely with the French squadrons, and repeatedly complained to his men that they had been unable to find the king of the English in open country. For, not knowing that the king was so near, he hurried with a distinguished force of knights to Nogent, since he hoped that on that same day he would gain that castle through a plot of treachery [Col. 0867A]. But matters turned out very differently: victory in battle separated those swelling with pride and eager for war from their equals in war, and pursued those who had marched forth in triumphal pomp once they had been cast down and put to flight. Burchard of Montmorency and other prudent men advised Louis against making war in Neustria; but the furious men of Calvimont compelled him to enter the contest. William the Chamberlain also tried to draw Henry back from battle; but William de Warenne and Roger of Bienfaite encouraged him manfully.

Then it became openly known, through messengers passing between them and rumour-mongers spreading the report everywhere, that both kings had advanced with their companies and, if they wished to fight now, could meet at close quarters. The French had already approached Nogent and burned the storehouse of the monks of Buscheron [Col. 0867B]; the English had seen its smoke rising high as a signal. Near the hill called Guarcliva lies open country and a very broad plain, called Brenmula by the inhabitants. There Henry, king of the English, dismounted with five hundred knights. The warlike hero put on his arms and prudently arranged the iron-clad battle-lines of his combatants.

There were there his two sons, Robert and Richard, excellent knights, and three counts: Henry of Eu, William de Warenne, and Walter Giffard. Roger, son of Richard, and Walter of Alfage, his kinsman; William of Tancarville and William of Roumare; Nigel of Aubigny and very many others attended the king [Col. 0867C]. They were comparable to the Scipios, the Mariuses, or the Catos, Roman censors, because, as the outcome proved, they possessed great strength of secular judgment and knightly valour. Edward of Salisbury, a stout champion whose proven strength was widely known and whose steadfastness endured unto death, bore the standard there. When King Louis saw what he had long desired, he assembled four hundred knights whom he could then have ready, and ordered them to act courageously in battle for the preservation of justice and the liberty of the realm, lest the glory of the French perish through their cowardice.

There William Clito, son of Robert, duke of the Normans, took up arms in order to free his father from long imprisonment and claim for himself his ancestral inheritance. There too Matthew, count of Beaumont [Col. 0867D], Guy of Clermont, Otmund of Calvimont, William of Garland, commander of the French knighthood, Peter of Mantes, Philip of Montbray, and Burchard of Montmorency stood ready for battle. Among the Normans, Baldric of Bray, William Crispin, and many others joined the French. All these men, swollen with pride, assembled at Brenmula and began vigorously to fight against the Normans.

At the first encounter the Gauls began to strike fiercely, but, rushing forward without order, were defeated; quickly exhausted, they turned their backs. Richard, the king’s son, and one hundred knights mounted on horseback stood prepared for battle. The rest fought on foot in the field with the king. In the first line William [Col. 0868A] Crispin and eighty horsemen charged against the Normans; but when their horses were immediately killed, all were surrounded and held fast. Then Geoffrey of Serran and other men of the Vexin struck bravely and forced the whole line to waver somewhat backward. Yet the hardened warriors recovered courage and strength, and captured Burchard, Otmund, Alberic of Marolles, and many other Frenchmen after throwing them down.

Seeing this, the French said to the king: “Our eighty knights who went forward are nowhere to be seen. The enemy surpass us in number and strength. Burchard and Otmund, and other foremost champions, have already been captured; and our squadrons, wavering in great part, are diminished. Therefore withdraw, we beseech you, lord, lest irreparable loss [Col. 0868B] befall us.” Louis accepted their advice and fled swiftly with Baldwin of the Wood. The victors captured one hundred and forty knights and pursued the rest as far as the gates of Andely. Those who had come proudly by a single road fled in confusion by many winding paths.

But William Crispin, surrounded with his men as has been said, when he caught sight of the king, ran through the midst of the battle-lines toward the man whom he hated most and dealt a deadly blow with his sword upon his head. But the collar of the distinguished prince’s special cuirass kept his head unharmed. Immediately Roger, son of Richard, struck the rash assailant, captured him after he had fallen, and, lying upon him, protected him lest the friends standing about should at once kill him in revenge for the king. For he was attacked by many men and was scarcely saved by Roger [Col. 0868C]. He had indeed undertaken a wicked rashness: he had raised the right hand that struck with a spear against the head which had been anointed with holy chrism through pontifical ministry and had borne the royal diadem while the peoples rejoiced and sang thanks and praises to the Lord God.

In the combat of the two kings, in which there were nearly nine hundred knights, I learned that only three were killed. For all were everywhere clothed in iron, and, from fear of God and from recognition of their fellowship, they spared one another in turn; nor did they strive so much to kill those fleeing as to capture them. Christian warriors, indeed, did not thirst for the shedding of their brothers’ blood, but, by God’s gift, rejoiced in a lawful triumph for the benefit of holy Church [Col. 0868D] and the peace of the faithful. There the valiant Guy and Otmund, Burchard and William Crispin, and many others, as stated above, were captured and taken that same day by the returning men to Nogent. Nogent is three leagues from Andely, and at that time, while wars raged, the whole region was deserted. In the midst of it the rulers suddenly met; a mighty clamour of fighters rang out, the tumultuous clash of arms roared, and the overthrow of noble barons inspired horror.

The king of the French, fleeing, wandered alone in the wood; but a peasant who did not recognize him happened to find him. The king earnestly begged him, and moreover promised him much under oath [Col. 0869A], that he should show him a shorter road to Andely or, for a great reward, accompany him there. Assured of excellent payment, the man consented and led the trembling prince to Andely. The king feared both that his guide might betray him and that pursuing enemies might seize him. At last, when the countryman saw the king’s imperial retinue courteously meeting him at Andely, he set little value on whatever reward he had received and bitterly lamented, condemning his own dullness, once he realized how great a profit he had lost through ignorance of the man.

King Henry redeemed the standard of King Louis from the champion who had captured it for twenty marks of silver [Col. 0869B], and retained it as testimony to the victory granted him from heaven. On the following day, however, he sent the king’s horse (*mannum*) back to him, with saddle, bridle, and all its equipment, as befitted a king. William Atheling also sent back to his cousin William Clito the palfrey which he had lost in battle the previous day, and, at his provident father’s prompting, dispatched other gifts necessary for the exile.

The king distributed the prisoners among towns; and he completely released Burchard, Hervé of Gisors, and several others, because they were men of both kings, allowing them to depart free from bonds. The renowned Guy of Clermont fell ill at Rouen and died, to the grief of the king, who had kept the famous champion in prison. But Otmund, a worthless old rascal, was banished to Arques, where, as he deserved, he was held fast in iron fetters and chains until the kings’ reconciliation [Col. 0869C]. His ill repute was reported as far as Illyricum, because he supported thieves and robbers in increasing their crimes. He despoiled pilgrims, the poor, widows, unarmed monks, and clerics, and was not ashamed to assail them in many ways.

Peter of Mantes and some other fugitives threw away their identifying marks lest they be recognized; cleverly mingling with the pursuers, they shouted the cry of the victors and proclaimed, with feigned praise, the greatness of King Henry and his men. Robert of Courcy the younger pursued the French as far as the borough, and there was detained by those whom he supposed to be his fellow soldiers. He alone among the Normans was captured—not as a coward, since he was alone in an enemy town, surrounded by many men and shut up in prison [Col. 0869D].

The misfortune that had befallen the French in Normandy was spread far and wide, and throughout every province on this side of the Alps was everywhere repeated by mourners or mockers. The arrogant were ashamed; the fighters who had been present in the battle sought various evasions against their scoffers; and different men advanced different lies to excuse their disgrace.

### VIII. King Louis Renews the War

King Louis, saddened by the capture of the one hundred and forty knights whom the jubilant victors had brought to Nogent, went to Paris. There Amalric, who had not been present in the battle, visited him to offer consolation. As the king lamented the flight and capture of his men and turned many matters over in his mind, Amalric said:

“My lord should not be saddened by an adverse outcome, for such are the chances of war, and they have often befallen the greatest and most famous emperors. Fortune, or her wheel, is changeable. For the one whom she suddenly raises she casts down in a moment; conversely, she raises with better hope one who has been overthrown and trampled upon. Therefore now, considering the resources of Gaul and gathering immense forces from every side, rise up and accept the sound counsel that I offer for repairing the losses to our honour and power. Let the bishops, counts, and other powers of your kingdom assemble with you; and let the priests, with all their parishioners, go with you wherever you command, so that a common army may inflict common vengeance upon [Col. 0870B] the public enemies.

“I, who was absent from the expedition recently completed, shall take part with my men, and shall furnish you counsel and assistance while preserving my duchy. I have a strong fortress at Cintray, where Waleran of Tani and other most faithful companions await me and protect the surrounding country against the townsmen of Breteuil. There we shall assemble in safety, and from there we shall attack Breteuil, which lies in the heart of Normandy. If we can gain it, we shall restore it to Eustace, who has been disinherited on our account; and Ralph of Conches, my nephew, will join us with all his men and fortifications. He possesses the strong castles of Conches and Tosny, Portes and Acquigny; proven barons hold his lordship, and through him alone they will greatly increase our numbers [Col. 0870C]. For he is now hemmed in by Breteuil and does not support us because he does not dare, lest his whole land be immediately devastated.”

Cheered by these words, the king decreed that everything should be done as the aforesaid hero had proposed. He therefore sent swift couriers and communicated his edict to the bishops. They gladly obeyed him and placed the priests of their dioceses, together with their parishioners, under anathema unless they hastened at the appointed time for the king’s expedition and crushed the rebellious Normans with all their strength.

Thus Burgundians and men of Bourges, Auvergnats and men of Sens, Parisians and Orléanais, men of Vermandois [Col. 0870D] and Beauvaisis, Laonnais and Étampois, and many others, went greedily like wolves toward prey. As soon as they had left their homes, they began even in their own regions to seize whatever they could. This untamed people hungered insatiably for plunder and irreverently despoiled churches along the way, oppressing neighbouring monks and clerics as enemies. There was no royal justice among these criminals; episcopal severity was then wholly inactive, and each person did with impunity whatever chance impulse suggested to him. The bishops of Noyon and Laon, and many others, were on that expedition and, because of the ill will they bore toward the Normans, permitted every wickedness to their men. They even allowed holy places to be violated as if by divine authority [Col. 0871A], in order that, by indulging their forces in many ways, they might multiply their legions, and, approving both right and wrong, might urge them on against their enemies.

King Louis therefore brought to Breteuil numerous divisions from Péronne and Nesle, from Noyon and Lille, from Tournai and Arras, from Gournay and Clermont, and from all the provinces of France and Flanders, in order to restore what had been lost to Eustace and recall to their former honours the others who were in exile together with the exiled William. But Ralph the Breton boldly advanced to meet them with his troops, received them in fierce fighting, and, dealing terrible blows with spear and sword, inflicted grievous losses upon them. He ordered all the gates of the castle opened; yet, although the gates stood open, none of the enemy dared enter, because the extraordinary force of those resisting effectively drove them back [Col. 0871B]. A savage engagement was fought at three gates, and valiant champions on both sides were frequently thrown down.

When the king of the English learned of the renewed incursion of the French into Neustria, he sent his son Richard with two hundred knights to aid Ralph of Gaël, appointing Ralph Rufus and Rualo of Avranches, bold and capable scouts, to guide them. As they fought most fiercely, the royal household arrived; at the sight of it, the strength of the now-weary French began to fail. The distinguished Ralph ran from gate to gate and frequently changed his arms so as not to be recognized. That day he threw down many famous champions and, after unhorsing their riders, generously gave their horses to comrades [Col. 0871C] in need. Thus, through knightly valour, he deserved to be praised among the foremost champions for ages.

A handsome and most worthy Fleming threw down Ralph Rufus, Luke of La Barre, and other vigorous knights; carrying off their horses, he swelled with arrogance and did not prudently guard against the sad fate near at hand. He confronted the unconquered Breton, as though he were some common fellow, in his usual fashion; immediately he fell, mortally struck by him, was captured before many witnesses, and died after fifteen days in Breteuil prison.

The king of the English followed his son Richard and his other advance troops with a great host, prepared again to fight the thousands of French if he found them in his land. But they, who had thought to take the town by a long siege, returned to France on that same day, their swelling hope frustrated, driven back with disgrace and wounds. By a just judgment God likewise brought back the priests without glory, filling them with trembling, losses, grief, and confusion: they had shamelessly surrendered holy places, which they ought to have protected by priestly censure, to be polluted by foul and greedy ruffians [Col. 0871D].

Then William of Calvimont, the king’s son-in-law, and other proud young knights, angry that they had gained nothing at Breteuil, turned aside, nearly two hundred strong, toward the castle of Tillières, in order to win some advantage or glory for themselves. Gilbert, castellan of Tillières, lay hidden with his retainers in a concealed place and watched the roads lest brigands ravage his lands [Col. 0872A]. When the French arrived, he suddenly sprang out and captured William, the king’s son-in-law, obtaining two hundred silver marks for his ransom. He captured some of William’s companions and put the rest to flight in disgrace.

Thus Gaul, its children’s stiff-necked pride broken, groaned deeply enough when it reckoned the disastrous events it had recently endured in Neustria—events to be reproached by its future generations. But King Henry, because he was a lover of peace, flourished happily. God mercifully heard the Church praying for him and graciously granted him repeated victories over his enemies. Renewed prosperity, gently favouring him, greatly terrified the savage partisans and instilled bitter repentance for their ill-fated faction in the enemies of the commonwealth.

[Col. 0872B] On 17 September [1119], Richer of l’Aigle seized Odo and all the booty from Cisei, on the day when King Louis advanced upon Breteuil with many thousands; but he gained nothing except disgrace and wounds. The aforesaid young man performed in that expedition a deed worthy of lasting memory. While country people from Vacei and neighbouring villages pursued the raiders and considered how they might recover or ransom their herds by any means, the spirited knights turned back upon them, charged them, and pursued them as they quickly gave way. Since the country people had no strength by which they could defend themselves against an iron-clad line, and no nearby refuge to which they could flee, they saw a wooden cross beside the road [Col. 0872C], before which all together prostrated themselves to the ground.

When Richer saw this, he was moved by fear of God and, for sweet love of the Saviour, reverently honoured His cross. He ordered his men to leave all the terrified people unharmed and themselves to continue the journey they had begun, lest they suffer some hindrance. Thus, through fear of the Creator, the nobleman spared nearly one hundred villagers, from whom he could have exacted a great price had he rashly presumed to seize them. In the same week, through his uncle Rotrou, he was reconciled to the king and obtained all his father’s land in England and Normandy.

Afterward the king entered the district of Ouche with an army and visited his enemies who held Glos and Lira [Col. 0872D]. Roger, son of William son of Barno, then held the keep of Glos, while Ernald of the Wood was castellan of Lira. When they saw that royal power was trampling everything underfoot and that all assistance from Eustace and Amalric had failed them, they spoke with Ralph, who was their neighbour, and through him made an acceptable peace with the king, surrendering to him the castles which they had long held faithfully. The king restored these to Ralph of Gaël; and, now that the district of Ouche had been pacified, he returned to Rouen and gave thanks to God.

Meanwhile, because the same hero regarded Ralph of Conches with suspicion and could not reach his own estates beyond the Seine except through Ralph’s land, he granted, with the king’s counsel, Pont-Saint-Pierre and the whole valley [Col. 0873A] of Pîtres, so that Ralph might be faithful to him and defend the commonwealth with all his efforts against the public enemies. He also granted Ralph Rufus the revenues of Glos, having found him necessary in many matters and judging that he would still be useful.

### IX. The Council of Reims Held by Pope Calixtus, at Which the Controversies between the Emperor and the Apostolic See Are Considered

In the middle of October [1119], Pope Calixtus came to Reims with the Roman senate. Remaining there for fifteen days, he held a council and diligently deliberated with the shepherds of the Lord’s flock concerning the welfare of the Church. There were fifteen archbishops and more than two hundred bishops, with many abbots and other ecclesiastical dignitaries. Summoned by apostolic command from Italy [Col. 0873B] and Germany, Gaul and Spain, Britain and England, the islands of the Ocean, and all western provinces, they gathered for love of the Saviour, prepared gladly to obey His commands. The archbishop of Mainz hurried to the synod at Reims with seven bishops, securely escorted by a company of five hundred knights. When their arrival was learned, the pope rejoiced and sent Hugh, count of Troyes, with troops of knights, to meet them amicably.

The king of the English permitted the prelates of his realm to go to the synod, but strictly forbade them to make any complaint whatsoever against either party. For he said: “I shall grant complete justice in my land to everyone who complains. Every year I pay to the Roman Church the revenues established by my predecessors, and I retain likewise the privileges granted to me in the same manner from ancient times. Go, greet the lord pope on my behalf, and humbly hear only apostolic commands; but do not seek to introduce superfluous innovations into my kingdom.”

The synod was held in the metropolitan church. There, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November, the pope sang the Sunday Mass and consecrated Thurstan of Bayeux as archbishop of York, granting him a privilege that he should be subject not to the metropolitan of Canterbury as to a master, but as though to a fellow bishop. On the following Sunday he blessed Frederick, brother of Count Herman of Namur, as bishop of Liège. Within three years he died after being poisoned by his rivals, and now happily shines forth through miracles [Col. 0873C] occurring at his tomb.

In the basilica of the Blessed Virgin Mary, before the crucifix, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, seats were set for the bishops, and each metropolitan sat in due order, as had anciently been determined for them by the Roman pontiff. Ralph surnamed the Green, archbishop of Reims; Leotheric of Bourges; Humbert of Lyons; Geoffrey of Rouen; Thurstan of York; Daimbert of Sens; Gilbert of Tours and his successor Hildebert of Le Mans; Baldwin of Dol; and eight other archbishops, with their suffragans and the delegates of absentees, together with many abbots and a multitude of monks and clerics, prefigured the coming judgment. Seeing this in the spirit and pointing to it as if with his finger, Isaiah cries out with awe and eagerness of mind: “The Lord will enter into judgment with the elders of his people and their princes” (Isaiah 3:14) [Col. 0874A].

The apostolic see stood on a lofty platform before the doors of the church. When Mass had ended, Pope Calixtus took his seat, and in the foremost rank before him stood the Roman senate: Cono, bishop of Palestrina; Boso of Porto; Lambert of Ostia; John of Crema; and Hato of Viviers. These above all others examined questions with subtlety and, endowed with remarkable learning, offered abundant responses. The deacon Chrysogonus, clothed in a dalmatic, stood beside the pope and held the canons in his hand, ready to produce the authoritative opinions of the Fathers as the matter required. Six other ministers, dressed in tunics or dalmatics, stood around [Col. 0874B] and frequently commanded silence when a tumult among disputants arose.

First, after the litany and the formal prayers, the pope began simply and devoutly to expound in Latin the Gospel passage in which Jesus commanded His disciples to go before Him across the water (Mark 6:45). He eloquently recounted how, when evening had come, a contrary wind arises and the ship of holy Church is endangered amid the waves of this world and tossed by the manifold storms of temptations and tribulations; but the raging blasts of the wicked suddenly grow calm at the Saviour’s visitation, and the desired tranquillity returns to the children of peace.

When the pope had finished his sermon, Cardinal Bishop Cono rose and most eloquently admonished the holy archimandrites concerning pastoral care. From the book of Genesis (chapters 29–30) he also recited from memory Jacob’s words and declared that the prelates of the Church ought spiritually to show toward the Lord’s flock the same care which Jacob showed toward the sheep of his uncle Laban [Col. 0874C].

King Louis entered the synod with the princes of the French. He ascended the assembly platform, where the pope sat pre-eminent above all, and set forth his complaint reasonably. He was eloquent in speech, tall in stature, pale, and corpulent.

“I come,” he said, “to this holy assembly with my barons to seek counsel. Lord pope, and you, venerable fathers, hear me, I beseech you. The king of the English, who long ago entered into alliance with me, has inflicted many attacks and injuries upon me and my subjects. He violently invaded Normandy, which belongs to my kingdom, and has treated Robert, duke of the Normans, detestably, against every right and law. He grievously harassed my man, though Robert was his brother and lord, in many ways; at last he seized him and has held him in long imprisonment to this day. Behold William, the duke’s son, who has come here with me to you: he has utterly disinherited him [Col. 0874D]. Through bishops, counts, and other persons, I have demanded that he return the captive duke to me; but I have been able to obtain nothing from him in this matter.

“He seized Robert of Bellême, my envoy through whom I had communicated to the king what I wished; he put him in chains and has kept him confined to this day in a harsh prison. Count Theobald [Col. 0875A] is my man, but at his uncle’s instigation he has wickedly risen against me. Inflated by his uncle’s wealth and power, he rebelled against me, waged cruel war against me in bad faith, and disturbed my kingdom to the loss of many. He seized Count William of Nevers, a lawful and upright man whom you know well, as he returned from besieging the castle of a certain excommunicated robber—a place truly a den of thieves and a pit of the devil—and has committed him to prison until this day.

“Religious bishops rightly opposed Thomas of Marle, a seditious robber of the whole province. Therefore they ordered me to besiege this general enemy of pilgrims and all simple people. They themselves, together with me and the lawful barons of France, assembled to restrain the outlaws; and with a common levy of the Christian army they fought out of zeal for God. As the aforesaid hero was returning peacefully from there with my permission, he was captured and has been held by Count Theobald to this day, although a multitude of nobles on my behalf have often humbly sought the count’s release, and his whole land has been placed under anathema by the bishops [Col. 0875B].”

After the king had said these and similar things, and the French assembly had affirmed the truth of his speech, Geoffrey, archbishop of Rouen, rose with his suffragan bishops and abbots and began to answer reasonably on behalf of the king of the English. But a tumult of opponents arose and interrupted him; he fell silent because many enemies were present there, to whom a defence of the victorious prince was unwelcome [Col. 0875C].

Meanwhile Hildegard, countess of Poitou, came forward with her retainers and, in a loud, clear voice, eloquently unfolded her complaint, which the whole council carefully heard. She said that her husband had abandoned her and had placed in her bed Malbergion, wife of the viscount of Châtellerault. When the pope asked whether the count of Poitou had come to the synod in accordance with his summons, William, the most eloquent young bishop of Saintes, and several bishops and abbots from Aquitaine rose and excused the duke of Aquitaine, asserting that he had set out for the council but had been detained on the road by illness [Col. 0875D]. The pope accepted illness as an excuse, granted a postponement, and fixed a definite date by which the count was to appear for judgment in the pope’s court and either take back his lawful wife or incur a sentence of anathema for his unlawful repudiation.

Then Audin, the bearded bishop of Évreux, made a complaint against Amalric, declaring that Amalric had shamefully expelled him and abominably burned his bishopric. Immediately, in reply, Amalric’s chaplain boldly spoke publicly and plainly called the bishop a liar before the whole assembly: “It was not Amalric,” he said, “but your own wickedness that deservedly expelled you and burned the bishopric. He whom the king disinherited through your deceitful malice recovered his due honour as a most valiant knight, strong in arms and friends. The king besieged the city with many bodies of his men, set fire to it by your command, and burned all the churches together with the buildings. After inflicting such great damage he withdrew, and still has not obtained the citadel or the city. Let this holy synod consider and judge: who deserves greater condemnation for the churches that were burned, Audin or Amalric?” [Col. 0876A]

As the French supported Amalric against the Normans, a great altercation of words arose. At length silence was made, and the pope spoke:

“Do not, I beseech you, my dearest ones, contend uselessly through a multitude of words; rather, seek peace with all your strength as children of God. For the Son of God descended from heaven for peace’s sake and mercifully assumed human flesh from the inviolate Virgin Mary, in order devoutly to quell the deadly war which arose from the fault of the first-created man; in order, having become mediator, to establish peace between God and man; in order to reconcile the angelic and human natures. We must follow Him in all things, we who, whatever our worth, are His vicars among His people. Let us strive in every way to secure peace and salvation for His members, because we are ministers and stewards of God’s ministries [Col. 0876B].

“By the members of Christ I mean the Christian people, whom He redeemed at the price of His own blood. Who, placed amid the disturbance of secular tumults of war, can worthily contemplate spiritual things or fittingly meditate upon the law of God? Warlike sedition stirs up and disrupts the peoples and compels them to wander fatally amid the precipices of vices. It violates churches, defiles sacred things, and irreverently multiplies many wicked acts. It violently disturbs the clergy and in many ways calls them away from religious study. It terrifies those engaged in the worship of God, wickedly assaults them with troubles, and weakens them, so that from fear they do not know what to do. It confuses and destroys regular discipline and drives the undisciplined headlong into every crime. Thus ecclesiastical strictness is dissolved, deadly laxity spreads everywhere, and the modesty of chastity is lamentably exposed. The fury of evil men spreads abominably, and the host of the wicked is daily carried miserably down to hell [Col. 0876C].

“Therefore we must eagerly embrace peace everywhere and in all things, peace which we plainly see to be the nurse of good things; we must preserve it without ceasing, command it upon all, and preach it by word and example. Christ Himself, hastening toward His Passion, left it to His own, saying: ‘Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you’ (John 14:27). The same Christ, rising from the dead, presented it again, saying: ‘Peace be unto you’ (Luke 24:36). Great rest and security exist where peace reigns; grief and tribulation wear down and torment all whom anger gnaws and discord provokes. Peace is the gentle and health-giving bond of those dwelling together, and a universal good for every rational creature. Bound indissolubly by it, the heavenly beings rejoice; and earthly beings likewise continually need to be joined in a similar bond. Without it, pestilent persons both are feared and fear others, and, never secure, are troubled and mourn.

“Therefore I shall labour vigorously, with God’s help, to seek this virtue which I desire, which I most highly praise on the authority of the holy Scriptures and with the general approval of the public good, and to spread it throughout the whole Church of God [Col. 0877A]. I command the Truce of God to be observed, as Pope Urban of holy memory decreed at the council of Clermont, and I confirm by the authority of God, of the apostle Saint Peter, and of all God’s saints the other decrees there enacted by the holy Fathers.

“The emperor of the Germans has instructed me to go to the castle of Mouzon and there make peace with him for the advantage of holy mother Church. I shall now go there to labour for peace, and I shall take with me my fellow bishops of Reims and Rouen and certain others of our brothers and fellow bishops, whom I judge more necessary than the rest for this settlement. I order all the other bishops and abbots to await our speedy return here, with our Creator’s help. I command all to wait here and do not permit even Geoffrey, abbot of Saint-Thierry, to depart, although his lodging is nearby. Pray for us, that God our Lord may grant us a successful journey and graciously direct all our efforts toward the peace and welfare of the whole Church. When I have returned, I shall carefully examine your complaints and arguments as justly as I can, with the Lord’s aid, so that this holy assembly may be sent home in peace and joy [Col. 0877B].

“Then I shall visit my spiritual son and cousin by blood, the king of the English. By prayers and exhortations I shall admonish him, Count Theobald—namely, his nephew—and the other disputants, that they render justice to all in all things and receive that same justice from all in the love of God; and that, reconciled according to God’s law, they may cease from every clamour of war and rest and rejoice in security with the peoples subject to them. But those who refuse to obey our persuasions and stubbornly persist in their audacity against justice and the public peace, I shall strike with the dreadful sentence of anathema unless they repent of their perversity and make canonical satisfaction for offences already committed.”

When he had said this, the assembly of the faithful was dismissed.

### X. The Council of Reims Continues

[Col. 0877D]

On the following day, Wednesday, he set out for Mouzon with a distinguished retinue, and returned to Reims on the following Sunday, weary and ill from exertion and fear. Meanwhile the multitude of church officials awaited the pope’s return with anxiety. Those who had gathered there from distant regions at the apostolic command were accomplishing nothing, fruitlessly spending their resources and sorrowfully neglecting the care of their households. At last, after his return, the pope held the synod for four days and dealt with various affairs of the churches.

Accordingly, on Monday, after the pope had taken his seat, John of Crema, a learned and eloquent priest, rose and began to set forth in order the events of the journey that had been undertaken [Col. 0878A]:

“It is known to Your Holiness,” he said, “that we went to Mouzon. But, with misfortunes rising against us, we accomplished nothing advantageous. We went there in haste, but returned thence in greater haste. For the emperor arrived at the aforesaid place with a huge army, having with him, as though about to fight, nearly thirty thousand armed men. When we observed this, we shut up the lord pope in the aforesaid castle, which lies in the domain of the archbishop of Reims; and, going out ourselves to the appointed conference, we altogether forbade him to leave it. We sought many times to speak more privately with the emperor; but as soon as, separated from the crowd, we moved aside with him, countless retainers—aware of his will and treachery—[Col. 0878B] surrounded us and, brandishing their spears and swords, struck great fear into us. For we had not come equipped for war, but unarmed, seeking peace for the universal Church. The deceitful emperor quibbled by various evasions and dealt craftily with us; yet above all he waited for the pope to appear, that he might seize him. Thus we spent the whole day to no purpose; but we carefully hid the Father of Fathers from his sight, remembering how deceitfully this same man had entered Rome and seized Pope Paschal before the altar in the basilica of the apostle Saint Peter. At last the grim night separated us, and each returned to his own quarters. We, indeed, fearing that worse might befall us, promptly set out on the road of return—or rather, of flight. [Col. 0878C] Indeed, we greatly feared lest the formidable tyrant, with the many legions which he led with him, should pursue us.”

It is enough for the present to have said this concerning those events.

The archbishop of Cologne sent envoys and letters to the lord pope; professing submission, he made peace and friendship with him. He also freely restored, as a token of goodwill, the son of Peter Leon, whom he held as a hostage. Saying this, and as if in extraordinary exultation and remarkable joy, he pointed with his finger to a black and pale young man, more like a Jew or an Agarene than a Christian, dressed indeed in excellent garments but deformed in body. The Franks and many others standing by the pope looked upon him with derision and wished him disgrace and swift destruction [Col. 0878D], because of their hatred for his father, whom they knew to be a most wicked moneylender.

Then the archbishop of Lyons rose with his suffragans and began to speak thus:

“The bishop of Mâcon brings a complaint before this holy synod: that Pons of Cluny has inflicted losses and many injuries upon him and his church; that he has forcibly taken away his churches, tithes, and the obedience due to him, and has denied him the appropriate dignities and the ordinations of his clerics.”

When the primate of Lyons had completed complaints of this kind, many bishops, monks, and clerics followed up, raising clamorous cries about things violently taken from them and about the unjust encroachments they had suffered from the Cluniacs. [Col. 0879A] Very many were greatly agitated and, continuing their uproar for a long time, vomited forth the bitter things they had been brooding over.

At last, silence having been made, the abbot of Cluny rose with a great company of monks, and with a brief reply, a modest voice, and calm speech subdued his complaining assailants. For he was a high-spirited monk from the Valley of the Bruttii (Valle Brutiorum), son of the count of Melgueil and godson of Pope Paschal, and had been brought up among the Cluniacs under Paschal’s authority. Young in age and of medium stature, yet teachable from childhood, steadfast in virtues, and agreeable in his cheerful dealings with those around him; handsome in fair complexion, distinguished, as has been said, in character and lineage, closely related by blood to kings and emperors, endowed with religious devotion and literary learning—and therefore adorned with the prerogatives of so many graces [Col. 0879B]—he stood firm and stern against hostile rivals. Assailed in the synod by many cries, as has been described, he replied:

“The church of Cluny is subject to the Roman Church alone and is the pope’s own; and from the time of its foundation it has obtained from the Roman pontiff privileges which these accusers endeavor by violence to abolish and render void. Let it be known to all of you, blessed Fathers here present, that I and our brothers strive to preserve the monastic possessions which we have undertaken lawfully to maintain, just as the venerable Hugh and our other holy predecessors possessed them. We have inflicted losses or injuries upon no one; we have not plundered another’s property, nor do we in any way desire to plunder what belongs to anyone. [Col. 0879C] But because, for the love of God, we stubbornly defend against robbers the property given to us by the faithful, we are called invaders and unjustly endure many reproaches. Excessive concern about these matters does not belong to me. Let the lord pope, if he wishes, defend his own church, and let him protect and guard the churches, tithes, and other possessions which he himself has entrusted to me!”

The pope therefore ordered that judgment on all that he had heard from both sides be deferred until the day after next. On the following day John of Crema rose and began the preface to his address in this manner:

“Just as it is right that the lord pope should diligently hear your complaints and, like a father to his sons, help you in every way without pretence, and should owe you such service not once but daily [Col. 0879D], so indeed it is fitting and right that he himself should possess some property in your dioceses, and should freely have, by his own choice or by the offering of the faithful, a church, a house, or some possession.”

After this had been gladly conceded by all, John continued:

“More than two hundred years have passed since the church of Cluny was founded; and from the very beginning of its foundation it was given to the Roman pope, who plainly distinguished it with useful privileges in a Roman synod before many witnesses of different rank. It is established, and it clearly appears to those reading the charters in which it is entered, that Gerald of Aquitaine built the monastery of Cluny upon his own allodial land and, while going to Rome [Col. 0880A], most devoutly entrusted it to the Roman pontiff. Nor did he wish this to be done without purpose: for he then offered the pope twelve gold pieces and decreed that the same number should thereafter be given every year. Thus the aforesaid church has until now been subject to no prince or bishop except the pope; and, through God’s abundant help, it has happily grown in estates and religious inhabitants. Hence the sweet fragrance of its praiseworthy fame has spread far and wide through the world, and the example of its holiness has abundantly supplied wholesome discipline to those who devoutly seek it. The community of monks elects an abbot according to the Rule of the holy Father Benedict, sends the elected man to the pope with attesting letters, and he consecrates and blesses him according to ecclesiastical custom.

“The whole multitude of believers believes and bears witness [Col. 0880B] that he who, by God’s command, presides over the apostolic see has the power of binding and loosing. For he is the vicar of Peter, prince of the apostles, to whom it was divinely said: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven’ (Matt. 16:18). Therefore the apostolic see is the hinge and head of all churches, established by the Lord and by no other. And as a door is governed by its hinge, so all churches are governed, by the Lord’s ordering, through the authority of the apostolic see. Behold, it was granted to blessed Peter by the Son of God that he should surpass the other apostles; hence he is called Cephas [Col. 0880C] (John 1:42), because he is the head and first of all the apostles. What came first in the head must fittingly be followed in the members. Who can resist him to whom such power has been granted by the Lord? Who dares loose one whom Peter has bound, or bind one whom he himself has absolved? Therefore, since the abbey of Cluny is subject to the pope alone, and since he who, by God’s command, is above all on earth protects it, Roman authority confirms the privileges of the Cluniacs and, by the power of God, commands all the sons of the Church that no one rashly deprive them of their ancient liberty, strip them of possessions long held, or burden them with unprecedented exactions. Let them possess everything in peace, so that in tranquillity they may always be able to serve God!”

As John spoke these words, several bishops and others neighboring the Cluniacs became agitated; and although they did not dare openly oppose the pope’s commands, they did not concede the statements firmly uttered by the cardinal. [Col. 0880D] In the disputes, abundant arguments were hurled back and forth, flowing freely from the deep spring of rich wisdom. But I cannot recount individually all the proceedings of the council. Keen sophists treated subtly of many affairs of the Church and clearly imparted much instruction to attentive hearers. There Girard of Angoulême, Hato of Viviers, Geoffrey of Chartres, and William of Châlons thundered forth above the rest as leaders of speech, and shone conspicuously among witty scholars and ardent lovers of Sophia, “Wisdom.” [Col. 0881A]

A messenger spoke of the death of the cardinal-bishop of Tusculum, who had recently died on the journey; and a letter from Clementia, the pope’s sister, was read on behalf of her son Baldwin, count of Flanders. For these, and for all the faithful departed, the sorrowing shepherd prayed to God with the venerable assembly.

On the last day of the council, the bishop of Barcelona—of medium and thin body, but outstanding in learning, eloquence, and religious devotion—delivered a subtle and sufficiently profound discourse on royal and priestly dignity, which all who were able to understand it drank in with the greatest eagerness. Then the pope sorrowfully excommunicated Emperor Charles Henry, “the God-fighter,” Burdinus the false pope, and their supporters [Col. 0881B]; and he associated with them other wicked men who had often been openly reproved but persisted incorrigibly, and struck them with the same blow of anathema until they should amend themselves. Finally, he ordered the decretal chapters of the synod of Reims to be published. John of Crema composed them by counsel of the Roman senate. John, a monk of Saint-Ouen of Rouen, wrote them down in a charter, and Chrysogonus, deacon of the holy Roman Church, read them distinctly and clearly. The text of the council is as follows:

“We confirm, by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and the authority of the apostolic see, the provisions established by the ordinances of the holy Fathers concerning the wickedness of simony. [Col. 0881C] Therefore, if anyone sells or buys, either personally or through any intermediary, a bishopric, abbacy, deanery, archdeaconry, priesthood, provostship, prebend, altars, or any ecclesiastical benefices, promotions, ordinations, consecrations, dedications of churches, clerical tonsure, seats in choir, or any ecclesiastical offices, both seller and buyer shall be liable to loss of his dignity, office, and benefice. Unless he repents, pierced by the sword of anathema, he shall in every manner be cut off from the Church of God which he has injured.

“We utterly forbid the investiture of bishoprics and abbeys by a lay hand. Whoever among laymen henceforth presumes to invest shall be subject [Col. 0881D] to the punishment of anathema. Moreover, whoever has been invested shall entirely lose the honor with which he was invested, with no hope whatever of recovery.

“We decree that the possessions of all churches granted to them by the liberality of kings, the generosity of princes, or the offerings of any faithful persons shall remain forever unshaken and inviolate. If anyone takes them away, invades them, or holds them by tyrannical power, let him be struck with perpetual anathema, according to that chapter of blessed Symmachus. Let no bishop, priest, or cleric of any kind leave ecclesiastical dignities or benefices to anyone as though by hereditary right.

“Adding this also, we command that no payment whatever be demanded for the reception of baptism, chrism, holy oil, or burial [Col. 0882A], or for visiting or anointing the sick.

“We altogether forbid priests, deacons, and subdeacons cohabitation with concubines and wives. If any are found to be such, let them be deprived of ecclesiastical offices and benefices. If even thus they do not correct their impurity, let them be deprived of Christian communion.”

Pope Calixtus II, with the whole council, enacted these decrees on 30 October [1119], and blessed in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit all who had gathered there. Then that sacred assembly was dissolved, and each person returned home praising God.

## XI. King Henry brings several rebellious Normans back to obedience. On Old Rouen

[Col. 0882B]

Meanwhile King Henry vigorously besieged Évreux, and his nephew Theobald, count palatine, labored to reconcile those at variance. By prudent counsel and persuasion he brought Amaury to the king, and Amaury, immediately reconciled, voluntarily surrendered the castle to the king; he himself joyfully received back the whole county of his uncle. Eustace and his wife Juliana, having taken counsel with their friends, hastened at their urging to the siege; entering barefoot, they fell at the king’s feet in his tent. The king at once said to them:

“Why have you dared enter upon me without my safe-conduct, when you have provoked me by so many and such great injuries?”

Eustace replied:

“You [Col. 0882C] are my natural lord. Therefore I come safely to you, my lord, to render you my service faithfully and to make complete amends for my faults, according to the judgment of your mercy.”

Their friends were present, pleading for the king’s son-in-law. Richard also, the king’s son, approached as a suppliant for his sister. Clementia softened and kindly turned the king’s heart toward his son-in-law and daughter. Thus the appeased father-in-law said to his son-in-law:

“Let Juliana return to Pacy, and you will come with me to Rouen; there you shall hear my judgment.”

Without delay the king’s command was fulfilled, and the king spoke thus to Eustace:

“For the honor of Breteuil, which I gave to Ralph the Breton, your kinsman—whom I have found faithful and most upright in my necessities against enemies—I shall compensate you in England with three hundred marks of silver each year.”

Thereafter the aforesaid nobleman fortified Pacy in peace with ditches and walls and, abounding in much wealth, lived for more than twenty years. Juliana, moreover, after some years changed the wanton life which she had led and her habit; becoming a nun in the new monastery of Fontevraud, she served the Lord God.

Hugh of Gournay, Robert of Neubourg, and the other rebels, seeing that they themselves, though stronger, had been defeated and that the king had surpassed all in strength and wisdom, repented of their previous acts and, both personally and through friends, sought the king’s mercy. He at once—being one who feared God and cultivated peace and justice [Col. 0883A]—spared the barons who pleaded for forgiveness of their error and, pardoning their offences, kindly received them into friendship.

The king assembled an army against Stephen, count of Aumale, who alone still resisted; and in the place called Old Rouen he began to build a castle, which he named Mata-Putena—“the subduer of the harlot”—in contempt of Countess Hadwisa. For at her instigation the aforesaid count had rebelled against his lord and kinsman the king, and had for a long time aided William Clito and Baldwin of Flanders, whom he had received in his castles. When he learned that the king was advancing against him with an army, he took counsel with prudent friends, humbly made satisfaction to the king, and the king, forgiving everything, departed in triumph and peace. [Col. 0883B]

Concerning Old Rouen, of which mention has now been made, I shall touch upon what is related in ancient histories of the Quirites, the Romans.
