Gaius Julius Caesar besieged Calète, from which the district of Caux still retains its name, and assailed it long with all his strength. Since irreconcilable enemies from all Gaul had assembled there—men who had offended by slaughter, arson, and frequent outrages and had provoked Caesar beyond forgiveness—he persistently attacked the city, captured it with its inhabitants, and utterly destroyed it. Yet, lest the province be left without a garrison, he built there a fortification which, from his daughter Julia, he called Julia Bona; but barbarian speech, corrupting the name, called it Lillebonne. He then crossed nine rivers: Guitefleda and Tala, now called the Dun; Sedana and Belnaius and Seda; Guarenna, Deppam, and Eara [Col. 0883C]; and he surveyed the shore of the Ocean as far as the river Auc, commonly called the Ou [Eu]. At last, after this industrious prince had investigated the advantages of the country and provided for his own people, he determined to build a city for the assistance of the Quirites, which he called Rodomum, as though “the house of the Romans.” Having summoned craftsmen, he measured out its extent and, having stationed stonecutters and masons there to carry out the work, departed.

Meanwhile Rutubus, a powerful and savage tyrant, held an apparently impregnable stronghold upon a hill beside the Seine, by which he controlled the surrounding province [Col. 0883D] and ships passing on the nearby river. Hearing this, Caesar hastened there with an army and stormed the castle called Rutubus’s Port. A knowledgeable native can clearly discern the traces and ruins of that town. Caesar then recalled the masons and other craftsmen from the aforesaid place and founded the noble metropolis of Rouen on the Seine; to the former settlement on the Auc he left, down to this day, only its name.

I have added these particulars from the accounts of the ancients, for the knowledge of posterity, because I mentioned Old Rouen, where King Henry began a castle against his enemies but, being immediately reconciled with them, abandoned the work begun. Now I shall return, as I began, to events recently done and, following ancient writers to the measure of my ability, offer my labor to the age to come. [Col. 0884A]

All the Normans who, as stated, had rebelled against the king, having experienced him to be stronger than themselves in every respect and taking better counsel than formerly, sought pardon both personally and through their friends; and, after their offences had been forgiven, they were received as suppliants by the king. Against their will they left William Clito with his tutor Helias in exile, but otherwise they could not obtain peace with that most powerful prince.

## XII. (1119) King Henry has a conference with Pope Calixtus. Peace is arranged between the kings of France and England

In November Pope Calixtus came into Neustria and held a conference at Gisors with the king concerning peace. The magnificent king honorably received him and [Col. 0884B] approached prostrate at his feet, reverently honoring one whom he recognized as shepherd of the universal Church and as his kinsman by blood. The pope kindly raised the humbled king, blessed him in the Lord’s name, and, after the kiss of peace had been given, each rejoiced in their mutual embraces. At last, when the proper hour for the conference had come, the pope began to address the king thus:

“At the council of Reims I treated, with the holy bishops and other great men and sons of the Church of God who had gladly assembled there at our invitation, concerning the welfare of the faithful; and I solemnly promised that I would labor for the common peace. Therefore, glorious son, I have hastened into these regions and pray the mercy of almighty God that He may graciously regard our efforts [Col. 0884C] and beneficially direct them toward the general good of His whole Church. First of all, I beseech your magnificence to agree with us devoutly and, as heir of the true Solomon, to become a peacemaker toward your enemies who seek peace through us.”

When the king had promised that he would gladly obey the apostolic commands, the pope began his address in this fashion:

“The law of God, providing wisely for all, commands that each person should lawfully possess his own right; but that he should not covet another’s possessions nor do to another what he would not wish done to himself. Therefore the synod of the faithful generally decrees and humbly asks of Your Highness, great king, that you release your brother Robert, whom you have held in chains for a long time, and restore to him [Col. 0884D] and to his son the duchy of Normandy which you have taken away.”

Hearing this, the king replied:

“Reverend Father, I shall reasonably obey your commands, as I promised from the beginning. Yet I ask now that what I have done, and in what manner, be diligently heard. I did not deprive my brother of the duchy of Normandy; rather, I recovered by arms the hereditary right of our father, which neither my brother nor my nephew possessed for themselves, but which most wicked robbers and sacrilegious scoundrels were miserably devastating. No honor was rendered to priests or other servants of God; rather, almost paganism was spreading everywhere through Normandy. The monasteries founded by our ancestors for their souls were being destroyed, and religious cloister-dwellers, deprived of sustenance, were dispersed. The churches were plundered, and most were burned; their inhabitants were dragged out from hiding places. Savage parishioners slaughtered one another in mutual blows, and the survivors, lacking a defender, lamented amid so many desolations. Thus for almost seven years such misery afflicted Neustria and allowed no one secure safety either within or without. [Col. 0885A]

“Frequent entreaties from religious persons came running to me, urging me for the love of God to aid the desolated people, and with many prayers begging me not to allow the most wicked robbers any longer to rage against the innocent. Compelled by this, I crossed into Normandy and was received by the illustrious counts William of Évreux and Robert of Meulan and by other lawful magnates. Seeing the desolation [Col. 0885B] of my paternal right, I grieved; yet I could not assist those in need except by military arms. For my brother protected the instigators of all wickedness and eagerly embraced the counsels of men through whom he was held cheap and contemptible. Gunher of Aunay, Roger of Lacy, Robert of Bellême, and other criminals ruled the Normans; and under the guise of the duke they lorded it over bishops, the whole clergy, and the unarmed people. Those very men whom I had driven out of the region beyond the sea because of their wicked factions, he made his intimate counsellors and set over innocent settlers as governors. Countless killings and burnings were everywhere committed, and dreadful deeds which those unacquainted with them would think almost unbelievable. [Col. 0885C]

“I repeatedly commanded my brother to use my advice, and I would have supported him with all my strength. But he despised me and employed my enemies against me. Seeing such crimes prevail, I was unwilling to withhold my service from holy mother Church; rather, I strove profitably to carry out the office divinely imposed upon me. Therefore, fighting stoutly by arms and fire, I took Bayeux from Gunher, Caen from Enguerrand son of Ilbert, and recovered other towns after subduing the tyrants in battle—towns which my father had possessed in his own lordship but which my brother had handed over to perjured traitors, himself remaining so poor that he needed the alms of his dependants. At last I besieged Tinchebray, the den of demons [Col. 0885D], whither William, count of Mortain, brought my brother against me with a great army. Against them I fought in the field of Falaise, in the name of the Lord and for the defence of the country. There, indeed, with God’s help—He who knows my well-intentioned efforts—I overcame my adversaries and captured both counts, my brother and my cousin, with many of our deserters. I have guarded them carefully to this day, lest through them scandal arise for me or my kingdom. Thus I recovered my father’s inheritance and all his dominion, and have labored to observe my father’s laws according to God’s will for the peace of His people.

“But I did not consign my brother to chains as an enemy captive; I placed him, like a noble pilgrim broken by many sorrows, in a royal castle [Col. 0886A], and supplied him abundantly with every abundance of food and other delicacies, and with varied furnishings. I entrusted his five-year-old son to Helias, the duke’s son-in-law; abandoning the whole honor of Saint Sidonius which he possessed, he fled abroad, desiring that he might in understanding and every growth of virtue and power be made equal in all things to my own son. But Helias, at the instigation of his accomplices, stole my nephew away from me; he fled abroad and troubled me as much as he could by many raids, but, God preventing it, he has not yet prevailed. He stirred up the French, Burgundians, and other peoples against me, but, unless I am mistaken, brought more harm upon himself than upon me. I summoned my nephew many times and through many envoys amicably asked him to come safely to my court and share royal wealth with my son. I also offered him three earldoms in England, to rule them; and I proposed that, brought up among the courtly speakers, he should clearly learn how greatly his intelligence and integrity toward rich and poor alike would be valued in the future, and how strictly he should embrace princely justice and military discipline. [Col. 0886B] But he rejected what I offered and preferred to live as a beggar in exile among foreign thieves rather than enjoy abundance with me. The uncultivated fields, burned houses, devastated villages, ruined churches, and peoples mourning for the killing of friends and plundering of their wealth are witnesses to all the evils I have recounted. [Col. 0886C] Let Your Holiness, lord pope, examine these things wisely and diligently give profitable counsel to those who rule and those who are subject!”

Having attentively heard the king’s words, the pope was astonished and praised his actions as he had related them.

“Now,” he said, “we have heard enough concerning the duke and his son; but, saying nothing of these for the moment, let us turn to other matters. The king of the French complains that the treaty between you has been wrongly broken and that many injuries have been unjustly inflicted upon him and his kingdom by your retainers.”

The king replied:

“The pact of friendship between us was first violated by him. In many ways he strengthened my enemies against me and encouraged my men, by promises and persuasion, to raise their necks against me. Yet if he wishes to make amends for what has been done and henceforth keep the covenant of friendship inviolate [Col. 0886D], I am ready to obey your admonitions in every respect.”

Delighted by this, the pope added:

“The king also complains of the injury which Count Theobald, your nephew, did to him when he seized the count of Nevers as he was returning from the siege which the king himself, with the bishops of France, was maintaining against Thomas of Marle, in order to restrain him from the wicked acts he was inflicting upon the innocent.”

“I shall seek no pretexts,” said the king, “for refusing to obey your fatherly admonitions toward tranquillity and peace; and I shall submit my nephew Theobald, who is a true lover of justice, to you for every good purpose. I also exhort my other nephew William to keep peace, and through Your Sublimity I still offer him those things which I have already offered often through others [Col. 0887A], because I desire both to satisfy you in all things and to secure the common peace of the people and my nephew’s prosperity as though he were my own child.”

Finally the pope sent his envoys to the king of France and his magnates, and conveyed the English king’s responses suitable for peace. All therefore rejoiced. It seems superfluous to me to prolong the narrative by expounding at great length how great was the joy of a people shattered by wars when, the storm of war having been calmed, the gentle serenity of long-desired peace returned. The concord of the princes having thus been confirmed, castles captured by force or guile were restored to their lords; all soldiers captured during the war on either side were freed; and they were joyfully permitted to return from prison to their own homes. [Col. 0887B]

## XIII. Council of Rouen. Clerics rise against the archbishop

But envious and restless Satan, who deceived the first human being through the serpent (Gen. 3), grieved to see the kings and warriors, mighty champions, reconciled by God’s grace; and he sowed the tares of deadly discord among the priests in the temple of God. For Archbishop Geoffrey, after returning to Rouen from the council of Reims, held a synod in the third week of November; sharpened by the apostolic enactments, he burned fiercely against the priests of his diocese. Among the other chapters of the council which he put forward, he entirely forbade them all association with women [Col. 0887C] and launched against transgressors a terrible sentence of anathema.

Since the priests intensely recoiled from so grievous a burden and muttered complaints among themselves concerning the danger to their bodies and souls, the archbishop ordered a certain eloquent Albert to be seized, because he had begun to say something or other, and immediately confined in a prison cell. The aforesaid bishop was a Breton, indiscreet in many things, obstinate and irascible, severe in expression and bearing, harsh in rebuke, rash, and full of wordiness. When the other priests, astonished by the unprecedented occurrence, saw the priest dragged from the church to prison like a thief without an accusation of guilt or lawful examination, and, terrified beyond measure, did not know what should be done—uncertain whether to defend themselves or flee—the furious bishop rose from his chair, hurried out of the synod, and summoned his retainers, whom he had previously instructed for this very purpose. At once they rushed with clubs and weapons into the church and began irreverently to beat the gathering of clerics who were conversing together. [Col. 0887D]

Some of them, clothed in their long robes, ran through the muddy streets of the city to their lodgings. Others seized benches or stones which they happened to find there and tried to resist. But the retainers were ashamed that they had fled, beaten by an unarmed choir of tonsured men; in anger they quickly summoned cooks, bakers, and neighboring followers and renewed the fight, a relapse, within the sacred sanctuary. [Col. 0888A] Whomever they found in church or cemetery, just or unjust, they struck, shoved, or otherwise injured. Then Hugh of Longueville, Anschetillus of Cropus, and several other mature and religious old men were waiting in the holy building and speaking in turn of confession or other useful matters, or were duly chanting the daytime Hours in praise of God. But the foolish servants stupidly attacked them, abused them with insults, and scarcely spared them from slaughter—hands having been drawn back—because they themselves, on bent knees, tearfully begged for mercy. Released at once, they fled from the city as quickly as possible with the companions who had gone before, without waiting for the bishop’s permission or blessing. [Col. 0888B] Instead, they brought grim reports to their parishioners and their concubines, displaying their wounds and bruised injuries on their bodies to prove the truth of the matter.

The archdeacons, canons, and respectable citizens grieved over the unspeakable violence and sympathized with the worshippers of God, who had undergone unheard-of disgrace. [Col. 0888C] Thus priests’ blood was shed in the bosom of holy mother Church, and the holy synod was turned into a scene of frenzy and mockery. Greatly disturbed, the archbishop withdrew and hid himself in the dining hall. But a little later, when his anger had subsided after the clerics had fled, as described, he came out, blessed water after putting on a stole, and reconciled, with the sorrowful canons, the church which he had defiled. The abominable outcry of sedition reached the prince’s ears, but occupied with other affairs, he postponed rendering justice to those injured.

## XIV. King Henry crosses to England. The terrible shipwreck of the White Ship

King Henry, [1120], having after many labors put affairs in Normandy in the best order, resolved to cross the sea, distribute generous rewards to the newly enlisted soldiers and leading knights who had served laboriously and faithfully, and raise certain men to high rank by granting them great honors in England. He therefore immediately ordered a fleet prepared and a plentiful military force of every rank to accompany him.

Meanwhile Ralph of Gaël, fearing the treachery of the Normans over whom he exercised lordship—though they had formerly been unwilling because of their support for Eustace—and considering that he possessed Gaël, Montfort, other towns, and great holdings inherited from his patrimony in the Breton region, arranged, by the king’s counsel and will, the marriage of his daughter to Richard, the king’s son; and with her gave Breteuil, Gloz, Lire, and the whole honor due to himself in Neustria. [Col. 0888D] But this plan was weak and futile, because God, who governs all things well, ordered otherwise. For the girl mentioned afterwards married Robert, count of Leicester, and lived with him for many years.

With a great fleet prepared in the harbour called Barfleur, and a noble company assembled in the king’s train as the south wind blew, on 25 November [1120], at the first watch of the night, the king and his counts embarked; they raised their sails aloft and entrusted them to the winds upon the sea, and in the morning those to whom God granted it reached England.

On that voyage a grievous disaster occurred, drawing forth much mourning and countless tears. Thomas, son of Stephen, approached the king and, offering him a mark of gold, said:

> “My lord king, my father was Stephen, son of Airard; throughout his life he served your father at sea. For he conveyed him in his own ship to England when he went there to fight Harold. By faithfully performing this office until his death, he pleased him; richly honoured by him with gifts, he flourished magnificently among his fellow-countrymen. I claim this fief from you, my lord king; and I possess, duly fitted out for royal service, the vessel called the White Ship.”

The king replied:

> “I willingly grant what you ask. I have chosen a ship suitable for myself, which I shall not change; but I now entrust to you my sons William and Richard, whom I love as myself, together with much of the nobility of my realm.”

On hearing this, the sailors rejoiced. Flattering the king’s son, they asked him for wine to drink; and he ordered three measures of wine to be given them. When they had received it, they drank and abundantly shared it with their companions, and, drinking too much, became drunk. At the king’s command many barons embarked with their sons, and, as I think, nearly three hundred persons were on that ill-fated ship.

Indeed, two monks of Tiron, Count Stephen with two knights, William of Roumare, Rabellus the Chamberlain, Edward of Salisbury, and many others went ashore, because they saw that the ship contained an excessive multitude of frivolous and ostentatious young people. There were fifty skilled oarsmen aboard, as well as fierce passengers, who had already taken their seats in the ship, puffed up and so forgetful of themselves through drunkenness that they scarcely acknowledged anyone with respect. Alas, how many of them had minds empty of devout reverence toward God,

> Who governs the boundless fury of sea and air.

Therefore they mockingly and disgracefully drove away the priests who had come to bless them, and the other ministers carrying holy water; but shortly afterward they received the penalty for their derision.

Men alone, together with the king’s treasure and vessels carrying wine, filled Thomas’s ship; and they urged him with all speed to pursue the royal fleet already ploughing the waves. But, rendered senseless by drink, he trusted in his own strength and that of his attendants, and boldly promised that he would overtake all who had gone before. At last he gave the signal to sail. The ship’s crew seized the oars without delay; others joyfully fitted the rigging, not knowing what hung before their eyes; and they caused the ship to race across the sea with great force.

As the drunken rowers strove with all their might, and the wretched helmsman misdirected the ship’s course over the sea, the port side of the White Ship was violently struck against a huge rock, daily exposed when the tide withdrew and covered again by the incoming sea. Two planks were shattered; suddenly, alas, the vessel overturned. All cried out together in that great peril; but the water immediately filled their mouths, and they perished alike.

Only two men grasped the spar from which the sail hung; hanging there through much of the night, they waited for whatever help might come. One was a butcher of Rouen named Berold; the other a noble boy named Geoffrey, son of Gilbert de l’Aigle.

At that time the moon was in the nineteenth degree of Taurus, and for almost nine hours illuminated the world with its rays, making the sea bright for the sailors. After the first submersion, Thomas the captain recovered his strength, remembered himself, raised his head above the waves, and, seeing the heads of those somehow clinging to the timber, asked: “What has become of the king’s son?” When the shipwrecked men answered that he had perished with all his companions, he said: “Wretched that I should live from now on.” Having said this, in evil despair he preferred to die there rather than face the fury of the enraged king for the destruction of his children, or suffer long punishment in chains.

Those hanging in the water called upon God, encouraged one another mutually, and tremblingly awaited the end appointed for them by God. That night was bitterly cold with frost. Thus the tender fair-haired boy, after long endurance, lost his strength from the cold; commending his companion to God, he fell back into the sea and died, and was never seen again. Berold, however, poorest of them all, clothed in a garment of rams’ skins, alone of that great company saw daylight. In the morning he was taken aboard a small boat by three fishermen and alone reached land. After recovering somewhat, he carefully unfolded the sequence of the sad event to those eagerly asking; afterward he lived cheerfully for nearly twenty years.

Roger, bishop of Coutances, had brought onto the ship condemned by God’s judgment his son William—whom the king had already made one of his four principal chaplains—his brother also, and three distinguished nephews; although they made light of it, he had blessed them and their companions according to the episcopal rite. He himself and many others still standing together on the shore, as well as the king and his companions, who had already gone far out into the Channel, heard the terrible cries of those in danger. But not knowing the cause until the following day, they wondered and discussed it among themselves as they sought an explanation.

The mournful report, swiftly flying from mouth to mouth among the people, resounded along the maritime shores and reached the knowledge of Count Theobald and the other great men of the court. Yet on that day no one dared tell the anxious king, despite his many inquiries. The nobles wept copiously apart, mourning inconsolably for dear kinsmen and friends; but before the king they could scarcely hold back their tears, lest the cause of their grief be revealed.

At last, on the next day, by Count Theobald’s ingenuity, a weeping boy fell at the king’s feet; from him the king learned that the wreck of the White Ship was the cause of the mourning. Overcome at once by excessive anguish of spirit, he fell to the ground; but his friends raised him and led him into an inner chamber, where he uttered bitter lamentations. Jacob was not more sorrowful over the loss of Joseph, nor did David pour forth more grievous complaints over the killing of Amnon or Absalom. Since so great a ruler mourned, all the sons of the realm were free to weep openly, and this mourning lasted many days.

All universally lamented William Ætheling, regarded by the English as the lawful heir of the kingdom, so suddenly fallen together with the flower of a select nobility. He was now approaching manhood, nearly seventeen years old. He had already taken as wife the noble Matilda, almost his own age. At his father’s command, he had gladly received the homage of all the magnates of the realm. In him rested a father’s love and the people’s confident hope.

Yet sinful human dimness cannot investigate or behold what the heavenly Majesty blamelessly ordains concerning His own creation, until wicked human captivity has been entangled like a fish by a hook or a bird by a snare and is hopelessly engulfed in miseries on every side. For while it awaits long life, happiness, and exaltation, it suddenly encounters swift destruction, misery, and abasement—as in daily events from the beginning of the world to the present day we may plainly see demonstrated by proofs both modern and ancient.

[Col. 0891C] The grieving king mourned his sons, the chosen young knights, and the chief barons; above all he lamented Ralph the Red and Gilbert of Eu, often recalling their valour with tears. Nobles and subject commoners mourned lords, children, relatives, acquaintances, and friends; brides mourned bridegrooms, and beloved wives their sweet husbands. I do not care to multiply unavailing dirges. I shall record here only the brief poem of one distinguished versifier:

> A grievous hour befell, and most wretched was Thomas’s ship,  
> Ill steered: she struck the rock and perished.  
>
> A lamentable event, when that noble youth  
> Was plunged alike into the sea and destruction.  
>
> The noble offspring of kings is tossed upon the deep;  
> Those whom leaders mourn, sea-monsters devour.  
>
> O immeasurable grief! Neither nobility nor wealth  
> Restores to life those killed by the sea’s wave.  
>
> Purple and fine linen rot in the liquid abyss;  
> Even he whom a king begot became food for fishes.  
>
> Thus Fortune mocks the powerful who trust in themselves:  
> Now she gives, now takes away; now raises, then crushes.  
>
> What could the number of nobles, what wealth, what worldly glory,  
> What, William, could your beauty avail you there?  
>
> That royal splendour withered, and the sea took away  
> What you had become and what you were to become.  
>
> Amid these waters a grievous condemnation awaits them,  
> Unless heavenly mercy freely spares them.  
>
> If, in exchange for their bodies, their souls obtained gifts of salvation  
> And rejoiced, sorrow would be far away.  
>
> The sure salvation of the soul truly gives cause for rejoicing  
> To those who fittingly remember their own beloved dead.  
>
> Hence there is great grief, because the human mind does not know  
> Whether rest belongs to those whom the wet Thetis tosses.

[Col. 0892A] What mortal could adequately recount how many people of the earth wept for so disastrous an event, or how many estates were left without their natural heirs, to the loss of many? For William and Richard, the king’s sons, perished, as has been said; so did their sister Matilda, wife of Rotrou, count of Mortain; likewise Richard, the young count of Chester, praiseworthy for much excellence and generosity, with his wife Matilda, sister of Theobald, count palatine.

Othver also, his brother, son of Hugh, count of Chester, tutor and, it is said, instructor of the royal children, when the ship suddenly overturned and the nobles were irreparably submerged, immediately embraced the young prince and fell with him beyond recovery into the depths. The boy Theodoric, nephew of Emperor Henry of Germany; two handsome sons of Ivo of Grandmesnil; and William of Rodelent, their cousin—who were crossing by the king’s command to receive their fathers’ estates in England; William called Bigod, with William de Pirou, the king’s steward; Geoffrey Ridel and Hugh de Moulins; Robert Malconduit; the worthless Gisulf, the king’s clerk; and many others of high birth, were swallowed by the waves. Their pitiable fate was mourned by parents, close relations, companions, and friends, who felt the desolation and losses caused by their deaths throughout diverse regions. There perished, it is said, eighteen women who flourished as daughters, sisters, nieces, or wives of kings or counts.

Compassion alone compelled me to recount these things, and diligence urges me to set them down in clear writing for the age to come, since that dark gulf swallowed no one of my own blood for whom I might shed tears from kinship, but only from compassion.

When the coastal inhabitants learned the certainty of the disaster, they dragged the broken ship, with the whole king’s treasure, to shore and found everything that had been aboard entirely safe, except the people. Then, on 25 November 1120, while the Christian people were celebrating the feast of Saint Catherine, virgin and martyr, swift men eagerly ran along the seashore seeking the bodies of the lost; but, finding none, they were deprived of the rewards they greatly desired. Wealthy magnates earnestly sought out skilled swimmers and renowned divers, promising them great sums if they would return the bodies of their loved ones, so that they might commit them to worthy burial.

The people of Mortain sought theirs more earnestly than the rest, because nearly all the barons and chosen men of that county had died. The count alone, as has been said, left the vessel because he was troubled by diarrhoea, together with two knights, Robert de Saucqueville and Walter; by God’s will, while those who remained perished, they successfully crossed in the king’s ship. Count Richard and a few others, however, were found many days later far from the place of destruction, having been carried away as the raging waves drove them each day; they were recognized by acquaintances from the various garments in which they had been clothed.

## XV. Pope Calixtus Returns to Italy. King Henry’s Marriage. Various Events. Dissensions Arising in the Abbey of Cluny

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1120, in the thirteenth indiction, Pope Calixtus, having well ordered ecclesiastical affairs in Gaul, went to Italy with a great company of nobles of both orders. Received favourably by the Romans, he governed the Apostolic See for five years. With God’s aid he performed many good works and shone in our age as a light and example of virtues especially for the Church.

He seized Burdinus, the false pope, who was exercising tyranny against the Church at Sutri, and confined him in the monastery called Cava, so that he might not in any way snarl against the peace of Catholics. There is there a community of religious monks, who possess, according to their rule, an abundance of food and a plentiful supply of all things required by human necessity. The place itself is inaccessible from outside, and no one can enter except by a single approach; consequently that monastery is aptly called Cava, “the Cave.” For just as lions, bears, and other untamed beasts are confined in a cage, lest, roaming freely at will, they cruelly ravage people or livestock, so the wild and undisciplined—who, like wild asses of the desert, roam wantonly and harmfully in various directions—are compelled to live regularly beneath God’s yoke in this scholastic enclosure.

King Henry, having lost his wife and child, decided on the advice of wise men to take a wife. He betrothed the distinguished girl Adeliza, daughter of Godfrey, duke of Louvain. Adorned splendidly with royal insignia, he joined her to himself by the Christian rite; and the queen, consecrated through the ministry of priests, flourished in the kingdom for fifteen years, but though abundant in other blessings she remained until then without the desired offspring. The prudent king carefully distributed among the living the honours of the dead. He joined their wives, daughters, or nieces, together with their inheritances, to his young knights; and thus he consoled many and liberally raised them above hope.

Ranulf of Bayeux obtained the earldom of Chester with the entire inheritance of Count Richard, because he was the nearest heir, being a nephew through Matilda, sister of Count Hugh. He had as wife Lucy, widow of Roger son of Gerold; by her he begot William Ranulf, to whom at his death he left the earldom of Chester and his entire inheritance on both sides of the sea.

Fulk, count of Anjou, after making peace with the king of the English and strengthening their friendship through the union of their children, as has already been said, became concerned for his salvation and greatly desired to be reconciled also to God. He therefore strove to do penance for the crimes he had committed. Entrusting his land to his wife and his young sons Geoffrey and Elias, he went to Jerusalem and remained there for some time in association with the Knights of the Temple. Returning with their permission, he voluntarily became their tributary and bestowed on them thirty pounds of Anjou money every year. Thus, prompted by God, the noble hero granted an annual revenue to those venerable knights, whose life serves God in body and mind and who, scorning all worldly things, prepare themselves daily for martyrdom; by this example he laudably encouraged many other great men of Gaul to a like work.

After the Council of Rheims, concerning which much has already been written, the primate of Lyons, the bishop of Mâcon, and several other bishops became very troublesome to the Cluniacs. They took away many things that others had given them and supplied the clergy—who always envy monks—with material for rebellion. In their dioceses they inflicted insults upon them and harshly oppressed them both personally and through subordinate officers. Therefore the brothers, unable to bear losses and injuries, were distressed and fled, like sheep from wolves’ jaws, to the folds of the monastery.

A great dissension also arose among them within the cloister’s inner precincts. Some, stirred by zeal against Pons, the archimandrite, accused him before Pope Calixtus at Rome: they alleged that he was violent and prodigal in his conduct, and squandered monastic resources excessively on useless causes. Hearing this, he became very angry and, rashly abandoning his abbatial office before the pope, departed abroad. He remained for some time in Palestine, at Jerusalem, on Mount Tabor, and at other holy places where the Lord Jesus had lived bodily among the poor Nazarenes.

The pope was angry because Pons had imprudently left without his permission and blessing, and ordered the Cluniacs to choose for themselves a suitable ruler. They therefore made Hugh, an aged man of thoroughly tested life, their abbot. When he died three months later, they buried him in the northern part of the enclosure; on the stone arch constructed above him they inscribed this epitaph:

> Here lies Hugh the Second, abbot of Cluny,  
> Besançon his father’s land, Lyons his mother’s;  
> Distinguished in religious life, aged, loving, and ever rejoicing  
> In holy worship, he clung to you, supreme Creator.  
> May he now live blessedly with you in eternal rest!

Then the Cluniacs chose as their master Peter, a religious monk, noble and learned, whose governance they have now borne for a very long time.

Abbot Pons, however, was held in high esteem in Judaea, and the fame of his religious life and distinction spread even among foreign peoples. Then, as human instability has it, freely abandoning the seats of prophets and apostles, he returned to Gaul, where his arrival disturbed many minds. After coming back from the eastern regions, he went to Cluny to visit the brothers and friends. Then, at Satan’s instigation, a shameful dissension arose among the brethren. Bernard Grossus was then prior and, it is said, the source and instigator of the sedition. Some resolved to receive Pons honourably as their abbot; others, opposing them, resisted vigorously.

The knights and local people, both peasants and burgesses, rejoiced at his coming, for they loved him greatly because of his affability and generosity. Learning of the monks’ schism, they rushed into the monastery and forcibly brought in Pons and his supporters, although he himself did not wish it. Alas! The frenzied men burst into the monastic enclosure and, as though an enemy force had captured a city by arms, ran to plunder, wickedly carrying off the household goods and utensils of God’s servants. The dormitory, the *crontochium* [term uncertain], and the remaining hidden places of the monks, hitherto concealed from laypeople, now lay open to men and women—not merely respectable persons, but buffoons and prostitutes as well.

On that very day a terrible portent occurred there. The great nave of the basilica, recently built, collapsed; but, God protecting them, it injured no one. Thus the merciful Lord terrified all by an unexpected collapse for their rash invasion, yet by His immense kindness preserved them all. The populace scattered everywhere, running about and shamelessly committing unlawful acts. Yet whoever was saved unharmed by God’s hand from the destruction of that terrible fall, and was preserved in this miraculous manner, was afterward able to repent.

Abbot Peter was absent, having gone to distant regions for the benefit of the many brothers entrusted to his care. The monks of his party hastened to him and recounted in order the losses and the injuries shamefully inflicted upon God’s servants. He, however, went diligently not to Cluny but to Rome, and explained the event to the pope [Honorius II], monks who had suffered these things bearing witness. The pope, hearing it, was deeply grieved both by the monks’ disgrace and by the guilt of the people who had transgressed God’s law. He immediately summoned Pons, ordered him to appear before the judgment of the Apostolic See, and to give an account of the matters charged against him. But Pons came to Rome, delayed approaching the pope, and, though summoned to appear at an appointed hearing, refused to come.

The Roman pontiff therefore sent Peter to Cluny with apostolic letters and dignities, commanding the monks to obey him in all things according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, their holy father. They obeyed the orders, received their abbot in triumph, and have borne the yoke of his authority ever since, laudably serving the divine law. A few days later the pope sent his officers, seized the contemptuous Pons, and imprisoned him. Not long afterward, afflicted with overwhelming grief, he fell ill there and died, mourned by many.

Therefore, as someone says:

> The beginning often seems unlike the end.

Everyone ought from the depths of the heart to commend himself by prayers and vows to God, who is the highest good: that He who began good in us may bring it to completion, strengthen it, and protect it amid adversity and prosperity, so that the faithful combatant may happily receive the prize of the heavenly inheritance.

## XVI. On the Monasteries of Crowland, Ouche, and Certain Others. On the Archbishopric of Canterbury. The English People’s Great Favour toward Monks

[Col. 0896A]

In the thirteenth indiction, on Sunday, about the third hour, while Masses were being sung, on 28 September [1119], a great earthquake occurred in England, and the walls and masonry of churches were cracked throughout four counties. Chester, Shrewsbury, Hereford, and Gloucester, with the neighbouring regions, saw and felt this; their inhabitants, pale with overwhelming terror, trembled. In the time that followed, several prelates of churches in England or Neustria died and, by God’s ordering, left to others the burden of prelacy which they had eagerly borne.

Geoffrey of Orléans, abbot of Crowland, a devout and pleasant man, died on 5 June; he was succeeded by Wallevus, brother of Earl Gaius, of noble English stock. Albold of Jerusalem, a monk of Bec and abbot of Saint Edmund the King and Martyr at Bury St Edmunds, also died suddenly. After him Anselm, nephew of Archbishop Anselm, held the office for a long time.

When Robert de Limesey, bishop of the Mercians, died, Robert surnamed Peccatum succeeded him. On Robert’s death Roger, nephew of Geoffrey de Clinton, assumed the office. After the death of Turold, abbot of Bourgueil, the distinguished Matthias of Mont-Saint-Michel presided. John, a monk of Sées, highly learned in letters, succeeded him. When he died, King Henry entrusted Bourgueil to his kinsman Henry, who had been abbot of Saint John the Baptist at Angély, but had been expelled by the monks and by William, duke of Poitou.

After Fulchered, who as the first abbot had arranged the monastery of Shrewsbury for God’s worship, Geoffrey, a monk of Sées, undertook pastoral care. When he was shortly afterward overtaken by sudden death, Herbert assumed the governance of the immature abbey. When Guntard, vigorous ruler of the church of Tournai, died, Robert of Pruneres was substituted. Because he was well educated, eloquent, and honourable, he was taken from the monastery of Ouche to govern that church.

In Pope Paschal’s time, Ralph, archbishop of Canterbury, came to the king in Neustria and from there began a journey to Rome, although he was already disabled by swollen feet. But when reports of the pope’s death reached him on the road, he sent envoys to Rome. He himself returned to Rouen and lived in Normandy for nearly three years.

Once, while staying there, during the Translation of Saint Benedict, which the monks celebrate festively, he was struck suddenly by a sharp illness after Mass, while being divested of his vestments; he lost his speech. After a few days, despite manifold medical treatment, he began to speak, but never afterward fully recovered the use of his tongue. He then suffered paralysis for two years and, conveyed in a suitably adapted carriage, took to his bed at his see in the hands of his own people.

At last, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1123, in the first indiction, Archbishop Ralph died at Canterbury on 20 October. After some years he was succeeded by William of Corbeil, a regular canon.

Behold how the ancient custom was corrupted through the envy with which clerics burned against monks. Augustine, a monk who first preached Christ in England and converted King Æthelberht and his nephew Sæberht, with the peoples of Kent and London, to Christ’s faith, flourished by Pope Gregory’s command as metropolitan primate of all Britain. Thereafter, down to Ralph, archbishop of Canterbury, all were monks except Frigeard, Oda, and Stigand.

Frigeard, chaplain of King Lothair, was elected to the episcopate and sent to Rome to be consecrated by Pope Agatho. The pope granted him a ten-day postponement; while awaiting the blessing, he took to his bed and gave up his spirit without the anointing of episcopal office. Oda, on account of his nobility and goodness of character, was chosen from the clergy and consecrated archbishop. When he learned that all his predecessors had been monks, he willingly and devoutly changed his habit, and served God as a religious monk and archbishop until death.

Stigand, chaplain to Queen Emma, was very worldly and ambitious. He first seized the see of London and afterward that of Canterbury. Yet he never received the pallium from the Roman pope; indeed, being under interdict from Pope Alexander, he profaned Harold when he should have blessed him as king. Accordingly, as he had been puffed up by raising himself, so, humbled and confounded by God, he groaned; for, after William I had been established in the kingdom, his offences became clear and he was deposed by a synod’s judgment. Thus he is not even to be counted in the catalogue of pontiffs.

The English continually loved and honoured monks because through them they had been converted to God; the clerics themselves rejoiced reverently and kindly that monks were placed above them. Now, however, customs and laws have changed, and clerics exalt clerics in order to refute and trample upon monks.

Around this time Roger, abbot of Ouche, broken by age and illness, declined from his former strength and greatly desired to be relieved of the burden of pastoral care. He therefore sent two honourable monks, Ernald of Telliol and Gilbert of Sées, into England, and sent to the king through them the following letter, which he had ordered Ralph Laurence to compose:

> To his glorious lord HENRY, king of the English, ROGER, humble and unworthy servant of the monks of Ouche: may he be saved by Him who grants salvation to kings!
>
> Since, as the Apostle says (Romans 13:1), “there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been ordained by God,” provision for the welfare of God’s house must be made in an orderly manner by every authority. Therefore I, my lord, who until now, though unworthy, by God’s ordering, under the noble rule of your governance, have served the brethren of the church of Ouche in the place of an abbot; who, supported by your aid, have for a long time applied myself to adversities and prosperities, more as a burden than as an honour; now, worn out by old age and weakened in body, fearing that I may harm rather than benefit the Church, since human character changes with the vicissitudes of time, humbly beseech your clemency, following the counsel of spiritual fathers—the archbishop of Rouen, the bishop of Lisieux, many abbots besides, and various men of ecclesiastical rank—that, pitying me, whom you have shown yourself to love until now, however little it may be, you may henceforth free me, useless and less fit as I am, from so great a burden, and provide for God’s house, according to the wisdom given you by God, a suitable and worthy shepherd.
>
> Yet, lest under such a pretext I should seem to be seeking my own repose by evading the rage of the intractable, I bear witness before God to their charity, obedience, and simplicity. For, nourished abundantly both on milk and on solid food from the breasts of mother Church, they are found ready to obey all the commands of God and of their spiritual father, and peacefully obedient. Most excellent king, setting before you only the misery and incapacity of my weakness and old age, I beg you not to delay carrying this out; I earnestly pray, sinner though I am, the King of kings that He may deign to cooperate with you in this very matter. Farewell.

The kindly king, hearing of the frailty of this simple and religious old man, sympathized and sent letters commanding the community of monks to choose a good abbot acceptable to him. When the envoys returned, sixty-six monks assembled in God’s name and carefully heard Saint Benedict’s chapter concerning the appointment of an abbot. Then the venerable Abbot Roger and his spiritual sons deliberated about the salvation of souls and chose one of themselves in the Lord’s name to take the abbot’s place.

They set over themselves as abbot Guarin of Sées, surnamed “the Little,” and in this imitated the apostles, who by divine direction selected Matthias the Little of God to complete the sacred number of twelve. The two aforementioned elders presented the elected brother, by command of the community, to John, bishop of Lisieux. With his permission, they crossed the sea amid winter’s cold and storms and sought the king, who was then travelling through Northumbria, by long and muddy roads. They found him at York on the feast of Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra.

The illustrious king, hearing what the monks had done, confirmed the election and, on the counsel of Thurstan, archbishop of York, granted the abbey to the chosen brother, Stephen, abbot of Chartres—later patriarch—being witness. The king then granted him all monastic possessions, dignities, and privileges that his predecessors had hitherto held, and issued against adversaries the following charter, sealed with the royal seal:

> HENRY, king of the English, to JOHN, bishop of Lisieux, STEPHEN, count of Mortain, ROBERT de la Haye, and all his barons and faithful men of Normandy, greeting.
>
> Know that I have granted to Abbot Guarin the abbey of Saint Evroul. I will and firmly command that he hold it well, in peace, quiet, and honour, with its churches, tithes, lands, woodland and open land, and all its possessions, as any of his predecessors ever held it more well, quietly, and honourably.
>
> Witnesses: Thurstan, archbishop of York; William de Tancarville; and William d’Aubigny.
>
> At York.

Guarin therefore, strengthened by the exalted authority of the powerful sceptre-bearer, returned to Normandy, kept the Lenten observance with the brothers, and on Ascension Sunday received the blessing from John, bishop of Lisieux. From then on he learned to endure the labours and sorrows of pastoral care.

He is especially to be praised for kindly serving the venerable old Roger and, during the three years that Roger lived thereafter, obeying him in all things as a son obeys a father and a disciple a master. The gentle old man continued, as formerly, to occupy himself in his chamber with psalms, prayers, and pious conversations. He had a suitable priest as his chaplain and companion, from whom he heard Mass and the canonical office in the oratory of Saint Martin, and with whom he discussed, by questions and answers, the mystical enigmas of Scripture and the flowers of collections of writings. Since he had always judged the burden of external cares harmful and unbearable to himself, he now, freely, wholesomely, and honourably gave thanks to God; and, the freer he was, the more secure he became, joyfully awaiting the goal of his final day.

At last, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1126, in the fourth indiction, the aforementioned elder fell more gravely ill than usual. Anointed with holy oil and having fully completed the other rites appropriate to a servant of God, he died on 13 January. His disciple and successor, with his fellow brothers, commended the teacher’s soul to God and duly celebrated the solemn funeral rites. On the following day his body was carried to the chapter house and reverently buried there beside Abbot Osbern.

I composed a brief hexameter epilogue concerning him, in which I preferred truth to elegant sound. Praying thus for him to the kindly Saviour, and recalling the good qualities divinely bestowed upon him, I poured forth:

> Save, Christ the King, the gentle and sincere father Roger,  
> For he patiently endured much for your sake.  
>
> Poor, he abandoned lands, houses, and his own will,  
> And eagerly strove to follow you on the path of virtue.  
>
> Gervase was his father, and Emma his mother;  
> In them shone the radiance of character and ample distinction.  
>
> Roger, a priest trained in learning, gladly took up  
> The monastic yoke of blessed Benedict.  
>
> For long, great uprightness possessed his character,  
> By which he deserved to be set over his companions as ruler and abbot.  
>
> When Serlo was made bishop of Sées,  
> He assumed the governance of the holy monastery of Evroul.  
>
> As a monk he flourished well for fifty-five years,  
> Whence he became shepherd of the flock at Ouche for thirty-three years.  
>
> Here he received ninety monks into discipleship  
> And taught them to serve the strict King in monastic life.

Simple and gentle, resplendent in pursuits of goodness,

Those whom he instructed by words he helped by holy examples.

At length, worn out by old age, he laid down his limbs

upon the earth, when the twelfth day of January had passed.

O good King, his sins wiped away, grant him the joys of light.

He was a lover of peace; I pray that he may now rest in peace! Amen.

XVII. New rebellions against King Henry.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1122, in the tenth indiction, the storm of wars arose again, revived by the spirit of malice; and, as senseless slaughter was bestially stirred up, human blood was miserably shed. The most wicked Erinys, having found herself a dwelling in the hearts of pestilent men, rages; and again she purposes and urges men to rise up for the destruction of themselves and their own. [Col. 0900B] For the restless are distressed by peace and by the tranquillity of the people; and while they strive to cast down the pride of others, they themselves are often destroyed by their own missiles, through the just judgment of God. Truly blind and senseless are those who desire wars amid peace, who seek misery amid happiness as a thirsty man seeks drink, and who do not know what a good thing is while they possess it; but, when they have lost it, seek it with all their might, yet, afflicted by miseries, cannot discover it again. Hence they become sorrowful over an irrecoverable loss, and weep inconsolably.

Thus many men, seeing that the lawful heir of King Henry had died and that the king himself, declining into old age, lacked legitimate offspring, embraced his nephew William with entire affection and bent all their efforts toward raising him up. The king himself lovingly reared after their father’s death, as though they were his own children, the sons of Robert, Count of Meulan, whom he had greatly loved and by whom, at the beginning of his reign, he had been very substantially aided and comforted; and, when the twin brothers Waleran and Robert came of age, he gave them military arms. Waleran possessed all his father’s patrimony on this side of the sea: namely, the county of Meulan in France, and Beaumont in Neustria, together with the patrimony subject to it. His brother Robert, moreover, held the county of Leicester in England. To him the king gave Amicia, daughter of Ralph de Gaël, who had been promised to his son Richard, and added Bristol with the estates belonging to it. [Col. 0900C–D]

The same king treated his daughter-in-law Matilda with the utmost kindness and retained her in England, with the greatest honour, for as long as she wished. Yet after some years, desiring to see her kinsfolk, she went to Anjou and there remained for a while, attached by love to the land of her birth. At last, at the urging of Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, ten years after her betrothal she left the world; and, as a nun in the monastery of Fontevraud, she freely cleaves to and serves her heavenly spouse. As has been said, she married, I think, when she was twelve years old in the summer; and before six months had elapsed her beardless husband perished in a shipwreck. But the benevolent king reared her as his own daughter and kept her with himself for a long time, so that [Col. 0901A] he might join her to a husband of exalted power and raise her in wealth and honour above all her kindred. Yet she adopted the better counsel, being united to her heavenly spouse, the Son of God and of the Virgin. For she was prudent and beautiful, eloquent and well behaved, adorned fittingly with many virtues. May her end in good things prove desirable to humankind and pleasing to God!

At the same time Amaury, Count of Évreux, bore excessive bitterness in his heart because he saw the provosts and *gravarii* in his land raging too violently. They imposed unheard-of exactions and perverted judgments at their pleasure; they inflicted many oppressions upon great and middling persons alike. Yet they did this not by their own strength, but by fear of the king and by his authority. [Col. 0901B] For the king himself, unaware of such acts, was staying in England; nevertheless, his fear restrained military boldness, while he grieved that so great a fury of the *gastalds* was ravaging the inhabitants. Wicked officials are worse than robbers: country people can avoid petty thieves by fleeing or taking a detour, but they can in no way evade crafty bailiffs without loss.

Therefore the spirited Amaury sought out Fulk, Count of Anjou, his nephew, and with persuasive words urged him to unite his daughter Sibylla to William, son of Duke Robert, whose worth, beauty, and highest nobility were fit for sovereignty. [Col. 0901C] Fulk readily complied with his uncle; summoning the young man with his tutors and attendants, he betrothed his daughter to him and granted him with her the county of Maine until he should obtain his hereditary right. Then Amaury drew into partnership with his faction everyone he could, and found many easily inclined and ready for this purpose, such being the fickleness of the Normans.

Accordingly Waleran, Count of Meulan, William de Roumare, Hugh of Montfort, Hugh of Neufchâtel, William Louvel, Baldwin de Bré, Pagan of Gisors, and many others, whispering deceitfully, first took counsel in secret; but shortly afterwards they burst forth into open rebellion, to their own ruin. Count Waleran eagerly desired to display a specimen of his military apprenticeship; but he unquestionably began this foolishly, when he rebelled against his lord and foster-father and, as an ally of that lord’s enemies, first raised arms against him with his deadly hand. He had given his three sisters in marriage to three leading castellans, so that they might be lawfully provided for and he himself might thereby be strengthened among all his kinsmen on every side, men who possessed men, strongholds, and abundant wealth. One was given to Hugh of Montfort, another to Hugh of Neufchâtel, son of Gervase, and the third to William Louvel, son of Ascelin, who after the death of his brother Robert Goël obtained, with the entire patrimony, the castle of Ivry. [Col. 0901D]

William de Roumare claimed his mother’s land, which [Col. 0902A] his stepfather Ranulf of Bayeux had surrendered to the king in exchange for the county of Chester; he also demanded another possession in England called Corfe. But the king did not agree to his request; indeed, he answered him insultingly. Angered, the young man at once crossed to Neustria and, having found a favourable opportunity, withdrew from the king. Relying on the aid of many men, he waged a most fierce war against the Normans from Neufmarché. For two years he satisfied his anger with plunder, burnings, and the capture of men, nor did he cease from this enterprise until the king gave him adequate satisfaction and restored a great part of the right he had demanded.

In September Amaury and Waleran, together with the others whom I have named above, assembled at the Cross of Saint Leufroy [Col. 0902B] and there jointly made a general conspiracy.

The king was not unaware of the secret treacheries. Therefore in October he summoned a great host at Rouen; and, setting out from the city on Sunday after he had eaten, while no one knew where he meant to go or what he intended, he called Hugh of Montfort. When Hugh promptly came before him, the king ordered him to surrender the fortification of Montfort castle. But Hugh, conscious of his treachery, became suddenly anxious when the deception was exposed; and, not knowing what to do in so short a moment of time, he finally assented to the royal commands. For he feared that, if he refused, he would immediately be put in chains. The king then sent faithful friends with him to receive the keys of the fortifications. [Col. 0902C] But as soon as Hugh had vanished from the king’s sight, riding swiftly on a charger, he left his companions at the entrance to the forest. Then, by a shortcut which he knew better, he got ahead of them. He did not dismount, but ordered his brother, his wife, and the other retainers to guard the castle carefully. “The king,” he said, “is coming here with his force; hold this stronghold bravely against him.” From there he hurried to Brionne and, reporting what had happened, armed Count Waleran for open conflict.

When the king’s friends returned, grieving that Hugh’s trickery had deceived them, the spirited king swiftly ordered his knights to arm and attack the unprepared garrison. In the first two days the whole town was burned, and the outer fortification was captured as far as the citadel. Robert the king’s son and Nigel d’Aubigny brought a great force from the Cotentin and other districts; Ralph of Gand and the other besieged men were sharply harassed within by repeated assaults. At last, when they saw themselves deprived of every aid from the conspirators, within a month’s siege they adopted the wiser course, made peace, and, received into the king’s friendship, surrendered the tower to him. The king then went to Pont-Audemer and besieged the castle vigorously for six weeks. [Col. 0902D]

Because Adelina was the daughter of Robert, Count of Meulan, the king granted Adelina and her son Waleran the open country on this condition: that Hugh should return peacefully to him and thereafter be his faithful and intimate friend. Hearing this, Hugh rashly rejected it, and preferred to be disinherited and deprived of everything he possessed rather than, reconciled to the king by whom he had been fostered and raised, remain happily attached to him. [Col. 0903A]

XVIII. Death of Serlo, bishop of Sées.

In the same month [1123], the venerable Serlo, after ruling the bishopric of Sées for thirty-two years, sang Mass in the church of Saint Gervase the martyr on 26 October, the seventh day before the Kalends of November. When it was finished, he summoned the clergy and ministers of the church and said: “I am being broken by age and weakness, and I see that my end is now at hand. I commend you to the Lord God, who set me over you as His vicar, and I beg you worthily to pray to Him for mercy on my behalf. Henceforth let a place of burial be prepared for me, because the time of my dwelling among you is now shortened.”

Then he went with the clergy to the altar of Saint Mary, Mother of God, and there [Col. 0903B] marked out, before the altar and with his pastoral staff, the space for his coffin. Having poured out prayers to the Lord, he sanctified the grave with the sprinkling of holy water. Immediately workmen dug the pit with mattocks and removed the soil with shovels. Masons and stonecutters hollowed out the sarcophagus with hammers and arranged every furnishing for the bishop—still walking and speaking—as though he already lay lifeless on the bier.

On the following day, Friday, he came into the basilica. He wished to celebrate the Mass which he had customarily attended; strong rather in spirit than in bodily strength, he placed the amice over his head, but, with his limbs trembling, feared to begin so solemn a service. He therefore ordered his chaplain William to perform that office. When Mass had been celebrated, [Col. 0903C] he summoned all the canons and said: “Meet before me after dinner, because I wish lawfully to distribute, for the Church’s benefit, the treasure which I have accumulated for human uses from the revenues of the Church. With God’s grace, I greatly desire to avoid any possibility that the wicked party may find anything concerning me by which it could justly accuse me in the sight of my Lord. For as I entered this world naked, so it is fitting that I depart naked, that I may deserve, free from encumbrance, to follow the footsteps of the Lamb, for whose love I long ago joyfully left all worldly things.”

At the ninth hour the bishop sat again at table; but, already longing for the things above, he ate nothing of what was before him. Those others, however, who did not eat eagerly because they were filled with sorrow, he abundantly instructed while feeding them with the nourishment of doctrine [Col. 0903D] and, as a plentiful sower of the word, scattered the seed of God’s word generously. I think that Normandy produced no offspring more elegant or eloquent than Serlo. His stature was moderate, and he was handsome in every respect, insofar as human form requires and as befits an earthborn man filled with many miseries. In adolescence he was red-haired; in youth he quickly became grey; and for almost fifty years before his death he shone white as snow. He was most learned in both secular and sacred letters, and most ready to answer every question put to him. He was exceedingly stern toward the obstinate in evil, but most merciful toward one confessing sin with tears, and, like a pious father toward a sick child, most gentle. I could say many good things about him; but [Col. 0904A] my words cannot remove death from him. Wearied, I turn to other matters and am eager to bring the book I have begun to its end.

As those ready to rise from table after the meal, a messenger arrived and reported that the Roman cardinals Peter and Gregory were present. For the vigil of the holy apostles Simon and Jude was then being observed. Immediately the bishop said to his clerics and stewards: “Go quickly and serve the Romans diligently, giving them abundantly everything that is necessary, because they bear the legation of the lord pope, who after God is the universal father; and, whatever kind of men they may be, they are our masters.” The industrious old man therefore sent his attendants to meet them, while he himself remained seated alone in his chair, without pain or visible illness, as was his custom. [Col. 0904B] All the others, as he had commanded, went out to meet the cardinals, received them honourably as guests, and honoured them in every way, as was fitting, in accordance with the pontiff’s command. Meanwhile, while suitable service was being rendered to them, the bishop, seated in his chair, died as though he had fallen asleep.

Then the ministers, once everything was completed, returned to their old master; but they mourned him tearfully, now dead in his seat. On the following day his body was buried in the grave prepared, as I have said, on the third day, by John, bishop of Lisieux, whom the king had sent from the siege of Pont-Audemer to perform this office.

After Serlo’s death, the young John, son of Hardouin and nephew of the aforesaid John, obtained the bishopric. As he was younger in age, so he must be judged far inferior to his predecessor in literary learning. [Col. 0904C] He was consecrated in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1124, after Easter, and by his uncle’s command first began to exercise the pontifical office in the diocese of Lisieux. For at Cisay, on 4 May, the fourth day before the Nones of May, he dedicated the church of Saint Albin and came from there to Ouche on the same day. Then, on 5 May, the third day before the Nones of May, a Monday, he blessed a new crucifix and dedicated the church and altar of Saint Mary Magdalene, which Ernald, a noble and ancient monk, had built from his own administration and from the gifts of the faithful.

When the king’s retainers heard of the sudden death of the aforesaid prelate, as related, they immediately rushed from the fortress which they were guarding, like ravens to a corpse. They transferred to the king’s treasury all the treasure and everything found in the episcopal residence, distributing nothing to the churches or the poor. [Col. 0904D]

The king himself was then besieging an enemy castle and regarded as suspect several of those who flattered him as intimate followers; knowing their secret deceits, he judged them truly unfaithful. Louis of Senlis, Harcher, the cook of the king of France and a distinguished knight, Simon Trenel of Pexey, Luke de Barra, and other fierce warriors were inside, resisting the besiegers in many ways. But the king burned the entire town, which was very large and rich, and fiercely attacked the castle. He himself attended prudently to everything; like a young recruit, he ran everywhere, energetically applied himself to what had to be done, and encouraged all. [Col. 0905A] He instructed carpenters making a siege tower, reproved with mocking insults those who failed in their work, and by praising those acting stoutly urged them on to greater efforts. At last he raised his engines, injured the garrison by repeated assaults, and forced them to surrender. Louis, Ralph son of Durand, and their accomplices then made peace with the victor; having surrendered the fortification, all were permitted to depart safely with their possessions. Some of them went with the French to Beaumont, where the count was.

There Simon de Parrona, Simon de Neaufle, Guy surnamed Malvoisin, and his nephew Peter de Manli, as well as William Aculeus [“the Needle”], and nearly two hundred other fighting men from France served the count. At his command they ranged through the neighbouring countryside and inflicted enormous losses upon the king’s supporters by plunder and fire. [Col. 0905B]

On the very day when the aforesaid castle was surrendered, news was brought to the king that a grievous crime had been committed elsewhere. For while he was occupied, as has been said, with military affairs around Ry, the treachery of perjurers was devising the following scheme near the Epte.

XIX. Henry pacifies Normandy after punishing rebels and traitors.

An assembly was appointed, on Monday [1123], the day on which the market is held, in the house of Pagan of Gisors. Robert de Candos, keeper of the royal keep, was invited to it, in order that he might suddenly be cut down unarmed by assassins deceitfully armed there, [Col. 0905C] while the town itself was at once invaded on every side by hidden bands. On that day the knights, mingled with crowds of peasants and women hurrying to the market from the neighbouring hamlets, entered the borough freely. Since very many of them had long been known to the burgesses, they were innocently received as guests into their houses; their number filled a great part of the town. At last, at the hour of treachery, frequent messengers urged Robert to hurry, but his pious wife Isabel detained him a long while to discuss domestic matters. This indeed happened by God’s will.

While Robert delayed, Baldwin arrived last at the assembly. While the others were still waiting silently under arms, he was first to cast off his cloak; putting on his mail, he cried out in haste: “Come, knights! Begin what must be done, and act bravely!” Immediately the treachery was discovered by the townsmen, and, when a loud uproar arose, the gate nearest to them was forcibly seized by Pagan’s men. [Col. 0905D] When Robert mounted his horse and, unaware of the treachery, came to the market, he saw armed robbers plundering the town and heard the terrible din of war on every side. Terrified, he fled as quickly as possible to the refuge from which he had not yet gone far. There Count Amaury and his nephew William Crispin, armed with their companies, climbed the hill opposite the stronghold and dared to terrify the garrison more with threats than deeds. All who were certainly known to have taken part in this crime were declared public enemies and guilty of perjury against the king.

But when Robert saw that he could not expel them by his own forces from the strongly fortified town, he set fire to the nearest houses; the devouring flame, driven by the wind, seized the entire borough. Thus he drove the enemies from the town’s enclosure and repelled them from assaulting the stronghold. In so great a confusion of affairs, the generous and honourable burgesses of Gisors lost much; their houses and possessions consumed, they were reduced to poverty. The church of Saint Gervase, which Archbishop Geoffrey had dedicated a few years earlier, was also burned. [Col. 0906A]

When the king heard rumours of these events, he hurried from Pont-Audemer to Gisors with his army, eager to fight boldly against his traitors if he found them. But when they learned that the conqueror, whom they still thought occupied in the siege, was hastening there, they fled in fear and toil and with great disgrace. Then the king’s justices seized the county of Évreux and all the lands of the traitors and subjected them to the king’s lordship. Hugh, Pagan’s son, was then with Stephen, Count of Mortain; unaware of his father’s crimes, he served the king. The king therefore granted him his paternal honour and completely disinherited the perjured old man together with his son Hervé. From that time the treaty which the pope had made between the kings three days earlier was broken, and revived war, fatally blazing up, broke out on both sides. [Col. 0906B]

The winter was then rainy. But the king, wisely considering the labours and anxieties of the common people, spared them, lest, exhausted beyond measure, they should fail like beasts of burden worn out by excessive toil. Therefore, after he had taken the two most strongly fortified towns, Pont-Audemer and Montfort, with the estates belonging to them, he ordered the people to rest in peace during the Advent of the Lord. [Col. 0906C] He stationed his household troops with their principal commanders in castles and entrusted to them the protection of the districts against robbers. He placed Ranulf of Bayeux in the tower of Évreux; Henry, son of Goscelin de Pommerey, at Pont-Authou; Odo, surnamed Borleu, to guard Bernay; and other worthy champions in other places to protect the region from enemy incursions. William, son of Robert of Harcourt, also remained attached to the king’s service. [Col. 0906D]

In the following Lent, Count Waleran summoned his confederates and, on the night of the Annunciation of the Lord, went to reinforce the tower of Vatteville. He had with him his three brothers-in-law: Hugh of Neufchâtel, son of Gervase; Hugh of Montfort; and William Louvel, son of Ascelin Goël. Count Amaury was pre-eminent among them all. The military band under these leaders conveyed provisions to the besieged and unexpectedly attacked at dawn the king’s fortification that hemmed in the castle. They ensnared Walter, son of William of Gualicheriville, whom the king had made captain of the guards, [Col. 0907A] while he stood in armour at the palisade upon the earthwork, fiercely defending the castle. With iron hooks they drew him out without release and carried him away captive.

Count Waleran had entrusted the castle to two brothers in whom he trusted, Herbert of Lisieux and Roger, with eight retainers. He then devastated the surrounding countryside, seized from houses and churches whatever was suitable for food, and brought it into the tower for the support of the guards. On the same day the enraged count, like a foaming boar, entered the forest of Brotonne. Finding peasants cutting wood in the woodland, he seized many of them, cut off their feet, and made the captives cripples; thus he profaned rashly, though not with impunity, the emblem of that holy feast.

Meanwhile Ranulf of Bayeux, keeper of the tower of Évreux, learned through scouts that numerous enemy forces had gone by night to Vatteville. He immediately sought out his comrades Henry, Odo, and William, zealously informed them of the enemy’s passage, and urgently persuaded them, on the enemy’s return, to contest with the sword the royal road of their lord. [Col. 0907B] They gladly agreed, with the hundreds subject to them; splendidly armed, they assembled with three hundred knights near Bourg-Theroulde. On 26 March, the seventh day before the Kalends of April, they waited in the field for those coming out of Brotonne and returning to Beaumont. When the royal knights saw them and considered themselves inferior in valour and strength, they began to fear men of such prowess. [Col. 0907C]

Yet some dared to encourage the fearful. Odo Borleu said: “Behold, the king’s adversaries rage through his land in security and carry off captive one of his nobles, to whom he entrusted the defence of his realm. What shall we do? Shall we allow them with impunity to lay waste the whole country? Some of us must dismount for battle and strive to fight on foot, while another part must mount their horses for combat. A body of archers must stand in the first line and force the hostile column to halt by wounding the horses. In this field today the courage and strength of every warrior will be plainly revealed. For if we, benumbed by cowardice, allow a baron of the king to be led away bound by enemies without striking a blow, how shall we dare stand before the king’s face? We shall deservedly lose our pay together with our honour, and, in my judgment, ought no longer to eat the king’s bread.”

Accordingly all the rest were heartened by the exhortation of this distinguished warrior, and his fellow soldiers consented to dismount with their men. He did not refuse, but, on foot in arms with his men, who loved him greatly, cheerfully awaited the conflict. Waleran, a youth eager for warfare, when he saw his opponents, danced childishly as though he had already defeated them. But Amaury, more mature in age and judgment, dissuaded both him and the others, who were less prudent, from battle: “By all nations!”—for Amaury swore thus—“I advise that we avoid battle. For if we few presume to fight against the many, I fear that we shall incur disgrace and loss. See, Odo Borleu has dismounted with his men; know that he is determined to prevail. This warlike knight, now on foot with his men, will not flee; he will either die or conquer.” [Col. 0907D–0908A]

But the others said: “Have we not long desired to meet the English in the open plain? See, they are here. Let us fight, lest shameful flight be reproached to us and our heirs. Behold, the military flower of all France and Normandy stands here. Who can withstand us? Far be it from us to fear these countrymen and commoners so greatly that we should turn aside from the road because of them or hesitate to fight them!”

They therefore drew up their lines. First Count Waleran wished to charge them with forty knights, but his horse was wounded beneath him by the archers and fell. For forty bowmen in the first line killed the horses, and before the count’s men could strike, they were thrown down. Then the count’s party was quickly shattered and turned to flight; they abandoned their arms and whatever burdens they carried, and each, as he could, saved his life by the protection of flight. There Count Waleran, his two brothers-in-law named Hugh, and nearly eighty other knights were captured. Bound tightly in the king’s prison, they long paid tearfully the penalty for their rashness. [Col. 0908B]

William of Grandcourt, son of William, Count of Eu, a worthy knight of the king’s household, was in this battle and captured Amaury as he fled. But he pitied a man of such prowess with human compassion, knowing very well that, if he were detained, he would scarcely—or never—leave the king’s chains. He therefore chose to go into exile, abandoning the king together with his land, rather than bind an eminent count in inextricable knots. Thus he escorted him to Beaumont and remained honourably in France as an exile with him, as his deliverer. [Col. 0908C]

William Louvel, captured by a peasant, gave him his arms as the price of his ransom. Shorn by him like a squire, carrying a stake in his hand, he fled to the Seine; unknown at the river crossing, he gave his stockings to the boatman as fare and returned barefoot to his own home, rejoicing that he had somehow slipped free and escaped the enemy’s hand.

After Easter 1124 the king held a judicial hearing at Rouen concerning those accused men who had been captured.
