There he deprived Geoffrey de Tourville and Odard de Pin of their eyes for the crime of perjury. He also ordered Luke de Barra to be deprived of sight for his mocking songs and reckless enterprises. [Col. 0908D] Then Charles, Margrave of Flanders, who had succeeded the young Baldwin in the duchy, attended the king’s court with many nobles. He compassionately grieved over the condemnation of the unfortunate men and, bolder than the rest, said: “Lord king, you do something unknown to our customs when you punish knights captured in war, while in their lord’s service, by mutilation of limbs.”

The king replied: “Lord count, I do a just thing, and I shall prove it by manifest reasoning. Geoffrey and Odard were my lawful men with the consent of their lords; freely committing the crime of perjury, they lied to me concerning their faith, and therefore deserved to be punished by death or deprivation of limbs. To preserve the fidelity which they had sworn to me, they ought rather to have abandoned everything they possessed in the world than adhere in any way to any man against right, betray their faith wickedly, and break the compact with their lawful lord. [Col. 0909A] Luke, however, never did homage to me; but he recently fought against me in the castle of Pont-Audemer. Finally, once peace was made, I pardoned whatever he had done outside it and allowed him to depart freely with his horses and property. Yet he immediately joined my enemies, renewed hostilities against me in their company, and added worse deeds to his former ones. He even composed indecent songs about me as a witty minstrel, sang them publicly to my dishonour, and repeatedly provoked my ill-wishing enemies to laughter. God has now delivered him to me to be punished, compelled to desist from wicked deeds, so that others, hearing of the correction of his reckless audacity, may be suitably corrected.”

On hearing this, the duke of Flanders fell silent, because he had nothing that he could reasonably object against it. The executioners therefore carried out the commands. But when Luke learned that he was condemned in this life to everlasting darkness, the wretched man preferred death to living blinded. While the executioners pressed upon him, he resisted to his own hurt as much as he could. At last, as though mad, he struck his head against walls and stones in their hands, and so, to the sorrow of many who had known his courage and wit, miserably gave up his life. [Col. 0909B–C]

Meanwhile Morin de Pin, the count’s steward, fortified his castles and courageously urged all whom he could to resist the king stubbornly. But the strong king, having assembled a great army, besieged Brionne in April. There he immediately built two castles, by which he shortly compelled the enemy to surrender. The madness of fools would not permit that peace to be made without great injury to the innocent, for the whole town, including its churches, was first burned. Those in the castle of Vatteville were reconciled to the king after surrendering the fortification; shortly afterwards the king ordered it razed to the ground by princely authority. [Col. 0909C]

Finally, after the king had subdued to himself all the count’s strongholds except Beaumont, he informed the count, who was in chains, of the outcome of his actions. Through the same messengers he ordered him to command that Beaumont be peacefully surrendered to him. [Col. 0909D] Seeing that he had been deceived by the empty hope of youthful fickleness, justly cast down from the height of his former power because of his perversity, and fearing that, if he offended the high-minded judge by further obstinacy of any kind, an even more dangerous calamity would fall upon him, the count sent faithful envoys and earnestly commanded Morin, administrator of his affairs, without delay to submit that often-mentioned castle to the triumphant sceptre-bearing king of the English.

Morin then, though late, carried out the commands, but could in no way obtain the king’s favour. He had been appointed the young man’s tutor by the king and had freely suggested to him the wicked counsel of rebellion. He lost the wealth through which he had swelled excessively in Normandy; puffed up above himself and seeking more than was fitting, he had insolently introduced a disturbance that would harm many innocent people. Therefore, cast off his paternal soil by royal judgment, he lived in exile among foreign lands until his death. [Col. 0910A] The king acquired the entire possession of the very rich count in Neustria and held the count himself with his two brothers-in-law under close guard. After some time all three were sent to England; the count and Hugh, son of Gervase, were confined in prison for five years. Hugh of Montfort, however, already groaned in chains for thirteen years, and no friend dared to petition the king for him, because he had offended more grievously without grave cause. [Col. 0910B]

Blessed be God, who orders all things well, directs the courses of mortals more beneficially than they themselves desire, and showed the balance of justice in the territory of Red Monastery to pious observers! For in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1124 He granted victory to lovers of peace, confounded the rash disturbers of the whole province, and swiftly dissipated the criminal plots of their accomplices by their own hindrance. During that week, the inhabitants of seven castles situated in the district of Lisieux or Ouche, on their border, had determined to join them to the detriment of many. [Col. 0910C] Hugh of Le Plessis had already deceitfully seized Pont-Erchenfroi and confidently awaited aid from the confederate rebels. Thus the inhabitants of Sap, Bonne-Faite, and Orbec, as well as many others, made an agreement with them through fear, since they lacked the strength and courage to defend themselves against their great power.

But when the leaders of wickedness had been crushed, as stated, their sworn associates fell silent and were exceedingly afraid to be exposed before the justices and men learned in law merely for consenting to treachery. It was then a leap year and, as we heard it commonly said, the leap-year truly fell upon the traitors. As their strength gradually failed, Amaury and Louvel, with the other enemies, sought the king’s peace and, unwillingly, abandoned the exiled William, whom they were wholly unable to help. At last they humbly made satisfaction to the king, recovered his friendship with pardon for their past offences, and regained their former honours. [Col. 0910D]

When these things had been done, William’s agreement with the Angevins was broken; and he, with his tutor Elias and Tirel de Mainers, wandered through foreign lodging-places in great fear and poverty. The long and powerful arms of his uncle were to be feared, for the renown of that man’s authority, wealth, and power stretched everywhere from West to East. That boy was born for hardship, from which he was never fully delivered while he lived. He was likewise bold and proud, handsome and ruinously ready for military enterprise; deceptive hope commended him to the people more than his own merit did. [Col. 0911A] In monasteries of monks or clerics, where he was accustomed to lodge, despite being an exile he was more a burden than an honour because of his extravagance, and, with innumerable men attached to him, he brought them more misery than safety. Many people’s opinion concerning him was mistaken, as afterwards became clearly apparent by heaven’s judgment, as I shall truthfully declare at the end of this little book.

## XX. Rainald, Archbishop of Rheims. Pope Honorius II. Death of the Emperor Charles-Henry. Lothair is elected emperor.

In those days many changes were made among the princes, modern successors being substituted in their places. Ralph, surnamed the Green, archbishop of Rheims, pre-eminent among the fathers in learning and eloquence [Col. 0911B], laudably devoted in our time to worthy studies, father and instructor of monks and clerics, patron and defender of the poor and of all subject to him, died in a good old age after many praiseworthy works. After him Rainald, bishop of Angers, a very different man from his predecessor in many respects, obtained the see. Ulger, whose life was renowned for religion and learning, assumed the government of the church of Angers, and offered the peoples the light of truth.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1125, in the third indiction, Pope Calixtus died, and Lambert, bishop of Ostia, was raised to the papacy as Honorius. This most learned old man was zealous in the observance [Col. 0911C] of the sacred law, and governed the Roman Church for six years. In the same week in which Pope Calixtus departed this life, Gilbert, archbishop of Tours, who had gone to Rome on ecclesiastical business, died there. When the people of Tours heard this, they chose for themselves Hildebert, the approved bishop of Le Mans, and, with Pope Honorius’s permission, joyfully translated him to the chair of the metropolitan see of Tours. He lived there honorably for nearly seven years and benefited those subject to him. At Le Mans he consecrated Guy, a Breton, as bishop.

In the same year, during Whitsun week, Charles-Henry V, emperor, died and was buried at Speyer, the metropolis of Germany. As he lay dying, the Caesar left the imperial insignia to the Empress Matilda; [Col. 0911D] afterward, since no offspring survived him, Lothair, duke of the Saxons, succeeded, enthroned by the general decree of the people. For the archbishop of Mainz, eminent in power and energy, and taking precautions through his foresight lest schism or an irregular seizure of the Empire should occur, summoned the bishops and nobles of the whole realm with their forces. When they had assembled, he deliberated with them concerning the appointment of an emperor. He had obtained from the empress the insignia and ornaments of the Empire before presuming to speak of so great a matter:

> “Most excellent barons,” he said, “who stand upon this plain, listen to me attentively, I beseech you; and, giving prudent heed, obey what I shall say. I labor for the benefit of you all and of the many who are absent; anxiously I reflect by night [Col. 0912A] and by day. There is no need now for many speeches. You know well that our emperor has died without issue. A successor faithful and devoted to God, and most useful to the children of the Church, must wisely be sought for him. Let forty wise and lawful knights from among you therefore be chosen; let them withdraw apart and, according to their faith and conscience, elect the best emperor—one who, by merit of his virtues, may be set over the Empire and may give the fullest protection to all the people subject to him.”

This was granted by all. Indeed, more than sixty thousand fighting men were present there, each striving in different directions and considering the outcome of the affair.

At length the distinguished arbiters, who had been separated from so many soldiers, returned after a long discussion [Col. 0912B] and said:

> “We commend Frederick, duke of the Alemanni; Henry, duke of Lorraine; and Lothair, duke of the Saxons, and declare them honourable men worthy of the Empire. We say this certainly not because we have been swayed by private favour, but because, having considered the welfare of all, we affirm what has seemed right to us. In the name of the Lord, choose whichever of these three you wish, for all, as has long been proved, are praiseworthy persons and, in our judgment, deserve by their valour to be preferred to the whole world.”

On hearing this, the archbishop said:

> “You glorious princes who have been named, go eagerly and choose one from among the three of you. Whomever [Col. 0912C] you elect, we shall submit to him in the name of Almighty God. But if any one of you departs from the common decree, let him immediately be beheaded, lest through one man’s insolence the holy assembly of Christians be disturbed.”

The stern condition imposed by the spirited prelate was dreadful to all, and among so great a multitude no one dared utter a word against the prelate.

Accordingly the aforesaid dukes withdrew apart and, surrounded by a ring of legions, stood in the midst. Looking at one another, they were silent for some time. At last, while the other two were silent, Henry first broke the silence:

> “What are we doing here, lords? Have we been sent here to devote ourselves to silence? A great business has been entrusted to us. We have assembled here not to be silent, but to discuss the greatest good. [Col. 0912D] I have waited long enough for you to speak. Shall we spend the whole day mute? Consider the deliberation entrusted to us, and say what pleases you.”

When his companions assented that he should state what seemed good to him, since he was the eldest, he said:

> “It is fitting that our counsel should now be of the best kind, because at this moment the whole Latin world looks to our decision. Let us therefore pray to the Lord God, who set Moses over the Hebrews and revealed to him Joshua as a victorious successor, that He himself may graciously work with us, as He was with Samuel when he anointed David king.”

Having said this, he chose his son-in-law Lothair. The third feared to object, apprehensive of the sentence enacted by the chief prelate. They then returned to the assembly. Henry, giving careful [Col. 0913A] attention to all, said:

> “We elect Lothair, duke of the Saxons, endowed with many virtues and long proved in the high rank of a prince by military prowess and justice, as king of the Alemanni, Lorrainers, Germans, and Bavarians, Lombards and all the peoples of Italy, and as emperor of the Romans.”

All heard this, and many willingly assented.

The archbishop of Mainz, as I have said, was then the chief and organizer of this assembly. He immediately ordered all the highest nobles, before departing from that field, at once to do homage to Lothair before all. Straightway Henry, rejoicing, Frederick, grieving, and all the chief magnates after them bent the knee before Lothair, did him homage [Col. 0913B], and set him over themselves as king and emperor.

When the assembly had broken up, Frederick’s army attacked Lothair, wounded him and many on his side, and put them to flight. For Frederick had brought with him nearly thirty thousand armed men, because through fear or favour he supposed that he himself would become king. But since, as has been said, he was forestalled by the ingenuity of the worthy pontiff and could not accomplish his will, he afterward waged a very great war through his brother Conrad. Lothair, however, with God’s help prevailed, and by the merit of his valour and commendable piety had now reigned for ten years.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1126, in the fourth indiction [Col. 0913C], the pontifical church of Saint Gervasius, martyr of Milan, at Sées, was dedicated on 21 March by Lord Geoffrey, archbishop of Rouen, and five other bishops. King Henry of the English was present there with his nobles and granted to that church an annual income of ten pounds as an endowment. Present there were Gerard, bishop of Angoulême and legate of the Roman Church; John of Lisieux; John of Sées; Geoffrey of Chartres; and Ulger of Angers.

In October the church of Saint Peter the Apostle in the suburb of Rouen was dedicated; there the body of Saint Ouen, archbishop and confessor, was honourably laid to rest.

[Col. 0913D] In the same year William of Poitiers died. William, duke of Apulia, son of Roger Borsa, also died without sons. Pope Honorius sought zealously to subject his duchy to the lordship of the Apostolic See. But Roger the younger, count of Sicily, rose against this, engaged in many battles with the pope’s army, and claimed by military force the principality of his cousin; having done homage to the pope, he possessed it until the present day. This man was the son of Roger the elder, son of Tancred of Hauteville, and of the valiant Adelaide, who had been the wife of Boniface, a powerful marquis of Italy, and who, after the death of her first husband—the brother, that is, of Guiscard—married Baldwin I, king of Jerusalem.

## XXI. King Louis again undertakes the protection of Henry Clito, son of the duke of Normandy, and attempts to defend his rights against the king of England.—The duke of Flanders is killed by Burchard of Lille and other conspirators.—Henry Clito receives the duchy of Flanders.—Wounded in battle, he dies.

[Col. 0914A]

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1127, in the fifth indiction, Louis, king of the Franks, addressed the magnates of the realm at his court on Christmas Day and earnestly entreated them to pity and assist William the Norman. For he was a distinguished young man, handsome, bold, and worthy, but beset by many misfortunes from infancy. While still an infant, his mother Sibylla of Apulia was killed by poison. His father Robert, duke [Col. 0914B] of the Normans, was captured in the battle of Tinchebray, and Henry, his brother and king of the English, obtained the duchy of Normandy. The boy himself was entrusted by order of the king to be brought up by Elias of Saint-Saëns, his maternal uncle; through fear of the aforesaid king and his supporters, Elias took him into France. There, among strangers, he was brought up in great poverty and not without much fear. Many enemies sought him, in many ways, in order to kill him; many others, on the contrary, sought him out in order that he might be restored to his paternal honour. Human purpose vainly attempts what divine ordinance has otherwise disposed.

King Louis and the chief magnates of the French kingdom; the very energetic young Baldwin and Charles, princes, with the nobles [Col. 0914C] of Flanders; Amaury of Montfort, count of Évreux; Stephen, count of Aumale; Henry, count of Eu; Waleran, count of Meulan; Hugh of New Castle; Hugh of Montfort; Hugh of Gournay; William of Roumare; Baldwin of the Wood; Richer of Laigle; Eustace of Breteuil; and many other Normans and Bretons; together also with Robert of Bellême and the forces of the Angevins and men of Le Mans—all undertook to assist the exiled William. But, God opposing them, who had preferred King Henry above all those named in depth of understanding, military strength, and abundance of resources and friends, they achieved nothing. Many of them were captured, disinherited, or slain for their criminal undertaking. Many rebellions also arose against King Henry [Col. 0914D] on this account, and castles and rural districts were burned. The city of Évreux and the episcopal church of Saint Mary, the abbey of nuns at Brionne, Montfort, Laigle, Pont-Audemer, Bellême, and many other places which perished in devouring fires bear witness to this.

At length, when the exiled William was twenty-six years old and no one had been able to support him against his uncle in recovering his paternal inheritance, Queen Adela gave him her uterine sister in marriage, namely the daughter of Count Rainier. King Louis gave him Pontoise, Chaumont, and Mantes, together with the whole Vexin. This was done in January, and shortly before Lent [Col. 0915A] he came to Gisors with a military force to press his claim upon Normandy; but the Normans respected him as their natural lord.

On 1 March, Charles, duke of Flanders, son of King Cnut of the Danes, came to the church at Bruges with Tesnard, a townsman of Brothburg, and twenty knights, to hear Mass. There, while he was bowed to the ground in prayer to God, he was killed by Burchard of Lille and thirty-two other knights; and nearly all who were with him there were cruelly killed. On hearing of so grave a crime, William of Ypres immediately besieged the castle of Bruges and shut in the murderous killers on every side, until Louis, king of France, came with William the Norman. After a month-long siege, he crushed, captured, and hurled the savage executioners from the highest [Col. 0915B] tower of Bruges. He then gave the duchy of Flanders to William the Norman and took back the Vexin with the towns which he had given him. Yet William, after obtaining the duchy of Flanders by gift of the king and hereditary right, ruled it laboriously for only sixteen months.

First, he rose against the traitors of Duke Charles, pursued them with all his efforts, and spared none for any consideration of noble birth, power, rank, or penitence. He condemned nearly one hundred and eleven and cruelly punished them by being cast down or by other kinds of death. The relatives of those killed were therefore deeply grieved and plotted loss and destruction against him. He gave the castle of Montreuil to his guardian [Col. 0915C] Elias of Saint-Saëns, who had long been in exile for him and had endured disinheritance with Tirel of Ménerville. In August he led an army against Stephen, count of Boulogne; wishing to subject him to himself, he began fiercely to ravage Stephen’s land with sword and fire. At length trustworthy envoys of peace were sent, and because they were cousins they pledged their hands to one another; a truce for three years having been granted, they were reconciled.

Meanwhile, while Duke William was occupied in this expedition and fortune attended him variably, at times happily but more often sadly, Iwan of Ghent and Daniel of Tenremonde, nephews of Baldwin of Ghent, cunningly sought vengeance for their friends and attempted to carry out their plotted crime, to the lamentation of many [Col. 0915D]. For they approached Thierry, count of Elsass, reproached him for neglecting and relinquishing his hereditary right without pressing his claim, and promised that they and many others would assist him if he asserted that right. Thierry of Elsass and Lambert, count of Ardres, therefore entered Flanders and recovered, with the support of the Morini, the very celebrated castle called Lille, Furnes, Ghent, and many other places. On hearing this, William granted a truce to Stephen of Boulogne and fought against his domestic enemies until death. For they were powerful and noble men, commendable for courage and great valour, formidable through wealth, friends [Col. 0916A], fortifications, and the favour of their fellow-countrymen.

In July the duke, having assembled an army, besieged the castle of Aalst and pressed it with Godfrey, duke of Louvain, for several days. Many came to him from Neustria. So deeply did many love him, and so great was their confidence in him, deceived by false hope, that they freely left their native land with their natural lords, relatives, and friends. Others, polluted by perjuries or killings, attached themselves to the exile.

William of Ypres, son of Robert, margrave of the Morini, at first opposed him; but, fortune betraying him, he fell into William’s hands at Trie, a castle of the Vexin. William immediately entrusted him to Amaury of Montfort [Col. 0916B] for safe keeping. Not long afterward, however, the duke received this same man into favour through the intervention of friends and released him from his bonds.

At Ypres there were three fortresses, one belonging to the duke, another to William, and the third to Daniel and Iwan. There the duke’s enemies conspired to kill him. They decided to rush upon his citadel by night and stationed four companies outside, so that he might by no means escape destruction. But the duke, unaware that so deadly a plot was prepared against him, came to a certain young woman whom he loved. She washed his head as usual, and, having learned of the hostile conspiracy, wept as she washed him. The young man asked his beloved why she was weeping and, by prayers and threats, carefully [Col. 0916C] compelled her to disclose in sequence all that she had learned from his enemies concerning his death. Immediately, with his hair still uncombed, he and his men seized their arms. He took her with him lest she should somehow be endangered, and sent her to William, duke of the Poitevins, his contemporary companion-in-arms, through a certain abbot; he begged that duke to give her in honourable marriage, as though she were his own sister, in reward for her liberation of him. This was done.

William then passed safely through all the snares and angrily condemned his public enemies. The warlike young man next gathered forces from every side, besieged the castle of Aalst, attacked it vigorously, and strove with all his strength to compel the townsmen to surrender. He often performed both the office of duke and that of common soldier [Col. 0916D], for which his loving guardians, fearing for him, frequently rebuked him. Often, like a keen commander, he summoned hundreds; but more often, like an ardent novice, he fought.

One day [1128], an enemy formation came to the crossing of a certain watercourse and sought to aid the besieged. Against it the du[ke suddenly] dispatched three hundred knights.

> [Note: [Col. 0915] Thus the learned man Le Prévost restored this passage, lacking in the manuscript.]

But as the conflict [was too] prolonged and the enemy’s strength increased greatly, the duke’s knights began somewhat to fall back and waver. Seeing this, the duke roared in anger, hurried to their aid, fought boldly, greatly strengthened his men, and put the enemy to flight. Returning from there, he suddenly charged the gates of the castle; at his arrival [Col. 0917A] the troop of retainers which had sallied out scattered and fled, some of them leaping over the rampart. When the duke saw them there and seized the lance of a foot-soldier standing in his way, he was by chance grievously pierced by the iron point which he tried to grasp in his right hand. The wound ran through the fleshy part of his hand between thumb and palm as far as the pulse of his arm. Thus severely wounded, he withdrew, showed the wound to his household, and began to lament in heartfelt grief; not long afterward he took to his bed. For the disease called the sacred fire entered the wound, and his whole arm as far as the elbow turned black like charcoal. He was ill for five days, repented of his sins, sought the monastic habit, and, fortified by confession and reception of the Lord’s body, died.

[Col. 0917B] Elias and Tirel, with the other members of the duke’s household who had always been faithful to him, concealed the mortal wound of their young lord from the Flemings and all outsiders, and compelled the townsmen to surrender by force of arms. Iwan, the lord of the castle, was reconciled; after hostages had been given and peace established, he became a trusted friend. Then the Normans led him into the duke’s tent and sorrowfully showed him their lord lying dead upon a bier:

> “Look,” they said, “you can see what you have done. You have killed your lord and thereby brought mourning upon countless knights.”

Seeing this, he trembled and burst into tears of violent grief. Elias said to him:

> “Cease, I pray you, [now to weep, for] henceforth your tears are useless [and are no] help to the duke. Go; take up your arms [and make] [Col. 0917C] your knights arm themselves, and have the dead duke’s body honourably conveyed to Saint-Bertin.”

> [Note: [Col. 0917] This passage, defective in the manuscript of Saint-Evroul, was thus restored by the often-praised Le Prévost from the Puteanus manuscript, Imperial Library of Paris, no. 875.]

This was immediately done. A community of monks came out to meet it and received the corpse into the church. There it was buried beside Duke Robert, and the following epitaph was inscribed on the stone laid over it:

> William, famous knight, noble man,  
> Margrave of Flanders, lies here, a monk of Saint-Bertin.  
> Robert was his father, and Sibylla his mother;  
> They held the reins of the Norman race.  
> On the fifth day before the Kalends of August returned,  
> The warrior died, struck by iron in battle at Aalst.

John, son of Odo, bishop of Bayeux, first approached King Henry, announced to him the fate of his nephew [Col. 0917D], and humbly offered sealed letters on William’s behalf. In these, the dying young man asked his uncle’s forgiveness for the wrongs he had committed against him, and begged him kindly to receive all those who had taken refuge with him, if they returned to Henry. When the king received this, he assented. Many who had been distressed by their lord’s death took up the cross of the Lord and, exiles for Christ, sought his tomb in Jerusalem.

Thierry of Elsass was made duke of the Morini and was allied in confidential friendship with Louis, king of the Franks, and Henry, king of the English. King Henry, by royal justice, subjected to him Stephen, count of Boulogne [Col. 0918A], and the other Normans who held lands in Flanders. At length Thierry’s very beautiful wife, whom he then had, died some years later; on the advice of the king of England, he married Sibylla of Anjou, the betrothed of his predecessor William.

## XXII. King Henry forgives the supporters of his nephew Henry Clito.—Normandy is restored to peace.—The prophecies of Merlin.

Relying on the help of the heavenly Dispenser, King Henry remained firm in his high position amid so many adversities. He received rebels who had abandoned their rash enterprise and humbly returned to him, and with careful kindness consented to be reconciled with them. First, therefore, as was said above, William of Roumare was honourably [Col. 0918B] reconciled to the king and thereafter became his familiar table-companion and friend. The king also gave him as wife the noble Matilda, daughter of Richard de Redvers; she bore him a handsome son named William Elias. This knight had been morally unstable in youth and excessively devoted to lust; but, to be chastened by divine punishment, he fell into a most severe illness. Having spoken with Archbishop Geoffrey, he vowed to God a reformed life. He then returned to Newmarket and, when he had recovered, established seven monks in the church of Saint Peter the Apostle, where four secular canons had served. Beyond what Hugh of Grandmesnil had given there to the monks of Saint-Evroul, he gladly added much more. He dictated a charter confirming the possessions which [Col. 0918C] he had given, and rebuilt the church screen and the monastic dwellings.

Thus, in the twenty-eighth year of King Henry [1128], William, the young count of Flanders, died. With him fell the strength and courage of all who supported him against his uncle. The rashness of the arrogant had no one to whom it could attach itself after it lost the young leader for whose sake it had troubled Normandy’s countryside with fire and arms. Then Duke Robert, who was held prisoner at Devizes, saw in a dream that his right arm was struck by a lance and immediately taken from him. On awakening in the morning, he said to those standing by:

> “Alas! My son is dead.”

The report had not yet reached that place by messengers’ mouths when [Col. 0918D] his father, taught this in dreams, told those assembled. He himself died at Cardiff six years later and, then released from prison, was buried at Gloucester.

Behold the prophecy of Ambrosius Merlin, which he uttered in the time of Vortigern, king of Britain, and which has been visibly fulfilled in many particulars during six hundred years. I should therefore like to insert into this little work certain matters which seem applicable to the times of our own age. Merlin was contemporary with Saint Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, who in the time of Emperor Valentinian crossed into Britain twice and disputed against Pelagius and his followers, who prated about the grace of God. Having performed many signs in the Lord’s name, he refuted the heretics. Then, after he had devoutly celebrated the Easter feast, he fought against the Anglo-Saxons, who were then pagans and were attacking the Christian Britons. Stronger in prayers than in arms, with an army of newly baptized men crying “Alleluia,” [Col. 0919A] he put the heathen host to flight. Whoever wishes to know these things and other matters concerning the fortunes of the Britons more fully should read the books of Gildas the Briton, historian, and Bede the Englishman. In them a lucid account shines forth to readers concerning Vortimer and his brothers, and brave Arthur, who waged twelve wars against the English.

It is reported that Merlin showed Vortigern a pool in the middle of the pavement, two vessels in the pool, a folded tent in the vessels, and two worms in the tent [Col. 0919B], one white and the other red. They immediately grew very large and, becoming dragons, fought one another cruelly. At last the red dragon won and drove the white to the edge of the pool. As the king watched these things, he wept sadly with the Britons. Asked by the astonished spectators for an interpretation, Merlin, speaking by a prophetic spirit, explained that the pool in the midst of the pavement represented the world; the two vessels, the islands of the Ocean; the tent, the cities and villages of Britain in which men dwell; and the two worms, the two peoples of the Britons and English. They would afflict each other in terrible conflicts until the bloodstained Saxons, signified by the red dragon, should drive the Britons, figured by the white worm, as far as Cornwall and the shore of the Ocean. The Britons are white because they were made white by the font of baptism from the days of King Lucius and Pope Eleutherius.

The aforesaid prophet set forth in order the things that would happen to the northern islands and committed them to written memory in figurative language. Then, after speaking of the German worm and the decimation of Neustria—the massacre at Guildford inflicted on Alfred, brother of Edward, son of King Æthelred, and Alfred’s companions—he thus prophesied concerning the instability of the present age and the turbulent changeability of events:

> “A people shall come in wood and iron tunics, who will exact vengeance for that man’s wickedness. They will restore dwellings to their former inhabitants, and the ruin of foreigners will be revealed. His offspring shall be cut away from our gardens, and the remnant of his race shall be decimated. They shall bear the yoke [Col. 0919D] of perpetual servitude and shall wound their mother with mattocks and ploughs. Two dragons shall succeed, one of whom shall be choked by the dart of envy, while the other shall return beneath the shadow of a name. A lion of justice shall succeed; at his roar the Gallic towers and the dragons of the islands shall tremble. In his days gold shall be drawn from the lily and the nettle, and silver shall flow from the hooves of bellowing beasts. Men with curled hair shall wear varied fleeces, and the outward dress shall signify the inward parts. The feet of the barking creatures shall be cut off. The beasts shall have peace; humanity shall grieve at punishment. The form of commerce shall be divided: half shall be round. The rapacity of kites shall perish and the teeth of wolves shall be blunted. The lion’s cubs shall be changed into fish of the sea [Col. 0920A], and his eagle shall nest upon Mount Aravius. Venedotia shall grow red with maternal blood, and the house of Corineus shall kill six brothers. The island shall be wet with nightly tears, whence all shall be provoked against all. Descendants shall strive to fly beyond the heights, but the favour of newcomers shall be exalted. Mercy from the wicked shall harm its possessor, until he puts on his begetter. Then, girded with the tusks of a boar, he shall surpass the mountain-peaks and the shadow of the helmeted man. Albania shall be angered and, summoning those from beyond the sea, shall devote itself to shedding blood. A bridle shall be placed in his jaws, forged in the Armorican gulf. The eagle of the broken treaty shall gild it and shall rejoice in a third nesting. The ruler’s cubs shall awake and, abandoning the woods, shall hunt within the walls of cities [Col. 0920B]. They shall make no small slaughter among those who oppose them and cut off the tongues of bulls. They shall load the necks of the roaring creatures with chains and renew the times of their forefathers. Thereafter, from the first to the fourth, from the fourth to the third, from the third to the second, a thumb shall be anointed with oil. The sixth shall overthrow the walls of Ireland and turn its woods into a plain. He shall bring diverse portions into one, shall be crowned with a lion’s head; his beginning shall yield to wandering desire, but his end shall fly up to the heavenly ones. For he shall renew the seats of the blessed throughout the lands and set pastors in fitting places. He shall clothe two cities with pallia and give virginal gifts to virgins. Thereupon he shall deserve the favour of the Thunderer and be crowned among the blessed. From him shall come a plague penetrating all things, by which the ruin of his own people shall threaten. For through it Neustria shall lose both islands and be stripped of its former dignity. Then the citizens shall return to the island.”

I have excerpted this small reading from Merlin’s little book and have offered a small drop of it to students to whom it has not been revealed. Some part of it I have understood in events which have occurred. But, unless I am mistaken, those yet to be born will experience much more of it with grief or joy. Those skilled in histories will readily be able to understand his sayings if they know what happened to Hengist and Catigern, Pascent and Arthur, Æthelberht and Edwin, Oswald and Oswiu, Cædwalla and Alfred, and the other princes of the English and Britons down to the times of Henry and Geoffrey, who still await under uncertain fortune the things hanging over them, ordained for them by divine and ineffable [Col. 0920D] disposition.

For it is clearer than daylight to the informed reader what is said of William’s two sons:

> “Two dragons shall succeed”—that is, lustful and fierce lords—“one of whom shall be choked by the dart of envy”: namely William Rufus, who in hunting will be slain by an arrow. “The other,” that is Duke Robert, “shall perish beneath the shadow” of prison, bearing the emblem of his former name, that is, duke. “A lion of justice shall succeed”—this refers to Henry—“at whose roar the Gallic towers and the dragons of the islands shall tremble,” because he surpassed in wealth and power all who reigned in England before him.

Let interpreters explain the rest plainly in the same way. I could say much in explanation, if I undertook to compose a commentary [Col. 0921A] on Merlin. But setting these matters aside, I shall return to the order of my narrative and truthfully pursue the fortunes of our own people.

## XXIII. Gormond, Patriarch of Jerusalem. Ecclesiastical Affairs. The Council of Rouen. Affairs Conducted in France and in the Kingdom of Jerusalem.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1128, in the sixth indiction, Gormond, patriarch of Jerusalem, died. Stephen of Chartres governed holy Sion for two years after him. When he departed, William of Flanders succeeded. In the seventh indiction, Geoffrey, archbishop of Rouen, fell ill and, after a prolonged illness, departed this life on 26 November. Meanwhile, while the aforesaid chief prelate was ill and, solicitous for the salvation of his soul [Col. 0921B], wisely distributed all that he possessed, Matthew, monk of Cluny, bishop of Albano and legate of the Roman Church, came to Rouen to King Henry and discussed ecclesiastical interests with him. By the king’s order, therefore, the bishops and abbots of Normandy were summoned; in the chapter at Rouen, with the king present, they heard the decrees proclaimed by Pope Honorius’s legate as follows:

That no priest shall have a wife. But whoever refuses to abstain from a concubine shall not hold a church, receive a share in ecclesiastical benefices, or have his Mass heard by any of the faithful.

That one priest shall not serve two churches, nor any cleric possess prebends in two churches; rather, he shall serve God in that church whose benefices he enjoys, and daily pray there for his benefactors.

That monks or abbots shall not receive churches or tithes from the hand of laymen. Laymen shall restore to the bishop what they had usurped, and monks shall receive offerings from the bishop in accordance with the wishes of the possessors. Yet whatever they had formerly acquired in any fashion, they shall peacefully possess by papal indulgence; but in future they shall not presume to usurp anything of this kind without the permission of the bishop in whose diocese it lies.

Then the Roman legate absolved all from past transgressions, and in the following month, as has already been said, the archbishop died. Present there with [Col. 0921D] the legate were Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres; Goscelin Rufus, bishop of Soissons; and all the bishops of Neustria: Richard of Bayeux, Turgis of Avranches, John of Lisieux, Richard of Coutances, and John of Sées. There were also many abbots: Roger of Fécamp, William of Jumièges, Ragenfrid of Saint-Ouen, Warin of Saint-Evroul, Philip of Saint-Taurin, and Alan, elect of Saint-Wandrille [Col. 0922A], as well as many others. Their supporter, King Henry, was present and did not allow the bishops to impose any burden upon them.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1129, in the seventh indiction, the boy Philip was chosen by his father Louis and crowned king at Rheims on Easter Day by Rainald II, archbishop of Rheims. But two years later, having fallen from a horse and been grievously crushed, he died at Paris.

In the same year, King Henry gave his daughter Matilda in marriage to Geoffrey, Count of Anjou; Turgis, the aged bishop of Avranches, joined them in marriage with the episcopal blessing. After their wedding had been lawfully celebrated, Count Fulk again departed for Jerusalem, married the daughter of King Baldwin II, and easily acquired the kingdom of Jerusalem and the principality of Antioch—things which the most famous warriors had scarcely obtained. [Col. 0922B] His mature father-in-law also offered him the crown, but the younger man refused to wear it during the elder’s lifetime. Nevertheless, for the one year that the elder thereafter survived, he exercised authority securely throughout the whole realm as son-in-law and heir.

At first he foresaw the future less wisely than he ought, and, being too hasty, irrationally changed provostships and other offices. For the leading men who had from the beginning fought strenuously against the Turks, and who with Godfrey and the two Baldwins had laboriously subjected cities and towns to themselves, the new prince removed from his familiarity. He obeyed newly arrived Angevins, and other inexperienced persons who had recently [Col. 0922C] come; and, rejecting the old supporters, he placed these recent flatterers over the counsels of the kingdom and the custody of fortresses. Hence great resentment arose, and the obstinacy of the magnates was damnably aroused against this inexperienced changer of offices. Inflated by a spirit of wickedness, they long directed against their own vitals the zeal for warfare which they ought unanimously to have exercised against the heathen. Each side even gathered heathens against the other. Thus they lost many thousands of men and several towns.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1130, in the eighth indiction, Baldwin II, king of Jerusalem, died on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September [15 August], and Fulk of Anjou had already possessed the kingdom for six years.

[Col. 0922D] In the same year, Hugh of Amiens, a Cluniac monk and abbot of Reading, became archbishop of Rouen.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1131, Pope Honorius died at Rome, and immediately an excessive schism arose in the Church of God. For Gregory the deacon was elected pope by some and was called Innocent; while Peter Anacletus was consecrated by others.

## SUMMARY OF THE THIRTEENTH BOOK

[Col. 0923]

I. Various events. The Franks go to Spain to aid King Alfonso against the Saracens. Many of them settle in Spain. Numerous affairs of those regions. II. The battles of King Alfonso, aided by the Franks, against the Saracens of Spain and Morocco. Disorders in Spain. The death of King Alfonso. III. The tribulations of the Church of God. Bishoprics and monasteries are disturbed. The schism of the antipope Anacletus. The arrival of Pope Innocent II in Gaul. IV. An assembly of prelates gathered at Cluny. Various events in Italy and Normandy. V. Disturbances and various events in Apulia and Sicily. VI. Portents and heavenly scourges. The ruin of many churches and cities. The deaths of very many people and princes. VII. The Council of Piacenza. Hugh, archbishop of Rouen. King Henry suppresses or punishes many lords. The illness of Louis, king of the Franks. VIII. The death and funeral of Henry, king of the English. Disturbances in England. IX. Stephen, the new king of the English. Disturbances in Normandy. The plundering of the borough of Ouche. X. Various events in England and Normandy. XI. The invasion and plundering of Normandy by the Angevins. XII. Pious meditations. The death of various lords and prelates. Drought. XIII. Stephen, king of the English, receives Normandy as a fief from Louis, king of the Franks. Stephen punishes rebels. Angevin attacks upon Normandy. XIV. The death of Guarin, abbot of Ouche. The death of Louis, king of the Franks. Disturbances and wars in Normandy. A Breton invasion of Normandy. King Stephen crosses the sea into England. XV. Various events in the kingdom of Jerusalem. XVI. John, emperor of Constantinople, attempts to gain possession of the city of Antioch. Raymond, prince of Antioch, voluntarily becomes the vassal of Emperor John. XVII. Various events in France, England, Apulia, and Normandy. The Count of Anjou renews war against the king of England. XVIII. King Stephen quells and punishes rebellions. XIX. Peace between the kings of England and Scotland. Wars in Normandy. Plundering by the Angevins. XX. A Roman council. Andinus, bishop of Évreux. The deeds of the bishops of Salisbury and Ely. Matilda, countess of Anjou, crosses the sea into England. Various events. XXI. Disturbances and rebellions in England. King Stephen is captured in England by the Angevins. XXII. Various events after King Stephen’s capture. The end of this work. Pious meditations.

## THE THIRTEENTH BOOK

### I. Various events. The Franks go to Spain to aid King Alfonso against the Saracens. Many of them settle in Spain. Various events in these regions.

[Col. 0923A]

While western pilgrims were often fighting the pagans in Palestine and were dedicating Jerusalem and other cities to Christ through frequent battles and long sieges, Geoffrey, Count of Mortain, son of Count Rotrou—a man worthy of praise for many virtues—fell sick unto death. Having summoned the nobles of Perche and Corbonnais, who were subject to his county, he wisely arranged his affairs. He instructed his wife Beatrice, daughter of the count of Rochefort, and his leading men prudently, asking them to preserve, without deceit, the tranquillity and security of peace [Col. 0923B] and faithfully to keep his land and its strongholds for his only son Rotrou, who had gone abroad on pilgrimage to Jerusalem.

> [Note: [Col. 0923B] Aegidius Bry more correctly states, on the authority of Hermann of Laon, that this Beatrice was born to Hilduin, count of Ruciaco [Rochefort]. He nevertheless rightly rebukes Hermann for calling Beatrice the wife of Rotrou, rather than of Geoffrey, Rotrou’s father and count of Mortain or Perche, to whom she was in fact married. (Dom Bouquet.)]

Finally, after duly completing everything, the vigorous hero became a Cluniac monk and died and was buried at his castle of Nogent in the middle of October. There his father had begun a monastery in honour of St Dionysius the Areopagite, and he himself had greatly enriched it with lands and possessions. In the same month William de Moulins, a most daring margrave, died and was buried in the chapter-house of St Evroul.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1100, when the affairs for which they had gone to Jerusalem had been accomplished, the leading men returned and recovered their own possessions. Then Robert, duke of the Normans, Robert of Flanders, Rotrou of Mortain, and many others returned prosperously; and, deservedly congratulated by their kinsmen, they possessed what was theirs. Not long afterward Alfonso [Col. 0924B], king of Aragon, was heavily attacked by the pagans and exceedingly harassed by frequent engagements and many losses.

> [Note: [Col. 0924B] Alfonso did not succeed Peter in the kingdom of Aragon until the year 1104. (Id.)]

He therefore sent envoys to his kinsman Rotrou [Col. 0925A], humbly requesting him to come to his aid while he fought against the heathen and to bring with him Frankish auxiliaries, whose aid they had praiseworthily experienced in many emergencies. He also promised abundant pay to the Gauls who gave assistance, and rich estates to those willing to remain with him. Immediately the most worthy count summoned his fellow-soldiers, brought aid to his royal kinsman, and helped him without deception or pretence; but he did not find unbroken good faith among the Iberians. For, while he had acted vigorously in many matters with his companions and fellow-countrymen, and their assistance had greatly terrified the Saracens, the Spaniards plotted treachery against them and, as is believed, with the king’s agreement, planned the death of their own helpers. When this crime became known to the Franks through their accomplices [Col. 0925B], Rotrou left the king with the treacherous Iberians and returned to Gaul with his comrades, having received no worthy reward for such great labours.

At the same time a great quarrel arose between Rotrou and Robert of Bellême over certain claims which those same margraves advanced concerning the boundaries of their estates. They therefore waged cruel war against one another, committed plundering and arson in each other’s lands, and piled crime upon crime. They despoiled the unarmed common people, repeatedly afflicted them with losses and fear of loss, and distressed with many calamities the soldiers and country-dwellers subject to them. Nevertheless Rotrou prevailed: he routed the defeated Robert [Col. 0925C] of Bellême, seized many of his men, and confined them in prison. They were cousins, and therefore disputed over the estates of their forebears.

Guarin of Domfront, whom demons strangled, was an ancestor of Rotrou; and Robert of Bellême, whom the sons of Walter Sori butchered with axes in prison at Ballon like a pig, was the uncle of Mabel, Robert’s mother. Robert therefore alone possessed Domfront, Bellême, and every right of his kindred, and refused to have a sharer in his wealth or a partner in his power; indeed, he insatiably desired to heap up more possessions by fraud or force.

Thus the neighbouring counts Geoffrey and Rotrou [Col. 0925D] had often vehemently contested their share of the inheritance; but they had not been able forcibly to take their right from the aforesaid tyrant, who possessed thirty-four strongholds, even though they inflicted countless losses upon him. But King Henry of the English, having learned Rotrou’s worth, gave him his daughter Matilda, born out of wedlock, as wife, and greatly increased his lands and wealth in England.

### II. The battles of King Alfonso, aided by the Franks, against the Saracens of Spain and Morocco. Disorders in Spain. The death of King Alfonso.

When the Saracens learned of the departure of the Franks, they became bolder and, attacking the regions of the Christians anew, displayed their strength in the savage slaughter of many. [Col. 0926A] The Aragonese, ashamed and oppressed by the enemy’s strength, again summoned the Franks, made satisfaction to them for their former insult, and, by oath, specified the lands and honours that they would give them. The count, therefore, forgetting the former dispute and injury, accepted the embassy of his friend and cousin, brought with him a huge army gathered from every direction, and boldly entered the land of the pagans to fight them. The Spaniards, rejoicing at such assistance, eagerly received the Franks; and, wishing to make amends for their former offences, lodged them in their cities of Toledo, Tudela, and Pamplona and in their towns, and gave them extensive honours and possessions. Avoiding idleness, they assembled at the beginning of summer, drove the heathen from [Col. 0926B] their borders with bloody blows, and, intending to repay them in kind, crossed into their territory. With God’s favour they exacted manifold vengeance for the injuries and insults inflicted, and, finding great abundance of food and all things in those regions, waited there through the winter.

Then Rotrou, Count of Mortain, with the Franks; the bishop of Saragossa with the brothers of Palms; and Guarzo of Biara with the Gascons fortified Penecadel, where there are two impregnable towers, and held it for six weeks. At length they gathered to fight Amorgan, king of Valencia, by way of the city of Xàtiva. But the pagans fled before they were struck. Leaving sixty retainers in the fortification of Penecadel [Col. 0926C], they returned.

But the Almoravids and Andalusians, sent from Africa by King Alis, son of Insted, met them and besieged them for three days in the castle of Serraliis. During these three days the Christians did penance for their sins, fasted, and invoked God. On the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September [15 August] they fought; aided by heavenly power, after a prolonged battle, at sunset they conquered. Yet, fearing the dangers of the night, they did not dare long to pursue the fleeing pagans by unfamiliar routes.

The day before the general battle, Guarin Sancio, a man highly praiseworthy in many respects, went up into the mountains with the brothers of Palms. There, while the Christians fought by the power of God, King Alamin fled in defeat with 154,000 foot-soldiers. Countless men from such vast legions of pagans perished, whether by the weapons of their pursuers, precipices, overwhelming exhaustion, thirst, or other kinds of death. Thus the Africans who had come to support the idolatrous Iberians were destroyed; cast down to Orcus by the missiles of Christ’s worshippers, they suffer the punishments of Gehenna with their kings.

Thereafter some Normans and Franks sought out places suitable for themselves and chose homes there in which to live. But Silvester of Saint-Calais, Rainald of Bailleul, and many others returned to their native soil, preferring their patrimonies to the acquisition of foreign possessions. Then [Col. 0927A] the Norman knight Robert de Culci,

> [Note: [Col. 0927D] Or Aculeus, d’Agilon, as Baluzius observes in *Marca Hisp.* col. 489: “In the year 1147, among the foremost men who followed King Louis VII to the East, William Agilons of Trie is named” (in his *Life and Deeds*); “in the Appendix to Aimoin he is called Willelmus Anguillon. … From this,” Baluzius continues, “it is certainly inferred that Robert de Culeio sprang from the most noble house of Trie in Normandy or the Vexin.” (Dom Bouquet.)]

surnamed Burdet, resolved to remain in Spain and withdrew to a certain city called Tarragona in ancient manuscripts.

There, in the time of the Emperor Gallienus, the holy martyrs of Christ, Bishop Fructuosus and the deacons Augurius and Eulogius, are recorded to have suffered. First thrown into prison and then cast into flames, they obtained what they prayed for: when their bonds were burned away, they stood with hands outstretched in the form of a cross and were burned while praying. Aurelius Clemens Prudentius composed a metrical poem about them in his *Book of the Martyrs* and unfolded their contest in splendid verses. Tarragona was a metropolitan see, and Oldegarius, a most learned old man, flourished as archbishop and exercised the office entrusted to him in the villages and boroughs of his diocese. Indeed, oaks, beeches, and other lofty trees had by then grown in the episcopal basilica itself and had occupied the space within the city walls from ancient times, since its former inhabitants had been slaughtered or driven away by the savagery of the Saracens.

Finally Robert, at the bishop’s prompting,

> [Note: [Col. 0928D] The bishop of Tarragona, Oldegarius.]

went to Pope Honorius, disclosed his intention, received from the pope the county of Tarragona as a gift free from every secular exaction, and, after returning and seeking out strong companions to attach to himself, guards it to this day and resists the heathen.

Meanwhile, while he was going to Rome and then had returned to Normandy to gather comrades, [Col. 0927C] his wife Sibyl, daughter of William Capra, guarded Tarragona. She excelled no less in courage than in beauty. While her husband was absent, she kept vigilant watch: every night she put on a coat of mail like a soldier, carried a staff in her hand, ascended the wall, went around the city, roused the guards, and wisely warned all to guard cautiously against the enemy’s snares. Praiseworthy was this young lady, who served her husband with such faith and devoted love, and piously governed God’s people with unwearied diligence.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1125, after Count Rotrou had returned with his retainers and auxiliaries to Gaul, the king of Aragon, seeing the notable deeds which the Franks had accomplished against the pagans in Spain without him, became envious. Eager for praise, he arrogantly gathered a great army of his own people. He also travelled through distant [Col. 0927D] regions as far as Córdoba and remained there with his army for six weeks, striking great terror into the inhabitants, who believed that the Franks were present together with the Iberians. The Saracens hid in their fortifications, though they allowed herds of cattle and flocks of sheep to roam freely through the fields. No one came out of the castles against the Christians; but the Christian host plundered at will everything outside the defences [Col. 0928A] and afflicted the provinces with severe devastation.

Then nearly ten thousand Muceranians assembled and humbly approached King Alfonso. “We,” they said, “and our fathers have hitherto been reared among the heathen; and, having been baptized, we willingly maintain the Christian law. But we have never been able to learn the perfect doctrine of the holy religion. For, under the subjection of unbelievers, by whom we have long been oppressed, we did not dare to seek Roman or Gallic teachers, nor did they come to us because of the barbarity of the pagans whom we formerly obeyed. But now we rejoice greatly at your arrival and desire, leaving our native land, to migrate with you, our wives, and our possessions.” [Col. 0928B] King Muceran accordingly granted what they asked. A great multitude therefore departed from their territory and, for love of the sacred law, went into exile under severe want and hardship.

When the Aragonese returned, they found the whole region stripped of every good thing, and before reaching their own homes were grievously afflicted by extreme scarcity and hunger.

The people of Córdoba and other Saracen peoples were greatly enraged when they saw that the Muceranians had departed with their families and goods. Accordingly, by common decree, they rose against those who remained, cruelly despoiled them of all their belongings, and grievously harassed them with beatings, chains, and many injuries. They put many of them to death by horrible tortures [Col. 0928C], and banished all the others into Africa beyond the Atlantic strait, condemning them to harsh exile out of hatred for the Christians, a great part of whom they had accompanied.

But when King Alfonso returned to his kingdom, he was disturbed by many great disorders, both public and domestic. His wife Urraca, daughter of Alfonso the Elder, king of Galicia, had rebelled against her husband at the counsel and instigation of the Galicians; plotting his destruction alike by poison and by arms, she had caused the ruin of many. Finally, when the Galicians saw the grave dissension between husband and wife and were unable to persuade them to make a fitting peace, they set up as their king Peter-Alfonso, son of Count Raymond the Frank [Col. 0928D] by the daughter of Alfonso the Great. Calling him to this day “the little king,” they stoutly defend under him the liberty of the kingdom.

A fierce war continued for a long time against the aforesaid kings and brought many losses upon the peoples subject to them. The aforesaid woman raged against her husband in every way and supported her grandson, who ruled his paternal inheritance. At last, by God’s disposal, like Egla, David’s wife, she perished after prolonged slaughter [reading uncertain], through difficulty in childbirth. Upon her death, clear peace joined the warlike kings in friendship, and a shared zeal for fighting armed them against the heathen.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1133, in the eleventh indiction, Alfonso, king of Aragon, assembled an army against the pagans, besieged and took the very strongly fortified and wealthy castle of Mequinenza. He ordered its proud inhabitants, who gloried in their riches, abundance of food, and what they believed to be impregnable strength, to surrender unharmed and depart peacefully with all their possessions. But they resisted fiercely and scorned his threats and promises. The vigorous king pressed them hard for three weeks and forcibly gained the outer part of the fortification. Then the frightened defenders [Col. 0929B] offered the king the inner fortress and begged that he allow them to depart freely with all that was theirs. The angry king answered them: “What you now request I offered you freely from the beginning. But you, despising and rejecting the power of Christ, the faith of the Christians, and valour, did so. Therefore now, by my head, I assure you that you shall not depart from here save with the loss of your lives.” Then he commanded his men to raise the prepared siege-engines and make vigorous assaults upon the town. This done, they took the castle, cut off the heads of all the heathen, and thereby struck great terror into the neighbouring people.

The victorious king then led his army against the city of Fraga [Col. 0929C] and enclosed it in a siege lasting a year. The citizens immediately sent envoys to Africa and requested King Alis of Africa to aid them. He sent them across the sea ten thousand Almoravids. Arriving in Spain, these ordered the king through four nobles to withdraw hastily from the siege of the city. Immediately the king commanded the holy relics of his chapel to be brought to him; when they had been brought, he swore before all that he would not abandon the siege unless the city were surrendered to him, or death forestalled him, or he were put to flight. He also commanded twenty of his nobles to swear this.

The envoys returned and reported this to the Almoravids, who immediately gathered all their comrades and came together for battle. Then the strongly arrayed battle-line of the heathen met the king’s army and began to fight fiercely. Finally, when the king saw a most formidable contest impending, he swiftly sent messengers and begged all his friends and neighbours to assist him. He himself, with his troops, skilfully withdrew on foot to a neighbouring hill. There he fought the opposing Almoravids for three continuous days and nights. But Robert surnamed Burdet, count of Tarragona, and other faithful men, hearing reports of the king’s attack, quickly armed and came flying with loose reins. Crying aloud the name of Jesus, they struck [Col. 0930A] the weary heathen in a sudden onslaught, overthrew them, and routed them in defeat. They captured many, killed more, and, once victory was won, grew exceedingly rich from the enemy’s spoils; rejoicing, they gave thanks to God the victor.

Yet, because in this declining age no mortal power endures long, adversity, by the ordinance of God the just ruler, swiftly followed prosperity. The citizens of Fraga—the city besieged by the king, a refuge for every kind of worst person among heathens and false Christians—feared the anger and irresistible efforts of so great-hearted a prince, as well as the army of Christians marked with Christ’s cross and strengthened by unconquered valour. They sought peace from him [Col. 0930B] and promised submission upon agreed conditions. But he refused their agreement with an obstinate mind, scorned to receive an annual payment from them, and confirmed by oath his threat that he would obtain them by siege. Hearing this, the Saracens became fiercer in desperate desperation, again sent envoys to Halin, king of Africa, and urgently procured assistance for themselves in their great peril from other kings and princes of the heathen.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1134, in the twelfth indiction, Robert II, duke of the Normans, died in February at Cardiff in Britain, in the twenty-eighth year since he was captured at Tinchebray and held in his brother’s prison; he rests buried in the monastery of the monks of St Peter the Apostle at Gloucester. [Col. 0930C]

Then Buchar-Halis, son of the king of Morocco, gathered numerous forces of warriors from every side and came to Spain to fight the Christians. Alammion of Córdoba, Alcharias of Dalmaria, and other leading men of Libya and Iberia joined him with many thousands, and they cunningly arranged their forces for battle. Gathered together, they aided Fraga and led there five divisions. The first division drove two hundred camels laden with provisions and many necessary goods, with which they attempted to relieve the besieged and lure the needy Christians into an attack upon the foremost troops, eager for plunder. The other companies [Col. 0930D] lay hidden at a distance in separated ambushes, cautiously waiting to catch those who pursued the fleeing enemy.

Two rivers run to Fraga: the Segre from Lleida, and the Ebro from Saragossa, at Campo Dolente. Between these rivers battle was fought in July, and much blood was shed. When King Alfonso heard that an enormous multitude of heathen were coming against him, he summoned the leaders of the Christian army and magnificently urged them to battle. Count Bertrand of Laon,

> [Note: [Col. 0929] This Bertrand was born to Count Theobald of Risnel and Heliarde, daughter of Hilduin, count of Rulciacum [Rochefort]. (Dom Bouquet.)]

count of Quadrion, Rodrigo of Asturias, Aimer of Narbonne, Centulf, son of Gaston of Biara [Col. 0931A], Garsio Adramis, and many other warlike nobles fought at Campo Dolente.

When King Alfonso saw the first division driving the camels laden with provisions, he commanded Count Bertrand to engage them first. Bertrand said to him: “My lord king, let us allow the first troops to pass, so that when they approach the city we may be fully prepared; then, if they return laden with plunder, we may strike them, while carefully protecting our ranks against the enemy’s ambushes. Meanwhile, let us wait for their companions following behind and receive them ready for battle.” Then the angry king exclaimed: “Where is your greatness of spirit, brave count? Until now I have never found cowardice in you.” At these words the high-spirited count blushed and fiercely charged the heathen with his forces. They immediately turned their backs and attempted to take refuge among the countless masses following them. Then innumerable divisions rose against the Christians and killed Bertrand, Aimer, and Centulf with many thousands.

The king, with the survivors, fought for a long time on a certain hill and, enclosed by the overwhelming multitude of enemies, lost almost all his men. There he resolved to fight unto death for Christ. But the bishop of Urgell commanded the king to withdraw. Overwhelmed with grief for his men’s destruction, he refused. The bishop said to him: “By the authority of God Almighty I command you to leave this field immediately, lest, if you fall, [Col. 0931C] the whole region of Christians be subjected to the heathen and a general slaughter befall every Christian dwelling in this province.” Finally, constrained by the episcopal command, he consented to obey; but, surrounded by countless thousands of pagans, he looked in every direction for a difficult way out. Nevertheless, with his fierce sword and sixty knights who remained with him in the struggle, he opened a path for himself through the thinner enemy line. With the utmost difficulty he escaped with ten fellow-soldiers, leaving behind the aforesaid bishop slain with fifty fighters.

The heathen exulted in this outcome, and the Christians were greatly distressed. When the king returned in deep mourning to his friends, he met the men of Saragossa, the Franks, and other faithful men hurrying to battle [Col. 0931D]; but, on hearing the grievous news of the disaster, they were shattered and mourned bitterly. Seeing the king, however, they sought to strengthen themselves and willingly offered themselves to obey his command.

Burning with anger and possessed by grief, he longed intensely for at least one act of vengeance from the Lord upon the pagans before he died. He therefore led the Christian divisions that met him by winding byways to the coast, [Col. 0932A] where he found ships carrying a multitude of Saracens, rich with Christian captives and spoils. He suddenly rushed upon them, when they suspected nothing of the kind, inflicted a vast slaughter upon them, and somewhat satisfied his raging anger. There was a ship laden with Christian heads, which King Buchar was sending to his father, the king of Africa, as evidence of his victory. The lover of vain glory was also sending about seven hundred captives and distinguished trophies.

But King Alfonso, as stated above, suddenly arrived by God’s disposal. Having slaughtered the enemy, he recovered the heads of his slain companions and gave them back to the Church of God for honourable burial. The captives [Col. 0932B], already lying bound in the ships, heard the uproar, raised their eyes, and, seeing what they had not dared to hope for, were exceedingly joyful. Their strength revived; heartened, they eagerly loosed one another’s bonds, while the Christians on shore fought the Saracens, and leaped down from the sterns to aid their own men. Taking the weapons of those who had been killed, they sought to kill the surviving heathen. Thus grief followed in the place of the pagans’ rejoicing, and the Christian host blessed God in all its deeds.

Strong King Alfonso, worn down by labours and hardships, fell ill shortly afterward; lying in bed, he gave up his spirit after eight days. On his death [Col. 0932C], because he had no son, conflict over a successor held his subjects in turmoil amid the clamour of war for some time. At length the Aragonese chose Remigius, priest and monk, because he was the king’s brother, and made him their king.

> [Note: [Col. 0931D] Because Ramiro, or Ranimiro, says Rodericus (*bk.* VI, ch. 1), had been a monk and priest in the monastery of St Peter of Thomaris—that is, the monastery of Thomières in the district of Narbonne—and had indeed lived as a monk in that monastery for forty years and more, the kingdom could not fail to be disturbed by tumults after Alfonso’s death. As Rodericus states in the same place (ch. 2), the Aragonese wished to substitute for the dead king a certain noble named Peter of Tarazona [read: Atherasia]; but two great men, resolved to preserve their allegiance to the natural lord, turned the minds of many away from their first purpose and made diligent efforts to bring the monk Ranimiro out of his monastery. … Having brought him out of the monastery, they placed him on the royal throne at Huesca. These final words overthrow the invention of more recent writers who maintain that he was bishop of Roda and Barbastro. (Dom Bouquet.)]

But the Navarrese set Garsio, a satrap, over themselves as king.

### III. The tribulations of the Church of God. Bishoprics and monasteries are disturbed. The schism of the antipope Anacletus. The arrival of Pope Innocent II in Gaul.

The Roman Church, troubled from the death of Pope Honorius by the two contenders for the papacy, saw an immense abundance of tribulations and dissensions spread throughout the world. For in many monasteries two abbots arose, and in bishoprics two prelates contended for the episcopate: one adhered to Peter Anacletus, while the other favoured Gregory Innocent. In a schism of this sort, excommunication is fearful, because it can scarcely be avoided by some when each bitterly attacks the other and lethally anathematises his opponent together with his supporters. Thus, whenever anyone desires to do something but, hindered by impossibility, cannot bring it to effect, he at least invokes God against his rival by means of his own imprecation. [Col. 0933A]

Peter, through the power of his brothers and relatives, held the city and consecrated Roger, duke of Apulia, as king of Sicily; through Roger’s assistance he attached almost the whole of Italy to himself. Gregory, however, made for Gaul with the clergy of the Quirinal and was first received by the people of Arles, whence he sent envoys to the Franks. When the Cluniacs learned of his coming, they sent the pope and cardinal-clerics sixty horses or mules with all suitable equipment and honourably conducted them as far as their basilica. There they retained the pope and his company for eleven days, and caused the new church in honour of St Peter, prince of the apostles, to be dedicated by him amid great rejoicing and a vast crowd of people. [Col. 0933B]

Thereafter he gained great authority among the western peoples because the Cluniacs had preferred him to Peter. For Peter himself had grown up under their care in childhood and had been a monk in their habit and profession. Gregory, therefore, received amicably by the Cluniacs—whose authority especially excels among the monks of our countrymen—as the Father of Fathers, shone in Gaul with the splendour of the pontifical office. Thereafter, being received by the western princes and bishops, he quickly acquired great power. At Chartres King Henry of the English humbly fell at his feet and, on the Ides of January [13 January], willingly showed him the reverence due to a pope, bestowing many gifts upon the Roman clergy with royal munificence. There, lodged in the house of Helisendis the viscountess, he remained three days amid the rejoicing of Franks and Romans. Then throughout that whole year the aforesaid pope travelled through France and imposed an immense burden upon the churches of Gaul, since he had with him Roman officials and many retainers and could obtain nothing from the revenues of the Apostolic See in Italy. He spoke with Emperor Lothair, who treated him and his companions as a venerable master. He appointed a council to be held at Reims in October and summoned to it all the bishops and abbots of the entire West. [Col. 0933C]

Meanwhile, the boy Philip, whom King Louis had caused to be consecrated king two years earlier and who, by the honeyed sweetness of his simple character, had pleased all who knew him, was playfully pursuing a certain squire through the streets of Paris. He fell from his horse, was horribly broken in his limbs, and died the next day. Thus, without confession or viaticum, he died before [Col. 0934A] his father and mother on the third day before the Ides of October [13 October], and was buried amid great mourning among the kings of France.

On the following Sunday the pope dedicated the basilica of St Medard, bishop, at Soissons, and then hastened to Reims for the council. There, examining many cases concerning persons of high rank, he remained for nearly fifteen days. Thirteen archbishops and 263 bishops were present, along with a great multitude of abbots, monks, and clerics. The king and queen, and all the nobility of France, gathered there; through Rainald, archbishop of Reims, they made their request to the whole synod, asking that the boy Louis be consecrated king in place of his brother Philip. Accordingly Pope Innocent, on 25 October, consecrated the king’s son as king. This consecration [Col. 0934B] displeased certain Frenchmen of both orders. Some laymen hoped, after the prince’s death, to increase their own rank; while certain clerics sought to claim the right of electing and appointing the ruler of the kingdom. For these reasons, therefore, some murmured about the boy’s appointment; and, without doubt, had they been able, they earnestly wished to prevent it. But when King Louis learned that unprecedented attempts at a new rite were arising in his realm, he angrily desired to exact deadly vengeance upon some who had tried to exclude his offspring from the summit of royal power. Hence the malevolent rashness of certain men ran more recklessly into crime, and proved, alas, a horrible ruin to some; while it brought grief to others who burned with love for God and their neighbour.

[Col. 0934C] For after John, the aged bishop of Orléans, abandoned his bishopric, Hugh the dean, who had been elected to the episcopate, returned from the king’s court and was struck down and killed on the road by reckless men. The bishopric, without a shepherd, long tossed like a ship without a helmsman at sea. At that time Thomas also, a canon of St Victor’s, a man of great authority, was murdered; Stephen, bishop of Paris, standing by, beheld his killing with immense grief.

[Note: [Col. 0933D] Thomas, prior of St Victor’s at Paris and Bishop Stephen’s assistant in administering the diocese, had long been hated by Theobald Notier, archdeacon, because Thomas had branded him with the charge of avarice. But Thomas incurred his greatest hatred because he was believed to have advised Stephen to relax the interdict which Theobald had imposed upon his archdeaconry, owing to goods taken by him from a canon passing through it—this being done to vindicate episcopal authority, which Theobald had violated by issuing this thunderbolt secretly, without the bishop’s knowledge, although he was then in that archdeaconry. Theobald’s anger finally went so far that he marked Thomas for death; two of his nephews undertook the task of committing the crime. Thus, after laying an ambush, they attacked and murdered Thomas Kala as he was returning with the bishop near Gournay [Col. 0934D] on 20 August, as is recorded in the necrologies of St Victor’s and of St Guinailus at Corbeil; and indeed it was a Sunday, Stephen himself testifying to this in the letter which St Bernard wrote to Pope Innocent II in Stephen’s name: “The religious man, Thomas, prior and master of St Victor’s … on the Lord’s day … had his brains cruelly dashed out by wicked men before my very hands for righteousness’ sake” (St Bernard, Letter 159). It follows that Thomas’s death must be assigned not to 1131, when 20 August fell on a Thursday, but to 1133, when that date coincided with Sunday. (Dom Bouquet).]

For the strength of the mad executioners prevailed: they neither revered the Creator of all things nor, for His sake, revered the bishop as His faithful servant.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1132, in the tenth indiction, [Col. 0934D] Pope Innocent, having withdrawn from Gaul, where he had found obedience and immense friendship, sought Italy; but, rejected by the Romans, he retired to [Col. 0935A] the rich province of Picenum. There for several years he exercised the apostolic dignity, and from there dispatched decretal rulings throughout the world.
