Then the strictness of holy life greatly increased among churchmen, and the canonical order, much beloved in France and England, flourished in many ways. The zeal of abbots also presumed to surpass the bounds set by their predecessors, adding heavier requirements to ancient institutions and imposing burdens sufficiently hard upon weak shoulders.

#### IV. An Assembly of Prelates Convened at Cluny. Various Events in Italy and Normandy.

Peter, abbot of Cluny, then sent couriers and letters throughout all his dependent houses, summoning the priors of all the houses in England, Italy, and other kingdoms [Col. 0935B] and commanding them to be present at Cluny on the third Sunday in Lent, to hear precepts for a monastic life more austere than those they had hitherto observed. These archimandrites obeyed his commands, and 200 priors assembled at Cluny on the appointed date. On that day 1,212 brethren were present there; they went in procession chanting according to the ecclesiastical rite and, joyfully raising their eyes to God, devoutly praised Him together. I report this confidently because I was joyfully present, saw so glorious a company gathered in the name of Christ Jesus, processed with them on Sunday from the basilica of St Peter, prince of the apostles, and, entering through the cloister into the church of the Virgin Mother, prayed.

[Col. 0935C] Then Ralph, bishop of Auxerre, and the abbots Alberic of Vézelay and Adelard of Melun, monks of that same monastery, enlarged the gathering and confirmed Abbot Peter’s undertaking by their presence and exhortation. But he increased the fasts imposed on his subjects, abolished conversations, and removed certain aids for infirm bodies which the moderated clemency of the reverend Fathers had until then permitted them. The brethren, accustomed always to obey their master and unwilling to resist him contrary to religious custom, accepted these harsh commands; yet they reasonably pointed out that the venerable Hugh, and his predecessors Majolus and Odilo, had followed the narrow way of life and sought by that same way to lead the Cluniac brethren to Christ. They likewise respectfully and humbly maintained, with good reason, that it ought to suffice to run with hearts enlarged in the way of God’s commandments by following the footsteps of men whose holiness had been publicly demonstrated by the shining evidence of miracles. But the severe master, forgetting Solomon’s command, “Do not remove the ancient boundary which your fathers have set” (Prov. 20:28), emulated the Cistercians and other adherents of novelties, persisted in untried ventures, and was then ashamed to abandon his undertaking. Later, however, softened, he assented to the judgment of his subjects; mindful that discretion is the mother [Col. 0936A] of virtues, he compassionately came to the aid of the weak, and abandoned very many of the severe regulations he had proposed.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1133, Emperor Lothair laboured, for the love of God, to reconcile the bishops and other faithful who, after Gregory or Peter, were wandering in dissension. He ordered Peter either to yield to the other or to submit his appointment to judgment. Peter gladly accepted the command and agreed to come before the emperor himself for an examination by righteous men. Then the emperor gave Innocent similar instructions; but Innocent refused to come to the settlement unless everything pertaining to the episcopal office were freely restored to him. When the emperor heard this, he was angered against Gregory, left Peter in possession of everything he held, and, with the affair unfinished, withdrew after seven weeks [Col. 0936B].

In the same year Richard, bishop of the city of Bayeux, died in Easter week. Two years later he was succeeded by Richard, son of Robert, count of Gloucester, the king’s son. At Pope Innocent’s command Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, consecrated him. At this time Richard of Bellafago, the king’s honoured chaplain, also received the bishopric of Avranches, and the aforesaid metropolitan consecrated him.

#### V. Disturbances and Various Events in Apulia and Sicily.

About this time a great disturbance arose in Apulia. To explain its origin, it is necessary to recount [Col. 0936C] the earlier lineage and the fortunes of the persons concerned.

After the death of the aged Roger, count of Sicily, son of Tancred of Hauteville, his wife Adela perceived that she could not govern such great possessions with her little son. Anxiously, she diligently considered, both by herself and with her advisers, what was to be done. For the aforesaid count and his eleven brothers had acquired vast provinces by military valour and had vigorously subdued the barbarians beneath the mighty hand of the Most High God in Apulia and Sicily. At length the aforesaid woman allied herself with Robert, son of Robert, duke of Burgundy, and gave him her daughter [Note: [Col. 0935D] Dom Bouquet corrects this to: “niece,” that is, the daughter of a brother or sister.] in marriage, together with the whole principality of Sicily.

For Robert’s father was a son of Robert, king of the Franks, and of Queen Constance; his nobility sprang from the blood of kings and emperors, and he shone exceedingly in many lands through illustrious deeds and remarkable virtues. This was the man whom his powerful mother, after the death of his father, wished to set over all Gaul, and whom she strove by every means, as I have briefly mentioned above, to prefer to Henry, the first-born. Finally, justice rightfully raising Henry to the throne of the kingdom, Robert long held the duchy of Burgundy and begot three sons, Henry, Robert, and Simon [Note: [Col. 0935D] “To these three sons of Duke Robert,” says Dom [Col. 0936D] Bouquet, “a fourth, Hugh, must be added; concerning him the short Chronicle of Auxerre, under the year 1057, says: ‘Hugh, son of Duke Robert, set fire to the village [Col. 0937D] of St Brice, and 110 men, women, and children perished inside the church; and in the same year he himself was killed.’ Plancher considers him Robert’s first-born son (History of Burgundy, vol. I, p. 269).]. His first-born Henry, at his father’s command, [Col. 0937A] married a wife, by whom he begot three sons—Hugh, Odo, and Robert, bishop of Langres [Note: [Col. 0937D] Orderic likewise omits a fourth son of Henry, bearing his father’s name. He went to Spain in 1095, became count of Portugal through marriage to Theresa, illegitimate daughter of Alfonso VI of Castile and León, and became the ancestor of the kings of Portugal. On this matter see Pagi, under the year 1108, no. 6. (Dom Bouquet.)]—and died during his father’s lifetime. After his death the father lived a long time, and, in old age, set his sons above his grandsons, granted them his duchy, and ordered all the magnates to adhere completely to his offspring. Hearing this, the boy Hugh remained silent and patiently awaited a suitable time. Yet he placed fixed hope in the Lord and said privately to those who agreed with him: “The just Lord, who took my father from this world, will not deprive his offspring of their rightful inheritance.” When the duke’s death came, he summoned all the officials and barons and imperiously commanded the officers of the principal court swiftly to adorn the royal residence for himself and his magnates [Col. 0937B]. They wondered at the audacity with which so young a man issued such an order, but immediately, in alarm, obeyed his commands and hastened a splendid preparation at Dijon for the new duke. Thus the spirited young man acquired his ancestral dignity without war or bloodshed; and, after his uncles Robert and Simon had gone into exile, he held his paternal inheritance with distinction for three years. Distinguished for justice, he pleased the gentle and the just; but he descended like lightning, terrible to the irreligious and lawless. At the end of three years he voluntarily surrendered the duchy to his brother Odo, and himself, for love of heaven, left the world. Becoming a monk at Cluny [Note: [Col. 0937D] Pope Gregory VII (Letter 17, book VI) complains to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, that he received Duke [Col. 0938D] Hugh, because, he says, scarcely any good prince can be found. (Dom Bouquet.)], he gloriously served God for fifteen years. His brother Odo [Col. 0937C] long possessed the duchy of Burgundy; by Matilda, daughter of William Testard, count of Burgundy, he begot Duke Hugh and Hela. She first bore Pons, count of Tripoli, to Bertrand, count of Toulouse; afterwards she bore Guy, count of Ponthieu, to William Talvas, and produced a plentiful offspring of both sexes by both men.

But Robert of Burgundy, as stated above, married the daughter of the Norman Roger and defended the principality vigorously against all opponents for ten years. Meanwhile his mother-in-law reared the boy Roger; and when she recognized that the youth was fit to bear arms and govern his father’s right, she poisoned her son-in-law, that excellent Frenchman and worthy knight, with a poisonous draught. Thus, after the noble marquis had been destroyed [Col. 0937D] by a woman’s deceit, Roger succeeded and flourished for many years in great prosperity. Yet, stained by many crimes, he deserved, I think, to be purified [Col. 0938A] by great torments. His crafty mother, who had been the daughter of Boniface the Ligurian, had amassed for herself a huge treasure from money gathered from every source after the death of her husband.

When Baldwin, the earlier king of Jerusalem, heard this, he coveted her wealth and sought her by distinguished envoys in order to marry her. But she, insatiably greedy for pomp and honour, accepted the noble marriage-brokers and, surrounded by a multitude of retainers and carrying a vast treasury, hastened to Jerusalem. King Baldwin gladly received the rich wealth and distributed it among the paid soldiers who laboured in fighting the pagans for Christ’s name; but he repudiated the woman, wrinkled with age and notorious for many stains of crime. Thus the old woman, disgraced as her sins deserved, [Col. 0938B] returned to Sicily and thereafter grew old among her people, despised by all.

Roger, prince of Sicily, became exceedingly powerful and surpassed all earlier members of his family in wealth and honours. After the death of Duke William, as stated above, he acquired the duchy of Apulia despite the unwillingness of its inhabitants. Then he attacked all who attempted to resist him and cruelly crushed them with great forces. He spared no one, but cast down kinsmen and strangers alike, trampling them dishonourably after stripping them of their goods.

Tancred of Conversano was vigorously besieged by Roger the Sicilian at Matella; fleeing thence to a town called Montepeloso, he was captured there by his arrogant [Col. 0938C] pursuer. Geoffrey of Andria, too, was captured with his wife by the same man in a stronghold situated beside the city of Potenza. Roger subdued the town and seized there a treasure containing fifteen mina of gold or silver. He also seized Grimald of Bari, a Lombard, a generous and valiant man, and grievously humbled him after taking away his possessions and fortresses. He disinherited his cousin Richard, prince of Capua, and by unjust force compelled him into exile. Thus, by violent oppression, he ruined near and distant alike; shedding much blood and cruelly wringing many tears, he grew exceedingly powerful. He was the first of Tancred’s line to mount the royal throne and bear the sceptre, diadem, and other [Col. 0938D] insignia of kingship. He married the daughter of Peter Leo, sister of Pope Anacletus [Note: [Col. 0938D] Romuald, archbishop of Salerno, a contemporary historian, enumerates in his Chronicle the wives of Roger, first king of Sicily: namely Alberia, whose origin he does not mention; Sibylla, sister of Hugh II, duke of Burgundy; and Beatrice, daughter of Gunther, count of Rethel in French Champagne. Therefore Alberia was the sister of the antipope Peter-Leo, named Anacletus, and consequently daughter of Peter-Leo, a Roman citizen—not of Alfonso, king of León and Castile, as modern writers assert without any foundation. (Dom Bouquet.)], and, crowned by him, now bears the royal emblem.

#### VI. Heavenly Portents and Scourges. Destruction of Many Churches and Towns. Deaths of Very Many People and Princes.

[Col. 0939A]

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1134, in the twelfth indiction, many grievous things happened in the world. Some were afflicted by them, as their sins required; others, seeing dreadful and unprecedented things, trembled pale with terror.

For on the feast of the Holy Innocents a heavy snowfall fell, covering the whole surface of the earth and so blocking the entrances of houses by its mass that on the following day people and beasts could scarcely leave their shelters or procure in any way what they needed. Many faithful did not enter church on that feast, nor in most places could even the priests, impeded by [Col. 0939B] piled snow, cross the thresholds of the basilicas. Six days later, when the west wind blew, the snow melted and an immense flood of waters suddenly arose. The rivers swelled excessively, overflowed the boundaries of their channels, and inflicted enormous losses and hardships upon mortals. In adjacent villages and towns they filled houses and drove people from their dwellings. They swept huge haystacks from meadows and carried barrels full of Falernian wine and other storage vessels, with many spices and precious goods, from their places. Many therefore lamented their losses, while others, conversely, rejoiced at unexpected gain.

In June a violent heat scorched the world for fifteen days [Col. 0939C] and compelled earth’s inhabitants to flee humbly, by fasting and prayer, to the mercy of almighty God, lest they perish burnt by flames like the people of the Pentapolis. Indeed, the Titan heat, then passing through Gemini, dried up springs and pools, and a grievous thirst afflicted herds of living creatures. Then, on a certain Saturday, many suffering from the heat sought the refreshment of water, and in almost a single hour many were drowned in waters in different places. In our own neighbourhood, from which reports easily flew to us, thirty-seven persons perished in ponds or rivers. I do not know how to investigate the divine judgment by which all things occur, nor can I disclose the hidden causes of events; but, asked by my companions, I simply recount the history of the year. Who can search out [Col. 0939D] the unsearchable? As I have seen them, I kindly record events for posterity and glorify almighty God in all His works, which are truly just. Let each person consider according as divine inspiration is given to him, and let him beneficially gather whatever he judges useful to himself.

In August, on the vigil of St Lawrence the martyr, after None a violent whirlwind arose; terrible thunder, with an excessive downpour of rain, followed it toward evening. Then lightning fell with tremendous roaring and killed several women in different places. Yet I heard of no male killed by that stroke; only the female sex, among both human beings and brute animals, bore the weight of the threatening scourge.

[Col. 0940A] In the village called Planches, on the border of the dioceses of Lisieux and Sées, a young man named William Blanchard was driving a cart from a nearby field. His sister stood in it with bundles of oats. As the young man feared the exceedingly loud rain and hastened with all speed toward his mother’s nearby cottage, lightning immediately struck the haunches of the mare drawing the cart. It killed at once the mare, her wandering filly which was following, and the young woman in the vehicle. The young man, who sat on the saddle and guided the beast with a bridle, fell down in extreme fright but, by God’s mercy, escaped unharmed. There was a tremendous outburst of rain; nevertheless the fire consumed the two-horse cart and the sheaves. [Col. 0940B] On the following day I saw their ashes and the corpses of the dead placed on a bier, for, while staying at Merlerault, I went there so that I might know beyond doubt the truth of the occurrence and report this divine stroke to posterity.

In the village called Gaspraie, when reapers saw the clouds darkened by gloomy blackness, they said to a girl who was perhaps gathering ears of grain in the field: “Run quickly, daughter, and bring us our cloaks and tunics against the rain.” She willingly accepted the instruction and immediately began to go. But, at what I think was her first step, lightning struck and, hitting her, killed her instantly. Many similar things occurred in that same hour, as I later learned by truthful report, but I cannot set down every one of them separately in writing.

[Col. 0940C] In the first week of September the Lord our God punished many sins with fire and burned the households of sinners, along with treasures unjustly amassed over a long time. Le Mans and Chartres, ancient and wealthy cities, were burned. Alençon, Nogent-le-Rotrou, Verneuil, and other towns and many villages likewise perished, as the flame of God’s wrath ran through the world. Then the episcopal basilica at Le Mans, which was exceedingly beautiful, was burned; and the shrine containing the body of St Julian, bishop and confessor, was with difficulty transferred to the monastery of St Vincent the martyr. The bones of the holy virgin Scholastica, with many other relics, were also burned; after the fire, their ashes were found in their places [Col. 0940D] by devout searchers. At Chartres, the monastery of St Peter the apostle was burned, and the venerable community of monks, its cloister and remaining buildings destroyed, was scattered.

In these storms, the inhabitants of different places experienced marvellous and various events, endured diverse and mournful causes of fire, and could recount lengthy narratives to their fellow-sufferers, either in amazement or lamentation. But I was not present at these events, nor have I chosen to lengthen the book by relating doubtful matters.

In the same month the just Judge wrought terrors through the contrary element in another region, and checked wicked pirates in the crimes by which the earth had been polluted under Noah.

In Flanders, the sea overflowed at night and, suddenly spreading for seven [Col. 0941A] miles, covered churches, towers, and cottages alike, and swept away countless thousands of persons of both sexes, ranks, and conditions in one common peril. There indeed [Note: [Col. 0941D] Thus in the Chesnian edition. Perhaps “level,” or “of the plain.”] neither swiftness aided the runner, nor strength protected the fighter, nor abundance of wealth saved the rich; rather, the flood enveloped handsome and ugly men and women alike, and, closing their mouths with water, immediately handed them over to death. Thus the sea accomplished the punishment of the wretched in an instant and immediately returned at God’s command to its place. A poor woman, who had recently given birth to an infant, heard the roar of the rushing water. Terrified but of sound mind, she sprang at once from bed, seized her infant and a hen with her chicks, and quickly climbed a small haystack outside her cottage [Col. 0941B]. The force of the invading water, overwhelming everything, lifted the hay and carried the mound far away, tossing it this way and that. Yet by the mercy of the merciful God the woman was saved and, in such close proximity to death, was divinely snatched from it with the little creatures she had with her. A boy of twelve told me that he immediately climbed onto the ridge of a house-roof and there escaped the danger of destruction, while his father and mother perished below.

In the same year illustrious princes died. For, as stated above, Robert II, duke of the Normans, died at Cardiff in February. Alfonso, king of Aragon, died at the beginning of autumn, after the battle of Sées, in which the deaths occurred of the noble barons Bertrand [Col. 0941C] and Rodrigo, and of other magnates.

At that time the Welsh Britons were grievously afflicted by all the peoples who were under King Henry’s rule, and very many of their territories were given to Flemings. Wherever the Welsh themselves were found in woods and hiding places, the Flemings killed them like dogs, without the least regard for humanity. Seeing this, their more spirited men were greatly angered, recovered their courage, and took up arms. Inflicting much damage in revenge, they rose fiercely against King Henry. They burned the castle called Cans, belonging to the son of John the pagan, and mercilessly slaughtered all the men and women whom they found inside. Having committed this deed, all the inhabitants, together with outsiders, sought the densely wooded tracts like wolves and waged open hostility through slaughter, robbery, and arson [Col. 0941D].

#### VII. The Council of Picenum. Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen. King Henry Suppresses or Punishes Numerous Lords. Illness of Louis, King of the Franks.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1135, in the thirteenth indiction, Pope Innocent held a very great synod at Picenum [Note: [Col. 0941D] Commonly Ancona, but not Pisa, as is stated in V. C. Guizot’s French translation.] [Note: [Col. 0942D] This council is mentioned nowhere else, unless perhaps it is identical with the Pisan council held in the preceding year. (Dom Bouquet.)], and discussed ecclesiastical interests at length [Col. 0942A]; but, hindered by misfortunes, he could not accomplish everything as he wished.

Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, gave him very substantial assistance and, honoured by him, received primacy over many bishops. Thus occupied by the affairs of apostolic service, he for some time neglected the concerns of his own episcopate; remaining too long in the regions of Italy, he diligently dealt with the business of others. This greatly displeased the king.

Moreover, after the death of Richard, bishop of Bayeux, the king gave the bishopric of that city to his nephew Richard. The archbishop long refused to consecrate him because he was illegitimate, postponing it until it was granted by apostolic decree out of fear of the king. At last, when the legates returned with [Col. 0942B] the pope’s decrees, the Church of Bayeux was given to Richard, son of Robert, count of Gloucester, and on the same day the bishopric of Avranches was entrusted to Richard of Bellafago.

In the same year King Henry, greatly angered by dire reports concerning Welsh factions, prudently put Normandy in order and made three attempts to cross the sea with picked archers and a warlike force. But opposing circumstances arose, his journey was prevented, and God, who wonderfully contains all things, did not permit him to see England alive again.

His son-in-law Geoffrey of Anjou coveted the great treasures of his powerful father-in-law and demanded the castles of Normandy, asserting that the king had stipulated this to him when he married the king’s daughter. [Col. 0942C] But the spirited bearer of the sceptre, while he drew breath, wished to set no one over himself or to make anyone his equal, whether in his household or kingdom, carefully pondering the divine saying of Wisdom: “No one can serve two masters” (Luke 16:13). Consequently the swollen young man, in anger, offended the king with threats and proud acts, rashly despised his admonitions and counsels, and so insolently provoked him that the king wished to take his daughter away and carry her with him to England, had God so decreed. For the king bitterly resented that Geoffrey besieged his son-in-law, the viscount Rozcelin, and utterly burned Beaumont; nor did Geoffrey ever spare the king’s son-in-law out of reverence for so exalted a father-in-law.

[Col. 0942D] Thus the origin of very great dissensions among the magnates of Normandy was springing up. Some of them favoured the Angevin, but did not dare openly to declare rebellion, because they feared the king, a man experienced in many things. They rightly dreaded provoking to arms against themselves one whom they knew well to bind culprits in lasting chains as punishment.

William Talvas and Roger of Tosny were especially suspected and therefore feared to come to the king’s court. For this reason the king postponed his voyage to England and sent his own knights to guard the fortress [Col. 0943A] of Conches. Having introduced them, he retained the well-walled town around it and restrained the young Roger from rebellion. He repeatedly summoned Talvas to himself, but waited a long time for the man who did not dare come because his guilty conscience terrified him. Finally, after many summonses, he disseised him of all his lands. In September, stripped of all his honour, Talvas went over to the count of Anjou; received by him, he lived in the towns of Piret and Mamers, which belonged to that count’s fief. From the beginning of August until the feast of All Saints, the king ranged through the district of Sées and brought Alençon, Damfront [Almaniscas; reading uncertain], and Talvas’s other castles under his own control. Gathering a multitude of labourers, he enlarged the ditches of Argentan and strongly fortified that town, unaware of future events, though shortly afterwards it gravely harmed the neighbouring inhabitants.

On 28 October, while the feast of the holy apostles Simon and Jude was being celebrated and the devoutly watchful morning office was offered to the divine Majesty, a violent wind arose about the fourth watch of the night. Lasting throughout the day until None, it roared loudly and thundered terribly with a great crash; it stripped the roofs from countless houses, churches, and lofty towers, and, throwing down multitudes of trees, laid open the woods. Seeing these things, human hearts were terrified and men expressed various opinions. Certain acute [Col. 0943C] thinkers investigated the mysteries of events closely; cautiously inferring the future from the past, they said that God’s anger was threatening the world because of its sins, and that it would shortly strike down the princes of the earth with their subject peoples like forest trees.

At that time Louis, king of the Franks, was in the twenty-eighth year of his reign and lay ill, weakened by the draining effects of diarrhoea. Fearing death, he put his household and all that he possessed in order. He summoned the chief magnates of Gaul, Theobald of Blois and Ralph of Péronne, and reconciled them because they were at odds. He also entrusted the kingdom of Gaul to his son Louis Florus, whom three years earlier he had made king at Reims and caused Pope Innocent, together with a synod of thirteen archbishops and 263 bishops, to crown on 23 October [Col. 0943D], amid the rejoicing of the crowd present. When the physicians despaired of the king, almighty Adonai, who granted King Hezekiah fifteen additional years of life, prolonged the span of the sick Louis’s life and unexpectedly gave him an improvement from his former condition, so that he might amend his life.

#### VIII. Death and Funeral of Henry, King of the English. Disturbances in England.

Meanwhile King Henry of the English came to the castle of Lyons-la-Forêt on 25 November and arranged for hunters to go hunting in the forest on the following day. But when night came, he immediately fell ill, and from Tuesday until Sunday suffered from a mortal disease.

[Col. 0944A] First he confessed his sins to his chaplains. Then, after Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, had been summoned, he discussed spiritual counsel. Admonished, he pardoned all offenders their transgressions, granted exiles permission to return, and restored ancestral inheritances to the disinherited. He ordered his son Robert, who was illegitimate, to take sixty thousand pounds from the treasury which he maintained at Falaise and distribute wages and gifts to his servants and paid knights. He commanded that his body be carried to Reading, where he had founded a monastery of 200 monks in honour of the holy and undivided Trinity. Finally, the Catholic king begged all to preserve peace and protect the poor. After receiving confession, absolution, and penance from the priests, anointed with holy oil [Col. 0944B] and strengthened by the holy Eucharist, he commended himself to God. Thus, on Sunday, 1 December, at the beginning of night, he departed this life.

Five counts were present: Robert of Gloucester, William de Warenne, Rotrou of Mortagne, Waleran of Meulan, and Robert of Leicester, along with other magnates and knights and noble townsmen. Hugh the archbishop, with Audin, bishop of Évreux, bound them all by oath not to abandon their lord’s body except by common counsel, but to escort it in honourable formation all the way to the sea. Therefore, on Monday, they carried the king’s bier from the castle of Lyons-la-Forêt to Rouen; and twenty thousand people accompanied it, lest honour be lacking to him in his funeral rites. It was received in the metropolitan basilica of Holy Mary, Mother of God [Col. 0944C], with immense solemn celebration, while a great abundance of tears was shed by every order of both sexes. There, at night, in the archbishop’s chamber, a skilled butcher opened the fat corpse and embalmed it with fragrant balsam. His entrails, however, were carried in a vessel to the village of Ermentrudes and deposited in the church of St Mary of the Meadow, which his mother had begun but he himself had completed.

Then, by the prudent counsel of the wise, Rouen and the district of Caux were entrusted to William de Warenne, who for some time defended them effectively. William of Roumare and Hugh of Gournay, with other march-lords, were sent to guard the borders of the country. Roger of Salisbury, moreover, with certain other clerics, Robert [Col. 0944D] de Vere, John Algaso, other knights from England, and the king’s attendants and servants were assembled; and by way of Pont-Audemer and Bonneville they conveyed the king’s bier to Caen. There they waited almost four weeks for a favourable wind for sailing. Meanwhile the king’s body was kept in the choir of St Stephen the Protomartyr, until, after Christmas, monks having been sent there, it was placed aboard a ship and carried across; and by the successor to the kingdom, the bishops, and the princes of the land it was honourably buried in the basilica at Reading.

Now that I have truthfully described how the glorious father of his country died, I shall briefly compose in dactylic verses the sufferings of unruly Normandy, which its wretched mother endured so pitiably at the hands of her viperous offspring. Indeed, [Col. 0945A] as soon as that offspring learned of the fall of the stern prince, in the first week of the Lord’s Advent, on that very day, like ravening wolves it ran most eagerly to plunder and impious devastation.

The unconquered bearer of the sceptre, wise duke, renowned hero,  
Who fostered many peoples by just governance,  
Alas, has fallen. Hence arises a universal grief;  
Public disaster at once threatens both Normans and English.  
In wealth and justice, judgment and integrity,  
His energy shone manifestly everywhere.  
No better prince rules in the world than he—  
At a time when excessive wickedness rages throughout the world.  
As I judge, among all men he was one of the best.  
His distinctive deeds bear witness to this.  
Guardian of the Church and serene lover of peace,  
May he live for ever with Christ, King of the heavens. Amen.

King Henry died at the first light of December;  
A mournful ruin presses upon the limbs of the country.

[Col. 0945B]

Now everyone everywhere desires to seize another’s goods.  
Behold, each loosens the reins for unjust deeds.  
See how infernal Furies menace mortals.  
They prepare arms, summon men to war, and supply missiles.  
The Normans persist in thefts and robberies;  
They now kill, capture, and bind one another.  
They burn houses and everything held in them;  
They spare no monks and respect no women.  
The noblewoman groans, stripped by the frenzy of robbers;  
The common law of the Quirites affords her no protection.  
The beardless boy is struck down; the thief has no pity on a child.  
Though this Roman host is pagan, it does not do these things;  
It is clear in broad daylight that peace is bitter to them—  
Peace which they promptly despised when fate took away the king.  
For the death of their father-ruler the wicked thieves rejoice;  
Eager plunderers run about, ready for evil.  
And now they suppose that henceforth no lord will lawfully  
Restrain them; but, I say in reply, they are gravely mistaken.  
The everlasting right of the almighty King remains;  
[Col. 0945C] and He will soon give the Church a good protector.  
The prince having been taken away, the order of monks prays,  
Bending Wisdom by tears toward pardon for sins.  
O highest God, restrain them, lest they be able to commit  
The savage acts which, mad servants of destruction, they desire.  
See, madness rages, calls, and draws all men to crime.  
Suppress it, lest they have power to accomplish what they seek.  
Christ, provide a leader who may love  
And uphold peace and justice, and lead Your people to You.  
With the rod of justice strike the swelling backs,  
That Your people may always serve You in security.  
Amen.

Stephen, count of Boulogne, having heard of the death of his uncle, immediately crossed the sea. Received by William, archbishop of Canterbury, and by the other prelates and princes of the land, he ascended the royal throne; and, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January, he was crowned king, the fourth [Col. 0945D] ruler of Norman stock.

The Normans, however, meeting his brother Theobald at Neubourg, wished to set him over themselves. But in that very assembly they heard from a certain monk, Stephen’s envoy, that all the English had accepted Stephen, wished to obey him all, and to establish him as their king. Immediately all, with Theobald’s assent, resolved to serve one lord, because the barons possessed honours in both regions. Theobald, therefore, being the elder, resented not having obtained the kingdom; he hastened to important affairs pressing upon him in France, and negligently allowed Normandy to be trampled down for a long time. Meanwhile, since the king was occupied in England, Normandy was without a ruler.

[Col. 0946A]

In the first week of December, Geoffrey of Anjou, as soon as he learned of King Henry’s death, promptly sent his wife Matilda into Normandy. Guigan Algaso, a man indeed of very low birth but of great power, received her as his natural lady and subjected to her Argentan, Exmes, Domfront, and the other towns over which, by the king’s command, he presided as viscount. Then the count followed with William Talvas, count of Ponthieu, bands of Angevins, and men of Maine; and he was received by the men of Sées and other castellans who held of Talvas’s fee. His army, dispersed through the surrounding province, perpetrated cruelties, violated churches and cemeteries, oppressed its hosts with injuries, and inflicted many losses and wrongs upon those by whom it had been [Col. 0946B] kindly received.

But the Normans, in whom native fierceness and boldness reside, when they painfully felt the enemy’s wickedness raging against them, nevertheless took up arms in anger. They pursued the fugitives through villages and woods and, as common report relates, slaughtered more than seven hundred by fire or sword. The survivors, terrified by the bloody attacks of the Normans, fled back to their homes in disgrace; and, having been harshly chastised by their sharp blades, they did not thereafter venture to test them again. Robert of Sablé, son of Lisiard, and other magnates also rebelled against Count Geoffrey; by keeping him occupied in civil wars, they prevented his return to Neustria.

[Col. 0946C]

Yet Normandy, although not troubled by foreigners, enjoyed no security of peace, because it was wickedly afflicted by its own sons and, as if in labour, suffered the unceasing distress of its womb. If the Norman people lived according to God’s law and were united under a good ruler, they would be invincible, equal to the Chaldeans under Nebuchadnezzar, the Persians and Medes under Cyrus and Darius, and the Macedonians under Alexander—as the frequent victories in England, Apulia, and Syria bear witness. But because discord separates them from one another and lethally arms them against their own entrails, conquerors of foreigners are conquered by themselves; while neighbouring enemies look on in mockery, [Col. 0946D] they mercilessly cut one another’s throats with mutual blows. Hence the eyes of their mother frequently weep.

## IX. Stephen, the new king of the English. Disorders in Normandy. The plundering of the borough of Ouche.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1136, the fourteenth indiction, while Stephen, king of the English, delayed in crossing the sea into Neustria, and that province lacked both patron and prince, quarrels arose among the restless magnates of Normandy, and excessive evils increased through the sons of iniquity.

At the beginning of Lent, Eustace of Breteuil died at Pacy; and after Easter his son William assailed the honour of Breteuil with sword and fire. Then King Stephen gave his two-year-old daughter, still in the cradle, to Count Waleran of Meulan. After Easter the count promptly returned to Normandy. A violent war was fiercely waged between Roger of Tosny and Robert, count of Leicester, and a great desolation of the whole country miserably arose.

Between Rogationtide and Pentecost, Roger secretly entered the king’s fortress at La Vallée-de-Rouen. But after three days Count Waleran, with the united force of Rouen, rushed there and restored the town to the lord king. Then, on the Monday after Pentecost, he invaded Acquigny with a strong force and burned the whole town. On the following day, nevertheless, Roger rushed upon him and suddenly burned three of his villages. These and many similar acts the Normans committed, devouring one another with their own teeth.

[Col. 0947B]

From Christmas until the octave of Pentecost, because of the king’s absence—he was occupied beyond the sea by the manifold affairs of his kingdom—Count Theobald had received a truce from the count of Anjou; meanwhile the Norman host eagerly awaited the king’s arrival. But when the term of the truce ended, all the people were dismayed and, bereft of a ruler, did not know what to do. For malicious thieves longed to see the day on which they might freely steal or seize the goods of others. The unarmed, kindly, and simple greatly feared what the rapacious sons of Belial desired without fear of God.

Robert called Boethus, a notorious [Col. 0947C] archer, adhered to Richer of L’Aigle and enlisted many vagabonds and unruly serving-men for the daily perpetration of slaughter and robbery. The greater his skill in archery, the more detestable he was in wickedness. He rashly profaned the week of Pentecost—which the Holy Spirit sanctified by the sevenfold grace given to Christ’s disciples—with impious deeds; ignorant of the future, he thirsted for worse. For just as the good were beneficially kindled by the flame of the Paraclete Spirit to love God and neighbour, so the wicked, raging under a demonic spirit, were swept toward every crime.

Therefore, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June, plunderers ran like wolves toward prey. They did not invade the lands of warlike [Col. 0947D] knights, but immediately attempted to drive off herds peacefully grazing in the fields of the hooded monks. Yet, just as they themselves had been swift to shed blood, so by God’s just judgment they suddenly found ruin and misery in their paths. At Ouche thirty brigands plundered the property of simple folk; but when the herdsmen raised an alarm, the townsmen rushed out and captured twelve, seven of whom they hanged from one oak. There Robert Boethus, with his six accomplices, was raised up by the onrush of the furious populace; thus he immediately received such a triumph for his crimes. Behold: those who had not feared to defile the seven consecrated days of Pentecost, and had burned with savage rashness to oppress their defenceless neighbours by robbery and murder, perished together by hanging in the same number on the following [Col. 0948A] Monday.

When the men of L’Aigle heard this on the same day, they gathered in excessive fury to avenge their companions, flew at once to Ouche, and unexpectedly set fire to the borough of St Évroul. Eighty-four houses there were reduced to ashes in an instant. The weeping monks rang the bells and sang psalms and litanies in the basilica, fearing that the destruction of the monastery was imminent. Others went out to meet the knights, pleaded with tears, excused themselves from punishment of the guilty, and implored them with humble words; they also offered lawful redress and satisfaction for the offence. But the attackers raged like madmen; blinded by fury, they snarled against the monks and paid heed to no sound reasoning. Indeed, some [Col. 0948B] of them wished to injure God’s religious servants after throwing them from their horses. At last, without reverence for God, they assaulted the town; violently entering it, they carried off plunder and, as has been said, utterly burned the dwellings within the gates.

This sort of soldiery was deservedly turned into disgrace as avengers of brigands: it armed itself against innocent monks and their people, and avenged the vilest kidnappers, who were striving to perpetrate every crime.

Richer, the monks’ godson, rendered such service to his godfathers; thus he prayed for the soul of Boethus, the notorious thief and murderer, and of the other impostors, and offered such an oblation to the church in which he had been baptized. Baldwin, the priest of L’Aigle, likewise led his parishioners into this execrable crime. He was the first to cast fire into another priest’s lodging, and thus, as their guide, dragged his own followers headlong with him into the abyss. The violence of the flames reached even the basilica; but, through God’s mercy, a contrary wind arose and drove the balls of flame elsewhere, in the sight and joy of many. Thus the basilica and the monastic workshops, with the books and church vessels, were saved [the supplied verb is *fuerunt*, “were”]; to them the desolated country people fled with their little families, awaiting better times in accordance with God’s providence.

The men of L’Aigle, however, became rich and swollen with the spoils of the men of Ouche, but did not rejoice for long. For in the same month they rushed upon Sées and Gacé [Col. 0948D] and repeatedly fought against Roger of Tosny. Yet after the devastation of the town of St Évroul, they obtained no successful outcome; rather, by God’s judgment, they frequently suffered losses through the destruction or capture of their men. Deservedly: having fought against the naked and simple, and having spared them nothing out of fear of God, they later encountered very strong and warlike champions who did not seek them out; from the knights who met them they repeatedly heard, with reproach and derision: “Come here, soldiers. We are not hooded monks or tonsured clerics; we are armed knights challenging you to battle. We are your comrades; you must learn what we can do.” They often blushed at such reproaches, and many of them, suffering hard blows, fell. Thus some [Col. 0949A] were stirred toward repentance by the downfall of others.

## X. Various events in England and Normandy.

After Pentecost, King Stephen prepared his fleet for crossing the sea. While he awaited a favourable wind near the harbour, a messenger came, through whom he heard that Roger, bishop of Salisbury—whose uncle had long ago entrusted to him the guardianship of all Albion, and Stephen himself had later done likewise—was dead. He therefore interrupted his voyage and returned to Salisbury; finding the bishop alive, he was vainly delayed from his journey until Lent. Meanwhile Gilbert de Clare made an expedition into the district of Exmes and burned Neubourg, which King Henry had recently enlarged, together with the church of the Holy Mother of God. [Col. 0949B] He also pressed vigorously to burn the old borough; but Count Talvas and other knights suddenly rushed upon him, defeated him, and he escaped with difficulty. There Henry de Ferrières was captured, and a great capture or slaughter was made of men who favoured the king.

At that time Counts Waleran and Robert sought aid from Count Theobald of Blois and hired him against Roger of Tosny for one hundred marks of silver. On the feast of St Barnabas the Apostle they entered Roger’s land with an enormous multitude and burned the humble dwellings of many poor people in three villages. At length they rushed upon a large village called Bulgy; at the prompting of the count of Leicester, they set fire to neighbouring homes [Col. 0949C] and burned the beautiful church of St Mary Magdalene together with men and women.

On that same day Richer of L’Aigle and Alvered of Verneuil, while passing before New Ferrières with their men, were stoutly defeated and put to flight by Robert of Bellême [Note: [Col. 0949D] This Robert of Bellême—whom Orderic elsewhere surnames *Poardus*—is distinct from Robert [Col. 0950D], count of Bellême, father of William Talvas. (Dom Bouquet.)], by the Mauvais-Voisins, and by other French knights who were assisting Roger. With many of their companions captured or killed, they barely escaped. In the third week of June Count Theobald besieged Pont-Saint-Pierre and laboured greatly in attacking it for a whole month. For William de Fontaines, with other most proven knights and retainers who adhered to Roger, defended the town fiercely against the enemy.

[Col. 0949D]

Meanwhile, the venerable Boso, abbot of Le Bec, after laudably ruling that monastery for nearly ten years, died on the feast day of St John the Baptist, after a long illness which this most learned man had borne patiently. Theobald, prior of the church, succeeded him by the ecclesiastical election of the monastic community.

On the day after the feast of St John, Ralph, archdeacon of the church of Évreux, while returning from Pacy, was attacked by the sons of Simon Hareng and barely escaped. He himself was saved by fleeing to a certain church, but his servant and travelling companion, who fought for his lord, was killed.

This tumultuous year was truly a leap year, and then the last leap-year cycle in the order of concurrents ran its course; and, as common speech has it, the leap year fell upon the king and his people in Normandy and England.

In the third week of September Rouen was suddenly consumed by fire, and immense damage was inflicted upon the faithful people by God’s judgment. Alas, the noble monastery of St Ouen was consumed by devouring flames, though it had scarcely been brought to completion through the labour of many over eighty years. By an equal misfortune the monastery of nuns, constructed in honour of St Amand, bishop and confessor, was desolated.

## XI. Invasion and devastations of the Angevins in Normandy.

[Col. 0950B]

Then, on the following Sunday, the eleventh day before the Kalends of October, Geoffrey, count of Anjou, crossed the River Sarthe and entered Normandy with an enormous armed force. He had with him Duke William of Poitiers, Geoffrey of Vendôme, young William son of Count William of Nevers, and William, count of Ponthieu, surnamed Talvas. These men, together with many other tribunes and centurions, joined their forces to the Angevins and rushed upon the Normans in every kind of wickedness, whether for the prince’s favour or for greed of plunder. Hence those whom they shamelessly injured gave them, in hostile hatred, the contemptuous name “Helle-beccers.”

First the count besieged the town of Verneuil, [Col. 0950C] and in three days stormed the castle held by the knight Walter; but shortly afterwards that same townsman recovered it when the adversaries departed. The inhabitants burned Scorcheville and fled, leaving smoke and ashes behind them as the enemy slowly approached. The townsmen of Auneau made a treaty for one year. Robert of Neubourg, lord of the aforementioned castle, was known to Count Geoffrey and had long been attached to Count Amaury in friendship and familiarity. The Angevins approached the castle of Montreuil and assaulted it twice; but because those within resisted stoutly, they gained nothing but wounds and, after many of their men had been killed, withdrew.

Richard [Col. 0950D] surnamed Basset, whose power in England during King Henry’s life had been great, as that of a chief justiciar, wished—swollen with English wealth—to raise himself above his native equals by the magnitude of his works on the small Norman fee he possessed by hereditary right from his parents. He accordingly built a very strong square-stone tower at Montreuil. But after the king’s death, William de Montpinçon promptly entered it, fortified it with arms and men, and courageously repelled the raging Helle-beccers, as has been said. From there they made for the castle called Hubert’s Monastery; having defeated Paganellus, the townsman who had perpetrated many wicked acts [Col. 0951A] in that disastrous year, they took the town and severely constrained the aforesaid townsman and thirty knights by a vast monetary ransom.

Then, while the feast of St Michael the Archangel was being celebrated, the hostile army prepared to besiege Lisieux. But as they hurried there, Count Waleran of Meulan and other Norman magnates who were there with many knights appointed Alan of Dinan, with the boldest defenders, to guard the city. They themselves went out in order more freely to bring aid from outside to the besieged, and waited anxiously at a distance for the outcome. The Bretons and others who ought to have defended the fortress, however, were terrified when they saw the enemy’s multitude from afar and despaired of advancing to meet them or fighting hand-to-hand. They therefore set fire to the city entrusted to them and burned it, thus forestalling their enemies by their own destruction, lest worse things happen.

When the enemy approached and saw the city burning with its abundant wealth, they were grievously angry and distressed because they were wholly disappointed in their hope of plunder; they lamented the loss of booty perishing in the flames. Thus, mourning, they learned the Norman people’s resolution and marvelled at the bitterness of their implacable hostility: they saw them prefer their own resources to perish by conflagration rather than, resources intact, submit their necks to the yoke of foreign lordship.

[Col. 0951C]

But because of the exceedingly fierce fire, they could neither approach the fortress nor undertake an assault in any way. Turning their horses back, they immediately returned to Sap and attempted to storm that town to its depths. A tall tree called a fir had stood from ancient times near the church of St Peter the Apostle, and popular speech used to call the village Sap from it. That name survives to this day in the borough or castle. The Angevins, returning from Lisieux, unexpectedly came there and found the inhabitants boldly coming out against them and raging fiercely. While they fought hotly, flames were set among the buildings by both sides, that is, natives and foreigners alike; hence the townsmen’s strength was immediately exhausted. Then the church [Col. 0951D] of St Peter the Apostle was burned with the whole village, and, after many who tried to resist had been wounded, the shattered tower was taken.

Walter de Clare and his brother-in-law Ralph de Coldum held it and resisted their opponents for some time with thirty knights; but overwhelmed by the immense force of the opposing host, they failed, and, their strength spent, were captured in the castle. For nearly three thousand archers harassed them with arrows, while many slingers hurled a hail of stones against the townsmen and fatally overwhelmed them in a great storm.

The Angevins remained in Normandy for thirteen days, and by their savagery earned lasting hatred from the Normans, not dominion over them. Since the Normans then lacked a prince, they encountered no general battle; [Col. 0952A] nevertheless, while engaging here and there in rapine and arson, they were beaten by country people. Diminished as their companions fell in different places under varying fortunes, they finally fled. They committed innumerable evils beyond expression and deservedly suffered like things in return. They showed no reverence for sacred things; indeed, they wickedly trampled the Lord’s sanctuary and, after the fashion of pagans, abused priests and other ministers of God. Some they irreverently stripped before the holy altar; others, ringing bells and calling upon God, they slaughtered. Nine priests together ran to the count and made a tearful complaint concerning the violation of their churches and the plundering of sacred objects; all honourable and God-fearing men who heard it were deeply grieved.

[Col. 0952B]

The leaders therefore proclaimed at Sap to the whole army that sacred things must not be defiled; but rash plunderers amid so great a multitude made light of the magnates’ decree. Common soldiers and unruly pirates had gathered like wolves to devour others’ devourers; wandering and undisciplined, they had flown together like kites from diverse and remote regions, desiring nothing except plunder and the striking down or overcoming of anyone they met. The magnates, who ought to have led their separate companies on the expedition under lawful command, knew nothing, in my judgment, of the strict discipline of Roman warfare; nor did they regulate even military enmities with the moderation proper to heroes. Consequently almost all of them, I think, were stained by shameful deeds, without [Col. 0952C] any regard for good; through every crime they rushed into a double ruin, of body and soul, and appeared hateful to God and men.

They slaughtered very many herds of cattle and flocks and ate the meat raw or half-cooked, without salt or bread. They tried to carry the hides home to their own country in many carts. Although the autumn season abounded in supplies of food, and the province’s fertility—after a long peace under a good ruler—smiled upon its inhabitants and provided every abundance of grain and meat, such a multitude lacked the services of cooks and bakers; amid the commotion of war, provisions of very many things most needed for human necessity were unavailable. Therefore the Helle-beccers, because after profaning sacred things they intemperately consumed ill-prepared food, by God’s just judgment almost all fell sick with flux of the belly; distressed by flowing diarrhoea, they left foul traces as they went, and most could scarcely regain their homes.

At last, on the Kalends of October, while they attacked the castle of Sap and its garrison resisted most fiercely, Count Geoffrey was severely struck in the right foot by a spear; with a grave wound to his foot and the rout of his men, he experienced somewhat of Norman resolution.

His wife came to him that same day toward evening and brought many thousands of fighters with her in vain. For early the next morning, while the inhabitants everywhere trembled, [Col. 0953A] the Angevins suddenly withdrew; fearing those by whom they had been greatly feared, they fled obstinately, devastating the whole country alike of allies and enemies. The Normans learned of their flight too late and were greatly grieved that they had not driven them from their country by pursuit. Only Enguerrand de Courte-Odmard, with Robert de Mesdavit and a few other knights, occupied the crossings of the Orne. There he detained many men, horses, and wagons laden with bread, wine, and much equipment, and compelled the Angevins, who in fear of death dared to enter the river where there was no ford, to suffer death in the deep Orne.

The count, who had entered Normandy mounted on a foaming horse and with many threats, returned pale and groaning, [Col. 0953B] lying in a *badivola*. [Note: [Col. 0953] The manuscript of Ouche reads *badinola*, that is, a litter or a bed carried on a journey. (Dom Bouquet.)] Yet on that very return he endured greater losses from his own men than from his enemies. For in the wood called Malassise the count’s chamberlain was killed, and his wallet, containing comital garments and precious vessels, was stolen.

Meanwhile, while the Angevins, as already related, devastated the district of Lisieux and, raging in pagan fashion without fear of God, perpetrated abominations, Roger de Conches ravaged the surrounding region in the diocese of Évreux, delivering everything to slaughter and devouring flames. He had with him William de Pacy, son of Eustace, Roger the Bald, and Count Ferric; and he kept Count Waleran and all the knights of the district of Ouche occupied, so that they could not advance in arms against the Angevins. Roger fiercely attacked the castle which the count of Meulan had built at La Croix for the country’s defence, but failed to take it. Yet Roger and his fellow-knights violated the abbey that St Ouen had formerly built, dedicated in honour of the holy Cross which he had seen in heaven, and entrusted to Blessed Leufredus to govern; he did not long go unpunished for this. He burned the monks’ borough and attacked the church, seized fugitives hiding there in the inner precincts of the monastery, and plundered the possessions of the monks and of those who had fled to them. But shortly afterward, through the vengeance of God, the most righteous judge, he lost everything [Col. 0953D]; for, on the day after the Angevins’ flight, that is, the third day of October, Roger was unexpectedly defeated.

In the valley of the Andelle he devastated a fertile province, devoted himself without reverence to slaughter, plunder, and arson, and thus made many people miserable with his accomplices by taking away their possessions. He burned the church of St Stephen, for which offence he received retribution that very day. For on Saturday about evening, as they returned leading with pomp an immense spoil and many captives, Count Waleran and Henry de Pommeraye came out from a neighbouring wood with five hundred knights and stood ready for battle against the hostile force. Roger, who was very bold and valiant, fought strongly but vainly against the enemy with the few knights whom he had with him—for he had sent William de Pacy and Roger the Bald, with their forces, booty, and captives, ahead to Acquigny. Overwhelmed and defeated by numbers, he yielded; captured with Count Ferric and Robert of Bellême, surnamed Poardus, he groaned, and by his misfortune brought great joy to his enemies and security to the neighbouring country people.

Meanwhile, while Ferric de Étampes groaned in prison, his wife—by whose lineage he himself was called count—went to King Louis at Paris. As she returned while pregnant, she was injured while riding and shortly afterward died in difficult childbirth.

## XII. Pious reflections. Deaths of various lords and prelates. Drought.

[Col. 0954B]

How mutable are the vicissitudes of this present life! Secular joys swiftly pass away and in a moment desert those who most ardently pursue them. Worldly honour, like a bubble, suddenly bursts and fails, mocking and deceiving those who gape after it. Lovers of the world pursue corruptible things and, walking along the precipices of vices, are thus corrupted; suddenly, when seated on high, they slip down into the depths. While with toil they scarcely attain lofty pride, from that height, swollen with vanity yet retaining nothing, they are cast down in a moment. Only well-shaped tales about them are widely disseminated by eloquent men among those left behind who still enjoy the vital air.

Therefore the omnipotent Creator instructs those who dwell on earth and beneficially teaches them in many ways not to fix the anchor of their hope in this sea of a fragile age, nor lethally cling to transitory pleasures or gains. “For we have no continuing city here,” as the Apostle says, “but we seek the one to come” (Hebrews 13:14).

Behold, in this leap year, after the death of King Henry, many changes occurred in the world, and many persons of clerical and lay rank, together with people of middling and lowest estate, died.

Then Gerard, bishop of Angoulême, a most learned man, passed away; in the Roman senate he had been of great name and power in the time of Popes Paschal, [Col. 0954D] Gelasius, Calixtus, and Honorius.

Guy de Étampes, bishop of Le Mans, died; Pagan, archdeacon of Saint-Calais, succeeded him. Moreover, in place of Gilbert, surnamed “the Universal,” bishop of London, who had recently died, Anselm, nephew of Archbishop Anselm and abbot of St Edmund the King, was appointed. William, archbishop of Canterbury, died, and Henry, brother of King Stephen, was chosen to govern the metropolitan see. But because, according to the decrees of the canons, a bishop cannot be transferred from his own see to another church without the authority of the Roman pontiff, the aforesaid bishop of Winchester [Col. 0955A] crossed the sea during the Lord’s Advent; after sending envoys to Pope Innocent at Piacenza, he himself spent the winter in Neustria.

He learned from those who mourned of the impious crimes committed by the faithless in the leap year—crimes full of affliction and tears; he heard sad complaints concerning Normandy’s wretched misfortunes and could see with his own eyes sure signs: houses burned, churches unroofed and desolate, villages laid waste and bereft of their own cultivators, and peoples deeply afflicted in their mother’s bosom, insolently deprived of every necessity and plundered by both their own countrymen and foreigners without fear of a protector, and not yet gladdened by the presence and aid of a suitable ruler. Thus an even graver blow still threatens Normandy through many kinds of suffering.

In the diocese of Sées, an interdict struck the whole land of William Talvas. The sweet melody of divine worship, which softens and gladdens the hearts of the faithful, was silenced. Laypeople were forbidden to enter churches for God’s service, and the doors were locked. The bronze bells fell silent; the bodies of the dead decayed unburied, striking fear and horror into those who saw them. The joy of marriage was denied to those who sought it, and the gladness of ecclesiastical solemnities was humbled. In the diocese of Évreux too, a like discipline resounded, and throughout all the land of Roger of Tosny it strove to restrain the disorderly by fear. He himself is confined in bonds in prison, helpless to do his own will, weeping and lamenting; and even by the Church he is cursed for the violation of sacred things which, fully in command of himself, he had committed through insolence. His entire land is punished by a terrible anathema. Thus the stubborn and excessively rebellious are crushed by a double affliction; but, alas, the hard hearts of the others who behold these things are not corrected, nor are they turned from their perverse purpose toward amendment.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1137, in the fifteenth indiction, there was a great drought throughout the whole world, such as no one in our times had seen. In many places springs dried up, lakes and cisterns were drained, and certain rivers ceased to flow. Men and beasts of burden suffered from the distress of thirst; and in some regions [Col. 0955D] they sought water as far as seven leagues away. Some of those who carried water for themselves and their households upon their shoulders succumbed to the extremity of the excessive heat.

### XIII. Stephen, king of the English, receives Normandy as a fief from Louis, king of the French. Stephen punishes rebels. Angevin attacks upon Normandy.

In the third week of March King Stephen came into Normandy and landed at Ogas [place-name uncertain] with a great retinue. When news of his arrival was heard, the common people, oppressed and desolated for a whole year, rejoiced.

At the same time William, duke of the Poitevins, mindful of the evils which he had lately wrought in Normandy, was moved by repentance and set out as a pilgrim for Saint James’s shrine. [Col. 0956A] Then, on Good Friday, the fifth day before the Ides of April, strengthened by holy communion, he died devoutly before the altar of the blessed Apostle. He ordered his daughter to be given in marriage to Louis the Younger, king of the French, and appointed that king heir to all his rights; and this was afterwards done.

Certain Norman magnates were hostile to King Stephen, against whom he summoned Frenchmen and Flemings. In May King Stephen held a conference with King Louis; he received from him the duchy of Normandy by right and made a treaty of friendship, as his predecessor had maintained. He therefore returned more secure, attacked the rebellious Raoul with military force, besieged his towns of Lillebonne, the villeries, and Odo’s residence, and, either personally [Col. 0956B] or through auxiliaries, subdued them with their households by sword and fire.

Then Geoffrey of Anjou came into Normandy with four hundred knights and, acting as a mercenary in his wife’s service, committed enormous outrages. From the beginning of May he waged cruel war and laboured zealously to ravage the district of Exmes by fire, plunder, and the slaughter of men. He burned Bazoches, the town of Roger de Mowbray, together with its church, and there the fire killed six men. The monks of Dives agreed to pay one hundred and ten marks of silver to the count of Anjou for their protection; thus they protected their land from utter destruction. Likewise, the monks of Fécamp paid a hundred marks for Argences. [Col. 0956C]

Then Robert, count of Gloucester, and certain others were suspected of turning to the enemy. But the townsmen of Caen adhered firmly to the king’s loyalty; while they guarded the fortress, Geoffrey and his men returned from Le Val-Bérenger having gained nothing. There William of Ypres and his men wished to fight the Angevins; but since the Normans, through jealousy, refused loyally to aid them, he withdrew with his followers. Leaving behind his faithless associates, he went to the king across the Seine. The king, having made peace with Raoul, entered the Évreux district and released Roger de Conches from prison in the sixth month after his capture, imposing severe terms upon him so that his rash wickedness might be punished. [Col. 0956D] He attached to himself Rotrou, count of Mortain, and Rotrou’s nephew Richer de l’Aigle, granting them what their greed had eagerly demanded: to the count he granted the town of Moulins, and to Richer Bonmoulin. Thus binding them to himself, he set them against the enemy on the borders of Normandy, judging it more useful to give up lesser things in order to preserve greater ones than greedily to embrace everything and thereby deservedly lose friends and their support. He warmly embraced William of Ypres and the other Flemings, placing especial trust in them. Therefore the Norman magnates were greatly angered, cunningly withdrew their service from the king, and, envying them, laid snares in many ways. Then a band of country people was everywhere engaged in plundering amid very many disasters; for the hostile sword devoured many, [Col. 0957A] while sudden death pressed upon many others from another quarter.

In June King Stephen came to Lisieux and assembled a large army, intending to besiege Argentan or another town where he had learned that Geoffrey of Anjou was, with whom he desired to engage at close quarters. But his nobles shrank from such a contest and strongly dissuaded the king from battle. Then, during that expedition, a most serious riot arose between Normans and Morini, and a deadly slaughter of men on both sides took place.

> **Note:** [Col. 0957D] On account of one hose of wine—that is, a wine-skin full of wine—which a certain Morin, or Fleming, had taken from an esquire of [Col. 0958D] Hugh of Gournay. R. de Monte. (Dom Bouquet.)

As a result the entire army was thrown into confusion, and the greater part of the princes departed without taking leave of the king. Every troop of retainers also followed its own leader.

[Col. 0957B] When the king saw his columns fleeing without battle, he was exceedingly angry and hastily pursued the deserters as far as Pont-Audemer. There he detained Hugh de Gournay, the young William de Warenne, and other haughty young men, and calmed them as far as he could by threats and inducements; but he could not sufficiently pacify the resentful hearts of these crafty men. Since he regarded them as suspect on certain grounds, he did not venture to lead them back to war; instead, having adopted what seemed to some a sounder policy, he accepted a two-year truce from the enemy. Thus in July, with God’s help, the tranquillity of peace revived Normandy. The unarmed people, who had been scattered, returned to their cottages and, for a while [Col. 0957C] after the excessive storms of disorder, remained quiet amid great want and rested in somewhat greater security.

### XIV. Death of Warin, abbot of Ouche. Death of Louis, king of the French. Disorders and wars in Normandy. Breton invasion of Normandy. King Stephen crosses to England.

Meanwhile Warin, abbot of the church of Ouche, after serving God in monastic life for forty-three years and having now reached the age of sixty-three, died happily. For on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of July he reverently sang Mass in the morning, buried a certain deceased knight, and on that same day took to his bed. He was gravely ill for five days and, while sick, heard daily the Mass which he himself, as priest, had celebrated very frequently for thirty years. [Col. 0957D] Seeing, therefore, that he was about to enter upon the way of all flesh, he devoutly sought the provision for so great a journey; and, about to go to the court of the supreme King of Hosts, he prepared himself by tearful confession, constant and earnest prayer, anointing with holy oil, and the saving reception of the Lord’s body. Finally, equipped with such and so great protections, he departed on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July. Having fulfilled in himself, as has been said, all that befits a faithful athlete of Christ, he departed; and in the fifteenth year of his rule, commending his spiritual sons and himself to the Lord God, he fell asleep. Gilbert, abbot of the monastery of Sées, was present and, with his companions mourning for their father, celebrated the funeral rites in tears. [Col. 0958A] Thus, while the rains of tribulation poured upon the entire province, Abbot Warin, son of Robert and Gisela, was taken away and buried in the chapter house beside the tomb of Abbot Osbern.

After his death the monks of Ouche assembled together and held a common deliberation, lest the condition of their church should decline. Then, while they were celebrating the feast of Saint John the Baptist, and on that very day deliberating together in chapter, they considered the rule of the holy father Benedict, the authority of their charter—which Duke William, later king, had confirmed with the bishops and magnates of Normandy—and the privilege and ancient custom of the church. They unanimously elected Richard of Leicester, a monk learned, devout, eloquent, [Col. 0958B] and endowed with many good and notable gifts. He was absent, and had no kinsman connected with him in that assembly. He suspected nothing of this; indeed, he was toiling in England at rural labours for the service of the brethren. For his abbot had sent him there long before, and for six months he had diligently administered the affairs of the church there. He knew the English people and language, since he had been a canon of Leicester for nearly sixteen years and, before his conversion, had long lived at the court of Robert, earl of Meulan. He had been distinguished as a judge of cases, confidant of secrets, and intimate counsellor in practical affairs. The monks, considering these and other proofs of worth [Col. 0958C] suitable to a ruler, chose him to govern the church; and King Stephen and his magnates gave their approval to the election.

The monks of Ouche, always faithful to their teachers and rulers, placed a white stone over the tomb of the venerable Abbot Warin. Upon it, out of love for my once beloved companion and afterwards father, I composed this epitaph to be engraved:

> Beneath this stone are covered Warin’s body and bones,  
> Who was a monk at Ouche for forty-four years,  
> A strong combatant against the temptations of the flesh,  
> Who, by God’s gift, shone renowned in gracious virtues.  
> For his merits he was taken from the flock by the brethren  
> To bear particular help to his companions as their governor.  
> Twice seven years he flourished as abbot in reverence,  
> Thirsting amid present ruins for eternity.  
> When June had completed its twentieth course of the sun,  
> This father departed this life, while those subject to him wept.  
> May the God who rules all things grant him light above the heavens.

In July and August the excessive heat of summer scorched the inhabitants of the earth and endured until the Ides of September; a manifold pestilence made mortals sick. Then King Louis summoned his son Louis Florus, entrusted him to the guardianship of Count Theobald the Palatine and his cousin Raoul de Paronne, and sent him with the army of France into Aquitaine, that he might marry the daughter of the duke of Poitou and bring the whole duchy under his rule, as Duke William had ordained. Meanwhile King Louis fell ill from the excessive summer heat in the forest of Aquilina, [Col. 0959A] and, as his sickness worsened, died on the second day before the Nones of August; he received royal burial among the kings in the church of Saint Denis the Areopagite. On the following Sunday the boy Louis was crowned at Poitiers and thus obtained both the kingdom of the Franks and the duchy of Aquitaine, which none of his fathers had possessed.

> **Note:** [Col. 0959D] Suger and other contemporary historians report that Louis the Fat died of diarrhoea on the Kalends of August themselves. Henry of Huntingdon, moreover, censures the gluttony of Louis and of his father Philip in his letter *On Contempt for the World*, to Walter, chapter 5, in these words: “What shall I say of Philip, king of the French, and Louis his son, who reigned in our times, whose god was their belly—indeed, it was their deadly enemy? They devoured so much that they lost themselves in fatness and could not support themselves. Philip formerly died of fatness; Louis, though still young, is nevertheless already dead of fatness. And what of their good fortune? Was not Philip often defeated by his own men and often put to flight by utterly insignificant persons? Was not Louis driven from Martiocampus by King Henry, and, as is plain, often put to flight by his own men?” Do not place excessive trust in an Englishman who thus abuses the kings of France. (Dom Bouquet.)

In Normandy Roger the Bald, himself turbulent, disturbed the peace. Against him King Stephen led an army and seized his stronghold, called Grandis-Silva, in the Évreux district. Thus the rebellious robber was subdued, made peace with the king, and that region rested for a little after great oppression. Then in the Vexin the king destroyed the fortress of Chitry, which was a den of robbers. Thereupon William [Col. 0959B] de Calmont, with his son Odmond, rose against the king and resolved to wage war because his house had been overthrown. In the Avranchin Richard, surnamed Silvanus, fortified a very strong castle at Saint-Patern; gathering robbers from every side, after King Henry’s death he inflicted a most savage slaughter upon the people of God. After his long career of violence, the most just avenging hand of God cast him down without delay when it pleased.

For the aforesaid robber once went out to plunder, while a troop of knights from neighbouring towns set the village of Saint-Patern on fire. When Silvanus saw the smoke of his village, he hurried back with his men by a circuitous path; [Col. 0959C] but, riding more swiftly than his companions, he encountered the enemy first and was killed in their meeting, pierced by a knight’s lance. The royal knights then approached the castle and demanded that its inhabitants surrender the tower to the king. When they refused, the royal men disgracefully threw the corpse of their slain lord before the gate and displayed it to them. On seeing this grave misfortune, the guards were terrified. They surrendered themselves and the fortress to the king’s knights, remained mournfully silent, and buried the body of the “Twice-Dead” beside the road outside the cemetery.

At the same time the Bretons, whose leader in committing this crime was Galduin of Dol, rose up and burst into the lands of Saint Michael the Archangel at Mont-Saint-Michel and into the neighbouring possessions. [Col. 0959D] Repeatedly carrying off plunder, they inflicted immense losses on innocent people. But after innumerable injuries had been brought upon the country folk, their wicked leader was struck down by divine vengeance and they dispersed. For one day the fierce Galduin led one hundred and forty knights, with many foot-soldiers, on an expedition; he seized enormous booty and many people and began to return triumphantly. [Col. 0960A] But the rising sea held all of them at the shore. Meanwhile, at the outcry of the poor populace, twenty Norman knights pursued the raiders. When Galduin heard shouting behind him, he turned back against the pursuers with ten knights, protected only by their shields. The Normans attacked them boldly, pursued the Bretons as they turned their backs, and killed Galduin before he could rejoin his fellow-knights. Thus the raiders, thrown into confusion, lost their booty; fleeing, they carried grim news back to their own people.

Thus unhappy Normandy was disturbed by various storms, wounded by the mutual swords of her own children, and filled everywhere with much mourning for innumerable killings. She endured most dreadful misfortunes and daily feared still harsher ones, because she sorrowfully saw the entire province deprived of an effective governor. [Col. 0960B]

Meanwhile King Stephen heard rumours of internal disturbances among the English. Therefore, at Advent, he hastily crossed into England, taking with him Counts Waleran and Robert and nearly all the other magnates. He had appointed as justiciars of Neustria William of Roumare, Sheriff Roger, and certain others, commanding them to do what he, being absent, could not do: namely, to administer justice to the inhabitants and provide peace for the unarmed people. But upon returning to England, he found the kingdom in turmoil and perceived the foment of excessive cruelty [Col. 0960C] and bloody treachery. Certain pestilent men had formed a conspiracy and, by secret plots, encouraged one another to crime: on an appointed day they were to kill every Norman and hand over the rule of the kingdom to the Scots. This great perversity was first made known to Richard Nigel, bishop of Ely, by associates of the sworn conspiracy; through him it was published to the other bishops of the realm, the magnates, the officials, and the king’s retainers.
