Many of the wicked conspirators were therefore exposed and convicted, paid the penalty for so great a crime, and deservedly perished by the gallows and other forms of death. Others, conscious of their guilt, fled before accusation and, convicted by their own conscience, went into exile, leaving behind all [Col. 0960D] their wealth and honours. The more powerful men who knew of the rebellion were rashly emboldened to resist; they made a league with the Scots and Welsh, and with other seditious and faithless persons, for the destruction of the people.

### XV. Various events in the kingdom of Jerusalem.

At that time pilgrims arrived from the eastern regions [Col. 0961A] and spread grievous reports through the western world, causing great sorrow to the hearts of the faithful who burn with love for God and neighbour. They reported that Pons, count of Tripoli, had fought against the heathen in that same year and had himself fallen by the sword of the gentiles along with many others. Encouraged by this, Amir Sanguin, king of Aleppo, assembled his military forces and, in autumn, entered the Christian territories with a vast Turkish army. Ready for battle, he challenged the Christians. Hearing this, Fulk, king of Jerusalem, sent messengers throughout his kingdom, summoned all fit to bear arms to battle, and led almost six thousand men to the encounter. He left only women and unarmed clergy to defend the towns and ordered all others, [Col. 0961B] without any excuse, to go to the contest.

At length the two sides met, and a fierce engagement was fought on both sides. Countless thousands of pagans fell. But by the judgment of God, whose judgments are just and true, almost the whole Christian army was destroyed, except for thirty knights. The king alone, ten knightly companions of his household, and eighteen Knights of the Temple escaped and fled to a certain castle facing Damascus, built by Baldwin I and called Mont-Royal. There they remained shut in for some time and resisted stoutly. All therefore fell confessing Christ, apart from the few who, as has been said, barely escaped with the king. Though Sanguin [Col. 0961C] had lost many thousands of his own men by the Christians’ swords, elated by the victory he had desired, he immediately pursued them, besieged the castle, and hard pressed the survivors who had escaped the battle and were defending the stronghold, attacking them in many ways. Although the besieged suffered many hardships, they were especially weakened by the distress of hunger and, for want of bread, were compelled to eat horseflesh and other unclean and unfamiliar meats. The king himself, because of the scarcity, acted as food-server and distributed portions of donkey or dog meat to each man.

Meanwhile Raoul, prelate of Jerusalem, heard of his people’s calamity and was grieved. He pondered deeply how he might aid the martyrs enclosed in the castle. First he went round the faithful recluses [Col. 0961D] who devoted themselves to heavenly contemplation within the walls of Jerusalem, and begged them and all the other Jerusalemites to pray more earnestly to the Lord, Saviour of all, for the common safety of His people. Then he exhorted clergy and laity alike, proclaimed a three-day fast for all, and imposed this observance, after the fashion of the Ninevites, not only on matrons but even on infants and beasts of burden. When the fast had been willingly and devoutly completed, the patriarch went to the seaport and, by God’s will, encountered what he had greatly desired.

For he saw four ships laden with men approaching the shore from afar and, from the saving sign of the cross which he observed upon their dress, recognized that they were Christians. Rejoicing, [Col. 0962A] he waited for them to put in at the harbour and reverently greeted them as they disembarked. When they had come out onto the open plain, he began to address them thus:

> Truly you are blessed and friends of God, for whom the heavenly court waits as participants in its blessedness. Behold, if steadfast faith burns within you, then without doubt the cause of martyrdom is offered to you, that cause for which the holy athletes of Christ—George and Theodore, Demetrius and Sebastian—laboured in battle against Satan and his followers, fought fiercely, conquered gloriously, and, triumphant, received an everlasting crown from the King of Hosts. I pray that a like fortune may attend you and that God may grant you no unequal reward. Behold, fierce Sanguin and the gentile army have lately invaded our lands. Having destroyed the army of Christ, they have stubbornly besieged the king of Jerusalem with a few men in a certain castle [Col. 0962B] and strive by many means to compel those shut in to surrender. But our countrymen, hoping in God, endeavour manfully to resist their assault; mindful of God’s wonders, they await His swift help, choosing in the Lord’s name rather to follow their companions through death than to be subjected in life, with disgrace, to the profane. You have heard enough of the situation. Since you are prudent and courageous men, you understand well what I desire and what must be done in such a matter.

When they heard this, all eagerly offered themselves against the pagans and desired with their whole strength to assist their besieged brethren. The joyful patriarch said:

> We give thanks to God, the most mighty *Adonai*, who ever deigns swiftly to raise up His own by consolation. Now therefore, you who have left your native soil for heavenly love, abandoned beloved wives and long-sought riches, and arrived here through many hardships by sea and land: take the examples of the saints and hold forth the shield of faith; steadfastly succour the sanctuary of God which you have sought from afar. The Lord is with you: He swiftly comforted the besieged in Bethulia through a woman. By the widow Judith He cut off the head of proud Holofernes; after crushing the Assyrians, He mercifully refreshed the thirsty people, enriched them with victory and countless spoils, and magnified them above all the nations round about. He also sent assurance through the prophet Isaiah to King Hezekiah, shut up in Jerusalem, [Col. 0962D] and on the following night destroyed one hundred and eighty-five thousand Assyrians through an angel; after his blasphemies and savage threats, He put the haughty King Sennacherib to shameful flight.

> Consider these and many other similar things in the works of God, and, trusting in God’s power, undertake the contest.

With these salutary admonitions the bishop instructed the Christian company and led the armed men against the Turkish ranks. The scouts of the pagans saw a great army coming from the sea and immediately reported it to their prince. He sent quick and eloquent envoys to meet them and diligently asked through them who they were and where they were going. They answered: “We are Christians. [Col. 0963A] We desire with all our strength to aid our brethren whom we have heard are besieged by pagans. We also ardently desire to avenge in battle those others who have already been killed.” The reply was given that they should remain quietly where they were for the present and be ready for battle on the third day.

Meanwhile the crafty Sanguin summoned King Fulk to a conference and, amid many sly evasions, said to him:

> I pity your nobility greatly, and because you are a king I desire, if you wish, to spare you. I know very well your circumstances and the failure of your strength. The distress of hunger grievously oppresses you together with all those enclosed with you, and you expect assistance from no quarter. Therefore make peace with me. Surrender the castle to me with all who are within it, and I will allow you to go free.

Fulk answered:

> [Col. 0963B] Far be it from me to become the betrayer of my brethren. I will by no means do this; rather, I shall persevere with them until death and patiently await the end of the struggle.

Sanguin said:

> Consult with your men and take counsel advantageous to yourself and them. I shall spare you because you are a king and ought to be honoured. Surrender the castle and all the captives from our people whom you hold; receive all those of your people whom we have, and then depart gladly with all your men under a peace secured by oath.

Hearing this, Fulk returned to his men, told them all that he had heard from the tyrant, and asked what ought to be done in circumstances so constrained. Not knowing that help was near, they anxiously gave quick counsel. They urged that the tower be surrendered for the rescue of the Christians, that the town of Mont-Royal be opened to the Damascenes, [Col. 0963C] lest the besieged incur the danger of death and the holy city of Jerusalem lie open, without a defender, to the mockery of the gentiles. Thus King Fulk, terrified, agreed to his men’s counsel and made with the heathen the peace they had demanded, confirmed by oath. Sanguin received the garrison and his nephew, whom they had captured; he likewise restored to the Christians those of their men who were in bonds, as had been agreed. Then the tyrant, triumphing and mocking, said to Fulk: “You have been deceived, king,” and pointed out the Christian camp which had come to its aid. Yet although the faithful were sorrowful over this trick, the decision could not be altered. When safe-conduct had indeed been granted, the king, patriarch, and faithful men met from [Col. 0963D] both sides and asked the tyrant to permit them to bury their brethren killed in the battle. With his assent, they sought out the bodies of the slain and honourably buried those they found. When they wished to remove the golden rings from their fingers, they could not. Therefore the living devoutly praised almighty God and reverently buried Christ’s martyrs with their ornaments.

### XVI. Emperor John of Constantinople seeks to obtain the city of Antioch. Raymond, prince of Antioch, voluntarily becomes the vassal of Emperor John.

At the same time, when the Jerusalemites were mournfully afflicted by the heathen, as has been said, [Col. 0964A] and Raymond, prince of Antioch, with other valiant knights, hastened to assist them upon learning of their brethren’s need, John, emperor of Constantinople, gathered a huge army from all his extensive dominions and besieged Antioch, the metropolitan city of Syria, claiming that it belonged to his empire.

The aforesaid Raymond, who then held the principality, was the son of William, duke of the Poitevins. After King Henry’s death he went to the eastern lands and married the daughter of the younger Bohemond, given to him by favour of his cousin Fulk. By God’s grant he acquired the broad principality in Syria. While, as I have said, he was hastening to assist the king of Jerusalem against the pagans, he heard on that journey that the emperor had arrived to besiege the city. Troubled by so great a tempest, [Col. 0964B] he immediately returned with his companies of companions and hastened to aid his own people, who were trembling and shut up in the city without a protector. When he had approached the city and was anxiously afraid that he could neither break through the surrounding army nor enter the city, he began to deliberate with his men about the pressing situation. One of them, whom I consider truly high-spirited, said to him:

> It is well known that the Greeks excel in prudence and surpass other nations in eloquence, but lack boldness and courage in difficult affairs. Therefore, my worthy fellow-knights and proven champions, if you deem it fitting to follow my counsel, take up your arms bravely. Armed as though you belonged to the imperial companies, go silently as far as the tent of Augustus himself [Col. 0964C] and penetrate the Ionian legions. Then shout terribly near the emperor’s ears and boldly make known who you are.

Hearing this, the others were encouraged for the difficult undertaking and at night admirably followed the high-spirited knight’s advice. The Franks reached the imperial tent, shouted, and began to strike those who opposed them. The emperor’s army, unsuspecting, unexpectedly heard the sudden cries of the fierce Franks and, exceedingly terrified, confused, and without counsel, took flight. Leaving everything behind, it fled for three miles, as though it saw a sword hanging over its necks. [Col. 0964D] But Duke Raymond stood fast while the Pelasgians fled with their emperor. He did not wish to pursue countless men for long with only a few followers; instead, putting a limit to his rejoicing, he entered his city and, by God’s gift, brought great joy to the Antiochenes. At sunrise the citizens came out, found great riches in the tents and storehouses, eagerly plundered them, and joyfully carried the spoils into the city. The emperor, wearied by flight, rested with his men. Ashamed and angry, he asked who had put him to flight; recognizing the boldness of the Aquitanians and their successful exploit, he blushed. He assembled his army again and invited the aforesaid prince to a conference. The high-spirited hero who had earlier offered the counsel to fight again advised the duke not to reject the conference concerning peace, [Col. 0965A] saying that it was now honourable and very advantageous to negotiate peace.

Raymond agreed and went to the assembly. The emperor said to him:

> The city of Antioch belongs to the empire of Constantinople. Prince Bohemond did homage to my uncle and, together with the other magnates of the West, promised that, should he recover all that the Turks had taken, he would restore it to the sacred empire. I therefore demand this agreement from you, who now rule, and reclaim the city of our empire which you usurp.

Raymond replied:

> I do not wish to debate ancestral arrangements with you. I received this city from the king of Jerusalem with the daughter of its prince, and I promised him faith as my lord. I shall therefore lay your arguments before him and obey his decisions in all things; I shall make no determination in this matter without his counsel.

[Col. 0965B] When this had been said, the emperor approved Raymond’s keeping faith with his lord. He granted a truce so that Raymond might consult the aforesaid king and lawfully ascertain from him what ought to be done. When this embassy had been sent to the king, who was then ill, he disclosed the matter to his close friends and replied:

> We all know well, as we have long learned from our elders, that Antioch belongs to the empire of Constantinople and was withdrawn from Augustus and subjected to the Turks only fourteen years ago. The emperor’s remaining assertions concerning the agreements of our predecessors are true. We ought not deny truth or resist what is right—certainly not when I am held by a grave illness. Therefore [Col. 0965C] I cannot aid my kinsman. For owing to the heat, cares, and labours which I have endured, and the poor food which I unhappily ate while recently shut up in Mont-Royal, I have contracted a deadly illness together with my companions. Therefore I am now prevented from giving aid in battle to my cousin. Recognize our excuse, then, go, and tell your lord on my behalf to make peace with the emperor; by my command, let him receive from the emperor the city that belongs by right to the emperor and hold it lawfully. For the emperor is a Christian, of great power, and honoured by the Franks. If he wishes, he is very able to help them.

The returning envoys duly delivered the response, and the two princes confirmed between themselves a peace advantageous to pilgrims and to all believers in Christ dwelling [Col. 0965D] in Greece or Syria. Raymond therefore became the emperor’s man and received Antioch from him; the emperor promised him friendship and assistance against Damascus and all the gentiles. Thus this war, which had continued ruinously for almost forty years, had arisen and been waged against Alexius by the Bohemonds and their successors, and had brought bondage, destruction, and many losses upon countless thousands, now ceased, by God’s favour, under the princes Emperor John and Raymond of Poitiers, to the rejoicing of many on both sides.

### XVII. Various events in France, England, Apulia, and Normandy. The count of Anjou renews war against the king of England.

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1138, in the first indiction:

> **Note:** [Col. 0965D] Observe that Orderic begins the year from Christmas Day. (Dom Bouquet.)

Louis the Younger, king of the French, was crowned at Bourges on Christmas Day. There an immense court of nobles and men of lesser rank from all France, Aquitaine, and the neighbouring nations was assembled. Metropolitan bishops and their suffragans gathered there. Counts and other dignitaries flocked there and rendered their service to the new king.

Peter Anacletus, who had usurped the apostolic see for nearly seven years, died suddenly while seated in the chair on the eighth day before the Kalends of February. It is said that [Col. 0966B] his brothers—the sons of Peter Leo, who possess very great power in the city of Rome—concealed him so thoroughly that it is unknown where his body was buried. In the following month too, a report resounded far and wide that Roger, duke of Apulia, had died:

> **Note:** [Col. 0966D] A false report; it is certain that Roger died only in the year 1154, on 26 February. (Dom Bouquet.)

The aforesaid schismatic had consecrated him king of Sicily and, by giving him his sister, had enlisted him to disturb the rights of the Church. When Emperor Lothair heard of Roger’s supposed death, he hastened into Apulia and sought to subdue it to himself according to ancient custom and the established order of the Romans.

Stephen, when he had come to England and learned of the machinations of certain persons against the common welfare of the kingdom, was angered against the rebels, took up arms precipitately, and, while his brother Henry, bishop of Winchester, forbade it, besieged Bedford. There, with the winter rains setting in, he laboriously spent Christmas and achieved nothing. For the sons of Robert de Beauchamp held the stronghold stoutly and did not in any way submit to the king until the aforesaid bishop, his brother, was present. They had not determined to withhold the submission or service due to their lord; but, having heard that the king had given Simon de Beauchamp’s daughter, together with her father’s honour, to Hugh surnamed the Poor, they feared the loss of their entire inheritance and, on their friends’ counsel, offered stubborn resistance. At last they yielded to the bishop when he arrived after five weeks; by his counsel and assistance, which they considered advantageous, they made peace with the king and surrendered the town.

[Col. 0966D] In Normandy, Rainald de Dunstanville, the illegitimate son of King Henry, was disturbing the district of Cotentin; favouring his sister, he adhered to the Angevins. He also had with him Baldwin de Redvers, Stephen de Mandeville, and other enemies of King Stephen. But Roger the viscount opposed them vigorously and, protecting his country, resisted the hostile and perverse designs with distinction. At first he seemed exceedingly formidable to his enemies; but in the sea of this world no power endures long. His enemies, excessively envious of his prosperity, laid snares for him [Col. 0967A] and plotted his destruction. One day they sent out raiders to carry off plunder, while certain knights lay concealed in ambush, eager to shed blood. When the cry was raised, Roger and his men seized their arms; pursuing the robbers with their spoil, he fell into the hands of those lying in wait. They sprang from ambush like hungry lions, struck down the unsuspecting men, and mercilessly cut Roger’s throat, though he cried out for his life and promised much. Thus, when their ruler had been killed, the whole district was laid waste, and the frenzy of robbers, raging without restraint against the country people, became utterly unbridled.

In January Simon Rufus, Baldwin’s son, with the permission of Robert son of Geroy, entered the castle of Échauffour [Col. 0967B] and, having gathered a band of retainers around him, began to devastate the lands of Count Robert of Leicester in the diocese of Évreux. He was an exceptionally fierce knight, bold and ready with his hand, generous toward his fellow-soldiers and resolute in severe exertions; hence he was rash in difficult and savage enterprises. Once he had begun the devastation of the country, his brother Ribald joined him in the crime and received him into the fortress called Pont-Erchenfroi. But William Fraxinellus and his six brothers, Alan de Tannet, Ernald the count’s steward, and the townsmen of Glos rose up, burned Pont-Erchenfroi, the little monastery, and the surrounding villages. Such deadly fury seized both sides and drove them all into such wickedness that [Col. 0967C] they showed no reverence for holy places, spared neither religious persons nor innocent peasants and widows, and did not restrain their hands or their zeal for crime even during the holy days of Lent.

The two-year truce agreed between the king and Geoffrey of Anjou was violated in many ways. During Lent the countess’s retainers seized Ralph de Axon, a powerful man, and delivered him to their lady to be tightly bound. She held him for a long time and did not permit him to depart until he surrendered his fortresses. Conversely, Engelram de Soria and other royal men stubbornly encountered Rainald and Baldwin outside the castle of Ulmo (the Elm); fighting hand-to-hand, they captured Baldwin and many others. There, indeed, while the battle was at its height [Col. 0967D] and it was still uncertain to whom victory would fall, some kinsmen and friends of Viscount Roger, having found the place and time for vengeance, drew their swords against their own side, killed several of Roger’s slayers, and thus secured the triumph of victory for the opposing party. Behold, as the Lord says: “Whoever takes the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matthew 26:52). The frenzied company which a little earlier had cruelly butchered Roger, son of Nigel, was unexpectedly struck down among its own men by his friends.

[Col. 0968A] At the same time Theodoric, ruler of Flanders, gave his daughter in marriage to the son of King Stephen, resigned the entire duchy of Flanders, and then took up the Lord’s cross.

> [Note: [Col. 0967D] The Utica manuscript adds: “And he went to Jerusalem; returning from there, he trained in warfare the boy to whom he had promised his daughter.” Besides, this marriage of Theodoric’s daughter to King Stephen’s son appears fictitious. (Dom Bouquet.)]

In May Count Waleran and William of Ypres crossed to Normandy and attempted to assist the greatly troubled country. First they took up arms against Roger de Conches; but fortune changed, and they found him a warlike knight, prepared to resist them. Therefore they directed their fury against the country people; both sides rushed to plunder, devastated the district with fires and robberies, carried off necessary goods, and subjected the unarmed population to desolation.

Geoffrey of Anjou came to Normandy in June [Col. 0968B] with an armed force. By entreaties and promises he won Count Robert of Gloucester to his side; through him he brought Bayeux, Caen, and many towns of Normandy under his power. In England, moreover, many bishops and townsmen, hearing that the aforesaid count, whose power was great in both realms, was supporting the Angevins, brought forth the malice they had concealed within themselves and rebelled against the king.

In July Count Waleran and William of Ypres, grieved that their enemies had prevailed through domestic treachery and had now for the most part trampled underfoot the Normans, who in foreign lands had overcome foreign enemies, summoned Ralph de Perronne with two hundred knights to assist them. Calling together other [Col. 0968C] auxiliaries from every side, they resolved to march against the Angevins. But Robert de Courcy immediately sent word to Count Geoffrey and revealed to him the scheme of his own party, advising him to leave Normandy quickly and await a more favourable opportunity. Hearing this, Geoffrey at once withdrew fearfully with his men. The assembled multitude of his adversaries was greatly distressed that the enemy army had escaped by a sudden departure. Yet, lest a thousand knights should appear to have assembled in vain and return home without any exploit, they went to Caen, laid waste the district on every side, and attempted to draw the garrison out of the fortress. But Count Robert greatly feared the factions of both parties and therefore cleverly concealed himself inside with a hundred knights. [Col. 0968D] Only forty horsemen came out, met the enemy on a narrow path above the Orne, and the two sides fought with extreme ferocity. There Robert Bertran and John de Jorra, noble and handsome knights, were killed, and many men on each side were wounded; many grieved at their sad misfortune.

The aforesaid Count of Gloucester, through whom the occasion of great disturbance had arisen, possessed power in England through the gift of his father King Henry and flourished in wealth, towns, and fierce men. For [Col. 0969A] he held the fortress of Gloucester and Canterbury, and also possessed the very strongly fortified towns of Brighton, Lyds, and Dover.

> [Note: [Col. 0969B] In the name of his wife, who had succeeded Robert son of Haimon, Robert possessed the earldom of Gloucester, as is evident from the following genealogy:
>
> “This Lord Robert took as his wife Sibyl, sister of Robert de Belesme, earl of Shrewsbury, and begot by her four daughters: Mabel, Hawise, Cecily, and Amice … This venerable Robert, son of Haimon, after founding this famous monastery [of Cranborne] and accomplishing other deeds vigorously, paid the debt of death in the month of March, in the year 1117 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the seventh year of King Henry the First, and passed to the heavenly realms … But King Henry the First, after the death of Robert son of Haimon, unwilling that so great and distinguished a lordship—namely, the honour of Gloucester—should be divided among the sisters, caused Cecily and Hawise to be made abbesses, Cecily at Shaftesbury and Hawise at Winchester. He gave the third, Amice, in marriage to the count of Brittany, reserving only the eldest, Mabel, whom he gave in marriage to his illegitimate son Robert, together with the entire honour of her father, the said Robert son of Haimon, [Col. 0969D] creating him earl and count of Gloucester after the first Conquest …
>
> “This illustrious count died in the year of the Lord 1147, on the day before the Kalends of November, and in the twelfth year of King Stephen … He was succeeded by his son and heir, Count William, who, having taken as wife Hawise, daughter of the count of Leicester, begot by her Robert, who was forestalled by death before his father … He also begot three daughters: namely, the eldest, Mabel, married to the count of Évreux in Normandy; from her was born Amalric, who possessed the earldom of Gloucester briefly after Isabella’s death in King John’s time, but soon died without children. He begot another daughter named Amice, whom he gave in marriage to Lord Richard de Clare, earl of Hertford. He also had a third daughter named Isabella. Yet after her father’s death King Henry II retained the honour of Gloucester in his own hands for six years. In the final year of his reign, he gave Isabella, daughter of the said Count William, to his son John [Col. 0970B] (called Lackland) in marriage, with the entire honour [Col. 0970C] of the whole earldom of Gloucester; John held that honour throughout the reign of his brother King Richard … and, after the death of his father and brother, was elected king. But because he had no children by Isabella, their marriage was dissolved after one year; nevertheless, he retained the honour of Gloucester for himself, etc. He gave Isabella in marriage to Geoffrey de Mandeville, earl of Essex, together with the earldom of Gloucester. After Geoffrey’s removal by death, the aforesaid Isabella, during the same king’s reign, when King Louis of France had occupied England, was, with the king’s assent, married to Hubert de Burgh, justiciar of England; but she too died shortly thereafter. The noble Count William of Gloucester died in 1173 … Robert, his son, was born at Cardiff and died there in the year of the Lord 1176 … Thus, when Count William’s two daughters had died without children, the inheritance passed to Amice, daughter of Count William and wife of Richard de Clare. She gave her entire inheritance to Gilbert [Col. 0970D] her son by the said Richard. Richard died in the year of the Lord 1206 and was buried at Clare, etc.” (*Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 155). (Dom Bouquet.)]

Consequently, many who favoured him offended the king by rebelling; driven by frenzy, they disturbed the neighbouring provinces and ravaged them in many ways. First Geoffrey, surnamed Talbot, seized the city of Hereford and, gathering criminal accomplices there for wickedness, rebelled against the king. Walchelin, surnamed Maminot, held Dover; Robert, son of Alured of Lincoln, held the castles of Warham and Moreton; Walchelin held Uckham; William de Moun held Devizes; and the young William surnamed Puerellus held four towns—namely Brampton, Ellesmere, Overton, and Whittington—and, puffed up by these, enlarged [Col. 0969B] the band of rebels. Ralph Lupellus held the fortress called Cary. William, son of John, fortified Harptree and, joining himself to other rebels, strove to disturb his native land. Moreover David, king of Scotland, either because of the deceitful invitation of factional men, by whom he had been provoked to his country’s harm, or because of the oath which, at King Henry’s command, he had already sworn to his niece, assisted the destructive disturbers of the kingdom in favour of the Angevins. He held the very strong town of Carlisle (Carduilum), which, they say, Julius Caesar founded, and stationed there a most ferocious force of Scots. They cruelly invaded England [Col. 0970A] and attacked the neighbouring peoples in war, exercising their barbarity upon them in a bestial manner. They spared no one, but killed young and old alike; they also slew pregnant women by ripping open their wombs with the savage sword.

## XVIII. King Stephen suppresses and punishes rebellions

King Stephen employed the sharp sword against so many insurgents, and by gifts, promises, or the strong hand of fighting men brought his enemies under his control. He made Robert de Stuteville, an upright and very litigious knight, earl of Derby, and raised Gilbert de Clare to be earl of Pembroke; through them he won over Walchelin Maminot, Lupellus, and many others who were their friends or kinsmen. Since, as I have said, very many were rebelling, the spirited king was moved to anger and attempted with three armies to storm the enemy strongholds. First he besieged the city of Hereford, which lay on the river Wye, on the border between the English and the Welsh. Received gratefully by the citizens and inhabitants as their natural lord, he took the town; having put Geoffrey Talbot to flight, he mercifully spared the others within. The queen, meanwhile, besieged Dover by land with a strong force and ordered the men of Boulogne, her friends, kinsmen, and dependants, to restrain the enemy by sea.

> [Note: [Col. 0970D] The wife of this pious King Stephen was the most noble Lady Matilda, daughter of the vigorous Count Eustace of Boulogne, born of Mary, daughter of Christina, sister of Margaret, queen of the Scots. These two, namely Margaret and Christina, were sisters of Edgar Ætheling, kinsman of Saint Edward, king and confessor. William, count of Warenne and Boulogne, was the son of the said King Stephen and his wife Matilda. The said Queen Margaret bore her husband King Malcolm of the Scots six sons and two daughters: namely Matilda, who married King Henry I and bore Matilda, who first married the emperor and afterwards Geoffrey, count of Anjou, by whom she conceived King Henry II; and Mary, of whom mention has been made above. (*Monasticon Anglicanum*, vol. I, p. 706). (Dom Bouquet.)]

The men of Boulogne gladly embraced their lady’s commands, [Col. 0971A] rendered her their service, and covered the narrow strait with a multitude of ships, lest the garrison might obtain any assistance. Meanwhile Robert de Ferrières, whom the king, as stated, had appointed earl of Derby, spoke with his son-in-law Walchelin, made peace between him and the king, and brought the aforesaid fortress under the king’s authority. Gilbert de Clare besieged the castle of Exceedes and pressed the townsmen until they surrendered.

William son of Alan, burgess and sheriff of Shrewsbury, who was married to the niece of Count Robert of Gloucester, wished to support him, rebelled against the king, and held the aforesaid city against him for almost a month. At last, defeated by royal power in August, he fled, and the king subdued the fortress by a strong assault. Arnulf de Hesdin, uncle of the aforesaid young man, a warlike and rash knight, repeatedly arrogantly rejected peace offered by the king, moreover presumed to hurl insulting words at him, and compelled others who wished to surrender to persist stubbornly in rebellion. Finally, when the fortress had been taken, he was captured with many others and brought before the prince whom he had despised. Since the king, because of his mildness, seemed contemptible to the defiant, and many nobles summoned to his court disdained to come, he angrily ordered Arnulf and nearly ninety-three others who had resisted to be hanged on the gallows [Col. 0971B] and others to be swiftly punished by different forms of death. Arnulf, though repenting too late, and many others begged the king for themselves and promised a large sum [Col. 0971C] of money for their ransom. But when the king set the price of vengeance at many weights of gold, they were immediately put to death. Their puffed-up accomplices, hearing of the king’s severity, were exceedingly frightened; trembling, they hurried to the king within three days and invented various excuses for having delayed so long. Some even brought the keys of their fortresses and humbly offered their service to the king. When the seditious deserters had been somewhat restrained, the lovers of peace rejoiced.

## XIX. Peace between the kings of England and Scotland. Wars in Normandy. Angevin ravaging

That same week a like fortune smiled upon King Stephen in another part of the kingdom. For the count of Aumale [Col. 0971D] and Roger de Mowbray fought against the king of Scotland and, after killing a multitude of Scots, put the king to flight. They avenged the savage slaughter which the Scots had previously inflicted upon the English without any regard for the Christian religion.

> [Note: [Col. 0971D] This is the battle called by English writers the most famous Battle of the Standard. (Dom Bouquet.)]

The Scots, fearing the threatening sword, fled to the water and rushed without a ford into the great river called the Zeda; fleeing death, they were at once swallowed by death. After the long war of the two kings, fiercely waged by both to the injury of many, envoys of peace were divinely raised up. They travelled between the two kings, now exhausted by losses, killings, continual cares, and labours, and brought them back to concord. Henry, son of David king of Scotland, approved this friendship, loved Adelina, daughter of William, count of Surrey, and sought her in marriage. Bound by such a tie, he adhered wholeheartedly to the friendship of the Normans and English, perceiving on the counsel of wise men that this would be wholesome and very advantageous for himself and his people.

Meanwhile the Normans raged within their mother’s bosom, and acts of wickedness were perpetrated everywhere. On the seventh day of September Roger of Tosny assembled a distinguished body of knights and, striving to avenge many injuries formerly done to him, stormed Breteuil. He had with him Count Baldwin IV of Hainaut [Col. 0972B] with eighty knights, Peter de Maule with forty, Simon Rufus with twenty, and a strong troop which he himself had gathered from all his dominions. The ardent Roger, surrounded by this notable company, unexpectedly attacked the town; setting it on fire, he inflicted enormous damage upon the unprepared townsmen. Threshers were cutting the harvest in the streets, and great heaps of straw and chaff lay scattered before the houses, as autumn requires; from these the flames readily took their welcome nourishment. Thus the prosperous town was burned in an instant. The church of Saint Sulpicius, bishop and confessor, was also burned, alas, with much property of the townsmen and with people who were inside it. When the castle’s knights saw that they had been forestalled by the enemy, many fled toward the stronghold and were overtaken by the enemy’s sword. In the same year peace was made between Roger and the brother counts—

> [Note: [Col. 0972D] That is, the twins: Waleran, count of Meulan, and Robert, count of Leicester and Breteuil. (Dom Bouquet.)]

—who also brought him to King Stephen in England, where he was honourably reconciled with him.

On the Kalends of October, Geoffrey of Anjou besieged Falaise. He laboured there much but vainly for eighteen days and departed on the nineteenth day without gaining anything. Richard de Lucy, leader of the knights, was in the town and stoutly defended the fortification with its inhabitants. With the gates thrown open, the besieged daily mocked the besiegers by their boldness; shut in with an abundance of food and weapons, they defiantly challenged them to assault [Col. 0972D] as a jest. The enemy, however, ravaged the surrounding countryside, irreverently entered churches, took sacred vestments and vessels without fear of God, polluted holy places, spared no one, and plundered the possessions of the common people and whatever else they could seize. At last, terrified by God, they fled by night, leaving behind tents with clothing and weapons, as well as wagons laden with bread, wine, and other necessary things. The townsmen rejoiced in these and became very rich. But ten days later the count of the Angevins unexpectedly returned and, ranging about Falaise with many [Col. 0973A] thousands, plundered the goods of those returning and resting securely, inflicted enormous damage on Normandy by slaughter and robbery, and did not cease from his deadly operations for three weeks.

At the beginning of November he came to Touques, found a wealthy borough there, and greatly desired to storm the neighbouring fortress of Bonneville on the next day. Then the enemy found large but empty houses in the aforesaid town, where, exulting, they rashly lodged and prepared splendid feasts for themselves. Meanwhile, in the depth of night, while the hostile force rested securely in separate houses, William, surnamed Trossebot, the defender of Bonneville, cleverly forestalled the enemy’s rashness. He rallied the townsmen assembled with him to great deeds by an urgent exhortation, sent contemptible boys and prostitutes into Touques [Col. 0973B], and carefully instructed them what to do according to a well-considered plan. As instructed, they secretly dispersed through the borough and boldly set fire in four quarters of the town, at forty-five places. The Angevins had already entered the town and had taken their hosts sitting in their own homes and chairs. Awakened by the great roar of flames and the shouting of the watch, they were greatly frightened and fled, abandoning arms, horses, and many other necessary things. The aforesaid William, armed with his men, came out to meet the enemy; but the thickness of the smoke darkened everything, so that they could neither see nor recognize one another. At last the troubled count halted in a cemetery, [Col. 0973C] gathered his men there, and, confused and alarmed, waited for daylight. At dawn he fled as quickly as possible and, having experienced something of Norman audacity, came to Argentan not without disgrace. The weak common people of Normandy trembled in sorrow and, lacking a defender, invoked the aid of the Most High. The leading men of the people engaged in deceitful and malicious feuds; many treacherously favoured the enemy and did not defend their own people, but oppressed them after taking away their goods and wickedly preyed upon them.

At that time Theobald, abbot of Bec, was raised to govern the metropolitan see of Canterbury in England; and Letald, a monk of good life, was appointed in his place to govern the church of Bec.

## XX. Roman council. Audin, bishop of Évreux. Deeds of the bishops of Salisbury and Ely. Matilda, countess of Anjou, crosses to England. Various events

In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1139, in the second indiction, [Col. 0974A] Pope Innocent II held a great council at Rome in mid-Lent and commanded the assembled multitude of prelates to observe inviolate the statutes of the holy Fathers. Men summoned from many lands had come to the synod and, for this purpose, undertaken a dangerous journey in winter; thus, at great loss of their possessions, they had seen the walls of Rome. The pope disclosed to them much from ancient books and compiled an eminent body of sacred decrees. But the excessively abundant wickedness of men throughout the world hardened their hearts against ecclesiastical ordinances. Therefore, when the teachers returned home, apostolic decrees were published throughout the kingdoms. Yet, as is manifest, they brought no benefit to the oppressed and to those desiring assistance, because princes and [Col. 0974B] magnates of kingdoms, together with their subject peoples, held them in little regard.

Audin, bishop of Évreux, travelled to England in Easter week and died and was buried there at Milton, in the community of canons, on the sixth day before the Nones of July. Born in the district of Bayeux, he pursued literary studies and, trained in the liberal arts, became one of the most learned men. Having become familiar to King Henry, he pleased him among his chief clerks.

Then, advanced from the king’s chapel, he held the diocese of Évreux for twenty-four years, instructed the clergy and subject people in observing God’s law, diligently promoted the worship of the Church, and restored from its foundations the basilica of the Blessed Mary, Mother of God, which had been burned [Col. 0974C] at that time. Rotrou, son of Henry, count of Warwick, archdeacon of Rouen, was elevated to the bishopric of Évreux and consecrated by Lord Hugh, archbishop of Rouen. In the same year, I believe, Thurstan, archbishop of York and brother of the aforesaid Audin, died.

> [Note: [Col. 0973D] When Thurstan perceived that the end of his life was at hand, he laid aside his mitre and went to the Cluniac monastery of Pontefract in England. On the feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul, says John, prior of Hexham, he solemnly received the monastic habit and blessing; throughout the remaining days of his life he was not negligent concerning his soul’s salvation. Therefore, continues the same writer, in the year 1140 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the seventy-fifth from the coming of the Normans into England, and the twenty-sixth year and sixth month of his archiepiscopate, on the eighth day before the Ides of February, Thursday … he rendered up his spirit. These chronological indications, adopted from those English writers, denote the following year as beginning on the Kalends of January, in which year the eighth day before the Ides of February did in fact fall on a Thursday, and the seventy-fifth year from the Normans’ entry into England, and the twenty-seventh of Thurstan’s pontificate, were then in progress. (Dom Bouquet.)]

At the same time a great disturbance arose in England. Roger, bishop of Salisbury, relied greatly upon wealth, powerful friends, and fortresses; since he had presided over all England throughout King Henry’s life, he was accused above all the magnates of the realm of being unfaithful to his king and lord and of favouring the Angevin party. He was supported also by indispensable accomplices: namely, his son, who was the king’s chancellor, and his very powerful nephews, one bishop of Lincoln and the other of Ely.

Moreover, from the abundance of their many riches, such exalted men possessed great boldness and presumptuously troubled neighbouring magnates with various attacks. [Col. 0975A] Therefore many, agitated by furious stings, conspired against them; having seized an occasion, they rose together and attempted to repay them in kind for the disturbances inflicted. The two brothers, Counts Waleran and Robert, Alan de Dinan, and many others began a sedition at Oxford against the household of the bishops. After many had been killed on both sides, Bishops Roger and Alexander were captured. But the bishop of Ely, who had not yet come to the king’s court, but had lodged outside the city in a village with his attendants, heard the dire rumours. Since he was conscious of guilt, he suddenly fled to the very strong town of Devizes; assembling the surrounding district, he occupied the fortress in advance and resolved to fortify it against the king with all his strength. [Col. 0975B] Hearing this, the angry king advanced with an army and sent William of Ypres ahead with many threats, swearing that Bishop Roger should eat nothing until the hostile stronghold was surrendered to him. He also seized Roger, the bishop’s son, surnamed the Poor, and ordered him to be hanged before the gate in sight of the rebels. His mother Matilda of Ramsbury—the bishop’s concubine—was holding the principal fortress.

At last the bishop of Salisbury, having obtained the king’s permission, spoke with his nephew and severely rebuked him because, seeing sedition arise, he had not returned to his own diocese but had rushed madly into others’ affairs and, by a raging conflagration, caused hunger to many thousands. Since the arrogant nephew [Col. 0975C] persisted stubbornly in rebellion with his followers, and the angry king ordered that the aforesaid Roger be promptly hanged on the gallows, the fearful mother, hearing her child’s grievous plight, came forth and said, anxious for her son: “I gave him birth, and I must by no means deserve his death; but if this is necessary, I ought to save him through my own death.” She immediately sent a messenger to the king and offered the strong fortress which she held as the ransom of her friends. Thus the bishop of Ely, broken in spirit, sorrowfully accepted surrender with his remaining accomplices. Finally, when all had been reconciled, the town was surrendered to the king and the bishops returned peacefully to their dioceses. Not long afterwards Bishop Roger died, and the bishop of Ely became a public enemy of the whole country [Col. 0975D].

In autumn Matilda, countess of the Angevins, crossed to England with her brother Robert of Caen, Guy of Sablé, and many others. Having been received at Arundel by the king’s permission, she proceeded peacefully to the towns favouring her party. In this permission one may note the king’s great simplicity—or negligence—and prudent men ought to lament that he was forgetful of his own safety and the security of his kingdom. For he could easily then have extinguished a great fuel of excessive wickedness, had he imitated the cunning of the wise and expelled the wolf at once from entering the sheepfold; had he saved the sheep, forestalled malignant wickedness at its very beginning, and, in the manner of his forefathers, cut off with the sword of justice the deadly forces upon the heads of those who sought robberies, killings of men, [Col. 0976A] and the devastation of their country.

In November Count Rotrou of Mortain, hired for a price, came to Pont-Erchenfroi. Since eight ordinary knights inside, who were dying of hunger, surrendered, he recovered the fortress, allowed the wretched garrison to depart, and entrusted the town to Roger de Platanis. Then Ribald, Simon Rufus, and the other nephews of Ralph Rufus were swiftly expelled and suddenly lost control of the castle which they had hitherto held.

Robert of Caen lodged his sister Matilda, now received into England, in his residences. With Welshmen summoned to assist him, excessive wickedness was multiplied everywhere. For more than ten [Col. 0976B] thousand barbarians, it is said, were scattered throughout England. They spared neither holy places nor the reverence due to religion, but continually pursued robbery, arson, and the slaughter of men. I cannot relate individually how great was the affliction suffered by God’s Church in her children, who were daily butchered like cattle by the swords of the Britons.

In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1140, in the third indiction, King Stephen convened a council and sought to deliberate with his magnates on the condition of the commonwealth. Then a dispute arose among the magnates concerning the appointment of the bishop of Salisbury. Henry, bishop of Winchester, wished to install his nephew Henry de Sully; but, unable to prevail against stronger opposition, he angrily left the king’s court. [Col. 0976C] For Count Waleran of Meulan had chosen Philip de Harcourt, archdeacon of Évreux, and the king readily agreed to him for several reasons. He granted the aforesaid young man the monastery of Fécamp, in which great religious devotion had flourished in the time of the four preceding abbots.

In the same year Richard, abbot of Ouche, after returning from the Roman council, crossed promptly to England after Christmas, compelled by circumstances. Worn out by many labours, he fell ill with fever in Lent. Greatly afflicted by it for many days, he fortified himself well with confession and prayer; after Easter he took a draught from the physicians, but overcome by its excessive strength, he died on the seventh day of May. [Col. 0976D] Thus, in the third year of his rule, he died on the Ides of May, in England, was carried to Torvay, and was buried before the crucifix in the church of Saint Mary by Lord Robert, abbot of that same monastery. When the monks of Ouche heard this, they assembled together and elected as abbot Ranulf, prior of Nogent, who had already lived honourably in monastic life for forty years. The brother-elect crossed to England with letters from Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, and John, bishop of Lisieux, concerning the brothers’ unanimous election. Having seen the pontifical letters, King Stephen granted him the abbey and confirmed its ecclesiastical possessions. On returning from England, he approached Bishop John with royal letters and, graciously received by the venerable bishop, received his paternal blessing on the eighth day before the Ides of November [Col. 0977A].

## XXI. Disturbances and rebellions in England. King Stephen captured in England by the Angevins

In the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1141, in the fourth indiction, a great disturbance arose in the kingdom of the English, followed by a sudden reversal to the injury of many.

Rannulf, Count of Chester, and William de Roumare, his uterine brother, rebelled against King Stephen and treacherously seized the castle which he possessed at Lincoln for the defence of the city. For they had shrewdly observed the time when the servants of the tower were scattered in different directions, and then had sent their wives ahead to the castle, ostensibly for amusement. At length, while the two countesses were staying there and playing and conversing with the wife of the knight who was to guard the tower, the Count of Chester followed, unarmed and without a cloak, as though to fetch his wife, accompanied by three knights; and no one suspected any evil. Having thus entered, they suddenly seized the bars and such weapons as were there, and violently expelled the king’s guards. Then William and armed knights with him entered, as had previously been arranged. Thus the two brothers brought the tower and the whole city under their control.

Bishop Alexander and the citizens reported the event to the king. On hearing it, the king was greatly angered and wondered that his closest friends, whom he had advanced to great honours and dignities, had committed so great a crime. Then, after the Nativity of the Lord, he assembled an army, hastened immediately to Lincoln, and, with the help of the citizens, unexpectedly captured by night nearly seventeen knights who were stationed in the city. But the two counts were in the castle with their wives and household friends; suddenly surrounded, they anxiously did not know what to do. At last Rannulf, who was the younger, more impulsive, and most daring, went out by night with a few men and made his way to his own people in the county of Chester. He laid his complaint before his father-in-law Robert, Count of Gloucester, and his other friends and kinsmen; he stirred up the Welsh and other disinherited men against the king, and gathered forces from every quarter to assist those shut up under siege. Above all he sought out Matilda, Countess of the Angevins, earnestly requested her aid, pledged his allegiance to her, and obtained her favour as he wished. Therefore, with a mass of armed men assembled, the two counts, of Chester and Gloucester, approached the siege and prepared to fight their opponents. The king, however, hearing daily reports of the enemies’ approach, made little of them and did not believe that they were such men as would undertake so bold an attempt; meanwhile, he compelled those in the castle, who begged for his mercy, to be attacked with engines of siege.

At length, on Sexagesima Sunday, while the holy solemnity of the Lord’s Hypapante [Presentation] was being celebrated, and the king himself saw that the enemy battle-lines were already present, he summoned his nobles and asked their advice as to what he should do. [Col. 0978A] Some accordingly urged him to station a strong body of troops with the loyal citizens to defend the city, while he himself should withdraw honourably in order to assemble an army from all the regions of England, and should return at a suitable time, if the enemy remained there, to attack them with royal severity. Others also advised that the reverence due to the holy Purification of St Mary, Mother of God, should be observed, and that the time of battle should suitably be delayed while messengers of peace went between the parties, so that, with a postponement interposed, neither side might be defeated and human blood might not be shed to the grief of many. But the obstinate prince disdained to heed prudent counsel, considered it unworthy to defer battle for any reason, and immediately ordered his men to arm for war.

The battle-lines of the combatants therefore met near the city, and, troops being drawn up on both sides, they joined battle. The king formed three divisions for himself, and the opposing side likewise arranged three. In the first line of the royal army were Flemings and Bretons, commanded by William of Ypres and Alan of Dinan; opposed to them stood the frenzied host of Welshmen, commanded by the two brothers Mariadoth and Kaladrius. The king himself dismounted with certain men and fought bravely for his life and the state of his kingdom. Count Rannulf, on the other side, likewise dismounted with his men and greatly encouraged the valiant legion of Chester foot-soldiers to make slaughter. Robert, Count of Gloucester, who was the greatest figure in that expedition, ordered the Bassians and other disinherited men to strike the blow of battle for the recovery of the inheritances which they claimed.

At first the fighting on both sides was exceedingly fierce, and much human blood was shed. The king’s battle-line contained distinguished knights, but the enemy prevailed through their excessive multitude of infantry and Welshmen. William of Ypres with the Flemings, and Alan with the Bretons, were indeed the first to flee, making the enemy more courageous and their own allies more fearful. In that conflict treachery raged wickedly; for certain magnates accompanied the king with a few of their own men, while sending a troop of their retainers ahead to the enemy, so that the latter might prevail. Thus they broke faith with their lord and may deservedly be judged perjurers and traitors. When Count Waleran and his brother William de Warenne, Gilbert de Clare, and other eminent Norman and English knights saw the first division flee, they too took fright and fled. But Baldwin de Clare, Richard son of Urse, Enguerrand de Say, and Ilbert de Lacy remained loyally attached to the fighting king and fought manfully with him until the end. King Stephen, mindful of the brave deeds of his predecessors, fought boldly; and as long as he had three champions fighting with him, he did not cease to fight with sword or with a Norwegian axe, which a certain young man there had handed him. At last, weary and abandoned by all, [Col. 0979A] he surrendered himself to his cousin Count Robert, was captured, and shortly afterwards was presented by him to Countess Matilda. Thus, thus, as Fortune’s whirling wheel turned, he was hurled from the throne of the kingdom and, groaning and miserable—alas!—imprisoned in the great fortress of Bristol. Baldwin de Clare and the other distinguished young knights whom I have said dismounted with the king and fought conspicuously were captured.

On the preceding night, while the people of God celebrated vigils in honour of the Virgin Mother and awaited the general assembly of Matins to be solemnized according to ecclesiastical rite, in the western regions—that is, in Gaul and Brittany—there was a violent fall of hail and rain, and with tremendous flashes of lightning a dreadful roaring of thunder was heard. On the very day, while the king, about to fight, was hearing Mass and was inwardly troubled, I believe, by many thoughts and anxieties, a blessed candle broke in his hand and, as many watched, fell three times. To certain interpreters this appeared plainly an unlucky omen, and on that same day it was manifestly fulfilled in the ruler’s fall.

## XXII. Various Events after the Capture of King Stephen. End of This Work. Pious Meditations

The king’s misfortune produced grief among clerics, monks, and simple people, because the king himself was humble and gentle toward the good and mild; and, if deceitful magnates had allowed it by abandoning their evil designs, he would have been a generous and kindly protector of his country. But the citizens of Lincoln, who had supported the king, their lord, as they ought, as soon as they heard that victory had fallen to his adversaries, abandoned in despair their houses and wives with all their possessions and fled to the neighbouring river, seeking safety in exile. When they suddenly crowded together at the boats, filled the vessels by their excessive numbers, behaved disorderly in terror of death, and those behind rushed violently upon those before them, the little boats immediately capsized. Almost all who had embarked perished—according to some, nearly five hundred noble citizens. Not so many fell in the military engagement. A certain renowned William, a *optio* [officer] on the king’s side, was killed; he was a nephew of Geoffrey, Archbishop of Rouen. Of the others, according to those who were present, not more than one hundred died.

Count Rannulf and the other victors then entered the city, plundered it all like barbarians, and slaughtered the remaining citizens whom they could find or capture, like cattle, by various forms of death and without any regard for pity.

Once the battle had been fought and the king captured, a great division arose in the kingdom of the English. Henry, Bishop of Winchester, immediately turned to the Angevins; after the countess had been favourably received in the royal city, he utterly abandoned his brother the king and all who were on his side. Count Waleran, William de Warenne, Simon, and many others, however, adhered to the queen and promised that they would fight bravely for the king and his heirs. Thus wickedness multiplied greatly and everywhere on both sides, and England was filled with robbery, arson, and the slaughter of men; that land which had once been most rich and abundant was now miserably laid waste.

When Geoffrey, Count of Anjou, heard that his wife had prevailed, he immediately came into Normandy, sent envoys to the nobles, and lawfully demanded that they surrender their fortresses to him and remain at peace. In the following Lent, Rotrou, Count of Mortain, was the first to make peace with him; breaking the treaty which he had made with the king, he gave his aid to the Angevins. He had recently acquired a cause for anger against the king because he had requested his assistance in rescuing his nephew Richer, but had obtained nothing from him. Richer de l’Aigle was travelling peacefully to England with fifty knights on the Sunday in September when the Nativity of Blessed Mary was celebrated. When he arrived unarmed at the borough called Lira, he was suddenly captured by Robert de Bellême, who lay in ambush for his journey and with whom he had hoped to maintain firm peace.

> [Note: [Col. 0979] This Robert is the man who was surnamed Poardus, and is therefore distinct from Robert, Count of Bellême. (Dom Bouquet.)]

At Bristol he was imprisoned for six months; and the aforesaid robber, with excessive tyranny, without cause devastated his land by plundering and burning. His uncle Count Rotrou grieved greatly over such fury and desired to rescue his nephew from chains and his honour from his enemies. He therefore took great care frequently to seek an encounter with him, accompanied by armed men. At last, [Col. 0980C] at the end of October, by God’s will, he encountered the robbers with a strong force, captured Robert and his brother Maurice and many others, and, having severely imprisoned them as was just, gave great security to the innocent country people.

In the middle of Lent the leading men of the regions of Mortain assembled and held a conference concerning affairs of state. There Hugh, Archbishop of Rouen, and the Normans approached Count Theobald and offered him the kingdom of England and the duchy of Normandy. But he, prudent and devout as he was, refused to be burdened with the weight of such great cares; yet, subject to certain conditions, he granted the royal right to Geoffrey, son-in-law of King Henry: namely, that Geoffrey should surrender to him the city of Tours, which was held of his fief; release his brother the king from captivity; and restore in full to him and his heir the former honour which he had held during his uncle’s lifetime. Then Robert, Count of Leicester, made an alliance with Rotrou and, at the request of the counts who were present, released Richer de l’Aigle. He also secured peace for himself and his brother Waleran with the Angevins until he returned from England. The townsmen of Verneuil, among whose community thirteen thousand people were counted, who had formerly raged and threatened terribly for the king, observing that many who had lately opposed the Angevins were now yielding to them, began to soften from their former harshness. Having surrendered their fortress, they accepted the lordship of Count Geoffrey and Matilda. The townsmen of Nonancourt did likewise not long afterward.

John, Bishop of Lisieux, now old and long experienced, unwilling to endure the Angevin war so long without hope of any assistance—especially when he saw them everywhere predominant on this side of the Seine and peacefully bringing many neighbouring towns under their control—made peace with the count in the last week of Lent, upon the advice of his friends. Then, before Pentecost, after returning from Caen to Lisieux, he became ill from excessive heat and exertion; after an illness of one week, in the thirty-fourth year of his episcopate, he died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June [21 May]. [Col. 0981B] Then Rotrou, Bishop of Évreux, Rannulf, Abbot of Ouche, and the other abbots of his diocese assembled and buried his body in the basilica of St Peter the Apostle, before the altar of St Michael, on the north side.

Then Louis the Younger, King of the Franks, assembled a great army and went to besiege Toulouse for the feast of St John the Baptist, seeking to make war upon Count Alfonso, son of Raymond.

Behold, worn down by old age and infirmity, I desire to finish this book; and evident reason demands that this be done for several causes. For I am passing the sixty-seventh year of my life in the service of my Lord Jesus Christ; and, while I see the great men of this world crushed by grave misfortunes very contrary to themselves, strengthened by God’s grace I rejoice in the security of submission and poverty. Behold, Stephen, king of the English, is held groaning in prison; and Louis, king of the Franks, conducting an expedition against the Goths and Gascons, is repeatedly troubled by many anxieties. Behold, the bishop having died, the see of Lisieux lacks a bishop; and I do not know when or what sort of bishop it will have.

> [Note: [Col. 0981D] In the same year Arnulf, nephew of John and archdeacon of Séez, a man distinguished by integrity of character and learning, was elected by the clergy and people. When Geoffrey, Count of Anjou, opposed his election, Peter the Venerable wrote on behalf of the elect to Pope Innocent, with high praise, asking him to confirm the election and not admit the opposition of the Count of Anjou. The pope granted the prayers of Peter the Venerable and confirmed the election and ordination of the most deserving bishop Arnulf. St Bernard likewise wrote to Innocent on behalf of Arnulf, the elect, against Count Geoffrey. Mabillon, *Annals of the Benedictine Order*, vol. VI, p. 337. (Dom Bouquet.)]

What more shall I say?

Meanwhile, almighty God, I turn my speech to you and doubly implore your mercy to have pity on me. I give you thanks, highest King, because you made me freely and ordered my years according to your good pleasure. For you are [Col. 0981D] my King and my God, and I am your servant and the son of your handmaid, who have served you, according to my ability, from the earliest days of my life. For I was baptized on Easter Saturday at Atcham, a village in England situated upon the great river Severn.

> [Note: [Col. 0982D] Commonly: Saverne.]

There you regenerated me through the ministry of the priest Ordric from water and the Holy Spirit, and gave me the name of that same priest, namely my godfather.

Then, when I was five years old, I was sent to school at the city of Shrewsbury and offered you my first services as a cleric in the basilica of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul. There the distinguished priest Siward taught me for five years the letters of Carmenta, daughter of Nicostrata, and devoted me to psalms and hymns and other necessary instruction. Meanwhile, you exalted the aforesaid basilica, situated upon the river Meole, which belonged to my father, and through the pious devotion of Count Roger built the venerable monastery. It was not your will that I should serve there longer, lest among relatives—who are often a burden and hindrance to your servants—I should suffer disturbance or incur any loss in observing your law through carnal affection for my family.

Therefore, glorious God, who commanded Abraham to depart from his land, his father’s house, and his kindred, you inspired my father Odelerius to renounce me entirely and subject me wholly to you. Thus, weeping, he gave me, also weeping, to the monk Rainald and sent me into exile for love of you; nor did he ever see me afterwards. As a tender boy, I did not presume to oppose my father’s wishes, but willingly submitted to him in all things, because on your behalf he promised me that, if I became a monk, I should possess paradise with the innocent after my death. Gladly accepting this agreement made between you and me through the words of my father, I left my homeland, parents, all my kindred, acquaintances, and friends. Weeping and bidding me farewell, they commended me to you in kindly prayers, O highest God Adonai!

I beseech you, receive their prayers and graciously grant, O King Sabaoth, what they wished for me.

Thus, at ten years of age I crossed the British sea, came as an exile into Normandy, unknown to all and knowing no one. Like Joseph in Egypt, I heard a language which I did not know. Yet, aided by your grace, I found every gentleness and kindness among strangers. In the eleventh year of my life I was received into monastic life by the venerable Abbot Mainerius in the monastery of Ouche; and on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October [21 September], a Sunday, I was tonsured according to clerical rite. The name Vitalis was also given me in place of my English name, which was thought discordant to Norman ears; it was changed from the name of one of the companions of St Maurice the Martyr, whose martyrdom was then being celebrated.

In the aforesaid monastery I have lived for fifty-six years, with your favour, and have been loved and honoured by all the brethren far more than I deserved. Having endured heat and cold and the burden of the day, I laboured in the vineyard of Sorech among your servants and confidently awaited the penny which you promised, because you are faithful. I reverenced as fathers and masters the six abbots who were your vicars: Mainerius and Serlo, Roger and Warin, Richard and Rannulf. These lawfully presided over the community of Ouche; they kept watch over me and the others as men who would render account; they applied diligence within and without; and, with your accompaniment and help, provided us with necessities. On the Ides of March, when I was sixteen, Bishop Gilbert of Lisieux ordained me subdeacon by command of Serlo the elect. Then, two years later, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April [26 March], Bishop Serlo of Séez placed the deacon’s stole upon me. In that rank I gladly ministered to you for fifteen years. Finally, in the thirty-third year of my life, William, Archbishop of Rouen, burdened me with the priesthood on the twelfth day before the Kalends of January [21 December]. On that same day he ordained 244 deacons and consecrated 120 priests; with them I devoutly approached your holy altar in the Holy Spirit, and for thirty-four years now I have faithfully rendered you the sacred ministries with gladness of mind.

Thus, thus, Lord God, my maker and giver of life, through different ranks you freely gave me your gifts and rightly apportioned my years to your service. In every place to which you led me long ago, you caused me to be loved by your servants, not through my merits but through your gift. For all your benefits, [Col. 0984A] gracious Father, I give you thanks; with all my heart I praise and bless you; and for my innumerable offences I tearfully implore your mercy. Spare me, Lord, spare me, and do not put me to shame. In your inexhaustible goodness look mercifully upon your creature, and forgive and wipe away all my sins. Grant me perseverance in your service and unfailing strength against the malice of many-shaped Satan, until, by your gift, I attain the inheritance of everlasting salvation. And the things which, gracious God, I ask may be given me here and in the world to come, I earnestly wish also for my friends and benefactors. I desire these too, according to your providence, for all your faithful, that they may obtain the eternal goods toward which the desires of the perfect ardently strive, since the efficacy of our merits is not sufficient.

[Col. 0984B] O Lord God, almighty Father, creator and ruler of angels, true hope and everlasting blessedness of the righteous: may the glorious intercession of the holy Virgin and Mother Mary, and of all the saints, aid us before you, through our Lord Jesus Christ, redeemer of all, who lives and reigns with you, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## A.D. 1151–55. GUERRIC, ABBOT OF IGNY

[Col. 0983]

## NOTICE

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimae aetatis*, vol. III, p. 123)

Guerric, formerly a canon of Tournai and master of the school, became a Cistercian monk and about the year 1140 a disciple of St Bernard, and afterwards Abbot of Igny in the diocese of Reims. He died about A.D. 1155, on 19 August. He was the author of *Sermons*, which, after the first edition by Jean Cagnæus—Paris, 1539, octavo, reprinted there in 1547, octavo, and corrected by Jean Coster at Antwerp in 1546—were subsequently published more than once by Jacques Merlon, Horst, and Mabillon with the writings of St Bernard.

> [Note: [Col. 0983] See the works of Rivet, vol. III, p. 677; Labbe, vol. I, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 400; Maittaire, vol. III, *Annals of Typography*, p. 677.]

Combefis calls them truly golden and honeyed, and gave them a place in his *Library of Preachers*. They are also found in the Cologne *Library of the Fathers*, vol. XIII, from the edition of Jean Coster; in the Lyons edition, vol. XXIII; and separately at Lyons in 1630, edited by the Benedictine Maur Raynaud; and in French, translated by Jean Gagnæus, Paris, 1547. Trithemius also mentions letters of this Guerric, chapter 588. Sander, p. 105 of the *Bibliotheca Belgica*, records manuscript *Postils on the Psalter* at Tournai, 2 folio volumes. Charles Visch, in the *Cistercian Library*, p. 131, records much more: works on the Gospel of Matthew, on Paul’s Epistles and the Catholic Epistles, and also a treatise *On the Sickness of the Loving Soul*.

[Col. 0985]

## BLESSED GUERRIC’S SERMONS

They are extant among the works of St Bernard in Mabillon’s edition of 1719. See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXV, at the beginning.)

## A.D. 1153. ATTO, BISHOP OF PISTOIA

[Col. 0985]

## NOTICE

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimae Latinitatis*, I, 146)

Atto, Vallombrosan abbot and afterwards Bishop of Pistoia from A.D. 1133 to 1153, wrote the *Life of St John Gualbert*, founder of the Vallombrosan order, which is printed in the *Acts of the Saints*, 12 July, vol. III, p. 365. But the *Life of St Verdiana*, which some attribute to this Atto, is by a later writer, since Verdiana died in 1242. See the *Acts of the Saints* under the calends of February; Raphael Badius’s notes on Lorenzo Jacomini’s Tuscan translation of that Life, published at Florence in 1692, octavo; and the *Journal of Men of Letters* at Modena, year 1692, p. 315 ff.

[Col. 0985]

## LIFE OF ST JOHN GUALBERT, BY ATTO

(See *Patrologia*, vol. CXLVI, col. 667, in the *Acts of St John Gualbert*.)

## A.D. 1154. ANASTASIUS IV, ROMAN PONTIFF

[Col. 0985]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(Mansi, *Councils*, XXI, 773)

Anastasius IV, a Roman citizen from the Suburra district, son of Benedict, formerly called Conrad, an elderly man experienced in the practice of the Roman Curia, according to book II of Freising’s *Life of Frederick*, was raised from Abbot of St Anastasius in the diocese of Velletri and Cardinal-Bishop of Sabina to the highest rank in the Church in the year of the Lord 1153, on the seventh day before the Ides of July [9 July], in the reign of Emperor Frederick I. So the continuator of Sigebert states. Dodechin is therefore mistaken in the appendix to Marianus Scotus, where he writes that Adrian succeeded Eugenius. Anastasius offered the Lateran church a chalice of great weight. A lover and supporter of the poor, he not only built most elegant houses and a most magnificent palace by the church of St Mary Rotunda, but also, during a famine in which almost all Europe was afflicted, supplied food most generously to the needy, even to those living outside the walls of Rome. After he had borne the pontifical office for one year, four months, and twenty-four days, he died at Rome on the fourth day before the Nones of December [2 December] and was buried in the Lateran in the year of the Lord 1153. In his time flourished Richard of St Victor, Gratian the compiler of the *Decree*, Peter Lombard, and Peter Comestor, the latter two being eminent theologians. St Bernard, abbot, aged sixty-three, died on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September [20 August] in the year of Christ 1153.

[Col. 0987]

## DIPLOMATIC NOTICE

(Philipp Jaffé, *Regesta of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 652)

In Anastasius’s bulls one finds Florentine years of the Incarnation and the imperial indiction; this phrase: “KEEP ME, O LORD, AS THE APPLE OF THE EYE” (Psalm XVI).

## LETTERS AND PRIVILEGES OF ANASTASIUS IV, ROMAN PONTIFF

For the books used, see the bibliographical index prefixed to volume CLXXXIX of the *Patrologia*.

### A.D. 1153

[Col. 0989A]

### I. Privilege for the Church of St Mary of Pisa  
*(Lateran, 8 September)*

[Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, III, 395.]

Anastasius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Leo, archpriest, and the other canons of the Pisan church of Blessed Mary, both present and future, canonically entering, for ever.

A pious request ought to be fulfilled by the ensuing effect of the will, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the requested benefit may undoubtedly gain force. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we willingly assent to your just petitions and, following in the footsteps of our predecessors of happy memory, Callistus and Eugenius, Roman pontiffs, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the Church of Blessed Mary, Mother of God, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that same church now justly and lawfully possesses for the support of your brotherhood, or may, God favouring, acquire in future through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain unimpaired to you and your successors and, through you, to that church. We have judged the following to be expressly named:

The church of St Viviana at Soarza, with all property belonging to the canonry of St Mary and its appurtenances; the church of St Christina at Chinsica; the church of St Martin at Guasolongo; the church of St Mary at Mezzana; the church of St Mary at Villarada; the baptismal church of St Mary at Arena, with its dependent chapels and tithes; the church of Vaticaria; the church of Pusignano; the church of Fasiano; the church of St Bartholomew of Zumulo; the fortress of Comitello with its appurtenances; whatever you possess in the castle of Jupalli [variant: Tripalli] and its appurtenances; the castle of Scannello with its appurtenances; and other castles with their appurtenances, as they are known to have been granted to the Church of Pisa by Countesses Beatrice and Matilda of revered memory.

Whatever you possess in the estate called Pappiana; whatever you possess in the estate of Populogna; the *Rubus* of the city of Pisa; one hundred solidi from the riverbank, customarily paid for the candle; whatever you possess in the castle and estate of Castelnuovo and of Camajano Vecchio; the land at Carraja Gunduli, which Cajetanus of good memory granted you out of devotion, and on which, with your assent, he built a church in honour of St John the Evangelist; the land which you possess at Petriano [variant: Pesciano], with the church of St Margaret and its appurtenances; the rent paid to you by the *sontiarii* [variant: *lontriarii*], who fish in the lagoon.
