I, Oddo, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Roland, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June [20 May], in the second indiction, in the year 1154 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Anastasius IV.

### LXXIX. He receives the prior and monastery of Saint Saviour at Venice under Saint Peter’s protection and confirms its privileges.  
*(Lateran, 27 May.)*

[CORNELII, *Ecclesiae Venetae*, XIV, 94.]

ANASTASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GIRARD, prior of the church of Saint Saviour situated at Rialto, and his brothers, present and future, professing the canonical life, in perpetuity.

The care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us by God, the provider of all good things, so that we may love religious persons and strive by every means to advance religion pleasing to God. For no service is ever rendered acceptable to God unless, proceeding from the root of charity, it is preserved by the purity of religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and, after the example of our predecessor of blessed memory Innocent, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church of Saint Saviour, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present document.

And because you have vowed to observe the canonical order and to live according to the Rule of Saint Augustine, we gladly assent to your wishes and, by apostolic authority, ordain that this order shall remain inviolate in that church for all time; establishing that whatever possessions or goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, with God’s favor, acquire by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

> [Note: Here Mozzagrugnius ends; he omitted the remainder of the charter.]

We likewise confirm to you the share of tithes from your parishioners which belongs to your church according to the sacred canons and the enactments of the holy Fathers. We further forbid anyone to be put in charge of that church by any contrivance of fraud or violence, except one whom the brothers of that place collectively, or the sounder part of their counsel, shall canonically provide to be elected. We establish that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while the right of the mother church is nevertheless preserved. You may also receive, without anyone’s objection, for conversion clerics or free laymen fleeing from the secular world. But we forbid any brother, after making profession in that place, rashly to leave the cloister without the prior’s permission. Let no one dare to retain one who departs without a common letter of authorization.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, harass it with any molestations, or unlawfully receive or retain that church’s parishioners. Rather, let all things remain whole and unimpaired, for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If anyone therefore, etc.

I, Anastasius, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. I, Imarus, bishop of Tusculum, have subscribed. I, Ugo, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed. I, Cencius, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina, have subscribed. I, Guarinus, bishop of Palestrina, have subscribed. I, W., cardinal priest of the title of Calixtus, have subscribed. I, Guido, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, have subscribed. I, Girardus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill, have subscribed. I, Octavianus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia, have subscribed. I, Julius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, have subscribed. I, Guido, cardinal priest of the title of Pastor, have subscribed. I, Bernardus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Clement, have subscribed. I, Henry, cardinal priest of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Martin on the Mount, have subscribed. I, Guido, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, Odo, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Roland, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church.

> [Note: [Col. 1075D] He later became Pope Alexander III.]

On the sixth day before the Kalends of June [27 May], in the second indiction, in the year 1154 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Pope Anastasius IV.

### LXXX. To Ulric, bishop, and the canons of the Church of Halberstadt.  
*(Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 14 June.)*

[Leuckfeld, *Antiquit. Poeldenses*, 281.]

ANASTASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother ULRIC, bishop, and to his beloved sons the canons of the Church of Halberstadt, greeting and apostolic blessing.

A possession which has been adjudicated to a church by canonical judgment ought to be left to it without any opposition. It has indeed come to our attention that the Church of Goslar, at a place called Slanstede, held a certain possession adjudicated to it in the synod of Halberstadt, of which it had for a long time been violently despoiled. Since it is unjust that the aforesaid church should henceforth be troubled concerning this matter, we command you by these present letters that, if any lovers of injustice should decide to harass the said church concerning the same possession, you shall defend the aforementioned church against their attacks, as your office requires, and cause it to possess that possession peacefully.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July [14 June].

SAINT PETER. PAUL. POPE ANASTASIUS IV.

### LXXXI. He undertakes the protection of the hospital of Altopascio and confirms its goods and privileges.  
*(Rome, at Santa Maria Rotonda, 3 July.)*

[*Memorie e documenti del principato Lucchese*, IV, I, 25.]

ANASTASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GUIDO, rector of the hospital of Altopascio, and his brothers, present and future, devoted there to divine service, in perpetuity.

It is fitting readily to grant assent to religious desires, so that the devotion of the faithful may obtain a swift result. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and, after the example of our predecessor of blessed memory Pope Eugenius, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid hospital, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present document. We establish that whatever possessions or goods that hospital now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, with God’s favor, acquire through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you, your successors, and Christ’s poor. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names.

The tithes which Anselm, bishop of Lucca of blessed memory, granted to that hospital; the land and possessions of Valle-cava; the possessions which you have in the valley of the Arno and in the plain of Lucca, or in other places. Certainly, concerning the produce which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or the increase of your animals, let no one presume to exact tithes from you.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid hospital, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but let all things remain whole and unimpaired, to benefit in every way your use and that of Christ’s poor, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical reverence due to the diocesan bishop.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person in the future, etc.

I, Anastasius, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Place of the sign of Pope Anastasius IV. “Guard me, O Lord, as the pupil of the eye.”

I, Guido, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico, have subscribed. I, Oddo, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have subscribed. I, Gregory, cardinal priest of the title of Calixtus, have subscribed. I, Guido, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, have subscribed. I, Bernardus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Clement, have subscribed. I, Octavianus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia, have subscribed. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, of Pammachius, have subscribed.

Given at Rome, at Santa Maria Rotonda, through the hand of Roland, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the seventh day before the Kalends of July [25 June], in the second indiction, in the year 1153 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Anastasius IV.

### LXXXII. Special privilege granted to Marquard, abbot of Fulda.  
*(3 July.)*

[SCHANNAT, *Dioeces. Fuld.*, 262.]

ANASTASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son MARCHUARD, abbot of the venerable monastery of the Church of Saint Fulda, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Among all the churches of the German kingdom, confirmed by privileges and decrees from ancient Fathers and from our predecessors, holy and apostolic men, the monastery of Fulda is known to have flourished in wealth and eminence of dignity. The most holy Roman Church has always provided for it more kindly in its affairs; and in proportion as she has seen it belong more especially to her right and protection and remain more steadfast in its devotion, she has taken greater care to assist it in its needs.

Knowing, therefore, by how many assaults of storm it is shaken, contrary to the commands of the holy Fathers; how many pressures and molestations it suffers through the wickedness of secular men; and how harsh and how lax you often find certain of our brothers and fellow bishops when justice is to be rendered to you against those wrongdoers: from the benevolence of the Apostolic See we have decreed that this authority be granted to your person. If, concerning wrongdoers against the church entrusted to you and invaders of its goods, wherever situated within bishoprics, you bring your complaint a second or third time to those bishops to whom their spiritual care belongs, and they refuse to do you justice, you may, after a second and third warning, bind those wrongdoers with a sentence of excommunication by our authority, unless they make satisfaction to you and your church. Nor may that sentence be relaxed beforehand by any bishop, until they render you suitable satisfaction for the claims which you have against them.

You therefore, beloved son Marquard, shall be so devoted and faithful to your mother, the most holy Roman Church, for the favor granted you, and shall use the authority granted you in such a way, that you may appear not undeservedly to have obtained this benefit and may be shown fitly to rise to the obtaining of others. And since we know your oversight to be necessary to the monastery of Fulda, we establish by the authority of our Apostolic See that all which you have recovered in the revenues of the Church, and all which you have restored to your monastery from things previously taken away or unjustly possessed, shall remain secure to it forever.

Given on the fifth day before the Nones of July [3 July], in the second indiction.

### LXXXIII. He receives under protection the house of the Hospital at Jerusalem and confirms its possessions and privileges.  
*(Lateran, 21 October.)*

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 780.]

The religion of the Christian faith devoutly believes and truthfully confesses that our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, though rich in all things, became poor for our sake. Hence, promising fitting rewards of consolation to his imitators, he says: “Blessed are the poor, for yours is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5). The same Father of orphans and refuge of the poor, exhorting us in the Gospel to hospitality and beneficence, says: “What you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matthew 25). And, to demonstrate the excellence of such great goodness, he asserted that he would render a reward even for a cup of cold water.

We therefore, upon whom by the office entrusted to us rests the duty of providing with paternal concern for those who are far away and those who are near, embrace your devotion with due kindness. As requested, after the example of our predecessors of blessed memory Innocent, Celestine, Lucius, and Eugenius, Roman pontiffs, we receive the hospital and house of the holy city of Jerusalem under the guardianship of blessed Peter, and fortify by the privilege of the Apostolic See the persons and property belonging to it. We establish that whatever possessions and goods have been reasonably acquired for that hospice by the watchfulness of your care, for sustaining the needs of pilgrims and poor persons, in the parishes and territories of cities of the Church of Jerusalem or of other churches; whatever has been offered by any persons, or shall hereafter happen to be offered by grants of kings or princes, through the Lord’s bounty, or acquired by other just means; and whatever has been lawfully granted by the venerable brethren, patriarchs of the See of Jerusalem, shall be preserved forever in peace and integrity for you, your successors, and the brothers charged with the care of pilgrims.

If any places have been bestowed upon that venerable house by anyone in devotion, you may build villages there and construct churches and cemeteries for the use of those living there, provided that there is no neighboring abbey or community of religious men which may be disturbed by this. But when lands are conferred upon you under any just title, you shall have the faculty and permission to establish oratories and make cemeteries there for the use of pilgrims and only of brothers who are of our table.

We decree, therefore, that the collectors of your fraternities or collections, saving the right of their lords, shall stand under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves and shall have peace throughout the lands in which they are present. Likewise, we establish that anyone received into your fraternity, if the church to which he belongs should happen to be prohibited from divine offices and he should die, shall not be denied ecclesiastical burial, unless he has been excommunicated or specifically interdicted. Moreover, if any of your brothers sent by you to receive those fraternities and collections come to a city, castle, or village which happens to lie under an interdict from divine offices, then, out of reverence for almighty God, at their welcome arrival the churches shall be opened once in the year and, excommunicated persons being excluded, divine offices shall be celebrated there.

Since all your goods ought to be devoted to the maintenance of pilgrims and poor persons and therefore ought by no means to be applied to other uses, we establish that no cleric or layman may presume to exact tithes from you on the produce which you cultivate at your own expense. We establish that no bishop may pronounce a sentence of interdict, suspension, or excommunication in churches subject to you. Nevertheless, if a general interdict is pronounced in those places, divine offices may be celebrated plainly, behind closed doors and without ringing bells, with excommunicated and specifically interdicted persons excluded.

So that nothing may be lacking to you for the fullness of salvation and care of your souls, and so that ecclesiastical sacraments and divine offices may be furnished more conveniently to you and Christ’s poor, we establish that you may receive clerics and priests coming to you from anywhere—after first obtaining, so far as lies within your knowledge, suitable testimony by letters or witnesses concerning their honorable character and ordination—and retain them with you both in your principal house and in the obediences subject to it, provided that, if they are from nearby, you receive them from their own bishops [lacuna], and that they are not bound to any other profession or order. But if the bishops should perhaps refuse to grant them to you, you shall nevertheless have authority, by the authority of the Holy Roman Church, to receive and retain them. Those clerics shall be subject to no person outside your chapter, except the Roman pontiff.

We likewise grant you the faculty, without anyone’s objection, to receive free laymen into the religious way of life and the service of Christ’s poor. But we forbid your brothers, once received into [lacuna] and into your sacred college, after making profession and taking up the religious habit, the faculty of returning to the secular world. Nor shall it be lawful for any one of them, after making profession, to cast off the cross of the Lord once assumed and the habit of your profession, or to transfer to another place or monastery on the pretext of a stricter or less strict religious life, against the will or without the consultation of the brothers, or without the permission of him who is master. Nor shall any ecclesiastical or secular person have leave to receive or retain them.

The consecrations of altars or churches, the ordinations of clerics to be promoted to sacred orders, and the other ecclesiastical sacraments shall be received from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favor and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to administer them to you freely and without any improper exaction. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested. Upon the death of you, the present steward and provost of that place, let no one be put in charge there by fraud, contrivance, or violence, except one whom the brothers there elect according to God.

Moreover, we confirm to you, for your zeal in the work of hospitality, and through you to the aforesaid hospice, all honors and possessions which it now justly holds beyond or on this side of the sea, in Asia or Europe, or may hereafter, with God’s favor, reasonably acquire.

Let no one therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Roland, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November [21 October], in the fourth indiction, in the year 1154 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Pope Anastasius IV.

### LXXXIV. He confirms for the Church of Trondheim the metropolitan rights established under Eugenius III by Nicholas, bishop of Albano, legate of the Apostolic See.  
*(Lateran, November.)*

[THORKELIN, *Diplom., Arna-Magn.*, year II, 3.]

To all to whom the present letters shall come: Sueno, dean; Ulpho, archdeacon of the Church of Nidaros; Ingewaldus, prior of the Regular Canons of Saint Augustine at the holy see near Nidaros; and Peter, prior of the Friars Preachers in the same place: eternal greeting in the Lord.

Be it known that we have seen and carefully read the letters written below of Pope Anastasius IV, of happy memory, neither cancelled nor erased nor damaged in any part, under brown silk cords and a leaden seal, with the subscription of that same supreme pontiff Anastasius and of the cardinals. Their tenor, together with the subscriptions—although the signs appended there by the same subscribers are here omitted—follows word for word and is as follows.

ANASTASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother JOHN, archbishop of Trondheim, and to his successors canonically appointed, in perpetuity.

Although the same power of binding and loosing has been granted to all the disciples, and although one and the same command has come to all, to preach the Gospel to every creature, nevertheless a certain distinction of rank has been established among them. One alone singularly received the care of the Lord’s sheep, which lay equally upon all, when the Lord said: “Peter, do you love me? Feed my sheep” (John 21). He also obtained among all the apostles the title of primacy and received from the Lord a special command concerning the strengthening of his brothers, so that succeeding authority might understand by this that, although many may happen to be ordained for the government of the Church, one alone nevertheless holds the place and summit of supreme dignity, and one presides over all both with the power of judgment and with the burden of governance.

Accordingly, after this pattern, diverse persons in the Church have been appointed in diverse orders to render diverse ministries. Some are ordained for the ordering and government of individual churches; others, for individual cities. In each province, moreover, others have been established whose judgment has precedence among their brothers and to whose examination the questions and affairs of persons subject to them are referred. Over all, however, the Roman pontiff is known to hold the first place, as Noah did in the ark. By the privilege bestowed upon him from above in the prince of the apostles, he judges and disposes of all causes and does not cease to strengthen throughout the world the children of the Church in the firmness of Christian faith, continually striving to show himself such a one as seems to have heard the Lord’s voice saying: “And you, once you have turned, strengthen your brothers.”

After blessed Peter, those apostolic men who, through the succession of times, rose to bear the care of the Apostolic See took unceasing care to fulfil this duty. Throughout the world, now in person and now through their legates, they exerted the utmost effort to correct what needed correction and establish what needed establishment. Following their footsteps, our predecessor Pope Eugenius of blessed memory was concerned, as the duty of his office required, to correct matters in the kingdom of Norway which seemed to demand correction and to sow there the word of faith. What he could not accomplish in person, because the care of the universal Church prevented it, he committed for execution to his legate, our venerable brother Nicholas, bishop of Albano.

When Nicholas came to those regions, he employed at interest the talent entrusted to him, as he had received in command from his master, and, like a faithful and prudent servant, strove to return it multiplied in fruit. Among the other things which he accomplished there for the praise of God’s name and the commendation of his ministry, he granted the pallium to your fraternity, as our aforesaid predecessor had commanded him. So that the province of Norway might not thereafter lack metropolitan care, he established the city of Trondheim, entrusted to your governance, as the perpetual metropolitan see of that province. He decreed that the bishoprics of Aslo, Hamar, Bergen, Stavanger, the islands of Orkney, the islands of Guthraie, the islands of Iceland, and Greenland should be perpetually subject to it as to their metropolis, and that their bishoprics should obey you and your successors as their metropolitans.

Therefore, lest anyone at any time presume to violate this establishment, we confirm it by apostolic authority and fortify it by the privilege of this present document. We establish that the city of Trondheim shall be regarded for all time as the metropolis of the aforesaid cities, and that their bishops shall obey you and your successors as their metropolitans and receive the grace of consecration from your hand. Your successors, however, shall go only to the Roman pontiff to receive the gift of consecration, and shall always remain similarly subject to him and to the Roman Church.

Moreover, your fraternity, having received the pallium—that is, the fullness of the pontifical office—shall use it only within the church, at the sacred solemnities of Mass, throughout your entire province, and only on the following days listed below: the Nativity of the Lord, Epiphany, the Lord’s Supper, the Resurrection, Ascension, Pentecost; the feasts of the holy Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary; the feast of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul; the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist; the feast of blessed John the Evangelist; the Commemoration of All Saints; at consecrations of churches or bishops, blessings of abbots, ordinations of priests; on the anniversary of the dedication of your church; the feasts of the Holy Trinity and Saint Olaf; and the anniversary day of your consecration.

Let your fraternity, therefore, having received the fullness of so great a dignity, strive so vigorously to perform all things that the adornments of your character may fittingly accord with it. Let your life be an example to your subjects, so that through it they may recognize what they ought to seek and what they must avoid. Be outstanding in discernment, pure in thought, blameless in action, discreet in silence, useful in speech. Let it be more your concern to benefit men than to rule them. You must consider in yourself not the power of rank but the equality of your human condition. Strive that life may not fail doctrine, nor, conversely, doctrine contradict life. Remember that the governance of souls is the art of arts. Above all, let it be your care firmly to observe the decrees of the Apostolic See and humbly to obey it as your mother and mistress. Behold, dearest brother in Christ, among many other things these are the obligations of the pallium, these the obligations of the priesthood. You will easily be able, with Christ’s help, to fulfil them all, if you possess charity and humility, the mistress of all virtues, and if you have inwardly what you show yourself outwardly to possess.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the same Church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but let all things remain whole and unimpaired for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See.

If anyone therefore, etc.

I, Anastasius, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Imarus (Imarus), bishop of Tusculum. I, Nicholas, bishop of Albano. I, Hugo, bishop of Ostia. I, Centius, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Guido, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus. I, Manfredus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Savina (Sabina). I, Aribertus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Ascaldus (Astaldus), cardinal priest of the title of Saint Prisca. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, of Pammachius. I, Henry, cardinal priest of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus. I, Guido, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, John, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Roland, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the [lacuna] day before the Kalends of December, in the third indiction, in the year 1154 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Anastasius IV.

Furthermore, we, the aforesaid dean, archdeacon, and priors, have seen six other apostolic letters, namely of Adrian IV, Clement III, Innocent III, Gregory IX, Innocent IV, and Clement IV, bearing seals and entirely free from every suspicion. We have thought fit to append, under the same tenor of words, the same privileges granted in every respect to the aforesaid Church of Nidaros, with similar subscriptions of those supreme pontiffs and cardinals.

Given at Nidaros, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July [28 June], in the year of the Lord 1629.

### LXXXV. Privilege for the monastery of Longpont.  
*(Lateran, 24 November.)*

[MABILLON, *Annal. Bened.*, VI, 725.]

ANASTASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son THEOBALD, prior of Longpont, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We desire that those things which noble men and princes of the world bestow upon pious places and religious persons out of regard for piety and due charity should remain firmly established; and, lest hereafter they should be disturbed by the opposition of any persons, it is fitting that we strengthen them by the authority of the Apostolic See. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord Theobald, we readily grant assent to your just petitions. We confirm to you, and through you to your church, by this document of our authority, the Abbey of St. Peter of Mont-Lethéric, with all that pertains to it, which our most dear son Louis, king of the Franks, with the consent of Abbot John, who then governed that church, and of the canons dwelling there, as is contained in the privilege of that same king, reasonably bestowed and confirmed in writing upon the church over which, by God’s authorizing, you are known to preside, in order that monks might be placed there to advance the divine offices and the condition of the church for the better. This gift was also granted in our presence by our venerable brother Theobald, bishop of Paris, in whose diocese that church is situated [Col. 1084C]; and we decree that the said donation shall remain ratified for all time. Therefore let no person presume, with rash boldness, to infringe this document of our confirmation or in any way oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he shall incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed Apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, the eighth day before the Kalends of December [24 November].

LXXXVI. He informs the bishops of Sweden that he has joyfully received news that the people have advanced in apostolic teaching, etc. (Lateran, 28 November.)

[LILJEGREN, *Diplomatarium Suecicum*, I, 679.]

[Col. 1084D]

ANASTASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable bishops of Sweden: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We rejoice, most beloved brethren, and render thanksgivings to Almighty God, because we now see the Church long ago promised unto the ends of the earth brought forth, and behold the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts so enlarged that what the Prophet said long before now truly seems fulfilled: “He extended his branches even unto the sea, and his shoots unto the river” (Psalm 79 [80]). For as the apostles preach, a faithful people is daily begotten for the Lord, and the barren womb which did not bear children is so increased with natural sons that, according to the voice of the Psalmist, the sound of the apostles seems to have gone forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world [Col. 1085A]. This is plainly shown by the fact that the people entrusted to your governance cries to the Lord from the ends of the earth; abandoning the nets of the Gentiles, it glories in receiving apostolic teaching.

Indeed, when our venerable brother Nicholas, bishop of Albano, returned to the Apostolic See, he declared that this same people had gladly received the word of the Lord from his mouth, and that both you and the whole people had unanimously shown him that reverence, devotion, and obedience which are due to the legates of the Apostolic See out of veneration for the apostles. Therefore, the more readily that people has shown itself disposed to hear the word of the Lord [Col. 1085B] and eager for apostolic teaching, the more earnestly do we desire always to devote ourselves to its instruction and formation. And because we cannot visit it bodily, we wish to visit it by affection and letters.

Accordingly, even now we send them, through our writings, the address of apostolic blessing, and by our letters admonish them to observe those things which our aforesaid brother established among you. Therefore, lest—God forbid—that which the prophet laments should happen among them: “The peoples asked for bread, and there was none to break it for them” (Lamentations 4), let your frequent exhortation not fail, so that, as they have well begun, they may persevere immovably in reverence for the most holy Roman Church [Col. 1085C], and with devout minds and unceasing diligence observe the constitutions of our aforesaid brother.

Take heed, for you have been appointed watchmen to the house of Israel: let the trumpet be in your throat, and give Him no silence. Announce to the people of God their crimes, lest perhaps, if you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, he indeed die in his sin, but his blood be required from your hands. Set yourselves before them as an example of good works, and show them by life and deeds, not merely by words, what they must do, so that you may seem to keep the commandments of the Lord in memory in order to do them, and may be proved ministers and disciples of Him of whom Scripture says: “For He began to do and to teach” (Acts 1). For the speech of a teacher is held in contempt [Col. 1085D] when the example of a good life does not accord with his preaching.

For we trust in the mercy of the Creator that, if according to the obligation of your office you diligently cultivate the Lord’s field and devote yourselves in word and deed to the instruction of His people, and humbly remain in the observance of apostolic teaching and obedience to the most holy Roman Church, you shall both receive here an increase of virtues and, at the final judgment, continually attain with all the saints the reward of eternal blessedness.

Although it has been established in a general council that whoever lays violent hands upon a cleric shall remain subject to excommunication until he comes to make satisfaction before the Apostolic See, nevertheless, because of the great remoteness of the lands, we have judged that this constitution should be mitigated [Col. 1086A], namely: only those who within that people may put a cleric, monk, or convert to death, or cut off one of his limbs, shall be sent to the Apostolic See to make satisfaction. Others, after suitable satisfaction has been imposed upon them by you, shall be absolved from the bonds of excommunication, provided that they first swear that they will obey your command. You shall afterward impose an ecclesiastical penalty upon them, so that they may neither in deed, nor counsel, nor consent, cause a cleric, monk, or convert to be beaten or seized.

Furthermore, we admonish and exhort your charity in the Lord that each of you shall faithfully endeavor, every year, to collect from his own bishopric and transmit to the Apostolic See the tribute which your kingdom and people had established as annually payable to blessed Peter [Col. 1086B].

Given at the Lateran, the fourth day before the Kalends of December [28 November].

LXXXVII. He exhorts King Sverker and the magnates of Sweden to continue following the commands of Nicholas, legate of the Apostolic See, etc. (Lateran, 28 November.)

[LILJEGREN, *Diplomatarium Suecicum*, I, 56.]

ANASTASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved sons in Christ, S., king, and all the magnates of Sweden: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Among the other ways in which divine mercy deigns to honor the ministry of the most holy Roman Church over which, by God’s authorizing, we preside [Col. 1086C], there is nothing for which our mind is more earnestly exercised in thanksgiving and praise of the Creator than if He grants that, through us or our brethren, the boundaries of His Church may be enlarged and that the seed of the divine word, through the provision of the Apostolic See, may bring forth fruit pleasing to Him. Since we see this fulfilled by the grace of the Almighty in the coming of our venerable brother Nicholas, bishop of Albano, among you, we render thanksgivings to the author of all good things and in every way commend His benefit, both in respect to us and to you: He called you out of darkness and the shadow of death into His wonderful light, and, when you were dead in sin, made you alive together with Christ [Col. 1086D].

We pray, moreover, that He who began a good work in you may complete it, and may always cause you so to cleave to apostolic teaching, so to establish and confirm you in the body of Christ, which is the Church, through the bond of charity, that you may continually strive to fulfill, for the salvation of your souls, what you have faithfully believed; and that, after the laying aside of this corruptible tabernacle, when the Lord comes for judgment, you may be able to meet Him with all the saints, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ. And we firmly believe, God bringing it about, that this will happen if, always holding before the eyes of your minds the apostolic teaching and preaching of our aforesaid brother, you strive to be doers of the word and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves. For if anyone, as the Apostle says (James 1) [Col. 1087A], is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he shall be like a man considering the face of his birth in a mirror: for he considered himself and departed, and immediately forgot what sort of man he was.

Therefore, lest this happen to you, we admonish and exhort you in the Lord: watered through this same brother of ours by the rain of sacred speech, strive to bear the fruit of life. Consider among yourselves how, whereas you were once darkness, you are now light in the Lord; set your minds on things above, not upon things on earth; and, gathered through the true Noah and His ministers out of the flood into the ark of the Church, firmly observe the commandments of the Lord and the decrees of our aforesaid brother concerning the liberty of your churches, the prohibition of carrying arms, and other matters pertaining to the people’s salvation [Col. 1087B].

Behold the animals perishing outside the bounds of the ark; and, gathered within it, render immense thanks to Him who gathered you. Consider among yourselves His kindness: in order to redeem you from the hand of the enemy and gather you from the regions, He did not disdain, for your sake while you were still sinners, to be clothed in flesh, disgraced upon the cross, and punished by death. And since by His free goodness He has made you sons of the apostles and members of His body [Col. 1088A], persevere immovably in the unity of that body and in the truth of the Catholic faith. With all diligence, as you have begun, venerate the most holy Roman Church, mother of all the faithful; and though you are separated from her by a great interval of lands, always be present to her through devotion and pious longing.

For we hold firm and undoubted that, if you remain until the end in her obedience and subjection and endeavor to fulfill the statutes of our aforesaid brother and apostolic teaching, you shall attain from earthly things to heavenly, and from things falling and transient to things eternal and ever abiding. Cause the tribute which, as a token of your devotion, you have established as yearly payable to blessed Peter from your lands [Col. 1088B], to be given to our brethren the bishops, so that through them it may be sent to the Apostolic See. Indeed, we exact it not so much for our own advantage as for the salvation of your souls, since through this service of inward devotion we desire that you obtain the patronage of blessed Peter.

Given at the Lateran, the fourth day before the Kalends of December [28 November].

ANNO DOMINI 1154: ANSELM, BISHOP OF HAVELBERG

[Col. 1087]

NOTICE

(FABRICIUS, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, I, 114)

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, or Avelberg, from the year 1126 to 1154, in the March on the river Avel or Havel, under the archbishop of Magdeburg, wrote a book *On the Order of the Regular Canons of St. Augustine*, to which he himself was also devoted. It is extant in Bernard Pez’s *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. IV, part II, p. 75. Dachery published the same author’s three *Dialogues*—one on the various forms of the Christian religion and two containing disputations against the Greeks—in vol. XIII of the *Spicilegium*, p. 88 (new edition, vol. I, p. 161). See Oudin, vol. II, p. 1429 ff. Eisengrein, p. 97, mentions several Lives of saints by him in lengthy volumes, and many letters to various persons.

[Col. 1089]

SECOND NOTICE

(OUDIN, *Commentary on Ecclesiastical Writers*, II, 1429.)

[Col. 1089A] Anselm, bishop of Havelberg in the margraviate of Brandenburg, renowned for learning and achievements, wrote a learned work against the Greeks. Lucas Dachery published it from a manuscript codex of the monastery of Cîteaux in vol. XIII of his *Spicilegium*, where in the prefatory matter he speaks of Anselm, bishop of Havelberg. Havelberg is a city of Germany and was formerly a bishopric under the archbishop of Magdeburg in the March of Brandenburg, as Philip Ferrarius testifies in his geographical lexicon.

In that place Anselm flourished in the year 1150; and earlier, having been not moderately imbued with every kind of literature, both sacred and secular, and with the writings of the holy Fathers, he had, from the time of Emperor Lothair II, whose envoy he was, been sent as legate to Constantinople to the emperor of the Greeks. Anselm was also sent by Pope Eugenius III to Conrad, king of the Romans, then residing in Lombardy, as appears from Pope Eugenius’s letter in these words: “After we learned that you had arrived safely in the regions of Lombardy, we judged that certain of our brethren should be sent to Your Serenity, as we notified you through our venerable brethren Hartwig, archbishop of Bremen, and Anselm, bishop of Havelberg [Col. 1089B], so that they might set forth to you the affection and goodwill which we bear toward you,” etc. Otto of Freising reports Eugenius’s letter in Book I of *The Deeds of Frederick*, chapter 61. Likewise, in Book II, chapter 4, Anselm subscribed, together with several bishops, to the agreement between Emperor Frederick and Pope Eugenius.

Sent to Constantinople, he was challenged there by the wiser Greek bishops and entered into a celebrated assembly or colloquy, in which the controversies between Greeks and Latins were keenly debated on both sides, yet with the utmost moderation. Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, himself recounts this to Pope Eugenius III in these words: “I was once the legate of the great Lothair Augustus, emperor of the Romans, to Constantinople [Col. 1089C]; and while I stayed there for some time, I held many discussions and inquiries concerning such matters of doctrine and rite, now in private, now in public gatherings, both of Latins and Greeks. Your Holiness was pleased both to request by commanding and to command by requesting that I collect into one body the things which I had either said to them or heard and received from them, and compose, in dialogue form, as it were an *Anticimenon*, that is, a book of oppositions.”

And after a few intervening words: “So far as memory supplied, I preserved the course of the Dialogue which I held in a public assembly near the city of Constantinople with the venerable and most learned Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia. This Archbishop Nechites was foremost among the twelve teachers,” etc. “But I prefaced it with a book on the one form of believing and the manifoldness of living, from righteous Abel to the last Elect, compelled by the many requests of certain brethren,” etc.

How humbly he thought of himself is shown by the words he adds: “Indeed, whoever reads these things should know that I wrote them, not so much in order to teach anyone or to display what I have learned, as to obey the holy command of Apostolic Blessedness,” etc. “If in writing my lack of skill commits any fault, the obedience laid upon me and humbly fulfilled excuses it.”

[Col. 1090A] Then in the second book of the *Dialogue* he treats of the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father together with the Son, which the Greeks deny. He shows how the disputation began, and at the beginning of Book II, chapter 1, names the Latin and Greek men present in this manner: “When I was stationed in the imperial city and frequently received various questions from the Greeks, and proposed others to them there, it pleased Emperor Kalojohn, and also the patriarch of the city N., a religious man, that a public assembly should take place. A day was appointed so that, in the hearing of all, the things said on either side might be spoken aloud. Therefore, when very many learned men had assembled in the quarter called that of the Pisans, beside the church of Hagia Irene, which in the Latin tongue is called Holy Peace, in the month of April,” etc. “And when recorders had been appointed faithfully to take down and commit to writing everything said on either side, the whole multitude which had eagerly assembled to listen became silent. There were also present not a few Latins, among whom were three learned men, skilled in both languages and most learned in letters: James by name, a Venetian by nation; Burgundio by name, a Pisan by nation; and a third, distinguished among the rest, renowned among both peoples for his learning in Greek and Latin letters, Moses by name, an Italian from the city of Pergamum [Col. 1090B]. He was chosen by all to be interpreter of the faith for both sides. Thus, when all things had been arranged,” etc.

In the third book he treats of the different rite of the Eucharist among Greeks and Latins—namely, unleavened and leavened bread—and of the authority and prerogative of the Roman Church. This final disputation was held in the basilica of Holy Wisdom, in the presence of Greek learned men, as Anselm relates in Book III, chapter 1. By learned replies and the force of his arguments, he dissolved the Greeks’ objections, stoutly defended the Latin Church, and finally defeated and disarmed them so thoroughly that he induced the archbishop of Nicomedia to request a general council, by which the schism might be abolished and the two Churches reconciled.

Thus speaks the bishop of Havelberg in the final chapter, whose words, I think, will not be unwelcome to the reader. Nechites speaks: “With the utmost diligence, as I have said above, efforts ought to be made that a general council be held at a suitable place and time, where all matters that separate us and you from the same rite may be brought into a single confirmed concord, and where Greeks and Latins alike may become one people under the one Lord Jesus Christ, in one sacramental rite.” Finally, Anselm of Havelberg concludes the whole disputation and all the discussions, answering Nechites: “You who desire a general council appear to intend that which is catholic; and therefore I too desire a universal council to be held, where your wisdom, maturity, and discernment [Col. 1090C] may shine forth before the face of the whole Church for the salvation and instruction of all,” etc. All cried out, “Δόξα σοι τῷ Θεῷ” (*Doxa soi tō Theō*), that is, “Glory be to God,” etc. “Calos dialogos,” that is, “a good discourse between two persons.” “Autographs, autographs”: that is, “Let it all be written down, let it all be written down.”

This work is also extant in manuscript in the Pauline Library at Leipzig, as appears from the catalogue of that library’s manuscripts, printed at Leipzig in 1686 through the care and effort of its librarian Joachim Feller, p. 412.

[Col. 1091]

BOOK OF ANSELM, BISHOP OF HAVELBERG, ON THE ORDER OF REGULAR CANONS

(Edited by R. P. PEZ, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, IV, II, 74.) (G)*

EDITORIAL NOTE.

As soon as the illustrious order of Regular Canons, living under the generally received Rule of St. Augustine, either arose or was restored, it acquired various adversaries because of the novelty of its institution, as they supposed. The first to attack it seem to have been the clerics called secular, though not all of them, but for the most part men of inferior character: concubinaries, pursuers of pomp and vanities. Opposed to the rule and rigor of apostolic life, they raged against the backs of those whose virtue and holiness they were weary and ashamed to imitate and emulate. Against this kind of adversary Gerhoh, provost of Reichersberg, wrote a sharp and forceful apology to Innocent II, supreme pontiff; we published it, having drawn it from the library of Rottenbuch, in vol. II, second part.

Other and more powerful adversaries of the Regular Canons, under the appearance of a holier life and doctrine, were certain monks. Having no bowels of compassion, they not only do not return to their brother his ox or ass which has gone astray, but even endeavor to steal it away. They not only do not assist a brother wounded and left half-dead by robbers, but inflict wound upon wound; and, doing to others what they would not have done to themselves, they endeavor to draw away the sons and disciples of the canons from those masters under whom they could be saved and to attract them to themselves—as though Christ were found among them alone, as though the kingdom of God had proceeded from them or come to them alone. Thus one almost hears it said, as was once said in the times of heresies: “Behold, here is Christ,” or “Behold, He is there,” etc. These matters may be read more fully and advantageously in Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, in the present splendid little work, which elegantly and solidly refutes monks who disparage the order of Regular Canons.

Chapter XVIII is worthy of note: in it Anselm believes that, both for propriety and for the purpose of practice, Regular Canons ought in manual work to discuss matters of necessity and usefulness not in the vernacular but in Latin. Concerning the length of psalmody, he states in chapter XX: “Just as I do not require a multiplication of customary psalms, so I do not forbid speaking in tongues in such matters. I especially approve that those who sing psalms and pray should apply themselves so that what is uttered with the mouth may be pondered in the mind, and that the exercise of work and reading, or the turtledove sacrifice of secret prayer, should not be excluded by the prolongation of common prayer and psalmody—since these things ought to be done and those not omitted.”

In chapter VIII he offers several examples of Regular Canons endowed with extraordinary virtues and heavenly gifts. In chapter XXIX he raises to the skies with the highest praise Hugh of St. Victor, Rupert of Deutz, Bernard of Clairvaux, and Norbert, archbishop of Magdeburg, all of whom were contemporaries of Anselm. I owe this little work to the distinguished and most learned Georg Eccard, who informed me that it had been copied from a codex in the library of Hamersleben. The name of Anselm appears both at the beginning and at the end of the copy communicated to me, and I do not doubt that a later scribe faithfully reproduced the old title of the little book as it appeared in the Hamersleben exemplar.

Yet this can never prevent me from strongly suspecting that the author of the present little work was very different from Anselm of Havelberg. Certainly, no one can read chapters VIII and XXV attentively without immediately suspecting that this composition proceeded from the diocese of Salzburg or Passau rather than from any other. But those who at some time have been permitted to inspect more ancient codices will judge how much weight should be given to my conjecture. In good faith I gave to print what I received from a most learned man, very experienced in such matters.

Besides the book *On the Order of Regular Canons*, Anselm also transmitted two other monuments of his talent to posterity. The first is the notable work *Against the Greeks*, first published by our Lucas Dachery in vol. XIII of the *Spicilegium*. The other, not yet printed, is preserved among my papers and bears this title: *Treatise of Lord Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg, on the Order for Chanting the Litany, addressed to Frederick, Archbishop of Magdeburg*. I would gladly have added this treatise to the little work *On the Order of Regular Canons*, had it not been sent to me too late by my most learned friend. But what could not be done in this edition will be done in the following volumes. [Note: [Col. 1091] He did not fulfill this promise.]

[Col. 1093] Here begins the Treatise on the Order of Regular Canons, edited by the reverend presbyter and lord in Christ, Lord Anselm, bishop of the Church of Havelberg, of the same order, who flourished in the time of Bernard.

CHAPTER I. On the Decline of the Canonical Order.

[Col. 1093A]

Fathers and sons of the canonical order, have pity on yourselves and on us; have pity on the canonical order, at least you who are its friends, for the hand of the Lord has touched it. When the Church was in its beginnings, it was great among all the sons and daughters of the East, strong with the sevenfold Spirit and the faith of the Holy Trinity; it possessed fine oxen and sheep, asses and camels, in thousands of converts from Jews and Gentiles, and daily made feasts of holy banqueting with rejoicing in the breaking of the Lord’s bread.

Then Satan demanded it, that he might sift it as wheat, beginning with the persecution which took place in Stephen. Thus also in our time, through the sluggish negligence of certain masters [Col. 1093B] and the watchful treachery of false brethren, power over it was given to Satan by the Lord. He destroyed all its substance and its children; so that in most places where it once flourished, our canonical order—instituted not by men nor through men, but by God—has been reduced almost to nothing.

CHAPTER II. From Whom the Canonical Order Arose.

It flourished prefiguratively in Aaron’s priesthood and Levitical ministry; in Christ, His apostles and disciples, and in those first believers themselves, in whom there was one heart and one soul in God, it brought forth the fruit of sweetness and salvation. In the holy Roman pontiffs, from blessed Peter the Apostle down to Pope and Martyr Urban, the sixteenth after him [Col. 1093C], and in almost all the clergy of those times—as that same blessed Pope Urban testifies—it brought forth to the world the shoot of righteousness’ planting; and afterward likewise in the holy confessors and pontiffs Hilary, Ambrose, and Augustine.

CHAPTER III. On Its Rivals.

It had indeed died some time ago, but came to life again; it had perished, but was found. Through its music and choirs, behold, the house of the Church is now gladdened. Therefore our brethren the monks ought to rejoice, and not insult this order as it dies in some of its members, nor seize the inheritance of one half alive. If its enemy—the assembly, that is, of acephalous clerics [perhaps “headless” clerics]—had cursed it, it would surely have borne it; and if he who hated it, seeking his own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ, had spoken great things against it, perhaps it would have hidden itself from him. But now the sons of its mother fight against it; and the man who was its guide and intimate companion, of one mind with it, who together with it took sweet food from the word of God and walked in the house of God in harmony (Psalm 54 [55]), its man of peace in whom it trusted, has greatly increased his treachery against it (Psalm 40 [41]); so that it may now say with the Apostle: “I can glory not only in dangers from the Gentiles, but also in dangers from my own people and dangers from false brethren” (2 Corinthians 11) [Col. 1094A].

But let the mark of false brotherhood be laid only upon those who, having no compassion, not only do not restore to their brother his wandering ox or ass, but even endeavor to steal it away; who not only do not help a brother wounded and left half dead by robbers (Luke 10), but inflict wound upon wound; and who do to others what they would not have done to themselves, while they endeavor to withdraw their sons and disciples from those masters under whom they could have been saved and attract them to themselves—as though Christ were among them alone, as though the kingdom of God had proceeded from them or come to them alone. Thus one almost hears it said, as it was said once in times of heresy: “Behold, here is Christ,” or “Behold, He is there” (Matthew 24) [Col. 1094B].

But we do not wish to go, nor shall we follow. For Christ is not so poor or so harsh as to have only monks who live by the labor of their hands; as to delight in the deadly cold of those lacking a garment of skins, or to desire that His servants be burdened to collapse by a multitude of woolen tunics, or to command them to be bitten by multiplied worms—all of which are practices of bodily destruction through their very use, with no sparing of the body. But in the house of God are many dwellings, and the Lord knows those who are His (2 Timothy 2); and let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity. And pure and undefiled religion is this: to visit the sick, orphans, and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained from this world (James 1) [Col. 1094C].

Certainly, insofar as our lords and brethren the monks, whatever color of clothing they use, share with us in these and other observances of true religion and exercises of piety—whether they go before us, accompany us, or follow after those who go before—they are truly our lords and brethren. And we love all among them who are wise and recognize their brethren and household; who, as cherubim and seraphim in heaven, so on earth sing with us in harmonious unison, “Holy, Holy, Holy,” and celebrate the God of Hosts in shared rejoicing.

Nor do we envy them their flight of six wings under the name of seraphim [Col. 1094D], provided they also permit the canonical order, under the name of cherubim, to join them in shared rejoicing. Otherwise—to say nothing of cherubim and seraphim—they cannot even be reckoned among the company of angels. For the kingdom of heaven does not belong to the proud, who boast of their supposedly surpassing holiness in disparagement of others, chanting a superlative “Holy of holies, Most Holy,” and thus disturbing the Church’s harmonious accord. It belongs to little ones and the humble; and whoever wishes to become greater in it must become the least of all, the servant of all [Col. 1095A].

Now, since it is necessary to boast, though it is not expedient, let the canonical order also boast—but boast not in itself, but in the Lord—and say: “In whatever anyone dares, I speak foolishly, I dare also. Are they followers of Christ’s poverty? So am I. Are they emulators of apostolic perfection? So am I. Are they professed adherents and observers of the common and cenobitic life? So am I.”

CHAPTER IV. On the Glory of Tribulation.

“Are they ministers of Christ? I speak as one less worthy, yet wisely: I am more so. In many labors, more abundantly in prisons, beyond measure in beatings, frequently in deaths. From Jews and Gentiles alike I have been handled countless times with scorpions and bull-whips, weighted scourges and lashes; I have often been beaten with rods, more often stoned, suffered shipwreck, often given over to fire, often immersed in water, often exposed to beasts, a hundred times raised upon the rack, a hundred times stretched upon the scaffold, often endured iron combs, more than once roasted on the gridiron, and a thousand times subjected to the sword. Often in journeys: dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from my own people, dangers from Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, dangers at sea, dangers from false brethren; in labor, hardship, many vigils, hunger and thirst, many fastings, cold and nakedness” (2 Corinthians 6) [Col. 1095B]. “Besides those things that are without, my daily pressure: concern for all the churches.” In all these labors, dangers, distresses, and sufferings, it is clear how this has been manifested in priests and Levites and in other confessors and martyrs of Christ belonging to my profession, in time of persecution [Col. 1095C].

CHAPTER V. Monks Brought Forth in Solitude.

For when, in the time of persecution, it sought the wilderness, necessity having been turned into choice, the monastic order was at last brought forth and grew strong. But if it recognized itself as the son of priest and confessor, why should the son, however vigorous and noble, exalt himself above his parent’s head, virtue, dignity, and nobility? Or how do we all call upon one Father, God? Yet we are all brethren: we are two, namely the canonical and monastic orders, like two brothers born of the same womb, true sons of Jacob. Of them that same patriarch Jacob said to his ten sons: “You know,” he said, “that my wife bore me two sons. One went out, and you said: ‘A beast has devoured him’; and until now he has not appeared. If you take this Benjamin also, and any misfortune befall him on the way, you will bring down my gray hairs in sorrow to the underworld” (Genesis 44) [Col. 1095D].

Let us be, I say, two orders, like these two sons of the patriarch Jacob: brothers born of the same womb, both sprung from one noble mother Rachel, both eager to behold truth and pursue piety. And let me, the canonical order, be—as has already been said—the elder Joseph, growing in priestly dignity and ecclesiastical governance for the Lord; while let the younger monastic order be Benjamin, who was called by his mother “son of sorrow,” but by his father “son of the right hand” (Genesis 35). For Mother Church, in the sorrow of her suffering, as said above, and of her death, turned love of solitude and necessity into choice for him. Yet by the Father he was accounted a beloved son of the right hand, as heir of eternal goods. For I, Joseph, the elder of these sons—that is, the canonical order—was sold into Egypt by my brethren during the time of persecution, and endured prisons, when the iron of manifold suffering passed through both my soul and flesh, until my word reached the testimony appointed by God and the world was brought beneath the yoke of faith [Col. 1096A].

CHAPTER VI. Canons Nourished with Joseph in Egypt.

But in the time of Pope Sylvester and Emperor Constantine, when peace was restored to the Churches of God through that devout prince, and when in the aforesaid pope and the clergy I was wonderfully exalted even among men, I was not merely brought out of prison like another Joseph: I also sat in Pharaoh’s chariot and became lord of Egypt, prince of the world, and ruler of kingdoms. This was almost fulfilled historically and literally in Pope Sylvester himself, when the emperor, as he sat upon an imperial horse in the city of Rome, performed for him the office of groom through the middle of the city [Col. 1096B].

CHAPTER VII. On the Persecution of Heresies.

But in the time of heresies, who was weak, and I was not weak? Who was scandalized, and I did not burn? [Col. 1096C] (II Cor. XI). Meanwhile, I—Joseph, the firstborn of the true Jacob and Rachel—was devoured by a most evil beast. For at that time too, in my Hilary and Athanasius and the other bishops, priests, and ministers of that age, I was driven into exile and, innocent, cast into the pit. But when the impious king Constantius died in the midst of this departure, and Julian the Apostate, the true Antichrist, was removed from among us—he who was also crushed without hand and slain by the Spirit of God’s mouth—the kings again sent for me and released me; the princes of the peoples dismissed me. At that time likewise, through my archimandrites Hilary, Augustine, Ambrose, and the other teachers of my school, such an abundance of spiritual crops, gathered from the nations, was stored [Col. 1096D] in the granaries of Egypt, in the libraries of the Church, that it even now suffices to repel the famine and want of this age.

But, as someone says:

> Nothing is blessed in every respect.  
> —Horace

For, as has been said, once peace for God’s Churches, together with an abundance of riches and the glory of dignities, had been restored, secular display and the vanity of this world again devoured me, the canonical order, Rachel’s firstborn, as has been said. Thus the heavenly Father may rightly say over me in lament: “A most evil beast has devoured my son Joseph” (Gen. XXXVII). Meanwhile, as charity grows cold and iniquity abounds, Benjamin also—that is, the monastic order—being absent from his father [Col. 1097A], sets out as a stranger for the Egypt of this world, and Father Jacob’s sorrow is increased.

But behold: in our time, by God’s disposition, the canonical order flourishes, and it is announced to my father, the true Jacob, that his son Joseph lives. And he, as though awakening from a heavy sleep, says: “If my son Joseph still lives, it is enough for me: I shall go and see him before I die” (Gen. XLV). That is to say: If I see my canonical order living, then in a sense I shall not die in my posterity. Yet even now, though revived and flourishing, it is not easy to set forth briefly how much I, the canonical order, have suffered from impious kings in these last times for the defense of ecclesiastical liberty.

## CHAPTER VIII. On persecutions of canons

[Col. 1097B]

Indeed, amid the disturbance of the schism, in my Erlebaldo of Milan I endured the horror of death; in Popes Gregory VII and Urban, persecution. In Pope Paschal and his clergy, in Manegold of Lautenbach, and in many others, I was captured and imprisoned. In my Eppo of Salzburg I was deprived of my eyes. In the brethren of Passau, of the church of Saint Nicholas, and in many others, I suffered persecutions. Moreover, to the horror of those who saw it, in some members of the aforementioned household I was beaten with rods, when, as in the time of Mattathias Maccabee, each of my people, fleeing the defilements of excommunication by which the princes of that time were bound, could scarcely [Col. 1097C] appear in public without immediately being denounced by everyone as an abominable monster.

Nevertheless, this little flock of mine did not thereby lose confidence in the truth that reigns; but, confessing the truth before kings and princes, it was not ashamed of Christ’s words. Therefore the heavenly Father will not be ashamed of it. Yet in that tempest my brother, the monastic order, consulting its own repose, either kept itself within the enclosure of its own silence or—what was worse—even assented to iniquity, while I, the canonical order, struggled in my sons, privately and publicly, unto death. For who then was scandalized, and I was not weak? (II Cor. XI). If it is necessary to boast, though it is not expedient, I shall come to visions and revelations of God.

I know some persons of my institution, still living in the flesh, who wear not woolen but linen tunics and shirts, taking care that their dress not be conspicuous, and seeking to please by their conduct rather than their clothing. Amid zeal for fasting, reading, prayer, and the other practices of spiritual exercises, they have more frequently and for longer periods inhaled with their nostrils paradisal fragrances; sometimes, carried beyond bodily sensation, they have heard with a most divine hearing sounds of heavenly hymnody, full of honeyed sweetness. At times, amid songs of God’s love and praise, they have inwardly received in their souls the kisses of God’s word; at the perceptible touch of the spiritual Bridegroom, stirring them to spiritual work, their bellies have often [Col. 1098A] trembled. To their spiritual eyes, golden pendants inlaid with silver were many times made by the friends of the Bridegroom: that is, visible forms, corresponding to the spiritual gift bestowed upon them, were shown to their minds through the ministry of angels.

I know such a man, a disciple of my school, still living in the flesh: Theophilus, fourteen years ago. Having entered into agony and singing psalms and hymns at length (Luke XXII), amid paradisal fragrances he was caught up into an unfamiliar trembling of flesh and spirit exulting in God, so powerful and sweet that, because of its power, his soul could scarcely contain itself within the sheath of flesh; and because of its sweetness, being almost dissolved, it might have dwelt in paradise. Thus he may not vainly boast [Col. 1098B] that he was anticipated by blessings of sweetness and crowned at the gate of paradise.

And I know such a man who, after public and private vigils, prayers, and morning praises, wished, in bitterness of soul, while seated within the enclosure of the cloister in a place apart from the congregation of brethren, to give his limbs to rest. While his heart was awake, he was divinely put to sleep, and received from the Lord no small experience of that miracle which was shown to the disciples sitting in the upper room on the fiftieth day after the Resurrection. For suddenly he heard a sound from heaven, as of a mighty wind (Acts II), which began gently, grew stronger, approached the house in which he was, and poured itself in through the window beside the seated man’s head. In the rush of that spirit, a certain fiery substance—not burning, but shining, like an alloy of gold or brass in a furnace—struck with great force against that window, which was glazed with glass. Entering within, it immediately dissolved as though into a thin mist and filled the whole house where he sat. The atoms of that mist, full of sweetness and blessing, poured themselves with a certain force into the body and soul of the seated man through every pore, until the force of this river, abundantly filling his soul, had made the city glad. Then he too, returning to himself, went away within himself into a holy fullness, wondering and praising God, who thus consoled him. For a long time afterward he perceived, even in the outermost [Col. 1098D] parts of his body, the sweetness of so great a fullness and the fullness of such sweetness. The grace of this experience, not idle, has continued to stir him toward holy pursuits; as he himself is accustomed to confess in his secret communings in Christ, he perseveres, walking in the strength of that food amid the temptations of this life to the present day, and, as he hopes, will walk in it until the end of a good consummation. “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change nor shadow of turning” (James I).

There is also another member of my household, of my institution, from whose mouth certain persons of undoubted faith saw something like a fiery tongue continually proceed while he expounded the word of God in church; he himself, however, felt nothing except a good grace from God in speaking.

[Col. 1099A]

At another time, the finger of an invisible hand was seen continually marking that same man’s mouth with the sign of the cross as he expounded the word of God. At another time, having entered into agony and praying at length (Luke XXII), he experienced, in no small miracle, the power and grace of what seemed like sparks coursing through him and especially filling his face.

On a feast day of blessed Ambrose, while he was celebrating the solemnities of Mass, blessed Ambrose himself was seen standing beside him as he offered the sacrifice, and consecrating the offering together with him.

At another time, while he stood more deeply absorbed at the altar [MS. “altius,” perhaps *altari*], about to celebrate Mass, when the Canon and the actions of the heavenly mysteries had been reached, something like fire was seen rising about him. Gradually increasing, it finally enveloped the whole priest [Col. 1099B], so that nothing but fire could have been seen in him. And, wonderful to tell, the wall which stood between did not prevent a certain faithful person, to whom this was granted, from seeing it: in a double miracle, both in what was seen and in the seer, the divine fire appeared through the obstacle of the wall no differently than if nothing intervened.

At another time something secret concerning this same priest was revealed to the same person of good faith and love, which perhaps is not unworthy to be known. This priest was among the tents of Kedar, surrounded by the darkness of what appeared to be some alien wickedness. To keep silence concerning it would have been unsafe for him, so far as God was concerned; yet to expose it was not possible without danger of persecution. [Col. 1099C] And as he spoke of this matter among his own people, declaring with intense grief of heart that each alternative was praiseworthy—namely, when no cause existed, or when the cause for which one must fight was altogether hidden, to enjoy peace in Christ; and, when the cause required it, to suffer persecutions for Christ’s sake—he distinguished, in accordance with the saying of the Wise Man, “a time of peace and a time of war.” The intermediate sluggishness, in which neither peace is secure nor persecution glorious, he declared must be wholly rejected by an ecclesiastical man, lest he himself deserve to be rejected by the Lord, who says to the angel of the church of Laodicea: “Would that you were either cold or hot. But because you are neither cold nor hot, I shall begin to vomit you out of my mouth” (Apoc. III).

While, I say, [Col. 1099D] the aforementioned priest spoke such things and encouraged himself by these and other like words to endure persecution, the aforesaid person, not ignorant of Christ and of this priest beloved in Christ, and devoutly reflecting in faith that Christ both exists and speaks in his chosen ones, while contemplating the man’s abundant speech conceived the desire to wish and say in his heart: “Oh, if only I might be able to recognize some visible proof of Christ dwelling and speaking in you!” And while he revolved this thought within himself in silent meditation, the speaker’s face became radiant with the Lord, like that of Moses, and was clothed with a certain divine splendor of countenance (Matt. XVII); beyond perhaps what can be spoken or believed, it was changed into the radiant [Col. 1100A] and glorious face of Christ himself. Thus the aforementioned person, beholding and greatly delighting in these things, was not disappointed of his pious desire, by which he had longed to see Christ in his priest. Meanwhile the priest himself experienced nothing but a certain divine fervor of good zeal within himself, though greater than usual—just as, while sacrificing, he perceived no other thing around him than the good grace of God present within him.

And these are your gifts, Christ; this is the abundance of your gifts toward us, Holy Spirit, God the Paraclete. You so comfort the humble that you are accustomed to offer strong drink to those who mourn, according to what your mother asked of you, O Lemuel—that is, “man in whom God is,” Lord Jesus Christ—saying: “Do not, O Lemuel, do not give wine to kings, because there is no secret where drunkenness reigns, [Col. 1100B] lest perhaps they drink and forget judgments and alter the cause of the sons of the poor. Give,” she says, “strong drink to those who mourn, and wine to those bitter in soul. Let them drink and forget their poverty, and remember their sorrow no more” (Prov. XXXI). It is not now necessary to discuss these words one by one.

And I give thanks to you, Lord God, Father of heaven and earth, who have hidden these things from the wise and prudent—that is, from kings, or from those already mentioned who possess the consolations of this world, neither seeking this consolation nor able providently to receive it—but have revealed them to little ones (Matt. XI). Thus it pleased you. Even in such outwardly appearing visitations, which declare the Holy Spirit’s presence, you visibly work within holy souls, while, according to the form of these visions, you infuse into them some spiritual gifts—for example, a word of wisdom and knowledge, steadfastness in strength, or another such gift. In these your humble ones possess consolations, and, while they are exercised in them, forget their poverty and remember their sorrow no more. Through those who speak or write, when any of the others hears the voice of the Holy Spirit, he does not know whence it comes or whither it goes [Col. 1100C] (John III).

But I refrain from boasting of such things; for it is not expedient, lest it perhaps be said to me: “Behold, the dreamer comes; come, let us kill him” (Gen. XXXVII). Indeed, even while I kept silence and served the Lord in humility, certain evil husbandmen said to me: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Matt. XXI). For in episcopal sees the black or gray monastic order, clothed in trousers or stripped of them, is not feared; nor is the clergy, dressed in woolen tunics, so feared as an innovation that it should sit in those sees as the legitimate heir. But among my household—clothed in wool and skins for necessity, and in linen both for the dignity of their order and for the significance of the mystery—the white linen of Aaron’s garments and the white tunic of the apostle James are greatly feared. Hence it is said of him as well: “This is the heir,” and so forth. Nor should my sheep, that is, the souls of my household, therefore abhor the dress of their innocence because they have seen very many wolves clothed in it, since the Lord is powerful to make lambs from wolves, or, having expelled wolves, to bring in lambs.

[Col. 1101A]

Perhaps the devil hates this too in that order: that, after the likeness of the apostles’ primitive institution, it has been so moderately and communally established for all that not only companies of men but also companies of women live together in their respective groups, separated by fitting enclosure; little boys and girls also, old people together with the young, praise the name of the Lord (Ps. CXLVIII). As was foretold through Isaiah in a figure, the lion with the kid, the calf also with the bear, and the wolf with the lamb were to dwell together, and their young likewise were to rest together (Isa. XI). Thus our true Jacob moderates the progress of his journey according to what he sees his flocks and little ones can bear; for if he compelled them to labor beyond measure in walking, all the flocks would die in one day.

And while Moses—my household men, true Israelites—sings to the Lord, gloriously magnified, especially as they lead the choirs of common life together with women, the musical melody celebrates the song, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified” (Exod. XV). One might see them standing near the Lord’s cross: on this side the disciple in the male sex, on that side the woman in the female sex, committed to the disciple. Let princes see and be angry; let pains seize the inhabitants of Philistia; let trembling seize Moab; let the inhabitants of Canaan grow stiff with fear; let dread and terror fall upon them, O God, by the greatness of your arm, while true [Col. 1101C] Israel, led by you, advances toward the land of promise, terrible as an army drawn up in battle array (II Paral. XX).

Perhaps the devil, the enemy of every good, also hates in my household the fact that, according to the Lord’s command, they zealously guard against a twofold leaven.
