On the one hand, they abstain from the pomp and allurements of worldly excess, as from Herod’s leaven; on the other, they guard against the superstition of novelty, as against the leaven of the Pharisees (Matt. XVI), judging that the Church’s ancient usage must be maintained in dress as well as in abstinence, fasting, and the forms of divine offices. They do not easily turn either to the right or to the left, so that, in accordance with the careful injunction of Father Augustine’s rule, they appear to avoid making their dress conspicuous, whether in softness or austerity, whether in costly or cheap clothing.

## CHAPTER IX. On tonsure

For in the tonsures or shavings of their heads, my household members of whom I speak, made participants in royal and priestly anointing, desire also to be marked in visible form as belonging to Christ their head, the supreme King and true Priest, whom God the Lord anointed as king, priest, and prophet above his fellows. Therefore they do not merely shave a small circle at the crown of the head, as was once the custom of heretics—a misuse that persists among some even to this day—but, according to the determination of the Fathers, shave the whole upper part of the head, leaving below only the circular crown. Thus the shaved or flat portion of the head represents the priestly tiara, while the circle of hair displays the emblem of the royal crown. This is so that no one among them, like Absalom, may be made conspicuous by burdensome long hair while also weighed down by the mass of sins; nor may he go about, after the manner of Jews who still have a veil over their heart, not crowned and mitred but covered in skins.

[Col. 1102A]

Now, as has been said, the shaved part of the head is rightly in us a sign of priestly holiness: just as no intervening obstacle lies between the crown of our head and heaven, so no hindering concern should be able, at the time of prayer, to cover our mind, stripped of earthly cares, and prevent it from clinging immediately to God.

Yet although in these matters we do not wage war according to the flesh, we nevertheless walk in the flesh. In it, as our heavenly Father knows, we need all earthly supports. In the perfect man it is fitting that these same earthly supports be subordinated to the mind’s proper dignity, according to the saying: “His left hand is under my head” (Cant. II). That is, they should not burden or darken the mind, but crown the ordering of prudent disposition, so that, by wisely contemplating on the one hand and prudently arranging or acting on the other, they may rightly be adorned with the insignia of a priestly kingdom.

But since this perfection and the preservation of perfection are not the work of one day, for the hairs of our affections, not uprooted from the root but shaved by the razor of holiness once undertaken, grow again from the remnants of our wretched mind innate and remaining in us. This happens when, making provision for the flesh or managing temporal matters, we exceed the limits of necessity and multiply cares that burden the mind, according to what is written: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. IX). Hence the frequent renewal necessary to us through daily repentance and mutual confession, in which our youth is renewed like the eagle’s. The Psalmist, seeking this, says: “I was exercised, and I swept out my spirit” (Ps. LXXVI). For the sake of this inward renewal, according to the Lord’s saying, “Cleanse what is within, and what is without shall be clean” (Matt. XXIII), we also customarily admit frequent renewals to the heads of our bodies by washing, razor, and scissors, so that in this respect too the hands of the priestly or clerical order, as of the Church’s Bridegroom, may be “turned,” golden through mystical heavenly meanings and full of hyacinths (Cant. V).

[Col. 1102D]

Once this pattern of the heavenly coinage has been well begun in us, it belongs to the diligence of the father of the monastery, lest it be disfigured through the negligence of barber or shaver, to inspect the heads at every time of shaving, or to entrust the faults of the tonsure, to be examined and corrected, to another diligent inspector. He will see to it that the whole upper part of the monk’s head is shaved, that the lower edge of the crown reaches only the top of the ears, and that the entire ear remains uncovered.

We derive this form of tonsure or shaving, after its legal authority among the Nazirites and evangelical authority among the apostles, also from the Third Council of Toledo, whose fortieth canon reads as follows:

> “All clerics and readers, like Levites and priests, having shaved the entire upper part of the head, shall leave below only the circular crown. They shall not do as readers appear hitherto to do in parts of Gaul, where, like laymen, with long hair they shave a small circle only at the top of the head. For this rite has hitherto been that of heretics in Spain. Therefore, for the removal of scandal from the Church, this mark of disgrace ought to be removed, and there should be one uniform tonsure or habit, as is the usage of all Spain. Whoever does not observe this shall be guilty against the Catholic faith.” [Col. 1103B]

## CHAPTER X. On surplices

Likewise, in the white linen, full-length and ample garment which we call the surplice, retaining the Church’s ancient usage and displaying in it the pattern of the Lord’s cross, they admit nothing novel. In the whiteness of the linen garment they signify innocence of life and purity of flesh achieved by much chastisement; in its fullness, the generosity of charity; and in its length down to the ankle, perseverance in good work unto the end. At the same time they show themselves blessed and peaceable, because Roman nobles too formerly wore the full-length toga in peace.

The tongue or flap of this tunic is always loose and open, showing that we should always be ready to give an answer and teaching to one who asks us for a reason; to refute opponents; and to be useful in speech for edification, teaching and instructing at every time of speaking. But the tongue or flap of the shirt is always closed and fastened upward, signifying the perpetual guard or closure of our heart and mouth against idle talk and evil speech. Indeed, we must sometimes abstain even from edifying conversations for the sake of silence, so that we may truly say to the Lord: “My secret is for myself; my secret is for myself” (Isa. XXIV); and again, “I was dumb and silent even from good things” (Ps. XXXVIII); and: “I set a guard upon my mouth when the sinner stood against me” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XI. On the shirt

[Col. 1103D]

For I have seldom repented of having kept silence; often it has harmed me to have spoken. Death and life also are in the hand of the tongue, and “the man who does not offend in word is a perfect man.” “No human being has been able to tame the tongue” (James III). Yet what is impossible with men is undoubtedly possible with God (Matt. XIX). Therefore the tongue or flap of our heart and mouth is fastened upward, so that in the measure in which it is closed against earthly and human speech, it may be opened to the secrets of divine utterances and soliloquies with God. For as man does not live by bread alone but by every word proceeding from God’s mouth (Matt. IV), so the tongue is shut as a minister not only of human utterance but also of divine speech or converse [Col. 1104A]. Nor does it refuse an immoderate silence among human beings, since it has been granted to mingle in conversation with God and angels through prayer.

## CHAPTER XII. On the fur garment and cowl

Certainly, what is called the tongue or *snalla* on the fur tunic seems to pertain not so much to mystical meanings as to practical necessity. But the cowl, a woolen garment belonging to our habit, which Augustine, the steward of my household, calls a *birrus*, encloses and wraps the body on every side in a black, almost funereal covering, and signifies in us the humility of mortification and renunciation of the world. For just as one clothed in a cowl is in a sense shut out from the world and almost sepulchrally enclosed within himself, so that he cannot easily look backward, free his hands to fight or strike back, or stretch them out to worldly embraces—for this garment, shortened and narrowed, cannot be opened on either side—so my household members should remember that they must live as dead to the world and removed from all worldly displays, works, and allurements.

We use this garment almost daily, but especially during Lent or penitential times, so that we may know that we ought to be not only righteous but also penitents for our daily sins. Furthermore, if you count the two wings of this garment covering us on either side with the four parts of the full-length tunic—namely, front and back and the two sleeves—you will find in the holy character of our own habit what you wonder at in the flight of the six-winged cherubim. [Col. 1104C]

## CHAPTER XIII. On the form of fasting

In fasts and abstinences too, striving to retain the Church’s ancient observance, they discipline themselves at times by fasts of two or three days, and at times even by daily fasts. Easter and the other chief feasts of the Lord, as also the celebrated feasts of apostles and martyrs, are excepted from the observance of fasting on account of the twofold meal. Thus, even according to the flesh, they share for the time being in the mystery of the festal joy of those whose sufferings and sorrow they seem to have mourned in the preceding vigils and fasts, lest they appear vainly to profess in the Apostles’ Creed the communion of saints, whose sufferings they do not share in sorrow and whose joy they do not share in rejoicing.

## CHAPTER XIV. On abstinence from meat

It must also be said that it is good not to eat meat. Thus in common refectories they abstain from its consumption, yet they do not deny its use to the sick until their strength is restored, nor to children, the weak, or guests at suitable times and places.

Neither have they forbidden poorer monasteries, less well supplied with fish and milk, to use animal fat as seasoning [Col. 1105A] for vegetables and legumes on alternate days. They judge that the resources of possibility must be weighed not only in individuals but in communities as well. Yet they do not condemn other cenobites who abstain wholly from these things, deny such consolations to their sick and children, and bind guests to the strict observance of regular abstinence, although they charge them with a certain lack of discretion because they exceed the limits fixed by the Fathers. For anyone in our age wishing to be holier, better, wiser, and more discerning than Augustine and Benedict is to be reckoned as belonging to superstition rather than religion, since it is enough for the disciple to be like his master, lest he be marked by that apostolic rebuke: “Do not touch; do not even handle,” and so forth (Col. II).

## CHAPTER XV. On the grace of certain Churches

Nor, constrained by apostolic holiness, do we dare to despise those who eat meat and moderately permit its use once or twice a week at the tables of regular brethren, especially if they live in regions where the greater number of brethren of the same order, who live more strictly, do not require otherwise. For while in every profession the better are to be imitated, just as I consider it a kind of superstition for some monastery presumptuously to dictate new regular precepts and not to be encouraged by the examples of its elders, so I judge it shameful for others to remain below the good custom [Col. 1105C] preserved among them, especially if no reasonable cause exists requiring this to be done.

## CHAPTER XVI. On silence

Knowing too, my scholars, that silence is a practice of piety, at night and by day, at times assigned to the divine office or reading, and in secluded places—that is, the oratory, dormitory, and refectory—they so strive after silence that they restrain their tongues even from good speech, unless the superior must arrange something. Even then he shall arrange it, so far as possible, in fewer words and with less noise.

## CHAPTER XVII. On manual work

[Col. 1105D]

While seated at their work, my household members keep silence from morning until Terce, unless the necessity of the work requires someone to speak. I strive so to regulate such speech that the practice of piety—that is, silence—is not excluded, while each person speaks without vocal noise with the fellow worker beside him solely about what is necessary for the work. So, as the Gospel relates, Martha called her sister Mary quietly, saying: “The Master is here” (John XI), where both fewness of words and moderation of voice did not exclude the grace of silence. But if anyone considers that more must be said, he shall lead outside the gathering of workers the person with whom he must speak, unless perhaps the superior judges that something should be said to all in common.

After prayers also, once Mass has been completed, if the arrangement of time permits—and provided it is not a day of regular fasting—they likewise sit at their work until Sext. From Sext they devote themselves to reading until None, unless, during summer days, some of this time must be taken away for the midday rest and rest for the eyes. For if it is a day of two meals, they are to devote themselves to reading either in the morning before Prime, as is customary for some, who also delay Prime until the second hour; or, after Mass has been said, before Sext. But after the brethren have eaten following Sext, together with those serving the tables, and after the midday rest on summer days, once None has also been said, they are to assemble for work, whether in the garden or wherever necessary. The same is to be done if the brethren have eaten after None. [Col. 1106B]

## CHAPTER XVIII. That we should not speak German

In this work, indeed, we believe that it pertains both to propriety and to the purpose of the exercise that they should converse about matters of necessity and usefulness not in the vernacular but in Latin. All must jointly guard against much talking or idle talk beginning to spread, or any frivolous word being heard. If anyone, after warning, does not immediately cease from such things, he shall be subject to regular discipline. But if something concerning the divine office must be discussed, they shall do so briefly, either sitting in chapter, after chapter, or at least after None, once *Benedicite* has been said, and standing. If external work is lacking even after None, they shall sit diligently at their work until Vespers, as in the morning.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the signals for the hours

So that the course of our daily regimen may proceed properly and in order, they take no little care to observe the signals of the hours and ring them at the proper time. Thus they rise for the nocturnal vigils at midnight; in winter, Prime is rung at the first dawning of day, but in summer as soon as the sun has risen; in winter Terce is rung near the end of the third hour, but in summer around the middle of that hour, so that time may remain from the end of Mass, which follows Terce, for reading until Sext. Sext itself is not to be rung before the beginning of that hour, lest the time for reading be excluded, cut short beforehand or afterward, and the regimen of the divine office be, as it were, blind.

For reading after prayers and the Lord’s praises is a certain eye of this regimen of ours; if it is absent or dark, the whole body of the regimen will be dark in that respect. Likewise, it is judged maimed if those able to work neglect manual labor.

None too is to be rung, on days free from labor, when the hour itself begins; on other days, when the eighth hour has passed its middle, so that sleep during summer days may be shortened and the meal on fasting days may be brought forward in winter for the sake of weaker age or sex. Yet it must not be rung before the beginning of the hour itself. Vespers likewise is to be rung during summer days when the eleventh hour begins; in winter, when daylight begins to fail those doing work. After Vespers, where the community must proceed or sit, two or three lanterns are to be brought according to the size of the gathering. [Col. 1107A]

## CHAPTER XX. On the singing of psalmody

In psalmody also I prescribe this: that it be performed moderately—that is, neither too quickly nor too slowly—yet with articulation and according to the tones, and not in a voice too lax or too loud. It will also belong to the ruler of the order, sometimes to omit the silence of the medial division and sing more rapidly for the gathering of the people or another reasonable cause; or, when the people are absent, to prolong it somewhat for the sake of solemnity. For this seems also to be the point of the command of the Law in which the Lord said to Moses: “When a prolonged and a short trumpet blast sounds, the camp shall move” (Num. X). And a few verses later: “But,” he says, “when the people are to be assembled, there shall be a simple sound of the trumpets, and they shall not sound a short alarm” (ibid.).

Just as I do not require a multiplication of familiar psalms, so neither do I forbid speaking in tongues in such matters. I especially approve that those who sing psalms and pray should take pains that what is uttered by the mouth be turned over in the mind; and that the exercise of work and reading, or the turtledove sacrifice of secret prayer, not be excluded by a prolonged common recitation of prayer and psalmody, since these things ought to be done and those not omitted. [Col. 1107C]

## CHAPTER XXI. When prayer is to be made

Our work, as has been said, is arranged in the morning and before the meal so as to consist of things that can be carried out indoors in silence and quiet. We do not expend that time on outside work unless some greater necessity requires it, knowing what the Apostle said to his disciple Timothy: “Exercise yourself unto godliness. For bodily exercise is useful for a little, but godliness is useful for all things, having promise not only of the life that now is, but also of that which is to come” (I Tim. IV). Nor are we unaware that Pope Sylvester established holidays for clerics for the same reason.

But neither should we despise rustic and servile tasks in their proper time, knowing that the Apostle worked with his own hands and commanded, saying: “If anyone does not work or labor, let him not eat” (II Thess. III). Therefore, lest idleness find a place among us, we urge the elderly, the weak, and those unable to work to sing psalms quietly; while we recall young and stronger persons who are able to work—if any withdraw themselves from work or distract others—to labor by the discipline of the rule, and especially by silence and fasting [Col. 1108A]. We also forbid young people to join one another at work or converse together, unless senior brethren are present as witnesses.

## CHAPTER XXII. On Fasting and Other Matters

Indeed, my own household customarily regulates its fasts and abstinences according to the most judicious prescription of Father Benedict, concerning which Augustine, steward of my household, spoke very briefly. From his institution they have likewise customarily borrowed the methods of excommunicating the disobedient and the beneficial midday rest during summer days, together with other practices established by him. This is almost my daily and my community’s occupation: fasting, abstinence, prayer, reading, and work; besides these, the care of everyone and the administration of many churches. While my household goes about laboring in these churches—preaching the word of God, visiting the sick, burying the dead, instructing catechumens, and baptizing—I consider my ministry no less acceptable to God than the monastic quiet or agricultural labor of monks [Col. 1108B]. Nor do I judge this fragrance of my garments to be so far inferior to the fragrance of prayers, since the Bridegroom himself says to the bride: “The fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense” (Song IV).

## CHAPTER XXIII. On Forbidding Private Property and Correcting Sins

Let those know themselves excluded from this defense of mine [Col. 1108C] who, under the profession of common life in the clergy, claim anything as private property for themselves; who, restless and talkative, pursue wandering idleness; and likewise those so-called monasteries which freely allow such conduct among them. Moreover, they let capital sins pass in them, as though unpunished, without an appropriate penalty and without what is called the greater penance, although punishment, if there is any, ought to be corrective. Unless, therefore, they take care to correct such persons justly, I exclude them from this defense of my sons.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On Receiving Clerics from Outside

In compensation for these more contemptible persons, I receive under the protection of my defense priests or clerics who live commendably even outside cenobitic enclosure while administering churches [Col. 1108D]. Bishop Prosper, follower of my steward Augustine, had previously received them under the patronage of our defense, writing as follows:

> [Note: [Col. 1107D] *On the Contemplative Life*, book II, chapter 11.] “A priest entrusted with the duty of stewardship should receive from the people, for distribution, not only without greed but even with praiseworthy piety; and he faithfully distributes what he has received, if he has either left all that was his or joined it to the possessions of the Church, and has placed himself among the poor out of love for poverty, so that from the same source from which he supplies the poor, he himself also lives as a voluntary poor man. Clerics likewise, whom either choice or birth has made poor, receive the necessities of life, whether living in their own houses or in a community, with perfection of virtue; for it is not desire of possession that leads them to receive these things, but the necessity of life compels them” [Col. 1109A].

Thus Prosper. Where he says “in their own houses,” this must be understood not of houses possessed by hereditary or proprietary right, but by ecclesiastical justice or benefice. Thus it is written of the disciple whom Jesus loved that he received the Lord’s mother “into his own” (John XIX). Yet he possessed nothing by proprietary right, but possessed, from the distribution of common goods, his own portion to administer, through a sharing disposition and use. Persons of this kind, then, are not only free from the bond of greed, but are also worthy of the praise of perfection belonging to those who leave everything for Christ—provided, however, that they otherwise lead a life free from crimes and vices, devote themselves to ministry or leisure for the word, and do not lend assistance, through shared service and participation, to others in forbidden occupations, lest, with those with whom they have one communion, they also have a common cause [Col. 1109B].

Of such people, as Prosper himself seems to say, the Apostle says: “Those who labor in the sanctuary eat what belongs to the sanctuary, and those who serve at the altar share with the altar” (I Cor. IX). Unless he had meant this concerning those who have renounced their possessions, he would never confidently have added: “Thus God also ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live by the Gospel”: those who wish to have nothing of their own, who neither possess nor desire to possess, but are holders not of private goods but of common goods.

Accordingly, in keeping with Prosper’s reasonable teaching, which agrees with apostolic doctrine [Col. 1109C], it is not improper that priests and clerics living commendably even outside monasteries should be received under the protection of my defense.

I have taken care to sketch these matters concerning the daily course of the brethren, as common life speaking for itself in the clergy and glorying in the Lord. I have become foolish—but compelled by those who glory beyond measure in their singular holiness, striving to make one proselyte from the canonical to the monastic order; and, when they have made him, they will doubtless make him a son of Gehenna. He has condemnation because he has made void his first faith, and he is also shown disobedient to the holy Roman Church through Pope Urban II, who commands and says:

## CHAPTER XXV. That No Regular Canon Is to Become a Monk

We command—and, in commanding, usefully forbid—that no canon who has made regular profession be made a monk, unless, God forbid, he has publicly fallen. If anyone, presuming to act contrary to our decree, attempts to do so, we command that he return to the canonical order; afterward, as a memorial of his presumption, he shall wear the cowl as a memorial of his presumption, and remain last in choir [Col. 1109D].

And indeed there is among some dispute or uncertainty concerning this word: whether the command says that he should *wear* (*deferre*) or *lay aside* (*deserere*) the cowl. We do not contend over the word [Col. 1110A]; yet we know without doubt that Urban II himself, the giver of this command, and after him other Roman pontiffs, stripped the cowl from presumptuous persons of this kind.

Pope Innocent II agrees with this in a letter which he wrote in defense of our order, in these words:

> “INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable CONRAD, Archbishop of Salzburg: greeting and apostolic blessing.”
>
> “On the dignity and excellence of the life of canons,” etc. See Innocent II, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXIX, no. 565.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On Maintaining the Canonical Order

[Col. 1110B]

Likewise, the Council of Autun, supported no less by the authority of the Roman see, restrains the presumption of abbots and monks in such matters, saying:

> Let no abbot or monk presume to recall canons, as regulars, from the purpose of their canonical profession, or to receive them by drawing them into the monastic habit so that they may become monks, so long as they can find a church of their own order in which, living regularly and canonically, they are able to serve God and save their souls. But if they dare to undertake this by rash boldness, let them be bound by the bond of anathema.

These sayings of the Fathers, advanced with the weight of authority and reason, could suffice both to repress the presumption of monks [Col. 1110C] and to restrain the insolence of our own members, lest they “be carried about with every wind of doctrine” (Eph. IV), were it not that the love of their own superiority drives the former more vehemently, while the foolish desire to try novelty drives the latter. In this they are at once found transgressors of the Lord’s command, who instructed his followers not to go from house to house, but commanded that, whatever house they entered, they should remain in it (Luke X).

## CHAPTER XXVII. On Moderation in Abstinence

Perhaps among men holiness clad in rags, stripped of breeches and fur garments, and sweating in rustic labor seems more precious because it exempts neither the Lord’s days nor the apostles’ feast days from the severity of fasting [Col. 1110D]. But to me, and to anyone of sound understanding, it is a very small matter that we should be judged by men or by a human day. Nor do we judge ourselves; rather, we glory in the Lord, and this is our glory: the testimony of our conscience (II Cor. I). In accordance with the most divine command of the Lord, we avoid the leaven of Herod and the Pharisees (Mark VIII)—on the one side crimes, on the other superstitions. “Instead of the saltwort shall come up the fir tree, and instead of the nettle shall grow the myrtle” (Isa. LV), when divine contemplation and heavenly conduct succeed worldly greed, which fixes its roots in the stream of passing things; and when novice fervor transforms unrestrained abstinence, so that there need be no flight [Col. 1111A] in the winter of excessive rigor, nor on the Sabbath of worldly or Jewish laxity.

We have therefore been called to liberty, provided only that we do not make liberty an occasion for the flesh, but serve one another through charity. For neither a habit nor the lack of a fur garment or breeches is anything, but the keeping of God’s commandments. Nor is the kingdom of God food and drink, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit (Rom. XIV). Yet I rejoice meanwhile that the excessive deviation of some to the right exposes the excessive deviation of others to the left, and that in the meantime we too learn how firmly we ought to hold to divine commands, since we recognize others as self-restrained even for the sake of human institution. But one thing grieves me: that so much discretion is attributed to our Fathers Augustine and Benedict [Col. 1111B], while they themselves are represented as authors or teachers of such severity.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Having Linen and Fur Garments

For Father Augustine never forbade linen clothing among clerics; nor did Benedict, a most discerning man, take fur clothing away from his monastic disciples. Indeed, he himself used a sheepskin cloak (*melota*), and although in the Rule he spoke with regard to the climate of his own region, he nevertheless permitted monks a shaggy tunic in winter. What else, indeed, is the fur tunic which we customarily use but a shaggy tunic? For it is plainly shaggy, and it cannot be denied to be a tunic, since Genesis records [Col. 1111C] that the Lord gave Adam and his wife tunics of skins (Gen. III).

But let each person abound in his own judgment; and would that all things might be done for edification and not for the ruin of some! And if any think otherwise, God has revealed this also to them. Yet I have said these things not to disparage those brethren of whom I speak, who seem to me in almost all things worthy of admiration and praise for humility, holiness, and patience; among them I also reverence and embrace certain distinguished men as heavenly lights.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On Distinguished Authors

For just as in our order Hugh, magnificently illumined by the gift of knowledge, shone forth in our times [Col. 1111D] like the morning star; and just as, in the Cluniac order, Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, the renowned interpreter of nearly the entire Old and New Testament, adorns that golden order like a topaz; so Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, endowed with the gift of humility and wisdom, is in the Cistercian order a great light of the heavenly court and an outstanding ornament of that order. Likewise Norbert, archbishop, eminent in the gift of splendid learning, undoubtedly also shone as a brilliant light in the Church of God.

Yet those very persons among them whom I know to be wiser and whom I honor do not think differently from us in these matters. Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, disapproves of deserters from our order to his [Col. 1112A]; and Father Norbert, who introduced woolen tunics among clerics, afterward became a disapprover of his own institution. For when he was younger, he girded himself and went where he wished (John XXI), and by novice fervor and youthful vigor was thus led into that affectation. But when he had grown old and had become archbishop of the Church, yielding both to authority and to ancient custom, he himself accepted linen tunics, as though girded by another. He also instructed his disciples, who obeyed him, to wear them, desiring to effect this in all the clergy of his institution; but death forestalled him, and a custom received by many could not suddenly be removed. So much for these matters [Col. 1112B].

## CHAPTER XXX. On the Mystical Kinship of the Two Orders

Meanwhile, a certain trace of this saying appears to me in what the Lord foretold in John’s Apocalypse: “I will give to my two witnesses, and they shall prophesy for one thousand two hundred and sixty days, clothed in sackcloth” (Rev. XI). Since martyrs and confessors are rightly understood in the two witnesses, these two orders also—namely, clerics and monks—may not inappropriately be understood through them. Even in our time, by wisdom divinely given to them, their mouths have been opened to prophesy and preach the mystery of God; and this for one thousand two hundred and sixty days, that is, during that time [Col. 1112C] when the iniquity of Antichrist abounds.

That abundance of iniquity is signified by the excessive number 1,260, concerning which it is not now necessary to speak in detail. They prophesy and are clothed in sackcloth—that is, in every kind of penitential humiliation—which both clerics and monks also display outwardly in humble and lowly dress. In their gray and black, woolen and linen garments, they seek not splendor or softness, but what suffices necessity with propriety. They jointly ensure, indeed, that their dress is not conspicuous.

But perhaps someone may think that the canonical order follows after the monastic order. This is not surprising, for there is some difference between the two orders in profession and witness [Col. 1112D].

## CHAPTER XXXI. The Monk Is a Witness of the Lord’s Death

The monastic order, by mortifying itself to the world in mournful dress, proclaims to us Christ’s death and how we ought to die with him to vices and desires.

## CHAPTER XXXII. The Canonical Habit Is a Witness of the Resurrection

The clerical order, in white dress, shines with the angel as a witness of Christ’s resurrection, showing how, rising with Christ, we ought to walk in newness of life.

Perhaps the uninstructed also object to us because of the softness of wool in sheepskins [Col. 1113A], as though we appeared blameworthy in light of the Lord’s saying concerning John the Baptist’s clothing: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A man clothed in soft garments? Behold, those who wear soft garments are in kings’ houses” (Matt. XI). But they do not properly observe that in this saying the Lord reproves not every softness of clothing, but especially that softness accompanied by costliness: such as garments made of the skins of foreign mice, woven of silk, and other such things in which costliness joined with softness exceeds the simplicity and humility of Christian poverty.

Luke the evangelist indicates this more clearly, saying: “Behold, those who are in costly clothing and luxury are in kings’ houses” (Luke VII). Therefore, since Matthew the evangelist calls them soft garments, while Luke, as stated, calls them costly clothing, it is clear what softness in garments the Lord reproves. Thus the innocence which they strive to attack through the evangelist may also be defended through the evangelist, both in us and in monks who do not use costly dress [Col. 1113B].

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the Origin of Sacred Vestments

In sacred vestments, however, we admit costliness without blame; and those who rightly understand the monastic order customarily admit it as well. By adornments of this sort, possessing a mystical rationale, we fittingly cover the nakedness of our Noah, mocked upon the cross [Col. 1113C]. Moreover, by the beauty of such vestments we prefigure the glory of the future resurrection which shall be revealed in us (Rom. VIII), proceeding on the highest solemnities clothed in copes of rich cloth.

These two orders should run together in the Church as twins, witnesses of twin grace: neither should prefer itself to the other, but they should outdo one another in honor, although one may in some respects run ahead of the other.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the Running of the Two Disciples and of the Two Orders

This course is beautifully prefigured in the Gospel by the running of the two disciples, Peter and John. We know where it is written: “The two ran together, and that other disciple ran faster than Peter and came first to the tomb. Yet he did not enter, but, seeing the linen cloths, stood outside. Then Peter came following him, entered the tomb, and saw the linen cloths; and then the disciple who had come first to the tomb also entered” (John XX) [Col. 1113D].

Truly, a course worthy of the admiration of a spectacle! Two disciples of Christ run together: one loving more than the rest, the other more loved; one called from a wedding, the other from work upon the sea; one sweetly reclining on Christ’s breast, the other walking with Christ upon the waves of the sea; one a beholder of marvelous heavenly things, the other made a spectacle to the world; one more accustomed to quiet and contemplation, the other more ready for the ministry of the word. They ran together not only in that brief race to the tomb [Col. 1114A], but throughout the course of their lives. They ran together: one more vigorous in youthful body and mind, the other steadier through the gravity of age. They ran together, and the one who outran the other did not thereby prefer himself to him, but rendered to the elder the precedence in recognizing mysteries. For though he came first to the tomb, he did not enter, but, seeing the linen cloths, stood outside; Peter, however, following him and coming to the tomb, entered first.

## CHAPTER XXXV. An Allegorical Interpretation

In every person, intention and action run together: the one more beautiful and lovable, the other more patient and fruitful; the one free to attend to the word by seeing, the other devoted to ministry [Col. 1114B]. They run together; nor should intention, which runs ahead of the ministry of the word, therefore be judged the worthier. For often in the ministry of the word mysteries are revealed which, before the ministry, when contemplation alone existed, lay hidden. This is Peter’s entering the tomb first; hence the saying: “The unfolding of your words gives light and gives understanding to the little ones” (Ps. CXVIII).

Nor should we reason from Mary’s part being preferred by the Lord to Martha’s part that intention is worthier than ministry of the word. Otherwise Peter, recognizing through contemplation in the sheet-vessel the ministry of the salvation of the Gentiles, would have to be judged worthier than himself when preaching the word of life to Cornelius—an enormous absurdity. Especially since Peter executed in the ministry of action nothing other than what the preceding contemplative vision taught him; whether that vision was merely a sign of the action, or even its efficient cause, I do not know [Col. 1114C].

Thus the rest of Mary listening seems worthier than the office of Christ preaching. Yet there is not much difference between Martha’s ministry and Christ’s: Christ refreshes by the word of life a soul that will live eternally, while Martha sustains with earthly bread flesh destined to die. Martha, serving, is anxious because she is troubled about many things while ministering to Christ; Mary is occupied with one thing and about the one thing necessary (Luke X).

Of this ministry Christ himself says: “I am among you as one who serves” (Luke XXII). Of the dignity of this ministry Peter says: “It is not right for us to leave the word of God and serve tables” (Acts VI). And Luke says in the Acts of the Apostles: “While the apostles were ministering and fasting, the Holy Spirit said: Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work,” etc. (Acts XIII). Again, at the beginning of his Gospel, Luke says: “As those who from the beginning themselves saw and were ministers of the word delivered them to us” (Luke I), joining vision to the ministry of the word as John to Peter [Col. 1114D].

But vision precedes the rationale of ministry in time, and John runs faster than Peter. And, lest you doubt that the intention or vision that comes first is signified in John, and the ministry of the word that follows in Peter, after the Lord’s resurrection, while seven disciples were fishing together, Jesus appeared to them and stood on the shore. The disciple whom Jesus loved, recognizing the Lord first, said to Peter: “It is the Lord.” Simon Peter, therefore, when he heard that it was the Lord, girded himself with his tunic—for he was naked—and threw himself into the sea. But the other disciples came by boat, dragging the net of fish (John XXI) [Col. 1115A].

Behold: the disciple whom Jesus loved recognized him first, yet did not throw himself into the sea. But Peter, who recognized him later, being more steadfast in mind, threw himself into the sea. Thus you may know that John signifies the endeavor of knowing and the gift of contemplation, which are first in order; while Peter, as has already been said, expresses the ministry of the word. In this ministry the waves of the world must often be borne and trodden underfoot; and, moreover, they often undergo the bitterness of death, so that through martyrdom they may come to Jesus. The other disciples come in the boat of enclosure or quiet, drawing the net of fish through application to prayer and the intention of pious desire, as though by a certain rope [Col. 1115B].

Yet Peter and John—intention and action, vision and ministry of the word—run, press on, and hasten together on land and sea, though differently, around and toward the one thing necessary, which shall not be taken from us. For as vision is eternal, so too the ministry of the word that enlightens us will be eternal, the Lord promising us that, having girded himself, he will make us recline and, passing by, will serve us. This ministry is also signified in the banquet celebrated with the seven disciples [Col. 1115C], when the Lord Jesus, after his resurrection, standing on the shore and remaining in the repose of eternal sanctification, invites them to breakfast, saying: “Come, children.” There he takes bread and gives it to them, and likewise fish.

We may therefore devoutly believe that, in eternal life also, the ministry of the word will not be lacking, now shared with the Lord alone and with the angels and holy souls who are companions of his banquet. We too shall know when we hear him say: “Come, dine” (ibid.); “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV).

These two orders too, monastic and canonical, run together in the Church as John and Peter [Col. 1115D], both beloved and both loving God. As Ambrose says in his letter to the people of Vercelli: “One rests in a cave, the other struggles in the theater; one flees the world, the other conquers the world; one reclines with John on Jesus’ breast, the other walks with Peter upon the sea of the world; one is more accustomed to contemplation, the other more devoted to ministry; one, with John, beholds marvelous things, the other, with Peter, is made a spectacle to the world; one is more patient in bodily discipline, the other more fitted for moral instruction.” Let them run together, and let neither prefer itself to the other, though one may appear to outstrip the other in some respects. For even if the monastic order surpasses our order in the humility of endurance and in bodily discipline [Col. 1116A], it does not for that reason take precedence also in the stewardship of God’s mysteries.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. The Canonical Order Dispenses God’s Mysteries

But in these matters, just as John yields precedence to Peter, so the monastic order yields precedence to the clerical order, to which it was said in Peter: “Feed my sheep” (John XXI). This order also has authority, as the first together with Peter to draw the net, to clothe and summon from the boat those companions belonging to the monastic order whom it recognizes as fit for this task, so that they may come and help him, laboring with him in the Gospel of Christ.

These orders, although somewhat different from one another in the purpose of their profession and in variety of habit, are nevertheless not opposed to one another; but like the two cherubim they look upon one another with fraternal intimacy, their faces turned toward the mercy-seat [Col. 1116B]. Thus they also usefully converge in one person: when clerics retaining private property are converted, leaving all things behind, to monastic and cenobitic perfection; or when men of proven learning and conduct within monasteries are admitted to the ministry of the altar or summoned to govern churches.

From such men Gregory I and Gregory VII, Roman pontiffs, became brilliant lights of the Church. Even now the Church glories in the holiness of Eugene, its Roman bishop; and many other pontiffs and priests of the same order are found to have presided most beneficially over the Church in various places and times. They shone both by the power of miracles and—no less than this—by the prerogative of learning [Col. 1116C].

Therefore, in the Lord Jesus both things, that is, the power of miracles and the grace of teaching, are equally commended in the Gospel. It is written that two walking together on the road said of Jesus that he “was a man, a prophet, mighty in deed and word” (Matt. XXI). Likewise in the Acts of the Apostles: “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts I). And Luke himself makes this clearer in his Gospel, writing the words of the Lord Jesus to John’s two disciples: “Go, tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise” (Luke VII). Finally, equating the grace of evangelizing with miraculous power, he added what is no less than these: “The poor have the Gospel preached to them” [Col. 1116D] (ibid.).

Let those, therefore, who wish marvel at the power of miracles in Martin and Benedict. I shall no less marvel at and venerate the grace of teaching and learning in Ambrose, Hilary, and Augustine, joined to holiness of life, for the Lord himself bears witness that it is no less great. Through that grace many poor have received the Gospel, many blind in soul have been illumined, lepers cleansed, and dead persons raised. These miracles, assuredly, are not doubted by sound judges to be greater in proportion as they are more spiritual.

God distributes his gifts: one person shines through miracles, another through gifts of wisdom and knowledge or through learning in doctrine. In all these things the two disciples—Peter, that is, the canonical order, and John, the monastic order—run together [Col. 1117A], when they are praiseworthily united in one person: when men for whom it is permitted become monks from clerics, and proven monks become clerics; when the grace of evangelizing among clerics is no less sublime than the power of miracles among monks; when the apostles’ ministry in the word is no less worthy than the silence of Mary listening and obeying; when these, drawing the net of fish, walk upon the waves of the sea with Peter no less bravely than those sweetly recline upon Jesus’ breast with John; when, among clerics who are ministers of the word, victory over tyrants and deaths with Peter and Paul is no less exalted than retreat into the wilderness, and the frequent and manifold revelation of heavenly visions, among monks with John exiled on the island of Patmos (Acts I) [Col. 1117B].

In all these matters, I say, and in many others too lengthy to enumerate now, these two orders run together praiseworthily in the Church and do not cease to run together until the end of the age, both beloved by God and both loving God.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Therefore It Is Heretical Persistently to Maintain That Monks Should Not Govern Churches

Which of the two should be preferred is placed not in human judgment but in that of God alone—except that he is believed to be greater in the kingdom of heaven who is found to have lived more holily, humbly, and commendably, whether in their order [Col. 1117C] or in ours. There also many widows and married women are set above many bishops and monks; they are great not in the estimation of men, each person receiving a reward according to his own labor.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On Lay Converts

[Col. 1118A]

Moreover, in our own monasteries these two orders, namely canons and monks—John and Peter—still run together, when unlettered persons, leaving secular life and everything else in order to take up Christ’s yoke, are converted among us. They neither can nor wish to be promoted to clerical order; rather, they live commendably in every degree of monastic perfection, working with their hands and crucifying their flesh with its vices and desires in penitential dress. In certain cloisters, according to monastic custom, they also customarily gird themselves for labor with the garment called a scapular, so that in the respect in which some appear to glory, they may be thought to lack little, in this similitude, of the flight of the six-winged cherubim [Col. 1118B].

In all these matters, the two orders of which we speak run together, walking in combined step. So too it is written of Peter and John that they advanced with their steps joined—not one outrunning the other, but walking together. Thus it is written: “John was going up with Peter into the temple at the ninth hour of prayer” (Acts III). There the crippled man received the power of walking through their words; immediately leaping, with his feet and ankles strengthened, he walked and entered the temple with them, walking, leaping, and praising God.

And truly, where priestly authority, understood in Peter [Col. 1118C], and monastic holiness, signified through John, are united either in one community or in one person, such walking together will undoubtedly redound to the praise and glory of God and will bring salvation to many imitators. Amen.

[Col. 1117] Here ends the treatise on the order of regular canons, by the reverend father and lord in Christ, Lord Anselm, bishop of the Church of Havelberg, a contemporary of Eugene III.

[Col. 1117]

# APOLOGETIC LETTER OF ANSELM, BISHOP OF HAVELBERG, IN DEFENSE OF THE ORDER OF REGULAR CANONS

(Eusebius Amort, *Vetus disciplina canonicorum regularium et saecularium*, etc., Venice, 1747, quarto; vol. II, p. 1048.)

## EDITORIAL NOTICE

Concerning Anselm, Oudinus writes as follows in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*:

> “Anselm, bishop of Havelberg in the margraviate of Brandenburg, [lacuna] was sent by Emperor Lothair II as envoy to the emperor of the Greeks at Constantinople. There, challenged by the wiser Greek bishops, he entered into a celebrated assembly or colloquy, which he describes to Eugene III. Anselm was also sent by Pope Eugene III to Conrad, emperor of the Romans, etc. He likewise subscribed to the agreement between Emperor Frederick and Eugene III.”

Thus Oudinus. But since Emperor Lothair had already died in the year 1138, and Conrad succeeded him, and then Frederick, it is probable that this apologetic letter was written before 1138. For after undertaking the embassy to Constantinople, he does not seem, amid continual business, to have had time remaining for matters of this sort. That excellent work against the Greeks would, for example, certainly have absorbed his attention; I also found a manuscript copy of it among our canons at Neustift in Tyrol.

The present little work was communicated to me from a manuscript codex through the kindness of the Reverend Lords Augustine Eichendock, who is now performing with highest praise the office of general in the Windesheim Congregation.

**Letter of the venerable Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, to Ecbert, abbot of Huysburg, against those who importunately contend that the monastic order is worthier in the Church than the canonical order.**

[Col. 1119A] Anselm, a poor man of Christ, called bishop of Havelberg, to Ecbert, venerable abbot of the monastery of Huysburg: greeting in that peace for which we are called Christians and are Christians.

Just as one who handles and administers the things of charity according to the law of charity ought to be embraced, so likewise, on the other hand, one who has attempted to strive against charity ought to be admonished by the duty of charity, lest, while deceived by the appearance of what is right—calling light darkness and darkness light, sweet bitter and bitter sweet, and saying that evil is good and good evil—he fall from good into evil, abandon the light and seize darkness, and, rejecting what is sweet, choose for his unsound palate to taste what is bitter.

Recently, while, as is my custom, I was sitting alone and happened to be reading the Letters of blessed Jerome [Col. 1119B], a certain brother came in and brought me a written work. When I took it up and, eager as I am for new writings, read it through at once, I found that writing not merely idle but burdensome. Immediately I was greatly astonished at the judgment of so great a man, who had begun, arranged, and ended this work in such a fashion. And behold: the title of the work unexpectedly appeared and made known that you were its author. Then, rereading it attentively and observing every point, I found certain superstitious and useless things to say, which nevertheless you endeavoured to establish by certain little arguments drawn from opinion and by certain authorities bent round to your own meaning [Col. 1119C].

How great an evil it is to make even Holy Scripture subject to one’s own interpretation, rather than adapting one’s own understanding to divine Scripture, ought to be unknown to no one accustomed to devote himself to sacred reading. For you strive, by divining from divine Scripture, to set it against divine Scripture; and, so far as may be gathered from your words, you maintain that all the faithful, of both Old and New Testament, were monks. Nor do you hesitate openly to say that the passage recorded by Luke the Evangelist—“They had one heart and one soul,” etc., etc. (Acts IV)—belongs to the society of monks, rather than to the apostles and their followers, among whom at that time even the name “monks” was unknown. Hence that same book is entitled Acts of the Apostles [Col. 1119D], not Acts of the Monks.

You also cite certain words of blessed Augustine on Psalm 132: “Behold how good and pleasant it is to dwell together in unity”; in these he plainly commends the apostolic and common life [Col. 1120A], yet you, with considerable lack of understanding, endeavour to twist them toward the monastic profession alone. Tell me, brother: were those five hundred who saw the Lord after the Resurrection—as the Apostle Paul recalls—monks? Were the one hundred and twenty who were gathered together in one place after the Lord’s Resurrection and Ascension into heaven, when, as they stood together in one place, the Holy Spirit, sent from heaven on the day of Pentecost, came upon them—sent as he had been promised—were all these, I ask, monks? Yet it was pleasant for them, as brothers, to dwell together in unity.

You also insert certain passages from the writings of John Chrysostom, which for this reason you cannot rightly understand: you seem to have charity confined only to monks, rather than extended to all Catholics [Col. 1120B]. Finally, I do not know whose teaching you append—that of a certain Robert—whose authority, because it is unknown in the Church, is as easily despised as it is established. Perhaps, however, he is accounted great among you, not because he wrote anything great, but because he was an abbot of monks. I confess that I have read some of his writings for their curious novelty; I also knew and saw the man himself. But in him I found true the well-spoken Greek proverb: “A fat belly does not produce a subtle mind.”

But, dearest brother, I ask you: why do you labour so much to your own detriment? Why do you beat the air so fiercely? Why do you argue with such zeal on behalf of the monastic order, which no wise person attacks? Doubtless you do it in order to please certain persons by what you say and become known to many more [Col. 1120C]. But, as the common saying goes, do not sell bladders as lanterns. Yet you do this only to simple, unlearned, or even ignorant children who marvel at every novelty. Why, by writing, do you dig cisterns that cannot hold water? With what rashness do you presume to offer muddy water in writing to the children of God? Sharing as they do in Christ’s flesh and blood, and eating the whole lamb roasted—not raw, as you do—they are accustomed daily to draw from the divine utterances the fountain of living water.

I fear for you; and for God’s sake I fear concerning you: lest, while you vainly and idly defend the venerable garment which no Christian unless mad attacks, you should lose Christ’s garment—that is, the robe of charity—by wishing to tear it [Col. 1120D]. Yet I wonder whether you would do these things if you were not a monk. I am not a monk; nevertheless, I am prepared to defend the monastic order with you. For so many saints, so many blessed persons, so many elect, so many perfect persons, so many full of the Holy Spirit are recorded as having served under that rule [Col. 1121A], that it is beyond doubt that anyone who should presume to disparage an order so praiseworthy and so deserving of embrace is a man of mad mind and a limb of the devil. For monastic life, when maintained in its proper course, is altogether beyond reproach: it is to be undertaken, revered, desired, embraced, strengthened, fortified, preserved, and in every way raised and set up toward heaven as a ladder for sinners and penitents.

Nevertheless, far be it that the perfection of monks should in any way diminish the perfection and holiness of clerics. Nor do I agree, sweetest brother, with the words which you have gathered and amassed for this purpose [Col. 1121B]: to prove that the life of monks, as more worthy, ought to be preferred to the excellence of clerics. But before I answer this opinion of yours, I wish to preface only a few things by which my judgment may shine more clearly upon you.

I do not call a monk good because he is a monk; rather, because he is good, I declare him good. I do not call a cleric good because he is a cleric; rather, because he is good, I call him good and love him as good. I do not judge a layman good or bad because he is a layman; rather, because he is good or bad, I approve him as good or disapprove him as bad. For God is not a respecter of persons, but “in every nation whoever fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts IV); and he also, as the Apostle says, “wills all people to be saved” (1 Tim. [Col. 1121C] II).

Was it therefore the act of a wise man to disturb by a writing the hearts of so many monks, long since calmed from the storm of the world, summon them into disputation, and, as you say, rouse them for battle on behalf of the dignity of the monastic order—though, to speak the truth, against no one—in vain? I think that, if you could, you would have summoned all the monks of Egypt and Mesopotamia—Pauls, Anthonys, Hilarys, Macariuses, and even that father Benedict, blessed no less in holiness than in name—from the sleep of peace into a useless war. You would not have feared what you ought especially to have feared: that, if they were alive, they would prove you blameworthy; not only would they not support you, but they would become stern and exacting judges of your ignorance. For they were so much more worthy of the heavenly life as they are found to have been humbler under the clerical order through which the Church of God is governed [Col. 1121D].

I greatly wonder with what face and with what rashness you call them your teachers and glory that you are their disciple, when neither you seem to have anything to do with them nor they with you, apart from the common law of Christianity by which we are all one in Christ. They were content with rags, scarcely enough to cover the shame of the flesh and in some measure temper the harsh cold; but you act otherwise. They, hungry and seeking their food by their own hands, bent over hoes and rakes; but you do not act thus. They were needy; you abound. They were afflicted; you have consolation. They were pressed by distress; you lead a tranquil life [Col. 1122A]. They wandered in deserts, etc.; you sit secure among your own people upon a lofty throne.

I have said all this briefly, lest, if I set forth the bare truth in comparing you and them, I should destroy the charity which I intend to build up, and seem to wound more deeply the wound I have undertaken to heal. I would rather that, while I am silent, you yourself should examine yourself by considering their comparison, than that you should be troubled and angered by my speaking and showing with an unwelcome finger what is true, cutting too sharply to the quick with my tongue. For I desire always to see, hear, and embrace you gentle, cheerful, pleasant, kindly disposed, peaceable, and never disturbed.

Yet in all these things I do not intend to take away either the name or the merit from you or from any monks of the present day [Col. 1122B], especially since I, a sinner with a head beset by many fears, desire to be saved with the aid of all of us and to be found, in name and merit, among Christ’s poor. But now let us return to the words of your writing.

“You say that the dignity of the monastic order is confused because a certain Peter, provost of the canonical clerics at Hamersleve, who were leading the common life in the profession of the apostolic institution, is sought after as a monk and recalled to his former order, which certainly, as I affirm, he was not permitted to leave without evident cause.”

O Christian unworthy of every dignity, contentious about some iniquitous dignity! But perhaps you meant heavenly dignity [Col. 1122C]. For one dignity is heavenly and another earthly. If you contend concerning earthly dignity, you are earthly, and certainly show yourself unworthy of dignity and worthy of every righteous indignation of good people. But if you thought it necessary to speak of heavenly dignity, why do you lament that it is confused? It is altogether alien from every confusion and completely free. It follows, therefore, that neither is that dignity which is earthly to be sought by a good Christian, nor is that which is heavenly in any way to be believed or said by any Christian to be confused.

You also find fault with the name “regular canon,” and say that it is new and therefore contemptible [Col. 1122D]—as though this consequence were necessary: if new, then contemptible. How contemptible that contemptible argument is, no one who knows how to reason syllogistically can fail to know. Certainly, everything that has acquired antiquity or age was at some time new. Therefore, a thing is not more or less contemptible because it is new or was new; nor is it more or less acceptable because it is old or will be old. Whether something is old or new, if it is good and useful, it ought rightly to be acceptable to all good people. There are ancient goods and new goods; there are ancient evils and new evils. Certainly, just as the antiquity or novelty of evils adds no authority to them, so likewise no antiquity or novelty of goods takes away their dignity [Col. 1123A].

It seems also that there you have not simply, but craftily, as if by insinuation, employed the common name “cleric”—flattering clerics and drawing them to your side—and praised it for its antiquity. I fear that you did this not so much truly to praise them as, if I may say so without offence to you, freely to disparage these others. Yet I confess I do not know how to answer you concerning this term, since the expression “regular canon” seems to mean the same thing as if someone said “regular regular” or “canon canon.” Unless perhaps modern usage has become accustomed to double the same word in Latin and Greek, so that this doubling of meaning may be a firm affirmation of an ancient religion now restored, or a manifest distinction from certain persons who do not live so regularly [Col. 1123B].

But if the aforesaid priest Peter, after long professing the apostolic life and being clothed in the garb of poverty, at last wished or caused himself to become a monk by human fickleness—not by divine election—descending, not ascending, ought he not rightly to be recalled and invited back to the first pledge which he had made void? Especially since the authority of the holy Fathers forbids this to be done and judges that, if it has happened, it must be reversed, and commands this forcefully. Whoever thinks, in the arrogance of his superstition, that he need not obey them irretrievably condemns himself. For, as blessed Ambrose says: “Whoever does not agree with the Roman Church is plainly a heretic.”

Pope and martyr Urban says thus: “We command, and in commanding universally forbid, that no canon who has professed the regular life shall become a monk, unless—God forbid!—he has publicly fallen. But if anyone, presuming to act contrary to our decree, attempts to do so, we command him to return to the canonical order; and henceforth, as a memorial of his presumption, he shall wear the cowl and remain last in the choir” [Col. 1123C].

Likewise Bishop Gelasius: “Certain brothers who had professed the canonical life came to us and said that their father, having cast aside both paternal care and the canonical habit which he had professed, had entered a monastery of monks against the wishes of all his brethren. Disturbed by the presumption of so great a novelty, we decreed—and by decreeing command—what Pope and martyr Urban of blessed memory had decreed before: namely, that the same abbot should return without opposition to the cloister from which he had departed most disorderly. Yet, as the mark of so great a presumption, he was to wear the monastic cowl in that same place or cloister until his death. Since we saw that this pleased all the brethren assembled before us, we command that this very rule be observed perpetually in the canonical order by the authority of God Almighty, of the apostles Peter and Paul, and of ourselves” [Col. 1123D].

Likewise Urban II: “We decree that none of the canonical profession, after he has set a man over his head in God’s stead, shall dare, through an impulse or prompting of frivolity [Col. 1124A], or under the pretext of a stricter religion, to depart from the cloister without the permission of the provost and of the entire community. We forbid, by the authority of God and our own, that one who departs be received by any abbot, monk, or bishop without the assurance of letters common to them all.”

Likewise elsewhere: “We have learned that among certain canons a blameworthy practice, deserving ecclesiastical correction, has taken root: contrary to ecclesiastical custom they put on cowls, which monks alone ought to use. Certainly they ought not wholly to usurp the dress of persons whose mode of life is approved by no authority for their use, but rather is rightly censured and rejected by those of sound judgment. Henceforth this must be utterly forbidden.”

Likewise: “Clear authority makes it evident that the canonical institution surpasses the other institutions. Therefore it is necessary that those designated by the name of this profession should endeavour to adorn that institution in themselves by life and conduct, rather than dishonour it [Col. 1124B]. For those who possess an institution of such great authority and ought to make themselves examples for others must fear lest, should they—God forbid!—depart from their purpose, they be made unworthy of the kingdom of God.”

Likewise, from the Council of Autun: “No abbot or monk shall presume to receive a regular canon or make him a monk as long as he can find a cloister of his own order in which he may be saved.”

Therefore, beloved brother—for we are both fellow-servants of God [Col. 1124C]—I should like to know, and to be taught by you, by what reasoning or authority you wish one who is a good cleric to become a monk. For indeed a cleric of good life may well, boldly, and confidently say with the prince of the apostles and with that whole primitive and holy fellowship: “Lord, behold, we have left all things and followed you; what then shall we have?” (Matt. XIX).

What if he has sold all things and given to the poor, and now follows Christ naked? What if he already carries his cross and, prepared for every persecution, imitates Christ and his apostles? What if he has said or done nothing as his own in this world, except perhaps sin? What if he has already renounced all that he possesses, and, hearing the words of life and embracing the discipline of righteousness, has made himself Christ’s true and perfect disciple [Col. 1124D]? If, I say, a good cleric—for I speak of a good cleric—has fulfilled these things which I have written and likewise the other commands of the Gospel, will not that very man sit with the Twelve judging the twelve tribes of Israel? (ibid.) Will not Christ the Saviour himself, giver of perfect salvation, make him recline among the disciples and, passing by, minister to them? “Where I am,” he says, “there also shall my servant be” (John XII).

Say then, if you can: has the faithful God anywhere promised to a monk something which he has refused to give to a cleric unless the latter becomes a monk? I certainly do not recall having read this either in the promises of the Gospel or anywhere in the whole sea of divine Scripture, nor do I remember having heard it from anyone who has read it. Therefore, I beg you, let everyone, with your permission [Col. 1125A], remain in the calling in which he was called. Do not presume, under the pretext of religion, to disturb the ecclesiastical order, divinely established according to the pattern of things seen upon the mountain. Rather pursue peace, with every humility and Christian fellowship, with all who are in the house of God, lest, while religion on the occasion of yourself or anyone else judges religion on the other side, house fall upon house according to the words of the Gospel, and a destructive scandal arise in the Church of God.

But perhaps you say that you have often seen, often heard, and moreover frequently read that certain clerics have passed over to the monastic order and habit, and conversely that certain monks have been admitted into the clerical estate. I confess, my dearest, that I too have seen, heard [Col. 1125B], and read of such occurrences. But one must carefully consider not only what has been done but also how it has been done, or is daily done in the Church of God. For if a cleric passes to a monastery, this has been done or tolerated only by discretionary permission, not by the law or rule of the ecclesiastical institution—when at times that man has been either truly necessary or useless, or a proud despiser of ecclesiastical discipline and canonical obedience, or a slippery follower of secular life and an insolent transgressor, or perhaps harmful to himself and others in the Church. Such persons are not forbidden to become monks by the Fifth Council of Toledo, canon 49.

But many examples of the saints teach in what manner, according to the strict and ancient norm of ecclesiastical institution, it is necessary for a cleric to become a monk [Col. 1125C]: clerics who are criminal and infamous are found degraded by ecclesiastical censure from holy orders, or even suspended, shut up in a monastery thereafter to mourn their sins. From this it is plainly evident, and no one with a sound mind can doubt, that the order of canons is higher in the Church than that of monks, since criminals are cast out from the former as guilty persons and confined in the latter as condemned persons, unwilling, sorrowing, and weeping, for punishment and penitence.

Who is so mad as ever to say that he has seen criminal and infamous monks—for sons of darkness may arise among them too [Col. 1125D]—cast out from the monastic order as from a higher order and received into the canonical order as into a lower and more abject one? Therefore, whenever a cleric bound by canonical profession and tied by the pledge of his own mouth to the cross of obedience—what have I to do with wandering, unbound, and headless clerics? For “the wicked walk round about” (Ps. XI)—if, I say, as I have often said, a good cleric, led by some frivolity, as can happen, flees the narrow way that leads to the homeland (Matt. VII), seeks a monastery, and asks to be made a monk, I say plainly, I say openly, and, if anyone does not know this—though I suppose there is no such person—I teach it confidently: he is not to be received, but is to be freely sent back to his own stall, from which, wandering and fugitive after breaking the rope of obedience [Col. 1126A], he had strayed.

But if, either through ignorance—for knowledge is not everyone’s possession—or, what is worse, through presumption and usurpation, he has been received and made a monk, then with the holy Roman pontiffs, in the Church and with the Church, I state most openly and proclaim confidently that he must be recalled and, according to the ordinance laid down by the holy Fathers who forbade this to be done, restored to the former order which he had abandoned through foolish and superstitious devotion.

Conversely, if a monk has kept inviolate the purpose of his religious life; if he has served obediently under the Rule of blessed Benedict; if, exercised by frequent reading in the understanding of divine Scripture, he has made himself useful to the Church of God: following the example of blessed Gregory, the great theologian, when summoned by clergy or Church, he may beneficially be advanced to the priesthood or even to the pontificate [Col. 1126B], so that the mouth which he had formerly humbly closed may thereafter be usefully opened in the midst of the Church, and that, as a good man, he may bring forth good things from a good treasury (Matt. XII).

Yet whenever this is done, it must be done according to the ordinance of the preceding Fathers: namely, he must by no means cast off the monastic habit, but wear it hidden; instructed in canonical learning, he must always put on over it the stole and orarium. He shall lay aside the “Song of Ascents,” which formerly he sang mournfully, crying to the Lord out of tribulation; and, passing from the octave of “Blessed are the undefiled” (Ps. CXVIII) into the true eighth day, he shall become accustomed to and exercise the divine offices with the clerics [Col. 1126C]. In every respect, both by habit and by office, he shall regularly show openly that he has now become a cleric: the black garment hidden beneath and within, on account of the sorrow of the human condition, or of weakness and mortality; but the linen and white garment shown outside and always visible, on account of newness of life and the brightness of the resurrection. This, indeed, he ought henceforth to preach to the people of God with all the greater ardour because it is more truly evident that he has merited, by good works above others, to be set over them.

Let our and your Jerome now come forward: ours as a priest, yours as a monk; truly “not thinking high things, but consenting to the humble” (Rom. XII); not a follower of a third tongue, which at this time hisses in detraction among most people, but a most learned investigator of three languages [Col. 1126D]. Let him, I say, come forward, declare publicly what he has taught ought to be thought concerning clerics and concerning monks, and open without shame his volume for me, for you, and universally for everyone to read.

For thus he writes to Heliodorus: “Far be it from me to speak anything sinister about those who, succeeding to the apostolic rank, make Christ’s body with their sacred mouth; through whom we too are Christians; who, holding the keys of the kingdom of heaven, in a certain manner judge before the day of judgment; who preserve the Lord’s bride in sober chastity. But, as I touched upon above, the case of monks is one thing, that of clerics another. Clerics feed the sheep; I am fed. They live from the altar. For me, as for a fruitless tree, the axe is laid to the root if I do not bring an offering to the altar; nor can I plead poverty, since in the Gospel he praised the aged widow who cast in the two small coins that alone remained to her. I am not permitted to sit before a presbyter; they, if I sin, may hand me over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord Jesus Christ” [Col. 1127A].

And below: “But if the pious entreaties of the brethren invite you also to the same order, I rejoice in your ascent; I fear your fall.”

Likewise blessed Augustine: “A perfect monk scarcely makes a good cleric.”

See to it, brother, that you too read humbly the things written humbly by such great men. But perhaps, after so many authorities [Col. 1127B], your mind prefers still to be doubtful rather than certain about matters which it believes unwillingly. Therefore, so that nothing may be lacking for you, slow and difficult as you are, in coming to belief, let firm truth of unshaken reason follow where the authority has gone before.

Grant, then, for the moment that what you say is true, and attend for a little. You maintain that the monastic profession is worthier than all other professions. You further add that, by the example of blessed Gregory and of very many others, monks may lawfully pass into the order of clerics. You speak well—indeed, you seem to speak well—but you are justly ensnared by the words of your own mouth. For either it is true that the monastic order is worthier than the other orders, and one may not pass from it into the clerical order [Col. 1127C]; or, if passage is permitted, it follows that the order from which one passes is truly not worthier. No one judges that a person should pass from a worthier to a less worthy order, unless perhaps he has publicly fallen.

Choose, then, what you wish. Either live wholly stripped of ecclesiastical orders and content with monastic dignity alone and simply; or, if you think you are allowed to ascend from that dignity to ecclesiastical orders and dignities, confess humbly, with me and with the whole Church, that you are meanwhile lower and that the cleric is now truly higher. Otherwise you are necessarily forced into the position of saying and teaching that a monk who desires to be a cleric is striving altogether to become vicious. How absurd and blameworthy this is, let both monks and clerics judge [Col. 1127D]—they who until now were proclaimed nearer to holy orders in proportion as they were found to be of better life.

Therefore at last change this opinion, which you seem rather to have dreamed than proved by any authority or reason. And as for your boasting in your writing about the miracles of blessed Benedict, though miracles ought not to be adduced as examples, I wonder why you do not marvel at the apostles and their countless multitude of imitators, who cling to their footsteps, through whom God performed and performs so many and such great miracles that no minds could ever suffice to enumerate them.

As for what you wrote from the Dialogue of blessed Gregory, that the same venerable Benedict, a priest who had been troubled by a devil before assuming the priesthood [Col. 1128A], had forbidden [someone] the service of the altar: certainly he did this not by authority to judge, but by the practical benefit of counsel, as one prophetically foreseeing in the spirit that evil would befall the man who disregarded so salutary a counsel of so great a man.

And as for your further citation from the same Dialogue, that he excommunicated certain holy sisters, and your inference that he therefore possessed this authority of ecclesiastical censure: you have not considered it rightly. Faithful Benedict imposed that sentence of excommunication not by pronouncing it, but by threatening it.
