Later he absolved these sisters—rather, he learned that God had absolved them and informed others of it—not by ecclesiastical law, since they were dead, but by the offering which he made for them, through true priestly authority.

Some time ago, when I was in the Roman Church [Col. 1128B], I saw and heard a certain abbot of Clairvaux, rough-clad and worn away by emaciation, truly a man worthy of God, no false but a genuine disciple of blessed Benedict. By command of Innocent II, Roman pontiff, a great and incomparable man, he sat among the clerics and delivered an exposition of words of divine Scripture. Yet he did this more by pontifical obedience than by priestly office.

Moreover, that I may not be silent about myself also—for I ought humbly to think of myself as a sinner, unable to break the seal of divine Scripture—the same pontiff of the holy Roman Church, while celebrating the collects and the solemn rites of Mass on the Nativity of Mary, Mother of God, called me, as I happened to be present [Col. 1128C]. After the archdeacon had read the Gospel and fallen silent, he ordered me to ascend the lectern or ambo and, with him present and all eager to listen, deliver a word of teaching and exhortation. This I did, according to my measure and according to the grace given me by God, not so much by my own authority—although I was a bishop—as by the authority of him whom I was bound humbly to obey in all things.

Therefore, are things that are sometimes done by a useful dispensation, sometimes by a discerning permission, and sometimes even by a special command, to be drawn into precedent against things established by an immovable law and invincible authority? Far be it!

It has also been reported to us that you do not fear to insinuate into the ears of certain persons, or even at times are not ashamed to say before some, that regular canons [Col. 1128D] ought neither to hold parishes nor to exercise the care of souls among the people. If this is true, I am utterly astonished at your prudence; for whoever strives to maintain this—though I judge that no wise person thinks it—plainly does so from envy of the canonical order rather than love of truth. For one who thinks rightly invites all priests rather to the regular life than wholly removes from the guardianship of the Lord’s sheep those who live regularly. The wrongdoing of others ought to displease them all the more because they are known to have departed further from wrongdoing of their own; and the amendment of another’s life should be entrusted to them all the more securely because they have applied greater diligence to the amendment of their own. No unworthy injury should be inflicted upon the canonical order in the Church, like an olive tree [Col. 1129A] bearing abundant fruit.

The common practice of the whole Church is likewise clear: just as no monk is appointed to an archdeaconry, archpriesthood, or any parish, so no regular canon is removed from ecclesiastical judgments, synodal cases, the administration of the care of souls, or any ecclesiastical office or dignity. Indeed, often sought even by an uneducated people, he is elected and appointed; and, like a lamp shining in a dark place, teaching both by word and example, he is loved and honored. Therefore whoever, wishing to satisfy his own ill will, attempts in this matter to disparage the canonical order, plainly either does not know what he says, why he says it, or against whom he says it, or else, as one most ignorant of all writings, maliciously boils over solely with [Col. 1129B] envy of what is good. When the occasion is suitable, I shall answer opponents more fully concerning this assertion, according to what shall be revealed to me from above, so that “their teeth may be broken in their own mouths” (Psalm 57), and, laying aside the darkness of envy or ignorance, they may come to their senses and be corrected.

But let us now proceed, and answer both your words and those of certain monks who boast that they are exclusively contemplative. In this way at least, as though divine Scripture favored them—as they suppose—they arrogantly set themselves above clerics who now labor in the active life and who will then be raised into the contemplative life. May it please the Lord that they might either be so active as not to trample upon contemplatives, or so both contemplative and active as to despise neither the latter [Col. 1129C] nor themselves; but rather, in the time of holy contemplation, love good active persons, and again, in the time of good action, cherish holy contemplatives.

Yet both you and I, dearest brother, have great cause for fear: lest, while on opposite sides we dispute in writing concerning matters treated within fixed limits by the holy Fathers who made progress in the highest theology, we offend both against the contemplative life and against the active life, and destroy by provoking one another the charity which we ought mutually to build up. But I trust in the Lord, because the charity poured into our hearts through the Spirit dwelling within us (Romans 5) “is patient, is kind, is not jealous, is not puffed up, is not provoked, thinks no evil, [Col. 1129D] rejoices with the truth, bears all things,” etc. (1 Corinthians 13).

If, because you are a monk, you presume to offer the sacrifice of turtle-doves, do not regard it as base or less contemptible if I, a cleric and poor man of Christ, humbly offer in the temple of the Lord the offering of the poor, namely young pigeons. Let us therefore see whether the distinguished heralds of either the Old or the New Testament, though commendably living in the active life, were in any way devoid of what is called the contemplative life, so that they could be termed active in such a manner that they plainly could not also be called contemplative.

Abel, the first righteous man, a shepherd of sheep and a type of shepherds of souls, must be believed to have been by no means devoid of divine contemplation; his good offerings are said to have been accepted by the good God (Genesis [Col. 1130A] 4). Noah the righteous man (Genesis 6), ruler of the ecclesiastical ark—how could he have been alien to divine contemplation, through whom and with whom God arranged the salvation of those whom He did not wish to perish in the flood? Abraham, father of many nations both in flesh and in faith (Genesis 17), is read to have contemplated the Lord now in Ur of the Chaldeans, now upon one of the mountains, now in the land of Canaan, or in other places, and to have been blessed by His familiar address. Jacob, father of the twelve patriarchs, bearing in Rachel and Leah the figure of the two lives, namely contemplative and active, is read to have seen the Lord face to face (Genesis 32), and to have beheld from heaven angels ascending and descending by the ladder, and the Lord Himself leaning upon the heavenly ladder [Col. 1130B] (Genesis 28).

When Moses was tending the sheep of Jethro, his father-in-law, priest of Midian, and had driven the flock into the inner wilderness, he came to Horeb, the mountain of God. The Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire from the midst of a bush; and he saw that the bush burned and was not consumed. Therefore he said: “I will go and see this great sight” (Exodus 3). O great vision! O mighty contemplation! How was he not contemplative, who foresaw so far in advance the beginning of our salvation in the bush burning and not consumed, as though in the blessed Virgin Mary herself, pregnant without carnal desire?

The same Moses, later made leader of God’s people, was called up the mountain, while darkness stood between him and the contentious people. There he was instructed by divine contemplation and discourse concerning the law and the governance of the people, the ordering of the priesthood, and [Col. 1130C] the arrangement of the tabernacle of the covenant. As a servant in the whole house of God, through contemplation of heavenly things he was divinely taught and made fit for earthly action; and the Lord is read to have spoken with him as friend with friend. “See that you make everything according to the pattern of those things which you saw on the mountain” (Exodus 25).

Joshua and Caleb, leaders of that same people, when they went to explore and behold the land of promise, fittingly bear the figure of contemplatives searching out the secrets of the heavenly country. Returning to the people and carrying back a cluster of grapes upon a pole, they courageously stirred all hearts to take possession of that most fertile land, and, like good teachers in the Church of God, gave themselves as an example of virtue by going before the people [Col. 1130D] (Numbers 13).

David, king and prophet, neither neglected the kingdom over which he ruled well on account of prophecy, nor lost the prophecy with which he humbly abounded because he administered the kingdom well. Thus, with grace repeatedly coming upon him, he was at one time a perfect contemplative, at another a perfect man of action. This is confirmed by divine testimony: “I have found,” says the Lord, “David, son of Jesse, according to my heart” (Acts 15). Who can believe that Daniel, “a man of desires,” was wholly alien from divine contemplation in the midst of Babylon? (Daniel 2.) Who can judge the three youths cast into the furnace of fire not to have been contemplatives, when they deserved even to have the Son of God with them in the furnace? (Daniel 3.) And Ezekiel says of the holy living creatures [Col. 1131A]: “They went and returned” (Ezekiel 1): they went by devoting themselves to contemplation; they returned by serving action.

The Lord likewise says to the same prophet: “Go out into the plain, and shut yourself up in the midst of your house” (Ezekiel 3). What is it to go out into the plain except to go forth into the midst to preach to the people? And what is it to be shut up in the midst of one’s house except, in preaching itself, to keep guard over the mind and preserve inwardly, by contemplation, the spiritual joy of life as though enclosed?

See: you observe that the earlier Fathers, without any ambiguity, held at times the contemplative life and at other times the active life, both in complete perfection. Hence some of them, because of the frequent visions of God’s secrets which they saw and announced to the people as either already accomplished or yet to come, [Col. 1131B] were called Seers. They went before, carrying the precious cluster on the pole of the Old Testament behind their backs; although they did not see many things, they nevertheless knew of Him figuratively and believed faithfully in Him.

But what do you think of those who followed and bore before themselves, on the pole of the New Testament, that same most sweet cluster now to come at the end of the ages, and, as followers, looked upon Him set before their blessed eyes? What, I ask, do you think they knew, how great was their joy, and with what longing for contemplation they burned? To them the cluster itself, filled with every sweetness of divinity—namely the Son of God, trodden in the winepress of the cross—was at one time read to have said: “Blessed are the eyes which see what you see; [Col. 1131C] many kings and prophets desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Matthew 13). He plainly teaches that the things which happened to those men figuratively are seen by these with face now unveiled.

Accordingly, Jesus Christ Himself, Son of God and man, head of the Catholic Church, head of contemplatives, head of all active persons, strict judge of all the proud, lover and preserver of all the humble, willing, gracious, and spontaneous giver of spiritual grace, and generous, munificent, sufficient, and abundant rewarder of grace bestowed—He “who worked salvation in the midst of the earth” (Psalm 74)—do you think Him contemplative or active, or rather both contemplative [Col. 1131D] and active?

Let your charity attend, and consider carefully and humbly with me. Our Lord Jesus Christ, according to the truth of the Gospel, and yet according to a tropological interpretation well known and commonly used in the Church, was received as a guest by the two sisters Martha and Mary. Martha, while busily occupied with much serving, suitably signified the active life. Mary, sitting at the Lord’s feet and listening most eagerly to His word, fittingly represented the contemplative life. When the Lord said of her, “Mary has chosen the best part, which shall not be taken from her” (Luke 10), did He mean the best part in comparison with Himself and Martha, or rather in comparison not [Col. 1132A] with Himself but with Martha alone?

Jesus Christ sat and taught; in teaching, He bore the role of teachers. Mary sat silently and devoutly listening to His word; Martha, troubled by many things, served anxiously. Let your charity attend: Christ teaching, Mary listening, Martha serving—there are three persons. Which of these three seems to you more worthy? There are three offices: which of the three seems to you more worthy? But I know, and without any doubt am certain, that you confess the person of Jesus to be more worthy than either of the others. Since, therefore, the person of Jesus is admittedly more worthy than both, no one can doubt that His office too was most worthy. How, then, Mary could have chosen the best part in comparison with Jesus, who was present there—show this if you can. Therefore I think that this word proceeding from the mouth of Truth, concerning Mary and addressed to Martha, was spoken with reference to Martha herself [Col. 1132B]. For I would not readily—indeed, in no way—believe that Mary, who listened, rather than Jesus, who taught, chose the best part. Yet it must also necessarily be true upon the testimony of Truth that Mary chose the best part, provided the saying is referred to those who in the Church of God are only in the order of hearers, not of teachers. Hence it is suitably said, “she chose”: subjects may commendably choose for themselves silence, quiet, and a place for hearing; but they ought not of themselves choose the office of teaching, but must be chosen for it by others, if they are worthy.

Thus, as the former is praiseworthy in some, so the latter is blameworthy in most. Nevertheless [Col. 1132C] I now fear for you, since “the thoughts of men are vain” (Psalm 94), lest you be deceived and perhaps suppose Christ to have been neither contemplative nor active, especially since He appears to have held neither the office of Mary listening nor that of Martha serving, but the office of a master teaching. But if you consider more carefully “what Jesus began to do and to teach,” it will plainly appear that the great prophet who arose among us, through whom and in whom God visited His people (Luke 7), was for us most perfect in action and, for us, contemplative above the heavens.

The Gospel says [Col. 1132D]: “Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led in the Spirit into the wilderness for forty days” (Matthew 4). Again: “Jesus went up alone upon the mountain to pray” (Matthew 14). Again: “Lifting up His eyes to heaven, He said: ‘I confess to you, Father,’” etc. (Matthew 11). Again: Jesus went out according to His custom to the Mount of Olives; withdrawing from the disciples about a stone’s throw away, He knelt and prayed, saying: “Father, if You will, remove this cup from me; nevertheless, not my will but Yours be done.” Then an angel from heaven appeared to Him, strengthening Him; and, being in agony, He prayed more earnestly (Luke 22). Again: Jesus took Peter, James, and John his brother, led them up a high mountain, and was transfigured before them, etc. (Matthew 17).

O divine contemplation! O great revelation of the secrets of God! O manifest [Col. 1133A] confirmation of the blessed resurrection in Moses and Elijah, who appeared there! O rare, wonderful, and beyond speech delightful presentation of future and inestimable glory! Surely, if you—who so greatly and so often glory in your contemplative life—had been there and beheld the Son of God in such glory, you would not have kept silent for so long at the Lord’s command, as did the other apostles worthy to be there. Instead, you would have gloried more in yourself and about yourself, because you had seen it, than in Him who brought it about—especially since you seem not even now to refrain from despising your fellow servants on account of many lesser visions, of whose sight and contemplation you know absolutely nothing.

Again, the Gospel says of Jesus that He taught the crowds in the temple, on the mountain, or in a boat; gave sight to the blind, cleansed lepers, healed the sick, cast out demons (Matthew 11), cured paralytics (Matthew 4), rebuked the scribes and Pharisees, and, in divine zeal, reproved others, saying that they were of their father the devil (John 8).

Behold: the Son of God, the pattern of highest contemplation and of perfect action, bore in His one person the example of both lives and presented Himself, in deeds and words, as the rule of right living to all Christians and especially to His apostles. It does not seem necessary, after Christ, the head of all Christians, to describe the life of the apostles to you; for, since they clung most fervently to His commands and footsteps, we must believe [Col. 1133C] that they ordered their lives according to their Master’s teaching: so that, like the blessed pure in heart, they might behold in contemplation the God of gods in Zion; and at other times, like the blessed merciful desiring to obtain mercy, might take charge of their neighbors by preaching, healing, tending, and evangelizing.

Thus the Apostle Paul, teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth, who confidently dared to say, “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 4), sometimes forgets what lies behind and stretches himself toward what lies ahead, surpassing himself in mind toward God in contemplation. Sometimes, in caring for those subject to him, he is sober from that heavenly, intoxicating cup of divine contemplation—neither losing the heavenly Friend whom, in burning charity, he had already delightfully embraced [Col. 1133D] and held, nor neglecting his neighbor, whom because of that same charity he now endeavored to attend and provide for. For, as it is written, “There is a time to embrace, and a time to be far from embraces” (Ecclesiastes 3). The same Paul, laboring for all and actively sowing the Gospel of Jesus Christ from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum, says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3).

John the Apostle and Evangelist, who, like an eagle flying aloft and beholding with unblinking eyes the rays of the true sun, drank most abundantly from the fountain of the Lord’s breast, and, filled with the spirit of wisdom and understanding and endowed with the special privilege of divine love, penetrated by contemplation the secrets of the Godhead and the mysteries of the heavenly beings—he too passed into active life. At Ephesus and in many [Col. 1134A] other places he taught the Gospel, founded churches, ordained bishops, and appointed presbyters.

Behold, God’s holy living creatures burn and shine like flashing lightning: they go into contemplation and return into action; and they are not diminished but increased both in merit and in reward. But you, once entering the Holy of Holies—if indeed you have yet entered it—while high priests enter at one time and go out at another, you alone, as it seems to you, have never gone out. O immense, great, sublime, incomparable merit! You entered the Holy of Holies once; if indeed you entered, and thereafter, as you imagine, did not leave. What a singular privilege of continuous and unending contemplation in the flesh—granted neither to Aaron himself, nor to any high priest, nor to the apostles themselves, who saw the Lord in the flesh!

O man of ineffable blessedness, worthy only of heavenly suns! You have chosen the best part: without interruption you have been filled with complete joy; already you are fulfilled with gladness at the face of God; already you possess pleasures at His right hand for ever (Psalm 16)—indeed, before the end! What then remains for you to await? If this is so, it is well: blessed are you, whose remaining thoughts keep festival for the Lord each day (Psalm 76). But take care not to be deceived. Satan is often accustomed to transform himself into an angel of light; and while you, or any devout person, strive to contemplate Him who dwells in inaccessible light (1 Timothy 6), that envious one swiftly runs to the soul tending toward higher things and deceitfully and fraudulently presents himself to one seeking the truth. Since he always wishes to be like the Most High, he wickedly feigns himself to be the Most High. By a likeness of the true, he unjustly deceives the hearts of the simple, still darkened by earthly dwelling, and spirits seeking the supreme good of spiritual goods and most ardently investigating where life and truth are. For his food is choice, and he is confident that the Jordan will flow into his mouth. Therefore see that you too are not deceived: “Have you found honey? Eat only what is sufficient; for the searcher into majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory” (Proverbs 25).

Perhaps you are angry with me because I have dared to write such words, especially since you, caught up into the third heaven [Col. 1134D] and carried into paradise, are accustomed alone after Paul to hear secret words which it is not lawful for a human being to speak (2 Corinthians 12). But it seems to me that light from heaven has shone around you from God and has cast you to the ground by its illumination, so that, trembling and astonished, even with open eyes you see little or nothing. You must therefore be led by the hand and guarded by your familiars, because you need Ananias, who, at the Lord’s command, may visit you and lay upon you the hand of correction. Thus, when the scales of misty darkness, which until now seemed to obstruct bright light for you, fall from your eyes, you may recover sight, be filled with the Holy Spirit, and, receiving the nourishment of divine Scripture, be strengthened to defend what, as a zealot for monastic traditions, you appeared to attack not justly but rashly [Col. 1135A].

But shall we find an Ananias whom you judge sufficient for yourself? Ananias means “the grace of God.” May that hand of good action, I pray, be laid upon you; may it raise you as you lie fallen; may it open for you the eyes of serene contemplation; may it instruct you in rational service within your profession; and may it preserve you from a useless and vain imagining of truth.

Moreover, as I think—or rather, as I more truly believe—this opinion of yours is not that of all monks. For what wise person, even if he is a monk, doubts that monks are not contemplative when they can scarcely, or not at all, be called active? Some of them go about marketplaces abroad; they dispute about possessions and involve themselves in secular affairs; they harass their tenants with extorted money. Others at home, breaking silence, weave together tales and idle talk, and, sitting in judgment, pass judgment on every religious order. Some, to confess the truth, kindly receive Jesus coming in His least ones, as they ought, and devoutly labor much in Martha’s service. Finally, others are busy with some good work useful to the monastery: writing, reading, singing, or serving musical chant.

Among them, unless I am mistaken, some are so simple that, while others labor abroad and watch usefully and commendably over the monastery’s common needs, they imagine the contemplative life consists in sitting idly in the cloisters with hands clasped and sleeves rubbed thin; having idle food, receiving idle clothing, sleeping securely and idly, wandering at will from corner to corner with slow, affected pace [Col. 1135C]; cunningly investigating the abbot’s departure and arrival, and the prior’s absence or presence; inquisitively seeking from newcomers what happens outside; confusing everything by the tangled multiplicity of signs, while the tongue is silent but the restless hand usurps its office; and, to sum it up, abounding idly in everything beyond necessity, and living idly by abundance.

If they see the course of their own will hindered at any time, they immediately grow angry, either murmuring secretly or stubbornly protesting openly. Often they even withdraw into hiding places with perhaps feigned patience; they choose for themselves proud silence under the appearance of religion; they impose upon themselves, for a time and without profit, fasts arising from wicked indignation rather than pious devotion. While they inwardly seethe with the miseries and faults of their temptation and do not disclose them outwardly through confession and repentance, they drink as punishment the cup of their own bitterness.

Yet among them are some who ascend the tower of strength and humility, taste most abundantly and eagerly the sweetness and banquet of contemplative life, are sometimes intoxicated with the wine of compunction, and at other times delight spiritually as though filled with marrow and fatness (Psalm 60). Indeed, my purpose in this part of the letter is not to examine the order, life, or habit of canons or monks, nor to describe again what has long since been described. Rather, provoked by the occasion of your letter, I wished plausibly to demonstrate [Col. 1136A] that the contemplative life is neither the exclusive possession of monks nor, always or without distinction, a life that can belong to all monks, as they themselves claim, and on that account arrogate to themselves above others the special name and title of contemplation. I wished also to show that the profession of canons does not hinder them from sometimes being devoutly raised, by the drawing of grace, to the highest citadel of contemplation—a grace which they commonly deserve, so that they may better exercise care for their neighbors.

Therefore, that we may now see plainly, and that it may appear clearly even to a person of little understanding, whether the canonical order or the monastic order—whose manner of life is different, though both are good—is more useful or necessary in the Church of God, let us suppose for the moment that every kind of monk is entirely stripped and without ecclesiastical orders, as it is agreed they were in ancient times and as no person skilled in letters doubts; and let us meanwhile remove every kind of cleric. Tell me, brother, how will the Church stand, since without archbishops, bishops, presbyters, deacons, and the lower orders of clerics, it cannot even be called or be a Church?

Conversely, remove for the moment every kind of monk, and let the Church of God possess, according to Christ’s ordering and according to the Apostle, some prophets, some apostles, others evangelists, others pastors and teachers, and other orders of clerics. Will these not suffice “for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up [Col. 1136C] of the body of Christ” (Ephesians 4), which is the Church? Though the Church could stand well and in good order without monks, it is nevertheless built up and adorned more fittingly and beautifully, “clothed round about with variety” (Psalm 45), by diverse orders of the elect. In it, just as a good and perfect monk is to be loved and imitated more than an incompetent cleric, so a cleric living well and according to rule is undoubtedly always to be preferred even to the best monk.

For my part, I should judge it just and good that all clerics live according to rule, and that none of them become monks; but those who refuse to live according to rule should either be corrected and reformed within their own order, or else lawfully become good monks everywhere.

Now let us choose two credible persons from the two orders; and, that the truth of what has been said may become most plainly clear, let us compare them and their pursuits, offices, and merits with one another. For example: Paul the Apostle is the standard-bearer of the eternal King, leader of the word of God, a vessel of election to bear the Lord’s name before kings and rulers. Always disputing and persuading concerning the kingdom of God, he gathered many Jews, very many Greeks, and some Romans, whether through speech or through letters, into the orthodox faith. He served vigorously not himself but God; he built and planted the Church of Christ as though anew from its foundation; like a mighty warrior he subjected many of the Gentiles to Christ’s laws; and he ascribed the name and title of triumph not to himself but to the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God. Three times beaten with rods, once stoned, three times shipwrecked, fighting the good fight, finishing the course, keeping the faith, knowing that a crown of righteousness was laid up for him and faithfully awaiting it, certain in whom he had believed (2 Timothy 4), he finally consummated a glorious martyrdom at Rome, leading many with him to glory. Even today, through his admirable epistles, he teaches in the Church, bears fruit, and draws many believers after him.

Paul the monk was simple, humble, devout, solitary, silent, God-fearing, severe in fasting, sparing in food, rough in clothing, diligent in prayer, worn down by vigils and labor, seeking nothing but Christ, sufficient to himself in Christ [Col. 1137B], penitently weeping over past sins, most diligently guarding against future sins as far as he could, steadfast in purpose, useful to himself alone, persevering in labor, and at length falling asleep in peace in the Lord (Acts 7). He aided no one by teaching or writing, unless perhaps he invited someone by the example of his eremitical life.

Let us therefore compare these two Pauls of Christ. Which of them seems to you more exalted in the Church of God, or more worthy, when his labors are ended, to possess the Lord’s glorious inheritance? Does it seem good in your eyes that our Paul should abandon the apostleship and neglect the ministry which he had received from the Lord and honorably exercised among the Gentiles, descending into a desert or monastery, where, although he might avoid idle speech, he perhaps would not be free from idle silence? On the contrary, how much better and more useful it would be if your Paul, leaving solitude—if indeed he were suitable and chosen for preaching—had, where our Paul had begun the vineyard, cooperated with Christ, for whom are all things and through whom are all things, in bringing forth and nurturing just as many children for the Church of God [Col. 1137C]!

Now weigh the labor of each, and also the fruit or reward of each, and surely you will judge Paul the Apostle incomparably preferable; otherwise you alone will disagree, which would be impious, with the judgment of the communion of the whole Church. For “each shall receive his reward according to his labor” (1 Corinthians 3). But if perhaps you tell me that neither I nor any of those who are now of the canonical order resembles our first Apostle, I confess it: you speak truly. Yet I think that I too speak truly in saying that neither you nor any of the modern monks known to me resembles your first monk. Nevertheless, in saying either thing, I do not dare to block for any believer the fountain of divine grace, most lavish then, now, and always; rather, because it is so open and abundant for all, I rejoice and shall always rejoice.

But because of the importunity of certain persons, who always promise the highest things only to themselves, though they are not the highest—or not alone the highest—the letter has become longer than I had expected. Yet charity, which necessarily [Col. 1138A] compelled me to write to you on this occasion, will give you leisure for reading and, by your reading, will take away weariness at its length.

It remains, therefore, that the holy humility of blessed monks may rest content; and, because God “has shut up all things under sin, that He may have mercy upon all,” and yet there is no one who can at times hide himself from His heat (Psalm 19), let us all lament our imperfection. Since “a person does not know whether he is worthy of hatred or love” (Ecclesiastes 9), let us humble ourselves under the mighty hand of God (1 Peter 5); and, while we have time (Galatians 6), let us “come before His face with confession” (Psalm 95), carefully guarding against contending so disorderly over an order that we deservedly fall from every order of the blessed. Let us not, fallen into pride and deceived and led away by Satan into rivalry with our brethren, be Christians in vain. Let us know this [Col. 1138B]: as in the Church which is in heaven there are diverse orders of blessed spirits, so in the Church still upon earth there are diverse orders of believers; and as there none fell except the proud and envious, so none shall ascend into their place except the humble and those possessing charity.

Therefore you, brother most dearly beloved in Christ, together with your penitents who mourn both their own sins and those of the whole people, “enter into the rock; hide yourself in a pit of earth from the fear of the Lord and from the glory of His majesty, when He rises to strike the earth.” Exercise your heart by fasts, prayers, vigils, tears, and continual meditation; sweep your spirit clean; confidently implore the Lord Jesus, comforter of all who mourn; and meanwhile, as a suppliant, embrace and hold [Col. 1138C] the feet of His humanity until He has mercy on you—He who has mercy on all and hates none of the things He has made, overlooking human sins for the sake of repentance (Wisdom 11).

But I, with my brethren, the poor of Christ, the least of God’s servants, a poor little vessel in the Lord’s temple, the last of those who serve the tabernacle of the covenant, will according to my strength carry the ark of the covenant with the other priests of God. I will faithfully serve with those who minister. I will humbly summon with the trumpets of divine Scripture the Christian people hastening toward the promised land, to conquer carnal desires and defeat the hosts of spiritual wickedness, until, our enemies overcome, the walls of Jericho fall; until Hittite and Amorite [Col. 1138D], Canaanite, Perizzite, Hivite, Girgashite, and Jebusite perish by the divine sword; until Midian, Sisera, Jabin, Oreb, Zeeb, Zebah, and Zalmunna fall under the divine blow (Psalm 83); until, the Philistines and all other adversaries overcome, we all ascend with joy to the heavenly Jerusalem above, according to our tribes, to give thanks to the Lord’s name (Psalm 142); and until we celebrate the solemn day in the temple of peaceful Solomon “in dense throngs” (Psalm 118).

There the vessel of election and those vessels made for honor, not dishonor, fulfilled their office. There, when the figures of the true things have ceased and the veil has been laid aside, we shall enter the Holy of Holies with the great High Priest, never to leave it once entered [Col. 1139A]. There the book of each individual will be opened, that we may know as we are known; there we shall always see face to face the King in His beauty (1 Corinthians 13), and always seeing, we shall always desire to see. There knowledge will be without error; there memory without forgetfulness.

Meanwhile, as long as we are pilgrims away from the Lord (2 Corinthians 5), whether we write, say anything, admonish one another or are admonished, or do anything, let us do all things in the Lord’s name (1 Corinthians 10). Let us not pass judgments against one another [Col. 1140A], carefully guarding and praying that Satan, whom we must resist in faith (1 Peter 5), not in contention, may not tempt us. For God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (James 4). Therefore, in all that either my littleness or your brotherhood dictates, may charity always remain superior: always enduring, always whole, always unshaken, always untouched, always ratified, always sound, always firm. Amen.

[Col. 1139]

# Dialogues of Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg

(Dom D’Achery, *Spicilegium*, vol. I, p. 161.)

## Prologue: To Pope Eugenius III, Supreme Pontiff

> [Note: Col. 1139C. Manuscript: “Here begins the prologue of Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, to the *Antikeimenon* [‘Contrasting Opposites’], composed in dialogue form, addressed to the venerable Pope Eugenius III, in the year 1145, during the time of Saint Bernard.”]

[Col. 1139B] To Lord Eugenius, most blessed Pope of the holy Roman Church, ever to be regarded and embraced: Anselm, poor man of Christ and inadequate bishop of the Church of Havelberg, offers absolute obedience in the Lord.

When I was in the presence of Your Blessedness in the month of March at the city of Tusculum, among the many matters which it pleased Your Holiness to discuss with me, you told me that a certain bishop, bearing an embassy from the emperor of Constantinople and a letter written in Greek characters, had recently come to the Apostolic See. You also said that this bishop, thoroughly trained in Greek letters and endowed with and confident in an eloquent manner of speech, had put forward many things concerning the doctrine and ecclesiastical rite of the Greeks [Col. 1139C], which in no way agree with the teaching of the Roman Church and differ greatly from its rite. [Note: [Col. 1140C] “And from its rite.” Thus Baluzius corrected it; formerly it was read “and from its outcome.” In this prologue we have added within brackets certain words that were altogether necessary.] And he, indeed, by forcibly twisting certain authorities of the Holy Scriptures to his own meaning, seemed to affirm as correct everything in which the Greeks disagree with the Latins; while he seemed to discredit as incorrect those things in which the Latins differ from the Greeks. That which was his own, precisely because it was his own and not because it was true, he approved in every possible way [Col. 1140B]; but that which was ours, because it was ours and not his own, he rejected altogether. Among these matters he argued especially, as you said, concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit: the Greeks believe and say that he proceeds from the Father alone, whereas the Latins from the Father and the Son; and [concerning] the rite of the sacrifice at the altar, which the Latins celebrate with unleavened bread, but the Greeks with leavened bread; as well as certain other matters, rather ingeniously raised as questions.

Therefore, since I was once the envoy at Constantinople of the august Lothair the Great, emperor of the Romans, and while staying there for some time held many discussions and disputations on such doctrine and rite, sometimes in private and sometimes in public assemblies of both Latins and Greeks, [Col. 1140C] it pleased Your Holiness both to request by commanding and to command by requesting that I should gather into one work the things which I had said there and which I had heard and received from them, and should compose them in dialogue as a kind of *Antikeimenōn*, that is, “book of things set in opposition,” so that all things said by them on these subjects, and those reasonably set against them, might be subjected to the freer judgment of your discernment, insofar as they might more truly become known to your discrimination [Col. 1141A]. For some Latins are often misled by Greek statements when they hear merely the outward sound of the words rather than understand their examined meaning, imagining that the Greeks affirm what they do not affirm, or deny what they do not deny at all.

Accordingly, I did what apostolic authority commanded, to which obedience is always owed—not only through devoted humility but also from the necessity of eternal salvation. So far as memory supplied it, I preserved the course of the dialogue which I had in a public assembly at the city of Constantinople with the venerable and most learned Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, adding certain matters no less necessary to the faith than suited to this work. This Archbishop Nechites was foremost among the twelve *didaskaloi* [teachers], [Col. 1141B] who, according to the custom of Greek sages, direct the studies both of the liberal arts and of the divine Scriptures; they preside over the other learned men as surpassing all in learning, and all the most difficult questions are referred to them. Their solutions are thereafter accepted and written down without reconsideration, as settled judgments.

I have prefaced it with a book on the one form of believing and the many forms of living, from righteous Abel to the last elect person, compelled by the many requests of certain brothers. They said that it is no slight scandal to many little ones, and also to the learned, that in the Church which is one, while holding one faith, so many innovations of such diverse religious observance emerge everywhere in manifold ways through the succession of times [Col. 1142A]. Although the judgment of Your Blessedness, filled with the most precious treasury of the Holy Scriptures and surpassing all else, is abundantly sufficient to answer the Greeks, with the Lamb revealing—or opening—the seal of divine Scripture, the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world; and although, after the excellence of so great a teacher, other Latin scholars too may assemble many arguments against them that are stronger, nevertheless let not what I have woven in this *Antikeimenōn* in dialogue be rashly judged superfluous. Perhaps some humble people, whose minds are not very quick at once to discover something, will gladly read these things in order more truly to know what the Greeks say, and [to] find here, to some extent, what may be answered to them [Col. 1142B].

Certainly, whoever reads this should know that I wrote it not so much in order to teach anyone, or to display what I have learned, as to obey the holy command of Apostolic Blessedness. I judge that not to obey this is a greater sin than obediently to write things that may be less useful or less convincing. Thus I did what I could, though less than I ought or wished; and what I ought, by obeying plausibly enough, though writing less plausibly. For the fault of not obeying a command is more serious than writing, in obedience, even things of whatever quality, provided only that the rightness of faith is preserved; for if inexperience sins in writing, obedience that has been imposed and humbly fulfilled excuses it.

# BOOK I. On the unity of faith and the multiplicity of ways of life, from righteous Abel to the last elect person

[Col. 1141]

## CHAPTER I. On the fact that some are accustomed to wonder at the very diverse forms of the Christian religion

[Col. 1141C]

Many people are accustomed to wonder, to raise the matter as a question, and by asking questions to cause scandal not only for themselves but also for others. For they say, and inquire as slanderous questioners: “Why do so many innovations arise in the Church of God? Why do so many orders arise within it? Who can count so many orders of clerics? Who would not marvel at so many kinds of monks? Finally, who would not be scandalized and afflicted by a wearisome scandal amid so many and such diverse forms of religious observance, differing from one another? Indeed, who would not despise the Christian religion, subjected to so many variations, altered by so many inventions [Col. 1141D], agitated by so many new laws and customs, fluctuating with rules and practices renewed almost every year? What, they say, is now commanded by certain persons for the sake of the kingdom of heaven is immediately forbidden by the same or by others for the sake of the kingdom of heaven [Col. 1142C]. What is now prohibited as sacrilegious is suddenly allowed as holy and salutary.”

When idle, such people introduce questions and pervert the hearts of the simple, saying that every religious observance is the more contemptible the more changeable it is. “For what,” they say, “is so movable, so variable, so unstable—how can it be worthily imitated by any wise person? By its very diversity it proves itself fit to be rejected.” “Look,” they say, “we see certain persons arise in the Church of God who clothe themselves, as they please, in an unusual habit; choose for themselves a new order of life; and, whether under the title of monastic profession or under the vow of canonical discipline, take for themselves whatever they wish. They devise for themselves a new manner of chanting [Col. 1142D], a new measure of abstinence, and limits for food. They imitate neither the monks who serve under the Rule of blessed Benedict nor the canons who live the apostolic life under the Rule of blessed Augustine. Rather, doing everything anew as has been said, according to their own pleasure [Col. 1143A], they are law to themselves and authority to themselves. Under the pretext of a new religious observance they gather into their society whomsoever they can. They are thought more religious if they are found separated from every habit and discipline of religious people, and are pointed out with the finger as conspicuous above the rest.”

These and similar things they say, troubling some by frequent questions, not openly but secretly and insidiously tearing at religion. As though they loved and embraced religion, they say: “Would that we could find somewhere something certain, upon which we might confidently rest our heads in expectation of eternal salvation!” They are such troublesome slanderers that, if they happen to see anyone depart from his professed religious observance [Col. 1143B], they immediately rage against all religious observance; they ascribe the evil of one person to all. [Note: [Col. 1143D] “The evil of one person.” We chose to print this; the earlier edition read “a lesser evil.” In the following chapter we have printed “within with us,” where it had read “among with us.” Concerning the little words which we have added [Col. 1144D], it is enough to warn the reader once that they are distinguished from the rest in a definite way: they are enclosed in brackets.] Because of one wandering apostate, they despise and reject all others who persevere in the fear of God and in a holy purpose. They do not heed what is written in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea, gathering fish of every kind; when it was filled, they drew it out, sat down by the shore, chose the good into their vessels, and threw the bad outside” (Matt. 13:47–48). And in the parable of the tares: “Let both grow together, lest perhaps, while gathering the tares, you uproot the wheat with them” (ibid., v. 30).

But if these people who argue and slander religion on account of its diversity wished themselves to be numbered among religious persons, then all the things which now serve them for scandal and destruction would themselves become for their correction and edification, as it is written: “Great peace belongs to those who love your law, and there is no stumbling-block for them” (Ps. 118:167). And: “All things work together for good for the saints” (Rom. 8:28).

## CHAPTER II. That the one body of the Church is ruled and governed by one Holy Spirit, having diverse distributions of graces

Therefore, so that such questioners may no longer wonder at the diversity existing in the Church of God, and so that their troublesome and importunate questions may no longer have any place; finally, so that they too, having laid aside scandal and falsehood and recognized the true way of religious observance, may no longer be able to wander because of diversity, but may be found truly religious with those who are truly religious, and be within with us rather than outside against us [Col. 1143D], let us see—and invite them to see with us—what according to the Catholic faith or the Holy Scripture ought to be done and maintained concerning this: namely, how the Church of God is one in itself and according to itself, and how it is multiform according to its children, whom it has formed and forms by diverse ways, laws, and institutions, from the blood of righteous Abel to the last elect person [Col. 1144A].

For it is said in the voice of the Bridegroom: “My dove, my perfect one, is one; she is the one of her mother, the chosen one of her who bore her” (Song 6:3). She is one: one in faith, one in charity, one by the singleness free from the stain of impious unbelief and from the wrinkle of perverse duplicity. There is one generation of the righteous, of which it is written: “The generation of the upright shall be blessed” (Ps. 111:2). And there is one body of the Church, brought to life, ruled, and governed by the Holy Spirit—the Holy Spirit who is united to it, manifold, subtle, mobile, eloquent, undefiled, certain, sweet, loving the good, keen, hindering nothing beneficial, humane, kindly, steadfast, secure, possessing all power, overseeing all things, and able to receive all spirits; intelligible and pure. That is, in the Holy Spirit, [Col. 1144B] according to the Apostle: “There are divisions of graces, but the same Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:4). And: “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for usefulness: to one, through the Spirit, a word of wisdom; to another, a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, gifts of healing in the one Spirit; to another, the working of powers; to another, prophecy; to another, discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, interpretation of utterances. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, dividing to each individually as he wills” (ibid., vv. 7–11).

See clearly that the one body of the Church is brought to life by one Holy Spirit, who is both one in himself and manifold in the diverse distribution of his gifts [Col. 1144C]. Yet this body of the Church, enlivened by the Holy Spirit and distinguished and differentiated through diverse members in diverse times and ages, began with the first righteous Abel and will be completed in the last elect person: always one by one faith, yet manifoldly differentiated by a multiple variety of ways of life.

## CHAPTER III. On the diverse rite of sacrifices by which the same one God was propitiated from Abel to Christ

For Abel, being a shepherd of sheep, in faith offered to God from the firstborn of his flock and from their fat. He was the first to do this in faith, commanded by no special divine order and instructed by no written law as yet, but taught by the law of nature alone, which advised that the Creator should be honoured by the creature. God looked upon him and upon his gifts, although no rite of sacrifice is yet there recorded as having prescribed that this or that should be offered in this or that way [Col. 1144D]. It is rightly said that God looked first upon Abel himself and afterward upon his gifts, because it is believed that both he and his gifts pleased God not because of the gifts but because of righteousness.

By faith Noah, having received an answer concerning things not yet seen, was fearful and prepared an ark for the salvation of his household. Having gone forth from the ark, he was the first to build an altar to the Lord; and, taking from every clean animal and bird, he offered a burnt offering upon the altar [Col. 1145A]. But there an altar is not named: there the offering is said to have been made from clean birds, while here it is said to have been made from the firstborn of the flock; yet here too no order of sacrifice had been prescribed.

By faith Abraham offered sacrifice to the Lord, instructed by no written law as yet but admonished by a special divine vision. For thus the Lord spoke to him, teaching for the first time the order of sacrifices, not in writing but only by a command of the living voice, so that this appears to have been something to be done at that time by Abraham alone, not a written command left to his descendants: “Take for me,” he says, “a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old she-goat, and a three-year-old ram, as well as a turtledove and a pigeon.” Taking all these, he divided them through the middle and placed the two portions opposite each other on either side; but he did not divide the birds. “And birds came down upon the carcasses, and Abraham drove them away” (Gen. 15:9–11) [Col. 1145B].

By faith Abraham offered his only son Isaac to the Lord who commanded and tested him. He also believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness; and he was the first to receive the law of circumcision as a seal of faith. By faith Jacob, on his journey to Haran, after the vision in which he saw the Lord leaning upon the ladder, awoke from sleep in the morning, set up as a memorial the stone which he had placed beneath his head, and poured oil over it—taught by no law, but doing this by devotion of faith alone. Dying, he likewise blessed each of Joseph’s sons in faith.

Should not these, and many others approved by the testimony of faith, be considered members of the unity of the Church [Col. 1145C], even though, with one faith, they worshiped one God by diverse ways of life and by diverse rites of sacrifice? How many faithful persons were there from Adam to Noah, not numbered here, who followed the natural law, knew and worshiped God the Creator of all, and did not inflict upon any neighbour, to give offence, those things which they did not wish done to themselves? From Noah to Abraham, moreover, very many faithful persons were found who, following the law of nature, served not the creature but God the Creator alone in diverse ways; and, abstaining as far as they could from every injury to their neighbour, humanely bestowed upon their neighbours those things which they themselves would have desired.

Furthermore, from Abraham to Moses there were by no means few who, similarly following the natural law and sometimes also receiving from the Lord a law of obedience [Col. 1145D], are reckoned among, and belong to, the unity of the Church. They devoted themselves not to lust but to the posterity of children to be begotten; sometimes they even took as concubines handmaids whom their own wives had given them in hope of children. They used them as obediently as their own wives, not incontinently. They also believed with the most certain faith that in their seed, which is Christ, all tribes of the earth would be blessed. In their time also the rite of circumcision was announced, which they received from the Lord’s command as a seal of faith.

Then, from Moses to David, when circumcision was already customary, the chosen people of God, separated from fellowship with foreigners and led by Moses, their most faithful leader, were gathered into one Church [Col. 1146A]. The written law was established by the finger of God; a new rite and new rules of sacrifices were instituted; the law of burnt offering, the law of sacrifice, and the law of the offering for a vow were formed in manifold variety. A new order of life, new commands, new precepts, and new prohibitions were written for that Church. Thus, by the diversity of the written law, the people of God were set apart from the uncircumcised and from all other nations; they were governed and ruled by chosen judges.

At that time the famous Gentile Job is thought to have lived: outstanding in the virtue of patience; most clear in his faith in the future resurrection; most courageous in enduring the shameful temptation caused by his own wife; most prudent amid the burdensome consolation of his friends [Col. 1146B]; strongest in faith under the most crushing weight of every temptation; and approved by God himself through the true testimony that no one like him existed on earth. Rising early, he sanctified his children and offered burnt offerings for each one. [Note: [Col. 1145] “For each one.” “On behalf of each one” would be preferable; and shortly afterward, where the text reads “to propitiate God,” it is read “to preach God.”] I do not know by what rite—one not displeasing to God at that time—whether Job himself had then devised it, or whether the religion of that nation had then chosen it for itself to proclaim God, or whether perhaps God had at that time appointed it for that Gentile people through someone; though certain Scripture does not report this to us.

## CHAPTER IV. That the ancient fathers, though they did not fully know every article of the Christian faith, are nevertheless believed to have been saved in faith in the One to come

[Col. 1146C]

Afterward, from David to Christ, when leaders had ceased, kings were chosen and anointed in the same Church; scribes and Pharisees are named; the most glorious temple, in which the ark of the covenant was to be placed, was built; prophets, men most worthy of reverence, arose; they spoke and wrote various prophecies, prophesying to that people future prosperity and adversity. To the law long since written were added new traditions, new ceremonies, and observances. Singers chanting on the psaltery were appointed, with tambourine, choir, organ, and every kind of musical instrument. Nazirites arose according to the times; many honorable things were most devoutly arranged for the adornment of the house of God. Thus among the ancient fathers, by many ways [Col. 1146D], the one God was faithfully served in one faith.

For all served in faith in the One to come, and in faith in the One to come they were saved. Although most of them did not possess such knowledge of the faith that they fully knew, article by article, all the sacraments of Christ and of the Church, and beheld with unveiled face the mystery of the incarnation, birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension, nevertheless it must be believed most firmly that, as those seeing from afar, greeting Christ who was to come, and awaiting the grace of the desired promise, they belong to the unity of the Catholic Church and pertain to the holy city, the new Jerusalem coming down from heaven, prepared by God like a bride adorned for her husband [Col. 1147A] (Rev. 21:2).

For how are we to understand what is written of very many of them: “This man began to invoke the name of the Lord” (Gen. 4:26); “This man invoked the name of his God” (Gen. 13:4); “This man built an altar to the Lord” (Gen. 12:7); and “He invoked the name of his God” (Gen. 21:23)? Is it not because he invoked the name of the Lord, believing that the name of the Lord is the Son of God who was to come in the flesh? The prophet, speaking of the incarnation of the Son of God—who is the Word of the Father and the name of the Lord—also fittingly suggests this: “Behold, the name of the Lord comes from afar, and his brightness fills the whole earth” (Isa. 30:29). For just as someone previously unknown becomes known to another through his proper name, so God the Father became known and was manifested to the world through his proper name: through his only Son, through his Word [Col. 1147B].

## CHAPTER V. That two famous transitions of religious observance took place—the Law and the Gospel—with the testimony of earthquakes because of the greatness of those events

It should be observed that two famous transitions of life and religious observance took place, also called the two Testaments, each accompanied by the testimony of an earthquake because of the greatness of the events themselves. The first occurred from idols to the Law, where there were thunders and lightnings, a very dense cloud, the blast of a trumpet, and a terrifying noise. The second occurred from the Law to the Gospel, where there was a great earthquake, the sun was darkened, rocks were split, tombs [Col. 1147C] were opened, and the bars of hell were broken. But a third earthquake is foretold, when, after these things are ended and completed, there will be a transition to things which will no longer be moved or shaken.

In these two transitions, or changes, divine Wisdom made use of such great variety by degrees that, first, cutting people off from idols, it permitted sacrifices; second, removing sacrifices, it did not prohibit circumcision; then, taking away circumcision, it commended saving baptism together with evangelical institution and teaching. Thus it made Jews out of Gentiles and Christians out of Jews; and, gradually taking away, transferring, and administering, it led humankind, as if by stealth, from the worship of idols to the Law, and from the Law [Col. 1147D]—which indeed did not bring them to perfection—to the perfection of the Gospel, pedagogically and medicinally. At last, removing every dispensation, it taught the whole perfection of the Christian law.

## CHAPTER VI. That the Old Testament openly proclaimed God the Father, but obscurely God the Son; while the New Testament revealed God the Son, but first suggested and gradually taught sufficiently the deity of the Holy Spirit

For what is the case? The Old Testament openly proclaimed God the Father, but not God the Son so openly: rather, obscurely. The New Testament revealed God the Son, but indicated and suggested the deity of the Holy Spirit. Later the Holy Spirit is proclaimed [Col. 1148A], granting us a clearer manifestation of his deity. For it was not fitting, before the deity of the Father had been confessed, that the Son should be openly proclaimed; nor, before the deity of the Son had been received, that the deity of the Holy Spirit should be proclaimed to us—lest human minds, dulled by dwelling on earth and weighed down by the burden of sins, be loaded with food beyond their strength and burdened beyond measure.

Nor was the transition easy from things which had come into veneration through long custom and extended time. Therefore evangelical and salutary medicine was received gradually, as by the weak, and through divine skill medicinally mixed with gentler remedies. Yet the Holy Spirit himself is everywhere set alongside the Son in the Gospel: the Son is begotten [Col. 1148B]; the Holy Spirit, going before in the conception, overshadows the Virgin; the Son is baptized; the Holy Spirit is present in the form of a dove with the testimony of the Father; the Son is tempted; the Holy Spirit leads and brings him back; the Son performs miracles; the Holy Spirit follows everywhere and enters into believers; the Son ascends to heaven; the Holy Spirit succeeds him in order to teach and supply all truth.

Thus faith in the Holy Trinity, measured gradually according to the capacity of believers, distributed as it were in parts, and growing into completeness, was finally made perfect. Accordingly, from Christ’s coming until the day of judgment—the sixth age, as it is distinguished—in which the one and same Church, now with the Son of God present, is renewed, there are found not one or uniform but many and multiform conditions [Col. 1148C].

There was indeed one appearance of Christian religious observance in the primitive Church, when Jesus, returning from the Jordan and led by the Spirit into the wilderness, after the tempter had left him following the temptations, passed through Judaea and Galilee and chose twelve apostles. He instructed these men by a special teaching in the Christian faith; taught them to be poor in spirit and taught them the other things written in the sermon which he delivered to them on the mountain; instructed them to trample underfoot this wicked world; and formed them by the salutary and innumerable precepts of evangelical teaching.

But after Christ’s passion, resurrection, and ascension, and after the Holy Spirit had been given, many people who saw the signs and wonders [Col. 1148D] done through the hands of the apostles gathered themselves into their fellowship. And it came about, as Luke writes: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul; no one said that anything was his own, but all things were common to them; nor was anyone needy among them. It was distributed to each according as each had need” (Acts 4:32–35). “But none of the rest dared join themselves to them, though the people magnified them” (Acts 5:13).

Thus a new Church of believers was gathered through the grace of the Holy Spirit, renewed first from the Jews and then from the Gentiles. The rite of both Jews and Gentiles was gradually laid aside, though certain natural and legal distinctions were preserved; these, selected and excepted from both the law of nature and the written law, were not and are not contrary to the Christian faith [Col. 1149A], but are salutary to all who observe them devoutly and faithfully.

At that time the complete faith of the Holy Trinity also began to be openly proclaimed, with testimony from the Old and New Testaments. Previously it had been disclosed as if under a shadow and by stages. New sacraments arise, new rites, new commands, and new institutions. Apostolic and canonical epistles are written. Christian law is established by teachings and writings; the faith called Catholic is announced throughout the whole world. The holy Church, passing through diverse conditions succeeding one another gradually, is renewed, as the youth of the eagle, down to the present day and always will be renewed, while the foundation of faith in the Holy Trinity remains secure [Col. 1149B]. Beyond this foundation no one can afterward lay another, although in the superstructure diverse constructions of diverse religious observances often grow into a holy temple for the Lord.

## CHAPTER VII. On the seven seals signifying the seven successive states of the Church; and that in the first state, when the white horse went forth, the primitive Church grew through the novelty of miracles and wonders

Certainly, the seven seals which John saw, as he himself relates in his Apocalypse (6:2), are seven successive states of the Church from Christ’s coming until all things are completed at the end and God is all in all. For “when the Lamb had opened one of the seven seals, behold [Col. 1149C] a white horse; and he who sat upon it had a bow, and a crown was given him, and he went forth conquering so that he might conquer” (ibid.).

The white horse is the first state of the Church, shining and most beautiful in the brightness of miracles, which all admired and magnified because of its novelty. He who sat upon it and had a bow is Christ, governing the Church and humbling and overthrowing the proud with the bow of apostolic teaching. “And a crown was given him” (Rev. 6:2), because “he went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom” (Luke 19:12). “And he went forth conquering, so that he might conquer” (Rev. 6:2), just as he himself says to his own: “Take courage: I have conquered the world” (John 16:33). See: in this first state of the Church being born, the multitude of men and women believing in the Lord increased more and more [Col. 1149D], and the Church of God daily became more illustrious through the power of miracles and the number of believers (Acts 5:14).

## CHAPTER VIII. That in the second state of the Church, when the red horse went forth, the most grievous persecution of the saints blazed forth

“And when he had opened the second seal, another, red horse went forth; and to him who sat upon it was given power to take peace from the earth, so that people might kill one another; and a great sword was given to him” (Rev. 6:3). See the second state of the Church openly revealed to the disciple whom Jesus loved. For what else does the going forth of the red horse mean but the blood of martyrs, shed in testimony to Christ, when peace was taken from the earth and the great sword of persecution was given [Col. 1150A] in the Church?

This state of persecution undoubtedly took its beginning from the glorious protomartyr Stephen, whom the Jews stoned. After his triumph, such persecution blazed up that the Church could no longer remain in one place, Jerusalem; rather, the apostles, scattered over the whole earth, preached the faith of Christ, and in preaching brought their lives to completion through martyrdom. Thus Peter and Paul adorned Rome, James Jerusalem, Andrew Achaia, Bartholomew India, Matthew Ethiopia, and the other apostles each a separate province, by their most glorious martyrdom. After them, very many other believers endured mockery and scourging, and moreover bonds and imprisonment, suffering the most grievous and exquisitely devised kinds of tortures. They happily raised the title of Christian profession to heaven [Col. 1150B] and left us their memory in blessing. Laws were written against the Christian name, so that whoever was found to be a worshiper of this religion might be dragged off to punishments and condemned without a hearing.

But the Church of God flourished in persecution as a palm tree in victory; and, like the cedar of Lebanon, the more it suffered, the more it multiplied.

But the dragon, that ancient serpent, who had stirred up such savagery against the Church of God, saw that he could not utterly swallow the woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars on her head, by the flood [Col. 1150C] that he had sent from his mouth. He was enraged against the woman and again set himself to make war with the rest of her offspring, who keep her commandments and bear the testimony of Jesus.

Therefore, when open persecution ceased, the law issued against Christians was relaxed; another law was promulgated for the peace of the Church; kings hastened to baptism; rulers of diverse provinces received the faith of Christ; and the whole world, which had formerly persecuted the Christian name, now humbly venerates it. The cross of Christ, formerly an occasion of stumbling and derision, is now raised up for honour and veneration. Churches are magnificently built everywhere; bishops, priests, deacons, and clerics of the remaining orders, formerly cast aside, are called back from exile; teachers of the faith are sought everywhere [Col. 1150D]; and the most sacred order of bishops and clerics is dispatched and spread throughout all lands to preach the Gospel of God.

## CHAPTER IX. That in the third state of the Church, when the black horse went forth, the greatest dangers from heretics troubled the Church beyond measure

“And when he had opened the third seal, behold a black horse; and he who sat upon it had a balance in his hand” (Rev. 6:5). See the third state of the Church, in which the black horse emerged. The black horse is the dark doctrine of heretics, whom the aforesaid great dragon stirred up against the Church of God so that the Church which he had previously been unable to swallow by the shedding of martyrs’ blood [Col. 1151A], he might now throw into disorder by the utterly perverse teaching of heretics.

Heretics therefore arise, bearing the character of the beast stamped upon their hearts; and while they hold in their hands a deceitful balance for weighing, they propose equity while disputing concerning the faith, but deceive the less cautious by the slightest weight of a single, even the smallest, word, and draw them into the share of their error. Among these are Arius, that most notorious presbyter and most hostile heresiarch of the Church of God, and his followers. Disputing over the name of consubstantiality and separating themselves from the Church on that account, they counted diverse substances in the Trinity, falsely affirming—impiously supposing diverse substances where we piously believe diverse persons. [Col. 1151B] There was also Sabellius, who, because he rightly believed there to be one substance in the Trinity, thought that one person likewise ought to be believed there among the three—namely, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. There was also Nestorius, bishop, who judged that a double nature could not exist without a double person; and therefore, although he rightly confessed a double nature in Christ, he wrongly believed there to be a double person, foolishly preaching one Son of God and another son of man. There was also Eutyches, an archimandrite abbot, who did not think that a double nature could exist without a duplication of person; and, since he did not confess a double person in Christ, he judged that it followed that there should appear to be one nature. Thus Nestorius, [Col. 1151C] rightly believing that there are two natures in Christ, the divine and the human, confessed with sacrilegious mouth that there are two persons there. Eutyches, on the other hand, most rightly believing that there is one person in Christ, falsely believed that there is also one nature there. Opposed to one another, they were deceived and deceived others.

There was Macedonius, bishop, faithlessly asserting that the Holy Spirit is a creature and not God. There was Donatus, who taught in proud contention that the Son is less than the Father and the Holy Spirit less than both. There was also Photinus, bishop, most shamelessly attributing Christ’s beginning from Mary to sexual intercourse. There was Manes of Persia, from whom come the Manichaeans, stubbornly teaching two principles and perversely denying that God’s Only-Begotten is eternal.

[Col. 1151D] There were also very many other heretics, each of whom, teaching false doctrines in his own time and, like enemy men, sowing pestilential tares among the wheat of apostolic teaching, cruelly plucked and tore apart God’s dove—simple in faith, holy and immaculate in deed. Against them many councils were held in fitting places and times; heretical perversity was condemned, the leaven of malice and wickedness was purged out, and Mother Church was strengthened in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. For in the Council of Nicaea, and those of Antioch, Ephesus, Chalcedon, and Constantinople, and in very many other synodal assemblies of holy Fathers held in diverse provinces, the serpentine poisons of heretics were so utterly destroyed, crushed, [Col. 1152A] stilled, and emptied out that they now no longer dare to sprout or bubble up in any corner of the Catholic Church. Orthodox faith itself, after so many assaults, has been so strengthened, founded, and established that henceforth, with the Lord’s favor, it ought by right always to remain unshaken and unmoved: wholly entire, so that nothing may be added; and wholly inviolate, so that nothing may be taken away. Therefore the holy Fathers have fittingly forbidden anyone henceforth publicly to dispute about the faith, as though concerning something already defined and which ought to be doubtful to no one; for it is the height of madness to seek an imaginary light in broad and manifest day. Whoever, after truth has been found, learns something further, [Col. 1152B] seeks falsehood and deservedly entangles himself.

Once the Catholic faith had been rooted, various rules were added to shape the discipline of the Church. Since the holy Fathers enacted them, they were worthily called canons. In them are found precepts, prohibitions, dispensations, rigor, necessity, indulgence, remission, terror, admonition, and the other means through which, in this state, the Church increased by a wonderful wisdom against heretics just as, in the preceding state, she increased by victorious patience amid the persecution of martyrs. But behold: the roaring lion does not cease or sleep, but still prowls about seeking someone to devour (1 Pet. 5:8).

## CHAPTER X. That in the fourth state of the Church, when the pale horse went forth, the Church of God labored beyond measure because of false brethren; and that in this state many and varied religious orders also increased.

[Col. 1152C]

“And when he had opened the fourth seal, behold, a pale horse; and he that sat upon him, his name was Death, and Hell followed him” (Rev. 6:7). This is clearly the fourth state of the Church, in which the gravest and deadliest danger lies in false brethren. For just as a pale color is mixed of white and black, and does not show itself wholly white but falsely contains both, so likewise false Christians, or false brethren—whose multitude is now beyond counting—publicly confess Christ with their mouths, [Col. 1152D] but deny him in their deeds. They attend church, receive the ecclesiastical sacraments, show their prelates due reverence, and, according to the Apostle, outdo one another in showing honor. They build churches and fittingly adorn both them and their altars for the beauty of God’s house. They celebrate the solemnities and feasts of the saints with what seems the greatest devotion; they greatly commend long offices of Mass and the ordered processions of the clergy; they sometimes impose upon themselves fasts and distinctions of food; they extend alms to the poor with their own hands; when holy and truly religious men happen to meet them, inwardly proud in heart but outwardly bowing the head, they greet them, often receive them as guests and treat them humanely, and commend themselves to their prayers. Some even visit [Col. 1153A] the glorious tomb of the Lord at Jerusalem, the thresholds of the apostles, or other holy places. In every cause, whether another’s or their own, they call God to witness for themselves; whatever they say or do, they declare that they say or do it in the Lord’s name. In brief: in decent dress, decent speech, decent appearance, decent gait, and every decent movement of the body, they bear and outwardly display a religious, honorable, disciplined person. With them and among them the state of the Church seems peaceful: she is neither openly attacked by the sword of persecutors nor wearied by the deceitful importunity of heretics.

Yet the Church labors so greatly among false Christians, or false brethren, who have put on the name and habit of Christian religion, [Col. 1153B] that the one sitting upon the pale horse is rightly called Death—a death sparing no mortal—and is also aptly called Hell, which never says, “Enough.” For what is there in false brethren but the death that kills souls, pale in hypocrisy and pretense, followed by Hell with open jaws, utterly ready to devour? Of them the Lord says in the Gospel under the name of scribes and Pharisees:

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who shut the kingdom of heaven before men. You yourselves do not enter, nor do you permit those entering to enter. Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who devour widows’ houses while making long prayers; therefore you will receive a greater judgment” (Matt. 23:13–14).

“Woe [Col. 1153C] to you, scribes and Pharisees, who tithe mint, dill, and cumin, and neglect the weightier matters of the law: judgment, mercy, and faith” (ibid., 23).

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who cleanse the outside of cup and dish, while within you are full of robbery and uncleanness. Blind Pharisee, first cleanse what is inside the cup and dish, that what is outside may become clean. Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who are like whitewashed tombs: outwardly they appear beautiful to men, but within they are full of dead men’s bones and filth. So you also outwardly appear righteous to men, but within you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity. Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who build the tombs of the prophets and adorn the monuments [Col. 1153D] of the righteous, and say: ‘If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have been their partners in the blood of the prophets.’ Thus you bear witness against yourselves that you are sons of those who killed the prophets. And you—fill up the measure of your fathers! Serpents, brood of vipers, how will you escape the judgment of Gehenna?” (Matt. 23:25, 33).

Behold, dearest brethren, we have heard terrible threats against hypocrites. Let us fear the pale death of souls, and Hell following and gaping wide; let us flee detestable hypocrisy.
