Let us cleanse and purify what is within by sincere confession, and wipe it clean by frequent outpourings of tears. [Col. 1154A] But outwardly, each in the order to which he has been called, let us in no way depart from the rule of ecclesiastical discipline, if we do not wish either to commit or to suffer scandal.

### Invective against the hypocrite

Woe to you, wretched hypocrite, most wretched of all wretches: pretender to good, lover of evil, enemy of God, enemy of yourself, seducer of yourself, deceiver of yourself, defrauder of yourself, flatterer of yourself, mocker of yourself, deluder of yourself, slanderer of yourself, condemner of yourself, betrayer of yourself, judge of yourself, murderer of yourself; displayer of truth, maker of falsehood; thief of your own treasure, persecutor of your own conscience; wicked fox, restless worm, twisting serpent, biting cancer, whitewashed wall; most foolish of all other fools; martyr of the devil; walking among the living without life; already dead and buried; most ruined of all [Col. 1154B] men; worthless servant; inwardly bound, inwardly chained, inwardly pierced through, inwardly imprisoned, inwardly concealed, inwardly most rotten, inwardly most foul; most shameful, most unhappy, most criminal, most wicked, condemned, deceitful, puffed up, empty, windy, pale, blinded, dark, timid, suspicious, swollen, full of demons, steeped outwardly and inwardly in magical arts; desperate, leaning wall, cast-down fence, having no foundation, near to ruin; muddy, filthy, unclean, most foul, confused, hateful, treacherous; seller of holy oil, extinguished lamp, most deceitful, excluded and alienated from every good, already thrust into Hell, most false and devoid of all truth, and in every way detestable to God and angels [Col. 1154C] and men!

Woe to you, wretched hypocrite! You have mounted the pale horse; your name is Death; Hell follows you, entirely certain to devour you. Woe to you, wretched hypocrite! Would that you might turn in heart and become a trampler of falsehood and lover of truth, so that what you have hitherto done in pretense you may henceforth do in truth. Do not change the quality of your good works, but change the wicked intention of perverse pretense; and so, from works now made good, dare to await or hope for the merit for which previously, as a pretender, you ought to have awaited worthy punishment. For a good or evil intention gives a work its name and demands either merit or punishment in just recompense.

In this state of the Church appeared religious men, [Col. 1154D] lovers of truth and restorers of religion: Augustine, bishop of the Church of Hippo, the envoy of the province of Numidia in Africa. Gathering brethren who were not false, he chose to live the apostolic life; and he prescribed for them a Rule for communal living. Afterwards it was promulgated and approved throughout the whole world of the Catholic Church, inviting and gathering very many into the holy fellowship of common life, in imitation of the apostles and according to the pattern of so great a man; and it gathers them still today. Following in his footsteps, a certain most religious N. [Note: [Col. 1153] “Most religious N.” indicates Arberius; concerning him see vol. IV of *Gallia Christiana*, p. 802.] of Saint-Ruf in Burgundy arose in the time of Pope Urban. He gathered brethren in the same canonical [Col. 1155A] profession, first enlightened that entire province, and gradually spread the same religious observance into different regions.

There also arose in the same profession and imitation of the apostolic life a religious presbyter named Norbert, in the time of Pope Gelasius. Because of his religious devotion and the many enormities and schisms then occurring in the Western Church, he received from Gelasius, the Roman pontiff, letters and authority to preach. In his own time he was most illustrious and renowned in religion; he traversed diverse provinces in preaching, gathered no small multitude of religious persons, established many communities, and by word and example formed them to the perfection of apostolic life. He also had such favor before God and men [Col. 1155B] that those able to attach themselves to him truly called themselves blessed. Afterwards he was made archbishop in the Church of Magdeburg. His holy and venerable body rests in the church of Blessed Mary in his metropolitan see, where he had established brethren of his religious order. The religious observance renewed through him therefore began to have very great growth and spread throughout the world, so that scarcely any province in the western regions lacks communities of that same observance: France, Germany, Burgundy, Aquitaine, nearer Spain, Lesser Brittany, England, Denmark, Saxony, Leuticia, Poland, Moravia, Bavaria, Swabia, Pannonia—which is Hungary—Lombardy, Liguria, and Etruria, which is Tuscany. All these provinces, [Col. 1155C] I say, possess communities of the aforementioned observance and continually trust to be aided by their examples and prayers. This same holy society also extended its branches into the East: for there is one community in Bethlehem and another in the place called Saint Habakkuk.

There also arose in the monastic order, after many Fathers of monks dwelling in Egypt, blessed Benedict, a man worthy of God and full of the Holy Spirit. Drawn out from the wilderness of Nursia, where he had been hidden, he became abbot of monks in Campania, on Mount Cassino. Most fervent in religious life, he prescribed a Rule for his followers at the Holy Spirit’s dictation and renewed and strengthened the monastic order, already wavering at that time. Both in person and through [Col. 1155D] his Rule, he afterwards established many monasteries of monks in diverse regions.

There also arose in recent times in Tuscany, at the place called Camaldoli, a religious man named John [Note: [Col. 1155D] “Named John.” The reference is to Romuald, well known by this name.], who, under the title of monastic profession, put on a new habit with his brother monks in a new fervor and had many disciples who followed his pattern. Not long ago, in another place called Vallombrosa, near the mountains of Perugia, a very religious new congregation of monks arose, differing from the others called monks by a new order and new habit, and it has many followers of its pattern.

[Col. 1156A] Accordingly, in Burgundy, in the place called Cîteaux, another new congregation of monks arose almost in our own times, differing in order and habit from all who are called and are monks. Because they seem to surpass and excel others in the virtue of patience, the plainness of their clothing, diligent observance of the Rule, love of holy poverty, and most ardent religious devotion, they have innumerable imitators of their observance and pattern. Among them in our times appeared an abbot named Bernard, in the place called Clairvaux: a most religious man, distinguished by the power of miracles, famous from West to East for his holiness. Pope Eugenius, venerable and formerly a monk of Bernard’s monastery, [Col. 1156B] often honored him with fitting reverence in councils of many bishops.

Likewise, a little before these times, a certain new religious institution began in Jerusalem, the city of God. Laymen, religious men, gathered there and call themselves the Knights of the Temple. Having relinquished their possessions, they live [Note: [Col. 1156D] “They live”: perhaps “they live in common”? That indeed seems to me to be the sense.] under obedience to one master; they have cut away superfluity and costly clothing, being ready to defend the glorious tomb of the Lord against the assaults of the Saracens. At home they are peaceful; abroad, valiant warriors. At home they obey regular discipline; abroad, they obey military discipline. At home they are trained in holy silence; abroad, they are fearless amid martial tumult and assault. In brief, in everything they are commanded [Col. 1156C] to do, within and without, they are perfected in simple obedience. Pope Urban first confirmed their life and purpose by the counsel of many bishops whom he had convened for that very purpose in council, decreeing that all who joined this society in hope of eternal life and persevered in it faithfully should receive remission of all sins. He declared that they were not of lower merit than monks or canons of common life.

Likewise, in the Eastern Church, among Greeks, Armenians, and Syrians, there are diverse kinds of religious persons. They agree indeed in the one Catholic faith, yet differ from one another considerably in customs, order, habit, diet, and the office of psalmody. When I was in the imperial city Constantinople as apocrisiarius [envoy] [Col. 1156D] of Lothair the Great, most Christian Roman emperor, to Kalojoannes, emperor of that same imperial city, and was an eager observer and diligent investigator of diverse religious observances, I saw many orders of Christian religious life there. In the monastery called Pantocratoros—that is, “of the Almighty”—I saw almost seven hundred monks serving under the Rule of blessed Anthony. In the monastery called Philanthropou, “of the Lover of Man,” I saw no fewer than five hundred monks serving under the Rule of blessed Pachomius. I also saw very many communities devoutly serving under the Rule of blessed Basil the Great, that most learned man.

[Col. 1157A] Now all these things—so divine, so holy, so good—in diverse times and diverse orders are wrought by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills (1 Cor. 12:11). The Holy Spirit, who governs the whole body of the Church from the beginning, now, and always, knows how to renew men’s sluggish minds and believers sated with long-familiar religious observance through the beginning of some new form of religious life. Thus, when they see others mounting ever higher to the loftier citadel of religion, they may be stirred more strongly by new examples and, abandoning the sloth and love of the world that held them, may eagerly and without fear attain and imitate what is perfect. For all people are generally more inclined to wonder at what is unfamiliar and unaccustomed than at what is familiar and customary. By God’s wonderful ordering it comes about that, as ever-new religious observance grows from generation [Col. 1157B] to generation, the youth of the Church is renewed like the eagle’s, so that she may both fly more sublimely in contemplation and gaze more keenly, as though with unblinking eyes, upon the rays of the true sun.

Do you then suppose that, in so great a multitude of good persons, no scandal can be found among false brethren? Would that it were so—would that it truly were so! But I fear; I am by no means secure. For when I hear the Lord saying in the Gospel, “Have I not chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil?” (John 6:71), when, I say, I hear this, I am greatly afraid. If in the company of the apostles, few though they were and chosen by the Lord himself, a devil was not lacking, how can one suppose that false brethren are lacking in so great a multitude of good persons? They are certainly [Col. 1157C] members of the devil. For there have also been false prophets and false apostles. Therefore let us not wonder if false brethren are with us and among us. Let us bear them in charity and wait in prayer for them to become true, laying aside pretense. We are together in one net, but when drawn to shore we shall not together be gathered into the vessels of the saints. We grow together in one field, but at harvest-time we shall not together be gathered into one granary. They indeed with us, and we with them, though by different ways and with different intention, run together until this fourth state of the Church is ended. Then the saints shall follow the Lamb wherever he goes; but those who bear the name of the pale horse and of death shall be buried in Hell.

## CHAPTER XI. That in the fifth state of the Church the souls of the saints beneath God’s altar cry: “How long, O Lord, holy and true, do you not avenge our blood upon those who dwell on earth?” etc.

[Col. 1157D]

“And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw beneath the altar the souls of those slain for the word of God and for the testimony which they held. And they cried with a loud voice, saying: ‘How long, O Lord, holy and true, do you not avenge our blood upon those who dwell on earth?’ And white robes were given to each of them; and it was said to them that they should rest yet a little while, until their fellow servants and their brethren, who are to be killed as they also were, should be completed” (Rev. 6:9–11). This is the fifth state of the Church. [Col. 1158A] The Church labored in persecution and increased in patience; she labored under the subtle deceit of heretics and increased in wisdom; she labored among false brethren and hypocrites and increased in endurance. Now the souls of the saints, who by the shedding of blood have merited to rest beneath the altar, which is Christ, seeing the countless miseries of the struggling Church, cry out for her with a great voice, as it were of compassion: “How long, O Lord, do you not avenge our blood?” and the rest that follows there, pertaining to the fifth state of the Church.

## CHAPTER XII. That in the sixth state of the Church, when a great earthquake has occurred, a most powerful persecution will come in the time of Antichrist.

[Col. 1158B]

“And when he had opened the sixth seal, a great earthquake occurred” (Rev. 6:12). This is the sixth state of the Church, in which a great earthquake indeed occurs: that is, the most powerful persecution, which will come in the times of Antichrist. And it will truly be great, because, as the Lord says, “Then there will be tribulation such as has not been since nations began to exist” (Mark 13:19). In other times of persecution, although many kinds of torments were prepared against the Christian name, sound and undoubted faith was still held. Here, however, torments are proposed and a false faith is urged under Christ’s name. For it is said: “Behold, Christ is here; behold, Christ is there.” And there will be tribulation such as has not been (Matt. 24:21), not only in the extent of persecution but also [Col. 1158C] in the overthrow of faith, men not knowing what they ought either to believe or to hold.

“The sun became black as sackcloth of hair,” because Christ, the Sun of righteousness, and the Christian name will then be in abjection, contemptible and obscure blackness; both Christ himself and Christians will be vile and despised in the eyes of Antichrist and his followers, like haircloth, the vilest of all garments. “The whole moon became as blood,” because persecution unto blood will rage against the Church in every part of the world; the moon, alternately waxing and waning, plainly signifies her. “And the stars of heaven fell upon the earth.” The stars of heaven are the saints who appeared to shine as teachers in the firmament of the Church; under that most powerful persecution they will depart from the faith and fall to earth, because they will cling to earthly pleasures and from love of earthly things fall into iniquity. Hence it is added: “As a fig tree casts its unripe figs when shaken by a great wind” (Rev. 6:13). Although in the Gospel the fig tree signifies the Synagogue, here it signifies in particular the whole Church, from which those who were unfruitful and empty of good works will then fall. *Grossi* are the fruits of the first season, which, before reaching maturity, are shaken by the wind and fall to the earth. So too those who have not yet reached the maturity of good works and are empty are shaken by the wind—that is, by the final persecution—and will fall to earth (Acts 22:7), that is, into earthly pleasures. [Col. 1159A] This wind is rightly called great because, as stated above, the persecution will overtake even the elect. “And the heaven withdrew like a scroll being rolled up” (Rev. 6:14). Heaven, that is, the Church, in which ecclesiastical sacraments are hidden, wrapped up, and enclosed, will withdraw from Christians’ use and be concealed from public and solemn rite, as men wither from fear of Antichrist and expectation of those things that shall come upon the whole world (Luke 21:26). “And who shall be able to stand?” (Rev. 6:17), and the other things found in that sixth state of the Church.

## CHAPTER XIII. That in the seventh state of the Church, after many tribulations, there will be great silence, and the octave of infinite blessedness will be restored; and thus the Church of God, one in faith, one in hope, one in charity, is manifold through the variety of her diverse states.

[Col. 1159B]

“And when he had opened the seventh seal, silence occurred in heaven for about half an hour” (Rev. 6:1). The seventh seal is the seventh state of the Church, in which silence will occur because, after the Church’s tribulations—through which she bore the sons of God in great sorrow—after the judgment which will take place at the coming of the Son of God, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, when all things have been consummated, there will be the silence of divine contemplation. The jubilee year will be restored; the octave of infinite blessedness will be celebrated; the Holy of Holies, now that the veil of the law has been removed, will be opened to the faithful; the Song of Songs will be sung before the throne of God and of the Lamb with infinite joy; the solemn day will be established unto the horn of the altar—that is, [Col. 1159C] unto the highest citadel of contemplation—in dense throngs or assemblies; the truth of all figures and sacraments that have existed from the beginning of the world in diverse times will be revealed, and all things will be consummated through him and with him.

But by the statement that silence occurs for half an hour, I think this is certainly signified: although all the elect contemplate God in his glory, nevertheless no creature is thought capable of being granted a knowledge or vision by which it comprehends the full divine substance as it is. For he is incomprehensible and dwells in light inaccessible to every rational creature, whether human or angelic. Thus “half,” and not a complete, hour is rightly said: for although one may attain sufficient blessedness, none is granted to attain the complete knowledge of God himself by which his immeasurable divinity might be comprehended.

Therefore let no one wonder or complain that the Church of God has been distinguished by the unchangeable God through varied laws and observances before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. For it was fitting that, according to the progress of times, the signs of spiritual graces should increase, declaring truth itself ever more clearly, and that knowledge of truth should thus, with the effect of salvation, receive growth from time to time: so that first good things, then better things, and finally the best things were set forth. This variety [Note: [Col. 1159] “This variety.” Anselm certainly wrote *haec varietas*, “this variety,” not, as Acherius had printed, *haec veritas*, “this truth.”] came about not because of a changeableness in the unchangeable God—who is ever the same and whose years do not fail (Ps. 101:29)—[Col. 1160B] but because of the variable weakness of humankind and its temporal change from generation to generation. For there is one Church of the elect, subject to one God: one in the faith by which it faithfully believes the things to be believed, whether concerning the past or the future; one in the hope by which it steadfastly hopes for the things the faithful are to hope for; and one in the charity by which it loves God and its neighbor in God, and which in its breadth extends even to enemies for God’s sake.

Therefore the glory of the King’s daughter, who is the Church, is inwardly the beauty of faith and the testimony of a pure conscience, but she is “clothed round about with golden fringes in variety” (Ps. 44:14), in the diversity of religious observances and activities; and she is the chariot [Col. 1160C] of God, ten-thousandfold, thousands of those rejoicing. Henceforth, therefore, let no believer suspect that there is any scandal in the fact that the Church, whose faith in what is to be believed is always the same, does not always have the same form of life. But for now it is enough to have answered those who censure so many varieties within the holy Church. If, although they take this perversely, they can receive pious answers to their questions, I hope that no scandal will henceforth arise for them through which they might either despise any form of religious life or withdraw their foot from any religious community—provided that they themselves are willing, and that God, who draws all things to himself, is willing to grant this to them.

The first book ends.

## THE PROEM TO THE SECOND BOOK BEGINS, which is called *Antikeimenōn* [Ἀντικειμενῶν], that is, the Book of Contrasted Matters.

[Col. 1159]

[Col. 1159D] I thought that in the preceding pages I had sufficiently answered those who complained of so many varieties, so many forms of religious life, so many changes, so many novelties, so many kinds of profession in the holy Church. But, as it seems to me, although what I have said appears sufficient for them—as is evident from the fact that they no longer assail me over this question—they turn to other questions and do not cease to trouble me. What they formerly seemed to do with an evil zeal, they now, changed for the better, seem to inquire into with a pious and humble spirit. Therefore I shall answer them all the more willingly with whatever is given me from above, since they have shown themselves to inquire more humbly. For God, who resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (1 Pet. 5:5), wishes us to be humble, so that in asking and answering he may not resist us as proud persons, but may truly give grace and grant understanding to the humble.

They say that I have sufficiently answered [Col. 1161A] the question proposed, and say that I could easily have done this, and that they themselves could easily have approached and assented after so many and such weighty arguments and authorities—especially since it does no harm to have diverse customs within one faith, provided that the rite of ecclesiastical sacraments and the general institutions of ecclesiastical order always remain unchanged; neither of these may lawfully be altered by anyone on his own authority, unless he is caught up in the madness of a rash mind.

“But,” they ask, “what does it mean that some in the Church appear to differ in the faith of the Holy Trinity and in the rite of the sacraments, as the Greeks differ from the Latins? If, while preserving unity of faith and one rite of the sacraments, they were unlike in every other respect, this might somehow be tolerated and would seem to involve less scandal [Col. 1161B] or danger. But since they seem to disagree concerning the faith, without which it is impossible to please God, and are recognized not to agree in a single rite of the sacraments, it is necessary that you answer us on this point: what ought we think concerning them, or what ought we ourselves hold?”

“We indeed confess that we are not a little scandalized when we hear that Greek men, most wise and learned in every knowledge of the Scriptures, are said neither to believe nor to say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, just as he proceeds from the Father. If this is so, it is deservedly a very great occasion of most serious scandal. Yet the names of so many thousands of Greeks are found in the catalogue of saints: [Col. 1161C] some whose bodies were buried in peace in Christ, others who gave their bodies to punishments for God’s sake and washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb, thereby meriting to have everlasting crowns. In their honor and reverence many churches have been built and dedicated, and their annual feasts are solemnly celebrated throughout the churches.

“Moreover, in the holy Roman Church many pontiffs of Greek nationality have sat in the chair of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles. Guiding well, in Peter’s stead, the Church, which is Peter’s little ship, by the rudder of right faith and the oar of sound doctrine, they are rightly numbered among the saints. The holy Roman Church herself, mother of all churches, [Col. 1161D] received from the Lord this privilege: that she was so specially founded upon the firm rock that she could never be moved by any wind of heretical perversity. It is astonishing how Greeks can be numbered among the saints, and Roman pontiffs chosen from among them, if they erred so gravely in the faith of the Holy Trinity as to say and believe that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone and in no way from the Son—unless perhaps someone dares to say [Col. 1162A] that it makes no difference to Christian faith and the salvation of believers whether one says or does not believe this or that; as if the article of faith by which the Holy Spirit is believed either to proceed or not to proceed from the Son were necessary for no Christian.

“Accordingly, how,” they ask, “could it happen that a Roman pontiff who was Greek by nation believed, according to the Greeks, that the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Son, while in the Roman Church he preached, according to the Latins, that the same Spirit does proceed from the Son? For it is wicked to say that they believed one thing and preached another. But if what they believed was also what they preached, how did the Roman Church patiently hear those whose doctrine—namely, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone and not from the Son—she neither approved then [Col. 1162B] nor approves today?”

These and similar matters they often raise in discussion; and sometimes in private, sometimes openly before the brethren, they rouse me when I would be silent. At length, overcome by their importunity and repeated requests, I am compelled to reply; and because of their excessive insistence, I must now set my foot where formerly, in reading the divine Scriptures, I was accustomed to pass over with a plain sense. Yet I do not see that I am adequate to resolve the statement of so weighty a question. Nevertheless, lest I seem wholly to keep silence, to give no answer to those who inquire, and by silence to wound the charity of the brethren—when I may please them by speaking—I prefer to say something, even though it may afterwards need correction, [Col. 1162C] rather than offend by silence the charity of those to whom an answer is owed.

Above all, I am compelled to do this by the command of the Lord and of the most blessed Pope Eugenius. And as I ought to deny nothing to the just and devout requests of the brethren, so—indeed, much more—I do not dare to disobey such great commands. It will surely help make this question clear if I gather into one account the disputation which I held in the imperial city of Constantinople with Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, and arrange it as a dialogue, so that the reader may see more plainly what either Greek or Latin thinks concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit. For the aforesaid archbishop was among them of great religious standing, most acute in intellect, most learned in Greek letters, most eloquent in speech, [Col. 1162D] and most cautious both in giving and receiving an answer. In disputation or conference he omitted nothing by silence which seemed capable of strengthening his own opinion or overthrowing ours—especially since at that time he was foremost among the twelve chosen *didaskaloi* who, according to Greek custom, preside over their studies, and had been chosen by all for the office of disputing against me.

> [Note: [Col. 1161D] Although it is by no means unlikely that Anselm himself wrote the Greek words in Latin characters, [Col. 1162D] it seemed best to print them in Greek letters, lest they deceive anyone as they deceived Achéry.]

## BOOK TWO. On the Procession of the Holy Spirit: whether, according to the Greeks, he proceeds from the Father alone, or, according to the Latins, from the Father together with the Son.

[Col. 1163]

## CHAPTER ONE. How the dialogue concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit was held in the city of Constantinople between Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, and Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia; and concerning the method of interpretation between the speakers.

[Col. 1163A]

Accordingly, when I was stationed in the imperial city and frequently received various questions from the Greeks, while likewise putting others before them, it pleased the most devout Emperor Calo-John, and also the patriarch of that city, a religious man, that there should be a public assembly. A day was appointed so that, in the hearing of all, the things said on either side might be voiced.

Therefore, when a great many learned men had assembled in the district called that of the Pisans, beside the church of Hagia Irene—which in the Latin tongue is called Saint Peace—in the month of [Col. 1163B] April, on the tenth day, if I remember correctly; when silence-keepers had been stationed, as is the custom there; when arbiters had been appointed; and when notaries were seated to faithfully take down and commit to writing everything said on either side, the whole crowd, which had eagerly gathered to listen, fell silent. There were also present quite a few Latins, among whom were three learned men, skilled in both languages and exceptionally well educated in letters: James by name, a Venetian by nation; Burgundio by name, a Pisan by nation; and a third, pre-eminent among the others, Moses by name, an Italian from the city of Pergamum, renowned among both peoples for his learning in Greek and Latin letters. He was chosen by all to be a trustworthy [Col. 1163C] interpreter for both sides.

When all had thus been arranged, seats placed facing one another, silence imposed, and all eagerly and attentively listening, Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, said:

“Reverend fathers, I have not come for contention, for thus the Apostle says: ‘Not in strife and jealousy’ (Rom. 13:13); and again: ‘If anyone is contentious, we have no such custom’ (1 Cor. 11:16). Rather, I have come to inquire into and learn concerning your faith and mine, especially because this was your wish.”

Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, said:

“What you say is pleasing, and your humility is pleasing to us. For in conversation and humble conference truth shines forth sooner than if we contended proudly and greedily for victory.”

Anselm, [Col. 1163D] bishop of Havelberg, said:

“We ought not to forget what is written in the Gospel: that Jesus joined himself to two disciples as they were going from Jerusalem to the town of Emmaus and speaking about him; and he went with them, and they recognized him in the breaking of bread (Luke 24:35). If we likewise wish to travel together and converse together concerning truth without disputation, [Col. 1164A] Truth itself will draw near by joining itself to us, and we shall recognize it in the breaking of bread—that is, in the divine Scriptures. Let us therefore walk together upon the way of charity, not contending by proud reasoning, but together investigating truth through humble inquiry.”

Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, said:

“It seems to me that the chosen interpreter should faithfully render word for word what we are going to say, because in this way we may understand one another better and he can perform the task more easily.”

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, said:

“I am not accustomed to such a manner of speaking; moreover, such interpretation is suspect to me, because I may be caught on a word if it is translated differently, and it does not become us to contend over words. Rather, let there be used between us an interpretation which takes in and sets forth the continuous discourse of each side with the full and connected sense of the words. For in this manner of speaking or interpreting, we shall appear not as guardians of words but as investigators of meanings.”

Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, said:

“Let it be as you say; for this too pleases me, because it pleases you.”

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, said:

“I still wish to preface a few points. We intend to address a difficult question; I was summoned suddenly to this assembly, and since yesterday and the day before yesterday I have given none of these matters prior consideration. I ask the reverence of all who sit and stand by [Col. 1164C] that, should some word perhaps escape me—as sometimes happens in such situations—which offends the ears of any of you, you do not at once cry out against me with clapping and uproar, but, in accordance with your gentleness, patiently await the course of my speech, remembering that I am a guest among you. Indeed, I had previously feared this very thing in that method of word-for-word interpretation, and for that reason then removed it from our conference. Let there therefore be no quarrel over words among us, but a careful search for the truth of the meanings.”

Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, said:

“You have spoken well, and I ask the same.”

All said:

“It is good, it is fitting; let it be so, let it be so.”

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, said:

“Following holy and apostolic teaching, we believe [Col. 1164D] and teach that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God in substance, three in persons. We also believe that the Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeding from both—that is, from the Father and the Son. This we believe and teach.”

Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, said:

“What you say is catholic and to be accepted. But when you say [Col. 1165A] that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son as from the Father, we do not assent to or accept this, especially since no reasoning, no authority of canonical Scripture, and finally no general council says or teaches it.”

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, said:

“Since you have put forward three things—reason, the authority of canonical Scriptures, and general councils—and since you placed reason first, I should first like to know by what reasoning you are prohibited from believing or saying that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son as also from the Father.”

Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, said:

“In all philosophy, and especially in the highest theology, one must be cautious. The wisest of the Greeks have until now avoided saying *polyarchia* (πολυαρχία), that is, many principles; they have also avoided *anarchia* (ἀναρχία), which means ‘without a principle’; but they chose, revered, and taught us to revere *monarchia* (μοναρχία), that is, one principle. They refused to admit into God that which is *polyarchon* (πολύαρχον), ‘having many principles,’ because they said that what has many principles is contentious. They also refused to admit into God that which is *anarchon* (ἄναρχον), ‘without a principle,’ because they said that what is without a principle is disordered. Reasonably fleeing these two alternatives, they turned to venerable *monarchia*, which we too revere and embrace, and from which no one who holds the orthodox faith ought to depart.

“For if there were two principles, either both would be deficient or one would be superfluous. For [Col. 1165C] if one lacked something possessed by the other, it would not be supremely perfect; but if one lacked nothing which the other possessed, then, since all things were in one, the other would be superfluous.

> [Note: [Col. 1165] ‘One lacked nothing.’ We have chosen to emend thus; for the reading of the earlier edition, *nihil unde esset* (‘nothing from which it might be’), is wholly inept.]

“Therefore we believe that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God: the Father unbegotten, the Son begotten from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father alone and not from the Son. For if we said that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, since the Father would be a principle of the Holy Spirit and likewise the Son would be a principle of the Holy Spirit, the consequence would immediately follow that there are two principles, and we would fall into *polyarchia*, that is, many principles—which is contrary to all reason. Therefore we believe and teach that the Father is the principle of the Son whom he begot, [Col. 1165D] and that the same Father alone is the principle of the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from him alone. We say that the Father is the principle of both, not in time but in causality: for both are from the Father as from one principle, the one by generation, the other by procession—not temporally, but causally.”

## CHAPTER TWO. That in the Lord there is not *anarchia* (ἀναρχία), that is, no principle; nor *polyarchia* (πολυαρχία), that is, many principles; but *monarchia* (μοναρχία), one principle.

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, said:

“I agree with you in denying many principles in God—which you call *polyarchon*—because this is contrary to all reason. Yet a certain heresiarch, a Persian by nation, named Mani, from whom the Manichaeans derive their name, who polluted almost the whole of Africa, was deservedly condemned by the Catholic Church because he maintained that there are two principles and taught certain other things contrary to the Christian faith. Likewise, what you call *anarchon* (ἄναρχον) in God—that is, without a principle, or not a principle—I do not at all admit in God, any more than you do. For unless God were the supreme principle, he would be without himself; and if he were without himself, he would not exist at all. Therefore, in God neither are many principles to be asserted, because that would be contentious; nor is no principle to be asserted, because that would be disordered. Both alternatives threaten dissolution and destruction. For whether [Col. 1166B] it is said that, because there are many principles, there must also be many conflicts; or that, because there is no principle, nothing is ordered—whether, I say, this or that is asserted—either is utterly absurd, because, as I said, each lies close to dissolution and destruction: the one because of the conflict found there, the other because of the disorder found there.

“I accept with you in God the one principle which you call *monarchon* (μόναρχον), because God is the supreme and complete principle, the principle, that is, which he himself is to himself. What is without a principle is that which exists apart from him and outside him; and that is absolutely nothing. Thus in God there are not many principles, nor is there no principle; rather, he himself is one principle to himself within himself, holding through himself and in himself the most free sovereignty properly belonging to monarchy. And as he is to himself the life by which he lives, so he is to himself the principle by which he rules.

“Yet as to your claim that, if the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, there are therefore two principles: I judge that this argument of yours, so hastily formed an enthymeme, is by no means to be accepted. For the false conclusion drawn does not follow from the true premise stated. It is true that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son; but it is false that there are two principles. Therefore there is no connection between them. Let your charity attend: [Col. 1166D] we say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, but we do not therefore concede that there are two principles, because the Father and the Son are one principle, just as they are one God. As we say ‘God from God,’ yet not two gods; and as we say figuratively ‘light from light,’ yet not two substantial lights; and ‘wisdom from wisdom,’ yet not two wisdoms: so certainly we say ‘principle from principle,’ yet not two principles. Hence, when the Lord was asked in the Gospel, ‘Who are you?’, he answered concerning himself: ‘I am the principle, who also speak to you’ (John 8:25), showing that he is one and the same [Col. 1167A] principle with the Father in the unity of the same substance, though he is from the principle by the property of his filial person.

“One must consider what is said, of what, why, and in what respect. For when he says, ‘I am the principle, who also speak to you,’ and does not say, ‘I am the principle, which also speak to you,’ he sufficiently indicated that he is one with the Father in the same consubstantiality, though he is not one with the Father in personal property. For the Son is the same principle as the Father himself according to substance; but he is not the same as the Father according to person. Yet what he said, ‘I am the principle, who also speak to you,’ can also be understood otherwise: as intending to show himself to be Creator [Col. 1167B] and principle of the creature, just as the Father is the principle of the creature, since all things are from him. Hence in Genesis: ‘In the beginning God created heaven and earth’ (Gen. 1:1). And that he is principle in the beginning and with the principle, hear the evangelist John: ‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God; all things were made through him, and without him nothing that was made was made. In him was life’ (John 1:1–4). And in the Psalms: ‘With you is the principle on the day of your power’ (Ps. 109 [Vulgate 109:3]).

“Accordingly, the Father is called principle relatively to the creature, from whom are all things; the Son also is called principle relatively to the creature, through whom are all things; and the Holy Spirit likewise is called [Col. 1167C] principle relatively to the creature, in whom are all things. Yet there are not three principles, just as there are not three creators, because the works of the Trinity are inseparable. Therefore God is called one principle with reference to the creature, not two or three.

“But if the persons of the Trinity are referred to one another, then, if the begetter is a principle relative to the one begotten, the Father is a principle relative to the Son because he begets him. Whether the Father is rightly called principle relative to the Holy Spirit because the Spirit proceeds from him, and whether the Son is rightly called principle relative to the Holy Spirit because the Spirit also proceeds from him, is a matter of some question among certain persons. But if the one who is given—that is, the Holy Spirit—has as his principle him from whom he is given, since he received from nowhere else what proceeds from that source, it seems not unfitting to acknowledge the Father and the Son to be principle [Col. 1167D] of the Holy Spirit. Yet they are not two principles; for just as the Father and the Son are one God, so, in relation to the Holy Spirit, they are one principle. For the Holy Spirit is given and proceeds not from elsewhere but from the Father and Son, who are one principle.

“Moreover, the Father as principle and the Son are the same principle; for if the Son were a principle other than the Father and not the same principle as the Father, then precisely in being other he would cease to be principle. Therefore, whatever we ascribe to the Father, let us ascribe also to the Son. For if the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, and all that belongs to the Father belongs to the Son and all that belongs to the Son to the Father, surely the Father’s principle is the Son’s principle. That is: the principle which the Father [Col. 1168A] is is the principle which the Son is; and thus the Holy Spirit, proceeding from both—the Father and the Son—has not two but one principle of his procession. For in God ‘principle’ is said in three ways: substantively in reference to himself; relatively to one another in the Trinity, as the Father to the Son; and again relatively, with respect to the creature, as Creator.

## CHAPTER THREE. That what is eternal is not thereby without a principle, just as the Son is coeternal with the Father but is not without a principle, because he is from the Father.

“And perhaps you wonder why those who are together coeternal are not called *synarcha* (σύναρχα), that is, simultaneous principles or co-principles. But it must be noted that what is without a principle is also eternal; yet what is [Col. 1168B] eternal is not thereby without a principle. For the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—all three persons—are coeternal and coequal with one another; but not all three alike are without a principle. The Father indeed is *anarchos* (ἄναρχος), that is, without a principle; and he is the principle of the Son, who is coequal, coeternal, and consubstantial with him: principle as cause, as fountain, and as eternal light. But the Son—

> [Note: [Col. 1167] ‘But the Son.’ In the earlier edition only *lumen* (‘light’) was read here; even if that reading is admissible, it is certainly mutilated. There is no doubt that Anselm wrote it as we have printed it.]

—although coeternal and consubstantial with the Father, is by no means *anarchos*, that is, without a principle, because he has the Father as his principle and cause; and he himself is the principle of all things. But when I say ‘principle,’ do not admit time, nor insert any interval between begetter and begotten; nor divide [Col. 1168C] the nature by some ill-conceived, ill-introduced interruption interposed between those who are always coeternal with one another. For if time were older than the Son, then the Father would be the first cause of time, not of the Son; nor would the Son be maker of times, if he were subject to time; nor would he by nature be Lord of all things, but would have been assumed into lordship by the Father’s grace, or indeed would not be Lord at all. Thus the Son would altogether be cast out from deity as not coeternal with the Father but placed under time.

“The Father, then, is principle of the Son as cause; and the Father together with the Son is principle of the Holy Spirit as cause. It is evident, however, that a cause is not altogether older than those of whom it is the cause, just as the sun is not older than its own light. Hence it is evident that all [Col. 1168D] three persons are together coeternal and coequal with one another, but that all three are not together without a causal principle. Therefore, as has been said, the Father is *anarchos*, that is, without a temporal or causal principle, because he is not from elsewhere but from himself. The Son, however, is not *anarchos*, since he has the Father as the cause of himself: a principle not temporal but causal. But if you understand ‘principle’ as that which arises in time, then the Son too is *anarchōs* (ἀνάρχως), and the Holy Spirit is *anarchos* (ἄναρχος), that is, without a temporal principle; for the Trinity, which makes times, did not begin with time or under time.

“Certainly the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—the whole Trinity together—just as it is one God, so is one [Col. 1169A] and the same substantial principle, which you call *monarchon, pantokratoun* (μόναρχον, παντοκρατοῦν), that is, one principle, or one all-holding sovereignty; but in no way two or three principles, which you call *diarchon* (δίαρχον) or *triarchon* (τρίαρχον). For thus one reads in the Athanasian Creed, venerable throughout the whole Church:

> ‘The Father eternal, the Son eternal, the Holy Spirit eternal; and yet not three eternals, but one eternal. The Father immeasurable, the Son immeasurable, the Holy Spirit immeasurable; and yet not three immeasurables, but one immeasurable. And God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit; and yet not three gods, but one God. And Lord the Father, Lord the Son, Lord the Holy Spirit; and yet not three Lords, but one Lord.’

“So likewise the Father is principle, the Son is principle, the Holy Spirit is [Col. 1169B] principle; and yet not three principles, but one principle. All three together are one principle, and each individually is that same complete and perfect principle. And just as the three persons are rightly called consubstantial, yet are not rightly called three substances, so perhaps the three persons may rightly be called co-principial; yet they are not rightly called three co-principles—which the Greeks call *synarcha* (σύναρχα), while the Latins have no such term in any usage of Latin.

“Perhaps someone, deceived by a plausible but false opinion, thinks that two principles may be spoken of because, when one says ‘principle without principle,’ and again says ‘principle from principle,’ two principles seem to be posited. But he does not rightly observe that God not from God—namely, the Father—is rightly said, and again God from God—namely, the Son—is rightly said; yet there are not therefore two gods. Likewise, light not from light is rightly said, and light from light is likewise rightly said; yet there are not two lights. But if someone should say, ‘The principle who is the Father is not the principle who is the Son; and the principle who is the Son is not the principle who is the Father,’ and should wish to infer from this that there are two principles, he is wholly mistaken. For when it is said, ‘The principle who is the Father is not the principle who is the Son,’ and when it is said—

> [Note: [Col. 1169D] ‘And when it is said.’ From this passage we have removed the word *patet* (‘it is clear’), which an unskilled copyist had added after the word *et* (‘and’), thereby disturbing the sense.]

—‘The principle who is the Son is not the principle who is the Father,’ nothing else is said or understood except that the Father is not the Son and the Son is not the Father; this always distinguishes the distinction of the persons. [Col. 1169D] Thus, according to the distinction of persons, it is rightly said negatively: ‘The principle who is the Father is not the principle who is the Son,’ and ‘the principle who is the Son is not the principle who is the Father.’ So, according to the identity of the same essence, it is rightly said affirmatively: ‘The Father is the same principle as the Son, and the Son is the same principle as the Father.’ Though this one is not that one, this one is what that one is; though he is not that identical person, he is nevertheless the same identical thing; though this one is not the person that this one is, this one is nevertheless this very thing that this one is. He is not he; but they are the very same thing, always one God, always one principle—never two [Col. 1170A] gods, never two majesties, never two principles.

“Accordingly, if the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Son, as you suppose, show, if you can, how it can be true that he proceeds from the Father. For if, according to you, one must believe that he does not proceed from the Son, then according to you one must also believe that he does not proceed from the Father, since the Father and the Son are one, as he himself says: ‘I and the Father are one’ (John 10:30); and again: ‘I am in the Father and the Father is in me’ (ibid., 38). Therefore, whoever says that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father who is in the Son must also say that the same Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son who is in the Father; [or, if he denies

> [Note: [Col. 1170D] ‘Or, if he denies.’ We have added the words enclosed in brackets, being certain that Anselm wrote them; perhaps, in his usual manner, he also added ‘who is in the Father.’]

> proceeding from the Son,]

he is compelled also to deny that the same Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father who is in the Son. For the Father and the Son [Col. 1170B] are one; and when it is reciprocally said that the one is in the other, it is by no means one thing in another as something substantially other, but that which is substantially one and the same is meant. Hence, to Philip asking, ‘Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us,’ the Lord says: ‘Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father, because I am in the Father and the Father is in me’ (John 14:8–9). This was said because of the unity of the same substance. And when it is said, ‘I and the Father are one,’ *one* is said, because of unity of substance, against Arius; *are* is said, because of plurality of persons, against Sabellius—as if he said: ‘I and the Father are one: that which he is, that am I according to substance.’

“Thus it seems established that, while you wish to persuade [Col. 1170C] me not to believe that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son lest I fall into two principles, you too are now compelled to deny what you previously believed—namely, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone. You have thus fallen into such a snare that you, who formerly denied one thing, namely procession from the Son, and affirmed the other, namely procession from the Father, must now either dare to confess neither according to your own view, or rightly confess both with me according to the Catholic faith and the reasons set forth.”

Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, said:

“What you have argued concerning principle seems sufficiently acceptable. But since you say that the Holy Spirit proceeds [Col. 1170D] from the Father and the Son, yet do not admit two principles, and prove this because the Father and the Son are one, it can by the same reasoning be proved that the same Holy Spirit proceeds from himself, just as from the Father and the Son. For the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one essence of divinity; and thus, if he proceeds from those with whom he is substantially one, it is necessary to say that he also proceeds from himself, with whom they too are substantially one.”

## CHAPTER FOUR. That as the Father begot, but not himself, and as the Son was begotten, but not by himself, so likewise the Holy Spirit proceeds, but not from himself.

[Col. 1171A]

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, said:

“God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit; yet not three gods, but one God. And although it is rightly said that God the Father begot God the Son, since he is one God, it cannot rightly be said of God the Father that God the Father begot himself; nor can it rightly be said of God the Son that God the Son was begotten by himself. Likewise, although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, and the Holy Spirit is rightly believed to proceed from the Father and the Son, it is not rightly said for that reason that he proceeds from himself. For though he is substantially one with the Father and the Son, he is nevertheless neither the Father nor [Col. 1171B] the Son, and therefore ought not to proceed from himself as he proceeds from them.

“Accordingly, as the Father begot, but not himself, and as the Son was begotten, but not by himself, so likewise the Holy Spirit proceeds, but not from himself. This is also clearly proved from the Gospel of John, where it is written concerning the Holy Spirit: ‘For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak’ (John 16:13). He will not speak from himself because he is not from himself; and because he is not from himself, neither does he proceed from himself, for his being is the same as his proceeding. Whence he is, thence he proceeds; and whence he proceeds, thence he is. His being is nothing other than proceeding. As it is proper to the Father to beget the Son, and proper to the Son to be begotten from the Father, so it is indeed proper to the Holy Spirit [Col. 1171C] to proceed from both as from one principle.”

Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, said:

“We proposed to discuss the procession of the Holy Spirit, but in order to prove your position you introduced the Father as begetter and the Son as begotten—not inappropriately, I admit, for what you said is sufficiently pleasing. Nevertheless, answer briefly on this very matter: what, or of what kind, do you think is this procession of the Holy Spirit of which we speak? Does it seem true to you that the Holy Spirit proceeds according to the common substance, or according to his distinct and proper person?”

## CHAPTER FIVE. That, as it is unknown what kind the Father’s unbegottenness is and what kind the Son’s generation is, so it is unknown what kind the eternal procession of the Holy Spirit is.

[Col. 1171D]

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, said:

“Tell me what or of what kind is the Father’s unbegottenness, and what or of what kind is the Son’s generation; and I shall tell you what or of what kind is the procession of the Holy Spirit. Then both of us will be mad, searching out divine mysteries and wishing to investigate by reasoning matters which are known to be ineffable, above every understanding of rational creatures, and which by their depth or height surpass every human, indeed every angelic, capacity. But if you wish to press me and be troublesome about this question, let this suffice for you to hear which suffices for me to believe: [Col. 1172A] it is enough for me to believe that the Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit proceeding. But in what manner this one is unbegotten, or this one begotten, or that one proceeds, I think must be honored with reverent silence. Let it be a great thing for us to believe that it is so as it is, and let it not be our curiosity to investigate how it is; for how it is is not granted even to angels to conceive, much less to us.

“The Father who begot, the Son who was begotten, and the Holy Spirit who proceeds from both, together know—by a knowledge eternally known to themselves alone—the divine and eternal generation of the Son, the divine and eternal procession of the Holy Spirit, and the mode and quality of that generation and procession. This surely surpasses the dark cloud of our humility, to whom vanity sometimes presents itself as truth. Yet I think it may not unfittingly be said that the Father always was and is unbegottenly, the Son always was and is begettable, and the Holy Spirit always was and is processible. The Father’s begetting coincides with the essence of that same Father; the Son’s being begotten coincides with the essence of that same Son; and the Holy Spirit’s proceeding coincides with the essence of that same Holy Spirit. Neither this nor that is earlier or later.

## CHAPTER SIX. That in the highest Trinity, being is one thing, while being Father, Son, or Holy Spirit is another.

[Col. 1172C]

“Nevertheless, in that highest Trinity, to beget is not the same as to be; to be begotten is not the same as to be; and to proceed is not the same as to be. For it is not by that whereby he is that he is Father; nor is it by that whereby he is that he is Son; nor is it by that whereby he is that he is Holy Spirit. Rather, that whereby he is is the one substance that is there. But that whereby the one, as Father, begets; whereby the other, as Son, is begotten; and whereby the third, as the Holy Spirit sent forth, proceeds: by this there are no longer one but three persons. Thus the substance—or rather essence—by which the three are is one; and the personality by which the three are distinguished is three. For, as I said, being is not the same there as being Father; being is not the same as being Son; nor is being the same as being [Col. 1172D] Holy Spirit, or proceeding. Rather, being there is being God, being great, being good, being wise. Those three things individually belong properly and personally to the three persons; but this one thing is substantial to each individually and to all together.

## CHAPTER SEVEN. Why the Holy Spirit alone is called Holy Spirit and the third person in the Trinity; and why this is not a rank of dignity but an order of numbering and a designation of his proper person.

“And indeed the Father is spirit and is holy, but he is not the one who is the Holy Spirit, namely the third person in the Trinity. Likewise, the Son is spirit and is holy, but he is not the one who is the Holy Spirit, namely the third person in the Trinity. [Col. 1173A] So too the Holy Spirit is spirit and is holy, and he alone is rightly called simply the Holy Spirit, and the third person in the Trinity. Perhaps, moreover, he alone is rightly called the Holy Spirit because, by the sole breathing-forth of the same Godhead, he binds both the others and himself into one essence, ineffably distinguishing unity in Trinity and Trinity in unity, while wonderfully joining them; so that we believe in that supreme unity and Trinity, singularly distinguished and distinctly joined, something paradoxical—that is, alien or unexpected—to every human understanding. Therefore the Holy Spirit is the coeternal bond of the two, their communion, their concord, their love, their sweetness, their holiness. For how is the Father God, if not holy? And how is the Son God, if not holy? If you remove this holiness from God the Father or God the Son, then, once this holiness has been removed, you have removed the Godhead also. For what Godhead, or what kind of Godhead, is not holy? Is it not imperfect if it is not holy? Is it not altogether nonexistent if it is not holy? Therefore, since the Holy Spirit, as I have said, is the coeternal holiness of both, he is rightly called the Holy Spirit: by the common holiness existing as one with the Father and the Son, and by the property of his person completing the Trinity. Moreover, the unity of the same substance—undivided, simple, and one in itself—remains eternally undivided, simple, and one in itself, never having received any number; and this is for us the one [Col. 1173C] God.

“But the plurality of persons, arising from unity not temporally but eternally and causally, moved, so to speak, toward duality, and proceeding came to rest eternally in the coeternal Trinity, and in the number of the Holy Trinity coeternally, without any time having intervened. This is for us Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Although they are three in number, because the person of the Father is one thing, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another; and there is one person of the Father alone, two persons of Father and Son, and three persons of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—nevertheless, no successive rank of dignity is to be sought in this Trinity, coeternal with itself. For nowhere in any writing of those who have treated of the Holy Trinity, so far as I think, is the person of the Father found called first according to a rank within the Trinity, nor the person of the Son second; although the person of the Holy Spirit is sometimes found called the third person in the Trinity. [Col. 1173D] This is said not according to a rank of dignity, but according to the distinct manifestation or designation of the separate and individual person. For the Trinity is not ordered by a succession of rank in dignity, but continuous in number and equal in dignity, so that three persons truly and always exist there continuously and simultaneously. They are not, however, called first, second, and third person by degrees, because this indicates a rank of separate and ordered dignity. Number itself—namely, three—does not signify a rank of dignity, but the plurality of the Trinity in a plural way. Thus when the Holy Spirit is called the third person in the Trinity, he is not called so in relation to a first or second person as though inferior in dignity, but is called third—that is, one of three—by the particular designation of that person.

“Accordingly Augustine, [Note: [Col. 1173D] Augustine, Book I of the Various Questions of Orosius, questions 69 and 22.], bishop of the city of Hippo, an outstanding teacher, writing to Orosius, said: ‘And the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters, and he is the third person in the Trinity.’ Again, the same author, in chapter 113 of the book *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*: ‘Why the Son of God, and not another, was sent: after God the Father, the devil wished to be called god, [Col. 1174B] and even now persists in striving for this; though the matter did not belong to him, but this was the Son of God, who is second after God the Father—not by nature, but by order.’ Again, the same Augustine, in chapter 195 of that book, against Eusebius: ‘The Holy Spirit is third in order—not in nature, not in rank, not in divinity, not in person, not in knowledge. For just as the Son of God is second from the Father and is not lesser in divinity, so also the Holy Spirit, following from the Son, is not unequal but equal in the divinity of substance.’

“Likewise Hilary, [Note: [Col. 1173D] Hilary, Book XII, *On the Trinity*, near the end.] bishop of Poitiers, formerly a most renowned and eloquent defender of the Catholic faith, in Book XII of *On the Trinity*: ‘The Son, true God from you, God the Father, and begotten by you, is thus to be confessed after you [Col. 1174C] as together with you, because you are the eternal author of his eternal origin. For since he is from you, he is second from you; second, I say, by his mode of existence, not by a difference of dignity. For he subsists from God the Father as though in the first place, while the Holy Spirit subsists from the Father as though in the third place, but from the Son in the second place.’

“Accordingly Jerome, [Note: [Col. 1173D] Jerome in his commentaries on the Psalms, and [Col. 1174D] in his exposition of this verse of Psalm 50: ‘Confirm me with a principal Spirit.’] a presbyter learned in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew letters, calls the Father the principal Spirit in relation to the Son, speaking thus in his work on the three virtues: ‘David in the Psalm (50:12–13) asks for three spirits, saying: “Confirm me with a principal Spirit. Renew a right spirit within my inmost parts. Do not take your Holy Spirit away from me.” Who are these three spirits? The principal Spirit is the Father; the right Spirit is Christ; the Holy Spirit is the Holy Spirit himself. Thus the Holy Spirit is third from the Father, but second from Christ according to numerical order—as though this were said according to the ordered and fitting arrangement of calculation, namely according to the very mode of existence and the sequence of enumeration which exists in the persons themselves, not according to any ranks of their dignity. For the Father is from no one; the Son is from the Father alone; the Holy Spirit derives his being from both. Therefore observe, so to speak, no secondariness of nature or dignity, but only an order in the mode of existence and in the order [Col. 1175A] of speaking.’ Again Augustine [Note: [Col. 1175] Augustine and Jerome, in the same places, and in the letter to Cyril in exposition of the Creed.] says at the beginning of chapter 22 of the book *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*: ‘The Son differs in no respect from the Father—indeed, he differs in no respect in substance, because he is a true Son. Yet he differs in cause, or rank, because all power is in the Son from the Father. And although the Son is not lesser in substance, the Father is nevertheless greater in authority, as the Lord himself testifies and says: “If you loved me, you would rejoice because I am going to the Father, because the Father is greater than I” [John 14:28]. Maintaining this order, the Apostle Paul says: “One God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus, through whom are all things, and we through him” [1 Cor. 8:6]. Thus the first rank is he from whom are all things, the second he through whom are all things, and the third he in whom are all things. And because none of these is degenerate, they are signified in the unity of God, as the Apostle says: “For from him, and through him, and in him are all things; to him be glory for ages of ages” [Rom. 11:36]. Reason therefore requires, and the Catholic faith teaches, that in designating the Trinity this order of utterance be most rightly maintained: Father, Son, Holy Spirit. For those who are equal in dignity cannot be named simultaneously and equally in speech; and those who possess unity of the same majesty also possess a Trinity of distinct personhood, with every rank of distinct dignity removed, yet with a successive order of distinct enunciation allowed. The Son of God himself, who knows all things, openly taught this order [Col. 1175C] of enunciation in the Trinity when he said to his disciples: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” [Matt. 28:19].’

## Chapter VIII. That the names of the Trinity are found transposed

“Furthermore, some are accustomed to disparage the Holy Spirit, supposing him inferior because he is placed third in order. Yet there is such simplicity in the divine Scriptures that one sometimes finds the third placed first: they are arranged as the occasion requires. No injury is thereby done to any of them, because their divinity is one. Thus we read in Isaiah, with the Lord saying: ‘I am the first, and I am for ever; and my hand founded the earth, my right hand established heaven’ [Col. 1175D] [Isa. 48:13]. And in what follows: ‘I have spoken, I have called, I have brought him, and I have made his way prosperous. Draw near to me and hear these things: from the beginning I have not spoken in secret. When they came to be, I was there; and now the Lord has sent me and his Spirit.’ Who then do we think is the one who founded the earth? He is the one who says, ‘I am the first,’ and who says that he has been sent. Do we think this is the Father because he says, ‘I am the first’? Far be it! For what follows—‘And now the Lord has sent me and his Spirit’—plainly shows that it is the Son, who says that he has been sent by God and the Holy Spirit, and yet says, ‘I am the first.’ Behold, these things are equal between the Son and the Holy Spirit. For just as the Holy Spirit is read to have been sent by the Father and the Son, so Christ was sent by God and the Holy Spirit. It is peculiar to the Father alone that he is not said to be sent.

“Let us also consider the Apostle’s words, in which he embraces the Trinity in another order. Among other things he says in the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians: ‘May the Lord direct your hearts in the love of God and the endurance of Christ’ [2 Thess. 3:5]. Who do you think is called Lord here, except the Holy Spirit, who directs our hearts in the love of God the Father, who sends the Son, and in the endurance of Christ, who obeyed the Father unto death? And in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, departing from the order found in the tradition of faith, he begins from the Holy Spirit in recounting the workings of gifts and ministries, then adds [Col. 1176B] the Lord Jesus, and places God third, whom he says works in the Holy Spirit and in the Lord. Thus the Lord himself also says: ‘The Father abiding in me, he himself does the works’ [John 14:10]. For, because both the Holy Spirit and Christ are from God the Father, their operation is God’s work. Indeed, he calls the Holy Spirit the same as Lord, and the same Lord God; and this is because of unity of nature. Therefore, when in this passage he says that the same God, who is also Lord, works all things in all, he concludes further below: ‘But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each individually as he wills’ [1 Cor. 12:11].

“Behold, with the order of the personal names in the Trinity transposed, three are said to possess one operation, because, when one acts, the three are most rightly said to act. Why? Because they are of one divinity, in whatever order their names are found placed. David too, in Psalm 50, prays to and invokes God the Spirit, with the names of the three persons transposed in simple faith, believing the nature of the Godhead to be the same in all three: ‘Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right Spirit within my inmost parts’ [Ps. 50:11]. By “right Spirit” he meant Christ. Again: ‘Do not cast me away from your presence, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me’ [ibid., 12]. By “Holy Spirit” he meant the Holy Spirit himself. Again, below: ‘Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and confirm me with a principal Spirit’ [ibid., 13]. By “principal Spirit” [Col. 1176D] he meant the Father, who is his own principle and the principal cause, or the causal principle, of the Son and the Holy Spirit.

“And John says in the Apocalypse: ‘I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, says the Lord God, who is and who is to come, the Almighty’ [Rev. 1:8]. And below: ‘I am the first and the last, and I was dead, and behold, I am living’ [ibid., 17]. Again below: ‘Thus says the first and the last, who was dead and lives’ [Rev. 2:8]. Behold, we see the simplicity of Scripture: how it transposes the names of the Trinity, now placing the Father, now the Son, now the Holy Spirit before or after the others. This does no harm to the Catholic faith, which confesses that the three are of the same nature.

## Chapter IX. That Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not deficient but sufficient names, signifying no diminution or inferiority in substance

[Col. 1177A]

“And it must be known that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are by no means deficient names: it is not the case that, because the Father is not the Son or the Holy Spirit, he is deficient in this respect; nor that, because the Son is not the Father or the Holy Spirit, he too is deficient in this respect; nor that, because the Holy Spirit is neither Father nor Son, he too is deficient in this respect. Rather, they are unfailing and sufficient names, signifying no abatement or diminution with respect to substance. We say ‘this Father,’ ‘this Son,’ and ‘this Holy Spirit’ in order that the unconfused distinction of the three hypostases—that is, persons—may be preserved in the one nature and worthy Godhead. Although, when the three persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—are named, the plurality of persons follows for the mind from the meaning of the words, nevertheless the unity of the same essence must not be absent from the faith and understanding of right believers. And when one God is named, although the unity of the divine essence follows for the human mind, which is less sufficient in itself, from the proper meaning of the word in the singular, nevertheless the plurality of persons must by no means be absent from the faith and understanding of right believers. Thus we believe in the heart and confess with the mouth unity in the divine substance, [Col. 1177C] while preserving the Trinity of persons; and the Trinity of persons, while preserving the unity of the divine essence.

“Thus our ‘one’ is not Sabellian but Christian: it is not in a confused unity of persons, but in the true and simple unity of the same substance. Likewise, our ‘three’ is not Arian but Catholic: it is not in a plurality of substances, but in the right distinction of persons. Otherwise, striking upon either promontory of Arian or Sabellian impiety, we might be drowned in the depths, where many have been endangered and where those who sailed incautiously have suffered shipwreck in heretical condemnation. They frequently and extensively disputed concerning faith, but never attained the truth of faith, because they did not know either what they said or what they affirmed. If the poverty of human speech could have devised one single name which aptly and sufficiently signified in God both unity of substance and Trinity of persons, and did so with full and sufficient meaning, certainly the Church of God would not labour so greatly in speaking and believing, as it has so often laboured, faithfully and variously expounding many words or names concerning God.

“Yet Christian faith does not consist in the bare confession of names and words alone, but in the pure truth itself of Trinity and unity; and from that truth itself—by which the one God is truly true, and the Trinity of persons truly real—there arises a true and saving confession in words. Therefore, when Father God, Son God, and Holy Spirit God are named, let no one suppose that there is *tritheian* (τρίθειαν), that is, three godheads or a threefold [Col. 1178A] godhead. For those who are of the same nature also possess identity of the same divinity and honour, which among the Greeks, as I think, is called *homotimia* (ὁμοτιμία), “equality of honour.” Christians ought not to be called or be *tritheists* (τριθεΐτας), worshippers of three gods, but *monotheists* (μονοθεΐτας), worshippers of one God.

## Chapter X. That the Holy Spirit is called proceeding neither according to the common substance nor according to the person said absolutely, but according to relation

“As to what you asked—whether the Spirit is called proceeding according to the substance common to the three, or according to the distinct and proper person—the following answer must be given. [Col. 1178B] The Holy Spirit is consubstantial with the Father and the Son. For he is from the same substance and no other, since, just as it is common to them to be one and the same God, so it is common to them to be one and the same substance. Yet neither the Father is called unbegotten, nor the Son begotten, nor the Holy Spirit proceeding, according to substance or according to person. For if the Father were called unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit proceeding according to the substance by which they are one, then surely the Father would be called, according to the same common substance, unbegotten and begotten and proceeding; and thus there would arise a certain new and confused mixture of unbegotten, begotten, and proceeding. For whatever is said of the divine substance according to substance must be common to all three.

“Therefore, if the Father were called unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit proceeding according to substance, all things would necessarily be common simultaneously to all three: the Father would be called at once unbegotten, begotten, and proceeding; the Son likewise unbegotten, begotten, and proceeding; and the Holy Spirit likewise unbegotten, begotten, and proceeding. Thus, because of excessive confusion, neither the distinct Trinity of persons nor the undivided identity of the same substance would stand. Conversely, if unbegotten, begotten, and proceeding were said according to substance, then, since the one who is unbegotten is not the one who is begotten or proceeding; the one who is begotten is not the one who is unbegotten [Col. 1178D] or proceeding; and the one who is proceeding is not the one who is unbegotten or begotten—there would no longer be merely one substance, but three different substances, according to which they would be called distinct from one another: one unbegotten, one begotten, and one proceeding. Thus the Trinity would no longer be *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον), “of the same substance,” but *heteroousion* (ἑτεροούσιον), “of another substance.” In the one case, then, confusion and mixture of persons would cast us into the Sabellian abyss; in the other, plurality of substances would plunge us into the Arian deep.

“The Holy Spirit, therefore, is not called proceeding according to substance, although his procession is substantial. Further, if the Holy Spirit were called proceeding according to person, no less absurdity—but the same absurdity—would appear to arise from this. For in that supreme, ineffable, and incomprehensible Trinity, the name ‘person’ is said absolutely; but whatever is said absolutely is said according to substance. It follows that person must be said in substance; for it is clear that person is subject to nature, and that a person cannot be named apart from nature.
