Therefore in the Trinity, when we say ‘the person of the Father,’ we say nothing other than the substance of the Father; when we say ‘the person of the Son,’ nothing other than the substance of the Son; and when we say ‘the person of the Holy Spirit,’ nothing other than the substance of the Holy Spirit—although one substance is always named there, whereas three persons always exist and are named there. Because, then, person as well as substance is said absolutely, the Holy Spirit is not called proceeding according to person, just as he is not called proceeding according to substance.

“It remains, therefore, to say that, just as the Father is called Father in relation to the Son, and unbegotten in relation to the begotten; and just as the Son is called Son, begotten, Word, image, seal, character, and radiance in relation to the Father; so too the Holy Spirit is called Holy Spirit proceeding in relation, and sent by both who send, gift from both who give, love from both who love. It is certainly necessary to note what is said, of what it is said, in what respect, and for what reason. For things said absolutely are said according to substance, whereas things not said absolutely are said relatively in the very distinction of persons. Yet the name “person,” devised by the ancients because of the extreme poverty of words, is said in this sense—so that the Trinity may be understood in the Trinity—not relatively, but absolutely, like substance, or rather essence.

“Among the other names of Latin speech, those which belong individually to each one—such as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—are said not commonly but individually. But those which are common to all—such as substance, God, almighty, and others like them—are said not only individually but also commonly. For just as the Father alone is called Father, the Son alone Son, and the Holy Spirit alone Holy Spirit, each individually, [Col. 1179D] so indeed all three together and each one of the three are called God, substance, almighty, and the like—terms which belong both individually to each and commonly to all three. In this way, just as things differing in number and persons are expressed differently according to number, so things differing neither in number nor substance are expressed according to substance in the same and not a different way.”

## Chapter XI. Whether the Son, like the Father, is rightly called the sender forth of the Holy Spirit, which the Greeks call προβολεύς

[Note: [Col. 1179] They say προβολεύς, “sender forth”; this is the most correct reading, in place of which Acherius had everywhere printed *provolvens*, “rolling forth,” without any sense.]

Nechites, Archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “What you have said is quite pleasing; but I ask you: do you grant that the Father is the sender forth of the Holy Spirit who proceeds—what our Greeks call *probolēus* (προβολεύς)?”

Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg, said: “I do not know what *probolēus* (προβολεύς) means, since I am not Greek but Latin. Yet I readily grant that the Father is the sender forth of the Holy Spirit and that the Holy Spirit is sent forth; provided, however, that I likewise call the Son sender forth of the same Spirit. For the Gospel plainly says this of both. Of the Father: ‘The Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name’ [John 14:26]. Of the Son: ‘When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you’ [John 15:26]. And below: ‘But if I go, I will send him to you’ [John 16:7]. In this manner, therefore, the Father and the Son are senders forth of the Holy Spirit; but the Holy Spirit is sent forth by both, though promised by one alone, that is, the Son.”

Nechites, Archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “If the Father is sender forth and the Son too is sender forth of the Holy Spirit, then there are two senders forth, two givers; and so they seem to be two principles of the Holy Spirit.”

Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg, said: “As I see, you have cunningly wished to lead me into admitting two principles, and you bring back as though forgotten for fresh discussion matters which were settled above when we treated of the principle, in order to catch me unguarded and, as it were, forgetful of what was said. But I admit two principles nowhere in divine Scripture. Whether, however, two senders forth or two givers can rightly be called such is for you to say, since you introduced this Greek name *probolēus* (προβολεύς), which, as you say, means ‘sender forth’ among us. But because the proper meaning of this Greek name is uncertain, I do not wish meanwhile to define anything certain concerning it.

“Now I should like you to listen patiently to me. You say that the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Son. In saying this, you do the greatest injury to both, namely the Son and the Holy Spirit. For while the Father and Son mutually stand in relation as begetter and begotten, and likewise the Father and Holy Spirit mutually stand in relation as sender and sent, and as giver and gift, tell me, I ask: do you not do great injury to the Son and the Holy Spirit, to whom you attribute no mutual relation, indeed whom you separate, so to speak, from a shared communion of procession? For the Father and Son, so to speak, regard one another by generation; and again the Father and Holy Spirit, so to speak, regard one another by procession. But according to you the Son and the Holy Spirit remain without any reciprocal communion or relational connection by which they might regard one another. And what else is it to say this than, to some extent, to dissolve the supreme and venerable Trinity?

## Chapter XII. That the Holy Spirit is the σύμπνοια of both, that is, their concord, and the σύννευσις of both, that is, their mutual regard

[Col. 1181A]

“Indeed, the Holy Spirit is the *sympnoia* (σύμπνοια) of both, that is, their concord, and the *synneusis* (σύννευσις) of both, that is, their mutual regard. By holiness proper and natural, he communicates with the Father and the Son; he is the same in substance, not the same in person; and, so to speak, completes or embraces the Trinity in the Trinity, while dissolving unity on account of Trinity. Therefore consider what you say, see what you think, and take care not to offend against the Son and the Holy Spirit in such a manner that you lose both of them together with the Father. For whoever sins against the Son sins also against the Father, and whoever offends against the Son offends also against the Father. For the Son himself said: ‘Whoever despises me despises him who sent me’ [Luke 10:16]. Again: ‘Whoever does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him’ [John 5:23].

“Now it is certain that the one who denies the Son this honour—that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him just as from the Father—does not honour the Son. Again, it is certain that whoever separates the Holy Spirit in unsound faith from communion with the Son by removing the relation of procession inflicts no slight blasphemy upon the Holy Spirit. Thus he offends both: the Son, because he considers him unworthy—that from him the Holy Spirit [the source breaks off]; and the Holy Spirit, because he judges him too unworthy to proceed from the Son. Thus, gravely sinning against both and against the Father, he blasphemes the whole Trinity. For what greater blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is there than to believe and teach that the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Son? Certainly the text, ‘Whoever sins against the Father or the Son will be forgiven; but whoever sins against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come’ [Luke 12:32], seems not to have been spoken only about the Macedonian heresy, which said that the Holy Spirit was a creature and not God. Rather, it is evident that it was also written concerning this sin of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. Whoever commits that sin of blasphemy, unbelief, or impatience, unless he repents, will not be forgiven either in this age or in the age to come, although that passage of Scripture can also be expounded in many other ways.”

## Chapter XIII. That no one ought silently or patiently to endure being called a blasphemer, just as the Lord did not when he was told, “You have a demon”; and that the Holy Spirit receives diverse names because of diverse effects

[Col. 1181D]

Nechites, Archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “You have argued quite subtly on the proposed question. But what you finally added—namely, that we who deny that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son do injury to both, indeed offend the entire Trinity in this matter and, as you say, commit blasphemy—this we neither ought nor can hear with equanimity, especially since every form of rebuke calls for patience, whereas this calls for none at all. For who can patiently bear being called a blasphemer?

“For the Lord, the model of all patience, after patiently hearing all the insulting words which the Jews directed against him—when they called him a glutton and wine-drinker, a carpenter’s son, and many other such things—finally, when they said to him, ‘You have a demon’ [John 8:48], and, ‘By Beelzebub, prince of demons, he casts out demons’ [Matt. 9:34], replied: ‘I do not have a demon’ [John 8:49]. He thereby plainly taught that we ought patiently to accept every reproach spoken against us; but no one ought to pass over in silence an accusation that he is thought not Catholic but heretical, so that he might seem alienated from the Holy Spirit and a companion of demons. Therefore I shall answer what you have said, as the Lord also teaches me: in no respect do we offend the holy and indivisible Trinity. Rather, as true Catholics, we venerate it in the unity of the same substance with the honour due to divinity. We neither cut up and divide the divine substance as Arius did, nor confuse the persons as Sabellius did; nor, with Macedonius, do we separate the Holy Spirit from deity by calling him a creature; nor, like the Pneumatomachians attacking the Holy Spirit, do we inflict any blasphemy. For we worship God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit: three persons, one Godhead, undivided in glory, honour, dominion, and substance.

“Hear further whether we blaspheme the Holy Spirit. We believe that the Holy Spirit is to be worshipped with the Father and the Son: the one God who deifies and gives life through baptism; the Spirit of God; the Spirit of Christ; the mind of Christ; the Spirit of the Lord; Lord in himself; the Spirit of sonship—that is, of the Son of God, or of our adoptive sonship; the Spirit of truth; the Spirit of liberation; the Spirit of wisdom and understanding; the Spirit of counsel and strength; the Spirit of knowledge and godliness; the Spirit of the fear of the Lord. For the Holy Spirit, God, is the effective cause of all these things: filling all things in substance, containing all things, filling the world according to substance, incomprehensible to the world according to power; good, right, principal; sanctifying, not sanctified; giving life, not given life; measuring, not measured; participated in, not participating; filling, [Col. 1182D] not filled; containing, not contained; inherited after Christ by the apostles; clarifying, glorifying; numbered in the Trinity of persons; the finger of God; fire as God; love; charity; the Spirit who knows all things, who teaches, who breathes where he wills and as much as he wills; directing; speaking; tested in the wilderness; provoked to anger when Jesus cast those buying and selling out of the temple; troubled at the raising of Lazarus; illuminator; giver of life—or rather, light in himself and life in himself; maker of temples; deifying; perfecting, so as both to precede baptism through faith and to be sought after baptism through the laying on of hands; doing whatever God does; distributed by grace in fiery tongues; dividing charisms; making apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, [Col. 1183A] and teachers; intellectual, manifest, great, immeasurable, unimpeded, undefilable, equally powerful, most wise, and manifold in his activities; revealing all things; possessing his own power; unchangeable; almighty; *pantepiskopos* (παντεπίσκοπος), that is, bishop of all; passing through all intellectual, pure, most subtle spirits, angelic powers, as well as prophetic and apostolic powers, and other powers also distributed among various persons, according to the same Spirit and not in the same places—by which he is also shown to be uncircumscribable.

“Whatever is said of the Holy Spirit in more humble terms—such as being given, sent, distributed, chrism, gift, breathing upon, promise, intercession, or anything else of this kind—must be referred back to the first cause, so that it may be shown what is from what. Since we believe and teach such things concerning the Holy Spirit, we are confident that we are guilty of no unforgivable blasphemy. But if we do not readily believe that he proceeds from the Son, do not wonder: however many arguments you bring forward, we cannot suddenly come over to this view, especially since no authority of the Gospel, canonical Scriptures, or even holy councils persuades or teaches us to believe it.”

## Chapter XIV. That no one ought to adapt the meaning of Scripture, which has deserved to be called divine, to his own understanding, but rather ought to adapt his own understanding to it
Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, said: “If you demand authorities to persuade you of this [Col. 1183C], would that, when you have heard them, you might receive them with a right understanding! But I fear that the proverb current among us may apply to you: ‘A wolf was set to learn his letters; but he kept crying, “lamb, lamb, lamb,” paying no attention to what he heard outside from his teacher, but to what he carried within in his heart.’ But if you have hardened your heart and so shut fast your obstinate mind that, whatever may be said, you nevertheless refuse to yield, what good then is anything that we may say? It is better to be silent humbly than to speak uselessly and beat the air with idle words; for there is a time to speak and a time to be silent. But if you should strive to twist the authorities put forward to your own meaning, rather than take care to adapt your own meaning to the divine Scripture [Col. 1183D], I fear that in this matter also you may oppose and resist the Holy Spirit, since you are not ashamed rashly to overthrow, outside the understanding of the Holy Spirit, those things written at the Holy Spirit’s dictation, and to twist them to your own meaning. Yet we have met, not to conquer, but to investigate what is true. For Truth itself says: ‘The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life’ (John 6:64). And elsewhere: ‘The Spirit of life’ (Ezek. 10:17), who shall be in you—that is, the Spirit of the holy Scriptures.”

Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “How great an evil it is to distort by a kind of violent interpretation the meaning of Scripture, which has deserved to be called divine, toward one’s own opinion, rather than humbly to subject and adapt one’s own understanding altogether to divine Scripture [Col. 1184A], ought not to be unknown to anyone accustomed to devote himself to sacred reading; and therefore you have given good warning. Do then yourself what you have warned me to do. If you wish to propose sacred authorities, expound them in such a way that you do not appear, by a forced interpretation, to wish to prove your opinion because it is yours, rather than because it is true. For it is written: ‘He who presses the breasts hard to draw out milk produces butter; and he who squeezes violently draws out blood’ (Prov. 30:33). But now say whether you have any authorities favoring your opinion in the question proposed.”

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, said: “This still seems necessary to state beforehand: so long as we spoke in our own words, each of us could abound in his own opinion. But now that we have begun to treat divine words [Col. 1184B], it is fitting that we speak without contention, bear with one another in due reverence, and render honor to the Holy Spirit, who is the author of divine Scripture, so that he may deign truly to disclose to us what he himself wills us humbly and without contention to investigate. For there are some whom, when the truth of Scripture presses them, prefer even when defeated to quarrel in disputation and to resist truth with perverse utterances, rather than confess their own errors; and, when at last they cannot find what to answer, they nevertheless do not know how to be silent humbly.”

Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “You have spoken well; but this also ought not to be passed over in silence: if perhaps one of us should differ from the other in expounding Scripture—since this can often happen without damage to sound faith [Col. 1184C]—what is said should not immediately be called error. For from one Scripture several good interpretations are often drawn, and they are by no means to be despised, even though they may seem to have no bearing whatever on the present question.”

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, said: “You speak excellently. Only be well-disposed, neither slow nor reluctant to believe; and do not, as the common saying goes, seek a knot in a reed. For as wisdom will not enter a malicious soul (Wisdom 1:4), so divine wisdom of its own accord enters a well-disposed soul.”

Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “Take courage. I willingly believe what ought to be believed, provided I am suitably led to it; but now, speak.”

## CHAPTER XV. That the Lord, by breathing upon them, gave the Holy Spirit to the apostles; yet that bodily breath was not the Holy Spirit, but a sign of his procession; and how the words “Receive the Holy Spirit” are to be understood.

[Col. 1184D]

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, said: “After the resurrection, the Lord Jesus presented himself to his disciples, breathed upon them, and said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’ (John 20:22). What else, I ask, did that breathing signify except that the Holy Spirit proceeds also from himself? For that breath was not the substance of the Holy Spirit, but a demonstration that the Holy Spirit proceeds also from the Son.”

Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “I agree with you that that bodily breath was not the substance of the Holy Spirit [Col. 1185A]; but I do not agree with you that this breathing was a sign of the procession which is from the Son.”

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, said: “If, when Christ breathed and said, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit,’ the apostles received the Holy Spirit, why should that very breathing not be believed to be a sign of his procession? Again, if the Holy Spirit was given to the disciples by the Son as he breathed and said, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit,’ tell me, I ask, how he came from the giving Son into the receiving disciples except by proceeding from him—with whom he is always—and arriving at those to whom he was then given in the exercise of the gift? For the apostles to receive the Holy Spirit, there had to be one who gave; and thus he proceeded from the giver into those receiving. Yet even if there had not been any who received [Col. 1185B], there would no less have been one who proceeds; for his procession is eternal and substantial. Thus, although he would not then fittingly be called ‘given,’ he could no less be called a gift or gift-able (*donabile*). For that which can be given, even though it is not given, is called a gift or gift-able; but it is not called ‘given’ unless it is given.

“Indeed, by his own natural essence, whereby he is from the Father and the Son, the Holy Spirit is capable of proceeding and capable of being given; he exists only by proceeding, is given only by proceeding, is received only by proceeding, and works nothing except by proceeding. Therefore, when he is said to be sent or given, whether by the Father or by the Son, he is said to be given in no other way than by proceeding; for his giving or sending is his procession. [Col. 1185C] The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son in two ways. One procession is eternal, according to affection—that is, the love by which the Father loves the Son and the Son the Father. The other procession is temporal, according to effect—that is, his gifts which are given to human beings.”

Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “Since the Holy Spirit is everywhere by essence and was not absent even from the hearts of the apostles by presence, what do you suppose Christ gave by breathing, or the apostles received, when it was said to them, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’? For if they are said to have received the Holy Spirit, who is the third person in the Trinity, who is everywhere, and who was already in their hearts, how can it rightly be said that they then received him [Col. 1185D] whom they already had and who was already in their hearts by presence?”

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, said: “The Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and the Son, who is the third person in the Trinity, who is fully and perfectly God, who is everywhere and nowhere absent by the essence of divinity—he was in the apostles’ hearts by the presence of that divinity; afterward, as humble and chosen persons, they received him through indwelling grace. Thus he says of himself: ‘Upon whom shall I rest, except upon the humble and quiet person, who trembles at my words?’ Likewise: ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble’ (James 4:6).

“They therefore received the Holy Spirit now bearing fruit through indwelling grace, whereas previously he had been among them as if barren [Col. 1186A], merely everywhere through the essence of divinity. It was as though he said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit in grace, who was previously among you in essence alone; receive as a gift what had previously been among you as something foreign; receive in use and office what had previously been among you without reception of the gift; receive in the effect of spiritual grace what until now had been among you merely in the presence of essence; receive through sanctification what had previously been among you without the manifestation of any power.’

“It is as if someone possessing clear eyes but without visual power were told: ‘Receive eyes so that you may see—eyes which you previously did not have for seeing.’ Or as if a deaf person possessing ears were told: ‘Receive ears for hearing, which you previously had without the use of hearing.’ Or as if one possessing a tongue but mute were told: ‘Receive a tongue for the use of speaking, which you previously possessed without this use.’ Or as if one with withered hands were told: ‘Receive hands for working, which you previously possessed apart from the function of working’; and as if a lame person possessing handsome feet were told: ‘Receive feet for walking, which you previously possessed without the benefit of walking.’ [Col. 1186B] Or as if someone who had money belonging to another deposited with him were told: ‘Receive this money, and let it be yours for use; previously it was with you without any use for your need or benefit.’

“In this way, then, the words appear to have been spoken: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit in the use and gift of spiritual grace,’ whereas previously he was among you in the immensity of divinity. Nevertheless, before the solemn and so manifest bestowal of the Holy Spirit, the apostles were not altogether without spiritual grace. Thus the Lord said to Peter when he confessed Christ, the Son of God: ‘Blessed are you, Simon Peter, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.’ That is, as though he said: ‘You received this through heavenly and divine inspiration, not through a human revelation of flesh or blood.’ The other apostles too possessed faith divinely inspired before the Holy Spirit was given, but not so great a faith as he ought to possess who is to be saved through faith. Whatever they had in lesser measure was supplied through the solemn and manifest gift of the Holy Spirit.

“Why not? Was not Peter, leader of the apostles, who said that he was ready to go with Christ both to death and to prison [Col. 1186C], suddenly brought to deny Christ by the voice of a serving-girl at the door? Yet afterward, after the Holy Spirit had been given, clothed with power from on high, when the chief priests threatened and forbade him to preach in Christ’s name, he boldly answered: ‘We must obey God rather than men’ (Acts 5:29).

“This gift of the Holy Spirit was first made on earth by breathing, on account of love of neighbor; afterward it was made from heaven in diverse tongues, on account of love of God. Here we are also instructed, to some extent, that because the Holy Spirit was given twice, he must likewise be believed to proceed from two—not twice, but simultaneously and once. From heaven, indeed, as from the Father who is in heaven; but on earth, as from the Son who in his humanity lived on earth [Col. 1187A] among human beings. Yet when he gave him, the same Son was no longer then mortal on earth among mortals, but after the resurrection and before the ascension manifested himself to the apostles in the appearance that pleased him, abundantly bestowing the Holy Spirit on them.”

Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “When the discourse concerns the summit of highest theology, comparisons of this sort drawn from bodily things seem to have no place. Nor should likenesses of higher things be derived from lower; for the stable nature of immovable things cannot be fully known from the changing nature of things in motion. Certainly, to compare spiritual things to bodily things, or adapt divine things to human things—what else is this but to seek the living among the dead?”

## CHAPTER XVI. That spiritual things are sometimes compared with bodily things, and bodily things sometimes with spiritual things.

[Col. 1187B]

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, said: “I grant what you say. For it is impossible for any one of the things compared to attain an adequate and pure truth of the thing to which it is compared. A likeness is never introduced wholly, but only in some respect; otherwise it would no longer be called a likeness but rather identity. For nothing similar is altogether similar to that to which it is similar—not even among bodily things, whenever they are mutually compared by some likeness. But we offer or receive such likenesses as dramatic representations, not indeed as expressing the pure truth of the things themselves [Col. 1187C], but as drawing the hearer’s mind toward a greater knowledge of the thing itself. And it often comes about through instruction of this kind that what was previously unknown because of the great height of its nature becomes known. For the mind rises through the things it knows to the things it does not know. ‘The invisible things are understood and perceived through the things that have been made’ (Rom. 1:20), and much else in this manner.

“Just as spiritual things are often understood through likenesses of bodily things, so bodily things are also sometimes learned through spiritual things. Thus Moses is told: ‘See that you make all things according to the pattern of those things which you saw on the mountain’ (Exod. 25:40). There he is plainly commanded to arrange everything for the construction of the tabernacle in bodily form after the likeness of things he had first seen spiritually [Col. 1187D] on the mountain. Therefore, instructive likenesses of bodily or incorporeal things must not be despised, although they cannot perfectly express the truth of the things themselves.

“Very often, through visible concepts, words are invisibly formed inwardly in the invisible soul of one who does not know; visible letters are also visibly formed upon a visible parchment; and while silent they speak, while speaking they are silent. Again, through those same visible letters, an invisible understanding is formed in the reader’s soul. And it also happens that, if the first concepts after whose pattern those letters were originally made are erased when forgetfulness intervenes, they are reborn when the same letters are looked upon. Thus, in turn, discourses of words and visible letters are made in likeness of invisible concepts [Col. 1188A]; and again, in likeness of discourses or visible letters, new invisible concepts are produced—although visible and invisible things are found to be not of the same, but of utterly different natures.

“The Lord also often spoke in parables through likenesses, sometimes comparing bodily things with spiritual and sometimes spiritual things with bodily. Certainly, I think that no likeness drawn from creature to Creator can readily be found which may be applied with complete exactness.”

Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “I fully approve what you have just said on these matters; but if you have further authorities concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son, put them forward.”

## CHAPTER XVII. That, when the woman touched the Lord’s fringe, power went out from him; and that the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from him, is called by the name of power.

[Col. 1188B]

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, said: “Hear and attend to what the Son said concerning the woman suffering from an issue of blood, who touched the fringe of his garment and was healed: ‘Someone touched me, for I perceived power going out from me’ (Luke 8:46). That the Holy Spirit is here called by the name of power is clear, as is plainly known from that place where the angel, teaching Mary, said: ‘The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you’ (Luke 1:35). For after the angel had said, ‘The Holy Spirit shall come upon you,’ he fittingly added, ‘And the power of the Most High shall overshadow you,’ evidently to show that the Holy Spirit is the same thing as [Col. 1188C] the power of the Most High.

“And the Lord himself, promising him to the disciples, said: ‘But remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high’ (Luke 24:49). Again: ‘You shall receive,’ he said, ‘the power of the Holy Spirit coming upon you, and you shall be my witnesses’ (Acts 1:8). The evangelist must be understood to speak of this power when he says: ‘Power went out from him and healed all’ (Luke 6:19). Therefore it is manifest that the Holy Spirit proceeds also from the Son—unless perhaps you refuse to see, with eyes deliberately shut, what is clearer than light, and deliberately refuse with deaf ears to hear Scripture crying aloud and pressing itself upon you.”

Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “If, then, as you affirm, the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, why did the Son say, ‘He proceeds from the Father’ (John 15:26), and remain silent concerning his procession [Col. 1188D] from himself?”

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, said: “Why do you suppose, except because he customarily refers to the Father what is his own, since he himself is from the Father? Hence also he says: ‘My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me’ (John 7:16). If, then, his teaching is understood in this way—even though he says that it is not his own but the Father’s—how much more must the Holy Spirit be understood there also to proceed from him, where he says, ‘He proceeds from the Father,’ without saying, ‘He does not proceed from me’? From whom the Son has that he is God—for he is God from God—from that one he also has that the Holy Spirit proceeds from himself; and therefore the Holy Spirit has from the Father himself the fact that he proceeds also from the Son, just as he proceeds from the Father.

“This too is fittingly and plainly indicated in the Gospel, where he says: ‘Whom I shall send to you from the Father’ (John 15:16), showing that the Holy Spirit belongs both to the Father and to the Son. And when he had said, ‘Whom the Father will send’ [Col. 1189A], he added, ‘in my name’; yet he did not say, ‘Whom the Father will send from me,’ as he said, ‘Whom I shall send to you from the Father.’ He thereby showed that the Father is the principle of the whole divinity—or, if it may better be said, deity—being the author of generation and procession. Therefore, he who proceeds from the Father and the Son is rightly referred to him from whom the Son was born.

“The Holy Spirit, then, is the power of the Most High, namely the Father; and he is also the power of the Son, who is himself likewise the Most High. And because he belongs to both, he must rightly be believed to proceed from both; for as his communion belongs not to one of them but to both, so his procession is from not one of them but from both.”

Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “We confess that the Holy Spirit belongs to both. For we have the Lord himself saying: ‘It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you’ (Matt. 10:20). We also have the Apostle saying: ‘If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you’ (Rom. 8:11); here he plainly intended the Spirit of the Father. Likewise the Apostle says: ‘God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying: Abba, Father’ (Gal. 4:6). And elsewhere: ‘Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him’ (Rom. 8:9). For these reasons, then, and for many other testimonies by which we are instructed, we rightly confess, as I have said [Col. 1189C], that the Holy Spirit, who is the third person in the Trinity, belongs to the Father and the Son. Yet we do not dare to confess that he proceeds from both, because perhaps it is one thing for him to be from the Father and another thing for him to proceed.”

## CHAPTER XVIII. That, as for the Holy Spirit to be from the Father is the same as to proceed from the Father, so for him to be from the Son is the same as to proceed from the Son.

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, said: “The Holy Spirit, who is from the Father and proceeds from the Father, either is from the Father in the same respect in which he proceeds from the Father, or he is not from the Father in the respect in which he proceeds from the Father. But if, in the respect in which he is from the Father, he also proceeds from the Father, why, likewise, should he not proceed from the Son in the respect in which he is from the Son? For in the respect in which he is from the Father, he is also from the Son [Col. 1189D]; and in the respect in which he is from the Son, he is also from the Father. Therefore, he is from the Father and the Son—unless perhaps someone should dare to say that he has one being from the Father and another being from the Son. To say this is sheer madness.

“For he does not have one being from the Father and another from the Son, nor one procession from the Father and another from the Son; rather, he has one and the same being and one and the same procession from both Father and Son. He does not exist twice, nor proceed twice; he has neither two beings nor two processions; nor, what is most impious to say, are there two Holy Spirits proceeding. As it is certain that for him to be from the Father is nothing other than to proceed from the Father, so no one ought to doubt that for him to be from the Son is nothing other than to proceed from the Son [Col. 1190A]; for his procession is substantial.

“But if you grant him one being from the Father and another proceeding from the Father, you surely make him differ from himself, though certainly for him to be from the Father is nothing other than to proceed from the Father. For he exists by proceeding from the Father, and by existing from the Father he proceeds by a substantial procession and a proceeding, or processible, substance. Therefore show, if you can, that the Holy Spirit has another being from the Son. Again, show, if you can, that for him it is one thing to be from the Father and the Son and another to proceed; and thus you have made him differ from himself and have most shamelessly emptied the sound faith concerning the Holy Spirit.

“Again, if for him being from the Father is the same thing as proceeding, then, if his being from the Son is the same as his being from the Father, he proceeds also from the Son as from the Father. But if he does not proceed from the Son [Col. 1190B], then his being from the Son is likewise not the same as his being from the Father. If his being from the Son is not the same as his being from the Father, then he has either another being or no being at all from the Son; either conclusion is absurd. But if he is not from the Son, neither is he from the Father, for the Father and Son are one. But if he is not from the Father, neither does he proceed from the Father.

“Again: if he proceeds from the Father because he is from the Father processibly, then by the same reasoning he proceeds also from the Son because he is from the Son processibly. For it is equal—or rather the same—for the Holy Spirit to be from the Father and to be from the Son, and to proceed from the Father and to proceed from the Son, because it is written of him: ‘He shall not speak from himself, but whatever he shall hear, he shall speak’ (John 16:13). From where, then, he hears, from there he speaks; and from where he speaks, from there he proceeds. Therefore, from where he has essence, from there he has hearing; from where he has hearing, from there he has knowledge; from where he has knowledge, from there he has procession. Thus, for him to be from the Father and the Son is to proceed from both by existing, hearing, and knowing.

“But why the Son’s being from the Father is called being born from the Father, whereas the Holy Spirit’s being from the Father and the Son is not called being born but proceeding, and what difference there is between being that is being born and being that is proceeding—this is a most difficult question. Yet the Son himself is said to proceed from the Father, as there: ‘I came forth from the Father and came into the world’ (John 16:28). And again: ‘I proceeded from the Father’ (John 8:42). Yet that procession, namely of the Son, is wholly other, differing from the procession of the Holy Spirit. For the Son is sent by his own proper mission and procession in being born, and proceeds from the Father in being born; but the Holy Spirit proceeds by his own proper mission and procession in proceeding, and is sent in proceeding by both the Son and the Father [Col. 1190D].

“See, then, what you say, and beware lest by denying the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son you be convicted also of taking away from him the being he has from the Son. For since his being the Holy Spirit and his proceeding are the same, whoever denies that he proceeds from the Son also denies that he is from the Son; and whoever denies that he is from the Son denies also that he is from the Father, for they are one. Whoever denies both that he is and that he proceeds from the Son as well as from the Father denies that he is the Holy Spirit. Consequently, to say the one thing and the other amounts to nothing else than dissolving the whole Trinity [Col. 1191A]. How unjust and impious that is, you may judge.”

Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “I think this must first be answered: the Father is such as the Son is such as the Holy Spirit is, and this is according to substance; but the Father’s begetting is not such as the Son’s being begotten, nor is it such as the Holy Spirit’s proceeding. And although, as you said a little earlier, it is neither easy to investigate nor possible to define how the Father begets, the Son is begotten, or the Holy Spirit proceeds, nevertheless this is not said rashly: this one begets in one way, this one is begotten in another way, and this one proceeds in another. Yet no action or passion at all is to be conceived in these matters.

“And although the Father’s being, the Son’s being, and the Holy Spirit’s being are the same substantially, it is one thing personally for the Father alone to be, and not the Son or the Holy Spirit; another for the Son alone personally to be, and not the Father or Holy Spirit; and another for the Holy Spirit alone personally to be, and not the Father or the Son [Col. 1191B]. The former marks identity of substance in the three; the latter marks personal distinction in the same three.

“Therefore, when by argument you inquire whether it is the same thing for the Holy Spirit to be from the Father and from the Son, and again ask whether it is the same thing for him to be and to proceed, and thus strive to prove that, just as his being is the same from both, so also his proceeding is the same from both: when you say this, you ought surely to have considered that, although the Holy Spirit belongs to both and is from both, he does not seem to be from both equally, and consequently does not proceed equally. For he is from the Father as from one who is from no one and has from no one the fact that the Holy Spirit belongs to him and is from him. But he is from the Son as from one who is from the Father and has from the Father this very fact: that the Holy Spirit also belongs to him and is also from him. Thus it appears that the Holy Spirit truly belongs to both and is from both, but not that he belongs to both equally or proceeds equally from both.”

## CHAPTER XIX. Whether the Holy Spirit proceeds equally from the Father and from the Son, since the Father is from no one, whereas the Son is from the Father; and a comparison from Adam, the first formed being, from Eve’s division from that formed being, and from Abel’s descent from both.

[Col. 1191D]

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, said: “The Father, who is from no one, has nothing from either the Son or the Holy Spirit; nor does the Son, who is from the Father, have anything from the Holy Spirit. But the Son has everything from the Father, even that he is God; for he is God from God, and has from him also that the Holy Spirit proceeds from himself. Further, the Holy Spirit has from the Father himself that he proceeds also from the Son, just as he proceeds from the Father. Thus, whatever the Son is or has, and whatever the Holy Spirit is, is wholly and principally from the Father himself. The Father, as author and principle of generation and procession, is from no one and has nothing from anyone. Perhaps for this reason [Col. 1192A] it is thought that the Holy Spirit neither belongs equally to both nor proceeds equally from both.

“But what is this? Our discussion has undertaken to determine not how the Holy Spirit proceeds from each, but whether he proceeds from both. Once that has been granted, then, if you wish, the other question also may subsequently be investigated. Still, I would have you attend briefly to this point, since it pleases you. I say that the fact that one from whom he is and from whom he proceeds—the Father—is from no one, whereas the other from whom he is likewise and from whom he likewise proceeds—the Son—is from the Father, does not at all appear to take away from the Holy Spirit, as regards himself, equality of being and proceeding from both. For because of this he is neither earlier nor later, neither less nor more from, or proceeding from, one than the other; but he proceeds from both simultaneously and once, in no unequal manner but equally—that is, eternally in equality known to himself. Although some may seem rightly able to say that he is and proceeds more properly from the Father, as from the first cause, than from the Son, of whom the Father is the cause.

“For when it is said that the Father is from no one and the Son is from the Father, no priority or posteriority is to be understood there, nor greater rank in the one and lesser rank in the other; rather, in both there is equality of the same majesty [Col. 1192B]. Although the Father has no cause of himself and the Son has the Father as his cause, nevertheless the power and glory of the caused and the uncaused—that is, of the one having a cause and the one having no cause—are the same, so to speak. Therefore, since they possess the same eternity, majesty, power, strength, will, and equality, how should they emit the Holy Spirit proceeding from them not equally but unequally? For the Holy Spirit’s procession is substantial, just as the Son’s generation is substantial.

“This may be seen through whatever analogy may be suitable. Adam, by himself—that is, without any generating cause—was a formation of God alone. Eve was a division of that same formed being, as of a preceding cause. Abel descended from both, not through formation or division from a formed thing, but through the course of natural human generation. Adam was a human being, Eve a human being, Abel a human being, and therefore *homoousion* (ὁμοούσιον), that is, of like substance or the same nature; yet Adam was not Eve or Abel, Eve was not Adam or Abel, nor was Abel Adam or Eve. Do you not think [Col. 1192D] that Abel, as regards himself, descended equally by generation from father Adam, who had no generating or dividing cause, and from mother Eve, who had descended from Adam as her cause, not by generation but by division?

“For as it is true that Adam and Eve together and at once begot Abel, so likewise it is true that Abel was begotten equally from them, as regards himself. Although some dissimilarity may be assigned between the begetters—namely, formation and division from a formed being—yet in the one begotten the course of the same generation is not dissimilar but the same. Adam was not father earlier than Eve was mother; rather, he was father and she mother simultaneously, and Abel was simultaneously the son of both, descending from each by an equal course of birth. [Col. 1193A] Eve’s having come from Adam by division does not prevent Abel from being the son of one just as much as of the other, and not more or less the son of one than of the other. Eve indeed has from Adam both that she exists by division and that Abel, who is Adam’s son, is also Eve’s son by generation. Thus she has from Adam the fact that she is mother of Abel, whom she bore, while he is likewise father of the Abel whom she bore.

“But in this proposed comparison one must contemplate as in a stage representation. Therefore let no one say that the Holy Spirit is from the Father in one way—that is, by proceeding—and from the Son in another way—that is, not by proceeding—although the Father, from whom he is and from whom he proceeds, is from no one, while the Son, from whom he is likewise and from whom he likewise proceeds, is from the Father. For, as we have argued above, the Holy Spirit has the same being from both, and for him this same being is to proceed from both, as truly as it is ineffably. To believe this is as necessary to faith as it is near to salvation.”

Nechites, Archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “According to the arguments you have woven together with the support of reason, it does not seem absurd that the Holy Spirit should have the same being from the Father and from the Son; yet neither does it seem thereby proved that he proceeds from both, whether equally or unequally.”

Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg, said: “Since you grant that he has the same being from both, you must also confess that he has the same procession from both; especially since it has been shown sufficiently clearly above that, for him, to be from both is the same as to proceed from both, and to proceed from both is the same as to be from both [Col. 1193C]. Therefore he is the Father’s as he is the Son’s, and he is not the Father’s in one way and the Son’s in another. Now he is the Father’s by proceeding from him; and indeed the being which he has both from the Son and from the Father is nothing other than proceeding from both.

“Listen further. You grant that the Holy Spirit is sent by the Son—I know that you grant it, because this is plainly read in the Gospel, unless perhaps some impiety has removed it from your codices, which I do not at all suppose: ‘Whom,’ says the Son, ‘I will send to you.’ You also grant that he receives and proclaims from that same Son, whose very own he is. For this too is in the Gospel, unless, as I said, it has been erased from Greek codices: ‘He,’ he says, ‘will receive from what is mine and will proclaim it to you; for he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak’ [Col. 1193D] (John 16:13).”

Nechites, Archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “I grant all these things: namely, that he is from him, that he is sent by him, that he receives from what is his and proclaims it, that he hears from him, that he speaks from him. I grant all this because the Gospel teaches it. But I do not teach, nor presume to teach, that he proceeds from the Son—a procession which the Gospel does not teach.”

Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg, said: “I greatly wonder at your prudence: you so abhor this word ‘proceeds’ when used of the Holy Spirit from the Son, although you have expressions in the Gospel of equivalent force and identical meaning, and confidently grant them on the authority of the Gospel [Col. 1194A]. For what else is, or even can be, his being sent from the Son but his procession from him? For when the one sends, it follows that the one sent proceeds from the one by whom he is sent; yet the one sent is not absent from the sender, nor separated from him—always present from the one always present.

“Again, he who belongs to him, and who has from him all that he has from the Father—who is from him as he is from the Father, and has from him as he has from the Father—how can he be thought not to proceed from him? As has often been said, his proceeding is nothing other than his being; his being is nothing other than his proceeding; and his hearing and speaking are nothing other than his being and proceeding—and all this is not from himself. For he is by proceeding, and by existing he proceeds [Col. 1194B], since for him to be is to be capable of proceeding.

“Therefore, as is indisputably gathered from all that has been granted, the Holy Spirit is the Father’s and is the Son’s; he is from the Father and from the Son; he is sent by the Father and is sent by the Son; and thus he proceeds from the Father and proceeds from the Son.”

Nechites, Archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “I cannot deny that, by arguments and authorities most carefully sought out and suitably brought forward, you appear to have proved what you proposed; and I would not wish to resist the Holy Spirit. But I wish you still to hear what moves me greatly and most strongly frightens me away from this word ‘procession.’ Our Lord Jesus Christ, the saviour of humankind, founder of the faith, founder of the Gospel, and lover of our salvation, established for the apostles a faith sufficient [Col. 1194C] for the salvation of all. For he would not be a sufficient saviour unless he had been a sufficient teacher. Yet nowhere did he say anything concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son, as he did concerning his procession from the Father. Therefore it seems very rash to me for anyone to presume to add anything to, or remove anything from, the Christian faith already fully established and sufficient for salvation—especially in the faith of the Holy Trinity.

“And it seems to me that, in rendering due reverence to the Gospel, we ought to say of the Holy Spirit the word ‘processes’ or ‘proceeds,’ because it is attributed to him that he proceeds from the Father; but because it is not attributed to that same Holy Spirit that he proceeds from the Son, we ought by no means to say it. Thus, it seems, we may walk safely [Col. 1194D] in faith, adding nothing and subtracting nothing, but simply holding what we have learned from the Gospel. For just as it is unsafe to take anything away, so it is dangerous to add anything.”

[Note: Col. 1193. “For just as it is unsafe”: there can be no doubt that this is the correct reading; at least the earlier edition’s reading, “for just as it is to such an extent,” was inept.]

## CHAPTER XX. That, just as the statement “the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son” is not found in the Gospel, so too the statement “the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Son” is nowhere found in the Gospel; nor is it found that he proceeds from the Father alone.

Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg, said: “You have spoken as befits your maturity and the prudence of so great a man. Nevertheless, one must not tremble where there is no fear. Stand here, then, and attend carefully to what I say. If you fear to say that the Holy Spirit [Col. 1195A] proceeds from the Son because the words ‘proceeds from the Son’ are written nowhere at all in the Gospel, tell me, I pray, with what face or with what rashness you are not afraid to utter this negative assertion concerning procession, namely, ‘he does not proceed from the Son,’ when it is found written in no place of Scripture and nowhere in the Gospel.

“Why do you not keep silent where, as you think, the Gospel is silent? Whence do you get that negative ‘not,’ which the Gospel does not teach you? Who could ever have persuaded you to say ‘he does not proceed from the Son,’ when the Gospel does not say this, yet could not have persuaded you to say ‘he proceeds from the Son,’ when the Gospel neither denies nor forbids this? You reverence the Gospel so that you do not dare say ‘he proceeds from the Son’; yet you do not reverence the Gospel [Col. 1195B] so that you do not dare say ‘he does not proceed from the Son.’ There you fear where there is no need to fear, and there you do not fear where there is need to fear.

“I grant you that, among us, the words ‘proceeds from the Son’ are not found so simply in any place of Scripture. And you too must grant that the words ‘does not proceed from the Son’ are found nowhere in the same source. What then? Shall we dispute about words now signifying this, now that? Does it become us to follow letters, syllables, or verbal expressions, abandoning the truth of things? Let us leave that rather to children playing at grammar and dialectic. We, however, ought rather to investigate the meaning than cling to words.

“Accordingly, you say that the Holy Spirit proceeds either from the Father alone or not from the Father alone. If you say from the Father alone, you certainly do not have this from the Gospel [Col. 1195C]. But if you choose to say ‘not from the Father alone,’ you must confess that he proceeds from the Son as from the Father, or from some other source, I know not what. But perhaps you will not dare choose either alternative, especially since neither is found in the Gospel, to which you think absolutely nothing should be added.

“It remains, therefore, that with free faith, and without contradiction either of the Gospel or of yourself, we say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. For when the Gospel says ‘from the Father’ and not ‘from the Father alone,’ it allows us quite freely to say ‘not from the Father alone, but also from the Son.’”

Nechites, Archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “By saying ‘he proceeds from the Son,’ and by saying ‘he proceeds not from the Father alone’ [Col. 1195D], you compel me to say ‘he proceeds from the Father alone’; and you compel me rashly and outside the Gospel to deny what you seem rashly and outside the Gospel to affirm. For words belong no more to the speaker than to the one who compels another to speak.”

## CHAPTER XXI. That nothing should be affirmed rashly, and nothing refuted angrily.

Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg, said: “This was the Platonic doctrine in the schools of the Academics: to affirm without rashness and to refute without anger. For there is a fallacious reason, which is sometimes deceived by the likeness of truth; and there is a non-fallacious reason [Col. 1196A], by which the truth of things is comprehended through certain knowledge. And just as fallacious reason is rightly refuted without anger, so non-fallacious reason is rightly defended, not by proud rashness, but by humble assertion and praiseworthy humility.

“Therefore you ought to accuse your rashness, not mine. For I possess this procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son, of which we are treating, as proved by so many testimonies from the Gospel and other Scriptures; I establish it without rashness through non-fallacious reason, and faithfully believe it. But you have, and can have, no authority from the Gospel or other Scriptures for the negation. Therefore your rashness is rather to be accused, since you rashly deny what neither the Gospel nor any other Scripture denies, and rashly reject what you do not know whether it should be proved [Col. 1196B] or rejected. My faith, however, which I affirm and know, and which I prove by the testimony of the Scriptures—not through rashness but with the Holy Spirit’s aid—is not to be accused.

“Therefore, just as I do not rashly assert what is certain but faithfully believe it and truly prove that it ought to be believed, so you too should endure without anger the refutation of what is uncertain to you. Either then finally confess with me that the Holy Spirit proceeds also from the Son; or, if you do not yet dare, perhaps because you are too faint-hearted and tremble where there is no fear, do at least this: while I confess it, be silent; and do not deny with the shameless little monosyllable ‘not’ what you doubt and are uncertain about, but which I affirm with certainty and confidence [Col. 1196C].

“But if you wish to answer, answer this: that you simply do not know whether the Spirit proceeds or does not proceed from the Son. Then you would answer rightly: confessing meanwhile your own ignorance, but not denying my faith. For how can one judge rightly about what one does not know? But now you can no longer deny your ignorance on this matter.

“Let your judgment on this, therefore, cease; and do not presume any longer to deny what is uncertain to you, which until now you used rashly to deny as one who did not know. For it is incongruous that one who has gone astray off the road and does not know that he is astray should strive to correct one who walks knowingly and rightly on the road; and that one who is not certain should introduce uncertainty. Unless perhaps that fallacious opinion of the Academics still stands among you, or among some of you [Col. 1196D], by which they thought that the highest wisdom was a thoroughly investigated ignorance of all things. Hence they were called masters of ignorance, because they were accustomed to answer every question thus: ‘What if you are mistaken?’ Hence too Aristotle, called wise by some of them, says: ‘To doubt concerning each particular will not be useless.’”

Nechites, Archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “The wise men of the Greeks never said that opinion should be accepted as truth; and they preferred humbly to doubt concerning ambiguities of faith rather than rashly define anything, since what remains over—whether Scripture says too little, or human understanding is insufficient to grasp it—seems to be committed to the fire [Col. 1197A] of the Holy Spirit. For we are human beings; therefore, to think something otherwise than it is, is a human temptation. But through loving one’s own opinion too much, or envying those better than oneself, to proceed as far as the sacrilege of cutting off communion, founding schism, or heresy, is a diabolical presumption. To think in no respect otherwise than reality is, however, angelic perfection.

“Therefore, because we are human and often err and doubt, let us meanwhile beware diabolical presumption until we attain the perfection of angelic judgment. For our elders have hitherto humbly avoided the affirmative word concerning this procession, ‘he proceeds from the Son’: they did not know the truth of the matter and avoided the rashness of the expression. Yet they never said the negative words, ‘he does not proceed from the Son’ [Col. 1197B], fearing error and avoiding offence against Scripture, which plainly says neither. Unless perhaps they were provoked and stirred by the insolence of certain Latins rashly affirming this—men who came to us with superciliousness, speaking loftily, beating the air with clamorous disputations, wishing to display their little learning, and attempting through the mist of sophistry to obscure, or even, if possible, suppress, the great wisdom of the Greeks. To these we did not yield even for an hour, but always sent them away full of confusion, as they deserved.

“But you, most beloved servant of God, because you humbly and gently speak this word which can save our souls, and in the same way humbly and gently accept what we say, and serve not contention but reason and authority—therefore we gladly hear your sweetness. And, to confess the truth, in this disputation of ours something has been granted to you which until now has been granted to no Latin in this imperial city, in a public assembly, who walked above himself and exalted himself against the knowledge of God [Col. 1197C]. But let us proceed further.

“What is the reason that at the first Council of Nicaea, attended by three hundred and eighteen Fathers, nothing was discussed concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son? Certainly the creed composed at that council and confirmed by the authority of so many Fathers contains nothing of this kind. Whatever it contains has been sealed with the key of anathema in such a way that nothing can be added or removed without the greatest scandal to the Church and danger to the soul [Col. 1197D]. How then do you think to escape that anathema, when you do not fear to introduce there the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son, not previously stated, and add it to the faith—if, indeed, you have received the Council of Nicaea as venerable for all Catholics?”

## CHAPTER XXII. That it is not rash to add to the Gospel something which is not contrary to the Gospel, as was done at the Council of Nicaea and at many other councils.

Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg, said: “I embrace with due veneration the creed [Col. 1198A] of the Council of Nicaea, and I receive as a Catholic the twenty-two chapters of that council which have been able to reach us in copies. But when I affirm the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son, which is not forbidden there, I teach or append nothing contrary; and therefore I have no reason to fear that anathema. For what was there forbidden under anathema was the addition of anything contrary to that creed; it was not forbidden that nothing else be taught. Rather, teaching something else is permitted.

“But you are a student of the Gospel and, as you maintained above, say that the faith established by the Lord Jesus in the Gospel is sufficient for the believer’s salvation; and that whoever either increases or diminishes it makes himself in either case a transgressor of evangelical faith. You do not wish to add, remove, or even alter one iota or one stroke; nor do you wish the meaning of evangelical Scripture to be expounded in other words signifying the same meaning. Tell me: how could you ever be persuaded to accept the Council of Nicaea, or any other council, when in nearly all general councils so many enactments necessary to Christian faith have been established that are nowhere found in the Gospel? [Col. 1198B]

“Tell me also: if you refuse to receive the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son solely lest you seem to add to the Gospel something not plainly written there, why do you not for the same reason reject the faith of the Council of Nicaea, approved and received by the Catholic Church, when that faith too is nowhere set forth and explained in the Gospel with such distinctions? Do you believe in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit? Do you worship the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: one God in substance, three in persons? Do you believe the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be the Holy Trinity: one almighty God; the entire deity in the Trinity essential and consubstantial, coeternal and omnipotent, of one will, power, and majesty, Creator of all creatures? [Col. 1198C]”

Nechites, Archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “I believe these things, because I am not an Arian but a Christian.”

Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg, said: “Do you believe each individual person in the Holy Trinity to be one true God, full and perfect?”

[Col. 1198D] Nechites, Archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “I so believe because I am Catholic, not Sabellian. And this is the faith of right believers: that we neither divide the substance in God with the Arians nor confuse the persons with the Sabellians.”

Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg, said: “May your brotherhood not be angry, I pray, nor take offence if I question you a little further. For I ask not in order, like one laying a trap, to catch you in your answer; but that I may learn something from you, or perhaps, if it can be so, that you may learn something from me, and that we may forgive one another and come to know both your faith and mine.”

Nechites, Archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “Ask freely what you wish, for I welcome it.”

[Col. 1199A] Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg, said: “Do you believe that the very Son of God, the Word of God, eternal, born from the Father, consubstantial, omnipotent, and in every respect equal to the Father in divinity, was temporally born from the Holy Spirit and Mary ever-virgin, with a rational soul; that he has two births, one eternal from the Father and the other temporal from his mother; that he is true God and true man, proper and perfect in each nature, neither adoptive nor phantasmal; the only and one Son of God, in and from two natures, but in the singularity of one person; impassible and immortal in divinity, but in humanity suffering for us and for our salvation with a true suffering of flesh?”

[Col. 1199B] Nechites, Archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “I believe and accept all these things, because, after the Nestorian heresy, which held that there were two persons in Christ, and after the Eutychian heresy, which held that there was only one nature in Christ, and after very many errors briefly and distinctly put to rest in your proposition by its individual words, holy mother Church so decreed.”

Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg, said: “Do you also believe the Holy Spirit to be full and perfect, true God, coequal and coessential with the Father and Son, co-omnipotent and coeternal in every respect?”

Nechites, Archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “This is the Catholic faith, confirmed after the Macedonian heresy [Col. 1199C] and strengthened at the Alexandrian Council by many orthodox bishops, who, treating of the divinity of the Holy Spirit, included him in the consubstantial Trinity. Therefore whoever does not hold this faith whole and entire shows that he is not truly a Christian.”

Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg, said: “You believe well, worship well, and speak well. Tell me then, dearest brother, with charity laid as a middle path between us: where is this faith of yours found in the Gospel so distinctly stated? That you should believe in God the Father and in God the Son is indeed plainly taught there, when the Son says: ‘You believe in God; believe also in me’ (John 14:1). That you believe in the Holy Spirit, you rightly believe; but, to my knowledge, nowhere in the Gospel is this shown so plainly and simply in words [Col. 1199D].

[The Apostle, however, plainly proclaims that the Holy Spirit is God when he says: ‘Do you not know that you are the temple of God?’ And immediately he adds: ‘And the Spirit of God dwells in you’ (1 Corinthians 3:16). For God dwells in his temple; but the Spirit of God does not dwell in God’s temple as a minister, since elsewhere he says more plainly: ‘Do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own? For you were bought at a great price; therefore glorify God in your body’ (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). Again: ‘The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple’ (1 Corinthians 3:17).]

[Note: Col. 1199. “The Apostle, however”: I have chosen to enclose these words in brackets because they do not appear to be Anselm’s, since they interrupt the sequence of the discourse.]

“That you worship God the Father [Col. 1200A], you do rightly, because the Gospel teaches this too: ‘True worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth’ (John 4:23). That you also worship God the Son, you do rightly, because the one in whom you believe as God, you rightly worship as God; and this too is suggested by the Gospel: ‘I and the Father are one’ (John 10:30), and ‘I am in the Father, and the Father is in me’ (ibid., 38). Since each is truly one God in the other—consubstantial indeed, but not, if I may put it so, co-personal—each is rightly worshipped as one God in the other.

“But where, I ask, is it distinctly and plainly found anywhere in the Gospel that you worship the Spirit as to be worshipped and glorified together with the Father and the Son? Although a discerning reader, if he carefully examined what is written, ‘True worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth,’ would surely, I think, find the whole Trinity to be worshipped there. For when it is said, ‘True worshippers will worship the Father,’ immediately follows ‘in spirit,’ and then is added ‘in truth’: so that it may be understood plainly that the Father is to be worshipped in the Spirit and in the Truth, who is the Son; the Son in the Father and Holy Spirit; and the Holy Spirit in the Father and Son [Col. 1200B].

“Nevertheless, some heretics, passing over the Gospel text far too plainly and carelessly—indeed foolishly—and not searching out the spirit and life hidden in the Gospel words, refused to affirm that the Holy Spirit is to be worshipped. They said that they were restrained by reverence for evangelical Scripture, which did not plainly show either whether he is to be worshipped or not. See then how your position can stand: you say that you so revere the Gospel that you dare add nothing to the faith which you think it establishes sufficiently. For on this point you are convicted of speaking against yourself: first you thought and said that nothing was to be added to Gospel faith; afterwards, by Christian profession, you confessed the faith of the Holy Trinity, distinguished and handed down in the Council of Nicaea and other councils and strengthened against heresies [Col. 1200C].”

## CHAPTER XXIII. That the faith of the Holy Trinity was fully established in the councils over which the Holy Spirit, παντοσκοπος—“bishop of all”—presided; he who had earlier been author and founder of the Gospel.

[Col. 1200D] “Do not, then, henceforth restrict the faith of the Gospel so that the creed of the Council of Nicaea appears superfluous to you, or likewise the other councils of orthodox Fathers, over which presided their author, the Holy Spirit, whom a little earlier you called *Pantoscopus* [παντοσκοπος], that is, ‘bishop of all.’ In these councils the Catholic faith was so strengthened and confirmed that, if they had not been held, the faith itself which we hold—by which we confess and believe unity in Trinity and Trinity in unity—would either not exist today, or, if it did exist, would languish and fluctuate, subject to innumerable heresies.

“Therefore the Lord, knowing that much still had to be added for the restoration of the Catholic faith, after he had spoken to his disciples everything fitting for that time, added these words: ‘I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now; but when he, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will teach you all truth’ [Col. 1201A] (John 16:12–13). Your brotherhood remembers that the Lord says of himself in the Gospel: ‘I am the way, the truth, and the life’ (John 14:6). And here he says: ‘When he, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will teach you all truth’ (John 16:13).

“Behold the Holy Spirit: the love of Father and Son, the bond of both, the communion of both, the charity of both; the Spirit, I say, of the Son who is Truth, the Spirit of Truth teaching all truth, who himself, proceeding from the Son who is Truth, established the Gospel and instituted for the apostles a faith sufficient for its time. Behold: the Son, who says that he still has many things to say, promises that the Spirit himself will at the fitting time say what the Son said he still had to say.

“What else, then, do you think that this same Holy Spirit, the Spirit of Truth, taught, except what he knew the Son, who is Truth and from whom he proceeds, still had to say? He taught precisely this and nothing else: what the Son said he still had to say. For the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the mouth of Truth, which is Christ, first established the Gospel; afterwards he was present, as the author and teacher of truth—as he had been promised—at the councils of the holy Fathers. The faith which he himself had briefly established in the Gospel [Col. 1201B], he explained in the councils of the holy Fathers; and what the Son still had to say, he who proceeds from the Son truly set forth and fully taught, so that what the apostles alone could not then bear may now be borne by the whole Church spread throughout the world [Col. 1201C].

“Thus, as I said, the Holy Spirit—as he had been promised, that when he came he would teach then, now, and always all truth—was present at the councils of the holy Fathers and presided as teacher of all. Teaching the faith of the Holy Trinity which we hold, between the impiety of Arius, who separated the divine substance, and the impiety of Sabellius, who confused the persons, he gradually handed down all truth. He instituted the sacraments of the Church; arranged with fitting moderation the form of baptism instituted by the Lord; and established the rite observed by holy Church in the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood.

“He renewed patriarchs, metropolitans, archbishops, bishops, presbyters, deacons, and other lower ecclesiastical orders for divine ministry and the adornment of God’s house [Col. 1201D]. He distinguished, in a most holy and good order, chrismal anointings, the sacrament of penance, and the laying on of hands. He added the solemnities of Mass and the other divine offices for God’s praise. Through Catholic teachers, as through his own instrument, he opened to us the sacred Scriptures of the Old and New Testament—as it were raining from without. By familiar inspiration, as though by a dew from within, he made known to us divine mysteries mysteriously enclosed under the seal of the divine Scriptures [Col. 1202A]. Because he is the power of the Most High, he powerfully scattered heresies as they gradually arose. Through apostolic men he dictated ecclesiastical laws to preserve the Christian religion.

“And, to gather all into brief compass: instructing the whole Church in holy discipline, gradually teaching all truth, he illuminated it with the light of true knowledge; he still illuminates it, and will always illuminate it. For God, who does not lie, promised: ‘And I will give you the Spirit, that he may remain with you for ever’ (John 14:16). And again: ‘Behold, I am with you always, even to the consummation of the age’ (Matthew 28:20)—namely, through the indwelling grace of the Holy Spirit.

“Thus the same Holy Spirit dictated both the Gospel itself and the councils held by orthodox Fathers; and while gradually teaching all truth, he said nothing contrary to truth. Therefore you may now safely say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, since what the same Holy Spirit seems to have expressed less openly about himself in the Gospel, he afterwards plainly supplied in various councils as master of both Scriptures [Col. 1202B].”

Nechites, Archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “You have woven together the Gospel and the holy councils of the holy Fathers quite suitably, and have plausibly shown that the same Holy Spirit is the author of the Gospel and of those councils. This we also believe, and therefore we venerate those councils with equal veneration beside the Gospel. Accordingly, to tell you the truth, we and most of our learned men do not disagree with you as to the meaning of this procession [Col. 1202C]. But, as I have often said, the expression for this procession has hitherto been foreign among us. We do not shrink from the sense of ‘procession,’ because it is correct, but from the word ‘procession,’ because it is unfamiliar. Many Greek teachers also, who expounded the divine Scriptures, although they sufficiently and expressly indicated to us the same sense of this procession in appropriate words, nevertheless did not use this word ‘procession’ so clearly, nor leave it to us as a customary expression.”

## CHAPTER XXIV. That many Greek authors said that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, as from the Father.

[Col. 1202D] Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg, said: “Why do you say this? That most famous Archbishop Athanasius of Alexandria, a most vigorous disputant against the Arian heresy, perfect and most learned in the Catholic faith, in no way inferior to the wise Greeks, says thus in the creed: ‘The Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son’; and he adds, ‘proceeding.’ He plainly taught that the Spirit proceeds from both, since he referred ‘proceeding,’ just as ‘being,’ to both—especially since the Holy Spirit has being from the Father and Son in no other way than by proceeding.

“Didymus also, no small teacher among the Greeks, who produced many books, wrote three books on the Holy Trinity, and commented on Origen’s work *On First Principles*, that is, *Periarchon* [Περὶ Ἀρχῶν], leaving excellent explanations in them—this Didymus, I say, deprived of sight through an affliction of the eyes but perfectly illuminated within, plainly shows in the book *On the Holy Spirit*, which our Jerome, learned in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew, translated, that the Holy Spirit proceeds also from the Son. He says: ‘The Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of Truth and the Spirit of Wisdom, cannot hear from the Son speaking what he does not know, since he himself is that which is brought forth from the Son: that is, God proceeding from God, the Spirit of Truth proceeding from Truth, the Consoler abiding from consolation’ [Col. 1203A].

“So says Didymus. What that Truth is from which he proceeds, the creed of the Council of Ephesus, of two hundred bishops—which is also known to have been Greek—plainly determines in these words: ‘Although in his substance he is the Spirit of the Son, and is understood in personal property as Spirit and not Son, yet he is not alien from him. For he is called the Spirit of Truth, and Christ is Truth; therefore he proceeds from him in the same manner as from God the Father’ [Col. 1203B].

“Likewise Cyril, Bishop of Alexandria, in the eighth letter addressed to Nestorius, beginning, ‘To the most reverend and God-loving …’: ‘If the Spirit is in spiritual substance, or rather is understood in himself insofar as he is Spirit and not Son, nevertheless he is not alien from him. For he is called the Spirit of Truth and flows from him, just as indeed from God the Father.’

“Likewise John Chrysostom, Homily 26, *On the Holy and Adorable Spirit*, in an exposition of the creed, beginning: ‘The universal Church rejoices [Col. 1203C]. This is the Spirit proceeding from the Father and Son, who distributes his own gifts as he wills.’

[Note: Col. 1203D. Homily on the Holy and Adorable Spirit.]

“Likewise, in Homily 28, another exposition of the same creed, beginning:

[Note: Col. 1203D. The same, in the same work.]

“‘Upon the fabric of the whole Church.’ Therefore one must believe that the Holy Spirit is the Father’s and the Son’s. Likewise, we say that this Holy Spirit is coequal with the Father and the Son, and proceeds from the Father and the Son. Believe this, lest evil conversations corrupt your good morals.’

“Likewise:

[Note: Col. 1204D. The same, in the same work.]
