“‘See everywhere the mystery of the Trinity. Behold, we also believe in the Holy Spirit, who, proceeding from the Father and Son, is joined in charity.’

“Augustine also, Bishop of Hippo, legate of the province of Numidia in Africa, a distinguished man and the most eloquent African in all Scriptural learning [Col. 1203D], who attended many African councils, wrote not a few books against the heresies of the Manichaeans and Donatists, and produced many writings expounding the Old and New Testament. His innumerable volumes are read everywhere throughout the world in great authority. He himself inserted very many testimonies concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son throughout his writings.

“Likewise Jerome, Ambrose, Isidore, Hilary, and very many other teachers of the Latin tongue, as well as Leo the Great, supreme pontiff of the most extensive city of Rome, inserted much concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son in their writings [Col. 1204A]. I do not therefore set them before you with their writings, because perhaps Latin teachers among the Greeks do not have so great an authority in these times as they would have if they were Greeks. If this is so, it is by no means praiseworthy—though I say this with peace between us and you preserved. For ‘God is no respecter of persons’ (Acts 10:34), and ‘the Spirit breathes where he wills’ (John 3:8).”

Nechites, Archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “I am pleased that you have wished to bring forward our teachers. But I ask whether you, being a Latin, accept the authority of those whom you named and of our other teachers.”

Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg, said: “I deny the gift of the Holy Spirit to no Christian—Greek, Latin, or faithful Christian of any people. I despise none, reject none, and judge none to be rejected. Rather, with an open mind I receive and embrace every person who speaks rightly and writes things not contrary to apostolic doctrine [Col. 1204B].”

Nechites, Archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “I seem to myself to have found a Latin who is truly Catholic; would that such Latins came to us in these times! For if some do come, they walk in things too great and too wonderful for them, and speak to us not such things—neither so Catholic nor so humble—but proud and intolerable things. Accordingly, when our teachers wrote anything concerning the faith of the holy Trinity or the creed of faith [Col. 1204C], if, in passing and on the occasion of explaining a proposition, they said that the Holy Spirit proceeds or flows from the Father and the Son, they did not say this with the same meaning of procession or flowing as when He is said to proceed from the Father. For what proceeds from the Father proceeds properly; and because it proceeds properly, it is also properly said to proceed. But when we are found ever to have said that He proceeds or flows from the Son, this is by no means said properly, because He does not properly proceed or flow from the Father in that manner. Indeed, He properly proceeds as from Him who is the first cause and His principle; but if He is found or said at any time to proceed or flow from the Son, this is neither said nor is so proper, because what is from the Son, or proceeds or flows from the Son [Col. 1204D], is not or does not act as from a first cause. For the Son Himself also has from the Father, as from the first cause and principle, what He is, that He is Son, and that He sends forth from Himself the Holy Spirit proceeding or flowing. Therefore, as I said, the Holy Spirit is properly said to proceed from the Father as from the first cause.

“Thus the wisest among the Greeks have distinguished this procession of the Holy Spirit from both Father and Son: attributing properly to the Father the first cause of the procession, from whom the Son Himself is properly by generation, and from whom the Holy Spirit is by procession. [Col. 1205A] But to the Son they attribute the procession of that same Holy Spirit not so properly, since the Son is not from Himself and is not the cause of Himself; and therefore He is neither properly nor as first cause the cause of the Holy Spirit, so that the Spirit might properly proceed from Him as from the Father. Thus the Father is from no one; the Son is properly from the Father; the Holy Spirit is from both. Yet He is properly from the Father because the Father is from no one; but He is not so properly from the Son because the Son is not from no one, but is from the Father, and has from the Father that the Holy Spirit is from Him. Thus I grant that the Holy Spirit properly proceeds from the Father, who is from no one; but from the Son, because He Himself is from the Father, He does not proceed so properly. And this is what, as I have already said, the wisest among the Greeks have distinguished.”

## Chapter XXV. That, although the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, He is nevertheless found to proceed properly and principally from the Father, both among Latin and Greek writers.

[Col. 1205B]

Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg, said: “We do not deny that the Holy Spirit properly proceeds from the Father, because our teachers have taught us this very thing—whether they received it from yours, or yours from them. Hence our Jerome [Note: [Col. 1205] Jerome, *On the Explanation of the Faith to Cyril*, at the beginning and toward the end of the letter], expounding in his *Definition of the Catholic Faith* the Nicene Council, says: ‘We believe in the Holy Spirit who proceeds from the Father.’ Likewise: ‘We find in Scripture that the Holy Spirit is true God, and is properly from the Father.’ [Col. 1205C] And again: ‘The Son and the Spirit are properly from the Father, and truly from the Father and the Son, because He proceeds.’

“First, then, accept that the Holy Spirit is properly from the Father, Scripture saying: ‘By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of His mouth all their host’ (Ps. 32:6). And the Savior says: ‘The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father’ (John 15:26). Likewise blessed Augustine, the eminent teacher, in Book XV of *On the Trinity*, chapter 17: ‘It is not without reason that in this Trinity none is called the Word of God except the Son; none the gift of God except the Holy Spirit; and none He from whom the Word is begotten and from whom the Spirit proceeds principally except God the Father.’ The same, Book XV of *On the Trinity*, chapter 17: ‘And the Holy Spirit proceeds principally from Him from whom the Son was born. But I added “principally” [Col. 1205D] because the Holy Spirit is also found to proceed from the Son. Yet the Father gave this to Him not as already existing and not yet possessing it, but whatever He gave to the Only-begotten Word, He gave by begetting Him. Thus He begot Him, so that the common good should also proceed from Him.’

“Likewise Augustine, Book XV of *On the Trinity*, chapter 26: ‘As generation from the Father gives essence to the Son without any beginning of time and without any mutability of nature, so procession from both gives essence to the Holy Spirit without any beginning of time and without any mutability of nature.’ The same, in the same work: ‘The Son was born from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds principally from the Father, and, with the Father Himself giving without any interval of time, proceeds commonly from both.’ [Col. 1206A] And below: ‘He is not begotten from both, but the Spirit of both proceeds from both.’ Likewise, in the following chapter: ‘Nor can we say that the Holy Spirit is not life, since the Father is life and the Son is life; and therefore, just as the Father, having life in Himself, gave the Son also to have life in Himself, so He gave Him that life should proceed from Him, as it proceeds from Himself.’

“From these words of the blessed teachers Jerome and Augustine, I think it must sufficiently be granted that the Holy Spirit proceeds properly and principally from the Father as from the first cause, because He so proceeds from the Father as in the first place, since the Father does not have Him from another but from Himself. For the Father is the first cause, [Col. 1206B] and the first cause has no cause. But since the Son is not from Himself, but from the Father, He has from the Father—not from Himself—that this same Holy Spirit proceeds from Him also, from whom He Himself has being through generation. Therefore the Father is the principal author and causal principle both of generation toward the Son and of procession toward the Holy Spirit. Accordingly, although one does not read that the Spirit proceeds from the Son so properly and principally, nevertheless, just as it is true that He proceeds from the Father, so it is likewise, with every ambiguity removed, true that He proceeds from the Son. No inequality in His procession is admissible, since, as has been said, He is affirmed to proceed equally from both.

“Although the person of the Father, from whom He properly proceeds, is not the same person as the Son, from whom He nonetheless proceeds, one must by no means say that there are two distinct processions or two Holy Spirits, as there are two distinct persons, Father and Son. Rather, one must say that there is only one procession, and the procession of one Spirit, from both: because it is neither first from the Father and afterwards from the Son, but there is simultaneously from Father and Son one and the same eternal and substantial procession of the Holy Spirit. This Holy Spirit, proceeding substantially and eternally from both simultaneously and at once, constitutes the whole Trinity together with Father and Son personally—that is, by a plurality of persons.” [Col. 1206C]

Nechites, Archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “We now seem able sufficiently to agree, since neither our teachers nor yours are found altogether to differ in this view—provided the writings of those who are found to have written more carefully on this question, whether among us or among you, are rightly understood. But what do you say to this: that certain wise Greeks say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son?”

## Chapter XXVI. That certain Greeks and also Latins held that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son, adducing certain rather unsuitable comparisons.

Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg, said: “These words and whispered formulas are unfamiliar [Col. 1207A] to me; therefore for the present I have no answer to give on this point except what the Apostle warns: ‘Avoid novelties of words’ (1 Tim. 6:20). Yet let those who say this see in what sense they say it. I have indeed read in a certain book written by Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers, once a most celebrated teacher, in Book XII of *On the Trinity*, certain things similar to this. Thus Hilary himself speaks to God the Father [Note: [Col. 1207D] Hilary, Book XII of *On the Trinity*, near the end]: ‘Concerning Him and the Son, in Your Holy Spirit, who proceeds from You and is sent through Him.’ Likewise: ‘Your Holy Spirit is from You through Him.’ Likewise: ‘May I merit to worship Your Son together with You, and Your Holy Spirit, who is from You through Your Only-begotten.’ These things Hilary says, and I think they are quite to be accepted with the foregoing qualification: that the Father has this from no one, while the Son has it from the Father, and each sends forth from Himself the Holy Spirit who proceeds.

“But to say, or even to think, that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father into the Son and thus through the Son for the sanctification of creation, and does not proceed simultaneously from both, is utterly absurd. Yet some exceedingly foolish persons, theologizing foolishly on this subject, offer such an example of their folly. ‘Just as,’ they say, ‘a son of men proceeds from his father into his mother, and from his mother comes forth into this light, existing naturally from the substance of both, so surely the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father into the Son and through the Son for the sanctification of creation.’ [Col. 1207C] Those who say such things, because they are in time, speak temporally, and deceive themselves by assigning temporal things to eternal realities. For when a human son proceeds from his father into his mother, he does not then proceed from his mother into the light; and when he proceeds from his mother into this light, he does not then proceed from his father. Therefore, by drawing this inept comparison, they are themselves quite deservedly drawn into error and into the just condemnation of that same error.

“Others, stretching themselves beyond themselves toward theology yet remaining far beneath theology, devise for themselves another no less inept comparison. They say that, just as a lake is said to proceed from a spring—not from a stream, but through a stream—into which stream the water of that lake, issuing from the spring, passes and arrives at the pool; so likewise the Holy Spirit is said properly to proceed from the Father as from the supreme source, into the Son as into a stream, and then through the Son as through a stream, for the sanctification of men, as into the pool of this age. [Col. 1207D] But I marvel at and shudder at comparisons of this kind, raised from comprehensible things to incomprehensible things. Since they cannot attain to knowledge of the truth, they remain far below it; they impede the minds of those attending to them by their preoccupation, and often turn them away from right faith, because the mass of bodily creatures placed before them blocks the path of seeking truth in divine and spiritual things. [Col. 1208A]

“But just as those who walk by faith put all such things aside and cast them behind them, advance in faith by contemplative understanding, and humbly raise themselves above themselves to pass into higher things, so those who walk by reason and cling to a likeness of truth, burdened by the load of human ignorance and weighed down by the sleep of false opinion, remain behind. They deserve to remain behind faith, with reason left behind; and are unworthy to go before reason while faith leads. Therefore such ridiculous comparisons must by no means be introduced by wise men. Rather, as has, I think, been sufficiently determined above, the Catholic faith concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit from Father and Son must be maintained. And if perhaps some unusual writing is found which nevertheless, because of the authority of its author [Col. 1208B], ought to be received and read with reverence—as is that of the aforesaid Bishop Hilary, who holds great authority in the Church—then that writing, although it may seem to suggest something divergent, must be read and explained only so far as it is brought into harmony with those writings and a Catholic understanding reaches the law of charity.”

Nechites, Archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “This Hilary of whom you speak, Bishop of Poitiers, is found in ancient times to have attended many Greek councils, and he was and is held in high esteem among us. You have now produced his writings before us and cautiously defined them sufficiently. We too, whenever we find similar things in the books [Col. 1208C] of our teachers, define them by a similar qualification. For when a true proposition is established in the holy Scriptures, it is not difficult for an intelligent reader to incline words written in whatever manner toward the truth of the proposition.

“Accordingly, let your charity know that, after so many reasons have been set forth and so many authorities supplied, I and any wise Greeks stand with you in the same view concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit. Yet I do not wish you to think that we are now confessing this because in this debate of yours we have been defeated by you; for wise Greeks have always held this view. And whenever this same question has been humbly raised by wise Latins, they confessed with their mouths what they believed in their hearts; and, referring all that has been written on this question [Col. 1208D] to the law of charity, wise Latins and wise Greeks agreed together in one. But it is of no concern to us what foolish Greeks or proud Latins may say and dispute among themselves.”

## Chapter XXVII. On agreement in this question, and on removing the scandal from the midst of both peoples through the authority of the Roman pontiff by a general council.

Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg, said: “Let us give thanks to the Holy Spirit, who has willed that we should conclude this question in brotherly peace and a concordant confession, in the presence of so many men who also agree with us. Therefore nothing remains except that, as you believe, so you should teach and write without any hesitation that the Spirit proceeds from Father and Son; and that you should hold unity in the same faith with the holy Roman Church, which is the mother of all Churches and which teaches and writes this. [Note: [Col. 1209] ‘Of the same faith.’ We have emended thus, since the printed text read ‘of the same becoming.’]

“For he does not possess the charity of God who does not love the unity of the Church. Whoever disagrees with it, as blessed Ambrose, Archbishop of Milan, said, is plainly a heretic. For whoever, through presumption and obstinacy, persists when overcome by supporting reason and authority, sins without the excuse of ignorance and therefore offends more grievously. It also becomes your holiness and my humility, since we are bishops, not only knowingly to teach what we know, [Col. 1209B] but patiently to learn what perhaps we do not know.”

Nechites, Archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “Dearest brother, I embrace your humility; I admire and acknowledge the devotion which you seem to have toward the truth of faith. I cannot but be moved when you speak; I likewise assent to everything you have said, and I join you with my whole mind and body. Yet these words, ‘The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son,’ since they have not hitherto been publicly heard in the churches of the Greeks, cannot suddenly be introduced so as to be publicly taught or written without some scandal to the people or to certain less prudent persons. Rather, a general council of the Western and Eastern Church ought to be held under the authority of the holy Roman pontiff, with the consent of the most pious emperors, where these matters and certain others necessary to the Catholic Church might be defined according to God, lest perhaps you or we should run in vain. [Col. 1210A]

“Then all of us who are Christians in the regions of the East, together with the holy Roman Church and the other Churches which are in the West, would willingly receive, proclaim, teach, write, and establish for public chanting in the churches of the East, by common wish and equal agreement and without scandal to any among us, this statement: ‘The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son.’”

Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg, said: “Would that I might see this [Col. 1210B] and deserve to be present at so holy a council, where Peter, prince of the apostles, in the person of his vicar the Roman pontiff, sits together with the whole Church gathered into one, which has been entrusted to him by God; and where the Holy Spirit, of whom we have spoken, descending upon all and teaching every truth then and until the consummation of the age, may make all one in Christ with Peter and in Peter’s faith! Would that it might be so, would that it might be so, would that it might be so! May God will it, may God will it, may God will it! Glory be to God, glory be to God, glory be to God!” Others likewise cried out: “It is good, it is good, it is good. So be it, so be it, so be it!”

## Book Three. On the differing Eucharistic rite of Greeks and Latins, namely unleavened and leavened bread, and on the authority of the Roman Church.

[Col. 1209]

## Chapter I. On the conference held in the Basilica of Saint Sophia in the presence of Greek scholars.

[Col. 1209C]

Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg, said: “When in the past week we met in the place called the Quarter of the Pisans, and discussed the procession of the Holy Spirit, that same Holy Spirit, who teaches all truth, was present with us. Through our mutual conference He sufficiently taught us what we ought to think concerning Him and His procession; and, after many turnings of a non-contentious and brotherly discussion, He at last humbly brought us into the law of charity and harmony in one judgment. And since it pleased all your excellencies that we should again meet in this holy Basilica of Saint Sophia [Col. 1209D], in whose apse we now sit, just as one must believe that the same Spirit, who fills the world, is nowhere absent by His divine essence, so one must hope that He is now also present at this assembly of so many men [Col. 1210C] through His indwelling and abundant grace. For it is written: ‘Where two or three are gathered in My name, I am in their midst’ (Matt. 18:20), says the Lord.

“I see also that very many more venerable persons have assembled here, and I am greatly afraid and even ashamed to speak among so many teachers, among whom I count myself as nothing. If I say anything in my smallness, I do not know whether you will judge it worthy of praise or blame. Yet if, in the midst of teachers, I am found asking and listening, that will by no means be inglorious for me—especially since the Son of God Himself, the wisdom of God, sitting among teachers and asking and listening, offered Himself to us as an example of humility. [Col. 1210D] Indeed, I would rather say something good by asking questions than, through excessive shyness, keep silent when it is time to speak and, by keeping silent, remain ignorant of what I desired to know.”

Nechites, Archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “By the grace [Col. 1211A] of God, we brought the earlier question to its conclusion in peaceful words while preserving charity, so that it is now pleasant for us to confer with you, not in a dispute over words but in an inquiry into meanings. Therefore the presence of so many men need not frighten you, since they have not assembled here in order to bring you any accusation on any pretext, but to hear you speak with the customary gentleness of the Greeks. They heard of the question which you treated with us in the past week, and they greatly desired and still desire to hear the words of your sweetness. Whether in your questioning or your answering, they wish to apprehend something new that is good. For it is written: ‘A wise hearer will be wiser’ (Prov. 1:5).

“Far be it that anything should come from any of ours which would be unfitting to your honor or ours, or by which you might rightly be disturbed—unless this should occur in the course of discussion, which also ought carefully to be avoided. [Col. 1211B] Say, then, what you please.”

## Chapter II. That the universal Church is known to exist in three modes: by the authority of holy Scriptures, universal tradition, and particular institution.

Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg, said: “The universal Church spread throughout the world is known to exist in three modes. For whatever is maintained within it is either the authority of the holy Scriptures, universal tradition, or a particular and individual institution. The whole Church is bound by authority; it is likewise bound throughout by the universal tradition of its elders; but each Church is maintained and governed by private constitutions and particular regulations, according either to the diversity of places or to what seems good to each. [Col. 1211C]

“Thus I greatly wonder that the Eastern Church differs so much from the Western Church in the differing rite of sacrifice, in the sacraments of the altar, and in the preparation of the Lord’s body and blood—which you call the Eucharist—especially since this is a universal tradition of the elders; indeed, to say what is true and greater still, it is the inviolable institution of Jesus Christ our Lord Himself, always to be observed. For the holy Roman Church, rightly to be imitated by all Catholics, diligently uses unleavened bread in the sacrament of the altar [Col. 1211D] by ancient institution, and as mother of all Churches has handed down the same practice to all Western Churches.”

## Chapter III. That the Greeks separate themselves from the rite of the Roman Church against universal tradition, and sacrifice with leavened bread.

“The Eastern Church, separating itself from obedience to the most holy Roman Church and from unity in so great a communion, while preferring to devise something new and particular rather than maintain universal custom, wounds itself as though by the sacrilege of its own schism. In preparing the Lord’s body it uses leavened bread, and does so deliberately [Col. 1212A], as though by an ordinance of its own authority. When I say ‘deliberately,’ I mean this: a Greek is so intent upon having leavened bread in the sacrament of the altar that, should he happen not to have it and be wholly unable to obtain it, he would rather entirely abstain from the ministry of the altar than offer unleavened bread in consecrating the Lord’s body. Therefore, as I said, I greatly wonder, and I desire gladly to learn from you the reason or authority for this custom.”

Nechites, Archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “Our fathers, most religious, learned, and devout men in the divine law, who presided in this patriarchal church in which we now sit and governed this imperial city together with the whole East in ecclesiastical discipline [Col. 1212B]—whose memory is still with us and celebrated in blessing, and who also left us many writings of their sacred institutions—must not be thought to have lacked either reason or authority in this institution of leavened bread and sacramental rite. Out of reverence for them, we maintain inviolate and with due veneration the things they handed down to us, and we judge that they are not to be reconsidered by anyone, however eminent he may be in authority of office, holiness of life, or excellence of learning.

“Therefore, if the Roman Church holds or teaches that something else is to be held, it does what pleases itself. According to its own will it now chooses what it wishes, now rejects what it wishes, now approves what it wishes, now disapproves what it wishes, now establishes what it wishes, now changes what it wishes, now writes what it wishes, now erases what it wishes, now commands what it wishes, now forbids what it wishes. [Col. 1212C] In all these things it employs its own authority and finds persons to follow and imitate it, whether through good simplicity or through insufficiently instructed simplicity; perhaps this also sometimes occurs through the mere custom of obedience and sometimes through the necessity of obedience.

“But we have hitherto maintained and still maintain what we received as established and handed down by our holy Fathers; nor do we dare easily abandon it on any occasion. For if we presumptuously wished to relinquish or alter it, we would offend against the reverence for the holy Fathers, which must always be honored and never despised; we would render void the rite of the sacrament [Col. 1212D] which we have hitherto observed, as though it had been nothing and empty; and we would make ourselves blameworthy before the whole world for complete frivolity and instability. Rather, we wish to preserve and defend the finding and institution of our predecessors, and, now wearied, to recline upon the couch of so great an authority, than by further inquiry to disapprove even what is customary and labor to introduce novelties.”

## Chapter IV. That it is better to abandon an error, however long established by use, when a better reason has been considered, than obstinately to persist in it.

Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg, said: “No one should doubt that custom must yield to manifest truth, because reason and truth always exclude custom. It is better humbly to abandon an error, even though it has become customary through long use, once a better reason has been considered, than proudly to persist in it and defend it by stubborn contention. [Col. 1213A] For no one ought obstinately to contend for what he has once absorbed, but should gladly embrace anything better and more useful that he hears. Many good men are recorded to have done this.

“Cyprian, once the great bishop of great Carthage and a most precious martyr, was accustomed to baptize with a single immersion, abounding in his own judgment and considering one faith, one Lord, one immersion. But afterward, having seen a better reason, he abounded in a higher understanding by immersing three times and imitating the holy Roman Church, considering the sacrament of the three-day burial [Col. 1213B]: that the period of the resurrection is expressed when the infant is raised from the waters for the third time, and that the threefold confession reasonably requires a threefold immersion. Although a threefold immersion is rightly celebrated because of the mystery of the Trinity and the sacrament of the three-day burial, nevertheless one baptism is likewise rightly recognized because of the unity of the one faith and the one substance of the one God.

“I would not wish to hear such things from your prudence, because it is fitting neither for your religious profession nor for the honor of anyone wishing to be a Christian to speak so disparagingly of the holy Roman Church. Let it be for the moment as you have said it appeared to your eyes. Yet if I bore it calmly, you certainly ought not to be expected to bear it calmly from me. For I am a special son of the Roman Church, and I am not ashamed to be her servant; and you know this well. Therefore your prudence ought to have spared me and spoken more sparingly of her, since you knew that I could by no means patiently endure even the least injury to my mother and mistress, the Roman Church. [Col. 1213C]

“Certainly, dearest brother, I embrace with due reverence the holy Fathers who rightly governed the Eastern Church, as you do. For most of them were diligent investigators and steadfast defenders of the Catholic faith, although some who are found to have governed this imperial metropolis also are found at times to have erred greatly in faith.”

## Chapter V. On the primacy of the Roman Church; and that it was never contaminated by any heresies, but has always been Catholic.

[Col. 1213D]

“But if the authority of those who presided here has such weight among you that you consider their enactments, of whatever sort, inviolable, attending only to the bare authority of those who established them and not rather to the truth of what has been established, why do you not instead receive the decrees of the most holy Roman Church? Through God, from God, and after God, it has obtained the primacy of authority in the next place throughout the Church spread over the entire world. For this is what is read to have been decreed concerning it in the first Nicene council by the three hundred and eighteen Fathers:

“‘It must certainly be known, and no Catholic may be ignorant [Col. 1214A], that the holy Roman Church was not placed before others by any synodal decrees, but obtained primacy by the Gospel utterance of our Lord and Savior, where He said to the blessed Apostle Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build My Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I shall give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16:18–19; 18:18). The companionship of the most blessed Apostle Paul was added in the same Roman city. On one day and at one time, under Emperor Nero, he contended and was crowned with Peter by a glorious death; and both together consecrated the holy Roman Church to Christ the Lord by the shedding of their blood, and set it above all others throughout the world [Col. 1214B] by their presence and venerable triumph.

“‘Therefore, by heavenly favor, the Roman Church is the first see, dedicated by the martyrdom of the most blessed Apostles Peter and Paul. The second see is at Alexandria, consecrated also in the name of blessed Peter by Mark, his disciple and evangelist, because Mark too, having been sent by Peter, first preached the word of truth in Egypt and received glorious martyrdom; the venerable Abilius also succeeded him. The third see at Antioch likewise has honor through reverence for the blessed Apostle Peter, because he lived there before he came to Rome, appointed or established Ignatius as bishop there, and there the name “Christians” first arose for the new people. [Col. 1214C]

“‘Thus he consecrated the other sees—namely, the second at Alexandria and the third at Antioch—only by the memorial of his name. But Peter, prince of the apostles, honored the first see, which is in the most eminent and triumphant city of Rome, by the presence of his body. Moreover, the holy Roman Church, chosen by the Lord above the rest, was endowed and blessed by Him with a special privilege. By a certain prerogative it preeminently surpasses all Churches and excels by divine right. For while others at different times have been overtaken by various heresies and have wavered in the Catholic faith, she, founded and established upon the rock, has always remained unshaken. She could not be torn from the simplicity of the faith held by Simon Barjona—that is, “son of the dove”—by any false and sophistical arguments of heretics [Col. 1214D], because, by the Lord’s grant, she was always armed against deceptive questions with the shield of divine wisdom. Nor could she be shaken by any terrors or threats of emperors or powers of this age, because, strengthened by the Lord, she was secure against every attack with the shield of most steadfast patience.

“‘Therefore the Lord, knowing that the other Churches would be severely troubled by heretical assault, but that the Roman Church, which He Himself had founded upon the rock, would never be weakened in faith, said to Peter: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and when once you have turned, strengthen your brethren” (Luke 22:32). It is as if He were saying openly to him: You who have received this grace, that, while others [Col. 1215A] suffer shipwreck in faith, you may always remain immovable and steadfast in faith—strengthen and correct those who waver, and, as the overseer, teacher, father, and master of all, bear care and solicitude for all. Rightly, then, did he receive the privilege of preeminence over all, who had received from the Lord above all the privilege of preserving the integrity of faith.’”

## Chapter VI. That the Church of Constantinople was almost always troubled by being leavened with most grievous heresies.

“But the Church of Constantinople—if I may say this without offense to you and to all who sit here; for you ought not deny the truth, which, although it may sometimes be permissible to leave unspoken, may never be denied—has often, leavened by innumerable heresies [Col. 1215B], cast aside the sincerity of faith, swelled with hollow inventions against God and the apostolic Church, and stubbornly raised itself, so far as it could, against Peter’s faith and its sound teaching.

“Here flourished that detestable Arian heresy, which first sprang up in Alexandria and polluted nearly the whole East with its poisonous leaven, also drawing certain bishops from the West into itself. It said such disastrous things concerning the Son of God as: ‘There was when He was not’; ‘Before He was born, He was not’; ‘He was made from things not existing’; ‘He is of another substance or nature’; and ‘the Son of God is mutable and changeable.’ Among the chief adherents of this heresy was Eusebius, who, leaving the city of the heretics [Note: [Col. 1215D] ‘Leaving the city of the heretics.’ It should surely be read *Berytensium* [of the Berytians], as those versed in ecclesiastical history know], first desired [Col. 1215C] and obtained the Church of Nicomedia, then afterwards invaded this Church of Constantinople, infected it with the same leaven, and occupied it until his death.

“Here presided as bishop of the city of Constantinople a chief heresiarch, who spread everywhere the leaven of his heresy. He asserted that a mere man was born from the holy Virgin Mary, so as to make one person of the flesh and another of the Godhead; he did not recognize one Christ in the Word of God and the flesh, but proclaimed separately and severally one Son of God and another son of man. Here Macedonius presided, entangled in the Arian heresy, and contaminated with the same pestilential leaven all whom he could; he also asserted that the Holy Spirit is a creature. Here Eutyches, presbyter [Col. 1215D] and archimandrite, poured out the leaven of his heresy. For he confessed that our Lord was of two natures before the union; but after the union he confessed not two natures but one, thereby producing mixture and confusion. Here there were many greater and lesser followers of the Arian presumption.”

“This Eudoxius, first bishop at Antioch and afterwards, having invaded this city, its bishop, presided, having been led astray by Arian madness. Here appeared the heretic Eunomius, whom this same Eudoxius made bishop at Cyzicus after seeking to expel Eleusius. This Eunomius, that sophist, [Col. 1216A] presumed to speak profanely against God by sophistries; for he says: ‘God knows nothing more of his own substance than we do; nor is it known more to him or less to us. But whatever we know of it, he too knows in every respect. And conversely, whatever he knows, you will find unchangeably in us.’ An innumerable crowd of various heretics has also always been accustomed to spew forth here the leaven of heretical perversity.”

“Who, finally, could count all the heretics and all their errors that have existed in this city, who have leavened the holy and immaculate Church of God with false doctrines and attempted to tear Christ’s tunic by an impious schism? Either heresies arose here and were disseminated hence in every direction, [Col. 1216B] or, wherever they boiled up throughout the East, they flowed together into this city as into a bilge; and, gathered here, they made a muddy pool. Sitting in it like muddy frogs and making a din with argumentative and sophistical cries, they neither heard for themselves nor allowed others to hear what the word of truth is [Note: [Col. 1216D] *What the word of truth is.* This is the true and suitable reading, which we have printed in place of that which had entered the earlier edition: *qui . . . . fit*]. The multitude of the simple was also made drunk from this pool of heresies as from wormwood. Thus all the filth of heretical perversity has always had its dwelling here, as it were its own nest; here they mixed the leaven of their malice and wickedness, distributed it for sharing throughout the world, wherever they could, not only in words but also in deceptive writings, and from this [Col. 1216C] city, like the first and great Babylon, offered the deadly cup to emperors, kings, and princes.

“The emperor Constantius, son of the emperor Constantine the Great, drank from this cup, full of the Arian heresy, as appears in the dialogue held between him and the most reverend Pope Liberius, which Theodoret, bishop and writer of ecclesiastical histories, recorded. In that dialogue the faith of the most holy Pope Liberius—third after Julius following Sylvester—appears founded upon the firm rock, as does his admirable steadfastness. He refused to subscribe either to Arian madness or to the condemnation of Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, a great and incomparable man, although he suffered from the emperor many promises [Col. 1216D] and, as is read there, many threats. Because he was an immovable pillar, a defender of truth, and possessed the privilege of Petrine steadfastness, the same emperor ordered him carried into exile in Thrace. He was also aptly called *Liberius*, because then, with an unconstrained brow and an unconstrained voice, he confessed the truth, which is Christ.

“Therefore, while the Churches of Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, and nearly all the other Churches established throughout the East were suffering shipwreck in the Catholic faith, [Col. 1217A] Peter’s little boat alone, though battered by many waves of persecution and however violent the wind might be, suffered no shipwreck through heretical overthrow. Rather, to purge out the leaven of malice and wickedness by which heretics corrupted God’s Church, it has always laboured, both in its own person and through its legates, and labours still today. For blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, received this command from the Lord: ‘And you, once you have turned back, strengthen your brethren’ (Luke 22:32).

“Since, therefore, the most holy Roman Church, preserving the virginity of the right faith and aided by the Lord, deserved to be the mother of all Churches, all who wish to be called and to be children of God and of the Church rightly imitate her in all ecclesiastical sacraments with due humility. [Col. 1217B] Although different customs and ecclesiastical usages exist according to the diversity of each nation, and not all can conform to the Roman Church in these matters, yet in ecclesiastical sacraments, as I have said, there must never be any discord from the most sacred mother of all, the Roman Church. What then do you think? Is it safe for the Church of Constantinople not to receive, or rather, to despise, the decrees of the Roman pontiff? If you do not wish either to be or to be called children of the Roman Church, see to it yourselves; judge for yourselves. But if you wish to be called and to be children of the Church, consider what is written: ‘My son, hear the discipline of your father, and do not forsake the law of your mother, that [Col. 1217C] grace may be added to your head and a necklace to your neck’ (Prov. 1:8). In pure charity I have spoken pure truth sincerely and without any leaven of falsehood. You likewise, in that same charity—would that you would set aside the leaven—answer whatever you wish.”

Nechites, Archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “You have spoken very great and exalted things concerning the dignity of the Roman Church; but your modesty could have spoken more sparingly about the things you added concerning this Church. Yet it is fitting both for you and for me, out of reverence for those who are present and who have patiently heard you speak, that you should hear me answer with the same equanimity with which I heard you. For this is what the charity in which we meet requires.”

## CHAPTER VII. That the Greeks say that the three patriarchal sees were once sisters, among which they do not deny the primacy of the Roman Church

[Col. 1217D]

“I do not deny or reject the primacy of the Roman Church, which you set before me as so eminent. Indeed, our ancient histories state that three patriarchal sees were sisters: Rome, Alexandria, and Antioch. Among these, Rome, the most eminent seat of the empire, held the primacy, so that it was called the first see; appeals concerning doubtful ecclesiastical cases were made to it from all the others, and matters not governed by fixed rules were subject to its judgment. [Col. 1218A] Yet the Roman pontiff himself was called neither ‘prince of priests’ nor ‘supreme priest,’ nor anything of this kind, but only bishop of the first see.

“For Boniface III, a Roman by nation, bishop of the city of Rome, son of John, obtained from the emperor Phocas that the apostolic see of blessed Peter the apostle should be head of all Churches, because the Church of Constantinople at that time styled itself first of all on account of the transfer of the empire. Nevertheless, lest the Roman pontiff, the Alexandrian, or the Antiochene should teach or institute anything in their Churches that differed either from the faith or from harmony with the others, and so that all might say and preach one thing, it was established that two legates, instructed in faith and sound doctrine, should always be sent from the Roman [Col. 1218B] Church. One was to attend the Alexandrian and the other the Antiochene patriarch, diligently observing them while they stood in the *anologion* [Note: [Col. 1217D] *Anologion*: that is, a pulpit or raised platform.] and preached publicly concerning the faith.

“Likewise, two were to be sent from Alexandria: one to attend the Roman pontiff and the other the Antiochene, for the same duty. Again, two were to be sent from Antioch: one to attend the Roman pontiff and the other the Alexandrian pontiff, for the same duty. Thus whatever Catholic doctrine was preached in one of these Churches would be confirmed by the authority and testimony of the others. But if anything contrary to the faith, discordant with communion, and alien to the truth should be taught in any of these Churches, the legates [Col. 1218C] of the others were to correct it with brotherly charity and humble admonition. If they could not correct it, and the person, acting rashly and presumptuously, wished obstinately to defend his error, the matter was immediately to be brought through those same legates before the hearing of the other sister Churches. If he could be recalled to the concord of sound doctrine through canonically sent letters, that was well; otherwise, a general council was to be held concerning it.

“Now because, by the divine will, the empire was transferred to this imperial city, which became the head in the East and was called New Rome because of imperial authority, it was also decreed by the one hundred and fifty bishops who gathered in this city, when blessed Nectarius was ordained bishop of this [Col. 1218D] see, after the condemnation of Maximus the Cynic, who was infected by the contagion of Apollinaris. Then, I say, through the efforts of the most devout Emperor Theodosius the Great, it was decreed that, just as ancient Rome had from ancient times obtained from the holy Fathers primacy in ecclesiastical causes because of the honour of the empire, so this younger and New Rome should likewise hold ecclesiastical primacy after her because of the dignity of the empire; that it should be called and be the second Rome and the second see; and that it should preside over all the Churches of Asia, Thrace, and Pontus, handle ecclesiastical causes, and determine them by its own authority.

“Therefore the legates who were guardians of the Catholic faith, and who had formerly preserved the faith by reciprocal and brotherly oversight while visiting the Roman, Alexandrian, [Col. 1219A] and Antiochene Churches, were also sent to this imperial city; and likewise other legates were sent from here to them for the same ministry, so that all might say one thing and differ in no doctrine of truth.”

## CHAPTER VIII. That the Greeks say they withdraw from councils of the Roman pontiffs because the latter divided the monarchy of the Roman Empire

“Yes, dearest brother: this is what we find written in our ancient histories. But the Roman Church, whose primacy among these sister Churches we indeed do not deny, and to which we acknowledge the first place of honour when it presides at a general council, separated itself from us because of its own exaltedness when it usurped the monarchy, which was not its office, and divided the bishops and Churches of West and East by dividing the empire. Therefore, if it sometimes holds a council with the western bishops without us, let those receive its decrees and observe them with due reverence whose counsel dictates what it judges should be dictated, and with whose concurrence it establishes what it decrees should be established. [Col. 1219B]

“Although we do not differ from the Roman Church in the same Catholic faith, because in these times we do not hold councils with it, how could we receive its decrees, which are written without our counsel—indeed, without our knowledge? If the Roman pontiff, sitting upon the lofty throne of his glory, wishes to thunder at us and, as it were, cast down his commands from on high; if he wishes to judge—indeed to command—concerning us and our Churches not by our counsel but by his own decision, according to his own pleasure, what brotherhood, or even what fatherhood, could this be? Who could ever bear this with equanimity? Then indeed we could rightly be called and be true slaves, not children, of the Church. If this were necessary and such a heavy yoke threatened to be laid upon our necks, nothing would remain except that the Roman Church alone should enjoy whatever freedom it wished; it should itself make laws for all others, while itself being without law; and it would appear and be no longer the pious mother of children but the harsh and imperious mistress of slaves. [Col. 1219D]

“What then is the use to us of knowledge of the Scriptures? What of literary studies? What of the instructional discipline of teachers? What of the most noble talents of the Greek sages? The authority of the Roman pontiff alone, which, as you say, is above all, abolishes all these things. Let him alone be bishop, alone teacher, alone instructor; let him alone answer to God, as the sole good shepherd, concerning all entrusted to him alone. But if he wishes to have fellow-labourers in God’s vineyard, let him, while retaining his primacy, be exalted and glory in his humility; and let him not despise his brothers, whom the truth of Christ has begotten in the womb of Mother Church not for slavery but for freedom. For, as the Apostle says, ‘We must all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, that each may receive according to what he has done, whether good or evil’ (2 Cor. 5:10). He says ‘all’: it was the Apostle who said it; he did not except himself, nor did he except any mortal. He says ‘all,’ and he does not even except the Roman pontiff. Accordingly, [in] no creed do we find that we are commanded to confess the Roman Church specifically; rather, everywhere we are taught to confess one holy, catholic, and apostolic Church. [Col. 1220A]

“I have said these things about the Roman Church, preserving peace with you. I venerate it with you, but I do not follow it with you in all things, nor do I judge that it must necessarily be followed in all things. You have proposed its authority to us as so exalted that, abandoning our rite, we should accept its form and imitation in the sacraments without examination by reason and the authority of Scripture, and should follow it as blind men with closed eyes follow a guide, wherever it, led by its own spirit, might go before. Let wise Latins and Greeks alike judge how safe or honourable that would be for us.”

## CHAPTER IX. A commendation of the Roman Church: how exceedingly diligent it is in examining and deciding ecclesiastical cases

Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg, said: “Let not your charity be burdened if I interrupt the course of [Col. 1220C] your words. You seem to me to employ much excessive and foolish irony against the Roman Church; and so, unable to endure your mockery, I have forestalled your speech, lest you add still more useless things to things already useless. For if you knew the Roman Church’s religious devotion, sincerity, fairness, gentleness, humility, piety, holiness, wisdom, discernment, benevolence, compassion, constancy, justice, courage, prudence, moderation, purity, charity toward all, and, above all, its most diligent investigation in examining ecclesiastical cases and its most unconstrained truthfulness in rendering judgment—if, I say, you knew these things in the Roman Church by sure experience as I do—then you would never have said or even thought such things. Rather, without anyone inviting you, you would at once and of your own accord pass into its full communion and hasten to obedience to so great a holiness, in which it shines in itself, and to such fairness, by which it extends itself toward others. Nor would you listen to anyone wishing to hold you back—if, that is, you wish to be as much a lover of another’s holiness as a defender of your own custom. [Col. 1220D]

“We know, indeed, that the one hundred and fifty bishops gathered in this city under Theodosius presumptuously decreed that the Church of Constantinople, as a second Rome, should also be called and be the second see; that it should govern by its own authority the Churches of Pontus, Asia, Thrace, and those in barbarian lands; and that it should itself determine cases brought before it. We also know that all the bishops of the Council of Chalcedon, two hundred and thirty in number, wrote to Pope Leo, asking him, in deference to the emperors Marcian and Valentinian, to grant this privilege to the Church of Constantinople above the other metropolitan sees: that it might ordain the metropolitans of the provinces of Asia, Pontus, and Thrace. But the most reverend Pope Leo replied by confirming all the acts of the holy Synod of Chalcedon, while annulling and wholly invalidating only those acts undertaken through the presumptuous ambition of the Constantinopolitans, because they were contrary to the decrees of the Council of Nicaea. [Col. 1221A]

“Thus the prudence of so great a man is remarkable: you wished to advance as authority a decree—or rather, a presumption—made by the one hundred and fifty bishops in this city, particularly when the ecclesiastical rule commands that nothing presumed apart from the judgment of the Roman pontiff should have force, and that acts not ratified by him through apostolic authority and subscription should have no validity. Unless perhaps you have read that decree but have not read the apostolic letters written by the most blessed Pope Leo against the same decree, in which it is utterly annulled and rendered void as contrary to the Council of Nicaea.”

Nechites, Archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “Does it seem to you that the Lord said only to Peter, rather than to all the apostles: ‘Whose sins you remit are remitted to them, and whose sins you retain are retained’ (John 20:23)? And again: ‘Whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven’ (Matt. 16:29). On the contrary, it is believed that the Lord spoke this not to Peter alone but to all with Peter, and to Peter with all, without distinction. Nor did the Holy Spirit, sent by the Lord, descend at Pentecost upon Peter alone, though it had previously been promised equally to all the apostles; rather, it kindled all of them together and, not with an unequal gift or unequally, but with an equal gift, bestowed it alike upon all, as had been promised. [Col. 1221C]

“Let us therefore acknowledge the authority Peter received from the Lord in such a way that we do not suppose the authority of the other apostles diminished. All of them equally, without mutual prejudice or usurpation, truly meek and humble in heart, received the same Holy Spirit and, in the same Holy Spirit, received the same authority of binding and loosing. Nor does it seem right to attribute to Peter alone a privilege which the Lord himself, in giving it, made common to all. Care must be taken that the others, possessing the same prerogative in the same authority, are not deprived of their due while an authority belonging to all is ascribed to one alone. Let Peter, the twelfth among the apostles, be honoured in such a way that the other eleven apostles are not excluded from the authority of their apostleship, which they certainly received not from Peter but from the Lord himself, as did Peter, by an equal and not dissimilar dispensation.” [Col. 1221D]

## CHAPTER X. That, although the authority of binding and loosing was given not to Peter alone but also to the other apostles, and although the Spirit descended not upon Peter alone but also upon the other apostles, Peter’s primacy is nevertheless superior to all the rest

[Col. 1222A]

Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg, said: “I grant that the Holy Spirit descended not upon Peter alone but upon all the apostles, and that it was said not to Peter alone but also to all the others: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you remit are remitted to them, and whose sins you retain are retained’ (John 20:23). Yet, addressing this saying especially to Peter and appointing him, as it were, gatekeeper of heaven, he said: ‘And [Col. 1222B] I will give to you the keys of the kingdom of heaven’ (Matt. 16:19). And again: ‘Feed,’ he says, ‘my sheep’ (John 21:17). To him also, who before all others confessed and said, ‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,’ he said: ‘Blessed are you, Simon Peter, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven’ (Matt. 16:16–17). He thereby plainly taught that Peter was first instructed by heavenly inspiration in the truth of faith, which the other apostles afterward learned through his open confession.

“For the Lord Jesus entered not Andrew’s boat, nor John’s, nor James’s, nor that of any other, but Peter’s alone; sitting in it, he taught the crowds. This figuratively showed that evangelical and apostolic doctrine would flow to the multitude of peoples throughout the world from the holy Roman Church, over which Peter, prince of the apostles, was to preside. [Col. 1222C] The apostles themselves likewise recognized that a primacy had been conferred personally and principally upon blessed Peter, as appears quite plainly in the book of Luke entitled *The Acts of the Apostles*. For when a dispute arose at Antioch among certain apostles as to whether circumcision should be imposed on believers who had come from the Gentiles, a delegation was sent to Jerusalem to Peter and the other senior apostles who were with him concerning this question. When all had assembled and engaged in much debate, Peter, as one holding the primacy, rose in the midst of all and pronounced that circumcision should not be imposed on the Gentiles. By the authority given him by the Lord, [Col. 1222D] he determined what had appeared doubtful, proving it by the vision of the sheet shown to him and by the conversion of Cornelius and other Gentiles. James, bishop of Jerusalem, and all the apostles and elders present humbly acquiesced in and obeyed the same judgment.

“Peter was the elder among the apostles, firmer in faith, simpler in hearing the words of eternal life; hence he was called Barjona, that is, ‘son of the dove.’ He was readier in giving and returning answers between Christ and the apostles, and more effective in healing the sick even by the shadow of his body. After the Lord’s ascension, he received in Christ’s place that new and primitive Church. He expelled Ananias and Sapphira, who lied to the Holy Spirit and were struck dead by the breath of his mouth, from the Church and from that holy fellowship. He condemned Simon Magus with his money and, greater everywhere in virtues and miracles through the Lord’s cooperation, humbly honoured the primacy of his apostleship among the other apostles. [Col. 1223A] Therefore no one among the faithful ought in any way to doubt or question, but ought most firmly to hold, that Peter was appointed by the Lord as prince of the apostles. Just as the Roman pontiff alone, in Peter’s place, performs Christ’s office, so surely the other bishops perform the office of the apostles under Christ; they act in Christ’s place under Peter, and in Peter’s place under the Roman pontiff, his vicar. In this no derogation whatever is made from any apostle, if each person is humbly assigned his own office.”

## CHAPTER XI. That heresies which arose in Constantinople or anywhere in the East were also extinguished there

[Col. 1223B]

Nechites, Archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “What you say may be so. Yet a little earlier you said that the Church of Constantinople—indeed, almost the whole East—was contaminated by various heresies. You said this, and you said it partly truly, since I too, being a servant of truth, ought not deny the truth. But tell me, I pray: where were those heresies condemned? Who condemned them? If they arose here from wicked and unrighteous men, they were also condemned here by good and Catholic men. For when the Emperor Constantine the Great was converted to the faith and wrote laws pleasing to God [Col. 1223C] for Christians, Rome with its West and Constantinople with its East hastened to the faith by imperial decrees.

“Since a new faith, unheard by many, was suddenly being publicly preached; since in this city the studies of the liberal arts flourished; and since many wise men skilled in logic and subtle in dialectical reasoning excelled, they began to examine the Christian faith by argument, and in examining and reasoning they failed. Searching out searches and claiming to be wise, they became foolish and vain in their thoughts, because they did not humbly investigate that which they ought piously and humbly to have believed. While in the proud reasoning of human knowledge they stretched upward, they fell into the depths of unbelief. Many became heretics, made many sects for themselves, and the Christian faith was confused and torn apart, divided into many and very diverse heresies. [Col. 1223D]

“Accordingly, seeing such persons abuse secular learning and the heads of heresiarchs boil up in different places at different times, the Eastern Church, sending synodal letters everywhere and assisted by most devout emperors, held many councils. The first was at Nicaea in the province of Bithynia, where the Arian heresy was condemned and the creed of faith, inviolable for all Catholics, was composed and confirmed by the authority of the Holy Spirit and of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers. [Col. 1224A]

“Then, as time passed and various heresies followed, many other councils were held for the destruction of the various heresies and the building up of the Catholic Church. General councils were solemnly held in the Church of Chalcedon, in this Church of Constantinople, at Ephesus, Antioch, and Alexandria, for the condemnation of heretics and the strengthening of the faith and unity of all Churches. Thus, as I said, if heresies arose here, they were extinguished here also. It appears that God’s Church grew more and more in knowledge of the Scriptures through the occasion of heresies and acquired greater strength of faith after heresies had been extinguished. [Col. 1224B] Indeed, now that the Catholic faith has been defined and fully completed, the holy Fathers have rightly forbidden anyone further to dare publicly dispute concerning the faith, especially since henceforth nothing is to be taken away from or added to it. Once truth has been found, what does one who seeks further deserve to find except falsehood?

“Someone may certainly humbly investigate by questioning, so that something concerning the faith which he previously did not know may come to his knowledge; provided only that he does not contentiously call into doubt what has been defined by the holy Fathers within a certain boundary of faith. No mortal may reopen this, since it has been prohibited under a most severe anathema. Therefore let this reproach which you wished to cast upon us concerning heresies now cease, because among all wise persons the truth and virtue of the good ought to carry more weight than the lies and vices of the wicked. Tell me, I pray, where are the heretics now? They are not here; their very name is heard nowhere in the East. Rather, everywhere in the East Catholics render to God worship worthy of him in plain and sound faith. [Col. 1224C]

“Perhaps heresies did not arise in the Roman city because there were not there persons as wise, subtle, and investigative of the Scriptures as among us. And just as the vain wisdom by which those heretics among us were seduced is blameworthy, so Roman lack of learning is surely praiseworthy: they said neither this nor that concerning the faith, but with a simplicity that was, as it were, less learned, they heard others speaking and teaching about it. This seems to have occurred either from excessive negligence in investigating the faith, from the gross slowness of a dull intellect, or from the preoccupations and burden of secular impediments. For just as it belongs to learned persons either to think or speak wholly well or wholly badly, so it belongs to foolish and unlearned persons neither to think nor to speak well or badly. [Note: [Col. 1223D] *He speaks of these persons.* What is enclosed in brackets appears to have been sewn onto this passage by an unskilled and inept copyist; for it does not cohere with what precedes. [Col. 1224D] Moreover, the final clause has been brought here from Book II, chapter 21.] Of these the Apostle says: ‘Not knowing either what they say or what they affirm’ (1 Tim. 1:17). Of the former a certain wise man says: ‘It will not be useless to doubt about every individual thing.’”

## CHAPTER XII. That there is only one head of the Church on earth, namely Rome, and not two or more, as the Greeks say; and that Greek heresies were destroyed not by the authority of Greeks but of Roman pontiffs

[Col. 1225A]

Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg, said: “The Apostle says: ‘Christ is the head of the Church, and God is the head of Christ’ (Eph. 5:23; 1 Cor. 11:3). But Christ, the head of the Church, ascending on high entrusted his office on earth to Peter, prince of the apostles. Peter, following Christ’s footsteps unto martyrdom, appointed Clement as his vicar; and thus the Roman pontiffs, successively substituted in Christ’s place, are the head of the Church on earth, whose [Col. 1225B] head in heaven is Christ. Do not therefore make two or many heads in the one body of the Church, for this is altogether unfitting, unseemly, monstrous, contrary to perfection, and near to corruption in any body.

“When you say that the one hundred and forty Fathers assembled in this city decreed that Constantinople, as a new and younger Rome, ought to hold primacy in the East over all Churches and be able to determine ecclesiastical cases by its own authority, what else do you do except erect two heads in the one body of one Church, build altar against altar, and establish and renew, as it were, another Manichaean *bema*? For just as those heretics, separating themselves from the Church by heretical perversity, once erected in Africa their own *bema*, that is, a separate place for offering sacrifice, and celebrated as Easter the day on which Mani was killed, in the festival of that *bema*, with a tribunal or altar furnished with five steps, adorned with costly cloths, set in the open, displayed to worshippers, and honoured with great honours—[Col. 1225C] so you in the East, now maintaining a distinctive rite of sacrifice and setting yourselves against the Roman Church, raise the horn of singularity.

“If you think this should be done because the empire has been transferred by right, you are thereby shown to rely not on divine but on human judgment. If, because of the authority of a city—because you say the seat of imperial rule is there—you judge that the head of the Churches has also been established here, then by the same reasoning you can establish a third head of the Churches in Antioch, which is known to have been no less a seat of imperial rule. Likewise, you can establish a fourth head of the Churches in Babylon, which is the metropolis of Egypt and a seat of royal rule, provided you can add it to your empire and subject it to Christian laws. By the same reasoning you can establish a fifth head of the Churches in the great city of Baldach, said to be the seat of the great Persian kingdom, if you can conquer it and subject it to ecclesiastical laws. Thus the same reasoning for establishing ecclesiastical heads may be extended to each capital of other kingdoms, and there would no longer be one Peter, one prince of the apostles, but many Peters and many princes of the apostles. [Col. 1226A] How absurd this is, you may see; let those present, who hear both me and you, judge.

“It is therefore certain, and beyond doubt for anyone of sound mind, that just as there is one Church, so there is one head on earth of the one Church, namely the Roman pontiff. Not only the authority of human empire but chiefly the majesty of divine judgment has willed him to preside over all. All who wish to be saved in Peter’s faith under his obedience ought especially to imitate his form and institution in ecclesiastical sacraments. Thus blessed Ambrose, Archbishop of Milan, says: ‘Whoever differs from the Roman Church is without doubt a heretic.’

“You said that heresies arose here and died here, and that this happened by the authority of holy Fathers who were in the East and gathered at the Council of Nicaea and many other councils. I marvel at your prudence in ascribing to the members what belonged to the head, and in attributing to those who sat beside the presider what is known to belong to the presider. [Col. 1226B] If all those holy Fathers who attended those councils were alive today, not one of them, nor all of them together, would claim for themselves the authority of any council. Rather, they would acknowledge all conciliar authority in the Roman pontiff, either presiding in person or confirming all things through his legates. For the ecclesiastical rule, which they did not fail to know, commands thus: that councils ought not to be held apart from the judgment of the Roman [Col. 1226C] pontiff. It must therefore be understood that the heresies arose here through the error of Greeks; but although they were indeed destroyed here, they were destroyed not by Greek authority but by the authority of Roman pontiffs.”

Sylvester, bishop of Rome, a Roman by birth, ordered the Council of Nicaea to be held under the Emperor Constantine, with three hundred and eighteen bishops assembled. There, by apostolic authority, the unimpaired faith was set forth, and Arius, Photius, Sabellius, and their heretical followers were condemned. Victor and Vincent, presbyters of the city of Rome, presided over that council in the place of Sylvester, the Roman pontiff, and subscribed first. He himself also assembled two hundred and seventy-seven bishops in the city of Rome, and again condemned Calixtus, Arius, and Sabellius. Innocent, [Col. 1226D] bishop of Rome, an Albanian by birth, condemned the heretics Pelagius and Celestius. Pelagius maintained that one born of a Christian mother ought not to be born anew through baptism. Leo, bishop of Rome, a Tuscan by birth, decreed that a council be held at Chalcedon under the Emperor Marcian, where six hundred and thirty bishops assembled. There, by apostolic authority, the Catholic faith was set forth: namely, that two natures are believed to exist in Christ, those of God and of man. Eutyches the archimandrite, Nestorius, bishop of this city, and Dioscorus, archbishop of the Alexandrians, were condemned. This council was presided over by Paschasinus, bishop of Heraclea; Lucentius, bishop of the church in the city of Ascoli; and Boniface, presbyter of the holy Roman Church, vicars of Lord Pope Leo; and [Col. 1227A] they subscribed in his stead. Felix, bishop of Rome, a Roman by birth, having held a council at his own see, [Note: [Col. 1227D] “At his own see.” Baluze emended this thus, since the text was read as *in fide sua*, “in his own faith.” Below, where it reads “which is called Boezanas,” the same Baluze observed that, following Anastasius, *Boetianum* should be printed.] condemned Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, and Peter, bishop of Alexandria, because they were Eutychians. Gelasius, bishop of Rome, an African by birth, discovered Manichaeans in the city of Rome; he had them deported into exile, and burned their books before the doors of the basilica of Saint Mary. Having held a synod and sent letters throughout the East, he again condemned Acacius and Peter.

Agapetus, bishop of Rome, a Roman by birth, came to Constantinople to the Emperor Justinian and was received with honor. In the emperor’s presence he convicted and condemned Anthymus, bishop of this city, who, misled by the Eutychian heresy, refused to acknowledge two natures in [Col. 1227B] Christ. Anthymus too was sent into exile by the emperor. Theodore, bishop of Rome, a Greek by birth, condemned Pyrrhus, bishop of Constantinople. Pyrrhus had first come to Rome and, before the pope, condemned the heresies in which he had been entangled; yet, like a dog, he returned again to the vomit of his condemned heresy. The same pope, having sent legates to this city, condemned Paul, bishop of this city, because he would confess neither one nor two wills or operations in Christ the Lord. Martin, bishop of Rome, a Tuscan by birth, held a synod in the Lateran patriarchal residence with one hundred and five bishops and condemned Cyrus of Alexandria and Sergius, Pyrrhus, and Paul, patriarchs of Constantinople, who had presumed to devise novelties against the undefiled faith. [Col. 1227C] He made copies and sent them throughout all the East and West by the hands of the orthodox.

Donus, bishop of Rome, a Roman by birth, found in Rome, in the monastery called Boezanas, Nestorian Syrian monks. He dispersed them among various monasteries and established Roman monks there. Agatho, a Sicilian by birth, at the request of the most pious emperors Constantine, Heraclius, and Tiberius, sent his envoys to Constantinople for the making of unity between the Churches: Abundantius of Paterno, John of Reggio, and John, bishop of Porto; Theodore, a presbyter of Ravenna; Theodore and Gregory, presbyters; John, a deacon; and Constantius, a subdeacon. When they entered the [Col. 1227D] city, they were received with great honor on the Lord’s Day and were summoned to a procession to the holy Mother of God at Blachernae, with such honor that imperial piety even sent richly caparisoned horses from the palace for them, attended by a retinue, in order to receive them in this manner. Presiding at a synod in the basilica called the Trullus, with one hundred and fifty bishops, and representing the place of the most blessed Pope Agatho, while the emperor sat in royal splendor, they condemned Macarius, patriarch of Antioch, and his followers, who asserted one will and operation in [Col. 1228A] Christ. The emperor sent him into exile at Rome. They also decreed that two wills and two operations be affirmed in Christ. At the same time John, bishop of Porto, on the octave of Easter, celebrated the public Latin Mass in the church of Saint Sophia before the emperor and the patriarchs; and all unanimously acclaimed, in Latin voices, praises and victories for the most pious emperors.

Behold, you see that whatever heresies arose here and elsewhere were crushed and destroyed by Peter the Apostle, through the Rock of faith. Therefore, not only from the councils already mentioned, but also from many other councils held in the East, and likewise from very many African councils in which various heresies were condemned, it is evident [Col. 1228B] that the Roman Church possesses by divine gift two divine privileges: first, an incorrupt purity of faith above all others; and second, authority to judge over all. Since it is so exalted in authority, who is so imprudent as not to choose to accept its authority and its decretal enactments, and to imitate its rite in ecclesiastical sacraments? Therefore let so great an authority at last suffice for you: lay aside the use of leaven, employ unleavened bread in the sacrifice of the altar, and in this as in the other sacraments show yourself conformed to the holy and undefiled Roman Church, as a devoted son obedient to his mother.

Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, said: In this archive of Hagia Sophia we possess the ancient acts of the Roman [Col. 1228C] pontiffs and the proceedings of councils, in which are found these very statements that you have made concerning the authority of the Roman Church. It would therefore truly be no small shame for us if we denied things which we have before our eyes, written among us by our Fathers. Yet neither the Roman pontiff himself nor his envoys would have possessed any authority in any council, or in the condemnation of anyone in the East, without the consent, vote, and assistance of the orthodox bishops established throughout the East. In zeal for the faith, these bishops sometimes condemned heresies together with the Roman Church, and sometimes even without it; and they confirmed the rightness of the Catholic faith. But since you so insistently invoke the authority of the often-mentioned Roman Church, tell me, I ask you: which of the Roman pontiffs decreed that unleavened bread must be used in the sacrifice of the altar, so that necessity should compel us to adopt it, and so that, if we do not adopt it, we should incur a just condemnation?

## CHAPTER XIII. That the Greeks say they use leaven in the sacrifice of the altar by the authority and institution of the Roman pontiffs Miltiades and Siricius.

Anselm [Note: [Col. 1228D] “Anselm.” In the earlier edition this entire chapter was attributed to Nechites; we have restored it to Anselm, since no one can deny that it is his.] bishop of Havelberg said: [Col. 1229A] I confess that in the ecclesiastical books that are among us I have nowhere found this written.

Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, said: Certainly Pope Miltiades, an African by birth, decreed that on the Lord’s Day consecrated offerings should be sent through the churches from the bishop’s consecrated bread; this is what is called the *fermentum* (“leaven”). And Pope Siricius, a Roman by birth, issued a decree that no presbyter should celebrate Mass throughout the week unless he received a portion of the consecrated bread of the designated local bishop, called the *fermentum*. If the authority of Roman pontiffs seems sufficient to you against me, it ought also to suffice for me against you. You put before me the rite of sacrificing with unleavened bread, which the Roman Church has maintained by long custom; but I put before [Col. 1229B] you a writing of Roman pontiffs concerning the ancient institution of the *fermentum*. If, then, you judge me to be a transgressor of custom, I nevertheless judge you in the same way to be a transgressor of apostolic institution. Yet it is graver and more presumptuous to offend against an institution than against a custom. For the former is shown to be binding by authority and by the reason of its author; whereas the latter is maintained merely by use, wherever it arose and however it may be maintained.

For no one who has come to know the acts of the Roman pontiffs and their various enactments by reading them can doubt the decree of the Catholic Roman pontiffs Miltiades and Siricius concerning offering leavened bread. Moreover, I think more truly—and this may be inferred from the custom of certain people who certainly possessed the same authority—that in ancient times the Roman Church did not differ from the Greeks in this matter, nor the Greeks from it. Rather, both the one and the other used now leavened and now unleavened bread indifferently in the ministry of the altar, as the convenience of those making the offering advised; nor did any Greek or Latin who wished to communicate suffer scandal over this matter. This is rendered still more credible by the fact that, while a multitude of Greeks and Latins dwelt together in the city of Rome, not only Latins, but also a great many Greeks, are recorded to have presided over the holy Roman Church. Anacletus, bishop of Rome, was Greek by birth; his successor Evaristus was Greek by birth; so too were Telesphorus, Hyginus, Eleutherius, Anterus, Sixtus, [Col. 1229D] Eusebius, Zosimus, John; likewise John, son of Plato; and Zacharias, son of Polyoenus.
