All these, and very many others whose names do not now occur to memory, Greeks by birth, eminent in Christian religion and sound doctrine, are known to have presided over the Roman Church.

Do you suppose that among these Greek prelates and their Latin subjects there was a daily contentious disagreement over offering unleavened or leavened bread? That the pontiffs themselves, as Greeks, never offered anything but leavened bread, and that the Roman Church did not communicate with them in this matter at all? And again, that the Roman Church, through Latin priests, used nothing but unleavened bread, and that the Roman pontiffs likewise withdrew themselves from communion with their Latin subjects because of the [Col. 1230A] unleavened bread offered? Who could believe this? Who would dare to affirm it? How could they have been Catholic prelates if equally Catholic subjects did not communicate with them? Or how could they have been Catholic subjects if equally Catholic pontiffs did not communicate with them? How could such a Church rightly be called a Church, in which no harmony existed between prelates and subjects in communicating?

Rather, I think it must be believed that, as I have said, in antiquity all used indifferently now leavened, now unleavened bread, according to the decision of the presiding minister or of the offerer; and all scandal among communicants, Greek or Latin, was removed. Hence, even within the walls of spacious Rome, there is to this day at Saint Caesarius a community of Greek monks; and outside the walls, along the Latin Way in Roman territory, at the place called Crypta Ferrea, there is another such community of Greek monks. These still, as I have reliably learned, offer leavened bread. This occurs without scandal to the Roman pontiff or to the Latins among whom they live and with whom, in mutual communion, they communicate.

## CHAPTER XIV. That it may be believed that the apostles and their successors used now unleavened and now leavened bread indifferently; and that the Western Church gradually abandoned one entirely, while the Eastern Church abandoned the other.

[Col. 1230C] I think that the apostles of Christ themselves did this: in the consecration of the Lord’s body, according to the rite they observed at that time, when the Church was being born, they must be believed to have used now unleavened and now leavened bread. For as they travelled through various provinces preaching the Gospel, whenever they turned aside to a Church of Christians and wished to offer the holy sacrifice to the Lord for the brethren’s communion, it seems quite credible that they did not seek leavened bread or unleavened bread over-zealously—or even, if I may venture to say it, over-curiously. Rather, whatever lay ready to hand, whether the one or the other, they offered devoutly without distinction. I think that this manner of offering or communion was handed down in ancient times [Col. 1230D] by the apostles both in the Roman Church and in all other Churches, although no definite Scripture tells us so.

But the same Roman Church gradually laid aside one, namely leavened bread, and adopted only the other, namely unleavened bread; and it did this on its own authority. The Eastern Church likewise gradually abandoned the other entirely, namely unleavened bread, and chose only the other, namely leavened bread. Yet on this account neither the wise Greeks of old nor the wise Latins of old thought one another deserving of contempt. Although they were less uniform in this matter, they nevertheless loved and cherished one another faithfully in Christ, with mutual peace and brotherly charity; and, without mutual condemnation, whenever it was appropriate, they held councils together.

[Col. 1231A] Now the modern rashness of certain Latins, exalting themselves above themselves, arose, according to the account of history found in the *chronicles*, that is, the annalistic books, about [before] three hundred years ago. That rashness often stirred up many scandals between Latins and Greeks. For at that time a certain Charles, king of the Franks, arose; he violently seized the Roman Empire and caused himself to be called patrician of the city of Rome. In his time the monarchy was divided—or rather torn apart—against the majesty of the Empire. From this there arose no few scandals between Latins and Greeks, not only through diversity in imperial arrangements but also through difference in ecclesiastical rules.

Thus, when the Latins revile our leavened bread, judge it unworthy of the sacrifice [Col. 1231B] of the altar, call us heretics from the arrogance of their self-exaltation rather than from an assertion of truth, and exclude us from their altars and refuse communion with us, we too, provoked by them and replying to them in equal measure, care nothing for their unleavened bread, judge it unworthy of the sacrifice of the holy altar, call them not “unleavened-bread heretics” (*azymitae*) from arrogant pride but in the name of just retribution, exclude them from our altars and refuse communion with them. As they put us to shame, so we put them to shame with an equal balance; and whatever sin we commit in this matter, we do under grave provocation.

But if they wished to restrain themselves from such reproaches, to walk with us in brotherly charity [Col. 1231C] and not to tread upon us from the height of their power, we would indeed rejoice with great joy. We would not only cease from this foolish reply, but, judging none of them and excluding no one from the right of our communion because he thought differently, we would gladly render due reverence with the most willing spirit of brotherly charity, and, in accordance with the Apostle, anticipate one another in fitting honor.

But the proverb is true: “Where foolish provocation comes first, an unworthy reply follows not undeservedly.” It should always be considered, and not readily forgotten, that the authority of the Greeks was once so great among learned Latins that even the names of ecclesiastical [Col. 1231D] offices and solemnities were arranged under Greek names, as they are still called today in the Roman Church itself and throughout the West: patriarch, metropolitan, archbishop, bishop, chorepiscopus, presbyter, deacon, subdeacon, acolyte, exorcist, canon, cleric, abbot, monk, church, monastery, cenobites, hermit, basilica, baptism, exorcism, catechumen, Epiphany or Theophany, Hypapante, Parasceve, Pentecost. From this it is plainly evident that the Greeks, from whom the Latins themselves long ago received the names of ecclesiastical dignities and solemnities, must not be regarded as possessing a negligible authority—since the Latins were then as wise as they are now, or wiser.

## CHAPTER XV. That the authority of many Roman pontiffs ought to prevail more than that of two; that one synod may annul another; and that Popes Miltiades and Siricius seem to have legislated not concerning the host, but concerning *eulogiae*.

[Col. 1232A]

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, said: If you judge the decree of Pope Miltiades and Pope Siricius concerning *fermentum* to be observed because of the authority of those who decreed it, then much more must be observed what is known to be frequently practiced in daily use by very many Roman pontiffs, and to be customary by celebrated observance in all Churches, both at Rome and throughout nearly the whole world. I said “nearly,” [Col. 1232B] however, only because of you Greeks, those who live in Pontus and Thrace, certain people in Asia, and the Ruthenian people, who, like unlearned persons ignorant of all divine Scriptures, imitate your rite as irrationally as they do simply, because they are your neighboring inhabitants and bear the yoke of this empire in servile fear.

Yet, if the aforesaid popes perhaps decreed by the authority of the apostolic see that something must be observed in their own times, was it not equally lawful for very many pontiffs, exercising the same authority of the same apostolic see over which they too presided, to change it reasonably for the better as the Church grew and daily advanced toward greater discernment? If you consider the authority of the apostolic see in two persons, know that the same authority prevails in many. For greater is the authority of very many holy Fathers who say and do what is good than that of two who exercise the same authority, even though those two are good, say what is good, and do what is good.

Furthermore, as you know, one synod sometimes annuls another because a better reason has been considered; sometimes from necessity, sometimes from utility, sometimes from the circumstances of the times. All this is done according to the discernment of those set over the Church, whom God has willed to preside over his Church then or now, and to whom he has entrusted the keys of discernment and authority in every divine work, while the foundation of the Catholic faith always remains safe and unmoved.

Moreover, as I think more truly, this decree [Col. 1232D] of the Roman pontiffs Miltiades and Siricius seems to be understood not of a leavened host, but rather of the *eulogiae*, which are ordered to be distributed through the churches every Lord’s Day. As for what you said about the harmony of the wise Latins and Greeks of old, among whom, as you maintain, there was no scandal in offering unleavened or leavened bread: I do not dislike what you say. Nevertheless, I think the judgment of my elders, and especially of the Roman pontiff, must be awaited on this question. For not my own judgment, but theirs, ought to please me—those to whom authority has been given from above to judge both me and my judgment. We ought to imitate not only diligence in teaching, but also modesty in learning.

## CHAPTER XVI. That Constantinople and the entire Eastern Church were under the obedience of the Roman Church, and ought rightly to be so, and ought to imitate it in the sacramental rite.

[Col. 1233A]

Further, as to your complaint of the modern and almost novel rashness of the Latins against the Greeks, do not be surprised. Since all histories relate and prove that in antiquity you were under the obedience of the Roman Church, which is Latin, you have now, not very long ago, despised the sweet yoke of obedience and rejected the subjection which your ancestors humbly rendered to the Roman Church. You, wise in your own eyes and thinking lofty thoughts of yourselves, have done this. It is therefore no wonder if they are angered with you and criticize your rites, lamenting that you have withdrawn from their [Col. 1233B] obedience to your own harm.

And as to your almost boastful assertion that the Latins have Greek terms for ecclesiastical dignities and solemnities: do you suppose, I ask, that the Latins sent here to the Greeks in order that Greeks might invent such names for them, as though they were unskilled, deficient in Latin speech, and unable to form them? Please do not think so. Rather, the ancient Greeks frequented mighty Rome as mistress and head of the world; they were subject to its empire, as were the other nations throughout the world, and rendered due reverence and obedience to the Roman pontiff. The holy and praiseworthy humility of the Roman Church gladly admitted their counsels, both in arranging ecclesiastical names and solemnities and in many other matters, [Col. 1233C] because they were wisely humble and humbly wise.

Italy too was anciently called Greater Greece, as writers of ancient histories say. In the city of Rome, the speech of both languages was commonly in use and vigorous; Latins in turn used Greek, and Greeks Latin, and neither language was foreign to Rome’s inhabitants. Thus it seems to have happened that some things in the Church are called by Latin and others by Greek names. Hence it was also instituted in the Roman Order that, at the solemnities of Mass on the highest feast days, the readings and Gospels should be recited in Latin and Greek, because both peoples, educated in both languages, were present. [Col. 1233D] Would that modern Greeks were as humble and obedient to the Roman Church as those Greeks were! How gladly—how gladly, I say—the Roman Church would even today admit their counsels and, according to its customary humility, listen to their wisdom! For it was never so proud or envious as arrogantly and contentiously to insist excessively even on its own institutions, whatever their character; or enviously to disparage or oppose the institutions of others, provided that they were good.

This is evident because its own institutions were often changed when better institutions were added above them, and it humbly adopted the good institutions of others for imitation. For example, the bells of the Church, which were first invented in Campania near the city of Nola—whence they are called *nolae* or *campanae*: the Roman Church adopted this because it is good, and did not despise it because it was another’s invention. The Greeks, by contrast, wise in their own judgment, abounding in their own opinion, wise in their own eyes, and considering themselves self-sufficient, have always been accustomed to glory in their own inventions, whatever they may be, while enviously disparaging the ordinances of others, however good. They assert that what is theirs is good because it is theirs, and that what is not theirs is not good because it is not theirs. Against them the Apostle says: “Not that we are sufficient to think anything of ourselves as from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Cor. 3:5). Yet he also says of himself, [Col. 1234B] humbly as well as confidently: “I think that I too have the Spirit of God” (ibid.).

Thus the Latins use now Latin and now Greek terms in ecclesiastical orders: in Greek, *episcopus*; in Latin, *pontifex* (“bishop”). In Greek, *presbyter*; in Latin, *senior*, that is, “priest.” In Greek, *diaconus*; in Latin, *minister* (“servant”), as translators’ diligence has rendered terms from Greek into Latin, from Latin into Greek, or from Hebrew into Latin or Greek.

Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, said: Enough has been said by both sides concerning the authority of the Roman Church. But since you said that, after a better reason had been considered, apostolic authority enacted and commanded—or handed down—the use of unleavened bread universally to all Churches, I should now like to hear the reason [Col. 1234C] why this was done: why the use of leaven, instituted by Pope Miltiades and Pope Siricius, was abolished, and the use of unleavened bread was instituted and handed down by other apostolic men. If the reason you promise is added to the authority already advanced, what you endeavor to assert will seem more credible. And if, as I have said, reason and authority support one another, what remains except that all of us immediately agree with your assertion and, laying aside the leaven that two seem to have instituted, agree with the many who have established something else above it, and adopt unleavened bread?

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, said: I would not readily accept as having suddenly persuaded me what you think I said so casually—namely, that the Roman Church once used leavened bread and, after laying it aside, adopted unleavened bread. But because you advanced the decree of Pope Miltiades and Siricius, I had to answer you with what I thought on this point, led by a reasoning that is not false, though preserving the authority of such great Fathers. Therefore now attend to the reason why our unleavened bread ought rather to be used than your leavened bread in the sacrifices of the altar.

## CHAPTER XVII. That Christ consecrated unleavened bread at the Lord’s Supper; and that nowhere in the Old Testament is leavened bread commanded to be offered, but unleavened bread.

Our Lord Jesus Christ, who came into this [Col. 1235A] world to save sinners and who presented himself as the pattern of all truth, must himself be believed first to have had unleavened bread in the consecration of his most sacred body. He distributed it to his disciples and left them its form to imitate and to perform in remembrance of himself. For, in distributing the sacrament, he said: “Take, this is my body” (Luke 22:19); and, in instituting the form of the sacrament, he said: “Do this in remembrance of me” (ibid.).

He said “this” because of the error of certain people who do not think that the same body is consecrated in the sacrifice of the altar which he consecrated at the Paschal Supper and handed to his disciples. Instead, adhering far too foolishly to the subsequent words, “in remembrance of me,” they think that he instituted only that the sacraments of the altar should be celebrated merely in remembrance, and not in the reality of that same body. “This,” he says, “is my body; do this” (ibid.): do this—that is, consecrate that very body, not merely in remembrance but in the pure reality of the body itself. And when he said, “in remembrance of me,” he intended this to be understood: that the sacrament of the true body ought to be celebrated by the faithful for no other purpose but simply in memory of his Passion and for the salvation of souls. Thus the Apostle says: “As often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you will proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Cor. 11:26).

It must therefore be believed that Christ at the great Paschal Supper had only unleavened bread and handed that which he had consecrated into his body to his disciples, [Col. 1235C] because he himself said of himself: “I have not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5:17). But the Law says in Exodus, which in Hebrew is also called *Hellesmoth*: “In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month at evening, you shall eat unleavened bread until the twenty-first day of the same month at evening. For seven days leaven shall not be found in your houses. Whoever eats leavened bread, that soul shall perish from the assembly of Israel, whether a stranger or a native of the land. You shall eat no leavened thing; in all your dwellings you shall eat unleavened bread” (Exod. 12:18). Since, therefore, during those seven Paschal days no leavened bread was found in any house of Israel but only unleavened bread, and Christ had come not to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, it is clear that at the Paschal Supper, when he consecrated his body, he had unleavened bread and consecrated it: thus bringing the old Passover to completion and initiating the new Passover. For whence could he have obtained leavened bread, which in all houses of Israel during those seven days was forbidden by the Law, prohibited and forbidden both to strangers and natives under a definite penalty of condemnation? Unless perhaps you wish to devise for yourself the opinion that, as Almighty, he then created new leaven for himself to complete this sacrament. But this plainly runs contrary not only to the Gospel but to all probability.

[Col. 1236A] Does this reasoning seem sufficient to you? Let Christ, the author of this sacrament, whom one must imitate in all things, suffice for you as example and model. If his authority is insufficient for anyone, let him seek another person with whom to speak; for I wish, as the Apostle directs, to avoid him as a heretical person after the first and second admonition (Titus 3:10). Let your charity consider this: nowhere in the Old Testament is leavened bread commanded—or even permitted—to be offered in the Lord’s sacrifice. Indeed, it is altogether forbidden and, as unacceptable to God, is everywhere prohibited by the Law from being offered.

For it is written thus in Leviticus (2:11), which is also called *Vaicra* in Hebrew: “Every offering which is offered to the Lord shall be made without leaven; neither any leaven [Col. 1236B] nor honey shall be burned in the Lord’s sacrifice.” Again, in Leviticus (7:11): “This is the law of the peace offering: if the offering is for thanksgiving, they shall offer breads without leaven, mixed with oil; and unleavened cakes anointed with oil; and fine flour baked.” Again (Num. 6:13): “This is the law concerning consecration: when the days which a person had appointed by vow are fulfilled, he shall offer an offering to the Lord: an unblemished lamb for a whole burnt offering, an unblemished ewe of one year for sin, an unblemished ram as a peace offering, and also a basket of unleavened breads mixed with oil and cakes without leaven anointed with oil.” Again (Lev. 6:14): “This is the law of the sacrifice and the libations. The priest shall take a handful of the fine flour mixed with oil and shall burn it on the altar as a most sweet odor; but Aaron with his sons shall eat the remaining part of the flour without leaven, and shall eat it in the sanctuary. It shall not be leavened, because a portion of it is offered as incense to the Lord; and it shall be most holy.” Again, in Exodus (23:18): “You shall not sacrifice the blood of my victim upon leaven.” Again (29:2): “You shall take unleavened loaves and a cake without leaven, mixed with oil, and cakes spread with oil” (Lev. 24:5). Likewise, the twelve loaves of presentation, baked from pure fine flour, which were placed six on each side before the Lord upon the most pure table and changed every Sabbath—no one with even some acquaintance with that Scripture can doubt that they were unleavened.

[Col. 1236D] You see, therefore, by how evident a reason and how firm an authority it has been established that unleavened rather than leavened bread ought to be used in the sacrifice of the altar. Everywhere the leaven of corruption is rejected and forbidden from sacrifice; everywhere the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth is approved, and by its offering God is made propitious to the people.

Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, said: You have presented the reason you promised sufficiently fittingly and plausibly, supported as it is by great authorities. I too do not dare deny what is plainly true, lest I suddenly assume the conspicuous face of one ashamed and blushing, lose the countenance of calmness, take on the disgraceful expression of confusion, and [Col. 1237A] be caught in a lie while laboring contentiously against what is true. For one who speaks truth does not labor, whereas one who speaks falsehood speaks from himself. Let what you have said, then, for the moment be true. Yet in the Gospel we read: *Εὐλόγησεν ἄρτον*, that is, “he blessed bread.” Since it says *ἄρτον*, [Note: [Col. 1237] “It says *ἄρτον*.” This is certainly the correct reading, not, as in the earlier edition, *arton, id est panem*—“arton, that is, bread.”] it seems to mean bread simply: ordinary bread, namely leavened bread, which people universally use and which they call *ἄρτον*, “bread,” in customary speech. But if they wish to speak specifically about unleavened bread, they do not use the word *ἄρτος*, “bread,” at all; rather, they use the distinct expression meaning “unleavened bread.” For Greek *ἀ-* means “without” in Latin, while *ζυμός* means “leaven.” Thus I too understand “leavened bread” in its simple, ordinary sense when I read in the Gospel: *Εὐλόγησεν ἄρτον*, that is, “he blessed bread.”

What concern is it of mine that I should write or read there, *Εὐλόγησεν ἄζυμον* (“he blessed unleavened bread”), when the Evangelist has written *Εὐλόγησεν ἄρτον*, which plainly seems to mean ordinary bread? Again, what you introduced from the Old Testament, demonstrating that leavened bread may nowhere be offered in sacrifice, appears to be a very acute observation; yet I can by no means deny it, and it is, I confess, a weighty argument for your assertion. But it seems to me that the same Leviticus of the Old Testament contains a reference to the offering of leavened bread, where Moses says to the children of Israel: “You shall therefore count from the day after the Sabbath on which you offered the sheaves of firstfruits, seven full weeks, until the day after the completion [Col. 1237C] of the seventh week, that is, fifty days; and thus you shall offer a new sacrifice to the Lord from all your dwellings: two firstfruit loaves from two tenths of leavened fine flour, which you shall bake as firstfruits to the Lord” (Lev. 23:15). Here leavened bread plainly seems to have to be offered to the Lord—unless there is some interpretation which compels us to understand this otherwise than it appears to be written.

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, said: “Thus I believe that Holy Scripture must be read: it never disagrees with itself, but always agrees with itself. And this ought to be the earnest endeavour of a prudent reader: [Col. 1237D] that he may then know that he has rightly understood the Scripture of the divine law when he has brought it into harmony with the other Scriptures and with the law of charity. For such an offering as this—in which two loaves of firstfruits are offered, from two tenths of leavened fine flour—has nothing at all to do with the order of those things specially offered to the Lord. For it is neither made upon the altar, nor in the place of the sanctuary, nor within the Holy of Holies; nor is it made by any rite belonging to the other offerings. Rather, when the priest has received from the offerer the loaves of firstfruits of leavened fine flour, and has lifted them up before the Lord in thanksgiving for the fruits of the earth, he does not there offer them by any rite of oblation; [Col. 1238A] instead, they immediately pass wholly into the use of the priest himself.

“Therefore, dearest brother, that you may know I have spoken truly, investigate most carefully, and nowhere will you find in the Law that leavened bread is to be offered to the Lord in sacrifice; rather, always unleavened bread or the purest fine flour, without any leaven. Accordingly, in conformity with this form of offering—which the Lord everywhere instituted in the Old Testament, and by which he willed to be propitiated for his people—we must believe that the Son of God himself, who knows best how God the Father is to be propitiated, also used unleavened bread in the consecration of his most sacred body. Thus he neither abolished the figure of the Law in offering unleavened bread, nor failed to fulfil and bring to completion the truth of that same Law in consecrating his true body.”

## CHAPTER XVIII. That leaven is nowhere taken in a good sense in Holy Scripture; and that it is less suitable for handling with due care.

[Col. 1238B]

“Accordingly, throughout all Holy Scripture your leaven is nowhere found taken in a good sense, as our unleavened bread is. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel of Luke (chapter 12:1): ‘Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy.’ Likewise, in the Gospel according to Matthew (Matt. 16:6): ‘Look to it and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.’ Likewise, in the Gospel according to Mark (chapter 8:15): ‘Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and [Col. 1238C] the leaven of Herod.’ And the Apostle says: ‘Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened. For Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed. Therefore let us keep the feast, not with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth’ (1 Cor. 5:7).

“Furthermore, if you consider rightly, your leaven is by no means as suitable for reverent handling as our unleavened bread. This was handed down to us through Moses, who was faithful in all God’s house and who ordered everything according to the pattern of those things which he saw on the mountain, and finally through Christ himself. For leavened bread, when it is handled, broken, and distributed, very easily crumbles into many fragments; and it cannot be guarded so carefully, nor [Col. 1238D] altogether without negligence, as it ought. Since even the smallest particle, so to speak, is the true and entire body of the Lord, anyone guilty of however slight a negligence concerning it incurs the Lord’s grave curse, as it is written: ‘Cursed is the man who does the work of his God negligently’ (Jer. 48:10).

“But our unleavened bread, chosen by God the Father in both Old and New Testament, and approved and consecrated by God the Son through the most holy consecration of his body, is firm, pure, valid, unstained, incorrupt, not porous, not puffed up, not soft; it does not easily break into the tiniest fragments. [Col. 1239A] Rather, it is in every respect manageable and most suitable for consecrating, breaking, and distributing with every care. It is also reverently prepared among religious Latins by the hands of deacons, from selected grains and the cleanest fine flour, in the sacristy for the future host, with the chanting of psalmody; and it is kept under careful guard until the time of sacrifice. Therefore, when reason, authority, and the suitable practical character of the sacramental host itself have been considered, it ought plainly to be evident to all Greeks living throughout the East that unleavened bread should be used rather than leavened.”

## CHAPTER XIX. That because of their long use of leaven, the Greeks cannot readily pass to unleavened bread; but that, after a general council has been held, they may adopt either practice quite indifferently, once the scandal to both peoples has been removed.

[Col. 1239B]

Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “I have seen and learned this use of leavened bread in the churches of the East from the beginning, and I know that it has been handed down from our predecessors. I revere the usage, so long established, of so great a Church; I do not dare rashly to judge it, nor do I see that it can easily be changed. Yet this is what I think and say personally, and I believe that all learned Greeks do not differ from my judgment.

“If, therefore, I should happen to be somewhere where I could have no leavened bread whatever, but unleavened bread were at hand and prepared, and I wished to sing Mass and offer to the Lord the sacrifice of the altar, [Col. 1239C] I certainly would not shrink from unleavened bread. Rather, I would confidently consecrate it for offering to God as an immaculate sacrifice, receive communion faithfully, and, if Greeks happened to be present, give it to them for communion—provided that it were a day of public communion, whether Easter or any other solemnity on which the Church customarily receives communion universally by established rule. On such days no Christian may withdraw himself from communion at the altar, unless perhaps he has been excluded because bound by public penance.

“But because the weak-minded are more numerous than those instructed and steadfast in faith, and the crowd which does not know the law of discernment is very easily scandalized, it would be worthwhile for all Latins and Greeks to labour most earnestly in the Lord, [Col. 1239D] so that, gathering together in one place at a fitting time, they might hold a general council and either all universally adopt in uniform fashion the rite of unleavened bread, or all universally the rite of leavened bread. Or, if either course could not universally be taken without the slightest—or without excessive—scandal to the other party or people, at least they should agree upon this: that neither should these rashly judge those on account of unleavened bread, nor those these on account of the leavened bread which they customarily use. Instead, they should mutually grant one another peace, and holy charity should not be destroyed on this occasion—a charity which, to the grave danger of both peoples, is seriously weakened among both.

“For although, according to the authorities and arguments set forth above, and also according to the rite of the sacrament itself, [Col. 1240A] as you have said, an unleavened host seems rather to be the one that should be offered; nevertheless, because the Greeks’ long-standing use has long prevailed for the leavened host, and because changing it seems impossible without the greatest scandal to the multitude—indeed, to the whole people—it is rightly judged that what has so long been customary among us should be permitted. This is especially so because both the leavened host and the unleavened host are equally bread. Though they differ in form, there is no difference of leaven or unleavened bread in the substance of bread; and, while the integrity of faith is preserved, either seems capable of being offered in a sufficiently catholic manner. This is especially true because the living bread which came down from heaven (John 6) can fittingly be figured equally in either.

“Let, therefore, the destructive scandal of discord between the two peoples be removed; and in offering unleavened or leavened bread there will be no danger to right faith, [Col. 1240B] because, as I have said, with sound faith the host of the Lord our Saviour Jesus Christ can lawfully be made from either, for the salvation of those who believe and faithfully offer it, and not for the salvation of those who contend wickedly. For it is written: ‘God is a God of peace and not of dissension’ (1 Cor. 14:33). And from on high the angels announce: ‘On earth peace to people of good will’ (Luke 2:14).

“For the sacred host, whether leavened or unleavened, made from many grains gathered into one, signifies the whole people of the Church gathered into one and the same charity in Christ. Anyone who separates himself in any way from brotherly charity, which is in Christ Jesus, [Col. 1240C] participates in that host only at great danger to himself, however secure he may think himself.

“Indeed, the rash perversity of unjust judgments by which we devour one another seems a greater sin than the diversity of sacraments over which we disagree. For the latter, as I said above, seems capable of being done in the Lord with sufficient indifference. But the former—namely, the rash prejudgment of those who maliciously disagree with each other—is never permitted to any Christian. God is offended by discord, as by a sin full of evil; but he is appeased by the saving host, as by perfect devotion. The former sharply accuses those to be condemned; the latter profitably excuses those to be saved. The former provokes God the Judge by offending him; the latter appeases the merciful God by propitiating him. The former sends to hell; the latter to the heights above. Through the former we are alienated from God; [Col. 1240D] through the latter we are incorporated into God. Through the former we become earthly; through the latter heavenly.

“Whatever, therefore, may be the case regarding the diversity of the sacred offering, all must have recourse to unity in charity. For, just as charity in the sacred offering, so the sacred offering in true charity, covers a multitude of sins. And just as the saving host does not effect salvation without charity, so perfect charity is not scandalized by the diverse offering of that same host. In the absence of this charity all other goods are possessed vainly; in its presence some goods may be lacking without mortal fault.

“Therefore, if a general council should be held after consultation with all, with the most pious emperors supporting it, and it should happen that my insignificant person were present, [Col. 1241A] I would plainly and confidently say these very things before everyone. I would fear neither Greek nor Latin in this judgment, and with due humility and reverence I would admonish the gentleness of the Roman pontiff, that, with his help, every occasion of hostility and discord might be removed and we all might become one in the observance of the sacraments, as we have always been one in the catholic faith.

“And I hope that he would patiently hear my humble admonition, as Peter, though prince of the apostles, once humbly heard Paul steadfastly rebuking him. There both the constancy of Paul, rebuking confidently and justly, is commended, and the humble patience of Peter, enduring in meekness, is highly praised—although I am far inferior to Paul, and he ought not to be inferior to Peter. [Col. 1241B] Thus it might indeed happen that the Roman pontiff, Latin to the Latins, Greek to the Greeks, and made all things to all, would gain all, and by the humble authority of the Apostolic See would harmonize all the matters over which we disagree: either by abolishing one practice altogether and universally establishing the other, or by removing the scandal of both and restoring both practices indifferently.”

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, said: “Enough seems to have been said on this question, but something still remains which I should like to learn from your prudence.”

## CHAPTER XX. On the mixing of wine and water in the chalice, which Greeks and Latins do differently.

[Col. 1241C]

“Tell me, then, why you do not offer in the sacrifice of the altar wine and water poured and mixed together in the chalice. Why do you consecrate unmixed wine without water? For after unmixed wine, when offered, has been sacrificed, only then do you pour plain and unconsecrated water into the chalice and mix it with the most sacred blood; and so you receive communion. By what reasoning, I ask, do you do this?”

Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “It is not recorded that Christ consecrated water mixed with wine in the chalice at that great supper of his which is especially called the Lord’s Supper. Therefore we likewise follow its pattern; and we have no greater reason than imitation of the Saviour himself.”

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, said: [Col. 1241D] “Although nothing explicitly concerning water is written in the Gospel, so that it is read there either as having been added or as not having been added, nevertheless it does not seem absurd to understand that Christ himself sacramentally consecrated wine mixed with water, according to the custom of the Jews and Palestinians, who always drink wine mixed with water. If you say that it is rash to affirm that the wine at the Lord’s Supper was mixed with water because this is not read in the Gospel, I nonetheless say that it is rash to affirm that water was not added to the wine there, since that too is nowhere read in the Gospel.

“And if you think it incautious to say something which that Scripture nowhere says about the matter, why do you not likewise think it incautious to deny what that Scripture [Col. 1242A] nowhere denies about the same matter? I do not contentious­ly affirm that the wine in the Lord’s chalice was mixed with water; but neither ought you contentious­ly deny it, especially since evangelical authority neither affirms nor denies either alternative. In doubtful matters nothing should be affirmed rashly, and nothing rejected indignantly. Therefore, when you affirm something, beware of rashness; and when you reject something, beware of indignation. For just as rashness in affirming is presumptuous, so anger in rejecting is usually quarrelsome. Both must be most prudently avoided by those who investigate truth.

“Yet since, as the Gospel expressly says, blood and water came forth from the Lord’s side on the cross [Col. 1242B] (John 19) for the redemption of our salvation, it seems right that wine and water mixed in the chalice should be offered in remembrance of the Lord’s Passion and for the forgiveness of our sins. Thus, in the blood of the new and eternal covenant, the water which signifies the people may not be absent: the people who are redeemed and saved in communion with that same blood of the new and eternal covenant, and are incorporated, united, sanctified, and offered as one body of the Church with their head, who is Christ. For it is written: ‘Many waters are many peoples.’

“For this reason Latins offer wine and water mixed together in a single chalice, so that the blood of Christ may be signified by the wine and Christ’s people, which is the Church, by the water; [Col. 1242C] and so that they may be sanctified not separately or singly, as though divided, but mixed together, as though into one body. But when you offer unmixed wine alone without water in the chalice, you no longer sanctify the Church, which is Christ’s body, together with Christ its head; rather, you offer Christ alone, the head of the Church, consecrated without the members. This indeed seems to lack all reason. And what is consecrated is rightly said to be consecrated not singly but together.”

Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “As you have said: ‘Many waters are many peoples.’ But we, following the pattern of the Lord’s Supper, offer unmixed wine alone in the chalice, which through divine operation and power, and through the ministry of the priest, [Col. 1242D] is consecrated as the blood of the new and eternal covenant. Afterwards, fittingly and reasonably, we add water to it, so that the people, not sanctified in themselves, may be sanctified by the union through which they are united to the blood already consecrated. Thus, in the consecration of unmixed wine, we celebrate with due reverence and deepest devotion the consecration of Christ’s blood alone. Nevertheless, we do not neglect the salvation of the Christian people when we add the water afterward, so that it too—which is the people—may be sanctified through participation in the same sacrament.

“For it would seem less fitting that the sanctifier and that which is to be sanctified should possess equal rank in one and the same consecration. It is enough if the water, which is the people, is sanctified through participation in the divine consecration, and does not possess the full dignity of that same consecration. [Col. 1243A] For from the beginning we were not sanctified with Christ except through the Holy Spirit and communion in the Holy Spirit; and we began to be sanctified through participating and communicating in the holy sacraments of Christ and the Church.”

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, said: “I would not have you separate the head from the members, nor the members from the head. For, as the Apostle says, ‘Christ is the head of the Church’ (Eph. 5:23). If by separating them you remove Christ, where, I ask, is the head of the Church? Or how can there be a Church where Christ, who is the head, is absent? But if by separating them you remove the Church, where, I ask, are the members of the head? Or how can Christ be called the head of the Church [Col. 1243B] where there are none of its members?

“Take care, then, brother, lest by some contrivance of deceptive reasoning you think the head should be separated from the members, or the members from the head. For that is to remove both Christ and the Church from the midst and to throw everything into confusion. Certainly Holy Scripture is accustomed to say many things about the head, which is Christ, that do not apply to the Church; and likewise it often speaks in the person of the Church things which do not apply to the head. Yet it does not intend thereby in any way to separate the one from the other.

“For as Eve was fashioned from the side of Adam as he slept, so the Church was fashioned from the side of Christ suffering on the cross. Therefore, in the offering and consecration of the Lord’s most sacred body and blood, celebrated in remembrance of the Lord’s Passion, the water must not be absent: [Col. 1243C] the water which, flowing from Christ’s side together with the blood, figured the Church and watered and baptized her by sanctifying her. Thus the whole that flowed from the Lord’s side may give life to our human being, renewed by these two things, so that if he has contracted any stain of sin after baptism, he may have in this a flood of pardon by which he may be washed and again renewed from day to day.

“For if wine is offered without water, Christ’s blood begins to be without us, as though the head were without members. But if water alone is offered, the people appear to be without Christ, as though the members were without a head. But when both are mixed, then surely the mystery of Christ and the Church is rightly accomplished spiritually, because Christ and the Church are shown to be one body. [Col. 1243D] Thus they are no longer, as it were, two—wine and water—but the wine, namely Christ’s blood, becomes that by which children receiving communion obtain both the flood of sacred purification and renewal, drink the blood which is the price of Christian salvation, and pass into the unity of Christ’s body, which is the Church, through spiritual purification and being made alive together.

“Do not wonder that two liquids—water and wine—consecrated together are changed by divine operation into one thing, namely blood, for the spiritual quickening of our souls, since every day, however many liquids we drink, are changed into our blood for the sustenance of our bodies. [Col. 1244A] For this reason wine and water are not inappropriately mixed mystically beforehand, and yet after the consecration nothing but blood is drunk; because, having first been baptized in it through water, afterwards we drink him spiritually by hungering and thirsting for him.

“For who has ever presumed to receive communion in the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood unless he had first been reborn through the water of baptism? To do so would not be to receive communion, but, by acting outside the order, to place oneself outside the communion of Christians. No one is incorporated into Christ by drinking this cup unless he has first, in baptism, been buried together with Christ and made a member of him. We therefore rightly mix water with wine before consecration, and, consecrating them together, receive the blood alone after consecration, because one must first be baptized in water and afterward be nourished and satisfied by Christ’s blood.

“But you seem rather ineptly to withhold water from being consecrated together with the wine. In this way, what belongs to both as though to one you do not bestow on both as though to one; but, removing the one, you think it ought to be granted to the other alone. In the very offering you offend him whom you ought to propitiate, while you rightly seek to offer but strive wrongly to divide what is offered or is to be offered. For one sins no little who does not rightly separate things rightly joined; and you carelessly separate improperly things which were rightly joined upon the cross and mystically flowed from the Lord’s side, as though instituting something better on your own authority, while contemptuously [Col. 1244C] altering what was then divinely done.”

Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “I do not attempt to separate the members of the Church, divinely united to their head Christ.

> [Note: [Col. 1243] ‘Divinely united.’ Acherius had printed *diu conjuncta* (‘long united’); since that was nonsensical, we have restored the reading as you see it.]

“Rather, I join them fittingly in a suitable way, so that the members, having received the sanctification of the head, may themselves also be sanctified and may be more worthily fitted to Christ through the union of sanctification. And I can demonstrate by many arguments that this is how it should be done.”

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, said: “‘Always answering those who always answer leads on to infinity. You are indeed subtle in intellect for discovering a new opinion, and eloquent in Greek speech for defending it; but in matters of this kind, [Col. 1244D] modest and sober wisdom is more commendable—wisdom for which the limits laid down by the holy Fathers suffice—than an excessively ingenious and excessively searching cleverness that tries to extend itself above itself and beyond the limits of the holy Fathers. For thus the Apostle warns: ‘Do not think more highly than you ought to think, but think soberly’ (Rom. 12:3).

“What is so false that speech cannot make it seem true? Or what is so true that speech cannot make it seem false, if cunning cleverness and persuasive eloquence are not lacking in the speaker? See to it yourself if you have spoken falsehood as truth. I know, and do not doubt, that I have spoken truth. For, with the Gospel as witness, we know and believe without doubt that blood and water flowed together from Christ’s side upon the cross for the redemption of our salvation and that of the whole human race. [Col. 1245A] Therefore we too offer wine and water mixed and consecrated together in one chalice for the remission of all sins; for this reason we teach this rite of offering; and it suffices us to imitate the pattern of Christ’s Passion, because we do not wish to be hindered by new inventions.

“Whatever we do, whether in this or in other ecclesiastical sacraments, we do according to the figure which preceded or according to the truth which appeared in Christ. We consider that we do nothing from ourselves, but everything from God, who sanctifies all things sacramentally and truly.”

[Col. 1245B]

Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “The reasoning pleases me; the authority pleases me; the truth pleases me; the rite pleases me; your humility also pleases me; your graciousness pleases me; the ordered gravity of your words pleases me. Yet above all these things I desire to see a general council, so that, with all agreeing in one, we may all say the same thing in Christ Jesus our Lord.

“And as both the unleavened and the leavened host are made from many grains of the purest wheat, and as wine pressed out is gathered from many grapes collected into one, so may one harmonious Church, holding the same belief, be established from many multitudes of Greeks and Latins. Let neither your unleavened bread become for us nor our leavened bread for you a judgment of condemnation on the day [Col. 1245C] of the Lord, while we rise into contention against one another over that which has been established for salvation for both. For dangerous contention is more to be feared by us and by you than differing custom in the same observance.”

## CHAPTER XXI. On the various and differing baptism of Greeks and Latins.

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, said: “I find you wise and discerning in all your words; therefore I ask you not to be unwilling to answer a little further and to resolve for me, who am greatly perplexed, the matter which moves me. As I hear, it is your custom that if a Greek wishes to marry a Latin wife—as often happens, and as is known also frequently to have happened [Col. 1245D] among imperial persons—you first bathe her with sanctified oil poured into some vessel and wash her all over the body; and then at last, as one passing into your rite and law, she is joined in marriage. I should very much like to know why this is done, if indeed it is done. For it seems to be a kind of rebaptism.

“And if it is so—that you judge our Latins, or indeed any Christians baptized in any manner under the invocation of the Holy Trinity, to require rebaptism—then this is plainly [Col. 1246A] a most manifest heresy, akin to a certain sect of Arians. Councils ought to be held with you not as fellow participants but against you; and, without any question or hearing, you ought to be anathematized. Everything you do or say is altogether abominable, detestable, and execrable before God and human beings—especially if you take the Lord’s name in vain and presume to invalidate the invocation of the Holy Trinity, by which we are baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

“Eusebius, once bishop of Nicomedia, wholly leavened with Arian heresy, as the history written in Greek by the venerable bishop Theodoret and translated into our Latin by Epiphanius Scholasticus from Cassiodorus relates, rebaptized the great emperor Constantine into the Arian doctrine. [Col. 1246B] For the following is read there: ‘Constantine, having fallen ill, departed from the city of Constantinople as though for the hot baths; and when he was staying at Nicomedia, overcome by sickness and not ignorant of the uncertainty of this life, he received the grace of holy baptism.’

“This same emperor Constantine, as the *Ecclesiastical History* relates—

> [Note: [Col. 1245D] ‘Ecclesiastical History.’ He had in mind the Acts of Pope Sylvester, circulated under the name of Eusebius of Caesarea, as we say both from other evidence and from Ratramnus’s Book IV of the *Counter-arguments against the Greeks*. These Acts are still preserved in the Library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.]

—written by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, had earlier been baptized at Rome, at the beginning of his conversion, within the Lateran palace by the most blessed Pope Sylvester. Both histories, that of Eusebius and that of Cassiodorus, deserved to be called *Ecclesiastical* because of the truth of events carried out in the Church at different times.

“Likewise Constantius Augustus, son of the great Constantine, [Col. 1246C] leavened with the same heresy and rebaptized by the aforesaid Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, recalled the venerable Pope Liberius from exile and requested and commanded him to agree with him and to be rebaptized with the heretics. The most blessed pope did nothing of the kind. Although he publicly opposed the heretic Constantius in this matter, he nevertheless tolerated and passed over many heretical things in many respects for his sake.

“The same Emperor Constantius ordered Pope Felix, Liberius’s successor, beheaded because Felix had declared him a heretic, rebaptized a second time by the aforesaid Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, near Nicomedia at the estate called Aquilone. If the dregs—

> [Note: [Col. 1246D] ‘If the dregs.’ Baluzius corrected the text thus; Acherius had printed *sex* and conjectured that *secta* (‘sect’) should be read.]

—of that same heresy still remain among the Greek people, namely, that they rebaptize in their own rite those who come to them after having been baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity, [Col. 1246D] why, I ask, should they be called Christians? Whoever thinks a person must be rebaptized denies the power of the Holy Trinity, in which catholic baptism is administered, and is already condemned.”

Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “If Latins knew the Greek rites in their entirety, they would not so readily slander them or so readily take offence at them. Yet it is unsurprising that they judge this matter wrongly, even though what they do not know is right. [Col. 1247A] Far be it from the orthodox faith of the Greeks that we should judge any Christian baptized under the invocation of the Holy Trinity to require baptism again. To do this, or to preach that it ought to be done, is heretical.

“Certainly, we have certain purifications involving anointing with sacred oil. When foreign persons, men or women, come to us and desire to enter our rite and our communion, we anoint them with consecrated oil because we do not know whether they have previously received the sacrament of anointing. But we by no means baptize again those whom we have learned were baptized before; nor do we anoint those whom we do not doubt were already anointed, sanctified by chrismal anointing through the laying on of hands, and confirmed in the Christian religion. What is not known to have been done before is not said to be repeated.”

## CHAPTER XXII. On the concord of Greek and Latin scholars.

[Col. 1247B]

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, said: “I give thanks to God, who has removed this scandal also from me and has taken from me the reproach against the Christian name which until now I had suspected in the most learned Greek people.”

Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia, said: “If our faith and our rites, which we possess in the law of God, please your prudence, we greatly rejoice. But since we seem to differ somewhat not in great matters but in the least matters, which, although they do not impede the salvation of souls, nonetheless do not build up charity, [Col. 1248A] it would be necessary to labour with utmost diligence, as I said above, for a general council to be held in a fitting place and at a fitting time. There all the matters which separate us and you from the same rite might be brought back into a single concord, and Greeks and Latins alike might become one people under one Lord Jesus Christ, in one faith, one baptism, and one sacramental rite.”

Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, said: “It belongs to heretics to seek corners and hiding-places. But since you desire a general council, you seem to aim at what is catholic. Therefore I too desire that a universal council may be held, where your wisdom, [Col. 1248B] eloquence, holiness, gravity, discernment, meekness, modesty, religion, steadfastness, piety, and perfection may shine forth before the face of the whole Church for the salvation and instruction of all. My humility, moderation, littleness, devotion, affection, and desire will never cease to pray for this.”

All cried out together: “Δόξα σοι, ὁ Θεός, δόξα σοι, ὁ Θεός, δόξα σοι, ὁ Θεός”—that is, “Glory be to God, glory be to God, glory be to God.” “Καλὸς διάλογος” (*kalos dialogos*), that is, “a good dialogue.” “Ὁλόγραφοι, ὁλόγραφοι” (*holographoi, holographoi*), that is, “let it all be written down, let it all be written down.” Here it ends. Thanks be to God.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1154: GILBERT OF POITIERS, BISHOP OF POITIERS

[Col. 1247]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE

(*Gallia Christiana nova*, II, 1175)

[Col. 1247C] Gislebertus Porretanus, a native of Poitiers, is described in the code of Walter of Roucy as lord of the district [Note: [Col. 1247C] Our Sammarthani maintain that this is incorrectly written. For, they say, during Porretanus’s lifetime this lordship had from ancient times borne lords of the same name, whose heiress Leonora transferred that castle as her dowry into the noble Poitevin family of Volvire.]; but this was written in a very recent hand. From being a canon of Saint-Hilaire-le-Grand and a most subtle philosopher and theologian, he was made bishop [Col. 1248C]; for at the time of his election, namely in 1141, or rather 1142, he was teaching theology at Poitiers. [Note: [Col. 1248C] For his predecessor, Bishop Grimoard, occurs “in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1142, indiction II, in the reign of King Louis,” in a charter of Renald Claret, in the presence of Lord P., abbot of Saint-Maixent.]

At that time the theology called Scholastic was in vogue. In handing down the doctrine of the faith and explaining the divine mysteries of the Trinity, the Incarnation, and so forth, it began to employ terms hitherto unknown: abstractions of the mind, real and virtual distinctions, second intentions, and the like. Gislebertus Porretanus and Peter Abelard, whom Saint Bernard sharply attacked, embraced this theology in their schools and seemed to depart from the faith and introduce a novel and foreign teaching. Saint Bernard especially, whose theology had been drawn from Holy Scripture and the holy Fathers, charged these theologians with error and with novelty—most dangerous in matters relating to religion.

But Otto of Freising should be heard speaking of Gislebertus:

> “In those days, in Aquitaine, at Poitiers, a city of Gaul, there was a bishop named Gilbert. A native of that same city, from youth to extreme old age he had cultivated the study of philosophy in various places in Gaul; and, both in fact and in name, he had discharged the office of master. Shortly before these events he had been raised to the episcopal dignity in the aforesaid city [Col. 1249B]. Because of the greatness of his subtle intellect and the sharpness of his reasoning, he was accustomed to say many things beyond the common manner of men. Once, therefore, as he was holding a large assembly of clergy from his diocese and introducing into an exhortatory sermon certain matters concerning faith in the Holy Trinity, two of his archdeacons, Arnald and Calo, appealed against him, alleging that he was teaching contrary to the rule of the Catholic Church, and summoned him to the judgment of the supreme pontiff and the Roman See. Thus both parties set out and met Pope Eugenius, bishop of Rome, as he was travelling from the city toward Gaul, at Siena, a city of Tuscany. Having heard them and learned the purpose of their journey, the Roman pontiff briefly replied that he was entering Gaul and wished there to examine the matter more fully, because, owing to the abundance of learned men residing there, he would have a more suitable opportunity for investigation. The archdeacons returned to Gaul [Col. 1249C] and, after consulting Bernard, the above-mentioned abbot of Clairvaux, inclined him to favor their case against the bishop. Now that abbot, both zealous from fervor for the Christian religion and in some degree credulous through habitual gentleness, so abhorred teachers who relied too much upon human reasoning and secular wisdom, and so readily lent an ear if anything discordant with the Christian faith was said to him concerning such men.”

When Saint Bernard learned through the aforementioned archdeacons what was being reported about Gislebertus, he immediately worked diligently with them that the heresies said to be taught by Gilbert should be condemned by apostolic judgment. The case had first been heard at Auxerre, afterward at Paris; but so that the judgment might be more solemn, Gilbert was compelled to appear before the general synod at Reims and answer the charges circulated concerning him.

Otto further recounts the accusations brought against him, while describing the formation of our bishop’s life from youth, in book I, chapter 50:

> “The aforementioned archdeacons, having enlisted Abbot Bernard, a man of such great authority and esteem, attempted to condemn Bishop Gilbert by the same course as the aforesaid Peter [Abelard]; but neither the cause nor the subject matter was the same. For Gilbert, from youth subjecting himself to the instruction of great men and trusting more to their weight than to his own intellect—such as first Hilary of Poitiers, then Bernard of Chartres, and lastly Anselm and Ralph of Laon, brothers—had drawn from them no light but a weighty learning. His hand had not been hastily removed from the rod; he had applied his mind to learning not at variance with moral discipline and gravity of life, not to jokes or amusements, but to serious matters. Hence he preserved gravity in gesture as well as voice, and showed himself as difficult in speech as in action, so that what he said could never be grasped by childish minds, and scarcely even by minds learned and trained.” [Col. 1250A]

Thus far Otto. These teachers of Gislebertus, Hilary and Bernard, are entirely unknown to us. We do not think that Hilary means that holy Doctor of the Church who was the glory of the see of Poitiers and of the entire Gallican Church, although Mabillon holds this view; and this appears also to have been the opinion of Dean Laurence, discussed below.

Otto records that the following charges were made against Porretanus: that he maintained that the divine essence is not God; that the properties of the persons are not the persons themselves; that the theological persons are predicated in no proposition; that the divine nature was not incarnate; and, besides these, other lesser charges—that, by diminishing human merit, he said that no one except Christ merits anything; that, by invalidating the sacraments of the Church, he said that none is baptized unless destined to be saved; and so forth.

Otto continues in chapter 51:

> “Accordingly, when Pope Eugenius was presiding with cardinals, bishops, and other venerable and learned men in the already mentioned city of Paris [Col. 1250B], Bishop Gilbert was brought before the consistory to answer these articles. Two masters were produced against him: Adam of the Little Bridge, a subtle man, and Hugh of Champfleury, the king’s chancellor and recently made canon of the Church of Paris. They asserted, and as it were pledged themselves under oath, that they had heard some of these things from his own mouth—to the great amazement of many present, that men of such stature and practiced in rational disputation should offer an oath as proof.”

In the same place:

> “While many things were objected to him from both sides, and he was compelled by the attacks of many to answer concerning so ineffable a matter, he is reported among other things to have said: ‘I boldly confess that the Father is one thing as Father, another thing as God; yet He is not this thing and that thing.’ Master Joslen, bishop of Soissons, received the obscurity of this saying—as a profane novelty of expression—so impatiently that, in avoiding the middle, he ran into the bank,” as the proverb has it. [Col. 1250C]

Yet this manner of speaking, employed by Gislebertus, is approved on Augustine’s authority, who says: “Thus it is one thing for God to be, another to subsist; just as it is one thing for God to be, another to be Father or to be Lord. For what He is is said of Him in relation to Himself; but ‘Father’ is said in relation to the Son, and ‘Lord’ in relation to a serving creature.”

Pope Eugenius, observing the difficulty of the case, granted Gislebertus a reprieve until the general council to be held at Reims in Lent of the following year. In that celebrated assembly, overcome by the force of Saint Bernard’s arguments, he retracted and abjured his former doctrines. Besides Otto of Freising, one should read Geoffrey in the *Life of Saint Bernard*, Bernard himself, volume I, Sermon 80, and Mabillon in the preface to the new edition of Saint Bernard’s works. Let us briefly note the remaining acts of this bishop.

He is mentioned in the records of Fontenay-le-Comte in 1148 and 1153. [Col. 1250D] In 1149 he attended a certain synod at Bordeaux, mentioned in charter 21 among the documents of the Church of Bordeaux, where he yielded certain matters to the abbot of Saint-Cyprian. In 1150, together with the archbishop of Bordeaux, he settled a dispute which had arisen between Matilda, abbess of Fontevraud, and Julius, abbot of La Couronne, concerning certain fiefs. He departed this life in 1154. The appendix of Robert of Mont-Saint-Michel to Sigebert says of that year:

> “On the sixth day before the Kalends of December [26 November] . . . . . Gilbert, bishop of Poitiers, dies, a religious man and of manifold learning, who lucidly expounded the Psalms and the Epistles of Paul.”

Concerning his death, Laurence, dean of Poitiers, composed a lament, published by Bessius from a manuscript codex, at whose end these words are read:

> “He slept in a good old age, an old man and full of days, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1154, the thirteenth of his episcopate, Anastasius being Roman pontiff, Louis king of the Franks, Henry duke of the Aquitanians, [Col. 1251A] in the month of September, on the day before the Nones of September [4 September]. He was buried by Geoffrey, bishop of Bordeaux, and the other bishops, B., bishop of Saintes; Hugh, bishop of Angoulême; and Elias, bishop of Périgueux, in the church of Blessed Hilary, his father and patron. For it was deemed especially fitting and appropriate that he should obtain the inheritance of the one whose doctrine he had followed and whose office he had held. May his soul rest in peace. Amen.”

The following epitaph is inscribed in a manuscript codex of the library of the Discalced Carmelites of Paris, and is appended to his work *On the Trinity*:

> In our times that most celebrated master  
> Received this work, a vigorous and wise servant.  
> He flourished and surpassed all other masters.  
> A logician, ethicist, theologian, and sophist;  
> Astronomy alone of the seven arts he lacked;  
> Preeminent in the arts and in divine philosophy.  
>
> [Col. 1251B] How eloquent he was in speech and how profound  
> In meaning is attested by those known to have read him well.  
> In the books of that great Boethius were his discoveries.  
> He was rightly called another Boethius indeed,  
> Though his proper name was Gislebertus.  
> Poitiers bore him, and chose him as its bishop;  
> Truly ennobled [perhaps *enriched*, *ditata*] by so great a patron.  
> May he enjoy eternal rest in the peace above.

[Col. 1252A] Another inscription in the necrology of the Church of Le Mans gives:

> Here Gislebertus, bishop of Poitiers,  
> An outstanding teacher, finished life’s struggle;  
> His living fame in the world now surpasses his understanding;  
> May his spirit live joyfully for ever.

On the day before the Nones of September, an anniversary observance is held in the cathedral church for Bishop Gislebertus, “buried at Saint-Hilary.” Thus the old necrology states; and in the church of Saint-Hilaire-le-Grand, near the sacristy, his tomb is still displayed, skillfully made of marble, though largely broken by the Calvinists, who burned his bones. On the same day annual prayers for him are marked in the calendars of Holy Trinity, Poitiers; Saint-Maurice, Angers; and Saint Mary, Chartres. In the latter church he is recorded as having first been canon, then chancellor, [Col. 1252B] and finally bishop of Poitiers. Perhaps while a canon of Chartres he heard that master Bernard of Chartres whom, as we said, Otto of Freising mentions. In the appendix to Guibert of Nogent, page 564, there survives Gislebertus’s letter on the Eucharist.

[Col. 1251]

## LITERARY NOTICE

(*Literary History of France, by Benedictine Religious*, vol. XII, p. 471.)

Gilbert, surnamed de la Porrée, is the author of a large number of writings, of which at most four or five have been published.

The first is a commentary on Boethius’s books *On the Trinity*. It appears in the general edition of Boethius’s works, published at Basel in one folio volume in 1470. This commentary gave Gilbert’s opponents their greatest opening. Extracts from it were produced at the Council of Paris, and he repudiated them as inaccurate; at that of Reims, he himself brought an authentic copy, whose reading the Pope, after examining it, prohibited until it had been corrected by the Holy See. Its style is compact, harsh, and convoluted, so that, far from dispelling the obscurities of the text, the gloss itself would need another gloss to be understood. In a manuscript of the Library of the Discalced Carmelites of Paris it is followed by a verse encomium of the author, reported in the *History of the University of Paris* and in the second volume of the new *Gallia Christiana*. [Note: [Col. 1251] See above.] Another manuscript—that of Saint-Amand—presents a portrait of our author at the head of the same work, with this inscription:

> Master Gislebertus, bishop of Poitiers, reveals the higher secrets of philosophy to four diligent, attentive, and knocking disciples, whose names are written below, because they are worthy.

Below the portrait are those of three of his disciples; the fourth appears in the initial letter of this commentary. The inscribed names are Jourdain Fantome, Yves, dean of Chartres, Jean Belet, and Nicolas of Amiens.

The second published work from Gilbert’s pen is a letter to Matthew, abbot of Saint-Florent at Saumur and subsequently bishop of Angers. It answers a letter written by that abbot consulting him on the following case. A priest of his monastery had pronounced the sacred words over an empty chalice after consecrating the bread; discovering this at the breaking of the host, he made a new consecration of both species. Matthew asked what penance this priest’s fault deserved. Gilbert answers that, because a similar case had already arisen in his time, he could do no better than conform his decision to that rendered then by wise and enlightened persons. Accordingly, he considers that the priest in question should abstain for some time from celebrating Mass; that fasts and other bodily mortifications should also be imposed upon him; and that he should be directed to prayers in expiation of so great a fault. He adds that, besides the fact that the priest should not have repeated the consecration of the bread, he could have omitted that of the wine and communicated only under the first species, since Christ is wholly present under either species. He cites as proof the Church’s practice of communicating children only under the species of wine, and the sick only under that of bread. A nearly similar decision in such a case may be found in a letter (Epistle 69) of Saint Bernard to Guy, abbot of Trois-Fontaines.

[Col. 1253] There are three editions of this consultation of Gilbert: the first in Dom D’Achery’s Notes on Guibert of Nogent (p. 564); the second in the first volume of Dom Martène’s *Anecdotes* (p. 427); and the last in the sixth volume of the *Benedictine Annals* (bk. LXXVII, no. 113).

The third work of our author made public is his *Treatise on the Six Principles*, a philosophical work found among Aristotle’s works translated by Hermolaus Barbarus, immediately after that philosopher’s *On Categories* in the old editions. [Note: [Col. 1253] It is also part of an old Gothic quarto edition of philosophical books whose title reads: “Authorities of Aristotle, Seneca, Boethius, Plato, Apuleius, Porphyry, and Gilbert of Poitiers.”] For several centuries this work was highly esteemed in the schools. Several learned men did it the honor of commenting on it. Among them were Albert the Great, whose work entitled *Eight Treatises on Gilbert of Poitiers’s Six Principles* appears in the first volume of his works, Lyons edition of 1651; Geoffrey [FABR., *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, bk. VII, p. 195] of Cornwall, a Carmelite religious of the fourteenth century, who wrote an unpublished gloss on this text; Antony Andrew [NIC. ANT., *Bibliotheca Hispana*, bk. XIX, ch. 4, no. 190], a Spanish Franciscan of the same century, whose commentary on the *Six Principles* is included in the collection of his works published at Venice in 1481, 1509, and 1517; and Bonagratia of Ascoli, a Dominican, among whose works, also printed at Venice in 1481, one sees *Commentaries on Gilbert of Poitiers’s Six Principles*.

The fourth published work of our author is a commentary on the Apocalypse. The preface appears at the head of Nicholas of Lyra’s *Postils* on that book, and the body of the work was used in a compilation of various ancient interpreters of the Apocalypse, published at Paris in 1512 in one octavo volume.

We guarantee the printing of a fifth work by Gilbert, a commentary on the Psalms drawn from the ancient doctors, only on the authority of Lipenius (*Theological Library*, vol. II, p. 585), who cites a folio edition of 1527 without naming place or printer. Fabricius did not know it, and we have made fruitless searches to discover it. Whatever the case, this commentary exists in manuscript in several libraries: specifically, those of the King (no. 2577); the abbeys of Saint-Amand (SANDER., *Manuscripts of Belgium*, pt. I, p. 45), Braine in the diocese of Soissons (HUGO, *Premonstratensian Annals*, vol. I, p. 412), Selincourt in the diocese of Amiens, and the Church of Saint-Omer (*ibid.*, vol. II, p. 558). In the copy at the latter repository Gilbert’s commentary is intermingled with another by his disciple Nicholas of Amiens, intended to explain it; this shows that the former is not very clear by itself.

Geoffrey of Clairvaux, in his letter to the Cardinal of Albano (*Councils*, vol. X, p. 1125), reports a passage in Gilbert in which, speaking of the adoration due to the flesh of Jesus Christ, he plainly says [Note: [Col. 1253] “I do not mean that adoration which is *latria*, owed to the Creator alone, but that which is more worthy than *dulia*. For the adoration of *dulia* is also paid to a creature; and it has two kinds: one offered indiscriminately to human beings, the other offered to the humanity of Christ alone.”] that it is not an adoration of *latria*, such as is owed to the Creator alone, but only an adoration higher than that of *dulia*. “For,” Gilbert adds, “the adoration of *dulia* is rendered even to a creature, and two kinds are distinguished: one whose object is human beings without distinction; the other rendered only to the humanity of Jesus Christ.” This doctrine, of which Gilbert appears to be the author, subsequently had many adherents, as will be seen under Peter Lombard.

The writings of our author that have not yet been published are:

1. Various questions on all Holy Scripture, existing at the abbey of Saint-Ouen in Rouen and at Saint-Bertin (MART., *Anecdotes*, vol. III, p. 662).

2. Glosses on the prophet Jeremiah, of which there are two copies in the King’s Library (nos. 148 and 278).

3. Glosses on the Song of Songs, preserved in the public library of Utrecht (SANDER., *ibid.*, pt. II, p. 85).

4. Glosses on the Gospel of Saint John, known to us only by the testimony of Henry of Ghent (*Writers*, ch. 8).

5. Glosses on the Epistles of Saint Paul, of which copies occur in the King’s Library (nos. 2579, 2580, and 2581); those of Saint-Germain-des-Prés (LE LONG, *Sacred Library*, vol. II, p. 911), Saint-Victor, Vauclair, the Dunes in Flanders, Magdalen College at Oxford, and the Pauline Library at Leipzig. In this work Gilbert teaches, as Geoffrey of Clairvaux observed (*Councils*, vol. I, p. 1125), that the name of God and Son of God is given to the man in Jesus Christ only by adoption.

Moreover, all these glosses are merely an extension of those of Anselm of Laon, which served, so to speak, as the framework for all subsequent glossators of Scripture in the later ages.

6. A very lengthy and rather unintelligible commentary, in the manner of almost all Gilbert’s works, on Boethius’s treatise *On the Two Natures in Jesus Christ*. This work predates the Council of Reims to which Gilbert was summoned; for shortly before its meeting he sent a copy to Pope Eugenius, who gave it to Gothescalc (MAB., *Annals*, bk. LXXIX, no. 1), then abbot of Mont-Saint-Martin near Arras and later bishop of that city, to examine. The latter did not judge it favorably. He extracted several propositions that seemed erroneous to him and opposed passages from the Fathers to them. A copy of this work by Gilbert exists at Saint-Amand (SANDER., *ibid.*, pt. I, p. 51).

7. A commentary on the work attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, *On Hebdomads, or on the Dignity of Theology*. This commentary, together with the text on which it comments, is in the library of the Church of Tours; it is also in the King’s Library (no. 2178).

8. A book *On Causes*, found in the library of the Dunes (SANDER., *ibid.*, pt. I, p. 199).

9. Oudin additionally attributes to our author a treatise in the form of a work *On the Trinity* (*Writers*, vol. II, p. 1286), which he says is in the Library of the Discalced Carmelites of Paris. What we can affirm is that it is no longer found there. It perhaps does not differ from the commentary on Boethius.

10. At the Library of Saint-Ouen in Rouen there is *Little Glosses of Master Gislebertus Porretanus on Matthew*, in a manuscript from the end of the twelfth century. The same work is also found, but under the name of Geoffrey Babion—whose article was previously given (vol. IX, p. 520)—at the abbey of Saint-Germer. The latter copy is less ancient than the first. Nevertheless, its attribution is strengthened by the authority of another copy found at Cîteaux under the title *Of Geoffrey Babion on Matthew*. Whatever the case, the work, divided into eighty chapters, begins with these words [Col. 1255]: “Our Lord and Redeemer, for commendation, etc.,” and ends: “may have merited to possess Christ as a dweller in the lodging of their heart.”

11. Gilbert had composed a rhymed prose piece on the Trinity (OTTO OF FREISING, *Deeds of Frederick*, bk. I, ch. 52), which was produced against him at the Council of Paris. But we believe this piece lost, since we know of no copy of it.
