12. Among Gilbert’s productions lost to time must also be counted his sermons, which Peter of Celle (bk. VII, ep. 19) valued so highly that he did not hesitate to compare them with those of Saint Bernard.

Such are the known works of Gilbert de la Porrée. Their number and extent show his constant love of labor; the great number of citations they contain testifies to his learning; and several important difficulties of dogma and morals, well resolved in them, display the depth of his intellect. But the lack of method prevailing in most of these works, and their apparent affectation of reducing everything to the sophistical opinions of the School—not to mention the dryness of their style—have caused them to fall almost wholly into oblivion.

[Col. 1255]

## LETTER OF GISLEBERTUS PORRETANUS, BISHOP OF POITIERS, TO MATTHEW, ABBOT OF SAINT-FLORENT AT SAUMUR

### How a priest offering sacrifice with bread alone and without wine is to be punished, and concerning certain other questions

[Note: [Col. 1255B] We found this letter of Gislebertus, bishop of Poitiers, to Matthew, abbot of Saint-Florent at Saumur, in which he answers several questions put to him, in an old codex of the monastery of Grandmont in the district of Limoges. Our Acherius published the answer to the [Col. 1256B] first question in his notes on Guibert, omitting the other three, which were absent from his manuscript. Here we give it complete.]

(MARTÈNE, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. I, col. 427, from a Grandmont manuscript.)

[Col. 1255A] GISLEBERTUS, by the grace of God bishop of Poitiers, to his beloved brother in Christ [Note: [Col. 1256B] Matthew, abbot of Saint-Florent at Saumur, became bishop of Angers in 1156.] MATTHEW, by the same grace abbot of Saint-Florent: greeting in Christ.

You have seen fit to consult our insignificance concerning an instance of forgetfulness which is said recently to have occurred in your church: namely, that, bread having been placed upon the altar for consecration in the Eucharist and the chalice being empty, a priest pronounced all the words pertaining to the sacrament of bread and wine as far as the breaking of the bread. When, upon uncovering the chalice, he realized that he had erred, he put wine and water into the chalice and repeated the sacred words of consecration not only over the chalice but also over the consecrated host of bread. You ask what should be done concerning this act by yourselves, by that priest, and concerning that host.

[Col. 1255B] We offer, not something new from our own judgment, but the counsel which we once heard from prudent men concerning a similar case, in answer to your inquiry. When a similar event had come to the ears of certain prudent men, they judged that the priest should be rebuked for negligence and arranged that the community should pray for him. Following this example, therefore, we advise that your priest abstain for a time from offering the host, and meanwhile, after he has been expiated by such fasts or other bodily disciplines as you shall provide, and not only by his own prayers but also [Col. 1256A] by yours and those of the whole community, may he be worthy to offer again. Yet since this case of forgetfulness befalls him not from a consciousness of error—which, when obstinate, is called heresy—but from delusions that often fill the loins of those who rightly believe, the punishment of this discipline may be shorter in duration and milder in severity.

Since, however, in either sacrament, whether of bread or of chalice, after the customary blessings made by the priest, Christ is whole and entire, he should altogether have refrained from reconsecrating the already consecrated bread; and he could sufficiently have refrained from pouring wine and water into the previously empty chalice, and, without that repetition of the sacred words, have communicated in Christ under the sacrament of bread. For baptized children often receive communion in the sacrament of the chalice alone, and the sick in that of bread alone [Col. 1256B]; and in respect to the reality itself and the sacrament of future incorruption they receive nothing less than those who receive Christ at the Church from the Lord’s own table in both the sacrament of bread and that of the chalice.

We answer your inquiry, if not fully, yet faithfully, trusting in your charity, which regards what is small as great and what is incomplete as perfect. We add what we ourselves customarily do, lest we be deceived by such forgetfulness, either of our ministers or of ourselves. When our ministers have poured wine into the chalice which they are to offer, we do not trust them concerning the mixing of water with the wine, unless, once the bread has been offered to us and the chalice is being offered, they themselves pour in the water before our eyes, or, after giving us the water vessel, we add it to the chalice. Thus both minister and priest remain free from doubt and unharmed by any occurrence of forgetfulness.

### On Natural Pollution

It is asked whether, after nocturnal pollution, the body of Christ ought to be consecrated or received by anyone. To this we say that there are three kinds of nocturnal pollution. One pollution arises from persistent thoughts; another from drunken excess; another from nature. If someone is polluted at night through persistent thought which he had during the day concerning some woman [Col. 1257B], he is forbidden to consecrate or receive the body of Christ. If someone is polluted at night through drunken excess, he is similarly forbidden. But if a person’s receptacles are full, and nocturnal pollution occurs naturally from that superfluity, then, after a penance has been imposed, his body washed, and his clothes changed, he may consecrate or receive the body. Here ends.

### Another Question

[Col. 1258A] It is asked concerning those who have committed some criminal act, known to the priest: if they request the body of Christ from that priest, should it be denied them or not? To this we say, Augustine being our witness, that they ought to be admonished, not barred. We have Christ’s example, who gave His body and blood to Judas the traitor, knowing him to be unclean and about to betray Him; for Judas was not yet publicly denounced, nor placed outside the communion of the Church. Therefore, although we know someone to persist in some criminal act, we ought not deny him the body of Christ if he asks for it, unless he has been excommunicated and placed outside the communion of the Church.

### Another Question of Master Gislebertus

[Col. 1258B] It is asked whether, if a robber is led away to be hanged and requests the body of Christ in order to escape, it ought to be given to him. To this we say that, out of reverence for the body and blood of Christ, it ought not be given to him, because it would be shameful if he were hanged after communion. But after penance has been imposed, if he repents from his whole heart and confesses his sins, we ought to hope for his salvation.

[Col. 1257]

## COMMENTARIES OF GISLEBERTUS PORRETANUS ON BOETHIUS

(See *Patrology*, vol. LXIV; vol. II of Boethius’s Works, cols. 1255, 1301, 1313, 1353.)

[Col. 1257]

## GISLEBERTUS PORRETANUS’S BOOK ON THE SIX PRINCIPLES

(*Works of Aristotle*, translated by Hermolaus Barbarus; Paris, from the press of Prigent Calvarin, at the Twin Cypresses, in the Cloître Brunel, 1541.)

[Col. 1257C] A ratio, or form, is that which comes upon a composite, consisting of a simple and unchanging essence. It cannot itself be composite, since it is separated from the nature of a composite. For a composite coming upon a composite makes it greater by its addition; a form coming upon a composite does not make the mixture greater by its addition. A white body, indeed, is no greater or smaller than itself when not white; nor, if it is conceived as not white, does the composite thereby suffer destruction or diminution of magnitude [Col. 1258C], but only alteration.

And because it may seem that this also applies to souls, we said that its essence is unchangeable; by this term souls are excluded from our definition, since they are evidently affected by contrary movements, now of joy, now of sorrow. And because there are philosophers who think that the soul of the world is something unchangeable and simple, wishing to exclude it from our account, I added: “coming upon a composite.” Therefore that definition contains all the required elements, so that, if one examines it closely, there is nothing one might desire or find superfluous. [Col. 1259A]

But it may be asked whether this is perpetual—that every form is said to be unchangeable—for several forms appear otherwise. A statement changes from true to false; whiteness, from bright, becomes somewhat dark or dark; and the same opinion is capable both of truth and of falsehood. But this is not so. The brightness of daylight whiteness is nothing other than the whiteness itself being called bright. Likewise, neither a statement nor an opinion is itself subject to contraries; rather, words are signs of the impressions held in the mind. But these matters have been discussed elsewhere.

I call “essential” whatever confers their own being upon things joined and constituted by any composition and, for the most part, can in no way be absent—for example, sense, reason, and the continuous and the discrete, which contain things like these [Col. 1259B]. One essential element, moreover, has the role of matter; another, that of form. Thus, in a human being the body is matter and the mind form. Accordingly, both mind in relation to body and rationality in relation to a human being are essential. But these matters have been explained more fully in the book entitled *Categories*.

Of forms, some exist by nature, others by art: reason exists by nature, colour and certain other affections by art. Some are doubtful, whether they have their origin by nature or by art, such as the shaping of sections, where there is no addition, but only a drawing apart of the parts. Perhaps the shaping itself is ascribed to nature, but art is required in order that it be perceived by sense. [Col. 1259C] For that form which grows together by the conjunction of parts undoubtedly subsists through art; but this is evident, whereas the other is more obscure.

Should those forms which are said to range over many things appear to exist by nature, or by art? They cannot exist by art, since no action seems possible by which one may reach a form established in many things; nor do they appear to exist by nature, because things produced by nature took their beginning from some created and fashioned thing. Yet these forms are not fashioned things, for no account can be given why they should be of this sort. Or is nature itself that fashions those forms, obscurely and secretly? For just as, when several parts are joined, a certain whole arises which surpasses the magnitude of each part, so from individual things held separately [Col. 1259D] a single form is conceived which, as it were, embraces them all and surpasses them in its predication. Thus universality is constituted by nature, since it proceeds from individual things, while singularity itself, if I may so say, advances and coheres together with the act of creation.

But whoever investigates this with careful subtlety will discover that, just as nature exercises its powers in actions hidden from us, so the Creator of nature displays His own powers in nature itself. This is known from His works, since He established nature by a determinate number. Enough of these matters, for they belong to another undertaking.

One kind of form is in a subject and is predicated of a subject: for example, knowledge, which is both placed in the soul as its subject and predicated of a subject—grammar. Another is indeed in a subject, but is not predicated of any subject: for example, Socrates’ baldness, and generally whatever is numerically one in this manner. Others are predicated of a subject and are not found in a subject, such as “mortal” and “rational.” Of those things which are in a subject and cannot be said of a subject, some are perceptible and others imperceptible. Perceptible are those comprehended by sense, such as whiteness, noise, smell, heat, blows, sweetness; imperceptible are those perceived by the mind, such as disciplines. Likewise, whatever is predicated of some subject cannot be called perceptible.

From what has been said it is clear that some forms can be seen as situated in some place, as blackness in the eye; others are such that it is difficult to show where they are located, such as knowledge, servitude, dominion, the relation by which one is called a father, and the relation by which one is called a son—unless someone places them [Col. 1260A] in the very constitution of those who beget and fashion.

All the forms which I have just set forth, represented singly—that is, apart from a connected statement or sequence of speech—each signify by their own marks either substance or accident, that is, something supervening. Of those which supervene upon things already existing, some are regarded simply within substance, such as line, surface, and body; others come from without, such as acting, being acted upon, being composed, where, when, and having. Those things which subsist through themselves, and likewise those which require merely a subject in which to be placed, have been discussed in the work entitled *Categories*; the rest must now be treated.

Action, or making, is the form through which we are denominated as acting or making upon subject matter. For example: one who cuts, in so far as he cuts, is denominated “cutting.” One kind of action is said to belong to the body; another pertains to the mind. The latter differs from the former because bodily action necessarily moves the very body in which it exists: the same body is both agent and mobile. But the action, or operation, of the mind does not move that in which it itself exists, but something joined to it. For while the mind acts, it is at rest and unmoved; and although it continually moves the body, it nevertheless, as I have said, remains unmoved. For the mind is not seen to be moved either through place or by any other motion, except insofar as it undergoes alteration.

First, indeed, it experiences no motion of increase, diminution, or local conveyance; for place belongs to body, and the soul is not body. [Col. 1260D] But how can that which is not body be moved through body? Therefore there is no soul able to change place from place to place; only body is moved from place to place.

Someone may say: “When mirrors remain in place, does not the reflected image move about in them in response to the movement of the object set before it?” Either the question cannot be entertained, once we admit that the image which appears truly subsists in the mirror; or, if we deny this, an error intolerable to ordinary people will result. It may be more convenient, however, to say it thus.

Moreover, one must know that everything which is in motion anywhere is in action; for to be moved is nothing other than action. Therefore everything which is moved also acts incidentally; for every action is in motion, and every motion is understood as constituted in action. Hence it is proper to action [Col. 1261A] to be in motion, just as it seems proper to motion to be in action.

This is plainly true of actions through which things are created and brought forth; but it seems doubtful in actions through which things happen to be overturned or destroyed. For one who demolishes something is indeed in motion, yet seems to do nothing, since nothing is produced upon it, but what has been made is overthrown. Yet action requires and concerns itself not with what thing it acts, but with the thing upon which it acts. Nor is motion a species of action, but a quality, because rest itself is also referred to the genus of quality. In general, whatever things are contrary to one another receive predication within the same genus.

The chief property of action is certainly that it produces and impresses a passion upon the subject matter. Every action produces passion, and whatever can inflict passion is action. It may indeed occur that action is produced and inflicted from action. For the action of something moved through itself produces the action which is brought in through another; for example, the action which an animal impressed upon another took its awakened beginning from the first action which that same animal performed. It makes no difference whether the principle is said to have been the action or the passion of the animal which impressed action upon another; or whether action is held to be the pure and unmixed principle, and passion a mixed one. Accordingly, that first operation or act must be called productive both of action and of passion.

Quality itself produces from itself that which is making: [Col. 1261C] heat itself, which is admittedly a quality, generates from itself the action called “heating.” Particular quantities too are produced by the genus which we have named “being composed”; and it is evident that certain qualities also flow from it. Such are roughness, smoothness, and the like, which are certainly qualities. Likewise line, surface, and body have both substance and origin from position itself. Quantity and quality are also productive of quantity and quality: line produces length, plane surface breadth, body thickness, and heat heat. Position itself too is fashioned by action and passion. For the generation of position requires a certain genesis, as it were, of simple things—that is, the arrangement and ordering of parts. Every such genesis consists in the action or operation of that which composes and places them. “When” proceeds from time; “where” from place.

That which I call “having” is constituted by body; for only things placed around a body are said to be had. The destruction and passing-away of individuals, which do not subsist in any subject, is primary; but generation occurs in those things which are next after the primary things. Whatever is predicated of individuals comes into being and coheres from things which are in no way predicated—for example, the common term “man” proceeds from individual men.

Moreover, acting and being acted upon admit contraries, and likewise differences of more and less. Thus to what I call “cutting” its contrary is “joining together”; and to what I call “burning” its contrary is “sprinkling.” Things are also said to become more or less heated, cooled, dried, moistened, gladdened, or saddened. [Col. 1262A]

Passion is an effect and a certain impressing of fire, and an accompaniment of action. Some things receive it more readily, others stubbornly reject it. Therefore what is more animate, so to speak, is distinguished from what is less so: a brute animal from a shrub, and a human being from brute animals. Whatever has been said concerning action may also apply to passion, with the term alone changed.

The word *passion* has several meanings. The operations of the soul which we have nevertheless placed under the genus of action are also called passions: love, hatred, joy, grief. This class of qualities is sometimes called the passive actions of the soul. [Col. 1262B] Passions are also called those things which afflict human health, such as infirmities and diseases and the other qualities of this kind which we have elsewhere set forth and classified.

Passion itself, as we have stated, is the first work which proceeds and is generated from action; yet it is not situated in the agent itself, but in that to which it is applied, and it receives the motion produced by the maker. For that which strikes is not itself said to undergo passion, but the matter subjected to the striker. Enough of these matters. Whoever desires more should reread the treatise *On Action*.

“When” signifies an account derived from the occurrence of time, not time itself, although they are plainly akin and related. Accordingly, “when” is not past time, but its event and, if I may say so, a certain affection in things through which things are said to have been; nor is it the time joined with things, by which certain things are said to be simultaneous or contrary, but an affection of time through which things are said to be in conjunction. [Col. 1262C] Nor is consequent time identical with “when,” but is that which is necessarily going to come to pass, from which things are said to be future, whether tomorrow, the day after tomorrow, or otherwise.

Therefore one “when” flows from the past, another proceeds from the present conjunction, a third from the future. It has been said in the *Categories* that past and future are continuous quantities, since they are bound to the instant—not because the past has a permanent essence, but because at its exit or boundary, by which it is joined with the instant, it has not yet passed away and is not entirely elapsed. Nor did we call the future continuous because it remains and subsists, but because it seems wholly and necessarily about to be born and to emerge—as though it were altogether present. In this respect there is no difference among the three, past, instant, and future.

Therefore people often deliberate about future things and do not decide about them otherwise than about present things. Terms belonging to things which subsist in reality are also applied to future things: “The sun will rise the day after tomorrow”; “a naval battle will take place tomorrow”; and likewise to past things: “Socrates died the day before yesterday.” Things are also predicated as necessarily about to occur in the future, as though born from the present: “Callias will, or will not, be disputing tomorrow.” For the word “about to dispute” signifies a future action, although as yet nothing of it exists in reality. [Col. 1263A]

“When” and “where” differ in this: in whatever thing time itself either is, was, or will be, its own “when” also either is, was, or will be, proceeding from that time to which each thing separately corresponds. But that “when” which is considered in things that are always accompanies the very present instant, and both subsist in the same subject. Yet those “whens” which arise from past and future time are never simultaneously with their own future or past.

But “where” itself and the place from which “where” derives never subsist in the same subject, [Col. 1263B] because “where” itself is situated in that which is bounded and enclosed by place, whereas place is in that which bounds and encloses. A “when” born from the past differs from that which is born from the future: what is born from the past is later than the future; what is born from the future is earlier than the past. If you take one and the same “when,” you will find that it flows first from the future, then from the present instant, and lastly from the past, just as time itself is first future, then present, and finally past.

Further, just as one kind of time is simple and punctual, another composite and extended—the simple measures a simple action, as its attendant; the composite, a composite action—[Col. 1263C] so one “when” is simple, as being at a point or instant, another composite, as being in an hour, day, month, year, and the like. And just as the parts of time itself never stay, so the parts of “when” continually and perpetually flow away. For the “when” generated from the past is bound and linked at the instant with the “when” generated from the future.

There is, however, a difference between “when” and time, because certain things can be measured by periods of time, such as “of this year,” “one year old,” “two years old,” and “three years old.” Similarly, a motion is called great as though it lasted a long time. But nothing can be measured by “whens” themselves, although things are said to be, to have been, or to be going to be at some time, according as “when” itself varies in things of which time is the follower and companion. [Col. 1263D]

“When” itself does not admit more and less, because neither a year itself nor a one-year-old thing seems able to be more a year or more one year old. Nor can one year be called more or less than another year, nor one one-year-old thing more or less than another. Nor does “when” admit contraries, since one and the same “when,” as we have said, proceeds from future, present, and past; and the same indivisible thing cannot receive two contraries predicated of it. Contraries, moreover, cannot be held together in the same subject at the same time. But all three “whens”—of the joined, the elapsed, and the consequent—are understood to subsist together and simultaneously in the same thing. For of the same thing which now survives, it is true both that it stood in the past and that it will stand in the future. Contraries, however, cannot subsist in the same individual or be predicated at the same time. [Col. 1264A]

“When” subsists in every generated thing. Thus the whole human body is at some time—that is, in time—for it experiences the divisions of time: spring, summer, winter, and autumn. The mind experiences them too; whence it happens that some study by night better during winter, others during summer, and some during spring or autumn, according to each person’s bodily temperament. For the soul joined to the body takes on the nature and constitution of that body. Those whose bodily constitution is dry or cold generally find their minds more stirred than usual during autumn; those in whom blood abounds are more tried in spring. The same is observed in other things according as the natures of living beings either agree with or differ from the turning-points of the seasons. Thus whatever undergoes the changes of time and turns and sways with its moments must necessarily exist in time. Such are the things we have mentioned. Nor can one readily find other things of which this may be affirmed more truly or more clearly. [Col. 1264B]

“Where” itself is said to be the bounding of a body, proceeding from the boundary of place; place itself is constituted in the body which receives and encloses. Therefore whatever is bounded by place appears to be in place. Thus it is clear that being situated in place is not the same as what they call “where”: place is contained in the surrounding body, while “where” is situated in the body which is surrounded.

Nor does every thing appear to have its own “where” joined to it. The soul is nowhere, since it neither occupies nor fills a place. For a place in which the soul is said to subsist could receive another living thing; but the place occupied and inhabited by any other thing cannot be occupied by another thing unless the first departs and moves elsewhere. A grain of wheat poured into a measure could not be admitted so long as the air filling the measure remained in it; once the air is expelled, the grain immediately succeeds and enters. [Col. 1264C] Therefore neither can two things occupy the same place, nor one thing different places. Hence neither can the soul be bounded by place, nor indeed anything else which appears foreign to the nature of body.

Someone may say: “Can not one thing be situated in several places? For a single persisting sound is received by different persons. Whether sound is air, or is not air but cannot subsist without air, the same air will certainly be in many places; therefore the same body must be thought to be in different places. For since a sound is numerically one, it cannot be believed to be divided into different parts of the air, so that it then disperses, as it were, into the ears of many.” Therefore those who grant that one and the same sound reaches the ears of many must necessarily confess that the same portion of air also enters the ears of many—a thing which cannot occur in any way.

Accordingly, since one must choose either to acknowledge that the things perceived by different persons are different, or to judge that one and the same body is in many places, we must choose the less objectionable alternative: it is not the same sound that is perceived, [Col. 1265A] but different sounds which spiritually generate and express one another. Thus it may be granted that a certain sound is not uttered by an animal: for the sound which is echoed spiritually and shaped in the likeness of the first is not the animal’s sound, since it is not struck forth by the animal. Otherwise every sound is uttered by an animal; for who has ever perceived any sound amid the silence of animals? Accordingly, sounds which proceed from an animal’s mouth are called an animal’s sounds. Thus the sound of one animal will indeed reach many, but it will not be one single sound.

One “where” is simple, another composite. The simple arises from a simple place; the composite from a composite place. A simple place is the beginning and origin of continuous things. A composite place is that which Aristotle defines as having parts joined to the same boundary to which the parts of the body themselves are joined; but the parts of a body meet at a point of place. Thus portions of place enclose portions of body; for simple places do not contain body at all. Therefore no place will exist without its body, nor any body without place.

But the outermost surface of heaven, beyond which there is nothing, calls this into doubt. [Col. 1265B] It may be said to be its own place, as the ancients established, when that which is enclosed is other than and distinct from that which encloses. Therefore, if we are to grant that that outer sphere is in a place, we cannot deny that there is some further body in which the outer surface of heaven is enclosed. But there is nothing further; therefore that surface is not in a place. Yet to decide these matters is both obscure and unusual, and indeed contrary to sense.

“Where” itself can neither be relaxed nor intensified. One thing cannot be said to be more or less in a place than another, even though it occupies a larger or smaller place. Moreover, more and less are found neither in “where” itself nor in quantity; but this genus will be without contraries, because place has no contrary: one place cannot be opposed to another as its contrary. Nobody doubts this concerning other cases of “where.”

The question is whether these two, being above and being below, appear contrary to one another. Things which are at the top are known to be very far from things below, just as an upper place is from a lower. [Col. 1265D] Therefore the two “wheres,” being above and being below, like the places themselves, seem liable to be contraries. But whoever made them contraries would establish contraries in the same subject. For what I call being above and being below can be present in the same thing: the same thing is said to be both above and below, though not in relation to the same thing. Thus the heights of towers are above in relation to us, below in relation to the face of heaven. Further, the same thing would become contrary to itself. If the same thing can be both above and below, then, once these are set down as contraries, the same thing immediately becomes contrary to itself. From what has been said, being in a place is held free from contraries.

Position is a certain arrangement of parts, and the ordering produced by generation itself: through it things are said either to sit, stand, lie down, and likewise to be rough, smooth, or otherwise composed. [Col. 1266A] For sitting, standing, and lying down are not themselves positions, but are denominatively named from positions.

Yet it is customary to ask concerning straightness, curvature, roughness, smoothness, four-sidedness, three-sidedness, two-cubit size, three-cubit size, largeness, smallness, shortness, length, and the like, since they seem to signify a position of parts and scarcely any different nature. A thing is called rough or uneven whose parts partly project and partly recede; smooth, when all its parts are flattened straight and evenly. You will find the same in the other cases. Are not all these positions, then, but qualities concerned with position? For from the fact that parts are arranged, joined, and fashioned in this or that way, sense judges them to be rough or smooth, two cubits or three cubits—not conversely. The same judgement must apply to the other things of this kind. Thus each of them must be held not as a position, but as a quality proceeding from, and constituted around, position. [Col. 1266B]

This genus does indeed seem to admit contraries. We might suppose sitting and standing to be contrary, if contraries are things which cannot be present in one thing at the same time, but alternate in turn. The person who sits can immediately stand, and the one who stands can sit, though not at the same time. But if we decide that sitting and standing are contraries, we must immediately accept the inconvenience that not one contrary but several are assigned to one thing. For by that argument sitting and standing are no more proved contrary than sitting and reclining, since no one can sit, stand, and recline at the same instant, though one can do so successively. Therefore positions of this sort must be established as not contrary to one another.

Perhaps, however, it is not altogether unprecedented that several contraries should at times correspond to one thing, if both whiteness and blackness are known to be contrary to pallor, since they fall under the same genus and also change mutually into one another. Or are whiteness and blackness not contraries to pallor? For pallor and the other intermediate colours cannot subsist unmixed; rather, all are blended and compounded from blackness and whiteness. Therefore wherever [Col. 1266D] pallor or another colour of this sort appears, both blackness and whiteness must be understood to be there.

Further, contraries concern the same genus of nature. Sitting and reclining do not concern the same genus, because sitting is especially proper to human beings, while reclining is more widely shared: a horse no less reclines or lies down than a man does. Nor can they be intensified or diminished, because position is not more or less sitting than reclining, nor is someone who sits or reclines more or less sitting or reclining than another.

The particular feature of every position is that, among forms which come upon a thing from without, it most closely pertains to substance. For position seems to be nothing other than the natural ordering of the parts of a substance: either an ordering which belongs to certain things immediately from their origin, as to rough and smooth, hairy and hairless things; or an ordering not natural in that sense, but born from a frequent and customary movement of nature, such as reclining and sitting. [Col. 1267A] Therefore whatever comes upon a thing from without and most closely pertains to substance must be position. Conversely, whatever is position must come upon it from without and closely pertain to substance.

Having is the application of both the body and the things around the body, through which the former is denominated as having and the latter as being had. These terms are not applied from the covering of the whole body, but only from the covering of its parts: for example, being trousered, armed, shod, or wearing a broad-brimmed hat. Such things, however, are not named by primitive and simple terms but by derived and artificial ones: armour, footwear, sandals; and whenever usage demands them, such words must be coined in the same fashion.

Having admits more and less. An armoured cavalryman seems more armed than a light-armed skirmisher or infantryman; and someone who wears both *gallicae* and shoes seems more shod than one who wears only shoes or only *gallicae*. Some cases, however, do not admit more and less, such as being clothed or wearing a tunic. Nor is one state of having contrary to another, such as being armed, shod, or sleeved, because one and the same person can be armed, shod, and sleeved. [Col. 1267B]

The property of having is to exist in more than one thing—that is, both in the body and in the things around the body. For having, as I have said, is the application of the body and of things around the body, named not from the whole of them but only from the covering of parts. Very few other categories bear this distinction, namely quantity and relation alone. For similarity and dissimilarity subsist in many similar and dissimilar things, and the same number concerns many numbered things, constantly increasing through the accession of multiple units, so that nothing seems distributed among more things than number. Yet the difference is that not every quantity and not every relation shares this feature, whereas every having does: namely, that it is the same in many things. [Col. 1267C] Therefore whatever is both in the body and in the things which surround the body is called having. Hence the most distinctive property of having will be that it is present, as it were, in several things—both in the body and in the things which surround the body part by part.

The verb “to have” is understood in many ways. A quality is said to be had, as whiteness or blackness; likewise quantity and measure, as thickness or tallness. For to have blackness or thickness is nothing other than to be black or thick. Containers are also said to have what they contain—for example, a sextarius has wheat. Many things are said to be had in parts, as a ring on the thumb; this means nothing other than that the thumb is in the ring. A husband has a wife, and a wife a husband; but this manner of having is unusual and foreign, in that the one who has is also said to be had. Yet this signifies nothing other than a wife’s cohabitation with her husband. [Col. 1268A]

Thus it is clear that the most familiar meanings of this word fall within five classes. Others may perhaps be noted, but they must be left to the diligence of investigators. We are content to have spoken thus far concerning the six principles; those who seek the rest must be referred to the book entitled *Analytics*.

Things are thought to admit more and less in one of three ways. Some say that intensification and diminution consist in the increase and decrease of subjects; some, in the increase and decrease of the things received and contained in subjects; others make both of these the causes. We shall consider which of the three opinions [Col. 1268B] is most true. It must be understood that, if the first and second are overthrown, the third, which is compounded from the association of the two, will immediately be overthrown as well.

First, we cannot maintain at all that increases and decreases of subjects cause a thing to be described as more or less with distinction. Otherwise, when people assert that man, animal, or substance of that sort admits more and less, no answer could be made. For if we admit that intensification and diminution arise from increases and decreases of subjects, the same horse can both increase and decrease and consequently will be called greater or smaller than a stone, although the stone has never undergone increase or diminution. A mountain too is called greater than another mountain, though certainly neither grows nor diminishes. Likewise a pearl is called whiter than a horse, one white thing than another; yet there is no doubt that the pearl does not exceed the horse in magnitude.

Thus this conclusion will stand: either a pearl is whiter than a horse through the pearl’s magnitude and the horse’s smallness; or it is rashly asserted that a pearl is whiter than a horse; or absolutely nothing admits more and less through the magnitude and smallness—the increase and decrease—of subjects. But neither the first nor the second is true. Therefore the third remains: nothing at all admits more and less through increase and decrease of subjects. [Col. 1268C]

Nor can the second opinion be defended, which holds that intensification and diminution consist through the magnitude and smallness of the things received and contained in subjects. For if one thing could be whiter than another through a greater magnitude of whiteness, then both man and horse would be called whiter than a pearl; the area and extent of whiteness are greater in man and horse than in a pearl.

Further, if more and less do not arise from the measure of subjects, as we have proved, how will they arise from the measure of accidents? For the measure of what is received is contained and limited within the measure of its subject, and cannot be extended beyond it; the limit and boundary of each measure is generally the body itself. “Great” and “small” are terms of measure. Therefore, so to speak, smallness cannot be considered beyond the small body itself, because as much as is removed from the thing extended, so much also perishes from its measure. From this [Col. 1269A] it is apparent that differences of more and less arise neither through increase and decrease of subject nor of accident. If this is certainly not so through either separately, neither is it so through both together. Therefore another account must be offered for why some things seem capable of intensification and diminution.

These are things which happen to bear the name of some accidental form, not through the magnitude of the subject but because they are either nearer to the form whose name they have acquired or more remote from it. Thus “more” is said of what has approached the definition of the name; “less,” of what has receded from it. For example, a thing in which pure whiteness is present is called white without qualification. The nearer any thing affected with white comes to the force of this name, the whiter it is called. But “small” and “little” exist solely by comparison. For whatever, when compared with other things, is surpassed in bodily size, we call small and little. Therefore whatever is surpassed in extent is immediately judged smaller and shorter; and likewise in the other cases.

But it is asked why these admit more and less, while substances do not. Perhaps because terms applied to substances do not stand open-ended, but indicate things always fixed at a limit and, so to speak, at a summit beyond which nothing can proceed. Some accidents also do not admit more and less, such as quadrangularity, triangularity, and the like. This occurs either because they are represented in describing substance—for we call both body itself and quantity triangular—or because, like substances, they are always at a limit beyond which they cannot advance. [Col. 1269C] The same appears in superlatives: “whitest” and “blackest” seem free from the differences of more and less, because they possess the highest degree and a boundary beyond which they cannot advance.

From what can be, it does not follow that what cannot be can be. Therefore, if all points are joined, no magnitude is produced, because points added to points contribute nothing by accumulation. Simple generation and simple destruction occur not by the approach or departure of indivisible particles, which they call atoms, but because, for example, a whole body of air passes and changes into another whole.

Every subject has two things: matter and form. Whenever both are changed, then properly speaking simple generation and simple destruction occur, although the generation of fire is even simpler than that of earth. Fire contains the character, as it were, of form; earth is nearer to matter. But when a musical man is said, as it were, to perish or be corrupted, and an unmusical man, as it were, to arise or be generated, the subject—the man himself—remains. [Col. 1270A] Otherwise, if these were not qualities, namely being musical and being unmusical, but substances, then their generation and destruction too would be completely simple.

But they are qualities and certain affections of man, not substances. Thus both the generation and the destruction of the musical and unmusical man appear not to be generation and destruction without qualification, but a certain quasi-generation or coming-to-be and a certain quasi-destruction or perishing, since musical and unmusical, as I have said, are affections of the surviving and remaining man. Nor should a change of this kind be called generation or destruction, but only alteration. Matter itself, however, is properly the subject of generation and destruction.

But why is one who is being taught not said simply to be made or generated, but said to be made learned or generated learned? Perhaps this has been explained in the volume entitled *Categories*: some terms signify this particular thing and substance, others quantity, others quality. Therefore whatever does not signify substance will not be said simply to perish or arise, but only in a qualified sense. [Col. 1270C] Some accidents nevertheless belong naturally to substances according to the nature of each: for example, the downward tendency of earth and the upward tendency of fire.

## In the Year of the Lord 1157: Hugh Metellus, Regular Canon

[Col. 1269]

## Historical-Literary Notice

(Mabillon, *Analecta*, new edition, p. 476.)

The letters of Hugh Metellus in a manuscript codex of the Clermont Library at Paris number more than fifty-five. This codex was most kindly made available to us by the learned and religious John Hardouin, second librarian of that same library, who is devoting vigorous effort to the correction of Pliny. From these letters one may learn who Hugh Metellus was and at what time he lived. Born at Toul in the territory of the Leuci, he studied under Tiecelin and was also a pupil of Anselm of Laon. He had as a fellow-student a certain Humbert [Col. 1271], to whom he addresses Letter 40 thus: “To Humbert, once a philosopher, now a theologian.” And below: “We grew up together; together we put our hands beneath the rod; together, as time advanced, we toiled over grammar; together we served in Aristotle’s camp. At Toul I declaimed with you; in arithmetic I counted with you; in music I mused with you; beneath Gemini I was born with you.”

When already of advanced age, he turned to the Regular Canons of Saint Augustine in the abbey of Saint Leo, in the diocese of Toul, under Abbot Siebaud, in whose name he wrote Letter 18 to Abbot William. He mentions this conversion of his in Letter 11, addressed to Gemma, a son of Saint Benedict, in these words: “I changed my mind; I changed my dress. Instead of a little fur cloak smelling of a foreign mouse, I am wrapped in sheep’s skin; instead of marten skin, I am clothed in goatskin; instead of delicate foods, choice products of earth and water, cheap little vegetables, rustic legumes, and the bean akin to Pythagoras please me; instead of nectar-like drink, the drink of oats and the drink of water please me.” And in the first letter to Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, he says that, having shorn his hair and drawn up a written bill of repudiation, he had given notice to his former way of life. “After all this,” he says, “I devoted myself to the Rule of Blessed Augustine and shut myself in the cloister of the white Nazareans.”

From this it is clear at what time this Hugh lived; and this is confirmed by his other letters, which he wrote to Pope Innocent II, Albero of Trier, Stephen of Metz, Guilencus of Langres, Henry of the Leuci, and Embrico of Würzburg, bishops; likewise to Peter Abelard and Heloise, abbess of the Paraclete. In Letter 4, to Innocent, against Peter Abelard, he says: “After the death of Anselm of Laon and William of Châlons, the fire of the word of God failed on earth”; although he praises Saint Bernard and sets him against Peter Abelard. Worth noting is the heading of Letter 21: “To Embrico, venerable bishop and duke of Würzburg, Hugh Metellus [wishes him] worthily to administer to God the dignity of each office”; it shows that even at that time this bishop possessed ducal dignity. In Letter 41, addressed to the cardinals, he attacks the Norbertines for the extravagance of their clothing; and, reproaching them with novelty, explains, according to his own understanding, the origin of his own order.

He dedicates Letter 34 to “Hugh of Chartres, venerable master,” a title customarily used of teachers of letters. Thus at that time there were five Hughs of some distinction in letters: foremost Hugh of Saint Victor; then Hugh of Fouilloy, Hugh Farsitus, Hugh of Chartres the master, and Hugh Metellus—apart from Hugh of Fleury, surnamed “of Lady Mary,” who was older than the others.

Letter 33, written to Gerlandus, is directed—if the author deals honestly with his opponent—against certain remnants of the Berengarian heresy. Metellus had likewise sent him another letter in which he had assembled examples concerning the most holy sacrament of the Eucharist. Among all Metellus’s letters, only one can be referred to this matter, namely Letter 26, addressed to Gerard, a monk of tested spirit. This Gerard was undoubtedly the same man as Gerlandus, and the copyist has erred in one of the two names. In Letter 26 Gerard asks whether Christ’s body ought to be received daily; then whether that which is consecrated on the altar is the true body of Christ, or a figure of the body reigning in heaven. Metellus answers the first question by the authority of Ambrose and Augustine; the second as follows:

“For the differing—indeed, not to say opposing—opinions of different people compel you to doubt and pull you in different directions. For Augustine says that those Gospel words are figurative: ‘Unless you eat,’ etc. (John 6), and that they signify nothing else than that Christ suffered. Likewise: ‘Why do you prepare tooth and stomach? Believe, and you have eaten.’ You therefore raise the question why Blessed Augustine calls these words of the Lord figurative, when the Church, faithful Zion, believes that the consecrated bread is Christ’s true flesh. But the man filled with the Spirit of God turned his eye toward Christ’s intention, and under the designation of body and blood, by figurative speech, wished the faith of his Passion to be veiled from unbelievers and revealed to friends: namely, faith working through love; namely, the fellowship of head and members, and their union; namely, spiritual eating, not sacramental eating; the reality of the sacrament, not the sacrament; the power and efficacy of the sacrament, not the sacrament. Truth itself subsequently makes this plainly understood when it adds: ‘He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood’ (ibid.)—he prepares a dwelling for me. This plainly excludes sacramental eating, which some receive to their own condemnation.”

And below: “It is certain, because the outcome proves it, that the faith of the Roman Church, according to God’s promise, has never failed nor been corrupted by any heresy. The Roman Church has held to the aforesaid faith concerning Christ’s body and has faithfully persevered in it; through its preachers it has spread that faith far and wide.”

In this letter Gerard’s faith was not yet suspect to Metellus, since he calls him a monk of tested spirit. He recognizes only a doubt put before him, not an error. These words prove it expressly: “You therefore raise the question why Blessed Augustine calls the Lord’s words figurative, when the Church, faithful Zion, believes that the consecrated bread is Christ’s true flesh.” Gerard therefore acknowledged the Church’s faith. But because perhaps he was not entirely persuaded by Metellus’s answer to the doubt raised on Augustine’s testimony, Metellus—whose moderation no less than whose gravity of judgment is otherwise to be desired in his remaining letters—rashly accused Gerard, or Gerlandus, of error.

[Col. 1273]

# LETTERS OF HUGH METELLUS

## I. To Saint Bernard.—He elaborately pursues Bernard’s praises.

[Col. 1273A]

(It appears among the letters of Saint Bernard. See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXV, col. 687.)

## II. To the same.—He attempts to clear himself and his associates from an accusation.

(See ibid., col. 688.)

## III. To Abbot William, in the person of his own abbot.—He excuses his somewhat harsh reply to the calumnies of his Herbert.

(See the place cited above, col. 690.)

## IV. To Gerlandus.—On the most holy sacrament of the Eucharist.

(Mabillon, *Analecta*, new edition, p. 475.)

[Col. 1273B]

HUGH METELLUS TO GERLANDUS, burdened and honoured with knowledge of the trivium and quadrivium: may you thresh and carefully sift the words of Holy Scripture.

Physicians maintain that a swelling in the flesh arises from an excess of humours. Scripture writers assert that pride grows in the mind from an overabundance of knowledge. It is certain that you possess very great ability; it is manifest that you excel in manifold learning. You must therefore beware lest the knowledge in which you excel defile you and mingle fault with your praise.

[Col. 1273C] Understand what I say. The words that you sow among the people concerning the body and blood of the Lord savour of heresy, and, under your leadership, have drawn very many into the abyss of error. You put confidence in Augustine’s words. Do not put confidence in them. He is not with you in this opinion. You err throughout the whole way. You maintain with Blessed Augustine that the Lord’s words, spoken to his disciples concerning his body and blood, are figurative. For the Lord’s words have one sound and another figurative meaning. You assert what he asserted, but you do not understand what he understood. For he understood that the Lord spoke and meant spiritual eating, which is shared only by the good; not sacramental eating, which is shared by good and evil alike. This is made clear by the Lord’s following words: “He who eats my body and drinks my blood” (1 Cor. 10). For many eat [Col. 1273D] Christ’s flesh and are not members of Christ.

When one head of the hydra is cut off, many more things contrary to orthodox faith spring up again. Again, you object: “What takes place on the altar is a sacrament; a sacrament is a sign of a sacred thing; but the sign is not the thing signified.” Granted: I agree. Sacramental incorporation into Christ [Col. 1274A] is a sign of the union by which we are united and shall be united with Christ; it is not that union itself, but sign and thing signified differ from each other. Hence Augustine: “A sacrament is the visible form of invisible grace.” Or: the word *sacrament* is derived from a secret, and what takes place on the altar is secret. For what it is, or what it signifies, does not appear. It is indeed something other than what the outward appearance represents.

As I see it, you gnaw the crust but do not touch the crumb. You lean upon Augustine’s authority, but you are deceived. For Augustine, whom you have procured as your advocate, if you investigate carefully, you will find to be against you. Hear him proclaiming in a certain psalm, to the confusion of you and your like: “That very blood which the Jews shed while persecuting, the Jews afterwards [Col. 1274B] drank when believing.” Observe also what David did before Achish, king of Gath: how he carried himself in his own hands; and how Blessed Augustine explained it in his exposition of the title of Psalm 33. Do not be King Achish; do not say, “How can it be? How can anyone carry himself?”

Do not say: “If it is Christ’s true body, it cannot be in different places at the same time.” For if you say this, you will condemn yourself by your own mouth. You will not deny that the Virgin gave birth; you will not deny that Christ entered the disciples while the doors were shut. For if the former is denied because it does not accord with nature, these things too must be denied because nature resists them. Yield; rest. [Col. 1274C] For if you seek parallels, they are not singular; if you seek reason, they are not wonderful. “Faith,” as Blessed Gregory says, “has no merit where human reason provides proof.” And Blessed Augustine says: “Do not seek the order of nature in Christ’s body when his birth itself was from a virgin. Here nature is astonished and loses its order. Christ from a virgin; Christ from bread. The law of nature is disturbed.”

But if the sanctified bread is not Christ’s body but a figure of Christ’s body, as you assert—as many believe with you, or rather as the great error of many erring persons holds—I greatly wonder why the Apostle so earnestly forbids anyone to approach it unworthily. “Whoever receives unworthily,” he says, “eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (ibid.). Why is this? Because he does not discern the Lord’s body [Col. 1274D] but compares it, as it were, to common foods. Therefore many who receive unworthily become weak, and many die.

But if the bread of the altar is simply bread, as you say, sanctified by God’s word and the priest’s prayer, and possesses such power that it can weaken and bring one to the sleep of death—why [Col. 1275A] can bread at our table, sanctified by a priest’s prayer, not do this? Of it the Apostle says to Timothy: “Every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving. For it is sanctified through God’s word and prayer” (1 Tim. 4). The word sanctifies; the prayer obtains. That bread is bread, and this too is bread; that one is sanctified, and this one too is sanctified. Why can that one do more than this? Why can that one forgive sins, and not this one? If you do not know, I shall explain. Upon the altar, the one who sanctifies and the one sanctified are the same. The priest and the offering are the same; the one who sacrifices and the one sacrificed are the same; God and man are the same. These are God’s mighty works, exalting his name: not impossible, but fearful; not to be examined by arguments, but venerated by faith. [Col. 1275B] What is more fearful than that, at the prayer of Blessed Gregory, the bread of the altar assumed the appearance of flesh? This was done by the Lord to remove your doubt. Return, then.

Hear further what your patron Augustine still says. Hear what he says on that verse of the Psalmist: “Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but you prepared a body for me” (Psalm 39): “One sacrifice,” he says, “has been prepared in place of the many legal sacrifices. What one sacrifice? Namely, Christ’s body, which you know—which not all of you know; and may those of you who know it not know it to judgment!” He sets forth three things: that some know Christ’s body, some do not know it; and he wishes that those who know it may not know it to judgment. For “he who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.” And a little later, in the same place: “We know what we receive; and [Col. 1276A] may you come to know him whom you do not know, and, when you have learned it, may you not receive it to judgment. For he who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.” Do not suppose that he said this of the sanctified bread of the altar, but of Christ’s true body. For if it were merely bread, who would not recognize bread? Why is bread spoken of, and yet not all are said to know it? But without doubt he understood Christ’s body to be present under the appearance of bread, and therefore said that those who receive unworthily receive it to judgment.

Return to yourself, brother; return. Recall your mind, which has journeyed abroad into a far country. Do not eat the husks of swine; do not eat the refuse of wheat. Do you not see that, when the sun rises in the morning, mountains are illuminated first and valleys afterwards? Do you not see religious men and teachers of great renown [Col. 1276B] standing in this opinion and persisting in this faith: that the sanctified bread of the altar is no longer bread, but the true body of Christ? If this is true—indeed, because it is true—that Christ prayed to the Father for the support of Peter’s faith; and if it is true—indeed, because it is true—that Peter’s faith concerning the Lord’s body and blood, derived from him, has flowed down to our own times, uncorrupted, through the succession of apostolic men: because this is true, cease from your error—indeed, your horror—and hasten to restore in yourself the faith of Peter, the faith of the Roman See, which through you has been stripped of its crust; and hasten to reunite yourself to Mother Church. I could bring forward many examples from the holy Fathers of the Roman See concerning this faith; but because I assembled and collected them in another letter to be made known to you, I considered it best to refrain here.

# A.D. 1145–1159: BLESSED AMADEUS, BISHOP OF LAUSANNE

[Col. 1277]

# HISTORICAL-LITERARY NOTICE, BY DOM ABBOT J. GREMAUD

(*Mémorial de Fribourg*, Fribourg, 1854, first year, April, p. 126)

[Col. 1277A] Saint Amadeus, bishop of Lausanne, was born at the castle of Chaste, near Saint-Antoine, in the Dauphiné (department of Isère). He was the son of Amadeus of Hauterive and Petronilla, sister of Guigues VII, Dauphin of the Viennois.

[Note: [Col. 1277B] Haller, *Bibliothek der Schweizer-Geschichte*, III, 339, following the *Lives of Several Saints of the House of Tonnerre*, Paris, 1698, among which is the Life of Saint Amadeus. This Guigues VII is doubtless the one designated as Guigues IV in the *Art de vérifier les dates* (1770 edition, p. 759), and as Guigues III by Duchesne and Baluze. He was the first count of Albon to be surnamed Dauphin. We do not know on what Haller’s and the author of the *Lives*’ assertion rests, but it does not agree with the original biography of Amadeus the father, who is there called the nephew, not the brother-in-law or son-in-law, of the count of Albon. (Manrique, *Annales Cistercienses*, vol. I, p. 134.) We lack the books and documents needed to clarify this difficulty.]

Amadeus of Hauterive was lord of six towns or castles, and bore the name of the principal one, where he was born.

[Note: [Col. 1277C] Manrique, *loc. cit.*, p. 103. The Life of Amadeus the father was written shortly after his death by an anonymous author, at the request of Burno of Boiron, prior of Bonnevaux and afterwards abbot of Liuncelle. Manrique [Col. 1278B] reproduced part of this Life in his *Annals of Cîteaux*; it is our principal source for the early years of Saint Amadeus’s life, which the anonymous author relates together with that of his father.]

His biographer and several documents tell us that he was related to the emperors of Germany.

[Note: [Col. 1278B] Manrique, *loc. cit.*, and a diploma of Emperor [Col. 1278C] Frederick I, from the year 1455.]

Amadeus appears to have had only two children: a son bearing his father’s name, and a daughter whose name is unknown.

[Note: [Col. 1278C] Manrique, *loc. cit.*, and *Mémoires et Documents Romands*, VI, 44. (Since we shall often cite, in this) collection, the memoirs and documents published by the Society of History of French-speaking Switzerland, we shall cite them by the abbreviation: *Mém. et Doc. Rom.*—Since the Society of History and Archaeology of Geneva also publishes its works under the same title, we shall designate them by the abbreviation: *Mém. et Doc. Gen.*]

The birth of the younger Amadeus must be placed about the year 1110, as what follows will prove.

Amadeus of Hauterive shone among the lords [Col. 1277B] his neighbours. “He was courageous in war, illustrious in arms, far-seeing in his designs, cheerful, affable, of commanding stature, kindly toward his own people, and terrible to his enemies.”

[Note: [Col. 1278C] Manrique, *loc. cit.*]

Despite these advantages and his power, he decided to leave the world and embrace the religious life in the Order of Cîteaux, which was then beginning to flourish in neighbouring regions. Desiring to restore the exact observance of the Rule of Saint Benedict, some religious, led by Saint Robert, a gentleman [Col. 1278A] of Champagne, withdrew to a wilderness called Cîteaux, five leagues from Dijon, in the diocese of Châlons. They settled there on 2 March 1098. The convent maintained its full regularity under the following abbots, Alberic and Stephen; but as the monks dwindled through death and no one came forward to replace them because of the austerities and poverty of the convent, Abbot Saint Stephen despaired of leaving successors. Then, in 1113, Saint Bernard entered Cîteaux with thirty companions. The virtues of these religious touched the hearts of many people, who imitated their example. It became necessary to consider building new monasteries, and they multiplied so greatly that fifty years later [Col. 1278B] there were five hundred abbeys dependent upon Cîteaux. The order was based on the literal observance of the Rule of Saint Benedict, and it was definitively constituted in the year 1119.

[Note: [Col. 1278C] *Dictionary of Religious Orders*, by Fr. Hélyot, Migne edition, I, 920 ff.—Manrique, *Annales Cistercienses*, I, 6 ff.—*Life of Saint Bernard.*]

Like many other lords, Amadeus of Hauterive felt himself drawn toward this life of penitence and virtue, but he did not wish to embrace it alone. Having made his decision, he remained another year in the world and devoted this time to winning companions in penitence; nor was this in vain. In the Dauphiné itself a monastery of the Order of Cîteaux had recently arisen: Bonnevaux, founded in 1117 through the care of Guy of Burgundy, archbishop of Vienne.

[Note: [Col. 1279D] Manrique, *loc. cit.*, p. 93.]

There, in 1119, Amadeus appeared with sixteen knights and his young son. All were admitted as novices except the younger Amadeus, who, still a child, could not be received because of his age. He was nevertheless kept in the convent in order to apply him to the study of letters. The following year, Amadeus and his companions, having completed their novitiate, all irrevocably dedicated themselves to the Lord by religious vows. Meanwhile the younger Amadeus gave himself to study; but his father, seeing that his education was not carefully enough provided by [Col. 1279B] the monks of Bonnevaux,

[Note: [Col. 1279D] In the Order of Cîteaux, studies occupied only a secondary place; the monks’ principal occupations were chanting in choir, meditation, and manual work.]

left that convent with his son in 1121 in order to go to Cluny,

[Note: [Col. 1279D] The abbey of Cluny, one of the most famous in France, was situated in the territory of Mâcon, on the river Grosne. It was founded in 910 by William the Pious, duke of Aquitaine. Blessed Berno was its first abbot; his successors included Saint Odo, Saint Mayeul, Saint Odilo, Saint Hugh, and others. Abbot Pons, who governed the abbey at Amadeus’s arrival, did not imitate the holiness of his predecessors.—The Order of Cluny followed the Rule of Saint Benedict, but at that time less rigorously than Cîteaux, and allotted a greater place to literary study. *Dictionary of Religious Orders*, by Fr. Hélyot; Migne edition, I, 1002 ff.]

where he was received with the highest honours. A few days later, the younger Amadeus was sent to Germany to his relative Emperor Henry V. The emperor received him kindly, gave him the most renowned teachers, and cared for him as though he were his own son. Seeing his son’s education thus secured, Amadeus returned to Bonnevaux in the same year. The son remained with the emperor until the latter’s death in 1125. Having then been instructed in sacred and secular learning, and having reached the required age for entering religion, he left the court for the cloister and presented himself that same year at the abbey of Clairvaux. There, received with joy and honour, he took [Col. 1279C] the religious habit.

[Note: [Col. 1280D] Manrique, *loc. cit.*, pp. 104, 121, and 159.]

Clairvaux, a monastery dependent upon Cîteaux, was situated fifteen leagues from Langres in Champagne. It had been founded in 1115 by Saint Bernard in the midst of a wilderness called the Valley of Wormwood, and had been given to Cîteaux by Hugh, count of Troyes. Saint Bernard was abbot of Clairvaux for thirty-eight years and ended his life there.

[Note: [Col. 1280D]

Manrique, *loc. cit.*, I, 78 ff. *Life of Saint Bernard*, in Godescard, under 20 August. Original Life of the saint, among his works.

> Hidden amid the mountains lay a valley, covered then  
> with lofty woodland and green bramble.  
> The men of old deservedly called it Clairvaux;  
> they changed your name, bitter valley.  
> Although shady mountains surround it on every side,  
> none in the whole world was more renowned.

Nic. Hacqueville, president of the Paris Senate, in the works of Saint Bernard, Paris, 1513.]

There Amadeus the son spent the first years of his religious life, under the guidance of that house’s holy abbot. He made rapid progress in Christian perfection and early acquired a great reputation for learning and holiness. Thus, despite his youth, he was soon [Col. 1280A] judged worthy to direct others in the practice of religious virtues. Saint Bernard himself chose him as abbot of Hautecombe.

This monastery, situated on the shores of Lake Bourget in Savoy, had been founded by Amadeus III, count of Savoy. Historians disagree about the year of its foundation: Guichenon

[Note: [Col. 1280D] *Genealogical History of Savoy*, Turin, 1778, I, 223.]

and Besson

[Note: [Col. 1280D] *Memoirs for the Ecclesiastical History of the Dioceses of Geneva, etc.*, p. 129.]

place it in the year 1125, and Manrique

[Note: [Col. 1280D] *Annales Cistercienses*, I, 301.]

in 1135; the latter date is based on an ancient chronology of the Order of Cîteaux. The original foundation appears truly to go back to 1125, and for about ten years the convent was occupied by Benedictine monks

[Note: [Col. 1280D] Not monks of Saint Basil, as Guichenon, *loc. cit.*, says.]

who had come from the nearby abbey of Aulps. In 1135 Hautecombe adopted the reform of Cîteaux, whence monks came [Col. 1280B] to teach the practices of the new order. The first abbot of Hautecombe was Blessed Vivien, a close friend of Saint Bernard. Wearied by the exercise of his office, Vivien left Hautecombe in 1139 and retired to Clairvaux. The monks requested Amadeus to replace him, and Saint Bernard, with the monks’ consent, gave him to them as abbot.

The condition of the convent entrusted to Saint Amadeus was then far from flourishing. Recently founded, it was still poor; and its location in a deserted and barren place, together with the barbarity of neighbouring peoples, hindered its prosperity. When Amadeus the father came to visit his son at Hautecombe, he was alarmed by the difficulties confronting the convent. [Col. 1280C] He advised the abbot to leave so disadvantageous a site. “The soil is barren,” he told him, “and if through great labour you manage to make it yield some fruit, you see it taken away from you by greedy neighbours.” “If they take away,” the son replied, “our temporal goods, they cannot likewise deprive us of the eternal goods obtained by our labours. Since these eternal goods are what we seek, we shall find no place and no population more favourable.” Thus our holy abbot courageously remained at the post assigned him. Soon his virtues, and those of the monks whom he formed by [Col. 1281A] his example, drew temporal goods to the convent along with heavenly blessings. In seeking the kingdom of God, he found the prosperity of his house.

[Note: [Col. 1281D] Manrique, *loc. cit.*, p. 377.]

We know no particular facts about Amadeus’s administration; only one document relating to his time as abbot has come down to us. Amadeus III, count of Savoy, grants to Amadeus the abbot and to the brothers of Hautecombe the allodial land which he possesses on the shore of the place called Castellion (Lake Bourget), land formerly called Charaya and then Hautecombe. The other persons who owned part of this land likewise gave it to the said religious.

[Note: [Col. 1281D] Guichenon, *History of Savoy*, IV, 31.]

Guichenon gives us this document as the foundation charter of Hautecombe, but it is evidently only confirmation of an earlier donation; such confirmations were often made in the form of a simple gift, and we shall find an example below. The same author maintains that this document is from the year 1125, but admits that the original bears no date.

[Note: [Col. 1281D] Ibid., I, 224.]

To assign it to that year and regard it as a foundation document, it would have to have been made in favour of the first abbot, Vivien, rather than Amadeus, his successor.

Saint Amadeus governed Hautecombe only for a few years; soon he was called to a higher dignity. In 1144 Guy of Marlanie, bishop of Lausanne, was obliged to resign the episcopate because of his misconduct.

[Note: [Col. 1281D] *Mém. et Doc. Rom.*, VI, 42.]

His last known [Col. 1281C] act is dated 24 February 1144.

[Note: [Col. 1281D] Mathile, *Monuments of the History of Neuchâtel*, no. XI.]

Amadeus, abbot of Hautecombe, was chosen to succeed him; clergy and people accepted him with unanimous acclamation.

[Note: [Col. 1281D] Manrique, *loc. cit.*, p. 463.]

By his qualities and virtues, he appeared to them most worthy of the episcopate. The extent of the diocese, and the then-frequent violence and usurpations, required of the bishop of this see a high degree of activity, firmness, and self-denial. Amadeus combined piety and prudence with these qualities. But, deeming himself unworthy of so great an honour, he refused the dignity to which he was called. Nevertheless, he was enthroned despite his resistance; and, to secure his final acceptance, the supreme pontiff was asked to confirm his election. The pope, knowing Amadeus’s virtues, ordered him to accept the episcopate, allowing no excuse to be accepted.

[Note: [Col. 1282D] Manrique, *loc. cit.*]

He was consecrated on 21 January 1145, the feast-day of Saint Agnes. If the tradition preserved by Conon of Estavayé is reliable, this day was a privileged day for our bishop.

[Note: [Col. 1282D] *Mém. et Doc. Rom.*, VI, 43.]

It was on this feast day that he was born, first applied to the study of letters, entered [Col. 1282A] monastic life, and was made first abbot and then bishop.

In the same year Eugene III ascended the papal throne. This pope, formerly a monk of Clairvaux and a disciple of Saint Bernard, honoured Amadeus with particular confidence and entrusted him with the conduct of several affairs.

From his promotion onward, the new bishop of Lausanne gave free course to his zeal. He exercised the ministry of preaching with talent, for he was eloquent and spoke with unction. He visited the many districts of his diocese, some of which, situated in Alpine regions, were difficult of access. At Grindelwald in the Oberland, 3,510 feet above sea level, he consecrated a church built [Col. 1282B] of wood.

[Note: [Col. 1282D] Notes of M. Dey.]

By prayer he implored God’s blessing upon his labours, and he always had a tender devotion to the Blessed Virgin Mary. Here is how the biographer of his father presents Amadeus in the midst of his pastoral duties:

> “As soon as he was raised to the episcopal see, he reflected on the Apostle’s statement that a bishop must be blameless, and on the saying of a doctor that the greater the gifts, the stricter will be the account to be rendered for them. Therefore each day he examined his actions and governed himself, as well as his diocesan people, with as much care as though he had to appear before God at every moment. He was just in his judgments, far-seeing in his designs, faithful to his word, defender of widows, support of orphans, comforter of prisoners, promoter of the good of the poor, avenger of injustice, enemy of envy, friend of justice, chastity, and thrift, zealous for vigils and fasts, diligent in visiting the sick and relieving the poor, restrained in correction, full of zeal, discreet in speech, and fervent in piety.”

[Note: [Col. 1282D] Manrique, *loc. cit.*, p. 463.]

We find the same praises of Saint Amadeus in a letter sent to him shortly after his election by Nicholas, then a monk of Cluny and later of Clairvaux, and secretary to Saint Bernard. This letter shows that the holy bishop had retained his taste for study amid pastoral occupations. Nicholas [Col. 1282D] sends him Master Anselm’s treatise on the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 1282D] We reproduce this letter below.]

Amadeus’s father had the consolation of seeing his son raised to episcopal dignity. He died about the years 1148–1150, leaving in the Order of Cîteaux the reputation of a saint.

[Note: [Col. 1282D] Manrique, *loc. cit.*, II, 312.]

Since the temporal possessions of the bishopric of Lausanne depended directly upon the Empire, Amadeus sought [Col. 1283A] confirmation of them from Emperor Conrad II, then only king of Germany. By a diploma issued at Worms in 1145, he took under his protection the Church of Lausanne and its possessions, namely Murten, Lutry, Carbarissa (Chexbres), Corsier, Cubizacha (Cully), and Lugnorre. He granted to the bishop all that Rudolf of Rheinfelden and his family had possessed between the Sarine, Mount Saint Bernard, the bridge of Geneva, the Jura, and the Alps, just as Emperor Henry IV had already granted these possessions to the same Church. Moreover, he declared void all alienations made by Bishop Lambert.

[Note: [Col. 1283C] See this diploma in *Mém. et Doc. Rom.*, VII, 13; Gerbert, *De Rodolpho Suevico*, p. 157; Schoepflin, *Historia Zähringensis Badensis*, V, 86. M. Verdeil provided a translation in his *History of the Canton of Vaud*, 2nd edition, I, 82. He translates *Carbarissa* as Corbières; we believe this is mistaken, since the bishops of Lausanne never held sovereignty over Corbières, whereas they did hold it over Chexbres. Even if our translation is not certain, it is at least more probable.]

Three years later, by a bull dated the third of the Ides of April 1148 (11 April), Pope Eugene III likewise took under his protection, and that of Saint Peter, [Col. 1283B] the Church of Lausanne and all its goods; ratified the grants of Emperor Henry IV; and annulled the alienations of Bishop Lambert.

[Note: [Col. 1283C] Manuscript of Monsignor Lentzbourg.]

Confirmed by pope and emperor in the temporal possessions of the bishopric, Amadeus turned to regulating his relations with his subjects and clergy. As a temporal prince, he depended only on the emperor through the feudal bond and, apart from that dependence, was sovereign lord in his lands. But this power was not arbitrary among the bishops of Lausanne; relations between lord and subjects were regulated by customs that had acquired the force of law through the bishops’ practical sanction. It was under Amadeus’s episcopate that the first written record of these customs, [Col. 1283C] which has come down to us, was drawn up. By the counsel of the canons, barons, and burgesses, Arducius, [Col. 1284A] bishop of Geneva, acting as provost of the chapter of Lausanne, caused these customs to be formally acknowledged in the presence of Bishop Amadeus. Here are found the foundations of Lausanne’s temporal constitution. Subsequently enlarged by new articles, this acknowledgement became, in the fourteenth century, a true constitution, divided into 172 articles and known as the *Plaict-général* of 1368. [Note: [Col. 1283C] See *Mémoires et Documents Romands*, VII, introduction, p. XX.]

We give here the translation of this first act. [Note: [Col. 1283C] It is the Cartulary of Lausanne that has preserved this act for us; it is reproduced in *Mémoires et [Col. 1283D] Documents Romands*, VI, 426, and VII, 7. In vol. VI, Amadeus’s name is omitted; we presume that this is through oversight, since vol. VII, which gives it, drew upon the same source. Mgr Verdeil gave a translation of it, *History of the Canton of Vaud*, I, 79, but it is far from accurate.]
