## General acknowledgements of the rights of the bishops of Lausanne and of the customs of the said city

Since justice requires, and custom prescribes, that the lord’s rights and customs be acknowledged to him within his jurisdiction, this acknowledgement [Col. 1284B] was made to the bishop of Lausanne by the clergy, the barons, [Note: [Col. 1283D] In the Middle Ages, the word *baron* had a very broad meaning. In France and England it was used for a citizen. See Du Cange, *Glossary*, under *Barones civitatis Londinensis*. In the *Plaict* of 1368, the word *baronibus* is in fact replaced by *civibus*, “citizens.”] the knights, and the burgesses. [Note: [Col. 1283D] At Lausanne, citizens and the city must not be confused with burgesses and the borough, or primitive town. See the notice on St Marius, p. 52 ff.]

The whole city of Lausanne, both the city proper and the borough, is the endowment [Note: [Col. 1283D] In ecclesiastical matters, *dos* means landed endowment granted to a church for its maintenance and that of its ministers. See Du Cange, *Glossary*, [Col. 1284C] under *Dos ecclesiae*.] and the allod [Note: [Col. 1284C] An allod generally denotes a landed estate, and more particularly land held in full ownership—that is, direct lordship—which is subject to no payment or service, whether real or personal. In this sense it is the opposite of a fief, which is held in another’s name and is subject to payments and services. See Du Cange, under *Alodis*.] of the Blessed Virgin Mary and of the church of Lausanne.

The canons have free election of the bishop and owe the king [Note: [Col. 1284C] “King” here denotes the sovereign, who was the emperor.] only processions and prayers. [Note: [Col. 1284C] We have translated this article word for word, but we believe that this is not its precise meaning, nor is it the meaning assigned to it by the anonymous Commentary [Col. 1284D] on the *Plaict-général* of 1368, printed in *Mémoires et Documents Romands*, VII, 315 ff. According to this Commentary, composed at the latest at the beginning of the fourteenth century, *regere* should be read in place of *regi* in the Latin text; the article would then have the following meaning, which seems to us the true one: “The canons ought only to direct the processions and prayers.”]

The lord bishop of Lausanne holds the regalian rights from the king. These rights are: the public highways, [Note: [Col. 1284D] And the common pastures, according to the anonymous Commentary, p. 318.] tolls, transfer dues, [Note: [Col. 1284D] A right of four deniers per pound, which the bishop levied on sales. The burgesses and citizens of Lausanne and certain inhabitants of the surrounding district were exempt from it. Anonymous Commentary, p. 319.] the Black Joux, [Note: [Col. 1284D] The term *joux noires* ordinarily denotes mountains covered with forest. Those of the bishopric lay above Lake Joux and La Part-Dieu. Anonymous Commentary, p. 319.] coinage, markets, measures, public usurers, the old *ban* fines and new ones established by common agreement, watercourses, thieves, and abductors.

[Col. 1284C] On account of these rights, the bishop is subject to the king in this respect: if the king, summoned for affairs of the bishopric [Col. 1285A] or of the city, arrives, he is owed provisions [Note: [Col. 1285C] That is, his expenses must be supplied.] in the evening and morning. The king has no other right or jurisdiction in the city of Lausanne. The aforesaid expenses must be paid by the burgesses dwelling outside the walls of the city and by the bishop’s three territories: Avenches, Curtilles, and Bulle. These provisions must be purchased by two members of the bishop’s household [Note: [Col. 1285C] *Familia*, “household,” generally denotes the whole body [Col. 1285D] of subordinates and servants attached to one lord and dependent upon him on various grounds. The members of the household could therefore have very different conditions or status. See Du Cange, under *Familia*.] and by two burgesses. For other matters, the bishop owes the king the customary service.

The advocate [Note: [Col. 1285D] The advocate, *advocatus* or *defensor*, was a lay lord to whom bishops and monasteries entrusted the custody and defence of their temporal possessions. Advocates acted as the churches’ legal representatives before courts and were obliged to defend ecclesiastical lands by arms. The advocacy will be discussed in greater detail in the second part of this work.] holds the advocacy from the bishop’s hands, with respect to what lies outside the city walls and the bishop’s aforesaid lands—Avenches, Bulle, and Curtilles—for which he must be the bishop’s liege man. [Note: [Col. 1285D] A liege man, *homo ligius*, is one who gives fealty to a lord against and for all persons. He must assist him against all who may live and die. (*Assizes of Jerusalem*.) Whoever has performed liege homage may not bind himself to another lord except with reservation of the first lord; and it is the latter [Col. 1286C] whom he must defend should war break out between the two lords. See Du Cange, under *Ligius*.]

[Col. 1285B] To the advocate’s right belongs a third of the *ban* fines in the borough of Lausanne and in the three lands designated above. The advocate has no share in escheats. [Note: [Col. 1286D] Confiscations.]

Burgesses capable of bearing arms must follow the *fuercri* [Note: [Col. 1286D] *Al-fuer-cri*, *al-for-cri*, *al-foris-cri*: “at the cry, ‘outside!’”] of the mayor, the seneschal, or the *sautier*, [Note: [Col. 1286D] The mayor, seneschal, and *sautier* were officers of the bishop’s household; they exercised a defined jurisdiction and were chiefly charged with enforcing sentences pronounced by the superior authorities—the bishop, the *plaict-général*, etc. For their rights and functions, see the anonymous Commentary, p. 367 ff.] under penalty of a *ban* fine of three sols; but this must be done in such a way that they may return home on the same day, unless by common counsel it is necessary to remain longer.

But if, by common counsel, the bishop himself or his lieutenant (*nonce*) proceeds against the enemies of the Church, anyone who has not followed him shall pay a *ban* fine of fifty sols.

[Col. 1285C] But if the lord bishop, by the advice of the leading men of his city, goes to the king on Church business, or if the king summons him to an announced court, two or three burgesses whom he wishes to take with him must supply the expenses going and returning. The bishop must reimburse them, and the expense shall be recovered in the borough of Lausanne and in the three aforesaid territories.

The burgesses must aid the lord bishop in acquisitions and in other affairs.

Moreover, the burgesses must give him credit for forty days for provisions and horses’ shoeing, provided that one of his *mestraux* [Col. 1286A] [Note: [Col. 1286D] *Ministerialis*, an officer of the episcopal household. The *mestraux* did not administer justice, but enforced judgments.] stands surety for him. If the debt is not paid on the fortieth day, a pledge shall be given for the debt; this pledge must be kept for a year and a day without being sold.

The canons and knights are entitled, on their pledge, to fifteen days’ credit for provisions and shoeing.

In return for these services and the others, the lord bishop must defend the burgesses and their property by both the material and the spiritual sword.

Whoever falsifies the measure, weight, or ell shall pay sixty sols.

Whoever violates the city shall pay sixty sols.

Within the city all must be safe, except thieves, forgers, and traitors.

[Col. 1286B] In the borough, sixty sols shall be paid for shedding blood, or for drawing outside a house a sword, knife, lance, or another kind of weapon.

The canons, the chapter’s household and the servants of the canons, the bishop’s household, clerics, knights, and their servants are, in their own houses, exempt from the common law.

Whoever seizes the pastures must pay the fine as fixed by the *plaict-général*, and neither the bishop nor the advocate must defend him.

Having thus acknowledged the bishop’s rights and the city’s customs, Arducius further acknowledged the laws and privileges of the church and chapter [Col. 1286C] of Lausanne. We likewise give their translation below. [Note: [Col. 1286D] This document is found in *Mémoires et Documents Romands*, VII, 11. It is translated in the *Conservateur suisse*, III, 25, and in Mgr Verdeil’s *History of the Canton of Vaud*, I, 81, where Bridel’s translation is reproduced; that translation contains some inaccuracies.]

## Acknowledgements and statutes concerning the bishop and chapter of Lausanne

1. Whenever the lord bishop celebrates Mass at the high altar, the chaplain, deacons, subdeacons, and churchwardens who have served him must dine with him that day.

2. On the second feria—Easter Monday—the bishop must give a meal to the canons, the clerics who attend choir, and the canons’ household.

[Col. 1287A] 3. Offerings made to the bishop at consecrations which he performs in his diocese and wherever he celebrates Mass belong to the canons who accompany him on horseback, except wax and candles, which are his; grain and bread, which belong to the churchwardens; and eggs, cheese, and hemp, which belong to the custodians. [Note: [Col. 1287C] The churchwarden, *matricularius*, attended to the temporal affairs of a church; the custodian, *custos*, cared for the bells, linen, lamps, furnishings for church use, and so forth. These offices, distinct in themselves, were sometimes combined, and the churchwarden performed several functions of the custodian.]

4. Offerings made to the bishop, after his consecration, when he takes possession of the bishopric, at the first Mass he celebrates, belong to the canons.

5. The servants of the canons are obliged to pay the fine only to their lords, however grave and heinous the crime they have committed.

6. The household of a capitular who receives the latter’s prebend [Col. 1287B] must pay a fine only to the chapter in the event of an offence.

7. One third of the fines from our men arrested in this city for theft belongs to the provost, and the other two thirds to the chapter.

8. Judicial combats must take place in the presence of the provost. [Note: [Col. 1287D] Judicial duels—that is, ordeals or judgments of God—are meant here; medieval legislation tolerated them.] Thieves must be judged in the chapter, which has the right to sentence them. Half the fines from judicial combats belongs to the provost.

9. In the great church there must be only thirty canons: namely, ten priests, ten deacons, and ten subdeacons. Upon a canon’s death, every priest-canon must say three Masses, and a canon who is not a priest must recite the Psalter. Every [Col. 1287C] day until the thirtieth, the conventual Mass shall be celebrated for the deceased at the altar of St John; if he has been buried in the cloister, a procession to his grave shall take place every day for the same period.

10. No person may be distrained upon in the house of a canon or knight, except the master of the house alone.

11. When the bishop goes to the emperor’s court [Col. 1288A] on common business, two or four burgesses must pay the expenses; they shall be reimbursed by the burgesses of this city and by those of Avenches, Curtilles, and Bulle.

12. When the bishop purchases land or an estate given as a pledge, the burgesses owe him the legally prescribed aids, [Note: [Col. 1287D] A monetary contribution.] but the citizens do not.

13. If any canon refuses to pay the rent due at the expiration of its term, or wrongs the chapter, the other canons, after warning him, must no longer communicate with him in choir. The same shall be done with regard to the bishop. If they do not make satisfaction within eight days, their prebend may be withheld, and they remain debtors until satisfaction has been made.

[Col. 1288B] St Amadeus twice received Pope Eugenius III at Lausanne. The first occasion was in 1146, when that pope, leaving Rome because of disorders in that city, made his way to France. According to Briguet, [Note: [Col. 1287D] *Vallesia Christiana*, p. 147.] he consecrated, while passing through, the church of St Maurice in Valais on Christmas Day; according to M. Boccard, [Note: [Col. 1287D] *History of Valais*, p. 407. In June 1146 the pope was still in Italy, for on 23 August he addressed letters from Brescia in Lombardy to the bishop of Bologna. Sigonius, *De regno Italiae*, book XI, under the year 1146. Eugenius therefore crossed western Switzerland only toward the end of that year.] this consecration took place on 25 June. Eugenius III passed through Lausanne again when, in 1148, he left France to return to Italy. At the beginning of that year the pope presided over the Council of Reims. It was in that city that, on 9 April, he issued a bull in favour of Humilimont Abbey, [Note: [Col. 1287D] *Datum Remis . . . V Idus Aprilis*—“Given at Reims … the fifth day before the Ides of April.” Archives of Humilimont.] and, on the 11th of the same month, the bull mentioned above in favour of the church of Lausanne. [Note: [Col. 1287D] The place where this bull was issued is not specified, but the date shows that it was at Reims.] On 5 May he was [Col. 1288C] at Besançon, where he consecrated the high altar of the church of St John. [Note: [Col. 1287D] Dunod, *History of the Church of Besançon*, I, 155.] From there he proceeded to Lausanne, where he was on 17 May [Note: [Col. 1287D] We have two bulls issued at Lausanne by Eugenius III on that day: one in favour of Moutier-Grandval and the other of Bellelay. *Datum [Col. 1288C] Lausanne . . . XVI Kal. Junii . . .*—“Given at Lausanne … the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June …” Trouillat, *Monuments*, I, 308 and 311. Two further bulls dated from Lausanne in June 1148 are also mentioned: one of 20 June, in favour of the chapters of St John and St Stephen at Besançon (compare Trouillat, I, 310, note 4, and Richard, *History of the Dioceses of Besançon and Saint-Claude*, I, 363); the other, concerning the anniversary [Col. 1288D] of the consecration of the high altar of Besançon cathedral, was issued on 5 June according to Richard, *loc. cit.*, and on 21 June according to Dunod, *History of the Church of Besançon*, I, 155. We do not possess the text of these acts and therefore cannot see whether Richard’s and Dunod’s statements are correct; but these dates do not accord with those of the acts cited below, issued at Saint-Maurice and Martigny. One must assume either an error in these statements or that the pope retraced his steps from Martigny, which is unlikely.] and where he probably remained several days. On 26 May he was at Saint-Maurice, [Note: [Col. 1288D] Bull in favour of Payerne. *Datum apud S. Mauritium . . . VII Kal. Junii*—“Given at Saint-Maurice … the seventh day before the Kalends of June.” *Solothurner Wochenblatt* for 1829, p. 617, and *Archives of the Historical Society of Fribourg*, I, 375.] and the next day at Martigny. [Note: [Col. 1288D] Bull in favour of Rüggisberg. *Datum apud Ottodorum . . . VI Kal. Junii*—“Given at Octodurus [Martigny] … the sixth day before the Kalends of June.” *Solothurner Wochenblatt* for 1829, p. 555.]

During his stay at Hautecombe, St Amadeus acquired the particular friendship and esteem of Count [Col. 1289A] Amadeus III of Savoy and of the lords of the country, as is proved by the important office to which he was later called. On setting out for the crusade, Count Amadeus entrusted his son Humbert to the bishop of Lausanne and charged him with watching over the honour of the young man’s rank and the integrity of his lands. [Note: [Col. 1289D] Guichenon, *History of Savoy*, IV, 38.] On his return from the Holy Land, the count died at Nicosia on 1 April 1149. His son Humbert III succeeded him; but as he was then too young to govern alone, he took counsel with members of his family (*cum suis*, “with his own people”), and afterwards summoned Bishop Amadeus to him. When he arrived, he was informed of the purpose of this summons: he was to be counsellor to the young count and protector of his states. Amadeus refused; they pressed him: “If [Col. 1289B] we choose a duke, a count, or some other secular person instead of a faithful guardian,” they said to him, “we may have only a wicked and avaricious man, who will seek above all his own advantage and leave his ward only a ruined inheritance.” Urged by these entreaties and by the affection that had bound him to the father and which he then transferred to the son, Amadeus accepted this difficult charge and endeavoured to fulfil its duties well. [Note: [Col. 1289D] Ibid., IV, 39.]

“One could expect only great things,” says Guichenon, [Note: [Col. 1289D] Ibid., I, 234.] “from this education, because this prelate was one of the great men of his age. . . . The care which he gave this young prince became apparent in the fine qualities and rare [Col. 1289C] virtues with which the latter was endowed. Foremost among these was that profound piety and great love of God which made him, throughout his life, so steadfastly despise the perishable things of this world in order to attach himself to heavenly and incorruptible things. And although this prince’s heroic nature served as a step by which he attained this high degree of perfection, nevertheless the example of his tutor, his wise counsels, and the guidance of so excellent a hand contributed no little to it.” Humbert III was later numbered among the blessed by the Church, and his feast is celebrated on 13 March.

During this prince’s early years, we see Amadeus taking part in the count’s acts. St Maurice Abbey in Valais found itself [Col. 1289D] invaded by Raynald, who had violently seized the office of provost; Amadeus addressed a letter to the young Humbert, urging him to [Col. 1290A] protect the abbey. [Note: [Col. 1289D] Ibid., IV, 38.] When he set out for the crusade, Amadeus III, in order to meet the expenses of his journey, borrowed from the religious of St Maurice a gold table worth sixty-six marks. The bishop of Lausanne took care that the religious should receive the value of this table back. Accordingly, on Amadeus’s advice, Count Humbert promised to pay the abbey one hundred marks of silver and two marks of gold within four years, and granted it the revenues he received in the valleys of Bagnes and Octier. The deed of donation was executed in the abbey church of St Maurice in the year 1150, in the presence of Bishop Amadeus; Louis, bishop of Sion; Hugh, abbot of St Maurice; and several other witnesses. [Note: [Col. 1289D] Ibid., IV, 38 and 40.]

[Col. 1290B] Amid his dignities, Amadeus did not forget Hautecombe. His protection was highly advantageous to the convent; it was especially then that its buildings and possessions increased, and the number of its religious multiplied. [Note: [Col. 1289D] Manrique, *Annales Cistercienses*, I, 463.] The former abbot appears as witness to a donation which Count Humbert made to that convent. [Note: [Col. 1289D] Guichenon, *loc. cit.*, IV, 43.]

During the first half of the twelfth century, numerous convents were founded in the diocese of Lausanne. They were objects of our bishop’s concern. Being himself a religious, he loved and held monastic orders in particular affection. He knew how closely they conformed to the counsels of Jesus Christ and how suited they were to bring [Col. 1290C] humanity to Christian perfection; he also saw with his own eyes how useful convents were to the intellectual cultivation and material prosperity of populations, and how civilising their role was in the true sense of the word, since their activity contributed as much to spiritual happiness as to temporal well-being. [Note: [Col. 1289D] “One likes to inquire into these religious communities, which were the first to clear our forests, sow our plains, and plant vines upon our hillsides . . . One takes pleasure in seeing them draw blessings upon their labours through prayer, and deserve, by working, that heaven should answer their prayers . . . And in ascending through the centuries that have passed, [Col. 1290D] one offers to their memory the tribute of respect and gratitude owed them by posterity, enriched by their hardships and their sweat.” (Bridel, *Conservateur suisse*, VIII, 44.)] He did not believe that these institutions ought to be abolished because, like all institutions in which human beings play a part, they could give rise to abuses.

In 1147 and 1154 St Amadeus confirmed donations made to the convent of Théla by various benefactors, and himself gave a vineyard to the same religious. [Note: [Col. 1290D] *Mémoires et Documents Romands*, XII. Cartulary of Montheron, by M. de Gingins, pp. 10, 12, 16, and 20.—Théla, or Montheron, a Cistercian abbey two leagues north of Lausanne, was founded in 1135 by Guy, bishop of Lausanne.]

[Col. 1290D] He likewise confirmed donations made to the Premonstratensians of Fontaine-André [Note: [Col. 1290D] Matile, *Monuments*, no. XVI.—Fontaine-André Abbey, situated half a league from Neuchâtel, was founded in 1144 by the counts of Neuchâtel.] and Humilimont. [Note: [Col. 1290D] Archives of Humilimont.—Humilimont Abbey [Col. 1291D] or Marsens Abbey, half a league from Vuippens in the Gruyère, was founded in 1136 (new style, 1137) by three brothers of Marsens, of the Everdes-Vuippens family.] Later, he gave the latter abbey [Col. 1291A] the churches of Vuippens and Villardvolard. [Note: [Col. 1291D] Necrology of Humilimont, in the said archives.]

In 1154 Amadeus confirmed to the religious of Hautcrêt everything which Guido, his predecessor, and other persons had given them. He recalls the gift made by his predecessor and himself to this convent of the uncultivated and deserted land of Dézaley, to plant vineyards there and enjoy their produce in equal shares; moreover, the bishop promised to pay them twenty pounds within four years for this cultivation. After the bishop’s death, the religious were to own half these vineyards as a free allod. [Note: [Col. 1292D] *Mémoires et Documents Romands*, vol. XII, Cartulary of Hautcrêt, by J.-J. Hisely, p. 6.—Hautcrêt, a Cistercian abbey near Palézieux in the canton of Vaud, was founded in 1134 by Guido, bishop of Lausanne.] Amadeus further confirmed for this convent donations made by Louis, his officer, and by Bon-Fils of Chexbres. [Note: [Col. 1291D] *Mémoires et Documents Romands*, *loc. cit.*, 181 and 143.] He gave the abbey thirteen sols owed to him by [Col. 1291B] Ulric, son of Bon-Fils of Chexbres. [Note: [Col. 1291D] Ibid., 24.] He took care to have the donations which their father Amadeus had made to Hautcrêt confirmed by Gaucher and William of Blonay. [Note: [Col. 1291D] Ibid., 133.] This convent, as we see, had a large share in St Amadeus’s care. It owed this to the particular affection the bishop bore toward the Cistercians, the order to which he had himself belonged before his episcopate. Thus he liked to live at Puidoux [Note: [Col. 1291D] *Mémoires et Documents Romands*, VI, 43.—On a hill near Puidoux, the ruins of the old castle of the bishops of Lausanne may still be seen.] in the neighbourhood of Hautcrêt, where he rediscovered the life of Clairvaux and Hautecombe.

The Cistercians of Hauterive [Note: [Col. 1292D] Hauterive Abbey, founded in 1137 (new style, 1138), on the banks of the Sarine, one league from Fribourg, by William of Glâne.] likewise shared in Amadeus’s liberality. Renaud, lord of Estavayer, and his son Conon returned to the bishop of Lausanne the fief [Col. 1291C] which they held from him at Onnens and which comprised one quarter of that place’s territory and of the forest of Buchille. At those lords’ request, the bishop gave this fief to the religious of Hauterive. [Note: [Col. 1292D] Archives of Hauterive.]

In those times, the numerous complications of seigneurial rights produced by the feudal system sometimes gave rise to difficulties among various convents or ecclesiastical lords. Amadeus settled them more than once as judge or arbitrator. When he took possession of the bishopric, he found a dispute pending between the Church of Lausanne and the convent of Romainmôtier. [Note: [Col. 1292D] Romainmôtier, a priory of the Order of St Benedict in the canton of Vaud, dates in its original foundation from about the middle of the fifth century.] He brought it to an end by an act of the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January (16 December) 1148, leaving the convent [Col. 1292A] in possession of the churches of Apples, Morlens, Barlens, and Torclens; he gave the religious the church of Vallorbes and allowed them, under certain conditions, to have oratories near Orbe and Goumoens. [Note: [Col. 1292D] All these localities are in the canton of Vaud.—See the act in *Mémoires et Documents Romands*, III, 486.]

The monasteries of Great St Bernard and Melleraie [Note: [Col. 1292D] Melleraie, in Chablais, deanery of Alinge, in the former diocese of Geneva.] were inhabited by Regular Canons of St Augustine and united by an alliance that did not exclude the superiority of the former. These insufficiently defined relations caused conflicts. In 1154 Bishop Amadeus, acting by virtue of the commission entrusted to him by Pope Eugenius III, restored harmony between these two houses and regulated the reciprocal rights and duties both of the religious and of their superiors. [Note: [Col. 1292D] *Mémoires et Documents Genevois*, II, second part, p. 34.]

[Col. 1292B] A religious of the abbey of St Oyan, [Note: [Col. 1292D] St Oyan Abbey, in the department of Jura, France, was first called Condat, then St Oyan, and, since the thirteenth century, Saint-Claude; it was founded in 425 by St Romanus.] Dom Poncet (*Pontius*), had withdrawn to the deserted wildernesses of the Joux valley in the canton of Vaud, where he built a cell and cleared some land, which St Oyan Abbey inherited at his death. When Lac de Joux Abbey [Note: [Col. 1292D] This Premonstratensian abbey was founded in 1126 by Ebald, lord of La Sarraz. It was situated on the eastern shore of Lake Joux, while Lieu-Poncet was on the western shore of the same lake.] was founded and began to prosper, religious from St Oyan came to resume possession of Dom Poncet’s cell, which was called Lieu-Poncet. Disputes arose between these religious and those of Lac de Joux Abbey concerning fishing rights in the lake, from which they derived their principal subsistence. Peter, archbishop of Tarentaise, and Amadeus, bishop of Lausanne, were charged by the pope with intervening [Col. 1292C] and establishing a mode of life for the two convents. By a judgment pronounced at Lausanne in 1155, the prelates decreed:

1. That the number of religious dwelling at Lieu-Poncet must not exceed ten, who would be subject to the authority of the bishop of Lausanne;

2. That they must admit into their convent no religious who had left other monasteries;

3. That they must not keep animals;

4. That they could fish with nets in the lake only one day and one night per week, but might fish otherwise whenever they wished;

5. That the bishop might consecrate an altar for them and bless a cemetery;

6. Finally, that if the brethren abandoned Lieu-Poncet, it would belong to Lac de Joux Abbey. [Note: [Col. 1293D] *Annals of Lac de Joux Abbey*, by Fr. [Col. 1293D] de Gingins-la-Sarraz, in *Mémoires et Documents Romands*, I, 15, and ibid., first book, p. 181.]

It seems that new [Col. 1293A] difficulties arose, for the following year a second settlement had to be made. The same prelates, on 27 August 1157, settled an agreement between the abbots of St Maurice and Hautcrêt concerning one third of the chapel of Châtillens, the perpetual ownership of which the abbot of St Maurice surrendered to the abbot of Hautcrêt. [Note: [Col. 1293D] *Mémoires et Documents Romands*, XII, second part, p. 14.]

A dispute also existed between the bishop of Lausanne and the Church of Besançon. To settle it, the pope delegated Ortlieb, bishop of Basel, who summoned the parties to Neuchâtel in 1154 and delivered there his judgment, subsequently recorded in an act issued at Moutier-Grandval on 10 July of the same year. On the testimony of Arducius, bishop of Geneva, and several ecclesiastics of the two [Col. 1293B] churches, Ortlieb declared:

1. That the mayor (*villicus*) [Note: [Col. 1293D] The mayor, *major* or *villicus*, was a judge of lower jurisdiction and received seigneurial dues. See Du Cange, *Glossary*, and *Mémoires et Documents Romands*, IX, 384 ff.] of Lutry had no right over the lands of Cully belonging to the canons of St John and St Stephen of Besançon;

2. That the men of Cully would pay certain dues—*septem syleya et septem minas avene*, “seven [uncertain unit: *syleya*] and seven measures of oats”—to the bishop of Lausanne for the use of the woods;

3. That the bishop of Lausanne must protect them and, if he went to Cully, judge their disputes without demanding emoluments; while there, he would make use of the services owed him, but neither he nor his men should give cause for complaints;

4. That both parties would grant full liberty, for purposes of marriage, to their men who passed from one land to the other. [Note: [Col. 1293D] Zapf, *Monuments*, p. 94.—Matile, *Monuments*, no. XVII.—Trouillat, *Monuments of the History of the Bishopric of Basel*, I, 324.]

[Col. 1293C] Saint Amadeus was, as we have seen, related to Emperor Frederick I. On several occasions he was found among the dignitaries of his court. In 1153 he attended the Diet of Speyer, and appears as a witness in the diploma issued in that city on 17 January in favour of the bishop of Geneva. [Note: [Col. 1293D] Spon, *History of Geneva*, III, 10.—Besson, *Memoirs*, 358.—Guichenon, *Bibliotheca Sebusiana*, century 2, no. 33.] On 15 February of the same year he was at Besançon in the emperor’s retinue; he is named among the witnesses of the diploma granted in favour of Payerne. [Note: [Col. 1293D] Schoepflin, *Alsatian Diplomatic Collection*, no. 290.—*Solothurn Weekly Journal*, 1829, p. 620.—Archives of the Historical Society of Fribourg, I, 377.] Amadeus himself shared in the emperor’s benefactions: he was appointed his chancellor; at the same time he received the right to grant and revoke benefices, confirm donations, and summon before his court not only ecclesiastics but also lay barons, in the capacity [Col. 1293D] of imperial vicar. Frederick granted him these privileges because of his virtues and the ancient dignity [Col. 1294A] of the Church of Lausanne. [Note: [Col. 1293D] We possess only an extract of this diploma: we publish it below.—See *Memoirs and Documents of French-speaking Switzerland*, [Col. 1294D] I, first part, 76, where M. de Gingins places it under the year 1155.] These prerogatives ought, it would seem, to have secured the bishop of Lausanne against every hostile attempt; unfortunately this was not so. Amadeus found himself persecuted by those very persons who ought to have defended him. Yet the events which follow are only partly known, for the documents we possess are too incomplete and disclose only a portion of these facts—nevertheless among the most important of the episcopate with which we are concerned. [Note: [Col. 1294D] The principal of these documents is a letter addressed by Saint Amadeus to his beloved sons of the Church of Lausanne. It will be found after this notice.]

Every Church in the Middle Ages had its advocate or defender, charged with representing it in courts of law, administering justice in its name or defending its interests there, and protecting its temporal possessions by arms against its enemies’ attacks. [Col. 1294B] The ecclesiastical lord had to remain faithful to his mission of peace; for this purpose he chose a representative for litigation and armed defence. Various advantages were attached to the office of advocate; at Lausanne the advocate enjoyed one third of the proceeds from fines. The ecclesiastical lord entrusted this office to the lay lord whom he himself chose. Originally it was merely temporary; later, however, when regarded as a fief, it followed the laws of fiefs. This fief naturally depended upon the ecclesiastical lord, to whom the advocate accordingly owed fealty and whose man he became. Advocates did not always acknowledge this dependence in their conduct: [Col. 1294C] more than once they became the persecutors of those whom they were bound to protect and attempted to seize the authority of their ecclesiastical lords. This happened repeatedly at Lausanne, especially during Saint Amadeus’s episcopate.

The episcopal advocacy of Lausanne was then entrusted to Amadeus, count of Genevois, who had already exercised this office under the two preceding bishops, since the death of his father Aymon [about 1126]. [Note: [Col. 1294D] We have seen no document in which Count Amadeus bears the title of advocate, but the fact follows from the following circumstances: the count exercised authority in the diocese of Lausanne, since in two charters (*Memoirs and Documents of French-speaking Switzerland*, XII, part II, pp. 10 and 13) concerning the diocese, his name appears among those of the sovereign powers of the land, the emperor and the bishop. This proves that the count also enjoyed there a general authority, nevertheless dependent upon the bishop, since he owed homage to the latter (see Saint Amadeus’s letter: *Obliti dominii nostri, hominii sui*—“forgetful of our lordship and of their homage”). This authority can have been none other than that bestowed by the advocacy. In his learned *Memoir on the Rectorate of Burgundy*, p. 77, M. de Gingins distinguishes at Lausanne a protectorate (*consulatus*) from the episcopal advocacy; and he [Col. 1295D] bases this distinction on the name *consul* given to the count of Genevois in one of the charters cited above, and on the designation “advocate” given to Emmo of Gerenstein in an act of 1157 (*Memoirs and Documents of French-speaking Switzerland*, VII, 17; see also XII, part II, p. 14). For this assertion to be well founded, it would be necessary, first, that the word *consul* denoted this protectorate—which it does not, since *consul* never appears with that meaning, but was used in the Middle Ages as a synonym for “count” (see Du Cange, *Glossary*); secondly, Amadeus of Genevois and Emmo of Gerenstein would need to appear at the same time, the one as protector and the other as advocate—which again is not the case. The charters in which Amadeus appears belong to 1154 and 1155, whereas Emmo appears only in 1157. After 1155 the count of Genevois exercised no authority in the diocese of Lausanne, except as lord of certain lands; he therefore lost his office, which [Col. 1296C] probably occurred in 1156, as what follows will show. It must consequently be admitted that Amadeus and Emmo were not simultaneously, one protector and the other advocate, but exercised the latter office successively. Besides, it must be acknowledged that these [Col. 1296D] facts have not yet been sufficiently clarified; we hope to find light on this subject in a memoir recently announced to us by a learned professor of Lausanne.] Hardly had the count been invested with his office when he already had disputes with the bishop, as Saint Amadeus’s letter tells us. During the episcopate of Gerard of Faucigny, his kinsman, the count of Genevois destroyed the castle of Lucens [Col. 1294D] belonging to the bishop and erected another intended to dominate the Church of Lausanne. Gerard opposed the count’s hostilities [Col. 1295A] in vain: neither ties of kinship, nor tears, nor prayers, nor curses could move him. Soon afterwards, however, God undertook to punish these injustices.

Renaud, count of Burgundy, having refused to render homage to the emperor, had been deprived of his fiefs, which were awarded to Conrad of Zähringen, who was also invested with the rectorate of Cisjurane and Transjurane Burgundy (between 3 April and 22 May 1126). Conrad was to conquer the fiefs granted to him. He crossed the Aar with an army and attacked Renaud, to whom a great many lords of the two Burgundies had joined themselves; among them was Amadeus, count of Genevois. Conrad was victorious; Amadeus fled, and a [Col. 1295B] great number of his men remained on the battlefield. Crushed by this reverse, the count sought peace from Conrad, who nevertheless continued ravaging Genevois lands. Amadeus then appealed to Saint Bernard, who wrote in his favour to Duke Conrad. [Note: [Col. 1296D] Müller, *History of the Swiss Confederation*, book I, ch. 14.—De Gingins, *Memoir on the Rectorate of Burgundy*, in *Memoirs and Documents of French-speaking Switzerland*, I, 54 ff.—Works of Saint Bernard, letter 97.—Letter of Saint Amadeus.] When and how did these disputes end? Nothing makes this precisely known. An agreement doubtless took place with the bishop of Lausanne, since Count Amadeus continued to fulfil the functions of advocate. Later he had many difficulties with the bishop of Geneva, whose advocate he also was and whose authority he likewise sought to usurp. Bishop Amadeus intervened in this struggle as arbitrator or mediator. [Note: [Col. 1296D] Spon, *History of Geneva*, Documentary Proofs, no. III.] The affairs of Geneva were [Col. 1295C] not yet concluded when the Church of Lausanne again became the target of the same count’s attacks. He built a fortress above Lausanne, intended to dominate the city, openly rebelled against the bishop, and drew subjects of the bishopric into his party. Saint Amadeus, no longer safe at Lausanne, left the city and took refuge at Moudon; but there too he found himself among enemies. They resorted to [Col. 1296A] violence against him: his life was threatened; his garments were torn by weapons; one of his companions was struck even within his arms, and his blood spurted upon him. Wounded and despoiled himself, he left the castle of Moudon and fled barefoot. Thus condemned to exile, he was separated from his Church for some time. Around Easter he wrote to his beloved sons of the Church of Lausanne a letter in which he recounts the evils he had suffered, pronounces his curse upon the town of Moudon, which had betrayed its bishop, expresses wishes for the conversion of the count of Genevois, and ends with exhortations to his beloved sons, preparing them to celebrate the Easter feasts in holiness. [Note: [Col. 1296D] This letter has remained unpublished until now and almost unknown. It is found in an old manuscript of the abbey of Hauterive, together with the Homilies of Saint Amadeus and of Henry, abbot of Hautcrêt. A copy exists among the manuscripts of Monsignor de Lenzbourg.] We do not know how long the bishop’s exile lasted or how [Col. 1296B] he succeeded in overcoming the count of Genevois. The cartulary of Lausanne says only that it was by his prudence, and that he compelled the count himself to demolish and raze to the foundations the fortifications he had erected. [Note: [Col. 1296D] Letter of Saint Amadeus.—Cartulary of Lausanne, p. 42.] Nor is the year in which these events occurred specified; it appears, however, that they should be placed about the year 1156. In 1155 the count of Genevois still possessed his authority at Lausanne; in 1157 we find another advocate, Emmo of Gerenstein. The year 1156 may therefore be assigned as the most probable date.

Saint Amadeus had to contend not only with the claims of the count of Genevois, but also with those of a lord whose power was far more [Col. 1296C] to be feared. In 1155 or 1156 Berthold of Zähringen received from Emperor Frederick I the imperial advocacy [Note: [Col. 1296D] The imperial advocate was the emperor’s representative, or vicar.] and investiture with the regalian rights in the episcopal cities of Geneva, Lausanne, and Sion. By this grant the emperor injured the rights of these bishops, who had long been immediate vassals of the crown and thus could not be subject to any intermediate authority. They consequently had to oppose Berthold’s taking possession of the [Col. 1297A] advantages granted him. [Note: [Col. 1297D] Memoir on the rectorate by M. de Gingins, in *Memoirs and Documents of French-speaking Switzerland*, I, 68 ff.] Was the struggle at Lausanne as serious as at Geneva, and did Berthold take part in the count of Genevois’s hostilities against the bishop? Nothing tells us so. There remains to us from this struggle only one document, which makes its result known. It is an agreement between Duke Berthold and the bishop, which the duke promised by oath to observe. Its terms are as follows. [Note: [Col. 1297D] This agreement, preserved in the Cartulary, is found in *Memoirs and Documents of French-speaking Switzerland*, VI, 434 and VII, 16; Schoepflin, *History of Zähringen-Baden*, V, 106; and more completely in the bull of Pope Alexander III (1178), *Memoirs and Documents of French-speaking Switzerland*, VII, 24. The agreement is undated, but must clearly be placed around 1157.]

The duke undertakes to leave the election of the bishop of Lausanne free. He will not seek to acquire the fiefs dependent upon the bishop; neither he nor his heirs will demand the dues owed upon changes of bishops for Chexbres and Lutry, but these fiefs, together with the regalian rights, shall be surrendered to [Col. 1297B] the bishop by the duke without any entry payment. He will assist him, as far as he can and in good faith, to recover the possessions which the Church has lost and which have long been alienated. The duke’s men shall not go to seek lodging in the Church’s boroughs or demand hospitality there, any more than in the bishop’s palace or in the houses of clerics or knights (vassals); nor shall they take anything from them by force.

By this agreement, Saint Amadeus sought, as may be seen, to secure the freedom and independence of his Church. This was the last important act of his administration. There remain only some secondary facts to mention. Saint Amadeus gave the chapter of Lausanne the church of Ursins [Col. 1297C] (district of Yverdon), directing that henceforth the feast of Saint Agnes should be celebrated with a double rite. He further gave the same chapter, for the celebration of his anniversary, the churches of Yvonand and Gressy (district of Yverdon). During his episcopate he granted only four divorces. [Note: [Col. 1298D] *Memoirs and Documents of French-speaking Switzerland*, VI, 43 and 44.—It is known that among Catholics divorce is not a dissolution of marriage, but a mere separation which does not destroy the marital bond.]

During his final illness, physicians advised our holy bishop to use a remedy that would have violated his vow of chastity; he refused to preserve his life through sin. When he was near death, in the presence of the clergy and people assembled around him, he granted absolution to all whom he had excommunicated, except Humbert, lord of Aubonne, whom he summoned to the day [Col. 1297D] of Last Judgment because of the wrongs he was committing against the Church of Saint-Livre, near Aubonne. He died on 27 August. [Note: [Col. 1298D] *Memoirs and Documents of French-speaking Switzerland*, VI, 44.] Historians disagree as to the year of his death: most place it in 1158, and others in 1159. Since his successor was not consecrated until February 1160, [Note: [Col. 1298D] Richard, *History of the Dioceses of Besançon*, etc., I, 395.] the latter date does not seem improbable. The cartulary says that he ruled fourteen [Col. 1298A] years; since he was elected only about the end of 1144 and consecrated in January 1145, these fourteen years can have been complete only if he died in 1159. Saint Amadeus was buried in the nave of Lausanne cathedral, before the crucifix, beside Bishop Henry. At his death he gave his Church a gold ring adorned with a large and very beautiful sapphire, which his successors were to use when officiating in the cathedral, but which was not to leave that church. [Note: [Col. 1298D] *Memoirs and Documents of French-speaking Switzerland*, VI, 44.]

All writers who have spoken of Saint Amadeus have praised his talents and virtues; to beauty of body he joined qualities of mind and perfections of soul. Public veneration accordingly placed him among the blessed; it is under [Col. 1298B] that designation that he is mentioned in the Cistercian Menologium, in the Saints’ Calendar of that order, and elsewhere. The Congregation of Rites permitted Cistercian religious to celebrate his office with a double rite, and this permission was confirmed by Pope Clement XI on 25 September 1710. At the request of Hubert de Boccard, bishop of Lausanne, Pope Benedict XIV, by a brief of 12 December 1753, extended to the diocese of Lausanne the authorization to recite this office; since then the feast of Saint Amadeus has been celebrated among us on 28 January.

There remain to us from this holy bishop eight homilies in honour of the Blessed Virgin. If they cannot be compared with the masterpieces of the early [Col. 1298C] Fathers of the Church, they are nevertheless not inferior to the authors of his own age, whether in the nobility and piety of their thoughts or in the elegance and sweetness of their style. They do, indeed, share the defects of their century; one sometimes wishes for greater simplicity and less artifice in their ideas and expression. Despite these defects, they have often been reprinted. They are found in various editions of the *Library of the Fathers*; separately they were published at Basel in 1517, at Saint-Omer in 1613, at Lyons in 1633, at Douai, and elsewhere. Cousin published a French translation at the end of his *Lives of Several Saints of the Houses of Tonnerre and Clermont* (1698). Some fragments [Col. 1298D] were inserted into the old Lausanne breviary, as well as into the new one of 1787. Thus they were formerly read publicly in Lausanne cathedral. Despite their numerous editions, Saint Amadeus’s homilies are now rare; it would be appropriate for them to be reprinted.

Abbé J. GREMAUD.

[Col. 1299]

## LETTER OF BLESSED AMADEUS TO HIS SONS OF THE CHURCH OF LAUSANNE

(This letter, from a very ancient manuscript codex of the monastery of Hauterive, was first recently published by J. GREMAUD in the collection entitled *Mémorial de Fribourg*, first year, Fribourg, April 1854, p. 182.—The aforementioned codex also contains Homilies of Blessed Amadeus and of Henry, abbot of Hautcrêt.)

[Col. 1299A] AMADEUS, bishop, to the beloved sons of the Church of Lausanne: may you be filled with every blessing.

Though absent in body, I am present in heart and am moved day by day by love for you, desiring to be an exile for your freedom. What is burdensome I count light, what is harsh smooth, what is long brief, so that at last, with the Author of peace granting it, freedom of the highest honour having been restored, we may rejoice in tranquil peace. Indeed, it is more bitter than death for me to endure that, for the snaring of the clergy, the dishonour of the citizens, and the ruin of the people, foundations should be laid in the city of Lausanne, wicked buildings raised, and proud battlements threatening the Church appearing above it. I am ashamed to speak of the shamelessness of men rising against us unjustly, deceitfully, and ruinously. Forgetful of our lordship and of their homage, swift to wrong and slow to favour, [Col. 1299B] they plotted against our life without any reverence. I pass over much else: innocent blood was shed before our pallid face. The bishop’s garments, torn by weapons, cry out to the Lord, as does the indecently spattered stream of a companion’s blood. Hands often raised to holy things—though unworthily—still breathed of recent sacred rites; with these I had celebrated Christ’s mysteries, with these I embraced my friend. By sacrilegious daring, through the devil’s minions, he was wounded within the arms clasped around him; his blood ran into my bosom.

My dearest friends, do not believe that what I count the highest honour is misery. Christ’s humiliation is to be preferred to every worldly glory. I walked bloodied by my friend’s blood; he, sprinkled with his own blood, cleansed his friends [Col. 1299C] and cleansed his enemies also. “That your foot,” says one, that is, your humanity, O good Jesus, “may be dipped in the blood of your martyrdom; and the tongue,” that is, the preaching, “of your dogs”—formerly barking at you, now preaching you, made by God friends from enemies—so that this preaching itself may be adorned with the blood of martyrdom. Therefore, Christ’s humanity having been dipped in blood, the tongue of his dogs, converted from enemies, was dipped by that same blood, so that their first task was to preach the Gospel, provided that they did not fearlessly die in witness to the truth. I would wish our enemies likewise to be converted from Bashan—that is, from confusion—and, dwelling in the depths of the sea, to be converted from the most bitter wickedness of this surging age. Would that they might be so converted that, once the worst serpent has been killed in them, they may cast off their old skins in the narrow cleft of the rock, renewed in the garb of holy religion. But if they cannot do this, then, the serpent being nailed to the cross of the conqueror, may they be banished into perpetual exile; yet not excluded from heaven, let them pay the last farthing in punishment.

[Col. 1300A] But to return to the matter from which we have digressed: dragged away, beaten, and torn, we left the castle of Moudon, bearing the reproach of him who suffered outside the camp. Walking therefore barefoot, we shook from ourselves upon the ground its defilement, according to the Lord’s word, shaking off the dust as a testimony against them. And lest anyone be angry with me over this act, listen simply to its reason. The ancient Fathers, beset by distress of heart, prayed with the soles of their feet bare in order more swiftly to appease the Lord’s wrath. Thus we read that David acted, and thus many saints acted; hence the custom has grown up that we observe it at the beginning of fasts and on Good Friday. Therefore, stunned in mind by this unforeseen event in that hour of darkness, I took up the weapons of humility and fled to the aid [Col. 1300B] of prayers. For I knew well that by humble prayer every evil is driven away and every saving benefit bestowed. Prayer joined to pure humility, like a gem set in a ring of gold, obtains whatever it wills. The one who asks shall receive the practice of good works in the active life; the one who seeks shall find the embraces of Abishag—that is, wisdom—in the contemplative life; to the one who knocks heaven shall be opened in eternal life. Humble prayer washes away sins, repels adversities, gathers useful things, procures the best things, and ascends to lofty things. Humble prayer joins human beings to one another and joins them likewise with angels; it makes offerings acceptable, contemplates mysteries, brings upright life near to God, begins in fear, and is perfected in love. Therefore, as Solomon testifies (Eccles. VII), the end of prayer is preferred [Col. 1300C] to its beginning.

Behold the two wings of the dove, that is, of the simple soul: one is humility, the other prayer. A man disturbed by the voice of an enemy and exhausted by the persecutor’s tribulation asked for these to be given him: “Who will give me wings like a dove,” and so forth (Ps. LIV). Elsewhere it is said of this dove: “If you sleep between the two lots, the dove’s wings are silvered, and her hind parts are in the pallor of gold” (Ps. LXVII). The two lots are the two Testaments: one in the letter, the other in the spirit; one in shadow, the other in image; one promising, the other bestowing every good. These are the bride’s breasts in the Song of Songs (Cant. VII), likened to clusters of grapes. To become drunk from these through reading, meditation, and contemplation, and among them even to fall asleep to love of the world, worldly prudence, and the tumult of affairs, is as sweet as it is excellent. Let those who thus sleep keep watch in spirit, so that the wings of virtues may bear the dove aloft. The dove’s wings are silvered, [Col. 1301A] so that virtue may be clothed in example, made graceful in speech, shine in deed, and resound in preaching. Its hind parts are in the pallor of gold: its foreparts are beautiful indeed, but its hind parts, which consist in the pallor of gold, are more beautiful. For gold signifies God’s wisdom, which took hold of the dove’s hind parts when, at the end of the ages, it assumed mortal flesh and grew pale. Thus through silvered wings, after silver doves, one goes to the pallor of gold and ascends to the golden couch of the true Solomon.

But what are we doing, delighted by the dove’s image? We have clung too closely to the dove, whereas our soul has rather been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the men of Moudon. Castle of Moudon, may neither the dew of mercy nor the rain of grace come upon you, since you bestowed neither mercy upon the priest nor grace upon your bishop! [Col. 1301B] You crept from your cave, hissing dragon, to destroy; you rushed from your den, base lion, to spare no one. Mad sheep against your shepherd, people murderous toward your Father, you mingled the blood of a victim with chrism. Stock of Ham, generation of Canaan! Noah, uncovered in his tent, cursed Ham’s posterity. Your posterity, Moudon, is perpetually devoted to a curse because of the reproaches inflicted on Christ the Lord. You acted deceitfully in the sight of the Lord; treachery has been found in you. Your blood be upon your own head! You were founded in injustice, fortress of the devil. You grew by plunder and gained strength by iniquity. Many waters cannot wash you; you cannot be washed except by being destroyed. You cannot be justified until you are uprooted from the ground, until your wings, with which you flew to plunder, are completely torn away.

[Col. 1301C] We wish to commit to the memory of posterity that Amadeus, count of Genevois, unjustly destroyed the castle called Lucens, situated on the allodial land of the Church of Lausanne, and unjustly erected another, in the territory of the aforesaid Church, against that same Church. To Gerard, venerable bishop of Lausanne, neither his kinship with the count, nor opposition, nor cursing availed anything; neither tears nor prayers availed to prevent the strengthening of that castle hateful to God. Hence we believe it occurred by God’s wondrous judgment that, after a short interval had passed, when he fought with noble Duke Conrad, he feared Conrad’s face and turned his back, not without great loss and the death of very many of his men. But the Lord’s hand is not shortened. His eyes look upon all the ways of the children of Adam.

For liberty, justice, and truth, the aforesaid [Col. 1301D] count has turned cruel against me. David patiently endured Saul and mourned piously when he was slain. Elijah encountered Jezebel; John, Herod. My Jesus, by speaking justice, stirred up against himself the Pharisees’ assemblies. I know that truth produces hatred, but in the souls of the reprobate. No virtue lacks envy; the righteous have never lacked an enemy. Justice will not triumph where it lacks conflicts. Certainly I love the count, not his error; I love in him the sacraments of faith, the fellowship of nature, the fact that he is called a Christian and that he is human. Nevertheless I curse the evils he carries on in secret, the crimes he commits in public, the ravaging of clerics, the plundering of monks, and the despoiling of churches. He is confident that [Col. 1302A] the Jordan will flow into his mouth. He spews out a river after the woman who, in the Apocalypse (ch. XII), having taken wings, flies with her offspring to the Lord. I speak from conscience: would that his sins might be wiped away even by my blood! Far be it from me to commit this great sin by ceasing to pray for him! For what then? If he were converted, he would be useful for good work. “Take away,” says Solomon, “the rust from silver, and there will come forth a most pure vessel” (Prov. XXV). Would that the rust of every vice were removed from him! Would that, according to the prophet, the Lord’s fire refined his dross until pure! (Isa. I.) May he finally hear from the Lord: “I have compared you, my beloved, to Pharaoh’s chariots” (Cant. I), so that, as once his proud soul drew the devil’s chariot, so, humbled, it may willingly draw Christ’s chariot. But if—God forbid!—he proves unconvertible, hard, stony, [Col. 1302B] setting his face firmly against us, trusting in our weakness and mocking, as is his custom, our simplicity, let him hear what the Lord says to one who lawfully contends: “I have made your face stronger than their faces and your forehead harder than their foreheads. I have made you like flint; I have made you like adamant” (Ezek. III).

Meanwhile, beloved, let us not murmur like servants, but wait patiently as sons. If we consider what we have done, what we suffer is slight. If our sins were weighed by justice alone, even the torments of hell would scarcely suffice. It is therefore better to be scourged with human beings than tortured with demons. Yet woe to us if we are crushed by a double crushing! I shudder to have seen some who, if a return from hell were granted them, would bear witness to us concerning that place of torments, [Col. 1302C] warning that your flight should not take place in winter, because, when sickness prevails, the limbs grow cold unto death; nor on the Sabbath, when after death it is not permitted to work. Christ rose from the dead (Rom. VII): listen to him (Matt. XVII). Receive his new commandment: love one another; forgive everyone, if you wish your offences to be forgiven. “Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. LII). Let your loins be girded (Luke XII) with the belt of chastity; washed in the fountain of tears, put on the breeches of modesty. Do not bring strange fire when you enter the holy places, lest the fire of God’s wrath consume you. Let fornication, or any uncleanness, not even be named among you, as befits saints. “But know this,” says the Apostle, “understanding that every fornicator, or unclean person, or covetous person has no share [Col. 1302D] in the kingdom of God” (Eph. V). The same Paul commands that one must not associate with such persons. For he condemns those devoted to shameful gain, watching for opportunities, buying cheaply and selling dearly. Blessed Jerome says: “Avoid a cleric who is a trader, made rich from poverty, as a kind of plague.” The use of dice is diabolical; we forbid our clerics to play them, for the sacred canons depose clerics who gamble. Therefore, having put aside every old thing and purged out the old leaven, be renewed in the spirit of your mind (Eph. IV), so that you may be a new conversion, as you are unleavened: without stain of flesh and without corruption of mind. Put on, therefore, the new human being; celebrate Easter joyfully and joyfully receive Christ who has been sacrificed. Therefore let us feast: [Col. 1303A] the bread of life and the cup of redemption have been set before us. Eat, friends, the bread of angels; drink with Jesus of the fruit of his vine in the kingdom of the Father. Be made drunk with joy in his resurrection, in which is our resurrection. Therefore rejoice aloud, lead the choirs, frequent the church, [Col. 1304A] cherish the altars, glorify God, and remember the poor with gladness. Farewell in the Paschal passage, in the Lord’s ascent, in the rising of the one who rises again, in the glory of the one who ascends, filled with sevenfold grace in the jubilee of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 1303]

## EIGHT HOMILIES OF BLESSED AMADEUS, BISHOP OF LAUSANNE, ON MARY THE VIRGIN MOTHER

(According to the edition of Richard Gibbon, theologian of the Society of Jesus, Antwerp, duodecimo, 1613.)

## PREFACE OF RICHARD GIBBON

To the Very Reverend Father Dom MORAND BLOMNE, most worthy abbot of the Cistercian monastery of Clairmarais near Saint-Omer, greetings and peace.

While I was seeking the ancient writers on divine matters for the composition of my work, which has long been in hand, I came upon, among others, Amadeus, a religious of the Cistercian family and an equally excellent and most holy bishop of Lausanne near Geneva. He wrote no more than eight homilies on the praises of the Virgin Mother of God; but—good God!—with what ardour of mind, with what spirit! I read and reread them; and, as my mind was so moved by them that I hoped they would benefit not myself alone but very many others, I resolved to bring them again to light, though they had been printed a hundred years ago.

Nor indeed was there long deliberation about under whose name and patronage I should issue them. For I thought of Your Very Reverend Paternity, both because of the remarkable kindness with which you are endowed—which I have experienced most frequently, since your distinguished library, filled with ancient manuscript books, has always stood open to me—and because of your zeal for religion and regular observance, which, as I have observed, you desire to be as great as possible first in yourself and then in the flock entrusted to you. I say nothing of the fact that this author belongs to your order and brings it no small honour, though this has hitherto been unknown, whether one considers his learning or his piety.

If the singular favour which Your Very Reverend Paternity has shown toward us English—especially those who reside in the English College at Saint-Omer—by many proofs has any influence with me, I shall not fail to ensure that it may be permanently evident that you have not bestowed your affection and love fruitlessly either upon myself or upon them. What I repay is slight, I confess; nevertheless, with your favour and encouragement, it will someday be granted me to bring forth greater things. For that great—indeed, great—Aelred of yours, abbot of Rievaulx, not unlike Saint Bernard in style and piety, is now in hand; I still keep unpublished various works, gathered from place to place and copied out in my own hand. He deserves to see the light and to be handled by all. He awaits a Maecenas. I hope that he will find you, most Reverend Father, favourable and kindly disposed toward him.

Until you see him making his way to you, I commend to you and yours this Amadeus—what a man, and how great a man! Receive, then, best Father, this son of your house, sent to you by me as a pledge of my love for you; and live safe and well for many years with the holy community entrusted to you.

Antwerp, from the College of the Society of Jesus, 22 July—the very feast day of Blessed Mary Magdalene—1613.

Of Your Very Reverend Paternity,

your unworthy servant in Christ,

Richard GIBBON.

## HOMILIES OF BLESSED AMADEUS

[Col. 1303]

## HOMILY I. ON THE FRUITS AND FLOWERS OF THE MOST HOLY VIRGIN MARY

[Col. 1303B]

Every holy and rational soul, investigating the secret mysteries of heaven and distinguishing the orders of the heavenly spirits, finds, first after the Redeemer, that woman blessed among women, full of grace, who bore God and did not lose the glory of virginity. This blessed Virgin, brighter than every light, more pleasing than every sweetness, and higher than every dominion, illumines the whole world; renewing all things by the outpouring of the finest ointment, she surpasses the hosts of cherubim and seraphim in power and majesty. May the King, therefore, through her glorious merits, bring us into his chamber; and may the offspring of David, who shuts and no one opens, opens and no one shuts (Rev. 3), disclose to us the hidden mysteries. May he reveal to us the joys of his Mother, the beauty of his chosen mother. Moses and the prophets bore witness to her; afterward the evangelists and doctors of the Church received her life, conduct, and grace, so that truth might be rendered consonant with itself, and what those foretold as future these might recall as accomplished.

Therefore, stirred by so many and such great praises, let us run after the fragrance of her ointments (Song 1); and, drawing in the breaths of her graces, while we are delayed and held back from her most sweet sight, let us rest among the flowers with which she commands herself to be supported in the Song, saying: “Support me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love” (Song 2). What are these flowers, if not the divine mysteries in her praise and the sacraments once hidden from the ages, now appearing in the flesh and disclosed in the Spirit, which have burst forth from the sayings of the Fathers as from certain jeweled trees? The Apostle explains the apples, saying: “The fruits of the Spirit are charity, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, long-suffering, gentleness, faith, modesty, continence, chastity” (Gal. 5). She is supported with flowers when the foretold oracles appear; she is surrounded with apples when that which is written is fulfilled: “Give her of the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates” (Prov. 31). But since discourse has turned to true flowers and the everlasting fruit of righteousness, we must, aided by the gift of the Spirit, treat these flowers and fruits more fully.

Let us therefore observe two, as it were, golden baskets full of fruits and adorned with flowers: the New and Old Testaments, standing on either side, left and right, of the Virgin. Their antiquity passes to the left, while new grace shines on the right. Rightly, indeed, is the law of death on the left and the law of life on the right: for the former makes one a transgressor, while the latter removes transgression. The Virgin herself, blooming among virgins with flowers and delighting in the sweetness of fruits, appears in the midst; and like a tree planted in the middle of paradise, she raises her top to the height of heaven and, conceiving from the heavenly dew, bears saving fruit: the fruit of glory, the fruit of life, of which whoever eats shall live forever.

That what has been said may become clear: paradise is the garden to which the Church invites her Beloved: “Let my Beloved come into his garden, that he may eat the fruit of his fruit-trees” (Song 5). For she calls herself the garden of the Beloved, watered by the fountains of the Savior and made drunk by streams of gifts, so that, wedded in the love of the Spirit, she may rejoice, budding under his droplets, and may delight in the offspring of many children as in the abundance of her fruits. She calls upon her Beloved to eat the fruit of the fruit-trees because she has kept for him new and old fruits (Song 7), namely, the sayings of both Testaments. Or these are the perfected dispositions of her heart, which she bears between her breasts, as we read: “Your breasts shall be like clusters of the vine” (ibid.). Or, certainly, they are all good spirits, both angels and human beings: some persevere in newness of life, while others bear from their former state and corruption that which causes them grief.

By the new and old fruits may also be signified the new and ancient Fathers, among whom the Bridegroom’s love feeds until the day breathes and the shadows incline (Song 2). In the midst of these and among them rises the saving tree of which we spoke, producing the food of life and heavenly manna—manna containing every delight and every sweetness. Had the first Adam touched it, he would not have tasted death forever. In the Gospel the Son of Man declares himself to be this bread, saying: “I am the living bread which came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he shall live forever” (John 6).

To return, then, to the aforesaid baskets, and to consider the flowers of the left and the fruits of the right: what the Law promised in flower, grace supplied in deed; there what was to come is put forth, here perfected power is praised; there is the sacrament, here the reality of the sacrament. Let us attend to these same baskets, displaying Christ’s glory and the Virgin’s childbirth. For this is the sum and end of the Testaments: to speak beforehand of Christ, to show Christ, to announce Christ, and Mary the Virgin. This is now covered by sacraments, now wrapped in enigmas or likenesses, now celebrated in festal rite, now shadowed in sacrifices, now declared by prophecy or confirmed by evangelical testimony.

And in this dense forest of Lebanon, on this shadowy and thick mountain, the Bridegroom’s condescension reveals itself to us, together with the chamber of his coming forth: the Savior of the nations and the earth bringing forth the Savior; the star from Jacob and ruler from Israel; the rod from Jesse’s root and the flower from his root. Elsewhere we read that Christ was to be born of a Virgin, suffer in the flesh, rise in glory, ascend amid rejoicing, and bestow the gifts of the Spirit upon believers; elsewhere, that he was born, suffered, rose, ascended, and pours the gifts of the Spirit into his own.

Thus in the Scriptures of truth it was announced concerning his holy Mother that a virgin would conceive and a virgin bear a son, whose name is Emmanuel (Isa. 7), and whose going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity (Mic. 5). The Virgin alone merited to receive him, alone to bear him, alone to nurse him, amid the vows and ardent expectation of the praying Church, which says: “Who will give you to me as a brother, sucking the breasts of my mother, that I may find you outside and kiss you, and no one may henceforth despise me?” (Song 8).

“I may find you,” she says, “outside in the light—you who are the Father’s secret; I may find you appearing in the flesh—you who lie hidden in invisible majesty; I may find you as the Bridegroom coming forth from his chamber” (Ps. 18), “you who were conceived in the virginal womb by the Holy Spirit. And I may kiss you: I may kiss you, united to you in receiving your flesh and blood, so that we may no longer be two but one flesh. I may kiss you, cleaving to you in one Spirit, because ‘he who cleaves to God is one spirit’” (1 Cor. 6). “And let no one henceforth despise me”: not God the Father, seeing his own Son incarnate; not the holy angel, worshipping God made man; not the proud demon, grieving that he has been overcome by Christ.

[Col. 1307A]

Moreover, let us add some matters from the Gospel. We read (Luke 1) that the Virgin was greeted by the angel, betrothed by God, conceived by the Holy Spirit, and bore true God and true man, who would save his people from their sins (Matt. 1), and whose kingdom shall have no end (Luke 1). He is the one promised to Abraham, that in his seed all nations would be blessed (Gen. 22). Of him the Apostle fittingly says: “Consider how great this man is” (Heb. 7), who comes to save the nations. Truly great is he whom the Father sent into the world as his only-begotten, whom the Virgin brought forth bodily, whom the Virgin conceived and bore, and after whose birth she remained a Virgin. He is announced by the archangel, conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the sacred Virgin, and foreshown by John while John was still enclosed in his mother’s womb (Luke 1). He is received by the aged Simeon with ineffable joy; Simeon proclaims him the light of the nations and the glory of the people of Israel (Luke 2).

Do you see, then, Wisdom reaching mightily from end to end and ordering all things sweetly (Wis. 8), producing for herself such fitting witnesses from a child not yet born to a decrepit old man, and harmonizing the instruments of truth with so sweet a concord? Hence it is said through the Prophet: “There is none who can hide himself from his heat” (Ps. 18). His going forth is from the Father; his return, to the Father; his course, to hell; his return, to the throne of God. For who can hide himself from his heat, when an infant felt him in the womb and a cold old man burned for him in the Temple? The former, as though signifying that he wished to meet the Lord, leapt with such movement as he could. The latter, receiving into his arms Jesus so incredibly long awaited, drank in divine love to the marrow; unable in frail flesh to bear the most sweet fragrance of the supercelestial essence and the power of the word flaming in his bones, he prayed for the dissolution of his body, so that, his mortal dwelling broken open, he might more freely enjoy the sweetness he had already tasted and might announce to those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death the newborn Savior whom he proclaimed among those above.

But what are we doing, or where are we being carried? Behold, while we desire to proclaim her blessed among women, we exalt the blessed fruit of her womb; and while we seek to praise the tree’s appearance, we are detained by the fruit’s excessive sweetness. For every tree is known by its fruit (Matt. 7) and assessed by its own abundance. As the palm by the sweetness of its dates, the vine by the liquor of its wine, the wild olive by the richness of its olive: so indeed the praise of the one born overflows to his mother, and the divine birth increases the honor of the woman who gave birth.

Beloved, I would gladly repeat what has been set forth in another sense and confirm it by another argument, so that blind unbelief may be reproved by the light and the faith of Christ may present itself as tangible and without offense. Let us enter the Holy of Holies and behold the mercy-seat, having above it two cherubim looking upon it with faces turned toward it and overshadowing it with outspread wings (Exod. 25). There, among other things, shines a golden vessel containing the hidden manna. There is Aaron’s rod which budded (Num. 17; Heb. 9).

Understand the mercy-seat as that of which the Apostle says that Christ himself “is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2). The two cherubim signify the two Testaments. For *cherubim* means “fullness of knowledge,” and fullness of knowledge is in the Testaments. Rightly, therefore, do the cherubim look upon the mercy-seat with their faces turned toward it and cover Christ, whom the Testaments unanimously proclaim and veil with figures and enigmas. The golden vessel is blessed Mary: golden through excellence of life, golden through integrity and purity, golden through fullness of grace. This vessel contained the hidden manna, for she bore in her most holy womb the bread of angels, who descended from heaven and gives life to the world.

She is also called a rod, as being gracious and straight, slender and extended. Gracious through modesty and beauty; straight through judgment and equity; slender through aptitude for contemplation; extended through the merit of life. She flowered by the Holy Spirit, as Aaron’s rod flowered by miracle. That rod produced almond fruit; this one also produced the best almond, having kernel and shell: kernel, that it may refresh; shell, that it may cover. The kernel is his divinity; the shell, his humanity. Do you wish to know the kernel? Hear: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1). Do you desire to know the shell? Hear: “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid.). You see, therefore, that the Word incarnate is kernel within the shell.

And because the shell also has a husk, understand the husk as the bitterness of the flesh, the shell as the resurrection, and the kernel as the Godhead. By the husk Christ heals us; by the shell he strengthens us; by the kernel he provides eternal nourishment. May this kernel, this Word, enlighten us between the two and bring us even into the chamber of his Mother—he who lives and reigns with the same God the Father, in the unity of the same Holy Spirit, God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY II. ON THE JUSTIFICATION OR ADORNMENT OF THE VIRGIN MARY

Since, with God’s assent, we have once begun the praises of the most blessed Virgin, it remains for us to render her praises with the inmost devotion of heart and the service of our voice. Let us fix our attention upon her glory; and, entering the abyss of so great a light, let us run with expanded heart and ineffable joy through the gleaming splendor of her paths, saying with Solomon: “Her ways are beautiful ways, and all her paths are peace” (Prov. 3). And if, as the same prophet says, “The path of the righteous is as a shining light, advancing and increasing unto the perfect day” (Prov. 4), who could suffice to describe the light and splendor of her paths? Yet we shall endeavor partly to explain the course and increase of these ways, so that she may be recognized as glorious in her degrees and proclaimed through each of her degrees.

For she had distinct degrees and divided advances, that she might proceed in the most beautiful order of chastity, and, advancing from virtue to virtue, might see the God of gods in Zion (Ps. 83), transformed from glory into glory as by the Spirit of the Lord (2 Cor. 3). First, therefore, she deserved to be adorned with the beauty of every virtue. Second, she was joined to the Holy Spirit by a marital covenant. Third, she was found to be the Savior’s Mother. Fourth, a sword passed through her soul, and, flesh having been taken from her flesh, the ruin of the lost world was repaired. Fifth, she rejoices in her Son rising again and ascending above the heavens of heavens to the Father’s right hand. Sixth, she is taken from this world and, as the Lord comes to meet her, is placed above all the heavenly beings. Seventh, finally, she will be perfected when the fullness of the nations has entered and all Israel is saved (Rom. 11). For she rejoices, beyond what it is lawful to say or believe, in the common salvation of the elect, knowing that for their sake the Son of God assumed flesh from her. Then, therefore, she will be perfected, God having provided something better, lest they should be made perfect without us (Heb. 11).

Let us now consider the names of these degrees. The first may be called justification or adornment; the second, union or covenant; the third, the Virgin’s childbirth or new offspring; the fourth, strength of mind or martyrdom; the fifth, joy or wonder; the sixth, assumption or exaltation; the seventh, fullness or perfection. The aforesaid justification or adornment proceeds from fear of God. Such a union and covenant likewise arise from incredible loving-kindness. For the Virgin’s childbirth and new offspring poured out the light of knowledge upon the universe. The work of strength was displayed when Christ died and his Mother looked on. But when he rose again, the utterly profound and inscrutable counsel by which he deceived the crafty enemy and redeemed the world flowed forth into joy and wonder. Then, with heaven opened, invisible goods are disclosed; and something marvelous comes to pass: as God, in man, learned human sufferings by experience, so the human being assumed into God perceives God’s glory with full understanding. Finally, Wisdom will bring fullness and perfection, so that the perfect may appear in the Perfect and glory in fullness.

Let us repeat what has been said, and, lingering again over these same degrees, contemplate the Lord leaning upon the ladder and the angels also ascending and descending to the Virgin. For they marvel at the most chaste maiden, soon to be the Mother of the Lord and Queen of Heaven, and break out in these words of wonder and praise: “Who is this” (Song 3) “who rises up whitened?” What is “whitened” but adorned with white garments—adorned, that is, with the ornament of beauty and honor, righteousness and holiness?
