These breasts are fragrant with the best ointments when the aforesaid Testaments of the Church become known to the perfect through their utterances: according to the capacity of their senses, they nourish some with the historical surface, instruct others with moral sweetness, and lift others to lofty things through mystical understanding. [Col. 1333D] They are also fragrant with the best ointments when to these same Testaments are added the grace of spiritual understanding and the power of divine charity, so that, like certain lilies, they may shine by the gift of understanding and give fragrance by the sweetness of love. Among these lilies the Beloved feeds, as it is said in the voice of his beloved: “My beloved is mine, and I am his, who feeds among the lilies” (Cant. II). For he feeds among lilies when he satisfies the reader’s mind in the Scriptures with the inward sweetness of his Word. Therefore, surrounded by these lilies, the Mother of God heard from Solomon’s mouth: “Thy belly is like a heap of wheat surrounded by lilies” (Cant. VII).

The souls of the saints may also be designated by lilies: white through the merit of their life, fragrant through the example of their virtue. Of whiteness the Psalmist says to God: “Thou shalt sprinkle me, O Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; thou shalt wash [Col. 1334A] me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. L). Of fragrance he declares: “My heart has poured forth a good word” (Ps. XLIV). And the Apostle says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (2 Cor. II). Thus, surrounded by lilies, the Mother of the Redeemer could most fittingly utter this word suited to them: “My joy and my crown” (Phil. IV); all of you were purchased by my blood and by flesh taken from my flesh. He was also enclosed by these lilies when he rescued the souls of the righteous from hell and blessed them with the endowment of his glory.

For the true Jacob crossed the Jordan of mortality on the staff of the cross (Gen. XXXII), and returned with two companies. By the two companies I understand circumcision and uncircumcision, those who were under the Law and those before the Law. Therefore he died alone and rose again with multiplied increase. For he himself is the life of all, and the life of all rose with him. “For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all shall be made alive” (1 Cor. XV). By whose death we sprouted, by whose blood our root grew, by whose resurrection the body flowered.

[Col. 1334B] It flowered not as grass, but as the Word; not as a day of this age, but as the day of heaven. Hence the voice of the supreme Father says of the seed of David: “I will establish his seed for ever and ever, and his throne as the days of heaven” (Ps. LXXXVIII). Therefore the eternal flower rose from his root: it withered in the Passion, but flowered again in the Resurrection. Yet it flowered again not in order to fall anew, like a field-flower, but that the Word of the Lord might remain for ever. For “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John I).

Therefore Daniel, the man of desires (ch. VII), declares that the Son of Man came even to the Ancient of Days, in order that he might show the Son of Man. The Psalmist, looking well upon him, says: “Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the rod of righteousness is the rod of thy kingdom” (Ps. XLIV), and what follows. Behold, he calls him God and declares that his throne is for ever and ever. Afterwards he relates that this same one was anointed by God with the oil of gladness above his companions (ibid.). For as God he is from eternity with the Father and reigns for ever and ever; as man, in time, he is anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions. Truly above his companions, to whom the Father says: “Thou art my Son; this day I have begotten thee” (Ps. II), and: “Sit at my right hand until I make thy enemies [Col. 1334D] thy footstool” (Ps. CIX). That you may understand him to be equal to the Father in divinity, hear him saying in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one” (John X), and, “He who sees me sees the Father” (John XIV).

The Apostle also says of him: “Because God exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name” (Phil. II), and the rest which follows. Truly the knee of those in hell bends to him through terror, the knee of those on earth through redemption, and the knee of those in heaven through blessedness (ibid.). Upon the first he threatens punishments; the second he led out from misery; the third he lifts up in glory. To the first he is terrible in judgment, to the second merciful in help, and to the third bountiful in reward. For he subjects demons with his sword, redeems human beings with his blood, and satisfies angels with his countenance.

[Col. 1335A] Therefore those in hell bend the knee, trembling at his power; those on earth bend the knee, praising his mercy; those in heaven bend the knee, crying: “Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God of Sabaoth” (Isa. VI). He is your Son, O Mary; he is your love; he rose for you on the third day and in your flesh ascended above all heavens, that he might fulfil all things. Therefore, O blessed one, you have your joy; your desire has been granted to you, and Christ is the crown of your head. He has brought you supremacy over heaven through glory, kingship over the world through mercy, and the subjugation of hell through power. To your glory, so great and ineffable, all things respond with differing affections: angels in honor, human beings in love, demons in trembling. For you are venerable to heaven, lovable to the world, [Col. 1335B] and terrible to hell.

Rejoice, therefore, and be glad, because your defender has risen—your glory, who lifts up your head. You rejoiced at the conception, were afflicted in the Passion; rejoice again in the Resurrection, and no one shall take your joy from you. “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. VI). Therefore he calls to you: “Arise, make haste, my friend, my dove, my beautiful one, and come. For now winter has passed; the rain has gone and withdrawn; flowers have appeared in our land; the time of pruning has come” (Cant. II). “My friend,” through union; “my dove,” through unity; “my beautiful one,” through beauty and harmony. Arise from grief, affliction, humiliation, and dust, which are signs of sorrow. Make haste: cast off delays, shake off the burden, put away heaviness, put on lightness, take up your course, assume flight, and come. [Col. 1335C] Come, that you may rejoice in the glory of God, the firstfruits of the resurrection, the firstborn from the dead.

Now winter has passed—the winter in which Peter, numb with cold, denied him; in which the hearts of the Jews, frozen, extinguished for themselves the sun of righteousness, while kindled by the coals of their own desires. The rain has gone and withdrawn: the turbid, muddy, destructive rain mixed with snow and hail has gone and withdrawn. The rain of those crying and saying, “Crucify him, crucify him” (John XIX), has gone and withdrawn. The rain also has gone by which the threshing floor of the Gentiles deserved to be dried and the fleece of the Jewish people likewise. Flowers have appeared in our land: namely, the flowers of blessed spirits and angels, flourishing in turn [Col. 1335D] and filling with most sweet fragrance the place where the Lord was laid.

The ancient Scripture signified these when it established two carved cherubim upon the mercy seat, at either end (Exod. XXXVII), and depicted them with palms upon the doors of the tabernacle (3 Kings VI). The reason is evident: it was shadowed forth in figures and is now displayed in reality. Palms bear the emblem of resurrection; the doors and the mercy seat designate him who is the open entrance into the kingdom and the propitiation for human sins (John II). For the two cherubim are two angels, one of whom sat at the head and one at the feet where Christ’s body had been laid (John XX). They are rightly called flowers, because the eternity of the supreme God gives them an eternal spring, [Col. 1336A] so that they always bloom, never wither, never fall, and remain the same in inviolable beauty.

Flowers also appeared in our land when, as the Lord ascended, two men stood beside the apostles and said: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand wondering as you look into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you, will so come as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts I). The time of pruning has come: hell was pruned, and the devil was cut away from the heart of believers. The mouth of the Lord separated precious things from vile, cutting branches from the vines (Jer. XV) and gathering tares from the harvest, that he might store the grain in barns (Matt. XIII), handing the tares over to fire to be burned.

O mournful separation, grief and joy mingled everywhere! O sweet and bitter day, when the just Judge, [Col. 1336B] returning from hell, turned his back upon some and showed his desired face to others; left some in punishment and raised others as co-heirs in the kingdom; dismissed those to burn with the devil and lifted these up to be crowned in heaven! The wicked saw and groaned without hope; the good saw and rejoiced with full heart. O wretched ones, whom mercy did not assist! O good ones, whom it met in glory! O wretched ones, whom the Passion of the Only-Begotten itself did not help! O good ones, whom it rescued from perpetual death! The wicked saw and groaned without hope; the good saw and lifted up their voice in jubilation.

Likewise, you beheld your glorious Son ascending from the lower world; with your most blessed eyes you gazed upon the glory of your Son, and you saw and fainted. Your flesh and your heart failed [Col. 1336C] (Ps. 62); you melted (Song 5), when you heard the voice of your beloved Son speaking with you. His word became like a blazing fire in your bones. Therefore, kindled by divine converse, you became wholly as fire, and offered yourself to God as a holocaust most sweetly pleasing. O Phoenix, breathing fragrance more pleasing than cinnamon and balsam, delighting the King in your sight more sweetly than nard! O Phoenix, gathering every kind of spice, and surrounded by superessential fire, so that you fill the heaven of heavens and the angelic powers of heaven with incense of wondrous sweetness. This is most sweet incense; this well-compounded perfume rises from the censer of Mary’s heart (Exod. 30) and surpasses every sweet fragrance. Moreover, the censer, following the incense and raised by the Lord’s hand, ascends even [Col. 1336D] to the throne of Him who presides. It ascends attended by the escort of angelic spirits, crying aloud in the heights and saying: “Who is this who comes up through the wilderness, like a little column of smoke from the spices of myrrh and frankincense, and from every powder of the perfumer?” (Song 3.) But let this discourse, now brought as far as the Ascension, be concluded, so that another may, with God’s help, set forth this Ascension more fully. He lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## Homily VII. On the Death of the Blessed Virgin, Her Assumption into Heaven, and Her Exaltation at Her Son’s Right Hand

As I reflect upon and repeatedly reconsider in my mind the Assumption of the Mother of God, a question presents itself—one worthy of inquiry, useful when discovered, and exceedingly delightful [Col. 1337A] when clearly communicated. For the question is why, when the Lord ascended into heaven, his Mother, who embraced him with such affection, did not immediately follow him. Since she was weighed down by no cloud of sin, stained by no blemish of life; since she glowed above fire through charity, was brighter than light through chastity, and was splendid even to the citizens of heaven themselves through the novelty of her virginal childbirth, it seemed wondrous that she was not at once borne up with her Son to the heavens.

Certainly Enoch walked with God in purity of heart and was seen no more, because God took him away (Gen. 5). Elijah likewise, exceedingly inflamed by the fire of charity, is said to have been carried off in a fiery chariot and by fiery horses (4 Kings 2). But she, surpassing Enoch in purity of heart and greater than Elijah in the prerogative of love—why was she not immediately borne into heaven with him whom she bore? For she was full of grace and blessed among women (Luke 1). She alone merited to conceive the true God from true God; as Virgin she gave birth to him, as Virgin she nursed him, cherishing him in her lap and ministering to him in all things with loving service. Finally, she suffered more in spirit than in body with him as he died; she came to life again through the Spirit of God with him as he rose; and why did she not ascend with him as he ascended? For her most sacred flesh, which was made pregnant by the Holy Spirit, which swelled with the shoot of the magnificent King—in which God became man, the Word was made flesh (John 1), and through Christ the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily in her (Col. 2)—seemed, once the Lord had been assumed, fit to be brought into heaven.

Why then was she delayed, even for a moment? [Col. 1337C] Why did she suffer separation from her Son? Why was her most holy desire, burning with a more ardent fire, deferred? Because this delay was no small consolation to Christ’s disciples. It diminished nothing for the Mother and bestowed remedies of salvation upon the world. For the Lord Jesus wished that, when he himself returned to the Father, the apostles might enjoy maternal consolation and instruction. Although they had indeed been taught by the Spirit, they could nevertheless be taught by her who brought forth for the world the sun of righteousness and produced for us from her virgin meadow, her undefiled womb, the brow of wisdom.

In wonderful mercy provision was thus made for the primitive Church: though it no longer saw God present in this flesh, it might be refreshed by the most delightful sight of his Mother. For what could be so [Col. 1337D] pleasing, so beautiful and delightful, as to see the Mother of the Maker and Redeemer of all? If the tomb of our same Redeemer, which remains even today, is so desirable to behold; if the stone upon which the holy stock of Jesse rested is sought with such reverence that it draws to itself the affections and minds of all and, by a certain art of devotion, attracts everything to itself—what, or how great, was the joy of seeing the Mother of God, while divine mercy allowed her to live among us upon earth under the common lot?

Blessed was the nation and happy the generation that deserved to be illuminated by such a sight. Blessed indeed was that people in whose midst stood the tree, producing the fruit of life for those who believed and enjoyed it; the Mother of the true Light shone forth; that closed and sealed fountain appeared, from which came forth the spring of David’s house, open for the washing of the sinner and the menstruous woman (Zech. 13). This outstanding privilege, this heavenly gift, this special grace, were granted to the Church of the first believers.

Finally, the Virgin Mother bore in herself the commerce of every charism. By her very first appearance, sparkling with the fires of sacred love, she gently burned the hearts of her neighbors; she instilled faith into souls, commended modesty, gave beauty to uprightness, and bent them toward mercy. She breathed the flower of virginity, sowed the fresh field of chastity, portrayed before their eyes the bearing of humility, and displayed the sign of truth. “An unfailing brightness was around her, and a burning fire went forth from before her face” (Ps. 17). A fiery and swift river went forth from her (Dan. 7), to set enemies aflame, cherish friends, aid neighbors, and consume foes.

Those acquainted with the nature of animals report that the venomous basilisk, by its look alone and its deadly breath, kills everything near it. So she, on the contrary, violently enkindled by the heat of divine fire and scattered with the flames of the blazing Word, breathed out the fragrance of life-giving grace upon those who remained far off and those who were near (Isa. 57).

To some—namely, those of the adverse party—she was an odor of death unto death; but to others, namely those who believed in her Son, an odor of life unto life (2 Cor. 2). For as all die in Eve, so all shall be made alive in Mary. And as Eve’s crime brought about the condemnation of the world (Gen. 3), so Mary’s faith brought about the restoration of the world. The former was infected by deadly poison, which she transmitted [Col. 1338C] to her descendants; the latter was infused with a life-giving antidote, which in faith she conveyed to all. The former fell by wickedly believing the serpent; the latter rose and, according to the word God spoke in Genesis, crushed the serpent’s head (Gen. 3): foretold from the beginning, granted now to the primitive Church, promised from that time, and manifested at the end of the ages.

Who then would not hasten? Who would not run from the ends of the earth to behold the glory of such reverend majesty, to see that countenance endowed with every sweetness, imperial dignity, and singular power? Nothing like her was found among the sons and daughters of Adam. Nothing like her appeared among prophets, apostles, or evangelists. Heaven and earth gave nothing like her. “For who among the clouds shall be equal to her?” (Ps. 88), or who among the sons of God could be like the Mother of the Lord? And see in what fitting order her wonderful name shone throughout the whole earth before the Assumption, and her most celebrated fame was spread everywhere, before her magnificence was exalted above the heavens.

For it was fitting that the Virgin Mother of the Lord, in honor of her Son, should first reign upon earth, and then at last be received into heaven with glory; that she should be extended among those below, so that in holy fullness she might penetrate also into the things above—translated, as it were, from strength to strength and from brightness to brightness by the Spirit of the Lord (2 Cor. 3). Therefore, while present in the flesh, she tasted beforehand the first fruits of the kingdom to come: now approaching God with ineffable sublimity, now condescending to those near her with unutterable charity. On the one hand she was surrounded by angelic ministries; on the other she was revered by human service. Gabriel, the bridegroom’s friend, stood by her with the angels; John, rejoicing that the Virgin Mother had been entrusted to him, a virgin, at the cross, ministered to her with the apostles (John 19). The former rejoiced to see their Queen, the latter their Lady; and both rendered service according to the affection of their devotion.

But she, seated upon the loftiest citadel of virtues and overflowing with an ocean of divine charisms, poured out upon the believing and thirsty people, in most generous streams, the abyss of graces by which she surpassed all others. She brought health to bodies and healing to souls, being able to raise the deadness of flesh and soul. Who ever left her sick, sad, or ignorant of heavenly mysteries? Who did not return [Col. 1339B] joyfully and gladly to his own home, having obtained from the Mother of the Lord what he desired? Mary’s presence brought the pleasant mildness of spring; wherever she graciously turned, there was paradise.

“Your shoots,” says the Bridegroom, “are a paradise of pomegranates with the fruits of orchards; Cyprus with nard; nard and saffron, calamus and cinnamon, with all the trees of Lebanon; myrrh and aloes, with all the choicest ointments. A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, flowing in abundance from Lebanon” (Song 4). The paradise of the glorious Virgin has pomegranates in the variety of her virtues, fruits of orchards in the perfection of her works. It has also Cyprus with nard: the former fruitful in grapes, the latter an aromatic herb of marvelous fragrance—representing the sober intoxication of the senses [Col. 1339C] and the sweetly fragrant reputation of virtues. To these are added saffron and nard of joy; calamus, representing the stripping away of the flesh; cinnamon, representing sweetness; and all the trees of Lebanon, by which the totality of virtues is signified. There are also myrrh of mortification and aloes of incorruption, with all the choicest ointments poured forth in prayer, from that ointment which, resting upon the head, descended upon the beard, the beard of Aaron (Ps. 132)—not of that old Aaron who signified, but of the new Aaron who was signified. And it descended to the hem of his garment, which is the Church; that Church, according to Paul, presented to Aaron himself without spot or wrinkle (Eph. 5).

Thus the Bride, mother of the only Bridegroom, overflowing with these and such great goods, sweet and most dear amid delights, like a fountain of rational gardens and a well of living and life-giving waters flowing in abundance from Lebanon (Song 4)—from Mount Zion even to every surrounding and foreign nation—poured forth streams of peace and emanations of graces by heavenly infusion. Hence Blessed David, when speaking of her Son, our Lord, said: “In his days righteousness and abundance of peace shall flourish”; and then fittingly added of her, “until the moon be taken away” (Ps. 71). She herself is the moon, irradiating heaven and earth and shining far beyond the stars of the saints. “Until,” he says, “the moon be taken away”—she who, when the sun of righteousness was raised aloft, stood in her place (Josh. 10) and first shone upon the primitive Church. The faith of the fathers, in accordance with the truth of history, hands down that, from the Savior’s birth until the departure of his glorious Mother, the inhabitants of the lands rested in unbroken and tranquil peace, the frenzy of arms having been stilled. We have said these things in resolving the proposed question, to show with what benefit the Mother of our King was delayed.

It must also be observed from this delay that every faithful soul, wounded by charity and pierced by the arrows of love, should learn not to murmur if it should not be granted to depart hence according to its desire. Behold, the Mother of the Lord is delayed: who would dare to murmur? She is delayed in order to advance; she advances by persevering. For perseverance joined to love or to work creates fullness and produces perfection.

Hence the Psalmist says of the righteous: “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree; he shall be multiplied like the cedar of Lebanon” (Ps. 91). The palm tree is said to flower after a long passage of time, and the cedar of Lebanon is multiplied by the progress of years; so the righteous person, growing gray in spirit, shall flourish like the palm through long endurance. Hence the aforementioned Psalmist suitably adds a few words: “They shall still multiply in a fruitful old age” (ibid.). It should therefore be observed that Mary, of most excellent merit and singular righteousness, who deserved to be exalted above the angels, first had to be multiplied here in a fruitful old age. When this came about by the divine gift, her hidden honor and the form which she had borne in secret, becoming brighter than light and more excellent than all beauty, turned toward herself the faces and minds of the citizens above with wondrous love.

But who could fittingly extol in praises her most sacred Assumption? Who could explain how joyfully she departed from the body, how joyfully she saw her Son, [Col. 1340C] how gladly she hastened to the Lord, surrounded by choirs of angels and supported by apostolic service, when she beheld the King in beauty and saw her Son awaiting her with glory—as she who was free from every corruption was also immune from every affliction? She was led out from the dwelling of the flesh to dwell forever with Christ. She passed into the vision of God, and breathed forth to the Lord that most blessed soul, brighter than the sun, higher than heaven, worthier than angels.

Indeed, in her glorious departure Mount Zion is made radiant, where she, advanced in days, died in a good old age. There she fulfilled the office of life, giving the full and perfect consummation of all virtues. There the camp of God came out to meet one who was rather rising than dying, rather departing than perishing; and the armies of the heavenly host rushed forth to meet her. O how precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his Mother! What life can equal her death? What joys can equal her funeral? Add, if you will, worldly honors; add banquets and festive triumphs; add everything that delights and charms the whole world: yet her death is more joyful and more sweet than all these. For it is release from the flesh, a way to life, containing no pain, no bitterness, no fear. Instead of pain it comforts, instead of bitterness it delights, and instead of fear it strengthens upon the shore of faith’s resting-place. It does not bring darkness, since it opened eternal light; nor does it take away life, since it directs life to the author of life.

By this glorious death she departed—if it is permissible to call a passage into life “death.” Rather, to speak truly, it is life, where death alone dies, where the body of death [Col. 1341A] is put off, where the life of the flesh, devoutly ended in repose, is kept for the future with manifold increase. Is it not life, when one goes to the fountain of life and eternal life is drunk from life by an unceasing stream? The Virgin Mother was anticipated by this unfailing draught before her departure, so that in that very passage she might not be touched even by the slightest taste of death. Going forth, therefore, she saw life, so that she might not see death. She saw her Son, so that she might not grieve at the body’s departure. Thus, escaping freely into so most blessed a vision and obtaining the desired countenance of God, she found the venerable citizens of heaven ready to serve and escort her.

They marvel that a soul of singular merit, freed from eternal stain, bears no blemish of flesh or world. They marvel that, stripped of its limbs, it shines with the grace of complete purity. For what should they first praise in her: integrity or humility, prudence, strength of mind or long-suffering, the honor of motherhood or the novelty of childbirth? But complete virtue and full grace are more greatly praised in her.

Therefore the Lord, standing by as she leaves the body, proclaims her praises thus: “You are wholly beautiful, my mother, and there is no stain in you” (Song 4). “Wholly beautiful,” he says: beautiful in thought, beautiful in word, beautiful in deed; beautiful from birth to end; beautiful in virginal conception, beautiful in divine childbirth, beautiful in the redness of my Passion, beautiful in the distinguished brightness of my Resurrection. “Arise therefore, my friend, my dove, my beautiful one, my immaculate one, and come. For now the winter of my absence has passed; the rain of your tears has gone and departed; and, with the returning sun [Col. 1341C] of righteousness, angelic flowers have appeared for you. Your voice, O most chaste turtledove, has been heard” (Song 2). The time of Assumption has come.

Therefore, when the Virgin of virgins was being led by God and her Son, the King of kings, while angels exulted, archangels and heaven rejoiced together, and praises resounded, the prophecy of David was fulfilled, speaking to the Lord: “The queen stood at your right hand, in a garment of gold, surrounded by variety” (Ps. 44). Then, according to Solomon’s words, “Daughters rose up and called her most blessed, and queens together praised her” (Prov. 31; Song 6). “Who is this,” say the heavenly powers, “who comes up whitened, leaning upon her beloved?” (Song 8.) Or again: “Who is this who comes forth like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun?” (Song 6.) And again they said: “Who is this who comes up through the wilderness, like a little column of smoke from the spices of myrrh and frankincense, and from every powder of the perfumer?” (Song 3.) “This radiance is new and wondrous to us; this order of Assumption is new and glorious; this most sweet fragrance is new and pleasing.”

But led with such great praises, she herself could not cease from praise, as she saw the Son of God, begotten from herself, seated at the right hand of the Father’s majesty and receiving her into glory. “You have held my right hand; in your will you led me, and with glory you received me” (Ps. 72). And again: “He is at my right hand, that I may not be moved; therefore my heart has rejoiced and my tongue shall exult; moreover my flesh also shall rest in hope. For you have not abandoned me [Col. 1342A] in the world, nor will you allow the body of your Mother to see corruption” (Ps. 15).

But why do I linger over these things? To gather much into few words: there was present to the most glorious one the simple and manifold Word, the intelligible Word containing every word of praise, by which she herself honored the Lord and her Son with ineffable praise. Raised therefore amid cries of exultation and praise, she is placed, first after God and above all the citizens of heaven, upon the throne of glory. There, having resumed the substance of flesh—for it is not lawful to believe that her body saw corruption—and clothed in a double garment, she contemplates God and man in each nature, with the eyes of mind and body, as much more brightly than all others as more ardently than all.

Thereupon, condescending to the human race with unutterable charity and turning toward us those most merciful eyes by which heaven is illumined, she raises a common prayer for clergy, people, and both sexes, for the living also and the dead. From heaven she is present, most glorious and most powerful in prayer; repelling every harmful thing and bestowing every good thing, she grants to all who pray to her from the heart protection in this present life and the life to come. Mindful of the benefit through which she became Mother of the Redeemer, she most willingly receives the prayers of every sinner and intercedes with her own Son for the whole guilt of those who repent. Certainly the dearest Mother will obtain whatever she wills, through whose most chaste womb the Word of God came to us—Jesus Christ our Lord, who was to wash away the sins of the world and the bond of ancient sin by his own blood; [Col. 1342C] who lives and reigns with God the Father, God in the unity of the Holy Spirit, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## Homily VIII. On the Fullness or Perfection, Glory, and Patronage toward Her Clients of the Virgin Mary

Many days, most beloved, have passed during which, burdened by the episcopal charge and weighed down by immense cares, I have not been able to provide to your eager desire the banquet I promised concerning the praise of holy Blessed Mary. Now therefore, with that same Virgin herself favoring us, I shall not fail you, withdrawing myself a little from business and yielding to your devout desires. Let us therefore diligently celebrate in worship the Queen of heaven, Mother of life, fountain of mercy, overflowing with delights and leaning upon her beloved [Col. 1342D] (Song 8); and let us proclaim her with praise, though unequal to her worth.

Let us lift our minds on high, attentively considering how the most graceful rod sprung from the root of Jesse (Isa. 11) spread itself throughout all lands by the marvelous extension of its branches, in order to protect the scattered children of Adam from heat, storm, and rain by its desirable shade, and to nourish the hungry with its most health-giving fruit. Thus raised above all the trees of paradise and exalted above the lofty summits of the highest mountains, it penetrated the very heavens by immeasurable greatness, surrounded by choirs of heavenly orders and adorned with choirs of virgins. O beauty, glory, and magnificence of this tree, whose unfailing fruit and immortal food provide to citizens of heaven and earth an unceasing banquet, continual exaltation, and happy, everlasting praise! “Blessed are those who eat bread in your kingdom; blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord: they shall praise you for ages of ages” (Ps. 83).

In you too shall be praised, not Eve, the giver of death, but Mary, the giver of life, mother and nourisher of those joined to the life that lives. In you your Mother shall be praised. “Let the meek hear and rejoice” (Ps. 33). The glorious and arrogant Lucifer, wounded, fell to the depths: let the proud hear and be humbled. The humble Virgin ascended, crowned, to the throne of glory: let the humble hear and rejoice. He fell, exalted by great self-confidence; Mary entered in holocausts, entrusting her whole self to the fullness of grace. Hardened in wickedness, he shall add no more so as to rise again; strengthened in charity, she shall no more be moved so as to fall. For, clinging to an immovable center with unconquerable firmness, she can never be moved by any changeableness.

He, exceeding the most splendid bounds of angelic dignity while striving after that to which a created spirit cannot attain, pursued emptiness, was swept away over precipices, covered in dreadful darkness, and flowed down into the depths of the pit, to suffer forever and pay in torments the penalties of a most just condemnation. He is deservedly called the devil—that is, “the one flowing downward”—because he flowed down from the heights and, envying those who stand, still drags down with himself into the lower regions those whom he can.

He prompts his followers to seek honors, dignities, and eminences; to think lofty thoughts; to raise their horn on high; to love the acclamations of the crowd, greetings in the marketplace, the first seats in assemblies; to despise inferiors, prefer themselves to equals, envy superiors, forget God’s glory, subject some to themselves through flattery and others through threats or punishments, set themselves up as an idol, and do everything for human display and praise. When he has thus raised these wretched, haughty, puffed-up, bewildered, and deranged people to the clouds, then he cruelly bends them, utterly enervated, toward every shameful and dishonorable thing; and, without any pity, he hurls them down with himself into the lowest hell.

But the most glorious Virgin, most perfect in body, most serene in mind, gentlest toward the living—because she was humbler and holier than all, was raised above all, and was received most honorably into heaven by the citizens of heaven, and in imperial manner by the supreme Father. In the kingdom of eternal brightness and on the most excellent throne of glory, she was commanded to sit first after her Son, whom she bore incarnate from herself. Great God, terrible and mighty, of ineffable goodness: you raise and exalt the humble handmaid to the place from which you formerly expelled the rival enemy! Let humility triumph with increases of grace and with the illustrious crown with which you adorn it; but let empty and dark pride fall apart.

Therefore the most blessed one stands before the Creator’s countenance, singularly eminent in merit, ever making most powerful intercession for us. Taught by that light to which all things are naked and open, she sees all our dangers; and, as our merciful and gentle Lady, she pities us with maternal affection.

The holy living creatures of whom Ezekiel writes (Ezek. 1) [Col. 1344A] that they are full of eyes before and behind, within and without, and round about, cannot examine human labors and sorrows, misfortunes, failings, blindnesses, illnesses, extreme dangers, uncertain outcomes of life, and every evil of humankind as fully as the Mother of God can; nor can they, through heavenly aid, dissolve and repel them as she does. For the more sublimely she looks upon the heart of the immeasurable King, the more deeply, through the grace of divine mercy, she knows how both to pity the afflicted and to help the wretched.

Hence Mary was called, by God’s provident counsel, the “star of the sea,” so that her name might declare what she herself shows more clearly. For from the time she ascended to reign in heaven with her Son, clothed in beauty and likewise clothed in strength, she has girded herself to restrain by her nod alone “the wondrous surges of the sea” (Ps. 92). For she rescues those sailing upon the sea of this present age, who call upon her with full faith, from the force of the storm and the fury of the winds; and she brings them, rejoicing with her, to the shore of their most blessed homeland.

It cannot be said, beloved, how often some would strike upon most rugged rocks and suffer shipwreck, others would fall into the worst quicksands never to return, these would be swallowed by the fearful gulf of Scylla, those would be sweetly drawn to destruction by the songs of the Sirens, unless the perpetual Virgin Mary, Star of the Sea, had opposed them with most powerful aid and, when their rudder was already broken and their vessel shattered, had borne her own people—destitute of every human counsel—under heavenly guidance to the harbor of eternal peace.

Thus exulting in new triumphs, the new rescue of the lost, and new increase of peoples, she rejoices [Col. 1344C] in the Lord. Not content with the spoils of one portion, but desirous of human salvation, she drives the envious enemy farther away and continually acquires spoil after spoil for herself. Therefore with mighty hand and exalted arm she goes beyond the bounds of tyrants, attacks even the most fortified houses, makes hell tremble beneath her feet, and causes the prince of death, struck by overwhelming terror, to recoil. Finally, at her command, he violently vomits forth the prey that he had swallowed into the belly of his host, casting out in pain what he had held with immense pride. The fallen rise; penitents return: “The sinner shall see and be angry” (Ps. 111). His jaw pierced by the hook of the Lord’s cross, he gives back as free those whom he had formerly held captive, gnashing and wasting away with his teeth (ibid.). Through the Mother they are reconciled to the Son; through the Virgin, to the God of life; they are wholly withdrawn from death. “The desire of sinners shall perish” (ibid.), but the desire of Blessed Mary is fulfilled when those bound are daily brought out from the pit of misery and the mire of filth (Ps. 39), so that, released from sin’s prison and the depth of iniquity by the gift of forgiveness, they may breathe the air of everlasting freedom. Thus she gathers the scattered, calls back those who have turned away, rescues those being led to death, and never ceases to free those whom she sees being dragged to punishment.

She provides and heals with devout care not only for the salvation of souls but also for the health and needs of human bodies. In places dedicated to the memory of her holiness, she obtains movement for the lame, sight for the blind, hearing for the deaf, and speech for the mute, curing every kind of disease and granting innumerable benefits of healing. Guilty people come to her thresholds, beating their breasts and confessing their sins; having received pardon, they return joyfully to their homes. Those deprived of reason also come: persons sick in mind, frenzied, manic, possessed, deluded by nocturnal terror or another phantom, or by an actual assault of the evil one. Having recovered health, they obtain the bounty of the divine gift.

Likewise there come to her feet those who are bitter in spirit, sad, needy, afflicted, desolate, burdened with debt, and—what is most grievous—living under the stain of disgrace. She willingly receives the prayers of these and of all who cry out in whatever tribulation; pleading with her Son, she mercifully turns every evil away from them. For as wax melts at the touch of fire and ice melts in the sun’s heat, so the battle-line of enemies perishes before her face; and at her command nothing adverse endures.

It should indeed be noted and attentively considered with what affection and how great a kindness she embraces and loves those akin to her in purity of mind—she who, as has often been said, ceaselessly frees wicked and criminal people by her intercession from the death of sin and eternal pains. Distinguished and radiant with a twofold love, she is fixed most ardently upon God, to whom she cleaves as one spirit (1 Cor. 6); on the other hand, she gently consoles and draws the hearts of the elect, distributing to them excellent gifts through the bounty of her Son.

[Col. 1345C] Therefore, extending her six seraphic wings with swiftest motion, she now delights in the love of the Godhead at the fountain of life; now, illuminating the earth with signs and mighty works, she comes everywhere to her own as a most joyous and wondrous Mother. Some, by her presence, she makes victors over subdued vices; some she causes, by her devout intervention, to attain great virtues; to others she opens the bosom of inward contemplation; to others, at life’s departure, she provides a safe road, so that no power of the adversary may terrify those whom the Mother of God’s Only-Begotten guides to Christ.

There are very many examples of these assertions, which we pass over briefly as most familiar and widely known. Yet it must be known with certainty that the most frequent miracles, innumerable benefits, spiritual visions, heavenly revelations, and lofty consolations of the gracious Mother of the Lord will shine continually over the whole world until this aging world reaches its end and the kingdom whose end does not exist shines forth (Luke 1).

But amid these matters, that famous [Col. 1346A] day of judgment returns to mind—a day whose dread the holy prophet David declares that he fears (Ps. 55), and whose continual approach no believer fails to know. At that moment of terrible judgment, with angels, archangels, and the whole host of the heavenly army in attendance, the King of heaven will appear with the aforementioned most merciful Mother, to judge the world in righteousness and peoples in equity (Ps. 97). Then she shall shine with most splendid light, she through whose untouched womb and closed gate God, the King of glory, shed his light upon the world.

At that time the truth of the patriarchs and prophets will be made manifest—the patriarchs and prophets who long ago bore divine witness to the Virgin’s childbirth. The apostles too, her sons, imitators and witnesses of her virtues, will bring her glory and honor because, enlightened by her teaching and strengthened from heaven by the incoming Spirit of wisdom, they filled the Church with the splendors of the true Sun. The martyrs shall exult in the beauty and grace of their poured-out blood, possessing as their most excellent reward God from God, who deigned to be born of her.

The confessors will rejoice, seeing glorious her whom they loved while dwelling on earth and whose merits they pursued with most celebrated praise throughout their lives. They will rejoice, I say, beholding that singular diadem which, on the day of solemnity and joy, on the day of Assumption and glory, Christ placed upon his most beloved Mother—remembering that diadem with which she crowned him on the day of his espousal (Song 3). Virgins shall run in the fragrance of her ointments (Song 1), [Col. 1346C] hastening to enter the wedding with her, so that, joined forever to the true Bridegroom in the heavenly bridal chamber (Matt. 25), and with Mary leading the song, they may sing in response the new song (Rev. 14), which no one can utter unless one is a virgin in mind and body.

Finally, every sex and age, every rank and dignity, shall proclaim her most blessed; and an innumerable people shall acclaim her in joy, saved by her merits and prayers and crowned in the right hand of the merciful Lord. May it be granted that we belong to their number and company, O merciful, O loving, O sweet Mary, so that, when the day of wrath, tribulation, and distress comes, we may not be punished for guilt, but through you, Lady, may be found worthy of the mercy of him who ascended to the Father to prepare a place for his servants (John 14), that he might set them in the most delightful region of heaven, in the brightest dwellings of paradise among the blooming fiery stones: our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong beauty, honor, power, glory, and magnificence, with the same Father and the Holy Spirit, through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1347]

## Extract from the Diploma of Emperor Frederick I, Granted in Favor of Blessed Amadeus

*(Mémorial de Fribourg.—Plantin manuscripts. Given by Lord Baron de Gingins.)*

… Therefore we entrust our functions to our most dear chancellor Amadeus, bishop of Lausanne—who is acknowledged to be bound to us by lineage and nobility, and likewise by fidelity—in gathering, administering, and revoking grants; in confirming what is necessary; and in summoning ecclesiastical persons and barons to the court, in view of the man’s integrity and of the ancient dignity of the Church of Lausanne.

[Col. 1347]

## Letter of Nicholas, First a Monk of Cluny and Then of Clairvaux, Secretary to St Bernard, to Blessed Amadeus

*(Manrique, Annals of the Cistercians, under the year 1144, vol. I, p. 464.)*

[Col. 1347A] Brother Nicholas, at the feet of his father, offers himself. It would be great presumption, were it not that my love is great, for me to venture to write to your exaltedness; for affection draws me—an affection that cannot obey laws and over which kings cannot rule. I do not know how it happened, but from the time I saw you, your love poured itself richly into the innermost chambers of my soul; nor was there any delay between sight and affection, though I had spoken with you later.

If therefore I write confidently, it is because I love faithfully; if I am bold, I am nevertheless not false. Love does not recognize a lord; it recognizes a friend. Even amid mitres it is ignorant of rank; rich in condescension, powerful in affection, effective in persuasion, clear-sighted in purity. What then if you have gone up on high, my lord—indeed rather, my beloved? Even above the wings of the winds you cannot withdraw from my affection; and if you ascend to the heavens, I shall follow you wherever you go. For I love not the pontiff but the man, who bestowed the zeal of the Law upon the chair, rather than received it from the chair.

[Col. 1348A] What vigor is that, what keenness of spirit, which by the leap of its subtlety breaks through every obstacle, and which can philosophize concerning each of the arts, even with each individual master of an art? Therefore your generosity, even amid mortality, is pre-eminent: according to the orator, it shows itself gentle toward children, gracious toward young men, grave toward old men; strengthening all, adapting itself to all, common in conversation, equal in companionship, outstanding in counsel, and greatly to be desired because least of all ambitious. For I have seen you noble without pride, powerful without envy, devout without superstition, learned without boastfulness, grave without dullness, witty without affectation, steadfast without harshness, and sociable without fickleness. I marvel at this: that you possess a consciousness superior to eminent learning. Such does my spirit believe you to be; such does my affection declare you, continually whispering to me of the spirit of your sweetness.

[Col. 1348B] I send you Master Anselm’s book *On the Holy Spirit*, well punctuated, unless I am mistaken, and corrected. I, I say, who am yours and shall be yours as long as I exist, most loving Father.

## A.D. 1154–1159: Adrian IV, Roman Pontiff

[Col. 1349]

## Historical Notice

(Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 785)

[Col. 1349A] Adrian IV, an Englishman by nation, called Nicholas before his pontificate, cardinal of the Church and bishop of Albano, was sent by Eugenius into Norway. After spreading the Christian faith there and converting the barbarian people, he returned to Rome. Formerly the apostle of Norway, he was a man very gracious—these are the words of the Vatican manuscript—mild and patient, skilled in Greek and Latin, eloquent in speech, polished in rhetoric, exceptional in ecclesiastical chant, an excellent preacher, slow to anger, quick to forgive, a cheerful giver, generous in almsgiving, and distinguished in every aspect of moral character. On the third day before the Nones of December [3 December], in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1154, during the reign of Emperor Frederick I, he succeeded Anastasius in the pontifical see.

In his time, adherents of the heresiarch Arnold—who was protected in the City by the influence of the Arnoldists among the Romans and by the authority of the senate—attacked on the road Lord Gerard, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Pudentiana, as he was going to the pope, and wounded him mortally. For this reason the city was placed under interdict and was not absolved until they expelled Arnold and his followers from the walls and jurisdiction of the City. Once they had done so, the censure of interdict was removed and the citizens themselves were restored to the reception of the sacraments.

Arnold the heresiarch, banished from the City, was captured in the territory of Tuscany near Otricoli by Gerard, cardinal of Saint Nicholas. The viscounts of Campania then snatched him from his hands; they honored him in their land with every distinction as though he were a prophet. At the pope’s insistence, Frederick—still only king—punished one viscount severely and put the others to flight, thereby restoring Arnold to pontifical jurisdiction. Finally, the prefect of the City, at the pope’s command while he was present in Rome, put him to death by the gibbet; and, after his corpse had been reduced to ashes on a pyre, cast the ashes into the Tiber, lest his body be held in veneration by the foolish populace.

[Col. 1349C] He bound William, king of Sicily, with the bond of anathema because the king had rejected pontifical letters on the ground that they were not addressed to him with the royal title which he had assumed, and because he had occupied certain lands of the Church. Learning that Emperor Frederick had entered Italy with numerous forces, he went out to meet him and advanced as far as Sutri. When they met, the emperor dismounted from his horse and treated him with the honor due to him. Accompanying him to Rome, the emperor received the imperial crown. Without delay he restored to the pontiff the city of Tivoli, whose inhabitants had submitted to the emperor, because he understood it to be a patrimony of the Church; he then returned to Germany.

Thereafter, summoned by the leading men of the kingdom, Adrian went to Benevento and recovered the greater part of it from William’s control. While he was staying there, the emperor of the Greeks, through ambassadors, offered the pontiff fifty thousand pounds of gold [Col. 1350A] and promised, at his own expense, to drive William from Italy, provided that three maritime cities in Apulia should in the meantime be given to him. Stirred by this news, William attempted through intermediaries to make peace with the pontiff. He promised to restore everything that he had occupied—indeed, much more—if he were invested with the title of king of both Sicilies. The pontiff would immediately have granted his request had not the greater part of the cardinals dissuaded him. But after William had subjected all Apulia to himself with a strong army, Adrian, angered by the cardinals’ resistance, granted William everything that he had requested and conferred the aforesaid titles upon him.

After these matters were settled, Adrian went to Orvieto, which he was the first Roman pontiff to ennoble by making it his residence. Returning to Rome, he reproached Emperor Frederick by letter because the injury inflicted upon the archbishop of London had not been avenged. From these letters, wrongly understood, arose that dangerous dispute between Adrian and Frederick concerning the Empire, which Radevicus describes at length. The discord was calmed when the pontiff, in a second letter, explained that by the conferral of a *beneficium* he had meant nothing but the imperial coronation and the consecration conferred upon Frederick with it. It was revived when the pontiff refused to confirm the bishop whom the emperor had appointed at Ravenna.

[Col. 1350B] While residing at Rome, he was troubled by the citizens and returned to Anagni, where, after a short interval, he died from the illness of quinsy, as William of Tyre writes, after conducting himself praiseworthily in the pontifical office for four years and ten months. His body was brought to the City and buried near the tomb of Eugenius.—These details are summarized from the Vatican manuscript in Baronius, Otto of Freising, and William of Tyre. Dodechinus, in the appendix to Marianus, says: “Adrian had resolved to excommunicate the emperor on account of the marital dispute, but death forestalled him in October 1159.” Otto of Freising, who lived and wrote in these times, reports in Book VII, last chapter, that the venerable pope died in the eighth year of Emperor Frederick, which coincides with the year of Christ 1159.—“In the year 1160, on the Kalends of September [1 September], Pope Adrian died,” says the continuator of Sigebert.

Radevicus, *De gestis Friderici imperatoris*, Book II, chapter 43: “At that time,” he says, “Pope Adrian ended his final day at Anagni on the Kalends of September [1 September], and on the second day before the Nones of September [4 September] was honorably buried in the church of Saint Peter, in the presence of the clergy, senate, and Roman people, while the royal envoys were still there.” Therefore, the story which the heretics slanderously report is not merely non-miraculous but downright fabulous; without doubt it arose from a misunderstanding of the illness of quinsy from which Tyre writes that he died. John of Cremona, a shadowy schismatic author, is cited by Abbot Urspergensis, a supporter of the schismatics, in his *Chronicle*, in these words:

> “When he came to a certain spring, he drank from it; and immediately, as is said, a certain fly entered his mouth and clung to his throat, and could not be removed by any skill of physicians until he breathed his last.”

[Col. 1351A] It is not likely that so unprecedented and extraordinary a death would have gone unmentioned by the writers of his time whom I have listed above, if—God forbid—such an end had befallen the supreme pontiff. If, according to Pope Adrian’s judgment, no writer was silent that Emperor Frederick was swallowed by a river and his army miraculously destroyed by God, [Col. 1352A] who would believe that all writers would have been silent about a similar death of Adrian, had it occurred? No less a slander is the assertion by each supporter of the schismatics that Adrian was bribed to excommunicate Frederick—as though there had not been sufficient reason to condemn with a sentence of anathema one who had repudiated his lawful wife and taken another, and who, after being once reconciled with the Apostolic See, had again spewed forth against it the injuries described by Radevicus.

Adrian left posterity an admirable example: he gave not even an obol to his relatives, so much so that he would not spend anything even on his own mother, whom he left to be supported by the alms of the Church of Canterbury (as John of Salisbury testifies in Letter 24 to Saint Thomas).

[Col. 1351]

## Life of Pope Adrian IV, by Cardinal of Aragon

(Muratori, *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, III, I, 441.)

[Col. 1351B] Adrian IV, an Englishman, from the town of Saint Albans, who had been Nicholas, bishop of Albano, reigned four years, eight months, and six days. In his youth, in order to advance in literary studies, he left his country and kindred and came to Arles. While he was engaged in study there, it came about by the Lord’s providence that he entered the church of Saint Rufus and received there the religious habit, after making canonical profession.

Thus, advancing with God’s help from good always to better, he first obtained the priorate in that house and afterwards, by the common will of the brethren, rose to the summit of the abbacy. It happened that, because of matters concerning the Church entrusted to him, he came to the Apostolic See. When all the business for which he had come had been completed and he wished to return home, Pope Eugenius of blessed memory retained him with himself and, by the common counsel of his brethren, consecrated him bishop of Albano.

After a short time, when his integrity and prudence had become known, Eugenius sent him as legate of the Apostolic See from his own side into Norway, so that he might preach the word of life in that province and strive to win souls for almighty God. He, as a minister of Christ and a faithful and prudent steward of the mysteries of God, diligently instructed that barbarous and uncultivated people in Christian law and formed them by ecclesiastical teaching.

[Col. 1351C] Then, by divine disposition, before the day of his own apostolic office had arrived, Pope Eugenius died, Anastasius was appointed in his place, and Adrian returned, with the Lord as his guide, to his mother, the most holy Roman Church. He left peace to kingdoms, law to barbarians, quiet to monasteries, order to churches, discipline to clergy, and to God a people acceptable, zealous for good works. After a short interval Anastasius also died. On the second day thereafter, when all the bishops and cardinals had assembled at the church of Saint Peter to elect a shepherd for themselves, it came about, not without the disposition of divine counsel, that they unanimously agreed upon him. Clergy and laity alike acclaimed him Pope Adrian, and, though unwilling and resisting, enthroned him in the see of Saint Peter, God bringing it about, in the year 1154 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the third indiction.

[Col. 1352B] He was a man very gracious, mild and patient, skilled in English and Latin, eloquent in speech, polished in rhetoric, exceptional in chant and an excellent preacher, slow to anger, quick to forgive, a cheerful giver, generous in almsgiving, and distinguished in every aspect of moral character.

In those days Arnold of Brescia, a heretic, had presumed to enter the City and, spreading the poisons of his error, sought to turn the minds of the simple away from the path of truth. The aforesaid Roman pontiffs Eugenius and Anastasius had already labored greatly for his expulsion. But, protected and secure by the favor and power of certain perverse citizens, especially of the senators who had then been appointed by the people to govern the city, the aforesaid heretic remained insolently in that city in defiance of Pope Adrian’s prohibition and began to plot against him and his brethren and openly and savagely oppose them.

[Col. 1352C] For certain of those heretics, with impious audacity, presumed to attack on the Sacred Way the venerable man Master D . . . ., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Pudentiana, as he was going to the presence of the pontiff, and wounded him unto death. For this reason the pontiff placed the Roman city under interdict, and the whole city ceased from divine offices until Wednesday of Holy Week. Then the aforesaid senators, compelled by the Roman clergy and people, came into the presence of the same pontiff and, at his command, swore upon the holy Gospels of God that they would without delay expel from the whole city of Rome and its territory the oft-mentioned heretic and all his followers, unless they returned to the pope’s command and obedience.

Thus, after they had been expelled and the city absolved from the interdict, all were filled with great joy, together praising and blessing the Lord. On the next day, namely Maundy Thursday, when an immense multitude of people flocked from every quarter after their delay to receive the grace of the annual remission and to celebrate the glorious feast, [Col. 1353A] that same gracious pontiff, together with his brother bishops and cardinals and an immense throng of nobles and citizens, left with great honor the Leonine City, where he had been staying from the time of his ordination. Passing through the middle of the city, while all the people rejoiced with him, he arrived joyfully at the Lateran patriarchal palace. There, on that day and on the following Friday and Holy Saturday, and likewise on Easter and on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday, he solemnly celebrated the divine mysteries; and in the Lateran palace, according to the ancient custom of the Church, he festively ate the Paschal meal with his disciples. When the feast had been celebrated with joy, each returned home rejoicing.

At the same time William, king of Sicily, insolently raised his horns against his mother and lady, the most holy Roman Church. Having assembled an army, he caused the land of Saint Peter to be invaded in hostile fashion. [Col. 1353B] His army besieged the city of Benevento for some time and burned its boroughs. Then, entering the territory of Campania by force, it also burned the town of Ceprano, the castle of Babucum, and other undefended places. For these and other offenses, Pope Adrian drew Peter’s sword and struck the king himself with the sword of excommunication.

Meanwhile Frederick, king of the Germans, entered Lombardy with a great army and besieged the city of Tortona for a long time. Once it had been conquered and brought under his power, he hastened swiftly toward the City with such urgency that one might rightly believe an enemy rather than a protector was approaching. When this became known, Pope Adrian, who was then residing at Viterbo, after deliberating with his brethren and with Peter, prefect of the City, and Oddo Frangipane, sent to meet him John, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul; G., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Pudentiana; and G., cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. [Col. 1353C] He also gave them the remaining articles and prescribed the manner and form in which they were to come to terms with him for the Church.

Having received their instructions, they departed quickly, found him at San Quirico, approached him, were honorably received, and conducted into his tent. After the greeting they presented him with apostolic letters and explained to him the command of the lord pope. Among other things, these contained the demand that he return to those cardinals the heretic Arnold, whom the viscounts of Campania had taken from Master O., deacon of Saint Nicholas, at Bricole, where he had captured him; they honored Arnold in their country as a prophet.

When the king heard the lord pope’s commands, he immediately sent officers, seized one of those viscounts, and the latter, greatly terrified, at once restored the heretic into the hands of the cardinals. Before the arrival of those cardinals, however, the king had sent ahead Arnold, archbishop of Cologne, and Anselm, archbishop of Ravenna, to the presence of the oft-mentioned pontiff, to negotiate with him concerning the king’s coronation and to settle other matters together. Therefore he could give the cardinals no answer until he had first received those archbishops.

[Col. 1353D] The pontiff had intended, because the emperor’s arrival seemed exceedingly suspicious, to go to the city of Orvieto and wait for the emperor there. But because of their sudden and unexpected arrival he fell into greater uncertainty. Since he could no longer safely go to that most secure place, he hastened up to the city of Castellana, where, if the king had evil designs upon his person, he could safely avoid the king’s anger and easily frustrate his wicked plans.

The archbishops followed him, setting forth the king’s good will toward him and the whole Roman Church and likewise presenting the other matters entrusted to them. The pontiff said to them by the counsel of his brethren: “Unless I first receive my brother cardinals [Col. 1354A] whom I sent to the king, I shall give you no answer.” Thus the cardinals returned from the king and the archbishops from the pontiff, their business unfinished, and met one another, saying mutually that because of their absence an answer had been delayed on both sides. Therefore, after taking more prudent counsel together, they came jointly into the king’s presence in the Viterbo plain, where he had pitched camp.

Octavian, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia, had come to him—not sent by the pontiff, but dismissed by him—and was already breathing schismatic sedition. After the aforesaid cardinals had entered the king’s presence and had deliberated concerning their embassy and the fulfillment of the Roman pontiff’s command, Octavian began to spew forth the poison that he had imbibed and to disturb the peace. But he was shortly suppressed by his brother cardinals with cogent reasoning and, as he deserved, covered with much confusion.

At last, after the opponent had been refuted and sound counsel approved, [Col. 1354B] the king assembled the great court of all his nobles and soldiers. In the presence of those cardinals, sacred pledges were brought forth: the cross and the Gospels. A certain noble knight, chosen from among the others, was sworn and ordered to swear three times; he swore upon his own soul and that of the king himself that neither the life nor limbs of Pope Adrian and his cardinals would be taken but preserved; that no evil seizure would be made; that their honor and goods would neither be taken away nor permitted to be taken away; and that, if anyone should wish to take them away, he would wholly prevent and oppose it. He further swore that, after any injury inflicted upon them, he would to the utmost of his power cause it to be avenged and redressed, and would henceforth preserve inviolate the concord long before made through the principal persons of the two courts.

When this oath, as has been said, had been given by the king and gladly received by the cardinals, they immediately took leave and returned at a rapid pace to the supreme pontiff, [Col. 1354C] carefully reporting to him and his brethren all that they had done. It pleased the pontiff and those at his side that such security had been given them by the king and firmly confirmed by the counsel of his princes. Therefore, with every evil suspicion removed, he graciously assented to the royal request that the imperial crown be placed upon him. A suitable place and a fixed day for them to see one another were appointed by both sides.

The king accordingly advanced with his army into the territory of Sutri and pitched camp on the plain called Grasso. The pontiff descended to the town of Nepi. On the second day, many German princes coming to meet him, he was joyfully conducted, with a great multitude of clergy and laity and with his bishops and cardinals, to the presence of the aforesaid king, even to the king’s tent. But because the king did not, according to custom, perform for the pope the service of *strator* for the pope and hold his stirrup, the cardinals who had come with him, disturbed and greatly alarmed, withdrew and returned to the aforesaid Castellan city, leaving the pontiff at the king’s tent.

[Col. 1354D] The lord pope, therefore, greatly troubled with astonishment and uncertain what he ought to do, nevertheless dismounted sorrowfully and sat upon the faldstool prepared for him. Then the king came to his feet and, having kissed them, wished to proceed to the kiss of peace. The pontiff immediately addressed him in these words:

> “Since you have withheld from me that customary and due honor which your predecessors, the orthodox emperors, have been accustomed, out of reverence for the apostles Peter and Paul, to render to our predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, down to these times, I shall not receive you to the kiss of peace until you make satisfaction to me.”

The king replied that he ought not to do this. Accordingly, while the army remained in the same place, the whole following day passed in various discussions of this matter. At last, after the older princes had been consulted, especially those who had come with King Lothar to Pope Innocent, and the ancient custom had been diligently investigated, the judgment of the princes, confirmed by the common approval of the entire royal court, decreed on the basis of their report and ancient records that the king himself should, in reverence for the blessed apostles, render Pope Adrian the service of *strator* and hold his stirrup.

[Col. 1355A] On the next day the king’s camp was moved and transferred into the territory of Nepi, beside the lake called Jaula. There, as the princes had ordained, King Frederick advanced a little way; and, approaching the lord pope’s tent, he came by another road, dismounted from his horse, and met the pope at a distance of a stone’s throw. In sight of the army, he cheerfully performed the service of *strator* and firmly held the stirrup. The pontiff then first received the king to the kiss of peace. Afterwards they proceeded together toward the City. Since the Roman people were hostile to them, although the pontiff held the fortress of Saint Peter in his power, it was nevertheless decided that the king should enter the Leonine City with a strong force.

Having therefore pitched their camps outside and quickly taken counsel and arranged what pertained to the coronation, on that same day before the third hour the king, surrounded by a very great multitude of armed men, came to the steps of Saint Peter’s. There he laid aside the garments which he wore, clothed himself in more solemn attire, and went up to the church of Saint Mary in the Tower, where the pontiff awaited him before the altar. He bent his knees before him and, placing his hands between the pontiff’s hands, publicly rendered to him the customary profession and full security, in accordance with what is contained in the rite.

[Col. 1355B] Leaving the king there, the pontiff ascended to the altar of Saint Peter. The king followed his steps in procession. Before the silver doors, another of our bishops pronounced over the king the prayer, within the church, at the *rota*. A third bishop likewise conferred upon the king the third prayer and the anointing before the Confession of Saint Peter. When Mass had begun and the gradual had been sung after the Epistle, the king came to the pontiff to be crowned. The imperial insignia having been presented, he received from the hands of the pope himself the sword, sceptre, and crown of the Empire. Immediately the loud and powerful cry of the Germans, shouting in a voice of praise and joy, resounded so that a terrible thunderclap seemed suddenly to have fallen from heaven.

After these things had been completed in peace and tranquillity before the ninth hour, the Roman people, who were armed and stationed behind closed gates near the Castle of Crescentius, unaware of what had happened, began gradually to ascend toward the Leonine City without consultation or deliberation of their elders. Violently plundering the spoils of those who had remained in the Portico, they drove into flight all whom they found, pursuing them as far as the emperor’s camp.

[Col. 1355C] As the cries increased and an unexpected tumult resounded everywhere, the German army swiftly rushed to arms; swords were drawn, and fierce fighting took place on both sides. Why say more? Many were killed and very many captured. At last the people themselves, not without great loss among their own number, withdrew behind the gates of that castle.

But the pontiff, like a most gracious shepherd and loving father, was deeply troubled and grieved by so great an offense, and compassionately regarded that people as his own flock with the charity due to them. Wishing to relieve their plight, he labored long with the clemency of the emperor for the liberation of his sheep and did not cease earnestly to offer heartfelt prayers until he had secured the release of all the captives of the City from German hands and their restoration to the custody of Peter, prefect of the City.

Thereafter the emperor and the pontiff, leaving the territory of the City together, proceeded across the plains beside the Tiber as far as the ford of Magliano. There they crossed the river with the whole army and entered the Sabine county. Passing through Fara [Farsa] [Col. 1356A] and the castle of Poli, they arrived at the bridge of Lucano on the vigil of Saint Peter; and there, indeed, they decided to remain for the celebration of so glorious a solemnity. So that the Church of God and the Empire might shine with greater splendor, it was determined by common deliberation that, for the praise of God and the exaltation of the Christian people, the aforesaid Roman pontiff and Augustus should proceed together, each crowned, to the solemnities of the Mass on that day.

For it was entirely fitting that the two supreme rulers of the City should celebrate with joy and great gladness the feasts of those two princely apostles, who, having received from the Lord the power of binding and loosing, close and open the gates of heaven for whom they will. Then the people of Tivoli, as faithless and contumacious persons, wishing to withdraw themselves from the lordship and jurisdiction of Saint Peter, and setting aside the fidelity which they had recently sworn to Lord Pope Adrian and his successors, presumed to come into the presence of the emperor. [Col. 1356B] Having handed him the keys of their city, they gave themselves, together with the city of Tivoli, into his right and lordship.

The pontiff and the entire Roman Church regarded this deed as exceedingly grave and altogether intolerable. He complained to the emperor concerning so great an injury inflicted on Saint Peter without reasonable cause and earnestly begged him, as the proper advocate of the Roman Church, to restore to him the city which from ancient times was known to belong by right to Saint Peter. The Augustus, having taken counsel with his princes and learned the truth, immediately restored the city to him and, by the letter copied below, ordered the people of Tivoli faithfully to obey and in every way strive to serve the pope as their lord and father.

### Letter sent by the Emperor to the Citizens of Tivoli, ordering them to obey the Pope

[Col. 1356C] **FREDERICK**, by the grace of God emperor of the Romans and ever Augustus, to all citizens of Tivoli: his favor and good will.

We wish your community to know that, out of reverence for blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, we have relinquished the city of Tivoli to our most beloved and revered father in Christ, Pope Adrian, while preserving unimpaired in every respect the imperial right. For this reason we absolve all and each of the citizens of Tivoli from the allegiance which you recently swore to us. We earnestly command and direct you faithfully to support that venerable Pope Adrian, serve him devoutly, and strive to obey him devoutly as your lord; knowing, as has already been said, that you are absolved from the oath of allegiance which you recently made, while in all matters the imperial right remains reserved.

And because the heat of summer had already grown excessive, and a very great multitude of that army, owing to the unhealthiness of an unfamiliar climate, had incurred either the danger of death or a deadly [Col. 1356D] illness, the common will and urgent petition of the princes was that the emperor should return without delay to his own lands—which indeed he did. At the same time the aforesaid king of Sicily, after being struck by the sentence of excommunication, began to be held in contempt by his own people; and, since he scorned the salutary counsels of his faithful men concerning the satisfaction he should make, he was left almost alone in his pride and folly. For his leading counts and barons, together with the greater cities of Apulia, when they could by no means recall him from such great perversity, abandoned him and sent their envoys to the lord Pope Adrian as their principal lord, begging him to deign to come into those regions and receive into his hand and power the land itself—which is recognized as belonging by right to Blessed Peter—as well as their persons and goods.

Then the pontiff, having taken counsel with his brethren on these matters and assembled a splendid force of counts and other nobles from the City, Campania, and the surrounding places, came down to San Germano about [Col. 1357A] the feast of Saint Michael. There, having received fealty and homage from Robert, prince of Capua, Count Andrew, and other nobles of those parts, he sent them ahead of him to prepare his way and make the crooked straight and the rough places into level roads. A few days later he himself, passing through the castle of Mignano and the city of Capua, proceeded in the company of the count-lord as far as Benevento; and in that city he received almost all the barons of those regions, their lands, and the surrounding cities into fealty to Blessed Peter and to himself, as their principal lord.

Meanwhile the emperor of the Greeks sent a large sum from his treasury to Ancona through one of his princes, named Palaeologus. He also wrote to the same pontiff, asking and requesting that he grant to that emperor three of the coastal cities of Apulia, on the condition that he would unfailingly furnish the pontiff with sufficient forces, both in money and in soldiers and other armed support, for attacking the aforesaid king and expelling him from the whole of Sicily [Col. 1357B]. Moreover, he promised to give five thousand pounds of gold to the same pope and his curia.

Therefore the king, greatly alarmed by the measures daily being taken against him, and moved by repentance for his error, resolved in all humility to return to the bosom of his mother, the most holy Roman Church, and to the obedience of his lord and father, the Roman pontiff himself. Accordingly, he sent as far as Salerno the elect of the Church of Catania, together with several of the leading men of his court, who were to appear before the pontiff; he gave them full authority humbly to seek the lord pope’s grace and peace, and to render him the full satisfaction set out below, with firm security.

First, he sought absolution according to the custom of the Church; then he promised to perform homage and fealty to the pontiff. [Col. 1357C] He would restore all the churches in his lands with full liberty. As compensation for the damages inflicted, he would likewise give to Blessed Peter and the Roman Church, as their own hereditary property, the three castles of Padule, Montefusco, and Mortone, with their appurtenances. Moreover, he would subject Rome, which was then hostile to the pontiff, to the pope’s lordship by arms or by money. After recovering the favour of the lord pope and of the Church, he would bestow as much money as the Greeks had offered.

When these offers had been heard, the lord pope, by the common counsel of his brethren, sent as far as Salerno the venerable man Hubald, then cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes and now bishop of Ostia, so that he might inquire of the aforesaid envoys whether the things offered rested upon assured truth, and report to him what he found. This was done; and when the cardinal returned, everything promised on the king’s behalf was found to be true and ready for fulfilment.
