It therefore seemed good to the same pontiff [Col. 1357D] that so advantageous a concord and settlement, bringing great honour to the Church, ought to be accepted. But because the greater part of the brethren, judging the terms too lofty and wholly uncertain, would not consent at all, the whole offer was set aside and utterly rejected.

And because, according to the evangelical saying, “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, and he who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 14), after the king had thus humbled himself and his satisfaction had not been received, he marched with an army against the Greeks and Apulians who had occupied his land. Coming as far as Brindisi, where they had assembled, he fought them in the field; and having at last overcome, decisively defeated, and put them to flight, he won a complete triumph over them. Consequently such fear and trembling suddenly seized all Apulia and its borders that thereafter no one dared resist him. All fled before him and immediately restored to his lordship, without arms or compulsion, cities and very strongly fortified castles.

For this reason, after the pontiff [Col. 1358A] recognized that he had been deceived and utterly abandoned by all who had sworn to stand firmly with him, he sent the greater part of his brethren into Campania and himself remained at Benevento with a few men, awaiting the king’s arrival. After a few days had passed, the king himself moved with his army from the upper parts of Apulia and approached within two miles of Benevento. Then the aforesaid pontiff sent to the king the venerable men Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes; J., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus; and B., cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mark and chancellor of the Apostolic See, that in the name of Blessed Peter they might earnestly admonish him wholly to cease from his offences, make satisfaction for the damages inflicted, and peacefully preserve the rights of his mother, the most holy Roman Church.

Received and treated kindly by the king, they debated various articles in mutual discussion. Through their mediation the king and pope reached agreement; [Col. 1358B] and the king came to the church of Saint Marcian, situated near Benevento, humbly prostrated himself at the pontiff’s feet, and performed liege homage and fealty to him before a very large crowd of bishops, cardinals, counts, barons, and others standing around, Odo Frangipane administering the oath. The king was then received to the kiss of peace, and having bestowed great gifts in gold, silver, and silken cloths upon the pontiff, his brethren, and his whole curia, they departed from one another joyful and rejoicing.

The most gracious pope then left the city and territory of Benevento and directed his journey toward the city of Rome. Passing through Monte Cassino and the Marsican mountains, he came to the city of Narni. Since the city of Orvieto had for a very long time withdrawn itself from the jurisdiction of Blessed Peter, but he had recently acquired it with much effort and diligence and subjected it to the lordship of the Roman Church, [Col. 1358C] it seemed good to him and to his brethren to go to that city and honour it by his presence. For, until his time, as everyone said, none of the Roman pontiffs had ever entered that city or exercised any temporal power there. Therefore the clergy, people, and knights of that place received the pontiff with the greatest eagerness and highest reverence, and honoured him in every way they could. Remaining there for some time, he affectionately honoured great and small alike as a new household of Blessed Peter, and rejoiced in the sight of them. As winter approached, he went down to the pleasant and populous castle of Viterbo, and thence returned to the City and the Lateran consistory with due glory and honour.

This blessed pontiff thoroughly repaired in the church of Saint Peter the roof of Saint Processus, which he found dilapidated; [Col. 1358D] and, raising a wall on three sides above the oratory of Saint John at the Font, he made it level with the nave of the same church. In the Lateran palace he also diligently caused a very necessary and capacious cistern to be made, and repaired many other things in the same palace that had fallen into ruin through excessive age. In the church of Saints Cosmas and Damian, in mid-Lent, he dedicated the high altar by placing a stone upon the stone which the blessed Pope Gregory had consecrated with his own hands.

He greatly enlarged the patrimony of Blessed Peter through extensive properties and buildings. He purchased the castle of Corchiano from Buccaleone for one hundred and forty *afforciati* pounds. He likewise purchased from Ildebrand and Bernard, sons of Count Ugolino of Calmangiare, two excellent mills situated near Saint Christina, for one hundred and ninety pounds of the same currency. From the same counts he received, in pledge, Rocca Santo Stefano with half of Proceno and Repeseno, for one hundred and forty [Col. 1359A] eight *afforciati* pounds and five solidi, upon the terms written in the public instrument. He also received, through their voluntary donation, all the land of those same counts, as is contained in their public instrument deposited in the archives, as Blessed Peter’s own hereditary property. In the same manner and upon the same terms he likewise acquired all the land of Odo de Poli as Saint Peter’s own hereditary property.

He made at the castle of Radicofani a fortified enclosure with towers and a deep ditch. He also populated the deserted castle of Orta, which had been a den of robbers, for the peace and security of that district, and fortified it with a wall and towers at no small expense. At Ponte Lucano he caused a chapel to be built, in which he gave a six-ounce chalice, a bell, books, and priestly vestments for the celebration of Masses. Near that bridge he also bought from the wife of John de Benedicto, a citizen of Tivoli, two *modii* of land for seven *afforciati* pounds, and one from Raynald for twenty-eight [Col. 1359B] *afforciati* solidi; and from Gregory and Milo de Vallomontis, one and a half *modii* for twenty-five solidi of Pavia currency. He also bought [Col. 1360A] near the same bridge six *modii* of land from Odo de Insula and his wife for twenty-four *afforciati* pounds.

Moreover, he bought from the daughters of Raynald de Guardeja half of four castles—namely Castiglione, Cinciniano, Canapino, and Bulsignano—for [lacuna] *afforciati* pounds. He received a public instrument for this, and corporal investiture, through Antimus his marshal, from Vitalis, guardian of the aforesaid women, in the presence of Alexius the notary, the pope’s cupbearer; Peter de Arture, knight; Gallesano Malavolte; John Ferri; and many others.

He held two ordinations, in December and March: seven deacons, five priests, and bishops in various places, numbering [lacuna]. He died at Anagni on the Kalends of September [1 September], was carried to Rome, and honourably buried in the church of Blessed Peter beside the body of Pope Eugenius. Recorded by Boso, cardinal priest of the title of Pastor, whom this pontiff had appointed his chamberlain from the beginning of his pontificate [Col. 1360B], and whom he had ordained deacon in the church of Saints Cosmas and Damian; Boso remained constantly in familiar attendance upon him until his death.

[Col. 1359]

[Col. 1361]

# Letters and Privileges of Adrian IV

For the books consulted, see the bibliographical index prefixed to volume 179.

## Year 1154

[Col. 1361A]

### I. He confirms the possessions of the monastery of Aniane.  
*(Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 12 December.)*

[*Histoire du Languedoc*, II, preface, p. 549.]

**ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son WILLIAM, abbot of Aniane, etc.**

Whenever [requests are made] by religious men, etc. . . . We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, and whatever has been canonically bestowed upon the aforesaid monastery of Aniane through the monastery of Gordanic, from the donation of our brother Raymond, bishop of Uzès, shall remain secure [Col. 1361B] and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The church of Saint John of Aniane, etc.; the fisheries which the same monastery possesses in the sea and in the lagoon at Frontignan; finally, the gift of Aribaticus, with the water of the river Aniane, from the royal mill to the bridge of Vérone, which Raymond and Aienius, Bernard and Beatrice, counts of Melgueil, are known to have granted to that monastery; likewise the fief of Adaliz, etc.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of Roland, cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, on the second Ides of December [12 December], third indiction, in the year 1154 from the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 1361C], in the first year of the pontificate of the lord Pope Adrian IV.

### II. He confirms the arrangement made concerning the churches of Saint Geneviève, while preserving the rights and reasonable customs which the bishop of Paris possessed in them.  
*(Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 16 December.)*

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 829.]

[Col. 1362A]

**ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother THEOBALD, bishop of Paris: greeting and apostolic blessing.**

That our predecessor Pope Eugenius of blessed memory directed the churches of Blessed Geneviève to be administered by regular canons, as we have learned from his letters, was not done by him, nor did he intend it, [Col. 1362B] so that you or your successors should lose anything of your right which you are known to have possessed in those churches, or so that he might think the jurisdiction of your Church ought to be removed or diminished. Rather, it was so that those churches might be served by honourable and religious men rather than by lax and scandalously living persons. Therefore, confirming by the authority of the Apostolic See what he ordained in this matter, we wish all rights and reasonable customs which your predecessors are known hitherto to have possessed in the aforesaid churches to be preserved for you and your successors without any diminution. Let no person whatsoever therefore be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or rashly to oppose it. If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His apostles, the blessed Peter [Col. 1362C] and Paul.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January [15 December].

### III. He orders Hugh, abbot of Saint Remigius of Reims, and Master Fulk, disputing over the mastership of the schools in the borough of Saint Remigius of Reims, to return before him “after a period of two years, after the next Sunday on which ‘Laetare Jerusalem’ is sung.”  
*(Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 19 December.)*

[Varin, *Archives administratives de Reims*, I, 1, 334.]

[Col. 1363A]

**ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HUGH, abbot of Saint Remigius, etc.**

[Col. 1364A] You and our beloved son Master Fulk, canon of the Church of Reims, acting on behalf of our beloved son Leo, dean and master of the schools of the Church of Reims, came before the judgment of the Apostolic See and laid before our hearing that controversy which was being conducted between you concerning the mastership of the schools in the borough of the church of Saint Remigius. But since you had not come sufficiently prepared for the conduct of the case, we could not impose its due conclusion. Therefore, after a period of two years, following the next Sunday on which *Laetare Jerusalem* is sung, we have thought fit to appoint for you a date for hearing the case, so that, when each party has returned to the Apostolic See and is sufficiently furnished with its documents and witnesses, the same case may receive its due end under judgment of the Apostolic See. In the meantime, let your monastery possess as it possesses, and let its possession in no way be disturbed by the other party.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January [19 December].

### IV. He confirms the possessions of the monastery of Saint Remigius of Reims.  
*(Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 19 December.)*

[Varin, *ibid.*, I, 1, 328.]

[Col. 1365B]

**ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to HUGH, abbot of Saint Remigius of Reims.** . . . . . . . . .

A pious request ought to be fulfilled by a favourable result, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the benefit requested may undoubtedly acquire force.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests, and strengthen the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of Blessed Peter and ourselves and by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods it now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future acquire, by grant of pontiffs, bounty of kings [Col. 1365C] or princes, offering of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. [Col. 1366A] Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

[Note: This bull contains only a provisional judgment in favour of the schools of the abbey of Saint-Remi. Despite our investigations, we have been unable to discover the definitive judgment. Lacourt nevertheless seems to have known of it, unless he regarded as definitive a provisional judgment which was followed by no other. Here is Lacourt’s passage [Col. 1363B]:]

> “Hugh, abbot [of Saint Remigius], had a great dispute with Leo, schoolmaster of the Church of Reims, in 1154. The abbot maintained that the monks of Saint Remigius possessed the right to teach and open schools within their ban, without permission from the schoolmaster; and this suit was finally decided by decree of the supreme pontiff Adrian IV, whereby the monks of Saint Remigius were maintained in possession of the right to teach or permit the exercise of schools, in accordance with the ancient custom of Saint Benedict. Afterwards, too, in 1434, under Abbot John Cannart, it was adjudged by the bailiff of Vermandois, against the schoolmaster (*scholarcha*) of the Church of Reims, that masters teaching in schools within the ban of Saint Remigius should obtain this licence from the abbot and monks of Saint Remigius, and not from the schoolmaster of the Church of Reims.”  
> (Lacourt, Marlot, annotated notes, fol. 38.)

We shall place alongside Adrian IV’s bull [Col. 1363C] a document three centuries older, which, like it, concerns the schools of the abbey of Saint-Remi. It will also help complete what Mabillon’s *Annales Benedictini* . . . and the *Histoire littéraire*, passim, say about these schools. Anquetil, *History of Reims*, I, 229, and the *Almanac of Reims*, p. 75, had already spoken of our document. We shall take what we say concerning it from a letter and notes by Father Égée found in the King’s Library, Reims manuscripts, carton VI, and in Lacourt, Marlot, annotated notes I, note fol. 27.

**Letter of Father Égée, subprior of the abbey of Saint-Remi, to Monsieur Tranchant.**

> “If I did not know you to be as sincere as you profess to be, Sir, I would tell you that you carry obligingness a little far in writing that you have read with every possible satisfaction the inscription discovered here a month ago, and that you regard it [Col. 1363D] as a precious monument of monastic studies, capable only of greatly illustrating the abbey in which they flourished. To tell you the truth, that is what I thought myself . . . It is indeed clear proof that public schools once existed among us; and it seems to have been made only to be set above the entrance of the place in which these schools were established, in conformity with what Charlemagne had ordered by his capitularies concerning bishoprics and the more important abbeys. Until now, there had been only simple conjectures that the sciences had once been publicly taught at Saint-Remi. The illustrious men who came from it, the great number of ancient manuscripts still preserved there, together with [Col. 1364B] the great reputation of this arch-monastery, made this believable, it is true; but one did not dare assert it for want of proof. Now, by contrast, no one can reasonably call this truth into doubt any longer . . . This inscription was found engraved in large Roman letters upon a flat stone

[Note: This stone was six feet long, two and a half wide, and five inches thick. It covered a stone coffin decorated with panels, in which human bones and remnants of small boots were found. It had been turned over—that is, with the writing underneath—and, lest anyone think it had been placed there for the person buried, almost all the letters had been partly erased and hacked with a hammer. Here is the inscription:]

> In this cloister, places suitable for the study of computus flourish,  
> strengthened by Sicfarius’s aid:  
> adorning the office of provost with his genius, he established,  
> laying a renowned foundation, this foremost building that you see on the eastern  
> side. If you wish to know the other things,  
> they are adorned with saving ordinances, in which are contained *dindima* [sacred mysteries].

[Col. 1364D]

[Translation supplied in the source: “The study of computus, for which Sicfarius gave sound rules, flourishes in the schools of this monastery. By his intellect he brought distinction to the office of prior; and by constructing the splendid apartment seen toward the east, he restored the library, where are found, through his salutary orders, those authors who have written best on our sacred mysteries, for those who wish to gain understanding of them.”]

> which covered a stone coffin four feet below ground. It was found on 1 April 1713 by mason-workers digging the foundations of the new cloister toward the east, on the side of the chapter-house door opening onto that cloister, between that door and a door of the church also opening onto the cloister. As for Sicfarius, who is praised there in such high terms, I shall tell you, in answer to your question, that he was made provost, or cloistral prior, of Saint-Remi a little before the middle of the ninth century. He succeeded Baldwin in that office, and his immediate successor was Rodefroy, who held it under Archbishop Hincmar. For [Col. 1364C] the archbishops of Reims, from Tilpin to Hugh of Vermandois, all called themselves abbots of Saint-Remi; but they always appointed a provost or cloistral prior, charged with the care of regular observance. Sicfarius, or Soifarius, seems to have joined to the dignity of provost that of master; and he had all Saint Gregory’s *Moralia* on Job copied at Sicfarius’s order, as is stated in the volume containing books 17 through 22 inclusive. Nothing, it must be admitted, agrees better with our inscription. All these volumes of Saint Gregory, like all the works of the Fathers on Scripture, are nothing other than those divine books which treat of our highest mysteries; this is what the word *dindima* used in the inscription means. (See Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, onomastic index, century III, vol. I.) One need have only a slight acquaintance with the practices formerly observed in cloisters [Col. 1364D] to know that the monks’ most ordinary work was copying books. More than three hundred manuscripts remaining in the library of Saint-Remi prove that this kind of work was much practised there. Among the oldest are the book of the *Origins* of Saint Isidore, written about the year 700; Tilpin’s pontifical, written in 780; and Saint Gregory’s sacramentary, written in 799. [Col. 1365C] Accordingly, among the dues owed by those who cultivated the abbey’s lands, it is noted that they had to provide a specified amount of vermilion every year.

> “From the Polyptych of Remigius: At Saint Hilary there is a church in his honour . . . total rent: 106 *modii* of wheat, 411 of spelt, 257 of barley, 325 of mixed grain . . . twelve ounces of vermilion. At Rauciacum . . . the resident tenants give each year 545 *modii* of spelt, 40 *modii* of barley, 25 ewes with as many lambs, 323 chickens, 12 pasture-dues, 582 eggs, two pounds of silver, and three ounces of vermilion. At Avention . . . Bernold, a serf, and his wife Gifagdis pay a goose, eight denarii [Col. 1365D], and twelve ounces of vermilion.”

> “From so many manuscripts, most of which are commentaries on Holy Scripture, one may infer with some basis that this divine science—which constituted all the theology of that age—was taught at Saint-Remi; and the inscription seems to suggest this by the words *si noscere quaeras* [‘if you wish to know’]. But it states the matter yet more expressly concerning computus and the science of times. Paschal computus, as it was understood in that century, was properly a treatise of astronomy, comprising everything that could serve to draw up the ecclesiastical calendar and determine the date of Easter Day. Indeed, it is known that this knowledge was considered so important, after disputes had arisen in the Church concerning the time at which the feast of Easter ought to be celebrated, that not only did the emperors prescribe the study of computus in their capitularies, but almost [Col. 1366C] all bishops ordered priests and clerics by their synodal statutes to learn it. Hence, among the liturgical books possessed by each church for its use, one almost always finds a volume or booklets of computus.”

> “From the Polyptych of Remigius: Baina; in the aforesaid estate there is a church in honour of Saint Medard . . . one lectionary, one collection of prayers, from Easter to the Lord’s Advent, one psalter, etc. . . . In the village of the same estate there is a church dedicated in honour of Saint Remigius . . . one missal with Gospel and readings or antiphonary, one volume; the Epistles of Saint Paul, the seven Catholic Epistles, and Revelation with commentary, one volume; Jerome [Col. 1366D] on Matthew, one volume; one volume of canonical penitential; one psalter; quires concerning computus . . .”

> “Archbishop Hincmar, moreover, expressly ordered in an article of his capitularies of the year 852 that the priests of his diocese be fully instructed in computus. It was also, as the inscription states, in order to teach computus that public schools were established at Saint-Remi; and Provost Sicfarius, a good astronomer and skilled computist, explained the system of which he was the author and gave sound rules for acquiring this science. A great number of manuscript treatises on this subject from that century are found in the library of Saint-Remi. This confirms that these schools were celebrated and very well attended. That, Sir, is the closest to the truth that I have been able to discover concerning the inscription which you value so highly.

> “Accept, etc.”

The borough outside the castle in which blessed Remigius rests, with all jurisdiction and authority, as it was granted to you by the kings of the Franks and likewise confirmed by their charters: namely, that it shall remain exempt from every outside jurisdiction and authority, and that no one save the abbot and his monks shall exercise any judicial power there. Rather, the abbot and his brethren may there have breweries, ovens, mills, fisheries, and orchards; and, whenever circumstances and the time require, a market; shops, the ban, a butcher’s market, and every craft and all other things whatsoever known to belong to a borough; and whatever may seem suitable to their [Col. 1366B] pleasure and use . . . . the church of Saint Mary . . . . outside the walls of the castle of Rethel . . . . as Count Hugh gave it to you through the hand of Archbishop Rodulf . . . . together with the rent of the borough, the schools, and its other appurtenances; namely, Gerson with its church . . . . Baisne with its church and parsonage, and the chapel of Muscherio, and Noire with its appurtenances . . . . Champfleury with its chapel . . . . Sacy with its church, parsonage, and chapel of Les Maisneulx . . . . the chapel of Sarney and the mother church of Brool; Taisnières with its churches and appurtenances . . . . the church of Saint Thomas near the castle of Vienne, with the chapel of that castle; the church of Saint Oricle with its appurtenances; the church of Autry, [Col. 1366C] the church of Mathigy, the church of Neuville, the church of Cambuslia, the church of Ardullio, the church of Virisiac, the church of Vallis, [Col. 1367A] the church of Orisy, the church of Cheverees, with everything belonging to those churches; Terny on the Aisne, with its church and appurtenances; the land of Deonna with its mills; a fourth part of Hermundiville; Givey, Exy, the lord’s estate . . . . the freehold of Seven Willows . . . . the fishery which Count Henry gave you throughout the whole ban of Condé. At Joinville, all the land of Guy of Autry and of his nephew Geoffrey. At that same village, three ovens; the village called Saint-Martin on the river Suippe, with its mills and all other things belonging to the use of the poor; the manor of Belloverio, with the lands, meadows, pastures, mills of Hugh, and all other things belonging to the use of the poor.

In the territory of [Col. 1367B] Soissons: the village of Montigny with its appurtenances, and the land and tithe which Milo of Verneuil restored to you. In the territory of Laon: the manor of Corbeny with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Victor (Saint Viteny); the village of Cravennes with its tithe, all its ban, and its other appurtenances; Muncel with its church . . . . In the territory of Châlons . . . . the village of Beloy; Braux with its church . . . . Furneium, Walerios, the church of Vernol . . . . ; the land and tithe which you hold at Valray, and all other things belonging to the use of the poor. In the bishopric of Toul: Saint-Remy with its church; the tithe of Tronville. In the territory of Langres: Condedas [Col. 1367C] with its church and tithe; the village of Darmannum with everything belonging to those same villages. In the territory of Arras: the abbey of Saint John the Baptist of Hasnon with its appurtenances; Belgim with its church; the altar of Monci . . . . the church of Sueres . . . . In the bishopric of Aix . . . . the castle of Ventabren, with the church of Saint Michael of Finistella, now called Volta; the land and tithe of Fara. In the bishopric of Mainz . . . . Bigehen, the chapel of Glanna, Perferelenbac, Osterna, Kerembac . . . . In the county of Kiribere, the village called Brucca . . . . In the duchy of Thuringia, the villages named Scaunistrat, Nortus, Adistat, Lobach, and Promere . . . . In the district of Roslinxe, in the county of Blois, the manor called Berna . . . . Bischopfeselim. [Col. 1367D] In the village of Buppura, the freehold which Albert the advocate, having become a monk, bestowed upon your church. In the bishopric of Liège . . . . Clumam with its church and parsonage; the church of Sckina, Huleberge, the chapel of Ambe, the chapel of Skimorte, and the chapel of Heusta; likewise the villages of Covorna . . . . Herta and Beccha, as they were given to you by the kings of the Romans. In England, in the bishopric of Chester: Lapeleia, Estona, Merestona, half of Bigvifort, Milifort, and the village of Riduara. In the bishopric of Hereford: the village of Silvitona, the tithe of Beroniac . . . .

We also grant that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who have resolved to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, saving the rights of the mother church. Moreover, in the parish churches which you hold, priests shall be chosen by you and presented to the bishop; if they are suitable, the bishop shall entrust the care of souls to them, so that they may answer to him for the pastoral care of the people, but render to you the due submission for temporal matters belonging to the monastery.

When you, the present abbot of that place, beloved son, or any one of your successors, dies, no one shall be placed over it by any craft of intrigue or violence, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall determine ought to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of Saint Benedict.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, [Col. 1368B] take away its possessions, retain things taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations whatsoever; but that all things shall be preserved undiminished and intact for the benefit, in every respect, of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the canonical rights of the Apostolic See and of the diocesan bishops.

Therefore, if in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this document of our decree, should rashly attempt to act contrary to it, and, having been warned a second and third time, should not amend his offence by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment for the iniquity he has perpetrated; let him be cut off from the most sacred [Col. 1368C] body and blood of God and Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and at the last judgment let him be subject to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place, may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good works and, before the strict Judge, find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church, have signed. I, Imarus, bishop of Tusculum, have signed. I, Hugh, bishop of Ostia, have signed. I, Gregory, bishop of Sabina, have signed. I, Guy, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, have signed. [Col. 1368D] I, Bernard, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Clement, have signed. I, Manfred, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Sabina, have signed. I, Octavian, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia, have signed. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, have signed. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Sylvester, have signed. I, Guy, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Mary in Portico, have signed. I, John, cardinal deacon of the title of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, have signed. I, Odo, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison, have signed.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of Roland, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the third indiction, [Col. 1369A] in the year 1154 of the Incarnation . . . . and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Adrian, Pope IV.

## V. Privilege for the Monastery of Tulle  
*(Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 25 December.)*

[BALUZE, *History of Tulle*, Appendix, p. 484.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GERALD, abbot of Tulle, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

Whenever that which is recognized as fitting to religion and uprightness is requested of us, it becomes us willingly to grant it and to afford suitable support to the desires of petitioners. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, graciously assenting to your just petitions, we receive the aforesaid monastery of Tulle, over which, by God’s ordering, you preside, [Col. 1369B] under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify it by the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions or goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by the grant of popes, the gift of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, by God’s favour acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to set down the following by their proper names:

In the adjacent borough: the church of Saint Julian and the church of Saint Peter; the church of Aquina; the church of Montaigu; the chapel of Roca; the chapel of Marco; the chapel of Bosqueto; the chapel [Col. 1369C] of La Garda; the church of Spaniac with that chapel itself; the chapel of Clergo; the chapel of Spinaciis; the chapel of Autoire; the chapel of Monsalvi; the church of Viam; the church of Gransania; the chapel of Vetulo Tilio; the chapel of Monedeira; the chapel of La Valeta; the chapel of Sanciac; the chapel of Madranges; the church of Aureillac; the chapel of Boltiac; the chapel of Planis; the chapel of La Genesta; the chapel of Caunac; the chapel of Cornil; the church of Palaguangis; the chapel of Auriol; the chapel of Bellopodio; the chapel of Marcocella; the chapel of Capiac; the church of Saint Michael and the chapel of that castle; the church of Saint Peter of Baneries; the churches of Vairac; the chapel of Saint Mary of Macheriis; the church of Saint Denis; [Col. 1369D] the church of Faurgas; the church of Saint Peter of Cusantia; the church of Mairona; the church of Vogairo; the chapel of Bellocastello; the chapel of Castel; the church of Mairinac; the church of Riallac; the church of Rocamadour with all its appurtenances; the church of Saliac; the church of Donziac; the church of Marciliac; the church of Saint Aredius; the church of Saint Maurilius; the church of La Garda; the church of Saint Fortunata; the church of Albutiac; the church of Novavilla; the church of Molseo and the chapel of that castle; the church of Saint Amantius; the church of Saint Michael of Faorzes; the church of Saint Silvanus; the church of Saint Bonitus del Vernt; the church of Saint Pardulf of Crozilla; the church of Saint Martin, which lies between Dustram and Dordoniam; the church [Col. 1370A] of Mordelgue; the church of La Mazeira; the church of Sadra; the church of Saint Maxentius; the church of Saint Bonitus of Avalofa; the church of Saint Medard; the villages of Vairac and Aquina with all their appurtenances.

If any churches, ecclesiastical goods, or estates belonging to the monastery of Tulle have hitherto been unlawfully given to laymen by irreligious abbots or monks, or have been seized by laymen for the benefit of other monasteries before the lawful term, we command that they be restored entirely to your monastery. We further decree that the monastery itself shall not be excommunicated for the misdeeds of the knights dwelling in the castle of Tulle, on the condition, however, that if those knights are excommunicated, they shall not be admitted to divine offices there. [Col. 1370B] By apostolic authority, we also forbid any persons to ravage or molest the possessions of the monastery of Tulle on account of the offences of those knights. We decree that burial in the same place shall be, and shall remain, altogether free according to ancient and canonical custom, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who resolve to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated on account of their own offence.

We strictly forbid anyone to take away from you or interrupt, contrary to the custom of your church, the burial of the knights and their wives—namely, of Gimel, Bar, Boltiac, Correzia, Mairinac, Saint Augustine, Utmalros, Dent, Doitrant, Bellomonte, Saliac, Saint Clement, Saint Germanus, Saint Ferreola, Favars, Cornil, Saint Fortunata, La Garda, [Col. 1370C] Saint Amantius, Navis, Rocca, Marciliac, Clergor, Campaniac, Ladiniac, Pandrina, Clementiac, Saint Aredius, Saint Michael, Vairiac, and the castle of Tulle—and of all the viscounts of Turenne, Comborn, Ventadorn, and Gimel, and of their wives and children.

When you, the present abbot of that place, or any of your successors, dies, no one shall be set over it by any craft of intrigue or violence, except one whom the brethren by common counsel, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall elect according to the fear of God and the Rule of Saint Benedict. We further decree by this present ordinance that no one whatsoever shall dare diminish or take away the tithes belonging to your churches or their right thereto. We likewise decree that in the castles, villages, and possessions of your monastery no one shall ever presume to build new fortifications. Moreover, no one at all may exact or take tithes from the work cultivated by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the produce of your animals.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, etc., saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. Therefore, if in the future any ecclesiastical person, etc. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church. [Col. 1371A] I, Imarus, bishop of Tusculum. I, Hugh, bishop of Ostia. I, Cencius, bishop of Porto and Saint Rufina. I, Gregory, bishop of Sabina. I, Guy, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus. I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Sabina. I, Aribert, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Bernard, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Clement. I, Octavian, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, Astald, cardinal priest of the title of Saint [Col. 1371B] Prisca. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, of Pammachius. I, Henry, cardinal priest of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saints Sylvester and Martin. I, Guy, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint Mary in Portico. I, John, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Odo, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of Roland, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, [Col. 1371C] on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, in the third indiction, in the year 1154 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Adrian, Pope IV.

## VI. To Eraclius, Archbishop of Lyons, he affirms the “primacy over the provinces of Gaul—Lyons, Rouen, Tours, and Sens”—and confirms the possessions of his church.  
*(Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 26 December.)*

[*Primacy of Lyons*, second petition, Proofs, p. 6; attested by Bréquigny, *Chronological Table*, III, 224.]

## VII. He commends to Wibald, Abbot of Corbie, the affairs of the Roman Church before the emperor and its legates who are to negotiate with him.  
*(Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 29 December.)*

[MARTÈNE, *Amplified Collection*, II, 591.]

[Col. 1371D]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the Abbot of Corbie: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The devotion and reverence which you have hitherto rendered to the most holy Roman Church, your mother, are known both to us ourselves and to our brethren, who know them more fully and have reported them to us more fully. It is indeed fitting and consonant with reason that you should constantly show yourself devoted and subject to that Church, which labours for your salvation as well as for that of all the faithful; and that you should diligently consider its honour and benefit always, as you are known to have done hitherto. It remains for you to carry out so praiseworthily the good undertaking and purpose you have begun that we and our brethren, who bear good witness concerning you, may plainly recognize your fidelity and devotion by the very result of the matter. Therefore, by apostolic letters, we command and exhort your belovedness in the Lord to strive with all your might to honour the Roman Church, to which you owe every obedience and submission, and to show yourself without hesitation most ready for its advantage and service.

Having therefore found [Col. 1372B] this favourable opportunity, be so diligent in supporting that same Church before our beloved son Frederick, illustrious king of the Romans; so constantly commend it to him; and so confer with him concerning its advantage and advancement, that your mother Church herself may plainly recognize you by the result as her special and most devoted son, and that you may with greater confidence seek the assistance of the Apostolic See whenever it is expedient for you. Furthermore, we earnestly commend to your prudence our venerable brother C., [Note: [Col. 1371D] Cencius, first created cardinal priest of Saint Lawrence in Lucina by Eugenius III, and thereafter bishop of Porto by Anastasius IV.] bishop of Porto, and our beloved sons B., [Note: [Col. 1371D] Bernard, formerly a regular canon of Lucca and prior of the Lateran monastery, was granted the purple by Eugenius III and appointed by him and by Adrian [Col. 1372D] to many legations to Emperor Frederick.] cardinal priest of the title of Saint Clement, and O., [Note: [Col. 1372D] Octavian, first created cardinal deacon by Innocent III and then cardinal priest of Saint Cecilia by Eugenius.] cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. They are serving, by our command, as legates before the aforesaid Frederick, illustrious king of the Romans, and are to treat with him, God being the author, concerning the honour and [Col. 1372C] exaltation of the Roman Church and the welfare of the realm. We ask that you receive them honourably as ourselves, endeavour by every means to honour them, and make honourable provision for them in their needs. For if you recognize the Roman Church itself as your mother and strive to render it the service and honour due, it too will recognize you as its special son and will take care more promptly and easily to grant your petitions.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June [read: January].

## YEAR 1155

[Col. 1372D]

## VIII. He commands the clergy and laity of the Church of Saint Peter of the Mount to observe firmly “the Order of Blessed Augustine, with surplice and black capes, established in their church from ancient times.”  
*(Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 2 January.)*

[D. CALMET, *History of Lorraine*, II, Proofs, p. 337.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1373A] sons, the clergy and laity of the Church of Saint Peter of the Mount: greeting and apostolic blessing.

As we have learned from the tenor of the letters of our predecessor Pope Eugenius, of holy memory, in order that the canonical order established in your church from ancient times might be reformed there for the better, he sought to appoint over you a certain abbot of the Premonstratensian Order, namely Philip. Among other instructions, he wished to command him, after laying aside the garb of the Premonstratensian Order, to put on a surplice and, according to the ancient custom of your church, to use black clothing. But now, as we have learned by a manifest report, he has changed his vestments contrary to the prohibition of Pope Eugenius of holy memory; and in changing his clothing he did not fear to violate the unity of charity among you, since, as they say, he presumed to expel certain of your brethren from the cloister because they would not accept Premonstratensian garments or alter the habit they had assumed.

Since every cause of scandal must be wholly removed from those wishing to serve the Lord, we command you by apostolic letters to endeavour firmly to observe the Order of Blessed Augustine, established in your church from ancient times, with surplice and black capes; and henceforth to labour, in the calling in which you were called, in accordance with the vow you made, to render services pleasing to God, so that you may be crowned with blessed Augustine in heavenly glory. Furthermore, because the bearers of these letters are believed to have laboured for the common benefit of your church, we likewise command you [Col. 1373C] to reimburse them without any contradiction for the expenses which they are known to have incurred in coming to the Apostolic See, and which, as they assert, they borrowed from your common goods after a mutual oath had been interposed; and in no way to neglect recovering other things dissipated or alienated from the goods of that same church.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the fourth day before the Nones of January.

## IX. He confirms certain laws and privileges of the Premonstratensian Order.  
*(Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 3 January.)*

[LE PAIGE, *Premonstratensian Library*, 627.]

[Col. 1373D]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HUGH, Abbot of Prémontré, and the abbots and provosts of the same order, and their successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

Just as the human body is known to have many members, and some are held in greater honour because, by reason of the dignity of their excellence, they are pre-eminent, so in the body of Christ, which is the Church, many are gathered for the honour and praise of the Lord. Yet some, abiding more earnestly in his praises and service, are reckoned among the more excellent members in Christ’s body; they are as lights in the firmament of heaven, illuminating those on earth and diligently striving, by the fragrance of their own ointment, to draw others to Christ’s service. But you, most beloved sons in Christ, since we know that you are among their number, love you with sincere affection of charity and wish to grant favourable consent to your just petitions, so that you may labour the more ardently in the Lord’s vineyard as you perceive that you have found greater favour with your mother, the most holy Roman Church.

Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, acceding to your prayers, we decree and establish by the authority of the Apostolic See that all abbots and provosts of the Premonstratensian Order shall come annually to the general chapter at Prémontré, unless they are prevented by bodily illness or have leave to remain by common counsel. Thus, when you are all assembled in Christ’s name, [Col. 1374B] you may uproot what ought to be uprooted, firmly establish what ought to be planted, and deliberate most diligently concerning the common welfare of the order. We also decree that no archbishop or bishop may by any means prevent any member of your order who wishes to come to that chapter. Furthermore, by this present decree we establish that the canonical order known to have been instituted in your churches according to God, the Rule of Blessed Augustine, and the custom of the brethren of Prémontré, shall be observed inviolate in those churches for all time.

For the stricter observance of your order, we grant you leave to excommunicate your fugitives. We also forbid anyone to dare retain any of those fugitives without the permission of his superior. And so that you may always advance from good to better and preserve your order more effectively in its rigour, we confirm by the authority of this present decree that you may depose from the office of abbot abbots found guilty of an offence, and those whom you find altogether unfit, and place them, by decision of the chapter, in some church of your order. We also prohibit any abbot of the Premonstratensian Order from being transferred from one abbey to another without common counsel. But the brethren of the Church of Prémontré, which is recognized as mother of the others, may receive an abbot from any of the churches of the same order and install him in the church of Prémontré. We further establish by apostolic authority that whatever shall reasonably be ordained by your common counsel concerning the observance or discipline of your order [Col. 1374D] shall remain unshaken and be infringed by no one whatsoever.

We therefore decree that no person may rashly dare to infringe this document of our constitution or in any way oppose it, saving the authority of the Apostolic See, etc.

Therefore, if in the future, etc.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hugh, bishop of Ostia. I, Gregory, bishop of Sabina. I, Guy, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus. I, Guy, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. [Col. 1375A] I, Julius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, Henry, cardinal priest of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saints Sylvester and Martin. I, Odo, cardinal deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, through the hand of Roland, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the third day before the Nones of January, in the third indiction, in the year 1154 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Adrian, Pope IV.

## X. He directs B[ernard], Bishop of Paderborn, and Gi., Abbot of Liesborn, to hear the case of the bearer of these letters.  
*(Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 3 January.)*

[MARTÈNE, *Amplified Collection*, I, 596.]

[Col. 1375B]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother B., Bishop of Paderborn, and his beloved son Gi., Abbot of Liesborn: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Note: [Col. 1375D] Liesborn is an ancient Benedictine monastery in the diocese of Münster, founded, it is said, by Charlemagne in favour of his sister Roswindis; in the twelfth century it passed to monks and still flourishes under the Bursfeld Congregation.]

We have received the complaint of the bearer of these letters, who has come to the clemency of the Apostolic See: namely, that he has been unjustly despoiled by a certain priest of a church which he possessed canonically. Therefore, lest this poor man be compelled to suffer loss through failure of justice, we command you by these present letters [Col. 1375C] to cause both parties to appear before you and, after carefully hearing and examining the arguments of both parties, to settle the case through canonical justice.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the third day before the Nones of January.

## XI. He receives the monastery of Prémontré under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges.  
*(Rome, at Saint Peter’s, 5 January.)*

[HUGO, *Annals of the Premonstratensian Order*, Proofs, p. 18.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HUGH, Abbot of Prémontré, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

[Col. 1375D]

It is fitting that apostolic protection be at hand for those leading a religious life, lest an assault of any rashness either call them back from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of their sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive the church of Prémontré, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify it by the privilege of this present document. We decree that whatever possessions or goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, through the grant of popes, the gifts [Col. 1376A] of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, with the Lord’s aid acquire, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to set down the following by their proper names:

Namely, the precinct of the valley of Prémontré, as it is marked out by fixed boundaries, with its ponds and mills, free from every tithe and exaction; the wood for your use from Halierpré to Humbert’s Bridge, and on the other side through the middle of Rohard’s valley as far as the vicinity of Monand; the manor of Fontenelles with its appurtenances; the manor of Penencourt with its vineyards and other appurtenances; the manor of Merlin with its vineyards; the manor of Roteriis with its dependencies and appurtenances; the manor of Vercigny [Col. 1376B] with its appurtenances; the manor of Souppy with the mills lying beneath it on the river called the Aisne, and its other appurtenances and dependencies; two parts of Crépy; a third part of the tithe of Chavus.

At Valavergny, ten modii of wine from the tithe of the same village; the tithe together with the *terrage* of Vrevin; and the *terrages* of Concivilla, except for two modii which must be paid from it to the church of Blessed Mary of Nogent; also the fishpond and mill near the same village, as Ingelrannus, son of Thomas of Marle, had held them in his own demesne in the aforesaid two villages; the rent of Poilly; the mill of Rochis; the mill of Proisel; the mill of Achery; the mill of Cortun; the mill of Cenceny; the wine-dues of Bourguignon; the land of Carenni; [Col. 1376C] two parts of the mill of Aquila; vineyards of Broiencourt, Ursignicourt, Brummont, Lizy, Valavrigny, Montarcenne, and Monthavin; vineyards of the castle of Coucy and of Concivilla; wine-dues and vineyards of Novavilla.

In the bishopric of Soissons: in the suburb of the city, a manor and place, a winepress, and vineyards. At Pomerias, wine-dues; the money-rent of the castle of Brana and of the village of Branella; the manor of Bucy with its vineyards and other dependencies; the mill of Rupibus below that same village; the manor of Clamecy with its winepress, vineyards, and other dependencies; at Sorny, two winepresses, vineyards, and other revenues; the estate of Tenselva with its dependencies; the manor of Luilly and half a mill with its other [Col. 1376D] appurtenances; at Bethencourt, wine-dues and other revenues. At Pinon, a certain rent, a third part of the small tithe from the court, a sixth part of a certain mill, and the tithe which Josbert held there; the chapel and manor of Rosel, with mill, fishpond, winepress, vineyards, and all its appurtenances.

On the hill of Trosly: one manor with its lands, vineyards, and other appurtenances; and the part of the village with its appendages which Andrew of Baldimenento granted to you, as he held it in his demesne; and certain other things offered by other faithful persons of God. The manor of Biucy with its appurtenances; [Col. 1377A] the manor of Attechi, two parts of the tithe, vineyards, and its other appendages. At Cauny, a rent and wine-dues. In the village called Pont-Saint-Medard, a fourth part of the tithe; at Margival, half a mill; half the chestnut groves of Vausaillon.

In the bishopric of Noyon: the altar and manor of Bonolio with its appurtenances; the manor of Bolmont; the manor of Calveni; the freehold of Germainnes; the manor of Montisel; the manor of Thory; the manor of Landricourt; and in the suburb of Noyon, land, vineyards, and meadows, with a manor and what belongs to it; the mills of Despeville and half the tithe of that village; two parts of the tithe of Destoily; a sixth part of the tithe of Dury; the mills of Oflois and two parts of the tithe of that village; [Col. 1377B] a third part of the tithe of Grecy; half the site of a certain mill at Dinisa and half the tithe of that village; two parts of the tithe of Saint Radegund; two parts of the tithe of Calveni; a third part of the tithe of Caullincourt; two parts of the tithe of Gricourt; three parts of half the tithe of Leherwes; a third part of the tithe of Lancy; the tithe of Kivres; land at Omencourt; land of Liencourt and Curcy; three jugera at Greum; the free chapel of Saint Nicholas at Saint-Quentin; the manor of freeholds with its appurtenances; the manor of Voiana with its appurtenances; the manor of Hanapiis, held in freehold, with its tithe; two parts of the tithe of Bechincourt; two parts of the tithe of Cartigny; the whole tithe of Falvi, [Col. 1377C] except the small tithe; a fourth part of Aldeni; the mills of Escauly with their appurtenances; the mills of Hamel; the site of a certain mill at Pieton.

We have also considered it consonant with humanity, and establish by this present decree, to be valid in perpetuity, that the sisters who, through the labour of our brother Norbert, Archbishop of Magdeburg, of good memory, and through your exhortation, have entered the service of almighty God and offered themselves to the Lord, shall receive suitable maintenance from the goods of your church. No small part of those goods is known to have come to that place through them. Moreover, no one may presume to exact from you a tithe of your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or of the produce [Col. 1377D] of your animals. We also decree that no bishop may, without reasonable cause, forbid divine services in your churches.

Furthermore, you shall receive the ordinations of canons, the consecrations of churches, and the other ecclesiastical sacraments from the bishops in whose dioceses your churches are situated, provided that they are Catholic and enjoy the favour of the Apostolic See; otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you wish, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested. If any nobleman should resolve to be buried in your churches, no one may oppose his devotion and last will, saving nevertheless the right of the mother church.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, [Col. 1378A] take away its possessions, retain things taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations whatsoever; but that all things shall be preserved undiminished and intact for the benefit, in every respect, of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical rights of the bishops.

If anyone therefore, etc.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hugh, bishop of Ostia. I, G[regory], bishop of Sabina. I, Guy, cardinal-priest of the title of St Chrysogonus. I, Julius, cardinal-priest of the title of St Marcellus. I, Henry, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints Nereus [Col. 1378B] and Achilleus. I, John, cardinal-priest of Saints Sylvester and Martin. I, Guy, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Portico. I, Odo, cardinal-deacon of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, through the hand of Roland, cardinal-priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the Nones of January, in the third indiction, in the year 1154 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian IV.

XII. He receives the church of St Mary and St Evodius of Brana into protection, and confirms its rule and possessions. (Rome, at St Peter’s, 5 January.)

[HUGO, ibid., I, 324.]

[Col. 1378C]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons RADULPH, abbot of the church of Blessed Mary and St Evodius of Brana, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: for ever.

Those who choose the regular life ought to have apostolic protection at hand, lest an assault of any rash person either turn them from their purpose or—God forbid—weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, most beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests [Col. 1378D], and receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church of Blessed Mary, Mother of God, and St Evodius, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order which you have professed according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine and the institution of the Premonstratensian brethren shall be inviolably observed in that church for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions and goods you now justly and canonically possess, or may hereafter, God favouring you, acquire by grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and undiminished for you and your successors. [Col. 1379A] Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

Namely, the chief tenants, vineyards, wine-dues, rents, land-dues, and whatever you possess in the castle of Brana; the whole village of Vacinni, excepting the land of St Medard; the land of Spiritelli; at Converella, a rent of ten solidi and a certain cultivated plot; the entire tithe from the estate of Maceni; four sextaries of grain from the mill of Hugh, son of Radulph, near the Mount of St Mary; four sextaries of grain from the mina and rent; at Quincy, rents; at Yonne, ten solidi of rent and seven from householders, together with oat-revenue and land-dues. At Lui, rents, wine-dues, and land-dues. At Cerseolium, the altar and the entire tithe from the dovecotes of the lord of that [Col. 1379B] village, vineyards, arable land, and a mill. At Limet, vineyards and wine-dues. At Legia, rents and land-dues. From the tithe of Cury, a modius of grain. At Cremella, rents; at Villers, rents and land-dues; at Bestiti, rents; at Villare-sur-Aisne, wine-dues, rents, and land-dues; at Arseium, wine-dues and rents; at Ducellum, rents, land-dues, and wine-dues; at Curcellas, rents, land-dues, wine-dues, and meadow.

At Brainella, wine-dues, rents, land-dues, meadows, and a winepress. At Ay, rents and ash-trees; four sextaries of grain from a certain mill; the re-tithe of the lordship of the castle of Brana, namely of its wine, vineyards, presses, wine-dues, and all its produce—in ovens, mills, its own cultivated lands, [Col. 1379C] land-dues, revenues of oats and hay—and the re-tithe of the entire produce of three villages, namely Villers and the middle village, and of the oats owed to it for the use of woodland; provided, namely, that wherever possession of the lordship is transferred, its re-tithe is reserved to the aforesaid church; and whatever it possessed in the fishing-rights of the mills of Brana. The estate of Bruneries with its appurtenances; the mill of Joi; the tithe, land-dues, and rents from certain cultivated plots belonging to the church of St Peter of Hannon, at an annual rent of five solidi. This also has been granted to you by that same lord: that all his vassals may freely make alms to you from the fiefs which they hold from him.

A fourth part of the pastures of Granges and three arable plots; at Ancy, one mill, two parts of the great tithe of Blansi, arable lands, vineyards, vineyards, a mill, meadow, and woodland; the whole estate of Sarteas and everything belonging to that estate; a fourth part of the tithe of Vailly. At Vergelli, rents; the estate of Curtiali and everything belonging to that estate in the city of Soissons; a modius of salt, a modius of wine, and ten solidi of rent. In the diocese of Laon, two mills and arable land given to you by Bishop Bartholomew at a rent of twelve denarii. At Bergam, five thousand herrings and ten weights of cheese. Further, no one at all shall presume to exact tithes from you on the noval lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the increase of [Col. 1380A] your animals.

Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, all things shall be preserved whole and intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical rights of the diocesan bishops.

If anyone therefore, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, through the hand of Roland, cardinal-priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the Nones of January, in the second indiction, in the year 1154 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate [Col. 1380B] of Lord Pope Adrian IV.

XIII. He receives the monastery of Vallis Serena into protection and confirms its goods and privileges. (Rome, at St Peter’s, 5 January.)

[HUGO, ibid., II, Preface, p. 646.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons STEPHEN, abbot of Vallis Serena, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: for ever.

The unity of the authority and fraternal charity of the Apostolic See, in which by the Lord’s bounty we serve, urges us [Col. 1380C] to consent to the just wishes of religious persons and graciously to grant their reasonable requests. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves the church of Blessed Mary, Mother of God and ever-Virgin, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, God favouring it, acquire through grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and undiminished for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The valley itself, with the mill of Succi (in French [Col. 1380D] *Souccy*) and the right of use in the adjoining woodland, as granted to that church by John Rufus and his sons; the church of St Clotildis of Vivarium, free and exempt from every exaction, together with the appurtenances belonging to that church, its two fishponds, and the mills commonly called Becherer and Crievecor; also the customary dues of the aforesaid village, as held by your predecessors; likewise, the tithes and land-dues belonging to that church, with the freedom of the adjoining wood; the church of St Mary of Javagium with its mills and appurtenances; the land of Pont Robert; the land of Lord Lupus; the land of Peter of Oigny, which he conveyed to the aforesaid church for his daughters; the land [Col. 1381A] of St Anianus with its mill and appurtenances; the tithe of that place, as you hold it from the monks of St Denis and Guy of Margival; the land of Odo Rufus; the land of Pigmellis with its appurtenances; the land of the Tenants; the land of the Castle with its appurtenances; the land of Matthew of Loistris; the tithe of Bonolio; and what you possess in the tithe of Burenville.

Further, no one shall presume to exact tithes from you on the noval lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the increase of your animals. We also decree that no one shall receive your fugitives without the permission of the abbot and his chapter, and without the security of letters. We likewise decree that the burial-place of that house shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final wishes of those who choose to be buried there, [Col. 1381B] unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; the canonical right of those churches from which they were taken being nevertheless preserved.

Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; rather, all things shall be preserved free, whole, and intact for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If anyone therefore, etc.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Guy, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in [Col. 1381C] Portico. I, Burdo, cardinal-priest of the title of St Chrysogonus. I, Hugh, bishop of Ostia. I, G[regory], bishop of Sabina. I, Odo, cardinal-deacon of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Julius, cardinal-priest of the title of St Marcellus. I, Henry, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints Sylvester and Martin.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, through the hand of [Col. 1381D] Roland, cardinal-priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the Nones of January, in the second indiction, in the year 1154 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian IV.

XIV. To the people of Piacenza.—He confirms the election of Hugh as bishop of Piacenza and releases their city from interdict. (Rome, at St Peter’s, 9 January.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 819.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the entire clergy and people of Piacenza: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

When the church of Piacenza had long laboured before the Apostolic See to restore its position [Col. 1382A], and had in our hearing lodged a complaint against its bishop concerning certain matters, we strove, with the common counsel of our brethren, to call him strictly to account and carefully and diligently to confront him with the accusations. But he, wishing to spare himself this labour and to pursue rest and tranquillity, renounced the church of Piacenza in our presence. After taking counsel with our brethren, we granted our beloved sons, the clergy and laity of your city whom you had sent concerning this matter, free authority to elect as bishop some honourable, suitable, learned person who was in no respect disqualified by the sacred canons.

Accordingly, as was divinely inspired in them through the lofty and hidden counsel of the majesty of supreme providence, [Col. 1382B] they unanimously agreed upon and elected as bishop of Piacenza our most beloved son, Hugh—son of Hugutio, son of Peter Leo—a noble, discerning, suitable, and learned cleric. Although we were reluctant, and wearied by their many urgent entreaties, because we wished to retain him near us as necessary and most useful to the Holy Roman Church, we nevertheless at last scarcely granted him to them; and, the Lord being author, with the assent of our brethren, we confirmed that election.

Moreover, moved by the prayers and requests of this same beloved son Hugh, your elect, and of his noble parents, through whose counsel and aid the Roman Church is especially supported and defended against the attacks of enemies; and wishing also to show favour to you and your church, [Col. 1382C] we have by apostolic authority restored that church to the condition in which it is known to have been in the time of Arduin, bishop of Piacenza, of good memory. Likewise, at the request of these same sons of ours, after receiving an oath from your aforesaid citizens that the citizens of Piacenza had in no way committed the robbery on account of which your territory had been subjected to interdict, and that it is established that you have no spiritual or temporal jurisdiction over those robbers, we absolve you and your city from the obligation of the interdict and permit you henceforth to celebrate all divine offices.

It will therefore now be your concern to receive kindly and honourably, and to honour magnificently, the aforesaid son of ours Hugh, your elect, to whom the care of your souls has been entrusted; [Col. 1382D] and likewise to render him the reverence and obedience due in all things, so that we may not have cause to regret the great mercy which we have shown you by grace alone, and he may truly be able to commend your devotion and diligence in this matter.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the fifth day before the Ides of January.

XV. He confirms the privilege granted by Eugenius III to the canons of the church of St Peter (at Rome). (Rome, at St Peter’s, 20 January.)

[*Bullarium Vaticanum*, I, 53.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons BERNARD, cardinal-priest of St Clement and archpriest of the church of Blessed Peter, and the other canons of that church, present [Col. 1383A] and those to be canonically appointed in future: for ever.

The fellowship of the blessed Peter and Paul is so eminent and so glorious that both are teachers of the nations, authors of martyrs, and princes of priests. Although they surpass all the apostles by a certain distinctive prerogative, they experience no inequality of merit in heaven. To Peter were entrusted by our Saviour himself, the Lord Jesus Christ, the keys of the kingdom of heaven; Paul was chosen by God so that through his preaching he might fill the kingdom of heaven from the multitude of the nations. Peter is the rock and foundation of faith, sustaining us firmly by his solidity lest we fall; Paul arms us with upright conduct and the invincible reasoning of faith, lest we be wounded by the perverse doctrine of heretics. [Col. 1383B] Peter, holding primacy, binds and looses by his power; Paul, a zealous preacher, wonderfully fortifies us by exhortation lest anything blameworthy or deserving of binding appear in us. Peter is our support and the house of strength; planted and rooted in his faith, we are secure. Paul, the vessel of election, has summoned those predestined and chosen by God with the sounding trumpet of heaven; and by ceaseless prayer for us and intercession with God, he protects us lest we depart from faith and truth.

Since, therefore, these two greatest luminaries, illuminating God’s Church, shine forth with equal and friendly splendour and fraternal love, reason of equity and justice persuades us—who, though unworthy, act in Christ’s stead on earth [Col. 1383C] and are seen to sit in the chair of the same prince of the apostles—to cherish Blessed Peter’s household with paternal affection and to aid it in its needs with loving provision. Moved by the obligation of this reasoning, beloved sons in the Lord, following the example of our predecessor Eugenius of holy memory, with the consent of our brethren the bishops and cardinals, we grant you by authority of the Apostolic See, and confirm by this present writing, one fourth of all offerings which accrue from the altar of Blessed Peter the Apostle, from the chest, and from all the ministries of that church, except the ministry of Blessed Leo.

That is, whenever you wish, you shall always have free authority to retain and keep that offering in your own hands, or, with the consent of ourselves and our successors, to sell it to whomsoever you wish. In all other matters, however, the free disposal and custody of the church itself is preserved and retained in the hands of ourselves and our successors. [Col. 1383D] We have judged it fitting to do this so that, zealously labouring day and night in God’s praises, and diligently and fittingly chanting the Masses, Matins, and other Hours for the salvation of living and dead, you may honour the aforesaid church of Blessed Peter with the service due to it; and so that God’s faithful, visiting the thresholds of the apostles with fitting devotion, may always hold that place in greater devotion and reverence.

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may, with rash daring, infringe or in any way disturb [Col. 1384A] the text of this our grant.

If anyone therefore, etc.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Imarus, bishop of Tusculum. I, Hugh, bishop of Ostia. I, Gregory, cardinal-priest of the title of St Chrysogonus. I, Hubald, cardinal-priest of the title of St Praxedes. I, Manfred, cardinal-priest of the title of St Sabina. I, Aribert, cardinal-priest of the title of St Anastasia. I, Julius, cardinal-priest of the title of St Marcellus. I, Hubald, cardinal-priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Guy, cardinal-priest of the title of the Shepherd. [Col. 1384B] I, Astald, cardinal-priest of the title of St Prisca. I, Gerard, cardinal-priest of the title of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Henry, cardinal-priest of Saints Nereus and Achilleus. I, John, cardinal-priest of the title of Saints Sylvester and Martin. I, Guy, cardinal-deacon of St Mary in Portico. I, John, cardinal-deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Hildebrand, cardinal-deacon of St Eustace beside the Temple of Agrippa. I, Odo, cardinal-deacon of St Nicholas in the Tullian Prison.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, through the hand of Roland, cardinal-priest [Col. 1384C] and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the third indiction, in the year 1154 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian IV.

XVI. Privilege for the monastery of St Mansuetus at Toul. (Rome, at St Peter’s.)

[D. CALMET, *History of Lorraine*, II, Preface, 346.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons JOHN, abbot of the monastery of St Mansuetus at Toul, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: for ever.

Those who choose the religious life ought to have apostolic protection at hand, lest an assault of any rashness [Col. 1384D] either turn them from their purpose or—God forbid—weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service; and we fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by God’s favour acquire through grants of popes, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and undiminished for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names.

The cell situated at the castle of Rinellum, with all [Col. 1385A] its possessions. The church of Moruncurt and two parts of all the tithes of that church; likewise two parts of the offerings—namely at the Nativity of the Lord, Epiphany, Easter, Pentecost, the feast of St Peter in Chains, and All Saints’ Day; of offerings made during the year, one half, excepting private masses; of the endowment of that church; and of lands given as alms or which may hereafter be acquired, two parts, the vicar receiving the third part.

The cell of St James of Sionna and the mill of Evucurt; the cell of St Mary of Novo-Castro; the chapel of St Nicholas and the chapel of Unaucurt; the church of St Christopher and the altar-gifts of the three aforesaid churches, from all revenues, [Col. 1385B] of which you shall receive two parts and the vicar the third. The church of St Amand, situated in the suburb of Toul; and the altar-gift which Pipo, bishop of Toul of good memory, is known to have bestowed upon you at the request of Hugh, archdeacon and cantor, with the boundaries of the parish, namely: from the first gate closing the Bourg, where part of the stream Angruxia flows alongside that wall; and as the wall occupies and encircles the whole Bourg, and all habitation outside it lies on the left-hand side as the road divides southward, as far as the stream Iserella; and Iserella itself directs its course eastward on the left side as far as the public road, where, outside the gate of Uvel, it joins the stream Angruxia.

From the revenues [Col. 1385C] of that church, forty solidi assigned to the clothing of your brethren; likewise throughout the year, two parts of the offerings and alms of that church; and according to the provisions made concerning this by our most holy predecessors, the apostolic cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, or the bishops of Toul, especially because of the love and veneration of the relics of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, by which that place is distinguished and is venerated under apostolic authority.

We confirm these things, decree that they shall remain valid and inviolate for future times, impose perpetual silence, and, with every claim concerning the aforesaid church of St Amand set aside, decree by this present sanction that your monastery shall peacefully possess that place with its appurtenances.
