Your magnificence thinks praiseworthily and fruitfully of spreading the glorious name upon earth and accumulating the reward of blessedness in heaven, since, as a Catholic prince, you intend to enlarge the bounds of the Church, make the truth of the Christian faith known to unlearned and uncultivated peoples, and uproot the nurseries of vices from the Lord’s field; and, for the more fitting accomplishment of this purpose, you seek the counsel and favour of the Apostolic See. In this undertaking, the more lofty your counsel and the greater your discretion, the happier, with the Lord’s help, will be the success which we trust you shall have; for those things which take their beginning from the ardour of faith [Col. 1441C] and love of religion are accustomed always to attain a good outcome and end.

Indeed, there can be no doubt that Ireland, and all islands upon which Christ, the Sun of righteousness, has shone and which have received the teachings of the Christian faith, belong by right to blessed Peter and the most holy Roman Church—as your nobility also acknowledges. Therefore we the more willingly introduce into them a faithful planting and a shoot pleasing to God, because, upon inward examination, we recognize that this is more strictly required of us. You have informed us, dearest son in Christ, that you wish to enter the island of Ireland in order to subject that people to laws, uproot from it the nurseries of vice, pay to blessed Peter an annual rent of one penny from every household, and preserve whole and intact the rights of the churches of that land.

We therefore, favourably pursuing your pious and praiseworthy desire and giving benign assent to your petition, hold it pleasing and acceptable [Col. 1441D] [Col. 1442A] that you enter that island for the enlargement of the bounds of the Church, the restraining of the course of vice, the correction of morals, the planting of virtues, and the growth of the Christian religion; and that you perform what pertains to the honour of God and the salvation of that land. Let the people of that land receive you honourably and venerate you as lord, while ecclesiastical right remains whole and intact, and while the annual rent of one penny from every household is preserved for blessed Peter and the most holy Roman Church.

If, therefore, you bring to completion in deed what you have conceived in mind, endeavour to instruct that people in good morals; and act, both through yourself and through those whom you employ and whom you have found fit in faith, word, and life, so that the Church may be adorned there, the religion of the Christian faith planted and [Col. 1442B] increased, and matters pertaining to the honour of God and the salvation of souls so ordered through you that you may deserve to obtain from God an abundance of everlasting reward and may be able to possess in ages to come a glorious name on earth.

[Note: [Col. 1441D] This privilege is reported both by Matthew Paris under the year 1155 and by Gerald of Wales, *The Conquest of Ireland*, book II, chapter 6; Cossart has prefixed to it the following, plainly necessary for understanding the events: “Meanwhile, although the king of England was chiefly occupied and detained by martial exercises, he was nevertheless, even amid these activities, not forgetful of Ireland. Having obtained, through exertion, the previously mentioned letters concerning its abominations at the Synod of Cashel, he sent envoys to the Roman curia and obtained from Pope Adrian—an Englishman by origin, then presiding—a privilege by his authority and assent, both to rule the Irish people and to instruct that people, exceedingly uncultivated in the rudiments of faith, in ecclesiastical rules and disciplines according to the customs of the English Church [Col. 1442D]. The privilege was then sent to Ireland through Nicholas, then prior of Wallingford and afterwards abbot of Malmesbury, both installed and deposed, and through William, son of Aldhelm. A synod of bishops was at once assembled at Waterford; in public hearing, with the consent of the whole assembly, a solemn reading of this privilege was made by John of Salisbury, afterwards bishop of Chartres, sent to Rome for this purpose. Through him the same pope also presented the king with a golden ring as a sign of investiture. The ring was immediately deposited, together with the privilege, in the archives of Winchester.” G. Cossart.]

**LXXVII. To the monks of Corbigny for the reform of the monastery.** (Benevento.)

[New *Gallia Christiana*, IV, Documents, 90.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the whole chapter of the monastery of Corbigny: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Those who, after Pharaoh had been drowned, deserved by divine aid to free their necks from [Col. 1442C] Egyptian slavery, and who now seem to have crossed the Red Sea on dry ground, must take anxious care lest they be overthrown by the crafty suggestions of the devil and long to return to Egyptian food when they have begun to loathe manna. For spiritual food produces nausea only in those who, deceived by diabolical fraud, are found lax or lukewarm in the Lord’s service—persons whom Scripture declares are certainly to be vomited out of the Lord’s mouth because they can be found neither cold nor hot.

We say this, sons, because the vigour of the monastic order is not observed within the cloister of your monastery with the diligence required by the Rule of blessed Benedict, and some of you do not endeavour to perform those things by which they ought to please almighty God [Col. 1442D]. Therefore, lest you seem to run in vain, so run, sons, that you may obtain the prize of the eternal inheritance and receive with blessed Benedict an everlasting reward [Col. 1443A]. So that you may do this more fully and perfectly, we command your whole body by apostolic letters to endeavour to show due obedience and reverence to our beloved son Hu., your abbot, and so afford him aid and counsel for reforming religion in the monastery entrusted to him that, with your cooperation, he may reform within it the rule of religious life and restore it to a state of goodness.

Furthermore, by these letters we wish you to know that if any one of you proves obstinate and rebellious toward the aforesaid son of ours, your abbot, in his reform of religious life in the monastery entrusted to him or in other matters which are there to be ordered according to God, we shall, with God as author, hold ratified the sentence which that same son of ours, your abbot, may canonically promulgate against him for this reason [Col. 1443B], and shall cause it to be observed inviolate until due satisfaction has been made.

Given at Benevento.

**IN THE YEAR 1156.**

**LXXVIII. For St Mary of Frasinaria and St Peter of Pompeniano.** (Benevento, 13 January.)

[Muratori, *Writers of Italian Affairs*, II, ii, 1014.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother the bishop of Gino: greeting and apostolic [Col. 1443C] blessing.

Our beloved son Leonas, abbot of the monastery of St Clement, complains that the sons of Gentilis of Brittoli hold the church of St Mary of Frasinaria, and the sons of Rao of Puliano the church of St Peter of Pompeniano with its possessions, against the right of the monastery of Penne. Therefore, since the sanctions of the sacred canons forbid churches and their administration to be held by laypersons, however religious they may be, we command your brotherhood by these present letters not to delay in admonishing the aforesaid men to relinquish the churches promptly. But if they scorn to obey your admonitions, do not omit to administer canonical justice against them.

Given at Benevento, 13 January.

**LXXIX. He commands Silvester, abbot of St Augustine’s, Canterbury, to make a profession to Archbishop Theobald.** (Benevento, 13 January.)

[Twysden, *Historical Writers of England*, I, 1378.]

[Col. 1443D]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son SILVESTER, abbot of St Augustine’s: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The office of the supreme pontificate enjoined upon us by God and the governance of the dignity we have received admonish and invite us in every way to preserve whole and unimpaired for every person—and especially for our brothers the archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of churches—their rights, so that they may be the more solicitous for the flock committed to them as they perceive themselves the more strongly fortified by the aid of our protection [Col. 1444A]. Therefore, lest our venerable brother Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury, complain that he suffers any diminishment of his right, so far as lies with us, we command you by apostolic letters, strictly ordering that, according to the command of our predecessor Pope Anastasius of good memory, when requested by the said brother of ours you shall not refuse to make him a profession—provided, indeed, that it is established that your predecessors rendered the same profession to his predecessors.

Given at Benevento, 13 January.

**TO THE SAME PERSON**

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son the abbot of St Augustine’s, Canterbury: greeting and [Col. 1444B] apostolic blessing.

The more faithfully and devotedly our venerable brother, the archbishop of Canterbury and legate of the Apostolic See, is known to have been toward the most holy Roman Church from the very time of his promotion, the more earnestly ought we to love him and the church entrusted to him, and to preserve for him his rights whole and unimpaired. Therefore we command your affection by apostolic letters, strictly ordering that, just as it is established that one of your predecessors at some time rendered obedience to a predecessor of the same brother of ours, the archbishop, so likewise, setting aside every appeal and pretext, you shall not delay to render it to him within thirty days after receiving [Col. 1444C] these letters.

**LXXX. To the archbishop of Braga—That he obey the primate of Toledo.** (Benevento, 19 January.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 819.]

If you considered with due vigilance how great is the virtue of obedience, and if with careful solicitude you took thought how great an advantage it brings, you would endeavour to show due reverence and obedience to our venerable brother JOHN, archbishop of Toledo, so that the sincerity of your devotion would appear commendable both in the sight of the Lord and in the eyes of men. But in this matter you seem both to have lost the sense of humility [Col. 1444D] and to have departed from the path of justice: for, through some arrogance unknown to us, you neglect and despise obedience to him. Therefore, lest you be further charged with presumption or contumacy, we command your brotherhood by apostolic sentence to render the aforesaid brother of ours, the archbishop of Toledo—whose primacy throughout the whole kingdom of Spain we have confirmed by apostolic authority—due reverence as to your primate and complete subjection.

Otherwise, we hold ratified and firm the sentence of suspension which our beloved son Hyacinth, deacon-cardinal and legate of the Apostolic See, is known to have pronounced against you; and we establish that it shall possess the force of perpetual validity. For, following in the footsteps of our predecessors of blessed memory, Eugenius and Anastasius, Roman pontiffs, in accordance with the sentence of the aforesaid son Hyacinth, cardinal [Col. 1445A], unless you approach the aforesaid archbishop in all humility and take care henceforth to obey him, we order you suspended from every pontifical office and absolve all your suffragans from obedience to your person.

Given at Benevento, 19 January.

**LXXXI. He praises Theobald, bishop, C., dean, and the whole chapter of the Church of Paris because they granted to Hugh, chancellor, the income of a prebend in the Church of Paris.** (Benevento, 20 January.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 804.]

[Col. 1445B] ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother T., bishop, and his beloved sons C., dean, and the whole chapter of the Church of Paris: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We consider it pleasing and acceptable, and we greatly commend your charity for its provision in matters pertaining to the advancement of ecclesiastical interests, that you have granted to our beloved son Hugh, chancellor of our dearest son Louis, king of the Franks, the revenues of his prebend in your Church. Therefore, holding this grant ratified and confirming it by apostolic authority, we command you by these present letters to cause those revenues to be assigned to him in full wherever he may be. Thus he may always be bound in obligation to you and to your Church on this account [Col. 1445C], and we may the more willingly admit your petitions.

Given at Benevento, 20 January.

**LXXXII. At the request of Bishop John, he confirms the privileges of the Church of Olivolo, or Castello (Venice).** (Benevento, 25 January.)

[Cornelius, *Churches of Venice*, XIII, 219.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother JOHN, bishop of the Church of Olivolo [Note: [Col. 1445D] Although Henry Contarenus changed the title of the Church of Olivolo and wished it to be called Castello, nevertheless both the church and its bishops were very often called by the old title.] or Castello, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

By the office of apostleship enjoined on us by God, we ought to love our brother bishops both near and far [Col. 1445D], and preserve their rights for the churches in which they are known to serve the Lord, so that, just as we are called fathers in name, we may likewise be proved such in deed. Therefore, venerable brother John, bishop in Christ, we graciously assent to your reasonable petitions and have judged that the Church of Olivolo, over which by God’s authority you are known to preside, should be protected by a privilege of the Apostolic See, following the example of our predecessor Pope Lucius of blessed memory.

For the decrees of the holy pontiffs are known to have established that no one shall usurp another’s boundaries or presume to judge or excommunicate another’s parishioners; that no primate, no metropolitan, and none whatsoever of the other bishops shall enter another’s city or approach a possession which does not belong to him and lies in another bishop’s parish [Note: [Col. 1446D] Here *parochia* means “diocese.”], in order to dispose, order, or adjudicate anything there concerning anyone, unless invited by the person to whose jurisdiction it is known to belong [Col. 1446A].

Accordingly, by this page of the present document we prohibit and, in prohibiting, establish that in the Church of Olivolo, also called Castello, or in its diocese, no patriarch or fellow-provincial bishop may presume, without permission of you or your successors, to consecrate churches or bless clerics or nuns [Col. 1446B]; nor shall he have power there to prepare chrism, confirm children with chrism, or pronounce excommunications or absolutions. We further add that bishops are not to be summoned indiscriminately in the same diocese without your consent, except for the purpose of a provincial council; and even this shall be arranged with the permission of your charity. Nor shall they remain there beyond the limits set by the canons, except in case of grave necessity. Moreover, none of them without your permission shall dare to ordain or retain, there or elsewhere, clerics of your Church, or impose penances for public crimes.

Furthermore, both the church of blessed Mark and the other churches, or the clerics of the churches, within that same diocese shall remain under your obedience and governance. Those who are disobedient shall be restrained at your discretion according to the sanctions of the holy canons [Col. 1446C]. We decree that the same obedience shall continue to be owed to you from the monasteries of St Hilary, St George, St Nicholas, Holy Cross, St Zacharias, St Lawrence, St Erasmus [Note: [Col. 1446D] The monastery of St Erasmus was that which is now called St Secundus; it was formerly cultivated by Benedictine nuns.] and St Servulus, as your predecessors are known to have possessed. Moreover, abbots established in your diocese shall by no means presume to celebrate public Masses in churches not their own. We also establish that those who reside permanently in your diocese, and to whom you administer spiritual ministrations both personally and to their households, shall pay you tithes without anyone’s objection. But we prohibit any bishop or abbot, without consulting you, from daring publicly to impose penance upon them, whether healthy or sick [Col. 1446D], except perhaps when the moment of death is pressing.

Furthermore, we decree that whatever possessions and goods that same Church justly and lawfully possesses at present, or may hereafter, with the Lord’s help, be able canonically to acquire, shall remain secure and inviolate for ever to you and your successors, saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See.

If anyone therefore, etc.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church. [Col. 1447A] I, Imar, bishop of Tusculum. I, Centius, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Guido, priest-cardinal of the title of St Chrysogonus. I, Hubald, priest-cardinal of the title of St Praxedes. I, Manfred, priest-cardinal of the title of St Sabina. I, Julius, priest-cardinal of the title of St Marcellus. I, Ubald, priest-cardinal of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Octavian, priest-cardinal of the title of St Cecilia. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of SS. Sylvester and Martin. [Col. 1447B] I, John, priest-cardinal of SS. John and Paul, title of Pammachius. I, Oddo, deacon-cardinal of St George at the Golden Veil. I, Guido, deacon-cardinal of St Mary in Portico. I, Hyacinth, deacon-cardinal of St Mary in Cosmedin.

Given at Benevento [Note: [Col. 1447D] Adrian IV had been expelled from the city of Rome by the Roman citizens themselves and wandered through various cities of Italy [Col. 1448D], in order to bring relief to the afflicted Church. Thus Oldoinus, notes on Ciconius, vol. I, p. 1061.] through the hand of Roland, priest-cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, on 25 January, in the fourth indiction, in the year 1155 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian IV.

**LXXXIII. He asserts for John, archbishop of Toledo, the primacy of Spain.** (Benevento, 9 February.)

[Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 818.]

[Col. 1447C]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother JOHN, archbishop of Toledo: greeting and apostolic blessing.

When, because of pressing affairs of the church committed to you, your brotherhood had presented itself before us, it humbly requested from the Apostolic See—which has always been accustomed to grant the just desires of petitioners—that the privilege and letters of our predecessors of blessed memory, Paschal, Calixtus, Honorius, and Eugenius, be renewed for it; in these, the primacy of the Spanish realms is acknowledged to have been granted to the church of Toledo [perhaps: “the primacy of the Church of Toledo is acknowledged to be granted,” Col. 1447D]. But because we love you with sincere charity in the Lord, and have resolved by every fitting means to honor your person—since it is an unshaken pillar and support of the Church—we have judged your request worthy of acceptance and have not allowed your desire to be deprived of its effect. Therefore, after consultation with our brethren, by authority of the Apostolic See we decree that the said privilege, together with the letters, is to be renewed in accordance with your proposed petition; and that, just as your church has from ancient times possessed primacy throughout the whole region of the Spanish realms, so you and the Church of Toledo, which by the Lord’s appointment you are known to govern, shall possess that same primacy over all forever.

Moreover, we add that the privilege which our brother Pelagius, archbishop of Compostela, is said to have obtained from our predecessor Pope Anastasius of happy memory—namely, that he ought not to be subject to you by right of primacy—shall henceforth have no force and shall inflict no prejudice upon you. Rather, we decree that the privilege granted to you concerning the concession of primacy by our aforesaid predecessor Pope Eugenius of holy memory shall in every way prevail against it; especially since that of Anastasius was obtained neither by common counsel nor by the counsel of the sounder part of the brethren. We therefore decree that the archbishop of Compostela himself, as well as the other bishops of the Spanish realms, shall henceforth render to you and your successors obedience and subjection as to their primate by right of primacy; and that this dignity shall always remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors, for all time.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly infringe this page of our concession and confirmation, or in any way oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Benevento, on the fifth day before the Ides of February.

## LXXXIV. Privilege for the convent of the Paraclete. (Benevento, February 13.)

*[Works of Abelard, p. 354.]*

[Col. 1448C]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughters in Christ, HELOISE, abbess, and the other sisters of the Paraclete: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Both the office of the apostolate laid upon us by God impels us, and the fragrance of your good manner of life exhorts us, graciously to grant assent to your just requests and willingly to fulfill what pertains to your advantage and peace. Therefore, beloved daughters in the Lord, wishing to provide for your needs, by apostolic authority we grant to you and to those who succeed you free permission to bury at your abbey your brethren who have no burial-place of their own. Let no person whatsoever, therefore, infringe this page of our constitution or rashly oppose it. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Benevento, on the Ides of February.

## LXXXV. To Hillin, Archbishop of Trier. (Benevento, February 15.)

*[GUENTHER, Diplomatic Codex, 353.]*

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HILLIN, archbishop of Trier and legate of the Apostolic See: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Certain grave matters, which we hear not without astonishment and report not without great pain of mind, concerning our venerable brother Ar., archbishop of Mainz, have reached our hearing. Neither the authority of the Apostolic See, over which by God’s appointment we preside, nor the force of equity and justice permits us to leave them uninvestigated and uncorrected. For L., Her., Ul., and B., canons of the church of Saint Martin in the city of Mainz, came into our presence and declared that he had granted their prebend as a benefice to laymen who themselves retain it; that, without consulting clergy and people, he had sold gold, silver, and other ornaments of the church; and that, after an appeal had been made to us, he had taken many things from their property. They further added that this same brother of ours, having summoned a synod, publicly caused it to be forbidden that anyone should presume to appeal to the judgment of the Apostolic See. If these things are true, they grieve us all the more because we had least expected him to undertake anything of this kind against us and against the most holy Roman Church.

Therefore, in order that the matters stated may come to light, we have commanded him in our letters either to appear before you, if he can, to establish his innocence and to give those men, under your examination, full satisfaction in justice; or to present himself before us at the approaching feast of blessed Luke, to answer under our judgment concerning all these matters. Accordingly, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood to summon before you both the aforesaid canons and others who may wish to stand against our aforesaid brother in this case, as well as that same brother of ours; and, after carefully hearing and fully examining the canons’ accusations and his defense, to cause their prebend, which was taken from them after the appeal, to be restored to them. Whatever truth you discover in this matter, do not fail to report to us by your letters and through those same canons, so that, after duly examining it, we may determine what is just; for, just as we do not wish to be blamed for severity, so neither should we be liable to be charged with leniency or negligence in such grave offenses.

Furthermore, because the aforesaid Her. complains that many things from his property have been unjustly and violently taken from him by certain persons, namely Ul., Rod., Fed., Edelr., and Her., we likewise command you to strike them with the penalty of excommunication unless they restore what was wrongfully taken from him.

Given at Benevento, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March.

## LXXXVI. To John, Archbishop of Toledo: confirms the diocese of Complutum, the primacy of Spain, and use of the pallium. (Benevento, February 16.)

*[MANSI, Councils, XXI, 816.]*

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother JOHN, archbishop of Toledo, and to his successors canonically appointed in his place, forever.

How great was the dignity and glory of the Church of Toledo in ancient times; how renowned and illustrious it was both in the Spanish and Gallic regions; and how many benefits and advances in ecclesiastical affairs came through it—we believe this is sufficiently evident to all who examine the enactments of synodal decrees. But after the city of Toledo, once distinguished and held in high repute among the cities of the Spanish realms, was taken by Saracen violence—as the sins of the people demanded—the liberty of Christian religion there was reduced so completely to nothing that for many courses of years no dignity of pastoral office is reported to have remained active there.

Afterward, however, as the mercy of divine majesty willed, through the zeal of the illustrious and magnificent King Alfonso and the labor of the Christian people, the Saracens having been expelled, the aforesaid city was restored to the rule of Christians. Since it was worthy and altogether consonant with reason that, after that city had recovered its lost liberty, both it and its church should be restored to the condition of their former dignity, our predecessor Pope Urban of blessed memory—during whose time the city was rescued from Saracen hands—established that an episcopal see should be there and ordained a bishop in the aforesaid church, as had been the case in antiquity. We, therefore, though unworthy successors to him, wishing in no respect to diminish the rights of that church but rather to increase them, earnestly desire, with the Lord’s help, to establish the condition of that city, so far as lies within our power, in the glory of ecclesiastical dignity.

We therefore confirm forever to you and your successors, and through you to the Church of Toledo, the diocese of Complutum with its boundaries, and all other things which the Church of Toledo now justly and canonically possesses. Accordingly, both out of due reverence for the Church of Toledo and in response to the petitions of our most reverend son, the most excellent King Alfonso—by whose valor and prudence the suffragan sees have indeed been restored to their former liberty—we decree by authority of this present privilege that you, venerable brother, shall be primate throughout all the kingdoms of the Spanish realms, in accordance with the enactments of our predecessors of holy memory, Urban II, Paschal, Calixtus, and Eugenius, Roman pontiffs, just as the bishops of that city are established to have been in ancient times.

You shall use the pallium only in celebrations of Mass, especially at the following feast-times: on the three days of the Nativity of the Lord; at Epiphany; Hypapante [the Presentation]; the Lord’s Supper; Holy Saturday; the three days of Easter; Ascension; Pentecost; the three feasts of Saint Mary; Saint Michael; Saint John the Baptist; all feasts of the apostles; and those martyrs whose relics rest in your church; also Saints Martin and Ildefonsus, confessors; and the Commemoration of All Saints; at the consecration of churches, bishops, and clerics; on the annual anniversary of your consecration; and on the feasts of Saints Isidore and Leander.

All bishops of the Spanish realms shall look to you as primate, and shall refer to you whatever matter worthy of inquiry may arise among them, while preserving the authority of the Roman Church. Therefore, by the canonical tenor of this privilege, we confirm forever to you and, if divine grace grants it, to your successors, the Church of Toledo together with all churches and dioceses which it is known to have possessed by its own right from antiquity. Concerning those presently subject to Saracen rule, we command that, whenever it shall please the Lord to restore them to the power of the Christian people, they be returned to the due obedience of your church.

We have also subjected to your authority, on this condition, the dioceses of those cities which lost their own metropolitans when the Saracens invaded: so long as they remain without their own metropolitans, they shall be subject to you as to their proper metropolitan. But if any metropolitan see is restored to its former condition, each diocese shall be restored to its own metropolitan. Nevertheless, your brotherhood should not for that reason be less zealous that the glory of its proper dignity be restored to every metropolitan see.

All these things, and everything else that can be proved to have belonged to the ancient dignity and nobility of the see of Toledo, we grant and confirm by the authority and assured concession of the Apostolic See, to be possessed forever by you and your successors. We exhort you, venerable brother, with deepest affection always to show yourself worthy of so great an honor of the episcopate, taking care always to remain without offense toward Christians and Saracens, and striving, by words and examples, with the Lord’s gift, to convert unbelievers to the faith. Thus, while you excel outwardly in the dignity of the pallium and the prerogative of primacy before the eyes of all people, may you flourish inwardly in excellence of virtues before the eyes of the heavenly Majesty.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly, etc.

Given at Benevento through the hand of Roland, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March, indiction IV, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1154, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian IV. [Col. 1451D]

## LXXXVII. To John, Archbishop of Toledo: directs him to investigate charges against the Bishop of Pamplona. (Benevento, February 18.)

*[MANSI, ibid., col. 818.]*

Though our merits do not support us, we sit, by the Lord’s appointment, in the chair of the Prince of the Apostles so that we may be concerned for the condition of each church and may restore its pastors to the state of rectitude whenever they depart from the way of truth. Moved, therefore, by this consideration, we command your brotherhood by apostolic decree to summon the bishop of Pamplona—concerning whose life many unfavorable reports are brought to our ears—at a suitable place and time before you; or that you yourself hasten to his city or neighboring places. When the canons of Pamplona, as well as the above-mentioned [lacuna] bearer of the present letters, and the bishop himself, are present before you, carefully hear and examine the charges on which those canons accused him, and the homicide [lacuna] in respect of which the same above-mentioned persons, in accordance with the tenor of the letters of our predecessor Pope Eugenius of happy memory which he sent to that bishop, accused him. [Note: Col. 1451D. Corrupt text.] You shall also carefully hear and examine the depositions of witnesses, removing the impediment of appeal. Once these have been examined, diligently report them to us in your letters and send us the depositions of the witnesses under your seal, so that you may be more fully instructed by us as to how you are afterward to proceed against him. But if, when summoned by you, he scorns to come and submit to judgment, suspend him from the administration of both spiritual and temporal matters.

Given at Benevento, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March.

## LXXXVIII. To Nigellus, Bishop of Ely

Under penalty of suspension, Adrian directs Nigellus, bishop of Ely, “that within three months from receipt of the letters he shall without any delay restore the possessions of the church—which he is known to have alienated and disposed of contrary to the promise made at his consecration—to the condition in which they had been when he was appointed to govern the Church of Ely.” He also makes this known in another brief of the same date addressed to the monks who had complained against him. When Nigellus had excused himself on the ground of the king’s absence, alleging that the king’s presence was necessary for making the restoration, the pope, in other letters issued to Theobald, archbishop of Canterbury, at the Lateran on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, states that he judged a respite ought to be granted to him for doing this from the next feast of Saint Lucy (I think “until the next feast” ought to be read). Meanwhile, he relaxes the sentence of suspension “which,” he says, “we have pronounced against him.”

[Col. 1452C]

*(Acts of the Saints, Bollandists, June, vol. IV, p. 581.)*

## LXXXIX. To the heads of the Roman fraternity.—Arnaldus, heresiarch, in the time of Eugenius III, among other detestable acts which he had presumed against the Roman Church, sought to detach from the cardinals the clerics subject to them. To remove this diabolical innovation, which had gained force, Pope Adrian decrees that chaplains shall promise obedience to the heads of the titular churches. (Benevento, March 18.)

*[MANSI, Councils, XXI, 804.]*

[Col. 1452D]

ADRIAN IV, to the heads of the Roman fraternity.

It has come to our hearing that the clerics of Saint Peter in Chains, in one of their chapels, namely the church of Saint Mary in Candiatore, have forbidden the celebration of divine offices because the people of that church oppose the rendering of the hand of obedience to the priest of the aforesaid church—that is, of Saint Peter’s. Since, therefore, we cannot and ought not to endure that the church of Saint Peter in Chains should be deprived of its right, by apostolic letters we command you strictly to admonish the aforesaid people that henceforth they cease altogether from that opposition and do not presume to withhold from the church of Saint Peter in this chapel what it possesses in its other chapels. If they cease from such folly, we wish the interdict to be relaxed, so that divine offices may be celebrated in the aforesaid church of Saint Mary. Otherwise, we decree that they shall endure the penalty which they suffer in respect of the offices.

Given at Benevento, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April.

## XC. Receives the Church of Tortosa under the protection of the Apostolic See and confirms its statutes and possessions. (Benevento, March 20.)

*[FLÓREZ, Sacred Spain, XLII, 303.]*

[Col. 1453B]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother GAUFRED, bishop of Tortosa, and to his successors canonically appointed in his place: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since, by the apostolic office laid upon us by God, through which by the Lord’s appointment we have precedence over all Christ’s faithful, we ought to attend to the peace and tranquillity of each person, we must be especially concerned for the peace of those endowed with pastoral dignity and raised to the episcopal office. For unless we, attending to their interests, preserve their rights intact as far as we can with God’s permission and defend them by apostolic authority from the attacks of wicked men, those who have been committed to them by the Lord’s ordering for governance cannot truly be secure concerning their salvation.

Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, Bishop Gaufred, graciously assenting to your just petitions, we receive you and the Church of Tortosa, over which by God’s appointment you are known to preside, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we establish that the canonical order known to have been instituted there according to the Rule of God and blessed Augustine and the customs of the church of Saint Rufus shall be observed inviolate forever. Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, with the Lord’s assistance, by grant of pontiffs, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their own names:

Granatella; Fabaria with its appurtenances; and what the aforesaid Church possesses in Bitem and Astech. We also confirm whatever our venerable brother Bernard, archbishop of Tarragona, is known to have granted you in tithes, offerings, and funeral dues, with the consent of the suffragan bishops and of the illustrious Count Raymond Berengar of Barcelona; and an annual rent of one hundred bezants, which the same count granted you for the clothing of the canons, and through you to your church. We likewise confirm the tithes of all things in that bishopric which ought to be tithed, the first fruits, and all ecclesiastical rights of the aforesaid church; we grant them in full and strengthen them by apostolic authority. We also establish that the episcopal see of Tortosa shall have and peacefully possess all the boundaries of its bishopric, just as fully as any king in the time of the Saracens ever possessed, or ought to have possessed, the kingdom of Tortosa. We decree, moreover, that the canons of that church shall promise, render, and make profession of due obedience and reverence to you and your successors.

We further decree that no one shall be elected bishop in the said church unless he is a canon clothed in the canonical habit, a lover of religious life and learned in letters, who knows both how to preside over and how to benefit the flock entrusted to him. Persons holding administrative offices in the aforesaid church shall not possess the administrations committed to them as though by hereditary right; rather, at the discretion of the bishop and brethren, they shall either reside in the cloister or accept other administrative offices obediently and without objection. Furthermore, we establish that both bishop and canons of the Church of Tortosa shall pay in full tithes from all their possessions and revenues to the hospital of Christ’s poor, established for the common benefit of those in need.

We also forbid any ecclesiastical or secular person, unless fortified by our authority, to build churches, possess churches already built, or usurp parochial rights anywhere in the whole bishopric of Tortosa without the permission of you and your successors. If any of your parishioners should presume to diminish or take away the possessions and goods of the oft-mentioned church, or should commit any offense for which he is bound by the bond of excommunication, you may, by our authority, constrain him by canonical sentence until he makes fitting satisfaction. We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things remain unimpaired and intact, serving in every way the uses for the governance and support of those for whom they were granted, while preserving the authority of the Apostolic See.

If, therefore, anyone, etc.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Guido, priest-cardinal of Saint Chrysogonus. I, Hisbald, priest-cardinal of Saint Praxedes. I, Imarus, bishop of Tusculum. I, Centius, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Odo, cardinal-deacon of Saint George in Velabrum. I, Guido, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Hyacinthus, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Odo, cardinal-deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Bernard, priest-cardinal of Saint Clement. I, Octavian, priest-cardinal of Saint Cecilia. I, Gherard, priest-cardinal of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Henry, priest-cardinal of Saints Nereus and Achilleus. I, John, priest-cardinal of Saints Sylvester and Martin.

Given at Benevento through the hand of Roland, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, indiction IV, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1155, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian IV.

Place of the + hanging seal.

## XCI. To H[ugh], Archbishop of Sens, and Henry, Bishop of Beauvais.—Concerning the Church of Ferrières and certain peasants. (Benevento, March–April.)

*[MARTÈNE, Amplified Collection, II, 641.]*

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren H., archbishop of Sens, and HENRY, bishop of Beauvais: greeting and apostolic blessing.

By this present communication we wish your brotherhood to know that, after the allegations concerning the Church of Ferrières and the brethren of La Charité had been seriously heard on both sides and fully understood, we rendered judgment in favor of the Church of Ferrières. We awarded to the monastery of Ferrières the church of Brusiac, concerning which the dispute between them had arisen, in accordance with the judgment of H. [Note: Henry of Aprus, whom Saint Bernard mentions in his letters.] of good memory, formerly archbishop of Sens; we annulled the second judgment; and, in accordance with the first judgment, imposed perpetual silence upon the brethren of La Charité [Note: La Charité, a notable cell of the Cluniac order, situated on the Loire in the diocese of Auxerre.].

Accordingly, by apostolic letters we command your brotherhood, within twenty days after receipt of the present letters, to restore the abbot and brethren of the Church of Ferrières to possession of the aforesaid church and to take care to invest them by our authority. Furthermore, we have learned from the complaint of the said abbot and brethren of Ferrières that certain peasants, incited by the monks of La Charité, after the judge had made an investiture of possession, and although those brethren of Ferrières had in no way disturbed that possession, formerly invaded the church of Brusiac by armed force. Wounding one of the brethren of Ferrières, they rashly presumed to beat other monks and their servants and to carry off one servant bound. Therefore, by this present notice we enjoin you that, if what is alleged is true, you shall declare the peasants who laid violent hands upon the monks to be bound by the bond of anathema until they present themselves before the Apostolic See with your letters, prepared to make satisfaction for so great an offense.

Given at Benevento, on the seventeenth day before the Nones of April. [Note: Thus in the text, corruptly.]

## XCII. Concerning confirmation of the judgments pronounced by King Louis against Odo, Duke of Burgundy. (Benevento, April 8.)

*[New Gallic Christianity, Documents, 178.]*

[Col. 1456B]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother GODEFRED, bishop of Langres: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Things known to have been settled by reasonable provision ought to remain stable; and lest they should return to the difficulty of renewed contention, it is fitting that they be strengthened by the protection of the Apostolic See. Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, Bishop, graciously assenting to your just petitions, we hold valid by authority of the Apostolic See and fortify by the protection of this present writing the judgment which our dearest son in Christ, Louis, illustrious king of the Franks, is known reasonably to have pronounced—after taking counsel with the archbishops who were present—concerning certain controversies formerly pending between you and the Duke of Burgundy, as is contained in the writing of that king. We likewise confirm to you and to your aforesaid church one half of the castle of Mont-Sallion, with all its appurtenances, both in demesne and in dependent holdings. We establish that no person may infringe this page of our confirmation or in any way oppose it; but if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Benevento, on the sixth day before the Ides of April.

## XCIII. Receives the monastery of Saint Stephen of Dijon under protection and confirms its possessions. (Benevento, April 9.)

*[History of Saint-Étienne of Dijon, Proofs, p. 101.]*

[Col. 1456D]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HERBERT, abbot of Saint Stephen of Dijon, and his brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life: forever.

It befits the clemency of apostolic governance to love religious persons and to fortify their places by holy protection. For it is recognized as worthy and consonant with honor that we, who have been appointed to govern churches, should both protect them from the malice of wicked people and foster them under the patronage of the Apostolic See. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests and receive the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, fortifying it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we establish that the canonical order known to have been instituted in that place according to the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be preserved there forever inviolate. Furthermore, whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God being favorable, by concessions of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their own names:

The cemetery of the same church within the wall of the castle of Dijon. [Note: [Col. 1457B] **The cemetery.** Concerning it there was a long-standing and ancient dispute between the canons of Saint Stephen and the monks of Saint Bénigne, from about the close of the sixth century of Christ and thereafter; on this matter the abbot of Saint Bénigne wrote to Pope John III.] The church of Saint Medard with its tithes; [Note: [Col. 1457B] **The church of Saint Medard.** This church was founded about the year 910, as we related in Part I, chapter 3 of this work, where we also recorded its destruction and the causes of that destruction.] the chapel of Saint Vincent; [Note: [Col. 1457C] **The chapel of Saint Vincent.** The chapel dedicated to Saint Vincent still stands today; we have treated of it at length in Part I, chapter 2. Both the church of Saint Medard and the chapel of Saint Vincent were always dependencies of the mother church of Blessed Stephen.] the church of Saint Michael with cemetery and tithes; [Note: [Col. 1457C] **The church of Saint Michael.** Formerly situated near and outside the walls of the old castle of Dijon, it was restored when collapsing from age by Garnerius II, abbot of Saint Stephen; and Anthony Chambellan, likewise abbot, had it rebuilt in a more elegant manner about the year of Christ 1525.] the chapel of Saint [Col. 1458A] Mary of the Market and of Saint James of Tremoledo; [Note: [Col. 1457C] **The chapel of Saint Mary of the Market and Saint James of Tremoledo.** Among the parish churches of Dijon, the church distinguished by the title of the Blessed Virgin Mary has long held an altogether pre-eminent place. Founded in the market-place of Dijon, it was otherwise called “of the Market,” and together with the church of Saint James formerly constituted one and the same, certainly very ancient, parish. Yet the little church of Saint James was the mother church, while the chapel of the Blessed Virgin Mary was its dependency; for that reason the pope here joins it to its mother church. But on these matters see more fully the *Polyptych of the Churches of Saint Stephen*, Part I, §1, chapter 1.] the church of Saint Martin of the Meadow with the chapel of Fontaines [Note: [Col. 1457D] **The church of Saint Martin of the Meadow with the chapel of Fontaines.** Here too the pope joins daughter to mother: the church of Saint Martin, which ceased to be a humble hermit’s cell, is now the mother church of the parish of Fontaines, formerly called “of the Meadow” and “of Champagne,” commonly Saint-Martin-des-Champs. It still stands on the right bank of the stream Susion, not far from the monastery of the Capuchin Friars Minor, in the northern district. Fontaines, moreover, is the village renowned throughout the world as the birthplace and cradle of Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, commonly Fontaines-lès-Dijon.] and cemetery; the church of Saint Anianus of Aqueduct with the chapel of Asnières [Note: [Col. 1457D] **Aqueduct, Asnières.** The common people have customarily declined the name *Aquaeductus* in various ways: formerly they called it *Aheuz* in the vernacular; now they pronounce it more softly, Ahuy. It is a village, as is likewise Asnières.] and cemetery; the church of Saint Mary of Gemeaux with the chapel of Pichanges [Note: [Col. 1458B] **Gemeaux, Pichanges.** In the village called Gemeau, formerly Jumeau, is the mother church; the chapel, or daughter of the mother church, is in the district of Pichanges.] and cemeteries; the church of Saint Florentius of Tille-Castle, [Note: [Col. 1458B] **Tille-Castle.** As if “a castle on the river Tille,” on which there was formerly a place called Tilechâteau, now corruptly Trichâteau.] with the chapel located in that castle itself and cemetery; the church of Saint Martin of Vitré [Note: [Col. 1458B] **Vitré, Bez.** These are villages in the prefecture of Langres; more recent usage calls and writes them Vitrey and Baiz.] with the chapel of Bez and cemeteries; the church of Saint Andrew of Ormancey [Note: [Col. 1458B] **Ormancey, Columier.** Villages also, which the common people [Col. 1458C] call Ormancey and Columier.] with chapels and cemeteries; the church of Saint George of Ugny [Note: [Col. 1458C] **The church of Ugny with the chapel of Saint Julian.** A very ancient town has dwindled into a small village. If we believe Balcurraeus, it was formerly called Ongne; he was the first, without evidence, to derive the French name of Burgundy from this town or borough, as he calls it, as if from *Bourg Ongne*. Ruins and remains of a more substantial town do indeed occur there; it has long been a village, which the common people call Ogny.] with the chapel of Saint Julian and cemeteries; the church of Saint George of Faverney with the chapel of Magny [Note: [Col. 1458C] **Faverney, Magny.** These places have often been discussed in the polyptych and in this work. Modern usage calls them Fauverney and Magny-sur-Tille, to distinguish this village from another called Magny-Saint-Médard.] and cemetery; the church of Saint Peter of Tart [Note: [Col. 1458C] **Tart.** A place very well known as the site of the first Cistercian nunnery, founded there about the year of Christ 1120, which the unlearned corruptly write *Tard*.] with chapels and cemeteries; the church of Saint Germanus of Couchey [Note: [Col. 1458C] **Couchey, formerly Cotchiacus.** The common people have long [Col. 1458D] called it Couchey. We discuss its chapels in the *Polyptych*, Part I, §2, chapter 5.] with [Col. 1458B] chapels and cemeteries; the church of Saint Maurice of Senecy [Note: [Col. 1458D] **Siliciacus, formerly Sélecey, now corruptly Sénecey**, discussed above.] with cemetery; the church of Saint Martin of Quetigny [Note: [Col. 1458D] **Quintiniacus.** The ancients called it Cutigny, more recent writers Quetigny. The village is well known at Dijon from the establishment of regular canons begun there and introduced into this church of Saint Stephen in 1116; it has been elucidated by the notes of the most learned Mabillon.] with cemetery; the church of Saint Martin of Arc [Note: [Col. 1458D] **Arc, Brecey.** In the village of Arc on the Tille, commonly called Arc-sur-Tille, stands the mother and parish church; in the hamlet of Brecey is the daughter and dependency of the mother church.] with cemetery and the chapel of Brecey; the church of Saint Peter of Mirebeau with cemetery; the right which you possess in the church of Saint Genesius of Darois [Note: [Col. 1458D] **Darois, Estaulles.** Concerning these churches, founded of old in the villages of Darois and Estaulles, there was a long and serious dispute between the canons of Saint Stephen on the one hand and the monks of Saint-Seine on the other; it is treated at length in Part II, chapter 1 of this work.] and the chapel of Estaulles; whatever you possess in the church of Savigny; whatever you possess in the church [Col. 1459A] of Autrey [Note: [Col. 1459B] **The church of Autrey and its chapels.** The pope distinguishes between the church of Autrey and the place called Valley-Autrey, of which shortly below. Here he speaks of the parish church itself, which is in the village of Autrey, and of its chapels or dependencies, founded in the districts of Poyans and Broyes, as is more fully set forth in the *Polyptych*, Part II, §2, chapter 11, and §3, chapter 13.] and its chapels; the church of Françaux [Note: [Col. 1459C] **The church of Françaux.** This is a village in the diocese of Besançon, not far from the church of Lantenay, commonly Lone. Latin writers always called that village *de Francis*; the common people first called it Franceis, then François, and finally, indeed corruptly, Françaux.] with its tithe and the right of that village; one fourth of the tithe of Avirra; [Note: [Col. 1459C] **Avirra, or Ajurra,** is a place now unknown.] the tithe of Bucerolles, [Note: [Col. 1459C] **Bucerolles, or Buceroliis,** commonly Bucerolles. Giey, commonly Giey-sur-Aujon, and Cucey, commonly Cucey, are also districts.] the tithe of Giey, of Cucey; the site of the chapel situated between Leuglay and Saint-Fal; [Note: [Col. 1459C] **The chapel between Leuglay and Saint-Fal.** That place called La Chapelle-entre-Leugley-et-Saint-Fal passed, in 1154, into the rights of Hugh IV, duke of Burgundy, by an exchange discussed in Part II, chapter 8 of this work.] the place of Puteau; [Note: [Col. 1459C] **The place of Puteau, of Agnin-Fontaine.** The places in which colonies of regular canons, originating from the school of Saint Stephen, formerly lived the canonical life have long been unknown.] the place of Agnin-Fontaine; the place of Valley-Autrey; [Note: [Col. 1459D] **The place of Valley-Autrey.** In the bull of Calixtus above, no. 134, and often elsewhere, this place is called Galdo-Altre, perhaps more correctly than Valle-Altre. For it lay in a wood, not far from the village of Altré, now Autrey, where the canons of Saint Stephen then possessed a cell or priory, granted to them by Geoffrey, knight of Bellimont, about 1120. *Galdum*, *Gualdum*, or *Waldum* is a word of low Latin meaning “wood,” from the Alemannic, German, or Old French word *Wald*, that is, “wood.” Since that place was in a wood, it appears more correctly to have been called Gualdo- or Waldo-Altré than Walle-Altré; and an Italian copyist, perhaps not understanding the German word *Wald* or *de Waldo*, distorted it into *Vallem* (“valley”). See Cange’s *Glossary*, under *Galdum*.] the place of Mont-Cigney; [Note: [Col. 1459D] **The place of Mont-Cigney.** Elsewhere it is always called Mont-Ciconiacus. In the fourteenth century [Col. 1460B] it passed into the rights of the Knights Hospitaller of Saint John of Jerusalem, who had there a commandery of their order, commonly Mont-Cigny, formerly Mont-Cigney, paying rent to the treasurer of Saint Stephen.] the place of Bonavalle in the Jura; [Note: [Col. 1460B] **The place of Bonavalle in the Jura.** This place too, together [Col. 1460C] with Galdo-Altré and Mont-Ciconiacus, lay within the bounds of the County of Burgundy and passed into other hands. It does not appear to be the cell of Bonneval near the town of Ornans, founded among the ridges of the Jura as a dependency by monks of Saint Vincent of Besançon at the end of the twelfth century; for Pope Nicholas IV, in 1290, also listed this place of Bonavalle in the Jura among the proper possessions of Saint Stephen of Dijon.] the village of Ahuy; [Note: [Col. 1460C] **The village of Aqueduct.** It was formerly also called Aquodium; in the vernacular first Aqueux, then Aheuz, and now Ahuy, as noted above.] the right which you possess in Potangey; [Note: [Col. 1460C] **Potangey, Espirey.** Villages commonly called Potangey or Potangy, and Espirey.] the place of Espirey; the place of the court of Betton; [Note: [Col. 1460C] **The place of the Court of Betton.** The hamlet commonly called Court-Beton was long ago granted to laymen, subject to an annual rent payable to the abbot of Saint Stephen, which he still receives.] the place of Marcilly; [Note: [Col. 1460D] **The place of Marcilly.** A district situated not far from Tille-Castle, commonly Marcilly; its church, formerly parochial, had long before—at least from the year 1033—been united to the church of Tille-Castle and has since been its dependency.] the place of Neuilly; [Note: [Col. 1460D] **The place of Neuilly.** A village near Dijon called Neuilly, in which there is a priory with cure of souls wholly by right of the abbot of Saint Stephen.] the place of Lugny [Note: [Col. 1460D] **The place of Lonvigneius, formerly Luvigneius or Luvigniacus,** commonly Lugny. Herbert, abbot, received this place from the brothers of Longivada, commonly Longuay or Longué; later Walter, bishop of Langres, acquired it and founded a Carthusian house there, where he was buried in 1179. See the discussion in Part II, chapter 1 of this work.] with the dependencies of those places; the place of Fage; [Note: [Col. 1460D] **The place of Fage.** This place passed to the rights of the monks of Theuley by an exchange made in 1224 with Peter, abbot, and the canons of Saint Stephen, discussed in Part II, chapter 6 of this history.]

Indeed, of your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or of the produce of your animals, let absolutely no one exact tithes from you. [Col. 1459B] We also decree that the burial of your parishioners shall be free, unless perhaps some of them have chosen to be buried in other churches, while the rights of your church nevertheless remain intact. We prohibit any one of your brethren, after having made profession in that place, from leaving the cloister without the permission of the abbot and of his whole chapter; and no one shall dare retain a departing brother.

Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for absolutely no person rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, or to take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved whole for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and to the canonical rights of the diocesan bishop.

If anyone therefore in the future, etc.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Odo, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Guy, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Guy, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus. I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes. I, Ubald, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. [Col. 1460B] I, Bernard, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Clement. I, Octavian, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, Henry, cardinal priest of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus.

Given at Benevento through the hand of Roland, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fifth Ides of April, in the fourth indiction, in the year 1156 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian IV.

### XCIV. He confirms the privileges of the monastery of Saint Lambert of Liège. (Benevento, 18 April.)

[REIFFENBERG, *Monuments*, VIII, 642.]

[Col. 1461A]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HELGOT, abbot of the monastery of Saint Lambert, situated in the place called Liège, etc.

Whenever that which, etc., is requested of us.

Given at Benevento through the hand of Roland, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the fourth indiction, in the year 1156 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian IV.

### XCV. He commends to the canons of the church of Pisa his chaplain R., “for cutting stones and small columns,” to be used by the canons of the church of Saint Rufus in building their monastery. (Benevento, 20 April.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, III, 397.]

[Col. 1461B]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons L., archpriest, and the other Pisan canons: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

Those whom we know to be bound to us by a more ample devotion, and whom we love with a greater affection of love, we naturally call upon with greater confidence in your affairs. Since the church of Pisa has shown devotion to our predecessors and has always [Col. 1461C] endeavoured humbly to obey them, we do not wish it in our time to suffer any diminishment in its relation to us or to our mother, since we are prepared to love your church and its persons with full charity and to preserve for you its right whole and inviolate.

Accordingly, we earnestly commend to your charity our beloved son R., our chaplain, who is sufficiently devoted to the church of Pisa, and certain brethren of the church of Saint Rufus, whom we send to your parts for cutting stones and small columns. We would also certainly have sent with them our beloved son P., our scribe, had he not remained behind on your business. We ask that you provide them—and us—with such welcome assistance and counsel, both in craftsmen and in other matters, [Col. 1461D] that they may accomplish the work which they intend, and that we may owe you fruitful thanks. For we wish a cloister to be made for the work of our beloved sons, the canons of the church of Saint Rufus; with your assistance we would have the execution of the work completed.

Given at Benevento, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May.

### XCVI. He takes the monastery of Saint Paternianus of Fano under protection and confirms its possessions. (Benevento, 5 May.)

[AMIANI, *Memorie di Fano*, II, *Sommario*, p. X.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons VIVIAN, abbot of the monastery of Saint Paternianus, and to the brethren, both present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

It is fitting that those choosing the religious life should have apostolic protection at hand, lest an assault of any rashness either turn them back from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and take under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid monastery in which you are devoted to divine service, fortifying it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and whatever goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future acquire, by grant of popes, gift of kings or princes, offering of the faithful, or other just means, with the Lord’s help, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The parish church of Saint Mary in Serra, with all its appurtenances; whatever you rightfully possess in the parish church of Monte Maggiore together with the parish church of Saint Damian; the parish church of Saint Mary of Urciano; the chapel of Saint Eleutherius with its appurtenances; the chapel of Saint Christopher; whatever you rightfully possess in the chapel of Saint Apollinaris, in the church of Saint Michael, and in the church of Saint George; the chapel of Saint Lawrence of Quercusfissa; the chapel of Saint Marinus; the chapel of Saint Felicity; the chapel of Saint Marcellus; the chapel of Saint Hippolytus; the whole castle of Quercusfissa with its court; [Col. 1462C] the castle of Lubacaria with its court, and the land of Serra with its inhabitants; three parts of the castle of Poggio with three parts of the court of that castle; one half of the castle of Urciano with everything that you possess in its court, and what you possess in the court of Saint Eleutherius at Suasano; a fourth part of the castle of Monte Maggiore, with everything that you possess in its court; the holding of Saltaria; the holding of Casaclore; the demesne vineyard of Rusciano; the vineyard of Marano; the vineyard of Spornagatto; the mill of Rupoli; the mill of Argilla; whatever you possess in the mill at the bridge of Trave; the Greater Field; the field of Contado; whatever you rightfully possess in the castle of Rubri, together with everything that you possess in its court, and what they possessed in the court [Col. 1462D] of Fractula; and whatever you rightfully possess in the church of Saint Sylvester.

Moreover, you may receive, without any opposition, clerics fleeing the world or free laymen who wish to enter your monastery; and if anyone wishes to confer any of his goods upon that monastery for the salvation of his soul, no one shall dare impede him. You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the consecration of altars or churches, and the ordinations of clerics to be promoted to sacred orders from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to supply these things to you freely and without any improper exaction. Otherwise, you may approach whichever bishop you prefer [lacuna], who, supported by our authority, may grant what is requested.

Upon the death of yourself, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it through any cunning of deceit or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected according to God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict, as has been observed hitherto.

Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for absolutely no person rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, or to take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved unimpaired and whole for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See [Col. 1463B] and to the canonical rights of the diocesan bishop.

If anyone therefore, etc.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Benevento through the hand of Roland, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the third Nones of May, in the fourth indiction, in the year 1156 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian IV.

### XCVII. He takes the monastery of Steingaden under protection and confirms its goods. (Benevento, 31 May.)

[HUGO, *Ord. Praem. Ann.*, II, 536.]

[Col. 1463C] ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ANSELM, provost of the church of Saint John the Baptist of Steingaden, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

It is fitting that those choosing the religious life should have apostolic protection at hand, lest an assault of any rashness either turn them back from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and take under the protection of Blessed Peter and of ourselves, after the example of our predecessor Pope Eugenius of happy memory, the aforesaid church, founded on the personal allod of the illustrious Duke Welf, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing.

First, we decree that the canonical order known to have been instituted in that place according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine and the institution of the Premonstratensians shall there be observed inviolate for all time. Nor shall any brother, after having made profession there, leave that cloister without the provost’s permission; and no one shall dare retain one who leaves. Furthermore, whatever possessions or goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future acquire, by grant of popes, gift of kings or princes, offering of the faithful, or other just means, by the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm [Col. 1464A] and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these, we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

In the diocese of Augsburg, the church of Ingenried, with tithes and other appurtenances, canonically granted to you by our venerable brother Conrad, bishop of Augsburg; the estate called Sibenich Blebem, and the tithes legitimately granted to you by the said bishop; and likewise a part of a certain benefice, namely eight holdings in the place called Morchlorf, which you, beloved son Anselm, provost, are known to have redeemed from the hand of Theoderic of Pounb for seventy talents, with the assent and concurrence both of our venerable brother Conrad, bishop of Augsburg, and of the canons and ministerials of that church, as is contained in the written instrument of that same bishop our brother. We nevertheless confirm these to you.

Indeed, let no one presume to exact tithes from you for your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the produce of your animals. You shall receive the consecrations of altars and churches, and the ordinations of clerics who are to be promoted to sacred orders, from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic and willing to supply them to you freely and without improper exaction. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested.

We also grant that the burial-place of that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict, while the rights of the mother church nevertheless remain intact. [Col. 1464C] In addition, we decree that your church shall have no advocate. Upon the death of yourself, the present provost of that place, no one shall be set over it through any cunning of deceit or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall provide for themselves to be elected in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine.

Furthermore, if a general interdict is proclaimed in the parish, you shall nevertheless have free faculty to celebrate the divine offices behind closed doors, without ringing bells, excluding the excommunicated and those under interdict, and in a low voice.

Therefore we decree that it shall be lawful for absolutely no person rashly to disturb the church, or to take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things be preserved unimpaired and whole for the use and benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice, of course, to the authority of the Apostolic See and to the canonical rights of the diocesan bishop.

If anyone therefore, etc.

I, Pope Adrian IV. I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the church of Saint Praxedes. I, Julius, cardinal priest of the church of Saint Marcellus. [Col. 1465A] I, Bernard, cardinal priest of the church of Saint Clement. I, Octavian, cardinal priest of the church of Saint Cecilia. I, Gerard, cardinal priest of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, John, cardinal priest of Saints John and Ulric and of the church of Pammachius.

Given at Benevento through the hand of Roland, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the second day before the Kalends of June, in the fourth indiction, in the year 1156 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian IV.

### XCVIII. He takes the monastery of Saint Afra of Augsburg under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Benevento, 1 June.)

[*Monumenta Boica*, XXII, 176.]

[Col. 1465B]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons HEZITO, abbot of the monastery of Saint Afra, and his brethren, present and future, professing the monastic life, in perpetuity.

The most holy Roman Church, recognized as the mother and head of all churches, ought so to bestow the grace of its provision upon its members and to fortify them with the shield of apostolic protection that they may always remain in a state of religion and uprightness and manfully resist the wicked. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously granting assent to your just petitions and wishing to provide kindly for the church committed to you, we take that church under the protection of Blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and fortify it with the protection of this present writing.

We decree that whatever possessions or goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future acquire by reasonable means, with the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors. But because many losses and burdens are customarily brought upon churches through the negligence of prelates, we decree and establish by the authority of this present decree that no bishop may alienate, grant in benefice, or in any manner dispose of the estates or goods of the church committed to you.

Furthermore, we apostolically confirm for you and through you for that church the tithes of grain and swine, granted to you by the pious gift of certain bishops, on the road called Straza and in the suburb called Harena, provided, however, that they belonged to the right of those same bishops. [Col. 1465D] We likewise confirm the offerings of the altars granted in our presence by our venerable brother Conrad, bishop of Augsburg, to you, son Hezilo, abbot, and through you to your monastery; and we decree that this confirmation shall remain valid and unshaken in future times.

Therefore let absolutely no person be permitted rashly to disturb that monastery, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations.

[Col. 1466A] If anyone therefore, etc.

Circular monogram. I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Guy, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus. I, Julius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, Octavian, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, Gerard, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill.

Given at Benevento through the hand of Roland, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the Kalends of June, in the fourth indiction, in the year 1156 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian IV.

### XCIX. To the clergy of Augsburg. He declares Conrad, bishop of Augsburg, innocent and condemns his accusers to a severe penalty. (Benevento, 6 June.)

(PEZ, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, VI, I, 381.)

[Col. 1466B]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the clergy and provost of Augsburg: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

Our venerable brother Conrad, your bishop, appeared before us with the other party concerning the controversy and discord carried on between him and his canons and certain monks; and we ourselves and our brethren carefully heard the arguments and allegations on both sides.

But after their long dispute, when witnesses from the side of our aforesaid brother had been heard and received, and his opponents had failed, we fully recognized his innocence. Therefore, we wholly absolve him from their accusation, and suspend all those same opponents from every divine office. We add that all who took part in this defamation must, barefoot, within eight days after their return, enter by whatever gate the bishop chooses and come to the cathedral church, seeking pardon from our aforesaid brother for their presumption. When this satisfaction has been received, he shall restore to them the divine ministries. We have judged this penalty to be imposed upon his opponents. But those who remained with him in his trials shall have the apostolic blessing and favour.

[Col. 1466D] Given at Benevento, on the eighth Ides of June.

### C. He takes the church of Saint Vincent of Bergamo under protection and confirms its goods. (Benevento, 8 June.)

[LUPI, *Codex diplomaticus Bergomensis*, II, 1149.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons JOHN, archpriest, and his brethren, present and future, living canonically in the mother church of Saint Vincent of Bergamo, in perpetual memory.

Both the force of equity and the order of reason require that just petitioners be granted their request, especially insofar as the piety of the petitioners assists their wishes and truth does not abandon them. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions and, following the example of our predecessors of happy memory, Innocent and Lucius, Roman pontiffs, take under the guardianship and protection of the Apostolic See the church of Blessed Vincent the martyr, together with the college of your congregation and all things belonging to that church, and fortify it with the page of this present writing.

We decree that whatever possessions in churches, towns, villages, tithes, revenues of fairs, or other things that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future reasonably acquire, with the Lord’s aid, by grant of popes, generosity of kings or princes, offering of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain firm and unimpaired for you and your successors forever.
