We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid Church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact for your use and for the use of the others for whose governance and maintenance they have been granted, wholly to their benefit, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and to the canonical respect due to the bishop of Ferrara. If anyone therefore, etc.; but to all, etc.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Gregory, bishop of Sabina. I, Ubaldus, cardinal priest of St Praxedes. I, Julius, cardinal priest of the title of St Marcellus. I, Ubaldus, cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Bernard, cardinal priest of the title of St Clement. I, Octavian, cardinal priest of the title of St Cecilia. I, Gerard, cardinal priest of the title of St Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, John, cardinal priest of SS John and Paul. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of SS Sylvester and [Col. 1549D] Martin. I, Ildeprandus, cardinal priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Odo, cardinal deacon of St George at the Golden Veil. I, Guido, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Portico. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin. I, John, cardinal of SS Sergius and Bacchus. I, Bonadies, cardinal deacon of St Angelo. I, Arditio, cardinal deacon of St Theodore. I, Boso, cardinal deacon of SS Cosmas and Damian. I, Albert, cardinal deacon of St Adrian.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, through the hand of Roland, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Ides of January, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1157 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Adrian IV.

## CLXXVI. He receives under protection the Hospital House of Misericordia at Piacenza.  
*(Rome, at St Peter’s, 21 January.)*

[CAMPI, *History of Piacenza*, II, 356.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to ALBERT, rector of the charitable hospital, and to his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

It is fitting readily to grant assent to religious desires, so that faithful devotion may obtain a swift result. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, moved by the prayers of our venerable brother Hugh, your bishop, and favourably concurring in your just requests, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the church of St Giles, together with the hospital in which you are devoted to divine services; and we strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing, decreeing as follows. (There follow the provisions set out in the privilege of Anastasius IV cited above.)

Moreover, we confirm by apostolic authority for your devotion the reasonable customs and liberties granted you by our aforesaid brother and strengthened by the guarantee of his document; and, as is contained in the writing of that same brother of ours, we decree that they shall remain ratified and unshaken for all future time. No one whatsoever shall presume to demand tithes from you on newly cleared land (*novalia*) which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the increase of your animals. We likewise confirm by apostolic authority the water-key or sluice-right (*clavica aquae*) which our aforesaid brother Hugh, bishop of Piacenza, granted you and confirmed by the guarantee of his document.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact, wholly for the benefit of those for whose governance and maintenance they have been granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and to the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If, therefore, in future any ecclesiastical or secular [Col. 1550D] person, etc.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church.

(There follow the subscriptions of the cardinals.)

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, through the hand of Roland, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February, in the eleventh indiction, in the year 1157 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian IV.

## CLXXVII. He receives under protection the Church of Ratzeburg and confirms its possessions and rights, at the request of Henry, duke of Bavaria and Saxony.  
*(Rome, at St Peter’s, 21 January.)*

[ORIG. GUELF., III, Preface, 42.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother EBERHARD, bishop, and to the beloved sons, the canons of the Church of Ratzeburg, present and future, canonically appointed: in perpetuity.

We ought readily to grant assent to religious desires, so that devout devotion may obtain a swift result and undoubtedly gain strength, when this has been granted through the prior charity of the Apostolic See. Therefore, beloved sons in Christ, inclining to your petition at the prayers of our dearest son Henry, duke of Bavaria and Saxony, upon whose land the aforesaid church is known to have been founded, we willingly assent; and we receive the aforesaid Church of Ratzeburg under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves and strengthen it by the safeguard of this present writing. We decree [Col. 1551B] that whatever possessions, whatever goods, the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future, with God’s favour, acquire by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

From the gift of the nobleman Henry, duke of Bavaria and Saxony: three hundred cultivated and uncultivated *mansi*, with all their appurtenances; mills; the whole and entire territories of Sadelbandia and Polabia, with the churches and their tithes, and the peoples subject to them. Furthermore, we decree that the canonical order which is known to have been established there according to God, the Rule of blessed Augustine, [Col. 1551C] and the habit of the brethren of Prémontré shall be observed inviolably in that church for all time. On the death of you, the present bishop of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it through any cunning of intrigue or by force; rather, the person whom the brethren of the Church of Ratzeburg, with the counsel of religious persons, shall have provided to be elected according to God and the constitutions of the holy Fathers.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid Church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved intact, wholly for the benefit of your use and of the use of others for whose governance and maintenance they have been granted. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person shall knowingly attempt in future rashly to contravene this page of our constitution, and, having been warned a second and a third time, shall not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honour; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred Body and Blood of God and of the Lord, our Redeemer Jesus Christ; and let him be subject to severe vengeance at the final judgment. But let all who preserve the rights of the same Church have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action [Col. 1552A] and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, through the hand of Roland, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1157 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian IV.

## CLXXVIII. He receives under protection the church of St Mary of Gariberto at Piacenza.  
*(Rome, at St Peter’s, 23 January.)*

[CAMPI, *History of Piacenza*, II, 356.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons HONESTUS, prior of St Mary of Gariberto, and his brethren, present and future, canonically appointed: in perpetuity.

Whenever something is requested of us which is recognized as consistent with reason and propriety, it is fitting that we grant it with a willing mind and afford suitable assistance to the petitioners’ desires. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, moved by the prayers of our venerable brother Hugh, bishop of Piacenza, we graciously assent to your just requests; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and of ourselves the aforesaid church, which belongs to the right and property of the aforesaid bishop, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions, whatever goods, the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future, with God’s favour, acquire by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: all the land that you hold in Rizolo and Uzano, and what you hold in Trabatiano, Carpeneto, Cerbole, Vezano, Aquensi, Clolano, and Octavello; the enclosed property (*clausum*) which you hold near the city at Faygliria; the enclosed property near the viscount’s mill; and another enclosed property beyond Fososta, near Gignola. Whatever you hold in Vivacario, St Paul, Casali Remissi, and Mamiliano; and all the houses which you hold around the church or within the city itself.

[Col. 1552D] We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid Church, etc.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hymarus, bishop of Tusculum. I, Gregory, bishop of Sabina. I, Hubaldus, cardinal priest of the title of St Praxedes. I, Julius, cardinal priest of the title of St Marcellus. I, Bernard, cardinal priest of the title of St Clement. I, Octavian, cardinal priest of the title of St Cecilia. I, Astaldus, cardinal priest of the title of St Prisca. I, John, cardinal priest of SS John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Henry, cardinal priest of the title of SS Nereus and Achilleus. [Col. 1553A] I, Ildeprandus, cardinal priest of the Basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Guido, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Portico. I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of St Mary in Cosmedin. I, John, cardinal deacon of SS Sergius and Bacchus. I, Albert, cardinal deacon of St Adrian.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, through the hand of Roland, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1157 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian IV.

## CLXXIX. He commands the provost and entire clergy of the Church of Piacenza to return to canonical discipline and obey Bishop Hugh.  
*(Rome, at St Peter’s, 25 January.)*

[IBID., p. 356.]

[Col. 1553B]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons, the provost and the entire clergy of the Church of Piacenza: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Clerics ought to differ from laypeople in life, conduct, and morals, so that the clerical order may shine forth and be shown to enjoy greater dignity when they strive to do those things which accord with clerical office. For the fragrance of honourable conduct and good repute ought to pass from clerics to laypeople, especially from those called canons, who have been gathered in the greater and more dignified churches to serve the Lord and provide for many persons. Therefore, sons, you must act diligently and reflect more attentively, so that you may restore yourselves and the Church entrusted to you to that ancient and praiseworthy condition from which it is known to have fallen; lest perhaps you appear to neglect honourableness and to think rather of earthly gain than of heavenly things. For, as we have learned from the testimony of many, the condition of the Church of Piacenza was once renowned and pleasing to God and men, so much so that among the other churches of the Italian kingdom it excelled in its abundance of decorum. Indeed, the canons of that church, according to an honourable and praiseworthy custom, ate together in one refectory and took sleep at the proper time in one dormitory. But you, at which we greatly wonder, have changed the condition of propriety into a less praiseworthy one; and—what we do not say without grave sorrow of heart—you seem almost wholly to have cast aside the pattern of clerical order.

And consequently it has come about that what formerly seemed to be an abundance of honourableness in the head may now deservedly be counted in the hindmost part. Therefore, that you may, with the Lord as author, be restored to your former condition of honourable conduct, we command you by this present writing: all of you shall eat from one cellar together in one refectory; sleeping in the common dormitory, you shall meet daily in chapter, so that you may be able jointly to deliberate concerning the spiritual and temporal affairs [Col. 1554A] of the Church entrusted to you. But since you ought to perform and put into effect these things and the other matters pertaining to propriety in accordance with [lacuna] of our dearest brother Hugh, your bishop, we further command you humbly to strive to obey that brother of ours as your father and the shepherd of your souls; to receive the orders required from the Church, if you are worthy; wearing round garments, to serve the Lord in church at the appointed hours according to the custom of canons; and, with the favour and help of that same brother of ours, your bishop, to order your household, God granting it, so that you may be called canons not only in name but in reality.

[Col. 1554B] Otherwise, we wish you to know that, by God’s authority, we shall hold valid any sentence which that same brother of ours may pronounce against any one of you on this account, and shall cause it to be observed inviolably.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, on the eighth day before the Kalends of February.

## CLXXX. At the request of Henry, duke of Bavaria and Saxony, he receives under protection the monastery of Blessed Pancras at Ranshofen and confirms its goods and rights.  
*(Rome, at St Peter’s, 29 January.)*

[ORIG. GUELF., III, 473.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons MEGENARD, provost of the Church of Blessed Pancras at Ranshofen, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

Those choosing the religious life ought to have apostolic protection at hand, lest an assault of any rashness either frighten them from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, moved by the prayers of the illustrious Henry, duke of Bavaria and Saxony, we graciously assent to your just petitions and receive the aforesaid church of the blessed martyr Pancras, in which you are occupied in divine office, under the guardianship and protection of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles; and we strengthen it by the privilege of the Apostolic See. First, indeed, we decree that the canonical order which is known to have been established in the same place according to the Rule of blessed Augustine [Col. 1554D] shall be observed there inviolably for all time. Moreover, whatever possessions, whatever goods, the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future, by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other means, obtain through the Lord’s favour, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: namely, the church of St Michael with its tithe and parochial right; chapels at Winkirchin, Hantinberge, and Geroltisberge; and the chapel of St Stephen at Brunove with their appurtenances; the chapel [Col. 1555A] of Hochberch with its appurtenances, in that liberty which our brother Eberhard, archbishop of Salzburg, reasonably confirmed for you by his own writing: namely, that no one except the archbishop himself and the provost of your church shall have authority to make any arrangement in them. Certainly, no one shall presume to demand tithes from you on your newly cleared lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or on the increase of your animals. You shall receive the ecclesiastical sacraments from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to administer them to you freely and without any improper exaction; otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested.

On the death of you, the present provost of that place, or if you are transferred to govern another church, or on the death of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by the craft of intrigue or by force, save the person whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the council, shall have provided to be elected in the fear of God and according to the Rule of blessed Augustine. Moreover, because your house is so established that the advocate of the goods of the aforesaid duke in those regions is also advocate of that place, we forbid either him or anyone in his service to oppress the same place with unjust burdens. Rather, that advocate must defend and protect you, your dependants, [Col. 1555C] and your possessions in the duke’s stead, as the duke himself established and confirmed by his writing, upon this condition: he shall hear both your complaints and those of your dependants, and administer fitting justice; but he shall demand no share from you on that account, receiving only from the granary of the aforesaid duke what is due to him in accordance with the ancient arrangement. For the said duke grants that advocate no authority to make dispositions in the cloister or over your dependants or possessions; rather, he is to protect you in his place and seek from this only eternal recompense. We also grant you all these things and confirm them by apostolic authority. But if that advocate attempts to contravene these provisions and, after a second and third admonition, does not amend, then, with the counsel and assistance of the aforesaid duke, that advocacy shall be removed from the unworthy man and another suitable person appointed in his place. We also grant that the burial-place of the same house shall be free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and final wish of those who resolve to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; but the rights of the mother church are preserved.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid Church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things shall be preserved unimpaired and intact, wholly for the benefit of those for whose governance and maintenance they have been granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See [Col. 1556A] and to the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If, therefore, in future, etc. But to all persons belonging to the same place, etc.

Given at Rome, at St Peter’s, through the hands of Roland, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Kalends of February, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1157 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian IV.

## CLXXXI. He addresses Emperor Frederick in sufficiently mild words; he excuses certain passages of his earlier letter (see above, no. 143), and commends his legates sent “to admonish Henry, duke of Bavaria and Saxony.”

[PERTZ, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Leges*, vol. II, p. 106.]

Since, by God’s disposition, as pleased Him, we undertook the care of the universal Church, we have taken care in all affairs to honour your magnificence in such a way that, day by day, your heart ought increasingly to have been kindled in love for us and in reverence for the Apostolic See. We therefore cannot endure without great astonishment that, when we had heard, through the report of certain persons, that your mind had been somewhat stirred against us, and had sent to your presence, to ascertain your will, two of our better and greater brethren—namely Roland, chancellor of the title of St Mark, and Bernard, of the title of St Clement, cardinal priests, who had always been zealous in the Roman Church for the honour of your majesty—they were treated otherwise than befitted imperial [Col. 1556C] dignity.

For your mind, as is said, was disturbed because of a certain word, namely *beneficium*; yet this surely ought not rightly to have disturbed the mind, not merely of so great a man, but not even of any lesser person. For although this term *beneficium* is taken by some in a meaning other than that which it has from its formation, nevertheless it ought on that occasion to have been understood in the sense in which we ourselves employed it and in which it is known to retain its original force. The word is formed from *bonum* (“good”) and *factum* (“deed”), and among us *beneficium* means not a fief (*feudum*) but a good deed. In this sense it occurs throughout the whole body of Sacred Scripture, in which we are said to be governed and sustained by God’s beneficium, not as by a fief, but as by His blessing and good deed. Your magnificence indeed clearly recognizes that we placed the insignia of imperial dignity upon your head so well and honourably that it may be judged by all to have been a good deed. Therefore, certain persons who have attempted to twist this word, and also the phrase, “we conferred upon you the insignia of the imperial crown,” into a meaning other than its own have done so not owing to the merits of the matter, but from their own inclination and at the prompting of those who in no way love peace between the kingdom and the Church. For by the expression “we conferred” we meant nothing other than what was said above: “we placed [it].”

Now, as to your having subsequently ordered ecclesiastical persons, as is said, to withdraw from the visitation owed to the most holy Roman Church: if this is so, your discernment, dearest son in Christ, recognizes, as we believe, how improper an action it was. For if you held any grievance against us, it should have been communicated to us through your envoys and letters, and we should have taken care to provide for your honour as for that of a most dear son. Therefore, at the admonition of our beloved son Henry, duke of Bavaria and Saxony, we have now sent to your presence two of our brethren, Henry of the title of SS Nereus and Achilleus and Hyacinth of St Mary in Cosmedin, cardinal deacons—prudent and honourable men—admonishing and exhorting your highness in the Lord to receive them honourably and kindly. Let your excellence know that what shall be communicated to your magnificence by them on our behalf has proceeded from the sincerity of our heart; and thus, through these same sons of ours and through the mediation of our aforesaid son the duke, let your highness strive to reach such an agreement that no seedbed of discord may remain between you and your mother, the most holy Roman Church.

## CLXXXII. He confirms the possessions and rights of the churches of SS John and Paul, St Martin, St Stephen Major, and St Stephen Minor, assigned for the maintenance of the canons of the Church of Blessed Peter (at Rome).  
*(Lateran, 10 February.)*

[Note: [Col. 1557C] The sacred buildings which Adrian IV in this bull, and Urban III, Innocent III, Gregory IX, and other Roman pontiffs in particular privileges issued on this subject, granted to the Vatican chapter or more firmly confirmed, have long since been listed in the revenue-registers or inventories of churches, hospitals, and monasteries subject to our basilica. From these are drawn clear proofs showing the complete servitude, obedience, and subjection of these churches to the Vatican chapter. [Col. 1557D] The said inventories and other manuscripts also record how many pounds, whether of saffron, pepper, wax, and so forth, or what sum of money each must pay to the Vatican basilica; likewise, they record many appointments of the same churches and grants of benefices attached to them, made by the aforesaid chapter of St Peter. With regard to sacred buildings in the City or situated not far from its walls, we always consider worthy of notice what we find written in the aforesaid inventories: namely, that on the recurring feast of the titular saint or patron, canons or some persons from the chapter went to them to celebrate the divine office in solemn procession, as is still customary. In some of them a sermon was customarily delivered; indeed, there was even a distinguished banquet which the rector of the church where the feast was celebrated was obliged to prepare. Consult the old parchment codex entitled *Sermons for Matins*, in our chapter archive, shelf-mark C, no. 107, where on pp. [Col. 1558C] 247–249 there is an index of churches under the jurisdiction of the basilica of St Peter. Compare also the paper codex compiled in 1489 by Demetrius of Lucca, a beneficiary of the same basilica, and held in the aforesaid archive under shelf-mark A.]  
*(Lateran, 10 February.)*

[Bullarium Vaticanum, I, 57.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the beloved sons BERNARD, cardinal priest of the title of St Clement and archpriest of the canonical basilica of the prince of the apostles, and the canons of that basilica; and to the rectors of the four monasteries of SS John and Paul, St Martin, St Stephen Major, and St Stephen Minor, present and future, canonically appointed: in perpetuity.

[Col. 1558A] It is clear to all worshippers of the Christian faith that blessed Peter was established by our Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ Himself, as prince of the apostles, and that the power of binding and loosing souls was entrusted to him by heavenly privilege. Hence it is said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church; and I shall give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16). And again: “If you love me, Simon Peter, feed my sheep” (John 21). Therefore we, although unworthy, who are the vicars of that same key-bearer of heaven and sit in his place in the holy Church of God, ought to cherish with our patronage his special ministers and the patrimonies of the Apostolic See, [Col. 1558B] and defend them against the assaults of wicked persons. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we grant your petitions with due kindness, and, following the example of our predecessors of happy memory—Sergius II, Leo IV, Leo IX, and Innocent II, Roman pontiffs—we strengthen by the page of this present writing the most holy churches of the blessed martyrs John and Paul, St Martin, St Stephen Major, and St Stephen Minor, assigned for your use and maintenance. We decree that whatever possessions, whatever goods, canonically belong to these venerable places, or may in future, through the Lord’s favour, be acquired by grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The church of Saint Mary in Catharina [Note: [Col. 1558C] On the church of St. Mary in Catharina, now called S. Catarina della Rota, discussion occurs below in connection with the bull of Urban III, issued in 1186.] with all appurtenances; the church of Saint Saviour [Note: [Col. 1558C] Monuments of no negligible antiquity, as we said on p. 23, note D, testify that this church of St. Saviour was erected by Charlemagne [Col. 1558D] and endowed with many revenues and estates. How, then, is Leo IV here asserted to be the founder of the sacred building? Perhaps the holy pontiff repaired it in such a manner and bound it to himself by so many and such great benefactions that it could not improperly be called constructed by him. James Grimaldi, in Turrigius, *On the Vatican Crypts*, p. 487, undertakes the following argument in order to defend the authenticity of the Carolingian diploma for that church, which presents the aforesaid Pope Leo IV and Charlemagne himself as contemporaries: “Leo III,” he says, “was also called Leo IV”; and he attempts to demonstrate this both from a manuscript chronicle by Richard, monk of Cluny, in the Vatican Library, no. 3765, and from Martin of Poland in his *Chronology of the Roman Pontiffs*, which place a certain Leo immediately after Sergius I. With what success, however, we shall consider below, when we discuss the Carolingian privilege itself more appropriately.] near the boundaries, which was constructed by our predecessor of holy memory, Pope Leo IV, [Col. 1559A] for the burial of all Ultramontanes, with all its uses and appurtenances; the church of St. Justin, constructed for the burial of all Lombards and Italians, with all its uses and appurtenances; the church of Saint Peregrine; the church of Saint Mary of the *Virgarii* [Note: [Col. 1559B] This sacred building is illustrated by the following words from the Roman Canon, title 47: “In the same square before the church of Blessed Peter, namely next to the church of Saint Mary of the *Virgarii*, there is another building, which by custom the school of the *Virgarii* prepares as a bed for the lord pope when, in the greater litany, [Col. 1559C] he comes to St. Peter’s.” Therefore those *virgarii*, as Cencius the chamberlain carefully noted in the Roman Order, no. 68, received ten solidi from the presbyterium. See p. 27, note d.]; the church of Saint Saviour of Cossa Caballi [Note: [Col. 1559C] Now called S. Giacomo Scosciacavallo. Cencius, chamberlain, in the Roman Order, ch. 18, no. 40, in Mabillon, states that six denarii from the presbyterium were given to St. Saviour of Scossa Caballi for a censer. See p. 25, note e.].

At the castle of Bucceia: the church of Saints Marius and Martha [Note: [Col. 1559C] William of Malmesbury, book IV, ch. 2, *On the Deeds of the Kings of England*, enumerates this among the churches situated along the Cornelian Way and mentions it in these words: “In the third church are Marius and Martha, and Audifax and Habacuc, their sons.” Compare the diploma of the aforesaid St. Leo IV, p. 16.]; together with the church of St. Lawrence of the castle of Bucceia; the castle of Bucceia [Note: [Col. 1559C] That the wealthy estate of Bucceia, which still remains under the right and ownership of the Vatican chapter, was given from his own patrimony by St. Leo IV to the canons of St. Peter, Peter Mallius and the Roman Canon [Col. 1559D] recorded in writing, title 2; and it is plainly inferred from the diploma of the same Leo, p. 16.] with its estates and hamlets, namely the Attician hill [Note: [Col. 1559D] St. Leo IX mentions this estate, as we saw above, p. 30.] and the estate of Paul; Olivetum with its other designated places, with the ruined church of Saints Cosmas and Damian; these estates being situated in the territory of Silva Candida; [Col. 1559B] the castle of Luternum [Note: [Col. 1559D] That we should look for the castle of Luternum nowhere other than in the territory of Cære is indicated both by the context of this bull, to be considered a little below, and by the previously cited privilege of St. Leo IX, p. 33.] with its estates, hamlets, and all its appurtenances; the church of Saints John and Paul within that castle itself; the oratory of Saint Nicholas, which is in the *Mesagna* [Note: [Col. 1559D] Is *Mesagna* the same as *mesagium*, namely a measure of land furnished with dwellings and farm buildings, as Cange says? See “Mesagium.”] of that castle; the church of Saint Andrew [Note: [Col. 1559D] The aforesaid diploma of St. Leo, p. 33, mentions the church of St. Andrew, as do other privileges to be produced below.] with all its appurtenances; the greater estate of Sessani, the lesser estate of Sessani, the estate of Pretoriola [Note: [Col. 1559D] Compare p. 33.] with houses, lands, and all its [Col. 1560A] appurtenances—these estates being situated in the territory of Cære near the castle of Luternum, thirty miles from the city of Rome; the church of Saint Anatolia [Note: [Col. 1559D] On the church of St. Anatolia, the *manicae*, and Trajan’s harbour, we spoke on p. 26, notes k, l, and m.] in the old city of Portus, with the fishery beside it, and with its lands and *manicae* at Trajan’s harbour; the church of Saint Sylvester of Sutri [Note: [Col. 1559D] Both St. Leo IX, p. 34, and Adrian IV in a special diploma [Col. 1560B] speak of the church of St. Sylvester of Sutri.] with the valley called Frictilli [Note: [Col. 1560B] Adjacent to Sutri is the valley of Frictilli, whose boundaries are defined on p. 67 in the aforesaid paper codex arranged by Demetrius of Lucca.], with its mills; the hospital of Ferento [Note: [Col. 1560B] I am aware that, according to more accurate geographers of the province, Ferento is in Basilicata. But the hospital [Col. 1560C] of Ferento enumerated here is placed by the rent-rolls of our basilica in the diocese of Ferentino.], with the oratory of Saint Lawrence and all its appurtenances; the hospital of Narni with all its appurtenances.

The monastery of Saint Benedict [Note: [Col. 1560C] The aforesaid inventories or rent-rolls place the monastery of St. Benedict, called de Scalocla, Scalocia, or Scalocchia, in the diocese of Città di Castello.] with all that belongs to it; the church of Saint Martin of Spello [Note: [Col. 1560C] In the diocese of Spoleto.]; the church of Saint Stephen of Runceia, situated in the bishopric of Attisium; the hospital of Traversa with the oratory of Saint Nicholas [Note: [Col. 1560C] A bull of Innocent III issued on the Ides of October, in the eighth year of his pontificate, and other diplomas to be cited below, place that hospital with the oratory of St. Nicholas in Campania, in the diocese of Assisi.]; the castle of Cassi [Note: [Col. 1560C] That is, Cascia, now a town in the diocese of Spoleto. Anyone comparing this bull with the paper book arranged in 1489 by Demetrius, beneficiary and chamberlain of St. Peter’s Basilica, and marked A in our chapter archive, must certainly hold this view. For the churches of St. Peter and St. Mary which the present bull connects with the castle of Cassi, that book frequently places at Cascia or Cassia, in the diocese of Spoleto. It is useful to produce one or two testimonies. The said codex records that Epiphanius, abbot of St. Eutychius, paid the Vatican chapter in 1472, for the church of St. Peter of Cascia, one ducat, I, col. 30, and for the church of St. Mary Annunciate of Cascia, col. 10; on p. 98 verso, it states: “In the same diocese of Spoleto, the church of St. Peter, in the square held by the convent of St. Augustine, pays annually one pound of the finest saffron as rent. The church of St. Mary Annunciate, held by Brother John of the Order of St. Peter Celestine, pays two pounds of wax as annual rent.”] [Col. 1560B] with the church of Saint Peter and the church of Saint Mary, with their estates, villages, and hamlets; the castle of Capracorum [Note: [Col. 1560D] On the castle of Capracorum, read p. 31, note a, and p. 33, note f.] with its lands, estates, and hamlets, with the ruined church of St. John, and with its watermills and millstones; the estate of Saint Cassian [Note: [Col. 1560D] It is certain from the constitutions of Leo IV and Leo IX, pp. 15, 26, and 30, that the estate of St. Cassian and most of the others immediately listed in this diploma are to be located on the Claudian [otherwise, Clodian] Way.]; the estate of Vicoli; the estate of Memoriense; the estate of greater Talianus and lesser Talianus; the estate of Casanillus; the estate of Casapindula; the estate of Cucumellus; the estate of Rotula; [Col. 1561A] the estate of Protelaris; the estate of Pritanella [Note: [Col. 1561D] St. Leo IX, in his diploma, p. 30, locates the estate called Pritanella on the Cornelian Way, on which we have spoken, p. 26, note e.]; the estate called Casa Lardaria [Note: [Col. 1561D] On the estate called Casa Lardaria, see again pp. 26, notes h and i.]; the estate of Cleandris, with the ruined church of Saint Agatha [Note: [Col. 1561D] See p. 26, note h.]; the estate of Cantulus; and the estate of Acqua Frigdula [Note: [Col. 1561D] This estate has now the same name and the same owner as formerly. For even today, called Acqua fredda, it remains under the ancient ownership of the Vatican chapter, outside the gate called Cavallegieri, about two miles from the City.], all mutually adjoining; the estate of Bravi [Note: [Col. 1561D] Pope Adrian I, as Maffeo Vegio testifies, book IV, no. 140, in Janning, vol. VII for June of the Bollandists, gave a very good estate called Bravi to the monastery of St. Stephen Major, of which we have spoken elsewhere.]; the estate of Pollini with all its designated places; the monastery of Saint Cornelius, situated in the territory of Veii, with all its appurtenances; six *pedicae* of land in the estate called the valleys of Pertica; the land of Macerano situated by the pierced rock [Note: [Col. 1562D] Namely, the estate which still preserves the same name; it is situated about eight miles from Rome outside the Flaminian Gate and belongs to the Vatican chapter.]; all the landed possessions which the monastery of Saint Sabas holds from your canonry in the territory of Galeria; likewise, half the rent of the houses and possessions of Saint Mary in Turri [Note: [Col. 1562D] On this, compare p. 18, note c, and p. 31.]; a third part of the offering which comes into the hands of the bishop of Portus [Col. 1561B] [Note: [Col. 1562D] The church of Silva Candida, or St. Rufina, was joined to the see of Portus in 1120 by a privilege of Calixtus II. The bishop of Portus thus enjoyed the same rights formerly possessed by the bishop of St. Rufina, including a share in offerings placed upon the altar of Blessed Peter. Consult the diplomas of John XIX, Benedict IX, and Victor II.] upon the altar, from which the chalice is placed upon the altar on Maundy Thursday, Good Friday, Holy Saturday, Easter Day, and Christmas Day.

You shall receive chrism, holy oil, the consecrations of altars or basilicas, and the ordinations of clerics in your churches from the diocesan bishops, provided that they are Catholic, enjoy the favour of the Apostolic See, and are willing to supply these things without any improper demand. Otherwise, you may approach whichever bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested. We further decree that no bishop, without the knowledge of the Roman pontiff, may presume, except when there is a general interdict, to prohibit divine offices in your churches or to exact anything from them for any reason; rather, let those churches remain freely under our protection [Note: [Col. 1562D] Peter Mallius and Maffeo Vegio, book II, ch. 3, no. 69, indicate that all the churches of the basilica, including those situated outside the City, possess such a privilege of liberty.].

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid Church, remove its possessions, retain those removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but let all things be preserved unimpaired and entire for the use, in every way advantageous, of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See.

If anyone therefore, etc.

But to all who preserve the rights of that place, etc.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Imarus, bishop of Tusculum. [Col. 1561D] I, Gregory, bishop of Sabina. [Col. 1562A] I, Hubaldus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedis. I, Julius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, Hubaldus, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Octavianus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, Astaldus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Prisca. I, Gerardus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, John, cardinal priest of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saints Sylvester and Martin. I, Ildebrandus, cardinal priest of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. [Col. 1562B] I, Oddo, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Guido, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. I, Bonadies, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo. I, Boso, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Albertus, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Roland, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth Ides of February, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1157 of the Lord’s Incarnation [Note: [Col. 1562D] By the style of bulls; but by common reckoning, 1158.], in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian IV.

### CLXXXIII. To Archbishop Hugh and Dean William of Vienne and their successors: he confirms the privileges granted by King Frederick I. (Lateran, March 15.)

[Bosco, *Bibliotheca Floriacensis*, left-hand column, 85.]

[Col. 1562C]

### CLXXXIV. He takes the church of St. Felicula at Parma under protection and confirms its possessions and rights. (Lateran, April 24.)

[AFFO, *Storia di Parma*, II, 369.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GERARD, prior of the church of St. Felicula, and his brethren, present and future, professing the canonical life: in perpetuity.

[Col. 1562D] Whenever that which seems consonant with reason and propriety is requested of us, it is fitting that we grant it with willing mind and render suitable support to the desires of petitioners. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests; and, following the example of our predecessor of holy memory, Pope Eugenius, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions or goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, by grant of popes, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The church of the Holy Sepulchre, with its hospital, situated in the suburb of Parma, with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Michael of Castiliculum with its appurtenances; the church of Saint James with its appurtenances, as Gerard, abbot of Saint John, is known to have granted it to you. We further decree that the canonical order, known to have been established in that place according to God and the Rule of Blessed Augustine, shall be observed there inviolate for all time. Certainly, no one may presume to exact tithes from you on your newly cleared lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense. Moreover, you may receive, without anyone’s opposition, clerics [Col. 1563C] fleeing the world or free laypersons for conversion. We likewise prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, from leaving the cloister without the permission of his prior upon any frivolous pretext; and no one may dare to retain those who leave without letters of authorization from the community.

Furthermore, we grant that the burial place of that establishment shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and last will of those who decide to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; without prejudice to the right of the parish churches from which the bodies of the dead are received. You shall receive the ordinations of clerics to be promoted to holy orders from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favour and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to administer them freely and without improper demand. Otherwise, you may approach whichever bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested. We also decree that you shall hold forever, free and unencumbered, the offerings of Masses celebrated in your churches by the bishop of Parma, just as our venerable brother Lanfranc, bishop of that city, granted them to you.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, remove its possessions, retain those removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but let all things be freely preserved for the use, in every way advantageous, of those for whose governance [Col. 1564A] and support they were granted, without prejudice in all things to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to contravene it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he corrects his presumption by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know that he is liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance.

[Col. 1564B] But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action, and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Imarus, bishop of Tusculum. I, Gregory, bishop of Sabina. I, Hubaldus, cardinal priest of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Octavianus, cardinal priest of Saint Cecilia. I, [lacuna] I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saints Sylvester and Martin. [Col. 1564C] I, Ildebrandus, cardinal priest of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Guido, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Callixtus. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustachius beside the Temple of Agrippa. I, Raymond, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Roland, priest of the Holy Roman Church, cardinal and chancellor, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, in the seventh indiction, in the year 1158 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian IV.

### CLXXXV. He takes the church of St. Samson at Orléans under protection and confirms its goods. (Lateran, May 10.)

[SAUSSEY, *Annales Ecclesiae Aurelianensis*, 446.]

[Col. 1564D]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the prior of St. Samson at Orléans and his brethren, present and future, living the regular life: in perpetuity.

A petition of pious will ought to be fulfilled by an ensuing effect, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth praiseworthily and the requested benefit may undoubtedly gain force. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. First, indeed, we decree [Col. 1565A] that the canonical order known to have been established in that place according to the fear of God, the Rule and institution of Blessed Augustine, and the church of St. Mary of Mount Sion, shall be preserved there inviolate for all time. Furthermore, whatever possessions or goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, by grant of popes, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. We grant and decree by apostolic authority that you may consecrate a cemetery in your church and bury there, without any opposition, both your brethren and your converts and all your household.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, remove its possessions, retain those removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but let all things be preserved entire for the use, in every way advantageous, of those for whose governance or support they were granted, without prejudice in all things to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop; and also without prejudice to the arrangement concerning the prebends of secular clerics, which is known to have been made by our predecessor of holy memory, Pope Eugenius.

If anyone therefore, etc. But to all, etc.

[Col. 1565C] I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church, etc.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Roland, priest of the Holy Roman Church, cardinal and chancellor, on the sixth Ides of May, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1158 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian IV.

### CLXXXVI. He takes the convent of Visbeck under protection and confirms its goods and privileges. (Lateran, May 11.)

[WURDTWEIN, *Subsidia diplomatica*, VI, 334.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved daughter THEMODIS, abbess of Visbeck, and the others with her who profess the canonical life: in perpetuity.

[Col. 1565D] A petition of pious will ought to be fulfilled by an ensuing effect, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth praiseworthily and the benefit may undoubtedly gain force. Therefore, beloved daughter in Christ, carefully considering the devotion which you bear toward the Apostolic See, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the monastery in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions or goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, by grant of popes, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just [Col. 1566A] means, God being favourable, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and to those who succeed you. We also grant by our authority unrestricted burial there for nobles of either sex, for your benefit and that of those who canonically succeed you.

We further enact that the monastery itself may never, under any pretext, be granted as a benefice to any person whatsoever, but shall always remain under the protection of the Roman pontiffs and the defence of emperors or kings. Moreover, we decree that within the precinct of the buildings or enclosures of the said monastery no cleric or layperson may at any time possess any dwelling by right of ownership or benefice; rather, the entire precinct of that place shall be open for the use and habitation of the abbess, the sisters, and other [Col. 1566B] religious persons. We prohibit any bishop other than the Roman pontiff from exercising any jurisdiction whatever in that monastery, so that, unless invited by the abbess of the monastery, he may not presume even to celebrate the solemnities of Mass there. Therefore, that all these provisions set forth above may henceforth have full force, we confirm them, by the authority of our favour, both for you and for those who succeed you.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, remove its possessions, retain those removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but let [Col. 1566C] all things be preserved entire for the use, in every way advantageous, of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice to the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If, therefore, in the future any ecclesiastical or secular person, knowing this page of our constitution, should rashly attempt to contravene it, then, after a second or third warning, unless he makes amends by suitable satisfaction, let him be deprived of the dignity of his power and office; let him know that he is liable before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and at the last judgment let him be subject to severe vengeance.

[Col. 1566D] But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that here they may receive the fruit of good action, and before the strict Judge may find the rewards of eternal peace. Amen.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubaldus, cardinal priest of Saint Praxedis. I, Adalbertus, cardinal priest of Saint Adrian.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Roland, chancellor, on the fifth Ides of May, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1156 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian IV [Note: [Col. 1565D] Read: the year 1158, the fourth year of the pontificate.].

### CLXXXVII. Privilege for the monastery of Saints Nazarius and Celsus at Verona. (Lateran, May 20.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, V, 798.]

[Col. 1567A]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons CLEMENT, abbot of the monastery of Saints Nazarius and Celsus, and his brethren, present and future, professing the monastic life: in perpetuity.

Whenever, etc. We fortify. First, indeed, we decree that the monastic order known to have been established in that monastery according to God and the Rule of Blessed Benedict shall be observed inviolate for all future time. Therefore, whatever [Col. 1567B] possessions or goods that same Church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire by grant of popes, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, through the Lord’s favour, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The church of St. Mary of Marcellitis with its appurtenances, subject to the annual rent of one Byzantine coin which you ought to pay for that church every year to us and our successors; the church of St. Sebastian with its appurtenances; the churches of Carliano; the church of St. Mary of Cluave with its appurtenances; the church of St. Cassian with its appurtenances; the church of St. Martin of Lavago with its appurtenances; the church of the Holy Sepulchre [Col. 1567C] with its hospital and appurtenances; the church of St. Vitalis with its appurtenances; the church of St. Felicitas with its appurtenances; the village of Cosiliani with all its rights; the land which you possess at Lenazzo; the land of Nodesola; the land of Portu; the land of Porcile; the land of Gepito; the land of Lavagno, with its vineyards and houses; the land of Grillana; the land of Mizano; the land of Monteauro, with its mills, irrigation channels, and vineyards; the land of Mizoli, with its olives and vineyards; land with olives in the territory of St. Mary in Selle; land and vineyards of Colignola; the lands of Lilasi; the land of Garda, with its olives; the island of Paquara, with meadows and all appurtenances.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your [Col. 1567D] successors, no one may be set over it by any cunning of deceit or by force, except the person whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall in the fear of God and according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict judge ought to be elected. Certainly, no one may presume to exact tithes from you on your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or upon the fodder of your animals. We therefore decree, etc., without prejudice, etc. But to all, etc. Amen.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubaldus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedis. I, Julius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, Octavianus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. [Col. 1568A] I, Astaldus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Prisca. I, Girardus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen. I, Hildebrandus, cardinal priest of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Guido, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus. I, Gulielmus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains. I, Oddo, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Rodulphus, cardinal deacon of Saint Lucy. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustachius beside the temple of Agrippa. I, Raymond, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Roland, [Col. 1568B] cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1158 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian IV.

### CLXXXVIII. He confirms the goods, possessions, and privileges of the church of St. John at Selbold. (Sutri, June 12.)

[WENCK, *History of the Land of Hesse*, III, p. 105.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son GERBODO, provost of the church of Saint John the Baptist at Selbold, and to his successors canonically appointed: in perpetuity.

The authority of our office urges us to cherish religious [Col. 1568C] places and to foster them under the protection of the Apostolic See. For this reason, beloved son Gerbodo in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests; and, following the example of our predecessors of good memory, Paschal and Innocent, Roman pontiffs, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the church of Saint John the Baptist, over which, by God’s appointment, you preside, and which belongs in a special manner to the right of the most holy Roman Church; and we fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. That church Ditmar, of good memory, formerly count of Gelnhausen, through the ministry of Rabenuld, a religious priest, devoutly and faithfully offered to blessed Peter and the holy Roman Church, and he arranged for regular canons to be gathered there.

First, indeed, [Col. 1568D] we decree that the canonical order known to have been established in that church according to the fear of God, the Rule of Blessed Augustine, and the order of the Premonstratensian brethren, shall be preserved there inviolate for all time. Furthermore, whatever goods or possessions that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, by grant of popes, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other just means, God being favourable, shall remain firm and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names: the parish church at Selbold, with its appurtenances, fields, and tithes on both sides of the flowing Kinzig, [Col. 1569A] provided that for it you shall answer to no person except the bishop; the church of St. Mary in the Valley, with the possessions of fields and vineyards on both sides of the stream, both in Hetenesheim and in Alta Villa, excepting the right due from ancient times to the episcopal table.

Certainly, no one may presume to exact from you tithes of your newly cleared lands, which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or of the fodder of your animals. We likewise forbid your brethren or converts, after making profession, to leave the cloister or move to another place without permission of their superior or brethren; and no bishop, abbot, ecclesiastical person, or secular person may dare receive or retain those who depart. [Col. 1569B] If, after a second or third warning, one of them scorns to return, you shall have leave to excommunicate him. You shall receive ordinations of clerics, consecrations of churches, and other ecclesiastical sacraments from the archbishop of Mainz, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favour of the Apostolic See, and is willing to administer them freely and without improper demand. Otherwise, you may approach whichever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested.

Furthermore, when there is a general interdict in the land, you may celebrate divine offices behind closed doors, excluding excommunicated or interdicted persons, without ringing bells and in a subdued voice. As a token of this liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay one Byzantine coin each year to us and our [Col. 1569C] successors. We further decree that no count, prince, advocate, or any ecclesiastical or secular person may exact undue or unjust exactions from you, or improperly impose burdens on priests residing in the aforesaid church or in its dependent churches.

We therefore decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church or its goods, remove its possessions, retain those removed, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but let all things be preserved entire for the use, in every way advantageous, of those for whose governance and support they were granted, without prejudice in all things to [Col. 1569D] the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If anyone therefore, etc.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubaldus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedis. I, Julius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, Bernardus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Clement. I, Gerardus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Ildebrandus, cardinal priest of the title of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Guido, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Callixtus. I, Guillelmus, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter in Chains. [Col. 1570A] I, Rudolfus, cardinal deacon of Saint Lucy in the Septa Solis. I, Boso, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Raymond, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata.

Given at Sutri, through the hand of Roland, cardinal priest and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the second Ides of June, in the seventh indiction, in the year 1158 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian IV.

### CLXXXIX. To the Archbishops of Tarragona and Narbonne.—He receives Raymond, Count of Barcelona, and his dominions under the protection of the Apostolic See. (Sutri, June 23.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXII, 828.]

[Col. 1570B]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers the Archbishop of Tarragona and [BERENGAR], Archbishop of Narbonne, legate of the Apostolic See, and to their suffragans: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We ourselves have learned through many proofs of events that our beloved son Raymond, the illustrious Count of Barcelona, has for a long time been exceedingly devoted and faithful to the most holy Roman Church, and has always shown himself solicitous and ready for its service; and we believe that this has without doubt come to the knowledge of your discretion. Therefore, in purpose and will [Col. 1570C] we intend to love him with sincere charity as our most devoted and special son; and, defending him more zealously against the attacks of wicked men, we are carefully intent upon supporting him in all his rights.

Moreover, our venerable brothers the bishops of Pamplona and Saragossa have taken care to represent to us on his behalf that the truce and peace between him and Lupus, king of Valencia, have been broken and entirely violated. Now the count himself, as he insistently declares, intends, with God's help, by every means to restrain and manfully attack the savage peoples and barbarous nations—that is, the fury of the Saracens, whose plague is most destructive to Christians. Yet certain persons professing Christianity [Col. 1570D] who oppose that count, led astray both by hostility and by greed for money, as we have learned, intend together with the Saracens to attack him and to divert his noble spirit from so praiseworthy a purpose. This is assuredly all the more grievous and distressing to us because we love his person with a more sincere affection, and recognize that those carrying out a deed so impious and foreign to the religion of the Christian faith are setting a pernicious example for posterity.

Therefore, so that whoever has presumed to attempt this may regret having undertaken a sacrilegious and profane act, we command your brotherhood by these apostolic letters that you do not delay, by our authority, to restrain with ecclesiastical censure all Christians who presume to hinder the aforesaid count—whose person and entire land we have received under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, so that we may defend him against [Col. 1571A] the incursions of wicked men, as the duty of our office requires—in his purpose; and all who, whether with the Saracens or without them, attempt to trouble him or his land while he remains in this purpose. Subject all their lands to sentence of interdict until fitting satisfaction has been made.

Given at Sutri, 23 June.

### CXC. He receives the Church of Saint Marcellus at Paris under protection and confirms its goods and rights. (Sutri, June 26.)

[FÉLIBIEN, *History of Paris*, III, 13.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1571B] sons NIVELON, dean of the Church of Saint Marcellus at Paris, and his brethren, present and future, canonically appointed: in perpetuity.

Both the force of equity and the order of reason require that just requests be granted effect; especially when piety supports the petitioners’ wish and truth does not abandon it. Therefore, beloved sons, moved by the prayers of Thomas, your fellow canon, we graciously assent to your just petitions. We receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify by the privilege of this present writing, the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service. We decree that whatever possessions and goods, whether vineyards, cultivated or uncultivated lands, pastures, meadows, and waters, that church now [Col. 1571C] justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, God being gracious, acquire by the grant of pontiffs, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other just means, shall remain secure and unimpaired for you and your successors.

Among these, we have thought proper to specify the following by their own names: namely, the borough in which the church itself is situated, with all its appurtenances; whatever you hold in the territory of the village of Judea; the land which you hold in the territory of Bertoldicourt; the land which you hold in the territory of Castrey; and the land which you hold in the territory of Chesi; the Church of Saint Peter of Ivry, with its cemetery; the Church of Saints Gervasius and Protasius of Vitry, with its cemetery and the tithes belonging to it; [Col. 1571D] the Church of Piro, with its cemetery and tithes belonging to it, and the chapel of Santrio; the Church of Asnières, with its cemetery and tithes belonging to it; and the Church of Charenton, with its cemetery, its tithes, and the lands which you hold there.

We further decree that, according to the ancient and reasonable custom of your church, you may freely elect a dean, who must continually serve the church. The clerics of that church who are to be promoted to orders shall be presented to the bishop by the dean of the same church. Furthermore, by apostolic authority we confirm to you all those liberties and ancient and reasonable customs which you have hitherto possessed within the precinct of the cloister, in the borough in which the church itself stands, in your villages and possessions, [Col. 1572A] and in the chapels of that borough—namely, Saint Martin and Saint Hippolytus—and in the chapel of Saint Hilary of the Mount.

Nor may anyone build a church in the parishes of the aforesaid church except with your consent and that of your bishop. Nor may anyone, against your will, withdraw or take away the serfs of the same church from your benefit and service. In the parish churches which you hold, you may freely, according to the ancient institution of your church and as you have done hitherto, elect priests and present them to the bishop. If found suitable, the bishop shall commit the care of souls to them; and those priests shall answer to you in temporal matters and to the bishop in spiritual matters. [Col. 1572B]

Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all things granted for the governance and support of those for whose use they were granted shall be preserved whole and shall benefit them in every way, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the Bishop of Paris.

If anyone therefore, etc. But to all, etc.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, cardinal priest of Saint Praxedes. I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of the Holy Cross. [Col. 1572C] I, Bernard, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Clement. I, Octavian, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Cecilia. I, Gerard, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, Hildebrand, cardinal priest of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Guido, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Calixtus. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Albert, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina. I, William, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Peter in [Col. 1572D] Chains. I, Odo, cardinal deacon of the title of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Bozo, cardinal deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Cinthius, cardinal deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Peter, cardinal deacon of Saint Eustace beside the temple of Agrippa. I, Raymond, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata.

Given at Sutri through the hand of Roland, cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, on 26 June, in the sixth indiction, in the year 1158 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Pope Adrian IV.

### CXCI. Having settled the dispute between the canons and the Bishop of Sutri concerning the Church of Saint Sylvester, he establishes perpetual concord by issuing a charter. (Vetralla, July 12.)

[Bullar. Vatic., I, p. 60.]

[Col. 1573A]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of the Church of Saint Peter: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Those matters which our brother cardinals, by command of the Apostolic See, establish reasonably or agreeably ought to stand in firm stability; and what has been determined must be strengthened by the safeguard of our authority, lest it be altered in the future by any rash action. But since formerly a controversy concerning the Church of Saint Sylvester was pending between [Col. 1573B] you and our venerable brother G., Bishop of Sutri—

> [Note: [Col. 1573D] G., Bishop of Sutri, etc. There is profound silence concerning this Bishop of Sutri both in Ughelli’s *Italia sacra* and in Labbe’s index of bishops subscribing to synods.]

—and since a complaint concerning it had been laid before us in our presence, we, wishing with the agreement of the parties concordantly to remove every ground of litigation, entrusted its amicable settlement to our beloved sons Roland, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Mark and our chancellor; Albert, of the title of Saint Lawrence in Lucina; William, of the title of Saint Peter in Chains, priests; and Raymond, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata. By the common will and consent of the parties, they terminated the controversy in the following manner, as is known to be contained in their written instrument: namely, that the payments or customary gifts [Col. 1573C] of meat which the Bishop of Sutri had been accustomed to receive from that church on certain feast days should henceforth be received at the same times in the same manner as he receives them from the churches of Saint Christina, Saint Paul, Saint John, or Saint Julian; and that he should show them the customary honour.

> [Note: [Col. 1573D] Understand gifts or offerings.]

Moreover, whenever a collection is to be made among the churches by the bishop for our reception and maintenance, that church shall furnish assistance to the bishop as one of the aforesaid churches. The clerics of that church shall attend the bishop’s synod and chapter, and shall come to the Church of Sutri for chrism and baptism, according to the custom of those churches, without objection. They shall firmly keep and observe the bishop’s general interdict and any sentence which the bishop has imposed upon one of his parishioners [Col. 1573D] for his offence, until fitting satisfaction has been made. If any cleric of that church falls into an offence so evident and manifest that he deserves suspension under the established canons, the bishop, without your knowledge, shall suspend him from office until fitting satisfaction has been made; but he shall not deprive him of ecclesiastical benefice. [Col. 1574A] But if anyone is accused of some crime and appears to have fallen into such guilt as seems to require judicial procedure, the bishop must investigate and judge the matter with you at Sutri.

When an archpriest is to be appointed in the church, you shall elect a person and present him to the bishop. The bishop shall confirm that election, unless an evident and manifest reason that ought to prevent it appears, and shall commit the care of souls to him. The person confirmed shall promise by his own hand that he will discharge and observe what has been set forth above; he shall make fealty to you and promise obedience, and both he and the remaining clerics shall obey you and answer to you concerning the administration and ordering of the church.

Therefore, that these arrangements may obtain perpetual validity and that what has been concordantly established between you may never be disturbed by anyone’s opposition, we confirm this settlement by apostolic authority and strengthen it by the protection of this present writing. We decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation or in any way oppose it. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Vetralla, 12 July.

> [Note: [Col. 1574D] Vetralla, 12 July. In what year of his pontificate Adrian issued this bull is not sufficiently clear, since he did not record it in his writings. Yet it seems probable that the charter was issued in the first year of his pontificate, A.D. 1155. For in that year, as is read in Baronius, the supreme pontiff was residing at Viterbo; departing for some unknown reason from that city to nearby Vetralla, he drew up these letters.]

### CXCII. He receives the Church of Saint Mary of Aachen under protection and confirms its possessions. (At the castle of Vicus Varius, September 22.)

[QUIX, *Diplomatic Codex of Aachen*, I, 31.]

[Col. 1574C]

### CXCIII. He confirms to Master Adam the mastership of the schools of the Church of Meaux, granted by Bishop M[anasse] of blessed memory. (Lateran, October 30.)

[DUPLESSIS, *History of Meaux*, II, 47.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son ADAM, master of the schools of the Church of Meaux: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[lacuna] We confirm to you by apostolic authority the mastership of the schools of the Church of Meaux, reasonably granted to you by M[anasse], formerly Bishop of Meaux, [Col. 1574D] of blessed memory. [lacuna] We decree that, according to the custom hitherto maintained by that church, no one may conduct schools in the city of Meaux without your licence and permission, etc. [lacuna]

Given at the Lateran, 30 October.

### CXCIV. To Hugh, Chancellor of the King of France.—He congratulates him for having usefully laboured to establish peace between the kings of France and England. (Lateran, November 4.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXII, 808.]

[Col. 1575A]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HUGH, chancellor of the illustrious King of France: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because, to the extent of your power, as we are told, you have been solicitous for peace and concord between our dearest sons Louis, the illustrious King of France, and Henry, the illustrious King of England, [Col. 1575B] and have devoted watchful labour and zeal to bringing this about, we hold it all the more pleasing and acceptable, and commend the prudence of your mind in this matter all the more earnestly, because this peace and concord are more pleasing to God and humankind and more beneficial both to those now living and to posterity.

For we have learned, both from the report of our beloved son Henry, messenger of the aforesaid our son, the King of France, and from the tenor of his letters, that through your zeal and diligence there is, by the grace of God, such unity and bond of charity between them, and such peace and concord have intervened, that nothing can break the covenant of their mutual friendship or in any way disturb the firmness of their love. Therefore we conceive all the greater joy, [Col. 1575C] and rejoice all the more with God and his angels, because we recognize that this friendship is necessary to both parties and see much advantage and abundant fruit proceeding from it.

Accordingly, we render immense thanks to almighty God, from whom all good things proceed and in whose hand the hearts of kings lie: through his mercy he has willed formerly discordant purposes and divergent wills to be so joined that nothing different can now be found in them, but they seem to will the same things and to think alike. We, indeed, who ought above all to desire the good of peace and concord among all people, beseech the divine clemency by continual [Col. 1575D] prayers that it may deign to preserve firm peace and perpetual unity between them.

Furthermore, we earnestly commend to your affection our aforesaid son Henry, a learned and honourable cleric, whom we know to be sufficiently faithful and devoted in your affairs. We ask you most earnestly, for the reverence of blessed Peter and ourselves, to hold him dearer than dear, and, in his needs, to provide for him with kindness and at our intercession in such a way that he may find our prayers effective on his behalf with you, and that we may consequently owe thanks to your devotion.

Given at the Lateran, 4 November.

### CXCV. He exhorts G[regory], prior, and the whole Camaldolese chapter to virtue and peace. (Lateran, November 24.)

[MITARELLI, *Camaldolese Annals*, III, 350.]

[Col. 1576A]
