ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons G[REGORY], prior, and the whole Camaldolese chapter: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We ourselves fully know, and the matter is everywhere proclaimed by widespread report, how greatly your monastery, in which you are gathered for the service of God, that you may confess his holy name and glory in his praise, has increased in both spiritual and temporal things through the past life, integrity, and religious observance of its priors. [Col. 1576B] For so long as the brothers of that monastery persevered in quiet, unanimity, and concord, seeking not their own interests but rather those of Christ; so long as they kept the monastic rule in habit, life, and conduct, they gave forth the grace and delight of spiritual blessings and abounded in temporal resources. So great was the fragrance of good repute issuing from that community that inferiors were drawn by such an example to more perfect things, so that they said: “Draw us after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song of Songs 1). Such rest, peace, and unity also prevailed in that place that men might deservedly say of it what is written: “Truly this is none other than the house of God and the gate of heaven” (Gen. 28).

Therefore, lest the monastery of Camaldoli, formerly distinguished by such religion and integrity and pre-eminent in such excellence of virtues, should in your time—God forbid!—seem in any way diminished from its former state, we exhort, entreat, and beseech you in the Lord wholly to abandon fleshly desires that wage war against the soul, trample underfoot worldly [Col. 1576C] lusts, aspire by good works to things eternal and enduring without end, strive by the zeal of a devout life toward the highest good and the rewards of eternal blessedness, and take care to remain so steadfast in the service of your Creator and so fervent in devotion to him that nothing may henceforth in any way separate you from the charity of Christ. Thus, because of the praiseworthy conduct of your life, that testimony of Holy Scripture may deservedly be applied to you which says: “A praiseworthy people, whom the Lord of hosts has blessed, saying: You are the work of my hands, my inheritance, Jerusalem” (Isa. 19).

For you must most diligently consider and ponder carefully lest your adversary the devil, who “goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5), draw you—God forbid!—by the poison of his cunning and the snares of his habitual and ancient deceit away from the embraces of the Bridegroom and from the service of your Creator. The more the enemy of the human race sees Christ’s faithful adhere to the law of God’s commandments and obey his saving counsels more diligently, the more he turns to crafty devices and labours anxiously to make them fall from the height of virtue [Col. 1577A] and abandon their holy purpose.

Yet we trust in you in the Lord, if we rightly know the charity of your inward person: as you imitate the footsteps of your predecessors and “do not seek what is your own, but what belongs to Jesus Christ,” who called you “out of darkness and the shadow of death into his marvellous light” (1 Pet. 2), the enemy’s cunning will by no means prevail against you, nor will his wicked persuasion be able to turn you away from the service of him to whom you are bound by indissoluble charity. Be strengthened, therefore, in the Lord and in the power of his might; stand firm in faith (Eph. 6); cast off the works of darkness and put on the armour of light (Rom. 13); overcome all the snares of the ancient enemy, divine aid accompanying you; and have mutual charity among yourselves.

Let it be so, indeed, that in nothing do you presume upon yourselves, according to the Apostle, but glory only in the Lord and in the Lord’s work, as it is written: “Let him who glories, glory in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1); for “it is not he who commends himself who is approved, but he whom God commends” (2 Cor. 10). [Col. 1577B] Yet it is reported—whereat we greatly inquire and grieve—that murmuring, a detestable vice, exists among you, and that you murmur against one another beyond what you ought. This vice has now so become associated with you that, as many have reported, it has reached the hearing of the Apostolic See.

Therefore we warn and earnestly exhort you to cease from this most deadly plague [lacuna] from murmuring, henceforth keeping a peaceful and tranquil mind, lest you incur displeasure in the sight of the eternal Creator and before the eyes of the divine majesty because of so great a crime. For you know, we believe, and certainly recognize how Mary, Aaron’s sister, was made contemptible before the Lord because she murmured against Moses, and how she was struck with the stain and foulness of grievous leprosy because she did not restrain herself from murmuring. Therefore she remained outside the camp until her flesh was restored to its former health. [Col. 1577C] Therefore, lest, as this same vice gains strength, you appear contemptible in the sight of the Most High and abominable in human eyes, guard your hearts with the vigilance that is fitting, lest they be further defiled by this foulness.

But that you may more easily fulfil, with God’s help, all that has been said above, you, beloved son prior, should show yourself to your brethren a gentle and approachable father; set before them saving counsels; always seek rather to be loved than feared; and endeavour to arrange and administer the affairs of the monastery entrusted to your governance according to the counsel of religious brethren who fear God, as is contained in the Rule of Blessed Benedict. You, beloved sons, monks, should render in all things due submission and obedience to your prior as to your proper shepherd and ruler of your souls. Neither in the reform of the order according to the ancient and reasonable custom of the Camaldolese, nor in any other matter concerning the welfare of that monastery and yourselves, should you presume to be rebellious [Col. 1578A] or contumacious toward him.

And we, who by the office of the apostolate laid upon us are debtors to all Christ’s faithful, if, through cooperating divine grace, you are steadfast in faith and effective in deed, shall provide for you with paternal affection and, to the extent that God grants us power, shall take care without interruption to assist you and your monastery in your needs.

Given at the Lateran, 24 November.

### CXCVI. Privilege granted to Hugh, Bishop of Piacenza.

[CAMPI, *History of Piacenza*, II, 357.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HUGH, Bishop of Piacenza, and his [Col. 1578B] successors canonically appointed: in perpetuity.

Seated by the disposition of divine clemency upon the summit of the Apostolic See, it is fitting for us to preserve unimpaired the rights of our brother bishops, and especially of those known to adhere more particularly to the most holy Roman Church, and to establish them by the protection of the Apostolic See in such a manner that they may not be rashly removed from their reasonable state. And since, venerable brother Hugh, Bishop in Christ, we love you with special preference because of your integrity, agreeing with willing assent to your reasonable petitions and following the example of our predecessors of blessed memory, the Roman pontiffs Paschal and Innocent, [Col. 1578C] we decree and enact by the present ordinance that clerics within the city or diocese of Piacenza belonging to the monastery of Blessed Sixtus shall be subject to you and your successors under episcopal jurisdiction: that is, they shall receive ordination from you; when called, they shall come to your council; they shall observe your directions concerning the government of the people; and, at an appropriate time, they shall receive from you or your Catholic successors chrism, holy oil, and the consecration of altars or churches within the diocese of Piacenza, provided that you enjoy the grace and communion of the Apostolic See and are willing to confer these freely and without corruption.

Likewise, following in the footsteps of our predecessor Pope Paschal of blessed memory, we enact that the monastery of Blessed Paul of Mezzano, with the cells or churches which it possesses [Col. 1578D] in the diocese of Piacenza, shall remain perpetually subject to you and your successors by episcopal right. Whatever abbot succeeds in that monastery shall in future receive the blessing of ordination through you; and neither he nor the clerics subject to him shall refuse to attend your synod. Moreover, any clerics or monks of that place shall be promoted to sacred orders through your ministry and shall receive from you chrism, holy oil, and the consecration of altars or churches, whether in the monastery itself, in its cells, or in churches situated in your diocese, provided that you enjoy the grace and communion of the Apostolic See and are willing to confer these freely and without corruption.

[Col. 1579A] Therefore we decree that no person whatsoever may infringe this page of our confirmation, etc.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hymar, Bishop of Tusculum. I, Gregory, Bishop of Sabina. I, Hubald, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Praxedes. I, Julius, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Marcellus. I, Gerald, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill. I, John, cardinal priest of the title of Saints John and Paul, of the title of Pammachius. I, Guido, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Portico. [Col. 1579B] I, Hyacinth, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, John, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. I, Bonadies, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo.

### CXCVII. He does not comply with Emperor Frederick’s request that Guido, subdeacon of the Roman Church, be placed over the Church of Ravenna, which desires him.

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 795.]

ADRIAN, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, FREDERICK, illustrious Emperor of the Romans: greeting and apostolic blessing.

How, out of regard for the heavenly Creator, and through the intervention both of your excellency and of our beloved son Guido, Count of Blanderade [reading uncertain], we formerly received our beloved son Guido, our subdeacon and son of that count, into our household and fellowship; how also, in consideration of his uprightness and for the honour and benefit of the most holy Roman Church, we assigned a church to him specially as though he had already been ordained deacon—we ourselves certainly remember these matters, and do not believe that they have escaped the memory of your serenity.

But now, considering his integrity and his advancement in learning, should life accompany him, and understanding how great advantages may yet accrue to the most holy Roman Church through him and through his noble and powerful relatives, [Col. 1579D] and to what height of dignity he may ascend in that same Roman Church if life accords with birth, we have been unable, after consultation with our brethren, to remove so precious a pledge from our side at the request of your excellency. For he has been promoted by the Apostolic See to the office of subdeacon, and a church has been specially assigned to him by us as if he were already a deacon, as stated above. Instead, when opportunity is given, with God’s help, we intend to ordain him in the Roman Church for the honour of that Church and of the empire, so that there he may someday, as divine grace shall provide, ascend to higher things, or from there, with the Lord’s assistance, attain the summit of another ecclesiastical dignity.

[Col. 1580A] For it is more fitting that one who is son and cleric of the Roman Church should not depart from her bosom; rather, while she confers upon him a place of dignity near herself, she should provide higher advancement for him from there. For she gladly summons to herself men adorned with character and learning, endowed with integrity and distinguished by nobility of blood; she is accustomed to receive them from elsewhere, and does not easily deprive herself of such men when she has them in her own bosom. Since, therefore, we see this to be more fitting and judge it more honourable, and since we trust also that this should be more pleasing, grateful, and acceptable to the imperial majesty, we have not thought your request admissible in this matter. We believe and hope that, when you have learned our will on this point, you yourself [Col. 1580B] will commend our intention and purpose.

## A.D. 1154–1159

### CXCVIII. He writes to the Archbishop of Thessalonica concerning the reconciliation of the Greek Church with the Roman Church. He commends to him Baldwin and Balditzion, messengers sent to Emperor Manuel.

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 796.]

ADRIAN . . . to his venerable brother, the Archbishop of Thessalonica: greeting, etc.

Since, through the envy of the ancient enemy, the See of Constantinople separated itself from the most holy Roman and Apostolic Church—something which we can scarcely utter without a flood of tears—[Col. 1580C] and the enemy of humankind poured out the peculiar poison of his malice, and the children withdrew from obedience to their mother, and duality took the place of unity, the successors of blessed Peter who preceded us employed much labour and effort that the schism might be removed and those who separated themselves from the Church might be restored to its unity.

For this reason, we also, who in this time have received, as God wills, the care of the Apostolic See for all the churches established throughout the world, though we possess nothing equal to the powers of blessed Peter, are nevertheless compelled to exercise this ministry. We have judged that we must take care lest we be numbered—God forbid!—among those whom the Lord rebukes through the prophet, saying: “You did not bring back what was driven away, you did not heal what was weak, you did not seek what was lost, and you did not bind up what was broken.” [Col. 1580D]

Therefore, let us hasten to bring the children into the place of the Church and unity, and to find the lost drachma. Prompted by the apostolic commandment, let us seek, through persuasion, to correct those who reject words of teaching, and let admonition be given to the faithful in season and out of season. Let us be instructed by the example of him who was the Lord of glory and had all things in his power, yet “bowed the heavens and came down” and, taking the form of a servant, emptied himself, so that the lost sheep might be restored to its flock.

Therefore, brother in Christ, by these letters we admonish your charity to take diligent care of this matter. For there is but one Church and one ark of sanctification, into which every one of the faithful must enter in order to be saved from the flood. Labour by every means for its union, and let your prudence reflect that the Church of God cannot stand divided; every living soul must be gathered out of the storms of the present flood into the one ark of the Church, to blessed Peter, governor of all the faithful. [Col. 1581A]

It has been handed down that the holy Fathers, illumined by the divine Spirit, decreed that the most holy Roman Church should absolutely hold the primacy over all churches, and prescribed that the judgment of all should be referred to its decision. To remove division, to bring about the Church’s unity, and to join the divided wall, give vigilant attention, for the love of God, for the salvation of the soul, and for the enjoyment of unfading glory. [Col. 1581B] First in yourself and then in others, so far as divine grace grants, labour that the flock may be united with the Church and that those who confess themselves the Lord’s sheep may return to the flock of blessed Peter, who received their care at the Lord’s command.

We, indeed, do not seek in this a temporal praise or passing glory, we who have undertaken the office of feeding. We confess ourselves servants of all the servants of God. But since we read that our Lord and Master went forth to raise one dead person in the body, wept at the tomb, and said, “Lazarus, come forth” (John 10), we judge it unworthy if we keep back the Lord’s talent [Col. 1581C] and neglect to raise in soul those whom we can. Finally, we earnestly commend to your charity our beloved sons Baldwin and Balditzion, the present messengers sent by a religious community to our most beloved son Manuel, Emperor of Constantinople. We ask that, through love of God, of blessed Peter, and of the Apostolic See, and through the practice of compassion, you give them consolation in their needs with a gracious countenance. We desire to be informed by letter concerning your health.

### CXCIX. He exhorts the consuls and the whole people of the castle of Grasse to defend the monks of Lérins against the Saracens and other enemies.

(*History of the Monuments of the Fathers*, Writers, II, 413.)

[Col. 1581D]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the consuls and the whole people dwelling in the castle of Grasse—“Grasse had not yet been honoured with episcopal dignity; for this reason he calls it a castle and not a city”—greeting and apostolic blessing.

When, by the office of apostleship laid upon us, we are bound to attend to the welfare of all Christ’s faithful, we ought nevertheless to love with a certain special prerogative, and to consider more earnestly the tranquillity and peace of, those who are distinguished both by religious life and integrity and are known to belong especially to the jurisdiction of the holy Roman Church. Moved therefore by this consideration, we commend with particular earnestness to your devotion our beloved sons, the religious brethren of the monastery of Lérins, [Col. 1582A] together with their possessions and goods; earnestly requesting, and enjoining this upon you for the remission of your sins, that, out of regard for piety and reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, you love and support them and strive by every means to preserve their rights for them. But if Saracens, enemies of the Christian name, or faithless Christians should perhaps presume to attack their monastery or any of their castles, stand by them manfully and furnish them, by every means within your power, both counsel and aid.

Given, etc.

CC. To Louis, king of the Franks.—He commends the king’s especially earnest affection toward religious men, and asks that the Premonstratensian brethren may experience it out of reverence for blessed Peter and himself.

(D. Bouquet, *Recueil*, XV, 688.)

[Col. 1582B]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The affection of paternal charity with which we embrace your nobility, most Christian prince, brings great joy to our heart whenever such reports of your deeds reach us as are undoubtedly known to concern the salvation of your soul. For we have heard, and know from experience of the result, that you love and honour religious persons, and, as a devoted son of the Church, zealously provide them with assistance through your favour. Indeed, the disposition which your magnificence inwardly bears in loving religious persons is clearly shown [perhaps *quem*; Col. 1582C], since in all persons you are proved to love religious life and foster integrity more earnestly. Therefore we commend to your excellence, with so much the greater affection and confidence, our beloved sons the abbot (Hugh) and the religious Premonstratensian brethren, because we ourselves love them with a purer affection of charity on account of their integrity and religion, and because we have greater confidence in the kindness of your royal disposition.

We therefore earnestly request your diligence by apostolic letters, that, for the love of God and out of reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, you support, foster, and defend them; and that, by the power granted you by the Lord, you preserve for them whatever your father Louis of good memory, or any other person, reasonably bestowed upon them out of regard for piety [Col. 1582D], and earnestly defend them against those who may wish to harass them on this account.

CCI. To Berengar, archbishop of Narbonne; Artald, bishop of Elne; and the barons established throughout the diocese of Elne.—Against Count Geoffrey of Roussillon.

(Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 829.)

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren BERENGAR, archbishop of Narbonne and legate of the Apostolic See, and ARTALD, bishop of Elne, and to all barons established throughout the diocese of Elne: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1583A] We do not wish what has been reasonably established by our predecessors to be disturbed by anyone’s rashness; rather, we command that it be observed by all unimpaired and inviolate. Our predecessor Pope Eugenius of happy memory bound Count Geoffrey and the adulteress whom he keeps in the bond of excommunication, namely because, having dismissed his lawful wife, he did not fear to unite the adulteress to himself in marriage. And since, as we are told, he still persists obstinately in his wickedness, confirming that same sentence as valid, we command it to be inviolably observed by all. We decree that it shall never be lawful for that count, even if his lawful wife should die, to unite in marriage to himself the woman whom he undoubtedly has defiled by manifest adultery.

Moreover, we decree that the sons [Col. 1583B] whom he has begotten of the adulteress in adultery, and who are judged illegitimate by law, shall for ever lack their father’s inheritance; nor may they at any time claim or possess any part of the said count’s inheritance by right of succession. If they should ever attempt this, let them know that they are to be bound by the bond of excommunication.

CCII. To Walter, bishop of Laon.—That he preserve the benefices bestowed upon the church of Prémontré by his predecessors, and neither inflict nor permit any trouble concerning those benefices.

(D. Bouquet, *Recueil*, XV, 687.)

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother GUALTER [Col. 1584A], bishop of Laon: greeting and apostolic blessing.

He who strives to imitate his predecessors in good works and to follow in their footsteps is accounted worthy of reward before the Lord and is, not without reason, commended by men. Your prudent discernment, as we believe, is not unaware how your predecessors Bartholomew and Walter, of good memory, supported and endeavoured by every means to preserve the benefices which are known to have been bestowed upon the Church of Prémontré, both by them and by others, out of regard for piety, and confirmed by apostolic authority. Therefore, by apostolic writing we command your fraternity that you yourself support and preserve those benefices granted to the aforesaid Church of Prémontré [Col. 1584B] through devotion of faith and love of charity, as your said predecessors are reported to have done; and that you inflict no molestation upon that Church concerning those benefices—

[Note: [Col. 1583C]

Bartholomew and Walter, bishops of Laon, had given several estates of their church to the Premonstratensians. Walter’s successor, Walter II, pressed for their restoration. The matter was brought before the Roman pontiff, as we learn from one letter of Bartholomew, who, having resigned the bishopric of Laon, was living as a private person at Foigny among the Cistercians. When he heard that he was being accused of having dissipated the Church’s patrimony, he cleared himself by the following letter at an assembly held at Laon before King Louis—not at Rheims, as is stated in collections of councils. The letter is as follows:

“To the VENERABLE and ever-beloved lord SAMSON, archbishop of Rheims, and to the holy assembly gathered in his presence, brother BARTHOLOMEW, a poor monk at Foigny: to love mercy and truth.

“The solemnity of this holy assembly commands my modesty to be silent; but the imminent danger to my reputation opens my mouth and urges me to speak openly [Col. 1583D]. For I cannot conceal what common report has spread among many and what has even flown to the ears of the lord Pope. There is a rumour that I have diminished episcopal revenues; and the bishop of Laon gives more credit than is right to this rumour. It is therefore mine, concerning these matters, to confess what is true; but it will be yours to discern what is just and to defend it.

“The see of Laon was sad and mourning when I first entered it, worn down by factions and burned by fires; the resources of the greater church likewise were distressed, and its revenues slight. If I stretched out my hand to it that it might rise again, God knows it, and the Church’s children know it. Yet I bestowed upon them nothing belonging to the bishop’s revenues, except pigs—commonly called breeding boars—which the churches paid to the episcopal household. These, I say, I granted for the prebend of the canons, because I could neither demand them without shame nor possess them without inconvenience.

“[Col. 1584C] Moreover, I found only five abbeys in our diocese, fallen away alike in resources and religious observance. In these, as God multiplied his mercy, the number of holy persons increased both in number and merit, and their property especially was enlarged. In addition, nine monasteries of the new religious life were founded here and there in the same diocese. Their number of persons almost surpasses number itself; their religious observance is a mirror of religious life; their property is so abundant that it fully suffices for so many. If I deny that I extended the hand of benefaction to old churches that they might rise again, and to new ones that they might stand up, I shall be lying. Certainly I benefited almost all the churches, though neither as much as I wished nor as much as I ought.

“Pope Calixtus entrusted to our faith lord Norbert, whose memory is blessed, that I might give him a place and assist his wishes. I therefore gave him land belonging to the bishop, though it would scarcely suffice for two ploughs. One part of it lies at Verciniac, another [Col. 1584D] near Anisy; yet it had lain barren and uncultivated for many years. Of what belonged to episcopal revenues, I remember having alienated nothing further. Yet, with our favour and consent, certain persons bestowed upon churches lands which they held from us in benefice; but I remitted to no one whatever the rents of those lands or the wine-dues.

“For the rest: if any advantage or honour accrued to that see through us, I do not wish it brought before human judgment; but if, as a man, I committed any fault, I do not refuse to be put to shame before men. I therefore wished to plead our cause before you as judges and to set it forth to you as witnesses; among you I do not fear an accuser while speaking the truth. Yet let it be permitted me also to venture something before you; let me speak something humanly. Did no titles and glory accrue to our see when it gave birth to so many and such great churches, when it multiplied for itself so many synodal persons? Since, then, as I hear, the lord bishop of Laon prepares war against his own vitals [Col. 1585D], why does he attempt what perhaps he may not be permitted to carry through? If I gathered together the children of God, if I received a righteous man in the name of a righteous man, let no one be angry with me; let another take care lest he scatter what has been gathered. May the Almighty preserve you all [Col. 1586D] for the honour of his name, and through you strengthen the religious observance and holiness of his Church.” (*From the Premonstratensian Library*, p. 430)]

—or permit it in any way to be inflicted by others, insofar as lies within your power.

CCIII. To the same.—On the same subject.

(Ibid., p. 689.)

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother GUALTER, bishop of Laon: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The more the brethren of the Church of Prémontré are known continually to adhere to the law of God’s commands and not to withdraw themselves from the service of their Creator, [Col. 1585A] the more sincerely we love them in charity and effectively commend them to those in whose devotion we have confidence. Therefore, by the authority of the Apostolic See, we earnestly request, admonish, and exhort your charity in the Lord on behalf of those brethren: for reverence toward blessed Peter and ourselves, love, support, and defend both them and the Church of Prémontré, in which they are devoted to divine service, with brotherly charity. Leave that Church, with all that belongs to it, in peace and tranquillity; do not permit it to be harassed in any way by any of your parishioners. But against those who presume in any way to trouble or disturb that Church, oppose yourself as a pious and watchful defender, and do not delay to restrain them from their wickedness by the spiritual sword [Col. 1585B].

CCIV. He confirms the goods and privileges of the Church of St John in the Vines.

(Louen, *History of the Abbey of Saint-Jean des Vignes*, p. 292.)

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ, GUIDO, abbot and canon of Saint John, called “of the Vines,” near Soissons, and to his brethren there established and to be established under the Rule of blessed Augustine: in perpetuity.

It is fitting that we grant assent to just wishes and lend our ears to just petitions, since, although unworthy, by divine dispensation we have been appointed heralds and guardians of justice in the lofty watchtower of the apostles Peter and Paul. Since, therefore, under the Lord’s inspiration, you have chosen the said community of canons according to the Rule of blessed Augustine, we rejoice with due devotion at your good and praiseworthy vow; and, so that more praiseworthy growth may follow your praiseworthy undertaking, with paternal affection we receive you, as most dear sons, with all your dependencies, under the protection of the Apostolic See and fortify you by the privilege of this writing. First, we decree that the canonical order established in that place according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine shall be inviolably observed there for all time [Col. 1585D].

Moreover, whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, God favouring, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Further, we forbid you to receive, without the consent of yourselves and your bishop, any tithes of parishes from lay hands; but the following proviso is corrupt in the printed text: *vos autem recuperandi … construere*, followed by “with the consent of [Col. 1586A] your bishop.” Nor may any of your brethren, after making profession in your church, leave your cloister without the permission of the abbot and brethren; and no one may dare retain a departing brother without a letter of common assurance. If he departs and, after being warned a second or third time, scorns to return, the abbot then in office shall have the power to excommunicate him. Upon the death of you, beloved son Guido, now abbot of this place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any deceitful contrivance or force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of their counsel, shall provide to be elected from the same order according to God and the Rule of blessed Augustine.

CCV. To the monks of Pontigny.—That they pay the tithes of a certain place.

(Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 830.)

[Col. 1586B]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son A., prior, and to all the monks of Pontigny: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since, by the Lord’s ordering, we have been placed upon an exalted watchtower, if the rights of all churches were not to be preserved whole and unimpaired, we should seem to hold the place of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, to no purpose and to act negligently in the duty of the dispensation committed to us. For the Church of God, under the governance which divine providence in grace has entrusted to us, is rightly directed on her course when we diligently correct every error [Col. 1586C] and endeavour to preserve for each its own right.

But our beloved son, a canon of the Church of Pont-Audemer, having laid before us a complaint against you [read perhaps: “having lodged complaints against you,” *vos conquaestiones*], showed us by his report that you violently take away certain tithes belonging to their right and harass them concerning those tithes with rash audacity. If you considered with attentive care the Rule of blessed Benedict, by which you say you are governed, and the monastic habit which you wear, you would not presume to stretch out your hands to plunder the goods of your neighbours or thus unlawfully to usurp for yourselves what belongs to another’s right.

Therefore, lest henceforth either the evil of avarice or, God forbid, the vice of rapacity accuse you, by apostolic writing we command and order you not further to presume to take away or disturb any ancient possession or tithe belonging to them, especially that which exists in the place called Ardennes [Col. 1586D]. And if this year you have withheld from them anything beyond the customary amount from those tithes, or if you hold any of their possessions by violence, do not delay in any way, all pretext being set aside, to restore them in full to those canons, according as the aforesaid Church is known anciently to have possessed them. For we have thought fit to allow religious men no tithes other than those known to arise from newly cleared land [Col. 1587A]. But if you dare to be despisers of this our command and a renewed complaint reaches the hearing of the Apostolic See, you must fear lest thereafter you feel the vengeance of ecclesiastical severity.

CCVI. He commands the bishops of Metz [Stephen] and Verdun to announce that Matthew, duke of Lorraine, is excommunicated.

(Baluze, *Capitularies*, II, 1559.)

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren the bishops of Metz and Verdun, and to his beloved sons G., provost, and R., dean, of the Church of Trier [Col. 1587B]: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We do not think your knowledge is unaware how the most holy Roman Church subjected Duke Matthew to excommunication and excluded him from the communion of the faithful because of the castle of Gondreville, which he built before the city of Toul. Yet although that son of iniquity ought at least to have amended when struck, he has added to the affliction of the same city by considering how to correct what he had done wrongly; and he has presumed to take from the Church of Toul Vischiriac and other villages, churches, possessions, and many other things, and does not cease to wear it down with many vexations and plunderings.

Therefore, by this present writing, we command and order you publicly to declare him excommunicated; and in his lands situated within your bishoprics to forbid the celebration of every divine office, except baptism for infants and penance for the dying, and to ensure that the same sentence is inviolably observed by all [Col. 1587C]. But if any person in clerical orders should presume to oppose that sentence, render him deprived both of his benefice and of his office until he comes to the Apostolic See with your letters to make satisfaction for so great an offence.

CCVII. He replies to Eberhard, archbishop of Salzburg, that marriages of serfs contracted without their lords’ consent are not to be dissolved.

(Augustine of Tarragona, *Works*, IV, 248.)

[Col. 1587D]

CCVIII. At the request of Bishop Henry, he receives the Church of Liège under protection and confirms its possessions.

(Chapeaville, *Deeds of the Bishops of Tongeren*, II, 105.)

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Henry, bishop of Liège, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

The office of apostleship imposed upon us by God, together with consideration for the Church’s welfare, exhorts and admonishes us to love with more ample charity, and continually to show greater honour and favour to, our brother bishops whom we know to excel in knowledge and integrity [Col. 1588A]. For then they can truly be concerned for the welfare of those subject to them; then they can apply themselves more effectively to the pursuit of their office, when they themselves perceive that we bestow more abundant honour upon them and love them with a more earnest affection of charity.

Therefore, venerable brother in Christ, Bishop Henry, granting willing assent to your just requests, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify by the privilege of this present writing, the Church of Liège over which, by God’s ordering, you are known to preside. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that Church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, the Lord providing, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful [Col. 1588B], or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The castle of Rode, its allod and household with all its entirety, in both spiritual and temporal matters; the castle of Belmont; the allod of Astenoit; the castle of Duras; the castle of Revonia; the castle of Esmerville; the castle of Burne; the castle of Fontaines, from the gift of the nobleman Cono; the three allods of Diepenbeche, Repe, and Scanz, which are known to belong to your table. Moreover, whatever the most Christian emperors Pippin, Charles, Louis, Lothair, Otto II and III, Henry, and the other kings bestowed upon that Church, we likewise confirm to you and your successors [Col. 1588C].

The abbeys of Lobbes with all their dependencies, Florennes, Brogne, St Hubert, Gembloux with its advocacy and all belonging to it, Fosses, Malonne, Namur, Dinant with its castle, Ceynac, Maffia, Tongeren, Huy, Amay, Maastricht, the monastery on the Sambre, Tournai, Aulne, Villers, Averbode, Hélecine, Castra, Thuin, Couvin, Bouillon, Givet, Hierges, Merlemont, Soture, the castle of Florennes, the castle of Fosses, Truinges, Evenes, Chaumont, Mirewart, Rochefort. Moreover, whatever right it has in castles, villages, boroughs, counties, and throughout the entire land of the count of Hainaut: Louvierval, Clermont [Col. 1588D], Franchiermont, Warsage, Argenteal, Casselin, Curtes, Berthehein, Coverne, Lentrechowe, Wentreluke, Semplovoir, Hoyn and Hoyz, Vervier, Nivelles, St Peter at Maastricht, Freres, Alleke, Hurle, Vileir, Seran, Ufey, Fronvile, Havelange, Thihange, Jamme, Methin, Maflines, Bavenchin, Hirwardes, Heiste, Turinnes, Herewardes, from the gift of the noblewoman Countess Ermengard. The allod of Woroime with all its dependencies. Also the peace which your predecessor Henry of good memory established in that bishopric.

We decree, therefore, etc.

I, Adrian IV, bishop of the catholic Church, have subscribed.

CCIX. He confirms the privileges of the Church of Saint Omer.

[Miraeus, *Diplomatic Works*, IV, 23.]

[Col. 1589A]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons JOHN, dean, and all the canons of the church of blessed Omer . . . .

. . . . We receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, and fortify by the privilege of this present writing, the aforesaid church of Saint Omer, in which you are devoted to divine service and where, namely, his venerable body is believed to rest. . . . . . . . . . . We also add . . . . . . that no priest in the town of Saint Omer may presume to celebrate Mass on the Purification of Saint Mary until the solemnities of Mass have been celebrated in the greater church. [Col. 1589B] . . . . Concerning the revenues and prebends belonging to the hospital of the poor, we decree that, when those who presently receive them die, they shall be granted neither to clerics nor laymen; but when they fall vacant, they shall henceforth serve only the table of the poor, etc.

CCX. He receives the monastery of St Michael in Peril of the Sea under protection and confirms its goods.

(*Monasticon Anglicanum*, II, 903.)

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ROBERT, abbot of the monastery of St Michael in Peril of the Sea, and to the brethren, present and future, professing the regular life: in perpetuity.

[Col. 1589C] Those choosing the religious life ought to have apostolic protection at hand, lest perhaps an assault of any rash person either recall them from their purpose or, which God forbid, weaken the strength of sacred religious life. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we mercifully assent to your just requests, receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in future acquire, God favouring, through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors [Col. 1589D]. Among these we have thought fit to specify the following by their proper names:

The churches situated in the Castle of the Mount, with its revenues and dignities, both ecclesiastical and secular; the village called Gornicum, with its churches and dependencies; the church of St Clement and the village called Drago with its church; the church of St Michael of Lupis; the church of Sarthitheyo; Ardenar with its church and all its dependencies; the village of Belneyr with its church; the village of Passibus with its church; the village of Cureyo with its church; the village of Husius with its church; the village called Crox with its dependencies; Ballene with its dependencies; the borough of Bremonis with its dependencies; the church of Cangeye [Col. 1590A] with its dependencies; the churches of Pontis Vixonis, with the tithes of the revenues of that castle; and the chapel of Hamelin with its dependencies.

In the diocese of Coutances: the village of St Paternus with its church and dependencies; the church of St John in the Fields; the church of St Pancras; the church of Coldevilla; the church of Fulquere-villa, with the village itself and its dependencies; the village of Eenoch; the land of Elleos; the church of Cartereth; the island of Chansye; whatever they possess on the island called Gerley; a fourth part of the island called Gurneie; and on that same island the church of St Saviour, the church of St Mary of the Castle, the church of St Michael of the Valley, the church of St Peter of the Wood, the church of St Mary of Lishon with its dependencies [Col. 1590B], and the chapel of St George; the island called . . . . . enchon, with its church.

In the diocese of Bayeux: the village called Donus Joannis with its dependencies; the village called Bretenvilla with its church and dependencies; the village called Bersum with its dependencies; and the church of Sear with its dependencies. In the diocese of Rouen: in the market of that city, the church of St Michael. In the diocese of Lisieux: certain meadows in the village called Pont-l’Évêque. In the diocese of Chartres: the village called Golcere, with its church and dependencies. In the diocese of Le Mans: the cell of St Victurius in the suburb of that city, with the borough of that suburb and all its lawful customs, [Col. 1590C] both concerning wine and other articles for sale, and its other dependencies. In the same suburb, the church of St John with its dependencies; the church of Lucare with its dependencies; the church of Pontenay with its dependencies; Vilarentum with its dependencies; the vineyards which you possess near the castle of Sillaim.

In the diocese of Tours: the lands and vineyards which you possess near that city. In the diocese of Angers: in that city, one house, vineyards, and land near the city; the church of Creant with its dependencies. In Brittany, in the diocese of Dol: Mount Randum with its dependencies; the village of Prastaam; Melnen and Lande in the diocese of Alet, and a certain church with its dependencies; the church of St Tigal with its dependencies. In [Col. 1590D] the diocese of St Corentin: the church of St Michael of Cornouaille. In the diocese of Rennes: the village called Villa Maris, with its church and dependencies; the church of Polleyo. In England, in the diocese of Exeter: the cell of St Michael of Mount Cornwall with its dependencies; the village of Ettonia with its church and dependencies; Sedewne and its church; the church of Endebrie; Viscumba; Estolleia; Ercumba and its church; the village called Hedrin. In the diocese of Winchester: three churches in the village called Basinges, Basingstoke; the church of Salisbury in the diocese of Salisbury; the church of Hetona in the dioceses of Wells and Bath; the church of Merthoc with its dependencies in the diocese of Ely; the church of Wem in the diocese of [Col. 1591A] York; and the village called Wath with its church and all things known to belong to that church.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken, diminish them, or oppress it with any vexations; but that all these things be preserved unimpaired and whole, to serve in every way the use and benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted—saving, of course, the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishops.

If anyone therefore in the future, etc.

YEAR 1155–1159.

[Col. 1591B]

CCXI. Privilege granted to Marchward, abbot of Fulda. (6 July.)

[Dronke, *Codex Diplomaticus Fuldensis*, 404.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son MARCHWARD, abbot of the venerable monastery of the Holy Church of Fulda: greeting and apostolic blessing in Christ.

Among all the churches of the German kingdom, the monastery of Fulda must be confirmed by the privileges and decrees of the ancient Fathers, our holy and apostolic predecessors. Therefore it is rightly established that this place has flourished in resources and has shone with eminence of dignity through the authority of the Roman curia and the protection of Peter, prince of the apostles [Col. 1591C]. The most holy Roman Church has always provided for it with especial kindness in its affairs; and the more it perceived that it belonged particularly to its jurisdiction and protection and remained more steadfast in devotion to it, the more diligently it took care to assist it in its needs.

Knowing, therefore, by how many attacks of storms that monastery is shaken contrary to the commands of the holy Fathers, and how great are the pressures and troubles it endures through the wickedness of secular men; and observing also how often you find certain of our brethren and fellow bishops harsh and remiss in rendering you justice against your wrongdoers, we have decreed, from the kindness of the Apostolic See, to grant your person this authority [Col. 1591D]: namely, that if, concerning your wrongdoers, those of the Church committed to you, and invaders of its goods situated in whatever bishoprics, you bring a complaint a second or third time before those bishops to whom their spiritual care pertains, and they refuse to render you justice, you may, after a second and third warning, bind those wrongdoers by our authority in a sentence of excommunication unless they make satisfaction to you and your Church as is right. Nor may that sentence be relaxed by any bishop before they have offered you fitting satisfaction concerning the matters you have against them.

You therefore, beloved son in the Lord [Col. 1592A], be so devoted and faithful to your mother, the most holy Roman Church, for the favour granted you, and use the power granted you in such a way that you may appear not undeservedly to have obtained this benefit and may be proved fit to rise to seek others. And because we know your oversight to be necessary in many respects to the monastery of Fulda, by authority of our Apostolic See we establish and confirm that everything which you have reclaimed from laymen among the Church’s revenues, and have restored to your monastery from things previously taken away or unjustly possessed, shall be ratified and stable for ever. Likewise, whatever you have established for your brethren as a consolation at supper, or bestowed upon your other communities in remembrance of your memory, shall remain firm and unshaken. Finally, we strengthen by apostolic authority the buildings of walls [Col. 1592B], the possessions of castles, and your other labours which you have undertaken in that monastery, so that no one may dare infringe what, through fear of God, you have endeavoured to acquire for your monastery and to preserve when acquired. Beyond all this, we decree and sanction by apostolic authority that whoever makes void these things or the other things handed down to that monastery by the holy Fathers shall be anathema.

Given on the second day before the Nones of July [6 July].

CCXII. To Hugh, archbishop of Rouen.—Concerning the case of Peter and his mother. (At Anagni, 13 August.)

[Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 642.]

[Col. 1592C]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother, the archbishop of Rouen: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have committed for hearing and final determination to our venerable brother, the bishop of Le Mans, the case known to be in dispute between Peter’s mother and Peter himself, and that between the woman who was the wife of the said Peter’s brother and her husband concerning a certain dowry.

[Note: [Col. 1591] William Passavant, who governed the Church of Le Mans from the year 1142 until about the year 1186.]

Accordingly, by apostolic writing we command your fraternity that, when requested concerning this matter by that bishop, you compel the woman who was the wife of the aforesaid Peter’s brother, and her husband, to appear before that judge and to accept and firmly observe what he shall judge according to the merits of the case [Col. 1592D], using every compulsion.

Given at Anagni, on the Ides of August [13 August].

CCXIII. To Louis, king of the Franks, who protects Pons, abbot of Vézelay: he gives thanks. He admonishes him to continue defending the monastery against the count of Nevers and to order the stone houses of the burgesses of Vézelay demolished.

(Mansi, *Concilia*, XXI, 814.)

We receive this with gratitude and acceptance, and we greatly commend Your Magnificence for the execution of pious undertakings, since, as the report addressed to us by our beloved son Pontius, abbot of Vézelay, has made clear, you have hitherto, out of love for God and reverence for our letters, diligently stood by him in accordance with the duty of royal dignity [Col. 1593A], and have supplied him counsel and assistance against his own persecutors and those of his monastery. And since the purpose of good men is directed all the more toward salutary works the more frequently they are reminded of them, we ask Your Highness by these apostolic letters, and enjoin this upon you for the remission of your sins, that, for love of God and reverence for blessed Peter and ourselves, you more earnestly love and honor the aforesaid abbot; and that you defend the monastery itself from the attacks of our beloved son the Count of Nevers and of all others, so that the brothers dwelling there may be bound continually to intercede with the Lord for the welfare of you and your kingdom, and that we may be bound to render thanks to your royal nobility. And because the burgesses of Vézelay, especially on account of their stone houses [Col. 1593B], which they possess fortified and elevated, behave so arrogantly against our aforesaid son the abbot and the Church of Vézelay that, because of their persecution, that same son of ours cannot even remain in the monastery: we ask Your Magnificence to have those houses demolished in such a manner that the arrogance of the burgesses may be checked and the Church of Vézelay may not be harassed on this account.

## A.D. 1157–1159

### CCXIV. He exhorts Abbot Odo and the monks of Saint-Denis to follow in the footsteps of Saint Benedict.  
*(Lateran, January 4.)*

[DOUBLET, *History of Saint-Denis*, 502.]

[Col. 1593C]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ODO, abbot, and the brethren of the monastery of Saint Denis: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Those who have professed the monastic life and devoted themselves to divine service ought to live religiously and according to the Rule, and to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. Therefore, since you have desired to serve God according to the Rule of blessed Benedict, strive with all the effort of your minds to fulfill your vow and observe pure religion. For it is fitting that you should be so rooted and strengthened in moral uprightness and charity that, through the fragrance of your good odor, very many others may run after the scent of your ointments. Wherefore, by these apostolic [Col. 1593D] letters we admonish and exhort you in the Lord to strive to adhere to the footsteps of your father blessed Benedict, so that, through the intervention of his merits and through your own care and zeal, your monastery may, by the Lord’s agency, prosper in temporal and spiritual growth, and you may deserve to receive an eternal crown in heaven.

Given at the Lateran, the second day before the Nones of January [4 January].

### CCXV. He confirms for Hugh, chancellor of the king of the Franks, the archdeaconry of Arras.  
*(Lateran, January 21.)*

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 803.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HUGH, chancellor of our dearest son Louis, king [Col. 1594A] of the Franks, and archdeacon of the Church of Arras: greeting and apostolic blessing.

If we readily assent to the reasonable petitions of our sons and support them with our protection in ecclesiastical benefices conferred upon them, we perform the action due to our office and provide effectively for ecclesiastical interests. For each man will be able to attend more fruitfully to the performance of his office in proportion as he sees every avenue for the assaults of wicked men’s rashness more carefully blocked. Therefore, beloved son Hugh in the Lord, wishing to provide henceforth for your peace and security, we confirm for you by apostolic authority, and fortify by the page of this present writing, the greater archdeaconry of the Church of Arras, with all that pertains to it, reasonably granted to you by our venerable brother Godfrey, bishop of that same Church [Col. 1594B]. Therefore let no one, etc.

Given at the Lateran, the twelfth day before the Kalends of February [21 January].

### CCXVI. He confirms the privileges granted to the monastery of Saint-Denis by Kings Robert and Dagobert.  
*(Lateran, February 5.)*

[DOUBLET, *History of Saint-Denis*, 504.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ODO, abbot, and the brethren of the monastery of Saint Denis: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Things which are bestowed upon religious men and most holy churches by the generosity of Catholic princes, out of regard for the Godhead, ought to remain in their established state and, lest in the course of time they be disturbed by anyone’s presumption, ought to be secured by the authority of the Apostolic See. Robert, formerly king of the Franks, of illustrious memory, desiring to provide for the peace of the brethren serving the Lord in your church, remitted, out of contemplation of divine mercy, to the brethren then living and to their successors forever, the solemn court which his predecessors, and he himself, had anciently been accustomed to hold in the castle of Saint Denis itself at Christmas, Epiphany, Easter, and Pentecost. Thus neither he nor any of his successors was thereafter to hold a solemn court in that place on the above-mentioned feasts, lest perhaps the gatherings [Col. 1594D] of the populace should afford an occasion of disturbance in the retreats of God’s servants and the church should incur heavy expenses through the influx of strangers.

Moreover, adding immunity to immunity, he decreed that the grant of his predecessor Dagobert, formerly king of the Franks, of illustrious memory, concerning fugitives, which had been issued to your monastery, should remain valid and unshaken for all time. Namely, that all which is known to be contained within the entire district extending to the place where those going to that church enter the bridge of Tricena; likewise as far as Montmartre; and further as far as the public road leading to Lupera—with judicial authority nevertheless, that is, the *ban*, and every fine for infringement, and whatever other customary legal dues may arise in fields [Col. 1595A], houses, public roads, or private ways—should remain in the right of your monastery without anyone’s objection.

Since you have requested that these matters be strengthened by our protection for their greater security, we, favorably assenting to your petitions, confirm these grants by apostolic authority and fortify them by the page of this present writing. We also confirm to that church, and to you and your successors, the fief which Matthew Bellus-Ligius, a man of your church, acknowledged that he held from your church at the request and upon the sworn charge of Suger, formerly your abbot, of happy memory, and committed to writing for the memory of posterity. We further ordain that you shall possess forever, without anyone’s disturbance, the Church of Holy Cross and the tithe of Vallis-Crisonis, as you possess them justly and canonically [Col. 1595B]. Let absolutely no person, therefore, be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or oppose it by rash presumption. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, on the Nones of February [5 February].

### CCXVII. To B. [Baldwin], bishop of Noyon, and Henry, bishop of Beauvais.—On behalf of the cantor of the Church of Péronne.  
*(Lateran, February 18.)*

[MARTEN., *Collection*, II, 643.]

[Col. 1595C] ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren B., bishop of Noyon, and HENRY, bishop of Beauvais: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son O., cantor of the Church of Péronne, came to the clemency of the Apostolic See and showed us in his complaint that W. of Inchy and his wife presume, under the protection of the nobleman J., count of Soissons, to take from him and unjustly retain one hundred pounds of Châlons currency, lands, and certain freeholds.

[Note: [Col. 1595D] The church of St Fursa, in which there is a distinguished college of canons.]

Accordingly, when our venerable brother the bishop of Cambrai had clearly learned that this was so, he bound them, as we have learned from his letters, with the bond of excommunication for so great a robbery, and subjected their land to an interdict. Since, however, we neither ought nor can endure that our aforesaid son the cantor should be deprived of his right, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters, under injunction, to take diligent care to summon the said count—by whose protection and assistance those goods were violently taken from him—within thirty days after receipt of these letters, so that he may compel the same W. and his wife, with every severity, to restore all that has been taken, and may no longer presume to furnish them assistance [Col. 1596A] or support in retaining it. Otherwise, without regard to appeal, do not delay to prohibit all divine services throughout the land of that count until full satisfaction has been made to our aforesaid son the cantor in all respects.

Given at the Lateran, the twelfth day before the Kalends of March [18 February].

### CCXVIII. He confirms certain possessions of the Church of Saint Ursus at Aosta (province of Tarentaise).  
*(Lateran, March 6.)*

[*History of the Patria Monuments*, Charters, I, 819.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son G., prior, and the entire chapter of the Church of Saint Ursus: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Whenever our confirmation is requested by religious men against the attacks of wicked persons concerning those things which they possess justly and lawfully [Col. 1596B], we ought not to prove reluctant to grant it, nor deny our consent to their reasonable petitions, lest we seem to give wicked men an opportunity for wrongdoing, whereas we ought rather to resist them. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, wishing beneficially to provide henceforth for your people and for the welfare of the church committed to you, and graciously assenting to your just requests, we confirm for you, and through you for the church entrusted to you, by apostolic authority, and fortify by the protection of this present writing, the Church of Saint Peter; the Church of Saint Andrew of Paone; the Church of Saint John of Carto with its appurtenances; and the tithe of Carto with its appurtenances, as they have been canonically granted to your church by our venerable brother Gui, bishop of Yporia [Col. 1596C]. We decree that absolutely no person may be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or oppose it in any way. But if anyone should presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at the Lateran, the second day before the Nones of March [6 March].

### CCXIX. To Henry, bishop of Beauvais.—On behalf of Master Nicholas.  
*(Lateran, March 8.)*

[MARTEN., *Collection*, II, 644.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, bishop of Beauvais: greeting [Col. 1596D] and apostolic blessing.

Whenever our intervention is sought from you by one of our sons in ecclesiastical matters, we grant our assent to his petition all the more readily because we trust that you can be more effectively induced to carry out the matter requested both by our admonition and by the duty of the office imposed upon you. Our beloved son Master Nicholas, who is very dear and welcome to us, a monk of Arremar, came into the presence of the Apostolic See and requested that we should admonish your brotherhood by our letters to give him support and grant his petitions in the affairs of that church.

[Note: [Col. 1595D] Arremar was a monastery of no small distinction of the Order of Saint Benedict in the diocese of Troyes. From it Nicholas the monk had gone to Clairvaux, later becoming the notary of Saint Bernard. When he had deserted that same Saint Bernard by apostasy, he returned to the monastery of his first profession and, being an astute man, brought it about that he was favored by the princes of the age. Hence I conjecture that this letter of Pope Adrian was written in his favor. [Col. 1596D–1597D]]

Therefore we ask your brotherhood by apostolic letters to love and honor more attentively, for reverence toward blessed Peter and ourselves, this same son of ours, who has been quite diligent and devoted in your affairs; and to assent continually and favorably to his petitions in the business of that church, and so furnish him your favor and assistance in his causes that your brotherhood may appear commendable for granting my petitions, and that we may be bound to grant your petitions more freely.

Given at the Lateran, the eighth day before the Ides of March [8 March].

### CCXX. To S., archbishop of Reims.—On behalf of the same man.  
*(Lateran, March 8.)*

[Ibid.]

[Col. 1597B]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother S., archbishop of Reims and legate of the Apostolic See: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Note: [Col. 1598D] Samson, who succeeded in 1140 Rainald, archbishop of Reims, after the latter’s death in 1137.]

Whenever our intervention is sought from you by one of our sons in ecclesiastical matters, we grant our assent to his petition all the more readily because we trust that you can be more effectively induced to carry out the matter requested both by our admonition and by the duty of the office imposed upon you. Our beloved son Master Nicholas, who is very dear and welcome to us, a monk of the monastery of Arremar [Col. 1597C], came into the presence of the Apostolic See and requested that we should admonish your brotherhood by our letters to give him support and grant his petitions in the affairs of that church. Therefore we ask your brotherhood by apostolic letters to love and honor more attentively, for reverence toward blessed Peter and ourselves, this same son of ours, who is quite diligent and devoted in your affairs; and to assent continually and favorably to his petitions in the business of that church, and so furnish him your favor and assistance in his causes that your brotherhood may appear commendable for granting our petitions, and that we may be bound to grant your petitions more willingly.

[Col. 1597D] Given at the Lateran, the eighth day before the Ides of March [8 March].

### CCXXI. To the archbishop of Reims and the bishop of Laon.—On behalf of the son of Ramald Cottella.  
*(Lateran, March 12.)*

[Ibid., col. 645.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren, the archbishop of Reims, legate of the Apostolic See, and the bishop of Laon: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Let your brotherhood know that it has come to the hearing of the Apostolic See that Ramald Cottella, when formerly setting out for Jerusalem [Col. 1598A], pledged as security to Henry of Teir a certain village of his called Boccumville, having borrowed money from him. That Henry, moreover, is said to have received from its revenues both his principal and more besides. Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if what is asserted is true, you shall compel the wife and children of the said Henry—for he has entered upon the way of all flesh—without regard to any appeal and with strictness, to restore the aforesaid village to the son of the said Ramald, setting aside every pretext and delay; otherwise, do not delay to pronounce against them a sentence of excommunication until suitable satisfaction has been made.

Given at the Lateran, the fourth day before the Ides of March [12 March].

### CCXXII. To Henry, bishop of Beauvais.—On behalf of the cantor of the Church of Soissons, that what was taken from him may be restored.  
*(Lateran, March 13.)*

[MARTEN., *Amplified Collection*, II, 645.]

[Col. 1598B]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, bishop of Beauvais: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved cantor of Soissons, appearing before us, lodged in our hearing a complaint against Odo of Angevilers, his wife, and his household: a certain man from his land had stolen from him five marks and thirty-one gold pieces, and the money had come into their hands; yet they were unwilling either to restore it or, as he asserts, to render him any justice concerning it [Col. 1598C]. Since therefore we can neither nor ought in any respect to fail the aforesaid son of ours in his right, we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters to take the utmost care to summon the said Odo, his wife, and his household, so that within forty days after your admonition they shall either restore in full the aforesaid money to the said cantor or without delay render him complete justice in your presence concerning it. But if they should refuse to do either, compel them by the bond of excommunication to perform one or the other.

Given at the Lateran, the third day before the Ides of March [13 March].

### CCXXIII. He asks A[lbert], abbot of Nonantola, to renew a certain precarial grant to Lot. and Turcl., noblemen.  
*(Lateran, A.D. 1157, March 21.)*

[TIRABOSCHI, *History of Nonantola*, II, 268.]

[Col. 1598D]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son A[LBERT], abbot of Nonantola: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Because we trust in your devotion, we do not hesitate to offer you prayers on behalf of our faithful friends. Therefore we earnestly ask your diligence [Col. 1599A] not to delay, for reverence toward blessed Peter and ourselves, to renew the precarial grant which our beloved sons, the noblemen Lot. and Turcl., your faithful men, are known to hold from the monastery of Nonantola; and to grant it to them henceforth as you have done until now, so that those same sons of ours may find our prayers made to you on this matter fruitful for themselves and may not be compelled to trouble us further on this account.

Given at the Lateran, the twelfth day before the Kalends of April [21 March].

### CCXXIV. He confirms the settlement concerning the subjection of the monastery of Vallis-Magna to Bonneval.  
*(Lateran, April 6.)*

[*Gallia Christiana*, VI, Instruments, 325.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son PETER, abbot of the monastery of Bonneval: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Controversies arising between ecclesiastical persons and brought before us ought to be terminated by means of justice; and, once decided, they ought to be committed to written records, lest they fall away from the memory of posterity. The Church of Cadouin, on account of the devotion which it had toward the monastery of Cîteaux, bestowed upon that monastery two churches that belonged to its right: namely, Ardurelles and the Church of Vallis-Magna, so that they might reform their life and habit according to its institution. The abbot of Cîteaux then granted both churches to the monastery of Bonneval. Thus it came about that, when Guigo, your predecessor, now bishop of Amélie, had organized both churches [Col. 1599C] with brethren from the monastery of Bonneval, the abbot of the aforesaid Church of Cadouin summoned him to judgment, strongly maintaining that the donation had been made neither with his own consent nor that of his chapter.

Thus, by the consent of both parties, the following agreement and settlement was reached between you: the aforesaid abbot of Cadouin was to possess the Church of Ardurelles peacefully and without molestation, while the Church of Magna Vallis was to remain freely with the monastery of Bonneval. The abbot of Ardurelles and the chapter of that place, by order of the abbot of Cadouin and of their own will, granted this settlement and promised that they would confirm it by the security of letters; they also promised that they would have it confirmed by the bishop of Albi, in whose diocese they are.

Some time later, however, when the said abbot of Ardurelles wished to infringe this settlement and summoned you to judgment concerning it, because he wished to compel you to take an oath against vexatious litigation, you, feeling yourself oppressed in this matter, appealed him to the Apostolic See. Accordingly, when both he and Ermengald, abbot of Vallis-Magna, sent by you concerning the same affair, were present before us, and the abbot of Magna Vallis had pleaded in our court the matters stated above, while the said abbot of Ardurelles strongly asserted that he and his chapter had assented to this settlement under compulsion [Col. 1600A] and not voluntarily, we nevertheless, having heard and carefully examined the arguments on both sides and taken counsel with our brethren, decreed that this settlement should remain valid and firm forever.

We further add that you shall be bound, within four months after proof has been made, to restore to them in full all movable goods presently appearing, which the abbot and brethren of the monastery of Ardurelles can demonstrate by lawful witnesses, in the presence of our brother P., bishop of Lodève, that they had conferred upon that church. And so that all these things may be observed inviolably forever, imposing perpetual silence upon the adverse party, we have judged them to be strengthened by apostolic authority [Col. 1600B] and secured by the protection of this present writing. We decree that absolutely no person may be permitted to infringe this page of our confirmation or oppose it in any way.

If anyone should presume to attempt this, let him, after a second or third admonition, unless he corrects his presumption by suitable satisfaction, be deprived of the dignity of his power and honor; let him know himself guilty before the divine judgment of the iniquity he has committed; let him be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and let him be subject at the last judgment to severe vengeance. But may all who observe these things have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find with the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace.

[Col. 1600C] Given at the Lateran, the eighth day before the Ides of April [6 April].

### CCXXV. To the bishops of Saint-Brieuc and Tréguier.—That they should prevent their priests, against the will of the archbishop of Dol, from celebrating divine offices.  
*(Lateran, April 11.)*

[MARTEN., *Anecdotes*, III, 902.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren, the bishops of Saint-Brieuc and Tréguier: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The office of the apostolate laid upon us admonishes and urges us by every means to preserve whole and unimpaired for our brother bishops their rights. Therefore, wishing to preserve for our venerable brother Hugh, archbishop of Dol, what is recognized as belonging to his right [Col. 1600D], we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters diligently to admonish, within fifteen days after receipt of the present letters, those priests who, in churches established in your dioceses and known to belong to the right of the Church of Dol, celebrate divine offices against the archbishop’s will, that they desist from so great a presumption and in no way presume henceforth to celebrate divine offices in the aforesaid churches against his will. If they should attempt to do so, pronounce an ecclesiastical sentence against them until suitable satisfaction has been made.

Given at the Lateran, the third day before the Ides of April [11 April].

### CCXXVI. He commands Eberhard, archbishop of Salzburg, and the bishop of Regensburg [(Hartwig)], to restore to Conrad, abbot of Biburg, the monastery which he had left because of the injuries of the brethren, and to punish the monks.  
*(Lateran, April 17.)*

[HUND., *Metropolis of Salzburg*, II, 212.]

[Col. 1601A]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren EBERHARD, archbishop of Salzburg, and the bishop of Regensburg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son Conrad, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary of Biburg, as we have learned from the testimony of your brotherhood, bishop of Regensburg, of your canons, of our brother the bishop of Bamberg [Col. 1601B], and from the assertion of many other religious men, was compelled by the malice and harassment of certain wicked brethren to depart from his monastery and visit the presence of the Apostolic See. When he intended to cross the sea and proceed to Jerusalem, in order there to remain permanently in some religious place in God’s service and for the salvation of his soul, we turned him aside from the purpose of his mind and sent him back to his own monastery, that he might have charge of the brethren hereafter as hitherto, and might exercise his ministry fully in the abbey.

Earnestly commending him, therefore, to your brotherhood, we command and enjoin you by apostolic letters to restore him, within twenty days after receipt of these letters, to the full possession of the abbey by our authority. Firmly charge the brethren of the same monastery to receive him honorably, treat him kindly, and render him in all things the reverence and subjection due to him as their own abbot and the ruler of their souls. If, meanwhile, anyone has been installed in that abbey, take care that he be wholly removed without obstacle of opposition.

You shall also remove from the monastery itself two monks of that church, namely Udo and Walth[er], and two lay brothers, namely Euch. [perhaps Eucherius or Eucharius] and Udal. [Udalricus], by whose hostility and repeated harassment the aforesaid son of ours, Abbot Conrad, declares that he relinquished the government of the abbey entrusted to him; and by our authority place them in obediences of the monastery, though outside the monastery [Col. 1601D]. They shall be compelled to remain in those obediences until, abandoning their malice and being corrected and reformed, they are recalled to their own monastery by the said abbot.

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of May [1 May].

### CCXXVII. He commands the monks of Biburg to obey Abbot Conrad.  
*(Lateran, April 17.)*

[Ibid.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the monks and lay brothers of Saint Mary of Biburg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1602A] Your beloved abbot Conrad, as we have learned from his own report and the testimony of many religious men, was compelled by the malice and harassment of certain wicked brethren to depart from your monastery and visit the presence of the Apostolic See. When he intended to cross the sea and proceed to Jerusalem, in order there to remain permanently in some religious place in God’s service and for the salvation of his soul, we turned him aside from the purpose of his mind and sent him back to his own monastery, that he might have charge of the brethren hereafter as hitherto and might exercise his ministry fully in the abbey.

Earnestly commending him, therefore, to all of you, we command and enjoin you by apostolic letters to receive him honorably, treat him kindly, and render him in all things the subjection and obedience due to him as your own abbot and the ruler of your souls [Col. 1602B]. Presume in no respect to be rebellious or disobedient toward him. If you should perhaps refuse to comply, know that any sentence which he canonically pronounces on that account against any one of you who proves contemptuous is to be held valid and firm by us.

Moreover, we command through our brethren, the archbishop of Salzburg and the bishop of Regensburg, that two monks of your monastery, namely Ud. and Gualch., and two lay brothers, namely Ud. and Euch.—through whose hostility and repeated harassment the aforesaid son of ours, Abbot Conrad, declares that he relinquished the government of the abbey entrusted to him—be removed from that monastery [Col. 1602C]. We decree that they shall remain in obediences of the monastery outside the monastery until, abandoning their malice and being corrected and reformed, they are recalled to their own monastery by the said abbot.

Given at the Lateran, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May [17 April].
