### CCXXVIII. He commands the bishop of Autun [Henry] to grant the abbot of Tournus investiture of the church of Pierre-Fitte within twenty days.  
*(Lateran, April 20.)*

[JUENIN, *New History of Tournus*, Preface, p. 165.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother, the bishop of Autun: greeting and apostolic [Col. 1602D] blessing.

Our beloved son, the abbot of Tournus, has shown us in a report sent to us that, although you had granted the Church of Pierre-Fitte to his monastery out of pious regard and had confirmed it by your own seal—a gift which we ourselves recall having confirmed by apostolic authority—you are unwilling to invest him with that church. Therefore we command your brotherhood by apostolic letters that, if the matter is as stated, within twenty days after receipt of these letters you shall grant to that abbot, setting aside every pretext and excuse, investiture of that church with all its appurtenances.

Given at the Lateran, the twelfth day before the Kalends of May [20 April].

### CCXXIX. To the archbishop of Narbonne and his suffragans—that they defend William, lord of Montpellier, and the possessions of him and of his brother, a pilgrim to Jerusalem, from the attacks of wicked persons, under threat of excommunication.  
*(Lateran, May 5.)*

[D. BOUQUET, *Collection*, XV, 683.]

[Col. 1603A]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren the archbishop of Narbonne and his suffragans, and RAIMOND, bishop of Maguelone; to R., prior, the archdeacons, and all the people of the Church: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We receive our beloved son William of Montpellier, with all that belongs to him, under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves; and we wish all his possessions to be preserved for him unimpaired and whole. Therefore we command all of you by apostolic letters to uphold, for reverence toward blessed Peter and ourselves, both him and his land and men, the castle of Castries, and the other honours of his brother William of Tortosa, who, for the forgiveness of his sins and the salvation of his soul, has visited Jerusalem and there proposed to devote himself for a year to divine service [Col. 1603B]. Where necessary, strive to defend them from the attacks of wicked persons. Restrain your parishioners from harassing and injuring William and his men, and do not allow any molestation or injury to be inflicted upon him, his possessions, or his men by those same parishioners of yours.

If anyone should presume contrary to justice to harass their land, or that of his aforesaid brother or of their men, pronounce a sentence of excommunication upon his person and a sentence of interdict upon his land. We further decree that divine offices shall not at any time be prohibited in the Church of Saint Mary and Saint Firmin, or in the other churches belonging to them, on account of the cause or fault of excommunicated persons who may happen to enter the castle of Montpellier. For it is unworthy that so great a people should be obliged to abstain from divine offices because of the fault and evil deeds of any person whatever.

Given at the Lateran, the third day before the Nones of May [5 May].

### CCXXX. To the canons of Holy Cross at Orléans.—He reproves them because they did not grant Hugh the chancellor the entirety of his prebend while he was absent. He orders them to do so henceforth and to restore what has been withheld.  
*(Lateran, May 9.)*

[Ibid., col. 805.]

[Col. 1603D]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the dean and the entire chapter of the Church of Holy Cross at Orléans: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We are greatly astonished and cannot but be moved against you, because although we formerly gave you orders that, even if our beloved son Hugh, chancellor of our dearest son Louis, illustrious king of the Franks, was not regularly present in your church, he should nevertheless possess the entirety of his prebend without any objection [Col. 1604A], you not only failed in this matter to carry our command into effect but even, what is worse, in contempt of us and the Apostolic See, after he had previously held it in full, have subsequently, as it is said, withheld one half from him. Unless the customary clemency of the Apostolic See softened our mind, you would feel the heavy hand of blessed Peter against you so severely that you would not presume again to attempt any such thing in contempt of us.

Therefore, lest we be compelled to exact from you, as your wickedness deserves, the gravest punishment, we command and, by commanding, enjoin all of you in repeated letters that henceforth you grant him his prebend entire, even though he is absent, as though he served regularly in that church [Col. 1604B]. Whatever has hitherto been withheld from him on that account, take care to restore to him in full within twenty days after receipt of the present letters, setting aside every pretext and excuse.

Given at the Lateran, the seventh day before the Ides of May [9 May].

### CCXXXI. To Hugh, chancellor of France.—He absolves him from the oath and unlawful condition by which the bishop of Arras had bound him when granting him the archdeaconry.  
*(Lateran, May 11.)*

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 804.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HUGH, chancellor of our dearest son Louis, illustrious king of the Franks: greeting and apostolic [Col. 1604C] blessing.

In view of the devotion and sincerity which you are known to have shown toward the most holy Roman Church and toward ourselves for many years past, and also in consideration of the worthiness and integrity of your person, we recall that we formerly conferred upon you in the Church of Arras the greater archdeaconry, after our brother G. [Godfrey], bishop of Arras, had first promised it to you, without any condition or obligation arising from any agreement. But that bishop of Arras, acting contrary to episcopal integrity and far too much according to merely human motives, wishing to place an obstacle in the way of this grant to you, bound you by an oath, as is said, that, whenever it should please him, you would resign the chancellorship without impediment of objection. Therefore, since so unlawful an oath ought to possess no binding force, by the authority of the Apostolic See we absolve you from the obligation of that oath; and we decree that the conditions imposed, contrary to our command, in the conferral of that archdeaconry are null in every respect.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Ides of May.

CCXXXII. To Godescalc, bishop of Arras.—He informs him that Chancellor Hugh’s oath has been annulled. (Lateran, 11 May.)

[Ibid., col. 806.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother . . . . bishop of Arras, greeting and apostolic blessing.

In view of the devotion and sincerity which our beloved son Hugh, chancellor of our dearest son Louis, illustrious king of the Franks, is known to have shown toward the most holy Roman Church and toward ourselves for many years past; and also in consideration of the worthiness and integrity of his person, we recall that we formerly conferred upon him in the Church of Arras the greater archdeaconry, after you too had first promised it to him, without any condition or obligation arising from any agreement. But you, acting contrary to episcopal integrity and far too much according to merely human motives, wishing to place an obstacle in the way of this grant to him, bound him by an oath, as is said, that, whenever it should please you, he would resign the chancellorship without impediment of objection. Therefore, since so unlawful an oath ought to possess no binding force, by the authority of the Apostolic See we absolve our aforesaid son, the chancellor, from the obligation of that oath; and we decree that the conditions imposed, contrary to our command, in the conferral of that archdeaconry are null in every respect. By these apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that you presume on no account henceforth to compel him to observe the oath he gave.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Ides of May.

CCXXXIII. To Samson, archbishop of Rheims.—That he restore to Chancellor Hugh the altar which he had taken from him. (Lateran, 11 May.)

[Ibid., col. 808.]

[Col. 1605C]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother SAMSON, archbishop of Rheims, legate of the Apostolic See, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son Hugh, chancellor of our dearest son Louis, illustrious king of the Franks, in a report sent to us, has shown that he possessed a certain altar in the bishopric of Arras by the gift of Alvisus, of good memory, formerly bishop of Arras; and he asserts that he possessed that altar quietly and peacefully until the time when he was to receive, by our command, investiture of the greater archdeaconry in the Church of Arras. But when the day was at hand on which, as we have said, he ought to have been invested in that archdeaconry according to our command, our brother the bishop of Arras, as has been represented to us, refused to grant him investiture unless the same altar were first restored to himself, and is said in this way to have extorted that altar from him. Since such circumvention is contrary to reason and wholly alien to the pontifical office, we have commanded that bishop, if the matter stands thus, to restore the said altar to our aforesaid son Hugh, chancellor, within forty days after receipt of these letters, all appeal being set aside. But if he should perhaps delay in doing so, by these apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that you yourself, in our stead, without allowing any appeal or pretext, do not delay to carry this into effect.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Ides of May.

CCXXXIV. He informs Gotescalc, bishop of Arras, concerning the foregoing letter. (Lateran, 11 May.)

[Ibid., col. 807.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable brother . . . . . bishop of Arras, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son Hugh, chancellor of our dearest son the king of the Franks, by a communication addressed to us, has shown that you took from him, without reasonable cause and without any judgment having intervened, the altar of Aslues, which had been canonically granted him by M., your predecessor of good memory, and which he is said to have held peacefully even during the time of your prelacy. Therefore, the more closely this chancellor is bound to the most holy Roman Church and to ourselves by greater devotion and fidelity, the more fitting it is that we should preserve his rights for him with greater care, unimpaired and entire. By these apostolic letters we command your brotherhood that, if this is so, you restore that altar to our aforesaid son without delay and without appeal.

Given at the Lateran, on the Kalends of November.

CCXXXV. He commands the dean, cantor, and whole chapter of Paris to grant to Hugh, chancellor of the king of the Franks, the provostship which becomes vacant in the Church of Paris. (Lateran, 11 May.)

[Ibid., col. 812.]

[Col. 1606C]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the dean, cantor, and whole chapter of Paris, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We ought to love with a certain special prerogative those ecclesiastical persons whom we know to be more devoted to the most holy Roman Church and whom we see to be more ready in its service; and, by rendering them the honor due to them, we ought to advance them by ecclesiastical benefices, as we judge expedient. Indeed, our beloved son Hugh, chancellor of our dearest son Louis, illustrious king of the Franks, is bound to us by a bond of devotion; and we ourselves fully know how faithfully, wherever need requires, he puts himself forward for the advantage and honor of his mother, the most holy Roman Church, and strives to promote her increase. We believe that this is not unknown to your discretion. Accordingly, loving him with sincere charity in the Lord, we endeavor, so far as we can with God’s help, to honor him in every way; and it is our purpose to provide usefully for him in his opportunities.

Therefore, placing the greatest confidence in all your devotion, by these apostolic letters we command and, in commanding, enjoin your whole body that you grant him, all contention and appeal set aside, the provostship which shall next become vacant in the Church of Paris and the houses in the cloister of that church which shall first thereafter become vacant; and that you permit him to possess what has been granted quietly and without any molestation.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Ides of May.

CCXXXVI. To the archdeacons of the Church of Trier. (Lateran, 11 May.)

[GUNTHER, I, 355.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the archdeacons of the Church of Trier, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Although unworthy, by the Lord’s authorship we sit in the exalted watchtower of the Apostolic See. We ought to preserve whole and unimpaired for our brothers the bishops and other prelates of churches their rights, so that they may be the more diligent in carrying out their office because they know themselves to be aided by the protection of the Apostolic See and supported in their justice. For this reason, we desire to uphold in his right our venerable brother Hy., archbishop of Trier, legate of the Apostolic See, whom we love with sincere charity in the Lord because of the integrity, learning, and religious character of his person; nor can we endure on any account that he should suffer diminution or loss in matters belonging to him.

Therefore, by these apostolic letters we command and enjoin your whole body that, rendering in all things to our brother the archbishop the submission and reverence due, you take care humbly to obey him as the proper shepherd and ruler of your souls. Whatever he shall reasonably ordain in the archbishopric entrusted to him, presume in no way to oppose. . . . Nor henceforth shall you grant priests investiture of churches without his knowledge and assent, as is known to be contained in the privilege granted to him by the Apostolic See. For we do not wish you to abuse the power granted you by him, so that because you are known to have received from him the power of investing, you ought to make investiture without his assent and concurrence. But if anything should be presumed by you in any way, we shall revoke as void whatever has been done, and decree that it shall obtain no validity thereafter.

Given at the Lateran, on the fifth day before the Ides of May.

CCXXXVII. To the clergy and people of Murmiralio [otherwise Murmurallio].—That they obey Hugh, archbishop of Dol. (Lateran, 27 May.)

[MARTÈNE, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, III, 902.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the clerics and laymen of Murmiralio, greeting and apostolic blessing.

The more deeply we love with sincere charity in the Lord our venerable brother H., archbishop of Dol, and desire to honor him as our dearest brother, the more we wish to maintain him in his rights and earnestly desire by every means that filial reverence and due honor be rendered to him by those subject to him. Therefore, by these apostolic letters we command and enjoin your whole body that you receive him honorably and graciously when he returns to you, as to special sons, with the fullness of our favor; treat him honorably; and, rendering him in all things the submission and obedience due to him as the proper shepherd of your souls, permit that same brother of ours to possess quietly and peacefully, without any objection, the entire revenues of your land, just as his predecessors, the archbishops of Dol, are known to have possessed them.

Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June.

## Year 1159

CCXXXVIII. Privilege for the monastery of the Holy Trinity of Monte Sacro. (Lateran, 1 January.)

[UGHELLI, *Italia sacra*, VII, 826.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot of the monastery of the Holy Trinity of Monte Sacro and his brethren, both present and future, professing the monastic life: perpetual greeting.

In choosing the religious life, apostolic protection has been granted, lest perhaps the assault of any rashness either turn them aside from their purpose or, which God forbid, weaken the strength of holy religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; and, following the example of our predecessors of venerable memory, Honorius, Innocent, and Eugenius, Roman pontiffs, we receive under the protection of this present privilege the aforesaid monastery of the Holy Trinity of Monte Sacro, in which you are devoted to divine service. We decree that whatever possessions and places that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, God being favorable, by grant of pontiffs, generosity of kings, liberality of princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. We have thought fit to specify these in their proper names:

Namely, the church of St. Mary situated in the place called St. Quirici, with its appurtenances; Rainiaria and the land which you hold in the territory of Riniani; the church of St. Matthias the Apostle within the walls of the city of Monte Sant’Angelo; the church of St. Simeon outside the city gate; the church of St. Vincent, situated among the appurtenances of that city in the place called Vota, with its properties; whatever you possess in the church of St. Luke and in the properties belonging to it; the parcels of land, vineyards, and other possessions which formerly belonged to the said city of Monte Sant’Angelo; and all properties belonging to your monastery both within the said city and in its territory.

The church of St. George at the foot of Monte Sant’Angelo, with its appurtenances; the saltworks and waters which you possess in the district of Siponto; the church of St. Martin of Porcarezza, with its territory; the church of St. Mary of Matinata, with all that belongs to it; and all other possessions which you hold in that same Matinata. Moreover, we grant to that monastery the estate called Matinatella and the church established in the same place; the parcels of land and courts which you possess in the place of Avanto. In the bishopric of Vesta, the church of St. Thecla, the church of St. Eugenia, and the church of St. Luke, with their appurtenances, and all properties belonging to your monastery in the aforesaid bishopric; the church of St. Peter and St. Mary near the castle of Caprelis, with its appurtenances; the fisheries and fishermen whom you possess at Barano; the mills in the valley of Monte Negro; the church of St. Pancras of Ischitella, with its hamlet and territories; the church of St. Vitus and the lands which you possess at Cannae; the church of St. James outside the gates of Baroli, with its appurtenances and all that belongs to your monastery both within that city and in its bishopric; the church of Saints George and Bacchus situated above the gate of Trani, with its appurtenances and all properties belonging to your monastery both within that city and in its bishopric; the church of All Saints situated in the place called Patiano; the donation to your monastery of all the properties written below, made by Immetatichus of the city of Vigiliae; the church of St. Fortunatus and the church of St. Thomas the Apostle, situated near the same city, with the properties belonging to them; the church of Saints Philip and James, with its appurtenances, situated near the city of Melfi, and all other properties belonging to your monastery both within that city and in its bishopric; the church of St. Procopius situated in the city of Bari, and all other properties belonging to your monastery both within that city and in its bishopric; the possessions and house which you possess in the city of Ruvo; and, in its bishopric, the church of St. Angelo and St. Nicholas below Ischitella, with their appurtenances, and whatever you possess in its territory.

Upon the death of you, the abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be imposed there by any cunning of usurpation or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of St. Benedict. The one elected shall come to the Roman pontiff to receive blessing. He shall have authority to receive free persons who wish to come to that monastery for conversion, and to have them live as monks according to the Rule of your Father St. Benedict.

We also decree that henceforth, for all future time, the seat of the abbacy shall remain in that place; and that no archbishop, abbot, or any person whatsoever may rashly disturb your monastery, place it under interdict, inflict any burdens or vexations upon it, remove its possessions, retain what has been removed, diminish them, or harass it with any rash vexations. Rather, all things shall be preserved entire for the benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving, however, the annual payment by you of a rent of two solidi to the monastery of Monte Cassino.

Furthermore, we add that you shall receive the consecration of altars and churches, the ordination of monks who are to be promoted to sacred orders, and all other ecclesiastical sacraments from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is suitable and enjoys the favor and communion of the Apostolic See and is willing to supply them to you without wrongdoing or exaction. Otherwise, you may request these from whatever Catholic bishop you prefer, who, by the authority of our See, shall grant what is requested. As a token of this liberty received from the Roman Church, you shall pay to us and our successors half an ounce of gold each year.

If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter knowingly attempts rashly to act against this page of our constitution, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not make amends by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honor; let that person know that he or she stands guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let that person be subject at the last judgment to strict vengeance. But upon all who serve the aforesaid place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Imarus, bishop of Tusculum.  
I, Gregory, bishop of Sabina.  
I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia.  
I, Julius, bishop of Palestrina.  
I, Hubald, priest-cardinal of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem.  
I, Astaldus, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Prisca.  
I, John, priest-cardinal of Saints John and Paul, title of Pammachius.  
I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saints Sylvester and Martin.  
I, Odo, deacon-cardinal of St. Nicholas in the Tullian Prison.  
I, Bozo, deacon-cardinal of Saints Cosmas and Damian.

Given at the Lateran by the hand of Roland, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the Kalends of January, in the third indiction, in the year 1158 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian IV.

CCXXXIX. He receives the collegiate church of St. Stephen in the city of Constance into the special protection of the Apostolic See. (Lateran, 29 January.)

[NEUGART, *Codex diplomaticus Alemannicus*, II, 91.]

[Col. 1611A]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son FOLCARD, provost of the church of St. Stephen situated in the city of Constance, and to his brethren, both present and future, professing the canonical life: in perpetuity.

The force of equity and the order of reason require that just requests be granted, especially when the petitioners’ will is aided by piety and is not unsupported by truth. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; receive under the protection of St. Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service; and strengthen it by the privilege of this document. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, the Lord granting it, by concession of pontiffs, generosity of kings, gifts of princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. We have thought fit to specify these in their proper names:

The courts and cloister-houses of the canons, one of which is situated close beside the chapel of St. George the Martyr, and the rest around the monastery; the tithes of Weinfelden; one at Emishofen; likewise two courts in the district of Linzgau, namely at Leustetten, and three holdings there, one mill, and four *scuposae* [a local landholding measure]; one court at Lupresreuti with half a holding; two holdings in the village of Uldingen; one *scuposa* at Menlichusen; one court at Hergershoffe; one court in the village of Rottvila with two mills; the village of Altinshusen; a certain allod in the village of Lengevillare; and other estates which you possess in the city of Constance, from which rents are owed to you.

Whatever rights you possess in the village situated in the district of Thurgau, namely Harprectisvillare, which belongs with all its rights—fields, pastures, and woods—to that church; likewise the courts, namely Salmasach, and five *scuposae* and newly cleared lands in the same village; one court at Lengevillare and the estate of a certain matron Gertrude with two *scuposae*; one court at Stadelhoffen with half a holding; also two holdings in the village of Buoch, one in the village of Turstorff, one at Anninhausen, one at Appishausen; one at Nuvilare and certain fields belonging to it; and one at Guntirhofen.

We also grant that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and final will of those who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict. We also decree that no parish priest shall be installed there except from among the canons. Moreover, because the resources of the aforesaid church are said not to be great, we decree that it shall be content with only nine canons and one provost, unless divine grace increases the resources of that church for the support of more persons. Upon the death of you, now provost of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any cunning of usurpation or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall canonically provide to be elected according to the fear of God.

We therefore decree that no person at all may rashly disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain things taken away, diminish things offered, or harass it by any vexations; rather, all things shall be preserved whole, for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance and support they were granted, while in all things the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop remain intact. If, therefore, any archbishop or bishop, emperor or king, prince or duke, count or viscount, advocate, judge, or any person great or small, secular or ecclesiastical, shall hereafter knowingly attempt rashly to act against this page of our constitution, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not correct such presumption by appropriate satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honor; let that person know that he or she is guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let that person be subject at the last judgment to strict vengeance. But upon all who preserve the rights of that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace. Amen. Fare well.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Gregory, bishop of Sabina.  
I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia.  
I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina.  
I, Hubald, priest-cardinal of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem.  
I, Octavian, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Cecilia.  
I, Astaldus, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Prisca.  
I, Heinrich, priest-cardinal of the title of Saints Nereus and Achilleus.

I, Arditio, deacon-cardinal of St. Theodore.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of Roland, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the fourth day before the Kalends of February, in the eighth indiction, in the year 1158 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian.

CCXL. Bull confirming the rights and possessions of the abbey of St. Augustine of Limoges. (Lateran, 8 February.)

[*Gallia Christiana nova*, II, *Instrumenta*, 180.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, abbot of the church of St. Augustine of Limoges, and to his brethren, both present and future, professing the monastic life: in perpetuity.

Whenever a request is made of us which is known to accord with religion and uprightness, it is altogether fitting that we grant it willingly; moreover, we decree that fitting support be afforded. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just petitions; receive under the protection of St. Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service; and strengthen it by the privilege of this document. First, we decree that the monastic order known to have been established in that monastery according to the fear of God and the Rule of St. Benedict shall be observed there inviolate for all time. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter acquire, the Lord granting it, by concession of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. We have thought fit to specify these in their proper names:

The monastery of Carovico with its appurtenances; the monastery of Ambazaco with its appurtenances; the church of Superbosco with its appurtenances; the church of Colongis with its appurtenances; the monastery and chapel of Castro-Lucio with their appurtenances; the church of Bonaco with its appurtenances; the church of Fagia with its appurtenances; the church of St. John of Rillaco with its appurtenances; the church of St. Paul with its appurtenances; the church of Buissolio with its appurtenances; the church of St. Christopher with its appurtenances; the church of St. Symphorian with its appurtenances; the church of St. Praejectus with its appurtenances; the church of St. Lazarus with its appurtenances; the church of Femmoreth with its appurtenances; the church of Vernaco with its appurtenances; the church of St. German of Ledros with its appurtenances; the church of La Vaisse with its appurtenances; the church of Saints Peter and German with its appurtenances; the church of Vegrine with its appurtenances; the church of St. Peter of Lascoube with its appurtenances; the chapel of St. Michael of Triguant with its appurtenances; and the chapel of St. Michael of Chasteluts with its appurtenances.

Moreover, by apostolic authority we confirm to you the tithes of the entire parishes of St. Christopher and St. Symphorian, which you have peacefully possessed for forty years. We also grant that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may obstruct the devotion and final will of those who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; the rights of parish churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken nevertheless remaining intact. In the parish churches which you hold, you may present to the bishop priests or rectors whom you have elected; if they are found suitable, the bishop shall entrust the care of souls to them. With respect to the care of the people, those priests shall answer to the bishop; but with respect to temporal matters, they shall answer to you. Upon the death of you, now abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be set over it by any cunning of usurpation or by force, except one whom the brethren by unanimous consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of St. Benedict.

We therefore decree that no person at all may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain what has been taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; rather, all things shall be preserved entire for the benefit in every way of those for whose governance or support they were granted, while in all things the authority of the Apostolic See and the appropriate right of the diocesan bishop remain intact. If, therefore, any ecclesiastical or secular person hereafter knowingly attempts rashly to act against this page of our constitution, and, having been warned a second or third time, does not correct the offence by suitable satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of power and honor; let that person know that he or she is guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let that person be cut off from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, our Redeemer; and let that person be subject at the last judgment to divine vengeance. But upon all who preserve their rights for that place may there be the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find before the strict Judge the rewards of eternal peace.

Thus signed in the margin of the original.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Hubald, priest-cardinal of Holy Cross in Jerusalem.  
I, Irmarus, bishop of Tusculum.  
I, Gregory, bishop of Sabina.  
I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia.  
I, John, priest-cardinal of Saints Sylvester and Martin.  
I, Hildebrand, priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles.  
I, Odo, deacon-cardinal of St. George at the Golden Veil.  
I, Hyacinth, deacon-cardinal of St. Mary in Cosmedin.  
I, Ardicio, deacon-cardinal of St. Theodore.

Given at the Lateran, by the hand of Roland, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Curia and Church, on the sixth day before the Ides of February, in the seventh indiction, in the year 1158 of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian IV.

CCXLI. He praises the plan of Louis, king of the Franks, who contemplates “hastening into Spain together with Henry, king of the English, in order to defeat the barbarism of the pagans.” Yet he dissuades him from excessive haste and urges him “first to examine and consider, through the princes of that kingdom, the necessity of the land, diligently to ascertain the will both of that Church and of its princes and people, and to receive counsel from them, as is fitting.” “For,” he says, “your serene highness ought to remember how, when both Conrad, formerly king of the Romans, and you yourself undertook the journey to Jerusalem with insufficient caution, without consulting the people of the land, you did not obtain the hoped-for result.” Accordingly, he postpones the apostolic exhortation to the people, requested through Rotrou, bishop of Évreux. But he receives the king’s realm into protection. (Lateran, 18 February.)

[MANSI, *Concilia*, XXI, 810.]

[Col. 1615A]

[Col. 1615B]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ LOUIS, illustrious king of the Franks, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Your magnificence appears to be giving a sufficiently praiseworthy and fruitful thought to the propagation of the Christian name on earth and to the accumulation for yourself of the reward of eternal blessedness in heaven. For you intend, together with our dearest son Henry, illustrious king of the English, to hasten into Spain, in order to extend the boundaries of the Christian people, to defeat the barbarism of the pagans, and to bring under the yoke and dominion of Christians apostate nations which flee from the Catholic faith and do not receive the truth. You also diligently strive to assemble an army and the necessities of the journey, so that this undertaking may attain a happy outcome. And, in order to carry it out more fittingly, you request the counsel and favor of your mother, the most holy Roman Church. We regard this purpose as all the more welcome and acceptable, and commend it the more highly as it deserves to be commended, because we believe that such an intention and so praiseworthy a vow have proceeded from a more sincere root of charity, and that your purpose and desire have taken their beginning from a greater ardor of faith and love of religion.

Yet, although your excellence is prudent in the maturity of its counsel and enlightened by the light of wisdom, it appears in ordering this matter to be excessively hasty. Consequently, it has left many astonished and anxious; for every good which is performed in its proper time and fitting order is in every way pleasing and acceptable to the eternal Creator, whereas otherwise it cannot be agreeable to His will. That this may appear more clearly, and that what we propose may be somewhat more fully evident, we have thought it not unhelpful to add an example. No one of sound judgment is ignorant that to consecrate Christ’s body and offer the sacrifice upon the altar of the Lord is good—indeed, salutary. Yet if it is not offered at its proper time and appointed hours, that which was expected to bring glory is now reserved for punishment; and one who offers sacrifice outside the appointed time will grieve that condemnation is imposed upon him for that very act from which, had he offered at the appointed time, he would rejoice to have his merit and reward increased.

Moreover, to enter another’s land appears neither prudent nor safe unless counsel is first sought from the princes and people of that land. Yet you, as we have learned, intend to go there and hasten thither without consulting the Church or the princes of that land; although you should on no account attempt this unless the necessity had been made known by the princes of the land and you had first been requested by them to do so. Therefore, because with all the devotion of our mind we desire your honor and advancement, and would not have you undertake anything of this kind unless reasonable cause requires it, we urge Your Highness by this letter first to examine and consider, through the princes of that kingdom, the need of the land [Col. 1616B]; to investigate carefully the will both of that Church and of the princes and people; and, as is fitting, to receive counsel from them. When this has been done, if you see that the land’s need is indeed pressing, if the counsel of the Church is favorable, and if the princes of that land themselves ask for the aid of Your Highness and give their counsel, then, in accordance with their request and advice, you may proceed with the undertaking and, with divine aid accompanying you, fulfill your laudable vow. Otherwise there would be reason to fear that your expedition might prove fruitless and fail to reach its desired result. Moreover, the princes and people of that land might be burdened by so great a force of yours if perhaps no necessity [Col. 1616C] pressed upon them; and we ourselves might in many ways appear blameworthy in this affair.

For the loftiness of Your Serenity ought to recollect and call to mind how, on another occasion, when both Conrad, of good memory, formerly king of the Romans, and you yourself undertook the journey to Jerusalem with insufficient caution and without consulting the people of the land, you did not obtain the hoped-for fruit or desired advantage; and how much loss and injury thereby befell the Church of God and nearly the whole Christian people. The holy Roman Church too, because it had given you counsel and support in this matter, suffered no slight reproach in the event itself; and all cried out against her in great indignation, saying that she had been the author of so great a danger [Col. 1616D].

Therefore, as all these alarming considerations occurred to us in our anxious reflections, we have thought it necessary to defer our apostolic admonition and exhortation to the people of your kingdom, in accordance with what our venerable brother [Rotrodus] . . . bishop of Évreux, presented to us on your behalf. For we observe that what is deferred for a time is not wholly removed. But at last, by the Lord’s agency, we shall send exhortatory and admonitory letters promising remission of sins, in accordance with the desire of Your Glory, when, by the counsel and request alike of the princes and people of that land, as was said above, you wish to undertake the journey and have prudently and laudably resolved to fulfill the vow conceived in your mind at a time of need [Col. 1617A], whereas perhaps at present no necessity presses.

We have judged it proper for the present, in accordance with the petition of the royal dignity, to grant letters in which we receive your kingdom under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves, declaring apostolic wrath and indignation against those who might presume to attack that kingdom until your return. For even if you had kept silence and made no request of us whatsoever, because of the ardor of the affection which we have for Your Highness, we would eagerly endeavor to effect and put into practice whatever honor and exaltation we could bestow upon you and your kingdom. Let your discretion, however, consider with provident deliberation our dissuasion, which we believe we have reasonably offered [Col. 1617B], and examine and weigh the other grounds upon which you so eagerly aspire to that journey. Finally, choose for yourself, concerning the matter, that counsel which you recognize, by the judgment of reason, to be the more fitting choice. Furthermore, receive without any hesitation whatever our aforesaid brother the bishop may set before the royal dignity on our behalf, as though it proceeded from our own mouth; and do not hesitate to place faith in his words, as though we ourselves were uttering them. For he has carried out the legation entrusted to him so prudently and diligently that by the zeal of his integrity and discretion he has obtained from us everything which any other person ought to obtain through careful and provident vigilance [Col. 1617C].

Given at the Lateran, 12 Kalends of March [18 February].

## CCXLII. Privilege for the Church of Hamburg.  
*(Lateran, 21 February.)*

[LAPPENBERG, *Hamburg. Urkund.*, I, 200.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son HARTWIC, archbishop of Bremen, and to his successors in perpetuity.

Since, by the office of the apostolate entrusted to us by God, through which by the disposition of the heavenly judgment we preside over all Christ’s faithful, we ought to give attention to the peace and quiet of each one, we must be especially solicitous for the tranquillity of those who are endowed with pastoral dignity and promoted to the pontifical office [Col. 1617D]. For unless, by attending to their interests, we preserve intact, insofar as God permits us, their dignities and rights, and defend them by apostolic authority from the assaults of wicked people, those who have been entrusted to them by the Lord’s disposition to govern cannot truly be secure in their welfare.

Moved therefore by consideration of this matter, brother archbishop, we graciously assent to your just requests. We receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid Church over which, by God’s authoring, you are known to preside, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that Church now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future acquire, by the grant of popes, the generosity of kings or princes, the offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, by the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors [Col. 1618A].

Moreover, by apostolic authority we likewise confirm the immunities and boundaries: namely, from the river Elbe downstream to the Ocean Sea, and upstream through the province of the Slavs to the river Peene, and along its course to the eastern sea; likewise, the cultivated and uncultivated marshes situated within or beside the Elbe, as Louis, the emperor of good memory, formerly reasonably granted them to the Church of Hamburg and as that Church possesses them.

We decree, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Roland, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, 9 Kalends of March [21 February], in the seventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1158, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian IV [Col. 1618B].

## CCXLIII. Privilege for the monastery of Jerichow.  
*(Lateran, February.)*

[Ibid., p. 202.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons ISFRID, provost of the Church of Jerichow, and his brethren, present and future, professing the canonical life, in perpetuity.

The authority of the apostolic see, which by the Lord’s bounty we serve, and the unity of fraternal charity urge us to assent to the just desires of religious persons and graciously to grant their reasonable petitions [Col. 1618C]. Accordingly, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests. We receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing.

First, we decree that the canonical order which is known to have been instituted in that place according to the Rule of the Lord and blessed Augustine and the ordinances of the Premonstratensian brethren shall be preserved there inviolably for all time. Further, whatever possessions and goods the same church now justly and canonically possesses, or may, by God’s favor, acquire in the future through papal grants, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors [Col. 1618D]. Among these we have thought fit to specify by name:

The estate upon which the aforesaid church stands, with all its appurtenances, which Hartwic—then provost and now archbishop of Bremen—by consent of his mother, Countess Richarda, granted to you from his patrimony out of devotion, together with the three villages, namely Wulkow, Wulkow, and Nitzentorp, also called Gardekin; two manses at Erkschleve for the lights of the same church, from which an annual rent of twenty-five solidi is paid to you; the manor of Burcwardo Kobelitz, also called Marienburgk, situated within the old rampart, with its pond and the village likewise called Kobelitz, with tithes and all its revenues [Col. 1619A]; the tithe of the village of Jerkow; the tithes of the villages of Wulkow, Wulkow, and Netzentorp; also the parish church of the village of Jerchow with its appurtenances; and the income of all tithes belonging by right to the diocesan bishop, which that diocesan bishop has reasonably granted you from cultivated and uncultivated lands lawfully accruing to your ownership, as is known to be contained in his written instrument concerning this matter. We confirm these things for you by apostolic authority.

We further decree that no advocate shall under any circumstances be appointed in your church except one whom the brethren by common consent have determined should be chosen. We decree that the archpriesthood of the whole territory—whose boundary is the river Elbe on the west, the river Havel on the east, the river Strumen on the south, and the final boundary of Buckwardi Klitzen on the north [Col. 1619B]—which was granted to you by Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, of good memory, shall be held in perpetuity by your church. You may receive into your church free and unfettered clerics or laypersons and retain them without any objection.

We also prohibit any of your brethren, after making profession in that place, from leaving the cloister on any frivolous pretext without the permission of his prior; and no one may dare retain a departing brother without a common letter from the canons.

We decree, therefore, etc.

## CCXLIV. To William, bishop of Le Mans.—He entrusts to him the settlement of a controversy long disputed between the Cluniac monks and the canons of Périgueux concerning the church of Roche-Boviscurt.  
*(Lateran, 27 February.)*

[BOUQUET, *Rec.*, XV, 691.]

[Col. 1619C]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother WILLIAM, bishop of Le Mans, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Concerning the case of Roche-Boviscurt, which is contested between the Cluniac monks and William of Atta-Faia, we have learned plainly how much labor each party has undertaken and how often each has approached the apostolic see concerning the same business; and we believe that this has become known to many. Since on this occasion the case itself was argued in our presence, yet could not receive its due conclusion through us because neither party was able to prove what it alleged, we have finally thought it proper to entrust the same case to your discretion. Thus, after both parties have been summoned to appear before you at a suitable place and time: if W. or other clerics who believe that they have some right in that church can lawfully demonstrate in your presence that they were ordained canons in the aforesaid church before the Cluniac monks were expelled from it, unless they were ordained to other churches [Col. 1620A] or can lawfully be excluded from judgment on other grounds, admit them to litigate concerning proprietary right and bring the case to its proper conclusion. Nevertheless, preserve the privileges granted by the apostolic see to the monastery of Cluny and the instruments of that monastery. If the clerics should prevail in the case concerning proprietary right, the church must return to the monks’ hands after their deaths, so that the privileges may retain their force. But other clerics introduced into the same church after the expulsion of the Cluniac brethren, and those appointed to other churches pursuant to the tenor of the letters of our predecessor Pope Eugenius, of holy memory [Note: For the letters of Eugenius, see *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXX.], and of our own letters, shall by no means be admitted.

But if the aforesaid W. and the others delay coming [Col. 1620B], or perhaps cannot prosecute the case, then, without impediment of appeal, absolve the aforesaid monks by authority of the apostolic see from their claim; adjudge the church itself to them; impose perpetual silence upon the others; and cause the monks to possess it peacefully.

Given at the Lateran, 3 Kalends of March [27 February]. [Note: In the year 1159, as may be seen in the letters of William of Le Mans below.]

## CCXLV. To the monks of Roche-Boviscurt.—He states that their case with the canons of Périgueux has been entrusted to the judgment of the bishop of Le Mans for settlement.  
*(Lateran, 27 February.)*

[Ibid.]

[Col. 1620C]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the prior and monks of Roche-Boviscurt [Note: There is another letter of Adrian to William of Alta-Faia, of the same purport and composed in the same words.], greeting and apostolic blessing.

Concerning the case contested between you and William of Alta-Faia, we have learned plainly how much labor each party has undertaken and how often it has approached the apostolic see concerning the same business; and we believe that this has become known to many. Since on this occasion the case itself was argued in our presence, yet could not receive its due conclusion through us, because neither you nor the other party could prove what it alleged, we have finally thought it proper to entrust the same case to our venerable brother, the bishop of Le Mans.

Accordingly, we command you by apostolic writings that, when you are summoned by him concerning this matter, you shall appear before him. If the aforesaid W. and other clerics who believe that they possess some right in your church can lawfully demonstrate in his presence that they were ordained canons in that same church before you were expelled from it—unless they were ordained to other churches or can lawfully be excluded from judgment on other grounds—he shall admit them to litigate concerning proprietary right and bring the case to its proper conclusion. Nevertheless, the privileges granted by the apostolic see to your monastery and the instruments of that monastery are to be preserved. Yet if [Col. 1621A] the clerics prevail in the case concerning proprietary right, the church must return to your hands after their deaths, so that the privileges may at last retain their force. But those introduced into the same church after your expulsion, and those appointed to other churches according to the tenor of the letters of our predecessor Pope Eugenius, of holy memory, and of our own letters, shall by no means be admitted.

If the aforementioned William and the others delay coming at the summons of our same brother the bishop, or perhaps cannot prosecute the case, he shall, without impediment of appeal, absolve you by authority of the apostolic see from their claim; adjudge the church itself to you; impose perpetual silence upon them; and cause you to possess that same church peacefully.

[Col. 1621B]

Given at the Lateran, 3 Kalends of March [27 February].

## CCXLVI. He confirms the possessions of the monastery of Saint Magloire at Paris.  
*(Lateran, 4 March.)*

[*Gallia Christiana*, vol. VII, *Instr.*, 67.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, abbot of the monastery of Saint Magloire at Paris, and his brethren, present and future, professing the monastic life, in perpetuity.

Apostolic protection should be present for those choosing the religious life, lest perhaps an assault of any rashness either turn them from their purpose or, God forbid, weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore [Col. 1621C], beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests. We receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by this present privilege. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or that you may by the Lord’s favor acquire in the future through grants of popes, generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify by name:

The land adjoining the monastery on both sides, free and undisturbed; the church of Saint Magloire [Col. 1621D] in the city of Paris with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Saturninus of Nogent with its appurtenances; the church of Blessed Mary of Reiis with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Denis and Holy Cross of Briis [lacuna]; and the tithe of Unvillaris and the tithe of Sancivri. In the diocese of Chartres: the church of Saint Lawrence with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Nicholas with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Denis of Madriaco with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Martin of Basethis with the whole tithe belonging to it; the church of Saints Cornelius and Cyprian of Novalibus; the church of Saint Peter of Pugneis with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Bartholomew of Bussoria with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Martin of Grosso Robore with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Martin of Galleis [Col. 1622A] with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Martin of Marolio with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Martin of Bainna with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Stephen of Vernoilo with its appurtenances; the church of Orvillaris with its appurtenances; and the church of Saint Cyricus of Baiolo with its appurtenances.

In Brittany: the church of Saints Peter and Paul and Saint Magloire in the district of Léhon, with the churches and chapels belonging to it—namely, the church of Saint Peter of Juram with its chapels; the church of Saint Juvat with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Judoc with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Lawrence of Treveron with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Magloire of the castle of Trivan with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Cophilus [Scophilus] above the sea with its appurtenances; and the meadows which Louis, illustrious king of the Franks [Col. 1622B], lawfully granted you in the marshes of Saint Opportuna. The tithe of the whole wood called Eulina, and the tithe of the pannage of that same wood. No layman, monk, or other person may take from you the tithe and the villages which you have held quietly and peacefully for forty years.

We decree that no bishop or any other person shall exercise unjust or undue exactions in the aforesaid churches belonging to you. In the parish churches which you hold, you may choose priests and present the chosen persons to the bishop; if they are found suitable, the bishop shall commit to them the care of souls. Those priests shall answer to the bishop concerning the care of the people, but to you concerning temporal matters [Col. 1622C]. If they refuse to do so, you shall have free authority, by apostolic grant, to withdraw from them the temporalities which they hold from you.

Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors, no one shall be placed over it by any trickery of surreptitious procurement or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren’s counsel, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict. We also prohibit any bishop from consecrating your churches without the assent of the abbot of that place. Further, no one shall presume to demand tithes from you of your newly cleared lands, cultivated by your own hands or at your own expense, or of the produce of your animals. We likewise grant that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may hinder the devotion and final will [Col. 1622D] of those who choose to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or under interdict; nevertheless, the right of the parish churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken is preserved.

We decree, therefore, etc.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church. Amen, amen.  
I, P., bishop of Tusculum.  
I, Hubald, priest-cardinal of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem.  
I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia.  
I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia.  
I, Walter, bishop of Albano [Col. 1623A].  
I, Abbo, deacon-cardinal of Saint George at the Golden Veil.  
I, Hyacinth, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin.

Given through the hand of Roland, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, 4 Nones of March [4 March], seventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1158, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian IV.

## CCXLVII. He receives under protection the monastery of the Valley of Saint Mary and confirms its possessions and privileges.  
*(Lateran, 4 March.)*

[*Orig. Guelf.*, III, 535.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons DUDELIN, abbot of the monastery of the Valley of Saint Mary [Col. 1623B], and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

Apostolic protection should be present for those choosing the religious life, lest perhaps an assault of any rashness either turn them from their purpose or, God forbid, weaken the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests. Following the example of our predecessor Pope Eugenius, of holy memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing.

First, we decree that the monastic order established there according to the fear of God, the Rule of blessed Benedict, and the ordinances of the Cistercian brethren shall be preserved there inviolably for all time [Col. 1623C]. Further, whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future acquire through papal grants, the generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, by the Lord’s favor, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify by name:

The place itself, namely the Valley of Saint Mary, devoutly offered to almighty God by the illustrious Frederick, count palatine, for the establishment of religious life there, together with twenty manses, meadows, pastures, and woods belonging to those manses; the manor called Steinthorp, with its appurtenances, namely pastures, meadows, and woods; by the gift of Countess Luchardis, the manor of Liutestorph with its appurtenances and tithes; the fourth part of the wood called Lapenwolt; by the gift of Marchioness Ermenchardis, four manses at Liutestorph with their appurtenances and revenues, and all that has been exchanged in that village with the brethren of the church of Walbech by the founder of the aforesaid church; by the gift of Countess Hoda, four manses at Aventorp with all their revenues; by the gift of Burchard and Willer, three and a half manses at Brandesleve; by the gift of Duke Henry, one mansi with woodland in that same [Col. 1624A] village; by the gift of Ludolf, seven jugera in the same village, with the assent of his heir, namely Frederick of Amfrideslove; four jugera and a meadow, purchased from Burchard of Gersleve.

Likewise, by the gift of the aforementioned Frederick, count palatine, half a mansi in that same village; by the gift of William of Ancersleve, three manses in that same village, and all that has been exchanged there with the sisters of the church of Quidenburg and of Wallebhec; a mill and half a mansi with a building plot, purchased at Greater Brandesleve; four manses at Offensleve and four manses at Mammendorp; half a mansi at Cowelle, in which the aforesaid count palatine granted the church half a mansi; by the gift of Countess Lucardis, two manses bought for a price in the same [Col. 1624B] village; by the gift of Albert, count palatine, son of that same countess, two manses at Nortgermesleve; by the gift of Frederick, ministerial of the aforesaid prince, half a mansi at Hoetmersleve; by the gift of Agnes, daughter of the duke of Linborch, three manses—one at Lesser Brandesleve and two at Wadentorp; by the gift of Beatrice, four manses at Ortorp; by the gift of Count Volrad, two manses in the same village and the tithe of your outlying estate at Brandesleve; by the gift of Eric, one mansi at Winninche; by the gift of the aforesaid Countess Lucardis, one building plot at Santorp with a certain woodland belonging to it; by the gift of the aforementioned count palatine, two manses, one at Somerstorp and another at Ekenbardenleve and Othmersleve; by the gift of Duke Henry, the village called Bardenbeke [Col. 1624C] with its appurtenances, namely meadows, pastures, and woods.

Likewise, by the gift of Agnes, daughter of the duke of Linburche, the fourth part of the woodland called Lapenwolt, Haskenroht, and Biscobroht, with all its appurtenances, namely meadows, pastures, streams, and woodland; moreover, the village adjoining that estate, with the tithe of that hamlet, and the wood called Lobectze. Halberstadt’s bishop canonically granted all these things to you at the request of his ministerial Notger of Godersleve, who held those same properties from him by right of benefice. Further, no one shall presume to demand tithes from you of your newly cleared lands cultivated by your own hands or at your own expense, or from the produce of your animals.

[Col. 1624D]

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things be kept whole and undiminished, for the benefit in every way of the uses of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving, of course, the authority of the apostolic see and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If anyone, therefore, etc.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Roland, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, 4 Nones of March [4 March], seventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1158, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian IV.

[Col. 1625A]

Among others, it was signed by:

Hyacinth, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin.

## CCXLVIII. To H. [Note: Hugh of Campo-Florido.] the elect and the chapter of the Church of Soissons.—On behalf of Vitto, dean of Soissons.

[MARTENE, *Ampl. Collect.*, II, 653.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons H., elect, and the whole chapter of the Church of Soissons, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We provide very usefully for churches when we enlarge ecclesiastical benefices for honorable men, especially churchmen and learned persons. In view of this consideration [Col. 1625B], we have by apostolic authority granted and invested our beloved son Vitto, dean of your church, with the prebend which you, son elect, are known hitherto to have held in that church, so that henceforth that prebend shall belong to the office of the deanery. For it was fitting that one who held the office of dean in a church should have sufficient revenues from which he might be honorably and suitably maintained. Therefore, by apostolic writings we command you to hold this grant valid and not presume at any time to disturb it.

Given at the Lateran, 3 Nones of March [5 March].

## CCXLIX. He receives under protection the monastery of Saint Clement of Pescara and confirms its goods and privileges.  
*(Lateran, 14 March.)*

[MANSI, *Concil.*, XXI, 827.]

[Col. 1625C]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons LEONATUS, abbot of the monastery of Saint Clement on the island of Pescara, called the Golden House, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

Both the force of equity and the order of reason require that just petitioners be granted the effect of their requests, especially when piety supports their will and truth does not abandon it. Accordingly, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests. We receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery [Col. 1625D], where the body of blessed Clement, pope and martyr, rests and in which you are devoted to divine service, following the example of our predecessor Pope Leo, of happy memory; and we fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree, etc.

We further forbid any bishop to hold a synod there. You may receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and ordinations of monks or clerics to be promoted to holy orders, from whichever bishop you prefer. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors [Col. 1626A], no one shall be placed over it by any trickery of surreptitious procurement or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of the brethren, shall provide to be elected according to God and the Rule of blessed Benedict, etc.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed.  
I, Gregory, bishop of Sabina.  
I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia.  
I, Julius, bishop of Palestrina.  
I, Walter, bishop of Albano.  
I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina.  
I, Hubald, priest-cardinal of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem.  
I, Octavian, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Cecilia.  
I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saints John and Peter [Note: correct: Paul], of the title of Pammachius [Col. 1626B].  
I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saints Sylvester and Martin.  
I, Hildebrand, priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles.  
I, Guido, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Callistus.  
I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia.  
I, Bonadies, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Chrysogonus.  
I, William, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Peter in Chains [Col. 1626C].  
I, Oddo, deacon-cardinal of Saint George at the Golden Veil.  
I, Hyacinth, deacon-cardinal of Saint Mary in Cosmedin.  
I, Ardicio, deacon-cardinal of Saint Theodore.  
I, Cinthius, deacon-cardinal of Saint Adrian.  
I, Peter, deacon-cardinal of Saint Eustachius beside the temple of Agrippa.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Roland, priest-cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, 2 Ides of March [14 March], sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1158, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Adrian IV.

## CCL. He receives the monastery of Muri with its appurtenances into apostolic protection and confirms its goods and rights.  
*(Lateran, 28 March.)*

[GERBERT, *Hist. Nig. Sil.*, III, 91.]

[Col. 1626D]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons CONO, abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin at Muri, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

The authority of our office admonishes and invites us to labor for the condition of churches and, with God’s help, to provide beneficially for their quiet and tranquillity [Col. 1627A]. For it is recognized as worthy and consonant with honor that we who, by the Lord’s disposition, have been appointed to their governance should both protect them from the malice of wicked people and fortify them with the patronage of blessed Peter and the apostolic see. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously assent to your just requests. We receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and fortify it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods the same monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may in the future acquire, through papal grants, the generosity of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful [Col. 1627B], or other lawful means, through the working of the Lord, shall remain secure and unimpaired to you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit to specify by name:

The church at Hermenstwillare; the church of Bousb; the church of Stanes; the church of Rische; the church of Pohwilo; the church of Egenwilare; the church of Rordorf; the church of Urtechun; the church of Tellewilare; and the church of Cohelinchon. When a general interdict has been imposed upon the land, you may celebrate divine offices with closed doors, without ringing bells, with excommunicated and interdicted persons excluded, and in a subdued voice. Upon the death of you, the present abbot of that place, or of any of your successors [Col. 1627C], no one shall be placed over it by any trickery of surreptitious procurement or by force, except one whom the brethren by common consent, or the sounder part of them, shall provide to be elected according to the fear of God and the Rule of blessed Benedict.

We decree, therefore, that no person whatsoever may rashly disturb the aforesaid monastery, take away its possessions, retain possessions taken away, diminish them, or harass it by any vexations; but that all things be kept whole and unimpaired, for the benefit in every way of the uses of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the apostolic see and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. If anyone, by any presumption, violates this privilege issued by the apostolic see, he shall be subject to the bond of anathema [Col. 1627D].

If anyone, therefore, in the future, etc. But to all those of the same place, etc.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church.  
I, Gregory, bishop of Sabina.  
I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia.  
I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina.  
I, Walter, bishop of Albano.

Given at the Lateran, through the hand of Roland, priest-cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, in the seventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1159, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Pope Adrian IV.

## CCLI. He receives the monastery of Prüfening under protection and confirms its goods and rights. (Lateran, April 1.)

[HUND, *Metropolis of Salzburg*, III, 134.]

[Col. 1628A]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Erbo, abbot of the monastery of St. George of Prüfening, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, for ever.

The care of the universal Church has been entrusted to us by God, the provider of all good things, so that we may love religious persons and strive by every means to promote religion pleasing to God. For no service is ever rendered acceptable to God unless, proceeding from the root of charity, it is preserved in the purity of religion. Therefore all lovers of the Christian faith ought to cherish religion and diligently foster venerable places, together with the persons devoted in them to divine service, so that they may not be harassed by the troubles of evil men or afflicted by burdensome exactions. For this reason, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously consent to your just requests; and, following the example of our predecessor Pope Eugenius, of holy memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery of St. George at Prüfening, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever goods and possessions have been justly and canonically bestowed upon your monastery by Otto, bishop of Bamberg of blessed memory, and by Egilbert and Eberhard, his [Col. 1628B] successors, and whatever may hereafter, by God’s grace, be conferred upon that place by their successors or by other faithful people, in like manner—whether by grants of pontiffs, liberality of kings, gifts of princes, offerings of the faithful, or by other reasonable means—shall remain secure and inviolate for you and your successors.

Furthermore, no one shall presume to exact tithes from you upon the newly cleared lands which you cultivate with your own hands or at your own expense, or upon the fodder of your animals. We also add that, in the churches or chapels situated upon the land of your monastery, you may choose honorable priests, who shall be presented by you to the bishop; and, if they are suitable, they shall receive from that bishop the care of souls, rendering account to him in spiritual matters and to you in temporal matters. If a general interdict is imposed in that land, then, with excommunicated and interdicted persons excluded from your church and its doors closed, you may celebrate the divine offices in a low voice. We also grant that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final will of those who determine to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted, while preserving nevertheless the rights of those churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, to take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all shall be preserved whole and intact for the benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If therefore in the future, etc. But to all, etc.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Roland, priest-cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, on the Kalends of April, in the seventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1159, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Pope Adrian IV.

## CCLII. He receives the monastery of St. John of Blaubeuren under protection and confirms its possessions and privileges. (Lateran, April 6.)

[PETRI, *Church of Swabia*, 180.]

[Col. 1629B]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Wernher, abbot of the monastery of St. John the Baptist, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, for ever.

Those who choose the religious life ought to have apostolic protection at hand, lest some assault of rashness either turn them aside from their purpose or—God forbid—break the strength of sacred religion. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, graciously consenting to your just requests and following in the footsteps of our predecessor Pope Urban, of happy memory, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid monastery, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that monastery now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by God’s grace, acquire through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit expressly to name the following:

The tithes of the church called Sussen and of the other called Laichingen, canonically granted to you; and all that Counts Henry and Hugh, and Countess Adelheid, have reasonably bestowed upon you. Count Hugh shall administer the advocacy of the aforesaid church while he lives. Should he perhaps prove harmful to the monastery, remove him and appoint another whom you judge useful. Moreover, under threat of anathema, we prohibit markets contrary to monastic religious life, all cohabitation of merchants, and every market transaction carried on to the detriment of the aforesaid monastery and to disturb the peace of the brethren in that monastery. If those merchants prove disobedient, no cleric in the place where the markets are held shall presume to celebrate Mass for as long as those markets continue.

In the parish churches which you hold, you may choose priests and present those chosen to the bishop. If they are found suitable, the bishop shall entrust them with the care of souls; and those priests shall be accountable to the bishop for the care of the people, but to you for temporal matters.
