You shall receive chrism, holy oil, consecrations of altars or churches, and ordinations of monks promoted to holy orders from the diocesan bishop, provided that he is Catholic, enjoys the favor and communion of the Apostolic See, and is willing to provide these things freely and without improper dealing. Otherwise, you may approach whichever bishop you prefer, who, supported by our authority, shall grant what is requested. We also grant that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final will of those who determine to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted, while preserving nevertheless the rights of the parish churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

[Col. 1630B] We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid monastery, to take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all shall be preserved whole and intact for the benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop. As a token of the protection received from the Apostolic See, you shall pay one Byzantine coin annually to us and our successors.

If therefore in the future, etc.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church, have subscribed. [Col. 1630C] (Fare well.) I, Hubald, priest-cardinal of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Roland, priest-cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, on the eighth day before the Ides of April, in the seventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1159, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Pope Adrian IV.

## CCLIII. He receives the church of Sainte-Opportune in Paris under protection and confirms its goods. (Lateran, May 12.)

[FÉLIBIEN, *History of Paris*, III, 33.]

[Col. 1630D]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the canons of Sainte-Opportune, present and future, canonically appointed, for ever.

A pious petition of the will ought to be fulfilled by a favorable outcome, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the benefit sought may undoubtedly acquire strength. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously consent to your just requests; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by God’s grace, acquire through grants [Col. 1631A] of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit expressly to name the following:

The Church of the Holy Innocents, and the watery land called the Marshes, lying near the city of Paris, which Theobald, formerly bishop of Paris and of blessed memory, and our dearest son Louis, illustrious king of the French, are known to have confirmed to you and your church and strengthened by their writings. We also confirm by apostolic authority the *capiceria* of that church, as the same bishop reasonably adjudged it to you.

[Col. 1631B] We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all shall be preserved whole for the benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, useful in every way, saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If therefore in the future, etc.

But to all in that place, etc.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Gregory, bishop of Sabina. I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. I, Julius, bishop of Palestrina. [Col. 1631C] I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Hubald, priest-cardinal of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Astald, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Prisca. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saints Sylvester and Martin. I, Bonadies, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Chrysogonus. I, Hildebrand, priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. I, Odo, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. [Col. 1631D] I, Hyacinth, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Cosmedin. I, Arditio, cardinal-deacon of Saint Theodore. I, Boso, cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of Saint Eustace near the temple of Agrippa. I, Raymond, cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary in Via Lata.

Given at the Lateran through the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and scribe of the lord pope, on the fourth day before the Ides of May, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1159, in the seventh indiction, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Pope Adrian IV.

## CCLIII bis. He confirms the settlement made between Hugh, abbot of Prémontré, and Walter, bishop of Laon. (Tusculum, May 30.)

[LE PAIGE, *Library of Prémontré*, 433.]

[Col. 1632A]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Hugh, abbot, and the brethren of the Church of Prémontré: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Those arrangements which are reasonably established by means of a settlement or agreement between ecclesiastical men ought to remain stable; and, in order that they may possess greater firmness in the future, they must be fortified by the protection of the Apostolic See. Therefore, [Col. 1632B] beloved sons in the Lord, granting favorable consent to your just requests, we confirm by apostolic authority and strengthen by the protection of this present writing the agreement made between you and our venerable brother Walter, bishop of Laon, concerning the possessions set down below. It was reasonably arranged, with the consent of both parties, through the mediation of our dearest son Louis, illustrious king of the French, our venerable brother Samson, archbishop of Reims and legate of the Apostolic See, and certain other bishops and princes. This agreement, as is known from the document made concerning it, is as follows:

It is the duty of pastoral office to provide for the peace and quiet of religious persons, to attest what has reasonably been done, and, lest it be obscured or weakened by any cloud of forgetfulness, to commit it to writing and convey it to the knowledge of posterity. Therefore I, Walter, called by God’s grace bishop of Laon, wish it to be known to both future and present persons that in our time a dispute arose between us and Hugh, abbot, and the brethren of the Church of Prémontré concerning the possessions listed below, because episcopal goods seemed to us to have been alienated without proper order. At last, through the mediation of the king of the French, the archbishop of Reims, bishops, and princes, the controversy reached a settlement in the following manner.

The brethren of Prémontré, so that, their privileges and possessions preserved, they might acquire firm and perpetual peace, handed over to us and our successors for ever three hundred pounds of revenues for the restoration of the estate, together with five hundred sheep, twenty cows, twelve beasts of burden, and seven pigs. We, however, granted to them the free and peaceful possession henceforth of everything about which the dispute had arisen and which they had held in the time of our predecessors Bartholomew and Walter; and, with the common consent of our chapter, we confirmed it by the authority of the present writing. We have also thought fit to specify these things individually by their proper names:

The valley of Prémontré, in which the church stands, free and released from every exaction by any person, together with the vineyards, lands, woods, pastures, meadows, streams, and mills which they have constructed there; and the slopes of the hills on every side, with the adjoining valleys, from the streams toward Vois as far as Hubertipont, Molnantvoisin, the valley of Rohard, and Halierpré. Within these boundaries, in that part where formerly there was common pasture beyond the stream toward Molnantvoisin, it is now occupied by ponds and mills. The brethren pay us two solidi annually on the feast of St. Remigius.

The estate of Fontinelles, free except for six denarii paid to the canons of St. Mary of Laon for the small tithe; one ploughland given by the bishop; and land capable of receiving fourteen *galetae* of seed, from the alms of Brother Udo, together with one modius of grain of the small measure payable to the mill of Tacerel. Also, other land at Belmont, capable of receiving about two and a half modii of seed by the measure of Laon and owing us annually thirteen and one-half denarii, gathered from the alms of Harduin, Gerard, Rufus, Emehard and his brother Thomas, Dordo, Ragner, Harduin, and Geoffrey of Guez; likewise a field capable of receiving a modius of seed and paying Hermentrude of La Ferté two solidi; nine meadows, amounting to about twelve mower’s strips: namely, two meadows of the brothers of Udo at Bruil; two meadows of the same toward Pinon; likewise at Bril, two meadows from Bertrada and Ralph Cholet, and the meadow of Hugh Lupus; also the meadow of Gelric of Montarcenne.

Two parts of the mill of Baretel, and a fifth part of the land for guarding that mill, with the adjoining fishpond and meadow; the mill of Guez and the pond which Ermengard gave, subject to an annual rent of four modii by the small measure; and a garden owing us one-half denarius, and a meadow owing two denarii to the Church of St. John of Bourg. The estate of Penencourt, comprising seven modii of seed by the measure of Laon, gathered from the alms of many persons: Amsard, Eilde, Gelric, Constantius, Walter, Hermund, Widelo, Odo, Robert, Berenger, Gelric, Robert Hugh, Dodo, Thomas, Robert, Elvidis, Berard, Berinvidis, Lauwin, Anselm, Dudo, and Terric.

Also the adjoining vineyards at Gislenval: Elwin’s vineyard; Legardis’s vineyard in the place called “at the two fields”; Hersendis’s vineyard; Renold’s vineyard at Ocemont; Theodoric’s vineyard at the winepress; and the vineyard gathered from the alms of Bernuidis, Ralph Spailart, Dudetiche, Hugh, Reinald, Roland, Ysembert, Hermene, Hermund, Brimel, Walter, and Alda. At Solarium, the vineyard of Hanimi and Roland; at Rahier, Dodo’s vineyard; at Marval, the three vineyards of Robert and Gualric, and the vineyard gathered from the alms of Warner, Thomas, Robert, Baldwin, Matilda, Widelo, Emehard and Thomas, brothers, Robert, Aggeus, Rainer, Odo and Gerard, brothers, Odo, Aggeus, Anselm, and Odo; in the ditch, Alda’s vineyard; in the *quartariae*, the vineyard of Ralph and Hugh; at Larris, the vineyard of Gelric and Robert; at Lomprei, Aggeus’s vineyard; at Lauis, Thomas’s vineyard; above the spring, the vineyard of Robert and Gelric; at the willow, the vineyard of Rascendis and the sons of Robert Cordele; at Warponval, Ralph’s vineyard; at Gerardon, Hermundis’s vineyard; at Larris, half of Ydo’s vineyard; at Cantaplora, the vineyard formerly of Odo; at Buimont, the two vineyards of Terric and Hugh.

Twelve portions of meadow: namely, above Aquila, the two meadows of Pagan and Brother Robert; at the bridge, the meadow of Robert Camec; at Toluci, two meadows of Brother Ydo and the meadow of Odo, son of Amelina; at Commupe and Bu, two mower’s strips of meadow belonging to Alda and Robert Catus; at Buimont, the meadow of Stephen and, at Escorni, the meadow of Brother Gelric; at the Golden Ford, two meadows of Robert Cordele. The wood outside Broiencourt, for which, with two vineyards from the meadow, they pay us nine and one-half denarii of good coin and twelve sextarii of wine; half a modius of wine from the men, and three [sextarii] from Ralph Spailart; likewise half a modius at Latre from the sons of Aggeus.

The estate of Merlin and its dependent vineyards: namely, the vineyard of Briars, the vineyard of Cohart, the vineyard of Lestolt, and the vineyard on the rock of Hadua, with the field and wood of Balescans, and the field at Kartaria and the wood at the knot, which had belonged to Brother Liger and his heirs, converts in the Church of Prémontré. The free enclosure of Lizy and Descapholt, acquired for the church both by alms and purchase.

At Escorni: two vineyards from the alms of Brother Udo; Baldwin’s vineyard; Aggeus’s vineyard; the vineyard of Alberic of Rua; and the vineyard of John Albus. At Esteroi, Gislebert’s vineyard; at Caperon, Burdin’s vineyard; on the rock of Hadua, the vineyard of Bernuidis and the vineyard of Albert Rua; at Laperche, Udo’s vineyard and three vineyards of Gerard—one at Valorcenois, another at Butem, and the third at Biars. Likewise at Biars, the vineyard gathered from Ermengard’s, Gerard’s, Ydo’s, and Ralph’s alms; in the valley of Valaurigny, Rascendis’s vineyard at Fulcherolles and Duda’s vineyard; in the valley itself, Robert’s vineyard; in the valley of Monbavain, Hemund’s vineyard.

About six meadows, comprising six mower’s strips: namely, at Bruil, the meadow of Gerard of Merli, owing us one denarius; at the new mill, two mower’s strips of meadow owing us six and one-half denarii, and half a mill-site from Brother Robert of Montarcenne; at Bulipré, the meadow of Brother Hugh of Testam; at Tanecel, the meadow of the knight Odo; one field at Lizy; two parts of the fields in the valley of Merli; the free estate of Vercigny; and one ploughland which Bishop Bartholomew originally granted them. Also about two other ploughlands, which, as the number of brethren increased, he himself added, partly from cultivated and partly from uncultivated land, with a meadow subject to a rent of two solidi; there he also ordered a church with an atrium to be built for the commemoration of himself and his successors. Also another newly cleared land made by the brethren after the custom of the other inhabitants, subject to a rent of two solidi; the mill of Achery, and fishing in any water whenever they wish; and one holding of land, paying us annually a modius of grain by the measure of Laon; and an estate free from every exaction, without right and judicial duel; one ploughland on the hill of Caspiac, given by the bishop; two modii of wine-rent on Mont Nantol; the land of Alberic and Beatrice of Bertolcourt; on Mont Brai, the land of Hersendis of Brai and her sons; two parts of the mill of Aquila, subject to an annual rent of ten solidi of good coin, payable to the treasurer of the Church of St. Mary of Laon.

In order, therefore, that all these things may obtain the strength of perpetual stability, we have considered them to be confirmed by the authority of the Apostolic See and fortified by the protection of this present writing.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever [Col. 1635B] to violate this charter of our confirmation or to oppose it in any way.

But if anyone presumes to attempt this, and, having been warned a second and third time, does not correct his presumption by suitable satisfaction, let him incur the indignation of almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and we decree that he shall be bound by the bond of excommunication. Amen, amen, amen.

Sealed:

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church.

And a little lower:

I, G[regory], bishop of Sabina. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto, of the title of Santa Rufina. [Col. 1635C] I, Walter, bishop of Albano. I, Astald, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Prisca. I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saints Sylvester and Martin. I, Odo, cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Arditio, cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint Theodore. I, Cinthius, cardinal-deacon of Saint Adrian. I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint Eustace near the temple of Agrippa.

Given at Tusculum through the hand of Hermann, subdeacon and scribe of the lord pope, on the third day before the Kalends of June, [Col. 1635D] in the seventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1159, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Pope Adrian IV.

## CCLIV. To Emperor Frederick—on the twofold injury inflicted by him upon the Apostolic See. (Palestrina, June 24.)

[MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 796.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Frederick, emperor: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Just as the divine law promises length of life to those who honor their parents, so it imposes the sentence of death upon those who curse father and mother. Moreover, the voice of Truth teaches us that “everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled” (Matt. X). Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, we are not a little astonished at your wisdom, since in the letter sent to us you appear not to show blessed Peter and the Holy Roman Church entrusted to him the reverence you owe. You place your name before ours, thereby incurring the mark of insolence—indeed, not to say arrogance.

What shall I say of the fidelity promised and sworn by you to blessed Peter and to us? How do you observe it, when you demand homage from bishops—those who are gods and all sons of the Most High—exact fidelity from them, join their consecrated hands to your own hands, and, openly made hostile to us, close not only churches but also the cities of your realm against cardinals sent from our side? Come to your senses, then, come to your senses: we counsel you, for, since you have received consecration and crown from us, while you seize what has not been granted, we fear that you may lose what has been granted, to the harm of your nobility.

Given at Palestrina, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July.

## CCLV. He receives the church of Utrecht under protection and confirms its goods. (Anagni, June 28.)

[MIERIS, *Cartulary*, I, 107.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Godfrey, bishop of Utrecht, and to his successors canonically appointed, in perpetual remembrance.

Since, by the office of apostleship entrusted to us by God—through which, by the Lord’s authorship, we stand above all God’s faithful—we ought to devote ourselves to the peace and tranquillity of each person, we must especially be solicitous for the repose of those endowed with pastoral dignity and raised to pontifical office. For unless, attending to their interests, we preserve their dignities and rights intact as far as we can, God permitting, and defend them by apostolic authority from the assaults of the wicked, they could not truly be solicitous for the welfare of those entrusted to their governance by the Lord’s disposition.

For this reason, venerable brother bishop in Christ, moved by your just requests, we grant favorable consent; and, in discharge of the apostolic office laid upon us by God, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid Church of Utrecht, over which you are known to preside by God’s appointment, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by God’s grace, acquire through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors. Among these we have thought fit expressly to name the following:

The county of Frisia; the castle of Enforde (variant reading: Euforde); the land of Drenthe; the nineteenth [share] in Holland; the estate of Valkenberg; Grutem in Utrecht; Marescalkerwerth (variant readings: Mareskalkerwetdh and Coppelwethe) and Coppelwetse; the castle of Benthem; Bruel of Voluho; Biddebueroke (Biddelmerbroke); and the churches of blessed Martin situated in Holland, which are known to belong to your right.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, or harass it with any vexations; but that all shall be preserved whole for the benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, useful in every way, saving in all things the authority of the Apostolic See.

If therefore, etc.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Hubald, priest-cardinal of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. [Col. 1637B] I, Hubald, bishop of Ostia. I, Bernard, bishop of Porto and Santa Rufina. I, Walter, bishop of Albano. I, Arditio, cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint Theodore. I, Boso, cardinal-deacon of the title of Saints Cosmas and Damian. I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of Saint Eustace. I, Hildebrand, priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles.

Given at Anagni through the hand of Roland, priest-cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, in the seventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1159, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Pope Adrian [Col. 1637C] IV.

From the archives of Hainaut, p. 142 verso.

## CCLVI. He receives the church of St. Mary of Rees under protection and confirms its goods. (Anagni, July 30.)

[LACOMBLET, *Charters*, I, 275.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Theobald, provost of the Church of St. Mary of Rees, and his brethren, present and future, professing the canonical life, for ever.

A pious petition of the will ought to be fulfilled by a favorable outcome, so that the sincerity of devotion may shine forth commendably and the benefit sought may undoubtedly acquire strength. Therefore, beloved sons in the Lord, we graciously consent to your just requests; and we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves the aforesaid church, in which you are devoted to divine service, and strengthen it by the privilege of this present writing. We decree that whatever possessions and goods that church now justly and canonically possesses, or may hereafter, by God’s grace, acquire through grants of pontiffs, gifts of kings or princes, offerings of the faithful, or other lawful means, shall remain firm and inviolate for you and your successors.

Furthermore, we decree that both the aforesaid church and its clerics and servants shall remain for ever in the liberty in which Anno, formerly archbishop of Cologne of good memory, is known reasonably to have placed them at the request of Countess Irmintrud, as is contained in the document made concerning it. We likewise confirm for you and your successors the power of exercising and determining legal matters over the household of that church, which Irmingard of blessed memory is known reasonably to have conferred from devotion; the tithes of the pigs of that same countess fed at Rees, Emmerich, and Stralen, as Sigewin, formerly archbishop of Cologne, is known to have confirmed to the aforesaid church; also the mint and four holdings granted by the same archbishop to supplement the prebends of your church. Whatever rights you have in Wileka, Darnouwe, and Winetre, and whatever you possess by the lawful gift of Benno, formerly bishop of Osnabrück, and Ennel, ministerial of Cologne, we likewise confirm for you and your successors. We further will that the tithes of newly cleared lands in the territory of Dager[n]ov, and the beer-grain together with one holding, as they were canonically granted to the same church by Frederick, formerly archbishop of Cologne of happy memory, and peacefully held until now, shall be preserved firm and unshaken for the oft-mentioned church in times to come.

We therefore decree that it shall be lawful for no person whatsoever rashly to disturb the aforesaid church, take away its possessions, retain those taken away, diminish them, [Col. 1638C] or harass it with any vexations; but that all shall be preserved whole and intact for the benefit of those for whose governance and support they were granted, useful in every way, saving the authority of the Apostolic See and the canonical right of the diocesan bishop.

If, therefore, in the future, any ecclesiastical or secular person knowingly attempts rashly to violate this charter of our constitution, and, having been warned a second and third time, does not correct his presumption by fitting satisfaction, let that person be deprived of the dignity of office and honor; let him know himself guilty before divine judgment for the iniquity committed; let him be separated from the most sacred body and blood of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Redeemer; and let him be subject to strict vengeance at the last judgment.

But may all who preserve the just rights of that place have the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that they may receive here the fruit of good action and find, before the strict Judge, the rewards of eternal peace. Amen, amen, amen.

I, Adrian, bishop of the Catholic Church. I, Gregory, bishop of Sabina. I, Bernard, bishop of the Church of Porto. I, Walter, bishop of Albano. I, Hubald, priest-cardinal of the title of Holy Cross in Jerusalem. I, Hildebrand, priest-cardinal of the basilica of the Twelve Apostles. [Col. 1639A] I, John, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Anastasia. I, Oddo, cardinal-deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil. I, Odo, cardinal-deacon of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. I, Peter, cardinal-deacon of Saint Eustace near the temple of Agrippa.

Given at Anagni through the hand of Roland, priest-cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and chancellor, on the third day before the Kalends of August, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1159, in the seventh indiction, in the fifth year of the pontificate of Pope Adrian IV.

## CCLVII. He receives the monastery of Reichersberg under protection and confirms its goods. (Anagni, August 16.)

[HUND, *Metropolis of Salzburg*, III, 238.]

[Col. 1639B]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Gerhoh, provost of the Church of Reichersberg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Both the force of equity and the order of reason require that effect be granted to just petitioners. Therefore, beloved son Gerhoh in the Lord, giving favorable consent to your petition, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and ourselves that church, together with all the goods which it now justly and canonically possesses or may hereafter, by God’s favor, acquire through lawful means. In particular, we confirm by apostolic authority and strengthen by the protection of this present writing Munsture and Steine, [Col. 1639C] with all their appurtenances, for that church, as our venerable brother Eberhard, bishop of Bamberg, is known reasonably to have given them in exchange; and the parish of Munsture, which our venerable brother Conrad, bishop of Passau, granted to the Church of Reichersberg by reasonable provision.

We also grant that burial in that place shall be free, so that no one may oppose the devotion and final will of those who determine to be buried there, unless they are excommunicated or interdicted, while preserving nevertheless the rights of the parish churches from which the bodies of the dead are taken.

Therefore let no person whatsoever be permitted to violate this charter [Col. 1639D] of our protection, confirmation, and grant, or oppose it in any way. But if anyone presumes to attempt this and, having been warned a second and third time, does not amend his offence by fitting satisfaction, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of His blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and that he is to be bound by the bond of excommunication.

Given at Anagni, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September.

CCLVIII. (Lateran, March 19.)

[PERTZ, *Archiv* IV, 428.]

[Col. 1640A]

[Note: [Col. 1639D] *Dubia*.] He writes to H(ilinus) of Trier, A(rnold) of Mainz, F(rederick) of Cologne, and all their suffragans that “a necessary division must be made between spirit and soul, between themselves and King (Frederick), whose portion lies outside the Lord’s inheritance; for the schism which he has stirred up against us will rebound upon his own head.” For, he says, at his first entrance, when he had met with us concerning his advancement through the Duke of Saxony and through you two metropolitans, the one of Trier and the late one of Cologne, you know whether he fulfilled what he promised—indeed, he stirred the whole City against us, because he laid upon our neck the blood of the Romans which he abundantly shed against us. We shall publicly strike him with an anathema. Behold, one greater than Jeroboam is here: he seeks to impose upon you the yoke of his iniquity and to draw you into the ruin of his condemnation.---He boasts that he is our equal, as though our power were feared, embraced, and loved only in his own little corner, namely the German kingdom, and not equally in other kingdoms.---Was not the empire transferred from the kingdom of the Greeks to the Alemanni, so that the king of the Germans was not called emperor until he had been consecrated by the apostolic see? Mark the words: before consecration, merely king; after consecration, however, Augustus and emperor. Whence, then, does he have the empire except from us? Through us he rules.---This man says that we transferred Viterbo from the royal chamber into a new Rome and apostolic see, although all Apulia belongs to our authority and not to his. Therefore, we are divided: we on this side of the Alps, he beyond the Alps.---Does he not have his seat at Aachen in the Ardennes, just as we have ours at Rome? By as much as Rome is worthier and greater than Aachen, so much greater and worthier is the apostolic see than your king.---Could we not transfer the empire from the Germans back to the Greeks?---What does your king boast of, as though he could reclaim the empire from foreign nations, when he can scarcely restrain any one of his princes by force of arms? Could the German emperors pluck Rucherus [perhaps Roger] from Sicily, or from Calabria and Apulia? Could this man tear those same lands—from whom the true poetic saying is:

[Col. 1640D]

“The mountains are in labour; a ridiculous mouse will be born.” (HORACE, *Art of Poetry*, 139.)

—from the hands of his son? How will he bind Greece, when he could not [alternatively: could] subdue Dacia? When, by the force of his own prowess and the strength of his army, he was unable in the previous year to defeat the duke of Saxony and Bavaria?---We have written these things to you so that you may bring your king back to his senses.

[Col. 1641]

VARIOUS LETTERS TO ADRIAN IV.

I. The Bishops of Germany to Pope Adrian.

(MANSI, *Councils*, XXI, 792.)

[Col. 1641A]

Although we know and are certain that the Church of God, founded upon the firm rock, cannot be cast down either by winds or by the floods of storms, nevertheless we, being weaker and faint-hearted, are shaken and tremble whenever assaults of this kind occur. Therefore we have been grievously troubled and terrified by those matters which appear likely to provide the seedbed of great evil, unless God avert it, between your Holiness and your most devoted son, our lord the emperor.

Indeed, by those words contained in your letters, which you sent through your most prudent and honourable envoys, Lord Bernard and Lord Roland the chancellor, venerable cardinal-priests, the whole commonwealth of our empire was moved. The ears of the imperial power could not patiently hear them, nor could the ears of the princes endure them. All so stopped their ears that we, saving the favour of your most holy fatherhood, neither dare nor can defend those words because of the adverse interpretation of their ambiguity, or approve them by any consent, since they were unheard-of and unprecedented until these times.

Receiving and embracing with due reverence the letters which you sent us, we admonished your son, our lord the emperor, as you commanded; and from him, thanks be to God, we received such an answer as befitted a Catholic prince, in this form:

**Frederick the Emperor’s reply to the bishops of Germany.**

Two things must govern our empire: the holy laws of the emperors and the good custom of our predecessors and fathers. We neither wish nor are able to go beyond these limits of the Church; whatever departs from them we do not accept. We gladly show due reverence to our Father; we ascribe the free crown of our empire solely to divine favour; we acknowledge the first voice in the election to the Archbishop of Mainz, then what remains to the other princes according to their order; the royal [Col. 1641D] anointing to the Archbishop of Cologne, but the highest, which is imperial, to the supreme pontiff. Whatever goes beyond these things is superfluous; it is from evil.

We compelled the cardinals not to depart from the borders of our land, not out of contempt for our most beloved and most reverend Father and consecrator, but because of those things which [Col. 1642A] they had brought, both written and to be written, to the dishonour and scandal of our empire; we would not allow them to proceed farther. We have neither closed by edict, nor wish in any way to close, entry into and departure from Italy to pilgrims or to those reasonably going to the Roman see for their own necessities with the attestation of their bishops and prelates. But we intend to resist those abuses by which all the churches of our kingdom have been burdened and assailed, and by which almost every monastic discipline has died and been buried.

At the head of the world God exalted the Church through the empire; at the head of the world the Church—though, as we believe, not through God—now demolishes the empire. It began with a picture; the picture advanced to writing; the writing seeks to advance into authority. We shall not permit it; we shall not endure it. We shall put our crown before it, rather than consent that the crown of the empire be thus laid down along with us. Let the pictures be erased and the writings withdrawn, so that everlasting monuments of hostility may not remain between kingdom and priesthood.

These things and others—such as the agreement with Roger and William of Sicily, and other compacts made in Italy, which we do not dare fully recount—we heard from the mouth of our lord the emperor.

But while the Count Palatine was absent, having been sent ahead to prepare the expedition into Italy, we heard from the chancellor, who was still there, nothing except what concerned humility and peace, save that he had supported them to the best of his ability because of the danger to their lives threatened by the people, as all who were present bear witness.

For the rest, we humbly ask and implore your Holiness to spare our weakness; that, as a good shepherd, you may soften by your letters the greatness of spirit of your son, sweetening your earlier writings with honeyed gentleness, so that the Church of God may rejoice in tranquil devotion and the empire may glory in the condition of its sublimity, through the mediation and help of him who was made the mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus.

II. Emperor Frederick to Pope Adrian.—For confirmation of the bishop-elect of Ravenna.

(MANSI, *ibid.*, 794.)

[Col. 1642D]

FREDERICK, by the grace of God Emperor of the Romans and ever Augustus, to ADRIAN, venerable pontiff of the Roman Church.

Since our beloved and faithful Anselm, the venerable bishop of the Church of Ravenna of blessed memory, had died, [Col. 1643A] lest our court should long lack so great a prince, we took care that a person should be substituted in his place who seemed suited to repairing the losses of that Church and carrying out our service.

Above all, keeping before the eyes of our mind and hearing with no deaf ear what is written, “Outdo one another in showing honour” (Rom. XII), we intend in return to raise more highly, for your honour and that of the holy Roman Church, the son of the Count of Blanderate, whom we recall that you received, at our request, as a cleric and son of the Roman Church. This is especially fitting in that Church which, after the holy Roman Church, we regard as either the greatest or one of the greatest. With divine mercy favouring the purpose of our will, the whole Church of Ravenna unanimously and willingly agreed upon the election of that person, in the presence of highly honourable men—our legate and yours: on the one side Hyacinth the cardinal, on the other Hermann, bishop of Verden.

Since learning and morals, together with birth, commend the person of the aforesaid bishop-elect, he has now become more commendable and acceptable to us because of the reverend testimony of your fatherhood; and we rejoice and desire that he should also be loved and honoured by you, though according to that reason and order in which fathers are accustomed to love their sons, whom in due time they also free and permit to provide for their own household.

Indeed, it is most fitting for the holy Roman Church, as mother of all churches, to gather her children, who are the fruit of her womb, [Col. 1643C] and, having gathered them, to distribute them among houses and households for the adornment of God’s house; and our empire likewise ought and wishes to confer fitting honour upon them as those proceeding from the womb and bosom of [Col. 1644A] our mother. Therefore let your prudence weigh with deeper consideration what in this matter befits both your majesty and honour and ours.

III. The Consuls of Genoa to Adrian IV.—That he protect Genoese rights in the eastern regions.—(See Adrian’s Letter 75 above.)

(Caffaro, *Genoese Annals*, in MURATORI, *Italian Historical Writers*, VI, 266.)

Most reverend Father and lord, on behalf of the consuls of Genoa I make complaint to God and to you concerning the king of Jerusalem, the count of Tripoli, and the prince of Antioch, who daily take away and diminish the justice which the Genoese ought to enjoy [Col. 1644B] in the eastern regions, although their predecessors granted it to the Genoese and confirmed it by oath and privileges.

They did this because the Genoese, with many and great engines and expenses, and with much shedding of blood, captured by siege and battle the cities and places of the East, as is made known to you by these present writings. Moreover, I make a formal complaint concerning the men of the king of Jerusalem, who unjustly took Genoese ships and money with galleys. I further make this complaint concerning certain provincials of Bernard Atton and his companions. Therefore, most holy Father and lord, I humbly entreat your excellence that the staff of the apostolic see may strike with the bond of anathema all who take away the rights of the Genoese.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1156: ODO, ABBOT OF MORIMOND

[Col. 1643]

NOTICE

(FABRICIUS, *Bibliotheca medii et infimae Latinitatis*, IV, 159.)

Odo, formerly abbot of Belleprairie and later abbot of Morimond, in the diocese of Langres in Gaul, of the Cistercian order, died in 1161, according to the testimony of the Sammarthani, vol. IV, p. 674, where they note certain of his short works listed by Philip Seguin in the *Library of Manuscripts*. They are also mentioned by Visch, p. 254 of the *Cistercian Library*: *On the Meanings of Numbers*; *On Numerical Figures*; *On Free Appellations*; *On the Mysteries of Figures*; *On the Rules of Generations*; *On the Knowledge and Interpretations of Numbers*; *On the Meaning of Unity*; *On Relations and Their Mysteries*.

In Leland, ch. 180, p. 213, he is called “of Morimond,” where Leland reports his book *On the Analyses of the Ternary*, preserved in the library of Corinium, or Cirencester. Bale, III.19, moreover attributes to this Odo—though Leland had doubted the attribution—a *Dialogue on the Christian and Jewish Religion*, with Leo and Odo as interlocutors; further, a *Chronicle*, more rightly assigned to Otto of Freising; and *Analyses of Numbers*. Distinguishing this latter from the little book *On the Triad or Ternary*, Jacobus Faber, in his preface to Euclid, praises this Odo as an expert mathematician.

There are also: *The Book on the Three Hierarchies and the Three Degrees by Which Salvation Is Attained through Them*; and an *Enchiridion*, or dialogue between master and disciple, with a *Micrologus of the Art of Music*, manuscripts according to Labbe; to which add a treatise *On the Translation of the Relics of St Benedict to the Monastery of Fleury*. In Feller’s catalogue of the manuscripts of the Pauline Library at Leipzig, p. 161, Odo, abbot of Morimond, is mentioned as the author of *On the Passing of Bernard*. In Labbe, p. 208 of the *Library of Manuscripts*, there are *Sermons of Odo of Morimond, of the Cistercian Order*. Some of these are found in Combefis’s *Preachers’ Library*.

[Col. 1645]

SERMONS OF ODO.

(COMBEFIS, *Bibliotheca concionatoria*, vol. I, pp. 25, 259, 797; vol. VI, p. 311; vol. VIII, p. 121.)

FIRST SERMON. ON THE FIRST SUNDAY IN ADVENT. On the words: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord” (Isa. II.2).

[Col. 1645A]

Isaiah, most elegant of the prophets, foreseeing in the Spirit the coming of the Saviour, urges us in mystical speech to hasten with him to meet him, by the steps of conduct and the strides of virtues. “Come,” he says, “let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and to the house of the God of Jacob.”

Let those who are sluggish and inactive, walking difficult paths—or rather wandering off the path—hear, “Come.” Let those who indeed walk, but turn aside; who are not strong but fall, hear, “Let us go up.” To those lying below in the valley of tears it is said, “To the mountain of the Lord.” To strangers and pilgrims who have no abiding [Col. 1645B] city here it is said, “To the house of God.”

The mountain of the Lord is the height of perfection or the summit of virtues; or it is the King of glory himself, the Lord of hosts. This mountain is luminous, rich, and fragrant. For it is written: “You shine wonderfully from the everlasting mountains” (Ps. LXXV); and again, “The mountain of God is a rich mountain” (Ps. LXVII); and elsewhere, “I will go to the mountain of myrrh” (Song IV); and, “Upon the mountains of spices” (Song VIII).

It is luminous, in opposition to that mountain of which it is said: “Raise a standard upon the dark mountain” (Isa. XIII). It is rich, not producing thorns and thistles but offering most abundant pastures, so that lambs may feed according to their order, as it is promised: “I will feed [Col. 1645C] them in most abundant pastures, on the mountains of Israel” (Ezek. XXXIV). It is fragrant, so that there may be “an aroma of life unto life” (II Cor. II), and “in the fragrance of his ointments let us run” (Song I).

It is luminous that it may shine; rich that it may feed; fragrant that it may draw. Luminous, purifying hearts with the light of faith; rich, intoxicating them with the abundance of virtue; fragrant, stirring desire with the scent of sweetness.

In this bright, fertile, fragrant world is situated the house of God—not the earthly dwelling that is to be dissolved, but the eternal heavenly dwelling not made with hands (II Cor. III). God himself, leaning upon the ladder of virtue, stretches out the hand of grace to those who ascend (Gen. XXVIII), drawing us to the Son, as the Son himself says: “No one comes to me unless the Father draws him” (John XVI).

When we have come to him who draws us with the Father, [Col. 1645D] he will teach us his ways (ibid.); and we, adding grace to grace, shall walk in his paths (Isa. II). “Blessed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord, and teach out of your law” (Ps. XCIII). “Show me your ways, and teach me your paths” (Ps. XXIV). May I know how many they are and what they are like.

“All the ways of the Lord are mercy [Col. 1646A] and truth,” says the Prophet (ibid.). Mercy pardons one who acknowledges sin; truth corrects transgression. Each of these ways is straight, singular, unobstructed, beautiful, safe, and abundant.

It is straight because, following the rule of truth, it is not twisted by the winding paths of errors. “The ways of the Lord are right, and the righteous shall walk in them” (Hos. XIV). It is singular—that is, either excellent or unique—so that among the byways of many paths which seem right to people, it may stand out distinctly, according to the Apostle who says: “I show you a still more excellent way” (I Cor. XII).

It is unobstructed, lest the steps of the walker be hindered and delayed by intervening folds of any unevenness. It is beautiful, that it may soothe the traveller’s mind with delight, lest, wearied by the hardness of the beginning and overtaken by tedium, the horse pant at the threshing-floor. [Col. 1646B] “Her ways are beautiful ways” (Prov. III).

It is safe, so that the traveller may not fear attacks of enemies or dread the loss of his goods. It is abundant, because it overflows with every good thing.

SECOND SERMON. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD.

“The glory of God is to conceal a matter; the glory of kings is to investigate a saying” (Prov. XXV). The reason for this venerable solemnity requires not so much learned speech for its expression as the attentive purpose of a devout heart for its contemplation. For the matter is difficult and hard to utter, but wonderful and delightful to consider.

What is more wonderful than that the Word became flesh by assumption of humanity, not by consumption of divinity; and that divine and human things were joined, not changed into human things? Thus they were united without being divided.

This is the reason for the veneration of the present day: that the Son of God, covered with the veil of undefiled flesh, came visibly to us, yet did not depart from the bosom of the Father’s substance, while the immeasurable power of his majesty remained. He accepted the neediness of our poverty into himself, and did not lay aside from himself the riches of his glory. He bent down that we might be raised up; he emptied himself that we might be filled.

His poverty, abasement, and weakness confer upon us riches, exaltation, and salvation. For he who became poor possessed in himself all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col. II), in order to enrich us; he who humbled himself remained in the glory of the Father’s exalted majesty, in order to lift us up; he who deigned to become weak remained the power [Col. 1646D] of God, in order to save us. Thus he took what was ours while retaining what was his. Therefore, in what is his and from what is his, he is rich, exalted, and strong; in what is ours and from what is ours, he chose to be poor, humble, and weak.

For our instruction it is fitting to apply reflection to this work of our salvation. In it human nature may see what it is and what it ought to do. The former [Col. 1647A] will be seen when its worth and abasement are known; the latter when its profit and loss are known.

Its worth is inferred from God’s work performed for it; its abasement, from the reason for that work. This is what the Prophet considered and at which he was astonished, upon which Augustine says: “Your work, O God, is that the Word became flesh.” By this work the dignity of our nature is commended and its worth recognized.

He surely valued us greatly, since in order to grant the healing we needed, he raised the frailty of our substance into unity with his own person. He who was in the world, through whom the world was made (John I), came into the world to save sinners (I Tim. I); and not only this, but “deliverances from death belong to the Lord, the Lord” (Ps. LXVII).

The reason for this work was our misery. For human nature, corrupted at its very root through free choice, was enveloped in such darkness of error, bound by such entangled cords of iniquity, and separated by so great an interval from the blessedness of the heavenly homeland that it could neither be enlightened, justified, nor redeemed by its own powers, nor could angel or prophet assist it.

Finally, a law was given which could not give life, in order to make sinners also transgressors and to increase transgression, not erase it. But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made in the likeness of sinful flesh (Gal. IV), so that the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us (Rom. VIII).

He is the one who was handed over for our offences and rose again for our justification, enlightening the blind, freeing the bound, and bringing back those who had gone astray, through his teaching, death, and resurrection.

Behold the depth of sickness that oppressed humankind, for whose healing so great a physician had to come. Hence one may especially recognize the wretchedness of our abasement: the greatness of our weakness could in no way be restored to health unless the medicine for the sick were made by the blood of the healer, and the death of the physician restored life to the patient.

Therefore the honour of human dignity is inferred from the assumption of our humanity into God; the abasement of our wretchedness from the mass of our weakness; and this from the difficulty of the remedy.

After this, it is fitting that in our conduct we attend to our loss and gain: loss, if it is blameworthy; gain, if it is praiseworthy. Great indeed and immeasurable is the loss of suffering, extending even to the division of soul and body and beyond, for one who has trampled the Son of God underfoot, regarded the blood of the covenant as defiled, and insulted the Spirit of grace (Heb. X).

He tramples the Son of God underfoot who does not believe him; he regards the blood of the covenant as defiled who lives a life full of defilement; he insults the Spirit of grace who arrogates righteousness to himself. Loss threatens such a person.

But whoever is devout in faith, holy in conduct, and pleasing in humility possesses a gain which is believed by faith, inferred by reason, and will be proved at the end. For God is faithful, who by the gift of present things makes known the expectation of future things.

Moreover, the place, time, and testimony of the Lord’s Nativity offer illustrious lessons in conduct. The place: outside the homeland; the time: at night; the testimony: angelic, from heaven.

The place bears a twofold form of instruction, teaching us to acquire merit and to lament exile. We acquire merit when we devote ourselves to virtues; we lament exile when we long for our homeland. Yet the place for these actions is only the present age, while we are in the body and away from the Lord (II Cor. V). Therefore, when we practise righteousness and long for glory, we are, as it were, carried outside our homeland, showing that we have here no abiding city but seek the one to come (Heb. XIII).

We are likewise instructed by the time in a twofold lesson, teaching us humility and caution. Night is representative of adversity and productive of obscurity; adversity humbles, and obscurity conceals.

Therefore we are taught by night caution and humility: caution, that we may conceal what we love, lest we lose it by exposing it; humility, lest confidence in our work inwardly generate the vice of pride. Both are useful for driving away and uprooting the pattern of pride: the former of outward boasting, the latter of inward vanity.

Finally, in the testimony one must consider who testifies, what he testifies, and to whom. One worthy person testifies to worthy things before worthy persons: an angel testifies of Christ to shepherds; the messenger of truth proclaims the joy of salvation to humble persons; the minister of brightness proclaims the rising of light to those solicitous in heart and devout in mind.

In three respects this witness presents himself as commendable and worthy of imitation. He appears alone, to teach the firmness of unity; standing, to teach constancy of firmness joined with the affection of charity. Fittingly, first one and afterward many appear, because unity can pass into increase, while multiplicity can flow away into fewness.

And although the authority of the messenger dispels the mark of unbelief, a sign appropriate to the dignity of the one being born is nevertheless given. “You will find,” he says, “an infant,” as weak; “wrapped in swaddling-clothes,” as poor; “and laid in a manger” (Luke II), as humble.

Learn from Christ, O Christian, weakness: lay aside presumption in your own strength; despise perishable possession; trample down worldly ambition. Finally, a multitude praising and saying, “Glory to God in the highest” (ibid.), bears witness to the announcement of one.

This is the glory of which it was foretold: “The glory of God is to conceal the Word” (Prov. XXV). For the tabernacle of a human body veiled and concealed the eternal Word of the Father, and the unfailing radiance of the eternal sun was covered by the bright and light cloud of flesh: bright through innocence, light through power.

This is God’s glory, by which the glorious Father appeared, whom the Son glorified upon earth. But “the glory of kings is to investigate a saying” (ibid.). Those shepherds are rightly called blessed kings, who governed themselves and what was theirs most excellently. Investigating the saying, they came and found, as had been spoken concerning this child (Luke II), who is God blessed for ever. Amen.

THIRD SERMON. ON SEPTUAGESIMA SUNDAY.

[Col. 1649A]

“The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning” (Matt. XX), etc. The Gospel discourse compares the kingdom of heaven to a householder who went out at dawn to hire labourers for his vineyard.

To understand this comparison, one must chiefly ask what the vineyard signifies, where it is situated, what the hours are, and what sort of cultivation is meant. When these four have been discovered, the way to understanding the remaining points will be not difficult.

Different people indeed say different things about these matters, and the opinions of each should be set forth, so that from their various meanings the significance and rationale of vineyard, place, time, and work may be gathered.

David says: “You brought a vineyard out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it” (Ps. LXXIX). When he says this, he shows us that the vineyard is the discipline of renunciation, transferred from the darkness of the world to the light of religious life when, after the thorns of vices are expelled from the human mind, the shoots of virtues are planted.

Therefore the vineyard is the discipline of renunciation; if a person undertakes it, he goes and sells all that he has (Matt. XIII), and plants it. Here one must carefully observe that such a precious shoot ought to be entrusted to rich soil, lest the industry of the working farmer be frustrated, by the barrenness of the ground, of the expected abundance of fruit.

Thus we read in Isaiah: “A vineyard was made for the beloved on a horn, son of oil” (Isa. V). This is the place of the vineyard of the Lord of hosts: a fertile and rich place, “a horn, son of oil.”

The horn signifies eminence and firmness, upon which the foundations of the discipline of renunciation are laid. For this purpose stands out, and, going out from the world as though proceeding from the flesh, is set apart from the contagion of human life and conduct and is raised on high—not through the arrogance of pride against the Lord, but through loftiness of life and an affection of devotion toward the Lord.

Because this occurs by the gift of the Holy Spirit, it is called a horn, son of oil, as though an affection of spiritual grace. Therefore, whenever someone is called to undertake the discipline of sacred religious life, with the glory of an unfading crown set before him as his reward (I Pet. V), God hires his labourer into his vineyard. Our householder is himself so by authority, reason, and benefits.

[Col. 1649D]

Labourers are sent into the vineyard at five hours: early morning, the third, sixth, ninth, and eleventh hours. Early morning is the illumination of faith, for the second morning will be the beginning of contemplation.

It is the first because faith is one, as the Apostle commends its unity thus: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. IV): one Lord by whom we are governed, one faith by which we are enlightened, one baptism by which we are sanctified. Whoever is led by the power of faith to work well is, as it were, hired into the vineyard early in the morning.

The second hour, called the third, is hope, which follows faith. The third hour, placed second, is fittingly likened to hope, because hope consists in two things and derives its origin from three.

Pardon and glory are hoped for; remission and promise constitute these. It arises from consideration of human dignity and condition; from consideration of divine mercy in redemption; and also from experiences of the same goodness in the granting of benefits.

Hence it is written: “There are three that bear witness on earth: the Spirit, the water, and the blood” (I John V). In the blood is signified the nobility of our race; in the water, the flux of mortality; in the Spirit, the distribution of power.

Therefore blood bears witness to our salvation because we were made in the image of God; water because we were redeemed by the death of the Son; and the Spirit because we have freely been enriched with the abundant wealth of spiritual gifts.

Reflection on these things strengthens our hope in every danger; and strong hope invites us without sluggishness to the work of the vineyard.

[Col. 1650B]

At the sixth hour are expressed the disposition and effect of mercy and compassion; and evangelical authority teaches that mercy consists in six works. These are: feeding the hungry, giving drink to the thirsty, taking in the stranger, clothing the naked, visiting the sick, and coming to the imprisoned (Matt. XXV).

Although their outward performance is rewarded with the possession of the kingdom of heaven, their spiritual performance brings a more excellent fruit. Whoever shows a brother, languishing and hungry for good works, the way of righteousness by the example of his own works, feeds the hungry. If he teaches by deed and word one who is ignorant of the way of truth and desires it, he has given him to drink from the saving water of wisdom (Ecclus. XV).

There is one who, caring for his salvation, refuses to become entangled in the arts of worldly business; he seeks quiet, loves silence, perseveres in prayers to the Lord, and his soul refuses to be consoled (Ps. LXXIII). He delights only in exercises of virtue and remembrance of God, being free for God and dwelling with himself.

What is he except a stranger and pilgrim upon the earth (Heb. XI), having here no abiding city but seeking the one to come (Heb. XIII)? To embrace such a person in the arms of charity, cherish him, and reverence him with humble affection is to take in the stranger.

Many ridicule such persons, call them idle and dull, and suspect them of hypocrisy; the rashness of their judgment is rebuked by the Apostle’s rebuke: “But why do you judge your brother? Or why do you despise your brother?” (Rom. XIV). Such people do not take in the stranger but drive him out.

Certainly naked is the person whom the garment of righteousness does not cover, whose shame is uncovered by committed fault. But he must be covered with the garment of silence and the disposition of compassion; one must feel for him and not judge him rashly.

For there is a person who, when he sees his brother sinning, does not say to himself, “He today, and I tomorrow,” as some saints are recorded to have done; rather, he slanders, accuses, judges, and defames him, as though the crimes of others were his own praises.

Such a person does not cover his neighbour’s nakedness but makes his disgrace public. But one who has compassion, conceals it, or rebukes him fittingly and privately, covers the naked.

The fifth work of mercy is to visit the sick: a pious work and one of great merit. Yet sickness of the soul is more dangerous than disease of the body. Therefore to visit it and provide it with healing is a more difficult labour, but its fruit yields a more abundant reward and praise.

For pitiably sick in mind is the one who sluggishly carries out his purpose, who is unstable in will, frivolous in zeal, undisciplined in action, yields to corrupt suggestions, is overwhelmed by rushing temptations, and lies half-dead upon the bed of idleness under the various sicknesses of vices.

The spiritual physician visits such a person. Bringing with him the ointments of exhortation and the medicines of the divine Scriptures, he draws near, binds his wounds, pours in the oil of consolation and the wine of correction (Luke X), and with the help of his own works, as though upon the burden-bearing beast of his own body, calls him back to the rest of stability as to an inn—strengthening the sick, steadying the unstable, gathering together the scattered.

The labour of such a person truly surpasses the ministry of bodily visitation, since he has visited and healed a better and enduring substance, effectively fulfilling the office of visitation because he fulfils it spiritually.

Now one must come to the imprisoned both in deed and word. The confinement of prison signifies tribulation and sorrow. Whoever is placed in it suffers the darkness of grief, lacking the light of joy.

If someone directs affection toward one so afflicted, proves that affection in deed, and meets and relieves the tribulation of his brother by works, words, and prayers to the Lord for him, that person comes to the imprisoned not so much by the approach of his feet as by the disposition of compassion.

If by his effort the sufferer is rescued from the narrowness of sorrow into the breadth of joy, from the darkness of tribulation into the light of prosperity, he not only comes to him but also brings his soul out of prison, that it may confess the name of the Lord (Ps. CXLI).

The fruit of this labour is most abundant, and the reward for so great a deliverance is plentiful in heaven (Matt. V). Therefore preparation of will and work for fulfilling these deeds spiritually, and certainly also bodily, is the going forth to the vineyard at the sixth hour.

The ninth hour is assigned to humility. For nine approaches ten, which is a perfect number and in which is the first progression of numbers, with no number between. Thus humility through action approaches perfection, although in its own estimation it remains below it. Whoever, therefore, humbles himself in all things in proportion as he is greater is a labourer of the ninth hour.

But eleven, which passes beyond ten, sometimes signifies transgression of the commandments, sometimes a voluntary exceeding of them: the latter here, the former elsewhere. Therefore whoever, beyond what has been commanded, offers something to God by pious will with the joy of the Holy Spirit, adds to ten and goes out to the vineyard at the eleventh hour.

He receives a reward not unequal to that of the labourer of the first hour, who bore the burden and heat of the day; for he has borne fruit more than all—not, I say, laboured more.

Accordingly, the supreme householder sends laborers at these five hours to cultivate the vineyard of heavenly discipline [Col. 1652A]: at the first hour through the unity of faith; at the third through confidence of hope; at the sixth through works of love; at the ninth through the virtue of humility; at the eleventh through the fullness of perfection. But after the laborers have been sent, idleness must not be pursued; rather, the work of the vineyard must be carried out. The prophet Isaiah teaches what that work is: “The Lord fenced it about”—there can be no doubt that it was His vineyard—“and chose stones out of it; He built a tower and constructed a winepress, and made it choice” (Isa. 5).

A fence is a firm interweaving of different rods, which keeps swine and wild beasts from entering the vineyard. It is likened to the interlacing of diverse virtues, which are joined together in one bond for the safeguarding of holiness. For virtues are linked to and chained together with one another; and he who serves Christ in them pleases God (Rom. 14). But without faith it is impossible [Col. 1652B] to please God (Heb. 11). The work of righteousness must first be built upon the foundation of faith, so that action may give life to faith and faith may uphold action. For faith and action must walk on one path. Thus the meaning of the first hour accords with the first work. When anyone has been sent through the unity of faith into the vineyard of heavenly discipline, he must first of all strive to fortify his purpose with the defense of every virtue, so that, according to the prophet, he may be called “a builder of fences, turning paths into rest” (Isa. 58). Thus the other four hours may be referred to the other four works, each to its own.

When the vineyard has therefore been fenced, stones must be chosen out of it. Stones signify hardness, roughness, and heaviness, which must be uprooted from our hearts so that [Col. 1652C] we may become gentle, yielding, and ready for every good work, and that the plant of virtues may be set in the place of stones. Yet the greatness of the reward hoped for makes one undertake that labor, and the hope of recompense consoles the laborer who is growing weary beneath the burdens of stones. Thus he does not fail until the stones fail. When they have been cast out, he builds a winepress to crush grapes and press out wine. The winepress is aptly compared with the affection of compassion, by which the soul of one who feels with another is pressed, as it were, by the press of the sufferer’s misery. From this flows the wine of love: wine sweet and strong, which gladdens the human heart (Ps. 103).

Finally, having tasted this flavor, the cultivator of the vineyard applies more watchful protection. He therefore builds a tower, from whose height he may foresee thieves [Col. 1652D] and wild beasts approaching, in order to prevent them from plundering the vineyard’s fruits. Clear reasoning teaches that the height of the tower corresponds to humility, for the Lord says: “Whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Matt. 23). Humility is the mother and guardian of all virtues. Hence, after its acquisition, the vineyard is called choice, because it is perfect; for by the same humility by which it is begun, it is brought to perfection.

Therefore the laborers of our householder, going out into the vineyard at the first hour, fence it through faith; at the third, through hope, they choose stones out of it; at the sixth, through love, they build the winepress; at the ninth, through humility, they erect the tower; at the eleventh, the work is completed. Then, when evening has come, the householder’s steward appears and, beginning with the last and continuing to [Col. 1653A] the first, gives each one a denarius (Matt. 20).

The time of each of our rewards is the last day of his life. Then, with the angel standing by, each receives the reward of his work, according as he has done in the body, whether good or evil (2 Cor. 5). But let us take examples from the good. “They received each one a denarius” (Matt. 20). In the denarius are considered its shape, image, and inscription. Its shape is roundness; its image is adorned with the likeness of a king; its inscription conveys knowledge. Roundness signifies eternity; the image, likeness to God; the inscription, knowledge. We shall therefore receive in reward a denarius: “When this corruptible shall have put on incorruption” (1 Cor. 15); and, “When we shall be like Him, because we shall see Him as He is” (1 John 3); and we shall know Him as [Col. 1653B] we ourselves are known (1 Cor. 13). Thus eternal life, likeness, and knowledge await the laborers in God’s vineyard. This reward is rendered to them in justice by the merciful and just Lord (Ps. 114), who called them through grace, and who is blessed forever. Amen.

## SERMON IV. ON THE THREE BIRTHS AND THE CORRESPONDING THREE VIRTUES OF BLESSED MARY, BLESSED JOHN, AND THE LORD THE SAVIOR

The celebrated days on which many saints entered the kingdom of heaven have brought us venerable joys for the world. Yet the excellence of three won the privilege that not only their return to the Father of lights, but also their entrance into the world should be celebrated in solemn remembrance. This must not be believed to have been appropriated by presumptuous human license, but established by the ordering of the divine will [Col. 1653C]. We commemorate the venerable births of blessed John the Baptist, who came in the spirit and power of Elijah, of the Son of God Himself, and of Mary. “Blessed the wombs that bore such persons, and blessed the breasts that gave themselves to such persons” (Luke 11). Singular is their prerogative, to which no mortal can be compared. [lacuna] “She was seen neither as having one like her before, nor as having one after her.” Among those born of women none arose greater than he. But “who shall declare this one’s generation?” (Isa. 53).

We cannot imitate the deed, but the mystery of the deed is imitable. We cannot be the parents of such persons; [Col. 1653D] we can be their imitators. And indeed it is more beneficial to bear them in the mind than in the womb, through the offspring of virtue rather than through a mass of flesh and blood. In every way we more greatly conceive virtues which will kill sin than we beget children who will die because of sin. If the fruit of moral action is greater than that of physical generation, let us examine the character of their holiness and reproduce their natural virtues in ourselves. Therefore, with the favor of the Trinity of the Godhead, we shall assign to each a trinity of virtues—not that we give a part to those to whom we grant fullness, but that from their totality we select what is more commendable and more fit for imitation.

Among the virtues in which the Virgin’s singular prerogative excels, her faith, obedience, and chastity are most worthy of proclamation. The deeds and words furnish exceedingly credible proofs of these three [Col. 1654A]. When the archangel Gabriel was sent to her from heaven and announced a work without precedent, conception contrary to custom, and birth beyond nature, she did not waver in disbelief; rather, she was strengthened in faith, knowing that God is able to do what His messenger proclaimed (Rom. 4). A holy woman of the same race and faith bears witness to this faith, saying of her who was present: “Blessed is she who believed” (Luke 1). She displayed obedience: embracing the promise entrusted to her, she followed it through to its fulfillment. “Behold,” she says, “the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (ibid.). She who declares herself a handmaid promises obedience; she who sighs for it to be done to her by us does not herself refuse to do it.

Why is it necessary to praise chastity in her, who shone so brightly that she became the temple of the Lord and the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit; who, with mind incorrupt and body untouched, begot from virginity Virginity, and from flesh gave birth to Divinity? Thus the blessed Virgin had faith against seduction, obedience against transgression, and chastity against corruption. She was not seduced, did not transgress, and was not corrupted. Let us likewise be steadfast in temptations, lest we be seduced; whole in chastity, lest we be violated; and obedient in commandments, lest we transgress. By this imitation we have set forth the virtues of the Virgin’s birth [Col. 1654B].

Likewise the Savior’s forerunner shone in three virtues: his speech was rational, his life religious, and his disposition humble. Examples confirm these statements [Col. 1654C]. Among the crowds flocking to him, soldiers also came to consult him about their way of life. He did not command them to unfasten their belts or renounce military service, but to extort from no one and to be content with their pay. But he sharply rebuked the Pharisees, who sought to establish their own righteousness, calling them “brood of vipers” (Luke 3). Thus reason required both that he give moderate counsel to those seeking it and that he show severity toward the presumptuous.

There are as many examples of his religious life as deeds. His place, clothing, food, and conduct are marks of religious devotion: his place, the desert; his clothing, poor; his food, harsh; his conduct, chaste. The place was suitable for quiet; the clothing fitted for mortification; the food apt for purity; the conduct appropriate to holiness. In short, whatever belongs to his life also belongs to religious devotion. An evident proof of his humble disposition is that, though he was of such excellence that he was thought to be Christ, he “confessed and did not deny” (John 1): “The one whom you suppose me to be,” he says, “I am not” (ibid.). He confessed what he was not, so that he might be what he was. He was not Christ; he was Christ’s friend, the bridegroom’s friend: “But the friend of the bridegroom who stands,” etc. (John 3). Therefore, as the foregoing examples show, John the Baptist possessed reason in speech, religious devotion in life, and humility in disposition. Let us likewise possess them, so that our life may reproduce his nativity [Col. 1654D].

It remains for us to extol the Nativity of the Lord and Savior with new praises and imitate it through virtues. But what shall we say about [Col. 1655A] the virtues of the Lord of virtues? His whole life was virtue. Yet he shone above all others in three virtues, by which he “worked salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. 73). They are not especially difficult to imitate and are most fruitful in their benefit: kindness toward the needy; patience toward enemies, enduring injuries; and toward friends, revelation of mysteries. The testimony of apostolic and evangelical history confirms these things. “He went about,” it says, “doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil . . .” (Acts 10). And speaking of Jesus and His works: “The blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, and the poor have the Gospel preached to them” (Luke 7). It would take too long to recount each of His works of beneficence. Whatever He did was a benefit; as many deeds, so many benefits [Col. 1655A].

How great [Col. 1655B] His patience was, the injury of the scourges proves; the insults of His shameful death bear witness. Since it was by His will, not by necessity, that He endured all these things, He preferred to maintain patience rather than exercise power. His glory toward His friends is proved by the glorification displayed on the mountain: He revealed His majesty to His friends and did not conceal from them His gifts and good things. It is a notable proof of extraordinary love not to deny friends knowledge of our good things, to make all things common, and to conceal from them nothing that may benefit them. That the Lord did this, He Himself, and no other, bears witness: “All things whatsoever I heard from the Father I have made known to you” (John 15). And again: “The glory which You gave Me [Col. 1655C] I have given them” (John 17). Finally, when they asked Him concerning the day of judgment, He postponed teaching what it would not benefit them to know. So greatly did He provide for their advantage rather than their wishes.

Thus we prove that the Lord Jesus showed kindness to the needy, patience toward enemies, and glory to friends. In these things the Lord and Master gave us an example, that we also might do to one another and emulate the mystery of His nativity through virtues. But, to draw together what has been set out above in scattered fashion, we worthily celebrate and imitate the three nativities, each with its three virtues, if we possess faith, obedience, and chastity, as in Mary; if we have rational speech, a religious life, and a humble disposition, as in John; and if we do good to the needy, endure enemies, and glorify [Col. 1655D] friends, as was shown in the Lord.

## SERMON V. ON THE FEAST OF ST. BENEDICT

On the words of Ecclesiasticus: “Beloved by God and men, whose memory is in blessing.”

“Beloved by God and men, whose memory is in blessing, He made him like the saints in glory” (Ecclus. 45). It is natural, and consonant with virtue, to honor one’s own originating principle and not to wander by a degenerate path from one’s origin. “All rivers enter the sea, and return to the place from which they come forth” (Eccl. 1). It is altogether salutary to follow the footsteps of one’s founder and not, with most wicked presumption, to follow one’s own will as teacher. Whatever in us draws the beginning of perfection, any virtue, or any model of religious life, derives its form from our blessed father Benedict. He, our lawgiver, gave order to our life and discipline to our conduct. To encourage our imitation of him, Scripture assigns him three virtues of holiness and bestows the testimony of glory: “Beloved by God and men,” it says, etc. Although these words were spoken of another, they are nevertheless aptly applied to his praise, because what suits one saint through unity of virtues and harmony of character is not unsuited to another like him. If, then, they apply to him, they must not be at variance with our character and purpose, lest we be convicted as degenerate sons if we are found unlike our Father in deeds [Col. 1656A].

First, it is fitting to know for what reasons and in what respects we are to be loved by God and by human beings. Nor should we seek to be loved by God but not by human beings, as is the habit of certain persons who misuse the Apostle’s testimony: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1); and, “If I still pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ” (Gal. 1). In proud rashness, they strive to displease people and disdain to be loved. But it happens to them that they are neither loved by God nor, hateful to people, harassed by the suspicious reproach of a bad reputation. To be loved by people but not by God is not merely useless but harmful, since it is an occasion of boasting and fuel for pride. We must therefore join both together, and desire and strive to be loved by God and by people.

But since God is Spirit, one who would be loved by God must reckon the beginning of love in the spirit and carry on this work inwardly: “The light of God’s countenance is marked upon us” (Ps. 4). God especially loves the seal of His own image. Therefore He loves the soul, especially if it emulates His form. This will be so if it is pure, steadfast, and fervent. God supremely and unchangeably is all these things. He is pure, whose Wisdom “reaches everywhere because of her purity, and nothing defiled enters into her” (Wis. 7); steadfast, with whom “there is no change, nor shadow of turning” (Jas. 1); fervent, who, as Moses teaches, “is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4).

Let the soul which was made in God’s image likewise be pure, lest it receive into itself any alien admixture, but through the diligent practice of virtue increase within itself its native beauty. Let it be steadfast, lest it be carried about by every wind of fickleness and return from evil to good and from good to evil; rather, let it persevere firmly and steadily, adhering by an undeviating path to the good it has attained. Let it be fervent, lest, made lukewarm by harmful indolence, it be vomited from God’s mouth (Rev. 3); rather, let it walk in a glowing spirit from virtue to virtue, and, even if it does not always attain the result of progress, never lose the desire for it.
