Let it be pure, that it may not be foul; steadfast, that it may endure; fervent, that it may progress. Such persons are deservedly loved by God, and God comes to them and makes His dwelling with them (John 14) [Col. 1656B].

There are likewise three ways and reasons why we are loved by people, who see faces and behold outward things: namely, life, moderation, and kindness. First, our actions ought to be just, our pursuits honorable, our mind composed, and indeed our entire life adorned with such beauty of honorableness that it draws even the affection of opponents. For no one but the most perverse can hate what is good, even when unwilling to imitate it. Yet moderation must necessarily be observed in all things; whoever exceeds it incurs the charge of singularity and offends the eyes of observers.

To a praiseworthy life moderation must be added, setting fixed bounds to virtues, so that there may be nothing excessive, but rather the measure described by the pagan poet be observed:

> There is a measure in things; indeed there are fixed bounds,  
> Beyond or short of which right cannot stand.  
> —Horace, *Satires* I.107

One who is conspicuous in life and outstanding in discretion is deservedly to be loved. Let a person be loved, but let kindness add the fullness of love, so that he may help his neighbor [Col. 1657B] in deed, word, or prayer. Service makes friends. Whoever has this world’s substance under his control and sees his brother in need must not shut his heart against him (1 John 3), but must show mercy cheerfully. Or, if unable to do so, let him offer helpful counsel, the support of consolation, and a good word beyond an excellent gift. If the law of silence restrains him from this service, he shows by evident signs that the will to help is present, though the means are lacking. For whoever proves ready with benefits, diligent in service, and devoted in will toward neighbors cannot, I think, fail to be loved—especially when uprightness of life goes before and moderation accompanies it. Thus life will serve virtue, moderation beauty, and kindness need: [Col. 1657A] life to help, moderation to delight, kindness to bear fruit [Col. 1657C].

It follows: “Whose memory is in blessing.” There are different kinds of blessing. Laban, speaking [Col. 1658A] to Jacob, says: “God has blessed me at your coming” (Gen. 30), calling an increase of possessions a blessing. There is another blessing greater than this: when we are enriched with virtues and abound in spiritual goods. Thus the Apostle says to certain persons: “You have been made rich in every word and in all knowledge, so that you lack no grace” (1 Cor. 17 [as printed]). And elsewhere: “In all things you abound in faith and speech, knowledge and every diligence, and moreover in love” (2 Cor. 8): in faith certain and fervent; in speech discerning and eloquent; in knowledge for discernment; in every diligence by pursuing what is useful more earnestly; and moreover in love, loving one another and loving eternally. In these, abundance of virtue is denoted.

The most excellent blessing of these is when they receive from the [Col. 1658B] Lord’s hand the kingdom of beauty and the diadem of the blessed Father’s appearance. Concerning this blessing, the Apostle likewise, announcing future certainties with the force of things past, says: “God has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ” (Eph. 1). To define each by its own name: the first is multiplication of resources; the second, the supplement of virtue; the third, the crown of eternity. The first is given for consolation, the second for merit, the third for reward. In each of these blessings is the grace of Benedict and a memory in his name, so that he who received the name of blessing may be heir to the name.

In praise of him it is further added: “He made him like the saints in glory.” For he performed great signs like the saints and was made like the saints in the glory [Col. 1658C] of miracles. As we behold his glory, let us, as children, follow his life, that we may be heirs of blessing, through the favor of our Lord. Amen.

## A.D. 1157–1163: FASTREDUS, THIRD ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX

[Col. 1657]

## NOTICE

(*Literary History of France*, by Benedictine Religious, vol. XII, p. 625)

Fastrède, also called Fastrade and sometimes Flaster, was born into the noble house of Gaviamès or Gaviaumer in Hainaut [Note: [Col. 1657] *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. III, p. 171]. Educated in letters and virtue by capable masters, he went to dedicate himself to God at Clairvaux Abbey under the governance of Saint Bernard. The merit he displayed in that retreat is attested by the choice made by the abbot of Clairvaux of his person to govern the new Cistercian colony established at Cambron in 1148. The office was difficult to fill, because many obstacles opposed that foundation. Fastrède overcame them by prudence and wisdom.

He conducted himself so well at Cambron that the monks of Clairvaux recalled him in 1157 to make him their abbot. Having become Saint Bernard’s successor, he reproduced that great man’s zeal for the maintenance of regular discipline. We possess a valuable monument of this zeal in a letter which he [Col. 1659] wrote to an abbot of his filiation. Under the pretext of ill health, the latter permitted himself relaxations contrary to the Rule, and even superfluities in food and clothing. Fastrède urged him by the most pressing reasons to change his conduct.

“What a contrast,” he says to him, “between the life you lead and that of all the other houses—even your own! Everywhere in our monasteries people are fed on oat bread, vegetables cooked without oil or fat, peas, and beans: a regimen so exact that it permits not even an exception on Easter Day. You plead your headaches and stomach ailments to exempt yourself from it; but you are under a very gross illusion if you think that monks, in their illnesses, may in conscience allow themselves all the alleviations used by secular people. Saint Bernard used to tell us that a monk, if thoroughly aware of his obligations, would not eat a morsel of bread without moistening it with his tears, since his office is to expiate by his groans both his own sins and those of the people. Infirmities,” he added, “cannot authorize monks to live in laxity, since our first fathers deliberately sought out deep and marshy valleys in which to build monasteries, so that, often being liable to illness, monks might always keep the idea of death before them and not live in a fatal security.”

“If these fraternal remonstrances,” Fastrède continues, “cannot make enough impression upon your heart to lead you to amend yourself, I shall be forced to employ the remedy which my position as superior places in my hands.”

This letter stirred up, in the last century, a controversy between two devout and learned solitaries, who cited it several times in French, sometimes entire and sometimes in extracts. It is found in the original among the letters of Saint Bernard in the new edition of that Father (*Ep.* 440).

The interests of the Church ought to touch a solitary, and especially a leader of solitaries, even more keenly than those of his order. Filled with this truth, following Saint Bernard’s example, Fastrède exerted himself greatly, together with several abbots his colleagues, to extinguish the schism occasioned in 1159 by the election of Pope Alexander III and that of the antipope Victor [Note: [Col. 1659] *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. V, p. 800]. In the letter which he wrote to Omnibon, bishop of Verona, we have a detailed account of the measures and journeys he undertook on this matter. If Providence did not permit success fully to answer his efforts, it is clear that they were not wholly fruitless, and that neither he nor his colleagues were responsible for their failing to have all the effect they could have hoped for. The letter just mentioned is found in vol. X of Father Labbe’s *Councils* (p. 1407), vol. VI of Father Hardouin’s (part III, p. 1585), and vol. III of the *Library of Cîteaux*.

Lambert, abbot of Cîteaux, who had been one of Fastrède’s collaborators in the matter of the schism, abdicated toward the end of 1161 or the beginning of the following year. Our abbot was then elected, as the worthiest member of the order, to replace him. He did not enjoy that dignity for long. In the spring of 1163, having gone to Paris to see Pope Alexander on various affairs of his order, and especially to request Saint Bernard’s canonization, he died there on 21 April, mourned by the pope and the king, who even honored him with his tears. His body was brought back to Cîteaux and buried there in the cloister beside his predecessors. The order’s martyrologies count him among the saints [Note: [Col. 1659] *Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. IV, p. 987; Manrique, *Annales Cistercienses*, under 1163, ch. 1; Dubois, *Ecclesiastical History of Paris*, bk. XIII, ch. 4, no. 4; *Mirror of Cistercian Chronicles*, no. 317].

No other productions of his pen remain except the two letters just mentioned. Both works show that he knew how to write and was capable of producing formal compositions.

[Col. 1659]

## LETTER OF FASTREDUS

To a certain abbot of his order, on the observance of regular discipline.

(See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXII, col. 704, among the letters of St. Bernard.)

[Col. 1659]

## LETTER OF THE SAME AUTHOR

To Omnibon, bishop of Verona. On the Council of Toulouse, at which Alexander, Victor having been rejected, was recognized as pope; and on the conventicle at Pavia.

(See among the letters of various persons to Alexander and his legates, *Patrologia*, vol. CC.)

## ABOUT THE MIDDLE OF THE CENTURY: JOHN CIRITA, ABBOT OF THARAUCANUS IN SPAIN

[Col. 1661]

# THE LIFE AND LETTERS OF JOHN CIRITA

[Col. 1661A] *Bundle of Saints of the Cistercian Order* (bk. I, p. 267), comprising the heroic virtues of most illustrious bishops, the origins of monastic orders serving under the Cistercian institute, the contests of most steadfast martyrs, and the beginnings of various abbeys; by the Reverend Father Friar Chrysostom Henriques of Horta, monk of the same order and general historiographer of the Congregation of Spain.—Brussels: at the shop of Jean Peperman, sworn bookseller and city printer, under the sign of the Golden Bibles, 1623.

## CHAPTER ONE. Despising the honors of this age and bidding farewell to temporal soldiery, he embraces the eremitic life.

At the time when the empire of the Saracens extended far and wide through nearly all the provinces of Spain, while Alfonso VI, so named, held the kingdom of León, a nobleman named John [Col. 1661B] Cirita had devoted himself from his earliest youth to military affairs and had distinguished himself wonderfully in them. Lest he persevere any longer entangled in the vanities of the world, divine Providence mercifully called and set him apart by its grace. For when he entered battle against the Saracens, was wounded by them, and lay nearly dead, he found the way of eternal life.

Once restored to himself, he left his native country and came to the mountains of Galicia, where a priest of holy life most kindly received him and gave him no slight instruction in the reading of sacred Scripture. That priest also applied to his wounds the medicine they required. The virtue and holiness of this venerable man so captured and inflamed John that, seizing the time and opportunity, he desired to abandon the world and surrender himself wholly to God. Since he opened his ears to the priest’s voice, he won a triumph over himself, cast off his military belt, and transferred his mind from martial exercises to spiritual warfare [Col. 1661C].

Because knowledge of letters adorns and instructs the mind, and sacred Scripture soothes the soul’s affections, John, taught by the venerable priest, attained great knowledge of the divine law. Sitting humbly at his feet and receiving from his mouth the words of heavenly wisdom, adorned with every kind of virtue, he made remarkable progress. After some time had passed, the venerable priest of Christ happily exchanged death for life. His death brought no small sorrow to the blessed young man. In his longing for the eremitic life, John chose a deserted place to inhabit in the province lying between the Douro and the Minho. There he persevered unyieldingly while the devil assailed him with various temptations, though the devil marshaled all his efforts for John’s ruin, recalling to the young man’s mind the pleasures and freedom of his former life and representing to him the way of perfection which he had undertaken as altogether steep and difficult. Had the Lord not joined battle and fought in his contest, he would have fallen entirely into weakness [Col. 1662A] and returned, like a dog, to the vomit of his former vanity.

## CHAPTER II. Tempted by the devil in the form of a woman, he triumphs wondrously, is made abbot over anchorites, and shines with a prophetic spirit.

One day, while he was attending with devout affection to heavenly contemplation, delighting in a secluded place and sitting alone in his cell, a certain woman, wandering through the trackless paths of the vast wilderness and fleeing as though terrified, reached the blessed man’s hermitage [Col. 1662B]. With tears and sighs she earnestly begged him to save her from the hands of her husband, who, she said, was seeking her in order to kill her, by hiding her in his cell that night. When he heard this, the servant of God—because love does not know fear—did not dread the weapons of the ancient enemy. Moved by love, he opened the door and allowed the fugitive to enter his own chamber. Engaging with her in familiar conversation, perhaps more intimate than was permitted, he spent the greater part of the night.

Afterwards, desiring to give himself to sleep, he lay down upon his bed. The devil stretched his bow and made ready his arrows upon it; stirring up the heat of lust, he seized, scorched, and inflamed John’s whole body. He had almost subjected his mind to himself through consent to wickedness, had not divine grace supplied the heedless anchorite, who implored divine help, with the arms of steadfastness and strengthened him with spiritual powers. The blessed servant of God therefore rose, rekindled a fire that was almost extinguished, and set his left arm in its flames. He remained unmoving until his flesh, utterly burned, was seen to separate from the bones; and by the force of the material fire he escaped the burning of the flesh that solicited him. The devil, miserably defeated, vanished; and, crying out from the upper roof of the cell, began to heap insults upon him and say: “The time will come, O senseless man, [Col. 1662C] the time will come when fire will not be able to snatch you from my hands.” But John gave immense thanks to Him who had stood by him in battle and thereafter became more cautious against the devil’s assaults.

Later, when the report of the holiness and reputation for perfection of two athletes of Christ, who lived celibate lives upon the lofty rocky peaks of mountains watered by the River Nonga, reached his ears, he left the desert so that through their example and instruction in holy life he might advance more and more in the growth of virtues. He came humbly to them and threw himself at their feet. The holy man was kindly received by the holy men, who had already learned of his virtue and purity of conscience through a divine revelation granted beforehand. Through their holy life and companionship, he so excelled all the hermits of that wilderness in virtue that those who had newly renounced the vanities of the world and were seeking a life pleasing to God in the desert entrusted themselves to blessed John’s instruction, to be happily trained by him.

When death had taken those two most holy elders after they had praiseworthily completed the contest of this present life, John was appointed in the abbot’s place. Leaving the rocks in which they had lived, he arranged to build a hermitage near the River Barosius, on the summit of a mountain whose inaccessible height and ruggedness offer a steep and difficult ascent. There both he and the other brothers, inflamed by love for their heavenly homeland, began to lead a life more angelic than human [Col. 1663A].

The fame of the venerable man spread widely through the surrounding regions and reached the ears of Henry, count of Lusitania. Henry visited him in person and was no little edified by his humility and poverty. After various conversations concerning the heavenly homeland, he humbly begged John to obtain from God by his prayers a son whom he might leave as heir of his principality. The blessed man at once, filled with the prophetic spirit, replied: “Take courage, my lord, for you shall have a son distinguished in the works of war and peace. He shall win a great name among all the princes of the earth, and he shall be the terror of unbelievers and the scourge of pagans.” So he spoke, and so it afterwards happened. For Theresa, wife of the aforesaid count, conceived and bore Alfonso Henriques, who became the honor and glory of the Portuguese nation and the foundation of the kingdom of Portugal. When his father, after illustrious deeds, breathed his last, Alfonso was heir to his father’s piety as well as to his kingdom. He pursued Saint John Cirita with the highest affection and, in difficult matters, had recourse to him as to a divine oracle. He was always accustomed to say: “Abbot John more easily obtains from the Lord whatever he desires than I obtain it from my friends” [Col. 1663B].

## CHAPTER III. Saint John the Baptist appears to our father Bernard; he commands him to send monks into Spain to build a monastery; and Blessed John Cirita, warned by divine revelation, meets them as they approach on their journey.

[Col. 1663C]

At this same time the most glorious Father Bernard, illuminating the whole Christian world with the rays of his virtue and teaching, governed the monastery of Clairvaux with the greatest piety and gentleness. In the year of the Lord 1119, on the twenty-fourth day of June, after the praises at Vigils, while he was persevering in prayer in the choir, Blessed John the Baptist appeared to him in the dress and form in which he is commonly depicted by the Church, and said to him:

“For the salvation of many souls, who lack instruction and wander far from the way of salvation, it is expedient for you to send some of your monks into the more remote regions of Spain. Divine mercy will show them the place which it has already chosen for the construction of a monastery, where many souls will be offered to God as an acceptable sacrifice through the daily mortification of body and heart. As testimony of this matter, I affirm to you with certainty [Col. 1663D] that monastic strictness shall never fail in that place, and that the church shall be consecrated to my name.”

Having said this, he disappeared. But blessed Father Bernard, filled with utter wonder, persevered until the sixth hour, considering what had happened to him and giving thanks to God. Wishing to carry out Saint John’s command, he selected, from among the distinguished men of the monastery of Clairvaux who served God faithfully through the merit of an innocent life, eight men especially eminent in holiness and fit to accomplish so arduous a work: namely Bohemund, Aldebert, John, Bernard, Cisinand, Roland, and Alan; and Bohemund was appointed their abbot. Having called them apart, he related to them the words of Saint John and explained the divine will concerning the construction of a new monastery in the western parts of Spain, in the place which a heavenly sign should point out to them. He added:

“On the journey you will meet a certain holy cultivator of the desert, of blameless life, named John. Forewarned by divine revelation, he awaits the day of your arrival. By his direction and counsel all your works shall be guided, until the will of God is perfectly fulfilled.”

And because the province to which he was sending them lay almost wholly under the yoke of unbelievers, he exhorted them steadfastly to undergo death for Christ and promised them an eternal crown. Therefore, after the honeyed words which divine love supplied to him, and after embraces of sincere charity, he dismissed his beloved sons in peace, strengthened by their father’s blessing. Taking leave of their brethren, they departed from the sacred monastery of Clairvaux.

But let us now turn our discourse to our John. While these things were happening in Gaul, the Baptist appeared also to him, as to our Father, informing him beforehand of the arrival of those eight monks whom the holy abbot was sending to establish a monastery. He commanded him to bring their holy desires to their desired end and, by his authority, to commend them to [Col. 1664B] the prince and nobles of the land. He declared that this monastery would become a renowned nursery of virtues, and showed him the place where he would find the monks on their arrival. Having said this, he disappeared.

The blessed servant of God, full of exultation and joy, set out. After some days, during which he wandered here and there through the dreadful and vast solitudes of the wilderness, he encountered the Clairvaux monks coming toward him not far from the city of Lamego. Its king, having been defeated by the Portuguese a few years earlier, had cast aside Muhammadan errors and embraced the Catholic faith. Who could adequately recount the joy felt by Christ’s servants when, after the hardships of a long journey and their various tribulations and distresses, they found Blessed John, appointed for them by Blessed Bernard as their guide and father? After a humble greeting, they handed him a letter from our most holy Father Bernard, composed in the following terms.

[Col. 1664C] Letter of our blessed Father Bernard, abbot, to Blessed John Cirita.

It is found among the letters of St Bernard in our edition, no. 464. See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXII, col. 669.

Having read this letter, Blessed John, filled with the greatest joy, resolved to go with the Clairvaux monks to Prince Alfonso, who was then staying at Guimarães, in order to obtain from him permission to choose any place whatever for building a new monastery. When they arrived at court, they were received most graciously by the prince. Considering the poverty of their clothing, the gravity of their modesty, and their profound humility, he had scarcely understood the reason for the servants of God’s journey and arrival when, behold, he dismissed them in peace, furnished with the following privilege:

ALFONSO, most glorious duke and, by God’s grace, prince of the Portuguese [Col. 1664D], son of the illustrious Count Henry and Queen Theresa, and grandson also of the great Alfonso.

For the remedy of my soul and of the souls of my parents, I grant to you, Abbot John Cirita and the brethren who are with you, this charter and safeguard: let no one hinder you from going and establishing a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, of the new reform, in such a manner that the land on which you establish it shall belong to our dominion; and if it belongs to another, let it be purchased at our expense. And if any one of our vassals or knights should act against this, let him be cursed by God and tortured in hell with Judas the traitor.

The charter and safeguard made at Guimarães, on the Kalends of March, era 1158.

I, the aforesaid prince, confirm this charter with my own hand.

Blessed John and the monks then departed and returned by the same road. For the venerable abbot had been warned not to proceed farther, but to remain in [Col. 1665A] the inner wilderness and more secluded desert until God’s will should deign to be disclosed to them. After spending a few days on the road, they came to the river Barosus, which lies a mile and a half from the city of Lamego and waters the extensive places of that wilderness. Following its current, they reached very lofty mountains which encircle, like walls, a most pleasant valley, into which two streams flow their waters into the Barosus.

They resolved to choose this place, as though entirely removed from human society, for habitation, and to settle there, awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the great sign of God which had long before been promised to their holy Father Bernard. There they made four huts from the branches of trees and erected a very poor little church, dedicated to the name of the Holy Saviour, which remains to this day. They fixed their dwelling there for the time being. The venerable Abbot John, leaving the Clairvaux monks intent upon prayer and devout works [Col. 1665B], returned to his own brethren, until the divine will concerning the building of the monastery and the arrangement of its site should be revealed to them by some heavenly sign.

## CHAPTER IV. The monks build the monastery of Saint John of Tarouca in the place divinely shown to them by heavenly splendour.

Therefore Abbot Bohemund and his companions, giving themselves without interruption to divine praises, earnestly implored divine mercy with continual prayers, that they might deserve to see the heavenly sign promised to their Father Bernard. It happened on the thirteenth day of April, in the year of the Lord 1120, that Blessed Bohemund came out from his hut at about midnight and prayed to God to accept their service. Turning his eyes toward the nearer valley, he saw—and behold—a splendour of wondrous brightness, like lightning descending from heaven, remain motionless in the air [Col. 1665C] near the ground, making the dark narrow places of the forests and surrounding mountains bright on every side as with noonday light.

Astonished, the servant of Christ, not ignorant of the mystery of the divine light, called his brethren and showed them the sign promised by Saint John the Baptist. Immediately, setting aside every difficulty and believing it to be a sign of divine goodness, they resolved to choose that place for the building of a monastery. They exulted in spirit and rejoiced with spiritual gladness, as though saying: “This is our rest for ever and ever; here we shall dwell, because God has chosen it.”

They saw this heavenly splendour in the same place and at the same hour on the next eight nights. In order to obey the counsel of holy Father Bernard—who had appointed John Cirita, whom we left serving the Lord with his companions in the mountain rocks, as their guide and ruler—they explained in the following letter to the holy abbot what had happened and what had been shown to them by God:

To the venerable Father JOHN CIRITA, Brother BOHEMUND and the rest who are with him offer such small service as they can.

Know that, divine mercy so disposing, not I alone but all whom you left in this place have beheld with unworthy eyes a wondrous sign. Since twelve nights have now passed since we first saw it, and since we heard from our Father, who directed us here, of a similar prodigy, we thought it right to report this to you, lest perhaps the Most High wishes a monastery to be built in this region. May your fatherhood prosper, and may it keep us, its little sons, commended to God.

Two monks carrying this letter were sent out. After various perils of the journey, they reached the hermitage of the blessed man. Received by him with the greatest humility, they made the miracle known to him both by their report and by the letter itself. Then, kneeling and raising hands and eyes to heaven, he offered and rendered immense thanks to the Creator of heaven and earth [Col. 1666A] with the deepest affection of his heart. Afterwards, all together and with confidence, they began to deliberate about this miracle and the construction of the monastery. Following various conversations concerning the heavenly life, he gave them a letter like theirs and sent them back to their own abbot:

To the most beloved brethren in the hermitage above the river Barosus, at Curved Mountain, JOHN, the unworthy servant of Christ Jesus, desires salvation in Him.

“I shall sing for ever of the mercy of the Lord,” which He has willed to show toward His servants. Take courage and believe the words of your master, for through them the day of your joy is now drawing near. And lest you be led astray by a false vision, earnestly and with tears ask the Lord of all to show you this sign again; and, after you have said Masses, mark out and enclose the place where you see the brightness, so that, with the Lord’s help, we may build the monastery there. May eternal mercy preserve you, and in your holy prayers ask forgiveness for my sins.

Immediately, as humble sons ready to obey, they strove to carry out all that had been commanded them. By frequent vigils, fasts, sacrifices, and prayers, they begged for the renewal and confirmation of the former miracle. The Lord deigned to hear them, showing them again the divine light. They enclosed with a fence the whole area to which the divine brightness extended, so that they might erect there a church and the monastery’s buildings.

Then the venerable Abbot Cirita arrived, and all were filled with incredible joy at his presence. He too, devoting the whole night to prayer, deserved to see that splendour. He understood that this light signified the power of radiance and the rays of heavenly teaching with which those monks and their successors were to be adorned, so as to illuminate the whole country—indeed, the whole Church—by driving away the darkness of vices.

He therefore went to Prince Alfonso [Col. 1666C], taking Blessed Bohemund with him, and recounted to him the whole miracle. On hearing it, the Catholic prince was carried away in great astonishment. At length he dismissed them enriched with privileges, ornaments, money, and various gifts for constructing the monastery. Returning to the wilderness, they began to build the house of God. The prince himself laid the first stone on the twenty-first day of June, in the year of the Lord 1122, in the presence of the magnates of the kingdom and the bishop of Lamego himself, who blessed the stone and the foundations of the church. A few days later the monastery was completed. Blessed Bohemund presided there, as holy Father Bernard had directed. At last, full of virtues and renowned for miracles, he shortly afterwards fell asleep in the Lord; and, by the common consent of the brethren, Blessed Aldebert was elected, who had been prior under the same Father Bohemund.

## CHAPTER V. How Blessed John Cirita became a Cistercian monk; and concerning Queen Theresa, who assumed the habit of our Order.

[Col. 1666D]

Behold the humble beginning of the Cistercian Order in the remoter regions of Spain, namely in Lusitania. From this it was afterwards permitted to grow so greatly that a thousand monks lived together in the monastery of Alcobaça alone. We treated at length above, in the Life of our most holy Father Bernard, of its miraculous foundation.

When Blessed John saw the monks of Saint John of Tarouca—for this was the name which they had given the new monastery—shining with various virtues, and learned that they flourished in the school of spiritual virtues through zeal for regular discipline, he greatly desired to follow in their footsteps. Thus, with incredible exultation of mind, he received the Cistercian habit from the hand of Blessed Abbot Aldebert, and was the first in Lusitania to enter holy religion under our observance.

Observe the humility of the blessed man. From his youth he had been a master of others in the holy art [Col. 1667A], and was honoured by them as father and abbot; and behold, he became once more a disciple. After making his profession, he returned to his brethren dwelling in the wilderness and persuaded them to submit their necks to the yoke of so holy a religious life. There he built another monastery of the Cistercian Order, called Saint Christopher of Dafoens.

Among the other anchorites who gave themselves to the Cistercian Order, the following were especially distinguished: Peter Froila, Pelagius, Alvarus, Andrew, Luyba, Germanus, Rofendus, and Hermannus. Their lives are contained in an ancient manuscript book of the monastery of Saint Christopher, as may be seen in John Marquez, *On the Origin of the Hermit Brothers of Saint Augustine*, chapter 15, §11.

At this time Queen Theresa, daughter of Alfonso, emperor of the Spains, assumed the habit of the Cistercian Order from the hand of Blessed John Cirita. Soon afterwards, struck by illness and lying upon her bed, already near death [Col. 1667B], she wrote a letter to her son Alfonso Henriquez. Entrusting it to John Cirita, she departed this life, not without a reputation for sanctity.

And behold, the prince arrived at the city of Coimbra to seek his mother’s final blessing. But when he learned that she had already departed from this world, he was suddenly struck with the deepest grief and read the letter which Blessed John had kept, composed in the following terms:

To her most beloved son ALFONSO, THERESA, his mother, sends greeting and her blessing.

My end is near, most loving son, and now all things of this world have become worthless to me, except you, whom I would have wished to see. But let us see one another in a better homeland. I commend my servants and maidservants to you, and the brethren of the new reform, under whose habit and profession I depart. I pray that my burial may be beside your father, the illustrious Count Henry, so that those whom life saw joined together may be seen by death to be inseparable. Let your sisters and their children be dear to you. Govern your people in peace, and above all worship God. May He bless you and preserve you from your enemies. I leave you my blessing and favour, and I go to God and my Judge. Farewell in the Lord, my dearest son.

When Abbot Adelbert had happily completed the course of his life, so that even after death, shining with miracles, he was honoured by a great concourse of people, God’s servant John was called to preside over the monks of Saint John of Tarouca. Though reluctant, he accepted this dignity in the year of the Lord 1125. There he began to emit wondrous virtues and rays of holiness; wholly absorbed in virtue, and with all his hope directed toward God, he breathed after heavenly things with the innermost affection of his heart.

To preserve chastity and wash away the stains entering into his heart, he considered that his flesh must be chastised with the sickle of abstinence. Thus for the space of three days he tasted absolutely nothing; when these had passed, he took only a small morsel of bread, and nourished his body, worn out by old age and almost consumed by penitence as though by infirmities, with cold water [Col. 1667D]. With the greatest diligence he watched lest time slip away in vain. Thus one would find the venerable old man either persisting in prayer, occupied with divine praises in choir, or intent upon manual work with the monks. Apart from these things, judging himself removed from all other concerns and involving himself in no business, he became for his monks a rule through the example of his holy manner of life.

## CHAPTER VI. On the origin of the Order of Aviz, which serves under the Cistercian observance and received its laws and rule from Blessed John Cirita.

It happened, after Alfonso, the first king of the Portuguese, had defeated a vast multitude of pagans in the field of Ourique, that certain knights eager for glory made a league and pact among themselves: fighting for the Catholic faith and the liberty of their country, they would rather surrender their lives into the hands of unbelievers than abandon their holy purpose under the compulsion either of danger of death or of any necessity whatever.

Their reputation was great; as they repelled the attacks of the Moors through frequent victories, their fame spread everywhere day by day. King Alfonso, desiring to bring their pious purpose to the happiest conclusion, summoned Blessed John Cirita, that he might give these knights a norm and rule of life, so that, serving under some observance, they might fight more gloriously for Christ’s name. The holy abbot came and, with the consent of the apostolic legate, wrote down constitutions for them to observe.

Blessed Abbot John therefore composed this rule for the knights of Aviz, and all professed that they would observe it firmly and unanimously. Later the very famous Lusitanian city of Évora, made most noble by the frequent residence of Portugal’s kings [Col. 1668B], was granted to those knights by King Alfonso in the year of the Lord 1147. At length they moved to the castle of Aviz and dwelt there, and from Aviz they were called the Knights of Aviz. But more concerning this Order is found in the Life of Blessed Peter Alfonso, book II.

## CHAPTER VII. Blessed John Cirita, renowned for the prophetic spirit and various virtues, departs this life and shines forth through various miracles after death.

The venerable Abbot John, beloved by God and men, shone with such gifts of virtues that by his most fervent way of life he powerfully kindled into the love of God both his own monks and lay people, who frequently flocked to the holy man to drink from him the water of heavenly wisdom. Since he surpassed in holiness and learning all the religious men of that province, he was honoured with the highest affection by all: by Prince Alfonso of Lusitania [Col. 1668C], and by the magnates and nobles of that kingdom.

He was especially honoured by the most noble Egea Monio and his wife Theresa. To show their piety and affection toward him and our Order, they founded the monastery of Salzedas and gave it to Blessed John Cirita and the Cistercian household in the year of the Lord 1126, long before the establishment of the Order of Aviz. In the year 1145 he secured the union of the Benedictine monks of Saint Peter of Aquilis with the Cistercian congregation, subjected them to the monastery of Saint John of Tarouca, and obtained many privileges and resources from the king and the nobles of the kingdom. These benefits, and countless others, came through his merits to our sacred Order, recently planted in those regions.

As a true shepherd and father, he instructed and strengthened his brethren and showed himself a faithful minister. He was pious, merciful, humble, gracious, scorning no one and despising no one, venerable in age [Col. 1668D] and character. He was also visited by frequent heavenly consolations, and the Lord revealed to him the hidden mysteries of His wisdom. He shone with the prophetic spirit, so that he knew not only future events but even the thoughts of men. By streams of tears he strove to wash away the sins of his youth, as though he had not obtained forgiveness of his sins by the continuous mortification of his body and the martyrdom of monastic life.

When the venerable old man had reached the limit of decrepit age, weighing with true and ample judgment the burden of so grave an office, and judging that his failing strength could by no means bear it well, he resolved to relinquish the abbatial dignity, withdraw from every concern, and await the last day of his dissolution in the monastery of Saint Christopher, which he himself had begun before becoming a Cistercian monk. Calling together his brethren, the monks of Saint John of Tarouca, he explained his will to them and appointed in his own place [Col. 1669A] Blessed Monk Bernard as their abbot, one of the first founders sent by our most blessed Father. He was a man of proven virtue, so that both while living in this world and after his most happy departure from it, shining with various miracles, he was venerated by the people as a saint.

Accordingly, in the year 1161 the monks accepted his resignation, sorrowful indeed and not without tears. He returned to the ancient hermitage of Saint Christopher, where he was humbly received by Abbot Michael and the other brethren. For three and a half years, by frequent fasts and incredible mortification of the body, he strove to acquire new sheaves of merits.

But while his body failed, he exulted with wonderful serenity of soul and sweetness of spirit. When he was struck by grave illness, drew near to his departure and day of death, and knew it beforehand through the Lord’s revelation, he dictated the following letter to his sons, the monks of Saint John of Tarouca, whom he loved with the innermost affection of his heart, a few days before his happy death:

JOHN, poor in virtues and rich in failings, to you religious men who offer to the Lord an immaculate sacrifice: everlasting salvation and remembrance of me.

It has pleased the Lord Jesus Christ to bring me to the end which I desired: the day of my release and joy is drawing near. But because I know myself lacking in your virtues, and fear lest I appear before the Bridegroom without oil [Col. 1670A], you who have prepared your lamps in due time, help me while there is time, lest perhaps I hear that harsh saying: “I do not know you.” And if the Lord grants me, as I hope, the inaccessible light, it will be mine not to fail you in your needs, since I was your brother and companion in tribulations and shall not abandon you in the time of joy. And because sickness weakens my little body, my soul greets you; pray to the Lord for it.

When the structure of his outward dwelling was already loosened on every side and gave his longing soul free departure, all the monks assembled. Exhorting them with a pious discourse to perfection and to observance of the Rule, and blessing them, now strengthened by the Church’s sacred sacraments, he began in an intelligible voice to chant the hymn *Te Deum laudamus*—“We praise thee, O God.” When he reached its final verse and brought it to an end, he happily fell asleep in the Lord. Taken up by angels, he passed as a victor into glory on the twenty-third day of December, in the year of the Lord 1164 [Col. 1670B].

After his death, the Lord deigned to show through various miracles the purity of his conscience and the manifest character of his merits. Upon his tomb the following epitaph was placed, engraved in large letters:

JOHN, ABBOT OF CIRITA, GOVERNED THE MONASTERIES OF ST JOHN, ST CHRISTOPHER, SALZEDAS, AND ST PETER. RENOWNED IN LIFE, RENOWNED IN MERITS, RENOWNED IN MIRACLES, HE SHINES IN HEAVEN. HE DIED ON THE TENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF JANUARY, ERA 1202.

[Col. 1669]

## RULE OF THE MILITARY ORDER OF AVIZ, ISSUED BY BLESSED JOHN CIRITA.

(*Fasciculus SS. Cisterc.*, p. 273.)

[Col. 1669C] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: God one, true, and inseparable in essence. We, John Cirita, Abbot of Saint John, and Guiscardus, monk of the same monastery, in the presence of the most noble King Alfonso and the other men of his court, by the consent and authority of the lord Bishop of Ostia, now legate *a latere* throughout all Spain, establish and ordain a knighthood in honour of God and our Father Benedict, for the glory of our Cistercian reform, and in order that Christ’s faithful may be delivered from the raids of the Moors. Its knights are to defend religion in war, practise charity in peace, preserve chastity in marriage, lay waste the lands of the Moors by continual incursions, and wear a habit bearing before them the sign of religion: namely, a small hood with a scapular so made that it does not hinder them when fighting in battle [Col. 1669D]. They shall not quarrel about the colour of the other garments, but all things shall conform to the requirements of the season. The scapular, however, shall always be black.

In war they shall have coats of mail, swords, and lances according to the strength of each, carrying nothing marked with gold except their swords and spurs, and always placing their hope in the armour of faith. In peace they shall rise for prayer, hear Masses, fast on Fridays, and sleep in their small hoods. They shall keep silence when eating together. They shall receive pilgrims, honour elders, and receive the master of the knighthood as father and leader; and in all things they shall keep before their eyes the Rule of holy Father Benedict.

From what they acquire in war they shall give to the poor, widows, and churches; and they shall take care to lead the Moors whom they have taken captive to the faith by holy admonitions.

If they capture a castle or city, they shall inform the lord king and, at his command, dispose of everything [Col. 1670D], remaining subject to authority not only when it is good but also when it is harsh. Let the master, as leader of the others, take care to govern his subjects not only by words but also by examples, teaching not only in peace but fighting also in war.

If any knight has a grievance against him and, after an excuse has not been accepted, still considers himself wronged, he shall have recourse [Col. 1671A] to the abbot appointed by the Lord Abbot of Cîteaux, lay his complaint against the master before him, and await judgment. Only the Roman pontiff or his legate *a latere*, or the most reverend Father Abbot of Cîteaux and his visitor appointed for this purpose, and personally the Father Abbot of Clairvaux, may take cognizance of that judgment.

In elections of the master and other officials, the order established in the definitions of Cîteaux shall be observed. The newly elected man shall receive the insignia of his mastership from the hand of an abbot, and in his hands shall make oath and obedience in the following form.

### Form of the oath which the master of the Order of Aviz must make.

[Col. 1671B] I, N., newly elected master of the knighthood of Saint Benedict of the Cistercian Order, in my own name and in the name of this knighthood, swear and promise obedience to the Roman pontiff, to my lord the king of Portugal, and to you, Father Abbot, in the name of Cîteaux, and to all your successors who shall be for ever. I swear that I shall not sell or give away the goods of the knighthood, nor consent to their being sold, given away, or alienated. In war I shall not abandon my knights in danger in order to secure my own freedom, nor surrender castles, towers, or towns without the command and will of the king of Portugal. I shall not permit my knights to go into battle unarmed or to go about without the hood. I shall go at the king’s commands, pursue his traitors to the best of my ability [Col. 1671C], harass the lands of the Moors, defend the right of this kingdom in every place, and be ready for every war with horses and arms; and I shall never act against all these things. So help me God and these holy Gospels.

After the election of the master, he himself shall give the insignia to knights newly entering. If, however, the lord king or his son and heir is present, they shall perform the ceremony of admission to the order of knighthood. If at the time when anyone is admitted an abbot of the Cistercian Order should be personally present there, he shall give the insignia, and homage shall be made in his hand.

If any knight, while travelling, finds an abbot of the Cistercian Order, he shall leave his horse, approach humbly, request a blessing, and offer himself as a companion on the journey. If such an abbot passes through places, castles, or cities where knights of this fellowship are present, whether in peace or war, the commander of the castle shall offer him the keys; all things shall be governed according to his direction for the time he is there.

Cistercian monks shall be received as brethren, and every office of charity shall be shown to them. I, the above-named King Alfonso, ratify and confirm all these things by my authority. And I, Guiscardus, monk of Saint John of Tarouca, at the command [Col. 1672B] of Lord King Alfonso and of Father John Cirita, the aforesaid abbot, dictated and wrote all these things with my own hand at Coimbra, on the Ides of August, era 1200.

The Archbishop of Braga, on behalf of the kingdom, approve and confirm.

The Bishop of Lisbon, on behalf of the clergy, approve and confirm.

Peter, offspring of the king, peer of the Franks and master of the new knighthood, on behalf of myself and my knights, approve and confirm.

Ferdinand Roderici Monteyro, knight of the new knighthood, approve and confirm.

Gundisalvus Vanegas, knight of the new knighthood, approve and confirm.

[Col. 1672C] Ferdinand John, knight of the new knighthood, approve and confirm.

John Portarius, knight of the new knighthood, approve and confirm.

Peter de Sousa, knight of the new knighthood, approve and confirm.

Roderic Vanegas, knight of the new knighthood, praise and approve.

Julian Alfonso, knight of the new knighthood, confirm and praise.

[Col. 1671]

## APPENDIX TO JOHN CIRITA.

### I. The Cistercian Order of Saint Michael in Lusitania is established by King Alfonso under the correction and governance of the Abbot of Alcobaça.

(*Fasciculus SS. Cisterc.*, p. 262.)

[Col. 1671D] Among our number there must be counted certain other religious men who, serving in the regions of Lusitania under the Cistercian observance, owe their origin to the most illustrious King Alfonso Henriquez of the Portuguese [Col. 1672D]. Using the words of its founder himself, I shall describe the beginning and rule of life of this Order. For he says:

[Col. 1673A] “In the name of God, of Saint Michael the Archangel, and of the holy guardian angel. Since it is fitting to repay the benefits of almighty God by due services, therefore I, Alfonso, by God’s grace king of the Portuguese, wishing and desiring, in my lowliness, to acknowledge the divine favour, and that my descendants may remember His wonders by which He established our kingdom upon the earth, after the counsel and mature deliberation of the good men whom the Lord chose for Himself—namely Martin, Abbot of Alcobaça, Ranulph, master in sacred letters, and very many monks of the same monastery who were present, together also with the governors entrusted to our care—we establish a certain brotherhood of knights in praise and honour of our Lord Jesus Christ and of the most blessed Virgin Mary His mother, under the invocation of Saint Michael the Archangel and my guardian angel. The reason why it is established in this way is as follows.

“While I was in Santarém, Albarch, king of Seville, came against me with a huge multitude of knights, such that his multitude covered all the borders of my kingdom. He pitched camp beside the town in which I was shut up with a small band of my own men, awaiting the arrival of some assistance. But a messenger came, reporting that the king of León had arrived. Since there was suspicion between us, I feared him, believing that he had come to aid my enemies. Therefore I resolved to go out to battle against Albarch before he arrived, and ordered my men to be made ready on the next day [Col. 1673C].

“I prayed to my angel, whom God in His mercy had given me as companion and guardian, and to blessed Michael the Archangel, that they would come to my aid and rescue me from the hand of my enemies. This indeed happened. When in battle my standard had been captured by my enemies, I leaped down from my chariot in order to free it; and while I fought on foot in the press, a wondrous thing to see appeared beside me, sinner that I am: the arm of one fighting and helping me, armed as it seemed to me, and its upper part was covered with a wing like that of an angel. But I could not see the body, nor did anyone see it, although many of the Moors saw the hand, as captives afterwards said.

“When I saw the hand, I was strengthened within myself and leapt among the enemy; and behold, a thousand fell at my side and ten thousand at my right hand [Col. 1673D]. My enemy was defeated, and we gathered their spoils. We saw cast down upon the plains of Santarém the great hand which had pursued us, and we sang praise to our God: ‘For He is good, for His mercy endureth for ever.’

“Afterwards, when I was preparing to wage war against the king of León, I learned that he had come to help me and was returning in peace. Joyful and glad at this, I came to praise the Lord Jesus Christ at the monastery of Alcobaça. There I remained for thirty-three days, serving Him and considering the kingdom of God. And lest the help of Saint Michael and my angel be forgotten, by the counsel of those mentioned above [Col. 1674A], I resolved to establish an order and fellowship of knights who should wear over their hearts a purple wing adorned with gold and brilliance, such as that which I had seen in battle seemed to my eyes to have been. The conditions which the knights of this Fellowship must observe and swear when they receive the wing are these—”
are.

## Constitutions of the Knights of the Order of Saint Michael, or of the Wing

1. “No one who is not a nobleman of our palace and court shall wear the wing or be admitted to our Society.

2. All who fought in the conflict in order to recover my banner shall be admitted to the Society and shall wear the wing.

[Col. 1674B] 3. He who is admitted to the Society shall be beside the king, or beside his banner, in battle; and no one may bear that banner unless he wears the wing.

4. He to whom the wing is given shall swear, into the hands of the abbot of Alcobaça, fidelity to God, the Roman pontiff, and the king, in the customary form; and no one but the abbot of Alcobaça shall confer the wing.

5. A knight of this militia shall daily recite the number of prayers customarily recited by lay brothers of the Cistercian Order, whether in peace or in war.

6. When anyone receives the order, he shall give fifty solidi for the repair of the altar of Saint Michael in the church of Alcobaça.

7. All brothers of this militia shall go to Alcobaça, hear Vespers, Matins, and [Col. 1674C] Mass, and receive communion from the abbot’s hand, clothed in white capes in the manner of lay brothers.

8. The abbot of Alcobaça shall have jurisdiction over the knights and may excommunicate them if they live wickedly, and compel them to abandon concubines and their most wicked manner of life.

9. The knights of this Society, after their first marriage, if they have children, or a son who is heir, shall not enter into second marriages after the death of their first wife, but shall live in continence.

10. On their shields in war they shall bear the wing without any other device; and in peace they shall not go without it.

11. The knights of this brotherhood shall be gentle toward the humble, stern toward the proud, helpers of women—especially noblewomen—[Col. 1674D] virgins, and widows; in all things defenders of the faith, assailants of enemies, and obedient to their superiors.

12. The number of knights shall be according to the king’s will. Whomever he chooses he shall send to the abbot of Alcobaça; and the abbot shall give him the wing and a white cape with his blessing, receive from him the oath in the customary form, read to him these ordinances and the other ordinances of his order, and enter his name in the register.

And because this is my will, and because I desire to commemorate for my descendants the benefit of the Lord and of Saint Michael, I, King Alfonso, established this militia in the monastery of Alcobaça, in the Era 1205,” that is, in the year 1167 of our Redemption. BERNARD BRITO, *History of the Cistercians*.

## II. Privilege Granted by Alfonso, King of Portugal, to the Monastery of Saint John, after the Saracens Had Been Driven Away near the River Távora in 1122

(*Fasciculus SS. Cisterc.*, p. 215.)

[Col. 1675]

[Col. 1675A] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. I, Alfonso, most victorious prince of the Portuguese, son of Count Henry and Queen Teresa, and likewise grandson of the great Alfonso, emperor of the Spains, make known to those present and future that King Albucazan, king of Badalhonce [Note: [Col. 1675B] Pax Julia, in Spanish, Badajoz.], came with his people to devastate our lands. He besieged Trancoso, laid waste many other castles of my territory, and carried off captive [Note: [Col. 1675B] He reduced to captivity.] men, women, children, beasts of burden, and much livestock [Note: [Col. 1675B] Cattle.]; he inflicted great devastation [Note: [Col. 1675B] He caused damage.] and left the whole country ruined. Therefore [Note: [Col. 1675B] For this reason.] I gathered my men and went to where the brothers of Saint John of Barosa were. I found that they lived in great holiness; and because I recognized that the Lord was with them, [Col. 1675B] I took [Note: [Col. 1675B] I led with me.] from there Prior Aldebert, that he might pray for me and for my army [Note: [Col. 1676B] Army.] and celebrate Masses. He assisted me so effectively in battle that, when he prayed, I was victorious.

But one day [Col. 1676A] I left my army and went without him to fight with the Moors. In that battle I lost a cross which I had brought [Note: [Col. 1676B] Carried.] from the monastery, and many knights, because [Note: [Col. 1676B] On account of the fact that.] I fought without the prayers of that good man. Therefore I, the aforesaid prince, having understood the power and good assistance [Note: [Col. 1676B] Help.] which his prayers gave me, for the service of God and the salvation of my soul and of my parents, grant to the monastery of Saint John and to the brothers who shall serve God there, the hamlets of Reguenga which I possess near [Note: [Col. 1676B] Near.] Trancoso, that they may have them for food and clothing, with all their appurtenances, rights of entry, and rights of departure.

If, however, anyone, whether one of our own people or a stranger, should attempt to violate this covenant, let him first be accursed and, with Judas the traitor, [Col. 1676B] condemned in hell. This charter was made in the month of June, Era 1160. I, the aforesaid prince, confirm with my own hand this charter which I ordered to be made, and ratify it by my authority.

XXVI.—King Lothair. King Charles. Extinction of Charlemagne’s dynasty. 91.

XXI.—Luke. 184.  
XXII.—Martial of Limoges. 185.

### Part Two, Book Three

I.—Prologue. 229.  
II.—Foundation of the monastery of Saint Evroult of Ouche, and of various monasteries in Neustria. Invasions of the Normans into this province, where they settled. 230.

XIX.—On Saint Josse, son of Juthael, king of the Bretons. 290.

XXI.—Results of the battle. William subdues the country. He is crowned king of the English. 299.

### Book Four

I.—Deeds of King William in England. 303.  
II.—King William returns to Normandy. Archbishops of Rouen. 306.  
III.—The English are oppressed by the Normans. They plan rebellions. 308.  
IV.—King William returns to England. Rebellion of the city of Exeter. 311.  
V.—Other rebellions in England against the Normans. 313.  
VI.—Many Norman knights leave England and return to Normandy. Norman tyranny. Rebellions of the English. 315.  
VII.—The futile attempts of the sons of King Harold, the Danes, and the Saxons against the Normans. 316.

IX.—Council of Windsor. The piety and praiseworthy conduct of King William. On the origins of the monastic order in England. [Col. 1680] 322.

XI.—Peace and concord are gradually established between English and Normans. The unhappy fate of Earl Morcar. On William of Poitiers, the writer. 329.  
XII.—King William divides the lands of the English among his Normans. Pride and luxury of the Normans. 330.  
XIII.—Norman churchmen also seek riches. The commendable abstinence of the monk Guitmund. 335.  
XIV.—Dissensions among the heirs of the county of Flanders. Queen Matilda governs Normandy. 339.  
XV.—Council of Rouen. 341.  
XVI.—Abbeys in Normandy under King William. 343.  
XVII.—Pope Alexander II. Pope Gregory VII. On the bishopric of Le Mans. 346.  
XVIII.—Herbert, count of Le Mans. Disorders in Maine. 347.  
XIX.—The rebellion of Counts Roger of Hereford and Ralph of Norwich against King William. The execution of Earl Waltheof. 351.  
XX.—Life of Guthlac the hermit. 356.  
XXI.—Death of Blessed Guthlac the hermit. Miracles and wonders at the saint’s tomb. Construction of Crowland monastery. 361.  
XXII.—History of Crowland monastery. 362.  
XXIII.—Miracles at Waltheof’s tomb. 366.  
XXIV.—King William vainly attempts to subdue the Bretons. Ainard, first abbot of Saint Peter of Préaux. His successor Fulk. 368.  
XXV.—Dissensions among the sons of King William. 370.

### Book Five

I.—Prologue. 373.  
II.—Various events in Normandy. 376.  
III.—A pitiable event at Lisieux. Death of Hugh, bishop of Lisieux. 377.  
IV.—Gilbert Maminot, Hugh’s successor. 379.  
V.—John, archbishop of Rouen. William, his successor. 380.  
VI.—Council of Lillebonne. 381.  
VII.—On the city of Rouen. On the city of Évreux. Deeds of Blessed Taurinus. 386.  
VIII.—Mellonus and Avitianus, apostles of Normandy. Distichs in honor of the forty-seven first bishops of Rouen. 390.  
IX.—Continuation of the distichs. 394.  
X.—Continuation of the distichs. 400.  
XI.—Continuation of the distichs. Epitaphs of Rollo and William Longsword. 405.  
XII.—Succession of events in Neustria under King William. Rebellions of Robert, son of King William. 407.  
XIII.—Continuation of events. 410.  
XIV.—Other sons of King William distinguish themselves by good conduct. His daughter Adela. 413.  
XV.—The author returns to the history of the monastery of Saint-Evroult. Administration of Abbot Mainier. 415.  
XVI.—Survey of donations made to the monastery of Saint-Evroult. 417.

XXI.—The survey of donations continues. On the lords of Manlay. 441.  
XXII.—The surveys of donations continue. 445.

I.—Prologue. Various events. 449.  
II.—Digression. History of Blessed Count William, monk of Gellone. 452.

VII.—Continuation of the Life of Blessed Evroult. 472.  
VIII.—Continuation of the same Life. 475.

XVI.—Succession of the abbots of Saint-Evroult. 499.

### Part Three, Book Seven

I.—Brief compendium of events in the kingdom of the Franks, from the coronation of King Pippin to the end of Charlemagne’s dynasty. 507.

XI.—The author returns to the narrative of events. Wars between Normans and Franks over the Vexin. 541.  
XII.—Death of King William. 543.

### Book Eight

I.—Duke Robert succeeds his father in Normandy, and William Rufus in England. Numerous discords arise after King William’s death. 557.  
II.—Odo, bishop of Bayeux, is released from custody. Henry purchases from his brother Duke Robert a portion of Normandy. 559.

VIII.—Various events in Apulia, Normandy, and England. Deaths of certain magnates. William Rufus’s strict administration. 578.  
IX.—King William plans to attack his brother Robert in Normandy. The people of Le Mans rise against the aforesaid Robert. Count Fulk of Anjou. 582.  
X.—Count Fulk of Anjou devises a new fashion in shoes. Customs, clothes, games, and so forth of this period. 586.  
XI.—The people of Le Mans rise against the Normans. 588.  
XII.—Dissensions and wars among the magnates of Normandy. 591.  
XIII.—Discordant disturbances and wars in Normandy continue. 593.  
XIV.—Discordant disturbances in Normandy continue. War between the men of Évreux and Conches. 597.

XVII.—A remarkable occurrence involving a certain priest of the diocese of Lisieux. 607.  
XVIII.—Agreements concluded between King William and Duke Robert. Affairs of the bishopric of Lisieux. Roger, abbot of Saint-Evroult. 612.

XXI.—Conspiracies are formed against William Rufus in England. 622.  
XXII.—Discords and private wars among the magnates of Normandy. 625.  
XXIII.—Robert of Bellême harasses the monks of Saint-Evroult. 630.  
XXIV.—Religious life and death of certain knights. On Anfrid, first abbot of Préaux. Abbots, prelates, and monks distinguished in virtues and learning. 632.  
XXV.—On the new garments of monks: how and by whom they were invented. 636.  
XXVI.—Abbots and monks conspicuous for piety in new monasteries. On the founders of the new orders. 642.  
XXVII.—The distinguished Hugh of Grandmesnil, on his sickbed, receives the monastic habit from Geoffrey, prior of Saint-Evroult, and dies shortly afterward. On his children. 645.

I.—Prologue. Remarkable events of this period. 647.  
II.—Various omens. Council of Clermont. 649.  
III.—Councils held in regions of Normandy. The holy war is preached. 653.

VII.—Capture of Nicaea. Advance of the great army of crusaders. Battles against the Turks. 665.

IX.—Siege of Antioch. 672.  
X.—The siege of Antioch continues. The crusaders capture that city. 678.  
XI.—The Turks, led by Kerbogha, attack the Franks at Antioch. 681.

XVIII.—Jerusalem is captured by the crusaders. 708.

XX.—Battle of Ascalon. Victory falls to the Christians. On Baldric, archbishop of Dol. 712.

### Book Ten

I.—Urban II dies. Paschal II; Henry IV and Henry V, emperors. Their disputes with the supreme pontiffs. 717.  
II.—Narrative of English and Norman affairs. Character of William Rufus. Deaths of certain prelates. On Blessed Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury. 721.  
III.—Crusader knights, bishops, and abbots. 723.  
IV.—Frankish and Norman magnates contend with one another over the Vexin. [Col. 1683] 725.

IX.—Serlo and Roger, abbots of Saint-Evroult. Controversies arise between the monks and the bishop of Lisieux. Consecration of the church of Saint-Evroult. 741.

XI.—Bohemond recovers Laodicea. Duke Robert travels through Italy on his return to Normandy. New knights prepare themselves for the holy war. On the mournful event which occurred in the New Forest. 747.  
XII.—Evil omens concerning King William. The aforesaid king dies. 749.  
XIII.—Henry, brother of William Rufus, succeeds him on the throne. 753.  
XIV.—Count Elias recovers the county of Le Mans. 755.  
XV.—Rivalry and dissensions arise between King Henry and Duke Robert. On Ranulf Flambard, bishop of Durham. Duke Robert crosses into England with an armed force. 757.  
XVI.—Peace is arranged between the two brothers, Henry and Robert. 761.  
XVII.—The duke of Poitou, the duke of Burgundy, and many other magnates take the cross. Their disputes with the emperor of Constantinople. 763.  
XVIII.—Emperor Alexius’s treachery. The crusaders’ army is destroyed by the Turks in Asia Minor. 767.  
XIX.—Rule of Godfrey, king of Jerusalem. Baldwin, his brother and successor. Battle of Ramla. 770.  
XX.—Harpin of Bourges is captured by the Saracens. 773.  
XXI.—Bohemond is captured by the Saracens. Melaz, daughter of Prince Daliman, liberates him from prison by subtle ingenuity. 774.  
XXII.—Continuation. 778.  
XXIII.—Melaz becomes a Christian and marries Roger, son of Richard and kinsman of Prince Bohemond. 782.

### Book Eleven

I.—Prologue. Philosophical maxims. 785.  
II.—Various events in England and Normandy under King Henry and Duke Robert. 787.  
III.—Disputes and wars between King Henry and Robert of Bellême. This count is compelled to submit himself to the victor. 790.  
IV.—Robert of Bellême goes into Normandy and perpetrates many evils there. He rises against Duke Robert. On the death of certain men. 794.

VI.—Magnus, king of the Norwegians, is killed on an expedition. 801.

VIII.—Tribulations of the Church. Serlo, bishop of Sées, urges King Henry and his nobles to cut their beards and hair. 805.  
IX.—Bohemond, duke of Antioch, comes into France. Various events. King Henry and his brother Robert labor unsuccessfully to make peace. 808.  
X.—By which wicked persons discord between the two brothers is stirred up. King Henry joins battle with Duke Robert, defeats and captures him at Tinchebray. 812.  
XI.—Robert of Bellême again attempts to incite the Normans against King Henry. 817.  
XII.—Bohemond, aided by Robert of Montfort and many other barons, undertakes an expedition against the emperor of Constantinople. Death of Mark Bohemond. Antioch is defended against the Saracens by Baldwin. 819.  
XIII.—King Baldwin is captured by the Saracens. [Col. 1684] 822.  
XIV.—The singular fate of Baldwin and certain other knights. 826.  
XV.—On affairs conducted in the principality of Antioch. 829.  
XVI.—Events in Normandy and elsewhere. William of Rots, abbot of Fécamp. Roger of Rye succeeds him. John, archdeacon of Sées. On the deaths of certain persons. 832.  
XVII.—Various events. Abbots and priors outstanding in piety. 836.  
XVIII.—Philip I, king of the Franks, dies. His son Louis succeeds him in the kingdom. The count of Beaumont and the lord of Montmorency invade the lands of Saint-Denis. King Louis acts vigorously against the seditious barons. 838.  
XIX.—King Henry holds his brother Robert captive. Various events. Plague and other calamities rage in certain regions of Gaul. 841.  
XX.—Anselm of Canterbury, Hugh of Cluny, William, archbishop of Rouen, and several other distinguished prelates and doctors die. 843.  
XXI.—King Henry visits the monastery of Saint-Evroult. Wars between the peoples of the kings of France and England. The two kings hold a conference and make a treaty. 844.

I.—Pope Gelasius II and Burdinus, antipope. Disputes between the Apostolic See and the emperor. Wars between Louis, king of the Franks, and Henry, king of England. Various wonders. 849.

XVIII.—Death of Serlo of Sées. 903.  
XIX.—King Henry pacifies Normandy after punishing rebels and traitors. 905.

XXI.—King Louis again takes up the protection of Henry Clito, son of the duke of Normandy, and attempts to defend his rights against the king of England. The duke of Flanders is killed by Burchard of Lille and other conspirators. Henry Clito receives the duchy of Flanders. Wounded in battle, he dies. 914.  
XXII.—King Henry pardons the supporters of his nephew Henry Clito. Normandy is restored to peace. Merlin’s prophecies. 918.  
XXIII.—Gormond, patriarch of Jerusalem. Ecclesiastical affairs. On the Council of Rouen. On events in France and in the kingdom of Jerusalem. 921.

I.—Various events.—The Franks set out for Spain to aid King Ildefonsus against the Saracens; many of them establish themselves in Spain.—Various events in these regions. 923

[Col. 1685]

XII.—Pious meditations. The deaths of various lords and prelates.—Drought. 954

**In the year 1153**

I.—Privilege for the church of St Mary of Pisa. 989

III.—Privilege for the monastery of St Anthimus. 994

## DIALOGUES

Prologue. 1139

### BOOK ONE

Chapter I.—On the fact that some are accustomed to wonder at the many different forms of the Christian religion. 1141

Chapter II.—That the one body of the Church is ruled and governed by one Holy Spirit, while possessing diverse distributions of graces. 1143

Chapter III.—On the diverse rite of sacrifices by which the same one God was propitiated from Abel until Christ. 1144

Chapter IV.—That the ancient fathers, although they did not know each individual article of Christian faith fully, are nevertheless believed to have been saved through faith in what was to come. 1146

Chapter V.—That two celebrated transformations of religion took place, namely those of the Law and of the Gospel, accompanied by the testimony of an earthquake because of the greatness of those events. 1147

Chapter VI.—That the Old Testament openly proclaimed God the Father, but obscurely proclaimed God the Son; whereas the New Testament made God the Son manifest, first intimated the divinity of the Holy Spirit, and gradually taught it sufficiently. 1147

Chapter VII.—On the seven seals signifying the seven states of the Church; and that in the first state, when the white horse went forth, the primitive Church increased through the novelty of miracles and wonders. 1149

Chapter VIII.—That in the second state, when the red horse went forth, the most grievous persecution of the saints raged. 1149

[Col. 1689]

Chapter IX.—That in the third state of the Church, when the black horse went forth, the greatest dangers from heretics troubled the Church beyond measure. 1150

Chapter X.—That in the fourth state of the Church, when the pale horse went forth, the Church of God laboured beyond its strength amid false brethren; and that in this state also many and various religious orders grew. 1152

Chapter XI.—That in the fifth state of the Church the souls of the saints cry beneath God’s altar: “How long, O Lord, holy and true, will you not avenge our blood upon those who dwell on the earth?” etc. 1157

Chapter XII.—That in the sixth state of the Church, after a great earthquake has occurred, a most powerful persecution will come in the time of Antichrist. 1158

Chapter XIII.—That in the seventh state of the Church, after many tribulations, there will be a great silence, and the eighth state of boundless blessedness will be established; and thus the Church of God, one in faith, one in hope, and one in charity, is manifold through the variety of its different states. 1159

The prologue of the second book begins. 1159

### BOOK TWO

Chapter I.—How a dialogue was held in the city of Constantinople on the procession of the Holy Spirit between Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, and Nechites, archbishop of Nicomedia; and on the method of interpretation between the interlocutors. 1163

Chapter II.—That in the Lord there is not *anarchia* (ἀναρχία), that is, no principle; not *polyarchia* (πολυαρχία), that is, many principles; but *monarchia* (μοναρχία), that is, one principle. 1165

Chapter III.—That what is eternal is not thereby without a principle: thus the Son is coeternal with the Father, yet is not without a principle, because he is from the Father. 1168

Chapter IV.—That just as the Father begot, but not himself, and as the Son was begotten, but not by himself, so likewise the Holy Spirit proceeds, but not from himself. 1171

Chapter V.—That just as it is unknown what the Father’s unbegottenness is like, and what the Son’s generation is like, so it is unknown what the eternal procession of the Holy Spirit is like. 1171

Chapter VI.—That in the supreme Trinity, to exist there is one thing; to be Father, Son, or Holy Spirit is another. 1172

Chapter VII.—Why the Holy Spirit alone is called the Holy Spirit, and the third person in the Trinity; and that this is not a rank of dignity, but an order of counting and a designation of a distinct person. 1172

Chapter VIII.—That the names of the Trinity are found transposed. 1175

Chapter IX.—That Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not deficient but sufficient names, signifying no remission or diminution in respect of substance. 1177

Chapter X.—That the Holy Spirit is said to proceed neither according to the substance which is common nor according to the person which is spoken of in itself, but according to relation. 1178

Chapter XI.—Whether the Son, like the Father, is correctly called the sender forth of the Holy Spirit, which the Greeks call *probolēus* (προβολεύς). 1179

Chapter XII.—That the Holy Spirit is the *sympnoia* (σύμπνοια), that is, harmony, of both, and is the *synneusis* (σύννευσις), that is, the regard, of both. 1181

Chapter XIII.—That no one ought silently or patiently to endure being called a blasphemer, just as the Lord did not when he was told, “You have a demon”; and that the Holy Spirit receives different names because of his different effects. 1181

Chapter XIV.—That no one ought to adapt the meaning of Scripture, which has deserved to be called divine, to his own opinion, but rather ought to adapt his own opinion to it. 1183

Chapter XV.—That the Lord gave the Holy Spirit to the apostles by breathing upon them, yet that bodily breath was not the Holy Spirit but a sign of his procession; and how “Receive the Holy Spirit” is to be understood. 1184

Chapter XVI.—That spiritual things are sometimes compared to bodily things, and bodily things sometimes to spiritual things. 1187

Chapter XVII.—That, when the woman touched the Lord’s hem, power went out from him; and that the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from him, is called by the name “power.” 1188

Chapter XVIII.—That, just as for the Holy Spirit to be from the Father is to proceed from the Father, so for him to be from the Son is to proceed from the Son. 1189

Chapter XIX.—Whether the Holy Spirit proceeds equally from the Father and from the Son, when the Father is from none but the Son is from the Father; and the comparison of Adam, the first creature fashioned, Eve’s formation from a portion cut from him, and Abel’s descent from both. 1191

Chapter XX.—That, just as the Gospel does not state, “The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son,” so likewise the Gospel nowhere states, “The Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Son”; nor is it found that he proceeds from the Father alone. 1194

[Col. 1690]

Chapter XXI.—That nothing should be affirmed rashly, and nothing refuted angrily. 1195

Chapter XXII.—That it is not rash to add to the Gospel something that is not contrary to the Gospel, as was done at the Council of Nicaea and at many other councils. 1197

Chapter XXIII.—That faith in the Holy Trinity was fully formulated in the councils over which the Holy Spirit presided as *pantoscopos* (παντόσκοπος), “bishop of all,” who was also the earlier author and maker of the Gospel. 1200

Chapter XXIV.—That many Greek authors said that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son as from the Father. 1202

Chapter XXV.—That, although the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, he is nevertheless found to proceed properly and principally from the Father, both among Latin and among Greek writers. 1205

Chapter XXVI.—That certain Greeks and also Latins thought that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son, adducing certain insufficient analogies. 1206

Chapter XXVII.—On agreement in this question and the removal, by the authority of the Roman pontiff through a general council, of scandal from between the two peoples. 1208

Chapter I.—On the conference held in the basilica of Holy Wisdom, in the presence of Greek learned men. 1209
